en: Salutation to that True Self, from whom all beings appear and in whom they abide, and into whom they attain peace.

Salutation to that Self of the Knower, from whom arise the knower, knowledge, and the object of knowledge; the seer, the act of seeing, and the field of vision; and the agent, the cause, and the action.
Salutations to that essence of Brahman-bliss, from whom sprays of joy radiate in the sky and upon the earth, and who is the life-force of all beings.
A certain very sharp-witted Brahmin, his mind drawn by doubt, went to the hermitage of Agastya and respectfully questioned the sage.
Sutīkṣṇa said: "O Blessed One, knower of the essence of dharma, you who have reached certainty through all the scriptures, there is one great doubt; please explain it out of compassion."
Having determined with certainty whether action is the cause of liberation, or knowledge is the means to liberation, or both, tell me which one alone is the cause.
Agastya said: Just as the flight of birds in the sky is achieved by means of both wings together, even so is the supreme state attained through both knowledge and action.
Liberation does not arise from action alone, nor indeed from knowledge alone; rather, liberation comes from both. The wise know that both are the means.
In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history from the past: long ago, there was a certain Brahmin named Kāruṇya who had mastered the Vedas.
The son of Agniveśya, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, having completed his studies under his teacher, returned to his home.
Then Agniveśya, observing his son standing silently in the house at that time, having performed no work and being full of doubt, looked upon him who was devoid of action.
Agniveśya said: The teacher spoke these censurable words to his son for his own benefit: "O son, why do you neglect the performance of your own duty?"
Tell me, how will you attain perfection if you are not devoted to action? Let the reason for this cessation from action be explained.

Kāruṇya said: "One should perform the Agnihotra as long as one lives and should constantly observe the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā). This dharma, characterized by worldly engagement (pravṛtti), is enjoined by both Śruti and Smṛti."
Liberation does not come through wealth, nor through ritual action, nor through progeny; rather, some ascetics, through mere renunciation alone, partake of the nectar of immortality.
"O Guru, between these two scriptural injunctions, what should be done by me? Having fallen into such doubt, I remained silent regarding my duty.
Agastya said: Having spoken thus, O dear one, that compassionate brahmin became silent; yet, seeing his son in such a state, the preceptor spoke again to his son.
Agniveśya said: "Listen, my son, to a single story; having grasped its entire meaning from me within your heart, my son, do as you wish."
A certain woman named Suruci, the most excellent among the hosts of Apsarases, was seated upon a peak of the Himalayas covered with peacocks.
There, tormented by passion, the kinnarīs take delight with the kinnaras in the current of the celestial river, which is mingled with the great flood that destroys the torrent of sins.
She beheld Indra’s messenger traveling through the atmosphere; the highly fortunate Suruci, the best of apsarases, spoke to him.
Suruci said: "O illustrious messenger of the gods, from where have you come? Where will you go now? Please tell me all of that."
The divine messenger said: "Well asked by you, O fair-browed one; I shall relate it to you exactly as it is. The royal sage Ariṣṭanemi, having indeed bestowed the kingdom upon his son..."
Free from passion, that righteous-souled one departed for the forest to practice austerities; that king is now performing penance on Mount Gandhamādana.
"Having performed my duty there, I am now returning from that place; I shall go to the side of Śakra to report that news."
The Apsarā said: "O Lord, tell me what happened there; I am humble and desirous of asking, so you should not feel any agitation."
The divine messenger said: "Listen, O blessed lady; I shall tell you in detail exactly what occurred while that king was performing difficult austerities in that forest."
"Thus was I commanded at that time by the King of the Gods, O fair-browed one: 'O messenger, take this celestial chariot and go there with haste.'"
It was joined by hosts of apsarases, adorned with various musical instruments, and graced by gandharvas, siddhas, yakṣas, kinnaras, and others.
Having gone to that auspicious mountain Gandhamādana, which is covered with various trees and resounds with the sounds of palm-clapping, flutes, drums, and other instruments;
Having placed King Ariṣṭanemi upon a celestial chariot, O messenger, bring him to the city of Amarāvatī for the enjoyment of heavenly pleasures.
The messenger said: Having received this command from Śakra and taking that celestial chariot, which was equipped with all necessary implements, I went to that mountain.
Having arrived at that mountain and gone to the king's hermitage, I reported all of Mahendra’s commands to Ariṣṭanemi.
Having heard these words of mine, O auspicious lady, he spoke while still in doubt. The King said: "O messenger, I wish to question you; you ought to tell me that."
What are the virtues and what are the defects there in heaven? Tell me before you; having understood the conditions existing there, I shall act according to my preference.
The messenger said: "In heaven, supreme happiness is enjoyed through the fullness of merit; indeed, by means of the highest merit, one attains the most excellent heaven."
Likewise, by a middling [practice], a middling heaven is attained, and not otherwise; but by the least merit, a corresponding heaven is attained.
Intolerance of the excellence of others, rivalry even with equals, and complacency toward those who are inferior—these persist until the exhaustion of one's merit.
"When their merit is exhausted, these mortals enter this world again; such are the virtues and defects, O King, that reside in heaven."
Having heard these words, O auspicious lady, that king replied. The king said: "O messenger of the gods, I do not desire such a fruit as heaven."
Henceforth, having performed most severe penance, I shall indeed cast off this impure body, just as a serpent sheds its worn-out skin.
O divine messenger, take this celestial chariot and go back to the presence of Mahendra just as you came; homage be to you!
The divine messenger said: "O blessed lady, having been addressed thus, I went to report it before Śakra; after reporting exactly what had occurred, I was struck with great wonder."
Indra said: Mahendra spoke to me again with gentle and sweet words: "O messenger, go back there once more and lead that king to the hermitage."
"Deliver my message to the great sage Vālmīki, who has realized the ultimate truth and is free from passion, for the sake of his own awakening."
O Great Seer, O Great Sage, awaken this humble king—who is free from passion and does not desire heaven—to the ultimate reality.
"Afflicted by the suffering of saṃsāra, he will gradually attain liberation. Having said this, I was sent into his presence by the King of the Gods.
Having returned there, I informed King Mahendra that the king had provided the means for his own liberation, which had arisen from the anthill.
Then that one born from an anthill, with great affection, inquired after the king's well-being through a message of inquiry concerning his welfare.

The king said: "O Blessed One, knower of the reality of dharma, you who have known all that is to be known, best among the wise! I have achieved my purpose by the sight of you; that alone is my well-being."
Blessed One, I wish to ask; please tell me that without obstacle: how may I be released from the suffering of the bonds of saṃsāra? Tell me that.
Vālmīki said: Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the Rāmāyaṇa in its entirety; having heard it and grasped it with effort, you will become liberated while living.
O wise king of kings, having realized the true nature of reality, I shall relate the auspicious dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Rāma concerning the means to liberation; please listen.
The King said: "Who is Rāma? Of what nature is he? To whom does he belong—whether bound or indeed liberated? O best among the knowers of reality, tell me this with certainty."
Vālmīki said: By the very pretext of a curse, Hari, assuming the guise of a king, became possessed of ignorance; though he was the Lord, he became one who knows only a little.
The king said: "Tell me the cause of the curse upon Rāma, who is indeed the very nature of consciousness and bliss, the embodiment of pure awareness; and tell me who was cursed."
Vālmīki said: Sanatkumāra, free from desire, was dwelling in the abode of Brahmā; Viṣṇu, the Lord and Sovereign of the three worlds, arrived there from Vaikuṇṭha.
Honored there by Brahmā and the inhabitants of the world of Śalya, the Lord Īśvara, seeing that Kumāra was absent, spoke.
"Sanatkumāra, you have become paralyzed by pride through your desireless conduct; therefore, become one afflicted by desire, known by the name Śarajanman."
By him also Viṣṇu was cursed: "Since you possess omniscience, having abandoned that for some time, you shall become ignorant."
Seeing his wife slain, Bhṛgu, overwhelmed with rage, said: "O Viṣṇu, you too shall surely suffer the loss of your wife."
"Viṣṇu was cursed by Vṛndā because of the deception you practiced; therefore, at my word, you shall undergo separation from your wife."
For the wife of Devadatta, while staying on the bank of the Payoṣṇī river, met her death upon seeing Viṣṇu wearing the guise of Nṛsiṃha.
For Nṛhari, already afflicted by grief due to separation from his wife, was cursed by him: "Indeed, you too shall suffer separation from your own wife."
Having been thus cursed by the prince Devaśarman, who was himself a descendant of Bhṛgu, and having been cursed by Vṛndā, Viṣṇu consequently attained human status.
All this has been told to you regarding the cause of the pretext of the curse; now I shall tell you everything else—listen with an attentive mind.
Salutation to that Self of all, the pervasive Lord who shines as the nature of light within me—in heaven, on earth, in space, and both outside and inside.
Vālmīki said: He who possesses the firm conviction, "I am bound; may I be liberated," being neither utterly ignorant nor fully wise, is the one qualified for this scripture.
Having first investigated the means to worldly success, the wise person who then investigates these means to liberation is not born again.
O crusher of enemies, in this Rāmāyaṇa, having first established these means for the story of Rāma which possess great power in the past, I [shall proceed].
To that disciplined and wise disciple Bharadvāja, I gave the jewel with one-pointed attention, just as the ocean gives it to a suppliant.
Then these methods of discourse were proclaimed by the wise Bharadvāja in the presence of Brahmā, in a certain thicket on Mount Meru.
Then the Blessed One Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, being pleased with him, spoke to that noble-minded one: "Son, choose a boon."
Bharadvāja said: "O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, this boon is pleasing to me today: please declare that by which these people may be liberated from suffering."
The venerable Brahmā said: "Quickly and with great effort, request the preceptor Vālmīki here; by him this irreproachable Rāmāyaṇa was commenced."
Upon hearing this in its entirety, a person will cross over delusion by means of it, just as one crosses to the far shore of the ocean by means of a bridge endowed with boundless virtues.
Śrī Vālmīki said: Having spoken thus to Bharadvāja, the Supreme Lord, the Creator of all beings, arrived at my hermitage together with that Bharadvāja.
Quickly honored by me with offerings of water for the feet, guest-water, and other rites, that Great Being, who delights in the welfare of all creatures, spoke to me.
O blameless and excellent sage, because of this description of Rāma’s true nature, he must not be abandoned out of agitation until the conclusion [of the story].
By means of this treatise, this world will swiftly cross over the perils of saṃsāra, just as one crosses the ocean quickly by means of a ship.
"I have come here for this very purpose: to speak. For the benefit of the world, compose a scripture," so said the Unborn One.
From that meritorious hermitage of mine, he vanished in an instant, rising up again in a moment like a great wave from the water.
When that Blessed One had departed, I was filled with wonder; then, with a composed mind, I questioned Bharadvāja once more.
"What is this that was proclaimed by Brahmā? O Bharadvāja, tell me quickly!"—when thus addressed, that Bharadvāja spoke again to me.
Bharadvāja said: "This has been stated by your lordship: compose the Rāmāyaṇa for the benefit of all the world, as a means of crossing the ocean of saṃsāra."
And tell me, O Blessed One, how did Rāma and the high-minded Bharata conduct themselves in this narrow strait of saṃsāra?
Śatrughna, Lakṣmaṇa, and the illustrious Sītā followed Rāma, as did those sons of ministers who were possessed of great intelligence.
Tell me clearly how these have attained this state free from suffering, so that I may likewise become so, together with the people.
O Indra among kings, having been respectfully told by Bharadvāja, "Speak," I then proceeded to speak in order to carry out the command of the Lord.
Listen, dear Bharadvāja, for I shall speak to you according to what was asked; by hearing this, you will cast the stain of delusion far away.
O wise one, conduct yourself in such a way that you may live happily, just as the lotus-eyed Rāma conducted himself with an intellect entirely unattached.
Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, and the high-minded Śatrughna; Kausalyā, Sumitrā, Sītā, and likewise Daśaratha.
Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, and the other eight ministers were skilled in weaponry, free from enmity, and had attained the perfection of awakening.
Dhṛṣṭi, Jayanta, Bhāsa, Satya, and Vijaya; Vibhīṣaṇa, Suṣeṇa, Hanumān, and likewise Indrajit.
These eight ministers have been described as having minds free from passion; they were great-souled ones liberated while living, who followed whatever came to them.
O son, if you conduct yourself exactly as these have sacrificed, given, received, dwelt, and remembered, then you are indeed liberated from all distress.
Having fallen into the shoreless ocean of saṃsāra, the noble being who has attained supreme yoga does not fall into sorrow nor succumb to dejection; free from fever, he remains eternally satisfied.
Bharadvāja said: O Brahman, having first described the state of one liberated while living, tell me in due order how Rāghava [attained it], so that I may become eternally happy.
Śrī Vālmīki said: O virtuous one, for this worldly delusion that has arisen like the color of the sky, I consider its non-recollection to be better than mere forgetting.
Without the realization of the absolute non-existence of the visible world, that [Self] is never experienced by anyone at any time; therefore, let one's own consciousness be sought.
And that [truth] is indeed possible here; for this purpose, this treatise has been composed. If you listen to it, you will attain reality, and not otherwise.
O sinless one, through this inquiry, it is experienced without weariness that this delusion of the world, though visible, does not exist at all—just as color does not exist in the sky.
If, through the realization that "the visible does not exist," the cleansing of the mind's objects of perception is accomplished, then the supreme bliss of Nirvana has been attained.
Otherwise, for you who roll about here in the pits of the scriptures and possess unrefined ignorance, there will be no liberation even in aeons.
O Brahman, that supreme abandonment of all latent impressions without exception is called liberation; that alone is the stainless path.
When latent impressions are exhausted, the mind dissolves quickly, just as a speck of frost vanishes when the continuity of cold is exhausted, O Brahmin.
This body, a cage of elements, is sustained by latent impressions (vāsanā), just as a multitude of pearls is strung together by a fine thread woven within.
Impression (vāsanā) is said to be of two kinds: pure and likewise impure. The impure is the cause of birth; the pure is the destroyer of birth.
The wise declare that impure latent impression (*vāsanā*) is characterized by a dense form of ignorance, is possessed of thick egoism, and brings about rebirth.
Having abandoned the sprout of rebirth like a parched seed, she remains; though she sustains a body for its sake, she is called "Pure" because she has known that which is to be known.
In embodied beings who are liberated while living, there remains a pure latent impression that prevents rebirth; it persists within the body like the after-image of a whirling wheel.

Those of great intelligence whose latent impressions are purified and who are no longer vessels for the misfortunes of rebirth—having known that which is to be known—they are called liberated while living.
Listen as I shall tell you how the high-minded Rāma attained the state of liberation while living, for the sake of quelling old age and death.
O Bhāradvāja of great intelligence, listen to this auspicious method of Rāma; I shall speak it, and by that very means you will always understand everything.
Having departed from the schoolhouse, the lotus-eyed Rāma spent his days at home, free from all fear, in playful diversions.
Then, as time passed while the king protected the earth, the subjects remained free from sorrow and devoid of all affliction.
On one occasion, the mind of the virtuous Rāma became intensely eager to behold the series of holy fords and hermitages.
Having reflected thus, Rāghava approached his father’s feet and grasped them—those with their nails as their filaments—as a swan might grasp two fresh lotuses.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Father, O Lord, my mind is yearning to behold sacred fords, the abodes of the gods, forests, and shrines."
Therefore, you ought to make this former request of mine fruitful; O Lord, there is no supplicant in the world who has not been honored by you.
Thus entreated by Vasiṣṭha, the king then deliberated and released Rāma first, as he was the primary petitioner.

On an auspicious day under a favorable constellation, Rāghava, his body adorned with auspicious ornaments and having had rites for well-being performed by the twice-born, set out together with his two brothers.
Accompanied by the Brahmins sent by Vasiṣṭha who were well-versed in the scriptures, and together with only a few affectionate and excellent princes.
Having been adorned by his mothers, who repeatedly embraced him while pronouncing blessings, he departed from that house, intent upon a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
Departing from his own city, he was greeted by the citizens with the sounding of musical instruments, while being gazed upon by the eyes of the city women, which were as tremulous as swarms of bees.
He was showered with rains of parched grain scattered by the lotus-like hands of the village women, so that he appeared like the Himalaya mountain covered in snow.
Winning over the assemblies of brahmins, hearing the blessings of the people, and surveying the horizons, he wandered through the forested regions.
Then, proceeding from his own territory of Kośala-maṇḍala in due order, he beheld [the holy sites], preceded by bathing, giving, austerity, and meditation.
Sacred riverbanks, forests, and sacred shrines; jungles at the edges of inhabited lands, and the shores of oceans and mountains.
The Mandākinī, which resembles the moon; the Kālindī, with its stainless blue lotuses; the Sarasvatī, the Śatadrū, the Candrabhāgā, and the Irāvatī.
The Veṇī, the Kṛṣṇaveṇī, the Nirvindhyā, and likewise the Sarayū; the Carmaṇvatī, the Vitastā, the Vipāśā, and also the Bāhudā.
Prayāga, Naimiṣa, Dharmāraṇya, and likewise Gayā; Vārāṇasī, Śrīgiri, Kedāra, and likewise Puṣkara.
And he visited with reverence the Mānasa lake, Kramasaras, likewise Uttaramānasa, Vaḍavāmukha, and the multitude of other sacred fords.
The great sacred ford of Agnitīrtha, as well as Indradyumna-saras, the lakes, the rivers, and likewise the series of streams and ponds.
[He described] his master Kārttikeya, as well as Śālagrāma Hari, and the sixty-four sacred sites of Hari and of Hara.
And he saw the shores of the four oceans, variegated with many wonders, as well as the groves of the Vindhya and Mandara mountains, and the regions of the principal mountain ranges.
And likewise, he saw the auspicious hermitages that purify the great royal sages, as well as the brahmin sages, the gods, and the brahmins.
That bestower of honor wandered again and again with his two brothers through all the regions of the earth, reaching even to the four ends of the quarters.

Honored by gods, kinnaras, and humans, the joy of the Raghus, having surveyed this entire earth, returned to his own home like the Lord who, after wandering through the quarters, returns to the realm of Śiva.
Śrī Vālmīki said: Showered with handfuls of flowers by the city-dwellers, the glorious Rāma entered his home like Jayanta entering heaven.
Then Rāghava, having arrived first, bowed down to his father Vasiṣṭha, to his brothers and kinsmen, and to the brahmins who were elders of the family.
Rāghava, whose conduct was repeatedly embraced by his friends, brothers, father, and the assembly of brahmins, could not contain himself for joy.
In that house of the son of Daśaratha, the quarters of the sky seemed to reel from the mutual exchange of pleasant words, as if from the soft sounds of flutes.
Then, for eight days, there was a festival celebrating Rāma’s arrival, filled with the joyful clamor and shouting of people intoxicated with happiness.
From that time forth, Rāghava lived happily in his home, describing the various customs and manners of the different regions here and there.
Having risen in the morning and performed his twilight devotions according to the prescribed rites, Rāma beheld his father seated in the assembly hall, resembling Indra himself.
Having spent a fourth part of the day with Vasiṣṭha and the others, he remained there, honored by them with most varied discourses filled with wisdom.
Permitted by his father and surrounded by a vast army, he went to the forest teeming with boars and buffaloes, out of a desire for the hunt.
Then, having returned home and performed the sequence of rites beginning with bathing, he ate together with his friends and kinsmen and passed the night with his companions.
Rāghava, having returned from his pilgrimage with such daily conduct, stayed together with his two brothers at his father’s house.

O sinless one, he passed his days with this moonlight-like conduct, which was pleasing to the king’s worldly affairs, delightful to the hearts of the virtuous, and as tender as the essence of nectar for which he was praised.
Śrī Vālmīki said: Now, while the sixteenth year was underway, Rāma—the scion of Raghu—was accompanied by his followers, as were Śatrughna and Lakṣmaṇa.
While Bharata remained constantly at his maternal grandfather’s house in happiness, the queen protected this entire earth according to the law.
And while King Daśaratha—highly wise, knowledgeable in statecraft, and having deliberated daily with his ministers on the matter of obtaining sons for other purposes—was engaged in counsel;
When his pilgrimage was completed, Rāma remained in his own home; day by day he grew emaciated, like a stainless lake in autumn.
The prince’s large-eyed face took on a pallid hue, like a white lotus with blossoming petals ripened by the sun, encircled by a ring of rice stalks.
With his hands resting upon the surface of his cheeks, seated in the lotus posture, he became silent and inactive, entirely overcome by anxiety.
Emaciated in body, filled with anxiety, exhausted, and deeply dejected, he said nothing at all to anyone, appearing as if he were depicted in a painting.
Being entreated again and again by his attendants out of weariness, he performed his daily ritual with his lotus-like face faded.
Beholding Rāma, who was distinguished by such qualities and was a mine of all virtues, his two brothers fell into that very same state.
Likewise, seeing those sons emaciated and distressed, the protector of the earth, together with his wife, fell into a state of helplessness due to anxiety.
"O son, what is this heavy anxiety of yours? Thus he asked Rāma again and again with affectionate words, but Rāma did not say anything to him at all.
Having said, "Father, I have no suffering at all," Rāma, whose eyes were like lotus petals, sat upon his father's lap and remained silent.
Then King Daśaratha asked Vasiṣṭha, the best of speakers and knower of all affairs, "Is Rāma distressed?"
Having been addressed thus by the sage Vasiṣṭha, the king reflected: "O illustrious one, there is a reason for this; O King, let there be no sorrow in you."

The virtuous do not harbor anger, dejection, or widespread joy on account of a trivial cause; O King, in this world, great beings do not undergo transformation except through the processes of creation and dissolution.
Śrī Vālmīki said: When the lord of sages had spoken thus, the king remained filled with doubt, sitting in silence and waiting for some time in dejection.
While all the queens in the royal palaces were exhausted and remained on guard, keeping watch everywhere for every movement of Rāma.
At that very time, however, the great seer known as Viśvāmitra arrived to see that lord of men in Ayodhyā.
Then, it is said, the sacrifice of that wise man, who was devoted to the practice of dharma, was indeed devastated by Rākṣasas who were intoxicated by their power of illusion, heroism, and strength.
For the sake of protecting that sacrifice, he wished to see the king; for that sage was unable to complete the ritual without obstacles.
Then, intent on their destruction, the immensely radiant Viśvāmitra, a treasure-house of asceticism, went to the city of Ayodhyā.
Desiring an audience with the king, he said to the gatekeepers: "Quickly announce that I, Kauśika, the son of Gādhi, have arrived."
Having heard those words of his, all the gatekeepers went to Rājagṛha, their minds agitated, impelled by that speech.
Then those doorkeepers, having gone to the royal palace, announced to the king that the seer Viśvāmitra had arrived.
Then, approaching the king who was seated out of place and surrounded by a circle of royal attendants, that staff-bearer, acting with haste, addressed him.
O King, at the gate stands a glorious man of great splendor, radiant as the rising sun, his mass of matted hair crimson with flames.
He made that region, filled with horses, elephants, men, and weapons, as radiant as molten gold by means of his splendors, like the assembly hall of the Lord of the Gods.
While the King was looking on at the staff-bearer, Viśvāmitra announced his arrival with a voice free from arrogance, saying, "The sage has arrived."
Having heard these words of Yashṭika, that best of kings, together with his ministers and vassals, rose up from his golden seat.
On foot alone, he was suddenly garlanded by a multitude of kings; praised by the vassal lords, he was accompanied by Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva.
He went to the place where the great sage Viśvāmitra was; he beheld that tiger among sages stationed at the gateway.
For some reason, the sun had descended to the surface of the earth, overwhelmed by both the spiritual luster of a Brahmin and the great prowess of a Kshatriya.

His shoulders were covered by a mass of matted locks that was perpetually withered by old age and made coarse by the expansion of his ascetic penance, resembling a mountain enveloped in the clouds of twilight.
He bore a radiant body that was both tranquil and lovely, luminous yet unimpeded, modest yet majestic in appearance.
With a splendor that was both charming and extremely formidable, serene yet agitated, profound and overflowing, its radiance was colored by that majesty.
He held in his hand a single, smooth, stainless water-pot, which was the sole companion to his state of infinite life, while his mind remained unfading.
With a mind overcome by compassion, he was sprinkling these subjects as if with nectar through his glances and his clear, sweet words.
His limbs were properly invested with the sacred thread, and his white, uplifted *sruva* ladle seemed to bestow both infinity and wonder within the beholder.
Beholding the sage from afar, the king, his body bowed low, prostrated himself so that the jewels of his crest-ornament touched the ground.
There the sage also saluted the lord of the earth with sweet and noble speech, just as the sun salutes Indra.
Then all the twice-born ones, headed by Vasiṣṭha, honored him with due respect, following the sequence beginning with a welcome.
Daśaratha said: "O virtuous one, by this radiant appearance of yours, which has arrived unexpectedly, we have been graced as beds of lotuses are by the sun."
O Sage, through the sight of you, I have attained that blissful joy which is beginningless, unbroken, and free from all states of woe.
"Today we truly stand at the forefront of the fortunate in accordance with dharma, since we have become the object of your arrival."
Conversing thus, the kings and great sages, having reached their seats in the assembly hall, sat down together.
Seeing that best of sages adorned with splendor, the king was struck with awe; yet, with a joyful countenance, he himself offered him the guest-offering (arghya).
Having accepted the guest-offering from the king according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures, he honored the king by performing a circumambulation.
Honored by the king, he then, with a joyful countenance, inquired after the welfare and well-being of the lord of men.
Having met with Vasiṣṭha, that bull among sages smiled, honored him as was fitting, and then inquired after his well-being.
Having honored one another for a moment as was appropriate and having come together, they all, with joyful minds, entered the residence of the great king.
Seated upon their respective appropriate seats, their mutual splendors increasing, they all respectfully inquired after one another's well-being.
To that wise Viśvāmitra who was seated, he repeatedly offered water for his feet, the guest-offering, and a cow.
Having honored Viśvāmitra according to the prescribed rites, the king, with palms joined in reverence and a composed mind, spoke these words with a joyful heart.
Just as the attainment of nectar, just as rain in a time of drought, and just as the recovery of sight for one who is blind—such is your arrival.
The birth of a son to one who was childless through union with a wife as desired, the obtaining of wealth from an object seen in a dream, and likewise this arrival of yours—[all these have occurred].
Just as there is union with what is desired, just as there is the arrival of what is wished for, and just as there is the recovery of what was lost, so too is your arrival.
Just as there is joy when a dead man returns by traveling through the sky, so too, O Brahmin, is there joy from your arrival; welcome to you, O great sage!
Indeed, who would not find joy in dwelling in the world of Brahmā? O Sage, your scripture is likewise; I tell you this as the very truth.
And what is your supreme desire? What may I do for you? You have arrived as a worthy recipient for me, O Brahmin, being most righteous.
Formerly, you were known by the title of royal seer, your radiance illumined by asceticism; now, having attained the status of a brahmin seer, you are worthy of worship by me, O Blessed One.
Just as joy would arise in me from being sprinkled with the waters of the Gaṅgā, so does the joy from seeing you cool my inner self, as it were.
Free from desire, fear, and anger, devoid of passion and free from affliction—O Brahman, it is most wonderful that you have come to me.
O best among those who know what is to be known through the Vedas, I perceive myself as stainless, situated in an auspicious field, like the orb of the moon emerged from the water.
O Sage, I consider your arrival to be like the direct manifestation of Brahmā himself; I am purified and graced by your visit.
O virtuous one, because it has been graced by the merit of your arrival, my birth today has become fruitful; my life is truly well-lived.
Having seen you arrived here, and having honored and bowed to you, I bow within myself alone, like the ocean beholding the moon.
O bull among sages, whatever task you have come for or whatever purpose you have served, know that it is already accomplished; you are always worthy of my honor.
O Kauśika, you ought not to hesitate regarding your own duty; O Blessed One, there is nothing that I cannot give to you as it is requested.
"You ought not to deliberate upon this matter according to dharma; I am your agent for everything, and you are my supreme deity."

Having heard these exceedingly sweet words, spoken with humility by the knower of the self and pleasing to the ear, the bull among sages—distinguished by his virtues and renowned for his qualities—attained supreme joy.
Śrī Vālmīki said: Having heard those words of the lion among kings, which were so wonderfully extensive, the highly effulgent Viśvāmitra, his hair standing on end with joy, spoke.
O tiger among kings, this is truly worthy of you alone upon this earth—you who are born of a great lineage and follow the tradition of Vasiṣṭha.
O tiger among kings, carry out the decision regarding that matter which is in my heart; uphold righteousness.
"O bull among men, I am practicing the Dharma for the sake of attaining perfection; however, terrible Rākṣasas stand in my way, creating obstacles for me."
Whenever I worship the hosts of gods with a sacrifice, at that very time the night-stalkers destroy my sacrifice.
When that sacrifice had been performed many times by me, the leaders of the Rākṣasas covered the earth with flesh and blood.
When that assembly of sacrifices had thus become desolate, he, having exerted himself in vain, lost his enthusiasm and departed from that place.
O King, my mind does not incline toward releasing anger; for such was that deed that no curse can affect him.
Such was that initiation for sacrifice of mine in that great rite; by your grace, may I attain its great fruit without obstacle.
You ought to protect me, who am distressed and have come seeking refuge; for the despair of those who seek help, O most virtuous one, is indeed a defeat.
You have a glorious son, Rāma, who possesses the prowess of a proud tiger, who is equal to Mahendra in valor, and who is the destroyer of the Rākṣasas.
O tiger among kings, you ought to give me that eldest son, Rāma, whose valor is truth, the hero who still wears the side-locks of youth.
For, protected by me through my own divine splendor, he is indeed capable of crushing the heads of those Rākṣasas who have done him harm.
And I shall bring about for him manifold and infinite welfare, by which he will become worthy of worship even by the three worlds.
And having encountered Rāma, those night-stalkers will not be able to stand their ground, just as deer in the forest cannot remain upon seeing an enraged lion.
No other man than the enraged Kesarin is able to fight those descendants of Kakutstha, just as no one can fight rutting elephants except for a furious lion.
For those wicked ones, intoxicated by their prowess in battle, are like the Kālakūṭa poison; they are the servants of Khara and Dūṣaṇa, resembling the wrathful God of Death himself.
O tiger among kings, they will not withstand Rāma’s arrows, which fall incessantly like the showers from a cloud that sweep away the dust.
And you ought not, O King, to harbor affection born of [having a] son; there is nothing in this world that cannot be given away by those of great soul.
Ah, now I truly understand that those Rākṣasas have been slain; for wise men such as we do not engage in action when the outcome is uncertain.
I know the high-souled Rāma, whose eyes are like lotuses, as do the greatly effulgent Vasiṣṭha and those others who possess far-reaching vision.
If righteousness and great renown are established in your mind, then you ought to grant me the son whom I desire.
And my sacrifice shall last for ten nights, at which the Rākṣasas—my enemies who act as obstacles to my sacrifice—must be slain by Rāma.
In this matter as well, O Kakutstha, let all your ministers, headed by Vasiṣṭha, grant their permission; therefore, O Rāma, bid him farewell.
O knower of time, O Rāghava, act in such a way that this time does not pass me by; may prosperity be yours, and do not set your mind on grief.
Even a minute task, when performed at the right time, becomes a source of benefit; conversely, even a great service, if performed at the wrong time, comes to naught.
Having spoken these words, which were consistent with righteousness and purpose, the righteous and highly effulgent Viśvāmitra, lord of sages, became silent.

Having heard the words of the eminent sage, the high-souled one remained silent, for he was unable to speak words so perfectly fitting; indeed, a wise person finds no satisfaction except through speech endowed with logic, nor does the world find contentment when its heart's desire remains unfulfilled.
The Eighth Canto. Vālmīki said: Having heard those words spoken by Viśvāmitra, that tiger among kings remained motionless for a moment and then spoke thus with dejection.
This lotus-eyed Rāma is less than sixteen years of age; I do not see in him the fitness for battle with the rākṣasas.
"O Lord, this is a full akṣauhiṇī army of which I am the master; surrounded by it, I shall give battle to the flesh-eaters."
For these servants are brave, valiant, and skilled in counsel; and I myself, bow in hand, am their protector at the forefront of battle.
Together with these, I give battle even to heroes as great as Mahendra, like a lion against rutting elephants.
Rāma is but a child among armies; he does not know strength from weakness, for no ground of battle other than the inner apartments has ever been seen by him.
He was not equipped with the finest weapons, nor was he skilled in combat; he did not know the nine missiles used by millions of heroes on the fields of battle.
One should always practice exclusively in flower gardens, city parks, and in the groves and bowers of pleasure gardens.
He knows how to sport together with the princes upon his own courtyard grounds, which are strewn with offerings of flowers.
Today, O Brahmin, due to the reversal of my fortune, he has become exceedingly pale and emaciated, like a lotus turned white by frost.
Unable to address his own name nor to leave the grounds of his home, with his soul overwhelmed by inner distress, he remains merely silent.
O leader of sages, for his sake, I, along with my wife and servants, have surely become as devoid of essence as a cloud in autumn.
Such is this young son of mine, now overcome by mental anguish; how can I give him to you to fight against the night-stalkers?
O holy one of great intelligence, the affection for a son leads to true happiness even more than association with young women, even more than the essence of nectar, and even more than sovereignty.
Those things which have a miserable end, involve great undertakings, and bring weariness to the three worlds—even the virtuous perform them without doubt out of affection for their sons.
O tiger among sages, men may renounce their vital fluids, wealth, wives, and even happiness; yet they do not renounce a son, for such is the inherent nature of living beings.
The Rākṣasas were performers of cruel deeds and experts in treacherous warfare; Rāma fought them in this manner, for such a stratagem alone was exceedingly difficult to withstand.
Separated from Rāma, I cannot endure to live for even a moment, yet I still desire life; therefore, you ought to take me to Rāma.
"O Kauśika, nine thousand years have passed since my birth; these four sons were produced by me through great hardship."
Among them, the lotus-eyed Rāma is the preeminent one; without him, the other three cannot sustain their lives in this world.
If that very Rāma is being led by you toward the Rākṣasas, then know me to be as good as dead this very moment, deprived of my son.
Indeed, my supreme affection for my four sons is centered precisely here; therefore, you ought not to take away Rāma, who is the eldest and the very embodiment of dharma.
O Sage, if it is your desire to destroy the army of the night-stalkers, then lead forth the fourfold force together with me.
What is the prowess of those Rākṣasas? Whose sons are they, and how did they come to be? What is their size, and who are they? Describe this clearly to me.
O Brahmin, how should Rāma act toward those demons who fight with deceit—whether by means of my young children or by me?
"O Blessed One, tell me everything regarding how those of ill fortune must stand in the great battle, for the Rākṣasas are indeed arrogant in their prowess."
For it is heard that there is a Rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa of great prowess, the brother of Vaiśravaṇa himself and the son of the sage Viśravas.
If that evil-minded one indeed creates an obstacle to your sacrifice, then we shall not be able to withstand him in battle, O evil-souled one.
O Brahmin, at various times, beings of immense power and majesty arise among all creatures and, by the force of time, dissolve away.
But now, at this time, we are not capable of standing before our enemies, Rāvaṇa and the others; such is the certainty of destiny.
Therefore, O knower of dharma, show favor toward my little son; for you are indeed the supreme deity for me, who am so unfortunate.
The gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, birds, and serpents are not capable of fighting Rāvaṇa; how much less so, then, are mere men in battle?
In battle, the Rākṣasa seized the valor of those possessed of great heroism; because of that, we were not able to withstand him in combat even with our children.
This is one such time when even the virtuous are made fragile; for Rāghava too has fallen into a state of wretchedness, worn down by old age.
Or rather, O Brahmin, I will never release my son—him who is like salt, a destroyer of sacrifice, a son of Madhu, and resembling an asura.
Furthermore, the two sons of Sunda and Upasunda are like the son of Vivasvat; they cause obstacles to sacrifices. Tell me this, and I will not give you my son.
If you will not lead me away, O Brahmin, then I am truly slain by you; otherwise, I do not see any eternal victory for myself.

Having spoken these gentle words, that scion of Raghu’s line was submerged in the surging waves of doubt regarding the sages' doctrines; like one bewildered in an ocean with high-tossing billows, the great-souled one could not find certainty for even a moment.
Vālmīki said: Having heard those words of his, whose eyes were clouded with affection, Kauśika, filled with indignation, replied to the lord of the earth.
Having promised "I shall do it," you ought not to abandon your vow; having become a lion, you now desire the state of a deer.
This reversal of fortune for this lineage of the Raghavas is unworthy; never indeed do hot rays arise from the cool-rayed moon.
If you are unable to do so, O King, I shall depart as I came; O descendant of Kakutstha, you who have failed in your promise, may you be happy along with your kinsmen.
Vālmīki said: Then, when the high-souled Viśvāmitra was thus overcome with anger, the entire earth trembled and fear entered the gods.
Perceiving that the Great Sage, the friend of the world, was overcome by anger, the wise Vasiṣṭha—steadfast, firm in his vows, and intelligent—spoke these words.
Vasiṣṭha said: You, the illustrious Daśaratha, born in the lineage of the Ikṣvākus, are like another Dharma incarnate, adorned with the virtues of the three worlds.
Being steadfast and firm in your vows, you ought not to abandon dharma; you are renowned throughout the three worlds, endowed with both righteousness and glory.
Fulfill your own duty; you ought not to abandon dharma. You ought to carry out the word of the Sage, the Lord of the Three Worlds.
O King, since they have promised "I shall do it" but do not perform it for you, they shall forfeit the merit of their sacrifices and charitable works; therefore, send Rāma away.
Even though you are born of the Ikṣvāku lineage and are Daśaratha yourself, if you do not uphold your word, who else will?
Sentient beings do not abandon the boundaries established by the conventional usage formulated by you and others; therefore, you ought not to forsake them.
Guarded by that lion among men as the nectar is guarded by fire, the Rākṣasas will not be able to overcome him, whether he has mastered the divine weapons or not.
He is Dharma incarnate; he is the foremost among those possessed of valor; he excels the world in wisdom and is the ultimate refuge of asceticism.
He knows the various weapons in the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile; no other man knows them, nor shall anyone ever know them.
Neither gods nor any sages, nor asuras, nor rākṣasas, nor nāgas, yakṣas, or gandharvas, even when gathered together, are the equal of the Sage.
In former times, when he had attained the kingdom, Kṛśāśva gave to Kauśika this weapon, which is exceedingly difficult for enemies to conquer.
For those sons of Kṛśāśva, resembling the sons of Prajāpati—heroes, radiant and of great prowess—followed after him.
Jayā and Suprabhā were the two slender-waisted daughters of Dakṣa; their offspring numbered one hundred and were exceedingly difficult to conquer.
In former times, Jayā, having obtained a boon, gave birth to fifty sons for the purpose of slaying the armies of the gods; they were capable and able to move at will.
Suprabhā gave birth to fifty other sons, named Saṃgharṣas, who were invincible, formidable in appearance, and exceedingly powerful.
Such is the heroism and great splendor of Viśvāmitra, the sage of the world; you ought not to entertain a despondent thought regarding Rāma’s departure.

While this Lord of Sages, the most eminent of Great Beings, stands nearby, even though death has arrived for this virtuous man, he attains immortality; therefore, do not fall into despondency like one who is utterly deluded.
The Tenth Canto. Vālmīki said: While Vasiṣṭha was speaking thus, King Daśaratha, with a heart full of joy, summoned his son Rāma along with Lakṣmaṇa.
Daśaratha said: "O gatekeeper, bring quickly and without hindrance the mighty-armed Rāma, whose valor is truth, together with Lakṣmaṇa, for the sake of the sacred rite."
Thus dismissed by the king, he went to the inner apartments and, returning in just a moment, spoke to the lord of the earth:
O King, Rāma, who has crushed all his enemies with his arms, remains dejected in his palace at night, like a bee within a lotus.
"I shall return in a moment," he says, and yet he meditates all alone; with a weary mind, he does not wish to remain in the presence of anyone.
Thus addressed by him, the king consoled all those followers of Rāma and questioned them in due order.
When asked by the king, "What is Rāma like? Of what sort is he?", the dejected servants of Rāma spoke these words to the lord of the earth:
"O Lord, we who support this slender body of yours have grown weary with exhaustion as your son Rāma’s body has faded from fatigue."
Ever since Rāma, whose eyes are like lotus petals, arrived from his pilgrimage with the brahmin, he has been dejected in spirit.
Through our diligent entreaties, he—this very person with his unfading countenance—either performs or does not perform his daily duty.
Dejected during bathing, worshiping the gods, giving gifts, eating, and other such activities, the Lord does not eat even when requested, until he has reached satiety.
In the courtyard, he does not sport with playful dalliances alongside the amorous women of the inner apartments who have set up swings, just as a cātaka bird does not delight in showers of rain.
O King, the series of armlets and bracelets set with ruby buds did not delight him as much as the sky, which had come within the range of his gaze.
Amidst the glances of sporting young women, amidst winds carrying the scent of flowers, and within the bower-houses of creeping vines, he becomes exceedingly despondent.
Even that substance which is appropriate, delicious, delicate, and captivating to the mind causes one to suffer as if with eyes filled with tears.
"Why do these city women, who cause such suffering, move about so restlessly?"—thus he censured the amorous ladies amidst their playful dances.
Like one acting in a state of madness, he does not take delight in blameless food, bedding, vehicles, amusements, bathing, or seats.
"What is prosperity? What is adversity? What is home? What are gestures? Having declared that "all this is indeed unreal," he remains alone in silence.
He does not engage in jests, he does not immerse himself in enjoyments, nor does he remain occupied with worldly affairs; he maintains only silence.
Women with creeper-like tresses tossing about and eyes rolling in playfulness do not bring him joy, just as does a doe to a forest tree.
He finds delight in solitary places, at the ends of the earth, on riverbanks, and in forests, as if he were a creature sold among other beings.
By that very disposition of turning away from the giving of clothing, drink, and food, he further pursues the ascetic who follows the way of a wandering mendicant.
O Lord of Men, dwelling alone in a region devoid of people, he neither laughs with a singular mind, nor sings, nor weeps.
Seated in the bound lotus posture with a mind empty of thought, he remains alone, resting his cheek upon the palm of his left hand.
He does not assume pride, nor does he desire sovereignty; he neither rises nor sets amidst the fluctuations of pleasure and pain.
We do not know whether he goes, what he does, what he desires, what he meditates upon, what he approaches, how he acts, or whom he pursues.
Day by day he grows thin; day by day he turns pale; day by day he falls into despondency, like a tree at the end of autumn.
O King, Śatrughna and Lakṣmaṇa likewise followed him, standing there exactly like him, as if they were his very own reflections.
Although questioned again and again by his servants, kings, and mothers, he said nothing at all and remained silent, devoid of any desire.
"Do not set your mind upon enjoyments that are pleasing only at first sight"—thus does a friend advise a worthy person standing by his side.
Amidst women delightful with various luxuries and in the midst of social gatherings, one who lacks affection perceives only their destruction, as if they were standing right before him.
"Life has been spent in activities devoid of attaining the state free from weariness"—thus he sings repeatedly in a sweet, low-pitched tone.
When an attendant standing nearby says to him, "Become an emperor," the sage laughs with a distracted mind, as if at one who is prattling like a madman.
He does not listen when something is spoken, nor does he look at what stands before him; he shows contempt everywhere, even toward things that are most excellent.
Even regarding a lotus in the sky or a great forest in the sky, no wonder arises in him that "this is indeed the mind."
Even when situated among beloved women, the arrows of Love do not pierce his mind, which is as difficult to penetrate as a great rock by torrents of water.
"Do you desire wealth as the sole refuge in times of misfortune? Having thus instructed him, he bestows his entire possession upon the seeker.
"This is misfortune, this is prosperity"—such is the delusion born of conceptual construction that has arisen in the mind; thus he sings these verses.
Even while crying out, "Alas, I am ruined! I am helpless!", people do not attain dispassion; rather, they simply say, "How strange!"—so he says.
While Rāma, that slayer of enemies and a great śāla tree to the forest of the Raghus, remains in such a state, we have come to extreme distress.
O mighty-armed one, O lotus-petal-eyed one, we do not know what we should do for him whose mind is such; for you alone are our refuge in this matter.
O Lord, he laughs calmly at the king or the brahmin who stands before him as an instructor, as if they were ignorant, and thus treats them with contempt.
Having reached the firm conclusion that this which has arisen, known as the expansive world, is neither a real entity nor indeed the self, he remained established [in that realization].
O Lord, he has no reliance on women, nor on himself, nor on friends, nor on his kingdom, nor on his mother; he has no reliance on prosperity, nor on adversity, nor on anything external.
He has cast aside all attachment, he is free from hope, he is without desire, and he is without support; he is neither deluded nor liberated—because of this, we suffer intensely.

"What is the use of wealth? What is the use of mothers? What is the use of a kingdom? What is the use of worldly striving?"—with such a firm resolve within himself, he remained intent on giving up his life.
He fell into extreme distress regarding his wealth, life-span, kingdom, friends, father, and mother, just like a cātaka bird during a drought.
Thus, may he who is devoted to compassion arise to completely uproot this affliction that has descended upon his offspring, spreading like a branch with its many offshoots.
O Lord, for one whose nature is such, the expansive web of saṃsāra, though endowed with all its splendors, acts as a counter-poison.
Who indeed on this earth could be such a great being, capable of establishing him in this worldly affair?

Having cast aside delusion from his mind, the high-minded one indeed brings all the darkness of affliction to the state of goodness and fruitfulness, just as the sun, dispelling the gloom upon the earth, attains its status as the light-maker.
Viśvāmitra said: "If this is so, O highly wise ones, let you quickly bring the descendant of Raghu here, just as lions bring a deer."
This delusion of the Lord of the Raghus arose neither from calamities nor from passion; for one possessed of discernment and dispassion, awakening alone is the great exaltation.
"O Rāma, come here in an instant, and we too shall be here in an instant; we will dispel his delusion just as the wind disperses a thick cloud from a mountain."
When this delusion has been skillfully wiped away, that delighter of the Raghus will find rest in that supreme state, just as we have.
He will attain truthfulness, joy, wisdom, rest, and freedom from affliction; he will achieve robustness and a beautiful complexion, as if having drunk the nectar of immortality.
And with a fully satisfied mind, the honorable one will carry out his own traditional course of conduct, unbroken and in accordance with established custom.
There will be a Great Being who knows the high and low of the world, who is free from the conditions of pleasure and pain, and for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are equal.
When the Lord of Sages had spoken thus, the king, his heart filled with joy, dispatched a succession of messengers once again to bring Rāma back.
After this much time had passed, Rāma rose from his seat in his own home and went into the presence of his father, like the sun rising from a mountain.
Surrounded by a few servants and his two brothers, he went to that holy abode of his father, heaven, like the lord of the gods.
Then Rāma saw Daśaratha from afar, surrounded by a multitude of kings like Vāsava by the hosts of gods.
It was attended on both sides by Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra, and it was garlanded by a multitude of ministers who were experts in the meaning of all the scriptures.
He was attended by lovely women with beautiful chowries in their hands, standing in their appropriate places like the quarters of the sky personified.
Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and others, as well as Daśaratha and his kin, beheld from afar Rāghava approaching like Guha.
Like the Himalaya mountain occupied by a fetus that has seized a living being, as if by a thorn, he was resorted to by all who seek his service—both profound and manifest.
Gentle, equanimous, and auspicious in appearance, with a mind noble through discipline, his lovely and tranquil body was a vessel for the welfare of others.
The onset of youth has fully arisen, yet it is graced by the tranquility of the aged; it is a joy that does not agitate the mind, for one's desires are almost entirely fulfilled.
Having reflected upon the course of the world, which is the domain of pure qualities, he was as if inhabited by virtues themselves through his singular longing for great being.
He was displaying the unsurpassed, noble, and sublime state, which completely fills the hollow of the inner heart, through an undisturbed mode of being.
Thus filled with a multitude of such virtues, the scion of Raghu was visible even from afar, his sprout-like garments and necklaces being pure white with a faint smile.
He bowed with his head, which bore the shimmering rays of a moving and beautiful crest-jewel, possessing the splendor of a celestial mountain swaying upon the trembling earth.
While the Lord of Sages was speaking thus, the lotus-eyed Rāma then approached to perform the salutation at his father's feet.
First [he honored] his father, then the sages, both being highly revered; then the Brahmins, then his kinsmen, and then the groups of teachers and friends.
And then he accepted with his gaze, his head slightly bowed, and his speech that succession of prostrations performed by the circle of kings.
Having received blessings from the two sages, Rāma, his mind perfectly composed and as beautiful as a celestial being, approached the holy presence of his father.
Then that lord of the earth, intent on honoring his feet with a prostration, quickly embraced him upon his head and kissed him again and again.
Likewise, that slayer of enemy heroes, with deep affection, embraced Śatrughna and Lakṣmaṇa, just as a royal swan embraces two lotuses.
Then, as the king said, "O son, stay on my lap," he settled instead upon a garment spread by his attendants on the ground.
The king said: "My son, you have attained discernment and are a vessel for all that is auspicious; do not subject yourself to distress with an aged intellect like that of a fool."
By one like you who practices what has been proclaimed by aged Brahmins and gurus, the meritorious state is attained; it is not reached by one who pursues delusion.
O son, calamities remain far away and exceedingly fragile for as long as no opening is given to the spread of delusion.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O prince of mighty arms, you are a hero; by you these enemies that are the sense-objects—which are difficult to sever and difficult to assail—have been conquered.
Why do you sink, like one ignorant of this, into the ocean of delusion—fit for the unenlightened, turbulent with waves, and characterized by dullness?

Viśvāmitra said: "O you whose eyes possess the flickering beauty of a cluster of swaying blue lotuses, tell me: having abandoned the state of mind created by yourself, for what reason do you now become deluded?"
What is their basis? Who are they? By what means? How many are they? And for what reason do these anxieties plunder the mind, just as rats devour a house?
I believe you are not the ultimate abode of mental agonies that are inappropriate for you; yet even those lowly afflictions are not to be employed by you in times of calamity.
O sinless one, speak quickly whatever you desire, and you shall obtain it all; furthermore, by this means, mental afflictions shall no longer pierce you.

Having heard these words of his, which were pregnant with the beauty of appropriate meaning, the wise banner of Raghu’s lineage abandoned his grief, just as a peacock does when a rain-cloud thunders and it infers the fulfillment of its desired object.
Vālmīki said: Thus questioned by the lord of sages, Rāghava, having composed himself, spoke these words, which were beautiful, full of meaning, and delivered with measured gravity.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, as requested by you, I shall now relate everything exactly as it is, even though I am ignorant; for who can transgress the word of the virtuous?
"I was indeed born here in my own father’s house; in due course I attained growth, and having acquired knowledge, I remained established therein."
Thereupon, O leader of sages, becoming devoted to the conduct of the virtuous, I wandered over the earth girt by the oceans for the purpose of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites.
Then, after such a length of time, as this [worldly] attachment was being removed from my mind, this very reflection arose within me.
My mind being filled with discernment, I myself thereafter reflected upon this with an intellect that had become indifferent to worldly enjoyments.
What indeed is this happiness in this continuous succession of saṃsāra, wherein the world is born for death and dies for birth?
All these states of being, including the activities of the moving and the unmoving, are entirely unstable; they are the masters of calamities, evil, and the very grounds of worldly existence.
Like iron rods, phenomena do not adhere to one another; they merely cling together through their own mental construction.
This expansive world is seen as dependent upon the mind; yet the mind itself appears as if non-existent—by what have we been so utterly deluded?
Alas, we of deluded intellect have been dragged far away by that which does not exist, like bewildered deer in the forest lured by the water of a mirage.
We have not been sold by anyone, yet we remain as if sold; alas, we are all fools, even though we know the magic of Śambara!
What indeed are these so-called enjoyments within these manifold phenomena, they being so utterly wretched? For we have remained here in vain through delusion, fixed in our attachments.
It is now understood that for a long time we have been dwelling fruitlessly in the forest; deluded and fallen into infatuation, we are like bewildered deer in a pit.
What use have I for sovereignty, what use for enjoyments? Who am I, and what is this that has come? Let that which is false remain false; for whom indeed has anything ever truly come to pass?
O Brahmin, as I reflected in this way, a distaste for all worldly existences then arose within me, just as it does for a traveler in the deserts.
Therefore, O Blessed One, tell me this: what is it that perishes? What is it that is born again? And what is it that increases?
Old age, death, calamity, birth, and prosperity increase again and again through their manifestation and disappearance.
Behold, by those very same trivial enjoyments, we have indeed been reduced to a state of decay, like mountain trees battered by the winds.
Like insentient beings, people stand about fruitlessly, sounding through the winds called "breaths," just like hollow bamboo flutes.
"How can this suffering be stilled?"—with such thoughts I am tormented, like an old tree by a fierce fire dwelling within its hollow.
Although my heart is as solid as a stone due to the sufferings of saṃsāra, I do not weep with falling tears merely out of fear for my own world.
Those mental functions of mine, which have become empty and tasteless due to dry weeping, are perceived by Viveka alone as he dwells within my heart in solitude.
I am utterly bewildered as I reflect upon this state composed of existence and non-existence; like a fortunate man in poverty, I stand far removed from the activities of saṃsāra.
Prosperities, which are intent on deception, delude the functioning of the mind, shatter the string of virtues, and bestow a web of suffering.
Wealth, with its wheels of accumulated anxieties, brings me no joy; nor do homes, which bring forth wives, resemble anything but the dwellings of those facing dire calamities.
O Sage, my mind finds no peace through reflections on the various states of defilement, which are fashioned from fragile causes; it is like that of a forest elephant bound in chains.

From time to time, in this world where the light is obscured by the thick mist of sharp delusion during the night, the wicked ones—thieves of hundreds of sense-objects, exceedingly clever, active, and ever-exerting themselves in every direction to seize the very essence of discernment—have appeared as formidable warriors; who indeed, other than the wise, would abandon them?

The Thirteenth Chapter. Śrī Rāma said: "O Sage, this noble Fortune (Śrī) who is established here in this world has been fashioned for the sake of total delusion; she, too, surely brings about misery."
Like a river in the rainy season, it carries forth vast, dull, and agitated waves of fire, which are filled with intense exuberance and are infinite in their surging.
Her many daughters of anxiety, nurtured by manifold indulgence, become restless and prevail over her like the waves of a river.
For this unfortunate woman does not fix her step in one place; like one who is consumed by fire, she runs hither and thither with unstable conduct.
Producing an intense burning sensation when her limbs are touched, she brings about only her own destruction, like a streak of lamp-soot when it is wiped away.
Indeed, like the common folk of a king, fools—without any investigation into merits or demerits—cling to one who has mounted them, even if that person stands by their side.
Through this or that action, she follows after expansion, just as the milk of the venomous serpent's poison spreads out.
People are as cool and soft to the touch toward both strangers and their own kin only so long as they have not been made harsh by prosperity, like snow before a windstorm.
Those who are wise, heroic, grateful, skillful, and gentle—by their very splendor, they are rendered as if soiled by a handful of dust, like precious gems.
O Blessed One, prosperity does not lead to happiness; indeed, it increases only suffering. When guarded, it brings about destruction, just as a poisonous creeper leads to death.
One who is illustrious yet beyond reproach, one who is heroic yet free from boastfulness, and one who is a master yet possesses an even vision—these three types of men are rare to find.
For this is a treacherous and dense cave for those who experience suffering, a great slope of the Vindhya mountains for the lordly elephants of thick delusion.

The night-blooming lotus of the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause, the moonlight for the white water-lily of suffering, the gale for the lamp of right vision, and the river with its surging waves of turmoil.
The state of agitation, like a mass of clouds, increases the poison of despair; it is a small field for conceptual constructions, providing the food for the serpent of fear and weariness.
It is frost to the creepers of dispassion, a night of transformation for the owl of worldly attachment, the fang of Rahu for the moon of discernment, and the moonlight for the lotus of goodness.
Captivating with various shifting colors like a rainbow, it is as flickering as lightning—appearing and vanishing in an instant—and it rests upon the dull matter of the body.
The forest was conquered by the female mongoose through her agility; the fierce mirage was conquered by the female mongoose born there through her intentness upon deception.
Like a wave, she does not remain fixed in one form even for a moment; like the flickering flame of a lamp, her movement and domain are exceedingly difficult to comprehend.
Like a lioness, she crushes the host of lordly elephants with her limbs in motion; like the edge of a sword, she is cool yet possesses an extremely sharp disposition.
I see no happiness at all, only suffering, from this ill-fated Fortune who has been snatched away by misfortune and who clings tenaciously to those afflicted by evil diseases.
Driven far away by misfortune, yet once again with great respect—alas! the shameless wicked person always seems to embrace her.

The goddess of fortune (Lakṣmī) attracts the movement of the mind, yet she is difficult to secure and momentary; her body twists like that of a serpent in its coils, and she is like a flowering creeper rising from a pit.
Śrī Rāma said: The body, as fragile as a drop of water hanging from the tip of a sprout’s edge, departs prematurely like one intoxicated, abandoning it all at once.
For those whose minds are worn out by attachment to the venomous serpents of sense objects, and who lack mature self-discrimination, life is merely a cause of exhaustion.

But for those who have understood that which is to be known and have come to rest in the expansive state, for whom existence and non-existence are equally resolved, [that state] becomes their happiness.
O Sage, we have reached a certainty established through limited forms; yet, amidst this mass of lightning from the clouds of saṃsāra, we find no peace in our lifespan.
It is as appropriate to wrap the wind, to break the sky into pieces, and to tie together the waves, as it is to place one's trust in life.
Like an autumn cloud, like a lamp without oil, or like a wave, it is perceived as already gone, flickering and unstable.
I may exert myself to grasp a wave, the moon's reflection, a mass of lightning, or a lotus in the sky; but I do not strive for life, whose stability is destroyed.
With an unresting mind, the deluded person strives for a long, empty life only for the sake of suffering, just as a female mule carries a fetus within her womb only to her own destruction.
O Brahmin, in this ocean of creation where the world-process flows like foam, life does not please me, being as transient as water upon the creeper of the body.
That by which what is to be attained is fully attained, by which one no longer grieves, and which is the state of supreme bliss—that is called true life.
For even trees live, and deer and birds live; but he alone truly lives whose mind does not live by means of mentalizing.
Only those living beings in this world who are not born again here have lived a truly virtuous life; all others are but aged donkeys.
The scripture is a burden to the undiscriminating, knowledge is a burden to the passionate, the mind is a burden to the restless, and the body is a burden to one who has not realized the Self.
Form, life-span, mind, intellect, ego, and likewise one's endeavors—all these lead to suffering for the person of dull wit, just as a burden does for the bearer of the burden.
Life is restless and incomplete, the supreme abode of calamities, a nest for the birds of disease, and a firm seat of exhaustion.
Day after day, casting off weariness, slowly and incessantly, one is destroyed by time—just as an old white mouse is killed by a cat.
The body is consumed by fierce diseases that take refuge in its cavities and inflict the burning heat of poison, just as the forest breeze is swallowed by savage serpents.
One is torn asunder by cruel sufferings that flow incessantly from within like sap, just as an old tree is consumed by vile wood-boring insects.
Surely death watches him, as a cat watches a rat, with an insatiable and constant greed to swallow him up quickly.
By emptiness, which is like a courtesan devoid of power yet pregnant with qualities such as fragrance, food is completely consumed, just as by a voracious eater.
In just a few days, having been fully recognized as such, the wicked man is abandoned by youth with indifference, just as a good person is abandoned by a wicked one.
Form is constantly coveted by Death—the friend of destruction, the kinsman of old age and death—just as it is by the most excellent of libertines.

In this world, there exists nothing so utterly devoid of quality as this life, which is constantly abandoned by stability and pleasantness, and which is both supreme and fragile—a mere vessel for death.
Śrī Rāma said: It has arisen in vain through delusion, and it increases in vain; I am terrified by this enemy of false egoism, which consists of nothing but illusion.
It is solely through the power of egoism that this manifold cycle of existence subjects those who are most wretched to the torment of the treasury of defects.
Through the power of egoism come calamities; through the power of egoism come terrible anxieties; through the power of egoism comes worldly striving; indeed, egoism is my disease.
Relying upon that supreme and long-standing enemy, egoism, I neither eat nor do I drink water; how much less, O Sage, could I enjoy sensual pleasures?
The night of saṃsāra is long, and the illusion that deludes the mind is like a snare set by a Kirāta hunter through the fault of egoism.
Those sufferings which are long-lasting, harsh, and great—born from the sense of "I"—they have gone forth like *khadira* thorns.
I renounce the ego, which has the moon, the sun, and Rāhu for its face; which is a thunderbolt to the lotus of the qualities; and which is like the autumn season to the clouds of equanimity.
I am not Rāma, nor do I have desire for worldly phenomena, nor does my mind dwell upon them; I wish to remain in peace within my own self, just like the Victorious One.
Whatever I have enjoyed, offered in sacrifice, or performed under the influence of egoism—all that is indeed insubstantial; the only reality is the state of being empty of egoism.
O Brahmin, if there is an "I," then one is afflicted by suffering in times of calamity; if it does not exist, one is happy. Therefore, freedom from egoism is better.
O sage, having abandoned the sense of ego through a tranquil mind, I remain free from anxiety; for the flood of enjoyments has its foundation in that which is fragile.
O Brahmin, as long as the cloud of egoism expands, so long does the cluster of *kuṭaja* flowers of craving blossom.
When the dense cloud of egoism has subsided, craving—like a fresh flash of lightning—vanishes very swiftly, disappearing somewhere through the process of the extinguished lamp-flame.
In the great Vindhya mountain of egoism, the intoxicated great elephant of the mind roars with thunderous slaps, like a rain-cloud with its peals of thunder.
In this great forest of the body, that vast lion of dense egoism which exults has spread out this entire world.
The succession of many births, strung upon the fine threads of craving, has been fashioned into a necklace around the neck by the fierce hunter of egoism.
O Sage, this enemy that is the ego has here spread out its web of dependence upon sons, friends, wives, and the like.
When this state of "I" has been wiped away, even by oneself swiftly, all these mental afflictions are likewise completely wiped away.
When the water of the "I" has subsided, the mist of delusion in the sky of the mind, which gradually brings about the cessation [of suffering], vanishes somewhere or other.
O Brahmin, for me, whose mental state is devoid of ego yet who is sinking in grief due to my own folly, you ought to explain whatever is appropriate here.

O Great-souled One, instruct me with what remains: I shall not, even with effort, resort to this abode of egoity—which is the dwelling place of all calamities, unstable, situated within, and abandoned by the Supreme Being—and which is exceedingly painful on all sides.

Śrī Rāma said: Through the performance of virtuous deeds and service to the noble, the mind reaches a state of being worn down by its defects; yet, like a drop of viscous fluid within the wind, the flickering mind continues to waver.
He runs aimlessly and distractedly here and there, wretchedly further and further away, just like a dog in a village.
One never attains anything anywhere, even through the acquisition of great wealth; one does not reach internal fullness, like a basket with water.
O Sage, the mind is eternally empty, yet it is entangled in the snare of vain hope; it finds no peace, like a deer strayed from its herd.
Maintaining a state as flickering as a wave, it never remains even for a moment in the heart without becoming torn and shattered.
The mind, agitated by its own conceptualizing, rushes through the ten directions, like the water of the milk-ocean when churned by Mount Mandara.
I am not able to restrain this great ocean consisting of the mind, which is filled with waves and swirling eddies, and garlanded with the crocodiles of illusion.
O Brahmin, the deer of the mind, longing for the sprouts of grass that are sensual enjoyments and disregarding its fall into the abyss, runs far astray.
My mind never abandons its own state of being mangled and shattered, just as the ocean, through its agitated movement, never relinquishes its restlessness.
With its flickering mode of activity, the mind—restless with a multitude of anxieties—does not fix its steadiness upon any single point, just as a lion does not remain within a cage.
Mounted upon the chariot of delusion, the mind carries away the happiness of equanimity from the body—its agitation destroyed—just as a swan extracts milk from water.
O Lord of Sages, the fluctuations of the mind have dissolved upon the bed of manifold conceptualization and do not awaken; therefore, I am distressed and tormented.
O Brahmin, with my self situated within the cord of craving that has been drawn tight by a firm knot, I am bound by the mind as if a bird were caught in a net.
O Sage, I am consumed by my mind as dry grass is by fire—with the continuous smoke of indignation and the turbulent flames of anxiety.
O Brahmin, I have been liberated from my mind—which had become dull through cruelty and followed after its wife, craving—just as a corpse is abandoned by a dog.
O Brahmin, I have been carried away by the mind—insentient in nature, with a movement characterized by the tossing and surging of waves—just as a tree on a riverbank is swept away by a flood.
As if carried far away by a fierce wind, my mind has been led astray toward sudden falls or wandering in the void.
Constantly intent on crossing this ocean of saṃsāra, I have been blocked by my evil-minded self, just as a flood of water is dammed by a bridge.
As I was traveling from Pātāla to the earth, and from the earth back to Pātāla, I have been ensnared by that evil-minded one like a wooden post in a well by means of a rope.
Through investigation, this [world] is seen to be utterly false in its expansive form and fragile by nature; I have been seized by a wicked mind, just as a child is seized by a Vetāla.
O Brahmin, his mind-grasping power is hotter than fire, more difficult to traverse than even a mountain, and firmer than a diamond; it is truly hard to restrain.
The mind falls upon its objects like a bird toward its own prey; in an instant it reaches detachment, like a child with his toys.
O dear one, this ocean of the mind—insentient by nature, restless, possessing the movement of vast whirlpools, and devoid of any restraining serpent—carries me far away.
O virtuous one, even more difficult than drinking up the great ocean, or uprooting Mount Sumeru, or even consuming fire, is the restraint of the mind.
The mind is the cause of all objects; when it exists, the three worlds exist, and when it is exhausted, the world is exhausted. Therefore, that mind must be treated with diligent effort.

These hundreds of mental joys and sorrows have surely come to you like wild elephants from the forest; I believe, O Sage, that they are now skillfully dissolving away as they grow thin through the power of your solitude.
