I have risen with my mind intent on conquering that enemy against whom the great ones have bound their hopes for victory over all virtues; yet, due to an inner lack of delight, I do not welcome prosperity—which possesses the dull and impure charms of a streak of clouds—just as the moon does not welcome it.

The seventeenth canto. Śrī Rāma said: In this world, by means of insatiable craving—the night of the darkness within the heart—swarms of owls that are the various defects flicker in the sky of consciousness.
With my essence and tenderness entirely consumed by anxiety, which brings about an inner burning, I am being dried up like mud by the heat of the sun.
In the great forest of my mind, which is crowded with the darkness of delusion and empty, the demoness of hope has become a frantic dancer.
Surely the chickpea-cluster of anxiety, its frost composed of words and radiant with a grove of gold, is now coming into full bloom.
Enough with wandering within; your mind, agitated by craving, has come like a wave of treacherous splendor upon the ocean.
Here upon the mountain of my body flows the river of craving, surging with waves, its form flickering like ripples, and resounding with the roar of unrestrained turbulence.
Like an old blade of grass driven by a whirlwind, the mind’s cātaka bird has been led away somewhere by turbid craving, which rises up to swallow its momentum.
Whichever excellence of virtue I rely upon with the greatest devotion, that very thing thirst cuts away for me, just as a mole gnaws at a stringed instrument.
Like a withered leaf in a stream, like a decayed blade of grass in the wind, or like an autumn cloud in the sky, I wander in the cycle of my thoughts.
We, whose intellects are incapable of reaching our own proper domain, become utterly bewildered in the snare of thought, like birds caught in a net.
O father, I have been so scorched by the flame called craving that I do not hope for the cessation of my burning even through ambrosia.
Having gone far, far away from here, and having met again and again, the mare, maddened by thirst, wanders swiftly through the ends of the quarters.
Craving, which is associated with the insentient, causes one's movement up and down; it is perpetually agitated, knotted, and like the rope at the top of a waterwheel.
Like a powerful ox driven by a rope, people are swiftly led away by this craving, which is woven deep within the body and is impossible for anyone to sever.
By the thirst for sons, friends, wives, and so forth, which is constantly pulling [one down], this net is spread throughout the worlds by Kirātī, as if among birds.
Like a night of black craving, she terrifies even the steadfast, blinds even the discerning eye, and exhausts even the joyful.
Crooked, soft to the touch, and signaling the imbalance of poison, craving is like a black female serpent that bites even when only slightly touched.
Piercing the hearts of men, creating a web of illusion, bestowing misfortune, and wretched—thirst is like a black ogress.
O Brahmin, the lute of craving—its strings being the clusters of lassitude—does not shine in bliss, for it holds its hollow body wrapped around with them and is worn out by age.
Tṛṣṇā is a creeper in a deep abyss that is eternally and exceedingly filthy, bitter, and madness-inducing; it has long tendrils and is thick with clinging moisture.
Bringing no joy, empty, fruitless, and raised in vain, craving is inauspicious and cruel, like a withered cluster of blossoms.
Even when her heart is not won over, craving pursues everything; yet it obtains no fruit at all, like an aged woman seeking a lover.
In the vast multitude of saṃsāra, crowded with manifold flavors, craving is the aged dancer upon the stages of the world's expanse.
In the vast wilderness of saṃsāra, craving is a spreading poisonous vine, blossoming with old age and bearing a succession of fruits that fall and rise.
Even when it can no longer do so, thirst maintains its dancing gait; devoid of joy, it dances like an aged dancer.
When the mist thickens, she trembles violently; when light arrives, she becomes still; and when obstacles are difficult to cross, her thought, like a restless peacock, sets foot upon them.
Abounding with dull waves and long remaining empty within its depths, craving is like a river in the rainy season that rises in agitation for only a moment.
Leaving behind one who has perished, craving moves from man to man like a restless bird, seeking another tree as it stands.
She sets foot even upon that which is unassailable; though satisfied, she still seeks further fruit; she does not remain long in one place—thirst is a restless female monkey.
Having done this, that follows; everything is indeed inconsistent. And craving strives incessantly, like a divine impulse.

In one moment it descends to the underworld, in another it ascends to the vault of heaven; in a moment it wanders through the bowers of the quarters—such is craving, the bee within the lotus of the heart.
Craving alone is the giver of long-lasting suffering among all the faults of saṃsāra; it casts even one dwelling in the inner apartments into extreme distress.
The garland of clouds that is craving bestows supreme dullness; it obstructs the supreme light and is dense with the mist of delusion.
For all classes of living beings engaged in the activities of saṃsāra, craving is like a binding rope that threads together the garland of their minds.
Diverse in color, devoid of qualities, long, and existing in a state of impurity; empty, having emptiness as its ground, craving possesses the nature of Indra’s bow.
A thunderbolt to the virtues of the crops, a fruitful autumn for calamities, frost to the lotuses of consciousness, and a long night for the darknesses.
She is the actress in the drama of saṃsāra, the female bird in the aviary of the workplace, the doe in the forest of the mind, and the lute for the concert of Kāma.
It is a wave in the ocean of worldly affairs, a chain for the elephant of delusion, a beautiful creeper upon the banyan tree of creation, and moonlight for the night-lily of suffering.
She is a single jewel-casket for the sufferings of old age and death; she is a perpetually intoxicated courtesan of mental anguish and physical disease.
For a moment craving is like a cloudless sky, for a moment it is a fragment of darkness; for a moment it resembles the path of the heavens, and for a moment it is as dense as a mist.
Thirst subsides for the sake of calming bodily exertion, just as thick, black darkness subsides for the sake of warding off demons.
This mute world, its heart agitated, remains deluded only so long as the cholera-like poison of craving continues to pursue it.
This entire world abandons all suffering when freed from anxiety; indeed, the abandonment of anxiety is said to be the mantra for the cholera of craving.
Grasping at everything—grass, stones, wood, and so forth—with the suspicion that it might be food, craving quivers at the end like a female fish in a pond.
Disease, suffering, and thirst for women quickly bring even a man of profound depth to the surface, just as the rays of the sun cause a lotus to rise.
Hollow within, knotted, with long shoots for thorns, and ever fond of pearl-jewels—cravings are like reed-vines.
Oh, how truly marvelous it is that those of great intelligence cut through even craving—which is so difficult to sever—by means of their stainless and radiant discernment!
Neither the edge of a sword, nor the flame of a thunderbolt, nor the glowing sparks of heated iron are so sharp, O Brahmin, as this craving that resides within the heart.
Blazing, with a dark and sharp tip, possessing a long wick of attachment, luminous yet painful to touch through its burning nature—craving is like the flame of a lamp.
Even the best of men—though as wise as Mount Meru, heroic, and steadfast—a single craving makes as light as a blade of grass in the blink of an eye.

The great slope of the Vindhya mountains is the thirst [for existence]: its dense thickets are spread wide, it is terrifying, composed of masses of clouds and dust, and filled with blinding darkness and fierce mist.

Desire alone, having found its mark within all worlds, remains in the universe—though difficult to perceive, it is present within the very body itself; like the power of sweetness in the water of the Milky Ocean, it dwells amidst the shimmering, restless waves.
Śrī Rāma said: This body, dense with the strings of moist entrails, subject to transformation, and prone to decay, throbs within saṃsāra; yet it leads only to suffering.
Though ignorant, he resembles one who knows; through the wonder of his own turned-about nature, though capable, he is as if incapable; he is neither inert nor conscious.
Oscillating between the views of the insentient and the sentient, the undiscriminating person of deluded soul yields only to delusion.
With a slight [cause] one attains joy; with a slight [cause] one falls into distress. There is no object of grief equal to the body, which is base and devoid of virtue.
He was adorned at every moment by a flower of blossoming smiles, which was ever-changing and radiant with teeth for its filaments.
With arms as branches and a thick trunk, with a noble stance like a pillar of ivory, he was embraced by the playful bees of his eyes, and possessed the large fruit of his head upon its pedestal.
With its trunk and limbs like beautiful sprouts, possessed of clusters of branches, bearing a mass of fruits as its purpose, it was a tree providing a dwelling for birds.

This tree of the body, possessing its own shade, is the resting place for the multitude of travelers that are living beings; to whom does it belong as one's own, and to whom is it another? What reliance, indeed, can there be in this matter?
O dear one, when the boat of the body has been repeatedly grasped for the purpose of crossing over, who could possibly maintain the notion of "self"?
In this empty forest called the body, crowded with many pits and filled with countless trees of hair, who can find any sense of security?
O Father, like a cat, I remain here within this fragile body-drum, which is bound together with flesh, sinews, and bones, and from which the sound has departed.
Grown within the forest of saṃsāra, the monkey of the flickering mind has the appearance of a wish-fulfilling flower-cluster, yet it is gnawed by the woodworm of long-standing suffering.

The serpentess of craving has made her home here; the crow of anger has built its nest. This glorious tree, from which the merit of smiles emerges, bears the great fruits of both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
He had a mass of branches in the form of well-formed limbs, was beautiful with clusters of hands for blossoms, and possessed sprouts in the form of all his own bodily parts trembling in the wind.
He is the support for all the birds of the senses, with well-formed pillars of knees, lofty, endowed with the luster of a lake, and frequented by travelers in the form of desire.
A row of long grass-like hair has grown upon its crown; it is a hollow belly where the vulture of egoism has built its nest.
With its roots—the web of latent impressions—severed, this body-plakṣa tree has become difficult to grasp; devoid of the vigor of exertion, it brings me no pleasure.
O Sage, for me who am a householder within the great mansion of the body and the ego, let it roll about or attain stability; what does this matter to me?
This house of the body is not desired by me: its sense-organs are cattle bound in rows, its courtyard is the whirling thirst, and all its limbs are dyed with passion.
This house of the body is undesirable to me; it is a hollow space, cramped by the friction of the wooden beams of the spinal vertebrae, and bound together by the ropes of the entrails.
This house of my body is undesirable: it has spreading sinews for its strings, blood and water for its mire, and is whitened by the *maṅkola* flowers of old age.
I do not desire this house of the body, whose structural stability is seized by the endless activities performed by the servant-mind, and which has false delusion as its great pillar.
This house of my body is not desired by me; it resounds with the cries of children in distress, is made pleasant only by a comfortable bed, and its maidservants are consumed by wicked desires.

This house of the body is not desired by me; it is crowded with the vessels and utensils of the manifold objects of the senses, which abound in impurity, and it is encrusted with the salt of ignorance.
With ankles made of guggulu, knees resting upon pillars, and a head as its roof, this house of my body—though very firm with its long wooden arms—is not desired by me.
O Brahmin, this house of my body is pleasing to me; it has the open eyes for its windows, the courtyard of the house of wisdom where one sports, and anxiety as its daughter.
This body-house is not pleasing to me, for its moon-chamber of the ears is concealed by the covering of the hair on the head, and its turrets of long fingers are lacking.
With the sprouts of hair as thick as a wall covering all its parts, and possessing an interior like an empty, hollow chest, this house of a body is not desired by me.
This house of the body, with its navel as the central chamber, its interior filled with the humming of vital breaths, and winds that produce whistling sounds, is not desired by me.

That house of my body is not desired by me, for it is filled with windows in the form of wide-open eyes and is never at rest due to the force of the wind agitated by the constant coming and going [of the breath].
With its gateway to the mouth terrifyingly overrun by the monkey of the tongue, and with fragments of teeth and bones visible, this house of my body is not desired.
This house of my body, smooth with the plaster of skin, restless with the movement of its mechanical parts, and constantly burrowed by the rat of the mind, is not desired by me.
My body-house is not desirable; at one moment it is illuminated by the light of a lamp-like smile, beautiful with joy, and at another moment it is pervaded by floods of darkness.
The abode of all diseases, a city of wrinkles and grey hair, a dense thicket of every affliction—this house of the body is not desired by me.

This forest of my body is undesirable to me; it is uneven with the agitation of the senses and the constellations, empty, hollow and pithless, and its thickets and corners are the darkness of delusion.
O Lord of Sages, I am unable to sustain this body-abode, just as one of little strength cannot rescue an elephant mired in the mud.
What is the use of prosperity, what use of sovereignty, what use of the body, and what use of undertakings? In just a few days, Time cuts everything away.
O Sage, tell me: what beauty can there be in this body, composed of blood and flesh, both internally and externally, whose sole nature is destruction?
O dear one, tell me, what reliance can there be for the wise upon those ungrateful bodies which do not follow the soul at the time of death?
"As long as this body—trembling like the tip of an elephant's ear in rut and fragile as a dangling drop of water—does not abandon me, so long shall I abandon it."
This body-sprout, trembling with the movement of the wind, fragile, worn out, thin, and round, is harsh and tasteless; it is not desired by me.
Having enjoyed and drunk for a long time that which is as delicate as a young sprout, it eventually reaches a state of attenuation and pursues its own destruction without effort.
Indeed, this physical body feels no shame as it repeatedly experiences those very same pleasures and pains, consisting of both existence and non-existence.
Having exercised sovereignty for a very long time and enjoyed the glory of wealth and power, why is this body protected, when it attains neither height nor stability?
In the time of old age it undergoes decay, and likewise in the time of death it meets its end; the body is exactly the same, making no distinction between the wealthy and the poor.
Within the belly of the ocean of saṃsāra, in the hollow interior of the cave of craving, this mute tortoise of the body remains asleep, O seeker of liberation.
In this ocean of saṃsāra, numerous pieces of wood that are human bodies are fit only for burning; among them, they know of no man at all.
For the discerning person, there is no purpose whatsoever in the state of a physical body, which is a long-lasting circle of wickedness and which causes the falling of the fruit of one's downfall.
Plunging into the mire of the womb, it suddenly reaches old age; no one knows how or when this frog of a body will depart.
All undertakings are devoid of essence, and bodies are like fleeting winds; as they travel along the path of dust, they are not seen by anyone here.
O Blessed One, the movement of the wind, of a lamp, and of the mind as they go is known, but the coming of the body is never perceived.
Fie, fie again and again upon those who are attached to their bodies and attached to the stability of the world, who are intoxicated by the wine of delusion!
"I am not the body, nor is the body mine; likewise, this [body] is not I"—those whose minds rest thus, O Sage, are the supreme persons.
Abounding in honor and dishonor, and delightful through great gain, those who perceive only faults destroy a man whose attachment is bound solely to the body.
We have been deceived by the artifice of egoism, which acts like a demoness with a graceful form, lying in the hollow of the body.
All this wretched wisdom, bound to the body by this [craving], has been deceived—alas, all alone—by the wicked rascal of false knowledge.
Not even the slightest thing in this visible world is real; yet, by that deluded self with its painted body, the people are deceived.
In just a few days, this withered sprout of a body falls away effortlessly, like a drop from a mountain stream.
This body is soon to perish, like a bubble in the ocean; it vibrates fruitlessly and without result amidst the cycle of vain activities.

O twice-born one, I have no reliance for even a moment upon this body, which is a city conjured by the delusion of a dream and subject to the transformation of false knowledge, and whose destruction is all too evident.
He who has determined stability in lightning, autumnal clouds, and cities of the Gandharvas—let him place his trust in physical combat.

Having cast aside like a blade of grass this body—which is subject to a continuous succession of fragile activities, which possesses a triumphant birth amidst forceful tendencies, and which is full of powerful defects—I now abide in happiness.
Śrī Rāma said: Even having obtained birth in this ocean of worldly existence—which is fickle in form and surging with the waves of duties—childhood leads only to suffering.
Incapacity, calamity, craving, muteness, dull-wittedness, greed, restlessness, and wretchedness—all these prevail in childhood.
In states that are fierce with anger and weeping, and shattered by wretchedness, childhood is a bondage like the tethering-post for elephants.
Neither in death, nor in old age and disease, nor in calamity, nor even in youth, do those anxieties that tear at the heart during childhood cease.
The undertaking of animal births is despised by all; it is fickle, characterized by the conduct of children, and brings suffering even beyond death.
For whom could the dense ignorance of mental reflections—fragile with its manifold conceptualizations, and whose mind is cut down and shattered by childhood—bring any happiness?
What fear could there be in calamity for anyone else—that fear which, through lack of understanding in childhood, arises at every step from water, fire, wind, snakes, and garlands?
Falling powerfully into playful antics, wicked amusements, evil desires, and base intentions, the fool brings about supreme delusion.
Childhood, which begins with constructions imagined by conceptual thought, is difficult to traverse and provides no secure footing; it serves only to discipline a person, not to bring peace.
Whatever faults, whatever misconducts, whatever evil courses, and whatever wicked anxieties there may be—all of these reside in childhood, like owls in a ruined dwelling.
O Brahmin, fie upon those foolish men whose minds are stolen away and who, with their intellects rendered futile, imagine that childhood is delightful!
Wherein the mind, shaped like a swing, oscillates amidst its fluctuations—even that which is impossible within the three worlds—how can it possibly lead to contentment?
O Sage, for all sentient beings indeed, the mind attains a state of restlessness ten times greater in childhood than it does in all other conditions.
The mind is restless by its very nature, and childhood is the height of restlessness; when these two are joined together, who indeed can be a protector against the inner fickleness of the breasts?
O Brahmin, those whose minds were seized by childhood learned fickleness from the eyes of women, from masses of lightning, from clusters of flames, and from the waves.
Indeed, childhood and the mind, in all their various states of activity, are seen to be constantly unstable in their condition, like two brothers.
All forms of suffering, all faults, and all anxieties depend solely upon the fool, just as men depend upon one who possesses wealth.
If a child does not obtain something new and delightful every single day, he falls into a swoon caused by the distress of poison.
With a little he comes under control, and with a little he falls into transformation; the fool delights in impurity alone, just like a dog.
With a face streaming with incessant tears, his body smeared with mud and his mind dulled, the child resembled a parched plot of land drenched by rain.
Devoted to fear and food, wretched, desiring both the seen and the unseen, and possessed of a fickle intellect—one assumes childhood for nothing but suffering alone.
Having failed to obtain the objects desired by his own imagination, the weak-minded fool, his intellect tormented, falls into misery as if his very heart has been torn out.
O Sage, those sufferings of a child—whose aims are difficult to attain and whose many crooked ways are so intense—are not experienced by anyone else.
The fool is constantly tormented by his own powerful mind, which revels in its desires, just as a forest glade is scorched by the summer heat.
A youth who has entered the house of learning encounters great torment, as terrifying as the unevenness of poison, like a lordly elephant at its tethering post.
Infancy, with its tender disposition, consists of various desires and is a false conceptualization; it leads to suffering that is exceedingly long-lasting.
How could that folly by which one, being overjoyed, desires to consume the world and seize the moon from the sky, lead to happiness?
O one of great intelligence, what difference is there between an internal consciousness that is powerless to ward off cold and heat, and a child or a tree?
Devoted to eating, intent on fear, and constantly seeking food, the young ones possess the nature of birds, desiring to fly with their two wings.
In childhood there is fear of the teacher, as well as of the mother and the father; there is fear of people and of elder children—childhood is a temple of fear.

O Great Sage, for one whose disposition is struck down by the state of all faults and who delights in the play of non-discrimination, even taking refuge here does not bring sufficient satisfaction to anyone; it remains merely the impurity of childhood.
Śrī Rāma said: Having abandoned the miseries of childhood, a man whose mind is still afflicted by worldly desires ascends to youth with agitation only to fall from it.
There, experiencing the fluctuations of his own restless mind, which possesses infinite diversions, the dull-witted one goes from sorrow to further sorrow.
Helpless, one is overwhelmed by the demon of desire, which dwells within the cavity of one's own mind and causes manifold agitation.
Just as collyrium applies a covering to the eyes of the young, so does it involuntarily apply veils to the minds of children, whose thoughts are as fickle in their movements as those of women.
O Sage, those very faults arising from evil undertakings—those which are corrupted by that very same [mind]—destroy such a person of that disposition and of that nature.
Those people who have not been destroyed by youth—which, like the seed of the great hell, causes an unceasing wandering—have not been destroyed by anything else.
He by whom the formidable terrain of youth—composed of various flavors and filled with a multitude of diverse events—has been crossed, is called steadfast.
Youth does not please me; its form flashes for but a moment, it possesses the thundering of dense clouds, and like the glare of lightning, it is inauspicious.
Sweet, delicious, and bitter, yet corrupting and a mere ornament to the faults; youth, which resembles the surging waves of wine, does not please me.
Unreality appearing as reality, soon bringing about deception, and like union with a woman in a dream—such youth does not please me.
I do not find youth pleasing; though it charms the minds of all men for but a moment, it stands before everyone like a city of the Gandharvas.

Youth, which lasts no longer than the flight of an arrow, though it offers pleasure, is radiant with suffering and constantly provides fuel for the fire of burning passion; therefore, it does not please me.
Youth does not please me; it is delightful only at first sight, its inner nature is devoid of reality, and it is like union with a courtesan.
Whatever undertakings there may be, they all bring about every kind of suffering; they manifest in youth just as great calamities appear at the end of an eon.
Even the Blessed One fears the night of ignorance that is youth, which causes the darkness within the heart and assumes a terrifying form.
This agitation of youth causes one to utterly forget virtuous conduct, brings about a failure of the intellect, and bestows excessive delusion.
In youth, a living being is consumed in the heart by the fire of unbearable pain born from separation from a beloved, just as a tree is consumed by a forest fire.
For even an intellect that is perfectly pure, expansive, and holy becomes turbid in youth, like a river during the rainy season.
A river with its thick, surging waves may be terrifying, yet it can be crossed; but not so the river of youth, which is fickle and whose inner depths are agitated by craving.
"She is my beloved," "those are her full breasts," "those are her charms," "that is her face"—through such thoughts concerning youth, a person falls into a state of decay.
In this world, virtuous people honor a young man afflicted by the pain of restless craving, but they do not honor one who is cut down like a withered blade of grass.
For youth is indeed the eternal tethering post for the great elephant of pride, which, afflicted by intoxication and bearing the pearls of its own faults, leads only to destruction.
Alas, youth is a forest whose roots are the vastness of the mind, which harbors the venomous serpents of the faults, and whose trees are wasting and weeping.
Know that youth is a lotus flower: crowded with filaments of passion, filled with petals of false conceptualization, and frequented by bees of evil thoughts.
Fresh youth is the abode of the birds of mental and physical affliction, which frequent the shores of the lake of the heart and possess both formed and unformed wings of vice.
The ocean is in its prime youth, possessing playful waves that are insentient, beyond counting, and indifferent to all boundaries.
The fierce wind of youth is skilled at destroying the stability of all those whose creation of virtues has taken root, for it is thick with passion and darkness.
The fierce dust-storms of youth lead the face to paleness and cause the brows to become disheveled; harsh with age, they ascend to the highest peak of decay.
The exuberance of youth in men awakens the host of defects, cuts away the garland of virtues, and is the playground for the splendors of misdeeds.
This moon of fresh youth bewilders the bee of the mind by binding it to the pollen of the lotus-body.
The lovely creeper of youth, sprouted from a fragment of the body, intoxicates the bee of the mind as soon as it has attached itself and reached its full growth.
The deer of the mind, rushing toward the mirage of youth that arises from the heat of the body's winds, fall into the pit of the sense objects.
The moonlight for the night of my body, the mane of the lion of my mind, and the wave of the ocean of my life—this youth of mine brings me no satisfaction.
This youth has borne fruit within the wilderness of this body for only a few days; indeed, you should not place your trust in this autumnal season.
In an instant, the bird of youth immediately departs from the body, just as the wish-fulfilling gem slips from the hand of one of meager fortune in a mere moment.
Whenever youth ascends to its highest peak, the passions, feverish with longing, leap up only for one's destruction.
Right then do the demons of passion and hatred leap about; this entire host does not set until the night of youth has passed away.
O Youth, who are full of manifold transformations, wretched, and perishing in an instant—have compassion for me as if I were a son dying before you!
That utterly deluded man who, out of delusion, experiences joy because of youth—which is subject to momentary destruction—is indeed known as a "human deer."
The foolish person who, out of pride and delusion, longs for youth intoxicated by passion, will before long be joined with remorse.
They are worthy of worship, they are great-souled ones, and they alone are true men on this earth, O virtuous one, who have happily crossed over the peril of youth.
The ocean, though filled with formidable sea-monsters, can be crossed with ease; but youth that is tainted by vice and tossed by the force of its own surging waves cannot.

Adorned with discipline, the abode of noble beings, radiant with compassion, and encircled by virtues—indeed, O dear one, such a youth, so difficult to find here in this world, is like a forest situated in the sky.
Śrī Rāma said: In this cage of limbs, made of flesh-puppetry, fickle as a machine, and adorned with sinews, bones, and joints—what in a woman can truly be beautiful?
Having separated the skin, flesh, blood, and tears from the eye, look closely; if it is truly beautiful, why do you delude yourself in vain?
"Here are the hair, there is the blood"—this is the body of a woman; what does one of vast intention gain by censuring her?
O dear one, those very limbs of all embodied beings that were repeatedly cherished with garments and ointments are now being torn apart by flesh-eating scavengers.
On which breast the splendor of a pearl necklace was seen, resembling the rush of the Ganges water sparkling upon the slopes of Mount Meru’s peaks.
In cremation grounds and at the ends of the quarters, that very same breast of a woman is devoured by dogs in due time, like a small morsel of food.
Just as the limbs of a young elephant in the forest are smeared with blood, flesh, and bone, so too are the limbs of a passionate woman; for what attachment can there be toward her?
The mere fact that a woman is pleasing at first sight is imagined; O Sage, I believe that even this does not exist here, for it is solely a cause of delusion.
What difference is there between wine, which bestows expansive exhilaration preceded by intoxication and passion, and a woman who likewise causes transformation?
O Sage, the elephants of human beings, tethered to the hitching post of the tongue, do not attain awakening even with the firm goads of tranquility.
Bearing hair like soot, difficult to touch yet pleasing to the eye, women—like flames of the fire of evil deeds—burn a man like straw.
For women, though they be full of passion even when far away from those who are burning with desire, are yet devoid of essence; they are indeed a beautiful yet terrible fuel for the fires of hell.
Her braided hair was disheveled, her eyes were like shimmering stars, her face was like the orb of the full moon, and she smiled with a cluster of flowers.
With men agitated by her playful charms, she brings about the destruction of their undertakings; she is a long night of passion that utterly deludes the intellect.
Delightful and sweet with flowers, adorned with sprout-like hands, rich in the playful charm of bee-like eyes, and bearing clusters of blossoms that are her breasts.
With limbs as fair as the filaments of a flower, yet intent on slaying men, she brings about a state of frantic helplessness, like a lovely poisonous creeper.

By the mere sigh of her longing for union, she who is eager to crush [her lover] like a serpent, the man is drawn out from his cave by his beloved, as a snake is pulled from its hole by a female elephant.
Women are the snares for binding the limbs of those bird-like men whose minds are deluded, scattered by the hunter named desire.
O Brahmin, the intoxicated elephant of the mind remains bound by the chain of passion within the vast tethering post of the *lalanā*, as if mute.
For men who are like fish in the pond of birth, wandering in the mud of the mind, woman is the baited hook on a line made of the cords of evil latent impressions.
A beautiful-eyed woman is a tethering post for horses like a manger, and a bond for men like a spell for serpents.
O Sage, this variegated land of enjoyment, rich in manifold flavors, has indeed attained its supreme state here by depending upon women.
May I always be defiled by this woman, who is like a small casket for all the jewels of faults and a constant chain of suffering.
What use have I for breasts, or eyes, or hips, or the ground—this worthless thing whose sole essence is mere flesh?
O Brahmin, in just a few days, a woman goes to ruin, with flesh here, blood there, and bones elsewhere.
O Sage, those women who are fondled by stout men and are dear to them sleep upon the ground of their ancestors with their limbs well-proportioned.
O Brahmin, in the forest, a woman drinks from the mouth of her beloved the juice of leaf-sprouts that has become even thicker with affection.
The hair becomes the decorative fringe on the trees of the cremation ground, and the bones, shining like stars, appear upon the circle of the earth within a few days.
The dust drinks the blood, and many flesh-eaters devour it; the jackals consume the hides, and the vital breaths depart into the sky.
Thus have I described to you the imminent condition of the limbs of women; why do you still pursue delusion?

How indeed can one endowed with intelligence [regard] this structure, known as the *lalanā*, which is a configuration resulting from the contact of the five elements, as something that descends toward taste?
Anxious thought, following after its beloved, becomes like a dense thicket with spreading branches, garlanded with bitter and sour fruits, and reaches a state of extreme height.
Due to being utterly bewildered, the mind—obscured and agitated by dense craving—falls into supreme delusion, like a deer strayed from its herd.
A young man devoted to a young woman reaches the highest state of pitiability, like an elephant, lusting after a female, bound in a pit in the Vindhya mountains.

He who has a wife has a desire for enjoyment; for one without a wife, where is the ground for enjoyment? Having abandoned the woman, the world is abandoned; having abandoned the world, one becomes happy.

O Brahmin, I do not take delight in enjoyments that are difficult to transcend and charming only at first sight, flickering like the wings of a bee; out of fear of death, disease, old age, and the like, I shall strive with effort to attain the supreme state of peace.
Śrī Rāma said: "Childhood is indeed insufficient, for it forcibly drinks in youth; and later, old age consumes youth—behold their mutual harshness."
Old age destroys the body, just as a thunderbolt destroys a lotus, a whirlwind destroys autumnal water, or a river destroys a tree on its bank.
Old age, appearing in a decrepit form and causing every limb to become worn out, swiftly leads the body to deformity, just as a drop of poison does.
Lustful women look with indifference upon a man whose every limb is slack and torn, his body worn out by old age, as if he were a mere young camel.
When people have been seized by old age, which is both effortless and relentless, wisdom flees away like a woman who has been struck by her rival.
Servants, sons, wives, kinsmen, and friends likewise laugh at a man trembling with old age, as if he were a madman.
For greed approaches an aged man—who is difficult to look upon, wretched, and devoid of virtue and prowess—just as a vulture alights upon a tree that is not tall.
In old age, a longing that consists of the defect of wretchedness grows within the heart; it is long-lasting, brings burning pain, and is the sole companion of all calamities.
"What painful and most terrible deed must I perform for the sake of the next world? Indeed, in old age, a fear grows that is impossible to remedy."
"Who am I, this wretch? What indeed can I do, and how shall I remain? I shall simply maintain silence"—such is the dejection that arises in old age.
"How, when, and what kind of delicious food might I obtain from people?"—this constant thought, along with old age itself, burns the heart in one's later years.
In old age, greed arises with a longing to enjoy, yet one is unable to do so; indeed, the heart is consumed by the wretchedness of one's lack of power.
Like a female crane worn out by old age, the body-tree stands at its head, filled with the serpents of disease, crying out as long as it inflicts the suffering of physical torment.
O Sage, just then, the owl of death, desiring the thick darkness of blindness, was seen arriving swiftly from somewhere.
Just as darkness pursues the evening twilight that has arisen, so too does death pursue one upon seeing old age manifest in the body.
O Sage, as soon as the monkey of death sees from afar the tree of the body in full bloom with the flowers of old age, it rushes toward it with great speed.
An empty city appears; a tree with its branches lopped off appears; a region suffering from drought appears; yet a body worn out by old age does not appear.
In an instant, old age seizes a man with such force—causing him to cough and gasp as if to swallow him—that he is like a vulture snatching meat.
As soon as she sees him, as if filled with longing, old age seizes his body for a moment and places it upon her head, then swiftly shreds it, just as a young maiden plucks a white water-lily.
Making whistling sounds, this wind, harsh with dust, withers her body—already worn out—as a gale withers the sprout of a tree.
The body, struck by old age and having reached a state of decay, bears the beauty of a withered lotus strewn over by a mass of frost.
This old age, like the risen moonlight upon the peaks of the mountain of the head, forcefully causes the night-lotuses of coughing due to wind to blossom.
Beholding the pumpkin-like head of men, withered and grey by the alkali of old age, Time, it is said, devours it as its sovereign lord.
Exerted by the son of Jahnu (Yama), Old Age swiftly cuts away the roots of this tree of the body while its life-force is still moving.
The old cat, greedy for the flesh of the body, devours the mouse of youth with great ferocity and attains supreme delight.
There is nothing in this world so inauspicious as the female jackal born of the body that howls with old age.
This flame of old age blazes forth, consisting of the smoke and darkness of suffering, with coughing, labored breathing, and whistling; indeed, he by whom it is ignited is utterly consumed.
O father, the slender body of men, with its shoots of white hair, becomes crooked through old age, just like a flowering creeper bent down by its blossoms.
O Sage, the elephant of death surely uproots in an instant the camphor-tree of the body, which is as white as the camphor of old age.
O Sage, as King Death approaches, with old age as his white fly-whisk, his army of personal afflictions and diseases marches ahead.
O Sage, behold those who had entered the hollow of a mountain and were not conquered by their enemies in battle, now swiftly defeated by an old, decrepit ogress.
Within the interior of the body-dwelling, enveloped by the frost of old age, the infant senses are not able to move even slightly.
Stumbling repeatedly with the third part of her staff, coughing and emitting downward wind, old age dances like a woman on a drum.
In this Gandhakuṭī of the wandering through saṃsāra, the beauty of the fly-whisk named "Old Age" shines forth, resting upon the staff of the body as its crest.
O Sage, while the city of the body remains white with the rising moon of old age, the night-lotus of death blooms in an instant.
In the inner apartments of the body, which are white with the plaster of old age, women remain in comfort, though there exist incapacity, affliction, and calamity.
O Sage, where non-existence precedes and old age triumphs over living beings, what consolation can there be here for one of dull intellect like me?

What is the use of that wretched life and miserable grasp, even if one lives on until old age has arrived? For in this realm of old age, O father, all the desires of people remain unconquered and cast everything aside.

Śrī Rāma said: Through the manifold conceptualizations and much idle chatter of those of small intellect, delusion has been driven to a state of heightening within the pit of saṃsāra by means of various distinctions.
How could the wise ever find a place here in this cage of a snare? Only fools desire to seize the fruit reflected in a mirror.
Even here, for those whose cultivation of happiness is fragile, time cuts it away entirely, just as a rat gnaws through a thread.
There is nothing here that this all-devouring time does not swallow up; it devours the entire world that has been born, just as the submarine fire consumes the surging ocean.
As the Great Lord, Time is terrible in its universal uniformity; it is intent upon swallowing this entire existence of the visible world.
Even for the great, O Lord, Time waits not even a moment; having become the soul of the universe, it swallows the infinite world.
Manifesting slightly through forms known as ages, years, and kalpas, he who is the self of the unperceivable form stands pervading all things.
Those things which are delightful, those auspicious undertakings, and even those as massive as Mount Sumeru—all are swallowed up by Time, just as serpents are devoured by Garuḍa.
Merciless, hard, cruel, harsh, wretched, and base—there is nothing that this Time has not yet swallowed even to this day.
Time, whose mind is solely intent on devouring, eats even while swallowing; yet this great consumer is never satiated, even by the infinite floods of worlds.
Time takes away, destroys, creates, consumes, and slays; for it is like an actor who performs the dance of saṃsāra in manifold forms.
It incessantly breaks apart the seeds of the elements situated in their divisions within the world, due to its lack of substantiality, just as a parrot [breaks] pomegranate seeds.
The elephant that sustains the life-creepers of the abundant populace roams about, its tusks severing the sprouts of the people—both those who are virtuous and those who are wicked.

Encompassing the entire expansive forest of Brahmā—which has Viriñci as its root, the cosmic egg as its trunk, and the great gods as its fruit—it stands pervading the vast expanse of the supreme reality.
Filled with bees during the night and creating clusters of blossoms by day, the creeper of the arts of the Creator never grows weary.
O Sage, the crest-jewel of rogues is not split even when broken, nor is he burned even when burnt; he is not seen even though he is visible.
In a single moment, it is capable of raising something up slightly and destroying something else entirely; thus, from its vast extent, it is like a kingdom of the mind.
He remained there, causing people to revolve in a cycle of forms that produce only material wealth, through the conduct of a woman of wicked dalliance whose abundance is a source of misery.
Out of self-centeredness, he was intent on making everything his own—straw, dust, Mahendra, Mount Sumeru, a leaf, and the ocean.
Cruelty is fully present right here; greed is firmly established right here; all misfortune is found right here, as is unbearable fickleness.
He playfully impels the sun and moon across the vault of the sky, as if playing with two balls in his own courtyard like a child.
With his form encircled by garlands of the bones of all beings reaching down to his feet, he shines forth like Time itself at the end of an aeon, having seized upon every conceptual construction.
In the sky, Mount Meru trembles like a birch bark leaf tossed by the winds at the end of an eon, driven by the fierce movements of this [ascetic].
Having become Rudra, he becomes Mahendra and then the Grandfather; he also becomes Śakra and Vaiśravaṇa, and yet again, nothing at all.
Possessing immeasurable splendor, he bears within himself other creations that arise and perish like the waves of the ocean, appearing by day and night.
Shaking down from the trees called Mahākalpas, he stood like one [shaking] the clusters of ripe fruits—the hosts of gods and asuras.
This is the time when the great trees that are the cosmic eggs have reached their fall, resounding with the humming of the mosquitoes that are living beings.
Accompanied by his beloved Action, he alone delights his body with the night-lotus of pure existence, which is made to blossom by the moonlight of consciousness.
He remained established, leaning upon his own body as a seat that was boundless, shoreless, and limitless, as lofty as a great mountain.
In some places he remained contemplating his own nature as dark with deep blackness, in some places as pervaded by splendor, and in some places as devoid of both.
With his own being—whose essence is the condensed quintessence of countless transmigrations—he has come to a state of being firmly rooted, like the earth itself, heavy with its burden.
It does not weary, it does not exert itself, it does not come, nor does it go; it neither sets nor rises, even throughout hundreds of great eons.
Merely through the effortless play of initiating the world, with profound ease, he protects by means of his own self the vast Self that is free from egoism.
He remained there, as if placing upon his own lake the row of day-lotuses—now stained with the mud of night—and the whirling bees that were the clouds.
Having taken up his worn-out broom, the wretched man spends the night with Kṛṣṇā and brings back from all sides the gold dust that shines upon the mountain.
Moving the sun-lamp from corner to corner with his finger, he gazes about the house of the world out of miserliness, wondering, "What is there, and where?"
Beholding with his unblinking solar eye, he devours the ripe fruits of the world-guardians; this [world] is like a decayed forest.

Death, like a casket, gradually deposits the jewels of the world—strung upon the thread of the qualities (*guṇa*)—into its formidable interior, which is strewn with the dilapidated huts of the universe.
That very string of world-jewels which is abundantly filled with virtues, he cuts away further, having placed it upon his body as if for the sake of ornamentation.
The fickle moon constantly and excessively encircles the night-lotus garland that follows him day by day, with its stars as its filaments.
The butcher of the world—consisting of mountains, oceans, clouds, and mountain peaks—daily drinks even the red specks of the stars upon beholding them.
He is the moon for the lotus of youth and the lion for the elephant of life; there is nothing, whether trivial or significant, that he does not plunder.
Through the playful sport of cosmic manifestation, which grinds and casts down all living beings, non-existence delights in itself by means of its own self through the appearance of existence.
He is the creator, the enjoyer, and the destroyer; he is the rememberer who has attained the state of all things.
Indeed, the power of Time manifests here among men by suddenly revealing and then concealing the body—which, though possessing both beautiful and ugly forms, has no internal division between them.
Śrī Rāma said: Of this prince, whose play is so formidable, from whom all calamities have been cast far away, and who possesses unmeasured power over Time within this worldly existence;
As he thus practiced his sport of hunting with wretched and deluded multitudes of beings and wild animals, the thicket of the world’s jungle became worn out.
The great ocean at the time of the Kalpa’s end is a delightful pleasure-pool, wherein the beautiful submarine fire shines like a lotus in one corner.
The world is fashioned from those very same elements—pungent, bitter, sour, and so forth—which have become oceans of curd and milk, yet have become stale through the cycles of time.
Caṇḍī, who moves through the four quarters, accompanied by the entire host of Mothers, is stationed within the forest of saṃsāra; she is a tigress who destroys the multitudes of malevolent spirits.

The earth of consciousness is held in the palm of the hand; it is a vessel for drinking, filled with the essence of flavor, and adorned with a garland of swaying clusters of lotuses, water-lilies, and white lilies.
Roaring and slapping his massive limbs, Narasimha made him a captive bird in the cage of his arms; with his mane and broad, muscular shoulders, he was turned into a plaything.
Sweet with the lute of the bottle-gourd, possessing the radiant splendor of an autumnal sky, the Lord Mahākāla is indeed a playful young cuckoo.
The bow named Non-Contemplation (Abhāvanā), its form incessantly vibrating and discharging volleys of arrows of suffering, flashes forth in every direction.

Supreme indeed is Time, who is skilled in excessive playfulness; wandering, moving, and shimmering, he tears asunder this decaying world, acting like a restless monkey, and here he exerts himself with his body quivering.
Śrī Rāma said: "In this very world, another who acts as the crest-jewel of misfortunes is called 'Fate' (daiva) and 'Time' (kāla)."
Apart from mere activity, no other form is perceived for that which consists of its own vibration; it has neither action nor intended purpose.
Therefore, this entire succession of beings, as fragile as a garland of snow, has been brought to a state of extreme distress by this heat.
Whatever expansive circle of the world is seen here, that is his dance-hall; in it, he dances intensely.
And thirdly, bearing the exceedingly terrible name Kṛtānta, the intoxicated deity dances in the world in the form of a Kāpālika.
O Sage, as Kṛtānta dances like one utterly impassioned, he is constantly and intensely enamored with his beloved Niyati.

The remainder, Śaśikalāśubhra, and Gaṅgāvāha—these two are threefold; they exist both as the sacred thread (upavīta) and as that which is not worn (anivīta) upon the chest of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra).
O Brahmā, the orbs of the moon and sun are the golden bracelets at the base of his arms; the playful lotus in his hand is the pericarp of the cosmic egg.
Studded with stars like dewdrops, with the Puṣkara and Āvarta clouds as its trembling leaves, that single sky was the very canopy over the waters of the universal ocean.
Before such a person as he, Destiny, ever longing for him, dances with unremitting fervor through her various undertakings.
In the hollow of the pavilion of the world, she who is fond of dancing, whose nature is unimpeded movement, and who is restless with coming and going;
With beautiful ornaments upon her limbs, she was like a series of intermediate celestial worlds; her massive, circular braid hung down from the sky as far as the netherworld.
And Narakālī, a garland of anklets resplendent with a sweet, tinkling sound, is strung upon the thread of evil deeds and stands with her feet in the underworld.
On the tablet of Yama’s face, Citragupta has painted a musk tilaka-mark, fashioned according to the number of his deeds.
Having assumed a black countenance at the end of the eons, this goddess indeed dances again in agitation, making the solid mountains resound with her loud cries.
Behind them were the Prālambas, the Vibhrāntakas, the Kumārabhṛtas, and the Barhins, terrifying with the loud, resonant clamor from the vast openings of their three eyes.
With the heads of Śiva, whose moon was scattered among his long, dangling matted locks; and with the chowries of Gaurī’s beautiful, fair tresses, from which lovely Mandāra flowers were falling.
With skull-drums as vast as Bhairava’s belly, resembling mountains in their violent dancing, and with begging-bowls formed from the hundred-pored body of Indra that resounded with noise;
Filling the sky with the weight of her dry skeletons and skull-topped staffs, she, the bringer of universal destruction, terrifies even herself.
With a beautiful garland of lotuses that are the wheels on the heads of his universal forms, he shines as he leaps in the cosmic dances throughout the great kalpas.

It is said that at the end of the eon, even Tumburu and the other celestial musicians flee from her due to the terrifying sounds of her drums, which rival the tumultuous roar of the Puṣkarāvarta clouds.
Within the dancing Kṛtānta, who shines with the orb of the moon, whose peacock-feather crown is the sky made beautiful by the moonlight of the stars;
In one ear there was a blazing ring of bones from the Himalayas, and in the other, a beautiful golden earring from Mount Meru.
Right here, the two swaying earrings are the sun and moon upon the circles of her cheeks; and the range of the Lokāloka mountain serves as her girdle all around her waist.
Moving here and there, the lightning—its whorl like an earring—shines like a strip of cloud-cloth fluttered by the wind.
With maces, sharp-edged spears, lances, pikes, barbed missiles, and clubs—sharp weapons gathered like the Destroyer himself when he has finished consuming the world.
Upon this long noose of the bonds of saṃsāra, cast by the hand of Time, upon which the great thread of remaining enjoyments is strung, his garland shines resplendent.
The row of bracelets formed by the seven oceans is his ornament, radiant with the brilliance of the jewels in the makara-shaped clasps that shimmer with life.
The great whirlpool of worldly affairs, a succession of pleasure and pain, darkened by the dust of passion and the gloom of ignorance—this row of hair shines upon him.
At the end of the eon, Kṛtānta, being of such a nature, having brought to an end this dance born of Tāṇḍava along with Maheśvara, withdrew his creative activity.
Furthermore, she performs this dance-play consisting of *lāsya*, which is the very nature of creation, adorned with the overcoming of old age, grief, and suffering.

Again and again he creates worlds, forest interiors, and other realms, as well as the arrangement of the network of living beings; he fashions both the stable and the unstable, and the beautiful patterns of conduct, just as a tireless child constructs figures out of mud.
Śrī Rāma said: O great sage, since this world of these beings—time and the rest—is thus constituted, tell me: what reliance can those like me have here upon that which is called saṃsāra?
O Sage, we stand as if sold by these gods and others, like forest deer deluded by the constructions of a magical illusion.
This ignoble succession of time, intent upon devouring all, incessantly casts the world into the ocean of calamity.
The god [of love] burns within with his cruel deeds and evil desires, just as fire burns the world with its flames of hot light.
This destiny, which is naturally fickle due to its feminine nature and is ever intent upon its fixed course, now disturbs my fortitude—she who is beloved for her form as the boundary of conduct.
Like a serpent seizing the wind, Death—whose conduct is cruel—seizes the multitude of living beings without ceasing, leading the undecaying body to old age.
Yama, the king of the lords of the dead, is merciless; he does not show compassion even for one who is suffering. A person who is noble in his compassion for all beings has become rare to find.
O Sage, all classes of beings are indeed of feeble substance; these realms of enjoyment are for nothing but suffering and lead to an endless end, being truly dreadful.
Life is exceedingly fickle, death is invariably cruel, youth is extremely unsteady, and childhood is robbed by dullness.
The world is stained by the impurity of time; kinsmen are the bonds of existence; enjoyments are the great diseases of worldly life; and cravings are but mirages.
The enemies are indeed the very senses; truth has become untruth. The enemy, the mind, strikes at itself by means of the mind alone.
Egoism leads to blemish; intellects are frail; actions yield bitter fruits; and pastimes have become centered on women.
The true wonders, which were once the objects of longing, have been destroyed; women have become banners of vice, and the aesthetic sentiments have fallen into a state of flavorlessness.
When an object is known as non-existent, the mind is surrendered to the ego; when beings are pierced by the realization of their non-existence, the end of existence is not attained.
O virtuous one, the mind, its interior agitated, suffers in solitude; the disease of passion flourishes, while dispassion does not approach.
When the vision is struck by the quality of rajas, tamas increases further; and the reality of pure being (sattva) is not attained, being exceedingly remote.
Stability has become instability; death is facing its arrival; fortitude has fallen into despondency; and delight is constantly fixed on what is unreal.
The intellect is clouded by dullness, the body is intent solely on falling, old age seems to blaze within the frame, and past misdeeds flash back into consciousness.
With effort, youth passes away; association with the virtuous remains far off; no refuge whatsoever exists, and nowhere does truth arise.
The mind is as if utterly bewildered within; joy has gone far away; compassion does not arise with its former brilliance; and baseness approaches from afar.
A person who is constantly caught up in falling and rising moves from steadiness to instability; the embrace of the wicked is easily obtained, but association with the virtuous is difficult to find.
Phenomena come and go; meditation is the bond of existence. Only the perpetual succession of beings is led here and there.
For even the directions are no longer seen, and even place is subject to the designation of "other"; even mountains crumble—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
Even the sky is devoured by existence, and even the earth is woven [into it]; even the ground falls into desolation—what reliance can there be on a person such as I?
Even the oceans dry up and even the stars perish; even the perfected ones (siddhas) meet their end—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
Even the Dānavas are torn asunder; even Dhruva’s life is uncertain; even the immortals are slain—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
Even Śakra is assailed by crooked ones, and even Yama is brought under control; even Vāyu loses his nature as wind—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
Even the moon attains the state of the sky, even the sun goes to fragmentation, and even fire reaches a state of being submerged; what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?

Even Parameṣṭhin, though established in his final state, is carried away; even Hiraṇyagarbha, though unborn, is led off; even Bhava falls into non-existence—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
By whom time is measured and destiny is led, and by whom even the infinite sky is dissolved—what reliance can there be on a person such as I?
By some delusive being whose form is unknown through its nature of being inaudible, unutterable, and invisible, the worlds are mocked.
Having attained even a fraction of egoism, there is no one in the three worlds who is not afflicted by that which dwells within them all.
Like the sun upon the ridges of rocky mountains, one who has become like a horse is constantly driven along, as helpless as a forest stone.
The terrestrial globe, the abode of the hosts of gods and demons dwelling within it, is encircled by the wheel of celestial spheres, like a ripe walnut by its husk.
The gods in heaven, men on earth, and the serpents in the netherworlds—all are reduced to a state of decay in the mere span of a single kalpa.
And Kāma, having acquired his prowess through the battle with the Lord of the Universe, has leaped forth out of all due order and bounds about, having assailed the world.
Spring, like an intoxicated elephant, with its rutting ichor of falling blossoms that perfumes the entire circle of the quarters, renders the mind fickle.
Even great discernment is not able to restore the mind to its natural state when its form has been gazed upon by the tremulous eyes of an attached woman.
I consider only the Buddha to be truly happy, for his mind is cooled within itself, even while he acts for the benefit of others and is consumed by compassion for the suffering of others.
Who is able to count the waves in the ocean of life—waves that arise and perish, falling into the submarine fire of time?

All men indeed, through delusion, are bound by the snares of evil desires; like deer caught in thickets of vice, they are scattered throughout the wilderness of birth. By their wicked deeds here, the lifespan of people in this world is consumed away amidst the succession of rebirths.
We do not know what the fruit will be for those who have fashioned a noose from the trees and creepers of the sky, even though we are experts in discernment.

"This is a festival today; this is the season; likewise, there is a procession here; these are your kinsmen; this is happiness with its special enjoyments"—thus, falsely weaving a web of such discursive thoughts, the world falls away here with a mind that is wavering and fragile.
Śrī Rāma said: Furthermore, O Father, in this world-nature which is exceedingly beautiful and delightful, there is nothing whatsoever that comes forth by which the mind may attain supreme rest.

When childhood has passed and the deer of the mind—restless with its imagined play—is worn out in the caves of women, and when the little body has reached a state of decay, the world suffers only in grief.
Having cast far away the lotus-pond of the body, struck by the frost of old age, and once the bee of life has departed in an instant, the lake of worldly existence for all people is utterly dried up.

Whenever it surely reaches maturity, then and there this vine of the human body brings forth its delight; though laden with the weight of old age, it bears many fresh blossoms even as it becomes withered and decayed.

In this world, the river of craving flows on, its powerful current sweeping away the entire multitude of infinite objects; it is skilled at eroding the roots of the sturdy tree of contentment for those standing upon its banks.

Bound by the leather straps of the body-ship, tossed about and wandering in the ocean of existence, the unsteady vessel is churned by the five sea-monsters known as the sense-faculties as it sinks downward.

These deer of the mind, wandering through the forest of the creeping vine of craving and roaming among the hundreds of branches of the trees of desire, waste away their time without ever attaining the fruit.

In times of hardship, their dejection and delusion are cast far away; in times of well-being, they are not captivated by an arrogant mind. Such great men, whose inner hearts are unshaken by beautiful women, are exceedingly rare in this day and age.

Those who cross the ocean of battle, with its waves consisting of throngs of elephants, are not heroes in my view; those alone are heroes here who cross this ocean of the body and senses, with its waves of the mind.

No state whatsoever is seen for anyone that is delightful as its ultimate, untainted fruit—a state which, once attained, the world reaches rest, its mental fluctuations having been struck down by the cessation of vain hopes regarding action.

Those great ones who, bound by unshakable fortitude, fill the hollows of the world’s quarters with their fame, their dwellings with their majesty, and Fortune herself with the power of their goodness—such as these are not easily found in this world.
Whether situated within a mountain crag or inside a diamond fortress, all fortunes and calamities alike—along with the force of supernatural powers—constantly approach him from every side.
Sons, wives, and wealth are fashioned by the intellect, O dear one, appearing like an elixir; yet none of them provides benefit in the end, for therein lies a most delightful swoon of poison.

Overcome by despair and having reached a precarious state at the end of his body's life-span, a person here, remembering his own former states which were empty of Dharma, is consumed within by the fire of old age.
Having spent the first days in activities aimed at attaining sensual pleasures, wealth, and dharma, by what means can a man’s mind—fickle and restless like the tail-feathers of a peacock—attain rest?

Even by those results of past actions that have already appeared before one, yet whose form remains unattained—resembling the lofty waves of a river—and which arrive solely by the power of destiny, the world is mocked; for people have diverse tastes.
These and those activities, cultivated by them and infinitely enchanting, swiftly wear away the hearts of people toward the end of old age through the delighting of their wives.

Just as the withered leaves of trees, having come together at birth, quickly go to their dissolution, even so do worldly people, devoid of self-discrimination, go from wherever they have gathered by means of the days.

Having wandered here and there to a great distance and entered his home at the close of day, who can find sleep during the night—a time when the day is empty of the virtuous deeds performed by people of discernment?

When the entire host of enemies has been put to flight and prosperity has arrived from all sides, one may enjoy these pleasures for as long as they last—yet at any moment, death may arrive from somewhere unknown.

Alas, the people on this earth are being churned by these entities whose forms are increased from some source yet remain trivial, which are seen for a moment and then vanish; they do not realize whether this is a new attainment or a fall.

Bound by their wretched karma, those people and sheep make Kālamukha their prey with their own dear lives; having forcibly attained corpulence, they do not exist [any longer] due to the affliction of their bodies.
The restless multitude on this earth comes ever swiftly and goes away ever swiftly without ceasing; from wherever it arises, it is like a succession of waves, momentary in its destruction.

Intent solely on taking away the lives of men, women captivate the mind with their loveliness; like poisonous tree-creepers with red blossoms and restless bees for eyes, they entice all who behold them.
Coming from here and there, bound by a common convention though in vain, the illusory practice of men regarding wife and friend is like a temporary association during a journey.
Just as when lamps have gone out after consuming many wicks that were bound by excessive oil, so too in the flickering garlands of saṃsāra—which are unreal—their true nature is not known.

This wheel of the breast, which is the very engine of the turmoil of saṃsāra, though as fragile as a water-bubble in the monsoon rain, spreads a conviction of long-lasting stability in the mind of a heedless person.

Virtues, once radiant with splendor, have perished by the power of fate; now, existing only in a state of decay, they have retreated far beyond the reach of consolation, like the winter season for a lotus.

When a tree, having approached again and again by the power of fate, provides assistance with the very weight of its own body, what occasion is there for remorse when that same tree is cut down by axes? For in such a case, where is the room for consolation?
From association with this person—who, though charming, is of excessively wicked conduct and has arisen to cause internal ruin—one now experiences a swoon, just as from contact with a poisonous tree.

What are those directions in which no faults exist? What are those regions where there is no burning pain of suffering? What are those beings in whom there is no fragility? What are those actions in which there is indeed no illusion?

For the Viriñcis, who live for a single moment within the duration of a kalpa, are themselves counted by the number of kalpa-epochs; therefore, in the web of time which possesses all its parts (kalās), even the notions of shortness and length are unreal.

Everywhere the mountains are made of stone, the earth is made of clay, and trees are made only of wood; people are composed of flesh and possess a nature bound by human effort—there is nothing here that is unprecedented or devoid of transformation.

When perceived by consciousness as permeated by volition, this world—bound by water, possessing a downward-tending course, and situated in the sky—is seen through the distinct differentiation of the characteristics of objects; other than this, there is nothing else whatsoever.
O virtuous one, this wondrous marvel here, which causes wonder in the hearts of wise men, never at any time becomes an object for anyone, even in a dream—so strange is its nature.

Even now, though the magnitude of conceptual construction has vanished like the fruit of a creeper in the sky, for those struck by even a fragment of greed, not even a single word consisting of noble accounts arises.
Desiring to attain the supreme state, the world today is led astray by its own mind and falls fearlessly from the mountain peak, like a beast longing for the fruit of the blue vine.

With their useless parts cast aside within, possessing only the shadows of creepers, leaves, fruits, and flowers; like trees by a chasm whose prosperity is destroyed even in their very bodies—such are men of the present day.

In some places people move about in regions beautiful with softness, and in others in harsh ones, like black antelopes wandering through continuous forest tracts in the intervals between different lands.

Whose minds are not struck with wonder by the events of this world—events that occur day after day, whether terrifying or beautiful, whose ends are agitated and confused, and which, like actions whose results ripen into suffering, destroy all rising hope? Not even the mind of a corpse is moved.

People are attached to desire and intent on various base and unskillful activities; yet in this world, even such a virtuous person is not easily found today, even in a dream. All actions are surely distressed by attachment to suffering and utterly wretched; I know not how this state of living is to be brought to its end.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin, whatever is seen here—the entire world, both stationary and moving—all that is unstable, resembling a meeting in a dream.
O Sage, that which is seen today as a dug-out pit resembling a dried-up ocean shall become a mountain shrouded by clouds by morning.
That which is vast with its array of forests, having licked the very sky, though great, in just a few days reaches the level of the earth or even the state of a well.
That very limb which today is covered with silken garments, garlands, and ointments, tomorrow will be cast far away into a pit, naked as the sky.
In that very place where today a city was seen, bustling with diverse activities, there arises within days the nature of a desolate wilderness.
O King, that man who today stands as a radiant sovereign over the realms shall, in a few days, become a heap of ashes.
The great and terrifying forest, which resembled the vault of the sky and whose canopy of banners covered the heavens—that very place became a city.
That formidable forest grove, which today shines encircled by creepers, in just a few days will once again become a desert land.
Water turns into dry land, and the earth becomes a body of water; indeed, the entire world—including its wood, water, and grass—is utterly overturned.
Youth, childhood, the body, and accumulations of wealth are impermanent; states of being pass incessantly from one condition to another, like waves.
Life in this world is as flickering as the flame of a lamp in the wind; the splendor of all things in the three worlds is like the flash of lightning.
This vast succession of beings falls into perversion, like a heap of seeds that is being constantly replenished again and again.
With the heavy cloth of the dust of many beings tossed about by the wind of the mind, she is adorned with the dramatic gestures of falling, rising, and turning away.
This worldly state is perceived as a delusion produced, like an actress in the *ārabhaṭī* style of dramatic performance, manifesting through the frenzy of her dance.
It produces the delusions of a city of Gandharvas, yet it is enchanting through its grand social interactions, which are as fleeting as the flickering of a sidelong glance.
O King, the structure of saṃsāra, repeatedly casting forth a light as flickering as lightning, shines like one intent on a dance.
Those days were great; those were the prosperities and those the activities. Everything has passed into the path of memory, and we too shall depart in an instant.
Day by day it undergoes decay, and day by day it is born again; even today there is no end to this burnt-out cycle of worldly existence, whose form has been destroyed.
Men fall into the state of animals, and animals even attain the state of men; gods likewise fall from their divinity. O Lord, what indeed in this world is stable?
Creating night and day again and again with its web of rays, the sun, as Time, passes them by while watching for the limit of destruction.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and all classes of living beings alike rush toward destruction, just as bodies of water flow toward the submarine fire.
The sky, the earth, the wind, the ether, the mountains, the rivers, and the directions—all these are the dried fuel for the submarine fire of destruction.
Wealth, kinsmen, servants, friends, and all possessions—everything has become tasteless for one who is terrified by the fear of destruction.
These objects of existence continue to taste sweet for the wise man in this world only so long as the malevolent demon of destruction does not enter the path of his memory.
In one moment sovereignty arrives, and in another moment poverty comes; in one moment freedom from disease is attained, and in another moment the onset of disease occurs.
Who indeed among the wise has not been deluded by this world-illusion, which strikes down the self at every moment and bestows constant error?
For a moment the circle of the sky was smeared with the mire of darkness; for a moment it was beautiful with a soft radiance like a flow of molten gold.
For a moment its hollows were encircled by garlands of water-lilies blue as clouds; for a moment it resounded with a terrifying roar, and for a moment it remained as if mute.
At one moment it was adorned with stars, at another embellished by the sun; at one moment it brought delight through the moon, and at another it was entirely cast out from view.
For who, even if wise, would not fear this [saṃsāra], which consists of coming and going and whose momentary existence is subject to destruction?
Calamities come for a moment, and prosperity comes for a moment; birth is for a moment, and death is for a moment—O Sage, what indeed is not momentary?
"In this world, one person existed previously, yet another man is born after a few days; O Blessed One, there is nothing that is truly stable, for everything is always of a single, changing nature."
The state of a cloth is seen in a jar, and the existence of a jar is seen in a cloth; there is nothing that, having been perceived, does not undergo reversal within cyclic existence.
It expands, produces, consumes, destroys, and emits [the elements] in succession; they revolve constantly around a person, like night and day.
A hero slain by a coward, or even a hundred slain by one—when commoners attain power, the entire world is turned upside down.
This world continually pursues error, like a succession of waves arising from the perception of the movement of inert matter.
Childhood lasts but a few days, then comes the splendor of youth, and after that, old age; since even the body possesses no single fixed form, what reliance can there be on external things?
In every respect, the mind is like an actor: for a moment it attains joy, for a moment it falls into despondency, and for a moment it reaches a state of serenity.
Creating this thing here, that thing there, and yet another thing elsewhere, this Creator grows weary like a child at play.
It accumulates, produces, consumes, destroys, and emits in succession; it revolves incessantly toward every person, like night and day.
For people who participate in worldly existence and are subject to appearance and disappearance, neither calamities nor prosperities attain permanence.
Time generally plays, casting everyone into calamity, it being skilled in all four modes of conduct and capable of tossing everything aside with mere sport.

The floods of fruits from the succession of beings in the three worlds, distinguished by their diverse and uneven ripening, fall day after day from the vast trees of saṃsāra, driven down by the winds of time.
Śrī Rāma said: Thus, in my great mind consumed by the forest fire of faults, the hopes for enjoyments no longer flicker, like mirages in lakes.
Day by day this condition of saṃsāra turns toward bitterness, like the volatile juices of a neem vine under the power of ripening by time.
O King, wickedness increases and goodness diminishes day by day within the hearts of people, which have become as harsh as the *karañja* thorn.
Day by day, the boundaries on earth are shattered instantly, like a parched bean pod bursting without even a crackling sound.
O Lord of Sages, for one who is burdened by anxieties regarding kingdoms and heaps of enjoyments, a solitary life characterized by the absence of such anxiety is superior.
My garden is not for my delight, nor are my women for my pleasure; the hope for wealth brings me no joy; I am at peace along with my mind.
The world is impermanent and unhappy, and craving, my dear, is difficult to bear; the mind is struck by restlessness—how shall I attain peace?
I do not rejoice in death, nor do I rejoice in life; I remain just as I am, free from all feverish distress.
"What use have I for sovereignty, what use for enjoyments, what use for wealth, or what use for my endeavors? That very thing which was under the sway of egoism has dissolved within me."
Those who strive for the sake of liberation from those firm knots of the senses that bind them upon the rope of the succession of births—they are the supreme ones.
The minds of proud women were churned by the god whose banner is the sea-monster, just as a delicate lotus is crushed by the trampling of an elephant's hooves.
