O Lord of Sages, if this is not treated today with a clear intellect, then when indeed will there ever be another occasion for the treatment of the mind?
Poison is the inequality of sense objects; poison is not called mere [physical] poison. Sense objects destroy future births, whereas [physical] poison destroys only a single body.
Neither pleasures nor pains, neither friends nor kinsmen, neither life nor death serve to bind the mind of the wise man.
Therefore, O Brahmin, best among those who know what precedes and follows, instruct me quickly so that I may become a knower, free from sorrow, fear, and exertion.
Ensnared by the net of latent impressions and bristling with the thorns of suffering, this forest of ignorance is terrifying in form, filled with frequent falls and upheavals.
O Sage, I am able to endure the crushing impact of the saw’s edge—the calamity of sense objects and death arising from the worldly affairs of saṃsāra.
"This does not exist, this exists"—this delusion born of worldly convention shakes the flickering mind, just as the wind disperses a mass of dust.

The collection of living beings is like a string of pearls threaded upon the fine threads of craving; with consciousness as its translucent substance, it is eternally expanding, with the mind as its central gem.
I shall ruthlessly tear asunder this necklace of saṃsāra, adorned with the serpent of Time, just as a lion tears through a snare.
O best among the knowers of reality, by what lamp of wisdom may you quickly dispel for me the mist of the forest of my heart and the darkness of my mind?
O Great-souled One, those mental afflictions that exist here do not reach destruction unless they encounter the company of those with supreme minds, just as thick darkness is dispelled by the moon.

Life is as fragile as water hanging from a mass of clouds shattered by the wind; enjoyments are as flickering as lightning flashing amidst a canopy of clouds; and the flow of youthful pleasures is as transient as the current of a river—perceiving this, I have today swiftly and firmly sealed my mind with the seal of renunciation for the sake of lasting peace.
Śrī Rāma said: Having thus observed the world submerged in the mire of mental reflection, within the hollow of hundreds of millions of calamities that have arisen, my mind [is distressed].
My mind seems to reel as if it were spinning, and a great agitation arises within me; my limbs tremble like the leaves of an ancient tree.
A mind that has not embraced the highest contentment and fortitude is agitated; having no secure refuge, it fears in this world like a young girl under a weak ruler.
These fluctuations of the internal organ roll about amidst conceptual constructions, like deer enticed by a hollow mirage, deceived by insignificant objects of perception.
Lacking the basis of discernment, fallen and established in misery rather than the state of the virtuous, these wretched ones—the eye and the other senses—have fallen like blind men into a well.
Thought, dependent upon the Lord of Life, neither remains stationary nor proceeds according to its desire, like a beloved wife in the home of her husband.
Wearing down all things as she casts them away and yet continues to bear them, my fortitude has fallen into a state of distress, like a creeper at the end of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Having cast aside all objects and remaining without a fixed basis, existence remains established by repeatedly grasping and then abandoning the self.
My mind is mocked by my internal support, which wavers though it claims to be immovable, like the poverty of a tree whose roots have been severed.
The mind, flickering, expansive, and wandering through the ends of the world, does not abandon its agitation, just as the immortals do not leave their own celestial chariots.
Therefore, O virtuous one, what is that state of stability—substantial, effortless, free from conditions, and beyond delusion—in which sorrow is no longer found?
How did virtuous people such as Janaka and others, who were engaged in all kinds of undertakings and devoted solely to worldly activity, attain the state of supreme excellence?
O bestower of great honor, how could a person here not be smeared by the mire of saṃsāra, even though it has been repeatedly applied to their limbs?
Relying upon what view do you great-souled ones, free from defilement, live liberated while yet alive and wander here in this world?
How can those who are like serpents, devouring the enjoyment of sense-objects only to incite fear, ever attain a state of nobility, given that their power is of a fragile nature?
How can the lake of the intellect, trampled by the elephant of delusion and defiled within by stains, attain supreme clarity?
How is it that a person, even while engaged in worldly activity within the flow of saṃsāra itself, incurs no bondage, just as water on a lotus leaf?
How can a person attain supremacy while perceiving this entire world as being like himself or like a blade of grass, yet remaining untouched by the agitation of the mind?
Having recollected through his conduct that Great Being who has reached the further shore of the great ocean, people do not fall into suffering.
What is the appropriate highest good for him? What would be the appropriate fruit? And how indeed should one conduct oneself in this utterly inconsistent cycle of existence?
O Lord, tell me some truth by which I may understand the beginning and end of this world, for the activity of the Creator is unstable.
O Brahmin, act so that the cleansing of the impurities of my mind—the moon within the sky of the heart—may come to pass without obstacle.
What here might be accepted, what rejected, or what else? How may this flickering mind find rest, O Mountain-Dweller?
By what purifying mantra is this cholera of miserable saṃsāra—causing hundreds of labors—pacified without effort?
How may I intensely attain that coolness—the cluster of blossoms on the tree of inner bliss—which, like the full moon, is never diminished?
Having attained fullness within, I am now complete and do not grieve; may you virtuous ones, who know reality, instruct me here so that I may likewise never grieve again.

O Great-Souled One, why do conceptual constructions constantly and excessively torment you here—depriving you of rest in the preeminent state of unsurpassed bliss—as dogs might torment a small creature in the forest?
Śrī Rāma said: In this life-span, as fragile as a drop of water hanging from the trembling leaf of a tall tree, and in this body, as delicate as a digit of the moon, the lord of the cool rays;
The gathering of friends and virtuous people is like a circle of snares for a living being—fragile as the throat-skin of a frog croaking in a field of grain.
When the dense cloud of the fierce mist of delusion—fanned by the wind of latent impressions and made manifest by the lightning-flashes of evil desires—thunders and roars intensely.
The fierce peacock of greed dances a wild dance upon the trembling, wide-open, and rustling kuṭaja tree of misfortune, which is bursting with its blossoms.
In this cruel cat of Death, who carries off all living beings like mice, whose movement flows unceasingly, and who pounces from somewhere above;
What is the means? What is the way? What is the reflection? What is the refuge? By what means might this forest of life, which has such an inauspicious outcome, not exist?
There is nothing on earth, nor in heaven among the gods, anywhere at all, which the wise do not lead even this trivial thing toward a state of delight.
For how can this world, which is burnt by saṃsāra and agitated by incessant mental constructions, attain sweetness—being devoid of flavor—unless it is freed from delusion?
May you find delight in bathing with milk as the ripening reward for your hopes; it approaches you like the earth, bright with flowers, approaches the springtime.
By what means can the nectar-shining moon of the mind arise, its stains wiped away by cleansing, from that which is defiled by the mark of desire?
By one who has seen the course of saṃsāra and who has destroyed both the seen and the unseen, how indeed should one conduct oneself in the pathways of the forest of saṃsāra?
How is it that the great diseases of passion and hatred, the multitudes of enjoyments, and worldly powers do not afflict a living being wandering in the ocean of saṃsāra?
And how is it that one does not burn even when falling into the fire of the best of the wise, just as mercury is not consumed by fire because it is possessed of the essence of mercury?
For it is said that in this world, no stability is possible without the performance of worldly activities, just as there can be no water for one who has fallen into the ocean.
Free from passion and hatred, and devoid of pleasure and pain, there is no virtuous action here, just as a flame of fire is devoid of burning.
In the three worlds, there is no destruction of existence—which is characterized by mental ideation—without a logical means; state that supreme method clearly.
"Tell me that supreme method of worldly conduct by which suffering does not come to me; or else, explain that very method of worldly conduct."
How, by whom, or what was performed by that person of supreme mind in the past, by which his most purifying mind now attains this ultimate rest?
O Blessed One, as you know, please tell me for the sake of dispelling delusion that by which the virtuous have surely attained freedom from suffering.
Alternatively, O Brahmin, if such a logical proof does not exist, or if someone clearly does not state it to me even though it exists;
And yet, I myself do not attain that unsurpassed rest; therefore, having abandoned all worldly effort and attained a state free from egoism, I remain as I am.
I shall not eat, nor shall I drink water; I shall not put on a garment; I shall not perform any activity such as bathing, giving gifts, or eating.
I do not remain attached to my duties, whether in times of prosperity or in states of adversity; O Sage, I desire nothing at all except for the relinquishing of this body.
Free from doubt, devoid of the sense of "mine," and without envy, I remain here in silence alone, as if fixed in a painted image.
Then, having gradually abandoned the perceptions of exhalation and inhalation, I shall relinquish this useless structure known as the body.
"I am not this, nor is it mine, nor is there another; I shall become extinguished like a lamp whose oil is spent. Having renounced everything, I shall cast off this physical body."

Śrī Vālmīki said: Having spoken thus, Rāma—delightful as the stainless moon, his mind blossomed by profound reflection—became silent before the great ones, like a peacock ceasing its cry out of exhaustion before the massive clouds.
Śrī Vālmīki said: While that lotus-eyed prince Rāma was thus speaking words that bring about the cessation of the delusion of the mind, [the sage spoke].
All those present there became filled with wonder, their eyes wide open, as if their hair stood on end to listen to the words that were about to be uttered.
Those whose entire latent tendencies for worldly existence have been cast off by the latent tendency of dispassion are, for a moment, like those tossed about by the waves of the ocean of nectar.
Those songs of Rāmabhadra, when heard by listeners whose hearts were swollen with internal bliss, seemed as if they were fixed within them like paintings.
[He was surrounded] by sages such as Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra who were present in the assembly, and by ministers headed by Jayanta and Dhṛṣṭi, all of whom were experts in counsel.
By kings such as Daśaratha, by the citizens including the Pāraśavas and others, by vassal lords and princes, and by Brahmins who were exponents of the Veda.
Likewise, with servants and ministers, with birds confined in cages, with pet animals devoid of movement, and with horses that had ceased chewing;
And by the throngs of women led by Kausalyā, who stood at their own windows with the sound of their ornaments silenced and themselves motionless.
The garden creepers served as dwellings for birds that, though perched upon the very eaves of the houses, remained undisturbed in their flocks and ceased their chirping.
Together with the Siddhas and the sky-dwellers, as well as the Gandharvas and Kinnaras, and the preeminent sages headed by Nārada, Vyāsa, and Pulaha.
And those words of Rāma, which possessed diverse meanings and were most noble, were heard by others as well—by the lords of the gods, the Vidyādharas, and the great serpents.
Then, while the lotus-eyed Rāma—beautiful as the moon, the moon of the sky that is the Raghu dynasty—remained silent;
Accompanied by voices of acclaim uttered by the assembly of Siddhas, a rain of flowers fell from the sky like a canopy.
Resounding with the humming of pairs of bees resting within the buds of *mandārava* flowers, it delighted men who were intoxicated with joy by its sweet fragrance and beauty.
Like a succession of stars scattered by the wind in the sky, it was like a flash of laughter from a celestial woman fallen upon the surface of the earth.
It was like a row of falling drops from a cloud of *vṛṣyamūka* flowers, or like a succession of lumps of fresh butter being poured forth.
Noble as a rain from the Himavat mountains, resembling a mass of pearl necklaces, like a garland of moonbeams, and like a succession of waves of milk.
Enveloped by lotuses with their filaments, it was filled with swarms of wandering bees and stirred by sweet, fragrant breezes singing with the sound of *sītkāra*.
With its clusters of ketakī flowers swaying about, its masses of kairava lilies quivering, its circles of kunda blossoms falling away, and its abodes of blue lotuses trembling;
Filling the courtyards, the floors, the roofs, and the squares, it was beheld by the men and women dwelling in the city who craned their necks to look.
A rain from the sky, resembling a cloudless blue lotus, fell without agitation; it was something never seen before by any person, and it inspired wonder in all.
Stirred up by the hands of hosts of invisible Siddhas in the sky, that rain of flowers fell for a quarter of a Muhūrta.
When the assembly hall was filled with light and the rain of flowers had subsided, those who were present in the hall heard this conversation among the hosts of Siddhas.
Having wandered throughout the heavens for an entire kalpa among the hosts of Siddhas, we have heard this unprecedented elixir for the ears.
That which was indeed spoken so loftily by this moon of the Raghu dynasty—due to his state of freedom from passion—is truly beyond the reach even of the Lord of Speech.
"Oh, what great merit has been gained by us today through hearing these words issuing from the mouth of Rāma, which bring such immense joy to the intellect!"

Because the Joy of the Raghus has respectfully spoken that which is appropriate—having attained the state of supreme excellence and being beautiful with the nectar of tranquility—we have been instantly awakened by him.
The Siddhas said: "It is fitting that the great seers should state the conclusion to be spoken, in order to hear the purifying words uttered by the banner of the Raghus."
Let all the great sages, the preeminent among ascetics headed by Nārada, Vyāsa, and Pulaha, come without any hindrance.
Let us fly all around this holy assembly hall of the son of Daśaratha, which is densely packed and radiant with gold, like bees hovering over a lotus pond.
Śrī Vālmīki said: Having been addressed thus, that entire divine succession of sages, who dwell in their celestial abodes, descended there into that assembly.
Like a string of jewels, their limbs were adorned with various colors; like a string of pearls, they enhanced each other's exceeding beauty.
It was like a unique rain of moonlight, like a second solar orb, or like a succession of full moons accumulated over a vast expanse of time.
Where Vyāsa shines like a cloud amidst a host of stars, there Nārada shines like the moon amidst a multitude of stars.
Pulastya shines here like the lord of the gods among the deities; likewise, Aṅgiras shines like the sun among the gods.
Then, as this army of Siddhas descended from the sky to the earth, the assembly hall of the son of Daśaratha rose up, filled with sages.
Mingled together, those beings who move through the sky and those who move upon the earth shone forth, their bodily radiance intermingling with one another as they illuminated the ten directions.
With hands grasping bamboo staffs and holding play-lotuses, their hair-tips were entwined with sprouts of dūrvā grass, and their locks were adorned with crest-jewels.
They had tawny masses of matted hair, their heads were adorned with crowns and garlands, they wore rosaries on their forearms, and were encircled by wreaths of jasmine.
Some were clothed in rags and bark, while others were draped in garlands and silken garments; some had their waist-bands swaying, and others wore clusters of shimmering pearls.
Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra honored all those sky-dwellers in due order with offerings of water for the hands and feet, and with words of welcome.
Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra, along with the great hosts of sky-dwellers, honored him with reverence through offerings of water for the feet and guest-offerings, and with words of welcome.
With all due reverence, the king worshipped the assembly of Siddhas, and the assembly of Siddhas likewise greeted the king with inquiries concerning his welfare.
Having received mutual hospitality through various expressions of affectionate zeal, those who move in the sky and those who dwell upon the earth sat down upon their seats.
With words, a rain of flowers, and shouts of "Well done!", they honored Rāma from all sides as he stood bowed before them.
And there, Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha, and the ministers Vāmadeva and others sat down, resplendent with royal fortune.
Nārada, the son of a god, and Vyāsa, the bull among sages; then Marīci, Durvāsas, and likewise the sage Aṅgiras.
Kratu, Pulastya, Pulaha, Śaraloman, the lord of sages, Vātsyāyana, Bharadvāja, and Vālmīki, the bull among sages.
Uddālaka, Ṛcīka, Śaryāti, and likewise Cyavana.
These and many others, who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, were high-souled leaders established there, having realized all that is to be known.
Together with Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra, those learned sages, Nārada and the others, spoke these words to Rāma, whose face was bowed in humility.
"Oh! How wonderful that the prince has uttered speech endowed with auspicious qualities, most noble and filled with the essence of dispassion!"
It is thoroughly perfected in what is to be said, endowed with awakening, appropriate, clear, sublime, pleasing, worthy of the noble ones, and moreover, lucid and free from agitation.
Whom does these words spoken by Rāghava not fill with wonder—words that are clearly articulated, distinct, pleasing, and bring satisfaction?
Among a hundred [verses], the speech of even a single one becomes a magnificent marvel of all kinds, uniquely capable of bestowing the desired object.
O Prince, without you, whose [intellect] bears the fruit of discernment, in whom does the vast vine of wisdom reach its supreme blossoming?
That man is considered wise in whom the flame of the lamp of wisdom dwells in the heart, blazing like that of Rāma and producing incomparable illumination.
There are many, indeed exceedingly many, machines made of blood, flesh, and bone that draw objects toward themselves; yet among them, there is nothing conscious.
Bound by delusion like cattle, they repeatedly undergo the sufferings of birth, death, and old age, yet they do not reflect upon this cycle of existence.
Only rarely and in some place is one person seen whose intention is pure, who is worthy of reflection upon his past and future, such as this Arimardana.
Those who possess auspicious forms and yield the fruit of unsurpassed wonder are indeed rare in this world, like mango trees.
The course of the world seen with right vision, a marvel of one's own discernment—this very thing is seen today within this venerable system of thought.
In this land, trees that are auspicious, easy to climb, and rich in fruit and foliage grow in abundance; yet sandalwood trees do not.
In every forest there are trees that are always laden with fruit and foliage; yet the clove tree, with its unprecedented wonder, is not always easily found.
Like the cool moonlight from the moon, like a cluster of blossoms from a fine tree, or like a trail of fragrance from a flower—such was the wonder beheld from Rāma.
O best of the twice-born, in this burnt-out cycle of existence fashioned by the creation of a capricious and malevolent fate, the essence is indeed extremely difficult to find.
Those whose intellects, as repositories of glory, strive to attain the essence, are the fortunate ones, counted among the foremost of the virtuous; they alone are the supreme men.
No one equal to Rāma has been seen here in all the worlds; nor do we believe that anyone such as he, possessed of discernment and noble soul, will ever exist again.

Even though we have performed wonders that cause amazement to the entire world, if what is desired by the heart of Rāghava does not bear fruit, then it is clearly we sages ourselves who are of ruined intellect.
Vālmīki said: When these words had been uttered with such a great sound by those present in the assembly, Viśvāmitra, out of affection, addressed Rāma who stood before him.
O Rāghava, best among the wise, there remains nothing further for you to know; by your own subtle intellect, you have understood everything.
In your own mirror-like intellect, which is eternally pure by nature, mere cleansing is required only to a slight degree.
Like the intellect of Śuka, the son of the Blessed Vyāsa, your mind, though it has already known all that is to be known, requires only internal rest.

Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, how was it that Śuka, the son of the venerable Vyāsa, did not initially find rest even though the object of knowledge was before him, and how did he later find rest through his intellect?
Viśvāmitra said: O Rāma, listen to this account of the son of Vyāsa, which I shall relate in accordance with my own life story, and which is the cause of the end of births.
This venerable Vyāsa, who resembles a mountain of collyrium and possesses the radiance of the sun, is seated upon a golden throne at the side of your father.
To him was born a son named Śuka, moon-faced and skilled in statesmanship, possessed of great wisdom, and established like a sacrifice personified.
As he contemplated this worldly course of existence within his heart, this very same discernment indeed arose in him just as it has in you.
Therefore, by means of his own discernment, that high-minded one himself investigated for a long time what is beautiful and attained that which is the truth.
Though the supreme reality had been attained by himself, his mind remained unsettled; he did not reach the conviction within himself that "this is the reality."
His mind alone ceased its restless wandering; it turned away from enjoyments fraught with manifold calamities, just as a *cātaka* bird turns away from rain-showers.
Once, that one of pure wisdom, with devotion, questioned his father, the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, who was dwelling in perfect seclusion on Mount Meru.
O Sage, how has this grand display of saṃsāra arisen? How does it come to rest? To what extent, by whom, and at what time does it occur?
Thus questioned by his son, the sage Vyāsa, who knows the self, explained everything that was to be said to him clearly and exactly as it is.
"I already knew this before," Śuka then thought to himself; with his auspicious intellect, he did not hold his father's words in high regard.
The venerable Vyāsa, having understood his son’s intention in this manner, replied again to his son: "I do not know [this] in its true essence."
There exists on the surface of the earth a king named Janaka; he knows that which is to be known exactly as it is, and from him you shall obtain everything.
When told "Father," Śuka departed from the earth below Mount Sumeru and reached the city of Videha, which was protected by Janaka.
O King, that son of Vyāsa, Śuka, having been announced by the staff-bearers to the high-souled Janaka, was informed: "He stands here at the gate."
Having said, "Let this [instruction] remain as it was for the sake of Śuka's inquiry," Janaka then became silent for seven days out of contempt.
Then Janaka had Śuka enter the courtyard; there he remained for exactly seven days, dwelling in that same state of dejection.
Then Janaka had Śuka enter the inner apartments, and for seven days he thought, "The king is not to be seen."
There, Janaka doted upon Śuka, whose face was like the moon, with intoxicating women, sumptuous meals, and an abundance of enjoyments.
Those enjoyments and those sorrows did not shake the mind of Vyāsa’s son, which remained as immovable as a mountain with its base firmly fixed, like trees in a gentle breeze.
Utterly serene, composed, silent, and joyful in mind, Śuka remained there like the full moon.
Having recognized his true nature and seeing Śuka brought before him with a joyful heart, King Janaka bowed down to him.
"Having completed all duties for the world and attained every desire, what is it that you wish for? Thus he spoke to him, having quickly offered a welcome.
Śrī Śuka said: O Teacher, how has this grand spectacle of worldly existence arisen? How does it come to rest? Please tell me this correctly and quickly.
Viśvāmitra said: When Janaka was thus questioned, he then related that very same account which had previously been told to him by his high-souled father concerning Śuka.
Śrī Śuka said: "This very thing was previously understood by me through discernment; and it was explained in the same way by my father when he was questioned."
O best among those skilled in speech, you too have stated this very same point; and this indeed is the meaning of the sentence as it is observed in the treatises.

Just as this [world], arising from one's own conceptual construction, is exhausted through the exhaustion of that very conceptual construction, so too is saṃsāra—once it has been burnt away—exhausted; such is the certainty that it is devoid of essence.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, tell me this truly and unswervingly; for my mind, wandering through the world, finds rest only in you.
Janaka said: "O Sage, there is no other certainty higher than this; you have realized it yourself and have heard it again from a teacher."
In this world, there exists only the one, uninterrupted, conscious Self, and nothing else; bound by the power of its own volition, it is liberated when free from volition.
By this, it is clearly known that you, a great soul, have realized all that is to be known, such that detachment from enjoyments has arisen within you regarding everything visible here in the past.
O young Mahāvīra, your mind has turned away from enjoyments which are like long-lasting diseases; what else do you wish to hear?
The fullness of the great treasury of omniscience did not arise for your father while he remained in extensive asceticism in the same measure as it has for you.
I am indeed superior to Vyāsa; you are his disciple and his son. By the attenuation of your desire for enjoyment, you are even more distinguished than I.
Everything that was to be attained has been attained by you, whose mind is now fulfilled; O Brahmin, you do not fall back into the realm of the visible—you are liberated, so cast off delusion.
Having been thus instructed by the high-souled Janaka, Śuka remained silent, established in the pure, supreme reality.
Free from sorrow, fear, and exertion, effortless and with all doubts severed, he went to the faultless peak of Mount Meru for the sake of meditative absorption.
Having remained there for ten thousand years in a state of non-conceptual meditative absorption, he was extinguished within himself like a lamp devoid of oil.

Pure, with the stain of temporal distinctions removed, that great-souled one merged into oneness within his own stainless and purifying self, like a drop of water in the ocean, his latent impressions having dissolved away.
Viśvāmitra said: "O Rāma, the mere cleansing of that son of Vyāsa is exactly as much as you require; only that much is appropriate for you."

O lords of sages, by this [knowledge] everything that is to be known has been understood without exception; for him, worldly enjoyments do not provide pleasure, just as diseases do not please one of sound intellect.
This is indeed the characteristic of a mind that has known what is to be known: that all varieties of enjoyments no longer taste sweet to it.
Through the contemplation of enjoyments, bondage born of unreal things attains firmness; through that same contemplation being stilled, bondage in the world reaches attenuation.
O Rāma, the attenuation of latent impressions (vāsanā) is called liberation by the wise; the strengthening of the latent impressions regarding objects is designated as bondage.
O Sage, for most men, the realization of the truth of their own self occurs only after they have grown weary of sense objects through the hardships of worldly existence.
He who sees correctly is a knower of that; having known what is to be known, he is a wise man. To that great soul, enjoyments do not become palatable by force.
He for whom worldly enjoyments no longer hold any appeal on this earth, even without causes such as fame and the like, is called one liberated while living.
As long as that which is to be known has not been fully understood, so long does detachment from sense objects fail to arise in a living being, just like a creeper in a desert land.
Therefore, know that this scion of Raghu has already realized what is to be known, since these delightful lands of enjoyment do not delight him.
O lords of sages, upon hearing from the mouth of a true person that "whatever Rama knows within himself is the Reality," one surely attains rest for the mind.
The intellect of Rāma seeks only rest in the state of absolute oneness, just as the beauty of autumn seeks repose.
In this matter, may the illustrious and venerable Vasiṣṭha provide the means for the high-souled Rāghava’s mind to find rest.
He is the eternal lord and family preceptor of all the descendants of Raghu; he is omniscient, the witness of all, and possesses stainless vision of the three periods of time.
O venerable Vasiṣṭha, do you perhaps remember that which you yourself [said] previously, for the sake of pacifying the enmity between us and for the welfare of those of great intelligence?
On a peak of the Niṣadha mountain, crowded with *sarala* trees and inhabited by sages, much knowledge was taught by the Blessed One, the Lotus-born Brahmā.
O Brahmin, by means of that reasoned knowledge, this worldly latent impression surely comes to rest, just as darkness does before the sun.
O Brahmin, quickly instruct that which is logical for Rāma, who dwells at the end of time, so that he may attain rest.
And this is not at all a hardship, for Rāma is one whose impurities have been removed; just as a face reflects effortlessly in a stainless mirror.
That knowledge, that meaning of the scriptures, and your own irreproachable skill—O virtuous one, these are what are taught to a good disciple who is free from passion.
Whatever is taught to one who is not a disciple or who lacks dispassion becomes impure, like cow's milk poured into a dog's skin.
Wherever those like you—who are free from passion, fear, and anger; devoid of pride; and whose sins have dissolved—speak, there the intellect finds its rest in this world.
When this was said by the son of Gādhi, those sages, headed by Vyāsa and Nārada, honored that very point, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent!"
Then the illustrious sage Vasiṣṭha, possessed of great splendor, standing by the side of the king like Brahmā’s son Brahmā himself, spoke.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O Sage, I shall carry out what you command for me without hindrance; for who, even if capable, is able to transgress the word of the virtuous?"
For I shall quickly dispel the darkness of mind of the princes, Rāma and the others, with knowledge, just as one dispels the darkness of night with a lamp.
I remember all that knowledge, unbroken, which was formerly proclaimed on Mount Niṣadha by the Lotus-born One for the sake of quelling the delusions of saṃsāra.

Vālmīki said: Having spoken thus, that great-souled Vasiṣṭha—whose oratorical splendor was enhanced by his firm resolve—declared this for the sake of pacifying ignorance, as the sole means of awakening to the supreme state.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That knowledge which was previously spoken by the Blessed One, the Lotus-born, at the beginning of creation for the sake of the peace of the world—that very thing I shall now relate.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, you will indeed recount the extensive compendium on liberation; however, for now, dispel this doubt that has arisen within me.
How is it that Śuka’s father, the omniscient and high-minded teacher Vyāsa, was liberated while still possessing a body; and how was his son liberated?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Within the light of the supreme sun, the motes of dust of the three worlds, having arisen again and again, dissolve away; they do not admit of any calculation.
And as for those millions of multitudes in the three worlds that exist at present, not even one of them can be numbered by anyone.
There will be waves of the creation of living beings in the supreme ocean; indeed, there is no way even to enumerate them.
Śrī Rāma said: It is appropriate to investigate those successions of world-creations that have been and those that will be; but what indeed are those that are currently present?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Whether one is an animal, a human, a god, or another, that which is called the "self" perishes; yet at the very same moment and in the very same place where it perishes, it perceives this world.
Within his own heart, by means of the subtle body known as the *ātivāhika*, the unborn one—whose nature is space—experiences the three worlds within the void of the mental body.
In this way, millions have died, are dying, and will die—beings who individually pursued various hopes for the world.
Like a creation of mere imagination, like the play of a kingdom of the mind, and like a series of magical illusions, it is like the appearance of the meaning of a story.
Like a dust-storm or an earthquake, like a terrified young piśāca, like a string of pearls in the stainless sky, or like a tree and a vehicle that do not stir.
Like the perception of a dream, like the sound of a drum, like a memory, or like a flower in the sky, one who has died within their own mind experiences the wandering of the world by themselves.
There, through excessive transformation, that very [space] attains density; thus, "this world" expands within the space of the living soul (jīvākāśa).
Furthermore, one who experiences birth, death, and so forth in that very place imagines another world; having died there, he likewise [imagines] it again.
Within that [space] there are other persons, and within them others still; thus these appear as "saṃsāra," like the layers of a plantain tree.
Neither the collection of great elements such as earth and so forth, nor the sequences of the world, exist for those who have died; nevertheless, they still experience the delusions of the world.
For this ignorance alone is infinite, possessing manifold expansions; it is a long river for the dull-witted, whose waves are the successive creations.
O Rāma, in the vast ocean of ultimate reality, the waves of creation repeatedly arise—both those very same ones and many others in great abundance.
Some are similar in every respect—regarding lineage, conduct, mind, and qualities; some are similar by half; and others are entirely distinct.
I remember this thirty-second interruption there, as it was perceived by my consciousness according to its actual state of manifestation.
Among them, twelve are of small intellect and are equal to those who are intent on family and form; ten are all of uniform appearance, while the remaining ones are distinguished by their lineage.
In the future, there will likewise be others such as Vyāsa and Vālmīki, as well as Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, and yet others besides them.
Human beings, the hosts of celestial sages, and the gods arise together in great numbers, and at times they dissolve again, each separately.

The seventy-two triple-world systems of Brahmā—those that have been, those that are, and those that will be—I perceive as being that very same thing, as something else, as the worlds, as you, and as me.
Thus, in due course, this tenth incarnation of the far-sighted sage Vyāsa, whose deeds are wondrous, is clearly perceived.
Many times we were joined with Vyāsa and Vālmīki; and many times we ourselves existed individually and separately.
"We ourselves have become just like these others; we ourselves have become diverse in form, yet equal in intention."
Indeed, he must still undergo eight more births here; furthermore, he will once again compose the work named Bhārata, together with its histories.
Having divided the Vedas and established the lineage through him, and likewise having performed the office of Brahmā, the liberation of the people of Videha must be brought about.
Free from sorrow and fear, possessing peaceful nirvana, with all conceptual constructions gone, this Vyāsa is described as one liberated while living, having conquered his mind.
Sentient beings may at times be equal in terms of wealth, lineage, age, karma, learning, knowledge, and conduct; yet they are never truly equal in those respects.
In some cases, through hundreds of creations, these things either come to be or do not; yet this illusion is at no time thus devoid of an end.
This vast succession of beings continually restrains its own perversion, like a heap of seeds that is perpetually being replenished again and again.
In that very same configuration, and again in another, the forms of creation proceed repeatedly like waves from the ocean of time.
With an inner heart consoled, with conceptual fluctuations stilled, and consisting of the essence of his own true nature, the wise one remains unobscured, satisfied by the nectar of supreme peace.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as the state of being water remains the same in the ocean whether it is in the form of gentle waves or in the form of the water itself, so too is the liberation of the sage the same, whether he is without a body or with a body.
Liberation, whether with or without a body, does not exist within the realm of objects; for one who has not tasted enjoyment, how can there be experiences of what is to be enjoyed?
We behold before us this best of sages, liberated while living, who is indeed like a solitary object; there is no longer any obstacle within his inner heart.

What difference can there be between those liberated with a body and those liberated without a body, since they are both of the nature of pure consciousness? It is just like the water in the state of waves and in the state of stillness; it remains that very same water.
There is not even the slightest difference between liberation with the body and liberation without the body; they are like the wind itself, whether it is moving or still.
Whether with body or without body, liberation is not an object of valid cognition; for us as well, that [liberation] exists, and it is an indivisible oneness.
Therefore, listen to this very subject at hand, which is an ornament for the ears—the knowledge being taught by me, which destroys the blindness of ignorance.
For indeed, O descendant of Raghu, everything here in this world is always obtained by everyone through human effort when it is properly applied.
For here, just as from the moon, a cool refreshment arises in the heart; so too, in the attainment of the fruit of one's exertion, it comes from human effort alone and from nothing else.
Human effort is seen through direct perception to lead to results like the ripening of a vibration; as for "fate," which is imagined by the deluded and the dull-witted, it does not exist at all.
Whatever movement of mind or body is performed according to the path well-taught by the virtuous, that is manly effort; that alone is fruitful, while everything else is the behavior of a madman.
Whoever desires a certain object and strives for it with perseverance will certainly attain it, provided they do not turn back from their purpose midway.
Indeed, by means of human effort, a certain distinguished being attained the state of Śakra, beautiful with the sovereignty over the three worlds.
Only a certain flash of consciousness, by means of human effort alone, suddenly ascends to the state of Brahman, which has its abode in the lotus.
By his own essential human effort alone, a certain man indeed has attained the state of Puruṣottama, he whose banner is Garuḍa.
By human effort alone, a certain embodied being here, whose form was once encircled by women, has attained the state of having the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
Know that human effort is of two kinds: that which belongs to the past and that which pertains to this life. The former is quickly overcome by present human exertion.
By those who are diligent, firm in their practice, and endowed with wisdom and enthusiasm, even Merus are swallowed; what need is there to mention former human efforts?
That state of manhood which consists of human effort strictly governed by the scriptures is what leads to the attainment of the full weight of desired fruits; otherwise, it leads only to misfortune.

In one state, when a man is himself poorly situated, even a few drops of water from a single cup squeezed by the tips of his fingers may seem much; yet in another state, when he must provide for the distribution of what is fit to be maintained—dividing it among oceans, mountains, cities, and islands—the entire earth would not seem large enough.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For those who act in accordance with the scriptures, worldly engagement itself is the primary means for accomplishing all actions, just as light is the primary means for distinguishing colors.
Whatever one desires with the mind, yet does not accomplish through action according to the scriptures—that is the "intoxicating play" (mattalīlā); it is delusive and does not achieve any purpose.
Just as one exerts oneself by means of something, so too is it experienced by that very thing; it remains as one's own karma alone, and there is no other separate vision of destiny.

Human effort is traditionally held to be of two kinds: that which is contrary to the scriptures and that which is in accordance with the scriptures. Among these, that which is contrary to the scriptures leads to misfortune, while that which is in accordance with the scriptures leads to the supreme goal.
Two human goals, equal and opposing like two fighting rams—one pertaining to the past and the other to this life—struggle; therein, the one with lesser strength is subdued.
Therefore, by whatever means possible, a person should strive with human effort so that, through the Tantra and right yoga, he may quickly conquer this present existence.

Two human goals, equal and opposing one another like two fighting rams—one belonging to oneself and the other belonging to another—strive together; of these two, the one with superior strength prevails.
Where misfortune is encountered despite human effort guided by the scriptures, one should recognize that one's own personal power is the stronger factor in producing that misfortune.
Relying on supreme human effort and grinding teeth against teeth, one should overcome past human effort that was inauspicious and directed toward the inauspicious by means of what is auspicious.
The thought that "this past human effort compels me" must be forcibly cast beneath one's feet; for it is not superior to direct perception.
One should strive with great human effort for as long as it takes for past negative karma to subside of its own accord.
A past fault is undoubtedly pacified by present virtues; for here we see the illustration of how a fault of yesterday is destroyed by virtues of today.
Having cast aside false divinity with a mind perpetually uplifted, one should strive to establish within oneself that which leads to the transcendence of saṃsāra for the sake of ultimate prosperity.

One should not walk the path of those who lack exertion, for they are like human donkeys; rather, one should apply effort according to the scriptures for the sake of accomplishing success in both worlds.
One must emerge from this cavern of saṃsāra by one's own strength, relying on human effort, just as Hari [emerged] from the cage of his enemies.
Day after day, one should contemplate one's own body as perishable; one should cast it away like a mere beast and take refuge in that which is appropriate for the virtuous.
Having tasted something soft in the home, such as a mixture of pleasant food and drink, one should not let one's life be reduced to ashes like an insect in a wound.
Through auspicious human effort, an auspicious result is swiftly attained; through inauspicious effort, an inauspicious one is always obtained. That which is called "fate" is nothing at all.
He who abandons direct perception and resorts to inference is like one who, seeing these two as snakes by his own arms, flees away.
Seeing the mouths of those with scorched intellects—who perceive the unseen as supreme—claiming, "Fate impels me," Fortune turns away.
Therefore, through human effort, one should first resort to discernment; one should thoroughly investigate the scriptures whose great purpose is the knowledge of the Self.
Fie upon the wicked desires of those fools who, while contemplating their own goals in their minds according to the scriptures, fail to accomplish them through their own efforts!
Human effort is not infinite, nor is it sought through mere exertion; even with great effort, a jewel cannot be obtained from a stone.
Just as a jar is limited, and just as a cloth is limited, so too is the purpose of man fixed and established within a definite measure.

And it is its very nature that this [scripture] bestows its own fruit through the study of true scriptures, association with the virtuous, and right conduct; otherwise, it does not lead to the accomplishment of one's purpose.
This is the true nature of human effort; a person who acts in this manner never, at any time, finds their exertion to be fruitless.
Even other supreme men, though afflicted by the suffering of wretchedness and poverty, have attained a status equal to the lord of the gods through human effort alone.

Since one's own true purpose is attained through human effort by means of qualities such as the study of scriptures and association with the virtuous, which have been sufficiently practiced from childhood.
Those of wicked intellect who think that what has been seen, experienced, heard, or done by them was brought about by fate are themselves ruined.

If laziness did not exist as a calamity in this world, who would not be wealthy or highly learned? It is because of laziness that this earth, bounded by the oceans, is filled with human cattle who are destitute of wealth.

When childhood has passed—restless with incessant play—a man should, from the onset of the age adorned by powerful arms, strive through association with the virtuous to purify his intellect regarding words and their meanings, and conduct investigations into his own virtues and faults.

Vālmīki said: When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; at the end of the night, they returned together with the rays of the sun.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Therefore, since destiny is nothing other than one's prior human effort, one should cast it far away; rather, by means of the company of the virtuous and the sacred scriptures, one should forcibly uplift the living soul.
"In whatever measure there is effort, in that same measure shall the fruit quickly arise; thus, human exertion alone exists, and destiny is nothing but that."
Just as at the time of suffering one says, "Alas, what misery!", so too the expression "Alas, fate! is a synonym for the words "alas" and "misery."
There exists no such thing as "destiny" (daiva) that takes a form other than one's own prior karma; it can be overcome in this world by a fool, just as a powerful man overcomes another.
Just as yesterday's evil conduct becomes auspicious today through beautiful conduct, so too does one's past karma reach a state of purity.
Those who strive for its conquest, yet are not enslaved by even a fraction of greed, are wretched, vulgar, and deluded fools who remain dependent on fate.
When an action performed through human effort is destroyed by fate, it should be understood that in such a case, human effort is the more powerful force.
When, of two fruits on a single stalk, one is hollow and empty, effort is exerted there for the sake of experiencing its flavor.
Since even those worldly states that have attained perfection come to destruction, one should recognize that the power of the effort that causes such decay is indeed great.
Two human aims fight each other like two rams; whichever of them is stronger there, that one alone conquers in an instant.
That a king is forcibly made into a beggar by Maṅgalebha is due to the great power of the efforts of his ministers, elephants, and citizens.
Just as food is seized by the power of the teeth and ground to powder, so too is another person, relying on his own prowess, crushed by a hero.
For those who are great and exert themselves with diligence, even the insignificant become like food; they may be employed at will in various tasks, just like clods of earth.
Whatever human effort there may be of a capable person, whether visible or invisible, that is perceived as "fate" by one who is powerless and lacks self-awareness.

That which is the most powerful among beings is established as not being destiny; it is clear that this [power] is the presiding authority even over those [beings], while they exist in mutual relation.

The unhesitating, natural wisdom of the teachers, ministers, elephants, and citizens—that is what constitutes the kingdom of the mendicants, acting as both the creator and sustainer of the stability of its subjects.
When a beggar is made a king by the elephant Maṅgala at some time or other, it is either past human effort or powerful destiny that is the cause therein.
The present [action] overcomes the past, and the past [action] forcibly overcomes the present; in this regard, the person who is always free from agitation regarding human activity is the victor.
Of the two, that of the present day alone would be stronger through direct perception; for destiny can be overcome by efforts, just as a child can be defeated by a youth.
Just as the harvest acquired over a year is carried away by a cloud, so too is this human effort of the cloud surpassed by one who exerts greater exertion; thus, the latter triumphs.
Even when wealth acquired through gradual effort is lost, one should not feel distressed; for where my strength was powerless, what cause is there for lamentation?
If I cause suffering for the sake of that which I cannot avoid, then it is fitting for me—who have not conquered death—to weep every single day.
All these states of the world, manifesting through the power of place, time, action, and substance, are surpassed by one who possesses superior effort.
Therefore, relying on human effort and having brought one's wisdom to purity through the study of authentic scriptures and association with the virtuous, one should cross the ocean of saṃsāra.
These two fruits of human effort—the past and the present—have grown like fruit-bearing trees in the forest of humanity; of these two, the latter prevails.
The ignorant creature who does not destroy his trivial past karma through auspicious endeavors is not the master of his own happiness and suffering.
Impelled by God, he may go to heaven or even to hell; he is always dependent on another, a mere beast—of this there is no doubt.
But he who possesses noble wonder and dwells in virtuous conduct emerges from the delusion of the world, like a lion from a cage.
He who, abandoning the unseen [destiny], remains fixed in the useless and false imagination that "someone is impelling me thus," is a base person who should be shunned from afar.
Regarding the thousands of legal cases that come before you and pass away, you should adjudicate them according to the scriptures, having abandoned both pleasure and displeasure.
For one who does not abandon their own boundaries and remains unbroken according to the scriptures, all jewels attend upon them, just as they do in the ocean.

The wise have designated as "human effort" (pauruṣa) the state of being solely intent on exertion toward the action that achieves one's own goal; when constrained by the scriptures, that effort leads to success.

The capacity of action, which is characterized by vibration, to accomplish its own purpose is itself raised up by an intellect sharpened by the company of the virtuous and the study of authentic scriptures.
The wise know that the ultimate truth is infinite and a bliss of equanimity; those scriptures and virtuous beings from whom this is eternally obtained should be served.
Having come here from the world of the gods, it shall bring benefit to both worlds; that former human effort is indeed what is called by the term "destiny" (daiva).
This is indeed appropriate; we do not deny that this exists. Those who believe in fate as imagined by fools have come to their end.
Benefit for both worlds arises constantly from one's own human effort alone; for just as yesterday’s misdeed attains beauty through a virtuous act today.

Therefore, one who possesses a task should exert effort this very day, for that fruit is seen to arise from human effort alone, as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand; the fool, casting aside what is perceptible, sinks into the delusion of fate.

O one of auspicious intent, disregard that destiny which is devoid of all causes and effects, imagined merely through the power of one's own conceptual constructions; for it is unreal, and instead take refuge in your own human effort.

When that fruit which has been conceived by the scriptures and the long-established local customs manifested through virtuous conduct flashes forth in the heart, the mind attains a state of upliftment; they say that this subsequent bodily manifestation is what constitutes human effort (*pauruṣa*).

Having realized that this state of being a man is the fruit of human effort, one must always be devoted to personal exertion; then, by serving excellent scriptures, virtuous people, and the learned, that state may be led to its highest fulfillment.

Since this human effort, when practiced by those who have cultivated the conviction that "human exertion always triumphs" through their skill in discerning between fate and human endeavor, leads to success, one should apply oneself to the service of noble persons.

Having understood that this living being consists of a succession of births and is afflicted by disease, let him lead it to peace through the accomplishment of innate human effort in this life—by means of the unfailing, excellent medicine of serving satisfied and supreme scholars who have been refined.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having obtained a body free from disease and with minimal suffering caused by the afflictions, one should thus concentrate upon the Self so that one is not born again.
He who seeks to turn back fate through human effort shall have all his desires fulfilled in this world and the next.
Those who, having abandoned exertion, remain devoted solely to fate, destroy virtue, wealth, and pleasure; they are haters of themselves.
The vibration of consciousness, the vibration of the mind, and the vibration of the senses—these are the forms of the human goal; from these, the arising of results occurs.
Just as the mind experiences, so does it undergo its vibration; in that very same way the body moves, and in that very same way one becomes the experiencer of the fruit.
This is well-established even among children: wherever and however it may be, fate is never seen; therefore, in this world, human effort alone prevails.
By virtue of human effort, Bṛhaspati alone became the preceptor of the gods, and Śukra attained the status of preceptor to the lords of the Daityas through human effort.
O virtuous one, even those best of men who were afflicted by the suffering of wretchedness and poverty have attained equality with the lord of the gods through human effort alone.
Great beings, who were the refuge of various wonders through the enjoyment of their vast power, have become guests of hell solely due to the fault of their own human pride.
Through the power of their own human effort alone, the various classes of beings have ceased [their suffering] amidst thousands of existences and non-existences and diverse conditions.
Success is achieved through the scriptures, through the teacher, and indeed through oneself—these are the three means; it occurs everywhere through human effort, never through destiny alone.
One should diligently draw the mind away from unwholesome states and establish it in wholesome ones alone; this is the summary of the meaning of all the scriptures.
"O son, practice with diligence that which is beneficial, that which is not trivial, and that which is free from ruin"—thus stand the teachers.
"In whatever measure my effort is directed toward a result, in that same measure the fruit quickly follows; thus, I am the enjoyer of the fruit through human exertion alone, and not through destiny."
Success is seen to arise from human effort; through human effort, the wise achieve their course. Destiny is merely a consolation for those of feeble intellect when faced with suffering.

In this world, the sequence of human action—such as traveling to another country and so forth—is constantly seen to bear fruit through means of valid cognition, foremost among which is direct perception.
The enjoyer is satisfied, not the non-enjoyer; the goer goes, not the non-goer; the speaker speaks, not the non-speaker; thus human effort bears fruit for men.
Those of sound intelligence cross over insurmountable perils through human effort without exertion, but not by this futile means.
Whoever exerts effort in whatever manner, that very person alone partakes of the corresponding fruit; for no one here attains a result by remaining silent.
Through auspicious human effort, an auspicious fruit is attained; through inauspicious, an inauspicious one, O Rāma—do as you wish.
The attainment of the fruit from human effort here, occurring either after a long time or quickly due to the influence of place and time—that which is so attained is remembered as destiny (daiva).
Fate is not perceived by the eye, nor does it exist in another world; what is called "fate" is simply the fruit of one's own action in the heavenly realm.
A person is born in this world, grows, and then decays; yet fate is not seen therein, as it is in childhood, youth, and old age.
The wise have designated as the term "human effort" (pauruṣa) the state of being solely intent on the exertion required to achieve a goal; by means of this, everything is attained.
The movement from one place to another, the grasping of objects by the hand, and likewise the activity of the limbs, are accomplished through human effort and not through destiny.
But that single-minded devotion to an effort whose result is the attainment of what is useless is called the behavior of a madman; nothing at all is achieved by it.

The capacity of action, which is characterized by vibration, to accomplish its own purpose is itself raised up by an intellect sharpened by the company of the virtuous and the study of authentic scriptures.
The wise know the ultimate reality to be the bliss of infinite equanimity within oneself; therefore, those scriptures and virtuous teachers from whom this is attained through effort are to be served.

The quality of true scripture and the like increases through the intellect, and the intellect increases through the quality of true scripture and the like; they both grow by mutual practice, like two lotuses over time.
Through qualities such as the study of scriptures and association with the virtuous, practiced sufficiently from childhood, one’s own beneficial purpose is accomplished by human effort.
The Daityas were conquered by human effort, the activities of the world were established, and the worlds here were fashioned by Viṣṇu through exertion, and not by fate.

O Raghunātha, in this world where human effort is the cause, exert yourself long and diligently so that you may not, O fortunate one, fall without hesitation into the state designated as that of trees and reptiles.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: There is no form, nor actions, nor movement, nor prowess; what is it that is called "destiny" (daiva), which is merely established upon false knowledge?
Those words which state that "this has come to pass in this way as the result of one's own karma" have attained common renown under the name of "destiny."
In that very matter, those of deluded intellect have reached the certainty that "destiny exists," having grasped it through their poor understanding, just as one might seize a snake in a rope.
Just as yesterday’s misconduct attains beauty through virtuous conduct today, so too does today’s [misconduct] through that of the past; therefore, one should strive to be devoted to wholesome deeds.
If a foolish person of wicked mind believes that destiny is established by fallacious inference, he must go toward the fire thinking, "There is no burning from destiny."
If fate alone is the agent here, what is the use of human exertion? Fate itself will perform the bathing, giving, sitting, and evacuation.
What is the use of instruction from the scriptures, for this man is indeed mute? He is merely moved by destiny; what can be taught to whom here?
Moreover, no lack of movement is observed here in the world except in the case of a corpse; since the attainment of results follows from movement, destiny is therefore useless.
Furthermore, no cooperation whatsoever is observed between the formless divine and the embodied person; therefore, destiny is useless.
When the limbs of two [beings] come together with one another, each acts as the sole agent; even when the hands and other members are struck down, nothing is ever done by fate.

Moreover, this destiny is not experienced here in the same way as mental cognition; since it is not perceived even by cowherds, let alone by those of cultivated wisdom, destiny is therefore always non-existent.

If cognition and the object are distinct, then if that [cognition] is indeed the same as the object, how can there be any difference between them? If you claim that the means of knowledge for this conceptualization is human [agency], why is it not simply assumed?

There is no contact between that which is formless and that which possesses a body, just as there is none between the sky and a corporeal being; yet a corporeal object is seen to be joined [to another], therefore destiny does not exist.
If there is anything else in the three worlds that you can employ for the sake of living beings, let the multitudes of beings lie down; fate will accomplish everything.
"Driven by fate, I do such things as have come to pass; this is merely a word of consolation, for in the ultimate sense, there is no such thing as fate."
Fate is imagined by the foolish, and they, devoted to it, have gone to ruin; but the wise, through human effort, have attained the highest state.
Tell me, what indeed is the use in this world of those who are brave, those who are valiant, those who are wise, and those who are learned? For they all must await destiny.
If he whose extremely long life has been determined by those who know the times should live even with his head severed, then that indeed is supreme destiny.
O Raghava, if one who possesses the wisdom determined by those who know the proper time is not even taught, yet knows that [truth], then destiny is supreme.
O Rāma, by the sage Viśvāmitra, having cast destiny far aside, brahminhood was attained through human effort alone and not otherwise.
O Rāma, by us and other men who have attained the state of sages, the power of traveling through the sky for a long time has been achieved solely through human effort.
Having destroyed the hosts of gods within the belly of the three worlds, the lords of the Dānavas established their empire through human effort alone.
The lords of the gods, by means of their vigor and through human-like effort alone, forcibly seized from the Dānavas the vast world that had been mangled and shattered.
O Rāma, by means of human effort and skill, this beautiful water is held for a long time within a casket; fate is not the cause in that matter.
O Rāma, capacity for bearing burdens, taking up tasks, exertion, agitation, and exhaustion is seen in living beings, but not in destiny, just as it is not seen in a medicinal herb.

O you of auspicious intent, disregarding fate—which is devoid of all causes and effects, imagined through the power of one's own conceptual constructions, and composed of unreality—take refuge in supreme human effort.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, knower of dharma, you have attained the pinnacle of excellence; therefore, tell me, O Brahman, what is that which is called "destiny" (daiva) in the world?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, human effort alone is the agent of all actions and not anything else; it is the enjoyer of the fruit everywhere, and destiny is not the cause therein.
Fate does nothing at all; it neither acts nor enjoys, nor does it exist. It is not seen and is not heeded; it is merely such a mental construction.
In this world, the attainment of auspicious or inauspicious objects resulting from human effort that has reached fruition is designated by the term "fate" (daiva).
The constant attainment of desired or undesired objects brought about by human effort—whether that attainment is desirable or undesirable—is designated by the term "fate" (daiva).
But that future goal which is to be accomplished solely through human effort is what is designated by the term "fate" (daiva) within this collection of worlds.
Indeed, O Raghava, for any person in this world, destiny—which is of the nature of space—both brings about something and does not bring it about.
When the human effort has been accomplished, that expression regarding the arising of auspicious or inauspicious results—"this is situated thus"—is called destiny (daiva).
"In this way my thought occurred, and indeed such was my conviction; that expression used regarding the attainment of the fruit of karma is called 'fate' (daiva)."
That which expresses the attainment of desired or undesired results as "this is [it]"—a mere word for consolation—is called "fate" (daiva).
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, that which was previously accumulated as karma is called "fate" (daiva); how then has fate been set aside by you?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Well done, O Rāghava! You understand; listen, and I shall tell you everything by which your intellect will become firm in the conviction that "there is no destiny."
That mental impression which indeed existed abundantly in the past has itself undergone transformation into the form of karma for human beings.

O Rāma, whatever kind of latent impression (*vāsanā*) a living being possesses, he becomes its agent in an instant; for it is simply not possible that one could perform an action and possess a different nature.
One who intends to go to a village reaches the village, and one who desires a city reaches the city; whoever has whatever kind of latent impression always strives for that very thing.
Whatever action was firmly performed in the past with intense urgency, that very thing is here spoken of by the synonymous term "fate" (daiva).

Thus, actions reside in actions, and one's own latent impressions (vāsanā) are matured by action; the latent impression is nothing other than the mind, for the mind is traditionally held to be the person (puruṣa).
Since these actions are thus [performed], O virtuous one, action is indeed the mind; for the mind is the person (puruṣa), therefore it is certain that there is no destiny (daiva).
Whatever beneficial thing this mental being strives for, he obtains that very thing through fate itself, even though it has already been accomplished.
"O Rāma, the wise have declared that mind, consciousness, latent impressions, action, destiny, and resolve—these are the designations for what is difficult to determine."
O Rāma, just as a man of such a name exerts himself constantly with firm resolve, he obtains a corresponding result in full measure.
Thus, O descendant of Raghu, everything is attained here through human effort and by no other means; therefore, may that [effort] grant you prosperity.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Sage, just as the web of past latent impressions (vāsanā) impels me, so do I remain; being wretched, what can I do?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "For this very reason, O Rāma, you shall attain eternal welfare through human effort alone, brought forth by your own exertion, and not otherwise."
O Rāma, there exists for you a twofold accumulation of latent impressions—both auspicious and inauspicious—from the past, or perhaps only one of the two.
If you are led there today by a stream of pure latent impressions, then through that very auspicious sequence, you will attain the eternal state.
Moreover, if an unwholesome state should entangle you in distress, then that former habit must be conquered by you with effort and force.

You are the wise one, consisting of pure consciousness; you are not the body, which is insentient by nature. Where indeed could that state of being an object of cognition exist for you, apart from another mind?
If another causes you to perceive, who else is there to cause that other to perceive? Who would cause this one to perceive? Therefore, an infinite regress is not real.
The river of latent impressions, flowing along both auspicious and inauspicious paths, should be directed onto the auspicious path through human effort and exertion.
O best among the strong, by means of human effort and power, draw your own mind away from unwholesome states and establish it only in wholesome ones.

The mind of a living being, having moved away from the unwholesome, goes to the wholesome; from that as well, it moves to the other. Indeed, the mind of a creature flickers like a fish caught on a hook.
One should quickly pacify the child-like mind through equanimity, but not abruptly; rather, one should protect it gradually with human effort alone.
The flood of latent impressions, whether auspicious or inauspicious, was previously made dense by you through practice; today, make the auspicious one dense.
O crusher of enemies, know that when, by the power of prior practice, those [thoughts] of yours give rise to latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then the practice has borne fruit.
O sinless one, even now your latent impressions are reaching a state of density due to the power of habit; therefore, apply yourself to the practice of the auspicious.
If your latent impressions (*vāsanā*) did not become wealth in the past due to lack of practice, they will certainly not increase now either; therefore, my dear, be happy.
Even when there is doubt, cultivate only that which is exceedingly auspicious; for in this increase of latent impressions, no fault whatsoever arises from the auspicious.
"Whatever one practices in this world, one becomes permeated by that"—this principle, free from doubt, has been observed among the wise since childhood.
Therefore, being disciplined through yogic postures, strive here for your own welfare by relying on supreme manly effort and conquering the five senses.
As long as your mind is unrefined and you have not yet realized that state of reality, practice that which has been determined by the authority of the Guru and the scriptures.

Therefore, since your afflictions have been ripened and you have surely realized the true nature of reality, you, being free from suffering, must certainly abandon even this stream of virtuous mental impressions.

Having followed that which is exceedingly beautiful, noble, and auspicious with a mind perceiving its delightful nature, attain the state that is forever free from sorrow; and thereafter, having even relinquished that, abide perfectly.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The reality of Brahman as it truly exists is called the necessity of existence; that is the teacher's status as a teacher, and that is the disciple's state of being a disciple.
Therefore, relying on human effort for the sake of your ultimate welfare, which is your eternal kinsman, make your mind one-pointed and listen to these words of mine.
Quickly restraining the senses—which fall into intermediate states and mount upon the chariot of one's desires—bring them to a state of equanimity through human effort.

For the sake of attaining success in this world and the next, I shall proclaim this compendium, fashioned from the very essence [of knowledge], which bestows the fruits of human goals and consists of the means to liberation.
Having abandoned within him the latent tendencies of saṃsāra so that they would not be grasped again, he took up perfect tranquility and contentment with a noble intellect.
Having made the mind, which has been struck by the investigation of the meaning of preceding and succeeding sentences, equanimous and continuous within the Self;
O Rāma, listen to this means of liberation which I shall now describe; it brings about the destruction of pleasure and pain and is the sole cause of great bliss.
Having heard this discourse on liberation together with all those who possess discernment, you will go to the supreme state free from suffering, where no destruction exists.
This was spoken in a former age by Brahmā Parameṣṭhin; it brings about the destruction of all suffering and is the supreme consolation of Śrī.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahman, by what cause was this spoken formerly by the Self-born One? And how was it obtained by you? Tell me this, O Lord."

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: There exists the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), whose nature is infinite manifestation, all-pervading, the refuge of all, and imperishable in essence—the lamp within all living beings.
From that [source], which possesses the nature of both vibration and non-vibration, Viṣṇu was born, like a wave from the ocean filled with flowing essence.
From that lotus of the heart, which had Mount Sumeru as its pericarp, the cardinal directions as its petals, and the stars as its filaments, the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) was born.
Adorned by a circle of divine sages who were knowers of the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas, he created the entire flood of the world with its manifold conceptualizations, just as the mind does.
In the corner of Jambūdvīpa, in the land called Bhārata, he created a dense mass of human beings overwhelmed by mental and physical afflictions.

In this creation of the various classes of beings, which is filled with manifold calamities, the limbs of all creatures are despondent regarding existence and non-existence, and they are constantly intent upon arising and destruction.
Seeing that suffering of this people, the Lord, the creator of all worlds, was moved to compassion, just as a father is by the suffering of his son.
"Who could bring an end to the suffering of these whose hopes are destroyed and whose lives are forfeit? Thus he reflected with one-pointed concentration for a moment for their welfare.
Having reflected thus, the Blessed One, the Lord himself, created austerity, righteousness, charity, truth, and indeed the sacred fords.
Having created this, the Creator of beings reflected once more: "By means of this [creation], there shall be no end to the suffering of men," he thought to himself.
Nirvana is called the supreme bliss, by means of which one is neither born nor dies; it is obtained solely through that knowledge.
For a living being, knowledge alone is the means for crossing over saṃsāra; austerity, charity, and likewise pilgrimage sites are proclaimed to be non-means.
Therefore, for the sake of liberating these wretched people from suffering, I shall quickly reveal a fresh means of crossing over.
Having reflected thus, the Blessed Brahmā, seated upon a lotus, formed a mental resolve and brought me, this [universe], into existence.
O sinless one, having arisen from somewhere, I quickly appeared before my father, as swiftly as one wave rises from another.
The Lord, bearing a water-pot, was saluted and greeted by me, who also bore a water-pot; he, bearing a rosary, was likewise saluted and greeted by me, who also bore a rosary.
Having said to me, "Come, my son," he joined his hand to mine upon the northern petal of his own lotus, as white as the moon.
Clad in a deer skin, with his own garment being a deer skin, my father Brahmā spoke to me, as a noble swan might address a crane.
O son, for just a moment let ignorance seize your mind, which is as fickle as a monkey, just as the hare-mark seizes the moon.
Thus, having been cursed by him immediately after my deliberation, I indeed forgot my entire stainless true nature.
Then, having fallen into a state of dejection, I remained with an unawakened mind, tormented by suffering and grief like a man born into poverty.
"Alas! How has this defect called 'saṃsāra' come to be here? Having thought thus within himself, he remained silent.
Then my father said to me, "Son, why are you sorrowful? Ask me about the destruction of suffering, and you shall be forever happy."
Then, seated upon the petal of a golden lotus, I questioned that Blessed One, the creator of all worlds, regarding the medicine for the disease of cyclic existence.
"O Protector, how did this saṃsāra consisting of great suffering come to be? And how is it exhausted for a living being?"—thus was I questioned by him.
That knowledge has been declared in great detail, knowing which it is the supreme purifier; indeed, I have remained as if exceeding my father’s own intention.
Then the Creator of the world, the speaker and the cause of all things, spoke to me, who had realized what was to be known and had returned to my own true nature.
Having reduced you to a state of ignorance by means of a curse, I have made you my questioner, O son, for the sake of the spiritual accomplishment of all people through this essence of knowledge.
Now that your curse has been pacified and you have attained supreme awakening, remain in solitary oneness like me, O Kanaka, just as gold is distinct from its dross.
O virtuous one, go now upon the surface of the earth to Bharatavarṣa, situated within Jambūdvīpa, for the sake of favoring the world.
In that regard, O son of great intellect, you should instruct those devoted to the ritualistic section (kriyākāṇḍa) according to the sequence of the ritualistic section, following its proper order.
O virtuous one, those whose minds are dispassionate, as well as those of great wisdom who investigate reality, should be instructed by you with knowledge that bestows bliss.
Thus commissioned by my father, the lotus-born Brahmā, I remain here, O Rāghava, for as long as the succession of beings endures.
