Indeed, there is nothing whatsoever that must be done by me here; with the thought "I must simply remain," I am established upon the earth with a deeply tranquil mind. With a state of constant sleep-like mental activity, I perform actions here, yet I do nothing at all.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus have I related to you everything concerning the descent of knowledge upon the earth, as well as my own intended purpose and the deeds of the Lotus-born One.
O sinless one, today my heart is intensely yearning to hear this supreme knowledge, owing to the ripening of my great merit.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, how did the intellect of the Supreme Lord, the Parameṣṭhin, proceed toward the descent of knowledge in the world immediately after the creation?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Within the Supreme Brahman, Brahmā himself was born by the power of his own nature, eternally consisting of vibration, like a wave in the ocean.
Having thus beheld this afflicted creation and the entire course of that creation, situated in the past, present, and future, the Supreme Lord [reflected].
When the destruction of the Kṛta and other ages—the time characterized by active cycles—had arrived, the Lord, perceiving the delusion of the worlds, was moved by compassion.
Then the Lord, having created me and repeatedly endowed me with knowledge, dispatched me to the surface of the earth for the sake of pacifying the ignorance of the world.
Just as I have been dispatched by him, so too have other great seers in great numbers, headed by Sanatkumāra, Nārada, and others.

Through the sequence of ritual action and merit, as well as through the sequence of gnosis, these [teachings] have been proclaimed in order to uplift the world, which is bound by the disease of mental delusion.
Then, in ancient times, when the Kṛta Yuga had waned, those various great ṛṣis [established] the sequence of rites as the purity of the earth gradually diminished.
For the purpose of establishing the sequence of ritual actions and for the regulation of boundaries, kings were appointed according to the division of separate territories.
Furthermore, many treatises on Smṛti and treatises on sacrifice were composed on this earth as appropriate means for the attainment of dharma, kama, and artha.
While this Wheel of Time flows, and that sequence has dissolved, people are daily intent on eating and devoted to the acquisition of rice.
Conflicts broke out among kings for the sake of sense-objects, and living beings on earth were brought to the state of being punished in great numbers.
Then, unable to protect the earth without war, the kings were no longer capable [of ruling]; they fell into a state of wretchedness along with their subjects.
For the sake of dispelling their dejection and for the sake of the gradual attainment of right view, great perspectives on knowledge have therefore been proclaimed by us and others.
This inner science was first described among kings; subsequently, as it spread throughout the world, it was called the "royal science" (rājavidyā).
This is the royal science, the royal secret, the supreme knowledge of the inner self; having known this, O Raghava, kings have attained the state beyond all suffering.
Now, O Rāma, after many kings of stainless fame have passed away, you have been born today here on this earth from Daśaratha.
O crusher of enemies, this beautiful dispassion, which is pure and without external cause, has arisen in your mind because of your extreme serenity toward him.
O Rāma, for every virtuous person who possesses discernment, there first arises a passion-based dispassion (*rājasam vairāgyam*) preceded by a specific cause.
But this unprecedented detachment of yours, which produces wonder, is causeless, characterized by goodness, and born of your own discernment.
Who indeed would not become dispassionate upon seeing a loathsome object? For the supreme dispassion of the virtuous arises solely from discernment.
Indeed, for those great and highly wise ones in whom dispassion arises even without a specific sign, their minds are truly stainless.
Indeed, by means of an intellect detached through the contemplation of the wonder of its own discernment, a living being shines like a youth with a garland of bridegrooms.
Those who, having discerned this construction of saṃsāra through discrimination, attain dispassion—they alone are the supreme persons.
By the power of one's own discernment alone, having investigated this again and again, one must forcibly abandon this magical illusion, both externally and internally.
Who would not become dispassionate upon seeing a cemetery, misfortune, and wretchedness? That dispassion which arises spontaneously is the supreme good.
Having attained a state of great, natural dispassion, you are worthy of the essence of knowledge, just as soft soil is for a seed.
Through the grace of the Supreme Lord, the Master, the Supreme Self, a virtuous intellect such as yours pursues discernment.
Through a great sequence of ritual actions, through austerity, through observance of rules, through charity, through pilgrimages, and through long-term discernment;

When evil deeds have come to an end and one engages in the investigation of ultimate reality, the intellect of a living being proceeds by way of a chance occurrence, like the "crow and the palm fruit."
Those people who are devoted solely to ritual action remain fully ensnared by the whirlpools of saṃsāra as long as they do not behold the supreme state in this world.
Having seen this cyclic existence as it truly is, and having abandoned the mind absorbed in it, they go to the supreme state like elephants freed from their tethering posts.
O Rāma, this endless cycle of worldly existence here is full of peril; the great being endowed with a body does not perceive it without knowledge.
O descendant of Raghu, by means of the very raft of the yoga of knowledge, those of great intelligence have crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra, so difficult to traverse, in the blink of an eye.
Listen with an attentive mind and constant vigilance to this method of knowledge, which carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra.
For these worldly fears of suffering, with their endless turmoil, burn within for a long time unless one possesses blameless skillful means.
O Raghava, by what means can the sufferings of dualities, such as cold, wind, and heat, be endured by the virtuous without the power of knowledge?
Afflicting thoughts fall upon the foolish man at every step and at their appointed time, burning him like a flame of fire consumes straw.
The fires of mental afflictions do not burn the wise man who has understood what is to be known and possesses right vision, just as flames of fire do not consume a forest drenched by rain.
Even when the desert wind of saṃsāra—revolving with mental and physical afflictions—is turbulent, the knower of reality is not shaken, like the wish-fulfilling tree.
Therefore, a wise person who desires to know reality must, with effort and full of devotion, question one who is truly wise, authoritative, and awakened in soul.
The speech of a speaker who is authoritative, when questioned, and whose mind is excellent, should be received with effort, just as saffron is taken up by a fine cloth.
O best among those skilled in speech, there is no one more foolish than that man who questions a person whose words are not to be accepted because he does not know the truth.
There is no person more base than he who, when questioned with effort by an authoritative speaker who knows that [truth], does not carry out their word.
Having first ascertained through the effect whether the speaker is ignorant or possesses knowledge of that [matter], the man who then poses a question is a person of great intelligence.
The fool who asks a question without first determining the speaker is an inferior questioner; he is not a fit vessel for the great meaning.

When questioned by a wise person, one should speak to an irreproachable Buddha whose intellect is capable of reconciling what precedes and what follows; one should not speak to a base person who follows the nature of a beast.
The wise call that man the most foolish who speaks without first considering whether the questioner is capable of grasping the meaning that is consistent with valid authority.
O descendant of Raghu, you are exceedingly fond of praising virtues and are an inquirer; I too know how to speak, and this union of ours is a perfect match.
O you who are skilled in words and their meanings, whatever I say, you should determine with effort that "this is the matter" and keep it unbroken in your heart.
O great sage, you are dispassionate and a knower of reality regarding the condition of worldly beings; thus, what is spoken to you takes root within you, just as saffron water adheres to a cloth.
Devoted to focused attention and discerning the ultimate truth, your wisdom enters into the object of knowledge like the rays of the sun entering the midst of water.
Whatever I say should be accepted and diligently applied to the heart; otherwise, you should simply question me, for there is no point in remaining here in vain.
O Rāma, for the mind is fickle, like a monkey in the forest of saṃsāra; having purified it with effort within the heart, one should listen to the song of the ultimate truth.
Having kept for a long time at a great distance those who lack discernment, the ignorant, and people who delight in the company of the wicked, one should indeed honor the virtuous.
Through constant association with the virtuous, discernment arises; enjoyment and liberation are said to be the two fruits of the very tree of discernment.
At the gateway to liberation, four gatekeepers are proclaimed: tranquility, inquiry, contentment, and fourthly, association with the virtuous.
These four, two, or three should be served with diligence; they open the door to the royal palace of liberation.
Or else, one should resort to even a single person by every possible effort, even at the cost of sacrificing one's life; for when one is brought under control, all four likewise come under control.
For one who possesses discernment is the vessel for the treatises, knowledge, austerity, and sacred learning; he is like the sun, the form of whose ornaments is the very radiance of its beams.
For the dullness of wisdom among the mindless reaches a state of solidity, just as water, through its own inertia, attains the state of a stone.
But you, O Rāghava, with your inner heart blossomed by kindness, virtuous qualities, and insight into the meaning of the scriptures, stand like a lotus at sunrise.
O noble-minded one, you ought to raise your ears to hear and understand these words of wisdom, just as a living being raises its ears for the sound of a lute.
O Rāma, through the yoga of dispassion and practice, strive to acquire the wealth of equanimity and goodness, wherein no destruction is found.

At the outset, for the sake of liberation from cyclic existence, one should increase wisdom itself through the study of the scriptures, association with the virtuous, and the practice of austerity and self-restraint.
Know this alone to be the ultimate destruction of this Mauryan [kingdom]: that this scripture is being observed with some degree of refined intellect.
This poisonous tree of saṃsāra is the sole abode of calamities; it constantly deludes the ignorant, so one should strive to destroy this folly.
Through folly, which moves like the gait of a serpent of ill-hopes and leaps within the heart, the mind undergoes contraction, like leather placed in fire.
In one who possesses wisdom, this vision of reality becomes clear, just as the sight [is clear] upon the moon when its entire, stainless orb is free from clouds.
He whose mind is endowed with the fourfold analytical investigation, is possessed of the four analytical knowledges, and is expansive, is called a "man" in this world.
With your blossoming, white, darkness-dispelling heart—cool-rayed through its excellent discernment and endowed with virtues—you shine like the stainless moon in the sky.

The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, you are a person of perfected mind who knows how to inquire; you understand what has been spoken, and for that reason I have proceeded to speak with due respect.
Having established your mind within the self—free from passion and darkness and following pure goodness—remain steadfast to hear this knowledge.
"The entire array of qualities belonging to the questioner exists in you, and the qualities of the speaker exist in me, just as the wealth of jewels exists in the ocean."
O son, you have attained detachment born from discernment and non-attachment, just as a moonstone becomes moist when struck by the rays of the moon.
Since childhood, you have long practiced pure virtues; being yourself pure, they are as continuous and extensive as the fibers of a lotus stalk.
Therefore, listen; I shall tell you a story, for you alone are its worthy vessel. Indeed, without the moon, the white water-lily does not bloom in its pure splendor.
Whatever undertakings there may be and whatever views there may be, they all indeed come to complete rest when that state is seen.
If there were no resting of consciousness for one of noble mind, then in this cycle of existence, what virtuous person could endure such dullness of thought?
Upon reaching the Supreme, all mental fluctuations dissolve, like the rocks of the great mountain ranges when struck by the multitude of suns at the end of a kalpa.
O Rāma, this unbearable cholera-like affliction caused by the onset of the poison of saṃsāra is pacified by the purifying Gāruḍa mantra of yoga.
And that yoga is surely obtained through the investigation of the scriptures with virtuous persons; it is indeed the mantra for the knowledge of the ultimate truth.

Indeed, it must be understood that when inquiry is necessarily conducted here, there occurs the complete exhaustion of all suffering; therefore, those who possess the vision of inquiry should not be viewed with disregard.

By a person possessed of discernment, having completely cast off this cage of worldly existence—like a snake shedding its fully ripened skin—the entire world is viewed as a mere magical illusion for one's diversion, with a fever-free and cooled inner heart; for this world is a source of supreme suffering for one who lacks right vision.

For the passion for cyclic existence (*saṃsāra-rāga*) is exceedingly treacherous; like a serpent it bites, like a sword it cuts, like a spear it pierces, like a rope it entangles, and like fire it burns. Like the night it blinds, and like a stone falling unexpectedly upon men, it renders them helpless. It carries away wisdom, destroys stability, and casts one into the blind well of delusion. Thirst (*tṛṣṇā*) wears one down; there is no suffering whatsoever that a being in cyclic existence does not encounter.
It is said that this cholera of the sense objects is incurable; if it is not treated, it brings about various consequences that result in a multitude of cities of hell.

Wherein the fall of a sword sharpened on a whetstone is like the striking of a stone; where being burned by fire is like being sprinkled with snow; where the cutting off of limbs is like the application of sandalwood paste; where forests are like the gnawing of wood-worms; where the halo of a halo is like the rubbing of a limb; where the incessant falling of iron arrows shaken by the fire of battle is like the cooling of summer heat; where the shower of spray from a fountain-house is like the decapitation; where being silenced by a pleasant sleep is like the excellence of a seal upon the face; and where great accumulation is [the result].

Therefore, O Rāghava, one must not treat with contempt this machine of worldly existence, which is so dreadful with its thousands of such painful efforts; rather, it must certainly be restrained and understood in such a way that, indeed, through the investigation of the scriptures, the highest good is attained.

O moon of the Raghu dynasty, if these great sages, great seers, brahmins, and kings have their bodies enveloped in the armor of knowledge, how is it that—even while experiencing various forms of worldly affliction involving suffering—they remain with minds constantly joyful, despite being incapable of enduring such pain?

For here, just as Hari, Hara, Padmaja, and the others remain free from curiosity and devoid of the disturbances of conceptual construction, so too do those supreme among men, who have attained the lamp of the self, remain in this world with purified intellects.

When delusion is utterly exhausted, when the thick cloud of ignorance has dissolved, when reality is fully known and the infinite Self is realized; when, having deliberated with the noble ones, one perceives through the intellect that this worldly existence is merely a semblance of a moving body—then this wandering of the world becomes a source of delight.

Moreover, O Rāghava: when the essence of consciousness has become serene within the heart, when the Supreme dwells in the arising of tranquility, and when all perceptions of mental constructs have become the fullness of peace before one; then this worldly wandering, which is the sport of the perceived Reality, becomes equalized through the intellect, its flavor savored by the internal instrument of the mind.

Moreover: A chariot, a post, a body, the arrangement of horses, the movement of the senses, the vibration, the wind, the objects of pleasure resulting from riding, the supreme atom, or the embodied soul—when these are seen with a faultless intellect as they truly are within this world, this wandering of the world becomes a delight in the Reality.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having firmly grasped this vision, those of great intelligence who have realized the Self move about here in the world of transmigration like exalted beings.
They do not grieve, they do not desire, and they do not beg for good or evil; they perform everything, yet here they do nothing at all.
They remain indeed pure, they act with purity, and they proceed [in life] free from the dualistic notions of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, established in their own self.
They come and yet do not come; they go forth and yet do not go. They act and yet do not act; they speak and yet do not speak.
Whatever undertakings there may be and whatever views there may be—all those, whether as things to be abandoned or to be adopted, perish once the state [of the Self] has been realized.
Having abandoned all worldly attachment and possessing a sweet disposition of mind, one attains happiness from every side, like the orb of the moon remaining in its place.
Even the undertaking of a divine manifestation, in which every wonder is perfectly arranged, cannot be contained within oneself alone, just as an elixir cannot be contained within the moon.
He performs no magical illusions and does not pursue latent tendencies; having cast off the fickleness of a child, he shines forth even from the very beginning.
For such states of being are obtained from the perception of the reality of the self, and not otherwise.
Therefore, through inquiry, the Self alone is to be sought, meditated upon, and known by a person throughout his life, and nothing else.
Through the continuous practice of that which brings into harmony one's own experience, the scriptures, and the teacher, the Self is perceived.
One who disregards the meaning of the scriptures and treats great men with contempt should not, even when fallen into painful adversity, become equal to fools.
Neither disease, nor poison, nor calamity, nor likewise mental anguish on this earth causes such distress to men as the single folly residing within their own bodies.
Just as this scripture has been heard by those with some degree of refined intellect, there is no other scripture whatsoever that so effectively removes ignorance.
This treatise, which is pleasant to hear, brings happiness, and is as beautiful as its illustrations, is entirely free from contradiction through its connection with the meaning of the sentences.
Those calamities which are difficult to overcome, and those empty, wretched rebirths—they all spring forth from folly, just as thorns grow from the khadira tree.
O Rāma, it is better to wander for alms with a begging bowl in hand through the streets of outcaste dwellings than to lead a life destroyed by folly.
Better to be a blind worm in solitude within terrible dark pits or even in the hollows of trees than to possess the folly that brings such extreme suffering.
Having attained this light consisting of the means to liberation, no person shall ever again fall into blindness, even within the darkness of delusion.
Indeed, craving causes the lotus of man to contract as long as the stainless radiance of the sun of discernment has not arisen.

For the sake of liberation from the suffering of saṃsāra, together with kinsmen such as myself, one should realize the true nature of the self by means of the authority of the guru and the scriptures.
O Rāghava, conduct yourself here just as Hari, Hara, and others, as well as other Brahman-sages, move about as those liberated while living.
In this world, sufferings are infinite while pleasure is like a mere blade of grass; therefore, one should not fixate on pleasures that are followed by suffering.
That state which is infinite and effortless must be attained with diligent effort by a person who possesses discernment, for the sake of achieving the essential goal.
These very ones are the supreme persons, the vessels for the goal of human life, whose minds—free from all feverish distress—rest upon the unsurpassed state.
Know those of wicked mind who are satisfied with mere sensual enjoyment and the pleasures of kingship and the like to be blind frogs.
Those who are devoted to the deceitful, the malevolent, those intent on evil deeds, to enemies disguised as friends, and to those who indulge in sensual pleasures;
Those fools, whose intellects are dulled by delusion, go from the difficult to the more difficult, from suffering to suffering, from fear to fear, and from hell to hell.
O Rāma, because they are said to destroy one another, one should never abide in the pursuit of worldly well-being within the states of pleasure and pain, which are as fragile as a flash of lightning.
Know those high-souled men like you, who are dispassionate and perfectly secluded, to be worthy of veneration, for they are the sole vessels for both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Relying firmly upon discernment through the yoga of the practice of dispassion, one shall cross over this terrible river of saṃsāra and its calamities.
One who understands this world and possesses discernment should not sleep within the illusions of saṃsāra, for they bring about the stupor and delusion of being poisoned.
He who, having entered this saṃsāra, remains with indifference, is like one who sleeps upon a bed of straw within a house that is fiercely ablaze.
That state, reaching which they do not return and attaining which one does not grieve, is indeed attainable through wisdom; there is no doubt in this matter.
If that [self] does not exist, what fault could there be for you through such investigation? If it does exist, then you will have crossed over the ocean of existence.
When a person's inclination here is toward investigating the means to liberation, then he is said to be one who partakes in liberation.
A state of well-being that is unfailing, free from apprehension, and devoid of delusion does not exist within the three worlds without the state of absolute liberation (*kevalībhāva*).
Upon attaining that, upon attaining the supreme, no affliction arises; neither wealth, nor friends, nor kinsmen can be of assistance.
There is no moving of hands or feet, no traveling to other lands, no exhaustion from bodily mortification, and no reliance on sacred fords or shrines.
That state is attained solely through the conquest of that mind alone—by means of action whose sole purpose is human effort and whose function is the unification of latent impressions.
By abandoning the webs of suffering through solitude alone, which is achieved solely by the one-pointed certainty of inquiry, this [liberation] is attained by a man.
By one seated on a comfortable seat, reflecting upon that for oneself, no sorrow is felt once that state is attained; indeed, such a person is not born again.
The virtuous know that to be the ultimate limit of the essence of all happiness; they call that unsurpassed, motionless state the supreme elixir.
Because all states of existence are subject to decay, there is no happiness at all in either heaven or the human realm; it is like water in a mirage within these two.
Therefore, the conquest of the mind should be contemplated as the means for achieving tranquility and contentment; from that, infinite and equal union is attained, and through it, bliss is obtained.
Whether standing or walking, falling or wandering, whether it be a *rakṣasa*, a *dānava*, a god, or a human being.
That supreme bliss to be attained arises from the pacification of the mind; it is the fruit of the lofty tree of discernment, which bears the blossoms of expanded tranquility.
Even while devoted to worldly affairs and encountering a multitude of tasks, he neither abandons nor craves them, remaining like the sun stationed in the sky.
The mind that is profoundly peaceful, utterly transparent, rested, and free from delusion—being effortless and devoid of longing—is neither desirous nor does it reject anything.
Listen now to these gatekeepers at the door of liberation in their proper order; by devotion to even one of them, the door of liberation is entered.
The vast desert expanse of saṃsāra, which yields both pleasure and suffering and is long-lasting, becomes cool for a living being through its radiance equal to that of the moon.
Through tranquility, the highest good is attained, for tranquility is the supreme state; tranquility is auspicious, tranquility is peace, and tranquility is the warding off of delusion.
For a man who is satisfied by tranquility, whose self is cool and clear, and whose mind is adorned with peace, even an enemy becomes a friend.
For those whose inner disposition is adorned by the moon of tranquility, their supreme purity arises like that of the oceans of milk.
Those virtuous ones in whose hearts the lotus of tranquility has blossomed within the sheath of the heart-lotus are indeed like Hari, possessing two lotus-hearts.
Those for whom the beauty of tranquility shines upon their stainless moon-like faces are noble moons worthy of homage, having conquered the senses through their loveliness.
The splendors existing within the belly of the three worlds do not bring such joy as the manifestations of tranquility, which are the true likeness of imperial prosperity.
Whatever sufferings, whatever insufferable cravings, and whatever painful anxieties there may be—all of these perish within those whose minds are peaceful, just as darkness vanishes before the suns.
For the mind of all living beings attains such clarity as it does when curiosity is aroused in a peaceful person, which it does not do even toward the moon.
In a virtuous person who possesses tranquility and friendliness toward all living beings, the supreme reality reveals itself spontaneously.
Like a mother, all beings here place their utmost trust in one who is endowed with tranquility, whether they face hardships or gentleness.
One does not obtain such happiness through the drinking of elixirs nor through the embrace of Fortune as one obtains when the mind is pacified within.
O Rāghava, comfort with the sprinkling of the nectar of tranquility this mind, which is shaken by all manner of mental and physical afflictions and overcome by the triple wheel of craving.
Whatever you do and whatever you eat, if it is performed with a mind cooled by tranquility, O dear one, that alone tastes sweet in the mind; nothing else does.
O Rāghava, I believe that even those limbs severed by her whose mind has attained the bliss covered by the nectar-essence of tranquility will grow back again.
Neither piśācas nor rākṣasas, neither daityas nor enemies, nor even tigers or serpents, harbor hatred toward one who abides in tranquility.
Arrows cannot pierce one whose every limb is well-armored with the nectar-like armor of tranquility, just as they cannot pierce a diamond stone.
A king does not shine so much even when staying within his inner apartments as he does through a mind that is impartial, clear, and characterized by tranquility.

A person does not attain such satisfaction upon seeing something dearer than life itself as that which a person attains by beholding one whose disposition is peaceful and who has attained tranquility.
He who conducts himself well with a conduct that is disciplined and tranquil, and which is welcomed by the world, truly lives here; no one else does.
Whatever action a virtuous person performs with an undisturbed mind and in tranquility, all these beings rejoice in it.
Having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled that which is pleasant or unpleasant, he who neither rejoices nor desponds is called "peaceful."
He who is equal toward all beings, who desires what is to come and does not abandon it, and who has conquered his senses through effort—he is called "peaceful."
Having touched upon all things with a pure intellect, one for whom actions are seen exactly as they are both internally and externally is called "peaceful."
He whose mind is undisturbed, shining like the orb of the moon, is called "peaceful," even amidst death, festivals, or battle.
Even when remaining [in the world], he is as if not remaining; he neither rejoices nor is provoked to anger. He who is established in his own nature, equal to deep sleep, is said to be "peaceful."
He whose joyful gaze, lovely with the flow of nectar, extends toward all people, is called "the peaceful one."
He who has attained inner coolness, who does not sink into worldly objects, and who engages in worldly affairs without being deluded—he is called "peaceful."
Even in the midst of endless calamities, even at the great dissolution of the eons, he whose mind does not dwell upon the trivial is said to be "peaceful."
That man who engages in worldly affairs, yet whose mind remains unstained like space, is said to be "peaceful."
Among ascetics, the highly learned, sacrificial priests, and kings—among those who are powerful and rich in virtues—it is only the man of tranquility who truly shines.
For the great ones who possess virtuous qualities and whose minds are absorbed in tranquility, bliss arises from the heart like moonlight from the white-rayed moon.
The limit of all multitudes of virtues and the singular ornament of manliness—tranquility shines forth with glory in times of distress and in places of fear.

Having relied upon that supreme state—tranquil, immortal, unassailable, and guarded by the Noble Ones—the great-souled ones have gone to the highest goal; O descendant of Raghu, follow that very same path in due order for the sake of your own perfection.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: One who knows the cause should constantly perform inquiry into the self with a mind that is supremely pure and stainless through the understanding of the scriptures.
Having attained sharpness through inquiry, the intellect perceives the supreme state; for inquiry is indeed the great medicine for the long-standing disease of saṃsāra.
The forest of calamities, its form sprouting from endless striving, does not grow again once it has been cut down by the saw of discernment.
O one of great wisdom, everything—whether the loss of kinsmen through delusion, calamities, or states of tranquility—is pervaded by this; for indeed, discernment is the refuge of the virtuous.
For the wise, there is no means other than investigation; by means of investigation, the minds of the virtuous abandon the unwholesome and attain the wholesome.
Strength, intelligence, vigor, discernment, and the fruit of action—all these bear fruit for the wise solely through investigation.
Relying upon expansive investigation, which is a great lamp for what is appropriate and inappropriate and an achiever of one's desires, one shall cross the ocean of saṃsāra.
The lion named discernment, being a pure self, tears apart the great elephants of delusion whose lotus-hearts have been mangled.
That even the deluded, by the power of time, have reached the supreme state in this world is the unsurpassed manifestation of the lamp of inquiry.
Kingdoms, vast prosperity, enjoyment, and eternal liberation—these, O Rāghava, are the fruits of the wish-fulfilling tree of inquiry.
Those thoughts of the great ones here that expand through solitude do not sink in adversity, like hollow gourds upon the water.
Those who conduct themselves with an intellect that gives rise to discernment indeed become the recipients of most exalted fruits.
The clusters of flowers upon the karañja trees of non-investigation—those which stand in the forest of the fool’s heart and first obstruct hope—are the very ways of suffering.
O Rāghava, may that sleep—stained like powdered collyrium, possessing the nature of intoxication from wine, and consisting of a lack of discernment—come to an end for you.
A person devoted to right reflection does not sink into delusions, even when they are exceedingly long-lasting, just as a mass of light does not sink into darkness.
He in whose clear mental lake the multitude of lotuses that are inquiry has surely blossomed shines like the Himalayas.
For one whose intellect has become dull and is devoid of discernment, a thunderbolt arises from the moon as fruitlessly as a demon rising against a child.
O Rāma, a man who is devoid of discernment and is the lowest of men must be abandoned from afar; he is a fragment of suffering, unsubstantial, and the springtime for the creepers of ruined fortune.
Whatever undertakings are ill-conceived, whatever conduct is wicked, and whatever anxieties are base—all these appear without scrutiny like goblins in the darkness.
O scion of the Raghus, keep far away from him who lacks discernment, who is like a solitary forest tree, and who is incapable of performing virtuous deeds.
For when the mind of a living being is secluded and freed from the helplessness of desire, it attains supreme bliss within itself, like the full moon.
Discernment, when arisen within the body, thoroughly cools everything and adorns it exceedingly, just as moonlight does for the world.
For a living being, the investigation of the intellect—which is the white chowrie of the banner of ultimate truth—shines forth like the moon in the night.
Living beings who move with the grace of discernment, illuminating the ten directions like the sun, truly shine forth as further removers of the fear of worldly existence.
The life-taking vetāla conjured by the delusion of a fool’s own mind in the night sky dissolves through investigation.
All worldly phenomena are charming only when not investigated; their true existence is non-existent, and they fall apart under investigation.
The long-standing vampire of saṃsāra—which is imagined by a person’s own deluded mind and bestows manifold suffering—is dissolved through inquiry.
Know this state of absolute liberation to be equanimity, blissful, free from affliction, infinite, and independent—the fruit of the lofty mountain of discernment.
Through that [practice], which is noble due to its immovable stability and manifest with the splendor of its full extent, dispassion arises like coolness produced by the moon.
Through that great medicine of self-investigation, which is well-established in the mind and bestows the state of excellence, the virtuous person neither desires nor rejects anything.
The mind that takes that state as its support becomes expansive and luminous; it neither sets nor rises, like the sky which is utterly free from internal limits.
He neither gives nor takes, he neither elevates nor is he stilled; merely observing like a witness, he remains as one who experiences the world.
It neither subsides, nor does it abide within or without; it neither adopts inaction, nor does it sink into action.
He remains indifferent toward what has passed and follows after what has arrived; neither agitated nor unagitated, he shines like the full ocean.
Thus, with minds full [of contentment], these great-souled ones of noble intent—yogins liberated while living—dwell here in this world.
Having dwelt for a very long time, as long as they desired, those steadfast ones finally abandon that [state] and proceed to the pervasive state of absolute oneness.
Even in times of calamity, a wise person should diligently reflect with effort upon the question, "Who am I, and whose is this saṃsāra?"—and do so by means of a remedy for oneself.
O Raghava, a king understands the doubt regarding the difficulty of a task—whether it will be fruitless or fruitful—only through careful deliberation, and not otherwise.
The established tenets of the Vedas and Vedānta, which are the cause of stability, are determined through inquiry, just as the features of the earth are discerned at night by means of a lamp.
Investigation is a beautiful eye that sees even what is obstructed—unimpaired by darkness and undazzled by intense lights.

For one who is blind to discernment is like one born blind; such a person of wicked intellect is an object of pity for all. But he whose soul is discernment possesses the divine eye and triumphs over all things.
This wondrous power of discernment, which consists of the Supreme Self, is worthy of honor and the sole means for attaining great bliss; it must not be abandoned for even a single moment.
A person who is elegant in discernment is pleasing even to the great, just as a mango fruit that has reached full maturity delights all.
Men whose minds delight in reflection and who have understood the path of travel do not repeatedly wallow in the many abysses of suffering.
Neither does a sick man nor one shattered by hundreds of misfortunes wail as much as the ignorant man whose soul is ruined by a lack of inquiry.
Better is the state of being mud, better is the condition of a worm in filth, and better is dwelling in a blind cave than the lack of discernment in a human being.
One should abandon that which is the natural abode of all misfortune, despised by all the virtuous, the ultimate limit of all instability, and devoid of discernment.
A great-souled person must always be engaged in inquiry; for indeed, inquiry is the support for those falling into the blind well.
By supporting oneself through one's own self and investigating with discernment, one may cause the deer of one's own mind to cross over the ocean of delusion that is saṃsāra.
"Who am I? How has this defect called saṃsāra come upon me?"—such an inquiry according to reason is called *vicāra* (investigation).
The heart of the foolish and unreflective man has long been made like a stone—blind, leading from blindness to delusion, and resulting solely in suffering.
O Rāghava, for in this world, by those whose vision consists of grasping at existence and non-existence or of rejecting them, no reality whatsoever is properly known except through inquiry.
From inquiry, reality is known; from reality, there is rest in the Self. Therefore, when the mind is stilled, there is the complete destruction of all suffering.
Success indeed bears fruit upon the earth and attains its highest manifestation through action; when examined with the eye of clear discernment, may it shine forth for you who possess tranquility.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Contentment is indeed the supreme good; contentment is called happiness. O destroyer of enemies, one who is contented attains the highest rest.
For those who are happy in the sovereignty of contentment, whose minds have long found rest, and who are peaceful, even a universal empire seems like a mere scrap of withered straw.
O Rāma, an intellect characterized by contentment never declines, for it remains undisturbed even amidst the treacherous conditions of worldly existence.
For those who have attained peace and satisfaction by drinking the nectar of contentment, even this incomparable splendor of enjoyments acts like a potent poison.
These waves of nectar-like flavor do not bring such happiness as contentment, which possesses an exceedingly sweet taste and destroys all faults.

Having abandoned the desire for what has not been attained, having reached equanimity toward what has been attained, and being free from distress regarding what has not been seen, he is called "content" in this world.
As long as the mind does not attain contentment within itself by means of the self, calamities continue to arise from the cavity of the mind like creeping vines.
The mind, cooled by contentment, attains full expansion through the vision of pure discernment, just as a lotus blossoms fully under the rays of the sun.
In a mind that is helpless under the sway of desire, devoid of contentment, and withered, knowledge does not reflect, just as it does not appear in a bent mirror.
The lotus of man does not undergo contraction through the thick night of ignorance for him, in whom the sun of perpetual contentment has forever risen.
Even though he possesses nothing at all, that person enjoys the happiness of sovereignty, provided his mind is contented and free from mental and physical afflictions.
He who does not long for what has not been attained, and who enjoys what has been attained in due order, and whose conduct is very gentle—he is called "contented."
In the mouth of the great one who is devoted to contentment, fully satisfied, and whose mind is complete—pure like the ocean of milk—the Goddess of Fortune shines resplendent.
Relying upon the stainless fullness within one's very own self by means of the self itself, one should abandon craving everywhere through human effort.
For one filled with the nectar of contentment and possessing a mind that is peaceful and cool, the mind attains a natural and eternal stability, like that of the moon.
With minds nourished by contentment, those of great prosperity attend upon him like servants, having entered into a state of servitude.
When a person remains established in themselves, self-abiding and content within their own self, all mental anxieties are quickly pacified, like dust in the rainy season.
O Rāma, by means of a pure livelihood that is ever-cool and free from the breaking of family traditions, a person shines with fullness like the moon.
Just as people find satisfaction in beholding the face of a man, beautiful in its symmetry, they do not find such satisfaction through the accumulation of wealth.
O descendant of Raghu, even the great sages who roam the heavens bow down before that stainless king of men, who is adorned here with equanimity, wisdom, and the virtues of the virtuous.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O one of great intelligence, for men specifically in crossing over the ocean of worldly existence, the company of the virtuous everywhere provides assistance here in this world.
Those great-souled ones who protect the white flower of discernment, born from the tree of association with the virtuous, are the vessels for the glory of its fruit.
An empty place becomes crowded; even death turns into a festival; and misfortune appears like prosperity in the company of wise men.
Victorious in this world is the singular, virtuous association with the good—a wind that acts as a delusive mist for the lotus-pond of the heart, yet serves as a cooling frost to its heat.
Know that association with the virtuous is the supreme nourishment for the intellect, the felling of the tree of ignorance, and the complete expulsion of mental anxieties.
From association with the virtuous, the supreme lamp of discernment arises—truly captivating and radiant, like a cluster of blossoms after being watered.
The powers of association with the virtuous bestow an unsurpassed, eternal, and abundant bliss that is free from misfortune and free from affliction.
Even by men who have fallen into most miserable circumstances and have become helpless, association with the virtuous must not be abandoned even in the slightest degree.
In this world, associations with the virtuous are lamps for the true path; they are the rays of the sun of knowledge that dispel the darkness within the heart.
For one who has bathed in the Ganges of association with the virtuous—cool and pure—what need is there for gifts, what need for sacred fords, what need for austerities, or what need for sacrifices?
O sinless one, if there exist holy men who are free from passion, whose doubts are severed, and whose knots are untied, what is the use of penance or visiting sacred fords?
Fortunate are those whose minds are at rest; for the virtuous must indeed be sought out with supreme effort, just as jewels are sought by a poor man.
The intellect of the wise, graced by the beauty of association with the virtuous, shines forever like a lotus amidst a host of celestial nymphs.
By that fortunate man who did not abandon the company of the virtuous, the excellence of the state of stainless reflection was brought to its highest pinnacle.

Those virtuous ones who have severed the knots [of ignorance], who possess that knowledge, and who are honored by all—these should be served by every means, for they are the very means for crossing the ocean of existence.
These very people have become the dried fuel for the fires of hell—those virtuous ones who, with ease, beheld the fires of hell as if they were water.
The delusion regarding such objects as "poverty is death" and "death is suffering" is completely pacified by the medicine of association with the virtuous.
Contentment, association with the virtuous, inquiry, and likewise tranquility—these alone are the means for men to cross the ocean of worldly existence.
Contentment is the supreme gain; association with the virtuous is the supreme goal; discernment is the supreme knowledge; and indeed, tranquility is the supreme happiness.
These four are the stainless means for shattering cyclic existence; those who have practiced them have crossed over the ocean of existence, whose waters are delusion.
O best among the wise, when even one of these [four] has been practiced until the stainless state arises, all four indeed become practiced.
Even a single one among all these is a source of abundant progeny in this world; for the sake of complete success, therefore, one should diligently take refuge in one alone.
Association with the virtuous, contentment, and discernment—when well-considered—proceed like vehicles upon an ocean that is clear through tranquility.

Prosperities attend a living being who is endowed with discernment, contentment, tranquility, and the company of the virtuous, just as they attend one who has taken refuge under a wish-fulfilling tree.
In a person endowed with discernment, tranquility, virtuous association, and contentment, the qualities of excellence flow forth like beauty and other attributes in the full moon.

In one who possesses good company, contentment, tranquility, and discernment, and who holds right views, the glories of victory proceed, just as they do for an excellent minister in matters of statecraft.
Therefore, O descendant of Raghu, having conquered the mind—one of these which is eternal—by human effort, one should diligently cultivate virtue.
Relying on supreme human effort and having conquered the elephant-like mind, as long as even a single virtue does not reside within, there is no higher state.
With manly effort, you should grind your teeth against your teeth, O Rāma, until your mind is firmly resolved upon the acquisition of virtue.
Whether you are a god, a yakṣa, a human, or even a tree, O mighty-armed one, as long as that remains, there is no remedy whatsoever for you here.
When even a single quality that yields fruit gains strength, all defects of one whose mind is helpless quickly perish.
When virtue increases, virtues that overcome defects flourish; when vice increases, defects that destroy virtues flourish.
In this forest of mental delusion, the swift river of latent tendencies flows constantly among living beings, with its broad banks formed by the auspicious and the inauspicious.
For she, by her own effort, flows toward whichever bank she is cast; she carries you along with that very bank—do as you wish.

O you of excellent mind, gradually follow the auspicious banks within the forest of the mind by means of the speed of human effort; alas, by that, you will not be carried away even slightly by the great river of your own innate nature.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, he who possesses such internal discernment is great in this world; he is fit to hear the words of knowledge, just as a king is fit to hear the speech on statesmanship.
Pure, a great-souled one who has purified his discernment, free from attachment to the dull, he is fit, like the sky for the autumn moon.
Supported by this excellence of virtue, though it has been broken, you should listen to these words about to be spoken, which remove the delusion of the mind.
For that person for whom the wish-fulfilling tree of merit stands bowed under the weight of its fruit, this effort to hear [this teaching] arises for the sake of liberation.
One who is worthy becomes a vessel for words that are purifying, noble, and bestowing the singular realization of the Supreme; the base person does not.
This compendium, entitled *Mokṣopāya*, which measures the essence [of all teachings], consists of thirty-two thousand verses; when known, it bestows liberation.
Just as light proceeds from a lamp that has been lit while one is awake—even against one's will—so too shall nirvana come about through this [practice].

Whether known personally or heard from others, it grants the singular bliss of the cessation of delusion; when contemplated and described, it immediately bestows [liberation], just like the celestial river of heaven.
Just as the delusion of a snake in a rope perishes through inspection, so too does the suffering of cyclic existence come to rest through this contemplation.
In this [work], there are six chapters consisting of sentences whose meanings are logically consistent and individually formulated, containing the essence of examples and well-spoken verses.
The first chapter, titled "Dispassion," has been fully proclaimed; by it, dispassion increases like a tree in a desert through irrigation.

This determination of the true nature of destiny, together with its sequel, consists of one thousand and five hundred verses; when this is reflected upon in the heart, purity arises from illumination, just as it does in a well-polished gem.
Thereafter, the chapter titled "The Conduct of the Seeker of Liberation" was composed; it consists of approximately one thousand verses and is beautiful due to its logical arguments.
Indeed, the section concerning the origin [of the world], which consists of parables and narratives, describes the true nature of those men who seek liberation.
The world consists of seven thousand granthas that expound consciousness; its splendor takes the form of the notions of "seer," "seen," and "I-ness."
That in which it is described as being neither arisen nor even emerged, and upon hearing which this entire world is understood by the listener within his own inner consciousness.

That [universe], together with ourselves and you, in all its detail, including the space of the worlds and the mountains—being free from the grasping of a solid mass, without walls, and without mountains.
Devoid of the primary elements such as earth and the rest, it is like a city in one's imagination; it appears like the perception of a dream and is spread out like a kingdom of the mind.
It resembles a city of Gandharvas because it is a perception devoid of objective reality; it appears like the delusion of two moons, or the movement of water in a mirage.
Resembling a mountain shimmering on the surface of the ocean, yet devoid of the attainment of truth; appearing like a demon of mental delusion, it is seedless and yet radiant.
It appears like the meaning of a discourse and resembles a string of pearls in the sky; it is like the state of being a bracelet in gold, or like the state of being a wave in water.
Just as blueness, though always non-existent, arises in the sky—appearing charming to the perception even though it lacks a wall or a physical basis.
Just as a painted fire, though not made by an agent and appearing long-lasting in a dream or in the sky, possesses the nature of fire despite being no fire at all; so it is with this.

In this way, it projects the world—consisting of words, forms, and objects—which is unreal in nature, appearing like a garland of water-lilies upon waves, or like a dance that has arisen before one's eyes.
It was like a mass of water rising up, filled with the whirring of wheels; it was like a sapless forest in summer, with its leaves withered and its fallen parts destroyed.
With minds distracted by the fear of death, they dwell in stone houses and mountain caves; performing solitary dances in dark caverns, their behavior is that of madmen.
The mist of ignorance having been stilled, consciousness is like an autumnal sky; it is as if carved upon a pillar, or as a painting manifested upon a wall.
Just as [an image] fashioned from mud and so forth may be either sentient or insentient, the fourth chapter, concerning "Abiding," has thus been formulated.
Thus, consisting of three thousand verses and composed of commentaries and narratives, [this work] has attained the state of being the very ego-sense of the world.
In this regard, it is proclaimed that the sequence of seer and seen is fully developed; this delusion of the world shines forth, pervading the expanse of the ten directions.
Thus, it is said therein that he has long attained growth; thereafter follows the *Upaśāntiprakaraṇa* consisting of five thousand [verses].
The fifth purifying stage is proclaimed as beautiful with its continuous sequence of reasoning: the delusion has arisen that "this world," "I," and "you" are [identical].
In this manner, within this "Chapter on Quiescence" (*Upaśāntiprakaraṇa*), it is explained through a collection of verses that when it is heard, cyclic existence (*saṃsṛti*) comes to rest.
Like a fallen painting whose colors have faded, it becomes barely perceptible; with only a hundredth part remaining, its form is one of completely stilled delusion.

Abiding in a mind fixed on another's intention, she was like the splendor of a city that does not exist; she stood beside an unattainable object, like the long-drawn-out clamor of a battle in a dream.
Like the terrifying sound of a thunderbolt from a cloud filled with the intent for tranquility, it is comparable to a city conjured up in a dream that has been forgotten.
Her body was as pure as a jasmine flower blooming in a city garden yet to come; her tongue was like the experience of the meaning of a profound discourse being uttered.
Like a wall surface covered by a painting whose colors have not yet been applied, it resembles a city of conceptual constructions whose objects are being forgotten.

The movement of the forest trees, belonging to all seasons and yet not yet arisen, has an indistinct form; it is colored by the essence of spring, which will take the shape of future flowers and woods.
Like a river whose flood of waves has subsided within and whose water is tranquil, the sixth chapter, titled "Nirvāṇa," is thus proclaimed.

The remaining portion of the text is its measure, which bestows great meaning through knowledge; when that is realized, there arises the supreme good—nirvāṇa, wherein all conceptual constructions are stilled.

The self whose nature is the light of consciousness, beyond both the unmanifest and the manifest, is the pure essence of gnosis, free from ailment, as clear as the sheath of the supreme ether, and in whom all the delusions of existence have been stilled.

Having brought the wanderings of the world to rest, he remains well-established, having accomplished all that was to be done; like a diamond pillar for the undertakings of all people, he is as serene as the sky.
Having swallowed the entire web of the world according to its sequence and being fully satiated, he has made his mental engagement with the perception of all forms consist of nothing but space.
Abandoned by the views of cause, effect, agency, and what is to be rejected or accepted, he is as if bodiless though possessing a body, and though amidst saṃsāra, he is beyond saṃsāra.
Consisting of pure consciousness, resembling the interior of a solid stone, the sun of consciousness shines upon the worlds as if dispelling the darkness of night.

Though his nature is that of supreme illumination, he has entered as it were into a state of utter blindness; the wicked play of worldly existence is blocked within him, and the cholera of desire has been destroyed.

The world’s splendor remains upon a single tip of one of his pores—this embodied, lifeless corpse from whom the vampire of ego has vanished—just as a bee might rest upon a flower somewhere on Mount Mahāmeru.
Within the hollow of its own interior, the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) in every single atom contains thousands of world-glories; having created them, it then beholds them.

The vastness of the heart of the Great-minded One cannot be equaled even by hundreds of thousands of Hari, Hara, and Añjanaja, because it is exceedingly expansive, being the state of one who has attained liberation and is the unsurpassed reality.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Within this which is merely consciousness, awakening proceeds, just as from a seed that exists when sown, a good fruit necessarily arises.

Even a human-authored treatise is to be accepted if it conveys sound reasoning; conversely, anything else is to be rejected even if it is of divine origin. One who adheres solely to what is logical must maintain this principle.
"A word endowed with reason should be accepted even from a child; any other, even if spoken by the Lotus-born One, should be rejected like a blade of grass."
Who would not censure that excessively passionate man who, thinking "this is the well of my father," drinks water from a well while neglecting the Ganges water standing right before him?
Just as light will inevitably arrive when the dawn has broken, so too will excellent discernment arise within this state of mind-only.
When the [truth] has been heard from the mouth of the wise and understood by oneself as well, and when an impression has gradually arisen in the intellect through sustained inquiry;
First of all, there arises within him a mastery of refined speech, pure and well-constructed, which, like a lofty creeper, serves as an ornament for the assembly hall.
Supreme is that state of urbanity which is endowed with the quality of greatness, by means of which even kings and even the immortals enter into affection.
A man who knows what precedes and what follows becomes wise in all matters, just as one with good eyesight and a lamp in hand perceives objects clearly in the night.
Defects such as greed and delusion gradually diminish sufficiently, just as the mists of the quarters of the sky fade away when autumn is near.
The intellects perceive only the practice of discernment; no action whatsoever bears fruit without its own repeated cultivation.
The mind attains clarity like a great lake in autumn; it achieves supreme equanimity like the ocean when Mount Mandara has ceased its churning.
Like a crest-jewel that has cast off all blackness, or like a cloth of darkness that has been set aside, wisdom—discerning the nature of things—blazes forth intensely.
Gazes filled with the defects of wretchedness and poverty, though their inner intent is revealed, do not cut into the vital organs, just as arrows fail to pierce one who is clad in armor.
The terrifying fears of cyclic existence do not tear at the heart of the wise man, even though they stand before him, just as arrows cannot pierce a great boulder.
"How can there be a beginning for births, actions, fate, and human effort?"—this multitude of doubts is pacified just as darkness is dispelled by the sun.
At all times, in all things, perfect tranquility arises, just as when the night has become calm and the light of dawn has appeared.
Like the ocean, there is profundity; like Mount Meru, there is steadfastness; and like the moon, a coolness arises within the one who reflects.
That state of liberation while living gradually reaches its full fruition for him who has stilled all particularities; it becomes beyond the reach of words.
Cool toward all objects, pure, and bestowing supreme illumination, the intellect attains the highest light, like the autumnal moonlight.
In the stainless sky of the heart, where the sun of discernment shines with the light of tranquility, the comets that bring forth multitudes of misfortunes truly do not arise.
They become tranquil, attain purity, and remain gentle in their noble state; free from thirst, they abide in the unmoving water like rows of clouds in autumn.
Villainy, which acts recklessly and is cruel, ceases like the wretched dance of goblins at the arrival of day.
Mental anxieties do not shake the intellect that is firmly rooted in the foundation of Dharma and has ascended the yoke of fortitude, just as winds cannot move a painted creeper.
The wise man does not fall into the pit that consists of attachment to sense objects; for who, indeed, knowing the path, would run headlong into a chasm?

His intellect delights in whatever action comes to him that is not in conflict with true scriptures and the conduct of the virtuous, just as a noble woman finds pleasure in the courtyard of the inner apartments.
In as many millions of billions of worlds as there are atoms, one whose intellect is unattached perceives the creations situated within each and every one of them.
For a person whose inner self has been purified by the realization of the means to liberation, the flood of worldly enjoyments neither causes distress nor brings joy at any time.
He sees all the unimpeded classes [of beings] that fall and rise in every single atom, like the waves of water.
He feels no aversion toward things that have arisen, nor does he long for those that have ceased; though awakened, he performs his duties like a tree that is as if unawakened.
He appears like an ordinary person, following whatever comes to him; yet, in the attainment of desired or undesired results, his heart remains unconquered.
Let this entire treatise be read and analyzed by the wise; this is indeed to be experienced directly, and is not merely stated like a boon or a curse.
This treatise is indeed easy to understand and is adorned with poetic ornaments; it is a beautiful poem full of aesthetic flavor (rasa), explained through illustrative examples.
One who knows even a little of the words and their meanings understands this by oneself; however, he who does not know this by himself must listen to it from a learned scholar.
Once this has been heard, reflected upon, and known, nothing else—such as austerity, meditation, or recitation—is of any use for a person here in attaining liberation.
From the intense study of this treatise and from repeated contemplation thereof, there shall arise an unprecedented scholarship preceded by the purification of the mind.
The arrogant demon of the seer and the seen, which manifests as "I" and "the world," subsides of its own accord without effort, just as a ghost vanishes at the rising of the sun.
The delusion that "the world" and "I" exist subsides even while it persists; like a dream-delusion once fully recognized, it no longer causes one to wander excessively.

Just as the joy or sorrow of a person regarding a city of their imagination does not cause them distress once it is understood to be such, so too is it with this delusion of the world when it is thoroughly comprehended.
Just as a painted snake, when fully understood, does not cause fear of a snake, so too a perceived snake, when fully understood, does not bestow pleasure or pain.
Just as the serpent-nature of a painted snake perishes through full comprehension, so too does cyclic existence, though it remains as it is, become pacified.
In the crushing of a *sumana* blossom, there might be some slight disturbance; but in the attainment of the state of ultimate reality, not even the slightest disturbance occurs.
In the crushing of a flower petal, a physical part undergoes vibration; here, however, there is only the cessation of mental activity, not the movement of any bodily limb.
Seated on a comfortable seat, eating as much as is appropriate, and never remaining engaged in activities contrary to right conduct regarding the web of enjoyments.
One should contemplate this treatise, as well as other works, at every opportunity and in every place with ease, whenever one encounters the company of the virtuous as circumstances allow.
The awakening of great wisdom, which brings peace to saṃsāra, is attained; by means of this, one is never again born to suffer the crushing of the machine of the womb.

Even those base ones who remain unafraid in the midst of this, dwelling in the savor of sinful enjoyments, are not even worth mentioning—those lowest of men who are like worms in the excrement of their own mothers.
Listen now, O Rāghava, as I relate this expansion of knowledge, which is the most essential core of the intellect.
Listen now to that introduction as this scripture is being heard, just as its true meaning is investigated according to its technical terminology.
The wise know that to be an illustration (dṛṣṭānta) by which an object not yet experienced here is made known through a perceived object, yielding the fruit of assistance toward understanding.
O Rāma, without an illustration, a previously unknown matter is not understood, just as household goods and utensils in a house at night cannot be seen without a lamp.
O descendant of Kakutstha, whatever examples I have used here to awaken your understanding, let them all—though they possess their own causes—attain that which is eternally causeless.
The relationship of cause and effect between the objects of comparison and the things compared exists among all things whatsoever, with the exception of the Supreme Brahman.
In this instruction on Brahman, whatever example is stated here for you, it is understood to possess a commonality with only one part [of the subject].
Whatever illustration is given here for the purpose of awakening to the reality of Brahman, each of them should be understood as being like that which arises in a dream within the world.
This being so, how can there be an example possessing form for Brahman which is formless? Thus, the speculative utterances of fools do not arise.
Due to the refutation of examples seen to be unestablished, contradictory, and so forth, and because the world is like a dream, nothing at all arises.
It has been analyzed that the unreal exists neither in the past nor in the future; just as the waking state is, so too is the dream state—this is established even for children.

Through dreams, mental constructs, meditation, boons, curses, medicinal herbs, and so forth, examples that accord with reality are seen here, because the existence of the world possesses that same nature.
Among the other treatises composed by the author for the sake of the means to liberation, this alone is the definitive system for the awakening to that which is to be known.
The dream-like nature of the world is understood from the sacred scriptures; indeed, it cannot be explained quickly, for speech proceeds only step by step.
The world is like a dream, a mental construction, a city of the imagination, and so forth; since these alone are the appropriate analogies, no others exist here.
When that which lacks causal agency is compared to that which possesses it for the sake of awakening, a complete similarity of all attributes is not possible through such means of comparison.
The wise person, free from dispute, must accept that the object of comparison shares a common property with the standard of comparison in at least one respect, in order to achieve understanding.
Indeed, when perceiving an object, apart from the mere light emitted by a lamp, nothing else—such as its location, oil, or wick—is of any utility.

O dear one, because it possesses the capacity for only a portion [of its function], the standard of comparison brings about the cognition of the object of comparison, just as a lamp does so by means of the light of its object.
When the awakening of understanding arises through even a mere portion of the illustration, the determination of the meaning of the Great Sentence should be grasped as something to be adopted.
One should not, by falling into the state of a fallacious logician, destroy awakened consciousness through unholy conceptual constructions that end in the denial of direct experience.

Because it causes experience through investigation, the Vedic corpus follows us even among people like ourselves; yet a word spoken by a woman—even if it concerns the supreme truth of the Vedas—is merely the babbling of speech and not authoritative scripture.

O dear one, our view is that the unification of all scriptures into a single coherent statement bears fruit because there exists a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) other than the consciousness nourished by its own limbs [the senses] which perceives merely the apparent object; therefore, that [other means] is the authority.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In comparisons, the capacity of a specific quality is what is apprehended; for if there were total similarity between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison, what distinction would there be?

Through the realization of the meaning of the scriptures concerning the knowledge of the single Self, and through the awakening to illustrative examples, the attainment of the meaning of the Great Sayings is called peace and nirvāṇa.

Therefore, enough with the proliferation of conceptual distinctions between the illustration and the illustrated; rather, one should rely upon the meaning of the Great Sentence through whatever reasoning may be employed.
Know that peace is the supreme good; be diligent in attaining it. When the rice to be eaten has been obtained, what is the use of further deliberations regarding its preparation?

For the sake of awakening, that which lacks causes is compared to that which possesses causes; and the objects of comparison are compared by means of similes that are similar to them in certain respects.
One whose soul is devoid of discernment should not remain attached to worldly enjoyments, like a blind frog that has grown fat within the belly of a stone.
Relying on examples and exerting effort, one should conquer the supreme state; one should be possessed of discernment and enriched by the meaning of the treatise on peace.
Through the study of the scriptures, instruction from the virtuous, wisdom, and association with those who know it, he repeatedly engaged in the practice of acquiring the Dharma and its purpose.
The wise one should investigate until he attains rest within himself—that peace called the fourth state (turya), which is beyond further destruction.
For one who is established in repose in the Fourth State (turya) and has turned back from the ocean of existence—whether living or dead, whether a householder or an ascetic—[this applies].
He has no concern for what is done or left undone, nor for the confusions of the Vedas and Smṛtis; like the ocean without Mount Mandara, he remains as he is.

The similarity between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison should be understood through a single aspect for the sake of awakening to what is to be known; one should not remain fickle regarding that awakening.
By whatever means possible, you must understand that which is to be understood; those who are restless and eager for awakening do not perceive what is logical and what is illogical.
When the self of experience has come to rest within the heart, the space of consciousness, he who declares that there is no reality there is called one whose intellect is as clumsy as a crow's beak.
Through portions of its own conceit and conceptual constructions, the ignorant one conceptualizes pure awareness; it thus defiles its own inner awakening, just as a cloud defiles the stainless sky.
Just as the ocean is the abode of all existing waters, so too is perception the sole means of valid cognition here; therefore, listen to that.

The supreme ones know that direct perception (*vedana*) is the direct witness of the essence of all the senses; indeed, that which is established through the attainment of that [perception] is declared to be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
That which is called "direct perception" (pratyakṣa) here is simply experience, feeling, and cognition according to its designation; that alone is our "living soul" (jīva).
That very consciousness is the Person (puruṣa), whose nature consists of the notion of "I-ness" (ahaṃtā); that consciousness by which it arises is known as the objective category (padārtha).
Through the delusions of various sequences created by conceptualization, discursive thought, and the like, it manifests as the world, just as water manifests as waves and so forth.
At the beginning of creation, having first manifested as the causeless itself through the play of creation, it quickly became the manifest cause within its own self.

However, although it does not exist, the cause—the form of the world—remains as if real within this primordial nature (prakṛti), having attained manifestation for the individual soul (jīva) that arises from non-investigation.
But inquiry itself, having destroyed its own form that arose from itself, quickly brings about the supreme, great, and direct realization.
When one who possesses discernment understands even discernment itself as the Self, then that which remains is the supreme, beyond all conceptual description.

When the mind is rendered effortless and tranquil through its own faculties and actions, there is no purpose served by things done, nor by things left undone, because of the absence of mental cultivation.
When the mind is rendered effortless and stilled, those organs of action do not engage in activity at all, like a machine whose movement has not been set in motion.
They know that sensation is the cause for the movement of the mental machine, just as a rope is contained within the wooden ram of a waterwheel.
The world, agitated by forms, light, mental attention, and objects, exists within the perceiver like the movement of wind inside a bellows.
When the pure awareness of the self of all arises as being of that very nature, it shines forth, manifesting forms of body, internal and external, and the expansion of space and time.
Having seen the mere appearance of the visible, it remains maintaining its own essential nature; whatever form appears to it, in whatever place and in whatever manner, that is exactly how it is.
In whatever way and wherever that Universal Self attains manifestation, it immediately abides there and shines as if it were of that very form.

Because it consists of all things, it is as appropriate for the Seer to possess the state of being seen; yet, since the state of being seen exists only when there is a Seer, that state of being seen is not ultimately real.
Therefore, this Brahman is established as being indeed without cause; it is directly perceived as the creator, while inference and other means of knowledge are merely its parts.

O virtuous one, that supreme state which a devotee who has cast far away the meaning of the word "fate" (daiva) seeks through mere self-effort alone—that is indeed attained inwardly by a hero through his own human exertion (pauruṣa) alone.

First, investigate according to the truth and the white [teachings] of the lineages of teachers, until you yourself, through your own intellect, realize the supreme, formless state that is utterly pure.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: First, through the means of association with noble beings, one should forcibly lead one's wisdom toward growth; thereafter, through the characteristics of a great being, one attains the state of a great person.
Whatever quality by which a person shines forth here, that very quality remains; therefore, one should quickly cause that intelligence to increase.
For this state of being a Great Being, endowed with qualities such as tranquility and the like, O Rāma, does not attain any accomplishment whatsoever without perfect knowledge.
Through wisdom, qualities such as tranquility increase in the lineage of the virtuous; they are praiseworthy because of their internal fruit, like new sprouts from rain.
Supreme knowledge increases from virtues such as tranquility, just as an excellent rain of rice grows from sacrifices consisting of food offerings.
The qualities such as tranquility arise from knowledge, and from tranquility and the others likewise arises knowledge; these mutually increase like a lotus and a lake.
Knowledge arises from the conduct of virtuous persons, and the path of virtuous persons arises from knowledge; thus, both knowledge and the path of virtuous persons mutually increase one another.
And by means of the sequence of human effort skilled in tranquility, wisdom, and so forth, the wise person should practice the methods of knowledge and the conduct of the true person.
As long as both the path of knowledge and the sequence of the true person have not been practiced equally, my dear, not even one of these two will succeed for a man in this world.
Just as the joy of song is accomplished by a woman guarding the ripening rice, accompanied by the driving away of birds with a sustained rhythmic beat; so too is the bliss of the song achieved.
Through the application of knowledge and the effort of a true person, by means of one who is a non-agent yet appears as an agent, a person free from desire likewise attains the supreme state.
O descendant of Raghu, the sequence of right conduct has thus been proclaimed by me; now, in the same manner, the sequence of knowledge is correctly taught.
This true scripture, which bestows fame, longevity, and the fruits of human endeavor, should indeed be heard from a trustworthy person who knows it, by one who is wise.
Having heard this, through the purity of your intellect, you will by force attain that state, just as turbid water attains clarity through contact with the *kataka* nut.

For this mind of the sage, having known that which is to be known, indeed goes helplessly to the supreme state; once that unbroken, supreme reality is realized, it does not abandon it by the power of that realization.
Through the powers of speech, the knower of Brahman perceives Brahman within himself as if in a dream; whatever one knows through words arising from one's own [inner] sound, that indeed he knows.
By this reasoning, in this world where creation exists within the ether of Brahman, the objection—"What is this? Whose is it? Where is it?"—has been refuted.
I shall now speak all of this according to my knowledge, according to the facts, in due order, and according to their true nature; listen to this, O wise one.
One who knows the body to be the space of consciousness perceives the world as if in a dream; "I" and "you," along with everything else, are merely examples of the dream-like cycle of existence.
Following this treatise consisting of the discourse on the conduct of those seeking liberation, I shall now fully expound this treatise on the origin of the world.
