This bondage arises from the existence of the visible; with the absence of the visible, bondage is not possible. Now hear, in due order, how this visible world [is non-existent].
Whatever arises in the world, that indeed grows; that very same thing attains liberation, or heaven, or even hell.
Therefore, for the sake of your own understanding, I shall first explain how and by whom this birth within saṃsāra occurred.
O Raghava, listen briefly to this meaning of the section; thereafter, I shall relate it to you in detail according to your desire.
All this that is seen—the entire world, both stationary and moving—is like a dream in deep sleep; it perishes at the end of the aeon.
Then there remains something existent—calm and profound, neither light nor pervasive darkness, indefinable and unmanifest.
"Ṛta," "Ātman," "Paraṃ Brahma," "Satya," and so forth—these names of that Great Self have been devised by the wise for the sake of conventional usage."
That very self, though being such as it is, shines forth as if it were something else; it enters, as it were, into the state of living, constrained by its future name.
Then, having become agitated by the conceptualization of the meaning of the word "jīva," the self of the elements becomes the mind (manas), becoming sluggish through the act of thinking.
By that [mind], the mind arises from the Great Supreme Self—unsteady in form though originating from the perfectly stable one—just like a wave from the ocean.
That [mind] itself constantly and spontaneously conceives [its objects] at its own will; by that means, this vast splendor of a magical illusion is thus spread out.
Just as the referent of the word "bracelet" is not distinct from the gold, nor is the gold distinct from the bracelet, so too the referent of the word "world" is not distinct from the Supreme.

This world exists exactly as it is within Brahman alone, whose nature is infinite; the meaning denoted by the word "world" does not exist [apart from it], just as the nature of a bracelet does not exist apart from gold.
Whether real or unreal, like a shimmering wave upon a scorching river, this worldly splendor is spread out by the mind as a magical illusion.
Ignorance, cyclic existence, bondage, illusion, delusion, and the great darkness—these are the names assigned to it by those who know all things.
First, listen to this description of the nature of bondage being told; thereafter, O moon-faced one, you will understand the true nature of liberation.
The existence of the seer and the seen is called bondage; the seer is bound by the power of the seen and is liberated in the absence of the seen.
The world, the self, the "I," and so forth—the false nature called the "seen"—exists as long as this persists; until then, liberation is not found.
The disease of the visible world is not pacified by vain prattling such as "this is not it, this is not it," which only generates further conceptual constructions; on the contrary, it increases.
For those who investigate, the real world that is perceived does not pass away through the grinding of the burden of logic, nor through pilgrimages, religious observances, and the like.
If the world-appearance were real, it would never cease for anyone; for there is no coming into being of the non-existent, nor the passing away of the existent.
Wherever the Self, whose nature is neither insentient nor sentient, abides, there the splendor of its object of vision arises for the observer—even within the interior of an atom.
Therefore, this world-appearance exists; it has been wiped away by me through asceticism, meditation, and recitation, just as one who is satisfied with sour gruel [discards finer food].
O Rāma, if this visible world exists, it is reflected in this very mirror of consciousness, even within the interior of a single atom; for it is exactly so.
Just as whatever stands here or there is reflected in a mirror, so indeed are the sky, the ocean, the earth, the mountains, and the waters reflected in the mirror of consciousness.
Then, moreover, there is suffering therein: old age, death, and birth; the grasping and abandoning of existence and non-existence; and that which is gross and subtle, moving and unmoving.
This visible world has been wiped away by me, and I remain here; this very state is the inexhaustible seed for the recollection of cyclic existence within meditative absorption.

But while this visible world exists, how can there be non-conceptual meditative absorption (nirvikalpa-samādhi)? For if there were such absorption, consciousness and even the fourth state (turya) would be possible.
For upon emerging from meditative absorption, just as at the end of deep sleep, this entire world-suffering appears exactly as it is, in its unbroken state.
O Rāma, what indeed is gained by meditative absorptions (samādhis)? For when one is once again struck by misfortune, what happiness is there in a momentary state of equanimity?
Or if one should attain stability in non-conceptual meditative absorption, that should be considered the stainless state, resembling imperishable deep sleep.
When this visible world exists, nothing whatsoever is attained by anyone; for wherever the mind goes, there indeed arises the delusion of the world.
If, moreover, the observer remains by force contemplating the state of being a stone, even at the end of that [contemplation], the state of being an object of perception arises for him once again.
Furthermore, non-conceptual meditative absorptions, which are like a state of stone-like insensibility, do not remain for everyone; rather, they are experienced by some [only].
Nor do the meditative absorptions, which have become as firmly rooted as a stone, reach that supreme state which is peaceful, the unborn and inexhaustible nature of consciousness.
Therefore, if this visible world were real, it could never cease; that the visible world might cease through austerity, recitation, and meditation is merely the imagination of the ignorant.
Just as the seed of a lotus dwells within the hollow of a lotus-stamen in the form of a coiled sprout, so does the perception of the visible world reside within the seer.
Just as flavor exists in substances, as oil exists in sesame seeds and the like, and as fragrance exists in flowers, so does the cognition of the visible exist in the seer.
Just as the fragrance of camphor and other such substances arises wherever they may be situated, so too does the world arise within the belly of the element of consciousness (*cid-dhātu*).

Just as your dream, your volition, and the intellect that governs the kingdom of the mind are seen through your own direct experience, so too does the ground of the visible world exist within the heart.
Therefore, just as a piśāca residing within the mental constructions of a child utterly destroys that child, so too does this [grasping] which takes the form of the visible destroy the observer.
Just as a sprout situated within a seed manifests a radiant body according to place and time, so indeed does the perception of the visible expand itself.

Just as a substance possesses a wonder that is eternally arisen within its own interior—devoid of rising or setting—so too does the existence of the world reside within the interior of the substance whose body is pure consciousness, being its very nature.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen to this narrative called "The Birth from Space," an ornament for the ears, which is the section known as "Origination," by means of which you shall understand, O Rāghava.
For there is a twice-born man named Ākāśaja, who is supremely righteous, constantly devoted solely to meditation, and ever intent on the welfare of all creatures.
When he lived for so long, Death thought to himself: "I am indeed inexhaustible; I devour all beings one after another in due order."
"Why do I not devour this brahmin born of space? Against him my power is blunted, like the edge of a sword upon a stone."
Having reflected thus, he then went to that city to kill him; for no one who is intent on their own task abandons their exertion.
Then, as soon as Death himself enters that abode, fire—resembling the conflagration at the end of an aeon—burns him up.
Having burst through the great garland of fire-flames, he indeed entered within; seeing the twice-born man, he desired to seize him with his hand with great effort.
And although he was powerful, he was unable to seize with his hundred arms the Brahmin standing before his eyes, just as one cannot grasp a person created by mere thought.
Then Death, having approached Yama, the cutter of doubts, asked him: "O Lord, why am I unable to devour that which is born of space?"
Yama said: "O Death, you alone are not capable of slaying anyone by force; it is the deeds of one who is to be slain that bring about that result, and nothing else."
Therefore, having diligently investigated the deeds of this Brahmin who is to be slain, you shall devour him with their assistance.
Then Death wandered about, intent on searching for that deed, through circles, the ends of the quarters, lakes, rivers, and all directions.
Forests, thickets, and groves; mountains and ocean shores; other islands, wild tracts, cities, and towns.
Having thus wandered over the entire circle of the earth—including principalities, all kingdoms, and the dense forests within the various regions—he did not find anything whatsoever from any source.
Death exerted himself to obtain those actions born of space, but like a wise man seeking the son of a barren woman, or another seeking a mountain of mere imagination, he failed.
Then, having approached, he questioned Yama, who is skilled in all matters; for he is the ultimate refuge and the source of authority for his dependents in times of doubt.
Death said: "O Lord, tell me where the deeds of one born of space reside. Then Dharmarāja, having reflected for a very long time, spoke this:
The King of Dharma said: "O Mṛtyu, there are no actions whatsoever belonging to one born from space; this brahmin born from space was produced solely from the sky."
He who is born from space alone must be as stainless as space itself; he has no auxiliary causes, nor does he possess any actions whatsoever.
He has no connection whatsoever with his former karma, just like the son of a barren woman or like one who has not yet been born.
Because of the absence of causes, he is therefore nothing but space; he possesses no prior karma, just as there can be no great tree in the sky.
This mind of his is not subject to necessity because of the absence of prior karma; for today, he has not accumulated even the slightest karma.
Thus, the self whose nature is the treasury of space, eternally abiding in its own cause which consists of the clear void, has no causes whatsoever.
He has no past actions, nor does he perform any today; in this very way, he here consists of nothing but the space of pure consciousness.
The movement of his vital breath, which is perceived as action by people such as ourselves, is seen by us alone; however, he possesses no consciousness of action in this regard.
Established as if contemplating from the supreme state, she is indeed the very form of consciousness; her own distinct form is like a carved statue upon a pillar of consciousness.
In that very same way, O twice-born one, the friend exists as one's own self from the perspective of ultimate reality, just as liquidity exists in water and emptiness exists in space.
Just as there is vibration in the wind, so too is this [vibration] in the supreme state; for him, there are indeed no actions belonging to the present nor any that have been accumulated.

Because this [consciousness] does not have prior [moments] as its cause, it has not fallen under the power of saṃsāra; for that which arises in the absence of auxiliary causes [is not subject to such continuity].
It is experienced that this [entity] does not become different from its own cause; therefore, due to the absence of causes, it is self-arisen.
Tell me, how can this agent—who did not exist previously nor exists today—be said to "attack" when he is about to form in his intellect the conceptualization known as death?
He who possesses the firm conviction, "I am this earth and so forth," quickly becomes identified with the earth; moreover, he can be easily restrained.

Due to the absence of any conceptualization of earth and the other elements, this Brahmin has no form; it is not at all possible to grasp him, just as it is impossible to seize the sky with a strong rope.
Death said: "O Blessed One, tell me how indeed it is that [beings] are born from the void; and tell me how the earth and the other elements exist, or how they do not exist."
Yama said: This twice-born one was never born, nor is he ever non-existent; he remains as such, being merely the light of absolute consciousness.
When the great dissolution occurs, nothing whatsoever remains; only Brahman exists—peaceful, undecaying, the infinite Self, and absolute.
Then, following that, there arises near him a mountain-like radiance, which is empty, eternally manifest, subtle, free from limiting adjuncts, supreme, and established.
Because its essential nature is pure consciousness alone, it perceives "I am the body"; thus, it beholds a delusory form as if by chance, like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit.
That very Brahmin, at the beginning of that creation, remained within the belly of the sky, established in the form of the non-conceptual space of consciousness.
He has no body, no actions, no agency, and no latent impressions; he is the pervasive, dense mass of pure consciousness, the sky of pure awareness.
No web of past latent impressions exists for him at all, for he is of the nature of pure space, like a light of the nature of radiance.
When even mere sensation has completely subsided, such a thing is no longer seen; therefore, as is the space of consciousness, so too are its perceptions.
"From where indeed does the earth and the rest originate here, what is their nature, and how do they come to be? Therefore, O Death, do not exert yourself in attacking this."
"It is never possible for anyone to grasp the sky. Having heard this, Death was struck with wonder and departed for his own abode.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Grandfather, this god who has been described by you to me as Brahmā is, in my opinion, the self-existent, unborn, singular Self, the very essence of consciousness."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "It is even so, O Rāma; this Brahman has been described by me to you. Long ago, on account of this very matter, Death engaged in a dispute with Yama."
In that Manvantara, when Death, devouring all beings, was carrying away the creatures, he gained strength and, having overwhelmed the Lotus-born Brahmā, undertook the task himself.
At that very moment, he was exhorted by Yama, the King of Dharma: "Whatever is done constantly, therein alone delight is born."
How indeed can Brahmā, whose body is the supreme ether, be approached? For he is mere mind and volition, his form devoid of earth and the other elements.
Whatever wonder of consciousness appears as the experience of forms is indeed consciousness-space itself; it possesses neither causality nor the state of being an effect.
Just as a person created by imagination appears with a form shimmering in space, though devoid of earth and other elements, so too does the Self-born shine forth.

Just as a city appears in a cloudless sky, or as a string of pearls appears in a mental construction or a dream—though it is not composed of earth or other elements—so too does the Self-existent One manifest.
In the absolute Supreme Self, there is neither the visible object nor the seer; nevertheless, this self-existent one shines forth as its own consciousness.
This mind, which is nothing but mere volition, is called Brahman; it is the person of the space of volition, and for it, earth and the other elements do not exist.
Just as a bodiless figurine appears within a painting, so too does Brahmā appear from the ether of consciousness like a crystal jewel.

The self-existent one shines as Brahman—the absolute space of consciousness, infinite, without beginning or middle—by the power of its own mind; yet, though appearing as if possessing form or as if a person, in reality it has no body, being like the son of a barren woman.
Śrī Rāma said: "In this very way, the mind is pure and devoid of earth and the other elements; you have stated that the mind is Brahman, which is truly free from earth and the rest."
Therefore, O Brahmin, tell me this: why is past memory not the cause here for myself, for you, for others, and for all living beings?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For one who possesses a previous body today, accompanied by past karma, memory arises; that is the cause for the persistence of worldly existence.
When not even a single prior action of Brahmā exists, how and from where could his recollection of a previous state arise?
Therefore, it appears either as causeless or as having its sole cause in one's own mind; being non-different from its own cause, it is self-existent and possesses its own nature.
This body of the Self-existent One, O Rāma, is purely *ātivāhika*; for the Unborn, a material (*ādhibhautika*) body is not possible.
Śrī Rāma said: Is there one subtle body (*ātivāhika*) and another material body (*ādhibhautika*); or is there only one for all classes of beings, O Brahman?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For all beings whose nature is causal, there are indeed two bodies; however, for the Unborn (the Supreme Self), because of the absence of causality, there is only the one subtle body (ativāhika).
The one Unborn is the supreme cause of all classes of beings; there is no cause for the Unborn, and therefore he possesses a single body.
The body of the first Prajāpati is not material at all; consisting of space itself, he shines forth possessing a subtle, transportable body.
Having a body consisting of mind alone, this primordial Lord of Creatures, whose nature is not composed of earth and the other elements, and whose form is space, extends forth all creatures.
And these, being of the nature of the sky of consciousness, exist without any other causes; for it is experienced by everyone that whatever is, is that very thing.
Nirvāṇa alone is the Supreme Person; that itself is supreme awakening. That very thing remains as mind-only (cittamātra); it does not become the earth and so forth.
For all classes of beings engaged in the worldly course of saṃsāra, this first vibration is the mind-body that arises from itself.
Non-different from this prior vibration and having its very nature as that, this creation has issued forth like the creation of movement from the wind.
From this creative intuition (pratibhā), which takes the form of intuition itself, this creation shines forth as possessing a true experience, though it exists merely as the nature of intuition.
An illustration for this is found in the sexual union with a woman in one's own dream-city; though non-existent, it is radiant with the experience of reality through the fulfillment of its purpose.
Not composed of earth or the other elements, appearing with the form of space and bodiless, the Lord of Beings—who is one's own self—shines in the form of a person as if he possessed a body.
Because consciousness consists of conceptual construction, it neither arises nor emerges; because its own nature is self-dependent, it neither arises nor ceases.
Brahmā is the personification of volition, whose form is devoid of earth and other elements; consisting solely of the nature of mind, he is the cause for the existence of the three worlds.
Just as this volition of the Self-born One shines forth by its own nature, so too does this space-like self shine like a mountain of your own volition.
Due to a firm form of forgetfulness regarding its own subtle, transportive nature, it falsely appears like a ghost through the perception of a material body.
This is the first awakening of the great consciousness through effort; because of its nature as pure awareness, the forgetfulness of the subtle body does not arise.
No demoness born of the material world arises for him—unreal, like a mirage, falsely bestowing the delusion of dullness.
When Brahmā consists of mind alone and is not composed of earth and the other elements, then the entire universe is mind alone; for whatever has arisen is indeed that very mind.
Since there are no cooperative causes for that which is unborn, there are likewise none at all for that which is born from it; therefore, some [causes] do not exist.
The diversity of effects arises from the cause; therefore, there is nothing here [in the effect] that does not exist [in the cause]. It is established that as the cause is pure, so is the effect.
For here, the relationship of cause and effect is not at all tenable; for exactly as the Supreme Brahman is, so too are the three worlds.
The world is stretched out by Brahman, which has, as it were, attained the state of mind; it is non-different from the pure Self, just as fluidity is non-different from water.
All this that is spread out is woven by the mind; it is entirely unreal, like a city of imagination or a city of the Gandharvas.
There is no state of being material, just as there is no state of being a snake in a rope; how then can those who are awakened, such as Brahmā and the others, remain therein?
Indeed, for one whose mind is awakened, there exists only the subtle body (ātivāhika); for such a person, how and from where could there even be talk of a material body (ādhibhautikadeha)?
For the person named Manu, who assumes the form of Viriñci, the kingdom of the mind known as the world stands as if it were of the nature of reality.
The mind alone is the state of Viriñci, for it consists of volition; having brought its own form to expansion, this world is spread out by the mind.
Viriñca is the form of the mind, and the mind is the body of Viriñca; earth and the other elements do not exist here [in reality], and therefore earth and the others are merely imagined.

Just as within a lotus there is the lotus-stalk, so within the mind there exists the state of being an object; the mind and the perception of objects have never been distinct from one another by anyone at any time.
Just as here your dream, your volition, and the intellect’s sovereignty over the mind are experienced through one's own direct perception, so too the realm of the visible exists within the heart.
Therefore, just as a demon residing in a child's mental construction destroys that child, so too does this [demon] appearing in the form of the visible destroy the internal observer.
Just as a sprout situated within a seed manifests a radiant body according to place and time, so indeed does the intellect of the perceivable expand itself.

If the suffering of the visible world does not ever subside, and if the visible world does not subside, there can be no isolation for the knower. However, when the visible world is impossible, the state of being a knower subsides even while it persists; indeed, they call this his liberation.
Śrī Vālmīki said: While the leader of sages was thus speaking with unrestrained eloquence, the assembly became single-minded in its desire to hear, and all remained established in silence.
The tinkling sounds of the networks of small bells had subsided, and even the hārītas and parrots within their cages had ceased their play, no longer moving about.
Even while the women remained with their amorous gestures completely forgotten, the entire royal assembly hall stood as if fixed upon a painted wall.
The day, with its sweet heat, had but a single *muhūrta* remaining; all worldly affairs, along with the rays of the sun, began to diminish.
Fragrant with the scent of clusters of blooming lotuses, the breezes blew with sweet vibrations, as if they had come to listen.

Like the sun abandoning its confusion regarding the arrangement of day and night when it is time to contemplate what has been heard, he left his solitary place and went to the empty slope of the western mountain.
In the forest lands, coolnesses arose like the onset of mist; they were as if the very essence of tranquility, cooled within from hearing that [news].
People in all ten directions became scarcely mobile, as if they had abandoned all activity in order to listen with full attention.
The shadows of all things stretched out their long necks, as if to hear the sequence of words from Vasiṣṭha.
The doorkeeper, bowing low before him, said to the lord of the earth: "O King, the time for your bath and the worship of the twice-born has greatly passed."
Then the venerable Vasiṣṭha, having withdrawn his sweet voice, said: "O Great King, let this much suffice for you to hear for now."
"I shall say something else tomorrow morning," having said this, he became silent. Upon hearing this, the king said, "So be it," for the sake of increasing his prosperity.
With offerings of flowers, water for the feet, respectful oblations, honors, and the giving of sacrificial fees, he reverently worshipped the gods, celestial rishis, sages, and brahmins.
Then the entire assembly rose, including the circle of kings and sages, their faces surrounded by the halo of the mass of jewels strewn across the floor.
The armlets and bracelets jingled from the mutual friction of their limbs; the space between their broad breasts was covered by golden bands drawn down by the weight of their necklaces.
With the sounds of awakened bees resting upon the lap of their crests, they seemed to speak through their hair, which was filled with a humming drone.

The quarters of the sky were turned golden by the radiance of their golden ornaments, while the activities of their senses were completely stilled by the meaning of the Sage’s words held in their minds.
The sky-dwellers went to the firmament and the earth-dwellers to the circle of the earth; they all performed their daily routines in their respective homes.
In the meantime, the dark night appeared like a young woman secluded in her home, free from the company of people.
The lord of the day departed to illuminate other lands; for it is indeed the vow of the virtuous to act as a light-giver everywhere.
The twilight arose on all sides, bearing a multitude of stars, like the splendor of spring appearing with forests of blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees.
In the interior of the village shrines and houses atop the mango, nīpa, and kadamba trees, the birds settled like pure mental activities within the mind.

Adorned by fragments of clouds tinted with the light of the sun, as if with a slight hue of saffron, the western mountain appears like one clad in yellow garments; accompanied by the sky, it is graced by clouds and the necklace of stars.
Having taken the offerings at twilight, when [the time] had passed, the darknesses arose like vetālas in bodily form.
The cool breeze blew, causing the droplets of dew to quiver, with playful flashes of lightning as its sprouts; it was tender, promising the lilies, and refreshing.
The quarters of the sky, their stars indistinct, fell into utter darkness, like widowed women with long, hanging tresses of hair.
The moon, an ocean of milk, came to the world filling it with a flood of radiance; its form was composed of elixir as it traversed the sky.
Masses of darkness fled and vanished somewhere, like ignorance departing from the minds of kings upon hearing the words of wisdom.
The seers, the protectors of the earth, the sages, and likewise the brahmins, rested in their own abodes as if they were various objects within the mind.
There, for those [monks], the darkness departed slowly at dawn—dense as a dark body smeared with collyrium—and the vast mist gradually returned.
The radiant stars vanished from the sky, like showers of blossoms swept away by the morning breeze.
The sun, its rays now fully blossomed, appeared in the sky, like the newly arisen faculty of discernment within the minds of the great.

Adorned with fragments of clouds tinted by the sun’s radiance as if with the hue of saffron, the eastern mountain—clad in yellow garments and accompanied by clouds—united with the sky, which was graced by the necklace of stars.
The sky-dwellers and earth-dwellers returned once more to the assembly hall, having performed their morning rites in the very same manner as the previous day.
The entire assembly entered with their former arrangement; it became motionless in appearance, like a lotus pond when the wind has ceased.
Then, seizing the occasion, Rāma spoke with a sweet voice to Vasiṣṭha, the tiger among sages and the best of speakers.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, tell me clearly what the nature of the mind is, by which this entire cluster of worlds is stretched out.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, no form whatsoever is seen of this mind, except for its mere name, like the empty and inert appearance of the sky.
The mind does not exist as a real entity either externally or within the heart; know, O Rāma, that it is situated everywhere, just like space.
This form has arisen from this [mind], resembling the water of a mirage; yet through momentary conceptualization, it is like the delusion of a second moon.
Know that which appears as the manifestation of an object in the midst [of consciousness], whether it be existent or non-existent, to be nothing other than the mind.
That which is the manifestation of objects is designated as "mind"; there is never anything else whatsoever that exists by the name of mind.
Know that the mind is volition; it is not distinct from volition, just as water is not distinct from its fluidity, or as movement is not distinct from the wind.
Wherever there is conceptualization, O dear one, the mind is situated there in that same way; conceptualization and the mind are never, for anyone, distinct.
Whether the appearance of objects be real or unreal, know that it is merely the mind; that mind is indeed Brahman, the Grandfather.
The self consisting of the subtle body is called the mind; through its long duration, however, it assumes the nature of the material intellect.
Ignorance, transmigratory existence, mind, intellect, bondage, impurity, and darkness—these, the most excellent knowers understand, are the synonymous names for the visible world.
Indeed, there is no form of the mind whatsoever apart from the visible; and I shall further declare that this visible world has truly arisen and does not [ultimately] exist.
Just as a lotus vine exists within the seed of a lotus, so the visible world exists within the atom of the Great Consciousness.
Just as light belongs to illumination, just as mobility belongs to the wind, and just as fluidity belongs to water, so too is visibility perceived in the Seer.
Just as the state of being a bracelet exists in gold, just as water exists in a mirage, and just as a wall exists in a dream-city, so too does the perception of the visible exist within the seer.
In this way, even that impurity which exists as if non-different from the seer—the state of being an object of sight—I shall swiftly wipe away from the mirror of your mind.

Know that state in which the seer of this [world] becomes, by force, a non-seer due to the absence of the seen, to be the state of absolute isolation (kaivalya); for from that very state, the unreal becomes real.
When the state of reality has been attained, the latent impressions of passion, aversion, and the like subside, just as the turbulence of movement ceases when the wind is stilled.
When everything that can be illuminated—including all directions, the earth, and the forms of space—is no longer present, the nature of the light becomes pure, just as it is in itself.
When the visible world—including the three worlds, "you," and "I"—has attained non-existence, the seer of the pure self becomes that state of absolute isolation.
For indeed, when mountains and all other things are reflected therein, the nature of the mirror remains as it is—consisting solely of its own essential form.
When the agitation of the visible world—such as "I," "you," and "the universe"—has subsided, there arises that state of absolute oneness, wherein the Seer remains established without seeing.

Śrī Rāma said: If this world is real, it will never cease to be; for that which exists can never become non-existent. Yet we perceive no unreality in this visible world, which only bestows defects upon us.
Therefore, O Brahmin, how can this cholera of the visible world be pacified—it which causes the delusion of mental existence and bestows a continuous succession of suffering?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen to this mantra for the pacification of this demon of the visible world, by which, O Rāma, it will utterly perish and come to its end.
O Rāghava, that which exists can never perish; therefore, even when it has seemingly perished, it remains as a seed within the heart.
From the seed of memory, the perception of the visible world arises again in the space of consciousness and spreads its vast defect in the form of the earth, mountains, and sky.
Thus, there would be the fault of non-liberation, yet that is not possible here, because gods, sages, and seers are seen to be recipients of liberation.
If this world were beginningless, then liberation would not belong to anyone; whether the object of perception resides externally or within the heart, it serves only for destruction.
Therefore, listen to this most terrifying proposition of mine, which you will surely understand through the subsequent text.
This world, characterized as "I" and as the nature of space and the elements—is it not the case that there is actually no referent whatsoever for the name "world"?
Whatever collection of visible objects is seen here before one, all that is indeed the Supreme Brahman—undecaying, immortal, and immutable.
In the full, the full expands; in the peaceful, the peaceful is established. As space arises within space itself, so Brahman abides within Brahman.

There is no visible object possessing the nature of existence, nor is there a seer, nor an act of seeing; it is neither empty, nor inert, nor consciousness—it is simply this all-pervasive, tranquil reality.
Śrī Rāma said: A mountain is ground to powder by the son of a barren woman; a hare’s horn sings aloud; and a stone, stretching out its mass of arms, performs the Tāṇḍava dance.
"Sand flows oil, stone maidens recite, and painted clouds thunder"—such, O Lord, is this very statement.
This world consists of the mountain-like void of the sufferings of old age, death, and so forth; why do you tell me that even this does not exist?
O Brahman, tell me how this universe is neither established, nor produced, nor existent, so that this may become certain for me.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, listen; I am not one whose speech is inconsistent, for that which is being told appears as unreal as the son of a barren woman or a sound in the sky.
This was unproduced in the beginning at the start of creation; therefore, it does not exist at all. For this appears to the mind like a city in a dream or similar state.
And the mind alone, at the beginning of creation, was unarisen and of non-existent form; listen now as I explain how it is experienced in this manner.
The mind spreads this defect consisting of what is seen, which is by nature subject to decay; though unreal, it takes the form of the real, just as one dream follows another within a dream.
That [consciousness] itself spontaneously and swiftly conceives a body; by that means, this splendor of a magical illusion is spread out by its own expansion.
It throbbs, leaps, moves, begs, wanders, sinks, and withdraws by itself; it even assumes the state of another and merely flickers due to its own fickle power—such is the mind.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, tiger among sages, what indeed exists here in this delusion of the mind? How has the mind, composed of illusion, arisen, and from where does it come?
"O Lord, tell me in brief about origination at the beginning; thereafter, O best of speakers, you shall explain the remainder that is yet to be told."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the great dissolution has arrived and all things have ceased to exist, at the beginning of the entire visible creation, only the tranquil state remains.
The unborn, undecaying, and stainless Lord, the supreme Self and Great Sovereign, who is all, the doer of all, and eternal, remains ever unsetting like the sun.
That from which words turn back, which is realized by the liberated, and for whom designations such as "self" and so forth are merely conceptual constructs and not born of intrinsic nature.
That person who [perceives] the Sāṃkhya views, the Brahman of the Vedāntins, and the purely stainless consciousness-only of the knowers of consciousness—
He who is the emptiness of the proponents of emptiness, the illuminator of the suns' splendors, he is always the speaker, the thinker, the knower of truth, the enjoyer, the seer, and the agent.
Though present, it is as if non-existent in this world; though residing within the body, it is far away—this light of consciousness, for it is like the radiance of the sun.
For from him the gods, Viṣṇu and the others, emerge like rays from the sun; and from him the infinite worlds arise like bubbles from the ocean.
Into whom all visible multitudes dissolve like waters into the great ocean, and who illuminates both the self and objective phenomena like a lamp; [that is the Self].
He who is established in space and in bodies, in stones, in waters, and in creepers; in dust, in mountains, in winds, and in the netherworlds.
He who drowns the agitated group of eight cities here and there, by whom the deluded have been rendered mute, remaining as if fixed in meditation like stones.
By whom the sky was made empty, by whom the mountains were made solid, by whom the waters were made fluid—he under whose control is the sun as his lamp.
From this [source], the diverse rains of the essence-less cycle of existence flow forth, like rains from a cloud filled with inexhaustible nectar.
In that which is infinitely vast, the waves of the three worlds—consisting of manifestation and disappearance—quiver like mirages in a desert.
He whose nature is imperishable, whose essence is non-destruction, who dwells within all living beings, who is hidden yet transcendent, and who is established in all states of being.
By which wind does that creeper of primordial nature dance—born in the sky, bearing the cosmic egg as its excellent fruit, with the mind as its root and the senses as its leaves?
That jewel which shines within the casket of every body, in which moon these rays of the web of worlds quiver.
In that tranquil mass of consciousness, which rains down nectar, all beings flash forth like streams of water, and creations appear clearly like lightning bolts.
When objects marvel at one another through the light of that by which the unreal has become born as unreal, and by which the real has attained its state of being real.
The body of one who does not desire [sensual objects] trembles in the presence of another who is dull-witted and intensely attached; yet for one who abides in peace within the self, it remains still.
Destiny, place, and time, as well as movement, vibration, and action—by him who transcends all existence, these have been brought into being.

Because it consists of pure consciousness, that which is space becomes [manifest] through the thought of the void; yet, when presided over by the thought of objects, it remains as if it were the state of being an object itself.

Even while performing here the infinite multitude of great deeds for the worlds, he does nothing at all, nor does anything whatsoever; he remains alone, established in his own self, which is changeless consciousness that never sets, having abandoned both rising and abiding.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For this supreme God of gods, the Supreme Self, supreme perfection comes through knowledge alone, and not from the hardship of ritual performance.
In this context, neither knowledge nor ritual practice is of any use; rather, it has been established here that [the means] for quelling the delusion of water in a mirage is this [insight].
This is neither far away nor near, neither unattainable nor difficult to reach; having the nature of the manifestation of one's own bliss, it is obtained from one's very own body.
In this regard, asceticism, charity, vows, and the like do not provide any assistance; there is no means of accomplishment here other than resting in the ultimate nature alone.
Devotion solely to the company of the virtuous and to the true scriptures is the cause here; it is the genuine means for subduing the web of delusion.
Merely through the thorough realization that "the Noble One is indeed the God," suffering does not arise for a person, and he attains the state of liberation while living.
Śrī Rāma said: Merely by the thorough realization of this Self through the self, faults such as death and the like never again cause affliction.
Where is this great God of gods to be found from afar, and by what intense austerity or how much hardship can he be attained?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, that Divine One is known through the exertion of one’s own human effort and through blossoming discernment, not by means of austerities, ritual baths, or external rites.
O Rāma, without the abandonment of passion, hatred, delusion, anger, pride, and envy, austerity and charity are merely affliction; they are not real.

When the mind is afflicted by passion and the like, one deceives another to acquire wealth; the fruit of that [wealth] belongs to the one to whom it is given, while the act itself belongs to the one for whose sake it was acquired.
Whatever vows and other practices are performed when the mind is afflicted by passion and the like, that is called hypocrisy; its fruit is not even slight.
Therefore, by human effort, one should acquire the primary medicine: association with the true scriptures and virtuous people, which destroy the disease of worldly existence.
In this matter, apart from a single human effort, no other means whatsoever is found to lead to the attainment of the destruction of all suffering.
Hear what that human effort is like for the sake of attaining self-knowledge, by which the cholera-like plague of passion and hatred is entirely pacified.

With a mind satisfied by contentment, one should abandon even the mere scent of worldly enjoyment, acting according to one's capacity in a manner that does not contradict worldly custom or sacred scripture.
One should first, according to one's capacity, through diligent effort and with an undisturbed mind, devote oneself to the company of the virtuous and the study of authentic scriptures.
He who is content with whatever he has obtained, who disregards what is censurable, and who is devoted to the company of the virtuous and the study of authentic scriptures, is swiftly liberated.
For the Great Muni, who has fully realized the nature of reality through discernment, even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Śaṅkara become objects of his compassion.
In whatever region people who are for the most part virtuous declare someone to be a saint, he is distinguished; he is a true saint, and one should resort to him with diligent effort.

Among all branches of knowledge, the science of the inner self (adhyātmavidyā) is preeminent; they call that treatise which relies upon its discourse a "true scripture" (sacchāstra), and through its investigation, one is liberated.

Ignorances are forcibly destroyed by discriminations born from true scriptures and the company of the virtuous, just as the impurities of water are removed by contact with *kataka* nuts, and just as the minds of people are purified through spiritual practice (*yoga*).
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, tell me where this deity who was described—by the knowledge of whom one is liberated—is situated, and how may I obtain him?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This deity who has been described does not abide at a distance; he is eternally situated within the body, renowned as pure consciousness alone (cinmātra).
This [Self] is this entire universe, yet he is not the universe; he is all-pervading. Indeed, only he alone exists, for there is no perception of anything designated as "the universe."
The moon-bearer is pure consciousness alone; Garuḍeśvara is pure consciousness alone; the sun is pure consciousness alone; and the lotus-born Brahmā is pure consciousness alone.
Śrī Rāma said: If even children say that this world is merely consciousness alone, then what indeed would remain here for instruction?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That which you have understood as "the universe is pure consciousness and sentience" is not at all the knowledge that brings about the destruction of worldly existence.
O Rāma, volition is the cycle of existence; this living being is known as a beast. From this very source emerge the fears of old age and death.
For the ignorant person, though formless, is indeed a vessel for suffering; because it possesses consciousness, the mind—which is itself an object of consciousness—stands as its own misfortune.
That which is freedom from the object of thought, or rather, the state of being turned away from the objectless—that is its full state; having known that, one does not grieve.
The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut away, and one's karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen.
Furthermore, its orientation toward an object of thought cannot be restrained without the non-existence of that object; for how indeed can the visible object of thought be stilled?

Since that which is of the nature of the non-objectifiable consciousness cannot exist without the absence of objectification, how indeed could there be an orientation toward its own nature, given only the cessation of objects?
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, when which living being is realized does the cycle of worldly existence not perish? Where and of what nature is that ignorant beast who has the form of space?
O Brahmin, tell me: what is that Supreme Self like, which is perceived through the company of the virtuous and the true scriptures as the one who carries one across the ocean of worldly existence?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Those who desire this consciousness—the individual soul that has fallen apart in the wilderness of birth—are ignorant, even if they are learned men.
For the living being itself is indeed the cycle of existence—a continuity of consciousness and suffering. When this is known, nothing remains unknown anywhere.
O Rāma, if the Supreme Self is known, the continuity of suffering comes to an end, just as cholera ceases when the influence of poison has subsided.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, describe to me truly the form of the Supreme Self, by seeing which the mind will cross over all delusions.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That form which exists in the interval when consciousness, having traveled from one distant place to another, reaches its destination in a mere moment—that is the nature of the Supreme Self.
The absolute non-existence of saṃsāra as it appears exists within that great ocean of awakening which is the nature of the Supreme Self.
That in which the sequence of seer and seen, though present, has reached its setting, and which is space yet not space—that is the nature of the Supreme Self.
That which is empty yet as if non-empty, wherein the world remains empty, and that which is empty despite the flood of creation—that is the nature of the Supreme Self.
That which, though consisting of pure consciousness, remains like a massive stone—insentient within and indeed insentient in its very form—is the nature of the Supreme Self.
That by which everything, including the external and internal, having attained complete union, reaches the state of its own true nature—that is the form of the Supreme Self.
Just as light is the nature of illumination and emptiness is the nature of space, so too is this established state situated within that which is the form of the Supreme Self.
Śrī Rāma said: How indeed is it understood that the Supreme Self is of the nature of Reality (sadrūpa)? And how is it that this visible world, known as the "universe," is impossible?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: If there were a firm establishment of the realization of the absolute non-existence of this worldly delusion, which has arisen like the color of the sky;
That alone is known as the form of Brahman; it cannot be attained by any other action. Since the visible world is absolutely non-existent, there is no auspicious path other than this.
When this visible world has reached the state of absolute non-existence as it truly is, that ultimate reality remains; it is then realized, and from that, one is born [into that state].
Nowhere does a reflection exist apart from the absence of an object to be seen; indeed, a mirror never remains without a reflection.
Without the realization of the inherent existence of this visible world called "the universe," the supreme reality can never be understood by anyone at any time.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, how can there be non-existence for this entire range of visible things—the cosmic egg and the stability of the world? Where is Mount Meru within the interior of a mustard seed?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, if for a few days you remain with an undistracted mind, devoted to the company of the virtuous and the study of the true scriptures, then in an instant I shall [do so].
I cleanse your perception of the visible world as if it were a mirage; when the visible object ceases to exist, the state of being a perceiver also subsides, and pure awareness alone remains.

The state of being a seer exists when there is an object seen; the state of being an object seen exists when there is a seer. Indeed, unity exists when there is duality, and duality exists through the application of unity.
For when one is absent, the establishment of both does not indeed occur here; rather, when duality, unity, the seer, and the seen have ceased, that which is eternally present remains.
I cleanse from the mirror of the mind all the impurities—the world of perception consisting of egoism and the rest—by means of the realization of their absolute non-existence.
The non-existent has no being, and the existent has no non-being; since that which does not exist by way of intrinsic nature cannot exist, what affliction is there to be cleansed?
That which is seen spread out here, though unproduced at the beginning of the world, is merely expanded within its own stainless self by virtue of being the consciousness of Brahman.
That which is called the world has not arisen, does not exist, and is not perceived; it is like the state of being a bracelet or other ornaments in gold. Why, then, this labor of cleansing?
In this way, I shall explain this in detail through many logical arguments, so that the uncontradicted reality may be experienced by oneself.
For how could there be existence here of that which has never arisen from the very beginning? How could there be a river of water in a desert, or a grasp of a second moon?
Just as the son of a barren woman does not exist, just as there is no water in a desert, and just as a yakṣa in the sky does not exist, so too the delusion of the world does not exist.
O Rāma, that which is seen here is indeed Brahman itself, free from all affliction; this I shall explain later through reasoning, and not merely by words.

O one of noble intellect, it is improper to show contempt for that which those who know the truth proclaim here through reasonings; for they know that one who, being of deluded intellect, disregards what is consistent with reason, is a person of wretched persistence and is indeed ignorant.
Śrī Rāma said: By what reasoning is this known, and how is it established? When this is experienced through logic, nothing remains to be known.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This cholera of false knowledge, known as the world, has been rooted for a long time; it does not subside without wisdom, which is called inquiry.
"O Rāma, I shall relate these narratives for the sake of attaining awakening; if you listen to them, O virtuous one, you will indeed be liberated and wise."
If, due to your habit of agitation, you rise from the midst [of your task] and depart, then nothing at all will be accomplished today for you who possess the nature of an animal.
Whoever desires an object and strives for it in that manner will certainly attain it, provided they do not turn back out of exhaustion.
O Rāma, if you are devoted to the company of the virtuous and to the true scriptures, then in days, or even months, you shall attain the supreme state.

Śrī Rāma said: O best among those who know the scriptures, for the sake of awakening to the knowledge of the Self, what indeed would be that principal scripture by knowing which one no longer grieves?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O high-minded one, for those for whom self-knowledge is paramount, this auspicious Mahārāmāyaṇa is the supreme among all scriptures.
From this, the best of histories, our awakening proceeds; this is declared to be the essence of all histories.
Since the state of liberation while living arises spontaneously upon hearing this verbal scripture, it is therefore exceedingly purifying.
Through inquiry, the world of appearances, though seemingly stable, comes to an end; just as when a dream is fully recognized, its manifestation ceases right there within the dream itself.
Whatever exists here exists elsewhere; what does not exist here exists nowhere else. The wise know this to be the treasury of all the sciences of consciousness.
Whoever hears this constantly, the intellect of that person of noble wonder will undoubtedly attain the supreme awakening even beyond awakening itself.
For one who does not find pleasure in this due to the arising of evil deeds, let him examine whatever true scripture exists within the body of knowledge.
Upon hearing this, however, liberation while living (jīvanmuktatva) is experienced by oneself, just as freedom from disease is felt when a potent medicine has been drunk.
For when this scripture is being heard, the listener understands it within himself: "This has been correctly stated by us, like a boon or a curse."

This suffering of saṃsāra perishes for you through the mere discourse of inquiry into one's own self; it does not perish through wealth, charity, austerity, Vedic study, or even by hundreds of efforts arising from such discourse.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: With their minds fixed on that and their lives dedicated to it, awakening one another and constantly speaking of it, they find contentment and delight.
For those who are solely devoted to knowledge and who investigate self-knowledge, that state of liberation while living arises, which is indeed liberation without a body.

Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin, tell me the characteristics of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and one liberated after death (videhamukta), so that by means of them I may strive with an intellect guided by the vision of the scriptures.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: He for whom this world remains exactly as it is, even while engaged in worldly activity, and who has reached the state where the mind has set like the sky—such a person is called liberated while living (jīvanmukta).

He who has attained exclusive steadfastness in awakening, who remains as if in deep sleep even while awake, and who conducts himself in the world—such a person is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
He whose facial radiance neither rises nor sets in pleasure or pain, remaining as he has come to be, is called one liberated while living.
He who remains awake while in the state of deep sleep, for whom no waking state exists, and whose consciousness is free from latent impressions—he is called one liberated while living.
Even while acting in accordance with passion, hatred, fear, and the like, he who remains as pure as the inner sky is called liberated while living.
He whose state of being is free from egoism, and whose intellect is not defiled—whether he is acting or not acting—he is called one liberated while living.
He who, within half a blink of an eye, perceives the dissolution and creation of the three worlds as being identical to himself—that wise one is called liberated while living.
He from whom the world does not shrink, and who does not shrink from the world, being liberated from joy, envy, and fear—he is called one liberated while living.
He whose mental agitation regarding saṃsāra has been stilled, who, though possessing parts, is partless; who, though possessing a mind, is mindless—he is called liberated while living.
He who, though engaged in the practical affairs of all categories of objects, remains cool and whose self is complete even amidst material things—he is called one liberated while living.
Having abandoned the state of liberation while living when the body has come under the power of time, he enters the state of disembodied liberation, just as the wind enters a state of motionlessness.
The one liberated while in the body neither rises nor sets, nor does he cease; he is neither existent nor non-existent, neither far away, nor am I, nor is he another.
Becoming the sun, Viṣṇu blazes; as the protector, he guards the three worlds; as Rudra, he destroys all things; and as the lotus-born Brahmā, he creates the emanations.
Having become space, he supports the mass of wind along with the sages, gods, and asuras; having become the Kulācala mountains, he serves as the abode for the cities of the world-protectors.
Having become the earth, she sustains this unbroken stability of the world; having become grass, shrubs, and creepers, she yields a continuous succession of fruits.
Bearing the forms of both water and fire, the moon blazes and flows swiftly; it produces nectar, yet it also produces the deadly Hālāhala poison.
Fire manifests as brilliance; darkness becomes blindness; that which exists as empty space attains the state of the sky; and that which exists as a mountain effectively obstructs.
The mind makes itself mobile when it has a mobile form, and stationary when it has a stationary form; having become the ocean, it encircles the earth-woman like a bracelet.
Having become the body of the supreme sun, spreading light to its very limit, it remains utterly tranquil, like the mass of motes of dust in the three worlds.
Whatever appears here—whether it has appeared, is appearing, or will appear—all that visible object throughout the three periods of time is indeed this [Self] alone.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahmin, why do you speak thus? For my vision of this matter is indeed troubled; it is my firm conviction that this state is difficult to attain and hard to traverse."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, this is called liberation; this is declared to be Brahman; this is described as nirvāṇa. Listen now to how it is attained.
That which is seen here, endowed with the magnitude of the visible world and so forth, is attained by the intellect through the non-origination of even this [world] that exists.

Śrī Rāma said: "O best among those who know what is to be known, when those liberated while in the body (videhamukta) attain the three worlds, do they consider themselves as having merely entered into creation?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: If the three worlds exist, then let them go to that place where not even the slightest meaning of the word "the three worlds" can possibly occur.

Since this [world] has reached the state of being the three worlds, how can there be an understanding of the meaning of the word "Brahman"? Therefore, this conceptualization of the referent of the word "jagat" (the world) is not possible for us.
Through the awakening of true being, all this is understood as Brahman alone—the non-dual, peaceful, mere manifestation, as stainless as space—being the world.
For even after searching throughout the golden bracelet, I did not perceive anywhere that which is called "bracelet-ness," apart from the stainless gold itself.
Apart from water, I do not perceive anything at all in the waves of the ocean; for that very nature of being a wave is seen only where it does not exist [as something separate].
The state of vibration is never, at any time or place, other than the wind; the wind is always nothing but vibration, and therefore the world is not distinct from it.
Just as emptiness is in space, as heat alone is water in the desert, and as fire is always in the world, so too is Brahman the three worlds.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, instruct me in that supreme method by which liberation arises through the realization of the absolute non-existence of the world of appearances.
When the seer and the seen, which have mutually coalesced and are of a single number, reach a state where the duality no longer exists, only nirvāṇa remains.
Therefore, just as the visible world is absolutely non-existent, so too does Brahman alone exist abiding in its own nature; explain that to me.
How is this known through reasoning, and how is it established? O Sage, once this is established, nothing remains to be proven.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This cholera of false knowledge, which has been firmly rooted for a long time, is surely pacified and uprooted by the mantra of inquiry.
It is not possible to destroy this instantly in a moment, for it involves ascending and descending equally upon a mountain that falls away on all sides.
Therefore, so that the delusion of the world may be stilled through the yoga of practice, by means of reasoning and logical demonstrations, this is being told; listen.
O Rāma, I shall relate this narrative for the sake of attaining awakening; if you listen to it, O virtuous one, you will indeed be liberated and possessed of true understanding.
Now, this chapter on origination is being told by me to you; for whatever arises, O Rāma, one becomes liberated from that.
"This delusion of the world, which appears in this manner, is unborn and of the nature of space"; this is what is now being explained by me in this chapter on origination.
Whatever is seen here in the world, whether stationary or moving—everything, rich in all its various forms, including gods, asuras, and kinnaras.
When that great dissolution arrives, which brings about the transformation of Rudra and the other deities, it becomes non-existent, invisible in nature, and perishes, going somewhere unknown.
Then, neither light nor pervasive darkness remains; there exists only something that is indefinable, unmanifest, and yet real.
It is neither empty nor devoid of form; it is neither the object of sight nor the act of seeing; nor is it a flood of real entities, for it abides in infinity.
It is something whose nature is indefinable, a form more full than the full; it is neither being nor non-being, neither being-and-non-being, neither an entity nor a becoming.
It is pure consciousness alone, devoid of objects of thought, infinite, undecaying, and auspicious; it is without beginning, middle, or end—beginningless and free from all affliction.
In whom the world vibrates like a visible pearl upon a swan, he who is both this and not this—the God whose nature is both being and non-being.
Without ears, tongue, nose, skin, or eyes, he who hears, tastes, smells, touches, and sees is everywhere and at all times.
That very light by which the form of existence and non-existence is perceived, as well as the beginningless and endless variegated creation and one's own nature, is free from attachment.
He who perceives the world as a mere star within the space between his eyebrows—half-opened to view—and sees his own true nature as the ever-shining essence of the void; [he is liberated].
For that Lord, there exists no other cause, like the horn of a hare; and this world is His effect, like a mass of waves arising from water.
By the light of that lamp of pure consciousness—which blazes incessantly on all sides and abides in the seats of the mind—the three worlds shine forth.
Without whom even these luminaries such as the sun would be like darkness; in whose presence the three worlds proceed like a mirage.

In that which vibrates, the glory of the world arises as if it were emerging, yet when it has entered a state of motionlessness, it does not; therein, this splendor of the universe appears like the circularity of a whirling firebrand.
The Great Pervasive One, whose nature is the play of the creation and dissolution of the universe, possesses a pure and imperishable essence consisting of both movement and stillness.

The existence of that [reality], which consists of both vibration and non-vibration, is all-pervading like the wind; it appears as if divided merely by name for the sake of conventional usage, but not in reality.
He who is always awakened, he who is always asleep, and he who is neither asleep nor awakened, being everywhere and at all times.

That which is motionless is Śiva, the peaceful; that which is its vibration is the existence of the three worlds. He alone is the one whose form is full, whose nature consists of the play of both vibration and non-vibration.
Like fragrance in flowers that are destined to perish, it does not vanish; though present before the eyes, it is ungraspable, just like the whiteness in a white cloth.
He who, though like one mute, is not mute; he who, though like a stone, is a thinker; he who is an enjoyer, though eternally satisfied; and he who is an agent, though possessing nothing.
He who, though bodiless, possesses all limbs, and has a thousand hands and eyes; by whom, though abiding nowhere at all, this entire world is pervaded.
Even though he is devoid of the power of the senses, all sensory activities belong to him; even though he is without thought, these modes of mental creation are his.
Because it is not seen, there arise the fears of the serpent of saṃsāra and delusion; when it is seen, all hopes and all fears flee away.

In that which is the witness, the expansive and constant manifestation—like a lamp—it is within that which exists that all activities proceed, including the impulses of the mind preceded by vibration.
For from it arise hundreds of rows of objects in the form of jars, cloths, and so forth, just as the masses of waves, surges, and ripples arise from the ocean.
That very same [reality] arises as something else through the delusions of hundreds of objects, just as gold appears as bracelets, armlets, neck-ornaments, and anklets.
That which is the one self-luminous nature—whether it be you, or me, or these people; and that which is not you, being of an unawakened nature, nor me, nor these people; [that is the Self].
The world of appearances flashes forth from that which is neither distinct nor separate, yet appears as if it were; it is fragile and insubstantial, like a series of waves upon the water.
From whom comes the reckoning of time, from whom comes the visibility of the visible, by whom mental construction is made, and by whose light everything is illumined.
Action, form, taste, smell, sound, touch, and consciousness—whatever you perceive, that is this God; and that by which you perceive, that too is He.
Among the seer, the act of seeing, and the seen, that which remains as pure seeing—by focusing upon that, you shall realize your own self, which is the goal to be accomplished.

The unborn, undecaying, beginningless, eternal, constant Brahman—auspicious, stainless, unfailing, highly venerable, and irreproachable; devoid of all mental constructions, the cause of causes, experience itself, unknowable yet the knower, the universe within.
Śrī Rāma said: When the great dissolution occurs, that which remains here becomes formless; of this there is no doubt.
How could it not be empty? How could it not be luminous? Or how could it not be of the nature of darkness? Or how could it not be radiant?

Or how could it not be of the nature of consciousness? Or how could it not be the individual soul (jīva)? How could it not be the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva), or how could it not be the mind (manas)?
Or how could there be nothing at all, or how could there be everything? By this very turn of phrase, a kind of delusion has arisen within me.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This question you have posed is difficult; yet I shall resolve it for you without effort, just as the sun dispels the darkness of night.
O Rāma, listen as this is explained: that which remains at the conclusion of the great kalpa is not empty in the manner [of a void].
Just as a carved figure on a pillar remains uncarved [in its essence], so does the universe abide therein; therefore, that state is not empty.
This world, known as the universe, appears with such great abundance; whether it be real or unreal, wherever it exists, there is non-emptiness.
Just as a pillar that has not been carved with figures is not empty of those figures, so too the world appears as Brahman; therefore, that state is not empty.
Just as a wave in gentle water neither exists nor does not exist, so this world within Brahman has reached the state of being both empty and non-empty.
Because place, time, and so forth are quiescent, the fashioning of a wooden image occurs in a tree; since this is not [ultimately] possible, one is thereby deluded regarding the Infinite.
Therefore, this comparison of the world's existence to the figures on a pillar and so forth is similar only in a partial sense regarding ultimate reality, not in every respect.
This never arises from another, nor does it ever cease; thus established as the sole, eternal Brahman, it abides within its own self.
The conceptualization of the meaning of the word "empty" depends upon the non-empty; since it arises from non-emptiness, how could there be emptiness or non-emptiness?
Indeed, this light arising from the elements is not possible in Brahman; how then could it exist there in that imperishable one, where [the sun, fire, moon, stars, and so forth] are absent?
The absence of the manifestations of the great elements is called darkness; however, since that [darkness] arises from the absence of the great elements, there is no darkness whatsoever here.
Self-experience alone is the illumination of this [reality], which is of the nature of space; that which exists within is experienced by that very [self-experience] and not by anything else.
This undecaying state, which is free from both darkness and light—know it to be like the sheath of space, the very sheath within which the world exists.
Just as there is no difference whatsoever between the bilva fruit and the interior of the bilva fruit, so too there is not even the slightest degree of distinction between Brahman and the world.
Just as a wave exists within water, or as a jar exists within clay, so too where the existence of the world resides—how could that be of the nature of empty space?
The splendor of the earth, water, and so forth, ending with form, is equal-minded; but Brahman is as pure as space, and that [world] likewise resides within it.

Therefore, just as the space of consciousness is even purer than physical space, so too the world, which constitutes the referent of the word "world," exists within it as something of that very same nature.

Just as the pungency within a pepper is not perceived by one who does not eat it, so too is the state of pure consciousness in the space of consciousness not perceived without the element of the object of thought.

Therefore, even consciousness, though appearing as non-consciousness, is devoid of any object within itself; this world-nature is likewise exactly so, by virtue of its being essentially nothing but that.
Form, light, and mental attention are nothing other than that very [consciousness]; therefore, the universe as it exists is either deep sleep or the fourth state.

Therefore, the yogi, though engaged in worldly activity, remains with a tranquil mind as one whose nature is deep sleep; he abides in the non-manifest Brahman, which is the casket containing all manifestations.
Just as great waves abide within calm, formless water, so does the universe abide within the Supreme, which is likewise formless and of that same nature.
From the Full, the Full flows forth; that Fullness is formless. The universe has appeared from Brahman, for it is indeed perceived as its own purpose.
From the Full, the Full flows forth; that which is established remains the Full itself. Therefore, the universe is unarisen; and whatever has arisen, that is indeed the Full.
Since that which is perceived cannot exist within it, how can there be a single purpose for the world? Since a taster cannot exist, O mirage, what indeed is its pungency?
For others, this state of being the mind and its objects is both real and unreal; since that [duality] does not exist, how can there be the status of being a reflection for a reflection?
It is subtler than even the atom, for it is more minute than the minute; it is pure, subtle, supreme, and more tranquil than even the interior of space.
Because its nature is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, it is exceedingly vast; it is without beginning or end, a manifestation devoid of anything to be manifested.

Since neither the nature of consciousness nor the state of being a living soul is found therein, how could there be any latent impression (vāsanā) in the form of a mind that possesses a permanent nature?

Precisely because the nature of consciousness does not arise therein, there is no state of being a living soul (jīvatā), nor intellectuality, nor mentation, nor the state of being a sense organ, nor even latent impressions (vāsanā).
Thus, this state—though filled with great undertakings—is ageless; according to our vision, it is peaceful, empty, and more vast than space itself.
Śrī Rāma said: What is the nature of that supreme reality, which has the form of infinite consciousness? Tell me this again in detail for the increase of my understanding.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the great dissolution has occurred, that which remains is the supreme Brahman, the cause of all causes; this very thing is now described, so listen.
Having destroyed its own self through the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind, that which is of the nature of existence and inexpressible is the true form of that reality.
There is no visible world, and the seer, due to the absence of the visible, is as if dissolved; that which appears as "it shines" is the true nature of that reality.
That form of the individual soul which is turned away from the object of thought—pure consciousness, stainless and peaceful—is the very nature of the Supreme Self.
Even when wind and other elements touch the limbs, that form of the mind which exists in a living being without the experience of touch and so forth is indeed the Supreme Self.
O sinless one, that which remains is the very nature of that long sleep—the state of the mind which is dreamless, infinite, and non-inert.
That which is the heart of the sky, or that of stone and of wind—that is the form of the Supreme Self, the consciousness-ether which is beyond the reach of thought.
The state that exists by its own nature for one who is without ego-conception and without mental activity while living—this is the supreme, peaceful existence of that primordial reality.
That which is the center of the light of consciousness, or of light itself, or of space, and that which is the center of vision—that they know to be the form of Brahman.
That which is the beginningless and endless perception of feeling, light, the visible, and likewise darkness—that is the nature of the Supreme Self.
That nature which, though eternally unarisen, appears as if the world arises from it; and which, though non-different, appears as if divided—that is the ultimate reality.
That state of remaining like a stone even while engaged in worldly affairs, which is the very quality of space within that which is not space—that is the nature of the Supreme Self.
That state wherein these three forms—the object of knowledge, the act of knowing, and the knower—which arise and set before one's eyes, no longer appear; that indeed is most difficult to attain.

That in which this state of the object of knowledge, the act of knowing, and the knower is reflected within the great mirror of the non-intellect (abuddhi) and so forth—that is remembered as the supreme form.
That form of the Great Consciousness which remains when freed from the mind, dreams, and the senses—whether in the moving or the stationary—is all that remains at the end of everything.
If the nature of immobile beings were to consist of consciousness, being free from mind, intellect, and the like, it would be comparable to the Supreme.

Brahmā, Arka, Viṣṇu, Hara, Śakra, Sadāśiva, and the rest—this one supreme Śiva alone abides here in peace; through the cessation of all limiting adjuncts, it consists solely of consciousness, free from conceptualization and abandoned by all worldly attachment.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, when the great dissolution has arrived, where indeed does this radiant form, this visible world, cease to exist?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: From where does the son of a barren woman come, or what is he like? Where does he go? Tell me, where does the forest of the sky go, and from where does it come?
Śrī Rāma said: The son of a barren woman and a forest in the sky neither exist nor will they ever exist; what kind of visibility could he have, and what kind of non-existence?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as the son of a barren woman and the forest in the sky never exist at any time, so too this entire visible world, beginning with the universe, never exists at any time.
That which does not exist at the beginning neither arises nor perishes; what kind of arising could it have, and what talk can there be of the word "destruction"?

Śrī Rāma said: Indeed, the conceptualization of the son of a barren woman or a tree in the sky exists; just as that [conceptualization] is characterized by birth and destruction, why should this [world] not be the same?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The weighing of that which is equal yet incomparably situated by means of mental constructs is indeed like a disconnected utterance; such indeed is the existence of the world.
Just as this bracelet-ness clearly seen in a golden bracelet does not exist at all [as a separate reality], so too world-ness does not exist in the Supreme.
Just as emptiness does not exist in space as something distinct from it, so too the state of being the world does not exist at all within Brahman, even though it is perceived there.
Just as blackness is not separate from collyrium, nor coldness from snow, so too the world is not perceived as distinct from the Supreme State.
Just as coolness is not distinct from the moon or from snow, so too creation does not exist as something separate from Brahman.

Just as water does not exist in a mirage-river, and just as the nature of the moon does not exist in a second moon, so too this thing called "the world" does not exist at all here within the stainless Self, even though it is perceived.
For that which does not exist at the very outset because it lacks a cause of its own, does not exist even in the present; what kind of destruction could there be for such a thing?

How could insentience, which is impossible for that which has arisen from the elements, belong to an insentient entity such as earth? How could it possess cause and effect, just as shadow cannot possess sunlight?
Due to the absence of a cause, this effect has not arisen as anything at all; that which exists is the cause itself, and it remains established in this very manner.
That which appears as ignorance is nothing but the manifestation of consciousness; that which is seen as the world in a dream is nothing but the radiance of consciousness.
