Just as the delusion of the world in a dream is merely the manifestation of consciousness within, so too at the beginning of creation, the expansion of the world is the manifestation of consciousness within Brahman.
Whatever is seen here always abides within the Self; this world never sets nor does it ever rise at any time.
Just as liquidity is water, as movement is wind, and as radiance is light, so too is the triple world nothing but Brahman.
Just as one who possesses inner knowledge perceives a city within a dream-consciousness, so too does one's own self alone appear as the world within the Supreme Self.

Śrī Rāma said: If this is so, O Brahman, then tell me how this world of visible objects—which has become like a poison—can produce such a firm conviction, being as unreal as the experience of a dream.

When there is an object of sight, there is indeed a seer; when there is a seer, there is the state of being an object of sight. When both exist within a single being, there is bondage; when one of the two ceases, there is liberation for both.

As long as there is no absolute non-existence—that is, as long as the visible object has not ceased—so long is the state of being an object of vision present in the seer, and the wisdom of liberation does not arise.
If the visible world were to first come into existence and subsequently undergo destruction, then bondage—in the form of the uselessness of remembering that which was seen—would never cease.
Wherever consciousness may be situated, just as in the case of one's own mirror, a reflection consisting of all memories indeed adheres to it completely.
If the visible world has never arisen from the very beginning and does not exist by itself, then liberation occurs because the seer is of the same nature as the visible.
Therefore, O best among the knowers of the Self, dispel by means of reasoning my notion that liberation is impossible, until its absolute impossibility is established through discourse.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O Rāma, listen as I relate to you through this long discourse how the entire world, though non-existent, always appears as if it were real and as the self of all."
As long as that place is being described there with words of resolute discourse, your heart finds no rest, just as silt does not settle in a lake.
Having realized the absolute non-existence of this delusion of world-creation, you, whose self is established in the singular meditation of the Awakened One, shall carry out your worldly activities.

Views characterized by grasping and abandoning existence and non-existence, and by the gross, the subtle, the moving, and the unmoving, will not pierce you, just as arrows cannot pierce a great mountain.
This very Self is one alone; there is no second conceptualization. O Rāghava, I shall explain to you how the world has arisen within this.

Therefore, my dear friend, all these manifestations are his; that Great-Souled One, who is both with and without parts, himself arises and dissolves as the locus for the modes of perceiving forms and the mental reflections upon them.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen with a most excellent intellect to how this universe has arisen from this supreme, tranquil, and supremely purifying state.
Deep sleep appears like a dream, and Brahman alone appears as if it were creation; that state is the self of all—now hear the sequence regarding it.
Of that infinite jewel of consciousness, whose nature is infinite light, the universe—which by its very essence consists of mere existence—arises perpetually from its own inherent nature.
Then, within itself, consciousness—though its nature is ungraspable—comes as it were to attain a slight state of being an object of cognition, preceded by the reflective awareness of "I."
With the mental constructions of future objects, its form is slightly inferred; yet this pure awareness, subtler than space, shines within everything.
Then that supreme being, becoming conscious and oriented toward sentience, becomes fit for the name "consciousness" (citi) by virtue of being somewhat attainable in that manner.
Subsequently, there arises a dense self-awareness called the "living being" (jīva) and so forth, which possesses the grasping of objects; this occurs when one has abandoned the supreme state.
At that time, existence itself, whose essence consists solely in mental cultivation and which is oriented toward transmigration, does not arise from the perspective of the true nature of things.
Immediately upon this, its own existence arises as emptiness; it is the seed of the qualities such as sound, and it bestows the referents of future designations.
Immediately thereafter, along with the very existence of time, there arises from the seed—the primary cause for the persistence of the world—that which is designated as "the future."
Of that supreme power, this net—which is merely its own self-awareness—arises as something unreal, yet it flashes forth as if it were real.
Consciousness of this nature is the seed of the tree of volition; from it arises the atom of egoism, which, through its vibrancy, becomes the vital wind.
I, as consciousness, through the contemplation of the subtle element of sound within the ether, gradually condense by myself and become fully established as my own subtle element.
That seed of the tree of the flood of words, which has the nature of future objects, has blossomed forth as the collection of Vedas known as words, sentences, and means of valid cognition.
Therefore, the entire glory of the world will arise from the Supreme Self, which spreads forth through the transformation of the multitude of objects fashioned from the flood of sound.

That very consciousness, accompanied by such a retinue, is designated by the word "jīva"; it is the seed of the tree whose form is a flood of manifested objects and their corresponding verbal designations.
Then, indeed, the flood of the pit-like belly of the world will expand, its interior encircled by a fourteenfold web of living beings.

Not yet having attained the designation or activity [of touch], its body throbbing due to the speed of consciousness, that very [subtle element] becomes the subtle element of touch (sparśa-tanmātra) in an instant through meditative cultivation.
The seed of the tree of the flood of contact has the expanse of the mass of wind as its root; from it, the vibration of the activity of all beings will spread forth.
In that very state, through the play of consciousness, light arises from experience; that is the subtle element of fire (tejas-tanmātra), which serves as the designation for what is yet to come.
That seed of the tree of light, consisting of the unfolding of the sun, fire, and so forth, from it the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) will expand through the differentiation of forms.
As it is being cultivated until it reaches extreme subtlety, like the watery portion of a mass of water, that savoring of the assembly is called the subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra).
The essence of the future play of the world is the seed of that tree of aesthetic flavor; from their mutual enjoyment, saṃsāra will spread forth.
This [ego], consisting of conceptualization, which names the future form, perceives the state of the subtle element of smell through the qualities whose nature is conceptualization.
From that [Self], which is the support of all and whose form is the seed of the future terrestrial globe and the tree of the world, the cycle of existence will expand forth.
The subtle elements (tanmātras), being clearly perceived as they mutually transform by themselves, are like waters that flow continuously and without interval.
Likewise, these [elements], whether mixed or separate, are not found in their pure state; for indeed, they exist only until the destruction of all things.
Existing within the belly of space as forms consisting of pure consciousness, they become like the networks of banyan trees from within the interior of a tiny seed.
They perceive a hundredfold branching of emanations and they quiver; they shine within a single atom and in an instant become eons.
They rush toward manifestation, yet they remain without manifestation; pierced by consciousness, all things become condensed in an instant.

This group of subtle elements (tanmātras) would be that consciousness whose nature is volition (saṃkalpa); it perceives, though formless, as having the appearance of the minute particles of sensation (vedanā).

Indeed, the seed within the worlds is merely the pentad; the primordial power is the seed whose state remains unseparated from Parā. That very seed becomes [the world], as is eternally experienced as pure consciousness (cinmātra); thus, the glory of the world is unborn and beginningless.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, within the vast and equanimous Supreme Brahman, which is the conscious Self, there exists neither the state of the unarisen ether, nor light, nor darkness.

First, the conceptualization of "objectivity" arises from the consciousness of the objective aspect within that which exists; subsequently, the conceptualization of "mind" arises from the consciousness of the nature of the power of consciousness.

From that arises the manifestation of the individual soul (jīva) through the consciousness resulting from the conjunction with the object of thought; thereafter follows its manifestation as Māyā, by virtue of being solely intent upon the object of thought.

Then, from the transformation of the intellect (buddhi) through its stages of skin-sensation and egoity (ahaṃkāra), this very [intellect] possesses the states of mind (manas) and so forth, as well as the subtle elements (tanmātra) of sound and the rest.

From the swelling of that which consists of the other subtle elements (*tanmātra*), which possess the nature of the gross elements (*bhūta-rūpin*), this great thicket of the world and its beginning is perceived in such a manner.
In this manner, either instantaneously or through a gradual process, like a city constructed in a dream, it repeatedly arises and perishes within the great forest of the vast space.
This seed, born from the planting of the groves of the world’s karañja trees, requires nothing at all—neither earth, water, fire, nor anything else.

This [consciousness], consisting of pure intellect, will subsequently create the earth and other elements, which are essentially composed of consciousness alone, just as a dreamer creates a city within his own dream.
Wherever it may be situated, it releases the sprout of the world; the fivefold seed of the world is the imperishable consciousness (cit) of that fivefold [seed].
Know that whatever is the seed, that is the fruit; therefore, the world is composed of Brahman. Thus, at the beginning of creation, this group of five [elements] exists within the great space.

The self, which has become its own limb, is imagined by the power of consciousness (cicchakti) and is not real; it is by means of this that [consciousness], having attained a state of swelling, expands this [universe].
Even that [space], being conceived as having the nature of space, is essentially composed of existence; for nothing at all is ever established by means of that which is itself unestablished.
How could that whose nature consists of conceptual construction attain reality? Or, if the group of five is Brahman through the cognition that it has Brahman as its essence—
Know that quintet to be the mature Brahman itself, which is the sequence of the three worlds; just as it manifests at the beginning of creation, this arises from that quintet.
In the very same way, here in this present state of being, it itself becomes the cause; thus, nothing at all is born, and the world that has arisen is not perceived.
Just like a city in a dream or a mental construction, the unreal is experienced as real; within the supreme space of Brahman, the state of the individual soul's space is perceived in the Self.
Thus, because earth and the other elements do not exist, the self is pure like the funeral pyre; thus this living being is described as arisen in space like its own self.
Now hear how the living space (jīvākāśa) comes to occupy this body: that very living space exists within that Supreme Lord.
When it perceives through thought, "I am a minute particle of light," that very thing imagines itself to be swelling within the void of space.

Just as the moon, when conceptualized as being real though it is unreal, does not truly exist, so too, by contemplating that very [moon], one remains established in the form of both the seer and the seen.
Though it is one alone, it becomes twofold, as in the perception of one's own death within a dream; then, as if assuming a slight degree of grossness, it perceives itself as the "star" (tāraka).

Because he has cultivated the state of being the manifestor of all objects exactly as they are cultivated, through his universal form, he himself is that very Self; thus, even though it is eternal, he realizes by himself, "I am He."
From the mind it assumes a condition like that of a traveler in a dream; likewise, it takes on a form shaped like a star, designated as the "future body."
By meditating thus, the mind, having abandoned its state of being an object as it were, as well as that which is external to it, [remains] thereafter within the hollow of the *tāraka*.
Just as a mountain, though situated outside, appears within a mirror; just as the body is contained within a well; and just as speech is held within a casket.

The individual soul (jīvaka) perceives this consciousness within the subtle body during dreams and mental constructs; residing within the Tāraka [the Savior] which is its own true nature, this soul cognizes by itself.

This very thing, which takes the form of the existence of knowledge such as the intellect and the mind, is the space of the living soul (jīvākāśa) by its own nature, situated there within the treasury of the space of the stars.
With the thought "I shall see," it seems to expand into the sky in order to perceive; then, through those very two apertures, it again perceives that which is called the external.
That by which one sees shall be known by the name "the pair of eyes"; that by which one touches is indeed the "skin," and that which hears is "hearing."
That by which one smells is the sense of smell; he perceives it within himself. That is his own tasting, and subsequently the tongue will manifest.
That which vibrates is the wind; one should also contemplate that the host of action-faculties is the activity [of the wind], born from form, light, and mental attention.
The self of the subtle body remains in the sky within the sky; thus, one should contemplate the swelling of that spark of fire.
Though non-existent, it appears as if real, like the word "living being" applied to Brahman; thus the meaning of the term "living being" has fallen into the turmoil of conceptual construction.

The self whose nature is the subtle transportive body (ātivāhika-deha), having the form of the sky of the mental body, perceives the entire sphere of forms situated within the limits of its own imagination.
One perceives it as existing within water, another as having the nature of a universal emperor, and yet another beholds and even experiences the manifestation of future cosmic eggs.
The womb-chamber of the self is the mind; according to its own volition, it experiences the conceptualization of place, time, action, and substance.
Constructing words while meditating, the creator binds [beings] with conceptualized sounds; this is the delusion of an unreal world, wherein the body is merely a subtle vehicle (ātivāhika-deha).
Just as the flight of a bird appears in a dream though it is unreal, so too this self-arisen one has arisen by himself, though he is fundamentally unproduced.
The primordial Lord Prajāpati, whose self is the subtle spiritual body (ātivāhikadeha), remains even when this delusion, which takes the form of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), has come into being.
Nothing at all has been accomplished, nothing has been born, and nothing is seen; that Brahman is the infinite space, remaining as space alone.
This world has the form of a city of imagination; though it exists, it is not real at all. It is uncreated and free from passion—this indeed is the wondrous manifestation that has arisen.

That which is uncreated yet experienced is not [conventionally] real, though it stands as if real; for, within a great aeon (*mahākalpa*), it is undoubtedly liberated even for those beginning with Brahmā.
There is no prior memory, nor is there any cause for the Self-born; therefore, as the Self-born is, so is this world born from Him known to be.
However, the beginningless experience that exists here in the city and so forth is like the earth and other elements experienced in a dream, which appear in such a manner upon waking.
He is remembered as being of the nature of pure space alone, and the world is always remembered as being within him; wherever and in whatever way liquidity is differentiated within water.
In each and every case, there is no other creation within the Supreme Self; this creation is thus matured, yet He remains exactly as He is.
Thus indeed does this universe shine, as pure as the very nature of space; this visible world is thus peaceful, a delusion created by one's own self.
Without support and without that which is supported, non-dual and devoid of unity, nothing at all has arisen within consciousness, even when the world appears to have arisen.
The supreme space is established as immediately empty and utterly transparent; that which is so established is devoid of all the nature of saṃsāra.
Therein there is nothing superimposed, no substratum, no object of vision, and no state of being a seer; neither the cosmic egg exists, nor Brahmā, nor do any cavillers exist anywhere.
Neither the world nor the earth exists; everything remains only as peace. It is Brahman alone, pure and transparent, that shines thus by itself, through itself, within itself.

Due to its nature as consciousness, like water due to its fluidity, this world—which is in fact non-existent—revolves within itself in the form of a whirlpool; though non-existent, it appears here as if it were real.

In the end, that which is unreal perishes, just like one's own death in a dream; or rather, because it is its own true nature, this [reality] is indeed existent, free from affliction, undivided, without beginning or end, and the interior of the sky of pure consciousness alone.

In the supreme space itself, the first Lord of Creatures shines eternally by himself, equal to emptiness; for he possesses a subtle, transportable body and not a form composed of the elements such as earth, and therefore that which has not been born does not exist as a reality.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, this entire collection of perceivable phenomena—the world, the ego, and so forth—is nothing at all. Because it is unproduced, it does not exist; and that which does exist is only the Supreme.
In the beginning, the supreme space itself perceives its own living state, like water beginning to stir within the hollow of a motionless ocean.

Without ever abandoning its nature as space, consciousness thus experiences, as it were, a state of inwardness, like an internal mental modification within a dream, a mental construction, or a mountain.
The great body consisting of Virāj, which is devoid of earth and the other elements, is indeed the subtle body (ātivāhika), composed of pure consciousness and like the clear sky.
It is inexhaustible, resembling a mountain in a dream, and like a city seen in a steady dream; it has the appearance of an army depicted in a painting by an artist whose mind is fixed.
It is like a multitude of statues on great pillars that have not been fixed in the ground; the self, unattached within the space of Brahman, is like a carved figure on a firm pillar.
The first Lord of Creatures, renowned as the Self-Existent (Svayambhū), was without cause because of the absence of his own prior effects.
At the conclusion of the great dissolution, all the Grandfathers (Pitāmahas) of the initial time are liberated; therefore, what prior karma could there be for them?
Though not a wall, he is the very essence of the wall; visible yet invisible, he abides in himself. He is neither the object seen nor the seer, neither the creator, nor indeed anything at all.
This alone is the source of all words, meanings, and echoes; from it arises the multitude of living beings, just as a row of lamps arises from a single lamp.

Indeed, by its own volition, it moves from one volition to another, devoid of earth and the other elements; it is as empty at the beginning as it is at the end, just like passing from one dream to another.
Those living beings who emanate from this single vibration are, due to the absence of auxiliary causes, that very same [vibration].
In the absence of auxiliary causes, the effect and the cause are one and the same; therefore, this delusion of creation is nothing other than the Supreme.

The speaker of Brahman is the Virāṭ-self; the state of emanation is like the Virāṭ-self itself. He alone exists as the space of the individual soul (jīvākāśa), since from him the unreal earth and other elements arise.
Śrī Rāma said: Is the individual soul (jīva) finite, or is it an infinite mass? Or rather, is there an infinite self that constitutes a solid mass of souls as vast as a mountain?
Why do the living beings emerge like streams from a rain-cloud, like spray from the ocean, or like sparks from heated iron?
"Thus, O Blessed One, tell me the definitive determination regarding the web of living beings; this has been mostly understood by me, so please reveal that very thing."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: There is not even a single individual soul; how then can there be the arising of multitudes? Indeed, your words are like saying that the horn of a hare has flown away.
There is no individual soul, nor are there multitudes of souls, O Rāghava; nor does there exist any single mass of soul resembling a mountain.

Let your conviction be unwavering that here there exist no mental constructions whatsoever—not even those consisting of the conceptualization of the meaning of the word "jīva," nor any other mental constructions at all.
Indeed, there exists here the pure, stainless, and all-pervading Brahman, which, by virtue of its omnipotence, assumes whatever powers it chooses of its own accord.
Indeed, by means of the very sequence of pure consciousness, one quickly beholds that [reality] as if it were a blossoming creeper—whether manifest in form or formless.
The individual soul, the intellect, the vibration of action, the mind, duality, and even unity—all these employ that self-expressing existence for the purpose of cognition.
Thus, while remaining unawakened, one becomes Brahman itself through awakening; ignorance perishes upon investigation, yet it does not truly awaken.
Just as darkness perishes when observed by means of a lamp, yet its true nature is not known, so indeed it is with non-awakening.
Thus, Brahman alone is the individual soul (jīvātman), undivided and continuous, possessing all powers, without beginning or end, and having the nature of the essence of great consciousness.

Because it is entirely devoid of atomicity, no conceptualization of difference exists anywhere in it; for whatever conceptualization there may be, that is itself [the reality] through direct experience.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahman, how is it that all the living beings of the world do not act in accordance with the will of a single soul, given their subjection to the unity of the Great Soul?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That Great Soul, that Brahman, whose nature consists of all powers, exists here as it wills, undivided and continuous.
Whatever that Great Soul desires, that very thing comes to him quickly; first, he desires what was previously wished for, and from that, duality arises.
Subsequently, for those powers that have been divided into duality, a sequence of action is postulated by him [the Lord] in this manner: "By this, it becomes thus."
In the absence of that [prior cause], when these [powers] do not arise, it is the will of the Pradhāna alone that grows; for this restriction has been ordained by the unborn power of Brahman.
That [power] called the individual soul (jīva), which bears fruit in dependence upon another power, does not do so without the performance of the regulation of the primary power (pradhāna-śakti).
If the regulation of the power of the Pradhāna were not well-established, then the fruit of human endeavors would never come to pass anywhere, since they are dependent upon that power.
Thus, the Great Brahman exists as the Great Life-force (Mahājīva), devoid of end, beginning, or middle; it becomes the millions and billions of individual lives, yet is ultimately nothing at all.

Due to the perception of the object of thought, the living being comes into existence and enters the cycle of transmigration; through the non-perception of that, it returns again to its original state of equilibrium.

In this way, through the sequential and non-sequential processes of the younger and older vitalities (jīvas), the state of being the Self-vitality arises, just as the nature of gold emerges from copper.
In this interval, within the great void, even this non-existent multitude arises as if real, being nothing other than one's own self, consisting of the wondrous play of consciousness.
That which arises as a spontaneous wonder within consciousness—the future notion of "I" regarding the body, name, and so forth—is known by the wise as *ahaṃbhāvanā* (the sense of egoity).
Since consciousness is the substrate of consciousness and is infinite due to being identical with it, this entire expanse of worlds is reflected within that [consciousness].
That very same immutable consciousness, though inseparable from such forms, is awakened by its own power alone through words such as "transformation" and "modification."
That which is the self-experience of consciousness—whose nature is uninterrupted play—and the manifestation of the object of cognition, exists as the world itself.
This pervasive power of consciousness, subtler even than space, perceives this sense of "I" by its very nature.
When that which vibrates within her own self by herself alone, like water, perceives the subtle atom of egoity at the end of the world, then she beholds it clearly.
Because consciousness itself produces wonder within its own self through that which is beautiful and wondrous, it has therefore been given the name "the world."

O Raghava, the ego which perceives the object of thought is itself that mental construction; since even the subtle elements and so forth are consciousness alone, where then can duality or unity reside?
Upon abandoning the notions of "living being," "cause," and so forth, abandon also the ideas of "you" and "I. What remains between existence and non-existence shall become the true nature of reality.
Just as that self-existence was first conceived by the intellect, so it has arisen; it is seen as non-different from space. We do not know existence or non-existence.

The universe, the void, and that which is called the activity of the world—all this is the void, the abode of the wise; for it exists as a formal manifestation due to its nature as the wonder of consciousness, and indeed nothing else exists.
Whatever is a manifestation of something is never different from it; therefore, even that which has parts [is not different], so what need is there to mention that which is partless?
Whatever is the form of the world belongs to that whose nature is vibration, which is eternal, inconceivable, nameless, and of infinite form.
The mind, the intellect, the ego, the elements, the mountains, and the directions—whatever such arrangements exist for the persistence of the world, they arise from the reality of consciousness.

Know that the world is the consciousness of Cit; for there is no such thing as a world that is not consciousness. Since it is not a non-world, it would be non-consciousness if it were not consciousness; how then could there be a distinction of "world" through mere appearance?
The innate wonder that lies at the end of the seed-syllable *cit-marīci* is this very thing: it abides as the world consisting of nothing but the subtle element of the living soul (*jīva-tanmātra*).

The manifestation of its own power from consciousness, which is the consciousness’s sense of "I-ness," is indeed the individual soul (jīva); it has the nature of the activity of vibration and is designated as "that which is yet to be."

That which manifests as consciousness by its very nature, consisting of its own self-established designation, is differentiated from its own modifications; yet it is neither divided [in essence] nor non-existent.

There is no difference between the agent and the action, for both are of the nature of the vibration of consciousness; the action is merely vibration, and that alone is traditionally known as the person (puruṣa).

The life-force (*jīva*) is the vibration of the mind (*citta*), and for men, the mind is that very same thing; the intellect (*manas*), however, being the nature of the senses, attains as it were a manifold existence within the reality of pure being (*sattā*).
For the world is a flash of the light of consciousness in which all particularity has been stilled; therefore, nothing other than that exists, such as the states of cause, effect, and so forth.
"I am indestructible, I am unburnable, I am indeed unmoistenable and un-dryable; I am eternal, all-pervading, stable, and immovable"—thus it is established.
For in this matter they dispute, disputing as those who are deluded; yet we, while causing them to wander in delusion, have ourselves become free from delusion.

When the visible, embodied form is firmly established in the Knower, modifications and the like appear as distinct; but they do not exist when that form is absent from the Knower’s consciousness, within the sky of Consciousness whose nature is both being and non-being.

From the essence of the sap of consciousness within the tree of the mind, the beauty of the honey of consciousness expands its own cluster of blossoms—pure as the sky—which bears the name of power, time, and so forth.
The unstruck staff of consciousness vibrates with its own manifold splendor; the wind of consciousness, whose nature is born from the egg, possesses its own characteristic movement.

The water of consciousness itself manifests as a diverse shimmer, not residing in anything excavated; it itself constitutes the state of diverse elements, even manifesting as the most excellent limbs.
The moonlight of consciousness, ever-risen and radiant with its own manifold aesthetic flavors, is consciousness itself; it is the manifest, great-souled illumination of consciousness.
When the external has subsided of its own accord, consciousness arises from its own knowledge; it itself reaches the state of deep sleep through its own inertia within the insentient.
O Great Space of Consciousness, because the unmoving consciousness is itself vibrated, the world exists and does not exist through the illumination of the light of consciousness.
The world both exists and does not exist as the singular voidness of the space of consciousness; the world both exists and does not exist as the great form of the light of consciousness.
The world exists and does not exist as the vibration of the wind of consciousness; the world exists and does not exist as the blackness of the darkness within the mass of consciousness.
The world exists and does not exist as a day of light from the sun of consciousness; the sequence of the world is a particle of oil within the dust of the ink of consciousness.

The heat of the fire of consciousness is the world-line; the whiteness of the conch of consciousness is the world; the interior of the mountain of consciousness is the world; and the fluidity of the water of consciousness is the world.

The world is the sweetness of the sugar-cane of consciousness; the world is the smoothness of the milk of consciousness. The world is the coolness of the snow of consciousness; the world is the blazing of the flame of consciousness.

The world is the oil within the mustard seed of consciousness; the world is a wave upon the river of consciousness; the world is the sweetness of the honey of consciousness; the world is a golden bracelet of consciousness.

The world is the fragrance of the flower of consciousness; the world is the fruit at the tip of the creeper of consciousness. The very existence of consciousness is the existence of the world, and the existence of the world is the very body of consciousness.
Here, differentiation, transformation, and so forth reside like dirt upon a fingernail; thus, these three worlds, whether existent or non-existent, are composed of Being (Sat).
Because its nature is non-conceptual, existence and non-existence are indeed one; the relationship of part and whole, as well as word and meaning, are like the horn of a hare.
Fie upon those who imagine that there is a denial of experience—that world wherein neither mountains, oceans, earth, rivers, nor lords exist!

Since consciousness is one, such a consequence would follow; what room is there here for any other delusion? Though as solid as the heart of a stone, consciousness remains perfectly clear within its own space.
Just as a stone contains within it its entire tranquil internal structure, so too this impurity born of space exists within the space of the collection of objects.

For you, there are no attachments to existence, non-existence, selfhood, otherness, me-ness, or mine-ness; [all things] are spread out like the arrangement of a multitude of lines within the interior of a leaf.
By its very nature as consciousness, this Grandfather—the cause of all multitudes of causes—bears within itself that which consists of both difference and non-difference.
By its very nature, the mind is essentially the cause because it is experienced as consciousness; nor can the non-existence of the inconceivable consciousness be established even by words.
It is observed that whatever exists arises, just as a sprout [arises] from a seed and so forth.

O dear one, within that Great Consciousness which is like the sky, there exists the division of the three worlds as a profound void; for you have gained certainty through direct experience that this entire visible universe is composed of the Supreme State.

When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This world is indeed just like the sky; for just as a pearl shines within the pure void, so too the world shines as one's own self within the firmament of consciousness.
The Shalabhanjika statue of the three worlds appears as if carved, though it is not actually carved; it is carved by the pillar of consciousness alone, yet no carver exists here.

Just as the surges of waves in the ocean, though not deviating from their inherent nature, appear to move within the water, so too do those who perceive external objects appear to act, even while remaining unshaken by their own true nature.

The light of the sun passing through a lattice, as well as the particles of dust in the form of that lattice, appear gross in relation to the perception of the world, yet are as immovable as atoms in relation to a minute particle.
This appearance of the world does not appear as something separate from Brahman; yet, like the web of rays from the sun through a lattice, it provides the experience of appearing as distinct.

Even though these worlds, consisting of earth and the other elements, have been experienced, they do not exist at all within that which has the nature of space, just like dreams and mental constructs.
In this world, which is of the nature of the space of consciousness, the grasping of a solid mass does not exist anywhere, just like water in a mirage-river.

In this world, which consists of grasping at a solid mass and is like a city of one’s imagination, the appearance of visible objects shines forth like a river in a desert—having the nature of an illusion.
By what means has the splendor of the visible world—which is like a dream—been weighed on a scale? Released from all mental construction, it expands as the void.
Setting aside the knowledge of the knower, there is no actual difference in meaning between the words "world," "Brahman," and "self," for they all refer to the same objective reality.
This pure consciousness, devoid of objects, shines like the sky before the sun; it is as subtle as the cloud of one's own volition is to a rain-cloud.
Just as a dream-city appears clear in relation to the excellent city of the waking state, so too does this world appear clear in relation to a world created by mere volition.

Therefore, know that the world, being of the nature of consciousness and devoid of objects of thought, is nothing but the void; understand that the words "void" and "world" are synonymous, both consisting solely of consciousness.
Therefore, nothing whatsoever has arisen here in this world of appearances; it remains as it is, unnameable and unmanifest.
The sky of consciousness within the great space of the world is without a supporting wall; it does not fill even an atom's worth of space or the measure of a scale.
It is of the very nature of space, transparent and devoid of any grasping at solid form; it is a wondrous manifestation of space within space, existing like a city of one's own imagination.
In this regard, listen to this narrative of the pavilion, which is an ornament for the ears, so that this matter may find rest in your mind without doubt.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin, for the increase of true awakening, tell me quickly in brief the entire narrative of Maṇḍapa, by which my understanding may flourish.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: On this surface of the earth, there arose a radiant lotus of a lineage, a glorious king named Padma, who possessed many sons and was endowed with discernment.
He is an ocean for the preservation of moral boundaries, a sun for the darkness of his enemies, a moon for the night-lotus of his beloved, and a fire for the grass of his own faults.
He is Mount Meru for the hosts of gods, the moon of glory in the ocean of worldly existence, a lake for the swans of virtuous qualities, and the stainless sun for the lotuses.
A wind for the creepers of battle, a lion for the elephants of the mind, beloved of all branches of knowledge, and a mine of all marvelous qualities.

He is the Mandara mountain shimmering during the agitation of the ocean of the enemies of the gods; he is the honey from the clusters of flowers of his own play; he is the flower-armed god of love who is the very essence of good fortune.

Keśava is one whose hair is animated by the wind of the playful dance of the *līlātāla* tree; he is the moon for the white water-lilies of noble character and a fire for the creepers of wicked conduct.
He has a fortunate wife named Līlā, a playful woman endowed with every charm, who, like a lotus, has arisen upon the earth.
Her graceful movements were followed by all, her speech was sweet, she moved slowly with joy, and her smile was like the rising of a second moon.
Possessing a lotus-face as enchanting as a swarm of bees, with a fair body and limbs as pale as the *karṇikā* flower, she was like a moving lotus-pond.
Shining like a multitude of kunda flowers with the grace of creepers, full of aesthetic flavor, with sprouts for hands and the luster of blossoms, she was like the embodied splendor of spring.
With a pure white body, meritorious and bringing delight through her touch, she was like the Ganges descended to earth in embodied form, graceful as a swan.
To perform for a long time the service of that god whose arrows are flowers of the earth and who bestows all delight, another woman appeared like Rati herself.

When he is anxious, she is deeply anxious; when he is joyful, she is joyful; when he is agitated and distressed, she is likewise agitated and distressed. Like a reflection, the beloved is joyful when he is joyful, and when he is enraged, she is merely terrified.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Together with that earthly apsarā, whose husband was her sole beloved, he took delight with his wife in the essence of unfeigned love.
In the groves of garden trees, in the thickets of *tamāla* trees, in the delightful bowers of flowering canopies, and in the dwellings formed by circles of creepers.
Upon flower-strewn couches in the inner apartments, along pathways laden with heaps of blossoms, on swings in the spring gardens, and in the pleasure ponds.
Upon mountains of sandalwood trees, beneath *saṃtānaka* groves, in the dwellings of *kadamba* and *nīpa* trees, and within the hollows of *pāribhadra* trees;
In the groves of the spring forest, fragrant with the nectar of blossoming *kunda* and *mandāra* flowers, the birds and cuckoos warbled melodiously.
And upon patches of various forest grasses with soft luster, and at waterfalls raining down showers of shimmering spray as they flow;
And upon the slabs of mountains composed of gems and rubies, in the dwellings of divine sages and seers, and in hermitages of remote merit;
When the night-lotuses have blossomed, and the day-lotuses are smiling, and when the dark forest grounds are covered with flowering and fruit-bearing trees;

They were beautiful with their amorous dalliances that were crimson with passion, and they were lovely through their mutual desires, which were enriched by the essence of intense and tender love for one another.
With riddles, narratives, and likewise with "fistfuls of syllables," with chess-like grids, many kinds of gambling games, and likewise with those where the fourth [line] is hidden.
And by means of dramas and narratives, verses following the *vindumatī* meter, divisions of place and time, and the activities of cities and villages.
Adorned with garlands of flower strings and various arrangements of ornaments, they move with playful, restless steps and partake of diverse flavorful foods.
By chewing fresh saffron, camphor, and betel leaves; and by the nail-marks that concealed her body with blossoming flowers, creepers, and guñjā berries.
Through the playful acts of smearing each other with unguents, the sequences of throwing garlands, and the successive swings of flower-beds within the house, they amused one another.
By means of the coming and going of pairs of boats, elephants, horses, tamed camels, and other vehicles, and through the playful splashing of water during aquatic sports, they [enjoyed themselves].
With dancing, singing, artistic gestures, rhythmic clapping, and the *tāṇḍava* dance; with ornaments, musical performances, conversations, and the playing of the lute and the drum.
In gardens, by trees on riverbanks, along excellent streets, in inner apartments, and in palatial mansions, they engaged in swinging upon flower-decked swings.
Having been thus raised in comfort, that beloved and affectionate wife of his, who possessed beautiful eyebrows and was full of longing, once reflected:
This husband of mine, the lord of the world, is dearer to me than my own life; how might he, full of youthful vigor and endowed with splendor, become free from old age and death?
"With this husband, how may I, a beloved woman with high breasts, sport at will for a hundred yugas long within the flower-pavilions?"
Therefore, one should exert effort through austerity, recitation, and self-restraint, so that the king may become like the moon at its rising, free from old age and death.
I shall ask those twice-born ones who are advanced in knowledge, advanced in austerity, and advanced in learning: "How might death not occur for human beings?"
Having thus brought them and honored the twice-born, she bowed and asked them again and again: "O Brahmins, how might immortality be attained?"
The Brahmins said: "O Goddess, all the perfections and supernatural powers are attained through austerity, recitation, and self-restraint; however, immortality is never obtained."
Having heard this from the mouth of the brahmin, she, terrified of separation from her beloved, reflected again immediately by means of her own wisdom.
If, by fate, my death should occur before that of my husband, then, liberated from all suffering, I shall abide happily in my own self.
"Then, even if my husband should die at the beginning of a thousand years, I shall act in such a way that his life-spirit does not depart from the house."
While my husband’s life-breath wanders within this very inner apartment of my own, I shall dwell there at my ease, constantly beheld by my lord.
Starting this very day, for the sake of this purpose, I shall worship the goddess Jñapti Sarasvatī with recitations, fasts, and observances until she is fully propitiated.
Having thus resolved, that excellent woman, without even informing her husband, undertook a rigorous vow according to the scriptures and remained established in it.
At the conclusion of every three-night period, having broken her fast, she was devoted to the worship of gods, brahmins, gurus, the wise, and the learned.
Her body was constantly engaged in bathing, giving, austerity, and meditation; she practiced all forms of faith and right conduct, and she was the remover of afflictions.
Without her husband knowing her whereabouts, she pleased him according to the proper time, according to his efforts, according to the scriptures, and in due order.
Thus, for three hundred nights, that young woman, steadfast in her observances, remained incessantly devoted to asceticism through arduous exertion.
Then, at the end of one hundred three-night rites, having been worshipped and honored, the blessed Goddess Gaurī, the Mistress of Speech, being pleased, spoke to her.
The illustrious Sarasvatī said: "O child, I am well-pleased with you because of your uninterrupted austerity and your extraordinary devotion to your husband; accept the boon you desire."

The illustrious Queen said: Victory to you, O one who possesses the luster of the moon that removes the defect of the burning pain caused by the flames of birth and old age! Victory to you, O one who possesses the luster of the sun that dispels the mass of darkness within the heart!
O Mother, O Mother of the World, protect this wretched woman! O auspicious one, grant these two boons that I request.
"First of all, O Mother, let not the life-breath of my husband, the King of Videha, depart from this very pavilion of his own inner apartments."
O Great Goddess, I entreat you for a second boon: whenever I desire to see you or to seek a favor, then grant me your vision.
Having heard this, the Mother of the World herself said, "Let it be so for you," and then vanished, rising up like a wave in the ocean.
Then that queen, her chosen deity being well-pleased, became filled with joy like a doe hearing a song.
Then, the Kālacakra, consisting of moments and characterized by vibration, flows within the wheel of days, months, seasons, and years, as well as in the staff of the year and the hub of the instant.
The consciousness of her husband vanished from his body while it was still visible, like the sap of a withered leaf.
When he, his body mangled in battle, died within the inner apartments, she, like a lotus plant deprived of water, fell into a state of extreme withering.
With all her lower lip-sprouts withered by the hot, poisonous breaths [of the snake], she reached the state of death, like a doe pierced by an arrow.
When he had met his death, she fell into the blindness of darkness, like the beauty of a decorated house when the flicker of its lamp-flame has been extinguished.
In an instant, that young woman became emaciated and fell into a state of despondency, like a river whose current has failed, rendered grey with alkaline silt.
The proud woman, on the verge of death, quickly became one who cries out in distress and quickly became silent and mute like a separated female ruddy goose.
Then Sarasvatī, who dwells in the compassionate sky, felt compassion for her who was utterly overwhelmed, just as the first rain pities a small fish distressed by the drying up of its pond.
The illustrious Sarasvatī said: "O child, having covered this husband of yours who has become a corpse with a heap of flowers, place him there; you shall obtain a husband once again."
The flowers will wither, but he shall not perish; moreover, he will soon restore you to the status of being his wife.
And this life-breath of yours, as clear as the sky, shall not depart quickly from this pavilion in the inner apartments.
Having heard this from her kinsmen, she whose eyes were like rows of bees was comforted by their arrival, as a lotus plant is refreshed by waters.
Having placed her husband right there and concealed him beneath a profusion of flowers, she remained somewhat consoled, like a poor woman who has discovered a hidden treasure.
On that very day, at midnight, while all the attendants in that inner apartment were overcome by sleep, she—she herself—was there.
With a mind of great purity through meditative concentration, he summoned the Blessed Goddess Jñapti from the realm of suffering; she approached him and spoke to her.
"Child, have I been remembered by you? Why do you bear such grief? The delusions of saṃsāra appear just like the water of a mirage."
Līlā said: "Where is my husband staying, what is he doing, and what is he like? Lead me to his side; I cannot live alone."
The Goddess said: "The space of the mind, the space of consciousness, and the third, the [physical] space—know, O fair-faced one, that the space of consciousness is more void than the other two."

Through the contemplation of the singular nature of the space of consciousness, that which is essentially the sheath of the space of consciousness appears and is experienced instantly, even though it does not exist [as a separate entity].
O lady of excellent complexion, know that which is the very interval between consciousnesses when one reaches another place from one's own land in a mere instant—that is the space of consciousness.
If you attain stability in that state, with all mental constructs entirely cast aside, then you will undoubtedly reach that reality which is the state of the Self of all.
This is attained by the complete cessation of the world, and not otherwise; yet by my boon, O beautiful one, you shall attain it swiftly.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus, the goddess departed for her own divine abode; Līlā, however, remained effortlessly absorbed in unwavering samādhi.
In an instant, she abandoned her own body along with the cage of the internal organs, like a bird that has left its nest and flown into the sky.
Standing in the sky within that very palace-ether, she beheld her husband, the protector of the earth, seated in the assembly hall amidst many kings.
Seated upon the lion-throne, he was praised with cries of "Victory! and "Long live!", and was intent on undertaking the task of the mandala-host.
It was situated within the royal capital, which was strewn with clusters of banners, and there stood an immeasurable circle of sages, brahmins, and seers at its eastern gate.
The mandala of the countless kings and lords of kings situated at the southern gate; the mandala of the countless worlds of women situated at the western gate.
Crowded with countless chariots, elephants, and horses at the northern gate, it was a confrontation with the Deccan region decided by a single servant.
The eastern regions whose administrative procedures were established by Karṇāṭanātha, and the entire northern path of the Mlecchas determined by the lord of Surāṣṭra;
All the western tribes were overrun by the Mālava country, while the region was cheered by messengers from Laṅkā who had arrived from the shores of the southern ocean.

On the shore of the eastern ocean, he beheld the celestial river described by the Siddhas to Mahendra; on the shore of the northern ocean, he saw the Guhyakas described by the messengers who had arrived there.
Its entire courtyard was crowded with countless kings who had come from the shores of the western ocean to witness the sequence of his sunset.
The sound of the foremost musical instruments was surpassed by the brahmins reciting in the sacrificial enclosure, while the forest elephants echoed the joyous clamor of the bards.
The expanse of the sky resounded with the sounds of singing and instrumental music, while the atmosphere was thick with clouds of dust raised by the rows of horses, elephants, and chariots.
Rich with flowers, camphor, and incense, its mountains fragrant with perfumes, it contains many teachings arranged as the provisions for all maṇḍalas.
He was a mountain of exceedingly bright white garments like clouds of fame-sandalwood; he alone became a pillar for heaven and earth, having surpassed the sun with his own majesty.
The lord of the earth was preoccupied with grand undertakings that were slow to begin, while the sovereign master-builder was diligently engaged in the construction of various cities.
Then that great undertaking fell upon the assembly hall of the king—celestial in nature, like mist falling upon the forest of the sky.
There, no men at all beheld her wandering before them, for she was created by mere thought, like a woman fashioned from desire.
Thus they did not see her moving before them, just as one might not perceive a city fashioned by another's imagination.
He beheld all those very same people from his former life assembled in the hall, just as one who possesses perfect mindfulness perceives various cities within a single mountain.
Those regions, those customs, as well as those very boys, those same young women, and those very ministers;
Those very same rulers of the earth, those very same scholars, those very same ministers of pleasure, and those very same servants of such a kind.
Then he [inquired] about other scholars and friends who were unprecedented, as well as about other legal proceedings and other citizens likewise.
At midday, during that day, the quarters were filled with dense forest fires; the sky, along with the moon and sun, resounded with the roar of clouds and wind.
It was adorned with trees, rivers, mountains, cities, and towns; it was filled with the layout of various cities and crowded with wildernesses and villages.
The king was twice eight years of age and free from the aging of his former life; likewise, all the people and every inhabitant of the village were of that same former age.
Beholding them, that woman became overwhelmed with anxiety, wondering, "Have all those inhabitants of the city died?"
Again, through her awakening to conventional designations, she went to her former inner apartments and, in an instant, saw them there at midnight exactly as they were before.
Then she roused her companions who were overcome by sleep, and said, "I am in extreme distress; please grant me a place to stay."
"If I stand by the side of this lion-throne of my husband, I shall see a great assembly of my own people; only then will I live, and not otherwise."
Then, when she had spoken thus, the king and his retinue all became alert and attentive, each to their respective duties, in due order.
Rows of staff-bearers went forth to assemble the citizens and members of the assembly, like the rays of the sun upon the earth to bring about the day's business.
And the servants, acting with great diligence, swept the grounds of the assembly hall, just as autumn days clear the sky that had been soiled by the clouds of the rainy season.
Multitudes of lamps stood in the courtyard, having drunk up the waters of darkness, like rows of stars arrived as if to witness a marvel.
They filled the courtyards with floods of people, just as, at the beginning of a creation, the oceans—once dried up by the dissolution of the world—are filled with water.
The blameless ministers and vassals returned each to his own place, like the world-protectors returning to their respective quarters when the three worlds have been restored.
Winds blew, cooled by dense frost infused with camphor, and made fragrant by the rich scent exhaled by blossoming flowers.
At the edges stood doorkeepers dressed in white garments, like rows of clouds on mountains distressed by the heat of the sun upon Mount Ṛṣyamūka.
Masses of flowers, yellowish with radiance, fell upon the earth like clusters of stars scattered by a violent wind.
The followers of the king filled the assembly hall, just as swans fill a lake strewn with full-blown lotuses.
She sat down upon a new, gold-embroidered seat near the lion-throne, like Līlā herself seated within the mind of the God of Love.
He beheld all those kings, his elders, noble ladies, female companions, courtiers, friends, kinsmen, and relatives, exactly as they had been before.

Having observed everything exactly as before, she indeed attained supreme joy; and the king, along with the people of the realm, shone like the moon with the splendor arising from their restored life.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "In this way, I shall sufficiently divert this sorrowful mind"—having thus signaled her intention to the kings, she then rose from the assembly hall.
Having entered the inner apartments, she went to her husband's side in the inner pavilion and, while staying there, she entered into reflection upon Puṣpagupta with her mind.
"Aha! How wondrous is this illusion, that these people of our city are situated both there and here, as if in a place where there is a distinction between outside and inside!"
Even these mountains, garlanded with palm, tamāla, and hintāla trees, are just as they were there; alas, this illusion extends everywhere!
Just as a mountain is perceived both inside and outside in a mirror, so too is creation perceived within and without the mirror of consciousness.
In this regard, I ask the Mistress of Speech, having worshipped her: "Which creation is composed of delusion, and which is ultimate reality? She spoke without doubt:
Having thus resolved, she then worshipped that goddess, and beheld her arrived before her, assuming the form of a young maiden.
Seated before the Goddess who was seated upon a majestic throne, Līlā, remaining on the ground, questioned the Great Śakti of the Ultimate Reality.

Līlā said: O Goddess, even the most exalted ones feel supreme agitation for one who is worthy of compassion; indeed, it was by you alone that this supreme order was established at the beginning of creation.
O Supreme Goddess, tell me that which I ask you with such humility before you; surely let your grace toward me be fruitful.
This mirror named "the world" is even more stainless than the sky; its minute particle is [as vast as] millions upon millions of yojanas.
A mass of light from words free of seams, soft and very cool, known by the name "the inconceivable consciousness," it stands before one without a foundation.
Space, time, the divisions of space, light, necessity, and succession—these, having reached their ultimate transformation, are reflected within it.
The splendor of the reflection of the three worlds exists both outside and within; therein, what indeed could be artificial, and what could be non-artificial?
The illustrious Goddess said: "O beautiful one, tell me what is the nature of the non-artificiality of creation? What would its artificiality be like? Explain this to me exactly as it is."
Līlā said: "O Goddess, O Mother, since I remain here and you, O Sovereign of the Gods, remain there, I know that this creation is not artificial."
I consider that creation, wherein my husband now stands, to be artificial, because it is empty and does not fulfill the requirements of place, time, and so forth.
The Goddess said: An artificial creation never arises from that which is non-artificial; for an effect that is dissimilar to its cause never emerges from it anywhere.
Līlā said: O Mother, the effect is seen to be quite distinct from its cause; clay is unable to hold water, whereas the jar born from it is its receptacle.
The Goddess said: Indeed, whatever effect is produced by auxiliary causes, some diversity in the primary cause is observed therein.
Tell me, O fair-faced one, what is the cause of that creation of the Lord in the earth and other elements? From which portion of his body did that manifestation arise there?
If it has departed from here by flying up, how could it be here on the surface of the earth? What are the auxiliary causes, and what are the primary causes in this matter?
Even in the absence of [primary] causes, that which arises as a cooperative condition is experienced by everyone as nothing other than a result of those preceding causes.
Līlā said: "O Goddess, that memory of my husband has thus expanded; I know that memory is its cause, for this is the certainty: 'This is creation.'"

The illustrious Goddess said: "O gentle one, just as memory is of the nature of space, so too is that which is born from it; likewise, O lady, even though the creation of your husband was experienced, it was indeed only space."
Līlā said: Just as my husband has described this creation as consisting of the space of memory, so do I regard it; that very creation is the illustration here.
The Illustrious Goddess said: "It is even so; this unreal creation appears radiant through its lords. In that very same way, it appears here, O daughter; I perceive this."
Līlā said: "Tell me how this illusory creation arose from my formless husband, so that the delusion of the world may cease."
The Goddess said: Listen as this is explained—how this creation, which prior to memory consists of mere delusion, appears as having the nature of a dream-illusion.
Somewhere in the space of consciousness, there exists a pavilion of saṃsāra, its form concealed by a structural arrangement like a pane of glass within the sky.
With Mount Meru as its central pillar, the goddesses of the world as its statues, the fourteen realms as its inner chambers, the three hells as its pits, and the sun as its lamp;
Its corners were filled with termite mounds and crumbling earth from the mountains; it was the dwelling of many sons and of aged Brahmins who were lords of progeny.

It is filled with the silkworms that are the multitudes of living beings; it possesses the blackness of the upper surface of the sky; and it resounds with the humming of the swarms of mosquitoes that are the hosts of Siddhas dwelling in the firmament.
Its corners were enveloped by a fierce mass of smoke from houses of clouds; it was a tiny insect upon the celestial chariots situated on the great bamboo-poles of the paths of the wind.
It was filled with the tumultuous clamor of the playful antics of fools such as gods and demons, and it was packed full of the houses, villages, vessels, and utensils of other worlds.
Its surface was sprinkled by the waters of lakes, rivers, oceans, and ponds; its hollows shone with portions of the netherworld, the earth, and heaven.
There, in a certain corner within a hollow of the sky, upon the surface of a rock or a clod of earth, there was a single pit belonging to a mountain village.

In that place, sheltered by rivers, mountains, and forests, the twice-born man—possessing fire, accompanied by his wife and sons, free from disease, provided with cow's milk, released from fear of kings, hospitable to all guests, and devoted to dharma—dwelt.
The Goddess said: "In terms of wealth, dress, age, actions, learning, power, and conduct, he is indeed similar to Vasiṣṭha, yet his behavior is not that of a true descendant of Vasiṣṭha."
He had a wife named Arundhatī, who was as beautiful as the moon; by name she was Arundhatī, yet in both the earth and the sky she was indeed unobstructed (Arundhatī). Vasiṣṭha was his name.
She was equal even to Arundhatī in terms of wealth, dress, age, conduct, learning, power, and behavior, yet not in the quality of her inner consciousness.
Possessing the flavor of unfeigned love, moving with the languid grace of amorous play, and smiling like a white water lily, she was his entire essence within this worldly existence.
Once, while that Brahmin was seated upon the grassy plateau of that mountain covered with *sarala* trees, he beheld the king below.
He was proceeding with his entire retinue, desiring to hunt, amidst the great roar of the army as if wishing to split Mount Meru.

With yak-tail fans that resembled banners of moonbeams, it made the grove of creepers appear like the sky, and with circles of white umbrellas, it made the vault of heaven seem like a floor of silver mosaic.

The sky was filled with a flood of dust from the earth raised by the hooves of horses, while the elephants, with their trunks uplifted, concealed it like watchtowers with the wind blowing through them.
A circle of the spirits of the quarters was flowing like a great whirlpool of tumultuous noise, while another circle shone with necklaces, armlets, and golden rubies.
Beholding that protector of the earth, he thought this: "Oh, how delightful is sovereignty, illuminated by every form of prosperity!"
When shall I become a sovereign of the earth, filling the groves of the ten directions with foot-soldiers, chariots, elephants, horses, banners, parasols, and yak-tail fans?
When will the breezes, fragrant with the nectar of kunda flowers, drink the perspiration droplets from the women of my inner apartments, born of the fatigue of love-making?
When shall I make the faces of noble women as bright as the rising moon, by filling the quarters with my fame that is like camphor?
Thus, from that time forward, this brahmin became resolute; devoted to his own duty, he remained constantly diligent throughout his entire life.
Then, as if intent on shattering the lotus like a frost-bolt, old age approached the twice-born man, appearing as if it had already been worn away by the water.
Then, as his death drew near, his wife fell into a state of withering, like a creeper whose flowering season has ended due to the fear of summer heat.
Having propitiated me just as that woman did for you, she then chose this boon—immortality, which is so difficult to attain—after realizing its true nature.
"O Queen, because the life-force of my deceased husband seemed to have come from his own pavilion itself, I accepted that very [pavilion] as hers."
Then, by the power of time, that brahmin passed away; yet he remained within that very space of the house in the form of the vital breath.
By the power of his own former, manifold resolutions, this Lord, possessed of supreme power, has himself become one whose very body is space.
The king was the conqueror of the three worlds, having subdued the surface of the earth by his splendor, overwhelmed the heavens by his majesty, and protected the netherworld by his compassion.
He was like the fire at the end of an eon to the trees of his enemies, like the god of love to women, like Mount Meru to the winds of sensual objects, and like the sun to the lotuses of the virtuous.
It is a mirror for all scriptures, a wish-fulfilling tree for seekers, a footstool for the foremost of the twice-born, and the moonlight of the nectar of the full-moon dharma.

When that twice-born one, whose body was composed of the elemental ether, had become a corpse within the space inside his own house—that very self which consists of the space of the mind—[the world vanished].
His Brahmin wife, emaciated by grief, was as withered as a dried bean pod; her heart broke in two.
Having become a corpse along with her husband and casting off her body far away, she approached her husband by means of her subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*).
Following her husband like a riverbed that has been excavated, she attained freedom from sorrow, just as a vāsantī creeper puts forth its blossoms.
There, this brahmin possesses houses, lands, and other such wealth; yet today, the eighth day since his death was reached, his life-force remains within a cave in the mountain village.
The Goddess said: "That husband of yours has today become a twice-born man who has attained the status of a king; and she who was named Arundhatī, the Brāhmaṇī, is you, O lady."
"May you two, as a noble couple, rule this kingdom here, like a pair of young cakravāka birds, or like Śiva and Umā born upon the earth."
Thus has been described to you in its entirety this prior sequence of worldly existence; it is merely an illusion, like space itself, assuming the form of the individual soul.
From this delusion, this [other] delusion is reflected in the space of consciousness; though unreal, it appears as real, bringing about the destruction of worldly existence for both of you.
Therefore, what could there be that consists of delusion, or who could be free from delusion? No creation manifests other than the unimpeded perception of non-existence.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having heard this, Līlā, her eyes wide with wonder for a long time, spoke these words in a voice as graceful as a playful gait.
Līlā said: "O Goddess, how has your word become so false? Where is the life of the brahmin in his own home, and where are we standing here?"
How do such other worlds, that earth, those mountains, and those ten directions shine within the interior of my husband’s house, wherein he resides?
The intoxicated Airāvata was bound within the hollow of a mustard seed; a battle was waged by a gnat against a pride of lions within the cavity of an atom.
Mount Meru, situated within a lotus seed, was swallowed by the son of a bee; hearing the roar of the ocean in a dream, the peacocks dance in wonder.
This is indeed inconsistent, O Sovereign of all sovereigns; that the earth and mountains exist within a house is likewise inconsistent.
O Goddess of gods, tell this exactly as it is with an immaculate mind; for those of great luster, when favored by your grace, do not tremble.
The Śrī Devī said: "I do not speak this falsely; listen exactly as it is, O beautiful one. Indeed, the subversion of the laws of necessity (niyati) is not performed by those such as us."
I myself established that boundary which was being divided by another; once it has been breached by me, who else will maintain it?
The soul of the twice-born who had been in battle beholds this Mahārāṣṭra country within his own very home, as if it were the sky itself, for he is of the nature of space.
That former memory of yours has been lost and has arisen otherwise; O lady, this is like the memory of waking that occurs in a dream—this is death.
Just as the three worlds appear in a dream, just as the triple universe appears in a mental construction, just as a battle over the contents of a story, and just as water in a desert land.
This earth, including its mountains, forests, and cities, stands within that brahmin’s house like a mental construction or a reflection in a mirror.
This density of creation appears as if real, though it is unreal; therefore, within the hollow of the sheath of the sky of consciousness, which has the appearance of reality—
That which arises from the unreal, such as memory, is itself unreal; for even a wave does not truly exist in the river of a mirage.
Know this dwelling of yours to be situated within the space-receptacle of that house; know me, you, and everything else to be nothing but that pure sky of consciousness alone.
In this regard, dreams, delusions, mental constructs, and successions of one's own experiences are the primary means of valid cognition for awakening, like lamps.
The life-force of the twice-born remained within the house of the brahmin in that sky; the earth, with its oceans and forests, stood there like a bee upon a lotus.
Within a certain single, delicate corner-cavity of that [city], this body of the city and so forth exists like a tuft of hair in the sky.
O slender one, that very same abode is situated within this city; therefore, what is it but like a multitude of worlds situated within a mote of dust?
"O child, within every single atom of the conscious self there exist worlds within worlds; yet, is this not merely a name that is being doubted?"
Līlā said: "O Supreme Goddess, that Brahmin died on the eighth day; O Mother, how could so many years have passed for us? How can this be?"
The Goddess said: "O lady, just as there is no length of space, so too there is no length of time; listen as I explain this according to the proper reasoning."
Just as this manifestation of the creation of the world is mere appearance, so too is this manifestation of moments and eons mere appearance.
In a single moment, the entire world appears as "you" and "I" to those born from oneself; listen as I explain this sequence of its manifestation exactly as it is.
Having experienced for a moment the fainting swoon of false death, O lady of virtuous vows, the living being forgets its former state and perceives another.
By that very act of unfolding, although it is of the nature of space within space itself, this which is to be supported perceives: "I am situated here in the support."
One perceives this body, consisting of hands, feet, and so forth, as "this is my own"; whatever form one conceives of, that very thing one perceives.
"I am the son of this father; these years are mine; these are my delightful kinsmen; and this is my lovely abode."
"I was born as a child, and I have grown to be such as I am; all these kinsmen of mine likewise move about in this same manner."
Because of the oneness of the mind, space, and the cloud, those [states] exist both within oneself and in others; likewise, even when this fragment of cyclic existence arises in the mind, it is so.
Nothing at all has arisen or persists; it is like the stainless sky. Just as consciousness exists in the dreamer, so too is that same consciousness present in the object seen.
Because it perceives what was seen in a dream through its all-pervading unity, it arises in the same way through the perception of the next world and so forth, just as in a dream.
Just as it arises in the next world, so too does it arise here; thus, for people who are non-existent [in reality], both that dream-world and this world are equally existent.

There is not even the slightest difference [between them], just as there is none between waves and water; therefore, this universe has arisen [from that which is] unborn, and because it is unborn, it is indestructible.
But because it is its very nature, that which appears does not exist at all; it is consciousness alone, just as it is when devoid of objects of thought, having the form of the supreme ether.
Even when there is an object of thought, it is likewise of the nature of the supreme ether; therefore, the object of thought is not other than that, just as a wave is not other than the water.

The state of being a wave does not exist in the taste, for it is just like the horn of a hare; yet that very [taste], though never deviating from its own nature, appears as if it has become the object of cognition.

Therefore, the visible object does not exist at all; how, then, could there be the cognition of a seer and the seen? This occurs for the living being in the very twinkling of an eye, immediately following the delusion of death.
The splendor of the creation visible in the three worlds manifests as a mental appearance, according to place, according to time, according to its inception, and according to its sequence.

According to their birth, according to their mother, according to their father, according to their lineage, according to their age, according to their status, according to their position, and according to their conduct.
Like a kinsman, like a servant, and according to its setting and rising here, the one whose body is consciousness perceives: "I am born," though indeed unborn.
And place, time, action, substance, mind, intellect, sense organs, and so forth—[all these] he perceives in his body at the end of death as if it were suddenly in its youth.
"This is my mother," "This is my father," or "I was once a child"—such a sequence, whether actually experienced or not, consists merely of memory.
Afterwards, that [result] arises for him like the emergence of fruit from a flower; even a kalpa is experienced by me as passing in the blink of an eye.
For Hariścandra, separated from his beloved, that night lasted twelve years; for those parted from their lovers, even a single day stretches out like a year.

Just as in a dream, one thinks, "I am dead," "I am born," or "This is another father of mine," so too arises the notion that an experience has been enjoyed even though the enjoyment has not actually occurred.

Even when one has eaten, there is the perception that one has not; thus, among those who speak with such embellishments, what is seen becomes empty. Misfortune becomes equal to festivals, and even deception becomes a gain within the consciousness of intoxication, sleep, and the like.

Just as pungency resides within the tiny seed of a peppercorn, and a network of carved figures exists within a pillar, so too does this tranquil, non-differentiated world exist within the Unborn; for one who perceives the bondage and liberation of that [world], how and what could they possibly be?
The Goddess said: Immediately after the delusion of death, all worlds manifest clearly to the living being, just as all forms appear fully upon the opening of the eyes.
And composed of space, time, the divisions of direction, ether, phenomena, and karma, they flash forth infinitely and possess stability until the end of the aeon.
Even that which was neither experienced nor seen occurs to one as "this was done by me," and it immediately attains the state of memory, just like one's own death in a dream.
Thus, this infinite delusion shines within the void of the sky of consciousness; it is a city named "the world," consisting of mere imagination and devoid of walls.
This world and this creation expand as nothing but memory, whose singular form consists in the reversal caused by the habitual identification of what is distant with the kalpa and the moment.
Thus, cognition is of two forms: that which has experienced and that which has not experienced; yet, devoid of any prior cause, it proceeds as the very nature of consciousness alone.
Even when another experience has occurred, no consciousness of its having been experienced arises; it is like a father’s memory of his own father arising from a dream-delusion or the like.
Sometimes, having abandoned the state of memory, it appears as mere intuition alone; in the first creations, it shines forth in that form according to its sequence.

O slender one, this visible world, beginning with the three realms, which has been experienced, remains in the memory of some; for others, it has not been experienced and does not remain in their memory.
This lordship over creatures appears to some atoms of consciousness even without a refuge, occurring by mere chance, like the "crow and the palm fruit."
The complete forgetting of the universe is designated as liberation; therein, neither the desired nor the undesired exists for anyone whatsoever.
Without the attainment of absolute non-existence regarding the persistence of the "I" and the world, this liberation consisting of non-arising simply does not arise.
The delusion of a snake in a rope persists because the referent of the word "snake" is impossible; even though it is composed of non-arising and is inherently quiescent, it does not subside.
This is not "half-peaceful" but rather "peaceful" in the sense of being fully integrated; for in the case of one lacking wisdom, when one demon has ended, another demon arises.
