This worldly existence is entirely an expansion of the Supreme; this is the certainty. Due to the absence of a separate cause, that which appears here is nothing but the Supreme itself.
Līlā said: "How did the recollection of the cause arise for him in the form of the Brahmin and the Brahmin woman in this creation, since he was without anything to be remembered?"

The Goddess said: "In that case, the cause is the memory of the Grandfather (Brahmā), not his own memory; for such memory could not have existed previously, because he was liberated from his former birth."
Since it was previously impossible for anything to exist as a memory, consciousness itself comes to possess the nature of the lotus-born [Brahmā] and so forth, because it abides in that very manner.
Another knower of beings, distinct from Prajāpati, arises by chance—like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit—consisting solely of creative intuition.
Thus, when the world has dawned in this way, there is nothing whatsoever that has ever dawned anywhere; there is only the consciousness-ether (cinnabhas) abiding.
The supreme state is the cause of this twofold memory; this very relationship of cause and effect exists as one alone within the sky of consciousness.

Both the effect and the cause, together with their auxiliary causes, do not cease because of the identity of cause and effect; rather, they persist due to the absence of that [realization of non-duality].
Know that you are indeed the form of the Great Consciousness; [know] recollection as cognition. Therefore, the relationship of cause and effect exists, yet that term is not ultimately real.
Thus, nothing whatsoever has arisen, not even the visible world or consciousness; within the space of consciousness, the space of consciousness alone abides in its own self.
Līlā said: "O Goddess, what a supreme vision has been shown to me by you! The beauty of the world's form is like the radiance of the sun at dawn."
Now, O Goddess, as long as my vision has not reached full maturity in this regard without practice, so long must you dispel this curiosity of mine.
"Lead me to that mountain village, that place of creation, where that Brahmin dwelt together with his Brahmin wife in his home; I wish to behold it."
The Goddess said: "By relying upon that supreme, purifying vision which consists of the nature of consciousness beyond objects of thought, abandon this form and become stainless."
Then, like a man standing on the ground who perceives a city within the sky through his own mental resolve, you will undoubtedly attain the Self that is space, abiding in the ether.
This being the case, we shall behold that [Self] along with its creation without obstruction; for this body is indeed the supreme bolt upon the door to seeing it.
Līlā said: "O Goddess, why is it that another world is not attained by means of this very body? Out of your gracious favor, please tell me the reasoning for this."
The Goddess said: "These worlds, which are formless, have been perceived by you as having form through a vain grasping, just as one might perceive gold as a ring."
Just as the nature of a ring does not exist even in that which assumes the form of a golden ring, so too the world does not exist in Brahman, even though it appears in the form of the world.
This world is indeed the sky of consciousness; it is Brahman alone that is perceived here. Yet, something resembling a visible object is seen within it, like a speck of dust in the ocean.
This phenomenal world is indeed false; I am the non-dual Brahman, which is Truth. In this matter, the Vedāntas, the gurus, and personal experience are the authorities.
Brahman alone sees Brahman; that which is not Brahman does not see Brahman. This very nature of its own is what is celebrated by such names as "creation" and the like.
There is no arising of the relationship between cause and effect for Brahman and the worlds, due to the absence of all auxiliary causes.
As long as the cognition of difference has not been stilled through the practice of yoga, you certainly do not perceive Brahman, which is of a nature other than that [difference].
In this regard, those such as ourselves who have attained mastery through the practice of attaining Brahman indeed perceive that supreme reality.
The body of this city of my own conceptualization is composed of space; yet, within it, I perceive through this very body that state which is Brahman itself.
Likewise, these beings such as Padmajā and others are worthy of the body of pure gnosis; O lady, they abide as portions of Brahmā, Ātmaja, Jagadā, and the rest.
O child, without practice toward you, the form has not attained the state of Brahman; it remains as the nature of conceptualization, and for that reason, you do not perceive it.
Where even a city of one's own volition cannot be attained with one's own body, how could another body attain a city of another's volition there?
Therefore, having abandoned this body, you who are of the nature of the space of consciousness, O best among those who know what must be done, do today exactly what you perceive.
A city of imagination is real with respect to that which is imagined; it is neither a doubt nor a disembodied state, nor anything else whatsoever.
Just as this delusion of the world came to its present state at the time of the original creation, so too has destiny reached its full maturity from that very moment onward.
Līlā said: "O Goddess, you have said, 'O Brāhmaṇa and Brāhmaṇī, let us go to the world'; I say this: how, O Mother, is it possible to go?"
"Having left this body here, with a mind following pure beings, I am going to that supreme world; how will you go there?"
The Goddess said: Your tree of the sky of volition, though it exists, is of the nature of space; it is not of the nature of a wall, nor is it obstructed by a wall, nor does it destroy a wall.
That manifestation of the pure, single being is indeed the very form of consciousness; therefore, it differs only slightly from the Supreme Self.
Such as this body is, I shall not depart leaving it behind; by means of this very body, I shall reach that place, just as the wind carries fragrance.
Just as water mingles with water, fire with fire, and wind with wind, so too does this body merge with other bodies composed of mind.

For the cognition of "earthen-ness" does not attain identity with the cognition of "an earthen object"; how could there be a mutual impact between a mountain of conceptual construction and a [real] mountain?
This mental body of yours and those like you is indeed purely *ātivāhika*, yet it has been grasped as a material (*ādhibhautika*) entity due to long-standing habitual conditioning.
Just as in a dream, just as in long-term meditation, just as in a delusion, just as when there is a mental construction, and just as in a city of the Gandharvas.
When the attenuation of your latent impressions (vāsanā) has indeed reached its firm state, then the subtle body (ativāhika-bhāva) will once again enter this physical frame.
Līlā said: When the conviction that this is the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) becomes firm, does this [physical] body reach that same state, or does it perish?

The Goddess said: If that which exists were indeed subject to the process of destruction and non-destruction, then for that which does not exist at all in reality, what kind of destruction could there be?
When the delusion of a snake in a rope has vanished through the power of realizing the truth, O son, what talk can there be as to whether the snake was destroyed or not destroyed?
Just as a snake is no longer seen in a rope once the truth is fully understood, so too the physical body is no longer perceived through the knowledge of the subtle body.
Even conceptual construction would cease if it were imagined by someone; that which never exists here has already been cast aside like a stone.
"O blessed lady, we see this truth—that this body and so forth exist as the supreme, filled by the Supreme—but you do not perceive it."

When, at the beginning of creation, the state of being a mind arises as something fashioned by conceptual construction, from that time forward, each individual sentient being perceives the visible world.
Līlā said: When the supreme reality alone exists—tranquil, undivided by space, time, and so forth—whence can there be an occasion for conceptualization?

The Śrī Devī said: Just as the state of being a bracelet exists in gold, just as the state of being a wave exists in water, and just as reality exists in dreams, mental constructs, cities [of the mind], and the like; [so too does the world exist within Consciousness].

Just as there is no such thing in the experience of truth, so too there is nothing at all in Brahman—because its own nature is free from disease and consists of a self that is distinct from conceptual construction.
Just as there is no dust in the sky, so there is no part in the Supreme; this is the one, unborn, pervasive, and peaceful state, wherein there is neither part nor the perception of parts.
Whatever appears here is, like that [Self], indeed free from affliction; it is a mere manifestation, like the luster of glass or the brilliance of a beautiful gem.
Līlā said: O Goddess, tell us, by what means have we been led astray for so long a time, even regarding the names of the conceptual distinctions between duality and non-duality?
The Goddess said: O fickle one, you have long been deluded and distressed by a lack of inquiry. This lack of inquiry arises from one's own nature; it perishes through inquiry.
Non-investigation perishes through investigation in a mere twinkling of an eye; therefore, this very existence is internal ignorance, and it does not exist as true knowledge.
Therefore, there is no lack of investigation, no ignorance, and no bondage; there is no liberation—this world is unassailable, pure consciousness.
Since you did not investigate this for so long, you were not fully awakened; rather, you remained deluded and agitated.
From this day forward, you are awakened; you are liberated and discerning. The seed of the subtle tendencies has fallen away from your mind.
For when the visible world called "saṃsāra" has never arisen from the very beginning, how could it be perfumed by that [world], and what kind of latent impression (vāsanā) could there even be?

When the absolute non-existence [of all things] has been realized, and when the mind is firmly established in supreme, non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*), wherein the seer, the seen, and the act of seeing are unified;
When this seed of the exhaustion of latent impressions has sprouted even slightly within the heart, perceptions such as attachment and aversion will gradually cease to arise.
This arising of saṃsāra will reach a state of rootlessness; it will attain a foundation in non-conceptual meditative absorption.

Free from the stains of temporal impurity, by means of the pure support of the intermediate space of the sky, you shall, after a short period of time, become the end of all causal processes of manifestation.

The Goddess said: Just as the dream-body is not real despite being experienced through the thorough knowledge of the dream, so too this [waking world] is unreal due to the attenuation of latent impressions (vāsanā).
Just as the dream-body subsides through the thorough understanding of the dream, so too does the waking body subside through the thinning of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Just as this body is perceived at the end of a dream-body or a body of volition, so too does the subtle, transportable body (ativāhika) arise at the end of the waking-state mental construction.
Just as the state of deep sleep arises in a dream when the seeds of latent impressions are absent, so too does liberation arise in the waking state when the seeds of latent impressions are absent.

However, that which is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of those liberated while living is not a latent impression; it is called "pure being" (*śuddhasattva*), and is described as the universal essence of existence (*sattāsāmānya*).
That sleep in which latent impressions remain is known as *suṣupti* (deep sleep); that waking state in which latent impressions remain is called *moha* (delusion).
Sleep in which all latent impressions have been destroyed is designated by the term "the Fourth" (turya); it indeed occurs even during the waking state when the supreme state has been realized.

That state of existence while living, in which the latent impressions have been exhausted here, is called "liberation while living" (jīvanmukti), though it is not recognized by those who are unliberated.
The mind, when permeated by pure beings and its latent impressions attenuated, attains the state of a subtle body, just as snow turns into water through heat.

The mind, having attained the state of a subtle transportive body (*ātivāhika*), meets with other Buddhas and perfected beings (*siddhas*) who have entered into other creations and births; it does not meet anything else.
When this sense of "I" comes to rest through your own practice, then the expansive awareness that reaches to the end of all that is visible will arise within you of its own accord.
When the knowledge of the subtle body (ātivāhika) attains a permanent state, then indeed you shall behold the purifying worlds that are free from volitional thought.
Therefore, O blameless one, exert effort toward the attenuation of latent impressions; when that has reached maturity, you will become liberated while living.
As long as this cool moon of awakening has not been fulfilled, let the world look toward another realm while maintaining the body here.
A body of flesh will unite only with another body of flesh, and not with a mental body in the activities of worldly affairs.
This has been recounted by me exactly as it was experienced and as it stands, established from childhood and perfected through realization; it is not, indeed, like a boon or a curse.
Through the intense practice of awakening, as the latent impressions of worldly existence (saṃsāra-vāsanā) wane within this very body, the state of being a "mind-body" (citta-śarīratā) truly arises.
And that very [self], while about to arise here, is not perceived by anyone; rather, people perceive only the body as it is dying.
Furthermore, this body neither dies nor lives; for what indeed are death and life but delusions of dreams and mental constructs?
Just as life and death exist within a person created by imagination, so too, O daughter, do they appear—though entirely unreal—within this physical body.
Līlā said: "O Goddess, this stainless knowledge has been taught to me by you, upon hearing which the cholera-like affliction of the visible world comes to rest."
In this regard, be gracious and tell me: what is practice, or of what nature is it? How does it attain nourishment, and when it is nourished, what will come to pass?
The Śrī Devī said: Whatever is done by anyone, in whatever manner, and whenever it may be, that never attains perfection in this world without practice.
The wise know that practice to consist of reflecting upon that, speaking of that, mutually awakening one another to that, and being solely intent upon that.

Those noble beings who, being dispassionate, cultivate the attenuation of the tendency toward enjoyment within themselves for the sake of non-becoming—they, the fortunate ones, are victorious upon this earth.

The visible world was never produced even at the beginning of creation; it does not exist at all, always. "This is the world" and "this is I"—the practice of awakening is said to be the realization that this is so.

When passion, hatred, and the like have been attenuated through the realization that the objects of perception are non-existent, that delight which arises from strength is declared to be the practice of Brahman.

Without the realization that the object of perception is impossible, the attenuation of hatred and other afflictions cannot occur; therefore, that is called austerity, not knowledge, and it is merely suffering.

For the realization of the impossibility of the perceptible is called both knowledge and the object of knowledge; through its cultivation, there is nirvāṇa—thus, this cultivation is of great consequence.

In the mind, the entire sleep of the long night of worldly existence is dispelled by the constant sprinkling of the water of discernment, which is as cooling as frost—just as a great mist vanishes in autumn.

When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having thus conversed that night in the pavilion of the inner apartments, while her attendants were indeed asleep, O lady of excellent limbs.
In that mind which was clever, whose doors and windows were secured by all manner of firm bolts, and which was languid with the thick fragrance wafting from heaps of scattered flowers;
Seated beside a corpse adorned with unfading garlands and garments, his station illuminated by a face like the entirely stainless, full moon.
Having gone to the place for meditation, they stood with their limbs motionless, like figures carved from jeweled pillars or like images depicted upon a painted wall.
They both abandoned all their anxieties when contraction set in, like two lotus plants at the end of the day whose streaks of fragrance have spread abroad.
The two became intensely tranquil, pure, and devoid of movement, like a mountain in autumn when the wind has ceased and the garlands of clouds have fallen away.
Through non-conceptual absorption, the two abandoned external consciousness, just as the two beloved wish-fulfilling trees previously shed their sap at the end of a season.

When the delusory object of perception—namely, "I" and "the world"—is understood through those two [means of knowledge] to be of the nature of absolute non-existence from the very beginning, there is no arising of that which is seen through delusion.
Then, O sinless one, this visible demon has completely set for both of us; because it lacks substantiality, it is like the horn of a hare.
For that which does not exist at the very beginning likewise exists not even in the present; whether it appears or does not appear, the world is therefore like the water of a mirage.
Those two women became solely their own true nature, utterly tranquil, like the sky far released from the multitude of objects such as the moon and the sun.
The goddess of cognition moved about with that very body of knowledge, while the other, assuming a human form, moved swiftly in accordance with her meditative concentration and wisdom.
Having ascended by a mere span within the house itself through their consciousness, they both became like the sky of consciousness, possessing the form of sky-travelers.
Then those two playful women, with eyes full of grace, having by their very nature moved far away from the perception of objects, entered into the sky.
Remaining there, they then leaped through the sky by means of their mental activity (*cid-vṛtti*) across a distance of ten million *yojanas*, to a place far, even farther away.
Due to their inherent nature of pursuing whatever is visible, even though they both have bodies of space, they became companions here devoted to affection by gazing at each other's forms.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having leaped further and further away, as they slowly ascended to a high station, holding hand in hand, they beheld the sky.
It was swollen like a single vast ocean, profound and pure within, yielding the blissful enjoyment of contact with the most delicate, gentle breeze.
It is delightful and serene because it is immersed in the waters of emptiness; it is utterly pure, profound, and clear due to its association with the virtuous.

They rested upon the pure, full-orbed moon, which was like a dwelling of nectar within the swelling belly of the cloud resting on the mountain peak, and which was as stainless as the interior of the quarters of space.
In the sweet breeze, which issued forth from the lunar orb and was enchanting with the fragrance of the mandāra garlands of the Siddhas and Gandharvas, they took their delight.
At the end of the intense heat, they swam in the mass of clouds, which was like a lake filled with water and sluggish with its flow, crowded with red lotuses in the form of lightning flashes.

Like two female bees wandering at will among lotus ponds, they roamed freely through the quarters of the sky, upon the peaks of the great mountains that form the flood of the earth's surface, and upon the tips of its lotus-fiber sprouts.

Perceiving it as a shower-house, the two of them wandered within that pavilion formed by a circle of clouds agitated by the wind, which held forth the cascades of the Ganges like torrents from a mountain spring.
Then, moving gracefully and resting according to their strength, they beheld in the void a sky exceedingly sluggish due to its vast expanse.
Never before seen, it was a hollow of every kind of peril, neither filled nor emptied even by hundreds of millions of worlds.
Higher and higher, ever more aloft, it was filled with various distinct levels and excellent celestial palaces, adorned with diverse forms of ornaments.
Its interior was like the conflagration at the end of an eon, illuminated by the radiance from the ruby slopes of the principal mountain ranges, such as Meru, which filled the sky on all sides.
Beautiful as the peaks of the Himalayas due to the abundance of the luster of pearls, it was radiant with golden grounds from the splendors of the regions of the Golden Mountain.
The greenness of the grassy grounds was intensified by the luster of great emeralds, while the darkness arising from the exhaustion of the seer and the seen produced a deep blackness.
With its multitude of celestial chariots fluttering like *pārijāta* creepers, it served as a banner for that ground of lapis lazuli, which appeared as if covered in clusters of blossoms.

It possessed the coming and going of those who had conquered the winds through the great siddhi of mental speed; it resounded with the humming of celestial palaces, mansions, and the songs and instrumental music of divine women.

With no space between them due to the constant movement of the multitudes of the most excellent beings in the three worlds, it was crowded with hosts of gods and asuras whose movements were not seen by one another.
The perimeter was occupied by circles of *kūṣmāṇḍas*, *rākṣasas*, and *piśācas*, while a multitude of celestial chariots (*vaimānika*) moved with great speed upon the mass of wind.
It produced the whistling sound of moving celestial chariots with its thunderous roar graspable by the fist; its wind-machines were set in motion by the dense movement of planets and constellations.

The abodes abandoned by those who have attained only minor accomplishments, scorched by the heat close at hand, and whose charming celestial chariots are consumed by the winds from the mouths of the sun’s horses.
The sky was made restless by the movements of throngs of world-protecting deities and celestial nymphs, while its clouds were formed from the incense smoke rising from the queens' inner apartments.

It was darkened by the mass of fierce splendor from the multitude of common *siddhas*, while the ornaments fallen from the limbs of the celestial women summoned to their respective heavens were scattered about.

It was filled with dense clouds, shaken by the coming and going of throngs of powerful siddhas, which made the Himavat, Meru, and Mandara mountains appear as if they were draped in white silk at their sides.
It was surrounded by swarms of moving crows, owls, vultures, and hawks gathered in heaps, and by throngs of dancing ḍākinīs, like waves upon the ocean.
It was filled with throngs of active yoginīs with the faces of dogs, crows, camels, and donkeys, who were coming and going after having traveled fruitlessly for a hundred yojanas.
In that cloud-palace, smoky-grey with the smoke of the fires of the world-protectors, pairs of Siddhas and Gandharvas had commenced the festival of amorous play.
Its path was traversed by Madana, who was maddened by the songs and hymns of heaven; its wings were marked by the wheel of celestial mansions moving without ceasing.
The waters of the triple-pathed river flowed within it, its foundations dug deep by the masses of wind, while the children of the gods moved about, preoccupied with gazing at the wonders.

In some places, there were palaces moving with their physical bodies, equipped with vajras, wheels, tridents, swords, and spears; elsewhere, there were buildings without walls, where Nārada and Tumburu sang.
In some places, it was agitated by the great onset of vast clouds upon the path of the clouds; elsewhere, it resembled a painted cloud at the end of an eon, motionless and fixed in its form.
In one place, it possessed clouds as beautiful as a rising mountain of black collyrium; in another, it had clouds lovely like molten gold at the end of the summer heat.
In some places, the garment of clouds over Mount Ṛṣyamūka was enriched by the heat of forest fires; in other places, the water of emptiness possessed the turbulence of a windless ocean.
In some places, it has the blades of grass and shoots of the clouds of the wind-river; in other places, it is as stainless as the luster of the skin on the backs of swarms of moving bees.
In some places it was grey with dust stirred up by winds resembling the Meru river; in other places its surface was variegated by the radiance of celestial chariots and gods.
In some places it was garlanded by circles of Mothers dancing nakedly; in other places there were groups of Yoginīs constantly agitated by fresh intoxication.
In some places, it was garlanded by sages resting in peaceful meditative absorption; it was equally captivating to the minds of the virtuous, as all agitation had been cast far away.
In one place there was a circle of singing kinnaras, gandharvas, and celestial women; in another, it was filled with motionless cities; and in yet another, a magnificent city was flowing along.
In some places it was filled with the city of Rudra; in some places the great city of Brahmā; in some places a city created by Māyā; and in some places a city yet to come.
In some places there was a lake with wandering moons, in others a lake consisting of stillness; in some places a multitude of Siddhas was moving about, and in others the moon had risen.
In one place it consisted of the rising sun; in another, of the darkness of night; in some places it was tawny with the garments of twilight, and in others, grey with frost.
In some places white with snowy clouds, in others filled with rain-bearing clouds; in some places, as if on dry land, the world-protector rested even within the sky itself.
In some places, the hosts of gods and asuras were busily engaged in ascending and descending; in others, they were agitated by their movements toward the east, west, north, and south.

In some places there were mountains hundreds of thousands of yojanas away that were difficult to reach; in other places they were filled with indestructible darkness, resembling the interior of a stone.
It is indestructible and vast splendor, resembling the sun or fire in some places, yet as cool as the interior of a mass of snow in others, such as in the abodes of the moon and other luminaries.

In some places there were forests of kalpa-tree creepers appearing before one as they flowed along; in other places, there were cities of the gods falling from on high after being struck down by the daityas.
In some places it was marked by the tracks of celestial chariots descending, and in others it was scarred by the mutual collisions of hundreds of rising comets.
In some places, the foremost mandala was seized by a host of auspicious planets; in some places, it was pervaded by the darkness of night; and in some places, it was radiant with daylight.
In some places there were thundering clouds, in others clear and silent ones; and here and there, white fragments of cloud scattered by the wind served as an offering of flowers.
In some places it is utterly empty, pure, and boundless; like the heart of a wise man, it is spread forth—blissful, soft, peaceful, and transparent.
In some places, the field of the sky-dwellers resounds with the croaking of swarms of frogs mounted on semen, while elsewhere it is enveloped by the waters of emptiness.
In some places it was covered by birds such as peacocks with golden crests, and in others by the mounts of Vidyādharīs and goddesses that had taken up their stations there.
In some places there were circles of peacocks dancing amidst the clouds, while in others the ground was dark with fire-parrots, as if it were a patch of lush green grass.
In one place, a low-hanging cloud was mistaken for the buffalo of the Lord of the Dead due to its great size; in another, a dark cloud was seized by horses out of fear that it was a village of straw.

In some places it was pervaded by the cities of the gods, and in others it was filled with the cities of the Daityas; the cities could not reach one another, and the wind blew through the gaps between them.
In some places it was radiant with Bhairavas dancing with the form of the Kulācala mountains; in other places, Vināyakas were dancing together with the winged lords of mountains.
In some places, mountains were being tossed aloft by the wings of the gale-force winds; in other places, it was made beautiful by throngs of celestial women from the cities of the Gandharvas.
In some places, clouds rose high above millions of trees destroyed by flowing mountain torrents; in other places, it was as cool as the waters of a lotus-pond in the sky created by magic.
In some places, there was a breeze cool and refreshing, drawn by the rays of the moon; in others, there were trees, mountains, and clouds scorched by the heat of the sun.
In some places it was utterly silent due to the complete stillness of the wind; in other places, hundreds of mountain-like cloud-peaks were rising with their summits touching the sky.

In some places it resounded with the gurgling roar of clouds intoxicated by the onset of the rainy season; in other places it was difficult to traverse due to battles waged by hosts of gods and asuras.

In one place, he saw the lotus-vehicled god (Brahmā) summoned by the cries of the female swans of the celestial lotus-lake; in another, he saw the breeze plundering the night-lotuses on the banks of the Mandākinī.
By the proximity of rivers such as the Gaṅgā to his own body, there were schools of leaping fish, crocodiles, crabs, lotuses, and tortoises.
In various regions, the orbs of the moon and sun appeared as if eclipsed by the flickering shadows of the earth cast down from the sun situated in the netherworld (pātāla).
In some places, there was a forest of illusory flowers shaken by the winds of creation, where the celestial women trembled at the falling frost-like showers of petals.

O excellent lady, having leaped high into the sky above that mass of beings contained within the three worlds—which move like gnats in the hollow of a fig tree—you are now ready to return once more to the surface of the earth.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: As those two women were traveling from the sky toward a mountain village, they beheld a certain patch of ground that appeared to their consciousness as if it were the surface of the earth.

The vast heart-lotus of the man of the universe has the eight directions for its petals; it is densely packed with the filaments of the mountains and is beautiful, laden with the abundance of its own fragrance.
In the midst of the stalks of the river-lions, there was a dewdrop, whirled around by the female bees of the night and swarming with the mosquitoes of the hosts of spirits.
It was filled with a multitude of internal qualities, covered with beautiful apertures and hollows, possessing the splendor of the light of day, and carrying floods of water.

Moist with nectar, it was a lotus stalk whose swan wandered in the sky, which became the vessel for the night’s contraction, and whose fibers were the lords of serpents submerged in the mud of the underworld.
At times, its base caused the quarters of the world to tremble with the shaking of the ocean, while its roots extended downward, where the Daityas and Dānavas acted as thorns.
With the creeper-like womanhood of the Asuras, which was tender with the enjoyment [of him], she whose seed was all beings reached the heart, which was the great seed of the mountain-king.
There, the vast pericarp known as Jambūdvīpa has the rivers for its filaments, the stalks for its stem, and the cities and villages for its pistils.

She is beautiful with the seven lofty seed-syllables of the lords of the principal mountain ranges, and she fills the expanse of the sky with the seed-syllable of the great Mount Meru situated at her center.
It was like a drop of frost upon a lake, or the pollen of a forest-born lotus; on the dry lands, it appeared as a swarm of bees surrounding a circle of people standing within its perimeter.
It was pervaded by oceans that resembled bees, extending for hundreds of yojanas, awakening every night, and possessing the splendor of the four directions.
She rests upon the eight petals of the directions, with the oceans and their gods as her bees, and is fashioned in nine ways by the nine royal brothers.
It was a hundred thousand yojanas in extent, filled with particles of dust, and steady with the spray of frost from the array of various inhabited lands.
Twice the size of the continent, it is encircled on the outside by the line of the salt ocean, which winds around it like a conch-shell encircling its outer whorl.
Beyond that, she assumes a body twice as large, circular in shape, which is pervaded by the world-surface vine known as the island-streak called Śāka.
Beyond that, she was encircled by a band of the ocean of fresh milk, twice as vast in form, which was sweet and cool.
Beyond that, it was encircled by the coastal range of the island named Kuśa, which was twice as large in form and adorned with various kinds of people.
Beyond that, it was encircled by a band of the Ocean of Curds, twice its size, which eternally satiates the multitudes of gods.
Then, by that very strip of land called the Krauñca island, it was encircled, appearing like a new royal city surrounded by a moat.
Beyond that, by a stripe of the ocean of ghee of the same measurement; and beyond that, by a stripe of Śālmalī Island filled with impurity.
Then, with a streak of the great ocean of wine, white as flowers, it was as if the form of Hari were enveloped by the body of Śeṣa.
Then, by means of a line [representing] the Gomedaka continent of that same measurement, and likewise by a line [representing] the ocean of sugarcane juice as pure as the slopes of the Himalayas;
Beyond that, it is bounded by the line of Puṣkaradvīpa, which is twice its size, and finally by the line of the ocean of sweet water (svādūdaka) of the same measure.
Then, ten times greater than that was the high circular trench leading down to the depths of Pātāla, appearing like a vast accumulation of chasms.
Turning back by the path leading to Pātāla, which is itself terrifying in nature, she was indeed ten times more formidable than all of this combined.
In the four directions, reaching to the very limits of the sky, it was terrifying with its mass of abysses, as if wearing a garland of blue lotuses clinging to its form of half-faded darkness.
With its lofty, vast, and magnificent garland of mountains—the Lokāloka range—adorned with peaks of various jewels and blossoming kahlāra, kumuda, and lotus flowers;
It was like the gathered tresses of the hair-knot of the Fortune of the Three Worlds; and from all this, it was ten times greater in nature.
It was garlanded by a forest named Ajñātabhūtasaṃcāra, which was ten times greater than all of that.
Just as the sky is pervaded in the four directions by incomparable water, so too [the ocean] is ten times greater in essence than all this [world].
Adorned with a mass of flames eager to melt Mount Meru and other peaks, [he is] ten times greater than all of this.
By that [wind] which carries away the mass of mountains such as Meru like blades of grass or dust, which causes the bursting asunder of the lords of mountains, and which robs one of their speed;
Because it is devoid of emptiness, it is surrounded on all sides by the soundless wind; then, from all this, it becomes tenfold in nature.

Then the sky was completely enveloped by a single, formless void; thereafter, it was pervaded for hundreds of millions of yojanas by a solid, golden wall of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) consisting of two layers.

Thus, beholding the interior of the world—encircled by the oceans, great mountains, the guardians of the quarters, the cities of the gods, the heavens, and the earth—the human woman suddenly saw her own dwelling-cavern upon the ground.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, O fair-complexioned one, those two women emerged from the sphere of the universe and reached another place where that abode of the Brahmin was located.
Then those two perfected women beheld their own abode, a pavilion that was the residence of Brāhmaṇas, invisible to the world.
With handmaidens overwhelmed by anxiety, the faces of the women drenched with tears, their countenances mostly ruined and resembling withered lotus petals.
It was like a city whose festivals have vanished, or like the ocean swallowed by Agastya; it was like a garden scorched by summer heat, or like a tree consumed by lightning.
Like a cloud scattered by the wind, like a lotus withered by frost, or like a lamp whose oil is nearly spent and whose light is fading.

That house, struck by the separation from its master, became like a forest of withered, decaying tree leaves whose beauty has faded due to the compassion of one whose death is imminent; it grew coarse and grey, like a region parched by the cessation of rain.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, through the long practice of pure knowledge, that beautiful woman became like a god, possessing the power of true resolve and true desires.
He thought: "Let my kinsmen see both me and this goddess for a moment, appearing in the form of ordinary women."
Then, while there, the householder saw two women who illuminated the palace like a pair of Lakṣmī and Gaurī.
Beautiful with various unfading garlands and garments brought from Āpāda, the forest was made fragrant like the pair of Vernal Splendors themselves.
Filling the entire forest of medicinal herbs with elixirs, they were like two risen moons, bestowing coolness, refreshment, and happiness.
With glances from eyes as tremulous as long, creeper-like tresses, she scattered heaps of jasmine flowers mingled with blue water-lilies.
The forest was turned to gold by the flowing stream of bodily radiance, which captivated all with its movement like a river overflowing with the essence of molten gold.
They sport upon the playful swing of the innate beauty of their bodies; they are the waves of the ocean of their own loveliness.
With her pair of tremulous, creeper-like arms and her reddish hands, she was scattering a forest of ever-new golden *kalpa* tree creepers.
Furthermore, with feet that were tender like uncrushed, unfading flowers and young shoots, and which resembled garlands of land-lotus petals, they did not touch the ground.
It was causing young sprouts to emerge through the nectar-like sprinklings of the sight of dried *tālī* and *tamāla* groves, which possessed pure luster.
Having said, "Homage be to the two forest goddesses," Jyeṣṭhaśarman then cast a handful of flowers along with his household.
A handful of flowers fell at their feet in the house, like a shower of frost-drops upon the two lotuses of a lotus-pond.

Jyeṣṭhaśarman and the others said: "Victory to you two forest goddesses, who have come for the sake of destroying our suffering! For the protection of others is generally the innate duty of the virtuous."
At the conclusion of those words, the two goddesses spoke with respect: "Tell us the cause of this suffering, by which these people are seen to be so distressed."
Jyeṣṭhaśarman and the others related their own suffering, consisting of the calamity that had befallen the couple, to the two goddesses in due order.

Jyeṣṭhaśarman and the others said: "O Goddesses, you have become affectionate Brahmin couples here; you are hospitable to all, founders of lineages, and the very pillars upon which the stability of the twice-born rests."
Since our parents, having abandoned their home along with their sons, cattle, and kinsmen, have gone to heaven, the three worlds are empty because of that.
Perching upon the house and scattering [their cries] at every moment, the birds mourn with sweet voices their body lying dead in the empty dwelling out of devotion.
Distraught by the wailing and lamentation of the deep, heavy roar from within its caves, the mountain weeps profusely with streams of tears as thick as rivers.

The quarters of the sky, causing cries of lamentation for their destruction, with their garments of clouds stripped away and their breasts of clouds exposed, were reduced to extreme emaciation by the scorching of their sighs.
With all its limbs wounded and mangled, harsh with piteous cries, the village remained dejected, devoted to fasting, and intent on death.
Day after day, warm drops of dew fall from the clusters of blossoms—which are like the sockets of their eyes—downward from the trees.
The street, where the movement of people has ceased, is grey with dust; it stands empty at heart, like a widow bereft of joy.
The creepers, cooing with cuckoos and bees, struck by the tears of rain, sighing most fervently with their heat, strike their bodies with their hands of tender shoots.
To divide themselves into a hundred forms upon the surface of the great rock in this vast chasm, these waterfalls fall down with bodies scorched by heat.
Deprived of their splendor, they have become fearless, mute, and disordered in heart; filled with blinding darkness, the houses have fallen into a state of profound desolation.
From the garden flower-beds, as they seemed to weep with the humming of bees, a foul odor issued forth, which bore the other name of "own fragrance."
Day after day, the vines that sported upon the mango trees become tasteless and wither away, their bud-cluster eyes closing in grief.
Agitated, they set out to cast their bodies into the ocean; like small streams, they moved restlessly with a tumultuous clamor, tossing their forms upon the ground.
The ponds remained within themselves in the bliss of motionlessness, perceiving even their own extreme restlessness—the movement caused by the falling of gnats—as free from fear.
"Surely today the sky has become adorned by our father with singing kinnaras, gandharvas, vidyādharas, and celestial nymphs."
Therefore, O two goddesses, please perform for us the destruction of our grief; indeed, the sight of the great is never without fruit.
Having spoken thus, she touched her son on the head with her hand, as a bending lotus plant touches its drooping root-knot with its leaf.
By her touch, he abandoned his distress, misfortune, and peril, just as a mountain sheds the heat of summer through contact with the clouds of the rainy season.
Then, by the sight of those two goddesses, all the members of that household became possessed of fortune and liberated from suffering, like those who drink the nectar of immortality.
Śrī Rāma said: "Why was her son Jyeṣṭhaśarman not granted a vision of his mother by her through such play? Dispel my delusion for now."

The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: For one who has awakened through the realization of earth and the other elements, the aggregate of earth and so forth assumes the nature of a solid body; for another, it remains as mere empty space.
O dear one, that which is non-existent appears as if it were existent because of the perception of earth and so forth; just as a ghost does not appear to a child when it is not perceived.
Just as that which appears as earth and so forth may in an instant become non-earth and so forth through the recognition of it as a dream, so too is it clearly evident even in the waking state.

Earth and the other elements, when perceived through the lens of space, are experienced as nothing but space; for indeed, in the case of those whose constituent elements are agitated, their efforts toward walls appear as if they were directed toward empty space.
In a dream, one perceives a city, the earth, or a void, as well as a pit; and even a woman who is non-existent in reality performs causal functions for men within that dream.
When space is perceived as earth and so forth, earth and the other elements arise in an instant; even the next world is directly experienced during a state of fainting.
The ignorant man perceives a phantom in the sky, while one who is dying sees a forest in the atmosphere; another perceives a mass of hair in the sky, yet another perceives pearls in the sky.
Those who are terrified, intoxicated, half-asleep, or traveling by boat shall always see and experience things such as vetālas, forests, and trees.
Therefore, the form of these objects appears as it has been cultivated through practice; it does not exist as a single entity from the perspective of ultimate reality.
But having effortlessly understood, according to reality, the non-existence of earth and the other elements, space alone shines forth through consciousness as that which has arisen as an error.
For the sage who possesses the realization that there is only the single space of consciousness—the Self which is Brahman—how, what, when, and from where could there be sons, friends, or wives?

The visible world is unarisen from the very beginning, and that which appears is indeed the Unborn itself; it is only for those possessing perfect knowledge that the perceptions of passion and hatred have been brought to an end.
That the hand was placed playfully upon the head of Jyeṣṭhaśarman was the fruit of his consciousness, which had awakened to the undertaking established by that power.

For consciousness perceives exactly as it intends; yet that which is subtle is even more pure than space. O Rāghava, in every respect, it is that very consciousness which constitutes the web of objects, as is experienced in dreams within imagined cities.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In that village on the mountain slope, within the hollow of his pavilion, those two women vanished right there while remaining present.
Then, while his household members—whose suffering had been pacified—remained occupied with their own duties, he thought, "A favor has been bestowed upon us by the two forest goddesses."
Sarasvatī spoke of Līlā, who was merged in the space of the pavilion, herself having the nature of space, as if remaining silent out of wonder at her who likewise had the nature of space.
In those cases where there is mutual conversation regarding intentions or dreams, that conversation produces a causal efficacy just as it does here in the waking state.

Even without the earth and other elements, the channels, or the vital breaths and so forth, that consciousness of conversation arises between those two, just as it does in dreams or in mental constructs.

Śrī Sarasvatī said: "That which was to be known has been known in its entirety through the consciousness of both seen and unseen objects. Such is this reality of Brahman; tell me, what else do you ask?"
Līlā said: "Why have I not seen that soul of my deceased husband where he rules his kingdom? Why am I seen here by this son?"

The illustrious Sarasvatī said: "O child, O lady of excellent complexion, without practice, your conviction regarding duality at that time certainly did not completely set; it was not entirely extinguished."
How can one who has not attained non-duality be joined with the practices of non-duality? For one established in asceticism, how could there be the experience of a shadow-body?
When the thought "I am Līlā" arose in you without practice, at that moment your power of true resolve (satya-saṃkalpatva) had not yet come to pass.
"O beautiful one, today you have become one whose resolve is true; therefore, let your son behold me—your cherished wish has borne fruit."
If you now go into the presence of that husband of yours, then your legal proceedings with him shall proceed as they did before.
Līlā said: "Right here, in the space of this very palace, my husband was a Brahmin; right here he died and became a lord of the earth."
Right here in this very cycle of existence, within that same region of the earth, I am established as a city matron in that royal capital.
Right here in this very inner apartment, my king has died; right here in the space of that inner apartment, in that very city, is the monarch.
Accomplished on the surface of the earth as the lord of various provinces, he remains established right here in this very state, possessing the swiftness of total uprightness.
Within this very space of the house, I believe all the lands of the universe reside, like heaps of mustard seeds inside a casket.
I always consider my husband’s realm to be not far away; act in such a way that I may see it as if it were situated right here at my side.
The illustrious Goddess said: "O daughter of Arundhatī on this earth, you now have three husbands by name, or perhaps there were many, numbering in the hundreds."
But of those three who were nearest, O twice-born one, he was reduced to ashes; the king remained as a corpse within the inner apartments, concealed inside a garland.
For in this mandala of saṃsāra, the third lord of the earth has fallen into the great ocean of saṃsāra and come to wander within it.
Deprived of the play of the waves of enjoyment, his consciousness is defiled; with the functions of his mind shattered by dullness, he is a tortoise in the ocean of saṃsāra.
Though performing various and even turbulent royal duties, he remains asleep and inactive through his dullness, failing to awaken from the delusion of worldly existence.
"I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am perfected, I am powerful, and I am happy"—thus entangled by the great rope of misfortune, one falls under its control.
Tell me, O woman of excellent complexion, whose husband do you intend to lead to your side, as a gust of wind carries a trail of fragrance from one forest to another?
For this cycle of existence is indeed one thing, and that pavilion of the cosmic egg is another; O child, the successions of worldly transactions are likewise entirely distinct.
Although those circles of cyclic existence stand here at one's side, the distance between them here is many millions of millions of yojanas.
Behold again this body of theirs, which is nothing but empty space; within them are situated millions upon millions of Merus and Mandaras.
In every single atom, all categories flash forth without obstruction from the Great Consciousness, like motes of dust shimmering in the rays of the sun.
For even though these cosmic eggs are heavy due to their vast undertakings, when placed on a scale, they do not weigh even as much as a single grain of rice.
Just as a forest shines in the sky with the stainless radiance of various jewels, so the world shines as consciousness, devoid of the elements such as earth, through contemplation.

"This world is merely a mental construct (jñapti) that shines forth"—such [a view] applies to the Self and not to the earth and so forth, for at the very beginning of creation, nothing whatsoever was produced.
Just as a wave in a lake, having arisen again and again, appears according to various forms, times, limbs, places, and commands, so too is that [consciousness].
Līlā said: "O Mother of the World, it is exactly as I have now remembered here: this birth of mine is rajasic, neither tamasic nor sāttvika."
"Since descending from Brahmā, eight hundred births of mine have passed through various wombs; now, as it were, I see them again."
O Goddess, in a certain part of the circle of saṃsāra in the past, I was a Vidyādhara woman, a bee among the lotuses of other worlds.
Then, defiled by evil latent impressions, I became a human woman in another sphere of worldly existence, the beloved of a lord of serpents.
Dwelling in a forest of kadamba, kunda, jambīra, and karañja trees, I then became a Śabarī woman, dark-complexioned and wearing garments of leaves.
Deluded by my dwelling in the forest, I then became arrogant; with eyes like flower clusters and hands like leaves, I was a playful maiden of the woods.
I, that very vine of the holy hermitage, purified by association with sages, was consumed by a forest fire and became the daughter of that same great sage.
Through the ripening of those karmas that yield the fruit of non-femininity, I became a glorious king in the Surāṣṭra lands for a hundred years.
Due to the fault of the king's misdeeds, I became a female mongoose with limbs destroyed by leprosy for nine years in the marshy thickets of the Tāla trees.
O Goddess, for eight years in the lands of Surāṣṭra, I assumed the form of a cow out of delusion, through the playful behavior of wicked, ignorant, and foolish cowherd boys.
Like a snare set by a hawk in the forest, it was severed with great effort, just as the lowest of latent tendencies (vāsanā) is cut away.
Together with her, she rested upon beds in the centers of lotuses, her body soiled by the pollen of the filaments enjoyed in private within the hollows of the lotus buds.
She wandered through the delightful forest glades on her lofty-horned antelope, whose eyes were captivating, while her vital organs were being struck by Kirātas.

As she was being carried away by the waves of the ocean when the cardinal points had vanished from her sight, she saw that her striking of her face against the leaping of fish, water, and turtles was in vain.
On the banks of the Carmaṇvatī, he drank the coconut-liquor at the conclusion of lovemaking from the lips of a Pulindī woman who was singing with a sweet voice.
The royal swan, his voice sweet with the sound of "sīt," was beautifully delighted by his mate, who was devoted to him and fond of lotus ponds, through their unrestrained amorous play.
In the groves of *tāla* and *tāla* trees, the beloved cast glances at her lover with trembling face and eyes, agitated by intoxicated gazes.
In heaven, the celestial bees were quickly delighted by the lotus-lake of the Apsarases, whose beautiful bodily frames were like a mass of flowing molten gold.
Upon a ground strewn with heaps of jewels, gold, rubies, and pearls, he took delight with his youth in the forest of wish-fulfilling trees on Mount Meru.
I remained for a long time as a tortoise upon the shores agitated by great waves, amidst shimmering clusters of creepers, and within the caves of the coastal forests of the ocean.
Upon the waves rising and falling in succession, I performed the sport of a female royal swan among the rows of moving wings of those sporting in the lake.
Having observed the wretched state of the mosquito, who was being worn out by the swaying of the *śālmalī* leaf, the female mosquito smiled piteously.
He wandered among the mountain torrents, where the waves rose higher and higher, kissing the tips of the dancing ripples, and played like water-reed stalks in the water.
In the Mandāra palace on Mount Gandhamādana, the young Vidyādharas, overcome by passion, previously fell at her feet.
Afflicted by passion, I have long wallowed upon beds filled with saffron and camphor, like the radiance of the moon upon the lunar orbs.

I have wandered through various wombs filled with hundreds of diverse sufferings, my mind agitated by rising and falling, carried along by the restless waves of the long river of *saṃsāra* like the flight of a doe pursued by an irresistible wind.
Śrī Rāma said: "O delicate one, how did you emerge from that wall of the cosmic egg, which is as solid as the core of a diamond, perfectly circular, and extended for ten million yojanas?"

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Where is the universe, where its wall, and where in this context is that adamantine hardness, when the two goddesses are surely situated within the space of the excellent inner apartments?
In that very mountain village, in that same celestial abode, that Brahmin named Vasiṣṭha enjoyed sovereignty.
He experienced that very same empty corner of the pavilion's space as the surface of the earth extending to the limits of the four oceans.
Upon the surface of the earth within the self of space is that royal city; there he experiences the royal palace, and she too experiences it as Arundhatī.
She was born as one named Līlā, and by her Jñapti was worshipped; together with Jñapti, she leaped through the sky, which was wondrous and enchanting.
In a space the size of a span within that very interior of the house, she reached another universe within the temple of the mountain village.
Having emerged from the cosmic egg, he returned to his own abode, just as a man lying on a bed passes from one dream to another.
All this is merely a flash of intuition, nothing but empty space; there is no cosmic egg, no cycle of existence, no walls or such things, and no distance.

It is one's own mind alone that shines forth as such a captivating thing for those two; when it is merely a vivid manifestation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), where is the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and where is worldly existence (*saṃsṛti*)?
This infinite space of consciousness is indeed unobstructed; it is merely stirred by one's own mind, just as the wind is set in motion by the principle of vibration.
The unborn and tranquil sky of consciousness indeed exists everywhere and at all times; yet, by virtue of its nature as consciousness, it appears as the world itself, by itself, within itself.

For one by whom the Buddha is perceived as empty, like something fallen from the sky, for him this [Buddha] is not truly the Buddha; for one by whom he is perceived otherwise, he is like a mountain of vajra-essence.
Just as a radiant city appears within one's very home in a dream, so too does this unreal world appear luminously within the element of consciousness.
Just as water is perceived in a desert mirage and the state of being a bracelet in gold, so too does this appearance of the visible manifest within the Self as if it were real, though it is unreal.
Thus conversing, those two women of graceful form emerged from the house and went outside with beautiful, measured steps.
While the villagers gazed at the mountain in front of them, which was visible, it kissed the hollow of the sky and touched the orb of the sun.
It was pure with various multicolored groves of all kinds of blossoming flowers, and it resounded with the noise of many waterfalls and the warbling of forest birds.
The circle of clouds was tawny with masses of various colorful flower-clusters, while birds and cranes rested upon the tips of their swaying, drooping branches.
Its entire riverbanks were concealed by a dense thicket of sturdy vañjula reeds, while its caves and stone fissures were filled with whirling breezes.
The sky was its inner chamber, covered by a vault of flower-tips; the clouds were its walls, and the long, falling streams of rivers were its shimmering clusters of pearls.
Its riverbanks were stirred by winds from the groves of swaying trees, and its vicinity was perpetually cooled by the shade of various forests.
Then those two women beheld there that mountain village itself, as if it were a fragment of heaven fallen from the sky.
It possessed a multitude of water-channels resounding with noise and clusters of full lotus-pools; its marshy banks were filled with the playful warbling of birds and the cries of cuckoos.
The entire grove was made formidable by the "hum" sounds of moving herds of cows; it was rich with clusters of thickets and bowers, and possessed dense, shady grassy meadows.
The interior of the street was difficult for the rays of the sun to enter, grey with the mist of the night, and tangled with a mass of lofty flower-clusters.
With waterfalls released by the splashing against the hollows of the rocks, they recalled the beauty of the waters of the Milk Ocean as it was churned by Mount Mandara.
The courtyard was crowded with trees that seemed to stand there having brought a mass of flowers, shining with the great weight of their fruits and blossoms.
It was covered by a rain of scattered flowers from trees agitated by sap, as well as by winds shaking the rippling waves and producing gurgling sounds.
The birds, though hidden and unsuspecting, let out a slight cry as they were startled by the sharp clinking sounds of water droplets trickling from the unexpected masses of rocks.
It was filled with birds that, agitated by tasting the spray from the leaping waves, moved in circles like the revolving of a moon upon the river.
The children, fearing the gaze of crows resting upon the tall palm trees, had hidden away the pieces of sugarcane molasses that they themselves had eaten until they were old enough.
It was cooled by the thickets of date palms, neem trees, and citron trees at its edge, and by village boys wearing flower garlands, carrying provisions, and dressed in fresh garments.
With her hands and garments made of fine linen, her ears filled with flower-clusters, emaciated by hunger, she—like a low-born village woman—had taken over the highway.

The tumultuous roar of the clashing waves of the rivers drowned out all conversation; there, one remained in solitary seclusion, yearning for relief from the dense terror born of the dullness of karma.
The courtyard was crowded with naked children whose faces, hands, and shoulders were smeared with curd, who had lips like glossy flower-vines, and who were marked with streaks of cow-dung mud.
Its sandy banks were marked with lines as it was carried along by waves that caused the grass, creepers, and vines on its shores to sway like swings.
The bees were sluggish and intoxicated by the thick fragrance of curd and milk; the children were broken by tears from the pain of being deprived of their desired food.
The people were laughing at a woman who was terrified and busy twisting her braided hair because she had become angry with a man who had smeared a circle of cow dung on his hand.
Where crows flew about with wings spread wide like the petals of *dānta* flowers, and where cruel *kuraṇṭaka* shrubs were strewn across the house-alleys, courtyards, and gateways.
Every morning, the courtyard was strewn knee-deep with flowers by the hollows and caves situated at the sides of the house, which shone with the luster of blossoming plants.
It was a forest tract filled with nets of deer, camaras, and antelopes, where young fawns slept upon the young grass grown within the thickets of *guñjā* shrubs.

Like those who have fallen into deep sleep, they were unmoved by the twitching of a single ear; like curd left over by a cowherd, they were free from flies and the twitching of gnats at the corners of their mouths.
The honey was scattered by flies that had exhausted themselves in every house; the dwellings were made crimson with lac from the gardens of blossoming aśoka trees.
The trees were perpetually moist and in full bloom due to winds carrying showers of spray, while all the grass covering the ground was pierced by the buds of the Kadamba flowers.
White with heaps of blossoming *ketaka* flowers from which the creepers were pruned, it carried the deep, heavy humming of swarms of bees moving through the air.
From its windows and caves issued clouds resting upon the white-washed walls; it was further distinguished by rows of full lotus ponds and vast royal palaces.
It possessed cool and pure grassy meadows shaded by dense foliage, where the stars were reflected in the dewdrops clinging to the tips of every blade of grass.
Its dwellings were white with an unceasingly falling rain of blossoming snow, and its trees bore wonderful clusters of blossoms, leaves, and excellent fruit.
The young women were fast asleep within the inner chambers of the house, sheltered by clouds; the lamps were rendered useless by the lightning flashing from the clouds resting upon the palace roofs.
The pavilion resounded with the thick, humming drone of the winds from the mountain caves, while the temple was enchanting with wandering cakoras, hārītas, and does.
With breezes moving slowly toward it, languid with the thick fragrance exhaled by blossoming kandalī plants, the tree’s tender leaves were swaying.
It was filled with throngs of women absorbed in the playful dalliance of quails and partridges, and it was tumultuous with the clamor of ruddy geese, cuckoos, and crows.
It was garlanded with the blue fruits of *śāla*, *tāla*, *tamāla*, and lotuses, and its trees were entwined with the graceful arrangements of encircling creepers.

Of those pleasure groves, whose windows were entwined by creepers with swaying shoots; which were fragrant with blooming *kandalas* and *śilīndhras*; which possessed pavilions where the leaves of *tālī* and *tamāla* trees performed a dance; and which were cooled by the blossoming trees of the gardens.

Of those [forests] where herds of cows were agitated by the movement of the wooden gates of the water-wheels; which were beautified by grounds of dark green crops and flowers; whose river-courses were concealed by rows of trees on their banks; and which possessed dense canopies formed by the tips of flowering creepers.

The ponds were fragrant with the nectar of the garden lilies; their lotuses were obscured by swarms of bees blinded by the scent; their rows of lotuses surpassed the splendor of Indra’s palace; and the sky was reddened by the pollen of the multitude of blossoms.

[It was a place] where mountain rivers flowed with a gurgling roar, radiant with the brilliance of clouds as white as kunda flowers; where there were dwellings of blossoming creepers shimmering atop palatial mansions, and where sweet-voiced birds moved about playfully and restlessly.

There, young men rested upon carpets of blossoming flower petals, while playful women wound garlands around their feet; everywhere, the paths were crowded with excellent creepers shimmering in beauty, bristling with beautiful new sprouts like teeth.

Of those places crowded with tender, newly sprouted lotuses; whose dwellings are veiled by hanging curtains of clouds; whose grounds are renowned for being green with necklaces of frost; and where the womenfolk are distressed by the lightning from clouds resting upon the palaces.

[The hermitage] of those who are beautiful with the shimmering fragrance of blue lotuses, where the cowherds look up expectantly at the sound of the "hum" of the peacocks, where the courtyards of the houses are filled with the playful deer resting in confidence, and where waterfalls and thick sprays of spray rise up as they dance.

Where the winds, intoxicated by fragrance, strike those who are distressed; where the lamps are forgotten amidst the blazing of medicinal herbs upon the ramparts; where the dwellings are crowded with flocks of birds agitated by clamor; and where the conversations of the water-birds along the streams are heard as a confused din.

Who is able to describe the splendor of those mountain dwellings, where the falling drops of water are as beautiful as a shower of pearls, cooling all the trees, creepers, grasses, and sprouts, and where the flowers never cease to bloom?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: There, those two goddesses fell into the village whose inner nature was cool—the Goddesses of Enjoyment and Liberation—just as the glories of worldly enjoyment and liberation fall upon a man who is tranquil and has realized the Self.
By that much time and through that practice, she became Līlā; because her sole body was pure knowledge, she possessed stainless vision of the three periods of time.
Then she spontaneously recalled, by her own natural power, all those previous states of transmigration from her former births, deaths, and so forth.
Līlā said: "O Goddess, having seen this place through your grace, I remember everything that occurred here in the past, as well as all other subsequent deeds."
In this world, I was once an aged woman, with limbs covered in visible veins, emaciated and grey; a Brahmin woman whose hands and belly were as rough as the tips of dried *darbha* grass.
A wife who brings prosperity to her husband's lineage, who is skilled in milking and churning, is like a mother to all sons and a bringer of joy to guests.

Devoted to the gods, the twice-born, and the virtuous, her limbs were moistened with ghee and cow's milk; she was the cleanser of frying pans, sacrificial vessels, water-pots, and all other household utensils.
She constantly had her forearms smeared with fragments of food and a single glass bangle; she was devoted to honoring her son-in-law, daughter, brother, father, and mother.
From the very moment she entered the palace until her body’s dissolution, she spent her days and nights wasted away, incessantly speaking with agitation, "Long! Long! for a very long time.
"What am I? What is this saṃsāra?"—such a conversation, even in a dream, is unheard of for the wife of a dull-witted Vedic scholar who possesses such a perverted intellect.
She was intent on a single goal: the gathering of cow-dung fuel for cooking; her head was wrapped in a faded woolen blanket, and her limbs were emaciated.
She was intent on extracting a worm from the root of a young calf's ear; she was hurriedly calling for a potsherd to water the vegetables growing in her house.
The young calves were satisfied by the grass at the edge of the dark blue waves of water; every moment, the doors of the houses were being smeared with fresh plaster and painted.
For the sake of policy, she never deviated from the reproachful words of the household servants, just as the shoreline of the ocean, due to its fixed boundary, never oversteps its limit.
She was marked by a single earring that resembled a withered leaf, swinging upon her ear like the livelihood of a living being terrified of old age, which must be struck with a wooden staff.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus, she moved about within the hollows of the mountain villages and, with a smile, showed them to Sarasvatī as she was wandering there.
This is my flower garden, adorned with clusters of *pāṭala* trees; this is my grove of *aśoka* trees, with its pavilions in the flowering park.
This is the calf tied to the branch of a tree on the bank of the Puṣkīraṇī; this is that very heifer named Karṇikā who has cast off her leafy fodder.
This is that wretched water-carrier of mine, so full of sloth; today, for the eighth day, she weeps with eyes drenched in tears.
"O Goddess, here I have eaten; here I have dwelt; here I have stayed; here I have slept; here I have drunk; here I have given; and here I have taken."
"This son of mine, named Jyeṣṭhaśarman, is weeping in the house; this milch-cow of mine is grazing on the grassy meadow in the forest."
Let us look upon this porch of mine, which is grey with coarse ash and lime, as if it were my own five-sensed body dwelling in the house, destined for the fire of destruction.
This kitchen area, surrounded by formidable and flourishing pumpkin vines, is like a second body of mine.
These kinsmen, their eyes copper-red from weeping, have become a bond upon this earth; with rudrākṣa beads placed upon their armlets, they carry fuel for the fire.
In the rocky clefts, its form was perpetually veiled by waves that snapped at clusters of flowers while their ripples brushed against the leaves of the creepers on the shore.
With its grassy plateaus on the edges strewn with spray from the excellent creepers, and with spray from blue lotuses frothing as they strike against the surfaces of stone slabs;
The clusters of the midday sun’s rays were turned into frost by the downpour of blossoming flowers, while the trees on the riverbanks resounded with the intense noise of the falling blooms.
It was pervaded by heaps of flowers that caused great brilliance, appearing like coral through the reflected luster of blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees.
By the village stream, intoxicated by its great whirlpool of clamor, its village children were utterly preoccupied with the abundance of fruit being carried along.
Its stone floor was washed by water tossed by the rippling waves, and it was perpetually cooled by the shade of dense-leaved trees that covered it.
This house-pavilion is now visible, beautiful with its winding flowering creepers, and its windows covered by clusters of blossoming leaves.
Here resides my husband, whose form is that of the vital ether, the lord of the earth girdled by the four oceans.
He remembered that this had indeed been his former desire; with a nature characterized by intense spiritual urgency, he thought, "May I quickly become a king myself."
O Supreme Goddess, with only eight dinars, he obtained a prosperous kingdom that granted him confidence for a long time.
O King, that lord of mine, my husband, remains here in the sky within his house, invisible like the wind in the air or like fragrance in the breeze.
Right here, within the space of the tip of my thumb, that very sky abides as the realm of my lord; it is fully understood to extend for millions of yojanas.
O Sovereign Mistress, we two are as if in the sky, and my husband’s kingdom is restored to its natural state; this vast Mahāmāyā has spread forth, filled with thousands of mountains.
Therefore, O Queen, it is my desire to go once again to my husband’s city; come, let us go there—for what distance is too great for those who are resolute?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus, that lady bowed to the Goddess and, quickly entering the pavilion, flew with her into the sky, which was as dark as a cloud, like a bird.
Resembling a mass of crushed collyrium, as beautiful as a single tranquil ocean, like the body of Nārāyaṇa, and possessing the pure luster of a bumblebee's back.
Having transcended the path of the clouds and likewise the region of the winds, he then ascended the path of the sun and passed beyond the path of the moon.

Having gone beyond the path of the immovable ones (dhruvamārga), having reached the path of those being perfected (sādhyas), and having completely transcended the earth of the perfected ones (siddhas), he leaped over the sphere of heaven.
Having gone beyond the world of Brahmā to the realm of the Tuṣitas, and having transcended Goloka, Śivaloka, and the world of the ancestors;
Having crossed over the worlds of the bodiless and the embodied, and having gone further and further away, she finally became somewhat awakened.
Afterwards, he looked back toward the expanse of the sky that had passed away, until not even a trace of the moon, sun, stars, or anything else was visible below.
It stood motionless and deep, filled with darkness that occupied the hollows of the quarters; resembling the interior of a single vast ocean, it was as solid as a mountain of rock.
Līlā said: "O Goddess, tell me, where has the light of the sun and other luminaries gone? How can darkness become motionless within the belly of a stone and graspable by the fist?"
The Goddess said: "O sir, you have come to such a height in the sky that even the lights of the sun and other luminaries are no longer visible."
Just as a firefly at the bottom of a great dark well cannot be seen by one following behind, so too, because of this, the sun cannot be seen below here.
Līlā said: "Oh, how far we have both come upon this path! Even the sun is not perceived in the least, appearing like a minute particle of dust beneath our feet."
"O Goddess, please tell me: what other path might there be beyond this, and of what nature is it? And how, O Mother, is it to be traversed?"
The Śrī Devī said: Beyond this, ahead of you, is the shell-like crust of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), from which the moon and other celestial bodies have arisen as mere particles of dust.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: While they were conversing thus, the shell of the universe arrived, like two bees reaching the dense pavilion on the side of a mountain.
Therefore, you have emerged from that without any affliction, as if from the sky; for that which is established in certainty is the Vajra Master, and nothing else.
Then, her consciousness being free from obscuration, she beheld that which was spread out everywhere—the exceedingly radiant water and other elements on the far shore of the cosmic egg.
Ten times greater than the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), water is situated there; it stands enveloping [the egg] like the skin on the surface of a walnut.
Therefore, fire is ten times [greater] than that; wind is ten times greater than that; space is ten times greater than that; and beyond that is the supreme ether.
In that supreme void, no conceptualizations of middle, beginning, or end arise at all, like talk of the son of a barren woman.
It is absolute, expansive, peaceful, beginningless, and free from delusion; devoid of beginning, middle, or end, it abides within the Great Self.

If a stone were to fall by force upon this [earth] with supreme power until the end of the eon, and even the king of birds were to fly up from there with force; even the wind, moving with a single impulse, would not find the space of a single yojana within that stainless sky during that entire eon.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: There, O Wind, having in an instant transcended the coverings of earth, water, fire, as well as space and the ether, each ten times greater than the preceding;
He beheld the supreme ether, devoid of all measurement; this entire world was spread out therein like a mere egg.
She beheld such creations, veiled within cosmic eggs, flashing by the millions in the sky like motes of dust in a sunbeam.
In the great ocean of space, within the waters of great emptiness, there arise bubbles of the nature of the great liquid of consciousness, possessing the radiance of a hundred million.
Some he saw falling downward, some ascending upward, others moving horizontally, and still others remaining motionless, established in their own consciousness.
Wherever and in whatever manner consciousness arises for whomsoever, there and in that very manner does their form arise.

It is not here, nor indeed there; neither above nor below, nor are there any comings and goings. That state is something entirely other than this; for that [state] is indeed beyond the arrival of the body.
There, by its very nature as consciousness, it arises again and again; yet through its own volitions, it comes to rest, like the web of volitions born from a child's imagination.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahman, tell me this: what would be below, what would be above, and what would be horizontal in that radiant realm, if it were not situated even here?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: All these cosmic eggs, together with their coverings, shine within the great, infinite void—due to faulty perception—like clusters of hair seen in the sky.
Since all categories of existence run toward [the Self] because they lack independence, that which is the earthly portion within the cosmic egg is below, while the other is above.
When large ants move upon a round clod of earth in the sky, their feet are said to be toward the ten directions and below, while their backs are above.
In the hearts of some, the surface of the earth was covered by a web of trees and anthills, while the stainless sky was surrounded by gods, humans, and demons.
