This world, together with its villages, cities, and mountains, has arisen along with that which has come into being; it is like a ripe walnut encased in its skin, produced by conceptual construction.
Just as female elephants flash about within the expanse of the Vindhya forest, so do the atoms of the cosmic egg flash within its vast interior.
In that [atom] is everything, from which everything arises, and which is everything in every respect; it is eternally composed of all things, and likewise exists even within each minute atom.
In that ocean of supreme light, which consists of pure consciousness, the waves known as world-eggs (brahmāṇḍas) come and go incessantly.
Some remain empty within, their nights of conceptual construction having come to an end; like waves in the ocean, they are carried along in the ocean of emptiness.
For some, a gurgling roar set in at the end of an intermediate eon; it was not heard by others, nor perceived by them, as their senses were overwhelmed by their own nature.
In others, at the first commencement, creation unfolds within the pure stages, like the subtle form of a sprout within the husk of moistened seeds.
At the onset of the great dissolution, the sun’s rays, lightning, and mountains began to melt away, like particles of snow under the heat.

Some who have not yet attained the spiritual stages fall [into lower realms] for an entire kalpa; indeed, they are born again only when their [karmic impressions] are finally exhausted, at which point they consist of pure consciousness.
Some remained as if paralyzed, like tufts of hair in the sky; those whose consciousness had thus arisen appeared like the vibrations of the wind.

When the very beginning of the Vedic scriptures has been set forth otherwise than through traditional practice (ācāra), then the undertaking of others as well is likewise established as being of an impermanent sequence.
Some are beings such as Brahmā, some are creators and protectors such as Viṣṇu, some are other lords of creatures, and some are beings without a protector.
Some are lords of diverse creations, some are of the nature of animals, some are filled with a single ocean, and others are devoid of birth.
Some were masses of solid rock; some had worms within them; some consisted entirely of deities; and some had humans within them.
Some are filled with eternal darkness, and likewise inhabited by beings; some are filled with eternal light, and likewise inhabited by beings.
Some are filled with mosquitoes, possessing the splendor of the udumbara fruit; some are eternally empty within, while others are sentient beings whose very nature is the vibration of emptiness.
Other such creations, which here exist within the internal consciousness, do not even enter the realm of conceptualization, just as a mountain filling the sky does not.
Their garment is such a vast expanse of great space, spread out, which is not measured even by Viṣṇu and the other gods as they proceed throughout the duration of their lives.
Residing within each individual egg-sphere like a jewel on a bracelet, the elemental nature of earth, by its own inherent character, acts as an attractor of beings.
O Great-minded One, since that which is our all-encompassing majesty does not fall within the range of my intellect, I have no power to describe that world.

Just as intoxicated yakṣas dance within a vast, dense forest of terrifying darkness without seeing one another, so do many great worlds flash forth within the expanse of the supreme, far-extended sky.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having thus reflected, as they emerged from their own world, they suddenly beheld the inner apartments once they had departed.
The great royal corpse was filled with flowers standing in full bloom; beside the corpse sat the body of Cittalīlā.
Crowded with people in deep slumber due to the dense darkness of night, it was languid with the fragrance of incense, sandalwood, camphor, and saffron.
Beholding that other world of her husband, Līlā, intent on departing for the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), fell from that very sky into this world with a body formed by her resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
Having pierced through the shell of the cosmic egg and repeatedly breaking through the veil of worldly existence, he entered his master’s slightly expanded world of conceptualization.
Together with that goddess, he reached once again the vast pavilion of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), which was surrounded by protective enclosures; having entered it with such speed, he proceeded.
She beheld the mire-pool of her husband’s world-creating imagination, like a lioness entering a mountain cave darkened by clouds.
O Goddesses, you two entered that void which is the self of the void of the universe, just as an ant enters a ripe bilva fruit within the shell of the cosmic egg.
There, having passed beyond other worlds, mountains, and the intermediate space, they reached the earth's surface, which was crowded with mountain ranges and oceans.
Having gone to Jambudvīpa, which is adorned by Meru and has the interior of nine petals, one then reaches the mandala of Līlānātha in the land of Bhārata-varṣa.
In the meantime, in that very circle on the adorned ground, a certain neighboring king, swollen with pride, launched a sudden assault.
Because of that, the sky became utterly congested with beings from the three worlds who had gathered there for the sake of witnessing the fury of the battle.
While they were thus unawares, those two goddesses beheld the sky, crowded with hosts of sky-dwellers and garlanded as if by clouds.
It was accompanied by hosts of Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, and Vidyādharas, and surrounded by Apsarases from the heavenly realm who were eager to seize the heroes.

It was filled with blood-drinking, flesh-eating, and blood-thirsty bhūtas, rākṣasas, and piśācas who were frantic for prey, while the women of the vidyādharas held their hands full of showers of flowers.
It was surrounded by vetālas, yakṣas, and kūśmāṇḍas, who, out of a desire for duels and eager observation, had seized mountain slopes as shields to protect themselves from the falling of weapons.
The circle of beings fled through the expanse of the sky along the path of the missiles, while the spectators, agitated by their own vanity, were filled with intense excitement.
There, rumors of the imminent battle with Bhīma circulated among one another, while beautiful women, eager for playful laughter and amorous gestures, held chowries.

[I praise] the hymn of auspiciousness by the Supreme Sage, which is applied through the contemplation of phenomena; [I praise] the hymn on the occasion of the many perfected goddesses of the world-lords.

It was radiant with the soldiers of Indra, who were busily engaged in bringing back heroes worthy of heaven; it possessed the tall elephants known as the World-Guardians (Lokapālas), adorned for the sake of the brave.
The Gandharvas and Cāraṇas were intent on honoring the arriving heroes, while the noble warriors were gazed upon by the side-long glances of the celestial women who were eager for the brave.
It was a source of throngs of women eager for the embrace of the staff-like arms of heroes; and by the white glory of its warriors, it turned the sun into the moon.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, what kind of warrior is designated by the word 'hero' (śūra)? Who would be the ornament of heaven, and who would be a mere child-warrior (ḍimbhāhava)?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: He who, for the sake of his lord engaged in conduct prescribed by the scriptures, dies or becomes victorious in battle, is a hero and a partaker of the world of heroes.
Otherwise, a man who meets his death in battle with his limbs severed by living beings is said to be one slain in a tumultuous fray; such a person becomes an inhabitant of hell.
The man who fights for the sake of one whose conduct deviates from the scriptures shall go to an inexhaustible hell when he dies in battle.
One who fights while conforming to the meaning of the scriptures as far as possible and to worldly conventions, and who is likewise devoted—such a person is called a hero.

O noble-minded one, for the sake of a cow, for the sake of a Brahmin, and for the sake of a friend, he died through his effort to protect one who had sought refuge; thus, he became an ornament of heaven.
Those kings who remained ever devoted solely to the protection of their own country when it was to be protected, and those who died for that purpose, are heroes who attain the world of heroes.
Those who die in battle for the sake of a king who is intent on harming his subjects, or even for a lord who is no king at all, surely go to hell.
For those who, whether belonging to kings or even to those who are not kings, die in battle with their limbs severed while acting contrary to the scriptures, they indeed go to hell.
If the battle were conducted in accordance with righteousness, then order would prevail; otherwise, intoxicated and devoid of fear of the next world, they would utterly destroy everything.
"Wherever a hero is slain, he goes to heaven"—such are the common sayings; however, the definitive conclusion of the scriptures is that one who fights for the sake of dharma is a hero.
Those who endure the edge of a sword for the sake of those who possess virtuous conduct are called heroes; all others are merely children slain in a brawl.
For their sake, celestial nymphs stand in the sky during battle with longing hearts, uttering words to the great beings who have become heroes.

The sky shone forth as if its splendor were raised in celebration, filled with the sweet and languid songs of Vidyādharīs, crowded with amorous women busy arranging garlands of Mandāra flowers, and graced by rows of celestial chariots where lovely Suras and Siddhas rested.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then Līlā, standing upon the earth endowed with vidyā, beheld from the sky the world where the Apsarases were dancing out of longing for Vīravara.
Within his own kingdom, protected by his lord and adorned with military strength, there was a certain vast forest as terrifying as a second sky.
The two armies stood agitated, resembling two gentle oceans; dense with great undertakings and intoxicated, they remained under the command of two kings.
Ready for battle and well-armored, he was as wonderful as a blazing fire; his eyes were marked by agitation at the sight of the onset of the first blows.
It carried people along by means of a downpour from the edge of uplifted, stainless swords, and it was filled with gleaming battle-axes, spears, slings, lances, and mallets.
It was shaken by the falling of forests agitated by the flapping wings of Garuḍa, and it possessed shimmering golden armor that gleamed under the light of the rising sun.
With weapons raised in fury as they glared at one another’s faces, they were fixed in mutual stares as if painted upon a wall.
Its established order was maintained by long-drawn-out boundaries of writing, while the clamor of its irresistible great armies drowned out all conversation.
The drum had long since fallen silent from the pride of the previous blows, and the entire army was rendered sluggish by the stationary positions of the bound warriors.
It was divided by a single bridge in its center, which was two bow-lengths wide and empty within, like a single ocean agitated by the wind at the end of an eon.
The body is a master over which anxiety, distress, and agitation hold sway; its throat-skin is that of a croaking frog, and the cavern of its heart is frail and afflicted.
It possessed countless soldiers ready to sacrifice their very lives and all their possessions, and its archers held bows drawn back to their ears, intent on discharging floods upon floods of arrows.
Countless soldiers stood motionless, watching for the fall of the blows; the scene was crowded with the frowns of those whose brows were hardened by mutual longing and intensity.
The armor produced a harsh clanging sound from the mutual friction [of weapons], while the hollows sought by cowards were scorched by the mouths of heroic warriors.
Its existence was rendered uncertain by the mere sight of its mutual configuration; it possessed tall, aged elephants whose every hair was attached to all its limbs.
Because of that state in which his life-force was distracted by the anticipation of the previous blow, the sound of the waves was completely stilled, and it resembled a city sealed in sleep.
The clamor of the multitude of conchs and trumpets was stilled, and the drums were hushed; all the clouds of dust settled upon the earth and into the sky.
Abandoned from behind by those intent on flight, it shone like an ocean filled with countless fish in the form of a spreading *makara* array, with its finger-jewels serving as its islands.
The clusters of flower-bunches on the banners surpassed the stars in the sky, while the trunks of the elephants raised aloft turned the interior of the firmament into a forest.
With all its weapons on the same side as the flood of shimmering, trembling light, the interior of the sky was blown upon by breaths that were gasping with the sounds "dham-dham."
It was radiant with gods whose wicked conduct had been trampled by the formation of the wheel-array, and it contained multitudes of nāgas fleeing in terror from the fury of the garuḍa-array.
With its front ranks shattered by the falcon-array (śyenavyūha) and its excellent sounds [of battle], there were vast multitudes falling down in heaps as they struck one another.
It resounded with the fierce cries of excellent heroes emerging from the arrangement of various arrays, and it was filled with circles of intoxicated mallets brandished and raised aloft by hands.
The sun was darkened by the clouds formed by the rays of Kṛṣṇa’s weapons, while the sound of his arrows resembled the whistling of dry leaves tossed by the wind.
It stood like a multitude of many kalpas and the highest kalpas gathered together, like a single ocean arisen and agitated by the winds of universal dissolution.
It quivered like the two wings of Mount Mahāmeru severed all at once, resembling a mountain of collyrium shaken by a turbulent wind.

It was like turbulent darkness rising from the caverns of Pātāla; its banks were restless with the frantic dancing of intoxicated beings, resembling the Lokāloka mountain; it appeared as if the earth itself had risen up, having burst through the mass of the great hells.

With floods of water in the form of the sunlight of the day turned dark by the rays of their swaying spears, maces, swords, and axes, he seemed for a moment to be preparing to turn the entire vessel of the world into a single ocean with his bottomless and infinite torrents.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, among the kings eager for battle, the warriors, the ministers, and the spectators in the sky, these words broke forth:
The sky, strewn with the heads of heroes, shone like a lake with swaying lotuses and like a river carrying birds, appearing as if it were filled with stars.
Behold: at midday, these clouds and sunbeams appear as if they were twilight, reddened by the winds carrying floods of blood-stained droplets and vermilion.
"O Blessed One, what is this? Is the sky filled with straw? This is not straw; O heroes, these are clouds of arrow-showers."
As many drops of dust as are moistened by blood upon the earth, for so many thousands of years shall those warriors have their dwelling in heaven.
"Do not fear; these are not swords with the luster of blue lotus petals; these are the playful glances from the eyes of Lakṣmī, who gazes upon heroes."
The flower-armed god began to loosen the girdles upon the hips of the celestial women, who were eager for the embrace of their heroes.
With their creeper-like arms swaying, their hands like red shoots, their eyes intoxicated by flower-clusters, and fragrant with the scent of honey;
The deities of the Nandana grove, singing with sweet voices, have begun to dance in anticipation of your arrival.
This army breaks its own adversaries from within with harsh axes, just as a village woman breaks her lover’s heart with her glances and gestures.
Alas! My father’s head, adorned with flaming earrings, has been carried by my broad-headed arrow to the vicinity of the sun, like the eighth planet [Rāhu] drawn near the sun by Time.
With his arms raised high, he whirled with speed the wheel known as the *citradaṇḍa*, upon which two large stones were fixed by their feet and ankles and spun around.
This warrior shines like Yama; he comes from the direction of the realm of Yama. As he withdraws his army from all sides, come, let us go back the way we came.
Headless trunks, crowded with flocks of herons wheeling in confusion over freshly severed heads, dance wildly on the battlefield, reaching as high as palm trees.
In the assemblies of the hosts of gods, conversations were held among themselves: "When will these wise ones go to the other world? How will they go? Who will go? From where?"
He swallows the approaching armies as the ocean swallows rivers; alas, how formidable is that warrior, with his battle arrays of fish and sea-monsters!
Rows of sharp iron arrows were strewn upon the temples of the elephants, like full-fledged showers of rain fallen upon the peaks of mountains.
As he was about to say, "Alas, my head has been carried away by the spear," the sky resounded with the cry "I live! from his head, like the warbling of a bird in the air.
"Let this army, which drenches us with a rain of mechanical stones, be forcibly restrained by means of a network of iron chains."
Free from wrinkles and grey hair, his former wife, who was an Apsaras, recognized her husband as slain in battle and accepted him.
The splendors of the forests of spears, their forms fashioned from the very beginning, were like rows of steps for the heroes to ascend to heaven.
On the chest of the warrior, whose body was as lovely as beautiful gold, that beloved woman—a celestial nymph—was seen, intent on searching for her husband.
"Alas! Our army has been destroyed by warriors with uplifted fists, just as the plateau of the celestial mountain is overwhelmed by the great waves of universal dissolution."
"Fight at the front, you fools! Carry away the half-dead men; do not strike down your own with kicks, you lowest of men!"
While the throng of Apsarases is intent on braiding their hair and filled with intense longing, let this soldier, possessing a divine body, be observed as he approaches their side.
On the banks of the celestial river, where golden lotuses are in bloom, gladden him who has come from afar with the shade, the cool waters, and the breezes.
With the tips of their fierce bones shattered by the clashing of various weapons, they flew through the sky like scattered stars, emitting shrill cries.
In the sky, which is like a life-giving river flowing with the water of arrows and whirling with circular eddies, even mountains are reduced to the state of minute mud.
With the heads of heroic kings whirling on their orbital paths, the thorns of sword-blades became entangled in the stalks of the creepers that were the rays of their weapons.
With the banners of its lotus stalks and petals having drawn in bees, the sky was turned into a lotus pond where the lotuses swayed in the moving wind.
Like ants on a mountain covered with a heap of dead elephants, the timid women shrink away, as if from the broad chests of men.
Breezes blow, causing the tresses of the Vidyādhara women to flutter, heralding their union with a beloved whose unsurpassed beauty is unprecedented.

As the parasols flew upward and remained poised in the sky, they attained the state of moons; indeed, by means of his fame incarnate, he brought about the whiteness of those royal umbrellas as if by the moon itself.
At the end of his fainting from death, the soldier, in the blink of an eye, attained an immortal body fashioned by the artisan of his own karma, like a city in a dream.
Showers of spears, javelins, double-edged swords, and discuses were released with joy; their fragments remained in the ocean of the sky, crowded like fish and sea-monsters.
The expanse of the sky, filled with white umbrellas severed by arrows like swans, shines as if covered by hundreds of thousands of gathered full moon discs.
With fly-whisks flying through the sky and making beautiful gurgling sounds, it possesses the splendor of a mass of waves whose movement is checked and stirred by the wind.
Umbrellas, chowries, and banners, shattered by weapons, are seen scattered across the field of the sky like stalks of the rice-plant of fame.
Behold, O fortunate one, the shower of spears being carried through the sky and brought to destruction by my arrows, like the beauty of the crops being destroyed by locusts as they approach.
This clashing of sword-blades from the soldiers with outstretched staff-like arms, produced from their hard armor, is like the fierce roar of Death itself.
Shattered by the wind of sophistry and crushed by the torrents from their tusks, the elephants lie broken like mountains in this age of the destruction of mankind.
The chariot-division, with its horses yoked to the lord of the wheel, is cast into a great lake of blood; its movement overcome by cries of "Alas! Alas!", it struggles in distress.
By the clanging sounds produced by the collision of shields, armor, walls, and swords, the Night of Doom, as she dances, plays a war-lute as it were.
Behold how the quarters of the sky are reddened by the wind sprinkled with droplets from the streams of blood shed by men, elephants, donkeys, and horses.
In the sky, which was like a cloud of sword-blades and as dark as Kālī’s hair, she appeared like lightning amidst clouds heavy with a garland of arrow-buds.
With weapons whose blades were smeared with fresh blood clinging to them, the world shone like the agitated realm of fire, as if ablaze.
Showers of *bhuśuṇḍīs*, spears, tridents, swords, clubs, and javelins fell from their hands in profusion, being cut and shattered by one another.
The battle, where the Yātudhānīs were struck down by Akṣobhya alone and their mutual activities ceased, was perceived through the wisdom of his wrathful gaze as if it were a dream.
The terrifying clamor of battle, arising from the agitation of wounds, seems to sing as it is struck by the incessant clashing of unceasing weapons.
The ocean of battle, filled with the fierce powder of weapons from mutual clashing, became as if composed entirely of sand, with severed umbrellas for its waves.

This mountain of battle, its world of the guardians of the quarters filled with the echoes of musical instruments spreading forth with impetuous passion, seemed like the mountain of the cosmic dissolution moving through the sky with fierce wings, expert in its retrograde course.

Alas, alas! Woe! These iron arrows—scorched by the manifest flashes of lightning leaping forth from the mouths of their formidable shafts, whirring as they are impelled by strings vibrating with a twanging sound—carry away a multitude of mountain rocks.
"Before these arrows, blazing like a flaming fire, can sever our limbs with a sharp *chhitti* sound, come quickly from here, O friend! Let us go; this fourth watch of the day is passing away."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then that ocean of battle became like one intoxicated, as if performing a frantic dance, with its waves of horses intent on leaping upward.
With its white fish-swarms of arrows resting upon the foam of parasols, and its hollows agitated by the surging, restless waves of the cavalry;
It possessed the swirling eddies of armies led by rivers of various weapons, and its moving great mountains were the seats of herds of rutting elephants.

With his head whirling as it moved through the hundred revolutions of the whirling discus, he was like a blade of grass; the water-like luster of his brandishing sword was swallowed by the clouds of dust.

The two ships, whose multitudes of soldiers were neither broken nor unbroken as they shattered the expansion of the crocodile-array, caused the mountain caves to resound with the great gurgling roar of their whirlpools.
The mustard seeds were the flood of arrows emerging from the array of fish, and the circles of waves were the banners torn away by the surging currents of weapons.
His earrings were like whirlpools in a sea formed by weapons and water; his army, with its dense movement of fury, was like the great timi and timingila fish.
The army was terrifying with its waters consisting of black iron armor, while its ornaments—the troops and their leaders—were bound within the lines of whirlpools formed by headless trunks.
The quarters of the sky were thick with the mist and spray of arrows, while the singular, dense roar of the tumult drowned out every other sound.
The spray from fragments of heads was agitated by falling and leaping; wooden fragments of soldiers whirled about amidst the circular arrays of whirlpools.
Fierce in its agitation from the churning of the curved bows that produced harsh twanging sounds, it rose up as if from the netherworld with waves of soldiers surging forth without hesitation.
It was foaming with the parasols and banners that rose and fell in endless succession; the rushing current of the flowing rivers of blood swept away the trees that were the chariots.
It was filled with great bubbles of blood resembling elephants, and its aquatic creatures were the horses and elephants moving within the flowing current of the army.
That battle, like the battle for Ambaragrāma, was a marvel to men; it was as restless as mountains shaken by the earthquake at the time of universal dissolution.
With birds in its tossing waves, with the flanks of its banks formed by herds of falling elephants, and with the terrified troops of timid deer uttering loud "dhur-dhur" cries;
His army was as fragile as hundreds of locusts amidst rows of autumn reeds; his arrows were like leaping waves, and the earth was covered by the forest of his arrowy burden.
With the humming of moving bees as its sound, the caves serving as its deep-toned musical instruments, the army-cloud at long last arrived, with the leaping warriors as its lions.
A cloud of spreading dust, with falling armies for its mountain peaks, with the excellent bodies of chariots for its thunderbolts, and with the flashing circles of swords for its lightning.
A mass of flowers fell from their feet; banners and parasols became clouds; and elephants, like rafts, were swept away by the surging flood of rivers of flowing blood.
That battle became like the end of an aeon, agitated by the devouring of the world, with its banners, umbrellas, flags, chariots, and infantry scattered about.
He was like the sun, intensely radiant with the mass of falling rays of his stainless weapons, while the minds of all were scorched by the heat of his fierce vital force.
It was incessantly filled with showers of arrows from bows like Puṣkarāvarta clouds, while the sky was encircled by lightning in the form of streaks of sword-blades flashing like stone-slabs.
The mountain ranges of elephant herds fell into the ocean of blood that had been severed; the stars, scattered across the sky and falling down, produced a tinkling sound like pearls.

The sky was filled with clouds resembling the whirlpools of the waters of the Cakrakulyā river; the weapons were like the fire of cosmic dissolution, consuming the armies as if they were other worlds.

The pure mountain [of his body] covered the surface of the earth with a rain of thunderbolts in the form of weapons; the multitude of people was crushed by the falling mass of mountains that were the king of elephants.
The earth and sky were shrouded by clouds consisting of dense masses of arrow-showers; the solid ground was formed by the impact of the agitation of the great ocean of the vast army.
It was pervaded by those [soldiers] who, like a mountain by aquatic monsters stirred up by a fierce wind, were intent on crushing one another, appearing like a sudden eruption of weapons.

Pikes, swords, discs, arrows, spears, maces, *bhuśuṇḍīs*, and lances, clashing against one another with a roar as they were shattered, blazed forth in the ten directions by the hundreds, whirling about like the spectacle of objects tossed about by the winds at the end of an aeon.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, while those heaps of arrows stood like mountain peaks, all the cowards were broken and fled in the ten directions.
Upon mountains of elephant carcasses where rows of clouds rested, and amidst Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas sporting in an ocean of blood;
Of the great ones, steadfast in Dharma, endowed with virtue, vigor, and courage—pure lotuses of noble lineage, heroes who never turn back.
Duels broke out like the thundering of clouds; eager to swallow one another, they clashed like the surging floods of rivers.
A cage met with a cage, a multitude of elephants with a mass of elephants, a forest with a forest, and a mountain with a mountain, as they collided with force.
The flood of horses, with its mass of neighing steeds moving with rapid speed, was like a surge of waves upon the ocean, possessing a roar like the rush of billows.
One division of men fought against another division of men with equal weapons, like a current of reeds against a current of reeds, or as a wind-stirred force against a mass of air.
And a flood of chariots crushed the entire body of the enemy's chariot-force, just as a city, driven by fate, crushes an asuric city that has been cast up into the air.
With its archers as its banners, the army fought, covering the sky with a previously unseen rain-cloud formed by the downpour of autumnal arrows.
When warriors of feeble resolve flee by some stratagem during battles with uneven weapons, as if in the fire of the end of the world;
Wielders of the discus clashed with wielders of the discus, archers with archers, swordsmen with sword-fighters, and those armed with *bhuśuṇḍī* missiles with those armed with *bhuśuṇḍīs*.
The great wielders of maces fought with maces, the Kuntis with their spears, those armed with double-edged swords with sword-bearers, and those with darts in hand against those with darts.

Those with mallets were with those wielding mallets; those shining with clubs were with those bearing clubs; those who fought with spears were with spear-wielders; and those skilled with pikes were with those armed with pikes.
Those skilled in spears fought with spears; those praised for their axes fought with battle-axes; those wielding clubs fought with raised clubs; and those armed with stones fought with stones.
With nooses they were bearers of nooses; with spikes, bearers of spikes; with knives, they were knives; and with slings, they were equipped with them.
They hold adamantine fists and are raised up by adamantine hooks; they possess the knowledge of plowing with plows and are armed with tridents.
With nets of chains and with chains as delicate as bees, they were like masses of waves from the agitated ocean, tossed about by the onset of the dissolution of the world.
The single ocean of the sky shone forth, with the whirling fragments of the shattered discus as its eddies, the spray of arrows as its wind, and the revolving weapons as its sea-monsters.
With its aquatic creatures consisting of the heads of surging waves of upraised weapons, that ocean within the cavity of heaven and earth became impossible for even the gods to cross.
The army of the eight divine classes, divided into two wings, stood thus, with each half enraged by the two kings.
Listen now to the enumeration of the regions such as Madhyadeśa, which have come from the eastern directions; these are the provinces on the side of Padma, the Lord of Līlā.
In the east are the Kosalas, Kāśis, Māgadhas, Mithilas, Utkalas, Mekhalas, Karkaras, Mudras, and likewise the Saṃgrāmaśauṇḍakas.
The Mukhyas, the Himas, those headed by Rudra, the Tāmraliptas, as well as the Prāgjyotiṣas, the Vājimukhas, the Ambaṣṭhas, and the man-eaters.
The Varṇakoṣṭhas, the Saviśvotras, those who eat raw fish, the Vyāghravakras, the Kirātas, the Sauvīras, and the Ekapādakas;
There is a mountain here named Mālyavat, as well as Śivira, Añjana, Vṛṣaladhvaja, Padma, and others, along with the mountain Udayakara.
Now, to the southeast, these dwellers of the Vindhya mountains and other regions reside: the Cedis, the Vatsas, the Daśārṇas, and the Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, and Upavaṅgas.
The Kaliṅgas, Puṇḍras, Jaṭharas, Vidarbhas, Mekhalas, as well as the Śabaras, Anavarṇas, Karṇātras, and Purupūrakas.
The Kaṇṭakasthala people, the Pṛthagdīpakakomala, the Karṇāndhra, the Caulika, and likewise the Ārmaṇvata.
The Kākakas, Hemakuḍyas, and likewise the Śmaśrudharas; the Baligrīvas, Mahāgrīvas, Kiṣkindhas, and Nālikerins.
Now, these kings belong to the southern region of this Lord of Līlā: Vindhya, Kusumāpīḍa, Mahendra, and likewise Dardura.
Malaya and Sūryavān, as well as the Gaṇas who were prosperous in their kingdoms, were renowned as the Avantīs and likewise as the Śāmbavatīs.
The Daśapūraka, Kathācakra, Āreṣika, Ātura, and Kacchapa mountains; the Vanavāsa and Upagiri mountains, as well as the Bhadragiri mountains.
The Nāgaras, the Daṇḍakas, the Gaṇarāṣṭras, the Nṛrāṣṭrakas, the Sāhas, the Śaivārpyas, the Mūkas, the Karkoṭas, and the Vanavimbalas.
The Pampānivāsins, the Kairakas, the Karkavīrakas, the Sverikas, the Yāsikas, and the Dharmapattana-pañjikās;
The Kāśikas, Tṛṣṇakhallūlas, Yādās, Tāmraparṇakas, Gonardas, Kanakas, and those belonging to Dīnapattana.
The Tāmrīkas, those filled with deceit (Dambharākīrṇas), the Sahakauraṇakas, as well as the Vaituṇḍakas, the Tumbavanālas, the Ajinadvīpas, and the Karṇikas.
The Śivayas, who shine like the pericarp [of a lotus], the Kauṅkaṇas, the Citrakūṭakas, the Karṇāṭas, the Maṇṭavaṭakas, and likewise the Mahākaṭakikas.
The Āndhras, the Kolagiris, the Avantikas, the Vicerikas, the Caṇḍāyattas, the Devanakas, the Krauñcas, and likewise the Vāhas.
Śilākṣārodabha, Nanda, and Mardana—those known as the Malayas are remembered as the peaks of Citrakūṭa belonging to the hosts of Rākṣasas in Laṅkā.
Then, in the south-western direction, there are the Mahārājya and Surāṣṭra peoples, as well as those known as the Sindhu, Sauvīra, Śūdra, Ābhīra, and Draviḍa.
There are the Kīkaṭas, those known as Siddhakhaṇḍa, and also the Kāliruhās; here is the Hemagiri mountain, as well as the Raivataka mountain.
The Jayakacchas, Mayavaras, Yavanas, Bāhlīkas, Mārgaṇāvantas, Dhūmras, and those named Tumbakas are the living beings there.
Likewise, there were the hosts of Lājagas and those who dwell upon the mountains; then there were millions of people from Abdhitoṅka—these were the subjects of Līlāpati.
Now, hear of these districts situated as an antidote to that: first, in the western direction, there are these great mountains.
The king of mountains named Maṇimān, as well as Kurārpaṇagiri, Vanārkaha, Meghabhava, Cakravān, and Astaparvata.
The people known as the Pañcajanas are those who end the practice of brahmacarya at Kāśa; likewise, there are the Bhārakṣatas, the Pārakas, and the Śāntikas.
The Śaivyas, Āramarakas, Ākhyās, Guhas, as well as the Niyanas, Haihayas, Suhmagas, Tājikas, and Hūṇakas.
The Karkas, Giriparṇas, and Avamas dwelling in the regions of Pārśva and Kataka—those castes who have abandoned the boundaries of dharma are Mleccha tribes.
Beyond that is a land devoid of human habitation extending for two hundred yojanas; beyond that is the peak of Mount Mahendra, whose ground is composed of pearls and gems.
Beyond the hundreds of mountains is the mountain named Aśva; beyond that lies the formidable great ocean on the slope of Mount Pāriyātra.
In the northwestern direction lies the region of Girimati; likewise Veṇupati, and beyond that, the great earth ruled by Narapati.
Likewise, there were the Phalgunas, the Mandavyas, the Ekanetras, the Purukundas, and the Parashas, who meditated upon the solar orb.
Vanmilās, Nalinās, Dīrghās, those with long hair and long limbs, Raṅgās, Stanikās, Guruhās, and likewise Caluhās.
Beyond that is the incomparable kingdom of women, where cows, bulls, and offspring are their food. Then, in the north, there is the Himavat, then the Krauñca, and then the Madhumān mountain.
Kailāsa, Vasumān, and Meru; in their foothills dwell the people of both [regions]: the Madras, Āravas, Yaudheyas, Mālavas, and Śūrasenikas.
The Rājanyas are likewise to be known, as well as the son of Arjuna; and the Trigartas, the Ekapādas, the Kṣudrās, the Abalās, and those dwelling in Asvastava.
The Abalas, Prakhalas, Śākas, Kṣemadhūrtis, Daśadhanas, Āgāvas, Anyadaṇḍas, and likewise the Ahanyasanas—these are the ten [clans].
The Dhānadās, the Sarakas, and likewise the Vāṭadhānas; the Gāndhāras of the inner islands, and likewise the Avantīs and Suras.
Then there was the city named Takṣaśilā, and beyond that Vīlavagodhanī; then the land of Puṣkarāvarta, and after that the earth of Yaśovati.
Then there are Nābhimati, Bhūmi, Tikṣā, Kālavarā, as well as the city of Kāhaka and the city of Surabhūti.
Likewise, there were Ratikādarśa and Antarādarśa; then Piṅgalapāṇḍavya, and the Yātudhānakas on the Yamunā.
The Mānavas, the Nāgas, the Hematālas, and likewise their own respective faces; Himavān, Vasumān, Krauñca, Kailāsa, and similarly the Agas.
Beyond that is a land devoid of human settlements, measuring eight thousand yojanas; now hear in order about the inhabited regions to the northeast.
The Kālutas, the Brahmaputras, the Kuṇidas, and likewise the Khadinas; the Mālavas, the Randhrarājyas, and similarly the Vanas and the Rāṣṭras.
The Keḍavastās, the Siṃhaputras, and likewise those who have become dwarfs; the Sāvākaccas, the Āpalavas, the Kāmiras, and the Daradas.
Then there were the Abhisāsakas, the Jārvākās, the Palolas, the Kuvikas, the Autukas, and the Kirātās; these were the lowly peoples of the Golden Land.

Following that was the ground of the divine groves, then the splendor of Viśvāvasu’s exalted palace, then Mount Kailāsa with its lovely forests—a terrain equal to the celestial chariots of the Vidyādharas and the gods.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In that battle, which was terrible with men and elephants violently torn apart, and in which throngs of warriors rushed forward crying, "Me first! Me first!"—
These and many others there were reduced to ashes as they entered with great effort, like moths into a fire.
Other people from the Middle Country have not been cited by me here; listen to these as I shall describe the various positions of King Līlā.
The Taddehikas, Śūrasenas, Guḍas, Aśvaghanāyakas, Uttamajyotis, Bhadrāṇis, Madamadhyamikas, and others [are there].
The Sālūkas, Ākodyas, Mālās, Daujñeyas, Pippalāyanas, Māṇḍavyas, Pāṇḍunagaras, Saugrīvas, and others are the Gurus and Grāhas.
The Pāriyātras, Kurāṣṭras, Yāmunas, Udumbaras, Rājyāhvās, Ujjihānas, Kālakoṭikas, and Māthuras.
The Pāñcālas and those from Dharmāraṇya, likewise those from the north and the south; the people of Pāñcālaka, Kurukṣetra, and the Sārasvatas.
Driven by the forces of Avantī, Syandana, Śreṇī, Kunti, and Pañcanada, the army, quivering and fleeing, fell into a great abyss.
And the royal treasuries, ending with the Brahmā-wealth, were plundered like garments by the people; having fallen to the ground, they were trampled upon by rutting elephants.
The brave men of Daśapura, their bellies and necks severed by weapons, were attacked by arrows from the ground and cast into the lake at Yojana.
Bound by the strings of their own entrails emerging from their torn bellies, these *śāntika* spirits, their movements stilled, were devoured at night by *piśācas*.
By the Udravas and Bhadragiris, consecrated for the sacrifice of battle, the Maragas were cast into the pits of the earth like tortoises.
Fleeing with their blood streaming, their great speed brought to a halt, the Daṇḍikas were scattered by the Haihayas like deer driven by the wind.
The Daradas, whose teeth were shattered by the tusks of elephants and who had crushed their enemies, were carried away by the great river of blood like the sprouts of trees.
Devoured by iron arrows, the Chinese, their lives worn out and shattered, cast off their bodies in the ocean as if they were merely burdensome weights.
With their necks struck by spears hurled by the brave warriors of Karṇāṭa, the heroic Naladas were shattered like clusters of stars.
With their weapons bristling with the force of arrays of elephants and crocodiles, and engaging in hand-to-hand combat, the Dāśakas and Śakas roared aloud.
The people of Daśārṇa, like timi fish among reeds, were freed from their fetters and chains yet remained terrified of the net, hiding in the blood-stained mire.
By destroying the Gurjara army, the plucking of the hair of the Gurjara women was accomplished in battle by hundreds of the lofty, spear-like noses of the Tangana warriors.

From the streams of blood flowing from their ears, the warriors' wounds dripped like drops from clouds; the showers of their weapons were like rainforests, and the luster of their heroic arms was like the radiance of the sun.
Upon the Ābhīras, who were terrified by the ominous appearance of the dark sun shining from the circle of *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons, the enemies fell like herds of cows upon green pastures.
O Aṅga, that army, beautiful with its lovely golden ornaments and flowing with coppery [blood], was enjoyed by the Gauḍa warrior through the dragging of nails and hair.
In the battle, the Taṅgaṇas were scattered in pieces by the slicing of their armor with countless discuses, while vultures, eagles, arrows, and hawks [scattered] their remains.
Hearing the "guḍuguḍa" sound of the Gaudas flying up as they were churned by clubs, the Gandhara cattle fled ahead like Dravidians.
Resembling the ocean of the sky and carrying a multitude of banners, it created a dense, nocturnal darkness for the Pārasīkas.
Within the interior of the pure Ocean of Milk, which surged at the blow of Mount Mandara, he deposited his weapons like forests upon the snowy peaks of his enemies.
That multitude of weapons, which had flown through the courtyard of the sky like clouds, was seen as if it were leaping upon the ocean by means of the rolling waves.
The forest of the sky was seen filled with hundreds of moons by means of white parasols, dense with locust-like arrows, and indeed packed solid with spears.
The Kekayas were made to utter cries of distress like those of heroes drinking the liquor of death; their heads were covered in dust as they were overwhelmed by flocks of herons that filled the sky.
The daughters of the Kirāta army, having reduced their limbs to a state of passionlessness through the tumultuous clamor of their cries, seemed to roar as if with terrible thunder.
Those whose bodies were made of kāśa grass were overwhelmed by invisible birds through illusion, just as dust is scattered by agitated winds that have shaken their wings.
Maddened, thoroughly shaken, having cast aside their weapons and armor, the Narmadās—creators of jests—danced, laughed, and sang.
The shower of spears, accompanied by a network of tinkling bells, was driven by the wind of Śālva’s arrows and took on the appearance of a spray of water droplets.
The followers of Śibi, mangled by the Kauntas and struck down by whirling spears, were seen becoming corpses and being carried to heaven like Vidyādharas.
By the steady army, whose nature was to support the earth, the cities of the Pāṇḍus were plundered by the mere thrill of its movement.
Those soldiers were crushed by the intoxicated men of Kāśī from the land of the Five Rivers, like trees with trunks as formidable as tree-stems are by elephants.
The Brahmāvatsanaka trees, cut down by the wheels, fell to the earth; along with their horses, they were severed by the krakaca-saws like flowering trees.
The grove of white crows, mowed down by axes driven from bellies, was set ablaze by Bhadreśa, who stood at its side, with the fire of his arrows.
Against the wooden warriors, the aged elephants sank down, their tethering posts gone; they met their destruction in the battle, like fuel in a blazing fire.
Having wandered upward from Trigarta as far as Mitragarta, which was like a blade of grass, they entered the depths of Pātāla with their heads cast down in order to flee.
In the Māgadha army, radiant as an ocean stirred by a gentle breeze, the Mandas were submerged like old elephants in the mud.
On the field of battle, the Cedis seized the consciousness of the Taṅgaṇas, just as the heat of the sun takes away the delicacy of flowers scattered upon a path.
The people of Kausala, unable to endure the roar of the Pauravas, became like the Destroyer himself; they unleashed a torrential rain of maces, spears, arrows, and javelins.

With their limbs mangled by arrows, they became motionless like coral trees on a mountain; yet, with their forms drenched in thick, fresh blood that resembled the sun, they seemed to run away in terror.
With their forms shaken by the wind of the great weapons—the showers of iron arrows—they whirled about like clouds radiant with swarms of bees.

The clouds were like rain-bearing clouds, the rams were filled with wool as thick as arrows, the trees were covered with arrow-leaves, and the elephants roamed about, driven by the roar of that [battle].
The creatures dwelling in the hollows of the forest trees, worn out by old age and the decay of the forest kingdom, snapped as they were violently pulled away, like fragile threads.
When the wheels of the chariots were shattered and their riders pinned beneath them, throngs of people fell like clouds upon forested mountains.
Having reached the forest of *śāla* and *tāla* trees, which agitates the people, there was the cutting off of arms in that lofty grove of *sthāṇu* trees.
Beautiful women from the Nandana gardens, intoxicated by their youth and resorted to by the best of heroes, dwelt upon the forested slopes and groves of Mount Meru.
The excellent forest of the army shone with the sound of "tāra" cries for as long as it had not been reached by the enemy, which was like the flame of the fire at the end of an aeon.
Severed and joined with the Piśācas, their weapons snatched away by Bhūtas, the Daśārṇas fell before Karṇa like young calves.
Those whose lords were broken fled, desiring to conquer that splendor with their vigor, just as Kāśa grasses lose their luster when the vigor of the river's current has dried up.
Strewn with husks, embers, arrows, spears, swords, and mallets, even the deceptive snares of the necklets were cast away by the fleeing hell-beings.
The Kauntakṣetra people, having remained surrounded by warriors dwelling in Prastha, clearly fell into a state of powerlessness, like virtues overwhelmed by the wicked.
Dvipaya, having seized the heads of the Bāhudhānas in an instant with his broad-headed arrows, they quickly fled like lotus plants whose stalks have been severed.
Having debated with one another from beginning to end, the Sārasvatas achieved victory; like scholars in philosophical disputations, they were neither agitated nor defeated.
Dwarfish, mangled, and insignificant, they were turned back by the Yātudhānas; yet they attained supreme splendor, like fires extinguished by fuel that have now been kindled anew.
O Rāma, even Vāsuki, though agitated by his mass of tongues as he licks the nectar of the earth, would not be able to describe this excellent battle in its entirety.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, while the battle was exceedingly tumultuous and crowded with the terrifying sound of arm-slapping, as the sun was shrouded by increasing darkness and the hard armor was being shattered to pieces.
The waters flow as showers of stones fall, while the rivers are choked by the tossing of reeds and rows of lotuses.

And as the autumnal rivers arrived and receded far away, emitting sprays of fire produced by the friction of their mutual impact against the tips of the fruits; and as the autumnal rivers arrived and receded far away, emitting sprays of fire produced by the friction of their mutual impact against the tips of the fruits.
The ocean of the sky was filled with the swirling eddies of the lotus-faces of severed heads, rippling with waves, while the multitude of weapons formed a series of celestial Ganges rivers.

With thick clouds filled with weapons that resounded with the whizzing of the wind, which caused the perfected ones at the ends of the world-regions to suffer from the irritation of *kapikacchu* bristles.
With his majestic form softened by the remaining eighth part of his life-span, he became emaciated like a hero whose vigor has been spent by the force of a weapon's blow.
With their horses and elephants exhausted, their ranks broken, and the brilliance of their massed weapons dimmed, the armies, along with the very day itself, lost their former splendor.
Then, after the two commanders-in-chief had deliberated together with their ministers, they dispatched messengers to one another with the message: "Let the battle be called off."
There, due to exhaustion, the strength of their machines and weapons was diminished; consequently, at that time, everyone agreed to the cessation of battle.
Then, a certain warrior alone ascended the high flagpole-tip of a great chariot, like the Pole Star (Dhruva) mounted upon the edge of the two armies.
He brandished his white silken garment across the entire circle of the quarters, as if to say, "Let the battle cease," like a long, pure white ray of light against a dark sky.
Then the kettledrums resounded, their echoes filling the quarters of the sky, like the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds at the conclusion of the great dissolution.
When the vast sky was filled with the rivers of arrows and other weapons, they proceeded to come forth easily, like rivers flowing from a lake.
The movement of the soldiers' weapons gradually subsided, like the trembling of trees at the end of an earthquake, or like an ocean that has ceased its agitation.
Then the two armies began to emerge from the battle, like a flood of water flowing in the four directions from the single ocean at the time of universal dissolution.
With its faces as agitated as the churning Ocean of Milk when Mount Mandara was lifted up, the army gradually attained calmness as its whirlpools subsided.
Gradually, in a mere moment, the battlefield became as terrifying with its bloated corpses as it was empty when the ocean was swallowed by Agastya.
It was filled with a continuous succession of corpses, agitated by flowing rivers of blood, and resembled a forest of crickets filled with the humming and chirping of insects.

It resounded with the gurgling roar of waves from the currents of many great rivers of blood; it was filled with men who were frantic—some calling out in lamentation, some half-dead, and others still clinging to life.

A torrential waterfall of blood flowed from the masses of corpses, some dead and others half-dead; it caused the illusion that the living men standing upon the backs of the corpses were themselves trembling.

It was like a great forest torn apart by the wind, where fragments of clouds rested upon the peaks of the mountain-like heaps of lordly elephants, and masses of shattered chariots lay scattered about.
Horses and elephants were being swept away by the force of the flowing rivers of blood, while the field was crowded with arrows, spears, double-edged swords, maces, clubs, darts, and scimitars.
The ground was covered with saddles, blankets, armor, and mail; the corpses were shielded by a multitude of banners, yak-tail whisks, and silk streamers.
The wind whistled through the groves of quivers whose hoods were opening wide, while piśācas slept upon beds made of heaps of corpses and masses of straw.
It was covered by the rainbow-like luster of crowns, necklaces, and armlets, while its long ropes of thick entrails were being pulled by the hands of dogs and jackals.
It was bristling with the teeth of men whose lives were barely lingering, jingling slightly in the field of blood; it was filled with living men who, like frogs, were submerged in the mire of gore.
It bore hundreds of terrible rivers of blood, flowing from the mass of wood-like arms and thighs, with their hundreds of eyes protruding like excellent armor and body-plates.
It was crowded with wailing kinsmen and men who were half-dead or dead; its interior was blocked by arrows, weapons, chariots, horses, elephants, and saddle-cloths.
The sky was bent low by the circles of the staff-like arms of dancing headless trunks, while the cavities of the nostrils were moistened and oppressed by the stench of rutting ichor, fat, and marrow.

The lives of few were spared as they were held back by elephants, horses, and men who were themselves half-dead from the intense carnage; the drums were struck down by the forceful impact of the waves of rivers flowing with blood.
It was a hundred rivers of blood from slain elephants, horses, and crocodiles, with channels of blood hissed forth by the hosts of dying men.

It had a mouth filled with arrows and small living creatures, its sound was like that of a beautiful woman’s voice, and it was red with blood from the impact of the wind carrying the scent of the bodies of wives and their husbands.

It contained headless trunks (kabandhas) trampled by the trunks of great elephants whose noses were half-raised, and high headless trunks brought down by elephants and horses that were no longer under control.
[He saw] women weeping and wailing, fallen down, agitated, and vomiting blood; and noble ladies whose husbands were dead, who had cast away their weapons and surrendered their lives.
It was crowded with many travelers who had just departed from their camps, and it was filled with the living attendants being dragged away by the hands of corpse-carriers.
[He saw] a hundred rivers with hair for moss and curved lotuses for whirlpools, and a great river of flowing blood rich with high surging waves.

It was filled with half-dead men struggling to pull weapons stuck in their limbs, and with elephants and horses whose bodies were being offered as oblations amidst the wailing of those who had died in a foreign land.

It is known by such names as "the end of life," "recollection of sons," "sacrifice for a mother," and "supreme devotion to the deity"; it is described as the piercing pain that severs the vital organs, accompanied by cries of "Alas! Alas! and "O, what woe!"

Then he beheld one who was dying, whose accumulation of past actions (*prārabdha*) had been exhausted by his enemies, who was incapable of fighting elephants, and whose tutelary deity resided in the bodies of the deceased.
It is the flight of those who rely on the great heroism of contempt for death, yet it is the eager departure from a terrifying abode where whirlpools of unexpected blood swirl.

Aware of their misdeeds through the agony of being struck by arrows that pierce the vital organs, they began to be overrun by headless trunks like the mouths of vetālas that had commenced their assault.
It bore aloft banners, umbrellas, beautiful chowries, and lotuses; it scattered a crimson glow like that of twilight in all directions, possessing the splendor of a red lotus.
It was like an eighth ocean of blood, with the revolving rims of chariot wheels for its whirlpools, rich with clusters of foam from the banners, and beautiful chowries for its bubbles.
With its chariots overturned, resembling a city submerged in the mud of the earth, it was like a vast forest whose trees have been blown down by a cataclysmic wind.
It resembled a world consumed by the fire at the end of an eon, like the ocean drunk up by a sage, or like a region devastated by excessive rain and abandoned by its people.
It was crowded with bundles of spears and whirled with circles of *bhuśuṇḍī* missiles; it was filled with corpses resembling hundreds of rutting elephants, along with *tomara* lances and mallets.
It was like a spreading grove of palmyra trees grown upon a rocky peak; it had the tall trees of spears rising from the banks of flowing rivers of blood.
The sky was filled with trees of weapons woven from elephant hide and strewn with flowers of cloth, while the atmosphere was webbed with clusters of tongues of entrails dragged out by herons.
The raised forest-trees of spears grew upon the banks of the rivers of blood, and the clusters of lotuses were the banners standing above the lakes of gore.
Men submerged in blood-red mud call out to their friends; the sight of broken people emerging from the falling carcasses of lordly elephants is beheld by all.

With trees stripped of their branches by wild beasts, it appeared as if filled with half-severed headless trunks; and with heaps of elephant hides and rags being carried away like rivers of blood, it was as if a multitude of boats were flowing along.
It was a mass of white foam-like garments shimmering within the stream of blood, where men were incessantly carried away by the swift current of the moving tide.
Here and there fell headless trunks like Rākṣasas; the fleeing soldiers were cut down by the mass of upward-pointing, thick axles and wheels.
It resounded with the blood-like roar of *bhāṅkāra* and *phetkāra*, and the cries of those half-dead; it shook the dust from the birds with streams of blood dripping from the stone mortars.
It was a scene of perilous *tāṇḍava* dances by *vetālas* as swift as the wind, amidst the clattering of broken chariots whose wooden frames lay overturned, obstructing the path of noble warriors.

It strikes terror with the throbbing movements of the internal, ready warrior that is the individual soul; its mouth is filled with the mire of blood, and it is a corpse toward which there is not even a trace of compassion for living beings.

In some places, dogs and crows were seen suffering as they strained their necks for a living; in others, it was agitated by the clamor of carnivorous beasts fighting over a single piece of meat; and in yet others, it was crowded with scavengers who had died while contending for that same morsel.

With streams of blood gushing from the necks of camels, horses, elephants, men, chariots, and leaders of troops as they were overturned, that battlefield became a garden of Death; with its weapons like unwithered creepers, it was like the entire world at the end of an aeon, overturned along with its mountains.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, like a hero whose blood has been drained, the sun was eclipsed by time; its majesty withered by the heat of the weapons, it was cast into the ocean.
Beautiful with the glow of blood from the battle, reflected in the mirror of the sky, the streak of twilight momentarily appeared as if it were the severed head of the sun.

From the earth, the netherworld, the sky, and all directions, the Vetālas arrived like the surging waters of the ocean at the time of universal dissolution, their rhythmic clapping sounding like bracelets.
Upon the head of the lordly elephant of day, which was smeared with the sword-like darkness of the night, there lay scattered the pearls of the starry host, reddened by the glow of twilight.
In those beings devoid of essence, blinded by darkness, yet possessing the flavor of passion, the lotuses of nectar-like hearts contracted as if they were closing.
With their wings closed and sleeping for a moment, their necks raised with difficulty, the birds in their nests became like weapons upon the limbs of corpses.
The worlds, made beautiful by the nearby moon, became like rows of blossoms with throbbing hearts, like the glories within the factions of heroes.
With its waters consisting of blood, its bees hidden within its limbs, and its lotus-faces closed, the lotus-pond became like a battlefield.
Above was the lake of the sky, adorned with the lilies of the stars; below was the lake of water, with shimmering lilies in the form of stars.
In the darkness, the beings, freed from fear, gathered together in great numbers, spreading out in every direction like waters breaking through their banks.
The battlefield was crowded with throngs of singing vetālas, and it was filled with the play of kaṅkas and kākolakas perched upon the laps of rattling skeletons.

Then, there was a fire consisting of fat and flesh, blazing with the light of the stars from the flames of the wood-pile, resounding with the sound of "pacat-paca-paca," and burning away the marrow and flesh.

With the entire mass of its bones cracking and bursting asunder, it was on the verge of revealing its collection of consciousness, yet it was concealed by the water-sports commenced by the female Vetālas.
It was intense with the clamor of dogs, crows, yakṣas, vetālas, and tālas; it resembled a forest where birds were taking flight due to the coming and going of spirits.
O Ḍākinī, intent on extracting blood, flesh, fat, and marrow; O Piśāca, with blood, fat, and flesh dripping from your gnashing teeth!
In the midst of it, the funeral pyres revealed a multitude of corpses and blood made manifest; Virūpikā was being led away, carrying a great corpse placed upon her own shoulder.
Its interior was made terrifying by the frantic dance of a circle of fierce Kumbhāṇḍas; it ended with the "chamicchami" cries [of the demons] and had fat, blood, and tears for its clouds.

It was filled with the forms of land-dwelling beings carried away by the surging currents of rivers of flowing blood, and it resounded with the confused cries of a multitude of *vetālas* as they dragged along skeletons.
A young vetāla sleeping within a casket made from the belly of a dead elephant; a rākṣasa engaged in the sport of drinking at a secluded spot for ritual practice.
It was illuminated by the flaming funeral torches of the quarreling intoxicated vetālas, while its wind was made fragrant by the scent of flowing blood and fat.
It resounded with the clamor of jackals vomiting up baskets of corpses, while the Yakṣas, greedy for the taste of half-cooked carcasses, frolicked amidst the strife.

It was filled with birds perched upon the peaks of the Tuṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, Aṅga, Taṅgaṇa, and Aṅgala mountains, and it bore the appearance of flames blazing directly toward one another like the falling of stars.
It was disfigured by blood amidst the exultation of falling *vetālas*, and its vicinity was filled with the sound of *yoginī* throngs being heard by *piśācas*.
He played musical instruments consisting mostly of large lutes made from entrails stretched out, while men who had been possessed by female spirits were now freed from those demonic influences.
In some places, good soldiers were half-dead from the terror caused by the sight of the Rūpikā; in others, the Madra country was incomplete due to the presence of Vetālas and Rākṣasas.
The night-stalkers were terrified by the garments falling from the shoulders of the *svarūpikās*, and the sky was crowded with a multitude of unprecedented hosts of spirits that had collided there.
It was like a heap of corpses scattered among birds that look only for their own food—a human carcass snatched away with great effort while the man was still dying.

With its red-colored parts appearing like fragments produced by the flames of the fire from Śiva’s mouth, it was as if covered on all sides by clusters of newly blossomed Aśoka flowers that had flown upward.
It had young vetālas busily engaged in binding the necks of headless trunks (kabandhas), and it was like a ball of fire in the sky due to the flashing teeth of yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and others.

It filled the seat of the dark clouds, adorned with masses resembling the interiors of mountain thickets and caves in the sky; it was like a basket of shattered potsherds for the world, shaken by the winds of the kalpa agitated by the impetuous onset of wandering spirits.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, on that battlefield long made terrible by the conduct of night-stalkers, the two watches of the night remained engaged in their duties, like the day in the conduct of men.
In the night-house, where the walls are clearly visible even to a ball easily grasped by the hand, a host of spirits leaps about, their eyes darting in greed for gain.
In the silence of the wandering darkness, when the quarters of the sky were blocked by sleep, the noble-souled husband of Līlā appeared as if somewhat dejected in mind.
Having quickly deliberated upon the morning duties with ministers skilled in counsel, [he lay] upon a bed shaped like a long crescent moon and cool as snow.
In that beautiful dwelling resembling the interior of the moon, within a cool cave, he fell asleep for a moment with his lotus-like eyes closed.
Then those two playful women, abandoning that sky, entered that house through the openings like two streaks of wind entering a lotus bud.
Śrī Rāma said: O best among those who know speech, how large is this gross body, and how, O Lord, did it quickly enter through an opening as thin as a thread?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O sinless one, he whose mental delusion consists in thinking, "I am this physical body," is not able to pass through a minute aperture.
"He has obstructed me," "I am not at ease here"—for one who possesses such a thought, it is experienced that she (the mind) becomes an experiencer of what has already been experienced.

How can one who has experienced the thought "I am going" with respect to the first half [of the journey] possess a consciousness intent on going with respect to the second half? That person would be performing that very same action.
For fire does not go upward when obstructed, nor does it go downward; in whatever manner consciousness has proceeded, in that very same manner it remains established.
For one seated in the shade, how can there be experiences of heat? For him, no other object is experienced within his own consciousness by anyone else.
As is consciousness, so is the mind; it has reached such a state of being, yet by supreme effort, it is led once again to another condition.
The cognition of a snake regarding a rope is forcibly subverted by the cognition of "no snake"; otherwise, however, it remains exactly as it was.
As is consciousness, so is the mind; as is the mind, so is one's striving. This is well-established even for a child; who has not experienced it?
Furthermore, how and by whom can that person—who is like a man in a dream or a mental construction, whose form is merely like an image and whose nature is as empty space—be obstructed?
For indeed, the body of everyone consists entirely of mind alone; because it is experienced as such, it appears as if it were moving from somewhere within the heart.
In the original creation, the rising and setting of this [world] occurs exactly as desired, arising from its own inherent nature; subsequently, it becomes the cause for both duality and unity.
Know that these three—the space of the mind, the space of consciousness, and the third, the [outer] space—are one, by virtue of their inseparable nature.
Know this state of being the body of consciousness to be the arising of all-pervasiveness; it arises according to one's perception and desire, just as it arises according to one's perception.
He dwells within a mote of dust, he is withdrawn into the belly of the sky; he dissolves into the sheaths of sprouts and becomes sap within the leaf.
It glimmers as the state of water-waves, it dances within the heart of a stone; having become a rain-cloud, it pours forth, and having become a stone, it remains still.
He travels at will through the sky and even into the bellies of mountains; possessing a body of infinite space, he then assumes the state of a subtle atom.
It bore forest down upon both its interior and its exterior.
Space contains millions of abodes of the lotus-born Brahmā, which are non-different from its own self, just as the formations of whirlpools are non-different from the ocean.
At the beginning of creation, this one—whose body is the mind—awakens without agitation; having become the great Self of space, it then perceives its state as primordial nature (prakṛti).
In that same way, non-existence itself arises as if it were existence through the intellect, just as a person in a dream experiences the delusion that "this son of a barren woman exists."
Śrī Rāma said: What is this mind? Or how does it come to be for us? How is it that, upon being observed, it becomes neither existent in nature nor anything else?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Each individual mind possesses such power; thus, for every single mind, the delusion of the world arises separately.
The multitudes of worlds arise and dissolve in a single moment for some, and in an eon for others; hear now the sequence of these.
O wise one, know that this fainting which is experienced by each individual at death and other such times is the night of the great dissolution.
At the end of that, everyone individually expands their own creation—born of innate habit, dream, and mental construction—like the dancing of men on a moving mountain in a state of confusion.
Just as at the end of the night of the great dissolution, the body of the Self and the mind gradually unfolds this universe, so too does it unfold for each individual immediately after death.
Śrī Rāma said: Just as the creation after death is experienced through memory, so too does one experience it after a long time; therefore, the universe is not without a cause.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, during the great dissolution, all beings beginning with Hari and Hara attain the state of disembodied liberation; how then could there be any possibility of memory?
Since even someone like me, having awakened to the Self, is surely liberated, how could those born from the lotus—being bodiless—not be liberated?
But for those other living beings who are like you, memory becomes the cause in their births and deaths here, due to the absence of liberation.

The mountain, the support of the earth, with its firmly established base and its peak reaching the sky, exists as if awakening within, yet remains unawakened at the end of the swoon of death; that is designated as Pradhāna.
That is declared to be the nature of space; it is the unmanifest, both insentient and sentient. This is the sequence in the arising of existence, occurring through remembrance and non-remembrance.
For when that [intellect] becomes oriented toward awakening and is fully awakened, then from the void (kha) arise the subtle elements, space, time, action, the gross elements, and so forth.
That very pentad of senses becomes swollen and awakened; that alone is what perceives within the body, and this is its subtle, transportive body (ātivāhika).
Through long-standing habituation, this [mind], thickened by conceptual construction, brings about the perception of external objects, just like a child.
Then, the divisions of space and time, existing as its substratum, arise without ever having truly arisen, like the act of vibration in the wind.
Thus has this wandering through the worlds increased in vain; though experienced, it is composed of unreality, like union with a woman in a dream.
Wherever a living being dies, he immediately perceives that very place; right there, he sees this entire expanse of the world situated in just this manner.
The void itself experiences the delusion that "I am the clear world"; being of the nature of space, the living soul, though possessing a self, appears as if born from the form of space.
Beautiful with its cities of the gods, mountains, suns, and clusters of stars, yet hollow with the perils of old age, death, distress, and disease.

The exertion of the absence of intrinsic nature, encompassing the gross and the subtle, the moving and the unmoving, along with the oceans, mountains, earth, rivers, the directions, day and night, the kalpas, and the destruction of moments.
"I was born here by this father"—thus having a firm conviction; "this is my mother, this is my wealth"—thus having arisen latent impressions (vāsanā).
"This is my good deed and this is my evil deed"—such is the conceptual construction made by the mind; "I was a child" or "I am young today"—thus does the heart sport.
Thus, each individual forest-thicket of cyclic existence has been described: it is blossomed with the flowers of the Tārās, and its trembling shoots are like dark blue clouds.
Moving with the herds of deer as its horses, with gods and asuras as its birds, with light as its pollen-dust, and with dark thickets and groves as its forest retreats;
The ocean is filled with lotus ponds, and Mount Meru and other mountains are but clods of earth; yet within the seed of the lotus of the mind lies the sprout of experience.
Wherever this living being dies, there it sees [the world] in an instant; thus it is with each of the numerous fragments of the world that arise individually.
Tens of millions of Brahmās, Rudras, Indras, Maruts, Viṣṇus, and Vivasvats have passed away, as have those who beheld mountains, oceans, spheres, islands, and other worlds.
These views that have passed, those that will pass, and those that are passing away have lost their true form; who is capable of counting those [views] that are richly augmented by Brahman?
Thus, this universe consisting of walls does not exist at all apart from mental construction; it is merely moving within the mind—consider this now!
That which is the space of consciousness is itself known as the mind; and that which is the space of consciousness is itself the supreme state.

That which is a whirlpool is merely water; it is not a real substance that is the whirlpool. Likewise, the seer remains as if he were the object of sight, yet there is no such thing as a real, existent object.
The manifestation of the sky of consciousness within the elemental ether is like that of a gem; it is the world, appearing as various existing entities, like a cavity in the atmosphere.
The word "world" (jagat) exists as the supreme nectar when understood through my intellect; however, when understood through your intellect, it does not exist at all, even in the words "you" or "I."
Therefore, Līlā and Sarasvatī abide as the very embodiment of space within the all-pervading Supreme Self—which is pure, omnipresent, unobstructed, and stainless.
Since they always rise wherever they desire and wherever they wish within the sky, their path lies in that house.

The sky of consciousness exists everywhere; here, it is that which is true perception, conceptualization, and reflection, spreading forth. They call this body "ativāhika" (subtle/transcendental) and indeed wall-less; tell me, how could it be obstructed, and by what? How so? Speak!
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When those two goddesses had entered, that lotus-palace became beautiful, its interior radiant and white with the light of the rising of two moons.
By its power, the king, along with the other men and women, fell asleep amidst the soft, pure, and fragrant breezes from the gentle *mandāra* trees.
It was like a forest in springtime, filled with blossoming lotuses on its banks, where the pain of disease has fled and the joy of good fortune abounds.
Refreshed by the floods of light from their bodies, which were as cool as the flow of moonlight, he awoke as if sprinkled with nectar.
He beheld two celestial nymphs resting upon two seats, like two lunar orbs risen upon two peaks of Mount Meru.
Having reflected for a mere moment, the king, his mind filled with wonder, rose from his bed like Śeṣa, the bearer of the discus and mace.
With his garlands, necklaces, and lower garments hanging down and well-restrained, he took up a handful of blossoms like a mass of flowers in full bloom.
Emerging from the hollow of his own garment, which was folded upon the ground where he had been seated in the lotus posture, he spoke these words with humility.

Victory to the two goddesses who possess the luster of the moon in dispelling the defects of birth, worldly existence, and the fever of passion, and who possess the luster of the sun in driving away the darkness of both the external and the internal.
Having spoken thus to them, he offered a handful of flowers at their feet; it was like a blossoming tree on the bank offering itself at the feet of two lotuses.
Then, in order to explain Līlā’s birth as a king, the Sovereign Goddess Sarasvatī, through her creative power (saṃkalpa), enlightened the minister standing at her side.
Seeing that the two celestial nymphs had awakened, he prostrated himself, offered a handful of flowers at their feet, and entered before them with his body bowed low.
The queen said, "O King, who are you? Whose son are you? When were you born here? Having heard this, the minister spoke these words:
O Goddesses, by your grace, I am able to speak even before you both; therefore, O Goddesses, let the birth of my lord be heard.
There was a king born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, lotus-eyed and illustrious, named Kunda-ratha, whose shadow-like arms covered the earth.
He had a son named Bhadraratha, whose face was like the moon; his son was Viśvaratha, and his son was Bṛhadratha.
His son was Sindhuratha; his son was Śailaratha; his son was Kāmaratha; and his son was Mahāratha.
Viṣṇuratha was his son, and Nabhoratha was his son; this lord of ours is his son, possessed of a perfectly pure form.
Filling people with nectar like the moon from the Ocean of Milk, he was known as Vidūratha on account of his great accumulations of merit.
Born of his mother Sumitrā like a second Guha born of Gaurī, his father, when he was ten years old, gave him the kingdom and departed for the forest.
From that time forth, he has protected the surface of the earth in accordance with righteousness, now that the tree of his good deeds has borne fruit upon the arrival of this auspicious occasion.
"O two goddesses, whose sight is difficult to obtain even through hundreds of hardships from long asceticism—this lord of the earth known as Vidūratha [seeks you]."
"Today, by your grace, I have attained supreme purification. Having spoken thus, the minister and the king likewise remained silent.
O King, as he stood on the ground with palms joined, face bowed, and seated in the lotus posture, remember by yourself through discernment your former birth.
As she spoke, Sarasvatī touched him on the head with her hand; then the darkness of the heart, the delusion of the lotus, went to its destruction.
And at the moment of the arising of the touch of that request, his heart became fully blossomed; he remembered his former history as if it were pulsating within him.

Having understood that the abandonment of the body and the sole sovereignty was accompanied by the playful manifestation of *līlā*, and that it was the unfolding of the event of *prajñapti* through *līlā*.
He became like one being swept away in the ocean by his own account; he said to himself: "Alas! This illusion has spread throughout this worldly existence."
"By your grace, I have now fully understood the two goddesses here. The King said: "O two goddesses, what is this? It is as if a single day has passed for me who am dead."
Seventy years have passed since I was born here; I remember many deeds, and I remember my great-grandfather.
"I remember childhood, youth, friends, kinsmen, and attendants. Jñapti said: "O King, immediately after the swoon of the great delusion of death,"
When that intermediate world had passed away, in that very moment, in this very house, and even in this very dwelling within the sky;
O King, this pavilion is indeed within the house of that brahmin from Girigrāma, situated as it were in the inner space of that very dwelling.
Within that, this world-house shines forth individually; indeed, the living soul within the house of Brahmā is present before me.
Right there on that floor, within that very pavilion, and inside that very house, this entire circle of worldly existence was situated.
