Therefore, this house of yours does not exist as something solidly established; it resides only within your own mind, which is as pure as the clear sky.
This world, spread out by the delusion of worldly activity, has come into my presence through intuition: that such is my name, such is my birth, and such is my lineage of the Ikṣvākus.
"These were my grandfathers of such-and-such names in the past; I was born as a child, and when I was ten years old, my father passed away."
"Having consecrated me here in this kingdom, the wandering mendicant has gone to the forest; thereafter, having conquered the quarters and made the kingdom free of thorns,"
With these ministers and citizens, I protect the earth, performing the sequence of sacrificial rites while upholding the subjects in righteousness.
Seventy years of my life have passed away; now this enemy force has arrived, and for me there is a terrible conflict.
"Having fought this battle, I have returned home as it was before; these two goddesses have arrived at my house, and so I shall worship them."
For when worshipped, deities grant their own desired objects; of these two, this one of mine shall bestow knowledge and the recollection of past lives.
"Here the Goddess has bestowed upon me what brings about blossoming, like that of a lotus; now I have accomplished my purpose and am free from all doubt."
"I am at peace, I am fully extinguished, and I abide in absolute bliss"—this is the vast and greatly agitated delusion of yours.
Rich in various modes of conduct and dwellings, and traversing other worlds, it was at that very moment when you previously met your death.
At that very moment, this intuition arose spontaneously in your heart; it is like leaving behind one swirling eddy and taking up another.
Just as the current of a river flows swiftly, and likewise its spreading stream, so too does a whirlpool arise when it is joined with another within the eddies.
At times, the splendor of creation increases, both mixed and unmixed; at that moment of your death, such an intuition arose within you.
This unreal net has appeared before the sun of consciousness, just as within a single moment of a dream there occurs the delusion of a hundred years.
Just as life and death again occur within a creation of one's own imagination, and just as one perceives walls and ornaments in a city of the Gandharvas.
Just as trees and mountains tremble during the turbulence of a ship's voyage, so do the eastern mountains dance when their own elements are disturbed.
Just as the severing of one's own head in a dream is entirely false, so too is this matured delusion, which takes on the form of continuity, purely illusory.
In reality, you have never been born, nor have you ever died; you are of the nature of pure consciousness, peaceful, and abide within the Self.
You see all this, yet you do not see anything at all; as the self of all, you shine eternally by yourself within yourself.
Noble like a great jewel and radiant like light, in reality this is neither the surface of the earth nor are you this [person].
These mountains are not villages, nor are these [trees], nor indeed are we; for they are merely within the space of the pavilion belonging to the Brahmin of the mountain village.
The world shines brilliantly, enriched by the wives of the Lord of Līlā; therein lies the royal capital of Līlā, its form adorned with pavilions.
Thus, this world is known to shine within its belly, like the sky; and within that world is a house, inside which we are situated here.
Thus, for those pavilions, the sky was as stainless as the sky itself; likewise, within those pavilions there was neither earth nor any city.
Neither forests, nor mountain ranges, nor clouds, rivers, and oceans exist; people dwell there in their homes alone in that utter void.
"Neither people, nor kings, nor even the mountains see [them]. Vidūratha said, "If this is so, O Goddess, how is it that these followers of mine are here?"
Are they perfected within themselves, or do they not exist within themselves? To them, the world appears like the objects of a dream, and for them, dream-people and the like [are real].
"Tell me, how could they be real or unreal when the Self exists? Śrī Sarasvatī said: "O King, among those who have known what is to be known and whose nature is solely pure awakening,"

This world, which has the nature of existence, does not exist at all within those whose self is the sky of consciousness; it appears only to the one whose self is pure awareness—so how can there be such a thing as the delusion of the world?
When the delusion of a snake in a rope has subsided, how can the delusion of a snake arise again? When its non-existence is fully realized, how can there be existence in the delusion of the world?

Once a mirage is fully understood, how can there again be the notion of water? When one's own dream is fully understood during the time of dreaming, how can there be death in that dream? For one who has died even in their own dream, the fear of death arises only as a dream.

For the Buddha, who is pure and possesses the splendor of the autumnal sky, whose intention is transparent, bright, and utterly expanded—“I” and “the world” are merely the objects of false words; in reality, my dear friend, they do not exist, for that [duality] is merely verbal.

When the sage had spoken thus, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the performance of evening rites; the assembly, having offered salutations, departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For that fool of unawakened intellect who is not established in the expansive state, this world—though non-existent—is as if real, being as hard as a diamond.
Just as a ghost causes suffering to a child until his death, so does this world appear real to the deluded mind, though it is unreal.
Just as a mirage of water causes delusion for deer, so too does this world appear real to the deluded mind, though it is utterly unreal.
Just as the death of a living being in a dream appears to be real and performs a causal function despite being unreal, so too does the world appear to those of deluded intellect.
Just as for one who is unacquainted with gold, there is only the cognition of a bracelet in a golden bracelet, and not even the slightest thought of gold; so it is here.
Likewise, for the ignorant person, there exists only this perception of the visible world, and not any other perception of ultimate reality.
Just as in the sky, rows of pearls, peacock feathers, clumps of hair, and optical illusions appear as if they were real though they are unreal, so too does this world appear to those of poor vision.
Know this entire universe to be a long dream, joined with the sense of "I" and so forth; hear how other people within it are as real as those in a dream.
There exists the all-pervading, tranquil, and pure essence of the ultimate truth, whose body is pure consciousness beyond the reach of thought—an expansive supreme space.
That is all-pervading, possessed of all powers, everything itself, and the self of all; wherever and in whatever manner it arises, it truly abides there in that very way.
Therefore, those inhabitants of the city whom the observer perceives in that dream-city are indeed men who become such for him in an instant.
That which is the consciousness-nature of the seer resides within the space of the dream; for it is conceived as appearing like the mind within the space of the dream to human beings.
Due to the unity of the nature of the knower, one perceives as if it were a human being; thus, by the power of consciousness within the Self, both [the self and the other] attain reality.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, if even in a dream the dream-persons were not real, tell me, what fault would there be in that which has a body consisting of mere illusion?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In a dream, the inhabitants of a city do not exist as real entities in fact. Hear from me the proof in this matter, which is perception itself and nothing else.
At the beginning of creation, the Self-born Lord appears as the nature of experience resembling a dream; this entire universe is merely a fragment of His volition, and thus it is indeed like a dream.
Thus this entire universe is a dream; therein, you are real to me. Just as you are, so too are all others—the best of dreams for men—within that dream.
If those inhabitants of the city in the dream were not real, then here too, in that same form, there is not even the slightest bit of reality for me.
Just as I am your very self of truth, so may everything of mine be true; such is my resolve for mutual success within this worldly existence, which is like the perception of a dream.
In this vast dream that is saṃsāra, "I am real to you," and "you too are real to me"—all things are thus in dreams; such is the sequence.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, it is my conviction that for one who is awake and sees a dream, that city of dreams exists in its very form of reality, just as it appears to the dreamer."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: It is exactly so; it remains just as it is because of its reality, like a city seen in a dream, appearing as clear as the sky even to the dreamer who is not asleep.
Let this matter rest for now; however, know that what you consider to be like waking reality is actually but a dream within, not filling out space, time, and so forth.
Thus all this appears; it is not real, yet it stands as if it were real. It delights the mind even though it is false, like union with a woman in a dream.
Everything exists everywhere, both inside and outside the body; whatever one perceives in whatever manner, one's own consciousness sees it exactly as such.

Just as whatever substance exists within a treasury is obtained by the one who sees it, so too does everything exist within the space of consciousness; it is indeed perceived by that very consciousness.
Immediately thereafter, the goddess Jñapti, having made Vidūratha beautiful with the sprouts of discernment through the sprinkling of the nectar of awakening, spoke this:
This very thing has been described by me, O King, for the sake of sport. May it be well with you; we shall depart now that the perspectives of these illustrative examples have been seen.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When these words had been spoken by Sarasvatī in a voice of sweet syllables, the wise king Vidūratha spoke these words.
Vidūratha said: "O Goddess, even my sight of you would not be in vain for one who does not seek a reward; how much more so, then, will it be for you, who bestow such great fruit?"
O Goddess, having cast off this body, I shall go from here to another world, as one goes from one dream to another dream.
Behold me quickly, O Mother, for I have come to you as one who has sought refuge; neglect toward a devotee, O Giver of Boons, does not befit the great.
"Wherever I go, may this minister and this maiden, though she is but a child, come with me; have mercy on me."

Śrī Sarasvatī said: "Come, O Lord of the circle of former births; enjoy without hesitation this kingdom, beautiful with the play of appropriate wealth. Know this: we have never at any time seen the rejection of the desires of a supplicant."
Śrī Sarasvatī said: "O King, you must now die in this excellent battle; the entire kingdom you were destined to obtain in the past shall now be manifest before your very eyes."
The maiden, the minister, and you must go to the former city; you shall find that body reduced to a corpse.
The two of us shall go back the way we came; you, however, must go to that place in the form of the wind, along with the maiden and the minister.
The gait of a horse is one thing, while that of a donkey or a camel is another; the gait of an elephant with temples streaming with rut is yet quite different.
While this sweet conversation was thus proceeding between the two, a man entered in a state of agitation and, standing upright, spoke.
O Lord, this great enemy force, raining down arrows, discuses, swords, maces, and clubs, has arrived like a surging, single vast ocean.
Joyfully, he released a rain of maces, spears, and *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons, resembling the rocks of the Kulaparvata mountains tossed up by the winds at the end of an aeon.
In the city that resembled a mountain, a fire broke out, pervading the quarters of the horizon; burning with crackling and popping sounds, it was toppling down the excellent city.
In the sky, great mountains of smoke, resembling jars of clouds at the end of an eon, began to rise up with force like Garuḍas.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Even as the man was speaking thus with agitation, a great clamor arose outside, filling the quarters with its harsh sound.
Of bows drawn forcibly to the ear and raining arrows, and of powerful, exceedingly rutting elephants in full musth.
With the crackling sounds of fires burning brightly, and with the great tumultuous cries of the citizens whose wives had been consumed by the flames;
The sound of the fragments of fire as they cross over is described by the roar [of the flames], while that of the blazing rays due to their flickering is "dhagaddhag."
Then, from the window, the two queens, the minister, and King Vidūratha beheld the great city resounding with loud clamor in the dead of night.
It was filled by the supreme force, surging with waves of clouds and fierce currents, possessing the momentum of a single full ocean agitated by the fire of universal dissolution.
It was being consumed by great tongues of flame that filled the sky, blazing like Mount Meru melting under the fire at the end of an eon.
With the fierce, thundering roars of great clouds graspable by the fist, and with the terrible, tumultuous clamor of the fleshly prattlings of bandits;
The sky was covered by smoke-colored clouds resembling the Puṣkarāvarta clouds, and it was filled without interval by masses of flames that shone like the tips of soaring gold.
The sky was made turbulent by fierce stars resembling fragments of flickering firebrands, while masses of houses in various regions blazed like mountains of fire.

The city fell with its armies destroyed, as hollows of clouds like flying embers rained down, while the fierce roar of the fire consumed the throngs of people who were crying out in harsh lamentation.
The sky was rendered almost seamless by sparks from fires and iron arrows, while heaps of burnt cities lay scattered amidst a dense mass of many weapons and stones.
Where fierce and noble warriors were crushed by the collision of trumpeting elephants, and where great wealth was scattered upon the roads as fleeing thieves were cut down.
There, men and women wailed piteously as they fell upon heaps of glowing coals; the burning wood crackled with loud *caṭacaṭa* sounds as it crumbled and tumbled down.
The surface of the sky was filled with hundreds of suns from the mass of vast, whirling firebrands, and the entire surface of the earth was strewn with glowing embers.
The bamboo was burning with the crackling sound of firewood in a conflagration; all the soldiers were crying out as they wailed like dense masses of living beings being consumed by fire.
He was a great eater whose fire was never satiated by the royal glory that had been reduced to mere dust, and who was as if a massive mouth for the fire that was ever-ready to swallow everything.
By chance, there was a house where fire crackled with harsh sounds, desiring fuel consumed by the fire that devours infinite living beings as its food.
Then King Vidūratha heard there the cries of the warriors whose wives had been burned, as they stood watching and rushed forward.
Alas! The trees of the house, standing high in the wind-blown embers, crackle with a harsh *khara-khara* sound; the travelers on the path of the sun's heat are enveloped in a net of dust.
Alas! The frost-cold tears of those whose wives have been consumed by fire sink into the bodies of the elephants, like the eloquent expressions of wisdom submerged within the minds of the great.
Alas, father! Your weapons have struck the grass of the young woman’s braid; they blaze like heaps of dry leaves fanned by the wind of heroes.
Long as the river Āvartanī, this Dhūmayamunā flows with towering waves; behold, it rushes toward the celestial Gaṅgā.
Behold! The river of smoke, ascending upon the logs of burning embers, blinds the denizens of celestial chariots with its bubbles of fiery sparks.
Her mother, father, brother, son-in-law, and nursing infant were all consumed by fire in this house, burnt as if by the fuel of the wicked.
"Alas, alas! Come quickly to this house of coals; from here you shall fall as Mount Sumeru falls at the time of universal dissolution."
Ah! These weapons—arrows, stones, spears, lances, darts, and swords—enter [the enemy] like moths into a web, twilight, or a mass of clouds.
Alas, the streams of flames enter the sky at the end of time, like masses of water from the ocean entering the blazing submarine fire.
Great clouds are smoking and flames erupt from the mountain peaks; even the lakes dry up like the hearts of those filled with passion.

As if out of anger at being used as hitching posts, these rows of trees are felled by the elephants with a crackling sound produced by their snapping trunks, while the elephants themselves utter cries of distress.

With their branches once laden with abundant flowers and fruit now stripped of their splendor, the house-trees have fallen into a state of wretchedness like householders whose entire possessions have been consumed by fire.
Deprived of their parents, these children, sinking into a mass of darkness on the streets, alas, are struck down by the falling of walls upon their limbs.
At the head of the battle, Kīraṇya, trembling with fear from being driven by the wind, let out a bitter cry as he bore the weight of falling embers.
Alas, what misery! A stone from a mechanical device has fallen upon his shoulder—which was already pierced by a sharp, firm firebrand—just like a thunderbolt striking a man.
Alas! With cows, horses, buffaloes, elephants, camels, dogs, jackals, and sheep, the road was blocked by these fierce and agitated creatures, as if a battle had begun.
With their garments making a rustling sound like a swarm of bees hovering over a mass of lotuses, the women go along wailing, appearing as if covered by land-lotuses.
Behold, the sparks of flame lick the creeper-like tresses of women, making them resemble *aśoka* flowers like female serpents with their trunks.
Alas, alas! Upon the eyelashes of the fawn-eyed maiden, which are marked like wings, the flame of fire finds rest as if upon evil paths.
Even while being consumed by fire, a man does not depart without his wife; alas, how difficult it is for living beings to sever the snares of affection!
The elephant, having violently uprooted trees with their glowing coals and scorched the lotuses, plunged in anger into the Puṣkarada lake.
Having reached the stage of clouds, smoke—possessing flickering streaks of lightning within—showers down a multitude of blazing embers like a rain of iron arrows.
O King, with smoke flickering and sparks of fire whirling in circular motion, the sky stood like an ocean filled with jewels, bearing a crest-like garland.
The white garment shines with the brilliance of the crest of flames, like a casket smeared with saffron bestowed by Death himself at a festival.
Alas! How truly distressing is this situation, devoid of all propriety; for even the noble wives of kings are being held captive by enemy heroes with weapons raised.
With their garlands of loose flowers serving as a path and a boundary wall, their breasts were strewn across their chests by their half-burnt braided hair.
Their hips and loins were visible through their swaying garments, and the circles of the earth were encircled by their falling ruby bracelets.
Pure pearls were scattered from the networks of broken pearl necklaces, while golden luster shone from the sides of breasts that were now visible and now hidden.
The clamor of battle was drowned out by the harsh cries of female ospreys; their flanks split open by the incessant flow of blood, they lost consciousness.
Their garments were soaked and tied together by the mud of blood and the water of tears, as they were being dragged away by force by men who had placed their arms under their armpits.
With cries such as "Who indeed might be our protector in this [calamity]?", the soldiers were made to weep by those who perceived the impending disaster, like a row of blue lotuses being rained upon.
With masses of thighs as delicate as lotus stalks and utterly stainless, visible against the clear expanse of the sky, they resembled celestial lotuses.

With their garlands, garments, ornaments, and body-unguents no longer swaying, and with the creepers of their long, flowing tresses disheveled and clouded by tears, they appeared like the royal fortunes emerging from the ocean of passion, which was being incessantly churned by the Mandara mountain of joy.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In the meantime, the queen, intoxicated by her youth, entered that house like Lakṣmī entering the hollow of a lotus.
With her garlands and garments disheveled and her strings of pearls scattered in disorder, she was followed by her companions and maidservants, overwhelmed with fear.
With a moon-like face and pure-limbed body, her breasts trembling with her breath, and teeth like stars, she stood there like the sky incarnate.
Then one of her companions addressed the king, as an apsaras addresses the lord of the gods when he is intent on the battle of the elements.
O King, together with us, the queen has fled from within the inner apartments and come for refuge to Your Majesty, like a creeper, distressed by the wind, seeking shelter at a tree.
O King, those wives of yours were carried off by powerful men with uplifted weapons, like the trees and creepers on the shores of great oceans swept away by masses of waves.
All the masters of the inner apartments were crushed by the arrogant enemies, who fell upon them unexpectedly like winds upon choice trees.
Our city has been seized by enemies who approached unsuspected from afar, just as lotuses are carried away at night by waters during the rains through their surging currents.
Our city has been assailed by numerous enemy warriors and by fires that emit smoke, roar loudly, and possess licking, fierce tongues of flame.
The playful queens, along with their retinues, were forcibly seized by their hair and led away while wailing like female ospreys captured by fishermen.
Thus, this branch of ours that has arrived, flourishing with its spreading tendrils, possesses the power only of the Lord to uproot the stainless [impurity] that has been reached.
Having heard this and looked upon the two goddesses, he said: "I am going forth for battle; may this wife of mine, who is a bee at your lotus-feet, be forgiven."
Having spoken thus, the king, his eyes reddened with anger, went forth like a lion from its mountain cave after having torn through a forest with a rutting elephant.
Then Līlā beheld Līlā, whose form resembled her own, appearing like a beautiful reflection come forth in a mirror.
Prabuddhalīlā said: "O Goddess, tell me, what is this? Why am I standing here? She who was 'I' previously—how is it that she is now standing here as 'this'?"
The ministers and others, the citizens, and the warriors with their forces and vehicles—all these very same ones stood there in that very same manner.
Furthermore, O Goddess, how do all these abide both here and there—both outside and inside—as if in a mirror; are they conscious?

The Goddess said: Just as a cognition arises within, so does it experience [its object] in an instant; consciousness attains the state of being the perceived object, just as the mind attains the state of being the mental content.
In whatever form an object exists in the world, it arises in that very same way at that very moment; there is no distance of space or time, nor any diversity born of material objects.

The external and the internal appear [within consciousness]; here, the object of a dream serves as the illustration, for that which is within—the city of dreams and mental constructs—is but a manifestation of consciousness.
Thus, through constant practice, this very state has become clearly established by its own name; it is just as the nature of your husband was when he died in that city at that time.
A being of such a nature, having arrived at that very place for that very purpose, is indeed distinct from these other beings, even though they too are of a similar kind.
Indeed, for this [consciousness], all that is experienced as the form of all objects is non-deceptive and exists as its very nature, like an army in a dream or a mental construction.
Tell me, then, what constitutes its truth, or of what nature it is; or else, because it perishes at a later time, it must be a non-entity.
And since all this is exactly like that, what further room is there for the notion of non-existence? In a dream, the waking state is unreal; in the waking state, the dream is composed of unreality.
Death is unreal in relation to birth, and birth is likewise composed of unreality in relation to death; this is because of their perishable nature and because they are merely experienced, O Rāghava.
Thus, O sinless one, this world—which is neither existent nor non-existent—appears as mere illusion, whether it be now in this age or at the conclusion of a great kalpa.
That which never does not exist is Brahman alone; that is this world. Within it, these delusions called "creations" shine forth.
Like clusters of hair in the sky, they do not truly shine; as waves are in the ocean, so are these creations in the Supreme.
Arising again and again, they dissolve like dust in a great wind; therefore, I recognize the falsity within myself regarding this appearance consisting of delusion.
What reliance can there be on the mass of water in a mirage, or on the ashes of creation? There are no other delusions there; that alone is the supreme state.
In dense darkness, there is only the appearance of ghosts, but no ghost exists at all; likewise, birth and death are delusion, and this entire world is pervaded by such delusion.
All that remains at the end of that great kalpa is peace; therefore, this visible world is neither real nor ever unreal.
Alternatively, these two are indeed Brahman itself, because they arise within that very [Brahman], just as space exists within an atom, and as substance and so forth exist even within a dyad.
Wherever a living atom (jīvāṇu) is, there it perceives this world as its own body, just as fire perceives heat, which arises from the sequence of its own inherent nature.
In the same way, the pure consciousness perceives this self as its own nature, just as motes of dust swirl within a house at sunrise.
Thus, these atoms of the cosmic egg reside in the supreme space, just as vibration resides in the wind, fragrance in the air, and emptiness in the sky.

Thus the universe remains in the Supreme, liberated from the grasping of a solid mass; it consists of existence and non-existence, acceptance and rejection, the gross and the subtle, and the moving and the unmoving.
These such portions of Brahman, which are devoid of constituent parts, must now be understood by you for the sake of realizing that which possesses form.
Non-different from that Self, they are as if without parts; this entire universe, as it exists, arises through the sequence of its own inherent nature.
Empty of the meanings of all words, it abides as non-different from Brahman; it is neither real nor unreal, like the delusion of a snake in a rope.

Due to false experience, the real appears as unreal; yet that which is thoroughly examined is the supreme cause. Because it is consciousness, it is called "jīvatva" (the state of being a living soul)—this is sufficient.
Then, through such experience alone, one clearly attains the state of being a living soul; whether this world that shines in the sky be real or unreal, it remains as it is.
The individual soul indeed colors itself through its own volitions and experiences; it quickly experiences certain things based on previous experiences.

Some [verses] have never been experienced before; some are even (equal) and some are uneven; at certain times they are those very same [even ones], and in other cases they are even-uneven (ardhasama).
In the space of the living soul (jīvākāśa), there shine experiences that are unreal yet appear real; they possess their own lineages, their own conduct, their own births, and their own activities.
Those very same ministers and citizens become possessed of discernment; they alone are truly capable within themselves, being impartial regarding place, time, and beneficial outcomes.
Such is the established position regarding the intuition (pratibhā) whose nature is the self of all: just as an intuition consisting of pure being arises in the sky that is the self of the king.
Likewise, she arises foremost within the very sky of my intuition—she whose character is yours, whose conduct is yours, whose lineage is yours, and who consists of your very form.
Thus this play appears, born from the reflection of intuitive insight; within the all-pervading mirror of consciousness, intuitive insight reflects itself.

Whatever form it takes where it exists, that very form arises there continuously; whatever internal manifestation of the space of the living soul (jīvākāśa) produces itself, that same manifestation stands externally as a reflection in the mirror of consciousness (cidādarśa).

This sky, this world, and this earth—know, O dear one, that all this is merely the manifestation of Me alone, the interior of the bilva-fruit of the space of consciousness; therefore, remain here as you are, perfectly tranquil and pure.
Śrī Sarasvatī said: "This husband of yours, Vidūratha, having cast off his body on the field of battle, shall reach that very inner apartment and become such a self once again."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having heard these words of the Goddess, Līlā, who had previously resided in that city, stood before her with palms joined in reverence and spoke these words while bowing low.
The second Līlā said: "The goddess Bhagavatī Jñapti has been constantly worshipped by me; that goddess grants me a vision in my dreams during the nights."
O Goddess of gods, O Mother, you are exactly as she is; therefore, out of compassion for me, who am so wretched, grant me a boon, O lady of lovely countenance.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having been addressed thus, Jñapti then recalled her devotion and, being pleased, spoke these words to Līlā, who had been her dwelling place in the past.
The Illustrious Goddess said: "O child, I am well-pleased with you for your lifelong, undiminished, and single-minded devotion; receive the boon you desire."
Taddeśalīlā said: "Wherever my husband remains after abandoning his body on the battlefield, may I become his wife there with this very same body."
The Illustrious Goddess said: "So be it! O daughter, I have been worshipped by you for a long time without obstacle, with single-minded devotion and abundant offerings of flowers and incense."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, when the local pastime had blossomed due to the arising of that bridegroom, the goddess Pūrvalīlā, her heart agitated by doubt, spoke to the goddess.
Pūrvalīlā said: For those like you, who possess true desires, whose resolutions are thus firm, and who are of the nature of Brahman, everything they desire is quickly accomplished.
O Sovereign, tell me why I was not led by that very body to this other world—that village on the mountain.
The Goddess said: "O lady of excellent complexion, I do nothing for anyone; it is the individual soul (jīva) itself that swiftly accomplishes its own desired ends."
I am the beneficial proclamation, the presiding deity of pure consciousness; within each individual exists the power of consciousness, whose nature is that of the life-force (jīva-śakti).
Whatever power arises for a living being, in whatever manner it manifests for each individual, that power always yields its fruit for that person in exactly that same way.
As you were propitiating me, your vital energy (jīva-śakti) arose; at that time, you thought, "If he were here now, I would be liberated," and so it has long been for you.
In various ways, you have been fully awakened by me; through that reasoning, O woman of excellent complexion, you have been led to a stainless state of being.
Awakened by this very cultivation for a long time, you have then attained that very goal through the power of your own consciousness at all times.
Whatever effort of one's own mind arises for anyone over a long period, it yields its fruit in due time, exactly in that manner for each respective person.
Whether becoming austerity or even a deity, consciousness itself bestows the fruit in another way, or else it gives it according to its own will, like the falling of fruit from the sky.
Nothing other than one's own self-awareness ever yields any fruit at any time; therefore, act quickly as you wish.
Indeed, the inner self, which is the very nature of consciousness, enters into the state of creation; whatever it perceives and strives for, that very thing becomes its fortune.
Reflect upon whether it is indeed delightful or not; having understood that which is purifying, abide within that.
Śrī Rāma said: While they were thus conversing within that house, what did Vidūratha do, having gone out from the house in anger?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Vidūratha emerged from his palace, surrounded by a great retinue like the moon amidst a multitude of stars.
With all his limbs armored and adorned with clinging necklaces and ornaments, he went forth like the Lord of the Gods amidst great shouts of "Victory! Victory!"
Giving orders to his host of warriors, listening to the arrangement of the mandala, and surveying the ranks of heroes, the king ascended his chariot.
With a form like that of a peaked roof, adorned with pearls and rubies, and covered by five banners, it was like a supreme celestial chariot.
Its golden shafts shone as they were fixed into the wheel-rims, and its pole was beautiful with the tinkling sound of pearl nets and its swift-moving yoke-pole.
With well-proportioned, auspicious, flickering, and slender ears, they moved with the speed of flight as if carrying away the gods.
With strides that suddenly surpassed the wind in speed, they seemed to be dragging their hindquarters along while drinking in the very sky.
It was harnessed to eight horses that filled the quarters with their neighing, appearing as if they were full moons radiant with the luster of chowries.
Then there arose the sound of kettledrums, unrestrained like the roar of clouds driven by elephants, filling the air and made terrible by its echoes against the mountain walls.
It was filled with the clamorous din released by the intoxicated soldiers, echoing with the tinkling of networks of small bells struck by the clashing of weapons.
With the crackling sounds of bows, the whistling songs of arrows, and the jangling clatter of masses of armor crushed against one another's limbs;
With the crackling sounds of blazing fires, with the cries of those in distress, with the mutual challenges of warriors, and with the tumultuous lamentations of bards;
The terrifying sound, filling the bowers of the ten directions, became as if made of solid stone, compressing the entire hollow of the universe until it could be grasped by the hand.
Then it flew up toward the sky, as if intent on soaring into the heavens, while its dust-like form thickly obstructed the path of the sun and covered the surface of the earth.
Because of that, the great city became as if entered into the state of dwelling in a womb; its darkness reached a density like the delusion of youth.
Multitudes of lamps departed somewhere like stars with the day; restless throngs of nocturnal spirits arrived with their strength.
The two Lilas and that young maiden beheld that great battle, as if with their hearts bursting open, having been granted the great vision by the Goddess.
Then their weapons subsided amidst the rising clatter of their armlets, like tongues of fire extinguished by the surging waters of a single ocean.
Gradually withdrawing his army, he was perceived as a different force; like Mount Meru when its wings have been clipped, it entered as if into a single ocean.
Then there arose a clear, crackling sound of the strings, and successions of clouds composed of rays of light moved about.
Taking to the sky, various birds in the form of weapons flew forth; the lusters of the gleaming arms spread abroad, dark with the abundant life they had seized.
The flames arising from the clashing of weapons blazed like the fire of a brand; the heroic clouds rumbled as they rained down torrents of arrow-showers.
Weapons as cruel as saws entered the limbs of the heroes, and the fragments crushed by those weapons fell through the air with a crackling sound.
The darkness quickly subsided by means of the lamps of the fire of weapons; all the armies became bristling with new arrows as if with hair.
In that Yama-like procession, rows of headless trunks rose up like dancers; the Piśācī women, acting as war-maidens, sang aloud of the intensity of the battle.
The great rivers of dust raised by the elephants through the forceful clashing of their tusks were carried across the expanse of the sky.
The corpses whirled about like dry forest leaves cast down by a windless storm; rivers of blood flowed forth from the mountain of battle that rained down death.
The dust was stilled by blood, the darkness by the fires of weapons, the sounds by the single-minded focus on battle, and the fears by the certainty of death.
There occurred a battle that was purely devoid of vulgar speech and free from confusion; it resembled a cloudless sky, adorned with the shimmering ripples of sword-waves.

With floods of arrows whizzing with a *khadakhada* sound, with *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons falling with a *ṭakaṭaki* roar, and great missiles clashing with a *jhaṇajhaṇa* din—that battle became difficult to cross, like the deep ocean.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: While this terrible clash of battle was thus proceeding, the two Līlās spoke these words again to the blessed Jñapti.
Līlādvaya said: "O Goddess, why does our husband suddenly defeat us in battle? Tell us, for even though you are pleased, this elephant has fled."

The illustrious Sarasvatī said: "O daughter, I have been propitiated for a long time by this King Vidūratha, the enemy of kings, for the sake of victory; I have not been so propitiated by King Vidūratha himself."
Therefore, that very Vidūratha both conquers and is conquered; for consciousness, which is internalized cognition, is such as it is perceived by whomever, whenever, and in whatever manner.
I quickly bring about for him that which he impels me toward; in whatever manner one impels me, I abide as the fruit thereof for him.
"Intrinsic nature does not admit of change, just as heat is inherent in fire; through this realization, 'I am truly liberated,' such has been my conviction."
Therefore, O child, she who is the embodiment of eloquence shall be liberated; his own enemy is the lord of the earth named Sindhurāja.
"I shall be victorious in battle"—because of this [thought], I was honored; therefore, Vidūratha, having obtained that body along with his wife, [attained his goal].
In time, O child, he shall be released by you and her; his own enemy is the lord of the earth named Sindhurāja.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "Having slain him on the surface of the earth, the victor shall rule the kingdom. While the goddess was speaking thus, the two armies continued to fight.
As if to behold a marvel, the sun ascended the mountain of sunrise; the masses of darkness fled like armies in the form of enemies.
Other multitudes of living beings were created like stars at twilight; gradually, the mountain lands emerged from the dark sky.
The world shone as if tossed up from the ocean of collyrium; the rays of the sun fell like beautiful streams of molten gold.
Then the sky and the field of battle appeared like streaks of blood upon the foremost heroes who were like mountains.
With its arms it was filled with writhing serpents; with its splendors it was strewn with gold; with its earrings it was showered with heaps of jewels; and with its heads it displayed lotuses.
It was dense with swords as its weapons, thick with arrows like a swarm of locusts, rich with a steady twilight of blood-red luster, and filled with corpses accompanied by perfected beings (siddhas).

It was densely crowded with necklaces mixed with sloughed-off snake skins and with girdles blazing like flames; it was adorned with shimmering creepers in the form of banners and had great thighs fashioned into its archways.

With hands and feet it was like a forest of blossoming shoots; with arrows it resembled a grove of *śara* reeds; dark with the grass-blades of the luster of weapons, it was filled with *kaitaka* flowers in the form of a profusion of arms.
Strewn with garlands of weapons, it was as terrifying as one possessed by madness; it took on the appearance of a grove of blossoming *aśoka* trees through the fires produced by the clashing of arms.
With the leaders of the siddhas fleeing amidst loud, tumultuous shouts of "udaghuṃ," it took the form of a golden city, its weapons glittering like the rising sun.

The sky resounded with the clashing of spears, swords, javelins, discuses, double-edged swords, and mallets; it was filled with the force of flowing rivers of blood, carrying away a multitude of corpses.
It was crowded with *bhuśuṇḍī* slings, spears, lances, swords, tridents, and stones; it was filled with the falling of headless trunks covered by the blows of pikes and weapons.
In the empty arena of battle, amidst the tumultuous clamor raised by the Vetālas performing the Kāla-taṇḍava dance, the two flaming chariots of Padma and Sindhu moved forward.
Those two appeared like the sun and moon, the two signs of the sky, in the heavens; they were crowded with weapons such as discuses, spears, bhushundis, double-edged swords, and lances.
Surrounded by thousands upon thousands of heroes, they moved about as they pleased, executing wide-ranging circular maneuvers with loud roars.
With a whistling sound, they crush many beings with their great wheels, becoming both death and immortality; they cross the rivers of blood with the grace of elephants in rut.

In that river, where the hair of the body was like abundant moss, where the wheels were like whirlpools and the moon was the water, elephants were cast down and thrown into confusion by the agitation caused by the impact of the moving wheels.
There was the jingling sound of gems and pearls and the rattling of the chariot-poles; there was the flapping sound of the ends of banners struck by the wind.
They were followed by many great heroes and vast armies of cowards, who vomited forth streams of spears, arrows, and even bows.
There, amidst the flashing spears, spikes, and discuses in the battle, those two momentarily wheeled about in a circle upon the ground.
Both faced each other with their weapons raised, as they let fly showers of iron arrows, creating a sound like the roar of thunderclouds.
Roaring at one another like two intoxicated ocean-clouds, as those two lions among men struck each other with arrows, the earth—[shattered by their impact]—[resounded].
Some took the form of stone maces, spreading through the sky; others had faces like swords, while still others had faces like mallets.

Some had faces like sharp discs, some had faces like axes; some had faces like spears, some had faces like spikes and rocks; some had faces like tridents, while others were as massive as great boulders.

Then the feathered arrows fell like masses of rocks cast down by the winds of universal dissolution; at that moment, the encounter between the two became as tumultuous as the surging of the oceans at the time of the world's end.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having reached the ocean that had arrived before him with its surging waves, the king became expanded by a fury as intense as the midday sun.
He strung his bow, making the quarters of the sky resound for a long time, like the blast of the wind at the end of an eon striking the slope of Mount Meru.
The powerful king discharged a succession of arrows bound in the night of his quiver, like the rays of the sun at the time of universal dissolution.
A single arrow departs from his bowstring, yet as it flies through the sky, it becomes a thousand, falling by the hundreds of thousands.
The power and agility of Sindhudvīpa were likewise equal; thus, by the boon of Viṣṇu, the Giver of Boons, the archery of those two was identical.
Those arrows called *musalas*, shaped like clubs, covered the sky with a great roar, like the thunderbolts at the end of an eon.
Rows of golden arrows shone resoundingly in the sky, like crying stars falling, driven by the winds of the cosmic dissolution.
From Vidūratha, showers of arrows issued forth incessantly, like floods of water from the ocean or rays of light from the sun.
Like flowers from a great tree shaken by a fierce wind, or like showers of sparks struck from a heated iron ball;
Like streams from a rain-cloud, like spray from a waterfall, or like brilliant sparks from the great conflagration of that city's fire.
Hearing the crackling sound of the two bows being drawn, the two armies became as silent as the ocean at rest, watching in stunned silence.
In that battle, floods of arrows flowed through the sky like the currents of the Gaṅgā, rushing toward the ocean with a gurgling roar and great speed.
A continuous rain of whetted golden iron arrows, accompanied by the "śava-śava" sound of falling corpses, issued forth from the cloud that was the bow.
Seeing Bāṇa, who was like a flood of the Mandākinī, proceeding to fill the ocean, Līlā, a resident of that city, watched him from a window.
Perceiving victory for her husband through that multitude of arrows, she, whose lotus-face blossomed with joy, spoke these words.
Victory, O Goddess! Our Lord is victorious; look upon him! Moreover, by this shower of arrows, even Mount Meru would be reduced to powder.
While she was speaking thus, the two goddesses—distraught with cries of deep affection and intent on gazing at her—felt in their hearts a sense of pity for the mortal woman.
The submarine fire of the ocean drank up that surging sea of his body, just as Agastya, by the heat of his arrow, swallowed the Mandākinī.
Having cut that great cloud of arrows into fragments with a shower of shafts, and having reduced it to fine dust, he cast it into the ocean of the sky.
Just as the movement of an extinguished lamp is not perceived, so too the movement of that multitude of arrows was not discerned.
Having severed that dense cloud of a body which was a shower of arrows, he spread it across the sky like a mass of hundreds of corpses drenched in blood.
Vidūratha also swiftly shattered him with his finest arrows, just as the wind at the end of an aeon scatters a common, intoxicated cloud.
Thus, with their showers of arrows rendered futile by counter-strikes, the two lords of the earth delivered blows without further hesitation.
Then Sindhurāja, out of friendship for the Gandharva, discharged the Mohanāstra; by that weapon, all the worlds were rendered unconscious, with the sole exception of Vidūratha.
With their weapons and garments cast aside, mute, and with dejected faces and eyes, the warriors became like the dead, or as if they were figures depicted in a painting.
Just as delusion was leading anyone other than Vidūratha to dullness, King Vidūratha then took up the weapon of awakening.
Then the subjects regained consciousness like a lotus-pond at dawn, while Sindhu became enraged at the Rākṣasa like the sun at the demon Dhūmrākṣa.
He took up the terrifying Naga-weapon, which causes distress through the binding of nooses; by it, the sky became filled with serpents resembling mountains.
The earth was adorned with serpents like a lake with lotus stalks; all the mountains became as if covered by blankets of black snakes.
All these objects indeed reached a state of exhaustion from the heat of the poison; the earth, along with the expanse of its mountains and forests, fell into a state of helplessness.
Winds carrying glowing embers, proclaiming the calamities of poison, blew harshly with heat and mist, while dust blazed like fire.
Then Vidūratha, an expert in great weapons, took up the Sauparṇa weapon; by that Garuḍa-weapon, the Suparṇas rose up like mountains.
They have made all directions golden, fulfilling every hope; they have generated the winds of universal destruction through the violent agitation of their wing-mountains.
Circles of hissing serpents were drawn in by the force of the wind from their nostrils, filling the regions of the ocean with great "ghura-ghura" roars.
Like Agastya swallowing the ocean, that cloud-like Suparṇa swallowed the mass of serpents that filled the earth, hissing distressfully with the sound "śala-śala."
The circle of the earth shone, freed from its serpent-bedding, like the hollow of the earth after a long time, or like the ocean when its mass of water has vanished.
Then that army of Garuḍas vanished somewhere from sight, like a mass of lamps by the wind, or like a circle of clouds in autumn.
Like a mass of mountains and flights of birds out of fear of a thunderbolt, the array before him was like a world seen in a dream, or like a city of one's own mental construction.
Then Sindhu discharged the weapon of darkness, which produces blinding gloom; by that, the darkness increased until it was as black as the belly of the earth.
Spreading across the cavity of the earth, it became like a single vast ocean; the armies became like fish, and the stars became like jewels.
It was like an ocean of ink-paste set in motion by darkness, as if produced by the winds of the kalpa arising from the mass of the mountain of collyrium.
All the subjects were as if fallen into a blind well; all worldly affairs fell into confusion, like the quarters of the sky at the end of an eon.
Then Vidūratha, the best among those who know mantras, having fashioned the Mārtaṇḍa weapon—a lamp within the pavilion of the universe—set it in motion with a mantra.
Then, like the cloudless autumn season, Agastya drank up the ocean that had risen, just as the sun drinks up the dark clouds with its rays.
The stainless quarters of the sky, released from the garment of darkness, shone forth like beautiful women with lovely breasts standing before the lord of the earth.
All the forest ranges within became manifest, like the intellects of the virtuous when they are freed from the soot-like net of greed.
Then Sindhur, overwhelmed with anger, instantly unleashed the most terrifying Rākṣasa weapon, which consisted of arrows discharged by means of mantras.
Fierce and harsh forest-rākṣasas rose up from all directions like great oceans agitated by the trumpeting of the elephants of the underworld.
The fires, with their smoke-colored matted locks of Kapila hue, crackling with loud *caṭa-caṭa* sounds, were like blazing tongues licking at wet fuel.
Moving in whirlpools across the sky with terrifying whistling and clanging sounds, they were like great fires with blazing brands, tossing amidst thick columns of smoke.
With their faces, mud-pools, eyes, and bodies overrun by the sprouts of fangs as venom, they appeared like the banks of a foul pond where hair grows like moss.
Swallowing, rushing forward, and roaring like those who have been provoked, they were like water-laden clouds with masses of lightning amidst their matted locks.
In the meantime, Vidūratha, the lord of Līlā, bestowed the Nārāyaṇa weapon, which wards off wicked beings.
As this king of mantras was being uttered, the kings of weapons belonging to the Rākṣasas were quelled, just as darkness is dispelled at the rising of the sun.
The three worlds became devoid of the Rākṣasa host; it shone forth stainless, like the sky in autumn when the clouds have departed.
Then Sindhur released the fiery weapon (āgneya-astra), which set the sky ablaze; by it, the quarters of the world blazed as if ignited by the fire of cosmic destruction (kalpāgni).
All the directions became shrouded by a mass of smoke and clouds, as if the sky were agitated by the darkness of the underworld spreading upward.
The mountains appeared ablaze like mountains of gold, as if covered by dense groves of blossoming campaka flowers.
The sky, mountains, and forest thickets took on the appearance of masses of matted locks from a network of flames; they were as if smeared with saffron paste like garlands at the festival of Death.
And that populace, fearing for their safety, was set ablaze by that [fire] which touched the sky, as if it had been stirred from the ocean by the force of a thousand-formed ship.
Having conquered his enemy, Vidūratha, honoring him as he would strike again, discharged the Vāruṇa weapon.
Floods of water came from all sides like floods of darkness—from below, from above, and from every direction—appearing like mountains in liquid form.
Like portions of the sky, like clouds sustained in flight, like great oceans situated on high, and like the rocks of the principal mountain ranges.
They were like masses of *tamāla* trees flying up, like nights joined together, or like heaps of collyrium rising from the slopes of the Lokāloka mountain.
Like the vast expanses of the subterranean caves of Rasātala desiring to behold the sky, their forms were augmented by the force of a great, deep, and rumbling roar.
The stream of water, pervading the world, quickly swallowed up that intoxicated stream of fire at twilight, just as the night swallows the dark of day.
Having drunk that continuous stream of fire, the splendor of the waters filled the earth, like sleep manifesting once again after its body had been congealed.
Thus, while others were bewildered by the weapons, they created various illusions before them; they saw these illusory forms and experienced them as real.
Then the excellent protectors of the wheels of the ocean, who were like the weight of its causeway, were swept away by the waters as if they were blades of grass; and his chariot became submerged.
In the meantime, Sindhurāja remembered the drying weapon, that divine protection against calamity, which he had given him in the form of an arrow.
By that very sun, the water-based illusion was quelled; those who were dead remained indeed dead, and the earth became parched.
Then, like the wrath of a fool, a heat arose that tormented all creatures; it expanded with a harshness like that of a vast forest filled with decaying trees.
The luster of the bodies of the women of the quarters, beautiful with the flow of polished gold, was like a cosmetic ointment applied to their limbs.
Because of that, those who were his adversaries fell into a swoon born of the Dharma, like tender shoots scorched by a summer forest fire.
Then Vidūratha, in the height of battle, having bent his drawn bow with a loud twang, took up the Parjanya weapon.
Rows of clouds rose up like accumulated nights, moving slowly with water as if stirred by the frantic flight of swarms from the tamāla forests.
Dwarfish with their floods of water, moving about with a roar of unrestrained power, they serve as earrings for the entire circle of the quarters, which is made slow by their greatness.
Winds blew, swirling with rain-showers, piercing through the mass of clouds, and magnificent with the weight of scattered spray and mist.
Lightnings flashed in the sky like the gliding of excellent golden serpents, resembling the rolling side-glances of celestial women.

The quarters of the sky swayed, their mountain caves resounding with the swelling echoes of roars, and rumbling with the deep, gurgling sounds of the cries of elephants, lions, and bears that had been set in motion.
Torrential rains fell in streams like great clubs, harsh with painful clattering sounds, resembling the very glances of the God of Death.
First, a hot vapor, resembling fire, rose from the earth from the netherworld (pātāla), assuming the appearance of a mass of clouds as if for battle.
Then, in the mere twinkling of an eye, the mirages subsided, just as the latent tendencies of saṃsāra are dispelled by the overflowing essence of supreme awakening.
The entire circle of the earth became marked with mud and impassable; the ocean was filled with full torrents of water like the river Sindhu itself.
He discharged the Vāyavya weapon, which filled the hollow of the sky and was as terrifying as the roaring Bhairava intoxicated by the dance at the end of an aeon.

Winds blew from the quarters of the sky, their bodies pained by the falling of thunderbolts and scattering fragments of shattered rock; signaling the time of universal dissolution, they produced sharp, resonant clanging sounds that struck terror into the warriors.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Winds blew, swirling with frost and scattering the sprouts of the forest; they shook the multitude of trees and carried the pollen of playful flower-garlands.
Like birds, they rushed toward the masses of trees, fierce in their rising and falling; they shattered the fragments of watchtowers and pierced through walls as high as clouds.
Then, by that exceedingly fearsome wind, Vidūratha’s chariot was carried away like a withered leaf upon a river.
Then Vidūratha, an expert in great weapons, cast aside the mountain-weapon, as if the sky itself were striving to seize it with thick rain-clouds.
By that blow from the mountain-weapon, Virāṭ’s life-breath, like a pervasive wind, subsided as if through the cessation of consciousness.
Rows of trees situated in the sky fell to the earth like tens of millions of crows upon a mass of the corpses of various people.

The sounds of *sūtkāra*, *ḍāṅkāra*, *bhāṅkāra*, and *utkāraka* in the quarters of the sky were silenced, like the wailing cries of cities, villages, forests, and creepers when they have been utterly destroyed.
Like the ocean seeing mountains with wings—Maināka and others—falling here and there from the sky like colored leaves, Sindhu beheld them likewise.
Then the hosts of Vajras set forth, emitting the blazing Vajra-weapon, as they consumed the darkness of the great mountains like fires consuming a conflagration.
Thus hurled against the mountains, they shattered their peaks with the blows of their beaks, causing the heads to fall like fruits blown down by a violent wind.
Then Vidūratha, for the sake of neutralizing the Vajra weapon, unleashed the Brahmā weapon; thereafter, both the Brahmā and Vajra weapons were simultaneously extinguished.
Then Sindhu discharged the Piśāca weapon, dark as the night; by it, ranks of Piśācas, causing extreme terror, surged forth.
Then, as if out of fear of the twilight, the day turned to blackness; the Piśācas entered the world like masses of darkness.
Resembling pillars of ash, swaying with the grace of palm trees, they appeared to be of immense size, yet were nothing more than what could be grasped in a fist.
Some had upraised hair and emaciated limbs, while others were even bearded; with dark and soiled bodies, those sky-dwellers appeared like common villagers.
Terrified, with deluded vision, acting recklessly and wavering, they were wretched and cruel as if struck by a thunderbolt, like lowly village folk.
Moving through trees, mud, and the interiors of roads, they frequent empty houses; these beings, resembling hungry ghosts with black limbs, are flickering like restless tongues.
Then, intoxicated, they seized the remaining force of the enemy that had survived the slaughter; the soldiers there were broken, their weapons shattered, and their minds agitated.
Having cast aside their weapons, armor, and lives, they stumbled in their gait; with their eyes, limbs, faces, and feet, they displayed a multitude of contortions.
Having cast off their loincloths, with their lower garments submerged, they voided excrement and urine while maintaining a steady, commenced dance.
As soon as the queen of the Piśācas began to attack King Vidūratha, the wise king recognized that it was an illusion.
That lord of the earth knew the illusion that creates a battle with piśācas; by means of it, he deployed that army of piśācas against the enemy's host.
Then his own soldiers became healthy while the enemy warriors turned into ghouls; in his wrath, he quickly gave her another weapon, the Rūpikāstra.
From the earth and from the sky, the Rūpikās emerged, with hair standing erect on their heads, with sunken and terrifying eyes, and with trembling hips and breasts.
Some were old women whose youth had burst forth; some were stout-limbed, while others were decrepit; some possessed beautiful forms and hips, while others had deformed navels and blooming vulvas.
With human blood in their hands and human heads, their limbs were as ruddy as twilight clouds; their mouths were agitated by the flow of flesh and blood dripping from their lips, half-chewed.
They possess various movements of the limbs and various ways of bending one another’s bodies; they have stone-like arms, snakes, jaws, thighs, hips, sides, hands, and bodies.
They bore the corpses of infants made by women, with entrails pulled from their hands like ropes; they had faces like dogs, crows, and owls, with sunken mouths, jaws, and bellies.
They seized those Piśācas as if they were weak infants; thus, that army of female Piśācas became a single mass.
With faces, limbs, and eyes upturned from being submerged in their dance, they were trampling one another and rushing against one another.
With great tongues protruding and displaying various contortions of the face, it was thick with packs of *śarabha* beasts, while the limbs of corpses were being snatched away from one another.
Sinking and emerging in the blood-water, with a body shimmering in its heart, it had a protruding belly, long arms, and pendulous ears, lips, and nose.
They were struggling with one another in the great mire of blood and flesh, amidst the tumultuous, resonant clamor of the milk-ocean stirred by Mount Mandara.
Just as he had previously performed the movement of the illusion, so too did the other perform it for him immediately upon realizing it, with such agility.
Then he gave the Vetāla weapon, by which hosts of corpses arose—headless Vetālas and those with heads, swaying with their entrails.
Then that army became terrifying, like piśācas, vetālas, rūpikas, and fierce headless trunks (kabandhas), capable of swallowing the earth.
Then the other king also, having employed that illusion against his preceptor, discharged the Rākṣasa weapon, which was intent on seizing the three worlds.
Rākṣasas as massive as mountains, thick in every limb, surged forth from all sides; having taken hold of their bodies, they emerged from Pātāla like beings from hell.
Then there arose a terrifying army that struck fear into both gods and asuras—an army resounding with the great roars of shouting rākṣasas and filled with dancing headless trunks.
Abounding in snacks of fat and meat, and beautiful with blood and spirituous liquor; it was made lovely by the frantic dance of intoxicated *kūśmāṇḍa* spirits, *vetālas*, and *yakṣas*.

A bridge was established over the stream of blood by spirits whose brilliance rivaled the tips of the massed clouds of twilight, who were sprinkled with waves tossed up by the blood agitated by the staff-like feet of Kūśmāṇḍa performing his frantic dance.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: While that terrible confusion of battle was then occurring, for the sake of destroying the entire enemy army and for the pacification of his own forces, [he performed] one [act].
The mindful Ananta, possessing great nobility and supreme fortitude, called to mind the glorious Vaiṣṇava weapon, the lord of weapons, which was equal to Śaṅkara.
Then, from the tip of the fruit of that very arrow which had been consecrated with the Vaiṣṇava weapon when released by him, flaming meteors issued forth into the sky.
Rows of broad discuses made the horizons appear as if filled with hundreds of suns; approaching maces made the sky seem as if filled with hundreds of bamboo poles.
The sky was turned into a forest of grass by vajras with a hundred edges; the sky was turned into a grove of wretched trees by sharp-edged spears adorned with lotuses.
The sky was turned into a lattice of flowers by their sharp-edged arrows; the sky was turned into heaps of fallen leaves by their dark-hued swords.
Then the king, for the sake of neutralizing the second Vaiṣṇava weapon as well, discharged a Vaiṣṇava weapon that brings about the destruction of the enemy.
Then, from that [lake] also issued forth rivers consisting of arrows, spears, maces, darts, battle-axes, and other weapons, which had destroyed the weapons of their enemies.
A battle of those rivers of weapons and missiles took place in the sky, causing the destruction of the space between heaven and earth and shattering the great lords of the principal mountain ranges.
Arrows had felled the spears, and axes, swords, and battle-axes were hacked to pieces; maces, clubs, darts, and spikes had shattered the javelins.
The churning of the ocean of arrows was like Mount Mandara with its mallets, while the faces of the maces appeared like irresistible weapons.
The moon-like circle of his whirling spears pacified both misfortune and prosperity, while the violent advance of his darts provoked the risen God of Death himself.

It had upward-pointing weapons obstructed by its wheels, it caused the destruction of all other weapons, it shattered the cosmic egg of Brahmā with its roar, and it broke the great boundary mountains with its blows.
As the two fought with a torrent of weapons severed by their own streams, it was as if a thunderbolt were striking a mountain that had become ageless through the warding off of its own fluid.
It was filled with hundreds of stones that whistled like spikes as they were struck, and it contained a formidable circle of *bhindipāla* slings, their long handles subdued by the *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons.
With one hand holding a battle-axe and the other a trident, he brandished his severed enemy-warriors as they moved with their beaks still dripping blood.
The triple-pathed river and the sun were obstructed by the crackling *caṭacaṭa* sounds of bursting [bodies], while a great canopy of smoke arose from the mass of pulverized weapons and missiles.
From the clashing of their mutual weapons, lightning flashed from the whirling circles of blades; the cosmic egg of Brahmā burst with sound, and the principal mountain ranges were cast into the fire.
As the two fought with a torrent of weapons severed by their own streams [of power], the means for the immovable-souled one to bring about the end was simply the warding off of the other's missiles.
To see how much strength he possessed while standing effortlessly upon the ocean, Vidūratha discharged the Āgneya weapon with a sound like a thunderbolt.
He set the chariot ablaze like dry undergrowth in a forest; meanwhile, the interior of the sky was filled with a dense mass of weapons.
Like a rain cloud with its lightning-charges, or like a river during the monsoon, he [the demon] engaged in an exceedingly terrible battle for a moment against the weapons of the two kings.
When they had reached a state of mutual pacification, like two valiant warriors, in that interval Agni reduced the chariot to ashes.
Having burned the forest, he reached the Sindhu river as a lion emerges from a mountain cave; there, the Sindhu king, approaching him, neutralized the fire-weapon with a water-weapon.
Abandoning his chariot and reaching the ground, he brandished his sword; in the mere twinkling of an eye, [he struck] the hooves of the enemy's chariot-horses.
With agility, he cut [his opponent's] sword like lotus stalks with a blade; Vidūratha, now deprived of his chariot, drew his sword with a loud flourish.
Equipped with equal weapons and equal zeal, the two of them moved in circular maneuvers; as they struck one another, their swords became like saws.
As he was devouring the subjects with his row of teeth as if they were mere morsels of food, Vidūratha took up a spear and hurled it, casting aside his sword.
With a gurgling roar like the waters of the Indus, like a great portentous thunderbolt, it came on unceasingly and fell upon his chest.
Just as an unwilling wife [might strike] her unpleasant husband, by that blow of the staff he did not meet his death.
The Naga shed a mass of blood like water; seeing him broken, as darkness is dispelled by the moon, Taddeśalīlā was moved.
Filled with expansive and dense bliss, she spoke of their former pastime: "O Goddess, behold! This husband of ours has been slain by Nṛsiṃha."

With the tips of his crores of claws as sharp as spears, the Daitya, whose neck was raised like that of an elephant in the ocean, [shook him] like the water sprayed from the trunk of a lordly elephant standing on the shore of a lake.
As he was ground down, his blood flowed out with gurgling sounds; "Alas, what misery! The elephant, brought before the chariot, is now intent on mounting it."
"O Goddess, behold! This golden peak of Mount Meru has been pulverized by his mallet, just as if it were the Puṣkarāvarta cloud."
"By the falling of the whirling Pārtha, it was like a golden city; this husband of mine has arrived, brought here to mount the chariot."
Alas! Like a thunderbolt hurled by Indra or a mace cast by the Ocean, my husband has swiftly pursued the King of Sindhu, who bears a mace as his weapon.
Having deceived him with his gracefulness, he swiftly mounted the chariot; alas, what a tragedy! This Sindhu has, by his speed, overtaken the chariot of the noble son.
Like one mounted upon a lion’s mane, or like a tree being shaken upward by a flood, he tormented Vidūratha with showers of arrows after having sported with him.
His banner was severed, his chariot shattered, his horses slain, and his charioteer cut down; his bow and armor were broken, and with all his limbs pierced, he lay in utter distress.
Having pierced his broad-headed heart—firm as a slab of stone—with arrows as hard as thunderbolts, he surely casts him down upon the earth.
Then, having regained consciousness with great difficulty, behold how the shoulder of your master was severed by a sword as he was mounting another chariot that had been brought to him.
It sheds a stream of blood like the radiance of a mountain of rubies; alas, alas! Woe is me, by this ocean with its sword-like current!
My husband has been severed from my thighs like a tree cut by a saw; alas, alas! I am struck down, I am consumed, I am dead, and I am utterly ruined.
"Both my knees have been severed like lotus stalks by my husband," she said, and upon seeing that, she was overcome with fear for her husband's state of mind.
Like a creeper severed by an axe, she fell to the ground in a swoon; Vidūratha too, his knees giving way, collapsed while still striking at his enemy.
He fell beneath the chariot like a tree severed at its roots; even as he was falling, he was carried away by the chariot driven by the charioteer.
Whenever he struck him, the haughty Sindhu would deliver a blow to his throat; thus, with his throat half-severed, he was pursued by the Sindhu.

He entered the palace by chariot, just as the sun’s ray enters a lotus; yet, due to the power of Sarasvatī, he was unable to enter that house, just as a drunken gnat cannot enter the interior of a great flame.

With his body, garments, and armor smeared by splashes of fresh blood and froth trickling from the wound in his throat, which had been severed by a sword, the enemy was brought inside the house by the charioteer; having placed him upon a bed on the floor, the driver departed while the Blessed Lady remained nearby.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the cry "The king is slain! The king is slain by a rival king in battle! arose, the kingdom became overwhelmed with fear.

A multitude of carts was fleeing, heavily laden with vessels and household goods; it was filled with wailing and distressed wives, making the city difficult for its inhabitants to traverse as they fled.
With people fleeing in cries of distress, groups of women seized along the roads, and a great terror gripping everyone as they busied themselves plundering one another.
It resounded with the intense clamor of the dancing throngs of the enemy kingdom's people, while elephants, horses, and heroic warriors fell down, left without anyone to command them.
It resounded with the gurgling of bees flying from the interior of hives as the doors were shattered, and it was filled with fierce warriors clad in countless plundered silken garments.
The courtyard of the royal palace at Rājagṛha was filled with fresh entrails torn out by knives, while a multitude of Caṇḍālas and Śvapacas rested within the king’s inner apartments.
There were commoners eager to eat the food and rice stolen from houses, and children whose limbs were wounded by the feet of a multitude of heroes adorned with golden necklaces.
The women of the inner apartments were overtaken by youths of unprecedented beauty, while the paths were strewn with priceless jewels fallen from the hands of thieves.

The circle of vassal kings was preoccupied with the crowding of horses, elephants, and chariots, while the chief ministers stood at the forefront, intent on issuing the commands for the preparations of the consecration.
The master architect had begun the construction of the royal capital, where the king’s favorites were falling into the windows and chasms he had created.
It was filled with the roar of hundreds of shouts of victory from the kings of Sindhu, and its stability was maintained by the ocean-like multitude of his own innumerable royal hosts.
The royal favorites were fleeing, having been overtaken by the invasion from another village; plundering of towns and villages was occurring throughout the various districts.
The coming and going on the roads was blocked by the plundering of endless thieves and robbers; the heat of the sun was obscured by a mist caused by the absence of those of great majesty.
With the wailing of deceased kinsmen, the sounds of funeral drums, and the noise of horses, elephants, and chariots, there was a dense resonance that could be grasped as a single mass.
"Sindhudeva is victorious, the sovereign lord of the earth under a single umbrella!"—immediately after this, the kettledrums were then sounded in every city.
Then Sindhu, with his neck held high, entered the capital city like another Manu entering the world at the end of a Yuga to create new subjects.
Then, from the ten directions, the tributes set out to enter the city of Sindhurāja, appearing like elephants and horses carrying floods of jewels toward the ocean.
The ministers, in every direction toward the mandala, instantly established binding signs and instructions.
In a very short time, this rule regarding life, death, and honor arose in every land and in every city, just as follows.
Then, in the twinkling of an eye, the calamities and disturbances of the land subsided, like the movements of objects when the winds of a portentous storm have been stilled.
The region, encompassing the ten directions, quickly attained tranquility, like the Ocean of Milk when its turbulent whirlpools have subsided and Mount Mandara has been swiftly withdrawn.

The winds from the Sindhu region blew, tossing the masses of dark curls and agitating the swarms of bees upon the lotus-faces of the women; turbulent with the swirling of water droplets, they seemed in an instant to scatter all inauspicious qualities in every direction.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In the meantime, O Rāma, Līlā spoke to Sarasvatī, seeing her husband standing before her, stupefied and with nothing but his breath remaining.

"O Mother, this husband of mine has set out here to cast off his body during this battle of such great undertaking, amidst the turmoil of the kingdom. Jñapti said: "In a battle of such a form and great enterprise, in the agitation of the realm..."
Although it was prosperous and remained at its height, though it was slow to undertake various new enterprises, nothing at all was truly accomplished—neither in the kingdom nor upon the earth.
This world, consisting of nothing but a dream, does not abide anywhere at all; it exists within that pavilion, in the space near the corpse.
O sinless one, this kingdom of Bhū appears within the inner apartments of your husband’s residence; it is this very realm, with its interior filled by the countryside.
Within the house of the Brahmin Vasiṣṭha, situated in a village on the Vindhya mountains, the world exists within that house of the dead.
This world-house exists within the belly of the world-house of the corpse; thus is this great undertaking, the delusion consisting of the three worlds.
United with you, me, her, and him, the earth together with the oceans shall exist within the hollow of the sky, inside the body of a mountain village.
One's own self alone shines forth; that which is vain does not shine at all, nor anywhere. Know that to be the supreme state, devoid of destruction and origination.
Spontaneously manifesting, luminous, peaceful, and supremely free from affliction—indeed, within the pavilion-house, it arises as one's own nature within the Self.
Thus, even within those two pavilions which were so densely constructed, there exists only the empty space in their interior, and not the delusion of a world.
For in the absence of a deluded perceiver, what kind of delusion could there be in the delusion? Since the existence of delusion does not exist at all, that which exists is the unborn state.
Error is the appearance of that which does not exist; how can there be the state of seer and seen? Because of the absence of the sequence of seer and seen, that indeed is non-dual and innate.
Know that supreme state to be devoid of destruction and origination; it is self-luminous, manifest, peaceful, primordial, and free from affliction.
It is said that within the pavilion-house, people dwell there according to their own established order, within the Self that has arisen from their respective natures, as if in their own homes.
Neither the world nor any creation whatsoever is experienced there; therefore, I am the unborn space, and it exists as the world.
All consciousness of self is empty, like the network of mountains such as Meru; this is not made of bricks at all, just as a great city in a dream.
Even in a region the size of a span, those who know the world understand that there are hundreds of thousands of voids consisting of networks of mountains, yet possessing the essence of diamond.
Even within an atom, vast worlds arise in great numbers through their arrangement, like the leaves of a plantain tree.
The three worlds exist within the atomic point of consciousness like a city in a dream; within that too are atomic points of consciousness, and within each of those, there is a world.
O auspicious one, in that world where this lotus-king Śava resides, this Līlā, your co-wife, has already arrived long ago.
The very moment this Līlā fell into a swoon before you, she stood at the side of her husband Padma’s corpse.
Līlā said: O Goddess, how did she formerly become embodied there, and how did she come to abide in the state of being the wife of her co-wife?
Tell me briefly: what form do those who dwell in that excellent house see of her, and what do they say? Tell me this.
