The Śrī Devī said: Listen; I shall tell you everything in brief, exactly as you have asked—the account of my own play, O Līlā, which brings an end to the wretched vision of the phenomenal world.
That husband of Padmā beholds this vast delusion, consisting of the entire world, within that very same dwelling.
This battle is a battle of delusion; this person is a non-person, for they are merely delusion. Death exists here only through delusion, and thus it is of the nature of error.
By this very sequence of delusion, his beloved Līlā remains; both you and she, O beautiful woman, are merely a dream.
O beautiful woman, just as this [world] is for you two merely a dream, so too is this husband of yours, and I myself am likewise.
This world-appearance is such that it is called "the visible" here; when this very thing is fully understood, one abandons the meaning of the word "visible."
In this way, she is thus, and she is thus; so too is that king, and I have attained the state of truth within myself through the all-pervasiveness of the Self.
"We are here, having come together and been impelled by one another"—thus [they think], due to the state of the Great Mass of Consciousness which exists as the self-nature of all.
Thus did this queen remain, radiant with a captivating smile, her face playful with grace, and endowed with the bloom of fresh youth.
Sweet with her graceful conduct, speaking with words that were both pleasant and noble, her voice resembled the song of the cuckoo, and she moved with the languid grace of intoxication and love.
Her eyes were like the petals of a blue lotus, her breasts were round and full; she was lovely, with limbs as fair as gold, and lips like the ripe *bimba* fruit.
When this mental aspect of her husband, who consists of your own volition, abides within the wonder of consciousness, then she stands here with a form identical to yours.
Indeed, immediately upon the death of your husband, this very person was seen before you by him, whose self had become your own mental resolve.

When the mind itself experiences a material (ādhibhautika) state as its object of thought, that which is perceived is composed of pure being; therefore, it is a conceptualization of the subtle body (ātivāhika).
When the mind no longer perceives material existence as being composed of reality, then the conception of the subtle body arises as truth.
Furthermore, in this delusion consisting of rebirth through the perception of death, he has indeed been perceived by him, and he has likewise gone by you.
Thus he has seen you, and you have indeed been seen by him; for you also have become established within yourself, owing to the all-pervasive nature of the conscious self.
Since Brahman is all-pervading, in whatever manner and wherever it arises, it immediately becomes so there; one perceives it through the very power of dream.
Because it possesses all powers everywhere, whatever power may be raised up in a particular place, it remains there and shines forth in that manner due to the cause of intense momentum.
At the very moment the couple remained in a state of death-like stupor, they both perceived this within their hearts through the power of mental projection.
"These two are our fathers, and these indeed are our mothers; this is our country, this is our wealth, and such was our former occupation."
"We two have been married in this very way, thus having attained oneness; even that multitude of people has gone to truthfulness right there."
"In this very matter, there is a direct example: the experience of a dream. O Līlā, by contemplating in this way, I was then worshipped by you with playfulness.
"I shall not become a widow"—this was the boon granted by me as well; for this reason, indeed, the girl died here previously.
I am the conscious principle for you who possess consciousness; as the family deity, I myself always perform that which is to be worshipped.

Then Jīvaka, assuming the form of the vital breath (prāṇa-māruta) and having entered the state of movement by means of the mind, departed from her body while leaving his own physical frame at her mouth.
Then, at the end of the fainting spell caused by death, he was seen by this very living self within the intellect (buddhi) as being manifested in space right here in this house.

This fawn-eyed woman, endowed with the splendor of the moon’s orb upon her face, haughty with pride and fond of her lover's dalliance, desires to enjoy her beloved; with her face turned forward in haste through the memory of the past, she is united within the circle like a lotus-pond of extraordinary power awakened at the end of a dream.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, having obtained the boon, she set out through the path of the sky toward the celestial realm in order to reach her husband, the lord of the earth, with this very body.
Having reflected thus, she—her passion for the god of love unrestrained—leaped joyfully into the sky like a bird of delicate form.
There she found the maiden, sent by her very consciousness as a beneficial messenger, appearing as if she had emerged from the great mirror of her own imagination.
The maiden said: "I am the daughter of Jñapti; welcome to you, O beautiful one! I have been standing here on the path of the sky, awaiting none other than you."
Līlā said: "O Goddess with eyes like lotus petals, lead me to my husband; for the sight of the great is never in vain."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "Come, let us go right there," having said this, the young girl stood before her in the sky, intent on showing the way.
Then, following after him, she reached the hollow of the sky, as a streak of the lunar crescent reaches the tip of a garland of rays.
Then, having crossed the path of the clouds, she went into the midst of the wind-spheres; she approached the path of the sun and passed beyond the path of the stars.
By virtue of his lightness, having leaped over the worlds of Vāyu, Indra, the Suras, and the Siddhas, he reached the shell of the cosmic egg belonging to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa.

Just as the coldness of frost, though residing within, becomes manifest outside when a jar is broken, so too did she, perfected through her own resolve, emerge from the cosmic egg into the external world.
Having a body consisting of nothing but one's own mind, born from the nature of one's own volitions, one indeed experiences such a delusion within oneself alone.

Having ascended to and reached the station of Brahmā and the shell of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa-kharpara), one then [reaches] the coverings of water and the other elements situated beyond the cosmic egg.

Having leaped forward, he reached the interior of the great sky of consciousness, whose farthest limits are unseen even by Garuḍa flying with extreme speed from every direction for hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Therein exist hundreds of thousands of Brahma-eggs, innumerable and vast; they are unseen by one another, like fruits in a great forest.
There, having pierced a single vessel situated before him that was provided with an extensive covering, he entered within like a worm into a jujube fruit.
Again, having transcended the radiant worlds of Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and the others, he reached that glorious terrestrial sphere below the path of the stars.
Having reached that mandala, that city, and having entered that pavilion, she stood near the corpse of Puṣpagupta.
In the meantime, that fair-faced woman did not see the maiden; she had vanished somewhere like an illusion once it has been recognized.
Beholding the face of her husband in the form of a corpse, she realized through the power of intuition that this was indeed the truth.
This is that husband of mine, slain in battle by the Sindhu king; having reached these worlds of heroes, he lies for a moment at his ease.
"By the grace of the Goddess, I, being fortunate, have thus reached this state in my very body; there is no one whatsoever equal to me."
Having reflected thus, she took the beautiful chowrie in her hand and fanned him, as the moon fans the earth's surface with its light.
Prabuddhalīlā said: O Goddess, what will those servants, those female slaves, and that awakened king say, and with what speech and with what intellect?
The Goddess said: That king, those servants, and all of them [became one] with each other through the immersion in the unity of the space of consciousness and by the power of us two.
Because they are manifestations of the great consciousness and because of the certainty of the great fixed order, they see one another, reflected within each other.
"This is my co-born wife; this is my co-born friend; this is my co-born queen; this is my co-born servant."
Only you, I, and she shall know this marvel exactly as it happened in its entirety; no one else at all shall know it.
Prabuddhalīlā said: "Why did this Līlā, who speaks so charmingly, not go to her husband with this very body, even though she obtained him through a boon?"

The Goddess said: Those of unawakened intellect are not capable of reaching the worlds of the Siddhas—which arise through the power of merit—with their own bodies, just as shadows cannot reach the sunlight.
And at the beginning of creation, destiny was established by the enlightened ones, such that truth never at all mingles with falsehood.
As long as a child possesses the conceptualization of a ghost, how and by what means can there be the arising of that [realization] for one whose mind is free from ghosts?
As long as the feverish heat of non-discrimination exists within the self, how can the cooling moonlight of discrimination sufficiently arise?
"How could one who internally holds the conviction, 'I am the body composed of earth and other elements; I have no supreme movement in the sky,' ever possess a different conviction?"
Therefore, by means of the discernment of knowledge, merit, and supreme excellence, they go to the higher world with this body of merit.
Just as a dry leaf is quickly consumed by embers, so too this body of mine, having reached [the end], falls apart.
This alone occurs through the manifestation of boons and curses: that memory arises such that one thinks, "I am exactly as I have intended. This is memory.
How can that cognition of a snake with respect to a rope perform the function of a snake? For how can there be causal efficacy for that which does not exist even in its own right?
But that which is falsely experienced as "this is dead" is merely the manifestation of a previously cultivated habituation.
In the web of the world experienced by oneself, the delusions of memory are easily understood; such a practice of creation and so forth is not indeed something imagined by another.
The transmigrations being experienced within are like the lunar orb appearing from afar to men who do not recognize what is to be known—the external networks of elements.

The Goddess said: Therefore, those who are knowers of the object of knowledge, or those who have taken refuge in the supreme Dharma, attain the worlds of the *ātivāhika* (conveying) state in this world, and no others.
How can the state of being a physical body, which consists of false delusion, attain stability in the Truth? How could shadows exist in the sunlight?
Līlā, who knows all that is to be known and has taken recourse to the supreme dharma, went to the city fashioned by her husband solely for his sake.
Prabuddhalīlā said: "O Mother, let her depart in this manner; behold my husband! He has begun to relinquish his life-force. What should be done here now?"
How has the necessity of entities come about amidst their existence and non-existence? And how is it that there is again a lack of necessity, as indicated by death, birth, and so forth?
How is intrinsic nature established? How does existence reside in categories of things? How is there heat in fire and the like, and how is there stability in earth and the like?
How can there be coldness in snow and the like? What is existence in time, space, and so forth? And how could there be the perception of existence and non-existence, or of the gross and the subtle?
How is it that things such as grass, shrubs, and humans do not attain ultimate height, even though their own causes for height remain present and have not ceased?
The Goddess said: When the great dissolution has occurred and all objects have set, only the eternal Brahman remains, as the infinite space extending to the ends of the quarters.
By virtue of its nature as consciousness, it perceives itself as "I am a spark of light," just as you do in a dream, perceiving such things as traveling through the sky.
This spark of radiance attains grossness within itself by itself; that which is known as this very universe is indeed unreal, yet it appears as real.
Therein, he knows that internal Brahman as "I am this Brahman"; then, his own self creates this very world as a kingdom of the mind.
In that first creation, whatever cognitions were manifested in whatever manner and wherever, they remain even today exactly as they were, unchanging.

In whatever manner the mind manifests, in that very manner it becomes the self-consciousness; being itself unrestricted, it may become this or that, for here there is nothing whatsoever [other than it].
Moreover, it is not logical that one who possesses all forms should be nothing at all; for how indeed could gold remain after having abandoned every configuration?
Just as at the beginning of creation, consciousness itself manifested within itself as snow, fire, and so forth, even now it remains so by its own inherent existence.
Therefore, it is not possible for that which exists to abandon its own being; since consciousness remains, this necessity does not perish.
Just as something reflected appears there as if it were made of earth, even though it is of the nature of space, so too its movement from the beginning of creation until this day is not possible.
Whatever way consciousness manifests, if one lacks knowledge of the antidote, it does not deviate from that state by itself due to the habitual tendency toward feeling.
That which is experienced here in the beginning of the world as unarisen is the manifestation of the space of consciousness, like the sexual pleasure with a woman in a dream.
"This manifestation stands as the very unreal appearing as real"—this is the perfection of intrinsic nature; such are the experiences of reality.

That continuous stream of the manifestation of consciousness which was established at the beginning of creation remains even now, unshaken by anything else; it is called *niyati* (the principle of necessity).

The sky of consciousness, having grasped the perception of space, has attained the state of space; the firmament of consciousness, having grasped the perception of time, has attained the state of time.
The sky of consciousness, which perceives the apprehension of water, exists like water itself; for just as in a dream, a person perceives within himself the appearance of water.
The consciousness of dream-appearance shines forth and exists just as it is; through the skill of the wonder of consciousness, it gathers together this which is unreal.
Consciousness itself internally perceives the state of being a bedstead, water, earth, fire, or even air, though these are unreal, just as it does in dreams, volitions, and meditations.
Listen now to the sequence of experiencing the fruits of karma immediately after death—the process that brings about the welfare of the deceased—for the purpose of pacifying all doubts.
In the primary creation (Rūḍhasarga), there is a fixed limit of one, two, three, or four hundred years for the lifespan of men in the eastern and other directions; hear from me that fixed rule.
The purity or impurity of place, time, action, and substance regarding one's own deeds, as well as their deficiency or excess, are the causes of the lifespan of human beings.
In this world, when the dharma of one's own karma declines, the lifespan of human beings declines; when it increases, it attains increase; and when it remains the same, it likewise remains the same.

A child meets death through actions that bring about the death of children; a youth through those that bring about the death of youths; and an old man through those that bring about the death of the elderly.
He who abides in his own duty as it has been undertaken according to the scriptures becomes a fortunate vessel for a lifespan in accordance with the scriptures.
Thus, according to their karma, living beings experience here at the final stage the agonizing sensations of the vital organs being severed as they reach the end of existence.
Prabuddhalīlā said: "O moon-faced one, tell me briefly about death: is death happiness or is it suffering, and what happens after one has died?"

The Goddess said: At the end of the body, there are three kinds of persons who are about to die: the fool, the one who practices concentration (dhāraṇā), and likewise the person possessed of skillful means (yukti).
Having practiced the concentrations and being devoted to them, one who has mastered concentration and is likewise endowed with skillful means departs from the body at ease and proceeds accordingly.
He who has not attained the practice of *dhāraṇā* and is not possessed of yoga is a fool; at the time of his own death, he meets with suffering, his mind being rendered helpless.

Contemplating the helplessness brought about by the onset of latent impressions, one whose mind is intent on sense objects falls into a state of extreme wretchedness, like a lotus severed from its stalk.
One whose mind is not refined by the scriptures and who is devoted to the company of the wicked experiences an internal burning upon death, as if fallen into fire.
When this one, whose nature is lacking in discernment, undergoes a hoarse throat and deformity arising from his complexion and appearance, then he becomes dejected in mind.
It was utter darkness, devoid of light, where stars appeared even by day; the expanse of the horizon was filled with clouds, and the sky was as dark as thick, black clouds.
His vision whirling, he was pierced by agonizing pain in his vital organs; the earth became for him like the sky, and the space of the sky became like the earth.
The circle of the quarters having been overturned, he was as if being carried away upon the ocean, as if being led through the sky, his mind awakening from its deep sleep.
As if fallen into a blind well, as if joined within a rock, his own complexion becoming dull, he felt as if cut out from within his very heart.
It was as if Tṛṇāvarta had been cast down from the path of the sky; indeed, it seemed as though he were mounted upon a swift chariot, intent on devouring the Himalayas.
As if explaining the nature of saṃsāra, as if not touching his kinsmen, he remained like a wind-machine set in motion by a whirling spindle.
He was whirled about as if by a whirlwind, or dragged along as if by a rope; he seemed to be spinning in a whirlpool of water, as if placed upon a mechanical weapon.
Like a blade of grass being swept away by the wind of the rain-cloud, he was carried along as if rising with a flood of water only to fall back into the ocean.
As if falling into a bottomless abyss in the infinite sky amidst a whirlpool of wind, the ocean remains as it experiences a state of total upheaval.
As if falling incessantly and as if leaping up on all sides, his entire multitude of sense-faculties were agitated by the sound of the *sūtkāra* noise, as if they were wounds.
Gradually, all his sensory perceptions reach a state of pure clarity, just as the quarters of the sky do when the sun sets, becoming dim in their light.

He no longer knows what is before or behind him, for his mindfulness has reached a state of exhaustion; it is just as when, at the end of the western twilight, one's vision of the eight directions has vanished.
Due to delusion, his mind loses its capacity for discernment; through that lack of discrimination, he sinks into the great abyss of ignorance.
When one takes hold of delusion, then the vital breath does not take hold; and when it does not take hold of the vital breaths, then one falls completely into delusion.
Through the delusions of perception and ignorance, which mutually reinforce one another, a living being attains the state of a stone; this has been established since the beginning of creation.
Prabuddhalīlā said: For what purpose does this body come into existence—though it possesses all eight limbs—only to experience pain, delusion, fainting, dizziness, disease, and unconsciousness?
The Goddess said: "If such action was thus ordained at the beginning of creation by the consciousness of vibration, then why is there such suffering at this time after so much time has passed?"
Thinking "may this be mine," one enters into that state which arises from its own nature like a thicket; one perceives what is produced by the expansion of the mind, for there is no other cause here.
When, due to the force of pain, the channels within the body seize the vital air through their own contraction and expansion, it then abandons its natural state.
When the winds enter and do not exit, and having gone in, they do not re-enter, because they have entered the *vināḍī*, then through that vibration, mindfulness arises.
When the wind does not enter at all and the breath does not exit due to the failure of the body's channels, then one is said to be dead.
The consciousness that has been previously known as "I must undergo destruction after such a length of time," being impelled by that [prior determination], brings about death.
The seed-potency of consciousness born of creation—such as "I shall become such-and-such by means of this"—never undergoes destruction.
The very nature of consciousness is that which is called "awareness," and it is inseparable from itself; therefore, death and birth are not other than this awareness of one's own nature.
In some places it is gentle yet obscured, like water in a river; in some places it is gentle, and in others it is conscious, possessing the nature of a living being.
Just as the nodes of a long creeper appear at intervals along its length, so too do births and deaths occur within the continuum of sentient existence.
The conscious person is never born nor does he ever die; he merely perceives this world as a delusion, like a dream or a confusion.
The person is nothing but consciousness alone; when and how could it ever perish? If it were distinct from consciousness, tell me, what else could the person be?
Tell me, who has died until this very day? To whom does consciousness belong, what is it, and how does it die? Millions of bodies perish, yet consciousness remains imperishable.
If the mind did not perish when that one [object] died, then upon the death of a single being here, there would be the death of all existence.

Whatever variety of latent impressions (vāsanā) the individual soul (jīva) experiences by itself, it is to that very [stream of impressions] that the names "birth" and "death" are conceptually attributed.
Thus, no one dies and no one is born; it is only the individual soul that wallows in the pits of the whirlpool of latent impressions.
And because the visible world is absolutely non-existent, that latent impression (vāsanā) does not exist at all; through such inquiry, it perishes once it has been firmly known as such.

Having correctly observed through spiritual practices that the continuous stream of the world is neither arisen nor ceased, and is free from the fear of existence, the living being whose latent impressions no longer arise becomes liberated; this is the true reality here.
Prabuddhalīlā said: O Goddess of gods, tell me how a living being dies and how it is born again, for the further increase of my awakening.
The Goddess said: When the flow in the channels is disturbed and a person encounters a state of wind-disorder, then indeed his consciousness seems to become extinguished.
For pure consciousness is eternal; it neither arises nor ceases. It abides in the stationary and the moving, in space, in the mountain, in fire, and in the wind.
When the movement [of the body] ceases solely due to the obstruction of the vital breaths, that body is called "dead" and is then designated as "insentient."
When that body has become a corpse and the vital air has returned to the state of mere wind, consciousness, freed from latent impressions, abides in the reality of its own Self.
The name "jīva" is given to that minute [entity] possessing latent impressions; yet it abides in that very place, like a corpse in a house, or likewise in the sky.
Therefore, he is designated by the term "preta" by those engaged in worldly discourse; his consciousness, mixed with latent impressions (vāsanā), persists like a fragrant breeze.
When one remains within another state of vision after abandoning this visible world, then that [state] appears in various forms, like a dream or a mental construction.
In that very place, remaining mindful as before, at the very moment the death-faintness ends, he beholds another body.
Within the self, there is neither a jar nor its absence; there is only the empty space of another. In the ground of the sky, it is together with the sky, like the hare-mark on the moon in the void.
There are six kinds of pretas; hear this classification of them: those who have committed ordinary sins, those who have committed middling sins, and those who have committed gross sins.

There is the one possessing ordinary qualities, the one possessing middling qualities, and the one possessing supreme qualities; among these, some possess one [type], while others possess two or even all three.
A certain person who has committed a great sin (mahāpātaka) experiences for a year a state of mental stupor; utterly bewildered within, he remains like one whose heart is made of stone.
Then, after a long time, having experienced for a long duration the inexhaustible suffering of hell arising from the womb of latent impressions, he became a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Having experienced hundreds of wombs and passed from one misery to another, one occasionally finds peace amidst the delusion of this dream-like saṃsāra.

Alternatively, at the end of the delusion of death, they experience that very state—agitated by hundreds of dull sufferings—which exists within the heart, as if it were a tree or similar object, in an instant.
Having further experienced sufferings in hell corresponding to their own latent predispositions, they are then born after a long time upon the earth in various wombs.
Now, he who is of middling evil, immediately after the delusion of death, experiences for some time a state of dullness accompanied by a belly made of stone.
Then, having awakened after some time or even at that very moment, he will enter the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) after experiencing births through the sequence of animal wombs and so forth.
A certain person who has committed an ordinary sin experiences [the result] even after death, assuming an unimpaired body in accordance with his own latent impressions (vāsanā).
He perceives it as such, like a dream or a mental construction; and at that very moment, his memory arises in this way:
There, having enjoyed beautiful fruits and entered the hearts of men, they preside over the seminal fluids within the womb, according to the sequence of their births.
Following their own latent predispositions, these hungry ghosts experience this arrangement within themselves, both sequentially and non-sequentially, at the end of their fainting spell.
At first, they perceive, "We have died," and subsequently, through the offering of funeral cakes and other rites for their kinsmen, they realize, "We have been reborn."
Then, thinking, "These are the messengers of Yama, equipped with nooses of Time," he proceeds in turn with them as he is being led to the city of Yama.
The merit-possessor repeatedly enjoys beautiful gardens and celestial palaces, which have been acquired through his own karmic actions and are truly divine.
The sinner reaches the great snowfields, thorny brambles, chasms, and forests of sword-leaves—all of which have arisen from his own evil deeds.
"This path before me is pleasant to traverse, with cool grassy patches, lush shade, and ponds"—this is the thought of one who is in the middle state.
"This is the city of Yama; here am I, the Lord of Beings; here is the deliberation upon karma performed"—thus he experiences.
Thus, the vast fragment of cyclic existence unfolds individually, radiant with the conduct of all things exactly as they are situated, without exception.
Like space, it is utterly void; though possessing consciousness, its very nature is emptiness. Though radiant with the vastness of space, time, and action, it is nothing at all.
Commanded from here to experience the fruits of my own actions, I shall go quickly—henceforth either to auspicious heaven or indeed to hell.
Whether this heaven has been experienced by me, or this hell has been experienced, these various wombs have been experienced; yet I am born again in the cycle of existence.
"This rice plant was born as me; gradually I have remained as the fruit"—thus, through the awakening of future understanding, he will come to realize this.
Thus, with his faculties completely dormant, he attains the state of a seed within the man; that seed, having fallen into the womb, becomes an embryo in the mother.
That embryo is born in the world according to its past karma; it may be fortunate or unfortunate, appearing as a child of graceful form.
Then she experiences youth, radiant as the moon and inclined toward passion; thereafter, O lotus-faced one, she encounters old age, like a fallen thunderbolt from the cold clouds.
From that state as well, there comes disease and death, followed again by the fainting of death; then, like a dream, one returns once more to the assumption of a body through the physical aggregates.
He goes again to the world of Yama and once more undergoes the cycle of wandering; he experiences this again and again as various other wombs arise.
Thus, possessing a form as ethereal as space, he repeatedly experiences this intensely radiant state of constant flux until liberation, even while remaining in the void of space itself.
Prabuddhalīlā said: O Goddess, please explain to me once more, out of your grace, how this delusion proceeds at the time of the original creation, for the increase of my understanding.

The Goddess said: The mountains are the solid mass of ultimate reality; the trees are the solid mass of ultimate reality; the earth is the solid mass of ultimate reality; the sky is the solid mass of ultimate reality.
Since that Lord of Consciousness, whose nature is the Self of all, arises in whatever manner, He becomes exactly so in each respective place, being the pure Self of the supreme ether.
At the beginning of creation, by the principle of the person in a dream, the primordial Lord of Creatures appeared clearly; even now, existence remains just as it was then.
This first vibration is indeed the archetype of all objects; that which has been reflected from it remains established even today.
The wind residing within those cavities that exist in bodies causes the movement of the limbs; for that reason, one is said to "live."

From the very beginning of creation, this state of existence has remained thus among moving beings; even though they possess consciousness, they are motionless, and for that reason these trees and other such things are called "immobile."
This very space of consciousness (cidākāśa) manifests as a portion arising from sentience; that alone becomes consciousness (saṃvit), while the remainder does not exist at all.
If the city of Nara has been reached, it leads the eye-socket to consciousness; yet that life, which is not perceived by the eyes, does not truly live from the perspective of phenomenal creation.

Just as space is space and the earth is attained as earth, and just as water is water, so too does the body perceive whatever it conceives of freely; it experiences that very thing in exactly that way.
Thus, with his entire body, he remained contemplating the moving as moving by its nature of mobility, and the stationary as stationary by its nature of stationariness, being the self of all.
Therefore, whatever is called "mobile" possesses the nature of its own cognition; by that [cognition] it is perceived, and thus it remains established as such even now.
Furthermore, that which was awakened under the name "tree" remains established even today as an insentient entity—such as stones, trees, and grass—which are indeed characterized by immobility.

But there is no such thing as insentience existing separately, nor is there any sentience; at the beginning of creation, there is no distinction whatsoever, due to the single nature of pure existence.
The internal cognitions residing within trees and stones are indeed produced by the intellect and other faculties; such is the established principle regarding them.

Because that intellect, which perceives internal objects such as stationary things and so forth, exists in such a state, other designations, locations, and purposes are established through different conventions.
Whatever internal cognitions exist within worms, insects, and moths, those very things constitute their respective intellects and so forth, as well as certain designations and objects.
Just as the people of the northern ocean know nothing at all of the people dwelling on the southern ocean, except through their own individual experience.
When all beings, both stationary and moving, are absorbed in the experience of their own perceptions and are solely intent upon their own conventions regarding one another;

Just as there is a perception of frogs situated within a stone as well as those outside it—perceptions that are unreal and insentient—the same applies to those dwelling inside and outside one another.
The entire all-pervading mind, which was awakened by the sky of consciousness at the beginning of creation, is that very wind which remains established here even today.
That which is conceived as a cavity is the sky; therein is the wind, whose nature is vibration—such are the desires for creation, like the movement [of thought] within objects.
But the mind, in the ultimate sense, abides within all that is stationary and moving; it is only the movements [of the body] that come to be and cease to be through the winds.
Thus, in this world consisting of illusion, all objects are fragments of consciousness; just as they were at the beginning of creation and so forth, even now they remain exactly as they were.
Just as the manifestation of the intrinsic nature of all diverse phenomena is unreal yet appears as real, so too has this been explained to you.
"Look, King Vidūratha has likely set; he is departing from the heart of your husband Padma, who lies there as a garland-wreathed corpse."
Prabuddhalīlā said: "O Queen of the Gods, by what path does this corpse go to the pavilion? O Excellent One, let us both go quickly so that we may see him."

The Goddess said: Consisting of consciousness, it proceeds by resorting to the path situated within human latent impressions (*vāsanā*), thinking, "I am this [person]; I am going to another world far away."
By this very path, as long as it is agreed upon by theft, there is no severance of mutual desire, for it is bound by the ties of friendship.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the fatigue from this discourse had subsided, and the supreme vision had expanded like the risen sun of awakening within the noble mind of the king’s daughter, Vidūratha became free from the dullness born of the mind.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In the meantime, the king’s eyes became fixed with dilated pupils; he remained with only the life-force in his single body, his white lips parched dry.
His complexion was like that of a withered leaf, the luster of his face was pale and wasted; he resembled the dark hue of a bumblebee’s hum, while his labored breathing caused his face to contort.
His mind has fallen into the blind well of the great swoon of death, while the functions of all his sense organs, such as the eyes, remain hidden within.
Like a figure depicted in a painting, he was visible only as a mere form and devoid of consciousness; with all his limbs motionless, he was like a statue carved from stone.
What need is there for much speaking here? With only a small portion of his body remaining, his life-force abandoned him, like a bird dwelling in the sky leaving a tree about to fall.
With their divine vision, those two young women saw him situated in the sky—life itself, consisting of vital breath, like a trace of fragrance in the wind.
That consciousness of the living soul, having merged with the wind in the sky, began to travel far through the ether, following the dictates of its latent tendencies.
Then he followed that very pair of women who were the consciousness of life, like a pair of female bees clinging to the wind or to a trace of fragrance.
Then, in just a moment, when the fainting spell of death had subsided, he was awakened in the sky by a wind carrying a trace of the fragrance of consciousness.
He saw the messengers of Yama leading away his body, and he perceived his own physical form as it had been produced through the offering of funeral cakes by his kinsmen.
On the way, he reached the city of Vaivasvata, situated at a very great distance, which was radiant with the fruits of karma and surrounded by living beings.
Then Yama, having reached the city of Vaivasvata, commanded: "There are never any inauspicious deeds whatsoever belonging to this man."
This man is always a performer of pure and auspicious deeds; he has been further strengthened by the boon of the Blessed Goddess Sarasvatī.
"In Kusumāmbara there exists his former body, now become a corpse; let him go and enter it, and then let this [body] be abandoned"—with such a thought, he resolved.
Then, abandoned on the path of the sky like a stone fallen from a machine, there arose a triad in the firmament: Jīva-kalā, Līlā, and Jñapti.
The streak of life, however, flew upward; she did not see those two embodied forms as they followed her, leaping across the expanse of the sky.
Having quickly passed beyond other worlds and emerged from the house of the universe, he reached a second world and approached its terrestrial sphere.
Those two, whose forms were composed of volition, united with the thread of life and reached the pavilion of the Līlā inner apartments in the city of Padmarāja.
In an instant, they entered at their ease, like two gusts of wind entering a lotus, like the rays of the sun entering a lotus, or like a fragrant breeze entering a flower.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahmin, how did he reach the house near the corpse? And how was the path recognized by him, who possessed a dead body?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, why indeed does he not reach that house, since all of that [house] resides within the corpse situated inside his own latent impressions (vāsanā)?
Who does not see that this world, consisting of nothing but innumerable delusions, exists within the belly of a single living atom like the banyan tree within its seed?
Just as one perceives within the heart the seed of the living body as the sprout, so too does the atom of consciousness perceive the entire collection of the three worlds as its own inherent nature.
Just as a person standing in one place constantly and incessantly perceives with their mind their own treasure situated in a far-off land.
In this way, even though the individual soul is beset by hundreds of births and enveloped in delusion, it perceives its desired object residing within its own latent impressions.

Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, what kind of state does a living being attain whose form is devoid of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of offering funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and so forth, and for whom no funeral cake is offered?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Whether the thought "the rice-ball is being given by me" or "the rice-ball has been given by me" is firmly rooted as a latent impression (vāsanā) in the heart, the person becomes the enjoyer of the fruit of that rice-ball.
Whatever the mind may be, the living being becomes that; such is the experience among those with bodies and those without bodies, and it is never otherwise.

Through the cognition "I am one who has a sapinda," even one without a physical body possesses a sapinda; through the cognition "I am one without a sapinda," even one with a sapinda does not possess a sapinda.
For the reality of these objects consists precisely in their being meditated upon, and meditation indeed arises from the objects themselves as its causes.
Just as poison becomes like nectar for a living being through habitual conditioning, so too does an unreal object attain the status of reality through the power of mental cultivation.
One never dispels anything for anyone by means of a cause; therefore, be certain that there is no such thing as cultivation at all.
Nowhere has an effect ever been seen or heard of without a cause, up until the great dissolution; indeed, nothing exists by itself except for the Single Origin.
Consciousness alone is the latent impression; it assumes the status of an object, as in a dream. It undergoes the state of cause and effect, and having come forth, it remains as such.
Śrī Rāma said: "If a deceased person who is possessed by latent impressions (vāsanā) thinks, 'I have no dharma,' and a friend, having performed abundant dharma, offers it to him—"
In this case, is that dharma then lost, or is it not? Is meditative cultivation more powerful when its object is real, or even when its object is unreal?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Through the perfection of place, time, action, and materials, a creative conception arises; wherever that conception has fully emerged, he who possesses it is the superior victor over the two.

If a latent impression proceeds from the realm of phenomena, then by that [impression] the mind of a hungry ghost is gradually filled; but if it does not proceed from the realm of phenomena, there is no impurity through the cognition of a hungry ghost.
Thus, by overcoming one another, the one possessing superior power triumphs here; therefore, with auspicious effort, one should practice the cultivation of the wholesome.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin, if latent impressions (vāsanā) arise through space, time, and so forth, then at the beginning of creation in a Great Kalpa, from where did space, time, and the rest come?
This [result] arises from those auxiliary causes acting together as its cause; in the absence of those auxiliary causes, how could there be any latent impression (*vāsanā*)?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "It is even so, O mighty-armed one, whose nature is truth; at no time whatsoever, at the beginning of creation following the great dissolution, do space and time exist."
In the absence of auxiliary causes, this perception of the visible does not exist; it has not arisen, nor does anything whatsoever manifest.
Precisely because the visible object is impossible, whatever this is that appears is nothing other than Brahman itself, abiding in its own nature of consciousness, thus free from all affliction.
We shall indeed explain this to you with hundreds of arguments further on; for that purpose, this effort is being made. Now, listen to the present narrative.
Thus they beheld the palace, with its beautiful interior, strewn with offerings of flowers, cool as if it were springtime.
There stood the corpse, adorned with garlands of mandāra and kunda flowers, situated evenly within that capital city where all agitation and activity had been stilled.
The great corpse was draped with garlands and wreaths of mandāra and kunda flowers; at the head of the corpse-bed stood the foremost auspicious objects, such as a full water-pot.

The house had its doors, windows, and bolts firmly fastened; the light of the lamps was fading, leaving the pure walls darkened; and it was made resonant by the breath from the mouths of those sleeping in one part of the dwelling.

It was as lovely as the splendor of the full moon rising in its entirety; it surpassed the opulence of Indra’s palace with its beauty; it possessed a charming radiance within the bud of Brahmā’s lotus; and it was like a stainless moonstone, cool and silent.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then they both saw there, lying on one side of the bed of corpses before Vidūratha, Līlā, who had arrived first and was now dead.
She possessed their former dress, former conduct, former body, and former latent impressions; she resembled their former appearance, beautiful in every form and limb.
There she remained alone, her former movements of limbs stilled, her former garments cast aside, and her former burden of ornaments laid down.
Holding a chowrie and gracefully fanning the lord of the earth, she adorned the surface of the earth as the rising moon adorns the heavens.
She was standing in silence with her moon-like face resting upon her left hand, appearing like a forest glade in full bloom with the flower-like rays of light from her ornaments.
Beholding her casting showers of *mālatī* and blue lotuses in all directions with her glances, she seemed to create from her own loveliness moon after moon risen in the sky.
She was like the goddess Lakṣmī who had come to Viṣṇu in the form of a protector of men, or like the splendor of spring risen from a mass of flowers.
With her gaze fixed upon the face of her husband, she performed her desired gestures; yet with her countenance somewhat faded, she was like a night whose moon has grown dim.
That woman was seen by those two, but they were not noticed by her; because their resolutions were true, she did not speak to them in that manner at that time.
Śrī Rāma said: It has been described how, in that region, having established her body for the sake of her former pastimes, she departed through meditation accompanied by pure consciousness (jñapti).
O Lord, tell me now: why was Līlā’s body not described there? What became of it, and where did it go? Please explain this to me.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Where was that body of play, and how can it possess reality? It was merely an illusion, like the perception of water in a desert.
This entire world is indeed the Self; whence comes the conceptualization of the body and so forth? That which you perceive as blissful Brahman is itself Consciousness.
Just as this playfulness reaches its transformation gradually within awakening, so too does it do so within the Supreme; therefore, that body has dissolved like a mountain of snow.
Whatever is perceived by the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) as the visible world, such as earth and so forth, is given the name "material" (adhibhautika), and that belongs to that very [subtle body].
In its actual form, however, that which consists of earth and so forth—the physical body—is neither through sound nor through its object a true self, like the horn of a hare.
If a man has the thought in a dream, "I am a deer," would he go searching for a deer once his own state as a deer has ceased?
Untruth quickly arises, and likewise truth dissolves; just as for one who is deluded, the illusion of a snake in a rope vanishes once the error has passed.
This entire world, born of the mind and belonging to the unawakened, is indeed false; it has attained the status of a delusion without any seed.

Experiencing everything that is called creation as a perception within a dream, he remains for a long time with his sense of self identified with the body, like the revolving of the wheel of the earth.
Śrī Rāma said: For the yogin who is traveling toward his own world of Brahmā while standing before the worlds, what kind of body is this subtle, transportive (ātivāhika) one that is perceived?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The transition from one body to another always occurs without the former body, for this subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) is as transitory as those in dreams.
Just as a speck of frost in the heat, or a white cloud in the autumnal sky, though visible, attains invisibility—so too does the body of a yogi.
Or else, suddenly, the body of the yogi is no longer perceived by other yogis, like a bird that has swiftly flown up into the sky before their very eyes.
Due solely to the delusion of their own latent impressions, some people at certain times and in certain places perceive even a yogi who is standing right before them as being dead.
The notion of the body as the self is merely an illusion for them; it subsides through the realization of truth, just as the perception of a snake in a rope ceases within oneself.
What is the body? Whose is its existence? Whose is its destruction? How and from where does it come? That which was has remained exactly as it was; only ignorance has departed.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Lord, tell me this: does the physical body itself attain the state of being a subtle vehicle (ātivāhika), or is it something else that is carried along?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O excellent one, I have told you this many times, yet you do not grasp it: there exists only the subtle body (ātivāhika); the material body (ādhibhautika) does not exist at all."
Even as he practices that very [meditation], the notion of the material world (sādhibhautika) passes away; when that [notion] subsides, then his former [spiritual] state proceeds.
Then, that vain grasping at heaviness and hardness will subside, just as the [grasping] of a person in a dream ceases through the healthy awakening of the knower.
Thereupon, the attainment of lightness like cotton arises for the yogi, just as one perceives the body as a dream within a dream.
Just as the body becomes light through the recognition of a dream within a dream, so too, through awakening, this body becomes capable of leaping like something solid.
For those whose selves have been transformed through the mental constructs of many days, once this corpse-like body has been burned, they attain their final abiding right there.
Likewise, the experience of a subtle body necessarily occurs for yogis even while they are still living, due to the excellence of their awakening.
When mindfulness has arisen there, the "I" consisting of volition is sufficient; whatever kind of body that [previous state] was, such is this one upon awakening.
Thus this delusion appears, like the form of a snake in a rope; when it is destroyed, what is lost? When it arises, what is born?
Śrī Rāma said: "O Lord, if those who dwell there subsequently witness the divine play, do they perceive it through the power of their own true resolve?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "The queens will understand it thus: 'This woman stands here in distress; she is some other friend who has come from somewhere to her.'"
What doubt could there be here regarding them? For they are indeed like animals, lacking discrimination; they act according to what they have perceived—how could they possess any deliberation?
Just as a rolling clod of earth quickly passes by avoiding a tree, so too, in the state of ignorance, there exist the non-recitation, the beasts, and the primordial city.
Just as I do not know where the body of a dream goes upon waking—because it is entirely unreal—in the same way, so too is this physical body.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, where does the mountain of a dream go upon waking? Cut through this doubt of mine, as the wind disperses an autumnal cloud."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In the delusion of a dream or in a mental construction, objects such as mountains and the like merge within consciousness, just as vibrations merge within the wind.
Just as movement enters fully into the motionless wind, becoming non-different from it, so too this dream-object is a defilement of consciousness, being non-different from it.

Through the manifestation of objects such as those in dreams, consciousness alone shines forth intensely; yet when it does not so shine, being of that very nature, it attains oneness with that [object].
The duality of consciousness and the object of a dream is never found, just as that of fluidity and water, or motion and wind.
Whatever lack of awakening might exist therein is that unsurpassed ignorance; this is said to be saṃsāra itself, arisen as the nature of false knowledge.
In the absence of auxiliary causes, what indeed is the nature of consciousness? The duality of objects in a dream is, within the dream itself, devoid of objective reality.
As is a dream, so is this waking state; there is no doubt about this. Just as an unreal city appears in a dream, so does the unreal world appear at the beginning of creation.
And an object arising from a dream cannot be real; for consciousness possesses eternal reality, whereas the objects of dreams lack reality.
Just as a dream-mountain becomes space instantly or gradually, so too does the material world become space within awakening.
Those standing nearby see him as either having flown away or being dead, because they are struck by their own nature and fail to perceive the wise one who has become the *ātivāhika* body.
These creations are indeed false views, views born of delusion; they are the perception of mere illusion, a delusion, empty, like experiences in a dream.

These experiences of dreams, appearing as the clear manifestation of creation, are seen through the delusion of error and its opposite at the moment of awakening from death; all of them, existing within the subtle body (*ativāhika-śarīra*), shine forth falsely, like the sequence of a mirage.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In the meantime, Consciousness again restrained the life-force of Vaidūratha through its volition, just as one restrains the vibration of the mind.
Līlā said: "Tell me, O Goddess, how much time has passed while I was absorbed in samādhi in this palace, and while the king remained as a corpse?"
Jñapti said: "One month has passed here; these two maidservants of yours have remained vigilant in the sleeping chamber for the sake of guarding you while you slept."
Listen, O woman of excellent complexion, to what has happened here to your body: your frame has been moistened by your tears for a fortnight.
Lifeless, fallen upon the ground like a withered leaf, the corpse has become as cold as ice, resembling a block of wood or a wall.
Then the ministers, having arrived and determined for themselves by the sight of her moisture that she was indeed dead, carried her out of the house once more.
What need is there for much speaking here? Having been carried away and placed upon a funeral pyre made of sandalwood, he was suddenly reduced to ashes along with his ghee.
Then, crying out loudly, "The queen is dead! your entire retinue performed the funeral rites with great agitation.
Now, seeing you arrived here in person, it will be a great marvel that you have returned from the other world.
But you, O daughter, by virtue of your power of true resolve, appear with that very body in its natural whiteness; it is a marvel that [the darkness] remains over you.
O child, whatever latent impression you had toward the body when you were previously non-existent, that very form has arisen for you; therefore, it appears to you as it did before.
Indeed, everyone perceives everything according to their own latent predispositions; the non-contradictory illustration for this is the vision of a child by a vetāla.
O beautiful Siddha, you have become possessed of a subtle, transportive body (ātivāhika-deha); indeed, that former body of yours has been forgotten, along with its latent impressions.
For the wise man who has firmly established the vision of the subtle body, the perception of the physical world subsides, even while it is being perceived, like an autumn cloud in the sky.
Every embodied being becomes established in the state of the subtle body (ativāhika), resembling a cloud without water and like a flower devoid of fragrance.
When the consciousness of the subtle body has taken root through virtuous impressions, the physical body falls into oblivion, just as it does for one dwelling in the womb during youth.
We arrived here in the sky on the thirty-first day; now, at dawn, these two maidservants have been stupefied by me with sleep.
Therefore come, O Līlā; by means of your creative will, let us both manifest ourselves to Līlā so that worldly activity may proceed.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: As soon as the thought arose, "Let us two behold this sport," the two of them became visible and radiant there through the power of the Goddess's consciousness.
Then Vidūrathalīlā, her eyes wide with agitation, beheld the house, which was radiant with a mass of that splendor.
It was as if carved out from the lunar orb, or washed with molten gold; it possessed walls of liquid light, as cool as a stream of flame.
Seeing the house before her and beholding those two who had issued their playful command, she rose up in agitation and fell at their feet.
"O Goddesses who grant life, may you be victorious! I have arrived here first, clearing the path for you both."
When she had spoken thus, those proud women, intoxicated by their youth, sat down upon the seats like [creepers] upon the peaks of Mount Meru.
Jñapti said: "Daughter, tell me how you first came to this place; what has happened to you, what have you seen on the way, and where?"
Vidūratha’s wife said: "O Goddess, in that place I then fell into a swoon; I was like a digit of the second moon struck by the conflagration at the end of a kalpa."
"I have not willed anything at all, whether even or uneven"; then, she closed her eyes whose lashes were trembling.
Then, O Supreme Goddess, at the end of the fainting spell caused by death, I saw that I had quickly risen up and leaped into the midst of the sky.
Then, having mounted a chariot of wind in the elemental ether, I was brought by him to this abode like a streak of fragrance.
"O Queen, I see the dwelling adorned by its master; it is illuminated by a shining lamp, secluded, and furnished with a costly couch."
I shall look upon this husband as long as this Vidūratha lies with his limbs covered by flowers, like the spring season in a flower grove.
"Furthermore, thinking, 'This man is exhausted by the fatigue of the fury of battle and sleeps sufficiently,' I did not ward off this sleep of his, O Queen of the Gods."
"Immediately after arriving at this place, these two queens [were seen by me], O you who bestow grace upon me; thus have I related it exactly as it was experienced."
Jñapti said: "O you two who move with the gait of swans, O Līlā of lovely eyes, let us raise this king from the surface of his bed of corpses."
Having spoken thus, she released her life-force like a lotus releases its fragrance; taking the form of a wind-swayed creeper, she went near his nose.
He entered within the cavity of the nose like the wind into the hollow of a bamboo, concealing hundreds of his own latent impressions within, as the ocean hides its jewels.
His face, which contained the inner soul, attained its natural luster, like a lotus when the obstruction is removed and it is well-sprinkled with water.
Gradually, all his limbs shone with vitality, like the clusters of creepers upon a mountain during the flowering season.
Then he shone like the lord of stars on a full-moon night, his digits complete, illuminating the world profusely with the rays from the moon of his face.
He caused his limbs to throb—limbs that were tender and full of passion, radiant with the luster of gold like the sprouts of spring.
He opened his eyes, which possessed pure and trembling pupils; they were captivating and possessed of auspicious splendor, just as the moon and sun [open] the world.
He rose up with his body radiating, like the Vindhya mountain increasing in height; he spoke in a voice as deep as a thundercloud, "Who stands there?"
Then he said to the two Līlās standing before him, "Let it be commanded. He beheld the two Līlās standing there, bowing low before him.
Equal in conduct, equal in appearance, equal in form, and equal in stability; equal in speech, equal in effort, equal in joy, and equal in attainment.
Looking about, he asked, "Who are you? Who is she? And from where has she come? To him, Līlā said, "O Lord, listen to what I shall tell you."
O Lord, I am your playful consort from former times; like the inseparable union of word and meaning, I abide in close embrace with you.
This second Līlā, a beautiful woman composed of a reflection, was easily acquired by me for your sake.
Seated at the head of this [assembly], protect her on the great golden throne; O Lord, she is Sarasvatī, the auspicious mother of the three worlds.
"O Lord of the Earth, she has come here in person through the accumulation of our merit; by her, these two were brought here from the other world."
Having heard this, the lotus-eyed king rose up, wearing hanging garlands and garments, and fell at the feet of Jñapti.
O Sarasvatī, salutations to you, O Goddess who bestows the welfare of all; O granter of boons, grant me wisdom, long life, and wealth.
When he had spoken thus, the deity Jñapti touched him with her hand; Sarasvatī said: "May you, endowed with prosperity, be enriched by all desired objects, O son!"

May all calamities, all misdeeds, and all wrong views come to rest for you, and may infinite, perfect happiness prevail. May the people always remain joyful, may the kingdom be stable, and may fortunes ever flourish.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having replied, "So be it," Sarasvatī vanished right there; at dawn, all the people awoke along with the lotuses.
And Līlā embraced her lover, and Līlā in turn embraced him, again and again with great joy, as he was repeatedly dead and then revived once more.
Then the royal palace was languid with intoxication and passion; its people were maddened with joy, and it resounded with the noise of musical instruments and song.

Resounding with the tumultuous, gurgling sounds of "Victory!", "Auspiciousness!", and "The Day of Merit," the courtyard was filled with contented and well-fed people and crowded by the circle of royalty.
It bore thousands of showers of flowers released by perfected vidyādharas, while mṛdaṅgas, murajas, kāhalas, conchs, and dundubhis resounded.
It was intense with the trumpeting of elephants whose massive trunks were tossed upward, and it resounded with the vibrant cries of women performing wild, exuberant dances throughout the courtyards.
Beautiful with the world as its essence, it was rugged with the gifts brought by people falling into mutual collision, and lovely with the abundance of flower-garlands.

The sky was strewn with silken cloths scattered by the ministers, vassals, and citizens, and became filled with large lotuses in the form of their hands as they danced in the red hue of their garments.
Where the earrings of intoxicated women swayed playfully as they turned their necks, and where the mud of the Puṣpa flowers was splashed up by the falling of their footsteps.

The courtyard of the palace was covered by canopies like autumn clouds made of fine silk, and its grounds were filled with the dancing faces of beautiful women that resembled hundreds of thousands of moons.
"The queen and her husband have been brought back from the other world"—thus did people sing in verses composed on the spot in that foreign land.
Having heard the brief account thus related, Padma, the lord of the earth, performed his ablutions with waters brought from the four oceans.
Then the brahmins, the ministers, and the kings consecrated him, who had attained his rise and possessed infinite energy, just as the immortals consecrated Indra.
Līlā, Līlā’s husband, and the king—those of great intellect who were liberated while living—delighted in recounting their past adventures as if in acts of love.
By the grace of Sarasvatī and through his own manly effort, that king Padma attained the highest welfare of the three worlds.
That king, perfectly awakened through the knowledge of realization and endowed with the two-fold play, ruled there for eighty thousand years, irreproachable.
Having ruled the kingdom for eighty thousand years as those liberated while living, they—whose consciousness was perfected—attained the state of liberation beyond the body.

Having long protected their own kingdom—which was radiant with prosperity, charming yet wise, appropriate, beneficial to themselves, and refined—the virtuous couple attained liberation, bestowing satisfaction upon all people.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, this sinless narrative of Līlā has been told to you for the sake of removing the defect of the visible world; abandon the density of the world.
The existence of the visible world is already quiescent; no further pacification of it is required. For there can never be the trouble of wiping away that which exists, nor that which does not exist.
Having perceived that the object of vision, which is of the nature of the knowable, has become one with knowledge—which is of the nature of space—the wise one remains like the sky.

If this world has been established by the self-existent one—who is devoid of earth and the other elements—as being nothing but the manifestation of consciousness, then it has been established within his own self.
In whatever manner consciousness exerts itself, it remains established in that very way; once released into the river of creative awareness, it continues until it is restrained by effort.
This world is understood as the manifestation of the space of consciousness; it exists within the very self, the clear sky of consciousness, even down to the smallest atomic particle.
Thus, regarding this futile delusion, tell me: what is its existence, or what is its latent impression (*vāsanā*); what is its state, what is its necessity, and what is said to be its inevitability?
All this remains exactly as it was perceived, thus unimpaired; this infinite world is indeed an illusion, yet no such illusion exists at all.
Śrī Rāma said: Oh, what a supreme vision has been shown by you, O Blessed One! It is like the cooling lunar ray for the quenching of the burning of dry grass consumed by a forest fire.
Ah! After a very long time, that which was to be known has today been known by me—unimpaired, as it is, what it is, of what nature it is, from whence it arises, and when it occurs.

O best of the twice-born, as I contemplate this, I feel as if I am becoming tranquil and as if I have attained liberation; for this is a wondrous narrative, an exposition upon the perspectives of the scriptures.
O Blessed One, knower of all things, explain this doubt of mine to me; I am not yet satiated by drinking the nectar of your words with the vessels of my ears.
For that time of the Lord of Līlā, through his yogic power, spans three creations; in one place it is but a day and night, and in another it is merely a month.
In some cases it lasts for many years; for someone else, is it perhaps fleeting? For one it is very long, while for another it remains but a moment.
"O Blessed One, please speak to me accordingly out of your grace; for what is heard but once does not remain, like water on a clod of earth."

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O sinless one, whatever is perceived by whomsoever, in whatever manner, as whatever, and at whatever time, that very thing is experienced by him in that same manner, as that very thing, at that very time.
Amṛta becomes poison through the constant perception of it as poison; an enemy becomes a friend through the perception of him as a friend.
Just as the intrinsic nature of these categories has been meditated upon, that very nature, through long-term practice, comes under the sway of necessity.
This consciousness, whose sole nature is like that of a mirror, becomes whatever it manifests itself as; it immediately assumes that very form because its sole cause is its own inherent nature.
If one attains the consciousness of a multitude of kalpas in a single moment, then that kalpa becomes a mere moment; of this there is no doubt.
If one perceives an eon as a mere blink of an eye, then even that eon quickly becomes a blink; for consciousness is of such a nature.
For one who suffers, a night is like an eon; for one who is happy, it is but a moment. In a dream, a moment may become an eon, and an eon may become a moment.
Just as one experiences in a dream: "Having died and been born again, I have become a youth established in my prime, and I have traveled a hundred yojanas."
Hariścandra experienced twelve years as a single night; Lavaṇa enjoyed a lifespan of one hundred years in the space of a single night.
That which is a single muhūrta for Prajāpati Manu is the lifespan of the sage; that which is the lifespan of Viriñca is indeed one day for the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu).
O Rāma, that which is a lifetime for Viṣṇu is but a single day for the one whose crest is the bull (Śiva); for one whose mind has been worn away through meditation, there are neither days nor nights.
For the yogin, neither objects nor the world are real within the self; sweet becomes bitter when contemplated with a sense of bitterness.
Bitterness turns into sweetness when contemplated as sweetness; an enemy becomes a friend through the perception of friendship, and a friend becomes an enemy through the perception of enmity.

O mighty-armed one, the world exists according to one's own perception; those categories of objects that have not been practiced—such as the recitation of scriptures and the chanting of mantras—[do not appear].
Through the repeated practice of those perceptions, one certainly attains equanimity; for the earth appears to turn to those traveling by boat who are afflicted by the illusion of motion.
Even for those afflicted by the delusion of non-feeling, this [delusion] does not cease; through feeling, the empty appears as crowded, just as in the dreams of a dreamer.
Due to sensation, yellow, blue, or even white is experienced; like a calamity, a festival causes distress through delusion.
Indeed, even on a wall, the conduct of one who does not investigate is seen to be like that in empty space; for a non-existent yakṣa robs even the lives of the deluded.
A woman seen in a dream bestows pleasure as if she were awake; in whatever manner something appears, it becomes stable in that very manner.
The sky is indeed non-existent, and the sky alone exists within the conscious Self; it is spread out like the dancing of a shadow cast by a hundred-cubit cloud.
Know that the world is a vibration of the mind in the sky; it is not a real substance. It is merely the appearance of the movement of the demon of false cognition.
This is merely an illusion, unobstructed and without foundation; it appears as luminous, existing like the vision of a dream.
The wise know that for one who is not asleep, it is like something unprecedented arising, as if a senseless pillar were to perceive a statue.
The Great Pillar of Ultimate Reality perceives a creation similar to this: just as that man by my side in the dream was agitated by great warriors.
Such is the heaven of Brahmā, which is indeed like the state of deep sleep; it is like the sap at the end of winter, still present within the grasses, shrubs, and creepers.
The springtime remains on the earth, and likewise the creation remains in the supreme state, just as fluidity exists within gold, unmanifested from within.
Thus situated in the supreme creation, from the atom to the atom, the arrangement of the limbs is non-different from the possessor of the limbs, as it is from the Self.
Just as a single man in a dream perceives himself as the world, as the bodiless god of love, or as Brahmā himself, so too does he perceive another man in combat.

Such is this world, existing within the void of one's own self, appearing both as real and unreal; from the beginning of creation at the end of a great aeon, this world is of the very nature of consciousness.

The state of being mutual causes does not exist subsequently as something real; for if, within this liberated Brahman, another [world] were to arise from memory, then even in that creation born of the cognition of memory, the state of pure consciousness remains established.
Śrī Rāma said: How was the lineage of Vidūratha’s family perceived by all those leading ministers of the city in exactly the same way?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: All primary consciousnesses follow along with the principal consciousness, just as ordinary gusts of wind follow a vast whirlwind.
In accordance with one another, those cognitions were manifested in such a manner by the protector of the people, the inhabitants, and the ministers.
"This king of ours was born from such a lineage, like the inhabitants of Vaidūryaratha city who are experts in their own dwellings."
When the nature of something is already manifest, it is not reasonable to search for a cause elsewhere than its own nature, just as one does not seek the source of the radiance of a great gem.
"I alone shall be king in this manner according to family custom"—such was the intuition that arose from the jewel for Vidūratha, just as it had arisen for Vīta.
However many beings there may be, in whatever creation, at whatever time—because the element of consciousness is all-pervading, they have come to be like reflections of one another.
That consciousness which is possessed of intense momentum and remains unshaken therein attains supreme stability, remaining of one form until liberation.
By following after the powerful play of consciousness, the various natures mutually reflect one another within the mirror of consciousness by their very nature.
There, through great effort, one conquers the true perceptions and assimilates them to oneself, just as rivers flowing toward the ocean merge into it.
Those who are equal therein strive by virtue of their conscious nature only so long as one prevails here and the second sinks away.
Thus, throughout thousands of creations—as things are being born, perishing, and existing in great numbers—even down to every single atom—
Nothing is pervaded by anything, nor does anything abide in anything; this is the peaceful sky of consciousness, and therefore everything is without a foundation.
This dream appears even while one is awake and devoid of [ordinary] vision; yet its awakening is inevitable, and though it was personally experienced, it consists of unreality.

Just as a single tree, established in its own nature, consists of the essence of leaves, flowers, and fruits, so too the all-pervading Lord is indeed one, consisting of the essence of infinite and universal powers.
The unborn state, whose nature is illusory—consisting of the knower, the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and so forth—is never forgotten by anyone who has realized it.

The reality of the arising and setting of emptiness is both darkness and light, and though it takes the form of space and time, it is eternally one, beginningless, and pure. Devoid of beginning, end, or middle, it remains as a single, transparent expanse of water, rich with the gentle undulation of its own waves.

The nature of the world, consisting of "I," "you," and so forth, shines as the singular manifestation of pure consciousness; it appears like its own emptiness within the expanse of space, beyond the conceptual constructions of duality and unity.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, please explain to me properly once more how this delusion that "I am the world" arises from something other than its true cause.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Since consciousness perceives all things as being essentially equal within itself, therefore the unborn [Self] is in every way, at all times, and in all respects, the essence of everything.

For all perceptions of word and meaning are indeed Brahman alone; they are not separate from it. Among these, there exists no form whatsoever that consists of the subtle essence of all objects and words.
Just as the state of being a bracelet cannot exist apart from gold, nor the state of being a wave apart from water, so too the world cannot exist apart from the Lord.

This very [Brahman] is the form of the world, but the form of the world does not exist in the Lord; just as gold alone is the nature of the bracelet and so forth, while the state of being a bracelet does not exist in the gold.
Just as the form of a composite whole consists of multiple parts, so too consciousness—which is partless—is that which consists of all things.
O Supreme One, that which is perceived as the totality of the sense-objects at the same time appears within as this world, as well as the notions of "I" and "mine."
Just as the arrangement of various inscriptions exists within the interior of a stone, so too the world and the "I" exist densely within the mass of consciousness as non-different from it.
Just as waves abide within water that is surging with waves, so too do creations exist within the Supreme, devoid of the words and meanings of "creation."
The supreme does not abide in the creation, nor does the creation abide in the supreme; for their existence is like that of a part and the whole, yet they are without parts.

By means of one's own self-awareness in the form of consciousness, one's own pure consciousness alone is manifested; it is one's very own form and heart, just as vibration is [manifested] by the wind.
At that moment, this atom of sound, assuming the form of the wonder of consciousness, perceives within itself like the sky, or like a mental construction by means of the mind.
That very [consciousness] itself knows its own nature as the state of wind, possessing an internal flavor of touch, like the vibration of the air.

That very [consciousness] itself attains the state of manifestation as its own essential being, just as light residing within a sheath attains clarity through even a small fragment of its own radiance.
Thus, it itself attains the state of water, which consists of its own essential being, possessing within it a particle of taste, just as water possesses fluidity.
Then he perceives the earth as consisting of the essence of his own mind, with the subtle element of smell residing within it, like the quality of stability itself.
That which is the manifestation of one's own consciousness—the perception of a hundred-thousandth part of a moment of equal duration—is the continuous succession of the flood of creation.
Pure, manifesting all at once from its own radiance, visible yet internal, free from disease, and liberated from rising and setting, Brahman remains unestablished in any location.
The Buddha is eternally liberation, and even his union with the world is like that liberation; the non-Buddha is the nature of emanation, and even his release from it is always that same state.
In whatever manner and by whatever means Consciousness-Brahman is perceived within itself by its own self, in that very manner it becomes all things, possessing the power of every limb.

That [Reality] is true because it is the play of consciousness and consists of eternal experience; that [world] is untrue because it has emerged from the mind, which is the sixth among all designations.
Just as this movement exists in the wind, so does creation abide in the Supreme; it is a mental construction within that which is like a non-existent, and it is like the unreal even within the Real.

Just as light and heat within fire appear distinct yet are not different from it, so too the splendor of the universe—consisting of both the real and the unreal—is present within the consciousness of Brahman.
Just as a figurine is uncarved in clay or in wood, and just as letters exist within a mass of ink, so do the creations abide in the Supreme.
In the desert of the reality of Brahman, which is non-dual, the mirage of the three worlds shines forth; though the Self is unreal, it appears as if real.
