By means of the Brahman consisting of consciousness, the Self is perceived as the very essence of creation; yet, due to its non-duality, it is not perceived [as separate], just as a tree is not perceived apart from the seed within which it resides.
Just as sweetness belongs to milk, pungency to black pepper, liquidity to water, and motion to the wind;

Just as another does not exist there as something distinct from that which is present, so too within the Self, the creation—though its nature is pure consciousness—is non-different; it is the Supreme Self itself bearing the form of the individual self.
That which exists as the world is but the golden essence of the jewel of Brahman; since it is without cause, it is not distinct from that.
Latent impressions consist of the perception of the mind, the individual soul, and so forth; such perception arises from that which is not perceived, through effort and human exertion.
Nothing ever sets nor does it ever rise anywhere at any time; everything is the peaceful, unborn Brahman, a mass of consciousness as solid as a block of stone.

Toward every atom, thousands of floods of creations flash forth from the consciousness; within each of those atoms, there are further atoms—what room for latent impressions is there here, and how could they exist?

Just as waves and other phenomena, as well as latent and manifest powers, exist within water, so too do the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the rest abide within the individual soul (jīva).
If a living being feels even the slightest lack of interest toward sense enjoyments, then by that alone he has attained the highest state; such is the sacred tradition.
From whatever one becomes dispassionate, from that one is liberated; therefore, how can one who lacks the consciousness of "I" attain the consciousness of birth?
Those who know the consciousness that is both supreme and inferior, unborn, formless, nameless, and consisting of the moving and the unmoving as its substratum—they are victorious.

The supreme consciousness is self-manifest and non-dual, like a ripple on the surface of water within its own fluidity; as that "I," it sustains these worlds, which neither exist nor do not exist, being of the nature of the Supreme Self.

The consciousness consisting of the "I," through the differentiation of its own volitions, expands the universe; though turned inward, it experiences the end of an eon as being no more than a fraction of ten million billion moments.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Even in the calculation of a millionth part of an atom or a moment, thousands of world-ages appear as if they were truly real.
Within those too, and likewise within each infinitesimal atom, this very same infinite delusion appears as "this."
These supreme beings carry away the tranquil successions of creations, like water flowing within, turning upon its own clearly manifest whirlpools.
In this great desert, the splendor of creation exists as nothing but a false self, like a river whose rows of flowers have been shed by its banks, trees, and creepers.

Like a dream, a city of Indra’s magic, or a castle in the clouds, and like a mountain in a story, the ground of the experience of creation appears as something unreal, just like a mental construction.
Śrī Rāma said: O best among the wise, when, through such thorough inquiry, the realization of the supreme Self arises as the oneness of the single Self, free from all conceptual construction—
For what reason do the bodies of even those who know the ultimate reality remain here? They are overcome by destiny alone; and what, in this case, could that destiny be?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: There exists here the divine destiny, the power of consciousness whose form is vibration; it is the sole reality of that which must inevitably come to pass, persisting throughout all kalpas.
For at the original creation, destiny—which is the inexhaustible variety of existents—attains its ultimate fulfillment in this way: "By this [cause], this [effect] must always come to be."
She is called the Great Being, remembered as the Great Consciousness; she is renowned as the Great Power, established as the Great Vision.
She is called Mahākriyā (the Great Action), remembered as Mahodbhavā (the Great Origin), the mature Mahāspandā (the Great Vibration), and proclaimed as Mahātmaikatā (the Unity of the Great Self).
Thus, until the end of the aeon, he established his abode, regarding the worlds as mere blades of grass—whether they be Daityas, Suras, Nāgas, or mountains.
Sometimes the deviation from the existence of Brahman is inferred; it appears as a variegated picture within the treasury of space, for otherwise the stability of the cosmic order would not exist.
For the sake of awakening those who do not know the Self, that very self of Brahmā is designated as Viriñci and other Buddhas; this necessity is called "this creation."
The immovable has been seen as if moving, established having filled the Brahman; this creation, without beginning, middle, or end, is like a tree in the sky.

By Brahman, who abides within himself according to the analogy of lines carved in the interior of a stone, the law of necessity and creation are perceived, just as the sky is perceived by one lacking awakening.
Then, with external objects stilled and having cultivated their meditative absorption in the state of Brahman, they remained until the end of the four ages, when the kalpa reached its destruction.
Then, as the eon waned and the mass of suns blazed forth, the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds rained down with a loud and harsh roar.
While the winds of the eon blew and they remained in the single great ocean, when the multitudes of beings had perished, they remained established exactly as before.
Then, O Lord, at the end of the night's course, having withdrawn that entire state of existence, when you abide as the Self, they likewise remain established in that very same way.
Now that you have awakened and desire to create the cycle of existence, they remain established in their respective positions, high above, just as before, in perfect ease.
Likewise, O Blessed One, these ten—Brahmā, Brahmans, and Brāhmaṇas—are these ten states of transmigration established within the space of the mind.
O Lord, among them, I am this Sun, stationed here in the palace of space, employed by you on earth for the work of the divisions of time.
This creation of the directions has been described to you; the origin of the Brahmās in the sky is now explained—do as you wish.

O Supreme One, this excellent world that has arisen, its sky enveloped by various conceptual constructions and its network of sense organs causing delusion—all of that is merely a delusion within one's own mind.
The venerable Brahmā said: "O Brahman, O best among the knowers of Brahman, having addressed me, Brahmā, with the words 'Brahmāṇaḥ, Brāhmaṇāḥ, Bhānuḥ,' he became silent."
Then, after reflecting for a long time in my mind, I said to him: "O Bhānu, O Bhānu, tell me quickly, what else shall I create?"
"O Bhāskara, tell me: if these ten worlds indeed exist there, what purpose would another creation of mine serve?"
O great sage, having been addressed thus by me, Bhānu reflected for a long time with his intellect and then spoke these appropriate words in this matter.
Bhānu said: "O Lord, what purpose is there for you, who are effortless and desireless, in creation? O Master of the World, this creation of yours is merely for diversion."
O Lord, creation proceeds from you precisely because you are free from desire, like the reflection of the sun in water or like a reflection in a mirror.
O Blessed One, when you are free from desire regarding both the rejection and the attachment to the configuration of the body, your state neither yearns for nor abandons it.
O Lord, O Protector of Beings, you create this world merely for sport, repeatedly withdrawing it again and again, just as the sun withdraws its light at the end of each day.
This world must always be regarded by you as something to be engaged with solely for the sake of diversion, never out of a desire for worldly exertion.
O Great Lord, Supreme Soul, if you do not perform creation, what unprecedented result will you obtain by abandoning your eternal duty?
For that which is to be done must always be performed by the virtuous person without attachment, just as a stainless mirror performs the function of reflecting an image.
Just as the wise have no desire for the performance of action, likewise they have no desire for the renunciation of action.
Therefore, with that intellect which is like deep sleep and free from desire, perform your duties as they arise, remaining in the state of one awakened from deep sleep.
O Lord of the World, you find satisfaction in the creations of the sons of the Moon; therefore, O Lord of the Gods, these creations shall satisfy you.
These worlds are led by the eyes of the mind; they are not seen by the eye of another. Who indeed can know that "this world was created by the eye" as a certainty?
O Supreme Lord, he alone by whom this creation was fashioned with his mind beholds it with his physical eye, and no other.
And no one is able to destroy these ten transmigrations, which arise from the ten dustless [virtues] and have long endured due to the firmness of the mind.
That which is performed by the organs of action may indeed be restrained; however, no one is capable of restraining that which has been determined by the mind.
O Brahmin, whatever firm resolve has taken root in the mind of a living being cannot be overturned by anything other than that very resolve itself.
That which has been practiced for a long time with a firm resolve by the mind suffers no destruction even by a curse, even when the body has perished.

Whatever form has been firmly established in the mind and has taken root there, that very form a person becomes in this world, and nothing else. Therefore, I consider any other means for awakening that [true nature] to be as utterly fruitless as watering a mountain with a flood of water.
Bhānu said: "The mind is indeed the creator of the worlds; the mind is the supreme person. In this world, that which is done by the mind is truly done, not that which is done by the body."
Having been ordinary Brahmins, it is said that through the cultivation of the mind, the sons of Indu attained the state of Brahmā; behold the power of the mind!

For when the subtle body is meditated upon by the mind, it attains the state of a physical body; yet one who is not joined with the contemplation of the body is not afflicted by the attributes of the body.
For one with an outward gaze inevitably experiences pleasure, pain, and so forth; but by being inward-turned, the yogi does not perceive what is pleasant or unpleasant within the body.
Therefore, this world with its manifold delusions has the mind as its cause; the story of Indra together with Ahalyā serves here as an illustration.
Śrī Brahmā said: O Blessed One, O Sun, who is Kāhalī here, and who is Indra, the dispeller of darkness? For indeed, the sight that comes upon hearing their account becomes purifying.
Bhānu said: "O Lord, it is heard that in ancient times there was a sovereign among the Māgadhas known as Indradyumna, who was like a second Indra."
He had a lotus-eyed wife named Ahalyā, who was like a reflection of the moon’s orb, just as Rohiṇī is to the Moon.
In that very city, there was another wise young Brahmin named Indra, who was a libertine and the crest-jewel of a multitude of libertines.
Once, during the course of a conversation, it was heard by the queen Ahalyā that she had previously been the beloved of Indra.
Upon hearing this, Ahalyā became enamored of Indra; she then grew anxious, wondering, "Why does he not come to me, Ahalyā, though he is attached to me?"
Upon beds of lotus stalks and plantain shoots, that young woman suffered intensely, like a creeper cut down in the forests.
She grew weary of all those royal splendors, like a fish scorched by the summer heat tossing about on parched ground.
"Is this Indra? Is this Indra?"—with such babbling born of her state, she even abandoned her shame, yielding to utter helplessness.
Then, her friend, distressed with deep affection, said to her: "My dear, I shall bring Indra here without obstacle."
Hearing the words, "I shall bring what you desire," her eyes blossomed with joy, and she fell at her friend Nalini's feet like one lotus falling upon another.
Then, when the day had passed and the arrival of night drew near, that female companion went to that young brahmin named Indrākhya.
Having awakened him as was appropriate, that woman then quickly brought Indra to the vicinity of Ahalyā during the night.
Then, adorned with many garlands and ointments, she took her pleasure with that libertine Indra in a certain secret chamber.
Then, by means of that youth, who was charming with necklaces and armlets, she was won over by passion, just as a creeper is drawn by the sap of honey.
Then, being devoted to him and perceiving the entire world as consisting of him alone, she did not hold her husband—who was endowed with every virtue—in high esteem.
Then, after some time, that lion among kings discovered her passion for Indra, she who was like moonlight in the sky of her face.
As long as she meditates upon Indra, her face shines forth like a full moon or a blossomed white water-lily.
And even Indra, his entire sensory apparatus agitated by attachment to her, could not remain for a single moment anywhere when separated from her—oh, how great!
Then, the king heard the painful account of those two, whose actions were characterized by excessive generosity, affection, and lack of restraint.
Having observed that their mutual attachment was so intense, the king then administered punishment to both of them with many severe penalties.
Both of them, having abandoned [their former lives] in that body of water during the winter, were content and laughed there; they did not fall into distress.
Then the king asked, "Are you both weary, yet not evil-minded? They replied to the protector of the earth, "We have been drawn out from the reservoir."
Remembering here our mutual, irreproachable beauty of face, we do not recognize ourselves, our love for one another having grown so deep.
O protector of the earth, we are delighted by that fearless attachment to the teachings; we would not be deluded even if our own limbs were cut to pieces.
Then, having been cast into the frying pan, the two of them remained undaunted; with joyful hearts and delighted by their mutual recollection [of each other], they spoke thus.
Bound by their feet to the elephant's legs, they remained there without even feeling weary; thus did they speak to the king, delighted by their mutual recollection.
Though struck by whips and yet undaunted, they spoke in this very manner, repeatedly responding to other commands devised by the king.
When questioned, Uddhṛtau spoke again and again on that very same matter; Indra said to the protector of the earth, "This world is dear to me."
No piercing pains or sufferings afflict me in the slightest; and for her, O King of the World, everything is indeed composed of my own self.
Therefore, according to other teachings, not even the slightest suffering exists; for I am mind alone, O King, and the mind is indeed remembered as the person (puruṣa).
This body is indeed nothing but mere conceptual proliferation (prapañca), for it is seen to be suddenly struck by a mass of staffs applied at the very same moment.
It is not possible to break the mind of the Hero even in the slightest degree; O Great King, who indeed are they, what are they like, and whose powers are they?
By these [thoughts], even those who possess firm conviction in what has been seen are divided; whether the body attains growth or goes to ruin.
The mind, having fallen upon the cultivated object, remains as before; when it has long been permeated by a desired object, that mind is said to be "steadfast."
O King, the existence and non-existence residing within the body are not able to cause affliction, O Lord of the Earth, for that which has been cultivated by the mind with intense velocity.
He beholds only that which is immovable, not the movements of the body, nor any actions whatsoever, O King, including even boons or curses.
For men are indeed able to move the mind when it is possessed of intense momentum, because it is endowed with such intense momentum toward what is desired.
Just as deer are unable to move a great mountain, this dark-eyed woman is incapable of moving my mind; she is firmly established within the treasury of my heart.
Just as the Goddess Bhagavatī is in the lofty temple of the gods, I do not experience suffering, for my beloved protects my life.
O King, wherever and in whatever manner I stand or move about, I am like a mountain scorched by the heat of summer that is encircled by a mass of clouds.
In that regard, I experience nothing other than union with my beloved; with the name of Ahalyā’s lover, my mind has become the very essence of Indra.
O King, this mind of the wise man, intent upon a single purpose, does not become attached to anything else except for its own essential nature.

It is not shaken even by the power of excellent boons or curses, like Mount Meru; for the body undergoes a change as if it were something other through boons and curses. Indeed, O King, the mind remains steadfast, established in its desire for victory.

And these fragments of bodies that have arisen here in vain, O King, are not the causes of the minds; for the mind alone is the cause within these little bodies, just as water is the cause among all the juices of the creepers in every forest thicket.
Bhānu said: Then, having been addressed in this manner by Indra, that lotus-eyed king spoke to the sage named Bharata, who was standing by his side.
The king said: "O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, I behold in the face of this most wicked-souled man, who has carried off my wife, an exceedingly bold and expansive arrogance."

O great sage, quickly bestow upon him a curse proportionate to his sin; for the sin incurred by killing one who should not be killed is indeed the same as that incurred by abandoning one who should be killed.
Thus addressed by that lion among kings, Bharata, the best of sages, quickly reflected upon the transgression of that evil-minded man exactly as it was.
"O evil-minded one, perish along with this woman of wicked deeds, who has been overcome by treachery toward her husband!"—thus he uttered a curse.
Then those two, Rāma and Bharata, replied with these words: "You two are of evil mind, by whom this difficult penance has been brought to ruin."
By this bestowing of a curse, nothing happens to either of us; for when the body is destroyed, nothing of ours perishes, as we exist in our own internal forms.
Indeed, the inner self can never be destroyed by anyone anywhere; know this from us, for it is so because of its subtlety, its nature as pure consciousness, and its being difficult to perceive.
Śrī Bhānu said: With their minds bound by intense affection, they both fell to the ground due to the curse, like two leaves fallen from a tree.
Then, having fallen into misfortune and entered the womb of deer, the two of them were once again born as birds while still remaining inseparable.
Then, O Lord, in our creation, there were born a Brahmin couple who conceived a mutual bond, were devoted to austerity, and possessed great merit.
O Lord, that curse of theirs was indeed effective against Bharata, yet it was capable only of assailing his body and not in restraining his mind.
For even now, by that very cause of deluded formative forces, wherever you two are born, there you become husband and wife.
Beholding that lovely affection of theirs, permeated with the essence of unfeigned love, even the trees became permeated with the essence of love and agitated by gestures of passion.
Bhānu said: "Therefore, O Blessed One, I speak thus: the mind, O Sage, is difficult to restrain at the wrong time, and it is impenetrable even by formidable curses."
Therefore, O Brahman, the destruction of the lineages of Aindavas through the process of creation is not fitting; this is inconsistent with the nature of that Great Soul.
O Lord, what is there in this world, or indeed in all the various worlds, that could lead even you, the protector of the great-souled ones, to such wretchedness?

For the mind is the creator of the worlds; the mind is indeed remembered as the person. Whatever is accomplished by the determination of the mind cannot be achieved by substances, medicines, or punishments.
The reflection of a living being cannot be destroyed, just like that of a gem; therefore, let these remain here with their radiant displays of creative activity.
Having created the subjects here, remain; for the space of the intellect is indeed infinite—the space of the mind, the space of consciousness, and space as the third.
These three alone are infinite, illuminated by the space of consciousness; O Lord of the World, create one, two, three, or even many worlds.
"Abide in yourself by your own will; what has been taken from you by the sons of Indu? Brahmā said: "Now, when the Sun had thus spoken regarding the net of the world of the sons of Indu,"
O Great Sage, this was spoken by me after long reflection; O Bhānu, what you have said is indeed logical, for the sky is truly vast.
The mind is expansive, and the space of consciousness is vast; therefore, I perform my daily rites according to my desired creation.
O Bhāskara, I quickly imagine many nets of beings; O Blessed One, become truly my first Manu at once.
"Create the world as you desire, being duly impelled by me. Then that immensely radiant Prabhākara [responded] to these words of mine.
Having divided himself into two parts, O best of those who practice austerity, he became the Sun in this present body with his former self.
In that creation, having assumed a second body in an instant, he, becoming my very self, spread out a succession of days through his movement across the sky.
He created that entire creation, each part according to my desire.
O Sage Vasiṣṭha, I have thus explained to you all this: the true nature, the agency of all things, and the power of that Great Soul residing within the mind.
Whatever appears as a manifestation to this mind indeed becomes manifest, attains stability, and achieves fruition.
Having been ordinary Brahmins, it is said that by the power of their realization they attained the state of Brahmā; behold the potency of the mind!

Just as those who were the sons of Indu attained the state of Brahmā because of their consciousness, so too have we attained the state of Brahmā because of our nature as consciousness and our state of being the mind.
For the mind is of the nature of appearance, and that which appears is this very body and so forth within one's own interior; there is no perception of a body other than this.
The mind is the self-manifestation of the Self, and it produces that [manifestation] from itself, according to its actual occurrence, within its own being like pepper and other spices.
This very thing, appearing as if endowed with consciousness and called the *ātivāhika*, is itself described as the dense delusion known by the name "body."

This mind, whose latent impressions have become attenuated, is called by the name "jīva"; know that the jīva is the supreme state, attained gradually after the wondrous display of the body has ceased.
Neither I nor anything else exists here; it is only this mind that persists, appearing as if it has attained a state of being, like the consciousness of Vasiṣṭha and Indu.
Just as the mind of Brahmā was lunar (maindava), so too do I stand here; and this which has been created by him is indeed myself alone, appearing as the very essence of volition.
This is merely a play of the mind: "I am Brahman, established here. Know that the body and so forth are simply its own nature, arising from the void of the Self.

Through the contemplation that "I am of the single nature of pure consciousness, which is the ultimate reality," the living soul, having again become the mind, falsely perceives itself as having a bodily form.
This entire world, appearing like the cycle of existence for the son of Indu, is the body of consciousness; it is a long dream born of its own power, whose nature is fully awakened.
The entire world arises from the mind alone, preceded by the appearance of those [mental] constituents; it takes on forms such as the illusion of two moons, established like the moon in the sky.

It does not have the nature of being or non-being, nor is it both being and non-being; through perception it has the form of existence, yet it is unreal because of its contradiction [with that very perception].

Know that the mind, whose nature is volition and whose form is vast, is both inert and non-inert: it is non-inert because its essence is Brahman, and it is inert by virtue of its nature as the perceived object.

That which consists of the experience of the visible world does not exist as a reality; it is merely a manifestation within true being, just as the state of being a bracelet exists within gold, so too is it established within Brahman.
Because Brahman is all-encompassing, everything—whether insentient or consisting of consciousness, from ourselves down to a stone—is neither purely insentient nor purely sentient.
Since wood and such things lack consciousness, perception of them is impossible; for perception arises only from a connection with something similar.
Know that which is perceived to be non-inert; for by that [perception], all this indeed [is known]. For perception arises from a relationship between two similar things of the same nature.
The wealth of meanings for words such as "insentient" and "sentient" does not exist in this state that is beyond description, just as foliage and creepers do not exist in the great desert.

That which is the cognition of objects by consciousness is declared to be the nature of the mind; here, the conscious aspect is the non-inert part, while inertness is indeed the state of being an object of cognition.

In this context, the conscious portion is the element of awareness, while the insentient is seen as the object of cognition; thus, the individual soul (jīva), perceiving the illusion of the world, falls into agitation.
This state of the mind alone is pure, yet it is made twofold; therefore, she alone is the entire world, and she alone is that which is perceived as duality.
Having perceived its own self as something else, consciousness perceives its own form as an object; though partless, it appears as if divided into parts, wandering as if afflicted by delusion.
There is no delusion, nor is there any subject of delusion; such is the certainty here. Consciousness remains thus, resembling a completely full ocean.

Everything would be insentience for this [consciousness], yet you know its sentience and its state of being consciousness; the conscious portion is a part of awakening, while the emergence of "I-ness" is its insentience.

In the supreme reality that transcends egoism and the like, not even the slightest trace exists [of such distinctions], just as waves and so forth do not exist separately from water; for that [reality] has consciousness as its essence.
Know that the object of cognition, which appears as the notion of "I," has arisen like water within a mirage; it certainly does not exist at all.

Know that the state of "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) is the end, while the state of the Self (ātman) is free from affliction; the wise know that "I-ness" and the like are merely the Self, just as coldness is nothing other than snow.

Within the mind itself, insentience is perceived like one's own death in a dream; yet, by virtue of being the self of all and exercising all powers, it never reaches a state of mere equivalence [with that insentience].
The mind unfolds in every form as the objects of perception and so forth; though it is not a manifold self, this body of consciousness has a form as clear as space.

By one who is existent while abandoning identification with the body and so forth—which are of the nature of a mere appearance—the mind, which is itself of the nature of appearance, must indeed be investigated by the mind itself.
When the copper of the mind has been purified and attained the state of the ultimate gold, there is uncontrived bliss; what then is the use of the fragments of stones that are bodies?
That which exists is purified; that is awakening. And what are sky-flowers? If ignorance regarding the body and so forth were real, then attachment toward it would be appropriate.
But those ignorant ones who, being attached to the unreal, teach here that the self is denoted by words such as "body" and so forth—they are merely rams among men.
Just as one contemplates this within one's own mind, so it becomes in an instant; the examples here are the convictions regarding the moon, Ahalyā, and the artificial Indra.

Whatever manifests in whatever manner within the well-illuminated mind of the self, that very thing arises as the body for the self; having realized that this body exists but "I" do not exist, and that the true nature is the one consciousness alone, remain free from desire.

"This is the body, and this indeed is that"—from such a nature does one think "this is the body," and thus all of this goes to destruction. Just as a child experiences fear through the power of imagining a yakṣa or similar being, even though he is actually situated in a yakṣa-less body, so too does one suffer by some such reasoning.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O scion of Raghu, having spoken thus, that blessed Lord Brahmā, the source of the lotus and protector of all beings, was questioned by me once again; he then set aside his previous words and spoke this further discourse.
O Blessed One, you yourself have declared that the powers of curses, mantras, and so forth are unfailing; how then have those very same powers been rendered futile once again?
Indeed, it is said that among living beings, even the mind, intellect, and senses are all seen to be utterly deluded by a curse or by the power of a mantra.
Just as wind and its movement, just as oil and sesame seeds, are inseparable, even so are the mind and the body; the one is indeed that.
Now, if there is no body here at all, but it exists solely through the mind, it is experienced in vain—like a dream, a mirage, or a double moon.
In this case, the destruction of both follows from the destruction of one; indeed, upon the destruction of the mind, the dissolution of the body necessarily occurs.
O Lord, how is it that the mind is not assailed by defects such as curses and the like? Or how indeed is it assailed? Tell me, O Supreme Lord.
Brahmā said: There is nothing within the treasury of the world that cannot be attained by people through pure human effort, provided they follow auspicious actions.
From Brahmā down to the stationary beings, at all times and of every species, all embodied souls in this world possess two bodies.
The one consisting of mind and body acts swiftly and is ever-fickle; the other, however, is a body composed of flesh that accomplishes nothing.
In that regard, the body composed of flesh is connected to everyone; it is assailed by all curses as well as by the accumulation of spells and the like.
For he is almost mute, incapable, wretched, and perishing in an instant; as fickle as a drop of water on a lotus leaf, his state is dependent on destiny and the like.
This second body, called the mind, belongs here to those who possess a body; though dependent upon it, it is not subject to the elements within the three worlds.
If, relying on his own manliness and taking hold of eternal fortitude, he stands firm, then that blameless one becomes inaccessible to sufferings.
In whatever way the mind-body of embodied beings exerts itself, in that very way it becomes, reaping exclusively the fruit of its own resolve.
No human effort regarding the body of flesh bears fruit; every action of the mental body, however, is fruitful.
When the mind is constantly engaged in pure contemplation, curses and the like become fruitless against it, just as arrows are wasted upon a stone.
Whether the body falls into water, fire, or mud, the mind attains at that very moment exactly that which it contemplates.
O Sage, every superior person, in the subduing of all states of being, bestows the fruit without obstacle; for the mind, indeed, [is the master] of the mind.
Having inwardly made his mind full of love for his beloved through the power of his manly resolve, that artificial Indra did not experience even the slightest pang of suffering.
Having made his mind free from passion and devoid of fever through human effort, Māṇḍavya conquered the afflictions even while standing upon the tip of a stake.
Even while situated in a blind well, the rishi Dīrghatapas attained the station of the gods through mental accumulations of sacrifice.
"Even by men who are sons of the Moon, through human resolve and meditation, the state of Brahman was attained; that [attainment] is not subverted even by me."
There are also other wise and steadfast great seers of the gods who, being vigilant, do not abandon the internal contemplation of their own minds even for a moment.
Mental anxieties, physical ailments, curses, and evil glances do not shatter his mind, just as blows from lotuses cannot break a stone.
And as for those who have been broken by curses and other such arrows of mental anguish, I consider their minds to be lacking in manliness and incapable of self-discernment.
Never at any time in saṃsāra, even for a moment or in a dream, has anyone been seen whose mind was attentive or who was obstructed by the webs of faults.
Therefore, with the mind alone, a person here should, by means of their own human effort, join their very own mind to the path of purification.
O Sage, whatever appears to him becomes perfectly as it truly is; in an instant, his mind becomes robust, like a child possessed by a vetāla spirit.
Immediately upon its manifestation, the appearance abandons its prior state, just as a pot abandons the state of a lump of clay immediately upon the action of the potter.
O Sage, the mind attains the state of being a mere appearance in an instant, just as water, whose nature is merely vibration, becomes high waves.
Merely through persistent mental construction, the mind with its impure faculties perceives night even in the solar orb, just as it perceives duality in the lunar orb.
Whatever this mind perceives, that very thing quickly comes to fruition; it experiences that very same thing along with joy and sorrow, and therefore it is that [mind] itself which is that [result].
Even upon seeing a hundred flames of fire in the moon at every step of his inspired intuition, the mind experiences burning; and being thus burnt, it suffers intense remorse.
Indeed, the mind, at every step of inspired eloquence, is like an elixir even amidst bitterness; having seen and drunk it, it attains supreme satisfaction, leaps, and dances.
With every word of inspired eloquence, he perceives even the sky as a vast forest; having seen it, he cuts it down, and having cut it down, he plants it anew in abundance.

In this way, O dear one, the mind perceives immediately that very magical illusion which it itself imagines; having understood that the world is neither non-existent nor existent, you must surely abandon this fragmented vision characterized by manifold diversity.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: Thus was it previously spoken to me by the Blessed One; that very same thing has now been told to you.
Therefore, from that inexpressible Brahman, everything inexpressible arises everywhere; having itself attained a state of density, it becomes the mind.

That [body] comes to have a configuration preceded by the conceptualization of the subtle elements (tanmātra) and the mind; from that, the person becomes composed of fire (taijasa). He then applied the name "Brahman" to this very self.
Therefore, O Rāma, know that this Parameṣṭhin is the reality of the mind.
The Blessed Lord Brahmā has the form of the principle of *samanā*; because he consists of volition (*saṃkalpa*), whatever he wills, that very thing he perceives.

Then, by that [Brahman], this ignorance was conceptualized, consisting of the conceit of a self in what is not-self; by that Brahman, this world—composed of mountains, grass, and oceans—was sequentially conceptualized.
Thus, this creation, having proceeded gradually from the principle of Brahman and so forth, appears as if it has come from something else entirely.
Therefore, O Rāma, the origin of all things existing within the belly of the three worlds is from Brahman, just as waves arise from the ocean.

Thus, while the world has not yet arisen, that [power] of Brahman which consists of the form of consciousness, having been conceptualized within the ego (ahaṃkāra), causes Brahman to attain the state of being Brahman.
As for those other powers of consciousness, they are conceived as being non-different from the all-powerful one.
When the world has been expanded by you in the form of the Grandfather (Brahmā), they flourish within the mind.
These are called beings who undergo transmigration even by the thousands.

Having arisen from the sky into the atmosphere, enveloped by the subtle elements (tanmātras), those fourteen types of beings who abide within the space and wind of the firmament and exist as part of the aggregate of created things—having entered the body, whether stationary or moving, through the gateway of the vital power (prāṇaśakti) of that very [deity], they attain the state of seeds.

Thereafter, they are born into the world from a womb; thereafter, by the principle of the "crow and the palm fruit" (coincidence), they become partakers of the fruits of karma corresponding to the flow of their arisen latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Then, their bodies bound by the ropes of karma entwined with latent impressions (*vāsanā*), they wander about and repeatedly leap upward.
These classes of beings are indeed desire itself.
Some, driven by the whirlwind of karma, fall like forest leaves at the edge of thousands of people, and they roll about in the hollows of mountains.
Some immeasurable beings, deluded by the ignorance regarding the knowledge of the existence of consciousness, have been born here for a long time, even for many hundreds of kalpas.
Some, having passed through a few delightful intermediate existences, dwell in this world devoted to virtuous deeds.
Some, having realized true knowledge, have gone to the supreme state, like drops of ocean water driven by the wind back into the midst of the sea.
The birth of all living beings here proceeds from the station of Brahman; thus, the state of worldly existence is characterized by the fragile nature of manifestation and disappearance.
It sustains the fever of being afflicted by the imbalance of the poison of latent tendencies; it brings about infinite perils, misfortunes, and the performance of unworthy deeds.
Wandering through various directions, countries, times, mountains, and caves, she was an unchaste woman who created the utmost variety and caused great agitation.
O Rāmabhadra, this withered creeper of the world’s wilderness, severed by the axe of perfect discernment, shall not sprout again—its mind and body agitated like a broken vine.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, listen as I describe this classification of the origins of objects—superior, inferior, and middling—as they arise here and there.
This is that which has arisen for the very first time in this very life; it is known as "the first occurrence," arising from the cultivation of virtue.

And that [consciousness] is the basis for auspicious worlds and is followed by the performance of auspicious deeds; yet it is also the one that operates through the diverse latent impressions of saṃsāra.

Having been told that liberation occurs after only a few more existences, she became thick with virtuous qualities; she was capable of inferring what ought and ought not to be done solely from the fact that it would yield such a fruit.
Therefore, O Rāma, it is called "possessing essence" by those of perfected self; yet, if it functions through the latent impressions of the manifold world-process, it is so designated.
Extremely turbid through thousands of births, it becomes a partaker of knowledge; such is that which grants the fruits [of action], providing the inference of dharma and adharma.
Therefore, he is rightly called by the virtuous "the lowest of beings"; for immediately after that [state], there follows a multitude of births beyond counting and infinite in number.
If that which is characterized by uncertain liberation is called "utterly dark" (atyantatāmasī), then birth from a non-recent life is of such a nature as to produce such results.
O Rāma, best of the Rājās, that birth of a person which occurs within two or three lifetimes is middling; such a birth in this world is characterized by rajas.
Even one whose birth is not yet distant is called "one who has perfected their intellect" by those seeking liberation; for such a person is fit for liberation merely through that death.
By inferring from such effects, she is declared to be rajasa-sattvika; if she is so, then through a few other births, one becomes a partaker of liberation.

For such a state is described by those who know it as "the most passionate among the passionate" (rājasarājasī); yet, if she desires liberation for a long time, she becomes a partaker of liberation through hundreds of births.

That very undertaking described by you as being of the nature of passion (rājasa) and darkness (tāmasa), even if it were to result in liberation after thousands of births, is regarded as doubtful by the virtuous.

That birth of men from Brahmā, which involves such an undertaking as has been described, is characterized by passion (rājasa) and extreme darkness (tāmasa), and it occurs after they have experienced thousands of previous births.

For that [birth] has been described by the great seers as liberation after a long time, being characterized by darkness; yet, if one is destined for liberation through that very birth, it is so designated.
If those who know [the truth] say that such a person, characterized by such undertakings and possessing a *tāmasa* nature, will partake in liberation after a few more births, then so be it.
"Consisting of the nature of tamas and rajas" means [endowed] with such qualities augmented [by them], even through thousands of previous births and hundreds of future births.

Therefore, those who are unfit for liberation are declared by the knowers of truth to be *tāmasa-tāmasī*; they have already passed through hundreds of thousands of previous births, and shall do so for hundreds of thousands of births hereafter as well.
That [state] in which liberation is uncertain is called "extremely dark" (atyantatāmasī); all these classes of beings come from Brahman.
Slightly stirred from their state of enjoyment like waves from the ocean, all the multitudes of individual souls (jīvas) emerged from Brahman.
Like rays from a lamp, all the successions of beings have arisen from Brahmā through the expansion of his own radiance.
Like sparks from a blazing fire produced by its own power, all the multitudes of individual souls (jīvas) have arisen from that Brahman.
All visible perceptions of Brahmā have arisen like rays from the lunar orb, appearing in the form of *mandāra* flower clusters.
Just as the various branches of a tree possess the beauty of those very branches, so too have all the successions of living beings arisen from Brahman.
O Rāma, all the multitudes of living beings have arisen from Brahman, just as bracelets, armlets, and earrings arise from gold.
O Rāma, all the conceptualizations of the succession of beings arise from the Unborn alone, just as drops of water arise from a fountain of stainless radiance.
Just as the space within a jar, a bowl, or a hole, and so forth, arise from the space [itself], so too all the mental constructs of the world arise from the state of Brahman.
Just as droplets, whirlpools, and waves arise from water, O Rāma, so do all perceptions of the visible world arise from Brahman.
Just as the waves of a mirage arise from the radiance of the sun, all objects of perception are not distinct in nature from the perceiver.
Just as the moonlight is the radiance of the cool-rayed moon, or as light is the manifestation of fire, so too are these various classes of beings that exist.

For it is from that very source that they emerge and into that same source they enter; some births are long-lasting, occurring at the end of thousands of lifetimes, while others remain fixed as forms of only a few past births.
Thus, in these diverse worlds, by the will of that Blessed One, various forms possessing worldly activity come and go, fall and rise like clusters of sparks arising from a fire.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The action and the agent are non-different, having emerged together from the supreme state, just as fragrance and the flower emerge from a tree.
In the stainless Brahman, which is free from all conceptual constructions, individual souls manifest like the blueness perceived by those with diseased vision within the vast expanse of the sky.
O Rāghava, wherever the conduct of unawakened people is observed, there the assertions that "living beings are born from Brahman" remain established.
O Rāghava, it is not fitting for those who follow the conduct of the fully awakened to say that this world was born from Brahmā or that it was not born.
O Raghava, as long as even a slight conceptualization has not been brought to its full manifestation, the splendor of the teaching and the teacher does not shine in the world.

Therefore, for those who are wretched due to their perception of difference, this sequence of speech is taught by provisionally accepting [the distinction]: "This is Brahman" or "these are indeed the individual souls."
Thus it is seen that the world arises from Brahman through non-attachment; born from That, it is That itself, yet it is attributed to That as its cause due to the difficulty of comprehension.
Many multitudes of living beings, resembling Mount Meru and Mount Mandara, having risen up again and again, dissolve back into that very same supreme state.
Then these infinite [beings] flash forth, being born by the thousands in various quarters and groves, like sprouts upon trees.
The streams of living beings will emerge like fresh sprouts in the springtime, and they will dissolve back into that very same source like sweet juices in the summer.
Those very same ones and many others remain incessantly throughout the ages; the multitudes of living beings are born and dissolve within the Supreme.
O Raghava, the person and his karma are inseparable like a flower and its fragrance; having emerged from the Supreme Lord, they both gradually dissolve back into Him alone.
It is observed here in this world that these Daityas, Uragas, humans, and gods arise through non-existences and manifest again and again through existences.
O virtuous one, no cause for their dwelling [in this state] is observed other than the forgetting of the self; nothing else is seen that bestows the fruit of another birth.

Śrī Rāma said: Whatever has been determined by those who have abandoned passion and possess the vision of authoritative persons, regarding a subject that is non-contradictory, is called a scripture (śāstra).
Those who are endowed with the qualities of a great being, who are steadfast and possess an impartial vision, and who are endowed with an ineffable nature, are declared to be the virtuous ones.
For the two views of the foolish lead to the success of all their actions; likewise, they always follow the conduct of the virtuous as well as the sacred scriptures.
He who does not conform to the treatises for the sake of proper social conduct is cast out by all, and he sinks into suffering.
In this world and in the Veda, O Lord, it is thus always heard: that action and the agent are joined here in succession.
The agent is produced by action, and the action is brought forth by the agent; this principle, such as that of the seed and the sprout, is indeed declared in both worldly experience and the Vedas.
A living being is born from karma, just as a new sprout arises from a seed; and from that living being, karma is produced again, just as a seed is produced from a sprout.
By whatever latent impression a living being is led into the cage of existence, a fruit corresponding to that very impression is experienced.
This being the case, how indeed can you say that the arising of beings from the state of Brahmā occurs without karma, which is the seed of birth?
O Blessed One, by this very argument, you have refuted the notion that birth and action are invariably concomitant throughout the world.
In this world, two things have been wiped away: the notion that Brahman is not the cause, O Brahman, and the notion that fruits exist for those beginning with Brahmā as the results of actions.
When confusion has arisen in the world and actions no longer yield their fruits, and the law of the fish prevails, only destruction remains.
O Blessed One, tell me truly what that [action] becomes; O best among those who know what is to be known, sever this vast doubt of mine.

The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: "Well asked, O Rāghava! You have questioned me with this auspicious inquiry. Listen, for I shall speak to you so that there may arise in you a profound awakening of knowledge."
This mental unfolding occurs through the process of manifesting the creative powers (kalās); this is the seed of all actions, and its very fruit is found therein.
For as soon as the reality of the mind arose from the state of Brahman, at that very moment, karma arose for living beings and the individual soul (jīva) became established as a body.
Just as there is no difference here between two distinct flowers and their receptacles, so too there is no difference between karma and the mind, for they are inseparable.
In this world, the vibration of action is called "karma" by the wise; since that [action] first involves the mind and the body, karma is indeed nothing but the mind itself.
There is no mountain, no sky, no ocean, and no world where the fruit of one's own performed actions does not exist.
Whether it be an action performed in this life or one from the past that now manifests, this supreme human effort is never without fruit.
Just as soot vanishes of its own accord when the darkness that produced it has been destroyed, so too the mind perishes when the karma characterized by vibration ceases.

Upon the destruction of karma comes the destruction of the mind; indeed, the destruction of the mind is the state of actionlessness. This occurs only for one who is liberated, never for one who is not liberated.
Just as fire and heat are always conjoined, so too are the mind and its activity; in the absence of either one of these two, both dissolve away.

Know, O Rāma, that the mind, having always attained the play of vibration, is indeed of the single nature of vibration; and action is the mind, for when both have reached the state of the action of Dharma, they are mutually one.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The mind is indeed nothing but ideation; ideation has the nature of vibration; action is the form assumed by that ideation, and everyone pursues its fruit.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, you ought to describe in detail to me, though I am dull-witted yet possess a conscious form, that nature of the mind which has ascended to the level of volition.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That form which is fashioned by the power of volition belonging to the infinite, all-powerful, and great-souled reality of the Self, the wise know that to be the mind.
That which moves between existence and non-existence, being mobile for men and tending toward conceptualization—that, the wise know, is the nature of the mind.
"I am not of the nature of the manifestation of the Vedas; I am acting"—this is the firm conviction. Therefore, the wise know that form of the mind to be the exclusive ideation of that [Self].
In this world, the mind devoid of the power of action consisting of conceptualization is not possible, just as a possessor of qualities cannot exist without those qualities.
Just as the existence of fire and heat is not possible if they were distinct, so it is with action and the mind, and likewise with the self and the mind.
By its own nature as the mind, characterized by the fruit of action, having volition as its sole body, and possessing manifold expansions;
This universe is manifold in nature, consisting of illusion, and without cause; it is devoid of any fixed arrangement and is agitated by latent impressions and mental constructions.
Whatever latent impression (vāsanā) is established by whom, where, and in what manner, that very thing yields its fruit for that person there in that same way.
Karma is said to be the seed and the vibration of the mind; its various activities are like the branches of a tree that bear manifold fruits.
Whatever the mind intends to connect with, all these functions of the organs of action accomplish it; therefore, the mind is known as "action" (karma).
Mind, intellect, ego, consciousness, action, as well as imagination, transmigratory existence, latent impressions, knowledge, effort, and memory itself.
The senses, primordial nature, illusion, and action—these and other various verbal designations, O Brahman, are the causes of the delusion of saṃsāra.

By a chance occurrence like the "crow and the palm fruit," the various synonymous functions have been attributed to the consciousness that has abandoned its expansive form of vision and no longer follows after objects of thought.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, how have these various functions of the supreme consciousness—which conceive of diverse objects—come to be established as conventional designations?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Once, as if having cast off its state of being entirely composed of conceptualization, the mind, existing in that very state, became manifold in the form of outward manifestation.
When she remains established, having ascertained the continuity of cultivation, then this intellect is said to be capable of grasping the full extent [of reality].
When one imagines existence for oneself through false pride, it is called the bondage of existence by means of the conceit of egoism.
When, like a child, she is fragile and abandons this for that, completely relinquishing discernment, then she is called the mind.
When, because its sole nature is vibration, the agent rushes toward the fruit of that vibration while proclaiming it to be empty, then that [activity] is declared to be "karma."

When, by a chance occurrence like that of the crow and the palm fruit, one abandons firm certainty and conceives of whatever object is desired, that is what is meant here by "conceptual construction" (kalpanā).
When one internally determines, "This was seen before," or "It was not seen before," or "It was seen previously," that is designated as memory (smṛti).

When the latent impressions (vāsanā) of the powers of objects—like those whose enjoyments have been exhausted—dwell in the void with all other activities subsided, it is then called "subsidence" (asta).
There exists the stainless reality of the self, marked by the second vision; for that which was previously non-existent has now arisen, and is thus called "knowledge."
Throbbing toward its own destruction, it causes that state to be forgotten; through a web of false conceptualizations, that impurity is imagined.
Having heard, touched, seen, tasted, smelled, and reflected, this [faculty] gladdens Indra; therefore it is known as an *indriya*.
Since all the web of perceptible phenomena is unmanifest within the Supreme Self, it is called "prakṛti" (nature) in the world because of its being the fundamental source of all things.
It quickly leads one from existence to non-existence, or directly from non-existence to existence; because this conceptualization of existence and non-existence occurs, it is called "māyā."
In the world, that which has entered into the state of cause and effect through the activities of seeing, hearing, touching, tasting, and smelling is called "action" (kriyā).
These are the synonymous designations for that which follows the subject and the object, which has fallen into a state of defilement, and whose nature is characterized by manifest form.
Having attained the state of pure consciousness and returned to its natural ground, [these tendencies] have reached full maturity through hundreds of their own volitions.

The conceptualization of numerical divisions, which follows the web of dullness due to being marked by the stain of what is to be willed, is like consciousness itself when it is agitated by its own deficiency.
In the world it is called the "living soul" (jīva), and it is also spoken of as the "mind" (manas); it is called the "consciousness" (citta), and likewise it is called the "intellect" (buddhi).
The wise describe this defiled [nature], which has fallen away from the Supreme Self, as a mass of synonyms, turbid with various volitions.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahman, O knower of reality, is the mind inert (jaḍa) or is it indeed conscious (cetana)? Thus, a single certainty does not arise within me."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O Rāma, the mind is indeed neither inert nor has it attained the state of pure consciousness; rather, that vision which is neither dull nor conscious is called 'mind'."
That which appears as a turbid form between existence and non-existence, known as the cause of the world, is called this very mind.
Without a stable, uniform, and certain nature, that which exists is called "mind"; from that, this world has arisen.
That which is a mental construction in the form of a swing between the dull and the non-dull, belonging to the consciousness whose nature is now withered—that is called the mind (manas).

O Rāma, that which is inert consciousness—stirred by movement, defiled, and internally characterized by blemishes—is called the mind; it is neither purely insentient nor composed solely of consciousness.
For that [Self], these various names have been fully designated, such as ego (ahaṃkāra), mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), the individual soul (jīva), and others as well.
Just as an actor assumes various roles with great skill, even so the mind, moving from one action to another, takes on many different names.
Just as a man goes according to the power of his karma, so does the mind go, assuming various and distorted designations through the force of its diverse habitual tendencies.
O Raghava, these very designations of the mind that have been described by me are stated otherwise by proponents through hundreds of conceptual constructions.
Having superimposed upon the intellect that which is regarded as its own nature, various systems of nomenclature for the mind, intellect, sense organs, and so forth have been constructed by the mind.
For the mind of one person is dull, while that of another living being is distinct; likewise, the ego-sense belongs to one, and the intellect to another disputant.
O descendant of Raghu, those views consisting of ego, mind, and intellect, which are conceptualizations of creation, have been described by me as being of a single nature.

The Naiyāyikas have postulated them in one way, while those of similar [disposition] have imagined them otherwise; the Sāṃkhyas have conceived them differently, and the Cārvākas likewise in yet another way.
By the followers of Jaimini, the Arhatas, the Buddhists, and likewise the Vaiśeṣikas; by those others as well who are diverse, such as the Pāñcarātras and so forth.
And all of them, arising from various places and times, must reach that ultimate state, just as travelers reach a single city by different paths.
Due to ignorance of the ultimate truth and because of their perverted understanding, these seekers who wish to ascend merely engage in disputes through conceptual constructions.
Proponents praise their own paths with a diverse perspective, just as travelers arising at various times and places praise their own respective routes.
O Raghava, those whose minds are intent on ritual action have falsely proclaimed their own various logical systems by means of objects projected by their own conceptual constructions.
Just as a person, while performing actions such as bathing, giving, and receiving, attains the diversity of being an agent, so too does this mind.
Due to the influence of various effects, the agency [of the mind] is designated by different names; it is called "mind" (manas), "living being" (jīva), "latent impressions" (vāsanā), and "karma."
This entire world is experienced as nothing but mind; for a person who is without mind does not see the world, even while looking at it.
Having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled what is pleasant or unpleasant, one who possesses a mind indeed experiences internal joy or dejection.
The mind is the cause of objects, just as light is for forms; for one whose mind is bound is indeed bound, while one whose mind is liberated is indeed liberated.
Know that the insentient is supreme among those things produced from it, by which the mind is said to be insentient; for the mind, being itself insentient, does not perceive that which is sentient.
When this mind arose, which is neither conscious nor inert, then the world emerged, consisting of various pleasures, pains, and egoism.
For when the mind is of a single form, saṃsāra dissolves; it is by those [mental states] that the world is presented through delusion as a turbid cause.
O Rāma, the non-inert mind is not the cause of saṃsāra; and that which is inert, possessing the nature of a stone, is likewise not the cause of saṃsāra.
Therefore, O Rāghava, in this world, the mind is neither conscious nor inert; it is the cause of all objects, just as the faculty of sight is the cause for the manifestation of forms.
If there exists anything other than the mind, how could that world belong to one who is mindless? For the entire aggregate of all created beings dissolves [into it].
Under the influence of various karmas, the single mind assumes various designations, just as time, though one, becomes manifold through its various seasons.
If indeed non-attention, egoism, the senses, and activity agitate the body, then let there be other factors such as the vital principle (jīva) and so forth.
However, those distinctions among the philosophical systems that have been proclaimed in the mind through reasoning—whether by proponents or indeed by critics—are found here and there.
For they, O Rāma, do not perceive [this], nor are they distinguished anywhere; for all powers exist in the Divine, since they are omnipresent.
Indeed, as soon as even a slight power of consciousness arises within the pure [state], it becomes as if inert, and then diversity comes into being.
Just as thread is produced from a spider through consciousness, so too does primordial nature (prakṛti) arise from the eternally awakened Puruṣa, who is Brahman.

Under the influence of ignorance, the various mental dispositions have come to abide [in the mind]; for these are merely synonymous terms for consciousness (citi) used by disputants here, though they appear distinct.

Indeed, this impure consciousness (cit), having attained such designations as the living soul (jīva), mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), and ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti), is called by the multitude of names—cetanā, citta, and jīva—in the world; truly, there is no dispute over this.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin, this entire internal display has been produced from the mind alone; for it is understood from the meaning of the scriptural statement that "action is that very [mind]."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: By the mind alone, when colored by firm conviction, the luminous covering is once again accepted, just as it is by the fierce heat of the sun.
In this world, which is the Self of Brahman, the mind has attained a single form; in one place it is established as a human being, and in another it arises as a celestial being.
In some places it shone forth as a Daitya, in some places it arose as a Yakṣa; in some places it attained the state of a Gandharva, and in some places it took the form of a Kinnara.
I believe that it is the mind itself that expands through its vast form, appearing in the guise of various modes of conduct, regions of space, cities, and towns.
This being the case, the flood of bodies is comparable to grass, wood, and creepers; what purpose is there in investigating them? It is the mind alone that we must investigate.
Therefore, this entire world, which is expansive and agitated, is pervaded by that [consciousness]; I believe that apart from it, nothing remains but the Supreme Self alone.
The Self transcends all states, is omnipresent, and is the refuge of all; by its grace, the mind runs and leaps about within saṃsāra.
I consider the mind to be the agent of action; it is the cause within bodies. For it is the mind that is born and dies, for such qualities do not belong to the Self.
I believe that through inquiry alone, the mind itself will come to dissolution; and by the mere dissolution of the mind, thereafter, the highest good will be attained.
When that which is called the mind has been completely exhausted—along with the karmic impressions deposited within it—the living being is said to be liberated; he is no longer born again.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, you have described the three types of human births; the primary cause of these is the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent."
How then can the mind—which is called pure consciousness, which is the reality itself and devoid of intellect—arise from it and expand into the world-creating painter?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O Rāma, there are indeed three expansive spaces that exist within: the space of the mind (cittākāśa), the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), and the elemental space (bhūtākāśa) as the third."
For these are common to all and are established everywhere; however, through the power of pure consciousness, they have attained the nature of being manifest as existing entities.
That which abides both outside and inside, which makes known existence and non-existence, and which pervades all beings—that is called the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).
He who is the supreme benefactor of all beings, whose nature is the measurement of time, and by whom all this is pervaded—he is called the space of consciousness (cittākāśa).
That which has an uninterrupted body pervading the expanse of the ten directions, which is the elemental self (bhūtātman), is space (ākāśa), the substratum of wind, water, and the rest.

The two, space and the space of consciousness, arise from the power of the space of consciousness; for consciousness is indeed the cause of the entire flood of effects, just as the day is [the cause] of all that appears.

The mind is that very thing which is the impure consciousness characterized by the determination "I am inert" or "I am not inert"; know that by it, space and the other elements are brought into being.

The conceptualization of the three spaces (ākāśatraya) pertains to the domain of the unawakened self; it is imagined for the sake of instruction, but it does not pertain to the domain of the awakened.
The Supreme Brahman alone is everything, filling all things; it is the eternal object of awakened consciousness, devoid of parts and the act of dividing.

The ignorant person alone is instructed by means of the various distinctions between duality and non-duality contained within the body of scriptural texts; the awakened one is never instructed in this way.
O Rāma, as long as you have not awakened from the conceptualization of the three spaces, for that long alone shall you be instructed by me for the sake of realization.
The ether of space, the ether of the mind, and so forth, have issued from that which is stained by the ether of consciousness, just as mirages arise from a forest fire in the desert.
Having attained the state of the mind, it accumulates a defiled form; with its nature agitated, it weaves the illusory nets of the three worlds.

Indeed, this state of being a mind is seen in this impure reality which is essentially consciousness by those devoid of awakening; it is like the appearance of silver in mother-of-pearl, but not so for those possessed of awakening. Bondage here arises through ignorance, while liberation comes through the power of awakening.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O sinless one, whatever mind has arisen from whatever source, one should always apply oneself with effort to its liberation into the Self.
When the mind is joined with the Supreme, it becomes pure and free from latent impressions; thereafter, O Rāghava, being void of conceptualization, it attains the state of the Self.
This entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is dependent upon the mind; O Rāma, since it is subject to the mind, both bondage and liberation are clearly dependent upon it as well.
In this regard, listen with great care, O Rāma, to this unsurpassed narrative concerning the mind, which was told of old by Brahmā as it is now being related by me.
There is a vast forest called Rāmāṭavī, empty, unpeaceful, and most terrifying, in which even a hundred yojanas appears as a mere atom.
In that [city], there stood a certain man with a thousand hands and eyes, terrifying with his agitated mind, possessing a vast form.
Taking up many iron clubs with his thousand arms, he strikes his own back and flees by his own self.
Striking himself with his own self by means of firm blows, he, with a terrified soul, flees even for hundreds of yojanas.
Crying out as he fled, having gone far away here and there, he was exhausted, helpless in appearance, with his feet and limbs shattered.
Helpless indeed, he quickly fell into a great blind well, terrifying with the darkness of the black night, within the deep cavity of the sky.
Then, after a long time, he emerged from the blind well; striking again with blows, he drove himself away by his own efforts.
Having gone even further, he entered a thicket of Karañja trees covered with thorns, like a moth entering a flame.
Therefore, having emerged from that thicket of karañja trees as if in an instant, he again strikes himself with blows and flees from himself.
Having gone even further, he entered a lovely grove of plantain trees, cool as the rays of the moon, as if smiling.
Emerging from that grove of plantains in an instant, he again flees from himself, striking himself with his own blows.
Having gone even further, that blind man quickly entered that very same blind well, his limbs and form shattered.
Having emerged from the blind well, he entered a grove of plantain trees; from the plantain grove, he entered a pit containing a thicket of *karañja* forest shrubs.
Entering from a grove of *karañja* trees into a well, and from the well into a grove of plantains, he struck out while remaining established within himself.
Having observed him for a long time with such personal conduct, I forcibly restrained him on the road and held him back for a moment.
He was asked: "Who are you? What is this? For what purpose do you do it? What is your name? What is your desire here? Why do you wander about in vain?"
Thus questioned, O descendant of Raghu, he said to me: "I am nothing, nor do I perform any action whatsoever, O sage."
"I have been defeated by you; alas, you are my enemy! I have been seen by you, and I am lost—both for my suffering and for my happiness."
Having spoken thus, looking at his own distressed limbs and feeling dissatisfied, he wept with a loud cry, dejected like a cloud pouring rain upon the forest.
In a mere instant, having ceased his weeping there, he looked at his own limbs and both laughed and roared.
Then, at the conclusion of his loud laughter, that man gradually cast off his own limbs from all sides before me.
First his head fell, most terrible to behold; after that his arms, then his chest, and following that his belly.
Then, in an instant, that man, having sequentially abandoned those limbs, was prepared to depart for some other place by the power of destiny.
Later, in a secluded place, I saw another man likewise; he too was himself inflicting blows upon his own body on all sides.
With his thick-set arms, he flees by himself; he falls into a well, and having risen from the well, he runs toward it.
Again he falls into the pit; again, afflicted, he flees; again he enters the abyss, and for a moment, the cool forest.
"Alas! Again and again he is pleased, yet again he strikes out himself; having observed such a common mode of conduct for a long time, I am filled with wonder."
Having firmly restrained him, I questioned him in that very manner; and so, following that same sequence, he today wept and then laughed aloud.
Having reached a state of disintegration through his limbs, he became invisible according to his power; then, having reflected upon the force of destiny, he prepared to depart.
Again, in another secluded place, I saw another man striking [someone] in that very same way, yet he himself fled.
While fleeing, I fell into a great, blind, and dark well; there I remained for a very long time, waiting for him.
When that rogue had not emerged from the well even after a very long time, I then rose up to depart and saw a man once again.
As he was falling in such a manner and with such a form, I immediately seized him just as before and spoke to him once again.
In that very same way, O lotus-petal-eyed one, he did not understand that; that fool merely thinks, "He knows nothing at all about me."
Having said, "O wretched, wicked twice-born man," he departed intent on his own business; meanwhile, I continued to roam about in that great forest.
Many such men who cause harm have been seen by me; some, when questioned by me, come to rest like the agitation of a dream.
Some do not welcome what I have said, like a corpse-like body; some, having fallen into the blind wells of rebirth, rise up from them once again.
Some did not emerge from the grove of plantain trees even after a long time; others vanished within the vast thicket of the *karañja* forest.
Those devoted to the Dharma do not find a place of rest anywhere; such was that vast great forest, O descendant of Raghu.

Even today that [nature] exists within which those persons are thus situated; and she was seen by you, O Rāma, acting here before you. Yet, because of the immaturity of your intellect, O Rāghava, you do not remember her.

That terrifying forest, with its limbs crowded with various thorns and dense with thick darkness, though formidable in this world, is frequented by those who have not attained the supreme awakening as if it were a bower of flowering shrubs.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin, what is that great forest? When and how was it seen by me? Who were those men there, and what were they striving to do?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O mighty-armed Raghunātha, listen; I shall tell you everything. That great forest is not far away, O Rāma, nor indeed are those men.
O Rāma, know that this path of saṃsāra—deep, with its boundless hollows, empty yet rich in transformations—is a vast wilderness.
When this [reality] is attained through the light of discernment by means of a single object alone, being full and not joined with anything else, then it is indeed as if solitary.
Know that those large-bodied men who wander about there are, in truth, the very minds fallen completely into suffering.
O Mahāmati, I am the observer of these things with discernment; by means of discernment, O sinless one, they were seen by me as something entirely other.
For by me, through discernment, those very minds are awakened, just as lotuses are constantly awakened by the well-shining sun.
Some do not welcome me due to their delusion regarding solitude; by virtue of their contempt for me, they fall headlong into wells.
O descendant of Raghu, those dark wells and dense hells that you have entered are now like groves of plantain trees.
You ought to know that the minds of those who find their sole delight in heaven are like those who have entered the depths of a blind well and never emerged.
O Rāghava, those minds are joined with great sins which have not yet emerged from their state within the plantain grove.
O Raghava, those thoughts endowed with the accumulation of merit are like those that have entered a forest of karañja trees and do not emerge from them.
O descendant of Raghu, among those human beings, some minds were fully awakened and thereby liberated from bondage.
Indeed, some minds, assuming many forms, enter from one womb into another; they remain there, and they fall down and rise up again.
They know that thicket of karañja trees to be the passion for one's wife; human existence, crowded with the thorns of suffering and filled with various desires, is likewise such a thicket.
But those minds that have entered the dense thicket of the karañja tree, once born in human form, remain full of passion for that very same thing.
O scion of the Raghus, know that place where the groves of plantain trees are cooled by the rays of the moon—that which brings delight to the mind—is heaven itself.
Some maintain their bodies through merit and through austerity characterized by self-restraint, remaining steadfast whether they are already established or have just arisen.
By those ignorant men who have disregarded my intellect and mind, their own discernment has been disregarded by those minds that know not the self.
"By you I have been seen; I am ruined! You are my enemy!"—this which was quickly spoken was indeed a lamentation uttered by a dissolving mind.
O Raghava, that great wailing which was wept by the man with much speed was the lamentation made by the mind as it abandoned the web of enjoyments.
For one who has attained partial discernment but has not yet reached the stainless state, there will be intense anguish as the mind abandons worldly enjoyments.
With compassion, he beheld their weeping limbs and thought in his mind: "Alas! Having abandoned these, why should I depart?"
For one who has attained partial discernment but has not yet reached the stainless state, anguish indeed increases as the mind abandons the limbs of the body.
But that laughter which is blissful, arising from a man's awakening to intoxication and attained through discernment—that, O Rāma, is the laughter of a contented mind.
For one who has attained seclusion and abandoned abiding in saṃsāra, as the mind relinquishes form, bliss indeed increases.
Those very limbs which were seen by a man while laughing in derision are now seen by the mind as the very grounds for his own deception.
"Alas! For so long we have been deceived by things fashioned by false conceptualization. Thus, with a sense of derision, he looked upon his own limbs with his mind.
For the mind that has attained discrimination and rests in the expansive state looks back from afar with a smile at its former vessel of dejection.
When he was firmly restrained and questioned by me with great effort, it was shown that discernment forcibly seizes the mind.
When the limbs have fallen apart and vanished before one's eyes, it is demonstrated that the hope for objects ceases without that mind.
That which was described as the man possessing a thousand eyes and hands is indeed shown to be the infinite form of the mind.
