Just as a man strikes himself with a torrent of blows directed at his own body, so too does his own mind strike itself with the blows of its own evil imaginings.
When a person flees from striking himself with his own hand, it is because that mind flees from the blows of its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
It strikes its own mind by itself, according to its own will; and it flees away by itself as well—behold the manifestation of ignorance!
For all minds, scorched by their own latent impressions, flee of their own accord when they are fit to go to that state.
This very mind spreads out the extensive suffering that it has itself extended; yet, once it is utterly exhausted by that, it flees from it all on its own.
The mind comes of its own accord into bondage through the webs of volitional tendencies and latent impressions, just as the silkworm is bound by its own webs made of saliva.
Just as he incurs misfortune, so does he play restlessly; failing to see his own future suffering, like a child with its own wicked pranks.
Just as the monkey who pulled out the wedge suffered pain by treading upon the testicles situated in the cleft of the wood, so indeed does this mind suffer.
Through long-term protection and likewise through long-term cultivation, having attained insignificance through practice, one no longer grieves.
Through mental negligence, sufferings increase like mountain peaks; yet by the power of that very [mindfulness], they perish just as frost vanishes before the sun.

For as long as one lives, the mind indeed delights in blameless impressions born from the meaning of the scriptures, remaining silent toward passion and the like like a sage; subsequently, having attained that unborn, cool, and most purifying state, a person who abides therein need no longer grieve, even in the midst of great calamities.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This mind has emerged from the supreme state of Brahman, being both non-identical with it and identical with it, like a wave from the ocean.
O Rāma, for those who are awakened, the mind here is indeed Brahman alone and nothing else; just as for those who perceive the commonality of water, a wave is not something other than the ocean.

The mind is the cause of the delusion of saṃsāra for those who have not awakened to the nature of Rāmā; it is like one who fails to see the commonality of water and does not perceive the non-difference between water and its waves.
For those whose vision is unawakened, a distinction based on the relationship between the signified and the signifier is merely postulated for the sake of awakening them.
The Supreme Brahman is all-powerful, eternal, ever-full, and imperishable; there is nothing that does not exist within it, for everything is contained within that expansive Self.
For the Blessed One possesses all powers; whatever pleases him, the omnipresent one manifests that very power extended throughout.
O Rāma, the power of consciousness (cic-chakti) is perceived within bodies, the power of motion (spanda-śakti) within winds, and likewise the power of inertia (jaḍa-śakti) within stones.
Likewise, the power of fluidity resides in waters, the power of fire in fire, the power of emptiness in space, and the power of existence in the persistence of becoming.
For the all-pervading power of Brahman is seen extending through the ten directions: the power of destruction in things that perish, and the power of sorrow in those who grieve.
The power of bliss is in the Joyful [state], and likewise the power of vigor is in the Fierce; the power of emanation is in the Emanations, and at the end of the aeon, there is omnipotence.
Just as a tree exists within the seed of a tree—possessing fruit, flowers, creepers, leaves, branches, twigs, and roots—so too does this [universe] abide within Brahman.
By the power of appearance alone, the mind—which is situated between mental dullness and its opposite, and which is designated as either "living" or "other"—is perceived within the inner Brahman.
The various trees, creepers, shrubs, networks of vines, sprouts, and rice plants are but non-conceptual pure consciousness; their diversity is merely an unknown mental construction.
O Rāghava, behold today this very reality of the "I" as Brahman alone; it is the Self, all-pervading by name, whose great form is eternally manifest.

That power which, being of the nature of mentation, sustains itself as the mental organ is called the mind; it is like the illusion of feathers in the sky, or like the perception of a whirlpool in water.
The mind, which is merely a fraction of appearance, is likewise the living soul within the self; this very form of the mind that has arisen is essentially of the nature of mentation.
Therefore, O subduer of enemies, this is the power of Brahman; it is indeed Brahman itself. The distinction of "this" and "I am that" arises merely from appearance.
Nothing other than the mind is the supreme cause of delusion regarding Brahman; whatever exists, whether being or non-being, is contained within this very mind.
They know that power, which is designated as "all-pervading," to be the state of Brahman; it is called the essence of the existence of the mind, just as it resides within this mind.

Just as the powers of the seasons exist within the year, so do the activities of living beings reside within Brahman; they are like the earth, which, though pervaded by the flowers of all seasons, manifests through the distinctions of place and time.
Just as the Creator of the World places flowers here and there, so does He place various thoughts; for from Him, indeed, powers emerge at various times and in various places.

Due to the diversity of place, time, and other factors—just as rice plants [differ] on the surface of the earth—one perceives by means of one manifestation what was not produced by that very same [manifestation].
Know that those things which are conceptualized by mental words—such as the exclusion of opposites, number, form, and so forth—are born of Brahman; they are Brahman itself.
In whatever manner an appearance arises for this mind, in that very same way it comes to be; in this regard, the lunar mansions (the stars) are indeed cited as an illustration.
Just as movement occurs in the great ocean, which is itself unmoving and pure, so does this individual soul (jīva) exist within the Supreme Self (paramātman), being the cause of saṃsāra.
O Rāma, for the knower, everything perceived always revolves as Brahman alone within the Self, like the water of the ocean with its masses of surges, waves, and billows.
There is no second being, for existence consists solely of the activity of name-and-form; it is like a mental construction distinct from the water in an ocean where various waves arise.
That which is born and likewise perishes, that which moves and stands still—all this is Brahman; it is Brahman that evolves through Brahman.
Just as the intense heat within itself appears as a mirage, so too does the manifold Self manifest through its own manifold nature.
The instrument, the action, and the agent; birth, death, and persistence—all this is Brahman alone, for there exists no other conceptualization apart from it.
There is no greed, there is no delusion, there is no thirst, and there is no passion. What greed, thirst, or delusion could there be for the Self within the Self? Or from where could they arise?
This entire world is indeed the Self; the process of mental construction is the Self alone. Just as gold arises in the form of a bracelet, so does this Self arise in the form of the mind.
That supreme state which is unawakened is called the mind and the individual soul (jīva); when it remains unrecognized, it quickly turns from being a kinsman into a stranger.
By means of its own conscious self, though ignorant, through its own volition, the void was manifested by the living being itself, just as the sky is manifested by space.

In this world, the very Self shines as the individual soul (jīva) like one who perceives what is not the Self; due to faulty vision, both the existent and the non-existent arise, like the appearance of two moons.

Since these two—the perception of the meaning of delusion and the perception of the meaning of words—are utterly impossible, and because the Self alone is real, where is the bound self, and where is it liberated?
For one for whom bondage is eternally non-existent, the notion "I am bound" is a false imagination; for him, liberation is likewise imaginary and not real in truth.
Śrī Rāma said: "Whatever resolve the mind reaches, that very thing comes to pass and not otherwise. Therefore, O Lord, how can there be no bondage that is merely conceptual?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This conception of bondage is false and merely imaginary for fools; likewise, their other conception of liberation has arisen as nothing but a falsehood.
Thus, due to the non-remembrance of the vision of bondage and liberation arising solely from ignorance, there is in reality neither bondage nor liberation, O Mahāmati.
The unreality of conceptual construction is known to one whose mind is fully awakened; O wise one, it is like the snake in a rope, known to one whose mind has realized the truth.

No delusion regarding bondage, liberation, and so forth exists at all for the wise man; for it is only the ignorant person, O Rāghava, who possesses such delusions as bondage, liberation, and the like.

First is the mind, then the views of bondage and liberation, and afterwards the construction of conceptual proliferation known as the world; such is this established order, O fortunate one, which has become fixed like a narrative told by children.
Śrī Rāma said: O best of sages, what is this sequence called the "Account of the Child"? Tell me this in due order, for it is the cause for describing the mind.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, a certain child of innocent mind once asked his nurse, "O nurse, tell me some entertaining story."
O Great-minded One, for the amusement of that child, his nurse told him a narrative with clear and sweet syllables.
In some places, even where there is no city at all, there may be three auspicious princes of great soul, righteous and exultant in their valor.
In the vast empty city, like water-drops and stars in the sky, two were not born, and likewise one did not even remain in the womb.
Then, for the sake of obtaining the most excellent gain, they once gathered together; being separated from their kinsmen, with dejected faces and hearts stricken by grief.
Emerging from that empty city with their faces spread wide, they were like Mercury, Venus, and Saturn joined together as if emerging from the sky.
With limbs as delicate as the śirīṣa flower, scorched by the sun from behind on the road during the day, they were like tender leaves withered by the heat of summer.
With their lotus-feet scorched by the burning sands of the path, they lamented, "Alas, father! like deer strayed from the herd.
With their feet pierced by the tips of darbha grass and the joints of their limbs exhausted by the heat, they have traversed a long distance with bodies grey with dust.
On the way, they reached three trees that were thick with clusters of blossoms, garlanded with fruits and shoots, and served as a refuge for flocks of beasts and birds.
Among these three trees, two have not grown even slightly; as for the third, the self-climbing tree, its very seed does not exist.
Exhausted and weary, they rested there beneath a single tree, like Indra, Vāyu, and Yama at the foot of the Pārijāta tree in heaven.
Having eaten fruits that were like nectar and having drunk their juice, they fashioned garlands from clusters of blossoms, rested for a long while, and then departed.
Having gone even further, when midday had arrived, they reached a triad of rivers resounding with the rippling noise of waves.
There, one river was completely dried up, and not even a trace of water remained in the other two; their sight was like that of blind eyes.
In that [lake] which was utterly parched, they bathed with great devotion, like Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, afflicted by the summer heat, bathing in the Gaṅgā.
Having engaged for a long time in water-sports and having drunk water resembling milk, those princes themselves departed with joyful minds.
Then, at the end of the day as the sun was hanging low, they reached the city that was to be newly built, which resembled a mountain.
The lake of the dark blue sky was filled with lotus-pools of banners, and the circle of citizens resounded with the loud cries heard from afar.
There they beheld three beautiful, excellent mansions made of jewels and gold, like the peaks of a great mountain.
There were two unconstructed dwellings there, one of which was indeed without walls; those three men entered that beautiful, wallless mansion.
Having entered and quickly sat down, those fair-faced women, while sporting there, found three vessels fashioned from molten gold.
There, two of them turned into shards and one was reduced to powder; those long-witted ones took up that pot in the form of powder.
With those ninety-nine *droṇas* of that [grain] and one *droṇa* of the cooked rice, a hundred *droṇas* were consumed there by those who eat much.
Three Brahmins were invited by those princes; however, two were bodiless, and one had no mouth at all.
O son, there the blind man ate a hundred *droṇas* with his mouth alone; and what remained after the Brahmin had eaten was consumed by the princes.
Through these three [verses], the princes attained supreme peace; for those three princes who were to be born in that city are now dwelling happily today, engaged in the pursuit of hunting, my son.
O sinless one, this delightful narrative has been told by me to you; keep it in your heart, O wise one, and you will become truly discerning.
"O Rāma, this auspicious tale called 'The Child' has been told by the nurse; and the child became delighted by this auspicious narrative."
O lotus-eyed Rāma, this story of the young boy has been told by me to you in connection with the narrative concerning the mind.
This construction of saṃsāra has reached its present state through fierce conceptualizations firmly imagined, like a story told to children.
O sinless one, this net of conceptual construction, whose very nature is appearance, unfolds in the form of the mental fabrications of bondage, liberation, and so forth.
Nothing else exists here apart from mere volition; by the power of volition, something may appear as something, or it may not appear at all.
The sky, the earth, the wind, space, the mountains, the rivers, and the directions—all this is fashioned by one's own volition; thus, it is like a dream of the self.
Just as the three princes became rivers in the city, so indeed is this state of the world: it is merely a construction of conceptual thought.
Like the ocean consisting of mere water within its own waters, that which is restless and composed of mere volition flashes forth everywhere within itself.
At first, this world arose from the Supreme Self as mere volition; it then attained expansion through its activities, just as a day unfolds through its various functions.

The entire world is merely the manifestation of the web of volition; know that volition alone is the object of its play. Abandoning even this mere volition, take refuge in the state beyond conceptualization and, O Rāma, attain peace through certainty.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Through the power of his own volition, the fool falls into delusion, but not the wise man; for it is only the child who becomes bewildered by the notion of decay within that which is indestructible.

Śrī Rāma said: O best of the knowers of Brahman, who is this one conceived by whom, and for what purpose, was this destruction brought about—by which that which is truly non-existent has seized the great delusion, even though it is eternally existent?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This decay called egoism has been falsely imagined here by the unreal multitude of beings, just as a vampire was imagined by a child.
When everything exists within that single, supreme reality, from where does this thing called "I" arise, and how indeed has it come into being?
In reality, there is no ego-sense in the non-dual Supreme Self; it arises from imperfect vision, like a mirage on a riverbank in the intense heat of the sun.
The great undertaking of the mind-jewel is perceived as saṃsāra; resting upon itself by means of itself, it vibrates within like water.
Therefore, O Rāma, abandon false vision which is without support; take refuge in right vision, which has its support in truth and is blissful.
With an intellect characterized by discernment and free from the agitation of delusion, investigate now; abandon both the true and the false.
Having said that the unbound is bound, why do you grieve in vain? How, by what means, and in what manner can the infinite reality of the Self be bound?
In this entire reality of Brahman, which is the undivided Great Self, where there is no reckoning of diversity or non-diversity, what is bound and what is liberated?
Though free from affliction, one appears afflicted and suffers when a limb is severed; yet no such suffering arising from the modifications of difference and non-difference exists within the Self.
When the body is destroyed, wounded, or wasted away, no injury has come to the Self; just as when a bellows is burnt, the air filling the bellows is not destroyed.
Whether the body falls or rises, what loss has befallen us? When a flower is destroyed, what is lost? The fragrance remains, taking refuge in the sky.
Let the glories of the snows of pleasure and pain fall upon the lotus of my body; what injury can possibly befall us from those bees dwelling in the sky?
Let the body fall, or rise up, or go to the ends of space; what loss is that to me, whose nature is entirely different from it?
Just as is the relationship between the cloud and the wind, or between the bee and the lotus, so too, O Raghava, is the relationship between your body and your own self.
O Rāma, the mind is indeed the body of the entire world; it is the primordial power, consciousness itself, and the inner self, which never perishes.
O one of great wisdom, that Self which neither perishes nor departs never perishes at any time; why then do you grieve in vain?

Just as the wind goes to the infinite space when the cloud has dispersed, or as a bee goes to the infinite sky when the lotus has withered, so does the Self go to the infinite state upon the dissolution of the body.
Even the mind of a living being wandering in this saṃsāra does not perish without the fire of knowledge; what then can be said regarding the destruction of the self?
The same principle that applies to the pit and the jujube fruit, and the same sequence that applies to the pot and space, is the relationship between the perishable body and the imperishable self.
Just as a jujube fruit falls into one's hand when its husk bursts open, so too does the Self emerge into the sky when the body moves away.
Just as the space within a jar moves when the jar moves and remains still when the jar is destroyed, so too does this embodied soul remain free from affliction when the body has perished.
For the mental body of living beings is concealed by space and time, repeatedly shrouded by the cloth of death; O rogue, why this lamentation?
O mighty-armed one, when place and time have vanished at the moment of death, even a deluded man—what is there to fear? For here, no one perceives anything at all.
Therefore, O Rāma, abandon this latent impression that "I am" which exists as a mere falsehood, just as the king of birds abandons his egg when he longs to travel through the sky.
For this mental power is the cause of the desirable and the undesirable; by this very delusion, one falsely constructs [reality] as if in a dream.
This ignorance is endless; it increases for the sake of suffering. When not fully understood, it expands this world made of unreality.
This deluded one perceives the sky as something empty, like it were soiled by frost, because she has strayed from the natural state of her own true nature.
This world, though non-existent, appears as if it were real—slowly emerging from its inception, expansive, and imagined—just like a long dream through this [avidyā].
Its very nature, consisting of mere mental cultivation, has attained the state of agency; it is like the turbid eye of the world [perceiving] the reflection of rays of light in the sky.
O Rāma, lead her to the investigation of her own true nature through inquiry, just as the sun, the lord of day, leads a stone of frost to its dissolution by its heat.
Just as the sun, desiring the absence of cold, achieves its desired goal through its own rising, so too does one who seeks the dissolution of the mind achieve their desired aim through inquiry.
For ignorance, unawakened and spreading through difficult paths of misfortune, causes Śambara to rain down gold through various magical illusions.
The mind alone is fully capable of performing this act of its own destruction; for the mind dances the drama known as "the slaying of the self."
The mind beholds itself solely for its own destruction; for the one of wicked intellect does not realize that ruin is at hand.
By its own mere volition, the mind quickly accomplishes this for those who perceive their own destruction; affliction is of no use here.
Having abandoned the portion of its own volitions and conceptualizations, the mind—when endowed with discernment—casts off its expansive form and effects the realization of the Self.
The destruction of the mind is a great attainment; indeed, it is the dawning of the great eradication. Therefore, apply yourself to the destruction of the mind, and not to the impulse of the mind.

In this forest where dense groves of trees are pleasure and pain, and where the great serpent Kṛtānta (Death) lurks in wait, O fortunate one, this entire mind of yours, devoid of discernment, is the sole cause of great calamity for the Lord.

When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The mind, having arisen from the Supreme like a wave from the ocean, attains expansion and spreads this world here and there.
It quickly makes the short long, and leads the long to a state of being dwarfed; it likewise brings another part to its own state, and similarly brings its own state to the state of another.
Even that which is merely the size of a span, through the very cultivation of it as a reality, quickly becomes as radiant as the king of mountains, as if it had spontaneously attained that state.
The mind, having attained firm establishment and surging forth from the supreme state, in a mere moment creates the cycles of worldly existence and yet does not create them.
Whatever is seen here—whether the world is stationary or moving—all of it, in all its diverse forms, has arisen from the mind.
Agitated by the powers of place, time, action, and substance, the mind—like an actor due to its fickleness—passes from one state of being to another.

It quickly leads to existence what was non-existent, or it fully brings to existence what already exists; and being thus cultivated, it takes on exactly such pleasures and pains as have been habituated.
Just as the flickering mind itself takes up what has been obtained, so too does the aggregate of the hands, feet, and other limbs exert effort accordingly.

Then that very same action, whether it yields fruit or no fruit when the mind is concentrated, bestows its result in an instant, just as a creeper watered at the right time yields its corresponding fruit.
Just as a child in a house makes a variegated series of playthings out of mud, so too, O Rāma, does the mind create the world through its conceptual constructions.
Therefore, since the mind is like a mass of mud for the play of all people, why is this notion of "substantiality" imagined as being rooted in objects within the world?
Just as time, acting as the cause of seasons, brings about changes in the form of a tree, so too does the mind bring about an apparent alteration in the very nature of these objects.
In a mental wish, in a dream, and in the fabrications of one's imagination, even a vast array of leagues becomes like the footprint of a cow within the playful diversions of the mind.
Within, it makes an eon a mere moment; a moment it brings to the state of an eon. Since the mind is dependent on that, the wise know it to be the sequence of space and time.
Due to the intensity or mildness of their spiritual urgency, due to the distinction between their being many or few, and due to delay over a long period—but not because of incapacity versus capacity.
Delusion, agitation, misfortune, and the coming and going of place and time—these arise from the mind like shoots from a tree.
Just as the ocean is nothing but water, and fire is nothing but heat, so too this cycle of existence with its various upheavals is nothing but the mind itself.
Whatever has come into the range of cognition—along with its agent, object, and instrument, and enriched by the seer, the seeing, and the seen—all that is indeed nothing but the mind.

The mind itself perceives worlds, universes, and forest depths as its own manifestations; just as gold is seen by people through their notion of "gold" even while discarding the specific forms of armlets, crowns, and bracelets that constitute its shining appearance.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In this regard, listen as I relate to you this supreme account of how the splendor of the world’s illusion exists, entirely dependent upon the mind.
On this surface of the earth, there is a great and prosperous kingdom named Uttarāpāṇḍava, filled with various forests.
There, ascetics rested in dense, deep forests without any gaps, and the city-gardens contained groves where vine-swinging pleasure-grounds were presided over by Vidyādharīs.
Its mountains were tawny with masses of filaments from flowers shaken by the wind; it wore as its crest-ornament a forest garland consisting of shimmering clusters of blossoms.
Its jungles were bordered by groves and clusters of Karañja flower-stalks; villages were hidden within date-palm trees, and the sky resounded with a humming drone.
It was tawny with rows of *ekapiṅga* rocks and fields of ripening rice, and adorned with wild forests resounding with the unrestrained cries of peacocks.
Its golden forests resounded with the frantic cries of cranes, and its mountain villages were adorned with earrings of dark *tamāla* and pale *pāṭalī* trees.
The banks of the river were reddened by *pāribhadra* trees in full bloom, while a cacophony was produced by the warbling of flocks of various birds.
The god of love was captivated by the maidens in the rice fields as they sang; the clouds of blossoms were shaken down by the wind moving through the swaying flowers and fruits.
With siddhas, cāraṇas, and bards emerging from his palace like a cave, he was created as if beauty had been brought down from heaven itself.
It was a pavilion formed by groves of plantain trees and singing kinnaras and gandharvas, white with flower gardens stirred by the sound of gentle breezes.
There dwelt a king named Lavaṇa, supremely righteous, born of the lineage of Hariścandra, like a sun upon the earth.
There the mountains shine with their shoulder-masses white with the flower-crests of fame, like necklaces tossed about.
Having completely severed the entire circle of his enemies with fragments of his sword, he brings fever upon the world of his foes merely by being remembered.
Whose conduct—marked by noble undertakings and the protection of the world of the noble ones—people shall remember for a long time, as they do that of Hari.
Upon the peaks of the king of mountains, in the celestial abodes of the gods, the songs of his virtues are sung by the Apsarases with the thrill of bristling hair in rapture.
The songs of his virtues, sung by the celestial beauties and long heard by the world-protectors, are echoed by the swans of Brahmā through their own constant practice.
O Rāma, even in dreams, no action characterized by the fault of wretchedness has ever been seen or heard of in one whose noble genius is so extraordinary.
Once, when the lord of the day had reached the eighth part of the sky, he was seated upon his throne in the assembly hall.
While the king sat there comfortably like the moon in the sky, and the armies of the vassal lords were entering with great haste.
Then, while the lovely women were singing and the kings were well-seated, the joyful sound of lutes, flutes, and cymbals captivated the mind.
While the king—resembling the preceptor of the gods and asuras—was resting with his circle of ministers, [the women] stood with graceful charms, beautiful chowries in their hands.
When the royal affairs had been presented and entered upon by the ministers, and when the reports concerning the country were spoken by the skillful and excellent counselors;
While the sacred Itihāsas were being recited from the manuscript at the auspicious hour, and while the bards stood bowed before him chanting holy hymns of praise;
A certain magician entered that assembly with arrogance, like a rain-cloud entering the earth with a downpour that excites agitation.
Having approached the feet of the protector of the earth, whose shoulders were as noble as a mountain peak, he bowed to the beloved king like a fruit-bearing tree bowing to a mountain.
He entered before the king—who possessed a beautiful luster, broad shoulders, was laden with fruit, and radiant with flowers—just as a monkey might enter before the top of a tree.
Fickle and greedy for wealth, he spoke with his neck outstretched to the king, who was like a lotus, as a bee speaks to a lotus in the breeze of fragrant pleasure.
O Lord, while remaining seated upon your throne, behold for a moment this single, wondrous display of harshness here, like the moon in the sky gazing down upon the earth.
Having said this, he whirled his peacock-feather whisk, which causes confusion, like the Māyā of the Supreme Self, the seed of manifold manifestations.
The protector of the earth beheld her, radiant with a dust of splendor, just as Śakra, seated in his celestial chariot, beholds the vine of his own bow.
At that moment, the Saindhava vassal entered the assembly hall, like a cloud entering the path of the sky filled with a circle of stars.
And that gentle horse, possessing supreme speed, followed after him—just as Uccaiḥśravas follows the gratified Śakra when he is intent upon the world of the gods.
Taking that horse, he spoke to the king, just as the Ocean of Milk, possessing Ucchaiḥśravas, spoke to the Lord of the Maruts.
"O Lord of the Earth, this jewel among horses is like Ucchaiḥśravas; by its nature of swift flight, it is as if the wind itself were incarnate."
"O Lord, this horse has been sent to you by our master; for the auspicious splendor of an object truly shines when offered to the great."
When he had spoken thus, the magician replied to him, like a cātaka bird crying out to a rain-cloud once the thundering of the clouds has ceased.
O Lord, mount this noble steed and wander the world, just as the sun traverses the earth whose splendor is enhanced by its own radiance.
The king looked at the horse and spoke to him, like a peacock crying out at a cloud rumbling with thunder.
Then the king, whose form was like a painting, gazed at the horse with an unblinking eye, appearing as if he had been fixed in a work of art.
Having gazed for a moment, he remained seated upon his throne with his eyes closed; his vision was undisturbed, like the ocean with its fish and mountains when it is stilled by gentle rays.
For two moments he remained as if absorbed in meditation upon the Self; the sage, free from passion, stood like one agitated and yet established in supreme bliss.
He was not awakened by anyone else, for he was already aroused by his own majesty; rather, through his intellect, he further contemplated some profound thought.
There, the female chowrie-wavers remained merely with their white chowries motionless, like nights in which the rays of the moon have been paralyzed.
Those members of the assembly shone, filled with wonder and motionless, like lotuses whose filaments and petals have become rigid as if formed from mud.
The clamor of the people in the assembly hall gradually subsided, like the thundering of clouds in the sky when the rainy season has ended.
Immersed in an ocean of doubt, the excellent ministers fell into anxiety, like the gods when the Asura king Gadāpāṇi is despondent.
While the king stood with eyes fixed and motionless, his people—struck with wonder, paralyzed by fear, and despondent by delusion—bore the splendor of the lotus-like face of the Lord of Men.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, after two muhūrtas, the lord of the earth attained awakening, like a magnificent lotus released from the waters of the rainy season.
Awakened from his seat, he—adorned with armlets and a crest-jewel—caused the earth to tremble like a mountain whose peaks and slopes are covered by forests during an earthquake.
Then he awoke upon his seat, trembling like Mount Śaṅkara when the elephant of the netherworld is agitated.
The leaders supported that king as he was falling with their arms, just as the principal mountain ranges support Mount Meru when it is shaken at the time of universal dissolution.
Supported by those walking before him, the king, his mind deeply agitated, bore the splendor of the moon disturbed by waves.
"Who is this? Whose assembly is this? the king asked slowly, like a bee dwelling within the heart of a lotus sinking beneath the water.
Then the assembly spoke respectfully to the god, "What is this?", like a swarm of humming bees seeing the sun eclipsed by Rāhu.
Then the leading ministers questioned him, just as the gods once questioned Mārkaṇḍeya when he was terrified by the onset of the dissolution of the world.
O Lord, while you are situated thus, we are utterly distressed; for delusions, though groundless, shatter even the mind that is otherwise indivisible.
In which conceptual constructions has your mind become agitated—constructions that are pleasant at first sight but bitter in their final outcome, like sensual enjoyments?
Why does your mind, which has become pure and thoroughly cooled by discourses on constant and noble conduct, sink into agitations?
The mind, which has empty objects and is torn and shattered amidst worldly activities, takes on delusion; it does not manifest the splendor of greatness.
For whatever state of mind has arisen in him through constant practice, that very state continues to flow even when he is intoxicated by the pride of his body.
For even your mind—steadfast, awakened, possessing noble qualities, and directed toward a substantial object—is seen to be strangely mangled, as it were.
For the mind that has not practiced discernment follows the influence of place and time; it comes under the power of mantras and medicines, but not one whose activity is noble.

How could one who possesses constant discernment ever suffer from being cut or shattered? For such a person, the mind shakes off the pervasive [afflictions] just as a whirlwind shakes the mountain of the gods.
Thus, the splendor of the king, who had swallowed his grief upon the birth [of his son], adorned his face, just as fullness adorns the cool-rayed moon at the end of the month.
With his gentle face and eyes opened wide, the king shone like the month of Mādhava when the winter season has passed and a profusion of blossoms has burst forth.
Then, with his face devoid of memory due to extreme agitation, wonder, and distress, he appeared like the moon in the sky when death is near, beholding Rāhu.
Beholding the sorcery, he then spoke as if laughing, like Takṣaka in the form of a serpent upon seeing a predatory beast.
"O fool! What is this that has been done by you with your tangled web of nets, such that the ocean, which was motionless and serene, has in an instant returned to its placidity?"
Wondrous indeed are the hundreds of powers of the objects of the Divine; by these, even my mind, though possessed of great strength, has been cast into delusion.
Where are we, who understand the words of the Destroyer at the end of the world's cycle; and where are these widespread, inherent calamities that bring delusion to the mind?
Even when the mind has practiced great knowledge, it may remain within the body; at times, even for those possessed of intelligence, it may momentarily succumb to delusion.
"O members of the assembly, listen to this wondrous tale of what was displayed here for a moment by my magician."
I have observed within this many shifting states of affairs; for a moment, I was like the unborn Brahmā when his creation by Śakra had been destroyed.
Having spoken thus, while the members of the assembly looked up with wide eyes, the king, as if smiling, began to describe the wondrous event.

The king said: "In this world, which is crowded with various objects, filled with lakes, rivers, cities, and mountains, and where the principal peaks and oceans meet, there is this region distinguished by its abundance of wealth."
The king said: "There is indeed this region, endowed with various forests and rivers, like a younger brother born of the same womb as this circle of the earth."
And here I am the king, conducting myself in a manner pleasing to the citizens, seated in the midst of this assembly hall like Indra in heaven.
Meanwhile, a certain conjurer arrived from afar; this magician had risen up from the subterranean realm like Maya himself.
By this, the peacock-feather whisk has been whirled here today with intense brilliance, like a streak of Indra’s bow by the clouds driven by the winds at the end of an eon.
Beholding this restless mare standing before me, I, with a bewildered mind, mounted her back alone.
Then, as the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds [shake] a mountain agitated by the dissolution of the world, so did I mount my horse and set out after that moving mountain as it shook.
I set out alone for the hunt with extreme speed, like the surge of the ocean at the time of universal dissolution rushing toward the parched earth of one who has no protector.
By that horse, flickering like the wind, I was carried far away, just as an ignorant person is led astray by a deluded mind rendered inert through the practice of yoga.
The mind, devoid of anything and empty, was as utterly desolate as the heart of a woman; thereafter, it became as terrifying as the abode of the world consumed by the fire of universal dissolution.
Having reached this vast, boundless forest, which is free from salt, frost, trees, and water, my mounts are exhausted.
It was like a second sky, or like an eighth ocean, or like a fifth sea that has completely dried up, a hollow void.
His mind was as expansive as that of a wise man, yet as impetuous with anger as that of a fool; it had never seen the company of people, nor had it ever tasted the shoots of grass.
Having reached this forest, my mind has fallen into despondency, like a wanton woman who, having encountered poverty, finds herself without food, fruit, or kinsmen.
From sunrise until sunset, that day passed for me there in exhaustion, as the faces of the quarters were submerged in the waters of the mirage of the shimmering desert sands.
That forest was traversed by me with great difficulty and exhaustion, like a person seeking solitude views cyclic existence as having the nature of a void in its midst.
Having passed through this by means of it, I have gradually reached the Jangala forest, like the sun whose horses are exhausted reaching the peak of the sunset mountain as if wandering in a void.
In those regions abounding with rose-apple and kadamba trees, birds warbling sweetly flutter about like kinsmen to travelers.
Wherein rows of young grass tips appear scattered upon the ground, like the stirrings of joy within the heart of a crooked man who has attained ill-gotten wealth.
For that [pleasure] derived from a former forest retreat brings some slight happiness; indeed, among living beings, illness is better than death, which is absolute suffering.
There I reached the base of the Jambīra grove, just as Mārkaṇḍeya did when he wandered through the single ocean to see the Lord of Mountains.
There, scorched by the heat, I grasped a creeper entwined with the mountain's body, like a dark line of clouds clinging to a mountain.
While I was hanging down from this [branch], that horse galloped away, just as a mass of evil deeds departs from a man who has clung to the Ganges.
Exhausted from a long journey, I rested there for a long time, like the sun upon the slope of the western mountain at the foot of a wish-fulfilling tree.
Just as the sun has settled in the courtyard of the western mountain, as if to rest, along with the entire burden of worldly activities of saṃsāra.
When the entire interior of the world was gradually seized by darkness, and the nocturnal activities had fully commenced throughout the forest.
I was hidden within that fragile tree-stump with its hollow interior, my face long concealed, like a bird in its own nest.
Deprived of discernment by the poison of worldly attachment, like a miser whose memory is failing, he is as wretched as one who has sold himself away, and as if submerged in a blind well.
There, a night equal to a kalpa passed for me, submerged in delusion, like that of the sage Mārkaṇḍeya while being carried away by the single vast ocean.
I did not bathe, nor did I offer worship, nor did I eat at that time; for me, who stood at the forefront of calamities, that night passed away in vain.
For him who was sleepless, lacking fortitude, and trembling along with the sprouts, that night passed away with an excessively long duration.
Then, as streaks of darkness, along with the stars, the moon, and the night-lotuses, were being cast upon my face, it became utterly withered.

And as the shrieks of the vetālas subsided in that forest of swift-moving beasts, [the scene was filled] with the clattering of rows of teeth and the whistling sounds of those afflicted by the pain of the cold.
He saw me, submerged in distress, as if laughing, appearing like the eastern quarter reddened by the drinking of honey-wine.
In an instant, like an ignorant man perceiving knowledge, or a pauper perceiving gold, I beheld the sun in the sky, intent upon mounting an elephant.
Rising up, I flung aside each layer of the bedding and the cloth, like one fond of the twilight dance using the excellent hide of an elephant.
I set out to roam that vast wilderness, which was like the hut of the world when its hosts of living beings have been consumed by the fire at the end of an aeon.
Nothing real is seen there in that withered jungle, just as not even a trace of noble quality is found in the body of a fool.
Free from all fear, though restless with their circling flight, the birds roam about, uttering their cries of "cī-cī" and "kū-cī."
Then, when the lord of the day had reached the eighth part of the sky, and the creepers—having dried up their last traces of dew—seemed as if they had bathed;
As I was wandering about, I saw a girl carrying a vessel of boiled rice, holding a fine jar of nectar like the Mādhavī creeper seized by a Dānava.
I approached her there—she whose eyes were like shimmering stars, who was dark-complexioned yet clad in white garments—just as the moon approaches the night.
"O child, give me this rice quickly in my great distress; for through the removal of the suffering of the wretched, one's fortunes attain expansion."
This great hunger within me has grown to maturity, like a black female serpent dwelling in the hollow of an old tree that has given birth.
Yet, despite my entreaties, not even this much was given to me by her, just as wealth is not given to a wrongdoer by Fortune, however much he may strive and pray for it.
Only after a long time did I, following him most closely, fall from piece to piece as he stood before me like a shadow.
She said, "Know me to be a Caṇḍālī adorned with necklaces and armlets, as exceedingly cruel as a Rākṣasī who devours men, horses, and elephants."
O King, you shall not obtain food from me merely by honoring me, just as one cannot obtain beautiful nobility from a rustic person who lacks noble intent.
When she had spoken thus, as Khelā walked along, pausing at every step, immersing herself in the groves, and bending gracefully with playful charm, she said:
"I give you this food if you will become my husband; for the world does not benefit others with wealth unless there is a common bond of affection."
"In this field, my father—a Pulkasa, grey with dust like a hungry Vetāla in a cemetery—is driving my oxen."
This food belongs to him while he remains in the state of a protector, for beloved men are to be honored even at the cost of one's own life.
Then I said to her, "O lady of virtuous vows, I shall become your husband; for in times of distress, who takes account of caste-duties or family traditions?"
Then she offered half of that rice to me, just as Mādhavī formerly offered half of the nectar to Indra when he was in great distress.
I drank the juice of jambu fruits and ate the cooked rice of the forest-dwellers; there, with my mind carried away by delusion, I rested.
Having filled me there like the sun, that dark rainy season has passed away, as if taking hold with its hand of my life-breath standing outside.
He approached his father, who was of hideous appearance, of evil intent, and inspiring fear, with a massive form like the Avīci hell of torment.
By her, who was attached to me, her own purpose was communicated to that Mātaṅga, just as a bee clinging to a flower communicates its intent through its humming sound.
"O father, let this man be my husband; may it please you. Having said "So be it" to her, when the end of the day had arrived, he—

At the end of the day, as the quarters of the sky turned tawny with frost-clouds and were covered in rising dust, we set out from that place of Vetāla-binding, released like two bound servants by the God of Death.
In a moment, at twilight, they reached a hamlet from the Dīrghajaṅgala forest, just as Vetālas emerge from one cemetery to go to another great cemetery.
There were monkeys, cocks, and crows situated in their dismembered parts; swarms of flies hovered over the portions of the earth drenched with blood.
Where birds alighted upon the network of moist entrails spread out for drying, and where the cries of birds echoed from the fragments of jambīra trees situated in the garden groves.
In the courtyard, there were heaps of dried and heavy fat, birds fluttering about, and hides smeared with blood that had spread across the ground, dripping with drops of gore.
There, flies buzzed over lumps of raw meat held in the hands of children, while infants shrieked as they were threatened by a decrepit Caṇḍāla.
Having entered that terrifying settlement, strewn with severed heads and entrails, we were like the attendants of Kṛtānta entering a world that had become as if dead at the end of an aeon.
There, in my father-in-law’s new residence, I sat upon a spacious seat made of plantain leaves, which had been prepared with great haste.
But my mother-in-law, who was squint-eyed, with her bloodshot eyes said, "This is my son-in-law," and she welcomed that [statement].
Then, having rested upon a seat of antelope skin, he consumed the food of the Caṇḍālas, which had been gathered there in abundance like his own many misdeeds.
Those words of affection, though they were not even very pleasant to hear, were seeds of endless suffering; having heard them, they were truly enough to bring misfortune.
Then, on a certain day when the sky was cloudless and the stars were visible, through various preparations and the offering of their wealth of garments, [they set out].
Although that terrifying maiden was given to me by him, she is as black as a dark complexioned man gives torment through his evil deeds.

There, the outcaste Cāṇḍālas, who had consumed great quantities of flowing liquor, roared impetuously on all sides; they were accompanied by the beating of sharp-sounding drums and were full of merriment, like the great heaps of their own evil deeds personified.
The king said: "What is the use of saying more? From that time forward, with my heart won over by the festivities, I became a well-nourished Pulkasa there."
At the conclusion of the seven-night festival, after eight months had passed in succession, she became flowered; she then remained pregnant.
She gave birth to a daughter who brought her sorrow, like a calamity that brings the pain of misfortune; that girl grew quickly, becoming stout like the swelling anxieties of a fool.
After three years, that woman of evil intellect gave birth again to an unlovely son, who was like a calamity and a binder with the noose of hope.
Again I had a daughter, then again a son; thus I became a householder, an aged Pulkasa in the forest.
Many years were spent by me there with her, like the torments of hell experienced by a slayer of a Brahmin together with remorse.
Helpless against the afflictions of cold, wind, and heat, he has long been tossed about within the forest like an old tortoise in a small pond.
With a mind consumed by anxiety for his wife, he perceived his arduous undertakings as if the very quarters of the sky were ablaze.
Wearing a tattered garment made of many worn-out pieces of linen, he carried a load of wood in the forest like personified misdeed.
Clad in a foul-smelling loincloth that was tattered, old, and damp, he spent many years breathing beneath the shade of Dhavalīka trees.
Eager to fill his household with a wife, he was worn out by the icy winds; like a frog in winter, he had dissolved away within the depths of the forest.
Driven away by the spreading heat of the surging waves of various quarrels, drops of blood have been released from the eyes under the guise of tears.
In the drenched forest, those nights—distressed by the clouds—were spent within the hollows of stone-cave huts, while they fed upon the flesh of boars.
When the growth [of the world] has reached its end in time, and when it has attained the density of dark clouds, through the lack of affection among kinsmen and by means of incessant quarrels.
With suspicion arising at every turn, my heart rendered wretched by children clamoring for their share, I have spent years in the house of another.
The face has fallen into a state of decay due to the threats of fierce outcastes agitated by quarrels with other outcaste women, like the moon by the fangs of Rāhu.
The strips of panther flesh were chewed by him with his protruding lips, like the necklaces of hell-beings purchased from those very denizens of hell.
In the cold season, the fierce winter waves, emerging from the caves of the Himalayas, remained for a long time as dense masses of frost and a heavy downpour of spray.
In the land of Aṅga, where there was no clothing, arrows were endured as if they were liberated from death; [there,] by one deluded and aged with old age, the roots of withered trees were consumed.
As if by some single person who had performed many good deeds, numerous cooked meat pastries were respectfully placed in small bowls throughout the forest.
I, who possess a wicked wife and am prone to many facial contortions, have consumed food untouched by others in order to diminish my brilliance.
Like one's own merchandise sold elsewhere for a mere trifle, that skillful man repeatedly cut away the limbs from the body of that living being.
She was sold by her iron-hearted [husband] in the forest settlements of the Vindhya mountains, as if to increase her own sins arising from thousands of previous births.
With a gaze freed from attachment even at twilight, he beheld a spade lying scattered and covered with filth upon the grounds of a Caṇḍāla’s garden.
Like one fallen into the Raurava hell who has suddenly regained a sense of warmth, he felt as if he were entering into kinship with the thickets of the Vindhya caves.
There, they were presented by means of skillful yogic methods in the form of Pulindas, and were gratified by their speed in overcoming dogs with blows from wooden clubs.
With his wife and children sustained by meager food fit for village-dwellers, he spent his nights on the dry palm leaves that rustled under the heavy downpour of rain.
I was carried away by the forest monkeys together with Raṇitadanta, while my body was covered with bristles that stood on end from the cold.
During the rains, drops of water were held [in his mouth] like pearls by him whose belly was emaciated and ravaged by hunger, for the sake of filling the hollow of a cloud-fragment.
In the forest, a tumultuous quarrel was waged with his wife, who gnashed her teeth and squinted with eyes narrowed from cold.
With his body soiled by ink, acting like a kinsman to the Vetālas, he wandered along the riverbanks holding a fishhook for the sake of fish.
In that age, for the sake of the world's total destruction, he was like Yama with his noose; through many fasts, he had drunk the blood of a recently slaughtered deer.
That blood, warm as it was at that moment, was like the milk from a mother’s breast; yet I saw those dwelling in the cremation ground—drunk with blood, crimson-hued, and feeders on filth.
The forest-demons fled like those pursued by Caṇḍikā; snares were spread in the woods for the purpose of binding deer and birds.
Just as one increases hope for the sake of growth, so have I, through worlds composed of illusion and nets of threads, bound people and birds.
The quarters of the sky have been brought to ruin by the snares of one whose life is spent through evil deeds; even there, he has granted free rein to his mind for the arising of further misdeeds.
Hope has been stretched out far away, like a surging river in the rainy season; it has fled far off from the mind, as a female camel flees from a snake.
Compassion was cast far away from his body, like a slough by a serpent; and cruelty, roaring and raining down arrows of fury, took its place with ease.
At the end of the summer heat, it was accepted [by the people] like a dark cloud by the sky; though they were blooming, wounded, and salt-scorched, they were avoided from afar by the people.
Like withered jasmine flowers in a chasm, calamities have long been borne by me within the corners of my own lineage’s time, in the vast lands of hell.
While staying in the caves of the Vindhya mountains, I mercilessly sowed handfuls of the seeds of evil deeds through showers of delusion, using snares as my means.
Like Death himself among living beings, he pounced upon the deer; and I rested my head against the wall-like necks of the yak-cows.
With her feet and garments dangling, and with smoke rising from her mouth that was darkened by intoxication, she lay there as if asleep, devoid of discernment, like Śauri upon his remaining limbs.

For a long time, my body acted as a cave in the marshy thickets of the Vindhya mountains filled with snow; meanwhile, on the shoulder of my patched garment, which was teeming with lice, my dark-complexioned body remained.
In summer, I was endured as moving beings by the boar, like a furrow; many times I was [the witness] when the circles of living beings were scorched by forest fires.

Having followed the course of Time which consumes the world with the fire at the end of an eon, my wife gave birth there to sons who were like a difficult-to-grasp affliction—like greed appearing in the guise of a disease, bringing both sufferings and joys.
Then, as the only son of the king’s son, I was led by an unceasing fault through sixty years that were equal to kalpas.

O members of the assembly, for a long duration I was afflicted there, subjected to excessive abuse, weeping in times of calamity, eating wretched food, and dwelling in ruined hamlets; I remained bound by the shackles of evil impressions.
The king said: Then, as time passed and my life became worn out by old age, I came to bear a beard like a mass of young grass covered in frost.
As the floods of days fell away—driven by the winds of karma, whether full of flavor or devoid of it—like heaps of withered leaves.
Like a torrent of arrows in battle, amidst pleasures and pains that come without ceasing, and even amidst quarrels and improper acts that arrive and fall upon one.
O twice-born one, when the mind is dull and whirled about like the ocean with its mass of waves, it remains caught in the whirlpool of conceptual construction and imagination.
When the self has mounted the wheel composed of flickering thoughts and is whirled about like a blade of grass being swept away in the whirlpooling ocean of time;
Thus, as my store of merit was exhausted here, I became a two-armed donkey—a mere insect in the forest of the Vindhya earth, for whom a mouthful of fodder was my sole refuge.
When my status as a king was forgotten, like that of a corpse despite its great speed, and my state as a Cāṇḍāla became fixed, I was like a mountain with its wings clipped.
Like the end of an eon to cyclic existence, like a forest fire to a grove, like a wave of the ocean to its shore, or like a thunderbolt to a withered tree.

Then he arrived at the marshlands of the Vindhya mountains, where food, grass, leaves, and water were utterly absent, and which was filled with a swarm of fierce outcastes who swooped down like death upon him without warning.
When the mass of clouds does not rain, having vanished as soon as seen and remaining nowhere fixed, and when the wind blows carrying with it particles of glowing embers;
In the forest glades where the leaves were withered and rustling, and which were enveloped by forest fires—desolate places that seemed as if they had long since abandoned their worldly life.
Suddenly there arose a terrifying fire of unrestrained fury, which dried up every thicket and reduced all grass and shrubs to mere ashes.
The entire region was a circle of desolation, its inhabitants all grey with dust, every man famished, and devoid of food, grass, or water.
The earth was submerged in the mirage-water of the parched desert, while the sky was filled with forests of clouds that were but masses of spray raised by the wind.
A multitude of men, their ears longing for nothing but the mere sound of water, with all their people perishing from exhaustion due to the scorching heat of the sun.
His life-force had arisen, frantic with the impulse to devour leaves; his circle of teeth rolled about in a frenzy of gnawing at his own limbs.
It swallowed a mass of fierce khadira-wood embers mistaking them for meat, and it devoured fragments of forest stone thinking them to be balls of steamed rice.
A multitude of mothers, sons, and fathers were entangled with one another as living beings; excellent female sarika birds were swallowed by vultures while screaming from within their bellies.
The surface of the earth was drenched with blood from the mutual mangled limbs of warriors, while intoxicated and hungry elephants were frantic in their desire to devour lions.
It bore the terror of lions roaming one by one through deep caverns, and the spectacle of world-wrestlers intent on devouring one another.
The wind there was filled with glowing coals that flew up from trees stripped of their leaves; the ground along the mineral-rich slopes was licked by cats eager for the drinking of blood.
The forest wind whirled amidst a mass of flames like a dense cloud, while the jungle was turned tawny by heaps of fire blazing across every spot.
The thickets were dense with smoke rising from the groves of burnt pythons, while the sky was veiled by evening clouds as flames flickered, tossed by the wind.

It was filled with the tumultuous roar of agitated ashes, its circular pillars collapsed, and it resounded with the piteous cries of children being crushed by the tips of the trunks of weeping elephants.
It was a great corpse with the teeth and skin of a multitude of bewildered men, its own fingers—both red and not red—seized by the force of the stench of flesh.
With the hue of dense yellow smoke mistaken for blue-leafed creepers, it bore the deceptive appearance of blazing torches swallowed by circling vultures wandering through the sky.
It was agitated by the fleeing of people whose limbs were mangled by one another; its heart and belly were rent asunder by the crackling sounds of blazing fires.
It was filled with the leaping of terrifying forest fires accompanied by the whistling of winds from chasms, and with trees whose limbs were falling due to the hissing of frightened pythons.
Reaching that dry hollow, which caused the surrounding region to burst open at every moment, it took on the likeness of the world being consumed by the fire of twelve suns.

With the masses of people driven forth by the spreading winds from the groves of trees whose branches were ablaze with fire, the region took on the likeness of the pleasure-houses of the Fire-god, the Sun, and the Son of the Sun (Yama).
The king said: While that painful reversal of fate was occurring, like an untimely and violent end of an aeon, it brought extreme torment.
Some people, having departed with their wives and kinsmen, went to another land from the sky like clouds in the autumn.
With their sons, wives, and foremost kinsmen clinging to the limbs of their bodies, some there were shattered on the spot like trees broken in a forest.
Some devotees were carried away by tigers from their own homes, like fledgling birds that have not yet grown their wings when they emerge from their nests and are snatched by hawks.
Some entered the blazing fire like moths; others fell into chasms like boulders fallen from a mountain.
But I, having abandoned them—my father-in-law and the others—and taking only my wife, who was capable of managing herself, have emerged from this country with great difficulty.
Having escaped from the fear of death by deceiving even the fire, the wind, the devourers, and the Takṣakas, I have emerged together with my wife.
Having reached the edge of that region, he set down his sons from his shoulders beneath a palmyra tree, like various formidable calamities.
I am at last rested, having been weary for a long time, like one who has emerged from the Raurava hell, or like a lotus without water in summer, tormented by the heat of a long-lasting forest fire.
Then, while the Caṇḍāla girl rested at the foot of the tree, sleeping in the cool shade, he embraced his two children.
"One son of mine, named Pṛcchaka, stands before us; he is our youngest, most beloved, and full of innocence."
With a distressed soul and eyes filled with tears, he said to me: "Father, give me your flesh quickly, and let me drink your blood for a moment."
Speaking thus again and again, that foolish son of mine reached a life-ending state, crying out repeatedly from hunger.
Although I told him many times, "O son, there is no meat," that evil-minded man continued to say, "Give me meat nonetheless."
Then, deluded by parental affection and overwhelmed by excessive grief, I said to him: "My son, eat my cooked flesh."
That too was accepted by him as he said "Give," for his livelihood was exhausted and he subsisted on eating my flesh.
Out of affection and compassion, moved by the desire to dispel all suffering, and seeing his distress, I, burdened by grief, [acted].
Unable to endure that intense calamity, I, with a ruined soul, made a firm resolution within myself to seek death through a most trusted friend.
There, having gathered wood, I constructed a funeral pyre; and the pyre stood there, crackling with the sounds of *caṭacaṭa*, longing for me.
But while I was still casting myself upon that funeral pyre, the king suddenly sprang up from this throne with great speed.
Then, awakened by the sound of trumpets and shouts of victory, [he thought]: "This delusion has been produced for me by this magician."
When the lord of kings, Lavaṇa, possessed of great splendor, had spoken thus—"The state of the individual soul is endowed with hundreds of conditions through ignorance alone"—[the sage replied:]
The conjurer vanished there instantly in a moment; then those members of the assembly, their eyes wide with wonder, said this:
"O King, this man is not a magician who has no desire for wealth; rather, this is some divine illusion that makes one understand the nature of worldly existence."
In that [reality] wherein it is perceived that "the world is a play of the mind," for the world of the mind is indeed the play of the omnipotent and infinite [Brahman].
For the powers of the All-Powerful Creator are indeed manifold and hundredsfold, since even this discerning mind is deluded by his illusory power (māyā).
Where is this lord of the earth, who is well-acquainted with the ways of the world; and where is this vast agitation, which is fit for the mental disposition of an ordinary person?
Nor is this illusion, which deludes the mind, the mere whim of a magician; for it is said that magicians constantly strive for the accomplishment of their purpose.
"O sirs, they strive with effort for wealth; they do not vanish from sight. Thus we remain, agitated, at this time of doubt.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, I was indeed dwelling in that assembly hall at that time; this was seen by me directly, not heard from another.

Thus, O Great-Souled One, may your expansive mind, its faculties long nourished by manifold meditations, be victorious for a long time; when the nature of the "other" has been brought to rest, you shall attain that supreme, purifying state.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In the beginning, from the supreme cause, consciousness (citi) fell into the state of the object of thought (cetya); having reached the stage of ideation (kalanā), it became the manifold diversity of parts (kalā).

O Rāma, when one is immersed in such delusions—which consist of non-existent things and function in this manner—one becomes utterly stupefied for a long time, having reached a state of dense insignificance.
The mental activity, though itself non-existent and withered, spreads suffering extensively through thousands of defects, just as a young girl conjures up ghosts.
For indeed, even great suffering is brought to non-existence in an instant by a stainless mental state, just as the light of the sun dispels darkness.
It brings what is distant into proximity and leads what is near far away; the mind of the fool leaps among beings like a young bird among fledglings.
Fear exists where there is no fear for the ignorant mind possessed of latent tendencies; to the deluded traveler from afar, even a tree stump appears as a demon.
A mind stained by suspicion suspects enmity even in a friend; a creature whose intellect is possessed by intoxication perceives the very ground as spinning.
For when the mind is agitated, lightning strikes from the moon; nectar, when consumed with the perception of poison, produces the effects of poison.
Enveloped by latent impressions, the mind perceives the construction of a celestial city as if it were real when it is unreal; for even while awake, it is indeed like a dream.
The intense latent impression (vāsanā) of the mind, which is the sole cause of a living being's delusion, must be uprooted with effort by cutting it off at its very root.
Drawn by the snare of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the deer-like mind of men falls into utter helplessness within the thicket of the forest of *saṃsāra*.
The light of that person shines forth like the sun in a cloudless sky, by whose discernment the latent impressions of the knowable have been severed from the individual soul.
Therefore, know that this man is indeed the mind alone, not the body; for the body is inert, whereas they know the mind here to be neither inert nor non-inert.
O dear Raghava, know that whatever is done by the mind is truly done; O sinless one, know likewise that whatever is renounced by the mind is truly renounced.
The entire world is mind alone; the circle of the universe has the mind as its limit. The mind is space, the mind is earth, the mind is wind, and the mind is the Great One.
If the mind did not join the object with its own nature, then these objects would never be manifest, even when the sun rises.
The mind takes up delusion, and he who possesses it is called deluded; when the body has fallen into delusion, it is not called deluded, for it is a corpse.
Behold: the mind becomes the eye when seeing, it attains the state of hearing when listening; it reaches the condition of touch through feeling, and it attains the state of smelling through smelling.
In those various activities there, the tongue attains the state of being tasted; just as in a drama, it is the mind alone that follows along within the body.
It indeed makes the short long and bestows non-existence upon what exists; it turns the sweet into bitterness and brings the enemy to the state of a friend.
Whatever manifestation belongs to this mind as it proceeds through its activity, that alone is perception; for such is the experience here in this context.
Due solely to the power of a mental appearance, a night appeared to Haricandra, whose mind was agitated by a dream, as lasting twelve years.
By the power of the influence of his mind, an entire Yuga passed as a mere moment for Indradyumna, who resided within the city of Vairiñcyapura.
Through a pleasant mental disposition, even Raurava becomes a state of bliss, like the imprisonment of one who is firmly bound but expects to obtain the kingdom in the morning.
When the mind is conquered, the entire array of the senses is also conquered; it falls apart just as a string of pearls is destroyed when the thread is burnt.
By the power of consciousness (cicchakti), which is omnipresent, of transparent nature, changeless, eternal, subtle, and acting as the witness; by that which is ever-present and equal.

By means of the reality of the self, Rāma—which pervades all existents, yet is not an object of thought and is distinct from external objects—even that which is mute, inert, and like a physical body [is transformed].
The mind wanders aimlessly within, deluded by thoughts and desires, outwardly occupied with the play of mountains, rivers, sky, oceans, and cities.
While awake, it turns a desired object into something cleansed by nectar, yet it turns even nectar itself into poison for that which is undesired.
The mind creates within objects a form that possesses its own desired aspect—an excellence of self-manifestation in which all external states have been wiped away.
In the vital breaths, the mind—which is the vibration of the power of consciousness—attains the state of air; in luminous forms, it attains luminosity; and in fluids, it attains fluidity.
On earth, the mind—which is the vibration of the power of consciousness—attains solidity; in those with the view of emptiness, it attains emptiness; and everywhere, it attains the state of desire.
Behold the power of this mind: it makes white black and leads the black to whiteness, all without regard for place or time.
When the mind is attached elsewhere, even the taste of delicious food that has been chewed by the tongue is not experienced.
That which is seen by the mind is not truly seen; that which is seen is not perceived by the eye. Just as a form in darkness, so too is the sense-faculty a mere creation.

"Give me the mind through the sense-faculty, and the sense-faculty through the mind that is beyond the mind. The sense-faculties are produced from the mind; the mind is not produced from the sense-faculties."

Those great-souled ones who have known the knowable, being highly wise, abide in their minds with the realization that there is an identity between the mind and the body, though they are absolutely distinct.
With her braided hair radiant with flowers and her eyes moving playfully, the woman, though clinging to limbs as stiff as wood or a wall, was nonetheless absent-minded.
While his mind was distracted elsewhere in the forest by one free from passion, even his own hand, held in his lap and being devoured by a carnivorous beast, was not noticed.
O Sage, the extraordinary powers of the mind can easily and swiftly turn great sufferings into happiness and turn happinesses into suffering.
Alas, when the mind is attached elsewhere, even a story being told with effort is cut short like a creeper severed by an axe.
Even for a living being who is a householder, when the mind has ascended to the mountain slopes, the suffering of the delusion that white clouds are mountain caves is experienced.
When the mind is delighted in a dream, cities and mountains appear within the heart itself, like vast lands fashioned within the wide expanse of space.
When the mind is agitated in a dream, it projects a series of mountains and cities within the heart itself, just as a surging ocean projects a multitude of waves within itself.
Just as waves, surges, and ripples arise from the water within the ocean, so do the mountains, cities, and rows of palaces in dreams arise from the mind within the body.
Just as from a sprout there arises the splendor of leaves, creepers, flowers, and fruits, so too from this mind arise the various states of waking and dreaming.
Just as a golden ornament is not separate from the gold, so too the splendor of the activities of waking and dreaming is not separate from the mind.
Just as the beauty of the stream, droplets, waves, and foam is perceived in water, so too is this manifold variety of diverse manifestations perceived in the mind.

In this world, it is only the activity of one's own mind that arises as the states of waking and dreaming; through the immersion in aesthetic flavor (rasa), it assumes various roles just like an actor on a stage.
Just as the state of being a Caṇḍāla appears in salt through the power of perception, so too this expansive world is merely the mind's mental construction.
Whatever is perceived, by that very thing one quickly becomes; the mind is the creation of its own thinking—do as you wish.
Having assumed the forms of various cities, rivers, and mountains for embodied beings, this mind—which exists only within—expands as the world consisting of waking and dreaming.
Just as Lavaṇa attained the state of a Daitya from being a god, and the state of a non-serpent from being a serpent, so too the mind attains various states through the power of its own appearances.
Just as a man quickly attains womanhood from his own volition, or reaches the state of a son from being a father, so too does the mind.
Through volition one dies, and through volition one is born again; the mind, due to long-standing habituation, attains the state of living without a physical form.
The mind, deluded by the act of thinking and pervaded by ignorant latent impressions, enters the womb of volition and so forth, [experiencing] pleasure and pain, fear and fearlessness.
Pleasure and pain reside in the mind like oil in sesame seeds; depending on place and time, they may become intense or slight.
Just as oil from sesame seeds becomes manifest through pressing, so too do pleasure and pain become solidified when the mind is attached to its own mental fabrications.
O Rāma, it is indeed intention alone that is expressed by the mention of place and time; for it is under its influence that place and time attain their existence.
When the mental construction of body and mind has borne fruit, the mind becomes tranquil, exultant, joyful, delighted, and leaping; yet it is not the physical body that does so.
With various expansive manifestations fashioned by its own volitions, the mind frolics within this body like a virtuous woman in the courtyard of the inner apartments.
Therefore, he who does not allow his inner self to flow toward fickleness brings about the dissolution of the mind, just as a tethering post restrains an elephant.
He whose mind does not waver, like a supreme pillar of steel, is a man grounded in reality; all others are but worms in the mud.
O sinless one, he whose mind, having attained steadiness, remains fixed on a single point, is followed by meditation that leads to the unsurpassed state.
Through the restraint of the mind, the delusion of saṃsāra attains peace, just as the great ocean of milk becomes still when Mount Mandara has ceased its churning.
Whatever mental fluctuations arise through the delusions of conceptualizing enjoyments, these alone are the sources of the sprouts of the poisonous tree of saṃsāra.

These fools, sluggish with pride and delusion, circling around the flickering lotus of the mind—which possesses the great speed of utter dullness—fall like wretched bees into the whirling vortex of the mind, where thoughts are shattered and scattered in their rotation.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen, I shall tell you of a great medicine for the treatment of this great disease of the mind; it is within one's own power, excellent, most pleasant, and certain.
By one's own human effort alone—swiftly, in the form of self-awareness—and through diligent exertion, the vampire of the mind is conquered by abandoning the object of desire.
He who remains free from affliction while renouncing an object of desire has truly conquered his mind, just as an elephant subdues a rogue tusk.
The infant-like mind is nurtured through the effort of self-reflexive awareness; it is directed toward the unreal and the real, and is likewise awakened.

O Sage, with a mind made steady by the study of the scriptures and the company of the virtuous, and scorched by the heat of contemplation, cut through the iron-like mind with the very sword of the mind.
Just as a child is effortlessly led here and there by various objects, so too is the mind within; what, then, is difficult in this?
One should direct the mind, through its own conscious effort, toward a noble deed that brings about a future rise in prosperity.
Fie upon that worm of a man for whom the renunciation of his own desires—which is within his own power, absolutely beneficial, and yet most difficult to achieve—has become a task too hard to perform!
Having contemplated the forest as something delightful through one's own self-awareness, the mind is conquered without effort, just as a child is subdued by a wrestler.
By human effort, the mind is quickly conquered; by the state of no-mind and without effort, the station of Brahman is attained.
Fie upon those jackals among men who are unable to accomplish that which is within their own power, easily achieved, and requiring nothing more than the mastery of their own minds!
Without the mere pacification of the mind—which is to be accomplished solely through one's own effort and consists in the relinquishing of what is desired—there is no auspicious destination.

By means of the object to be accomplished, which is the mere slaying of the mind through the self-awareness of one's own nature, let that which is without rival, without beginning or end, and immovable be proclaimed here.
But apart from the pacification of the mind through the realization of what is desired, methods such as the teacher’s instruction, the meaning of the scriptures, and mantras are like mere straw.
When the mind has been severed by the weapon of non-conceptualization and has come to rest, it then attains Brahman—entirely, omnipresent, and tranquil.
In this teaching that dispels the miseries of conceptual construction—realizable through self-awareness—what possible torment can there be for a person once their body has become tranquil?
