Surely, disregarding destiny—which is fashioned by the deluded thoughts of the mind—bring your consciousness to the state of non-mind through human effort and realization.
Having long attained that certain, singular Great State, and having made the mind devoured by consciousness, become even beyond the mind.
Endowed with the cultivation of existence and joined with the supreme intellect, remain unperturbed and sustain yourself; thereafter, restrain the mind that has been seized by external objects.
Relying on supreme human effort and leading the mind to the state of non-mind, attain that great state where no destruction exists.
O Rāma, the mind—which is like an immovable intellect whose nature consists of the inversion of perception—can be conquered quickly only through manly effort.

Freedom from agitation is the root of prosperity; from freedom from agitation proceeds the conquest of the mind by a living being, through which the victory over the three worlds becomes as a blade of grass.
In that state where there is not even the slightest trembling or falling caused by the stroke of a weapon, what kind of torment could there be when only one's own nature has been turned away?
How will those lowest of men, who are incapable even of overcoming their own sensations, conduct themselves in the affairs of worldly life?
"I am a man," "I have died," "I am born," "I live"—such are the false views; they appear as flickering fluctuations of the mind, arising from what is unreal.
No one here dies, nor is anyone born; one knows for oneself that one's own mind has died and has become another world.
From here, the mind goes to the next world, manifesting in another form; since that [mind] continues for him until liberation, whence can there be fear of death?
May he wander through this world and the next; his mind remains until liberation, for no other form exists for him.
When a brother, a servant, or another has died, suffering is experienced falsely; it is my conviction that this is one's own mind, whose nature is turned away from its own consciousness.

While the pure and expansive state of well-being remained, yet apart from the pacification of the mind, it was investigated again and again across the horizontal, the upward, and the downward directions.
Indeed, there is no means for the pacification of the mind other than when the true, pervasive, pure awakening has dawned within the heart.
Through the mere dissolution of the mind, rest arises; one expands within the space of the heart by means of the stream of the wheel of consciousness within consciousness.
Kill the mind without hesitation; then mental afflictions will not bind you, provided that what was perceived as pleasant has been understood by you in its true nature as unpleasant.
It is my conviction that those limbs have indeed been severed from the mind; "this is I," "that is mine"—the mind consists of nothing more than this.
By the mere non-contemplation of that [object], it is cut away as if by a sickle; like a mass of clouds severed in the sky, it is dispersed in autumn.
In this way, the mind is agitated by the wind alone; wherever there are weapons, fire, or wind, there fear arises.
What fear can there be for one who is relaxed, gentle, and pure, and free from conceptualization? That "this is better" or "this is not" remains unharmed and established even in a child.

One should direct the mind toward the noble and supreme good, as one would a young son, [toward] that inexhaustible and peerless lion of the mind which destroys the nourishment of cyclic existence; those who do so are victorious here, bestowing the state of nirvāṇa.
Terrible calamities, which cause agitation and begin with the crushing of one's intentions, are produced [from desire] just as mirages arise in a desert.
Let the winds at the end of the aeon blow, let the oceans become one, and let the twelve suns blaze; for one who is free from the mind, there is no harm.
From the seed of the mind arise pleasure and pain, the auspicious and the inauspicious; these are the fragments of saṃsāra, the sprouts of the seven worlds.
Abiding firmly in that state, remain in the sovereign realm of non-conceptualization, which is accomplished solely by the mere absence of thought and bestows all perfections.
The mind, as it gradually wanes, bestows supreme bliss, just as the embers of wood that has been consumed grant satisfaction to one seeking the extinction of those embers.
Even if a hundred thousand Brahma-cells are the object desired by the mind, they are clearly perceived as distinct within the space of a single atom.

Having conquered the mind—which creates great misfortune through the power of mere conceptualization and accomplishes desired ends through the power of mere conceptualization—attain victory with that ever-arisen state of mere contentment, which is free from longing.

May that unborn state which remains—attained through supreme purity, through freedom from mental agitation, through equanimity, through the realization of those who know the Self, and through the pacification and diminution of inner egoism—be attained.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Upon whatever object, by whatever means, and in whatever manner, the mind—endowed with intense momentum—beholds its desired object.
This intense agitation of the mind arises and perishes; by its very nature, it is causeless, like a series of bubbles upon calm water.
Coldness is like that of frost, blackness is like that of collyrium; restlessness is the nature of the mind, appearing in forms both intense and non-intense.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin, how can the force of this exceedingly restless mind—which has momentum as its sole cause—be forcibly restrained from its flickering?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: A mind devoid of fickleness is not seen anywhere here; fickleness is the nature of the mind, just as heat is the nature of fire.
Know that this flickering power of vibration, which resides within the essence of consciousness, is the mental power whose nature is the manifestation of the world's grand display.
Just as the very existence of wind cannot be conceived apart from its vibration and non-vibration, so too there is no existence of the mind apart from its flickering movement.
That mind which is free from flickering is said to be dead; that very state is called austerity, the established conclusion of the scriptures, and liberation.
Through the mere dissolution of the mind, the cessation of suffering is attained; through the mere mentalizing of the mind, supreme suffering is reached.
The rakshasa of the mind, having arisen, produces intense suffering; therefore, with diligent effort, cast it down for the sake of happiness and infinite enjoyment.
O Rāma, this very flickering of his is called ignorance; destroy that which is known by the name of latent impression through inquiry.
Through that ignorance, through that latent impression, and through that internal existence of the mind—once these have dissolved by virtue of renunciation—the supreme good is attained.
That which is between existence and non-existence, that which is between consciousness and insentience—O Rāma, that is called the mind, its form oscillating between the two.
For, by the force of firm practice, the mind—struck by the contemplation of dullness and kindled by its own nature as dullness—attains a state of dullness.
Through the singular pursuit of discernment, the mind, by virtue of its nature as a portion of consciousness, attains oneness with consciousness here in this world by the power of firm practice.
By means of human effort, whatever state the mind is directed toward, it indeed attains that state through practice.
Furthermore, relying on human effort and mastering the mind with the intellect, take refuge in the state free from sorrow and remain steadfast, devoid of all doubt.
O Rāma, if the mind is not withdrawn by the mind itself from its immersion in the contemplation of worldly existence, there is no other means to forcibly uplift it.
The mind alone is capable of firmly restraining the mind; O Raghava, who other than a king would be capable of restraining a king?
For those seized by the grasping of craving, being carried away by the whirlpools in the current of the ocean of saṃsāra, their own mind alone is a boat far removed from danger.
Having severed with the mind alone the noose of the mind, that supreme bond—by whom the self has not been liberated, by no one else shall he be liberated.
Whatever latent impression (vāsanā) called "mind" arises, having perfumed the interior, the wise person should abandon each and every one; from that, the destruction of ignorance occurs.

Having abandoned the latent impressions of the flood of enjoyments, abandon the latent impression of duality; then, having abandoned both existence and non-existence, become free from conceptual construction and happy.
The non-cultivation of cultivation is indeed the exhaustion of latent impressions; this alone is called the destruction of the mind and the destruction of ignorance.
Whatever is perceived as something, therein non-perception is supreme; for non-cognition is nirvāṇa, while suffering arises from cognition.
By that very effort of his own, a person experiences in an instant the non-existence of all phenomena; therefore, one should constantly practice that meditation for the sake of prosperity.

Having understood that those things such as passion which are desired by the mind are, in this world, each of them devoid of substantial reality, abandon them; then, with the seed of its sprout destroyed, remain satisfied and do not undergo joy or sorrow.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "For this latent impression (vāsanā), which has arisen as something eternally unreal, is like the delusion of seeing two moons; therefore, O Rāghava, it is proper that it be abandoned."
Ignorance exists, as it were, only among those whose wisdom is lost; since its non-existence is accepted by those of perfect wisdom through mere name alone, how could it exist in them?
Do not be ignorant; become wise and investigate thoroughly, O village-dweller! There is no second moon in the sky; it is perceived in vain through delusion.
In this, apart from reality (tattva), there exists nothing whatsoever, whether real or unreal, just as in the vast ocean garlanded with waves, there is nothing apart from the mass of water.

Apart from your own conceptual construction, do not superimpose these entities—which are neither existent nor non-existent and are like an illusion—upon the Self, which is eternal, unchanging, pervasive, and pure.
You are not the agent; why do you possess this sense of "mine" regarding these actions? For when there is only the One, what is done by whom, and how?

Or rather, O wise one, do not become a non-doer; for what is desired is achieved through non-action? That which is to be accomplished is what must be attained; therefore, O sinless one, remain established in yourself.

O scion of the Raghus, because you are unattached, you are indeed an agent regarding existence and non-existence; yet because of that very lack of attachment, you are also a non-agent—how then can there be any vibration [of agency] in you, as if you were an agent?
If it were true, it would be worthy of adoption; if it were false, it would indeed be to be abandoned. Since one is solely intent upon what is to be adopted, attachment to action is indeed logical.
Since everything there is a magical illusion, consisting of māyā and devoid of substance, what basis could there be for views regarding what is to be rejected or accepted?
O scion of Raghu, this seed-atom of the cycle of existence is ignorance; for though it is truly non-existent, it has attained expansion as if it were real.
This wheel of the onset of saṃsāra, which is full of effort yet devoid of essence, should be understood as the latent predisposition (vāsanā) that bestows delusion upon the mind.
Like a beautiful bamboo stalk, it is hollow within and pithless in its core; like a succession of river waves, though unbroken, it is perishable.
Even when grasped with the hand, it cannot be held; though soft, its tip is exceedingly sharp, like a wave rising from a mountain torrent.
It appears as a semblance of a wave, yet it is not employed for the actual object; it is established in its own form, like the appearance of a wave within a river.
Though its color is pure like a flame, its hollow is soiled with soot; yet it leaps about through the favor of another, for it is given [its light] by looking toward that [other].
Faded in pure light, it yet shines even in darkness; like a mirage that has dried away, it displays the play of various colors.
Crooked, uneven, slender, soft yet harsh in its narrowness, fickle like a woman, greedy, and full of thirst—craving is like a black female serpent.
Like the flame of a lamp itself, it quickly perishes when the oil is exhausted; like a streak of vermilion powder, it shines even without color.
Flickering with momentary flashes, assuming various forms, and dull by nature, she arises like a crooked lightning bolt, striking terror into the simple-minded.
Having been seized with effort, it burns; having come into being again and again, it dissolves. For even when sought, it is not found; as fleeting as lightning, it is exceedingly fragile.
Though delightful, a fortune that arrives unasked brings misfortune; it is not welcomed by those seeking the highest good, like a garland of flowers out of season.
Completely forgotten, this [mind], which causes delusion even for the sake of great happiness, is conceived as leading only to misfortune, like the perception of a nightmare.
By the power of her manifestation, she produces these three great worlds in a mere moment and then holds them, swallowing them up.
By her, a single moment was made into a series of years for Lavaṇa, and a night was fashioned into twelve years for Hariścandra.
By her grace, for those separated from their lovers as well as for others who possess the splendor of their beloveds, the night shall become as long as a year.
Through its power, time becomes short for one who is happy and long for one who is suffering—a time that acts as the sole arbiter for those whose nature is entirely inverted.
In these activities, its agency exists by virtue of its mere existence, just as a lamp has agency regarding the effects of its light; it is not so in reality.

Just as a woman with breasts like ripe *śālī* grain, though adorned with colorful ornaments, is not truly a woman when she has reached her menses, so too this contemplation of forms is incapable of accomplishing anything at all.
Like a kingdom of the mind, though radiant in form and possessing hundreds of thousands of branches, it is devoid of reality and amounts to nothing from the perspective of ultimate truth.
Like a mirage in the forest, it is a mere false display; it deceives only those foolish deer and not human beings.
Like a mass of foam, it arises and perishes; it is devoid of continuity, inert yet flickering in form, and when scrutinized, it is nothing at all.
Moving with a terrifying form, grey with the spreading dust of the world, she forcibly traverses the interior of the universe like the whirlwind at the end of an aeon.
Like a column of smoke clinging to the body, causing the distress of burning, it pervades the worlds, having internalized the sequence of aesthetic flavors.
Like a very long stream of water produced from a cloud, this firm rope of unsubstantial saṃsāra is made of grass-like strands.
Like a garland of water-lilies upon a wave, it is described as mere imagination; like a lotus stalk with many holes, it is matured in mud and consists of water.
People see her intent on growth, yet she does not truly increase; like the taste of poison, sweet at first encounter but extremely terrible in the end.
Like the flame of a lamp that has gone out, I know not where it goes; like a mist seen at close range, though grasped, it is nothing at all.
Like a handful of dust scattered away, it is seen as consisting of ultimate atoms; this [world] is perceived as being merely the blueness of space, utterly devoid of causal characteristics.
Born from the delusion of seeing two moons, this confusion is produced like a dream; just as a stationary post appears to move to one traveling by boat, so too has it arisen here.
When the mind is afflicted by this, people who are as if agitated for a long time imagine the delusion of the dream of saṃsāra to be long-lasting.
When one's own mind is afflicted by this [ignorance], various delusions arise and perish, like waves in the ocean.
That which is pleasing and true is seen as both existent and non-existent; that which is unpleasant and untrue is seen as existent even while being non-existent.
Mounted upon the chariot of objective entities, this powerful mental construction swiftly assails the mind, just as a snare catches a bird.
With eyes overflowing with compassion and breasts dripping with streams of milk, she becomes a mother whose joy is radiant, just like a housewife.
The orb of the moon, though already exceedingly moist with nectar, quickly turns into poison, its outflow satisfying the three worlds.
Even the silent trunks of trees, through this blinding darkness, bestow a frantic agitation caused by the commencement of the dancing of Vetālas shrieking like madmen.
And at times such as twilight, even clods of earth, stones, and walls appear to those with the vision of serpents and pythons through her grace.
Even a single thing arises as a pair, just as when two moons are seen; it moves from distance to proximity, just as one's own death appears in a dream.
Just as a desired night seems long at first, time attains the state of a moment; yet to those separated from their beloveds, a single moment appears like a year.
There is nothing here that this arrogant woman will not do; O Raghava, behold the power of her who possesses nothing at all.
One should diligently restrain consciousness itself by means of consciousness; by blocking the flow of a river, this river of the mind dries up.
Śrī Rāma said: By this very non-existent, fragile-bodied, and utterly trivial thing called false imagination, the world has been wonderfully blinded.
By means of formlessness, by being devoid of a beautiful consciousness, and by being both non-existent and indestructible—how strange that the world has been rendered blind!
By the light that perishes while flickering amidst the darkness—possessing the nature of an owl's eye—the world has been wonderfully blinded.
It is strange that the world has been made blind by her who performs only evil deeds, who cannot endure even being looked upon, and who is unaware of her own body.
The world has been wonderfully blinded by her who possesses the nature of most wretched conduct, who is eternally beloved by the vulgar, and who never ceases to set.
Where the world has been rendered blind—by this [ignorance] which is always as if dead, agitated by endless suffering, and devoid of perfect awakening; how truly strange!
Strange indeed, the world has been blinded in no time by that bodiless [darkness], whose body is dense with passion and anger, and which moves crookedly through the spreading of gloom.
By means of this insentient [nature], which has its own form as its locus, which is worn out by dullness, and which utters long lamentations of suffering, the world has been wondrously blinded.
By this passionate activity, which clings to attachment for men and rushes headlong toward desires, man is wondrously rendered blind.
It is a marvel that a man is blinded by a woman who is a mere veil—she who is not even capable of enduring his gaze.
A man is wonderfully blinded by that harsh woman who possesses no consciousness at all, yet perishes even while she herself has not perished.

O Lord, by what means does this incomparable latent impression (vāsanā), which produces endless and difficult-to-restrain diversions, which partakes in pleasure and pain tending toward decay and rise, and which is bound within the dwelling of the cave of the mind, ever dissolve away?
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, how indeed is this dense and great blindness of a person, which arises from the expansion of ignorance, destroyed?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as a drop of frost perishes in an instant from the sight of the sun, so too, O Rāghava, does this ignorance vanish through the vision of the Self.
Meanwhile, it causes the embodied being, together with its own self, to oscillate within the abysses of saṃsāra, which abound with the dense thorns of suffering.
As long as ignorance has not been destroyed by that which brings about its exhaustion, there remains within oneself the desire to perceive the Self, which bestows the destruction of delusion.
O Rāghava, for her who perceives this [world] as supreme, her own destruction is brought about, just like that of a shadow seeking to experience sunlight.
When all-pervading awakening is seen, it dissolves of its own accord, just as the shadow of all desires vanishes when the twelve suns have risen.
In this world, ignorance is merely desire; its destruction is called liberation. And that, O Raghava, is accomplished simply by the absence of volitional thought.
When the night of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) in the sky of the mind comes to an end even slightly, the darkness diminishes due to the great rising of the sun of consciousness (*cid-āditya*).
Just as the night vanishes somewhere when the sun has risen, so too does ignorance dissolve somewhere when discernment has arisen.
Through firm latent impressions, the bondage of the mind attains density, just as a child's conceptualization of a ghost arises forcibly at twilight.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahman, whatever is seen here is ignorance, and that ignorance is destroyed by the contemplation of the Self. Of what nature, then, is that Self said to be?"

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That essence of consciousness which is free from the pursuit of objects of thought, which is universal and all-pervading, and which is inexpressible—that is the Self, the Supreme Lord.
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, whatever this world is, all that is at all times only the Self; O sinless one, ignorance does not exist.
Indeed, all this is Brahman—eternal, a mass of consciousness, and indestructible; no other conceptualization exists apart from that which is called "mind."
Nothing whatsoever is born or dies here in the three worlds; nor does the existence of the modifications of being ever exist anywhere.
Only the absolute, appearing as the absolute, the all-encompassing generality that is undiminished, pure consciousness alone exists here, free from the pursuit of objects of thought.

In that which is eternal, pervasive, pure, consisting of consciousness alone, free from affliction, tranquil, characterized by an even distribution of experience, and whose self has arisen as changeless;
That which, having itself conceptualized what transcends its own nature, runs toward it—the consciousness that withers by itself along with its objects—is known as the "withered mind."
From this all-pervading deity, the great-souled one who possesses all power, the capacity for differentiation has arisen like a wave from water.
In that one, vast, and peaceful [reality] where nothing whatsoever exists, she has attained perfection within the Supreme Self through mere volition.
Therefore, this [state] accomplished by mental resolve is destroyed by resolve alone—by that very same thing through which it was born, just as a flame of fire is extinguished by the wind.
The hope for enjoyment, having taken form through success achieved by human effort, dissolves by mere non-mentation; that is ignorance.
The mind is bound by the firm conviction that "I am not Brahman"; the mind is liberated by the firm conviction that "all is Brahman."
Volition is the supreme bondage; non-volition is liberation. Having conquered volition within, do as you wish.
There is no firm lotus pond here in the sky with golden lotuses, bees hovering over vaidūrya stones, and fragrant quarters of the sky.
With her circles of lotus-stalk arms, their stalks erect and their fullness manifest, she seemed to laugh at the orb of the radiant moon’s rays.
In this way, the net of conceptual construction, though non-existent, appears as if it were real; it is imagined by the childish mind for the sake of the play of its own objects.
In the same way, this ignorance here binds one to the fetters of existence; though flickering and not leading to happiness, it is grasped as firm by the fool.
"I am emaciated," "I am in extreme suffering," "I am bound," or "I possess hands, feet, and so forth"—one is bound by such worldly discourse that conforms to these mental conceptions.
"I am not suffering, nor do I have a body; for what self could bondage exist?"—by such conduct in accordance with this realization, one is liberated.
"I am neither flesh nor bones; for I am other than the body, the Supreme"—one who possesses such certainty within is said here to be one whose ignorance has been destroyed.
Or perhaps it is the splendor of darkness standing above, possessing the luster of the vaidūrya peaks on the summit of the lofty divine mountain, yet difficult to pierce even by the rays of the sun.
For just as blackness is imagined in the sky by a person standing on the earth through the impetus of their own conceptualization, so too is it conceived by nature.
Thus, O Rāghava, this ignorance is merely imagined as the conception of a self in that which is not the self; it belongs to the unawakened person, not to the awakened one.
Śrī Rāma said: "This is neither the shadow of the sapphire of Mount Meru nor the radiance of darkness; O Brahman, tell me, what is the cause of this blueness of the sky?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Indeed, blueness does not exist as a quality of the empty sky; nor is this [blueness] derived from the radiance of other jewels, nor is it the light of Mount Meru.
Because the cosmic egg consists of light, like the expansion of fire itself, and because its outer limit is luminous, there is no possibility of darkness existing within it.
O fortunate one, this emptiness alone appears manifold; it is like a fitting companion to ignorance, being composed of non-existence.
When there is the perfection of the destruction of one's own vision, darkness arises precisely in the eyes; because of the nature of things, that is perceived as the blackness of the sky.
Having understood this, just as the blackness perceived in the sky does not give rise to the cognition "this is blackness," so too it is with the cataract of ignorance.
For the wise have declared that the absence of mental construction is the suppression of ignorance; yet it appears as easy to accomplish as the blooming of a lotus in the sky.
O holy one, for this worldly delusion that has arisen like the color of the sky, I consider its non-recollection to be better than its remembrance; indeed, forgetting it is preferable.
Just as one perishes through the thought "I am lost" out of suffering, so indeed does a person attain happiness through the thought "I am awakened."
Thus, through intentions clouded by delusion, the mind indeed falls into a state of folly; but through intentions broadened by awakening, it pursues awakening.
For this eternal ignorance arises from a momentary recollection, whereas that which is perishable perishes within through forgetfulness.
She is the creator of all states of being, the deluder of all living beings; she is the bearer when her own self is destroyed, and the destroyer for the increase of her own self.
Whatever the mind intends to connect with, all the functions of the senses accomplish that in an instant, just as ministers carry out the command of a king.
Therefore, he who does not direct his mind toward phenomena through internal conscious effort attains peace.
That which did not exist in the beginning does not exist even today; that which appears here is Brahman—peaceful, one, and beyond reproach.
Therefore, there is nothing else to be contemplated—never, for anyone, in any way, or from any source. Remain without constraint in that which is changeless, without beginning or end.
Relying upon supreme human effort and with the highest intelligence, one should diligently uproot from the mind the cultivation of hope for enjoyments, together with its very roots.
That supreme delusion which arises as the cause of old age and death—that is the manifestation of latent tendencies (vāsanā) flourishing through hundreds of snares of hope.
"My sons, my wealth, this is I, this is mine"—it is this very latent impression alone that leaps forth like a magical illusion.
In this very empty body, which is as flickering as wind upon water, the serpent of egoism has been placed by a non-dual latent impression (*vāsanā*).

O Knower of Reality, from the perspective of the ultimate truth, notions such as "I," "mine," and "this" are quite enough; apart from the true nature of the self, which is like a series of rivers, nothing whatsoever is ever real.

Through the repeated creation of vision, this very ignorance—variegated and appearing as something else—continually revolves, manifesting as mountains, oceans, the earth, rivers, and rows of directions.
It arises through mere ignorance and perishes through mere knowledge; it is to be eliminated within pure Being, just as the notion of a snake is [eliminated] in a rope.

O Rāghava, this ignorance which exists for the ignorant is like the earth, the oceans, the mountains, and the rivers; but for the knower, there is no such ignorance, for that Brahman remains established in its own majesty.
The two conceptualizations of the rope and the snake are both constructed by the eye alone; however, by the knower, only the single, uncreated vision of Brahman is determined.
Do not be ignorant; be wise. Abandon the latent tendencies of saṃsāra. Why do you weep like an ignorant person by perceiving a self in that which is not-self?
O Rāghava, what is this dull and mute body of yours? For its sake, you are helplessly overwhelmed by pleasure and pain.
Just as there is no identity between wood and lacquer, or between a jujube fruit and its bowl, even though they are joined together, so it is with the body and the embodied self.
Just as when a bellows is burned, the fire does not belong to the air within it, so too, upon the destruction of the body, the self is not destroyed.
"O scion of the Raghus, the notions 'I am suffering' and 'I am rich in happiness' are delusions resembling a mirage; having understood this, abandon them and take refuge in the Truth."
Oh, how strange it is that the true Brahman has been forgotten by men, while that which is untrue, called ignorance, has surely entered their memory!
O scion of the Raghus, do not grant scope for ignorance; when the mind is obscured by this, there is suffering here that is difficult to overcome.
This [mind] is indeed false, causing harm, swollen with the mental brooding of the mind, bestowing suffering, and resulting ultimately in great delusion.
Even though the lunar orb is moist with nectar, by imagining it to be Raurava, one experiences the hellish suffering of burning and desiccation.
In lakes where the waves, lilies, spray, and ripples abound, the state of being filled with a mirage is perceived by the wind.
In dreams and other such states, one experiences various agitations caused by the creation, falling, and rising of celestial cities, which bestow both pleasure and pain.
If the latent impressions of saṃsāra do not indeed fill the mind, how could the frenzies of waking and dreaming lead one to calamity in this world?
The Raurava, Avīci, and other hells that inflict suffering are seen when false knowledge has increased within the dream-like realms of the forest.
Pierced by this [wisdom], the mind instantly perceives even within the thread of a lotus fiber the delusive misfortunes of the entire ocean of saṃsāra.
For when the mind is thus afflicted, even those established in sovereignty become such people as do not deserve to be treated by dog-cookers.
Therefore, O Rāma, having abandoned the latent impressions that bind one to existence and consist of all forms of passion, remain free from passion like a crystal.
While you remain engaged in your duties, let there be no attachment to passions, just as a crystal takes on various reflections without being stained by them.

If you always act with excellent conduct, having understood the assembly's curiosity and being perfected by it, and if you have abandoned vulgar actions through your noble intellect, then with whom can you be compared? For you are beyond comparison.
Śrī Vālmīki said: Having been thus addressed by the venerable and high-souled Vasiṣṭha, Rāma, whose eyes were like lotus petals, shone as if awakened.
With his inner heart blossomed, he attained a pure splendor, like a lotus refreshed when the darkness has faded at the sight of the sun.
With his face brightened by a gentle smile born of wonder at this awakening, he spoke these words, which were washed with the nectar of the light from his teeth:
Śrī Rāma said: Oh, how wonderful! Mountains are bound by threads produced from lotuses; indeed, all things are brought under control by that knowledge which is non-existent.
This very world, though consisting of mere straw, has attained the state of a vajra within the three realms; for even through ignorance, that which is non-existent appears as if it were existent.
Out of compassion, tell me once more the nature of this river of the illusion of saṃsāra within the courtyard of the three worlds, for the sake of my awakening.
O Great-souled One, there is another doubt that dwells within my heart: what kind of calamity did that illustrious Lavana encounter?
When the body and the embodied soul are either joined together or struck [by one another], O Brahman, who among them is the transmigrating being that alone experiences the fruits of good and evil?
Having thus brought about that unsurpassed calamity for Lavaṇa, where has he gone with his fickle undertakings, and who is this magician?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O sinless one, this body is like wood or a wall; it is nothing at all here, for it is merely imagined by this mind, like the world seen in a dream.
One should know that the mind, which has entered living beings and is adorned by the power of consciousness, is as restless as a young monkey and is the very impulse of saṃsāra.
For the embodied being, subject to the fruits of karma, assumes various forms of bodies; it is conceptualized by the names of ego, mind, and life-force.
O Raghava, for one who is thus unawakened—and not awakened—these endless pleasures and pains exist; they do not belong to the body at all.
The unawakened mind, constructing conceptualizations based on various perceptions, follows diverse mental fluctuations and assumes a manifold form.
As long as the mind is unawakened and remains asleep, it perceives delusion in a dream; once awakened, it never does so again.
As long as the living being, agitated by the sleep of ignorance, has not been awakened, so long does it perceive the delusive onset of saṃsāra, which is difficult to penetrate.
All darkness dissolves from the fully awakened mind, just as the interior of a lotus opens at the light of day.
That which is designated by the self-realized as mind, ignorance, mental life, and latent impression, and which is called the "doer of karma"—that embodied being is skilled only in suffering.

The body is inert and not deserving of suffering; it is the embodied self that suffers due to a lack of inquiry. This lack of inquiry arises from dense ignorance, and ignorance is the cause of suffering.
The living soul has become an object of both auspicious and inauspicious phenomena due solely to the fault of lack of discernment, just as a silkworm is enclosed within its cocoon.
Bound by the nature of non-discrimination, the mind, possessing manifold fluctuations, wanders like a wheel through various forms of existence.
It rises, it cries out, it kills, it eats, it moves, it leaps, and it reviles; it is the mind alone within this body, never the body itself.
Just as a householder performs various activities within his home, yet the house itself is insentient, O Rāma, so indeed is the living soul within the body.
In all pleasures and pains, and in all mental constructions, know that the mind is the agent, the mind is the enjoyer, and the mind is the human being.
In this regard, listen as I relate to you this supreme account of how that Lavaṇa fell into the state of a Caṇḍāla due to a delusion of the mind.
The mind experiences the fruit of its actions, whether auspicious or indeed inauspicious; O Raghava, listen now as I explain this exactly as you understand it.
O sinless one, in former times, Lavaṇa, born of the lineage of Hariścandra, sat down alone and reflected deeply in his mind for a long time.
My grandfather was a great officiating priest of the Rājasūya sacrifice; born into his lineage, I mentally perform that very sacrifice.
Having reflected thus in his mind and having prepared the necessary materials with reverence, the lord of the earth entered into the initiation for the Rājasūya sacrifice.
He summoned the officiating priests and honored the virtuous sages; he invited the gods and kindled the sacrificial fire.
According to the desire of the sacrificer, more than a full year passed within the garden while he honored the celestial rishis and the twice-born brahmins with his mind.
Having given away his entire possessions as a sacrificial fee to the beings, foremost among whom were the twice-born, the king awoke at the end of the day in his own grove.
Thus King Lavaṇa attained the Rājasūya sacrifice; indeed, he was endowed with its fruit through his mind alone, for it was accomplished by his contentment.
Therefore, know that the mind is the man who experiences pleasure and pain; O Raghava, apply that mind to the truth, which is the means for purification.
When the body is complete, the person is fully complete; when it is destroyed, he perishes. O wise ones, enough with those who hold the conviction, "I am the body."

When the mind, possessed of lofty discernment, is fully awakened, the sufferings of one whose intellect has become detached are utterly dissolved; for when the cluster of lotuses is revealed by the rays of the sun, the dullness and darkness born of their contraction are surely destroyed forever.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Lord, it is said that Lavaṇa obtained the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice; what indeed can be the proof in this matter, which is like a deceptive net of imagination?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the magician arrived at the assembly hall of Lāvaṇī at that time, I was dwelling there and witnessed it with my own eyes.
Then, when that sorcery of Śambara had come to an end, I was questioned with effort by the members of the assembly and by Lavaṇa, who asked, "What is this?"
Having reflected and seen it there, I have spoken of it; listen, O Rāma, as I shall explain to you that which was intended by the practitioner of sorcery (śāmbarika).
Indeed, those who perform the Rājasūya sacrifice undergo for twelve years the suffering of calamity, consisting of various forms of pain and disease.
Therefore, O Rāma, that divine messenger, appearing in the form of a juggler, was sent by Śakra from the sky for the purpose of causing distress to Lavaṇa.
Having bestowed the supreme station upon that performer of the Rājasūya sacrifice, he departed by way of the sky, which is frequented by gods and siddhas.

Therefore, O Rāma, this is indeed directly perceived; there is no doubt in this matter. For the mind alone is the agent and the enjoyer of diverse activities. By rubbing and purifying that very jewel of the mind—bringing it to dissolution through discernment like a frostflake by the heat of the sun—you shall attain the supreme good. Know that the mind itself is ignorance (*avidyā*), which creates the grand display of all beings. Under the influence of its various magical illusions (*indrajāla*), it brings this world into being. There is no difference between the words "ignorance," "mind," "living being" (*jīva*), and "intellect" (*buddhi*), just as there is none between the words "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) and "plant" (*taru*). Knowing this, perform only the mental construction of the mind itself. When the solar orb of the mind’s stainlessness has risen, O Rāghava, there is no darkness of defects arising from stained conceptualizations that is not dispelled; there is nothing that is not seen, nothing that is not made one's own, nothing that is not abandoned, nothing that does not die, nothing that is not one's own, and nothing that belongs to another—everything becomes everything at all times. This is the ultimate truth.
In the same way, the entire mass of objective existents and consciousness itself become a single unified whole, like a collection of various unbaked clay vessels placed together in water.

Śrī Rāma said: "O Great-Souled One, you have stated that by the complete dissolution of the mind, the end of all pleasure and pain is attained; how, then, does the non-existence of this mind—which is characterized by a flickering nature—come about?"

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O moon of the Raghu dynasty, listen to the method for the pacification of the mind, by knowing which you will attain a state of mental composure that stands far beyond your own habitual conduct.
For here, indeed, it has been previously stated that the threefold origin of all beings proceeds from Brahman.

In this regard, by means of that very first mental construction, [the Self], assuming the form of Brahman and consisting of volition, thinks "let there be a body"; whatever it thus conceives, that very thing it perceives, and by that, this grand display of the worlds is fashioned.

There, fashioning the cycle of transmigration consisting of birth, death, pleasure, pain, delusion, and so forth, this mental construction—having remained for a long time through the power of conceptualization—dissolves of its own accord, like a drop of frost when it encounters sunlight.

Arising according to its own momentum, it is born again through the power of volition in another form; that too dissolves again, and that very same thing arises once more—thus, wandering on repeatedly, it subsides of its own accord.

In this manner, infinite millions of Brahmās have passed away in this world-egg and in others, and there are others yet to come; furthermore, there are other infinite ones whose very number does not exist. In this manner, infinite millions of Brahmās have passed away in this world-egg and in others, and there are others yet to come; furthermore, there are other infinite ones whose very number does not exist.
While this state of affairs is thus occurring, listen to how the individual soul (jīva), having come from the Lord (Īśvara), lives and is liberated.
The mental power of Brahmā, having arisen and taking hold of the spatial power situated before it, follows the state of the wind located therein and attains a state of dense consolidation.

Then, having attained the state of the five subtle elements (tanmātras) that have reached the forefront, and having been led to the state of the internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa), she becomes the subtle primordial nature (prakṛti) characterized by sattva; through the volition of assuming the forms of ether, air, and fire, she takes on the form of frost, enters into rice and medicinal herbs, and attains the state of being the embryo of living beings.
From that it is born; from that the person is produced.
From the very moment of birth, that person must undertake the acquisition of knowledge from childhood onward and attend upon his teachers.
Then, gradually, a sense of wonder arises within the person themselves.
Through the vision of one's own clarity, there arises in the person—in whom the mental fluctuations have subsided—the discernment of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted.

When a person endowed with such discernment and free from accumulated egoism abides in the birth of the fire consisting of pure *sattva*, the sevenfold stage of yoga—which brings about the illumination of the mind—surely descends gradually for the sake of auspiciousness.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, what are the stages of yoga that bestow the seven perfections? Tell me this in brief, O best among those who know all principles.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The ground of ignorance consists of seven steps, and the ground of the knower likewise consists of seven steps; yet, there are innumerable other intermediate steps between these two.
Because they possess the essence of accomplishing their own efforts and are elevated by the weight of great being, these [virtues] take root at every step and bear fruit through their fruition.
In this regard, listen to the sevenfold ground of ignorance; thereafter, you shall hear of the sevenfold ground of knowledge.
Liberation is abiding in one's own true nature; its loss is the experience of "I-ness. This has been declared in brief as the defining characteristic of knowledge and ignorance of that [reality].

For those who do not deviate from the essential nature of pure consciousness, which is mere existence, there is no possibility of ignorance, because of the absence of the arising of attachment and aversion.
That the conscious principle sinks into the object of thought due to the loss of its own true nature—there has never been, nor will there ever be, another delusion greater than this.
When the mind moves from one object to another, that state which exists in between—devoid of mental construction—is called abiding in one's own true nature.

That state which is like the interior of a stone, in which all volitions have been completely stilled, yet which is free from the numbness of insentient sleep—that is known as abiding in one's own true nature.
When the portion of egoity is destroyed and stilled, and when duality has reached a state of motionlessness, that which shines forth as non-inert is established as the true nature of reality.
In that regard, listen to these stages of ignorance which have been superimposed: the seed-waking, the waking, and likewise the great-waking.
"Waking-dream," "dream-as-waking," "waking-in-dream," and "deep sleep"—thus delusion is sevenfold, each arising again from the others.
When conjoined, it possesses many names; hear now its definition: that which is the consciousness of the pure *cit* at the first stage is called "the Nameless."

That which exists as the seed-form, serving as the vessel for the meanings of words such as "future," "mind," and "living being," and which is awake [to its own nature], is called "waking within the seed" (bījajāgrat).
This is the ninth state of cognition; now hear from me about the waking cycle of one newly born, wherein there arises the notion: "this is another," "this is I," and "this is mine."
Thus, that cognition which is established in its own nature arises from the prior absence of waking; it is born in another birth as the notions "this is I," "that is he," and "this is mine."
A dense cognition, manifesting as the "great waking state," is thus described; whether it be unestablished or established, it is in every respect of the nature of that [reality].
That mental kingdom which belongs to one who is awake is called "waking-dream" (*jāgratsvapna*), categorized by such instances as the double moon, silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, and the mirage.
Through repeated practice, having attained the state of waking, a dream may become manifold; one thinks, "I have seen this for only a short time," and likewise, "this is not real."
Indeed, that cognition which occurs at the end of sleep regarding an object experienced during the time of sleep is called a dream; its great waking state resides within the heart.
Due to the absence of being seen for a long time, its great body remained unexpanded; yet, having become established as a waking state within a dream, it reached the stage of the Great Waking.
Whether the body is wounded or unwounded, that is indeed considered the state of dreaming or waking; it is the inert condition of the living being when the six states have been abandoned.
The state of deep sleep is said to be a condition rich in the awakening to future suffering; in that state, grass, clods of earth, stones, and so forth [are perceived as such].
O Rāghava, all objects exist as having the dimension of atoms; these seven states have been described by me as belonging to ignorance.
Each single branch here has a hundred sub-branches, appearing in various forms of manifestation; that which was long established as waking and dreaming eventually returns to the state of pure waking.
Through the differentiation of various objects, it expands and unfolds; even within its belly exist the perceptions of the great waking state.
In the midst of these as well, a person, through delusion, would go from one delusion to another; like a boat caught in a whirlpool within the water, it rushes into confusion.
Some cycles of existence remain as if waking from a long dream; others, moreover, are like waking within a dream, while still others are like dreams within a waking state.

I have described the stage of ignorance as consisting of seven steps, devoid of internal distinctions within the world of manifold transformations; you shall cross beyond it through beautiful investigations, once the stainless self has been perceived by itself through awakening.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O sinless one, listen to this sevenfold ground of knowledge; once this is understood, you shall never again sink into the mire of delusion.
Proponents of the stages of yoga speak in many different ways; however, these very [stages] are surely what I favor, as they bestow auspiciousness.
They know that awakening is gnosis (*jñāna*), and this consists of seven stages; liberation, it is said, is to be known as that which transcends the seven stages.
The realization of truth and liberation are indeed synonyms. This living being, upon the realization of truth, does not sprout again in this world.
The first stage of knowledge is proclaimed as that called "virtuous aspiration" (śubhecchā); the second is "investigation" (vicāraṇā), and the third is "thinning of the mind" (tanumānasā).

The fourth is the attainment of being (sattvāpatti); after that is the one named non-attachment (asaṃsakti). The sixth is the non-contemplation of objects (padārthābhāvanī), and the seventh is remembered as the state beyond the fourth (turyagā).
Liberation stands at the end of these; once it is attained, one no longer grieves. Now hear this definition of these stages.

"Am I truly a fool, standing here? I shall examine [the truth] through the scriptures and the company of the virtuous. Desiring this with dispassion as the primary motive is called *śubhecchā* (the desire for the auspicious) by the wise.
That engagement in virtuous conduct which is preceded by the study of the scriptures, association with the wise, and the practice of detachment is called *vicāraṇā*.
The absence of attachment to the objects of the senses through both investigation and virtuous desire—this state, arising from the attenuation of worldly existence, is here called *tanumānasā*.
Through the practice of the three stages, by virtue of detachment from objects in the mind, one's abiding in the pure Self is declared to be the attainment of *sattva*.
Through the practice of the four stages and by means of the fruit of non-attachment, and due to the blossoming wonder of established sattva, this state is called "Non-attachment."
Through the firm practice of the five stages, by delighting in one's own self, and by the non-contemplation of internal and external objects;
Through long-continued effort applied by another, because of the cultivation of the meaning, the sixth stage arises, which is named "cultivation of the non-existence of things."
Through the beautiful practice of the six stages, because no differentiation is perceived, that state of abiding solely in one's own true nature is to be known as the fourth state (turyagā).
For this fourth state (turya) exists here among those liberated while living; beyond that, the object of liberation after death (videhamukti) is the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta).
For those highly fortunate ones, O Rāma, who have reached the seventh stage—those great-souled ones who delight in the Self—have attained the supreme state.
Those liberated while living do not cling to the states of pleasure or pain; they may perform their necessary duties through natural inclination, or they may not.

Once awakened by those standing at their side, the virtuous indeed practice the conduct that has come down through the sequence of all traditions, remaining unimpaired like one who is perfectly enlightened.
Because they delight in the self, no worldly activities bring them any pleasure, just as the sight of forms brings no joy to women who are fast asleep.
And these seven stages are the domain of the wise alone; they are not for animals, stationary beings, and the like, nor for the minds of barbarians and such.
Even those such as animals and barbarians who have attained this state of knowledge—whether they possess a body or are bodiless—are liberated; of this there is no doubt.
For *jñapti* is the severing of the knot; when that occurs, there is liberation. It consists of the mere nature of tranquility, like the cognition of water in a mirage and so forth.
But those who have crossed over delusion yet have not reached the purifying state, remain established in these stages, intent upon the attainment of their own true self.
Some pertain to all stages; some pertain to two, three, or one stage; some pertain to six stages; and some pertain to seven stages.
Some have reached three stages, some have reached the final stage; some have traversed four stages, while others abide in two stages.
Some are vessels for a portion of the earth; some consist of three and a half stages; some consist of four and a half stages; and others consist of six and a half stages.
Discerning men move through the worlds upon these stages, established in the specific states of vision belonging to the asceticism of the sense-spheres.
For those wise and excellent kings who conquer in these ten ways consider here the defeat of armies of elephants from the quarters to be as insignificant as a blade of grass.

Those great ones who indeed conquer those stages are truly worthy of worship, for they have vanquished the enemy of the senses; since even the status of a universal monarch (samrāj) or a sovereign ruler (virāj) is to them as a mere blade of grass, they attain that which is supreme in the world.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as a ring of gold, having forgotten its nature as gold due to its perception as a ring, cries out, "I am not gold," so too does the Self [suffer] through this sense of "I-ness."
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, how does the emergence of the consciousness of a ring occur from gold? And how does egoism arise from the Self? O Lord, explain this to me exactly as it is.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O wise one, the coming and going of that which exists alone can be questioned, not that of the non-existent; for "I-ness," "you-ness," and the state of being a wave never exist as realities at any time.
If you are told, "Take gold and a ring," then whatever is given along with the ring exists [therein], of this there is no doubt.
Śrī Rāma said: "If it is so, O Lord, what would that be? And what is the nature of being a ring? By determining the meaning through this very inquiry, I shall know the body of Brahman."

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, if the formless nature of the non-existent were to be described as having form, then you might as well describe the physical features and qualities of the son of a barren woman.
The state of being a ring is a vain delusion; this is a mere illusion whose true nature is reality. Its very form is such that it is not seen when scrutinized.
In the water of a mirage, in the double moon, in the killer, in forms, and so forth—the only nature of these is that which, when scrutinized, is not found.
He who perceives the form of silver in mother-of-pearl never obtains even a minute particle of silver anywhere, not for even a single moment.
Without even being scrutinized, the real appears as if unreal, just as the nature of silver appears in mother-of-pearl, or water in the mirages of the desert.
The non-existence of that which does not exist appears when it is investigated; yet when not investigated, it manifests like an ocean of water in a mirage.

That which is non-existent indeed acts as a cause for an effect that appears to exist, and it remains stable; yet this delusive confusion, like the misconception of a Vetāla, leads only to the death of the foolish.
Excluding the single state of being gold, nothing else exists in gold, just as there is no such thing as being a ring or a bracelet in sand mixed with oil and other substances.
Herein there is neither truth nor falsehood; whatever appears in whatever manner, that acts as a causal efficiency in that very way, like the transformation caused by a yakṣa in a child's mind.
Whether it be true or even false, that which is firmly rooted in the heart performs its respective purposeful action, just as poison may perform the action of nectar.
This alone is the supreme knowledge: that this transmigratory existence is indeed an illusion, consisting of the cultivation of a sense of "I-ness" which is unreal and without foundation.

O King, the state of being a knower and so forth does not exist in the Self; nor does the sense of "I" (ahaṃtā) exist there. This reality, which is the absence of "I-ness," resides in that which is pure, tranquil, white, and supreme.
There is no such thing as eternity, nor is there anything belonging to Viriñci; there is no such thing as being the cosmic egg, nor is there anything such as being a son or the like.

There is no such thing as being another world, nor is there anywhere such a thing as heaven and so forth; there is no state of being Mount Meru, no state of being an asura, no state of being the mind, and no state of being the body.
There is no such thing as the nature of the great elements, nor is there any causality anywhere; there is no reckoning of the three times, nor is there the reality of existence or non-existence.

There is no such thing as "thou-ness," "I-ness," "selfhood," "that-ness," "existence," or "non-existence; there is no conceptualization of difference anywhere, nor is there any being or any attachment.
The entire world is peaceful, without support, eternal, and auspicious; it is free from affliction, without appearance, nameless, and without cause.
It is neither existent nor non-existent, neither the middle nor the end, neither all nor indeed all; it is ungraspable by mind or words, emptier than the empty, and more blissful than bliss.
Śrī Rāma said: "I have now fully realized that Brahman alone is everything and is uniform; nevertheless, tell me further: why is this creation perceived?"

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In the supreme, tranquil [Reality], that which is called the "Supreme" exists in this manner as "this-ness. Herein, there is neither creation nor any so-called creation at any time whatsoever.

Like water within the waters of the great ocean, [the individual soul] is established in the Supreme Lord; like water that is motionless despite its inherent fluidity, the supreme state is free from movement.
Light shines as if within its own self, yet that state does not shine at all; for the wise know that the essence of lights is shining, while that state is non-shining.

Just as water within the belly of the ocean quivers when the upper and lower regions are excluded, so too this world appears as if manifold within the Supreme due to its consciousness, though it is not different from that Supreme.

One who knows only slightly, by virtue of being conscious of himself, comes to experience as if there were an object of consciousness; he perceives "this is creation" and will thus remain established in that state eternally.

The firm conclusion is that creation is merely a designation for the ultimate reality; it does not exist as something distinct, nor is it absolutely non-existent, just as space is not different from space itself.
The emergence from the mind is the attainment of non-mind, and the cessation of that non-mind is the supreme peace; it is like the delusion of a bracelet in gold.
Only that which exists attains reality when the arising of mental tranquility occurs; that which does not exist attains existence by itself upon the arising of self-awareness.
Know that consciousness is the ego-sense, the agitation arising from the flurry of creation; know that non-consciousness is the supreme peace, yet it is not inert.

To the knower, this manifold creation is not diverse, for it consists of the single, auspicious Self; it is like an army of clay figures fashioned by craftsmen, appearing as male, action, and activity.
This is full, without beginning, infinite, and with a sinless interior; within the Full, it remains as the Full itself, through the supreme fillings of the Full.
That which is perceived as this creation is Brahman, abiding within Brahman; like space resting in space, it is the peaceful, auspicious [reality] resting in the peaceful Śiva.
Just as in a city of nine yojanas reflected in a mirror, there is neither distance nor proximity; so too is the sequence of "that" and "not-that" with respect to the Lord.
The universe arises from the non-existent, yet it always arises even as the existent; though appearing as real due to its manifestation, it consists of unreality because it lacks substantiality.
In this creation—which has the form of a city in a mirror, which shines like the water of a mirage, and which appears as the delusion of two moons—what indeed is real?
Just as a city appears to whirl in the sky due to the scattering of magical powder, so does saṃsāra—both substantial and insubstantial—appear within consciousness.

As long as ignorance has not been forcibly burnt down to its very roots by the fire of investigation—like a withered creeper—it continues to produce many diverse forests of pleasure and pain, dense with spreading branches.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, listen to what kind of greatness belongs to ignorance, which, though falsely described like a golden ring or similar trinket, is destined for destruction.
Having thus witnessed that delusion, King Lavaṇa set out for that great forest on the second day.
I remember that forest where I witnessed such suffering; for it might perhaps be found within the mirror of the mind, even beyond the Vindhya mountains.
Having thus resolved with his ministers, he set out for the Deccan, reaching the Vindhya mountain as if once again for the conquest of the quarters.
Out of curiosity, he wandered across the entire coastal land of the eastern, southern, and western great oceans, like the sun traversing the path of the sky.
Then, in one place, he beheld that formidable forest, standing before him like a personified thought, resembling the earth of the world beyond.
While dwelling there, he saw all those various events, questioned them, and having understood them, was filled with wonder.
And having recognized them as hunters born of the Pulkasa caste, he, bewildered by astonishment, wandered about again in great agitation.
Then, having reached the edge of the great forest, which was grey with smoke, he arrived at that very village where he had once been a well-fed Pulkasa.
There he saw various people, those women, those small huts, various types of reservoirs for water, and those various slopes of the earth.
And he saw those trees fallen unexpectedly, those following trails, those very same regions, and his many sons who had been struck down by disease.
To her elder friends, who were tearful-eyed, distressed, and filled with agony, she described the countless sufferings of her kinsmen scattered across untimely wildernesses.

An old woman, her eyes blazing with increasing tears, her breasts withered and her body emaciated—alas, distressed—wailed this lamentation there, like a cry of suffering in a land scorched by a fierce drought and thunderbolt.

Alas, daughter! Your entire body was once covered with sons; now, your limbs are withered by three days of fasting. Having cut through your armor with a sword, how and where were your life-breaths released from this worn-out body?

I remember the garland of *guñjā* berries worn by my Lord, who smiles with the moon as his crest-jewel; it hung from the palm leaves on the mountain of clouds, while its bright red fruits rested between his teeth.
When shall I ever again behold the terrifying leaps and bounds of my son as he roams within the groves of *kadamba*, *jambīra*, clove, and *guñjā* trees, where wild hyenas prowl?

Those playful splendors of desire do not exist even in the mouth of a wanton woman here, compared to the single portion of the chin on the son’s face, dark as a tamāla tree, which has taken the place of the prey upon his other face.

She, whose name was Yamunā, who resembled the Yamunā river, was led away by her husband Yama along with him, just as a Tamāla vine, together with its clusters of blossoms, is carried off by a favorable breeze in the forest.

Alas, daughter! You who wear a necklace of *guñjā* berries, whose limbs possess full and swelling breasts, whose complexion is as flickering as soot stirred by the wind, and whose teeth are like ripe *jambu* fruits amidst garments of leaves.

Alas, O Prince, whose splendor is like the moon! Having abandoned those beautiful women of the inner apartments, you have found delight in my daughter; yet even she has not attained stability for you.

O lord of men, what trivial thing indeed has not been done by the playful activities of the waves breaking upon the river of saṃsāra, which mock [the wise], if one has united with the daughter of a *puṣkasa*?

She, whose eyes were like those of a frightened deer, and he, whose valor was like that of a proud tiger—both went to destruction in a single step, just as hope perishes along with its object when great effort fails.

My husband has died and my own son is no more; I have traveled to a wretched land and am fallen into misery. I am born into a miserable birth and stand upon a great calamity; O, I am manifest fear itself, I am a great disaster!

I am a woman without a protector, the abode of manifold misfortunes: of pride born from the insults of the lowly, of the misery of one whose wife is afflicted by hunger, and of grief that moves with irresistible course through my daily life.

For one tormented by fate, deprived of kinsmen, deluded, and rooted in a great field of mental anguish, whatever constitutes life or death during that great calamity is the supreme means of sustaining the self.
For one who is deprived of people and dwells in a wretched land, endless sufferings arise, like grass on a mountain during the rains, teeming with thousands of branches and sap.
Having comforted his wife’s elderly nurse—who was speaking thus—with female servants, the king asked that woman: "What has happened here? Who are you? Who is your daughter? And who is your son?"
Then, with eyes full of tears, she said: "This village is named Puṣpasaṃghoṣa; here my husband was a Puṣkasaka, and he had one daughter who was like the moon."

By the turn of fate, she found her husband, who was like Indra, returned here as a king through the power of destiny; yet that wretched woman, like a solitary female camel finding a shattered jar of honey in the forest, [fell into despair].
Having enjoyed pleasures with him for a very long time, she gave birth to sons and daughters; they grew up in this forest thicket like a gourd vine clinging to a tree.
The Caṇḍālī said: "Then, after some time, O Lord of Men, in this village there occurred a terrifying misery of drought that broke the spirit of the people."
Due to this great suffering, all those people of the village departed and went far away; they have all met their death.
Therefore, O Lord, we here are empty and partakers of suffering; O gentle one, we grieve with noble tears that flow like a stream washing our eyes.
Having heard this from the mouth of the woman, the king was filled with wonder; looking at the faces of his ministers, he became as if fixed in a painting.
He reflected further upon that unsurpassed wonder; then, filled with amazement, he questioned him again and again.
Having brought about the destruction of their suffering through appropriate gifts and honors, he, being permeated with compassion, became the supreme lord of the desired worlds.
Having stayed there for a long time and reflected upon the courses of destiny, he returned home and, saluted by the citizens, entered his residence.
In the morning, at that place in the assembly hall, the king asked me: "O sage, how can a dream be such as this, appearing as if it were before one's eyes?"—thus he spoke in wonder.
Because it was spoken to him according to the actual state of things, that doubt of his was driven from his heart, like a cloud from the sky by the wind.
Thus, O Raghava, this great ignorance, which causes delusion, quickly leads the unreal to the state of reality and leads the real to the state of unreality.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahman, how can you speak thus? How has a dream attained the state of reality? This matter is like a grand delusion; it does not fade from my mind."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: All this indeed occurs within ignorance, O Rāghava; for instance, the appearance of cloth in jars is seen in dreams, delusions, and the like.
The distant appears as if near, like a mountain within a mirror; the long seems to become swift, just as the night becomes most excellent [at dawn].
And impossibility occurs, just as one's own death in a dream; and what is non-existent appears as if it were existent, like traveling through the sky in dreams.
That which is well-established moves excessively during a delusion, like the rotation of the earth; that which is immovable comes to seem moving, like a mind agitated by intoxication.
When the mind, enveloped by latent impressions, intensely contemplates something in a certain way, it immediately experiences that very thing accordingly; it is neither non-existent nor even unreal.
The moment the false knowledge consisting of "I-ness" and so forth has arisen, at that very moment the beginningless, middleless, and endless nature of delusion is said to have emerged.
By the power of mental appearance alone, everything undergoes transformation: a moment becomes an eon, and an eon becomes a moment.
A creature with a perverted mind perceives itself as a sheep; yet, by the power of its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), that sheep assumes the nature of a lion.
Unevenness, delusion, ignorance, infatuation, egoism, and so forth are all equal, because they are the causes for the perfection of the fruits of mental perversion.
Like the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit, worldly activities of great undertaking coincide with one another spontaneously through the power of mental impressions (*vāsanā*).
Whatever occurred previously in the salt-mining village of a certain king has appeared to him in his mind, whether it be true or false.
Just as the mind forgets even a vast mental action once performed, so too it certainly remembers what was done as if it were never done.
Likewise, even an ordinary person, upon waking from a dream in which they traveled to another land, perceives in their mind: "I did not eat," or "I have eaten."
In the village of Puṣkasa on the Vindhya mountains, such was the legal proceeding; it appeared to him as if it were a former account from a dream.
Or rather, that very same dream-delusion which was quickly witnessed by Lavaṇa has entered the consciousness of the Puṣkasas in the Vindhya mountains.

The aesthetic flavor (lāvaṇī) ascends to the intuition (pratibhā) in the mind of the Puṣkasa of Vindhya; or rather, the consciousness (saṃvit) of the Puṣkasa of Vindhya ascends to the mind of the king.
Just as the mental impression known as speech arises similarly for many people, so too do time, place, and action occur even in a dream.
Its existence is established through appearance within the course of worldly transaction; for the existence of all things is nothing other than their being cognized.
It appears as both consciousness and its opposite, like a wave in the union of waters, or like a tree situated in the past, present, and future within the seed of a tree.
Its existence and non-existence are established as being neither existent nor non-existent; for it is truly existent through consciousness, and non-existent through the absence of consciousness.
Ignorance does not exist at all, just as oil and the like do not exist in sand; for what state other than that of gold could there be for a bracelet apart from its being gold?
A connection between ignorance and the true nature of the self is not tenable; for a connection is clearly observed only between things that are similar, as is evident from one's own experience.

The relationship between lac and wood and so forth, which arises from the conjunction of the similar and the dissimilar, does not result from mutual experience; it is merely a single vibration of that [whole].

Everything consists of the ultimate reality; just as by that [consciousness], stones and other such things are perceived equally through the power of association, so too are they conceived by the mind as being identical.
When all things existing in the world consist of pure consciousness and pure existence, then they shine forth in mutual relation, established in their own self-experience.
A continuous connection between dissimilar things is not possible; nor can there be mutual experience without a reciprocal connection.
When a similar object encounters another similar object, it immediately attains complete unity; through that very unity, it manifests as a single form, and not otherwise.

When consciousness (cit) is joined with the object of thought (cetya), it arises as the perceiving subject; when the insentient (jaḍa) is joined with the insentient, it becomes a solid mass of insentience. And the unification of consciousness and the insentient can never occur anywhere, because of their essential difference.

The two aspects of consciousness (ciñcau) are diverse; they never meet together in one place. Because it consists of consciousness, the grasping of consciousness occurs through the grasping of consciousness, which is the act of knowing.
For these [objects] such as wood and stone are not of the nature of consciousness; indeed, one object is experienced by being transformed by another object.

Know that the tasting of flavors occurs by the tongue alone, arising from its own kind; and know that identity is the relationship [between them], for such a relation does not exist between dissimilar things.

Therefore, because of that [realization], the distinction between the insentient and the sentient does not exist; the stone and so forth are not considered insentient, for consciousness alone is measured by consciousness as having the form of stones, walls, and the like.
Having attained a state of oneness, it creates the delusion of the seer, the seen, and so forth—including everything from wood and stones—since it is composed of the ultimate reality.
Through its identity with that [Self], everything—rich in all modes and appearing as if infinite—is perceived with effort as an object of vision in relation to it.

O best among the knowers of reality, know that this entire universe is indeed nothing but pure existence; through hundreds of thousands of delusions, the universe appears only because of the failure to abandon non-existence.
The wonder of consciousness is filled, yet nothing at all is filled; the cities of men's mental constructs do not move against one another as they appear to do.

Thus, it is established that in the various creations there is no obstruction by space or time; for it is only when there is the cognition of duality that the state of being a creation arises, along with the emergence of delusions such as "I-ness" and so forth.

Just as there is the delusion of bracelets and such upon the relinquishment of gold-consciousness, so too the delusion of bracelets and such exists within the gold, moving from place to place and from birth to birth.
When seeing and the seen are abandoned, ignorance does not exist as something separate at all; it is like pure gold, which remains one despite the great diversity of bracelets and other ornaments.
Because this creation is one with consciousness, it is entirely non-existent; like a diverse army made of clay, it is merely earth, just as the perception of clay reduces it to mere earth.

Water is one, yet it appears as waves and the like; wood is one, yet it appears as carved figures; clay alone is one, yet it appears as jars and the like; Brahman is one, yet it is the delusion of the three worlds.
Among those who perceive the relationship between the seen and the seer, that which is the true nature of the seer—devoid of the seer, the act of seeing, and the seen—is indeed this supreme reality.
When the mind has moved from one place to another, that form of consciousness which exists in the interval—awake, conscious, and reflective—become absorbed in that at all times.
That which is your eternal form—neither waking, nor dreaming, nor deep sleep; neither insentient nor inert—be always absorbed in that.
Indeed, that heart of yours is like a stone, for it has abandoned all but its single quality of insentience; therefore, whether undisturbed or disturbed, always become absorbed in That alone.
For anyone here, nothing whatsoever arises nor does anything dissolve; whether unagitated or agitated, remain established in yourself as you please.
The person does not desire nor does he hate anything whatsoever in the body anywhere; remain established in yourself, free from apprehension, and do not fall into the activities of the body.
Just as one intent on the affairs of a village in the future does not dwell upon them now, so too, having attained the nature of reality, do not dwell upon the fluctuations of the mind.
Just as a person from another land, just as a piece of wood, and just as a stone—so too, O mind, view yourself as being without a self by means of the self.
Just as there is no water in a stone, and just as there is no fire in water, so too the mind does not exist within its own self; how then could it exist in the Supreme Self?
Thinking, "Whatever is done anywhere by that which is not perceived as 'this' or 'that' has not been done," one should transcend the mind.
Why does one not follow a border-dwelling barbarian, who follows a mind that is ultimately not one's own?
Constantly disregarding the mind, which is like a mere blade of grass, remain established in yourself, free from anxiety; you have been rendered as inert as mud.
"Indeed, my mind does not exist; it knows today only what is real or what is dead. Becoming one who possesses certainty, remain as motionless as a stone statue."
In the state of discernment, our mind does not exist; you are therefore devoid of it in reality. Why then are you tormented by that which is useless and brings only misfortune?
For those of feeble intellect who have been rendered helpless in vain by the non-existent yakṣa of the mind, [this work] has arisen from the mouth of the Moon.
Having cast the mind far away, remain firm as you truly are; be liberated through meditative cultivation and endowed with the supreme method.
