Fie upon those who follow after the unreal, whose minds take on the form of what is untrue—those for whom time is spent solely in the act of trying to kill the sky!

With a mind completely dissolved, O one of great majesty, become one who has reached the further shore of existence; be one whose self is stainless. Though investigated for a very long time, not even the slightest stain has been found within the stainless self of the mind.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: As soon as one is born, a person whose intellect has only slightly blossomed must be intent upon the company of the virtuous.
This torrent of the river of ignorance, fallen into an unceasing flow, cannot be crossed except through contact with the scriptures and virtuous people.
From that state of isolation, there arises in the person an investigation into what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted.
Then he has reached the stage of discernment called "the desire for what is auspicious."
Then, by the power of seclusion, there is investigation.
For one who abandons improper latent impressions through right knowledge, the mind attains attenuation due to the cultivation of mindfulness.
By that, he has descended to the stage of discernment called "the mind with attenuated mental fluctuations."
At the very moment that right knowledge arises for the yogin, at that very moment there is the attainment of pure being (sattva).
When, by virtue of that, his latent impressions (vāsanā) have reached attenuation, then he alone is called "unattached," meaning he is not bound by the fruit of action.
Then, through that attenuation, he practices the cultivation of the attenuation of the unreal.

As long as one does not act, nor engage in worldly affairs, even while remaining amidst the unreal objects of saṃsāra, because of the mind’s dissolution within one's own self through the power of practice, one does not perceive external objects even while acting upon them; one does not serve them with objective attachment, nor does one dwell upon them with longing. And because of the attenuation of latent impressions (vāsanā), like one who has just awakened from sleep, one performs what is to be done merely as a fool would. As long as one does not act, nor engage in worldly affairs, even while remaining amidst the unreal objects of saṃsāra, because of the mind’s dissolution within one's own self through the power of practice, one does not perceive external objects even while acting upon them; one does not serve them with objective attachment, nor does one dwell upon them with longing. And because of the attenuation of latent impressions (vāsanā), like one who has just awakened from sleep, one performs what is to be done merely as a fool would.
With his mind thus cultivated and refined, he ascends to the cultivation of the stages of yoga.

Having practiced for several years with the mind thus absorbed within, even while performing all external activities, he abandons mental identification with external objects; becoming the Self of the Fourth (turyātman), he is then called "liberated while living" (jīvanmukta).
He does not rejoice in what has been attained, nor does he grieve for what has not been attained; he simply follows what has come to pass, free from all anxiety.
O Raghava, you too have come to know the entirety of that which is to be known; surely, among all your activities, your latent impressions have been thinned away.
Whether your activity transcends the body or you remain within the body, do not give way to grief or joy; you are the Self, free from all affliction.
O Rāma, since you are the Self—pure, transparent, all-pervading, and ever-shining—whence can there be pleasure and pain, and whence can there be birth and death?
Why do you, who have no kin, grieve for the sorrows of relatives? For while this self stands without a second, what indeed are kinsmen to it?
Only a mere accumulation of atoms is seen in the body; because it undergoes changes in place and time, the Self neither arises nor perishes.
Since you are indestructible, why do you grieve, thinking "I am perishing"? For what kind of destruction could there be in the Self, which is pure and the abode of immortality?
Just as the space within a jar is not destroyed when the jar is reduced to shards, so too it is not destroyed even when this body perishes.
Just as the heat does not perish when a river of mirage-water has dried up, so too the Self does not perish when the body is destroyed.
Why does this desire arise within you? It is a meaningless delusion. Since you are non-dual, what second thing exists that your self could desire?
O Raghava, whatever is audible, tangible, visible, palatable, or olfactory—there is nothing in the world that exists apart from the Self.
All these powers, though omnipotent, abide entirely within that very Self; they reside in the pervasive Manifested One, just as emptiness resides in space.
O Rāghava, this world, which is called the ornament of the three realms, has arisen from the mind; through a threefold process here, it produces delusion by means of birth.
When the pacification of the mind—known as the destruction of latent impressions—is accomplished, this illusion known as karma perishes.
O Rāghava, sever with effort this latent impression (vāsanā), which is the rope for the mechanical carriage mounted upon this fierce water-wheel of saṃsāra.
When not fully understood, this [ignorance] bestows great delusion; but when fully understood, it is called "the Infinite," bestowing happiness and granting Brahman.
Having come here into this cycle of existence by way of sport after having enjoyed the state of Brahmā, one again recollects Brahmā alone and dissolves into Brahmā itself.
O Raghava, from Śiva—who is formless, immeasurable, and free from affliction—all beings have arisen, just as manifestations arise from light.
Just as a multitude of lines appears on a leaf, as a network of ripples in water, as bracelets and the like in gold, and as heat and so forth in fire; [so too does the world appear in Brahman].
Thus, these three worlds exist in the form of that very creative contemplation; they are situated within it alone, born from it alone, and are indeed identical to it.
He alone is called the Self of all beings and Brahman; when he is known, the entire world is known—he is the knower throughout the three worlds.
For the sake of conventional usage in the scriptures, names such as "Consciousness," "Brahman," and "Self" have been devised for this [reality] of expansive form by those of perfected soul.

When there is contact between the sense objects and the senses, that experience which is free from joy and resentment is indeed this pure experience; it is this very self, the imperishable consciousness.
In that Self of consciousness, which is clearer than the sky, the world is reflected as if it were separate, though it is indeed nothing but its own manifestation.

For greed, delusion, and the like cast those [beings] into that [state] by means of an unreal distinction from the Buddha; and those [afflictions] likewise cast him [the Buddha] into that [state] by means of that very same unreal distinction.
O Rāma, for you who are indeed bodiless and whose form is non-conceptual consciousness, from where has this delusion arisen—this delusion that stems from shame, fear, and despair?
O you who are bodiless, why are you, like a fool of poor intellect, overcome by these unreal constructs such as shame and the rest, which are born of the body?

When fragmentation occurs within the body of that which is of the nature of indivisible consciousness, even for one of imperfect vision there is no destruction; how much less so for one of right understanding?
Even when falling upon the path of darkness, the mind is not obstructed in its coming and going; that which is called "mind" should be known as the person, and not the physical body.
Whether the body exists or not, O Rāma, it is the person alone who remains throughout the three worlds—whether conscious or unconscious; when the body has perished, he does not perish.
All these various sufferings that you perceive belong to the body alone; they do not belong to the self of consciousness, which is ungraspable.
Since it has transcended the path of the mind and thus remains as if empty, how indeed could consciousness be grasped by either sufferings or celestial pleasures?
Having abandoned his own self from the ruined cage of the body, he entered into his habitual latent impression (*vāsanā*), just as a bee flies from a lotus into the sky.
O Rāma, if the reality of the self does not exist within this cage of a body, then what indeed could be lost when it perishes? Why do you grieve?
Cultivate truth; do not give way to delusion. For you, whose nature is stainless, there is no desire whatsoever for a self that is free from longing.
In the conscious Self—which is the witness, impartial, pure, and free from conceptual construction—the worlds are reflected without desire, just as reflections appear in a mirror.
Within the conscious Self—which is the witness, impartial, pure, and free from conceptual construction—the worlds appear of their own accord, like rays within a precious gem.
Just as there is a connection between a mirror and its reflection even without desire, so too here the distinction and non-distinction between the self and the world are established.
Just as the activity of the world arises by the mere proximity of the sun, so too is this world brought into existence by the mere existence of consciousness.
O Rāma, for this world-existence, the grasping at a solid mass has ceased; thus, it has become like space even within your own minds.
Just as light is the inherent nature of a lamp by its mere existence, so too is this worldly condition the inherent nature of the reality of mind.

In the beginning, the mind arose from the reality of the Supreme Self; by it, this world was spread out through the nets of its own conceptual constructions. Though empty, it was made empty by that [mind], just as the sky, though empty, manifests a most beautiful appearance of blueness.

When the mind has dissolved through the destruction of volitional constructs, the mists of worldly delusion vanish; within, there shines forth the one, unborn, primordial, and infinite pure consciousness alone, like the clear sky when autumn has arrived.

At first, the mind, whose nature is action, arises from volition; then, having approached the primordial matter of the Lotus-born, it vainly expands this world of manifold names, just as a deluded child imagines the body of a ghost.

Unreal yet appearing as real before one's eyes, it manifests again and then dissolves once more; the mind itself, its form flashing forth within consciousness, is like a series of circles of water in the great ocean.
Now, immediately after the section on origination, O Rāma, listen to this section on persistence, which, when understood, brings about liberation.
In this way, know for certain that this visible world is established as such; it is merely an illusion consisting of unreality, devoid of forms such as "I" and "this."
A painting has arisen in the sky without an artist and without colors; it is an experience without a perceiver, a dream-vision occurring without sleep.
The construction of a future city appears as if established within the mind; though unreal, it accomplishes its purpose, like the heat from a fire made by a monkey.
In Brahman, there exists nothing other than itself, yet it appears as something else, like a whirlpool in water; though its nature is existence, it is void, like solar radiance in the sky.
Like a mass of jewel-light seen in the sky without a foundation, it is like the city of the Gandharvas—visible yet eternally without a foundation.
Unreal like the water of a mirage, yet producing the conviction of reality; mature like a city of one's imagination, yet composed of non-existence—thus has it been experienced.

Consisting of the eloquence that manifests the meaning of discourse, it is neither situated anywhere nor non-situated; though devoid of essence, it possesses an extreme inner essence, resembling a mountain in a dream.
Like the elemental ether, it is radiant in form yet consists of mere emptiness; like an autumn cloud standing before one, it is stainless, inexhaustible, and unimpaired.

Like the appearance of impurity in the sky, it is perceived yet devoid of substance; like the form of dalliance with a woman in a dream, it appears to have a real object but is ultimately meaningless.
Like a painted garden in full bloom, it possesses the appearance of a lake yet lacks water; though luminous, it remains devoid of brilliance, like the sun or fire in a painting.
It was experienced as something unreal and unsubstantial, like a kingdom of the mind, devoid of essence and fragrance like a painted lotus pond.
Manifested within emptiness, possessing various colors and characterized by form, it arises like a rainbow—empty yet appearing as a solid mass.
By means of grasping, the elements, whose tender sprouts are withered, have been rendered inert, essence-less, and as hollow as the trunk of a plantain tree.
The turning of the wheel of darkness perceived by his darting eyes became an absolute non-existence, yet it remained as if directly present before him.
It is expansive like a water bubble, yet empty within; its form quivers, being both of the nature of essence and devoid of essence, with its arising and passing away occurring without interruption.
To some, it is like a spreading mist—grasped yet nothing at all; a void that is the locus of dullness and emptiness, like an atom.
"I am composed of something real"—thus it remains, though empty and unreal; even while being grasped, it persists as having no true nature, like a night-stalker.
Śrī Rāma said: At the dissolution of the great kalpa, the visible world remains like a sprout within a seed; it arises again from that very source in the Supreme. Tell me, how is this so?
Thus, O Blessed One, for the sake of pacifying all doubts, please explain clearly whether those who have awakened are ignorant or whether they are wise.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This visible world exists within the Great Abode like a sprout within a seed; he who speaks thus possesses ignorance, which is his childhood.
Listen to this: how can it be unrelated? How can it be unreal? This is a perverted understanding that causes delusion for both the speaker and the listener.
Listen now to how that deluded notion—which holds that the world exists within [Brahman] like a sprout within a seed—is merely a false prattle.
The seed itself becomes the visible object within the range of the mind and the sense faculties; just as it is logical for grains such as barley to give rise to leaves and sprouts.
How could the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) be the seed of the worlds—that which is exceedingly subtle, transcending the six senses with the mind as the sixth?
How and in what manner can there be the state of being a seed for the Supreme Self, which is subtler than even space, beyond all description, and unperceivable?

That subtle [cause] appears as non-existent, for it is indeed non-existent because it is not of such a nature; what kind of seedhood could there be therein? In the absence of a seed, whence can there be a sprout?
In that supreme state, which is clearer than even the expanse of the sky and is empty, how can the world, Mount Meru, the oceans, the sky, and so forth exist?
There is not the slightest thing whatsoever that exists as a real entity within that reality; if it did exist there, why would it not be seen?

Nothing whatsoever belongs to the Self; how, from where, or in what manner could anything come into being? Where, from what cause, or when could a mountain ever be born from the empty space within a jar?
How can anything exist within its opposite? It is like shade existing within sunlight. How can darkness exist in the sun, or how can frost exist in fire?
How could Mount Meru reside within an atom? For how can there be any unity between that which has form and that which is formless, any more than there can be between shadow and sunlight?
It is logical that sprouts exist within the husk of a grain such as rice; however, it is illogical to claim that this world, which possesses great form, exists within that which is formless.

Whatever capacity of the intellect and all the sense organs is seen in another person or in another place, that does not exist at all in the cognition of such an intellect; therefore, it is said to be "nothing at all."

He whose intellect is utterly deluded claims that the effect has itself become the cause; by what means, indeed, could that effect arise from it, except through its own causes and other auxiliary factors?

Having cast far away the notion of the relationship between cause and effect imagined by those of poor intellect, know that this very world—without beginning or middle—is established as that alone which is the Truth.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Now, O best among those who know what is to be known, I shall speak regarding this acceptance [of your view] within the stainless, great sky of consciousness, which transcends all mental constructs.
If the primordial sprout of the world exists therein, then tell me: by what auxiliary causes does it arise?
In the absence of auxiliary causes, the emergence of a sprout from you has never been seen here by anyone, just like the daughter of a barren woman.
O friend, if it has not arisen due to the absence of auxiliary causes, then the primary cause itself remains established in its own nature.
At the beginning of creation, Brahman itself abides within itself in the form of creation; as it remains without form, where is there any sequence of produced and producer?

Now, if the earth and other elements, or some others, assist here [in the production of cognition], that would constitute their status as auxiliary causes (sahakārikāraṇa); and this has already been refuted previously.
Therefore, the world remains quiescent within that state along with its auxiliary causes; the assertion that it "spreads forth from the mind" belongs to a child, not to a wise man.
Therefore, O Rāma, the world never was, does not exist, and will not be; it is merely the space of consciousness that shines swiftly in this manner within itself.
O Rāma, when the absolute non-existence of this world is realized, then all this is Brahman; it is not otherwise.
That which subsides through prior destruction, subsequent destruction, or mutual non-existence does not truly subside within the mind; yet it appears as if it has subsided.
Since this [world] subsides through its entities only as an absolute non-existence, and since it does not truly subside while the mind exists, where indeed can the visible world ever be stilled?
Therefore, the absolute non-existence of the perceived world in every respect is the only logical means for the complete destruction of suffering; no other method exists.
This world appears as the awareness of the space of consciousness; that which exists is simply "this," "I am he," or "I am not this," like a variegated story in the world.
This is today and so forth; this is the earth and so forth; likewise, this is the year and so forth; this is the eon (kalpa) and this is the moment (kṣaṇa); and these are death and birth.
This tumult at the end of the aeon is that very end of the great aeon; this is the commencement of creation, and this is the sequence of things yet to be and those already being.
These marks of the kalpas, these millions of cosmic eggs, these that have been encompassed and these that have come forth once more.
These are the networks of cognitive faculties, these are the divisions of space and time; yet the Great Consciousness is the supreme, unobstructed, and infinite void.
It shines by itself as "peaceful" and "remaining just as it was before"; these are but the radiance of a thousandth part of a single atom of the Great Consciousness.
This formless manifestation of creation appears as the wonder that is itself vomited forth by consciousness from within; it does not possess a material substratum.
They do not arise nor do they perish; they do not come nor do they go; they are as immovable as the carvings upon great rocks.
These creations manifest from the self within the stainless Self, like portions of space within space—formless within the formless.
Like the fluidity of water, like the movements in a constant wind, like the whirlpools of the ocean, or like the qualities inherent in those who possess them.
This entire world exists as a single mass of consciousness, infinite and pervasive, tranquil, and devoid of beginning, end, or commencement.
To claim that the world is empty in the absence of causes such as auxiliary factors, yet that the Self-Existent (Svayambhū) arises [from it], is indeed the babbling of a madman.

With all stains of the conceptualization of objects completely stilled, with the bed of all residual mental constructions cast away, and having long since dispelled the deep sleep of ignorance, he has awakened—the fearless one, the ornament of the earth.

Śrī Rāma said: At the beginning of creation at the end of a great kalpa, that first Prajāpati is born as the very essence of memory; therefore, I believe the entire world is likewise of the nature of memory.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O scion of Raghu, at the beginning of creation following the great dissolution, this very first Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) exists initially as the self consisting of memory alone.
Therefore, this world, which consists of the memory of that [Brahman] whose nature is volition, shines forth as a city of volition existing from before the time of Prajāpati.
Memory is simply not possible for the Supreme Self at the beginning of creation; since there is no birth, how or where could it exist, like a great tree in the sky?
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, is it not possible for there to be memory of the past at the beginning of creation? How is it that memory of the past is destroyed by the delusions of the great dissolution?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Those wise ones, beginning with Brahmā, who in former times attained liberation at the time of the great dissolution, have certainly reached the state of Brahman.
O observer of noble vows, tell me: who was the creator of memory in the past? For memory has become rootless, since the rememberer has attained liberation.
Therefore, in the absence of a rememberer, how or why could a tradition (smṛti) arise? For surely, at the end of a great aeon (mahākalpa), all beings must attain liberation alone.

Whether regarding what has not been experienced or what has been experienced, that memory which arises within the self-luminous sky of consciousness—that mature manifestation as the world is indeed the radiance of consciousness itself.
This very radiance of consciousness shines forth, illuminating that which is without beginning or end; it exists as both this world and as the Self-existent One.
That innate manifestation of Brahman, established from beginningless time, is the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) which takes the form of the cosmic Virāj.
Within the supreme atom, this triple world—along with its forests, clouds, and sky, and endowed with the sequences of space, time, action, substance, day, and night—shines forth.
The atom is expanded, and that [expansion] remains just as it was; yet again, a mountain range appears, possessing the same radiant quality.
Even there, that which appears as the visible object shines forth with such a form, following in succession; this nature of light, my dear, is not real.
Thus, there is no end anywhere for either right view or wrong view; yet, O sinless one, for this [right view], the Awakened has arisen, and not the Unawakened.

To one who has awakened, this is indeed only Brahman—solely peaceful and immutable; but to one who has not awakened, having perceived it through the intellect, it appears as the radiant [world] accompanied by the realms of existence.
Just as this radiant universe shines forth, expanding like an egg, so too do thousands of millions of others shine within every single atom.
Just as there is a figurine within a pillar, and within that figurine’s own limbs there is another figurine, and within that figurine’s limbs yet another, so too is the figurine of the three worlds.
Just as atoms on a mountain are neither indistinguishable nor countable, so too are the atoms of the three worlds within the vast Mount Meru, which is Brahman.
The subtle atoms may be counted within the rays of the sun; yet the atoms of the three worlds arise from the sun of consciousness.
Just as atoms move within the rays of the sun, within waters, and within dust particles, so too do the atoms of the three worlds move within the space of consciousness.
Just as this elemental space consists of the mere experience of emptiness, so too does this space of consciousness consist of the mere experience of creation.
When "creation" (sarga) is understood as the meaning of the word *sarga*, it leads one downward; when it is understood as the meaning of the word *brahman*, it becomes a source of supreme well-being.

The conscious self, the ruler, the seed of the universe, is Brahman alone—sufficient unto itself as the mere space of consciousness. One should know that whatever is born from it is that very same thing; the object of knowledge is merely the awakening of one's own internal awareness.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The ocean of worldly existence is crossed by means of the bridge that is the restraint of the collection of the senses; it cannot be crossed here by any other action whatsoever.
Through the study of the scriptures, association with the virtuous, and practice, one who possesses discernment and has conquered the senses realizes the absolute non-existence of this visible world.
O best of embodied beings, all this has been told to you regarding the nature of the successions of the ocean of saṃsāra, and how they come and go.
What is the use of saying more here? The sprout of the tree of mental karma—when that is severed, the world-tree, whose body is karma, is severed as well.
O Rāma, this entire world is the mind; when that [mind] is treated internally, the whole disease of the web of the world is indeed cured.
Thus, this world arises, agitated by the mind's own conceptualizing; apart from the mind, where indeed can a body be seen?
Apart from the absolute non-existence of the visible object, the demon of the mind does not come to rest even in hundreds of eons by any other cause.
And this is indeed possible for the treatment of mental disease; it is the supreme, most excellent medicine, consisting of the absolute non-existence of the visible world.
The mind takes on delusion; the mind dies and is born. Through the clarity of its own reflection, it is bound and again released.
This entire world throbs within the mind when it is swooned by thought, just as the city of the Gandharvas appears in the vast void of space, though it is utterly empty.
This entire expansive universe exists and vibrates within the mind; it is like fragrance residing in a cluster of flowers, appearing as if distinct from that which contains it.
Just as oil is in a sesame seed, or as a quality is in that which possesses the quality, or as a property is in its substratum, so too is this world in the mind.
Just as a web of rays exists in the sun, just as light exists in fire, and just as heat exists in the flame, so does this world exist in the mind.
Just as coolness is in frost, as emptiness is in the sky, and as flickering is in the wind, so is this world in the mind.

The mind is the entire world, and the world is likewise the mind; indeed, these two are always inseparable from one another. When the world is destroyed within the mind of these two, the world is truly destroyed, but when the mind is destroyed within the world, the world is not.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, best among those who understand the past and the future, how is it that this vast cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra) resides within the mind?
O sinless one, explain to me clearly through a vivid illustration how this vast samsara, as it vibrates, manifests within the mind.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as the worlds of the sons of Indu, though bodiless, remained firmly established in their minds, so too does this [universe] abide [within yours].
Just as King Lavaṇa attained the state of a Caṇḍāla when his form was confounded by Indra’s magical illusions, so too has this [state] remained fixed in my mind.
For a long time, due to his desire to enjoy the pleasures of heaven, Bhārgava attained both the lordship over those enjoyments and the state of being subject to worldly existence.
"Just as the state of being a lord of enjoyments remained thus in his mind," Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, [it happened] because of the son of Bhṛgu's desire to experience the enjoyments of heaven."
"How did his lordship over enjoyments and his state as a transmigrating being come to be? Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "Listen, O Rāma, to an ancient account, a dialogue between Bhṛgu and Kāla."
Long ago, on the peak of Mount Mandara, which was thick with tamāla branches and abounding in flowers.
The venerable Bhṛgu performed severe austerities in a certain place; his radiant and highly intelligent young son attended upon him.
Śukra, radiant like the full moon and shining like the light itself, remained established in meditative absorption within that excellent forest of Bhṛgu.
Like something carved at all times from the surface of a forest stone, Śukra remained [unmoving] upon beds of flowers and in courtyards of silver.
Upon the unrestrained swings of Mount Mandara, the child Śukra, through his playful sport, has fallen into great calamity between the two currents of knowledge and ignorance.
Then, like Triśaṅku, he remained distressed within the ocean of existence; this was at a time when his father had entered into a state of non-conceptual meditative absorption.
He remained undistracted in solitude like a king who has conquered his enemies; there he beheld an Apsaras passing through the path of the sky.
Like Janārdana [beholding] Lakṣmī churned from the midst of the Milk Ocean, she was encircled by garlands of Mandāra flowers, her tresses fluttering in the gentle breeze.
Her gait was resonant with the sound of her necklace, she perfumed the air of the sky, she was like a creeper upon the tree of loveliness, and her eyes were rolling with intoxication.
Beholding his beloved, whose very presence had been rendered nectar-like by the radiance of the moon that was her body, his mind became agitated with surging longing.
Just as the ocean is affected upon seeing the body of the pure, full moon, she too, beholding the face of Śukra, became utterly overcome.

Having awakened his mind—which had been repelled by those things born of the senses—Uśanas thereafter became, through his own self, one whose other functions had dissolved and who consisted entirely of his bride.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, meditating upon her with his mind, Uśanas remained right there with eyes closed and began this kingdom of the imagination all alone.
For this woman is here in the sky, the abode of the thousand-eyed one; and I have arrived in heaven, which is filled with restless celestial beauties.
These gods of yours are beautiful with crests of soft mandāraka flowers, their bodies possessing the playful luster of molten gold.
These are those beloved ones with gazes like blue lotuses that delight the eyes, playful with charming smiles, and possessing the glances of does.
These Maruts, radiant with flowers and appearing like intoxicated elephants, reflect one another and possess forms resembling those of Viśvarūpa.
These are those songs of the hosts of gods, sung in sweet, falsetto tones, heard by bees who have grown weary of the fragrance from the temples of Airāvaṇa.
This is that Mandākinī, where golden lotuses serve as the moving cranes for Brahmā, and where the leaders of the gods rest in the gardens upon its banks.
These are your world-protectors—Yama, Candra, Indra, Sūrya, Anala, Jala, and Anila—their bodies radiant with scattered, blazing flames of fire.
This is that Airāvaṇa, whose face was scratched by the bristling of his tusks during the course of battle, and who in combat had the circle of the lords of the Daityas impaled upon his teeth.

These, having moved from their positions on the earth's surface, have attained the state of stars in the sky; they are celestial beings traveling in chariots, with the beautiful radiance of moving gold.
These are those very waves of the Ganges' waters, strewn with Mandāra flowers, by which the deities are drenched with spray as they strike the surface of Mount Meru.
These are the avenues of Śakra’s grove, where rows of Apsarases sway upon swings, tawny with clusters of blossoming Mandāra flowers scattered about.
These are the breezes from the Pārijāta tree, fragrant with the nectar of the kunda and mandāra flowers, resembling a mass of moonbeams.
That Nandana grove was filled with throngs of vine-women eager to scatter the pollen of flowers like a fine cloud of incense.
These two, Nārada and Tumburu, have voices as melodious as the lute and cause the celestial maidens to dance with joy through the sound of their lovely songs.
These performers of meritorious deeds, adorned with many ornaments, are stationed within celestial chariots soaring through the sky.
These celestial women, their limbs intoxicated by passion and love, attend upon the Lord of Gods like forest creepers in a grove.
These are Indra’s stone-jewel flowers, clusters of wish-fulfilling gems, and these kalpa-trees, bristling with bunches of ripened fruit.
Here, first of all, I salute this Śakra seated upon his throne, as if he were a second creator of the three worlds.
Having reflected thus, the Lord of Śacī, with his mind alone, greeted him there; he appeared like a second Bhṛgu in the sky.
Then Śukra, having been honored by Śakra, rose up respectfully; taking him by the hand, he was led near and seated.
"O Lord, this heaven shines with splendor upon your arrival; O Śakra, may you dwell here for a long time. Thus he spoke to him.
Then, having sat down there, that descendant of Bhṛgu, with his face radiant, eclipsed the splendor of the entire stainless moon.

Worshipped by all the hosts of gods, that son of Bhṛgu, stationed at the side of Indra, attained incomparable satisfaction for a long time and became the cherished favorite of the most excellent of kings.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having thus reached the city of the gods by means of his own splendor, Śukra forgot his own former nature, except for his past affliction.
Having rested for a mere moment at the side of the Lord of Śacī, he, delighted by heaven, rose up to wander through the celestial realm.
Beholding the celestial splendor longed for by those with tremulous eyes, he went to see that host of women, just as a crane goes toward a lotus pond.
There, Bhṛgu beheld that beloved woman with eyes like those of a young deer, standing in the midst of the forest like a mango creeper.
She too, upon seeing that descendant of Bhṛgu, Rāma, fell under his sway; for she beheld him with a form graced by radiant and flickering charms.
With his limbs melting away like a moonstone in the moonlight, he gazed at that beloved woman as every part of his body dissolved.
Just as the moonstone draws in the cool, playful moonlight from the sky, she too, being gazed upon by him, became entirely devoted to him.
At the end of the night, she was surely called out to by the cakravāka like a beloved; having blossomed with passion, they were indeed mutually enamored.
The very same splendor that belongs to the sun and the lotus at dawn became theirs; and because she granted the desired object, she became known by that region as well.
Having rendered all her limbs powerless, she was surrendered entirely to desire; the arrows of Smara fell in abundance upon her tender body.
Like a lotus pond among *palāśa* trees, or like a stream from a rain-cloud, she became agitated by the arousal of passion, crowded with the swarms of restless bees.
She was the natural counterpart to a flower-cluster shaken by a gentle breeze; her eyes were like blue lotuses, and her gait was like that of a swan or a crane.
Madana agitated her like an elephant agitates a lotus pond; then, seeing her in such a state, Śukra attained his desired object.
Darkness, like the Destroyer who devours all beings, began to form its resolve; that region of heaven became overwhelmed with gloom.

Just as the world of mortals is surrounded by blinding darkness at the edge of the Lokāloka mountain, so too was that circle of gloom when he, the sharp-rayed sun, had dispelled the darkness of shame.
When that circle had reached its foundation, as if it were a pair of lovers, and when all those beings had departed toward their desired directions;

Then, from that place, at the end of the day, like birds returning to their nests, she—possessing long, tremulous outer corners of her eyes and with the agony of passion fully intensified—returned to the world of mortals.
Like a peahen approaching a rain-cloud, she came to the son of Bhṛgu, who was seated upon a prepared couch in the middle of a white chamber.
There Bhārgava entered, like Mādhava entering the Ocean of Milk; she, leaning upon his arms with her face cast down, entered after him.
And she shone like a lotus clinging to the heart of a celestial elephant; and she spoke these words in a sweet voice, moistened with passion and affection:
Behold his sweet speech, whose syllables are entwined with the playfulness of bliss; behold his face, like the orb of the stainless moon, which has drawn its bow into a circle.
"This Aṅgaka is indeed pursuing me, a weak woman; protect me, O Lord, for I am helpless, wretched, and here take refuge in you."
O noble one, know that comforting the miserable is a vow of virtuous conduct; it is practiced only by the foolish who do not understand the vision of true affection, O high-minded one.
Those who possess the power of discernment never disregard affection; for between two people who are mutually enamored, affection arises unexpectedly and spontaneously.
O beloved, she eclipses even the moon’s cooling radiance; yet this sovereignty over the three worlds does not gladden the heart as much as she does.
O giver of honor, just as there is mutual joy and affection between two people who have first fallen in love, so have I been comforted by the touch of your feet.
"Just as the night-lotus is touched by the moon's rays at night, O handsome one, I live through the drinking of the nectar of your touch."
Just as a restless female cakora bird longs for the drinking of the nectar of the moonbeams, so do you [long for] me, who am clinging to your feet, with your sprout-like hands.

"Embrace me and place me within your own lotus-heart, which is filled with nectar. Having spoken thus, she whose limbs were as soft as flowers fell upon his chest, her bee-like eyes rolling like a cluster of blossoms on a fine tree.
There, the couple, radiant with the splendor of their dalliance, entered those forest glades—lands shaken by winds white with lotus filaments—like two crimson bees entering among the lotuses.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, through those beloved expressions of affection long imagined by the play of his mind, the sage of Bhrigu’s lineage experienced a most perfect union that brought him great satisfaction.
Then, with her adorned with a garland of mandāra flowers and intoxicated by the nectar of the gods, he was accompanied by that second [companion], who was like the spotless moon.
He dwelt upon the banks of the celestial river, amidst golden lotus-beds where intoxicated swans sported, accompanied by Cāraṇas and Kiṃnaras.
The playful god, together with the deities, drank the elixir flowing from the moon’s crescent while dwelling within the bowers of *pārijāta* creepers.
For a long time, he sported with groups of restless Vidyadhara maidens upon a beautiful swing made of swaying creepers in the Caitraratha grove.
The expanse of the Nandana grove was violently churned by the first of Śambhu’s sons, just as the ocean was churned by Mount Mandara.
And he wandered through rivers thick with networks of young golden creepers, like the celestial groves of Mount Meru when they have been trampled by a mad elephant.
In the forest groves of Kailāsa, that lover spent nights as white as the moon with her, while the songs of the Gaṇas were sung.
Having rested upon the plateaus of Mount Gandhamādana, she was adorned by him from head to foot with golden lotuses.
O Rāma, he sported with her with laughter upon the shores of the Lokāloka mountain, which are enchanting with various wonders.
In the groves between the Mandara trees, together with the young fawns, he dwelt for sixty years in that constructed abode of the immortals.
On the shores of the Ocean of Milk, as he dwelt in the company of his consorts, half of the Kṛta Yuga was spent together with the inhabitants of Śvetadvīpa.
Through his playful creations of celestial cities and gardens, this creator of the infinite world-creation has come to imitate Time itself.
Then that Śukra dwelt again in the city of Purandara, happily with the fawn-eyed woman for eight cycles of four yugas.
Then, due to the exhaustion of his merit, he fell upon the circle of the earth with that very proud woman, his form impaired.
With all his limbs mangled by others, his chariot and its delights stripped away, he was overwhelmed by anxiety and ruined, like a soldier defeated in battle.
As he lay fallen upon the earth, his body shattered into a hundred pieces through long, agonizing thought, like a mountain torrent crashing against a rock.
When their two bodies were shattered and their minds were clouded by calamity, they wandered through the sky like two birds deprived of their nests.
There, those two entered the moon-like network of rays within his mind; having quickly attained the state of frost, they then became rice plants.
Having eaten those cooked rice grains in Daśārṇa, that best of the twice-born, Śukra, attained the state of semen and became the son of his wife.
Then, through association with sages, he established himself in fierce asceticism and dwelt in the thickets of Mount Meru for the duration of a Manvantara, O blameless one.
There, a son of a deer in human form was born to him; through affection for him, he again fell into a state of supreme delusion in an instant.
"May this son have wealth, virtues, and eternal life"—with such incessant anxieties, he abandoned his established state of truth.

Because he had fallen away from reflection on the Dharma and was preoccupied with thoughts of wealth for the sake of his son, Death carried him off as his lifespan was exhausted, just as a wind carries away a snake.
With his consciousness departed along with his singular preoccupation for enjoyments, he attained the status of a son to the lord of Madra and became the sovereign of the Madra land.
Having ruled for a long time in the land of Madra, having destroyed his enemies, he arrived here in old age, like a frost-bolt upon a lotus.
Together with his latent impression from asceticism, he abandoned the beautiful body of the King of Madra; because of that, he was born as this ascetic, the son of a forest-dweller.
O Rāma, having reached the bank of the great river Samaṅgā, that ascetic of great intelligence performed austerities, free from all distress.
Having experienced various states of birth and successions of bodies according to his diverse inclinations, that son of Bhṛgu remained happily on the bank of the excellent river like a firm tree.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: As Śukra was reflecting in this manner, a vast period of time consisting of many years passed before his father.
Then, after a long time, his body, withered by wind and heat, fell to the earth like a tree whose roots have been severed.
But the mind, its range flickering, wandered through those various and most diverse states, like a deer among the rows of forest trees.
His mind, wandering, reeling, and agitated as if cast upon a whirling wheel, found rest on the bank of the river Saṃgaṅgā.
Śukra remained as one devoid of a physical body, experiencing that state of worldly existence—which is dense with endless occurrences, yet both fragile and exceedingly firm.
Standing on the peak of Mount Mandara, the body of that wise one became withered by the spreading heat until it was reduced to mere skin.
Through the whistling sound of the wind flowing through the apertures of the body, his physical activity sings out like a sweet warble from the bliss of the destruction of suffering.
As if laughing at the wretched mind that wallows in the pits of the realms of existence, she smiles with her row of teeth white as bright clouds.
Displaying the natural emptiness of the world through her own form, she possessed the beauty of a hollow resembling a withered well in a forest clearing.
Scorched by the heat and now drenched by the weight of the rainwater, she sheds tears as if releasing the joy of remembering her former state.
In the forest lands, agitated by the playful movement of the moon and the wind, the ground was pierced by the falling showers at the arrival of the clouds.
On the bank of the mountain river, she was drenched by the form of monsoon torrents and covered with dust raised by the wind, as if defiled by her own evil deeds.
Trembling like dry wood in the winds, her form reduced to mere skin and bone, she stood in the forest as if performing penance amidst the whistling of the piercing gales.
Crooked, with a string of dried entrails, causing the shrieks of spirits, she is like the Fortune of the Forest in her youth—a hollow being whose belly is made of skin.
Because that holy hermitage was free from passion and hatred, and because of Bhrigu’s great ascetic power, it was not consumed by beasts or birds.

Her slender form emaciated by restraints and observances, she practiced austerities that captivated the mind of the descendant of Bhṛgu; then her body, its blood drained away by the wind, lay for a long time upon the vast rocks.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, after a thousand divine years, Bhṛgu, the supreme lord, ceased from his meditative absorption due to the attainment of ultimate awakening.
He did not see his son before him—his face bowed in humility, the leader of a host of virtues, standing there like merit incarnate.
He saw before him a great skeleton, solitary, appearing as if it were a body endowed with life, like misfortune or poverty personified.
Its body was withered by the heat; partridges were twitching within the openings of its skin; and frogs rested in the shadows of the hollows of its dried-out entrails and belly.
With newly hatched insects clinging within the sockets of its eyes, and swarms of silkworms threaded upon the cage of its ribs.

With her intestines washed away by the stream [of tears], she likewise possessed a garland of bones that was utterly parched, as if by the desire for past enjoyments that yield both desired and undesired fruits.
With his bright, smooth head-jar, radiant as the moon, he emulated the beauty of the top of a linga drenched in camphor.
With a straight neck, its veins withered away and nothing remaining but the bones, stretching upward as if to lengthen his very form.

He bore the appearance of having the boundary of his mouth defined by the bone of the tip of his nose, which was as pale as a lotus stalk and from which the flesh had been washed away by the stream [of blood].
Surely, with her long neck raised and her face turned upward, she was watching as if for the life-breaths departing into the expanse of the sky.
With his shanks, thighs, knees, and staff-like arms having attained double their length, he appeared like a foundation that had become unsteady out of fear of the exhaustion from a long journey.
With his belly excessively emaciated until it was mere skin, he seemed to demonstrate the extreme emptiness of the heart of a fool.
Beholding that tethering post of a garland of withered skeletons belonging to the elephant of suffering, he leapt from the precipice without reflecting on what had preceded or followed.
For at the very moment the light appeared, Bhṛgu’s eloquence arose; in an instant, he wondered, "Has this son of mine been dead for a long time? and then [realized he was not].
As he was thus reflecting upon his future son, a most terrible anger toward Time (Death) quickly arose within him.
"Why was my son taken away at such an untimely hour?"—thus provoked to anger, the Blessed One proceeded to cast a curse upon Time.
Then Kāla, having assumed a form and swallowed the subjects, approached the sage, having taken on a physical body composed of material elements.
The glorious one holds a sword and a noose; he wears earrings and is endowed with armor; he has six arms and six faces, and is surrounded by a vast army of servants.
With the leaping mass of flames arising from his body, the sky bore the splendor of a mountain covered with blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees.
With the circles of fire issuing from the tips of the tridents held in his hands, the quarters of the sky shone as if adorned with rising golden earrings.
The mountains, their peaks cast down by the force of his breath, swayed and fell, reeling as if mounted upon a swing.
By the radiance of the circle of his sword, the dark disk of the sun appeared as if it were clouded by the smoke of a world consumed at the end of an aeon.
Having approached that great sage, who was enraged and as deep as the ocean agitated at the end of an aeon, O mighty-armed one, he spoke to him with conciliatory words.

O Sage, those who have understood the nature of the world and have seen both the higher and the lower are not deluded even by means of a logical reason; how much less so, then, without a reason, O Supreme One?
"You are a brahmin of infinite splendor, while we are merely upholders of destiny; therefore, O virtuous one, you are honored as one worthy of honor, and not by the will of another."
O unwise one, do not exhaust yourself with penance through the great fires of the aeons; since I am not burned by them, what can you burn me with by your curse?
O Sage, we have swallowed and devoured millions of Rudras, we have consumed multitudes of Viṣṇus, and we have devoured the cycles of saṃsāra; where, indeed, are we not capable?
"For we, O Brahmin, are the eaters, while you and others are the food; this is indeed the fixed law of nature, not something intended by us."
Fire ascends by itself; waters flow downward by themselves; food goes to the eater, and the Ender himself brings about the dissolution of creation.
O Sage, this form of mine here is thus: the Self manifests by itself, within its own self, and of its own accord.
By the vision that has destroyed all taints, there is neither an agent nor an enjoyer here; yet by the vision that has not destroyed its taints, there are many agents here.
O Brahmin, agency and non-agency are merely conceptual constructs; they exist only for one with incorrect vision, not for one with correct vision.
Flowers in groves of trees and beings in the worlds come and go here of their own accord; they are conceptualized by means of names that serve as causes.
Just as the reflected moon possesses neither agency nor non-agency in its movement—being neither real nor unreal—so it is with Time in its creations.
The mind, through the engagement with false delusions, produces a conceptualization consisting of agency and non-agency, just as one with impaired vision perceives a snake in a rope.
Therefore, O Sage, do not give way to anger; such is the course of calamities. Whatever has happened, see it quickly as it truly is, without agitation.
We do not strive for the sake of reputation, nor are we overcome by pride; for, my dear, we are independent by our own nature and abide solely in destiny.
By the power of necessity, the wise proceed toward the inevitable course of worldly activity; it is not the great darkness of ego-inflation that leads them.
Those skilled in action must certainly and invariably perform their duty; however, you should never destroy it by resorting to the state of deep sleep.
Where is that vision consisting of wisdom? Where is your greatness? Where is your fortitude? Even though the path is well-known to all, why do you wander in confusion like a blind man?
O Sage, why do you wish to curse me in vain like a fool, without considering my current state, which has arisen from the ripening of the fruits of my own karma?
O Sage, for all embodied beings here, the body is of two kinds; do you not know that one is the physical body and the other is called the mind?
In this regard, the body is utterly inert and destined for destruction, and the mind is trivial; both are inevitably subjected to suffering for your sake.
O virtuous one, just as a chariot is driven by a skillful charioteer, so too should this body be guided by the mind out of some measure of affection.
An improper resolve is formed and the body is destroyed in an instant by the mind, just as a clay figure was destroyed by a child.
In this world, the mind alone is the person; what is done by it is said to be "done. Bound by the cause of conceptualization, it is bound; when freed from conceptualization, it is liberated.
"This body," "this limb situated here," "this head"—that which undergoes such expansive modifications is designated as the mind alone.

For the mind is called the living principle (jīva) because of its unity of resolve; it is the intellect (dhī) by virtue of its determinative nature, and it is the ego (ahaṅkāra) due to its sense of self-identification; indeed, its own manifoldness arises from itself.
If the mind, through the latent impression of a body and by its own desire, wishes for others, it perceives earthly bodies that do not exist.
If one perceives the truth, then the mind, consisting of that truth, abandons the conception of a body and attains supreme bliss.
While you were established in meditative absorption, the mind of your son traveled further and further away along the path of its own desires.
Having abandoned this body of Aushanasa in a cave of Mount Mandara, he departed for the abode of the gods, like a bird flying up from its nest.
There, among the Mandara and Guñja trees, at the foot of Pārijāta trees, in the groves of the Nandana garden, and in the cities of the World-Protectors;
O Sage, for eight cycles of four ages, that one of great splendor attended upon Viśvācī, the celestial beauty, as a bee attends a lotus.
Then, when his store of merit was exhausted—though he had fashioned it all from his own volitions born of intense spiritual urgency—it vanished like the nocturnal mist.
With his floral crest withered and the luster of his limbs and members faded, he fell along with her like a fruit ripened by time.
Having abandoned that divine body in the sky like a mere physical form, and having reached the elemental ether, he was then born upon the earth.
There was once a brahmin among the Daśārṇas, a king among the Kosalas, a fisherman in the great forest, and a swan on the banks of the triple-pathed river (Gaṅgā).
In the Solar dynasty there was King Pauṇḍra, the preceptor among the Sauras and Śālvas; then there was the glorious and wise Vidyādhara Kalpa, who was the son of a sage.
Then the protector of the earth, who was then a young ascetic, became known as Vāsudeva and dwelt on the bank of the Samaṅgā river.
Furthermore, by the power of his own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), your son wandered of his own accord through various other intermediate wombs that were indeed distressing.
He was again a Kirāta on Mount Vindhya and among the Kaikaṭas; then he was a Sāmanta among the Sauvīras and a Gardabha among the Trigartas.
The bamboo thicket is found among the Kirātas; the deer in the forests of Cīna; the reptile in the palm trees; and the wild cock in the Tamāla groves.
This very son of yours, having become the best among those who know mantras, formerly recited the lore that bestows the city of the Vidyādharas.
By that [means], O Brahmin, he became a great Vidyādhara in the sky, adorned with necklaces, earrings, and armlets, and with locks of hair falling in playful abundance.
He was like another flower-bowed god to the lotus-like heroines; he was the beloved of the Vidyādharīs and the ornament of the city of the Gandharvas.
Having reached the end of the eon within the splendor of the twelve suns, he was reduced to ashes, like a moth in a fire.
Then, in the vast sky devoid of the creation of the world, that latent impression of his wandered like a bird without a nest.
Then, when the time had arrived for the commencement of the construction of the world—a process involving manifold undertakings—at the end of the night of Brahmā, following its reversal.
O Sage, that latent impression (vāsanā) of his, though shaken by the wind, having attained the state of a Brahmin when [the age] was established, has today been born upon the surface of the earth.
O Sage, that young Brahmin named Vāsudeva was born among the wise, having studied the entirety of the Vedas.
O great sage, having become a Vidyadhara for a kalpa, your son is now performing austerities, stationed on the bank of the river Samaṅgā.

Driven by the persistence of various worldly desires, he has entered into the hollows of *khadira* and *karañja* trees, which are as formidable as caverns, and into the most dense forest regions within this world that serve as wombs for the belly.
Kāla said: "Today, on the very bank of the river, where the wind resounds with the crashing of a flood of wild waves, your son is performing austerities."
Wearing matted hair and a rosary of seeds, having conquered the delusions of all his senses, he remained there for eight hundred years, steadfast in his ascetic practice.
O Sage, if you wish to see that which is like a dream, a delusion of the mind, then quickly open the eye of higher knowledge and behold it.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When this had been spoken by the Lord of the World, Kāla, who regards all with an equal eye, the sage reflected upon the welfare of his son with the eye of knowledge.
And in a moment, by the power of his inspired intuition, he beheld the entire account of his son reflected upon the mirror of his intellect.
Then, having come from the bank of the Samaṅgā river, Bhṛgu entered his own body, which was situated on the ridge of Mount Mandara, healthy and established at the edge of time.
Gazing at Kāla with a smile of wonder, the beloved spoke these words; then the passionless sage, himself free from passion, replied with these words.
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, we are but children, lacking brilliance; for only those like you, O God, possess an intellect that perceives the three times with stainless clarity.
Abounding in various forms and transformations, appearing as unreal even while being real, this state of the world produces delusion even for the wise man.
O Lord, you alone know that form which exists within you and which acts as a magician’s trick for this mental activity of hers.
"O Blessed One, it is said that death does not exist for this son of mine; therefore, seeing him dead, I have become filled with agitation."
"O Lord, by the power of destiny, my time has been spent thinking, 'My son's life is not yet exhausted,' and thus even this trivial desire arose within me."
"O Lord, although we have understood the course of saṃsāra, we still fall under the sway of joy and resentment when encountering both misfortunes and successes."
"Anger toward one who acts improperly and favor toward one who acts properly—this, O Blessed One, is the established way of the world."

"This must be done" and "this must not be done"—as long as there is such activity, it is the delusion of the world. O Teacher of the World, the complete renunciation of this [delusion] is indeed what must be abandoned.
O Blessed One, because we became angry with you when we did not perceive that this was merely your own thought, may we be afflicted by that [anger].
"O Lord, I have now been reminded by you of what was intended for my son; therefore, this son was seen by me on the bank of the Samaṅgā."
In this world, the mind is the two bodies that pervade all beings; for the mind alone is the body by which this universe is perceived.
Kāla said: "O Brahmin, you have spoken correctly regarding the body and the mind; through volition, the mind creates the body just as a potter fashions a jar."
Through the delusion of the mind, by means of volition, the fool creates an uncreated form and destroys what has been created in an instant, just like a child [frightened] by a Vetāla.
And likewise, powers manifesting as agitation, dreams, false cognitions, and the like, appearing in the form of cities of the Gandharvas, are seen within the mind.
Relying, however, upon this gross perspective, O great sage, it is said that a person consists of two bodies: the mind and the physical body.
O Sage, these three worlds are merely a mental construction of the mind; they have arisen as a vast expanse that is neither existent nor non-existent, and nothing else.
Through the creeper-like limbs of the body of consciousness, fueled by the latent impression of duality, this manifoldness has arisen from ignorance, like the appearance of two moons.
The mind, through the latent impression of duality, perceives the entire collection of objects; it sees everything everywhere as distinct, such as jars, pits, cloths, and so forth.
"Emaciated, deeply miserable, and deluded—I am," and by cultivating these and other such notions arising from its own conceptual constructions, the mind undergoes the state of transmigration.
"Thinking is an artificial form; this is not my true nature, for I am that [Self]. Through the abandonment of that [thinking], the mind becomes tranquil—the eternal Brahman.
Just as in the vast ocean, which possesses many rows of waves yet remains tranquil in its movement, there is no single distinct wave.
In the Self, which is like water—equal, clear, pure, sweet, cool, indestructible, vast, of great majesty, and manifest;
A short wave, while manifesting its own form through the absence of intrinsic nature, produces the mental cultivation of "I am short" by means of conceptual construction.
A long wave, while manifesting its own form through the absence of intrinsic nature, creates the mental cultivation of "I am long" by means of conceptual construction.
Thinking, "I am short and my form has fallen away," one goes to the Talātala realm by means of that very contemplation.
Once arisen, one should cultivate the thought, "I have risen above the corpse"; then, a net of jewels with rays of light shines forth with radiant splendor.
Residing within the orb of the moon, he reflects the thought, "I am cool"; yet, as a reflection of the forest fire upon the mountain slopes, his body blazes with flame.
Alas, he trembles in silence, crying out, "I am burnt! while the trees on the slopes of the coastal mountains, reflected therein, appear to share his distress.
He shines with the thought, "I am engaged in the intense exertion of a great undertaking," even though his flickering body has been utterly destroyed by the violently surging winds.
Crying out as if in lamentation, "I have been torn to pieces," you roared; yet those waves are not distinct from the water-bearing ocean.
Not even a single form among these is either existent or composed of non-existence; nor are qualities such as shortness or length [inherently] in them, yet they are not absent from them.

For the norms are indeed established within the ocean, yet they are not non-established therein; they are merely rendered fragmented by the conceptual constructions residing in their own respective natures.
Perished and yet not perished, born again and again; though born and unborn repeatedly, they do not truly attain any state of difference through their mutual interaction.
Just as [beings] are indeed free from affliction, consisting of the commonality of water which is of a single form, so too in this vast, white, pure, and stainless [expanse].

In Brahman, whose sole body is pure Brahman, who possesses an expansive form, who is omnipotent, and who is without beginning or end, all things are non-different from him, even though they appear as if distinct.
The various powers, established [within Him], are restless due to their diverse modes of conduct; for indeed, the manifoldness of the many powers attains its station within His own body.
Brahman is expanded within Brahman like a circle of waves within water; as Brahman itself, it revolves in the form of female, male, and neuter.
There has never been, is not, and will never be any conceptual construction other than that which is called "the world"; not even the slightest difference exists between Brahman and the world.
"Indeed, this entire universe is Brahman; the world is nothing but Brahman alone. Meditate thus with effort and abandon everything else.
Though manifold in form yet single in essence, and producing hundreds of diverse appearances, destiny—fixed in its own nature—presides over all things.

The mind takes up both the insentient and the sentient and enters into that which consists of consciousness; it is the power in the form of latent impressions belonging to the self established in its own nature.
O sinless one, it is Brahman alone that expands in this vast form, filled with various manifestations like the ocean with its surging waves.
Through dwelling in various forms, it assumes diversity by itself; the self, by the self alone within itself, is like the water of the ocean within the water.
Just as various waves are not distinct from the water, so all conceptual constructions are not distinct from the Lord of All.
Just as there are the arrangements of branches, flowers, creepers, leaves, fruits, and buds within a single seed, so too does every potentiality always exist therein.
Just as a variety of colors is seen in the harsh sunlight, so too does a variety of powers—consisting of both the existent and the non-existent—reside in the Lord of Gods.
This world of diverse forms arises from the undifferentiated Śiva, just as a rainbow appears from a cloud of a single color.
From the non-inert, the state of inertness arises, caused by the contemplation of dullness, just as thread emerges from a spider or as deep sleep arises from a person.
When the mind is not purified, Śiva, by his own will, extends his power for the sake of its bondage, just as a silkworm weaves a cocoon of threads.
O Brahmin, by its own will, this self brings about forgetfulness of itself and undergoes a harsh bondage, just like a silkworm.
O Brahmin, by voluntarily contemplating one's own body as the Self, which is Brahman, one attains liberation from saṃsāra, just as an elephant is freed from its tethering post.
Just as one constantly cultivates the self, so too does it become itself; likewise, even though it is great, it is swiftly filled with power.
Cultivated power leads the self to its true nature in an instant, just as a great, all-encompassing mist at the onset of the rainy season [conceals] the infinite whole.
The unborn [Self], when impelled by that power, quickly attains identity with it; just as a tree, having reached the state of a particular season, becomes identical with that season.
There is no liberation for the Lord, nor is there bondage for the Self; I do not know from where these notions of bondage and liberation have arisen in the world.
There is no bondage, nor is there liberation; yet it appears as if composed of that very [bondage]. Alas, this world, consisting of illusion, is eternally swallowed by the impermanent!
As soon as the mind was conceptualized by this one who is himself devoid of parts, then this self was enveloped by it, like a silkworm in its cocoon.
Yet, these millions of mental powers, which possess entirely distinct forms and imagined bodies, emerge from this very source.
Born from that, abiding in that, yet appearing as distinct forms, like waves from the ocean; born from that, abiding in that, yet existing separately, like rays from the moon.

In this vast ocean of the Supreme Self, which consists of vibration, whose waters are consciousness, whose expansive expanse is spread wide, and which is garlanded with the essence of pure consciousness alone;

Some remain stable as Brahmā and Viṣṇu; some have attained the state of Rudra; some have reached the condition of a Puruṣa; and some have become deities. These surging waves, whose natures are manifested by their own inherent being, flash forth: some as Yama, Mahendra, Arka, Vahni, Vaiśravaṇa, and others. These waves, characterized by restless desire, kill, act, and stand still. Some appear as Kinnaras, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Suras, and so forth; these fierce waves leap up and fall down, tossing about. Some possess a somewhat stable form, such as the one born from the lotus (Brahmā); others are born and then destroyed, such as the gods, humans, and others.
Worms, insects, moths, snakes, mice, pythons, and so forth—some of these flash about in that great ocean like drops of water.
Some restless creatures—men, deer, vultures, jackals, and others—flit about in the mountain thickets like birds on the shores of the coastal forests.
Some have very long lives, while others have extremely short lives; some possess substantial mental capacities, while others have meager physical bodies.
In the turbulent dream of saṃsāra, some are imbued with a sense of stability, while others, struck down by false conceptualizations, imagine the world to be truly firm.
Some have very little cultivation [of the mind], being overcome by the fault of dejection; others are overcome by sufferings, thinking, "I am emaciated, extremely miserable, and deluded."
Some have attained the state of stationary beings, some have reached the state of deities; some have attained the state of men, and some have gone to the state of the ocean.

Some remain in this world for many hundreds of aeons, while others, pure as the moon, proceed to the supreme state; for the cognitions of consciousness—which possess "thinking" as their other name—arise from the ocean of Brahman like restless waves.
Kāla said: O Sage, these cognitions that take the forms of gods, asuras, and humans are non-different from the ocean of Brahman; this is the truth, and everything else is false.
O Brahmin, those defiled by their own conceptual constructions through false meditation have indeed fallen to lower states because of the internal conviction that "we are not Brahman."
Even those who have entered the ocean of Brahman, conceiving of themselves as distinct from Brahman, become deluded within the terrifying realms of worldly existence.
Know that these cognitions, though belonging to Brahman and yet stained solely by the act of thinking, are indeed non-action (akarma), even though they serve as the seed of karmas.
O sage, by means of this very internal mental construction in the form of volition—a terrifying handful of seeds for the *karañja* trees of the web of karma—[the world is produced].
These rows of stone-like bodies, spread throughout the world, remain still, leap about, weep, and laugh.
From the realm of Brahmā down to a blade of grass, like the wind through its vibrations, they surge forth, withdraw, wither, and laugh.
Among these, some are exceedingly pure, such as Hari, Hara, and others; some are abodes of slight delusion, such as the uragas, naras, and amaras.
Some remain in a state of extreme delusion, such as trees, grass, and the like; others, utterly bewildered by ignorance, have reached the state of worms and insects.
Some are carried away like straw, far from the great ocean of Brahman; these have not attained the [spiritual] stages, just like serpents, mountains, and so forth.
Perceiving only the presence of a living being, certain [beings] approach in this way; whether already born or yet unborn, they are buried by the aged rat of Death.
Having reached the inner core of the great ocean of the reality of Brahman, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Hara, and the others have attained that state together with their respective functions.
Some, whose nature is characterized by little delusion, remain supported by that very ocean of Brahma, which has an unfathomable shore and a flood of grounds.
Some classes of beings remain as barren, manifesting in the darkness, having exhausted millions of multitudes of births yet to be experienced and multitudes of births already experienced.
Some go from above to below, like a large fruit falling from the hand; some go further upward from above, while others go even lower from below.

This inexhaustible mine that produces much pleasure and pain has arrived here through the non-remembrance of the supreme state; it goes to destruction through the realization of the supreme state, just as the agony of poison vanishes through the remembrance of the Lord of Birds.
Kāla said: "Of these various and diverse classes of beings, as of waves from the ocean, or as of various creepers in the month of Mādhava."
Fortunate ones who have conquered mental delusion, who have perceived the higher and lower worlds, and who are liberated while living—yakṣas, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras—wander here in this world.
But others, whether stationary or moving, are as ignorant as wood or a wall; others have their delusion destroyed—what need is there to deliberate about them?
In this world, for the sake of establishing the self of living beings who are awakening, various treatises have been composed and promulgated by those who have realized the Self.
But for those whose intentions are fully awakened through the exhaustion of their misdeeds, their intellect proceeds stainlessly in the investigation of the treatises.
The delusion of the mind dissolves through the investigation of the true scriptures, just as the darkness of night vanishes from the sky due to the movement of the sun.
For a mind that does not diminish leads only to delusion and not to accomplishment; like a mist concealing it, it leaps about like a vetāla spirit.
O Sage, in this world, for all bodies whatsoever, it is the mind alone that is the vessel for pleasure, pain, and objects, and not the body composed of flesh.
This collection of flesh and bones that is seen, composed of the five elements—know it to be a mental construction; in the ultimate sense, it is not the body.
O Sage, this son of yours has quickly obtained exactly what he brought upon himself through his own mind and body; we are not at fault in this matter.
Whatever action a person performs according to their own latent tendencies, they obtain exactly that; in this world, there is no agency for anyone else.
Who indeed is there in this world, even the Lord of the Universe, who possesses the power to undo that which has been internally arranged by one's own mental impressions?
Those creations which are the expanses of hell, and those desires for birth and death—through the mental imagining of the mind, this [world], though motionless, bestows suffering.
What is the use of saying much more here regarding this compilation of words? Arise, O Blessed One; let us go to where your son is staying.
Having experienced everything with his mental body, Śukra remained for a moment as if motionless, like an ascetic who has become still through contact with the rays of the moon.
The vital breath (prāṇa-pavana), released from the mind like a ray of the moon, becomes the fruit through its state of distillation; by means of that vigor, it remains within.
Having spoken thus regarding the course of the world, the Lord Kāla, as if smiling, seized Bhṛgu with his hand, just as the sun seizes the moon with its ray.
Saying, "Oh, how wonderful is the established order of destiny! the venerable Bhṛgu slowly rose up like the sun from the mountain of sunrise.

O dear one, those two treasures of splendor, having risen together, then shone in the expanse of the sky filled with tamāla groves, like the sun and the full moon rising simultaneously in a cloudless firmament to sport amidst the rain-clouds.

Śrī Vālmīki said: When the sage had spoken thus, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then the two deities, Kāla and Bhṛgu, set out from a cave in the Mandara mountain to go upon the earth to the bank of the river Samaṅgā.
As they were descending from the mountain, those two of great splendor saw sky-dwellers sleeping within bowers formed by networks of fresh golden creepers.
[He saw] those who, playing in the courtyard of the sky with swings made of creeping vines, recalled blue lotuses by their gazes, as innocent and charming as those of a doe.
They sat upon high stone slabs used as seats by perfected beings (siddhas), appearing as if they were personified fortitude itself, having effortlessly beheld the three worlds.
The leaders of the elephant herds were immersed in a continuous downpour of falling flowers, while they raised their trunks as high as palm trees.
They were as if intoxicated, drowsy with pride, and standing there like personified forms of arrogance, their limbs reddened by the filaments of flowers and their tails crimsoned by the wind.
The restless yak-tails, the beautiful chowries of the circle of kings, were immersed in incessant showers of falling flowers.
He saw wild date palms inhabited by *kinnaras*, whose branches had become straightened and whose bamboo-like whistling was silenced as they struck one another’s fruits.

The mountain peaks were covered with thickets of *dhātupāṭala* and *durvakra* trees, where monkeys frolicked with great vigor; its plateaus were shrouded by canopies of climbing vines, and it contained groves that served as natural dwellings.
[He saw] the perfected ones being struck by celestial women with mandārava flowers, [their bodies] veiled by clouds as white as ash-red mineral pigments.

The rivers, with their masses of waves covered in *kunda* and *mandāra* flowers, appeared like Buddhist renunciants gathered on the riverbanks; as if out of longing for the ocean, they had donned the adornments of the spring season.
The trees, their limbs laden with a weight of flowers and shaken by the wind, reeled like drunkards upon obtaining honey, with bees for their eyes.
Beholding from here and there the vast splendor of the king of mountains, the two of them reached the earth adorned with cities and towns.
In an instant, they reached there the river Samaṅgā, which, with its waves shimmering with flowers, seemed as if it were composed entirely of blossoms.
Then, on a certain bank, Bhṛgu beheld his son, who had undergone a transformation of body and attained another state of being.

With his senses stilled and established in meditative concentration, the deer of his mind was motionless, as if having found rest after a very long time for the sake of quelling its long-standing weariness.
He seemed to be contemplating the infinite courses of the ocean of worldly existence—long enjoyed and recently abandoned—which are incessantly filled with joy and sorrow.
Surely it has attained immobility, like a wheel that has spun excessively, as if from the extreme whirling of the infinite cycles of the world.
He stood in a secluded spot, lovely and solitary, having taken refuge in solitude; his laughter was stilled, and the agitation and attachment of his mind were utterly broken.
