Established in non-conceptual samādhi, he had ceased from the activity of dualities and laughed at the entire course of worldly existence with a mind that was cool as ice.
Free from all occurrences, free from the state of being an enjoyer in its entirety, with the web of conceptual construction cast aside, it rests upon the supreme station.
In that state of infinite rest, one rests within the Self, like a white jewel that remains without grasping at reflections.
Bhṛgu beheld his son, whose intellect was fully awakened and steadfast, and who was entirely free from the conceptual constructions of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted.
Beholding that son of Bhṛgu, Kāla spoke these words to Bhṛgu, with a voice resembling the roar of the ocean: "This is indeed your son."
With the words "Awake!", he emerged from his meditative absorption, just as a peacock slowly rouses itself at the roar of thunderclouds.
Opening his eyes, he beheld at the end two powerful lords, Kāla and Bhṛgu, who had arrived together like the gods Śaśin and Divākara.
Then, rising from their seats of *kadamba* creepers, those two lovely brahmins, having come together as equals, bowed down like Hiraṇyakaśipu and Hari.
Having performed their mutual greetings, they sat down upon a stone slab, like Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, who are worshipped by the world, seated upon the summit of Mount Meru.
Then, O Rāma, that twice-born man, having completed his silent recitation on the bank of the Samaṅgā, spoke these peaceful words, beautiful as a flow of nectar.
By the sight of you two today, I have attained peace, like the world when the cool-rayed and the hot-rayed ones have appeared together.
That delusion of my mind, which could not be destroyed by scripture, nor by austerity, nor even by knowledge or learning—that has been exhausted by the sight of you two.
Showers of pure nectar do not bring such inner delight as these visions of the great ones bring rapturous joy.
"Who are you two of such immense splendor that, with your feet, you have sanctified this region of ours, just as the moon and sun sanctify the sky?"
To him who had spoken thus, Bhṛgu said to his son from a previous birth: "Remember yourself; you have awakened, O scion of Raghu—you are not ignorant."
Awakened by Bhṛgu, he remembered his own state in a previous birth for a mere moment, his eyes opened wide in meditation.
Then, with a face smiling from wonder and a joyful mind, that best of speakers uttered words slow with reflection:
The destiny of the Supreme Self has its beginning unknown in this world; under its power, this expansive wheel of the universe revolves.
My infinite past births, though unknown, have likewise had infinite results, like those experienced from the beginning of the eon until its end.
We have witnessed intense struggles for power and the delusions of acquiring wealth; we have also wandered for a long time upon the peaks of Mount Meru, free from all sorrow.
On the slopes of the mountain of the gods, there is the yellow, fragrant water of the Mandākinī, reddened by the filaments of mandāra flowers and filled with kahlāra lilies.
He wandered through the groves of Mount Mandara, where golden creepers were in full bloom, and upon the peaks of Mount Meru, beautiful with flowers and the shade of wish-fulfilling trees.

There is nothing that has not been experienced, there is nothing that has not been done, and there is nothing that has not been seen among the various occurrences of the desirable and the undesirable.
That which was to be known has now been known; that which was to be seen has been seen unimpaired. I am at rest, having long been weary; all my delusion has come to an end.
"Arise, dear father, let us go; let us see that body situated on Mount Mandara, which has already begun to wither like a dried-out forest creeper."
In this world, there is nothing desired by me, nor is there anything undesired; I merely wander about to behold the unfolding of destiny.

I follow that which is exceedingly beautiful and practiced by the noble ones with a mind of single-minded devotion; let this be my cherished resolve, while I continue to carry out these worldly activities as they have arisen.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Reflecting thus upon the courses of the world, those knowers of reality departed from that bank of the Samaga river, their lives moving with restless energy.
Gradually ascending into the sky and emerging from the hollows of the clouds, they reached the cave of Mount Mandara in an instant by way of the path of the Siddhas.
On the plateau of that mountain, the descendant of Bhṛgu beheld his own body from a previous birth, now withered but still covered by moist leaves.
And he said this: "O father, this slender body is indeed that very same one which was formerly cherished by you with pleasant enjoyments."
This is that body of mine, whose every limb the nurse once anointed for a long time with affection using camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood.
This is that very body of mine, for which a cool bed was prepared with heaps of Mandāraka flowers upon the grounds of the groves of Mount Meru.
Behold, this very body of mine, once caressed by hosts of intoxicated celestial women, now lies upon the surface of the earth, crushed by the mouths of crawling serpents.
This very body of mine, by which I long sported in the groves of the sandalwood garden, has now become a withered skeleton.
Today my body withers away, deprived of mental activity that once took the form of lofty amorous passion through contact with the limbs of celestial nymphs.
Amidst those various amorous pastimes and in those various conditions, you are so bound by the contemplation of them; how then, O little body, can you remain at ease?
"Alas! You whose name was 'Tana' have come to wither like an ascetic; you have become a mere skeleton, O ill-fated woman, and you terrify me."
By that very body through whose playful enjoyments I once delighted, I now feel fear because it has become a mere skeleton.
Behold, where that necklace formerly shone like a web of stars upon my chest, ants are now crawling there.
Behold, that very body of mine, which once captivated excellent women with its luster like molten gold, is now being dragged away as a mere skeleton.
Behold, with my wide-gaping mouth, its dry hide flayed by the heat, and with my skull-like face, I terrify the deer in the forest.
I see that the cave-like interior of my corpse’s belly, due to its state of complete desiccation, shines as if illuminated by the rays of the sun or by discernment itself.
This slender body, parched and lying supine upon the stone of the mountain, seems to lead the hearts of the virtuous toward dispassion by means of its own insignificance.
Through non-conceptual meditative absorption, which is liberated from attachment to sound, form, taste, touch, and smell, this very [state] is dried up upon the mountain.
With the demon of the mind surely liberated, her body remains as if in bliss; it does not fear even the slightest injury from the gods.
When the vampire of the mind has been completely stilled, the body attains a fraction of that bliss which cannot be reached even by sovereignty over the world.
Behold how he sleeps happily in the forest—his doubts at rest, all curiosity vanished, and the web of mental constructions cast aside.
The tree of the body, agitated by the frantic agitation of the monkey-mind, trembles with such force that it cuts itself away from its very roots.
On the mountain, my body—liberated from the miseries of the mind and established as if in supreme bliss—no longer perceives the conflict between elephants, clouds, and lions.
I see no other source of welfare for living beings than mindlessness (*acittatva*), which is like the arrival of autumn to the mist of delusion caused by the fever of all desires.
Those very ones of great intelligence, whose minds were once peaceful, have now reached the ultimate limit of the enjoyment of pleasure by becoming despondent.
By good fortune, I behold in this forest this body of mine, freed from all states of suffering, established in a state free from fever, and beyond mental agitation.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, it is said that at that time, many bodies were repeatedly consumed by the descendant of Bhṛgu."
Since this body was produced by Bhṛgu, what further great excellence could possibly have arisen in it? It is nothing but a cause for lamentation.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, that conceptualization of Śukra which had reached the state of a living being was born as the son of Bhṛgu, in the form of Bhārgava, consisting of the nature of karma.
For she, having first emerged from the supreme state and reached the state of the elemental ether, became agitated by the winds.
Entering the heart of Bhṛgu by means of the flow of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, it gradually attained virility and became the body of Uśanas.
Having received the sacraments prescribed for a Brahmin girl, she remained there before her father; in the course of time, she attained the state of a withered skeleton.
Since this body of Brahmā had arrived for the very first time, Śukra then uttered that lamentation directed toward it.
Though free from passion and devoid of desire, Śukra, assuming the form of Samāṅgā, grieved for his body; for such is the inherent nature born of the physical frame.
Whether for one who knows or for one who does not, this sequence persists as long as the body exists; this worldly transaction continues always, whether through attachment or detachment.
Those who have fully understood the course of existence and those who are ignorant, following the nature of cattle, both remain within worldly conventions like those caught in a net.

In worldly affairs, the ignorant man is exactly like the most learned scholar; here, the difference lies solely in their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which is the cause that bestows either bondage or liberation.
As long as there is a body, so long indeed is there suffering in suffering and pleasure in pleasure; yet the wise, whose minds are unattached, demonstrate [this] like those who are not awakened.
Great-souled ones are always happy amidst pleasures and sorrowful amidst painful conditions; for they appear just like those who are unawakened.
The reflections of the sun are disturbed, but not the sun itself; knowing this distinction between the moving and the unmoving, the knower abides amidst the activities of the world.
Like the sun remaining steady and composed amidst its reflections, he—though having completely abandoned worldly activities—is truly a Buddha, even while appearing to possess an unawakened intellect.

For one whose faculty of intellect is liberated is liberated even if the faculty of action is bound; likewise, one whose faculty of intellect is bound is bound even if the faculty of action is liberated.

In this world, the perceptions of pleasure and pain, as well as the perceptions of bondage and liberation, have the intellect and the senses alone as their cause, just as lights are the cause for illumination.
Maintain conduct appropriate for the world outwardly, while remaining free from internal worldly conduct; remain perfectly equanimous, with all desires completely stilled.
Remaining within yourself by means of your own self, which is liberated from all desires, perform the necessary actions; for the maintenance of the body is indeed required.
Do not fall into this pit of calamity, this fierce blind well of "mine-ness," upon the path of saṃsāra which is a deep chasm with great whirlpools of mental and physical afflictions.
You are not in things, nor are things in you, O lotus-eyed one; you are of the nature of pure awakening—remain as the self, firmly established within.
You are indeed the stainless, pure Brahman; you are the self of all and the creator of all. Contemplating the entire universe as peaceful and unborn, be truly happy.

O Great-Souled One, having attained the stainless state free from longing and with the great darkness of the notion of "mine" dispelled, if you prevail over the mind, homage to you, the one of supreme wisdom, the great and virtuous being!
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, having set aside the words of his son as well as those of Bhṛgu, the Lord Kāla spoke these words in a deep resonance.
Kāla said: "O Bhārgava, having cast off this body of a female ascetic, enter this [new] body, O virtuous one, just as a king enters a city."
O sinless one, at the proper time, you must again perform penance with that body of yours which was previously victorious, so that you may attain the status of lord of the asuras.
When the end of the great aeon has arrived, you must cast off this body of Bhārgava so that it is not taken up again, like a withered flower.
Having attained the state of liberation while living, remain, O high-minded one, performing the role of preceptor to the great lords of the asuras with this body of your former form.
May it be well with you both; we shall go to our desired direction, for there is nothing whatsoever that would not be pleasing to his mind.
Having spoken thus, as they shed tears, he vanished from them like the sun with its rays from the two worlds when their limbs are scorched by heat.
When the Blessed Lord Kṛtānta had departed, Bhārgava reflected upon destiny—the inevitable course of fate, which is determined and impossible to thwart.
Mādhava entered that youthful body—which was withered by the cause of Time yet destined for the auspicious emergence of future blossoms—just as a bee enters a beautiful creeper.
That body of the Brahmin woman, with its face and limbs turned pale, fell trembling quickly upon the ground like a creeper whose roots have been severed.
When the life-force had entered that body of a son, the great sage performed a nourishing rite for it with mantras and the waters from his water-pot.
Then all the channels of her body shone, filled to the brim, like rivers in the rainy season whose hollows are overflowing with floods of water.
Like a lotus pond in the rainy season or a fresh creeper in spring, when she was full, her banks appeared as if covered in new sprouts.
Then Śukra arose, his vital breaths flowing forth, like a cloud filled with water through the union of moisture and wind.
He first saluted his father, whose form was purifying, just as a cloud first risen in the sky greets a mountain with its thunder.
Then the father embraced his former body, his heart melting with affection, just as a cloud after a long time embraces the slope of a mountain.
The high-minded Bhṛgu beheld his former body with affection, and even as he laughed, he maintained the conviction: "This one was born from me."
At that time, the affection thinking "this is my son" even carried away Bhṛgu; for the sense of "mine-ness" regarding the body persists as long as its physical form remains.
Then the father and son became mutually resplendent, like the sun and a lotus pond rejoicing at the end of the night.
Like a pair of ruddy geese joined after a long separation, or like a peacock and a rain-cloud filled with affection at the arrival of the monsoon.
Having remained there for a moment with their long-standing and deep longing satisfied by that equal fitness, those two of great intelligence then arose.
There, they reduced that body of the twice-born Samaṅga to ashes; for who indeed in this world does not follow established custom?
Thus those two ascetics, Bhṛgu and Bhārgava, resplendent like the moon and the sun in the sky, dwelt together in that sacred forest.

The two masters of the world, liberated while living, were known for their miraculous powers and their realized wisdom; they remained perfectly equanimous and steadfast amidst the floods of various places, times, and circumstances.
Then, in due course, Śukra attained the status of preceptor to the Asuras, while Bhṛgu likewise remained in his own appropriate and painless station.

This Śukra was first born in that manner from that supreme state of reality, possessing noble fame; later, through his own swift wandering from the path of mindfulness, he became dispersed among other states of existence.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, just as this [vision] became fruitful for the son of Bhṛgu through the experience of its manifestation, why would it not be so for another?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This body first arose from the foot of Brahmā; it is the pure lineage of Bhārgava, unstained by any other birth.
That state of the pure mind which occurs when all desires have been completely stilled is called Truth; it is described as this stainless consciousness.
Whatever a being whose mind is pure contemplates in such a manner, that very thing quickly comes to be exactly so, just as water becomes a whirlpool.
Just as the delusion of the son of Bhṛgu arose spontaneously by itself, so too is the son of Bhṛgu the illustrative example for each individual case here.
Just as a seed produces its own sprouts, leaves, and so forth, in the same way, the fragments of delusion arise for all the multitudes of living beings.
This entire universe that is seen is exactly like this: each individual thing arises falsely and likewise sets in falsehood.
Nothing whatsoever in this world sets or rises for anyone; this is mere delusion, expanding like one bewildered by magic.
Just as one who dwells within a mental projection is himself a fragment of cyclic existence, so too do thousands of such [projections] exist for them, falsely perceived.
Just as the activities in dreams and imagined cities are not seen as distinct from one another, so too are these delusions of saṃsāra.
In this way, multitudes of cities exist in the sky as forms born of mental construction; they are not seen except by those with the vision of false cognition.
There are indeed Piśācas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas of such a form; their bodies consist of mere volition and are composed of pleasure and pain.
In this very same way, O delight of the Raghus, we and these others have come into being, possessing forms composed of our own volitions, appearing as both false and real.
For the continuity of creation exists for others in exactly this form; yet its substantiality is not real, for such substantiality is established only in that which is non-substantial.
Indeed, the entire universe rejoices individually in this very way, though in vain, just as the single essence of spring manifests in the form of forests and thickets.
Just as this first mental construction has come into manifestation, so too is it thus analyzed when seen through the ultimate reality.
The mind, which is individually delighted and situated within the belly of its own inherent nature, perishes as it perceives this world as being engaged in such-and-such undertakings.
By the power of appearance things exist, but by the observation of reality they do not; the world-net is a long dream, a tethering post for the elephant of the mind.

The existence of the world is the very existence of consciousness; the existence of consciousness is the very existence of the world. With the absence of one, both are destroyed, and that occurs through the investigation of reality.
For the manifestation of a pure mind is indeed true, just as it is logical that the impurity of a gem is removed here by means of polishing and the like.
Through long and firm practice, the purification of the mind occurs; for one who is not assailed by volitional constructions, intuitive insight arises in the mind.
Just as gold does not remain pure when it is in a soiled garment, so too a single vision does not remain stable when the mind is withered.
Śrī Rāma said: How did these sequences of time and action, along with their rising and setting, come to exist within the mind of Śukra, given that the world is of the nature of a mere appearance?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as this world was perceived by Śukra through his father’s teachings, so does it abide within the mind of someone else, like a peacock within a peacock’s egg.
This [world] resides within the treasury of its own nature; it has arisen through this sequence, just as from a seed there come forth sprout, leaf, and so on, up to the creeper, flower, and fruit.
Bound by whatever latent impressions (vāsanā), the living soul perceives that very thing within; and here, its own true nature is the illustration: this world is indeed a long dream.
O Rāma, each fragment of worldly existence surely arises individually; at night, it appears clearly within oneself like the web of dreams experienced by the men of an army.
Śrī Rāma said: This world-process arises from fragments that meet one another spontaneously; or perhaps they do not meet. You should explain this to me exactly as it is.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: A mind that is impure and lacking in vigor does not deserve to unite with another; yet when iron is heated, it merges with heated iron, provided both are pure.
Pure mental principles merge with one another; for just as waters that are of a single form attain unity, those that are turbid do not.

For the purity of the mind consists in being free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which is a uniform state of non-perception of the unreal. Through that swift purification, one becomes awakened and, by means of the yoga of those [pure] elements alone, attains union with the Supreme.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Within all the fragments of worldly existence, there is no distinction in the manifestation of that which consists of the subtle elements (tanmātra) and whose nature is the seed-potency of beings.
Whether it be engagement or withdrawal, for the entire class of living beings, it is preceded by the functioning of the subtle elements immediately following the state of deep sleep.
Those living beings who participate in phenomenal activity perceive only the subtle elements; because of their identity with those subtle elements, they see the creations as mutually imagined.
Through the single channel of the subtle elements alone, the diverse reservoirs of creation intermingle with one another and attain density on all sides.
Some abide in separate states and dissolve separately; some are joined together with one another, remaining as the unimpaired humming of the world.
That which consists of thousands of worlds, innumerable within every atom, yet not touching one another—that is the forest called Brahman.
Through mutual intermingling, these have attained a state of density; whatever is established in a particular place in a particular manner, that alone one perceives there, and nothing else.
The present kingdom of the mind having reached futility, that should be known as the cutting off of the mind's succession of lives.

As successive creations merge with one another and their latent tendencies become firmly established, the existence of the body becomes deeply rooted; conversely, the absence of the body is simply forgetfulness.

Because the gold of consciousness has forgotten its own nature by becoming fully developed as a body, ignorance—which is actually unreal—is experienced; yet, when purified, it is realized to be nothing other than the bracelet itself.

Just as the pure vital breath perceives the objects of knowledge through the sensation of the supreme vital breath and so forth, so too does it perceive the kingdom of the mind based upon other creations.
For all multitudes of living beings, the Self rests in three states known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; in this regard, the body is not the cause.
Thus, while the self exists as the principle of life (jīvatva) consisting of the three states, corporeality does not manifest within it, as the nature of waves manifests in water.

Having reached the state of the power of consciousness (citkalā) and abiding in the state at the end of deep sleep, the enlightened individual soul returns [to its source], while the deluded one proceeds toward creation.

Because it demonstrates its own benevolence toward both, the ignorant, unawakened, and non-enlightened individual soul (*jīva*) is of one and the same nature as the other; such a soul is a participant in the process of creation.
Because consciousness is all-pervading, some [consciousness] is led by a creation; in each creation there is a distinct form, and there are indeed other creations as well.
Within those as well, there are floods of internal creations, like the layers of a plantain leaf-stalk; they possess a thick, leaf-like structure that is not far removed from all other creations.
Brahman is by nature cool, like a pavilion made of plantain leaves; just as there is no difference between the plantain tree and its hundreds of leaves, so too there is no otherness within it.
There is no otherness within the reality of Brahman, even across hundreds of creations; just as a seed, having blossomed from its sap, becomes a seed once again.
Likewise, when Brahman becomes the mind through awakening, it becomes the supreme Brahman; the seed, having rasa as its cause, unfolds into the state of the fruit.
The individual soul, having Brahman as its cause, expands in the form of the universe; it is not appropriate to say what the cause of that essence (rasa) might be.
It is not tenable to say what the cause of Brahman might be; nor is it tenable to say that its nature is something else, because it is devoid of distinctions.

One should not investigate causes and so forth in what is causeless, nor the supreme reality in things that are merely conventional; for one must investigate the essence—what is the use of investigating the insubstantial?
The seed, having abandoned its form as a seed, is seen as the fruit; but Brahman, not abandoning its own nature, exists as both the fruit and within the seed.
Everything possesses the form of a seed, whereas the state [of Śiva] is formless; therefore, it is not possible to equate them. Consequently, there is no analogy for Śiva.
That which appears as "non-self" is born only from itself, yet it is not born as something perceived by another; therefore, know that Brahman—the world, like space—is neither born nor unborn.
While perceiving the visible world, one does not perceive one's own self as the seer; for whom, whose consciousness is overcome by conceptual proliferation (prapañca), can its innate state arise?
When the delusion of water in a mirage exists, what cleverness is there? But when cleverness exists, what is that mirage?
The seer, as clear as space, does not see even his own entire body; he does not see himself as if it were his own eye—alas, what a delusion!
The seer, as clear as space, does not see even his own entire body; he is like one who, though free from delusion, perceives his own self as if it were an object of sight.
Brahman, as pure as space, is not attained even with effort; yet when the visible is seen for what it is—mere visibility—the attainment of it is very far away.
Wherever something is not perceived without its specific nature, there too the visibility of even a subtle object remains far removed for the observer.
O Rāma, by that [means] the visible is seen, but the seer is not seen; for only the seer alone exists, while the visible does not exist here at all.
If the seer, who is the self of all, is situated within the seen, what indeed remains of the state of being a seer? It is just as when whatever is accomplished by a king endowed with all powers.
It experiences itself in that very way and immediately arises as such; just as a piece of sugar, when its sweetness is manifested, becomes radiant.

Just as a tree, though elevated by its fruits, flowers, and creepers, does not abandon its state of being sap, so too the living soul (jīva), which is the radiance of consciousness, again becomes embodied.
Without ever abandoning its state of pure consciousness, it perceives the world as a dream through its own internal experience, consisting of the act of seeing and the seer.

Just as the quality of being a fragment exists within the earth due to the taste of egoism and so forth, so too does it exist within the Self through thousands of diverse fragments, even though one's own Self is non-dual.
Just as the essence of the earth arises, so too does it arise without agitation within the trees of the effulgence of the essence of consciousness, as they shine by themselves within themselves.
In this world, no end can be perceived for those who are struck by hundreds of visible branches; each fragment here possesses its own distinct aesthetic wonder.
In this way, this consciousness experiences and perceives existence as distinct, according to whatever individual manifestation of the life-force arises for each being.
In that very manner, she [the Supreme Consciousness] exists as the world-form of her own self-consciousness; thus, certain individual soul-transmigrations meet one another.
Having wandered through saṃsāra themselves, they find peace after a long time; behold this with a subtle and supreme vision, with a mind of wisdom.
Thousands of world-conflagrations exist even within the interior of a single atom—in the mind, in space, in stone, in flame, in wind, and in water.
Existences in the cycle of birth and death exist throughout the entire universe like oil in sesame seeds; when the mind attains perfection, then the individual soul becomes pure consciousness.
And she is pure and all-pervading; therefore, their mutual union is the form of the bee of one's own essential being for all [beings], beginning with Padmajā.
This world is a long, great dream that has arisen within; certain successions of beings pass from one dream to another dream.

Therefore, this perception remains most firm in the case of walls and the like; whatever one contemplates there with consciousness, that very thing quickly and sufficiently comes into being right there.
Whatever is seen by her even in a dream is indeed real at that time; for within the atom of consciousness, all atoms of experience exist.

Just as leaves, creepers, flowers, fruits, and atoms exist within another seed, I consider that the atoms of consciousness exist within the world of atoms; space is latent within space—abandon the delusion of duality and unity.
Through its own space, time, action, and substance, consciousness experiences atoms within itself, yet it does not experience other atoms because they do not exist [within it].
The atom of consciousness itself, manifesting as the creation in a dream, is experienced through the perception of bodies, ranging from that of Brahmā down to that of an insect.
In reality, there is nothing here whatsoever that has been manifested; yet the atoms of consciousness themselves, being true, experience duality as their own flavor.
The fragment of the atomic consciousness itself shines forth with an expansive body, emitting the fragrance of pure awareness through the flower-like gateways of the eyes and other senses.
Someone perceives the jar of consciousness (ciddhaṭa) exceedingly as an external form, because consciousness—the seed of all that is visible—is omnipresent and indestructible.
Within [this world], a certain person perceives the entire impure universe; therein, due to the excessive passage of time, he repeatedly emerges and sinks.
Seeing thus again and again from one dream to another dream, he rolls falsely among the banyan trees like a stone fallen from a mountain peak.
Some are gathered together, while others remain in the cloudless state within their own selves; these fragments of bodies flash forth, submerged in the expansion of their own consciousness.
Those who perceive within themselves the delusion of the world and living beings maintain that this perceived world is spread out by various agents and is as unreal as a dream.
Because the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is the self of all, that which is visible exists as truth within the Self; for wherever the all-pervading [Self] is found, there indeed everything arises.
Furthermore, within every manifestation of a living being, a fragment of the living soul arises intensely, and within that as well, another still more internal one.

A living being is born within a living being, and within that too is yet another living being; for everywhere, like the fibers of a plantain leaf, a living being exists indeed within another living being.

Immediately upon the transformation of the intellect regarding the visible world, this [duality] perishes once it is fully understood, just as the nature of being a bracelet and so forth vanishes when gold is recognized.
For one in whom the inquiry—"Who am I? and "What is this?"—does not arise, the long-lasting delusion of the fever of living remains unliberated within.
The reflection of that person of right-mindedness should be known as fruitful, for whom the greed for enjoyments diminishes day by day.
Just as medicine administered to the body brings about health, so too, when the mastery of the senses is practiced, discernment becomes fruitful.
Discernment exists only in words, shining like fire in a painting; for one who possesses it, the lack of discernment is not abandoned, leading only to suffering.
Just as the wind makes its presence known through touch and not by speech, so too is his discernment awakened solely through the attenuation of desire.

Know that "wondrous nectar" is not truly nectar, and know that "wondrous fire" is not truly fire; surely a "wondrous woman" is not truly bodiless (Anaṅga). Such verbal discrimination is itself a lack of discrimination.

First, through discernment, passion and enmity become attenuated and then are uprooted entirely; subsequently, even effort itself is completely exhausted. That state in which there is discernment is truly purifying.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The Supreme Brahman is the seed of the living soul, existing everywhere like space; by that [Brahman], the living soul exists in manifold ways even within the world that is the belly of the living soul.

Because they are essentially one solid mass of pure consciousness, the various classes of living beings exist within the living soul like the layers of a plantain tree, or like insects within the belly of the earth.
Whatever indeed, just as a worm might arise from the heat of the body in summer, whatever is perceived in the pure space of consciousness, that becomes a living being by itself.
In whatever manner those Jīvakas strive for the realization of their own selves, in that very manner they quickly become [so] through various methods of worship.
Those who sacrifice to the gods go to the gods; the Yakṣas indeed go to the Yakṣas; those who sacrifice to Brahman go to Brahman; therefore, one should take refuge in that which is not vain.
For that son of Bhṛgu was indeed liberated through the purity of his own consciousness, yet he was immediately bound by nature by the object of perception seen for the first time.
Born on earth and withered, whatever form consciousness first attains before it, it becomes that very form; it becomes nothing else whatsoever.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, you should explain the distinction between the states of waking and dreaming; how is there waking within waking, and how is there dreaming that is a delusion of waking?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That which is endowed with stable conviction is called waking; that which possesses unstable conviction is declared to be dreaming.
In the state of waking, a dream may be seen for a moment, while in another time it persists; thus that which was waking becomes a dream, and a dream attains the state of waking.
The distinction between the states of waking and dreaming does not exist apart from stability and instability; for all experience of these two is always equal in every respect.
Even a dream attains the state of waking during the time of dreaming due to its stability; whereas that which remains unstable is merely waking, because it is perceived as such.
Even a dream follows the state of waking when it is perceived by the waking intellect; however, its dream-nature remains established according to how it is experienced by the dreaming intellect.
That which is perceived as stable for as long as it persists is called the waking state; however, because of its momentary destruction, it is like a dream—listen now to how that occurs.
The life-element exists within the body by which one lives; it is designated, O limb, as heat, vigor, the life-element, and so forth.
When the body is engaged in activity through mind, action, or speech, then the life-element (jīvadhātu), impelled by the vital breath (marut), flows forth.

As that [consciousness] spreads through the limbs, every perception indeed arises; for, being perceived, it moves toward what is called the mind—the internal delusion of the world that was previously latent within.
Flowing outward through the apertures such as the eyes, it perceives within itself a form rich with various shapes and transformations, consisting of the external world.
Because it is stable, that [state] is understood as being exactly thus; it is called the "sequence of waking. Now hear the sequence beginning with deep sleep.
When one's body is not agitated by mind, action, or speech, then this very element of life remains with a peaceful self, established in its own well-being.
When the winds have attained equilibrium, the heart-lotus is no longer agitated, just as a lamp in a windless chamber produces nothing but light.
Consequently, consciousness does not move through the limbs, and for that reason it is not agitated; it does not enter the eyes and other sense organs, nor does it go outside through the apertures.
The living soul vibrates within itself, just as the consciousness of oil exists in the sesame seed, the consciousness of cold in frost, and the consciousness of fluidity in clarified butter.

A certain subtle portion of consciousness, taking the form of the individual soul, attains within itself the state of deep sleep—a state that is tranquil, windless, and devoid of objective cognition—by virtue of its own transparency.

Having known this and ceased from mental agitation, even while engaged in worldly activity, one who remains equanimous throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep is remembered as the awakened one who possesses the fourth state (turya).
When that constituent of life is set in motion by the vital breaths which have attained a state of serenity during deep sleep, it arises as consciousness, and from that, it is manifested as the mind.
One quickly perceives within one's own mind the entire web of the universe, with its successions of existence and non-existence and its various delusions, as vast as a tree within a seed.
When the life-element (jīvadhātu) is slightly or intensely agitated by the winds, one then perceives within oneself the movement in space, thinking, "I am asleep."
When it is flooded by water, it then experiences within itself the agitation of the water and so forth, just as a flower experiences its own fragrance.
When one is overcome by bile and other humors, then the entire vast expanse of the summer season and so forth arises within oneself as if it were outside.
Just as one sees external regions and times filled with blood and red in color through the nature of experience, one likewise sinks into that very state.

Whatever latent impression (vāsanā) one cultivates, that one perceives within while asleep, just as [the mind] is stirred by the movement of the vital air through the apertures such as the eyes and perceives external objects.
Because his sensory gaps have not been overcome, he becomes agitated within; that which he experiences through consciousness immediately is called a dream.
When one whose sensory openings have been invaded by the agitated wind perceives [objects], the best of sages call that "waking."

Thus, by you who have now understood this, the truth known here as "reality" has been proclaimed within; for in this unreal world, it should not be cultivated, but rather that which cultivates the realization of death, destruction, and the defects of worldly existence.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, I have explained all this to you regarding the nature of the mind; it was not told by anyone else for any other reason whatsoever.
Whatever the mind, possessed of firm resolve, meditates upon repeatedly, it attains that state—just as a mass of iron attains the nature of fire through contact with flames.
Views that grasp at existence and non-existence or at acceptance and rejection are imagined by the conscious mind; they are neither unreal nor real, being merely the products of mental restlessness.
But the mind is the agent of delusion and the cause for the persistence of the world; it is the defiled mind that expands this [universe] in the form of the manifold world.
For that which is called the person is indeed the mind; by directing it onto the auspicious path, all prosperities in the world—which are to be accomplished solely through its conquest—are attained.
If the person were identical with the body, how could the great-minded Śuka have undergone the wandering through hundreds of different births in various forms?
Therefore, the mind is indeed the person, and the body is truly the object of perception; whatever this [mind] consists of, that it undoubtedly attains.
Exert yourself to pursue that which is non-empty, effortless, free from attributes, and beyond delusion; you shall attain its true nature.

The mind flies toward the body that resides within it, but the mind does not go toward a physical form that is merely practiced. Therefore, O fortunate one, let your mind fly here toward the truth; let it abandon all else that is untrue.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, this great doubt which agitates my heart like a restless wave in the ocean—[pray resolve it]."
In that which is unconditioned by space, time, and the like, all-pervading, eternal, and free from affliction—whence has this withered consciousness called "mind" arisen?
Since there is no other name, neither existing nor yet to be, how, of what kind, and in what manner could any blemish exist therein?
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: Well spoken by you, O Rāma! Your mind has become a partaker of liberation, flowing with the highest essence like a cluster of blossoms from the Nandana grove.
This mind of yours, devoted solely to the investigation of what precedes and what follows, shall attain that most exalted state which was reached by Śaṅkara and others.
But, O Rāma, this is not the time for this question now; this question is addressed only when the final conclusion is being stated.
At the time of establishing the final conclusion (siddhānta), you must ask me this supreme question; by that, your final conclusion will become as clear as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of your hand.
This speech of yours at the time of establishing the final doctrine shines forth; for the cry of the peacock is appropriate in the rainy season, while the song of the swan is fitting in autumn.
The innate blue hue in the sky shines at the end of the rainy season, whereas during the rains it arises from the mass of thick and towering clouds.
This supreme determination of the mind, which is the subject at hand and has been commenced, is that by whose power the birth of living beings occurs; listen to it, O observer of noble vows.
Thus, O Rāma, this nature, which possesses the quality of mental cogitation, has been determined by all seekers of liberation to be "action."
Listen to its name and the form it is conceived to have according to the different philosophical systems, as described by eloquent speakers through their various perspectives on the scriptures.
Whatever state the mind, flickering in its thought, assumes, it attains that very nature, just as the wind dwelling within a flower acquires its intense fragrance.
Then, having determined that very [object] and conceptualizing it as such, one colors one's own ego-sense with an internal passion.
Based on that certainty, one attains the essence in that very [state]; for the body consists of that, and from it, so too do the faculties of cognition.
For that which is the mind, O Rāma, the body follows it and is under its control; it attains the nature of that [mind], just as the wind within a flower attains the nature of fragrance.
When the sense organs are active, the group of action organs then vibrates of its own accord, like dust tossed by the wind.
When the group of organs of action is agitated, it fully exerts its own power; thus, extensive action is produced, like a mass of dust in the wind.
For thus the activity of the mind is the seed of action, and the mind is said to be its essence; the existence of the two is non-different, just as that of a flower and its fragrance.
Whatever state the mind assumes through the power of firm habituation, it accordingly sheds the branches of manifestation known as vibration and action.
Thus, one performs an action and brings about its fruit with diligence; then, having experienced that very relish, one is quickly bound.
Whatever state he assumes, he perceives that very thing as the reality; and the conviction arises in him that there is no other excellence than that.
For they always strive for the sake of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation; their minds are firmly resolved through their very own practice.
Having accepted the innate and pure understanding of the followers of Kapila as their own mind, they have formulated their philosophical perspectives based on the scriptures.

But regarding liberation, those whose minds are conditioned [to believe] that there is no other way to attain it, reflect their own view while remaining fixed in the delusions of their own restrictive rules.
The proponents of Vedānta, having determined through their intellect that "this is Brahman," have conceived liberation as being endowed with tranquility and self-control.

But those whose minds are convinced that liberation cannot be attained otherwise than through their own view, explain their own perspective by means of their own arbitrary delusions regarding restrictive rules.

The proponents of consciousness (vijñānavādins), having determined through their intellect—which is filled with shimmering errors—that liberation consists in being endowed with tranquility and self-control, have formulated this [view].
But those whose minds are convinced that liberation cannot be attained otherwise, reveal their own views through their own arbitrary delusions regarding restrictive rules.
Various philosophical views have been imagined by the Arhats and others, according to their own respective inclinations and whims, through diverse modes of conduct.
Indeed, these various styles (rītis), though established by themselves, arise like a multitude of gentle water bubbles rising from a signless source; thus they are matured in their diverse forms.
O mighty-armed one, the mind is the source of all these modes of being, just as the ocean is the source of jewels.

The neem tree and the sugarcane are not simultaneously bitter and sweet, nor are the moon and fire cold and hot; whatever has been intensely practiced and perceived in a certain way, it is experienced exactly as such.
But that bliss which is uncreated—men striving for its sake should lead their minds to consist of it, so that it may be fully attained.
The mind that avoids its own empty and tumultuous objects of perception is not necessarily dragged away by the pleasure and pain born from them.
O sinless one, contemplate the visible world as impure, unreal in nature, delusive, a cause of fear, a mere appearance, expansive, and bondage.
This is illusion; this is indeed ignorance; this is mental cultivation that brings fear. The wise know that karma is that state of consciousness which consists of being absorbed in that [object].
Perceiving that the mind is delusive when it is entirely intent upon the objects of sight, you should wipe away that falsehood, which is like a mire of great impurity.
This experience of identity with the visible world, which is perceived as being established in its own nature, is called the wine of saṃsāra, or ignorance, by the wise.
Afflicted by this, the world does not attain what is auspicious, just as one whose eyes are blinded by a cataract cannot perceive the brilliant light of the sun.
And that [mind] arises by itself from conceptualization, like a tree in the sky; O Mahāmati, it ceases through the mere absence of conceptualization in one's cultivation.
When [doubt] has been exhausted by its own inherent force through playful inquiry, non-attachment toward all objects has attained stability.
When the vision of truth has been attained and unreality has come to an end, that Self—the pure essence of non-conceptual consciousness—is fully realized.
He for whom there is neither existence nor non-existence, neither happiness nor suffering, but in whose interior only the state of absolute oneness is perceived.
He who has been abandoned by an unfit cultivation, and by the mind, the faculties, and the views—which, though not distinct from the self itself—has been utterly forsaken.

Just as the sky is obscured by endless rows of clouds, so too is the true nature of reality obscured by infinite latent impressions, like the essence of a snake perceived in a rope that is mistaken for one.
Bondage is imagined as being within the nature of the consciousness-space (cidākāśa) precisely through non-bondage; for every imagined object is rendered otherwise by means of a counter-imagining.
That very [Self] assumes otherness, like the sky [appears different] during day and night, when it is non-vacuous, effortless, free from limiting adjuncts, and devoid of delusion.
That which transcends every such conceptual construction leads only to happiness, just as there is fear when one thinks "there is a lion" in an empty granary.
Likewise, there is fear that "I am bound within this very empty body," yet when one looks into an empty granary, no lion is found.
Likewise, when this purpose of the bondage of saṃsāra is scrutinized, it is not found; the notions "this world" and "this I" have arisen as a delusion.

Just as the shadow of a palm tree appears during the middle of the day, so too do existence and non-existence, the auspicious and the inauspicious, arise for a living being through the power of conceptual construction.
In one moment they lapse into non-existence, and again in a moment they attain existence; just as a mother herself, having assumed the state of a wife, hangs from the neck [of her son].
Bestowing the joy of sexual union, she performs the duties of a housewife; embraced by her motherly affection, she remains like a beloved clinging to his neck.
Surely she causes one to forget even the god of love through her maternal affection, as she observes the multitude of objects that yield fruits according to one's inner disposition.
In this world, no single form can be declared for objects by the wise; rather, the mind, through the power of firm habitual cultivation, intensely conceives of them exactly as it does.
One perceives each respective fruit as having that form for that duration of time; there is nothing that is not real, and there is nothing that is not false.
In whatever manner and by whatever means something is determined, it is characterized as such; the mind, having cultivated the elephant of space, is perceived as a celestial elephant.
He pursues the female elephant of the forest of the sky who stands within the sky; therefore, you should understand that volition alone consists of the nature of all things.
O Rāma, remaining in deep sleep, become the self of the Self by means of your own self; for a gem is indifferent toward the act of rejecting reflections.
It is incapable due to its insentient nature, O Rāma, but not so for one like you; for here, O Rāma, the entire world is reflected within your own self.
Having determined that it is a non-entity, do not allow yourself to be colored by it; nor should you regard it as real, for it is non-different from the Supreme Self.

Realizing that you are without beginning or end, contemplate the Self by means of the self. O Raghava, those mental objects that reflect in your mind—let them not color you, as they do a crystal, due to your attachment to them as other than yourself.

Just as various colors enter a crystal without coloring it, because it remains manifest in its own nature, so too may the desires for worldly existence enter you here, O Dispassionate One, while you remain manifest in your true state.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For a person who has practiced inquiry, whose mind’s fluctuations have dissolved, who abandons discursive thought, and whose self has attained some degree of maturity through realization— Please provide the final answer in the following format: The final answer is: ...
For one who has abandoned the visible as something to be discarded, who has attained that which is to be accepted, and who perceives the Seer while not perceiving the visible as a seer;
While one must remain awake to the supreme reality, such a person lives as if vigilant, yet remains asleep upon the path of worldly existence, which consists of dense delusion.

For one who is dispassionate toward all enjoyments—whether they be flavorful or flavorless, and whether they be delightful in their fullness—due to ultimate and absolute detachment, and who is free from all desire;
When its dullness has worn away, the self attains complete oneness with the sky; it dissolves like a mass of frost in the heat when all attachment has vanished.
Then, as their cravings subsided like rivers at the end of the rainy season, with their inner waters once more restless with surging waves.
When the knot of the heart has been severed—like a bird's web in the snare of worldly tendencies by a mouse—and loosened by the force of dispassion;
Just as water becomes clear upon reaching the kataka fruit, so too does one's own nature become perfectly serene through the power of higher knowledge.
Free from passion, free from attachment, free from duality, and free from dependence, the mind emerges from delusion like a bird from a cage.
When the malice of doubt has been stilled and the delusions of curiosity have vanished, the mind, its interior completely full, shines like the full moon.
Having produced supreme beauty, and rising high from afar only to set, it ascends everywhere with equanimity, like the wind over a calm ocean.

Consisting of darkness, mute, and with its interior shattered by dullness, the latent impression of worldly existence (saṃsāra-vāsanā) reaches a state of attenuation at the dawn [of wisdom], just as the night does.
The lotus-pond of wisdom, with its shoots of merit, blossoms with the sun of realized consciousness; it shines with stainless radiance like the sky at dawn, yet in embodied form.
Wisdom, captivating the heart and capable of delighting the world, increases when attained by sentient beings, like the rays of the full moon.
What is the use of saying more here? The one of great intelligence, who has known that which is to be known, neither rises nor sets, being like the expanse of the non-existent sky.
For one whose own nature has been fully understood through inquiry and whose self has arisen, even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Śaṅkara become objects of compassion in this world.
Even when manifest in form, conceptual constructions do not reach that one whose inner mind is free from egoism, just as deer cannot reach a mirage.
Like waves, these worlds come and go according to the mind; they embrace the ignorant one at birth and death, but not the wise one.
Manifestation and disappearance constitute transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), and no other sequence exists; one who perceives them as such rejoices in them and becomes bound.
Just as the space within a jar is neither born nor dies when the jar is decorated or defiled, so too is the self here, even when the body is adorned or corrupted.
When the cool light of discernment has arisen, the latent impression born of false delusion perishes at its very peak, like a mirage in the desert.
As long as one has not investigated "Who am I? and "How is this?", the spectacle of saṃsāra remains like a mass of darkness.
He truly sees who perceives this body—which is the seat of calamities and arises from the weight of false delusion—not as a self.
He who perceives the pleasures and pains in the body as arising from the influence of place and time, and is free from the delusion that "these are mine," truly sees.
He truly sees who perceives everywhere: "I alone am that which is endowed with the infinite limits of space, the directions, time, and all activity."
He who perceives that "I am subtle," even though [the self] is conceived as being divided into millions of parts, each as small as a hundred-thousandth of the tip of a hair—he truly sees.
He truly sees who perceives both himself and everything else through a vision that is eternal and undivided, seeing all as nothing but the light of consciousness.
He who perceives that which is all-powerful, infinite in nature, abiding within all beings, non-dual, and consciousness itself—that person truly sees.
He who, though wise, does not perceive "I am the body"—which is subject to birth, old age, and death, and agitated by the fears of mental and physical ailments—he truly sees.
My greatness pervades horizontally, upwards, and downwards; he who perceives that "there is no second to me" truly sees.
All this is strung upon me like clusters of jewels on a thread; he who sees that "the mind is not indeed I" truly sees.
"I do not exist, nor does anything else; only the stainless Brahman exists. He who perceives thus in the midst of existence and non-existence—he truly sees.
Whatever exists in the three worlds is indeed a limb of myself; he who perceives it thus, as a wave in the ocean, truly sees.
"She is to be pitied and protected by me alone; she is my younger sister. He who looks upon the three worlds as fragile in this way—he truly sees.
He for whom the notions of "self" and "other," as well as "thou" and "I," have ceased with regard to existence—he, the one with beautiful eyes, surely sees clearly.
He who perceives the body consisting of the Bhairava of Consciousness—free from the pursuit of objects of thought and filling the entire web of the universe—he truly sees.
Whether one perceives pleasure, pain, existence, becoming, or whatever mental constructions of discrimination there may be as "I alone," one certainly does not fall away from [the truth].

Seeing that in this world—which is filled with both one's own self and others—one who exists as a mere fragment asks, "What is to be abandoned by me? What is to be accepted? and thus becomes a true ascetic.
He for whom the notions of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted have utterly ceased—this reality being merely Being, beyond reasoning and devoid of appearance—he indeed is the true man.
He who, like space, is the single Self even while pervading all states of being, yet does not undergo the coloring of those states—he is the Great-Souled One, the Great Lord.
I bow to that state which has attained the nature of Time, yet is free from the conceptualization of darkness and light; which is gentle, perfectly even, and established in its own self.

Salutations to that Śiva, the possessor of supreme awakening, whose infinite activity is ever directed toward the singular consciousness of all things, amidst the manifold and beautiful manifestations of the world’s rising and setting.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: He who rests upon the supreme state, remaining like the whirling of a wheel, is not defiled even while governing the kingdom of the city of the body.
For one who knows that, this great city of his own body—resembling a pleasure grove—is for the sake of enjoyment and liberation; it leads only to happiness, not to suffering.
Śrī Rāma said: O great sage, how indeed is the body called a city, and how is it that a yogi, while dwelling within it, becomes the sole enjoyer of royal happiness?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, this city of the body is delightful and endowed with all virtues; for the wise man, it is rich in infinite diversions and illuminated by the sun of self-perception.
The interior of the world was illuminated by the light from the windows of her eyes; the open spaces between her feet were reached by the expansion of the streets of her hands.

Her creeper-like line of body hair was a thicket of vines, her skin was garlanded with a network of veins, and the circles of her shanks, thighs, and pillar-like calves were firmly established upon her ankles and toes.
Its forefeet were fashioned first from stone, divided by lines; it was beautiful with the boundaries of the joints, sinews, and vital marrow of skin.

The rivers of her private parts were formed by the tips of the broad and slender portions [of her body], and she was covered by forested plateaus consisting of the foliage of her shimmering locks of hair.
Adorned with a garden-like face where the eyebrows, forehead, and lips provide a harmonious shade, her expansive cheeks were strewn with the blue lotuses of her falling glances.
The lake of her chest bore the budding lotuses of her breasts, and the mountain for her playful sport was her shoulders, shrouded by the thick line of hair.
Intent on devouring the food she had cast into the cavity of her belly, she was made to sound by the force of the wind expelled through the long hollow of her throat.
Adorned with the objects obtained as they came, determined by the marketplace of the heart, the city has its nine gates perpetually filled by the flowing serpents of the vital breaths.
With her mouth wide open, filled with fragments of teeth and bone that had never been seen before, the fierce goddess has her tongue lolling from its place in her mouth as she devours her food.
It was covered with hairy shrubs, its hollows were like deep ear-cavities, and its vast wilderness was bordered by the chains of the buttocks and the ridges of the back.
The ground of the garden of the mind is a rushing, endless mire arising from the water-wheel of the anus, where the excellent woman of self-reflection frolics.
The restless monkey of the sense-faculties is firmly bound by the rope of wisdom; she is delightful with the blossoming flowers of laughter in the garden of her face.
One's own body, which is pleasing to the mind and possesses all auspicious beauty, leads only to happiness and not to suffering, and is for the sake of the highest benefit.
For the ignorant, this is a garland of coffers for infinite sufferings; for the wise, however, it is a garland of coffers for infinite happinesses.

O subduer of enemies, when this [intellect] is lost, everything belonging to the knower is lost; when it is established, everything is established. Therefore, this [intellect] brings about the happiness of the knower.
Since the Knower, having mounted this [wisdom], dwells extensively within saṃsāra for the sake of both complete enjoyment and liberation, it is therefore remembered as the "Chariot of the Knower."
Since sound, form, taste, touch, smell, kinsmen, and prosperity are indeed obtained through this very [wisdom], it bestows gain upon the wise man.

O Rāma, that net of pleasure, pain, and action which this [consciousness] carries by itself, it is precisely this [consciousness] that is capable of bearing the weight of all things for the All-Knowing One.
Indeed, ruling his kingdom within that city of the body, the wise one dwells free from feverish anxiety and devoid of distraction, like Indra in his own city.
He does not cast the wild horse of the mind into the pit of arrogance, nor does he surrender the daughter of wisdom to the evil tree of greed.
And the enemy of ignorance does not see any vulnerability in him; rather, it cuts away the very roots of the fear of the enemy that is cyclic existence.

In this world, which is the revolving core of craving and is difficult to grasp due to the enjoyment of sensual desires, the one who is overturned does not sink, even amidst the tumultuous play of pleasure and pain.
With his mind fixed on his desires, he performs an uninterrupted bath at the confluences of rivers and sacred fords, both externally and internally, in due order.
Averse to the sight of pleasures invisible to all the senses, he dwells eternally in the bliss called meditative absorption within the inner sanctum of his heart.
This city is always a bringer of happiness to one who has realized the Self; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, just as Amarāvatī does for Śakra.
Everything remains established by that which is itself established; nothing is destroyed by that which is destroyed. How could that most magnificent city not bring happiness?
When the city of the body has perished, nothing at all is lost for the knower, just as when a jar is destroyed, the space within it—which pervades the jar—is not lost.
Just as the wind touches an existing jar but not one that is not present, so too does the embodied soul touch this city of its own body.
The person situated here, though being the all-pervading Self, enjoys the objects of experience fashioned by the creator of the universe, and thus partakes of the fruits attained by men.
Even while acting, he does not act; though intent upon all purposeful activity, he sometimes carries out all the various tasks at hand.
Sometimes, with a playful and restless mind, his pure heart, moving unimpeded, ascends a beautiful celestial chariot to wander about.
Abiding there, he constantly delights with Lokasundarī, whose limbs are ever cool; dwelling eternally within her heart, he rejoices through his loving-kindness.
Two beloved ones stood properly at his two sides—Satyavatī and Ekata—their hearts equally gladdened, like the two stars Viśākhā beside the moon.
He beholds all worlds—exhausted and torn by the saw of suffering—as if standing upon the back of the sky like the sun, surveying those situated within a forest of creepers.
Having long fulfilled all his aspirations and being beautiful with every excellence, he shines like the full-orbed moon, never again to suffer eclipse.
Even when indulging in a flood of enjoyments, no weariness arises for him; indeed, the Kālakūṭa poison, though in his throat, only serves to enhance the beauty of the Lord of Death.
For enjoyment that is fully understood and experienced leads to contentment; like a thief who is served after being recognized, he becomes a friend rather than an enemy.
To the wise man, the splendor of enjoyments—like a theatrical performance—is seen as a mere spectacle, even when men and women, those throngs of dancers, have departed far away in separation.
Just as travelers encounter a village procession that has arrived unexpectedly, so too do the wise regard all activities consisting of worldly affairs.
Just as the eye falls upon objects presented without effort with a mind free from passion, so too does the intellect of the steadfast fall upon its duties.
The wise one who is fully established never seizes an object already reached by the senses, nor does he grasp that which is not yet reached; thus he remains complete.

Those of wavering minds cannot shake one of noble intellect—whether they have not yet attained their goal or have already attained it and remain equanimous—just as flickering blows from a peacock's tail feathers cannot move a mountain.
With all doubts completely stilled, with all curiosity dissolved, and with the body of conceptual construction utterly exhausted, the knower shines like a sovereign emperor.
Not contained within itself, it expands by its own self within itself; full and without limit or end, like the ocean of milk within the great ocean.
One whose mind is not deranged and who is peaceful laughs at beings who are wretched in their craving for enjoyments and whose senses are miserable, as if they were madmen.
Just as one who desires another's abandoned wife is ridiculed by others, so too is he who desires sense-objects through his senses mocked by the wise.
One should bring under control, by means of discernment, the mind that has fled toward sense objects and abandoned its own gentle bliss, just as one subdues a great elephant with a goad.
That mental tendency which is allowed to flow toward enjoyments must be destroyed at the very outset, just like the sprouting of a poison plant.
For even that honor bestowed upon one who has been struck is infinite; like a meager watering of rice parched by the summer heat, it acts as nectar.
For one who is not in need, honor and great respect are not perceived; the flood of the rainy season does not shine when rivers are already full.
Even when full, the ordinary ocean still desires more; it continues to take in water sufficient to fill the entire world.
When the mind has been restrained, whatever subsequent enjoyment or adornment arises, it considers that very thing—failing to attain expansion—to be of great value because of its afflicted nature.
A ruler of the earth who is free from bondage is satisfied with a mere morsel; being unbound by others and unsubdued, he does not hold sovereignty in high regard.
Pressing hand against hand and grinding tooth against tooth, and as if crushing limb with limb, you should conquer the enemies that are the senses.
Those wise men here who are resolved to conquer others must first thoroughly subdue their own sense faculties, for they are the enemies of the heart.
On this vast expanse of earth, those men are truly fortunate and possess virtuous intentions who are counted among the elite of human arts and have not been conquered by their own minds.
I pay homage to that perfectly pure one, whose great serpent of the mind—rendered helpless by its coils within the hollow of the heart—has attained complete pacification and is fully delighted.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In the empire of the great hells, the enemies that are the senses are difficult to conquer; they are like elephants intoxicated by their own evil deeds, bristling with the barbs of the arrows of desire.
Those who, being ungrateful, destroy their own first refuge—the body—are the enemies of one's own senses, who are difficult to conquer and constitute a vast treasury for evil deeds.
Having reached the abode of the body, the vultures of the senses—greedy for the bait of sense-objects and possessing the fierce wings of what ought and ought not to be done—flit about restlessly.
Those rogues who have been captured by the net of the threads of discernment—no nooses can maim their limbs, just as [nooses cannot restrain] the strength of a serpent.
He who possesses the wealth of discernment finds delight in the objects of sense—which are charming only at first sight—within this city of the wretched body.
One is not helplessly overcome by the internal enemies that are the sense faculties in the way that kings dwelling in formidable cities made of clay are not so well-protected.

Just as those who have mastered their minds are lords of the city that is their own body—having subdued the servants that are the senses and having well-seized the enemy that is the mind—so too [is the state of the yogi].
Like blossoms in springtime, those of pure intellect flourish—those whose mental pride has been destroyed and who have subdued the enemies that are the sense faculties.
Like lotus ponds in winter, the latent tendencies for enjoyment wither away; yet until then, those tendencies leap about in the heart like midnight goblins.
As long as the mind has not been conquered through firm practice upon a single principle, it remains a servant because it performs desired tasks, and a minister because it accomplishes noble deeds.
I consider the mind of the discerning man to be a vassal overcome by the senses; yet it is cherished by the affectionate wife and protected by the purifying father.

I consider the mind of the wise to be the supreme confidence of their best friend; it is beheld within by one's own vision through the eye of scripture and realized through one's own direct experience.
Having abandoned the self, the father of the mind bestows supreme accomplishment when he is well-seen, well-grasped, well-firmly established, and well-awakened.
Joined with excellent qualities, this heart-pleasing jewel of the mind shines within the heart; it is like axes for the tree of rebirth and brings about future prosperity.
Thus the mind-mantrin directs its activities toward auspicious deeds; thus, O Rāma, is the jewel of the mind, though stained by much mud, purified.

Wash yourself with the water of discernment for the sake of perfection and become possessed of light; for one who dwells in the terrifying realms of worldly existence while devoid of discernment [is lost].
Do not fall, helpless like an ordinary person, into this illusory cycle of existence (saṃsāra-māyā), which is filled with calamities and crowded with hundreds of misfortunes.
Do not disregard this mist of great delusion; rather, relying upon supreme discernment and perceiving the truth with your intellect, [overcome it].
Having fully conquered the enemies that are the senses, cross over the ocean of existence; for this body is indeed unreal, and pleasure and pain are likewise non-existent.
O Rāghava, let not the logic of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa be yours; through the firm abiding of Bhīma and Bhāsa, you shall attain freedom from sorrow.

O Great-minded One, having thoroughly cast aside with your own intellect that vain certainty which thinks "I am this," take hold of that which is other than that; go to that state, drink, eat, and though possessing a mind, you shall not be bound.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For that wise one who delights in the world, who sports in this world, who abides for the sake of his own welfare, and who speaks of the supreme goal—[for him, there is no need for further effort].
"O Rāghava, let not the logic of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa befall you; through the firm stability of Bhīma and Bhāsa, may you be free from sorrow."
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahmin, you who remove the torment of worldly existence, why have you cited the analogy of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa? Let it not be so for you."
"O Lord, remover of the torment of worldly existence, what was said by you when you spoke, 'May you be free from sorrow through the firm abiding of Bhīma and Bhāsa'?"
Awaken me, who am pure, with this noble speech that removes the thick heat, as the rainy season does for the peacock.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, hear the analogy of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, which is firmly established by Bhīma and Bhāsa; having heard it, perform that which you deem best.
In the cavernous depths of Pātāla, which were delightful with every wonder, there was a lord of the Daityas named Śambara, a great ocean of the jewels of illusion.
He constructed the mansions of the asuras within gardens in a city of the sky; his own realm was adorned with artificial, supreme suns and moons.
The Immortal Mountain (Meru), filled with lotuses and other flowers produced from fragments of rock, satisfies the Dānavas by providing an endless array of magnificent riches.

The sound of the songs sung by the women in his jewel-adorned palace surpassed the voices of the celestial nymphs; and the trees in his pleasure groves were filled with the full orb of the moon’s reflection.
Its delightful abodes were made formidable by clusters of blooming blue lotuses; its golden water-lilies were summoned there by the calls of jewel-adorned swans.
He formed lotus buds from the tips of the branches of his golden trees, and he became a source of mandāra flowers falling like a swarm of karañja blossoms.
Therein dwelt Vāsava, who had been conquered by the infinite Daityas through the machine of logic; there he fashioned garden pavilions with flames of fire that were as cold as snow.

Everywhere he surpassed the joy of the Nandana grove with his flower gardens; he was the sandalwood of the Malaya mountains that steals away all the world's illusion and removes every serpent-like affliction.
The women of his inner apartments were surpassed by the splendor of golden beauty; the courtyards of his houses were knee-deep with heaps of various flowers.

For the sake of sport, he is the wielder of the discus and mace who has conquered the Lord of Clay; within his celestial city, the interior is enriched by stars consisting of masses of jewels that fly upward incessantly.
The surface of the sky was like a hundred moons for the entire underworld at midnight; it was intense with the songs sung by the world to its own statues and the clamor of battle.
The lordly elephant of the gods was put to flight by the illusory Airāvaṇa; the interior of his harem was filled with the excellence of the splendors of the three worlds.
Fortunate with every prosperity, honored by all who possess sovereignty, his formidable commands were saluted by all the vassal lords of the Daityas.
The circle of asuras rested in the shade of his great forest-like arms; he was adorned with a jewel-mandala that serves as the support for the entire host of the Buddha's faculties.
That demon, who had destroyed the gods and possessed a harsh and terrifying form, came to have a vast asura army capable of destroying the deities.
While that Māyābala was asleep and likewise gone to another land, the gods, having found a vulnerability, reportedly struck down his army with force.
Then, for the sake of protection, the Daitya Śambara appointed Muṇḍi, Krodhadruma, and others as his subordinate generals over his own armies.
Having reached them from within, the terrifying gods struck them down, like hawks swooping from the midst of the sky upon agitated sparrows.
Furthermore, the best of the asuras appointed other generals, who were as restless and loud-voiced as the waves of the ocean.
The gods quickly struck them down with that [weapon], and because of that, he became filled with wrath; he went to the full celestial realm, Triviṣṭapa, in order to destroy the immortals.
Therefore, terrified by her illusion, those gods vanished, like deer into the groves of the forests of Mount Meru when faced by a lion.
He beheld heaven empty, like a world exhausted at the end of an aeon, with the hosts of minor gods wailing and the faces of the apsarases drenched in tears.
Dwelling there in anger, he seized whatever beautiful things he found, burned the city of the world-protectors, and departed for his own abode.
When the hatred between the Dānavas and the gods had thus become more intense, the gods abandoned heaven and vanished from sight in all directions.
Then, whatever army commanders were appointed with great effort by the Daitya Śambara, those gods, intent on their own exertion, slew them.
Until he was overcome with agitation, Śambara, filled with intense rage, burned like a fire fed with excessive straw, sighing heavily.
Then, even after searching throughout the three worlds, he did not find the gods, despite his supreme effort, just as a man of evil deeds fails to find a hidden treasure.
By means of his illusory power, he created three terrible and exceedingly powerful Asuras, who stood like Time itself personified, arisen for the purpose of protecting Bala.
Manifested through illusion, those terrifying beings of great magic, carrying away the trees of their strength, rose up like mountains whose wings had been shaken loose.
Marked by the names Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, they are each the sole agent of whatever they encounter, possessing the nature of pure consciousness alone.
Because of the absence of past actions, those former latent impressions (vāsanās) do not exist; they possess as their sole characteristic the vibration of pure, non-conceptual consciousness alone.
