Having reached the rising of the inner impulse, they [perceive] the slender, essence-less, and artificial portion of the living being born of karma, which is a mere mental fabrication and remains unfulfilled within.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having thus resolved, the lord of the Daityas dispatched his army, accompanied by Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, to the surface of the earth to destroy the gods.
Armed with weapons, the Daityas emerged from the groves along the ocean and from the mountain caves with terrifying roars, moving with the ease of winged mountains.
The Dānavas, emboldened by Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, filled the hollow of the two worlds (Heaven and Earth), which had the sun struck down by the blows of their hands.
Then, from the groves and the caves of the celestial mountain, the formidable hosts of the denizens of heaven arose like the turbulent oceans at the end of a cosmic dissolution.
Between those two armies, which bore the banners of the gods and the asuras, there occurred a battle within the world that was terrifying like an untimely and violent dissolution of the kalpa.
Then their heads, with darkness swallowed by the brilliance flashing from their earrings, fell like the lights of the sun and moon overturned at the time of cosmic dissolution.
Resounding with the lion-roars emitted by the soldiers, the mountains trembled like they were breaking into loud laughter under the full force of the winds of universal destruction.

The dust was like the impact of weapons against mountain rocks; the walls were struck down by the blows of those weapons; and the circles of lions rested fearlessly upon the slopes of the great boundary mountains.
From the weapons struck down by their mutual blows, flickering sparks of fire arose like stars scattered at the end of a kalpa.
Upon the banks of that single ocean filled with floods of blood and flesh, there were Vetālas as tall as the palm trees of the Kalpa age, clapping their hands in rhythmic time.
In the sky, where the clouds of dust were stilled by showers of spurting blood, the tips of crowns and earrings of those struck and crushed by weapons lay scattered.

The quarters of the sky became devoid of gaps, filled with Daityas who resembled the sun, who bore the likeness of the wish-fulfilling trees of the kalpa age, and who had shattered the great lords of mountains with their blows.
With their walls toppled by the wind from the edges of the blazing swords, the mountains were reduced to a mass of fragments, as if shattered by the fire at the end of an aeon.
And those gods assembled like those invigorated by horse-sacrifices, [driving away] the Asuras who were deprived of their weapons, just as winds scatter the clouds.
Then, attacking them, they seized those [demons] as the seasons seize the trees when they have grown old; and they too seized those intoxicated ones, like trees climbed by bears.
With their weapons as sprouts and their radiant missiles as blossoms upon the trees of their arms, the gods and asuras shone like forest trees in full bloom, swaying in the wind.
They filled one another and the ten directions with floods of weapons, just as the wind fills the forests on Mount Sumeru with clusters of blossoms.
A terrible battle took place between the armies of the gods and the dānavas, like that of swarms of great mosquitoes within the hollow of the space between heaven and earth.
Then, amidst circles of world-protectors with upraised arms, there arose a dreadful roar of battle, resembling the thundering of clouds at the end of an eon.
Like a patch of earth on the ground grasped as a solid mass in the sky, it was thick and heavy, with a belly as slow-moving as a great cloud, yet capable of being seized by the fist.
The chariots crushed together like mountains of weapons, while the dancers shrieked; there was a gurgling sound from the harsh lamentations of those whose hearts were broken and devoid of strength.
It was amplified by the roar of the end of the aeon, surging forth from the dissolution of all conditions; it was like a mountain of gold melting under the impact of the twelve suns.
Emerging from the impact with the vessel of the universe through its reversal, it was like a great torrential flood of water, resembling a mine struck by living beings.
The sound of the mountain-king’s wings flapping as they quivered, and the mountain caves bursting open as they were filled by the hard [impact]; ||| 13 ||
His body resembles the agitation of the milk-ocean when churned by Mount Mandara; he is the source of the creatures of the islands, brought together by the loud, rhythmic slapping sounds of passion.
When the two armies were agitated, there occurred a battle characterized by the upheaval of dānavas, in which cities, villages, mountains, forests, and men were crushed to pieces.

The quarters were filled with the mountain-like Dānavas severed by hundreds of great weapons, while the interior of the sky was filled with the dust of weapons and other implements struck against one another.
The hundreds of peaks of Mount Meru were shattered by the impact of the circles of *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons, and the lotus-faces of the Daityas and gods were severed by the wind of his arrows.
The old grass of gods and demons was whirled about by hundreds of revolving whirlpools, while the sky was enveloped by the surging waves of the army's blows.

The multitude of celestial chariots was crushed and cast down by the fierce winds of his weapons, while the city of the sky was inundated by the surging flood of ocean waters unleashed by his missiles.
Carrying hundreds of rivers of great missiles, swords, spears, and pikes, [the battle] caused the pavilion of the universe to collapse under the violent blows from the wings of mountains.

The city of the world-protectors was being overwhelmed by the flood of blows from the heels of the Daityas, while the mansions resounded with the jingling of bracelets as women let out cries of lamentation.

It was filled with the waters of a surging flood of intoxicated blood arising from the hosts of Daityas; it was fierce with throngs of men washed in gore and filled with the cries of those fleeing in terror.
It was filled with Yama, who was both concealed and revealed by the lotus-like faces of the world-protectors, and it was once again crowded with hosts of troops seen by the gods and asuras.
It was terrifying with the loud clanging of many bells and the "sha-va-sha" sounds of flowing corpses, as they moved back and forth like the mountain-demons that take the form of similar mountains.
The entire earth, oceans, and mountains were reddened with blood from the cascades flowing from the fierce daitya-mountains, which had been split apart by the tips of weapons.
It was a place where kingdoms, cities, forests, villages, and caves were utterly destroyed, and where mountains of countless corpses of asuras, elephants, horses, and humans lay piled up.
The elephant Airāvaṇa was adorned with rows of iron arrows that pierced through its skin, and its shoulders were crushed by the blows of fists from those intoxicated by battle.
It shattered mountains with torrents of rain like the massed clouds at the end of an eon, and crushed the great boundary mountains so they flew apart by the impact of a massive thunderbolt.
The Danava was set ablaze by the mass of flames leaping from his provoked fire, yet he extinguished that fire by drawing up the ocean with a single cupped hand.
The great flames were turned to stone by the mass of the fierce Daityas; the fiery rays of the forest-arrayed fuel consumed the mountains and the flowing waters.
The night of the end of the eon, consisting of irresistible darkness created by weapons, had its vast veil of gloom consumed by the radiance of the multitude of illusory suns.
It pours down a rain that completely dries up the thick clouds of the kalās, like a rain of illusory fire; it rains down a mass of weapons emitting hissing fire.

It was filled with the agitation caused by the rain of mountain-weapon missiles dispelled by the rain of diamond-weapon missiles; it was rich in battles between the weapons of sleep and awakening, and it took recourse in the obstruction of mutual rivalry.

The tree-weapon with its moving saws was being carried away; the darkness, blinded by the recollection of water, fire, and missiles, was dispelled by the brilliance of the Brahmā-missile, which rendered that battle as fierce as a conflict with the weapon of Brahmā.
The entire sky was rendered dense with hosts of weapons disgorged by the stars, shattered by showers of stone-missiles and blazing with showers of fire-missiles.
In a mere moment, the chariots—with their banners touching the moon and thundering with the whirring of their wheels—leaped over both the mountain of sunrise and the mountain of sunset.
The great asura who does not die even when struck by the vajra; the great asura whose life is sustained by the great vidyā-mantra of the immortal seed-essence.
The hosts of gods were fleeing, while the immortals were exultant in victory; and here and there were the great comets of the auspicious planets.
It uprooted the neck of the intellect amidst floods of portents and auspicious signs; it was like an ocean of blood for the world, including its mountains, earth, and seas.
Due to irresistible enmity, he turned the forest of *kiṃśuka* trees into a mass of blossoms and created a great ocean filled with corpses, as numerous as mountains.

There hung from the tips of the branches of the trees a great corpse, swaying to and fro; it was illuminated by the shimmering plumage of birds, which were distressed by their own winds and adorned with glowing fruits.
The expanse of the sky was filled with showers of arrows falling like palm trees, while hundreds of headless trunks, resembling mountains, were seen with their hundreds of arms.
With dancing [warriors], it brought down clouds, celestial chariots, and the stars of the gods; with arrows, spears, maces, darts, and battle-axes, it pierced through mountains.
The sky was strewn with fragments of walls fallen from the seven worlds, while the firm kettledrums were struck incessantly by clouds as intoxicated as if in a state of rapture.
Thus, with the thundering of hundreds of sounds from the depths of the netherworld like the trumpeting of elephants, the long mountain-like Dānavas were drawn forth by the hand of Vināyaka.
The hosts of Maruts, whose success and goals were achieved through the movement of Ekadikkarani, fled, as did the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, gods, and Cāraṇas.

With their limbs mangled by the falling of thunderbolts and shattered into fragments of stone, the winds—announcing the time of universal dissolution and devouring the celestial trees with a gurgling roar—blow in the directions of the sky.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: While that terrible tumult of battle was then occurring, the bodies of the gods and asuras were like pits within the belly of a cloud.
While streams of blood flowed like the floods of the Gaṅgā descending from the sky, and while the multitude of gods, encircled by the noose, let out a thick roar of battle cries.
Upon a tiger that had crushed all the celestial abodes by pulling them with its own claws, and upon a mountain-slope where the immortals were destroyed in a battle of fierce fury.
When Airāvata, his roar silenced, was intent on flight, and the army of the Dānavas had swelled like the sun at midday;
Afflicted by the pain of fallen limbs and with blood flowing from them, the celestial armies fled like waters breaking through their banks.
Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, who had long been hidden, followed them like fires following fuel that has burst into a blazing roar.
Although they searched with great effort, the asuras did not find the gods, just as lions do not find deer that have flown up into a dense thicket of trees.
Then, when the hosts of immortals had not been captured, Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, with joyful hearts, went to the Lord residing in the treasury of Pātāla.
Then those gods, having been defeated, were despondent; but after consoling themselves for a moment, they went to Brahmā of immeasurable luster in order to find a means of victory.
To them, whose faces possessed the splendor of deep redness, Brahmā appeared, like the moon appearing to the oceans at evening whose waters have been turned crimson.
Having bowed down to him, those gods fully related to him the misfortune brought about by Śambara and the sequence of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa.
Having heard all that and reflected upon it, Brahmā, the discerning one, spoke these words of consolation to the host of gods:
The illustrious Brahmā said: At the end of a hundred thousand years, Śambara must be slain by Hari in battle; let him wait for that time.
"O best of the immortals, today, while fighting these Dāmas, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, you must flee from the Dānavas by means of illusory warfare."
Through the power of habitual practice in battle, the wondrous manifestation of egoism will enter into their hearts like a reflection in mirrors.
But these gods—Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa—having acquired latent impressions, will become easy for you to conquer, like birds caught in a net.
But today, these gods, being free from latent desires and devoid of pleasure and pain, have become invincible as they strike down their enemies with fortitude.
Those who are bound by the threads of latent impressions and brought under control by the snares of desire fall into subjection in this world, like birds tied with ropes.

Those steadfast ones whose latent predispositions have been shattered, whose intellects are unattached to anything, who neither rejoice nor are provoked to anger—they are the great-minded ones, difficult to conquer.
He whose internal knot of bondage is formed by the rope of latent impressions (vāsanā), though he be great and possessed of vast learning, is overcome even by a child.
One who constructs such conceptualizations as "this is I," "this is mine," or "that is it," becomes a vessel for calamities, just as the ocean is for waters.
He by whom the self has been cultivated as limited to only this much, even if he were omniscient, has fallen into the utmost wretchedness in every respect.
He who has imagined a limit for that which is infinite and immeasurable has, by that very act, brought his own self under control by himself.
Whatever exists in the three worlds that is distinct from the self—upon that, let the latent impression (vāsanā) be bound by way of being something to be grasped.
The wise know that mere attachment is the source of infinite sufferings; they know that mere non-attachment is the source of all happiness.
"As long as Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa remain established in worldly existence with such lack of resolve, we shall certainly not conquer them, just as fire cannot overcome gnats."
A living being, overcome by internal latent impressions that lead to wretchedness, is defeated; otherwise, even a mosquito would be like the immovable mountain Meru.
Wherever a latent impression exists, there it attains growth; for duality is observed in a quality-bearer when the quality is present, not when it is absent.
"O Śakra, act in such a way that they cultivate within themselves the latent impressions (vāsanā) of 'this is I,' 'this is mine,' and so forth, just as Dāma and the others did."
Whatever misfortunes befall people, and whatever states of existence and non-existence they encounter, these are the bitter yet tender blossoms of the thorny *karañja* vine of craving.
The world, bound by the threads of latent impressions (vāsanā), revolves; when these have increased, they lead to extreme suffering, yet when they are severed, they lead to happiness.
Though steadfast, though possessing vast knowledge, though of noble birth, and though great—a living being is bound by craving, just as a lion is bound by a chain.
For this bird of the mind that dwells in the tree of the body and moves toward the abode of the heart, this craving has been fashioned as a snare.
The world, wretched due to its latent tendencies, is dragged away by the End-maker, like a bird by a child with a string, gasping violently and utterly helpless.
Enough with the burden of weapons and with wandering about in battle; through reasoning, strive with effort to overturn the enemy's latent tendencies.
O leader of the immortals, when the enemy's fortitude falters in the midst of battle, neither weapons, nor missiles, nor treatises bring victory.
Moreover, these—Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa—being intoxicated by the force of their practice in battle, will seize an impression consisting of egoism.
When those ignorant persons created by Śambara take recourse to latent impressions (vāsanā), then they shall become conquerable.
O gods, you should awaken them through the battle of reasoning until, by the power of practice, they become possessed of latent impressions (vāsanā).
Then they will become submissive to you, their latent impressions bound; with hearts pierced by craving in this world, none shall remain weak.

This entire world, both even and uneven, has arrived at stability within its own latent impressions; just as the mass of trembling waves in the ocean subsides, so too must that very [instability] here proceed toward healing.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus to the gods, the Blessed One vanished right there, like a wave of water that has made its sound upon the shore of the coastal forest.
Having heard those words, the gods departed toward their desired directions, just as breezes carry away the fragrance of lotuses, taking with them a garland of forests.
For some days, they rested in their own lovely and ever-lustrous mansions, like bees among lotuses.
Having attained for a short time that auspicious state which brings about their own exaltation, they raised a roar of dundubhi drums resembling the sound of clouds at the dissolution of the world.
Then, a terrible battle that caused a long delay broke out once more between me and those Daityas, some stationed in the sky and others dwelling in the depths of Pātāla.

Multitudes of swords, arrows, spears, and mallets blew forth; likewise, clubs, maces, sharp axes, discuses, and conchs; as well as thunderbolts, mountain rocks, fires, trees, and weapons with the faces of serpents, Garuḍas, and other creatures.

A river created by magic, with a torrent of great waters like a mass of clouds and weapons fashioned by illusion, indeed rushed forth swiftly in every direction; it possessed a deep roar like the flood of waters agitated by hundreds of thousands of rocks, mountains, and trees, and it surged forth instantly.

With a torrential downpour of thunderbolts in all directions, accompanied by a celestial palace surrounded by waters like the Ganges, there was a mass of flaming brands, spears, rocks, darts, swords, lances, arrows, javelins, and mallets flowing in the central current. With a torrential downpour of thunderbolts in all directions, accompanied by a celestial palace surrounded by waters like the Ganges, there was a mass of flaming brands, spears, rocks, darts, swords, lances, arrows, javelins, and mallets flowing in the central current.

Even this formidable body composed of earth and other elements, though it receives and inflicts blows as if it were a dense mass of matter, subsides like an illusion when gods, asuras, and siddhas are present; yet the illusory form arises again, and it is not that very same [body] itself.

The faces of the quarters became like great oceans filled with floods of blood from mountains shattered by weapons resembling crags; they were overgrown with the corpses of the lords of gods and asuras, which served as rocks for forests of spears and palm trees.

Vomiting forth spears, arrows, javelins, maces, swords, and discuses, and playfully swallowing the mountains hurled by the gods and dānavas, a creation of iron lions—possessing rows of teeth and claw-tips like flaming saws—fell down still alive.

The line of venomous serpents shone forth like the ocean submerged by soaring, massive, and towering mountains, appearing as a host of suns at the end of an eon that set the quarters ablaze with the flood of heat from the fiery flames of their blazing eyes.

The entire world became a body of extreme distress, enveloped by the surging waves of the ocean agitated within by the harsh impact of the thundering vajras and makaras, by the mountain ranges being whirled about, and by the swirling currents of rivers of diverse weapons.

The sky, the courtyard of the great hosts of asuras, had its lofty serpents shaken by mountains, missiles, weapons, and Garuḍas; for a moment it was filled with oceans, for a moment with floods of fire, for a moment with suns, and for a moment with darkness.

With masses of mountain-like fires from weapons spread through the sky, agitated by the *guḍaguḍa* roar of Garuḍas, the world became as unbearable as at the time of universal dissolution, its interior space filled with the blazing abodes of the gods and the earth itself.

The Asuras flew up from the surface of the earth into the sky like birds from a mountain slope, while the gods fell to the ground by their own excessive force like the rocks of mountains shaken during the dissolution of the world.

Then, the gods and demons, consumed by the great conflagration clinging to the forest-like rows of trees formed by the lofty weapons fixed upon their bodies, assumed the appearance of mountains tossed by the winds at the end of an aeon within the expanse of the sky.

O dear one, the sky all around the mountain, filled with streams of blood released from the bodies of the lords of gods and asuras as they whirled about on every side, bore the likeness of the Ganges when its waters have been stained by the mass of rays produced at twilight.
Then they rained down mountains, showers of water, and likewise showers of various fierce weapons; they rained down terrible thunderbolts and, moreover, showers of fire upon one another.

Expert in the paths of both right and wrong conduct, and having shattered the walls of all the great mountains, they simultaneously rained down a shower of merit upon the temples of elephants from every direction.

The gods and asuras, agitated by the tumult of battle, their hands wielding weapons intent on crushing one another’s limbs, wandered through the sky scattering their splendor, grinding down the broad ranks of the army of the elephant-king’s offspring.

With severed heads, hands, arms, and thighs wandering like inauspicious locusts through the quarters of the sky, the belly of the world then became filled with those fierce fragments as if by masses of clouds, obscuring the mountain ranges at the horizon from the sun.
The earth was shattered into pieces as it was struck by the masses of flashing sword-blades, whirled forth by the shouting warriors who slapped their thighs, and fell down, shattered by mutual blows.

With mutual showers of weapons, stones, mountains, and trees, and through the friction of bodies as hard as Mount Meru, the battle took place with a crackling sound that rent the sky, its terrifying and heavy roars like those at the end of an eon.

The cosmic egg, with its two halves like the sun and fire stirred by the wind of intoxication, and containing a vast multitude of gods and demons, became as terrifying as the end of an aeon, with its walls and corners shattered to pieces.

The mountain peaks, whirling violently and filling the horizons, were struck by weapons as massive as themselves; they rattled and shrieked as if in agony from the fierce winds of the high caves, and roared loudly with the sounds of charging lions. The mountain peaks, whirling violently and filling the horizons, were struck by weapons as massive as themselves; they rattled and shrieked as if in agony from the fierce winds of the high caves, and roared loudly with the sounds of charging lions.

Within [the mind], there is constant wandering amidst illusions, rivers, oceans, armies, dense fires, and conflagrations; with trees, the corpses of gods and asuras, immovable mountains, and towering rocks; and with the arrows, swords, sharp spears, maces, and weapons of delusion—like forest leaves scattered by the wind.

With the bodies of the warriors falling—bodies as formidable as the strength of Durvāra’s elephant, capable of shattering the measurement of the wings of the lord of mountains—the ocean suddenly became filled with the flood of water from the city of the gods, as if it had been swept away by the wind from the falling mountain-like corpses.

Then the atmosphere was filled with a thick, humming roar, and the earth—with its mountains washed by blood—became like a cavernous expanse of the world filled with pools of gore, teeming with activity.

Then, indeed, that battle became truly like this worldly existence: it brought about transformations extending through infinite vision; it foretold pleasure and pain oriented toward decline and rise; and it was crowded with the friction of gods and asuras engaged in the act of combat.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, with such tumultuous undertakings, the life-taking Asuras, suddenly seized by fury, commenced a truly great battle.
By means of illusion, as well as by dispute, by alliance and by war, by flight, by fortitude, and by concealment and protection;
Through acts of treachery, combat with missiles, and frequent disappearances, that battle was maintained by the gods for thirty-five years.
For eighteen, seven, and five years, days, months, and years, there fell upon trees, fires, weapons, thunderbolts, and mountains a rain of these very things.
After such a length of time, through the firm habituation of egoism, Dāma and the others—whose minds were swallowed up by it—adopted the conviction that "I am [the body]."

Just as a mirror becomes like the reflected object due to the excellence of proximity, so too do those [elements] attain the state of being accompanied by egoism due to the excellence of habitual practice.
Just as an object situated at a great distance does not reflect in a mirror, so too the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of an entity does not arise from a lack of practice.
When Dāma and the others were born with the latent impressions of egoism and selfhood, they fell into a state of wretchedness, thinking, "This is my life; this is my wealth."
Seized by the latent impression of existence and consequently by the latent impression of delusion, they are bound by the snares of hope; therefore, they have fallen into a state of wretchedness.
For, like a deluded person, the sense of "mine-ness" (mamatva) is imagined by those devoid of egoism; it is like the perception of a snake in a rope by Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa.
"How may my body, from head to foot, become firm?"—thus did they fall into a state of wretchedness, made miserable by the craving of "mine-ness."
"May my body remain firm; may my wealth lead to happiness"—the fortitude of those whose minds were thus bound vanished within.
Because their bodies were possessed of latent tendencies and because they were of little strength, that intentness of the enemies of the gods upon striking quickly became as if wiped away.
Thinking, "How shall we exist in this world? they fell helplessly into a state of wretchedness, like lotuses deprived of water.
For those who possessed the conceit of "I," their delight in women, food, and drink became a terrifying state of being, rooted in worldly existence and leading them further into the cycle of birth.
Then, in that battle, out of fear, they fell into a state of hesitation, like little deer in a forest thick with rutting elephants.
Thinking "we shall die, we shall die," their hearts struck by anxiety, they indeed wandered very slowly in the battle against the enraged Rāvaṇa.
For those who desired only their own bodies and were terrified even of death, the enemy placed its foot upon their heads because of their lack of fortitude.
Then, their strength utterly spent, they were unable to slay the warrior standing before them, just as fires cannot consume an oblation when their fuel is exhausted.
Having attained the state of gnats for the striking gods, the common soldiers stood there in heaps, mangled by wounds and gashes.
What need is there for much speaking here? With their hearts terrified by death as the gods advanced, the Daityas fled from the field of battle.
While those famous ones known as Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa—along with the other Dānavas and their followers—were fleeing in terror from all sides within the abode of the gods;
Then that army of Daityas, having been devoured, fell in flight from the sky on all sides, like a cluster of stars scattered by the winds at the end of an aeon.
In the groves of the Immortal Mountain, upon the peaks of its summits, on the shores of the oceans, and amidst the masses of clouds;
In the whirlpools and chasms of the ocean, in ravines and surging rivers, in the wildernesses, at the ends of the quarters, and in the blazing forests.
In villages and cities where the land was devastated by his arrows, in forests with fierce predators, and in the forest fires of the desert lands;
On the mountains at the edge of the Lokāloka range, in the lakes, and in the cities of Andhra, Draviḍa, Kaśmīra, and Pārasīka.
In the waves of various oceans, in the masses of Ganges water, on other continents, in the nets, and upon the creepers of the Jambū region;
Those enemies of the gods fell from all sides like mountains, their limbs and feet shattered and their hands and arms torn apart.
With their entrails like strings clinging to the branches, shedding streams of blood, their heads with their crests scattered, they emerged with eyes full of rage.
Armed with weapons, their armor and missiles shattered by the power of Māyā’s arrows, their various garments and weapons fell scattered and overturned from afar.
Terrifying with the crackling sound of helmets dangling from their necks, they had hundreds of stone-tipped spikes protruding from their crests and hanging down from various parts of their bodies.

They were obstructed by the sharp, fierce, and hard thorns of the silk-cotton trees that struck them with a *kaṭat* sound; their heads were shattered into a hundred pieces by being dashed against surfaces of solid stone slabs.
Immediately upon the mere discharge of all their various weapons and missiles, the lords of the asuras perished in every direction, like dust in the waters of the ocean.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the gods were thus gratified and the Dānavas had been slain, Dāma, Vyāla, Kaṭa, and the others became dejected and overwhelmed with fear.
Enraged, Śambara—whose army had been destroyed—blazed forth like the fire at the end of an aeon, crying out "Where are you? against Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa.
Then, out of fear of Śambara, Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa abandoned their own domain and went to the seventh netherworld (pātāla), where they remained.
There, the servants of Yama, who are capable of terrifying even Time itself, stand out of curiosity as the guardians of the ocean of hell.
Then those fearless ones, having instilled fear in those who had departed, gave them maidens in succession who were like dense clouds in form and like anxieties in nature.
Together with them, Dāma and the others spent their time there for a period of ten thousand years, having taken up endless evil latent impressions (vāsanās).
"This maiden is my beloved; she is mine, for I am her master"—thus did time pass for those whose bonds of affection were deeply rooted.
Then, on one occasion, Dharmarāja arrived at that place by chance for the purpose of investigating the affairs of the great hells.
Because they did not fully understand this King of Dharma, three asuras did not bow down to him, treating him like an ordinary servant for their own destruction.
Then, by Vivasvat, these were cast into the blazing and terrible realms merely by the movement of a frown.
There, those cries of lamentation, along with their friends, wives, and kinsmen, were consumed like leafy branches of trees by forest winds.
Born through their own cruel latent tendencies, Kirātas and royal servants take on the forms of those who perform the work of bondage once again.
Then, having abandoned that birth, they were born as crows in ravines; at the end of that, they attained the state of vultures, and from there they reached the state of parrots.
Those evil-minded ones became pigs in Trigarta, rams in the mountains, and then worms in Magadha.
Having experienced various other diverse successions of births, O Rāma, today these fish remain in a small pond in the forest of Kaśmīra.
Drinking water that is like thin mud boiled by a forest fire, they neither die nor live, being worn out by the mire of old age.
Having repeatedly experienced the agitation of various wombs, they have come into being again and again, only to perish once more like waves in the ocean.

Caught in the ocean of existence and driven by the threads of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), they have long been carried like straw by the waves in the form of bodies; O Rāma, they have not yet attained peace—consider the infinite and terrible magnitude of these latent impressions.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: Therefore, O high-minded Rāma, I shall speak for your awakening; I do so as a mere play, lest you fall into the analogy of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa.
Due to its pursuit of non-discrimination, the mind effortlessly embraces such a calamity for the sake of the endless sufferings of existence.
Where, indeed, is the lordship over the host of Śambara, the destroyer of the gods; and where is the state of being a fish, withered by a net of mud scorched by the heat?
Where is that great fortitude capable of putting to flight the hosts of the immortals, and where is this state of being a lowly servant to the Kirāta king?
Where, indeed, is the noble fortitude of the mind’s purity free from egoism, and where is the wicked conceptualization of egoism arising from the influence of false latent impressions?
O Lord, this vast and spreading cluster of the miseries of saṃsāra, dense with its branches and tendrils, rises up with egoism as its sprout.
O Rāma, diligently cleanse the ego within yourself; by contemplating that "I am nothing at all," become happy.
The orb of the moon of ultimate reality, composed of elixir and cool, has become invisible, shrouded by the cloud of egoism.
Afflicted by the demon of egoism, the three—Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa—though non-existent, attained existence as demons through the greatness of Māyā.
O Rāma, today the fish remain in the great forests, lakes, groves, and ponds of Kaśmīra, greedily longing for bits of moss.
Śrī Rāma said: "The non-existent has no being, and the existent has no non-being. How then did those things, which are non-existent, attain existence? Tell me this."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "It is even so, O mighty-armed one; that which is non-existent never arises anywhere at any time. Even the most minute thing can become vast."
Tell me, what is established as non-existent, and what is that which is established as existent? By means of a correct illustration alone, I shall bring about your awakening.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahmin, it is indeed true that we who are here are virtuous; yet you say that even Dāma and the others, though not virtuous, are established as virtuous."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, just as Dāma and the others exist as products of illusion, they are indeed unreal, appearing as real like the flow of water in a mirage.
In the very same way, we too—along with the gods, asuras, and dānavas—are merely unreal as we move about, go, and come.
Your existence is indeed false, and my existence is likewise false; though experienced, it is unreal in nature, just like one's own death in a dream.
Just as a deceased kinsman experienced even in a dream is composed of unreality, so too is this world, if there were the realization that "this has died."
This statement, pertaining to the utterly deluded, does not shine at all; for [the truth] arises through practice, and there can be no denial of direct experience.
That certainty which has taken root within and become perfected without practice never perishes for anyone in this world at any time.
Even one who is utterly deluded laughs like a madman at that madman who says, "This world is unreal; Brahman alone is real."

Where indeed could there be unity between one who is intoxicated and one who is sober, or between one who is ignorant and one who knows the truth? It would be like the union of darkness and light, or of shadow and sunshine, within the same perception.
Even with effort, an ignorant person who has experienced an object cannot deny its reality, just as one cannot step over a corpse that lies within one's grasp.
It is not fitting for the ignorant person to say that "the entire world is Brahman"; for one who has not experienced austerity and knowledge, he has experienced only that [world].
For this speech, O Rāma, shines forth only within the domain of the unenlightened; in the case of a Buddha, there is truly nothing whatsoever that can be characterized by the form of "I am."
Experiencing that "this supreme, tranquil state is indeed Brahman," how could it be appropriate for that wise one to deny his own direct experience?
Apart from the other, there is nothing whatsoever of "I" within the self; just as there is no ring-ness or the like apart from gold, there is no distinctiveness in me.

Apart from reality itself, there is nothing at all in the deluded self; just as gold is not found apart from the cognition of waves and so forth, so too for the knower, there is no ultimate reality [other than that].
The fool consists of false ego, while the wise man consists of the one true Self; indeed, neither can ever be joined with the other, for that would be a denial of their respective natures.
How can there be a denial of that which consists of something else? For the statement "I am a pot" would indeed be the talk of a madman.
Therefore, neither we nor Dāma and the others are real anywhere; those [others] are unreal, and so are we, for indeed there is no origination for us.
Truth is pure consciousness, the stainless sky of awakening; truth is all-pervading, peaceful, and free from rising or setting.
Everything is peaceful and void, existing as if it were nothing at all; within that space, my dear, these creations shine forth as its own innate radiance.
Just as the innate visual perceptions of one with cataracts appear as clusters of hair and the like, so do these perceptions appear there.
In an instant, he experiences himself exactly as he perceives it; therefore, the sky of consciousness, though unreal, becomes real through that very perception.
"There is neither truth nor untruth; therefore, in the three worlds, in whatever manner the nature of consciousness perceives something, it arises exactly in that way, without a doubt."
Just as Dāma and the others were, so have we arisen; whether real or unreal, my friend, what conceptualization can there be regarding them?
In this infinite, all-pervading, and formless sky of consciousness, consciousness arises in whatever manner; in that very way, it shines forth abundantly therein.
Wherever consciousness itself manifests in the form of a rope or the like, it becomes established as such through the experience of that specific form.
Wherever consciousness arises by itself in the form of ourselves and others, it becomes established there in that very way, through the experience of having that specific form.

The designation "world" is applied to the manifestation of one's own dream, just as the state of being "deer-water" is attributed to the heat of the sky-like void of consciousness which has the nature of space.
Where the sky of consciousness is awakened, there the designation "the visible" is applied; where it is asleep by that very same [consciousness], there the designation "liberation" is applied.
And that [consciousness] is never anywhere asleep, nor is it ever awakened; let it be understood that the visible world is merely the sky of consciousness.
Nirvāṇa itself is the glory of creation, and the glory of creation itself is nirvāṇa; there is no difference in meaning between these two words, just as there is none between synonyms.
The ultimate reality perceives the world as its own form; it is just as a cataract-afflicted eye perceives a mass of floating hairs.
That hair-net is not anything at all; for that vision remains as it is. This visible world is nothing whatsoever; thus the sky of consciousness is established.

Everything exists everywhere, just as it is experienced; nothing whatsoever exists here that has not been experienced. This peaceful, singular, and all-pervading reality abides thus; therefore, remain with grief, fear, and duality abandoned.

This form of the great consciousness is inherently pure, tranquil, and dense like the interior of a rock; it neither exists nor does not exist in any particular way, yet whatever does exist shines forth as that very reality.
Śrī Rāma said: "How can there be an end to the suffering of Dāma, Vyāla, Kaṭa, and the others—who, though they were virtuous, became as if non-existent like children, yakṣas, and piśācas?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O scion of Raghu’s line, listen to this which was spoken by Yama when he was entreated by those servants of Yama along with the family of Dāma and Vyāla at that very moment.
When Dāma and the others shall experience separation and hear their own story, they will undoubtedly become liberated.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, where, when, and how will they hear this account of your own life? Or rather, please describe it to me in due order.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In a small pond on the shore of the Mahāpadma lake in Kaśmīra, he experienced a succession of births as a fish again and again.
With their minds agitated and fickle, they will meet their end in due time; right there in that lotus lake, they shall become cranes.
There, amidst garlands of white water-lilies and clusters of lotuses, among the excellent creepers of moss and the undulations of the waves;
Upon the swaying swings of blossoms and upon the creepers of blue lotuses, amidst the streaks of clouds formed by masses of spray, and within the cool whirlpools that swirl about.
Having enjoyed the delights of the lake, those cranes, the ornaments of the world, having sported for a very long time, have now returned with their purity restored.

Having attained awakening, they will become liberated and separated [from the body], just as the qualities of passion (rajas), goodness (sattva), and darkness (tamas) reach a state of separation by chance.
Within the region of Kaśmīra, there will be a city adorned by mountains, which shall be known by the name Adhiṣṭhāna and will be glorious.
In its center there will be a peak named Pradyumnaśikhara, like the small pericarp of a lotus within its calyx.
Upon the summit of that mountain, there will be a certain king’s palace, a great mansion reaching to the clouds, like one peak upon another.
In the northeast corner of the house, within a cavity in the wall above the head, near a blade of grass constantly shaken by an unceasing wind.
In the storehouse-consciousness (ālaya), the donor will become like a predatory beast or a sparrow; like a beginner who has heard little of the scriptures, he utters sounds devoid of meaning.
At that very time, there will be a king there named Śrī Yaśaskaradeva, like another Śakra in heaven.
O Dāman, there will be a *dānava* named Maśaka in his house; with a soft sound, he will pierce the back of a large pillar.
At that time, within that very city called Adhiṣṭhāna, there will also be a monastery known as the Ratnāvalī Monastery.
In that place, a minister of that land known as Narasiṃha will dwell, who perceives bondage and liberation as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of his hand.
In his house there shall be a pet bird, a *krakara*, named the illusory demon Kaṭa, who has fashioned for himself a royal cage.
That Nṛsiṃha, the minister of the king, will narrate this excellent story of Dāma, Vyāla, Kaṭa, and the others, composed in verses.
Having heard this and his own past life recalled through that story, Śakaṭa, the Krakara, will thus attain peace—the supreme, great tranquility of final Nirvāṇa.
The kalaviṅka bird dwelling on the edge of the Pradyumna peak will hear the discourse from those there and attain supreme nirvāṇa.
Even a mosquito, having come to dwell within a wound inside the wood of the royal palace, will attain peace by chance upon hearing [the teaching].
O Rāghava, the sparrow shall attain liberation from the horn of Pradyumna, the mosquito from the royal palace, and the lizard from the monastery.
Thus has this entire sequence of the story of Dāma and Vyāla been told to you; in this very way, Māyā is the void of saṃsāra, yet she is exceedingly radiant.
Due to lack of full understanding, one is whirled down from even a great state by the power of various forms of ignorance, just as one might be led astray by the waters of a mirage.
Deluded fools fall down like Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa; where is the crushing of Mount Meru and Mandara under the mere knitting of a brow?
Where is this state of being a mosquito in a wound inside the wood of Rājagṛha? Where is this state of having the orbs of the sun and moon struck down by a mere palm-slap from an arm?
Where is the state of being a bird in a hole in the wall of a house on Mount Pradyumna? Where is the tossing of Mount Meru with hands as light as play with flowers?
Or where, on the peak of the Man-Lion, does the state of being a young partridge exist in the house? It is the sky of consciousness itself, its radiance colored by the quality of passion (rajas).
Without abandoning its own nature, it perceives even that which is dissimilar, through the delusion of its own latent impressions (vāsanā), whether those impressions are real or unreal.
Just as a creature goes toward a mirage with the thought that it is water, so do those cross the ocean of existence with the very notion that it is their own natural flow.
Those who abide in nirvana perceive that which is to be seen as attained through the scripture; they [reject] the various transformations of suffering and the doctrines of dry logic.
They go to the abyss like waters, destroying their own gains by means of a path established through personal experience that leads according to the scriptures.
O noble one, there is no destruction for those who go to the supreme goal; O Mahāmati, this is because of the thought, "May this be mine, may that be mine."
Because of his own wretchedness and misfortune, not even ashes remain for him; yet he who is noble-souled regards even the three worlds as a mere blade of grass.
All calamities abandon him, just as snakes cast off their worn-out skins, within whom the wondrous manifestation of pure being (sattva) constantly vibrates.
The lords of the world protect him like the unbroken realm of Brahmā; even in the face of an endless calamity, one must never deviate from the proper course.

Even Rāhu, though drinking nectar in this manner by means of a non-sequential process, has died; [so too does one die] without the contact of true scriptures and holy men, which provide a light as fierce as the sun.
Those who take refuge do not fall again under the power of the blindness of delusion; those who were once powerless come under control, and all calamities go to their destruction.
The excellence achieved by one through virtues becomes inexhaustible—those who have no satiety with virtues and whose passion is for sacred learning.
Those men who are devoted to truth are superior to other beings; by the moonlight of their fame, the lakes of the hearts of living creatures are illuminated.
Surely Hari resides in the very form of those oceans of milk; everything that was to be enjoyed has been enjoyed, and all sights worth seeing have been seen.

What else [is needed] for the destruction of worldly existence than renewed greed for enjoyments? [One should act] according to the sequence, according to the scriptures, according to established custom, and according to the traditional order.
Remain steadfast; let go of the unreal web of internal enjoyments; cultivate intimacy with fame through virtues that reach the heavens.
For these two indeed protect one from death; they are never seekers of worldly enjoyments. The beautiful Siddha women sing of their fame, which is as white as the moon.
They live by means of songs and the expanse of the sky, while others are as if dead; having undertaken the supreme human effort and exerting excellent endeavor.
Who that practices without agitation according to the scriptures would not be a possessor of accomplishment? One who dwells according to the scriptures should not harbor haste for accomplishments.
Success ripened over a long period of time becomes a fruit of full nourishment—free from sorrow, fear, and exertion, and devoid of pride and constraint.
Let legal proceedings be conducted according to the scriptures; let them not perish, for the living being has reached the end within worldly existences that are like dilapidated blind wells.
O you who have many attachments, now that your senses have been subdued, do not go from here again toward the lower, base state.
Let this scripture be considered as a weapon for warding off calamities, even in battle where elephants are torn apart by hundreds of rows of sharp arrows.
What is the seal of life for one in the mud? Let the scent of worldly enjoyment be cast aside. Noble ones, what is the use of mere wealth? One should instead contemplate the sacred scriptures.
"This is the reflection, this is the reflection"—let this be truly investigated with the intellect, like cattle driven by another.
This deliberation, which bestows misfortune, is wretched and devoid of virtue; let this dense, long, and great sleep be abandoned, and let one awaken.
Do not remain asleep like an old tortoise in a small pond; resolve to rise up for the sake of pacifying old age and death.
The attainment of wealth leads to misfortune; a flood of enjoyments brings about the disease of existence; all prosperities are calamities; and victory everywhere consists in having no attachment.

For those engaged in worldly affairs, [this is] for the sake of successful results through action that accords with both worldly custom and the conduct prescribed by the scriptures, following from careful deliberation.

For one whose conduct is beautiful through right behavior, whose life is lived in solitude, and who has abandoned the pursuit of the fruits of worldly happiness and the states of suffering, his lifespan, fame, virtues, and prosperity flourish together like a blossoming spring creeper for the sake of good fruit.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Because everything is possible everywhere and at all times through the fulfillment of every excellence, you must not abandon your auspicious exertion.
Having approached the Lord of the Lake, who bestows joy and delight upon friends, kinsmen, and relatives, even death itself was utterly conquered.
Even the gods, though endowed with supreme excellence, were overwhelmed by the Dānavas—who were rich in the wealth of their purpose—just as lotus ponds are trampled by elephants.
At the sacrifice of King Marutta, by the great seer Saṃvarta, another creation was brought forth, including gods and asuras, as if by Brahmā himself.
The status of a Brahmin, though difficult to attain, was acquired through asceticism by Viśvāmitra, who was endowed with great excellence and repeatedly applied himself to it.
For one who eats such a difficult-to-obtain water-sediment as if it were an elixir of immortality, even a person of little fortune like Upamanyu attained the Ocean of Milk.
Consuming the Trailokyamallas, including Viṣṇu, Alajā, and the others, as if they were blades of grass, Kāla was himself brought to his end by Śveta through the firmness of his supreme devotion.
Having won over Yama through her affection and having established a conversation with him, Sāvitrī brought back her husband Satyavat from the other world.
There is no excellence in this world that does not have a manifest fruit; one who possesses every excellence must investigate within until the ultimate truth is reached.
Self-knowledge is that which scrapes away the very root of all perceptions of states of pleasure and pain; therefore, one should cultivate it with great excellence.

For one who has fallen into calamity and seeks its destruction, views such as the view of a visible object and so forth do not lead to the attainment of any happiness free from affliction other than suffering.
Non-quiescence is the supreme Brahman, and quiescence is the supreme state; even though this is so, nevertheless, know this Śaṅkara first.
Having abandoned conceit and resorted to eternal tranquility, one should investigate the state of nobility through wisdom and practice the service of the virtuous.
Neither austerities, nor sacred fords, nor scriptures prevail in crossing the ocean of saṃsāra without the service of the virtuous.
He whose greed, delusion, and anger diminish day by day, that virtuous person conducts himself according to the scriptures in his respective duties.
Then, through association with those who know the Self, there arises in that virtuous one the realization of the absolute non-existence of this visible world, just as it is perceived.
But through the absolute non-existence of the visible world, only the Supreme remains; by virtue of the absence of anything else, the individual soul quickly merges into that very [Supreme].
The visible world has not arisen, nor did it ever exist, nor will it exist; even in the present it does not exist at all, for only the supreme, unshakeable reality exists.
Thus it has been demonstrated by a thousand arguments; it is seen as well, and it is experienced by everyone—I shall now demonstrate it further.
Likewise, this stainless and peaceful sky of consciousness of the three worlds—how or in what manner could there be "reality" or "unreality" within it?
The beautiful, flickering consciousness manifests as a wondrous marvel within the unmoving Self; for by that very [consciousness], this world is realized to be nothing other than that itself.

The experience of the abundance of the three worlds is the orb of rays from the sun of consciousness; tell me, who can describe any distinction between the sun and its rays, for that state is free from conceptual construction?
The opening and closing of this consciousness-vision by its very nature are these two: the setting and the rising of the experience of the world-form.
The sense of "I," when unrecognized, is a stain upon the sky of ultimate reality; yet the sense of "I," when fully recognized, becomes the very sky of the Supreme Self.
When the sense of "I" is fully understood, it no longer exists as "I" at all; it becomes one with the self of the consciousness-ether, just as water becomes one with water.
The world of perception, beginning with the "I," does not exist at all in reality; therefore, by means of inquiry into the "I," that [reality] alone necessarily remains.

Even among those of pure intellect, the notion of a demon regarding one who is not a demon is suppressed; such is the case for children whose inner faculties are still shrouded in darkness until they reach the stage of inquiry.
As long as the moonlight of consciousness remains obscured within by the thick cloud of egoism, it does not cause the night-blooming lily of ultimate reality to blossom.
When this notion of "I" has been wiped away, and one is oneself devoid of self-interest, what room is there for the mere imagination of craving for hell, heaven, liberation, and the like?
As long as the cloud of egoism expands within the heart, so long does the cluster of *kuṭaja* blossoms of craving come into full bloom.
When consciousness is constantly overwhelmed by the cloud of egoism, only dullness persists; light never manifests.
This ego-sense, which does not exist, is falsely imagined by itself; it leads only to suffering and not to joy, like a yakṣa conjured by the delusions of a child.
The deluded sense of "I," falsely imagined through ignorance, bestows infinite saṃsāra, just as a wicked mind [perceives] a rope and other such things [as snakes].
From the vast delusion of thinking "I am this," there arises another darkness that is more harmful than any other; such a source of misfortune has never existed in saṃsāra, nor will it ever exist.
Whatever pure pleasure or pain arises here in existence, that is merely the unfolding of the expansion of the wheel of egoism.
The sprout of egoism, uprooted by the heart and planted [in its stead], destroys his cycle of existence—that tree which has a thousand branches and is difficult to cut down.
The sense of "I" is the sprout of those inexhaustible trees that are births; the expansive thoughts of "this is mine" are their branches by the thousands.
Objects such as latent impressions (vāsanā) appear like the bursting of a crow’s fall; they are like waves, excellent mud, or the charming sound of a bird when investigated.
The notion of "I" shines forth through the cultivation of egoism; therefore, free yourself from the sense of "I" and "you," and bring to a halt this turning of the wheel of saṃsāra for yourself.
As long as the darkness of the sense of "I" expands in the forest of birth, so long do these female demons of anxiety, intoxicated with thought, dance about.
For that lowest of men who is seized by the demon of egoism, neither the scriptures nor the mantras lead to the accomplishment of his true being.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, by what means does the ego-sense not increase? O Brahman, tell that to me for the sake of pacifying the fear of saṃsāra.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When one remains established in one's own stainless self, which has the form of a mirror of pure consciousness, the ego does not increase through such contemplation of one's true nature.
"This splendor of Indra’s net is false; what use have I for attachment or aversion?"—from such internal reflection, the sense of ego does not arise.
When one realizes for oneself that "I am not in the self, nor does the splendor of the visible world belong to me," egoism does not increase through such peaceful conduct.
For when the views of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted regarding "the world" have ceased within me, and equanimity has become serene, the sense of "I-ness" does not increase.

When the notions of "I" and "the world" have ceased within, and when the views of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted have perished, the sense of "I-ness" does not increase in that serene equanimity.
Śrī Rāma said: O Lord, what is the form of the ego, and how is it abandoned? Is it with a body or without a body, and what occurs when it is relinquished?
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, there are three kinds of egoism here in the three worlds; two are excellent, while the other is to be abandoned. Listen, for I shall tell you.
"I am this entire universe; I am the Supreme Self, the Infallible One; there is nothing else"—this indeed is to be known as the supreme ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti).
For one who is liberated while living, this [realization] leads to liberation and not to bondage; I am distinct from everything, as subtle as a hundredth part of the tip of a hair.
This consciousness which is thus described is the auspicious second form of egoity; it leads to liberation and not to bondage, for it belongs to one who is liberated while living.
That which is designated as "I-conceit" (ahaṃkāra) is merely a conceptual construction and not real; this conviction that "I am this [body] consisting of hands, feet, and so forth" is what it is.
This third one is egoism; it is merely worldly and utterly trivial. This evil-natured thing is to be avoided alone; it is remembered as the supreme enemy.
A living being struck by this powerful enemy, who bestows manifold afflictions, does not grow again.
The world, its intellect rendered miserable by this long-attached and false egoism, sinks indeed into calamities.

A living being who possesses the refined sense of "I" attains liberation through the Blessed One; whereas one who perceives this [body] as having a nature of defects, like the worldly sense of "I," remains bound.
Having determined "I am not the body," its renunciation is the doctrine of the great; first, one must accept the two types of egoism, both of which are worldly.
First, one should accept the two forms of ego that are non-worldly; the third form of ego, which is worldly and brings suffering, must be abandoned.
Indeed, through this wicked arrogance, Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa have reached such a state that it causes distress even when mentioned in stories.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin, having abandoned this third worldly form of egoism from the mind, what state of being must a person attain to obtain his own welfare?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This [mind], which bestows suffering, must first be abandoned; for in whatever manner a person remains after having relinquished it, in that very manner he attains the Supreme.
O sinless one, if a person should remain contemplating these two previously mentioned views regarding the ego, he attains that supreme state.
Then, having abandoned even those [notions] and being devoid of all egoism, he should remain established; thus he ascends to the exceedingly lofty state itself.
At all times and with every effort, mundane and difficult-to-abandon egoism must be avoided for the sake of realizing supreme bliss, by means of this wisdom.
The abandonment of attachment to the body, of disease, of demerit, and of evil egoism—this alone is the ultimate supreme good, this is the highest state.
Having abandoned this gross worldly egoism through contemplation, a person does not fall downward, whether remaining still or engaged in worldly activity.
O Great-minded One, for a being whose egoism has been completely stilled, enjoyments are like diseases; they do not taste sweet, just as poisonous liquids do not please one who is well-satiated.
When sensual enjoyments no longer provide satisfaction, the supreme good stands before a person; for when darkness has faded, what else indeed can the mind turn toward?
O Rāghava, it is precisely by abandoning the pursuit of egoism and through human effort that one crosses the ocean of worldly existence.

Thinking, "I am not [the body], nor does anything belong to me," and "everything is mine, and I am indeed all," the Great-Souled One, having established this praiseworthy consciousness within the mind and brought it to such a state, attains the supreme station.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In this regard, listen as I tell you what occurred after Dāma and the others had departed, within the city of Śambara, which was as vast as a mountain.
Thus, when the entire army of Śambara had fallen from the sky, its stability destroyed and utterly perished like a mass of clouds in autumn.
Having spent several years with his army conquered by the gods, that Dānava, intent on slaying the gods once again, reflected:
But as for Dāma and the others, those asuras who were created by me through my illusory power (māyā), they were filled with false pride in battle due to their own folly.
Now I shall create other Dānavas arisen through my illusory power; I shall also make them knowers of the inner science (adhyātma-śāstra) and possessed of discernment.
Then, through the thorough knowledge of reality, being freed from false conceptions, they will no longer fall into egoism and will conquer those gods.
Having reflected thus, the lord of the Daityas, by means of his intellect, brought forth through his illusory power (māyā) such Dānavas as the ocean produces bubbles.
The supreme ones are omniscient, knowers of what is to be known, free from passion, devoid of sin, performers of only that which has been attained, and those whose selves are cultivated.
Marked by the names Bhīma, Bhāsa, and Dṛḍha, they possessed purified minds and viewed the entire world as if it were mere straw.
Having reached the world, those Daityas covered the sky, roaring with weapons for lightning, like clouds in the rainy season.
They fought equally even against the gods for many groups of years; yet, through the power of discernment, they never succumbed to egoism at any time.
As long as the latent impression (*vāsanā*) "this is mine" arises within them, so long will the inquiry "who is this? and "what am I? fail to reach the state of unreality.
"O wise ones, who am I, this bodiless state?"—from such inquiry as this, fear and other such emotions did not arise within them.
"This body is unreal; it does not exist. Pure consciousness alone abides in the Self. There is no such thing as 'I,' nor is there anything else. Having thus resolved, the Asuras departed.
Then, by those who were free from egoism, fearless of old age and death, who accomplished their goals, steadfast, and followed the present moment;

By those whose intellects are eternally unattached, who have destroyed all other [notions of] agency, who are liberated from the net of latent impressions (vāsanā), and who, having accomplished their task, are non-doers; |||
Thinking, "This is the work of our Lord; this must be done," they were intent on their vow, free from passion, devoid of hatred, and always possessed of an even-minded vision.
That divine army was slain, devoured, carried off, and consumed by Bhīma, Bhāsa, Dṛḍha, and the others, just as the excellence of one's own food is experienced by its eaters.
Crushed by Bhīma and Bāṣpa, the army of the gods fled with great speed, like the Gaṅgā falling from the Himavat.
That army of the gods went for refuge to the god who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk, just as a row of clouds driven by the wind seeks shelter on a mountain.
Hari comforted that terrified army of the gods, as a lover might comfort a solitary woman surrounded by serpents.
Then that celestial host dwelt within the cavern of the Ocean of Milk for as long as the Blessed One had not yet set out for the purpose of dispelling it.
Then a fierce battle took place between Śauri and Śambara, like an untimely dissolution at the end of a kalpa, during which the principal mountain ranges were tossed up into the air.
In that battle, the Daitya Śambara, along with his army and mounts, was subdued; struck down by Nārāyaṇa, he departed for the city of Viṣṇu.
But those [enemies], though firm as Bhīma and Bhasa, were brought to rest by Viṣṇu alone in that uneven battle, like lamps by the wind.
For when they have attained peace, being indeed free from all latent tendencies, their destination is no longer known, just like that of lamps which have been extinguished.
Therefore, O Rāma, the mind is bound by latent impressions and liberated when free from them; attain the state of being free from impressions through discernment.
Through the correct perception of the Truths, latent impressions dissolve; and with the dissolution of latent impressions, the mind attains tranquility like a lamp [in the absence of wind].
Nothing at all here is real; one should thoroughly cultivate the realization that no entity exists. Therefore, "there is indeed no cultivation"—this is right vision.
This entire world is indeed the Self alone; who could imagine what, or where? That which is called "imagination" does not exist at all—this is the correct vision.
Where the two sounds named "vāsanā" and "citta," which are endowed with their respective meanings, have dissolved through the vision of truth—that is the supreme state.
The mind, enveloped by latent impressions, has attained a state of stability here; that very same mind, when liberated from them, is called "liberated."
That very mind, which has assumed the state of existence through various forms such as jars and cloths, should be swiftly brought to stillness, like a false yakṣa that has arisen.
Just as the mind was transformed by the forms of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, so too, O descendant of Raghu, your steadfastness remains unshaken by the formidable and firm logic of Bhāsas.
O Rāghava, let not the logic of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa be yours; O Rāma, this was told to me long ago by my father, the lotus-born Brahmā.

O Rāghava, since that which was spoken by me has been for you, my disciple of supreme intelligence, let there be no application of the "Dāma-vyāla-kaṭa" maxim for you; O sinless one, may the "bhīma-bhāsa-dṛḍha" maxim always prevail for you.

This path of worldly existence, beset by the dense crisis of pleasure and pain and reached through the heat of becoming, perishes for one who possesses worldly activity only through constant non-attachment upon reaching prosperity.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Victorious are those great heroes, the virtuous ones, by whom their own mind—tending toward sense objects through the swelling of the mire of ignorance—has been utterly conquered.
For this saṃsāra, which bestows all manner of afflictions and suffering, there is only one remedy: the restraint of one's own mind.
Listen to the essence of all knowledge, and having heard it, let it be firmly grasped: bondage consists merely in the desire for enjoyment, and its abandonment is called liberation.
What is the use of other compositions of treatises? Let this alone be done: whatever is pleasant here, let all that be viewed as like poison or fire.
The enjoyments of sense objects are unstable; having reflected upon them again and again, they bring happiness when cultivated after being renounced from above.
A mind enveloped by latent impressions gives rise to expansive defects, just as ground strewn with the seeds of thorns produces the proliferation of thorns.
The intellect, free from the web of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and devoid of mental proliferation, in which attachment and aversion are no longer seen, gradually attains supreme tranquility.
It always produces auspicious qualities, free from the ailments of the unwholesome; it is like the earth containing excellent seeds, which yields sprouts that grant fruit in due time.
When the mind has become serene through the continuous cultivation of virtuous states, and when the dense cloud of false knowledge has gradually subsided;
When his nobility increased like the white moon, and his holy discernment spread forth like the radiance of the sun in the sky;
She stood there, like a pearl released from its casing that has grown within it, or like the moon established in the springtime when its purpose has been fulfilled.
When the cool-shaded tree of association with the virtuous bears fruit, and when the straight tree of meditative absorption drips with the delicious nectar of bliss;
The mind becomes free from duality, devoid of desire, and without affliction; its restlessness, misfortune, sorrow, delusion, fear, and disease are all stilled.
With doubts regarding the meaning of the scriptures exhausted, with all curiosity vanished, with the web of conceptual construction cast aside, he was free from delusion and untainted.
It is effortless, free from reproach, indifferent, and without excess; it is with sorrow and mist thoroughly stilled, unattached, and devoid of knots.
Having destroyed the nest of his own wife along with its offspring—the fierce son of doubt—and together with its thirst, he accomplishes his own supreme self, which is the goal of sovereignty.
Remembering his sovereignty over these things, he abandons the conceptual constructions that cause the body's nourishment, and casts off his physical form like a blade of grass.
The rise of the mind is its destruction; the destruction of the mind is the great awakening. The mind of the wise man goes to destruction, while the mind of the ignorant man increases.
The wheel of the world is mind alone; the circle of mountains is mind. Mind is the sky, mind is the deity, mind is the friend, and mind is the enemy.

That forgetfulness of the true nature of the mind-essence (cittattva), which is turbid with conceptual construction, is called the "mind" (manas); this is the latent predisposition (vāsanā) that partakes in cyclic existence.

The principle of consciousness (cittattva), which consists of pure awareness alone but is slightly turbid with conceptualization and is affected by the descent of the objective world, is called the individual soul (jīva).
That which has fallen into the category of the cognizable, having acquired a fixed designation and reached a state of ignorance, is itself imagined by the internal mind to be even more substantial.
The transmigrating person is not the self, nor is it the body, nor the blood; everything such as the body is insentient, while the embodied one is like a lotus leaf, untainted.

When the body is cut into pieces, there is nothing else remaining apart from blood and so forth; when the trunk of a plantain tree is split open, there is nothing else remaining apart from its leaves.
Know that the mind is the life-force of man; it has assumed that very form. By itself, it grasps the self through the self, as it is imagined by its own conceptual constructions.
There, a person spreads out and constructs extensively from his own conceptual constructions a web for his own bondage, just like a silkworm.
Having abandoned this wandering through a body, it assumes bodily form again in another place and time, just as a sprout attains the state of a leaf.
Whatever kind of latent impression this mind possesses, such it is born; that mind which is born then sleeps, and thus it remains within a dream at night.
A sour seed, sprinkled with a sweet juice, becomes sweet; a sweet seed, sprinkled with the paste of *prativiṣā*, becomes pungent.
Through a great and auspicious latent impression, the mind becomes great; Indra’s sovereignty arises within his mental kingdom, and he experiences it as if in a dream.
Due to a base latent impression, one perceives even a slight baseness of mind; through the delusion of a demon, one sees demons in a dream at night.
In a lake of vast purity, turbidity finds no footing; likewise, in a state of vast turbidity, clarity finds no footing.
When there is vast turbidity in the mind, a fruit of that same nature arises; likewise, when there is vast purity, a fruit of that same nature arises.
Even when exhausted, the noble person never abandons their lofty course; like the moon, they strive unceasingly to fulfill their aspirations.
Here there is neither bondage nor liberation, neither non-bondage nor the state of being bound; this is merely an illusion arisen from delusion, like a vine of Indra’s net.
Having the appearance of a city of Gandharvas, arisen like a mirage, it manifests as the delusion of two moons, yet is devoid of both duality and unity.
"All this is indeed the reality of Brahman"—this is the ultimate truth; this world-process, being devoid of essence and composed of unreality, shines forth [as such].
Arising from the false conviction, "I am not infinite; I am a wretched being," one is dissolved by the firm conviction, "I am infinite; I am the Lord."
The notion "I am this" directed toward one's own all-pervading and pure self—this is that bondage in the world, fashioned by one's own conceptual construction.
Devoid of the states of bondage and liberation, and free from duality and unity—this entire reality is the existence of Brahman; such is the ultimate truth.
One who has attained purity through death, who is unattached to all views, and who has reached the state of mindlessness here, perceives Brahman; not otherwise.
The mind, having attained purity through the waters of a virtuous continuum, takes up the Brahma-vision, just as a white cloth takes up dye.
O sinless one, through the contemplation that "all this indeed is my self," when the power of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted is exhausted, let bondage and liberation be liberated.
For one whose mind has been purified by bodily discipline, scriptural learning, dispassion, and wisdom, the world appears as a mere flash of light, like a gem of noble birth.
Know that the one-pointedness of the mind, which arises from identifying with an object, is a vision of unreal knowledge that perishes in an instant.
When the mind, having abandoned everything external and internal as well as all perception of the visible, remains dissolved therein, it has then attained that state.
This clear perception of the visible world is necessarily composed of unreality; know that being composed of that [unreality] is the very nature of the mind, and nothing else.
Because it is perishable at its beginning and end, it is likewise unreal in the middle; therefore, those whose minds are ignorant suffer even while [the treasure] is held in their own hands.
If one lacks the realization that "this world is indeed the Self," the splendor of the visible world brings suffering; otherwise, however, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

The notion that "the water is one thing and the wave another" is ignorance due to perceived multiplicity; whereas the realization that "this wave is indeed the water" is wisdom, owing to the recognition of oneness.
That which consists of suffering and has the nature of what is to be abandoned or adopted arises as unreal; however, through the knowledge of its non-existence, infinity alone remains.

And because it is fashioned by conceptualization, the form of the mind is composed of unreality; tell me, O Rāghava, when that which consists of unreality has perished, what cause for grief can there be?
Just as a kinsman who lacks affection is seen with a mind free from attachment and aversion, so too do you perceive the reality of your own cage; behold!

Just as one who lacks affection for a kinsman is not stained by that kinsman's joys and sorrows due to a thorough understanding of the truth, so it is with the self, which consists of the accumulation of reality.
That beginningless and auspicious knowledge which lies between the seer and the seen—when that truth is realized, the mind becomes tranquil, like dust when the wind has ceased.
When the wind of the mind has become tranquil, the dust of the body subsides; once again, the mist does not arise in the city of saṃsāra.
When the rainy season of latent impressions had ended, when the state of stability had arrived, when dullness had produced a trembling in the heart, and when the mud had reached dryness;
When the pit of thirst has dried up, when the forest of the heart has become stilled and dull, when the grove of the senses has withered away, and the thicket of false knowledge has been destroyed;
The mist of delusion is dissipated like the night at dawn; that resulting dullness departs somewhere, just as poison destroyed by a mantra.
On the mountain of the body, the petty rivers of fear do not flow forth; nor do the peacocks of fierce volitions dance with their wings outspread.
Moving within the sphere of the sky of consciousness, it attains supreme purity; the sun of the living soul, exceedingly clear and of great glory, shines forth intensely.
Freed from the burden of dense delusion and having attained supreme solitude, the great quarters of space shine intensely when cleansed at the proper time.
The stainless Mañjarī of Joy shines intensely, cooling the quarters of the sky like moonlight in the autumnal firmament.
Through the manifestation of all prosperity, which bestows supreme bliss, the ground of discernment, when thoroughly purified, attains complete fruition.
The interior of the world becomes exceedingly beautiful with supreme light, possessing the expanse of mountains and forests, perfectly clear and cool in its shade.
The clear lake of the heart, expanded by the virtuous and broadened into the form of crystal, attains the state of a stainless lotus bud.
