The restless bee of one's own ego, soiled within the calyx of the heart-lotus, flies away somewhere beyond all hope of being seen again.
He becomes free from all projection, all-pervading, the leader of all; devoid of latent tendencies, with a tranquil mind, he is the sovereign in the city of his own body.

Having attained the lamp of the self through investigation, his steady intellect is as if completely dissolved within the mind; beholding the worldly states of existence as tasteless and subject to decay, he dwells free from feverish distress in the city of the body.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, tell me again for the sake of increasing my understanding how this universe exists within the consciousness-self that transcends the universe.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as future waves exist in water in an unmanifest state, yet do not truly exist as something other than their own nature, so too are all creations within the state of consciousness.
Just as space, though all-pervading, is not perceived due to its subtlety, so too the partless nature of consciousness, though all-pervading, is not perceived.
Just as an appearance exists within a gem, appearing as if established or as if non-existent—being neither real nor unreal—so too does this creation exist within the Self.

Just as the sky is not touched by clouds that rest within it and are supported by themselves, so too the supreme consciousness is not touched by creations that rest within it and are supported by consciousness.
Just as that light situated in the ocean is reflected, my dear, so indeed is consciousness perceived within bodies through the subtle octads (puryaṣṭakas).
Devoid of all conceptual constructions and free from all perceptions, this very consciousness is of an indestructible nature; it is designated by such terms as "the object of cognition" and so forth.

She is subtler than a hundredth part of space, possessing a form free from all parts; she perceives the single identity with the essential nature of the entire world, both in its manifest and unmanifest states.
Just as the vast diversity consisting of waves and so forth in the ocean of water does not exist as something separate from it, so too is the transformation of existence.
This vast diversity consisting of "thou-ness" and "I-ness" exists within the ocean of consciousness; apart from pure consciousness alone, it does not manifest at all.

It gathers the gathered and the gatherable; therefore, this world remains within the Self. But for each ignorant person, there arises the conceptualization that something else has arrived and something else exists.
Among the ignorant, she is the womb containing the multitude of the inherently fierce cycle of existence; among the wise, she is manifest as light itself, being the single essence of all that exists.
By virtue of experience, she is eternally the illuminator of the sun and other luminaries; she is the taster of all beings, and the bringer of existence for those who enjoy worldly life.
It does not set, nor does it rise; it does not emerge, nor does it remain; it neither comes nor goes, and it is neither here nor not here. It is consciousness (cit).
This very consciousness, pure in form, abiding by itself within itself, O Rāghava, thus expands through the phenomenal world known as the universe.
Just as light radiates through masses of light, and water through floods of water, so does consciousness manifest through its vibrations in the form of the delusive appearances of creation.
By its own nature, it is named Consciousness; it is all-pervading, arisen as the Self, both manifest and unmanifest, partless yet bearing parts.

By himself abandoning the infinite state through the expansion of his own mental constructs, and by gradually proceeding toward the state of pure consciousness with the sense of "I am," he attains it.

When this manifold diversity has taken root within the cycle of existence from time immemorial, one comes to abide in the state of grasping at existence and non-existence, and of accepting and rejecting.
Through hundreds of vibrations of the eightfold city, it both acts and does not act; like a mass of sprouts situated within the hollow of the earth’s womb, it attains growth.
Space assumes the quality of vacuity, which is not in conflict with any form; wind possesses the sole property of motion; and water exists in the form of taste.
The earth is firm, the splendor is manifest, and the worlds endure; time stands by means of its reckoning for the sake of restriction and permission.
In flowers, fragrance gradually emerges from the accumulated filaments; on the ground, the swelling sap within the hollow of a clod of earth returns to the state of a mere stump.
The delicate sprouts at the base yield fruit consisting of mere sap; these lines take their place within the rows of young leaves.
He favors youthfulness with his thunderbolt and bow, and whatever [form] he becomes, he does so incessantly through his shape and his forest [of attributes].
Heaps of flowers and sprouts attend upon the spring; the riches of divine fire arrive as the ritual of summer.
The dark masses of clouds long for the rainy season, and all the heaps of fruit pursue the autumn.
In winter, the ten directions become laughing with snow; in the cold season, the chilly winds turn the water into the state of stones.
Time does not abandon its own boundary consisting of these ages; creations pass away with the play of the surging waves of a river.
Destiny attains stability, bringing about steadfastness and skill; the wise remain until the final dissolution, possessing the nature of supporting the earth.
Within this world-system, there are fourteen kinds of beings, possessing various modes of conduct and dwellings, and various forms of manifestation.
Again and again they dissolve, and again and again they are born; like bubbles without water, they pass away in a continuous succession of streams.

It comes, it goes, it remains stationary, and through its playfulness it acquires great wealth; it runs about amidst births and destructions. Like one driven mad, this wretched mass of people, whose efforts are directed toward false conceptions, has been rendered helpless by Kṛtānta (Death).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In this manner, all the cycles of worldly existence, appearing so very stable on every side, come and go again and again by the very nature of Brahman.
All this has arisen from itself and has become the cause for one another; perishing through mutual interaction, it dissolves by its own very nature.
Just as there is no movement within the depths of unfathomable water, yet movement appears, so too is this very consciousness perceived as both the unreal and the real.
Just as rivers are seen [to vanish] from the heat into the formless sky itself, so too are these perceptions of creation perceived within the reality of the mind.

Just as the self, under the influence of intoxication, appears as something other than itself, so too the element of consciousness, by virtue of its nature as consciousness, remains that very same thing yet appears as if it were not.

This [world] is neither existent nor non-existent, because consciousness remains as it is whether that [world] exists or does not exist; nor is it something other than consciousness, just as the nature of gold is not distinct from the bracelets and other ornaments made of it.
O Raghava, that by which you perceive sound, taste, form, and smell—this is the Self, the Supreme Brahman, which abides pervading all things.
Because of the non-duality of the all-pervading, stainless Self, which transcends both unity and plurality, there exists no second conceptualization whatsoever; it is not otherwise anywhere.
Apart from the contemplation of Rāma, auspicious and inauspicious existences and non-existences are imagined as creations either within the non-self or within the self.

For desire proceeds toward an object that is established as distinct from oneself; where nothing whatsoever exists apart from one's own self, what could the self possibly long for, what could it remember, toward what could it run, or what could it approach?

Therefore, conceptual constructions such as "this is desired" and "this is undesired" do not touch the Self. Consequently, in the state of desirelessness, the Self does nothing at all, because of the identity of the agent, the instrument, and the object; nor does it abide anywhere, because of the identity of the substratum and the contained. Furthermore, the inactivity (*naiṣkarmya*) of the desireless Self is not something to be achieved, because there is no second conceptualization [of an alternative state].
"O Rāma, you do not know this other state, which is the abiding in Brahman; being liberated from all dualities, become an agent free from the fever of worldly distress."

Furthermore, O Rāghava, having repeatedly performed this manifold action with vigor, tell me what is it that can be attained by you through the creation of beings? Or rather, let your conviction rest in non-agency; being one who possesses the sacred scriptures, remain established in yourself, pure and still like a windless ocean. Furthermore, O Rāghava, having repeatedly performed this manifold action with vigor, tell me what is it that can be attained by you through the creation of beings? Or rather, let your conviction rest in non-agency; being one who possesses the sacred scriptures, remain established in yourself, pure and still like a windless ocean.

Thinking, "Even by traveling a very great distance with effort and speed, that which is here said to be 'fully complete' cannot be reached; therefore, do not pursue the multitude of objects with your intellect—you are not those objects, but you alone are the ultimate reality, the conscious self."

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This being the case, that agency which is observed among those who know reality regarding pleasure, pain, and so forth, or in yoga and the like, is non-existent for them, but not for the ignorant.

For what indeed is called "agency"? It is that determination of the internal mental activity, or the conviction regarding its acceptability, which is designated by the term "latent impression" (vāsanā); this is what is expressed by the word "agency."

Due to the power of activity, the person vibrates in accordance with his latent impressions (vāsanā) such that he becomes the enjoyer of such a fruit; he experiences the fruit in accordance with that vibration. The established conclusion (siddhānta) is that what is called "being an enjoyer of the fruit" is [in fact] "agency."
And so it is said: "Whether one acts or does not act, whether in heaven or in hell, whatever kind of latent impression this mind possesses, that very thing is experienced."

Therefore, agency belongs to those persons who do not know reality, whether they act or do not act; it does not belong to those who have known reality, because they are free from latent impressions (vāsanā).

For one who has realized the truth, whose latent tendencies have become slackened, does not even while acting pursue the fruit of action; moreover, with an unattached intellect, he performs only mere movement. Even though he experiences this entire fruit of action as the Self alone, he acts without acting, his mind being immersed [in the Self].
Whatever the mind does, that is done; whatever it does not do, that is not done. Therefore, the mind alone is the agent, not the body.

It was understood that this saṃsāra has come from mind alone, consists of mind alone, is merely mind, and resides in mind alone; and that the object, like a mirage, has entirely subsided, leaving only the latent impression (vāsanā), which is known to exist as such.

For the mind of those who know the Self has attained supreme tranquility; it remains having reached the fourth state (*turya*), like water in a mirage when a cloud rains, or like a drop of frost dissolved in the fierce heat of the sun. For the mind of those who know the Self has attained supreme tranquility; it remains having reached the fourth state, like water in a mirage when a cloud rains, or like a drop of frost dissolved in the fierce heat of the sun.
The wise know the mind of the knower to be neither blissful nor devoid of bliss, neither moving nor unmoving, neither stable, nor existent, nor non-existent, nor even the middle between these.

The knower of reality does not sink into the savor of vibration consisting of latent impressions, like an elephant in a puddle; he perceives only the terrain of the enjoyments of the fool's mind, and not the true essence of being.

Likewise, there is this further illustration here: even one who does not fall into a chasm, while resting on a bed or seat, experiences the suffering of falling into a chasm if his mind is permeated by the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of such a fall. Conversely, another person, even while actually falling into a chasm, experiences the comfort of a bed or seat if his mind has attained supreme tranquility (*upaśama*). Thus, between these two cases of the bed/seat and the fall into the chasm, one becomes a doer of the fall despite not being a doer, and the second becomes a non-doer despite being a doer—this is due to the power of the mind. Therefore, the established conclusion is that a person becomes what their mind is.

Therefore, let the mind of one who acts or does not act there remain eternally unattached; for there is nothing whatsoever apart from the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) upon which attachment could be conceived. Know that whatever exists within this world is all a mere appearance, due to the purity of the mind.

Thus, for this person who has known what is to be known, when the certainty arises that "the Self is not the object of pleasure and pain," and when the certainty arises that "there exist no views of container and contained apart from the Self," and when the certainty arises that "I am the agent, the enjoyer, distinct from all objects, as subtle as a thousandth part of the tip of a hair," or when the certainty arises that "whatever exists here, all that is indeed I," and when the certainty arises that "I, the illuminator of all beings, remain omnipresent," then—being free from the fever of anxiety—the mental state remains in worldly affairs with effortless ease, realizing: "I am not the object of pleasure and pain. Thus, for this person who has known what is to be known, when the certainty arises that "the Self is not the object of pleasure and pain," and when the certainty arises that "there exist no views of container and contained apart from the Self," and when the certainty arises that "I am the agent, the enjoyer, distinct from all objects, as subtle as a thousandth part of the tip of a hair," or when the certainty arises that "whatever exists here, all that is indeed I," and when the certainty arises that "I, the illuminator of all beings, remain omnipresent," then—being free from the fever of anxiety—the mental state remains in worldly affairs with effortless ease, realizing: "I am not the object of pleasure and pain."

For the knower of reality, even in the midst of adversity, there is only joy; like moonlight, it alone adorns the nature of the world. Since the knower is devoid of the mind, he is a non-doer even while acting, because the mind leaves no stain upon him. Thus, he does not experience the fruit of action—even of that performed with effort—such as the movement of feet, hands, and so forth. For the knower of reality, even in the midst of adversity, there is only joy; like moonlight, it alone adorns the nature of the world. Since the knower is devoid of the mind, he is a non-doer even while acting, because the mind leaves no stain upon him. Thus, he does not experience the fruit of action—even of that performed with effort—such as the movement of feet, hands, and so forth.

Thus, the mind is the seed of all actions, all intentions, all states of being, all worlds, and all destinies. When that [mind] is relinquished, all actions are relinquished; all sufferings are exhausted; and all actions go to their dissolution. Even by an action performed mentally, the Knower is not overcome, nor is he rendered helpless, nor does he undergo attachment, because he is non-different [from the Absolute]. Thus, the mind is the seed of all actions, all intentions, all states of being, all worlds, and all destinies. When that [mind] is relinquished, all actions are relinquished; all sufferings are exhausted; and all actions go to their dissolution. Even by an action performed mentally, the Knower is not overcome, nor is he rendered helpless, nor does he undergo attachment, because he is non-different [from the Absolute].

Just as a child, while mentally constructing and destroying a city, experiences that mental construction of a city as if it were uncreated, doing so with ease and not regarding it as something to be grasped; and seeing pleasure and pain as unreal, he sees the destruction of the city—which was mentally created—as merely created [and thus unreal]. Thus, even while experiencing suffering with ease, he does not perceive it as suffering. In this way, although he acts, he is not at all stained from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Just as a child, while mentally constructing and destroying a city, experiences that mental construction of a city as if it were uncreated, doing so with ease and not regarding it as something to be grasped; and seeing pleasure and pain as unreal, he sees the destruction of the city—which was mentally created—as merely created [and thus unreal]. Thus, even while experiencing suffering with ease, he does not perceive it as suffering. In this way, although he acts, he is not at all stained from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

Among all things in the world, whether they are to be rejected or accepted, what is the cause of suffering? Furthermore, among those things to be accepted, there exists nothing whatsoever that is indestructible or distinct from the Self. Therefore, this Self is neither an agent nor an enjoyer; it is only through ignorance that this agency is superimposed upon it. Among all things in the world, whether they are to be rejected or accepted, what is the cause of suffering? Furthermore, among those things to be accepted, there exists nothing whatsoever that is indestructible or distinct from the Self. Therefore, this Self is neither an agent nor an enjoyer; it is only through ignorance that this agency is superimposed upon it.

That right view is essential; it does not arise from delusion regarding reality, because through the investigation of things as they truly are, the states of being an agent and an enjoyer do not exist. Views such as aversion toward or desire for the senses and their objects are seen by those who hold such views, but not by those who do not hold them.
Liberation does not exist for those whose minds are attached here in this cycle of existence; however, for those whose minds are unattached, all of this indeed exists.

For the knower who abides as he truly is, only the reality of the Self shines forth; he brings about duality and unity as established by those who propound duality and unity, he brings about existence and non-existence, and he reveals to him the state of possessing all powers, which is non-different from the web of his own powers. For the knower who abides as he truly is, only the reality of the Self shines forth; he brings about duality and unity as established by those who propound duality and unity, he brings about existence and non-existence, and he reveals to him the state of possessing all powers, which is non-different from the web of his own powers.
There is no bondage, there is no liberation; there is neither the absence of bondage nor the act of binding. This suffering exists due to lack of awakening; through awakening, it dissolves away.

The thought of liberation in this world is conceived in vain; the thought of bondage in this world is likewise conceived in vain. O Rāma, having renounced everything, being free from egoism, established in the Self, and acting with wisdom while moving about the earth, remain firm.

Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, since the Supreme Brahman alone exists in this way, tell me, O Great-souled One, from where does the emergence of creation come—this creation which is like a painting without a wall?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Prince, it is this very reality of Brahman that revolves; because it is the all-powerful principle, therefore all powers are seen within Brahman.
Existence, non-existence, duality, unity, multiplicity, beginningness, and endness.
And that is not something other [than the source]; just as a body of water within a mass of water, by means of its surging and blossoming, attains manifestation while displaying various forms.

Likewise, the mass of consciousness (ciddhana), by being consciousness (cittvāt), gathers, displays, sustains, generates, and withdraws all powers—those consisting of action (karmamayi), those consisting of latent impressions (vāsanāmaya), and those consisting of the mind (manomayi). Likewise, the mass of consciousness, by being consciousness, gathers, displays, sustains, generates, and withdraws all powers—those consisting of action, those consisting of latent impressions, and those consisting of the mind.
The origin of all living beings, of all perceptions on every side, and of all objects in their entirety, occurs incessantly from Brahman.
From the transcendent world they emerge, and because it is consciousness, they enter fully into it; they are constantly composed of that very essence, like waves in the ocean.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, this expression of yours is exceedingly profound; indeed, even now I do not fully comprehend the meaning of your statement."

Where, indeed, is the reality of Brahman, whose nature transcends the functions of the six senses including the mind; and where is this fragile splendor of worldly objects born from it—such is the construction of these words. And if this manifestation has proceeded from Brahman, then it ought to be of a nature similar to Him.
Whoever is born from something becomes exactly like that thing.
Just as a lamp [is lit] from a lamp, a person from a person, or grain from grain.
Since it has come from that which is changeless and so forth, it must itself be changeless.
Then, having heard that this occurrence of blemish upon the stainless Supreme Lord—the conscious Self which is distinct from all else—the venerable Brahmarṣi spoke.
This world exists as Brahman alone; there is no impurity here, O sinless one. Just as water in the ocean manifests through masses of waves, yet no dust arises from it.
O scion of the Raghus, no second conceptualization exists here apart from Brahman alone, just as there is no heat apart from fire alone.

Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahman, Brahman is free from suffering and beyond dualities, yet this world born of it is full of suffering; O Brahman, I do not understand these words of yours, for their meaning is unclear."
Śrī Vālmīki said: When Rāma had spoken thus, Vasiṣṭha, the tiger among sages, reflected in his mind upon how to provide instruction to the descendant of Raghu.
Yet this mind of his has not reached its ultimate expansion; it has attained only a slight degree of purity and is still being carried away by this worldly object.
For that wise one whose mind is fully developed, who has known what is to be known, and who has reached the further shore of the words concerning the means to liberation through discernment;
No one has any fault whatsoever; for knowledge is fully established within the Self. O Rāghava, this [Self] does not come to rest as long as it has not been spoken of.

But for one whose intellect is only half-developed, this [teaching] is not clearly manifest and does not shine; indeed, by contemplating through this perception of enjoyment as something visible, he perishes.

For one who has attained the supreme vision, the desire for enjoyments does not arise; "All is Brahman" is the established conclusion, and at such a time, even his name becomes appropriate [to this truth].
First, one should purify the disciple through qualities consisting primarily of tranquility and self-restraint; afterwards, one should instruct him that "all this is Brahman" and "you are pure."
He who says "everything is Brahman" to one who is ignorant or only half-awakened casts that person into the snares of the great hells.
It is fitting to say that for the great-souled one—whose intellect is awakened, whose desire for enjoyment has perished, and who is free from expectations—the stain of ignorance no longer exists.
And he who, being of extremely deluded intellect, instructs a disciple without first examining him, goes to hell himself until the dissolution of all beings.
Having reflected thus, the Blessed One, the best of sages, Vasiṣṭha—the sun to the earth who dispels the darkness of ignorance—spoke to him.

The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: "O sinless Rāghava, whether the perception of a stain exists or does not exist within Brahman must be stated at the time of reaching the final conclusion; you shall know this for yourself."
Brahman is all-powerful, all-pervading, omnipresent, and "I alone am everything."

Just as you see magicians performing various deeds through illusion, producing existence from non-existence and bringing non-existence to existence, even so the Self—though devoid of illusion—is like a supreme magician who, appearing as if composed of illusion, turns a pot into a cloth and a cloth into a pot; he produces a creeper upon a stone, just as one might produce the Nandana grove on the golden slopes of Mount Meru; and he brings forth a stone within a creeper, just as one might place a cluster of jewels upon the wish-fulfilling trees, or superimpose a forest upon the sky. Just as you see magicians performing various deeds through illusion, producing existence from non-existence and bringing non-existence to existence, even so the Self—though devoid of illusion—is like a supreme magician who, appearing as if composed of illusion, turns a pot into a cloth and a cloth into a pot; he produces a creeper upon a stone, just as one might produce the Nandana grove on the golden slopes of Mount Meru; and he brings forth a stone within a creeper, just as one might place a cluster of jewels upon the wish-fulfilling trees, or superimpose a forest upon the sky.

In that world, it will become like a Gandharva garden; through mental construction, it produces the state of a city in the sky, as if leading the earth's surface into the atmosphere, which has lost its shadows and is like collyrium.
It places the sky upon the surface of the earth like a vast multitude of women in the royal palace of a city of the Gandharvas.
Like a reflection of the sky upon red mosaic floors, there is nothing in the world that exists, will exist, or has ever existed.
If God, having assumed a manifest form and attained diversity, displays [the world].
Since everything—in every way and everywhere—exists here as only a single reality according to its occurrence, O Rāma, where then is there any occasion for joy, resentment, or wonder?
One should always remain steadfast through equanimity alone.
The knower of that, enveloped in equanimity, never undergoes the transformations of wonder, derision, delusion, joy, resentment, or agitation.
Indeed, in this world that is infinite in space and time, diverse logical arguments are observed.
And this Self, by means of these logical arguments and names, diligently constructs its manifestation and does not reject what has arisen, just as the ocean does not reject its waves.

Rather, just as butter exists in milk, a jar in clay, a cloth in threads, and a banyan tree in its seed, so too do the powers (śaktis) reside within the Self alone; they are designated as such when they have come into manifestation, appearing spontaneously like waves.
In this, there is no agent, no enjoyer, and nothing that undergoes destruction.
When one remains thus, established in the true Self alone—which is the witness, free from affliction, equal, eternal, and undisturbed—then this state is attained.

When existence is present, light arises like a lamp; when existence is present, the day arises like the sun; when existence is present, fragrance arises like a flower; thus the world is established by itself.
This which is perceived is merely a manifestation; it is like the movement of the wind, neither existing nor non-existent.

From the perspective of ultimate reality, the Blessed One stands as if faultless toward the worldly views; he is neither the creator of things destroyed nor the destroyer of things created. He is merely like a heap of flowers or stars—sometimes manifest, sometimes slightly manifest, and sometimes unmanifest.
For that object which is not one's own self perishes here; how could that object which is one's very own self ever perish?
That thing which is not of the nature of the self does not arise at all; and that thing which is of the nature of the self arises indeed.
How can that which is one's own self arise from that [self] as something already identical with it?
Therefore, by the power of perfect knowledge, there is the manifestation of all categories of objects from Brahman.

And for those who have thus entered, at the very moment of their entry, ignorance arises and the knowledge of reality attains firmness; thereupon, the tree of saṃsāra—with its hundreds of thousands of trunks, its many branches, and its heavy burden of various fruits of good and evil—begins to expand.

Having severed with the sword of discernment this tree called saṃsāra—which has the form of a cluster of hopes, which bears fruitless results through harsh sufferings, which sprouts with worldly enjoyments, blossoms with old age, and shines with the creepers of craving—you, like a lordly elephant released from its post, wander here as one liberated from the fetters of the self.
Śrī Rāma said: O Lord, tell me in detail how the birth of these living beings occurs from the state of Brahman, and to what extent and of what nature it is.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as the various classes of beings arise from Brahman, just as they go to their destruction, and just as they indeed become liberated; [so it is].
And how they increase, and how they remain when they have disappeared—listen, O mighty-armed and sinless one, as I shall tell you in brief.
The stainless power of consciousness, which is Brahman, by its own will and possessing all powers, imagines for itself the object of thought, which consists of the act of conceptualization.
Having attained density through the process of time, whatever that [consciousness] itself subsequently imagines, it assumes that very form, reaching the state of the mind.
By the mere volition of the mind, like a city of the Gandharvas, it instantly expands this unreal appearance, as if abandoning its state as Brahman.
The nature of consciousness remains as nothingness alone; that which exists as the visible world is indeed the visible sky itself.
Having formed the resolve to become a lotus-born being, he beholds his form as the lotus-born; thereafter, he fashions the world, preceded by Prajāpati.
O Rāma, this creation, filled with the humming sounds of fourteen kinds of infinite beings, has thus come about through the construction of the mind.
Consisting of mind alone, it is empty, having a body that is mere space; it is a city of mere conceptualization, being in essence nothing but delusion.
In this world, some species of beings remain in great delusion; some have awakened knowledge; and some indeed falter midway.
Among all the classes of beings connected to the earth, these human races come to be designated as such.
They are beset by many afflictions, full of suffering, and distressed by delusion, hatred, and fear; of them, I shall first correctly describe those of the rājasa and sāttvika natures.
That which is the immortal Brahman, all-pervading and free from affliction, is the manifestation of consciousness known as the infinite, beginningless, and devoid of delusion.
The vibration of that [Reality], whose body is motionless, attains density through a portion of its existence, just as movement appears in the calm ocean like a ripple.
Śrī Rāma said: What is said to be a single portion of the infinite reality of the Self? How could there be transformation, or how could there be the transgression of duality?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Therefore, this arrangement of words—"born from that," "then born"—is for the sake of conventional usage in the scriptures, O Rāma, and not from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Transformation, having parts, spatial location, and so forth—succession is not possible in the Lord, even though its arising is observed [in other things].

Apart from that [reality], there is no other conceptual construction, nor will there ever be; how then could there be the sequence of words and their meanings, which arise from conventional discourse?

Whatever conceptualization there is here, whatever object, whatever word, and whatever collection of speech—because they are born from that and consist of that, each is regarded as being like that very state.

That which is born from it becomes that very thing, like fire arising from fire; the conceptualization of difference, such as "this is the produced" and "this is the producer," is merely a verbal designation.
"This has arisen from that"—this is the established order of the world; yet, regarding the capacity for action, there is either a superfluity, or that which is produced is itself the producer.
"The confusion regarding words and their meanings—thinking 'this is one thing' and 'that is another'—does not exist when speaking of the Lord, because there is no distinction in valid cognition."
By that very power of the mind, cognition arises spontaneously; therefore, through firm cultivation, the desired object is attained.
"The second [flame] of Agni's single crest is called Janaka"—this is merely a variety of expression; there is no truth here in the meaning of the statement.
Those expressions such as "the produced" and "the producer" do not apply to the Supreme; for since it is one and infinite, what could produce what, and in what manner?

This is the very nature of a statement that immediately after one statement there is another statement; it is not logical [to claim] that it serves purposes such as excluding a counter-correlate or indicating number.
The wise know that very Brahman which appears in the Supreme as sound in the form of the conceptualization of objects, like a network of waves in the ocean.
Brahman is consciousness and Brahman is the mind; Brahman is the object of discernment and Brahman is the referent; Brahman is the word and Brahman is the elements of consciousness.
This entire universe is Brahman, and that state transcends the universe; yet in reality, the world does not exist, for everything is solely Brahman alone.
"This is one part, this is another, this is yet another"—in the case of such conceptualizations arising from false cognition regarding the nature of space, what truthfulness can there be in speech?
Just as a flame arises from fire, this designation "flame" is a name for the mind; the splendor of conceptual constructions born of fickleness does not, in reality, achieve any established existence.

The expression of conceptual construction is indeed unreal, yet it is conceptualized as having a real nature; this is due to vision being impaired by darkness, like the defect of the cognition of two moons.
From that all-pervading, infinite Brahman, which is the supreme state, nothing else whatsoever can arise; whatever arises from it is that very same reality.
Without the reality of Brahman, nothing at all is possible here; and indeed, this entire world is but Brahman—this alone is the ultimate truth.
O wise one, your philosophical tenet will be of this general nature; therein we shall set forth the cage of words explaining the meaning of that tenet.
In this world, some things such as ignorance exist, but not in any other sequence; you will fully understand all objects once that respective ignorance has been destroyed.
When non-entities are eliminated, the real entity becomes clear as it truly is, just as the visible world appears when the darkness of night has vanished.

O Rāma, this entire world is pervaded by false views; when these are stilled, your vision will become stainless within the purity of the unerring state—it will indeed be unerring, and there is no doubt whatsoever in this matter.
Śrī Rāma said: By your diverse and profound words, which possess a cool and stainless luster like the waters of the Ocean of Milk, [I am filled] on all sides.
For a moment I fall as if into blindness, and for a moment I go toward clarity; like a day in the rainy season with its shifting clouds, my life is like a day whose rays of heat have subsided.
How has the conceptualization of the infinite, the immeasurable, the all-encompassing, the singular, the luminous, and that whose essence never sets, come to be?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: All my utterances have meanings that correspond exactly to reality; they are never ineffective, nor do they possess contradictory meanings, nor do they give rise to contradictions between what precedes and what follows.
When the vision of knowledge has become clear and awakening has fully dawned, you, established in your own nature, will know exactly as it is the strength and weakness of my words and perspectives.
For the sake of the teacher and the teaching, and for the realization of the meaning of the treatise, may you not become absorbed in the delusion of words, meanings, and syntactical constructions.
When you shall know in the future that truth which is absolutely stainless, then indeed you will abandon the distinction between the signifier, the signified, and the word-meaning.

This proliferation of speech that creates distinctions is imagined for the sake of those to be instructed; it exists for the purpose of instruction and for the comprehension of the meaning of the treatise.
This proliferation of words, meanings, and speech is constructed within the instructions for the sake of the ignorant; it does not exist as ultimate reality for those who know that [truth].
Not even the slightest impurity, such as time, passion, or delusion, exists within the Self; that supreme Brahman, free from attachment, is itself established as this world.
O sinless one, this must be explained at length once again with many various arguments on the occasion of the final conclusion.
However, without the elaboration of speech, it is impossible to make an effort to pierce this incomparable darkness of ignorance, which has arisen through mutual dependence.
O Rāma, it is by means of that very supreme ignorance—the desire for the effort to destroy one's own self—that knowledge, which removes all defects, is sought after.
For a weapon is quelled by a weapon, impurity is washed away by impurity; poison is neutralized by poison, and an enemy is slain by an enemy.
Such is this illusion, O Rāma, which gives joy through its own destruction; its true nature is not perceived, for it perishes the very moment it is scrutinized.
It conceals discernment and produces worlds in abundance; yet it is not understood what this is—behold this wonder of the world!
When not looked at, it throbs; when looked at, it utterly perishes. This illusion dances about only as long as its true nature remains unrecognized.
Oh, how truly wondrous is this illusion that binds one to saṃsāra! Though it is utterly unreal, it appears as if most real, and by it, one's own cognition is fashioned.
Because he spreads out the pervasive illusion of saṃsāra within that [reality] which is utterly devoid of differentiation, he is therefore the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).

This does not exist in the ultimate sense, yet it is not so when kindled by meditative cultivation; having become a knower and attained the object of knowledge, you will understand its underlying intention.
But as long as you have not yet awakened, let there be a firm and unwavering conviction in you based on my words alone: that ignorance does not exist.
Behold this great mental activity that has become an object of perception; for it is merely non-existent, being but the manifestation of the mind alone.

Even one who has the internal conviction that "the seven elements are Brahman" is a partaker of liberation; for whatever perception—whether of a moving or unmoving form—is held with firm cultivation, [that is the reality].
She is the snare that binds all beings and birds of the entire world; she who, like the realm of a dream, is a delusion of the unreal appearing as real, yet is determined to be one.

One whose self is unattached beholds the world and does not sink into suffering; for one who has the realization that these [objects] are not his true nature, that very realization is the realization of his own self.
Even for that which lacks its own true nature, it is indeed ignorance alone that exists; no defects such as mutability and the like reside in the Great Self.
Within the Supreme Self, these things—mental conceptions, words, and the coloring of word-meanings that pervade the world—exist like dust particles in water.
These views seen in the scriptures have arisen for the sake of conventional usage and are not distinct from the Self; without this conventional usage, they do not exist.
They do not attain stability, like cloths whose warp-threads have been removed; for the self, being carried away by ignorance, is not perceived here.

And that [liberation] is attained through the knowledge of the Self, which is acquired from the meaning of the scriptures; indeed, it is said that there is no crossing to the further shore of the river of ignorance apart from the attainment of the Self.
Indeed, that state which is called imperishable cannot be reached by this ignorance, which yields impurity, wherever it may arise.
Surely she has attained stability and remains established having reached her proper place; O Rāma, let there be no further deliberation for you as to whence she was born.
"How shall I destroy her?"—let this be your deliberation; once she has set and perished, you will know, O Rāghava.
Since this [world]—what it is, how it is, and how it has perished—is in reality undivided, it truly does not exist; yet it appears, though it is not seen when scrutinized.

Who could know from what source the delusion regarding the non-existent has the form of reality? Having arisen and reached maturity, this [delusion], being of a non-substantial nature, leads only to harm.
"Destroy her by force; you will surely come to know her then. Even those who are brave and exceedingly wise do not exist within the three worlds."
Those men who have not indeed been rendered helpless by ignorance—exert yourself to destroy this ignorance, which is by nature a disease.

So that this ignorance shall not again subject you to the sufferings of birth—uproot the impurity of ignorance, the sole companion of all calamities, the blossom of the tree of nescience, and the mother of a multitude of misfortunes.

Having forcibly cast away this false view—which bestows fear, despair, and unbearable calamity, and which is the sprout of the great cataract that deludes the heart—may you reach the further shore of the ocean of existence.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, hear now the remedy for this disease spread by ignorance—which, though it is unreal and provoked, is destroyed by mere observation.
O Rāma, listen now to that birth which is both rajasic and sattvic, concerning which I have begun to speak here for the purpose of examining the power of the mind.
That which is the immortal Brahman, all-pervading and free from affliction, is the manifestation of consciousness called the infinite, beginningless, and devoid of delusion.
Since its very body is the vibration of consciousness, it is indeed consciousness itself that vibrates; it attains density from a particular location, just as the gentle ocean does from its movement.
Just as the water within the ocean moves or remains still according to its impulse, so too does the All-Powerful One, though remaining one, assume the state of the power of movement.
Just as the wind moves within the sky by itself, so too does the self here experience agitation within its own self through its own power alone.
Just as a gentle lamp rises to a height by the power of its own flickering flame, so too does this Self move playfully within its own body.
Just as the ocean within its waters is restless like a dancing wave, so too does the possessor of all powers manifest the play of movement within his own body.
Just as the ocean of gold flashes with the circles of light from its waves, so does the ocean of consciousness quiver within itself through the vibrations of the senses.
Just as the shimmering of pearls is perceived in the sky where there is nothing to be seen by the eye, so does the radiant power of consciousness shine within the great expanse of consciousness.

That power of consciousness, having become slightly agitated within the great ocean of consciousness, flashes forth as pure consciousness consisting of that very [ocean], like a wave upon the ocean itself.
Though non-different from the Self, it remains as if different, having attained expansion like the glory of light within the hollow of a light-source.
For a moment, that Goddess flashes forth through her universal power; she herself perceives her own power, just as the moon perceives its own coolness.
This power of consciousness (cicchakti) of the Supreme Self, called "the Manifest" (prakāśa), having arisen, draws forth its companions—the powers of space, time, and action.
Having thus realized her own intrinsic nature and abiding in the state that is without beginning or end, she, though unmanifested, contemplates form as if it were limited.
As soon as form is thus permeated by that supreme reality, at that very moment, perceptions such as names, numbers, and so forth follow it.
This very consciousness is indeed without substance and distinct from the Self; yet it is infinite and resides within it instantly, like a wave from the great ocean.

Just as there is no difference in gold that is distinct from bracelets and armlets, so too there is no difference between the Self and the nature of consciousness for one who contemplates its own inherent portion.

Just as one lamp is related to other lamps that have arisen from it, so too is the distinction between cognitions merely a matter of place, time, and degree; this is the inherent nature of consciousness.
Then consciousness, ignited by the power of the movement of space and time, pursues its own volitions and enters the state of conceptualization.

O mighty-armed one, the form of consciousness, which assumes shapes fashioned by conceptual thought and serves as the locus of space, time, and action, is called the "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña).
They say the field is the body; he knows that field in its entirety, including both the internal and the external, and for that reason he is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
Even he, while perceiving latent impressions (vāsanā), again falls into the state of egoism (ahaṃkāra); and that egoism, when it becomes the determiner, is called the defiled intellect (buddhi).
Intellect, fashioned by conceptualization, enters the domain of the mind; the mind, filled with dense discursive thought, gradually attains the state of the senses.
The wise know that this body consists of hands and feet, as well as the sense organs; it is known in the world as burning, being born, and living.

Thus, the individual soul (jīva), indeed, being entwined by the rope of volitional tendencies and latent impressions, its self surrounded by a web of suffering, gradually attains the state of the mind (citta).

Just as a fruit gradually attains a different state through the process of ripening, so too does the individual soul, by its very condition and not by its essential nature, undergo change under the influence of impurity.

The individual soul (jīva) attains the state of ego (ahaṃkāra), and the ego attains the state of intellect (buddhi); the intellect, in turn, reaches the state of mind (manas), which is ensnared by the web of volitions (saṃkalpa).
For the mind consists of volition and is intent upon grasping forms; it is driven even by desired objects that are real attainments distinguished from their opposites.
The powers beginning with desire—such as the senses—run after the mind, which is like an intoxicated bull, for the sake of their own ruin, just as rivers flow toward the ocean.
Thus, the mind, consisting of creative power (*śakti*), having attained a state of dense egoity (*ahaṃkāra*), enters into bondage by its own will, like a silkworm.
Driven by its own volitions as if led by ropes, the self undergoes bondage within this body and suffers in distress.
Perceiving "I am bound," the principle of ignorance (avidyā-tattva), gradually abandoning [its own nature], generates within [the self] the world-demoness that devours the wilderness of existence.
And dwelling within the flames of those very elements imagined by its own volition, it falls into a state of supreme helplessness, like a lion bound in chains.
Under the influence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it assumes the agency of performing diverse actions, and likewise undergoes states fashioned by its own mere will.

In some places it is the mind, in some places the intellect, in some places knowledge, and in some places the creative powers; in some places this is called the ego-sense, and in some places it is known as the subtle body of eight constituents.
In some places it is called *prakṛti*, in some it is conceived as *māyā*; in some it is declared to be *mala*, and in some it is established as *karman*.

In some places it is clearly known as "bondage," in some it is distinctly called "mind" (citta); in some it is declared to be "ignorance" (avidyā), and in others it is established as "desire" (icchā).
Therefore, O Rāghava, this mind here is bound and afflicted; it is overwhelmed by craving and sorrow, and it is stretched out as a locus for passion.
It is struck down by the cultivation of existence within the delusion of old age and death; it is seized by what is desired and undesired, and stained by ignorance and passion.

Its form is agitated by desire; it is the sprout of the forest of the tree of karma; it has utterly forgotten its place of origin; and it is fashioned by the imagined misfortunes of conceptual construction.
Bound like a silkworm in its cocoon, it has entered a state characterized by sorrow; composed of a multitude of mere mental factors, it is the heat of infinite hells.
Though visible only to oneself, this poisonous and evil tree of saṃsāra brings fear with its weight as heavy as the king of mountains; it is richly laden with the branches of old age and death.

Just as a banyan seed contains within itself a banyan tree that is devoid of fruit, so too does one harbor this entire cycle of existence, which creates the snares of desire, yet remains inwardly barren of results.
Burnt by the flames of the fire of anxiety, devoured by the python of anger, struck by the waves of the ocean of desire, he has forgotten his own grandfather.
Like a deer strayed from its herd, its mind overwhelmed by grief; like a moth consumed by the flames of the fire of sensory objects.

Like a lotus whose roots have been severed, it has reached a state of supreme withering; its limbs severed from its own station, it remains in a state of distress due to its lack of specific attachment.
Remaining indifferent toward sense objects and the like, and toward enemies of various forms, it has wallowed through these endless and perilous conditions.
The world has fallen into terrible suffering, like a bird in the ocean, trapped in its own bonds within the net of existence, as empty as a city of Gandharvas.
O you who resemble an immortal, rescue my mind—which is being carried away in the ocean of non-reliance and is distracted by sense objects—just as one might pull an elephant from the mud.
O Rāma, forcibly pull out my mind, which is submerged like a bull in the pond of passion and whose limbs are torn and shattered.

O Rāma, he in whose mind no distress arises here in this world—his form struck by the expansion of the auspicious and inauspicious, and swooning from the poison of blazing old age and death—is a demon in human guise.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, living beings are manifestations of consciousness, nourished by the ideation of worldly existence; they arise from the imagined forms of Brahman by the hundreds of thousands and even by the millions.
O sir, countless [beings] have been born in the past, and they are being born even now; and they will continue to arise like a torrent of water droplets from a mountain spring.

Overcome by the power of their own latent impressions, they have fallen into a state of helplessness regarding their hopes; with their intentions bound by themselves, they find themselves in most diverse conditions.
Without ceasing, in every direction, in place after place, on water and on land, beings are born or die like bubbles upon the water.
Some have had only one birth, some more than a hundred births; some have had countless births, and some are within two or three existences.
Some belong to future births, some have arisen from past existences, some belong to the present life, and some have gone to the state of non-existence.
Some, being born again and again for thousands of eons, remain within a single womb; others have resorted to different wombs.
Some endure great suffering, while others remain with little prosperity; some are exceedingly joyful, and others have risen like the sun and other luminaries.
Some were kinnaras, gandharvas, vidyādharas, and mahoragas; some were the sun, the moon, Varuṇa, the three-eyed Śiva, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā.
Some were kūśmāṇḍas, vetālas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas; others stood there as groups of brāhmaṇas, kings, vaiśyas, and śūdras.
Some were Śvapacas, Cāṇḍālas, Kirātas, Āveśas, and Puṣkasas; some were grasses and herbs, and some were fruits, roots, and moths.
Some appeared everywhere like painted creepers, shrubs, grass, and stones; others were like kadamba, jambīra, śāla, tāla, and tamāla trees.
Some were ministers, vassals, and regional lords within the cycle of worldly existence; others, clothed in rags, had attained the silence of the sages.
Some were serpents, pythons, worms, insects, and ants; others were lions, buffaloes, deer, goats, yaks, and antelopes.
Some became cranes, ruddy geese, herons, ducks, and cuckoos; others attained the state of lotuses, white esculent lilies, water-lilies, and blue lotuses.
Some were young elephants, great tuskers, boars, bulls, and donkeys; others were bees, mosquitoes, gnats, and those born from stinging insects.
Some are overwhelmed by the force of calamity, some have attained prosperity; some reside in the city of heaven, while others dwell in hell.
Some are situated within the circle of the bears, others have entered the hollows of the bears; some remain as wind-beings, and some are established in the station of space.
Some abide in the rays of the sun; some abide in the rays of the moon; and some abide in the sweet essences of grasses, creepers, and shrubs.
Some here wander as liberated while living, vessels of auspiciousness; some remain as those long liberated; and others have surely reached final transformation.
Some will become auspiciously liberated after a long time; others, being of the nature of consciousness, hate their own state of isolation (kaivalya).
Some were vast quarters of the sky, some were rivers of great velocity, some were women with lovely eyes, and some were eunuchs and neuter beings.
Some possess awakened intellects, while others have extremely dull dispositions; some are instructors of knowledge, while others have attained meditative absorption.
Living beings, rendered helpless by the onset of their own latent impressions, remain established in these various states with fixed mental conceptions.
Some wander about in the world, falling and rising again and again, incessantly struck by Death as if they were balls with the hand.
Bound by hundreds of snares of hope and bearing the latent impressions of existence, they pass from body to body like birds flying from one tree to another.
By means of the illusion that produces the conceptualization of infinite and endless volitions, she spreads out this great world-illusion consisting of the universe.
Fools wander in saṃsāra like masses of whirlpools in water as long as they do not perceive their own blameless self.
Having seen the self as unreal and having abandoned it, and having attained true consciousness, they reach the supreme state in due time and are not born here again.
Having experienced thousands of births, some who are ignorant fall once again into the perils of saṃsāra, even after attaining discernment.
Some, even after attaining a high state of power, return again to the condition of an animal due to their base intellect, and from the state of an animal, they even go to the hells.
Some, being of great intelligence, having arisen from the state of Brahmā, immediately upon that very birth, swiftly and completely enter back into that same place.
In other cosmic eggs, there are other multitudes of living beings; some among them attain the state of being born from a lotus, while others even attain the state of being Hara.
Some go to the state of animals, others even to the state of gods; and others, O Rāma, do not return at all, just as it is here, so it is there.
For just as this world is the essence of existence, so too do other worlds exist—those that have passed away and those that will come to be in great numbers.
Through various diverse sequences and by means of different causes, their manifold creations come forth and fall away.
One becomes a gandharva, another goes to the state of a yakṣa; one attains the state of a sura, and another comes to the state of a daitya.
By the very same conventions by which people exist in this universe, they likewise exist in others, though differing in their specific arrangements.
Through mutual friction, driven by the force of their own inherent natures, creations revolve like the waves of a river.
Through manifestations and disappearances, through emergences and submergences, creations revolve like the waves of a river.
From that Supreme [Reality], multitudes of individual souls emerge incessantly; indescribable and self-cognizable, they flash forth rapidly right there.
Like light from a lamp and the like, like rays from the sun and the like, like sparks from heated iron, and like sparks from a fire.
Like diverse fragrances from flowers, like cool rains from a downpour, and like waves from the ocean, [the manifestations] arise according to the sequence of time and other conditions.
Arising again and again over time and experiencing a succession of bodies, the multitudes of living beings go by themselves to their final rest in the state.
This unceasing, vast, and lofty delusive illusion of the creation of the three worlds—perishing and flourishing in vain—is like a wave in the ocean within the supreme state.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, by what process does the soul, having attained its state through this sequence, assume a body—a cage of bones?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O Rāma, I have already told you this before; why do you not understand it? Where has your intellect, which ought to be capable of investigating what precedes and what follows, gone?"
For this world, consisting of bodies and so forth, whether stationary or moving, is merely a manifestation, arisen like an unreal dream.
O sinless Rāma, this long dream is indeed seen as a mere falsehood, like the appearance of a double moon or like a mountain wandering within a delusion.
But one whose sleep of ignorance has been stilled, whose mental constructions have dissolved, and whose mind is awakened, does not perceive the dream of saṃsāra even while seeing it.

O Rāma, for all living beings, this cycle of existence (saṃsāra) indeed exists within the self at all times until the attainment of the state of liberation, being imagined as having an intrinsic nature.
The body of the living being is as flickering as a whirlpool of water; it is like the swelling sprout within a seed, or like the leaflet within its own sprout.
Just as there is a flower upon a sprout and fruit within the calyx of a flower, so too does that body, which consists of mental construction, exist within the mind.
O Rāma, because it exists as manifold forms, that which is clearly one [appears]; indeed, it is that very appearance of this mind that arises.
That very [consciousness] quickly becomes this body, resembling a jar made from a lump of clay; at the time of the original creation, it was his first and most excellent manifestation.
Since this all-pervading Brahmā was situated within the interior of the lotus bud, it attained its existence from that very process of his volition.

"This creation is boundless, like an illusion produced by a dense illusion. Śrī Rāma said: "The individual soul (jīva), having attained the state of the mind, reaches the station of Brahmā (vairiñca)."
"O Brahman, tell me quickly and in detail everything just as it is. Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O mighty-armed one, listen to the sequence regarding the assumption of a body within the realm of Brahmā."
By that very illustration, you shall understand the state of the world: the reality of the Self, which is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, [manifests] through its own power.
When it assumes a body delimited by space and time as if in mere play, at that very moment it takes on the state of a living being, intent upon the immersion in latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
The mind becomes restless, intent upon the process of conceptualizing; at the outset, the power of the mind, while conceptualizing, brings about [the world] in an instant.

Then, from that mental state which is as clear as the meditation on space and oriented toward the essence of the seed-syllable of sound, the mind reaches a state of density through the process of dense vibration.
With those two—the sky and the wind—which are invisible, one contemplates through the eye of the mind the movement of the air, which is oriented toward the moisture of the seed of touch.
Fire is produced from the aggregate of the natures of sound and touch; the mind, having attained a state of density, then brings it into manifestation in an instant.
Through that light, the stainless illumination called *prākāśya* increases; it is the mind, directed toward the qualities (*guṇa*), which experiences the subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*).
Within half a moment, the coldness of the waters arises from the perception of water; thereafter, in an instant, the mind manifests that which possesses such qualities.
The earth will emerge with its own essential nature, possessing fragrance and grossness; then, having abandoned its subtle state, it will be enveloped by such subtle elements (tanmātras).
One perceives a body in the form of sparks of fire shimmering in the sky, joined with a portion of egoism and endowed with the seed of the intellect.

That is called the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka), which is like a bee in the lotus-heart of living beings; by means of intense spiritual fervor, one should meditate upon its radiant form within that [lotus].
Through ripening, the mind attains grossness like a bilva fruit; it shines forth in the stainless sky, resembling molten gold within a crucible.
That fire assumes a particular configuration by its own inherent nature; and within that very configuration, which consists of a mass of fire, [it exists] again.
He cultivates an expansive, certain, and all-pervading meditative absorption (bhāvanā), which consists of the seat of the head above and likewise the feet below.
With hands positioned at his sides and a belly in the middle, the child has manifest limbs and a form pure with garlands of flames.
Then, by the power of his mental resolve, he remains with a body assumed [at will]; thus, through the influence of his own latent impressions, the sage of the mind constructs a physical form.
Just as the season brings its own inherent nature to fruition, it leads the body to growth; in due time, it reaches full manifestation and becomes a stainless form.
Established in the power of intellect, goodness, strength, energy, wisdom, and sovereignty, he alone is the Blessed Lord Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds.
Resembling molten gold, he is born from the supreme space; just as he abides in that supreme space, he possesses no other form.
By the play of the mind, it sometimes generates within itself a delusion that resides in the self—the supreme, infinite space that is devoid of any limits.
At times it is water, pure and without beginning, middle, or end; at other times it is a shimmering orb of flames from the fire at the end of an aeon.
At times he was a forest, at times blackness, at times the dark fortnight, or a lotus bud; the Lord assumes various and manifold forms until the end of every birth.
He effortlessly maintains the world by manifesting various forms; therein, for the very first time, he [proceeds] from the station of Brahmā.
Having descended then from ignorance, he likewise remains in a state of blissful non-recollection; upon the departure of the sleep of the womb, he beholds his radiant body.
Rich with the flow of inhalation and exhalation, as if constructed from physical substances, it is covered with millions of pores and endowed with thirty-two teeth.
It has three pillars, five deities, and is marked at the base by feet; it consists of five parts, possesses nine gates, and its limbs are made smooth with an application of skin.
It is proportioned with twenty fingers, marked by twenty nails, possessing two arms, two breasts, and two eyes, yet also having many eyes and many arms.
It is the nest of the bird of the mind, the lair of the serpent of passion, the abode of the ogress of craving, and the cave of the lion of life.
Then Brahmā, beholding his own most excellent and lovely body, which served as a tethering post for the elephant of pride and was adorned by the lotus of his mind, [was filled with joy].
The Blessed One, whose vision of the three times is stainless, reflected upon this vast expanse of space, marked by bees.
Thinking, "What was there at first in this [world] whose further limit is unseen? Brahmā, having just been born, possessed the vision of the stainless Self.
He beheld the numerous multitudes of creations that had passed away many times over; then, he recollected all the various groups of dharmas in their proper sequence.
Like the spring season taking up flowers, he took up the well-praised Vedas and effortlessly fashioned creatures born of his diverse creative wills.
Having various modes of conduct and behavior like a city of the Gandharvas, for the sake of their heaven and liberation, and for the attainment of dharma, desire, and wealth.
He composed infinite and diverse treatises; O Rāma, this very view has thus attained stability in this creation, like the beauty of flowers from the mind of Brahmā, who is like the springtime.

O son of Raghu, by means of his mind alone—assuming the form of Brahmā through various compositions and playful acts of creation—the splendor of creation has been brought to an incomparable state of stability here in this world.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This world is indeed accomplished, yet nothing at all is truly accomplished; it is merely emptiness, a mere appearance, existing as the play of the mind.
Neither space nor time are encompassed by this cosmic egg, even though it possesses a vast form; for its true nature is that of space itself.
Consisting of mere volition, like a city seen in a dream, wherever it may be, that place is empty; there exists only the absolute void.
Even this painting, which lacks the application of pigment to a wall and is composed of nothingness, is seen as something created; it is a wondrous and variegated picture produced within the void.
Everything from the body to the three worlds is imagined by the mind; this is the cause for recollection, just as the eye is the cause for seeing light.

For the world, through its delusions of jars, wells, and cloths, is a mere appearance; it revolves without being separate from the nature of reality, just as walls and other objects do not exist apart from it.
For this body has been fashioned by the mind for the sake of latent impressions (vāsanā), just as a silkworm itself creates its own cocoon in the manner of a silken thread.
There is no object whatsoever that the mind’s resolve does not encompass like the sky; nor is there anything difficult or even exceedingly hard to achieve that it does not attain.
In the case of the God who possesses all powers, what indeed are those powers that do not exist [independently] but are resorted to within the cave of the inner mind?
For indeed, O mighty-armed one, the existence and non-existence of all things at all times occur only when the omnipresent and all-powerful Lord exists.
Behold, O son, how by means of meditation one attains a body through the mind alone; therefore, O Rāma, they know that mental construction to be endowed with all powers.
All gods, asuras, humans, and others are created by one's own volition; when that volition subsides, they are extinguished like a lamp without oil.
O one of great intelligence, behold this entire world as resembling space, a manifestation of mere conceptualization, like a very long dream that has arisen.
Nothing whatsoever is born or dies here at any time from the perspective of ultimate truth, O wise one; rather, everything exists only as a falsehood.
That which neither increases nor decreases, and which is never anything at all—what could possibly be diminished there, and for whom, or what, would there be any destruction?

O Raghava, seeing with your subtle vision that which has become the ground and arisen from your own body, why do you, like an ignorant man, become deluded within yourself because of what is not great?
Just as a mirage appears due to heat, so too do all these beings, from Brahmā downwards, appear as if they exist, though they are non-existent, through the mental determination of the mind.
All the multitudes of forms in the world are like the illusion of two moons, arisen like a daydream, and are dense masses of false cognition.
Just as for one traveling by boat there arises the false perception of the movement of a stationary post, so too this constant succession of mental images arises as something entirely unreal.
Know this to be a magical net, a cage constructed by illusion; it is a creation of the mind's own thinking, existing as if neither real nor unreal.
This entire world is indeed Brahman; therefore, whence can there be otherness? What kind of contingency could there be, what would it be, and where would that [otherness] abide?
"This is a mountain, this is a post"—such is the delusion of grandeur; through the firmness of mental cultivation, that which is non-existent appears as if it were existent.
This world is the beginning of a fall into conceptual proliferation for one who is heedless; O Rāma, abandon the mental preoccupation with desire and craving, and meditate on something else.
Just as a dream, though involving great undertakings, is merely an illusion and not real, know that this long dream is likewise produced by the mind.
Abandon this ostentatious display of cyclic existence, which appears as great enjoyment yet is grasped as being devoid of substance—the treasury of the serpents of desire.
Knowing that this is unreal, do not fix your mind upon it; for a wise person, having recognized a mirage, does not pursue it.
The deluded soul who pursues prosperity—which is rich in its own nature through his own imagination and consists merely of mental desire—is indeed a vessel for suffering alone.
If this world does not exist as a real entity, let it go as it pleases to what is non-existent; but he who abandons the real entity and goes toward the non-existent perishes.
This world is merely a delusion of the mind, like the fear of a snake in a rope; through the mere variety of mental cultivation, it revolves for a long time.
In this world, only the fool is deceived by phenomena that arise from the non-existent and are as unstable as the moon reflected in water; one such as you, who knows reality, is not so deceived.
That fool who, while cultivating this collection of virtues, desires happiness, merely rubs away his own dullness by means of the cultivation of fire itself.
This entire world, though non-existent, appears as an alluring snare of water, like a city conjured by the mind's own imaginings within the heart.
This arises by the will of the mind and dissolves by its lack of will; thus it is falsely perceived as vast, like a city of Gandharvas.
O Rāma, when this world perishes, nothing at all perishes; and even when this world is joined [with existence], nothing at all is joined.
When the city of the heart, constructed by the mind, is broken and yet has grown into vast proportions, tell me: what has increased, and what of whom has been destroyed?
Just as a mental representation arises in the hearts of children for the sake of play, so too does this world arise incessantly through the mind.
Nothing belonging to anyone has been lost, just as in the waters of a magical illusion; likewise, when this saṃsāra—which arises from falsehood—is fallen away or destroyed, nothing is truly lost.
If that which is non-existent were to remain non-existent, then what indeed would be lost for whom? Consequently, there would be no basis at all for joy or despair within this cycle of existence.
Since that which is absolutely non-existent does not truly exist, what indeed can be destroyed? For in the absence of destruction, O Mahāmati, what possibility is there for suffering?
Or rather, what can possibly perish of that which is eternally existent? This entire world is indeed Brahman; how then could pleasure and pain arise?
O Great-minded One, what kind of growth could there even be for that which is absolutely non-existent? In the absence of growth, what occasion is there for joy?
In this entire cycle of existence, which is unreal and characterized solely by conceptual proliferation, what is there for a wise person to accept that they might desire?
Since this entire triple world is everywhere real and consists of the essence of Brahman, what could there be that is to be abandoned? Let the wise discern that which should be relinquished.
Whether the world exists or does not exist for him, that fool remains inaccessible to pleasure and pain; yet he is distressed by its destruction.
That which does not exist in the beginning and at the end likewise exists not in the present; for one who desires what is non-existent, only non-existence is perceived.
That which is real in the beginning and at the end is indeed real in the present as well; for one to whom everything is real, only reality itself is perceived.
Only the ignorant, not the superior ones, long for such unreal things as the moon within water or the surface of the sky, which serve only to delude the mind.
For the fool attains satisfaction through vast forms and purposes that are empty of substance; this leads to endless suffering, and not to happiness.
Therefore, O lotus-eyed Rāma, do not be a fool; perceiving that which is imperishable here, take refuge in the eternal and most steadfast.

Do not fall into despondency by calculating that "all this, including myself, is non-existent"; and do not fall into despondency by observing that "all this, including myself, is existent" in this world.

Śrī Vālmīki said: When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: What occasion indeed is there for grief regarding delightful wealth, wives, and the like? When they are seen through the perception of a magical illusion and then vanish, what lamentation can there be?
When a city of Gandharvas is neither defiled nor adorned, what sequence of pleasure or pain can there be regarding its parts—such as sons and so forth—which are likewise merely portions of ignorance?
What occasion for joy is there indeed in pleasant wealth, wives, and the like? When a mirage has vanished, can those seeking water find any delight?
Suffering is appropriate toward wealth, wives, and the aged, but not contentment; when delusion and illusion have grown old, who here can find consolation?
By those very same objects of enjoyment which produce passion in a fool due to his excessive attachment, it is precisely those same enjoyments that give rise to dispassion in the wise man.
When wealth, wife, and so forth have perished, what occasion indeed is there for joy? But the virtuous, looking toward the further shore, attain detachment through these very things.
Therefore, O Raghava, you who know the truth regarding the worldly affairs of saṃsāra, disregard what is lost as lost, and accept what is gained as gained.
Not desiring future enjoyments and enjoying those that have arrived without artifice—this is the characteristic of a wise person.
In this turmoil of saṃsāra, where the self is concealed and acts as an assailant, conduct yourself as a perfectly awakened one so that you do not fall into delusion.
Those of perverted intellect who do not perceive this sequence, which is free from conceptual proliferation, within the grand display of saṃsāra, are truly destroyed.
Whosoever’s attachment to the visible world and such has departed by whatever means, his pure intellect does not sink anywhere, for it finds no basis therein.
Ignorance, which is unreal, cannot embrace that omniscient one from whom the conviction that "this world exists" has ceased with respect to all things.
He whose intellect realizes that "I" and this entire world are one and the same, having abandoned both attachment and aversion, remains established and does not sink.
Having supported yourself with the intellect upon that pure state which lies between existence and non-existence, neither grasp nor release the perceivable world, whether external or internal.
Utterly detached, established in your own nature, and free from all attachments, remain like the sky, O Rāma, devoid of passion even while engaged in your duties.
For the wise person who abides in action, neither desire nor aversion exists; his discernment is not defiled, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
Whether your senses and mind perform acts such as seeing and touching or refrain from them, you remain the master of yourself; even without desire, you are the self-possessed one.

Let not the mind, which conceives "this is mine" regarding the objects of the senses—though such a conception is unreal—be submerged; whether it acts or does not act, let it not be drowned once it has been submerged.
O Rāghava, when the splendor of the objects of the senses no longer pleases your heart, then you have realized true knowledge and have crossed over the ocean of existence.
