For you, whether possessing a body or being bodiless, liberation has been achieved by the power of reality itself, even though you did not desire it while tasting the objects of the senses.
O Rāma, by means of supreme wisdom, separate the mind from the multitude of latent impressions for the sake of the highest state, just as one extracts noble fragrance from a flower.
In this ocean of saṃsāra, flooded with the waters of latent impressions (vāsanā), those who have boarded the boat of wisdom have crossed over; others have merely drowned.
Having investigated the reality of the self with an extremely steady intellect, as sharp as the edge of a razor, you shall then enter your own state.
O Rāma, one should conduct oneself just as those wise ones who know reality do—their minds nourished by knowledge—and not like a fool.
The great-souled ones who are liberated while living, ever-contented and of vast intellect, are to be followed by their conduct; not the deceitful who are wretched for the sake of sensual enjoyment.
They neither abandon nor crave the worldly affairs of the world; those who know both this shore and the further shore conform to everything.
In this world, those great ones who perceive reality never become miserable on account of their power, pride, virtues, fame, or fortune.
Great men do not weary even in utter solitude, nor do they become attached to celestial gardens; like the suns, they do not abandon their destined course.
Free from desire and following worldly conduct as it occurs, they move about exalted, established in their own natural state within the chariot of the body.
O Rama, you too have attained this expansive discernment; by the power of this wisdom, O handsome one, you are established in self-abiding knowledge.
Firmly maintaining a clear vision, free from pride and devoid of envy, dwell upon this seat of the earth; you shall attain supreme perfection.
Established in yourself, renouncing all that is beneficial to the self, and desiring the vision from afar, wander, O sinless one, having taken up supreme coolness within.

Śrī Vālmīki said: Thus, by the pure speech of the sage whose heart was pure, Rāma immediately appeared as if cleansed; with his inner self radiant and filled by the sweet nectar of knowledge, he attained a coolness like that of the full moon.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, who has reached the further shore of all the Vedāṅgas; I stand as if consoled by your pure words.
I do not reach satiety in hearing your words as you speak—words that are noble, secluded, refined, and sublime.
In the course of discussing the birth of the one born from the lotus according to the scriptures, you have described the origin of her who is by nature rajasic-sattvic.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, many hundreds of thousands of Brahmās, hundreds of Śivas and Indras, and thousands of Nārāyaṇas have already passed away.
And in many other diverse cosmic eggs, they wander by the thousands, engaged in various modes of conduct and pastimes.
Simultaneously, and throughout infinite worlds existing at other times, many others will likewise arise in great abundance.
O mighty-armed one, the births of those dwellers of heaven, such as the one born from the lotus and others, within the cosmic eggs appeared like various wonders arisen.
Sometimes the creations belong to Śiva, sometimes they arise from the lotus-born Brahmā; sometimes they belong to Viṣṇu, and sometimes they are fashioned by the sages.
Sometimes Brahmā is born from a lotus, sometimes he is born from the waters; sometimes he is born from an egg, and sometimes he is born from the sky.
In one staff there was the three-eyed Śiva, in another the sun-god Arka, in another the lotus-eyed Viṣṇu, and indeed in yet another the three-eyed Śiva himself.
In one creation, the earth was densely crowded with trees; in another, it was densely crowded with men; and in yet another, it was covered by mountains.
One was made of earth, another was made of stone; one was made of gold, and likewise another was made of copper.
Right here, some worlds are variegated, while others are otherwise; some consist of single worlds, and some are even devoid of greatness.
In this great sky of the reality of Brahman, infinite worlds sink and emerge like the waters of the waves of the ocean.
Just as waves exist in the ocean, as a mirage exists in the desert, and as flowers exist on the mango tree, so do the glories of the universe exist in the Supreme.
The motes of dust in the rays of the sun can be counted, but the multitudes of worlds, with their flickering forms, cannot be numbered in truth by Brahman.
Just as swarms of mosquitoes, agitated by the rains and other elements, perish again and again as they arise, so too do these creations of the world.
Nor is it known from what time these successions of creations have come forth; they are characterized by a constant coming and going.
Beginningless and incessant, they flash forth like waves; indeed, each preceding one arose from the one before it, just as that which preceded it arose from what was even further back.
Having come into being again and again, all classes of beings—including gods, asuras, and humans—dissolve away like the breaking of waves upon a river.
Just as this egg of Brahmā exists, so too do the series of cosmic eggs, which have perished by the thousands like the channels [of breath] within years.
Others currently exist, possessing present bodies, at the edge of this city of Brahmā, in the vast domain of Brahman.
There will be others belonging to Brahmā, possessing the splendor of the city of Brahmā; yet they too shall perish again and again, just like spoken words.
Other successions of creations, destined for Brahman, remain within him like pots in a heap of clay, or like sprouts in a seed.
Just as within the sky of consciousness up to the realm of Brahmā, the splendors of the three worlds—though rich with vast forms and transformations—are seen to be nothing at all when scrutinized.
Emerging and submerging, these glories are neither real nor unreal; like wickedness itself, they spread forth as the undertakings of the dull-witted.
Possessing the nature of waves, their bodies appearing and then vanishing, all these streams of emanations exhibit diverse forms and activities.
Indeed, creations possess variegated forms and transformations, for all perceptions of creation, taken as a whole, are not distinct from [the creator] for everyone.
O Rāma, emanations flow toward one who knows reality from the Divine, like raindrops from water or like showers from a cloud.
The perceptions of creation for all beings are not entirely distinct from one another, just as the waters, the ocean, and the swallows of the *śālmalī* tree are not distinct from it.
O Raghava, within these creations—whether flourishing or degraded—the subtle elements (tanmātra) arise from the supreme ether as a mere garland of impurity.
Sometimes, first, he attains a foundation in space; from that, Brahmā is born—this Prajāpati who is born from space.
Sometimes first the wind attains a firm foundation; from that, Brahmā is born—this Prajāpati who is born of the wind.
Sometimes, first light attains a firm foundation; from that, this Prajāpati, the creator of light, is born.
At one time, water first attains stability; from that, Brahmā is born—that Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) who is born from the waters.
Sometimes first the earth attains expansion; from that, Brahmā is born, he who is the earthly Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati).
When this fifth [element] increases by compressing these four, then, having arisen from that very state, it performs the activity of the world.
Sometimes, in water, in air, or even in a vast expanse of fire, a person who has been conditioned by primordial nature (prakṛti) spontaneously manifests all at once.
Then, at times a sound arises from his mouth, sometimes from his feet, sometimes from his shoulders or his back, and sometimes from his eyes or his hands.
At one time, a lotus is produced from the navel of this Puruṣa; within it Brahmā develops, and he is celebrated as the "Lotus-born."
This is an illusion, a delusion like a dream, a false circle of fabrications; it is like a kingdom of the mind, as beautiful as a whirlpool in restless water.
Tell me, how could such a thing possibly occur here in this consciousness? This is merely a childish fantasy being put forward as an inquiry.
Sometimes, within the pure ether, through the coloring of the principle of the mind, the golden cosmic egg containing Brahman manifests of its own accord.
At some time, a person indeed creates vigor within the waters; from that, a lotus is born, or else the great cosmic egg.
From him Brahmā is born; at times he is also the Sun, at times Varuṇa, at times Brahmā, and at times Vāyu, the egg-born.
Thus, O Rāma, within these various creations that have arisen and passed away, diverse origins of Brahmā have occurred in manifold ways.
This origin has been told to you for the sake of illustration regarding the creation of me alone, the Lord of Creatures; there is no fixed rule in that regard whatsoever.
This world-process, commonly regarded as saṃsāra, is merely the manifestation of the mind; this sequence of creation has been described for the purpose of awakening you.

This sequence of creation has been described to you so that you may understand how the various classes of beings, such as those characterized by sattva and the rest, came into existence in this manner.
Again there is creation, again destruction; again suffering, again happiness; again the ignorant, again the knower of that [reality]; and again the perceptions of bondage and liberation.
Furthermore, those who create the world again, their vision free from attachment and aversion, like lamps that have provided light, they both extinguish and arise once more.
In the arising and destruction of both lamps and Brahmas, there is no difference whatsoever in their destruction once they have abandoned their temporal extension.
Again there is Kṛta, again Tretā, again that Dvāpara and Kali; the entire world revolves once more like the turning of a wheel.
Again and again begin the manvantaras, again and again the successions of kalpas, and again and again the states of activity, just as every morning the day begins anew.
The interior of this world, fashioned by the divisions of light and darkness and by time, is again and again perceived as this entire universe; yet, again and again, it is nothing at all.
Like sparks from fire on a heated iron ball, these phenomena always abide by their very nature within the space of consciousness.
Sometimes unmanifest and sometimes having attained manifestation, all this exists within the supreme reality like the seasonal growth on a tree.
The vibration of consciousness alone is the self of all, always possessing such a form; from it arises creation, just as the appearance of two moons arises from the eye.
All continuous perceptions of creation flow together into consciousness; though they appear not to reside within it, they are actually situated therein, like rays of light from the moon.
O Rāma, this saṃsāra is indeed never truly real, for within the all-powerful [Reality], there exists the power of non-saṃsāra.
And yet, O virtuous one, this world has never been otherwise than it is now; for within the power of all things, the power of saṃsāra is found to exist.
Due to the momentum of transmigration sustained over time extending for the duration of a great eon, it is logical that cyclic existence will no longer exist from this point forward.
O Mahāmati, through the vision of wisdom, all this is indeed Brahman alone; thus, it follows logically that there is no such thing as saṃsāra.
However, from the perspective of the ignorant, because saṃsāra is uninterrupted, this illusion of saṃsāra is established here as being eternally false, even though it is incessant.
"O descendant of Raghu, because it has been cultivated again and again, it is said that this world is never otherwise; this is not false."
The quarters of space, seen to be constantly falling away in form and subject to destruction—how is it not established that this entire world is perishable?
The quarters of the sky were seen with the sun and moon risen everywhere, and the mountains appeared motionless; that the entire world was imperishable was likewise an unfailing analogy.
There is nothing that does not exist within that single, all-pervasive Self; for in that ineffable reality, the web of conceptual constructions cannot possibly arise.
Again and again all this occurs: again death and birth; again pleasure and again pain; again the instruments and the actions.
Again the quarters, again the sky, again the oceans and the mountains; creation arises again, like the radiance of the sun in the sky.
Again there are Daityas, again there are gods, again the succession of other worlds; again there is the desire for heaven and liberation, again Indra, and again the Moon.
Again there was the god Nārāyaṇa, again the sons of Danu and others; again appeared the beautiful moon, sun, Varuṇa, and Vāyu, moving through the quarters of the sky.
Adorned with Mount Sumeru as its pericarp and graced by the Sahya mountains as its filaments, the lotus of the two worlds rises again, full and with a swelling interior.
Having ascended the forest of the sky and leaping with the multitude of his rays as claws, the lion-like sun advances once more to shatter the herd of elephants that is the darkness.
Furthermore, the moon, with rays as beautiful as swaying, clear blossoms, creates a delightful nectar that adorns the faces of the women of the quarters.

Furthermore, when the merit of those who have performed virtuous deeds has been exhausted by the wind, they fall from the tree of heaven here below with their limbs shattered, like heaps of withered flowers.
Furthermore, the partridge of time, having made some rustling sound through the various modes of causal activity known as the commencement of saṃsāra, departs.
When Indra and the others had departed, having merely taken their seats, another lord of the gods arrived at that lotus of heaven, like a six-legged bee.
Furthermore, the Kali age defiles even that time which has been purified, just as a violent wind of refuse defiles the ocean even when it contains the Discus-bearer.
Furthermore, the potter Kālaka turns the wheel—which is called "conceptualization"—with speed and without ceasing, having fashioned it from the clay of the elements.
The world, its auspicious state destroyed, returns once more to a state of saplessness, like a forest that has become parched through the habitual force of its own volitions.
Furthermore, when the solar cycles have passed, the world—its endless bodies consumed by fire and filled with the bones of all beings—attains the state of a cremation ground.
Furthermore, through rains like those of the Puṣkarāvarta clouds that resemble the boundary mountains, the world—its great foam being the dancing saṃsāra—returns to the state of a single ocean.
Furthermore, when wind and water have subsided and it is devoid of all things, the world returns to emptiness, becoming like that unprecedented space.
Furthermore, having spent several years with an equanimous disposition toward the flavor of existence, one dissolves back into one's own self through the body that has grown old.
Again, at another time, it likewise expands the multitudes of worlds within the void, just like a city of Gandharvas.
The commencement of creation occurs first, and at the time of dissolution, everything arises; O Rāma, all this revolves again like a wheel.
O Rāma, in this vast display of great illusion, which is as extensive as the sky, what is said here—whether it be true or false—is to be determined.
O Rāma, this wheel of saṃsāra is like the story of Dāśūra; its forms are fashioned by conceptual construction, and it is devoid of reality, not being real in itself.

This world is spread out without interval by those conceptual constructions which, though arisen from the unreal, are like the vision of two moons; it is fashioned as something unreal and lacking true existence. Therefore, what is the cause of this delusion?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When those whose intentions are destroyed by enjoyments and power engage in a multitude of ritual activities, they do not seek the truth; at that time, the deceitful do not perceive it.
But those who have gone beyond the intellect and are not enslaved by the senses—they behold this worldly illusion as clearly as a wood-apple held in the palm of their hand.
Having seen that worldly illusion to be hollow, the discerning living being casts off the illusion consisting of egoism, just as a snake sheds its skin.
Then, having attained non-attachment, O Rāma, one is not born again, even while remaining for a long time in the fields of rebirth, like a seed consumed by fire.
Ignorant people strive for the benefit of the body—which is beset by mental and physical ailments and destined to perish tomorrow morning—but not for the sake of the self.
Like one who is ignorant, do not fulfill the desires of this ignorant body for the sake of suffering; instead, remain solely devoted to the Self, which is your true nature.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Lord, is this wheel of the cycle of existence merely like the story of Dāśūra—a construction of imagined forms that is devoid of any real substance?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, listen as I relate the narrative of Dāśūra, which is told by way of describing the true nature of the world-illusion (jaganmāyā).
On this surface of the earth, there is a great and glorious country known as Māgadha, famous for its trees bearing variegated blossoms.
Its forests were graced by the playful expanse of kadamba groves, and it was enchanting with every wonder due to the flocks of various birds.
Its borders were crowded with grain, adorned with city groves, and its entire riverbanks were filled with lotuses, water-lilies, and white lilies.
There was the humming of songs sung by women sporting on garden swings; the ground of the paths was densely covered with flowers gathered during the night.
There, on a certain mountain slope thick with *karṇikāra* trees, it was adorned with dense groves of plantain trees and clusters of *nīpa* shrubs.

In that place where the wind was shimmering with a flood of flowers, where the pollen was reddish like filaments, where the *kāraṇḍava* ducks raised their cries, and where the *sārasa* cranes were warbling;
In that meritorious, excellent mountain, where the trees were filled with various birds, there lived a certain sage of great asceticism whose soul was devoted to the supreme Dharma.
Named Dāśūra, he was endowed with great power of austerity; residing on the slopes of Mount Kadamba, he was free from passion and possessed of great intelligence.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, for what reason did that ascetic come to the forest, and how did he dwell upon the back of the great Kadamba tree?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: His father was renowned as Śaraloma; like another Brahmā, O Rāma, he dwelt upon that very mountain.
He had an only son named Kaca, like that of the preceptor of the gods; together with that son, he spent his life in the forest.
Then, having eaten only a single Śaraloma for a multitude of ages, he cast off his body and went to the abode of the gods, like a bird that has abandoned its nest.
In that very forest, Dāśūra, having been deprived of his father, wept piteously all alone like a kurara bird.
With his heart tormented by grief due to the separation from his parents, he surely fell into a state of withering, like a lotus in the winter season.
O Rāma, that boy, whose soul was exceedingly distressed, was thus consoled in the forest by a forest deity whose body remained invisible.
O son of a seer, possessed of great wisdom, why do you weep like one ignorant? Why do you not understand the flickering nature of saṃsāra?
O virtuous one, in this world such is the ever-shifting course of transmigration: one is born, lives, and thereafter inevitably perishes.
O Sage, whatever is seen within this vision—from Brahmā downwards—all that must come to an end; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, do not indulge in useless despondency over the death of your father; the setting of one who has been born is inevitable, just as that of the sun at the end of the day.
Hearing the voice "I am bodiless," Śikhaṇḍin, his eyes bloodshot red, regained his composure as if from the sound of thunder.
Having risen and performed his necessary duties, he then, out of reverence for his father, formed a firm resolve toward asceticism for the sake of attaining the highest perfection.
As he performed austerities in the forest through brahminical rites, his status as a learned Vedic scholar became characterized by infinite resolve.
But for that Vedic scholar, whose intellect was still seeking to know what remained unknown, his mind found no rest even upon the sacred surface of the earth.
Seeing even this entire surface of the earth—which is in fact purely pure—as if it were impure, he indeed found no delight anywhere at all.
Then, by his own volition alone, he formed this resolve: "Only at the very top of a tree, perfectly pure, is my dwelling appropriate."
Therefore, I shall now perform such austerity by which I may attain, like a bird, the state of dwelling upon the branches and the leaves of trees.
Having reflected thus, he kindled an exceedingly brilliant fire and, having cut flesh from the surface of his own shoulder, offered it as an oblation into it.
Now, let not the entire throats of the host of gods be reduced to ashes by the consumption of Brahmin flesh through my mouth.
Having reflected thus, the seven-rayed Lord, the deity of that [fire], appeared before him with blazing splendor, like the sun appearing before the Lord of Speech.
He spoke these firm words, which were agreeable to the prince: "Accept, O virtuous one, this boon offered by me, like a jewel taken from the interior of a treasure chest."
Having spoken thus, the young Brahmin, having honored the Fire-god with a beautiful offering flower and with words of praise, spoke.
O Blessed One, I do not reach the sanctifying circle of the earth that was filled with the Tathāgatas; therefore, let my station be above the trees.
When the son of the sage had spoken thus, the Lord Śikhin, the mouth of all the gods, said, "So be it for you," and vanished from sight.
When that god had vanished in an instant, like the twilight light from a lotus, the prince, his desires fulfilled, shone like the full moon.

Filled with joy, he laughed at the moon, which had attained its full orb yet was surrounded by its digits, and at the blossoming lotus, which shone with white smiles; for he surpassed them both with the abundance of splendor from the circle of his own face, which had achieved the desired form.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Now, [he saw] a place situated in the middle of a forest, which kissed the circle of the clouds and whose circular ridges were frequented by the horses of the sun, exhausted at midday.
Like a canopy stretching across the belly of the quarters with its branch-arms, it gazes upon the directions with eyes of blossoming flowers.
With its hair of bees fluttering in no small measure, shaken by the wind, it was wiping the faces of the quarters with its hands of tender shoots.
The forest groves seemed to laugh with their mouths—the thick clusters of bright blossoms on the *uruguḍḍa* shrubs—which appeared like betel-filled lips.
With the playful splendors of creepers and the pollen of flower filaments, it formed a circular expanse like the full moon with its radiance.
The world was embraced by the towering height of the forest, which was like a secret path of the perfected ones, concealed by a creeper-covered thicket where the cakora birds warbled.
The sky was adorned by the hanging peacock plumages of those seated upon the pedestals of the *skandhas*, appearing like clouds accompanied by rainbows.
It was filled with white yak-tails resting upon every shoulder, now emerging and now submerging, appearing and vanishing like moons throughout the course of a year.

With the warbling of flocks of *kapiñjala* partridges, the melodious cooing of *kokila* cuckoos, and the cries of *jīvaṃjīva* birds, it seemed as if the mountain were singing aloud with its lofty peaks.
And with flocks of kadamba ducks sporting in their nests, and with siddhas resting within the hollows of heaven, the world seemed as if it were entirely covered.
It was frequented here and there by clusters of blossoms that resembled Apsarases with coral-like trembling hands and bee-eyes, as if it were heaven itself.
With the pollen from the clusters of night-lilies, it was dark and tawny with blossoms, like a cloud accompanied by lightning and the splendor of Indra’s bow.
It was known as the one with a thousand arm-branches, filling the hollow of the sky; it was like the Cosmic Form (Viśvarūpa) dancing, with the moon and sun serving as its earrings.
Seated upon that lord of serpents was [the deity], amidst a sky crowded with hosts of stars, like another circle of the firmament in its center composed of creepers and flowers.
Resplendent with all its mountains and forests like the Grandfather Brahmā himself, it was like a single treasury of fruits, shoots, and flowers upon the earth.
Bearing a mass of buds veiled by the pollen of flowers, it was like the sky at its edges, where the net of stars is obscured by the rays of the sun.
The surface of the earth was encircled by tree trunks filled with restless birds and crowded with numerous nests, appearing like the world filled with inhabited districts.
Abounding with flower-clusters and beautiful banners, adorned with circles of creepers, white with *maṅkola* flowers, and strewn with heaps of blossoms.
It resounded with the warbling of cakoras, bees, parrots, cuckoos, and sārikās; its caves were dense with thick clusters of blossoms, serving as formidable windows.
Abounding with birds in flight and having hollows where people moved slowly, it was like the supreme inner apartment of all the forest goddesses.
It was resplendent with swarms of humming bees and rows of flower filaments falling like rivers descending upon a mountain.
Its trunk was covered by swarms of flower petals whirling about, sported by gentle breezes and increasing in volume, like a mountain shrouded by white clouds.
With her knees braced and her broad hips rubbed against the elephant's back, she stood firmly upon him like a young woman clinging to a great mountain.
It was surrounded by a flock of birds with variegated-colored wings, moving within the hollows of their shoulders, like Śārṅgin surrounded by a multitude of spirits.
With his trembling web of fingers formed by clusters of blossoms, he seemed to be demonstrating the art of dramatic gesture to the forest creepers set in motion by the woodland breezes.
Thinking with satisfaction, "I have found at least one dwelling for those who seek me," it seemed to dance, as it were, with the swaying of its many richly adorned creeper-garlands.
Because it was the sole beloved of the creepers, it was overflowing with the sentiment of erotic love (śṛṅgāra-rasa), as if singing in the *kakali* register through the humming of intoxicated bees.
It seemed to offer a welcome, as it were, to the sky-dwelling Siddhas with flowers cast down in reverence, through the warbling of cuckoos and the humming of swarms of bees.
With the splendor of the creepers' flowers and fruits upon the trees at its edge, it seemed to laugh with the brilliant radiance of its flower buds.
With its neck held high, it seemed to run through the midst of the sky as if to conquer the celestial *pārijāta* tree, pursued by swarms of birds soaring above.
With dense rows of flower clusters, lofty in their swelling centers, it seemed as if striving to surpass Indra by attaining a thousand eyes through its peerless blossoms.
In some places, covered by a multitude of jewel-like gems upon hoods as clear as clusters of blossoms, it resembled the serpent Śeṣa risen from the netherworld with a desire to behold the sky.
His form was covered with dust, like a second Śaṅkara, yet he brought welfare to all people through his shadow, which was laden with fruit.

He beheld a *kadamba* tree in the sky, like a city, accompanied by young arbors of flowering creepers whose buds were burst open by the dense mass of its leaves, and crowded with flocks of birds like citizens.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, with a mind slow with bliss, he [beheld] him who was thus adorned with the blossoming shoots of the fruit of wisdom, resembling a mountain of flowers.
Śauri ascended the kadamba tree standing in the forest, which acted as a pillar for heaven and earth, just as he had ascended the lofty banyan tree situated in the single ocean.
There, upon the tip of a leaf at the end of a branch reaching toward the sky, he entered with freedom from fear and established himself in one-pointed ascetic practice.
Then, having sat down upon a soft seat of fresh sprouts, he gazed for a moment at the quarters of the sky with eyes flickering with curiosity.

The mountains are beautiful with their single-string pearl necklaces, their breasts are the buds of the lordly peaks, their braided hair is the stainless sky, and their locks of hair are the drifting dark clouds.
Clad in garments of blue shoots, adorned with ear-ornaments of abundant flowers, holding full jars of the ocean, and wearing many ornaments.
They bear blooming lotuses, their breath is fragrant, their low, humming warbling is blue, and the sound of their waterfalls serves as their anklets.
The heavens are their heads, the great earth their feet, the rows of forests their lines of body hair, the jungles their thighs and hips, and the sun and moon their earrings.
The fields of the cycle of existence are filled with rice, provided with saffron-colored bowls, and draped in the white silken garments of snow-clad clouds clinging to the peaks of the breasts.

They were mirrors for the fresh adornment of the floodwaters of the great ocean; they were the inner apartments of the world, where the hosts of stars were the horripilation caused by the heat [of their beauty].
Wearing garments dyed with the menses, they were stained with the saffron of the sun’s rays; adorned with various flowers, they were anointed with sandalwood white as the moonbeams.

Seated upon a leaf of a creeper suspended in the sky, he joyfully beheld the ten directions—adorned without interval by flowers—which appeared like a vast expanse of forest, earth, and water flowing forth.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: From that time forth, he became renowned there in the hermitage of ascetics as Kadambadāśūra, a hero in rigorous penance.
Standing upon that lotus leaf and gazing for a moment toward all directions, he assumed the firm *padmāsana* posture, withdrawing his mind from the quarters of space.
Not knowing the ultimate truth, abiding merely in ritual action, and with a mind possessed by a craving for results, he performed that sacrifice.
With his inner self established upon the leaf of the creeper situated in the sky, he performed all the sacrificial rites in succession with that very mind of his.
There, for ten years, he worshipped the gods with his mind alone through sacrifices such as those involving cows, horses, and human beings, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
When his expansive mind had attained purity over time, the knowledge born of his own serene confidence descended within him by its own power.
Then, his veils shattered and the impurity of his latent tendencies dissolved, he once beheld her standing before him upon that creeper.
He beheld the forest goddess, large-eyed, with flowers for her garments, a woman of lovely countenance whose eyes were rolling with intoxication.
The sage spoke to that woman of faultless limbs, whose face was cast down and who was exceedingly captivating, fragrant as a blue lotus.
"Who are you, O lotus-petal-eyed one, whose beauty agitates the God of Love, appearing like a forest creeper laden with *kokilā* flowers?"
"Why do you stand there like a flowering creeper, as if you were a female companion?"—when she was thus addressed, the fawn-eyed woman with her fair and full breasts [remained silent].
The charming sage spoke these words in sweet syllables: "Whatever things are desired on this earth that are difficult to obtain,"
Those various [objects] are quickly obtained only through the requests of the great. I am here in this place overgrown with creepers and adorned by your *kadamba* tree.
O Brahmin, in the forest that is the abode of the playful charms of Lakṣmī, there dwells a forest deity; and on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, during the festival of Smara—
A gathering of forest goddesses took place in the Nandana grove; there, O Lord, I went to that assembly of the beauties of the three worlds.
There, during the festival of love, I saw all my friends accompanied by their sons; because I was childless, I was therefore deeply distressed.
While you, the great wish-granting tree, stand as the caravan leader for the multitude of all goals, how is it, O Lord, that I, like one without a protector and childless, must indeed grieve?
"Give me your son, O Blessed One; otherwise, I shall offer my own body here as an oblation into the fire for the sake of quelling the burning pain of my son."
When the slender maiden had spoken thus, the eminent sage smiled and, filled with compassion, gave her a flower from his hand and said:
"Go, O slender-limbed one; in a month you shall give birth to a lovely son whose eyes are free of impurity—one worthy of worship, just as a fine creeper brings forth a flower."
However, since our son was requested by you while you were overcome by the impulse of death, he will come to know [this] after undergoing great hardship.
Having spoken thus to the slender-limbed woman, whose countenance was serene and who was longing with the prayer, "May I perform service for you," that sage dismissed her.
She went to her own abode, and he remained with his own self; time passed in due order, marked by seasons and years.
Then, after a long time, that very lotus-eyed woman approached the sage, bringing with her a son who was twelve years old.
Having bowed and sat before the sage whose face was like the moon, she spoke with a gentle voice, like a female bee humming around a mango tree.
"O Blessed One, this is our son, the prince Bhavya; indeed, I have made him proficient in all the arts."
O Lord, he has attained only this auspicious knowledge, by which he will no longer be tormented within this wheel of saṃsāra.
O Lord, you alone must now compassionately instruct him in knowledge; for who indeed would consign a son born into a noble family to the state of ignorance?
To her who was speaking thus, the sage said, "O weak woman, leave this son here with his good disciple," and having spoken, he dismissed her.
When she had departed, that wise man remained self-restrained in the presence of his father, like Aruṇa before the sun.
Having attained this realization, the sage thereafter instructed his son for a long time with various eloquent discourses.
By means of hundreds of narratives and legends, through parables fashioned from observation, as well as through historical accounts and the definitive conclusions of the Vedas and Vedānta;
Through constant and detailed discourses that inspire no weariness, and by means of experiences brought to full maturity, may [the truth] take firm root within me.

By virtue of his direct experience, the great-souled maharṣi, having had enough with the multitude of words concerning appropriate matters that were redundant to the aesthetic flavor (rasa), enlightened his son standing before him in the sky, just as a cloud awakens a peacock.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Once, traveling through the path of the sky with my form invisible, I went along that road to bathe at the abode of Kailāsa-dwelling [Pārvatī].
Having emerged from the hollow of the circle of the seven sages in the sky, O wise one, I reached the lofty tree of Dāśūra during the night.
I heard a voice from the hollow of a bough in the forest, like the sound of a bee clinging to a lotus bud.
Listen, O son of great intelligence, to this marvelous narrative of a single event; I shall describe it to you exactly as it occurred in reality.
There is a king of great heroism, renowned throughout the three worlds, the illustrious one named Khottha, who is capable of subduing the world.
The leaders in all the worlds hold his instruction high upon their heads with reverence, like seekers holding a crest-jewel.
This Great Soul, whose sole delight was in daring feats and who dwelt in various wonders, was not brought under subjection by anyone in the three worlds.
Who is able to count its thousands of undertakings that bestow both pleasure and pain, which are like the waves of the ocean?
The prowess of that one of great valor has not been overcome by anyone in the world, neither by weapons nor by fires, just as the sky cannot be grasped with a fist.
Even Śakra, Upendra, and Hara do not imitate in the slightest that playful activity of his, which is vast in its undertaking and radiant with creative power.
O mighty-armed one, he has three bodies capable of wandering; having pervaded the world, they remain as the highest, the lowest, and the middling.
Born in that very vast expanse of space, he became possessed of three bodies; and there alone he took his stand, moving like a bird at the fall of a sound.
Right there in the boundless sky, he created a city with fourteen great thoroughfares, adorned with three distinct divisions.
It was rich with rows of groves and pleasure gardens, beautiful with pleasure-hills, and adorned with seven ponds encircled by strings of pearls.
It was illuminated by two inexhaustible lamps consisting of cold and heat, and it was crowded with the paths of merchants characterized by upward and downward movement.
In that very same vast city, by that king, groups of deluded beings were fashioned as small, wretched apartments within the cycle of existence.
Some are appointed above, some below, and some in the middle; some perish after a long time, while others perish quickly.
Covered with black roofs, adorned with nine gates, with winds blowing incessantly, and provided with many windows;
Illuminated by five lamps, they have three pillars made of white wood; they are smooth, plastered, and soft, crowded with the arms of the city gateways.
By that high-souled king, great yakṣas who were created through illusion and who were perpetually afraid of light were appointed as guardians over them.
Then, as the throngs of inner apartments moved about, that lord of the earth engaged in various diversions, like a bird in its nests.
O son, having dwelt at will for a hundred triple-bodies among those yakṣas, he emerges once more and departs.
O child, at times a firm desire arises in that one of restless mind: "I shall go to some city that is yet to be created."
As if possessed by a spirit, he rises up from there with impetuosity and runs; then he reaches that city, which is as if constructed by the Gandharvas.
O son, a desire sometimes arises in that one of unsteady mind, "I shall bring about his destruction," and by that thought he quickly perishes.
It arises again swiftly, like a wave from its own source in the water; it expands worldly activity intensely, yet again, slowly through renewed effort.
Then, by that very same worldly activity, one is sometimes humiliated; one grieves, thinking, "I am a servant, I am ignorant, I am miserable."
Sometimes it attains joy, and at other times it itself falls into a state of wretchedness, like the current of a river that surges with the swelling floods of the rainy season.

Victorious is that lord of the earth, the master of the waters, possessed of great majesty; he moves, leaps, yawns, quivers, shines, and yet does not shine, radiant as he is, agitated by the speed of the wind.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, in the dead of night there in Jambūdvīpa, the son questioned his father, whose mind was purified, as he sat upon the crest of a kadamba tree.
The son said: "Who is this king known as Khottha, whose form is like that of my father? And what was it that you told me? Tell me this according to the truth."
Where will the manifestation occur? Where can one go while it is present? Since your words contradict both purposes, they serve only to confuse my mind.
Dāśūra said: Listen, my son; I shall tell this to you exactly as it is, so that you may realize the true nature of this wheel of saṃsāra.
Thus have I described this structure of saṃsāra: though non-existent, it has arisen from effort; though devoid of substance, it is vast in extent.
The volition born from the supreme ether is said to arise from space; it is born by itself and dissolves by itself.
This entire expansive universe exists as that very nature; it is born when that is born, and when that is destroyed, it perishes.
They know Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Rudra, and the others to be merely his limbs, like the branches of a tree or the peaks of a mountain.
In the empty sky, he created this city of the three worlds; having attained the state of Viriñci merely by following after appearances.
In this [world] are spread out the fourteen world-enclosures with their vast expanses of light, where there are ranges of forests and groves, and successions of pleasure gardens.
Where the Sahya, Mandara, and Meru mountains serve as pleasure peaks, and where the moon and sun, with their cool and fiery splendors, act as lamps in the form of fire.
There, the rivers bear moving strings of excellent pearls, lofty like pearls upon trembling waves that flicker like the rays of the sun.
There, the seven great oceans are like ponds whose waters consist of sugarcane juice, milk, and so forth; whose lotus stalks are precious jewels; and whose lotuses are the submarine fire.
Furthermore, in the vast expanse above and in the sky, there exist the wealth and splendor of merit and demerit for men, gods, and kirātas, wherein buying and selling take place.
In this very world-city, by the mountain of volition, various chambers in the form of bodies were constructed for his own sport.
Some, known by the name of gods (gīrvāṇa), were appointed only above; some, such as humans, nāgas, and others, were appointed only below.
Moving by the flow of wind-machines, they were composed of flesh and clay, with white bones made of wood; they were variegated, smooth with a coating of skin, and stainless.
Some perish after a long time, while others are subject to swift destruction; some possess the splendor of a covering fashioned from the lush growth of hair and grass.
Possessing nine openings, foremost among which are the ears, eyes, and nose, they [the breaths] are hot and cold, driven by the life-force wind that flows without ceasing.
Equipped with a multitude of windows such as the ears, nose, mouth, and palate; possessing the side-streets of the arms and other limbs; and having the five sense-faculties as its small lamps.
O Great-minded One, within those [realms] created by illusion, the great yakṣas of egoism are fashioned through conceptualization; they are utterly terrified of the supreme light.
Within the chambers of the body, he constantly plays excessively with the great yakṣas of egoism, which always arise from what is unreal.
Just as a cat is in a granary, or a snake in a bellows, or as a pearl is within bamboo, so is the ego-sense within the body.
In the houses of bodies, the waves of volition rise for a moment and subside for a moment like lamps, just as waves do in the oceans.
He then pervades that city with a new creation yet to be; for he beholds the conceived object in an instant.
By the mere absence of conceptualization, it perishes quickly as if by itself; yet its very existence serves for one’s supreme welfare through that very state of non-existence.
It arises by itself as a mere mental construction, like a ghost imagined by a child; it leads only to endless personal suffering and never to happiness.
This pervasive suffering of the world expands through the existence of the self; it is destroyed by its non-existence, just as dense darkness is dispelled by light.
He weeps because of his own actions which bring him suffering, like the monkey who pulled out the wedge while his testicles were pinned between two pieces of wood.
He stands with his neck upraised, tasting a mere fragment of the bliss he had imagined, like a camel that has suddenly fallen upon a drop of honey.
For a moment it attains detachment, for a moment it attains delight by itself, and for a moment it undergoes transformation through mere conceptualization, like a child.
Having diligently uprooted this [mind] from all objective entities, O son, act in such a way that the intellect enters the inner state.
That mother has three bodies—inferior, superior, and intermediate—which are designated as *tamas*, *sattva*, and *rajas*, and which serve as the cause for the persistence of the world.
For volition, being of the nature of darkness, through constant worldly activity, falls into extreme wretchedness and descends to the state of worms and insects.
For volition, whose nature is pure being and which is devoted to the knowledge of reality, presides over its own sovereignty, which is not far from the state of absolute liberation.
For volition, which is of the nature of passion, exists within worldly activity; it persists in saṃsāra, enamored with children and wife.
But having abandoned these three kinds of form, O Mahāmati, conceptual construction reaches the supreme state upon the exhaustion of the self.
Having abandoned all views and restrained the mind with the mind, bring about the destruction of all conceptualization regarding internal and external objects.
Even if you perform severe austerities for thousands of years, or even if you completely grind yourself to dust upon a stone;
Whether you enter the fire or even the submarine fire, or whether you fall into a chasm or upon the edge of a sword.
Whether Hara be your instructor, or Hari, or even the lotus-born Brahmā, or the ascetic Lord of the World who is overcome with supreme compassion.
Whether you are situated in the netherworld, on the earth, or even in heaven, there is no other means for that [liberation] than the cessation of mental constructs.
Exert yourself to the utmost through human effort toward the cessation of mental constructs, which is unassailable, changeless, supremely purifying, and blissful.
"O sinless one, it is said that all states of being are strung upon the thread of volition; when that thread is severed, I know not where those fragile things go."

The non-existent, the existent, and both the existent and non-existent—all these arise from volition alone and not from anything else. Since volition itself is thus both existent and non-existent, what can be called "reality" in this world?
Whatever is conceptualized in whatever manner, that very thing becomes so in an instant; therefore, O knower of reality, never form any conceptualization whatsoever.

Be free from conceptual construction and devoted to the worldly activities as they arise; for when conceptual construction is extinguished, consciousness indeed turns toward that which is beyond the object of thought.
Having arisen in the form of a being through a womb consisting of truth, this world is not a source of suffering for him; it is meaningless and unlike his own nature.
Therefore, O sinless one, what is the use of your dying to such great suffering? The wise in this world resort only to that which leads to the absence of suffering, and nothing else.

Having attained the state of ultimate reality and having forcefully cast aside the web of conceptual constructions, realize that peerless state with your mental activities stilled, like those in deep sleep, for the sake of expansive bliss.
The son said: "O father, what is the nature of this *saṃkalpa*, and how does it arise, O Lord? How does it attain growth, and how is it destroyed?"

Dāśūra said: They know that the mind's orientation toward an object of thought—which belongs to the infinite reality of the Self, whose nature is the universal existence—is the sprout of volitional construction (saṃkalpa).
Having attained a slight degree of existence, that very [state] gradually reaches density, filling the sky of the mind like a cloud for the sake of solidifying its dullness.
The consciousness, while contemplating the object of thought as if it were distinct from itself, attains the state of volition, just as a seed attains the state of a sprout.
For by means of volition, volition itself is produced; it grows by itself quickly, leading only to suffering and not to happiness.
For the world is merely a mental construction, just as the ocean is merely water; apart from such construction, you have no other worldly suffering.
Indeed, this has arisen in vain through a mere coincidence, like a mirage or the appearance of two moons; though unreal, it continues to expand.
Just as one who has swallowed a citron fruit perceives the appearance of gold within it, so too does your own mental resolve, having come of its own accord, become true within your heart.
You were born from the unreal alone, and you exist in the unreal as well; yet when this wisdom is known, the unreal indeed dissolves away.
"This is that very 'I,' these phenomena are mine, consisting of pleasure and pain"—thinking thus, "all this is indeed in vain," you burn within with various anxieties.
Though unborn, you appear as if born; from where does this play of birth arise? You are deluded in vain by your own power of volition.
Do not form a conceptual construction; do not dwell upon any state of being. By this much alone, through such a state of mind, one becomes fit for ultimate well-being.
By the effort to destroy conceptual construction, one does not pursue fears; conceptual construction itself is exhausted by the mere absence of mental cultivation.
In the crushing of a *sumana* blossom, there might be some slight interference; it can be easily accomplished by mere intent, but not so in the destruction of conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa*).
The effort of moving the hand when picking flowers is useful for the son; yet even that effort ceases to be beneficial once his conceptual constructions have come to an end.
By one who must destroy conceptual construction through the reversal of mental states, even that is effortlessly destroyed in half a blink of an eye.
O dear one, when one has attained stability within one's own self, which is perfected as mere being, what impossible thing could possibly be accomplished by you? What indeed could it be like?
O sage, having severed thought with thought and your own mind with the mind, remain established in your own self; what is difficult in this?
For when conceptual construction is stilled, O Mahāmati, this entire suffering of saṃsāra becomes stilled, even from its very root.
For volition, mind, the living soul, consciousness, and the intellect with its latent impressions—O best of those who know the truth, these differ only in name, not in their actual meaning.
Apart from mental construction, nothing whatsoever exists anywhere here; cut that very [construction] out from your heart—why do you grieve for this?
Just as this sky is empty, so indeed is the world empty; for both of these are spread out, having arisen from conceptual constructions consisting of what is non-existent.
All of this is unestablished, yet it has been established by that which is itself unestablished; since the world arises from mental construction, where could any objective reality possibly abide?

But if there is no firm conviction in reality, upon what would latent impressions (vāsanā) be based? Through the exhaustion of cultivation (bhāvanā), perfection is attained; therefore, nothing remains to be acquired. Consequently, one should effortlessly abandon all this as unreal through meditation.
Through that cultivation of the body's insubstantiality, one is not stained by pleasures and pains; and having determined that it is no real entity, attachment and longing do not arise.
When attachment is exhausted, joy and resentment, as well as existence and non-existence, do not arise; therefore, all this is unreal, consisting of the delusions of pleasure, pain, and so forth.
The mind, the living soul, vibrates intensely as the mental city of the world, revolving through the future, the present, and the past.
Enveloped by latent impressions (vāsanā), the mind—possessing a throbbing power and remaining in this world—creates this worldly order through its own disposition; it is turbid and restless.
The living being, like a monkey in the forest of the heart, performs playful antics resembling its own nature; having assumed a long form, it in an instant becomes short.
The waves of the water of conceptualization cannot be grasped; when seen even slightly, they swell and diminish along with their attendants.
Even by a mere blade of grass, intentions blaze up like the residue of a fire; though their forms are unmanifest in the world, they are ignited and perish in an instant.
O son, these volitions—which cause delusion, consist of dull matter, and are like fires of lightning—must be treated immediately with that very medicine which is their own nature.

There is no doubt in this matter: that which is non-existent never becomes existent anywhere. If a mental construction (saṃkalpa) were established as real, it would become incurable by its very nature.
However, if this [impurity] were truly non-existent, it would then be easily remedied; for if the impurity of saṃsāra were innate, like the blackness of charcoal, it could not be removed.
O virtuous one, what evil-minded person would proceed to wash this away? For it remains within the very grains of rice, like the husk.
O son, even that which is attained effortlessly and is natural may, through excessive exertion and human effort, be utterly destroyed once again.
To the knower, the pervasive impurity of saṃsāra is easily eradicated, just as the husk of rice or the blackness of copper [is removed].
Just as a man's impurity is destroyed by action, O son, so too is [this] destroyed; there is no doubt. Therefore, be one who exerts effort.
Since this saṃsāra has not been conquered in vain by these false conceptualizations, it will quickly dissolve with little effort; for how can a non-existent thing endure for long?
When examined through reasoning, this cycle of existence has no reality of its own; it is like the appearance of two moons to one with cataracts, or like the light of a lamp to a blind man.
He does not belong to you, nor do you belong to him; O son, abandon this delusion! Do not cultivate such a notion regarding what is seen as real when it is actually unreal.

Let there be no vain delusion within you that "these playful manifestations are the brilliant splendor of my teacher"; for you too possess these extensive manifestations, and this entire world shines as the essence of that very reality.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O descendant of Raghu, moon in the sky of the Raghu clan, having thus heard that conversation between the two there at night, I [spoke].
He fell with a thud at the top of the kadamba tree, which was thick with leaves, flowers, and fruit; silent and having shed his rain, he resembled a cloud resting upon a mountain peak.
There I beheld Dāśūra, a hero in the restraint of his senses, endowed with supreme austerity and like a sacrificial fire in its brilliance.
With his splendors issuing forth from his body, he was heating that region and making the earth golden, like the sun heating the world.
Then, seeing that I had arrived, the fisherman honored me with the ritual offering of water (argha) and worshiped me by providing a seat and honoring me with leaves.
Then, together with that radiant Dāśūra, he related former stories that awakened his sons and were capable of enabling them to cross over saṃsāra.
I saw that tree, its hollows filled with buds, surrounded by herds of deer who were all moving with speed at the command of Dāśūra.
Like a forest being enjoyed, adorned with circles of creepers, it seemed to bloom with a smile, its petals quivering with breath.
With chowries as beautiful as the moon, whirling at the tips of the creepers, it was covered as if by autumnal skies filled with masses of white cloud fragments.
It was adorned with a necklace of pearls in the form of a succession of frost-drops, and every limb of it was filled with an abundance of clear blossoms.
It was anointed with saffron and sandalwood paste, unblemished, and adorned with a vast covering of pure, expansive, and deep red garments.
It was compared to a city-dweller, burdened by an excessive weight of flowers in his attire for a wedding, who has become attached to a woman who is actually a creeper.
Adorned with creeper-arbors in the shape of huts built by sages, and graced with clusters of blossoms as if they were banners during a great city festival;
Dusty with the pollen of flowers shaken off by deer scratching themselves, it stood like a bull-bull with the surrounding forest cleared away.
With its peacocks, pale-red with the pollen exhaled from their plumage, the mountain seemed as if it had cast out the twilight clouds as seedlings for its own nursery beds.
With a hand as red as coral, beautified by a smile of flowers, reeling with intoxication, and possessing the glow of horripilation at its edge;
With its dense mass of flowers swaying in the forest breezes, it appeared as if it were a woman whose eyes were sleepy buds and who bore clusters of blossoms like breasts.
Clad in garments as reddish as saffron from the mass of pollen of flower-clusters, he leaned against the window that served as his dwelling within the canopy of creeping vines.
With playful grace, it performed a dance upon swings of blue-flowered creepers, having constructed its abode on all sides from the top of its head down to the soles of its feet.
Accompanied by a multitude of forest goddesses, who were rich in the warbling of cuckoos, radiant with eyes like bees amidst a cluster of doubtful blossoms.
Their fatigue from lovemaking was allayed by the morning dew; languid with passion, they were thickly entwined with one another, their bodies smeared with the pollen of flowers.
It was surrounded on all sides by pairs of clear, intoxicated bees dwelling within the interior of the flowers, humming something appropriate to their affection.
With a desire to hear the humming from the cities on the outskirts of the forest, he listened for a moment with ears pricked up by the beautiful warbling and tinkling sounds from all directions.
For a moment, they gazed at the ocean-girdled earth, which was like a silken garment for the moon, with their heads resting so charmingly upon the tips of the lotus petals.
The interior of the forest floor was filled with auspicious young deer resting within leaf-cups, appearing like the personified principles of policy embodied by the sons of the forest regions.
In the nests, birds were sleeping soundly and trustfully; on the edges of the trees, circles of tree-skins (sloughs) lay like fruits fallen during ripening.
It was filled with bees rendered silent by doubt, with clusters of rosaries used for worship, and its borders were darkened by nests adorned with young shoots.
The entire forest was made fragrant, the sky was turned into clouds of flowers, and the ground below was variegated with *kadamba* pollen and strewn with a profusion of fruits.
What is the use of saying more here? There is not even a single leaf on that tree where it neither grows nor is it joined.
In every leaf the deer slept, at every step they rested, and in every thicket the birds nestled, within that king of trees.
As I gazed upon him, distinguished by such qualities, that dark night became like a great festival for me.
Then, by means of delightful stories that were enchanting through the light of higher knowledge, I led his son once again to supreme awakening.
There, the night passed for us as we conversed with one another in various stories, like a mere moment for a couple in love.
As the morning dawned, the cluster of stars, resembling the limbs of celestial nymphs and dense with a wealth of blossoms, gradually faded away.
Having sent Dāśūra away with his son as they reached the region of the sky above the Kadamba tree, I then went to the celestial river.
Having reached that desired place and ascended to the vault of the sky, he entered the space in the midst of the sages and remained there as if established in his own self.
O descendant of Raghu, this story of Dāśūra has been told to you; it is like a reflection of the world, appearing real in form yet composed of unreality.
O Raghava, I have told you this story of Dāśūra for the sake of your awakening in the discernment of the true nature of the world.
Therefore, having abandoned both unreal and even real attachment, remain ever-noble and self-possessed through the vision of the Dāśūra Siddhānta.

Therefore, having shaken off the impurity of conceptual construction from yourself, behold the stainless reality of the Self; you will soon attain that state by which you shall become worthy of worship throughout the worlds.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having determined that "this does not exist," abandon attachment toward everything; for what reliance can there be here for those who investigate upon that which does not exist?
If this which is being perceived exists as something that has attained reality, then remain established in your own self; why indeed do you assume a sense of "selfhood" in this?
Even if you possess the certainty that "this exists" or "this does not exist," how can attachment to cultivation be appropriate toward that which is both moving and unmoving?
This world does not exist, O Rāma; it is not yours, O high-minded one. It is merely the pure [consciousness] itself that has thus expanded and assumed such a limited form.
This is not created by an agent, nor does it follow a sequence produced by an agent; yet, having reached the state of being both agent and non-agent, this manifests of its own accord.
Whether this web of the world be without a creator or with a creator, do not let your mind become clouded by such dualistic conceptualization.

Deprived of all sense faculties, that self is like an insentient object, as if it were an agent; yet I consider it then to be a non-agent, and the world to arise by mere chance, like the "crow and the palm fruit" coincidence.
Whatever occurs by chance, like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, that is merely something that has arisen; only a fool, and no one else, fixates upon the underlying reality within it.
O Rāma, this world is never peaceful, nor is it subject to destruction; for it is perceived incessantly and because it arises again and again.
This world, O Rāma, never exists, nor is it subject to decay; for by inference, it is because it is constantly perishing and because it is non-existent.
When the agent here has transcended the state of all the senses and is free from fever, he never experiences weariness while acting at all times.
Thus, this mature destiny, consisting of the states of existence and non-existence, is seen to be just such—stable, long-lasting, and yet arisen from falsehood.
Why does he pursue that which is a mere hundred autumns—a tiny fraction of infinite time—when it possesses such great wonders?
If the entities of the worlds were permanent, then attachment to reality would not be fitting; for how indeed could there be a mutual conjunction between the insentient and the sentient?
If the phenomena of the world are unstable, then even that reliance [upon them] is not fitting; for this [reliance], which is as unstable as water-foam, will bring you suffering at its end.
O mighty-armed one, the attachment to the world as being the self does not shine, whether the self be considered stable or unstable, any more than a mountain of foam can appear solid.
Although it is the creator of all, the Self does nothing at all; it remains thus indifferent, like a lamp with respect to its light.
Doing nothing, he does not act, just as the sun performs its daily work; moving, he does not move, remaining established in his own state like the sun stationed in its own sphere.
From some unknown source, this world appears as if it has come into being, spread out like the whirlpools of a flood on the banks of the Aruṇā.
If this has been ascertained by you, O Rāma, with skill, and investigated with a mind purified by valid means of knowledge;
Nevertheless, O virtuous one, you ought not to cultivate a conceptualization regarding an object; for what kind of cultivation can there be in the case of a firebrand-circle, a dream, or an illusion?
A creature who has arrived by chance is not a fit vessel for affection; do not rely on this web of the world, which arises from delusion—it is no such vessel.
Just as you do not conceive of a real existence in heat within the moon, in cold within the sun, or likewise in the water of a mirage, so too should you not conceive of existence in this world.
Just as you perceive the delusions of a person created by imagination, a person in a dream, or two moons, so too should you view this entire collection of existing things.
Having abandoned all intermediate states consisting of the cultivation of the splendor of existence, O sinless one, abide as you truly are in this world, sporting at your ease.
Having drunk the state of non-agency, and having drunk even desire, [one realizes] the Self which abides within all beings yet transcends all, and which acts even while drinking.
This necessity unfolds merely through proximity; just as light shines forth without any desire simply through the presence of a lamp.
Just as *kuṭaja* trees [blossom] by the mere proximity of clouds, so too do the three worlds [arise] by the mere proximity of the Self.
Just as the sun remains in the sky devoid of all desire, so too does activity arise when the Lord exists.
Just as light proceeds from a wishless jewel when it is present, so too does this multitude of worlds proceed by the mere existence of the Lord.
Therefore, both agency and non-agency reside within its own self; due to being devoid of desire, it is a non-agent, yet it is an agent by virtue of its mere presence.

Because he transcends all the senses and so forth, the true Self is neither the agent nor the enjoyer; however, because it is [conceived as] contained within the senses, that very Self is indeed regarded as the agent and the enjoyer.
O sinless one, two states indeed exist within the self: agency and non-agency. Relying upon whichever of these you perceive as better, remain steadfast.
Through this firm contemplation that "I am all-pervading and a non-doer," one is not tainted even while performing actions that have fallen into the stream of worldly flow.
A living being falls into a state of despondency when the mind ceases its activity, having reached the conviction: "I do not perform even the slightest action here."
Who, desiring the flood of enjoyments there, would either act or renounce? Therefore, one should kindle the meditation: "I am eternally a non-doer."
That which is called supreme nectar remains as equanimity alone; then, through that state of being the great agent, one thinks, "I do everything."
If you desire stability, O Rāma, they consider that too to be supreme; alas, that I do not bring this entire worldly delusion to an end!

In that case, how could there be a sequence of passion and hatred, since it is utterly impossible for one [person] to belong to another? For a body has been burned by one [person], yet cherished by another.

Since this is merely our own undertaking, what room is there here for either dejection or exaltation, given that it is the expansion of my friend’s bliss and the arising of the destruction of the world-web?
Thinking "I am the doer," what room is there within for the sequence of sorrow and joy? For in the play of sorrow and joy, one acts through this sense of being the agent of one's own self.
When [the mind] has itself come to dissolution, equanimity alone remains; that equanimity toward all beings is the true, supreme state.
The mind established in that state does not undergo birth even slightly; or rather, O Raghava, it possesses both universal agency and non-agency.
Having abandoned everything and drunk in with the mind, remain firm as to who you truly are: "I am He; I am He; this is not I; I do not do this or that."
Thus, a vision consisting of the contemplation of [conditioned] entities does not lead to satisfaction; it is the path to the Kālasūtra hell and the snare of the Mahāvīci hell.
That state of "I am the body," which is like a row of sword-leaf forests, must be abandoned with every effort, even if total destruction is imminent.
That [vision] is not to be touched by one who seeks excellence, like a *puṣkasī* woman covered in horse-flesh; it has been utterly cast away by that film-like streak in the sight.
O Rāma, the supreme vision arises like moonlight when the clouds have vanished; by its rising, the ocean of worldly existence is crossed.

Having clearly realized within yourself, "I am not the doer, nor am I that [agent]," or having reached the certainty that "I am indeed the doer and I am all that," or having resolved, "I am something, or rather, I am nothing at all"—O most excellent one, remain established in your own true state, where the virtuous knowers of the Way stand as the supreme.

Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahman, what you have spoken is true and beautiful in its expression: the Self is indeed a non-doer yet the doer, and though a non-enjoyer, it is the creator of beings and the enjoyer."
The Lord of all and omnipresent, the stainless state of pure consciousness alone—the God who dwells within all beings is present on earth as their very body.
O All-pervading Lord, through your words, this Brahman has now reached my heart, just as a mountain is relieved of its distress by torrents of rain from the ocean.
Due to indifference and lack of desire, he neither enjoys nor acts; yet, because he brings about the welfare of the entire world, the Lord both enjoys and acts.
But, O Blessed One, this vast doubt remains in my heart; O Brahmin, sever it with your words, as the moon dispels darkness with its rays.
"This is existent, this is non-existent; this is he, I am this, but not that; this is one, this is a second"—such is the nature of the world, consisting of conceptual constructions.
Just as mist does not exist within the sun, how could this [world] reside within the pure Self from the very beginning?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, at the very time of the final conclusion, I shall give you a firm answer to this inquiry, by which you will know it according to reality.
O Rāghava, until you have attained the definitive conclusion regarding the means to liberation, you will not be sufficiently qualified to hear these questions and answers.
O Rāma, just as a youth is the proper recipient for the songs of beloved women, so too is the doer of meritorious deeds the proper recipient for questions and sublime discourses.
Just as a discourse full of passion is in vain among fools, so too is a discourse arising from noble inspiration useless for those of meager understanding.
At a particular time, a certain quality shines forth in a man; the fruit of a tree appears only in autumn, not in the month of Mādhava.
The words of instruction take hold in an elder, as dye does on a clean cloth; and the discourse on sublime wisdom takes hold in one who has realized the self.
The answer to this question was previously stated by me in brief; because it was not given in detail, it was not clearly understood by you.
If you yourself perceive that self by means of the self, then you will rightly know this answer to the question; of this there is no doubt.
But when you have attained awakening at the time of the final realization, O virtuous one, the sequence of questions and answers must be explained by me in full detail.
The self alone knows the self; indeed, the self is made by the self through the self alone. Being perfectly serene, the self attains the self.
Thus, O Rāma, has been explained this investigation into the agent and the non-agent; yet, due to ignorance of it, one remains with unabated latent impressions.

For one is bound by being bound to latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and liberation is the destruction of those impressions. Having abandoned the latent impressions, abandon even the desire for liberation.
Having first abandoned the tamasic tendencies perfumed by sense objects, take up the stainless tendency known as the cultivation of friendliness and the other virtues.
Having abandoned even that internally, though still interacting with those [objects], remain with all internal attachment stilled and with consciousness alone as your latent impression.
Then, having abandoned even that [mind] along with the intellect, remain in the remainder with steady concentration; abandon that by which you abandon.

Consisting of pure consciousness, [it perceives] the time of mental construction, light and darkness, as well as the latent impression and the one who possesses it, all preceded by the vibration of the vital breath.
O one of noble intellect, may you—who have completely abandoned even the roots [of worldly existence] and whose mind is as serene and tranquil as the clear sky—be honored by all.
The one of great intelligence who, having completely renounced everything from the heart, remains free from agitation—he is liberated, he is the Supreme Lord.

Whether he practices meditative concentration or performs actions—or whether he does not—such a person of supreme disposition, having abandoned all mental objects through the heart, is indeed liberated.
For one whose mind is free from latent impressions, there is no purpose served by inaction, nor any purpose served by ritual acts, nor by meditative concentration or the chanting of prayers.
The scriptures have been thoroughly investigated and long debated among one another; yet there is no higher state than the silence born from the complete relinquishing of latent impressions.
Having wandered repeatedly through the ten directions, everything that is to be seen has been seen; yet only a few people perceive things as they truly are.
Whatever is perceived, none of it exists; other than what is desired and undesired, people do not strive for anything therein.
Whatever undertakings there may be, whatever sequences of actions people perform—all of these are for the sake of the body alone; they are not at all for the sake of the Self.
In the netherworld, in the world of Brahmā, in heaven, and on the surface of the earth, as well as in the sky, only a few are seen who have witnessed such sights.
He for whom the certainties—"this is to be abandoned" and "this is to be accepted"—have dissolved as they arise from the unreal, that wise one is exceedingly rare to find.
Let him rule the world, or let him enter the ocean or its waters; no living being attains rest except through the attainment of the Self.
Those of great intelligence who are wise and heroic against the enemies of the senses should be venerated by those of lofty intellect for the sake of destroying the fever of rebirth.
Everywhere there are the five elements; nothing else exists as a sixth. Whether in the netherworld, on the earth, or in heaven, where could one of steadfast intellect find delight?
For the wise one who acts with reason, saṃsāra is like the footprint of a cow; but for one who has utterly abandoned reason, it is like a vast, intoxicated ocean.
For one whose consciousness has expanded, the entire universe is equal to a *kadamba* flower bud; even when this whole world is attained, what does he give away, and what does he enjoy?
For this reason, O Rāma, I consider those great acts of war undertaken by the ignorant to be censurable, as they bring about the destruction of tens of thousands of lives in combat.
Even within that extremely fragile interior, which lasts for only a single eon, there occurs the destruction of even those who possess the highest and greatest intellects.
Since not even the slightest [notion] of creation and so forth has arisen for the wise Self, what could possibly cause that Self to become powerful when these three worlds are encountered?
This earth is covered here by hundreds of mountains and likewise there by masses of water; how small is its body that it might fill the vast [universe]?
There is nothing in this world—including the netherworld and the abode of the gods—that could be considered more worthy of being accomplished for a self-possessed and wise person.
For the wise one who has attained oneness, who is as pervasive as space, who is self-abiding, possessed of the Self, established in the Self with a mind free from mental constructs—
The vast bank of the three worlds is grey with the misty nets of bodies, its hollows empty, and it possesses the beauty of a tranquil saṃsāra.
All the great mountain ranges are but foam upon the vast and stainless ocean of Brahman; they possess the splendor of the mirage-water within the great radiance of the sun of consciousness.
The successions of creations are the waves of the great ocean of the reality of the Self; the perspectives of the scriptures are the rains from the ocean of the unsurpassed state.
The lights of the moon, fire, and sun are like a jar, wood, and so forth; they are objects to be illuminated by the radiance of the nature of consciousness, which is likewise like specks of impurity.
Men, gods, and asuras dwell as their own selves, roaming the forest of saṃsāra like deer that feed upon the mouthfuls of grass that are sensual enjoyments.
The bodies of the world are like houses with bones for door-bolts, skulls for roofs, and sinews for chains; they are filled with the blood and flesh of living beings worn down by old age.
Deluded forest deer, stationed for movement within the city, were fashioned as leather puppets for the amusement of those with childish intellects.
A person of great intelligence whose mind is thus noble does not waver even slightly before floods of enjoyments, just as a mountain does not move before gentle breezes.
O Rāma, it is said that in that most supreme state dwells the Knower, in which even the region of the moon and sun does not exist, as if situated in the netherworld.
By whose light the world-protectors become clearly visible and well-informed, they protect their bodies as if watching over them, yet remain deluded in the ocean of night.
None of these worldly phenomena can delight one who knows reality, even when they are encountered repeatedly; they are like clouds to the vast sky of his heart.
None of these worldly phenomena can please one who knows reality, just as dancing monkeys cannot please Hara, who desires the dance of Gaurī.
None of these worldly phenomena can delight one who knows reality, just as a jewel placed inside a jar cannot reflect the beauty of its former image.

Beholding the world as being like a reflection cast upon the water—unsubstantial, comparable to a bubble on a vajra-stone, and as fleeting as a wave—the one who knows reality finds no delight in the pleasures sought by the fickle, just as a royal swan has no interest in bits of moss and weeds.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, listen to the purifying verses concerning this very subject which were sung by Kaca, the son of Bṛhaspati, to his ancestors.
