Once, while staying in a certain thicket on Mount Meru, the son of the preceptor of the gods attained rest within his own self through the power of practice.
His mind, filled with the nectar of right knowledge, found no delight in this contemptible, fragile self, which consists of the five elements and is merely an object of perception.
Despondent as it were because he saw no state other than that of the eternal Self, he spoke these words alone with a faltering voice:
What shall I do? Where shall I go? What shall I grasp? What shall I abandon? The entire universe is filled by the Self, just as it is by the waters of the great dissolution.
Suffering, the self, and happiness—through the vastness of space and hope—I have realized that everything consists of the self; thus, by means of the self, I am one whose afflictions are destroyed.
Within the body, both externally and internally, below and above, and in all directions—the self is here and the self is there; nowhere does anything exist that is not composed of the self.
For the Self indeed abides everywhere, and everything exists as consisting of the Self; all this is the Self alone, and thus I exist within the Self itself.
Whatever is indeed called "name," all that is entirely myself, the inner one; filling the boundless sky, I abide everywhere as pure existence.
"I abide full, my nature one of joy, like a single ocean of bliss"—thus he meditated there in that bower of the Golden Mountain.

Uttering the syllable *oṃ* in succession like the sound of a bell—one that is merely a fraction of the *oṃ*-sound, trailing off as soft as a child’s hair—he should meditate upon it within the supreme heart, neither abiding inside nor outside.

Purified by being free from the stain of the divisions of time, with the fluctuations of the vital breath dissolved within his heart, resembling the clarity of an autumn sky when the clouds have vanished, that Kaca remained there, O Rāma, singing.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "In this world, there is nothing at all apart from food, drink, and the company of women; what great man, then, would desire anything else that merely promises 'may it be auspicious'?"
Those who are like animals and beasts, deluded and wicked, are not satisfied with enjoyments that are the very essence of the wretched—enjoyments that are fragile in their beginning, middle, and end.
Those in this world who place their trust [in her] are no better than human donkeys; for this body of a woman is merely "hair here" and "blood there."
By this [offering], dogs may find satisfaction, but not human beings; for bodies—whether made of earth, stone, wood, or trees—are composed of flesh.

The earth is beneath and the sky is behind; what is new about these? Yet they lead to pleasure. Sensations following from contact with objects are fragile, crumbling at the first touch of discernment.
All worldly perceptions remain entirely untouched by delusion; even at the ultimate limit of everything, they abide within the hope for happiness.
Thus, impurity and suffering are like soot from a flame; the activities of the six senses, with the mind as the sixth, are impermanent, arising and passing away.
Creeper-like women, crushed by the lordly elephants of passion, do not maintain their composure; they hold with reverence this son of red flesh, thinking, "This is my beloved."
Through the process of delusion, one clings to the heap of bones under the name of "one's own body. O Rāma, all this is indeed true, yet it is for the satisfaction of the ignorant man alone.
O Rāma, the instability and unreality of the world bring no satisfaction to the wise man; it is like poison that causes a toxic swoon even before it has been consumed.

Abandoning that attachment to enjoyments, resort to the state of oneness with your own Self. When the mind attains stability through the realization that it is not composed of the non-Self, then this world-web, which is insubstantial, is seen as unborn.
By the power of latent impressions, the body is imagined by the mind of Brahmā, just as the self appears golden due to its brilliance reflecting off a wall.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmā of great intelligence, having attained the state of Vairiñca, how does the mind gradually bring this world to a state of solid density?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having arisen from the bed of the womb, the first child born from the lotus uttered the word "Brahman"; therefore, he is called Brahmā.
Then, the Fortune of Saṃkalpa established her abode in him, who was of the nature of a web of volitions and whose form was fashioned by the mind.
Then he first willed forth a mass of great radiance, like a circle of creepers at the end of autumn that encircles the quarters of the sky.
With karma woven upon its wings, it is composed of letters of supreme quality; its edges are tawny with masses [of light], and its sky-like expanse resembles golden wisdom.
His own palace was dense with a network of golden creepers like lattices, and it was adorned with earrings in the form of shimmering, spreading gardens.
Then, within that radiant light, he fashioned that body—possessing the very form of the Self—to be luminous as well.
From that splendor, the sun rises there, situated in the midst of a circle of rays, with his earrings of blazing gold.
Bearing a mass of flaming matted hair with fire spreading at its edges, his limbs were vast with flames, filling the entire circle of the sky.
Then the highly intelligent Brahmā, having protected those other portions of his splendor, cast them aside like the ocean casts its waves.
They too, having attained their perfections through mere volition and possessing equal powers, beheld the object as it was intended right before them in an instant.
Forming various intentions, they created many diverse hosts of beings—some among those beings, others among them, and yet others of various kinds.
Having recollected the Vedas and thereafter the many qualities of the sacrificial rites, this Brahmā established the boundaries for the world.
Assuming a Brahmanic form, that great body called "mind" thus extends this vision, which is crowded with the succession of beings.

It was rich with oceans, mountains, and trees, having established a world-transcending order; its interior was a dense thicket of matted locks consisting of Mount Meru, the surface of the earth, and the forested corners of the quarters.
It is characterized by pleasure, pain, old age, birth, and death; it is agitated by passion and hatred; and its very nature consists of the three qualities (guṇas).
Whatever was fashioned of old by the hands of Manu, which arose from Viriñca, all that is seen even today through Māyā exactly as it was so ordained.
Thus, whether among all beings or only some of them, one imagines the cycle of existence; yet one perceives that which is supreme, abiding as consciousness.
Delusion itself, consisting of this [world], has falsely attained stability in the world; it was fashioned by its own mere conceptualization through the mind in an instant.
By the power of volition, all the activities of the world are produced; by the power of volition, even the gods emerge, though they abide within the constraints of destiny.
This Lord Brahmā, born from the lineage of the creation of the world which was provoked by the Lords of Creatures, sits upon his lotus throne and reflects deeply.
By the mere vibration of the mind, the wondrous consciousness arises; it is a vast creation, full of enjoyment, and subject to the transformations of worldly activity.

It contains Rudra, Upendra, Mahendra, and the other gods; it is crowded with mountains and oceans; and its hollows are the narrow passages of the netherworld, the earth, the quarters, and the heavenly realms.
This entire web of mental constructs was spread out by me on all sides; now I have desisted from this process of giving rise to conceptual fluctuations.
Having thus resolved, he desists from the perilous thicket of conceptual constructions and, by means of the self, remembers the self as the beginningless, supreme Brahman.
Having attained that state which shines forth when the mind has dissolved, the tranquil-souled one dwells in bliss, like a weary man resting upon a couch.
Free from possessiveness and free from egoism, having attained supreme peace, he remains within himself by means of the self, like an undisturbed ocean.
Sometimes the Lord, the Master himself, desists from meditation, just as the ocean ceases its flow of water due to its inherent tranquility, as if released from a bond.
He contemplates cyclic existence, which is fraught with pleasure and pain, bound by hundreds of snares of hope, and afflicted by passion, hatred, and fear.
Then, his mind overcome with compassion for the sake of the manifestation of reality, he composes here various treatises of great significance.
The Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, which contain the essence of inner knowledge, as well as the Purāṇas and other texts, lead all embodied beings to liberation.
Again, having taken hold of that state, emerged from supreme calamity, he remains established in himself with a tranquil soul, like the ocean without Mount Mandara.
Having observed the activities of the world and having established the boundaries of conduct, Brahmā, seated upon his lotus throne, abides once again within his own self.
Sometimes, being free from all volitional constructions, he remained as if following the worldly course, acting by chance for the sake of bestowing grace.
Therein is neither rectitude nor renunciation, neither the body nor its grasping; there is no diversity, no consciousness, and herein neither stability nor instability abides.
The undertaking of all existents is equal in all modes of activity; like the form of a full ocean, it remains with nothing remaining [to be done].
Sometimes, being entirely free from all conceptual constructions, he awakens by chance for the sake of bestowing grace upon the worlds.
O Mahāmati, this meritorious state of Brahmā which I have described is also that sattvic state which the hosts of gods and asuras have attained.
That which arises as the fruit of the mind of Brahman in the space where the creation of consciousness has ceased—that very first [state] attains the status of Brahmanhood.
But when the state of persistence has occurred during the creation, another conceptualization arises; that, having resorted to space and wind, enters into medicinal herbs and sprouts.
One attains the state of a god, another attains the state of a yakṣa; first she arises as this very [earth], and then she fully partakes in the state of Brahman.

Whatever sentient being a [disposition] accompanies, that very being quickly arises [with it]; and once born, by the power of association, that same being is bound or liberated in that very life through its own subsequent engagement.

O Rāmabhadra, such indeed is the nature of this creation, acquired through karma that is manifestly fraught with peril; it appears within the sphere of conceptualization, sustained by the intensity of the burden of various impetuous movements.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Brahman, O mighty-armed one, when this Blessed Grandfather had taken his fickle station and established the order of creation;
In this world, which is like a dilapidated water-wheel, the thirst for life functions according to its own mechanism, using as its rope the string of living beings who have become like buckets.
And while the beings, arisen from Brahman, were entering the cage of worldly existence—whirling within the eddies that revolve in the midst of the hair-like [spokes] of the sky of the Lord.
In other minds, like seeds struck by the wind and tossed about, some are incessantly departing while others enter from all sides in the same manner.
O Rāma, the multitudes of living beings are like waves in the ocean within Brahman; born from the state that is without beginning or end, they have entered the realm of conceptualization.
These multitudes of living beings enter the elemental ether, like the beauty of smoke entering a cloud; they attain oneness with Brahman through the winds of the ether.
Just as the gods are assailed by a fierce host of Daityas, so too is that day overcome by its own wind, which acts through the nature of its vital breath.
By means of that wind which carries the elements and living beings—that bearer of fragrance—the individual souls enter into bodies and attain vitality.
Then, O Rāma, there arise in the world beings that are unmanifest; another succession of living beings is born from the stage of smoke and so forth.
In the hollow of the sky, which is filled with those very elements and not empty of them, the Blessed Moon rises with its full, radiant orb.
The world was drenched by the shimmering, pale rays from the ocean of milk; then, those exceedingly beautiful moonbeams fell down.
The restless female bird makes her nest in the forest as if among the inner apartments of a servant; and even from those [seeds], they attain fullness by their own inherent nature alone.
The row of living beings, wounded by the rays of the moon, sets foot upon those fruits as if upon the mother’s breasts filled with milk.
Those circles of fruit will ripen by the rays [of the sun]; having received the vital essence within those very fruits, they remain there until they have attained enlightenment.

The glorious seed-syllable presides over the cage of the womb, which contains the living force of the network of dormant latent impressions (vāsanā), just as a seed with its leaves folded sleeps within a banyan tree.
Just as fire resides within wood and as pots reside within clay, so too do [all things] emerge from Maheśvara through the application of various successive stages.
He who does not boast when he has not seen the splendor of another's body—he alone may truly be said to be born with noble conduct.

If one possesses the factors conducive to liberation in that very birth, then that is the *sāttvika* [type]; however, having entered this womb, there is a succession of births through ritual acts (*kṛtyā*).
O Rāma, if one has taken birth for the sake of protection, being characterized by the qualities of tamas, rajas, and sattva, I shall now describe the subsequent births of such a person.
Primarily, he who has entered into saṃsāra as it comes to pass is one of sattvic nature; such a person, O sinless one, never arises as anyone at all.
O Rāma, men who are rajasic and sāttvika arise here in this world; having investigated them thoroughly, one should reflect upon them with an intelligent mind.
O Rāma, those men who have emerged preeminently from the Supreme Self are difficult to find; they are endowed with great virtues.

And as for those others who are various kinds of fools, mute, and born of the nature of darkness (tamas)—what indeed can be deliberated upon regarding them, O Rāma, who are equal to stationary objects?

A few among men and gods have not yet reached the contemplation of existence (*bhavabhāvanā*) within this natural cycle of birth; indeed, like me, they have attained the fitness for profound investigation, being characterized by both passion and purity (*rājasasāttvika*).
Since you are established in this way through the investigation of the great state, investigate that directly and truly today; here there is no duality.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Those who are born on earth with great qualities arising from the *rajas-sattva* nature are always joyful and luminous, like moons in the sky.
They do not succumb to exhaustion, like a portion of the sky with its impurities; nor do they wither through adversity, like a golden lotus at night.

They do not desire anything other than their own nature, nor do they stand for anything else, just like stationary trees; they delight in their own proper conduct, just as trees delight in their own purposes.
O Rāma, just as the moon-like beautiful woman reaches a state of being eternally filled with nectar when she possesses the qualities of *rajas* and *sattva*, so too does she attain liberation.
Even in adversity they do not abandon [their composure], remaining as cool as the moon; by their very nature, they shine with the beauty of virtues such as loving-kindness.
Like forest trees with creepers that will soon bear new clusters of blossoms, good people who are truly virtuous are always even-minded, equanimous, and gentle.
Those who possess a wondrous steadfastness like that of the ocean become equal to you; therefore, O mighty-armed one, their state is free from the taint of calamity.
One should always go there; one must not go into the ocean of calamity. In this world, one should wander about in such a manner, free from weariness.

And one's own spiritual advancements flourish like those characterized by the quality of goodness (sattva) rather than passion (rajas), provided one repeatedly investigates the true scripture through its inconceivable course.
One should quickly contemplate with one's own mind the various forms of impermanence that always exist throughout the three worlds, both at the beginning and at the end of all activities.
The wise person should quickly contemplate the objects of experience as being like illusions and nothing else, having abandoned improper views and the futile succession of ignorance.
This infinite knowledge of reality must indeed be properly contemplated: "Who am I? How has this grand display of saṃsāra arisen, O All-pervading Lord?"
Having investigated with effort in consultation with the wise and the virtuous, one should not plunge headlong into actions, nor should one dwell with that which is harmful.
One should always perceive the total cessation of everything that follows the cycle of existence; one should follow only what is virtuous, just as a peacock follows a rain cloud.
Having adorned oneself with self-inquiry regarding the ego, the body, and this raftless cycle of existence, one should behold only the truth.
Having completely abandoned the body, though it be unstable and possessed of great beauty, like a thread from which a string of pearls has been removed, one should behold pure consciousness alone.
In that state, which is eternally extended, all-pervading, and present in all things—within that auspicious reality, this entire universe is strung together like clusters of gems upon a thread.

That very same consciousness which exists in the sun within the sky—the ornament of the expanse of all worlds—is the very same consciousness that resides within the belly of an insect in a hole in the earth.
Just as there is no difference between jars and space in the ultimate sense, O sinless one, so too there is no difference among those abiding in bodies within consciousness.

Since the experience of all beings alike—whether they distinguish between bitter, pungent, and so forth—is indeed one, there can be no difference [in that experience] other than that which arises from the object itself.
In this world, while the reality that is pure Being alone remains eternally, your intellect perceives: "This has been born," and "This has perished."
And there exists no such thing that, having come into being, utterly perishes; this is merely a mental appearance, O Rāghava—neither existent nor non-existent.
With a mind suddenly arisen and unpacified, one remains [in this state]; here there is no end to delusion until liberation, for that which is not this [state] is a non-entity.
O Rāma, why indeed do you remain idle here while abandoning the snare of delusion? For whatever arises from attachment to associations is truly a cause of further delusion.

If the world does not exist, what joy can there be here; and if it does exist, my friend, why is it a cause of delusion? Therefore, amidst the conditions of birth and death, remain forever peaceful and as utterly equanimous as space.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: A wise and discerning person, from the very beginning, should—with great intelligence—examine the scripture by means of the scripture, through the instruction of a learned man, and in consultation with a virtuous person.
Having deliberated together with a virtuous, discerning, and great wise man, one attains the supreme state through the power of great yoga.
A person who has been refined by study of the scriptures, association with virtuous people, detachment, and practice shines like you, becoming a vessel for innate wisdom.
You, whose own conduct is noble, steadfast, and a mine of multitudes of virtues, abide free from suffering, having abandoned the outpouring of existence and purified the mind of its stains.
Surely you have become equal to the autumnal sky from which the clouds have been cast away; be free from worldly ideation and endowed with supreme consciousness.
The mind that remains free from the artifice of thought and free from conceptual construction, and which is devoid of all divisions, is undoubtedly liberated.
Now, on this earth, people will follow the conduct of your supreme majesty, which is free from passion and hatred.
People will indeed dwell in conduct appropriate for the external world; the wise, equipped with their small boats, will cross the ocean of existence.
That virtuous person who possesses a mind equal to yours and has an even vision is fit for the insights of knowledge described by me; he is one who possesses right vision.
As long as you have a body, remain with a mind free from passion and hatred; maintain conduct appropriate for the world outwardly, while inwardly abandoning all desires.
Attain supreme peace, just as other virtuous ones do; for those who are not free from deliberation here are like jackals in their nature.
By cultivating those inherent natures which belong to great-souled men born with a virtuous disposition, a person attains the status of one born into a noble lineage in a future life.
Whatever caste and qualities a person constantly cultivates in this world, even if born into another caste, he immediately comes to partake in those very qualities.
All previous states of being, having fallen under the sway of karma, pass away; yet even great mountain ranges are overcome by human effort.
With fortitude, one should uplift the intellect from the mire, just as one would rescue a bewildered cow; even if one has taken birth in a tamasic or rajasic class, or indeed any other.
By the power of their own discernment, the virtuous attain the state of sattvic birth; therefore, O Rāghava, that which is applied to the clear jewel of the mind—
Thus, being absorbed in that, one manifests accordingly; therefore, through human effort, one becomes endowed with highly precious qualities.
In this world, those of later auspicious births become seekers of liberation; there is nothing on earth, nor in heaven among the gods, nor anywhere else, that is so.

Though endowed with virtues, you do not attain through human effort that which you seek—neither by celibacy, nor by fortitude, nor by the force of vigor and dispassion—without indeed being joined by the appropriate means.

Having established the reality of the self through wisdom for the benefit of all beings by virtue of your great being, become free from sorrow; then, by your very example, these people will likewise be liberated and freed from grief.

O Rāmabhadra, in this final birth, endowed with the great majesty of discernment and delightful with all virtues diffused throughout you, establish yourself in action rooted in purity; let not this delusive anxiety regarding attachment to worldly existence trouble you.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Now, immediately following the section on "Abiding," hear this section on "Quiescence," which, when understood, brings about liberation.
Śrī Vālmīki said: While the autumn sky was filled with stars, and the assembly remained motionless as Vasiṣṭha spoke these such delightful and purifying words, [the sages were captivated].
In the midst of that assembly, while the king remained silent in his desire to hear, he was like a lotus pond where the lotuses are motionless in a windless place.
And among the wanton women, whose power of passion and delusion had been stilled, peace entered within them as if they were long-ordained renunciants.
As if from the ears of the swans resting upon his lotus-like hands, and as if from the trees where the crows had ceased their harsh cawing;
While those kings who were knowers of reality were examining the subtle portion of consciousness with the tips of their index fingers resting upon the ends of their noses.
When Rāma had blossomed forth like the lotus at dawn, the seat of darkness was abandoned, as if by the rising of the sun in the sky.
Daśaratha listened with rapture to the words of Vasiṣṭha’s daughter, just as a peahen listens to the rumbling of clouds that have released their rain.
Having withdrawn the mind, which is as restless as a monkey, from all enjoyments, one should, with effort and essence, remain fixed upon the mantra while listening, O Mantrini.

While Lakṣmaṇa—whose true self had been fully realized through the words of Vasiṣṭha, who was as pure as a digit of the moon, whose aim was ever-shining, and who was expert in the mastery of his training—was present;
When Śatrughna, the crusher of enemies, had attained fullness of heart and remained like the full moon of the Rākā night, having reached a state of sufficient bliss;
When Sumitrā’s mind, though accustomed to sorrow, attained a state of friendship, her heart blossomed like a lotus at that very moment.
While those other sages and kings were present there, their jewels of minds were thoroughly cleansed, and their hearts seemed to be overflowing with joy.
Then there arose the sound of midday conchs, equal to the roar of the ocean and as deep as the thundering of clouds at the end of an aeon, filling all the quarters of space.
By that great sound, the words of the sage were eclipsed, just as the calls of the cuckoo are drowned out by the roar of a rain-cloud.
Then the sage silenced his own speech in the assembly: "By what great quality is one whose essence has been conquered proclaimed?"
Having rested for just a moment and hearing the sound of midday, when the thick clamor had subsided, the sage spoke to Rāma.
O crusher of enemies, I have related this much of today's discourse to you; tomorrow morning, we shall speak further on what remains to be told.
This which has arrived by necessity must be performed by the twice-born: that which ought to be done when midday has arrived must not be neglected.
You too, O fortunate one, arise and perform all the rites of proper conduct, such as bathing, giving gifts, and worship, for which you are so skilled.
Having spoken thus, the sage rose up together with the lord Daśaratha, like the sun with the moon rising from the slope of the eastern mountain.
As the two of them rose, the entire assembly trembled to rise as well, like a lotus pond with eyes of blue lotuses stirred by a gentle breeze.
Adorned by a swarm of bees rising from her ear-ornaments, she rose up like the twilight mountain, its lotus-like peaks swaying with the rays of the sun.
With the circles of their armlets ground together by the mutual friction of their limbs, they indicated the hour of twilight with clouds reddened and filled with jewels.
The humming of bees wandering about her falling ear-ornaments filled the air, while the sky was turned into a rainbow by the intense radiance of her crown.
With the lovely hands of creepers as its beautiful chowrie-festoons, she was like a forest tract agitated by a herd of noble elephants.
With their respective garments reddened by the weight of glittering bracelets, they were like a garland from the Mandara forest whose flowers are shaken down by the wind.
With pure clouds formed from camphor-like snowflakes, it spread across the entire earth like a row of autumn lotus-stalks.

With the cavities of her sky-like garment reddened by the tips of the jewels on her swaying crest, she was like the twilight when the blue lotuses have not yet blossomed, bringing about the dissolution of all activity.

With its surface filled with the water-like rays of jewels and its lotus-faces in constant bloom, she was like a lotus pond encircled by swarms of bees, resonant with the sound of anklets as her cranes.
That assembly, crowded with hundreds of kings, rose up in continuous succession, appearing like a newly arisen creation agitated by a multitude of spirits.
Then, having bowed to the king, the monarchs departed from the royal palace like waves of the ocean made into rainbows by jewels.
Then Sumantra and the ministers, experts in discerning flavors, bowed down to Vasiṣṭha and the lord of the earth, and departed for their bath.
Vāmadeva and others, as well as Viśvāmitra and others, stood with Vasiṣṭha at their head, looking toward Avarjana with intent faces.
King Daśaratha, the subduer of enemies, having honored the assembly of sages there and being dismissed by them, then departed for the sake of his own purpose.
Those who dwell in the forest went to the forest; those who dwell in the sky went to the sky; and the city-dwellers likewise went to the city, all in order to return in the morning.
Requested out of affection by both the lord of the earth and Vasiṣṭha, the powerful Viśvāmitra spent the night in the residence of Vasiṣṭha.
Vasiṣṭha was being attended by the foremost of Brahmins, as well as by kings and sages, and by all the sons of Daśaratha, headed by Rāma.
The illustrious one, honored by all the worlds, went to his own hermitage, followed by a multitude of gods, like the lotus-born Brahmā proceeding to the world of Brahmā.
Then, from that place, he dismissed all the sons of Daśaratha—Rāma and the others—who were bowing at his feet, sending them back to their own homes.

Having dismissed those who move through the sky, those who move upon the earth, and those who move below—each within the scope of their praised virtues—the noble-minded one conducted that day’s ritual for the twice-born in his own home according to the proper sequence.

Śrī Vālmīki said: Having come together and returned home, those princes, who possessed the luster of the moon, performed the entire sequence of daily duties in their respective residences without exception.
Vasiṣṭha, Rāghava, the kings, the sages, and the twice-born performed their respective duties in that manner within the courtyards of their own homes.
They bathed in reservoirs that captivated with lotuses, white lilies, night-blooming water-lilies, and blue lotuses, and which were lined with rows of ruddy geese, swans, and cranes.
They gave gifts to the brahmins consisting of cattle, land, sesame seeds, gold, beds, seats, vessels, and fine garments.
In their own palaces, variegated with gold and jewels, they worshipped the gods beginning with Viṣṇu, Śiva, Agni, and Sūrya.
Together with their sons, grandsons, friends, servants, kinsmen, and circles of companions, they then partook of their appropriate meals.
At that time, it was day in this city; yet because only a small portion remained—being reduced to its eighth part—it appeared neither vast nor beautiful.
They passed the remainder of the day until evening with activities appropriate for that time, together with the rays of light, until the sun went to its setting.
They performed the twilight devotions well, recited the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn, chanted sacred praises, and sang captivating verses.
Then the dark-complexioned night arose, removing the sorrow of longing women, like the daughter of Indra emerging from the Ocean of Milk to bestow the dew of the moon.
The descendants of Raghu rested upon couches that were strewn with flowers, sprinkled with handfuls of camphor, and as delightful as the long orb of the moon.
Then, in the absence of Rāma, that beautiful night, occupied with the affairs of others there, passed away slowly like a single auspicious moment.
Rāma remained there, reflecting upon those very words of Vasiṣṭha—sweet and noble—just as a young elephant dwells upon the thoughts of its mother.
What indeed is this wandering in saṃsāra? Who are these people? What are these diverse beings? Why do they come, and why do they go?
What is the nature of the mind, and how is it pacified? From what does this illusion arise, and how indeed does it cease?
What benefit or what fault could there be from this cessation? And how has this contraction come upon the Self, which is all-pervading?
What might have been said by the Blessed One, the Sage, regarding the destruction of the mind; what was proclaimed concerning the conquest of the senses; or what was said regarding the self?
Through its pervasive forms such as the individual soul (jīva), the intellect (citta), the mind (manas), and illusion (māyā), the Self alone extends this unreal cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra).
When these [afflictions], bound by the mere threads of the mind, have thus come to an end, how can we easily treat them so that suffering may be pacified?
How can I separate this female crane of the intellect from this circle of clouds that are enjoyments, just as a swan separates a stream of water from the milk?
We are unable to renounce enjoyments, yet without their renunciation we have no power over calamities; alas, a great crisis has arrived!
This object to be attained is merely mind, and likewise this purpose; yet, due to our folly, it has become as heavy as a mountain to us, like a yakṣa to a child.
Having attained supreme peace and being freed from the agitation of saṃsāra, my mind will find no further object to grasp, like a young woman who has found her beloved.
May my mind become purifying—its agitation stilled, all curiosity vanished, free from evil, and resting in the Self.
When, having firmly established myself in that state which is cooler even than the moon—though it be full of all its digits—and having found rest therein, shall I wander through the world?
When will the mind, having cast off its form that is fragile due to conceptualization and having dissolved into the Self, attain peace—like a wave in water?
When, having crossed the ocean of saṃsāra—turbulent with the waves of craving and garlanded with the sea-monsters of hope—shall I become free from the fever of suffering?
On paths purified by the cessation of mental afflictions, we who are wise shall dwell, free from sorrow and possessing equal vision, for those seeking liberation.
When will this long-lasting fever of cyclic existence—by which all limbs are tormented and which strikes fear into all elements—come to an end?
O Buddha, when will the mind—like the trace of a lamp in a windless place—become free from affliction and attain peace within the dense interior of the brilliant light?
When will their senses, whose bodies are scorched by evil desires, easily cross over sufferings, just as Garuḍas cross over oceans?
"This is that same I, weeping and deluded"—such is a vainly conceived delusion; like a dark cloud in autumn, when will it go to its destruction?
That mind which once found delight in the rows of Mandāra groves now regards them as mere straw; when shall we attain that state for which we now pray?
Tell me this: will the stainless insights of knowledge proclaimed by those free from passion ever find a place within your mind?
O mind, may I never again become the recipient of such cries as "Alas, father! Mother! Son!"—the food of those who consume suffering.
O sister, fulfill my request to the Buddha quickly; for the sake of liberating us both from suffering, reflect upon the words of the Sage.
O virtuous one, O noble-minded one, having fallen at your feet with affection, I entreat you: for the sake of the cessation of existence and for the welfare of our son, remain steadfast.
First, the words concerning dispassion were spoken by the sage Vasiṣṭha; then followed the conduct of one seeking liberation, and after that, the sequence of the births.
Therefore, O Intellect, remember as it truly is the chapter on Stability, which is beautiful with its illustrations, easily accessible through the womb of consciousness, and endowed with wisdom.

Whatever has been resolved by one of cultivated intellect and examined hundreds of times, if the mind's understanding does not attain it, that becomes fruitless like an autumn cloud; therefore, the intellect alone is the essence of what must be accomplished.
Śrī Vālmīki said: Thus, with such expansive thoughts, that night passed for him there, as it does for a lotus longing for the sun.
When the stars in the sky had become sparse, as if the quarters of the horizon had been swept clean, and were tinged with a slight ruddiness while still somewhat browned by darkness;
Simultaneously with the sounding of the morning trumpets, the glorious Rāghava, whose face resembles the moon, arose like a lotus from a lotus-hand.
Having performed the ritual for the morning bath and reunited with his brothers, he departed with a small retinue sent ahead and proceeded to the residence of Vasiṣṭha.
From a distance, Rāma, with his head bowed, approached the Sage who was established in meditative concentration in solitude, devoted solely to the Self.
Having prostrated before him, they stood in the courtyard with humility until the darkness was completely dispelled and the circle of the quarters became clearly visible.
Then kings, princes, sages, and brahmins came to the silent assembly hall, like immortals to the world of Brahmā.
That residence of Vasiṣṭha became crowded with people, thronged with elephants, horses, and chariots, and graced by the conduct of kings.
In an instant, the venerable Vasiṣṭha emerged from his meditative absorption; with proper conduct and hospitality, he received the people who stood before him in prostration.
Thus followed by the sages, the illustrious sage, accompanied by Viśvāmitra, suddenly ascended his chariot like the lotus-born Brahmā ascending his lotus-throne.
Surrounded by a vast army, he went to the home of Daśaratha, like Brahmā proceeding to Indra’s city, garlanded by all the gods.
There he entered the beautiful assembly hall of the son of Daśaratha, bowing low, like a royal swan surrounded by a flock of swans entering a lotus pond.
Then, at those three words, the great hero King Daśaratha rose from his lion-throne and quickly went forth.
There, all those kings headed by Daśaratha entered, as did the sages led by Vasiṣṭha, along with the ṛṣis and the brahmins.
And there were ministers such as Sumantra and others, wise men such as Saumya and others, princes such as Rāma and others, and the sons of ministers such as Śubha and others.
The subjects, beginning with the ministers; the citizens, beginning with Suhotra; likewise the servants, beginning with Mālava; and the garland-wearers, beginning with the townsfolk.
Then, when they had each sat down upon their respective seats and were all seated with their eyes fixed upon Vasiṣṭha, [he spoke].
When the clamor of the assembly had subsided, when the bards were established in silence, and when the reports on current affairs had concluded, that interior of the assembly became tranquil.
As the flickering garlands of pollen entered from the hollows of the lotuses, they moved restlessly among the swaying strings of pearls.
As the sweet breeze blew, carrying a thick fragrance emanating from all sides from the large flower-swinging cradles.
While the matrons sat upon couches by the gentle windows, their feet resting on floors strewn with flowers, they gazed [outside].

Upon the courtyards of his palace, whose surfaces were as red as the rays of the sun reflected in the facets of pearls, a swarm of bees did not alight upon the heaps of flowers; instead, they wandered in confusion like a cloud in the sky, driven by the mistaken notion that they were the reflection of fresh sunlight.

That which was heard through merit, issuing from the mouth of Vasiṣṭha, has spread through the world of the noble with wonder throughout its lineage; it consists of mutually desired words, charming with soft syllables and phrases, delightful with many virtues, [uttered] upon meeting the virtuous.

From the quarters, from the city, from the sky, and from the forest, the hosts of Siddhas, Vidyādharas, noble Munis, and Brahmins entered silently and in whispers around Vasiṣṭha—who was observing a vow of silence—along with those who were full of reverence, as he had just begun to speak.

As the wind blew, turning tawny with the golden pollen of swarms of bees submerged within the tender buds of blossoming red lotuses, it drowned out the songs of nightingales with the melodic chiming of swinging bells.

When the smoke of aloe-wood and tagara, mingled with the fragrance of sandalwood, wafted through the air marked by the intense scent of fresh flower-garlands; and when the breeze blew, carrying a trace of the perfume from the lotuses of the canopy and bearing the marks of drifting floral pollen, with bees recognized by their humming.
Śrī Vālmīki said: With a voice as deep as a thundercloud, and with beautiful, confident words, Daśaratha spoke these words to the leader of sages.
"O Blessed One, I hope you have been freed from the exhaustion born of yesterday’s discourse, which was intensified by the emaciation resulting from your ascetic penances."
We have been comforted by that very collection of words spoken yesterday, which was full of bliss and solitary, as if by a rain of nectar.
Like moonbeams that dispel darkness, these pure words of the great ones, stainless as nectar, cool the inner being.
For the well-spoken words of the great indeed bestow unprecedented joy, lead to the highest state, and remove excessive delusion.

Worthy of veneration is that tree of virtuous people, from whom arises the creeper of the discourse on the restraints (yamas) and other virtues—a single lamp illuminating the jewel of the self, whose essence is fullness.
The well-spoken words of the virtuous wipe away every ill-performed or poorly executed deed, just as the rays of the moon dispel a mass of darkness.
O Sage, our thirst, greed, and other such fetters of saṃsāra have been diminished by your teaching, like dark clouds in autumn.
We have set out to behold our own selves freed from stain, like those born blind who, having been given eyes by Rasāñjana, seek to see gold.
The mist called the latent impressions of saṃsāra, which has arisen in the sky of our hearts, is beginning to thin out for us solely through the autumn of your speech.
O Sage, neither the blossoms of the Mandāra tree nor the waves of the nectar-water delight the inner heart as much as the words of those possessed of noble intellect.
O Raghava, whichever day passes while you are being honored by the great multitude, that day alone possesses light here; all other days are but blind abodes.
O Rāma, whose eyes are like lotus petals, awaken once more the sage who is established in grace—the imperishable one who knows the true meaning here.
Thus addressed by the king, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha, noble-souled as he was, stood facing Rāma and spoke these words.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, the sole moon of your lineage, O high-minded one, do you perhaps remember the meaning of what I have spoken, having reflected upon it from beginning to end?
O crusher of enemies, do you perhaps remember the classification of all those various births according to the distinctions of the qualities such as *sattva* and the others?
Someone may remember or indeed know that form—which is both everything and not everything, both existent and non-existent, and eternally arisen—as distinct from the supreme self.
O virtuous one, sole recipient of praise for your goodness, do you remember how this entire universe arose from the Lord of All alone?
O one of noble mind, do you correctly remember that form, which is fragile due to the power of ignorance, though extended and infinite, appears as if it had an end?
That it has been established through the investigation of characteristics and so forth that the person is nothing other than mind—do you remember that well?
O Rāma, have you reflected upon the entire meaning of the discourse? Has that which was considered yesterday been retained within your heart throughout the night?
When repeatedly reflected upon and firmly established in the heart, a purpose bears great fruit; it does not do so for one who remains in a state of casual neglect.
O Rāghava, with a heart that is itself secluded, you are a vessel for those words that are pure and refined, just as a neck is for pearls.
Śrī Vālmīki said: Having been thus granted the opportunity by the sage of great luster, the son of the Lotus-Seated One, Rāma spoke these words.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, this is indeed the manifestation of your own power, that I, who am most noble, have understood your words.
"Whatever you have commanded, all that is exactly so and not otherwise; with sleep dispelled, I have contemplated the meaning of your words in my heart."
O Lord, yesterday the delightful mass of rays from the speech-sun spoken by you was made to shine forth for the destruction of the darkness of worldly existence.
O noble-souled one, all that has passed away has been gathered within me—delightful, meritorious, and pure, like a collection of jewels.
Whose head, O Siddhas, does your instruction not bear—teaching that brings beneficial results, is pleasing to the heart, meritorious, and a means to bliss?
Dispelling the veil of the mist of saṃsāra here, we have become clear through your grace, like days at the end of the rainy season.
Your holy instruction is sweet at its inception, increases one's good fortune in the middle, and results in unsurpassed fruit at the end.
May the flower of your speech—ever-expanding, white, unfading, gladdening both the auspicious and the inauspicious, and eternally glorious—grant us its fruit.

O you who are expert in the investigation of all scriptures, a single great lake for the spreading waters of merit; O observer of extensive vows, now devote yourself intensely to the expansion of the lineage of those whose sins have been destroyed.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O you of beautiful form, listen attentively to this beneficial Chapter on Quiescence, which is beautiful with its supreme philosophical conclusion.
O Rāma, this long-lasting illusion of saṃsāra is constantly maintained by beings of rajasic and tamasic nature, like a pavilion supported by sturdy pillars.
By wise beings such as you, who are strengthened by virtues, this ripened illusion is cast off with ease, just as snakes shed their skin.
O virtuous one, those classes of beings who are wise, as well as those characterized by passion and goodness, reflect upon the succession of worlds from the past.
For those whose debts have been extinguished through association with the scriptures, the virtuous, and noble deeds, an intellect arises that resembles a lamp, beholding the essential truth.
By investigating the self with one's own intellect through inquiry itself, as long as the object of knowledge has not been realized, it is not attained.

O delight of the Raghus, you are the foremost among those who possess wisdom, who are guided by policy, who are steadfast, who are distinguished by their lineage, and who are of the noble Rājasa nature by birth.
O wise one, examine for yourself the views concerning the origins of saṃsāra: what is real and what is unreal? Be one who is devoted to the truth.
What reality can there be for that which does not exist at the beginning and at the end? That alone is called "real" which is eternal at the beginning and at the end, and nothing else.
For that deluded beast of a creature whose mind clings to an object that is unreal from beginning to end, by what means can discrimination be produced?
In this world, it is the mind alone that is born; it is the mind alone that grows; but through the vision of right insight, it is indeed the mind that is liberated.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahman, this has been understood by me: that in these three worlds, it is the mind alone that wanders in saṃsāra and is the vessel for old age and death."
Tell me with certainty that means for crossing over it; by you, the sun, the darkness within the hearts of the Raghavas shall be destroyed.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, first let the mind be led toward merit through the scriptures, through supreme detachment, and likewise through association with the virtuous.
When the mind, imbued with goodness, has attained detachment, then one should follow gurus—those who are masters of realized knowledge as well.
Then, having performed meditation, worship, and so forth according to his instruction, he gradually attains that state which is supremely purifying.
Through pure discernment, one perceives the Self by means of the Self, as one perceives the entire universe within with the cool light of the moon, as if with the brilliance of the sky.
In the great ocean of worldly existence, a person is carried away like a blade of grass until, through the mind, they find rest upon the shore of discernment.
The intellect of this person, who has thoroughly understood reality through investigation, subdues all mental afflictions just as gentle water settles sand.
This gold and this ash are clearly recognized as such, yet not in the same way as for a goldsmith whose very self consists of the knowledge of gold.
When this imperishable and subtle Self has been realized within oneself for a long time, how could there be any occasion for delusion in a person here?
For if the mind is deluded internally because the essence is not fully understood, then once the essence is known, delusion undoubtedly becomes non-existent.
O people, the self, when not fully understood, leads to the establishment of suffering for you; but when fully understood, it leads to infinite happiness and peace.
Having manifested your true self from this body which has defiled you as if by being mixed with it, become established in yourselves; do not delay.

O humans, there is not even the slightest connection between this stainless Self and the body, just as there is no connection between gold and a speck of mud, even when that gold is situated within it.
The self is distinct and the embodied one is distinct, like a water-lily and a drop of water; with arms upraised I cry out, yet no one hears me.
As long as the mind remains inert by nature, like a tortoise in a well, it is utterly deluded by the path of worldly enjoyments and has forgotten the inquiry into the Self.
Until then, the darkness of saṃsāra is not dispelled even slightly, even by the moon together with fire, or even by twelve suns.
For when the mind is fully awakened, it discerns its own state; like the rising of the sun at night, the darkness within the heart flees away.
One should constantly awaken the mind, resting upon the bed of yoga for the sake of supreme enlightenment, in order to transcend cyclic existence; for existence indeed bestows ultimate suffering.
Just as the sky is not defiled by dust and the lotus is not defiled by water, even though they are in close contact, so too the self is not defiled by the bodies with which it is associated.
Just as dross and other impurities, though joined with gold, remain separate and do not undergo internal transformation, so too does the inert body remain distinct from the Self.

One perceives that the experience of pleasure and pain belongs to the self, just as one might perceive the presence of water droplets or fading in the sky, though they are entirely non-existent there.

Pleasure and pain belong neither to the body nor to the Self, which transcends all; for these belong only to one who possesses ignorance, and when that ignorance is destroyed, they belong to no one at all.
There is no happiness for anyone, nor is there any suffering for anyone; behold everything as consisting of the Self, peaceful and infinite, O Rāghava.
These expansive perceptions of creation that are seen here are like waves in water, or like a peacock's plumage in the sky, or within the Self.
Just as a gem spontaneously reflects its own shadows without any external cause, even so does this Self bestow creations consisting of light.
O wise one, neither the self nor the world is truly one, nor is duality non-existent; this entire manifestation now unfolds as a mere appearance.
All this is indeed Brahman; everything is thus pervaded by the Self alone. O sinless one, abandon the delusion that "I am one thing" and "this is another."
O Rāma, within that eternal, dense mass of Brahman, no conceptual constructions arise; they are not real, just as the waves in the ocean of water are not truly existent.
In the single, all-encompassing reality of the Supreme Self, there is no conception of a second, just as there are no particles of frost in fire.
Meditating upon the self by means of the self as consisting solely of consciousness, the self indeed unfolds within itself, upright and radiant in its nature of pure consciousness.
There is no sorrow, there is no delusion, there is no birth, and there is no one who is born. Whatever exists here, that alone exists; be free from the fever of anxiety, O Rāghava.
Free from dualities, eternally established in purity, devoid of the pursuit of acquisition and preservation, self-possessed, peerless, sorrowless in nature, and free from fever—be thus, O Rāghava.
Equanimous, self-abiding, steady-minded, with a heart calmed of sorrow, silent, pure as a precious gem, and free from fever—be thus, O Rāghava!
Solitary, with peaceful intentions, firm-minded, and having conquered your inner disposition, follow what has come to you as it is, and be free from the fever of passion, O Rāghava.
Free from passion, free from exertion, stainless, and cleansed of impurity; neither a taker nor a renouncer—be free from fever, O Rāghava.
O Rāghava, having attained the state that transcends all, fulfilled by the attainment of all that is to be attained, remain free from feverish agitation like the full, unmoving ocean.

Freed from the web of conceptual constructions and devoid of the ointment of illusion, with your soul satisfied within the Self by the Self, become free from the fever of worldly existence, O Rāghava.
O best among the knowers of the Self, whose body is infinite, shoreless, and boundless; O Raghava, as steadfast as the summit of the mountain that supports the earth, be free from fever.
By experiencing only what has been obtained, by having no desire for anything anywhere, and by relinquishing both taking up and rejecting, become free from the fever of passion, O Raghava.
Cultivate magnanimity within yourself by means of yourself, like the full ocean; cultivate joy within yourself by means of yourself, like the orb of the full moon.

O Rāma, this world-appearance, which is composed of unreal forms, does not pursue that which is unreal for one who knows the Truth. You are a knower of that Truth; you are one whose mental fluctuations have ceased; you are free from affliction; you are eternally awakened. O handsome one, remain with your sorrow stilled.

Protect for a long time, with your vision, this kingdom under a single umbrella as it was properly taught by your father; may you delight the circle of kings with all your virtues, for neither hope nor passion for worldly actions is appropriate here.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: It is my conviction that he who engages in activities without the latent impression of "I am doing this movement of the universe" is liberated.
Having assumed a human body, some who are devoted to these activities go from heaven to hell, and again from hell to heaven.
Some, though delighting in non-action and having desisted from action, go from hell to hell, from suffering to suffering, and from fear to fear.

Some, bound by the threads of their own latent impressions and impelled by the fruits of their karma, go from the state of an animal to the body of an immobile being, and from there back to the body of an animal.
Certain blessed knowers of the self, whose vision of the mind has been scrutinized and whose fetters of craving are severed, proceed to the absolute state.
O Raghava, having experienced only a few previous births, one who is liberated in this very birth is therefore characterized by the quality of sattva.
Once born, he attains growth like the moon on its full-moon day; and as the *kuṭaja* tree does in the rainy season, so does good fortune attend him.
O Great-minded One, pure knowledges enter him whose birth is his last, just as pearls enter an excellent bamboo tube.
Nobility, amiability, loving-kindness, gentleness, compassion, and wisdom always attend him, just as women attend upon the inner apartments.
He who performs all actions, yet when their merit is exhausted and its fruit has vanished, remains equanimous toward all undertakings, neither rejoicing nor grieving.
Just as darkness vanishes by day, so do the pairs of opposites come to an end there; and just as clouds disperse in autumn, so do the qualities attain purity there.
All people desire one whose conduct is sweet with gentleness, just as the forest deer in the woods long for the bamboo that produces a sweet sound.
Such splendors of virtue pursue a man of his final birth from the very moment he is born, just as cranes follow a rain-cloud.
Then, that person, perfected in virtues, follows the guru alone; he, in turn, enjoins him to that very purifying solitude.
With a mind endowed with excellence and possessing detachment from discursive thought, one then beholds the Lord, or the Self, as a single form, free from all affliction.
With a beautiful and tranquil mind, he first expands his internal mental reflection through inquiry for the sake of awakening.
For those of great virtue first awaken the sleeping deer of the mind—devoid of qualities—who are destined for their final birth.

Having diligently served those of renowned virtue and great weight, and having scrutinized the jewel of the mind with a stainless intellect, those men attain a stainless state, beholding for a long time the supreme light within.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: This general sequence has been declared for all embodied beings; now hear this other specific detail, O lotus-eyed one.
O Rāma, for those embodied beings born into this tumultuous cycle of saṃsāra, there are these two supreme methods capable of leading to liberation.
First, one [type of mantra] is declared to bestow accomplishment either gradually over many lifetimes or even within a single lifetime, through the performance of practices as instructed by the Guru.
But for the second type, who possesses a mind somewhat developed by himself, the attainment of knowledge occurs swiftly, like the falling of a fruit from the sky.
In order to bring about the realization of the falling of the fruit from the sky, listen to this ancient account; I shall relate it to you.

Listen, O fortunate one, to this sublime tale: those of great power, for whom the flood of obstacles consisting of past merit and demerit has been removed, attain a stainless and supreme discernment in their final existence, like a fruit falling from the sky.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: There was a powerful king of the Videhas named Janaka, whose noble intellect was free from all calamities and blossomed with every prosperity.
He is the wish-fulfilling tree for the multitudes of supplicants, the sun for his circle of friends, the springtime for the flowers that are his kinsmen, and the god of love for women.
A cool-rayed moon to the night-lotuses of the twice-born, a sun to the darkness of his enemies, and an ocean of the jewels of benevolence, he stood upon the earth like Viṣṇu himself.
Once, during the intoxicating springtime, when the young creepers were in full bloom, tawny with clusters of blossoms, and resounded with the warbling of cuckoos;
He went to the lovely pleasure grove, its expanse filled with blossoming trees and its courtyards graced by graceful, vine-like women, just as Indra goes to the Nandana garden.
In that delightful, excellent forest, where the wind blew fiercely from the *kesara* trees, he wandered through the mountain bowers accompanied by his attendants stationed at a distance.
Then, in a certain thicket of tamāla trees, he heard words uttered in their own discourse by invisible siddhas.
O lotus-petal-eyed one, these songs, which take the self as their object of meditation, were sung by those who dwell eternally in solitude, roaming the mountain caves.

The Siddhas said: We worship that which arises from the reality of one's own self, which is motionless, and which is the certainty of the bliss of consciousness resulting from the union of the seer and the seen.
Others said: "Having abandoned the seer, the seeing, and the seen, along with all latent impressions (vāsanā), we worship the Self as the first manifestation of seeing."
Others said: "We worship that Self which, situated eternally between the two positions of 'existence' and 'non-existence,' is the illuminator of all things to be illuminated."
Others said: "That in which all is, whose all [is], from whom all is, for whom this [world] is, by whom all is, and that which indeed is all—that Truth we worship together."
Others said: "We worship that Self of ours which is headless, ending with the letter *ha*, established in every form, and eternally uttering its own sound."

Others said: "Those who, having abandoned the Lord who dwells in the cave of the heart, go to another god, are like those who desire a jewel while having cast away the Kaustubha gem held in their own hand."
Others said: "Indeed, by renouncing all desires, this fruit is obtained, whereby the very root-stalks of the poisonous vines of longing are severed."
Others said: "That dull-witted man who, even after perceiving the extreme insipidity of all objects, again forms an attachment to them—he is no mere donkey."
Others said: "One should strike these serpents of the senses—whether they have arisen or not—with the staff of discernment again and again, just as Indra strikes mountains with his thunderbolt."

Others said: "One who possesses excellent tranquility should attain the pure bliss of peace; the mind of the virtuous attains serenity. For one whose mind is calmed, there arises for a long time a supreme abiding in the happiness of its own true nature."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having heard these songs sung by the hosts of Siddhas, the lord of the earth immediately fell into despair, like a coward at the roar of battle.
He went toward his own home, drawing along his retinue, like the flood of a river following the trees on its banks as it flows toward the ocean.
Having dismissed his entire retinue to their respective dwellings, he alone ascended to the preeminent palace, like the sun ascending the mountain.
There, observing the movements of the world as flickering as the wings of birds eager to fly upward, he lamented thus, overwhelmed with agitation:
Alas, what misery! Amidst these most wretched states of worldly agitation, I am forced to wallow like one stone against other stones.
Only a tiny fraction of infinite time is lived by me; yet I fix my attachment upon it—fie on that wretched consciousness!
How insignificant is this kingdom of mine, lasting only as long as my life! Why do I, with a ruined intellect, remain in such misery without it?
I am infinite in the beginning and at the end, yet in the middle my life is fragile; like a child before a painted moon, why do I vainly maintain my composure?
Alas, what a pity! I am utterly deluded by this ensnaring net of Indra, devoid of conceptual proliferation; by whom have I been so thoroughly bewildered?
Whatever object there may be, whatever is beautiful, whatever is noble or unartificial—none of that exists here at all; upon what, then, can my mind be fixed?
"Even that which is far away is not far when it dwells within my mind"; having thus resolved, I completely abandon the contemplation of external objects.
The rushing and surging of the world is as fragile as a whirlpool in water; even now it is seen to lead only to suffering—what reliance can there be on happiness?
Year by year, month by month, day by day, and moment by moment, pleasures are but lumps of suffering, while sufferings themselves recur again and again.
For that which is grasped is seen as distinct, yet it is neither perceived nor cultivated; that which remains here does not exist for the wise, wherein their true abiding might be.
Alas, those who today stand at the pinnacle of the great will fall low within a few days; when the greatness of the mind has been destroyed, what kind of confidence can there be?
Bound by no rope, I am yet bound; unstained by mud, I am defiled; though standing above, I have fallen—alas, my own self has lost its true state!
Why has this delusion come upon me so suddenly, even though I am wise? It is like a dark cloud, shrouding the light, that has come before the sun.
What are these great enjoyments of mine? What are these kinsmen of mine? I am a fool, bewildered by this convention as if it were composed of a phantom.
Why do I myself bind this passion for old age and death—this very attachment that causes distress—to these things?
Whether it remains or departs, what concern do I have for it? For this, like the beauty of a bubble, has arisen thus as a mere illusion.
Those great riches and enjoyments, those virtuous and affectionate kinsmen—all have entered the path of memory; even though they exist [in my mind], what stability can there be?
Where are the riches of kings, or where are the worlds of Brahmā? Those of the past have passed away; what is this confidence of mine?
The virtuous will laugh at me, who am intent on preserving my life, as if at millions of Indras swallowed like bubbles in water.
Tens of millions of Brahmās have passed away; successions of creations have gone by; kings have vanished like dust. What stability is there in my life?
If I continue to maintain attachment toward this delusion consisting of the body—the object of perception within the nightmare of the night of saṃsāra—then shame on this state of mine!
"This is that I" is a futile conceptualization, its nature being unreal; why do I remain like an ignorant person, possessed by the demon of egoism?
"Slain! Slain is this [life] by this extended line of time; though I see it, I do not perceive the subtle stroke of Time."
Those who once treated my footstool as their seat and used the Śārṅga bow as a play-ball have now been swallowed by the Kāla-Kāpālikas; why do you leap about before me with such confidence?
These days come and go incessantly even now; yet not even a single day has been seen to perish as an existing reality.
Just as cranes in a lake, these very enjoyments alone flash within the minds of all people, but not the vision of their own true state.
Having fallen from misery to even greater misery, and having gone from suffering to even more intense suffering, I am still not dispassionate; alas, shame on me, whose intention is so base!
In whatever auspicious objects firm attachment is bound, those very things are seen to perish; what, then, is supreme in this world?
Whatever is pleasing in the middle, at the end, or upon first encounter—all that is indeed impure, defiled by destruction and filth.
In whatever objects a person fixes his resolve, in those very same things, the rise of their destruction is seen to be extreme for him.
Day by day this dull-witted person here enters into a state that is more sinful, more cruel, and more sweat-inducing.
Struck solely by ignorance in childhood, struck by passion in youth, and afflicted by anxiety for his wife in the remainder of life—what can this dull-witted man ever do?
Why does the fool look upon this saṃsāra—which is subject to coming and going, tasteless, corrupted by the inequality of conditions, and whose essence is devoid of substance?
Even by performing hundreds of sacrifices such as the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha, one attains heaven for a portion of time lasting until the end of a great kalpa, but no more than that.
What region of heaven, or earth, or even the netherworld (pātāla) exists, where these calamities do not overwhelm one like ill-behaved bees?
How indeed can these mental anxieties and physical ailments—these serpents within the hollows of one's own mind and these sprouts upon the ground of the body—be warded off?
Existence stands at the summit of non-existence; in delightful things lies the height of un-delight; in pleasures dwell sorrows at their peak—upon which single thing, then, shall I rely?
Ordinary, lowly creatures are born and die; by them alone the earth is densely packed, yet truly virtuous people are difficult to find.
With eyes like rows of blue lotuses and adorned with supreme love, these playful women exist only for the sake of laughter, as they are subject to momentary destruction.
There exist such persons by whose closing and opening of their eyes the dissolution and creation of the worlds occur; what need is there even to count those like me?
There are things more beautiful than the beautiful and more stable than the stable; yet this splendor of worldly objects ends in mere thought—what do you desire?
And as for those various prosperities which are approved by the mind—alas, I consider even those to be great calamities, given their vast undertakings.
Even those various calamities, if they are approved by the mind, I consider them to be great undertakings—indeed, I deem them to be riches within the mind.
In this world, which is a mere manifestation of mind and as fragile as the moon reflected in the ocean, from where has this unprecedented string of syllables "this is mine" arisen?

When the stability of the world has come about by mere chance, like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, the distinction between what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted has been fruitlessly fabricated by a rogue.
In these views, which are limited by finitude, scorched by suffering, and falsely named "happiness"—in which of them am I attached, like a moth to the flames of a fire?
It is better to wallow in the fires of Raurava during the eternal conflagrations than to remain within the cycles of worldly existence, where one never attains liberation.
It is said that saṃsāra itself is the very limit of sufferings; how, then, can happiness be found in a body fallen within its midst?
Those who are established in this uncreated great suffering of saṃsāra perceive other sufferings as being entirely sweet.
I too, standing on the same level as the lowest wood and clods of earth, have attained equality with the ignorant who grasp at the most excellent things.
Of this tree of saṃsāra, which abounds with thousands of sprouts, branches, fruits, and shoots, the mind is the great primary sprout that constitutes its root.
I consider that to be nothing but volition; therefore, by the cessation of volition, I shall dry it up so that the tree of saṃsāra reaches its withering.
Since the activities of the monkey-mind, though charming in their mere outward form, are now fully understood as being perishable, I take no delight in them this very day.
I have experienced the cycles of saṃsāra, which are pierced by hundreds of snares of hope and bring the affliction of repeated falls and rises; now I shall rest.
"Alas, I am struck down! I am ruined! I am dead!"—thus have I grieved again and again; that grief has now passed away, and I do not weep for it anymore.
I am awakened; I am delighted, for this thief of the self has been seen. This thing called "mind" I shall slay, for I have long been slain by the mind.
For all this time, this pearl of my mind remained unpierced; but now it has been pierced and is worthy of the string.
Surely this drop of frost upon my mind will soon dissolve through the heat of the sun of discernment, after having persisted for so long.
Well-awakened by various holy ones and perfected beings, I follow after the Self, which is the means to supreme bliss.
Having found the jewel of the self in solitude and beholding it with joy, I remain with all other worldly concerns subsided, like an autumnal cloud upon a mountain.

Having forcibly cast out from within the false manifestation of "I am this" and "this is mine," and having destroyed the exceedingly powerful enemy that is the mind, I attain tranquility; homage be to you, O Discrimination!
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: While he was reflecting thus, a doorkeeper entered before him, like Aruṇa at the front of the chariot of the supreme Sun.
The doorkeeper said: "O Lord, upon whose pillar-like arms rests the entire burden of the earth, arise and perform the royal duties appropriate for the day."
These women, carrying jars of water mixed with flowers, camphor, and saffron, stood ready in the bathing area like rivers incarnate.
These lotus ponds, where bees wander through groves of *kamala* and *kahlāra* flowers, have been fashioned as pavilions with canopies made of the silken garments of the *kamalinī* plants.
These grounds on the banks of the lotus pond are filled with parasols belonging to those who attended the occasion of his bath, as well as with fly-whisks, chariots, elephants, and horses.
Likewise, the temples for the worship of the gods were prepared with caskets filled with complete garlands and overflowing with food and medicinal herbs.
Having bathed, with purifying blades of grass in hand, and having recited the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn, O Lord, this assembly of twice-born men, worthy of sacrificial fees, gazes upon you alone.
The Supreme Lord is protected by women holding fly-whisks made of yak-tail hair; the cool dining areas have been prepared for him by those lovely ladies.
Arise quickly; may it be well with you; perform your duty without fail. Great men do not let the proper time for their own tasks pass by.
When the doorkeeper had thus spoken, the king then reflected in that very same way upon the wondrous nature of worldly existence.
"How small indeed is this so-called kingdom and its happiness!"—thus it stands; I have no need for this which perishes in an instant.
Having completely renounced the entire deceptive display of Śambara, I abide in solitude alone, like a perfectly tranquil ocean.
Enough with these manifestations of enjoyment of mine, which consist mostly of what is unreal; having abandoned all activities, I shall remain in pure happiness alone.
O mind, abandon this cleverness born from the agitation of habitual attachment to enjoyments, for the sake of pacifying the mire of the snare of birth, old age, and dullness.
O mind, whatever states you perceive as objects of agitation, from those very states you shall experience supreme suffering.
Whether engaged in worldly activity or withdrawn from it, the mind never attains satisfaction, again and again and for a very long time, across all the planes of experience.
Therefore, enough with this vain preoccupation with enjoyments which leads only to evil; pursue instead that through which unartificial contentment arises.
Having reflected thus, Janaka became silent; with his restless mind stilled, he was like a figure depicted in a painting.
The doorkeeper, too—being well-versed in the mental dispositions of kings—said nothing further, out of both respect and fear.
Then, having remained silent for a moment, Janaka again reflected with a mind endowed with tranquility upon the life of living beings.
What is there to be accepted here that I should strive to accomplish? Upon what object, free from destruction, shall I fix my steadfastness?
What use have I for being intent on action, or what use for inaction? For nothing that has arisen is ever exempt from destruction.
Whether this body be active or inactive, it arises from what is unreal; for me, who am the pure consciousness established in equanimity, what loss can there possibly be?
I do not long for what has not been attained, nor do I abandon what has been attained; remaining established in my own self, let whatever belongs to me remain mine.
I have no purpose here with what is done, nor any at all with what is not done; for whatever is obtained through action or non-action is composed of unreality.
Whether I am acting or not acting, my deeds—whether appropriate or inappropriate—have no desired object here that has attained the status of being worth pursuing.
Therefore, having arisen, let this body perform its natural activity as it has sequentially arrived; for what is the use of this [body] with motionless limbs merely wasting away?
When the mind is steady, free from desire, equanimous, and devoid of passion, the movement and stillness arising from the parts of the body are equal in their result.
When the mind conceives of itself as the agent and enjoyer regarding the glorious fruits born of karma, and when that mind has attained peace, then even what was done by men is as if undone.

Whatever firm resolve has taken root within a person regarding their actions attains the state of being identical with them; my intellect has reached the stainless state, so I cast off this intermediate state of both steadiness and unsteadiness.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having reflected thus, Janaka rose to perform his duties as they arose, remaining unattached, just as the sun rises at the beginning of the day.
Having himself abandoned, by means of his mind, all latent impressions regarding the desirable and the undesirable, he acted according to whatever arose, like one in deep sleep even while awake.
Having completed the duties of that day, preceded by the propitiation of the noble ones, he spent the night alone in the very play of meditative concentration.
Having made the mind equanimous and stilled the wandering toward sense objects, he thus awakened his consciousness as the night was waning away.
The flickering mind in saṃsāra brings no happiness to you; attain tranquility, for from tranquility the peaceful, essential bliss is obtained.
To the very extent that you effortlessly conceive floods of conceptual constructions, to that same extent does saṃsāra expand through your own thinking.
Just as a tree attains a hundred branches through watering, so too do you attain an infinity of mental afflictions through your desire for the enjoyments of the wicked.
The creations of birth and worldly existence arise from the play of the web of thought; therefore, having abandoned this manifold thinking, attain tranquility.
O handsome one, weigh this world against the instability of saṃsāra; if you find any essence within it, then take refuge in that alone.
Since you have abandoned all reliance [on the truth] out of a longing for the seen and the seer, do not grasp this, nor let it go; wander according to your own will and desire.
Whether this visible world be non-existent or existent, whether it arises or passes away, O virtuous one, even if you encounter adversity, do not be affected by its merits or demerits.
There is not even the slightest connection between you and an object of perception that lacks an existent form; what kind of connection is this?

This non-existence [of the relation] is not real, for a relation between two things can only exist when both are either non-existent or existent; thus, this sequence of syllables is truly marvelous and unprecedented!
Even if this unreal thing were real, O handsome one, tell me: what kind of attachment could there be between the existent and the non-existent, such as that between a mortal and his life?
If both the mind and the object of perception were truly real and eternally established, then from what source could the expansion of joy and sorrow arise?
Therefore, abandon this great delusion; bring forth the exuberance of the mute. Cast off this unworthy state, which has entered you like a turbulent ocean.
O noble-minded one, do not fall into the impurity of delusion and become dull-witted, burning away in vain by yourself like a ball of glowing embers.
