There is nothing here that is so exalted or supreme by which you might attain ultimate perfection; therefore, O rogue mind, relying on extreme fortitude by force, abandon your fickleness!
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Reflecting in this manner while there in his own kingdom, King Janaka performed all his duties and, being of steady intellect, was not deluded.
His mind did not leap forth toward any states of worldly pleasure; it remained forever established solely in the state of deep sleep.
From that time forward, he neither grasped at what was visible nor did he abandon it; he simply remained established in the present, free from all doubt.
By means of that constant seclusion, he immediately attained the eternal state, never again to incur any stain, just as the sky is never again defiled by darkness.
Through his continuous pursuit of self-discrimination, that lord of the earth attained a pure and stainless perfect knowledge of infinite luster.
The conscious self, free from disease and untouched by the rays of conceptual thought, arose in the space of his heart like the sun in the sky.
He, the infinite self, skilled in knowing the self of all beings, beheld all phenomena established within the power of consciousness as being identical with his own self.
He was never elated, nor was he ever deeply distressed; because worldly affairs are merely the functioning of nature (*prakṛti*), his mind remained always equanimous.
From that time forth, O giver of honor, Janaka became liberated while living—a sage of mature wisdom who had realized the higher and lower truths of the world.
While ruling the kingdom of the Videhas, Janaka, the life of his people, was not at all tormented by joy or sorrow, for he was no longer under their sway.
It neither sets nor rises through the fluctuations of virtues and faults.

He neither desponds nor exults because of gains or losses arising from his kingdom; even while acting, he does nothing at all anywhere. He remains eternally and always situated within the consciousness.
In the state of deep sleep, all mental impressions of King Janaka had entirely subsided from all objects of existence.
He does not connect with the future, nor does he dwell upon the past; rather, he follows the present moment while simply smiling.
O lotus-eyed Rāma, by the power of his own inquiry alone, he has attained everything that is to be attained, and not through any other desire.
To whatever extent the limit of investigations is reached, to that same extent one investigates by means of one's own mind alone.
That state which is attained from a heart made clear by inquiry arising from association with the virtuous—that is not attained through a guru, nor from the meaning of the scriptures, nor from merit.
O Rāma, the true state is attained through one's own beautiful intellect, as if through a companion who is wisdom itself; it is not reached by any other name or ritual action.
For one in whom the flame of the lamp of wisdom—sharp-tipped and traversing both the past and the future—is ever ablaze, the blindness of dullness never causes affliction.
O Mahāmati, those calamities which are difficult to cross over and which are crowded with waves of suffering are crossed by means of wisdom, as if by a boat.
Even a slight misfortune afflicts a fool who is devoid of wisdom, just as even a tiny gust of wind strikes down a sapless blade of grass.
O crusher of enemies, O Rāma, even one who is without a companion, lacking wisdom, and without weapons, surely crosses over the fragile ocean of saṃsāra.
One who possesses wisdom achieves the completion of his task even without assistance; whereas one of poor wisdom perishes despite undertaking even the most important business.

One should first increase one's wisdom through the study of scriptures and association with virtuous people, just as one nurtures a creeper toward the attainment of fruit by beginning its irrigation and protection.
With the great root of the power of wisdom, the tree of one's true purpose bears fruit that is exceedingly sweet in due time, like the reflection of the moon in the waters.
The very same effort that people exert in acquiring external objects should first be applied toward increasing wisdom.
One should destroy the dullness of wisdom—the boundary of all sufferings, the supreme treasury of calamities, and the seed of the trees of saṃsāra.
Whatever is obtained from heaven or the netherworlds, and whatever sovereignty or other attainments are acquired—all that is secured by the high-souled one from the treasury of wisdom.
O Raghava, one crosses over that terrifying ocean of saṃsāra by means of wisdom; neither by gifts, nor by sacred fords, nor by austerity is this achieved.
That even men who walk upon the earth have attained divine prosperity is the sweet fruit that has arisen from the creeper of wisdom and merit.
By means of wisdom, leaders of herds of rutting elephants were torn apart by their claws and defeated by jackals, just as lions are overcome by deer.
Even by means of common [means], kingship has been attained by men through the power of wisdom; indeed, it is observed here that the fitness for heaven and liberation belongs only to the wise man.
Through wisdom, all debaters—who sport with their own conceptual constructions—conquer even those men who are like formidable warriors yet are exceedingly timid.
This wisdom is a wish-fulfilling gem residing in the heart-treasury of the discerning; like a celestial kalpa-tree, it bestows the fruit of whatever is thought of.
One who is capable crosses the cycle of existence; the inferior person is cast away by wisdom. The trained one reaches the further shore, while the untrained one does not reach it with a boat.
Wisdom rightly applied leads a man to the further shore, while wrongly applied it leads him to calamity; like a boat tossing in the ocean, it causes a person to wander in saṃsāra.
Faults arising from the multitude of desires do not afflict the discerning man who is undeluded and wise, just as arrows do not strike one who is well-armored.
O dear one, through wisdom the entire world is seen here exactly as it is; for those who attain right vision, neither calamities nor prosperities exist.
The dull-natured, vast, and dark cloud of egoism, which conceals the supreme sun, is dispelled by me through the wind of wisdom.
For one who desires to attain the peerless state of a Buddha, this very intellect must first be nurtured; for surely, a farmer who longs for the fruit first ploughs the earth itself.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, by thus investigating the Self with the self as Janaka did, you will attain, without obstacle, the state of those who have known what is to be known.
For those wise people of later birth who possess both rājasa and sāttvika qualities attain what is to be attained by themselves, just like Janaka.
Having repeatedly conquered the enemies known as the senses to such an extent that this self, by means of the self alone, becomes serene within the self.
When the all-pervading God, the Lord of gods, the Supreme Self, is propitiated and beheld by oneself, all perceptions of suffering are extinguished.
When that Supreme and Lower One is seen, the fists of the seeds of delusion, the showers of various calamities, and false views all go to destruction.
O Rāma, like Janaka, always regarding yourself with wisdom as the source of all undertakings, become one who possesses true fortune and is most excellent.
For one who constantly reflects within and perceives the world as flickering, the Self becomes serene of its own accord over time, just as it did for Janaka.
Neither fate, nor actions, nor wealth, nor kinsmen provide refuge for men terrified by worldly existence, except for their own effort.
O dear one, those who rely on fate and are devoted to evil intentions regarding their duties possess dull intellects; they are not to be followed, for they lead to destruction.
This, O Rāma, has been described as the attainment of knowledge, which bestows happiness and fells the tree of ignorance, like the falling of fruit from the sky.
The manifold mental construction of saṃsāra dissolves through investigation, just as melting snow, once its solidity is overcome, vanishes under the heat of the sun.
When the destruction of this night of the thought "I am this very [person]" has dawned, there arises of its own accord the all-pervading, expansive, and self-luminous light.
When this contraction of "I am this very [person]" has dissolved, an expansion arises that pervades infinite worlds.
Just as Janaka abandoned the latent impression of egoism, so too should you, O one of noble intellect, abandon it after investigating within.
When the cloud of egoism has perished, in the vast and stainless expanse of consciousness, the supreme sun of one's own light surely attains full maturity.
The contemplation of the sense of "I" is nothing but profound darkness; when that is brought to rest, illumination arises.
When it has been cultivated that "I do not exist, nor does another exist, nor does [anything] not exist," the mind attains tranquility and no longer sinks into things to be grasped.
O Rāma, know that the mind’s pursuit of what is to be accepted and its absolute avoidance of what is to be rejected—this alone is bondage, and nothing else.

Do not indulge in grief regarding things to be abandoned; do not be intent on things to be accepted. Having relinquished the views of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, abide in the remainder and attain purity.

Those for whom there remains the fixed notion that "this is to be accepted" and "this is to be rejected" have not dissolved [into the ultimate]; they still desire something and thus renounce something here in this world.

As long as the mind has not ceased its discrimination between what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, equanimity does not shine forth, just as moonlight does not appear in a sky filled with clouds.
For one whose mind is agitated by the thought, "This is non-substantial" and "this is substantial," equanimity does not arise, just as a cluster of blossoms does not appear on a *śākhoṭa* tree.
Where there is the pursuit of what is proper and improper, delighting in gain and loss, how can equanimity and clarity shine there, illuminating dispassion?
While this single, stainless reality of Brahman exists, what is improper, and where is there any propriety, in the eternal state of both multiplicity and non-multiplicity?
Since the two restless female monkeys—suspected of being both desired and undesired—flit about upon the tree of the mind, how can there be any tranquility for it in this world?
Hopelessness, fearlessness, constancy, equanimity, knowledge, effortlessness, actionlessness, gentleness, and non-conceptuality.

Fortitude, loving-kindness, intelligence, contentment, gentleness, and soft-spokenness—these abide without any latent impressions in the Knower who is free from what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted.
One should forcibly withdraw the mind that is running downward by means of withdrawal (pratyāhāra), just as water falling downward is held back by a dam.
Having abandoned these external objects, whether standing, walking, sleeping, or breathing, investigate all internal things in every way and at all times.
The turbid net of latent impressions, with its fish-hook of grasping thirst, has spread across the waters of saṃsāra and is stretched out by the threads of anxiety.
O dear one, cut through this with this sharp probe of intelligence, just as a wind sweeping across the vast expanse at the proper time disperses a cloud.
One should uproot the root of this tree of saṃsāra—the seat of the sprouts of defects—by means of steadfastness and a resolute intellect characterized by fortitude.
Having severed the mind with the mind itself, as one would cut down a tree with an axe, and having attained the state of purity, become steady this very moment.
Having severed the mind with the mind itself, and having forgotten the final mind, and having severed even the present mind, attain the state of one whose saṃsāra is cut asunder.
When delusion has forgotten cyclic existence, it does not grow up again; when the mind has forgotten cyclic existence, it does not grow up again.
Whether standing, walking, sleeping, waking, sitting, rising, or falling, having internally resolved that "this world is indeed unreal," abandon all attachment to it.
Relying upon the stainless equanimity, performing the duties already attained, and not thinking of those not yet attained—thus indeed should you dwell here, O Rāghava.
Just as Śarva both bears and does not bear the various forms (liṅgas), so you alone, O sinless one, should here perform and yet not perform these actions.
You alone are the knower; you are the unborn, you are the Self, you are Maheśvara. Being non-different from the Self, this entire universe is thus spread out by you.

He who, because of the non-existence of the self and its objects of perception, has abandoned all mental cultivation on every side, is not seized by the defects born of joy, resentment, and despondency.
Freed from passion and hatred, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal, the yogi who has abandoned the latent impressions of saṃsāra is said to be "yoked."
Whatever he does, whatever he eats, whatever he gives, and whatever he destroys—in all that, his mind being liberated, there is equanimity toward pleasure and pain.

He who, having abandoned the mental construction of the desirable and the undesirable, engages in his duties with the thought that "what has come must simply be done," does not sink into anything whatsoever.
O Mahāmati, the mind that possesses the certainty that "this world is nothing but the mere existence of consciousness," having abandoned the conceit of enjoyment, attains tranquility.
The mind, by its very nature, pursues the principle of consciousness as something inert, just as a cat in the forest pursues a lion out of a craving for meat.
Just as a follower of the lion eats the meat obtained through the power of the lion's prowess, so the mind resorts to the visible world obtained through the power of the vigor of consciousness.
The mind, though thus unreal in its conceptual nature, lives by the grace of consciousness; even consciousness, having become thought, imagines itself as the one universe.
Since that which is inert and utterly devoid of consciousness is like a corpse, how could it—the mind—arise without the power of the lamp of consciousness?

The power of vibration (*spanda-śakti*), which consists of aesthetic relish (*rasa*) and is touched by the very nature of consciousness (*cit-svabhāva*), is described by those with scriptural vision as "mind" (*citta*) through the statement that "mind is conceptualization" (*kalpanā*).
That which is the hissing of the serpent of the mind is called mental construction (kalana); having realized "I am consciousness alone," that [construction] goes toward the mind itself.
That consciousness which is devoid of an object of thought is the eternal Brahman; that same consciousness, when accompanied by an object of thought, is called mental construction (kalana).
That Brahman whose form is slightly touched [by manifestation] is the steady mind; this conceptualization is always present in the heart as if it were truly existent.
As soon as this well-known state called "mind" arises through the emergence of mental construction, it immediately forgets its nature as consciousness and remains established as if it were inert.

It is fully developed and named "conceptualization" (kalanā); it conforms to volitional construction (saṃkalpa), possesses delimitation, is the foremost of speech, and has the nature of things to be rejected or accepted.
This very consciousness, as if having come forth from its own power into the worlds, does not perceive its true form so long as it has not been fully awakened.
Therefore, through inquiry into the scriptures, through supreme dispassion, and through the restraint of the senses, one should personally awaken from the mental construction of the world.
The differentiation of all beings occurs through consciousness and its cessation; when awakened, one attains the state of Brahman, otherwise the world wanders in delusion.
One should awaken only that mental construction which is intoxicated by the wine of delusion, wallowing in the pit of sense-objects, and fast asleep from the lack of self-awareness.
For when this [intellect] is unawakened, it perceives nothing at all; though appearing within as the movement of conceptual construction, it is composed of unreality.
By means of that supreme vision residing within, this mental construction shines forth among all objects, just as the power of fragrance manifests in a flower cluster.
That subtle form which is conceived as "limited cognition" (kalanā) throughout the three worlds indeed knows something, for it has knowledge as its sole inherent attribute.
O Rāma, this insentient mental construction, which takes the form of a stone, is awakened only by the Supreme, just as a lotus is awakened by the sun.
Just as a maiden made of stone does not dance even when urged, so this mental fabrication within the body perceives nothing at all.
Where has a battle with a gurgling roar ever been waged by kings who are but mere painters? And where have medicinal herbs ever been awakened by the rays of the moon?
Where was there the leaping about of corpses with limbs smeared in blood? Where was there singing with sweet tones by fragments of forest stones?
Where is the darkness of night dispelled by the suns created by men? And where is a shadow cast by forests of sky made of mere imagination?
Where can any action be performed by these minds—which are inert like stones, arisen from a burden of false delusion, and consisting of nothing but a mirage?
Just as a river of mirages appears in the vast expanse of sunlight when one's eyes are injured, even so does this mental construction flash forth within the Self as if it were truly real.
Know that this which is called "vibration" has been understood by the cunning as the power of the winds (maruts) residing within the body as the vital breath (prāṇa).
For those whose consciousness is not invaded by the determinations of even a fragment of conceptualization, this supreme self-luminous radiance remains with its aesthetic essence unassailed.
That conceptualization which manifests as "this is I" and "that is mine" with respect to the vital breath (prāṇa) and the principle of the self (ātmatattva) is designated by the term "jīva."
Intellect, mind, and the individual soul—these are considered names for the unreal volition; they are merely conceptualized by those who know that [reality], O Rāma, but not in the ultimate sense.
Neither mind, nor thought, nor intellect, nor even this body exists here in the ultimate sense; only one's own Self exists here at all times.
The Self alone is this entire world, and the Self likewise is the progression of time; it is clearer than space, as if non-existent, yet it truly exists, stainless.

Due to its transparency, it appears as non-existent; yet, by virtue of being the nature of consciousness, it is existent. The Self, which transcends all categories, is experienced through self-experience.
The mind is utterly exhausted where the consciousness of the Supreme Self prevails; there, darkness perishes where light arises.
Where the reflections of self-consciousness are considered to arise from volition, there occurs the forgetting of the Self and the remembering of that which is born of the mind.
The mind of another person is said to consist of volition; liberation arises from that [state] through the absence of volition, which is the state of being without mind.
This much is the birth of the mind—the seed for the perpetuation of saṃsāra—whether it be the consciousness turning toward volitional construction or, as they say, the Self itself.

The existence of the mind, when stained by the mark of conceptualization, is called "differentiation" (kalanā); therefore, the mind is understood to possess masculinity, like the faculty of intellect (buddhi).
O Rāma, when the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti) is restrained, the mind dissolves; for the mental [self] has the form of the vital breath, just as a substance follows the shadow of that substance.
The vital breath (prāṇa), abiding in the heart, perceives the experience of other places; that which [perceives] this through the sensation of vibration is designated as the mind (manas).
Through dispassion, through the practice of the causes, through reasoning, through the destruction of addiction, and through the realization of the ultimate truth, the vital breaths are restrained.
Stones may occasionally possess the power to move or burn; however, minds do not possess the power to initiate motion or cognition.
Vibration is the power of the vital breath and wind; it is essentially mobile and insentient. The power of consciousness, however, is the clarity of its own self; it is eternally all-pervading.

The mind is conceived as the connection between the power of consciousness (cicchakti) and the power of vibration (spandaśakti); having arisen from that [connection], it is indeed false, and that is called false knowledge (mithyājñāna).
This is indeed called ignorance; it is declared to be this *māyā*. This is the supreme nescience that bestows the poison of saṃsāra and the like.
If the conceptualization of volition is not formed through contact with the power of consciousness and the power of vibration, then these fears of worldly existence are utterly destroyed.

When that power of vibration belonging to the wind is perceived by consciousness, it becomes an object of perception; at that very moment, through its internal volitions and so forth, it attains the state of being the mind.
This state of mind is falsely imagined by consciousness, like a ghost conjured by a child; for it is consciousness itself that takes the form of a vibration appearing as an unbroken, circular shape.
How indeed can this very mind be obstructed by anything else? With whom could Indra, whose power is unimpeded, ever engage in combat?
Therefore, due to the absence of related entities, no relationship exists here; without a relationship, for whom is that mind established, and of what nature is it?
In the oneness of consciousness and its vibration, what indeed is called the "mind"? What is an army without the gathering together of horses and elephants?
Therefore, O Rāma, there is no such thing as a wicked mind in the three worlds; this destruction of the mind arises from thorough and correct understanding.
O sinless one, do not thus direct your mind toward what is useless and harmful; the mind arises falsely, for in the ultimate sense, it does not exist here.
O high-minded one, do not form any mental construction whatsoever within; for, O Rāma, the mind that constructs is nowhere to be found here at all.
O Sage, the conceptualization born of incorrect knowledge—like a mirage—has been completely stilled within the desert of your heart through right vision.
Because of its insentience and lack of intrinsic nature, the mind is always as good as dead; yet by that which is dead, the world is killed—wondrous indeed is this cycle of folly!
He who has neither self nor body, neither support nor form—he by whom all this is consumed; wonderful indeed is this snare of ignorance!
I believe that even he who is struck by the mind alone, which lacks all [other] causal conditions, has his head shattered by blows from the petals of blue lotuses.
I believe that fool who is struck even by a mind that is dull, mute, and blind, is scorched by the rays of the full moon.
Even when a hero exists, he is overwhelmed by the world; this [world] that does not even exist is destroyed through the delusion of the ignorant.
Composed of false conceptualizations and having attained a false state of existence, it is not seen even when sought; what power, indeed, can it possibly have?
Ah! How truly wondrous is this illusion-creating artifice; by it, even with a mind exceedingly fickle, this world is utterly overcome.
Folly is that which is pursued by calamities; for what calamity is not known to the ignorant? Behold, this entire creation is produced solely through ignorance on account of folly.
Alas, what a tragedy! Even the creation of the evil-minded has fallen under the sway of folly, since even by this non-existent life is such a thing brought about.
I believe this creation, consisting of ignorance, is exceedingly fragile; it is being shattered into fragments by the flow of the waves of speech.
By the very mechanism of its basin of blue collyrium, it is pulverized; by the touch of the rays of the full-orbed moon, it faints away.
When seen by enemies released from their eyes like threads, he is bound; he is overcome by the army of his own volitions, created by his conceptual constructions.
Therefore, it is said that this [mind] is struck down in vain by another [object] that is imagined—by something else that is wretched and not established anywhere by the mind itself.
This creation, consisting of a world of fools, has arisen from the mind alone as something unreal; he who is unable to bring it under control is not taught by Rāma.
This wisdom, though noble in its nature, is not capable of subtle analysis; it is not fit for the words of instruction, yet it remains as if perfectly complete.
Even this lute fears the slender sound of its stringed wires; it even fears the radiance of the face of its sleeping kinsman.
Even from an unreal person, she flees in terror when their song is raised high; indeed, this ignorant woman has been rendered helpless by her own mind alone.

Overpowered by a mere fragment of pleasure as if by an enemy, and with his intellect impaired by his own heart dwelling within him, he does not know the truth; how then is he so utterly and pointlessly deluded?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O giver of honor, by that very mind which is carried away by the insubstantial waves of the ocean of worldly existence, people have acquired the state of being mute.
In this treatise, that [reality] is not taught by means of these analytical statements, which possess the noble quality of attaining its own nature.
Who indeed would be so wicked-minded as not to see that the forest, with its variegated clusters of blossoms, presents a wondrous sight to one who does not look closely enough?
What senseless person, whose nose is wheezing with leprosy, would—despite lacking discernment for various fragrances—accept as authoritative a fool through his own instruction?
Who of sound mind would accept as authoritative for the determination of the law a witness whose senses are perverted, who is intoxicated, and whose eyes are rolling from wine?
Who would ask a corpse lying in the cremation ground about hundreds of matters of worldly discourse? And who would instruct a fool when doubt arises?

How indeed can one be instructed regarding that serpent of a mind, accompanied by evil thoughts, which has not been conquered even while residing in the cave of one's intentions, though one may be mute and blind?
Know that the mind is already conquered in reality because it does not exist; it is like a stone that is not found even nearby—it has long since ceased to exist.
O Rāma, he by whom the mind—which though non-existent—is conquered by the evil-minded, dies from the stupor of poison as if having swallowed actual venom.
O Rāma, the knower always perceives the Self; the vital energies perceive the throbbing, and the senses perceive their own respective functions—what then can be said of the mind?
The power that causes the vital breaths to vibrate is the power of knowledge belonging to the Supreme Self; it is the innate power of the senses—what single thing here can be bound?
Since all these constituent things belong to that Self who possesses every power, from where indeed has this notion of separateness or expressibility arisen for you?
What indeed is called "jīva," by which this world is blinded? Know that it is merely the mind and is non-existent; what power can it possibly have?
O Rāma, seeing the succession of sufferings of those whose vision has been consumed by their own minds, my heart, overcome with compassion, suffers like a bewildered woman.
What indeed is the cause for distress here, that a fool should suffer? For common people and young camels are born only for the sake of suffering.
Ignorant and foolish beings are born within bodies solely for their own destruction; like bubbles in the ocean, these sinners arise incessantly.
Behold, how many animals are slaughtered every day in every slaughterhouse by those who act like butchers! What lamentation can there be for this?
The wind daily destroys the tumors born within the earth among gadflies and mosquitoes; what cause for lamentation is there in this?
In every direction, upon the lords of mountains and in forest after forest, the Pulindas and others slaughter hundreds of thousands of deer; what lamentation can there be in this?
In the water, a large fish mercilessly tears apart the subtle shoals of aquatic creatures for the sake of a meal; what lamentation can there be in this?
The fly, emaciated by hunger, eats the tiny particles of a louse; the hungry spider eats that fly, and the gadfly eats even that restless spider.
The frog eats that gadfly, and the wild beast eats that frog; the bird kills the fierce serpent, and the mongoose tears that bird to pieces.
The cat kills the mongoose; the dog tears apart the cat; the bear kills the dog; and the tiger tears apart the bear.
The lion overcomes the tiger, and the śarabha devours the lion; yet the śarabha meets its destruction when leaping upon a rutting cloud-elephant.
The clouds are dispersed by the winds, the winds are overcome by the mountains, the mountains are crushed by the thunderbolt; thus the thunderbolt is subject to the will of Śakra.
By Viṣṇu, Śakra is created; Viṣṇu undergoes the state of a living being—this condition of pleasure and pain, governed by old age and death.
For even creatures of massive bodies, though equipped with spells and weapons, are indeed subsisted upon by lice clinging to their limbs.
Thus, this forest of living beings is perpetually being torn asunder and shattered; out of sheer delusion, they devour one another and likewise strive to protect one another.
Various kinds of living beings perish incessantly, and lice, bugs, and ants are born incessantly.
In the reservoirs of water, fish, elephants, sea-monsters, and others are born; within the earth, swarms of insects, scorpions, and the like are produced.
In the intermediate space, birds and other creatures of the sky are born; in the forest paths, lions, tigers, deer, and others are born.
Diverse [insects] are born even within the limbs of living beings in every direction; even among stationary things, wood-boring insects such as the *jaghanaka* and others are born.
Within stones, insects, frogs, woodworms, and the like are born; likewise, various swarms of insects are born even within excrement.
Thus, throughout these countless births and deaths, may those possessed of compassion rejoice or weep incessantly.
In this turmoil of saṃsāra, which is incessantly arising and incessantly passing away, neither contentment nor sorrow is appropriate.
In this very same way, these rows of beings, arising from the abundant birth of all creatures, fly up again and again only to dissolve, like the clusters of leaves upon a tree.
He who, compassionate toward those of evil intellect, has set out to wipe away their suffering, makes the sky weary by erasing the sun's rays with the parasol held over him.
Men on earth who possess the same nature as animals should not be instructed; what purpose would there be in speaking of the meaning of discourse in the presence of a tree stump in the forest?
What indeed is the distinction between those with expansive minds and cattle? Cattle are led by a rope; those of deluded mind are led by their own thoughts.
Seeing the calamity of fools who are submerged in the mud of their own minds and have begun actions leading to their own destruction, even stones weep.
For those who have not conquered their own minds, all conditions bring suffering from every side; therefore, one of perfected wisdom does not engage with them.
O descendant of Raghu, the sufferings of those who have conquered their own minds are to be thoroughly investigated; therefore, having known what is to be known, proceed in this matter.
The mind does not exist, O mighty-armed one; do not imagine it in vain. By this imagination, you are being struck down as if by a vetāla spirit.
As long as you, being deluded, have forgotten the reality of the self, so long has the serpent of your mind remained aroused from within.
Now you have understood it as it truly is, O subduer of enemies: the mind grows from volitional thought; therefore, abandon that very thing immediately.
If you take refuge in this visible world, then you possess a mind bound by kinship; if you renounce this visible world, then you possess a mind that has attained liberation.
This collection of qualities is relied upon only for bondage; when abandoned, it leads to liberation. Therefore, do as you wish.
Meditating that "I am not this" and "this is not I," remain immovable like a mountain; with a heart resembling the infinite sky, you are the Lord of the Heart.
O Rama, my dear friend, having abandoned the impurity of conceptualization regarding yourself and this world—the duality consisting of "I" and "this"—remain perfectly steadfast, abiding in the All.
Within yourself and within the world, amidst the various states of the seer and the seen, always cultivate your own self through that which is called "vision."
Abandoning both the object of taste and the taster, and contemplating the act of tasting alone as it exists between the two, become eternally absorbed in the Self.
Taking as your support that which is devoid of support—the middle way between the object of Rama’s experience and the experiencer himself—remain steadfast in the center.
Free from the cultivation of worldly existence, and abandoned by the states of being and non-being—cultivating the self in this way, remain established in the self. Be yourself.
O Rāma, when you abandon this sense of self-existence and yourself contemplate the object of thought, then you fall into the state of the mind, which brings extreme suffering.
O mighty-armed one, by means of the reasoning that knows its own true nature, release the lion of your own self from this chain of the mind, from the cave of the mind.
When you fall away from the state of the Supreme Self and move excessively toward the object of thought, it is then that you form a mental construction and perceive that object.
O dear one, through the consciousness that the mind is an entity distinct from the Self, the mind becomes afflicted with suffering; yet, by abandoning that [consciousness], it perishes.
When the realization arises within that "this entire world is indeed the Self alone," where is the knower and where is the mind? What is the object of cognition, and what is consciousness itself?
O Rāghava, the wise know that the mere thought "I am the self" or "I am a living being" is what causes this beginningless and endless suffering to expand.
"I am the Self; there are no other entities called 'living beings' anywhere"—this very stilling of the mind is said to be supreme bliss.
O Rāghava, when the certainty arises that "this world is indeed the Self," the non-existence of the mind follows; of this there is no doubt.

When this is realized through the awakening to truth, the state is that "this is indeed one's own self"; know that the mind has completely dissolved, just as darkness vanishes before the light of the sun.
As long as the serpent of the mind remains within the body, there is great fear; once it has been expelled through yoga, whence can there be any occasion for fear?
O sinless one, this exceedingly powerful vampire that has arisen from mere delusion within the mind must be forcibly cast down by means of the mantra of perfect knowledge.
When the yakṣa of the mind has departed from the house of the body, O best among the powerful, remain free from mental anguish and devoid of agitation; there is no fear for you.

"Thinking 'I am indeed free from passion and free from acquisition,' by this much alone the existence of your mind has dissolved. You have reached the supreme state, the highest goal, which is free from suffering; remain thus within, with all seeking utterly stilled."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, following this impure existence of the mind—the seed-syllable of saṃsāra and the snare that binds the individual soul—[one remains entangled].
The Self, having abandoned its own true nature, assumes a defiled appearance; it aligns itself with that perception and maintains the impurity of conceptualization.
Bestowing increasing great delusion and causing fear, craving—in the form of a poisonous creeper—brings about only fainting.
Whenever it arises, this craving—which bestows great delusion, is like the dark night, and causes the infinite self to undergo transformation—manifests.
Hara and the other gods are capable of enduring the burning of the flames of the fire at the end of an aeon; but no one at all is capable of enduring the burning of the flames of the fire of craving.
Sharp, black, and very long, it constantly carries away one's own limb; cold yet resulting in unhappiness, this terrible sword of craving is truly dreadful.
O Rāghava, those fruits of the creeper of craving—which are terminal, difficult to digest, and elevated—are these very sufferings here in this world.
Invisible, this hound of the forest of craving, hidden within the cave of the mind, devours the flesh, bones, blood, and other parts of the body of men.
The river of craving, though dull-witted, suddenly bursts its banks; in one moment it reaches a state of exaltation, and in the next it falls into emptiness.
Seeing his wretchedness, his heart struck down and his vigor destroyed, a person succumbs to baseness; overcome by craving, he becomes deluded, cries out, and falls.
The vital breaths moving within the cavity of the heart remain healthy for that man in whose hollow the black serpent of craving does not dwell.
Surely, wherever the dark night of craving has set, there merits increase like moons in the bright fortnight.
That tree of a man which has not been gnawed by the woodworm of craving always reaches a state of full bloom through the flowers of merit.
In the forest of the mind, the river of men blinded by craving flows on, filled with infinite and turbulent waves, and crowded with eddies and whirlpools.
Driven by craving, all these people are whirled about, shattered, and repeatedly gathered together, like birds on the strings of a mechanical puppet.
Craving, harsh due to its hard disposition, leaps forth like the edge of an axe and cuts down even the most subtle roots.
The deluded person, pursuing craving, falls into a pit, just as a young deer, following a blue blade of grass or a branch, falls into a chasm.
Even when one is not intoxicated, old age thus destroys the eye in an instant, just as emaciating thirst, which dwells within the heart, causes decay.
Through the deep-rooted and inauspicious craving of Kauśikī, which has taken hold in his heart, this Blessed One Viṣṇu has assumed the form of a dwarf.
Indeed, by this very thirst, which is somehow knotted within the heart by fate, one wanders through the sky day after day, as if bound by a rope, like the sun.
One who has gone far away should abandon craving—which consists of all forms of suffering and cuts short the life of the world—just as one would avoid a cruel female serpent.
By craving the winds blow; by craving the mountains stand firm; by craving alone the earth supports all; by craving the three worlds are sustained.
This entire course of worldly existence is strung together by the cord of craving; no one is ever released from the bond of craving, just as one is not released from the bond of a rope.
Therefore, O Raghava, abandon craving by relinquishing mental constructs; for it has been determined through reasoning that the mind does not exist when there is no conceptualization.
O mighty-armed one, first direct this evil desire, composed of darkness, toward me within your heart, thinking "this is you" and "this is I."
O Rāma, if you do not cultivate this notion of self in what is not-self—which gives birth to suffering—then you shall be counted among those who know reality.

O fortunate one, having severed this unmeritorious state consisting of the sense of "I" by means of the very probe of the "not-I," you shall reach the ground that ends existence, with all fear for living beings overcome by the mastery over becoming.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, these words of yours are profound by their very nature, in that you tell me, "Do not grasp at the thirst of egoism."
O Lord, if I were to renounce the ego-sense, then I would abandon this entire configuration known as the body without remainder.
Just as a great tree is supported by its massive trunk, so indeed is this body supported by the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
When the ego-sense perishes, the body indeed necessarily perishes, like a massive tree when its root is severed by a saw.
O Sage, best among speakers, having deliberated upon this matter, tell me: how may I abandon him, and how may I live?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O lotus-eyed Rāma, bestower of honor, the abandonment of latent impressions (vāsanā) in all respects is described by the knowers of truth as being twofold: that which is to be known and that which is to be meditated upon.
"I belong to these objects, and they are my very life; I am nothing at all without them, and they, it is said, cannot exist without me."
Having thus formed an internal certainty and deliberated with the mind, one contemplates: "I am not the object, nor does the object belong to me."
O Rāma, that which is truly the abandonment of latent impressions—performed with ease by a mind that is cool within—is declared to be the object of meditation.

Having understood everything through equanimity and having brought about the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), one who is free from the sense of "mine" abandons the body; this is to be known as the exhaustion of latent impressions.
Having effortlessly abandoned the latent impression consisting of egoism, he who remains as one who has renounced all objects of meditation is called liberated while living.

O descendant of Raghu, know that he who has attained tranquility by abandoning all rootless mental constructions and latent impressions, and who consists of the relinquishment of the knowable, is truly liberated.

Having abandoned all latent impressions (vāsanā), those great-souled and virtuous ones, such as Janaka and others, remain in a state of effortless ease, having that very abandonment as their object of meditation; they are liberated while living.

But having abandoned latent impressions (vāsanā) and attained tranquility, those who have realized the Knowable remain as liberated-in-body (videhamukta) within Brahman, both the higher and the lower.

O Raghava, there are only two kinds of renunciation that are equal and established in the state of liberation; both of these have attained the nature of Brahman, and both are free from the fever of worldly distress.
O sinless one, when the mind is settled in the pure and solitary Self, one remains with a throbbing body, while the other remains with a tranquil body.

One remains with the body, liberated and free from the fever of suffering; the other, having abandoned the body, exists as one who is fully emancipated and whose latent impressions are no longer knowable.
He who neither rejoices nor desponds when pleasure and pain incessantly arrive in their due time is said to be liberated.
He for whom neither desire nor aversion exists toward desired or undesired objects, and who moves about like one in deep sleep—he is said to be liberated.
He whose internal notions of "mine," "I," and "here" have completely perished regarding the calculation of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, is called one liberated while living.
He who is not internally touched by joy, resentment, fear, anger, desire, miserliness, or [wrong] views is said to be liberated while living.

He who always remains awake with a mind whose mental fluctuations have been stilled as if in deep sleep, and who is constantly attended by joy like the moon joined with its digits—he is remembered here as one who is liberated.

Śrī Vālmīki said: When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, those who are liberated while in the body do not at all remain within the range of my speech; therefore, listen to this liberation while living.
When ordinary actions are performed with a desire that has been abandoned by craving, the wise know this state to be liberation while living.
The teachers say that the state of a living being who remains with an attachment bound to external objects through craving is bondage—a firm shackle to saṃsāra.
Surely that latent impression which has abandoned all volitional thought, yet continues to dwell within the heart and externally, is here called the "embodied one liberated while living."
"O Raghava, craving that is swollen by the calamity of external objects is said to be bound; craving that is liberated from the calamity of all objects is called liberated."
That craving which, even while present, has been eternally free from suffering and devoid of fragmentation since the past is remembered by the wise as liberation.
"O Raghava, know that this internal notion, 'let this be mine,' is craving; O high-minded one, know it to be a chain and a mental construction."
Having forever renounced this [notion] regarding all things, whether they exist or do not exist, the noble-minded one, supremely magnanimous, attains the ultimate state.

Having abandoned the hope for bondage and the hope for liberation, as well as the states of pleasure and pain, and even the hope for existence and non-existence, remain like the unagitated great ocean.
O best among the wise, seeing yourself as undecaying and immortal, do not let your mind be troubled by fears of old age and death.

This reality of the categories of existence does not belong to you, nor are you this, O Rāghava; that [reality] is something entirely different, and you yourself, O Rāghava, are someone else entirely.

When all that is non-existent has arisen and all that is existent has come to rest within You, who have transcended the state of being—that which is both being and non-being—whence can there be the arising of craving?
Furthermore, O virtuous Rāma, as a person reflects in his mind, a fourfold determination of vast scope arises within him.
"From head to foot, I am created by my mother and father"—this is the single conviction, O Rāma, which leads to bondage through the perception of what is unreal.
"I am subtler than even the tip of a hair, transcending all existing things"—such is the second firm conviction that arises in the wise for the sake of liberation.
"I am the very soul of all things in the web of the world, the imperishable All"—this third conviction, O scion of Raghu, leads indeed to liberation.
"I, or the entire world, am always empty and equal to space"—this is another, the fourth certainty, for the attainment of liberation.
Among these four certainties, the first is said to lead to bondage; the other three, arising from pure contemplation, are declared to lead to liberation.
Of these, the first is said to be the state of being bound by craving; the three types of pure craving are clear and belong to those who sport as liberated-while-living.
O Mahāmati, my mind, having taken hold of the certainty that "I alone am all this," no longer goes toward despondency.
The greatness of the Self pervades horizontally, upwards, and downwards; by the internal conviction that "all is the Self," one is not bound.
That which is empty is its nature, illusion, and also the consciousness of Brahman; it is likewise called Śiva, Puruṣa, Īśāna, and the eternal Self.
All this is always indeed Being; here, duality or anything else is never found anywhere. The world is pervaded by knowledge, and not by any other cognition.
The ocean, whose self is infinite, has filled the space down to the netherworld with its waters; the entire world, from Brahma down to a blade of grass, is filled by the Self.
Therefore, truth alone is real and eternal; falsehood is never found anywhere. Just as the entire ocean is but water, waves and the like do not exist anywhere apart from it.
Just as bracelets, armlets, anklets, and so forth are not distinct from gold, nor are millions of forms such as trees and grass different from the self.
Through the play of creating the world by means of the distinctions between duality and non-duality, the power that consists of the Supreme Self manifests as nothing but non-duality itself.
Regarding everything—whether belonging to yourself or to others—at all times, whether that object has perished or increased, do not grasp at pleasure or pain.
Relying on the non-duality of existence and having the nature of the non-duality of being, disregard the non-duality of action and become one who embodies both duality and non-duality.
Do not fall, amidst the terrifying stages of existence, into the caves filled with calamities by means of the whirlwind of conceptualizing phenomena, like an elephant inside a cave.

O Great-Souled One, duality consisting of the mind is not possible; nor is unity within the Self, for the nature of the Self does not arise from duality. Non-duality is devoid of unity, eternally manifest, the Reality; therefore, they say that the true nature of all things is neither this nor that.

Neither do I exist, nor indeed do the worlds exist; yet all this that appears is surely changeless. It is mere consciousness that shines forth as peace; know that this world is neither non-existent nor existent, yet it is called "existent."

The supreme nectar, beginningless, the illumination of all illuminations, undecaying, unborn, inconceivable, partless, and changeless; free from the web of the senses, the life-force of the vital energy (*jīvaśakti*), devoid of all mental constructs, it is the cause of all causes.

O Lord, you are eternally joyful, established in the expansive light of consciousness, the seed of all experience, and to be taught as one's own true nature. Within you, the Brahman, there is always the tasting of all things—whether "you," "I," or the "world"—in a state that is not subject to worldly conditions; may this certainty dwell within me.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O mighty-armed one, this is the natural disposition of great souls whose intentions are disciplined, who move here in this world with ease, and who are not affected by false views.
Even while dwelling in saṃsāra, the sage whose mind is liberated while living should laugh at the worldly courses of existence, which are tasteless in their beginning, middle, and end.
Established in all ordinary activities, remaining impartial toward all views, he is to be meditated upon as one who stands firm, having relied upon the abandonment of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Free from agitation in all circumstances, nourishing all goals, having seen the self through the light of solitude, he dwells in the grove of awakening.
Taking as his support the state that transcends all things, with a mind as cool as the full moon, neither agitated nor overly elated, he does not despair within saṃsāra.
Remaining impartial toward all enemies, endowed with compassion and courtesy, and performing his duties as they arise, he does not perish in this world among the foremost of men.
He neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor desires; established in silence, initiating only what is natural, he does not sink in saṃsāra.
When questioned, he speaks of the matter at hand; when not questioned, he remains like a pillar. Free from both likes and dislikes, he does not sink in the cycle of existence.
One who speaks what is agreeable to all, who is eloquent when exhorted, and who understands the intentions of living beings, does not sink in the cycle of existence.
One who perceives what is appropriate and inappropriate knows that the world, its activities ruined by craving, is like a bilva fruit inside the hollow of a hand.
Having ascended to the supreme state, he gazes upon the fragile condition of the world as if laughing, with an intellect that is inwardly cooled.
O Raghava, you have been told that such is the inherent nature of those great-souled ones who have conquered their minds and have seen both the higher and the lower.
But as for us, we do not know the intended opinion of those fools whose own minds are unsubdued and who are submerged in the mire of sensual enjoyments.
The women desired by them were adorned with both existence and non-existence; they were the very flames of the fires of hell, yet possessed the luster of gold.
Meanings are dense with purposelessness, consisting of the torment of vain and harmful ends; they point toward the onset of suffering and cast down calamities on every side.
We are unable to describe those actions, which are joined with their fruits, consist of various modes of conduct, and are filled with pleasure and pain.

Firmly grasping the full vision that delights in the relinquishment of all objects of meditation, remain established in yourself through the state of liberation while living, and wander in the world, O Rāghava.
Internally having renounced all expectations, free from passion and devoid of latent impressions, yet externally maintaining all conventional conduct, wander in the world, O Rāghava.
Noble, of refined conduct, and following all proper behavior, yet inwardly renouncing everything—wander thus in the world, O Rāghava.
Having investigated all the stages and having taken as your object through true resolve that supreme state which is not insignificant, dwell in the world, O Rāghava.
Having taken up inner hopelessness while directing your outward actions toward hope, being scorched on the outside yet cooled within, wander in the world, O Rāghava.
Displaying outwardly a feigned agitation while being inwardly free from all agitation, act as an agent on the outside but remain a non-agent within; thus, O Rāghava, move about in this world.
You have thoroughly understood the inner nature of all things; therefore, O Rāghava, wander in the world according to your will, with such a vision.
Abiding in feigned enthusiasm and joy, expressing feigned agitation and reproach, and manifesting feigned exertion and zeal, wander in the world, O Rāghava.
Having abandoned egoism, with a mind at peace and as radiant as the sky, wander through the world, O Rāghava, free from the mark of blemish.
Freed from hundreds of bonds of desire, equanimous in all conditions of life, and engaged in outward worldly duties, wander in the world, O Raghava.
From the perspective of ultimate reality, there is neither bondage nor liberation for the embodied being; this revolving cycle of saṃsāra is a false display of magical illusion.
O Rāghava, this world is seen as mere delusion arising from ignorance, appearing vast and producing conviction, like water in the intense heat of the sun.
How could there be bondage for the Self, which is unbound, uniform, and all-pervading? And in the absence of that [bondage], for whom would liberation be prescribed?
This vast delusion of saṃsāra arises from the non-knowledge of reality; it comes to an end through the knowledge of reality, just as the perception of a snake in a rope vanishes.
You have realized the truth by yourself through a single, subtle intellect; you have become free from egoism, so remain stainless like the sky.
Since you are thus a knower, abandon all these latent impressions of friends and kinsmen; for what indeed can be the cultivation of that which is of an unreal nature?
Moreover, by this very fact, you are inferred to be possessed of courage, even more so than from the highest cause; this was obtained first.
The self has no connection with enjoyments, kinsmen, worldly states, or auspicious and inauspicious actions; why then do you grieve for these?

O Rāma, for you whose mind has arisen with the realization that "I am one whose sole essence is the reality of the Self," there is no connection with fears; why then do you fear the delusion of the world?
O Raghava, since your kinsman is unborn, what connection do you have with him through the delusions of his kinship's joys and sorrows, that you should mourn for these?
If you existed in the past, so will you exist now; you have understood with certainty that you are standing here this very day.
Why do you not grieve for the many other kinsmen who have passed away—those such as Prāṇa and others who were situated nearby and immediately preceding you?
O Rāma, if you were one thing in the past, yet have become another now, and will likewise become something else in the future, then why do you, who are of such a true nature, become deluded?
Even if you did not exist in the past, do not exist today, and will not exist again in the future, nevertheless, since your cycle of existence has been exhausted, why do you grieve?
Therefore, sorrow is not appropriate for one following the ordinary worldly course; likewise, joy is appropriate, as it is fitting to act in accordance with what must be done.
Do not go to sorrow, O Rāma, nor even to happiness; attain equanimity toward everything, for the Supreme Self is all-pervading.
You are infinite, the very nature of existence, with an inner expanse as vast as the sky; you are light, eternally pure, like the hollow interior of flames.
With a body whose nature is unseen by worldly objects, you reside within the heart, spread out like the single thread of pearls in a necklace.
This very state of saṃsāra is that which, having come into being, comes into being again; it belongs only to the ignorant, not to the knower. O Rāma, you are a knower; be happy.
O you of noble mind, you have realized that this very nature of cyclic existence, which is perpetually distressing, expands through ignorance.
What else could form (rūpa) be, apart from mere delusion, within delusion? For what other sequence can there be in a dream, apart from the dream itself?
O Rāma, this power of the All-Powerful is thus composed of mere delusion; yet this extremely radiant manifestation is indeed perceived.
Who might be the enemy of anyone here? No one at all. For by the will of the Lord of All, everyone is always everything to everyone.
This entire world, cut down and shattered, yet mutually dependent, flows incessantly like a torrent of waves upon the water.
Then it moves from the upper state to the lower, and likewise from the lower to the upper; thus it revolves all around this unstable cycle of existence, like the rim of a wheel.
Those dwelling in heaven go to hell, and those in hell go to the third heaven; living beings pass from one womb to another, and from one continent to another.
The wise fall into wretchedness, while the wretched attain steadfastness; living beings flutter about in the confusion of hundreds of falls and rises.
A wheel that is uniform in form, stable, transparent, and free from distress—nothing such as this can be found here, just as a grain of frost cannot remain in fire.
Indeed, those very many illustrious kinsmen who are seen have all perished within just a few days.
O mighty-armed one, the cultivation of notions such as "otherness," "one's own," "difference," "thou-ness," and "I-ness" is not real here, just like the vision of two moons and so forth.
"‘This one is a kinsman and that one is a stranger; this is I and this is you’—O Rāma, let such false views now fall away from you."
Engaged in worldly affairs for the sake of play with these [senses] whose vision is destroyed—move about outwardly with ease, while they are cut away from the very root within.
O you of noble vows, conduct yourself in this state of wandering through saṃsāra in such a way that you are not exhausted by fatigue, as if carrying the burden of latent tendencies (vāsanā).
In whatever measure this inquiry of yours arises, which brings about the destruction of latent impressions regarding all activities, in that same measure they are pacified.
"This one is a kinsman, this one is not"—such is the calculation of those with small minds; but for those of noble conduct, the intellect is indeed free from all obscuration.
"There is nothing where I am not, and there is nothing that is not mine"—having thus resolved, the intellect of the wise is indeed free from all obscurations.
He who is as vast as space neither sets nor rises; established in himself, he perceives everything, just as one standing on level ground sees the surface of the earth.
For indeed, O Rāma, all these classes of beings are your kinsmen; yet, O Rāma, none of them are ever truly joined with you.

In this world, where confusion has been accumulated through hundreds of diverse births, the perception of "friend" and "enemy" is merely the state of delusion that flutters about; in reality, the three worlds are neither long-term friends nor enemies.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In this very context, they cite this ancient history, the conversation between two sons of sages on the banks of the triple-pathed river (Gaṅgā).
"O Raghava, listen to this meritorious and wonderful history, which is remembered from the context of the discussion as to who is a kinsman and who is not."
In a certain mountain glade of this Jambūdvīpa, there is a mountain named Mahendra, the great crest-ornament of the forest array.
He whose lofty peaks reached out into the sky, where sages and kinnaras rested in the shade of groves of wish-fulfilling trees, surpassed even the heavens in height.
It seems to sing as it were, through the resonant *ghuṃghum* sounds of the Sāma Veda echoing from the peaks and caves frequented by those who have reached the intermediate realms of Brahmā’s world.
He who shines with clouds thick with water, shimmering upon the tips of his peaks like locks of hair entwined with the flowers of creepers.
With the gaping mouths of its caves, it thunders as if laughing at the clouds of the cosmic dissolution, while the yawns of the śarabhas, eager to leap upward from within, resound.
By means of the roar of its waterfalls flowing through the interior of the caves, it completely surpassed the playful splendor of the waves of the ocean's waters.
On a delightful, expansive jeweled peak of that mountain, the celestial Gaṅgā was brought down by sages for the purpose of bathing and drinking.
On the bank of that triple-pathed river, where the trees were in full bloom, it shone upon the slopes of a mountain of jewels, glowing with the golden-yellow hue of shimmering gold.
There was a sage named Dīrghatapas, whose wisdom had fully dawned, who was a mass of asceticism, and possessed noble intellect; he was like another asceticism incarnate.
That sage had two sons, as beautiful as the moon, named Puṇya and Pāvana, like the two hairs on the head of Bṛhaspati.
Together with his two sons and his one wife, he dwelt on the bank of that river, which was lined with fruit-bearing trees.
Then, in the course of time, one of those two sons became possessed of knowledge; O Raghava, he who was the elder, named Puṇya, was also the most eminent in virtue.
He became half-awakened like a lotus at the morning twilight; having reached the state through folly, he remained wavering, not having attained it.
Then, when immeasurable time had elapsed, the cause of calculation having been reckoned, and when a hundred years had passed—during which the lifespan of his long, vine-like body had withered away.
Abandoning delight in this cycle of existence, which is filled with fragile beings and terrifying with its hundreds of calamities, he whose life is worn out by old age [should depart].
The sage Dīrghatapas abandoned his body—the nest of the bird of time—within the dwelling of a mountain cave, just as a porter casts off a burden.

He attained that passionless state, the abode of consciousness devoid of objects of thought, where all mental constructions and their stirrings have been stilled, just as the fragrance of a flower pervades the sky.
Then the sage’s wife, seeing his body on the ground, deprived of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and the downward breath (apāna), tossed about like a lotus without its stalk.
Through the practice of yoga long cultivated and perfected by her husband, she cast off her unfading body, just as a female bee leaves a lotus.
Having vanished from the sight of the people, she followed her husband alone, like the light within the expanse of the sky following the moon that has set.
When his parents had passed away, Pavana remained unperturbed while performing their funeral rites; established in merit alone, he experienced sorrow.
With his mind struck by grief, wandering through the forest paths and not seeing his elder brother, Pāvana lamented.
Then, having performed the funeral rites for his parents, the noble-minded and virtuous one returned to the forest, which was purifying yet filled with the intensity of his grief.
Puṇya said: "Why, my son, do you bring grief to such intensity—a cause solely for blindness—as a terrible autumn cloud brings tears to a lotus?"
O one of great wisdom, your father, together with your mother, has gone to that very state of the Supreme Self which is called liberation.
That is the station of all beings, that is the form of those who have conquered themselves; since you have attained your own true nature, why do you grieve for your father?
Such a delusion-born conception has been formed by you here in this world, that you grieve for your father, who is not even to be grieved for within the cycle of existence.
She alone was not your mother, nor was he alone your father; you were not the only son of those two who had countless children.
O son, thousands of mothers and fathers have passed away for you, like many watercourses flowing down through forest after forest.
"Even though you have countless sons, you alone are not their son; O son, the multitudes of sons of men pass away like the waves of a river."
Countless hundreds of thousands of sons have passed away from our parents, like the leaves, buds, and stalks of a creeper upon its branches.
In birth after birth, the multitudes of friends and kinsmen pass away for a living being, just as the fruits of a great tree fall season after season.
O son, if parents and children are to be mourned out of affection, why then are those who have passed away by the thousands not mourned incessantly?
O illustrious one, this proliferation is seen within the delusion of the world; in ultimate reality, O wise one, you have neither friend nor kinsmen.
For destruction, O brother, does not exist in the ultimate sense, just as drops of water do not exist in a vast desert, even after it has been scorched for a long time.
O one of great intelligence, these splendors you behold, flickering with parasols and chowries, are merely a dream for three or five days.
But with the ultimate vision, my son, investigate the truth: neither you nor we are at all possessed of delusion; therefore, abandon it.
"‘This one has gone,’ ‘this one is dead’—such wrong views appear before us, arising from the fever of one’s own conceptual constructions, but they do not exist in reality."
In the vast desert of ignorance, this water of mirage—consisting of the waves of the flow of good and evil, together with latent predispositions—shimmers forth in infinite forms.
Puṇya said: Who is a father, what is a friend, who is a mother, and who are kinsmen? By one's own intelligence alone they are shaken away, just as the dust of the earth is dispersed by a whirlwind.
This conceptual proliferation is extended merely by one's own mental labeling, consisting of the states of affection, hatred, delusion, and so forth toward kinsmen and friends.

One who is cultivated as a kinsman becomes a kinsman; one who is cultivated as a stranger becomes a stranger. In this world, one's state of existence is bound by cultivation, like the conditions of poison and nectar.
Since the Self exists as a single, all-pervading entity, how can there be such a conceptualization as "this one is a kinsman" and "that one is a stranger"?
"O son, investigate within yourself with your own mind: 'Who am I?'—apart from this body, a mere collection of blood, flesh, and bones, a cage of skeletal framework."
But from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is neither you nor am I; it is only through false cognition that one exults, thinking, "This is merit" or "This is purifying."
Who is one's father, who is a friend, who is one's mother, or who is a stranger? In this infinite play of space, what may be called "not one's own" and what may be called "one's own"? Please tell me.
If you are such [a person], then when those others have passed away through many births, why do you not grieve for those who were your kinsmen and your riches?
On the flower-laden plains and in the animal wombs, you had many kinsmen and paths; why do you not grieve for them?
Those swans, the kinsmen of Haṃsa, dwelt upon those lotus-ponds with their flowering banks; why do you not grieve for them?
Your many kinsmen, the trees, have become sufficient for you elsewhere in the variegated forest groves; why do you not grieve for them?
Upon the most formidable peaks of the mountains, you had many lion kinsmen; why do you not grieve for them?
In the rivers, lakes, and lotus ponds, you had many kinsmen in the form of fish; why do you not grieve for them?
In the Daśārṇas you became a brown forest monkey; in Tuṣāra you were a prince, and in Puṇḍra a wild crow.
Among the Haihayas he was Mātaṅga; among the Trigartas, a donkey; among the Śālvas, the son of Saramā; and in the Sarala tree, a bird.

Having become a *pippala* tree on the Vindhya mountain, and having become a wood-boring insect in a great banyan tree, and having become a cock on Mount Mandara, you have now been born as a brahmin in a mountain cave.
Having been a twice-born man among the Kosalas, having been a partridge among the Vaṅgas, and having been a horse among the Tuṣāras, you were born at the sacrifice of Brahmā.
He who was a worm within the stalk of a palmyra tree, he who was a gnat in an udumbara fruit, and he who was a crane in the Vindhya forest—O son, you are that very one, my younger brother.
That ant which, for six months, dwelt within the hollow of a knot on the thin bark of a birch tree in a cave of the Himalayas—that very one is you, my younger brother.
O virtuous one, that scorpion which remained for a year and a half in the cow-dung of the village of Sīmāntaka is this very younger brother of mine.
He by whom you were embraced upon the breasts of the Pulinda women in the forest, like a bee upon lotuses—he is this very younger brother of mine.
O dear son, in these and many other births among various species, you have been born hundreds of thousands of times in this Jambūdvīpa in the past.
Thus, with a subtle intellect purified by right vision, I perceive the sequence of your own past latent impressions.
Many diverse wombs of mine, slowed by delusion, have passed away; today I remember them with a vision awakened by knowledge.
Having been a parrot among the Trigartas, having been a frog on a riverbank, and having been a quail in the forests, I have now been born here in this grove.

Having experienced the state of a Pulinda in the Vindhya mountains, and having become a tree among the Vaṅgas, I have even attained the form of a camel on the Vindhya mountain, and am now born here in this forest.
He who was the Cātaka bird on the Snowy Mountain, he who was the king in the Pauṇḍra region, and he who was the tiger in the thickets of the Sahya mountains—that very person am I, your elder brother.
He who was a vulture for ten years, he who was a crocodile for five months, and he who was a lion for a hundred years—he is indeed your elder brother here.
I, the partridge of the village of Āndhra, the king among those who have shed their impurities, the son of the teacher of Śrīśaila, relate this as if it were a mere display of artifice.
I remember all my various past lives in diverse realms of existence, with their manifold conducts and activities, as well as the playful diversions of birth and wandering.
This being the case, hundreds of kinsmen born within this world have passed away—fathers, mothers, brothers, and likewise friends.
Whom do we grieve for together, and whom do we not grieve for at all? We grieve excessively for our kinsmen; such indeed is the course of the world.
Infinite fathers pass away, and infinite mothers pass away, like the leaves of trees in a forest for men wandering here in saṃsāra.
Therefore, my son, what measure can there be here for either suffering or happiness? Consequently, having abandoned everything and attained clarity, let us both remain thus.
Having abandoned the mental cultivation of conceptual proliferation and the "I" established in the mind, go to that state—may you be blessed—to which those skilled in the goal proceed.
In this world, the wise do not grieve over the state of constant flux—this coming and going consisting of falling and rising—but rather they simply dance for a long time.
Free from existence and non-existence, devoid of old age and death—remember your own self with an undistracted mind; do not let your intellect become deluded.
For you there is no suffering, no birth, no mother, and no father; you are indeed the Self itself, for when the Buddha is truly realized, you are not anyone else at all.
In this journey through saṃsāra, only those who are ignorant are truly endowed with the noble sentiment, for they provide various dramatic performances.
Those with impartial vision, established in their own nature, seeing things exactly as they have been attained, are indeed observers who abide by the duty of witnesses regarding that knowledge.

Just as lamps at the onset of night are not considered "doers" with respect to the act of illuminating, so too those who know that [reality] are not "doers" regarding the maintenance of the world here.
Just as mirrors, gems, and the like do not appear as reflections even when situated within their own reflected images, so too do those of great intelligence not appear within their effects.

Free from the stain of the disease of all cravings, established in your own healthy self-nature within the center of the heart-lotus—O son, by means of this very Self, abandon all agitation and attain perfect contentment within yourself.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus enlightened by that holy man, Pāvana then attained awakening and clarity, like the surface of the earth at dawn.
Then both of them, having attained perfection and having reached the further shore of knowledge and discernment, wandered blamelessly through that forest for as long as they desired.
Then, after some time, those two from Videha, having reached the state of Nirvana and being free from all attachment, attained tranquility like extinguished lamps.
In this way, for bodies previously experienced, there has been an infinite succession of people and kinsmen; alas, O sinless one, what can be grasped from them, or what can be abandoned?
Therefore, O descendant of Raghu, for these endless cravings, the only remedy is their abandonment; certainly not their preservation.
Thought increases through further thinking, just as fire grows with fuel; it perishes through the absence of thought, like a flame without fuel.
Mounted upon the chariot of abandoning all objects of meditation, beholding the world with a gaze noble with compassion for those in distress, remain steadfast; arise, O Raghava!
This is the pure state of Brahman—free from desire and devoid of affliction; having attained this, O mighty-armed one, even one who was deluded is no longer bewildered.
Taking solitude as his friend and a mature intellect as his sole companion, he who wanders even amidst difficulties is not deluded.
When all means of rescue have been blocked and kinsmen have been cast aside, no one can deliver one from such a crisis except through one's own fortitude.
Then, through detachment, by means of the scriptures, and also by means of qualities such as greatness, one should personally elevate the mind with effort for the sake of overcoming calamities.
Neither from sovereignty over the three worlds, nor from a treasury filled with jewels, is such a fruit obtained as that which is derived from a mind augmented by greatness.
In this belly of the world, while men fall through the tossing and swinging of rising and falling, may their minds indeed be free from fever.
When the mind is full, the entire world becomes filled with the flow of nectar; for one whose feet are shod with sandals, the earth is indeed as if covered with leather.
Through dispassion, the mind, following the power of its own dissolution, attains fullness; through desire, it attains emptiness, just as a lake loses its impurities in autumn.
The heart becomes empty, its hollow exposed, like the ocean swallowed by Agastya, for those whose minds are rendered helpless by their desires.
He in whose vast mind-tree the restless monkey of craving does not leap, his heart-forest, though extensive, shines with great majesty.
To those whose minds are free from longing, the three worlds are but the calyx of a lotus seed, a distance of a league is but a cow’s footprint, and a great eon is but half a blink of an eye.
That coolness is not found in the moon, nor in the caves of the Himalayas, nor in rows of plantain trees or sandalwood; it resides only in minds free from desire.
Neither does the full moon shine thus, nor the full ocean of milk, nor the lovely face of Lakṣmī, as does the mind free from longing.
Just as a cloud-streak defiles the moon, or as ink defiles a surface smeared with nectar, even so does the demoness of desire corrupt a man within.
The branches of the tree of the mind, known as hopes, cover the horizons; when these are severed, the great tree of the mind returns to its true nature.
When the mind, which is like a tree trunk, comes to rest upon the great branch of severed craving, fortitude—though previously of a single form—attains a hundredfold branching.
O Rāma, when the mind has reached its dissolution through that undiminished fortitude, that state is attained wherein no destruction exists.
O Rāghava, if you do not allow these mental fluctuations and desires to take root within your supreme disposition, then there will be no fear.
When your mind, devoid of fluctuations, has attained the state of no-mind, then you reach that pervasive inner existence which consists of liberation.
O Rāghava, when the mind is agitated within by the bird-like *kauśika* of craving, inauspicious things come forth in abundance and impurity.

Thinking is said to be the activity; the mind functions through its latent tendencies (*āśaya*). Therefore, having abandoned the hope of one who possesses mental activity, proceed to the state of mindlessness (*niścittatā*).
