Whoever exists by means of a particular mode of activity perishes without that very mode; therefore, for the sake of the mind's tranquility, bring that mode of activity to its complete cessation.

O Great-Souled One, having stilled all desires and cast off the bonds of existence, become one whose mind is liberated; for when the wicked hopes that are the ropes of fetters have dissolved away from the mind, who is not liberated?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Or else, O full moon in the sky of the lineage of Raghu, may you attain stainless knowledge through the transformation of the intellect, just like Bali.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, by your grace, everything that was to be attained has been attained within my heart, and it rests in the stainless state."
O Lord, like a cloud from the sky in autumn, that great darkness called craving has entirely departed from my mind.
Filled with nectar, established in my own self, cool-natured and of great luster, I abide within, full of bliss, like the lord of stars at full moon in the evening.
O autumn season for the clouds of all my doubts, yet I do not reach satiety with these words as you speak.
O All-pervading Lord, tell me again of Bali’s attainment of higher knowledge for the sake of increasing my own awakening; for the virtuous do not grow weary of one who is humble.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen, O Rāghava, I shall tell you the supreme account of Bali; by hearing which, you will attain that eternal awakening to reality.
Within this treasury of the world, in a certain corner of the quarters, there exists a realm situated beneath the earth, renowned as Pātāla.
With female elephants born from the Ocean of Milk, with moon-like maidens, and in some places with the daughters of the Dānavas, it shines with no space between them.
In some places it was filled with serpents possessing hundreds of heads, their pairs of flickering tongues emitting fierce sounds from the tips of their tongues.
In some places it was filled with the sons of Danu, who, like moving Mount Merus, were voracious in their efforts to uproot the entire universe encircled by the mountain ranges of their bodies.

In some places, it was resorted to by the elephants of the quarters, whose massive bodies rested upon the peaks of the Kumbha mountain, their bellies as vast as the circle of the earth, and whose tusks were like trees growing on mountains.

In some places, there were circles of lower hells, terrifying with foul-smelling spirits and successions of beings terrified by the great *kaṭakaṭa* sound; in others, they were fearsome with spirits of putrid odor.
It was covered from the surface of the earth down to the seven circles of the netherworld (pātāla), being in some places filled with oceans of jewels as if by openings into the subterranean realms.
In one place, it was sanctified by that Blessed One, Kapila, with the dust from his lotus feet, upon which the heads of gods and asuras had rested.
In one place, he was protected by that Blessed One Hāṭakeśa, who desired the worship and play of infinite beings brought together by the daughter of Asura.
In that realm, where the great burden was sustained by the pillar-like arms of the Asura, there reigned as king the Dānava Bali, the son of Virocana.
Together with all the gods, Vidyādharas, and serpents, he was accompanied by Sākranda; even the king of the gods desired to massage his feet.
He is the treasury of the jewels of the three worlds, the protector of all embodied beings, and the sustainer of those who sustain the universe—he whose guardian is Hari.
By the mere mention of his name, the temples of Airāvaṇa withered away, while the heart-veins of the serpents underwent a state of distress, like those of a peacock.
By the fierce heat of his majesty, the seven oceans—as if at the time of universal dissolution—became prone to evaporation before him of wrathful aspect, as if they had become sevenfold.
The rows of clouds formed by the smoke from the foremost of sacrifices, which enveloped the oceans, have always served as armor for the hollow interior of this cosmic egg.
By the forceful blow of whose gaze the supporting kulaparvata mountains were driven down, so that all the quarters of space bowed like creepers bent by fruit.
Having effortlessly conquered the entire expanse of the world and adorned it as his own, that Daitya ruled the kingdom for one hundred million years.
Then, as many ages passed away in their revolving cycles, amidst the great floods of gods and demons rising up and falling down;
Bali, the leader of the Dānavas, felt a sense of revulsion toward enjoyments that were incessantly consumed and characterized by grand displays throughout the three worlds.
Once, standing at a window fashioned with jewels upon the peak of Mount Meru, he reflected for himself on the nature of existence within saṃsāra.
To what extent must this empire now be ruled by me, whose power remains unimpaired, and how long must I sport within these three worlds?
Of what use is my great kingdom, which causes wonder throughout the three worlds and captivates with its abundant enjoyments, if it is merely consumed?
This mere enjoyment and consumption of objects, which is sweet only at first sight and inevitably comes to an end—what kind of happiness can it possibly bring?
Again the passing of a single day, again the persistence of the night, and again those very same actions—these lead only to shame, not to satisfaction.
The beloved is embraced again and enjoyed once more; this play of children brings shame here to the great.
Why is the wise man not ashamed to perform, day after day, that very same flood of activities which has become tasteless once it has been experienced?
Again day, again night, again the succession of duties; again and again, I consider this to be the mockery of the wise man.
Just as water, having reached a state of wavering, returns again to a state free of waves, so too does this person undergo various such activities.
This repeated activity, characterized by the behavior of one who is mad, repeatedly causes even the wise person to laugh, as it is like the play of a child.
Even if this ritual action were constantly performed until its purpose was accomplished, what kind of goal could there be such that no further action would ever need to be undertaken again?
Or for how long must this great display be maintained by us here, and what indeed is gained by it?
This endless play of children is in fact devoid of any real substance; it is performed in vain by those who seek the proliferation of misfortune through repetition.
I do not see any single, magnificent fruit here whatsoever; nor is there any other task to be accomplished upon its attainment, for once it is reached, nothing remains at all.
"Apart from enjoyment, what else could there be that is auspicious and indestructible? Thinking thus, Bali quickly reflected, having realized this.
Then the lord of the Asuras said, "It is remembered," and in an instant, with a frown, he reflected upon the matter within his own mind.
Long ago, it is said, the Blessed One Virocana—my father, who knew the reality of the self and had seen the higher and lower worlds—was questioned here by me.
O Mahāmati, that wherein all delusions regarding both all sufferings and all pleasures have been stilled—what is that called the "limit"?
Where has the delusion of the mind been stilled by the pacification of anger, and where have all desires completely passed away? O Father, where is that long-lasting rest, free from interruption?
What can a person here find satisfaction in having obtained all that is to be obtained? And what, having seen it, would ever again sufficiently benefit one’s vision, O Father?
For even these extremely numerous enjoyments do not bring happiness; they agitate the mind and cause even the virtuous to fall into delusion.
Tell me of something that is beautiful with an unimpeded bliss like that, wherein I may find long-lasting rest.

Having previously heard these words from my father—who had been carried off to heaven but replanted in the courtyard of my home like a tree of the ocean—words equal to a potent elixir of immense form for the quelling of my delusion, spoken from beneath that place where the veil was formed by clusters of flowers falling from the moonbeams; *ityākarṇya purā niśākarakaraspardhālugucchaskhalatpuṣpāpūrakṛtāvaguṇṭhanapadasyoktaṃ tale tena me / pitrā svargahṛtasya sāgarataroḥ saṃropitasyājire sphārākārarasāyanāsavasamaṃ saṃmohaśāntyai vacaḥ //* Hearing this, I recalled those words spoken long ago by my father, who, having been taken to heaven, was planted in the courtyard like a tree of the sea; words resembling a vast, flavorful medicinal liquor for the pacification of my confusion, uttered from beneath that spot where the covering was made of a mass of flowers falling from clusters vying with the rays of the moon.
Virocana said: "O sons, there exists an exceedingly vast region with a wide hollow, wherein even many thousands of triple-worlds find room."
Where there are neither oceans nor seas, neither mountains, nor forests, nor sacred fords, nor rivers, nor lakes.
Neither the earth nor space, neither heaven nor the winds and so forth; neither the moon and sun, nor the lords of the world, nor gods, nor dānavas [are its support].
There were no spirits, yakṣas, or rākṣasas; no thickets nor the splendors of the forest; and neither stationary nor moving things, such as wood or grass.
Neither water, nor fire, nor space, nor above, nor below, nor the earth; neither the world, nor heat, nor I, nor Indra, Hara, and the others.
There is but one great king there, of immense splendor; he is the doer of all, the all-pervading, the All, and he remains established in silence.
The minister, directed by him and intent on all counsel, quickly brings about what was impossible and thoroughly dismantles what was already established.
He is unable to enjoy anything and knows nothing at all; yet, though he is ignorant, he always performs everything solely for the sake of the king.
He alone was the sole performer of all the king's duties; the monarch himself remained entirely at ease in private.
Bali said: "O high-minded one, what is that land free from mental and physical afflictions? How is it reached, and by whom was it attained, O Lord?"
Who was that kind of minister, and who was that king of great power, by whom we were not defeated even though he sportively tore asunder the very nets of the world?
"This narrative is unprecedented and strikes fear into the hearts of the immortals; tell it so that you may dispel the cloud of doubt from the sky of our hearts."

Virocana said: "O son, that minister there is so powerful that he cannot be overcome in the slightest, even by the hosts of gods and asuras gathered together, even if they were multiplied a hundred thousandfold."
He is neither the thousand-eyed Indra, nor Yama, nor the Lord of Wealth; he is neither a god nor even an asura, if my son is conquered.
There, weapons such as swords, clubs, javelins, vajras, discs, and maces become blunted, like the striking of a lotus against a stone.
He is not within the reach of missiles or weapons, nor of the deeds performed by warriors; therefore, all the gods and asuras have been brought under his control at all times.
Even without Viṣṇu, by him here the asuras such as Hiraṇyākṣa were struck down, like the wish-fulfilling trees of Mount Meru by the wind at the end of an eon.
Even the gods, beginning with Nārāyaṇa, though they were all-knowing, were overcome by him and cast into pits at his will.
By his grace, Smara, possessing five arrows, strides with pride through these three worlds, leaping about like a sovereign emperor who has conquered them all.
Even though he is grasped by the hosts of gods and asuras, devoid of virtues, evil-minded, and ugly in form, Wrath expands through his grace.
The repeated conflict between thousands of gods and asuras is but the sport of that minister who possesses the power of counsel.
O son, if that minister is conquered by that lord alone, then he is easily defeated; otherwise, however, he is like a mountain.
In the course of time, that very lord develops the desire to conquer his own minister; by that [desire], the minister is conquered without effort.
If you have the power to conquer the wrestler of the three worlds, who has caused the three worlds to gasp for breath, then you are truly possessed of valor.
When that sun has risen, these lotus-pools of the three worlds come into bloom; when it has set, they dissolve away.
If you, O wise one of noble vows, are thus able to conquer that [mind] with a single intellect free from delusion, then you are truly steadfast.
When that is conquered, even those worlds not yet conquered will be conquered; but if that remains unconquered, these remain unconquered, even if they have been held for a long time.
Therefore, for the sake of infinite accomplishment and for eternal happiness, apply yourself with effort—even through arduous exertion—to the conquest of that [mind].

Indeed, by that exceedingly powerful one, the entire triple world—including the hosts of fathers-in-law, younger brothers, nāgas, and yakṣas, as well as humans, mahoragas, and kinnaras assembled together—was brought under control with ease, as if in sport.
Bali said: "By what means, O father, is that powerful one overcome? Who is he of such exceeding great heroism? Tell me everything quickly."
Virocana said: "O son, listen as I speak of the means by which even he, whose position is eternally invincible, may be easily overcome through the counsel of his ministers."
O son, if this [power] is grasped through the proper method, it comes under control in an instant; without the method, it burns like a fierce, venomous serpent.
Those who, having entertained this king like a child, restrain him through skillful means, attain their goal upon beholding that monarch.
When that king is seen, the minister comes under his control; and when that minister is overcome, the king is seen once again.
As long as that king has not been seen, the minister is not conquered; and as long as the minister has not been defeated, the king is not seen.
When a king has a wicked minister, that [minister] bears fruit as extreme suffering; when the minister is not subdued, the king goes to utter invisibility.
Therefore, through practice, one should undertake both simultaneously: the king’s appearance before him and the defeat of his minister.
By means of human effort and through gradual, well-practiced exertion, having accomplished these two with diligence, you shall reach that auspicious land.
O Lord of Daityas, when your practice has borne fruit, you shall go to that realm; provided, however, that you do not grieve even slightly for it thereafter.
With all their exertions completely stilled and their intentions perpetually joyful, the virtuous dwell there, with every doubt entirely pacified.
Listen, O son, as to what that country is; I shall reveal everything to you. What I have described to you by the name of a "country" is liberation, which destroys all suffering.
But there, O Mahāmati, the Blessed One himself, who transcends all states, acted as the minister; the wise one named Manas was appointed by him.
This entire universe has undergone transformation through its dependence upon the mind, just as a lump of clay becomes a pot, or smoke becomes a cloud.
When that is conquered, everything is conquered; everything becomes attained. Know that it is difficult to conquer, yet it is completely conquered by mere speech.
Bali said: "O Blessed One, tell me clearly that method by which one may overcome that mind, so that I may conquer this terrible [demon]."
Virocana said: "O son, regarding all sense-objects in every respect, this supreme lack of reliance is indeed the method for the conquest of the mind."
This alone is the supreme method; by this very means, the great elephant of one's own intoxicated mind is swiftly and completely subdued.

For this, O Mahāmati, is exceedingly difficult to attain and yet easily attained; it is very difficult to attain for those who have not practiced it, but it is attained with ease by those who have practiced it well.
O son, this aversion to sense objects, when practiced gradually, attains full manifestation in every respect, just as a creeper does when watered by irrigation.
For even by one of deceitful nature who desires it, that which has not been practiced cannot be attained, just as rice that has not been sown, O son; therefore, apply yourself to this.
So long do these embodied beings wander through sufferings, dwelling in the wilderness of saṃsāra, as long as they do not attain detachment from sense objects.
Without practice, no embodied being—not even one of extreme strength—can attain detachment from sense objects, just as one cannot reach another country without travel.
By constantly abandoning the object of meditation while remaining embodied, one should increase through practice the lack of interest in enjoyments, just like a creeper.
O son, without human effort, no auspicious fruit of action can be attained here, nor can one reach the state free from joy and resentment.
In the world, it is called "fate" (daiva); fate is never embodied anywhere. It is that which is designated as "inevitability" and "destiny," brought about by one's own past actions.

It is said that by the word "fate" (daiva) humans alone are meant, and no others; whatever has been accomplished by someone here, at whatever time, and in whatever place, when it has reached its completion, that is [referred to as fate].
That which destroys both joy and resentment is called destiny; destiny, which takes the form of necessity, is sustained by human effort.
Just as the delusion of a mirage vanishes through the play of right knowledge, so too whatever is conceived by human effort comes to pass exactly in that way.
When it is grasped as possessing fruit, it bestows the happiness of possessing fruit; for here, whatever our mind imagines, that it becomes accordingly.
Whatever kind of destiny this [intellect] conceives, it becomes exactly so; it renders some objects determined, others undetermined, and even those that were previously undetermined.
It acts upon the mind; therefore, this mind is joined to destiny. By establishing destiny within destiny, it sometimes bears the name of its own purpose.
Within this shell of the universe, the individual soul vibrates like the wind in the sky; performing what is ordained by destiny, it sometimes moves against that very destiny.
The word "destiny" (niyati) shines forth like a mountain peak for the sake of conventional designation; therefore, as long as the mind exists, there is neither fate nor destiny.
O virtuous one, when the mind has set, let whatever happens be so; for the living being is born as a person, and he becomes exactly what he is through his own human effort.
Whatever one intends in this world happens exactly so for him and not otherwise; O son, nothing exists here apart from human effort.
Relying on supreme human effort, one should cultivate detachment toward enjoyments; for as long as detachment toward enjoyments—which destroys worldly existence—has not arisen.
Supreme liberation, which bestows victory, is not attained as long as delight in sense objects—which causes total delusion—persists.
O son, as long as the state of swinging on the swing of worldly existence remains unsteady, it will never cease to cause suffering without the practice [of yoga].
When will this evil hope, pierced by the weight of the serpent of enjoyments, ever turn back?
Bali said: "O Lord of all Asuras, how does this very lack of attachment to enjoyments—which bestows long life—attain a stable state within the living being?"
Virocana said: The creeper of self-realization clearly bears fruit; it produces in the living being a distaste for worldly enjoyments, just as a great vine does in autumn.
Through the contemplation of the self, this supreme detachment from sense objects takes its place in the heart, like the goddess Śrī within the hollow of a lotus.
Therefore, with extremely beautiful investigation through the whetstone of wisdom, one should perceive the deity and simultaneously extract delight from sensory enjoyments.
One who possesses some degree of proficiency should fill one part with enjoyments, two parts with service to the teacher, and one part with reflection on the meaning of the scriptures.
The soul that has attained goodness becomes fit for the sequence of discourse on knowledge; with its form purified, it receives the supreme dye, just as a cloth does.
One should nurture the child of the mind by gradually caressing it with skillful means and purifying words, protecting it through the internalization of the meaning of the scriptures.
When transformed by wisdom and its stubborn grasping has become relaxed, the mind shines forth coolly, like crystal free from the moon's heat.
Then, with supreme and straightforward wisdom, one should quickly observe the form of the body as being exactly the same as that of enjoyments and a lord.
O son, by the power of wisdom and discernment, one should always simultaneously cultivate the observation of the self and the relinquishing of craving.
Freedom from thirst regarding other views and the supreme vision when thirst is absent—these two views exist mutually, like light and the wick of a lamp.
When the multitude of enjoyments has lost its relish and the God who is both supreme and inferior has been seen, an eternal and infinite repose arises in the Supreme Brahman.
An infinite bliss arises from the joy that is no longer conditioned by sense objects; for living beings, this never occurs except through the hearing of the Self.
Happiness arises through sacrifice, charity, austerity, and visiting sacred fords; yet it does not arise through austerities alone, nor through charity, nor even through sacred fords.
A person’s detachment from enjoyments occurs only through the contemplation of their true nature; by no other means whatsoever can the intellect be directed toward the contemplation of the Self.
O son, without one's own effort, there is no way for a person to proceed toward their highest good, except through the attainment of the supreme goal by renouncing worldly enjoyment.
The supreme bliss of resting in the state of Brahman is not attained anywhere else in this world, from the realm of Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
In the same way, one finds rest when the Supreme Cause shines forth, by relying on human effort and casting destiny far away.
A wise person should revile enjoyments, which are the firm bolts barring the door to the highest good; when revulsion toward enjoyments has matured, discernment arises.

When the rainy season had passed, he was as radiant and stainless as the autumn season; through reflection arose a loathing for enjoyments, and from that reflection came a further loathing for enjoyments.
These two fill one another like the ocean and its waters: the reflection upon the contempt for enjoyments, and the eternal vision of one's own self.
Like very affectionate friends, they accomplish their mutual purpose by first disregarding fate and striving with human effort.
Pressing his teeth against his teeth, he should cultivate a lack of attachment toward worldly enjoyments, acting in accordance with local customs and in harmony with the consensus of his kinsmen.
At the outset, one should acquire wealth through human effort and gradual means; with that wealth, one should attract noble and virtuous people.
From attachment to them, there arises the censure of enjoyments; from that, reflection follows, and subsequently, knowledge, which is the summary of the meaning of the scriptures.
Then, in due course, the attainment of the supreme state arises, when, at the time of cessation, you have withdrawn from sense objects.
Then, through the power of inquiry, you will attain the supreme state; you will perfectly find rest within the utterly pure Self.
Furthermore, you shall not fall into the mire of conceptual construction for the sake of suffering; though you abide, you have no attachment—O Pure One, O Sadāśiva, homage be to you forever!

O dear one, acquire wealth through gradual means and with little reproach, and gain the favor of virtuous people with honor; then, by disregarding sense-objects and the like arising from that association, you shall attain the realization of the Self through the power of perfect discernment.
Bali said: "This was previously told to me by my father, who possesses beautiful discernment; now, by good fortune, it has been remembered, and I have attained full awakening."
Today this clear distaste for enjoyments has arisen within me; by good fortune, I enter the pure bliss of tranquility, cool as nectar.
Filling the quarters once more, bringing back my provisions once again, and winning over my beloved once more—I am weary of remaining in this state of worldly existence.
Oh, how truly delightful is this land of tranquility, its interior so cool! In this state of peace, all perceptions of pleasure and pain come to rest.
I am at peace, I am fully extinguished, and I dwell happily established in tranquility; within, I rejoice like the reflection of the moon set in water.
Alas, the acquisition of wealth is misery: it causes the body to waste away through the impetuous force of a mind in constant agitation, and it is never free from incessant turmoil.
That I was formerly delighted when pressing woman's limb against limb and flesh against flesh is but the manifestation of delusion.
Examples have been seen; what has been enjoyed remains to be enjoyed, unexhausted. All that has come into being has been traversed. What, then, could possibly be called beautiful?
Furthermore, those very same things, here, there, or elsewhere, moving from this place to that—there is nothing whatsoever that is new.
Having mentally renounced and abandoned everything by myself, I remain established in my own true nature, like the full emerging from the full within the Self.
In the netherworld, on the earth, and in heaven, there are women, jewels, precious stones, and the like; yet even that essence is swiftly swallowed up by fleeting time.
For so long a time in the past, I was utterly foolish, harboring hatred toward the immortals for the sake of this trivial worldly desire.
What purpose would there be in abandoning this great affliction called the world, which is merely a mental construction? Indeed, what passion could there be for it in one who is great-souled?
Alas! For a very long time, intoxicated by the pride of ignorance, I have pursued misfortune with the thought that it was a gain, serving it as my own self for so long.
What in this triple world has not been done by me, ignorant as I am and driven by ever-increasing craving, only to increase my remorse?
Therefore, let this trivial former anxiety be enough for me; human effort achieves its fruit through the treatment of the present.
Today, through the unity within oneself of the single cause of infinite forms, happiness comes from every direction, like an elixir in the ocean.
"What is this 'I', and what might the self be?"—this inquiry into the nature of the self, I shall surely pose to the Lord Uśanas for the sake of pacifying ignorance.

I contemplate the Supreme Lord Śukra, whose grace is swiftly aroused; then, instructed by his words, I abide by myself within my own self in that state of infinite splendor. Thus, the fruits of the words of instruction yield an inexhaustible purpose.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having reflected thus, the powerful Bali, with eyes half-closed, meditated upon Śukra, whose eyes were like lotus petals and whose abode was the sky.

Then Bhārgava, who was constantly engaged in meditation, perceived that his disciple Bali, who resided within him, was present in the city, contemplating all things and seeking to obtain wealth for his teacher.
Then the lord Bhārgava, whose conscious self is all-pervading and infinite, brought his own body to Bali’s palace, which possessed jeweled windows.
With his body touched by the mass of light radiating from the Guru’s form, Bali awoke in the morning like a lotus awakened by the rays of the sun.
There, he honored that descendant of Bhṛgu by offering precious gems and water for his feet, by scattering heaps of Mandāra flowers, and by prostrating at his feet.
Then Bali spoke to his preceptor, who was seated upon a costly throne, his limbs adorned with precious gems and offerings, and his head crowned with a wreath of mandāra flowers.
Bali said: "O Blessed One, this intuition arising from your grace impels me to speak before you, just as the light of the sun impels one to perform a task."
I am dispassionate toward enjoyments, which bestow great delusion; I desire to know that reality which removes great delusion.
How small is this web of enjoyments, or is it even this? Who am I, who are you, or what are these worlds? Tell me this quickly.
Śukra said: What is the use of speaking at length here? O Indra among all the Dānavas, I am striving to go to the sky; hear from me in brief the essential point.
Indeed, here there is only consciousness; this is composed of consciousness alone. Consciousness is the mind, consciousness is "I," and these worlds are consciousness—such is the summary.
If you are capable, then by this [instruction] you will certainly attain everything; if not, then even though much has been told to you, it is like an oblation poured into ashes.

The bondage of consciousness consists in the limitation of being an object of thought; liberation from that is called liberation. That consciousness is the non-objectifiable Self of all—this is the summary of all established doctrines.
Adopting this certainty, you look upon [reality] with ease; by yourself, through your own self, you shall attain the infinite state.
"O sages, I am departing from here; seven of you have gathered together for some divine purpose, and I must indeed dwell there."
O King, as long as this body exists, even for those whose minds are liberated, the abandonment of actions as they happen to occur does not please them by their very nature.

When the descendant of Bhṛgu had thus spoken, he leaped with great speed through the clear path of the waters into the midst of the sky, which was variegated by swarms of bees and agitated by the multitude of planets like restless waves.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When that son of Bhṛgu, the eldest in the assembly of gods and asuras, had departed, Bali, the best among the wise, reflected in his mind.

It was rightly said by the Blessed One: "This triple world is indeed consciousness; I am consciousness, these worlds are consciousness, the quarters are consciousness, and this action is consciousness."
In the ultimate sense, everything—both external and internal—is consciousness alone; apart from consciousness, there is nothing whatsoever here or anywhere else.
If this sun is not perceived as "this is the sun" because it is not cognized, then what distinction between light and darkness could possibly be apprehended here?
If this earth is not perceived as "this is earth" because it is covered over, then what indeed is the earth-nature of the earth? O fortunate one, that has become the state of being covered.

If these directions are not perceived as "this is this direction" and "that is that direction," then what indeed is the directionality of the directions, and what is the mountain-ness of the mountains?
If this world is not perceived as "world" by consciousness, then what is the world-ness of the world, or what is the sky-ness of the sky?
If this body, which has the form of a mountain, is not perceived as a funeral pyre, then what indeed is the "bodiness" of the bodies of embodied beings?

The senses are consciousness, the body is consciousness, the mind is consciousness, and the search of the heart is consciousness; consciousness is within, consciousness is without, consciousness is the void, and the existence of all things and the stability of worldly life are consciousness.
Indeed, I perform all this preceded by the desire for touch; I do not experience any contact with the body at all.
What is the use of this body of mine, which is like wood or a clod of earth? I am consciousness itself, the singular Self of the entire world, whose nature is pure awareness.

I am consciousness in the sun within the sky of consciousness; I am consciousness in the cage of elemental beings; I am consciousness among gods and demons, and in all things both stationary and moving.
Consciousness alone exists here; indeed, no second conceptual construction is found. Since duality is impossible in the world, who is an enemy and who is a friend?
When the radiant head of the body named Bala was severed, what of that [body] was actually severed, given that it had filled all the worlds?
Hatred that has been accumulated and intensified becomes hatred and nothing else; therefore, all states such as hatred, whether existent or non-existent, are of the nature of consciousness.
Indeed, even when thoroughly investigated, nothing whatsoever is found apart from consciousness, throughout the vast interior of these three worlds.

There is no hatred, there is no passion, and for this pure consciousness alone, there are neither mind nor mental modifications; how could there be any conceptualization for that which is utterly pure?
I am consciousness, all-pervading and omnipresent, consisting of eternal bliss; I transcend the construction of conceptual thought and am devoid of any second part.
That which is called "consciousness" (cit) is not a name for that which is nameless; this all-pervading power of consciousness, whose essence is sound, manifests itself.
Free from the seen and the seeing, possessing a solitary and stainless form, eternally arisen and devoid of appearances, I am the Seer, the Supreme Lord.
Its form is devoid of conceptual construction, consisting of the subtle luster of the dark time; it arises as mere appearance, yet is eternally free from appearing as an object.
I bow to this Great Self, who is liberated and devoid of the coloring of objects of thought, whose singular nature is light-form, and who exists by his own essential nature.

Salutations to You, whose nature is immediate consciousness, who are the very essence of Your own being; salutations to the pure awareness that is free from objects of thought, and who are joined with the appropriate means of reasoning.
Homage be to you alone, O lamp illuminating all things; you are the nature of consciousness, free from the object of thought, filling the entirety of the universe in every direction.
I am the Great One, pure Being and Consciousness alone, in which all that is perceivable has been completely stilled; I am infinite like space, yet more subtle than the subtlest atom, all-pervasive.
These perceptions of the states of pleasure and pain do not reach me; that consciousness is an unperceivable awareness, an inconceivable, pervasive sentience.
The states of existence and non-existence found in the world are not able to define me; nevertheless, let these worldly states define this very me.
Just as these [objects] are intended by me, they are not distinct from me, if one thing is led [to cognition] by means of a thing that has become its own nature.
Whether something is taken away or given, how indeed can there be any loss for anyone? For I am always everything itself, the doer of all, and united with all.
"I am indeed this consciousness; nothing at all has been produced here. What is the use of conceptualization and mental construction? Consciousness is this one alone."
"I shall first cause agitation; then I shall find peace within my own purifying self"—thinking thus, Bali, who was supremely wise, [proceeded].
Established in silence while contemplating the meaning of the half-mora of the syllable Oṃ, with all mental constructs completely stilled and the multitude of conceptualizations thoroughly pacified.

Free from doubt, with all thoughts of "this" and "that" cast far away, devoid of the meditator, the object of meditation, and the act of meditating, he is stainless and his latent tendencies are stilled.
Bali, having encountered great calamity, became like a lamp extinguished by the wind; with his mind stilled, Bali dwelt there for a long time in that jeweled window, as if carved in stone.
With this desire fully stilled, perfected, and freed from the state of the fault of conceptualization, Bali shone with stainless being, like the autumn sky with its cloudless clarity.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then those Dānavas, the followers of Bali, at that moment ascended the high crystal palace of his residence.
The wise ministers, beginning with Ḍimbha; the feudatories, beginning with Kumuda; the kings, beginning with Sura; and those who seize the army, beginning with Vṛtta.
Hayagrīva and others were his soldiers; Akrūra and others were his kinsmen; Laḍuka and others were his friends; and Valūka and others were his favorites.
Kubera, Yama, Śakra, and other gods brought offerings; yakṣas, vidyādharas, and nāgas waited, longing for the opportunity to serve him.
Rambhā, Tilottamā, and other excellent women who wield yak-tail whisks; the oceans, rivers, mountains, as well as the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Then, for the sake of serving him, many other Siddhas dwelling within the belly of the three worlds came to that region of Bali.
The rows of crowns of the prostrating kings beheld Bali with reverence, as he remained motionless in meditative silence and absorption, like a figure depicted in a painting.
Having seen him and offered their salutations after having fulfilled their duty, those great asuras became languid with despondency, wonder, joy, and fear.
Having deliberated upon what had occurred there, the Dānavas ministers reflected upon Bhārgava, their preceptor and the foremost among all who possess knowledge.
Immediately after their thought, the Daityas beheld Bhārgava in a radiant form, appearing like a manifested city of the Gandharvas.
Being honored by the hosts of asuras and seated upon a great throne, Bhārgava beheld the lord of the Dānavas established in the silence of meditation.
Having rested for a moment as it were, he looked with affection and, observing Bali, perceived that his wandering through worldly existence had come to an end.
As if casting the assembly into the Ocean of Milk with the radiance emitted by hundreds of rays from his body, the Guru smiled and spoke these words.
O Daityas, this is truly extraordinary: that by his own discernment alone, this venerable Bali has attained the state of a perfected one (siddha) and reached the stainless abode.
O best of Dānavas, let this one remain right here in this very way; let him attain stability within his own self and behold the state that is free from suffering.
O Danavas, one who is weary and has attained rest, whose mental wandering through existence has ceased, and for whom the mist of saṃsāra has been stilled, is not to be addressed.
By this, one's own light has been attained amidst the peril of ignorance; once this agitation has subsided, it acts like the mass of rays from the sun during the day.
For in due time, by its own self-awareness, it will itself attain the state of awakening, like a sprout emerging from its seed-capsule after having been in a dormant form.
"O leaders of the Dānavas, all of you perform the tasks of your master; Bali shall attain awakening from his meditative absorption after a thousand years."
Thus addressed by the Guru, the Daityas there cast off the anxiety born of joy, indignation, and despondency, just as trees shed their withered blossoms.
Having assumed the form of Vairocani according to the previously established rule, all the asuras then remained intent upon their own respective tasks.

Men, the earth, the lords of the earth, the netherworld, the planets, the hosts of gods in the sky, the celestial realm, the quarters, the mountains, the guardians of the directions, the caves, the forest-dwellers, and the sky-dwellers all went to the heavens.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, after a thousand divine years, the venerable Bali, the bull among asuras, was awakened by the sounds of celestial kettledrums.
When Bala was awakened, that city then shone like a bed of lotuses at the rising of a flood of suns from the realm of Brahmā.
Bali was already fully awakened; meanwhile, until the Dānavas arrived, he reflected for a moment in his chamber of meditative absorption.
Oh, how delightful is this ultimate path, so cool! Having stood upon it for but a moment, I have attained supreme rest.
Therefore, following this very path, I shall act; what need have I for external riches that are enjoyed only here in this world?
Even among all the joys of Indra, the surges of bliss do not satisfy me within as much as the prosperity arising from the attainment of spiritual perfection.
Thus, as his mind again became slackened in its effort to find rest, the Daityas obstructed Bali, just as clouds shroud the moon.
Beholding them, his eyes agitated by the desire to bow before them, he reflected once more; his body was as if enveloped by those [mountains] resembling the Kulaparvatas.

For me, whose mind is gathered and whose conceptual constructions have been exhausted, what is there to be grasped? Since the mind has fallen into that [state], it attains the state of being its very essence, free from impurity.
"I desire liberation; why am I bound? By whom was I bound in the past? Being unbound, I desire liberation—what kind of childish mockery is this?"
There is no bondage, there is no liberation; my ignorance has come to an end. What use have I for the play of meditation, or what could I gain from meditation?
Having abandoned the delusion of meditation and non-meditation, look at your own manhood; let whatever comes come, for there is neither increase nor decrease for me.
I desire neither meditation nor non-meditation, neither enjoyment nor non-enjoyment; free from all feverish distress, I remain in a state of perfect equanimity.

I have no desire for the supreme reality, nor do I have any desire for the maintenance of the world; I have no task to perform in the state of meditation, nor do I have any task to perform through worldly power.
I am neither dead nor alive, neither existent nor non-existent, nor composed of existence; this is not mine, nor is anything else mine—salutation to myself, for I am the Great One.
"Let this kingdom of the world remain; I shall stay established here. Or let the kingdom of the world not remain here; I shall stay cool within my own self."
What use have I for the vision of meditative absorption, or what use for the glory of royal power and wealth? Let whatever comes come; I am nothing, and nothing belongs to me anywhere.
Even if indeed there is nothing at all that must be done by me now, why then do I not perform this particular action at hand?
Having thus resolved, Bali, the full-souled one and best among the wise, looked upon the Daityas as the sun looks upon lotuses.
By distinguishing the range of their vision, he accepted the prostrations of all the Danavas with his head, just as the wind gathers the fragrance of flowers.
Then Vairocana, there, through his mind—which was composed of the abandonment of all objects of meditation—performed all the affairs of state.
He honored the twice-born, the gods, and his teachers with worship; he paid due respect to his friends, kinsmen, vassals, and virtuous men.
He satisfied his servants and groups of supplicants with wealth, and he cherished the women by bestowing upon them various riches.
Thus he grew up in that kingdom under complete governance; then, at one time, his mind became inclined toward sacrifice.
Having gratified the entire world and being honored by the hosts of gods and sages, he performed a great sacrifice together with the foremost figures, such as Śukra and others.
Having determined that Bali was not seeking the burden of enjoyments, Mādhava, the bestower of success, went to Bali’s sacrifice for the sake of accomplishing Bali’s desired goal.
Knowing what must be done, he gave this forest tract of the world to Śakra, who was the eldest by age but pitiable, being solely miserly for the sake of enjoyment.
Moving here by his power, Hari deceived Bali and bound the monkey within this subterranean dwelling at the bottom of the netherworld.
Today, O Rāma, he has established himself once more for the sake of the state of Indra; with his body liberated while living, he remains self-abiding, his mind perpetually absorbed in meditation.
Dwelling in the cavern of Pātāla, Bali, whose mind was liberated while yet alive, viewed adversity and prosperity with an equal eye and regarded them as identical.
That wisdom neither sets nor rises with respect to pleasure and pain; it is equanimous, steady-making, and like a row of suns drawn in a painting.
Having long observed thousands of appearances and disappearances among living beings here, his mind has attained detachment from these terrifying things.
Having ruled over the three worlds for ten billion years, at the end, Bala’s mind attained detachment and became completely stilled.
Thousands of conjectures and refutations, and hundreds of affirmations and negations have been scrutinized by the Powerful One; where, then, can he find consolation?
Having completely renounced his desire for enjoyments, Bali, with a fulfilled mind, remained eternally established in self-delight within the depths of the subterranean cavern.
Furthermore, O Rāma, this entire world shall be governed here by this powerful one in the capacity of Lord of the World for many groups of years.
No satisfaction arises in him from attaining the station of Indra, nor does any agitation arise in him from falling from his own station.
Equanimous toward all states of being, with his disposition always uplifted, he remains established in himself like space, taking what comes to him.
I have thus described to you this attainment of wisdom by Bali; having firmly grasped this view, may you also rise up.
O Rāghava, through solitude like that of Balarāma and by the certainty that "I am eternal," one should attain the state of non-duality solely through human effort.
Having enjoyed the three worlds for ten million years—specifically eighteen million—even Bali, the best among the Asuras, eventually fell into a state of weariness.
Therefore, O subduer of enemies, having utterly renounced the burden of enjoyments which inevitably leads to bitterness, proceed toward that state of truth and bliss which is free from bitterness.
O Rāma, these perceptions of what is seen, which produce various forms and transformations, should not be regarded as beautiful here, for they are like mountain rocks from afar.
Bind this mind that runs here and there and wallows in worldly activities, and establish it within the hollow of the heart.
You alone are the sun of consciousness, situated everywhere in the universe; who is another to you, and who is your own? Why do you stumble in vain?
O mighty-armed one, you are infinite; you are the primordial Puruṣottama. You, whose body is consciousness, manifest yourself through hundreds of forms of objective phenomena.
All this world, both stationary and moving, is strung upon you—pure and eternally awakened—just as clusters of gems are threaded on a string.
You are not born, nor do you die; you are the unborn, universal Person (Virāṭ Puruṣa). O pure consciousness, may the delusions of birth and death never befall you.
Having deliberated upon the relative strength and weakness of all the diseases of birth, abandon craving for enjoyments and become merely an enjoyer.
While you, the Lord of the World, the sun of consciousness ever-risen, abide, all this—the ornamentation of the dream of saṃsāra—shines forth.
Do not indulge in futile despair; this longing for pleasure and pain does not belong to you. You are the pure mind, the self of all, the illuminator of all things.

Previously, you conceptualized the desirable as undesirable and the undesirable as desirable; having abandoned that through the practice of such [reversal], now abandon even that [conceptualization] itself.
When the perception of the desirable and the undesirable is abandoned, eternal equanimity arises; by means of that which dwells within the heart, a living being is not born again.
From whatever objects the mind sinks, like a child, one should withdraw it from each of those and instead apply it to reality.
Having thus bound the intoxicated elephant of the mind through the practice of constant application, one attains the supreme good by means of every faculty.
Do not fall into equality with those fools—rogues whose intentions are destroyed by false views, who know the body as it truly is, yet have sold their resolve for profit.
In this world, there is nothing more painful than the ignorance of one who, though possessing nothing, remains fixed in his own convictions while hanging upon the words of others.
O high-minded one, quickly drive far away from the sky of your heart this cloud of non-discrimination that has arisen by means of the wind of discrimination.
As long as one does not bestow grace upon oneself through one's own effort for the sake of perceiving the Self, the arising of discernment will not occur.
Even through the perspectives of logic regarding the meaning of the Vedas, Vedānta, and the scriptures, this Self does not become manifest until it has been perceived by oneself.
O Rāma, you have established yourself in serenity through your own self by means of your own self; having attained expansive awakening, you understand it as if through my words alone.
By my word, you have grasped this pervasive pervasiveness of the Supreme Self, the sun of consciousness, which is devoid of any portion of conceptual construction.
With all mental constructs dissolved, with doubts and delusions stilled, and with the mist of curiosity exhausted, you have become one who is free from the fever of worldly existence.
Whatever you approach, protect, destroy, drink, marvel at, or increase—let that also be so by means of that [same nature] when, O Sage, you are free from the suspicion of the stain of ignorance.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Now, O Rāma, hear this supreme method for attaining higher knowledge, just as Prahlāda, the lord of the Daityas, attained perfection through his own self.
In the depths of the netherworld (pātāla) there was one named Hiraṇyakaśipu, who put both gods and demons to flight and possessed prowess equal to that of Nārāyaṇa.
Having pervaded the expanse of the world, he seized the universe from Hari, just as a royal swan plucks a large petal from a lotus for a six-legged bee.
Having overwhelmed the hosts of gods, he ruled over the worlds, just as an elephant, having driven away a swarm of swans, rules over a lotus pond.
Then that lord of the Asuras, exercising sovereignty over the three worlds, in the course of time begot sons, just as Mādhava produces sprouts.
Those children of fierce splendor grew in no time at all, like a thousand rays of ten suns sporting as they pervade the sky.
Among those most worthy ones, there was indeed one named Prahrāda, powerful and the foremost soul, like the Kaustubha gem among precious jewels.
With that son, who was endowed with every beauty, Hiraṇyakaśipu shone intensely, like the year with the spring.
Then that Daitya Mada, accompanied by his sons and endowed with an army and a treasury, arrived with elephants dripping from three temples.
By the heat of the spreading radiance of that [light], which was expanding through the three worlds, it was as if by the splendor of the rays of a multitude of suns at the end of an eon.
Then the gods, headed by Sūrya and Indu, were not distressed by him, just as kinsmen are not troubled by a child who is restless with wicked playfulness.
Then they prayed to the Unborn One for the slaughter of the lord of the Daityas, who was like a rutting elephant; for even the great do not tolerate repeated wrongdoing.
Then there arose a deep, gurgling roar like the world at the time of dissolution, produced by the thundering of vajra-claws that resembled the tusks of the elephants of the quarters.
The circle of his teeth shone like a dense net of steady lightning flashes, and his earrings were like blazing fires flickering within the hollows of the ten directions.
His vast belly is the formidable seat formed by the mass of all the great mountain ranges, and he has shaken off the shell of the universe with the trees of his arms.
The mountains were driven away by the wind issuing from his mouth and belly; he was proud with a wrath like the fire at the end of an aeon, intent on burning the three worlds.
The sun was pushed forward by the movement of his thick, formidable shoulders covered in hair; the mountains were turned tawny by the masses of fire flickering from the pores of his skin.
The edges of the quarters were made formidable by the construction of great walls like the principal mountain ranges, while pattishas, prāsas, and tomaras emerged from every part of its body.
Assuming the form of a man-lion, Mādhava slew the great asura, who let out a terrifying "kaṭakaṭa" sound, just as an elephant slays a horse.
He burned the hosts of Pauras and Māsuras with the flames of his eyes that he had vomited forth, just as fire consumes the web of the world at the end of an aeon of all beings.
When that Nṛsiṃhamāruta had become violently agitated, it was like a single ocean tossed about by the crashing of thundering clouds.
Those hosts of Dānavas fled like gnats before a blazing fire; they vanished from sight like lamps whose light has been extinguished.
Then, with the lords of the Daityas having fled and the circles of the inner apartments burnt, the surface of Pātāla became like the world crushed at the end of an eon.
When the Lord, who is worshipped by the frantic efforts of the gods, had slain the Daitya during the unseasonable dissolution of the kalpa and had slowly departed for some unknown place;
The surviving sons of Danu, protected by Prahrāda, came to that burnt region like birds to a dried-up lake.
There, having performed lamentations for their own destruction as was appropriate for the occasion, they offered funeral honors to their deceased kinsmen among the departed spirits.
They slowly consoled their own surviving people, whose kinsmen had been slain and whose circle of friends and relatives had been consumed by fire.

With forms as wretched as figures depicted in a painting, devoid of effort and dejected in spirit, those leaders of the asuras—resembling great lotuses whose minds were scorched by grief—remained free from all outward agitation like charred trees.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, his soul overwhelmed by grief because the Dānava had been slain by Hari, Prahlāda, remaining silent, reflected within the depths of Pātāla.
What means can there be for us against this sprout of the asuras, which, though sharp-tipped as it grows here, is devoured by every monkey?
Never did the Daityas, though possessed of mighty arms, remain stable in Pātāla; they were shattered like lotuses upon the Himalayas.
Arising again and again, they perish—those things with radiant forms and gurgling sounds—their flickering efforts exhausted like the waves of the ocean.
The enemies, who rob all the world of its light, have reached full maturity; they bring suffering both externally and internally, and their delusions are like unprecedented darkness.
With hearts filled with darkness and their wealth of petals closing, friends like lotus-pools at midnight fall into despondency.
Surely the realm of my father has been overrun by the gods, who, like deer trampling a great forest, have defiled it by using his footstool as a stepping-stone.
Devoid of effort, their prosperity gone, wretched and with their inner intentions laid bare, kinsmen do not shine, like lotuses whose petals have been scorched.
In the houses of the heroic Asuras, the grey clouds of ash, stirred by incessant winds, fluttered like dense masses of incense smoke.
Upon the walls of the Daityas' inner apartments, where the door-panels had been torn away, new sprouts of barley appeared like the luster of emerald.
Even the Dānavas, who were like intoxicated elephants in the lotus-pond of the three worlds, fell into such wretchedness as the gods; oh, what is impossible for Fate?
Even at the slightest movement of a leaf, they tremble with the fear of seeing an enemy; utterly shattered, they flee like female deer that have strayed into a village.
The trees, their clusters of jewel-like blossoms serving as earrings for the women of Asura, have been felled by Narasimha and have attained the state of mere stumps.
There, in the Nandana grove, the wish-fulfilling trees were replanted, possessing leaves like divine garments and bristling with clusters of jewel-blossoms.
Formerly, the faces of the captive Asuras were praised by the gods; today, the faces of the captive gods are beheld by the Asuras.
I believe that the great rivers of charity, having flowed forth upon the flanks of the celestial elephants' temples, will become like mountain streams cascading down the ridges of peaks.
Upon the temples of our elephants, the splendors of the flow of ichor shine like dust upon parched desert tracts.
Those Daityas, who were like the peaks of Mount Meru and who moved with winds reddened by the nectar of blooming white Mandāra flowers, have become difficult to find.
The beauties of the gods and gandharvas, who were accustomed to the inner apartments of the dānavas, have today taken up residence on Mount Meru like blossoms upon a tree.
Alas, father! The graceful charms of housewives, now withered like dried lotuses and devoid of essence, are being mocked by celestial women with their playful dances.
Alas, those very same chowries by which my father was fanned in heaven when he possessed a thousand eyes, now fan him [in this state].
This calamity, which brings us such wretchedness, has come upon us through the favor of that one Hari, whose course of manly prowess is difficult to fathom.
Having found rest in the dense shade of the forest of his arms, the gods are never distressed, just like the peaks of the Himalayas.
Taking refuge upon the highest peak of Śauri’s valor, they have acquired prosperity; yet they now oppress us like monkeys perched upon a branch.
Thus, for the wives of the asuras—who were ever adorned with ornaments—the tears remained upon their lotus-faces like frost upon lotuses.
This world, like a dilapidated pavilion with crumbling, broken, and falling walls, is supported solely by the pillars of sapphire that are his arms.
He is the upholder of the celestial army as it sinks in the ocean of calamity, like the tortoise supporting Mount Mandara when it was submerged in the belly of the Ocean of Milk.
All these, beginning with his father, those best of asuras, were struck down by him alone, like the principal mountain ranges by the turbulent wind at the end of a kalpa.
He alone is the glorious Madhusūdana, whose arm-fire is capable of the act of universal destruction; he is the incomparable teacher of the host of gods.
By the prowess of that one who is an axe to the staff-like arms of the Daityas, the heroic Śakra oppresses the Dānavas as a monkey torments young children.
The lotus-eyed one is difficult to conquer; even when his weapons have been cast aside, he—being as solid as a diamond—is not shattered by the severing of missiles and arms.
My grandfather has simultaneously engaged in many terrifying bouts of martial fury, in which he has mutually hurled mountains at one another.
He who was not afraid even now when those various, most terrible, and extensive battles were spread out—what need is there to speak of his fear [in the future]?
I clearly consider this alone to be the sole means for attacking Hari; apart from that, I believe there exists no other remedy.
With one's whole being, with every faculty of mind, and with the full force of all one's exertion, that very God alone is the refuge and the goal here; it cannot be otherwise.
There is no one superior to him within the three worlds; Hari has attained the state of being the cause of dissolution, maintenance, and creation.
From this very moment onward, I have eternally taken refuge in the unborn Nārāyaṇa; for everywhere, I am indeed composed of Nārāyaṇa.
The mantra "Namo Nārāyaṇāya" accomplishes all aims; it does not depart from the treasury of my heart, just as the wind does not depart from the sky.
Hari is the quarters, Hari is the sky, Hari is the earth, and Hari is the world; I am Hari, the immeasurable Self, for I have been born as one consisting of Viṣṇu.
One who worships Viṣṇu while not being Viṣṇu shall not partake in the fruit of that worship; having become Viṣṇu, one should worship Viṣṇu, for I abide as this very Viṣṇu.
Hari, who is named Prahlāda, is not other than me; Hari is not separate [from me]. Possessing this certainty, I am the all-pervading one within, everywhere.
Having filled this infinite space, the son of Vinatā, with his golden limbs, has become the seat for my own limbs.
All the birds of weapons rested upon the single branch of his hand; his nails were great emerald trees scattered with the blossoms of their own rays of light.
These are my four arms, their shoulder-regions smeared with garlands of soft mandāra flowers, and their armlets rubbed by Mount Mandara.
This Lakṣmī, who rose from the depths of the Milk Ocean, stands by my side, holding a beautiful chowrie that resembles the shimmering flow of the crescent moon.
This fame of mine, which delights the world with ease, is like a cluster of blossoms on the tree of the three realms; it remains by my side, immovable and shining with purity.
This illusion at my side, sporting with her own magical net, ceaselessly creates new webs for the world.
This is she, who effortlessly overcomes the groves of trees of the three worlds; Jayā shines at my side like a creeper from the Kalpavṛkṣa tree.
These two gods, the Moon and the Sun, who are eternally cool and hot respectively, have manifested the cycle of existence within my eyes situated in the center of my face.
This radiance of my body, dark as a blue lotus, beautiful as a full rain-cloud, and spreading so as to darken the circle of the quarters, [is upon her].
In my hand is this conch, Pāñcajanya, whose sound vibrates; it is like the sky incarnate, the very essence of sound, standing there like the Ocean of Milk.
This glorious lotus, born from the hollows of my own channels, rests upon the palm of my hand; within its pericarp is the bee that is Brahmā.
This is my heavy mace, its surface variegated with jewels, resembling the peak of Mount Sumeru, adorned with golden armlets, and the crusher of Daityas and Dānavas.
This Sudarśana of mine, with the form of the sun, rises with upward-pointing rays; its edges are matted with flames, turning the quarters of the sky a deep crimson.
This dark, blazing axe of mine, beautiful as a banner-bearing fire, stands ready as Nandaka, bringing joy and felling the trees that are the Daityas.
This Śārṅga bow of mine, which resembles the Puṣkarāvarta clouds for discharging showers of arrows, has the luster of a lordly serpent and is as beautiful as Indra’s rainbow.
Within my belly, I have long borne these infinite worlds—those already born and perished, and those existing now in their manifold variety.
This earth is my two feet; this sky is my head; this triple world is my body; and these directions are my flanks.
"I am this very Viṣṇu in person, possessing the luster of the interior of a dark cloud, mounted upon the mountain of Suparṇa, and bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace."
All these wicked-minded ones are fleeing from me together, like heaps of straw with flickering movements scattered by the wind.
This one, dark as a blue lotus, clad in yellow garments, bearing a mace, endowed with Lakṣmī, and mounted upon Garuḍa—this is I myself, Acyuta.
Who is this hostile being that seeks me out, like a moth rushing toward the fire of time—agitated and capable of consuming the three worlds—for its own destruction?
These gods and asuras standing before me are unable to obstruct my fiery creation, just as those with weak vision cannot withstand the glare of light.
Brahmā, Indra, Agni, Hara, and the others praise me, this very Lord Viṣṇu, with infinite speech arising from their many mouths.
"I have become one whose sovereignty is fully manifested, possessing an unconquerable form; indeed, by my supreme majesty, I have transcended all states of duality."

I bow to that singular form which fills the interior of the abode of the three worlds, which forcibly destroys all wicked beings, and which, though situated within dense mountains, grass, and forests, removes every fear.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having reflected thus and assumed the form of Nārāyaṇa, Prahlāda then further contemplated upon the worship of the Enemy of the Asuras.
Let there be no higher or lower form than this body of Viṣṇu; for through the flow of his vital breath, this other Viṣṇu stands outside.
Mounted upon Vainateya, possessing four quivering powers, with conch, discus, and mace in his hands, he has dark limbs and four arms.
The glorious one, whose eyes are the moon and the sun; the delighter of Kānta, Nandaka, and Nandana; lotus-handed and large-eyed; wielder of the Śārṅga bow and possessed of great splendor.
Therefore, I shall quickly worship him, together with his retinue, with a mental offering delightful in all its constituent parts.
Then I shall worship this Mahādeva once again with a great external offering consisting of many jewels.
Thinking "This is Prahlāda," he worshipped Mādhava, the husband of Kamalā, with a mind bearing the weight of his accumulated spiritual provisions.
With layers of bowls made from heaps of jewels, with ointments such as sandalwood and the like, with incense, lamps, various ornaments, and diverse displays of wealth.
With wreaths of mandāra flowers, clusters of golden lotuses, thickets of kalpavṛkṣa creepers, and circles of jewel-like blossoms;
With the sprouts of celestial trees, with garlands of various flowers, with *kiṃkirātas*, *bakas*, *kundas*, *campakas*, and blue lotuses;
With kahlāra lilies, night-lotuses, kāśa grass, date palms, mangoes, kiṃśuka trees, aśoka trees, madana trees, bilva trees, karṇikāra trees, and kirātaka trees;
With clusters of *kadamba*, *bakula*, *nimba*, *sinduvāra*, and *yūthaka* trees, as well as *pāribhadra*, *guggulu*, and *binduka* trees, it was filled with heaps of blossoms.
With clusters of *priyaṅgu*, with trumpet-flowers (*pāṭala*), with minerals that are crimson-red, with mangoes, hog-plums (*āmrātaka*), products of the cow, and with *harītakī* and *bibhītaka*.
With the creepers, flowers, and tender sprouts of the *śāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees; with clusters of buds; and with *sahakāra* mangoes together with saffron.
With ketaka flowers, śatapatra lotuses, and clusters of cardamom blossoms—each an embodiment of every beauty and an offering of its own self.
With supreme devotion, which was as magnificent as the splendor of the universe, Prahlāda mentally worshipped Hari, his lord, within the inner apartments.
Then, in that temple, the lord of the Dānavas worshipped Janārdana with an offering complete with all external requisites.
Having worshipped the Supreme Lord again and again with external substances in this very sequence, the Dānava became filled with satisfaction.
From that time forward, Prahrāda worshipped the Supreme Lord every day with complete devotion in that very same manner.
Then, from that time forward, all the Daityas in that city became devoted to Viṣṇu; indeed, they all became auspicious, for the king is the cause of conduct.
Then the slayer of enemies sent word to the sky and the world of the gods, saying: "The Daityas, having abandoned their hatred for Viṣṇu, remain as his devotees."
O Rāghava, Śakra and the other gods, together with the hosts of Maruts, were filled with wonder, wondering: "How is it that the Daityas have indeed taken up devotion to Viṣṇu?"
In the Ocean of Milk, seated upon the coils of the serpent, the gods, filled with wonder, abandoned the sky and approached Hari, who was resplendent in battle.
There, they recounted this account of the Daityas to him, and as he sat there filled with unprecedented wonder and amazement, they questioned him.
The gods said: "O Blessed One, what is this? Those Daityas who are always hostile to you have indeed become one with that [illusion]; it is considered to be a mere illusion."
Where, indeed, are the utterly wicked Dānavas who have shattered the mountains, and where is devotion to Janārdana, which is obtainable only through a great birth in the West?
"O Blessed One, this report that an ordinary man has been born as one possessed of virtues is like a garland of out-of-season flowers—pleasing at first, yet causing distress."
For that which is not appropriate in a certain place does not shine there, just like a highly precious gem in the midst of a heap of glass trinkets.
Whatever kind of qualities a living being possesses, he attains that very same state; even among unborn beings who are alike, a dog does not find delight anywhere in their midst.
Diamond needles, even when plunged into the body, do not cause such pain as these views of substantial entities, which are bound by way of dissimilarity.
Whatever is obtained here in its proper sequence, appropriate, and irreproachable—that alone shines there, like a lotus in water, but not one on dry land.
Where is that wretched, low-born Dānava, base in nature, always delighting in inferior actions and engaged in vulgar undertakings; and where indeed is Vaiṣṇava devotion?

Just as a lotus plant growing on harsh, saline soil does not bring happiness here because it has an unfavorable support, so too, O Lord, the story that even the son of Diti was devoted to Mādhava does not bring us such joy.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then Mādhava, the slayer of enemies, spoke these words to the one roaring with extreme fury, just as a cloud speaks to a flock of peacocks.
The Blessed One said: "O wise ones, do not be despondent because Prahlāda is a devotee; this is his final birth, for that subduer of enemies is worthy of liberation."
Therefore, he must not again perform the act of conception by this one born of the Danavas, who has been utterly consumed, just as a burnt seed cannot produce a sprout.
The wise know that "the virtuous has become devoid of qualities" is an unfavorable sequence; they say that "the one devoid of qualities has become virtuous" is the sequence that grants success.
O best of immortals, go to your own various worlds; this daughter of Prahlāda has not come here for your own pleasure, but for the sake of your virtues.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus to the gods there amidst the waves of the Ocean of Milk, the Lord vanished like a cluster of tamāla leaves upon the shore.
That host of gods, having worshipped Hari, ascended into the sky like a mass of spray driven from the ocean by Mount Mandara.
Then the gods felt affection toward Prahlāda; for where great beings are not agitated, there the mind becomes full of trust.
The devoted Prahlāda worshipped Janārdana, the God of gods, every day with his mind, his actions, and his speech.
Then, as he was devoted to worship, his virtues—foremost among them the power of discernment, bliss, and dispassion—increased over time.
He did not delight in the multitude of enjoyments, like a tree withered of its sap; nor did he take pleasure in his beloveds, as a deer does not among the inhabitants of the world.
He found no delight in worldly activities except for explaining the meaning of the scriptures; he felt no pleasure in visible objects, just as a deer feels none on dry land.
His mind found no rest in the attachment to the diseases of worldly enjoyments, just as a pure pearl that is not yet strung finds no rest in the luster of other pearls.
His mind, having abandoned the calculation of enjoyments and the like yet not having attained rest, remained as if suspended in a swing.
From his abode in the Ocean of Milk, the divine Viṣṇu perceived that state of Prahlāda through his all-pervading and supremely beautiful intellect.
Then, by way of the path to the netherworld (pātāla), Viṣṇu arrived at the temple of Prahlāda’s deity, which had been made radiant by Prahlāda himself.
Having recognized that the god had arrived, the lord of the Daityas honored the lotus-eyed one with a twofold-intensified worship, paying him homage with great reverence.
Prahlāda, filled with supreme joy, praised with nourishing words Lord Hari, who was present in person within the house of worship.

Prahlāda said: I take refuge in Hari—the unborn, the infallible Lord, the sovereign, the protector of the helpless, the worthy refuge, the supreme light that removes every blemish, and the treasury beautiful within the abodes of the three worlds.

I take refuge in Him who resembles the dark blue petal of a water-lily, who is like the hollow of the stainless autumn sky, who has the luster of bees, darkness, and collyrium-ointment, and who bears the lotus, the discus, and the mace.

I take refuge in Him whose limbs are as tender as a cluster of stainless lotus filaments, who possesses a conch-shell with the luster of a white-petaled lotus bud, in whom the bee-like Brahmā hums with the sound of the Vedas, and who dwells within the petals of the lotus of my own heart.

I take refuge in the autumnal sky of Hari, which is strewn with the stars of his white fingernails, possesses the full orb of the moon that is his broad face bright with a smile, and has the Ganges of the mass of rays from the jewel upon his chest.

I take refuge in that Child who lies upon the leaf of a tree; he who is the dissolution of all incessantly created worlds, yet is eternally unborn and undecaying; he who is vast, whose noble body is matured by hundreds of virtues.

I take refuge in him who is fair as the pollen of a newly blossomed lotus, whose limbs are adorned with the form of a radiant lotus, whose body is anointed with a reddish hue like the twilight at the end of day, and who is beautiful in garments resembling gold.

I take refuge in the All-pervading Lord, who is the frost-fall for the lotus-pond of the sons of Diti, the ever-rising solar orb for the lotus-pond of the gods, the flood of water for the lotus-pond of Brahmā, and whose abode is the lotus in the heart.

I take refuge in Hari, the white lotus of the lily-pond that is the three worlds, the foremost lamp for dispelling the darkness of delusion, the clearly manifest, non-inert reality of the conscious self, who removes the suffering of the entire universe.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus honored with words abounding in virtues, that Hari, the destroyer of asuras, whose shoulder was graced by the presence of Śrī, replied to the lord of the asuras—who was dark blue like the petal of a water-lily—with affection, just as a cloud responds to a joyful peacock.
The Blessed One said: "O treasure-house of virtues, O great crest-jewel of the Daitya lineage, accept this boon as you desire: a further birth for the sake of the cessation of suffering."
Prahlāda said: O Bestower of the fruits of all intentions, O You who abide within all worlds, O All-pervading Lord, command me that which You know to be the most sublime.
The Blessed One said: O sinless one, may your inquiry, culminating in rest in Brahman, lead to the complete pacification of all agitation and to the supreme fruit.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus to the lord of the sons of Diti, Viṣṇu vanished like a wave of the ocean that has emitted a gurgling roar.
When the god Viṣṇu had disappeared, the Dānava spoke these final words regarding the worship: "The handful of flowers, adorned with jewels and gems."
Seated upon an excellent seat in the lotus posture, filled with great joy, he sat down and reflected within his mind upon the procedure for reciting the hymn of praise.
"I have been told by the Lord, the enemy of worldly existence, 'May you indeed become one possessed of discernment'; therefore, within myself, I shall perform the investigation of the Self."
What indeed am I in this grand display of the world, such that I speak, go, stay, and strive to acquire?
This world—including trees, grass, and mountains—is not "I"; since that which is external is utterly impure, how indeed could I be it?
Non-existent at birth, mute, and for a moment animated by the vital winds, this body dissolves in a short time; I am not this unconscious thing.
Being produced by the inert auditory canal, momentary in its destruction, formless and born of emptiness—sound is not the "I," for it is insentient.
Whether attainable or unattainable, through the skin which perishes in an instant, I am not insentient, for I have attained the touch of the Self by means of the clarity of consciousness.
I am not the insentient taste, which is bound by the tongue, trivial, fickle due to its restless nature, characterized by minimal movement, and dependent upon material objects.
Dissolved in the seer—the one who remains when the seen and the seeing have perished due to their momentary destruction—is form; it has ceased, and I am not that insentient thing.
I am not the insentient fragrance, which is imagined by the nose—blind, dull, and perishable—which is fragile and of indeterminate form.
Free from "mine-ness," devoid of mental construction, peaceful, and with the delusion of the five senses gone, I am indeed pure consciousness alone, stripped of all parts and their perceptions.
I am this pure consciousness alone, devoid of the object of thought; I am the illuminator, pervading both the external and the internal, partless, stainless, and composed of light.
By this conscious being, all these things, from jars and cloths up to the sun, are illuminated by the lamp of supreme splendor.
Now I have remembered all this truth: I am this all-pervading Self, the manifestation of non-conceptual consciousness.
By this [consciousness], these various fluctuations of the senses flash forth here, through its internal radiance, just as rows of sparks [flash] by means of fire's heat.
By this all-pervading Nidāgha, these various rows of flickering sense-faculties are made to quiver here, just like mirages in a desert.
By this, the substantiality of these categories is established, just as the possession of qualities such as whiteness is [revealed] by a lamp for garments.
For this very Self alone, like a mirror, stands as the ground for the experience of all beings who are awake.
By the grace of that one non-conceptual lamp of consciousness, the sun becomes warm, the moon becomes cool, the mountain becomes solid, and water becomes fluid.
This is the primary cause of all things experienced continuously in the maintenance of the world; there exists no cause for it.
Through this [cognition], the status of being an object arises intensely for those things experienced continuously, just as heat arises from intense application of heat.
From this causeless cause, the cause of all causes, this world has arisen, just as coldness arises from snow and the like.
Of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Rudra—the causes for the maintenance of the world—this is the primordial cause; there exists no cause for it.
Salutations again and again to this Self of mine, which is devoid of names such as "citta," "thinker," "seer," and "seen," and which shines forth by itself all at once.
Within this Lord of Beings, whose nature is non-conceptual consciousness, all beings abide and enter as subordinate qualities.
