Whatever is indeed conceived by this conscious inner self, that very thing comes to be everywhere; nothing else exists, even though it may be present.
Whatever is grasped by the mind attains its own true state; but that which is not grasped by the mind here, though it be real, comes to an end.
These hundreds of rows of objects, appearing as jars, cloths, and the like, are indeed reflected in this vast mirror of the sky that is the world.

This [universe] arises as increasing within that which is more increased, and as decreasing within that which is decreasing; it exists both as being and non-being within the objective entity, like the reflection of the sun.
Invisible to all beings, yet attainable by those whose minds have dissolved, this supreme and utterly stainless void is beheld by the virtuous.
This tree of causes, rich with the bees of proper conduct, bears a manifold and beautiful cluster of blossoms that attains prosperity.
From this arises the lofty and unstable structure of saṃsāra, rich with diverse trees and shrubs, like a forest range rising from a mountain.
This self of consciousness, the illuminator, is undivided among all those existing within the belly of the three worlds, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
I am that one, without beginning or end, possessing all forms; I abide within all moving and non-moving beings as my own self-experience.
Of that very me, these many bodies—both stationary and moving, and beyond all calculation—have come into being.
This one is of the nature of experience; by virtue of its own self-experience, it is itself the thousand-eyed and thousand-rayed one, because it is the seer of all that is seen.
Here I am, moving in the sky with my beautiful solar body, and also with my other body, the wind, which is air itself.
This body of mine, dark-blue in hue and bearing the conch, discus, and mace, indeed dances within this world as the ultimate limit of all auspiciousness.
I am born here, always seated upon the lotus throne, established in non-conceptual samādhi, and have attained supreme bliss.
With the form of the three-eyed one, a bee at the lotus-face of Gaurī, I withdraw this universe at the end of creation, just as a tortoise withdraws its mass of limbs.
In the form of Indra, I protect this entire triple world, which has come to me by succession, just as an ascetic guards his small hut.
"I am indeed this woman and man; I am also this youth. Because of bearing a body, I am old; I am born with faces turned in every direction."
I exist as the sap within the network of grasses, creepers, and shrubs; from the ground of consciousness, I cause them to rise up, just as a well draws forth a subterranean creeper.
For the sake of my own play, this beautiful and vast display of the universe was spread out by me as a child, like a toy made of mud.
All this is obtained by me; existence comes to me when it reaches me. And this, once abandoned by me, is nothing at all, even though it exists.
Whatever reflection has appeared in me, the expansive mirror of consciousness, that alone exists and nothing else; for apart from me, nothing else is found here.
In flowers I am fragrance; in flower petals I am luster; in lusters I am the art of form; and in forms I am experience itself.
Whatever is seen here—the entire world of moving and unmoving beings—is devoid of all conceptual construction; that is the supreme reality of consciousness, which is I.
The primordial power consists of essence (rasa), by which a flood of essence is spread; just as it [pervades] wood and walls, so do I pervade all things.
Having attained that supreme state of existing within all other objects, I manifest the diversity of consciousness by my own will.
Just as ghee exists within milk, and just as the power of flavor exists within water, so too do I abide as the power of consciousness within all beings.

This entire world, existing throughout the three periods of time, is situated within consciousness, devoid of the mental constructs of objects of thought, like a collection of material things upon the earth.
Filling the bellies of all directions, having abandoned the delusion of limitation, I abide as the Virāṭ, the sovereign emperor, present in all things and the creator of all.
This vast sovereignty over the world has come upon me unbidden—an unprecedented realm where Indra is no longer bound and the gods have been crushed by weapons.
Alas! I am indeed vastly expanded; I do not even subside within myself by means of my own self, like the single ocean tossed by the winds at the end of an aeon.
I find no end within myself, though it is inherently healthy and self-savored; I am like a crawling cripple quivering within the ocean of milk.
This small Brahma-cottage named Jagat is extremely cramped; like an elephant in a wood-apple tree, my vast body does not fit within its own limbs.
Even beyond the abode of Viriñci, at the very end of the principles (tattva), it has established its station; my form continues to expand even now and does not turn back.
How could this internal notion "I am named so-and-so" be without support? Indeed, for me—who possess boundless form—this [notion] was but a trivial thing.
The delusion that "this is you" and "this is I" is entirely false; what is the body, or what is bodiless? Who is dead, and who lives?
Wretched and of feeble intellect were my grandfathers, who abandoned this universal sovereignty and took delight in the realms of worldly existence.
Where indeed is this great vision, filled with and expanded by Brahman; and where is this terrifying sovereignty, with its fearsome horizons crawling with creeping things?
Victorious among all views is this pure vision, consisting of consciousness, which possesses infinite blissful enjoyment and is characterized by supreme tranquility.
Salutations again and again to me alone, who am the innermost Self of all beings, whose nature is consciousness free from the object of thought, and whose form is inward awareness.
I, the unborn, having been born, have conquered the cycle of the decayed saṃsāra; this great-souled one has attained all that is to be attained, and thus he lives and he conquers.
Having abandoned this supreme, eternal sovereignty of awakening, I find no delight in the unpleasant splendors of kingship, which are nothing but suffering.
Fie on that wretched insect among evil demons, ignorant of the Self, who wallows upon the surface of the earth as if it were merely wood, water, or stone!
What indeed has been accomplished by that ignorant teacher who, with substances consisting solely of ignorance, satisfies his disciple with a limb made of ignorance?
Having spent a few years in this illustrious monastic seat of the world, what indeed did Hiraṇyakaśipu obtain that was truly fitting for him?
Without tasting this bliss, even one who tastes hundreds of worldly kingdoms would have tasted nothing at all in this world.
Nothing has been attained by that through which this supreme nectar is attained; for one who is completely filled within by its attainment, everything is attained as an undivided whole.
Having abandoned this position, the fool goes to a limited state, but not the wise man; for the camel, having abandoned the sweet grass, goes toward the thorn, but not the other.
Who, having abandoned this supreme vision, would delight in a burnt kingdom? What wise person, having discarded the juice of sugarcane, would drink bitter neem water?
Indeed, all those grandfathers of mine were fools; having abandoned this vision, they took delight in the perils of kingship.
Where is the blossoming grove of Nandana, and where are these scorched desert lands? Where are these peaceful visions of awakening, and where is the notion of a self in worldly enjoyments?
There is nothing at all in the three worlds that one desires even as a kingdom; everything already exists within the nature of the mind—why, then, is it not experienced?

By means of that consciousness which abides in all things, which is established in its own nature, which is changeless, and which is everything—by it, at all times, everything is rightly attained from every source.
The radiant power is Taijasī; the attainment of nectar is Aindavī; greatness is Brāhmī; and sovereignty over the three worlds is Śākrī.
The supreme fullness belongs to Śarva, and the fortune of victory belongs to Viṣṇu; mental power belongs to the mind, and swift movement as well as strength belong to Vāyu.
The Āgneyī is the burning power; the Pāyasī is the satisfaction of taste; the Maunī is the perfection of great austerity; and likewise, the Vidyā is the Bārhaspatī.
The celestial movement of the gods in their palaces, the stability of the mountains, the depth of the oceans, and the great height of Mount Meru.

The glory of tranquility belongs to the Sugata; it is gentle like the *mādirī* creeper, swaying with intoxication; it is composed of the blossoms of the *mādhavī*; and it resounds with the thunder of the rainy season clouds.
There is the illusory nature of a yakṣī, the stainlessness of the etherial realm, the coolness of frost, and the heat of summer’s scorching sun.
And these, as well as many others consisting of space, time, and action, arising from various forms and transformations, are situated within the belly of the three times.
The diverse powers, established in their own state by the changeless consciousness, are brought forth by the supreme consciousness through its union with the process of manifestation and withdrawal.
Free from conceptual construction, the entire consciousness falls equally upon the perception of hundreds of objects, just as the light of the sun shines everywhere.

Just as one experiences in a single moment the entire earth—the mass of objects resting within the treasury of all hopes, encompassed by the activity of the three periods of time—so too does one experience the Self.

In the same way, the stainless Consciousness, being of that very nature, perceives the splendor of the vast objective state of the entire phenomenal world as it exists throughout the three periods of time.
The pure consciousness, though touched simultaneously with hundreds of temporal calculations and the expanse of infinite worlds, remains entirely full.
For consciousness, which has grasped the three times and whose vision perceives the infinite, nothing remains but fullness, which is synonymous with equanimity.
When perceived at the same time, even by one that is both sweet and pungent, the mind attains a state of equanimity, just like the simultaneous experience of honey and the neem tree.
By means of that subtle state of consciousness which has abandoned all mental constructs, which pervades all existents, and whose singular form is the non-duality of pure being.
Even the manifold splendor of objects, though their internal natures are mutually entangled, is experienced with equality through simultaneous perception.
By relying on non-existence through existence, existence abandons its state of suffering; by observing existence through non-existence, existence abandons its state of corruption.
For the consciousness that does not perceive the three times, which is devoid of the bonds of objects of thought, and which remains indifferent toward the object of thought, only equanimity remains.
Because it is beyond the reach of words, it goes as if into eternal non-existence; it remains as if having attained the state of the established doctrine of selflessness.
The self is thus Brahman—neither nothing nor the whole; when it is not attached to anything in supreme tranquility, it is designated by the name "liberation."

But this world, fashioned by conceptualization, is seen by the consciousness-vision only as a dim reflection; it does not perceive this [world] correctly, just as a cataract-afflicted eye does not see clearly.
Enveloped by impurities consisting of both effort and non-effort, that consciousness is indeed unable to fly upward, like a bird bound by snares.
By the very movement of their own volitions, these people have fallen into the snares of delusion, like birds caught by a hunter.
Ensnared by the web of volitions and falling into the pit of sense objects, this path free from affliction was not seen even by my ancestors.
Within just a few days, those wretched ones quivered upon the surface of the earth and were destroyed by him, like mosquitoes in a cave.
If these people had known this reality, then, being seekers of the suffering of enjoyment, they would not have fallen into the blind wells of existence and non-existence with their hopes destroyed.
Through the delusion of dualities arising from desire and aversion, living beings have reached the same state as worms submerged in crevices of the earth.
He lives who has extinguished, by the rain-cloud of the realization of truth, the mirages of conceptualization that take the form of desired and undesired objects.
Whence indeed could there arise for this pure moonlight, of uninterrupted and stainless form, these slightly warm stains that are perceived as its blemishes?
Salutations to myself, to my own self whose nature is uninterrupted consciousness; O God, jewel illuminating the world, alas, you have been found after a long time!
You have been grasped, you have been found, and after a long time you have arisen; you have been drawn forth from conceptual constructions—whatever you are, you are that; homage be to you!
Salutations to me and to you, the infinite; salutations to me and to you, whose nature is auspiciousness; homage to the God of gods, the supreme, the Supreme Self.

I bow down to my own self, which is like the orb of the moon when its clouds have vanished—its very nature free from the veil of conceptualization; rejoicing in its own form, established in itself, arisen by itself, autonomous, and self-exultant.
Prahlāda said: "Om"—this single, appropriate form, devoid of all modification, is indeed the Self; it is this entire universe, whatever exists within the world.
This conscious being transcends even fat, bone, flesh, marrow, and blood; for like a lamp situated within, it illuminates the sun and other luminaries.
It makes fire hot, it tastes the nectar-like essence, and one enjoys the experiences of the senses like a sovereign lord of the earth enjoying his pleasures.
Though standing, he is not seated; though walking, he does not walk. Though engaged in worldly affairs, he is tranquil; though acting, he is not defiled.
Whether performed previously, today, or now, here or there—in both worlds—this [dharma] is the same in all modes of livelihood, whether it has been enjoined or not.
The fearless one brings forth existence from here and there; he remains, causing the world to revolve, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
He is eternally composed of constant vibration because he is the ever-moving deity; yet he is eternally inactive even as a pillar, and he is eternally untainted even as space.
This [mind] agitates the thoughts, just as the wind shakes the sprouts; it drives its own row of senses, just as a charioteer drives a team of horses.

Like one who is extremely impoverished, he is always engaged in action within the house of the body; yet, like a sovereign emperor, he remains established in himself, self-abiding, all-pervasive, and the enjoyer of experience.
This very one should always be sought, praised, and meditated upon; by means of this, one transcends the delusion of old age and death and proceeds to liberation.
This [Self] is exceedingly easy to attain and easy to conquer like a trusted kinsman; it is the bee within the lotus-cavity of the body for everyone.
Even when not reviled and not summoned, he is obtained from his very own body; even when merely slightly invoked, he appears face-to-face in an instant.
As he is served, though he possesses every prosperity, there arises in him no pride or arrogance, as might be expected of a lord of wealth.
As fragrance resides in flowers, as oil in sesame seeds, and as taste in various flavors, so does the Divine abide within bodies.

Due to a lack of discernment, this conscious being, though residing within the heart, is not recognized for a long time—just like a kinsman seen before one's eyes whom one has not perceived for a long duration.
When this Supreme Lord is fully known through inquiry, supreme bliss arises, just as it does when a beloved person is found.
When this supreme kinsman, who bestows unrestrained bliss, is seen, those various perspectives arise by which all fragmentation dissolves.
All bonds are severed from every side, and all enemies are destroyed; hopes do not cut through the minds, just as wicked rats cannot destroy houses.
When this is seen, the world is seen; when this is heard, everything is heard; when this is touched, the world is touched; and when this is established, the world is established.

This [wisdom] remains awake while others sleep; it strikes down those who lack discernment; it removes the calamities of the afflicted; and it bestows [liberation] upon those who are not yet great-souled.
This very *jīva* wanders through the worlds for the maintenance of the universe; it indeed revels in enjoyments and vibrates within all objects.
Therefore, the worldly being, experiencing the self by means of the self through tranquility, abides within all bodies like pungency in peppers.
Formless, consisting of volition and calculation, it rests upon both the external and the internal; it abides as the universal existence within the multitude of objects in the world.
This is emptiness in space, this is movement in the wind, this is light in fire, and this is the supreme essence in water.
Thus, hardness resides in the earth, heat in fire, coldness in the moon, and existence in the multitude of worldly beings.
Just as blackness is in a lump of ink, as coldness is in a particle of snow, and as fragrance is in flowers, so does the Lord of the Body reside within the body.
Just as existence is all-pervading, and just as time is all-pervading, so too is the power of his lordship present in every place upon the earth.
Endowed with form, light, and mental attention, he exists as both sentient being and self; this Mahādeva is eternal and the awakener of the gods themselves.
"I alone am; no other mental construction exists for me, just as the sky is untouched by a particle of dust or a lotus leaf by water."
Just as there is no connection between a stone and agitation, so too there is no connection with others in me; let the fortunes of pleasure and pain fall upon the body or not, as they may.
And what harm has befallen us by the streams falling upon the gourd? Just as light that has passed beyond the wick of a lamp cannot be bound with a rope.
Likewise, I am not bound, for I transcend the entire multitude of existents; what connection can there be between me and desires, with states of being and non-being, or with the senses?
With what is the sky connected, and with what is the mind obstructed? When the body has been shattered into a hundred pieces, what injury can there be for the embodied soul?
When the jar is broken, pierced, or worn away, what loss is there to the space within the jar? Likewise, the mind, which is invisible like a ghost, has arisen in vain.
When that inert thing is destroyed through awakening, what loss has befallen us? That which consists of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of pleasure and pain—that, for me, is the mind.
Formerly there was only one, who today has attained vast bliss; one person enjoys, another takes [the fruit], while yet another faces the perils of misfortune.
Another observes: "Oh, what folly! Whose wheel is this? Nature experiences it, while the mind and body merely undergo its distress."

The wicked-minded one says: "There is folly here; there is no harm at all in mere solitude. I have no desire for the maintenance of enjoyments, nor do I have any desire for the renunciation of enjoyments."
Let that which comes, come; let that which departs, depart. I have no expectation for pleasures, nor do I have aversion toward the occurrence of suffering.
Let pleasures and pains come or let them go; who am I in relation to these? Whether there be various latent impressions (vāsanās) in the body or their cessation, [it is all the same].
Let them go; I am not in them, nor do they belong to me in any way. For all this time, I have been struck down by the enemy that is ignorance.
Having seized the entire essence of discernment and crushed it in solitude by means of the beautiful grace of Viṣṇu arising from within himself;
Now that it has been thoroughly understood, this demon of egoism has been driven out by me from the hollow of the tree of the body.
By means of the mantra of awakening others, I have now driven away this yakṣa of egoism from the great tree of my body.
Having attained the stainless state of merit, he shines as if in full bloom; with the poverty of delusion stilled, he exists when the fault of evil desires has been destroyed.
I stand as the Supreme Lord, having accumulated the wealth of discernment; all that is to be known has been known, and all visions of the visible have been seen.
That has now been attained by me, through which nothing remains unattained; by good fortune, I have cast far away all misfortunes and am freed from the serpent of sensual objects.
It has the frost of delusion thoroughly stilled; it is the cessation of the mirage of worldly desires; all directions are free from the dust [of passion]; and it is a tree of cool tranquility.
Through praise, prostration, petition, tranquility, and self-restraint, I have reached the vast and exalted ground of ultimate reality.
This Blessed Self has been obtained, clearly seen, and fully realized; having transcended the sphere of egoism, it has finally come within the range of my recollection.
The Blessed One is the Self by his very nature; he is Viṣṇu, the eternal Brahman, amidst the pits of the serpents of the senses and upon the ground of the chasms of death.
In the thickets of the *karañja* trees of craving, amidst the clamor of desire, within the forest-nets of latent impressions, and inside the wells of rebirth;

Amidst the burning of the forest fire of suffering, which extinguishes that very forest fire of suffering, there are hundreds of thousands of states of falling and rising, with the delusions of sinking and emerging.
Through appearances and disappearances, and through the activities of the snares of desire, I have for a long time been utterly deceived by my enemy, the ego-sense.
Just as one of little strength in the forest might be overcome by a piśāca during the night, so now, indeed, he is overcome by his own power of action.
Through the mediation of Śauri, the glory of discernment was awakened; once the Lord Īśāna had become fully enlightened, he [confronted] that demon of egoism.
Just as one sees no darkness when the lamp of the sky is blazing, so too I see no trace of that yakṣa of egoism which dwells in the hollow of the mind.
Like an extinguished lamp, O Lord, I do not know your destination; for even as you were seen right before me, O Ishana, you became intent on flight.
When that false egoism has arisen like a demon, my perfected pride is like a thief at sunrise.
I stand firm when walking, composed like a tree without serpents; being fully awakened, I am at peace and enter final nirvana within this world.
Thinking, "I have been abandoned by the thief," I have returned after a long time; I have attained internal coolness, with the mirage of desire extinguished.

Having bathed in the abundance of rain-clouds during the monsoon, like a mountain whose forest fires have been extinguished, one reflects upon the true meaning of this word "I" through the investigation of its own nature.

What is delusion? What are the sufferings? What are the evil desires? What are the anxieties? The delusions of hell, heaven, liberation, and so forth, exist only when the sense of "I" (egoism) is present.

Just as paintings proceed only on a wall and not in the expanse of the sky, the wonder of knowledge does not shine in a mind tainted by the dregs of egoism, just as the coloring of saffron does not shine upon a faded garment.
In the autumnal sky of the mind—free from the clouds of egoism and devoid of the showers of craving—the clarity that possesses radiant beauty shines forth.
Salutations again and again to you, O Self, whose mire is free from egoism, whose interior is perfectly serene, and who is a lake of the nectar of bliss.
Obeisance again and again to You, O Self, who are the ocean of bliss—to You whose fierce crocodiles are the tranquil senses, and whose submarine fire is the extinguished mind.
Homage again and again to him who has dispelled the clouds of egoism, who is the extinguished forest fire of desire, the mountain of bliss for me, and who is free from delusion.
Salutations again and again within to you, O Self, who are my noble mind—a lotus of blossoming bliss—whose waves of thought have been stilled.

Salutations again and again within to my own self, who dwells in the hollow of the lotus, who belongs to the side of the manifestation of consciousness, and who is the swan in the lake of the entire mind.
Salutations again and again to you, the Moon, whose form is composed of digits yet who is partless, whose essence is nectar, who is eternally risen, and whose nature is fullness.
Salutations again and again to the sun of consciousness, which is eternally risen, peaceful, the dispeller of the great darkness of the heart, all-pervading, yet invisible.

Salutations again and again to the lamp of consciousness, which is without oil yet kindled by its own luster, whose wick has emerged from the realm of mental activity, and which is steadfast, supported by its own intrinsic nature.
My mind, scorched by the fire of passion, has forcibly broken my inner heart—which was already heated—just as cold iron might shatter hot iron.
Having repeatedly severed sense-faculty by sense-faculty, and mind by mind with the mind, and having severed ego-construction by means of ego-construction, I remain as the Residue; thus do I triumph.

Having severed non-existence by means of existence, and having abandoned craving through non-craving; having crushed ignorance with wisdom, you are the Knower who appears as the ignorant—O Truth, homage to you!
When the mind has been severed within the mind and egolessness has been attained, and when all objective existence has dissolved through being, I remain alone and pure.
Free from objective manifestation, free from ego, free from the mind, and free from desire, my body remains solely within the pure Self that is vibration.
This bliss has arisen within me, surpassing even the infinite Lord of the World who is compassionate by nature, and it is endowed with supreme tranquility.
With the vampire of delusion pacified and the rakshasa of egoism departed, I have become free from the fever of worldly distress, liberated from the demoness of wicked desires.
Having severed the cord of the rope of craving from the cage of my own body, I know not where the bird of wicked egoism has flown away.
In this tree of the body, whose nest of dense ignorance has been shaken loose, I know not where the bird of egoity has flown away.

By good fortune, my numerous latent tendencies—soiled by the long-standing wickedness of evil desires, smeared with the ashes of enjoyments, and frequented by the serpents of fear—have been destroyed.
For how long have I been such a strange being? By what means has this [ego] of mine, though utterly false, come to possess such firmness of self-identification?
Today I am truly born; today I am one of great intelligence, since I have been completely abandoned by the dark, great cloud of egoism.
This Blessed One, the Self, has been seen by me, and likewise realized; He has been grasped, experienced, and, O dear one, established within my own direct experience.

This mind has reached tranquility—devoid of a foothold, devoid of mentation, and devoid of longing; it is cast off by the delusions of clever egoism, free from striving, devoid of the coloring of passion, and stripped of curiosity.

The great calamities—difficult to cross, uneven, most hard to endure, and productive of long-lasting faults—have come to an end; Maheśvara has been attained as the non-dual consciousness, within which the state of being "non-mind" has vanished.
Prahlāda said: The Self, which transcends all states, has after a long time come back to my memory; by good fortune you have been found, O Blessed One; salutations to You, the Great Soul!
Having saluted you and gazed upon you for a long time, I embrace you; O Blessed One, who else in the three worlds could be a kinsman other than you?
You kill, you protect, you give; you praise, you go, you leap about. You have arrived, you are seen; what do you do? Where are you going?
O you who have filled the entire universe with your own existence, O friend of all people! You are perceived everywhere at all times; where can you flee now?
The vast distance between us, separated by many births, has today become no longer distant; by good fortune you have been seen, O kinsman!

Salutations to you who have accomplished all that was to be done; salutations to you, the creator and the sustainer. Salutations to the one who is the stalk of saṃsāra, the eternal, and the pure-souled.
Salutations to the one who holds the king of discuses in his hand; salutations to the bearer of the crescent moon; salutations to the lord of the wise; salutations to you, the lotus-born.
This distinction between us here, which arises solely from the perspective of the signified and the signifier, is a false conceptual construction, like that between a wave and the water of the wave.
You alone expand eternally through your infinite form, which consists of the manifold variety of endless objects and sports with both existence and non-existence.
Homage to the Seer, homage to the Creator, homage to the one of infinite expansion; homage to the nature of all things, homage to you, the soul of all.
Throughout many births for a long time, I have endured manifold and protracted sufferings, being consumed and robbed of my vital energy by you as you were instructed by me.
The ways of the world have been observed, and various perspectives have been seen; yet by this, you have not attained reality, nor has anything truly been achieved.
This entire world consists merely of earth, wood, stone, and water; O Lord, there is nothing here apart from you that one does not desire to attain.
O God, today you have been found; you have been seen and attained. You have been reached and grasped; salutations to you, for you do not delude me.
O Lord, how is it that he who dwells with his body pervaded by the network of rays from the pupils of your eyes is not seen here in the form of a vision?

Since this [consciousness] touches everything—skin and touch, as well as odor—just as oil exists within the sesame seed, and since it brings touch into its own interior, how is it that it is not experienced?
How can he be far away, who, upon hearing a sound, internally reflects upon the supreme power of that sound and causes his body's hair to stand on end?
He whose things taste sweet even before being tasted, as they cling to the sprout-like tip of his tongue—who would not find him delicious?
Who does not hold within their grasp that body which one gazes upon with affection, taking up its flower-like fragrance with the hand of the nose?
How indeed can that Self, which is sung of through the Vedas, Vedānta, established doctrines, logic, Purāṇas, and sacred songs, once known, ever fall into oblivion?
Even this very series of bodies and enjoyments, though so delightful, no longer tastes sweet within me today, now that You—the supreme and the inferior—have been beheld in Your own clarity.
Through you, the stainless lamp, the sun has attained its brilliance; through you, the cool frost, the moon has attained its chill.
By you these mountains, your gurus, were supported; by you these sky-dwellers were sustained; by you alone this earth was made firm; and by you alone the sky was held aloft.
By good fortune you have attained me, and by good fortune I have reached you; O Lord, I am you and you are I—by good fortune there is no difference between us.
Salutations again and again to you, the Great Soul, who are joined with the two synonymous words "I" and "you"—whether belonging to me or to you.
Homage to me, the infinite one, whose nature is free from ego; homage to me, the formless one; homage to the self that is perfectly equal.
Abide right here in your own Self—equal, pure, the witness, free from all attributes, and unconditioned by space, time, and the like.
The mind becomes agitated, the functions of the senses quiver, and the expansive power that flows as the prāṇa and apāna breaths surges forth.
The bodily machines, smeared with skin, flesh, and bone, and driven by the charioteer of the mind, are pulled along by the reins of desire.
I am this very embodiment of consciousness; I am not anything whatsoever, nor do I have any fixed abode. Let the body fall or rise according to whatever desire it pleases.
After a long time I have been born as "I," and after a long time this attainment of my own self has occurred; after a long time it comes to rest, just as the world does at the end of a kalpa.
Having traveled for a long time through the cycle of existence on the long path of saṃsāra, I am weary and have long rested, like a fire at the end of a kalpa.
Homage again and again to you who transcend all and encompass all; and homage also to those who speak of me and of you.
Victorious is the witnesshood of the Supreme Self, which possesses all infinite enjoyments, is untouched by the functions of defects, and is free from all agitation.
Like fragrance in a flower, like wind in a pair of bellows, and like oil in sesame seeds, you are situated everywhere within this body.
You strike, you protect, you give, you roar, and you leap; though your nature is devoid of ego, this illusory power of yours is truly wondrous.
I conquer as the blazing radiance of the Lord, opening wide the entire world; I conquer again with all undertakings stilled, closing the world once more.
Within a single atom of yours, this entire circle of the world-system has existed, exists, and will exist, just as the state of a banyan tree resides within a banyan seed.
Just as a cloud in the sky appears in the forms of horses, elephants, and chariots, so too, O Lord, are you perceived through the delusions of hundreds of objects.
For the sake of the non-existence and the existence of entities that possess manifold transformations, be one whose self is liberated from becoming, transcending both existence and non-existence.
Abandon pride, great anger, turbidity, and likewise cruelty; the great do not sink into the common mire of worldly qualities.
Remembering again and again his former state of long-standing wickedness, he laughed with a spray of white pearls, wondering, "Who am I? What was that which occurred?"
Those undertakings have departed; those days are gone in which you were strewn with the mass of flames from the fire of anxiety.
Today you are the king in the city of the body, with expansive desires; you are seized neither by sorrows nor by pleasures, just as the sky cannot be grasped by hands.
Having today conquered the horses of the senses and subdued the elephant of the mind, and having utterly shattered the enemy of worldly enjoyment, you now preside over universal sovereignty.
You are the traveler across the shoreless sky, forever rising and setting; you are the sun, eternally bestowing light both within and without.
O All-pervading Lord, you are eternally asleep, yet you are awakened by Śakti for the sake of the play of perceiving enjoyments, just as a lover is awakened by his beloved.
The honey of form brought from afar by the small bees of sight is drunk by you, having been taken possession of through the power residing in the window of the eyes.
By you, through the constant movement of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, the darkness within the hollow of the cosmic egg is observed every moment as it goes and returns to the city of Brahmā.
In the flower of the body you are its fragrance; in the moon of the body you are nectar beyond nectar; in the tree of the body you are its sap; and in the snow of the body you are its coolness.
In you there is a wondrous affection, like clarified butter within the milk of the body; you abide within the inner self like fire within wood.
You alone are the unsurpassed taste; you are the manifestation even of splendors; you are the knower of all objects, and you are the illuminator of all lights.
You are the vibration of all winds; you are the rut of the elephant that is the mind; you are both the radiance and the sharpness of the crest of the flame of wisdom.
Under your influence, this speech of mine dissolves away; yet, like a lamp, it arises again from somewhere else.
Likewise, the circles of objects existing within the cycle of transmigration reside in you, just as the arrangements of bracelets, armlets, and upper-arm ornaments exist in gold.
By means of such words as "Bhava," "Anaya," and "Aham" (I), you yourself praise and speak of yourself, the Self, for the sake of sport.
Just as a cloud driven by a gentle breeze is perceived in the sky by the sight of elephants, horses, and men, so too are you perceived by the sight of all beings.
Just as fire blazes with flames in the forms of horses and elephants, so too are you seen on earth within all created things, though you are not distinct from them.
You are the unbroken thread stretched across those liberated from the cosmic egg; you are the field for the crops of living beings, cultivated by the elixir of consciousness.
By you, reality—which was previously non-existent and unmanifest—is made manifest among all things, just as the taste of meat is experienced through the process of cooking.
Even though the splendor of an object exists, it does not abide when you are not present, just as the beauty and charm of a woman's form does not remain for one whose eyes have departed.
Even here, you have not directed any object toward the welfare of beings; nor has your own beauty, reflected in the mirror, served for your own satisfaction.
Without you, this body rolls upon the earth like a piece of wood or a clod of clay; though it exists, it is as if non-existent, its height lost, just as the sun is invisible during the dark nights.
The sequence of pleasure and pain, having encountered you, perishes—just as darkness, heat, or cold does upon encountering light.
These states, such as pleasure and the rest, attain their existence solely through the perception of you, just as colors such as white and others appear in the morning through the light of the sun.
Having attained their own nature, they perish at the very moment of their connection; like the darkness of a lamp, they vanish completely as soon as they are seen.
That darkness, which had become manifest through the absence of a lamp, arises and perishes at the moment of contact with the lamp.
Thus, upon seeing you free from ailment, the fortune of pleasure and pain arises; yet, as soon as it has arisen, it perishes through total destruction.
Because of its fragile nature, it is not capable of remaining here for even an atom of time, just like a minute fraction of time called a *nimeṣalakṣabhāga*.
The slender city of the Gandharvas, which consists of the mental constructs of pleasure, pain, and so forth, manifests through your grace, yet dissolves once you are seen.
Born from the sight of you and perishing at the sight of you—by whom can she be perceived, as if dead when born, and as if born when dead?
How could an object that is unstable for even a moment perform a function? How could a garland be perceived [as such] by means of waves that have the form of blue lotuses?
Or when a thing that has already arisen and perished is made into an object of action, then this world would rejoice in having fashioned a garland out of flashes of lightning.
Abiding within the minds of those possessed of discernment, you grasp this fortune consisting of pleasure and the like; yet you do not abandon your state of perfect equanimity.
O you who dwell by chance within the innate self of those lacking discernment—enough of describing that form of yours to me, for it is the locus of no small words.
By you—who are effortless, partless, and devoid of ego—agency has been accepted, whether you exist or do not exist.
Victory to you of formidable form! Victory to you who are devoted to peace! Victory to you who transcend all scriptures! Victory to you who are the foundation of all scriptures!

Victory to you, O born one! Victory to you, O unborn! Victory to you, O wounded! Victory to you, O unwounded! Victory to you, O existence! Victory to you, O non-existence! Victory to you, O conquerable! Victory to you, O unconquerable!
I rejoice, I am pacified, I abide, and I have attained; as a victor, I live for the sake of victory. Salutations to me, salutations be to you!

While you abide in me—my own self established in its true state, free from disease and untainted by the dye of passion—where is bondage, where are calamities, and where are prosperities? Where are existence and non-existence? I attain eternal peace.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: While reflecting in this manner, Prahlāda, the slayer of enemy heroes, attained a state of samādhi characterized by unwavering supreme bliss.
Established in non-conceptual meditative absorption, motionless as if depicted in a painting, he shone, abiding in his own state as if carved out of stone.
As he continued to practice in that manner, a great deal of time passed while he remained in his own home, like the enemy of the gods (Rāvaṇa) staying on Mount Meru in the world.

Even though the lords of the asuras were awakened, they did not perceive the one of great intelligence, just as a sprout does not emerge from its seed-capsule despite abundant watering at the wrong time.
Thus, for thousands of years, he remained with his body full and his gaze fixed on a single point; perfectly tranquil in the city of the Asuras, like the sun reflected upon a stone.
Through that state which is entirely transformed into the condition of supreme bliss, he has reached the state of manifestation as if it were a supreme radiance devoid of [ordinary] bliss.
After this much time, that realm of Rasātala became kingless, fierce, and oppressed by the law of the fish.
When Hiraṇyakaśipu had perished and his son remained absorbed in meditative concentration, there was no other king remaining in the abode of the sons of Danu.
Despite the efforts of those lords of the Asuras seeking him through meditation and even with the greatest exertion, Prahlāda did not wake.
The enemies of the gods did not attain their blossoming form—that husband—just as bees do not reach a lotus at night, which possesses a shimmering network of petals and stalks.
The doctrine of consciousness was not understood within him by those of unawakened intellect, just as the sequence of human activity on earth is not perceived when the sun has set.
Then, while the Daityas had departed in their desired directions in agitation, and while the city was previously wandering about as it pleased in the absence of a king;
For a long time, that netherworld (Pātāla) became devoid of kings, overturned by the "law of the fish" (mātsyanyāya), and its succession of virtues had come to an end.
The city of Balimuktābala was devoid of all order and restraint; it was filled with women distressed by every suffering, who were stealing each other's garments.
The city was filled with men wailing and lamenting; its interior was thrown into disorder, its gardens and palaces lay prostrate, and it was tormented by futile calamities.
The hosts of gods were overcome with anxiety, their kinsmen were deprived of food and fruit; they were helpless before an untimely calamity, and the circle of the quarters was destroyed.
It was humiliated by the children of the gods, overrun by outcasts, empty of spirits, devoid of fortune, and its hollows were almost entirely desolate.

That host of asuras became utterly distraught—a battle of spells fought for the sake of women whose loyalty was uncertain, resounding on all sides with the cries of those whose wealth and wives had been seized, appearing fierce and formidable according to the customs of the Kali Yuga.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Now, Hari, who delights in maintaining the sequence of the entire web of the worlds, was reclining upon his couch of Śeṣa in the city of the Ocean of Milk.
When the sleep of the rainy season had ceased, the destroyer of enemies once gazed with his intellect upon the course of the world for the sake of the gods.
Having mentally beheld both heaven and the earthly realm, he quickly proceeded to Pātāla, which was protected by his enemy.
While Prahlāda the Dānava remained there with steady concentration, he beheld the prosperity in Indra’s city that had reached its full maturity.
Of him who dwells upon the surface of his serpent-couch, reclining upon the Ocean of Milk, holding the conch, discus, and mace in his hands, and who moves within his own body.
Seated in the lotus posture, with a body of exceeding brilliance that was the great abode of the three worlds, his mind reflected thus:
Now that Prahlāda has found rest in his station and the leader has gone to Pātāla, alas, this creation has for the most part become devoid of Daityas.
In the absence of the Daityas, the host of gods will reach a state free from the desire for conquest and will come to rest, like a river among unseen masses of clouds.
Then, having emerged from duality, it will attain that state called liberation; like a creeper whose sap has been exhausted by the loss of its pride, it enters a state of complete witheredness.
When peace has come to the flood of gods, all sacrificial and ascetic rites on earth will undoubtedly come to rest, bearing as their fruit only the state of being non-gods.
Then, when all activities have subsided, the earthly realm (bhūrloka) will come to its end; upon its destruction, there will be no further involvement in saṃsāra.
This triple world, which has been fashioned by me until the end of the eon, will perish prematurely like a drop of frost in the heat.
Why have I thus dissolved into this mental effort and come to destruction? What have I done here, acting as one who brings about the end of my own play?
Then, in this void where the moon, sun, and stars have vanished, I too, having brought my body to rest, shall abide in that state.
Since the world has thus come to such a sudden end, I see no good in this; I think it better that the Dānavas should live.

Due to the exertion of the Daityas, the gods' performance of sacrifices and austerities was thereby obstructed; otherwise, the structure of the world and the course of worldly existence would not have been altered.
Therefore, having gone to Rasātala, I shall duly restore the lord of the Dānavas to his own position, just as the season restores the tree.
If, however, I do this for another lord of the Dānavas instead of Prahlāda, I think that he will surely attack the gods.
This body of Prahlāda is his final one; it is great and purifying, and he must dwell here with this very body until the end of the kalpa.
For thus is the divine destiny of the Supreme Lord determined: that an embodied being must abide here according to its allotted lot, just as Prahlāda did.
Therefore, having gone to that very lord of the Daityas, I shall awaken him, just as a cloud awakens a peacock sleeping by a mountain river with its thundering.
Established in the samādhi of one liberated while living, he may exercise lordship over the asuras, just as a gem that is free from mental activity reflects images.
This creation, together with the gods and asuras, shall not perish; that conflict will come to pass, and it shall be my sport.
Although these two—the destruction and the emergence of creation—are perfectly equal to me, nevertheless, let this proceed according to its established order; what does it matter to me otherwise?

That which is equal toward both existence and non-existence, whether in their destruction or their persistence—any effort directed toward that, due to a lack of understanding, constitutes the attainment of union with it.
Therefore, I shall go to the netherworld to awaken the Lord of the Asuras; I shall attain steadfastness and no longer engage in the play of worldly existence.

Having reached the city of the Asuras, which is terrible with its arrogant conduct, we shall awaken the Daitya as the sun awakens the lotus; we shall bring this entire world back to its own stability, as the monsoon season brings the shifting mass of clouds to rest upon the mountain.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having reflected thus, the Self of all moved forth from his own city within the Ocean of Milk, accompanied by his retinue like a mountain with its peaks.
Through that very opening at the surface of the Milk Ocean, where the waters were solidified, he reached the city of Prahlāda, which was like another world of Śakra.
Then Hari beheld the Asura within the treasury of the golden palace, hidden in a mountain cave like the Lotus-born Brahmā absorbed in meditative concentration.
There, those Daityas, shaken by the Vaishnava splendor, fled far away like owls terrified by the rays of the sun.
Accompanied by two or three principal asuras and surrounded by his retinue, Hari entered the abode of the asura, just as the moon enters the sky with its stars.
Seated upon the throne of Vainateya, with Lakṣmī waving the fly-whisks for him, surrounded by his own weapons and attendants, he was saluted by celestial sages and holy seers.
"O Great-souled One, awaken! Thus Viṣṇu spoke, and he blew his conch Pāñcajanya, making the quarters of the sky resound.
By that great sound, born from the life-breath of Viṣṇu, there arose a force equal in speed to the oceans and clouds agitated at the same time as the end of an eon.
The host of Asuras fell to the ground in utter confusion, like a row of royal swans by the sound of a cloud rumbling with the playful grace of a rutting elephant.
The Vaiṣṇava folk, their joy aroused and their agitation gone, rejoiced like a row of *kuṭaja* trees blooming at the roar of a rain cloud.
The lord of the Dānavas gradually regained consciousness, like a kadamba tree in full bloom in the forest at the end of the rainy season.
Then the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti), having risen from the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), gradually overpowered the demon as the Gaṅgā overcomes the entire ocean.
In an instant, the splendor of his vital breaths assailed the asura from all sides, just as the solar radiance, immediately upon its rising, pervades the interior of the world.
Then, as the nine apertures of his vital breaths began to function, his consciousness became directed toward objects of thought within, reflected upon the mirror of the vital breath.
Tending toward volition, consciousness attained the state of mind as an object of thought, O Rāghava, just as the beauty of a face reflected in a mirror appears as a duality.
When his mind had slightly sprouted and his eyes were about to open, they gradually became like two blue lotuses in the morning.
As his consciousness entered the hollows of the channels touched by the inhaled and exhaled breaths, a vibration arose within him, like that of a lotus flower shaken by the wind.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, the mind attained fullness, like a wave in water when it has been filled by the force of the vital breath.
Then, with his eyes, mind, breath, and body blossoming, he shone like a lake with quivering lotuses when the sun has half-risen.
At this moment, as soon as the Lord said, "Awake!", he became fully awakened like a peacock at the sound of thunder.
To him, whose eyes were blossoming, whose pride had arisen, and whose memory was robust, the Lord of the Three Worlds spoke as he had formerly spoken to the one born from the navel-lotus.
O virtuous one, remember Mahālakṣmī; remember your own form. Why do you bring about the cessation of this body so prematurely?
For you who are devoid of the conceptualization of what is to be rejected or accepted, what purpose do the existence or non-existence of bodily states serve? Arise, arise now!
"You must remain here with this body of yours for as long as a kalpa; for we know the blameless destiny exactly as it truly is."
Remaining here in the kingdom as one liberated while living, you should cast off this body, free from anxiety, until the end of the kalpa.
O sinless one, when your body has been shattered at the end of the eon, you must abide in your own majesty, just as the space within a jar remains in the sky when the jar has broken.
Abiding until the end of the aeon, pure, and having seen the higher and lower worlds, this body of yours has become a playful manifestation of one liberated while living.
The twelve suns have not been raised, the mountains have not dissolved, and the world has not been consumed by fire; O virtuous one, why do you abandon your body in vain?
The wind blows, not mad, grey with the ashes of the three worlds; why do you vainly cast away your body, which is marked by the skulls of fickle gods?
Like clusters of blossoms on an *aśoka* tree, or like the lightning of the Puṣkarāvarta clouds, they do not flicker within the vessel of the world; why then do you abandon your body in vain?
The quarters of the sky, where the mountains resound with torrents of rain and blaze with flaming fires, do not crumble; why then do you abandon your body in vain?
This world, consisting of the three known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, remains as nothing more than a remnant; why do you pointlessly abandon this body, which is like a withered old cloud?
Nor have the quarters of the sky here fallen into decay, their intervals inferred merely by the rows of mountain peaks; why then do you abandon your body in vain?
The solar rays roam in the sky with the thunderous roar of splitting mountain peaks; the clouds of the kalpa do not thunder—why do you abandon your body in vain?
I, whose banner is the bird, dwell with light amidst the beings scattered throughout the ten directions; do not disregard my body.
We are these, these are the mountains, these are living beings, this is your lordship, this is the world, and this is the sky; do not disregard the body.
For one whose mind is agitated by the application of excessive ignorance, sufferings cut him down; for such a person, death is a joy.
"I am emaciated, deeply distressed, and deluded"—these and other such reflections rob one's intellect; for such a person, death is glorious.
Bound within by the snares of hope, one is led here and there by the flickering movements of the mind; for such a person, death alone shines forth as the only relief.
For one whose heart is shattered by cravings that have carried away his cultivation of mindfulness, death shines forth like sprouts from a field of greed.
For one whose creeper of mental fluctuations has grown as high as a palm tree in the forest of the mind, death shines forth when it bears fruit through pleasure and pain.
For one whose body is this wretched tree, with its network of foliage being the line of body hair, death shines forth as it utterly sweeps away the flood of misfortunes.
For him whose forest of his own body is being consumed by the forest fires of mental anguish and physical disease, death shines forth as a welcome release for that flickering vine of a limb.
For him upon whose body the pythons of lust and anger writhe like those on a tree withered within, death alone shines forth as his glory.
This abandonment of the body is known in the world as death; it is neither existent nor non-existent, and therefore it is not the cause of the experience of what is to be known.
The life of that wise person who perceives reality as it truly is, and whose mind never departs from the contemplation of the reality of one's own self, is truly radiant.
He whose state of being is free from egoism, whose intellect is not defiled, and who is equal toward all things—for him, life truly shines.
He who, with an inner mind cooled and free from passion and hatred, beholds this life like a witness—his life indeed shines.

For one who, having correctly understood through thorough discernment, abandons both what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, and has placed the mind within the mind—that person’s life is truly radiant.
The life of one who has dissolved the mind—which is unattached to objects that resemble non-entities and free from the impurity of conceptualization—is truly beautiful.
Firmly grasping the true vision, this activity of the world is performed with ease; he by whom life is lived without latent impressions truly shines.
He who, even while engaged in worldly activity, feels neither internal satisfaction nor agitation upon encountering what is to be rejected or accepted—his life is truly radiant.
Just as a flock of swans emerges from a pure lake during the bright fortnight, so does the stream of virtues flow forth from him; his life is truly radiant.
When he has reached the path of hearing, been seen, or come to mind, living beings attain bliss; his life is truly radiant.

O Lord of the Danavas, when he rises, all the lotus-like hearts of people become possessed of life and full of joy; it is his very life that shines forth like the inexhaustible moon’s fullness, and not that of any other.
The Blessed One said: The stability of the body that has been seen is called "life" by people; the relinquishing of the body for the sake of another body is known as "death."
O Great-minded One, you are now liberated from both these two sides; what death can there be for you here, or what life remains to you?
O crusher of enemies, all-knowing one, I have spoken this merely for the sake of illustration; you do not die, nor will you ever die.

Though residing in a body, you are bodiless because of your lack of embodiment; you are the seer who is free from the body. Though residing in space, you are indeed like the wind in the sky, for you are unattached.
O observer of noble vows, because it brings about the perception of touch, the body alone exists [as the locus]; and by virtue of obstructing expansion, space is the cause of expansion.

Where is there room for a body here among those who are tranquil, since they have awakened to the true nature of reality? This single, limited form, however, remains poorly situated within the ignorant.

At all times, you are everything indeed—the supreme singular consciousness that is the light of the intellect. What is the body, and what is the bodiless state, which you grasp and from which you abandon?
Whether spring arises or the wind of dissolution blows, what has come to the Self, which is devoid of both existence and non-existence?
Even while mountains are crumbling, even while the fires of cosmic destruction are burning, and even while cataclysmic winds are blowing, one indeed remains established in one's own self alone.
Let all beings remain, or let everything pass away; whether they perish or increase, it abides solely within the Self.
The Supreme Lord does not perish when [the body] reaches destruction, nor does He increase when it increases; He does not quiver even while this body quivers.
When the mental delusion that "I am the body" and "I am the embodied one" has perished, why does this vain conceptualization arise: "Shall I abandon [the world] or shall I not abandon it?"
"Having done this, I shall do that; having abandoned this, I shall take that"—O dear one, such volitions have utterly perished for those who know reality.
The awakened ones, who are the agents of all things, will perform some action here; yet they do not fall into the state of eternal non-agency by virtue of their non-performance.
Since there is no agency, the absence of being an enjoyer follows by logical necessity; indeed, who in these three worlds has ever gathered what was not sown?
When agency and enjoyership have been stilled, peace alone remains here; that very peace, having reached full maturity, is called liberation by the wise.
Awakened, consisting of consciousness, and pure, they abide pervading everything; what is there to be abandoned that they should take up, or what is there to be grasped that they should abandon?

Devoid of the sequence of parts involved in the cognition of the relationship between the grasped and the grasper, and lacking the constituent parts of the object of knowledge, what could it grasp, and what could it abandon?
When the relationship between the grasped and the grasper has been exhausted, peace arises fully; this peace, having attained stability, is designated by the name "liberation."
Abiding there, ever peaceful, supreme persons such as you indeed move about by virtue of a similarity to the movement of limbs during deep sleep.
With your latent impressions stilled through the awakening of others, observe this worldly existence with a mind established in the Self, as if you were half-asleep.

For those whose intentions are fixed within their own self do not take delight in pleasurable things; they are not distressed by the sufferings of others, being absorbed in the singular elixir of the self.
Ever awakened and free from attachment, they undertake these activities just as they arise, without desire, like mirrors reflecting images.
Established in their own self, they are awake; yet while situated in the cycle of worldly existence, they are as if asleep. With dispositions resembling deep sleep, they tremble like children.

O Great-souled One, having entered the path of the Unconquered and having enjoyed for but a single day the prosperity of the Lotus-born, depart now from this world for that supreme, imperishable abode which is endowed with a multitude of virtues.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When Padmanābha, who beholds the wonders of the three worlds and is like a casket of jewels for the universe, had spoken thus with words as cool as moonlight, [the Lord continued].
That body named Prahlāda, whose lotus-eyes were radiant, spoke these words with joy, being firm and having mastered the sequence of reflection.

Prahlāda said: "O Lord, through deliberations on what is beneficial and harmful, and by means of hundreds of royal duties, I have become exceedingly fatigued; I have come to a state of rest for a moment."
O Blessed One, through your grace, my stability has been perfectly attained; whether in meditative absorption or non-absorption, I am always equal in form.
O Great God, after being beheld for a long time within by my stainless intellect, it is by good fortune that you are now seen again externally by my vision.
O Maheśvara, I existed within this infinite vision, which is free from all conceptual constructions, like space within pure space.
Neither by grief, nor by delusion, nor by thoughts of dispassion, nor by the act of abandoning the body, nor by fear of saṃsāra.
For when that One alone exists, whence can there be sorrow, whence destruction? Whence the body, where is saṃsāra, where is stability, and where fear or fearlessness?
Just as one might by mere pure will, arising entirely of itself, so indeed did I dwell in that vast and holy state.
"Alas, O Lord! This thought, 'I am dispassionate; I shall renounce the world,' belongs to those of unawakened vision and brings about the transformations of joy and sorrow."
"In the absence of a body there are no sufferings; my conviction is that sufferings reside in the body"—this serpent of poisonous thought devours only the fool.
"This is happiness, this is suffering; this does not exist for me, this exists"—a mind thus oscillating is indeed deluded, not wise.
The latent impression of those ignorant ones who think "I am one" and "this [other] is another" prevails here among living beings whose self-awareness has been cast far away.
"This is to be abandoned, this is to be accepted"—this false delusion of the mind does not lead one who knows the inner reality to madness, as it does the ignorant person of wicked intellect.
O lotus-eyed one, when you pervade the entire self, how can there be a second conceptualization consisting of the categories of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted?

The entire world, whether existent or non-existent, has arisen as a manifestation of consciousness; what here is to be rejected, and what is to be accepted—that which is neither abandoned nor not abandoned?
Investigating the seer and the seen solely through their own intrinsic nature, he rested for a moment within himself, the Supreme Self, by means of the self.
Freed from existence and non-existence, and devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted, I was thus formerly, and now I am established in this very way.
O Mahādeva, everything that has come into my possession has become my very self; I shall do for you whatever pleases you.
"You, O lotus-eyed one, are worthy of worship throughout the three worlds; therefore, you ought to accept from me this honor offered according to my nature."
Having spoken thus before the one who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk, the lord of the Dānavas took up the vessel for the arghya offering like a great mountain taking up the full moon.
Then he worshipped Govinda, who stood at the forefront of the three worlds, together with his weapons, the host of Apsarases, the gods, the lord of birds, and the entire triple world.
Having worshipped the Lord of the Worlds, who dwells within all worlds—both external and internal—and who remains there, the Lord of Kamalā then spoke to him.
The Blessed One said: "Arise, O lord of the Dānavas, and take your seat upon the throne; I myself shall soon bestow the consecration upon you."
May those Siddhas, Sādhyas, and hosts of gods who have assembled here upon hearing the sound of the Pāñcajanya conch, bestow auspiciousness upon you.
Having spoken thus, the lotus-eyed one seated the worthy Dānava upon the lion-throne, like a cloud upon a peak of Mount Meru.
Then Hari [honored] him with the waters of the great oceans, such as the Kṣīroda, and with the floods of rivers such as the Gaṅgā, as well as with the waters of all sacred fords (tīrtha).
Together with all the assemblies of brahmin seers and all the hosts of siddhas, he was again joined by the vidyādharas and accompanied by the world-protectors.
The one of immeasurable soul consecrated the great Asura in the sovereignty of the Daityas, while being praised by the hosts of Maruts, just as Hari was formerly consecrated in heaven.
While being praised by the gods and asuras, Madhusūdana spoke these words to Prahlāda, who was himself being praised by the gods and asuras at his consecration.

The Blessed One said: "O sinless one, as long as Mount Meru endures, as long as the earth remains, and as long as the orbs of the moon and sun exist, so long shall you be a king, praised for your unimpaired virtues."
Having abandoned the fruits of the desirable and the undesirable with a mind of equanimous vision, and being free from passion, fear, and anger, protect the kingdom.
In this kingdom, which is filled with enjoyments and where the supreme ground has been seen, you should not feel agitation whether regarding heaven or the human world.
Regarding the views obtained according to place, time, and action, attend to the task at hand; O sir, remain with a mind free from mental agitation.

Having transcended the body and being entirely free from the notions of "this-ness" and "mine-ness," you perform actions with equanimity toward both existence and non-existence; thus, you are not afflicted in this world.
Having perceived the various states of saṃsāra and having weighed the incomparable and comparable states, you know everything everywhere; what else remains to be taught?
While you, free from passion, fear, and anger, reign as king, this painful and stubborn knot shall no longer crush the Asuras.
The beauty of her tears will drench the clusters of flowers on Asura’s ears, just as a river with its broad, turbulent waves floods a forest grove.
From this day forward, the world remains as if at peace, like the ocean after the Mandara mountain has been removed, no longer subject to the conflict between demons and gods.
Let the wives of the gods and asuras, brought together from one another, place their trust solely in their own husbands and their own inner apartments.

Having dispelled the darkness of the profound sleep of the long night of worldly existence, and with the glory of your resolve ever-risen, enjoy for a long time the sovereignty of Ajita, which is as delightful as the amorous charms of the daughters of Danu.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus, the lotus-eyed one, together with the humans, gods, and kinnaras, departed from the abode of the asuras like a second world-system.
He was being filled by multitudes of handfuls of flowers released by Prahlāda and others, and by the clusters of feathers from the rear of the king of birds.
Having reached the Ocean of Milk in due course and dismissed the river of the gods, he sat upon the seat of the serpent’s coils like a bee upon a white lotus.
Viṣṇu remained upon the serpent’s coiled seat, Śakra in heaven with the immortals, and the lord of the Dānavas in the netherworld; thus they all stayed, free from anxiety.

O Rāma, this attainment of awakening belonging to the daughter of Prahlāda, which destroys all impurities without exception and is as cooling as the nectar of the moon, has been told to you in its entirety.
But those men in the world who, even if they have committed many evil deeds, shall reflect upon her with their intellect, they will attain the state without delay.
Through general inquiry, evil action comes to an end; through inquiry into the words of yoga, who does not attain the supreme state?
Ignorance is said to be evil; it is destroyed by inquiry. Therefore, one should not abandon inquiry, for it cuts through the very root of evil.
For those men who contemplate this perfect attainment of Prahlāda, the sins committed throughout seven lifetimes undoubtedly go to destruction.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, how was the mind of the great-souled Prahlāda awakened when it had become absorbed in the supreme state by the sounds of the Pāñcajanya conch?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O you of sinless form, two kinds of liberation exist in this world: one with the body and the other without the body; hear now this distinction between them.
Know that the state of one whose mind is unattached to the taking up or casting off of actions, and who is free from longing, is here what is called liberation while living (jīvanmuktatā).

O Rāma, that very state, when the body perishes, is called videhamukti (liberation without a body), which is devoid of rebirth; those established in it do not come within the range of the visible world.
Like parched seeds, devoid of the sprout of further birth, the pure latent impression (vāsanā) of those liberated while living resides within the heart.
Purifying, supremely noble, and following after pure being, she who consists of self-meditation remains eternally as if in deep sleep.
O descendant of Raghu, even at the end of a thousand years, those liberated while living awaken with that very same intermediate state as long as the body remains.
O mighty-armed one, Prahrāda attained awakening through his own internal latent impression of pure being, awakened by the sound of a conch shell.
For Hari is indeed the Self of all beings; whatever appears to Him becomes exactly so immediately, for the Self alone is the cause of everything.
As soon as Vāsudeva thought, "May Prahlāda awaken at this very moment," it happened in that very instant.
Indeed, for the sake of creation, he whose self is Vāsudeva assumed a body within himself, both without cause and as the cause of all beings.
Through the contemplation of the Self, Mādhava is swiftly beheld; through the propitiation of Mādhava, the Self itself is swiftly beheld.
Firmly grasping this view for the sake of perceiving the Self, O Raghava, quickly dwell as one whose nature is inquiry; you shall attain the eternal state.
O Rāma, the pervasive rainy season of saṃsāra, filled with the downpour of suffering, brings about extreme dullness for those who do not behold the sun of inquiry.
By the grace of Viṣṇu, his own self, this exceedingly radiant illusion does not afflict the wise, just as a yakṣī cannot affect one who possesses the protective mantra.

By its own internal will, it attains density; by its own internal will, it becomes thin again in due time. This weaving of the web of saṃsāra occurs here within the flames of infinite māyā, like the wind-circle of a fire.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, we have been refreshed by the pure rays of your words, just as medicinal herbs are by the rays of the moon.
Your words, which are pure, soft, and longed for by the ears, bring comfort when received, just like flowers.
If everything is attained through human effort, then why was Prahlāda not enlightened without the grace of Mādhava?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, whatever was attained by the high-souled Prahlāda was achieved by him through human effort alone, and not from any other source.
The Self and Nārāyaṇa are indeed not different, like sesame seeds and their oil; likewise, they are like whiteness and a cloth, or like a flower and its fragrance.
For he who is Viṣṇu is indeed the Self (Ātman), and he who is the Self is Janārdana; the words "Viṣṇu" and "Self" are synonyms, just as "tree" and "plant" are.
First, he himself, by his own self, was appointed to devotion for Viṣṇu by his own supreme power, under the name Prahlāda.
For Prahlāda himself had personally won this boon; having made his own mind subject to inquiry, he had known it by himself.
Sometimes the Self awakens itself by its own power; sometimes it is awakened through the body of Viṣṇu, which is attainable through devotion.
Even though he has been propitiated for a long time and is exceedingly pleased, Mādhava is not able to bestow knowledge upon one who lacks discernment.
In the realization of one's own self, inquiry arising from human effort is primary; causes such as divine grace are secondary. Therefore, be intent upon the primary cause.
Therefore, having first forcibly subdued the five sense-faculties, practice with every effort and make the mind possessed of discernment.
Whatever is attained by anyone, anywhere, is indeed obtained through the operation of one's own power; it is never obtained from any other source.
Relying on human effort and having leaped over the mountain of the senses, cross the ocean of saṃsāra and go to the further shore, the supreme state.
If Janārdana were visible without human effort, why does that unborn one not likewise deliver the multitudes of beasts and birds?
If a guru can rescue the ignorant person through his own power alone, why then does he not rescue a trained camel or a bullock?
Nothing great is obtained from Hari, nor from a guru, nor from wealth; for that which is attained by one whose mind is subdued comes from oneself.
That which cannot be attained by the self when the serpent of the senses has been subdued through the union of practice and dispassion, cannot be attained even throughout the three worlds.
Satisfy the self by means of the self; worship the self by means of the self; having beheld the self by means of the self, remain established in the self by means of the self.
For the sake of engaging fools who flee from the study of scriptures, effort, and inquiry in a state of auspicious stability, "Vaiṣṇava devotion" has indeed been devised.
First, the primary rule is said to consist of practice and effort; in its absence, however, there is the secondary method consisting of the sequence of worshiping the object of worship.
If there is no conquest of the senses, what fruit can be obtained through worship? And if there is no conquest of the senses, what fruit can be obtained through worship?
For Hari is not attained without inquiry and tranquility; and for one who is liberated through inquiry and tranquility, what need is there for the Lotus-handed One?
Cultivate your own mind, endowed with discernment and tranquility; when that is perfected, you are perfected, otherwise you are but a wild donkey in the forest.
Why is it that a request for affection is made by Madhava and others themselves, yet a similar request is not made to one's own mind?
Viṣṇu resides within every single person; those lowest of men who go outside, abandoning him, seek Viṣṇu externally.
The reality of consciousness dwelling in the cave of the heart is the primary, eternal body; the form with conch, discus, and mace in hand is the secondary manifestation of the Self.
For he who, abandoning the primary, pursues the secondary, is like one who, having discarded a perfected elixir, seeks to achieve something that must still be accomplished.
But he who, O descendant of Raghu, does not attain stability in this wondrous state of self-knowledge, his mind remains intoxicated.

One who has not yet attained discrimination regarding the self, whose inner nature is unknown, and who has not mastered the mind, should worship the Supreme Lord who holds the conch, the discus, and the mace in his hands.
O Raghava, through the worship of that [deity] and through arduous austerity which produces dispassion, his mind attains purity in due course of time.
Through constant practice and discernment, the mind quickly becomes serene; it gradually attains the state of a mango tree that bears its own fruit.
O destroyer of enemies, this spoken fruit is also attained by the self through the self alone, by means of the cause known as the sequence of Hari’s worship.
Even he who attains a boon from Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor has thereby obtained for himself the fruit of the tree of spiritual practice.
The restraint of one's own mind is the ground for all supreme states and for all long-lasting prosperities, just as the soil is the ground for the beauty of the harvest.
Even for one intent on digging up the earth or pulling up a mountain, there is no other means here than the restraint of one’s own mind.
Human beings wander upon this earth for thousands of births as long as the great ocean of the intoxicated mind does not reach tranquility.
Even though they have been worshipped for a long time, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Rudra, and the others—though full of affection—cannot protect one from the calamities of mental affliction.
Abandoning both the external and internal, which shine with various forms yet are unborn, quickly perform the contemplation of pure consciousness alone for the sake of ending rebirth.

Taste that which consists solely of the one, stainless consciousness, free from all objects of perception, infinite in form, and the essence of all existence; you shall thereby reach the further shore, the supreme beyond the river of birth.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, this endless illusion called saṃsāra comes to an end only through the conquest of one's own mind, and not otherwise.
O sinless one, listen attentively as I relate this history for the purpose of understanding the manifold variety of the world's illusory expansion.
On this surface of the earth, there is a province named Kosala; it is like a grove of wish-fulfilling trees on Mount Meru, a source of multitudes of jewels.
There lived a certain virtuous Brahmin known as Gādhi, who was a supreme Vedic scholar, wise, and stood like the very embodiment of Dharma.
