From his childhood, he shone with a mind free from passion, just as the world is illuminated by a stainless and pure sky.
Having set some desired undertaking within his own heart, he departed from his circle of kinsmen and went to the forest to perform austerities.
There, that king of Brahmins reached a lake filled with blossoming lotuses, like the moon reaching the sky which is bright, stainless, and filled with the essence of stars.
Seeing that lake, the twice-born man entered it for the sake of penance, submerged up to his neck in water like a lotus in the rainy season.
Eight months passed for him as he remained submerged in the waters of the lake, his facial complexion only slightly faded due to the closing of his lotus-like dwelling.
Then one day, Hari came to him who was heated by asceticism, just as a dark cloud comes to the earth’s surface when it is distressed by the summer heat during the rainy season.
The Blessed One said: "O Brahmin, arise from the midst of the milk and take your desired boon; the tree of your religious observance has borne the fruit you longed for."
The Brahmin said: Salutation to Viṣṇu, the bee within the hollow of the heart-lotuses of the innumerable beings of the world, who is the lake for the unique lotus-stalk of the three worlds.
O Blessed One, I wish to behold this supreme illusion fashioned by you, which bears the name of saṃsāra and causes nothing but blindness.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: "O unborn one, you shall see this illusion and then abandon it"; having spoken thus, he became invisible, like a city of the Gandharvas.
When Viṣṇu had departed, that lordly Brāhmaṇa rose up from the water, his form cool and stainless like the moon emerging from the waters of the Milky Ocean.
His soul became completely satisfied by the sight of the Lord of the World, like a night-lotus blossoming at the sight and touch of the moon.
Then, for that forest-dweller who was filled with the joy of beholding Hari, several days passed while he performed his duties as a brahmin.
Once, he began his bath in a lake filled with blooming lotuses, reflecting in his mind upon the words of Viṣṇu, like a great seer.
Then, during the ritual of bathing, he performed a submersion within the water for the sake of destroying all his sins, as if with his own body undergoing a complete transformation.

During that rite performed within the water, his mind having forgotten its meditation and mantras, and the expansion of his consciousness having become disoriented, he beheld from within the midst of the water:
He saw his own deceased self, fallen within his own dwelling into a state of lamentation, like a tree toppled by the force of the wind into the depths of a mountain cave.
With the flow of inhalation and exhalation ceased, it has reached the state of liberation; the vibration of its limbs is completely stilled, like a lamp-flame in a windless place.
With a pale face, withered like a sapless leaf from a tree, he was as if turned into a corpse, yet not yet decayed, like a lotus whose stalk has been severed.
The sky appeared as if its gaze were inverted at dawn, the village seemed shrouded by a drought, and everything was grey with dust on all sides.
It was surrounded by distressed kinsmen, their faces drenched in tears, uttering piteous cries of lamentation, like ospreys surrounding a tree.
He was supported at his feet by his wife, who resembled a lotus pond whose lotuses had their faces carried away by the waters gushing from the breach of the dam.
His mother, greedy for his cries, wailing, moaning, and chatter, seized him by the chin, which was marked with the signs of infancy.
He was surrounded by other wretched people standing at his side with tear-streaming faces, clinging to him like trees with withered leaves from which the frost is dripping.
It was covered by limbs that had stretched out far away as if they were not their own, as if intent on avoiding contact out of fear of separation.
With his white teeth biting his lips, which were not touching one another, he seemed to laugh at his own life with those unblemished teeth that appeared as if they had lost their passion.
As if entered into silent meditation, as if fashioned from mud, as if fast asleep for lack of awakening, and as if resting profoundly.
He seemed to be listening with effort to the voices arising from the tumultuous clamor of his kinsmen’s lamentation, as if in order to discern the nature of their affection.
Then, with gestures agitated by the outcries of that moment's waves, they were drenched by the streams of tears from eyes raised in a swoon as they beat their breasts.
Gradually, driven out by his agitated kinsmen with loud, hoarse cries of "Tārā! and other lamentations, that inauspicious being was indeed banished so as never to be seen again.
It was led to the cremation ground, defiled by the mire of flesh, entrails, and fat; drenched in both dry and fresh fluids, and crowded with hundreds of skeletons.

The sun’s rays were shrouded by vultures like clouds; the darkness was dispelled by the blazing of funeral pyres; and the earth was overspread with a network of flames from the mouths of jackals and corpses.
It was bathed in flowing rivers of blood, where fierce herons and crows were submerged; it was filled with aged birds bound by a spreading web of strings still damp with gore.
There, in that blazing fire, those kinsmen reduced the corpse to ashes, just as the oceans do with the submarine fire by pouring forth floods of water.
With crackling and popping sounds, that fire quickly consumed the corpse, its mass of matted flames swelling up like a great quantity of dry fuel.

The fire, pervading the mass of clouds with the fragrance released by the loud *kaṭakaṭa* crackling sounds rising up, shattered the heap of bones on all sides, just as an elephant crushes a bamboo grove full of holes while exuding its thick, rich sap.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then Gādhi, with his intellect made pliant by his own mastery, beheld [the truth] within the stainless self by means of the inner self, while remaining right there within the water.
He saw himself, agitated, situated within the womb of a woman of the *śvapacas*—outcastes dwelling on the outskirts of villages at the edge of the circle of living beings.
Oppressed by the burden of dwelling in the womb, his delicate limbs tormented, he lay within the heart of a dog-cooker woman, as distressed as if in his own excrement.
In due time, through gradual ripening, she gave birth to one of dark complexion, like a dark cloud born of the rainy season by a dog-cooker woman, enveloped in impurities.
In the house of a dog-cooker (śvapaca), there was a child, the darling of the dog-cooker, who was moving here and there like the river Yamunā when it is swollen with overflowing waters.
He had reached the age of twelve, yet remained in the bloom of sixteen; with broad shoulders and noble limbs, he was as full-bodied as a rain cloud.
Accompanied by a retinue of dogs, he roamed from forest to forest, slaughtering hundreds of thousands of deer and adopting the lifestyle of a Paulinda hunter.
Then he was approached by the beloved of a dog-cooker (śvapaca), who resembled a tamāla creeper, adorned with clusters of breasts like blossoms, and possessing hands like fresh sprouts.
She was dark-complexioned, with a row of teeth that appeared pure despite her soiled appearance; she was like a forest creeper, her limbs gracefully undulating with abundant charm.
He was sporting at the edges of the forests with his new bride—dark-complexioned as he was with her who was dark as well—just as a male bee sports with a female bee amidst the abundance of flowers.
Dwelling amidst the leaves of forest trees and creepers, he was afflicted by calamity, appearing like the formidable Vindhya wilderness itself personified.
Resting in forest thickets, sleeping in mountain caves, hidden among heaps of leaves, and making its home within shrubs.
Abounding with *kiṃkirāta* flowers as ear-ornaments, adorned with garlands of jasmine, made beautiful by *ketaka* flowers worn as crests, and filled with garlands of mango blossoms.
He was accustomed to reclining on beds of flowers and wandering among mountain slopes; he was an expert in the secrets of the forests and highly skilled in the hunting of deer.
Then, upon the mountains, he brought forth sons who were the sprouts of his own lineage, yet whose fortunes were exceedingly harsh, like thorns on a khadira tree.
Though possessed of a wife and endowed with wealth, he remains with his youth gone, gradually falling into decrepitude like a dry land deprived of rain.
Then, having gone to that birthplace of the village of *bhūta-grahas*, he stayed there like a lord of sages, having constructed a small hut from leaves at a distance.
Having reached a state of extreme decrepitude due to old age, his own body was like that of his son; he resembled a withered *tāla* tree in a ravine whose sap had almost entirely dried up.
He maintained a mature household life as a dog-cooker (śvapaca) with many kinsmen; though his name and its meaning were cruel, he had attained great prosperity.
Then Gādhi saw that his wife was old and had become a remover of her own delusions by serving among the dog-cookers (outcastes).
His entire family was completely swept away by death, just as a mass of forest leaves is quickly carried off by a torrential downpour.
Wasted by suffering in the wilderness, he laments all alone, like a deer separated from its herd—despairing and with eyes full of tears.
Having spent some days there with a mind overwhelmed by grief, he abandoned his own country, just as a bird leaves a lake whose lotuses have withered.
He wandered through many lands, free from attachment yet filled with anxiety, as if impelled by another, like a cloud driven by the wind.
Once, while wandering through the empty sky like a celestial chariot in the firmament, that sky-goer reached the glorious city of Kīra.
Its paths, trees, creepers, and courtyards were covered with dancing jeweled garments; it was strewn with flowers reaching down to the ankles and made beautiful by sandalwood and agallochum.
Surrounded on all sides by vassal lords, women, and citizens, he reached the middle of the royal highway, which resembled the path to heaven.
There he beheld a house constructed of precious gems, with an auspicious elephant inside, moving restlessly like the king of the immortals' mountain.
When the king had died, he wandered here and there for the sake of the kingdom, like a connoisseur of jewels seeking jewels, out of a desire to behold the wish-fulfilling gem.
That outcaste gazed for a long time at the elephant, which resembled a mountain possessed of movement, with eyes wide with curiosity.
Taking him who was looking on with his trunk, that elephant respectfully placed him upon its own shoulder, as Mount Meru bears the sun upon its slope.
When he had ascended the litter, the drums of victory resounded on all sides, like the great oceans when the clouds of the cosmic dissolution have risen into the sky.
The king shone with his desires fulfilled, while the sound of the people crying "Victory! arose like the warbling of birds that have awakened.
Then there arose from the throngs of bards a dense clamor, like the roar of oceans whose waters are tossed by the tide.
There, beautiful women surrounded him for the sake of adorning him, like the waves of the Milk Ocean agitated around Mount Mandara.
The proud women filled him with various jewels strung together by their virtues, just as the shores at dawn fill the coastal mountains with the rising sun through its manifold radiance.
They adorned him with necklaces whose touch was cool as frost, just as dark autumn rains adorn a lofty mountain peak with the floods of forest rivers.
With flowers of diverse colors and fragrances, women with their sprout-like hands moving restlessly surrounded him, as if they were the forest surrounding the beauty of spring.
They quickly anointed him with ointments of various colors, flavors, and fragrances, just as a mountain is covered by clouds with masses of mineral ores.
Beautiful as gold and jewels, he captivated the expansive mind, like Mount Meru filling the sky pervaded by twilight clouds, stars, the moon, and rivers.
Adorned and surrounded by playful young creepers, strewn with flowers of jewels and silken garments, he shone like a wish-fulfilling tree.
All the subjects, accompanied by their retinues, approached him who was in such a state, just as travelers approach a blossoming tree by the roadside.
There, they consecrated him in due order upon a lion-throne, just as the immortals consecrated Śakra upon the elephant Airāvata.
Thus that outcaste obtained the kingdom within Kīrapura, just as a crow seizes a fat wild deer in the forest that has lost its life-breath.
His lotus-feet were rubbed by the lotus-palms of Kīrī; his entire body was beautified with applications of saffron paste, resembling the clouds of twilight.
In the city of Kīra, that king, accompanied by a multitude of women, shone like a lion joined by a pride of lionesses in a forest in full bloom.

His body adorned with clusters of pearls fallen from the temples of elephants slain by Hari, his anxiety and dejection stilled, he took delight there in the company of the virtuous and in various enjoyments, like an elephant scorched by the heat of the sun's rays finding relief in the full waters of a lake.

With royal majesty spread abroad and his commands established in every direction, having secured the administration of the country within a few days, and having fully relieved the burden of all the nobles through his ministers, he became the king there by the name of Gavala.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Surrounded by playful women, honored by the circle of ministers, saluted by all the vassal lords, and graced by the royal parasol and fly-whisks;

He was beloved as a teacher of perfected instructions, one who understood the sequence of the qualities of sovereignty; his wisdom was free from sorrow, fear, and fatigue, and he had attained the great tenth stage.
Having forgotten his own true nature through constant hymns of praise and auspicious rites, he was as if utterly intoxicated by liquors, his state of being filled with bliss.
A Chandala ruled the kingdom over the Kiras for eight years; during that time, he maintained the conduct of an Arya in its entirety.

Then, once by chance, he remained there having cast off his ornaments, like the sky when it is free from darkness and filled with the splendor of the stars, the moon, and the sun, as well as the clouds.
He did not highly regard our necklaces, armlets, and bracelets; for a mind expanded by sovereignty does not take pleasure in what is merely acquired.
Clad in such attire, he alone went out to the outer courtyard, like the sun setting from the main part of the sky.
There he saw a group of dark-skinned, stout outcaste dog-cookers, singing softly like a flock of cuckoos at the onset of spring.
With the grace of his sprout-like hands, he shook the strings of the lute, producing soft sounds like a tree whose bees hum softly as they stir its swaying branches.
Then one man rose up from among them—an old man with bloodshot eyes, resembling the leader of a tribe of outcastes, like a glass horn filled with frost.
"O Kaṭañja! he said suddenly to King Kīra, "Is there perhaps a king here who knows the art of singing?"
Does he honor the red-throated cuckoo as if he were full of passion, or does he perhaps fill it with offerings of household garments and seats?
Just as a mango tree with its abundance of fruit and flowers delights the bees, so too have I attained supreme bliss today by the mere sight of you.
Just as the lotus [blooms] at the rising of the sun, and as the medicinal herbs [shine] at the rising of the moon, so too [is this the source] of all joys and even of great attainments.
"The meeting with a kinsman is the ultimate limit of endless rest"—as the dog-cooker (the outcaste) spoke thus, the king, by his very gesture of victory at that moment, showed him contempt.
Meanwhile, the beloved women who had gone to the windows likewise fell into a state of extreme dejection upon realizing, "This is a dog-eater."
The citizens did not shine, like villages afflicted by a downpour of frost, or like great mountains beset by forest fires.
The king disregarded each of those conversations concerning the outcaste, just as a lion ignores the yowling of a cat perched on the top of a tree.
He quickly entered the inner apartments, which were filled with dejected people, like a royal swan entering a lake whose lotuses are withering for lack of rain.
With all his limbs relaxed and suffering from a wasting disease, he became like a withered tree, as if consumed by the fire within the great cavity between his two knees.
There he saw all the people with dejected faces, like a net of saffron flowers whose base has been gnawed away by a rat.
Then the ministers, the citizens, and the women did not even speak to that lord of the earth while he stood right there in his own house, as if he were a corpse.
Then his servants, though filled with grief and bound by deep affection, abandoned him when he offered them no hospitality, just as children leave a corpse.
With a face devoid of joy, his body dark and stripped of its luster, they—free from agitation—regarded him as if he were a scorched wasteland.
As his body began to smoke, the people, overcome by a state of intense distress, did not approach his side, just as one does not approach a fire on a mountain.
Devoid of enthusiasm and deprived of the assembly of courtiers, their commands found no footing, like drops of water upon ashes.
Because he had the appearance of one who performs cruel deeds and brought misfortune to those who associated with him, people fled from him in particular, as if from a *rākṣasa*.
Though situated in the midst of people, he remained all alone, devoid of wealth and other such qualities, like a traveler in a foreign land.
Even though she spoke to them repeatedly, the city-dwellers gave no reply to her, just as travelers give no answer to a whistling bamboo flute, even when it is adorned with strings of pearls.
Now, having been defiled by the dog-cookers for a long time, we shall not be purified by expiatory rites; we shall enter the fire.
Having thus resolved, the citizens and the ministers in the city set fire on all sides to funeral pyres fueled with dry wood.
Then, with those [fires] blazing all around like stars in the sky, the entire city became filled with people whose supreme state was one of lamentation.
It was hemmed in by wives wailing piteously with cries of compassion and shedding rains of tears, while the people nearby wept bitterly at the edge of the blazing sacrificial pit.
With the weeping of the attendants for the ministers who had entered the sacrificial fire-pits, the forest seemed to cry out even more intensely, as if by the winds.
The air was thick with the pungent stench of the flesh of eminent Brahmins being consumed on the funeral pyres, while a portentous whirlwind arose, scattering dust like falling snow.
With wheels that were powerful like birds brought from afar by the scent of long-standing fat carried by the wind, the sky became covered as if by clouds, obscuring the sun.
The circle of the sky blazed with funeral pyres fanned by the wind; the horizons were filled with a shower of stars that were masses of flying sparks of fire.
With heedless thieves crying out and young children trembling, the city was filled with terrified citizens who had abandoned all hope for their lives, falling into total disorder.
The city was without its watchful guardians, its entire stores plundered by thieves, its sons and wives abandoned, and its citizens preoccupied with his death.
While that painful reversal of destiny was thus occurring, a state resembling the end of all kalpas for the entire mass of living beings prevailed.
Gavala, his intellect purified by association with virtuous people in the kingdom, reflected while his mind was agitated by grief.
For my sake, this calamity has come to pass in this land—an untimely dissolution like the end of an aeon, which shall bring about the destruction of all its leaders.
"What use have I for the suffering of life? Death is a great festival for me; for a wretched creature condemned by the world, death is better than life."
Having thus resolved, Gavala, in the blazing fire, fearlessly offered his body as an oblation like a moth.

When that body named Gavala had fallen into the mass of fire and reached a state of fragmentation of its limbs, Gādhi suddenly regained consciousness within the water due to the throbbing sensation of the burning fire scorching his own limbs.

Śrī Vālmīki said: When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, after two moments, Gādhi’s agitation, born from the delusion of worldly existence, subsided like the swelling of the ocean at the turn of the tide.
Due to his delusion regarding the mental creation, he desisted from it, just as Brahmā desists at the end of a kalpa from the creation of the world.
Having become tranquil, he gradually attained awakening to his own true nature, like one whose intellect has become alert after intoxication has subsided and whose disposition has reached maturity.
"This is I," "this is that task," and "this is not"—thus he perceived, just as the world sees clearly when the night has passed and the veil of darkness has faded away.
Then, remembering his true nature, he drew himself up from within the waters, like the month of Mādhava bringing forth a lotus whose face has blossomed at the end of winter.
Beholding this earth, with its gates, towers, and sky, as if it were another world, he was filled with the utmost wonder.
"Who am I? What do I see? What indeed have I done?"—reflecting thus, he remained for a moment in a state of wonder, with his eyebrows knitted.
"I became exhausted in that very instant upon seeing the commotion"; realizing this, he rose from the water like the rising sun.
And he thought on the bank: "Where is that mother? Where is that beloved, since I have met my death in the midst of both my mother and my wife?"
It is said that both parents of this ignorant child of mine have perished, like a leaf carried away by the wind from a tree or vine by a sword.
"I am unmarried, and I do not know even the true nature of women, who are as corrupting and agitating as wine, like a twice-born man [who has renounced the world]."
My own kinsmen have become exceedingly distant from my native land; who indeed are they among whom I should give up my life?
Therefore, what indeed have I seen arising from this—a flurry of various undertakings, like a city of Gandharvas?
Let this matter rest; for such is the state of death even among one's kinsmen. In this slight delusion of Māyā, nothing real is perceived.
Thus, the mind of embodied beings perpetually wanders among infinite delusive perceptions, like a maddened tiger roaming through forest thickets.
Having thus resolved this matter in his mind, Gādhi then brought him to his own hermitage for several days.
Once, a certain dear guest arrived there unexpectedly; weary from his journey, he took rest there like Durvāsas resting with Brahmā.
That guest was brought to the highest satisfaction by Gādhi with foods consisting of fruits, flowers, and juices, just as a tree is nourished by the spring season.
Having mutually saluted one another at twilight and both having performed their recitations, they reached their beds in due order and lay upon soft sprouts.
Then a peaceful conversation began between those two ascetics, appropriate to their own practice, like the beauty of flowers appearing on two trees at the arrival of spring.
Gādhi questioned that guest with words that arose in the course of conversation: "O Brahmin, why are you so emaciated in body, and why are you overcome by fatigue?"
The guest said: "O Blessed One, hear the cause of my extreme emaciation and fatigue; I shall tell you the truth as it is, for we are not speakers of untruth."
On this surface of the earth, in a bower of the northern quarter, there is a great and glorious country, highly renowned by the name Kīra.
There I dwelt for a month, being honored by the people in the city, my soul greedy for the taste of various sensual pleasures and deluded by the vampire of the mind.

Once, on a certain occasion during the course of a conversation there, one person said: "O twice-born, it has been told to me that a king who was a dog-eater (śvapaca) once reigned here for eight years."
Then, when questioned by him in the villages, all the inhabitants said to him: "A Śvapaca has been our king here for eight years."
Thus, having been fully understood at the end, he entered the fire with speed; thereafter, hundreds of brahmins here likewise entered the sacrificial flame.
Having heard this from their mouths, O twice-born one, I departed from that circle and performed a penance at Prayāga for the sake of purification.
Having performed the breaking of my fast today at the end of the third Cāndrāyaṇa penance, I have come here; because of that, I am exhausted and exceedingly emaciated.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having heard this, Gādhi then questioned that twice-born man again, and he explained this very same thing once more, and nothing else.
Then, filled with wonder, he spent that night there on Gādhi’s mountain; and when the sun, the great lamp of the world-house, had risen, he departed.
When his guest had performed the rites of the morning bath and departed after taking leave, he reflected upon this with a mind overflowing with wonder:
"That which was seen by me in my agitation has been declared by the twice-born to be real; what indeed could this be, other than the method of Śambara’s illusion?"
That death of my own which I witnessed in the midst of my kinsmen was surely an illusion; of this there is no doubt. As for the rest, I see it as belonging to him.
Therefore, with an undaunted mind, I shall go quickly to a village on the edge of the realm of spirits to see the account of that outcaste dog-cooker.
Thinking thus with reverence, he rose up to go to another mandala, as if the sun were striving to see the side of Mount Meru.
Even the kingdom of their desires wise and industrious men obtain; having gone there, Gādhi obtained in its entirety that which he had seen in a dream.
Through resolute determination, even that which is difficult to attain is obtained; Gādhi, perceiving the world as an illusion, was intent on making it an object of knowledge.
Having set out on the road with the speed of a monsoon torrent, he traversed many lands like a horse driven by the wind.
Then, having entered that circle of beings whose conduct was of such a kind, Karabha was alone like a thorn in a forest of *kārañja* trees.
There, by means of the very arrangement established within consciousness, he again beheld no one who could lead him astray, like a Gandharva seeing a city of his own making.
At its edge, he beheld that very same dwelling of the outcaste, like a multitude of hells in the netherworld beneath the earth.
He saw that supreme expanse conceived by his own mind, consisting of its very arrangement; like a Gandharva, he perceived himself as both a dog and an outcaste.
In that very same configuration, he saw the dwelling place of the outcaste seen before; it led his mind to an indescribable state of world-weariness.
It was battered by the downpours of the rainy season, with sprouts of barley growing from its walls, its roof-covering half-fallen and its beds barely visible.
Poverty was as if solidified, misfortune as if it had become a wall, wickedness as if its limbs were fallen away, and wretchedness as if it were shattered to pieces.
Its outskirts were covered with white bones of cattle, horses, and buffaloes, crushed by the tusks of elephants, standing as if there to bear witness.
The place was covered with those very skull-bowls in which he had previously eaten and drunk, now filled with the waters of motionless clouds as if full of drink.
It was completely encircled by those very entrails, shriveled and covered with membranes, like long-reaching thirsts.
Then, with self-possession, he gazed for a long time at his own former house, which had quickly come to resemble a dried-up corpse.
Filled with great wonder, he approached the village, just as a traveler, having crossed a city of barbarians, reaches a land of the Aryas.
There he questioned the people: "O good sirs, do you perhaps remember the former history of this village—the succession of the dog-cookers at its edge?"
For I have heard from virtuous people that all wise men clearly perceive even what occurred long ago as if it were right in the palm of their hand.
Do you not remember this excellent old outcaste living here in solitude, who is like a physical embodiment of sorrows?
"O virtuous one, if you know, tell me that in truth; O traveler, it is taught that the severing of another's doubt yields great merit."
Thus questioned repeatedly by the twice-born Gādhi, the villagers replied with no small measure of derision and agitation, like physicians to one who is afflicted.
The villagers said: "O Brahmin, as you say, so it is; it cannot be otherwise. There was here a dog-eater named Kaṭaṃja, of terrible appearance."
His retinue of sons, grandsons, friends, servants, kinsmen, and relatives was exceedingly vast, like the mass of leaves upon a great tree.
Death snatched away all the wives of that old man, just as a forest fire consumes a mountain filled with flowers and fruit.
Having abandoned that country, he went to the interior of Kīra’s city; there he became king for eight years without any agitation.
He who, having understood the truth therein, is shunned from afar by people, is like a heap of misfortune or like a poisonous tree in a village.
Then, as the people were entering the fire, he himself entered the consumer of oblations; for through association with the noble, he had attained nobility and thus entered it.
Why do you, O Lord, take such pains to question this dog-cooker? Is he perhaps a relative of yours, or did you yourself become so?
As he spoke thus, Gādhi questioned him again and again; he dwelt for one month among all those bordering regions.
Just as he had experienced that corpse-eating, so it was described by all those villagers to him exactly as it happened, without any omission.

Then, having heard this unimpeded account from the mouths of all those beings and having clearly observed it exactly as it had been experienced, Gādhi—whose heart was mounted upon the stainless moon and whose form was hidden—was struck with supreme wonder.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Gādhi’s mind, having rolled about in the house of a dog-cooker, again fell into amazement; for the mind never reaches satiety when beholding wonders.
There he surveyed the sites and dwellings, just as the Lotus-born Brahmā surveys the worlds overturned by the agitation at the end of an eon.
He spoke thus to himself in that forest where his dwelling lay in ruins, amidst a garland of withered bones, like a tree inhabited by a piśāca.
These rows of ivory from the tusks of dead elephants, which were fashioned as enclosures, remain even today for an eon, like the peaks of Mount Meru.
Here, in the past, the flesh of that female monkey was eaten along with cooked bamboo shoots by those intoxicated by liquor, together with their outcaste kinsmen.
Having embraced a woman as dark as a dog-eater (caṇḍāla) here upon a lion-skin, he lay down and drank the maireya wine, bitter with the ichor of elephants.
The female dogs of the household, nourished on oil-cake scraps, are tied here with leather thongs to the wooden post of the dead elephant.
Here you gave three pots of pearls from elephants, bound with the fierce hide of a buffalo that shone like a cloud.
On those various grounds here, he rolled for a long time with the children of the outcaste dog-cookers, like cuckoos among a heap of mango leaves.
Here, as if proceeding from the whistling of the flutes of the children's sighs, the song was drunk; the blood of the dog was consumed, and one adorned with a corpse was accomplished.
There, together with his family members at the wedding festivities, the householder performed a dance accompanied by loud shouts, like the surging waves in the ocean.
Here, for the sake of providing food at other times, a bamboo cage has been constructed and secured for the crows, vultures, and birds that are eager to fly up.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Recalling his former activities as a dog-eater in this manner, Gādhi, his head trembling with astonishment, reflected upon the supreme activity of the Creator.
Then, after a long period of time, he who understood what was to be done departed from that region, leaving behind the circle of living beings, and reached another land by degrees.
Having crossed over a continuous succession of rivers, mountains, regions, and forests, he reached, it is said, the jewel of the snowy mountain, the abode of people.
There, his soul weary from wandering through the world, he reached the city of Mahīpāla, which resembled a mountain, just as Nārada reaches the realm of the gods.
Then, seeing places in the city that he himself had previously experienced, seen, and frequented, he respectfully questioned the people.
"O virtuous one, do you remember anything here regarding a lord who was an outcaste? If you know the truth of it, describe it to me quickly and according to the facts."
The citizens said: "O twice-born one, for eight years there was a *śvapaca* here who became the lord of the earth; his kingship was bestowed by Maṅgalahastin."
And having been fully recognized before entering the fire, O ascetic, twelve years have now passed.
Whatever Gādhi asked people out of his curiosity, he heard from their very mouths and even savored it.
Then, in that city, he saw the king with his army and vehicles, as well as the god Viṣṇu, the wielder of the discus, emerging from the palace and going outside.
Seeing the sky covered by clouds of moving dust, and recollecting his former royal state, he spoke with great astonishment:
These are those Kīra women, whose skin resembles the interior of a lotus, who possess the hue of molten gold and eyes like trembling blue lotuses.
These multitudes of yak-tail whisks, white as a mass of moonbeams, resemble steady waterfalls or heaps of kāśa flowers.
Rows of yak-tail fans are being waved by lovely women; these are like the splendors of forest creepers now set ablaze.
These are those herds of rutting elephants that fill the horizons; they are like the successions of peaks of Mount Meru, appearing as the trees of one's own imagination.
These kings, whose prowess is equal to that of Yama, Varuṇa, and Kubera, are your vassals, like the world-protectors of Indra.
These rows of houses, beautiful with groves of wish-fulfilling trees and creepers, extend everywhere as floods of all manner of objects, bestowing everything desired.
This kingdom of Kīra, which was enjoyed by me in the past, has today come before my very eyes like the conduct of my own previous birth.
"This waking state has returned to me like a dream; I do not know by what cause this illusion has arisen and now unfolds."
Alas! Indeed, by this long and leaping delusion of the mind, I have been rendered helpless, like a small bird caught in a net.
Alas, what a pity! My mind, unawakened and struck down by latent impressions, perceives spreading webs of delusion like those of a child.
"Indeed, this great illusion was shown to me by that wielder of the discus; now I have clearly remembered it without any flaw."
Therefore, I shall now make such an effort in a mountain cave that I may know both the origin and the nature of this delusion.
Having reflected thus, he departed from that city and went to a cave in the mountain; having reached it, he stood there like a rested lion.
There, for a year and a half, that one of great splendor performed austerities, subsisting on a mere handful of milk, for the gratification of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Then the lotus-eyed one approached him in the form of water, dark as a blue lotus, like a great lake in autumn.
He came to that cave in the king of mountains, the abode of the twice-born; then he dwelt in the sky, possessing a complexion as clear and transparent as a water-bearing cloud.
The Blessed One said: "Gādhi, have you seen my most powerful illusion? Have you seen the workings of the web of the world, which consists of the nature of destiny?"
Since you have attained this state of mind, which is rightly praised as blameless, what else do you desire while performing austerities on this mountain slope?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Seeing Hari speaking thus, Gādhi, the best of the twice-born, filled his feet with a profusion of flowers as an act of worship.
Having offered the arghya water, strewn flowers, and quickly bowed with circumambulations, the twice-born spoke these words to Viṣṇu, as a cātaka bird addresses a rain-cloud.
Gādhi said: "O Lord, this illusion consisting of profound darkness which has been displayed by you—make it manifest to me, as the sun makes the earth clear at dawn."
O Lord, how is it that the delusion which the mind perceives—being garlanded with the impurities of latent tendencies—is seen even during the waking state, just as in a dream?
And how did that delusion of a dream within the water, perceived for but a moment, attain the status of direct perception for me, O abode of the stainless state?
Given the vastness of this time and the existence and non-existence of this body, how could the internal states not exist, even through my delusions regarding outcastes?
The Blessed One said: O Gādhi, this is the nature of the mind—which, though its true form has been shaken by its own afflictions and has not perceived reality—when it perceives manifold delusions.
Nothing exists externally at all—neither the sky, the ocean, the earth, nor the directions; these exist only within one's own mind, like a mass of leaves within a sprout.
Just as fruits and the like expand outward from a sprout, so too do earth and other elements manifest externally from the mind.
It is true that the earth and other elements reside within the mind and are never external; for the sprout contains the leaf, and from it comes the glory of the fruit.
The mind destroys and creates itself—consisting of form, light, mental attention, reality, time, and activity—just as a potter makes a jar.
This is experienced by all men, even down to children, in their perceptions of dreams, delusions, the intensity of intoxication, passion, disease, and so forth.
In the mind, which has acquired latent impressions (vāsanā), millions of mental states reside, just as fruits and flowers exist upon a tree rooted in the earth.
Just as a tree that has been abandoned by the earth does not produce leaves again, so too for a soul that has been divested of its substrate, there is no further rebirth or the like.
Since the entire web of infinite worlds is established by that splendor, if the state of a dog-cooker (outcaste) is manifested therein, what cause for wonder is there in this?
You have realized that the state of being a dog-cooker exists only through the power of appearance, just like the various afflictions that arise with great intensity.
In that very same way, you have seen the confusion caused by a twice-born guest who arrived, ate, slept, and told a story.
Rising up in that very manner, I went on until I reached a region of spirits; you have seen this agitation of these spirits and these villages.
In this very way, this former house of Kaṭañja was trampled; people said, "Have you seen the agitation of Kaṭañja?"
In that very manner, I arrived at the city of Kīra, and I was told by the Kīras: "You have witnessed with amazement the sovereignty of a Śvapaca."
Thus, O best of the twice-born, you have seen this entire web of delusion—both that which you perceive as truth and that which you understand as untruth.
What indeed does the mind, enveloped by latent impressions, not perceive within itself? Even a purpose that requires a year to accomplish is seen accomplished in a dream.
There were no guests, nor those beings, nor those Kiras, nor that city; O one of great intelligence, you saw all this through delusion.
O Brahmin, while traveling as a wayfarer to the land of the Bhūtas, you rested in a certain cave, like a deer in a forest.
In that very place, due to being deluded by exhaustion, one sees this circle of beings as "this is that house of a dog-cooker," but not as it truly is.
In that very same way, you saw the city of Kīra as it truly was; whether at that time or at another, O twice-born one, it was indeed for the sake of an illusion that you perceived it so.

O Sage, though you have always dwelt amidst all things in their completeness, you have nevertheless perceived a delusion within the mind, like one who is deranged wandering through the various directions.
Therefore, arise and remain performing your own duty with a tranquil mind; for in this world, human beings do not attain prosperity without performing their own prescribed work.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus, Padmanābha—being worshipped by the hosts of ascetics throughout the worlds and surrounded by throngs of gods and sages with pure hands—returned to his own abode in the ocean.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, after Viṣṇu had departed, Gādhi himself wandered through the elements and so forth in succession, like a cloud in the sky, for the sake of investigating his own delusion.
Having learned his own story from the people there, he returned to a mountain cave and once again propitiated Hari.
Then, in a short time, Janārdana arrived; for Mādhava becomes a kinsman through a single act of propitiation alone.
The Blessed One, being gracious, spoke to Gādhi like a cloud to a peacock: "What further do you seek through this austerity?"
Gādhi said: "O Lord, I have been wandering for six months through the lands inhabited by Bhūtas and Kirātas; there, my own account does not find its way even into their stories."
"O Lord, have you seen the world of beings through illusion? For the words of the great are for the destruction of delusion, not for its increase."
The Blessed One said: "By a chance occurrence, like the 'crow-and-palm' maxim, the state of being a dog-cooker (outcaste) reflects in the minds of all the Bhūtakīras just as it does in yours."
Therefore, my dear, they relate your story exactly as it happened; for once a manifestation has appeared, it does not return to a state of non-manifestation.
A certain dog-cooker (outcaste) had built a house at the edge of the village; you saw it possessed by a spirit and reduced to fragments of brick.
Sometimes a single intuition arises even among many; for the movement of the mind is indeed diverse, like the simultaneous perching of crows, palm trees, and date palms.
For instance, many people may see the same dream, like those whose minds are slowed by intoxication from sleep, delusion, or liquor.
Many children delight in a single play, just as deer do in a single dark woodland thicket.
And many people strive at the same time toward the ripening of their own fruits through the manifestation of their actions, which appear in an exceedingly vast variety of forms.
O Brahmin, that scriptural injunction which states "the time for prohibitions and permissions is the giver" is merely a mental construct; for time exists only within the Self.
The Blessed Time is formless and is indeed Brahman itself; they know it to be unborn. It neither gives up nor takes anything from anyone, nor at any time.
This worldly time, consisting of years, kalpas, and yugas, is conceptualized by means of the multitude of objects, and yet the multitude of objects is conceptualized by means of it.
With their minds deluded by the confusion arising from a common appearance, those crowds of Kīra people perceived him in that very way.
Devoted to your own duty, examine yourself with your intellect; O virtuous one, remain right here once the delusion of the mind has departed, for I am going.
Having spoken thus, the Lord Viṣṇu, the Sovereign, vanished; Gādhi remained in the cave with a mind heavy with anxiety.
Then, after several months had passed on that mountain, that twice-born man once again propitiated the one who holds the lotus in his hand.
And one day, seeing her Lord arrived, she bowed down to him; she honored him with her mind and speech, and spoke thus to the Lord:
Gādhi said: "O Blessed One, remembering this state of mine as a dog-cooker and this illusion of worldly existence, my mind is utterly bewildered."
Having spoken thus according to the facts, for the cessation of great delusion, employ me in a single, pure action alone.
The Blessed One said: "O Brahmin, this world is the grand display of the great illusion of Māyā; all manner of wonders arise here from forgetfulness."
"That you saw that [city] in Bhūtakīrapura out of delusion is indeed possible; for such an illusion is seen by people."
And the Kiras, like you, have likewise seen such an illusion; it appears real even though it is in vain, because it arises simultaneously with other perceptions.
But hear this which I shall speak to you as it truly is and beyond reproach, so that your anxiety may wither away like a creeper in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
He who was formerly that outcaste named Kaṭañjaka in the realm of beings, became exactly as he had been before, in that very same form.
In that very same way, having become deficient in his vows and gone to another land, he became King Kīra; thereafter, he entered the fire.
At that time, the conduct of Kaṭañja appeared to you in your mind alone as if it were actually taking place within the water.
The mind sometimes completely forgets even an object that has been seen and experienced; yet at other times, it perceives even what has never been seen as if it were actually seen.
Just as the delusions regarding the existence of realms in dreams and mental fantasies are perceived by the mind itself, so too, my dear, are they seen even in the waking state.
Just as one who perceives the three times sees that which resides in the future and the past, so too does the story of Kaṭañja appear clearly in his intuition.
The one who possesses self-knowledge does not sink into the thought, "This is he, I am he, this is mine"; the one who lacks self-knowledge sinks into the thought, "This is he, I am he, this is mine."
The knower of reality does not despair, thinking "I am indeed all this"; he does not grasp at objects with the conceptualization of distinctions that lead to suffering.
Therefore, even though he is immersed in the whirlpools of worldly existence that revel in pleasure and pain, he does not sink, like a gourd vessel upon the water.

For your part, your mind is seized by the net of latent tendencies and you are devoid of discernment; like one suffering from a great disease with only a little remaining, you have not yet attained well-being.
Because your knowledge is incomplete, you are unable to ward off the delusion of the mind, just as one who lacks proper effort cannot dispel a cloud.
Whatever suddenly appears to your mind alone, by that very thing you are instantly overcome, just as a tree is by a person of great stature.
The mind, it is said, is the hub of this wheel of illusion here; if one stands having taken hold of it, nothing can cause any affliction.
Arise and, with an unwearied mind, perform penance for ten years in a grove on the mountain; thereafter, you shall attain infinite knowledge.
Having spoken thus, the lotus-eyed one vanished on the spot, like a wind-blown cloud, like a lamp, or like the swelling of the Yamunā, in an instant.
Gādhi, having attained the state of dispassion born from the power of discernment, became like a tree at the end of autumn that has lost its sap.
With a mind released from the burden of wandering delusions, he gently censured his own wondrous and improper conduct, which had arisen like a mineral impurity.
With his heart moistened by compassion, he went to Mount Ṛṣyamūka for the sake of supreme splendor through self-restraint and for the sake of rest, as a cloud approaches a mountain.
Having cast aside all mental constructs, he performed austerities there for ten years; by that means, he attained self-knowledge.

Thereafter, having regained his own true nature, the Great-Souled One—freed from fear and sorrow, dwelling upon the lands of enjoyment—remained perpetually joyful in the state of one liberated while living; serene and tranquil, he was like the full moon, his mind no longer agitated by the influx of worldly desires.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, O descendant of Raghu, this exceedingly vast and difficult-to-comprehend illusion, consisting of great delusion, is the formidable nature of the Supreme Self.
On one hand, there is the perception by the world of a dream lasting for only two moments; on the other, the delusion of being a king among outcastes experienced for many years.
Where is there the state of being perceived through agitation, and where is direct perception? Where is unambiguous unreality, and where is the transformation of reality?
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, I say: this treacherous illusion daily entangles the heedless-minded person in calamity.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin, how can one effect the stopping of this wheel of māyā as it revolves with such force, cutting through all one's limbs?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, know that the mind is the great hub of this wheel of illusion that constitutes the form of this world, which, as it revolves, causes others to revolve as well.
When that [subtle body] has been swiftly seized through the intellect by means of human effort, the wheel of māyā is obstructed because the channel of the navel has been grasped.
The wheel of delusion, with the mind fixed upon the navel, does not move, just as a peg wrapped in a rope cannot move when the rope is held fast.
O sinless one, you are an expert in the single method of wheel-warfare; why then do you not know that a wheel remains under control when it is firmly fixed at the hub, and not otherwise?
Therefore, O Rāghava, do not allow the mind to overwhelm you; with effort, restrain the self that carries the wheel of saṃsāra.
Without this reasoning, one's own suffering is endless and immeasurable; behold how, within this very view, it reaches its end in an instant.
But without the supreme medicine that consists merely in the conquest of the mind, the great disease of saṃsāra is not pacified even by effort.
Therefore, O Raghava, setting aside the practices of visiting sacred fords, giving gifts, and performing austerities, bring the mind itself under control for the sake of supreme welfare.

Samsara exists only within the mind, just as the space within a jar exists within the jar; when the mind is destroyed, there is no samsara, just as when the jar is destroyed, there is no space within the jar.
Having destroyed the hollow of the sky of saṃsāra—the vessel of the mind—enter that form whose nature is the incomparable sky.
For a moment, by employing the outward-turned intellect toward the present without effort, the mind—having abandoned the past and the future—attains the state of non-mind.
If you abandon the pursuit of even the slightest portion of volitional thought at every moment, then you have indeed attained that purifying state of non-mind.
As long as there is the mental construction of volition, so long do the manifestations of the mind persist; as long as the expanse of clouds remains, so long do the drops of water in the sky endure.

As long as there is a conscious mind, so long is there volition and the conceptualization of mental constructs; as long as the world exists with its moonbeams, so long do the fragments of frost persist.
If volition is devoid of mind and cultivated, know that the roots of one's own worldly existence are burnt away from the very root, just like the roots of a perfected being.
Indeed, consciousness devoid of the mind is called direct consciousness; it is by nature without a mind, and therein no stain of conceptualization exists.
That is truth, that is auspiciousness, that is the supreme state of the Self; that is omniscience, that is the vision wherein the mind is no longer wounded.
But wherever the mind is directed, there hope arises, and there too sorrow and joy always draw near, like crows to a cremation ground.
Through the realization of the true nature of reality, all things are established; yet the seed of the creeper of worldly existence is produced by conceptual construction.
Through the continuous practice resulting from contact with the scriptures and virtuous people, the unreality of worldly phenomena is realized.
Having withdrawn the mind from lack of discernment by means of resolute efforts, it should be forcibly united with the teachings of the scriptures and the conduct of the virtuous.
The self alone is the primary cause for the perception of the Supreme Self; a jewel fallen into the bottomless depths is perceived by means of a jewel itself.
One's own self alone desires to abandon the sufferings experienced by itself; therefore, the self alone is remembered as the supreme and sole cause for the knowledge of the self.
Whether speaking, releasing, grasping, opening the eyes, or closing them, remain intent solely upon infinite pure consciousness, free from all mental constructs.
Whether being born, living, or dying, and engaged in action, remain steadfast in that aspect of consciousness which has attained purity within your own self.
Having completely abandoned the latent tendencies of "this is mine," "that is this," and "I am that," become intent solely upon the internal pure consciousness through one-pointed devotion.

Regarding the present and future states of existence, be intent upon the unification of your own self-awareness through the synthesis and concentration of the single cognition that grasps them as one.
Whether in childhood, youth, or old age; amidst sorrows or joys; and throughout waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—remain centered in your own self-awareness.
Having cast off the impurity of the object of perception and having released the mind into the Supreme, cut through the foul snare of hope and become intent upon your own self-awareness.

With the poisonous arrows of hope stilled by your own conventions regarding the auspicious and inauspicious, and with the view of desired and undesired objects destroyed, become intent upon the essence of pure consciousness.

Without touching the agent, the object, or the instrument, and without contact with anything else, become one who is free from conceptual construction, without support, and devoted solely to your own pure consciousness.

While remaining truly awake, contemplate that state which is as if in deep sleep and perfectly stable; thinking "I am everything," become one whose very body is the singular essence of pure existence.

Liberated from the states of diversity and non-diversity, joined with equanimity through liberation, and serving as a lamp for the calculation of all things, become intent solely upon your own pure consciousness.
Having abandoned both selfhood and otherness, remaining undivided within the state of the world, remain steadfast by supporting yourself like a diamond pillar.

Abiding within, with a noble intellect whose sole characteristic is fortitude, go forth toward the state beyond both dharma and adharma, having destroyed the mental fetters that take the form of desire.
For one who tastes the reality characterized by self-awareness, even the most virulent hālāhala poison will become nectar.
Then arises great delusion, the cause of the wandering in saṃsāra, when there is no awareness of consciousness—which is stainless and partless.
Then delusion, the cause of the wandering in saṃsāra, is completely destroyed when one abides in stainless and partless self-awareness.
For you who have followed your true nature and crossed the great ocean of hope, your consciousness will expand in every direction like the rays of the sun.
O Rāma, for one who beholds the intrinsic nature and abides in the non-dual state of bliss, even a delicious elixir acts like a potent poison.
We associate with those men who have attained their true nature; the rest, though bearing the name of "men," are merely long-armed donkeys.
They go from mountain to mountain like elephants before a mountain, for one who has reached the highest pinnacle and stands elevated by his own self-awareness.
Within the limit where the unseen meets the invisible, even all the lights beginning with the sun do not assist one who possesses the divine eye of self-awareness.
For one who has realized the Self through knowledge, these great lights such as the sun and others pass away into unreality, like lamps at midday.
Among those possessing splendor, power, strength, and even great majesty—all who are endowed with loftiness—the knower of reality is supremely exalted.
Just as the sun, fire, moon, gems, and stars shine here with their light, so do the best of men, who have known all that is to be known, shine resplendent in this world.
O Rāma, those humans who do not know the ultimate reality are considered more insignificant than insects in the crevices of the earth, than donkeys, and even than animals.
As long as one lacks self-knowledge, the embodied being is a vampire of delusion; those who know the truth maintain that only the knower of the Self is truly united with consciousness.
For one who does not know the Self, though he may struggle on the surface of the earth, he wanders like a corpse in great distress; but he who knows the Self remains truly conscious.
Self-knowledge recedes to a distance when the mind has become thick with density, just as the splendor of light vanishes when a great cloud has arisen on all sides.
The mind should be gradually emaciated by the rejection of enjoyment and non-enjoyment, by one who knows the method, through the removal of its flavors over time, like a withered leaf.
By this identification of the non-self with the self, and by this reliance on the mere body, along with sons, wife, and family, the mind attains fullness.
Through the transformation of egoism, by the effortless stain of "mine-ness," and by the notion that "this is mine," the mind becomes swollen with attachment.
The mind grows fat with the suffering of old age and death, which brings about useless exaltation and serves as a vessel for the venomous serpents of the defilements.
Through the indulgence in mental and physical afflictions, through the seeking of worldly consolation, and through the effort to reject or acquire things, the mind grows fat.
Through affection, greed for wealth, the gain of jewels and women, and that which is pleasant at first sight, the mind becomes swollen with attachment.
By drinking the milk of false hopes, by the force of the wind of enjoyments, and by the movement of grasping at existence, the serpent of the mind grows fat.
The mind grows fat through the terrifying expansion of enjoyments, which possess a nature of coming and going and indicate the instability of poison.

The body is a foul pit where [suffering] has long since taken root; it possesses the high-stalked blossoms of a multitude of anxieties, is bent low by the heavy fruit of old age, death, and disease, and has flowers in full bloom through the flood of sensual enjoyments.

With the saw of the essence of discernment, forcibly cut down here this poisonous tree of the mind—which is like a wondrous mountain, with hope as its great branches and conceptual constructions as its leaves—without hesitation.

With intoxicated eyes, seated on one bank, fierce and incapable of the pleasures of rest, longing for a sight [of you] through the lineage of the virtuous, and a boil of pleasure and pain belonging to the cruel Lakhaṇḍa.

O Rāghava, lion among kings, tear asunder with the row of sharp claws of your wisdom the elephant of the mind—which dwells in the forest of the body and possesses the long tusks of chronic distortions—by making it perform its proper task.
Always finding delight in improper places, nourished by devouring the flesh of the body, with a beak-staff harsh from wicked deeds, one-eyed, and most thickly coated with black soot.

Drive far away from the nest-like cavity of your body this crow of your own mind, which is a burden, misbehaving, harshly cawing, and emitting foul odors; do this for the sake of pacifying its defects.

Attended by the ogress of craving, it has rested in the great pits of ignorance and wandered for a long time through hundreds of bodies in the forest of its own cycle of existence, which is devoid of true consciousness.

As long as one does not expel this demon of the mind from the house of one's own conscious self by means of discernment, dispassion, effort toward the guru, and independent mantras, how can there be the attainment of the Self in this world?

It has a face of both auspicious and inauspicious, it destroys the flood of prideful men, and it possesses the poison of anxiety and the coarse armor of the body; it is a constant consumer of clear breath, and it bestows the destruction of various fears upon everyone.

O Rāma, having brought the great serpent of the mind to rest within the hollow of the heart’s śālmalī tree by means of the unfailing power of the mantra of consciousness, cast off all fear and become one whose nature is fearless of worldly existence.

Bearing an inauspicious appearance due to his constant attendance upon rows of corpses, exhausted by the toil of wandering through the quarters of the horizon, he frequents the cremation grounds with a body scarred by wounds.

Chasing after the bait of enjoyments in all directions, with neck outstretched and its greed intensified by the wise, the vulture of the mind flies away indeed from the tree of the body; therefore, may you be victorious through skill in that regard.

Wandering through forest edges and distant quarters in search of fruit, restless and with agitated limbs, he has gone from the land of birth to the very ground of birth, laughing at the worldly folk bound by the cycle of existence.

O dear one, for the sake of spiritual accomplishment, subdue within yourself that great monkey of the mind which leaps about in this tree whose trunk is the body, whose eyes and nose are its flowers, whose arms and other limbs are its branches, and whose webbed fingers are its trembling leaves.

It has arisen for the destruction of the fruit of wholesome deeds, flashing with the lightning of its radiant mouth; it rains down a torrent of misfortunes, tossed within by the whirlwind of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).

By the power of the formidable mantra that abandons all volitional constructions, destroy with vigor the cloud of the mind situated within the sky of the heart; having attained the great fruit, become the primordial Lord.
Knotted by its own created actions, impenetrable by mantras and unburnt by fires, it fashions supreme suffering within itself—a long cord of all the various classes of birth.
O Rāghava, having yourself severed the snare of the mind—which is a continuous chain of countless bodies—by means of the weapons of mere non-conceptualization, roam at ease, free from all fear.

A venomous serpent that has scorched all travelers with its hiss, making the awakening of others extremely difficult to attain; one that has withered the regions of the world and raised its staff-like body by gaping for prey.

Having swiftly consumed with the power of the great fire of desirelessness that sluggish python of volitional thought hidden within the caves of the body, may you become liberated from worldly existence.

O virtuous one, having swiftly brought the mind to tranquility with a pure heart—just as one neutralizes a terrible weapon through the skillful application of another weapon—abandon for a long time your fickleness, like a tree free from monkeys whose splendor remains unimpaired.

Considering everything from your very body to be pure, with a mind free of doubt and inwardly stilled, look upon it as light as a blade of grass; having reached the further shore of saṃsāra, drink, sport, and rejoice with ease through the vision of what is to be abandoned.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Do not abide within the fluctuations of the mind, which are exceedingly long-lasting, subtle, extremely sharp, and white, resembling the edge of a razor.
O you who are skilled in guidance, having after a long time produced this creeper of intelligence within the field of your being, lead it to growth by watering it with discernment.
As long as this creeper-like body does not wither under the sun of time, lift it up and preserve it before it falls to the ground.

O you who know the single reality of the meaning of my words, through the contemplation of that very meaning of my words, you shall attain happiness, just as the enemy of serpents [Garuda] does through the contemplation of the sound of clouds.
Having repeatedly torn apart and scattered the five elements like the seeds of the *uddālaka* plant, examine them within yourself with a steady and firm intellect.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, by what sequence did the sage Uddālaka, having dissolved that pentad of elements, investigate them within?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen, O Rāma, to how Uddālaka formerly attained the supreme, unimpaired vision through the investigation of the multitude of beings.
In a certain corner of this world-old house, situated in the northwestern direction, there is a place filled with mountain-vessels.
It is said that on the plateau named Gandhamādana, the king of mountains, there exists a certain region strewn with flowers and the camphor-like filaments of trees.
The riverbank was filled with birds of variegated colors and graced by various creeping vines; it was frequented by forest-dwellers and radiant with the filaments of flowers.

In some places it was filled with great jewels; in some places it had shimmering lotuses and water-lilies; in some places it was like a woman with hair matted by frost; and in some places it was like a mirror for the lake.
There, on a certain rising ridge covered with *sarala* trees, where flowers were strewn up to the ankles and great trees provided lush shade;
A sage named Uddālaka, who was silent, dignified, and possessed of great intelligence, lived formerly as a fierce ascetic before he had even reached his youth.
At first, however, he was one of little wisdom yet possessed of reflection; though not yet resting in the state [of realization] and not fully awakened, his intention was virtuous.
Then, through the gradual practice of austerity, the study of scriptural meaning, and disciplined observances, discernment came to him, just as autumn arrives upon the earth.
Then, dwelling in solitude with a tranquil mind, his intellect terrified by the disease of saṃsāra, he reflected upon this.
What could that primary goal be, upon reaching which one no longer grieves, and having reached which, no further connection with birth arises?
When shall I find long-lasting rest in that supremely pure state where the mind has been abandoned, like a cloud upon the peak of Mount Meru?
When will the perceptions of my internal enjoyments come to rest, like the waves in the ocean whose sounds are the noise of restless billows?
When, with an intellect resting in the state of the ultimate reality, will I inwardly laugh at the mental construction that thinks, "Having done this, that other thing must also be done"?
When will the web of conceptual construction no longer cling to my mind, remaining there without attachment, like water on a lotus leaf?
When shall I have completely crossed over this intoxicated river of craving, with its many surging waves, by means of the supreme boat of wisdom?
I shall mock this action, which is being performed by beings born of the earth and composed of unreality, as if it were the confused play of children.
When will my mind, which is overturned by conceptual construction and tossed about like a swing, attain tranquility—like a dizziness subsiding when the force of the wind has been stilled?
With the splendor of my form thus illuminated, laughing at the comings and goings of the world, I shall attain inner contentment like the Virāṭ Self of perfect intellect.
With an inner form of perfect equanimity, gentle and free from longing for all objects, when shall I attain peace, like the ocean of nectar released from churning?
Beholding the entire splendor of the visible world—immovable like a mountain yet consisting of hundreds of desires—as if in deep sleep, I shall become inwardly expanded.
When shall I perceive everything—both external and internal—as nothing but pure consciousness alone, through an intellect whose conceptual constructions have been stilled?
When my mind and self have become tranquil and I have attained supreme consciousness, I shall reach the highest light, as if from the departure of one born blind.
When shall I behold from afar this slender digit of Time with the beautiful light of consciousness, attained through long practice?
Freed from likes and dislikes, and devoid of that which is to be rejected or accepted, when shall I attain inner contentment, established in the state of self-luminosity?
When will this night of my faults—strewn with the owls of desire, its lotus-heart withered by dullness—come to an end, O Kṛṣṇa?
With my mind stilled of all agitation, in a mountain cave, I shall attain identity with a stone through non-conceptual meditative absorption.
When will my elephant of pride, intoxicated by the great rut of self-conceit, meet its destruction, slain by the deer of the awakening of sentient beings?
When will the forest birds build a nest of grass upon my head, as I remain mute, resting in partless meditation?
When will birds, their minds steady in meditation, rest fearlessly upon my chest, which remains as motionless as a mountain pillar?
When shall I depart, having abandoned this lake in the forest of saṃsāra, which is overgrown with the tangled thorns of craving and infested with the shrubs of birth and decay?
Thus, overcome by anxiety, the twice-born Uddālaka sat down again and again in the forest and practiced meditation.
But as his mind, as restless as a monkey, was being led away by sense objects, he did not attain the foundation of meditative concentration that bestows joy.
Once, immediately after abandoning external contact, the monkey of his mind became agitated as it moved toward the state of being established in the [true] nature of reality.
Sometimes, having abandoned internal sensations, the monkey of the mind, due to its restlessness, wanders toward external objects as if scorched by poison.
O lotus-eyed one, at one time, upon seeing a splendor within his mind that shone like the rising sun, his consciousness turned toward sense objects.
Having abandoned the inner darkness of ignorance and its attachment to sense objects, his mind sometimes flies away like a frightened bird.
Having abandoned external and internal contacts as well as sleep, that mind occasionally attained a permanent state in the proximity of darkness and light.
Thus, with his inner mind agitated, he indeed sank day after day into the fierce depths of meditative states, like a tree engulfed by a windstorm in deep ravines.
With his mind deeply rooted in meditation, he remained as if in a crisis, his body swaying like a wave upon the shore of trivial craving.
Then, with a troubled mind, the sage dwelt alone on the mountain, like the lord of day upon Mount Mahāmeru.
Once, the sage reached a cave that was difficult for all beings to attain, where all movement had completely ceased, like the state of liberation.
Unperturbed by winds, unvisited by beasts or birds, unseen by gods or gandharvas, it was as beautiful as the supreme ether.
It was covered with heaps of flowers and as soft as tender grass, appearing as if it were made of emeralds set within crystals of jyotīrasa stone.
It possessed a very pleasant and cool shade, made manifest by jewel-lamps, and was as well-guarded as the inner apartments of a forest goddess.
With its family as its object of focus, it was neither too hot nor too cold, like the golden-white radiance of the autumnal sun when it has just risen.
She was like a young *mālāvatī* creeper, withered by the light of the sun, possessing soft sounds and breezes, and entwined with clusters of blossoms.

It was, as it were, a fitting path to tranquility, a suitable form for the repose of the Lotus-born; it was delightful with its soft clusters of flowers and tender like the interior of a lotus on all sides.
The virtuous Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That righteous soul entered that cave of Gandhamādana, which he had reached by wandering through various paths, just as a bee enters a lotus-bud.
Intent upon attaining meditative absorption, he shone as he entered [his state], like the lotus-born Brahmā entering his own city when his activity of creation has ceased.
There he prepared a seat with unfading leaves and clusters of blossoms, like the soft cloud-creator forming a mass of rain-clouds.
He spread that beautiful deerskin upon his back, like Mount Meru with its slopes of sapphire, bearing the sky filled with stars.
There he sat down, bringing about a thinning of the mind's fluctuations, like a silent cloud upon a mountain peak, its inner form pure.
Firmly assuming the lotus posture like a Buddha and facing north, he pressed his heels against his testicles and formed the Brahma-añjali gesture.
Having drawn back the agitated deer of the mind from its habitual tendencies, he undertook this investigation for the sake of non-conceptual meditative absorption.
O foolish mind, what purpose is there for you in the activities of worldly existence? The wise do not pursue actions that yield only suffering in the end.
He who pursues enjoyments after abandoning the elixir of tranquility is like one who leaves the Mandāra grove and enters a forest of poison.
Even if you go to the subterranean realm or to the world of Brahmā, you will not attain Nirvāṇa without the nectar of cessation.
Since the fulfillment of hundreds of hopes bestows all such suffering, abandon them and go toward the supreme good, which is supremely and uniquely beautiful.
These various conceptual constructions, consisting of existence and non-existence, lead only to your own fierce suffering and never to happiness.
O fool, why do you wander ceaselessly and fruitlessly among these things—sound and the rest—which have destroyed your true nature, like a female frog in a cloud?
O mind-frog, what have you finally attained after wandering fruitlessly through the world for so long in your blindness?
O fool, why do you not fix your mind upon that tranquility from which you obtain everything and in which you find peace? Why do you not set foot there?
O fool, having come within the range of hearing, do not go to your destruction like a deer, following after sounds with a mind nourished by futile exertions.
O fool, do not become bound by a mind that, having come into contact with the skin, is intent on touch for the sake of pleasure, like the lordly elephant lusting after a female elephant.
Having come into the presence of the tongue, O you who are blinded by greed, do not go to your destruction like a fish greedy for a baited hook.
Relying on the visual function that is directed toward the accumulation of light-forms, O simpleton, do not go to your own destruction like a moth lusting after radiance.
Resorting to the path of the nose within the hollow of the lotus-body, do not cling to bondage out of a longing for fragrance, like a bee.

The deer, the bee, the moth, the elephant, and the fish are each destroyed by one [of these five]; O ignorant one, how can there be happiness for one who is overwhelmed by all these misfortunes combined?
This net of mental impressions (vāsanā) belonging to the mind is harmful for one's own bondage; it is innate to oneself, like foam, and therefore [is discarded] just as one would by a maggot.
If you come like an autumn cloud and, having abandoned the disease of worldly existence, become utterly tranquil and pure, then your victory shall be infinite.
Although you know that the creation of the world is a nurse that brings about both decay and rise, and that it causes ultimate torment, you will not abandon it; you shall perish.
Or for what purpose do I perform this service for you? For, O sinless one, a man who possesses discernment has no [need for such] mental activity.
As long as there is density of ignorance, so long is there density of mind; as long as there is the nature of a rainy-season cloud, so long is there an abundance of mist.
As long as there is a thinning of ignorance, so long is there a thinning of the mind; as long as the rainy season has not ended, so long does the mist persist.
As long as the pure mind continues to arise through investigation, for that long I consider it to be already exhausted, like an autumn cloud.
This instruction which is given to one who is non-existent or perishing is like striking the sky, water, or the wind.
Therefore, because it is wasting away, I abandon you, who are composed of unreality; they say that the highest form of folly is the instruction of one who must be abandoned.
I am the non-conceptual lamp of consciousness, free from the latent impressions of egoism; I am not bound by you, the seed of egoism, for I am composed of unreality.
"This is I"—thus has a false view been clung to by you in vain; it is a cholera-like poison of doubt for the destruction of the deluded.
The notion that the infinite reality of the Self is "minute" cannot abide in the mind, just as it is impossible for an elephant to reside within a wood-apple fruit.
"Alas, this mind of yours is like a deep, great abyss—profound, painful, and rooted in latent tendencies; therefore, I shall not follow after it."
What indeed is this vain delusion, like that of a child who does not investigate? This error of "this is I" is merely imagined through the notion of egoism.
From the big toe up to the head, it has been analyzed down to the smallest particle; that which is called "I" has not been found—what could this be that stands as "I"?
That which fills every corner of the directions, which alone exists throughout the three worlds, is consciousness—unperceivable by itself, yet omnipresent and devoid of a separate self.
That whose limit is not perceived, nor indeed its conceptualization; which has neither oneness nor otherness here, neither greatness nor minuteness.
I know you, who are self-evident and pervasive, to be the cause of suffering; by means of the awakening born of discernment, this very [ignorance] of yours shall be destroyed by me.
"This is flesh, this is blood, these are the bones in the body; these are your breath-winds—where is that 'I' who stands [there]?"
For the vibration of the powers of the wind is the awakening of the Great Consciousness; old age and death in this body are merely that which stands [in the mind] as "Who am I?"
O mind, flesh is one thing, blood another, and bones yet others; consciousness is one thing and movement another—wherein then does this "I" reside?
"This is the nose, this is the tongue, this is the skin, these are the ears; this is the eye, this is touch—what is this that stands as 'I'?"
