In accordance with reality, I am not the mind, nor you, nor even latent impressions; this alone—the Self, the manifestation of pure consciousness—expands in its absolute solitude.
"I alone am everywhere here, or else I am nothing at all here"—this indeed is the vision consisting of pure Being; no other sequence exists.
For a long time, I have been struck down by the rogue of ignorance through this sense of "I," like a young animal caught in the forest by a proud wolf.
By good fortune, I have now recognized this thief of ignorance; I shall never again take refuge in it, for it robs one of the true nature of reality.
Free from suffering, I am not that person who is subject to suffering, nor is he mine; I am to him as a cloud is to a mountain, even while remaining upon it.
Having become this, I speak, I know, I remain, and I go; yet, through the vision of the Self, I have attained a state free from egoism.
Surely I alone consider these—the eye and the other senses—to be the knowers; whether they go or remain in the body, they are nothing to me.
Alas! What is this thing called "I," and how, by whom, was it fashioned—a vampire for the children of the world, possessing a form as immense and incomparable as a palm tree?
For so long a time I have rolled in vain within this pit, like a deer upon a rugged mountain from which the grass has been stripped away.
If the eye has turned its face toward looking for one’s own self-interest, then who could this "I" be that is not deluded by this suffering?
If the skin has turned toward its own true essence for the sake of touching it, then what is this so-called "I" that has arisen like a wretched ghost?
While this gustatory faculty is thus intent upon its own sequence of tastes, from where does this contemptible delusion arise that "I am an eater of delicacies"?

When the wretched sense of hearing has entered into the power of sound and is oppressed by its own object, what source can there be for the suffering of ego-identification, which is now devoid of its seed?
When one's own scent reaches one's own nose through its being self-supporting, I do not recognize that thief who thinks, "I am the smeller."
This cultivation, proceeding like a mirage, results in a vain conception; the notion that there is a real entity within that which is unreal is merely a delusion.

Even though this [cognition] is devoid of latent impressions (vāsanā), it proceeds by itself through the sense organs such as the eye toward its external object; latent impressions are not the cause here.
O mind, surely action is performed free from latent impressions; indeed, the foremost perceptions of pleasure and pain are not experienced at all.
Therefore, O all you people, having abandoned these foolish senses and your own internal latent impressions, perform every action; you shall not encounter suffering.
In vain have you been conditioned by latent impressions for the sake of suffering, like children who become distressed by playing with mud as if it were a toy that might be destroyed.

O sinless one, all perceptions such as latent impressions (vāsanā) and the like are not distinct from the Self, just as waves and the like are not distinct from water; this is so for the knower alone, and not for anyone else.
O childish senses, you have been ruined by craving alone, in vain, just as silkworms are destroyed by the thread produced from themselves.
It is by craving alone that you wallow here in the peril of old age and death, like travelers on a mountain path with blurred vision falling into chasms.
In this world, latent impression alone is the cause of your bondage in one place, just as a rope strung through an empty space is the cause for those who have been released to remain extended.
For this [world] is truly fashioned by mere conceptualization and does not exist in reality; it is severed by the mere absence of conceptualization, as if by a sickle.
For this [doctrine] leads only to your own delusion and destruction, like a gust of wind to lamps, even though their flames are flickering with brilliance.

O mind, you are the sheath of all the senses; therefore, having surely attained oneness with all the senses, and having perceived the self as being of an unreal nature, remain in nirvāṇa alone, which is stainless awakening.

Having skillfully cast off the endless cholera of the poison of sense-objects—the latent tendencies of worldly existence—through the application of the mantra that abandons what is desired, may you become the Blessed One, the dissolution of worldly life and the ground beyond all fears.

Uddālaka said: Its body is both boundless and infinite, yet it is as subtle as an atom; since consciousness is beyond the object of thought, latent impressions and the like have no power to pervade it.
Through the mind, intellect, ego, and the reflections of the dull senses, beings are spread with latent impressions; though empty, they are intent on terrifying others like ghosts.
Even after those investigations have been performed and extensively experienced, I, indeed, as the untainted consciousness, experience them again within.
Let the body assume or even abandon the state of worldly existence fashioned by its own impure dispositions; for I am indeed the untainted consciousness.
Since birth and death do not exist for the all-pervading consciousness, what indeed is it that dies? Or by whom is anything ever killed?
There is no purpose in life for one who has lost his soul; all life belongs to the soul. What will this wretched soul gain, even if it should somehow regain its life?
The notions that "one lives" and "one dies," which are turbid with false conceptualizations, belong only to the minds; they do not belong to the stainless Self.

For he who has attained the state of "I-ness" (ahambhāva) is grasped by means of existence and non-existence; but for the Self, there is no "I-ness," so how could it have those states of existence and non-existence?
The sense of "I" is a vain delusion, and the mind is a mirage; the entire collection of insentient objects—whose egoistic conception could it possibly be?
The body consists of blood and flesh; the mind has perished through inquiry; all things such as the intellect are inert—whence, then, can there be the cultivation of the sense of "I"?
Since the senses have always been perfectly established in their own nature, and objects remain as mere objects, whence can there arise the cultivation of the sense of "I"?

The qualities function for the sake of the qualities within primordial nature; primordial nature itself remains established in Being alone. Since it rests in that which truly exists, whence can there be the conception of "I"?
All-pervading, residing in all bodies, consisting of all time, and great—the absolute Supreme Self alone exists here as the conscious self.
Thus, what is my form, or who am I? What is my instruction, and by what was I made? What is my nature, and of what am I composed? Who am I, what do I grasp, and what do I abandon?

Therefore, that which is called "I" does not exist here as something subject to the arising of being or non-being; for one whose nature is free from egoism, with what could there be a connection, and how?
When the ego-sense, which is unreal, has ceased, what relation can there be, for whom, and of what kind? Once the absence of all relations is established, the conceptualization of duality dissolves.
Thus, whatever exists in this world has Brahman as its self; I am that very Being, I am that very Being—why then do I grieve in vain?
When one alone, stainless, all-pervading, and established in the state of the ultimate ground, how and from where could there even be the arising of the stain of egoism?

Indeed, there is no such thing as the splendor of objects; here, only the Self exists, all-pervading. And even if the splendor of objects were real, there would be no connection whatsoever for anyone.

When the senses move among the senses and the limbs, and the mind moves within the mind, how can there be any connection for the consciousness whose body is untainted—of what, to what, or in what manner?

Just as there is no mutual connection between pebbles, shards, and sticks, so too there is no such connection among the body, the sense faculties, the mind, and consciousness, even when they are observed together in one place.

In this world, which has arisen from the non-existent and is a great delusion of futile egoism, this universe is perverted by such thoughts as "this is mine," "this is for me," and "this belongs to him."
This wondrous manifestation of egoism, which arises when the light of reality has not yet dawned, dissolves upon the light of reality, like a streak of frost under the heat.
Apart from the Self, nothing at all exists; "All is Brahman"—this is my truth, and I meditate upon it.
I consider the non-recollection of this arisen delusion of egoism—which is like the color of space—to be truly the best form of forgetting.
Having completely abandoned for a long time the delusion of egoism along with its root, I remain within my own self with a tranquil mind, like the autumnal sky in the autumnal firmament.
The sense of "I" (ahaṃkāra), when pursued, bestows a multitude of misfortunes, spreads forth evil deeds, and expands one's inner torment.
When the dense cloud of egoism throbs within the watery sky of the heart, the cluster of vices blossoms everywhere upon the kadamba-tree of the body.
Death is at the end of life, and life ends in death; existence is cut off by non-existence—how bitter is this painful sensation!
"This has been gained; this I shall obtain"—such is the torment of the foolish, which causes burning and is never extinguished, like the fire of sun-gems in the summer heat.
The thought that "this does not exist" or "this exists" runs toward the ego-sense, just as a dull-witted person, with a dull mind, pursues a mass of clouds as if it were a range of mountains.
When the sense of "I" is completely exhausted, the tree of saṃsāra withers; being sapless, it never again produces a sprout, just like a stone.
The black female serpents of one's own craving, which have made their dwelling in the tree of the body, flee somewhere when the son of Vinatā—the discerning mind—arrives.

When the entire universe has arisen from the unreal, consisting of the delusion born thereof and composed of the unreal, what sequence can there be for "I" and "you," which are likewise composed of the unreal?
This world arises at the beginning from a causeless source; how can that which has arisen without a cause be called "existent"?
Just as the form of a jar exists within the clay at an infinite time in the past, so too this body existed in the past, exists now, and will exist in the future.
Just as water, having abandoned its initial and final states of calmness, remains for some time as mere intermediate water, both moving and unmoving, in the form of waves; so too is this [mind].
Those of wicked intellect who place their reliance upon this body—which is subject to the vibration of moments and is intent on dissolution—and upon the wave, are truly destroyed.
All things exist neither before nor after; they do not exist from the center outward. What reliance can there be on these things whose very form is destroyed by their lack of clarity in the middle?
The mind was previously and is still before you as the tranquil field of consciousness; whether existent or non-existent, what indeed has been said by you regarding this "reins" in the middle?
Just as in dream-visions, just as in perceptions during a state of agitation, just as in the playfulness of intoxication, or just as in the disorientation caused by traveling in a boat.
Just as in cases of bodily humors being disturbed, as in the impairment of the senses, as in states of extreme agitation or joy, and as in conditions of possession by a malevolent spirit.
Form is seen and indeed perishes, being unstable in both its existence and non-existence; likewise, this very fluctuation between deficiency and excess occurs here in the course of time.
And that [thought] was constantly produced by you, O mind, at the arising of suffering and pleasure; just as thoughts of separation destroy one who is full of passion.
Through the habitual practice of the unreal here, you appear as false yet as if real; like a mirage, therefore, that which is done by you would be considered done by me.
Whatever is experienced as an object of cognition, all that is the circle of the visible; having determined that it is without substantial reality, the mind proceeds to the state beyond the mind.
When a firm conviction has taken root in the mind that "this world is unreal," the latent tendencies toward enjoyment wither away like blossoms in winter.
Surely, because of its nature as consciousness, the mind—having abandoned the perceived self through its lack of vigor—is itself established in its own natural state once it is free from passion.
When cast into the fire of the Supreme Self, the mind itself, having consumed its own constituent parts through the process of concealment, attains eternal purity.
Having perceived the body as something other [than the self], having abandoned the latent impressions of sense objects, and having accepted its perishability, one conquers the mind like a hero.
The mind is the enemy of the body, and the body is the enemy of the mind; through the absence of one, both perish, like a container and its contents.
For those who possess passion and hatred, which are eternally and utterly opposed to one another, their destruction by the complete eradication of their roots is supreme happiness.
The statement that death occurs when these two are situated together is equal to the claim that the sky has been enjoyed by a woman other than Dhārā.
Wherever both [opposites] are joined together in an innate state of contradiction, there a succession of misfortunes falls like torrents of rain.
For that base person who finds delight in association with those who are mutually antagonistic must be abandoned, like a fire falling upon a house smeared with straw.
Having nourished the mind with its own volitions, like a child-demon nourishing its body, it offers its own sufferings to that mind as its very food for life.
The body, tormented by the sufferings of old age, then desires to destroy the mind; even a son kills his father when the latter has attained the status of an assailant.
There is no one who is by nature an enemy, nor anyone who is always a friend; a friend is said to be one who bestows happiness, while enemies are known as those who cause suffering.
Experiencing sufferings, the body desires to destroy its own mind; in an instant, the mind makes the body a mere convention for its own sorrows.

Thus, when suffering and pleasure are joined together in this way, what possibility is there for the arrival of happiness, given that these two—the body and the mind—are by their very nature utterly opposed?
When the mind alone is utterly exhausted, the body is no longer a vessel for suffering; yet, out of an intense longing for that exhaustion, the body itself constantly runs about.
The body, whether lost or not lost, is a source of misfortune and the very seat of calamities; it is produced from a mind that has failed to attain discernment of the self.
For these two—the mind and the body—have indeed grown thick together, being insentient in nature like a cloud and a lake joined by their forms.
Though they have become one in nature for mutual suffering and yet remain divided into two, they are engaged in worldly affairs together like water and fire.
When the mind is diminished and utterly exhausted, the body indeed becomes uprooted; but when it increases, it proceeds like a tree with a hundred branches.

When the mind is exhausted, the body—its latent impressions (vāsanā) having been spent—is likewise destroyed; yet the mind is not destroyed when the body is destroyed. Therefore, one should exhaust the mind.
Having cut down the forest of the mind—the tree of volition and the creeper of craving—and having reached the vast expanse of the ground, I dwell in happiness as I please.
This very mind, which was previously active, no longer remains within the mind; with its web of latent impressions (vāsanās) being pacified, it is like a cloud at the end of the rainy season.
This configuration of the elements, known as the body, is my enemy; may it remain only so long as the mind is wasting away and dissolving.
That for whose sake the glory of enjoyments indeed desires its own body—neither that belongs to me, nor do I belong to it; what purpose, then, could there be for me in a mere fragment of pleasure?
Listen now to the reasoning for the view that "I am not the body": why is it that a corpse does not move, even though all its limbs are still present?
Therefore, I am transcendent of the body, eternal, and of undiminished luster; having attained union with the Radiant One, I perceive the Sun within the sky.
I am not ignorant, nor do I have suffering, nor misfortune, nor the state of being pained; let the body exist or let it not exist—I remain free from the fever of affliction.
Where the Self resides, there is neither mind, nor senses, nor latent impressions; the vulgar do not stand near a mountain.
I have followed that path; I am alone, I am victorious; I am extinguished, I am partless, I am motionless, and I am free from desire.
Now I am disconnected from the mind, body, senses, and so forth, like sesame oil separated from the sesame seeds by its trickling away.
Furthermore, as I moved effortlessly from this supreme station of my own, having set my mind apart, this auspicious retinue was indeed created.
Transparency, vigor, existence, loveliness, truthfulness, and wisdom; blissfulness, tranquility, and always speaking with gentleness.
Fullness, magnanimity, truthfulness, radiant beauty, one-pointedness, the unity of all things, fearlessness, and the state in which the dualistic conceptualization of duality has been exhausted.
Ever-arisen, equanimous, self-abiding, beautiful, and dawning with auspicious fortune, these beloveds, dear to my heart, are eternally the beloved consorts of me, whose nature is the single Self.
Since everything is possible in every way, at all times, and for everyone, in relation to everything, my desire and lack of desire, as well as pleasure and pain, have come to an end.
Free from delusion, free from mental distress, and with a mind devoid of conceptual construction, I clearly bring myself to rest within my own self, like a thick mass of clouds in the autumnal sky.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having thus resolved with that expanded and pure intellect, the sage sat in the lotus posture, his eyes half-closed.
Having thus determined that "Om" is the supreme Brahman, that sage then declared: "By whomsoever the syllable Om is uttered, by him the supreme state has been attained."
He uttered the syllable *oṃ* with a piercing sound whose resonance ascended upward, like the ringing of a bell struck firmly upon its handle.
As he utters "Om," while his consciousness is directed toward that reality, it extends up to the summit of the syllable Om, resting in the vast and stainless Self.
In the first part of the three-and-a-half-fold measure, when the sound of the *praṇava* becomes manifest, the body resounds with the intensely agitated vital breath.
The process known as *recaka*, by which the vital breath exits from the entire body, emptied it just as Agastya drained the ocean after drinking its waters.
Having abandoned the body and relinquished its nest, he remained in the sky filled with the essence of consciousness, his vital breath suspended like a bird in the air.
The fire of his heart, with its blazing flames, consumed his entire body, just as a forest fire driven by a cataclysmic wind consumes a withered tree.
To this extent, such was the state of affairs in the initial stage of the *praṇava*; for haṭha-yoga does not arise by force alone, as it is indeed a source of suffering.
Then, at the moment when the other parts were equalized within the *praṇava*, there arose a stage of the vital breaths known as the "unwavering *kumbhaka*."
Neither outside nor within, neither below nor above, nor in the intermediate directions—there your vital breaths did not undergo agitation, as if they were solidified waters.
The fire that had consumed the body was instantly extinguished like a thunderbolt; only white ashes, pale as snow, were seen remaining of the body.
Where the white, motionless bones of the body appear as if they had slept comfortably upon a bed of camphor.
The wind brought that ash along with the bones and joined them to its own body, which had been greatly wasted away, as if it were observing the vow of the Three-eyed Lord.
And that [debris], tossed by a fierce wind, having covered the sky in an instant, vanished somewhere like autumnal mist or clouds of ash and bone.
In this manner, this state of the *praṇava* arose through a gradual process; for haṭhayoga is indeed painful and does not come about by force alone.
Then, on the third occasion, there occurred the sequence of the vital breaths known as the "Fulfiller of Fulfillment," which brings peace to the *praṇava*.
At this moment, the vital breaths, dwelling within the nectar of consciousness, attained a coolness in the void as beautiful as the touch of snow.
Gradually, situated in the midst of the sky, the fumes attained the state of lunar discs, as if becoming cool clouds dwelling within the expanse of the heavens.
In that lunar orb, complete with its full array of digits, which was like a heap of merit or a great ocean of elixir, [he entered].
The vital breaths have become streams consisting of elixir, resembling jeweled pillars like the rays of the moon passing through lattices.
That stream fell from the sky onto the ashes of Śeṣa’s body, like the celestial river of elixir falling upon the head of Hara.
A four-armed body, radiant like the orb of the moon, emerged from her, like the Pārijāta tree rising from the ocean after Mount Mandara was churned.
That body of Uddālaka, having arisen as Nārāyaṇa, shone with its lotus-like eyes and face in full bloom, beautiful with radiance.
The vital breaths, consisting of elixirs, filled his body, just as floods of water fill a lake or sweet juices fill a tree.
The vital breaths, filled with reverence, filled the internal Kuṇḍalinī, which had spread out following the sequence of the cakras, just as waters fill a great river.
The body of that twice-born man returned to its natural state, like the surface of the earth washed clean when the rainy season has ended.
Then, seated in the lotus posture, having established a firm stability within the body, he bound the five senses as one ties an elephant to its tethering post.
He undertook a resolute effort for the sake of non-conceptual samādhi, just as the autumn season strives to lead the sky to its natural, stainless clarity.
With her thoughts, she drew his heart from afar toward herself, as a rope pulls a stake, he who was like a deer whose breath had stilled and who was wandering through the quarters of the sky.
He forcibly restrained the mind—which was running downward, intoxicated, pure yet agitated—just as a dam holds back swift-flowing water.
She closed her eyes, which were beautiful with their thick lashes and motionless pupils, like a lotus at twilight when its petals have half-closed.
The silent sage brought serenity to the breath moving in and out of his mouth, like an auspicious time that brings prosperity to a favorable place.
He diligently separated the senses from their objects, just as one extracts oil from sesame seeds, or as a tortoise withdraws its limbs.
That man of steady intellect utterly abandoned all external objects of touch from afar, just as a jewel covered by a cloth suddenly casts off its distant luster.
He dissolved internal sensations by abandoning visual perception, just as a tree in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa dissolves the sap contained within its buds.
Then, by contracting the anus, he obstructed the winds of the nine gates, just as a jar with its mouth sealed blocks the other apertures of its interior.
The steadfast one bore his neck, which was richly illuminated by the jewel of his own self, clearly marked with a flower, like Mount Meru bearing the peak of its summit.
He bore within the space of his heart a mind that had attained self-restraint, like a mad elephant brought under control by skillful means and confined within the Vindhya chasm.
Having attained a stainless and most gentle clarity like the autumn sky, he carried away the immovable splendor of the full ocean when it is sheltered from the wind.
He shook off the floods of excessive conceptual constructions that had come into appearance before him, just as the wind blows away gnats shimmering in front of one's face.
As the mental images appeared again and again according to his will, the hero cut them down with his mind, just as one cuts down enemies with a sword in battle.
When the flood of conceptual constructions had been utterly severed, he beheld within the sky of his heart that darkness which veils the sun of discernment, as black as flickering lampblack.
He too he wiped away completely with the sun of his own mind, which had arisen through perfect knowledge, just as soot is quickly cleared by the wind.
When the darkness had ceased, he beheld that lovely mass of light, like the lotus of the morning twilight appearing when the nocturnal gloom has subsided.
Like a young elephant, he trampled the forest of land-lotuses; and like a vetāla, he swiftly drank the flood of blood.
When his vital heat had subsided, the mind of that sage, reeling like a night-lotus, fell into sleep as unsteady as that of a drunkard.
Like a serpent to a garland of clouds, like the sun to a bed of blue lotuses, or like the hot-rayed sun to the night, he swiftly tore that [bow] as well.
When his sleep had passed away, his mind contemplated those beings with eyes as dark as the sky, like peacock feathers in the firmament.
Just as a rain cloud [removes] the *tāpiccha* tree, as the wind [dispels] the mist, and as a lamp [eliminates] darkness, he quickly wiped away even that [impurity], being of pure nature.
When the consciousness of space had vanished, his mind became deluded, as if intoxicated by liquor when sleep has dissolved away.
This noble-minded man wiped away that delusion of the mind, just as the sun dispels the dullness produced by the night from the world.
Then, having reached an indescribable state entirely free from light, darkness, sleep, delusion, and the like, the mind rested for a moment.
Having rested quickly, O dear one, he attained consciousness of his universal form, like the water of a lake dammed by a bridge returning to its own source against the current.
Through the power of long-term investigation and from the tasting of his own consciousness, he then attained the state of pure spirit, just as gold attains the form of an anklet.
Then, having completely abandoned its state as mind, the mind attained the nature of the true essence of mind; it quickly became something entirely different, just like mud remaining inside a jar.

Having completely abandoned the object of consciousness, pure consciousness attained the state of universal consciousness, just as the ocean, having cast off distinctions such as waves and the like, becomes a single unity of water.

Having abandoned the mental conception of the multitude of elemental beings, he then became that great sustainer of the universe; thereafter, having attained awakening, he became the pure space of consciousness.
There he attained bliss, free from the seen and the seeing, infinite and of supreme savor, like an ocean of elixir.
Inherent within his body, he descended to a certain earth; being of the nature of the universal essence of existence, he became an ocean of bliss.
This swan of the consciousness of the twice-born, dwelling in the lake of bliss, remained in the sky as clear as autumn, like the moon full of its digits.
He became like a lamp sheltered from the wind, resembling a figure depicted in a painting; he was like an ocean devoid of waves, with the stillness of a rain-stilled and silent cloud.
Then, while staying for a long time in that great world, Uddālaka beheld many sky-faring Siddhas and even immortals.
Various nets of accomplishments have arrived from all sides, bestowing the stations of Śakra and Arka, and are densely crowded with throngs of apsarases.
That twice-born man, profound in intellect and unperturbed, paid no heed to those throngs of perfected beings, just as one disregards the frolics of childhood.
Disregarding the caravan of supernatural powers, he then remained for six months in that temple of bliss, like the sun upon the northern horizon.
O twice-born one, while that man was still attaining the state of liberation while living, the Siddhas, Suras, Sādhyas, and the gods beginning with Brahmā and Hara were present there.
Having been transformed into bliss, he reached the state beyond bliss; neither in bliss nor in the absence of bliss did that consciousness then manifest.
Having found stability there for either a moment or a thousand years, the mind finds no pleasure in a flood of enjoyments, just as one who has seen heaven finds no delight in the earth.
That is the state, that is the peaceful goal; that is the supreme, eternal, and auspicious good. For one who has attained rest therein, delusion no longer causes affliction.
Having attained that state, the virtuous do not return again to this perception of the visible world, just as those who have reached the Caitraratha grove do not return to a garden of khadira wood.
Having attained that state of great bliss from their minds, embodied beings no longer value the visible world, just as kings disregard a state of wretchedness.
O sinless one, when the mind has found rest in that state, does it ever return to the state of the visible world through some misfortune, or rather, does it not return at all?
Having dwelt there for six months, Uddālaka cast far away the ground of supernatural powers; he emerged like the sun from the womb of the clouds at the onset of spring.
With his soul fully awakened, he again beheld those beings of supreme splendor, who were longing to offer salutations, affectionate, and possessing bodies with the form of the lunar orb.
Successions of celestial chariots appeared, delightful with fly-whisks made of bees and the pollen of white mandāra flowers, and adorned with fluttering clusters of banners.
[He saw] sages such as ourselves, whose lotus-like hands were marked by the sacred *darbha* grass, as well as lords of the *vidyādharas* surrounded by *vidyādharī* maidens.
They spoke thus to that high-souled sage Uddālaka: "O Blessed One, look upon us with favor through our prostrations."
"Ascend this celestial chariot and come to the city of the Thirty-three; for heaven indeed is the ultimate limit of all worldly enjoyments and prosperity."
O Lord, enjoy for an eon the desired pleasures that are appropriate for you; indeed, all the practices of austerity are solely for the sake of enjoying the fruits such as heaven.
Behold these excellent women of the Vidyādharas, bearing necklaces and chowries, as they wait upon you like female elephants attending a male elephant.
Desire is the essence of dharma and artha; well-favored women have desire as their essence. Like flower-clusters in springtime, they are indeed heaven itself.
Having thus addressed all his guests, the sage, having honored them according to tradition, remained composed and free from agitation.
That man of steady intellect neither rejoiced in nor abandoned that prosperity; saying, "O Siddhas, go," he became intent on his own affairs.
Then, after attending upon him—who was devoted to his own duty and had attained a lack of interest in worldly enjoyments—the Siddhas themselves departed within a few days.
And that sage, liberated while living, wandered at his pleasure as long as he desired through the forest regions and the hermitages of the sages.
Upon the peaks of Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Himavat, and Vindhya; on the islands, groves, cardinal points, bowers, jungles, and forest lands.
From that time forward, the twice-born Uddālaka, having attained his goal, dwelt in the caves within the recesses of mountains, absorbed in the play of meditation.
Sometimes after a day, sometimes after a month, sometimes after a year, and sometimes after a multitude of years, he, absorbed in meditation, would awaken.
From that time forward, although Uddālaka was occupied with worldly affairs, he remained perfectly composed, having attained oneness with the reality of the mind.

Through the practice of the single, solid mass of the essence of consciousness, he attained the state of Great Consciousness (mahācitta) and became, everywhere in the entire world, like the solar radiance upon the earth.
Through long practice of the universal consciousness, having attained the universal existence, he neither sets nor rises within this visible world, like the sun in a painting.

With his mind fully stilled through the attainment of the supreme state of peace, the bonds of birth dissolved, and the oscillations of doubt exhausted, he bore that body which was as clear, stainless, expansive, and powerful as the autumnal sky—tranquil, yet conscious.
Śrī Rāma said: O sole sun for the day of self-knowledge, O fire for the grass of my doubts, O moon for the burning away of ignorance—O Lord, what is this "universal existence" (sattāsāmānya)?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the mind is completely dissolved through the constant contemplation of non-existence, then there arises the state of universal existence belonging to that which is the nature of universal consciousness.

Indeed, when consciousness, devoid of the aspect of "this-ness," dissolves into itself, it then becomes the utterly transparent generality of existence (*sattāsāmānyatā*), appearing as if it were non-existent.
When the mind dwells having negated all this—whatever exists, including that which is external and internal—then it abides in the state of universal existence.
When all visible objects are perceived as the universal existence (sattāsāmānya), appearing as their own nature through their own nature, that is the state of universal existence.

Just as the limbs of a tortoise withdraw themselves into itself, when visible objects dissolve into the Self by the Self, being no longer cultivated [as separate], then they attain the state of universal existence.
For this supreme vision, which resembles the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), is indeed possible at all times for both those with a body and those without a body who are liberated.

O sinless one, this [wisdom] arises for both the one who has emerged from meditation and the one established in samādhi; it belongs solely to the knower, and does not arise at all in the ignorant person born of awakening.
Abiding in this vision, all these noble-minded ones are liberated while living; they are like perfected alchemical elixirs upon the earth, or like winds in the path of the sky.
O Raghava, all of us beginning with myself, as well as Narada and others, and Brahma, Vishnu, Ishvara, and the rest, have been seen established within this state.
Having taken hold of this path that destroys all fear, Uddālaka dwelt for as long as he desired in the house of the world.
Then, after a long time, his intellect became firm in this resolve: "I shall remain liberated from the body (videhamukta) once I have cast off this physical form."
Having thought thus, he remained in a mountain cave upon a seat of young shoots, seated in the lotus posture with his eyes half-closed.

Restraining the nine gates of the mind by the suppression of the anus, and discerning the contacts of the sense-objects, he becomes one whose wealth of consciousness is cultivated within his own limbs.
Having restrained the vital breaths, with his neck held in a balanced posture, the root of his tongue pressed against the base of the palate, his face radiant.
With the mind and vision joined together, neither externally nor internally, neither below nor above, neither upon an object nor in emptiness, one should keep the teeth from touching each other.
O dear one, with the flow of the vital breath restrained, his facial complexion became clear; his limbs were erect with consciousness, and his body was covered in horripilation.
Through the practice of the consciousness of the limbs, one attains the commonality of consciousness; from that practice, one obtains the supreme vibration of inner bliss.

Then, through the relishing of that, the universal sustainer, whose self is infinite, attained the state of the general existence common to all, which is the sequence of the stages of the contracted mind.
He remained with his physical form perfectly balanced, having attained supreme rest, his facial radiance charmingly and exquisitely beautiful with a bliss that was not merely ordinary joy.

With his horripilation arising from the bliss of perfect tranquility, he attained the stainless state; the delusion of worldly existence, such as discursive thought and the like, had long since been worn away.
That Great Being became like one fixed in a painting; he was equal to the spotless autumnal moon when its digit is not yet full.
In a few days, he gradually became tranquil in his own stainless state, having transcended the stage of birth, like the sap of a tree in the pure heat of the sun's rays at the end of autumn.

With all conceptual constructions gone, changeless and delightful, his form liberated from the limiting adjuncts of every trace of impurity, he attained that primordial bliss in which the splendor of Indra is swept away like a blade of grass in a mass of water.

He became that Brahmin—immeasurable, pervading the interior of the sky and pervading the directions, full, possessing the nature of sustaining the worlds, served by many who are fit for liberation, transcending the qualities of speech, truth, primordial bliss, supreme happiness, and infinite.

Once her mind had attained its first state of pure clarity, the body of that twice-born one, while remaining seated, became in six months a mountain-lute with the slender arms of trees for strings, delightful with the whistling of the wind and scorched by the rays of the sun.

Then, after a considerable time, the Mothers, accompanied by the daughters of the mountain, emerged from the lake; for the sake of accomplishing their desired goals, they all appeared with their hair turned tawny, like rows of flames united with fire.

The goddess Khiṅkhinī, who is worshipped by all the gods, instantly placed upon the tip of her crown—between her sword and skull-topped staff—that skeleton of the Brahmin, which had been dried by the rays of the sun, and at night she gave it a beauty like that of a fresh, dark-red lotus.

Thus, the highly blessed Khiṅkhiṇikā rests upon the Uddālakadehaka—a cluster of creepers that is a plaything of grace, shimmering with fresh clouds tossed by a multitude of brilliantly shining peacock feathers and garlands of Mandāra flowers—just as a bee settles within a mass of blossoms at the rear of a flower-cluster. She follows behind.

This creeper of the mental fluctuations of Uddālaka, which has spread through the forest of the heart with flowers that shine with the blossoming of the bliss of discernment, once it has taken root—even while wandering—does not suffer separation from its true shade, but attains a most exalted and fruitful union with it.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O lotus-eyed one, wandering by this sequence and investigating the Self by means of the self, attain rest in the expansive state.

One should investigate the meaning of the scriptures with a mind focused on the teacher to that extent, through the practice of dissolving all objects of perception, until the state [of liberation] is attained.
The meritorious state is attained through the sequence consisting of detachment, practice, the meaning of the scriptures, wisdom, and the guru; or else, it is attained by wisdom alone.
An intellect that is fully awakened, sharp, and free from blemish attains the eternal state, even if it lacks all other favorable conditions.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, is there anyone who, having attained samādhi, remains as tranquil as one who is awakened, even while engaged in worldly activity?"
Someone else, having resorted to solitude, remains fixed in meditative concentration; O Blessed One, tell me which of these two is superior.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For one who perceives this collection of qualities as not being the self, that internal coolness which arises is called samādhi.
Having determined that the connection with visible objects resides in the mind, one person remains engaged in worldly affairs, while another is established in meditative absorption.
O Rāma, these two are happy within if they are cool; that which is inner coolness is the fruit of infinite austerity.
If the mind of one established in the state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is still flickering with mental activity, then that concentration of his is equal to the wild dancing of a madman.
If the mind of one engaged in the frantic dance of madness has its latent tendencies (vāsanā) exhausted, then that madman's conduct is equal to the meditative absorption (samādhi) of a Buddha.
The one who is awakened while engaged in worldly affairs and the one who is awakened while dwelling in the forest—these two are truly equal; they have undoubtedly attained the same state.
Even while acting, this mind, when its latent tendencies are attenuated, does not act as an agent, just as a person whose mind has wandered far away does not truly listen to a discourse.

Even though it does nothing, the mind that possesses intense latent impressions acts as if it were the agent, just as one whose limbs are motionless in a dream feels as if they are standing on the edge of a precipice.
The state in which the mind has no agency is the supreme concentration; know that to be the state of absolute oneness, that auspicious and ultimate liberation.

The supreme cause of the mind’s wavering and non-wavering is traditionally held to be memory; therefore, by means of meditation and the vision of meditation, make that very [memory] free from the sprout of desire.
That very mental meditation is declared to be unwavering and stable; that indeed is the state of absolute liberation, and that is always peace itself.
The mind with subtle latent impressions is said to be striving for the highest state; therefore, by making the mind free of impressions, the state of the agent is attained.
This mind, thick with latent impressions (vāsanā), is the vessel for agency and the source of all suffering; therefore, one should bring those impressions to attenuation.
That state by which the self becomes established in itself—remaining within the world yet tranquil, with sorrow, fear, and desire removed—is known as samādhi.
Having completely renounced with your mind the sense of self-identity toward all things, remain as you are—whether on a mountain or in a house.
For those householders whose minds are well-composed and whose faults of egoism have been stilled, their very home is like the solitary forest lands.
To you whose minds and vision are composed, this forest dwelling is equal to the abode of great beings.
O Prince, even though the great cloud of his peaceful mind was present, the cities—though ablaze with the fires of the people—and even the forests became desolate.
O slayer of enemy heroes, even forests devoid of people appear as crowded cities to one whose mind is intoxicated by its own habitual tendencies.
The mind that has emerged from its state reaches the end of delusion, which is deep sleep; it then attains Nirvana—Nirvana! Do as you wish.
He who always perceives the Self as transcending all states of existence, yet as being the essence of all states of existence, is said to be concentrated in meditative absorption.

He for whom the desired and the undesired have perished, whose internal form is expanded, and to whom all states of being are equal—he is called one who is composed in meditative absorption (samāhita).
O Lord of Men, the mind perceives this world as being truly existent by means of its own nature of existence; just as it is in a dream, so too is it in this waking state.
With his mind always turned inward, even while asleep, awake, or walking, he beholds the city, the countryside, the village, and the forest as if they were a wilderness.
Everything attains the state of space through constant abiding within; for this world, agitated by the elements, is in every respect useless.
But once inner coolness has been attained, the world becomes cool for those who are free from the fever [of passion], as long as they remain alive.
For all living beings tormented by internal thirst, this world becomes like a forest fire; for that which exists within is what stands without.
The sky, the earth, the wind, space, the mountains, the rivers, and the directions are but portions of the reality of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa-tattva) existing as if external.
Just as a banyan seed contains within it that which is the eternal Self, so does that [Self] shine forth externally when it expands, like the fragrance of a flower.
Nothing whatsoever exists anywhere either outside or within; whatever appears in whatever manner, that very thing arises as reality because of the nature of consciousness.
The inner reality of the Self appears as the external world; though it is contracted, it expands like camphor through its fragrance.
The Self alone vibrates extensively as the world, as the ego, and as both the external and the internal; and that all-pervading one is neither non-existent nor existent.

By means of that which is external, one perceives the internal; by means of that which is internal, one perceives what resides within; thus this Self, according to its knowledge, beholds its own mind.

The entire world, both external and internal, is differentiated from the Self, yet it is peaceful; however, when differentiation persists through the notion of "I-ness" and so forth, that world becomes subject to the fear of manifold destruction.
For one whose mind is struck by mental anguish, heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions—all are set ablaze from the very beginning of the eon.
But he who, finding delight only within himself, performs actions with the organs of action, and is not subject to joy or sorrow—he is said to be composed.
He who, seeing the self as omnipresent, has a thoroughly pacified intellect, neither grieves nor broods; he is said to be concentrated in meditation.
He who, seeing the course of the world from its prior to its posterior limit, laughs at these views is said to be composed.
Likewise, there is no sense of "I" in others, nor is there any birth of the world in me; just as heated fruits do not exist in the sky, they do not exist within the multitude of waves.
He in whom the internal state of "I-ness" does not exist, nor division and the like, nor the mind, nor the states of consciousness and unconsciousness—he alone exists; all other people do not.

He who, as clear as the sky, conducts himself here in this world with perfect detachment from external desires, remains tranquil, like a piece of wood or a clod of earth amidst the fluctuations of joy and anger.
He who, by his very nature and not out of fear, regards all beings as himself and the property of others as a clod of earth—he truly sees.

An object, whether large or small, is not perceived in its form as non-existent; nor is it experienced by the ignorant as having the form of existence, nor is it experienced by the knower as such [in that limited way].
Endowed with such an intention and having attained the state of a Mahāsattva, whether he remains, arises, departs, or meets death, he does not abide in that [world].
One may dwell either in one's own home, which is rich with the finest enjoyments and crowded with people, or else in a vast forest that is devoid of all enjoyments and free from activity.
Let him dance, intent on drinking and with unrestrained passion; or let him go to the mountain, having renounced all attachments and attained equanimity.
Let him anoint his body with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, or else let him fall into a fire spreading with masses of flickering flames.
Whether he commits very great and abundant evil or merit, or whether he meets death this very day or after a multitude of kalpas;
There is nothing that he does not do, yet nothing is done by that Great-Souled One; he incurs no stain, just as gold remains untainted even when situated in mud.

That [consciousness] is defiled by the meanings of the words "consciousness" (saṃvit) and "person" (puruṣa), which are themselves stained by the latent impressions (vāsanā) of "I-ness" and "you-ness," resembling the silver perceived in a mother-of-pearl shell.

Through the complete pacification of all things by means of right knowledge, one abides in the state as it truly is; thus, the internal stain of one's own nature is pacified by its very non-existence.
From the consciousness-self, which gives rise to the misfortune of the latent impressions of "I-ness," there arise for the person in this birth various pleasures and pains.

Just as when the delusion of a snake in a rope has subsided, there is no fear of a snake and one attains peace, so too, when the notion of "I-ness" has completely subsided, internal equanimity is considered to be attained.
Whatever one does, whatever one eats, whatever one gives, or whatever one offers in sacrifice—that does not belong to the knower, nor is the knower therein; let him not act, or let him act.
For him there is no purpose in action, nor is there any purpose for him in non-action; through the realization of his own true nature, he remains established in the Self alone.
From him desires arise, not like blossoms from a stone; and all those that do arise are he himself, like waves in the waters.

All this and that—this entire world in its totality—is without any division here; he is the single form of the Supreme Person, the purifier, who is eternally existent as "Sat," while that which is non-existent is merely "Asat."

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as within the peppercorn of the Self there is the perception of sharpness due to its consciousness, so too are egoism, duality, space, time, and all else perceived from that [Self].
Just as saltiness is perceived within a fragment of salt because it possesses consciousness, so too do egoity, duality, space, time, and all else abide within Me.

From itself, for the inner self who beholds within, there arises from its nature as consciousness the experience of sweetness; that [experience] unfolds as the ego-sense, duality, the world, the principles of reality, and so forth.
When the stone of the self perceives its own hardness by virtue of its consciousness, that [perception] becomes the ego-sense (*ahaṃtā*) and so forth, as well as distinctions such as space and time.

When the mountain of the Self perceives its own insentience through the state of being a knower, that which is established as "I-ness" (ahaṃtā), duality (bhedādi), the worlds (bhuvanādi), and so forth, [arises].

When that which exists by itself, as the self, undergoes the state of being a flow of consciousness and so forth, it then appears as if taking on forms such as whirlpools or the distinctions of "I-ness" and the like.

When there is the perception of the branches and so forth of the tree that is one's own self, then that which consists of "I-ness" and differentiation shines forth as reality, like the world and its contents.
When there is the realization of emptiness within the sky of the self due to its consciousness, that is the contemplation [of it] as the ego, the various distinctions, the worlds, and so forth.
When there is the perception of hollowness within the sky of the self due to its being consciousness, then egoism, duality, the body, and so forth are illuminated.
When the wall of the self exists as a continuous, uninterrupted whole by its own nature, it appears as if situated outside the mind through the distinctions of "I-ness" and so forth.

Since it is by its own nature a consciousness (*citta*) possessing self-existence, its singular perception of existence—consisting of "I-ness" (*ahantā*) and so forth, as well as differentiation—is established like the state of being sentient.
The self-manifestation of the inner self’s own light, which consists of "I-ness" and so forth, as well as consciousness and the like—that is what he knows as the individual soul (jīva).
When the form of consciousness, the elixir of consciousness, which exists within the moon of the Self, is tasted by itself, then that [state] characterized by "I-ness" and so forth is dispelled.

That which consists of the arising of the sweetness of consciousness within the sugar-candy of the Supreme Self is what is tasted by Him; therefore, egoity and the like do not exist within Him by their own nature.
Because it is consciousness, that which is the internal manifestation of the jewel of the Supreme Self manifests by itself; and within the state of the conscious Self, it perceives "I" and so forth.
And he knows nothing within, because of the impossibility of an object of knowledge here; nor does he taste flavor, because of the impossibility of anything to be tasted.
And since nothing exists within that which is perceived, he perceives nothing at all; and because of the non-existence of anything to be known, he knows nothing.
The Self alone appears as the non-existent; infinite and full in form, it remains forever as a single solid mass within itself, like a great mountain.
O descendant of Raghu, by this turn of phrase, I have demonstrated to you that there is no distinction between the "I-ness" and so forth, and the "world-ness" and so forth.
There is no mind, no cognizer, and no delusion such as the world and so forth; it is merely the peaceful, silent, and cloud-like state of the rain-stillness that subsides.

Just as water attains the state of whirlpools and the like due to its fluidity within water, so too does the Knower attain the state of "I-ness" and so forth within the Self, which is pure consciousness, through the process of cognition.
Just as liquidity exists in water and motion in the wind, so do the notions of "I," space, time, and so forth, exist within the Knower, who is pure consciousness alone.
O Śiva, the Knower knows knowledge through the expansion of knowledge for the sake of knowing; that "I-ness" is known by the Knower through the vital functions such as living.
In whatever way it arises, and by whatever kind of knowledge the ignorant man finds satisfaction, once he perceives non-duality as duality, he expands himself accordingly.
Life is consciousness, the knower is life, and life is the very life of the living being; there is absolutely no difference between the knower and the living being in their nature as consciousness.
Just as there is no such thing as a difference between the knower and the individual soul, know that there is likewise no difference between the knower and Śiva—He who is peaceful and indivisible.

All is utterly tranquil, unborn, one, without beginning or middle, luminous, consisting of pure self-experience, and devoid of any mark of cognition. "All is utterly tranquil"—this view composed of words is indeed for the sake of awakening; otherwise, to call this "Om" would be in vain.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In this very context, they cite this ancient history, the account of the Kirāta lord Suraghu, which is a source of wonder.
It was like the fat of the northern quarter, or a mass of camphor from the earth, or the laughter of Śiva manifested, or the white radiance of the moon.
On this Himalaya mountain there is a peak, a mountain named Kailāsa, which is like the leader of a herd of elephant-like mountains that has shed its trunk-like [peaks].
That dwelling was like the Ocean of Milk for Viṣṇu, like heaven for the Lord of the Gods, and like the navel-lotus of the Lotus-born One for the Moon-crested Lord.
He shines with swings made of rudrākṣa trees and accompanied by celestial nymphs, like the ocean with its waves of shimmering jeweled rods.
Where the playful *aśoka* trees shine like actual *aśoka* flowers struck by the feet of intoxicated women from the retinues of the gods.
Moving through the quarters among the Bhrigus, Śaṅkara wanders where waterfalls flow forth and recede incessantly, as if they were the liquid essence of moonstones.
It was as if the universe itself were covered by masses of creepers, trees, and shrubs, by ponds, lakes, rivers, and streams, and by deer, herds of wild animals, and living beings.
On that land dwell the Kirātas known as the Hemajaṭas, like ants gathered within the hollow at the root of a banyan tree.
In the forests at the foot of Kailāsa, those base beings who live off what is nearby dwell like owls among the rudrākṣa trees and shrubs.
Among them there was a noble-souled king, a conqueror of enemy cities, who was like the right arm of both the Goddess of Victory and his subjects.
The powerful one named Suraghu was the destroyer of the pride of his formidable enemies; he was like the sun in prowess and like the wind incarnate.
The leader of the Guhyakas was indeed surpassed by him in royal power and wealth; the preceptor of Indra was surpassed in wisdom; and the teacher of the Asuras was surpassed in poetic compositions.
He performed his royal duties through the sequence of punishment and favor, as they arose, without weariness in his limbs, just as the sun performs its daily tasks throughout the days.
Then he was overwhelmed by the pleasure and pain born from that [state], like a bird whose limbs are entangled in the snares of its own flight-path.
Why should I afflict this suffering being with my power, like sesame seeds in a press? For all beings alike, suffering arises just as it does for me.
"I bestow wealth upon him; through wealth, every person becomes full of joy, just as I am. Therefore, enough of my excessive restraints."
Or rather, I shall indeed bring about the destruction of this world without him; for this creation cannot exist without him, just as a river cannot exist without water.
"Alas, what a tragedy! This one who was always to be favored by me is now to be punished. By fate, today I am happy; alas, today I am miserable."
Thus the king’s mind, oscillating, found no rest, wandering like one long-thirsting caught in a single great whirlpool of water.
Then one day, the sage Māṇḍavya came to his house, having wandered through every corner of the quarters of the earth, like Nārada to the abode of Vāsava.
Tamas honored that great sage, who was skilled in all things and an axe for the stubborn trunk of the evil tree of doubt, and questioned him.
Suraghu said: "O Sage, by your arrival I have attained supreme bliss, like one who has reached the surface of the earth during the month of Mādhava."
O Lord, today I stand at the forefront of the blessed by virtue of the Dharma, since I have been beheld by you as a lotus is by the blossoming sun.
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, you have long been at rest; therefore, sever this doubt of mine, as the sun dispels the darkness.
By association with the great, whose suffering indeed does not perish? Yet those who understand suffering say that doubt is the highest form of suffering.
Arising from the various acts of restraint and favor [toward my devotees], these anxieties—residing within the bodies of my servants—torment me intensely, like the claws of a lion upon an elephant.
Just as the sun's rays always rise with equanimity, O Sage, let there be no other thought in my mind; act accordingly with compassion.
Māṇḍavya said: O King, this flimsiness of mind dissolves away by one's own effort, established in oneself, and through one's own means, even as surely as the Himalayas might melt.
By one's own inquiry alone, the fever of the inner mind is quickly pacified, just as a great mist vanishes at the mere arrival of autumn.
With one's own mind, one should inwardly investigate one's own sense faculties as they reside within one's own body: what are they like, and what are they?
"Who am I? How did this come to be? What is it, and how do birth and death occur?"—by reflecting thus within yourself, you will attain greatness.
For you, whose true nature is fully understood through investigation, states of joy and resentment shall not cause your mind to waver from its immovability.
Having cast off the mind, it will attain peace, free from fever, becoming like a wave that has returned to its former state as water.
O sinless one, even while remaining in his celestial form, he will abandon his body at the time when it becomes marred by imperfection, as if during the course of a Manvantara.
All those illustrious people will become objects of compassion for you, who have seen reality and are content, just as subjects on earth are toward a father.
O King, having perceived the Self through the lamp of discernment, you will surpass even the greatness of Mount Meru, the oceans, and the sky—greatness which bestows the supreme goal.
O virtuous one, when your mind has attained greatness, it does not sink into the currents of worldly existence, just as an elephant does not sink into the puddles of a cow's footprint.
But a wretched mind, O King, sinks even into a trivial matter, just as an old-bodied gnat sinks into the water of a cow's footprint.
Through that wretchedness of your own, which clings to mere appearances, you sink into the mire like a worm, due to the mental impressions of the mind.
To that same extent, O mighty-armed one, everything is abandoned by itself, until only the Supreme Self remains as the supreme vision.
The ore is washed away only so long as the gold alone remains; everything is scrutinized only until the Self alone is attained.
Having completely relinquished everything—in every way, everywhere, and at all times—by means of an all-encompassing awareness, one perceives the Self by means of the self.
As long as everything has not been relinquished, the Self is not attained; when all states have been abandoned, that which remains is called the Self.
O virtuous one, as long as the other is not abandoned, the object remains merely a generality; what then need be said regarding the attainment of its own true nature?
O King, when one strives with one's whole being for the sake of attaining the Self, having abandoned all other activities, it is only that [Self] which is attained, and nothing else.
Therefore, for the sake of beholding one's own self, one should renounce everything; having renounced all things whatsoever, that which is seen is the supreme state.

Having completely cast aside the expansion of all things existing within the world—which consists of the entire succession of causes and effects—and having thereafter dissolved one's own body, that which the mind attains is indeed That alone.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus to Suraghu, O descendant of Raghu, the venerable Māṇḍavya departed for his own beautiful circle of silence.
When the supreme sage had departed, the king went to a blameless solitude and reflected within his own mind: "Who indeed am I?"
I am not Meru, nor is Meru mine; I am not the world, nor is the world mine. I am not the mountains, nor are the mountains mine; I am not the earth, nor is the earth mine.
This Kirāta territory is not mine, nor am I the territory; by mere personal convention, it is simply a region belonging to me.
"I have abandoned this convention; I am not the country, nor indeed is it mine. Now only the city remains—this is the certain conclusion here."
Abounding with rows of forests of banners, crowded with servants' groves, and filled with elephants, horses, and vassal lords—this city is not mine, nor is it my city.
The multitude of enjoyments and the wife, whose connection to convention is purposeless and destroyed when that convention ceases—neither am I these, nor is all this mine.
Thus, along with my servants, my army, my vehicles, and my city—neither do I possess this kingdom, nor does the kingdom belong to me; for this convention is indeed confusing.
"I consider the body alone—endowed with hands, feet, and so forth—to be the self; therefore, for now, I shall examine its interior."
Therefore, in this matter, I am not this flesh and bone, which are insentient; nor do they enter into union with me, just as water does not unite with a lotus.
Flesh is inert; I am not that, nor am I even the blood. The bones are inert; I am certainly not they, nor do they ever belong to me.
I am not the organs of action, nor do the organs of action belong to me; for whatever in this body is insentient, that indeed I am not, as I am pure consciousness.
I am not the objects of enjoyment, nor do I possess objects of enjoyment, nor do I possess the sense organs; for the sense organs are inert and devoid of reality, and I am not the sense organs.

The mind is the root of the defect of transmigratory existence, for it is not the "I," which is indeed insentient; furthermore, the view that "the intellect" or "the ego" is the self is merely mental in nature.
The sheath of the elements, consisting of the mind, intellect, senses, and so forth, is a moving body; I am not such a thing, for I perceive the Self as distinct from the body and its constituents.

But the remaining conscious being is the individual soul (jīva); if that [soul] perceives through an object of perception, or if it is awakened by another, it would not possess the nature of the reality of the Self (ātmatattva).
Thus I renounce all that is experienced and all that is thought, for I am indeed not that; remaining as the residual, free from conceptual construction, I abide as pure consciousness.
Wonderful! I have attained my true self and, in due time, have become one who fulfills his purpose. I am that very Self, infinite; there is no end to this Supreme Self.
In Brahmā, Indra, Yama, Vāyu, and likewise in the hosts of all beings, this very Blessed One, the Self, exists like a thread running through pearls.
This very power of consciousness is stainless, free from the disease of the objectified world, filling every corner of the quarters, and assuming the form of Bhairava.
Subtle and pervading all states of being, she is free from both existence and non-existence; abiding within the entire realm up to the world of Brahmā, she is the casket containing all powers.
She is the most beautiful and auspicious of all, the lamp illuminating everything; she is the thread in the form of a woven web for all those liberated from saṃsāra.
Richly endowed with all forms of transformation, yet devoid of all forms; she has become the flood of all beings and has always attained the state of being everything.
These fourteen kinds of elements exist within the belly of the world; this worldly conceptualization, consisting of them, is of the nature of sensation.
The course of states of pleasure and pain is merely a false appearance; all that consists of various forms and appearances is nothing but the Supreme Consciousness, which is the Self alone.
This very self of mine is all-pervasive; this is that awakening, which, having assumed a form with manifest limbs, produces the delusion of being a king.
By the grace of this very [intellect], the mind, situated upon the chariot of the body, gallops, leaps, and dances amidst the playful diversions of the web of saṃsāra.
This mind, body, and so forth are not anything at all in reality; when this fragile [complex] perishes, nothing whatsoever perishes.
This dance, consisting of the web of the world, is performed by the actors that are the minds; it is perceived by this single thread of intelligence, like a streak of light from a lamp.
Alas, my concern regarding the maintenance of restraint and favor was in vain; it was based on the body, yet there is no such thing as a body at all.
"Aha! I am awakened; my false vision has vanished. Everything that was to be seen has been seen, and this which was to be attained has been attained by me."
Whatever is seen here as this entire visible world, it is nothing other than a mere portion of the vibration of consciousness; there is no eternal thing whatsoever apart from that.

Where are those two, and of what nature are they? Upon what are they based, and what is their essence? Likewise, [explain] the processes of restraint and favor, as well as joy and resentment, in the world.
"What is pleasure, or what indeed is suffering? All this is the expansive Brahman. I was deluded in vain; by good fortune, I have realized that I was but a fool."
In such light as this, why is there sorrow? Why is there delusion? Why is one gazing, why is one acting, or why is one standing still or departing?
Something called "this" shines thus within the sky of consciousness; salutations, salutations to you, O reality-less one! By good fortune have you been seen, O Beautiful One.
Aha! I have indeed awakened; I have fully understood. Homage to myself, the infinite, and to the arising of perfect knowledge!

Free from passion and established in the state beyond sense-objects, having transcended the delusion of worldly existence and abandoned all that colors it, I have attained the state of steady, profound sleep; therefore, I abide in the Self, equanimous with all.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, the lord Hemajaṭa attained the unsurpassed state through his resolute discernment, just as the son of Gadhi attained the status of a Brahmin.
The Lord was not weary of his activities, which were purposeful and effective, even though he engaged in them again and again throughout the succession of days.
From that time forward, he remained forever free from distress, steadfast in his own duty like a mountain at the forefront of a flood of water.
Free from both joy and resentment, performing his daily duties, he—possessing a noble and profound form—stole away the splendor of the ocean.
He shone with a mental state possessing the quality of deep sleep—a state that was unwavering and luminous—just as a lamp shines with its own flame.
He was neither pitiless nor compassionate, neither dualistic nor envious; he was neither wise nor unwise, neither seeking gain nor seeking loss.
With a constant vision of equanimity, a steady and unflinching mode of conduct, and an inner tranquility, he shone like the full moon over the ocean.
Perceiving the entire world as a mere construction of the nature of consciousness, his intellect shone forth in its fullness, with the glory of pleasure and pain utterly stilled.
Whether exulting, expanding, full, standing, walking, entering, or sleeping, he remained established in perfectly equal samādhi; awakened, he had attained dissolution into consciousness.
Then that lotus-eyed king, ruling his kingdom free from attachment, remained for many hundreds of years with his form unimpaired.
Thereafter, he himself, overcome by that splendor, abandoned this bodily configuration, just as a drop of frost sheds its form.
He entered the Supreme Cause, the Lord of Causes, who is without beginning or end, just as a river’s water enters the ocean filled to the brim by its wisdom.

Having attained the stainless splendor of the singular form and having reached a state free from people, his sorrow stilled, that Great-Souled One was sufficient as the supreme nature itself, like a jar and space joined with the sky.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O lotus-petal-eyed Rāghava, thus, upon the reversal of the afflictions of worldly existence, attain the state that is beyond duality; be free from sorrow for the sake of your ultimate welfare.
By relying on this view, the mind does not suffer, like a child who has found a lamp while submerged in a terrible darkness.
Through the state of discernment, the mind attains such peace as if it were falling into a chasm while clutching a firm bundle of grass.
Furthermore, having cultivated this purifying vision and proclaiming it, remain perpetually established in one-pointed concentration, thereby adorning the surface of the earth.
Śrī Rāma said: O Lord of Sages, how is single-pointed concentration achieved, and of what nature is it? For the mind is as restless as the plumage of a peacock shaken by the wind.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen now to this wonderful dialogue between that very Suraghu, who had become awakened, and the royal sage Parṇāda at that time.
I shall relate to you this mutual conversation between the two of them, whose minds were awakened and united through their singular devotion to Rāghava.
There was a king of the Pārasis, a slayer of enemy heroes, renowned by the name Parigha; he was like a mace [parigha] upon his chariot.
O descendant of Raghu, Suraghu became his supreme friend, just as Mādhava is to Madana when he resides in the Nandana garden.
Once, there occurred a great drought over the realm of Parigha, like that at the end of an eon in this world, born from the fault of the people's evil deeds.
There, many people perished, their lives emaciated by hunger, like successions of living beings in a forest blazing with fire.
Seeing that suffering, Parigha fell into incomparable despair; he abandoned his entire kingdom instantly, like a traveler fleeing a village consumed by fire.
Incapable of remedying the destruction of his subjects and devoid of passion, he went to the forest to perform austerities like a great sage clad in deerskin.
In a certain distant forest unknown even to the ancients, he dwelt with a detached soul, as if in another world.
Practicing austerities with a tranquil mind and self-controlled, he dwelt in a mountain cave and there subsisted on withered, dry leaves that had fallen of their own accord.
Then, for a long time consuming only withered leaves like a fire, he acquired the name Parṇāda among the ascetics.
From that time forward, this best of royal sages became known as Parṇāda throughout Jambūdvīpa and among the dwellings of the munis.
Then, after a thousand years of asceticism performed with a resolute mind, he attained through the power of practice the knowledge born of self-purification.
He became free from dualities, devoid of desire, with a tranquil mind; passionless and without compassion, he was liberated while living, his intellect fully awakened.
O virtuous one, he dwelt at will in this hermitage of the three worlds together with the Siddhas and Sādhyas, like a bee among lotuses.
Once, he reached the palace of King Hemacūḍa, which was constructed of jewels and resembled another peak of Mount Meru.
There, those two former friends paid honor to one another; they were now fulfilled, having understood what was to be known, and had emerged from the womb of folly.
"Aha! Indeed, my auspicious and purifying deeds have now borne fruit, since I have encountered you!"—thus they spoke to one another.
With their bodies embraced and their forms gladdened by one another, they sat together upon a single seat like the moon and the sun upon a mountain.
Parigha said: "My mind has attained supreme bliss through the sight of you; like the orb of the moon emerging from the water, my heart has reached a state of coolness."
Natural love, when separated from its object, spreads into a hundred branches, like a tree with unbroken roots on the bank of a pond.
O virtuous one, remembering those confidential conversations, those playful gestures, and those former activities, I rejoice again and again.
O sinless one, this knowledge which has been attained by me—born from the grace of the Supreme Self—has been understood by you through the favor of Māṇḍavya.
Are you free from suffering today? Have you found rest, like the sovereign of the earth upon Mount Meru, the supreme cause?
O most virtuous one, does clarity arise in your mind through delighting in the self, like the water of a lake in autumn?
O fortunate lord of men, do you perform all necessary duties with a gaze that is perfectly serene and profound?
Are the wise people in your lands free from mental and physical ailments, endowed with abundant rice, and dwelling without the fever of distress?
I hope that your earth, like the *phalinī* creeper bending under the weight of its fruit, sustains your subjects exceedingly with the abundance of your fruits.
I trust that your purifying fame has spread to the ends of the earth like the moon’s lattice of rays, taking on the appearance of a mass of frost.

I trust that these quarters have been rendered free of gaps by you through your multitude of virtues, just as the grounds surrounding a lake are made gapless by its waters, leaving no space for lotus stalks.
I trust that in every village, your maidens are seen singing your gladdening fame in the corners of the fields and other such places during the season.
May you have well-being regarding your grain, your wealth, and your possessions; and may you have well-being regarding your servants, your wives, your sons, and your cities.
Is this creeper of your body free from mental and physical afflictions? Does it bear fruit for the sake of merit, as prescribed for both this world and the next?
Is your mind free from attachment toward the serpents of the sense-objects, which are pleasant at first sight but are in fact eternal enemies?
"Alas! For a long time indeed we have been separated; by the power of Time we have now been joined once more, like the spring season and the mountain slope."
O friend, those states of happiness and suffering born of union and separation, which are not seen by living beings, do not exist in this world.
In this same way, having reached a state of difference during these exceedingly long periods, we have once again become united; for the operation of destiny is indeed manifold.
Suraghu said: "O Blessed One, who indeed can understand the course of this destiny—divine, profound, and awe-inspiring—which is like the movement of a serpent?"
Having cast aside "you" and "I," though far apart and in distant conditions, we have now been united once more; oh, what is impossible for Fate?
But today, O Great Being, we stand exceedingly well; through the merit of your arrival, we have attained supreme purity.
Behold how the trees of merit have borne fruit for us in such a way that we are no longer distressed, our sins having been exhausted by your arrival.
O royal sage, all our prosperities, which were established in the city, have today branched out into a hundred directions through your arrival.
O one of great majesty, you scatter your sweet speech and auspicious gaze all around like a heap of elixirs; for association with the virtuous is indeed equal to the supreme state.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, after they had remained there for a long time in such confidential conversation, which was imbued with their former affection, the one named Ayudha spoke.
Parigha said: "O sinless lord of the earth, whatever action is performed within this web of worldly existence leads to happiness for one whose mind is concentrated, but not for another."
I trust you practice that supreme concentration, which is free from conceptual construction, the ultimate place of rest, the highest tranquility, and the highest good.
Suraghu said: "O Blessed One, tell me this: what is that which is free from all conceptual constructions, the supreme peace, the highest good—what indeed is called samādhi?"
O Great-souled One, for that knower who always remains whether acting or not acting, when indeed could he ever be of uncomposed mind, and who indeed is such a person?
