But those whose minds are perpetually awakened, even while performing worldly activities, remain ever established in the single reality of the Self and are always in a state of perfect meditative absorption.
Even for one who has assumed the lotus posture and joined his palms in the *brahmāñjali* gesture, what is meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and how can it exist for one whose very nature is restless?
"O Blessed One, the realization of reality—which is like a fire that burns away the grass of all desires—is what is designated by the term 'samādhi,' and not merely remaining in silence."
O virtuous one, that which is concentrated, eternally satisfied, and perceives the meaning of things as they truly are, is called supreme wisdom by the wise under the term "samādhi."
Unshaken, free from egoism, and not following after dualities—that which has a form more stable than Mount Meru is designated by the word "samādhi."
Free from anxiety, having attained the desired, and devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted, the complete movement of the mind is designated by the term "samādhi."
From the moment his mind became endowed with ultimate awakening, from that time forth, the meditative absorption of that great-souled one remained uninterrupted.
For once the mind has become awakened, meditative absorption is not severed again, even when drawn far away, like a lotus fiber pulled by a child.
Just as the inexhaustible sun ceases its illumination at the end of a full day, so too may our wisdom cease from beholding reality only at the end of our lives.
Just as a river is not obstructed by its constant carrying of water, so too, through the awakening of the vision of discernment, it is not obstructed for even a single moment.
Just as time never ceases to forget the movement of its own moments, so too the intellect of the wise never ceases to forget its own self.
Just as the ever-moving wind does not forget its course everywhere, so too, O wise one, the intellect does not forget the indeterminate pure consciousness.

Just as the divisions of time remain fixed while accumulating their respective courses, so too does consciousness—devoid of both the act of cognizing and the object of cognition—accumulate various states of existence.
Just as an entity devoid of existence is not perceived, so too for the knower, time devoid of self-knowledge is not found.
Just as one who possesses qualities cannot exist in saṃsāra if devoid of those qualities, so too one who claims to possess a self cannot exist if devoid of self-awareness.
I am always fully awakened; I am always stainless; I am always peaceful in nature; I am always composed in meditative absorption.
By what means is a distinction produced in my samādhi, or how could it be? Since it is non-different from the Self, its nature as the Self is eternally and ever-present.
Therefore, at no time has my mind been devoid of meditative concentration, nor has it ever remained merely concentrated, because it arises solely from the reality of the Self.
The Self is all-pervading, eternal, and indeed everything in every way; for what could there be that is non-concentration, and what is traditionally known as concentration?

The great ones, whose intellects are eternally concentrated and who are perfectly equanimous, abide free from the distinctions of the transformation of objects; therefore, where indeed is that proliferation of supreme speech, which is based on the distinction between the unconcentrated and the concentrated?
Parigha said: "O King, you have surely awakened; you have attained that state. With your inner self cooled, you shine like the full moon."
Filled with the honey of bliss and embraced by supreme Lakṣmī, you shine like a lotus—cool, tender, and sweet.
Stainless, expansive, full, profound, and with your intentions made manifest, you shine like the ocean when it is released from the play of the coastal winds.
Transparent, filled with bliss, with the cloud of egoism destroyed, you shine clearly, vast and profound, like the autumnal sky.
Everywhere you appear composed, everywhere you are fully content; everywhere you are free from passion, O King, and everywhere you shine.
Having reached the further shore through your great intelligence by discerning the essential from the non-essential, you know all this exactly as it is, without exception.
Your body stands liberated from the agitation of the states of coming and going, its disposition gladdened by the knowledge of the reality that discerns existence and non-existence.
O beautiful one, you are satisfied with the Supreme, as if by a non-entity with an entity, as if the ocean were filled by a mere drop that never again diminishes.
Suraghu said: "O Sage, there is no object whatsoever in which we find anything worth acquiring; for as far as this visible world extends, it is nothing at all."
Since there is no thing to be accepted, what indeed could there be that is to be rejected? Without a counter-correlative—that which is to be excluded—how can something be called "rejection"?
Because all things are empty, yet not empty in terms of time, my mental states regarding both the empty and the non-empty have long since been utterly exhausted.
In this world, it is solely by virtue of place and time that the trivial becomes non-trivial, and the non-trivial becomes trivial; therefore, the wise should avoid both censure and praise.
In this world, praise and blame arise from attachment; attachment is directed toward that which is desired, and by one of noble intellect, even the most sublime object is regarded as desirable.
In the three worlds, women, mountains, oceans, and rows of forests—all these beings are empty of substance; in reality, there is no essence here.
In this dilapidated world composed of flesh, bone, wood, earth, and jewels—devoid of anything desirable and utterly empty—what indeed is there to be desired?
When desire has ceased, there is the destruction of hatred and passion, just as light and heat vanish when the splendor of day has departed.

Enough with these excessively extensive elaborations of speech; here, this single view is sufficient for happiness. If the mind within is joyful—equanimous and with its passions stilled—that is the unsurpassed foundation.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having thus reflected upon the delusion of the world, Suraghu and Parigha, honoring one another and being satisfied, departed intent upon their own respective duties.
O Raghava, having heard that very [teaching] which is the supreme cause of awakening, become clearly established in this very awakening.
When the dark cloud of egoism has dissolved in the sky of the heart by means of supreme wisdom, sharp through the process of firm investigation, [the mind becomes clear].
When the autumn season has arrived—agreeable to all the world, fruitful, joy-giving, pure, and expansive—the mind [is likewise].
One abides in the Supreme Self, the sky of consciousness, which is the object of meditation, the refuge, the easy path, the perfection of all bliss, and is perfectly serene.
He who is eternally absorbed in the inner self, eternally turned inward, and ever happy; who is constantly united with consciousness, is not afflicted by the sorrows of the mind.
Though deeply engaged in worldly affairs and even filled with passion and aversion, he incurs no internal stain, just as a lotus situated in water remains untainted.
The sage who possesses right knowledge, who is pure and whose mind is inwardly tranquil, is not afflicted by the mind, just as the king of beasts is not harmed by an elephant.
The mind of the wise person does not exist as one that is wretched and finds sole refuge in worldly enjoyments; for the mind of the wise is like a great tree in the Nandana grove.
Just as a person who is detached from birth and death does not suffer, so too the mind that has fully understood all ignorance is not afflicted by suffering.
O virtuous one, he who has fully understood the delusion of the mind—which arises from the nature of worldly existence—is not touched by sin, just as the surface of the sky is untouched by dust.
This very [wisdom] is the great medicine thoroughly understood through the overcoming of ignorance; it is like a lamp for the darkness of the disease spread by ignorance.
For as soon as ignorance is thoroughly understood, it is utterly exhausted, just as the realm of enjoyment vanishes in a dream.
Even while intent on worldly affairs, the virtuous person whose mind is inwardly attached and whose intellect is one-pointed is not touched by sin, just as water does not touch the eye of a fish.
When the light of consciousness has dawned, the night of ignorance has perished; the intellect of the knower, having attained supreme bliss, shines forth.
When the sleep of ignorance has been stilled, a person awakened by the sun of knowledge attains that enlightenment by which one is never again deluded.
Those days are lived joyfully, and those sequences of actions are truly auspicious, in which the moonlight of consciousness rises from the moon of the Self within the sky of the heart.
A person who has crossed over delusion through constant reflection on his own self attains inner coolness, just as the moon does through its own nectar.
Those friends, those scriptures, and those very days—through them, the splendor of dispassion arises, and from these, the awakening of one's own mind clearly emerges.
Those wretched ones, whose sins have not departed, long mourn—like weeds in the jungle of birth—for they are indifferent toward the vision of the Self.
Bound by hundreds of snares of hope, greedily longing for the bait of enjoyments, his form worn out by old age, and tormented by sighs of grief.
Life in the wilderness of birth bears the heavy burden of accumulated suffering; it is smeared with the mire of evil deeds and lies stagnant in the pond of delusion.
Bitten by the swarm of the stinging insect of passion, dragged by the excellent rope of craving, dwelling in the house of the merchant of the mind, and rendered motionless by the bonds of kinship.
Worn out by sons, wife, and old age, sinking and surfacing in the mire of evil, exhausted and deprived of rest, one is broken upon the long and arduous path.
Exhausted by coming and going, wandering through the forest of saṃsāra, it has not found the cool shade and is tormented by intense heat.
His appearance was radiant yet wretched, his senses assailed by external objects; he was overcome by the ringing of the bell of karma and struck by the blows of his own misdeeds.
Bearing the yoke of the revolving wheel of manifestation and disappearance, it wallows in the vast forest of ignorance with its limbs utterly exhausted.
[He saw him] perpetually submerged in his own misfortune, sinking down, possessing nothing, with limbs exhausted by the burden of karma, and uttering piteous cries.
O Rāma, exerting the utmost effort for a long time, one should forcibly rescue this powerful bull of a living being from the pond of saṃsāra.
When the mind has been extinguished through the observation of reality, the individual soul is never born again; at that time, it has crossed the ocean of existence.
O Rāma, through association with those of great spiritual power, one obtains the clear means for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra, just as one obtains a boat from a navigator.
In that desert-like land where there is no tree of a virtuous person—fruitful and providing cool shade—the wise man should not dwell.
O Rāma, one finds great rest for a moment under the campaka tree of the virtuous man, which has the leaves of smooth and cool speech, the shade of integrity, and the flowers of smiles.
In the absence of that [discrimination], which bestows the attainment of the heat of great delusion, a wise person should not sleep here even with a slight degree of discernment arisen.
For the self alone is the friend of the self; thus, one should uplift the self by means of the self. One should not cast oneself into the mirey sea of rebirth through arrogance.
"What is this? How has it come about? What is its root? What is its destruction?"—thus should the wise examine the suffering of the body with great effort.
Neither wealth, nor friends, nor scriptures, nor kinsmen can assist men when they have sunk and must be raised up by their own selves.
Having reflected upon something together with the mind alone—its constant companion and co-resident—the self becomes fully uplifted.
By means of the boat that is the vision of reality, which arises from self-reflection through the efforts of dispassion and practice, one crosses the ocean of existence.
Though constantly pitied by people and burned by evil desires, one should not despise oneself; rather, one should lift oneself up with diligence.
One should uplift the elephant of the living being, which is submerged in the mire of birth, by using the great tethering post of ego, the rope of craving, and the intoxication of the mind.
O Raghava, by this much alone the self becomes saved: that egoism is wiped away once delusion has been cast off.
By this alone, the true path clearly attains its full manifestation: that the ego-sense is severed when the web of the mind is cast aside.
By this alone, O Lord of Gods, the Supreme Self is understood: when the body is viewed as being equal to wood or a clod of earth.
When the cloud of egoism has been dissipated, the sun of consciousness is seen; thereafter, through its transformation, that supreme state is attained.
Just as there is the perception of light itself when darkness is completely dispelled, so too is there the self-perception of the Self when the ego-sense is severed.
When egoism has completely perished, that state which arises from bliss and joy—that state, characterized by fullness, should be cultivated with diligent effort.
Resembling the full ocean, it does not fall within our range of perception; it admits no comparison and does not pursue worldly passion.
If the fourth state (turyā) is attained—that which is merely a spark of the light of consciousness that has reached stability—then it is compared to that [vision].
Because its similarity is not far removed, that state of deep sleep is characterized as having a full form, vast and expansive like the splendor of the sky.
When the mind and the ego dissolve, there arises that supreme body of the Lord, which consists of the highest bliss and abides within the interior of all states of being.
O Rāma, that state, which is perfected through yoga itself and occurs immediately after deep sleep, cannot be reached by words; it is experienced only within the heart.
Without experience, the reality of sugar and such things is not experienced; without experience, the form of the self is also not experienced.

When this entire infinite reality of the Self is established within the mind that has become firm and transformed, and when all external things have subsided, the God of gods—who is the soul of all moving and non-moving beings—is indeed experienced by oneself.

Following that is the destruction of the latent impressions of sense-objects; following that is the auspicious, supreme, and manifest light; and following that, by virtue of equanimity, is the transformation into one's own true nature, which is of an inconceivable form for the great.
Śrī Vasiṣ�ṭha said: O lotus-eyed one, if the Self is not beheld even after cutting through the mind with the mind itself, then one must abandon the notions of "mine" and "I."
The suffering of the world does not set, like the sun in a painting; calamity arrives with boundlessness, as vast as the great ocean.
Again and again it approaches, caused by the waves of water; the monsoon of cyclic existence is turbulent, dark as a cloud and deep blue as the gloom of night.
In this very context, they cite this ancient history: the dialogue between a friend, Sahya, and Vilāsa, on the peak of the Sahya mountain.
There is a mountain that has conquered the sky with its height, the surface of the earth with its base, and the netherworld with its foundation; it is a conqueror of the three worlds.
Filled with countless flowers, possessing countless pure waterfalls, its treasures guarded by Guhyakas, it is named Sahya and possesses unbearable splendor.
With its walls radiant with the light of the sun and filled with clusters of pearls, it was as brilliant as the temples of a celestial elephant with their golden flanks.

In some places there was a downpour of flower-clusters; in others, it was spread with the finest minerals; in some places there were the essences of blossoming lakes; and in others, it was composed of rocks abounding in gems.

From here comes the sound of waterfalls resounding through the woods; from here the whistling of the hollow bamboos; from here the howling of the winds in the caves; and from here the humming of the bees.

On the mountain peak, the songs of throngs of apsarases were heard; in the forest, the cries of deer and birds; on the plateau, the rumbling of intoxicated clouds; and in the skies, the calls of birds.
Guha was inhabited by Vidyādharas; it was a lotus-pool with bees for its song, with Kirātas for its surrounding shores, and forest trees whose song was that of birds.
Enveloped by the gods in its upper parts, enveloped by men at its feet, and enveloped by the nāgas in the underworld, it was like another house for the world.
It was inhabited by perfected beings (siddhas) in its caves, by treasures hidden within its interior, by elephants resting among its sandalwood trees, and by lions upon the peaks of its summits.
His body was enveloped by clouds of flowers; he was dusted with the pollen of flower-clouds; he wandered through the hearts of flower-storms; and he was as white as a flowering tree.
Tawny like a cloud of dust from the mountain elements, he was fully attended by the throngs of city women standing upon the surfaces of jeweled stones, as if they were celestial *mandārava* flowers.
Where the rocks, draped in garments of cloud-blue and adorned with ornaments of mute gems, appear as beautiful golden women going to meet their lovers upon the mountain peaks.
There, on a plateau on the northern shore, where the trees were bent down by their fruit and the waters of cascading waterfalls flowed through a network of jewel-filled lotus ponds.
In a place bristling with clusters of blossoms shed from mango trees and creepers, where the edges of the quarters were filled with full-blown *aṅkola*, *punnāga*, and blue lotuses;

Where the sun was shielded by the canopy of creeping vines, where it shone with the brilliance of the rays of jewels, where it was infused with the flowing juice of the jambu fruit, and which brought delight to its own world.

Equal to the world of Brahmā, as delightful as heaven, and comparable to the city of Śiva, there is the glorious and great hermitage of Atri, which removes the fatigue of those who have attained perfection.
In that great hermitage, there were two ascetics who were as learned as Śukra and Bṛhaspati in the path of the sky.
Then, from those two who shared a single dwelling, two sons were born who were like two blossoming sprouts with pure bodies upon a lotus in a lake.
Vilāsa and Bhāsa gradually attained growth, like two creepers upon the long sprouts of their parents, who were like trees.
Let them remain as two friends, mutually affectionate and dear to one another, clinging together like sesame seeds and their oil, and existing like a flower and its fragrance.
Though not actually joined, they were as if joined by their son; like a couple deeply in love, their minds became one, as if having attained duality within unity.
Thus, those two of most enchanting form, rejoicing in one another, remained in silence within their own hermitage like a pair of bees upon a lotus.
Having cast off childhood, those two new favorites attained youth in a very short time, like the sun and moon that have just risen.
Then those two parents, afflicted by old age, abandoned their bodies and ascended to heaven, like two birds flying up from a nest.
When their parents had passed away, the two of them became dejected in countenance; with their limbs scorched and their vigor gone, they were like two lotuses plucked from the water.
Having performed the funeral rites for him there, they both wailed in lamentation; for the ways of the world are indeed inviolable, O giver of honor, even for the great.

Having performed the funeral rites, they were then overcome by the pain arising from grief; lamenting with piteous voices of compassion, they remained there with all movement stilled like figures in a painting, their hearts not empty though they appeared vacant.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Overwhelmed by excessive grief, those two ascetics remained firm; with all their limbs withered by penance, they were like two trees in the forest.
Free from passion, the two brahmins spent their time in the forest, having reached a state of supreme detachment like two deer separated from their herd.
Then days, months, and years passed for the two of them; in due course, both gradually reached old age, like two trees at the edge of a chasm.
Once, those two ascetics—who had long been worn out by their penances and had not yet attained pure knowledge—met together and spoke thus to one another.
Vilāsa said: O fruit of the foremost tree of life, O ocean of nectar dwelling within the heart, O great kinsman in this world, Bhāsa, welcome to you!
"O virtuous one, tell me, where have you spent these many successions of days while separated from me? Has your asceticism been fruitful?"
Is your intellect free from fever? Have you become self-possessed? Has your learning borne fruit? Are you well?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: To him who had spoken thus, being so utterly distressed by the cycle of existence and having not yet attained great wisdom, his friend spoke with affection to that friend.

Bhāsa said: "O virtuous one, welcome to you this very day! By good fortune you have been seen, O giver of honor. But how can there be well-being for us who remain here in this cycle of worldly existence?"

As long as the knowable has not been fully realized, as long as the ground of the mind has not been exhausted, and as long as cyclic existence has not been crossed, how can there be any virtue for me?
As long as the creepers of hope arising from the mind have not been completely cut down by the sickle of discernment, how can there be well-being for us?
As long as knowledge has not been attained, as long as equanimity has not arisen, and as long as awakening has not dawned, how can there be any virtue for us?
O virtuous one, without the attainment of the Self and without the great medicine of knowledge, this cholera of miserable saṃsāra arises once again.
The wretched tree of saṃsāra comes again: sprouted in childhood, its new youth blossoming as tender leaves, and now flowering with old age.
From this body, which is like a decaying tree, there arises once more the cluster of blossoms that is death, while the cries of kinsmen act as its bees and old age serves as its flowering.
The succession of years, its seasons having exhausted their efficacy through past karma and being woven together with ancient days, is led away until it is almost devoid of flavor.
Furthermore, one wallows in the great caves of the mountain of the body, which are bristling with the thorns of craving, and in actions that are like venomous serpents waiting for their prey.
Nights come and go, their arrivals and departures never ending, filled with long-lasting and fleeting joys and sorrows that are both auspicious and inauspicious.
Life is wasted by base actions that fail to achieve their intended purpose—actions that are but sprouts of obsession with evil desires—and by such deeds, one's lifespan is destroyed.
The intoxicated elephant of the mind, its tethering post of the physical basis uprooted and awakened by the female elephant of craving, runs far astray.
Clinging to the flickering tongue within the great abode of the tree of the body, the aged vulture of greed increases as the wish-fulfilling gem falls away.
Lacking moisture, devoid of joy, and light, with limbs as delicate as falling petals and the hue of withered leaves, this succession of days is wasting away.
Defiled by the dust of humiliation and with the beauty of its form set, the face turns ashen, like a lotus struck by frost.
As the lake of the body dries up and the waters of youth flow away, the royal swan of life, once gone, flees in an instant and does not return.
From the tree of life, shattered by the force of the wind of time, the flowers of enjoyments and the leaves of days fall downward.
One sinks into floods that are dark wells of mental delusion, wherein frogs of inner suffering croak amidst those who are addicted to the enjoyment of worldly pleasures.
Untouched by various forms of attachment, craving—tremulous and fragile—ascends far aloft like a banner atop a shrine.
The rat named Death gnaws away the thread composed of the hope for life within this great web of saṃsāra, which has existed for a vast duration of time.
The difficult river of life flows on, with the surging waves of youth, foaming with the tossing sword, and possessing great whirlpools of reversals.
The boundless river of ritual action flows, agitated by the surging waves of the world’s activities arising from the assembly of arts (kalās), its hollows filled with turmoil.
Endless rivers of kinsmen fall incessantly into the vast ocean of time, into its deep abyss.
O Father, this jewel of a body is lost within the belly of the ocean of the mire of destruction; it is not known where it has gone from birth to birth.
Bound for a long time within the wheel of thought, the mind—restless in its addiction to the practice of evil deeds—wanders like a blade of grass in the whirlpools of the ocean's depths.
Carried away by the infinite great waves of mental activity, the mind—its inner disposition dancing with anxious thought—finds no rest even for a moment.
"This has been done, I am doing this, I shall do that"—the bird of the intellect is thus ensnared by the web of such calculations and falls into a swoon.
This great elephant of duality, which perceives "this one is a friend" and "that one is an enemy," cuts through my vital organs just as it would blue lotuses.
In the great whirlpool of the river of anxiety, amidst the mass of its waves, the fish of the mind for a moment swells with pride, and in the next moment it loses its way.
This person, perceiving with the notion of a self these many kinds of sufferings that do not belong to a self, falls into a state of wretchedness.

Falling into various kinds of pleasure and pain, shattered by the widespread winds of old age and death, this person rolls upon the mountain within the belly of the world and, like a sapless leaf, reaches a state of decay.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having thus exchanged inquiries regarding each other's welfare, they attained pure knowledge in the course of time and thereafter reached liberation.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, I say that for a mind bound by its own fetters, there is no way to cross the ocean of saṃsāra other than through knowledge.
This suffering, though infinite, is trivial for one of noble mind; to the ill-fated bird, the ocean that cannot be crossed becomes like a mere cow’s footprint.
The great-souled ones, having transcended the body, abide in their own self which is pure consciousness; they behold the body from afar, like a spectator observing a crowd.
When the body is violently agitated by suffering, what loss has befallen us? What injury is there to the charioteer when the chariot is overturned and broken?
When agitation arises in the mind, what has come to the nature of consciousness? Is there any change in the ocean when the continuity of its waves is disturbed?
What are swans to the waters? And what are stones to the waters? What indeed are rocks to pieces of wood? And what are worldly enjoyments to the Supreme Self?

O Illustrious One, what kind of connection could there be between a mountain and the distant ocean? And what connection could there be between the mind and the reality of consciousness amidst the dense obstruction of the mountains?
Even lotuses being carried along in the currents of rivers are eventually left behind; what, then, can be said of these bodies belonging to the self?
Just as sparks and the like arise from the friction of wood and water, so do these fluctuations of the mind arise from the conjunction of the body and the self.
Just as reflections of wood appear in water due to the connection between the wood and the water, so too do bodies appear within the Self.
Just as reflections in a mirror, a ripple, and so forth are neither unreal nor real in an ultimate sense, so too are the bodies of the self.
Just as one is never distressed by the clashing of wood, water, or stone, so too there is no injury to the five aggregates, whether they are joined together or separated.
Just as trembling, sound, and other qualities arise from water that has been infused with wood, so too do they arise from this body when it is awakened by consciousness.

These consciousnesses do not belong to the pure or the inert, for they are the body of consciousness; indeed, these belong only to ignorance, and when that is destroyed, for us there remains only consciousness.
Just as no one has any experience of the union between water and wood, so too no one has any experience of the union between the body and the embodied self.

Just as this cyclic existence appears to the ignorant and has attained the status of reality for them, so too does this cyclic existence not attain the status of reality for the wise, according to its true nature.
Just as moisture does not cling to a stone in water, so do the experiences of external enjoyments fail to adhere to one whose mental state is free from internal attachment.
Just as there is no internal connection between water and wood, even when they are together, so too is the internal connection between the body and the embodied soul.
The connection between water and wood is devoid of internal attachment; such is the relation between the body and the embodied soul, as well as between a reflection and the water.
Pure consciousness abides everywhere, free from any object of cognition; other than that which is marked by duality, no such thing as "bad consciousness" exists.
That which is not suffering clearly becomes suffering through internal perception; just as a corpse becomes a vampire when it is imagined as such.
Even that which is unrelated becomes related through internal determination, like sexual union with a woman in a dream, or like an encounter with a post or a ghost.
For a connection that is essentially non-existent is like that between water and wood; in the same way, the false connection between the body and the Supreme Self is likewise non-existent.
Without internal attachment, water cannot be held by the falling of wooden vessels; likewise, the Self, when free from attachment to the limbs, is not burned by the sufferings of the body.
The wise know that by the very cultivation of the body, the self remains under the sway of bodily suffering; therefore, by abandoning that [cultivation], it becomes liberated.
O friend, because they lack internal attachment, these things do not possess suffering, even though leaves, water, dirt, and wood are joined together with one another.

Those who are free from internal attachment attain supreme freedom from suffering; likewise, they completely transcend even their own selves, bodies, senses, and minds, though these remain closely joined.
For internal attachment, O Rāma, is the seed-cause for all embodied beings in this cycle of existence—the trees of old age, death, and delusion.
A living being who possesses internal attachment is submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra; but one who is liberated from internal attachment has crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra.
The mind that possesses internal attachment is said to have a hundred branches; the mind free from internal attachment is called dissolved.
Know my mind to be unattached and resembling an unbroken crystal; know that a mind which is attached is impure, like a broken crystal.
A mind that is unattached and stainless is clearly liberated even while wandering in saṃsāra; but one that is attached, even if engaged in long-term asceticism, remains bound by extreme fetters.
The mind bound by internal attachment is liberated when freed from that attachment; indeed, internal attachment alone is the sole cause of both bondage and liberation.
For one who is free from internal attachment, there is no sense of agency even while acting, just as a boat carrying timber on water is unaffected by the qualities or defects of the water.
Due to internal attachment, a living being experiences agency even though it is not the agent, just as one experiences a state of agitation in a dream involving pleasure and pain.
Even for that which is bodiless, agency exists within the mind as its agent; it is comparable to the perception of agitated pleasure and pain, as in dreams and similar states.
When the mind is not the agent, the agency residing within it becomes manifest; for a person whose mind is empty does not perceive even while acting.
You attain what is done by the mind, but not what is not done by the mind; the body is never the cause, nor does agency belong to the mind.
The wise know that the mind, though acting as if it were a non-agent, remains unattached; being unattached, it does not become an enjoyer of the fruits of action.

One who is not attached to both the killing of a Brahmin and the horse sacrifice is not tainted by them, just as one whose mind is absorbed in a beloved woman far away is not affected by the duties standing before him.
The living being, free from internal attachment and possessing a sweet disposition, is never truly an agent or an enjoyer, whether it is performing actions externally or not.
That mind which is free from internal attachment becomes a non-agent; it is liberated, tranquil, engaged [in its true nature], and untainted.
Therefore, one should certainly abandon the cruel internal attachment to all objects that are clung to externally, which causes all suffering.

The mind, freed from the internal defect of attachment and having attained primordial tranquility with a radiance as pure as the sky, attains oneness with the Self—which is liberated from all impurities—like a steady gem set in water that is itself blue as the waters.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, what kind of association leads to bondage for men, and what is said to lead to liberation? How indeed is this [bondage] to be treated?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Through the contemplation that completely abandons the distinction between the body and the embodied soul, placing one's trust in the body alone is called attachment, which is fit for bondage.
When there arises within a person a desire for happiness based on the conviction that the infinite reality of the Self is finite, that attachment is said to be worthy of bondage.
"All this is the Self alone; what do I desire, and what shall I abandon?"—know this state of non-attachment to be the condition of one liberated while living.
"I do not exist, nor does another exist; let there be happiness or let there be none"—the man who is thus internally unattached is said to be a possessor of liberation.
He who does not rejoice in inaction nor clings to actions, who is perfectly equanimous and has renounced the fruits of action—he is known as one who is unattached.
He whose mind, being solely devoted to the reality of the Self, does not fall under the sway of joy or resentment, and who is free from attachment—he is called one liberated while living.
He who skillfully renounces all fruits of action and the like by means of the mind alone, and not through physical action, is remembered as one who is unattached.
All various activities that have manifested here, when treated with non-attachment, become healing and bring about the highest good.
Under the power of attachment, all these vast heaps of suffering branch out into hundreds of directions, like a thorny tree growing in a ravine.
That a donkey, its nose pulled tight by a rope, carries a burden along the road with a terrified soul is the manifestation of attachment to that [burden].
That a tree sustains its body while seated in one place, enduring the afflictions of cold, wind, and heat, is the manifestation of attachment.
That a worm, submerged in a fissure of the earth with its limbs oppressed, passes its time in a state of distress, is the manifestation of attachment to that [world].
With a belly emaciated by hunger, his mind fearful of obstacles, he spends his life perched on the treetop like a bird; this is the manifestation of attachment to that [world].
That the deer abandons its body due to the affliction of a hunter's arrow, even while subsisting on a diet of durvā grass shoots, is the manifestation of attachment to worldly existence.
These worn-out multitudes of beings, being born again and again, become worms and insects; this is the manifestation of attachment to that [world].
Arising again and again, they dissolve like waves in the ocean; that the infinite elements manifest in this way is the unfolding of attachment to them.
That men, having become like creepers and grass, die again and again while devoid of movement, is the manifestation of attachment to that [world].
When grasses, shrubs, creepers, and the like produce a particular form through their union with the essence of the netherworld (rasātala-rasa), that is the manifestation of attachment (saṃsakti).
That the river of saṃsāra is intoxicated and crowded with hundreds of objects appearing as if they were distinct from one's own self is the manifestation of attachment.
Attachment is said to be of two kinds, O Rāghava: the venerable and the barren. The barren kind belongs everywhere to the deluded; the venerable kind is innate to those who know reality.

That firm attachment to the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), which arises from objects such as the body and is devoid of the realization of the reality of the self (ātmatattva), is called "barren" (vandhyā).
Indeed, that attachment which arises from the discernment of reality through the awakening to the truth of the self is said to be venerable, for it is further devoid of worldly existence.
The Lord, whose hands hold the conch, discus, and mace, protects the three worlds through various means, by virtue of his attachment to those worthy of worship.
Day after day, by virtue of his attachment to the one worthy of worship, the sun makes the sky—eternal, supportless, and vast—assume the state of a traveler upon its path.
Through the power of attachment to that which is worthy of worship, the Brahmic body indeed manifests—a construction conceived over a long time through the concentration of great eons.
The body of Śaṅkara stands adorned with ashes, playfully clinging to his beloved, remaining so by virtue of its attachment to that which is worthy of worship.
The lords of consciousness, the perfected ones, the world-protectors, and others likewise, remain in the courtyard of the world through the power of their attachment to that which is to be revered.
Another series of worlds maintains a multitude of bodily machines, free from old age and death, by virtue of their attachment to the venerable one.
The mind falls upon sense-objects like a vulture upon scraps of meat, due to its attachment to what is venerable and under the influence of a futile longing for the beautiful.
By the power of attachment, the wind blows within the hollow of the world; the five elements abide, and this is the sustenance of the world.
In heaven are the gods, on earth are human beings, and in the netherworld are the serpents and asuras; they all exist within the udumbara fruit of the cosmic egg like shimmering gnats.
Infinite beings are born and die, they fall and they rise, like waves upon a surging river.
Arising again and again, they dissolve; this is the manifestation of attachment to them—beings that repeatedly become tasteless, like droplets of water from a waterfall.
With their limbs swallowed by one another, the people, shattered by dullness, wander about in confusion, O dear one, like withered leaves in the sky.
The circle of constellations in the sky, the swarm of gnats on a tree, and the flood of waters in the netherworld, my dear, all quiver only by way of circular motion.
Even today, the moon does not abandon its body, which is as turbid as water and like a ball thrown by the child of Time—a ball worn out by the conditions of rising, setting, and waning.
The assembly of suffering gods does not cut the fragment of their own minds, which is hardened by the sight of the manifold sufferings of the cycles of the ages.
"O Rāghava, behold this wondrous and diverse painting created by someone in the supreme ether, solely through the power of latent impressions."
This variegated world, composed of the universe, which is fashioned within the void of space by the sole stage of mental attachment—that is never real.
For those engaged in worldly affairs with minds attached to this saṃsāra, craving devours their bodies just as a flame of fire consumes blades of grass.
Who is able to enumerate the bodies of a husband whose mind is deeply attached to them, any more than one can count the multitude of motes of dust in a beam of light?
For those whose minds are attached, these rows of beautiful inner apartments are fashioned as the Raurava, Vīci, Kālasūtra, and other hells.
Whatever web of suffering exists within this world, all of that is imagined by those whose minds are attached to objects.
All successions of suffering come upon one whose mind is attached, like great rivers surging with waves of water flowing into the ocean.
All is pervaded by ignorance, which consists of the association with the mind, which has become a body of light, and which seeks the states of decay and arising.
O Rāma, through non-attachment to enjoyments, all forms of prosperity reach their highest expansion, like great rivers during the rainy season.
Know, O Raghava, that internal attachment to the limbs of the body is like burning coals; know, O Rama, that the absence of such attachment to the limbs is an elixir of immortality.
Prakṛti herself is consumed by the internal attachment that arises from her own nature, just as a medicinal plant is burnt by the fire produced from its own essence.
Unattached everywhere, profoundly peaceful, abiding as if infinite, appearing as real though unreal—may the mind be thus for the sake of happiness alone.
He who abides with his own mind—having attained the dawn of the vision of knowledge, having reached the state of the destruction of ignorance, and being entirely free from attachment—is liberated.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: By one who understands, the mind must always be kept under control, even while abiding in all things, remaining with everyone, and engaged in every activity.
I am not attached here to activities, nor to thoughts, nor to objects; neither in space, nor below, nor above, nor in the directions, nor in the creepers.
It is not in the external vast expanse, nor in the activities of the senses; it is not within, nor in the vital breath, nor in the head, nor in the palate.
It is not between the eyebrows, nor at the tip of the nose, nor in the mouth, nor in the pupils; it is not in darkness, nor in light, nor in this space of the heart.
It is not in the waking state, nor in the dream, nor in deep sleep, nor in the stainless; it is not in the black, nor in the yellow, red, and so forth, nor in the variegated.
It is neither in motion nor in stillness; neither in the beginning, nor in the middle, nor elsewhere; neither far away nor near; neither in the object nor in the self.
It is not in sounds, touches, or forms; nor in the fluctuations of delusion and bliss; nor in the activities of coming and going, nor in the calculations of time.

Having come to rest solely in pure consciousness, let the mind—though still slightly leaning upon objects of thought—abide everywhere as if devoid of flavor, finding its true essence only in the Self.
Abiding therein, free from attachment, the living soul has attained the state of the non-living; let it perform all this worldly activity, or let it not perform it.
Even while performing actions, the living being who delights in its own self does not incur any connection with the fruits of those actions, just as the sky is unaffected by clouds.
Or else, having abandoned even that objective aspect, let the living being remain as the tranquil mass of consciousness, perfectly stilled within itself like a glowing gem.

O Rāmabhadra, the living soul (jīva), having attained Nirvāṇa within itself as its eternally risen nature, does not enter into attachment even while engaged in worldly activity; due to its state of being free from attachment, it is as if it bears the burden of the body together with the fruit arising from karma.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Those of expansive mind remain established in the practice of the bliss of non-attachment; though engaged in worldly affairs, they dwell within with sorrow and fear departed.
In one whose body is neither agitated nor unagitated, due to the non-contradiction of consciousness, the splendor of the fullness within is perceived in the face, like that of the moon.
When one’s mind is free from fever—having abandoned the object of thought and resting in pure consciousness—the people are gladdened by him, just as water is clarified by *kataka* fruit.

Though he is ever absorbed in the vision of the Self, the wise man remains established in his own nature even while being restless; though he appears agitated, it is in vain, like the reflection of the sun in water.

Delighting in the Self, these great souls are awakened and possess supreme exaltation; though they appear as flickering as the tips of peacock feathers on the outside, within they are as immovable as Mount Meru.

The mind, having attained the nature of a self through its coloring by pleasure and pain, does not truly undergo that change, just as a smooth crystal, though joined with colors, does not become them.
For one who has understood the higher and lower states of the world, the view of cyclic existence that has arisen does not stain the true mind, just as a streak of water does not stain a lotus.
One who is absorbed in meditation on the Self, awakened to the Supreme Self, and liberated from the impurity of conceptualization, is said to be "attached to the Self."
Through delighting in the Self, the living being attains non-attachment in this world; through knowledge of the Self, attachment becomes attenuated, and not otherwise.
O Rāghava, while remaining truly awake, the living being becomes established in deep sleep; having entered this vision, it is free from duality and eternally devoid of setting or rising.
Having attained maturity here, he reaches the state of the purifying sun, just as the moon, by the power of its transformation, becomes the sun on the new-moon day.

That state of those whose minds have been exhausted, wherein the mind remains devoid of its own mental fluctuations, is called the cessation of all mental construction; it is a state of deep sleep even while awake.
Having reached that state of deep sleep while living and conducting his affairs, a person is never again dragged by the thongs of pleasure and pain.
He who, while remaining in the state of deep sleep even while awake, performs the activities of the world, does not undergo the perception of pleasure and pain, being like a mechanical puppet.
The power that afflicts the mind, causing the torment of existence and non-existence—once the mind has attained the state of selfhood, what can afflict it, and how?
A living being who remains established in the state of liberation while alive, performing actions with indifference as if in deep sleep, is not bound.
O sinless one, relying upon the state of deep sleep, perform or do not perform whatever action born of nature has arrived and remains established by the force of its fruition.
Neither the undertaking nor the relinquishing of action is pleasing to one who lacks knowledge; those who have realized the Self remain following whatever comes to them as their lot.
Even while acting, you are not an agent through a mind established solely in deep sleep; and even as a non-agent, you are an agent—do as you wish.
Just as an infant on a couch does not stir when perceiving nothing at all, so too, O Raghava, perform your actions without perceiving their fruits.

Established in the state of the non-objective consciousness, possessing the intellect of deep sleep even while awake, whatever one who has attained the Self performs, there is no sense of agency for him in that regard.
Having reached the state of deep sleep within his own mind and being free from latent impressions, the knower attains inner coolness, just as the moon does through its essence.
Abiding in deep sleep, he is of great splendor, full like the orb of the full moon; he remains equanimous in all states, like a mountain through the changing seasons.
The wise-souled one, though established in deep sleep, comes out into the state of agitation; yet there is no trembling in his actions, like a mountain that has begun to quiver.
Having become established in the state of deep sleep and freed from all impurity regarding the body, either cast it down at once, or hold it steady for a long time like a mountain.
O Rāma, this very state of deep sleep, when it has become mature through the yoga of practice, is called the "Fourth" (turya) by those who are experts in the principles of reality.
Consisting of bliss alone, with all afflictions entirely extinguished within, the wise one of great exaltation becomes one whose mind has utterly set.
Abiding there, the wise one, joyful and reeling with supreme bliss, always perceives this creation as if it were a mere play.
Free from sorrow, fear, and exertion, with the agitation of saṃsāra gone, the self-possessed one who has ascended to the fourth state (turya) does not fall again.
Having attained his own holy state, the man of steady intellect looks upon this world as it revolves, smiling as one standing on a mountain peak gazes down at those below.
But having attained an imperishable state in this fourth stage, one has reached the state beyond bliss because of being entirely absorbed in bliss alone.
Indeed, because he has transcended even the stages of non-bliss and great bliss, the yogi who has reached the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta) is called "liberated."

Having dissolved all the bonds of birth and having caused all conceits consisting of darkness to melt away, the great-souled one attains an existence composed of the supreme essence, like a lump of rock salt dissolved in water.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O descendant of Raghu, as long as there is the awareness of the fourth state (turya), so long is that the state of absolute oneness (kevalatā), which is the domain of both the living liberated one and of words.
Beyond this, O mighty-armed one, there is no object of speech for those who are liberated and bodiless, just as the sky is not an object for ordinary men.
For that state of rest is more distant even than the farthest distance; it is accessible only to those liberated while in the body, like the path of the winds in the sky.
Having experienced the maintenance of the world for some time through the state of deep sleep, he thereafter attains the fourth state (turya), reeling with supreme bliss.
O scion of Raghu’s lineage, just as those who know that [reality] and are skilled in the Self attain the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), so too do you reach that state free from dualities.
O Rāma, subduer of enemies, engage in worldly affairs with the state of deep sleep; like the moon of a painting, you shall have neither decline nor agitation.
Whether the configuration of the body perishes or remains stable, do not grasp at it, for this is a delusion that expands as the notion "this is the body."
What purpose do you have in the destruction of the body, and what purpose do you have in its preservation? Engage in the activities of nature; let this body remain as it is.
You have known that truth; you have awakened to that state; you have attained your own true nature—be free from sorrow for the welfare of all beings.
Having abandoned both the desired and the undesired, it shines like the sky freed from darkness and clouds by the beauty of its cool light.
One who is endowed with mental praise and self-perfection does not run downward, just as a person perfected through yoga, mantra, and austerity does not fall from the sky to the earth.
Here, there exists only pure consciousness, devoid of near and far; let there be no delusion in you such as "this is he," "I am this," or "that is mine."

The designation "Self" is conceptually constructed for the sake of conventional usage regarding the All-pervading Lord; however, the differentiation of name, form, and so forth has long since departed from Him.
Just as the ocean is nothing but water and not separate from its waves and so forth, so too all this is only the Self and not separate from the elements such as earth and water.
Just as nothing other than water can be found within the entirety of the ocean, even so, nothing other than the Self can be found within the vast expanse of the world.
O wise one, where do you establish the notion "this is I"? What is that reality, and what would belong to you? What is that reality, and what would not belong to you?
There is no duality, nor are there bodies, nor does any connection with them exist; nor can any stain be conceived [in it], just as darkness cannot affect the sun.
Even granting, O Slayer of Enemies, that duality exists, I declare that there can be no connection of the All-pervading One with the body and other such things, even though they exist.
Just as no connection is possible between the spreading of shadow and sunlight, or between light and darkness, so indeed it is with the body and the embodied self.
Just as there can never be a connection between cold and heat, which are eternally opposed to one another, O Rāma, so it is between the body and the self.
But how can the relationship of inseparable concomitance between these two—the insentient body and the sentient embodied soul—be experienced?
The discourse that the Self, which is pure consciousness alone, has a connection with the body—this is a matter difficult to comprehend, like imagining an ocean within a forest fire.
Through the contemplation of truth, this false view perishes; by such contemplation, it is like an ocean evaporated by the heat of the sun.
The conscious self is stainless, eternal, self-luminous, and free from affliction; the body, however, is impermanent and impure—how then can it be connected with that [self]?
The body vibrates due to the wind or is made corporeal by the elements; therefore, there is not even the slightest connection between it and the Self.

Even if duality were established for the body, a connection [between two bodies] would be impossible; but if duality itself is not established, O wise one, how could such a conceptualization even arise?
Therefore, while that very [reality] exists, establish your abiding right within it; there is never, for anyone, anywhere, either bondage or liberation.
O Rāma, bring to firmness everywhere, both internally and externally, this clear conviction that everything is composed of the Self and is peaceful.
"I am happy," "I am miserable," "I am deluded"—these are known as false views. If you hold the notion of a real entity in these states, then you desire suffering for a long time.
The same sequence that applies to a mountain and a blade of grass, or likewise to silk and a stone, is said to apply to the Supreme Self and the body with respect to their equality.
Just as there is no connection nor any equality between light and darkness, O Rāma, so it is with the absolute difference between the self and the body.
Just as the unity of cold and heat is not seen even in mere discourse, nor is there a fusion between insentience and light, so too it is not [possible] for the self and the body.
The body moves by means of the wind; by that very wind it comes and goes. It produces sound through the wind that plays within the channels of the body.

Just as sound consisting primarily of the letters ka, ca, ṭa, ta, and pa vibrates within through the internal winds, so indeed does it arise from the cavities of the body, like [notes] from a bamboo flute.
The throbbing of the pupil is the throbbing of the eye caused by the vital air (māruta); that very vibration of the sense organ is merely the consciousness of the Self.
The state of the self resides everywhere—in space, stones, walls, and so forth; it is perceived here within the mind alone, like a reflection in a mirror.
Having abandoned the abode of the body, wherever the bird of the mind goes by the power of its own latent impressions, there alone the Self is experienced.
Just as where there is a flower, there the perception of fragrance is established, so too, wherever there is the mind, there the perception of a self is established.
Just as space, which is present everywhere, reflects in a mirror, so too the Self, though present everywhere, is perceived within the mind.
Just as the place where water settles is its locus upon the earth, so too the internal organ alone is the locus for the self's cognitions.
The consciousness of the Self, reflected within the internal organ, spreads out this form of the world—both real and unreal—just as the light of the sun spreads its radiance.
Therefore, it is the internal organ alone that is the cause in the transmigration of beings; but because the Self transcends all, though it is the reality, it is not a cause.
The great-minded declare that non-investigation is ignorance and folly; it is the essence of wandering in saṃsāra and the cause of the internal organ.
Due to improper observation and delusion, the mind grasps at the existence of the self; thus, the seed-particle of total confusion appears like darkness before the sun.
O Rāghava, through the thorough knowledge of the single reality of the self as it truly is, the mind utterly reaches non-existence in an instant, just as darkness does by means of a lamp.

One should personally investigate the cause of saṃsāra from this perspective: it is the mind (cetas), known by such names as the individual soul (jīva), the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), consciousness (citta), and the intellect (manas).
Śrī Rāma said: O Lord, O Brahmā, how have these designations become established in the mind? Tell me this, O giver of honor, for the sake of my spiritual perfection.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: All these states of being are eternally of the single nature of the reality of the Self, just as the multitude of waves are but water.
The Self, whose nature is solely vibration, resides here and there within them, just as the water of the ocean exists within its restless waves.
In some places, Maheśvara remains among them as one whose nature is motionless, like the state of water in waters that have not yet attained the condition of waves.
In that regard, entities such as stones are motionless and established in their own nature; however, beings such as humans are restless, possessing movement like the foam on wine.
Within those bodies, the power of that Self, though omnipotent, was conditioned by the fabrication of ignorance; therefore, that ignorance remained established therein.
That ignorance, adorned by the infinite Self, is called the individual soul (jīva); it is an elephant trapped within the cage of the great delusion of māyā in the cycle of transmigration.

That which lives is called *jīva*; through the sense of "I," it becomes the ego (*ahaṃkāra*). By virtue of its function of determining, it is the intellect (*buddhi*); by virtue of its function of volition, it is the mind (*manas*).
Nature exists as nature, and the body exists as a locus of attachment; the insentient exists by virtue of its nature, while the sentient exists by virtue of its own self-existence.
That supreme reality which lies between the perception of the insentient and the sentient is this very same [reality] that is spread out as manifoldness under various designations.
O sinless one, the true nature of the individual soul (jīva) has indeed been proclaimed in many ways and in numerous places within the Vedāntas, such as the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and others.
But regarding these designations, false conceptualizations have been fruitlessly established by ignorant and deluded sophists solely for the sake of deceiving the foolish.
Thus, O mighty-armed one, this living soul is the cause of saṃsāra; what has been done here by this mute and most wretched body?
When one of the two—the container or the contained—is destroyed, the other is not destroyed; just so, when the body and such are destroyed, there is no destruction of the self.
Just as when the sap of a single leaf has been consumed, the essence does not go to ruin, and just as the leaf-sap enters into the network of the sun's rays; so it is here.

Upon the dissolution of the body, the embodied soul does not undergo destruction for anyone; if it is free from latent tendencies (*vāsana*), it likewise abides in the state of the Self within the ether.
I believe that for one who possesses such delusion of ignorance as to think, "I am destroyed when the body is destroyed," a vampire has arisen from the slope of his mother’s breast.
For that which undergoes absolute destruction is declared to be this [state]; indeed, the destruction of the mind is destruction, and that is called liberation.
It is said that one is dead or lost; I consider that to be false and unreal, for having been separated by space and time, he is experienced again and again.
Thus they are perceived by people through the designation of "death," though hidden by space and time, like blades of grass within the waves.
The individual soul, abiding in its latent impressions, departs after casting off the body, like a monkey who, having left one forest tree, takes up residence in another.
Again, O Raghava, having abandoned even that, it goes elsewhere in an instant, to another vast region and at another time.
Driven here and there by their own latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), living beings are led about for a long time, just as children are led by a cunning nurse who lives off them.
Entwined by the ropes of latent impressions and worn out within the hollows of mountains, those who live by the lives of living beings exhaust their own lives with extreme suffering.

Bearing the heavy burden of suffering brought on by advanced old age, their lives shattered by decay, these beings fall for a long time into the weight of hell, following the persistence of latent impressions produced in their hearts.

Śrī Vālmīki said: When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the body is born, you are not born; when the body is destroyed, you are not destroyed. You are the stainless Self within the self; the body is nothing at all to you.

The analogy of the jujube fruit in a bowl, or the situation of space within a jar—when one of these is damaged or destroyed, the notion that "both" are [damaged or destroyed] is a futile conceptualization.
When this perishable body has been destroyed and has returned to its own state, fie upon that blind-minded person who grieves, thinking, "I am perishing."
Just as the relationship between two chariots and their reins is devoid of affection or agitation, such is the connection of consciousness with the body, mind, and senses.
O Rāghava, just as the relationship between the mud and the turbid water of a lake is one of mutual dependence, so too is the connection between the body, the senses, and the self.
Just as the path of those who have traveled the road is free from hope and lamentation, so too is the union and separation of the body and the embodied soul.
Just as those terrified by the transformations of an imagined vetāla are themselves falsely imagined, so too are affection, pleasure, and the like.
The various classes of beings, though fashioned from the same aggregate of the five elements, are distinct from one another, like diverse figurines carved from a single block of wood.
In a load of wood, nothing other than wood is seen; in the body, which is a mere mass of elements, nothing other than that is seen.
O people, when the five elements are disturbed, destroyed, or produced, why have you fallen under the sway of joy, resentment, and despair?
What excellence indeed is there in men toward this fragile aggregate of elements called "woman," which bears another name as well, yet acts like a calamity arisen for the people?
The diversity of arrangements and parts is for the satisfaction of the ignorant alone; but for those who know that [reality], there is the vision of the five elements as they truly are.
Just as there is no passion between two stone statues, even though they are joined together like two figures carved from a single rock, so too there is no passion between the mind and the body.
Just as the mutual disposition of clay figures might be when they come together, may such be the disposition of your intellect, senses, self, and mind when they meet.
O sons of stone, you do not possess the capacity for mutual affection; since the body, senses, self, and vital breaths are likewise insentient, who here is there to lament?
Just as waves thoroughly bind together masses of grass scattered here and there, so does the perception of a body bind together the various elements.
Just as blades of grass in the waters of the ocean are joined and separated, so indeed do the elements within the body unite and disunite with the Self once internal conceptualization has ceased.

The Self, existing as consciousness, remains embracing the elements that constitute the body, like the ocean surging with the turbulent movement of its revolving waves that encompass even the blades of grass.

Through awakening, having abandoned the state of being an object of thought, the Self spontaneously attains its own true nature, just as water, by the power of its own movement, abandons its turbidity and attains clarity.
Then, with the multitude of elements having separated, the living being, situated within the mass of wind, perceives the body just as one perceives the circle of the earth from the sky.
Having seen the collection of elements as separate, the unborn one transcends the body and attains supreme light, like the brilliance of the sun during the day.
Then he knows himself by himself, free from the maladies of the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge, recollecting his own consciousness within as if from a state of intoxication.
The Self alone vibrates as the entire universe, appearing as if arisen through a multitude of entities, just as the infinite waters of the ocean appear as waves, droplets, and surging billows.
Thus, having attained great awakening, free from passion and devoid of sin, they wander here as those liberated while living, having reached the state of great beings.
Just as great waves move by means of various jewels and gems, so do the supreme ones move, having cast off all latent tendencies and the conventional usage of the mind.
The ocean does not perish because of the wood on its shores, nor the sky because of dust; likewise, the self-possessed person here does not wither because of his own worldly activities.

For one who has realized the Self, there is neither attachment nor aversion toward the ocean of worldly enjoyments—whether they have passed away or arrived, whether they are clear or turbid, fickle or dull.
Whatever mental ideation exists in its entirety within the world, the wise know that to be the radiant play of the reality of consciousness directed toward an object.

That which is myself, that which is the elements and so forth, and that which exists throughout the three periods of time—all this unfolds through the expansions of the relationship between the seen and the seeing.

Whatever is seen, whether it be non-existent or existent, is based upon a single perception; anything else is merely a mental coating. Therefore, whence can there be the perceptions of joy and sorrow?
The unreal is indeed unreal, for the real is indeed always real; know that the real-unreal is the non-existent—why then do you become deluded regarding its meaning?
Abandoning false vision, see correctly, O one with beautiful eyes; the mature person who possesses right vision is never deluded in this world.
It expands through the elaborations of the relationship between the seen and the seeing; that which is the supreme spiritual bliss within the relationship of the seen and the seeing.
Therefore, Brahman is said to consist of pure experience; it is the unsurpassed consciousness of bliss within the relationship between the seen and the seeing.

To the ignorant, it grants the cycle of worldly existence; to the wise, it grants liberation that is ever-arisen. The knower perceives the blissful connection between the seen and the seer as the very body of the Self.
That which is enveloped by the visible is bondage; that which is free from it is called liberation. It is the healthy, blissful consciousness of the relationship between the seer and the seen.
If that liberation is said by the wise to be free from decay and excellence, then it is the experience within its own domain regarding the relationship between the seen and the seeing.
Free from both the seen and the seeing, by taking hold of that [state], one experiences existence and non-existence; for this is the state of deep sleep, which shines forth in this very manner.
In this way, it attains the state of the Fourth (turya), which is known as liberation, when the perception of the visible world has ceased through the application of the supreme intellect.
But in this consciousness of the relationship between the seen and the seeing, O Raghava, the Self is neither gross nor subtle, neither perceptible nor otherwise.
I am neither conscious nor insentient, neither non-existent nor composed of existence; I am not the self, nor another, neither one, nor many, nor possessed of multiplicity.
It is neither situated nearby nor far away; it neither exists nor does it not exist. It is neither attainable nor unattainable; it is neither all, nor is it all-pervading.
It is neither an entity nor a non-entity; it is neither fivefold nor five. That which has come into the state of being visible is the locus of the six sense-faculties, with the mind as the sixth.
That state which has transcended [all things] is, in this world, as if it were nothing at all, for one who possesses right knowledge and perceives this world exactly as it is.
The entire universe consists of the Self; nowhere does anything exist that does not consist of the Self, whether through its hardness, fluidity, motion, space, or perception.

The Self alone is everything within all beings—earth, water, air, ether, and fire. O Rāma, there is no existence of things whatsoever apart from Consciousness. Know that the notion "I am separate from That" is the prattle of a madman.

Alone are all the worlds, passing through the sequence of all times and kalpas in their coming and going; there is no other fabrication of parts whatsoever but the Self alone—O Great-Souled One, become one whose mind is thus resolved and who has transcended it.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, by such a vision of inquiry and through the abandonment of duality, the true nature is attained by those who know it, just as the wish-fulfilling gem is obtained by those who know how to seek it.
Now hear this other view, O Rāma; by means of it, you shall behold the immovable Self within the visible world and become one possessed of divine vision.
I am the earth, I am the sun, I am the quarters of space, and I am also that which is below; I am the Daityas, I am the gods, I am the worlds, and I am the Great Radiance.
I am darkness, I am the clouds, and I am the earth, the oceans, and so forth; I am dust, wind, and fire—indeed, I am this entire universe.
Since I am indeed the Self alone established everywhere throughout the three worlds, who am I? What is this body and so forth? How can there be duality for that which is one?
Thus, possessing this certainty that the world is contained within yourself as its very self, behold it; you shall not be helplessly overwhelmed by joy or sorrow.
O sinless one, since this entire world is indeed established as being composed of that [Brahman], tell me, O lotus-eyed one: what could be one’s own and what could be another’s? Please explain.
Apart from that Knower, what exists that has arrived to cause joy or dejection? For the Knower, who is identical with the universe, there is no dejection.
These two views of the ego are of the nature of sattva and are exceedingly pure; they proceed from the knowledge of reality, are ultimate in nature, and bestow liberation.
"O descendant of Raghu, the first form of egoism (ahaṃkṛti) is 'I am the Supreme Atom, whose form transcends all'; the other is said to be 'I am everything.'"
But there exists, O sinless one, a third view distinct from the ego-sense; know that it is the notion "I am the body," which leads only to suffering and not to peace.
Then, having abandoned even these three for the sake of attaining all perfections, take hold of that which remains and remain firm, intent upon it.
Although its essential nature transcends all things and it surpasses the existence of everything, the Self, the illuminator, truly exists, filling the world with its own non-existence.
Behold quickly through your own direct experience that you are indeed that which is eternally arisen; O best among the knowers of reality, abandon all latent tendencies and the knot of the heart.
O Rāma, the self does not exist through inference, nor through the words of authoritative persons and the like; rather, it is always, in every way, and entirely perceived through direct experience.
Whatever there is—be it contact, vibration, or even the slightest consciousness—all that is the Lord, the Self, devoid of both the seen and the seeing.
That deity is neither existent nor non-existent; he is neither an atom nor is he great. He is not the middle between these two states of perception, yet he alone is all this everywhere.
And he who speaks thus is not fit to speak; this is not something other than that, my dear—behold the self that is free from affliction.
"This is not the self, nor is this [other] the self; it is merely a difference in designation"—thus it is imagined by that very omnipresent power within its own self.
For that Sun is established everywhere throughout the three periods of time; yet, because of its subtlety and its extreme magnitude, it is not perceived as a whole.
While infinite categories of objects exist, the Self naturally reflects as a living soul within the mirror of the *puryaṣṭaka* by its own inherent nature.

Through the very emergence of the city-of-eight (puryaṣṭaka), the Self is experienced by itself at all times and in all states, like the wind in the sky which is perceived through the movement of clouds.
The conscious self is all-pervading and omnipresent; it is not established in any particular place whatsoever. Just as existence (sattā) belongs to all objects, so too is the Great Lord.
When that city-of-eight exists, the individual soul vibrates within it, as dust does when there is wind, or as sight does when there is a lamp.

This desire within the city of eight resides in the Self alone, established in its own nature; it manifests when that Self has arisen, just as the worldly cravings of people appear when the sun has risen.
If, while the sun remains in the sky, this worldly transaction perishes despite such a proper arrangement, what has happened to the sun?

If, while the Divine remains established in the self, the body—which exists only by virtue of attaining its status through that presence—should meet its destruction, then what in this world has been lost within the self?
This Self of everyone, at all times, is neither born nor does it die; it neither takes nor does it desire; it is neither liberated nor bound.
Arising from the lack of awakening to the self, it takes on the nature of a self where there is no self; having the form of the delusion that a rope is a snake, this error leads only to suffering.

Because it is beginningless, this Self is not born; because it is unborn, it does not perish. Furthermore, since nothing exists apart from the Self, it does not desire anything other than itself, for such a thing is impossible.

Because it is never delimited by space, time, and so forth, this [Self] is never bound; since there is an absence of bondage, where could there be liberation? Therefore, it remains in a state of non-liberation.
O Rāghava, this Self is distinguished by such qualities as these for everyone; yet, due to the power of non-investigation, this deluded world weeps away.
Having correctly perceived the entire sequence of the world, past and future, do not fall into grief, O wise one, like those people who have succumbed to folly.
Just as one who knows should abandon both mental constructions that consist of liberation and bondage, so should the wise man conduct himself with self-silence, as if under restraint.
Liberation is not on the back of the sky, nor in the netherworld, nor upon the surface of the earth; for liberation is indeed the stainless mind awakened by perfect knowledge.
The dissolution of the mind itself through non-attachment to all desires is what has been called "liberation" by the knowers of reality who perceive the Self.
O Rāma, as long as the stainless awakening has not arisen, so long is liberation desired out of delusion, wretchedness, and devotion.
Having attained supreme awakening, when the mind has become the very nature of consciousness, even the ten forms of liberation are not desired, let alone a single liberation.
"This is liberation, this is bondage"—having abandoned such fragile conceptualization, you, the great renouncer, become that very state which is both being and non-being.

Having reached a state where conceptual constructions have completely dissolved, and with all attachment cast away within, may you for a long time protect the circle of the earth—which bears the girdle of the ocean dug by the multitude of Sagara’s sons—possessing ever-risen glory.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Through the play of time, one perceives a body within oneself; it is like the notion of ugliness arising in the heart of one who beholds a beautiful face.
Under its influence, this great illusion (māyā), whose belly is full of fatness and whose power is great intoxication, has arrived here as if from a mere drop of the taste of wine.
By this very changing [nature], which consists of being that and not being that, all this has come to pass, like water in a desert arising from heat.
The mind, intellect, ego, latent impressions, and even the senses—thus, by means of these waves marked with various names, the ocean of the Self surges forth.

The duality between the mind (*citta*) and the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) exists only in words, not in reality; for that which is the mind is indeed the ego-sense, and that which is the ego-sense is the mind.
