Just as whiteness is conceived as being distinct from snow, so too is the difference between the mind and the ego falsely imagined.
When one of the two internal factors—mind and ego—is destroyed, both are indeed destroyed, just as when a cloth is destroyed, its whiteness is also destroyed.
Having abandoned the hollow notion of liberation, as well as the perception of bondage and worldly desire, one should solely exhaust the mind through one's own dispassion and discernment.
If the thought "May I attain liberation" arises within, the mind has been awakened; yet when the mind is intensely intent on such thinking, it leads only to physical defects.
Whether the Self has transcended everything or is pervading all beings, what is bondage and what is liberation? Render such thinking rootless.
Since its nature is to vibrate, when the vital air moves within the body, then the hands, limbs, and the row of sprout-like tongues quiver.
Just as the wind causes a row of sprouts on a tree to tremble, so too does the vital air cause the series of limbs in the body to move about.
Consciousness is all-pervading, subtle, unmoving, and cannot be moved; it does not undergo vibration of its own accord, like a mountain god unshaken by the winds.
Reflecting all objects while abiding solely within itself, it illuminates these worlds through its own cognitive light, like a lamp.

In this regard, what is this vain delusion of yours that brings such extreme suffering? It is the notion of "I am this," "these are my limbs," and "this is mine"—a delusion belonging only to those of perverted intellect.
Thus, by means of this ever-changing vision, which is struck by waves of fluctuation, the activities of knowing, acting, and experiencing are perceived.
In that regard, this latent impression (vāsanā)—arising from the heat of ignorance and being utterly vain like a mirage—is born as the notions: "I am there," "I am the enjoyer," and "I am the agent."
This ignorance, though unreal, yet appearing as if real, drags away the wild deer of the mind that thirsts for sense objects, like a mirage.
O limb of the form of truth, once recognized, he perishes or flees from the midst of the Brahmins, just as the daughter of a Caṇḍāla does when discovered.
When ignorance is fully understood, it no longer drags one away; when a mirage is fully understood, it does not draw the thirsty person toward it.
O Rāma, through the realization of the ultimate truth, latent impressions dissolve along with their very roots, just as the mass of darkness vanishes when light arrives like a lamp.
When the certainty that "ignorance does not exist" has arisen through the scriptures and reasoning, ignorance dissolves like a drop of frost under the heat.
With the firm conviction that "what is the use of enjoyments for this inert body," the knower shatters the impure cage of hope, just as a lion tears apart its enclosure.
O Rāma, when the surrounding enclosures of hope have truly been cast away from the heart, a person, having attained innate beauty, experiences joy like the moon.
He attains supreme coolness like a mountain washed by rain; he experiences the highest bliss like a lowly man who has obtained a kingdom.
He shines with supreme splendor like the vault of heaven in autumn; he cannot be contained within himself, as vast as the ocean at the end of a kalpa.
Free from agitation, he remains like a cloud silenced by rain; the knower abides within himself, as tranquil as the ocean.
He assumes supreme fortitude and possesses stability as immovable as Mount Meru; he shines with a pure splendor like a fire whose fuel has been extinguished.
He becomes extinguished within himself like a lamp that has been stilled; the man attains supreme satisfaction, as if he had drunk the nectar of immortality.
Like a jar containing an internal lamp, like a fire with its flame within, or like a gem radiating brilliance, it attains inner luminosity.
He beholds his own self as the essence of all, omnipresent, the lord of all, the leader of all, possessing all forms yet devoid of form.
Enough with laughing at those fragile successions of days past, during which the mind remained as fickle as a volley of Cupid’s arrows.
Having withdrawn from the arena of worldly conflict, with the fever of pride and mental agitation stilled, he sat delighting in the inner self, full and pure in mind.
The stains of the mire of desire have been wiped away; the bonds of one's own delusion are severed; he is liberated from the fear of the defects of dualities; he has crossed the ocean of saṃsāra.
Having attained supreme rest, having reached the unsurpassable state that cannot be further gained, he has arrived at the station from which there is no return, through mind, deed, and speech.
He undertakes every desired undertaking, yet he desires nothing at all; he rejoices in everything that is approved, yet he rejoices in nothing at all.
He neither gives nor takes, neither praises nor blames; he neither sets nor rises, neither rejoices nor grieves.
One who has renounced all undertakings, who is free from all limiting adjuncts, and who has completely abandoned all desires is known as one liberated while living.
Having abandoned all desires, become silent in mind, just as the ocean ceases its flow entirely once it has relinquished its waters.
O dear one, a woman of excellent complexion clinging to the body does not bring such happiness as does hopelessness, which is cool as the moon, brings happiness to the heart.
O Rāghava, even the moon pressed against one's neck does not bring such happiness as the complete coolness of hopelessness brings within.
Spring does not shine so brightly with its fresh creepers full of flowers as does a man of noble mind who observes silence and whose heart is equanimous through freedom from desire.
Neither from the Himalayas, nor from pearls, nor from plantain trees, nor from sandalwood, nor even from the moon is such coolness obtained as that which is attained through the absence of desire.
Even more than sovereignty, even more than heaven, even more than the moon, even more than Mādhava, and even more than union with a beloved—hopelessness is the supreme happiness.
O virtuous one, that supreme bliss is attained through desirelessness, wherein the splendors of the three worlds do not benefit one even as much as a blade of grass.
Take hold of hopelessness—the axe that fells the *karanja* tree of calamities, the very state of ultimate bliss, and the flower-cluster of the tree of tranquility.
O Rāma, for one whose form is adorned with hopelessness, the earth is but a cow’s footprint, Mount Meru a mere post, the quarters of space small caskets, and the three worlds a blade of grass.
In this world, actions such as giving, taking, gathering, dwelling, and possessing are ridiculed by the best of men who have become free from desire.
By whom can he be compared—he who has rendered the three worlds as mere straw, and in whose heart conceptualization never takes root?
How can people weigh that Lord of the Self, in whose heart there is no attachment such as "let this be mine" or "let this not be mine"?
Relying on hopelessness, one attains the end of all distress, freedom from danger, perfect happiness, supreme good fortune, and wisdom.
Know that the state of being a thief of hope is the false delusion of the world; it has arisen like the apparent revolution of the circle of the quarters seen by one standing on a moving chariot.
Why do you remain deluded, O mighty-armed one, like a fool even though you have been awakened, with a mind wandering in the thought, "This is mine," "This is that," and "I am this"?
This entire world is indeed the Self; no diversity exists here. Having realized that the world is of a single form, the wise are not distressed by names.
O Raghava, through the very vision of the flood of objects as they truly are, the intellect attains supreme consolation in the form of desirelessness.
Relying upon that nature which is free from contradiction regarding existence and non-existence and remains constant at the beginning and the end, establish the stability of all things.
This illusion, which utterly deludes the mind of the hero of dispassion, flees away like a doe from a lion, leaving the transmigrating being behind.
A man of steady intellect regards his beloved—though her passion be intense and her mind fickle like a forest creeper—as being equal to a crumbling doll made of stone.
Riches do not gladden the heart within, nor do calamities cause distress; O friend, the splendors of the visible world carry one away, just as winds blow down a mountain that is bent.
Even for a sage of noble intellect whose mind is devoted to the young wife of Raktavighna, the arrows of Love are reduced to mere particles of dust by his discerning wisdom.
One who knows his own true nature is not helplessly dragged away by passion and hatred; even their mere vibration does not affect him, so how much less could there be an actual assault?
With his gaze fixed upon the swaying creepers like graceful women, he, whose form is like a mountain rock, does not delight in sensual pleasures, just as a traveler finds no joy in desert lands.
With a mind unattached, the wise man enjoys the entire abundance of enjoyments that come to him effortlessly and with ease, just as the eye perceives light.

O dear one, a succession of enjoyments such as women and the like, which arrives by chance like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, brings neither sorrow nor satisfaction even when tasted by the steadfast man.
The slight notions of pleasure and pain cannot disturb that knower who has correctly perceived the path, just as two waves cannot shake the king of mountains.
Regarding worldly enjoyments with detachment, gentle, self-controlled, and free from feverish anxiety, he takes refuge in his own true state, which abides within all beings.
The Knower remains free from agitation even while associated with the agitated; creating the worlds, he is indeed Brahman alone, devoted solely to the Self.
As the seasons do not waver amidst the various states of pleasure and pain that arrive in due time, place, and order, so the mountain-like king does not experience agitation.

O Rāma, even for one who is deeply immersed in worldly affairs, if he is possessed of great knowledge and his mind is eternally unattached, he does not sink at all despite the delusions of the organs of action.
Gold is called "stained" because of an actual stain, and not otherwise; likewise, a living being is said to be "attached" due to attachment to worldly existence, and not otherwise.
For the discerning person who perceives the knower as distinct from the body, nothing at all is cut away even when the limbs are severed.
Once that which is pure and luminous is known, it remains known forever; for a kinsman who has been recognized does not again fall into the state of being unknown.
Just as when the delusion of a snake has ceased, the perception of a snake no longer returns to the rope—like a mountain torrent that has fallen from a cliff during the rainy season.
Gold whose body has been purified by heating does not return to its natural impurity; even when submerged in mud, it does not take on that filth again.
When the knot of one's own heart is destroyed, there is no further bondage by the qualities (guṇas); for who could bind again with effort a fruit that has already fallen from its stalk?
Who has the power to join together again a stone and a gem that have both been reduced to pieces on all sides through analysis and investigation?
Once ignorance has been fully understood, who would sink back into it? Once the livelihood of outcaste dog-cookers has been thoroughly discerned, what twice-born man would look upon it with favor?
Just as the perception of milk in pure water ceases upon investigation, so too the latent impression of saṃsāra ceases through the investigation of the intellect.
The best of brahmins drink it, suspecting it to be honeyed water, as long as it has not been fully understood; once it is fully understood, it is abandoned.
Even though she is endowed with beauty and charm, a passionate woman is viewed by those who know reality as being like a painted beauty, consisting merely of material substances.
Just as soot, saffron, and the like [are used] on a woman's painting, so too are her hair and lips [used] even while she lives; what indeed is this obsession with her?
Just as molasses, once experienced as sweet, cannot be made otherwise even by burning and cutting, so too is the light of reality for the self.
A woman devoted to another man, even while busily engaged in household chores, relishes within herself that very elixir of union with another.
Thus, when the wise one has attained rest in the supreme, pure reality, he cannot be shaken even by the gods together with Indra.
By what powerful husband was a woman devoted to another made to forget the great festival of union with the lover of her own imagination?
Who could cause the mind of a great-souled knower of reality to forget its reliance upon the light of consciousness, which is the bliss of the world’s equanimity?
Engaged in uninterrupted worldly affairs abounding in all manner of pleasure and pain, he remains dependent on his kinsmen, yet is vexed by his husband and father-in-law.
Just as the world of brides, slowed by bliss through union with the beloved of their imagination, is not afflicted by the multitudes of sufferings that arise from calamity.
Likewise, one whose ignorance has dissolved, though fully engaged in worldly affairs, possesses right vision and virtuous conduct, and thus attains joy within the inner self.
He is not cut, even when his limbs are severed; he does not weep, though tears flow from him; he is not burned, even when being consumed by fire; and he does not perish, even when destroyed.

Free from the encounter of pleasure and pain, and unmoved even by calamities that thwart one's plans, may he sport whether in his excellent palace in the city, on the vast mountain, in the forest, or in the grove of asceticism.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Janaka remained established in his kingdom, and although he was occupied with worldly affairs, he was always free from inner fever, his mind ever unperturbed.
Your grandfather Dilīpa, though fully intent upon all worldly undertakings, enjoyed the earth for a long time solely through his inner state of freedom from passion.
Being stainless, the Buddha protected the people for a long time; Manu, eternally appearing as one liberated while living, ruled the kingdom.
Engaged for a very long time in various battles of strength and in numerous legal affairs, Māndhātṛ indeed attained the supreme state.
Bali, residing on the seat of Pātāla, maintained his existence as if it were eternal; ever-renouncing and ever-unattached, he remained established as one liberated while living.
Namuci, the lord of the Dānavas, was always intent on creating strife between the gods; amidst various modes of conduct and deliberations, he never felt any internal remorse.
In battle against Vāsava, the proud Vṛtra, who was prepared to sacrifice his body and possessed an expansive mind, engaged in a conflict with the gods with an inner spirit of peace.
Performing the duties of a Dānava and protecting the depths of Pātāla, Prahlāda attained joy that was free from harm and devoid of reproach.
O Rāma, although Śambara was solely intent on the art of illusion, because he had realized his inner identity with that very illusion, Śambara abandoned this illusory world of saṃsāra.
Engaging in battle with the Dānavas with an unattached intellect, he attained supreme consciousness and, being skilled, abandoned this world.

Even one who is devoted to the entire network of ritual actions, like the fire that is the mouth of all the immortals, enjoys the prosperity of sacrifice for a long time and remains liberated even while staying here in this world.
Being drunk by all the gods, the Soma, whose nature is uniform flavor, never undergoes any attachment, just as the sky, though pervaded [by clouds], remains free from clinging.

Even Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, though already liberated, engaged in the pursuit of a wife with such diverse efforts in heaven that he appeared as if he were still subject to worldly bonds.
Śukra, illuminating the expanse of the sky, and Budha, the protector of all aims—the preceptor of the asuras, whose mind is free from perturbation, passes his time.
Even though it has long been moving through the limbs of the multitudes of beings in the world, the wind is always moving everywhere and is indeed liberated.
O Rāma, although Brahmā understands the agitation caused by the constant coming and going of the worlds, his mind remains undaunted; with an equanimous heart, he exhausts his vast lifespan.
Even though he is liberated, the Blessed Lord Hari wanders for a long time through the world as if in play, through the battle against old age, death, and other dualities.
Even by the liberated Three-eyed One, Gaurī—like a cluster of blossoms on the tree of beauty—is borne upon half his body, as if he were a lover carrying his beloved.
Even though he was bound by the neck with a pearl necklace by Gaurī, the three-eyed Lord appeared like a perfectly pure necklace of pearls, as stainless as the crescent of the moon.
The hero Guha, though liberated, being of profound intellect and a singular ocean of the jewels of knowledge, performed all the martial deeds against Tāraka and the others.
O Rāma, Bhṛṅgīśa offered his own blood and flesh to his mother with a mind that was liberated, steadfast, and purified by meditation.
Although the sage Nārada was by nature liberated, he wandered through this wilderness of the world with a cool disposition toward his duties.
This lord Viśvāmitra, whose mind is liberated while living and who is worthy of honor, is presiding over the performance of the sacrifice as prescribed in the Vedas.
Śeṣa supports the earth, the sun creates the succession of days, and Yama performs his duty as the Restrainer—all indeed by virtue of their state of liberation while living.
Moreover, in this triple world, hundreds of others—yakṣas, asuras, humans, and gods—who have attained liberation remain within saṃsāra.
Established within worldly affairs among those who maintain diverse modes of conduct, some are cool within, while others are as dull as stones.
Having attained supreme awakening, some have come to the forest, such as Bhṛgu, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, Śuka, and others.
Some remain in kingdoms protected by royal parasols and fly-whisks, such as Janaka, Śaryāti, Māndhātṛ, Sagara, and others.
Some abide in the sky, situated within the circle of celestial mansions, such as Bṛhaspati, Uśanas, Candra, Sūrya, and the lords of sages.
Some have gone to the state of the gods and are seated in rows of celestial chariots, such as Agni, Vāyu, Varuṇa, Yama, Tumburu, and Nārada.
Some who are liberated while living reside in the depths of the netherworld (pātāla), such as Bali, Suhotra, Andha, Prahlāda, Āhlāda, and others.
Even among those born as animals, there are always those of cultivated intellect; even among those born as gods, there are those who possess foolish minds.
For indeed, everything arises from everything, everywhere, in every way, and at all times, within the Self of all, which exists in the form of infinite variety.
The destiny of fate is manifold and its operation is slow due to endless undertakings; yet, through the diversity of its structural components, everything is seen everywhere.
"Ordinance," "Fate," "Ordainer," "Lord of All," "Śiva," and "Īśvara"—by these names our inner conscious Self is designated.
There exists something real within the unreal, like gold among grains of sand; there exists the unreal within the real, like impurity within specks of gold.
When examined through reasoning, the notion of propriety in what is improper is clearly seen; for it is out of fear of evil, O Rāma, that the world engages in dharma.
O virtuous one, eternal truth is perceived within the unreal; through the practice of meditation on emptiness, the eternal state is attained.
That which does not exist arises quickly through the play of place and time; indeed, even rabbits are seen possessing horns when Śambara is present.
Those things which appear to be as firm as the essence of a diamond have gone to destruction; just as at the end of a kalpa, the moon, the sun, the earth, the oceans, the gods, and so forth.
Seeing thus, O mighty-armed one, the sequence of existence through being and non-being, abandon joy, resentment, and dejection, and attain equanimity.
In this world, the non-existent appears as existent, and even the existent is seen as non-existent; therefore, having abandoned both reliance and non-reliance, quickly attain equanimity.

O Rāghava, in this world, the attainment of liberation is not at all possible for one who lacks discernment; indeed, millions of people are submerged in worldly existence due to the absence of such discernment.
O Rāghava, liberation is indeed always attainable in this world through the practice of discernment; for it is by means of discernment that the multitudes of beings are liberated.
Liberation becomes easy to attain through solitude, yet difficult to obtain through lack of solitude; since it is attained by the dissolution of the mind, therefore, kindle your discernment.
One who desires prosperity should exert effort in the contemplation of the self; through the illumination of the self, the severing of the head of all suffering occurs.
Free from passion and free from attachment, those of great intellect who are liberated while living appear frequently in this world, like Suhotra and Janaka.

Therefore, you too, with an intellect made steadfast by the wisdom arising from detachment and discernment, wander as one liberated while living, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal.
Two kinds of liberation exist in this world for those who possess a body: one is with the body (sadeha), and the other is without the body (videha). Hear now the distinction between these two.
Through non-attachment to objects, there is peace of mind and liberation; O sinless one, this occurs even while the body still exists.

O dear one, the wise know that the supreme state of liberation (*kaivalya*) is indeed the exhaustion of all attachment (*sneha*); that [liberation] occurs both when the body exists and when it has ceased to exist.
He who lives free from attachment is called liberated while living; he who lives with attachment is bound; and the third is indeed liberated.
Effort for the sake of liberation should be applied with diligence and according to reason; for one devoid of effort and reason, even a cow’s footprint becomes difficult to cross.
But one should not, out of sheer delusion, allow oneself to fall under the power of others for the sake of suffering that is vast and beyond one's control.

Relying upon great fortitude with a resolute mind, examine the self by means of the self for the sake of your own long-term accomplishment; for one whose determination is expansive, the world becomes like a cow’s footprint.

That supreme state which the Sugata attained, and that same state from which no mortal king ever fell away, and that highest station reached by the great ones—that is the great fruit of the wish-fulfilling tree of diligent effort.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, these worlds arise from Brahman; they attain stability through lack of discernment and are indeed pacified through discernment.
Who is able to count the movements of the whirlpools of the world-net within the ocean of Brahman, or the motes of dust in the rays of light?
Know that incorrect perception is the cause for the persistence of the world; O beloved, correct perception is the cause for the cessation of saṃsāra.
For this terrible ocean of saṃsāra is difficult for others to cross; O Rāma, it cannot be crossed without both skillful means and diligent effort.
This ocean of his is filled to the brim with the waters of delusion, its depths unfathomable, and its hollows turbulent with the waves and whirlpools of death.
The foam of its merit is scattered abroad; it is a blazing Vāḍava fire for the hells; its waves are tossed by craving; it is an elephant in the waters of the mind.

In this [body], the river of life is a casket for the jewels of enjoyment; it is crowded with the serpents of agitated diseases and resounds with the gurgling of the crocodiles that are the sense-faculties.
Behold, O Rāma, these waves spreading forth, beautiful and tremulous; they are known as charming women, capable of drawing one toward their peaks.
Rich with the lotus-gems of their lips, filled with the blue-lotuses of their eyes, strewn with the flowers and fruits of their teeth, and adorned with the foam of their smiles.
With their hair like sapphire bracelets, rippling with the playfulness of their eyebrows, expansive with the sandy banks of their hips, and adorned with conch-like necks;

They are adorned with the jeweled plaques of foreheads, teeming with the crocodiles of amorous play, possessing the deep waters of flickering side-glances, and having the golden sands of their complexions.
If one who is submerged can thus cross over the ocean of saṃsāra, which is terrifying with its restless waves, that would indeed be the supreme human effort.
When the great ship of wisdom exists and the navigator of discernment is present, fie upon him who has not crossed over this ocean of saṃsāra!
He who, having traversed from shore to shore and having measured it on all sides, plunges into the ocean of saṃsāra—he alone is remembered as a true person (puruṣa).
"O Rāma, after the noble ones have reflected upon and surveyed this ocean of saṃsāra with their intellect, only then does play appear beautiful; not otherwise."
O virtuous one, you are indeed capable here; therefore, with a mind intent on investigation, this very cycle of existence is now being scrutinized by you.
He who, like you, first reflects upon cyclic existence and then plunges into it with a most transcendent understanding does not sink here in this world.
O Rāma, these enjoyments, which bring fear even to the serpent-like world-creatures, should first be examined with the intellect; they should be enjoyed only at the very end, like serpents by Garuḍa.
Those prosperities which are pursued after one has reflected upon reality and perceived it, result in a future elevation for a living being; all others lead only to suffering.
The strength, intellect, and splendor of one who has perceived reality increase, just as the beauty and other qualities of a tree flourish in the springtime.

O descendant of Raghu, knower of all that is to be known, you shine forth with supreme splendor like the cool-rayed moon, constantly endowed with a pure, equanimous, and most cooling glory filled with the essence of the highest elixir.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, you who have experienced the wonder of ultimate reality, tell me once more in brief the noble account of your life; for who could ever be satiated by your words?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "The characteristics of one liberated while living have been described by me in many ways; yet again, O mighty-armed one, listen to this which is being told."
Free from desire, the self-possessed one constantly perceives this entire world as if in deep sleep—unattached and as if non-existent in every respect.
Having attained the vision of the Self, he remains as if having reached isolation (kaivalya), as if his mind were in deep sleep, and as if reeling with bliss.
He does not take up even what is not given, nor does he grasp with his hand even what has been taken, by means of a mind that is equanimous and noble in its inward-turned nature.
Observing this succession of people as the movement of mechanical puppets with a gaze withdrawn within, he of tranquil intellect laughs.
He does not depend on the future, nor does he abide in the present; he does not dwell upon the past, yet he performs everything.
Though asleep, he becomes awakened; though awakened, he is as if asleep. He performs all actions within, yet he does nothing at all.
Having renounced everything within, and always free from inner seeking, even while performing external activities, he remains perfectly equanimous.

Externally, he continues his ordinary worldly activities, intent on performing actions as they arise, and he follows the duties toward his kinsmen as they come to him in the course of his own life's work.
His very self being the enjoyment of complete happiness, as if established in all hopes, he performs all actions while having abandoned the delusion of agency.
Remaining as if indifferent toward the activities of the primary constituents (prakṛti) in their sequential operations, he neither desires nor hates, neither grieves nor rejoices.

While living beings were intent on their own attachments, he remained with a mind unattached; toward those devoted to devotion, he behaved like one devoted, and toward the deceitful, he stood as if himself deceitful.
Among children he is a child; among the elderly he is old; among the steadfast he is steadfast; among those engaged in the ways of youth he is youthful; and among the suffering, he is sorrowful.
His speech was set upon meritorious discourse; his disposition was free from dejection; he was wise, filled with joy at what was said, gentle, and one whose fame was rooted in virtue.
Wise, serene, and sweet, he is full upon the dawning of his own intuition; with weariness and misfortune cast away, he is a loving kinsman to all.
His conduct was noble in form; he was equanimous, a gentle ocean of happiness, exceedingly affectionate, and cool to the touch, like the risen full moon.
He has no need for his own good deeds, nor for enjoyments, nor for ritual acts; he has no need for misdeeds, nor for the renunciation of enjoyments, nor for his kinsmen.
Neither by the commencement of cause and effect, nor by purification, nor likewise by bondage or liberation, nor by the netherworld, nor by heaven.
When the world is seen as it truly is—as a single, uniform essence—then the mind never feels distressed by bondage or liberation.
For one whose webs of doubt have been burnt away by the fire of right knowledge, the bird of the mind has flown off for good, free from all hesitation.
He whose mind is free from delusion and abides in equanimity neither sets nor rises, remaining like space amidst all views.
Just as a child seated within a chest moves about, so indeed does that [yogin] whose bodily movements are devoid of any sequential coordination.
Reeling like one intoxicated with joy, with the impulse for rebirth stilled, he no longer remembers what was done or left undone, owing to his realization that nothing is worth grasping.
He grasps and abandons everything in every possible way; having no purpose for anything that is not to be accepted, he acts like a child.
Even while engaged in activities according to the sequence of place, time, and action, he is not affected in the slightest by the pleasure or pain arising from those activities.
Although externally engaged with all objects, he nevertheless, through inner desirelessness, does not attribute existence to objects nor does he pursue their fruits.
He does not disregard the state of suffering, nor does he depend upon the hope for pleasure; he feels no joy at the success of an undertaking, nor does he grieve at its failure.
Even when the sun is intensely hot with its cool rays, even when the lunar orb is scorching, and even when fire spreads below, no wonder arises in him.
For one who realizes that these powers manifest here in this manner from the conscious self (cidātman), no further curiosity arises regarding these nets of wonders.
He does not adopt the wretchedness of compassion, nor does he pursue cruelty; he does not maintain a sense of shame, yet he does not fall into shamelessness.
Never of depressed spirit, never of agitated mind; never heedless, never weary of soul; never anxious, and never full of joy.
In his mind, which is vast and as stainless as the autumnal sky, anger and other such passions do not arise, just as new sprouts do not grow in the open firmament.
In this world, whose existence consists of an unceasing stream of arising and perishing, where, how, and indeed who could possibly be happy or unhappy?

In the movement of a bubble, in the rapid flow of water, and likewise in the succession of beings—where indeed is this [world], from where does it come, and what connection is there here to pleasure and pain?
Those men who are capable of creating through vision do not perish nor do they arise, despite the endless and incessant births of living beings through existence and non-existence.
Just as other dream-visions within the night arise and perish in every moment, so too do these worldly perceptions.
In this world, which is consumed by saṃsāra and characterized by incessant arising and incessant destruction, what room is there for the sequence of compassion and bliss?

When the absence of pleasure has resulted from the absence of the beautiful, and one has reached a state of being devoid of characteristics, what are those perceptions of suffering like, how have they come about, or where do they reside?
How can this state of suffering—which arises at the end of the experience of pleasure and expands its own seed—be peaceful while that pleasure has already vanished?

When pleasure and pain have been exhausted, and with their exhaustion, what remains of the objects to be rejected and accepted? Furthermore, when the auspicious and the inauspicious have dissolved, where can the desired and the undesired exist?

When the desire for enjoyments has vanished due to the destruction of both pleasant and unpleasant sights, and when hopelessness has become constant and matured, the mind melts like snow upon the Himalayas.
When the mind has been extinguished from its very root, what talk can there be of volition? Where can there be a perception of oil in sesame seeds that have been thoroughly burnt?

Through the intense contemplation of the non-existence of all phenomena, the great-souled one remains like the sky, free from all mental construction; established in his own mind, joyful, pervasive, and of a single form, the wise one stays, sleeps, and lives, eternally satisfied.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as a circle of fire is perceived from the whirling of a firebrand, though it is unreal yet appears as real, so too does the world arise from the vibration of the mind.
Just as a circular whirlpool appears as if distinct from the water due to the movement of the water, so too does the world appear due to the movement of the mind.
Just as in the sky, due to the movement of the eyes, a mass of peacock feathers or pearls is seen as if real though it is unreal, so too does the world appear through the movement of the mind.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin, tell me that by which the mind vibrates and that by which it likewise does not vibrate; for I shall surely treat it with that very thing.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, just as whiteness is in snow, as oil is in sesame seeds, as fragrance is in flowers, and as heat is in fire; so it is with this.
In the same way, O Raghava, the two vibrations of the mind are indeed closely joined; they are non-different, and the distinction between them is merely a false mental construction.
When one of the two sides—the mind or the movement of the mind—is destroyed, both perish without a doubt, as the quality and the possessor of the quality remain together.
O Rāghava, there are two stages for the destruction of the mind: yoga and knowledge. Yoga is indeed the restraint of its fluctuations, while knowledge is correct discernment.

Śrī Rāma said: At what time, in what manner, and by what means—namely, through the practice called yoga consisting of the binding of the prāṇa and apāna breaths—does the mind attain peace that bestows infinite bliss?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That wind which vibrates everywhere within the channels of this body—like water upon the movements of the earth—is celebrated as *prāṇa*.
Due to the force of its vibration, as it attains a variety of internal activities, the names "apāna" and so forth have been devised and assigned by those of perfected self.
Just as a flower is the locus of fragrance and snow is the locus of whiteness, so too this essence has attained non-difference from its support, the mind.
O Rāghava, know that this consciousness which arises from the internal vibration of the vital breath and is oriented toward the formation of volitions—that is the mind.

From the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa) comes the vibration of consciousness (citi); from that very vibration arises the vibration of awareness (saṃvit), just as waves, which produce the turning of whirlpools, arise from the vibration of water.
Those adorned by the scriptures say that the mind is the vibration of the vital breath; when that [breath] is restrained, the mind will surely become tranquil.
Through the subsiding of the vibration of the mind, this saṃsāra dissolves, just as worldly activity ceases when the movement of the sun's light comes to rest.
Śrī Rāma said: How can the movement of the vital airs, such as prāṇa and the rest—which move through the sky within the body-temple and wander there incessantly—be restrained?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Through the study of scriptures, association with the virtuous, dispassion, and the practice of yoga, one develops a lack of reliance upon and a firm reliance upon the former states of worldly existence.
From meditating upon one's desired object for a long time with single-mindedness, and from the intense practice of a single reality, the vibration of the vital breath is restrained.

Through firm practice of breath-retention such as *pūraka* and others, performed without weariness, and through union with solitary meditation, the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is restrained.

Through the experience of the reality of sound at the conclusion of the utterance of the syllable *oṃ*, when consciousness arises in deep sleep, the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is restrained.

When exhalation has certainly been practiced and the vital breath, becoming expansive, has reached the ether, the vibration of the breath no longer touches the apertures of the limbs and is restrained.
When inhalation has certainly been practiced until the breath, having filled the mountain-like density [of the body], remains motionless, the vibration of the vital breath is restrained.
In the practice of *kumbhaka*, one remains for an infinite time like a water jar; when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is rendered motionless through practice, the vibration of the breath is restrained.
Having diligently pressed the uvula with the tongue so that it reaches the root of the palate, when the vital breath has entered the upper aperture, the vibration of the breath is restrained.
When consciousness has dissolved through meditation into that subtle space called "nothingness," which is free from all temporal divisions, the vibration of the vital breath is arrested.
At the tip of the nose, within a space of twelve finger-breadths in the stainless ether, when the vision of consciousness becomes tranquil, the vibration of the vital breath is restrained.
Through practice, when the vital breath has reached the "end of twelve" above the palate via the upper aperture and its movement has dissolved, the vibration of the breath is restrained.

When the light of the star [of consciousness] has reached its cessation between the eyebrows, and when the conscious mind has become awakened as the abode of awareness, the vibration of the vital breath is restrained.
When that knowledge which has arisen instantaneously is firmly relied upon—in its aspect free from the fragments of conceptual construction—the vibration of the vital breath is arrested.
O Sage, when the perception of the beloved sky has been withdrawn for a long time, the vibration of the vital breath is restrained through mental meditation free from latent impressions.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, what is that which is called the heart of all beings in the world, in which this entire universe is reflected as in a great mirror?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O virtuous one, it is traditionally held that the heart of beings in this world is of two kinds: that which is to be accepted and that which is to be rejected. Hear now this distinction between them.
Know that which is situated on one side of the body within the space between the chest—within the body limited by such dimensions—to be the heart, which is to be abandoned.
Pure consciousness alone is established as the heart to be accepted; it is remembered as being both within and without, yet neither without nor within.
That indeed is the primary heart; therein this [consciousness] is fully established. It is the mirror of all objects and the treasury of all prosperity.
For all living beings, consciousness alone is said to be the heart; it is not a mere portion of a bodily limb, like an insentient, worn-out stone.
Therefore, when the mind is forcibly restrained within the pure heart consisting of consciousness, the vibration of the vital breath is arrested once its latent impressions have been removed.
By these methods, as well as by others devised through various intentions and residing in the mouths of various teachers, the vibration of the vital breath is restrained.
Through practice, these various methods of yoga become free from obstacles and serve as effective means for a fortunate person to shatter cyclic existence.

When the regulation of the vital breaths (prāṇāyāma) has attained firmness through practice and is marked by dispassion (vairāgya), it is considered fruitful according to one's latent impressions (vāsanā).
When the vital breath is brought to rest through practice at the twelve finger-breadths located at the eyebrows, the nose, and the palate, it subsides like a mountain river flowing far away.
Through repeated practice over a long period, the uvula is touched with the tip of the tongue at the palate, whereby the vital breath flows upward with great force.

Although these meditative absorptions are initially abundant in conceptual construction, through their own repeated practice, they quickly lead to the state of non-conceptuality for the sake of supreme tranquility.
A person who delights in the Self becomes free from sorrow and possesses inner happiness through practice alone, and not through anything else; therefore, be devoted to practice.
When the movement of the vital breaths has come to an end through practice, the mind attains tranquility, and nirvāṇa remains as the only residue.
O Rāma, the mind, when enveloped by latent impressions (vāsanā), takes on birth; when free from latent impressions, it attains liberation. It also sustains the vital breath (prāṇa); do as you wish.
The vibration of the vital breath is the form of the mind; from that arises the delusion of saṃsāra. When that very vibration comes to rest, the fever of saṃsāra ceases.
Through the exhaustion of the portions of conceptual construction, that state remains for the living being, from which all words, together with every form of mental fabrication, turn back.

That wherein all is, from whence all comes, that which is all, and from which all proceeds; wherein this world is not, from whence this is not, that which is not this, and not of such a nature as this world.

Because it is subject to destruction, because it is conceptual, and because it possesses qualities, there is indeed no example whatsoever seen that is similar to the Self, which is devoid of qualities.
She is the savor of all rice-grains, the illuminator of all splendors, the fashioner of all desires, and the moonlight of consciousness arisen within.
For from the wish-fulfilling tree, many rows of fruits of worldly existence—possessing manifold flavors—are born and fall without ceasing.
That person of great intelligence who, relying upon that state which is the ultimate limit of all things, remains firm-minded and knows it—that one is called liberated while living.

With all longing and curiosity departed, with the conceptualization of benefit and harm thoroughly stilled, the Supreme Person, whose mind is liberated, remains engaged in all worldly activities while maintaining a state of equanimity.
Śrī Rāma said: "The pacification of the mind engaged in yoga has indeed been described; now, O Lord, out of your grace, tell me of perfect knowledge."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "The Supreme Self exists here as the essence of manifestation, without beginning or end"—this one expansive certainty is what the wise know to be perfect knowledge.
"These hundreds of rows of objects, appearing in the forms of jars, cloths, and so forth, are the Self alone and nothing else"—this certainty is right vision.
Birth arises from incorrect perception; liberation comes from correct observation. Due to incorrect perception, a rope is seen as a snake, but not so through correct observation.

Consciousness that is entirely free from the component of volition and devoid of any object of cognition is designated as "pure awareness" (saṃvitti); in this state of liberation, there is nothing other than this.
When that pure form is recognized, it is called the Supreme Self (paramātman); but when pure, yet appearing as impure within, it is called ignorance (avidyā) by the wise.
Consciousness itself is the object of consciousness; there is no conceptualization of duality between these two. O Rāma, the Self alone accumulates its own self; indeed, nothing else exists.
The vision of the self as it truly is in these three worlds is this much: having ascertained that the entire world is indeed the self, there is fullness.
O Rama, everything is indeed the Self alone; where are existence and non-existence said to be, and where do the notions of bondage and liberation reside? What else is there to be grieved for?

There is no object of thought other than the mind, nor is there any mind; this is all Brahman alone manifesting. Everything is the one supreme space—what is liberation, and for whom could there be bondage?
This Brahman, whose form is expanded and which exists as the vastest of the vast, has its duality extinguished through knowledge; you yourself, O Self, become that very Self by means of the Self.
When form is correctly observed, there is not even the slightest difference between wood, stone, and cloth; where then are you, intent on conceptual construction?
That which is peaceful in the beginning and at the end, whose nature is indestructible—that is what is called "reality," and even the self; O Rāghava, become absorbed in that.
Beyond this entire sky is the whole world of the moving and the unmoving; where is the sequence of pleasure and pain? Be free from fever, O Rāghava.
Through the delusions of old age and death arising from duality and non-duality, the Self alone manifests by means of its own diverse forms, like water through its various waves.
For one who remains constantly embracing the pure Self with an internal intellect, what enjoyments here are capable of binding that Self?
For one who has cultivated expansive discernment, the enemies such as mental enjoyments do not pierce him even slightly, just as gentle breezes cannot shatter a mountain.
In this world, those who lack discernment, are ignorant, deluded, and devoted to hope swallow up sorrows, just as herons swallow fish from waterless places.
"The entire world is indeed the Self alone; ignorance exists nowhere. Holding fast to this view, remain steady in your true nature.

In various mental constructions there is no diversity, nor is there any difference in reality between the waters and other elements in lakes of manifold kinds; one who consists of this single certainty, having perceived the true meaning correctly, is said to be liberated.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O dear one, for the discerning person who contemplates within this way of life, no longing ever arises even toward enjoyments standing right before them.
The eye exists merely for the purpose of seeing; the living being exists for the sake of pleasure and pain; the ox exists merely for the burden; and the enjoyer is the master of the material object.
When the eyes are submerged in forms, what agitation can there be for an embodied being? When a donkey is stuck in a puddle, what loss is it to the commander of an army?
O base one, do not relish this mire of form with the eye; it perishes in the blink of an eye and indeed destroys you as well.
By the very same means by which one’s lifespan is calculated and by which one’s horses are guided, so too is the wise man swiftly bound, or the cruel man, by his own actions.

O eye, do not rely upon this form—which arises and perishes, which is charming only for a moment, and which is composed of unreality—for your own destruction; rather, rely on that which is indestructible.
The eye remains as a witness, and form abides within the self; light exists by the power of time—why do you alone suffer?
O mind, like the shimmering of water or a tuft of down rising in the sky, you throb with well-formed bonds; what has come upon you?
Just as a minnow quivers in the waters of a kalpa, so does the egoism, characterized by its own flickering, manifest within the mind; from where has this "you-ness" arisen?
Since light and form are eternally insentient yet manifest in mutual dependence as support and supported, your mental agitation is futile.
Form, light, and mental attention are not mutually connected, yet they appear as if they were joined, like a face and its reflection in a mirror.
For these have become closely joined together by the ignorant creature; when ignorance is swallowed by knowledge, they remain separate, being composed of unreality.
For these—form, light, and mental attention—are bound together by the conceptualization of the mind, just as wood is joined by lac.
The thread of one's own mental conceiving is severed through diligent practice of the mind by means of inquiry; once severed, the cultivation of ignorance is destroyed.
When the mind has been exhausted through the destruction of ignorance, these factors—form, light, and mental attention—no longer collide with one another at all.
The mind alone is the awakener of all the internal senses; therefore, it is that which must be eradicated, like a demon from a house.
O mind, you prance about in vain; the end of you has been seen by me: you are utterly insignificant in the beginning and at the end, and you perish even in the present.
Why do you dance about within in vain through these five forms? You dance only for him who knows you as his own.
Your leaping about does not bring even the slightest satisfaction to my mind; like the flickering of a deceptive mind, you burn in vain amidst your own fluctuations.
Stay or go, O mind; you do not belong to me, nor do you live. By nature you are eternally dead; through inquiry, you are known to be thoroughly dead.

O you who possess the form of eternal death, you are devoid of reality, inert, deluded, and deceitful; only the ignorant man, not one possessed of discernment, is oppressed by you through your lack of command.
Through our folly, we failed to recognize you while you were swiftly dying; today you have become death for us, just as darkness is to lamps.
By you, who are deceitful, my body-house has for a long time been entirely obstructed and deprived of association with the virtuous.
Now that you, who are insentient, resemble a ghost, and are a rogue of a mind, have departed, this house of my body may be inhabited by all virtuous people.
"You did not exist previously, yet now the world has become deceitful; you will not exist even now—O Vetāla, are you not ashamed?"
Depart from this dwelling of my body, O vampire of the mind, together with the ogresses of craving and the guhyakas of anger and the rest.
By good fortune, through mere discernment, the intoxicated vampire of the mind has emerged from the temple of the body, like a wicked wolf from its cave.
Oh, how wondrous and great is this: by this dull, momentary, and deceitful mind, all these people have been rendered helpless!
What is your prowess? What is your strength? What is your refuge? If you leap about alone and oppress people as if they were dead.
O you of base mind, you shall by no means be killed by me; O ignorant one, today you are merely perceived as dead.
For so long a time, knowing you to be alive, I have remained attached during the long nights of saṃsāra amidst abundant attachments.
"Indeed, I have realized today that this mind is dead and does not exist; therefore, having completely abandoned hope for you, I abide solely in the Self."
"By good fortune, I have myself realized today that my mind is dead; I shall not spend the remainder of my own life with such a rogue."
Having expelled the deceitful "I" from the dwelling of the body in an instant, I remain established within myself as my own true self, entirely free from the Vetāla.
Having long ago possessed a mind like a vetāla, I myself performed various transformations upon my own self; remembering this now, I laugh.
By good fortune, the vampire of the mind—towering as high as a palmyra tree—has finally been struck down after a long time, tormented by the sword of discernment from the chamber of the heart.
Now that the vampire of the mind has been stilled and has reached the pure state, by good fortune I abide alone in happiness within the city of the body.
The mind is dead, thought is dead, and the demon of egoism is dead; by means of the mantra of inquiry, I remain established in equanimity, alone and at peace.
What mind is mine, what hope of mine, and what ego could there be for me? By good fortune, this wife of mine has been entirely lost and rendered useless.
Salutations again and again to me alone—to that one who has accomplished all that was to be done, who is eternal, whose nature is stainless, and who is known as non-conceptual consciousness.
There is no sorrow, there is no delusion, nor am I myself; neither am I not, nor am I another; salutations again and again unto me alone.
I have no hope, no actions, no saṃsāra, and no agency; I have no state of being an enjoyer and no body—salutations again and again to Me alone!
I am not the self, nor is there anyone else; I do not exist, nor does another. I am everything—salutation after salutation to this very Self.
I am the beginning; I am the sustainer; I am consciousness; I am the worlds. There is no limitation of me; salutations, salutations unto me alone.
Salutations again and again to me alone—the great Self who is changeless, eternal, partless, all-encompassing, and present at all times.
Salutations again and again to me alone—to the one who is formless, beyond description, luminous, the Great Self, who abides solely as the self by itself.
I have entered within that Being which is equal, all-pervading, subtle, and the sole illuminator of the universe; salutations, salutations unto myself alone!
This very one is the mountains, the oceans, the earth, and the rivers; it is not "I" alone, nor am I alone. To me alone, who am this entire world rich with all objects, salutations again and again!

I bow to that infallible Lord, whose body is free from mental construction, equally delightful, manifesting the universe yet not the universe, infinite, himself unborn and undecaying, transcending all qualities.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having thus reflected and understood within, O mighty-armed one, the knowers of reality further reflect in this manner; the Self is to be known by those great-souled ones.
The truth that "this world is indeed the Self alone" is cleansed by the mind; yet from where could the mind have arisen? Oh, how the mind is itself a non-entity!

Because it is ignorance, because it is non-mind, and because it is like an illusion, the mind is indeed non-existent; or rather, it certainly does not exist at all as anything other than a delusion, like a tree in the sky.

Just as the movement of a pillar is established for a child who has gone into the water, so too is the mind—which is composed of the non-existent—established for the unawakened, but not for the awakened one.
When the delusion of ignorance and confusion has subsided, we no longer perceive the mind, just as the shaking of a mountain ceases once the spinning of a wheel has ended.

For in this way, the mind does not exist at all; there is only Brahman, whose nature is such. Since the mental constructions of objective entities arise from the mind, they have been abandoned by me as being unreal.
I am born with my doubts stilled; I stand free from the fever of passion. Thus I remain, thus I abide, entirely devoid of longing.
In the absence of the mind, qualities such as childish craving are utterly exhausted, just as various named colors vanish when the light has ceased.
The mind has died and craving has departed; the cage of delusion is destroyed. Selflessness has arisen, and while this remains awake, one has become enlightened.
The entire world is indeed one and tranquil; even this diversity is not real. What else could I contemplate within? Enough with this talk!
I am the eternal Self, established as subtle, all-pervading, and gentle; I have attained that pure state which is free from appearances and without beginning or end.
Whatever exists here and whatever does not exist—be it mind, self, or any such entity—is more transparent than space, peaceful, infinite, ungraspable, and all-pervading.
Whether the mind exists or not, whether it dies within or remains; what purpose is there for my deliberation, since my self has long been arisen in equanimity?
Out of ignorance, I was a limited being with the form of a thinker; through inquiry, I have become infinite in form—where indeed is that "thinker" I once was?
Even when the mind has perished, this splendor of conceptual construction is meaningless; for what purpose does it arise, serving only the function of the mind-demon?
"I shall abandon this internal fabrication of conceptualization"—having thus resolved "so be it," I remain with a tranquil self within the Self, like one observing a vow of silence.
O Raghava, one who knows that [reality] should daily investigate with wisdom and with the mind, whether eating, walking, sleeping, or standing, in all circumstances.
Having investigated with their own minds, which are established in themselves and self-abiding, the virtuous remain free from agitation amidst their natural duties.

Free from pride and intoxication, with joyful dispositions and a radiance equal to the autumnal moon, those of great intelligence dwell here in happiness, engaging in their natural worldly activities.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "In this manner, inquiry was performed by the learned Saṃvarta in ancient times; it was recounted to me on the Vindhya mountain by him, who had realized the Self."
Firmly grasping this view, with an intellect intent on investigation, cross over this ocean of saṃsāra by means of gradual stages.
Now, O Rāma, hear this other perspective that bestows the goal, by which the sage Vītahavya remained free from doubt.
In ancient times, the highly effulgent Vītahavya wandered through the forests, traversing the long caves of the Vindhya mountains like the sun moving through the caverns of Mount Meru.
In the course of time, he became weary of this terrible sequence of actions, which causes the wandering of saṃsāra and takes the form of mental and physical afflictions.
Through a noble desire for others, attainable through a portion of non-conceptual meditative absorption, he brought to an end the succession of his own worldly activities that had worn out the world.
He entered his own leaf-hut, constructed by Rambhā, which was made white with fragrant substances and appeared like a blue lotus.
There, upon that level and pure seat, well-spread with a deer skin, he rested—immovable and tranquil, like a cloud that has ceased its rain.
He stood in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), with his fingers placed upon his heels; he remained with his shoulders clearly set and his movement as still as a mountain peak.
Slowly withdrawing his mind from the light scattered across the quarters, he entered the cave of Mount Meru at evening, just as the sun withdraws its mass of rays.
Gradually abandoning both external and internal objects of touch, he reflected upon this with a mind free from sin.
Alas! This mind is so restless that even when withdrawn, it does not attain steadiness for a moment, like a leaf tossed by powerful waves.
Agitated by the unrestrained forms of the eyes and other senses, it leaps up incessantly like a ball struck by the palm of the hand.
It abandons the deities and seizes upon the functions increased by the senses; for it runs toward that from which it is restrained like one who is insane.
From a pot it goes to a cloth, from a cloth to a formidable cart; the mind wanders among objects like a monkey among trees.
I shall now thoroughly examine these five gates of the mind, beginning with the eye, which are designated as the "burnt senses."
Ha! Ha! O hosts of sense-faculties, why do you not assist me here toward awakening? You are as fickle as the waves of the ocean that toss about its waters at the shore.
O you of fickle intent, do not act with rashness to your own detriment; remember the vast webs of suffering that have occurred in the past.
O forms, you are indeed merely inert and base; yet in that which is inert, vanity flutters in vain like a mirage.
This arrogance of the blind, which is always devoid of light regarding things whose essential nature is without substance, arises only for the sake of being seen.
"I, the Blessed One, whose nature is consciousness, perform everything as a witness; you, with your collection of senses destroyed, why are you agitated in vain?"
My formless eyes and other senses falsely whirl about, resembling a firebrand’s circle and like the delusion of a snake in a rope.
Therefore, the eyes and other [senses] have been fully understood by that omniscient Self; there is not even the slightest connection between heaven, the netherworld, and the mountains.
Like a traveler afraid of snakes or a twice-born man afraid of outcasts, pure consciousness—untainted and beyond the senses—remains far removed from them.
The mere existence of consciousness is sufficient for your mutual agitation to cease, just as those engaged in their daily tasks remain at ease when the sun is shining.
O mind, you who wander like a Cārvāka, a mendicant for the sake of filling your belly in the four directions—do not roam thus in vain for your own ruin, like a dog; O world, do not act so!
"‘I am like consciousness’—this desire of yours is vain and false; O rogue, there can be no identity between consciousness and the mind, for they are absolutely distinct."
"This wicked notion of 'I' of yours, that 'I indeed live,' has arisen as a mere falsehood for the sake of suffering; it is not real, being devoid of truth."
Upon the arising of the ego, abandon this agitation of thinking "I am that"; O fool, you are nothing at all, so why do you agitate yourself in vain?
Consciousness is the mind, beginningless and endless; nothing other than consciousness exists. O great fool, what else could that which is called "mind" be within this body?
O mind, this sense of being an enjoyer and an agent has arisen like an elixir that results in poison; alas, it is indeed in vain!
Do not become an object of ridicule by relying on the group of foolish senses; you are neither the doer nor the enjoyer, for you are inert and are awakened by another.
Who are you in relation to enjoyments, or what are these enjoyments to you? For one who is dull-witted, even a self does not exist; how then can there be kinsmen, friends, and the like?

That which is insentient is indeed non-existent, for it is characterized by existence-in-non-existence; this is because the qualities of knowing, acting, enjoying, and being other are impossible therein.

If you are of the nature of immediate consciousness, then your very self is your body; what kind of existence could your mind—composed of being and non-being—possibly have that would cause you suffering?
Just as you have understood agency and enjoyership to be entirely false, so shall they be wiped away by me; listen to how this is done gradually through reasoning.
First of all, you yourself are insentient; there is no doubt about this. What kind of agency can belong to that which is insentient? How could stones dance here?
Therefore, live for a long time upon that pure, divine portion; you live, you desire, you kill, you wander in vain, and you prance about.
Whatever is performed by whatever power, that is indeed accomplished by that very power; a sickle cuts by means of a man's power, yet it is the man who is called the reaper.
He who is slain by the power of another is indeed slain by that very [power]; the sword kills by the power of the man, yet it is the man who is called the slayer.
Whatever is drunk according to one's capacity becomes drunk by that very person; the drink is drunk with a vessel, while the man who drinks is called the "drinker."

By your very nature you are utterly dull-witted; you are awakened by the All-Knowing One. Therefore, it is indeed the Self that, by itself, gathers this [consciousness] for itself; such is our position.
The Supreme Lord, your very Self, awakens you incessantly; yet the deluded must indeed be awakened by the wise through hundreds of repetitions.

Indeed, it is the very existence of the Self alone that shines here, having the singular form of pure consciousness; and by means of that very [existence], you remain having accepted the referents of the word "mind."
Thus, O mind, you have come under the power of the self through ignorance; but in the face of intense knowledge, you have dissolved like snow in the heat of the sun.
In that [reality], you are nectar; you are not deluded, nor do you exist from the perspective of ultimate truth. "That very thing is I"—this is vain; therefore, let it not lead to your unhappiness.
The mental construction of the unreal is like the creepers of Indra’s net; here, it is consciousness alone that has manifested as the limb of Brahman.
The power of Brahmā arises fully in the forms of the world of men and gods; it surges like the waves of the ocean amidst its masses of spray.
O fool, if you are composed of consciousness, then since you are eternally non-different from that supreme state, why do you grieve for anything else?
That state is indeed all-pervading, abiding in all beings, and possessing all forms; O ignorant one, upon attaining that, everything is attained forever.
There is no "you," there is no body, and there is no great, vibrating Brahman here; when "I-ness" and "you-ness" flash within the motionless, whose suffering could there be, and for whom?

If you are the Self, then the all-pervading Self alone exists here and nothing else; if that which is other than the Self is insentience, then that [insentience] does not exist as reality, though its form appears to exist.

The Self alone is the entirety of the three worlds, and nothing else exists apart from it; whatever reality there may be, you are that Self, and if anything else were reality, it would be nothing at all.
Why do you strive in vain with thoughts such as "this is I" or "that is mine"? How can that which has no real substance manifest? Who is slain by the horn of a hare?
O fool, there is no third category other than the conscious and the insentient; it is like a third coloring between shade and sunlight.
When dullness of mind and vision has been destroyed through the contemplation of truth, that which arises is merely self-cognizing awareness born from that [destruction].
Therefore, O deluded one, you possess neither agency nor even the state of being an enjoyer; you are indeed that supreme Brahman itself. Abandon your ignorance and become established in the Self.
It is said that the Self acts by means of you, who have become its instrument, solely for the purpose of accomplishing the object of knowledge through the faculty of pure consciousness.
An instrument that is non-existent in its own nature, insentient, without support, and motionless would not function without being impelled by an agent.
No power whatsoever exists in this instrument which is itself a non-agent; for what capacity does a sickle have to act in the absence of a reaper?
O mind, the capacity for the action of severing with a sword-strike resides in the person, not in the utterly inert sword; nor does such capacity reside even in all the limbs [of the body].
Therefore, my friend, you are not the doer; do not become a partaker of suffering in vain. O fool, being afflicted for the sake of others does not look well among common people.
A lord such as this is not to be pitied, for he would be your equal; he has no concern here with what is done, nor any with what is left undone.
But out of pride, thinking "I am helping him," the person of small intellect merely suffers; for those who dwell [in this world], no purpose whatsoever is served.
If you thus conform to the purpose of the agent, the Lord of Enjoyment, then he has no desire whatsoever here, for he is eternally satisfied.
This entire world is filled by the one, all-pervading conscious self, which shines with an uncreated radiance; there is no other existence than this mere conceptual construction.
By means of the manifestation as one or many, through that entire self-nature, what within is made internal within the Self itself—what is desired?
But for one such as you, agitation is produced in vain by mere sight alone, just as it occurs in a young man upon beholding a queen intoxicated with passion.
O handsome one, you are the agent of the mind, which is connected with the self; however, you are not its inherent relation, just as a fruit is not the inherent relation of a flower.
That which is this oneness with the second is called the state of relation; it is oneness now, whereas previously there was duality.

Consisting of various kinds of arrangements and intent upon the performance of diverse forms of action, worldly existence is remembered as manifold, being the causeless source of states of pleasure and pain.

A relationship is observed between two equal things, as well as between two halves of equals; but when that [equality] exists, there is no other relationship between two dissimilar things within the three worlds.
Numerous substances indeed depend upon the qualities of other substances; the falling away from consciousness is suffering—do not fall away from consciousness.

By this much alone, through one-pointed meditation, one becomes a constant meditator or a seer of the Self; for, by means of inner vision, there is the absence of the objective world which bestows suffering.
Know that the tendency toward conceptualization is a fall from pure consciousness, resulting in suffering, directed toward the inert things such as the mind, body, and senses, which are like stones.

O mind, what kind of agency can there be? How could a flower exist in the sky, which is devoid of all mental constructs and consists of the destruction of thinking within the mire [of worldly existence]?

Furthermore, agency is not possible in the self, just as it is not in the limbs of the sky; this is merely the self alone appearing within itself through various forms of multiplicity and non-multiplicity.
Just as the ocean surges with its waters through foam, bubbles, and waves, so does everything manifest within this Self of Consciousness, which is mere appearance.
There is no second conceptualization, just as there is none for a glowing coal in the ocean; for the Lord who is devoid of conceptualization, whether in the body or in the inert mind.
O Sundara, that which is free from both consciousness and the object of consciousness is the essence, and nothing else; there is no "this" or "that," nor even anything auspicious or inauspicious.

Thus, this false conceptualization does not exist, just as a forest does not exist in the sky; this entire expanse is merely consciousness alone, devoid of anything to be perceived. In that state, how could there be the false construction of "this is I," "this is another," or "this is someone else"?
Who could attribute a conceptualization to that which is beginningless, formless, all-pervading, and the expansive Self? Who could draw the Ṛgveda in the sky?

When the Self—ever-arisen, the essence of all things and categories, established as pure consciousness, filling and overflowing the vast quarters—has perfectly entered me, appearing as if unreal due to its stainlessness, then the fragments of pleasure and pain have perished; indeed, that was my delusion.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Once again, the steadfast and excellent sage, with his pure and brilliant intellect, properly awakened his own group of senses while remaining guarded.
Listen clearly as I shall explain that for the sake of the group of sense-faculties; having heard it and attained its cultivation, proceed to supreme freedom from suffering.
This existence of yours leads only to suffering and brings about its own end; therefore, you should abandon this existence of a self when it does not truly exist.
I clearly consider that this existence of yours has already come to an end through my instruction; for you are born of ignorance.
O mind, your own existence becomes manifest for your suffering, like the glow of heated gold which only serves to burn one's own sides.
Behold: while you exist, the multitudes of the rivers of saṃsāra, crowded with the surging waves of delusion, enter the ocean of time.
Rows of sorrows fell from somewhere, like torrents of rain, driven by a mutual sense of competition as each thought, "I shall fall first."
The boundless, cruel cholera of existence and non-existence throbs forth, intent on uprooting the heart and causing lamentation.
Upon this tree of the decaying body, where the bees of coughing and labored breathing hum, the cluster of old age and death blossoms with a stainless radiance.
In the hollow of the body’s cave, which is coiled by the serpents of turbulent waves, the restless monkey of anxiety dwells within the mind amidst a sky thick with mist.
The bird of craving, shrieking as it dances, uses its sharp beak of duality to sever the fragments of virtue from this withered tree of the body.
The coarse, impure, and ill-behaved cock of desire scatters the refuse of the heart here and there.
In the great night of delusion, the fierce owl of ignorance flutters about within the tree of the heart, like a Vetāla in a cremation ground.
These and many other misfortunes, like female spirits prowling in the night, surge forth when you, the host of the senses, are present.
But if you were not here, O virtuous one, all auspicious glories would shine forth brilliantly with light, like lotus ponds at dawn.
The sky of the heart shines, its mist of delusion stilled, encompassed by stainless light, and its interior rendered utterly free from passion.
Like a turbulent flood falling unexpectedly from the expanse of the sky, the surges of conceptual construction do not fall for long, as they cause only a state of deficiency.
Loving-kindness, which gladdens all, is peaceful and supremely purifying; it arises from the heart, as delightful as a cluster of blossoms from a fine tree.
Inwardly riddled with flaws, itself possessed of both suitable and unsuitable qualities, anxiety withers away like a lotus plant scorched by frost.
When ignorance is destroyed, light attains clarity within; it shines forth like the orb of the sun in the sky when the clouds have subsided in autumn.
Clear, vast and profound, unagitated and unassailable, the heart attains equanimity like an ocean when the wind has subsided.
The person dwells within, filled with a flood of nectar and consisting of eternal bliss, like the cool moon.

Upon the destruction of ignorance, consciousness attains clarity within; the entire universe, including all that is moving and stationary, comes to rest solely within a single portion of consciousness.
One meditates upon a form full of splendor, languid with bliss; it does not belong to those attached to vital breaths who weave the snares of hope.
Just as sap returns to burnt leaves, so too does [the essence] return to men who have exhausted the great path of worldly existence, old age, and birth.
One rests for a long time within the tree of the self so as not to wander again; such and other perfections of virtue arise in this manner.

But when you, the consumer of all, who brings about the destruction of every hope, are absent, then for these two sides—the nature of which consists in the existence or non-existence of the mind—[all hope perishes].
Accept for a moment that very path by which you perceive the highest good; O best of men, I consider your own true nature to be happiness.
Cultivate that very non-existence; for the renunciation of happiness is indeed folly. If it were real, it would exist as a consciousness internalized within.
Who would desire the absolute non-existence of one who lives? But you do not exist; I tell you this in truth, O handsome one.
Therefore, do not be happy with the thought "I live" based on a false intention; you were non-existent from the very beginning, and your existence exists only through delusion.
That very [nature] has now reached utter decay through investigation; O virtuous one, your form consists solely of this non-investigation.
When investigation is correctly performed, it remains in a state of equilibrium, equal in form; yet that which is born from non-investigation is like darkness arising from the absence of light.
Just as darkness is pacified by light through investigation, O friend, for all this time you have possessed only slight discernment.
This swelling of yours has become a cause of nothing but suffering; through mere deluded imagination, it has come to be like a child’s phantom.
The duality, which existed as a decaying state with its beginning and end dissolved through conceptualization, has now arisen as eternal once its own prior form had reached exhaustion.
By the grace of discernment, salutations again and again to discernment; though you are awakened in many ways, you have been further enlightened by the mind.
When the state of being a mind has perished, you remain as the Supreme Lord; your manifestation in your primordial nature has come to abide for the sake of ultimate well-being.
Now you are the Great Lord, liberated from all latent impressions; he whose birth arises from lack of discrimination perishes through discrimination.
As you proceeded toward the end through illumination, the darkness of non-perception vanished; O virtuous one, even though you did not desire it, stability was attained in discernment.
This destruction has come from every direction for the sake of accomplishing happiness; therefore, by means of established principles and reasonings, it is determined that "the sword does not exist."
O Lord of the faculties of mind, may it be well with you; you have reached the end [of this world], for that which was eternally non-existent in the past is now likewise non-existent in form.
And there shall be no future rebirth; may it be well with your own mind. I enter final nirvana; I am at peace. By good fortune, I am now free from the fever of existence.
I abide in my own self, established in the state of the fourth form (turya); therefore, there is indeed no such thing as an unstable mind within saṃsāra.
