The self indeed exists and truly does exist, for it is found elsewhere; this self is I myself, that very one, and there is nothing else anywhere apart from me.
I am always situated everywhere as the very consciousness that is the nature of awakening; I do not perceive within my stainless interior the conceptualization "this is the self."

Since there is no conceptualization of a single entity as being distinct from its counter-correlate, how could there be the conceptualization "I am this Self"? Thus, without uttering such a notion, I remain silent within my own self, like a wave in water.

Having attained that state of perfect consciousness which is free from the impressions of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), devoid of any portion of dependent cognition, where the movement of vital breaths has ceased, and wherein the defects of partiality have set—being beyond all objects of perception—I am stilled within myself as Mauna, utterly free from desire.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having thus reached this certainty, the sage Vītahavya, freed from all latent desires, remained motionless in meditative absorption within a cave in the depths of the Vindhya mountains.
Beautiful with the bliss of consciousness in which all movement has ceased, his mind having set [into stillness], he shone like a tranquil ocean.
Within him, the succession of vital breaths gradually subsided, like a fire whose fuel has been consumed, its flickering mass of flames coming to rest.
When the external object has ceased to exist internally and no longer persists externally, and when only that which has attained internal stability remains, his eyelashes do not even blink.
With their eyes directed toward the tip of the nose as if in a faint gaze, they attained a beauty equal to that of lotuses half-closed in bud.
With his body, head, and neck held perfectly erect, that one of great intelligence sat as if carved from stone or as if depicted in a painting.
As he remained thus for three hundred years within a hollow of the Vindhya marshlands, it passed for him like half a muhūrta.
It is said that for all this time, that self-possessed man did not perceive [the passage of time]; being liberated while living and absorbed in meditation, he did not abandon that body.
For that duration, that fortunate knower of yoga did not awaken, despite the noble roars of clouds, rumbling with the weight of heavy rain-showers.
With the loud cries of birds and monkeys and the sounds of elephants slapping their trunks, which increased as they bowed down before the lord of the surrounding circle during his hunt;
With the roaring of lions in their fury, the hissing sounds of waterfalls, the clashing of fierce thunderbolts, and the dense clamor of people;
With the leaps of intoxicated śarabhas, the crashing of mountain slopes during earthquakes, the roaring sounds of forest fires, and the surging leaps of water-floods;
By the blows from the slopes of great boulders, by the earth, dust, and water upon the ground, by the surges of floodwaters, and by heats as harsh as fire;
It flows freely at its own will when the cause for its restraint has dissolved, like waves in water as the rainy season comes to an end.
For in that mountain cave, in a very short time, he was buried in mud on the ground by the force of a monsoon torrent.
There he dwelt in the hollow of a tree trunk with a narrow interior, his shoulders pressed down by the mud like boulders upon mountains.
Then, when three hundred years had passed, that self-effulgent Lord, whose nature is the Self, awoke while still confined within the hollow of the earth.
Consciousness alone seized that body which was being crushed by the earth; for the body is merely the vibration of the vital breath, which cannot exist without the movement of the life-force.
Having attained full development upon arising within the heart, that mental construction, taking the form of his own mind, was experienced by him as if right within his heart.
In the lovely forest of Kailāsa, at the foot of a Kadamba tree, he attained the state of a sage for a hundred years, his self purified through liberation while living.
For a hundred years, one shall possess the state of a Vidyadhara, free from mental afflictions; for five yugas, one shall hold the sovereignty of Indra, saluted by gods and celestial musicians.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, regarding these manifestations of his as Indra and others, how can there be both restriction and non-restriction in the determination of space and time?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This power of consciousness, which is the self of all, manifests in whatever manner and wherever it arises; accordingly, it immediately becomes that very thing, due to its singular nature as the Self.
Just as a restriction [of place, time, etc. exists within the intellect, so it remains there; for the sequential restrictions of space, time, and so forth, consist essentially of that [intellect].
Thus Vītahavya, free from latent impressions, beheld various other worlds within the space of consciousness in his heart.
For those possessing right awakening, this very latent impression is no longer a latent impression; for one whose seed has been burnt by the fire of knowledge, what seed-nature can remain?
For one kalpa, he served as an attendant to the Moon-crested Lord, being proficient in all branches of knowledge and possessing stainless vision of the three periods of time.
Whatever kind of firm mental impression one possesses, one perceives things accordingly; it was precisely through the state of liberation while living that Vītahavya experienced this.
Śrī Rāma said: "O best of sages, this being so, even for one whose mind is liberated while living, there remain perceptions of bondage and liberation, just as they did in the case of Vītahavya."

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This entire universe, as it exists, is peaceful and as pure as the sky; it is Brahman alone for those liberated while living—for them, how could there be any perception of bondage or liberation?
Wherever and in whatever manner this expanse of consciousness shines forth, there and in that very manner, it attains its pervasive state to that same extent.
O Rāghava, by that very [Brahman] which has experienced them, many worlds are indeed being experienced as its own self through the form of Brahman.
In those countless worlds, which were formless and composed of great souls whose conscious selves were the fire of Vitahavya submerged within the hollows of the earth;
He who was Śakra, unaware of his true self, has today become a king among the wretched; even at this very moment, he is engaged in hunting in the forest.
He who was the swan, his self unawakened, born from the lotus of Brahmā, is that very same one now established as the lord of fishermen in a forest grove on Mount Kailāsa.
That king who was unaware of his own self while in the Saurāṣṭra region of the earth, he is today stationed here in a village of the Andhras, abounding in trees.
Śrī Rāma said: "It is said that this was the mental creation of Vītahavya; if those embodied beings therein were merely objects of delusion, how could they have assumed physical forms?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O Rāma, if that world of Vītahavya consisted of nothing but a single delusion, then why does this world of yours appear so much more extensive?"
This too, my dear, is pure consciousness alone, like an illusion consisting of the mind; even that space is pure consciousness alone, the mind alone, and like an illusion.
In reality, O Rāma, that world does not exist, nor does anything else; even for you, there is no existence of a world, for this is only Brahman that shines forth.
Whatever is past, present, and future, and whatever else there is—all this visible world is composed solely of mind and is nothing but consciousness.
As long as this reality of such a nature has not been fully understood in this way, it remains as firm as the essence of a diamond; yet once known, it is realized as the supreme, ultimate space.
Through ignorance, this very mind expands in such a manner by means of its surges and playful manifestations, like water in the ocean.

By the very sky of consciousness as it truly is, one's own mind attains the designation "manas"; by that, the expansive world of the visible is made manifest. Thus, it is spread out, yet nothing at all is spread out.
Śrī Rāma said: Now, how did Vītahavya extract his body from within that cavity of the earth while remaining there, and what became of him, and how?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Immediately thereafter, the mind named Vītahavya, whose nature is infinite, realized that it was nothing other than its own self, a mere manifestation of the Self’s own wonder.
Once, as this attendant of Śarva was spontaneously remembering Prāgjyotiṣa, a desire arose within him that was intent upon beholding all his previous births.
Then he beheld all his own bodies, some destroyed and others undestroyed; from among those that were undestroyed, he saw each one situated within its respective hollow.
By mere chance, the thought occurred to him to lift up that body; he saw it there, lying like a worm in the mud.
The body known as Vītahavya was crushed within a cavity of the earth, with a mass of mud upon its back brought there by the floods of the rainy season.
Having seen the earth’s surface thus covered with a network of grass, its skin and back made of clay, and constrained within the cavity of the earth by that one of great splendor;
Once again, with his mind possessed of supreme awakening, he reflected: "Because all my limbs are so tormented, my body is deprived of its vital breaths."
Once liberated, he is unable to move or act even in the slightest degree; knowing this, I shall quickly enter the body of the Sun.
"His attendant Piṅgala will then extract my body from there; or rather, what need have I for him? I shall simply remain at peace without any obstacle."
"I shall enter nirvāṇa; I go to my own state. What purpose is there for me in this mere play of the body?"—thus did Vītahavya reflect in his mind, O high-minded one.
Having remained silent for a moment on the ground, he reflected further: "Indeed, for me, neither the abandonment nor the preservation of this body is to be accepted."
"I shall enter the sun stationed in the sky like a reflection in a mirror"—thus the sage, assuming the form of the wind, entered the sun.

Having assumed a body consisting of the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka), like fire emerging from the opening of a bellows, the Blessed One, the Sage, likewise beheld that leader of sages situated within his heart.
Having seen it, that noble-minded one, reflecting on the sequence of past and future events, beheld within the hollow of the Vindhya mountain the body of the sage.
Moving through the midst of the sky, Bhanu (the Sun), perceiving what the Rishi intended to do, saw him lying unconscious, covered by grass and stones.
To rescue the sage from the earth, he commanded a leading host; that consciousness of the sage Vītahavya took the form of the city-constituent (puryaṣṭaka).
Having quickly honored Ravi with a mind full of devotion, she prostrated before him; and being permitted by Bhānu with due respect, she moved forward to his presence.
That Piṅgala, having left the sky, entered the cave-dwelling of the Vindhya mountains, which was tawny-hued and as beautiful as a young elephant in a forest thicket.

He reached the Vindhya forest, which shone like a garment of clouds intoxicated by the rainy season; there, with his claws tearing up the surface of the earth, he uprooted it from the womb of the world.
Then, like a crane drawing a lotus stalk from the mud, he withdrew his own subtle body—the city of eight—into the silent physical frame of the sage.
Circling in the expanse of the sky like a bird returning to its nest, the embodied Vītahavya and the sky-dweller bowed to one another.
Those two treasuries of splendor became solely intent upon their respective tasks; Piṅgala went into the sky, and the sage went to the pure lake.
Vītahavya quickly sank into the lake, which was like a lotus with stars for its filaments and the sun’s rays for its form, as it was filled with blossoming lotuses.

Like a young elephant in a forest at the edge of a muddy pool, having bathed there, performed his recitation, and worshipped the sun, he shone once again with a body adorned by his mind, just as before.

Endowed with that loving-kindness, supreme equanimity, and profound peace, as well as with true wisdom, sympathetic joy, compassion, and glory, the Sage—his mind liberated from all attachments—delighted for a full day on the bank of a river in the Vindhya mountains.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: At the end of the day, that sage once again entered a certain vast and well-known cave in the Vindhya mountains in order to compose his mind in meditative absorption.
Without abandoning that very contemplation of the Self, he who had seen the higher and lower worlds perceived everything with his mind as equal to the senses.
Long ago, the collection of my senses was clearly abandoned by me; now there is no purpose for me in further reflection or expansion of thought.
Having severed the conceptualization of "it exists" and "it does not exist," like a tender creeper, I remain as the remainder, fixed in my form like the peak of an immovable mountain.
Like the risen sun that has set, or like that which has set yet has risen; equal, appearing as the flavor of equanimity, I abide, having attained clarity.

Though awakened, I remain as if in deep sleep; though situated in deep sleep, I am like one who is awake. Taking hold of the fourth state (*turya*), I abide within the body with a motionless stability.
Standing like a pillar in solitude, with my mind established in all things, I abide free from affliction in the state of equanimity where the commonality of existence is the same everywhere.
Having reflected thus, he remained again in meditation for six days; then he attained awakening, like a traveler who has slept for a moment.
Then that blessed Vītahavya, a man of great asceticism, having attained perfection, dwelt for a long time in the state of liberation while yet alive.
He did not rejoice in what was favorable, nor did he ever disparage it; likewise, he experienced neither agitation nor did he attain elation.
Whether walking or standing still, this thought arose in his heart: "For the diversion of my distracted mind, let me engage in a discourse with myself."
O Lord of the group of imperishable senses, tell me, what kind of pervasive bliss and happiness has been attained by you, who possess such tranquility of mind?
Therefore, O best among the fickle, you must constantly maintain this very state of passionlessness and abandon all restlessness.
O you thieves of the senses! O you whose hopes are destroyed and whose names are ruined! This self does not belong to you, nor do you belong to the self.
As you depart, your share of destruction approaches; your hopes have been rendered fruitless. You, whose very foundations are fragile, are not capable of maintaining your hold.
This latent impression of yours that "I am the self" has indeed arisen from the forgetting of reality, like the perception of a snake in a rope that has been seen.
This notion of self in what is not-self, and this notion of reality in what is unreal, has arisen through lack of inquiry and perishes through inquiry.

"You are one thing, we are another, and Brahman is something else, intent on agency; the enjoyer is one thing and that which is consumed is another—what fault is there, and for whom, and of what kind?"
Wood is produced from forests; ropes come from bamboo and hide; the adze has iron blades; and the carpenter is intent on his meal.

Thus, just as in this world a firm and excellent house-structure is produced by a combination of materials, each possessing its own inherent capacity, occurring by chance like the "crow-and-palmyra" coincidence; so too [is the nature of reality].

Those who have attained perfection through a chance occurrence, their senses restrained by their own power—likewise, in this world of strife, whose fragmenting of whom can there be, for all are as fickle as a flickering flame?

Forgetfulness has been forgotten far away; mindfulness has been clearly recollected. What is real has become real, and what is unreal has become unreal; the wounded has perished, and that which was stable remains stable.
In this manner, that tiger among sages, the Lord of great asceticism, remained here for many groups of years engaged in such contemplation.
He always dwelt there, where reflection had reached its end for the sake of non-rebirth alone, and where delusion was situated far away.
Relying on the mere consolation of meditative absorption—which arises from seeing the flood of phenomena as they truly are, yet remains purposeless—he dwelt forever in a state of bliss.

When the perception of attachment to what is to be abandoned and acquisition of what is to be attained, as well as the perception of their rejection and taking up, had ceased, the mind of the sage Vītahavya transcended both desire and aversion.

At the boundary of birth and karma, in the state of disembodied liberation (videha-kevalībhāva), there arises a desire for the drinking of the nectar of the renunciation of attachment to worldly existence.

Having perceived the web of the world as something from which there is no returning, he likewise entered a golden cave on the Sahya mountain at the end of his life, quickly departing for that state where there is no more rebirth.
Remaining there in the bound lotus posture, he spoke within himself to himself: "O passion, go to passionlessness; O hatred, proceed to freedom from hatred."
For a very long time, I have sported here with you both; O enjoyments, salutations to you, for hundreds of millions of births!
Just as a child is cherished in the world by those who fondle him, so too have I been cherished by you in this supreme and meritorious path to Nirvana.
Homage, repeated homage, to that by which I was made to forget; O Suffering, it is through you being heated by me that I have diligently sought out the Self.
Therefore, this path has been taught to me by you; salutations be to you! By your grace, I have attained this cool state.

Homage to you, O reality of suffering, whose very nature is to bestow happiness upon that which is called suffering! May there be well-being for you, O friend, whose life is the essence of this worldly existence.
"This body remains, yet we depart to our own abode; alas, how strange is the destiny of living beings regarding their purposes!"
Even after undergoing hundreds of births, I shall eventually be separated from this body; therefore, O friend, you who have been my long-standing kinsman are now being abandoned by me.
By you alone was that destruction brought upon yourself through the power of self-knowledge; having attained the realization of the Self, you have brought about your own destruction.
Your body was not broken by another; rather, this was brought about by you yourself, while I lay still, as you, wretched and alone, withered away.
"O Mother Craving, you must not cause me suffering; I am departing. O Blessed One Desire, you must forgive those offenses born of my perversity."
"O Mother Tṛṣṇā, since you have finally, after a long time, brought about the complete subsiding of our faults, grant us this blessing!"
This separation caused by the fault of yoga is my final salutation; let there be homage to you, the god of virtuous deeds, who were formerly served by me.
Having been delivered from the hells, I was appointed to heaven for him who has grown upon the field of evil deeds and carries the trunk of hell.
Homage to the one who bears the weight of the flowers of the Teaching and whose branches are the suppression of evil deeds—he with whom I have long ago experienced many common births.
From this day forward, salutations to him who is invisible, whose nature is delusion, who speaks with a voice as sweet as a sounding flute, and who is clothed in leaves.
Homage to you, the female ascetic of the cave, my companion in meditative absorptions; for me, who am weary on the path of saṃsāra, you are the cause of consolation.
My very affectionate companion, who removes all greed, has been forsaken by me—who was distressed by every calamity—out of my own faults.
You alone are my supreme friend, resorted to for the sake of destroying my grief, providing a hand to grasp when I am in the pits and thickets of distress.
Salutations to you, the staff of wood, the sole friend in old age; it is like my own skeleton, with its framework of bones and its threads of blood and entrails.
O body, take only this much essence and depart; let there be salutations even to you for your various ways of agitating the water in bathing.
Homage be to worldly conventions; homage be to you, the cycles of existence! These, O sirs, are my innate and ancient friends.
In due course, my vital breaths have been drawn out; may it be well with you, for I am departing. Together with you, I shall pass through many diverse wombs.
He rested in mountain groves, and he grew weary among the realms of the world; he sported within the courtyards of cities and dwelt upon the mountains.
Whether engaged in the play of worldly affairs or set out upon various paths, there is nothing within the treasury of the universe that has not been shared by me with you.
Nothing has been done, nothing taken, nothing gone, nothing given, and nothing relied upon. Now, dear ones, you may go to your own directions; as for me, I am departing.
All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall; all unions end in separation—all things on the path of saṃsāra.
May this visual light enter the solar orb; may the forest flowers enter the consciousness of the bliss of fragrance.
Let the vital breath today enter the wind that stirs; let the powers of hearing sound enter the hollow of space.
May the powers of the essence of taste enter the lunar orb, like the ocean without Mount Mandara, or like a day when the sun has set.

Like a cloud in autumn, or like the creation at the end of an aeon, my own mental activity subsides of its own accord within the Self by means of the Self at the conclusion of the syllable *Oṃ*. I am like a flaming fire whose fuel is consumed, or like a lamp devoid of oil.

With the entire succession of activities vanished, my state transcends all conditions of the visible world; with my intellect stilled by following the peace of the *praṇava*, I stand here, free from the stain of delusion.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having thus reflected within himself, with his thoughts and desires stilled, he gradually uttered the Praṇava loudly, having attained the [highest] stage.
The ascetic, recollecting the Praṇava through the division of its parts beginning with the *mātrās*, [discovers] the pure and immutable essential nature by means of superimposition and negation.
Having abandoned all internal and external parts—whether gross or even more subtle—arising within the three worlds and fashioned by the imagination and its lack thereof.
Standing with an unshaken form within himself like a wish-fulfilling gem, he was like the full moon or Mount Mandara at rest.
Like a potter’s wheel brought to rest after its spinning, it was like the ocean—full, motionless, vast, and pure.
With its mass of light, heat, and darkness stilled, and devoid of sun, moon, and stars, it was as infinite as the autumnal sky, clear and free from smoke, clouds, and dust.
Together with the long-sounding thread of his breath ending in the *praṇava*, he cast off the web of the senses and their subtle elements, just as the wind scatters a scent.
Then he abandoned the mere state of darkness, which was like a vision appearing in the sky; it rose up with a throbbing form, just as a wise man might abandon a trace of anger.
Then, having reflected for half a moment upon that manifested splendor, he abandoned it; and at that time, there was neither darkness nor light.
Having reached that state, he destroyed with his mind that very mind—which was as fragile as a blade of grass—even as it quivered slightly, within half a moment.
Then, O dear one, consciousness becomes established in its own state, having attained a manifestation that is as pure and subtle as the cognition of a newborn infant.

In a period of time equal to half of half a blink of an eye, the Lord abandoned the state of being an object of consciousness for his own consciousness, just as the wind abandons its power of movement.
Then, having reached the state of visioning and thereafter the state of pure existence, he took hold of the state of deep sleep and remained as immovable as a mountain.
Then the Lord, having remained for a short while in the state of deep sleep again and again, attained stability within that deep sleep and reached the form of the Fourth State (turya).
There he was both joyless and joyful, both being and non-being; he was neither something nor nothing, like the light of that [reality] which is like darkness.
That which is called "not this, not this," consisting both of the non-conscious and the conscious—thence was that born which is beyond the range of even speech.
Then he became that most pure, vast, and supreme state, which pervades the interior of all existents yet is devoid of everything.
That which is the Void for the proponents of emptiness, the Supreme Brahman for the knowers of Brahman, and the stainless state of pure consciousness for the knowers of consciousness—[that is this].

He is the Puruṣa for those who hold the Sāṃkhya view, the Īśvara for the proponents of Yoga, Śiva for those marked by the crescent moon, and Kāla for those who maintain that Time alone is the sole reality.

For those who know the self, it is the self; for those whose selves are such, it is selflessness; and for the Mādhyamikas, whose minds are perfectly equanimous toward all things, it is the Middle Way.

That which is the established conclusion of all scriptures, that which conforms to the heart of all, that which is everything, omnipresent, and universal—he remains as that very reality, both being and non-being.

That which is the unsurpassed, motionless radiance even among all splendors, which consists solely of self-experience—whatever that is, he remains established as that very reality, both being and non-being.
That which is both one and many, both with taint and without taint, both all and not-all—that Reality, He remains as that very Being.

Then, in an instant, that Lord, whose state is even more stainless than the nature of space, remained established in that single, pure state—which is unborn, undecaying, beginningless, manifold yet one, both with parts and without parts.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having reached the very limit of worldly existence and arrived at the further shore of the ocean of suffering, the sage Vītahavya thus became stilled, free from further mental cogitation.
For when he had thus become tranquil and attained supreme peace, he was like a drop of water in the ocean, merged into his own transforming state.
Remaining thus motionless, that body fell into decay, having reached an inner state of witheredness like a lotus at the end of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Leaving their nest within the tree of his body, his vital breaths flew away like birds released from a snare, taking refuge in the heart-cavity.
All beings are entirely established within the elements; yet he whose body was a machine of flesh and bone dwelt upon the surface of the forest and the earth.

The elements of consciousness are established in the ocean of consciousness; they abide within the [material] elements. When the Sage has attained tranquility, everything abides in its own essential nature.
This rest of Vītahavya, rich with hundreds of reflections, has been told to you, O Rāma; discern it through your wisdom.
Having thus perceived the truth through this beautiful and kindled self-investigation, discern its essence and abide in it; arise, O Rāghava!
O Rāma, all this that has been described by me to you, as well as what I am describing today, or what I shall describe in the future—[all this is for your benefit].
By me, who perceives the three times, who lives eternally and for a long duration, all of that has indeed been personally investigated and seen.
Therefore, O Mahāmati, relying upon this stainless vision, attain supreme gnosis; for through gnosis, liberation is indeed obtained.

Through knowledge one attains freedom from suffering; through knowledge comes the destruction of ignorance; through knowledge alone, O Rāma, the supreme perfection is attained, and not from anything else in reality.
Having completely cut away every direction with his wisdom, the lord of sages Vītahavya has shattered the entire mountain of the mind.
That consciousness, whose nature is Vītahavya, [perceives] the world as a product of its own volition; it has experienced this very visible world as that world itself.
Vītahavya said: "The mind alone is the measure; the mind is the state of 'I-ness,' just as the senses are. This entire world is the mind—wherein then are difference and non-difference?"

Having realized the ultimate truth, with defects such as passion exhausted, and free from all impurities, transformations, limiting adjuncts, and attachments, the discerning one—who has long pursued his own inner nature—has attained the stainless, infinite state, with sorrow stilled.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, having brought yourself to the state of one who has known all that is to be known, like Vītahavya, remain forever free from passion, fear, and agitation.
For thirty thousand years, Vītahavya dwelt at ease, free from sorrow; in that same manner, O Rāghava, do you dwell.
And other sages of great intellect, O King, who have known that which is to be known, dwell in their own kingdoms; even so, O high-minded one, should you abide.
The self is never grasped through the sequences of pleasure and pain; though it is omnipresent, O mighty-armed one, why do you grieve in vain?
Many who have realized the self dwell here upon this earth; none of them, my dear, fall under the power of suffering as you do.
Be established in yourself, noble one; be equanimous, be happy. You are all-pervading, you are the Self itself; for you, there is no further rebirth.
Those like you, who are liberated while living, do not fall under the sway of the transformations of joy and resentment, just as lions do not come under the control of peacocks.
Śrī Rāma said: "In connection with this very topic, this doubt has arisen in me; like the autumn season [clearing] a cloud, may you dispel it for me."
O best among the knowers of the Self, why are powers such as traveling through the sky not seen here in the bodies of those who are liberated while living?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O scion of the Raghus, these things such as traveling through the sky and so forth are indeed the innate powers of objects, as established by authoritative means of knowledge.
O Rāma, that various web of activities which is seen and again traversed is merely the nature of objective things; it is not the view of those who know the Self.
O Rāghava, even one who knows the Self and is liberated may, through the power of substances, actions, rituals, time, and capacity, attain such things as traveling through the sky.
This is not the domain of one who knows the Self; for the knower of the Self is himself possessed of the Self. Satisfied by the Self within the Self, he does not pursue ignorance.
Whatever worldly phenomena there may be, they are known to consist of ignorance; how indeed could one who knows the Self, having abandoned ignorance, immerse himself in them?
Those who, by means of reasoning, establish even ignorance as being of the nature of happiness, are indeed composed of ignorance; they are not knowers of the Self, following such a course.

Whether one is a knower of reality or even one who has not attained the knowledge of reality, if they exert themselves in due order through time, substances, and actions, their upward movement and other [spiritual attainments] will be accomplished.
One who possesses the Self here has transcended everything and is free from desire; for being satisfied in the Self alone, he neither acts nor strives.
He has no concern for traveling through the sky, nor for supernatural powers, nor for enjoyments; neither for majesty, nor for honors, nor for hope, death, or life.
Ever-satisfied, with a tranquil self, free from passion and devoid of latent impressions, the knower of That, whose form is like space, abides in the Self.
Free from attachment, he is satisfied with both suffering and happiness that arrive unexpectedly, and with both life and death.
Like the ocean with the rivers, he remains within, honoring himself, whether by means of even or uneven objects encountered in their proper sequence.
He has no purpose whatsoever here through action, nor any through inaction; nor does he have any dependence on any being for any object of interest.
But he who, even though his self is unrefined, desires the nets of supernatural powers, accomplishes them gradually by means of the substances used for achieving those powers.
"This [world] is established in this very way through logic alone; such is the sequence of necessity, which cannot be rendered void even by the best of gods, such as the Three-Eyed One."
This is the very nature of things: their establishment is from themselves and not from another; they never abandon their fixed character, just as the moon does not abandon its coolness.
Neither the Omniscient One, nor the All-Knowing One, nor Mādhava, nor even Hara—indeed, no one at all—is able to act otherwise than according to destiny.
O Rāma, these powers—such as traveling through the sky and so forth—are born from the inherent nature of substances, time, actions, and the application of mantras.
Just as poisons kill, honey intoxicates, and fermented liquids and *madana* fruits cause vomiting; [so too does this medicine act].
Likewise, by virtue of their inherent nature, substances, time, and the sequence of actions—when joined with proper reasoning—swiftly and certainly accomplish the application.
O sinless Rāghava, for one who has transcended this [world] and abandoned ignorance, there exists neither agency nor non-agency regarding self-knowledge.
The logical applications regarding substance, place, action, and time do not in any way assist those who possess right knowledge in attaining the state of the Supreme Self.
He who possesses some desire is fully capable of accomplishing spiritual success; however, for the self-knowing one who is complete, no desire arises anywhere.
O sinless one, since the arising of the attainment of the Self occurs only when the entire web of desires has been stilled, how and why could a desire, which is its opposite, ever arise?
In whatever way a person’s desire arises, he strives accordingly; and at the proper time, he attains that result, whether he be wise or even more ignorant than that.
Vītahavya did not strive at all for the desire for knowledge; however, one who desires knowledge strives quickly, just as he [the deer] rose up in the forest.

In this way, the various accomplishments (siddhis) born of time, ritual action, substances, reasoning, and intrinsic nature—each acquired through its own sequence—will be realized exactly as one desires.
O Rāma, those garlands of fruits called "accomplishments" (siddhi) which were obtained by someone have been attained by him from the tree of his own exertion.
For the great ones who are eternally contented, who possess that knowledge, whose selves are purified, and who have set out upon their true quest, supernatural powers do not provide any assistance.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin, I have this doubt: why was that body of Vītahavya not devoured by carnivorous beasts, and why did it not decay upon the surface of the earth?
O Lord, tell me exactly how that Vītahavya, having gone to the forest at that very time, quickly attained the state of disembodied liberation.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O virtuous one, that consciousness which is entwined by the thread of the impurity of latent desires becomes, in this world, a partaker in the burning experience of the states of pleasure and pain.
But that [body], consisting of pure consciousness alone and freed from latent impressions, remains as a subtle body; for once it is severed, no one here has the power to rejoin it.
Listen, O mighty-armed one, by what reasoning a yogi is not overcome even by delusions such as the dissolution of the body, even over many hundreds of years.
Whenever and upon whatever object the mind falls, it quickly becomes composed of that very thing at that very moment.
For when one sees an enemy, the mind undergoes transformation; likewise, when one sees a friend, the state of being well-disposed is experienced by oneself.
But when one encounters a traveler, a tree, or a mountain that is devoid of passion and hatred, it is experienced directly that one becomes likewise free from passion and hatred.
One develops greed for what is delicious, becomes indifferent toward what is unpalatable, and experiences a sense of distaste for what is bitter; this is experienced by oneself.
Whenever and wherever the predatory mind falls upon the body of an ascetic, which is enriched by the play of equanimous consciousness, it immediately attains a state of equanimity.
Because he is liberated from all attachments, he does not engage in cutting or other such acts, just as a traveler on the road does not engage in the village chores of a villager within the village.
Having gone near the body of the yogin, it indeed attains a predatory nature; whatever occurs there quickly takes on that very form—of this there is no doubt.
Thus, by predatory beasts—tigers, lions, insects, and reptiles—the body of Vītahavya, resting upon the surface of the earth, was not torn apart.
Consciousness exists everywhere—in wood, clods of earth, stones, and so forth—abiding in the form of the universal property of existence (sattāsāmānya), like one who is mute or a child.
The slender one is seen only as something floating and flickering within the subtle bodies (puryaṣṭakas), like reflections in water.
By means of that uniform perception of earth, water, air, and fire, O Rāghava, Vītahavya’s body was rendered free from modification.
Listen further to me, O Rāma: vibration is the cause of destruction; and that modification arises either from the mind or from the wind within the structure of the world.
The vitalizing of the vital breaths is their vibration; when that ceases, they become like stones. Since they remained steady through concentration (dhāraṇā), his body was not destroyed.
For one in whom neither mental nor physical vibration exists, internally or externally, both Prakṛti and Kṣaya remain far away.
O best among the knowers of reality, when vibration has become stilled both internally and externally, the elements never abandon their established state within the body.

When the vibration of the body, which consists of the wind of the mind, has thus become completely stilled, the bodily constituents attain a mountain-like stability, their nature being thoroughly congealed.
And so it is seen in the world that when vibration ceases, there is a firm stability; like wood, the limbs of the wise remain unshakable, like those of a corpse.
Thus, for thousands of years, the bodies of yogins in this world do not decay nor do they disintegrate, like clouds submerged in water.
At that very moment, listen, did not Vītahavya—knower of reality, the best among those who have known what is to be known—attain peace by casting off his body?
For those who have understood what is to be known, who are free from passion, and possess great intelligence—all of them, having severed their fetters, remain independent while abiding in the body.
Neither destiny, nor past actions—whether from previous lives or this one—nor even latent impressions (vāsanā) are at all capable of restraining their mind.
Therefore, my dear, for those who know reality, the mind—acting by chance like the "crow-and-the-palm-fruit" coincidence—quickly brings to full completion whatever it contemplates.
By a chance encounter, like the falling of a palm fruit upon a crow, Vītahavya’s consciousness was awakened to his life, and that very life was immediately made firm.

But when his intuitive insight (pratibhā) attained the state of being liberated from the body, he then became one liberated while in the bodyless state (videhamukta), established in absolute sovereignty.
The mind, freed from latent impressions, swiftly attains liberation; when it arises as the self, whatever it desires comes to pass in an instant, for Maheśvara is composed of all powers.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For when the mind, through inquiry, has become as if set, then indeed the qualities such as friendliness arose within Vītahavya.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Sage, O Lord, you have stated that when the nature of the mind has vanished through the dawning of inquiry, qualities such as friendliness (maitrī) arise. How is this so?"
O best among speakers, tell me: when the mind has dissolved into Brahman, for whom do qualities such as loving-kindness exist, or where do they manifest?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The dissolution of the mind is of two kinds: with form and indeed without form. That which is with form belongs to one liberated while living; that which is without form arises from liberation from the body.

The existence of the mind here leads to suffering, whereas the destruction of the mind leads to happiness; having brought the existence of the mind to exhaustion, one should cause the mind to reach its cessation.
Know that the mind which exists as the cause of birth, pervaded by the dark nets of latent impressions (vāsanā), leads solely to suffering.
That mind which, ignorant of reality, highly esteems its own past accumulation of qualities as "mine," is called the suffering *jīva*.
As long as the mind exists, how can there be an end to suffering? When the mind has set for a living being, saṃsāra has come to its end.
Know that the mind, which exists here as the very root of suffering, firmly grasped and motionless, is the sprout of the forest of the tree of suffering.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, whose mind is lost, or what would it be like when lost? What would its destruction be like, and what is the nature of that destruction’s existence?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O best among those who know how to inquire, O scion of Raghu’s lineage, I have already described the existence of the mind; now hear from me concerning its destruction.
They know the mind of that steadfast one to be dead, whom the states of pleasure and pain do not dislodge from equanimity, just as breaths do not move the king of mountains.
The thought "this is I" and "this is not I" diminishes the Supreme among Men; those whose minds are not destroyed within do not perceive this.
They know that the mind of one whom adversity, wretchedness, enthusiasm, intoxication, languor, or great festivity do not lead to deformity is lost.
O virtuous one, this is the destruction of the mind; here, the mind becomes destroyed. This state of the destruction of the *citta* belongs to the one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
O sinless one, know that state to be delusion; when that perishes, then the quality of goodness (sattva), which is designated as the destruction of the mind, fully arises.
O Rāghava, for that one who is a plaything of pure being, whose mind has perished, and whose nature is that of liberation while living, some have applied the designation "mind."

O sinless one, the mind that is endowed with qualities such as loving-kindness possesses the highest latent impression; it is liberated from further birth and is the mind of one who is liberated while living.
O Rāma, that state of the mind of one liberated while living, which is pervaded by a latent impression that is itself freed from rebirth, is called *sattva*.

Because it has been experienced right now and is attained as a reality, this dissolution of the mind—which is subtle, conjoined with the body, and possesses form—belongs to the one liberated while living (jīvanmukta).

Then, like the rays of the moon, the qualities beginning with loving-kindness and culminating in sympathetic joy remain at all times and in every way established within the dissolution of the mind of one liberated while living.
In the Himalaya known as Sattva—the dissolution of the mind of one liberated while living—the riches of virtue blossom like flower clusters in spring.
But that formless dissolution of the mind which I have described, O scion of Raghu, exists as the disembodied liberated one (videhamukta), consisting of the partless Self.
Even a being endowed with all the foremost qualities dissolves into the stainless, supremely purifying state that is liberation beyond the body.

In that state concerning the disembodied liberated one, which consists of the dissolution of the sattva-guṇa and the destruction of mental constructs—known as Virūpa—not even the slightest thing exists.
Therein there are neither virtues nor vices, neither prosperity nor adversity, nor any longing; there is neither rising nor setting, nor any cognitions of joy or resentment.
There is neither light nor darkness, neither twilight, day, nor night; there are no directions, nor space, nor below, nor the nature of misfortune.
There is no latent impression, no construction, neither effort nor lack of effort, no attachment; there is neither being nor non-being, for that state is indeed not something to be accomplished.

It was like a sky devoid of darkness, yet filled with splendor by the canopy of clouds, the moon, the sun, and the wind; it was equal to that [sky] in autumn, clear, free from twilight, and radiant without dust.
For those who have reached the further shore of both awakening and the wandering in saṃsāra, their vast abode is like the sky for the winds.

In that state where suffering is completely stilled, which is non-inert by nature, tranquil with bliss as if in deep sleep, and free from the qualities of rajas and tamas—there dwell the great ones, bodiless yet possessing bodies as vast as the expanse of space, in whom every fragment of the mind has dissolved.

Śrī Rāma said: [I saw] the mountain that is the treasury of the supreme ether, upon which grow the trees of the various worlds; it is variegated with the flowers of the stars and filled with the birds of gods and asuras.
Its borders were adorned with sprouts of dark clouds garlanded by flashes of lightning; it was delightful in all seasons, jagged with the beautiful clusters of the moon and sun.
It is encircled by seven oceans and lakes, enchanting with hundreds of rivers, and it is the source of sustenance for infinite beings of fourteen kinds.
O Brahmin, [this is the fruit] of the spreading vine of worldly existence (*saṃsṛti*), which has spread its net and taken root, having invaded the forest of the world.

Of this creeper whose joints are old age and death, which bears a succession of fruits that are pleasure and pain, whose roots are firmly established, and which is watered by the libations of delusion;
What is the seed? And what is said to be the seed of that seed? Furthermore, what is the seed of that [seed], and what would be the seed of that as well?
O best among speakers, please explain all this again in brief for the further increase of my understanding and for the attainment of the essence of knowledge.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, know that the body is the seed of the creeper of worldly existence, containing within it the great sprouts of good and evil whose dense development is yet to unfold.
Thick with the spreading of its branches and abounding in fruits and shoots, this earth has become flourishing through him, like the earth in autumn.
The mind, which follows the dictates of desire, is the seed of this body—the treasury of states of existence and non-existence, and the casket for the jewels of suffering.
From the mind alone this entire network of limbs, both existent and non-existent, arises intensely; likewise, this is experienced by oneself within the delusions of dreams.
Just as a city arises from the conceptualization of a gandharva, so indeed does a body—resplendent with its form and provided with windows—arise from the mind.

Whatever worldly object there is that is capable of being perceived and comes within the range of vision, that form is an expansion of the mind, just as the state of being a jar and so forth is an expansion of clay.
There are two seeds for the tree of the mind, which bears the creepers of its functions: one is the movement of the vital breath, and the second is firm conceptualization.
When the vital breath vibrates, intent upon contacting the channels, then the mind consisting of pure awareness quickly arises.
When the vital breath does not vibrate within the hollows of the channels of the head, due to the power of non-perception, the mind is no longer born within.

This very vibration of the vital breath is perceived through the gateway of the mind; it has come into being as that which is called the "world" within the void, appearing in such a manner like the blueness and other qualities [of the sky].
When the vibration of the vital breath has fallen asleep, its cessation is called peace; through the movement of the vital breath, consciousness moves like a ball that has been struck.
Consciousness flashes forth within bodies, awakened by the vibration of the vital breath, like a ball struck by the hand that rolls through the courtyard in a series of circular turns.
The existent, all-pervading consciousness is awakened by the vibration of the vital breath; its form is subtler than the subtlest, like a trace of fragrance carried by the wind.
Know, O Rāghava, that the supreme good lies in the restraint of consciousness; where there is the mastery over causes, there no agitation exists.
Consciousness itself, having quickly arisen, eagerly moves toward the object of cognition; from that act of perceiving, infinite sufferings then arise for the mind.
When consciousness abides for the sake of awakening within deep sleep, then that stainless state—the goal to be attained—has been attained.
Therefore, if you do not cause consciousness to swell through the vibrations of the vital breaths and the impulses of latent impressions, then you are unborn.
Know that the mind is the swelling of consciousness; by it this world is spread out—a web of misfortunes that cuts down and destroys the lives of living beings.
Yogins practice the restraint of the vital breath for the sake of pacifying the mind, through breath-control exercises, meditations, and applications devised by skillful means.
The wise know that the auspicious health of consciousness, which bestows the fruit of the mind's tranquility and is the supreme cause of equanimity, is the restraint of the flow of the vital breaths.
O Rāghava, hear now about this other origin of the mind, which has been revealed and experienced by those possessed of knowledge—a mind whose very life is its latent impressions (vāsanā).
The firm cultivation that involves abandoning prior and subsequent deliberation regarding an object, and the grasping of that object—this is proclaimed as *vāsanā*.
O mighty-armed one, whatever has been cultivated by him through intense spiritual urgency, that alone he quickly becomes, having lost all memory of other things.
A person of such a nature, rendered helpless by latent impressions (vāsanā), becomes deluded, thinking that whatever he perceives is a real entity.

Due to the helplessness caused by the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), that [mind] abandons its true nature; one with false vision perceives everything as delusory, like one under the influence of intoxication.
One who possesses incorrect knowledge alone becomes overwhelmed by mental anguish, being brought under its sway by the latent impression residing within, as if by poison.
Since false vision is the cultivation of the notion of a self in that which is not the self, know that, O Rāghava, it is the mind that perceives substantiality in what is unsubstantial.
Due to the singular latent impression (*vāsanā*) of objects resulting from firm habitual practice, the extremely restless mind arises as the cause of birth, old age, and death.
When nothing whatsoever is projected in the form of things to be rejected or accepted, and one abides having abandoned everything, then the mind is not born.
When the mind, due to the absence of latent impressions, no longer perceives anything at all, then the state of no-mind arises, which bestows supreme tranquility.
When nothing whatsoever flashes within consciousness, like a cloudless sky, then the mind is not born within, like a lotus in the ether.
When no entity is cultivated with regard to any object whatsoever in the world, then how can the mind arise within the empty expanse of the heart?
O Rāghava, I consider this alone to be the nature of the mind: that it conceives of an internal object as being a real entity through its own inherent relish.
Therefore, for one who meditates on the visible world as nothing fit for conceptualization, how could the arising of the mind occur in that which is as pure as the expanse of space?
That which consists in relying on the non-contemplation of something, the contemplation of the non-existence of that thing, and the seeing of things as they truly are—that is called "non-mind."
That mind which, having completely renounced everything within, abides in a cooled state—even while engaged in worldly activity—is declared to be of the nature of non-existence.
He for whom attachment does not exist due to the absence of relishing habitual tendencies—his mind has reached the state of non-mind; that is called true being (sattva).
He whose latent impressions (vāsanā) are no longer dense enough to cause rebirth is liberated while living; established in pure being (sattva), he remains like the whirling of a potter’s wheel.
Those whose latent impressions (vāsanās) are devoid of flavor—like parched seeds, free from rebirth—are indeed established as liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
Having attained minds whose nature is pure being (*sattva*), they have reached the further shore of gnosis; they are said to be "mindless," for at the end of the body they take on the form of space.
O Rāma, there are two seeds of the mind: the vibration of the vital breath and latent impressions. When one of these two is exhausted, both are quickly destroyed.
For these two are mutual causes for the birth of the mind, O Rāma, just as water and the vessel are for the production of a water-jar.
He for whom there is no dense latent impression (*vāsanā*) that brings about rebirth—these two [the seed and the sprout] exist like sesame and its oil.
Inseparable and eternal, as well as requiring time and sequence, this [reality]—which consists of consciousness and has the nature of awareness—produces everything.
When both bliss and breath, together with the vital breath and the senses, arise from the mind along with their latent impressions, at that time [the state of consciousness occurs].

Just as fragrance resides in a flower and oil in sesame seeds, so do latent impressions (vāsanā) reside [in consciousness]; from the force of these impressions comes the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa), and from that, the impressions arise once more.
Through that, the sequence of seed and sprout arises for the seed of the mind, due to the surging of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) by means of the activity that agitates consciousness.

It awakens the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa), and through that, the mind (citta) is born; because its nature is to vibrate, the vital breath vibrates when it has touched the quality of the heart.
Awakening consciousness through that, the childish mind is born; for thus, both latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*) are its two causes.
Upon the destruction of one of these two, O Raghava, there is the destruction of both for the mind; pleasure and pain are the vibration of the mind, which is the great fruit of the body.
It has the form of sprouting effects, is entwined by the creepers of ritual actions, is coiled around by the black serpent of craving, and is the dwelling place for the cranes of passion and disease.
Indeed, the tree of the mind—with its root of ignorance firmly established and its birds of the senses hidden within—has had its latent impressions destroyed in an instant.
The torrent of wind causes it to fall, just like a fruit ripened by time, turning all directions white and obscuring every sight.
This body has the appearance of a flickering cloud, arisen from the pit of ignorance; it is pervaded by the blades of grass that are craving, and it has the form of a pillar.
With its body throbbing and slightly agitated toward the upward leap of bliss, it perceives the great light situated within and dissolves away.

And by the cessation of the movement of the vital breath, O Rāma, the dust of the mind is instantly stilled; for these two—the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the movement of the vital breath—are mutually dependent.

The object of consciousness is said to be the seed, for from it those two—the vibration of the vital breath and the latent impression—emanate; having reached the object of consciousness within the heart, they then arise.

Therefore, that which is to be experienced arises; this is said to be the seed of these two. Through the complete relinquishing of the object of experience, the latent impressions of the vibration of the vital breath cease.
Know that consciousness and its object perish quickly along with their roots—like a tree when its root is severed—if there is no steadfastness, which is the seed [of liberation].
An object of cognition cannot exist, just as a sesame seed devoid of oil; nothing whatsoever exists as a separate object of cognition, neither externally nor internally.
Consciousness, vibrating through its own volition, perceives an object of perception from itself; just as one sees one's own death in a dream, so too does one perceive residence in another land.
Through the application of its own wonder, the object of perception belongs to consciousness; where the self-awareness of consciousness exists by virtue of its own volition.
Therefore, O descendant of Raghu, this entire web of the world appears just as a ghost might appear to a child, arising from its own imagination.

Just as the state of being a person is perceptible to a post, so too is it to consciousness; just as the stick-like form or the dust-like nature belongs to the rays of the moon and sun, so it is here.
Just as the movement of mountains situated on a boat is perceived [as real] by consciousness, so too is the object of perception; for this is indeed false, and through right knowledge it dissolves.

Just as the state of being a snake exists in a rope, or the appearance of two moons from one's own faulty vision, so too pure consciousness alone is the three worlds and all that is knowable; there is nothing else whatsoever.
The wise know that such an internally established certainty is right knowledge (samyagjñāna), whatever may appear to it, whether previously seen or unseen.
One who understands this must strive with effort to cleanse consciousness; for it is merely the failure to cleanse it that constitutes attachment to the great cycle of saṃsāra.
The mere cleansing of that [defilement] is experienced as liberation; whereas consciousness leads to infinite suffering, which consists of rebirth.

Be one who is non-cognitive yet not insentient, because you do not produce the nature of pleasure; be one who is sentient yet free from [worldly] bliss, having abandoned all perception. O scion of Raghu, you are that very Self which is awakened and beyond the reach of perception.
Śrī Rāma said: O Lord, what is one who is neither inert nor devoid of consciousness like? And how is it that inertia ceases when there is an absence of such consciousness?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: He who is established in non-abiding everywhere and finds rest nowhere at all, that living being perceives nothing; for he is indeed consciousness itself, not inert matter.
He for whom no objective support consisting of the perception of objects exists here is called non-conscious yet non-inert, even while performing hundreds of tasks.
The space of the heart is not tainted even slightly by that which is to be experienced; he whose consciousness is non-inert is called one liberated while living.
When nothing whatsoever is cultivated within oneself due to the state of being free from latent impressions (nirvāsana), one remains steadfast, like the consciousness of an infant or a mute.
Then the wise one takes refuge in that pervasive, pure perception which is entirely free from dullness, because of which he is no longer defiled.
For one who has abandoned all latent impressions through non-conceptual meditative absorption, a vast bliss unfolds, like the blueness [appearing] from the sky.

There the yogins abide, possessing consciousness yet free from [dualistic] cognition; because they have become one with that, even that [consciousness], which is without beginning or end, dissolves within.
Whether walking, standing, touching, or even smelling, he is called by that [name]: non-inert, with bliss dissolved, having abandoned all perception, and happy.
Relying upon this view, through arduous and diligent effort, cross to the further shore of the ocean of suffering, O ocean of boundless virtues!
Just as from a seed a great tree arises in time and pervades the sky, so too does this unreal world of perception arise from one's own volition.
Whenever consciousness, having repeatedly formed a mental resolve, assumes its own form, that very consciousness becomes the seed of this web of births.
O Rāghava, know that consciousness itself, having produced itself by itself and deluding itself again and again, leads itself inward to liberation.
Whatever she contemplates, that very thing she becomes in an instant; though liberated from the plane of existence, her body does not return for a long time.
He is neither a god, nor a celestial being, nor a rakṣasa, nor a yakṣa, nor a kinnara, nor a human; it is the Self alone that, through its primordial playfulness, performs the dance of the world.
Having bound itself and wept like a silkworm, consciousness eventually attains its solitary state by its own inherent nature after a long time.
The pure water of consciousness has entered the nets of the oceans of the world; it alone flashes forth as the unprecedented circle of directions, having attained a state of non-duality.
Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions—these are said to be the waves of this continuous expanse of the water of consciousness.
"The entire world is mere consciousness; there is no second conceptualization. By such right knowledge, consciousness does not pass into otherness.
When one finds nothing at all, neither throbbing nor trembling, and abides solely in one's own self, then consciousness is no longer stained.
Now, O Rāma, it is said that pure existence (*sanmātra*) is the seed of this consciousness; from pure consciousness alone does this [universe] arise, just as luminosity arises from light.
Therein, existence has two forms: one remains in various shapes, while the second is of a single form; hear now this distinction between the two.
That which exists in various forms through the differentiation of the nature of being is described as "pot-ness," "cloth-ness," "thou-ness," and "I-ness."
But having set aside its divisions, existence, which is extended through its nature as a single essence, is declared to have a single form by way of its universal alone.
Having completely abandoned all particularity, that which is pure existence alone, untainted, uniform, and the great form—that they know to be the state of Being.
Form, by virtue of its manifold shapes, can never exist as something not perceived within existence; therefore, this [notion of form] is without a real objective basis.
But that form which is of a single nature, whose essence is stainless existence, never undergoes destruction nor does it ever become subject to forgetfulness.
Whether it be the existence of time, the existence of parts, or this existence of objects—having abandoned the conceptualization of such divisions, become solely intent upon pure Being alone.
Although temporal existence and self-existence, being free from all mental constructs, are of the nature of the supreme reality, nevertheless, they are not ultimately real.
How can that which is seen to be the cause of manifoldness—wherein the calculation of divisions yields distinct categories—be purifying?
Cultivating the single universal existence that permeates your entire being, remain filled with perfect supreme bliss, pervading all the quarters of space.
O Lord of the Wise, that very limit which is existence as mere generality has become the seed of this [universe], and from that alone it proceeds.
That primordial state, which is devoid of all mental construction, which is without beginning or end, and which extends to the limit of universal existence—of that, no seed exists.
Therein existence enters into dissolution and remains changeless; having attained its footing there, a person does not return again to suffering.
It is the cause of all causes, yet no cause for it is found; it is the essence of all essences, yet from it no further essence is found.
Within that vast mirror, all these perceptions of objects are reflected, just as trees on the bank are reflected in a lake.
All these phenomena there become delicious to the ocean of the virtuous, and they manifest like the six flavors to the tongue.
Therefore, even for the sky of consciousness which is more transparent than the clearest, that is both the state and the sufficient tasting of all varieties of flavors.
O dear one, it is there that the multitudes of worlds are born, exist, grow, or are touched; they remain and eventually dissolve.
He is the heaviest among those who are heavy, the lightest among those who are light, the grossest among those who are gross, and the most minute among those who are minute.
It is the most distant for those who are far away, yet it is near to those who are close; it is the smallest among the small, and likewise the greatest among the great.
O dear one, that is the light even among lights, that is the darkness even among darknesses; it is the reality even among realities, and it is the supreme direction even among directions.
Therefore, that which is both nothing and something exists as it is and does not exist; that which is visible and invisible is both "I am that" and "I am not that."
O sinless Rāma, act in such a way that you may attain a firm standing in that most purifying state through every possible effort.

That is the stainless, ageless reality of the Self; upon realizing it, the mind attains peace. Having realized the nature of that vast oneness, you shall long ago become one who has reached the state liberated from the fear of worldly existence.
Śrī Rāma said: O giver of honor, these seeds have been described by you; by the application of which one is swiftly attained to that state?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Whichever remedy I have declared for each of these seeds of suffering, by the application of that very remedy, the supreme state is swiftly attained.
If, by means of human effort, one forcibly abandons latent impressions at once upon reaching that state which stands at the pinnacle of universal existence, [then liberation is attained].
O knower of reality, you maintain a state that is imperishable even for a moment; in this very instant, you shall fully attain that auspicious state.
Or if, my friend, you establish yourself in the form of universal existence (sattāsāmānya), you will attain that state here with only a slight additional effort.
O sinless one, if you remain with your meditation established in the principle of pure consciousness (saṃvittattva), then through that superior effort you shall attain that supreme state.
O Rāghava, meditation is not possible upon a solitary object of perception, because this consciousness is always present everywhere.
Whatever you think, whatever you go toward, whatever you stand upon, and whatever you do—in each and every instance, consciousness is present; it is consciousness alone that is that very thing.
And if you exert effort in the complete abandonment of latent impressions (vāsanā), then all mental and physical afflictions will instantly fall into a state of laxity.
Indeed, this abandonment of latent impressions (vāsanā) is considered more difficult than all previous efforts; it is harder to accomplish even than uprooting Mount Sumeru.
As long as the mind has not dissolved, there is no destruction of latent impressions; and as long as the latent impressions have not been destroyed, the mind does not come to rest.
As long as there is no realization of reality, how can there be tranquility of mind? As long as there is no pacification of the mind, there is no knowledge of reality.

As long as the destruction of latent impressions has not occurred, how can there be the realization of reality? As long as the attainment of reality has not occurred, there is no destruction of latent impressions.
Knowledge of reality, the dissolution of the mind, and the destruction of latent impressions have become mutual causes for one another; therefore, they remain difficult to accomplish.
Therefore, O Rāghava, having abandoned the desire for enjoyment far away with discerning human effort, one should diligently take refuge in these three.
In every respect, as long as these have not been repeatedly well-practiced, the attainment of the state does not occur even in hundreds of aeons.

O Mahāmati, O Sage, the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the destruction of consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the dissolution of the mind (*manas*)—when practiced for a long time, these become fruit-bearing simultaneously.
Even if these are practiced individually for a long time, they do not grant accomplishment, like mantras that have been bound.
Even though these have been cultivated over a long period and even by one of keen intellect, they are unable to be mastered individually, just like soldiers [who cannot be led alone].
For when these are brought to equal exertion by the wise man, they cut through the ocean of saṃsāra, just as waters erode the slopes of a mountain.

The exhaustion of latent impressions, the dissolution of the intellect, and the destruction of the mind must be cultivated with effort simultaneously for a long time; by that means, my dear son, you shall not be stained.
When these three are practiced for a long time, the firm knots of the heart are severed without remainder, just as fibers are cut by the snapping of a lotus stalk.
O Rāma, this state of worldly existence has been practiced for hundreds of previous births; it is never extinguished except through the yoga of long-term cultivation.
Whether walking, hearing, touching, smelling, standing, waking, or sleeping, remain devoted to the practice of these three for the sake of your supreme welfare.

The knowers of reality understand that the restraint of the vital breath is equal to the complete abandonment of latent impressions; therefore, one should practice it in this manner even at that time.
Through the complete abandonment of latent impressions, the mind attains the state of non-mind; and through the cessation of the movement of the vital breath—do as you wish.

Through long practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), by means of the method imparted by the guru, and through the application of postures and diet, the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇaspanda) is restrained.
Because one sees things as they truly are, habitual tendencies do not arise; that which remains non-deceptive throughout the beginning and end of all things is established.
Form is that which is seen; by that, knowledge and its latent impressions are exhausted, because of acting without attachment and because of abandoning the cultivation of existence.
Because one perceives the destruction of the body, latent impressions do not arise; when the manifestation of latent impressions is destroyed, the mind does not function.
Just as dust in the sky subsides when the movement of the wind has ceased, so too indeed does the movement of the mind cease when the movement of the vital breath has ceased.

Therefore, just as dust arises from refuse and the like in this world, [so do afflictions arise]; thus, a wise person should exert themselves with great effort to conquer the movement of the vital breath.
Sitting down again and again with a one-pointed mind, or else, having abandoned this sequence, if there is merely the act of seizing the mind;
Whatever one desires, one attains that state after a long time; yet it is not possible to conquer the mind without blameless method.
Just as a wild and wicked elephant cannot be controlled without a goad, so too is the attainment of inner knowledge and association with the virtuous [necessary].
The complete abandonment of latent impressions and the cessation of the movement of the vital breath—these, indeed, are the mature methods for conquering the mind.
Those who, despite these existing methods by which [the mind] is quickly conquered—just as dust on the ground is subdued by showers of rain—seek to restrain it through force, [act in vain].
Those deluded ones who strive to conquer the mind by force are like those who, having cast aside a lamp, seek to destroy darkness with collyrium; they only succeed in striking down the light.
They bind the intoxicated king of serpents with lotus fibers; or rather, they bind their own body, which is not far from the mind, to that very mind.
Those who seek to accomplish their goals by abandoning reason are known as *haṭhas*; they go from fear to fear and pass from affliction to affliction.
Like wretched beings, they find no relief; subsisting on fruits and sprouts, they wander among the mountain peaks.
With minds utterly bewildered and terrified like wretched deer, her delicate-limbed intelligence has its very body lopped off and shattered.
One should never place trust in them, just as a doe that has entered a village does not; their minds are as turbulent with waves as water in a calamity.

Like a blade of grass cast far away by falling into mountain torrents, one is carried off by the delusions of performing sacrifices, ascetic penances, giving gifts, visiting sacred fords, and worshipping deities throughout the course of time.
Some rare individuals, though long possessed by mental afflictions, eventually destroy them through the power of destiny, just as deer do.
Burning with hundreds of the defects of suffering, they—subject to coming and going, impermanent, and passing through hells, heavens, and human realms—either perceive or do not perceive [the truth].
Taking forms that rise and fall like balls, they go from here to hell, thence to heaven, and right back here again.
They return again and again like ripples upon a lake; therefore, O descendant of Raghu, abandon this false view.

Relying upon pure consciousness, become steady and free from passion; for only the one possessed of knowledge possesses happiness, only the one possessed of knowledge truly lives, and only the one possessed of knowledge is powerful—therefore, become composed of knowledge.

O Great-souled One, perceiving the single, primordial, and unsurpassed state of pure consciousness—which is devoid of all that is to be experienced and free from conceptualization—abide within your very heart, free from mental constructs. Having attained the state of non-agency while performing action, may you possess the glory arising from peace.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: He by whom even a slight restraint of his own mind has been achieved through even a moment’s inquiry has attained the fruit of birth.
This subtle spark of reflection that flickers within the heart, through the practice of yoga, comes to branch out in a hundred directions.
Pure qualities resort to a man of somewhat mature discernment who is preceded by dispassion, just as birds resort to a lake full of water.
Even vast manifestations of ignorance do not at all overcome the wise person who investigates correctly and perceives things as they truly are.
What do sense objects, as well as mental fluctuations, afflictions, or even physical ailments, do here to one whose mind is firmly established in right vision?
Where have the Puṣkarāvarta clouds—filled with swirling winds and rosy with masses of lightning—been grasped by the fists of children?
Where, by a charming woman, has the moon situated in the midst of the sky been bound with charming jewel-caskets, mistaking them for lovely blue lotuses?
Where are those elephants, whose heads are adorned with blue lotuses from which swarms of bees fly out from their temples, now being tormented by mosquitoes as sweet as the sighs of charming women?
Lions, enraged in battle and possessing rows of beautiful claws gleaming with pearls fallen from elephants' temples, were trampled by deer.
Where are the hungry pythons, who, having devoured the towering forest trees by consuming their resinous exudations ignited by poison, have now been swallowed by agitated young frogs?
How can a wise man who has attained his livelihood, who knows what is to be known, and who possesses discernment, be truly overcome by the bandits of the sense objects and the senses?
The enemies that are the sense-objects carry away the immature intellect, just as a fierce wind sweeps away a tender creeper whose stem has been severed.

Those of evil intent are unable to shatter even a small portion of his mature discernment, just as gentle breezes cannot move a mountain that remains utterly steadfast against the great upheavals of the cosmic dissolution.
The whirlwind of anxiety shakes the tree of the flower of inquiry only if it has not firmly grasped the great seat; it cannot shake that which is well-established in a steady state.
Whether walking or standing, waking or even sleeping, he whose mind is not composed of inquiry is said to be dead.
"What might this world be? What might the body be?"—pondering thus slowly and incessantly with the vision of the inner self, either by yourself or together with virtuous people.
Through discernment that swiftly dispels darkness, the supreme state—the stainless reality—is seen, just as by a radiant lamp.
Through knowledge, the destruction of all sufferings arises, just as darkness is dispelled by the sun through the play of its light.
When knowledge has become manifest, the object of knowledge arises in its full clarity, just as pure light appears upon the earth when the sun has risen.
That illumination by which the reality of Brahman is awakened through scriptural inquiry is said to exist as if non-different from the object of knowledge.
O dear one, the wise know that the self-knowledge arising from investigation is true knowledge; the object of knowledge exists within it, just as sweetness exists within milk.
A person who possesses the light of right knowledge becomes himself composed of the object of knowledge, just as one who has drunk *maireya* liquor is always permeated by intoxication.
The wise know that the supreme Brahman is the stainless, uniform essential nature; by the mere attainment of knowledge, it becomes manifest of its own accord.
