Possessing knowledge and risen in bliss, he does not sink anywhere; liberated while living and free from attachment, he remains like a sovereign emperor who is himself the Self.
The wise man remains indifferent toward pleasant sounds such as those of the lute and the flute, as well as the charming songs of a beloved woman, even when they are sullied by carnal passion.
And amidst the humming of bees intoxicated by the pride of spring, and amidst the thundering of clouds over the flowers blooming at the onset of the rainy season;
Amidst the crests of peacocks dancing wildly, amidst the soft warbling of cuckoos, amidst the rumbling of fragments of clouds, and amidst the cries of cranes;
Amidst the sounds of hand-drums and other instruments ending with the kartaṛī, and amidst the deep-toned drums, as well as the sounds of various stringed, percussion, and wind instruments;
O Rāma, he does not bind his affection to harsh sounds nor to sweet ones, nor to clamorous noises, just as the moon does not dwell upon lotuses.
The wise one [dwells] amidst the rows of young plantain shoots, and in the delightful sports with the vine-like limbs of the daughters of the gods and gandharvas.

O Rāma, the wise man, whose intellect is unattached even to things within his own control, does not form any bond with them; he finds no delight in sensory contact, just as a swan finds none on desert lands.
One who possesses knowledge [discerns] among dates, *piṇḍa*-dates, *kadamba* fruits, jackfruits, and so forth; among grapes, cucumbers, walnuts, *bimba* fruits, citron fruits, and *jātī* flowers.
In the realms of wine, honey-liquor, maireya, mādhvīka, and āsava; and in curds, milk, ghee, inspissated milk, fresh butter, cooked rice, and so forth.
Among the six diverse flavors, in various foods to be licked, drunk, or relished, and in other fruits, roots, vegetables, and even meats;
The brahmin, whose form is satisfied and whose intellect is unattached, does not form a bond with certain things, finding delight in tasting them as if they were mere fragments of his own body.
He, possessed of wisdom, dwelt in the abodes of Yama, Varuṇa, Indra, Rudra, and the Sun, as well as upon the peaks of Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Sahya, and Dardura.
Upon nets of silken leaves, upon the digits of the moon’s orb, and within groves of wish-fulfilling trees that delight with the splendor of their forms;
Upon walls of precious gold and those made of pearls and gems, and upon the vine-like limbs of Tilottamā, Urvaśī, Rambhā, and Menakā;
The illustrious one, whose intellect is unattached, does not desire to see anyone; he is full in mind, honorable, silent, and immovable even toward his enemies.
One who possesses knowledge [discerns] among the kunda, mandāra, kahlāra, and kamala flowers, as well as among the kumuda, utpala, punnāga, ketakī, aguru, and jāti.
Upon the Kadamba, Cūta, Jambu, Āmra, Kiṃśuka, and Aśoka trees, and upon the Japā, Atimukta, Sauvīra, Bimba, Pāṭala, and Jāti flowers;
And among sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, lac, and musk; and among saffron, water-fragrance, cloves, cardamom, kaṅkola, tagara, and so forth.

With a single-pointed mind and equanimity, undisturbed by the scents of liquor, he does not bind his attachment to fragrance in some things, just as a twice-born man [does not crave] the aroma of wine.
He is not disturbed even in the slightest by the gurgling roar of the ocean, the echoing resonance in a mountain, or the roar of the lions, the kings of beasts.
He is not afraid in the slightest by the roar of the enemy's kettledrums, the clangor of the war-drums, or the sound of the harsh bowstring.
He does not tremble even slightly at the trumpeting of rutting elephants, the clamor of vetālas, or the shrieks of piśācas and rākṣasas.
One who is perfectly absorbed in meditative concentration does not tremble at the roar of a thunderbolt, the sound of a mountain splitting, or the trumpeting of Airāvaṇa.
Though subjected to the friction of a whirling saw, the slicing of a sharp blade, and the falling of arrows and thunderbolts, it does not waver from its own nature.
He finds neither joy in the grove nor does he fall into weariness; he feels no weariness among the gods nor does he find joy there.
Even in arid wastes where the sands were as hot as glowing embers, there were patches of soft, verdant ground covered with heaps of flowers.
Upon sharp razor-edges and beds of fresh lotuses, upon the heights of lofty mountains and within the depths of wells;
Whether upon rocks rough with the rays of the sun or among soft women; in times of prosperity or in fierce calamities; and whether in the company of lovers or at festive celebrations.
Even while dwelling [in the world], he is neither agitated nor does he fall into delight; with a mind eternally liberated within, he remains as if performing his duties.
In the forest lands of hell where limbs are contracted by iron, amidst endless showers of spears and lances hurled at one another;
He does not fear, nor does he succumb to helplessness or dejection; equanimous, with a tranquil mind and observing silence, the steadfast one remains like a mountain.
Having eaten that which is impure, unwholesome, smeared with poison, or even filth, one digests it quickly if it is moist and decomposed, as if it were delicious food.

One who knows reality possesses an unattached intellect and remains equanimous toward the tasting of food, whether it be a reflection, a counter-poison, medicinal paste, milk, sugarcane juice, water, or grain.
With fermented liquors, wines, milk, blood, fat, and meat-broths, or with parched bones, grass, and hair-ends, he is neither delighted nor provoked to anger.
She gazes with an equal look—one characterized by graciousness and sweetness—upon both the taker of her life and the giver.
Regarding stable and unstable bodies, and objects that are pleasant or unpleasant, he neither rejoices nor desponds, always kindled by equanimity.

Because the world’s stability is devoid of any fixed foundation and its very nature is unreliable, and because you have certainly realized all that is to be known and your own mind is free from passion; [you remain unmoved].
A virtuous person, with a mind free from the influence of the sovereign afflictions, never at any time allows any sense faculty to find scope when it is directed toward its object.
Swiftly devouring the senses—those which do not know reality, which find no rest, which have not attained the self, and which are unstable—just as lions devour a sprout.
Being carried away in the ocean of existence, tossed by the waves of latent impressions, and crying out in great distress, one is swallowed by the crocodiles of the sense organs.
The floods of conceptual constructions do not carry away one who reflects, who is fit for the supreme state, and whose mind finds rest in the Self, just as torrents of water cannot move a mountain.
For those who have come to rest in the supreme state at the very limit of all conceptual constructions, and who have attained their true nature, even Mount Meru is regarded as mere straw.
To those whose minds are expanded and equanimous, the entire world is but a fragment of withered straw; poison is indeed nectar, and a single moment is equal to a thousand kalpas.

Realizing that the world is nothing but pure consciousness, those of joyful intellect dwell with their minds full of bliss, for they perceive the entire universe existing within themselves as being composed of consciousness.
In this cage of worldly objects, which is but the vibration of pure consciousness, what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted? This is the view of those who know reality.
O sinless one, abandon this other delusion that "all this is consciousness alone. What could that vast body composed of consciousness ever abandon, and what could it desire?
That which arises from the earth as a future sprout and leaf is nothing but consciousness that manifests; likewise, it exists as the sprout of reality.
That which does not exist in the beginning or at the end is likewise absent even in the present; its appearance as an existent for some brief moment is but an illusion of consciousness.
Thinking thus, abandon the intellect that follows after existence and non-existence; having reached the end of all states of being, become one whose nature is the light of unattached consciousness.
Whether performing action with the body, mind, intellect, or even with the senses alone, one who is free from attachment is not tainted, whether acting or not acting.
O mighty-armed one, even while acting with a mind free from attachment, one is not stained by pleasures and pains, as if they were merely states of a mental wish.
Maintaining a mind free from attachment even while moving his slender limbs, he is not stained by pleasures or pains, just as one is unaffected during the states of mere mental desire.
One whose mind is free from attachment does not see even while looking with the eyes; because the mind is fixed elsewhere, this is experienced even by a child.
A living being whose mind is free from attachment does not see even while seeing; he does not hear even while hearing, nor does he touch even while touching.
Even while smelling, he does not smell; even while opening or closing his eyes, he does not see; and though he falls upon an object, he does not fall there by force.
This is experienced even by those of immature intellect—whether they be fools or wise men—who, though residing in their own homes, have minds fixed on another land.
Attachment is the cause of worldly objects; attachment is the cause of saṃsāra; attachment is the cause of hopes; attachment is the cause of calamities.

They know that liberation is the renunciation of attachment; from the renunciation of attachment comes freedom from rebirth. Therefore, O sinless one, renounce attachment to all things and become liberated while living.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, you who are like an autumnal wind that dispels the mist of all doubts, tell me, O Lord, briefly: what is attachment (saṅga) called?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That impure latent impression (vāsanā) which, through the presence or absence of objects, produces the modifications of joy and resentment, is called attachment (saṅga).
For those whose bodies are liberated while living, their latent impression (vāsanā) becomes pure, free from joy and sorrow, and brings about the state of no further rebirth.
Know that which is called "attachment to darkness" (tāmasa-saṅga) to be present as long as the body exists; the action performed by one under its influence does not indeed lead to bondage again.
For those who are not yet liberated while living, who are wretched and of deluded mind, the latent impression of bondage arises through joy and sorrow.
That very [nature] is called by the word "attachment" (saṅga), for it causes rebirth; whatever action is performed by means of it leads solely to bondage.
Thus, having abandoned attachment to form which causes the transformation of one's own self, if you remain undisturbed, you are not tainted even while acting.
If you do not undergo any change of state due to joy, resentment, or despondency, then, O Rāghava, you are free from passion, fear, and anger, and thus unattached.
If you do not succumb to weariness through sufferings, nor rejoice in pleasures, having abandoned the helplessness of hope, then you are unattached, O Rāghava.
While dwelling amidst worldly affairs and in states of pleasure and pain, you do not abandon true equanimity; therefore, O Rāghava, you are unattached.
If the self were indeed perceivable, it would be perceived as equal within all that is experienced; and since you follow whatever occurs as it happens, you are unattached, O Rāghava.
O sinless one, having attained through effortless detachment a stable state of liberation while living, remain equanimous, self-abiding, and free from passion.
With a mind liberated while living, silent, and having restrained the grasp of the senses, the noble one remains free from feverish distress, devoid of pride, intoxication, and envy.

For even amidst the entire multitude of things, he whose inner being is undepressed maintains an equanimous disposition; through his innate activity that proceeds in its natural sequence, he performs nothing else whatsoever.

Whatever task is at hand, whatever is appropriate for his own station, he performs that very thing; doing it entirely free from attachment or worldly ties, he finds delight within through his intellect and feels no weariness.

Then, whether encountering adversity or great prosperity, the one of great intelligence does not abandon his own natural disposition, just as the ocean of milk does not lose its whiteness even when churned by Mount Mandara.

Having attained either universal sovereignty or calamity, or the state of a crawling creature or the lordship of the gods, he remains free from the arising of distress and devoid of joy, remaining uniform like the moon amidst its waning and waxing.

With undaunted spirit, investigate the self as one whose agitation has been cast out, whose sense of duality has been discarded, and whose various attractive appearances resulting from diverse fruits have been stilled; thus you shall become established in the highest goal.

By means of an intellect purified by the play of the expansion described above, and having taken hold of the stainless state free from fever, you shall not again be bound here by the fetters of birth, for you have attained the vision of the Self as the object of perception.
Śrī Vālmīki said: Immediately following the chapter on tranquility, hear this chapter on liberation, which, once understood, bestows liberation.
While the leader of sages spoke these unrestrained words, the prince remained established in silence, his sole delight being the act of listening.
The royal assembly remained motionless, as if depicted in a painting, their minds fixed on the meaning of the sage’s words and their ascetic practices suspended.
On the ground shimmering with the circle of sages, he respectfully reflected upon the meaning of Vasiṣṭha’s words, his fingers twitching in their excitement.
While the group of matrons, their bee-like eyes blossoming with the joy of a wondrous gaze, had attained the state of deep, ripened mango blossoms;
When the sun was situated in the fourth part of the day in the sky, and the gentle moon had attained a slight tranquility through the dawning of some knowledge;

While the wind was hushed as if for the sake of listening alone, its movement stilled and its garlands of ripples at rest, bestowing the sweet fragrance of the Mandāra flowers, [he remained] in silence.
The rows of great bees were fast asleep upon the flower garlands, as if they were truly possessed of perfect meditation because they had already realized all that is to be known.
In the inner chambers enclosed by clusters of pearl lattices, the water shone without a ripple, as if it had stood still to listen.
When the cool rays of the sun had entered the interior of the houses through the windows and had become short, as if seeking rest after their long journey through the sky;
The sunlight, its body fading as the day declines, seems to proclaim tranquility, its own self now dusted with the mass of light from the lattice of pearls.

[He placed them] upon his hands, which were like playful lotuses, and upon the crests of the mountains, as if they had entered their minds through the fragrance of the nectar [of the flowers], having heard [the news].
While the children, the ignorant folk, and the pet birds were respectfully and incessantly obstructing the womenfolk from their meals for the sake of food, [he spoke].
The dust was thoroughly settled by the wind arising from the wings of wandering bees; the moonlight had fully subsided, as did the movement of the eyelashes upon the chowries.
As if out of fear of the web of shadows released by Agastya from his rays, they seemed to fly up through the windows and enter the interior of the house.
There arose a sound of kettledrums, tabors, and conchs that filled the quarters of the sky, intent upon making known the existence of the fourth part of the day.
By that sound, even his loud speech quickly vanished, just as the cry of a peacock ceases before the roar of a thundercloud.
The rows of birds in their cages, though unagitated themselves, had their wings trembling as if they were a forest of palm fronds violently shaken by an earthquake.
Terrified by fear, the children fled into the space between their nurses' breasts with cries, just as clouds in the rainy season rush into the hollows of lofty mountain peaks.
From the crest-ornaments of the kings, garlands of bees flew forth, like droplets of water from rivers whose currents are slightly turbulent.
Thus, while that house of Daśaratha was in such agitation, the day drew to a close and the sound of the conch shells gradually subsided.
Withdrawing his discourse on the subject at hand, that tiger among sages spoke in sweet tones to the scion of Raghu in the midst of the assembly.
O sinless Raghava, this web of words has been spread out by me; having bound the bird of the mind with it, take it into your embrace and lead it to the state of the Self.
I hope you have grasped the meaning of my words in this way—having abandoned what is difficult to understand, like a swan extracting milk from water.
Having reflected upon this in its entirety with your own intellect again and again, O virtuous one, you must now proceed by this very path.
By this very wisdom, O Rāma, you shall not be bound while sporting; otherwise, you will quickly fall downward like an elephant into a pit in the Vindhya mountains.
O Rāma, if you do not act upon my words which have been well-grasped by your intellect, then you will fall into a pit like a blind man who has lost his lamp in the nights.
"May his worldly activity proceed without attachment exactly as it has arisen"—taking this very established conclusion of the scriptures, be noble-minded.
"O members of the assembly, O Great King, and you, the rulers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa—may all of you now attend to your daily duties."
For this day has mostly reached its conclusion; we shall deliberate on what remains once we have returned in the morning to consider it.
Śrī Vālmīki said: Having been addressed thus by that sage, the entire assembly then rose up, their lotus-like faces blooming like a bed of lotuses in full bloom.
Having praised the king and performed salutations to Rāghava, those kings, once Vasiṣṭha had been fully extolled, departed for their own dwellings.
Accompanied by Viśvāmitra, the illustrious Vasiṣṭha, to whom the sky-dwellers had offered salutations, rose from his seat to go to the hermitage.
Kings beginning with Daśaratha and likewise the sages, having followed that sage—the speaker who was worthy of them—for a long time according to their respective status, [departed].
Having taken their leave, some went into the sky, some into the depths of the forest, and some to Rājagṛha—those virtuous ones, like bees rising from a lotus.
Having offered a pure handful of flowers at the feet of Vasiṣṭha, the king, followed by his wives, entered the interior of the house.
Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Śatrughna, having arrived at their preceptor’s hermitage, reverently worshipped his feet with devotion and then returned to the royal palace.
Having reached their respective dwellings, all those listeners bathed, offered worship, and approached the gods, the brahmins, and likewise the ancestors.
In due order, together with their own servants and retinues consisting of Brahmins and others, they partook of the food prescribed by the sequence of the duties of their respective castes.
When the sun had set along with the activities of the day, and the maker of night had arrived together with the activities of the night.
Having remained upon couches, silken beds, and seats, those forest-dwelling kings of sages and great seers who were once princes [now lived as ascetics].
With single-minded focus and great reverence, they reflected exactly as it was taught by Vasiṣṭha upon the means for crossing over saṃsāra.
Then, after only a single watch had passed, their faces sealed by sleep, they reached the beauty of dreams, like lotuses longing for the day.
For three watches of the night, Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Śatrughna contemplated that unimpaired instruction of Vasiṣṭha.
Then, for half a watch, with their eyes closed, they fell into a sleep that dispelled their fatigue in an instant—a sleep like a dream within a dream.

Thus, for those of pure mind who possessed discernment and whose aspirations were elevated by their realization of the essence, the night then ceased its course; the moon, now stained, assumed a state of crookedness.

Śrī Vālmīki said: Then Śyāmā, her moon-like face wet with tears and her steps faltering in the thickest darkness, appeared as she was wasting away, like the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of discernment (*viveka*) when they are being dissolved.
When the eastern mountain was seen as light because it had already been destroyed [by darkness], the mass of heat assumed the likeness of an ornament for the reclining [western] mountain.
Drawing in droplets of frost, having touched the orb of the moon, and possessing a light that swallows the moonlight, the morning breeze shone forth.
Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Śatrughna, having risen together with their attendants and performed their morning devotions, went to the holy hermitage of Vasiṣṭha.
There, even as the sage—who had already performed his twilight devotions—was departing from the palace, they offered him a continuous stream of water for his feet and bowed at his feet.
In an instant, that palace became silent with sages, brahmins, and kings, and gradually reached a state of complete density with elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles.
Then that tiger among sages, followed by Rāma and the others, went at the proper time to the house of Daśaratha together with that very army.
There, the king, having performed his twilight devotions and traveled a long distance, honored him with great respect upon their first meeting.
Having entered the assembly hall, which was further and exceedingly adorned with clusters of flowers, pearls, and gems, they all took their seats upon the rows of thrones.
Then, at that moment, all those listeners from the previous day—both those who move through the sky and those who dwell upon the earth—arrived together.
Having entered that gentle assembly hall and exchanged mutual salutations, she shone amidst the gathering of kings like a lotus pond in a windless place.
As those brahmin-sages, seers, and royal sages quickly settled according to their respective places and at their ease in those locations, [the following occurred].
When the soft sound of "welcome" had gradually subsided, and the bards seated in the corners of the assembly hall had fallen silent.
As the sunbeams rose swiftly, as if hastening to hear [the news], they entered through the windows and the lattices.
As the tinkling sound of the pearl nets subsides like sleep, arising from the touch of the hands of listeners who have quickly entered [the assembly], it is as if they are falling asleep.
The prince was like Śaṃkara’s [Kārttikeya], as Kaca was to the preceptor of the gods, as Prahlāda was to Śukra, and as Suparṇa was to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Rāma slowly fixed his gaze upon the face of Vasiṣṭha, like a female bee hovering near the edge of the sky and alighting upon a full-blown lotus.
Then the sage, skilled in speech, addressed the descendant of Raghu—who was himself an expert in the meaning of words—with those very words he had previously considered.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: "O descendant of Raghu, do you remember the words spoken by me yesterday, which were of exceedingly profound meaning and intended to awaken one to the supreme reality?"
Now, O crusher of enemies, listen to this other matter being spoken by me for the sake of awakening and for the attainment of eternal perfection.
By the power of the practice of dispassion and likewise through the awakening to reality, one crosses over saṃsāra; therefore, apply yourself to the practice of those very things.
When the difficult-to-comprehend [ignorance] has reached its end through the realization of true reality, and the immersion in latent tendencies has dissolved, the sorrowless state is attained.
Unconditioned by space, time, and the like, and transcending the two extremes of the unseen, the one Brahman alone indeed exists as the world, having attained a state of duality.
Where Brahman alone exists, unconditioned by any entities, peaceful and appearing as an absolute equality—how could there be any otherness there?
Thinking thus, having inwardly abandoned the notion of "I," you, the Great One whose body is liberated, uniform and tranquil in soul, become directly the bliss of your own Self.
There is no mind, nor ignorance, nor the intellect, nor the individual soul; these, O Rāma, are merely the mental constructs fashioned by Brahmā himself.
Whatever prosperities, whatever perceptions, whatever thoughts, and whatever desires there may be—all that is but Brahman, without beginning or end, expanding like the ocean.

In the netherworld, on the earth, in heaven, in a blade of grass, in living beings, and even in the sky—that Supreme Brahman, whose nature is consciousness, is seen; for indeed, there is nothing else.
Having abandoned relatives—whether those to be rejected or accepted—as well as wealth and the body, Brahman alone, devoid of beginning and end, expands like the ocean.

As long as there is the fabrication of ignorance, as long as there is the meditation on [a limited] Brahman, and as long as there is attachment to the snare of the world, so long will there be the conceptualization of the mind and other factors.

As long as there is the sense of "I" in the body, as long as there is the perception of this visible world by means of the self, and as long as there is the attachment of "this is mine," so long does the delusion of the mind and its like persist.

As long as you have not risen high through association with the company of the virtuous, and as long as your folly has not been utterly destroyed, so long will there remain an inclination toward the mind and its objects.
As long as this creator of the world has not reached a state of looseness through the power of right vision, so long will the mind and other faculties remain manifest within.

As long as there is ignorance, blindness, and helplessness through longing for sense objects, so long does the conceptualization of the mind and its derivatives arise from the heightening of delusion due to folly.
As long as the poisonous fragrance of desire throbs within the forest of the heart, the cakora bird of discernment does not enter therein at all.
For one whose mind has no longing for enjoyments, who possesses cool and stainless bliss, and whose net of bonds of hope has been severed, the delusion of the mind comes to an end.
For that person whose consciousness is eternally cooled through the abandonment of craving and delusion, and whose mind is tranquil, the ground of the mind has been awakened and relinquished.
For one who perceives the body as something unfamiliar, unregarded, and unsubstantial—as if it were distant and non-existent—how can there be a "land of the mind"?

For one whose nature is the realized essence of infinite consciousness and who perceives the world as contained within his own mind, the delusion regarding the individual soul and other such categories ceases.
When false vision has been stilled—its nature being that which causes erroneous delusion—and when the supreme sun has arisen, the sole seer of ultimate reality;
Know that the mind has dissolved, never to be seen again, like a parched leaf consumed by fire, or like a drop of ghee in a flame.
The state of mind belonging to those great-souled ones who are liberated while living and who perceive both the higher and the lower is called *sattva*.
In the bodies of those liberated while living, the latent impression that engages in worldly activity no longer exists under the name of "mind," for it has attained the state of pure being (sattva).
For those who know reality are mindless and always established in the state of equanimity; they wander here at their ease, with the effortless playfulness of one whose nature is sattva.

Though engaged in worldly affairs, those who abide in the essence of being and have their senses restrained perceive that light constantly; for them, there is no latent impression of duality or unity.
For the sage who, through inward-turnedness, offers the entire three worlds like a blade of grass into the fire of consciousness, the delusions of the mind and other such distractions cease within.
A mind purified by discernment is called *sattva*; it no longer bears fruit in delusion, just as a burnt seed does not produce a sprout.
As long as there are sentient beings whose inner nature is deluded, that which is subject to rebirth—designated by the term "mind"—is inverted through the lack of awakening.
You have indeed attained what was to be attained; the mind that had entered the state of a sentient being has been consumed by the fire of gnosis and shall not sprout again.
The mind pierced by desire grows back as if struck by an axe or fire; but the mind that has been consumed by the fire of knowledge and purified by awakening does not.

Indeed, the world is the expansion of Brahman, and the world is the expansion of Brahman; there exists no difference between these two, just as there is none between consciousness and the mass of Brahman.

The three worlds exist within consciousness, just as pungency exists within a peppercorn; therefore, consciousness and the world are not distinct, and thus the categories of "existent" and "non-existent" are in vain.

In this state, there is no consciousness of the linguistic convention between word and its referent; because of its nature as the sky of consciousness, both appear as unborn, and thus the notions of existence and non-existence are abandoned.
Since you are not composed of consciousness, you are not your own self; why, then, do you weep? If the worlds were not composed of consciousness, from where could such a conceptualization arise?

If everything is always composed of consciousness, then investigate that state of consciousness: it is pure, sentient, and without beginning or end; in that state, my friend, whence could there be any conceptual construction?
You are the conscious self, partless and devoid of near or far shores; remember your own expansive form, and do not become limited by forgetfulness.
Having attained that state of your own being, you perceive everything as non-everything; you are of such a nature, you are peaceful, you are consciousness, and you are the form of Brahman.

You are like the interior of a sesame seed, yet you are not; you are manifold, and yet you are also not so. You are that which you are, yet you are not as if you were that; you are both being and non-being, self-luminous.
That specific object which exists within you does not exist as "you" at all; therefore, you are not that. Be established in yourself, O mass of consciousness! Salutations to you.

Devoid of beginning and end, with a body of dense consciousness compressed within the vast space between the stone slabs, you are as pure as the sky; established in your own natural state, O Conqueror who dwells playfully within the leaf-cup of Brahmā’s belly, victory to you—salutations to you!
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O sinless one, you are that very consciousness which carries forth infinite worlds, like a mass of water in the ocean carrying the many waves of the future.
O Self of Consciousness, you are liberated from mental cultivation and devoid of both existence and non-existence; tell me, how can impressions and the like remain established within you?
This living soul shines forth by itself as "this" through latent impressions; tell me, my friend, what occasion is there here for the meaning of any other statement?
The ocean of your own conscious self is vast, deep, and radiant; though it possesses waves known as "Rāma," it is stilled and remains as equanimous and serene as the sky.
Just as heat is not distinct from fire, fragrance from the lotus, blackness from soot, whiteness from snow, and sweetness from sugarcane;

Just as light is not distinct from the luminous organ and experience is not distinct from consciousness, so too the world is not distinct from the nature of consciousness; it is like a wave arising from water.
Experience is not different from consciousness, and the "I" is not different from experience; the individual soul is not different from me, and the mind is not different from the individual soul.
The mind is not distinct from the senses, nor is the body separate from the senses; the world is not distinct from the body, for there is indeed nothing other than the world.
Thus has this great wheel been set in motion for a long time; yet nothing has been set in motion, nor is it swift, nor is it slow.
One's own self-awareness is infinite and all-pervading; thus, everything exists as an undivided void within the void, which is in nothing and is nothing at all.
The Void is fully expanded within the Void; Brahman is magnified within Brahman; Truth unfolds within Truth, abiding like the plenum within the plenum.
Even while engaging with forms, light, and mental attention, the Knower does nothing at all; for there is no agency in the Knower regarding that which is not to be grasped.

Since you regard that which leads to suffering as pleasure through the notion of "what is to be acquired," yet that which is neither existent nor non-existent cannot be acquired and is not the agent of pleasure and pain, [it follows that nothing is truly yours].

Just as the collection of words such as "space," "in space," and "spaces" is neither diverse nor non-diverse, and though meaningful, is itself utterly empty in nature—such is the sequence of the self and the world.
Pure within like the inner sky, yet perfectly adept in external conduct, he remains as steady as a piece of wood or a clod of earth amidst the fluctuations of joy and anger.
He who perceives even that most extreme enemy, intent on killing him with haste, as an unfeigned friend—he truly sees.
He who scrapes away both friendship and envy, root and all, like a tree on a riverbank, is the one who destroys the faults of joy and resentment.

If the true nature of the transformations of passion and hatred is not contemplated, then even those things that exist will take on the form of non-existence; they will be as if never experienced, even though they have been experienced.
He whose state of being is free from egoism, whose intellect is not tainted—even having slain these worlds, he does not kill, nor is he bound.
The realization of the existence of that which does not exist has been described as "illusion"; through complete understanding, it undoubtedly perishes.
He whose internal burden of latent impressions has been stilled like a lamp devoid of oil—that wise and unchanging man has conquered, as if by a work of art.

For one for whom this entire collection of objects, whether existent or non-existent, is not to be grasped in any state, there is neither the burning of suffering nor even pleasure; such a person is truly liberated while still alive in this world.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O sinless one, the mind, the intellect, the ego, the senses, and so forth—all these are composed of consciousness beyond the object of thought; where, then, do your notions of "living beings" and the like reside?
This manifoldness was bestowed by the Great-Souled One through a single self, just as a single moon appears manifold through the media of cataracts, water, vessels, and mirrors.
As soon as the poisonous possession of craving for enjoyments has subsided, then likewise ignorance and blindness set, like darkness at the destruction of gloom.
Through the internal recitation of the treatise on the self, the cholera-like poison of craving is destroyed within, just as mist is dispelled by autumn.
O Rāma, know that when ignorance is destroyed, the mind along with its kin is likewise destroyed; just as dullness in the sky subsides without obstacle when the clouds have dissolved.
When the mind has reached the state of no-mind, the delusion of latent impressions is exhausted; O sinless one, it is like the entry of pearls into a necklace once the thread has been cut.
Those who contemplate the meaning of the scriptures for the purpose of obstructing Raghunātha unite in their minds with those destined for the state of worms and insects.
The tremulous beauty of her lovely eyes, shaped like fresh lotuses, remains unimpaired even when dullness has been stilled, just as the movement of a lake persists even when the wind has ceased.
You have attained steadfastness, free from both existence and non-existence, in a state of supreme expansion like a wind within the sky.
I believe, O scion of Raghu, that you have attained awakening through my words, like a king within whose sleep of ignorance has been dispelled by the beating of drums.
The words of a family preceptor indeed take effect upon ordinary people; O Rāma, how could they not take effect upon you, who possess such exceedingly noble intelligence?
Where the worthiness of my words has been cultivated by one's own mind, my speech enters deeply within, just as water enters a heated field.

"O noble one of great majesty, we are indeed the eternal family preceptors of you, the scions of Raghu's line. Therefore, O noble one, you must quickly take these auspicious words spoken by me to heart, wearing them like a necklace."
Śrī Rāma said: "Oh! By contemplating the meaning of your words, I have attained the state of consciousness; O Lord, this entire web of the world, though standing before me, has become stilled."
Reflecting thus, I have set out toward the supreme peace within the Supreme Self, just as the surface of the earth, scorched by a long drought, is refreshed by rain.
I am stilled, cool in nature, and abide in pure happiness; having attained serenity, I am like a lake free from all agitation.
O Sage, I now perceive this entire circle of the quarters as perfectly serene and free from mist, seeing it exactly as it truly is.
I am born free from doubt, with the mirage of hope extinguished; liberated from both passion and dispassion, I am as cool as a cleared wilderness.
I have attained that inner bliss within the self which is devoid of end; wherein, O Lord, the tasting of the essence of elixirs is regarded as a mere blade of grass.
Today I abide in my true nature; I am well, I am joyful, I delight in the world, and I am Rāma. Homage to me, and homage to you!
Those doubts and those mental constructions—all have set for me, like the world of nocturnal vampires at dawn when the sun has risen.
When my heart has become pure, expansive, and cooled by the frost of serenity, my mind has attained peace, like a lake in autumn.
Doubts such as "Why and how is there a stain upon the self? have surely been uprooted, just as darkness vanishes before the moon.
Everything everywhere and at all times is only the Self, whose form is ever-manifested; how can there be the false conceptualization that "this is one thing" and "that is another"?
"Who was I in the past? Such was I, bound by the shackles of craving. Thus, with a blossoming smile, I laugh at my very own inner self.
Now I have clearly remembered: I am indeed this very person who stands here, bathed by the flood of the nectar of your speech.
Aha! I have indeed ascended to the vast, purifying earth, while remaining right here where the sun stands as if it were in the netherworld.

Salutations eternally to the one worthy of homage; I bow down by means of the self within the self, to myself who has reached existence after crossing the ocean of becoming characterized by being and non-being.

O Lord, by the power of experience, having clearly attained the state of a bee within the calyx of my heart-lotus, I have reached a condition here that is free from sorrow and long filled with joy through your excellent words.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O mighty-armed one, listen once more to my supreme word, which I shall speak to you, who are pleased with me, out of a desire for your welfare.
Even if you accept their distinction, listen for the sake of increasing your understanding, so that even those of little awakening may not suffer.
Because the ignorant person, whose nature is ignorance, has conceived the notion that the body alone is the self, the enemies of the senses overcome him as if out of sheer rage.
For that wise one whose self is knowledge, who is established in the Self alone, and who is contented with the senses as his friends, no harms can strike that blameless person.
For one who finds no praise for an object other than through its censure as it appears before them, for what reason would such a person take on a body for the sake of bodily suffering?
The self is not connected with the body, nor is the body in the self; these two are mutually distinct, just like light and darkness.
Permanently liberated from all modifications of existence and untainted, the Blessed One, the Self, neither sets nor rises, but is ever-risen.
Let whatever happens to this body—which is inert, ignorant, trivial, ungrateful, perishable, and a mere heap of elements—be exactly so.
How can that which is always manifest as pure consciousness ever grasp [an object], when the thorough knowledge of one necessarily entails the presence of insentience in the other?
Of what nature was the equality of pleasure and pain between those two, who were always equal and possessed identical qualities; how could they ever be otherwise?
Furthermore, how could two things that are unattached to one another be mutually conjoined? How could that which is gross take the form of the subtle, and how could the subtle become gross?
When one thing arises, there is no existence of a second during the day or night; knowledge does not become ignorance, nor does shadow turn into heat.
The true Brahman does not become non-existent even amidst diverse perceptions; nor is there even the slightest attachment for the omnipresent embodied one.
Just as there is no contact between water and the lotus situated within it, so too there is not even the slightest attachment of Brahman to the existence of the body, despite being within the body.
Even for one who has gone there, old age, death, calamity, pleasure and pain, and existence and non-existence do not occur, just as the sky is unaffected by the wind.

Not even the slightest [defilement] exists here; therefore, be at peace. Even while remaining in the form of a body, there is the great delusion consisting of the rising and falling of transmigration.
Brahman alone is seen, just as a collection of waves is seen in water; for here, because it subsists upon its own existence, the Self indeed experiences itself.
The body-machine exists like a wave arising from the mere presence of water; O dear one, its agitation or lack thereof depends upon the movement of its support, and thus does existence arise.

Just as the reflection of the sun and so forth [is seen] by means of a body, so too, when the reality of things is correctly perceived exactly as it is, [insight] arises with respect to that very reality.

The stability consisting of the body is a delusion of knowledge and it dissolves; for through the knowledge of the body and the embodied one as they truly are, there is stability in the reality of things as they are.
From a lamp, the nature of both the lamp and its object arises as being both existent and non-existent; for one who lacks right vision, this occurs through the revolutions and cycles of the body.
Empty within, these trees of delusion—the Arjunas—tremble here, their own true purpose unexamined and their consciousness untouched.
Those of dull intellect, being devoid of consciousness, quiver like blades of grass; because their minds have no firm foundation, all these inert beings are tossed about by the winds of space.
Arising and descending here and there, they cry out and quiver; they seize and then let go of everything, including grass, wood, and the like.
Rich with sound, touch, and form, their limbs tremulous like waves; though inert, they possess a radiant nature and are filled with the abundant wine of aesthetic flavor.
For all these [beings], who are like those of dull intellect amidst great floods involving their dwellings, arrivals, and departures, this immutable consciousness remains ever-present.
However, due to the power of her ignorance, she has fallen into a state of supreme wretchedness; for her continuous streams of sighs are like those of an ignorant blacksmith’s bellows.
They are seen to act only for the sake of a mere display, quickly ceasing to be effective, like the threatening gestures and roaring of a fool, or like the string of a bow-staff.
It is heard that even the enjoyment of fruits from a fool leads only to death, for he is devoid of conscious awareness, like a tree in the forest.
Resting upon him would be like resting on a stone slab; association with him would be like encountering a lifeless stump in a desolate wilderness.
Whatever has been done for that purpose is like striking the sky with sticks; what is given to such a base person—why is it not as if thrown into the mud?
The conversation he had with him regarding the summoning of the dog into the sky was ignorance; for what calamity indeed does not befall one who lacks knowledge?
This stream of saṃsāra flows on due to the heedlessness of the ignorant; for the ignorant, there are both fierce sufferings and even firm pleasures.
They return again and again like mountains at the end of an eon, persistently clinging to attachment for the body, wealth, wife, and so forth.
This terrible suffering of the ignorant person never ceases, for they have conceived the notion of a self within this deceitful body that is not the self.

How indeed can even the name of illusion—which consists of the cognition of the non-existent—be destroyed for one of evil intent, whose mind is deceitful, who is blind regarding reality, and who is of wicked intellect?
For one who possesses eyes and stumbles at every step upon non-existent objects, poison arises from the moon, just as fragrance arises from flowers.

And as thorns emerge from the earth like sprouts of durva grass from the soil, so do these [sensual objects] arise from the milk of the body; they are the female serpents coiled around the silk-cotton tree of the body and the chains for the elephant of the mind.
The hopes of the ignorant spring forth like rice from well-tilled soil; here, ignorance is the glory of hell, entwined by the serpents of evil deeds.
She protected him with joy, like a peahen guarding a rain-cloud; her eyes were as restless as hovering bees, and her sprout-like lower lip quivered.
A woman is a poisonous creeper that blossoms only for the sake of a fool; with its delicate sprouts, it takes root only in the fertile soil of an ignorant man's heart.
There exists the evil tree of passion, which provides shade for birds; its leaves are the smoke of sighs, and its clusters of weapons are the firebrands of its roots.
In the desert of the heart, the forest fire of hatred burns, causing calamity to the body; it resides in the minds of the ignorant and the envious, cloaked by the slander of others.
The lotus-pond of envy, with anxiety as its bees, flourishes intensely; it is filled with the agitation of waves of fierce suffering, polished anew in every birth.
The submarine fire of death repeatedly approaches that which is inert; birth passes into childhood, childhood into youth, and youth into old age.
In this world-complex of a dilapidated waterwheel, the deluded person alone undergoes old age and death again and again by means of the rope that is worldly existence.

Through repeated submerging and emerging, the ignorant man becomes like a water-jar within the machine; yet to the intellect of the wise, this world is as fragile as the water filling a cow's footprint.
That very [world] is, for the Great-Souled One, shoreless, boundless, and unfathomable; yet for the ignorant man, it is as if invisible from within the long cavity of his belly.
They do not reach the further shore, like birds from a cage, for they are the hubs of the burden of latent impressions whose very nature has undergone transformation.
The spokes of the wheel of birth cannot be made clear by the ignorant man, who, for the sake of the vulture-like senses, hunts his own body out of passion.
In the forest of saṃsāra, the vision consisting of the mountain of the elements—which is merely a fragment of clay and flesh—is spread out like a lump of bait from afar.
Through delusion, it is perceived as a variegated array of objects and subsequent attachments; victorious is the wish-fulfilling tree of conceptualization, which brings about manifold volitions.
Since the succession of leaves that is the world has issued forth from ignorance, it is upon this [reality] that they stand, shine, enter, and sport.
Wherein the various births are the leaves, the web of karma is the bud, and the many birds of enjoyment are endowed with diverse arrangements.
Merits and demerits are the fruits, and worldly power and splendor are the blossoms; clearly, these women are medicinal herbs that sprout when the moon of ignorance rises.
In this forest grove of saṃsāra, they have attained supreme splendor; yet it is filled with the multitude of the web of births, where the darkness of time rises.
Victorious is the moon of ignorance, the lord of defects, whose nature arises from emptiness; through the grace of this lunar ignorance, which abounds in the nectar of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
The women, graceful as royal swans and with limbs cooled by frost, were enjoyed by him who was like a cakora bird whose hopes were satisfied, seeking the nectar of the jewel of his mind.
The lovely night-lilies of women shine, with their flickering eyes as bees, the luster of their braided hair as the darkness of night, and their glistening pale breasts as the moonlight.
That women shine like jewels is merely the manifestation of his own folly.

O Rāma, these are the various and abundant fruits that have spread forth from the tree of ignorance—fruits that are sweet only at first sight, whose essence is calamity, which have a beginning and an end, and which are fragile throughout their entire existence.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the moon of intoxication has risen, women adorned with pearl necklaces and jewel ornaments shine like the waves of the milk-ocean of passion that have been stirred up.
The glances of the women, flickering across the surface of their cheeks, bear the beauty of swarms of bees hovering over the interior of golden lotuses.
In the garden groves during the springtime, when the earth is moistened by rut, the lovely flowers shine like the servants of the god of love.
Flesh-eating vultures, jackals, dogs, ravens, and crows are compared to women, who are likened to the moon, sandalwood, and lotuses.
The row of a woman's breasts appears like golden jars, lotus buds, or citron fruits, yet it is red, putrid, and foul-smelling.
The fleshy fragment called the lip, smeared with saliva, is compared to the liquid of honey and wine flowing from the moon of elixir.
The arms, which have the appearance of small, knotted joints and are like cruel spikes of bone, are described by auspicious poets using the metaphor of great, creeper-like arms.
Likewise, the row of archways shines forth, filled with beauties as lovely as the trunks of plantain trees, providing the bliss appropriate for the splendor of their breasts.
Even prosperity—which is dull and sweet at first, fraught with the succession of dualities in the middle, and quickly vanishing and sparse at the end—is ardently desired.

The mind encounters both suffering and happiness, which branch out into a hundred directions; yet it is the branches of suffering that arise as the various fruits of karma, while prosperity is their result.
The words, dense with the form of a woven net like ropes for imprisonment, stand within the thicket of their own proliferation, resembling the thatch of a hut.
A continuous mist of delusion, spreading like the essence of a waterless cloud, comes for a long time like the Yamunā river in the rainy season, dark as the gloom of night.
With his inner heart made bitter by various pleasures, he indeed increases—though devoid of affection—the poisonous sap of rebirth.
The winds of one's own karma blow, scattering heaps of leaves that are the people shattered and worn out by old age, and carrying the dust of various refuse.
This Time, whose belly devours all things through its voracious nature, is not satiated even by kalpas, though it has swallowed this infinite world like a ripened fruit.
Having drunk the wind of delusion through their skin, these various serpents move restlessly here, quivering with a cool mountain-like luster.
Afflicted by the demoness of anxiety and lacking the rising moon of solitude, the night of youth passes away as if shrouded in darkness, devoid of light.
The tongue falls into decay through the fevers of vulgar affection, just as even a thread situated within the hollow of a lotus core withers from the frosts.
The firm śālmali tree of poverty, with suffering and grief as its massive roots and a thicket of hardships and thorns, spreads out a thousand branches.
Having made his dwelling in the temple of the mind—which is empty within and whose loftiness has been destroyed—the owl of greed prowls about during the night thick with illusion.
Having first seized it with her ears, the old cat, quivering with certainty, tears apart the mouse of youth that has grown decrepit with age.
This creation, which has gradually attained the height of the mountains, though devoid of essence, reaches its full development like a mass of foam.
The creeper of existence has blossomed, white with the flowers of radiance, adorned with the sprouts of the world, and bearing the fruits of dharma and artha.
The beautiful house of the three worlds is sustained, with Mount Sumeru as its great pillar, the moon and sun as its windows, and the sky as its roof.
In the vast lake of saṃsāra, the bees of the sense of smell move about within the lotuses of bodies, drinking the nectar of the nature of consciousness.
The lamp of the sun flashes within the beautiful interior of the belly of the world, shining exclusively upon the great sapphire pavement of the path of the sky.
The world is like an aged bird, its limbs bound by the thread of hope, trapped within the cage of the senses fastened inside the pegs of its own latent impressions.
The creeper of worldly existence, its succession of leaves consisting of beings whose flames of suffering fall without ceasing, has long been stirred and made to quiver by the wind.
For some time after creation, those of noble lineage were filled with joy; they cast down the mire of the fierce hells and were for a moment freed from all doubt.
Within the lake of the path to heaven, where moss-like dark clouds float and fragments of the moon’s orb serve as pebbles, the nectar-like flavors of the gods shimmer.

The lotus-pond of activity is darkened by various fruits and mangoes, garlanded with a web of latent impressions (vāsanā), abundant and filled with the fragrance of vibration, and blossomed by ritual actions.
The wretched fish of worldly existence, quivering in the pond of saṃsāra, is seized by the treacherous, aged vulture that is Death.
Like a series of waves and foam, that very same thing appears to be something else, fragile and ever-changing; day by day, a variety of forms arises like the successive crescents of the moon.
This wheel is being turned by the potter Time, who fashions the many beings as its clay shards, all subject to momentary destruction.
Countless eons have passed in the immovable state; the nets of the world's wildernesses have been consumed by the fire of the cosmic age.
Through endless states of existence and non-existence, and through hundreds of conditions of pleasure and pain, the worldly condition thus undergoes perpetual reversal.
The fortitude of the Buddha’s wisdom was not broken by the tossing of world-ages, nor by the chains of latent tendencies, nor by the falls of great thunderbolts.
The latent impression bears the form of Indra, which was praised by the sons of Danu when their enemies had fled by the hundreds, yet which now suffers from being shattered by worldly existence.
This whirlwind of destiny constantly enters the throat of the serpent of time, whereupon a continuous succession of dust from the creation of beings incessantly falls.
In the waters of objective entities, all fruits and froths fall from every direction with incessant impact into the mouth of the submarine fire of non-existence.
The powers of various substances, arising spontaneously and suddenly, manifest as if they were the very splendor of the movement of water, perfected by their own inherent nature alone.
The lion of Death, with his mane bristling, devours even the vast and numerous young elephants of the world, which are filled with the pearls of living beings.
The birds of the world—whose wings are masses of clouds, whose fruits are the great mountain ranges, and whose beaks are the straightening of the earth—are born, die, and are sustained.
Upon the wall of consciousness, which is bright with vibration, the painter Fate unfolds the paintings of saṃsāra using the five senses as its colors.
Ever-moving, effecting all transformations, possessing parts that are a hundredth of a moment, its sprout is difficult to accomplish through unreal means.
Having perceived through meditation this subtle calculation of time that brings about their own arising, these stationary species remain established.
All classes of living beings are worn out by the disease of old age and death, which arises from passion and hatred and consists of existence and non-existence.
On the surface of the earth, rows of insects, who practice the most wretched forms of meditation, are inevitably tormented for a fixed period of time by the power of destiny.
In an instant, this serpent of Time—whose hole is difficult to perceive, who possesses vast coils, and who is full of ease—swallows this entire world while remaining invisible.
At times, perceiving something, they were distressed by their own bodies; though buffeted by cold winds and heat, they shone with the brilliance of blossoming flowers.

In this world, those possessed of virtuous conduct move about, bestowing fruits [of their deeds], even though they have bodies as fragile as chasms, within the hollow of the lotus that is the three worlds, where the masses of water find their rest.
The venerable Kālī, whose very activity is the vessel for the alms-bowl of the universe, makes a great humming sound like a swarm of bees that are all living beings.
Having herself repeatedly given alms to the spirits, she now desires to seize them; she whose tresses are a false darkness and whose eyes are as flickering as the sun and moon.
She contains Brahmā, Upendra, Mahendra, and others, as well as the earth, the mountains, and the best of peaks; she is the single basket of the reality of Brahman, with her breasts hanging down.
The power of consciousness is the Mother, gross yet flickering, as unsteady as a dense cloud; she whose teeth are a lattice of stars, the earth made ruddy by the twilight.
Holding the entire lotus-forest in her hand, with the city of Indra as her face, she has the seven oceans for her pearl necklace and is draped in garments of blue.
Having become the great navel of Jambudvīpa and the line of hair on the body of the beauty of the forest, the aged mistress of the three worlds perishes again and again.
Having perished, she is born again and again, causing great delusion; she has been submerged by others and then raised up once more in the terrifying, vast ocean of time.
In time, which flows with unfathomable nectar, Brahmāṇḍas—bursting bubbles—perish every moment; having remained for a while again and again, they vanish.
The cranes that are the causal principles have flown away in the blink of an eon; the lightnings of creation, though scorched, perish again and again as they arise.
In the dark cloud of time, these efforts of the light of consciousness flash forth; like birds among falling beings, they descend with unceasing wandering.
From the fiercely beating rhythm of Time, the leaders of the gods—the guardians of the fruit that is the cosmic egg—bring forth the creations of Brahmā through their very opening of the eyes.
Somewhere there are some who bring about destruction in the blink of an eye; by the mere opening and closing of their eyes, they dissolve thousands of networks of kalpas.
Furthermore, even those certain Rudras who exist within that supreme consciousness come into being and cease to be in the twinkling of an eye.
Even such a Lord of Gods exists, for this state of activity is infinite within the void of Brahmā’s station, which consists of infinite volitions.

What powers indeed do not exist that fill the world with variety? Thus, this worldly conceptualization, which shines with the weight of objects obtained through unexhausted volitions, is the manifestation of ignorance.

Those which are called prosperities are, in fact, continuous calamities; they are the afflictions of childhood, youth, old age, and death; and that immersion in successions of pleasure and pain is the manifestation of the intense darkness of ignorance.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In this forest grove of worldly existence, situated upon the slope of the mountain of consciousness, what is this creeper called ignorance of creation like, and when did it blossom?
This slender body-staff of hers, which illuminates the three worlds, is rich with joints as large as mountains and is enveloped by the skin of the cosmic egg.
Pleasure, pain, existence, non-existence, knowledge, and ignorance—these are the extensive branches and the roots and fruits herein.
From pleasure, ignorance arises intensely, and it yields that very same [pleasure] at the end; from pain, ignorance arises intensely, and it fully bears that very fruit.
This ignorance arises from existence and clearly bears fruit for that very existence; it attains being from existence and bears fruit for that very existence in an instant.
Through ignorance, that very thing increases, and its fruit will clearly be the same; through knowledge, consciousness arises, and it bestows that very [consciousness] at the end.
Her body, full of various kinds of rapture and abounding in joy, expands, shimmering with dense, tender sprouts.
This [world-tree] has the days for its blossoming flowers, the nights for its restless bees, and it is constantly quivering as the sprouts of living beings fall away.
Coming again and again, it falls upon that which produces discernment; though its dust is shaken off and it is cleansed, it returns once more to its attachment.
Abounding with emerging coral sprouts, bristling with newly formed shoots, endowed with the flowers of every season, and rich in all essential juices.

It flows incessantly with the birth of new existences, it is eager for the openings of destruction, it is filled with the essence of the expansion of enjoyments, and it is eaten away by the woodworm of singular discernment.
The circles of the moon and sun blooming daily on all sides are indeed her flowers, fluttering in the wind within the sky.
O descendant of Raghu, the stars are the blossoms of this [night-blooming lotus], which have reached the state of buds with their throbbing forms, filling the hollow of the sky.
The light of the moon, sun, and fire is but the floral pollen of her; for by this, she draws the hearts of men like a fair-limbed woman.
Shaken by the elephant of the mind, with the warbling cuckoo of conceptualization, crowded by the serpents of the sense-faculties, and stained by the skin of craving.
Having attained loftiness by resting upon the body of the Tamāla tree against the blue sky, she serves as a firm pillar for the knees of Heaven and Earth, adorning the garden of the world.
In the lower regions of the cosmic egg, she is entwined by her own root-system and nourished by the watering of the waters of all the oceans, such as the milk-ocean and others.
The three Vedas are the restless bees upon this cluster of flowers that is woman; she is shaken by the wind of the vibration of consciousness, and her vast activities are the swarms of ants.
Enveloped by the python of evil deeds, it is a bower of flowers that is the glory of heaven; dense with the life-force of living beings, it bestows various kinds of joy and intoxication.
It shines with the variety of various tranquilities, resplendent with various flowers, pervaded by rows of various fruits, and blossoming through various seasons.
It possessed circles of various flower-beds, bore various kinds of birds, was rough with various pollens, and contained various networks of mountain peaks.
It was filled with the buds of various arts, arisen from various multitudes of forests, grown upon the slopes of various mountains, and densely covered with various leaves.
She is born and being born, dying and likewise dead; she is half-severed and likewise unsevered, and thus eternally indestructible.
The past and the present always appear as if non-existent even while existing; she is eternally and utterly youthful, yet eternally subject to decay.
For this is indeed a great poisonous creeper; when embraced with impetuosity, it causes the fainting spell of the poison of saṃsāra, but when touched [with discernment], it perishes.

In the vast [universe], she is dissolved within him; in the ignorant, she remains established within, endowed [with all things]: "Here is water, here are mountains, here are serpents, and here are gods."
From here she has come as the earth, and likewise from here she exists as radiance; from here she has attained the state of the moon and sun, and likewise from here she takes the form of the stars.
From here is darkness, from there is light; from here is the sky, from there is the fertile earth; from here is the scripture, from there are the Vedas; from here is that which is devoid of duality.
In one place she flew upward as a bird; in another, she rose up as a deity; in another, she stood firm as a pillar; and in another, she attained the state of the wind.
In one place she is absorbed in hell; in another, she sports in heaven; in one place she has attained the status of a god; and in another, she exists as a worm.
In one place Viṣṇu, in another Brahmā, in another Rudra, in another Ravi; in one place Agni, in another Vāyu, in another Candra, and in another Yama.

O dear one, whatever is visible in the worlds—whether pervaded by great majesty or reduced to the state of withered straw—even if it manifests as Hara and the other gods, know that to be ignorance; for the attainment of the Self occurs through the transcendence of that.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin, having heard that even the entire range of manifested forms, including Hari, Hara, and the rest, are merely ignorance, I have fallen into a state of confusion.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That which is untouched by any object of perception, which is peaceful, which is the self of all, and which consists of the manifestation of existence and consciousness, exists here, free from all mental construction.
Therefore, from itself arises the *kalā*, whose nature is that of conceptualization; it emerges as a shimmering fluidity, like a line of whirlpools arising from water.
It is conceived as threefold—subtle, intermediate, and gross; subsequently, by means of that mind, it is again known through its own form.
Abiding in these states, it is conceptually differentiated as threefold: sattva, rajas, and tamas; this very [state] is known as Prakṛti.

Know that ignorance (avidyā) is the primordial nature (prakṛti), characterized by the three qualities (guṇas). This very [ignorance] is the cycle of worldly existence for a living being; its further shore is the supreme state.
In this regard, those three qualities (guṇas) which have been mentioned to you are also remembered as being threefold; each quality—sattva, rajas, and tamas—is divided individually.
Thus, this ignorance is divided into nine types according to the distinction of its qualities; whatever is perceived here is entirely dependent upon it.
"O Rāghava, know that the seers, sages, perfected ones, nāgas, vidyādharas, and gods—such is the sattvic portion of ignorance."
Of this sattvic portion, the Nāgas and Vidyādharas are tamas; the Munis and Siddhas are rajas; and the gods, such as Hara and others, are sattva.
Among the class of beings born from the divine womb, those such as Hari, Hara, and others have attained the stainless state through the primordial qualities of pure *sattva*.
O Rāma, he who becomes a knower of that which is the primordial constituent of the quality of sattva does not arise again; therefore, he is called liberated.
Therefore, O Mahāmati, these beings such as Rudra and others remain liberated as long as the world endures, as long as they possess a body.
As long as they possess a body, these great-souled ones remain liberated while living; at the end of the body, they shall abide in the Supreme Lord, liberated beyond the body.
This portion of ignorance itself has thus attained the state of knowledge; the seed becomes the fruit, and the fruit attains the state of the seed.
Ignorance arises from knowledge like a bubble from water; indeed, ignorance dissolves into knowledge like a bubble into water.
Just as milk and its waves are distinct only through the perception of duality, so too are knowledge and ignorance distinct only through the perception of difference.
Just as, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is an identity between the milk and the waves, so too, here, neither the state of ignorance nor the state of knowledge exists at all.
O scion of Raghu, having abandoned the views of knowledge and ignorance, that which exists here truly exists; for this [existence] is established by way of the exclusion of its opposite.
The visions of knowledge and ignorance do not exist; remain firmly established in what remains. There is no ignorance and there is no knowledge; enough with this conceptualization.

That which exists as something and yet as nothing—that which is consciousness (cit) and awareness (saṃvit)—is established as such; that very same thing, when its manifestation is not recognized, is designated as ignorance (avidyā).
This very reality is known as the destruction of ignorance; due to the absence of true knowledge, the false conceptualization called "ignorance" arises.
When ignorance has dissolved within their mutual hearts—like shade and sunlight—the two conceptual constructions are utterly exhausted.
These two, O Rāghava, dissolve; only the unattainable remains. Through the destruction of ignorance, even the side of knowledge is exhausted, O Rāghava.
Whatever remains is either nothing at all, or this entire expanse is it; thus, within that, everything is seen, yet nothing at all is seen.

Just as a banyan tree exists within a banyan seed, possessing flowers, fruits, and so forth, so too is the "somethingness" (kiñcit-tva) endowed with all powers; it is indeed the casket containing all powers.
It is emptier even than the sky, yet it is not empty, for its nature is consciousness; just as fire exists within a sun-crystal, or ghee within milk.
In this regard, all this is established within the arising of the sequence of space and time, just as sparks arise from fire or as rays of light from the sun.
Therefore, these flickering cognitions emerge from consciousness just as waves arise from the ocean, or as rays of light from a pure gem.
The treasury of infinite cognitions and their radiant splendors is eternal; indeed, everything exists as a real entity within all things, both internally and externally.
The sky is always of an indestructible nature, just as the jar; and just as the magnet possesses agency in the movement of iron toward it.

For in that same way, agency is attributed to that which is actually non-agent; just as inert iron vibrates by the mere proximity of a magnet, so too does this body, though insentient in nature, appear to think through the existence of that [Self].

This entire world is situated there, within that single seed of the universe called Consciousness, through the conceptualization of what is imagined by consciousness; it appears in variegated forms like a mass of restless waves upon water, though it is formless even more than space, wherein nothing at all exists.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Therefore, know this: this entire world, both stationary and moving, is nothing at all; understand, O dear one, that whatever has attained the state of being an entity is in fact nothing whatsoever.
O Rāma, where there is no conceptualization whatsoever consisting of existence and non-existence, this entire world beginning with the individual soul is but a vain effort; why do you strive for it?
This connection which is designated within the inner heart—we do not find it, just as one does not find the snake in the delusion of a rope-snake.
When the self is not fully known, it becomes the source of delusion for those who wander; when known, it attains its true nature as the self, which is the ultimate limit of all consciousness.

In the world, it is called ignorance when consciousness, though inherently stainless, relies upon the object of thought; yet, when freed from all limiting adjuncts, it attains the state of a self that transcends the object of thought.
For the person is indeed mind-only; when that [mind] perishes, he perishes. When it remains, this self remains, like the space within a jar when the jar exists.
Just as a child, while walking, sees one who is walking, and while standing, sees one who is standing, so too this deluded mind perceives itself as agitated.
Like a silkworm, it encloses itself within the fine threads of its own latent impressions; thus, due to its childishness, the mind does not realize this within itself.
Śrī Rāma said: O Lord, what is the nature of that ignorance which has reached a state of extreme density and remains fixed, having attained the bodies of immobile beings and the like?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having neither attained the state of no-mind nor fallen away from the state of mind, this consciousness remains within immobile beings by resorting to a neutral, intermediate form.

In that regard, O best among those who know what is to be known, I consider liberation to be situated at a distance, where consciousness remains within the dormant *puryaṣṭaka*, bestowing suffering; there it abides merely as pure existence, like one who is mute, blind, and inert.

Śrī Rāma said: O best among those who know what is to be known, I consider that liberation is not far off for those in whom consciousness is established in the state of non-dual existence even within immobile things.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When, having investigated this through prior intelligence and by perceiving things as they truly are, there arises the realization of the universal existence (sattāsāmānya), that is liberation, which is infinite.

The supreme abandonment of latent impressions (vāsanās) through thorough comprehension—that which is the state of being the universal form of pure existence (sattāsāmānyarūpatva)—the wise know that to be the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya).

Having investigated and examined the scriptures together with the noble ones through the cultivation of inner spirituality, they know that which abides in the universal reality of existence to be the supreme Brahman.
Know that state of deep sleep (*suṣuptatva*) to be that wherein the latent impression (*vāsanā*) remains dormant and sluggish within, like a sprout within a seed, and which bestows birth once again.

With the mind withdrawn within and latent impressions dormant on all sides, deep sleep—though characterized by insentience—is nevertheless a source of hundreds of miseries for one born into this world.
For all these beings, beginning with the immobile, possess the nature of insentience; they have ascended to the state of deep sleep, yet remain fit for birth again and again.
Just as flowers and the like exist within seeds, and as a jar exists within a heap of clay, so too, O virtuous one, does one's own latent impression reside within stationary beings.

That state where the seed of latent impressions (vāsanā) exists is deep sleep (suṣupta), which does not lead to perfection; that state where latent impressions are seedless is known as the Fourth (turya), which bestows perfection.
Likewise, even a tiny remnant of latent impressions, fire, debt, disease, enemies, oil, enmity, or poison causes affliction.

One who possesses the nature of the universal existence of the seeds of latent impressions (vāsanā) that have been utterly consumed—whether still embodied or disembodied—shall never again be a partaker of suffering.

The power of consciousness (cicchakti), whose nature consists of the seeds of latent impressions (vāsanā) and which possesses the character of dream, exists eternally as sapidity within all things, from stationary objects onwards.
In seeds, it exists as radiance; in insentient forms, as inertia; in substances, as substantiality; and in others, as hardness.
Then, she exists in the form of ash; likewise, she exists in the form of atoms within the dust; she exists in the state of blackness among dark things; and she exists as the sharp edge upon swords.
The Self is the power within all things; likewise, it abides in jars, cloths, and so forth, everywhere relying upon the form of the universal "Being."
Thus, this entire state of the visible stands filling [all space], just as clouds and rainbows fill the expanse of the monsoon sky.
And thus its own nature has been explained and investigated: it is non-universal yet all-pervasive, appearing as if real while being composed of latent impressions.
This view of a self is a non-view that causes wandering in saṃsāra; when it is seen [as it truly is], it brings about the destruction of all sufferings.
The non-perception of this [reality] is called ignorance (avidyā) by the wise; for ignorance is the cause of the world, and from it everything proceeds.
To the extent that ignorance is observed as being devoid of form, to that very extent it quickly dissolves, like a particle of frost in the sunlight.
Just as when a man whose sleep is fading reflects for even a moment upon his intention through the faculty of discernment, his sleep dissolves away.
Just as darkness is dispelled by light, so too does ignorance perish for as long as one conceptualizes what this state might be like.
Just as one approaches with a lamp in hand out of a desire to see forms obscured by darkness, so too does all darkness dissolve through the heat, just like clarified butter.
And no determination of form by darkness is perceived in a lamp; rather, there arises only the destruction of gloom, possessing a stainless form.
Thus, when being observed, she flees and goes away somewhere; for she is of an unreal form due to her lack of substantiality, yet she is seen because of a lack of investigation.
