Just as darkness is perceived when light has arrived, so too is the unreality of ignorance perceived once its lack of substantiality is realized.
As long as it is not illuminated, nothing at all is seen; once illuminated, ignorance is understood for what it truly is.
As soon as one reflects for oneself, "Who am I in this machine of blood, flesh, and bone?", everything instantly dissolves away.
When that which is unreal in nature at both the beginning and the end has certainly been discarded by the heart, they know that which remains in all things to be the destruction of ignorance.
That is neither nothing nor something; it is that very eternal Brahman. That reality is to be accepted as the goal when ignorance is dispelled.
Form is known to be devoid of intrinsic nature by its very name; for the taste of what is being tasted on the tongue is not perceived through anything else.
Ignorance does not exist anywhere; this is the indivisible Brahman alone, by which the entire expansion of the conceptualization of existence and non-existence is adorned.
The certainty that "this is not Brahman" is itself ignorance; the certainty that "this is Brahman" is its very destruction.

When it is said that "the pervasive Lord is not the web of appearances consisting of jars, cloths, and carts," that is ignorance; but if it is said that "the pervasive Lord is the web of appearances consisting of jars, cloths, and carts," then that ignorance has indeed vanished.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, this is being stated by me again and again for the sake of awakening: without practice, O virtuous one, the realization of the Self does not arise.
This ignorance is powerful, known by names other than "avidyā"; it has arisen from thousands of previous births and has become dense and firmly established.
It is experienced by all the senses, both externally and internally; because of this, the body has attained an extreme density amidst both existence and non-existence.
Self-knowledge, however, is beyond the range of all the senses; it attains its sole existence when the six senses, with the mind as the sixth, have ceased to function.
How indeed can that which remains transcending the functioning of the senses, and whose nature is beyond direct perception, ever come within the range of a living being's direct perception?
For your own realization, sever with the strokes of the sword of the playful practice of wisdom this creeper of ignorance that has taken root in the tree of your heart.
O Rāghava, dwell just as King Janaka dwelt after he had known all that is to be known—remaining devoted to the practice of self-knowledge.
This was the firm conviction of him who dwells in what ought and ought not to be done: whether waking or even standing still, for him there is truth through that knowledge.
It is certain that Hari, by means of whom he assumes various modes of conduct while descending into different wombs upon the earth, is proclaimed as possessing knowledge of those respective states.
O Rāghava, may that certainty which belongs to the Three-eyed One as he dwells with his beloved, or that which belongs to Brahmā who is free from passion, be yours as well.
That which is the firm resolve of Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, and of Bhārgava; and that of the Sun, the Moon, the Wind, and the Fire.
Of Nārada, Pulastya, and likewise of myself, Aṅgiras; of Pracetas, Bhṛgu, Kratu, Atri, and Śuka.
O best of Brahmins, O Raghava, let that very resolve which belongs to other royal sages who are liberated while still living be yours as well.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, O Brahmin, tell me in truth by what certainty these wise and high-minded ones remain free from sorrow and firmly established.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: "O prince of mighty arms, you who have known all that is to be known, listen clearly to how this matter was asked; for this indeed is their settled conclusion."
Whatever web of the world appears as an object of experience, all that is established as being the stainless Brahman.
Brahman is consciousness, Brahman is the world, and Brahman is the succession of all beings; I am Brahman, my enemy is Brahman, and my good friends and kinsmen are Brahman.
Brahman is the three times, and that [triple time] is established in Brahman alone; just as the ocean increases within itself by means of its waves and billows.
In this way, through the splendor of the categories of existence, this Brahman increases; Brahman is grasped by Brahman, and Brahman is enjoyed by Brahman.

Brahman expands within Brahman by means of its own expansive powers, just like the power of Brahman itself; yet that Brahman, appearing in the form of my enemy, acts as an adversary to me, who am Brahman.
That which is established in Brahman within Brahman—what else has been done by anyone? The persistence of imagined passions and the like is like a tree in the sky.

For those who have perished through the absence of volitional thought, what occasion for increase remains here? Indeed, even within the entirety of Brahman, there is the movement of walking, vibration, and so forth.
The entire Brahman vibrates; how can there be happiness or suffering? Brahman is fully satisfied in Brahman; Brahman is established in Brahman.
Brahman vibrates within Brahman; "I am not this other self. A pot is Brahman, a cloth is Brahman, and I am this pervasive Brahman.
Therefore, when the Brahman of the body has merged into the Brahman of death, what false construction can there be here regarding passion and dispassion? They are merely arbitrary.
For those who are suffering, what else could there be but the delusion of a rope-snake? When Brahman is established as the Brahman of the body, where is there pleasure in enjoyment and the like?
"How has this been accomplished by me?"—such a vain conceit would be groundless; for it is not different from water, just as the waves and the water both possess motion.

In Brahman, whose nature is vibration, "thou-ness" and "I-ness" do not exist in the same way [as they appear]; for just as nothing ever dies anywhere when deprived of water, so it is with these notions.
When the Brahman of the body has indeed attained the state of the Brahman of death, then "thou-ness" and "I-ness" do not remain, just as [the notions of] motion and stillness do not persist in water.
Likewise, the forms of the insentient and the sentient do not exist in the Supreme Self, just as the state of being a bracelet does not exist in gold, nor as a whirlpool in water.
In this way, the nature of the self consists of both being that and not being that; for this [nature] is the living self, while this other becomes the form of the insentient.

Thus, there is delusion for one whose nature is ignorance, but never for one whose nature is knowledge; for the ignorant, the world consists of a flood of suffering, while for the wise, it consists of bliss.
To the blind man, the world is darkness; but to the one with sight, it is light. To the wise man, the world is of a single nature; to the fool, it is exceedingly painful.
Like a night in which yakṣas flicker for a child, yet is empty for an adult, so too is this single, eternal jar of Brahman situated everywhere.
Nothing indeed dies, nor does anything live; just as in the play of ripples, nothing perishes and nothing is born.

Just as waves and other phenomena exist within the great ocean, so too does the multitude of beings exist within the Self; the notion that "this does not exist" or "this exists" is merely a delusion of the Self regarding itself.
Power alone flashes forth within without cause, like the rays of a crystal; the Self itself, as the essence of the power of the universe, is Brahman abiding within its own self.
Just as dense water is not destroyed by a spray of water droplets and waves, how could there be the notion of death regarding Brahman through the destruction of the body?
For indeed, nothing such as a body exists apart from Brahman, just as waves and the like do not exist apart from the water in the great ocean.
Whatever drop or droplet, whatever ripple or wavelet, whatever foam or surge—just as water is within water.
Whatever body, whatever mental construction, whatever visible world, whatever decay and non-decay, whatever arrangement of phenomena, and whatever object—by all that, it is Brahman within Brahman.
The diverse arrangement of forms belongs to Brahman, like [ornaments] made from gold; it is not of any other nature. For the deluded, however, the perception of duality is merely false.
The mind, the intellect, the ego, the subtle elements, and the senses—all this is Brahman alone; there is no manifold self, nor does pleasure or pain exist.
Through speech arising from such meanings as "I am this" or "this is the mind," the self unfolds within itself like an echo of sound in a mountain cave.
Brahman itself, when unknown, remains as if it has arrived at a state of ignorance; for in this way, the self is seen by the mind through the self within a dream.
If Brahman is not cultivated through the state of being Brahman, it becomes the impurity of ignorance; just as gold that is not refined remains as earth.
The knowers of Brahman know that the Great-Souled One himself is indeed Brahman; that which is not fully understood by the ignorant is called ignorance.
When known as Brahman, the non-Brahman becomes Brahman itself in an instant; when known as gold, the non-gold becomes gold itself in an instant.
For Brahmā is the Self, possessing all powers; therefore, whatever he intensely contemplates, being himself without external cause, he quickly perceives that very thing through his own power.
Those who know Brahman know Brahman to be without action, without agent, without instrument, without cause, and free from affliction—the self-sovereign Great Self.
That which is not fully understood is called ignorance; when it is fully understood, it becomes knowledge, which brings about the total destruction of ignorance.
Indeed, even a kinsman, when not fully understood, is called a non-kinsman; once fully understood, he becomes a kinsman through the destruction of the delusion of being a non-kinsman.
Once duality is known internally to be unreal, this realization arises; and through that distaste for duality, one indeed becomes dispassionate.
When it is clearly known that "this is not I," the cultivation [of this realization] arises; through this, one certainly becomes dispassionate toward false egoism.
When the knowledge "I am indeed Brahman" is true, that realization arises; it dissolves within one's own true nature, just as [an object] is absorbed within its own interior.
When that [Brahman] has been fully expanded, I know this world as "This is Brahman"; when the notions of "you," "I," and so forth are sublated, that which pertains to the world is "That" and "Being."
I know that this Brahman is the truth, enriched with every excellence; for me there is no suffering, no karmas, no delusion, and no desire.
I am equanimous, established in my own nature, and free from sorrow; "I am Brahman"—this is the truth. I am liberated from all parts and stains; I am everything, free from all affliction.
I do not renounce, nor do I desire; "I am Brahman"—this is the truth. I am blood, I am flesh, I am bones, and I am the body.
I am consciousness, I am sentience, and I am Brahman—this is the truth. I am the sky, I am space, I am with the sun, I am the quarters, and I am the earth as well.
"I am the form of the jar and the cloth; 'I am Brahman' is the truth. I am the grass, I am the earth, I am the shrub, and I am the forest and so forth."
I am the caravan leader of mountains and oceans; indeed, the oneness of Brahman is established. The powers of the elements are preceded by taking, giving, and contraction.
I am indeed the all-pervading conscious self, assuming the form of the expanded Brahman within the creepers, shrubs, sprouts, and so forth that seek their own manifestation.
The Supreme Brahman, whose essence is bliss, is peaceful and resides within the conscious self; that in which all is contained, from which all proceeds, which is all, and which is everywhere.

The certainty is that He who is considered by all to be the one Self, the Supreme Brahman, is known by such names as the conscious Self (cidātman), Brahman, Being (sat), Truth (satya), Immortality (amṛta), and the Knower (jña).
The all-pervading reality is said to be pure consciousness alone, devoid of objects of thought; it is stainless mere manifestation, which awakens the self-awareness of all beings.

The conscious Brahman is experienced as abiding everywhere and being tranquil, yet it is endowed with the entire array of mental constructs consisting of the mind, intellect, and the collection of sense organs.
Having abandoned all differentiation, I am the stainless Brahman-consciousness, my own manifestation, the cause of all things such as sound and the rest that constitute the existence of the world.
I am the pure Brahman-consciousness that provides space for reality; there is no decay for me, for my nature consists of a dense torrent of pure consciousness flowing incessantly.
Light, the silence of the wise mind, I am the supreme immortal Brahman-consciousness; I eternally experience the nectar of realization, whose nature flows without ceasing.
I am the stainless Brahman-consciousness, in which all cycles of day and night have ceased; it is peaceful, resembling deep sleep, and its nature is pure light.
I am the supreme enjoyment, the manifestation of Consciousness-Brahman, free from latent impressions; the perception of the taste of sugar-candy and other sweets remains only as a slight trace.

When the mind and other faculties have been fully realized, one truly becomes that Brahman, the Imperishable; yet for one whose mind is attached to a beloved, even when the moon has risen, [that realization does not occur].
I am the stainless Consciousness-Brahman, existing by virtue of the moon as a condition, for those people standing on the earth who have their gaze fixed upon the moon in the sky.
Indeed, that power of consciousness which abides in the void is the stainless Brahman-consciousness; likewise, it is stainless and devoid of any conceptualization of pleasure, pain, and the like.
I am the eternal Self, the Brahman whose nature is consciousness and the experience of truth; while the mind is fixed elsewhere, I remain like a traveler in a world of strangers.
That consciousness which is free from fault—I am that all-pervading Brahman—just as it exists in the causal operations of the sprout during the conjunction of earth, water, air, and seed.

I am that pervasive Consciousness-Brahman, whose power resides within the *udgamanīya* [the inner garment]; I abide of my own accord within myself, like dates, nimba fruits, and bimba fruits [which remain within their own husks].

That which is the existence of one's own taste, dissolved within, is that Brahman; I am the Consciousness, equal [to all], with an inner awareness free from both sorrow and joy, arising from the dawn of contemplation.
I am the stainless Consciousness-Brahman, equal in the occurrence of gain and loss; as far as the earth and the sun extend, so far is the thread of vision stretched out.
Pervading that, I am the tranquil, stainless, and expansive Consciousness, similar to its very essence; it has arisen likewise in the waking state, in deep sleep, and also in the dream state.

I am the fourth state, formless, without beginning or end, the pure consciousness-Brahman, free from all affliction; I abide like the sweetness inherent in hundreds of sugarcanes that have arisen as individual fields for men.
That Consciousness-Brahman is of one form in all; I am that, established in equanimity. It is the inherent, transparent nature, like the radiance of the sun.
I am this pervasive Consciousness-Brahman, the beloved one who creates light, like a particle of the bliss of enjoyment and like the power of tasting nectar.

I am that immutable Consciousness-Brahman, which is known solely through one's own direct experience; though its limbs are spread throughout the body, its face remains hidden, like a fiber within a lotus stalk.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, those great ones, possessed of certainty and free from sin, being true, abide happily in the true, peaceful, and even state.
Thus, the wise ones of perfected intellect, whose minds are free from passion, neither revile nor rejoice in life, nor likewise in death.
Thus, possessing an inconceivable wonder like the arms of Nārāyaṇa, they were straight yet appeared as if stumbling, like other Meru mountains.
They gazed upon forest groves, islands, and cities, as well as rows of celestial gardens and heavens, like gods themselves.
They wandered among the flower-filled groves swaying on the swings, and upon the peaks of Mount Meru adorned with various forest ranges.
They established kingdoms that had conquered their enemies, were graced with fly-whisks and parasols, possessed diverse wealth, and were characterized by wonderful conduct.
They followed all these people, whose conduct and activities varied, regarding their duties as those prescribed by the Vedas and the Smṛtis.
Adorned with such enjoyments—delightful, captivating with the smiles of beautiful women, and charming with pleasure gardens and places of recreation—they revel in their abundance.
And they entered the grounds of the Nandana grove, filled with beautiful mango trees, entwined with mandāra blossoms, and resounded with the songs of apsarases.
Among all beings, both moving and unmoving, among all creatures resting therein, and among the various ritual acts of sacrifice within the stages of domestic life, in their proper sequence.
In the pathways of the ocean of battle, where lordly elephants were being slaughtered, where numerous jackals wandered about, and which were terrifying with the booming sounds of kettledrums;
They remained amidst all forms of dualistic conduct—whether harsh-minded, arrogant because they had seized wealth, or fierce with the agitation of fury.
But their minds were free from passion, unconditioned, devoid of delusion, unattached, liberated, profoundly peaceful, and had reached the supreme state of pure being.
They did not sink, even in any great perils, however immense they might have been, just as lotuses do not sink when great floods come upon them.
O scion of the Raghus, he shone with the most beautiful Śrī, who was like a playful woman, just as the mass of waters shines with the splendor of the full moon.
He did not wither through the sorrow of suffering, as a forest glade does not under the heat of summer; nor did he rejoice in floods of enjoyments, as medicinal herbs do not at the touch of dewdrops.
For they, O Rāma, being entirely undistracted while performing their actions, neither clung to nor abandoned the desirable or undesirable fruits of those kāma-mañjarīs.
They did not rejoice at the accomplishment of their tasks, nor did they sink when overcome by them; they did not exult upon attaining happiness, nor did they wither even in times of distress.
They did not become bewildered in times of delusion, nor did they sink under the weight of calamities; they did not rejoice in auspicious events, nor did they weep in sorrows as you do.
Performing only their duties as required by their natural conduct, they remained free from agitation, like other Meru mountains.
O Raghava, having firmly grasped that vision which destroys all evil, roam at your ease in due order, free from egoism and devoid of the sense of "I."
Beholding this very succession of creations as it truly is, remain equanimous and free from delusion, like one standing upon Mount Meru, as deep as the ocean.
All this is indeed pure consciousness alone that has come to appear in this manner; here, there is nothing whatsoever that exists as either real or unreal.

Relying on the stainless greatness [of the Self], abandon this world with indifference; O fortunate one, become one whose intellect is unattached everywhere and who brings an end to worldly existence.
"Why do you weep with such intense agitation, and why do you grieve like a fool? You wander with a bewildered mind, O gentle one, like a blade of grass caught in a whirlpool."
Śrī Rāma said: Oh, Blessed One! Truly, the destruction of my impurities has been perfectly accomplished; through your grace, I have awakened like a lotus at the touch of the sun.
My delusion has surely vanished like mist in autumn; with all my doubts completely stilled, I shall carry out your word.

O virtuous one, if you speak here with a mind that is clear and single-mindedly focused, free from intoxication and delusion, liberated from pride and envy, whose soul has long been joyful and whose sorrow has long since been stilled, and who no longer falls back into suffering—then I shall do it without hesitation.

Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin, through the manifestation of perfect knowledge, upon the arising of the dissolution of latent impressions, I have indeed found rest in the state of one liberated while living.
O Brahman, tell me how one rests in the state of liberation while living, when the dissolution of latent impressions arises through the cessation of the vibration of the vital breath.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The method for crossing over the cycle of existence is expressed by the word "yoga. Know that it is of two kinds, characterized by the pacification of the mind.
Self-knowledge is one method of this [practice] manifested on earth; hear now from me what is called the second, which is the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Śrī Rāma said: Of these two, which is the better—the one that is easily attained or the one that is free from suffering—by the mere understanding of which no further agitation afflicts one?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Although both modes are indeed expressed by the word "yoga," nevertheless, it has become firmly established in common usage primarily for that which is joined with the vital breath (prāṇa).
In the process of crossing over saṃsāra, yoga and likewise knowledge are the two equal means; both are said to bestow a single fruit.
For some, yoga is unattainable; for others, the certainty of knowledge. But for me, O virtuous one, the certainty of knowledge is considered easily attainable.
Furthermore, ignorance that remains unknown would not exist even in dreams; knowledge, however, always functions in all states.

Or perhaps yoga does not become easily accomplished because it must be achieved through the practice of *dhāraṇā*, the seat, the location, and so forth; yet such a conceptualization is certainly not sound.

"O descendant of Raghu, it is said that there are indeed only two paths of knowledge taught in the scriptures; therein, knowledge has been described to you as being inwardly situated and pure of the object of knowledge."
Established through the movement of prāṇa and apāna, dwelling in the cave of the firm body, this yoga bestows infinite accomplishments and wisdom; listen, O virtuous one!

O Prince, having attained stability through the cessation of the movement of breath from the mouth, you shall abide with an imperishable mind; through the practice of yoga, remaining concentrated here, you will dwell in the supreme state with all speech stilled.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Indeed, within that infinite [Brahman], there exists somewhere this vibration in the form of the world, like a mirage in a desert.
There, Brahmā, born from the lotus, became the cause; he stood as the Grandfather, his mind reeling under the weight of the created beings.
I am his mind-born son, Vasiṣṭha, whose conduct is preeminent; I dwell in the circle of the bears (Ursa Major), which is fixed upon the Pole Star, for every age.
Once, while I was staying in the assembly hall of Indra in heaven, I heard from Nārada and others a discourse concerning those who have lived for a very long time.
Then, during the course of a certain conversation, a sage named Śātātapa—silent, dignified, and high-minded—spoke there.
In the northeastern corner of Meru, in a celestial realm made of ruby, there stands a glorious wish-fulfilling tree on its peak, known as the Mango Tree.
At the summit of that wish-fulfilling tree, within a hollow in its southern branch, there exists a bird's nest woven with golden creepers.
In that vast hollow dwelt a glorious crow named Bhuśuṇḍa, free from passion, like Brahmā in his own lotus.
Just as he lives here for a long time within the treasury of the worlds, so shall Cirañjīvī live in heaven; no one has ever been, nor will there ever be, his equal.
He is long-lived, he is free from passion, he is glorious, he is of great intelligence; he is one whose mind is at rest, he is peaceful, he is beloved, and he is skilled in the knowledge of time.
If one lives here in this world just as that bird lives, then that life would be meritorious, long, and truly successful.
Thus, being questioned further by him, Bhuśuṇḍa described it exactly as it was, speaking the truth in the assembly of the gods.
When the assembly of gods had departed and the occasion for their discourse had subsided, I went out of curiosity to see the bird Bhuśuṇḍa.
Where Bhuśuṇḍa was stationed, there I reached in an instant that supreme peak of Meru, vast and composed of rubies.
With a brilliance as lovely as red chalk and possessing the splendor of fire, it colored the expanse of the quarters as if with the essence of honeyed wine.
It was like a mountain of accumulated masses of fire blazing at the end of an aeon, with the smoke from its sapphire crests reddening the sky with its light.
It stood like a mountain of heaps for all passions, and like a single dense mine for the entire web of twilight clouds.
As Meru undergoes its upward departure, the lovely submarine fire—the digestive heat—emerges through the Brahma-nāḍī and reaches his head.
Like a goddess of the Sumeru forest, she playfully extended her finger-tip into the sky to grasp the moon, which was stained with fresh lac-dye.
With its red garlands of flames, the sky—its face being the clouds—seemed as if it were quivering to go toward the mountain, like the submarine fire (Vāḍava) situated upon a peak.
With its three fingers—the tips of its shimmering rays—seeming to touch the sky as if to grasp the stars, it kisses the heights.
The pavilion of the mountains had thundering clouds for its drums, was rich with clusters of blossoming flowers that seemed to laugh, and resounded with swarms of humming bees.
With its rows of teeth-like palm leaves shimmering as if in playful laughter, it possessed a noble and intoxicated passion, with throngs of celestial nymphs swaying like cradles.
Its caves were inhabited by pairs of gods resting upon the rocks; it wore the excellent garments of deerskins and bore the white Ganges as its sacred thread.
He saw a mendicant standing like Piṅgala, holding a bamboo staff, amidst a bower of creepers resounding with the roar of the Ganges' cascades, like an immortal.

The tawny head of Mera, fragrant with the sweet breeze carrying the lovely songs of Gandharvas, adorned with crowns of blooming golden lotuses and decorated with stars like jewels, appeared as if it had reached the very limit of the sky.
With heaps of forest flowers in fresh colors—white, green, yellow, pale red, and white—the pure paintings created in the sky were the play-mountain of the assembly of celestial young women.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Upon his head, where the locks of hair were like clouds filled with flowers, I beheld the Great Kalpa situated like a wheel of branches.
Enveloped by clouds of flower-pollen and bristling with clusters of jewels, it seemed as if one peak were placed upon another, its height surpassing the very sky.
A mass of flowers double that of the stars, foliage double that of the clouds, a mist of pollen double that of the rays of light, and clusters of blossoms double that of lightning.
In its branches resounded the song of the kinnarīs, doubled by the humming of bees; its foliage was made doubly vibrant by the world of apsarases swaying upon their swings.
The birds there arose in numbers twice that of the throngs of Siddhas and Gandharvas; their bark-garments were doubled by a fine mist, shimmering with the luster of jewels.
Its large fruit was doubled in size by its embrace of the lunar orb; its joints were doubled by clouds that resembled those at the dissolution of the world, clinging to its base.
Its trunks were entwined with delicious creepers, and kinnaras rested upon its leaves; it was like a cloud within a forest bower, where gods and others slept by its marshy banks.

Having driven away the bees with the tinkling sounds of their bracelets, [the women]—who were like female bees among the Apsarases—held flowers within their hands that were as vast as their own forms.
It was accompanied by excellent Suras, Kinnaras, Gandharvas, and Vidyādharas, filling the infinite space in all ten directions like the web of the world.
It possessed a dense network of buds, dense and tender shoots, dense blossoming flowers, and was garlanded with dense forests.
It was a dense mass of flower clusters, a thick cluster of jewels, rich with garments and gems that were without gaps, and agitated by the playful movements of creepers.
Everywhere, with flowers in full bloom, everywhere with fruits and sprouts, and everywhere with masses of fragrant pollen, a supreme variety was attained.
In its armpits, in its bowers, upon the leaves of its creepers, at its joints, and among its flowers, I saw birds nestled within their dwellings.
The Brahman-swan-like ascetics were nourished by fragments of lotus stalks as delicate as a digit of the moon, and they fed upon morsels of the roots of the *arjuna* lotus-plant.
He saw the young swans of Viriñci, who chant the Sāman, who are friends of the Veda through the syllable Oṃ, and who are instructed in the knowledge of Brahman.
They vomited forth a multitude of mantras with sounds resembling the utterance of "svāhā," appearing like dark clouds filled with a mass of lightning amidst their bones.
He saw parrots, dark as the fire-god, perched constantly upon the leafy creepers of the sacrificial altars being gazed upon by the gods; and he saw young peacocks with crests like the tips of flames.
He saw excellent peacocks protected by Gaurī, belonging to Kumāra, who were experts in the entirety of Śiva’s knowledge imparted by Skanda.
He saw his kinsmen, who were like autumn clouds in appearance, having taken up residence in the sky—great celestial birds born and perished within the very heavens themselves.
There were others born from the swan of Viriñci, others born from Agni and Śuka, others born from the peacock of Kumāra, and others born from the bird of Ambara.
And he saw Bharadvāja birds with two beaks, golden-crested birds, sparrows, cranes, vultures, cuckoos, krauñcas, and wild cocks.
O Raghava, I saw there many other birds as well—parrots, blue jays, cranes, and the like—like a multitude of beings upon the earth.
Then, while standing in the sky, I beheld her situated far off on the southern branch of the tree, which was covered with lush foliage.
In time, Kāka appeared on the Lokāloka mountain, encircled by a garland of clusters of blossoms, like a mass of clouds at the end of an eon standing in the forest.
There, as far as I could see, in a hollow of a tree trunk at one side, strewn with various flowers and filled with diverse fragrances, I beheld [him].
In the assembly hall of the meritorious women in heaven, which was perfumed by clusters of beloved flowers, the crows stood with their forms entirely undisturbed.
The clouds, torn asunder by the wind, were dispersed as if by a gale; standing in their midst was the glorious Bhuśuṇḍa, of towering form.
And in the midst of the fragments of glass, he was as prominent as a sapphire—full-minded, dignified, equanimous, and beautiful in every limb.
By constant attention to the movement of the vital breath, he remains perpetually inward-turned and happy; he is renowned as "Cirañjīvī" (the Long-lived One) because of that long life.
Renowned throughout the world as Bhuśuṇḍa, he was celebrated for his long life; his mind was matured by witnessing the conditions of the arrival and departure of the ages.
And in every kalpa, he grew weary counting the succession of births of the world-protectors—of Śarva, Śakra, and the Maruts.
He was a rememberer of kings long past among gods and asuras, possessing a clear and profound mind, being elegant, and speaking with words that were tender and charming.

He is the speaker of the unmanifest, the knower, free from possessiveness and free from egoism; he is the well-wisher, the kinsman, as well as the friend, the son of Death, the teacher, and the lord; he is always and in every way truth, and everything in the praise of all.

Gentle, serene, sweet, and full of flavor, that great-souled one was heart-pleasing like a lake whose inner regions are cool; a knower of worldly conduct, he did not abandon his profound depth even within the hollow of his heart-lotus, for the glory of his intentions was manifest.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, with my body blazing, I fell from the sky before him like a star falling upon a mountain, causing a slight commotion in the assembly.
The crow-pen, resembling a lake of blue lotuses, was agitated by the gentle wind of my landing, like the ocean by an earthquake.
Although he had arrived unexpectedly, Bhuśuṇḍa understood immediately upon seeing me that this was Vasiṣṭha who had come.
Rising up from the heap of leaves like a young cloud from a mountain, he spoke in sweet syllables: "O Sage, welcome!"
With his two hands, which were produced by mere volition, he immediately offered me a handful of flowers, like a mass of gold from a cloud.
When the leader of the crows had dismissed his attendants and brought forward a fresh leaf of the wish-fulfilling tree, saying, "Please accept this seat."
When Bhuśuṇḍa had risen and his own flock of birds had departed, he saw the sage seated there, with his gaze directed toward his own seat.
Then, surrounded on all sides by a flock of birds together with Bhuśuṇḍa, I sat down upon a seat in that thicket of kalpa-trees.
Having prepared the water for honor, the water for the feet, and other offerings, Bhuśuṇḍa, possessed of great luster and a contented mind, spoke to me with friendliness in sweet syllables.
Bhuśuṇḍa said: "Oh! After a long time, the Blessed One has shown us his grace, for we, like noble trees, have been sprinkled by the nectar-dew of your vision."
O Sage, most worthy of honor, by whom you have now been impelled through the long-accumulated store of my merit—whence have you come?
I trust that while you have long dwelt in this great delusion, equanimity remains entirely unbroken within your pure mind.
Why have you troubled yourself with the hardship of coming here today? You ought to grant us an answer, for we are eager to hear your words.
O Sage, by the mere sight of your feet, everything has been known by me; through the merit of your arrival, we have been graced by you.
We have come to your memory through our long-standing discussions on longevity; therefore, you have now sanctified this abode with your feet.
O Sage, although the scripture is already known to you, I ask you this here because my longing for the taste of the nectar of your words is fully awakened.
Having spoken thus, that bird Bhuśuṇḍa, who has lived for a long time and perceives the stainless reality of the three times, said this to me there.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: "O great king of birds, what you say is true; I have come today specifically to see you, who are long-lived."
"By good fortune, you are safe with a cooled inner heart; you have not fallen, O soul of the Buddha, into the terrifying snare of worldly existence."
Therefore, O Blessed One, sever this doubt of mine according to the truth: in what family were you born, and how did you become one who has known that which is to be known?
O virtuous one, how long is your lifespan, and what conduct do you remember? By whom was this dwelling-place pointed out to you, O far-sighted one?
Bhuśuṇḍa said: "O Sage, I shall describe all that you ask; a story should be heard with effort by a high-souled person who is free from agitation."

That which persons of noble intellect and great stature like you—whose forms are worthy of worship by the lords of the three worlds—listen to, brings about destruction through its proclamation of impurity, just as the heat of the sun is dispelled by the presence of clouds.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Now, O Rāma, that Bhuśuṇḍa was neither delighted nor crooked-minded; he was beautiful in all his limbs, dark-complexioned like a rain-cloud in the monsoon season.
His speech was smooth and profound, and he always addressed others with a smile; he weighed the three worlds as easily as a bilva fruit held in his hand.

Having viewed everything as if it were a blade of grass, he has rendered the cycle of existence an object of knowledge; having seen the world’s state of constant flux, he has realized the higher and lower limits of gnosis.
Steady, firm, and of great form, having attained rest like Mount Mandara, his mind is perfectly fulfilled and pure, appearing like the ocean of milk arrived in person.
With his intellect fully rested and tranquil, reeling with supreme bliss, he is a knower of the manifestation and disappearance of worldly births.

With a form as delightful as a face full of impetuous joy, his speech was charming and pleasant, suited for song; he seemed to have personally assumed a new body, filled with great rapture and capable of removing all fear.
With pure speech and a flawless sequence of words, he spoke this stainless nectar; like a charming cloud revealing its entire nature through thunder, he declared his own true form.
Bhuśuṇḍa said: "In this world, there is a supreme one among all the inhabitants of heaven, the God of gods named Hara, who is saluted by the gods of gods."
She whose eyes were like rows of bees, and who possessed breasts like lofty clusters of blossoms, was like a playful creeper clinging to half the body of a mango tree.
The Gaṅgā, white as snow and moonlight, entwined with clusters of waves and her matted locks coiled about him, is his garland of flowers.
Born from the ocean of milk, a flowing cascade of nectar, the glorious moon, acting as a reflected image, serves as his crest-jewel.
He who has rendered the Kālakūṭa poison nectar-like through the incessant flow from the moon upon his head, wears it as an ornament upon his neck like a sapphire.
The white water of his knowledge consists of ashes made of atoms, born from the pure fire of the great whirlpool of lines of dust.
His very bones, stainless and surpassing the moon, were fashioned and wrought as jewels composed of the splendor of his body.
His garment is the sky, which is nourished by the nectar of the moon, possesses the sprouts of dark rain-clouds, and is variegated with the dots of stars.
The house of which has become an external cremation ground, white as snow, filled with the cooked human flesh and rice of female jackals wandering about.
Adorned with garlands of skulls, wearing yellow and red garments and smeared with fat and liquor, their bodies entwined with strings of entrails—these are his kinsmen, the Mothers.
Whose bracelets are serpents with smooth bodies and the luster of shining gold, moving about with the jewels upon their heads trembling.
His conduct as Bhairava—intent on devouring the world, which is like a great mountain consumed by the mere glance of his eye—terrified the asuras through his effortless play.
For him whose mind was established in his own duty after having restored the world to health, the movement of his hand by mere chance brought about the destruction of the cities of the asuras.
Those mountains, whose forms were one-pointed and who were free from affection, passion, and hatred, were like his own food—though full of sap, they were yet devoid of flavor.

Whose attendants—the Pramathas—playfully sport with those who have heads for hooves, hooves for hands, and hands, teeth, mouths, and bellies for faces; and who possess the faces of bears, camels, goats, and snakes.
With a face resplendent with three eyes, his retinue consists of other Mothers whose stainless radiance is just like that of his Gaṇas.
The Mothers dance before him, bowing down along with hosts of spirits; they are the sole consumers of the infinite multitude of beings belonging to the fourteen classes.
With faces shaped like those of donkeys and camels, drinking blood, fat, and marrow, wandering through the quarters of space, they wear garlands made of the limbs of bodies.
Upon the peaks of the Vindhya mountains, in the sky, and in other worlds; in chasms, in cremation grounds, and within the bodies of embodied beings.
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, Aparājitā, Siddhā, Raktālambusā, and Utpalā are the deities.
Of all the Mothers, these eight are indeed the principal leaders; others follow them, and yet others follow those.
O Leader of Sages, O Giver of Honor, among those highly esteemed mothers, there exists one renowned as the mother Alambuṣā.
And the one named Caṇḍa has a vajra for bones and a beak, resembling a mountain of sapphire; his vehicle is a crow, just as Garuḍa is that of Vaiṣṇavī.
Thus, those Mothers, endowed with the eight sovereign powers and characterized by fierce deeds, once gathered together in the sky for some reason or other.
Those who follow the Vāma stream, having taken refuge in Tumburu and Rudra, celebrated a supreme festival that reveals the ultimate truth.
Having worshipped the two gods Tumburu and Bhairava, who are themselves worthy of worship by the world, they engaged in conversations of diverse meaning, delighted by the intoxication of wine.
Then, in the course of their conversation, this speech arose: "Does the divine Lord of Umā regard us with such indifference?"
"Let us display our power to him so that he, whose great might has been seen by us for only a moment, will not treat us with contempt."
Having thus resolved, those goddesses, having brought Umā herself under their control, respectfully sprinkled her whose face and limbs were pale.

The goddesses gazed upon her, whose hair was disheveled, who had been carried away by Māyā from her husband’s side, who had come to the stage of performance, and who had now fallen into a state of weeping.
On that day of Pārvatī’s consecration, a great festival took place there, enchanting with the dancing and singing of all those women.
The sky shone with unrestrained sounds of excessive joy, while their hips and bellies expanded through the tossing of their long limbs.
Others laughed with unrestrained outcries and deep roars, their limbs quivering, while the mountains and forests resounded with their noise.
Others, delighted by the drinking bouts, sang from the mountain peaks; their voices, like water, filled the hollow of the world-mandala with resonant sound.
Others drank their fill, their limbs, heads, and hooves smeared with nourishment, as they made light, gurgling sounds that echoed through the hollow of the sky.

The goddesses drank deeply and exulted; they moved with haste, spoke, laughed, and offered oblations to the fire. They fell down, leaped high, danced incessantly, and ate savory meat. Having turned the three worlds upside down, they acted with the conduct of madwomen.
Bhuśuṇḍa said: While this festival was thus proceeding, their excellent mounts likewise became intoxicated; they laughed, danced, and even drank blood.
There, in one place, certain celestial swans (*rathahaṃsya*), intoxicated by the *āsava* liquor, danced in the sky; they were of the nature of Brahmā, and Kāka was their charioteer, Alambusa.
And as the female swans danced and drank the wine, they experienced perfect delight upon the surface of the ocean shores.
Having become impassioned and intoxicated, all those female swans took their turn; then, it is said, they even dallied with the crow while in that state of intoxication.
That crow was the beloved of seven noble female swans; he took his pleasure with them one after another until they were mutually satisfied.
Then those queens, having conceived, became exceedingly joyful; and having performed their dances, they returned to a state of perfect tranquility.
The goddesses transformed Umā, the beloved of the Lord, into the state of a frog—a great illusion—for the meal of the trident-wielding Śiva.
And when the moon-crested Lord, having understood that [the goddesses] had said, "She gave us food which is dear to us," became enraged toward the group of Mothers;
Then, having brought her forth once more by the gift of their own limbs, they gave Pārvatī again in marriage to the Moon-crested Lord.
Then the goddesses, Hara himself, and their respective retinues, all with contented minds, departed each toward their own direction.
O Lord of Sages, those divine female swans became pregnant and related to her exactly as it had occurred the entire account of the goddess Brāhmī.
Brāhmī said: "O calves, you who are currently like calves to me in the work of the chariot are no longer capable; therefore, roam about now according to your own will."
Having spoken thus to the swans who were sluggish due to pregnancy, the goddess Brāhmī, devoted to compassion, remained at ease in unwavering meditative absorption.
O Lord of Sages, those royal swans, languid from pregnancy, wandered within the lotus-pond of Brahmā, which was like a lake with its center at the navel of the Unborn.
Thus, when their wombs had matured, they gave birth upon the petals of the navel-lotus to soft eggs, just as creepers produce sprouts.
When the time arrived, those twenty-one eggs split into two by the entry of the embryo, like the substantial cosmic eggs of Brahmā.
"O Sage, it is from those very eggs that we were born in this manner—these twenty-one crows, brothers born of Caṇḍa."
They were born and grew up upon that lotus petal; having developed their wings, they became capable of soaring through the sky.
Then the Blessed Lady Brāhmī, together with her mothers who were like female swans, having long propitiated [the deity] and being perfectly devoted to meditative concentration, remained steadfast.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One herself, intent upon showing grace, favored us with her very limbs, so that we remain liberated.
With our minds thoroughly stilled and at peace, having resolved, "We shall remain established in meditation in solitude," we went to the side of our father.
Then, embraced by our father and honored by Alambusā, we were seen by her with favor and remained there, self-restrained.
Caṇḍa said: "My sons, have you truly emerged from this web of saṃsāra, which is enveloped by the threads of the cords of limitless latent impressions?"
If we do not entreat this Blessed Lady, who is so kind to her servants, [then how could it be that] you have reached the further shore of knowledge?
The crows said: "O father, by the grace of the divine Brāhmī, that which is to be known has been fully known; however, we desire an excellent place for dwelling in solitude."
Caṇḍa said: "There indeed exists a mountain named Meru, the support of all collections of jewels and the refuge of all the gods, possessing truly great height."
Within the pavilion of the cosmic egg, he is the pillar made of gold, for whom the moon and sun are the lamps and the multitude of living beings are the family ornaments.
Richly adorned with a golden moon-throne and jewel-encrusted peaks for its fingers, it was like an arm of the earth raised up, encircled by the sounding oceans and continents.
Surrounded by the neighboring mountain-kings, seated upon the throne of Jambūdvīpa, the king caused his eyes—the sun and the moon—to revolve within that assembly of mountains.

He whose garland is the multitude of stars and jasmine blossoms, who is the sole garment for the ten directions, whose self resides within the two species of serpents, and who is the ornament of the lord of heaven.
He is fanned on all sides by beautiful women from every quarter, who are like ornaments of the city, with cool, flowing yak-tail whisks as thick as clouds.
Sixteen thousand yojanas of his feet are situated beneath the earth, and they are worshipped by the nāgas, asuras, and mahoragas.
His body measures eighty thousand [yojanas], with the sun and moon as his eyes; he is worshipped in the celestial abode by gods, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras.
Just as kinsmen depend upon a householder, so do beings of fourteen kinds subsist upon him, having seen his former dwelling place.
In its northeastern direction, however, there exists a great peak made of ruby, like another sun risen from the horizon.
Upon his back stands a great Kalpa tree, surrounded by hosts of beings, appearing like a reflection of the world in the mirror of its summit.
On its southern shoulder there is a branch with golden shoots, densely covered with clusters of jewels, and bearing fruits that shine like the orb of the moon.
There, O sons, a nest was formerly built by me—a nest shimmering with jewels—wherein I indeed took delight while the Queen sat absorbed in meditation.
It was covered with petals of jewel-flowers, endowed with fruits that were elixirs, and its courtyards were fashioned with rods of wish-fulfilling gems.
Filled with young crows whose every movement was preceded by intelligence, its interior was cool and pleasant, and it was strewn with heaps of flowers.
Therefore, go, my sons, to that nest which is difficult even for the inhabitants of heaven to reach; staying there, you will surely attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation without any obstacle.
Having spoken thus, our father there kissed us and embraced us, and gave us that meat which the queen had brought for us.
Having eaten that and having saluted the feet of the goddess and our father, we leaped from that place, the marshy region of the Vindhya, away from Ālambusa.
Gradually ascending through the sky and emerging from the hollows of the clouds, they reached the mass of the wind and paid homage to the celestial wanderers.
"O Lord of Sages, having left behind the Lord of Day (the Sun) and gone to the city of the other world, we have transcended heaven and arrived at the world of Brahmā."
There, preceded by a prostration, he quickly reported those words of his father exactly as they were to his mother and to the divine Brāhmī.
Having been embraced affectionately by those two and encouraged by their command to depart, we offered our salutations and emerged from the world of Brahmā.
Having transcended the cities of the world-protectors, they move through the sky, radiant as the sun, fickle, and traveling upon the mass of wind.
"O Sage, having obtained this wish-fulfilling tree and entered our own nest, we remain here in silence, free from the afflictions that were once far away."

Just as we were born and have reached this state, having attained awakening with minds fully pacified, so has this been told by me to you in its entirety and in its perfection; O Great-Souled One, instruct me further with what remains.
Bhuśuṇḍa said: "In a former kalpa, there was a certain world that had existed for a long time; by its configuration, it remains even now, not far removed from this."
O Lord of Sages, this account has been described by me through practice while living in the present, for the sake of awakening, as one who perceives the similarity with my previous births.
Today, O Sage, my merits accumulated over a long time have borne fruit, since I behold you here without any obstacle.
This nest, this branch, myself, and this tree—all these have attained purification today through the sight of you.
"O sir, having taken this water for honor and this water for the feet offered by the bird, and having surely rendered it pure, quickly command what remains to be done."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, when that bird Bhuśuṇḍa had personally offered this water for honor and water for the feet once more, I spoke these words to him.
"O Lord of Birds, why are those brothers of yours—possessing such character and great intelligence—not seen here? For you alone are seen."
Bhuśuṇḍa said: "O Sage, O Sinless One, a vast amount of time has passed while we have remained here; the successions of ages have worn away like days."
After this much time, all my younger brothers, having abandoned their bodies like blades of grass, were transformed into the auspicious state.
Though they be long-lived, great, virtuous, or powerful, all without exception are swallowed up by Time, whose nature is beyond measure.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O dear one, as the masses of wind and violent gusts carry the sun and moon upon their shoulders, moving with incessant speed, I hope you are not distressed?"
O Father, I hope you are not weary from the rays of the sun, which have long been so close to you, burning the forest groves upon the great mountains of sunrise and sunset?
O Father, I hope you are not distressed by the cool rays of the moon, which turn the water into ice, and by the falling of nearby hailstones?
O Father, I hope you are not weary from these circles of kalpa-clouds that rest here incessantly, shedding frost-like mist that is as sharp as an axe's edge?
Established in such a high station amidst the turbulent upheavals of the world, how is it that this lofty wish-fulfilling tree does not succumb to agitation?
Bhuśuṇḍa said: "O Brahmin, this life of a bird among all living beings is without support or foundation, despised by the whole world, and utterly insignificant."
And in such beings and in these lonely forests, the Creator has established a fixed abode for you, as if in a void or upon the path of the sky.
O Lord, how can there be freedom from sorrow for this long-lived bird born in this world, who remains bound by the snares of hope?
But we, O Blessed One, always abide in self-contentment; we are never deluded by those whose confusion has arisen regarding that which is formless.
Content with our own nature alone, freed from hardships and exertions, O Brahman, we merely pass the time here in our own abode.
There is no obstruction of the body of karma by either life or death; we remain just as we were established, with all our desires extinguished.
The state of the world has been observed, and various illustrative examples have been seen; surely our flickering body has been abandoned by the mind.
In the self-luminous light that is free from passion, which is eternally without affliction, I always perceive the movement of the smallest units of time above the limit of an eon.
O Brahmin, within this house of the Kalpalatā, which shines like a cluster of jewels, I perceive an unbroken aeon through the flow of the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
For on this lofty mountain peak, where day and night are indistinguishable, I perceive through my own intellect the progression of the world and the sequence of time.
O Sage, my mind has attained rest through awakening; it discerns the essential from the non-essential, its fickleness is cast aside, and it is peaceful and well-stabilized.
Like a village crow emitting vomit, I do not fall into helplessness due to the illusory snares of hope arising from the worldly conventions of saṃsāra.
Beholding the world's illusion with an intellect that possesses the nature of supreme tranquility and is cooled by light, we have attained steadfastness.
O one of great intelligence, even when terrible conditions arrive in their proper sequence, those whose minds are unshakable remain like pure crystals.
This worldly condition, though charming in its undertakings and fickle, does not fail to cause affliction whenever it is scrutinized again and again.
O Blessed One, do all these nets of elements necessarily pass away and necessarily come together, or not? What cause for fear is there for us in this?
As the river of saṃsāra—wavy with its net of living beings—enters the ocean of time, we remain disregarded even though we stand upon its bank.
We do not cast off, nor do we grasp; we neither stand here, nor are we established here. With gentle feet but cruel eyes, we stand upon this tree.
We have been favored by you, the best of men, who are free from sorrow, fear, and fatigue; being satisfied, you have bestowed your grace upon us, and we now remain free from all affliction.
Furthermore, O Blessed One, our mind has been overturned and rolling about; it has not found its proper functioning, nor has it grasped the true meaning of reality.
When the self has become tranquil—changeless and free from agitation—we have awakened as waves of consciousness, like great oceans on a full-moon day.
O Brahmin, by your arrival, our hearts are now filled with joy, such that the Ocean of Milk—with all its limbs stirred by Mount Mandara—is being spread forth.
I consider nothing to be more beneficial for myself than this: that the virtuous, who have renounced all desires, are followed by me.
What is obtained from enjoyments that are pleasant only at the first moment? From the wish-fulfilling gem of association with the virtuous, the essence of all things is obtained.
With speech that is smooth, profound, gentle, sweet, noble, and steady, you alone act as a bee within this lotus-bud of the three worlds.

O Holy One, I believe that even for one who has realized the Supreme Self, this birth today has become fruitful through the sight of you, which has pacified my misdeeds; for the company of the virtuous removes all fear.
Bhuśuṇḍa said: Amidst the terrible upheavals of the ages and amidst harsh words, this Kalpa-tree remains perfectly steady; it never trembles.
This place is inaccessible to all beings who dwell in other worlds; therefore, O virtuous one, we remain here in true happiness.
When Hiraṇyākṣa swiftly carried away the surface of the earth encircled by the seven continents, even then the tree did not tremble.
When the divine mountain became unsteady in its form, not even a single tree on that mountain which had been made level on all sides trembled.
When Nārāyaṇa, with Meru bent down by the pressure of his arms, lifted up Mount Mandara, even then that tree did not tremble.
When the world was so violently agitated that the orbs of the sun and moon fell due to the turmoil of the gods and asuras, even then the tree did not tremble.
When the winds of portent blew, uprooting the rocks of the great mountains and shaking the trees of Mount Meru, even then that tree did not tremble.
When the rows of clouds at the end of an eon moved, shaken by the winds from the caves of the mountain that rolls upon the ocean of milk, even then the tree did not tremble.
When Mount Meru stood on all sides within the arms of Kālanemi, having been slightly uprooted, even then the tree did not tremble.
When the winds from the wings of the Lord of Birds blew during the battle for the seizure of the nectar, causing the Siddhas to fall, even then this tree did not fall.
When Rudra, whose form was now complete and whose single purpose was not yet fully accomplished, departed for the Brahmāṇḍa, Garuḍa likewise did not shake the tree.
When the flames of the fire at the end of the eon, fierce with all the mountains and oceans, were cast aside by the hoods of Śeṣa, even then the tree did not tremble.
O tiger among sages, how could there be any calamities for those who dwell upon such an excellent tree? For us, indeed, calamities arise only from our own wretched state.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O one of great intelligence, when at the ends of kalpas the winds of calamity are blowing, and when the moon, stars, and sun are falling down, how do you remain free from distress?
Bhuśuṇḍa said: When worldly activity collapsed at the end of the kalpa, leaving the stability of the world behind, I then abandoned my nest like an ungrateful man abandons a true friend.
I abide in space itself, free from all conceptual construction, with all my limbs rendered motionless by nature, just as the mind is when devoid of latent impressions.
When the suns blaze forth, shattering the mountains to pieces, then, having bound the Vāruṇī concentration, I remain with a steady mind.
When the winds of universal dissolution blow, shattering the great lords of mountains, I remain motionless in the sky, having fixed myself in the mountain-like concentration (pārvatī-dhāraṇā).
When the world, including Mount Meru and all else, dissolves and becomes a single ocean, one who possesses an unwavering mind should then fix the *dhāraṇā* on the element of air during that deluge.
Having reached the far shore of the cosmic egg at the end of the principles, in that stainless state, I remain for that long in the state of deep sleep, with an immovable form.
Furthermore, as long as the Lotus-born remains engaged in the work of creation, I shall enter that cosmic egg and abide there in the abode of birds.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Lord of Birds, why is it that other yogins do not remain unbroken by their meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās) throughout the ends of kalpas, as you do?
Bhuśuṇḍa said: "O Brahmin, this destiny of the Supreme Lord is indeed difficult to transcend; I must indeed become such as I am, and others must likewise become what they are."
Necessity cannot be weighed; for whatever is to happen will happen exactly so, for this is the certainty of intrinsic nature itself.
"By the power of my own resolve alone, in kalpa after kalpa, again and again, this very tree comes into being upon this very mountain peak."

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: You are one whose long life is for the sake of ultimate liberation; you are a leader who provides instruction, possessed of both knowledge and realized wisdom, steadfast, and one whose mental faculty is fit for yoga.
O auspicious one, having witnessed the coming and going of various minor creations, what wonders do you remember within this sequence of worlds?

Bhuśuṇḍa said: "I remember this earth below, which was even greater [in extent], yet devoid of rocks and trees, and lacking grasses and creepers; it was free from the multitude of mountains, forests, and trees."
For ten thousand years and ten hundred years, I remember the earth below as being filled with heaps of ashes.
I remember the earth below, where the sun had not yet arisen, where the orb of the moon was powerless, and where the light of day was undifferentiated.
With its hollows half-revealed by the radiance of the jewels of Meru, I recall the world of Mount Aṅgāḍhya as being like the Lokāloka mountain.
I remember this earth here, fleeing in every direction as it was being destroyed during the great war with the Asuras.
I remember this earth, which for four yugas was overrun by intoxicated Asuras and became the inner apartments of the Daityas.
I meditate upon the hut of the universe, whose outer boundary is entirely enclosed within the innermost limit, and which remains as the residue of the three non-inert deities.
I remember this earth as being dense with forest trees for another half of four yugas, its other creations unseen.
In this way, I remember this earth as being covered by dense, immovable [mountains] for more than four yugas, a time when the conduct of people had not yet come into being.
I remember this earth as being strewn all around and completely filled for ten thousand years with mountains of the bones of deceased Daityas.
I remember the sky, from which all the Vaimānika gods had vanished out of fear, and the earth, stripped of all its trees and enveloped in darkness.

O intoxicated one, I remember the hut of the world as having become a single mountain within the vast expanse of the Vindhya range, which had grown so tall that it reached the sky and was no longer the domain of Agastya.
I remember these and many other such events; what is the use of saying much more? Listen to the essence in brief.
O Brahmin, I remember hundreds of countless Manus who have passed away, as well as all the hundreds of cycles of four yugas, which were full of intense activity.
I remember a certain creation that was entirely alone, self-pure, devoid of men and asuras, and consisting of a single mass of light.
I recall a certain creation involving a drunken Brāhmaṇa who drank liquor despite being forbidden from it, as well as a Śūdra who likewise drank liquor, and a virtuous wife who had many husbands.

I remember a certain creation in which the surface of the earth was densely covered with trees, where there was no conceived great ocean, and where a certain person appeared spontaneously of his own accord.
I remember a certain creation that was without mountains or ground, where gods and humans stood in the void, and which was known as being without the light of the moon or sun.
I remember a certain creation where there was no Indra, no great king, no neutral party, and no superior or inferior; it was my own wheel of the quarters of darkness.
The calculation of the beginning of creation, the division within the three worlds, the configuration of the principal mountain ranges, and Jambūdvīpa situated separately;
The division of the creation of the castes, duties, and intellects; the configuration of the mandala of the earth; the arrangement of the circle of stars; and the formation of the Pole Star.
The establishment of Indra and Upendra by Janman, Indu, Bhāskara, and the others; the abduction of Hiraṇyākṣa; and the raising up of the earth by the Boar.
The imagining of kings, the bringing of the Vedas, the uprooting of Mount Mandara, and the churning of the ocean for the sake of the nectar of immortality.

"The Garuḍa with unformed wings," "the origin of the oceans," and so forth—those traditional accounts (smṛtis) which concern the sequence of the world as it existed long ago in its infancy, even children remember them, my dear; what cause for concern is there in those matters?

I, whose life is sustained, have conceived Him who has Garuda as His vehicle and the bird as His vehicle; Him who has the bird as His vehicle and the bull as His vehicle; and Him who has the bull as His vehicle and Garuda as His vehicle.
Bhuśuṇḍa said: "Then, O Blessed One, when you and others—Bharadvāja, Pulastya, Atri, Nārada, Indra, and Marīci—had been born in the world,"
Among Pulaha, Uddālaka, and others, as well as among Kratu, Bhṛgu, and Aṅgiras; and among Sanatkumāra, Bhṛṅgīśa, Skanda, Gajānana, and the rest.
In Gaurī, Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, Gāyatrī, and many others; on Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Himavat, Dardura, and so forth.
Among Hayagrīva, Hiraṇyākṣa, Kālanemi, Bala, and others; among Hiraṇyakaśipu, Krātha, Bali, Prahlāda, and others.
Among Śibi, Aṅku, Pṛthu, Lāṅgala, Vainya, Nābhāga, Keli, Nala, Māndhātṛ, Sagara, Dilīpa, Nahuṣa, and others;
Among Ātreya, Vyāsa, Vālmīki, Śuka, Vātsyāyana, and others; and among Upamanyu, Maṇiman, Aṅkī, Bhagīratha, Śuka, and others.
When [events] occurred only a short time ago, or when they are somewhat distant, or even in the creations of today—what counting can there be in such recollection?
O Sage, I indeed remember this Janmāṣṭaka of yours, the son of Brahmā; in that eighth creation, you were united with me.
Sometimes you are born from the sky, sometimes you are born from water; sometimes from the wind or from a mountain, and sometimes you are born from fire.
Whatever its nature, whatever its conduct, and whatever its configuration and direction, I remember this creation as being exactly like three other creations.
I remember ten creations that were simultaneous, possessing stable stability, and consisting of gods who maintained a uniform and entirely consistent conduct.
O Sage, the nurse disappeared for five days; she was raised from the ocean by the Tortoise himself during five creations.

I remember this twelfth [manifestation]: the churning of the ocean of nectar, which threw the gods and asuras into utter confusion by the force of the Mandara mountain being pulled [as a churning stick].
Then Bali, the grasper, together with Vāra-tṛṇa and Hiraṇyākṣa, took that earth endowed with the essence of all medicinal herbs from heaven down to the subterranean realm.
Having become the son of Reṇukā for the sixth time, this Hari brought about the destruction of the Kṣatriyas, even across many cycles of creation.
O Leader of Sages, I remember that for a hundred Kali Yugas, the state of Buddha was attained by Hari solely through his incarnation as the Boar King.
I remember thirty disturbances of the three cities, two destructions of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, and ten defeats of Śakra, all wrought by the moon-crested Lord.
I recall the eight battles between Hari and Śarva for the sake of the arrow—battles involving the mantras that afflict and subdue fever, during which the armies of the gods were thrown into turmoil.
O Sage, because the intellects of men vary in degree from age to age, I shall explain the Vedānta as it is endowed with various arrangements of ritual limbs and recitations.
O sinless one, the Purāṇas—which possess a single essential meaning, are complete, and exist in many recensions—have been set forth by me and have spread forth in every age.
Furthermore, I remember those very same ones, as well as others of their kind, throughout age after age—the histories composed by those learned in the Vedas and other scriptures.
I remember another history of great wonder called the Rāmāyaṇa, measuring one hundred thousand verses, which is a scripture of knowledge.
"One should behave like Rāma, not like the voluptuous Rāvaṇa"—where such wisdom is bestowed upon the intellect as if a fruit were placed directly in the hand.
"This has been composed by Vālmīki, and now you shall know whatever else he will compose; furthermore, you shall know from time to time all that remains manifest in the world."
Whether composed by that very soul named Vālmīki or by another, this work—which had been forgotten—is now being performed for the twelfth time.
I remember a second work of equal scope, known by the name Bhārata, composed by a former Vyāsa, which has been forgotten in the world.
Whether composed by that very soul named Vyāsa or by another, this [work], having been forgotten, is now being produced for the seventh time.
O Lord of Sages, I remember the narrative scriptures that appeared in each successive age, possessing diverse structures.
O virtuous one, again and again, in age after age, I behold and indeed remember those very same objects, as well as others.
For the destruction of the Rākṣasas, Viṣṇu will now undergo his eleventh incarnation on earth under the name of Rāma.
With his man-lion body, Hari struck Hiraṇyakaśipu three times, like a lion strikes an elephant.
O Lord of Sages, for the sake of relieving the burden of the earth, this will now be the sixteenth birth of Viṣṇu in the house of Vasudeva.
This delusion pervading the world never truly exists; yet it appears at times, persisting like a bubble upon water.
This illusory perception of the visible world, which resides within the self as consciousness, is impermanent; it arises and dissolves swiftly, flickering like a wave upon the water.
I remember the three worlds as having many even arrangements and many uneven ones, as well as those with forms that are half-equal.
I remember those very same deeds and such other actions of theirs, as well as those other beings here who performed similar deeds.
O Brahmin, at the end of every manvantara, when the order of the world has been overturned, when its arrangement has become otherwise, and when all people have passed away and perished;
My friends are indeed different, and my kinsmen are also different; my new servants are indeed different, and those who provide me shelter are also different.
At times I made my dwelling in a secluded spot on the slopes of the Vindhya mountains; at times my abode was on the Sahya range; and at times my home was in Dardura.
Sometimes he was a dweller of the Himalayas, sometimes the Malaya mountain; at other times, he remained on the mountain in his former very same configuration.
And having reached a branch of a mango tree, O leader of sages, I build my nest within it as the beginningless and endless ages pass away.
"O virtuous one, this tree has been born with its very same configuration as before; it has simply cast off its body and attained happiness, rather than undergoing a transformation."
This tree has grown with the very same configuration as it possessed while its father was alive; the splendor of this son-tree is exactly as it was then.
Having established my former dwelling, I have come to abide here; previously, neither this northern quarter nor this mountain existed here.
Formerly, there was another mountain, superior in its quarters, whose very form consisted of individual bodies, and from which the night of Brahmā had departed.
At the conclusion of my meditation, having perceived this very creation as it truly is, I know the directions, such as those of Meru and others, from the movement of the sun and the constellations.

While that [consciousness] remains, its configuration changes and the directions appear otherwise; I consider the world to be neither existent nor non-existent, merely causing the intellect to wander.
This manifestation of the wondrous power of the Self's own vibration unfolds: a son attains the state of a father, and likewise a friend turns into an enemy.

I remember hundreds of women who have become men, and men who have become women; I remember those practicing the conduct of the Kṛta Yuga during the Kali Yuga, and those abiding in the state of the Kali Yuga during the Kṛta Yuga.
O Lord of Sages, I remember that even in the Tretā and Dvāpara ages, there were those who had not seen the Vedas or understood their meaning, and who lived according to their own conventions.
O Brahmā, while meditating upon the Creator, I remember certain beings here and there from the unimpeded acts of creation—the world including gods, asuras, and humans.

At the end of a thousand cycles of the four yugas, I remember the world as empty; I remember ten creations devoid of the forms of earth and fashioned by the mental conceits of Manas, pervaded by beings composed of air.

I remember all those [worlds] during the days of Brahmā—possessing various specific configurations and locations, containing the storehouses of living beings busy with diverse activities, and adorned with various arrangements, pleasures, and costumes.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: Then, O mighty-armed one, that best of crows was questioned by me once more for the sake of inquiry regarding this very tip of the creeper on the wish-fulfilling tree.
O King of Birds, how is it that death does not afflict the body of those who move within the treasury of the world, even though they are engaged in worldly affairs?
Bhuśuṇḍa said: "O omniscient Brahmin, although you already know [the answer], you ask me as if out of a desire to know; for masters always incite their servants to speak."
Nevertheless, I shall explain to you that which you ask me: they say that the primary way of honoring the virtuous is simply the carrying out of their commands.
Death does not seek to slay him in whose heart the continuous thread of latent impressions is not strung together with the pearls of his faults.
Death does not seek to slay him whom mental agonies do not pierce—agonies that are saws to the tree of exhalation and woodworms to the creeper of the entire body.
Death does not seek to slay him whom the serpents of worldly desires—whose hoods are the thoughts fixed upon his body—do not burn within.
Death does not seek to slay him whom the serpent of greed—filled with the poison of passion and hatred, dwelling in the cave-dwelling of one's own mind—does not devour.
Death does not seek to slay him whom anger—acting as a submarine fire in the ocean of the body—does not utterly consume, for that anger has drunk up the entire water of discernment.
Death does not seek to slay him whom the bodiless god of love cannot crush—that firm heap of sesame seeds as turbulent as a fierce press.
Death does not seek to slay him by whom the rest of the mind has been taken refuge in that one, stainless, and supremely purifying state.
Death does not seek to slay him whose mind is not fickle, like a monkey that has fallen upon a fragment of its own body and remains there.
O Brahmin, these great defects, which are the causes of the disease of saṃsāra, do not disturb even in the slightest degree a single mind that is concentrated in meditative absorption.
Sufferings arising from mental and physical ailments, stirred up by the great delusion, do not overwhelm a single mind that is composed in meditative concentration.
For one whose mind is composed, there is neither setting nor rising, neither recollection nor forgetfulness, and it is neither asleep nor awake.
The anxieties born of the transformations of desire and anger do not afflict the mind of one whose mental space has been blinded and whose consciousness is composed.
He neither gives nor takes, he neither abandons nor begs; he simply performs his duties, his mind being thus composed in meditative concentration.
Those things which are ill-meaning, ill-initiated, of evil quality, poorly expressed, and of bad sequence do not cut the mind of one whose heart is composed.
All things—vast in meaning, great, and endowed with excellence—shine forth for one whose mind is concentrated and who pursues them all.
One should direct the mind toward that supreme Truth which is beneficial in its ultimate result, imperishable, free from delusion, and liberated from the vision of evil intentions.
That which is unseen by the impure mind—which brings about mental agitation and is like a demon of manifoldness—should cause the mind to direct itself toward that supreme state.
In the beginning, middle, and likewise at the end, one should direct the mind toward that which is supremely appropriate for the long term—be it beautiful, sweet, and wholesome.
One should direct the mind toward that which is infinite, beneficial to the mind, true, devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and cherished by all the virtuous; that is the supreme [object].
One should direct the mind toward that which is the supreme light of the intellect, the primordial, the ultimate nectar, and the unsurpassed good fortune.
In heaven, along with the gods, asuras, and gandharvas, together with the vidyādharas, kinnaras, and hosts of celestial women, there is nothing whatsoever that is stable or auspicious.
O dear one, on this earth—along with its hundred kings, its mountains, cities, and villages, and including the oceans—there is nothing whatsoever that is beautiful or stable.
In Pātāla, together with its array of nāgas and asuras, and likewise with the hosts of asura women—indeed, throughout it all—nothing whatsoever is beautiful or stable.
In this entire world—whether in heaven, in the realm of the gods, in the netherworld, or on the slopes of the quarters—there is nothing whatsoever that is beautiful and stable.
In activities that are restless with mental and physical ailments, enveloped by floods of suffering, and eternally trivial, there is nothing whatsoever that is stable or auspicious.
In thoughts that cause the mind to tremble, that delight the heart, and that are fluctuations of the intellect, nothing at all is stable or auspicious.

Even amidst the shifting Mandara mountains of the heart’s surging milk-ocean, within the fluctuations of one's own volitions and conceptual constructions, there is nothing whatsoever that is stable or auspicious.
Even amidst these various activities, which are as unstable as the tips of swords and subject to incessant coming and going, there is nothing whatsoever that is stable or auspicious.
