Neither is sovereignty over the entire earth desirable, nor is the form of a celestial deity among the gods desirable, nor even residence in the depths of the netherworld; for that alone is desirable where the minds of the virtuous find their rest.

Neither is the investigation of confused scriptures better, nor the deliberation on the affairs of others; nor is the description of the sequence of eminent discourses superior—wherever the minds of the virtuous find their abiding place.
Neither is a long life consisting of mere desire excellent, nor is death excellent, nor is stubborn delusion; neither is hell excellent, nor is heaven, for the mind finds no stable footing anywhere.

Thus, all these various sequences of the world appear delightful to a man only because of his mental delusion; how could the great ones find lasting stability in objects that consist of such extremely unstable processes?
Bhuśuṇḍa said: There exists but one vision—sole, free from harm, and devoid of delusion—which is the most excellent and exalted among all forms of knowledge.
Contemplation of the self brings an end to all sufferings; it removes the long-accumulated nightmare of wandering in saṃsāra.
Moving through the vast courtyard of the stainless path of the mind, she likewise destroys all sufferings, anxieties, and misfortunes.
O Blessed One, that contemplation of one's own self, which is free from all conceptual constructions, arises fully within, just as light overcomes darkness.
It is easily attained by those such as you, yet it is difficult to attain for those such as we; it transcends all mental constructs and has reached the supreme pinnacle.
O Great Sage, how can those of ordinary intellect attain this state, which is the companion of that [wisdom] which delights in the contemplation of the Self?

O Lord of Sages, those who have attained some degree of equanimity and are cooled by the moon of discernment are equal to those absorbed in contemplation of the Self, though they are of various kinds.
From among my companions who contemplate the self, I have chosen one that brings about the destruction of all suffering and increases all prosperity.

"The cause of life here is based on the concern for vital breath. Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: To the bird Bhuśuṇḍa who had spoken thus, I, though already knowing this, calmly questioned the sage once more as a mere sport.
O you who sever all doubts, O one of exceedingly long life! Speak to me truthfully, O virtuous one: what is meant by "reflection on the vital breaths"?
Bhuśuṇḍa said: "O sage, you are a knower of all the Vedāntas and the destroyer of all doubts; yet you ask me about a crow merely for the sake of jest."
Or rather, O Blessed One, let me train myself further by responding to you once more; what harm could possibly come to me?
Listen to this "Concentration on the Vital Breath" (prāṇasamādhi) which I am about to describe; it restores life to Bhuśuṇḍa and grants Bhuśuṇḍa his own self-realization.
Behold, O Blessed One, this entire body-house, so enchanting, with its three kinds of great pillars and its nine doors completely covered.
It is protected on all sides by the householder ego, together with its wife, the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), and its kinsmen, the subtle elements (tanmātra).
Within, you see [the body] which has the ear-cavities as its attic-chambers, the hair as its roof-covering, and the large eyes as its windows.
The mouth was its principal gateway, the arms were the side-chambers, and the hollows of the doorways were adorned with the garlands of the rows of teeth.
With the gatekeepers of form, taste, and touch ever vigilant, it is surrounded by the bustling crowd of sensory perceptions and takes its stand upon the terrace of the stars.
Smeared with blood, flesh, fat, and the like, bound together by a network of sinews, joined by the timber of thick bones, it is well-constructed and firmly established.
O leader of sages, when the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* of this body are well-positioned, soft, in the middle, and closed within the side cavities;
The yantra consists of three pairs of lotuses composed of bone and flesh, soft, with stalks extending upward and downward, and possessing delicate, true petals that meet one another.
With its petals opening by means of sprinkling, and with its leaves moving gently as they are pervaded by the wind that travels through the entire sky.
As those leaves fluttered, that wind increased, like the wind outside when a mass of vine-leaves is struck by the breeze from all sides.
Having been increased and having established itself in many ways within the channels, it then spreads throughout this body as it moves upward and downward.
Then, that wind of the heart is designated by those who know it through technical terms such as prāṇa, apāna, samāna, and so forth, according to its various modes of conduct and activity.
Within the threefold mechanism of the heart-lotus, all the vital energies (prāṇa-śakti) extend upward and downward through the body, like rays from the orb of the moon.
These powers of the vital breath go forth and come back, draw out and carry away, sport about, and swiftly fly up and fall down.
This very breath, situated within the heart-lotus, is called *prāṇa* by the wise; O Sage, a certain power of this [breath] causes the eyes to blink.
One perceives touch; another carries [the breath] through the nose; one digests food; and another utters words.
What need is there for much speaking here? Within this very body, the Blessed Lord Vāyu performs everything, just as a mechanic operates a machine.
Therein, O Sage, the two winds that have issued forth with the dual convention of upward and downward are renowned as prāṇa and apāna; these two are the manifest and excellent winds.
O Sage, I remain constantly following the course of those two, who are eternally of cool and warm nature, and who are ever travelers through the sky.
Of the body and the great machine, which are free from fatigue; and of the sun and moon in the sky of the heart, whose nature is fire and soma.
Of this mind, which is the guardian of the city of the body; of these two chariot wheels, which are the praised and beloved horses for this king, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra); [of these two...]
As I followed those two winds known as prāṇa and apāna, I observed the movement of the bodily breaths from the moment of birth until the dissolution of the body.
O Brahmin, for those who are always equal in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, the days pass as if they were established in the state of deep sleep.
The movement of these two, though existing, is even more subtle and difficult to perceive than a lotus fiber that has been split into a thousand parts.

Having understood the movement of the two winds that flow without ceasing, and having followed that movement impelled within the heart, O Great-souled One, a man of joyful mind, his bonds destroyed, is not born here again.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, while the bird was speaking in this manner, I questioned him there once more, asking: "Of what nature is the movement of the vital breath?"
Bhuśuṇḍa said: O sage, although you know everything, why do you ask me as if in play? Nevertheless, I shall speak according to what was asked; listen to my words on that matter.
O Brahman, this prāṇa is the power of vibration, ever-moving; this prāṇa is situated above within the body, both externally and internally.
O Brahmin, the apāna too is a power of vibration that is always in motion; this apāna is situated downwards within the body, both externally and internally.
O Knower of Reality, listen now for the sake of your highest good regarding that from which this supreme prāṇāyāma proceeds, both while one is awake and while one is asleep.
The wise know that outward movement of the vital breaths from the cavity of the heart-lotus, occurring spontaneously and without effort, is *recaka* (exhalation).
When the breaths extend downward, reaching as far as twelve finger-breadths outside [the body], that contact of the breaths with the limbs is called *pūraka* (inhalation).
That filling touch which, free from effort, flows inward from the exterior into the internal vessel—they know that too as *pūraka*.
When the apāna has set and the prāṇa has not yet arisen in the heart, that state which is experienced by yogis is the state of kumbhaka.
Exhalation (recaka), retention (kumbhaka), and inhalation (pūraka) exist in three ways; they are located at the site of the arising of the apāna, twelve finger-breadths below and outside [the navel].
O Mahāmati, listen to those intrinsic natures which have been described by those of expansive intellect as abiding at all times and devoid of correct effort.
O Lord, for that wind which has arisen from outside at a distance of twelve finger-breadths, the inhalation and other [breath-movements] occur right there by its very nature.
That state which exists externally, at a distance of twelve finger-breadths from the tip of the nose and directly in front, like a jar that has been manifested within the heart;
The wise know that retention of the apāna wind within the ether to be *kumbhaka*; it is the movement of the outward-tending air reaching as far as the tip of the nose.
Those who know yoga understand that first [breath] to be the external inhalation; its movement extends even beyond the tip of the nose, reaching as far as the *dvādaśānta*.
The wise know that [state] of the wind to be the "external filling" (bāhyapūraka), which occurs when the prāṇa has subsided outside and the apāna has not yet arisen.
They know that to be the full, balanced, and external *kumbhaka* wherein there is an inward-turning of the breath even without the rising of the *apāna*.
One should know that external exhalation, when contemplated, bestows liberation; it is that which, having arisen from the "end of the twelve," possesses a supreme fullness of form.
They know that the external [breath] of the apāna is the subsequent pūraka; these, such as kumbhaka and the rest, both external and internal, should be practiced incessantly.
Having understood that [reality] which has the nature of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, one is not born again; O Greatly Wise One, these eight are to be recollected day and night.
I have described the natures of the bodily winds as bestowing liberation, whether one is walking or standing, waking or even sleeping.
These [senses], being by nature exceedingly fickle like the wind, come to cessation; therefore, one should be fully mindful through the intellect alone regarding what one does and what one eats.

In that state, the person is not at all an agent within himself performing breath-retentions and the like; rather, he remains undistracted in this activity, having completely abandoned the external mind.
In just a few days, a person who practices this attains the state of absolute oneness, even while external mental functions toward sense objects persist.
The mind does not find delight in this, just as a brahmin does not find delight in a dog's skin; those of perfected intellect who remain established by grasping this view [do not find delight].
Indeed, they alone have attained everything that is to be attained, for they remain unwearied—whether standing, walking, sleeping, or likewise waking.
If this view is observed, then that bondage is not attained, for those who possess the awakening resulting from following the inhalation and exhalation of breath.
With his impurities and delusion completely stilled, the wise person, being healthy and ever pure, will internally abandon all undertakings, even while performing them.

Having attained the movement of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, one who is well-established prospers in happiness; O Brahmin, the emergence of the prāṇa occurs from the lotus-petal situated within the heart.
O great sage, this prāṇa sets outside at a distance of twelve finger-breadths, while the apāna rises from the external "end of twelve" (dvādaśānta).
Then, the setting occurs within the lotus situated in the heart; there, the vital breath (prāṇa) arrives at the twelve-finger space in the realm of the sky.
Immediately after that step, this apāna draws [the breath] inward; then the prāṇa, directed toward the external space, flows upward like a flame of fire.
The apāna wind, directed toward the space of the heart, flows downward like water; this apāna, which is the moon, nourishes the body from the outside.
The vital breath (prāṇa), whether as the sun or as fire, digests this body within; for the prāṇa, heating the space of the heart at every moment, [performs this function].
The supreme sun causes the sky at the tip of the mouth to feel remorse; however, the moon of the downward breath (apāna), having flooded the sky of the heart, [fills] the tip of the mouth.
Immediately after the closing of the eyes, this [prāṇa] causes nourishment; the digit situated within the moon of apāna is made to swell by the sun of prāṇa.

Having reached that state where [the breath] is swallowed, one no longer grieves; likewise, when the sun of the vital breath (prāṇa) situated within is seized by the moon of the downward breath (apāna).
Having attained that state, the person who has been swallowed by it no longer undergoes birth; the vital breath itself attains the nature of the sun within the space both external and internal.
Thereafter, the vital breath itself, having abandoned its lunar nature which nourishes the body, presides over the state of being the moon, which brings about nourishment.
In an instant it attains the state of the sun, the position that causes complete drying; yet, having completely abandoned its solar nature, it does not reach the state of the moon.
First, the vital breaths are investigated; one does not grieve over [the loss of] place and time, having known the eternal setting and rising of the moon and sun within the heart.
When the mind has returned to its own innate support, the Self, it is no longer born; together with its rising and setting, its moon, its rays, and its coming and going.

He who perceives the divine Sun within his heart perceives truly; for the darkness that exists externally is neither diminished nor entirely exhausted, and thus it does not lead to spiritual accomplishment.
One should destroy the darkness within the heart; when that is destroyed, supreme perfection arises. When external darkness is completely exhausted, the Lokāloka mountain is revealed.
O Sage, when the darkness within the heart has been exhausted, one's own light arises; that which brings about the destruction of the darkness of the heart, when fully understood, bestows liberation.
With effort, one should observe the sun of the prāṇa until its setting with the udaya; for the moon of the apāna sets within the hollow of the heart-lotus.
From that state, the sun of the vital breath (prāṇa) rises within, facing outward; when the downward breath (apāna) has set, the prāṇa rises from the lotus of the heart.
When the shadow has dissolved its limbs, just as the heat [vanishes] right there instantly; when the prāṇa has set, apāna arises from the exterior in an instant.
O noble-minded one, know that just as a shadow vanishes immediately when the sunlight has disappeared from all sides, so too does the apāna vanish upon the ground of the birth of prāṇa.
Know indeed that the prāṇa has perished in the birthplace of the apāna; for when the prāṇa has set, the apāna is oriented toward its own rising.
By relying on external kumbhaka for a long time, one no longer grieves; when the apāna has set and the prāṇa is slightly inclined toward rising.

By relying on internal retention (*antaḥ-kumbhaka*) for a long time, one no longer grieves; by relying on the exhalation of the vital breath (*prāṇa-recaka*), it reaches the furthest limit of the downward breath (*apāna*).

By practicing the pure *kumbhaka* (retention), one no longer suffers; [this occurs] when the support for exhalation (*recaka*) is in the *apāna* and situated within the interval between the filling of the *prāṇa*.
Having perceived the inhalation established within itself, a person is not born again; for therein both the prāṇa and apāna have reached dissolution.
Taking that peaceful state as his support, he does not regret himself, even when the *apāna* breath is intent on consuming the vital breaths, for he perceives both place and time as partless.

Whether one investigates internally or externally, one no longer grieves, for the vital breath (prāṇa), intent on consuming the downward breath (apāna), is thus present both within the heart and outside.
Having fully observed both place and time, the mind is no longer born; for there, the prāṇa is indeed merged with the apāna, and the apāna with the prāṇa.
Behold those two, space and time, swallowed both externally and internally; for a moment, the breath has set and is devoid of the rising of the downward breath (apāna).
They know that external *kumbhaka* which is accomplished without effort to be that state; for internal *kumbhaka*, likewise accomplished without effort, is the supreme state.
This is that very form of the Self; this is pure, supreme consciousness itself. This is that which is eternally manifest; having attained this, one does not grieve.
Like fragrance within a flower, it dwells within the vital breath; we worship that conscious Self which is neither the prāṇa nor the apāna.
Like the taste within water, we worship the conscious Self (cidātman) abiding within the vital breath (apāna)—neither possessing breath nor devoid of breath.
We worship the conscious self (cidātman), situated at the end of the exhaustion of prāṇa, reaching the limit of the exhaustion of apāna, and existing in the middle between prāṇa and apāna.
We worship the conscious Self, the foremost bearer, who is the supreme vitalizing force of the vital breath, the ultimate life of the living soul, and the sustainer of the body.
We worship the conscious Self—the reality that is the thinking of the mind, the singular awakening of the intellect, and the ego-sense of the ego-maker.
We worship that reality of consciousness (cittattva), in which all exists, from which all proceeds, which is all, and from which all arises; it is eternal and consists of everything.
We worship that reality of the mind, which is the light of lights, the merit that purifies all that purifies, and which is not merely an object of meditation.

We worship that essence of consciousness where the *apāna* has set and the *prāṇa* has not yet arisen for even a moment—devoid of parts and free from blemish. We worship that essence of consciousness where the *apāna* has not yet arisen and the *prāṇa* has reached its end—the swirling vortex in the space at the tip of the nose.
We worship that essence of consciousness where the prāṇa sets, where the apāna also sets, and where both have not even arisen.
We worship that reality of consciousness (cittattva), which is the support for the state of the yogi, abiding externally and internally at the place of origin of the prāṇa and apāna breaths.

We worship that reality of consciousness (cittattva), which is the form of power among all powers, mounted upon the chariot of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, yet whose prāṇa and apāna are not extended outward.
We worship that Reality of Consciousness which is the Lord as the kumbhaka of prāṇa within the heart, as the kumbhaka of apāna outside, and as that which is released from the portion of pūraka.

We worship that reality of consciousness (cittattva), which is attained through the contemplation of the vital breath (prāṇa), which consists of the reflection upon the out-breath and in-breath (prāṇāpāna), which is the awakening to existence, and which is formless.
We worship that Reality of Consciousness (Cittattva), which is the vibration of the vital breath, which brings about the bliss of vibration, and which is the cause of all causes.

I take refuge in that supreme, ultimate state, which is free from the stain of all mental constructs, yet eternally encompassed by the multitude of arts; it is the glory of self-realization, the foremost station, and that which all the gods bow down to.
Bhuśuṇḍa said: "Indeed, this rest of the mind has been attained by me through the samādhi of the vital breath, gradually, within my own stainless self."
"Relying upon this view, O Great Sage, I stand firm; I do not waver even for a moment longer than the blink of an eye, nor would I move from Mount Meru."
Whether walking or standing, waking or even sleeping—even in a dream—this perfect meditative absorption of mine does not waver within my self.
Firmly established amidst the ever-changing and unstable conditions of the world, I remain inward-turned, abiding by my own will within the Self through the Self.
Even the wind might be restrained, or even water from its course; yet I do not recall anything contrary to this state of perfect concentration.
Through following the inward and outward breaths and beholding the Supreme Self, I have attained the sorrowless, primordial state of great austerity.
O Brahmin, even today, with a steady mind, I live observing the emergence and submergence of beings until the great dissolution.
I never think of what has been nor what will be; relying solely on direct perception, I abide here by means of my own self in the present.
Just as when duties have arisen, having abandoned all desire for their fruits, I abide solely in the state of pure consciousness, like one in deep sleep.
Having reflected upon the thought consisting of existence and non-existence, accompanied by the desired and the undesired, I abide within the Self; free from affliction, I live for a long time.
Constantly recollecting the occasion of the union of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, I find contentment within myself; I live long and free from affliction.
"This has been gained by me today; this beautiful thing I shall obtain"—such thoughts I have none; therefore, I live long and free from affliction.
O virtuous one, I neither praise nor blame anything or anyone, whether myself or another, at any time; by that, I have attained auspiciousness.
I am not elated by attaining the auspicious, nor do I feel distressed by the inauspicious; my mind is always equanimous, and for that reason, I have attained the auspicious.
Relying upon supreme renunciation, I have indeed always relinquished everything, including my very life; by that means, I have attained auspiciousness.
O Sage, my mind is stilled of its restlessness, free from sorrow, established in itself, and composed; it is peaceful, and by that I live free from affliction.
I see wood, a graceful woman, a mountain, grass, fire, snow, and the sky as equal everywhere; therefore, I live free from affliction.
"What has been accomplished for me today, or what will happen again tomorrow?"—such a fever of anxiety does not exist for me; therefore, I live free from ailment.
Amidst the sufferings of old age and death, and amidst the pleasures of attaining sovereignty, I neither fear nor rejoice; by that I live free from affliction.
"O Brahmin, I do not know, 'This one is my kinsman, this one is a stranger, this one is mine, and that one is from elsewhere'; by that [lack of such knowledge], I live free from affliction."
I know that all things, appearing as all objects, are without beginning or end and free from affliction; because I am Consciousness, I live free from affliction.
Whether eating, moving about, standing, sitting, breathing, or sleeping, I do not perceive "I am the body"; by that, I am long-lived.
Abiding like the state of deep sleep regarding this undertaking of saṃsāra, I perceive it as if it were non-existent; therefore, I live free from affliction.
"Since gain and loss, occurring at their proper time through skillful means, are equal to me—like my two hands situated upon my body—I live free from affliction."
With a steady power of vision, gentle and innocent, I look straight ahead everywhere; by that, I live free from affliction.
I have abandoned all sense of "mine" regarding this body from its feet to its head; having cast off the mire of egoism, I live free from affliction.
Whatever I do and whatever I eat, having renounced that even while possessing it, my mind attains a state of actionlessness; by that means, I live free from affliction.
Whenever I understand even a little, O Sage, at that very moment my mind does not become agitated; by that means I live free from affliction.
Though I am a lord, I do not commit aggression; though I suffer, I am not dejected; though I am poor, I have no longing; therefore, I live free from affliction.
Behold: within this body composed of form, the Self resides as the locus of consciousness among the elements; through its identity with the aggregate of elements, I live, free from affliction.
Being composed, I do not allow my mental state—which is driven by the snares of hope—to come into contact with internal objects; therefore, I live free from affliction.
I perceive the non-existence of the world and the existence of the Self, like a bilva fruit held in the palm of my hand; having awakened from sleep, I see this, and therefore I am long-lived.
I see everything as worn out, broken, slackened, decayed, agitated, crushed, and gone to ruin; yet, seeing it all as ever new, I live free from affliction.
I am happy when people are happy, and sorrowful when they are sorrowful; because I am a dear friend to everyone, I live free from affliction.
In adversity I am immovably steadfast, and in prosperity I am a friend to the world; I do not exist in the presence or absence of states, and therefore I live free from affliction.
"I do not exist, nor is there another for me; I do not belong to anyone else"—thus has my mind been cultivated, and by that I live free from affliction.
I am the world, I am the sky, I am the sequence of space and time; I am action—such is my understanding, and therefore I live free from affliction.

The pot is consciousness, the cloth is consciousness, space is consciousness, the forest is consciousness, and the cart is consciousness; "all is consciousness"—this is my conviction, and by it I live free from affliction.
Thus, O tiger among sages, I am known as Bhuśuṇḍa, the crow, a long-lived one who is like a bee to the lotus of the three worlds.

Beholding and contemplating for a long time the ocean of Brahman—with its waves of the three worlds tossed about, their forms differentiated by creation, destruction, and other processes, sometimes submerged, sometimes rising, and appearing as a chaotic spectacle—I have remained here.

Bhuśuṇḍa said: "O Brahmin, O you who have reached the further shore of knowledge, I have told you this—both who I am and how I exist here—out of boldness, solely for the sake of accomplishing your command."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "Oh, how wonderful! O Blessed One, this account of your own self that you have narrated is an ornament for the Vedas and a cause of supreme amazement."
Blessed are those who behold you, the Great-Souled One of exceedingly long life, as if seeing a second Brahmā born from the lotus.
Today our eyes have become blessed, since you have related in its entirety, exactly as it was, this purifying account of your own life, which is so conducive to awakening the intellect.
At dawn, when the glories of the gods were seen in all directions, no one else was beheld in this world as great as you.
Someone may perhaps be found after much wandering, like a great multitude; but a noble-souled person such as you is not easily found anywhere in the world.
Just as a pearl is produced within a certain section of a bamboo stalk, so too is one like you seen within a certain fragment of the world.
Indeed, a most great and auspicious task has been accomplished by me today, since you, whose soul is liberated from this meritorious body, have been beheld by me.
May it be well with you; enter your auspicious inner chamber, for it is now midday and I must depart for the abode of the gods.
Having heard this, Bhuśuṇḍa rose from his seat and, with his two hands as previously resolved upon, grasped the golden sprout.
With the pollen from the flowers of the wish-fulfilling creepers and with the moon as its cool radiance, the one of perfected intellect filled that vessel with a libation of pearls.
With that water for the guest-offering, water for the feet, and flowers, my elder brother worshipped me with devotion from head to foot, as if I were the three-eyed Lord Śiva.
Saying, "Enough, O Lord of Birds, with this hardship of following me," I rose from my seat and then leaped up like a bird.
Having followed me for a distance of one yojana in the sky, that bird was forcibly restrained by grasping his hand with my own hand.
In the very instant I had departed, becoming invisible upon the path of the sky, that king of birds turned back; for the company of the virtuous is difficult to abandon.
Sometimes, like waves in the ocean, we were seen by one another; at other times, through the memory of our former lives as birds, we beheld the sages in the sky.
Having reached the circle of the Seven Sages and being honored by his wife, two hundred years passed at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga in ancient times.
I met with Bhuśuṇḍa on a tree atop a peak of Mount Meru; O Rāma, now that the Kṛta age has waned, the Tretā age is currently prevailing.

O crusher of enemies, you were born in the midst of this Tretā Yuga; and again today, in your eighth year, Bhuśuṇḍa met with me right there upon that mountain, possessing a form that is likewise ageless.
Having heard this wonderful and excellent account of Bhuśuṇḍa’s experience as it was thus related, and having reflected upon it within yourself, perform whatever is appropriate.

Śrī Vālmīki said: Thus, whoever of pure intellect shall here contemplate this excellent discourse of Sumati and Bhuśuṇḍa—which concerns a state agitated by the manifold fears of worldly existence—shall forcefully cross over the river of unreality.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, O sinless one, I have related to you the story of Bhuśuṇḍa; by means of this wisdom, Bhuśuṇḍa crossed over the perilous strait of delusion.
O mighty-armed one, relying upon this view preceded by the practice of [controlling] your own vital breaths, become like Bhuśuṇḍa—one who has crossed the great ocean of saṃsāra.
Just as Bhuśuṇḍa attained that state which is to be attained through knowledge and yoga born of continuous practice, so too do you reach that same state.
All those whose intellects are unattached, observing the prāṇa and apāna breaths, attain a state of abiding in the supreme reality like Bhuśuṇḍa.
You have heard these various philosophical views; now, relying upon your own intellect, do as you wish.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, by you—the sun of the earth—with the rays of your wisdom, all the darkness of unruly wickedness within my heart has been wiped away.
We are awakened; we are delighted; we have entered our own abode. We stand with all that is to be known now known, like you who are yourselves unsurpassed.
"Oh, how wondrous is the life of Bhuśuṇḍa! O Blessed One, you have related it, which brings about the realization of the supreme goal."
O Brahmin, regarding this account of Bhuśuṇḍa told by you, that which was described as the house of the body, constructed of flesh, skin, and bone—
By whom indeed was it created, or from where did it arise? How has it come to abide, or who dwells therein?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, listen to this which I shall speak to you in its true essence, for the sake of awakening to the supreme reality and for the removal of defects.
O Rāma, this dwelling of the body—with bones for its pillars, nine gates, and plastered with blood and flesh—was not created by anyone.
This is merely an appearance that manifests in this very way; it has the form of the delusion of two moons, established as both existent and non-existent.
In the process of seeing two moons, there is indeed always a duality of moons; yet in reality, there is only one moon, and the body likewise exists in that very same way.
For at the time when the body is perceived, this body remains present; yet it is non-existent, and therefore it is said to be of the nature of both existence and non-existence.
When one recognizes a dream within a dream, that [previous dream] is indeed rendered false; for a bubble is real when it is in the state of being a bubble, yet false at other times.

The body is real in the context of being a body, but unreal in the context of anything else; likewise, water exists as such during the appearance of it, but otherwise it is neither existent nor non-existent.
In the process of appearing, the body is considered to exist and yet not to exist at other times; thus, this which appears now is merely a manifestation.
"This is my name, I am this"—thus remains the internalized reflection; "I am a physical body composed of flesh and bone"—this is the delusion.
Abandon [this body]; there are thousands of bodies constructed by mere conceptualization, by means of which one, while lying upon a comfortable bed, traverses the horizons with a dream-body.
O Rāma, you wander about; where is that body of yours situated, by which you [perceive] the interior of the city of heaven within the kingdom of the mind during the waking state?
You wander about Mount Meru; where, then, is that body of yours situated? For even in dreams, there is a dream within a dream, by which one traverses the slopes of the earth.
O Rāma, you wander about; where is that body of yours situated? It is a kingdom of the mind within the mind, amidst lands of great splendor.
By what means do you wander here? Where is that body of yours situated? As for those various worldly activities in the kingdom of the mind, they are performed by bodies that have already passed away.
O mighty-armed one, you perform [this]; where are those bodies of yours situated, by which you were united with that beloved of your imagination, the playful and passionate woman?
"You are attaining liberation with this body; where, then, does that body abide? O Rāma, these bodies are merely products of the mind, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent."
In the same way, this body, which possesses such conduct, is known to be [a product] of the mind; the delusion consists in thinking, "This is wealth," "This is the body," or "This is the country."
All that is the manifestation of the mental energy of volition; know this to be either a long dream or a prolonged delusion of the mind.
O descendant of Raghu, when you awaken by your own supreme will, you will realize that even this long-cherished kingdom of the mind is but saṃsāra.
Then you will see this clearly, just as at sunrise, that the state of the world is entirely different from what is produced by the web of dreams and mental constructs.
For this very process of conceptual construction is indeed of such a nature, just as I previously described the birth of the Lotus-born One.
Arising from the mind itself through the mental construction of internal volitions, the mind there assumes delusion, endowed with manifold arrangements.
This manifestation is merely the activity of conceptual construction, just as the imagined appearance of the mind attained the state of being born from a lotus.

Just as one body is contemplated, another body likewise remains present—specifically that which has been long practiced in the prior stream of existence through the intensity of latent impressions (vāsanā).
In that very same way, the body is seen through the arising of its form; for this very volition, brought about by human effort, is indeed consciousness itself.
O Rāma, one thing is conceived in one way, yet it manifests here quite otherwise; for when one conceives, "This is that," "This is mine," and "This is saṃsāra," [it appears accordingly].
O Rāma, that which is cultivated becomes true, arising from the firmness of its contemplation; for whatever is contemplated with intense force, that alone quickly comes to pass.
O Rāma, it is seen everywhere like a beloved daughter, exceedingly dear; just as the rotation of days is seen practiced within dreams.
In this way, when cultivated through meditation, even this cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is perceived such that it quickly appears like the day within the realm of a dream.
In the same way, this [universe], though existing for only a short time, appears to be stable; just as a river is seen in the sky when scorched by heat.
Even though the earth does not exist, it is seen due to conceptualization; it is seen through a distortion of vision, just as a peacock-feather whisk is seen in the sky.
In the same way, this fortune of the world appears due to false cognition; it is seen by an impartial vision, just as a peacock-feather whisk is not seen in the sky.
Through right view, this worldly glory does not appear [as it truly is], so that a timid person does not fall into agitation amidst their own mental constructions.
For in this world which is one's own mental construction, the wise person does not feel fear in that way; for it is simply one's own nature that now appears in this manner.
In this state of wandering through the stream of saṃsāra, why should anyone fear anything? That very self must be somewhat purified; through purification, it attains stainlessness.
O Rāma, this delusion of the world is not seen therein; by the mere sight of reality as it is, one's own nature attains purity.
It does not take on further impurity, just as gold does not become tarnished; this triple world is merely an appearance, neither existent nor non-existent.
Thus, the wise know that the abandonment of all other mental constructions is perfect vision; it is death, it is life, it is heaven, and it is both knowledge and ignorance.
"There is nothing apart from the manifestation of consciousness"—this is the correct vision of oneness. For me, the world of "you" and "I" does not exist as the ten directions.

The wise know that the correct vision is the realization that everything is indeed nothing but one's own manifestation, through seeing things as they truly are within this saṃsāra composed of both the existent and the non-existent.
Through correct vision, the mind neither sets nor rises, having ascertained that all phenomena are neither non-existent nor existent.
Through right vision, the mind becomes free from desire and attains peace; it neither censures nor praises, neither rejoices nor grieves.
Through right contemplation, the mind attains a cooling state of truthfulness: that indeed all kinsmen must inevitably die.
Thus, why do you grieve in vain over separations from kinsmen? It is a certainty that I, too, must inevitably die.
Thus, when the death of oneself has arrived, why do you grieve in vain? For one who is born, some degree of prosperity and the like is inevitable.
"What is to be attained by a man"—what occasion indeed is there for joy in this for every man engaged in worldly affairs within saṃsāra?
Since you have come for the sake of a purpose, what occasion indeed is there for grief? It swells, rises, and surges like a mass of bubbles in the ocean.
For this is but a net of worlds; what lamentation can there be in this? That which is real is always real, and that which is unreal is always unreal.

If it is merely the diversity of actions that is lamented, what else remains to be grieved? I do not exist now, nor did I exist in the past, nor shall I exist in the future; and he [the other] does not exist now.
This body arises from manifold defects; what else is there to lament? O friend, if I am indeed other than the body, being merely the reflection of consciousness, then [why grieve]?
"Wherein do existence and non-existence reside, such that one suffers?"—such was the mind of the sage, whose nature was perfect knowledge, as it became possessed of certainty.
Established in the unsurpassed state, he neither sets nor rises; he is not tranquil, yet he does not suffer; he perceives only transcendence, not non-tranquility.
The partridge seizes even a soft, pure tip of grass; for this reason, not even the slightest reliance should be placed upon this unreality.
Just as an ox is bound by a rope, a living being is bound by its attachment; therefore, you must firmly resolve this through your intellect.
O sinless one, you should conduct yourself here with a mind free from attachment; that which is to be done must indeed be done, while that which is not to be done is disregarded.
Having abandoned both the real and the unreal with ease through his great intelligence, that for whom all this appears as a mere manifestation—[to him belongs this state].
Just as the world attains inner coolness at the end of the day, so too does he attain it by abandoning the appearance of the multitude of objective entities.
O sinless one, behold this as a mere commonality of appearance; O Rāma, it is a mere appearance, defiled by the mental grasping of the mind.
Then, having abandoned even that, O Supreme One, become free from appearances—eternally composed of the space of consciousness, all-pervading, and devoid of everything.
When appearances are relinquished, existence becomes entirely stainless; once it is realized: "I do not exist, nor do my enjoyments truly exist."
This empty ostentation does not appear for the sake of anything harmful, once it has been contemplated thus: "I alone am indeed all this consciousness."
This display is not in vain; it does not appear for no purpose. Both of these systems of philosophy are true and grant ultimate perfection.
O Rāma, O sinless one, resort to that one of these two perspectives which you find more pleasing; for here, there are indeed only these two ways of seeing.
Dwelling thus, O virtuous one, bring about the complete destruction of passion and hatred—whatever has arisen in this world, whether in the sky or in heaven.

All that is attained, O Rāma, through the complete destruction of passion and hatred; for whatever kind of action is performed, O Rāma, with a mind afflicted by passion and the like, such is the result obtained.
That very same thing quickly turns into its opposite for the deluded; for when the fluctuations of the mind are obstructed by waves of hatred and fault-finding, virtues do not take root.
Like deer treading upon scorched ground, passion and hatred—those two serpents—have not dissolved within the hollow of the mind.
Indeed, what indeed cannot be obtained from that wish-fulfilling tree for those who are wise, self-controlled, clever, and learned in the scriptures?
Those who are filled with passion and hatred are indeed jackals; fie upon them! My wealth has been consumed by another, and my wealth has been given away by me to another.
Thus, what are these worldly pursuits, these sequences of passion and hatred? Wealth, kinsmen, and friends come again and go away.
Why would a wise person feel attachment or aversion toward these things? These manifestations of existence and non-existence are the illusory power of the Supreme Lord.
The entire structure of saṃsāra is fully capable of causing one who is attached to it to fall; in reality, O Rāghava, neither wealth, nor people, nor even the self is true.

It is clearly perceived that this is entirely false, falsely determined; everything is non-existent at the beginning and the end, and even in the middle, it is unstable for one possessed by mental affliction.
Where indeed would a wise man find delight in a tree in the sky imagined by another? One person imagines a woman in the sky, while another, far away, enjoys her.
Thus, my dear friend, this is the structure of saṃsāra; do not be deluded by this vast and agitated state of constant coming and going of beings.
The wise know this world to be as unreal as a city of the Gandharvas or a magical creation; it has arisen as something entirely non-existent, like a dream or a city of one's imagination.
Everywhere this world exists as if fallen into deep sleep; you behold it as the city and trees within the long dream of saṃsāra.
O Acyuta, you who are by nature prone to rolling in the sleep of ignorance, you remain here deluded by the dream of saṃsāra.
Therefore, abandon this expansive sleep, which consists of dense ignorance, just as a supreme man, having obtained a treasure, casts away the goddess of misfortune.
Awaken and behold your own Self, ever-risen, free from conceptual construction, the manifestation of consciousness—just as the morning lotus beholds the sun.
Awake! Awake! Again and again you are being awakened by me, O mighty-armed one; behold the stainless sun of the Self.
O Rāma, you have indeed been awakened by this very cool water of knowledge that I have showered upon you, which is endowed with beautiful sound.
Attain the supreme awakening; let there be enlightenment this very day, O Rāghava! Behold the truth, having abandoned this false delusion of the world.
There is no birth for you, no suffering for you, no defects for you, and no delusions for you; having abandoned all conceptual construction, remain well-established in the Self.

You have cast off the net of defects born from conceptual construction; you possess the gentle vision of the essence of deep sleep. For the sake of supreme purity, O Great Soul, abide in the self that is total tranquility, which is most expansive.
Śrī Vālmīki said: While Rāghava was thus listening, composed and even-minded, resting in his own self at ease and having attained supreme bliss;
And while all those present there were characterized by tranquility, he spoke these nectar-like words for the sake of establishing Rāghava’s inner repose.
The sage’s speech ceased, like rain from a cloud falling upon crops; then, when half a muhūrta had passed, Rāghava was awakened.
Again, Vasiṣṭha, the best among speakers, spoke on that very same matter. Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O Rāma, you are perfectly awakened; you have attained your own Self."
In this very way, rely upon the ultimate meaning and remain; do not set foot here in this world. For this wheel of saṃsāra has its hub in mere conceptual construction alone.

O descendant of Raghu, when the mind at the navel is obstructed by being held steady, this wheel of saṃsāra is brought to a halt. However, when it is agitated, the wheel of saṃsāra continues to revolve.
Even if obstructed with effort, it continues to flow with force, provided one applies supreme human exertion along with strength and wisdom through proper means.
One should extinguish the mind itself at the hub of the wheel of saṃsāra, by means of that which is endowed with wisdom and gentleness, and conjoined with the sacred teachings.
That which cannot be attained through human effort is not to be found anywhere; one must abandon reliance on fate alone, which is devised by the understanding of the childish.
Relying on one's own effort, one should first restrain the mind from the delusion consisting of ignorance that has been active since the time of Brahmā.
O sinless one, this world is perceived as being real though it is truly unreal; O sinless one, its forms consist merely of the expansion of the delusion of ignorance.
These bodies wander here, having arisen from all dharmas; yet, for the sake of the body, volition may indeed arise at some time.

O Rāma, a wise person should not concern themselves with the investigation of pleasure and pain; for one whose face is withered by sorrow becomes distressed, whereas one who is serene is free from such distress.
Moreover, the human being made of flesh is considered far more insignificant than a painted man, for it withers under mental and physical afflictions, is itself subject to decay, and is perishable.

The stability of the body of a person in a painting is not as [lasting] as that of the [actual] person; for indeed, the body depicted in the painting perishes when destroyed, whereas the other does not perish in that way.
The body, whose nature is flesh, inevitably perishes; yet, when well-nourished, it assumes a remarkably stable beauty, like a wondrous person.
Even when highly nourished, the physical body perishes and does not truly flourish; therefore, the excellent body is the "painted" body (the mental image), not this body of conceptual construction.

Indeed, those qualities that exist in a painted body do not exist in a body of mere imagination; for this [imaginary body] is surely far more insubstantial than even a painted body, being as it is merely inert.
O sinless one, what reliance can you have on this body composed of flesh? O high-minded one, this body is merely a body of long-standing mental constructs; do not place your trust in it.
For this body, born of a mere thought, is indeed more insignificant than even a body born of a dream; being produced by a small conception, it is not overwhelmed by long-lasting pleasures and pains.
Born from long-standing volitions and afflicted by long-lasting suffering, this body is indeed composed of volition; it neither exists nor does it not exist for us.
Why is this effort in vain? For this fool is merely a vessel for suffering; just as when a man made of a painting is wounded or destroyed, there is no injury to that [reality].
Likewise, when the person of one's own conceptualization is wounded or perishes, there is no real injury; just as when a kingdom of the mind is wounded or perishes, there is no real injury.

Just as when the second moon is wounded or diminished, there is no injury to that [actual moon]; just as when something undertaken in a dream is wounded or diminished, there is no injury to that [dream].

Just as when the water of a river is damaged or diminished by the heat of the sun, that [river] suffers no real loss, for it is merely constructed from conceptualization and is by its very nature subject to destruction.
Likewise, when this bodily machine is wounded or worn out, there is no injury to that [Self], for it consists of a long dream fashioned by the volitions of the mind.
Whether the body is adorned or defiled, there is no injury whatsoever to the consciousness; the consciousness does not reach its end, nor does the Self move, O Rāghava.

Brahman does not undergo transformation, nor is it harmed by the destruction of the body; for it is like a wheel standing above a revolving wheel, remaining as the original wheel while the subsequent wheels turn.
Just as one who is utterly deluded sees the circle of the directions spinning, due to a false cognition that has suddenly arisen and is leaping about.
Remaining there, one perceives this wheel of the body exactly as it is: as something whirled and appearing to whirl, and as something falling and having fallen.
The wheel of the body is seen both destroyed and being destroyed; relying on pure fortitude, one should abandon this dense delusion.
The body, which is both existent and non-existent, is created by false knowledge through mental construction; since it is produced by what is unreal, it can never be real.
The body, arisen from the unreal like the perception of a snake in a rope, performs the activities of the world even while being unreal, as if it were real.
O Rāma, that which is done by the insentient is not said to be "done" [by the self]; for even while acting, the body is never at any time the agent.
For the body is indeed inert and devoid of effort; it has no desire of its own. Since there is no agent whatsoever, the Self is merely its witness.
Just as a lamp placed in a windless spot remains steady within itself, so should one abide amidst the conditions of the world like a witness toward all phenomena.
Just as the sun performs its daily tasks while remaining in its own state, so too, O Rāma, perform this royal duty.
In this empty house of a body, which has arisen from non-existence and attained a semblance of reality like a yakṣa imagined falsely by a child;
Having come from somewhere unknown, this essence-less and wicked vampire of egoism, shunned by all virtuous people and named "the mind," has entered [me].
O Rāma, do not enter into the service of this one who is evil-minded with egoism; by serving him, the fruit obtained is rebirth in hell.
Within the house of the body, by the play of its own volitions, the hideous Vetāla of the intoxicated mind leaps about with ease.
Having entered the empty house of the body, that which was created by the yakṣa of the mind causes even the great ones, though established in meditative concentration, to be terrified.
Having expelled the vetāla of the mind from the temple of his own body, he never again fears anything within the empty city of saṃsāra.
In this house of the body, which is overcome by the element of consciousness, why do those who delight in it still remain today as if possessed of a self, as if they were something wondrous?
O Rāghava, those who have died while their body-dwelling was seized by the demon of the mind possess a consciousness like that of a demon, not unlike a non-demon.
O virtuous one, you dwell without attachment in this body, which is like a house inhabited by the great yakṣa of egoism; for indeed, it is not at all stable.
Having abandoned the habit of following egoism with an expansive intellect, and having attained the non-recollection of egoism, let one's own self alone be firmly grasped.
For those who, seized by the demon of egoism, seek only hell, and who are blinded by the intoxication of delusion, there are neither friends nor kinsmen.
Whatever action is performed with an intellect impaired by egoism, its fruit shall be like that of a poisonous creeper—consisting of death.
Know that the fool by whom the great festival of his own ego is maintained, being devoid of discernment and fortitude, has already perished instantly.
Those wretched ones who have been brought under the sway of the demon of egoism, O Rāghava, have become fuel for the fires of hell.
The tree of one's own body, in whose hollow the serpent of egoism writhes, is quickly felled by the undisciplined.
O best among the great, whether this demon of egoism remains in this body or departs, observe it with your mind, but do not identify with it.
For once you have become an Avadhūta—despised and mentally disregarded—the demon of egoism will do nothing to you here.
O Rāma, while this demon of the mind manifests within the abode of the body, what indeed has happened to the Self, which possesses infinite play?
The extensive calamities that befall men who are overcome by the yakṣas of the mind cannot be fully enumerated even in hundreds of years.
"Alas, alas! I am dead! I am consumed!"—these are indeed the modes of suffering belonging to the demon of egoism; they do not belong to another, O sinless one.
Just as space, though all-pervading, has no connection with anything here, so too the self, though all-pervading, is not joined with the ego-sense.
O Rāma, whatever this moving machine of a body performs and whatever it grasps is the activity of egoism, joined to the rope of the vital breath.
Just as space, though itself a non-agent, is said to be the cause for the growth of a tree, so too the Self, abiding within itself, is the cause for the activities of the mind.
By the mere proximity of the Self, the mind, having assumed a form, shines forth—just as a pure reflection on a wall appears by the mere presence of a lamp.
O Rāma, what connection can there ever be between one's own mind and oneself when they are separated, like heaven and earth, or like light and darkness?
O descendant of Raghu, through delusion the mind—which is enveloped by these restless vibrations of its own powers—is perceived as the self.
The Self is indeed of the nature of light, eternal, all-pervading, and omnipresent; know that the mind is deceitful egoism, while the Greatest One resides within the heart.
In reality, you are indeed the Self, the omniscient one; the mind is not [the self]. Cast far away the delusion of the mind; why are you so attached to this?
O Rāma, even a Piśāca dwelling in the empty house of the body, this wicked-minded one, while touching upon supreme silence, contemplates it within his mind.
Having cast off the demon of the mind—which brings about existence, is unwholesome, and robs one of the very essence of fortitude—be firm in who you truly are.
When a person is firmly seized by the yakṣa of the mind, neither scriptures, nor kinsmen, nor even teachers are able to protect that human being.
The teachers, the scriptures, and their meanings act as kinsmen who are able to rescue one whose mind-ghoul has been thoroughly pacified, just as one might pull a deer from a small puddle of mud.
In this empty city of the world, everything has been utterly corrupted by the intoxicated yakṣa of the mind, which leaps about within the house of the body.
This entire forest of the world, composed of fragments of bodies and haunted by the vetāla-demon of the mind, being utterly empty—of whom would it not cause fear?
In this city of the world, however, the house of the body—whose demon of the mind has been stilled—is inhabited by only a few virtuous ones.
O descendant of Raghu, it is heard here that every direction whatsoever is filled with the corpse-cemeteries of bodies and with the Vetālas of intoxicated delusion.
In this vast wilderness of the world, one who is deluded like a bewildered child should, by his own effort, propitiate the hope for fortitude and rescue himself by means of the self.
O Rāma, do not seek stability through the juices of grass in this forest of worldly decay, where herds of living beings roam like young deer.
In this forest upon the surface of the earth, young deer roam; having devoured the elephant of ignorance, you should adopt the conduct of a lion.
Other foolish deer roam in their own jungle within Jambudvīpa, O Rāma; do you likewise roam, O sinless one.

One should not plunge into a pond that is like a kinsman—though it appears beautiful—when its cold is extremely brief and it only serves to smear one with mud, just as one would not do in the case of a buffalo.
One should cast away the enjoyment and non-enjoyment of external objects and follow the path of the Noble One; having investigated the great purpose, one should take refuge in oneself alone.
One should not plunge into this most terrible and fierce whirlpool of anxiety for the sake of this body, which is impure, trivial, unfortunate, and misshapen.
The body is fashioned by one, inhabited by another yakṣa, and the sufferer of its pain is yet another; wonderful indeed is this cycle of folly!
Just as a stone possesses a solid mass of a single form within itself, so too does the Self, because existence alone is the sole universal, and nothing else is possible.

Just as solidity belongs to a stone, so do the mind and other faculties belong to the self; for they are non-different from mere existence, and since this [self] has no established form, it is non-existent.

Just as the nature of a stone is not distinct from the stone itself, and the nature of a jar is not distinct from the jar, so too the mind and other faculties are non-different from the Self by virtue of their mere existence.
In this regard, listen to this other vision that destroys great delusion, which was previously told to me in a cave on Kailāsa.
For the sake of pacifying the suffering of saṃsāra, there exists one who has gone beyond heaven, resplendent with a mass of moonbeams, whose crown bears the crescent moon, by the grace of the Lord.
There is a king of mountains named Kailāsa, the abode of Gaurī’s lover; there dwells the blessed Lord Hara, who bears the digit of the moon.
In former times, while worshipping that Great God on that very mountain, I once dwelt upon the bank of the Gaṅgā, having constructed a hermitage there.

For the sake of asceticism, he had long maintained a firm standing in the conduct of a *tāpasa*; surrounded by hosts of perfected beings (*siddha*), he had mastered the essential meaning of the scriptures.
Carrying a sewn pouch for flowers and a collection of many books—such was he, distinguished by these qualities, within a forest grove on Mount Kailāsa.
O Rāma, as I was engaged in ascetic practice, time passed by; then once, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight.

When the first part of the night in the fortnight of Śrāvaṇa had passed and was drawing to a close, the quarters of the sky appeared perfectly tranquil, as if they were standing in the silence of wooden statues.
In that interval, when the first watch of the night had passed, amidst thickets and dense forests where the darkness was as deep as if it could be cut with a sword.
Having extended my concentration and remaining with my gaze fixed on the external, I suddenly beheld a radiance arising in the forest.
Beholding it, which resembled hundreds of bright clouds and was like a multitude of moon-disks, illuminating the quarters and groves, I was filled with wonder.
As I gazed with an outward glance that was inwardly radiant, I saw that the bearer of the crescent moon had reached that mountain peak.
With his hand placed in the hand of Gaurī, his front led by Nandin, and being well-restrained, he took the *arghya* offering and, having instructed the disciples standing there, [proceeded].
With a joyful mind, I approached him, purifying my path with my gaze; there, even from afar, the three-eyed Lord offered a handful of flowers before him.
Having offered the guest-water, I bowed down and paid homage to the Lord with that straight, cool, and moon-like radiance.
For a long time, I have been made the abode of his glance, which removes all suffering, for him who sits upon the flowery mountain slopes and is the witness of the three worlds.
Having approached, I offered water for honor, flowers, and water for the feet; many handfuls of mandāra flowers were scattered before him.
Śiva was worshipped with various kinds of prostrations and hymns of praise; thereafter, the blessed Gaurī was likewise honored with such same ritual service.
Thus honored, together with her companions and the circle of the Gaṇas, she spoke at the conclusion of the worship in a voice as cool as the rays of the full moon.
To me, as I sat there, he who bears the crescent of the moon spoke: "O Brahmin, you who possess tranquility and have attained rest in the supreme state."
I hope that your virtuous companions remain steadfast in the higher realms; I hope your auspicious austerity proceeds without obstacle.
"Has that which was to be attained been attained? Are all fears now stilled?"—thus spoke the Lord of Gods, the sole creator of all the worlds.
"O Raghunandana, O Maheśvara, I spoke with words full of conciliation to those here who possess the auspiciousness of the recollection of the Three-eyed One."
For those whose minds are reeling with the bliss of recollecting you, nothing at all is difficult to attain, nor are there any fears whatsoever.
Those regions, those districts, those directions, and those mountains do not exist within the treasury of the world, nor do they bow down again and again.
Wherever people abide with minds solely intent on recollecting you, it is the fruit of past merit and the nourishment of present merit.
O Lord, the remembrance of You sows the seed of what is yet to come; You are the unique vessel of the nectar of knowledge and the moon that causes the light of fortitude to shine.
O Lord, mindfulness of you is the gateway to the city of liberation; by me, who possesses the noble wish-fulfilling gem of mindfulness of you, [all desires are fulfilled].
"The foot of the Lord of Beings has been placed upon the crest of all calamities"—having spoken thus to the Blessed Maheśvara, who was exceedingly gracious.
Having bowed down, I said: "O Rāma, listen to this: O Blessed One, by your grace all the quarters are filled for me."
But I ask you, O Lord of Gods, for a resolution regarding that doubt; speak with a gracious mind, free from agitation and free from affliction.
O Lord, what is the procedure for the worship of the gods that brings about the destruction of all sins and the increase of all that is auspicious?
Īśvara said: Listen, O best of the knowers of Brahman, to this unsurpassed worship of the gods; I shall describe it, by the mere performance of which one is indeed liberated at once.
"Do you know, O mighty-armed twice-born one, who might be the god? Neither the lotus-eyed one is the god, nor is the three-eyed one the god."
Neither is he the god born from the lotus, nor the god who is the lord of the thirty-three, nor the god Wind, nor the Sun, nor Fire, nor the Maker of Night.
There is no Brahmin, no king, no "I," and no "you," O best of the twice-born; for there is no god in the form of the body, nor is there a god who assumes the form of the mind.
The deity is not one who has the form of a lotus, nor is the deity the intellect; that which is uncreated, without beginning or end, and divine in nature is called "Deva."
How can they know that uncreated, beginningless and endless Divine, which is Consciousness-Śiva, within an object that is limited and measured by its forms and so forth?
That very [reality] is expressed by the word "God"; one should worship that, because it alone exists as everything, assuming the nature of both being and non-being.
For those who do not know the true principle of Śiva, worship through forms and other such means is performed; for one incapable of traveling the path of a *yojana*, a path of a *krośa* is devised.
The fruit obtained from Rudra and others is limited by such measures as "this much" and so forth; the fruit of the Self is bliss, which is uncreated and without beginning or end.
He who abandons natural fruit and pursues artificial fruit is like one who leaves the grove of Mandāra trees and goes to a forest of Karañja bushes.

Awakening, equanimity, and tranquility are the flowers and the foremost [offerings] therein; those who know what is to be worshipped recognize that the stainless, pure consciousness alone is the auspicious object of worship.
Know that when the divine Self is worshipped with the flowers of tranquility, awakening, and so forth, that indeed is the worship of the Divine; the worship of forms is not true worship.
But those people who, having abandoned the worship of the deity in the form of self-realization, are attached to artificial images, undergo long-lasting suffering.
O Brahmin, those virtuous ones who have known what is to be known regard the worship of gods as being like children's play, except for their meditation on the Self.
The self alone is the divine Lord Śiva, the supreme cause; he should always be worshipped incessantly with the offering of knowledge.
Know this conscious space—the self, the imperishable living being—to be your own nature; there is no other to be worshipped, for worship is the worship of the Self.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Lord, just as this world is essentially nothing but the space of consciousness, so too let that state of being the individual soul (jīva) and so forth, which belongs to consciousness itself, be explained.

Īśvara said: Indeed, it is only the sky of consciousness (cidvyoma) that exists here, devoid of near or far; it is that which remains at the end of the kalpa, wherein no object of thought (cetya) can possibly exist anywhere.
Whatever shines forth by itself, that which is its own self-expression—the very vibration known as "itself"—by that alone is this world sufficiently constituted.
Thus, like a city in a dream, the world appears as consisting of consciousness; thus, the world is purely of the nature of the space of consciousness, transparent and without foundation.

Because an object of cognition is absolutely non-existent, the visible world is nothing but the space of consciousness; that which shines forth due to its nature as consciousness at the beginning of creation is known as the "world."
Therefore, since this world appears in the form of a dream-city, what kind of otherness could there be therein, and from where, within that which is essentially the void of consciousness?

The mountains are pure consciousness alone; the world and the sky are pure consciousness alone; the self and the individual soul are pure consciousness alone; and the succession of all beings is pure consciousness alone.
Tell me, apart from the mere void of consciousness, what else could possibly exist at the beginning of creation, whether in a distinct heaven or a city? Tell me!
"Space, supreme space, the space of Brahman, and the consciousness of the world"—these are synonymous names for that [reality], just as the words 'pāda' and 'vṛkṣa' refer to a tree.
Thus, through dreams, mental constructs, and illusions, two [worlds] are experienced by oneself; at that time, it is said that the space of consciousness alone shines as the world.
Just as this space of consciousness appears in the form of the world within a dream, so too does that very same thing appear to us in what is called the waking state, which is itself a dream.
Just as in a dream-city nothing whatsoever can exist anywhere apart from the space of consciousness, so it is in the waking state with respect to the Great Consciousness.
Since no other object of cognition whatsoever exists, therefore this entire world, though appearing as both the mind and its objects, remains established as the non-objective mind alone.
Know that the three worlds, which have arisen of their own accord as a manifestation within the supreme space, exist like a dream within the sky of consciousness; they do not exist as a duality.

Just as objects such as pots and cloths in a dream consist of nothing but the space of consciousness, so too this creation at the very beginning of creation consists of nothing but the space of consciousness.
Just as nothing exists other than pure consciousness alone in a city of dreams, so it is in these three worlds.
Whatever perceptions there may be, and whatever existents or non-existents belong to the three times—all that, together with space, time, and the mind, is nothing but the void of consciousness.
This very God has been described, who is supreme from the perspective of ultimate reality; he who is you, he who is I, and he who is the entire world in its entirety.
For the entire multitude of things, for this world, for you, and for me, the body is indeed nothing other than the Supreme Self within the space of consciousness.

Just as in a city of dreams within one's imagination, there exists no body whatsoever other than the space of consciousness, so too, O Sage, from the very first moment of creation, there has been no form other than that.
The Lord said: Thus, this entire universe is nothing but the Supreme Self alone; it is Brahman itself, the supreme ether, remembered as the highest deity.
This worship is the highest good; from it, everything is obtained. It alone is the ground of creation; all this is established within it.
Therefore, that bliss which is unartificial, without beginning or end, non-dual, indivisible, and not to be accomplished by external means, is attained.
O best of sages, you are enlightened; therefore, this is being told to you: a vast abundance of flowers and incense is not suitable for the worship of the Supreme Deity.
For those whose intellects are undeveloped and whose minds are as fragile as those of children, the worship of deities is said to consist of artificial images.

For in the absence of tranquility, awakening, and so forth, they indeed worship with flowers and other offerings; thus, they worship a mere imagined form within an imagined nature, all of which is purely false.
Having performed worship through the sequences created by their own imagination, children attain satisfaction with offerings of flowers, incense, and fragments of food.
Having performed the worship of the deity in vain with objects created by their own imagination, they lead themselves to nothing but false results from whatever source.
O Brahmin, the worship with flowers and incense is intended for those of childish intellect; I shall now describe that form of worship which is suitable for those such as yourself.
O best among the wise, this deity who is such as we and others are is none other than the Supreme Self alone—the God who is the support of the three worlds. It is not anything else.
Śiva transcends all states and surpasses all conceptual constructions; though encompassed by all conceptualization, he is neither the whole nor the possessor of all.
O Sage, that which is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth; which effects the illumination of all undertakings; and whose form is pure consciousness alone—stainless—is called the God.
Consciousness transcends all parts; it abides within the interior of all beings. She is the Goddess who bestows existence upon all and who takes away the existence of all.
Brahman is that which is said to be between existence and non-existence; it is called the Supreme Self (Paramātman) and is designated as "Sada" and "Om."
By its nature as the Great Being, it has attained equality everywhere; it is proclaimed as "Great Consciousness" (mahācit) and is heard of as the "Ultimate Reality" (paramārtha).
Yet everything exists everywhere, just as sap exists within all creepers; it exists both in the form of the universal essence of being and as the nature of the Great Being.

O sinless one, that which is the reality of the mind in Arundhatī, that which is the reality of the mind in you, that which is the reality of the mind in Pārvatī, and that which is the reality of the mind in the Gaṇas;
Those of supreme intelligence who know reality understand that this consciousness-essence of mine and the consciousness-essence within the three worlds are one and the same God.
O Brahmin, tell me truly: what essence can there be in whatever other god is conceived as possessing feet, hands, and so forth, if he is apart from pure consciousness alone?
Pure consciousness alone is the essence of transmigratory existence; having attained the state of being the essence of all, that Lord is the "I am All," and from Him everything is obtained.
O Brahmin, he does not stand at a distance, nor is he difficult for anyone to attain; he is eternally established within the body, as well as everywhere in space.
He acts, he eats, he maintains himself, and he departs; he breathes out, he is the knower, and he knows each and every limb.
O Lord of Sages, he dwells within this city, which manifests through various activities and, by virtue of that [power], is bound to his own essential nature.
And by his grace, he dwells within this body-abode, which is unstable and possesses a deep inner treasury—a cave-like heart—as the Lord of the Cave.

For that stainless Self, which transcends the existence of the activity of the six senses including the mind, the designation "consciousness" (cit) has been conceptually fashioned for the sake of conventional usage.
This very one, consisting of consciousness, subtle, all-pervading, and stainless, produces this radiant manifestation and yet does not produce it.
Though it is exceedingly pure, that consciousness colors this worldly activity for the sake of the world, just as a wise man colors a sweet creeper with juice.
Those beautiful wonders which, as they truly exist within consciousness, cause it to marvel—by that very fact, some indeed are called "spaces" (nabhas).
Some are designated as "living beings" (jīva), some are designated as "mind" (citta), some are designated as "artistic skill" (kalā), and some are designated as "regions" (deśa).
Some denote actions, some denote substances, and some denote states such as the modifications of being, as well as classes and propriety.
Some are designated as "Light," some as "Mountain" or "Darkness"; some are designated as "Sun," "Moon," and so forth, while others are designated as "Yakṣas."
Just as a sprout is extended by the spring season through its own nature of desirelessness, even so is this splendor of the world extended by the conscious Self.
Indeed, even when all these [bodies] are complete, this single network of bodies is always but one, situated within the ocean of the three worlds.
The Sovereign Consciousness tastes the essence of the honey of volition, which is gathered by the bee of the mind wandering within the lotus of the body.
The world, including the gods, asuras, and gandharvas, along with its mountains and oceans, remains within consciousness yet flows onward like water in a whirlpool.
The wheel of saṃsāra, consisting of the conduct of a bound mind and characterized by a clever circle of deceitful associates, revolves within the wheel of consciousness as a vessel of delusion.
In the form of a four-armed being, he struck down the host of asuras, just as the sun destroys the heat with a mass of rain clouds armed with lightning.
O Brahmin, by virtue of having variegated eyes marked with the bull and the moon, he has become like a bee for the face-lotus of Gaurī, who is herself a lotus-pond.

Having attained the state of being adorned by the lotus of Viṣṇu, with her mind dependent on the meditation of consciousness, the Triple Veda maintains its position as the lake of the lotus born of Pitāmaha.
O Brahmin, various bodies manifest here in great abundance from the conscious principle (cit), just as leaves from a tree or as bracelets and other ornaments from gold.
She whose feet are worshipped by the entire host of gods bears the status of the crest-jewel of the three worlds through her effortless sovereignty.
Having attained the state of pure luminosity within the vast expanse of the three worlds, it falls, rises, and moves within its own self alone, like the water of the ocean.
The moonlight of consciousness, spreading its radiance in the four directions, causes all the night-lotuses of living beings to blossom.
The Great Lakṣmī, who is the mirror of consciousness, receives the reflection of the three worlds within herself through her grace, just as a pregnant woman carries her own embryo within her womb.
The glorious water brings about the great mandalas of the fourteen elements, just as the ocean produces its own treasures.
With its flowers of diverse perceptions and sprouts of dense volitions, it has ascended the field of the sky and bears the fruit of the flood of sentient beings.
Stained by the aesthetic flavor of the latent impressions of the mass of motes in the web of living beings, enveloped in the skin of sensation, it is agitated by the sprouts of mental desire.
She whose radiant form is the filaments of the three worlds throughout countless past ages; she who laughs with the exuberant play of incessant vibration.
Roughened by the joints of all seasons, with its shrubs like inert mountains, entwined with the knots of physical forms, and turned upside down from root to tip.
This mind is blossomed, delicate, and composed of both the real and the unreal; it is a manifold flower of visible objects, variegated and unable to endure scrutiny.
For here, by means of this [imagination], everywhere a semblance of reality is produced like a shadow; the object is conceived, expanded, described, and even brought into being.
By means of this great funeral pyre, the sun and other luminaries shine eternally; and bodies take pleasure in one another through the delusions of existence, consciousness, and insentience.
Whirled by the eddying vortex of consciousness, the very reality of the world—the mere dust-streak of the net of existence—dances as a visible body.
Consciousness fully manifests this entire undertaking of the world, just as a lamp with a flame that illuminates the three worlds reveals the objects resting upon its colors.
Just as the moon obtains union with the stainless lunar orb, so too does the splendor of all things existing in the world attain visibility everywhere.
