By the sprinkling of the elixir of consciousness, the series of objects of experience attains both its true form and its fruit, just as a beautiful creeper does when drenched by the rains.
And by its shadow alone, the dullness of this entire body arises perfectly, just as darkness arises here within a house.
If these wonders of consciousness did not exist within the body, they would surely not touch any form, having abandoned the body of the three worlds.
In this luminous expanse of consciousness, the restless young bride of the family of action—bearing the infant of volition—shines forth within the house of the body.

Without the light of consciousness, how, when, or where could any aesthetic flavor (rasa) become manifest, even if it were vibrating at the tip of the tongue? Or rather, by whom has such a flavor ever been seen?
Listen, my dear friend: even if it possesses beautiful branches and is fully covered by the creepers of tresses, how can the tree of the body shine without immersion in consciousness?
Consciousness alone expands, rolls about, and devours, acting as both the moving and the unmoving; consciousness alone exists, nothing else exists—this entire world has arisen as mere consciousness.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, having spoken thus at that time with a voice as clear as the moon, the Three-eyed Lord was questioned by me once again with a voice as clear as the moon.
O Lord, if consciousness is all-pervading and this world is of the nature of that single consciousness, then why does it not perceive this expansion of the earth as being like itself?
"How can this conceptual construction—that 'this [person], having previously possessed consciousness, now remains devoid of consciousness'—be based on direct experience in the world?"
Īśvara said: "Listen, O Brahman, to all this that you have asked; I shall speak it to you. You have posed a great question, O best among the knowers of Brahman."

For here in the body there exists Consciousness (cit), which consists of the nature of all beings; yet that which is turned toward movement, being one, is remembered as the supreme, non-conceptual state.

That very [consciousness], though conceived as the Buddha within, exists as something else entirely; like a woman who has fallen into misconduct, she has become both what was conceived and its opposite.

For that very same person, just as here [in this world] becomes another in an instant due to anger and so forth, even so consciousness—marked by conceptual construction—attains a state of otherness from its own essential nature.
O Brahman, that which is imagined by conceptual construction falls away from the nature of consciousness; gradually manifesting insentience, it reaches the state of objective manifestation.

Consciousness itself attains the state of being an object of cognition, reaching the condition of a subtle atom of space; subsequently, consisting of the seed of sound, it moves toward the subtle element of air.

Ending with the divisions of space and time, and enveloped by the subtle elements (tanmātras) in succession, it first becomes the individual soul (jīva), then quickly becomes the intellect (buddhi), and thereafter the ego (ahaṃkāra) and the mind (manas).
Having attained the state of the mind, one clings to saṃsāra; just as a twice-born man becomes an outcaste through the thought, "I am an outcaste."
Unawakened by its own conceptualization, and not awakening the entire world due to its dullness, it assumes a variegated form and incessantly undergoes conceptualization and the like.
Composed of infinite volitions and thickened by the volition of dullness, consciousness attains the state of inert matter through delusion, just as water attains the state of stone.
Then, O Sage, that which is designated as "mind," "mental delusion," and "illusion" arises in saṃsāra by resorting skillfully to dullness.
She has fallen into the dullness of delusion, is oppressed by the fetters of craving, is possessed by desire, anger, and fear, and wanders excessively between existence and non-existence.
Having abandoned her own infinite enjoyments, subject to the transformations of limitation, scorched by the forest fire of suffering, and her heart emaciated by the inauspiciousness of grief;
By the thought "I am this," she was rendered destitute by emptiness; clinging to the body alone as her refuge, she has fallen into supreme wretchedness.
Sunk in the great mire of delusion like an aged forest elephant, she swings upon the cradle of the creeper of existence and non-existence, her body trembling.
It deals with the transformations and worldly activities of a coreless and shoreless saṃsāra; its heart is scorched by suffering, and it is colored by the radiance of passion.
Like a doe strayed from her own herd, she has fallen into a state of helplessness; her form arises when manifest and sets when concealed.
She flees from those women who, summoned by her own imagination, appear with terrified and agitated glances, just as a young girl flees from Vetālas.
Like a camel seeking a sweet drop of conditioned pleasure, one who has fallen away from the intermediate state falls further down from fault to fault because of that very fault.
She has indeed fallen into extreme adversity; having gone from crisis to crisis, she has fallen from suffering to suffering, remaining in calamity after calamity.
Possessed by a multitude of various misfortunes, her disposition subject to compulsive impulses, she has fallen from misery to even greater misery, tormented by burning anguish.
Having gradually acquired proficiency through constant practice, she attained the status of a master of artistry and reached the pinnacle of skill in composing various poetic meters.
Terrified and having reached the brink of death, she was suspicious of everything, like a small fish in dwindling water, intent only on darting about.

In childhood, all her faculties were powerless; in youth, she was overwhelmed by anxiety; even in old age, she was afflicted by extreme suffering; and when dead, she was brought under the sway of karma.
She is born as a Nāgī in the city of heaven, as a Pātālī in the hollows of the netherworld, as an Āsurī in the caverns of the Daityas, and as a human woman on the surface of the earth.
A rākṣasī on the support of a rākṣasa, a vānarī in a hollow of the forest, a siṃhī on the peak of a king of mountains, and a kinnarī on a kulaparvata.
A Vidyādharī on Devagiri, a female serpent in Vanagartaka, a creeper on a tree, a female bird in a nest, a plant upon a mountain peak, and a doe in the forest.
Nārāyaṇa reclines in the ocean; the lotus-born Brahmā is absorbed in meditation in the city of Brahman; Hara has gone to his beloved on the mountain; and Hari, the best of gods, is in heaven.
The sun of sharp rays creates the day; the cloud rains water; and consciousness creates the wind, along with the mountains and the great oceans.
The wheel of seasons swiftly revolves as the circle of time; it attains the state of day and night, and gradually assumes the nature of light and darkness.
In one place, there is the swelling of the sap of seeds; in another, the silence of stone; in one place, a river full of water; and in another, the spreading of night-lotuses.
In some places by the ripening of rows of fruits, in some by wood fires and the like; in some by coolness, snow, and water, and in some by eating nothing at all.
In some places it has a blazing form, in some places it is a harsh rock, in some places it is blue, in others green; in some places it is fire, and in others the earth.

Because she is the self of all, because she is omnipresent, because she is endowed with all powers, and because she is everything—thus, that supreme [reality] is of such a nature, even clearer than the sky.

Just as water, by its own movement, constructs for itself a state such as that of waves and so forth—according to how, by what means, where, and when—it experiences those very things in that same way.

The female swan, the female curlew, the female crane, the female crow, the female saras crane, the female horse, the female wolf, the female heron, the female egret, the female deer, the female monkey, the female kinnara, and the female dog.
Vaṭīkā, Piṅgalī, Śālī, Makṣikā, Bhramarī, Śukī, Dhīḥ, Śrīḥ, Hrīḥ, Prītī, Ratī, Śambarī, Śarvarī, and Śaśī.
He wanders through these and other various wombs, revolving in saṃsāra like a blade of grass in a whirlpool of water.
Then she fears her own mental construction, like a female donkey from its own braying; there is no other girl so deluded, fickle, and weak as she.
O great sage, this has been described to you as the power of life (jīvaśakti)—miserable, subject to the sway of natural impulses, and possessing the nature of a bound soul (paśu).
Having assumed the designation "the self of karma," this [individual soul] of the Supreme Self is to be pitied; it has itself resorted to delusion, which is endless and full of suffering.
This innate impurity, which is non-existent yet pervaded by this [consciousness] and subject to destruction, is inseparable and persists like the husk upon a grain of rice.
Deprived of infinite prosperity and tormented by misfortune, she grieved for her life, like a heroine who has lost her husband.

Behold the power of the movement of the insentient: here, without the remembrance of its own state, the intellect falls miserably toward the lower realms, like the heavy wooden base of a water-wheel's bucket.

Īśvara said: In this way, consciousness accumulates what is utterly false through the mental cultivation that "I am suffering," having fallen into the delusion of the intoxication of a dream-consciousness, as in a state of agitation.
Just as a young woman, her mind deluded, weeps thinking "I am dead" even though she is not dead, so too does the consciousness (citi) weep, thinking "I am destroyed," even though it is not destroyed.
Just as this world is perceived by a distorted mind that is causeless, deluded, and yet seemingly stable, so too does consciousness perceive through the delusion of "I-ness."
For the mind is indeed the cause of this consciousness's experience of saṃsāra; yet it has no other cause whatsoever, because nothing distinct from consciousness is possible.
For in this way, due to the absence of a cause, that which is to be cognized is impossible; therefore, that mind by which the object of cognition is diligently cognized does not exist.
It does not possess the nature of the seen, the seeing, and the seer, like oil in a stone; nor does it possess the nature of agent, object, and instrument, like darkness in the moon.

The knower, the known, and the means of knowledge do not exist [in it], just as a new sprout does not exist in the sky; nor do consciousness, the conscious subject, and the object of consciousness, just as a khadira tree does not exist in the Nandana grove.

The states of "I-ness," "you-ness," and "that-ness" do not exist in reality, just as the nature of a mountain does not exist in the sky; nor do the states of having one's own body or another's body exist, just as the nature of a conch shell does not exist in soot.
They are neither diverse nor non-diverse, nor are they distinct like Sumeru mountains; nor is the splendor of the word for "meaning" like a great creeper in a barren wasteland.
It is not so, it is not so; nor is there night in the orb of the sun, nor is there heat in frost, just as there is neither reality nor unreality [in the Self].
Neither emptiness nor non-emptiness exists, like a tree within a stone casket; that which is called "the emptiness of emptiness" is as vast as the uncarved void of space.
Only the purity of the state of absolute oneness remains; this is not attained by anyone through any defect of the mind.

This misfortune that has arisen remains present merely through the non-cultivation of that [reality]; yet for one who knows it, that misfortune is pacified merely through the cultivation of that [reality].

Even for one who knows that [truth], nothing else is of use except the mere cultivation [of that knowledge]; for here, the state of self-mastery consists in the realization that neither a blade of grass nor the three worlds exist [independently].

This goal is indeed within one's own power, yet it is difficult to accomplish when one remains merely at the level of mental cultivation. If that which is not accomplished by a person is not achieved, how and where could it ever be obtained?
That consciousness which is non-conceptual and non-dual, which pervades all things, is the supreme, singular, and ultimate reality; it is the direct illuminator even of lights.
This very [reality] is the illuminator, all-pervading, eternally pure, perpetually arisen, devoid of mental activity, changeless, and stainless.
She is established in the pot, the cloth, the banyan tree, the wall, the cart, the monkey, the donkey, the asura, the ocean, the spirit, the man, and the serpent.
The existent reality stands like a witness; it does not vibrate anywhere. Like a lamp for the purpose of illumination, it performs no further action.
Though impure, this [intellect] is rich in non-conceptuality yet conceptualizing; though inert, it appears as non-inert; it is not all-encompassing, yet it is indeed all-pervasive.

Non-conceptual, supreme, and subtle, consciousness perceives its own self-awareness, just as the movement of the wind [is felt] in the limbs, vital points, and so forth during the winding of a machine.
Consciousness, when enveloped by form, light, and mental attention, becomes either existent or non-existent sleep, depending on whether there is awareness or a lack of awareness.

That supreme consciousness itself, through its own awareness, becomes exceedingly clear as thought; just as a virtuous person may become like an evil one when influenced by the desires of wicked people.
Just as gold, through the removal of impurities, loses its copperiness and regains its state of pure gold, so too does the supreme consciousness.

Just as one's own mirror returns to its state as a mere reflection through the cessation of its own superimpositions, so too, having entered into what appears to be creation, it returns to its own true state through awakening.
From the perception of non-existence, this saṃsāra proceeds; but from the perception of intrinsic nature, it is extinguished as something unreal.
When, due to its nature as consciousness, it gathers within itself another unreal state, then, having attained as it were a sense of "I-ness," that which is indestructible seems to perish.
Just as a fruit falls from the edge of a cliff or a tree with only a slight tremor, so too is this great downward fall from consciousness.

But this existence of form and the rest is nothing other than the stainless consciousness itself; for when duality and unity—arising from non-awakening—have dissolved through awakening, [nothing remains but consciousness].
The awakening of the mind toward the mental faculties and so forth occurs by the mere presence of the mind, just as worldly activity proceeds by the mere presence of light.
The throbbing of the pupil due to wind is called its radiance, which is known as sight; however, the cognition of the form of that object existing externally is the supreme consciousness.

The skin and the vital air are inert and insubstantial; their conjunction is called touch. The cognition of touch is mental activity, while the awareness of that [mental activity] is the supreme Consciousness.
The connection between the subtle element of smell and the wind is the consciousness of smell; however, the perception of these [objects] when devoid of the mind is supreme consciousness itself.

When there is contact with the wind of hearing the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra) even without the mind, consciousness that resembles deep sleep is declared to be the supreme Consciousness (cit).
The tendency toward action arises from volition; volition is the process of mental reflection; reflection is the turbidity of the mind; and the Self is consciousness, which remains stainless.
Consisting of the light of consciousness, eternal, and abiding solely within itself, it contains this internal world as a configuration, just as a stone [contains its internal structure].
Maintaining this non-dual state, which is devoid of modification and the like, it neither sets nor rises; it does not vibrate, nor does it increase.

Having attained the state of living through volition, yet by means of its own self which is devoid of volition, it contemplates its own condition as being neither conscious nor insentient, remaining established in itself.

The vital breath (prāṇa) is the chariot of this consciousness (cit); the ego (ahaṃkāra) is the chariot of the vital breath; the intellect (buddhi) is the chariot of the ego; and from that, the mind (manas) is the chariot of the intellect.

The chariot of the mind is the vital breath; the chariot of the vital breath is the collection of senses; the chariot of the multitude of senses is the body; and the chariot of the body is the vehicle.
Vibration is action within saṃsāra, the cage of old age and death; thus has this wheel been set in motion, born from primordial manifestation.
It appears within itself as something vast and unreal, like a dream; it does not possess even the slightest degree of reality, being situated like the water of a mirage.

O Lord of Sages, in this context, the vital breath (prāṇa) is considered the chariot through mental construction; wherever there is the wind of the vital breath, there the faculty of thought (manana) is firmly established.
Wherever the glory of light is established, there form shines; wherever the vital breath is firmly situated, that very thing trembles.

Just as a gust of wind that blows into a forest causes it to tremble, so too does the vital breath (prāṇa) quiver when the mind is not dissolved into the space [of the heart]. However, when the mind is merged into the space [of the supreme self], the vital breath does not tremble.
When the fire has ceased to exist, it no longer shines, just as its form does not appear; when the vital breath has subsided, there is not even the slightest trace of the mind within the wind.
When the whirlwind has subsided, the dust no longer stirs; wherever the vital breath (prāṇa) and the wind (marut) go, there the mind (manas) remains.
Wherever the chariot follows, there the charioteer is; likewise, the mind impelled by the vital breath reaches another place in an instant.
Otherwise, it would perish there like a stone released from a sling; where there is a flower, there is fragrance, and where there is fire, there is heat.

Wherever the vital breath (prāṇa) goes, there the wind (marut) moves; wherever the moon (indu) is, there is its luster. Consciousness arises from the vibration of the wind, and that is the contact with the channels (nāḍīs).

The expansion of consciousness is the mind, and that [mind] resides within the cavity of the vital breath; everywhere, consciousness exists, as clear as the sky, throughout both the insentient and the sentient.
Yet it is experienced as if it were trembling due to the vibration of the vital breath; though established within insentient things, its true nature is pure existence alone.

Awakened by the vital breath (prāṇa), consciousness perceives within the insentient through its nature as feeling, as it previously leaped about with various expansive manifestations; but when the breath has passed away, that very same consciousness, free from mentation, does not tremble.
O Sage, the Supreme Self is reflected within its own city of eight (puryaṣṭaka); just as a reflection is seen in a mirror and not in stones or other such things.
Know the mind to be the city of eight constituents (puryaṣṭaka), the sole cause of all effects; it is described by others through various distinctions imagined according to their own inclinations.

Know that the entire universe is that Supreme Reality, from which arises the web of perceived objects cluttered with mental constructs, in which it is intensely experienced as if established, and from which the mind revolves through the perception of a body.
The Lord said: O Sage, listen to how she, who is active and characterized by vibration, moving through the bodies of men, attains the supreme designation.
By means of those various accumulations of karma from the past—consisting of the desires of one's own mental constructions—which have grown exceedingly full, they are indeed struck down.
O Brahman, the power of consciousness has become like something insentient through its state as the mind; yet it vibrates by means of this [mind], which is appropriately its own manifested power.
O Sage, by her grace, this Citkalankavatī here creates and yet does not create the world, which is like a city of Gandharvas.
Due to the absence of the mind and other faculties, the body remains mute like a wall; for it is through their presence that it vibrates, like a stone propelled by the wind.
Just as this extremely inert iron moves when in proximity to a magnet, so does this individual soul (jīva) move when the all-pervading Supreme Being is present.
This individual soul shines forth abundantly by its own inherent power alone, just as a mirror receives a reflection even from an object situated outside its own substance.

Due to the forgetting of its own true nature, this individual soul has fallen into a state of insentience, just as a noble twice-born man falls into the status of a śūdra through delusion and the forgetting of his own being.
For consciousness, having forgotten its own true nature, has fallen into the state of the mind; due to its heart being struck by delusion, it experiences a profound sense of wretchedness.
The body, insentient and powerless, is moved by the force of the vital breath (vāta), just as water is moved by a succession of waves.
By this wretched living being, whose nature is karma and who possesses this mind, the machines of bodies are set in motion, like stones by the wind.
O Brahmin, for the purpose of pulling the chariot of the body, the Supreme Self has created the mind and the vital breath, which are firmly established in their respective functions.
Having made the insentient body its chariot and having attained the state of a living being, it mounts the chariot of the mind and drives the horses of the vital breaths.

In some places there is the state of having arisen entities; in some places, the state of having perished entities; in some places, the state of having many entities; and in some places, the state of having a single entity.

Just as water exists whether in a state of flowing or broken into waves, so too that very [reality], not abandoning its own nature, appears as both the existent and the non-existent, like water appearing as wave-form.
The supreme form of the Self shines forth within its own mental modifications by depending upon them, just as the beauty of forms appearing in objects depends upon this light.
When the stainless supreme Self, which is the nature of consciousness, is present, the individual soul lives with its light, just as a house does when a lamp is present.
Mental anxieties and physical ailments indeed swell for him, just as the state of waves arises from water and the state of foam arises from those very waves.
The living being, like a bee in a lotus-body crowded with mental and physical afflictions, undergoes instability, just as water assumes the state of waves.

Because the power of consciousness possesses all powers, through the contemplation "I am not consciousness," that very power falls into helplessness here, just as the sun is obscured by radiant clouds.

Due to its lack of autonomy and its accumulation of impurities, as well as its dullness, it does not perceive self-awareness, just as one overcome by dense stupor does not feel the crushing of his own limbs.
And having attained this contemplation, delusion perishes, just as a person who is devoted to thick delusion loses the memory of his own purpose.

When the power of the movement of the vital wind (vāta) within the consciousness of the limbs is lost through impairment, one does not perform synthesis [of experience], just as a leper cannot seek out movement.
Due to the vibration of non-awareness within the body, the lotus situated in the heart does not manifest when it is not touched, just like a wooden vessel outside that does not vibrate.
When the lotus petal is motionless, these vital breaths within attain peace, just as the powers of the external wind cease when the palm-leaf fan is still.
When the vital breath has ceased and other sensations have subsided, the living soul enters a state of complete silence, just as dust is no longer visible when the wind in the sky has stilled.
O Sage, when the mind is free from passion and devoid of support, it remains, having attained its own state, like the seed of a tree within water.
Thus, when the multitude of causes that have arrived in a state of deficiency have completely subsided within the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), the physical body falls motionless.
Due to the delusion of thinking "I am the thinker," latent impressions (vāsanās) undergo vibration; impelled by that, the mind within remembers one thing and forgets another of its own accord.

Through the throbbing of the petals of the heart-lotus, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*) becomes manifest; when the movement within the mechanism of the heart-lotus is obstructed, the subtle body perishes.
O twice-born one, as long as the city-of-eight (puryaṣṭaka) exists within the body, so long does that [being] live; when the city-of-eight has ceased, the body is said to be dead.
When, due to the awakening of conflicting impurities and by virtue of the states of cutting and piercing, the mechanism of the heart-lotus does not vibrate within;
Then the city of eight (puryaṣṭaka) gradually attains peace in the void, like a succession of winds when the mechanism of the wind is obstructed.
By the power of self-awareness, the individual soul falls into a state of helplessness; the lotus-machine situated within the body is perpetually set in motion.
Those from whose hearts pure latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have not departed, who possess a stable and uniform life-force, are liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) and long-lived.
When the lotus-machine is restrained and the vital breath has attained peace, this body, losing its fortitude, falls upon the earth like a piece of wood or a clod of earth.
O Sage, just as the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) becomes merged in the wind within the sky, even so does the mind then attain dissolution right there.
But the mind, long practiced in such states and inscribed with latent impressions (*vāsanā*), wanders here and there and perceives the manifold world of heaven, hell, and so forth.
Deprived of mind and vital breath, the body becomes a corpse, just as a house falls into utter desolation when its inhabitants have gone far away.

The all-pervading consciousness, having become a living soul through the act of conscious thought, resides in the mind; having assumed the body of the subtle octad (*puryaṣṭaka*), it becomes the possessor of the transportable body (*ātivāhika-dehin*).
Having embraced the five subtle elements within the mind, it remains established there; through its own nature, it perceives a gross form, like the delusion of a dream.
Through firm cultivation, one who is thereafter filled with aesthetic relish (*rasa*) forgets everything regarding the subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*) in an instant.
While this body is indeed unreal, the cultivation of artificial conceptions leads the unreal to the state of reality, and even the real to the state of unreality.
For, becoming individualized as a living soul through its conscious aspect, it becomes the mind; the mind then mounts the chariot of the city of eight constituents, and from that, the world arises.
It fully raises up the body composed of the eightfold city and consisting of wind; then, like a Vetāla animated by the beating of the heart, it is said to "live."
When the eightfold city has been exhausted and the mind dissolves into the ether, then this body throbs and is also said to be dead.
By the power of its own nature, the living being falls into forgetfulness and reaches a state of helplessness through the force of time, just as a leaf reaches a state of decay.
O Sage, when the lotus-machine is seized and obstructed by the power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti), and when the vital breath (prāṇa) has come to a complete stop, the human being dies.
Just as various leaves, having grown one after another over time, fall from a tree, so too do the bodies of men perish.
The bodies of embodied beings are born and they die, just as the leaves of trees; what cause for lamentation is there in that?
In the ocean of consciousness, these rows of body-bubbles surge forth—some here, some there; the wise man places no reliance upon them.
Although consciousness is all-pervading, it reflects within this mind; for no other thing can take up an object except through a mirror.

In the vast, pure sky of consciousness, efforts in the form of exertion flash forth—though not identical with it—as clamorous and clearly delightful, for the sake of tormenting the delusions of various embodied beings.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O you who bear the crescent moon as your crest-jewel, how has duality come to that infinite, singular Great Soul, the essence of consciousness?
And how, O Mahādeva, does that which is rooted and crowded with synonyms lead to the affliction of suffering, and how is it warded off by wisdom?
Īśvara said: When that Brahman exists as the one Reality, possessing all powers, then this arising of the conceptualization of duality and unity is indeed rootless.

If duality exists, then indeed there would be unity; if unity exists, then there would be a dual form. Since both parts are of the nature of consciousness, that [dual form] is also unreal because it is of the nature of consciousness.
Due to the absence of one, there is an absence here of both oneness and duality; without the one, there is no second, and without the second, there is no oneness.
Because cause and effect possess a single essence, they have a single form; thus, here, the transformation of the seed and so forth is conceived as extending even to the end of the fruit.

The nature of consciousness itself vibrates spontaneously as that which consists of it, through the non-duality of subject and object; even its transformations and so forth do not differ from it, because they are essentially identical to it within.
This conceptualization of modifications and so forth, arising from that [consciousness] with respect to objects, attains meaningfulness through various relations of cause and effect and the like.
The waves that exist in water are equal to those on a mountain; even he for whom a rabbit's horn is real is like a rabbit's horn himself.

The realization of the reality of things is what truly unites here; therefore, enough with verbal conceptualizations. O twice-born one, distinctions and the like are difficult to sever, for they are indeed [merely] derived from words and their referents.
The omnipotence of Brahman does not, in reality, differ from [Brahman] itself; it is like the waves, droplets, and billows [not differing] from the mass of water.
Just as flowers, sprouts, leaves, and so forth belong to the creeper and nothing else, so too do duality, unity, the state of being the world, "thou-ness," and "I-ness" belong to consciousness alone.
Any distinction made in consciousness due to changes in place, time, and so forth, is declared to be unreal; therefore, this question of yours is not appropriate here.
The powers of space, time, action, existence, necessity, and so forth, are indeed of the nature of consciousness; they have descended spontaneously from the very being of consciousness itself.

The reality of consciousness—consisting of the mind and its objects—is known by such designations as "consciousness," "Brahman," and so forth; it is just as a wave of water remains the same water while being fit for the designation "wave" and the like.
To the extent that there is a state of being wavy in the great ocean of the play of consciousness—which is itself without waves—that is precisely what constitutes attachment to objects of thought.
This very supreme Brahman is celebrated by such names as Satya, Īśvara, Śiva, Śūnya, Eka, Paramātman, and so forth.
Thus, that form of the Supreme Self which transcends the category of form, and that stainless "I" which is not an object of speech—[that is the reality].
Whatever is seen here belongs to that great consciousness, which is like a creeper; for it is not distinct from its fruits, shoots, flowers, and so forth, since it is composed of that very essence.
When consciousness, being called "existence," undergoes the acquisition of great ignorance, it perceives externality through its state as a living soul, just as one sees two moons.
Having meditated by its own nature that "I am indeed other," it itself undergoes, as it were, a state of otherness consisting of its own conceptual construction.
That form which, though possessing a stainless nature, appears as if stained upon reaching the river of saṃsāra, is perceived by consciousness alone.

By this very means, the conscious body itself attains oneness with the state of being a living soul; through the manifestation of the principle of consciousness, the living soul lives, being composed of that.
Even the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha), having entered into living beings and become the fivefold contemplation (bhāvanā-pañcaka), fully realizes, "I am the substance."
That substance, once consumed by a living being, quickly attains the state of *vīrya* (potency); from that, I am born endowed with life-force—this is the nature of experience, which knows.

Through the rapid delusion of experiencing the five [elements] in the sequence beginning with egoity (ahaṃtā), one perceives everything—both the stationary and the moving—and thus becomes fully established as each of those very things.

Through a chance occurrence like the "crow and the palm fruit," and by the exhaustion of firm habitual practice, it abandons its subtle form due to its merging with another latent impression (*vāsanā*).
Through its own cognition of duality, duality arises even for a single person, just as a radiant vampire appears due to a man's volitional thought of a vampire.
Through the realization of non-duality, even the duality of the self ceases, just as a person's agency vanishes through the resolve, "I do nothing."
Through the conceptualization of duality, duality arises even for that which is one; through the cognition of non-duality, duality perishes even for that which is manifold.
Indeed, duality does not exist within the Self by virtue of its nature as the Supreme Self, because it is eternally unchanging and so forth, and because it is omnipresent at all times.
For that which is fashioned by one's own volition ceases indeed with the cessation of volition; O Sage, it is like a kingdom of the mind or a city of the Gandharvas.

Likewise, there is suffering in the act of conceptualizing, not in the destruction of that conceptualization; the yakṣa of conceptualization exists in the creation of a city of Gandharvas, but not in its dissolution.
Since this suffering that has arrived came about through the mere formation of a wish, it can be destroyed by the mere absence of such a wish; what cause for distress is there in this?
By forming even the slightest mental construct, a person sinks into suffering; by not forming any mental construct at all, one enjoys imperishable happiness.
When your consciousness is not liberated from the serpent of conceptual construction, you do not shine brightly in the Nandana grove.
Having exhausted the clouds of conceptualization with the winds of your own discernment, attain supreme purity like the expanse of the sky in autumn.
Dry up the intoxicated river of conceptualization with the jewel-mantra; there, having comforted yourself while being carried along, remain free from mental constructs.
Shaken by the wind of volition and wandering like bits of leaves and straw, behold the conscious self by taking refuge in the elemental space.
Having warded off the turbidity of your own mental constructs by yourself, and having attained supreme clarity, become possessed of supreme bliss.
For the Self consists of all powers; in whatever way it intensely contemplates something, it then perceives that very thing as a manifestation of its own volition.
This world has arisen as mere volition and is false; O Brahman, it dissolves somewhere by mere non-volition.
The cluster of the web of births, stirred by the wind of volitional thought, comes to rest in the supreme state through contact with the wind of non-volition.
Dry up this creeping vine of craving, which has grown so strong, by uprooting its foundation: conceptual construction.
The arising of appearances and the exhaustion of appearances—just as a city of the Gandharvas, so too is the delusion of saṃsāra.
The lord of the earth grieves as long as he has forgotten that "I am the Lord," and as long as the realization "I am merely a man of the earth" has not arisen in his heart.
O Brahmin, his innate memory of the past was not dispelled by the present [memory], just as the rainy season is not driven away by the autumn that has arrived.
By means of a continuous flow, that very desire suddenly increases within the mind; just as it is the high-pitched sound of the lute-string itself that strikes the ear.
Cultivate this single contemplation: "I am alone; I am the Self. Endowed with that contemplation, you will surely become that very [Self].

For thus, this which is impossible—this reality that shines forth as non-detachment—is the supreme state, the one supreme God; in acts of worship, he possesses the forms of the worshiper, the act of worshiping, and the object of worship, yet being like something that is neither something nor nothing, he is the single embodiment of the state of consciousness.

Īśvara said: Thus this universe exists, consisting of both the real and the unreal, and having the nature of the gods; it is free from the state of duality and unity, and yet, for that very reason, it is endowed with both duality and unity.
The stain and deformity of the intellect have come to constitute the state of saṃsāra; that which is stainless and beyond saṃsāra is the nature of non-dual identity.
The mind, having incurred the stain of the thought "I am this," becomes bound; by realizing that this very part is non-different from itself, it is liberated.

Because it lacks the form of the objects of consciousness and because it is dualistic, the existent (sattva) abandons its being; it does not maintain the state of "being" as true for even a moment when conjoined with pleasure and the like.
Whether it be pure, partless, real, or unreal—and so forth—it is liberated from all names, words, and meanings, even though it is the self of all, like space.
All this is incomparable, peaceful, and traversed by the three paths; this is Brahman, expanded by Brahman through its power that unfolds like space.

When the mind has been severed within the mind itself—the self consisting of one's own senses and limbs—and when the web of the world, through the light of truth, has been shrouded and gone to dissolution;
The conceptual nature of the mental construction of cyclic existence is severed; the being known by the name "jīva" is like a parched seed.
Known as Paśyantī, she casts off the chewing of mental objects once they have been grasped; freed from the clouds of mental delusion, she is like the expanse of the autumnal sky.

Pure, abiding solely in the state of consciousness, yet having attained the restlessness of the objectified mind, she becomes possessed of all universality and has crossed the ocean of worldly existence.
Having attained the supreme state, she—plump with the expertise of the state of deep sleep from which there is no rebirth—rests, truly rests, in that vast expanse.
This first step has been explained to you when the mind is stilled; now hear, O best of Brahmins, the second step of this most purifying Śakti.
This very power of consciousness, liberated from the mind, is radiant with peace; it is free from all light and darkness, as beautiful as the vast expanse of space.
It is like the trace of deep sleep within a dense cloud, like the internal structure within a stone, like the latent flavor within salt, and like the power of movement within the wind.
When, in due course, it reaches its ultimate transformation right there, it then goes to the supreme space like the power of emptiness within the sky.
Surely it abandons its orientation toward the objective aspect, just as water abandons its turbulence, as a gust of wind abandons its movement, or as a streak of flowers abandons its fragrance.
Having abandoned both temporality and spatiality, she who is both with parts and without parts in all things—neither inert nor non-inert, expansive—bears a nameless existence.

She has attained the state of Great Being (mahāsattā), which is unconditioned by space, time, and the like; she is endowed with the fourth part of the fourth state (turyaturya), stainless, and free from disease.
O large-eyed one, it is that certain [consciousness] which stands like a witness, which is everywhere and at all times, and which is intent upon the sweetness of the light of all things.
This second state of the word has been explained to you, O observer of excellent vows; now listen, O best among those who know the words, as I shall speak the third state.

This vision, by ceasing the movement toward objects of thought, reaches the state of being beyond names and meanings; it arises as the absolute alone, transcending the referents of words such as "Brahman" and "Self."

Through steadfastness over time, she becomes established in her own state, stainless by virtue of the Supreme Self; and because she transcends even the names such as "the Fourth" (turyātīta), she attains the supreme state.
That is the supreme, the ultimate limit, the primary state by virtue of its nature as Śiva; it is the one, indivisible consciousness, the third, purifying state.
O dear one, that [reality], which has long been established in this foundation and which transcends all paths and travelers, does not come within the range of my words.
"O Sage, you have described that which transcends the reckoning of the three paths; remain eternally in that state," so said the eternal Lord.

O Sage, this entire universe consists of that [Self], because it is known as being identical with that; through the realization of Truth, O Lord of Sages, this world neither exists nor does it not exist.
Nothing here proceeds, and nothing here ceases; peaceful and appearing as absolute equality, it manifests like its own sheath.

Due to its non-dual unity, its lack of agitation, its nature as a solid consciousness, and its possession of qualities such as changelessness, it has long been characterized by both permanence and impermanence.
Because they consist of the density of consciousness, there is not even the slightest difference between infants, stones, and the sheaths of worlds, whether they be existent or non-existent.

The entirely auspicious, peaceful, and transcendent state that lies beyond the play of speech is that supreme goal, which consists of the mere essence of the syllable *oṃ* and is the fourth state (*turyā*).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, in a moment, Hara, intent upon the blossoming of Gaurī’s lotus-pond, spontaneously assumed an outward state of expansion.
Arising from the surface of the space of his face, the mass of his vision illuminated [all things], like a mass of rays risen from the sun within a casket of awakening.

Īśvara said: O sage, summoning your faculty of reflection (manana), let your own true being be immediately measured; do not discard the reality of "you" (tvam-artha) for what is worthless, just as the wind does not abandon its own vibration.
Whatever is to be seen here has been seen; what is there that is equal to delusions? For I see nothing here to be abandoned or acquired for one who knows that.

The sword [of wisdom], shattering these conceptual constructions consisting of both the peaceful and the non-peaceful, is itself the hero; having stood otherwise by means of that sword, become you yourself the seer of the Self.
Either quickly resort to this state of perception for the sake of external cognition, or else listen to what I have said; for what is the use of remaining silent?
Having said this, the wielder of the trident [said], "Do not become one whose consciousness is directed outward"; by means of the vital breath (prāṇa), this house of the body vibrates like a machine.
Having abandoned movement, it remains like one who is mute, devoid of vital breath; it is the power that stirs, the power that purifies, the power that perceives, and the consciousness itself.
That [consciousness], though embodied, is clearer than even the ether; its true existence alone is the cause here, just as the vital breath departs from the perishing body due to their separation.

The conscious self is clearer than even the sky and does not perish; what is the use of delusions? It is within the body composed of mind and vital breath that the essence of consciousness fully manifests.
For a reflection arises in a mirror of pure luster; yet even though an object is present before it, it does so without performing the actual function of a reflection.
Just as there is no reflection in a mirror covered with grime, O Leader of Sages, so too there is no [reflection] when the vital breath has departed from the body, even though the body still exists.

Although consciousness is all-pervasive, through the swelling of awareness and its vibration and so forth, it becomes free from the stain of [duality] by virtue of that very awareness; thus, consciousness alone is the supreme Śiva.
Know that he is the God who appears as all those [deities], bestowing the welfare of all beings; he is Hari, he is Śiva, he is the Unborn (Aja), he is Brahmā, and he is the Lord of the Gods.
That Supreme Lord has the wind, fire, moon, and sun as His body; He is this all-pervading Self, remembered as the mine of consciousness and pure awareness.
The Lord of gods, the sustainer of the gods, the Creator, the God of gods, the Sovereign of heaven—none indeed fail to be bewildered by the great radiance of his splendor.
Those who are indeed known in this world as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the rest—these very ones, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the rest, have emerged from the Supreme One.
Like sparks from heated iron, like droplets from the ocean, they arise as if from delusion or as if produced from the supreme state.
While the seeds of delusion—the creators of the web of conceptual construction—remain present, this thick ignorance arises with its hundreds and thousands of branches.
The mass of tangled roots of the multitude of living beings consists of the Vedas, the meaning of the Vedas, the Vedāngas, and so forth; from that infinite [mass], it has spread out again and again.
What sequence could there be in descriptions of those for whom place and time are perfected? Therefore, he is the supreme father of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others.
Mahādeva is the root-seed, like a tree is to its sprouts; he is everything designated as all sentient beings, the one who brings about the perception of all.
It bestows all existence, is radiant, venerable, and worthy of worship by those who know it; its object is a directly perceived reality, and it is ever-arisen everywhere.
Since it has reached the range of all things by virtue of its nature as pure awareness, no invocation, mantra, or the like is of any use for it whatsoever.
Constantly invoked, abiding in all things, and attainable everywhere by one's own consciousness—whatever state of objects it enters, from that very state, O Sage, comes auspiciousness.

He attains His own essential nature, which is the primordial Lord of the gods—the one who is to be worshipped, saluted, praised, and honored with offerings, and who is the very form of the perception of forms by the mind.

Know this to be the ultimate limit of all that is to be known, even among the great; having beheld this Self, which removes old age, grief, and fear, a living being does not sprout again, like a roasted seed.

That which bestows fearlessness upon all living beings, known as the primordial and effortless object of worship—you are that unborn, supreme state residing within the self; why then are you deluded by [external] perceptions?

Īśvara said: Thereupon, they know the Lord Rudreśvara to be the one whose nature is consciousness alone, who abides within the existence of all beings, who consists of self-experience, and who is pure.
Know that the stainless element of consciousness is the seed of all seeds, the essence of the wandering in saṃsāra, and the supreme action among all actions.
It is the cause of the floods of causes, yet itself causeless and untroubled; it is the cultivation of the floods of cultivations, yet itself uncultivable and devoid of the nature of becoming.

He is consciousness among the floods of consciousness, consciousness within the self of consciousness; he is his own object of thought and the unconscious, the supreme object of thought, and the manifold creative contemplation.
The wise know that stainless light—which is beyond the reach of sight and yet born of light, the flood of seeds of all seeds—to be the pure mass of consciousness.

Know that which is unreal yet composed of reality, peaceful, and devoid of both truth and untruth; from the existence of the Great Being down to the existence of all beings, know it to be pure consciousness alone and nothing else.
One becomes passionate oneself, becoming the impassioned subject and the passion that impassions; even though it is itself like space, one quickly becomes a decorated wall.
Within this vast consciousness, millions of world-illusory mirages have flashed forth, will flash forth, and are flashing forth.
In this self-luminous state, there exists nothing other than that which is perfected as its own mere existence, just as in fire there is nothing else besides its inherent heat.
They know that which contains Mount Meru within it to be equal to an atom; they know that which covers Mount Meru to be equal to an atom.
This blink of an eye is said to contain within it a great kalpa; yet, even while occupied by this kalpa, its nature as a blink of an eye is not abandoned.
By this [knowledge], which is subtler than the tip of a hair, the entire earth—even this earth clothed by the seven oceans—is pervaded; yet it does not reach its end.
Without even acting, he has attained the state of being an agent of the construction of saṃsāra; yet while performing great deeds, he does not do anything at all.
Though possessing substance, he is without substance; though without substance, he indeed possesses substance. Though bodiless, he has a great body; though having a great body, he is bodiless.
Even now this [world] is always "morning," yet it has reached the state of being "today"; it is neither "today" nor "morning," yet it is both "today" and "morning" at all times.
Bhiṇḍiṃ bhiṇḍiṃ; intoxicated in the grove, with a mass of human hair; always shining amidst the flickering light; the play, the gulugulu sound, the stone.
Such meaningless statements as these are likewise true; for there is nothing that is not true, and there is nothing that is not he.
Salutation to that Self of All, in whom is everything, from whom is everything, who is everything, who is everywhere, and who eternally consists of everything.

There, by the dense thicket of the intermediate space, which was like a pair of dark, playful, and trembling clouds produced by Vilāsavatī, the creeper of Fortune—adorned with garlands of pure sprouts and petals—was as if seized in a clenched fist.
Īśvara said: O you whose form is truth, the wealth of meaning for words such as these resides in that Lord of All, who is the casket for the jewels of all existence.
What indeed are those stainless luminosities that do not shine within that supreme jewel of consciousness, they which discern the manifold worlds?
This consciousness-existence (citsattā), residing within the seed and the grain, having obtained its own body consisting of earth, time, water, and so forth, produces the sprout and the plant.
Existing within the revolutions and transformations of the foam-whirls, she who is of the nature of essence produces the movement of the waters when in contact with the solid sense-faculties.
This [nectar] exists within the clusters of flowers in the form of sap; it shines forth through the nostrils and brings about full blossoming.

The Lord of Mountains, by the play of his stability, supports the state that is the foundation of creation—the unreal yet appearing as real, situated upon his rocky limbs, resembling his rocky limbs, and the very abode of truth.
Like the sense of touch, whose nature is the sheath of the vibration of the wind, he brings about his own son through this [body] as if out of a paternal affection.
Having meditated upon the self as the condensed essence of all things without exception for its own realization, it thoroughly renders that self into the state of space, as if it were nothingness.
Within the hollow of the mirror of space, which reflects the image of its own existence, it bears a stainless body called Time, marked by the twinkling of conceptual thought.
These [worlds] consist of transformation up to the fifth great lord; "this is thus" and "this is not so"—necessity itself becomes such.
In that Witness, which is a vast manifestation, the successions of the world’s variegated forms shine forth like actions within a house illuminated by a lamp.
In the grounds of the theater-pavilion of the city of supreme space, she stands like a witness, observing the cycle of worldly existence as the unfolding of her own power.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Lord of the World, what are the powers (śaktis) of this Śiva, and how do they abide? What is his witnesshood (sākṣitā), what is their activity, and how far does it extend?
Īśvara said: Of the immeasurable, peaceful, auspicious Supreme Self—gentle one, whose nature is pure consciousness alone, who is all-pervading, and who is formless.

O observer of noble vows, there is the existence of desire, the existence of space, and likewise the existence of time; similarly, there is the existence of necessity and the existence of the Great One.
The power of knowledge, the power of action, agency, and even non-agency—there is no end to such powers belonging to the one whose self is Śiva.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O Lord, from where do these powers arise? How is there multiplicity within them? How does their emergence occur, and what is the nature of their difference and non-difference?"
Īśvara said: This very power is said to belong to Śiva, who possesses infinite forms and whose nature is pure consciousness; therefore, it is not different from him even in the slightest degree.
Through the manifestation of knowerhood, agency, enjoyership, witnesshood, and so forth, the powers assume various forms, like water in many vessels.
Thus they dance in the world, within the cosmic theater of the universe, having been gradually trained by Time as if by a dancer.
This very manifestation as another is called necessity (niyati); it is given such names as action, agency, will, or time, and so forth.

Because this world, from the great Rudra down to a blade of grass and up to the movement of Brahmā, exists in such a fixed manner, that which constitutes this restriction is known as Niyati (the principle of necessity).
Fate is eternally devoid of agitation and remains unstained; it indeed performs this dance, the drama of the web of the world.

Rich with the playful display of various sentiments, accompanied by the dramatic gestures of transformation, it resounded with the roar of many Puṣkarāvarta clouds struck down in a single moment by the fire at the end of the aeon.
It was strewn with flowers of every season, a temple of rain-showers, where a great mass of perspiration-like water fell again and again.
It created the illusion of a dark blue garment fluttering like the leaves of clouds, and it was filled with the mass of jewels from the seven pure oceans forming its girdle.
The sky was illuminated by the side-glances of the watches, fortnights, and days, while the crests of the mountain ranges were busily engaged in repeatedly sinking and emerging.
It possessed three pearls of the Gaṅgā strung upon moonstones shimmering with its radiance, and its sprout-like hands were agitated by the clouds of twilight, whether visible or invisible.
[He is] the delicate ornament of the world, which is ever-restlessly surging; he whose footsteps traverse the vast surface of the earth, the netherworld, and the expanse of the sky.
It possessed a multitude of great, rising and falling drops of sweat like stars; its face was the sky, made manifest by the smile of the movement of its moon and sun earrings.

It has for its canopy the door-panels of the many imagined Brahmāṇḍas; it possesses pearl-like sprouts that resound as the clusters of world-systems roll about; and it contains within it the various flavors of the presence and absence of the conditions of pleasure and pain.

In this essence of the long drama called saṃsāra, which is a play of necessity (niyati) veiled by these transformations, this one Supreme Lord remains as the eternally manifest witness; he is neither separate from that [necessity] nor separate from it.
The Lord said: This is the God, the supreme one, who is always to be worshipped by the virtuous; he is pure consciousness, whose nature is experience, all-pervading, and the refuge of all.
Abiding in the pot, the cloth, the banyan tree, the wall, the cart, and the monkey, he is Śiva, Hara, Hari, Brahmā, Śakra, Vaiśravaṇa, and Yama.
The Blessed One, who is the self of all and exists both outside and within, is always worshipped by those of excellent intellect through various successive rites.
O Great Sage, first listen to how [the deity] is worshipped externally in sequence, O Knower of Reality; thereafter, you shall hear the internal procedure.

In all sequences of worship, the body-house is the object to be purified; however, one must strive with great effort to purify that which is the supreme self, consisting of the realization of the body.
Meditation itself is the internal worship; there is no other worship for it. Therefore, one should constantly worship the support of the three worlds through meditation.

One should take refuge in one's own essence of "I-ness," which is the nature of consciousness, radiant like a million suns, the illuminator of all appearances, and the internal light of consciousness.
His neck possesses the vast expanse of the infinite, supreme sky; his lotus-like feet are the treasury of the endless space below.
Adorned by a circle of arms that span the vast expanse of the infinite quarters of space, he wields various supreme weapons grasped from the great worlds.
Within the corner of the cavity of the heart rests a continuous succession of multitudes of universes; its form is boundless, having reached the further shore of the supreme space of light.
Below, above, in the four cardinal directions, and in the intermediate directions, it was filled without interval by a circle of immortals headed by Brahmā, Indra, Hari, Rudra, and Īśa.
One should contemplate this line of hair on his body as the true glory, the ropes of the machine of the three worlds that initiate various undertakings.
His powers, beginning with Will (icchā) and residing within his body, should be meditated upon; he is that supreme God, who is always to be worshipped by the virtuous.
Pure consciousness, whose nature is experience, is all-pervading and the refuge of all; it resides in a pot, a cloth, a banyan tree, a wall, a cart, or even in a monkey.
Śiva, Hara, Hari, Brahmā, Śakra, Vaiśravaṇa, and Yama—he whose sole body is pure existence, supported by the one-footed Ananta.
Time, which revolves the web of the world, is its gatekeeper; this entire sphere of the cosmic egg contains the expanse of the worlds along with their mountains.
One should contemplate Mahādeva, who possesses a thousand ears and eyes, as having become a certain corner of the body and a part of one's own limb.
He has a thousand heads and is peaceful, adorned with a thousand arms; he is enriched with the power of vision everywhere and possesses the power of smell in every direction.
It consists of touch everywhere, is endowed with the sense of taste on all sides, is filled with hearing everywhere, and is accompanied by the faculty of thought in every place.
It transcends all conceptualization, it is the supreme auspiciousness in every respect; it is the eternal creator of all and the bestower of all conceived objects.
Having reflected thus—that the Lord of Gods dwells within all beings, is everything, and is the sole means for accomplishing all—thereafter one should worship Him according to the prescribed rite.
O best among the knowers of Brahman, hear this procedure for worship: this deity, whose nature is one's own self-consciousness, is not worshipped with material offerings.
Not by means of lamps, nor incense, nor the offering of an abundance of flowers; not by the giving of food and other gifts, nor by the anointing with sandalwood paste.
Nor by the enjoyment of saffron, camphor, or various other [luxuries], but rather by that which is eternally obtainable without affliction, cool, and imperishable.
He is worshipped by means of that very single nectar, which is his own awakening; this alone is the supreme meditation, and this alone is remembered as the supreme worship.
One who perceives that uninterrupted internal awareness of pure consciousness alone—while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, moving, sleeping, and breathing;
While speaking, releasing, and grasping, one should remain composed of pure consciousness; having worshipped oneself as the Lord with the nectar of meditation.
With flowers offered by one who is liberated and endowed with supreme relish, his very self is the offering of meditation, for meditation is indeed what he desires.

Meditation is the water for the guest-offering and the water for the feet, consisting of pure self-awareness; the flower is the awareness of meditation; those who know all this are devoted to meditation.
Without that other [virtue], this self cannot be attained at all; through meditation, one attains clarity regarding all enjoyments, pleasures, and splendors.
O Sage, this self, in the form of the body, experiences [objects] within the house of the body; O wise one, by means of this meditation, it does so for thirteen moments (nimeṣas).
Even a fool, by worshipping the Lord for a single hundred moments, shall obtain the fruit of giving a cow. By worshipping the Master for even one hundred nimeṣas, he gains this reward.
A person obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) by worshipping his own self as the Lord for even half a ghaṭikā.
A person obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices by offering the oblation of meditation upon the self by means of the self.
He who worships for even one *ghaṭikā* shall obtain the merit of a *rājasūya* sacrifice; by worshipping at midday in this manner, one becomes the possessor of a hundred thousand *rājasūyas*.

Having thus worshipped during the day, a person shall dwell in the supreme abode. This is that supreme yoga; this is that supreme ritual. This is declared to be the external worship, which is most excellent for the self.

Any man who, without weariness, practices even for a moment this purifying teaching—the cause of the destruction of all sins—the multitudes of the worlds of gods and asuras shall honor him, for he has attained his station in this world like me, liberated in the Self.
Īśvara said: That which is the purifier of purifiers and the destruction of all darkness—that internal worship of the Self, I shall now proclaim.
Whether walking or standing, waking or even sleeping—this worship, which consists of constant meditation, pervades all modes of conduct.
One should constantly meditate upon this supreme Śiva, who resides within the body, the agent of all perceptions, as one's very self by means of the self.
Whether lying down or rising, walking or standing, touching that which is to be touched or abandoning it on all sides;
He who enjoys and renounces enjoyments that are abundant even without effort, who cuts away external objects, and who bestows the true nature of all undertakings.

In the case of deha-liṅgas (liṅgas consisting of the body), which are established in a state of peace and have abandoned other external liṅgas and so forth, one should worship the bodha-liṅga (the liṅga of consciousness) through the realization of whatever objects are encountered.
Abiding in the reality that has entered the current of the flow, purified by the bath of one's own awakening, one should worship the Linga of consciousness through the constant offering of awareness.

He is radiant, having filled the sky through the expansive cultivation of the nature of the sun; he has arisen as the moon, having attained the state of the moon through the expansive cultivation of the nature of the moon.
[He is] the consciousness that eternally perceives the flood of appearing objects, flowing through the bodily gateways in the form of the vital breath at the mouth.
Having made the vital essence (rasa) its charioteer, with the breaths as its noble steeds, it is mounted upon the chariot of prāṇa and apāna, hidden within the cave of the heart.
The knower of all objects of knowledge, the doer of all actions, the enjoyer of all things to be enjoyed, and the rememberer of all cognitions.

One should meditate upon Śiva, who is the flood of limbs fully and correctly cognized, cultivated through the cultivation of both existence and non-existence, vast, radiant with light, and all-pervading.
It is both partless and possessed of parts, residing within the body yet moving through space; it is unstained and yet stained, eternally the consciousness of the limbs and the whole.
Abiding in the power of mental reflection, arisen between the prāṇa and apāna, situated in the heart, throat, and palate, it rests upon the seats of the brows and the nostrils.
[He is] situated within thirty-six crores of steps, transcending the state of Unmanī; he causes the internal sounds and so forth to arise, impelling the bird-like mind.
It abides in two kinds of verbal paths: the conceptual and the non-conceptual; it dwells within all limbs like oil within sesame seeds.
Free from the stain of the arts yet firm with the multitude of arts, it is situated in one part within the lotus of the friend and throughout the entire body.
Pure consciousness alone, appearing as stainless, is the conceptualization of parts and their arrangements; it is directly perceptible everywhere, consisting essentially of one's own experience.
The individual conscious self, abiding again as a seeker of its own objects, quickly approaches all things and, in an instant, becomes as if it has attained duality.
One should contemplate: "This deity, appearing as the manifestation of the consciousness of one's own body, possesses hands, feet, and limbs, along with hair, nails, and teeth."
Many diverse powers, whose modes of conduct vary according to the state of the mind, incessantly attend upon me, as wives do for an excellent husband.
This mind of mine is the gatekeeper who announces the three worlds; this thought of mine is the female usher, pure in form, standing at the door.
My own nature is power, my intellect is action, and the various forms of knowledge are the ornaments adorning my limbs, O beautiful woman.
The organs of action, together with the groups of sense organs, are merely gateways; I am that infinite Self, whose form is devoid of all limitation.
"I abide as the single, filled self, full and filling all things"—thus one should rely upon that divine, pure, and wondrous nature of the Self.
Fulfilled in his divinity, he remains inwardly with a non-depressed soul; he neither sets nor rises, and he neither rejoices nor is angry.
He experiences neither satiety nor hunger; he desires nothing and abandons nothing. He is equanimous, with equal conduct, equal appearance, and equal form.
Having attained pure gentleness and possessing a beautiful disposition on all sides, he alone remained throughout his life with an uninterrupted great intelligence.
He indeed performs the worship of the deity day and night for a very long time; his body, though not moved from the essence of consciousness (cittattva), is declared to be the deity.
With every object as it is obtained, he honors Him with equanimity and with his entire intellect—the supreme consciousness of the Divine, which is pure awareness alone.
One should worship with all things arising in the sequence as they are obtained; no effort whatsoever should be made here regarding anything that is not already present.
One should worship the auspicious Lord constantly by means of having attained his body, through this very purposeful activity, and by the enjoyment of desires.
One should worship Śiva with various kinds of food and drink, possessing manifold opulence, as well as with beds, seats, and vehicles, according to what has been obtained.
With every form of happiness—delighting in the abundance of beloved food, drink, enjoyments, and so forth—one should worship the Self through perfect awakening.
One who is overcome by mental and physical ailments, possessed by delusion and agitation, and afflicted by every kind of calamity and suffering, should worship the Self.
One should worship the Self through all the various activities of the world—through death, life, dreaming, and so forth—which have been attained for the sake of the world's maintenance.
Whether in poverty or in sovereignty, with a self surrendered to the current of worldly flow, one should worship the pure Self with the flowers of various activities.
One should worship the serene Self with the playful display of passion and aversion, which is graced by the splendor of women amidst the surging waves of various quarrels.
One should worship the Self residing within the heart with a loving-kindness that reaches the hearts of the virtuous, which is firmly rooted, cool as the moon, and characterized by sweetness.
One should worship oneself with equanimity, compassion, and constant joy within the heart, by means of the pure path of power and through awakening.

One should worship oneself with whatever has been obtained—whether it arrived unexpectedly, whether it remains unstable, whether it is the sole enjoyment of wealth or non-wealth, and whether it was acquired by chance.
One should worship one's own pure self by either renouncing all enjoyments—both those that are prohibited and those that are not—or by practicing non-attachment toward them at all times.

One should worship the Lord of all objects by means of the multitude of desired and undesired things—whether appropriate or inappropriate—which are characterized by the self, and by wealth that has been both relinquished and acquired.
One should remain indifferent toward what is lost and gather what is gained; for this state of changelessness is indeed the supreme worship of the Self.
Always maintaining supreme equanimity toward all perceptions, whether they be desirable or undesirable, one should observe the vow of constant worship of the Self.

One should perceive everything as exceedingly auspicious; one should know that all is both auspicious and inauspicious. One should make everything consist of the Self and should constantly observe the vow of worshiping the Self.

Having understood that everything which is pleasant at first sight and everything which is extremely difficult to endure at first sight are all exactly the same, one should practice the vow of worshiping the eternal Self.
One should completely abandon the distinction of "this is I" and "this is not I"; having resolved that "all is Brahman," one should practice the vow of constant self-worship.
At all times, in every form, and through every mode of transformation, one should worship the Self by means of everything, in every possible way.
Having repeatedly renounced both the undesired and likewise the desired, one should always worship the Self by relying upon both.
Neither desiring nor rejecting, one should enjoy the objects of enjoyment as they arrive by fate through the very nature of things, just as rivers are received by the ocean.
One should not experience agitation amidst views, whether trivial or profound, for they are like the various objects appearing in the vast expanse of the sky.
Whatever auspicious or inauspicious result arises from the conjunction of place, time, and action—one should worship the Self with that very thing as it is received, without modification.
Whatever materials and riches have been prescribed in this ritual for the worship of the Self, all these should be thoroughly infused with a single equal amount of mercury.
They were neither sour nor pungent, nor bitter nor astringent; though smeared with various flavors, they were said to be truly sweet.
Equanimity is sweet and delectable; the power of its flavor transcends the senses. Whatever object of thought is permeated by it becomes nectar in that very instant.
Whatever indeed is contemplated in the form of the nectar of equanimity, that attains a sweetness like that which has flowed from the supreme moon.
When the mind has become like the sky of equanimity—dissolved, unchanging, and effortless—that alone is called true worship.
One should become full like the full moon, possessing an equal and uniform luster; transparent, consisting solely of the mass of consciousness, and though a knower, appearing in the form of a stone.
Clear as the intermediate space, performing external natural functions, free from the mist of passion, the knower is a perfect worshipper.
When the clouds of ignorance have dissipated, the knower shines like the autumnal sky—free from the mental impressions seen even in dreams and with the mist of egoism and its like stilled.

Beholding the mind as the setting sun and moon, where subject and object have vanished; seeing the expansion of consciousness like the sensation of a newborn infant; and perceiving the seed of the conscious mind as utterly tranquil—you remain established in the unsurpassed state even while living.

Constantly worship the Lord of the Body with all the delusions of pleasure and pain arising from objects, time, place, and causal conditions; remain with a mind in which all cravings have been stilled.
The Lord said: Whatever you do, whether at the proper time or according to your undertaking, that very act is the worship of the Self within the Śiva who is pure consciousness.
By that very means, the Lord himself experiences delight and likewise attains manifestation through his own inherent form, abiding as he is.
In the stainless Self, the objects denoted by words such as "attachment" and "aversion" arise as distinct forms, like sparks from a fire.

Whatever perception there may be—whether of royalty, wretchedness, pleasure, pain, and so forth—whether belonging to oneself or to another, each and every one of those is an act of worship toward the Self.
The universal consciousness itself is the worship, as is the eternal Self; likewise, Brahman is itself the Self by virtue of being the essence of pots and other objects.
Auspicious, peaceful, without appearance, one, and luminous—having attained this state, all this world, appearing as it does through cognition, stands as the very form of the Self.

Oh, how wondrous! It is the Self alone that appears established as something else, such as a jar; it is the very nature of the individual soul (jīva) and so forth within, as if surely possessed of forgetfulness.
Since Śiva is the self of all, infinite, and indeed the innermost Self, how could the delusion known as the worshipper, the worshipped, and the act of worship ever arise?
O Brahmin, a fixed form does not exist in the tranquil Īśvara, wherein the sequence consisting of the worshiper and the worshiped is conceptualized.
The deity who is delimited by worship, the object of worship, and so forth, is not the vessel of the lordship of the eternal, stainless Self, who is omnipotent and infinite.
O Brahman, it is indeed not appropriate to apply a designation of form to the Lord, whose nature is pure consciousness pervading the three worlds.
Those for whom the Supreme Lord is limited by space and time are to be instructed by us; they are not wise among the wise.
Having abandoned that view and likewise having taken recourse to this one, he becomes equanimous, pure-minded, peaceful, free from passion, and free from affliction.
Worship yourself with offerings of sensual pleasures as they arise from all sides, remaining undaunted in mind amidst happiness and suffering, and the auspicious and inauspicious.

And since you, the virtuous one, have attained that single, appropriate state wherein life itself is stirred [toward liberation], not even the slightest suffering of birth or the like can cling to you; it is like a stain failing to adhere to a spotless lap of crystal in a newly built house, which is entirely void within and transparent in every part.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Lord, what is called Śiva? What is called the Supreme Brahman? O Protector, what is called the Ātman? And what is called the Paramātman?
O Blessed One, Lord of the Three Worlds, why are such distinctions as "that," "existent," "something," "nothing," "emptiness," and "consciousness" spoken of?
Īśvara said: There exists here a certain Reality that is without beginning or end and devoid of appearance; because it is inaccessible to the senses, it remains as if it were nothing at all.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Lord, since the senses have attained invisibility even though they are joined with the intellect and other faculties, how can that [state] be approached without hesitation?

Īśvara said: He who desires liberation, being a portion of ignorance yet purely sattvic, [is characterized] by those very portions of ignorance known by such names as "scripture" (śāstra) and so forth.
Washing away ignorance with the supreme [knowledge], he remains here as the most excellent one, just as a skilled washerman removes dirt with dirt through skillful means.
When the destruction of ignorance occurs later, like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, the self perceives the self by means of itself; this is the certainty of its own nature.
Just as a child, by somehow rubbing [a mirror] against charcoal and washing it, attains the purity of its surface when the blackness of the charcoal is removed; so too does one attain purity.
One should investigate each part through various means such as the scriptures; thus, there is the *sāttvika* portion, the *tāmasa* portion, and likewise the arising of the Self within both.
The Self alone perceives itself and investigates by means of itself; that "only the Self exists here, not ignorance" is what the wise know as the destruction of ignorance.
Whatever various objects exist here, let them be understood as not being the Self; furthermore, the sequence beginning with the teacher's instruction is not the cause of the knowledge of the Self.
