The guru is the self whose nature is the functioning of the senses; Brahman is attained through the cessation of all the senses. Whatever object is to be reached upon the cessation of something else cannot be attained while that thing still exists.

O twice-born one, even those things which are not causes have become powerful causes for the attainment of self-knowledge, such as the instructions of the guru and so forth, through a gradual process.
When the succession of the guru’s instructions proceeds through the awakening of the disciple, the Self—though inexpressible and invisible—becomes gracious of its own accord.

The Self is not understood through the meanings of the scriptures, nor is it understood from the words of a teacher; rather, it is understood by oneself alone through the power of one's own awakening.

Without the meaning of the scriptures and the instructions of the guru, the Self is not realized; it is only through the existence of this conjunction that the knowledge of one's own Self is illuminated.

Through the long-standing association and presence of the teacher, the meaning of the scriptures, and the disciples, self-knowledge proceeds just as the conduct of people proceeds through the passage of days.

When there is the complete cessation of karma, the faculties of cognition and action, and the extremes of pleasure, pain, and so forth, the Self is called "Śiva" by such names as "Tat," "Sat," and others.
That in which this entire world does not exist, yet exists precisely in that form—it is indeed like existence itself, infinite and clearer than space.
In this [state], seekers of liberation who possess only slight knowledge remain without rest, their souls marred by the stains of various impure mental conceptions.

Standing not far away, within the range of vision of one liberated while living, they exist for the sake of awakening those who aspire to liberation and for the composition of the meaning of the scriptures.
By the world-protectors headed by Brahmā, Indra, and Rudra, who were highly learned and whose selves were purified for the sake of establishing the doctrines of the Purāṇas and the Vedas.
"Cit," "Brahman," "Śiva," "Ātman," "Īśa," "Paramātman," "Īśvara," and so forth—these are conceptual designations imputed upon this Lord who is beyond all designations and distinct [from them].
Thus is this reality of the world, one's own reality named Śiva; in every way, at all times, as the totality of all things—O, enjoy that bliss!
Terms such as "Śiva," "Ātman," and "Supreme Brahman" were fashioned by the ancients to denote distinctness; yet in reality, there is no difference in him.
O leader of sages, the wise one who thus performs the daily worship of the deity goes to that supreme state where we and others like us serve as attendants.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O Blessed One, you should explain to me in brief how this [world], though non-existent, appears as if it were existent."
Īśvara said: Know that which is the referent of words such as "Brahmā" and so forth to be pure consciousness alone; even the clear ether is gross compared to it, like Mount Meru is to an atom.
Moving here toward the state of the knowable, she attains fitness for consciousness; yet, being truly devoid of the knowable, she stands at the ultimate stage of Unmanā.
Because its object of experience is realized in an instant, it follows after the sense of "I," just as a man, by virtue of being human, assumes the state of a forest elephant in a dream.
Having attained the state of space and time within this form consisting of "I-ness" and so forth, those [mental constructs] consequently become friends whose very nature is emptiness.
That very existence, when conjoined with those [attributes], becomes designated as the "living soul" (jīva), characterized by vibration and consciousness, like a streak of wind.
The power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti), being of such a nature and delighting solely in certainty, follows the state of the intellect; thus it remains situated in the plane of ignorance.
It is followed by the power of sound, the power of action, and the power of knowledge; each of these vibrates within, manifesting its own form.
When this group [of elements] has quickly united and brought about mindfulness, it becomes the mind—the elemental self that is the seed of the tree of volition.
The wise know that to be the vehicle of the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha), which, through the power of Brahman residing within, perceives the Self by means of its own nature as the form of the Knower.
For these powers exist only within the mind as they are being accomplished; later, even though they have not yet arisen externally, they manifest here as external entities.
The existence of wind, the existence of vibration, the existence of touch, as well as the existence of the skin and the existence of light—thus is the illuminating nature of existence.
The existence of form, the existence of water, and likewise the existence of taste; likewise the existence of flavor, and likewise the existence of fragrance.

She is the essence of the earth, the essence of gold, and the essence of the gathered mass; she is the plump one, the essence of space, the essence of time, and is devoid of all forms of worldly opulence.

Having embraced this entire multitude of beings as its own nature, it vibrates while depending upon the petals and other parts, having attained the state of being the seed from which the seed-syllable arises.

Know this to be the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka), and this body is the subtle, transportable one (ativāhika). This, my dear, is boundless consciousness itself, which manifests as if possessing divisions.
Thus, it is endowed with the primary factors, yet it is not endowed with anything at all; it is neither knowledge, nor is it form, nor is it consciousness, nor is it cognition.
The Supreme alone shines forth in the Supreme; it is the absolute reality, the very self of the Absolute, like the play of liquid water within the belly of a mass of water.
This world, which is essentially one with consciousness and its perception, becomes something insentient and separate when fully understood; it is like a city of one's own imagination.
Through sensation and thorough knowledge, one attains the state of Śiva; but how can that which remains unknown attain the status of a reality?
Then, through its own internal volition, this atom spontaneously attains the state of being a part; it perceives within the body this existence consisting of those subtle elements alone.
He quickly perceives that very [subtle essence] as having attained a state of grossness; he perceives its apertures of the subtle elements according to their respective locations.

Then, by virtue of the singular contemplation of the form of the Puruṣa, having seen [the deity] in human form—just like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit—one becomes exceedingly satisfied and nourished.
One perceives this body remaining in such a state as if it were alive, though it is utterly non-existent, like a city of Gandharvas or a person in a dream.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The world has the appearance of a city of Gandharvas and is like a man in a dream; since it exists for the sake of suffering, what logic is there here for its destruction?
The Lord said: Suffering arises through the power of latent impressions (vāsanā), and those impressions exist even though the world is non-existent, like the shimmering water of a mirage.
Therefore, what is being perfumed, by what, whose perfuming is it, or from where? How, my dear, can the water of a mirage be drunk by a man in a dream?
But when there is a true seer, along with the ego, mind, and mental faculties, that which exists in the world is perceived as such.

Where there is neither latent impression (*vāsanā*), nor an impressioner, nor the state of being impressed—there is only the state of absolute oneness (*kevalībhāva*), in which the delusion of mental construction has been completely stilled.
For one for whom even the Yakṣa—whether real or unreal—is indeed empty and dissolved through absolute liberation (kaivalya), what else remains?
For this mental impression called "the world" has arisen in this way as something entirely empty, like a ghost; when it is stilled, peace remains unimpaired.
He who places his trust in egoism, in the world, and in the water of a mirage—that man of delusion should not be instructed in this teaching.

Those who know reality teach that the soul here is discerning, whereas they declare the ignorant to be deluded, unreal, and devoid of nobility. Indeed, he who instructs the ignorant is like one who gives his daughter to a man seen in a dream, whose complexion is as bright as gold.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, O Blessed One, that living being, situated in the sky during the first creation, beheld the turmoil of the body; for what state indeed does it attain?
Īśvara said: In the supreme void beyond the supreme, the individual soul perceives a body produced according to the previously mentioned sequence, just like a man in a dream.
Because the mass of consciousness is all-pervading, even as a man in a dream performs an action instantly, so too does the living being (jīva) who currently sustains a body.
Then, he quickly bestows upon himself the designation "I am the eternal, unmanifest Person"; by that, he becomes celebrated as the First Person.
Thus, in one creation he was the first Sadāśiva, while in another he was called Viṣṇu; the Grandfather (Brahmā) was not born from his navel.
That Grandfather [Brahmā] was in one place, and the other was in another; he was that personification of volition who had assumed a physical form through his own will.
When the first resolve has been nourished, it takes on the form of the mind; whatever one imagines, that very thing one experiences immediately and fully.
The entire world, though its true nature is emptiness like a ghost conjured by magic, appears as a real entity through the vision of delusion; thus arises the worldly course of egoism.
Indeed, that person who thus becomes himself the seer and so forth, rises up into the void at every moment and is then led away.
In a mere blink of an eye, one fully experiences a succession of great eons through the simple reversal of appearances.
In every atom, in every void, and in every moment, there arise for you the existence and non-existence of creations, kalpas, and great kalpas.
Some are seen by one another due to the similarity of their latent impressions (*vāsanā*); others are not seen by each other because of their perceived nature as distinct selves.
Creations arise everywhere through the process of creation, yet they do not exist within you, O Auspicious One; for in the supreme ether, they are themselves of the nature of ether.
And being themselves of the nature of both existence and non-existence, they dissolve like mountains in a dream; by these creations, neither space, nor time, nor agency is ever occupied.
These are neither identical to its own nature, nor is it to be conceptualized, nor is it momentary; nothing whatsoever is born here, and nothing whatsoever perishes.
Everything manifests as a wondrous play of consciousness within consciousness through the form of volition; the world is like the creation and the falling and rising of a city in a dream.
And it does not undergo even the slightest succession of space and time, just as the infinite [expanse] of space, time, and so forth [is traversed] by a mountain created by mere volition.
Though it was traversed by the world of beings, it remained as if untraversed; yet, though not traversed, it was as if traversed by the Mount Meru of one's own conceptual constructions.
Just as the place, time, and other conditions are high, so too does the world exist; for that which is this Puruṣa is the agent of all.
By this very sequence, the hips are produced here in an instant; indeed, the four classes of beings that remain stationary are likewise produced here in this manner.
From Rudra down to a blade of grass, beings come into existence at every moment; some are like atoms, while others are even subtler than atoms.
This is indeed the sequence for them, whether creation exists or not, because of the cultivation of such objects within this illusion of saṃsāra.
Through the cessation of differentiation resulting from practice, one attains Śiva; the supreme consciousness lasts for no more than half of a hundredth part of a moment.
If it were to move by its own nature, that very instability would arise; yet it remains established in its own conscious self, like the space within a stone, having the nature of the Knower.
That which is of the nature of beginningless manifestation is denoted by the word "Brahman"; yet when this creation has reached maturity, there is no further illumination of the Great Consciousness.

The state of atoms, characterized by the conjunction of direction, space, time, and constituent parts, comes to exist as living beings through the successive evolution of the elements and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
O dear one, the deer, plants, insects, gods, asuras, and so forth, exist within that which is eternal, pervasive, infinite, and firm, like a garland upon it.

The universe, woven from both being and non-being, resides within the all-pervading Viśvakarman; it is neither far nor near, neither above nor below, nor is it distinct from him. It was not in the past, nor is it today, nor in the morning; it is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor is it anything intermediate.

When the nectar of the time of experience has been realized, the mother [of cognition] no longer exists amidst all conceptual constructions; the garland of means of knowledge, though possessing the vast power of its fruit, finds no footing, just as fire does not exist in water.
O Sage, you have answered as asked; may prosperity be yours. We shall now depart for our desired direction; arise, O Pārvatī!
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus, while I remained with my handful of flowers still held, that Nīlakaṇṭha, together with his retinue, ascended into the expanse of the sky.

When that Lord of Umā, the sovereign of the three worlds, had departed, I remained for a moment; then, following that very recollection, with a mind newly purified by faith, I accepted the worship of my own deity, while he, possessed of tranquility, renounced it.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This supreme truth was spoken by him, and I myself know it; O Rāma, you too understand how this world is truly situated.
In this illusory cycle of existence, where the unreal is perceived by means of the unreal within that which is itself unreal, what is real and what is unreal?
Just as and by whatever conceptualization something is described, so too is it experienced even when not present, through that very same mental construction of its nature.
Just as liquidity exists in water, as movement exists in the wind, and as emptiness exists in space, so does the nature of creation exist within the Self.
From that time onwards, I have remained here until today, performing the worship of myself in that very same sequence with an undistracted mind.
"O Rāma, by means of this ritual of worship, these days are passed by me without weariness, even though I am occupied with worldly affairs."
The worship of oneself with the flowers of ritual conduct as they are attained—though it may seem interrupted—is never truly interrupted, day or night.
In the relationship between the grasped and the grasper, which is common to all embodied beings, that state of attentiveness which the yogi maintains is the worship of the Self.
O Lord of the Raghus, with this vision and a mind liberated from attachment, roam in this sparse forest of saṃsāra; you shall not suffer.
When great suffering has arisen, born from the loss of wealth and kin, hold fast to this view and engage in reflection, O observer of noble vows.
One should not take pleasure in the arising of wealth or kinsmen, nor feel grief at their loss; for all such perceptions within cyclic existence are constantly of this nature.
You surely know the manifold course of the sense-objects that agitate the mind—how they come, how they go, and how they overwhelm us.
In this very way do affections and riches arise; and in this very way they perish through unexamined causes.
They are not yours, nor are you theirs; they are the stainless internal activities of the world. This world is merely such as it is—why do you suffer in vain?
You here are the form of the universe, O you whose nature is the expansion of pure consciousness; when your own limbs are withdrawn, what room is there for joy or sorrow?

O dear one, you are of the nature of pure consciousness; this world is not distinct from you. Therefore, how and where could there be for you any conceptualization of what is to be rejected or what is to be accepted?

Thus, in the ocean of the world which consists of consciousness, where the flickering of the wheel of consciousness is like a mass of waves upon the sea, what room is there for the sequence of joy and sorrow?
Having attained a state of one-pointed consciousness and reached the condition of deep sleep, O Rāma, from this day forward, may you become one whose very nature is the fourth state (turya).
Equanimous, appearing as equal and even, with a radiant body and noble intellect, remain always devoted to the worship of the Self, like a perfectly full ocean.
Having heard all this, you stand here with a perfected intellect; O descendant of Raghu, ask whatever else you wish to inquire.
"Whatever was asked in the first chapter, that please prompt me to explain today. Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahman, my doubt has now been particularly dispelled."
Everything that was to be known has been known; natural contentment has arisen. O Sage, there is no impurity, no duality, no object of thought, and no conceptualization.
"At that time my ignorance was [present], but now it has been stilled; however, the notion that 'there is a stain upon the self' arose through the power of that ignorance."
That delusion has now ceased through your grace; the self is neither born nor does it die, nor is it ever defiled.
And indeed, I have been sufficiently awakened by all questions, doubts, and desires from every side, that "all this is composed of Brahman."
My mind has become pure and stainless, as if polished by Tvaṣṭṛ on a lathe, regarding all instructions on conduct received and proclaimed by the virtuous.
I remain within myself free from longing, like Mount Sumeru amidst gold; there is nothing where hope exists, and there is nothing that is desired.

There is nothing among the moving and the unmoving that is to be taken up, rejected, or regarded as neutral; there is nothing that is "this is to be rejected," "this is to be accepted," "this is real," or "this is unreal."
"Thus, O Sage, my confusion of thought has been stilled; I do not long for heaven, nor do I loathe Raurava."
For I abide in the Self alone, like the cloudless Mount Mandara, amidst the flow of the milk-ocean of the three worlds scattered into fragments.
O Rāma, Mandara, having long been bewildered, is now at rest and free from delusion; the conceptualization that "this is non-substance" and "that is substance" has utterly ceased.
O Lord of Sages, his heart was intensely inflamed by a web of false doubts as to how this world is known to be "thus" and "so."
Whatever state of wretchedness he encounters in the world cannot be found in that which is dull, devoid of activity, and characterized by various turbulent waves of agitation.
"O Blessed One, by your grace we have crossed over the ocean of existence; the limit of prosperity has been known, and the boundary of calamities has been seen."

O Supreme Lord, we are undaunted even in the face of all essential hardships; we are fulfilled. Our mind has attained true heroism within the ocean of worldly existence—a state that cannot be pierced by others and which crushes the elephants of unfulfilled desires.

My mind has attained a state free from conceptual construction, its desires have utterly dissolved, and its essential strength is undaunted; it is supremely joyful within, possessing a most serene form throughout the three worlds.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Whatever you do with the senses alone, engaged with present objects, by means of a mind that is unattached—that is not truly done.
Just as an object at the moment of its attainment brings satisfaction for the first time, so it does not do so after that single moment of attainment; who has not experienced this?
Just as an object brings satisfaction at the time it is desired, but not otherwise, therefore the fool, and no one else, binds himself with attachment to momentary pleasure.
At the time of desire, that which leads to satisfaction is desire itself; yet satisfaction ends in dissatisfaction—therefore, abandon desire.
If, through the passage of time, you should ever attain that state, you must never again be immersed in the form of egoistic conceit.
O Rāma, you have found rest upon the peak of the mountain of self-knowledge; you ought not to fall again into the great abyss of egoism.
For one who abides upon the summit of the Meru of knowledge, possessing the infinite and true vision of mindfulness—how could there be a fall again into the underworld that resembles the womb?
This nature of yours is seen to consist of the truth of equanimity; I consider you one whose conceptual constructions are exhausted, born with the darkness of ignorance destroyed.
"O gentle Rāma, your stainless equanimity, resembling the full ocean, seems to inform me that you are established in your own true nature."
May hope turn into hopelessness, and may the sense of existence turn into non-existence; may the mind turn into mindlessness for you who live without attachment.
Whatever perception of an object you may have, in each and every one of them resides Brahman, the mass of expanded consciousness, in the form of the universal nature of existence.
One who does not know the Self is bound; one who knows the Self is not bound. Therefore, O Rāma, by all means awaken your own Self through your own self.
Know that state to be freedom from latent impressions (*avāsanatva*), as gentle as the sky, wherein an object does not taste sweet to oneself, yet tastes sweet as it comes.
Perform your activities with internal faculties free from latent impressions; you shall not undergo transformation even by hundreds of disturbances, remaining like the sky.
The knower, knowledge, and the object of knowledge—these three are unified within the Self; through the experience of the peaceful Self, you are incapable of being subject to existence again.
The creation and dissolution of saṃsāra occur through the opening and closing of the eyes of the mind; by restraining the latent impressions and the vital breath, make the mind unblinking.
The emergence and dissolution of saṃsāra occur through the opening and closing of the vital breath; by means of practice and application, render that [breath] devoid of its opening.

The dissolution and emergence of karmas occur through the opening and closing of the eyes of ignorance; dissolve that [ignorance] by force through the restraint of the senses and the meaning of the scriptures taught by the Guru.

Just as the sky appears as the perception of phenomena due to the vibration caused by contact with wind and dust, so too does this world arise from the vibration of consciousness through its state of being an object of cognition.

This movement of the world flashes forth through the vibration of the relationship between the seen and the seeing, just as the perception of color arises from the contact of light with a wall or other objects.
In the absence of the vibration of the relationship between the seen and the seeing, no sensation arises that appears as existence, just as [no such sensation arises] within the minds of painted men.
Illusion arises from the vibration of the mind; in its absence, it dissolves. A wave arises from the vibration of water; in its absence, it perishes.

When the mind has attained a state of motionlessness through the abandonment of the portion consisting of latent impressions, through awakening, or through the restraint of the vital breath, how can there be the possibility of movement?
By the mere cessation of the vibration of non-awareness, the mind reaches the state of no-mind; or else, by the restraint of the vital breaths, that very same supreme state is attained.
In the relationship between the seen and the seeing, that which is the ultimate happiness is the dissolution of the mind through the vision of Brahman, which is the final and absolute realization.
Wherever the mind has not arisen, there that happiness is unconditioned; it does not exist even in heaven and the like, just as a house of ice does not exist in a desert.
The bliss born from the pacification of the mind is expansive and inexpressible by words; free from decay and excellence, it neither arises nor ceases.

Through awakening, the end of the mind occurs; through lack of understanding, there is the perception of a mind. Like a child’s ghost, by that [perception], the splendor of delusion has reached density.
For even though this mind exists, it dissolves through awakening; though real, it appears as if unreal, just like copper when it has been turned into gold.
The mind of the Knower is not called "mind"; the mind of the Knower is called *sattva*. Through awakening, the mind undergoes a change in its name and substance, just as copper becomes gold.
The state of being mind is not possible; therefore, it dissolves away. Delusion is stilled by awakening, for there is no non-existence of that which exists.
Mind and the rest are indeed non-entities, consisting of conceptual construction like the horn of a hare; therefore, all that belongs to the self dissolves through awakening to that [reality].

The mind, having attained the state of *sattva* for a certain period during the maintenance of the world, dwells there and thereafter becomes the *turyātīta* (the state beyond the fourth) within the *turya* (fourth) stage.

Brahman alone, through the flood of delusions arising from its manifold manifestations, thus exists as the one and the many in perfect equilibrium. It arises as the self of all; nothing else whatsoever exists, my dear, not even the mind and so forth, for they are like a mental construction within the heart.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In this regard, O Rāma, listen to this unprecedented and beautiful story in brief, which brings about awakening and causes the joy of wonder.
There exists a great bilva fruit, thousands of yojanas in extent, vast, stainless, and radiant, which remains undecaying even through the ages.
It possesses the essence of imperishable flavor, like the sweet core of nectar; though ancient, it is as beautiful and soft as the crescent of the new moon.
It was like Mount Meru in the midst of the array, as immovable as Mount Mandara, and unshakable even by the force of the winds at the end of a great aeon.
In its vast extent, it is immeasurable even by hundreds of millions of billions of tens of thousands of yojanas; it is the primordial root of the world's existence.
The vast cosmic eggs, when brought near to this great bilva fruit, lose their splendor beneath it, appearing like a mere trail of mustard seeds at the foot of a mountain.
O Rāghava, there is no one who surpasses him in the wonder of his sweet flavor, which is filled with a flowing essence and possesses all six tastes.
That which is never equalled by cooking—that which, my dear, though always cooked, is not afflicted by old age—is the highest state.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Rudra, and others—only some among them are aged; they do not know his origin, nor his root, nor even his stalk.
Of this fruit of great magnitude, whose sprout and tree have not been seen, whose form as a flower has not been observed, and which possesses neither stem, root, nor branches.
It possesses a single, solid, and expansive massiveness, and no transformation such as arising or alteration is observed in it.
Of this great work, which is the fruit containing the essence of all fruits, there is neither pith nor seed; it is expansive, changeless, and stainless.
Like a solid rock without interstices, yet like the flowing orb of the moon, it is as if distilling the nectar of its own self-awareness, which is to be tasted as ambrosia.
It is a treasury of all happiness, creating a cool light; resembling a mountain and like a mass of nectar, it is the marrow situated within its own fruit.
Therefore, that which is the supreme marrow—the wondrous manifestation of one's own self—is eternally protected as non-dual; having attained the fruit of glory, it remains forever unchanging.
By that slender girl, though she was very young and stout, her own physical arrangement reached a state of variety that resulted in a sense of distinctness, yet she did not abandon it.
Through the conceptualization "I am this," that which is non-existent and other than [the Self]—being stainless and impossible as a distinct entity—is produced by itself and thus cultivated.
Immediately upon the emergence of the power of the ego (ahaṃkalā), she [the primordial nature] was enveloped by the atoms of the three worlds, whose limbs consist of the sounds of space.
Thus, proceeding in this sequence, consciousness attains the nature of its own power; the marrow, having first reached its own prior arrangement, then completely abandons it.
By means of that power of consciousness, which assumes various shifting forms therein, the vision is thus extended toward its own very nature, which is equanimity.
This is the infinitely vast void; this is the digit consisting of time; this is called necessity; and this is action, whose form is vibration.

This is the expansion of conceptual construction; this is the wandering among various hopes; this is the abiding in passion and hatred; and this is the intellect that discriminates between what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted.
This is you, this is I, and this very one is established as "this" by itself; this flood of cosmic eggs stands above, yet it is itself both above and below, O dear one.
"This is in front, this is at the side, this is behind, this is near, or this is far; this is a past entity, this is present, and this is also future."
This is the circle of the pleasure-pavilion for the crown-jewel of the pavilion of the universe, containing within it the abode of the lotuses of manifold mental constructions.
This pericarp of the heart-lotus of Hari, which has blossomed from the reality of infinite time, is the rosary of lotus-seeds of the world.
This long path of clouds, its hollows filled with throngs of scattered great Rudras, is powerful enough to destroy those who wander astray.
This is Mount Meru, the pericarp of the lotus of the world situated here in the cardinal directions, where the gods act as bees, greedy for the joy of the honey of the shimmering moon.
This cluster of blossoms from the celestial glory of unrestrained fragrance belongs to the world-tree, which has the dust of hell for its roots and is ancient and withered.
And this lotus-pond of the play of the sky stands upon the shore of the ocean of Brahma, with stars for its filaments, extending to the very limits of the boundless and the bounded.
This is a succession of waves, flickering and unstable, which grasps at activity; it is a vast series of beings situated within the formation of the whirlpools of creation.
The lotus of time spreads forth to such an extent, with its sprouts being moments and eons; it has brilliance for its lion and the sky for its lotus.

These views on the meaning of the scriptures are rich in the modifications of existence, abounding in the cholera of old age and death, and filled with the playful manifestations of knowledge and ignorance.
Thus, that wonderful essence of the wood-apple tree remained established within the very interior of its own volitional formation.

Peaceful, self-abiding, free from affliction, and gentle, it is devoid of mental cultivation; having rendered both agency and non-agency as if they were neither done nor undone, it remains established in suchness.

This very one, though appearing as manifold and diverse, is indeed neither of a single nature nor manifold; it is that very same one, established in truth, possessing the uniform form of universal peace, the all-pervading, most great power whose nature is consciousness.

Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, knower of the essence of all things, it is my understanding that you have here described this [reality] which takes the form of the Bilva tree, as the very being of the mass of Great Consciousness.
This entire expansion, beginning with the ego-sense, has the form of pure consciousness; there is not even the slightest distinction consisting of the conceptualization of duality or unity.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as the existence of Mount Meru and other features resides within the marrow of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), so too does the existence of the world, beginning with the cosmic egg, reside within the marrow of this wood-apple (vilva) of consciousness.

The consciousness of emanation is the marrow of the bilva-fruit of the Self; yet, since it is impossible for its own support to be other than itself, this destruction of the all-pervading cannot possibly occur.
The wonder called the world resides within the seed of the *citermarīca* (the chiliarch of consciousness), like the internal structure of a stone, remaining within the tranquility of deep sleep.
In this regard, O moon-faced one, listen to another delightful and wonderful narrative, full of amazement, which I am now recounting.
There exists somewhere a great rock—glossy, clear, soft to the touch, possessing vast dimensions, dense, and eternally unshakable.
Within it, there are indeed many beautiful lotuses in full bloom, as numerous as those in a lake, truly infinite in number.
Their petals were interlaced with one another, yet they were also mutually separated; they were both hidden from each other and concealed, as well as manifest.
Some have their openings facing downward, some upward, and others sideways; their bases are joined together, and their openings are likewise interlaced.
The roots of the network of pericarp-spokes have their tips at the pericarp; some have their roots above, some have their roots below, and others are rootless.
And in their vicinity there are conchs by the hundreds of thousands, as well as massive masses of wheels arranged like lotuses.
Śrī Rāma said: "This is true; I have seen that great stone of such a kind. It exists in Śālagrāma, the abode of Hari, surrounded by its retinue."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "Thus you understand this; you have seen that stone, and whatever vital breath was there, it was entirely of the same nature as yourself."
But I have described this unprecedented stone to you here, within whose vast interior everything both exists and does not exist.
This "cicchilā" (consciousness-stone) has been described by me to you, within which the worlds indeed exist; by virtue of its nature as a single, solid unity, this consciousness is itself the stone.
Even within one whose body is exceedingly dense and whose form is without any gaps, the multitude of worlds exists within, just as vast wind exists within the sky.
The sky, the earth, the wind, space, the mountains, the rivers, and the directions—all exist within that stone, yet there is not even the slightest cavity in it.
Within this very dense-bodied self, the lotus of the world unfolds; in reality, there is nothing other than this, nor anything else that is of a pure nature.
Just as the world of conch shells, lotuses, and so forth is engraved upon stone, so too are the past, present, and future [worlds] like figures carved in relief upon a rock.
Likewise, all those various forms exist there in reality, just as the internal arrangement within a stone exists as a single mass despite having many distinct natures.

Just as it was grasped, so this [consciousness] becomes a single, dense mass in the form of a lump of clay; just as a lotus is not distinct from its sheath of stone, so too is that body composed of it.

Likewise, although the creation is non-different from the form of consciousness, it consists of the body; just as the lines of wheels and lotuses exist within a stone by way of the state of deep sleep.
Just as it exists within consciousness, so does this series of worlds exist—like a row of lotus designs within a stone, or a flash of pungency within a peppercorn.
Just as creation neither rises nor sets within consciousness, so too does the mortal man exist within the woman, like the marrow within a wood-apple fruit.

Likewise, the multitude of cosmic eggs within consciousness, though rich with infinite modifications, is that very same [consciousness]; thus, the statement that "modifications and so forth exist" is merely vain and purposeless talk.
It quickly attains that very nature, like a drop of water in water; because consciousness is infinite, these modifications and so forth are indeed consciousness.
That which is attained through speech dissolves by merging into that; this is indeed Brahman, free from modification and the like, and devoid of the objects of modification and the like.
Through the power of its own infinity, Brahman alone effects the rejection or acceptance of objects; Brahman itself abides as transformation and so forth, and Brahman alone is produced in succession.
Know this to be for another purpose here, like the water of a mirage: the seed that exists within the flower and fruit has no other nature than that which is within the seed itself.

Just as the existence of a seed develops and proceeds further and further, so too the density of consciousness within the mass of consciousness—that very process constitutes the sequence of the three worlds.
The oneness of these two is their duality; in the absence of one, both are lost. The arising of the world from any other source never occurs; such is the nature of reality.

Consciousness and the unconscious are never dual within, yet they are mutually non-dual; just as there is much internal division in the form of lines within a massive rock, so too the three worlds—neither different nor non-different from it—exist within the density of consciousness, like marrow within a bone.
Just as a single massive stone is encircled by lines and sub-lines, so too is the one Brahman seen as encompassing the three worlds.
Just as these lotuses and other forms within a stone are eternally in a state of deep sleep, neither setting nor rising, so too is the ego and the course of the world.

Just as an inscription within a stone is not distinct from the interior of the stone because it is of the same essence as it, so too the creator of the world and the world itself, such as its agency, are not distinct from Consciousness (cit).
Just as the arising and ceasing, the movement and stillness of lotuses within a rock do not become objects [of perception], so too the creators of the world do not become objects.
This is never created, nor does it ever perish; like a mountain, its nature consists of the experience of the playful manifestation of creative power.
Just as it is in whatever form and wherever it may be, so indeed is that very thing; everything consists of the essence of Brahman’s existence, remaining as if situated in deep sleep.
Know that this great delusion of the world, which is rich with manifold transformations of states, is indeed like deep sleep, comparable to a lotus and such within a stone.

The play of the world is eternally the state of deep sleep itself, because its true nature is the self, which is perfectly tranquil, uniform, and a mass of consciousness; thus, the states of creation are seen to be as insubstantial as lotuses within a stone, and they never truly enter into the body.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as there is a fruit from the essence of a tree, so too, through the sequential process of the consciousness's own sleep, that which exists by virtue of the arrangement of its own being is established as "creation."
Since even space, time, action, and so forth consist of that very nature, it is not tenable here to say, "this is one thing" and "that is another."
For one who knows how to grasp the impressions (*vāsanā*) of all words and their referents as being of a single nature, how can it be said that "this is non-existent"?
Just as the internal arrangement of a fruit exists according to its name and sequence, so too does the density of consciousness’s own being exist as non-dual yet appearing as manifold.
Neither non-different nor different, as if agitated yet unagitated; just as fruits exist within their own seeds, so do accomplishments exist within consciousness.
In the mirror of the city of the world, one's own reflection is gathered; it shines as if it were not shining at all, like the internal arrangement within a stone.
Within the supreme jewel of consciousness, even hundreds of millions of worlds exist, just as infinite fruits are fully contained within a wish-fulfilling gem.
This entire world appears like a pearl inlaid upon that expansive casket of consciousness; though composed of its very essence, it shines as if distinct from it.
Day and night, thoroughly transforming one sensation after another, the radiant sun of consciousness remains, illuminating the substances of the world.
Like the playful movement of water in the whirlpools and hollows of the ocean, consciousness is both non-dual and manifold, like the internal arrangements within a rock.
That which exists is a statue within the stone body; that which does not exist is a statue within the stone body.

That which is the truth amidst existents and non-existents is like the very marrow of consciousness; for the splendor of all objective phenomena has the essence of marrow, and it is indeed composed of that alone.
Just as the meanings of various words such as "lotus" and so forth are abandoned within the interior of a stone, so too this world is manifold; yet that which consists of all this is non-dual.
Just as a lotus-form and the interior of a stone are neither different nor non-different, being essentially indivisible, so too is this [universe] within the mass of consciousness.

Just as the sun’s radiance, though present within a vessel of pure water, appears as if absent to those with a limited perception of the physical ground, so too you, whose nature is both being and non-being, are not consciousness itself.
Just as the mass of water within the hollow of a cloud, though poised for movement, vibrates without actual motion due to its fluidity, so too is this interior of the density of consciousness.

Know that consciousness is like a mass of stone, conch, and lotuses; even while being identical with them, it is not identical with them. Know the world, including objects such as lotuses and so forth, to be within consciousness, which is like a mass of stone.

Though this is a mass of great stone, it is like the interior of a rock situated within a mass of consciousness—without apertures, non-dual, transparent, unborn, profoundly tranquil, yet possessing a structured form.
This world-Brahman shines like the stainless autumn season; this world-Brahman vibrates like the gentle, flowing moon.
This world is like deep sleep within Brahman; it does not exist, yet it is indestructible, like a lotus in a stone. Just as the nature of Brahman exists within Brahman, so too is this world situated.
No difference exists between these two, just as there is none between the words "taru" and "pādapa"; whatever worlds exist here, they are nothing other than the form of consciousness.

For these [phenomena], there is never any existence or non-existence, as in the case of that [illusion]; the world-appearance is Brahman alone, just as water [is not real] in the mirage of the wind-blown heat.
Just as water becomes pure by the sight of the sun, so too does Brahman become pure through contemplation—whether it be Mount Meru or a blade of grass, a shrub, the mind, or even the entire world.
They know that form which exists through the supreme division of water to be the Supreme; its collection is likewise the mind, whether it be as high as Mount Meru or as small as a blade of grass.
For that which is essential even in its subtlety is indeed more essential in its grossness; just as, O sinless one, the power whose nature is rasa exists as the ultimate atom.
Likewise, the state of Brahman exists within all objects of the world as milk; it is like the power of sap [present] in various grasses, shrubs, creepers, and waters.
In this way, that very state of Brahman arises as manifoldness, appearing as "this" and "not-this," just as the atoms of light constitute the playful display of forms.

The supreme nature of these [energies], which consist of the essence of qualities, the qualified, objects, and existence, resides within consciousness and the mind, just as Mount Meru and other such things exist within that which manifests them.

Just as the hardness of the mass of feathers and wings exists within the fluid of a peacock’s egg, so too does multiplicity exist within the principle of consciousness (citi-tattva), which is of the nature of manifesting that [multiplicity].
Just as a cluster of variegated peacock feathers exists within the fluid of a peacock's egg, so too does that which consists of various selves exist within the fluid of the peacock's egg.
When seen through the vision of discernment, both Brahman and the world exist in that same way: though appearing diverse, they are not diverse, just as the egg, its fluid, and the peacock [are one].

The delusion of Brahman and the world has as its essence the existence of both non-duality and duality; it is like the equality in which the existence of both the existent and the non-existent abides.

Therefore, know that the form of both the existent and the non-existent is the Supreme abiding within all beings; this world, consisting of diversity and non-diversity, is experienced as being without origin.

Behold the movement of the entire world within the egg of the peacock; as the principle of consciousness (cittattva) is in the world, so is the world in the principle of consciousness. It is both manifold and non-manifold, yet one, just like the fluid within a peacock’s egg.

The primordial consciousness, which is the essence of the egg of the world-peacock and is filled with the plumage of the delusions regarding various objects, takes the form of a peacock; yet know that within it is the state of pure existence, devoid of peacock-form—how then can there be any duality?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In that [Reality], where this entire expanse exists as its own unmanifest form—just as a peacock exists within its seed—therein reside egoity and all else.
Where nothing whatsoever has arisen, there everything exists; even here, O Aṅgiras, that [reality] reflects the essence of the bliss of heaven.
And so the sages, gods, hosts, perfected ones, and great seers, relishing their own true nature, are ever established in the state of the Fourth (turya).
These are they whose gaze is fixed with steady eyes and unblinking; they are established in the relinquishing of the vibration of attachment to the seen and the seeing.

Those for whom there is no cultivation of mental states, even while engaged in activities, and who remain established in the relinquishing of the vibration of the relationship between consciousness and its objects, [are liberated].
The breath of those does not stir, like figures in a painting; the mind of those does not stir, like figures in a painting.
Having abandoned attachment to the mind and its objects, they abide in their own true state; through subtle vibration, they accomplish their purpose just as a lord does by his mere will.
In the same way, through the vibration of mind, objects of thought, and so forth, they maintain their existence, just as a clear lunar ray gladdens a sprout.
In the same way, the Self gladdens within at the union of the seer and the seen, even though it has moved far from the original object and has not fallen upon the wall.
That which is the form of the sun's radiance is the form of pure consciousness; it is not an object of sight, nor is it fit for instruction, neither too near nor too far.

The pure nature of the Self is of the form of consciousness, attainable through solitary experience; it is neither the body, nor the senses and vital breaths, nor the mind, nor even latent impressions.
There is no living soul, nor vibration, nor consciousness, nor indeed the world; it is neither existent nor non-existent, nor the middle, nor indeed empty or non-empty.
Neither that nor anything else exists as place, time, substance, and so forth; it is entirely free from all these, as well as from the hundredfold sheaths within the heart.

Wherever this visible world vibrates, that is the state of the Self; it is neither the beginning of the day nor the end of the kalpa, and it is not a substance composed of earth, air, and the other elements.
In this world and the next, things sometimes exist in a different form from their true nature; thousands of bodily jars are born and die.

O best among the knowers of the Self, there is no fragmentation of this space of the Self, which encompasses both the internal and the external; indeed, all of that—the body and so forth—is itself the Self.
The entire universe, which is everywhere identical with the Self, appears as if slightly separate only due to the deformity of cognition; yet it is known by a perfectly perfected intellect.
Though blazing amidst worldly affairs, remain extinguished and free from the sense of "mine"; for whatever is seen here, this entire world of moving and unmoving beings—[is but a reflection].
All that is Brahman—devoid of attributes, devoid of qualities, pure in essence, changeless, without beginning or end, eternal, peaceful, and of a uniform nature.

The performance of death, the agent of action, the primary cause, the effect, birth, maintenance, dissolution, recollection, and all else—since you have seen that all this is Brahman through the vision of the Self, O dear one, why do you wander further, even though you are perfectly sound?
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahman, if there is no modification or the like within the expanded Brahman, then how does this world, consisting of existence and non-existence, appear?"

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O dear one, that which is the reversal of its own nature and the non-returning to its previous state—that is what constitutes modification and so forth, as it exists in milk and other such substances.
Milk returns again to the state of curd, but curd does not return again to milk; likewise, the pure Brahman remains as Brahman alone in the beginning, middle, and end.

Therefore, Brahman possesses no quality of being subject to modification, unlike milk and other such substances; for it is devoid of the distinction between beginning and end, nor does it undergo the process of becoming a composite whole.
Know that this transformation seen at the beginning and end of a problem is merely the agitation of consciousness; there is no actual modification in that which is changeless.
Neither the object of cognition nor the act of cognition exists there in that Brahman; it is designated by the word "Brahman" and is like the nature of consciousness devoid of all relations.
Whatever the nature of a thing is at its beginning and end, that is exactly how it is said to be; whatever difference appears in the middle is a manifestation arising from ignorance.
The Self, however, is equal everywhere and at all times—in the beginning, the end, and the middle; it never attains even its own otherness, nor does the reality of the Self ever change.
Because he is formless, because he is one, and because he is eternal, this Lord never comes under the power of the transformations of states of being.
Śrī Rāma said: Since the one, eternally singular, and absolutely pure Brahman exists, from where does ignorance arise, which is by nature a delusion of consciousness?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This entire universe is the reality of Brahman; it has been, it is, and it will be. It is changeless, without beginning or end, and it is certain that ignorance does not exist.
As for the sequence of the signified and the signifier in the word "Brahman," even there, that sequence exists only to teach the non-existence of any difference between them.
You, I, the worlds, the quarters, the sky, the earth, fire, and so forth—all are nothing but Brahman, without beginning or end; there is not even the slightest trace of ignorance.
The wise know that this so-called "ignorance" (avidyā) is merely an error and is unreal; for how indeed could that which does not exist be real?
Śrī Rāma said: "O Lord, in yesterday’s discourse on the section concerning tranquility, you stated that this ignorance is to be investigated in such and such a manner."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O scion of Raghu, you have remained unawakened for all this time; indeed, you have been awakened by these very constructs of your own reasoning.

This sequence of conceptual constructions, such as "this individual soul (jīva) consists of ignorance," has been devised by the best among those skilled in speech for the purpose of awakening the unawakened.
As long as the mind remains unawakened, it does not attain awakening even through hundreds of reproaches, provided there is no delusion.
Only by means of reasoning is this living being awakened and joined to the Self; if a goal is attained through reasoning, it cannot be achieved even by hundreds of other efforts.
He who says "everything is Brahman" to an unawakened person of dull intellect acts like a well-wisher reporting pain to a stump.
The fool is awakened by means of reasoning; the wise man is awakened by means of the reality itself. The fool attains wisdom not without being awakened by reasoning.
For so long you were unawakened; now you have been awakened by me through reasoning, by which you are being brought to full realization.
I am Brahman; the three worlds are Brahman; you are indeed Brahman, as is the ground of all that is perceived. There is no second conceptualization; do as you wish.
Though you internally bring about the three worlds as nothing more than the pinnacle of great consciousness that is beyond perception, you remain unstained.
"I am the Supreme Self—luminous in form, conscious, and all-pervading"—remaining within this realization of Rāghava, stay, move, breathe, and sleep.
If you are wise and virtuous, being free from "mine-ness" and free from egoism, then become that peaceful Brahman-knowledge abiding within all beings.
That very reality, which is beginningless and endless, is the supreme state; you abide as that, consisting of pure consciousness, the one self that pervades all.

That which is Brahman, the Self, and the Fourth (turya), as well as that which is ignorance and primordial nature (prakṛti)—the eternally one Self is non-different from all these, just as clay is the common essence in hundreds of jars.

The primordial nature (prakṛti) is not different from the Self, just as the state of being made of clay is not different from a jar; and just as pure clay alone exists within it, so does the primordial nature abide as the very Self.
This very vibration of the Self, which is like the swirling of water, is designated here by the word "prakṛti" (nature); for it is that alone which is so described.
Just as the single wind of movement is divided by name but not by reality, so too the one self-nature is divided by name but not by reality.

The distinction between these two arises from ignorance and dissolves through awakening alone; due to ignorance, it appears as if composed of reality, just as the delusion of a snake in a rope vanishes [upon knowledge].
When this seed of mental construction, vibrating, falls upon the field of consciousness, from it arises the sprout of the mind, which is the future fragment of saṃsāra.
This very [semen], once burnt by the knowledge of the Self, is not capable of sprouting again even if it is diligently sprinkled with the waters of latent impressions (vāsanā).
If the seed of conceptualization does not fall into the field of consciousness, then the sprouts of the mind—the trees that bear the fruits of pleasure and pain—will not arise.

Duality in this world is unreal, born of ignorance; abandon it, for you have attained awakening which is the destruction of ignorance. Through the power of the singular nature of the Self, you have become one whose essence is fearless existence; "there is no suffering at all"—this is the essence of our ultimate truth.

Śrī Rāma said: Everything that is to be known has been known, and everything that is to be seen has been seen unimpaired. We have become completely filled by you with the nectar of the knowledge of Brahman.
From the Full, this Full arises; from the Full, the Full is produced. The Full is filled by the Full, and the state of fullness abides within the Full.
O Brahmin, I ask this again merely as a play for the further increase of my understanding; you ought not to be angry with me, just as a father would not be angry with his child.
O Brahmin, although the ear, eye, sense of touch, tongue, and nose exist and are clearly perceived, [they do not perceive the Self].
How is it that a deceased being does not perceive its own sense objects, and how is it that while living, one perceives all of them?
How is it that the sense organs, though insentient, experience the externality of jars and other objects within the body, yet do not experience them again [as external] when they are inside?
Regarding the eye and other sense organs, which are indeed like iron rods—unjoined and separated from one another—how could that [consciousness] be said to be produced by them in mutual contact?
Although you already know these particulars in their hundredfold details, I ask them again; therefore, please explain them to me in their entirety out of compassion.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O dear one, neither the senses and so forth, nor the mind and so forth, nor even objects such as jars, exist here separately from the stainless consciousness.

Even more transparent than the sky, that mind, by its own nature, having conceived of form as itself through its very essence of consciousness, has manifested as the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*) solely through the activity of its objective tendencies.

And that very [principle] has become the primordial nature (prakṛti) for the persistence of the world; from its constituent parts are born the sense organs and so forth, as well as jars and other objects.
The mind, which by its own nature has attained the state of the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka), reflects objects such as jars within its own constituent parts.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, tell me what the nature of the mirror is, which possesses the majesty of creating a thousand worlds, and what the form of the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) is like.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That Brahman which exists as the seed of the universe, without beginning or end, is free from affliction; it is of the nature of light, pure consciousness alone, and devoid of all parts or mental constructions.
When it becomes oriented toward temporal activity, it is known as the inner *jīva*; indeed, that *jīva* clearly accumulates [karma] and vibrates within this body.

From the sense of "I" it is called *ahaṃkāra* (ego); from the act of thinking, it is called *manas* (mind); from the determination of cognition, it is *buddhi* (intellect); and likewise, from the perception of Indra, it is the *indriya* (organ).
Through the contemplation of a body, it becomes a body; through the contemplation of a jar, it becomes a jar. This very self-nature is remembered by people as the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka).
That consciousness which falls within the range of knowerhood, agency, enjoyership, witnesshood, and so forth, is called the *jīva*; indeed, the wise know that to be the *puryaṣṭaka*.

Then, from time to time, the living being itself becomes something else by its own nature, through the arising of minute particles of infinite latent impressions (vāsanā) that have been cultivated into specific forms.
By means of its nature as the city-of-eight (puryaṣṭaka), it assumes a form through time, just as a seed becomes a sprout through watering according to its latent impressions (vāsanā).
"I am the form, the body and so forth, the stationary and the moving; I am not the primordial conscious Self"—thus one perceives through false knowledge.
Enveloped by latent impressions, the living soul wanders for a long time in this world, moving up and down like a piece of wood struck by waves in the ocean.
Someone, due to the purity of their birth, immediately after being released from the bondage of existence, realizes the Self and attains the state that is devoid of beginning and end.
Someone who, after a long time, has become weary of the cycle of rebirths through various wombs, attains the supreme state of the Self by the power of self-knowledge.
O wise one, listen now to how this soul, having assumed such a form as a body, perceives through the eyes and other senses, just as one perceives the interior of a jar and so forth.

When consciousness, which is the limit of all calculation, has departed, this body remains, consisting of the collection of the six sense-faculties with the mind as the sixth, while life still persists.
When another [element] falls from all bodies into the sky in the form of the imperishable, then, through contact with that life-force, it attains oneness with the individual soul.
In the perception of external objects, the constant connection of the sense organ with the mind is the causal factor; never that of one who is dissociated from the mind.
Whatever is clearer than that reflects within it, like the sky; joined with the individual soul (jīva), even the external soul lives.
When the pupils of the eyes possess the luster of freshly polished jewels, then external objects are reflected within them.
Because it becomes joined with the individual soul (jīva) by way of being its reflection, O Rāghava, the external object comes to be known by the soul.
For even a child perceives that which comes into contact [with the senses]; why then should a living being—whether an animal or even an immobile thing—not perceive it?
Furthermore, the rays of the clear eye, enveloped by the living soul (jīva), fully embrace the visible object; the soul perceives it through its true nature.

This very same sequence applies to touch; the arising of cognition is the connection [between sense and object]. This has been explained for taste and smell as well, originating from the contact with the living being (jīva).
But sound, because it resides in space, reaches the space within the ear in an instant; thus, the perceptions of the sense organs enter the inner space of the living self (jīvākāśa).
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahman, tell me, what is the nature of this which is seen reflected in the mirror of the mind, as well as within machines, wood, and bellies?"

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O best among those who know what is to be known, understand that this mutual reflection between these two, which are as utterly inert as two living beings, is merely an illusion of the eye.
Let there be no conviction in you here that this world is merely that much; the wave beginning with "I" is always the water that is present.
In the supreme ocean, however, there is no such thing as space, time, action, and so forth; because of its eternal identity with that, the Self is omnipresent everywhere.

Always with an unattached mind and a joyful soul, knowing within yourself that peace is free from both false pleasure and pain, remain with your intellect settled in equanimity, having cast off all the delusions and maladies of existence.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "The eyes and other senses did not exist for you previously, just as all this has been heard by you regarding the Lotus-born One."
Just as the consciousness of objects arises at the beginning of the eightfold city of Brahmā, so too does it arise at all times for every eightfold city.
Know that the "city of eight" is the living soul (jīva), which is the emergence of the senses within the womb; whatever it conceives of, it immediately perceives as exactly that.
Know that the senses and what is called the objects of the senses constitute one's own perception; and how it becomes perfected, as was explained to you during the initial state of the mind.
Pure consciousness, arising as irreproachable self-awareness, then becomes endowed with the awareness of "I" and the infinite subtle bodies (puryaṣṭakas) of individual souls.
But because it is one, infinite, unknowable, and free from affliction; because it is non-existent, manifold, and not empty, it stands supreme.

Through the cognition of "this is the body" and so forth, that [consciousness] does not become the mind, nor does it attain the state of the individual soul (jīva), nor does it consist of the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka).
There is no play of ignorance and the like; he who always exists as if he did not exist is called the Supreme Self, transcending the mind and the five senses.

Therefore, the individual soul (jīva), whose form is consciousness and whose nature is thought, arises from that; [the statement] "it is merely an illusion" and so forth is proclaimed for the purpose of instruction.
When the disease consisting of ignorance has arisen from whatever cause, it dissolves through inquiry by means of instruction for the one being instructed.
There remains only that knowledge in which all forms have been completely stilled, wherein even space appears as gross as a great mountain within an atom.
Abandoning the objects of the world—which, though appearing as active and even existent, remain as if non-existent—abide within your own stainless body.
That which is composed of the intellect is indeed the very form of ignorance; for once it is truly perceived, it surely perishes and is no longer seen.
How indeed can that which is called "seen" be obtained as a real thing? Even when attained with great effort, it is like the water of a mirage.
The unreal appears as real due to ignorance; through knowledge, the object is seen as it truly is, and delusion perishes.

This investigation into ignorance—consisting of the individual soul, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and so forth—is a conceptual construction of one whose nature is itself imagined, even though [ignorance] is absolutely unreal.
This conceptualization of the individual soul and so forth has been fashioned by the scriptures for the purpose of instructing him and awakening him; listen to it with a one-pointed mind.
Abiding in the state of the *puryaṣṭaka*, consciousness—like one who has attained the condition of a living soul—is marked by the stain of *kalā* and is oriented toward awakening.
Whatever one meditates upon, that very thing one experiences quickly and fully—whether it be real or unreal, such as a yakṣa conjured by a child in the night.
It conceives of the five subtle elements (tanmātras) as having existence; likewise, it perceives the apertures within that self as they have arisen there.
From these very [elements] arises the five external elements; one perceives them as non-different [from consciousness], yet appearing as different, just as a sprout [produces] a hundred branches.
Then, possessing the conviction that "this is internal" and "this is external," the living soul (jīva) takes on a state of being, and subsequently solidifies it exactly as it has grasped it.
When the manifestation of the self appears like a web of rays from the moon, it is by that very [manifestation] that it is falsely accepted as having external tangibility.
Just as the heat of a mirage, or as the emptiness of the sky, so too the experience of the self exists as if it were something else.
Having formed a firm resolve right here, the discipline was made very firm; it was determined that "by this, it must be thus; by that, it must be so," leaving no room for deviation.

This [world], consisting of its own volitions, appears at some time as having the name of "intrinsic nature" or "other than intrinsic nature"; it exists by way of intrinsic nature alone, and not otherwise.
All this duality has arisen from the non-dual Self alone, just as a piece of sugar is produced from sweet juice, or a great jar from clay.

Because of the occurrence of spatial arrangement, transformation, and so forth, as well as place, time, and other factors, these are possible here [in the world]; however, they are not possible in the case of Īśvara, because place, time, and such factors do not apply to him.

Just as one who has arisen with the thought, "The flower is here, the leaf is there," perceives duality within their own undivided self, so too does the essence of existence carry duality within non-duality.
"This is the cloth, this is the wall, and so forth"—knowing Brahman as the Self within yourself through its universal nature, do not entertain duality.
"Just as a cloud remains as it is—today a sprout, today the brilliance of the sun, and today a rain-cloud—so too does the Self abide, possessing both existent and non-existent forms."
Thus, when this entire universe is pervaded by the Lord of All through such contemplation, who indeed in this world possesses the power to break its sequence?
In a space as clear as a mirror, one's own self does not reflect at all; because no separation is possible, it simply shines forth in its own right.
In Brahman, however, the Self alone remains and shines as the Self; though bodiless, it appears as a duality by its very nature, owing to its consisting of consciousness.
In whatever manner one knows that manifestation of the self, let it be so for oneself; even though it is unreal, it never deviates from truth in this world.
Just as the two states of being gold and being a bracelet exist in gold when it has become an ornament—one real and the other unreal—so too do consciousness and non-consciousness exist in the Self.

Because consciousness is all-pervasive, the nature of consciousness is eternally present in the mind, just as the nature of gold is present in a bracelet; yet its state of insentience remains at other times.

The mind, which consists of both consciousness and insentience, perceives and contemplates itself; in whatever manner and at whatever time it contemplates a particular state, it becomes that very thing at that time.
From time to time, the living being itself becomes variously manifested, assuming diverse forms within due to the arising of the buds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Just as a village seen in a dream moves away upon the opening of the eyes, so too this body, which is of the nature of a mental projection, passes from one body to another.
Just as in a dream a person may perceive a wall or a cloth, so too this other body exists by its own nature, though it is entirely unreal.
That which is unreal indeed dies, yet the unreal is born again; the living being, through its own manifestation, appears like a dream, as if possessing a form other than its own.
In the course of time, this form indeed does not undergo any change from its original state established by certainty; it is these beings themselves who wander through existence by their own nature.
A real object, whether seen or unseen, is experienced in a dream; O best among those who know what is to be known, understand that the form of the world is likewise in the dream of the living soul.
That which is seen by one who is not awake, though impelled by its own name and so forth, is not a dream; therefore, the pure self is mere consciousness.
Just as one perceives something called "unprecedented" in a dream and not otherwise, so too does consciousness perceive an object that has never been seen before.
Even long-standing past tendencies are overcome by human effort; indeed, through exertion today, yesterday's evil deeds are transformed into virtuous actions.
Apart from liberation, the eyes and other senses of living beings do not find peace; they merely emerge and submerge according to time and place.
Due to its own mental fabrication, the consciousness of that being exists as a body that is fierce, unreal, and composed of five elements, like a great yakṣa imagined by a child.
The mind, the intellect, the ego, and likewise the five subtle elements—this is declared to be the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka); this is the subtle, transmigrating body (ātivāhika-deha).
The mind-essence is indeed formless; its extreme density is like the nature of space. Its state as wind is a great tumor, and its state as a body is Mount Sumeru.

One who is free from passion becomes, through a gradual process, established in the state beyond all conditions and thus partakes in liberation; by this [state], even those who are inert are embraced within its single condition of deep sleep.
Likewise, this state called "dream," characterized by the perception of a body, wanders here until liberation among all things mobile and immobile.
For at times this subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) of everyone remains in a state of deep sleep, and at other times it remains as if in a dream.
When one abides in the state of deep sleep, pierced by the portents of future suffering dreams, then one remains like the fire of cosmic destruction, though its form has not yet arisen.
In states such as those of stationary objects and in the conditions of the wish-fulfilling tree, one remains indeed in deep sleep, dense as a solid stone of delusion.

Its state of deep sleep is insentience, while this cycle of worldly existence is its waking from that dream; that which is its awakening is liberation, and that which is its waking state is the fourth state (turyatā).

For liberation comes from the awakening of the individual soul; through that awakening, it attains the state of the Supreme Self, just as copper, when its impurities are washed away, attains the state of gold.

The liberation that arises from the awakening of the individual soul (jīva) is said here to be of two kinds: the first is liberation while living (jīvanmukti), and the second is liberation from the body (dehamukti).

For liberation while living is indeed the state of the Fourth (turya), and beyond that is the state transcending the Fourth (turyātīta). The individual soul (jīva) is consciousness; this awakening (prabodha) arises through the effort of the intellect.
The living self, whose measure is known, which knows as its inner controller, being composed of that [consciousness], perceives here this very fear as the delusion of a very long dream.

When one's own heart is firmly established in its natural state, that which was falsely uttered ceases; for within living beings, there exists nothing else whatsoever apart from the spark of consciousness.
Seeing that very [Self] as something else, one grieves in vain; for within the living atom (jīvāṇu), there is nothing other than the Supreme.
Wherever the world is perceived, alas, it is the unfolding of illusion, just as various whirlpools arise within the water boiling in a pot.

In the same way, there arises within living beings (jīvas) the emergence of false transmigration; their bondage is the bondage of latent impressions (vāsanā), while liberation is the dissolution of those impressions.

The state of deep sleep ends with latent impressions (vāsanā), while in the dream state, that condition manifests clearly; this living being (jīva), deluded by dense latent impressions, partakes in the states of stationary beings and so forth.
When the animal and human beings possess middling and thin latent impressions respectively, then objects such as jars are born externally through the internal life-force.

Then, due to the identity of the living self (jīva) in both, there is the existence of both the grasped and the grasper; when consciousness (cit) externally and internally encompasses both the self and the non-self.
Then the cognition of the grasped and the grasper, like a mirage with its heat, is abandoned; nothing here is relinquished, and nothing here is grasped.

The single conscious self shines forth as the form of both external and internal moments; the three worlds are but the wonder of consciousness, so enough with conceptualizations of duality! We have long been adorned within consciousness, wherein neither "external" nor "internal" exists.

Just as the waters cast off all distinctions become the sky-like, pure, entirely liquid, and singularly clean ocean; so too, this primordial, supreme state, having discarded the entire collection of distinctions, is realized as being solely free from affliction.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Know that this world-process is that very dream of the individual soul from the beginning, tender with its various mental constructions; it is neither real, nor is it composed of unreality.
A dream is never possible for the individual soul (jīva) as it is for a man; therefore, these states of being here are produced by both waking and dreaming while one is awake.
O best among those who know what is to be known, understand this long dream of the living soul to be unreal because it lacks substantiality, even though it appears to possess rapidity.
Moving from one dream to another, O sinless one, living beings perceive that which is unreal as if it were solid reality.
O dear one, insentience arises in the sentient, and sentience is proclaimed in the insentient; and unreality appears as reality due to the delusion regarding the experience of living beings.

Perceiving the entire threefold world as existing within even the sun, living beings wander about like those deluded by a dream, following after the swarms of bees that represent the perception of duality.
Because it is all-pervading and infinite, whatever one contemplates and perceives as one's own living soul, that very thing one quickly attains as a reality.
O mighty-armed one, that auspicious state of non-attachment was pointed out by Puṇḍarīkākṣa; embracing which, the great sage became liberated while yet living.
Arjuna, the son of Pāṇḍu, will spend his own life happily and free from suffering; therefore, spend your life in the same way.
Within that stainless [reality], this delusion of saṃsāra is seen, just as bracelets and the like are seen in gold, or waves and the like in water.
The fourteen types of living beings quiver intensely within this web of saṃsāra, like birds caught in a net.

In that regard, these—Yama, Candra, Arka, Śakra, and the others—whose sequence is highly praised, have attained the state of world-protectors within the cycle of existence consisting of the five elements.
"This is merit to be adopted; this, however, is evil to be abandoned"—such is the established order they have posited based on a cognition constructed by their own conceptualization.
O sinless one, until this very day, his mind has remained steady and firm upon his own karma, which has fallen into the stream like a mountain.
That Blessed One, Yama, at the end of every fourth yuga that has passed, performs austerities out of fear of sin resulting from the destruction of living beings.
Sometimes for eight years, or ten, or even twelve; sometimes five, seven, and so forth, and sometimes even sixteen.
While he remains seated like one indifferent, established in self-restraint, death does not harm any living beings within the web of the world.
