Because of that, the surface of the earth becomes impassable due to the dense mass of beings, like a sweating elephant amidst mosquitoes during the rainy season.
Then, O Rāma, these gods, by means of many stratagems, cause these various beings to perish for the sake of removing the burden of the earth.
In this way, thousands of ages and hundreds of worldly transactions have passed away, as well as infinite beings and worlds.
But today, O virtuous one, this Yama, the son of Vivasvat and leader of the ancestors, has now [arrived] when certain [of our merits] have been exhausted.
In each age, for the sake of destroying sins, one must perform the practice of vows here in one's own person for twelve years, having cast far away wife and children.
Therefore, this earth will become densely crowded with mortal beings who are as if immortal; oppressed by those who have become a burden, it will be like a thicket of shrubs.
Her body overwhelmed by the burden of the earth, she will seek refuge in Hari, just as a beloved wife, distressed and overcome by bandits, seeks her husband.
Then Hari shall descend to the earth in two bodies, together with all the portions of the gods who have entered into Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
The son of Vasudeva alone shall be known as Vāsudeva; he will be one body of Hari, while the second shall be the Pāṇḍava Arjuna.
Known as Yudhiṣṭhira, he will be the son of Dharma; that knower of dharma, the son of Pāṇḍu, will be the king of the earth girt by the oceans.
He will have a brother born of his paternal uncle known as Duryodhana; between them there will be a firm enmity, like that between Bhima and the mongoose over the snake.
As those two, eager for battle, seize each other’s thighs, eighteen terrifying akṣauhiṇīs will clash there.
Upon their destruction, Viṣṇu will bring about the division of the earth through the bodies of Rāghava and Arjuna, the wielder of the great Gāṇḍīva bow.
In the case of Viṣṇu and those named Arjuna, the body, having first assumed a natural state, will possess human attributes, filled with joy and indignation.
Seeing his own kinsmen within both armies on the verge of death, he will fall into despondency and will not exert himself for battle.
O Rāghava, for the sole purpose of accomplishing the task at hand, Hari will awaken that body named Arjuna by means of the body of Buddha.
It is never born, nor does it ever die; having come into being, it will not cease to be. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.
He who thinks this [Self] is a slayer, and he who thinks it is slain—both of them do not understand; this does not slay, nor is it slain.
For the Supreme Lord, the Self, who is infinite, of a single form, subtle even than space—what can perish, how, and by what means?

O Self of consciousness, behold the Self—endless, unmanifest, and without beginning or middle! You are the expansive form of consciousness, free from defect; you are unborn, eternal, and beyond all affliction.
The Blessed One said: "O Arjuna, you are not the slayer; abandon this impurity of egoism. You are yourself the eternal Self, liberated from old age and death."
He whose state of being is free from egoism, and whose intellect is not tainted—even by killing these worlds, he does not kill, nor is he bound.
Whatever consciousness arises within is experienced as "this is he," "I am this," or "that is mine"; abandon such internal consciousness.
And because of this very [identification], O Bhārata, you are distressed on all sides by pleasure and pain, being helpless and thinking, "I am joined with this" and "I am destroyed."
Actions performed by the qualities through their own constituent parts are [perceived] individually; one whose self is deluded by egoism thinks, "I am the doer."
Let the eye see, let the ear hear, let the skin touch this, and let the tongue experience taste; what is the status of "Who am I? in this regard?
Even when the mind of the Great-Souled One is engaged in the activity of time-keeping, there is no sense of "I" therein; what portion of affliction could possibly belong to you?
O Bhārata, when something is accomplished by many through their collective effort, a single person who seizes the credit for it out of pride is seized only for ridicule.
Yogis perform action with the body, mind, intellect, and even with the senses alone, having abandoned attachment for the sake of self-purification.
Those whose bodies have not been slain by the powder of the poison of "I-ness"—even while they are taking or giving—have not yet become free from the cholera of worldly existence.
Nowhere does this body shine, for it is defiled by the impurity of self-attachment; it is like a man who, though wise and deeply learned, is ruined by his lack of moral conduct.
Free from possessiveness and free from egoism, equal in suffering and happiness, and patient—he is not defiled even while performing what ought to be done or what ought not to be done.
And this, O son of Pāṇḍu, is your own duty as a Kṣatriya, most excellent; though it may appear cruel, it is for the highest good, leading indeed to happiness and prosperity.
Even if it be contemptible, or even something else consisting of unrighteousness—whatever your own task may be, O best of men, become one who speaks the truth here in accordance with it.
Even for a fool, one's own action alone leads to the highest good; how much more so for one of noble mind? When the intellect has its egoism dissolved, it is not defiled even when fallen.
Established in yoga, O Dhanañjaya, perform actions while abandoning attachment; being free from attachment, you shall not be bound by the actions you perform as they arise.
Having become one whose body is the peaceful Brahman, perform action consisting of Brahman; through the practice of offering everything to Brahman, you shall become Brahman itself in an instant.
With all your purposes surrendered to the Lord, with your self absorbed in the Lord, free from affliction, you—the soul of all beings—become the Lord who adorns the surface of the earth.

Having renounced all volitional constructs, equanimous, with a peaceful mind, a sage whose self is united with the yoga of renunciation—performing your duties, remain one whose intellect is liberated.

Arjuna said: O Blessed One, [please explain] in every respect the renunciation of attachment, as well as that which consists of offering to Brahman, and that which takes the form of offering to the Lord—namely, renunciation.
Likewise, O Lord, what is the distinction between knowledge and yoga? Tell me this in due order for the sake of dispelling great delusion.

The Blessed One said: When all volitional constructions have subsided and dense latent impressions are stilled, that which possesses no form of mental cultivation—that they know to be the supreme Brahman.
Those of perfected intellect know that exertion to be knowledge and yoga; they know the offering to Brahman to be the realization: "Brahman is everything—the world and I."
Empty within and empty without, like a heart of stone; peaceful, as clear as the expanse of space, it is neither the visible object nor beyond the faculty of sight.
Then, that slight emergence which arises as a slight otherness—this manifestation of the world—is like space, being emptiness itself.
This notion that "I am an entity" arises in each individual consciousness as a mere infinitesimal fraction of its infinite parts; what kind of attachment could there possibly be toward such a thing?
This [Self], though indeed non-different, remains as if it were different; for one does not perceive "I" as being separate, since separateness has no ultimate limit.
Just as there is "I" here, so too is there a jar and so forth here; likewise, the ocean exists in this very way. Why then is there such a grasping toward the ego?

When the various forms of conceptual construction flash forth within the self whose essence is pure consciousness—even though it is diverse in its manifoldness—why is there no apprehension of its underlying unity?

For one who has thus understood the distinction, there is the total destruction of that [ignorance] within the intellect; the wise know that renunciation (saṃnyāsa) to be the relinquishing of the fruits of actions.
Renunciation is said to be the absence of attachment to the web of mental constructs; it is the contemplation of the oneness of the Lord within the entire web of conceptualizations.

This very offering to the Lord, in which the appearance of duality has dissolved, is [the true state]; yet, due to the power of ignorance, there is a distinction among these [offerings] within the conscious Self that exists only in name.
The meaning of the word "Bodha" (Awakening) is indeed the one world; of this there is no doubt. I am the quarters, I am the world, I am the self, and I am also action.

I am Time; I am non-duality, and I am duality; I am the universe. Fix your mind on me, be my devotee, sacrifice to me, and bow down to me. Thus, with your self disciplined and making me your supreme goal, you shall come to me alone.
Arjuna said: O Lord of gods, you have two forms—the supreme and the non-supreme. Of what nature is that [supreme] form, and at what time shall I abide by resorting to it for the sake of perfection?
The Blessed One said: "O sinless one, know that my two forms are the common and the supreme; the common form is endowed with hands and other limbs, and bears the conch, the discus, and the mace."
My supreme form is without beginning or end, unique and free from affliction; it is expressed by such terms as Brahman, Ātman, and Paramātman.
As long as you remain unawakened, dwelling in the state of not knowing the self, so long remain devoted to the worship of the four-armed deity.
Through that sequence you shall become fully awakened, and from that you will know that which is supreme—my form without beginning or end, by means of which one is not born again.
Or if, O crusher of enemies, there is a being known through cognition as an object of knowledge, then quickly take refuge in that very self of mine as your own self.
When I declare, "I am this" and "I am that," it is this very reality of the Self (ātmatattva) that I am indeed instructing you upon.
I believe you have awakened rightly; you have found rest in the ultimate state. You are now liberated from all mental constructs; become one whose sole essence is truth.
Behold the Self abiding in all beings, and all beings within the Self; with your mind disciplined by yoga, see the same everywhere.
One who perceives the Self abiding in all beings and attains oneness with that Self, even while engaged in activities in every way, is not born again.

Oneness is the meaning of all words, and oneness is the meaning of the word "Self"; and for one who quickly realizes that even the Self is neither existent nor non-existent, that [oneness] belongs to him.
The certainty that "I am that Self which has ascended to direct experience—that illuminator which is the inner light within the minds of the three worlds"—is the conclusion.
O Bhārata, that experience of flavor which exists within the waters of the three worlds—both those produced from cows and those born of the ocean—is this very Self.
That subtle experience which resides within all bodies, being liberated from anything to be experienced, is this all-pervading Self.
Just as ghee exists within milk when it is complete, so does the Supreme abide within all objects and bodies.
Just as the radiance of all the jewels in the oceans exists both within and without, so do I exist within bodies, yet remaining as if unestablished therein.
Just as space exists within and without thousands of jars, so do I, the Self, abide within the bodies of the three worlds.
Just as a thread remains unperceived while its body is strung with hundreds of streams of pearls, so does this Self remain unperceived while abiding within hundreds of thousands of bodies.
In this multitude of objects, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, that which is the universal existence (sattāsāmānya) is known as the unborn Self (ātman).
That Brahman, its form slightly vibrating, remains as Brahman alone; yet, through a succession of delusions, it appears as "I-ness" and so forth, and as the world and so forth.
This entire world is indeed the Self; what is it here that is killed or kills? O Arjuna, how can this Self be tainted by the auspicious or inauspicious sufferings of the world?
He who sees that which remains like a witness, like a mirror amidst reflections—unperishing while things perish—he truly sees.
"This is mine and this is not mine"—this is what is said by me. "In this way I am the Self, the Self of all; know Me thus, O Pāṇḍava."
All these transformations of creation and dissolution proceed within the Self, residing in the mind as the sense of "I," like the ripples of water in the ocean.
Just as there is stoneness in mountains, woodness in trees, and waterness in waves, so too is there the nature of the Self in all entities.
He who sees the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in the Self, and likewise sees the Self as the non-agent—he truly sees.
Just as water exists within waves of various forms and transformations, or as gold exists within bracelets and other ornaments, so too, O Arjuna, does the Self exist within all beings.
Just as various groups of waves are restless in water, or as bracelets and other ornaments are [manifested] in gold, so too are all beings in the Supreme Self.
O Bhārata, know that the entire collection of objects, the elements, and the Great Brahman are one and the same; there is not even the slightest degree of difference between them.
Is there anything in the three worlds that can be perceived as a transformation of those states? Where are they, or where is the world itself? Why do you delude yourself in vain?
Having heard this and having internalized it with firm certainty, the virtuous, liberated while living, move about here with minds of equanimity toward all things.

Free from pride and delusion, having conquered the fault of attachment, constant in the inner self, with desires turned away, liberated from the dualities known as pleasure and pain, the undeluded go to that imperishable state.
The Blessed Lord said: Listen again, O mighty-armed one, to my supreme word, which I shall speak to you, who are pleased with me, out of a desire for your welfare.
For the contacts of the senses with their objects, O son of Kuntī, which give rise to cold and heat, pleasure and pain, are transitory, coming and going; endure them, O Bhārata.
But they are not distinct from the one Self; where, then, is suffering and where is happiness? In that which is without beginning or end and without parts, how can there be filling or breaking?

Established in that which is called the mere contact of the senses, consisting of the delusion regarding the contact of those sense-objects, the wise man who remains equanimous toward pleasure and pain is fit for immortality.
Since the self is all-pervasive, these [distinctions] exist as if they were distinct divisions; yet, being unreal in nature, how can that which is unreal be unable to endure?
Pleasure and pain do not exist even slightly, nor in any way at all; since the reality of the Self is all-pervasive, how could there be the existence of a non-self?
The non-existent has no being, and the existent has no non-being; pleasure, pain, and the like do not exist at all, for the omnipresent Supreme Self alone exists.
Having abandoned the notions of existence and non-existence regarding these two—the world and the self—and having abandoned everything in between, remain established in that which remains.
The self does not rejoice in pleasures nor does it languish in sorrows, O Arjuna; for although it is the conscious self that perceives what is seen, it remains within the body.
The insentient mind and so forth, having attained the state of a body, are the vessel of suffering; yet, when this [body] is injured or destroyed, there is no injury whatsoever to the Self.
O dear one, know that this insentient body and so forth—which exists as the experiencer of suffering and the like—is merely an illusion of māyā, arisen through the power of ignorance.
Nothing whatsoever, such as the body and so forth, nor suffering and so forth, exists as something separate from the self; therefore, what could be experienced by whom?
O Bhārata, that which I speak of here perishes by that very [speaking]; for delusion, which arises from ignorance, is suffering, and it is dispelled by perfect awakening.
Just as the fear of a snake in a rope, born of ignorance, perishes through knowledge, so too do suffering and the like regarding the body and so forth, born of ignorance, perish through knowledge.
"Brahman, which is everywhere, the universe, and unborn, neither perishes nor is born; know this to be the supreme truth—this is the highest awakening."
Having become a mere wave in the ocean of Brahman, you dissolve; now you shimmer within the whirlpool of Brahman—you are indeed Brahman itself, free from all affliction.
Just as you, I, and the soldiers are like the passing away of time, and just as vibrations are to Brahman, so too do the delusions of existence and non-existence not exist here.
Abandon pride, intoxication, grief, fear, desire, and pleasure and pain; this duality is of an unreal nature—become one, possessing the nature of reality.
Through the destruction of the akṣauhiṇīs of men, which consists of experience, make the pure Brahman—which has been expanded by Brahmā—consist of Brahman.
Without perceiving pleasure or pain, gain or loss, victory or defeat, attain oneness with pure Brahman; for you, O Bhārata, are indeed the ocean of Brahman.
Becoming equal toward gain and loss, and indeed possessing nothing at all, remain motionless like a windless spot and perform your natural duty.
Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give, and whatever you shall do, O son of Kuntī—regard all that as the Self; remain steadfast in this conviction.
Whatever one is inwardly composed of, that one undoubtedly attains; therefore, to attain the truth of Brahman, become composed of the truth of Brahman.
Having become Brahman, which is the fruit independent of anything else, and having realized "I am Brahman," the knower of Brahman performs action only as it comes, without any personal motive.
He who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, he is wise among men; he is called a performer of all actions.
Do not let the fruit of action be your motive, nor let there be attachment to inaction; established in yoga, perform actions, O Dhananjaya, having abandoned attachment.
Without relying on attachment to action, nor likewise relying on delusion, and even without relying on inaction, remain established as you are.
Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action, ever-contented and independent, even though fully engaged in action, he does nothing at all.
They say that attachment constitutes agency; even for one who is not the agent, that [agency] arises when the mind remains in a state of ignorance. Therefore, one should abandon ignorance.
By relying on a supreme knower of reality, the great-souled one who has attained freedom from desire experiences no sense of agency whatsoever, even while engaged in all worldly activities.

From the absence of agency comes the absence of being an enjoyer; from the absence of being an enjoyer comes equanimity and oneness; from equanimity and oneness comes infinity, and from that, the pervasive state of Brahman.
Having cast off the stain of manifoldness and attained oneness with the Supreme Self, you are not truly the doer, O Arjuna, whether performing what is to be done or what is not to be done.
The wise call him a learned man whose every undertaking is free from desire and purposeful intent, and whose actions have been consumed by the fire of knowledge.
He who remains equanimous, gentle, steady, self-abiding, peaceful, and free from desire for any object—even while appearing distracted, he has attained a state of complete undistractedness.
Free from dualities, eternally established in purity, indifferent to acquisition and preservation, and self-possessed, become one who follows whatever comes to you, adorning the surface of the earth.
He who sits restraining the organs of action while dwelling on the objects of the senses with his mind is a deluded soul; he is called a hypocrite.
But he who, O Arjuna, having restrained the senses with the mind, engages in the yoga of action through the organs of action while remaining unattached—he is preeminent.
Just as the waters enter the ocean, which remains full and established in immovability, even so all desires enter him; he attains peace, but not the one who hankers after desires.
The Blessed One said: One should not renounce enjoyments, nor should one cultivate a preoccupation with enjoyments; one should remain perfectly equanimous, following whatever comes to pass.

Do not conceive of a self in the body, which is non-self, nor of a self in worldly existence, which is non-self; rather, conceive of the self only in the true Self, whose nature is the cessation of becoming.
O mighty-armed one, upon the destruction of the body, nothing at all is destroyed; for the destruction of the self would indeed be destruction, yet the self is eternal and does not perish.
For he whose self is mindless and who has renounced all possessions does not perish; even though fully engaged in action, he truly does nothing at all.
They say that attachment constitutes agency; even for one who does not act, that [agency] may arise. For when the mind is established in ignorance, therefore one should abandon ignorance.
By relying on the supreme knower of reality, the great-souled one who is free from desire, the sense of agency never arises, even while he is engaged in all activities.
The wise know the Self to be indestructible, without beginning or end, and undecaying; let there not be for you the painful misconception here that "the Self perishes."
The supreme ones who have realized the self do not perceive in that way; those who imagine themselves to be the self perceive the self within their own [bodies] as a non-self.
Arjuna said: "If this is so, O Lord of the three worlds, O bestower of honor even upon the ignorant, then when the destruction of the body occurs, nothing desired is lost at all."
The Blessed One said: "It is so, O mighty-armed one; nothing whatsoever perishes anywhere. The Self alone exists as an imperishable essence; what of it could perish, and where?"
Apart from the delusive confusion of thinking "this is lost" or "this is gained," I do not perceive anything else in that way, just like the son of a barren woman.
The unreal has no being; the real never ceases to be. The truth regarding both of these has been perceived by the seers of reality.
But know that to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded; no one is able to effect the destruction of this immutable.
These bodies are said to have an end, belonging to the eternal, indestructible, and immeasurable embodied self; therefore, fight, O Bhārata!
The Self is one; there is no duality. How could that which is non-existent come into being? It is indestructible and infinite; for that which is existent, destruction does not exist.
When duality and unity are abandoned, that which remains as the residue—tranquil, between existence and non-existence—that is the supreme state here.
Arjuna said: "O Blessed One, since I am as good as dead, what is the purpose of the worldly condition of men? And how, O Lord, do heaven and hell exist within that condition of the worlds?"
The Blessed Lord said: Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, and intellect—this aggregate consisting of these subtle elements constitutes the individual soul (jīva) that dwells within bodies.
He is dragged along by latent impressions as if a young animal by a rope; he remains within the body like a bird in a cage.
Due to the influence of latent impressions, that [consciousness] passes away from the body—which has reached a state of decay through time and place—just as sap flows out from a fig leaf.
Having taken hold of these—the ear, the eye, the sense of touch, the tongue, and the nose—it departs, just as the wind carries fragrances from their source.

This body belongs solely to one who possesses latent impressions (*vāsanā*); it does not arise from any other cause. When latent impressions are abandoned, the body perishes; once it has perished, that supreme state is attained.
Possessed by latent impressions and nourished by the Supreme, the individual soul wanders through various wombs, burdened by the weight of its delusions, like a puppet of Māyā.

Under the influence of latent impressions (vāsanā), the individual soul (jīva) departs from the body, taking with it all the senses in their essential nature, just as the wind carries fragrance from a flower.
O son of Kuntī, when the life-force has departed, the body becomes motionless, its limbs and form devoid of movement like a tree when the wind has ceased.
Devoid of activity and rendered invisible by defects such as cutting and piercing, the body, being bereft of life, is therefore called "dead."
Wherever that living being, whose form is breath, abides in space, it perceives each respective extended form through the habitual practice of its own latent impressions.
For this body is perceived by the living soul as if it were non-existent; upon its destruction, you too should view yourself in this same way, or else remain like one in deep sleep.

Just as he perceives their forms, so too does he perceive their destruction; for it is said that at the beginning of creation, through meditative cultivation, he perceived these very things in this manner.
For at the moment of its sudden emergence, whatever appears before it, that very thing remains inseparably connected to this consciousness until its final fall.
The root of past latent impressions is overcome by human effort through present exertion, just as one quickly overcomes a dwelling place from yesterday with today's effort.
That very portion of the preceding and succeeding distinction which is perceived by a powerful person in an instant clearly triumphs.
Even if the Vindhya mountain were to split asunder or the wind of universal destruction were to blow, a wise person must never abandon human effort in accordance with the scriptures.

Under the influence of latent impressions regarding the creation of hells, heavens, and so forth, the living being—whose intellect is clouded by long-standing, deep-seated delusion—perceives these things all around itself.
Arjuna said: O Lord of the World, tell me what is the cause of this world's existence—the agitation consisting of the creation of hell, heaven, and so forth—for the living being.

The Blessed One said: "In this world, the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā) for the sake of the highest good is like a dream; yet, through the force of long-standing habituation, it becomes matured and causes the delusion of saṃsāra."

Arjuna said: "O Lord of the gods of gods, from what does it arise, and how is latent impression (vāsanā) destroyed? The Blessed One said: "Latent impression, which arises from the delusion of ignorance and consists of the conception of the self in that which is not the self, goes to its dissolution through the great awakening of self-knowledge."
O son of Kuntī, you have cultivated your self and have realized the truth; abandon the latent impression that "this is he," "I am this one," or "these people are mine."

Arjuna said: Upon the dissolution of latent impressions (vāsanā), the individual soul (jīva) dissolves of its own accord; for whatever has become swollen through the existence of something else, that dissolves upon the destruction of that thing.
When the individual soul has undergone dissolution and the conditions of space and time have been altered, who is it that becomes the vessel for birth and death?
The Blessed One said: O Mahāmati, know that the very self-form which is turbid through its own imagined conceptualizations is the individual soul (jīva) characterized by latent impressions (vāsanā).
O Bhārata, know that liberation is that immutable nature of the self which is independent, free from volition, and released from latent impressions through awakening.
O mighty-armed one, even while living, perceive reality as it truly exists; one who is liberated from the teacher of latent impressions is called "liberated."
He who is not free from latent tendencies is certainly not one who is devoted to all dharmas; even if he were omniscient, he would be bound on all sides like a bird confined in a cage.

He whose subtle latent impression (vāsanā) flickers within like a peacock feather in the sky of the difficult-to-perceive mind becomes liberated in this very world; for indeed, latent impression alone is bondage, and its destruction is surely liberation.
The Blessed One said: O Arjuna, by means of this state of being free from latent desires and thus liberated while living, attain inner coolness and abandon the impurity of grief for your kinsmen.
O sinless one, you are free from fear regarding old age and death; your mind is as pure as space; having abandoned all thoughts of the desirable and the undesirable, you are devoid of passion.
This task has fallen into the stream of events just as it came; perform your duties and actions, for nothing here is ever lost.
Whatever action is performed that has simply fallen into the natural flow, this is the very nature of one liberated while living; such is liberation while living.
The determination that "I shall abandon this action" or "I shall resort to this" is the nature of the deluded mind; for the wise, however, there is equanimity.
Performing actions as they flow along with the current, those whose minds are tranquil—liberated while living—vibrate here like those in deep sleep, remaining in a state of deep sleep.
The senses of one whose [mind] naturally remains within the heart, withdrawn from the objects of the senses, attain a steady state on all sides, like the limbs of a tortoise.
In the same way, the painter of the mind creates within the Universal Self the picture of the three worlds—devoid of a wall and consisting of the three periods of time—as the universe arises.
In the sky, although it is of the nature of space, a manifold painting has been spread out clearly by the painter of the mind, using the various activities as its pigments.
"Alas, what a delusion! This wall behind me has been made of the nature of space; yet this auspicious wall made of grass and mud is truly unprecedented and a great illusion."
There is not even the slightest difference between these clearly perceived walls produced by the mind’s painting; they are both equally apprehended as such.
O lotus-eyed one, know that those [worlds] are more empty than space, just as the arising and passing away of worlds appear in an instant within the mind during delusion.

The self and this world, including all that is internal and external, are like the sky; they are merely the kingdom of ancient mental constructs, and it is from this that their so-called reality arises.
However, even when not perceived, truth does not exist at all within delusion; through gradual perception, truth is dissolved by that very perception.
Though appearing, it is as insubstantial as a circle of clouds in autumn; like painted figures situated within a painting created by the artist that is the mind.
Due to the absence of walls, those things such as the three worlds are formless and exist outside; they do not exist, nor do you exist—what is being obstructed by what?
Having abandoned the delusion of the obstructed and the obstructor, become stainless in the void; for there is no activity of the sky, and activity itself is of the nature of the sky.
Therefore, the sky—pure and free from time, action, walls, and parts—is established within the mind; like a painting, it possesses form and consists of everything.
Know this entire world to be even more empty than the sky; it is a painting created upon the wall of the mind by the painter that is consciousness.
Through universal emptiness, it does not differ from space even in the slightest; just as the manifestation and dissolution of the world's emanations occur within the radiant mind.
Know, O friend, that in an instant these two were likewise situated upon the earth; today, within the kingdom of the mind—which consists of various experiences—they have perished.
Conceptual construction is imagined through a delusion that arises in an instant; it is capable of creating a mental kingdom that is utterly non-existent, just as the mind can do.
In the same way, when a powerful mind transforms a moment into an eon, it turns that single moment into an eon; thus, it makes the small into something vast.
"This is a delusion that has arisen, thinking that what is non-existent quickly becomes existent; in an instant, a kingdom of the mind appears by its very nature."
That which is of a manifold nature is established as this web of the world; because it culminates in nirvāṇa at the time of creation, it has arisen as consisting of moments.
The quality of being as solid as a diamond is here merely imagined through the power of creative intuition; for it is simply a reversal of appearance for one who has not understood its true nature.
Whether in engagement or in withdrawal, what indeed is this adamantine essence? When has the variegated world, painted by the mind, ever existed as something residing within the consciousness?
Even though there is no wall here, this [vision] appears before me as if vast and richly colored; oh, how marvelous! A brilliant painting has arisen without any supporting surface.
The world is clearly a painting that deludes the vision; it is a composition of various pigments of darkness and a coloring with various rays of light.
It possesses the limbs and members of various ritual procedures, is colored by various passions, is rich with the play of various views, and has eyes that perceive various experiences.
The sky is a lake of blue water, with various planets as its fierce ripples, diverse forms as its foremost and final features, and the stars, moon, and sun as its blossoming lotuses.

The leaf-patterns were formed by rows of clouds intent on various arrangements; the walls of the sky were like young women painted with the figures of gods, asuras, and human princes upon their forearms; and the supreme light was like the face of a maiden.

This charming little daughter, who captivates the three worlds, is fashioned out of space alone as a single stage for her manifestation; she colors all the worlds with the wheel of pure consciousness, and is made restless by the playful artist that is the flickering mind.

Her vine-like limbs are of gold, her mass of hair is thick, and she surveys the world with the movement of eyes like the sun and moon; she is clothed in the scriptures that govern dharma, artha, and kāma, and her feet move through the underworld while her high hips rest upon the earth.

Her four arms are as formidable as those of Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, and Hari; her slender body shines with breasts that are high and covered by living beings; she sits upon a lotus-throne on the surface of the earth encircled by great serpents, and the interior of the vast world, including its mountains, has become her leaf-like garment.

Her eye-movement dispels the flickering darkness of night; her hair stands on end like formidable stars; her row of teeth is like a circle of thunderbolts; she causes horripilation to arise in the fourteen kinds of incomparable beings as they tremble; and she is like the Kadamba flower at the time of universal dissolution.

The three worlds, endowed with living beings, fashioned out of space itself and diverse in nature, were created by the mind—which is of the nature of space—as a supreme puppet by a long-time, extraordinary painter skilled in the art of painting.
The Blessed One said: O Arjuna, know this to be a great marvel, for it is indeed strange that the painting appears first and only afterwards does the wall arise.
When a painting has been produced without a wall, a vast wall is seen; oh, how wonderful is this illusion! A gourd sinks and a stone floats.
In the three worlds, which are like a painting situated within the mind and whose nature is space, why has this "I-ness" arisen in you, whose own nature is space?
Everything is made of space; by space, in space, space dissolves. Space is experienced in space; space is spread throughout space.
Bound by the rope of latent impressions (vāsanā) like a long tethering-cord, O Arjuna, it is unraveled here precisely by the unraveling of those latent impressions.
Just as a reflection appears in a mirror, so does this [universe] appear within Brahman itself; it is inaccessible to cutting, piercing, and the like, because it is non-different from its substratum.
In Brahman, which is the sky of the Brahmas, there is no other, nor any cutting or breaking; by what, how, of what, or by whom could it be cut, or where could it be divided?

Therefore, through awakening, the absence of latent impressions has indeed been accomplished for you; for one who is not free from latent impressions is surely not truly devoted to all dharmas, even if they are so intent.
Even one who is omniscient remains bound by the self, like a lion confined within a cage, provided that even a very small seed of latent impression (vāsanā) exists within the soil of consciousness.

For him, the forest of cyclic existence arises again and again; however, when the seed of latent impressions has been utterly consumed by the fire of the awakening to truth—which has taken root in the heart through constant practice—it does not sprout again.
But when the seed of latent impressions is burnt, one does not sink into objects such as pleasure and pain; one remains pure, like a lotus leaf in water.

With a tranquil self, free from fear, having abandoned immeasurable desires, extinguished, and with the great delusion of the mind dissolved—having understood that purifying truth heard [in the scriptures]—abide within yourself as one whose nature is singular peace, free from all injury.
Arjuna said: "The delusion is destroyed; memory has been regained by me through Your grace, O Acyuta. I stand firm, my doubts dispelled; I shall do as You command."

The Blessed One said: "If the mental fluctuations have clearly subsided within the heart through awakening, know that the mind has indeed become tranquil internally and has attained the state of pure being (sattva)."

In this context, that which is devoid of "that" and "this," which is named direct consciousness (*pratyak-cetana*), which is entirely free from all [limitations], which is everything, and which is present everywhere—[that is the Self].
None of these worldly beings know that state, just as those on the ground cannot perceive a bird soaring high in the sky.
Know this Self to be inwardly conscious, appearing as a reflection, pure, devoid of volition, and inaccessible—just like the distant [object] in the case of visual perceptions.
That which transcends all, being utterly transparent and pure, cannot have its state perceived by one’s own habitual tendencies, just as the vision of ordinary people cannot perceive atoms.
When that [state] is attained, all these things such as jars and cloths are utterly exhausted; what then can the wretched latent impression (vāsanā) do there in the supreme state?
Just as a trace of frost dissolves upon reaching a mountain of fire, so too does ignorance dissolve upon encountering the pure reality of the mind.
Where is this wretched, trivial, and dusty latent impression that binds one to enjoyment, and where is the vast wind of the true nature of consciousness that fills the entire web of the universe?
This ignorance, which undergoes various forms of transformation, continues to manifest only so long as this pure self is not fully realized by the self through itself.
All perceptions of the visible have ceased, and thus pure transparency alone has arisen; it is like the sky within that state, one's own self, which fills everything.
That supreme reality, which possesses all forms yet is devoid of all forms, and which transcends speech—by what indeed can it be compared?

Therefore, having skillfully cast away the latent tendencies toward existence—which are like cholera caused by the poison of sensory objects—through the application of the mantra that abandons what is desired, become a lord of liberation, O Blessed One, a ground no longer subject to fears.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the Lord of the Three Worlds had spoken thus and remained silent before them for a moment, then the son of Pāṇḍu addressed these words there, like a bee approaching a cluster of dark lotuses.
Arjuna said: O Blessed One, by your word, this mind of mine has reached its supreme exaltation, having shed the entire burden of sorrow, like a lotus-plant awakened by the sun, the lord of the world.
Having spoken thus, Arjuna, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow who has the monkey as his charioteer, rose up; free from all doubt, he will perform the sport of battle.

He will make the earth a land of great rivers flowing with blood from wounded elephants, horses, and charioteers; and he will make the sky a place where the eye of the sun is obscured by the vast dust-storms spreading from the multitude of his arrows.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, maintaining this vision which destroys all evil, remain established as one whose nature consists of non-attachment, renunciation, and the offering of all to Brahman.
Know that Supreme Self to be the one in whom all exists, from whom all proceeds, who is all, who is everywhere, and who eternally consists of all.
Though situated at a distance, it is not distant; it is all-pervading and yet remains right where it is. Abiding in that, you attain its very existence; that indeed is it, free from doubt.
Know that supreme state to be the manifestation of consciousness (cidābhāsa) which is free from the object of cognition, uncreated awareness, and liberated from all that is thinkable.
She is the supreme, the ultimate limit; she is the unsurpassed vision among all visions; she is the greatness of all greatnesses, and likewise, she is the teacher of all teachers.
That is the Self, and that is consciousness; that is emptiness, that is the supreme Brahman; that is the highest good, that is Śiva, the peaceful; that is knowledge, that is the ultimate state.
This Self within consciousness, whose nature is universal experience, is that wherein all objective substances are relished through their very existence as one's own essence.
He is the essence of the sesame oil within the world; he is the lamp for the house of the world; he is the sap of the tree of the world; he is the protector of the cattle of the world.
He is the thread upon which the pearls of liberated beings are strung, and he is the supreme sharpness of the multitude of black peppers that are the elements.
He is the substantiality in an object, he is that supreme reality; he is the existence of an existing thing, or the non-existence of an existent thing by its own nature.
He who is himself attained as the very Self through the diversity of his own experience—indeed, all the states of the world are beautiful when left unexamined.
Existing entities are non-existent, crumbling under analysis within the web of the world—the very essence of which is a mass of false delusion—beginning with the notion of "I."
Having become what, do I persist? How has the intellect attained its state? I am the beginning, middle, and end; I am the measures and the mental constructions of volition.
"The space of Brahman is without beginning or end; what limit could there be to my own Self?"—one who possesses such internal certainty conducts oneself correctly in external affairs.
Always remaining within, free from rising and setting, that mind which abides in perfect equanimity neither sets nor rises.
He whose emptiness is like that of space, that great-souled one here possesses such a body; having ascended to the state of non-dual existence with an intellect as profound as deep sleep.
Even while engaged in worldly activity, he does not undergo agitation, just like a man reflected in a mirror; for even though he performs activities, he is like the person within the mirror.
He whose heart is not even slightly scarred by mental impressions partakes of liberation; he is reflected within the jewel of consciousness as if without division, like an image in a mirror.
Due to the supreme purity of consciousness, worldly activity proceeds as it does; this world appears as nothing other than the very wonder of consciousness.

Herein there is neither unity nor duality; even my instruction is composed of that [reality]. Through the wonders of the expressed and the expresser, of the disciple and the teacher’s words, [this is realized].
Within consciousness itself, the tranquil consciousness alone manifests as wonder within consciousness; for the vibration of consciousness is saṃsāra, while its non-vibration is the supreme state.

This cycle of existence is pacified by the stilling of the vibration of consciousness; when the Great Consciousness is bowed to, there is no objective referent, and that which is the exhaustion of mental cultivation is the state of partless being.
Even though it has no intrinsic nature, the vibration of its cognition is described as emptiness; that which is non-inert is said by the wise to be the supreme body of consciousness.
In reality, this cycle of existence is experienced as dependent upon mental cultivation; and through the mere dissolution of that cultivation, it becomes essentially void.
Through the state of absolute isolation, that very consciousness remains in its pure form; the wise know that the vibration of consciousness alone is what sets the wheel of saṃsāra in motion.

Just as bracelets and other ornaments do not exist separately from gold, the knower, the measure, and the object of knowledge do not exist apart from consciousness; nor does the movement of consciousness constitute transmigratory existence.

The mind alone is the vibration of consciousness; indeed, the lack of awareness of that [consciousness] is transmigratory existence. In the mere absence of awareness, the vibration of consciousness arises like the state of being a bracelet.

O Rāma, when this [mind] has dissolved into mere awareness, pure consciousness alone remains; by the mere awakening to one’s own true nature, the latent impressions of worldly enjoyment are exhausted.
In this world, the non-cultivation of enjoyments is itself the supreme characteristic of one who possesses knowledge; for by their very nature, all enjoyments are undesirable to the knower.
For who is ever so satiated as to desire bad food? Know this alone to be another characteristic of true wisdom.
It is certain that the non-desire for enjoyments exists by its very nature as the vibration of the mind itself, which is the form of the Self of all.

That internalized and well-practiced habit which has taken root within is known by the term "knowledge. He who does not enjoy even the objects of enjoyment while they are being experienced is truly wise; for the sake of conforming to worldly conventions, he strikes at the sky with sticks.
Without an artificial intellect, success is not attained.

Even when perceiving itself through the wounding of its own limbs, consciousness—remaining at the limit of the object of thought—perceives delusion as long as it stands within the sphere of the thinkable.

This [universe], whose nature is until-enlightenment, vibrates as the form of vibration; yet when perfect enlightenment arises within, there occurs the sequence of states of both vibration and non-vibration.
And that which is designated as the lamp of consciousness, by its very nature, goes somewhere when it has become completely extinguished, like a lamp whose flame has been stilled.
Here, there is not even the slightest talk of vibration or non-vibration; for that which is the non-vibrating wind is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor something intermediate.

That very form is the subsiding of consciousness within the vibration of non-awareness; the vibration of consciousness would be non-different from consciousness itself, assuming the form of the expansion of pure consciousness.
If consciousness (citi) abides solely within the Self, neither for bondage nor for liberation, and does not perceive any objectless cognition, it finds no nirvāṇa.

Even the names of such categories as bondage and liberation do not exist here; the internal realization that "let there be liberation" is itself fullness, which is the cause of the exhaustion [of duality].
Even the thought "let there be equanimity" is a bond for you; the supreme good is the non-perception [of objects]. Know that which is without appearance and is not inert to be the supreme state.

The nature and configuration of the intellect consists in its being oriented toward that which is not an object of cognition; it is the vibration of the Great Consciousness whose form is the conceptualization of words and their meanings.

This [self], which is subject to bondage, liberation, and so forth, perishes when it is scrutinized; for by that very scrutiny, the ego-sense (ahaṃbhāva) becomes pacified and remains without a substrate.
We do not know by what, what, or for whom one is bound or liberated; for the wise man who is free from conceptual differentiation, it is merely a mental construction.

Therefore, all that has arisen is without volition and without vibration, being unrestrained; for within the wind consisting of vibration, it is always one with consciousness because it is composed of that.

When [the mind] has been utterly exhausted, there is no longer saṃsāra; for when the mass of consciousness remains motionless, the very energy of consciousness is recognized as being incessantly the vibration of consciousness.

Apart from consciousness, no vibration whatsoever remains. While traversing one dream within this long dream composed of the visible world, the knower does not incur delusion, because his own self-awareness is all-pervading.

Within that wherein the existence of the consciousness of creation rises forth incessantly and forcefully, and wherein all these stains of the forms of manifold mental constructions dissolve; within that wherein all perceptions arise as blissful to relish—realize that inner Self through meditation alone.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, the primordial supreme reality is the mass of consciousness, the highest state; Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others are those great forms established therein.
People, like kings, rejoice with great splendor, shining intensely through their powers; they sport for a long time in pastimes such as traveling through the sky.

Just as the inhabitants of heaven rejoice here when someone from among their own people has gone there, so too, my dear, having attained that, one does not die; having attained that, my dear, one does not grieve.
Having attained that, my dear, one lives; having attained that, my dear, one is no longer obstructed—the Supreme Self, whose nature is the shoreless, supreme space.

If even a slight perception of the universal form of existence (*sattāsāmānyarūpa*) is cultivated, then in a mere moment the living being becomes a sage whose mind is liberated; performing the activities of worldly life, you shall no longer suffer.
Śrī Rāma said: Where the mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness have reached their dissolution, and only the universal being (sattāsāmānya) shines forth—who is that called a man of wisdom?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That Brahman which resides within all bodies—eating, drinking, moving about, taking up, and destroying within—is consciousness devoid of any object of consciousness.
That which is all-pervading, devoid of beginning or end, stable, and unacquired—the universal existence of all—is here called the reality of things.
It exists as space within the ether, as sound within sound; it exists as touch within touch, and as the sense of touch within the skin.

It is perceived as taste through its nature as taste and is absorbed in the tongue through its nature as that [taste]; it is seen as form through its nature as form and is absorbed in the eye through its nature as sight.
The nose is seen as nasality; fragrance is declared to be fragrance; the body is nourished as the body, and even the earth is seen as the element of earth.
It exists as liquidity in water, as airiness in air, as heat in fire, and as intellectuality in the intellect.

Through its nature as mind, it is established within the mind; through ego-making, even within the ego; through consciousness, it is rooted in consciousness; and through the state of being the intellect, it has arisen in the intellect.
It is fixed as a tree in a tree, manifested as cloth in cloth, established as a jar in a jar, and arisen as a banyan tree in a banyan tree.
In the stationary as the stationary, in the moving as the moving; in the stone as the state of being a stone, and in the conscious as the state of being conscious.
By being immortal among mortals, by being human among humans, by being an animal among animals, and by being a worm while existing as a worm.

In the sequence of time, the all-pervading Lord exists as time; likewise, in each season, he exists as that season; and in moments such as the *truṭi*, the *kṣaṇa*, and the *nimeṣa*, he is established as their very essence.
In the white, it is born as whiteness; in the black, it abides as blackness; in actions, it exists in the form of vibration; and in destiny, it exists through necessity.
The Supreme Lord abides as stability in that which is stable, as destruction in destruction, and as the nature of arising in that which arises.
One rests in childhood by means of childhood, in youth by means of youth, in the state of old age by means of old age, and in death by means of death.
Thus, the Supreme Lord is non-different from all objects, just as the mass of water in the ocean is non-different from its waves, spray, and ripples.
This diversity of theirs is indeed unreal; for by means of this very reality, it is imagined by the nature of consciousness, just as a ghost is imagined by a child.

"O Great-Souled One, having realized that this entire universe is pervaded everywhere by Me—who am established in all things, free from affliction, and possessed of manifold play—through the very nature of Consciousness as the self-conceived imagination, remain with a tranquil mind in happiness."

Śrī Vālmīki said: When the sage had spoken thus, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.

Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, if the assumption of a body by the lotus-born Brahmā and others is just like our own experience of a circle of dream-cities and towns, [then what is the difference between them and us]?
If all this has arisen in exactly that way as being composed of non-existence, then how has such a firm conviction arisen in us?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The previous creation of Prajāpati appears like our own creation; it consists of the appearance of living beings, yet it does not exist in reality.
Because consciousness is all-pervading, the individual soul is everything and transmigrates everywhere; and that [transmigration] arises from incorrect vision and is destroyed by correct vision.
This manifestation that has arisen before him, which is like a dream and whose sole essence is the notion of "I," remains exceedingly firm.
Just as a man does not perceive the rapid destruction [of objects] within a dream, so too is this [nature of all things] perceived here by the Brahmins in every dream.
This dream belongs to this person who is the manifestation; and Rāma, who is the self of all beings including ourselves, is exactly like that as well.
That which is born from a dream-person consists of that dream-person; for it is experienced that whatever is the seed, such is the fruit, just as in the case of a seed and its result.
Know that to be unreal which is accomplished by means of the unreal; even if an object is capable, it is not proper to cultivate a dense mental impression toward what is unreal.
Whatever arises from a person seen in a dream or similar context—though it be firmly believed in—it must be relinquished as a mental cultivation of what is unreal.
This very creation and so forth appears as a firm conviction within the self; this ancient dream of creation standing before us lasts but a moment.
In that very instant, the state of an eon is imagined, just as this long fragment of a dream arises for Prajāpati.

Thus, for every single living being, that which is called "creation" has arisen; the succession of the various classes of creation exists solely through the nature of the principle of consciousness itself.
Just as water quivers through its fluidity by means of the swirling of eddies, so too this splendor of creation is merely of the nature of a dream and is not real.
Then indeed this world arises; that state has reached dissolution. Just as, in whatever manner, and of whatever nature it was seen, so does it exist in that very same way.
For the ways of dream-delusions are not to be questioned; there is nothing in this world that cannot occur within a delusion.
Diverse perceptions of objects are seen throughout the three worlds, such as fire burning in the midst of water, like the submarine fire in the ocean.
Just as cities exist in the sky as the abodes of those who dwell in celestial palaces, so do lotuses grow upon rocks and trees upon the Golden Mountain.
In that solitary place, all merits reside just as they do in the wish-fulfilling tree; the rocks bear fruit like fruit-bearing trees, and are like clusters of jewels.
Living beings exist within stone, like frogs inside a rock; or water issues forth from stones, as from a moonstone.
In a mere moment, a jar becomes a cloth within the consciousness of sleep; even that which is unreal may be perceived, just as one perceives one's own death in a dream.
Just as water existing within living beings is held spontaneously in the sky, so does the water remain in the atmosphere like a canopy, like the celestial river.
Large rocks fly up like winged mountains; indeed, everything is found within the rock, just as it is with the wish-fulfilling gem.
O Raghava, thoughts bear fruit quickly, just as they do within the celestial gardens; however, those very same thoughts do not bear fruit quickly for liberation and the like.
Even though devoid of consciousness, it performs action like a mechanical man; such are these and other various delusions of undertaking activities.
Even by the playful arts of the Gandharva Śambara, such things were never seen to occur—those things arising from the movement of space, time, action, substances, and jewels.
Objects produced by Gandharvas are infinite and arise from reality; this very impossibility is also established as a possibility.
Arising and non-arising are equally for the sake of perfect accomplishment; it is like the delusion of a dream. There is nothing that is not true, and there is nothing that is not false.
In a dream designated as a creation, everything appears as everything everywhere; a creature whose intellect is immersed in that dream perceives it as if it were stable.

With a mind immersed in the dream of creation, the living being perceives stability in that same way; moving from one delusion to another, passing from one dream to another, the jīva becomes utterly bewildered here by participating in the conviction of extreme stability.

Just as a bewildered deer, encountering the interior of a pit due to the fault of falling into it, falls into delusion; so too does the living being, a vessel for transmigratory existence, fall into delusion consisting solely of the nature of falling.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "In this regard, O Rāghava, I shall tell you this ancient history; listen to it, which concerns a certain mendicant who was possessed of great contemplation."
There was once a certain great bhikṣu who was devoted to the practice of meditative concentration; he spent his entire day constantly engaged in his own religious duties.
That mind of his, purified by the practice of meditative concentration, instantly contemplates whatever it thinks of and quickly attains that state, just as water becomes waves.
Once, having ceased from his meditative absorption, he remained with a one-pointed mind; seated upon his own seat, he reflected for a moment on the sequence of ritual actions.
As he was reflecting, this thought arose within him spontaneously: "I shall quickly manifest the conduct of an ordinary person for the sake of sport."
Having reflected thus, his mind remained for a while in an intermediate state, like water returning to its source merely by abandoning its vibration and configuration.
Then, by that man of the mind, out of his own desire, the name "Jīvaṭa" was suddenly assumed; it remained so, as if by the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit.
Then Jīvaṭa, that man created in a dream, wandered for a long time through the streets of a certain city constructed within a dream.
There, intoxicated as a bee drinking the nectar of a lotus, he drank the beverage; then, with great joy, he fell into a deep sleep as if in sport.
In a dream, he beheld his own state as a Brahmin, satisfied with study and ritual practice, endowed with mere intuitive insight, appearing in his mind like the attainment of another land.
Once, that best of the twice-born, through his dedication to daily duties, fell asleep with his internal faculties withdrawn, like a tree whose essence has returned to its seed-state.
Then, in a dream, the twice-born man himself saw that he had attained the status of a feudal lord; having taken his meal as a lord, he once fell into a deep sleep.
In a dream, he beheld her possessing royal splendor as she protected the circle of the quarters, cherished by a multitude of enjoyments like a creeper graced by a profusion of flowers.
Once, that king, having set aside all desires and being at ease, fell asleep; his own future conduct was present before him, as if it were its own cause manifesting within its effect.
In a dream, he beheld within himself the irreproachable state of a celestial woman, appearing like the blossoming of a flower-cluster upon the swelling sap of a tree’s bud.
Exhausted by passion, that celestial woman fell into a deep sleep; she naturally transformed herself into a female deer, just as water turns into ice.
Once that doe with trembling eyes was overcome by sleep; in a dream, through the firm power of her own habitual practice, she perceived herself as a creeper.
Even animals perceive dreams due to the nature of the mind; the recollection by the consciousness of things seen and heard remains unimpaired.
She became a forest goddess, adorned with the flowers, fruits, and tender shoots of creepers, sporting in the bower-creepers of the forest garden.
By means of an internal consciousness that had ascended to the form of a sprout situated within a seed, she clearly perceived her own cutting.
Having remained in deep sleep for some time and experienced a dense state of insentience through his subtle essence (kalā), he then beheld himself as a steady bee.
Then that six-footed one roamed in the forest among the forest creepers and in the blooming lotus ponds, like a lover among young women.

In those places where swarms of bees hovered over clusters of blossoms, where they sported upon creeper-like strings of pearls, and where the floral honey tasted as sweet as the nectar of a beloved’s bimba-fruit lip.
He became one who, having entered the stalk of a lotus, was distressed within the lotus-pond; for even the mind of a dull-witted person finds delight only in some particular thing.
An elephant came to that lotus pond to agitate it; for the step of the foolish flourishes only for the destruction of beautiful things.
That very lotus-pond was crushed along with him, and he, like a six-legged bee, entered between the tusks and was reduced to powder like a grain of rice.

From the sight of the elephant and through the mental cultivation of that sight of the elephant, the bee perceived itself as having arisen in the state of an elephant intoxicated with the scent of ichor.
The elephant fell into a pit as deep as a dried-up ocean, like a living being in the empty world-cycle, dense with thick darkness.
He became the king's favorite, a destroyer of great enemy forces; always intoxicated by the power of liquor, that night-stalker seemed as if he were reeling.
Once, severed by a sword, he went to his end, like the individual soul within the self when its form has been blown away by the wind of discernment.
Seeing the bees rising from the frontal globes of the elephants' temples, the elephant, due to his constant practice of [mistaking] bees for those on his own temples, became once again a bee.

While enjoying the forest creepers, he returned once more to the lotus pond; for those who lack awakening, the habitual tendencies of past impressions are difficult to abandon and difficult to overcome.
There, crushed by the trampling of an elephant's hoof, he was reduced to powder; yet, through the perception of a swan standing nearby, he became a *kalahaṃsaka* (a type of small crane).
Having wallowed for a very long time in other wombs, Kalahaṃsa eventually came together with many swans and sported with them.
Consciousness, consisting of the Brahma-goose, possesses the subtle essence of both word and meaning; therein, its internal fullness is like the peacock within the egg-fluid.
Pondering that thought, he died, severely struck by disease and woodworms; through the continuous connection with that very awareness, he was born as a crane in the lake of the Lotus-born One.

There, one who possesses constant solitude and has been awakened by aesthetic graces, having abandoned the perception of worldly objects and remaining liberated—even as he stands at the moment of the end of the age—what indeed remains to be contemplated by him, who is already liberated from the body? What further could possibly occur for him?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, on one occasion, that bird beheld Rudra in the city of Rudra, having effortlessly attained the playful grace of the stalk of Brahmā’s lotus.
Thereupon, the thought "I am Rudra" arose in him with certainty, reflected instantly like an image in a mirror.
There, that being, whose body was composed of Rudra and the Bhūtas, cast off his physical form, just as a fragrance released from a cluster of flowers as it passes into the wind.
That Rudra sported at will in the abode of Rudra, distinguished by tens of millions of attendants and engaged in those various practices of the city of Śiva.
But Rudra, by virtue of that singular splendor of his unsurpassed knowledge, perceived with his intellect the entire previous account as if it were but a remnant of a dream.
Then that Blessed One, whose body is consciousness free from obscuration, spoke of his own accord in private, amazed by the hundreds of his own dreams.
Oh, how wondrous is this illusion, which deludes the entire world; though it is unreal, it appears real, like water in desert lands.
Thus, for the first time, I who am consciousness have attained the state of the mind, through the contemplation of the sky-like nature of the all-perfect and omniscient one.
Abiding by chance, the individual soul, colored by the subtle elements of the beings, became in a certain creation a monk who was entirely unperturbed.
When, through that union of limbs, she wanders freely outside with a playful and unagitated form, she is "Rati" by virtue of her inner state.

At that time, through the force of that practice and by the dissolution of all objective existents, the monk experienced only that [emptiness], having abandoned the arising of any other mental construction.
Whatever wonder has taken root in the mind, that alone unfolds; the summer creeper does not shed its leaves even when it drinks the water of spring.
Having become that monk Jīvaṭa, a living being with matured latent impressions, he wandered through those bodies like an ant through its holes.
Then, due to his devotion to the twice-born within himself, he perceived the state of being twice-born; for in the reversal of existence and non-existence, that which is powerful alone increases.
That brahmin attained the state of being constantly contemplated; for the sap, when continuously present, becomes the fruit upon the tree.
Because he performed acts of righteousness for the sake of the kingdom, he became a king; yet, due to his lustful nature, that king attained the state of a celestial nymph.
Lured by her eyes, that fawn became full of passion; alas, the delusion of latent tendencies leads to suffering for living beings!
Alas, that doe remained fixed in mind upon a creeper in the forest; she, the little creeper, inevitably experienced being cut down.
Then, through that crushing pressure, she—being permeated by that state—perceived within herself the condition of being a bee, which had been long practiced through internal consciousness.
Having experienced the crushing of the hooves of wild elephants, he then wandered again and again through the tumultuous whirlpools of great worldly existence.
At the end of hundreds of cycles of saṃsāra, I stand here as that very Rudra, amidst this frantic activity of saṃsāra which is a delusion consisting solely of one's own mind.
Thus, in these many and exceedingly variegated forest lands of saṃsāra, I have wandered greatly, as if they were not empty, for a long time.
In one creation I was named Jīvaṭa; in another, I was an eminent Brāhmaṇa; and in another, I was a lord of the earth.
Having been a swan in a lotus grove and an elephant on the slopes of the Vindhya mountains, I have now reached this state as a deer within the machinery of a body.
Here, infinite thousands of years and hundreds of four-age cycles have passed away, along with the movements of days and seasons.
Even before I first departed from the supreme state, the sequence of my fitness for the life of a mendicant was firmly established through my realization of reality.
Having transcended even further again and again, he attained the state of a Brahman-swan; that very same former practice had borne fruit through the arising of his spiritual union.
Whatever habitual practice has arisen for this living being without obstruction, even if it be utterly flavorless, that alone he quickly pursues.
Sometimes, through a chance occurrence like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, due to meeting with a virtuous person, the soul's habitual practice of unwholesome mental cultivation ceases.
And this prior habituation of latent impressions, acquired through association, depends solely upon its own arising; it awaits the effort of the abandoner.
That which is practiced here incessantly and also in another body, though unreal in both waking and dreaming states, is nevertheless experienced as real.

That which performs various purposeful actions for the sake of both suffering and happiness arises from mental cultivation; therefore, victory consists in the cultivation and non-cultivation of that [cultivation].
Meditation alone perceives its own self as "this body," which is merely an expansion of non-existence, just as a sprout develops into a thicket.
Upon investigation, this cultivation is seen to leave nothing behind here; nor does it even exist. Therefore, let us have enough of that delusion.
May the mere non-perception of this worldly delusion—which has arisen like the color of the sky—be sufficient for our cleansing.
This supreme Being alone, whose nature is not composed of material elements, is to be cherished; if She exists for the sake of sport, She will do nothing else.
Having arisen, I behold all those individual streams of my own saṃsāra; by bestowing perfect illumination, I unify them with myself.
Having reflected thus, Rudra went to that creation where the mendicant, staying in his monastery, lay asleep like a corpse.
Then, having awakened that monk through his own mind and intention, he joined him [in meditation]; the monk also remembered his own delusion.
Beholding Rudra as his own self, and likewise as consisting of Jīvaṭa and the others, that mendicant, though not subject to wonder through his awakening, nevertheless experienced amazement.
Then Rudra and the mendicant, both rising together, departed for some unknown place—the world of Jīvaṭa, situated in a single corner of the space of consciousness.
Having gone there to that palace, that island, that mandala, that region, that city, and having grasped him by the hand with a sword in his grasp;
They beheld Jīvaṭaka lying asleep, his consciousness lost like a corpse, having set aside his physical form and its worldly existence within the realms of becoming.
Having quickly awakened him and directed him through both his mind and his conscious will, those [beings]—Rudra, Jīva, Ṭa, and Bhikṣuka—became either uniform or threefold in form.
Though they were awakened, they appeared as if unawakened; though filled with wonder, they remained without wonder. For a moment, standing in silence, they appeared like figures in a painting.
Then they all went to a certain place situated in the sky, where a vast assembly of brahmins had begun their discourse, resounding with a great tumultuous noise.
Having gone there to that world, they reached that island, that region, that district, that village, and that brahmin’s dwelling.
They saw the Brahmin sleeping in his house, surrounded by his wife; he was held by the neck by the Brahmin woman, appearing as if he were still alive.
Having quickly awakened him and directed him with both mind and consciousness, many others who were situated there likewise became filled with wonder and yet free from it.
Then they went to the royal realm of the world, which was filled with the sky of consciousness, perceived by the intellect, and beautiful in its expansive scope of wandering.
Then they reached that world, that island, and that region; there they beheld the intoxicated Sāmanta sleeping upon a lotus-bed.

Like a female bee resting upon the hollow of a lotus bud, she—golden-limbed and radiant as gold—placed him within the hollow of her breast, as if he were a honey-bee sleeping in the interior of a lotus.
Surrounded by beloved women like a tree entwined with blossoming clusters, he stood amidst the lattice of lamps like a mass of gold set with heaps of jewels.
Having quickly awakened him and engaged him with both mind and consciousness, those many who were situated there became as one—some filled with wonder, others free from it.
Then, having awakened him there, they entered the royal cycle of existence; thereafter, they wandered through other realms of saṃsāra by means of their minds alone.
Having attained that state of Rudra—the desire for the Brahman-swan—all of them came together and shone as the hundred supreme Rudras.
That form of the Supreme Lord is of a single nature yet appears manifold; its body is differentiated by a single consciousness, though it is enveloped by diverse activities.
Then, that hundred-fold [state] of the Rudras is composed of unobscured consciousness; it abides as the connection to all saṃsāra and is situated throughout the entire world.
"O Rāma, there are indeed hundreds upon hundreds of great Rudras here; know that this is the eleventh, established as the cycle of worldly existence."
Whatever arises on all sides from that is indeed the transmigratory existence of the individual soul; therein, the multitudes of unawakened souls do not perceive one another.
For those awakened in mind meet together like waves in the ocean; but those who are unawakened, resting solely on that [mind], remain like clods of earth.
Just as water, due to its fluidity, merges completely with one another in waves, so too do the multitudes of awakened living beings merge thoroughly with one another because of their consciousness.
When each of these has arisen within saṃsāra, the multitudes of living beings exist as if real, though they are unreal, because the element of consciousness is all-pervading.
Whatever is excavated from the earth, that very thing is called "space"; likewise, whatever is projected by the all-pervading consciousness, that is exactly so for consciousness itself.
Just as you perceive all beings here within the realm of conceptual proliferation, so too is the nature of the self of all beings—the state of consciousness—found everywhere here.
Just as a carved statue is seen upon a tree, on a mountain, or in a chasm when one has gone toward the end, so too is the single Self perceived as the world situated within consciousness.
In the supreme, pure state beyond sensation, that which exists as sensation in the world is without cause and lacks consciousness, being like space by virtue of its emptiness.
Feeling exists as the bondage of the visible, while non-feeling is liberation; whatever may be pleasing to you, that very thing should be quickly made firm.
Creation and non-creation, bondage and liberation, consisting of sensation and non-sensation—both are non-different from the perspective of awakening; therefore, do as you wish.
But for that which does not exist due to lack of perception, what distress is there when it perishes? Know that whatever is to be attained through silence has already been swiftly attained.
That which consists of mere cognition is indeed the destruction of the non-cognition of its parts; one should practice that cognition of sensation which is desired as the [true] nature of sensation.
Just as a ripple is a vibration of water, so too is the world a vibration within consciousness; O descendant of Raghu, this alone is the difference between them here.

While place, time, and intrinsic nature exist in the case of water with its waves and so forth, at the beginning of the world, however, place and the rest do not exist, even though the world is perceived.

The triple world shines as the luminous Ābhāsvara; one's own consciousness, which is pure awareness, is the very nature of the intellect (*citi*). This [nature] exists within speech, yet it becomes afflicted by differentiation through conceptualization; however, when speech is stilled, the supreme self is auspicious (*śiva*).

"All is consciousness"—in this view, these two [consciousness and its object] are never distinct from one another, whether in terms of word or meaning; it is not a fitting statement to say that "the wave and the water are two," though for one who is ignorant, such a claim might seem appropriate.
Śrī Rāma said: O Lord of Sages, what occurred after this for Jīvaṭa, the Brāhmaṇa, and the others—the swans and so forth—whose bodies were merely those seen in the dream of the mendicant?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having come together with Rudra, they all became awakened; having mutually perceived the nature of saṃsāra, those portions of Rudra remained in a state of happiness.
Having observed that illusion as it had been described, Rudra sent his own partial manifestations back once more to maintain the state of transmigratory existence.
