Śrī Rudra said: "Go quickly to your own abode; having enjoyed pleasures there together with your wives for some time, you shall come back into my presence."
"You shall become my portions, those hosts who are the ornaments of my city; then, after the great dissolution, we shall go to that supreme state."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus, the blessed Lord Rudra vanished from their sight and entered into the midst of the Rudras who were enumerating the final stages of worldly existence.
Then Jīvaṭa, the Brāhmaṇa, and the others also departed for their own abodes; having spent their lives together with their wives, they eventually cast off their bodies through the passage of time.
Having reached the world of Rudra, they shall become the foremost of the Gaṇas; at times they are seen in the sky, assuming the form of stars.

Śrī Rāma said: "Those [beings] such as Jīvaṭa and the Brāhmaṇa were merely of the nature of the mendicant’s mental resolve; how did they attain reality? Wherein lies the reality of an object of resolve?"

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Abandon the notion that the reality of one's intentions pertains to even a portion [of existence]; abandon the reality of intentionality therein, for that which does not exist there does not exist at all, since that state is the self of all.
Whatever is seen in a dream and whatever is perceived through mental constructs exists in that very way there, being of that nature at all times.

Just as one goes to another place by way of having that [other] place and time as one's own nature, so too there is no going from one place to another without the self and other factors whose nature is motion.
A dream is not found [externally], nor is it found apart from that [dreaming]; everything exists within the treasury of consciousness, exactly as it perceives it.
O dear one, because it is the self of all, the mind attains that state unimpaired; for by whatever state of consciousness one reaches a mental resolve, one attains it even in a dream.
But this is not obtained without supreme practice and yoga; however, for those whose visions of the knowledge of yoga have borne fruit and remain steadfast, [it is attained].
Since Śaṅkara and the others see everything everywhere, this object standing before me has been conceived by me in such a way.
Nor does he incur the loss of both, because he relies upon both; for every desired task is accomplished by one who is devoted to a single goal.
Who, while going toward the southern quarter, reaches the northern direction? The object of one's intention is understood only by those who are intent upon the object of their intention.
Those intent on the object situated at the forefront perceive the object established before them; he who desires to attain the mental resolve resides in the intellect situated at the forefront.

Then, because of the absence of being established in a single [reality], he would destroy that pair; therefore, by being established in the single object, the life of a monk attains the state of Rudra.

Having attained everything with their whole being, and having likewise obtained all things as they exist, those monks live according to their own intentions; thus, each of them perceives that world as distinct.
And these do not perceive one another except through the knowledge of Rudra; therefore, being unawakened, living beings are born with their consciousness limited to the end of individual life.
By his will, they quickly assume those forms or many forms here; "May I be a Vidyadhara here," "May I be a scholar here."
Thus, the fruitfulness of single-minded meditation is the illustration for this state of action: whether it be oneness or multiplicity, or even folly or wisdom.
Through the effort of concentration and meditation, one is fully capable of simultaneously assuming both divinity and humanity by means of the sequences of place, time, and action.
Because its nature consists of all powers, the individual soul possesses a single power; by its very nature, its essence is both infinite and yet connected with an end.
O dear one, whether expanding or contracting, the living being who is non-violent toward that conscious Self attains for itself whatever it desires.
By means of these very sequences of place, time, and action, which they accomplish themselves, yoginīs and yogins abide here and wherever else they may be.
This has been seen many times through experience here and in the hereafter: while staying in his own home, Kārtavīrya became a source of fear for everyone.
Viṣṇu, remaining in the Ocean of Milk, is born as a person on earth; for the sake of the sacrificial animal, the Yoginīs remain within the host of Yoginīs and go forth.
While Śakra remains seated upon his heavenly throne, he descends to the earth for the sake of sacrifice; likewise, Janārdana becomes one thousandfold within this world.
Hundreds of devoted men attain human birth by bowing to him; likewise, this Janārdana becomes a thousandfold for one who honors him.
Through the playful acts of partial incarnations, he alone maintains the stability of the world, simultaneously embracing thousands of beloveds like the blinking of an eye.
In this way, those monks, Jīvaṭa the Brahmin, and the others, by the power of Rudra’s consciousness, went to the city of their own mental constructs.
Having enjoyed pleasures there for a long time and subsequently reached the city of Rudra, they shall dwell as attendants (gaṇas), remaining there together with their retinues.

Then, in dwellings of ever-blossoming new kalpa-lattices, amidst clusters of great jewels, throughout the various worlds, and in the cities of Śiva, the Vidyādharīs, wearing the crowns of the immortals, shone together with Rudra.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as that delusion was slightly perceived by the mendicant in his mind, he now perceives it clearly by separating it from actual reality through diligent effort.
The state consisting of birth and death of every living being who appears [within it] truly exists as having taken on form within the very nature of the space of consciousness.
Having separated itself, one's own self becomes the fragment of saṃsāra; every living being, once dead, realizes that its nature was like a separate dream.
Thus, although the embodied soul possesses such a nature, it remains distressed until liberation; this host of living beings has been described by me to you through this narrative.
"O Rāma, it is not only monks who think 'the self is moved by another'; for us, the individual soul goes from delusion to further delusion day after day."
Just as a stone fallen from a mountain peak descends lower and lower, so too does the individual soul (jīva), having strayed from the Supreme Self, perceive this firm dream.
From this dream one goes again to another dream; falling from dream to dream, this world is indeed certainly and utterly false.
The individual soul, worn out by illusion, perceives within itself—sometimes, by means of something, in this world, or even at some time—by its own accord.
When the notion of "I" regarding the body ceases, one is liberated and attains one's own true nature. Śrī Rāma said: "Oh, how terrible is this delusion that arises in this living being!"

Just as for one who is asleep, [the mind] falls completely under the sway of illusion—a fierce night of false cognition characterized by various forms and transformations—by means of even a slight [distraction].
"Alas! Indeed, there is a terrible disparity; O Blessed One, everything is always said to be like one's own [body] for the sake of the world's stability at all times."
"It was said by you that it arises, and it is experienced accordingly; such is the self distinguished by these qualities, yet that mendicant is of a deluded nature."
"Look within and tell me quickly whether it exists somewhere or not. Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "Last night, while established in samādhi, [I beheld] this small hut of the three worlds."
"Having observed whether a certain monk exists or not, I shall speak of him tomorrow morning. Vālmīki said: "While the sage was speaking thus, the midday drum resounded outside."
There arose a sound as deep as the thundering of clouds agitated at the time of universal dissolution; and successions of handfuls of flowers were offered at his feet.
Like flowers shaken from trees by the wind, the citizens rose from their seats after having honored the best of sages, though they were already [as if] departed.
Thereafter, the assembly rose with a succession of salutations; then, in the same manner as the previous day, the sky-dwellers and earth-dwellers departed.
In their respective abodes, all of them, diligently engaged in daily activities according to the scriptures, performed their own duties as was appropriate for their stage of life.
Reflecting upon the knowledge proclaimed by the Sage, those who move upon the earth and those who move through the sky passed their nights as if they were moments, yet also as if they were eons.

In the morning, when the people had again become intent on a succession of activities, the assembly of beings moving through the air and those dwelling upon the earth remained just as before, honoring the venerable ones through mutual conversation and the composition of popular narratives.
Vālmīki said: The hosts of sky-faring Siddhas, joined by the sage Vasiṣṭha and accompanied by Viśvāmitra and others, remained there, while the leaders of the kings rested.
Then that same assembly hall shone with Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, gentle and of even expanse, like a lotus pond in a calm wind.
Then the lord of sages, disregarding the words of the questioner, spoke; for the virtuous, being compassionate, awaken others by their very power.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O King, moon of the sky that is the Raghu dynasty, joy of the Raghus, yesterday that mendicant was observed by me for a long time with the eye of knowledge.
For a long time, desiring to see such a monk, I wandered through the seven vast continents and the great mountain ranges along with their principal peaks by means of meditation.
Indeed, nowhere has such a monk ever been found; for how could a kingdom of one's imagination possibly be perceived even in the external world?
Then, when a third of the night remained, I again set out toward the northern region by means of my intellect, like a shore-wind moving across the ocean.
There exists that great and glorious region named Jinanāma; there, upon an anthill, stands a monastery that serves as a refuge for people.
In that monastery, within his own small cell, a monk named Dīrghadṛśa, who had tawny hair, remained standing for the sake of meditative concentration.
And for twenty-one nights, as he remained thus established, beings fearing the disruption of his meditation did not enter his house, which was secured by firm bolts.
Indeed, his servants were dear to him while he remained thus as a mendicant; yet today, such is the nature of destiny that he must experience its reversal.
Twenty-one nights passed for him while he remained absorbed in meditation; yet, in his mind, they seemed like thousands of years.
In a certain former eon, he was previously a monk; today, however, he is the second in this [eon], and a third is not to be found.
But I, like a bee within the lotus of the world, have again searched with my fourfold mind for another such third monk.
From that creation, a third one was obtained with a similar disposition; thereafter, other creations were envisioned by me through my creative play.
As long as that creation exists, resting within the hollow of space, there exists a third monk who is equal in rank to Brahmā.
In this very manner, with that very same arrangement, all things have come to be and have been so many times over throughout the succession of creations.
In this assembly as well, those sages and brahmins who are present—many others besides them—must likewise behave with perfect equanimity.
"This one must be Nārada, and that other one must be this [other person]; thus, by means of such mental constructions and actions, he was joined with many others in abundance.
Thus Janma and the others were to be born, as were Vyāsa and Śuka; furthermore, Śaunaka was to be born, as were Kratu and Pulaha.
By Agastya, Pulastya, Bhṛgu, and also by Aṅgiras—these and others likewise were the locus for such ritual actions.
After a long, long time, this illusion will expand, because there will arise many others—both those born with conduct similar [to yours] and others besides them.
Again and again they revolve in successive creations like waves in water; some are entirely identical, while others follow a sequence that is only half-similar.
Some are slightly equal [to others], while some are never again so; thus is this vast delusion that bewilders even the great.
In this world, O sinless one, our karma does not exist for even a moment, for our spiritual practice unfolds; how much less so for twenty-one days and nights, which possess infinite forms?
Where indeed is their perception? Oh, how formidable is the course of the mind! This is merely a flash of intuition that has thus blossomed and remains.

Just as a lotus in the water at dawn, this [world]—originally pure—becomes impure through the very act of perception, giving rise to the waves of various conflicts; thus the entire web of saṃsāra arises from pure consciousness like sparks from a flame.

Thus, each manifested fragment is proclaimed as such, and within other fragments there are likewise diverse fragments; surely all of them are not false among themselves, for they flash forth within this Cause of causes, which is the Self of all.
Daśaratha said: "O leader of sages, let these men sent by me go quickly and awaken that mendicant, and bring him from his hut."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O King, the body of that great mendicant, deprived of life, has become moist and discolored; it is no longer capable of sustaining life.
Having become the life-force of that monk, this soul became a swan born from a lotus; remaining liberated while yet living, it was no longer a vessel for the cycle of worldly existence.
At the end of the month, their bolts were forcibly removed from that house; yet the servants remain in the intermediate space, desiring to see the distribution of alms.
Then, having restored their severed limbs, they will cast their bodies into the water; they will abandon one [monk] and choose another monk whose mind is unshaken.
By this very means, the monk remains liberated even while possessing a body; how then could that perished little body within the monastery be awakened?
This illusion, composed of the gunas, is difficult to overcome for one who lacks understanding; it is easily transcended by one who constantly possesses the realization of truth.
Just as the state of being a bracelet is produced in gold while [the gold] itself remains unchanged, its arising is caused solely by a reversal of appearance.
Thus, this Māyā is inferred within the Supreme Self, perishing merely upon observation, like a series of waves in water.

For the Knower, by virtue of being an object of perception, passes from one long dream to another; thus, through the lack of discrimination, everything that perceives itself comes to have the state of a living soul.
Whatever appears as an appearance to someone is that very self, by virtue of its own cognition; it is that very thing which arises as saṃsāra, like the perception of a *karañja* forest thicket.
The entire circle of cyclic existence has arisen from each individual element; to the monk, it is like a dream or like the extreme fragility of a bubble upon the water.
Just as the dream of the world was described by the Lotus-born Lord himself, so too has this dream arisen from an impure mind and become established for all people.
The creation appears like the sport of a grandfather in a dream; thus, each one that has arisen is like millions of cosmic eggs.
Whether throbbing or otherwise, the living soul perceives delusion within this heart; it is capable of experiencing a long, internal dream-like state.
Having attained mere existence as consciousness, and by the mere fact of being fallen from realization, it has become, in some instances, a vessel for the sufferings of old age and death.
Adorned with her own virtuous deeds, she remained as if having repeatedly reached the netherworld or the world of Brahmā by the mere vibration of a portion of her mind.

Taking the form of the vibration of consciousness, she clings to the self that has assumed the name and form of the individual soul; then, moving elsewhere, she wallows there, captivating all with her agitation.

Is the mind the Supreme Self, or is it not the Supreme Self, or is it neither? For this [mind], which bears names such as "living being" (jīva) and "body," its fitness [to be the Self] is like that of a reflection or the like.
The Supreme Brahman exists as Brahman alone, appearing as the world through mere perception, like pure space within space, or like stainless water within water.

This world exists as nothing other than Brahman itself, abiding in the forms of the universe; yet, due to a lack of realization, it fears its own manifestation as something else, just as a child fears his own reflection.
When vibration is rendered non-vibrant here, consciousness dissolves by itself; that too, through complete transformation, dissolves like ghee in fire.

The vibration of consciousness alone unfolds within the vibration of consciousness, which is the self of all; thus, movement and stillness, unfolding and so forth, are merely conceptual constructs and not real here.
Here there is neither vibration nor non-vibration, neither unity nor duality; it is the pure essence of consciousness alone, abiding exactly as it is.
But through essential inquiry, when both all words and their referents are found to be equal, this which is known as pure consciousness alone remains; even "it does not exist" is no longer found.

Duality arises from the perception of difference; this is the characteristic mark of primordial nature (*prakṛti*). When everything has dissolved through the realization of non-duality, the Supreme alone remains.
Its very multiplicity is its awakening, for that awakening consists in non-contemplation; and thus the questioner indeed exists, whereby there is supreme fearlessness.
Consequently, there is neither dreaming, nor waking, nor deep sleep, nor the fourth state; there is neither bondage, nor liberation, nor anything consisting of conceptual construction.
Peace alone is what is called the world; peace is established in this very way. Since non-awakening is thus unreal, where can there be the seer, the seen, and the act of seeing?
Even vibration would be non-vibration for you due to the absence of volition; consciousness, being devoid of volition, is not distinct from either vibration or non-vibration.

Devoid of the conceptualization of duality and unity due to the absence of the mental construction of forms, that [consciousness], through mere contemplation, reaches the state where Brahman alone remains.
That which appears like a shimmering stain of conceptualization upon the disc of consciousness is not a stain at all; know it rather to be the dense body of the mass of consciousness itself.

"Abide in that state of the one whose essence is consciousness, which is neither existent nor non-existent"—thus has been composed this compendium of the essence of great awakening, free from all defects.
The immortal form of the moon’s orb, free from the stain of conceptual construction, has been touched by you, who are worthy and whose nature is the destruction of both existence and non-existence.
Having brought all conceptualizations of existence, non-existence, and the like to the state of pure consciousness, rest at ease within the spontaneous play of the radiance of the Intellect.

Know that vibration and non-vibration, or conceptualization and non-conceptualization, are the tradition of the mind called by the name "Ocean"; for cessation in all its forms, the reality of peace, whether full or not full, abides as one and the same.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having become one who maintains the silence of deep sleep, having abandoned the playfulness of the mind, and being liberated from the impurity of conceptualization, remain established in that firmly grasped state.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Lord of Mauna, O Brahman, I understand vocal silence, sensory silence, and wooden silence; but tell me, what is called the silence of deep sleep?"

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, here in this world, sages are declared by the best of sages to be of two kinds: one is the ascetic who practices penance like wood, and the other is the one liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
When spiritual practice remains uncultivated and withered, one who is firmly resolved yet forcibly subdues the collection of senses becomes a silent sage who is merely a wooden ascetic.
Having understood this as it truly is, one whose self is cultivated and who abides within the self—even if like the world—is inwardly satisfied; he is remembered as a liberated sage.
That state which belongs to these two lords of sages when they are at peace—a nature consisting of the certainty of the mind—is designated by the word "mauna" (silence).
Those who know silence say that it is of four kinds: silence of speech, silence of the senses, wooden silence, and the silence of deep sleep.
Vāṅmauna is the restraint of speech; balāt-indriya-nigraha is the forcible suppression of the senses; akṣamauna is the abandonment of all physical movements; this is designated as kāṣṭha-mauna.

The fifth is mental silence (manomauna), which exists in the wooden ascetic (kāṣṭhatāpasa) at the time of death; the sixth, called deep-sleep silence (suṣuptamauna), the one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) lives in.
Among the three specific types of silence, the wood-ascetic is the object; that very state of deep-sleep silence is the fourth (turyā), which is the intellect of the liberated.

Silence of speech is indeed called silence, yet it is the mind that is truly established therein; for when the mind is impure, it leads to bondage for the living soul, and thus the wooden ascetic remains fixed within it.
Neither recollecting us, nor touching our visible forms or words, he remains as one observing while not seeing, silent as a piece of wood.
This triad of silences is known as the vibration of the flickering mind; those who are established there through the play of that state are sages, not merely knowers of it.
It is said that in these three forms of silence, there is no cognition of anything to be adopted; this was spoken by him as a mere play. Therefore, let those who know it be angry or not.
This is indeed the silence of deep sleep, established as the state of one liberated while living; listen to this ornament for the ears regarding the person who is not subject to rebirth.
Here the vital breath is neither restrained nor joined in the threefold way; the perceptions of all the senses neither exult nor grow weary.
This reckoning of multiplicity neither stirs nor subsides; it is neither mind, nor non-mind, nor not non-mind; it is neither being, nor non-being, nor anything else.
That state which is undivided, beyond practice, and established as being without beginning or end—whether one is meditating or not meditating upon it—is called the silence of deep sleep.
Having understood this delusion of the world's diversity as it truly is, that state which remains exactly as it is, free from doubt, is indeed the silence of deep sleep.
"This entire universe is spread out by Śiva alone, whose nature consists of manifold consciousness"—this established state which is infinite is called the silence of deep sleep.
Space is neither space nor is it everything; it both exists and does not exist. That mind which is thus even and peaceful is silence, like deep sleep.
All is empty, without support, the mere representation of peace; that in which one abides as neither existent nor non-existent is the supreme silence.
That which is the non-appearance of consciousness through the distinctions of existence and non-existence, place and time, all of which arise falsely—that the wise know as the supreme silence.
When the mind, its activity obstructed, perceives within itself that which is absolutely non-existent, the non-recurrence of the movement of consciousness—that is imperishable silence.
"I am not, nor is there another; there is no mind, nor anything mental"—this awareness of non-awareness is uninterrupted supreme silence.
"I am in this world merely the referent of the word 'well-being,' nothing more than the universal of existence (sattāsāmānya)"; this is called the silence of deep sleep.
Since there is only pure consciousness, how could there be any conceptualization of "self," "other," and so forth? Therefore, the entire infinite state of deep sleep is pervaded by silence.
Know that this very state of deep sleep and silence, because of its infinity, is like awakening; it is the pure fourth state (turya), and even that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta).
Whether it be the single absorption of deep sleep, the absorption of the fourth state (turya), or the absorption beyond the fourth (turyātīta), these indeed occur even while one is awake.

O Brahmin, O virtuous one, it is indeed the state of the Fourth (turya) that possesses the entirely pure and peaceful functioning; even while acting skillfully and fully in the waking state, whether still embodied or indeed disembodied, it truly exists as the very nature of space, O holy man.

Saying "Oṃ," remain as the one who has cast off the latent impressions of worldly existence; neither you, nor I, nor anything else here exists as reality. Yet, all this indeed appears within as a mere internal reflection; therefore, O Knower, abide established solely in the single digit of the treasury of the sky of consciousness.
Śrī Rāma said: O leader of sages, from where did the hundredfold nature of the Rudras arise? Are those who are the Gaṇas the same as the Rudras, or are they not? Tell me this quickly.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "The mendicant saw a hundred dreams involving a hundred bodies; he understood them all in their general outline, and therefore they were not described by me."
Those forms which were seen in the dream as those various hundreds of hosts—this is indeed the hundred of Rudras; for even the Rudras are hosts according to the ritual rule.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, how was a hundredfold mind produced from a single mind? It was done by Rudra while dreaming, just as a hundred lamps are lit from a single lamp."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Indeed, those whose consciousness is veiled by the objects of taste experience exactly that which they imagine according to their own unobstructed state of being.

Since the Self is all-pervasive and omnipresent, whatever is conceived in whatever manner and in whatever place, that is experienced there in exactly that way by the intellect through its faculty of knowing.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin, can the Lord be one who wears a garland of skulls as an ornament, is smeared with ashes, is naked, dwells in cremation grounds, and is a lustful man?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For the great lords, the perfected ones, who possess bodies while already liberated in life, there is no restrictive rule of action here; for such a rule is devised only for the ignorant.
But the ignorant person, because his mind is distracted, proceeds according to the "law of the fish" toward supreme suffering, unless he restrains his actions.

Being well-versed in wisdom, they do not sink into objects whether desirable or undesirable, because their senses are restrained, because they have attained Buddhahood, and likewise because they are free from latent predispositions.
They always perform actions that have become habitual like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence; yet they do not actually perform anything at all, for they have no attachment whatsoever to anything.
By a chance occurrence like that of the crow and the palm fruit, Viṣṇu was impelled to such action in the past; likewise the Three-eyed One performed such deeds, and so did the Lotus-born One.

For the one who possesses wisdom, there is never anything in the sphere of their experience that is blameworthy or blameless, nothing to be accepted or rejected, and neither "one's own" nor "another's" action.

Just as heat and other qualities became inherent in fire and the rest at the beginning of creation, so too did the activities of Hara and others, as well as the castes of the twice-born, become established.
When creation has reached full development, through the power of convention, various wonders resulting from experience are imagined; indeed, they are imagined by oneself.

Therefore, O scion of Raghu, I have not described to you that supreme silence of the fourth state (turya-mauna), which pertains to one liberated while in the body (videha-mukta); rather, this [silence] concerns the disembodied state.
One should consume with extreme clarity the space that is one's own self, which is of the nature of consciousness. The attainment of that state is the supreme good; hear now how it is attained.

Those who have awakened through the realization of right knowledge by means of constant one-pointed concentration, having understood [reality] through enumeration itself, are remembered as Sāṃkhya-yogins.

Those who, through skillful means, have attained the state where the vital breaths such as prāṇa and the rest are completely stilled, and which is free from affliction and without beginning or end—they are remembered as the yogis of yoga.
But that which is to be adopted by all is the peaceful, unconditioned state; some have attained it through enumeration, and others from the body through yoga.
He who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one truly sees; for the supreme state that is attained by the followers of Sāṃkhya is indeed the very same as that attained by the followers of Yoga.
Where the activity of breath and mind is not perceived at all, and where one has escaped the snare of latent impressions—know that to be the supreme state.
They say that the mind itself is the latent impression (*vāsanā*), for it is indeed the cause of saṃsāra; when it dissolves within both types of karma, it reaches the state of being without cause.
The mind indeed perceives the body as a child perceives a ghost; having brought its own self to dissolution, it no longer perceives it.
The mind has arisen in vain and is indeed unreal because it is not observed; like one seeing the form of one's own death in a dream, it does not exist when scrutinized.
But the existence of the mind is cyclic existence; where is "I" and "mine," and where is the continuity of rebirth? Where, then, can there be the teacher and the taught, or bondage and liberation?
The intensive practice of a single reality, the dissolution of the vital breaths, and the restraint of the mind—this is the summary of the meaning of the word "liberation."
Śrī Rāma said: "O Sage, if indeed the dissolution of the vital breaths is the cause of liberation, then I consider all living beings to be liberated simply by dying."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Among these three practices, know that the pacification of the mind is the best; understand that it alone is to be accomplished quickly, so that it may become auspicious.
When the vital breaths depart from this body toward Nirvana, they experience union with the subtle elements in the ether.

Know that the subtle elements (tanmātras) are indeed permeated by latent impressions (vāsanās). They unite with those vital breaths (prāṇas) that possess a mental nature and are composed of those [impressions], and not with others.
Arising together with their latent impressions (vāsanās), the vital breaths (prāṇas) abandon the body; they then enter into union with the wind in space for the sake of suffering, like a fragrance.
The mind, along with its latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), does not subside like water in the ocean; nor can vital breaths exist without the mind, just as rays cannot exist without the sun.
The mind never abandons the vital breaths without knowledge, just as a partridge does not leave a blade of grass without first grasping it with its own beak.

Through knowledge, the mind attains the state of being devoid of latent impressions and reaches its own dissolution; it no longer draws from the vital breath its movement, and thus peace alone remains.
From knowledge, the non-existence of all objects fully arises; from that, my dear, follows the dissolution of latent impressions and the separation of the vital breath and the mind.

Then the mind, being utterly tranquil, no longer perceives the state of embodiment; having attained the supreme state through its own dissolution, the wise know that the mind is nothing but latent impression (*vāsanā*).
For the mind consists merely of latent impressions; in their absence, there is the supreme state. Knowledge becomes the reality itself; they say that knowledge is investigation.
Thus, O Rāma, the end of this cycle of existence proceeds through mere self-discrimination, like the cessation of the delusion of a snake in a rope.
The practice of a single object, the restraint of the vital breath, and the dissolution of the mind—when even one of these is fully accomplished, they all become perfected through mutual influence.
Just as the wind is stilled when the movement of a palm-leaf fan ceases, so too the mind is stilled when the vibration of the vital breath ceases.
Upon the dissolution of the body, the vital breath (prāṇa) passes into the state of space-wind; there it perceives everything exactly as it has been perfumed.
Just as the Videhas perceive their bodies in the ether, so too do they experience all conduct together with the mind.
Just as fragrance subsides when the movement of the wind has ceased, so too do the vital breaths subside when the movement of the mind has ceased.
The vital breath and the mind are eternally inseparable in living beings; they exist as if mixed together, like the fragrance of a flower and its scent, or like sesame seeds and their oil.
The vibration of the mind is the vital breath; the vibration of the vital breath is the mind. These two always move together, like a chariot and its driver.
Like the container and the contained, these two perish when one is absent; and through their own destruction, they bring about the supreme effect known as liberation.
Through the intense practice of a single reality, the mind becomes thoroughly stilled; because its very nature is absorbed therein, the vital breath is also stilled by that means.
Having investigated that reality of the infinite Self, lead the mind to absorption in it; through that dissolution, the mind becomes firmly established as that very reality.
Since that which is truly superior is found neither in non-perception nor in perception—both of which are unreal—remain steadfast in that which remains as the residue.
One should contemplate existence within a single, firmly established reality until, through thorough practice, that existence reaches the state of non-existence.

For those who possess the power of sensory withdrawal (pratyāhāra), the mind dissolves of its own accord—as if due to the exhaustion of objects of enjoyment—along with the vital breaths; only the Supreme remains.
When the mind becomes one-pointed, it instantly becomes that in which the entire flood of diverse objects has been stilled, by virtue of its nature resulting from long-term cultivation.
Having realized through reasoned intellect that this ignorance does not exist, the supreme attainment comes from knowledge alone; thereafter follows its cultivation.
When the mind is stilled, this mirage of saṃsāra subsides, just as the mist composed of it vanishes when the cloud has reached its dissolution.
Know that ignorance is mind-only; therefore, bring about its destruction by that very means. O Rāma, the supreme state is of that same nature as the self of the mind, for it is not non-existence.
If the mind attains nirvāṇa in the supreme state for even a moment, know that it has been transformed into that very state and has found its true relish therein.
If your mind has found rest through Sāṃkhya or even through Yoga, having attained the state of pure being for even a moment, it will not be born here again.
The mind from which ignorance has dissolved is described by the term "sentient being" (sattva); having burnt the seed of saṃsāra, it does not provide an interval for rebirth again.

A certain person whose ignorance has dissolved, who is established in being and whose latent impressions are stilled, suddenly beholds the supreme light, which is like emptiness, and becomes tranquil.

O fortunate one, that in which the state of the self has dissolved and the mind has dissolved is here called "pure being" (sattva); it does not return again to the state stained by the parts [of worldly existence], just as copper that has attained the state of gold does not revert [to its former condition].
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The living soul quickly becomes non-living, and the mind attains the state of being no-mind; liberation is defined as the end of ignorance through the sun of inquiry.
The mind, ego, and so forth are perceived like the water of a mirage; though they are non-existent and merely slight, they dissolve through investigation.
Listen to these auspicious questions uttered by the Vetāla during the delusion of the dream of saṃsāra, which have come to my mind through this present occasion.
In the great Vindhya forest there was a Vetāla of massive form; out of pride, he came to a certain circle with the intent to kill.
Formerly, that Vetāla dwelt in a certain abode of the virtuous; he was happy, being constantly satisfied by the offering of many sacrifices.
Even when hungry, he did not kill a man who had arrived before him without cause or offense; for the virtuous are indeed observers of justice.
In due time, that forest-dweller went to another city, driven by hunger, to consume people through fraudulent means.
There he encountered the king who had gone out on his night patrol; that fierce night-stalker addressed him with a deep and terrible voice.
The Vetāla said: "O King, you have now been captured by me, the Bhīma Vetāla! Where are you going? You are ruined; become my food this day!"
The king said: "O night-stalker, if you devour me here by force, though it be unjust, your head shall split into a thousand pieces; of this there is no doubt."
The Vetāla said: "I shall not devour you, for this is unjust; indeed, this is the principle I am stating: you are a king, and all the desires of those who seek you must be fulfilled by you."
O King, fulfill this request of mine which seeks a meaningful outcome; you ought to correctly explain these questions that I have posed.
To what sun are the universes but tiny atoms compared to its rays? In what wind do the great particles of the vast sky flutter?
Moving from one dream to another by the hundreds and thousands, who is it that abandons or does not abandon its own pure and luminous essential nature?
Just as a plantain trunk consists of nothing but layers of leaves, repeated again and again, so too does that very same subtle atom consist of layer upon layer within its interior.
For which atom, without relinquishing its atomicity, could the Brahma-egg, space, the flood of elements, the solar orb, and Mount Meru be [merely] atoms?
Within the solid, singular core of the rock of a great mountain—an atom that is indeed partless—the three worlds exist as its very marrow.

If you speak thus to me, O evil-souled one, then I shall swallow you here, you self-destroyer, and having approached you by force, I shall devour your entire circle like a fruit, just as the God of Death devours the world.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the Vetāla had spoken thus, the king, whose garment was made white by the luster of his teeth, smiled and spoke these words in order to answer the questions.
The King said: "If this cosmic egg, which is an undecaying fruit, should ever exist, it would be surrounded by successive layers of bark, each ten times the size of the one before."
Indeed, there were thousands of such fruits upon it; its branches were exceedingly high, vast, and possessed trembling foliage.
Furthermore, there exists a great tree of vast form, difficult to perceive, upon which there are thousands of such branches.
Where there are thousands of such trees, that forest is exceedingly lofty, filled with infinite trees and shrubs.
Where there are thousands of such forests, there stands the great mountain Bṛhacchṛṅga, exceedingly high and vast in form.
Furthermore, there is a vast region with expansive hollows where there exist thousands of such peaks.
Furthermore, where there are thousands of such regions, there exists a great island (Bṛhaddvīpa) likewise endowed with large lakes and rivers.
Furthermore, there exists a terrestrial foundation endowed with various wonderful arrangements, wherein thousands of such islands are situated.
Where there exist thousands of such earths, there likewise exists that vast, expansive, and grand display of the great world-system.
Furthermore, there exists a vast cosmic egg (aṇḍa) as formidable as the seat of the sky, wherein there are thousands of such worlds.
There exists a vast ocean, a sea devoid of movement, wherein thousands of such eggs are contained within caskets.
There exists a pure, great ocean, wherein even a hundred thousand such oceans would be but a faint ripple, and which is itself the essence of its own playful manifestation.
Suppose there were some man of such exceedingly lofty stature that the waters of thousands of oceans like those would fill his belly.
There exists a Supreme Person, the foremost of all beings, upon whose chest a garland made of hundreds of thousands of such men rests.
Within whose mandala thousands of such great-souled men flash forth like the network of hairs upon his own body.
There exists such a Great Sun within hundreds of perceptions; all these various mental constructions are but its own radiance.
The atoms of the weapons of the universe are but the rays of this sun; I have called him the Sun of Consciousness, for he illumines all of this.
The supreme sun, whose intention is purified, is indeed the very self of consciousness; these expansive worlds are but its motes of dust.
By the light of the supreme sun of consciousness, these splendors of the day of the world appear and come into being, just as the splendors of the sun shine forth at times.

O you who dwell within the self that is pure consciousness alone, amidst this multitude of living beings who do not expand the jewel of the pavilion of the three worlds—alas, these scribbles of worldly delusion between the birth of consciousness and its end exist here; indeed, there is not even the slightest peace, so remain at rest!

The King said: "The existence of time, the existence of space, the existence of vibration, the existence consisting of consciousness, and the existence of pure awareness—all these and so forth are purifying."
In the great wind of the Supreme Self, the restless dust vibrates; like fragrance in a flower, it is by its very nature both identical with and distinct from that [wind].
In this great dream called the world, as one passes from one dream to another, the tranquil form of Brahman—which is the expansion of peace—does not abandon its state of peace.
Just as a plantain trunk consists of nothing but layers within layer, so too does this entire universe, though it is a transformation of Brahman, consist of nothing but layers within layer.
That which is praised by these words such as "Being," "Brahman," and "Self" is, according to you, a void beyond description; it is neither anything at all nor something specific.
Whatever existence is conceptualized is fashioned by experience; like a plantain trunk, it is merely this pure, pervasive consciousness alone.

Because of its subtlety and its unattainability, the Supreme Self is the supreme atom; yet because of its infinity, it alone has attained the state of being the foundation for Mount Meru and all else.
Even for this person who is subtler than the subtle and infinitely vast, the world and so forth appear like atoms, because they are perceived as being devoid of form.
This Person is subtler than an atom because he cannot be grasped, yet he is like a great mountain because he fills all space; though he consists of all limbs, he is devoid of limbs.
O virtuous one, know that these three worlds are merely the marrow of this consciousness-only; indeed, know that the three worlds have consciousness-only as their very core.

The worlds, perceived through the conceptualization of mere consciousness, are of a peaceful nature, delicate, and infinite in form; they are like the state of a child-ghost, utterly impossible to transcend. Thus, experience this for yourself and remain in peace.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having heard this from the mouth of the king, the Vetāla attained peace through his purified mind and an intellect capable of discernment.
Having become tranquil in mind and perceiving solitude as blameless, he became one whose meditation was unshakable, forgetting his agonizing hunger.
O Rāma, this web of questions from the Vetāla has been told to you by me; in this manner, this entire world is situated within that atom of consciousness.
Through inquiry, the universe contained within the sheath of the atom of consciousness dissolves; that which remains is the state of the body being like a corpse animated by a vetāla.
Withdrawing the mind from all sides with a tranquil inner self, remaining desireless and abiding in its own natural state, stay with a peaceful intellect.
O Sage, having made the mind itself as clear as space, remain with a self that is uniquely stilled and tranquil, perceiving equality everywhere.

For a king who possesses steady intellect and is free from delusion, following the course as it presents itself—just like King Bhagīratha—even that which is difficult to accomplish becomes successful.

For one whose mind is completely tranquil, whose conduct is fully satisfied, and who always abides within the self that is equanimous and composed of bliss, even the most difficult-to-attain desired objects are accomplished, just as the descent of the Gaṅgā and the excavation of the ocean were achieved [by Bhagīratha].
Śrī Rāma said: O Lord, please tell me how King Bhagīratha’s descent of the Gaṅgā was accomplished through the wondrous power of his mind.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: There was a most righteous king named Bhagīratha, who was like a tilaka ornament upon the circle of the earth bounded by the oceans.
Immediately upon their resolve, those who seek his favor obtain whatever they desire from him, whose face is as serene as the moon, as if from a wish-fulfilling gem.
He who constantly gave away his wealth for the sake of establishing the righteous took up only a blade of grass at times, like a wish-fulfilling gem.
Like a blazing rim threaded through the very essence of a diamond, he shattered the iron machine of the jewel below—the conduct of all wicked men.
Though his body was weary from the lack of smoke and fire, and though he was utterly destitute, he dispelled the darkness of men, just as the sun dispels the nocturnal gloom of houses.
Scattering a shower of sparks born from his own prowess in all directions, he blazes among his enemies like the fire produced by a sun-crystal at midday.
That which has a soft and cool touch, gladdening the mind of the wise, melts like a moonstone at the sight of the affectionate moon.
By him, the third quality of this stream of the Gaṅgā—which serves as the sacred thread of the world and flows through both heaven and the netherworld—has been fulfilled in this [earth].
The ocean, which had been dried up by Agastya, was filled again by the flood of the Gaṅgā—just as a great caravan of supplicants, though difficult to satisfy, is replenished.
By him, the friend of the world, his kinsmen dwelling in the netherworld were led up the stairway of the Gaṅgā to the realm of Brahmā.
Worshipping Brahmā, Śaṅkara, and Jahnu through ascetic penance, he experienced exhaustion again and again, yet his resolve remained unfailing.
While that lord of the earth was still in his youth, he reflected upon this worldly course of life, which is so full of turmoil.
Yet, by the power of fate, even in my youth, a tiny spark of reflection on the wonder of dispassion arose within me, like a creeper in a desert.
In solitude, this lord of the earth reflected thus: "This course of the world is eternally inconsistent and agitated."
Day after day, night after night, and again and again with hundreds of acts of giving and taking, that very same cycle appears tasteless to those performing their karmic duties.
I consider that to be a true deed well-done by which, once attained, nothing remains in this world yet to be attained; all other action is merely indigestion.
Repeatedly performing a despicable deed without shame—who indeed would do such a thing, being of deluded intellect and lacking wisdom, like a child?
Then once, his mind agitated and fearing worldly existence, Bhagīratha questioned his guru Tritala in private.
Bhagīratha said: "O Lord, having wandered for a very long time within these forest-like courses of worldly existence, which are utterly empty within, we are deeply exhausted."
O Blessed One, how does the end come about for all sufferings—such as old age, death, and delusion—which produce existence?

Tritala said: "O King, by means of that full awakening to the object of knowledge—which has arisen from the self through long-standing equanimity, which delights in non-differentiation, and which fills the very self."
All sufferings are exhausted, the knots are completely severed, doubts reach a state of equanimity, and all actions come to rest, O sinless one.
The wise know the Self to be the object of knowledge, perfectly pure and consisting of consciousness; it is omnipresent and eternal, neither setting nor rising.

Bhagīratha said: "O Lord of Sages, I know that there exists only pure consciousness—devoid of qualities, tranquil, stainless, and infallible—and that nothing else, such as the body and so forth, exists."
Why does my practice there become clear and not the other? O Blessed One, how may I possess this much realization alone?
Tritala said: Through knowledge, the mind attains absorption in the object of knowledge within the sky of the heart; thereafter, having become the universal body, the living soul is not born again.
Non-attachment and absence of clinging toward children, wife, home, and so forth; and constant equanimity of mind amidst the occurrence of the pleasant and the unpleasant.
Constant meditation upon that through the yoga of non-difference from the Self; resorting to solitary places; and a lack of delight in the company of worldly people.
Constancy in the knowledge of the inner self and the vision of the goal of the knowledge of reality—this is declared to be knowledge; that which is otherwise than this is ignorance.
O King, knowledge is attained when the sense of "I" is stilled; it takes the form of the destruction of passion and hatred, and serves as the medicine for the disease of saṃsāra.
Bhagīratha said: "O highly fortunate one, the sense of 'I' has long been established in this body like a tree upon its own mountain; tell me, how is it to be abandoned?"
Tritala said: By human effort, having abandoned the perception of the flood of enjoyments and having attained the blossomed state of being, the ego dissolves.
As long as the entire cage of constraints—such as shame and the like—is not shattered by the state of possessing nothing at all, so long does the ego remain manifest.
If you remain motionless, having abandoned all this through the intellect, then, upon the dissolution of the ego, you yourself are the supreme state.

Having abandoned all prosperity, you have gone forth into absolute poverty among enemies; with all distinctions stilled, fear departed, and every desire relinquished; with pride at peace and the notion of a body destroyed, you wander for alms even among them and have utterly forsaken me—if this is so, O Bhava, you are truly exalted.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, having heard this from the mouth of his guru, Bhagīratha, having resolved upon what was to be done in his mind, became intent on his own task.
Then, after only a few days had passed, he performed the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice for the sole purpose of attaining perfection through the renunciation of everything.
Discerning between those with merit and those without, he gave away his entire wealth—cows, land, horses, gold, and so forth—to the twice-born who were his own kinsmen.
Within merely three days, having relinquished everything, King Bhagīratha remained with nothing left but his life-breath.
Then, his kingdom being devoid of all purpose and its subjects and citizens exhausted, he gave it away to his enemy like a blade of grass to a borderer.
When his kingdom, palace, and circle of vassals were seized by his enemy, the sage, leaving nothing but his lower garment, departed from his own realm.
Where he was not known by name, where he was not known from his appearance—there, in villages, in forests, or in distant places, the steadfast one dwelt.
Thus, in a very short time, having stilled all desires through supreme tranquility, he attained rest within his own self.
Wandering over the islands upon the surface of the earth, he once, by the turn of fate and against his will, reached that very city of his own which had been seized by an enemy.
There, the peaceful Śamī begged for alms from various houses, from those who had fallen into calamity, and from the citizens and ministers alike.
The citizens and the ministers beheld King Bhagīratha; then, filled with despondency, they honored him with respectful service.
Although entreated by his enemy, "O Lord, accept the kingdom," the sage did not accept it, having disregarded everything except for food, which he would not take even as a blade of grass.
Having spent a few days there, he departed elsewhere; Bhagīratha was lamented by the people, crying out, "Alas! What a tragedy!"
Then, elsewhere, with his self pacified and his intellect fully at rest, that happy man once reached his guru Tritala, who delights in the Self.
Having offered his own hospitality, Bhagīratha dwelt for some time with him on mountains, in forests, in villages, in cities, and among the people.
Having attained equanimity, the teacher and disciple remained as equals; established in themselves, they regarded the maintenance of the body as a mere diversion.
Why is this body maintained, or what is gained by us if it is abandoned? Let it remain as it is, according to its natural state, following the proper sequence and conduct.
Having thus resolved, the two remained traveling from forest to forest, experiencing neither joy nor supreme bliss, neither unhappiness nor anything intermediate.
Wealth, the eightfold sovereignty beginning with the power of horses, even when offered by satisfied Siddhas, they both regarded as mere withered grass.
Thinking, "This body must be maintained by one's own karma alone as long as there is life, even against one's will," they both remained there by means of their own karma.

The two supreme sages, who were by nature perfectly equanimous and free from desire for pleasure or pain, welcomed his arrival with joy, arising from their own practice of the path; for they were self-restrained and remained ever equal toward both happiness and suffering.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Now, once upon a time, in a certain excellent city within a particular region, death took away a childless king like a fish seizing its prey.
There, the subjects, weary and having lost the traditional order of their land, sought out a king endowed with vast excellence and glory.
Having approached that steadfast sage Bhagīratha as he was wandering for alms, they recognized him, brought him back, and installed him as the lord of the army.
In an instant, Bhagīratha, surrounded by his heavy army like a lake filled with water during the rainy season, swiftly mounted his elephant.
With the clamor of the people crying, "Victory to Bhagīratha, the Lord of the World!", the great caves of the kings of mountains became completely filled.
While he was protecting that kingdom there, the original subjects, showing him great respect, approached the king and spoke thus to the lord of men:
The subjects said: "O King, that lord of ours who was chosen by you has been swallowed up by Death, like soft meat by a fish."
It behoves you to show favor so as to protect each respective kingdom; moreover, it is not proper to abandon wealth that has come unasked.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus entreated, the king accepted those words and became the lord of the earth marked by the seven oceans.
Equanimous, with a tranquil mind, observant of silence, free from passion and devoid of envy, he performed only those actions appropriate to the occasion, having concealed all sense of wonder.
He heard that the water of the Gaṅgā was capable of delivering his ancestors, who had perished in the depths of Pātāla and had once been like the ocean itself.
At that time, it is said, the celestial river did not flow upon the earth; therefore, the handful of Gaṅgā water was known as the "offering for the ancestors" (pitṛ-añjali).
And from that time forward, King Bhagīratha maintained a vow in order to bring the Gaṅgā down from heaven to the earth.
Then the king, having become peaceful and desiring what is to be done for the sake of asceticism, abandoned his kingdom along with his ministers and went to a solitary forest.
There, having propitiated Brahmā, Śaṅkara, and Jahnu again and again for thousands of years, he established the Gaṅgā upon the earth.

From that time forth, the triple-pathed river, possessing waves of pure ripples and clinging to the moon-adorned body of the Lord of the World, falls from the vault of heaven to the earth like the vast succession of great merits belonging to noble souls.

With its shimmering waves breaking and its mass of foam appearing like a smile, the triple-pathed river (Ganges) then became, upon the surface of the earth under King Bhagīratha, a thoroughfare for the spread of his fame—like a continuous stream of Dharma joined with a cluster of blossoming, pure merits.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Holding fast to this vision maintained with the wisdom of Bhagīratha, remain equanimous and self-abiding; perform whatever duty comes to you with a tranquil mind.
Having first abandoned this [world] and having brought the bird of the mind under control, remain peaceful within yourself, immovable like Śikhidhvaja.
Śrī Rāma said: Who was this one named Śikhidhvaja, and how did he attain that state? O Brahman, tell me this further for the sake of increasing my understanding.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In the past, during the Dvāpara age, and now in the future, a husband and wife shall attain affection for one another in that very same configuration.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, that which existed previously is indeed exactly the same now; why will it be so in the future? Tell me this, O best among speakers.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This state of the consciousness of Brahmā and others, which constitutes the fixed order of the creation of the world, is eternally established as arising from an irresistible nature.
That which, having existed many times, becomes manifold again; that which comes into being as something else without having previously existed, and then ceases to exist entirely once more.
Another [form], rich in its prior arrangement, vibrates forth through similarity, just as similar and dissimilar ripples arise in a lake.
Just so, various other conditions are seen in the cycle of existence; therefore, like a king, the Lord will once again [act] as in the story about to be told.
He will be possessed of great splendor; hear this account of him. It occurred previously in the Dvāpara age, when the seventh Manu had passed away.
In this fourth creation of the four-yuga cycle, in the lineage of the Kurus, there was a place situated not far from the renowned Vindhya mountains in Jambūdvīpa.
In the city of the Mālavas, there was a glorious lord named Śikhidhvaja, endowed with the qualities of fortitude and generosity, and possessed of patience, tranquility, and self-restraint.
He was a hero of auspicious conduct, silent, a mine of multitudes of virtues, a performer of all sacrifices, and a conqueror of all archers.
The doer of all deeds, the sustainer of the earth in his former body, he was charming, affectionate, sweet, clever, and an ocean of love.
He will be handsome, peaceful, fortunate, majestic, and devoted to righteousness; he will be a speaker on the matters of discipline and a bestower of all forms of prosperity.

He was an enjoyer who remained in the company of the virtuous, a fine listener of all sacred revelation; he was one who honored the Vedas without pride, treating even the company of women as lightly as a blade of grass.
When his father had ascended to heaven, he, though still a youth, being self-controlled and possessed of supreme vigor, personally undertook the conquest of the quarters for sixteen years.
Surely, through the perfection of his imperial sovereignty, he united the circle of the earth; he remained free from all fear, protecting his subjects in accordance with righteousness.
Then, as the years passed and spring blossomed forth in full splendor, that wise king, together with his ministers, whitened the quarters of the sky with his glory.
While the flowers were blooming and the moonbeams were shimmering, within the inner sanctum of the tree-branches, there were swings formed by clusters of blossoms.
In that place where the door-panels were made of revolving petals white as camphor-dust, and where the canopy was formed by clusters of blossoming flowers exuding fragrance;
While pairs of bees were humming loudly together in the dense thickets, and while a sweet breeze, cool with the spray of moonbeams, was blowing;
His heart, dwelling upon his beloved, became intensely eager for her who was reclining amidst the young shoots and leaves of plantain and kandalī trees on the riverbank.
Intoxicated by the sweet liquors made fragrant with an abundance of flowers, his mind found no other resting place, as if it had arisen together with the spring.
When shall I [behold] my innocent beloved, whose breasts are like golden lotus buds, upon the swings in the garden groves and amidst the playful lotus ponds?
When shall I place her, marked with saffron, upon my lap on a couch, like a female bee upon the swings of lotus creepers?
Gazing intently at that young girl, who clings to her creeper-like arms and yearns for a garland of lotus stalks, jasmine, and clusters of moon-bright flowers, I shall remain motionless.
"Will Indusundarī ever become tormented by love on my account?"—becoming absorbed in this thought, he set about gathering flowers.
He dwelt in the forest edges and in flowering groves, along the borders of the woods and gardens, and by the playful lotus ponds.
In houses encircled by creepers, in various garden grounds, and in places adorned with descriptions of the arrangement of forests and groves;
His mind was distracted by stories filled with the sentiment of love (śṛṅgāra-rasa), while in his heart were the swaying vine-like tresses of women whose bodies shimmered with pearl necklaces.
He worshipped the maidens whose breasts were like golden jars; I believe that wise ministers understand this to be the king's resolve.
The supreme position of a minister consists precisely in the ability to understand gestures and facial expressions; then, the circle of ministers deliberated upon his marriage.
He requested the daughter of the lord of Surāṣṭra, who was endowed with youth and possessed of fresh bloom, as his most excellent wife according to the prescribed rites.
He married her, who was like his own image; she was a beauty fit for a king, renowned on earth by the name Cūḍālā.
Having obtained that husband, she shone like a lotus pond in full bloom; and Śikhidhvaja gazed upon that Cūḍālā, whose eyes were like blue water-lilies.
Just as the divine sun causes the lotus-pond to bloom through its affection, so did the love between those two, whose hearts were offered to one another, increase.
With her limbs rich in gestures, emotions, and charms, she was like a young creeper; he, having entrusted all affairs to his excellent minister, lived happily with his subjects well-established.
Like a royal swan with a lotus-plant, he took delight with that beloved wife in the inner apartments, upon swings, and amidst artificial lotus-pools.
In gardens and monasteries, in the gathering of creepers and flowers, in the rows of Kadamba groves, and along the paths of sandalwood and aloe-wood.
Upon the swaying clusters of mandāra flowers and the plantains and kandalī stalks, in the city outskirts, at the edges of the forests, at the ends of the quarters, and upon the lakes;
In the forests and at the outskirts of towns, among the *jambu* and *jambīra* trees, everything they did for one another was full of delight.

Because they were like the splendors of heaven and earth, the best among those bearing the burden of the six years, they were constantly separated from one another due to their mutual affection and their respective duties.
They both became experts in the entire range of arts with one another; having attained friendship, they maintained as their very nature a single identity.
As if transferred from one heart to another, the master’s mastery of the meaning of all scriptures—even his artistic skill—emerged from his mouth unimpaired.
Like a child grasping at time and other such things, she became learned in all subjects; and from the mouth of Cūḍālā, she [learned] everything up to dancing, instrumental music, and so forth.
Then he studied and became exceedingly proficient in the arts, like the moon and the sun on the day of the new moon, their splendors mingling with one another.
Abiding within each other's hearts, both of them attained oneness; those two beloveds remained together, sharing a single essence with one another.
Like the fragrance inseparable from the flower, like Śiva and Pārvatī dwelling upon the earth, they possessed minds beautiful with cleverness and were experts in the meaning of all the scriptures.
And for the sake of their mission, Kamalā and the Consort of Kamalā arrived upon the earth; out of affection, they were gracious and sweet, speaking with words of perfect wisdom.

Devoted to following the ways of the world and well-versed in its affairs, they were perfected in the full range of arts and possessed the elixir of radiant aesthetic flavor; with limbs cool, smooth, and charming, they appeared like two risen moons.

He abandoned that peerless couple, who were radiant with the splendor of passion, enjoyment, and luxury within their inner apartments; they moved slowly with blooming pride and love, like a pair of royal swans within the hollows of the cosmic egg.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, for many years, the couple took delight day by day in the unrestrained sports of youth with intense longing.
Then, after many years had passed in their cycle of recurrence, his youth gradually ebbed away like water from a broken jar.
In this world of worldly activity, which is as fragile as a mass of shifting waves, death is as unavoidable as the falling of a ripe fruit.
Like a frost-bolt upon a lotus, old age is poised to fall; life flows away incessantly, like water from the palm of the hand.
Like a gourd-creeper in the rainy season, the single craving has grown long; like the current of a mountain river, youth indeed flows away.
Life is as unreal as a magician’s illusion, its stability decayed; pleasures flee away like arrows shot from a bow.
Mental sufferings fall upon the mind like a vulture upon meat; the body is as momentary in its destruction as a bubble in the waters during the rainy season.
Worldly activity, when examined, is as devoid of essence as the interior of a plantain tree; youth quickly passes away, like a beloved woman who acts against the wishes of her lover.
By force, a lack of interest has come upon me, like saplessness upon a tree; therefore, what here could be auspicious in form, stable, and exceedingly beautiful?
For a long time he reflected upon the scripture esteemed as supreme inner knowledge; by the sole means of self-knowledge, the cholera known as saṃsāra was cured.

Having resolved that "it shall be pacified," the two remained devoted to that; their minds were fixed on it, their lives were directed toward it, they were established in it, and they took refuge in those who knew it.
Then, intent on that worship and engaged in its practice, the two of them shone there, having become exceedingly proficient through constant exercise as they enlightened one another.
In their mutual delight, the two of them engaged in that same undertaking; then, O Rāma, she [sang] verses with charming cadences without ceasing.
Having heard from the mouths of those who know the inner self the meanings of the scriptures capable of delivering one across [suffering], he reflected upon his own self in this manner day and night.
Whether unoccupied or occupied with the intellect, one should purify it with a bright mind; then one should personally examine one's own self, thinking, "What might I become?"
Whose is this delusion that has come? How has it arisen, or where? The body is indeed inert and deluded; "I am not [this]"—such is the certainty.
This is well-established even among children and is experienced within the mind; furthermore, the group of organs of action consists of parts that are non-different from this [mind].
There is no difference between the parts and the whole, and they are indeed insentient; likewise, the collection of intellect and sense organs is seen to be nothing but insentient.
Since the mind is impelled by [the Self] like a clod of earth on the ground by a staff, I consider the mind itself to be inert, for its power consists merely of volitional construction (*saṃkalpa*).

Just as a stone is propelled by slings, so is the intellect impelled by determinations; the intellect is thus of the nature of determination, for it is insentient, while existence alone is determination.
Just as a river is surely carried along by its own channel, so too am I carried away by egoism; yet even this egoism is devoid of essence, insentient, and essentially like a corpse.
The Yakṣa is produced by the *jīva*, like a delusive phantom created by a child; and the *jīva* is the space of consciousness, whose nature is wind, situated within the heart.
This delicate being lives on by some internal means; oh, how this has been realized by him who is stained by the conceptualization of "I" and "mine"!

The individual soul lives by means of that which has become aged—the form of the Self consisting of consciousness; the soul lives by the very nature of consciousness, even while possessing the delusion of objects of thought.

Just as fragrance [is carried] by the wind, or as the current of a river [is drawn] by a hollow, the body of consciousness becomes inert through the accumulation of the unreal, insentient, and objective portions.

For just as fire submerged in a great flood abandons its own form, so too, when mental absorption (*citsamādhi*) occurs spontaneously, whatever appears—whether existent or non-existent—abandons its own nature.

Just as that very [mirror] becomes [stained] in an instant by casting off its own natural purity, so too does this nature of consciousness itself become [limited] through its own orientation toward objects of thought.
Thinking, "The insentient, which is void and like a non-entity, is awakened by consciousness," Cūḍālā wondered: "By whom was this consciousness made conscious?"
Thus he reflected, and after a long time he awakened in this way: "Aha! After a long period, that which is to be known—the state free from affliction—has finally been realized."
Indeed, once that which is to be known has been realized, no one falls away again; for these—the mind, intellect, senses, and so forth—are merely the play of consciousness.
Alas, all that exists is non-existent, like the appearance of a second moon; here, there is only one Great Consciousness, which is called "Great Being."
Stainless, equanimous, pure, and characterized by the absence of ego, it has the form of pure consciousness; it is Śiva, pure existence alone, and imperishable.
Shining forth once for all, stainless, and eternally risen, she is celebrated by such names as Brahman and Paramātman.

The objects of thought, the insentient, the mind, and so forth, are not different from this [consciousness] in terms of valid cognition. By her, this glorious consciousness (cicchrī) is perceived; she is remembered as the primordial consciousness (cid).
That which is this consciousness is the indestructible form of that [Reality]; it alone unfolds through the forms of the mind, intellect, senses, and their objects.
This manifestation of the existence of all objects in the form of the world is like the movement of waves, droplets, and billows within the Mother, the conscious Self.
This is that supreme form of that Great Consciousness; for she is indeed like a pure jewel of consciousness, arisen in perfect equanimity.
Indeed, that existence which persists as the unfolding of the world through its own non-dual power cannot possibly exist here as anything other than Māyā.
Just as the variety of vessels is indeed due to their being gold, so too does that [consciousness] arise in such a form; it perceives itself as that very form.

Just as the state of being waves and so forth arises in water through its own fluidity, so too does the world arise from the Great Consciousness by means of the individual mind, or rather, it does not even arise.
Just as the ocean itself, through its fluidity, assumes the form of a wave, so too am I pure consciousness alone, expanded yet devoid of the sense of "I."
For that sky of pure consciousness, there is neither birth nor death, nor any course of existence or non-existence; for it, no destruction ever occurs anywhere.
This sun of consciousness is indivisible, unburnable, and exceedingly pure; oh, how after a long time I have become peaceful and attained final liberation!
I am extinguished, free from delusion, like the ocean after Mount Mandara has been removed—unreal yet appearing, utterly clear, infinite, unborn, and immutable.
This space of the Self is unobstructed, stainless, supreme, eternal, and infinite; it is this very space, wherein the floods of fruits, beginning with the "fruitless" (aphala), reside.
This entire universe, including the gods and demons, is composed of me and is uncreated; the army consisting of men and their karma is entirely like a mere lump of clay.
Existence consists of both the seer and the seen, and likewise consists of the unity of pure consciousness; it is expressed as "this is unity," "this is duality," "I," and "not-I."
What delusion or confusion could there be? How, for whom, from where, or where [could it exist]? I am established in my own infinite, effortless, and perfectly tranquil state.
He who appears as the conscious one that perceives—whether it be unconscious or conscious—is one who has gone beyond to Nirvana and final extinction, free from fever, and devoid of volition.

That form, whose nature is appearing, is the void established within the Great Consciousness; it is not "this," nor "I," nor "another," nor the arising of existence and non-existence. All is peaceful, without support, and the Supreme alone remains.

Thus intent on inquiry, having realized through supreme awakening this reality of the Supreme Self as it truly exists, she became peaceful—her play of passion, fear, delusion, and darkness completely stilled—like a streak of cloud in an autumn sky.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Day after day, through that state of delighting in her own self and through her constant inward-turned nature, she remained established in her true essence.
Free from passion, free from attachment, free from dualities, and free from desire, she neither abandons nor grasps, moving according to her natural conduct.
Having crossed the ocean of existence and stilled the web of doubts, he was one whose inner self was completely filled by the supreme attainment of the Great Self.
Having rested for a very long time, weary though she was, she entered a state beyond all description, having found her footing within the dense [reality] that transcends every comparison.
Thus, in a very short time, that passionate Cūḍālā of excellent complexion attained the state of one who has known all that is to be known.
Just as this wandering delusion of worldly movement has somehow come to be, so too does it all dissolve of its own accord within one who possesses the knowledge of reality.
Having attained rest in that tranquil state where all the unseen is absent, she shone like a streak of autumn cloud, free from all agitation.

Unperturbed, she remained gazing upon herself by means of her own self, due to the absence of external connection, like an old cow that has reached a mountain peak covered with grass and stands there at rest.
By the power of her intense practice of self-discrimination and through the dawning of the Self, that beautiful woman shone like a splendid flowering creeper newly sprouted.
Then, on one occasion, having beheld that woman of faultless limbs and unprecedented splendor, Śikhidhvaja spoke with a smile:
O slender one, you shine all the more, as if endowed with renewed youth and adorned again and again, just as the world shines when it possesses a king.
O beloved, you shine intensely, as if having drunk the essence of nectar, as if having attained the state that is to be attained, and as if filled with a flood of bliss.
Bearing a beautiful body that is both tranquil and lovely, O passionate woman, you surpass the moon and possess an indescribable splendor.
O beloved, I behold your mind as free from worldly attachment yet compassionate, tranquil yet powerful, attained to equanimity, profound, and utterly serene.
O beloved, I behold your mind—tranquil yet infinitely wild—which treats the three worlds as a mere blade of grass and has tasted the essence of the entire universe.
O illustrious lady, no object of worldly prosperity or pleasure can equal your mind, which is as beautiful as the ocean of milk in a desert.
With those very limbs, tender as young plantain trees, lotus stalks, and sprouts, which have now attained stability, you appear as if you have reached full growth.
Thus, remaining in that very same configuration, you have attained another state, like a creeper at the change of season.
Have you drunk the nectar of immortality, or have you attained universal sovereignty? Or have you reached deathlessness itself through the application of yoga and its practice?
O lady with eyes like blue lotuses, what have you not already attained that is superior to sovereignty, or even the wish-fulfilling gem, or the three worlds? What remains for you to obtain?
Cūḍālā said: "I have come having abandoned this form which is neither 'nothing' nor 'something'; therefore, I remain as the Illustrious One, who is neither 'nothing' nor 'something' in form."
Having renounced all this and having relied upon everything else that is both true and untrue, I remain established as Śrīmatī by means of that.
