Whatever exists and whatever does not exist, I know that as it truly is—how it arises and how it perishes; by this, I abide as the Illustrious One.
I am satisfied by enjoyments as if they were already consumed, even when they are far away; I neither rejoice nor do I become angry, and for that reason I remain possessed of prosperity.
I delight in the solitary heart, which is like the infinite sky; I do not delight in royal pastimes, and for that reason I remain possessed of glory.
For I abide in the Self alone, whether in my seats, gardens, or palaces; I dwell neither in enjoyments nor in modesty, and thus I remain possessed of glory.
"I am indeed the sovereign of the worlds, not one whose form consists of even the slightest thing"; thus I find satisfaction in the Self alone, and by that I abide as the Illustrious One (Śrīmatī).
"I am this, and I am not that; I am truth, and yet I am not even that. I am everything, and yet I am nothing; therefore, I abide as the Illustrious One."
I do not seek pleasure, nor wealth, nor misfortune, nor any other state; I rejoice in whatever comes to me, and by that I abide in prosperity.
I delight with my companions—wisdoms that possess subtle discernment and vision of the scriptures; it is for this reason that I remain possessed of glory.

"O Lord, when I look here with the rays of my eyes, or with the sense-faculties, or even with the mind, I see nothing at all; yet, when I am devoid of those, I see nothing within. Thus, seeing correctly, I have long since arisen [from delusion]."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: To that fair-faced woman who was speaking thus, resting within her own self, the king—failing to understand the meaning of her words—smiled and spoke.
Śikhidhvaja said: "O fair-complexioned one, you are a child who utters incoherent prattle; you take delight in royal pastimes—enjoy them, O daughter of a king!"
How indeed can he shine, who, having abandoned something, has gone to nothingness, yet remains established in direct perception—having abandoned the true nature of what is directly perceived?
How indeed can he who abandons enjoyments, saying "I am content even with enjoyments not experienced," appear dignified, as if out of anger renouncing his seat, bed, and other necessities?
How indeed can he shine, who, having abandoned both enjoyment and non-enjoyment, delights in the empty sky alone, having renounced everything?
How indeed can he shine who, having abandoned all things such as clothing, food, and bedding, remains alone by himself with a steady intellect?
"I am not the body," "otherwise I am," "I am nothing," and "I am everything"—how indeed can he who has such prattle appear beautiful?
That which I see, I do not see; that which I see is something else entirely. How indeed can such idle chatter be considered beautiful, when one has not renounced it?
Therefore, you are a child, you are deluded, and you are fickle, O playful one; I play with you through various conversations and dalliances—play, O beautiful one!
Laughing aloud with a boisterous laugh at his beloved, Śikhidhvaja rose at midday to bathe and departed from the women’s quarters.
"It is a pity that he did not rest within himself and did not understand my words," Cūḍālā thought, dejected because the king had failed in her purpose.
Then, my dear friend, as those two shared such dispositions, much time passed there in those royal pastimes.
Once, although she was eternally satisfied and free from desire, Cūḍālā herself felt a longing for the playful act of traveling through the sky.
Then, for the sake of attaining the power of moving through the sky, that princess disregarded all enjoyments and went to a secluded place.
Devoted solely to solitude, her body established in its own posture, she practiced for a long time the upward-moving vital breath.

Śrī Rāma said: How is it that this entire world, consisting of the stationary and the moving, which is seen here, is experienced as being devoid of vibration, even though it is called by the name "action"?
Tell me, O Brahmin, what playful movement of intense practice is this, for one who possesses singular effort, that has resulted in such things as traveling through the sky?
Whether one knows the self or does not know the self, or whether it is for the sake of spiritual accomplishment or even as a mere pastime—O Lord, tell me how this is accomplished.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O dear one, O Rāghava, every object to be accomplished here in this world arises in three ways: as that which is to be accepted, that which is to be rejected, and likewise that which is to be disregarded."
That which is beneficial to oneself is to be accepted with effort; that which is to be abandoned is relinquished once known; and that which is neutral between these two is to be disregarded.
Whatever causes delight is to be accepted according to the sound view; that which is contrary to it is not to be accepted. The wise know that which is neutral to be something to be disregarded.
When everything for the wise and learned man of right discernment consists of the Self, then none of these three positions can possibly arise.
At times, she may simply regard all of this with indifference, having cast it aside as a mere sport, or she may not look upon it at all.

That which is characterized by equanimity for the wise becomes something to be rejected by the ignorant; it is to be abandoned by one of expansive dispassion—listen now to how the sequence of accomplishment proceeds.
All accomplishments, achieved through the means of place, time, action, and material substances, delight living beings here in this world, just as spring delights the earth.

O virtuous one, among these four, the emphasis on action is conceived as being in the middle stage; for, in the accomplishment of the attainments (*siddhi*) and so forth, those stages consist of that very action in succession.

The description of the sequence of practices involving pills, collyrium, swords, and so forth, as well as the faults therein for those who are unqualified, would be too extensive here and would detract from the subject at hand.
Let alone this detailed exposition on gems, medicinal herbs, austerities, mantras, and ritual procedures; such elaboration would indeed detract from the subject at hand.

Whether by residing on Śrīśaila, in a land of the Siddhas, or on Mount Meru and the like, even the expansion [of practice] called "attainment" (siddhi) destroys the primary purpose for one who has already achieved their goal.
Therefore, listen to this practice of training in the vital breaths and other winds, which yields the fruit of supernatural powers, as it arises in the context of the story of Śikhidhvaja.

For having abandoned all latent impressions other than those concerning the goal to be accomplished, one remains within, contracting the openings such as the anus through the sequential performance of actions beginning with the [proper] postures.

Through purity of food and seat, through contemplation on the meaning of the scriptures of the virtuous, through one's own proper conduct, through association with good people, through total renunciation, and through a comfortable posture.

O Rāma of noble vows, through the intense practice of breath control over some period of time, and by abandoning anger, greed, and the like, as well as renouncing worldly enjoyments, [the mind becomes purified].

In matters of relinquishing, acquiring, and restraining, all the vital breaths come completely under the control of that man who knows [the truth], just as servants are subject to their master's authority.
O Rāghava, all prosperities, from sovereignty up to liberation itself, are attainable by everyone because they depend upon the body and the vital breaths.
Circular in shape and resting upon a vital point (marmasthāna), the channel named Āntraveṣṭanikā is supported by hundreds of channels.
It resembles the whorl at the tip of a lute, is like a whirlpool in water, has the shape of the letter *ṛ* with its dot, and is situated in the form of a spiral earring.
It is declared to exist among gods, asuras, and humans; among deer, crocodiles, birds, and the like; and among all living beings, from insects up to those born from lotuses.

Her hair is bound in a circular coil like the body of the lord of serpents sleeping from the cold; her white locks are wound in curls like the moon melting away before the fire of the end of the aeon.
Touching the thighs, the space between the eyebrows, and the apertures, she remains restless in her movement, constantly vibrating with the vital breath.
Within that [lotus], which is as delicate as the sheath of a plantain tree, there vibrates the supreme power (parā śakti), whose movement is as shimmering as the resonance of a lute.
And she is called by the name Kuṇḍalinī, flowing in the form of a coil; she is the supreme power of living beings, bestowing the vitality of all powers.
Constantly sighing like an enraged female serpent, she remained with her face upturned, having become motionless.
When the vital breath enters the seat of Kuṇḍalinī in the heart, then consciousness arises within, born from the seeds of the subtle elements (tanmātras).
Just as the Kuṇḍalinī vibrates within the body like a bee upon a lotus, so does consciousness arise within through the awakening brought about by the power of subtle touch.
There, through the mutual embrace with soft touch between the two instruments, the Kuṇḍalinī rises swiftly so that consciousness may arise intensely.
In that [space], all the channels connected to the cavity of the heart arise and dissolve, like rivers into the great ocean.
Constantly eager to fall and oriented toward entry, she alone is declared to be the common seed of all consciousnesses.
Śrī Rāma said: Since consciousness (*cit-saṃvit*) exists as everything, uninterrupted until the end of the kalpa, for what reason does its manifestation clearly arise from the sheath of Kuṇḍalinī?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O sinless one, everywhere and at all times, everything exists as consciousness and pure awareness; however, its manifestation occurs in certain places due to the influence of the elements and their subtle constituents.
Although it exists everywhere within bodies, it appears as flickering; though the solar light pervades all, it indeed manifests upon walls and such.
In some places it is lost, in some it is manifest, and in some it has reached a state of disappearance; thus one object is seen within another object, manifested by the various states of existence.
O sinless one, listen further as I shall explain to you in due order how the process consisting of pure consciousness arises intensely within one's own body.

All that has arisen from the elements—whether sentient or insentient—and likewise the entire expanse of space, is all nothing but pure consciousness, nothing but pure existence, and nothing but emptiness, just like the sky.

For that indeed—which is pure consciousness, pure existence, changeless, and consisting of its own name—is nothing other than consciousness itself abiding somewhere as the five subtle elements (tanmātras) of the gross elements.
You perceive that duality as having become fivefold within your own self-awareness, with modifications and the like contained therein, just as hundreds of lamps arise from a single lamp.
By their own mere existence, which takes the form of a tiny fragment of volition, certain groups of five here attain the state of being a body.

Some [refer to] the state of being animals and so forth, some to the state of being gold and so forth; some to the state of being locations and so forth, and some to the state of being substances and so forth.
For thus it is established that the world is merely the vibration of the five elements; O descendant of Raghu, the consciousness of the intellect (citsaṃvit) is present everywhere here.

It is solely by virtue of the five [elements] that there is the designation "sentience" in the body and so forth; the designation "insentient vibration" occurs in some cases, and the designation "insentient" in others, such as in stationary objects.
Just as a wave stands motionless like dry land, so too does this consciousness, though possessing a flickering form, become endowed with inertia within the five [elements].

Just as one might wonder, "Is this the ocean, O gentle one, or is that the restless one?", so too is this pentad of the insentient and the sentient [distinguished] through conceptualization and the like.

O sinless one, by the power of its own nature, the fivefold group beginning with the body is the living soul (*jīva*), while the mountain and so forth are inert; yet the stationary and other things are moved by the vital wind.
O descendant of Raghu, words must be questioned regarding their intrinsic nature; for speech is observed to manifest as cold and heat, as snow and fire, and so forth.

Indeed, when subjected to critical inquiry, the persistence of the five [aggregates], which have grasped portions of latent impressions and undergo transformation due to the absence of nourishment, must be accounted for.
However, these distorted latent impressions can be easily directed from here to there by a wise person through systematic inquiry.
Whether it be impure or even pure, it is questioned by that; and another pentad exists with awakened latent impressions (*vāsanā*), while [this one] has dormant latent impressions.
One should apply that [method] where the fruit of inquiry is experienced; one should not strike at empty space with one's fists.

Indeed, the aggregates of the five elements range from Mount Meru and the like, which are established upon the tips of blades of grass, down to insects and the like; these are the stationary and moving beings, all of whom are established in discernment.
Some have dormant latent impressions (vāsanās), such as the species of stationary beings; others have awakened latent impressions, such as humans, gods, and so forth.
Some are turbid with latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), such as these animals and others; some have their latent tendencies cast off, such as these who are destined for liberation.
Then, within their own respective cognitions, mind, intellect, and so forth were fashioned, along with the designations associated with hands, feet, and the like, by means of the fivefold aggregates.
Other designations have been devised by others, such as animals and so forth; other various perceptions have been established by still others, such as stationary beings and so forth.
Thus, O virtuous one, these various pentads of dispositions manifest themselves through forms that are moving or unmoving, sentient or insentient, in their beginning, middle, and end.
O Lord of the Earth, the single volitional resolve of these [beings] is the seed of the cosmic trees of creation; within those [trees], however, are all these [worlds].

The senses are indeed like flowers, and the fragrances of their objects are like the filaments; the flickering desires shine as the bees, and the restless activities are like the clusters of blossoms.
The clear intermediate spaces between the worlds are its thickets; Mount Meru is its root; the dark clouds are its sprouts; and the ten directions are its swaying creepers.
O descendant of Raghu, those innumerable fruits—the beings that exist now and those that will exist in the future—are victorious.
O Rāma, these five seeds are indeed the five trees; they arise by their own nature of themselves and perish by themselves in the course of time.
They themselves undergo diversity and manifest for a long time due to their inertia; yet, being distinct from themselves, they come to rest like waves in the ocean.
From here they go toward height, and from here they go toward stillness of their own accord; these [states] arise through dullness and discernment, like waves in the ocean.

O Rāma, those who have gone to the abode under the power of discernment, though they were once heaps of the play of the five senses, thereby attain a stable state here; others, however, wander repeatedly throughout the world.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This seed of the five elements resides within that Kuṇḍalinī; it vibrates perpetually within her in the form of the vital breath (prāṇa).

The stainless digit of consciousness is the touch of the internal vibration of Kuṇḍalinī; it is called "Kalā" because of its quickening, and it is declared to be "Cit" (consciousness) by virtue of its awareness.
From life it becomes the living soul (jīva), from mentation it abides as the mind (manas), from volition it is volition itself, and through awareness it is known as the intellect (buddhi).
Having attained the nature of the ego, this very one called the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka) abides in the body as the unsurpassed power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti), known as Kuṇḍalinī.
The *apāna* wind, having reached the lower part, flows constantly downward; the *samāna*, situated in the center of the navel, and the one called *udāna*, located above, [flow respectively].
Below, it exists in the form of apāna; in the middle, it is always purely saumya (lunar); and though nourished, it remains in its own form as udāna within the person himself.
If it moves downward despite every effort and cannot be held back by exertion, then the man meets his death because of that [fluid] having been forcibly expelled.
If it is not restrained by means of yoga, the entire [vital energy] moves upward; then, due to that forceful exit, the person meets death.
If one should abide entirely within the self, having abandoned upward and downward movement, then that person's disease is destroyed due to the obstruction of the internal vital air.
From the impairment of the general channels, general diseases arise; from the impairment of the primary channels, primary diseases arise.

Śrī Rāma said: O Lord of Sages, what is the cause of their destruction and what is the cause of their arising in this body—both mental afflictions and physical diseases? Please tell me this correctly and quickly.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Mental anxieties and physical ailments—these two are the causes of suffering. One should know that their cessation is happiness; the destruction of those two is called liberation.
In the physical body, mental anguish and physical disease sometimes arise separately, sometimes simultaneously, and sometimes in alternation.

They know physical suffering to be disease, and that which is called mental suffering to consist of latent impressions (vāsanā); for they understand both to have ignorance as their root, and thus their destruction occurs through the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna).
Due to the power of ignorance regarding reality, without the subduing of one's own senses, one incessantly abandons the attenuation [of the mind] within the heart amidst passion and hatred.
"‘This has been obtained,’ ‘this has not’—from such dullness or dense delusion, mental anxieties arise like mist in the rainy season."
When desires throb violently and the mind has not been conquered by folly, through the consumption of bad food and the traversing of evil lands, [the body perishes].
Through the conduct of an evil age, through the manifestation of wicked deeds, through the fault of association with the base, and through the arousal of evil intentions;
When the continuity of the openings of the channels has either diminished or become fully filled, and when the vital breath has fallen into disorder, the body becomes impaired.
Due to the fault of instability, disease arises in the body; it is like the transformation of a river's form caused by the rainy season and the summer heat.
Whether it be from a previous life or this one, whether auspicious or inauspicious, whichever cognition is predominant, that very one directs the person accordingly in that sequence.
Mental afflictions and physical diseases arise within the five elements; hear now, O upholder of the Raghu lineage, how they are destroyed.
In this world, there are two kinds of disease: the common and the essential. Conventional usage is considered the common [disease], while the essential is said to consist of birth.
Worldly concerns perish simply by obtaining what is desired; mental afflictions are destroyed by the exhaustion of their objects, and even physical diseases are thoroughly subdued.
O Raghava, without the knowledge of the Self, the essence does not perish; for it is only through the realization that it is a rope that the snake in the rope is destroyed.

O Rāma, the destruction of the core of the afflictions of mental anguish and physical disease is the eradicator of the root of them all, like a river in the rainy season [uproots] the creepers on its banks.

However, diseases not born of mental afflictions are destroyed here either by means of substances, mantras, and auspicious rites as prescribed in medical treatises and other sciences, or by other methods.
The bathing rites, mantras, medicinal remedies, and the methods of the teacher—all the treatises on medicine have been mastered by you; what else remains to be taught?
Śrī Rāma said: How does disease arise from a latent impression (*ādhi*), and how is it destroyed by means other than medicinal substances—namely, through methods such as mantras and merit?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the mind is agitated, the body undergoes extreme turmoil; for instance, a person who is enraged does not even see what is right before him.
Without looking at the path ahead, he runs off-course like a deer afflicted by an arrow that has abandoned its natural track.
Due to agitation, the vital breaths abandon their equilibrium and flow through the body, like waters on a riverbank when an elephant has entered it.
When the vital breath flows unevenly, the channels fall into disorder, just as the order of the castes and stages of life collapses when the king is improperly situated.
Some channels reach fullness while others become empty, throughout the body when it is deprived of the vital breath, just like rivers in every direction.
Food leads only to disorder—whether through under-digestion, indigestion, or even over-digestion—due to the improper movement of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
Just as the current of a river carries logs toward the eastern region, so does the internal vital breath carry food to its own seat.
Those foods which remain within the body through the process of digestion, undergo disease by their very nature of transformation.
In this way, disease arises from the underlying affliction (ādhi), and it perishes through its absence; hear now the method by which diseases are destroyed by means of mantras.
Just as *harītakī* fruits cause purgation by their very nature, so too do the letters *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, and others affect the body through the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
O virtuous one, through pure and meritorious action and service to the holy, the mind attains purity, just as gold does by means of a touchstone.
O Rāghava, when the mind is pure, bliss increases within the body, just as there is clarity throughout the world when the full moon has risen.
Through the purification of the *sattva*, these vital breaths flow in due order; likewise, they digest the foods, and by that means, disease is destroyed.
The sequences of the destruction and arising of mental and physical afflictions have been declared to you; now, through the discourse on Kuṇḍalinī, hear that which is relevant to the present topic.
Know that Kuṇḍalinī, who is called by the name Prāṇa, belongs to the individual soul (jīva) known as the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka), just as a flower-cluster belongs to its fragrance.
When one remains in equilibrium after filling that [channel] through the practice of inhalation (pūraka), then the stability of Meru is attained, as well as the fullness of the body.
When the vital breath, drawn inward and filled by inhalation, is led upward by consciousness itself to endure the exhaustion and fatigue of the heat, [then that state arises].
Like a snake, it moves swiftly upward, assuming the likeness of a staff; taking hold of all the channels that bind the body like a creeper, it ascends.
Then this entire body is made to float, like a leather bag filled with air and submerged within water, its interior completely sealed.
Thus, through yoga that moves through the sky by the play of repeated practice, yogins attain a lofty state, just as the wretched [gods] attained the status of Indra.
When the Kuṇḍalinī energy, by means of the flow through the Brahma-nāḍī, moves outward and upward to the top of the skull, at a distance of twelve finger-breadths above it;
By means of the practice of exhalation (*recaka*), which restrains the other channels, one attains stability for a moment; then, there is the vision of the sky-like state.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, what kind of vision can there be without the multitude of rays from the eyes? How indeed can there be the true nature of the senses for those who are not divine?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O mighty-armed one, no beings moving upon the earth can perceive those who move through the sky by means of their human senses, unless they are endowed with divine knowledge.
O Rāghava, by means of the eye of the intellect situated far beyond consciousness, the sky-faring Siddhas are seen like dreams, even though they grant their own desired objects.

The vision of the perfected ones (siddhas) is just like the observation of a dream; however, this is the sole distinction: that upon attaining the state of a perfected one, there is stability of purpose.
By means of the practice of exhalation (*recaka*), when the vital breath is brought to remain for a long time outside the mouth at the *dvādaśānta*, it enters the supreme city.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahman, tell me how the nature of one's own being remains unshakably established; for compassionate speakers do not feel weary even when asked a difficult question."

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: It is certain that the power known as inherent nature (svabhāva), which manifests from the Self during creation and so forth, proceeds in exactly the same manner during its maintenance.
Since ignorance is not a real entity, its power over objects may also vary in some cases; for indeed, my dear, autumnal fruit is seen [to ripen] in the springtime.
All this is indeed Brahman, existing through both diversity and non-diversity; it unfolds for the sake of worldly transaction, its state being described as purely conventional.
Śrī Rāma said: For the purpose of passing through subtle apertures and the like, or for the purpose of filling space, how is this body brought to either minuteness or grossness?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as a cutting proceeds from the contact of wood and a saw, so fire is born from the friction of two things by its own nature.
Flesh situated within the belly of a wretched machine, with its ends joined to one another, is like reeds in water, thickly intermingled from top to bottom.
His Kuṇḍalinī Lakṣmī was hidden within her own abode, like a string of pearls within the casket of a ruby box.
Like a garland of fruit from a whirlpool, it is constantly shimmering; like a female serpent struck by a staff, it coils upward with rising undulations.
Abiding between heaven and earth like action itself, characterized by vibration, consciousness is a bee within the hollow of the heart-lotus, a sun that awakens the honey.
All that—the power, the lotus, and so forth—is shaken on all sides by her internal and external winds within the heart, like a cluster of leaves.
Just as, my dear, winds arise spontaneously within the sky and violently devour whatever there may be—whether strong or weak, soft or hard—so it is here.
Struck by the winds, that lotus and the rest tremble; it moves to various other places within the heart through its function, just as the sprouts and so forth of a tree do.
Day after day, the vital air within bodies causes all the essences to generate fire through mutual friction, like bamboos in a forest.
Then his body, whose nature was cool and windy, attained heat through that [fire] which had arisen in all its limbs, just as the world is warmed by the risen sun.
That radiance, in the form of a star, should be visualized by yogis as having entered the golden bee within the heart-lotus, moving everywhere throughout this [body].
When that knowledge, consisting of light, is contemplated, it bestows [the power] by which an object situated even a hundred thousand yojanas away is indeed seen constantly.
For that fire dwelling within the sheath of the heart-lake, the water was like the dried-up fuel of the submarine fire (vāḍava), while the lake itself was rich with the lotus-clumps of flesh.
That which is its clarity and coolness is called its lunar self (ātman); thus, that fire has arisen from the moon, for the body consists of both Agni and Soma.
They know that all that is of the nature of heat is designated as the sun, fire, and so forth; that which is of the nature of cold is called the moon. By these two alone is the world created.
Whether by way of the nature of knowledge and ignorance, or as the essence of both the existent and the non-existent, that very [principle] by which the entire world is produced is thus divided.
The wise know that the light of consciousness, beginning with knowledge (vidyā), is the sun and fire; the learned call the darkness of unreal insentience the moon.

Śrī Rāma said: "O Lord of Sages, best among speakers, you have stated that fire arises from the self of wind and from the moon; now tell me, O foremost of those who speak, about the origin of the moon."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Fire and moon are established as mutual cause and effect; in alternation and in equilibrium, these two sustain one another.
Just as the seed and sprout are related to the body of a living being, and as day and night are related to each other, so too would their existence alone be like shade and sunlight.
This coexistence of shadow and light occurs because they are perceived at the same time; it is a state enriched by the perception of only one [of two things], like the existence of day and night.
And the causal relationship between these two is said to be of two kinds: that which arises from the transformation of an existing form, and that which arises from the transformation of destruction.
The occurrence of a second from one, like a sprout from a seed, is this relation of cause and effect, which arises from the transformation of an existent nature.
When one perishes, the existence of the second occurs like day and night; this is the relationship of cause and effect, born from destruction and transformation.
Since the transformation into the form of an existent—such as the sequence of clay and jar—is perceived by the senses, no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is required.

Even the non-existence of the sequence of day and night, which consists of destruction and transformation, has attained the status of a primary means of valid cognition when it resides in a single entity.
Those who argue with fallacious logic, claiming there is no attachment and no agency, and who deny their own direct experience, should be excluded with contempt.
O descendant of Raghu, even non-existence is indeed a valid means of knowledge (pramā) like direct perception; for all living beings, the absence of fire is a proof of cold.
Fire, through its state as smoke, goes toward the sky and attains the nature of a cloud; by means of this transformation of its true form, that fire becomes the cause of the moon.
Because fire, through its loss [of heat] and its resulting coldness, passes into that very state by way of transformation into destruction, that fire becomes the cause of the moon.
Having drunk the waters of the seven oceans, the submarine fire, through its emission of smoke that has assumed the form of clouds, produces once again exactly those same waters in abundance.
Having drunk the lord of the night again and again on the new moon day, the sun vomits it up during the bright fortnight, just as a crane spits out a lotus stalk.
Having drunk the cool nectar-like soma at the onset of the breath from the mouth, the vital force (prāṇa), having attained fullness, fills the body upon the arrival of the clouds.
Even water, through its enjoyment as the source of all things, attains the state of the sun’s rays; by transforming into its true form, that water becomes the cause of fire.
For water attains the state of fire through its nature of destruction, due to its heat; by way of the transformation of destruction, that water becomes the cause of fire.
Upon the destruction of fire, the moon is a transformation of its true nature; upon the destruction of the moon, fire is a transformation of its true nature.
Just as fire, having reached its destruction, becomes the moon, and just as the day, having reached its end, becomes the night.
Between darkness and light, between shadow and sunshine, and between day and night, a form that is distinct from both is not perceived even by the wise.
The junction as well would be non-cessation; that is the very nature of these two. For just as existence and non-existence are established in a single locus, so too are these two.
Indeed, all beings manifest through the two qualities of consciousness and inertia, just as day and night appear upon the earth through darkness and light.
This establishment of the world has been brought forth by the two forms of consciousness and insentience, just as the lunar body is cool due to the mixture of water and nectar.
O Rāghava, know that the luminous fire and the sun are of the nature of consciousness; know that which is insentient by nature and of the form of darkness is the body of the moon.
When the stainless sun of consciousness is seen, the arising of worldly existence is destroyed, just as the darkness of a black night vanishes when the sun is seen in the sky outside.
When the inert body is perceived, one's own consciousness appears as if real, just as the mass of the sun's radiance shines upon a lotus at midnight.

Fire reveals the moon of Soma, which is the long-lasting radiance of the body of consciousness; and the moon, being composed of one's own awareness, is the form born of the sun that resides within the body of consciousness.
But that consciousness, being actionless and nameless, is not perceived in its isolation; it is apprehended only through the body, just as light is apprehended by means of a lamp.

The mind’s acquisition [of objects] through its orientation toward the cognizable is itself cyclic existence; the auspicious acquisition of that which is free from the cognizable is indeed Nirvana itself.
Having thus received good counsel from one another, these two—Agni and Soma—should be understood as the body and the embodied soul, joined together like a wall and its light.
O dear one, when there is an excess of nirvāṇa and an excess of inertia, the state of Agni and Soma remains alone.
Prāṇa is fire, hot by nature; apāna is the moon, cool. Like shadow and sunlight, these two are situated, moving along the pathways of the mouth.
When the apāna becomes cool, the hot fire of prāṇa attains existence within it, just as a reflection appears in a mirror. And that [coolness] likewise exists within it in the same manner.
The fire of consciousness, by means of its radiance and through experience, generates here the moon consisting of speech situated upon the lotus-leaf, just as one perceives the light outside a wall.

Just as at the beginning of cyclic existence, a certain consciousness, consisting of the nature of cold and heat, attained the designation of Agni and Soma, so too does that very same [consciousness] exist here in the creation of men.
Where the sixteenth digit of the moon is swallowed by the sun for a moment, and where there is a space of one span from the mouth—at that place, take your firm stand.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen now to this which shall be explained in detail—how the body of yogis attains either minuteness or even grossness.
Above the sheath of the lotus and wheel in the heart, a spark of fire flashes forth, like a golden bee or a fragment of twilight lightning in a cloud.
Through the consciousness of growth, he increases rapidly like a whirlwind; indeed, by virtue of his nature as consciousness, he rises like the sun.
Resembling the first sun of twilight clouds, having attained growth in an instant, it melts away the entire body along with its limbs, just as fire melts gold.

One who is unable to endure the touch of water should dissolve it even from the tips of the toes through yogic method; for fire exists externally through touch, but within the heart through the particularity of the object itself.
Having subsequently shaken off the two bodies, he dissolves somewhere, just as mist is dispersed by a whirlwind when the vital breath is agitated.
Devoid of the foundational channels, the Kuṇḍalinī power remains situated in the void, having emerged like a streak of smoke from a fire.
Having embraced the ego-sense consisting of mind, intellect, and the living principle (jīva), she is a flash of inner wonder, like a streak of smoke from a firebrand.
Whether on a pillar, a mountain, grass, a wall, a stone, in heaven, or on the earth—just as it is applied wherever it may be, by that means it is fully brought forth.

O dear one, that very consciousness proceeds through the sequence beginning with *rasa* and ending with *anta*; it attains fullness by means of *rasa*, like the resonance of a lute's strings when drenched with water.
O Rāma, whatever form one contemplates as filled with aesthetic flavor (rasa), it quickly assumes that very appearance, just as a line in the mind of a painter takes on a particular shape.
Then, by the power of its firm disposition, it reaches the internal bones, remaining there like an extremely subtle sprout within those situated in the mother's womb.
O Raghava, the power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti) attains whatever form it desires as its object of knowledge; it perceives everything from Mount Sumeru down to a blade of grass.

You have heard how the attainment of powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and others is accomplished through yoga; now hear that which is accomplished through knowledge, which is an ornament for the ears.
There exists here only one pure, gentle, and unperceived pure consciousness; subtler than the subtlest, it is peaceful—neither the world nor the activity of the world.
When it turns toward volitional ideation and, by means of itself, gathers itself together, having fallen into a state of turbidity, it is then called the "individual soul" (jīva).
Through the delusion of mental construction, this body—which is indeed unreal—is perceived by the foolish-souled individual as if it were a real entity, just as a child perceives a towering phantom.
But when the perfect illumination has arrived by means of the lamp of knowledge, the delusion of conceptualization in the individual soul perishes like an autumn cloud.
This body attains peace through the total destruction of all volitional thoughts; then, O Rāghava, it is completely extinguished, just as a lamp is when its oil is exhausted.
Just as a living being does not see a dream once sleep has passed away, so too the individual soul does not see the body when the Truth has been cultivated.
The individual soul, enveloped by the body, abides perceiving the unreal as real; yet, through the singular contemplation of reality, it becomes bodiless, illustrious, and happy.

O dear one, that conception of a self within the body and other things which are not the self is a terrible darkness of the heart, difficult to dispel even by the light of the sun and other luminaries.
By the sun of knowledge that "I am the stainless, pure consciousness alone, all-pervading and untainted by its very nature within the Self," [ignorance] perishes.
And others who have realized the self cultivate whatever [object] in whatever manner; by means of that firm cultivation, they see it exactly as it is, swiftly.
O Rāghava, by maintaining a firm state of being, even those who are deluded transform poison into nectar and nectar into poison as well.
Thus, whatever is cultivated here through firm meditation, that very thing indeed comes to be quickly; for this has been observed repeatedly.
When this body is viewed through the contemplation of reality, it truly becomes a body; however, when viewed through the contemplation of unreality, this physical form attains the state of space.
O virtuous Rāma, you have heard from scripture that the method of knowledge leads to the attainment of powers such as *aṇimā*; now hear this other method from me.
By means of the practice of exhaling (recaka), the individual soul is drawn out from the abode of Kuṇḍalinī and joined [to its source], just as fragrance is extracted from the wind.

This body, its vibration ceased, is abandoned like a piece of wood or a clod of earth; yet there remains a regard for both the body and the living soul, like that of a gardener toward his watering-pot.
Whether in a stationary or a moving object, according to one's desire and will, the individual soul is properly introduced within it to enjoy its prosperity.
Thus, having enjoyed the glory of accomplishment, if that body remains, one may re-enter it, or enter another body, or whatever else pleases you, my dear.
Likewise, having pervaded all bodies and so forth with consciousness, one remains fully complete after having filled the entire universe.

O Rāma, having known that which is eternally risen and free from defects, whatever the Lord—the light of consciousness—desires in whatever manner, he attains that very thing in no time; the wise know the state of perfection to be nothing other than this state of being unobstructed.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Endowed with the sovereign powers of the *aṇimā* and other qualities, that royal lady Cūḍālā became thus, being a virtuous woman possessed of intense practice.
She traveled by way of the path of the sky, entered the hollow of the ocean, and moved across the surface of the earth like the Ganges, pure and cool.
She did not depart from her husband’s chest for even a moment, nor from his heart; she dwelt in all his realms as if she were Lakṣmī dwelling in all the worlds.
Moving through the sky, dark-hued and adorned with flashes of lightning, she wandered over the surface of the earth like a garland of clouds or a range of mountains.
Wood, grass, stone, the elements, space, wind, fire, and water—all entered him without obstruction, just as a thread passes through a pearl.
Upon Mount Meru, he wandered at his pleasure among the peaks, the cities of the world-protectors, and the hollows and openings of the quarters and the sky.
She carried out her dealings with animals, piśācas, and the like, as well as with nāgas, gods, and asuras, and with vidyādharas, apsarases, and siddhas.
With great effort, Cūḍālā repeatedly instructed her husband toward the nectar of self-knowledge, yet he did not understand it.
"She is skilled in the arts, yet innocent and young; she is my wife"—in this way alone did the king perceive Cūḍālā.
Even after such a length of time, that king did not recognize Cūḍālā, who was endowed with such virtues, just as a child does not recognize a magical spell.
Because she had not yet attained rest in her own self, she did not reveal that glory of her spiritual perfection to the king, just as the performance of a sacrifice is not revealed to a Śūdra.
Śrī Rāma said: Even Śikhidhvaja did not attain awakening despite his efforts toward that great Siddhayoginī; O Lord, how then can another awaken?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, the sequence of instruction is merely the preservation of established order; the cause of true knowledge, however, O Raghava, is solely the pure intelligence of the disciple.
The object of knowledge of the Self is not known through learning nor through merit; the Self alone knows the Self, just as a snake [alone] knows its own tracks.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, this being so, how is it that in the maintenance of this world, the sequence known as the instruction of the Guru is the cause of self-knowledge?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: There was a certain extremely miserly Kirāta, possessed of wealth and grain, who lived as a householder with a family in a thicket of the Vindhya forest like a Brāhmaṇa.
Once, O Rāma, as he was walking through the Vindhya jungle, a single cowrie shell fell from him into a place covered by a thicket of grass.
Out of miserliness, he diligently shook everything—grass, husks, and so forth—for three days in every direction to obtain even a single cowrie shell.
"Let there be four cowries for you at the first time, and eight at the second; then a hundred, a thousand, and a thousand again—so [he said] in his mind."
Wandering through the forest, miserable and unwearied day and night, he did not perceive even the thousands of people's laughs, let alone anything else.
Then, at the end of three days, he obtained from that forest a great wish-fulfilling gem, resembling the orb of the full moon.
Having attained that, his heart was satisfied; having returned home in happiness, he remained with all the prosperity of the world obtained and with all things pacified.
Thus, just as that merchant obtained that jewel, which is priceless to the world, by searching for cowrie shells day and night without weariness; so too [is this attained].
In this way, through the instruction of the scriptures, knowledge of one's own self is attained; for by following the lineage of the Guru, one seeks one thing and indeed obtains another.
Brahman transcends all the senses; therefore, O sinless one, the reality of the Self is not attained through instruction consisting of the cognitions of the ears and other senses.
And without the instruction of a guru, there can be no attainment of the reality of the Self; by whom has the wish-fulfilling gem been obtained without searching for cowrie shells?
The oral instruction from the guru regarding this great reality has been attained; that which is causeless has become the cause, just as a cowrie shell [is transformed] by a jewel.
Behold, O Rāghava, this delusive illusion which confounds even the great: one thing is sought with effort, yet another result is obtained.

A person performs one action yet obtains quite another result, as is observed throughout the three worlds; therefore, the best way to navigate this worldly delusion of successive existences is through non-attachment and desirelessness alone.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thereupon, King Śikhidhvaja, being without the state of knowledge of reality, fell into a supreme delusion, like a child entering the blinding darkness.
With his mind inflamed by the fire of suffering, he did not take even the slightest delight in those prosperities brought before him, as if they were flames of fire.
In solitary places, at the ends of the horizon, by waterfalls, and in caves, that creature found delight like a hunter whose arrow has been released.
O Raghava, like you, all kings, when entreated by their servants with conciliation, persuasion, and instruction, are made to perform their daily duties.
Always possessing unrestrained dispassion and a tranquil mind like a wandering mendicant, he is distressed even while remaining in the midst of great enjoyments and royal splendor.
O giver of honor, you bestowed exceedingly great gifts—cows, land, gold, and so forth—upon the gods, the brahmins, and your own kinsmen.
He practiced austerities such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* vows, and he wandered through sacred fords, forests, and hermitages.
Even so, he did not obtain even the slightest freedom from sorrow, just as one seeking treasure who digs the earth finds no treasure.
Day and night, this great [body] withers indeed by the fire; thus he reflected again and again upon the medicine for the disease of saṃsāra.
Overwhelmed by anxiety and dejected, he did not perceive his own kingdom—even with its great splendor—as anything but poison before him, due to his distressed mind.
Then, on one occasion, Śikhidhvaja spoke these words in a sweet voice to Cūḍālā, who had come into his lap while they were in a secluded place.
Śikhidhvaja said: "I have enjoyed the kingdom for a long time and experienced the grounds of prosperity; now, joined with dispassion, I am going to the forest."
Neither pleasures nor pains, neither misfortunes nor successes, embrace the sage dwelling in the forest, O slender-limbed one.

There is no confusion caused by the ruin of one's country, nor is there the destruction of people in battle; I consider the happiness of those dwelling in the forest to be even greater than that of sovereignty.
Bearing clusters as breasts, with red shoots for hands, they wore the swaying white clouds as garments and carried garlands of blossoms.
They are colored by the pollen of their own and others' bodies, adorned with floral ornaments, and graced by the slopes of their hips which resemble golden rocks worthy of being enjoyed.
Enveloped by pearl necklaces in the form of rivers threaded with pearls that are the waves, they were surrounded by their companions, the creepers, and by their most charming young fawns.
Possessing a natural fragrance that is unrestrained, they offer food in the form of ripened fruits; their eyes are the rows of bees, and their bodies are creepers laden with a profusion of flowers.
O fair-faced one, these forest paths, with their cool and pure-limbed trees that have reached a state of flowing sweetness, delight me just as you do.
As the mind becomes secluded, solitary, and tranquil in a remote place, it does not do so even amidst the orbs of the moon, nor in the abodes of Brahmā and Indra.
O slender one, you ought not to create an obstacle to this consultation; for noble women do not thwart the desire of their husband even in a dream.
Cūḍālā said: "O Lord, an action performed when the time has arrived shines, and nothing else; a flower shines in spring, and fruit shines in autumn."
Resorting to the forest is appropriate for those whose bodies are worn out by old age, but not for the young such as yourself; therefore, this does not please me.
O Great King, as long as we have not been abandoned by youth, we shine in our home like trees with a profusion of flowers.
Accompanied by Puṣpamitrā, who has grown old along with me, we shall go together from our home to the forest, like swans departing from a lake.
For a king who abandons the protection of his subjects at an improper time, a great sin will accrue to that very ruler who has become vulnerable.
The subjects indeed restrain a king who acts prematurely; likewise, servants restrain their master from improper deeds, and they do so for one another.
Śikhidhvaja said: "Enough, O lotus-petal-eyed one, with this obstacle to my desired goal; know that I am already gone from here to a distant, solitary forest."
"You are but a child, O lady of faultless limbs; you must not come to the forest. For even for men, O soft-limbed one, this forest retreat is difficult to penetrate."
Even women who are hardy are not capable of dwelling in the forest; for clusters of flowers in the woods are unable to endure a row of weapons.
"You must remain here, protecting this supreme kingdom; for when a husband has departed, it is the vow of a wife to bear the burden of the household."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus to his beloved, whose face was like the moon, the self-controlled king rose to bathe and performed all his daily duties.
Then, having abandoned all activity for his subjects, the sun went to the western mountain, as Śikhidhvaja had gone to the forest, which was inaccessible to all people.
Having withdrawn her expanded form, the radiance followed that very Lord who had departed from his palace, like a devoted female crest-ornament following its master.
The dark night arrived, making the world grey with ash; like the Yamunā, it embraced Śiva, who bore the celestial river upon him.
The quarters of the sky stood as twilight clouds with teeth [of lightning], having formed a circle; they were marked by the rising smile of moonlight, adorned with the young tamāla trees.
As the couple proceeded toward the further shore, they reached the region of Meru, which was like a celestial garden for the divine Day-Goddess and the Lord of Day to sport in.
This shore was indeed abandoned by the fierce-rayed sun as the two approached; yet for the couple—the night and the lord of the night—it was once again Mount Merau.
Then the host of stars was seen scattered upon the pavement of the sky, like a handful of auspicious parched grain released by the maidens of the quarters.
The night, moon-faced, dark as the gloom, weary yet smiling with flowers, reached her youth, her breasts being the buds of the lotuses.
Having performed his evening rituals together with Cūḍālā, he slept again upon his bed like Mount Maināka in the ocean.
Then, at the hour of midnight, when the region had fallen into silence and all people were nestled within the solid stone-caskets of deep sleep;
While she was fast asleep on that bed of soft silk, utterly overcome by slumber like a female bee within a lotus, he—
King Śikhidhvaja gently, very gently, released his sleeping beloved from his lap, just as Rāhu releases the moonlight from the direction of the sky.
Hari rose from his bed, from which the edge of the garment was half-hidden by his clinging bride, like the ocean of milk rising with its surging waves of Lakṣmī’s radiance.
Thinking, "I shall go for the sake of the Vīrakrama," that one of perfected intellect departed from the city after setting his entire retinue of followers upon that very path.
Having said, "Obeisance to you, O Fortune of the Kingdom," he departed from the circle [of vassals] and entered the fierce forest alone, like a river entering the ocean.
That vast forest of night, thick with dense darkness and harsh with swarms of petty spirits, was passed away together with him.
Having led him through the empty wilderness for the long day, he rested with the sun upon a certain woodland floor.
When the sun had become invisible, she performed her bath and other preliminary rites there, ate some fruit and such, and spent that night.
Again at dawn, the king swiftly crossed over cities, high mountain ranges, and rivers for twelve nights.
Then he reached a forest situated on the slope of Mount Mandara, inaccessible to people and far removed from any human settlement.

The trees were encircled by ponds whose water flowed from gurgling conduits; it was a hermitage of twice-born sages known in former times, where the sacrificial altars and dwellings had fallen into ruin.
It was a dwelling of creepers frequented by siddhas and free from small creatures, filled with trees and vines, and abounding in fruits that provide sustenance for living beings.
There, on a certain level, pure, water-encircled spot—cool, dark with green grass, lush, and filled with fruit-bearing trees—
With creepers bearing clusters of blossoms, he constructed a leaf-hut, like the rainy season building a cage of dark clouds accompanied by lightning.
A smooth bamboo staff, a vessel for eating fruit, a water-offering bowl, a flower-basket, a rosary, and a water-pot.
O King, having brought a patched garment to ward off the cold, as well as a grass mat and a deer skin, he arranged them within that small hermitage cell.
Whatever other object was suitable for the duties of an ascetic, he established that there, just as the Creator places his footstep upon the earth.
In the first watch of the morning, he performed his recitation preceded by the twilight prayers; in the second, however, he gathered flowers, followed by bathing and the worship of the deity.
Afterwards, having eaten some forest fruit, wild tubers, lotus stalks, and the like, that self-controlled man, intent on his recitations, passed the night alone.

Thus, within a hut constructed on the marshy shore near Mount Mandara, the lord of Mālava spent the day without weariness; he did not even remember that splendor of his new kingship—for what indeed do the glories of sovereignty not captivate when discernment flickers in the heart?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus Śikhidhvaja remained in the forest at Pūrṇamaṭhikā; now hear what Cūḍālā did meanwhile at home.
There, at the time of midnight, when Śikhidhvaja had gone far away, Cūḍālā woke up in fear like a doe sleeping in a village.
Deprived of her husband, she beheld the bed fallen into emptiness, like a sky devoid of the sun, lacking the full moon, and its beauty stilled.
She rose up with her face somewhat withered and full of weariness, like a great creeper poorly watered, its sprouts—the limbs of her body—devoid of vigor.
Neither clear nor pure, having fallen into agitation, she remained like the beauty of day turned grey by mist.
Seated upon her bed for a moment, she reflected with deep anxiety: "Alas! Having abandoned his sovereignty as lord, he has gone from his home to the forest."
"What task remains for me here today? I shall go into his presence; for destiny has ordained that the husband alone is the refuge of women."
Having thus reflected, Cūḍālā rose up to follow her husband; emerging through a crevice in the wind, she ascended into the sky.
The yoginī wandered through the path of the sky by means of the wind-current, creating the illusion of another moon with her face before the caravan of the Siddhas.
Then she saw her husband returning as he had come, wandering alone at night in a secluded spot, bearing a sword, as prescribed by the convention of the Vetālas.
Beholding such a husband, she remained within the hollow of the sky and reflected upon everything that would happen to her husband without fail.
O Raghava, one must proceed by that [path] in such a manner, at such a time, in such a place, for as long as the task requires, according to its arising, and until the vast liberation is attained.
Realizing that it was inevitable for her husband to see him standing before him, she turned back from her departure in order to confirm that very fact.
Let my departure for now remain aside; for before much time has passed, I must go to his side—this is the certainty of destiny.
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā entered the inner apartments once more and lay down upon the bed of Śambhu, like the lunar digit at the head of the moon.
"The king has gone away for some reason at this moment"; having thus consoled all the citizens, the woman remained there.
She protected her husband’s kingdom through impartiality, just as a female guardian of the *kalama* rice protects a ripened field in due season.
While the couple remained thus, with the king protecting the kingdom and the forest-dweller guarding the woods, time passed for them as they did not see each other’s faces.
Then a day passed, and then a fortnight, a month, a season, and a year went by—Śikhidhvaja’s time in the forest and Cūḍālā’s in her own palace.
What need is there for much speaking here? For eighteen years, Śikhidhvaja lived with the woman Cūḍālā in her dwelling amidst the forest thickets.
Then, after many years had passed, Śikhidhvaja—dwelling in a cave on the slope of a great mountain—was overtaken by old age.
Then, having observed that the ripening of his husband's asceticism had been long protected, and as those years passed in the forest through old age;
Then, because the fulfillment of her own purpose was destined to occur in that manner, she thought, "Now is the time for me to go to my husband."
Having reflected, she made up her mind to go to the vicinity of Mount Mandara; she departed from the inner apartments at night and traversed the path of the sky.
Traveling through the sky by means of a gust of wind, she beheld [the trees] adorned with clusters of jewels covered by the silken garments of the Kalpa-trees.
Residing in the Nandana grove, these red-hued women, like *siddha* maidens going to meet their lovers, grasp fragments of the moon that rain down droplets of frost.
He caused the winds to touch him—winds possessing the supreme fragrance of the Siddhas—as if they were a succession of great waves from the ocean of the nectar of the moon’s orb.
He saw the stainless moonlight spread across the expanse of the sky, as well as lightning flashes moving through the midst of the clouds and clinging to them.
Not separated from her husband, she gazed at him again and again, and said to herself: "Alas! For embodied beings, this lasts as long as life."
My own mind, too, finds no peace; it is filled with longing: when shall I again see that lion-shouldered one, so devoted to my affection?
"When you said, 'I see my beloved,' my mind too yearns; the creepers, entwined with clusters of blossoms, long for their own tree as their husband."
My mind also yearns, thinking that they do not leave for even a moment, as this elder sister goes to her beloved like a perfected woman on a tryst.
Likewise, my mind was fixed on this: "When shall I also come? These breezes are gentle, and these are the rays of the moon.
Alas, these very things that delight the king of the forest now cause me anxiety! O mind, you who are ignorant of the truth, why do you dance so wildly within me in vain?
O virtuous one, where has that discernment of yours gone, which was as pure as the sky? Or rather, O friend, does your mind yearn for its own master?
"Stay! Why do you distress yourself with longing for me, who am already so full of longing? Or why do you long in vain, O perverse one? Your husband has reached old age."

He has become an ascetic with emaciated limbs and free from all worldly desires; I believe that his mind has reached the state of being entirely uprooted from pleasures such as sovereignty and royal enjoyments.

Like a river in the rainy season that has entered the ocean, the creeper of latent impressions (vāsanā) is stilled; he is devoted solely to solitude, unified in self, devoid of worldly flavor, and with his impressions extinguished.
I think my husband stands like a withered tree; nevertheless, my heart is filled with longing because of your longing for him.
Having awakened my intellect through yoga, I shall unite with my husband, having purified all worldly attachments and made my mind equal to that of the sage.
"I shall appoint you to the kingdom itself; we two shall dwell happily for a long time. Oh, after such a long period, this auspicious desire has finally been fulfilled!"
I shall attain that which my husband has long contemplated; this indeed stands above all multitudes of joys.
Thinking, "What happiness lies in tasting the union with the uniform activity of the mind," Cūḍālā leaped over the mountains through the sky.
She traveled across countries, oceans, and the ends of the quarters until she reached a cave of Mount Mandara; remaining invisible while stationed in the sky, she entered the depths of the forest.
Like a whirlwind, her movements known only by the swaying of trees and creepers, she dwelt in a leaf-hut built in a certain part of the forest with her husband.
Having seen him through his yogic power, he understood that he was as if situated in another body, adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, earrings, and other ornaments.
She beheld there that very same one who once possessed the splendor of Mount Meru, now with emaciated limbs and darkened complexion, standing like a withered leaf.
He stood alone, bathed in a flood of collyrium-water, as dispassionate as Bhṛṅgīśa, wearing garments of bark, and peaceful.
Seeing him seated on the ground, weaving flowers and marked by matted locks, Cūḍālā, whose limbs were faultless and whose breasts were full, [approached].
With a slight sense of despondency having arisen, she spoke thus to herself in her mind: "Alas! How terrible is this folly, which consists in not knowing the Self!"
Such conditions as these arise through the favor of folly: "This is that same prosperous king who is my very dear husband."
Having fallen into this state, crushed by the thick cloud of delusion within my heart, I must therefore certainly approach the Lord, who knows all that is to be known, this very day.
I shall lead you here, of this there is no doubt, to the glory of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; having cast off this form, by means of some other form.
I shall go into his presence to grant him unsurpassed awakening; for this woman, though she is my beloved, does not sufficiently heed what I have said.
Therefore, in the form of an ascetic, I shall awaken my husband in an instant; for my husband’s mind has now reached full maturity through the ripening of his austerities.
Thinking, "Today, my own true nature is reflected in this stainless mind," Cūḍālā became a young brahmin boy.
Having become slightly altered from her former state in an instant, like a wave upon the water, she fell into that forest in the form of a Brahmin’s son.
With her face radiant with a gentle smile, she approached the presence of her husband; Śikhidhvaja saw that son of a brahmin walking ahead of him.
He had come from within the forest, appearing like asceticism incarnate, with limbs as fair as molten gold and adorned with a necklace of pearls.
Śikhidhvaja saw before him a lovely man walking ahead, his body adorned with a white sacred thread, clothed in a pair of white garments, and carrying a water-pot.
He stood there with a beautiful rosary, twice the length of his forearm, which did not touch his body and measured exactly one cubit.
With his head covered by locks of hair like a lotus encircled by bees, he illuminated that region with circles of radiance emanating from his body.
His face was adorned with earrings like the newly risen sun; with a mandāra flower fixed in his topknot, he resembled a mountain with the moon resting upon its peak.
He possessed a body that was both lovely and tranquil, yet powerful and with senses fully conquered; adorned with a tilaka of ash as white as snow, he was beautiful to behold and graced the world.
Beholding that son of the twice-born, who was as restless as the full moon resting upon the golden slopes of Mount Meru, Śikhidhvaja rose up.
Having completely set aside his sandals with the thought that he was a son of the gods, [he said]: "O son of the gods, pay homage; please be seated on this seat."
Thus he showed him a seat of leaves with his hand, and placed a handful of flowers into the palm of the brahmin’s son.
"Like the moon to a cluster of water-lilies, or like frost upon a sprout—O royal sage, salutations to you! thus spoke the son of the twice-born.

Having taken flowers from it, he sat down upon a seat of leaves. Śikhidhvaja said: "O son of a god, O illustrious one, from where have you come? I consider this day fruitful, since I have seen you today."
This is the water for honor, this is the water for the feet, and these are the flowers, O giver of respect; let these woven garlands be accepted—may prosperity be yours.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus, O sinless one, Śikhidhvaja offered all of that—the water for the feet, the respectful oblation, the garland, and the flowers—to his beloved queen.
Cūḍālā said: "I have wandered through very many regions upon the surface of the earth; yet this honor that I have received from you has not been obtained by me from anywhere else."
O sinless one, by this charming, fitting, and humble demeanor of yours, I believe you will surely become an exceedingly long-lived man.
O virtuous one, have you perhaps accumulated the austerity for the sake of nirvāṇa, with a mind that is peaceful, noble, and free from conceptual construction?
O gentle one, this vow of yours is as peaceful as the edge of a sword, since you have renounced a flourishing kingdom to dwell in the great forest.

Śikhidhvaja said: "O Blessed One, you know everything; you are a god—what wonder is there in this? You are recognized by your world-transcending splendor itself, which serves as your identifying mark."
It is my conviction that these limbs of yours are fashioned from the moon; or rather, why else do you drench them with nectar as soon as they are beheld?
"I have a beloved wife who now protects my kingdom; O handsome one, her limbs are seen here exactly like yours."
Cover this body, tranquil and lovely from head to foot, with this flower, as a mountain peak is covered by a white cloud.
I believe that your body, which resembles the stainless moon and is as delicate as a petal of a flower, must be suffering from exhaustion due to the splendor of the sun.
O dear one, this white garment has been prepared by me in this manner for the worship of the gods; let it now attain its purposeful fulfillment through contact with your body.
One's life attains fulfillment by honoring a guest who has arrived; to the virtuous, a guest is to be honored even more than a god.
Who are you? Whose son are you? By what grace have you come here? O you whose face is like the stainless moon, dispel this doubt of mine.
The Brāhmaṇa said: O King, listen; I shall tell you without omission what you have asked. For what man would deceive one who asks with such humility?
In this world-receptacle, there exists the sage Nārada, whose self is pure; he is like a camphor tilaka-mark upon the lovely face of auspicious fortune.
Once, that divine sage was established in meditation within a cave; there, on the golden slope, the Ganges flows with its vast waves.
They shone like shimmering pearl necklaces upon the beauty of Mount Meru. Once, on the bank of a river at the conclusion of his meditation, the sage Nārada [beheld them].
Hearing the tinkling sound of jingling bracelets—a playful and melodious clamor—he, his curiosity somewhat aroused, wondered, "What is this?"
Glancing casually at the river today, he saw a host of women, mostly Rambhā and Tilottamā, who had come out for water-sports.
She was playing, divested of her garments, in a place devoid of men, with her rounded breasts resembling golden lotus buds.
Like trees with beautiful fruits entwined with one another, they shone with expansive forms filled to the brim by the flowing liquid of molten gold.
He was creating, with his thighs, a multitude of pillars for the temple of desire, while the sky-dwelling goddess was pervaded by him who had purified the moon.
With the flood of the essence of its loveliness, it seemed to threaten the rivers with its walls, which were like the chariot wheels of the God of Love from the celestial gardens.
With the waters of the Gaṅgā diverted from their course by embankments along the slopes of its hips, it stood as if the Universal Form itself, with every limb visible everywhere.
With every limb reflected therein, it attained the state of being a mutual mirror, like a leafy sprout from a branch of the kalpa-tree of Time that rains down [its fruits].
From the forest of the sky, born from the pollen of the flowers of light, which is crowded with the buds of the splendor of day and possesses a network of various curling creepers.
From the single time-snake that pierces the seven oceans with its throbbing waters, it [the world] is filled with intense passion, as if in rivalry with the clusters of her budding breasts.
Repeatedly lifting up her face, which was like a fully blossomed lotus petal, with its trembling curls, hair, eyes, and pupils acting as bees;
By those who accumulated a treasury for the sake of warding off the calamities of death, there was a blooming golden lotus, difficult for the multitudes of living beings to attain.
In a secret cave within Mount Meru, concealed by the shoots of lotus plants, cool on the bank of the celestial river, its impurities washed away by the waters of the gods;
Beholding that beautiful woman, whose form was like the fullness of the lunar orb gathered together in one place, the mind of the sage was suddenly overcome.

When the mind was agitated by waves of bliss and the vital breath (prāṇānila) remained steady, it became radiant and joyful, having attained a state of discernment that was no longer dependent on external objects.
Then, as he rejoiced, there occurred a slip of speech caused by passion, like a cloud at the end of summer that is filled with rainwater.
O noble one, the sage was like a fresh tree with its creepers and stalks cut away, or like the moon quivering with drops of dew.
The poison became like a double-dropped [elixir], its essential essence flowing away.

Śikhidhvaja said: Even such a sage—though possessed of great knowledge, liberated while living, free from desire, devoid of sin, incomparable in every respect, and eternally as clear as the sky both within and without—[remained thus].
O Brahmin, how did even Nārada become so infatuated with passion?
Cūḍālā said: O royal sage, for every species of living being in the three worlds, even for the gods and others, this body is by its very nature dual in essence.
Whether it be ignorant or knowledgeable, as long as there is the body and the mind, my dear friend, everything in this world is known to consist of nothing but pleasure and pain.
Happiness increases through some object such as satisfaction, just as light does by means of a lamp, or as the great ocean does by means of the moon.
For suffering indeed arises from some particular object, such as hunger; here, its own inherent nature (svabhāva) is the cause, just as darkness is caused by a veil of clouds.
When one's own nature—pure and true—is forgotten for even a moment, the visible world attains its full expansion, like a cloud in the rainy season.
Even through uninterrupted continuity, as long as one does not forget one's own nature, this demon of the visible world does not manifest in the mind.
Just as day and night exist by means of darkness and light, so too does the body exist by means of pleasure and pain.
For in this way, both pleasure and pain, through the observation of the causes of birth, become firmly fixed upon the sense-faculty, just as saffron is firmly fixed upon a cloth.

But for one who knows that, my dear friend, even if it touches [the mind] slightly, he does not come under its influence; just as the auspicious and inauspicious [powers] do not overcome a gem through passion and the like.

Just as a crystal does not undergo coloring through the presence of an object standing before it, so too the sage whose mind is liberated while living does not undergo such coloring due to his realization of reality.
The intellect becomes intensely colored by the mere attachment to an object; even when that object has passed away, the mind remains firmly tormented by it.
Just as a cloth, even after the saffron has been removed, does not relinquish its dye, so too the fool does not relinquish his attachment to sense objects.
By this very sequence, these two—bondage and liberation—are established: liberation is the attenuation of mental cultivation, while bondage is indeed firm cultivation.
Śikhidhvaja said: "O Lord, tell me how suffering or happiness arises for those who are far away when they encounter the causes for their own birth."
Your speech is exceedingly noble, extremely clear, and full of meaning; I do not reach satiety in hearing it, just as a peacock never tires of the sounds of thunderclouds.
Cūḍālā said: "Having obtained the heart-pleasing cause of her own birth through her body, senses, and hands, this young girl surely exults of her own accord in this experience of bliss."

Having reached the heart, Kuṇḍalinī causes agitation; she reaches the life-force residing within the Kuṇḍalinī. The channels of the life-force, which are fixed, have established their separate positions throughout the body.
The pulsating life-force enters the channels filled with vital breath.
With his self awakened solely by sensory contact, like the sap in trees and creepers, he remains thus during the movement of pleasant awakenings as well as the arrival of painful awareness.
The channels of the living being are fixed and extend separately throughout the body; they vibrate with joy for the fortunate, but not quickly for the miserable.

For those paths—whether well-adorned or poorly adorned—are not auspicious for you. Know him to be truly liberated for as long as this life remains stilled and motionless; know him from my perspective to be bound for as long as there is further throbbing with agitated breath.

The vibration of the subtle parts of pleasure and pain is the bondage of the individual soul (jīva), and nothing else; for when that is absent, there is liberation—thus is the twofold established order.
As long as the states of pleasure and pain have not been brought in by the deceitful senses, the gentle soul remains like one who is peaceful, equal in happiness.
Whether beholding happiness or suffering, the life-force within, though its body is subject to change, surges forth like the ocean upon seeing the moon, having transcended the senses.
O dear one, the living soul is agitated by perceived objects such as pleasure and the like, just as a cat is drawn by bait; in this matter, ignorance alone is the cause.
Through pure awakening to awakening, consisting of the knowledge of one's own self, there is no longer pleasure, pain, or the like; by that, he attains a state of serenity.
"Neither those pleasures and so forth, nor that [body], nor this 'I' who stands here are mine"—when the living being awakens thus, he attains nirvāṇa and becomes tranquil.
Since pleasure and the like are non-entities and lack that [conscious] nature, the individual soul does not turn toward them through internal awareness; rather, it simply becomes tranquil.
When the firm conviction that "all this is indeed the sky of consciousness, Brahman" has been attained, the individual soul comes to rest, like a lamp devoid of oil.

Just as a lamp goes out when the oil of happiness and other attachments is exhausted, so too does the individual soul [attain liberation] through the knowledge that "all is thus" and by contemplating non-duality.
Having realized that everything is indeed space alone, one does not fall into agitation; for what delusion of agitation can there be for this empty living being?
In this very manner has one lived since the first creation; by that same path, which was self-realized, one still travels even today.
Śikhidhvaja said: "O son of a god, while the vital breath moves through the channels suitable for its easy passage, how does that emission of semen occur?"
Cūḍālā said: "The individual soul (jīva), when agitated, stirs the series of vital breaths beginning with prāṇa, by means of consciousness alone, just as a king [stirs] his army."
By the movement of the wind, the fat within and the marrow-essence situated therein quickly abandon their fragrance, as do the pollen, petals, fruits, and so forth.
When it moves, it descends toward the truth, like thunder from a cloud in the sky.
Through the channel of the body's veins, the semen flows out spontaneously.

Śikhidhvaja said: "O son of a god, you are of great wisdom; you know the former state of affairs and how they existed. You are known by your very speech alone; for what more can be said of one's true nature?"

Cūḍālā said: Just as in the primordial creation, Brahman immediately manifested within Brahman itself in the form of pots, trees, cloths, and so forth, even so has it been established from the very beginning.
The wise know that nature to be like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, like the arising and perishing of water bubbles, and like the accidental letter carved by a woodworm.

In this world that has grown forth by the power of its own nature, various bodies wander about, subject to manifold transformations; some, through the exhaustion of their latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), do not come into being again, while others, possessing dense attachments, arise once more.
