Cūḍālā said: This great world is born from the power of the nature of the Self; having attained its stability through latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it remains subject to merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*).
"O Sage, our view is that once one has brought about the diminution of latent impressions (vāsanā), one is no longer grasped by dharma and adharma; consequently, a living being is not born again."

Śikhidhvaja said: "O best among speakers, you speak that which is most noble and of great significance; it has reached the level of direct experience, yet it is profound and like the supreme reality itself."
O beautiful one, by this power of your speech heard today, I have attained an inner coolness as if I had drunk nectar.
Therefore, tell me briefly and quickly that account of your own birth; thereafter, I shall listen with diligence to your speech, which is pregnant with wisdom.
Tell me today, exactly as it happened, where that heroic deed was performed by that noble sage Nārada, the son of Padmaja.
Cūḍālā said: Then, by him who was binding the intoxicated elephant of the mind to the vast tether-post of discernment with the pure rope of wisdom, [the mind was restrained].
That potency is like the liquid of the moon melted by the fire at the end of an eon; it is the coloring agent for mercury and other divine essences.
The Sage placed his form, melted away as it were, into a wondrous crystal pitcher standing at his side, which shone with brilliant luster like the moon itself.
There, on that mountain of vast beauty, it was massive on all sides, with deep hollows, very firm, and capable of withstanding the impact of stones.
That jar was filled by him with the milk he had intended, just as the ocean of nectar was filled by the Creator with the overflowing flood of ambrosia.

There, after a month had passed, the auspicious embryo—its growth following the sequence of the sage’s meager offerings—increased in the ocean of nectar like the moon’s younger brother, the moon itself.
In due time, Ghaṭa gave birth to a lotus-eyed child, just as the moon is born full from the month, or as the spring brings forth a flower.
With all his limbs fully formed, the embryo emerged from the jar like another moon, free from waning, rising from the subtle ocean.
In just a few days, he attained full growth, his bodily beauty becoming immeasurable like the moon in its bright fortnight.
In that sage Nārada, who was perfected in all accomplishments, he [the Lord] conquered the entire wealth of knowledge, as one might transfer its contents from one vessel to another.
In just a few days, having mastered the entirety of all branches of knowledge, the best of sages made him his very own reflection.
With that son who was a sage, the Leader of Sages shone like the moon risen at twilight upon a mountain of jewels, reflected therein.
Then, taking his son with him, Nārada went to the world of Brahmā and paid homage to his own father, Brahmā.
Then Brahmā, having received the salutation from his grandson—who had himself first offered salutations to the Vedas and other sacred texts—took him upon his lap.
Then, by means of a mere benediction, the Lotus-born Creator made that grandson named Kumbha omniscient and one who had reached the further shore of knowledge.
"O holy one, I am he; this is the pitcher. I am the grandson of the Lotus-born Brahmā, the son of the sage Nārada; I am named Kumbha, born from a pitcher."
I dwell at ease with my father in the city of the Lotus-born; the four Vedas are my friends, sporting in playful delight.
Gāyatrī is my maternal aunt, Sarasvatī is my mother; my home is in the world of Brahmā, and there I, as a grandson, am well-established.
I wander through all the worlds at will and without exception; yet, because I am fulfilled by playfulness, it is not for the sake of any particular task.
My feet do not touch the earth as they fall; dust does not stain my limbs, and my body feels no exhaustion.
"Today, traveling through the path of the sky, I saw you before me; therefore, my dear, I have come here and have told you everything."

"O you who know the life in the forest, I have indeed described everything exactly as it was experienced by me, including 'this I am. For the virtuous, being skilled in auspicious conduct, find great delight in conversing with the most excellent among noble people."

Śrī Vālmīki said: When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned together with the rays of the sun.

Śikhidhvaja said: "I believe you have been sent here by my own merits, which are manifesting at the time of creation—merits that are otherwise imperceptible, like a cloud driven by great winds upon a mountain."
O virtuous one, by virtue of having met you today with words that distill the nectar of immortality, I stand at the forefront of the blessed.
No entities whatsoever cool my mind in the way that association with the virtuous cools it, even including such things as the acquisition of a kingdom.
Where the unimpeded flavor unfolds in its universality, that state—free from the mental constructs of passion and the like—brings about the bliss of imagination.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the king had spoken thus, Cūḍālā, who was in the form of the sage’s son, interrupted his words and spoke again.
Cūḍālā said: Let this story rest for now; I have described everything to you. Tell me, O virtuous one, who are you on this mountain, and what are you doing?
To what extent will this forest-dwelling of yours continue? It is true that ascetics know how to speak both what is beneficial for us and what is untrue.
Śikhidhvaja said: "You are a son of the gods; you know everything exactly as it is. You are an expert in the ways of the world; what else shall I say?"
Out of fear of the cycle of existence, I dwell in the depths of the forest; O Noble One, although you already know me, I shall nevertheless tell you something of myself.
"I am King Śikhidhvaja; having renounced my kingdom, I have come here. O knower of reality, I am deeply afraid of birth again within this cycle of existence."
"O knower of reality, because happiness is followed again and again by suffering, and by death and birth once more, I am tormented while wandering through the forest paths."
Though wandering to the ends of the earth and though roaming as a scorcher of foes, I find no rest, like a poor man who has not found a single treasure.
O holy one, though effortless, fruitless, solitary, incomplete, and devoid of companionship, I wither away here in this forest like a tree gnawed by woodworms.
Even while perfectly accomplishing this unimpaired practice, I pass from suffering into a flood of suffering; for me, the nectar has become poison.
Cūḍālā said: "O Grandfather, I once asked this of you in the past: 'O Lord, tell me which is superior—ritual action or knowledge?'"

Brahmā said: Knowledge is indeed the supreme good; through it, one fully realizes absolute liberation (kaivalya). Ritual action has been prescribed merely for the purpose of passing the time and for diversion.
For those who have not attained the vision of wisdom, ritual action is centered on their offspring; how can one who possesses neither a garment, nor a cloth, nor a woolen blanket, give anything away?

Because they consist essentially of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), all actions are fruitful for the ignorant; for the wise, however, they are entirely fruitless due to the complete dissolution of those very latent impressions.
For in the absence of latent impressions (vāsanā), all actions become fruitless—whether they be unwholesome or even those that bear fruit—just as creepers wither in the absence of watering.
Just as the seasonal growth of the previous season dissolves at the change of seasons, even so the fruit of action comes to an end when latent impressions are destroyed.
Just as the fruit of the *śarala* reed does not ripen by its own nature, so too, O son, an action devoid of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) does not bear fruit in that way.
A fool whose habitual tendencies are those of a yakṣa sees a yakṣa, and not otherwise; a deluded person whose habitual tendencies are those of suffering sees suffering, and not otherwise.
An action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, though brilliant in form and exceedingly lofty, yields no fruit for one who knows its true nature, just like a blossoming *śaralata* creeper.
In this state, there is no such thing as latent impression (vāsanā) consisting of egoism and the like; it has arisen as something unreal through ignorance, like a sea of water in a desert.
For one whose ignorance has been destroyed through the contemplation that "all is Brahman," no latent impression arises, just as the ocean does not exist in a desert for a wise man.
By the complete abandonment of mere latent impressions (vāsanā), the living being attains within itself that state which is free from old age and death, and further, devoid of rebirth.

The mind accompanied by latent impressions (vāsana) is to be known as the object of knowledge; the mind free from latent impressions is knowledge itself. Having reached the object of knowledge through knowledge, the living being is not born again.
Cūḍālā said: "O royal sage, even Brahmā and the other great ones have declared that knowledge alone is the supreme good; why then do you remain in ignorance?"
"Here is a water-pot, here a wooden staff, and here a grass mat; O Lord of the Earth, why do you take delight in this display of useless things?"
"Who am I? How was this world born? And how is it extinguished? O King, why do you not investigate these things; why do you remain like one who is ignorant?"
O King, why do you not serve the feet of those who know the further and near shores, while they raise these questions: "What is bondage? What is liberation?"
Why do you remain like a stone-insect in the hollow of a mountain cave, wasting your life with this activity of barely perceptible consciousness?
That yoga is attained through inquiry, service, and association with the virtuous who possess equal vision—by means of which one is liberated.
Eating your morsel of food only with the virtuous, stay in the hollow of a forest tree, suppressing your wicked impulses like a worm in a crevice of the earth.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus enlightened by his beloved wife of divine form, Śikhidhvaja, with his face filled with tears, spoke these words.
Śikhidhvaja said: "O son of a god, today at long last I have been awakened by you! Out of folly, I abandoned the company of noble beings and dwelt in the forest."
"Aha! I believe my evil has entirely come to an end, since you yourself have come here and awakened me."
"You are my guru, you are my father, and you are my friend, O fair-faced one; as a disciple, I now bow at your feet—please show me your compassion."
Teach me quickly that Brahman which you know to be most sublime, by the knowledge of which one no longer grieves, and through which I may become liberated.
Within consciousness, there are numerous divisions such as the cognition of a jar and so forth; among these cognitions, which one is the supreme knowledge that serves as a savior?

Cūḍālā said: "O royal sage, if my words are worthy of being accepted by you, then I shall speak this to you; however, I will not speak of this knowledge in the manner of the woodpecker and the pillar."
The words of a speaker whose speech is not to be accepted become fruitless when questioned in jest, just as visual perceptions are fruitless in the darkness.
Śikhidhvaja said: "Whatever you say is to be accepted by me like the injunction of the Veda; this word of mine is true, and must be acted upon immediately without hesitation."
Cūḍālā said: Just as a child accepts his father’s word even when it is devoid of reasons and supporting arguments, so too should you accept these words of mine.
Immediately after hearing it, contemplating with your intellect that it is indeed auspicious, listen to my words as if they were a song, setting aside your desire for logical reasons.

Listen as I relate this delightful sequence of discourse, which accords with their own conduct, which brings about the awakening of the intellect after a long time for those who arise in such a way, and which makes the fear of existence easily crossed by those of great intelligence.

Cūḍālā said: Is there some illustrious man who is the abode of two eternally opposed qualities and fortunes in their entirety, just as the ocean is the locus of both the submarine fire and the waters?
Possessed of the arts, skilled in weapons, and proficient in worldly affairs, he has reached the limit of all conceptual constructions, yet he does not know that supreme state.
He set out to accomplish that which is achieved only through infinite effort—the attainment of the wish-fulfilling gem—just as the submarine fire strives to dry up the ocean.
For him who persevered with great effort over time, the wish-fulfilling gem was attained; indeed, what is not accomplished by those who apply themselves with diligence?
If one applies effort, exertion, and wisdom without weariness, then even if possessing nothing, one attains capability without obstacle.
He saw it standing almost at the tip of the jewel, within reach of his hand, like a sage situated on the peak of Mount Meru beholding the risen moon.
Although he was among the sovereign lords of jewels, he did not possess any certainty regarding the kingdom that had so suddenly come to him, appearing like a wretched commoner.
He reflected thus with a mind full of wonder, characterized by equanimity attained after the agitation of long-standing suffering.
"This is a jewel; this is not a jewel—if it were not so, it would not be that [jewel]. I touch it, I do not touch it; at some point, it passes away through contact."

It is said that the supreme jewel is not accomplished by this much time alone; rather, according to the sequence of the scriptures, it is accomplished through effort that may even end with one's life.
Miserable, with one eye squinted, I behold the light of the jewels like the flickering of a fly-whisk, as if seeing two moons through delusion.
Whence has such vast and abundant prosperity come to me, that even now I obtain this sovereign jewel which grants all perfections?
Indeed, only some great souls become truly fortunate, for whom the goddesses of prosperity become manifest in a short time.
"I am indeed a mere human, a wretched man of little austerity; how can supernatural powers come to me, who am the sole vessel for misfortune?"
Thus, for a long time, the ignorant man, reflecting with conceptual constructions and mental fabrications, did not make an effort to grasp the jewel, being deluded by his own folly.

When something is not to be obtained by someone at a certain time, he does not obtain it then; even though the wish-fulfilling gem has been acquired, it is cast aside with indifference by one of dull intellect.
While he remained thus, the jewels and supernatural powers departed; for those who treat them with contempt abandon them, just as an arrow leaves the bowstring once it has been released.

It is said that the supernatural powers (siddhis) come to a man once he has slain the state of wisdom; having arrived, they bestow everything, yet they depart when one is no longer able to endure them.
The man again exerted effort toward the acquisition of the supreme jewel; for resolute people do not falter in their own undertakings.
Then he saw a piece of unbroken glass, shimmering in form, placed before him by invisible, laughing, and deceitful siddhas.
Thinking, "This is a wish-fulfilling gem," the fool perceives substantial reality in that [clod]; for the ignorant person, deluded, sees clay as gold.

The delusion residing in the mind makes eight things appear as their opposites: it turns the sixth [sense] into two, a friend into an enemy, a rope into a serpent, and land into water; it turns the two moons into one, and nectar into poison.
Taking that burnt gem and abandoning his former fortune, he reflected: "Since everything can be obtained from this *cintāmaṇi*, what is the use of other riches here?"
"This land is unpleasant and harsh, filled with sinful people; why has my home almost vanished, and what indeed have become of my kinsmen?"
"Having gone far away, I shall dwell happily according to my desire in prosperity"—thinking thus, the fool took the jewel and went to the empty forest.
There, by means of that fragment of glass, he met with that calamity; for its appearance was just like that of ignorance, my dear, which resembles the luster of a mountain of collyrium.

Those sufferings which arise through the power of folly are neither calamities nor even old age and death; for folly alone stands at the head of all misfortunes, like the mass of black hair upon the bodies of people.
Cūḍālā said: Now, O protector of the earth, listen to this other delightful account, which is a supreme awakening for the intellect and worthy of yourself, O virtuous one.
In the Vindhya forest, there was an elephant, the leader of a great herd, who had risen up by himself from the Vindhya range as if through the pure intellect of Agastya.
Her two fangs were sharp, long, and white as vajra-flames; they were equal to the crests of the fire at the end of an aeon and capable of uprooting Mount Sumeru.
Bound by the elephant-trainer with a net of iron, he was tormented like Mount Vindhya by the Lord of Sages, or like Bali by Upendra.
Bound and tormented by weapons and jars, the elephant endured that agony which a steadfast man experiences when entering a new fire.
When his enemy, the elephant-driver, was seen from afar, that elephant entered the iron chest in which he had been confined for three days.
Then, out of weariness, that elephant made an effort to break his fetters; at another time, he produced the tinkling sound of small bells by tossing his head.
With those two teeth, he exerted himself for two moments and broke the network of chains, just as an Asura breaks the bolt of heaven.
From afar, his enemy beheld that severing of Bali's fetters, just as Hari saw the shattering of the heavens from the summit of Mount Meru.
When his bonds were severed, the enemy fell upon his head like a palm tree; step by step, Hari ascended to heaven, as Bali did from Mount Meru.
Falling from his two lotus-feet, yet failing to reach the elephant's head, he fell agitated to the earth like a ripe fruit struck down by the wind.
Seeing him fallen before him, the great elephant was moved by compassion; for the virtuous, whose noble qualities are ever-vibrant and expansive, exist even among those of the animal realm.
"What manliness is there in my merely crushing one who has fallen? Thinking even this much, he did not slay that enemy, though he was an elephant."
Having shattered the array of fetters, he advanced alone, like a vast flood of water sweeping away a wide-spreading dam.
Relying on compassion, Mātaṅga broke through the net and departed, like the sun in the sky after rending a mass of clouds.
When the elephant had gone, the mahout rose up with his body and mind restored to health; his pain vanished entirely along with the elephant itself.
Even though he fell from the peak of that lofty palm tree, he did not suffer any injury; I think the bodies of the wicked are indeed difficult to break.
The strength of the wicked increases in evil deeds like a cloud in the rainy season; and at that time, he was exceedingly zealous in his wandering.

When the enemy of elephants (the lion) had departed, the elephant, his limbs unaccomplished, returned in sorrow; but when he arrived, the lion vanished, like a treasure that increases only when it has been brought forth.
He diligently searched for the elephant hidden within the thickets of the forest, just as Rāhu seeks the moon in the sky to devour it when it is gathered with the clouds.
After a long time, he obtained the lord of elephants dwelling in a certain forest, resting at the foot of a tree as if he had just emerged from battle.
Then, at the place where the elephant was stationed, [he employed] a supreme collection of royal forces, consisting of troops eager for the elephant hunt, capable of capturing it.
In the forest, that elephant trainer constructed a circular trench all around; it was as if the Creator had fashioned a ring of ocean upon the earth in every direction.
That rogue covered it from above with a mass of young creepers, just as the autumn season covers the sky with a web of thin clouds.
Within just a few days, while roaming in that forest, the elephant fell into a pit like a mountain falling into a dried-up ocean.
As he was walking, he fell into a circular well as terrifying as the depths of Pātāla, located beneath a dry, excavated ocean and serving as a casket for the jewel among elephants.
Thus, having been bound even more firmly by that elephant-keeper, he remains even today in suffering within the abode of the earth, like Bali.
If he had slain the enemy who fell before him earlier, he would not have experienced that sorrow from having his own tethering post dug up by an elephant.
Out of folly, a man who does not purify his future time through the sequence of present actions goes to suffering, just like the elephant of the Vindhya mountains.
The elephant was indeed delighted, thinking, "I am freed from the shackles of the weapon," yet though he stood at a distance, he was bound once again; where, indeed, does folly not cause affliction?

O Great-souled One, know that ignorance is indeed the supreme bondage; yet one who is bound thinks "I am not bound" in his mind, so that he may seek liberation from it. For one established in ignorance, the entire rise of the self—comprising the three worlds—is suddenly [realized as] the ground of all.
Śikhidhvaja said: "O son of an immortal, please reveal once more to me that web of stories you have indicated, beginning with the acquisition of the jewel, Vindhya, and the binding of the elephant."

Cūḍālā said: "Through the completion of the vision of the meaning of words, within the house of the heart upon the walls of the mind, listen as I myself relate this wondrous tale; I shall open the picture for you."
O Lord of the Earth, you alone are he who is described as one skilled in the meaning of the scriptures yet unlearned in the knowledge of reality—a seeker of jewels.
You are a knower of the scriptures, like the sun upon the slopes of Mount Meru; yet you have not found rest in the knowledge of reality, just as a stone finds no rest in water.
Know, O virtuous one, that the wish-fulfilling gem is the unartificial renunciation of everything; you, of pure intellect, shall accomplish that which is the end of all sufferings.
O sinless one, through pure renunciation of everything, everything is attained; for the renunciation of all is indeed sovereignty—what could possibly be greater than that wish-fulfilling gem?

O virtuous one, through your practice, the renunciation of everything has been perfected; likewise, the rise of the Self as knowledge has occurred, whereby the splendor of the world has been diminished.
You have renounced your kingdom, along with your wife, wealth, and kinsmen, just as Brahmā abandons the task of creating the world at the onset of his own night.
"You have come to my hermitage from a place very far from your own country, like Garuda with the tortoise came to the end of the earth for rest."
In the renunciation of everything, only the notion of "I" has been left behind by you, like the pure essence of space by the wind, once all impurities have been wiped away.
When the mind alone is abandoned within the heart, the world attains fullness; yet you are obscured by the conceptual fluctuations of renunciation and non-renunciation, like the sky by clouds.
"This is not that supreme bliss, the great awakening of total renunciation; it is something else entirely, lofty and vast, which can only be accomplished over a long period."
When thought, having been seized by volition, gradually increased like a gust of wind fanning the movement of a tree, your renunciation flew away and vanished.
Whence can there be renunciation for one who even allows anxiety to envelop him? Whence can there be stillness in a tree that is possessed of the movement of the wind?
They say that thought itself is the mind, which has no name other than "volition" (saṃkalpa); while that very [volition] is vibrating, how could the mind be abandoned?
But when the mind has seized upon the house of thought within the web of the three worlds, O holy one, how can the stainless renunciation of everything be attained in an instant?
By grasping at mental constructs, O dear one, your internal renunciation has flown away like a village bird upon hearing a sound.
Having attained supreme freedom from anxiety through total renunciation, that being has departed; having been invited and honored, why would he cause you any suffering?
O lotus-eyed one, since all jewels of renunciation have thus departed, you have beheld with the eye of resolve the glass trinket of asceticism.
By you, in that very asceticism which arose from the delusion of vision, a single-pointed cultivation was fixed upon suffering, just as one might fix it upon the moon’s reflection in water.

Austerity performed without latent impressions and without attachment is infinite; yet austerity performed with latent impressions, which is uneven in its beginning, middle, and end, leads only to suffering.
He who abandons immeasurable bliss that is easily attained and exerts himself toward a limited object that is difficult to achieve is considered a fool and a destroyer of his own self.
Having undertaken the renunciation of everything, you have not accomplished it by remaining bound to the knowledge of the oneness of suffering in the dwelling of the forest.
O holy one, having escaped from the bonds of kingship which are filled with spreading suffering, you have now been bound by the visible fetters known as forest-dwelling.
For those who do not understand forest life, I consider the anxieties regarding cold, wind, heat, and so forth to be twice as great as the sufferings of imprisonment.
"You have thought enough that you have obtained a wish-fulfilling gem; O virtuous one, you have not even obtained a fragment of crystal."

Thus, O lotus-eyed one, I have correctly explained this to you, which is like the story of the effort regarding the jewel. Having understood this stainless truth for yourself, you must awaken to it; then, whatever you know, bring that to fruition within the treasury of your mind.
Cūḍālā said: Now, O tiger among kings, for the sake of understanding the true nature of things, hear the account of the events at Vindhya, which is full of wonder.
That elephant which was in the Vindhya forest is you here upon this earth; that dispassion and discernment are its two white tusks.
And that elephant-driver who stood intent on mounting the elephant—that ignorance of yours, intent on mounting [the world], brings you suffering.
O King, though you are exceedingly powerful, you are led by your own folly from sorrow to sorrow and from fear to fear, just as a mighty elephant is led by a feeble mahout.
Just as an elephant is bound by a tether made of adamantine iron, so you are encompassed by the calamities of existence within the snare of the noose of desire.
For hope is more treacherous than iron ropes; it is vast and firm. Iron may decay over time, but craving only increases.
That ignorance which an enemy, unobserved from afar, watches as a pair—the elephant and the driver—watches you, bound alone for the sake of sport.
Just as an elephant breaks the binding of a network of chains belonging to its enemy, so have you abandoned this thornless kingdom, a land of worldly enjoyment.
Sometimes it may be easy to break free from the bonds of weapons or chains, but for a virtuous person, it is not so easy to restrain this mind from its longing for worldly enjoyments.
Just as the elephant driver fell when he violently tore apart the bonds, so too did ignorance fall away when you renounced that kingdom.
When a person who has become dispassionate desires to abandon the hope for enjoyment, then ignorance trembles like a demon in a tree that is about to be cut down.
When the discerning person remains having completely renounced enjoyments, then ignorance flees like a demon from a felled tree.
When the flood of enjoyments has surely been released, the state of ignorance falls away, just as a nest situated in a tree falls when the tree is cut by a saw.
When you departed for the forest, ignorance was wounded by you; though it fell down, it was not slain by the great sword of the renunciation of the mind.
Rising up once more and remembering the insult he had suffered, he has cast you into this dense pit dug by the elaborate display of his asceticism.

If you had known the Tathāgata in that way at that very time, you would have caused him to be killed; for had you known the truth regarding the renunciation of the kingdom, he would not have allowed you to perish.
That the enemy caused you to be placed within a circular pit was because all that suffering from his asceticism was offered to you through ignorance.
O best of kings, that royal splendor which belonged to the enemy of the elephant (the Lord Śiva), O King, now dwells within the thoughts of you who disregard him.
O virtuous one, you are a lordly elephant, yet here in this vast forest you are like one who is no elephant at all; you have been cast away from here with such force by that enemy, ignorance.
The circle of the moat, shrouded by young creepers, is like the hardship of asceticism covered over slightly by the conduct of the virtuous.
Thus, even now, O King, you remain in this most dreadful pit of suffering created by your own penance, bound in the depths of Pātāla like Bali.

You are the elephant; the directions are the fetters; delusion is the enemy; the stake is a fierce bondage once again; the surface of the earth is the Vindhya mountain—such is the report concerning you. Now do whatever you must do.
Cūḍālā said: "Why was that knowledge not accepted at that time by Cūḍālā, who was possessed of noble conduct and had realized that which is to be known?"
For she is the foremost among those who know reality; whatever she says and whatever she does, my dear, all that is indeed true and should be practiced with reverence.
O King, if you did not carry out her word, why then did you not skillfully practice the renunciation of everything?

Śikhidhvaja said: "The kingdom has been abandoned, the home abandoned, and likewise the country; even the wife has been abandoned. Yet, my dear friend, why has total renunciation not been accomplished?"
Cūḍālā said: "Wealth, wife, home, kingdom, land, the royal parasol, and kinsmen—all these are not yours, O King; for what is your renunciation?"
There remains for you an unsurpassed portion that has not yet been relinquished; by renouncing it entirely, you shall attain a state free from sorrow.
Śikhidhvaja said: "If my entire kingdom were not mine, then even this entire forest—abounding with mountains, trees, and shrubs—would be mine; yet even that I renounce."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, even as he was speaking thus, impelled by the words of Kumbha, the self-controlled hero Śikhidhvaja—in the mere twinkling of an eye—[attained his goal].
Having made a very firm resolve, he completely wiped away that attachment to the forest, just as the flood of the rainy season washes away a streak of dust on its bank by itself.
Śikhidhvaja said: "Even from the forest with its trees, mountains, groves, and chasms, my latent desire has surely been abandoned; renunciation now abides within me."
Kumbha said: "The mountain slope, the forest, the chasm, the water, the trees, the ground—none of these belong to you; how then can there be 'renunciation of everything' for you?"
There remains for you an unsurpassed portion that has not yet been relinquished; by renouncing it entirely, you shall attain supreme freedom from sorrow.
Śikhidhvaja said: "If all this does not belong to me, then my hermitage—with its pond, its grounds, and its leaf-hut—is mine; I shall abandon it immediately."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, while speaking thus, the self-controlled hero Śikhidhvaja, awakened by the words of Kumbha, [attained his goal] in a mere moment of meditation.
With pure consciousness, he thoroughly wiped away that state of worldly exertion within his heart by means of its very vibration, just as the wind disperses a streak of dust by its own movement.
Śikhidhvaja said: "Surely that tree, the hut, the creepers, and even my own hermitage have been abandoned by me; indeed, total renunciation has taken its place within me."
Kumbha said: "A tree, a pond, dry land, a thicket, a hut, or a fence of creepers—none of these belong to you; how then can you have 'renunciation of everything'?"
You have another supreme portion that has not yet been relinquished; having renounced it entirely, you shall attain the highest state beyond sorrow.
Śikhidhvaja said: "If all this does not belong to me, then I shall abandon all these things of mine—the vessels and so forth, as well as my leather bags, walls, and huts."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus, that tranquil sage of pure soul rose from his seat with an undisturbed mind, like an autumnal cloud from a mountain peak.
But Kumbha, observing those actions himself with a smile, remained seated in his office of state affairs like the sun upon its chariot.
"Whatever he does, let him do it; this is his supreme purification. Having said this, Kumbha remained silent and gazed at Śikhidhvaja.
Śikhidhvaja, however, brought all that household furniture and equipment from the hermitage to one place, just as the ocean brings the waters of the earth.
Having established it, he kindled the fire with dry fuel, just as the sun, moving through its rays, ignites the surface of a sun-crystal.
Having cast that collection of vessels and utensils into the fire, he entered Dhvaṃsikā, like the sun upon the peak of Mount Meru after it has consumed the world.
"O beloved of your husband, since you have lived for all this time with an undivided intellect, let it be so for you by that very fact."
But now that delusion has been dispelled, you no longer benefit me; for long have I wandered in the forest of mantras and roamed along the paths of ritual action.
"I have seen the sacred sites; now I shall rest, my friend," Śikhidhvaja said, and having spoken thus, he cast his rosary into the fire.
As the wind carries the pure row of stars through the sky at the end of an eon, so have you been carried for a long time by me, the man-lion, from the forest deer.
This very deer-skin was worn by you out of ignorance upon your seat; now go, and may your paths to that which is trivial be auspicious.
"Go to the state of fire; the sky with its stars is equal to you. Having grasped him by his arms from that bull's body, he cast off the hide.
Just as fire from the ocean, wind from the mountain, or forest fire from a tree, so have you, by means of your great conduct, held back my waters.
O virtuous water-pot, you have not been properly requited for your charming friendship, your kindness, and your steadfastness.
And you alone are the supreme abode of all excellence, by which very fire you have purified your body and come to me.
"Go by that very path, O friend; may your ways be auspicious. Having spoken thus, he then gave the water-pot to the Vedic scholar.
Whatever is good should be given even to a great fire; for like the intellect of a fool, that which is kept hidden always falls downward.
"That same destination is fitting for you; O Bṛsikā, turn to ashes! Having said this, he took both Bṛsikā and Mṛdvikā and cast them directly into the fire.
For the sake of purification and for the sake of a seat, he indeed cast it upon the radiant funeral pyre; for that which ought to be abandoned must surely be abandoned at once.
It is the established rule that the virtuous provide detailed explanations regarding what is to be adopted; [yet] I shall quickly abandon all these vessels as they are submerged in the fire.

Fire burns its fuel only once, yet it serves for one's satisfaction; O virtuous one, I renounce these instruments of action for the sake of the inactive state. No distress should be felt therein—for who indeed would carry what is unfit?

Having spoken thus, the king instantly offered into the fire his entire collection of vessels and utensils suitable for the pleasures of forest life; he cast that multitude of implements into the flames all at once, like Time himself when the world blazes at the end of an aeon.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, having risen, he burned that dry grass-hut, which had been vainly constructed by the conceptualizations of his own ignorant mind.
Whatever remained, all of that Śikhidhvaja, with a mind free from agitation and observing silence, gradually [performed] with a composed intellect.
He burned it, threw it away, abandoned it, or broke it; he even took pleasure in his own belongings, clothing, food, and so forth.
That hermitage of his became a place where people were seen and then vanished, resembling the hermitage of Dakṣa’s sacrifice after it had been destroyed by the army of Vīrabhadra.
The herds of deer fled from the hermitage, abandoning their chewing of the cud, like the terrified people fleeing from a great city consumed by fire.
The king, who was satisfied with mere outward form and devoid of affection, said: "That collection of goods, along with the dry fuel, is being consumed by the fire."
Śikhidhvaja said: "Having abandoned all latent impressions therein, I indeed stand as one who has renounced everything. Oh, after such a long time, O son of a god, I have finally been awakened!"
I am perfected, absolute, pure, and awakened through bliss; what indeed could this reality be, other than a sequence born of my own volition?
To the extent that the various causes of bondage are abandoned, to that same extent the mind attains supreme peace.
I am at peace, I am fully extinguished, I am happy, and I am victorious; my obstructions have been destroyed, and I have accomplished the relinquishment of everything.
Naked, with the quarters as my garment and equal to the quarters themselves, I stand here; O son of a god, through such great renunciation, what else remains?
Kumbha said: "O King Śikhidhvaja, you have not renounced anything at all; do not vainly pretend to the supreme bliss that comes from the renunciation of everything."
There remains for you an unsurpassed portion that has not yet been relinquished; by renouncing it entirely, you shall attain supreme, sorrowless peace.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O mighty-armed Rāma, lotus-eyed one, having heard this, the king reflected for a moment and spoke as follows.
Śikhidhvaja said: "O son of a deity, when all has been completely renounced, only this body remains for me—a mass of wild beasts that are the senses, with a form composed of blood and flesh."
Having risen from that state, I shall again bring my body to its state of destruction by leaping from the Bhṛgu cliff without obstacle, and thus become one who has renounced everything.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus, as he was making a sudden effort to rise in order to cast his body into the pit standing before him, Kumbha also spoke.
Kumbha said: "O King, why do you cast away this innocent body in the great forest? For even a bull, when enraged, kills a young calf though it be ignorant."
This wretched body is indeed inert, mute in nature, and miserable; it is nothing at all belonging to you, so do not abandon your body in vain.
This silent self remains absorbed in meditation within itself alone; it is moved only by another, just as a piece of wood is moved by a wave.
Another person alone, who is worthy of restraint, repeatedly and forcibly agitates him, just as a drunken thief disturbs an ascetic dwelling in solitude.
Indeed, the body is not at fault for the occurrence of pleasure, pain, and so forth; nor is the tree at fault when the self experiences its fruit through the movement of the self.
The wind, throbbing, causes the falling of fruits, heads, and flowers; what offense has the young man committed against himself by being virtuous toward the steadfast?
O lotus-eyed one, it is said that even though you have cast off your body, the renunciation of everything has not yet reached completion for you, for that is indeed difficult to achieve.
O Bhṛgu, you are needlessly casting away this innocent body; by abandoning the body, one does not truly become a renouncer.
If you utterly renounce that evil by which this body is shaken, like a tree by a rutting elephant, then you are one who possesses great renunciation.
O King, when that [desire] is abandoned, everything beginning with the body is abandoned; otherwise, even though submerged, this [desire] sprouts again and again.
Śikhidhvaja said: "By what is this body moved? What is the seed of births and karmas? O handsome one, when what is abandoned does everything become relinquished?"

Kumbha said: "O virtuous one, O King, the renunciation of everything does not occur through the abandonment of the body, nor by the relinquishing of a kingdom, nor by the withering away of one's hut and such things."
When everything—whatever it may be and from whatever source—is completely renounced within that single cause of all, then the relinquishment of everything has been accomplished.
Śikhidhvaja said: "Everything is all-pervading, yet everything must always be abandoned and renounced. Tell me, O best among those who know the truth of all things, what is meant by 'everything'?"

Kumbha said: O virtuous one, that which has a universal form and is designated by names such as "jīva" and "prāṇa"—which is neither inert nor non-inert, yet deluded—is traditionally known as the "all," namely, the mind (citta).
Know that the mind alone is delusion; know, O King, that the mind is the person. Know that the mind is the web of the world; it is remembered that everything is the mind.

O Lord of the Earth, the mind is the seed of everything—of kingship and the like, of the body and the like, and of the stages of life and the like—just as the seed of a tree is the source of the tree itself.

When the seed of everything has been completely abandoned, everything becomes truly abandoned; O King, through the realization of both existence and non-existence, there occurs the renunciation of all.
Whether all phenomena or non-phenomena, whether kingship or the forest, for one with a mind there is supreme suffering; for one without a mind there is supreme happiness.
All this revolves as nothing but the mind appearing as the world, through the web of forms such as the body, just as a seed appears as a tree.
Just as a tree is moved by the wind, a mountain by an earthquake, and a bellows by the weight of its contents, so too is this body moved by the mind.
Know that the exceedingly firm mind of the Great Sages is like a casket for all the enjoyments of beings, as well as for their birth, old age, and death.
All this proceeds as nothing but the mind appearing as the world; through the web of forms such as the body, the mind becomes the individual soul (*jīva*) composed of mentation (*manomaya*).

O Sage, that which is peaceful is designated by such functional activities as "intellect," "the great principle" (mahat), "ego" (ahaṃkāra), and "vital breath" (prāṇa), according to their respective functions.

They say that the mind is everything; when it is relinquished, O Lord of the Earth, the abandonment of all things is accomplished, which marks the boundary beyond all mental anguish and physical disease.

O best among those who know renunciation, the wise understand that the renunciation of the mind is the renunciation of everything; when that is accomplished, O mighty-armed one, what truth remains that is not experienced?
When the mind is relinquished, duality and unity everywhere dissolve; there remains only the supreme peace, transparent, one, and free from ailment.
They know her mind to be the field for the continuous harvest of worldly existence; once the field has become non-field, how could there be the arising of rice?
Mind alone, sporting with existence and non-existence, manifests here in diverse forms as objects, just as water manifests as waves.
O King, by means of total renunciation, which takes the form of uplifting the mind, everything is properly attained at all times, just as through universal sovereignty.
O King, just as there is another object for your total renunciation, so too do you become an object for another; indeed, O King, you give away while you yourself receive.
By him who has renounced everything, the entire web of the world throughout the three times has been contained within, like a pearl within its casing.
By whom all has been relinquished, even while abiding in that void, the entire world situated in the three times remains like a string of pearls upon a thread.
By him by whom everything has been abandoned, as if by a lamp without oil; by him everything is illuminated, as if by a lamp with oil.
Having renounced everything that remains, he who sleeps like a lamp devoid of oil shines with a luminous nature, remaining equanimous like a lamp filled with oil.
Just as you alone remain when all things have been removed, so too does primordial wisdom remain when every form of grasping has been relinquished.
Just as you, O King, are not like others even when all things have been consumed by fire, so too, my dear, is Nirvana said to arise from the renunciation of everything.
For total renunciation is empty of self, yet it is the basis for all cognitions—just as space is the support for the infinite and sublime [forms] of the celestial beings.
For one who drinks the nectar of total renunciation, no fears of old age or death cause any affliction, just as streaks in the sky do not affect the void.
The renunciation of everything is the cause of greatness and stainless radiance; for if you renounce all, there arises the most vast stability of intellect.
The renunciation of everything is supreme bliss; all else is most grievous suffering. Having accepted this with the word "Om," do whatever you desire.
For one who renounces everything, everything indeed comes to him; just as water enters the fire, so too does it return to the ocean.
Within every act of renunciation lies the knowledge that brings clarity to the self; for indeed, it is within the emptiness of a vessel that jewels and such are contained.
Even in this degenerate age, at a time when all was being swept away, the Śākya Sage remained as firm as Mount Meru, free from all fear, solely by virtue of his total renunciation.
O Great King, the relinquishing of everything is the foundation of all prosperity; for since he does not grasp at anything whatsoever, everything is bestowed upon him.
Having renounced everything, being peaceful, self-abiding, and like the sky, you have become gentle; O King, remain in that very state.

Having renounced everything, O Great Being, you must now renounce that by which [renunciation] is abandoned; and having cast off the stain of pride in renunciation, become one whose nature is liberated, O Protector of the Earth!
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: While Kumbha was thus speaking repeatedly about the renunciation of the mind, the gentle king, reflecting within himself, spoke these words.
Śikhidhvaja said: "The bird of the space of my heart, the monkey of the tree of my heart—though repeatedly driven away, my mind indeed returns again and again."
I know how to seize this mind like a fish from a tangled net, but I do not know how to relinquish it, like a supreme treasure.
O Blessed One, tell me truly the original nature of the mind; thereafter, O Lord, tell me truly how to relinquish that mind.
Kumbha said: O Great King, know that latent impressions (*vāsanā*) alone are the very nature of the mind; indeed, the word "mind" (*citta*) is cited as a synonym for latent impressions.
Its renunciation is exceedingly easy and simple to accomplish, even more so than the stilling of the mind; it brings greater bliss than sovereignty and is more beautiful than a flower.
But for a fool, the renunciation of the mind has indeed become difficult to accomplish, like sovereignty for a commoner or like being Mount Sumeru for a blade of grass.

Śikhidhvaja said: "I know the true nature of the mind to be agitated and composed of latent impressions (vāsanā); I consider its abandonment to be more difficult to accomplish than even swallowing a thunderbolt."
Of the flower that is the fragrance of cyclic existence, of the fire that burns with suffering, of the lotus-stalk that is the world, and of the sky that is the wind of delusion;
Tell me how the effortless relinquishing of the mind occurs—of the mind that drives the machine of the body and acts as a bee within the lotus of the heart.

Kumbha said: O virtuous one, that total destruction of this mind which brings about the end of saṃsāra is precisely what has been called "the renunciation of the mind" by those of far-reaching vision.

Śikhidhvaja said: "I believe that through the renunciation of the mind, the destruction of the mind leads to perfect accomplishment. How can its absence be experienced even a hundred times over the course of this illness?"
Kumbha said: The tree of the mind has "I" as its seed, along with its branches, fruits, and sprouts; uproot it together with its very root, and become one whose heart is like space.
Śikhidhvaja said: O Sage, what is the root of the mind? What is its sprout? What is its origin? What are its branches, and what are its trunks? And how is it to be uprooted?
Kumbha said: O high-minded one, know that this arising of the sense of "I," which consists of the perception of the mind, is the seed of this tree of the mind.
The state of the Supreme Self is the field; that field belongs to the one composed of Māyā. From this [field], when first sprouted, there arises the sprout whose form is experience.
That which is of the nature of certainty and formless is called "intellect" (buddhi); it is the swelling of this very sprout designated as intellect.

Consisting of volitional constructs, it is designated by the names "mind" (*citta*) and "intellect" (*manas*); the living soul (*jīva*), whose nature is false perception, is indeed empty in essence, like a stone.
This body is a pillar, composed of sinews, bones, and flesh; its latent impression (*vāsanā*) is the movement of time within the region of the sprout in another place.
The branches of the tree of the mind are long, far-reaching, and spread out; they are the sense faculties, which yield meager enjoyment and have existence and non-existence as their source.
The great trunks of this tree-like mind, which is filled with both auspicious and inauspicious fruits, [arise] at every moment.

"Cutting away the branches of the treatises, apply yourself to the scraping away of the root. Śikhidhvaja said: "I am performing the lopping off of the trunk, branches, and so forth of the tree of the mind."
"O Sage, how shall I perform the complete eradication of the root? Kumbha replied: "The various latent tendencies (vāsanās) are the branches, endowed with fruits, movements, and so forth."
Those who have not cultivated [the mind] are cut down within by the power of their own perceptions; yet the sage remains with an unattached mind, his speech and deliberations stilled.
He who acts upon what has been attained becomes one whose mental creeper is severed within; he cuts away the web of the tree and creeper of the mind through human effort.
He who remains would be fit for the testing of the root; the lopping of branches is secondary, while the cutting of the root is primary.
Therefore, O Great Buddha, be intent upon scraping away the roots of the tree of the mind; for that is the primary task, so thoroughly perform the burning of the root.

"In this manner, the state of mindlessness arises for one who has severed the thorn of the mind. Śikhidhvaja said: "O Sage, what fire could be effective in this task called 'burning' for the seed of the tree of the mind, which is the self-sense of 'I'?"
Kumbha said: O King, this inquiry into one's own self—taking the form of "Who am I?"—is considered the fire for burning the seed of the wicked tree of the mind.
Śikhidhvaja said: O Sage, I have reflected upon this many times with my own intellect, as far as the world adorned by the circle of earth and forests extends.
Neither the mountain slope, nor the forest, nor the rustling of leaves and such; neither the body and so forth, nor the flesh, bones, blood, and so forth, because of their insentience.
Neither are the organs of action, nor the organs of perception; neither is the mind, nor the intellect, nor the ego, because of its insentience.
Just as the state of being a bracelet exists in gold, so does the state of "I-ness" exist in the conscious self; but since the insentient is unreal by nature, it does not exist at all, O Sage.

In the supreme state, the self that consists of the arrangement and dwelling of all objects and so forth exists; nothing else exists because of its otherness, just as a great tree does not exist in the sky.
"O Blessed One, although I know that you are capable of cleansing the stain of egoism, I do not know the Knower within; for that reason, O Sage, I have long been tormented."
Kumbha said: "O lord of the earth, if you do not possess even this much [wisdom], then tell me, O sinless one of great intellect, why you are so dull-witted."
Śikhidhvaja said: "O best of the wise, I am pure consciousness, the awareness of my own stainless self—that by which objects are relished and that by which they are determined."
For one such as I, this attachment is surely groundless; or even if it has a cause, I do not know that state which is called "I."
O Sage, because I am unable to wipe away this evil, non-self-defiling impurity from my soul, I suffer most grievously.
Kumbha said: "Tell me, O mighty-armed one, what is that great stain clinging to you, by which you remain a transmigrating being, whether through the existent or the non-existent?"
Śikhidhvaja said: "I do not know how to abandon that which is the seed of the tree of the mind and the impurity of my sense of 'I'; for though it is abandoned again and again, it returns to me."

Kumbha said: An effect arises from a cause; therefore, that [effect] may exist everywhere. But that which is other than this, being non-existent, appears like a second moon; though seen, it does not truly exist.
"The effect arises from a cause; the sprout of existence arises from the sense of 'I. Having thus investigated the cause, tell me now."
Śikhidhvaja said: "O Sage, I know that the perception of 'I' is the cause of this defect; tell me, O Lord of Sages, how that may be brought to rest."
"O Sage, tell me how to bring about the cessation of the object of thought, so that this 'I' may cease to exist in a state of suffering through its orientation toward objects of thought."
Kumbha said: You are a knower of causes; tell me quickly the cause of this sensation, and then I shall instruct you in the sequence of causes and non-causes.
Tell me this: how did you, who are without cause, become the cause for me—who am of the nature of the object of knowledge and the knower, and consist of the thinkable and the thinker?

Śikhidhvaja said: O Sage, this existence of objects here, such as the body and so forth, which consists of the nature of the perceivable and the perceiver and takes the form of the known and the knowing, has its cause in the body and the like.
Sensation arises through the reality of the body and so forth by way of the existence of objects; it is like a movement caused by the appearance of what is unreal, such as a streak of wind.
Just as I do not perceive the non-existence of the existence of things, so too does the seed of the mind—the perception of "I-ness"—become completely stilled.

Kumbha said: If the existence of entities such as the body and so forth were real, then that [existence] would belong to you; but since the existence of the body and the like is non-existent, upon what is your perception based?
Śikhidhvaja said: How could that which has some perceivable nature consisting of conceptualization be of an unreal form? How could light be darkness?
O Sage, how can it be said that this body—which is endowed with hands, feet, and so forth; which possesses the play of the fruits of action; and which is constantly being experienced—does not exist?
Kumbha said: O protector of the earth, that effect for which no cause exists does not exist here; the perception of it is merely an illusion.
A body, which is an effect, never exists without a cause; how indeed could that substance be born which has no seed?
But know that which is a non-cause yet appears as if it were an effect before one's eyes to be like the water of a mirage, arising from the delusion of the observer.
Know that this which has arisen from false delusion is indeed non-existent; even for one who exerts great effort, the water of a mirage cannot be obtained.

Śikhidhvaja said: It is not logical to seek a cause for that which is non-existent, such as the double moon or its reflection; for whom does the decoration of every limb of the son of a barren woman shine?
Kumbha said: "O King, know that this body—the skeletal cage of bones and so forth—is entirely non-existent, for it exists without a cause due to its inherent impossibility."
Śikhidhvaja said: O Lord of Sages, why is the father not considered the cause of this body, which is endowed with hands, feet, and other limbs, and is constantly perceived as such?
Kumbha said: O King, because of the absence of a cause, that which is called "father" does not exist; for that which is born from what is non-existent is itself said to be non-existent.
The seed is said to be the cause of things and their effects; for indeed, my dear, no sprout can arise in this world without a seed.
Therefore, for that effect whose cause is not established here, it does not exist when the seed is absent; the cognition of it is merely an illusion.
Indeed, that which is necessarily non-existent and seedless is a delusion of the mind, equal in nature to the appearance of two moons, water in a mirage, or the son of a barren woman.
Śikhidhvaja said: "In the three worlds, among the grandfathers, sons, and fathers, why is the Primordial Grandfather not the cause of the initial creation?"
Kumbha said: O King, even he who would be the primordial Grandfather does not exist at all; for when no entity ever comes into being due to the absence of a cause, how could there be an origin?
Because its own seed, the cause, is eternally absent, O Grandfather, that which appears as something else does not exist as anything other than an illusion.
Like the water of a mirage, it appears only as an illusory form; even its capacity to fulfill the purpose of the grandfather is of the nature of delusion.
Your dense persistence in the womb of the Grandfather, based on false conviction, has indeed ceased; I shall now cleanse away the remainder.

Therefore, O King, because he is of the nature of consciousness, this God of gods eternally shines by himself within the self through the mind; for that very reason, the Self has declared itself by itself as "the Lotus-born" (Brahmā) and as its own essential nature—thus all this is peaceful.

Śikhidhvaja said: "If this delusion shines forth from the highest Brahma down to a blade of grass, and if it is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-samartha*), then how can it be the cause of suffering?"
Kumbha said: Thus, the manifestation of this delusion of the world has spread out, like the hardness of water that has turned to ice due to the cold.
The wise know that ignorance is thus destroyed when it has become slackened; for there is no emergence [of knowledge] without the destruction of the departure from its former state.
Indeed, that very attenuation of all cognition is the cause for the attainment of the cessation of manifestation when one has entered the supreme state.
When attenuation is observed in that [mind], its cessation also occurs naturally through the gradual disappearance of its prior configuration.
In this very sequence, O King, you should understand that even the Primordial Person (Ādipurusha) is a manifestation of the form of delusion, existing like the water of a mirage.

Even in the absence of a grandfather, this lineage of beings is non-existent; it has never been established that what is unestablished can be established by means of something else that is unestablished.
For this perception of a real entity has arisen like the water of a mirage; through investigation, it dissolves just as the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell does.
As for the claim that an effect comes into being from the absence of a cause after having not existed, its nature cannot be established except through false cognition.
But that which is perceived through false views never exists at any time; by whom could jars ever be filled with the water of a mirage?
Śikhidhvaja said: Why is the supreme Brahman—the infinite, unborn, unmanifest, ethereal, peaceful, and infallible—not the cause of the First Creator?
Kumbha said: Because it lacks the state of being a cause, and likewise because it lacks the state of being an effect, the Self transcends non-duality; it is neither effect nor cause.
How could Brahman, which is without agent, object, or instrument, without cause, and without seed; which is beyond reasoning and unknowable, be an agent?
Because it is without cause, that world would be devoid of the nature of an effect; it is non-dual unity, without beginning or end, the primordial perception.
How, for whom, by what means, as an agent, as an enjoyer, or at what time could that Śiva—who is inconceivable, unknowable, peaceful, and immutable—ever exist?
Therefore, nothing here has been created; the world and so forth do not exist. You are neither an agent nor an enjoyer; everything is peaceful, unborn, and auspicious.
Due to the absence of a cause, this world is not the effect of anything; because it lacks a cause, know that this world is an effect only through delusion.
And because it is not an effect, this creation does not exist; thus it is not found. When the world is not the effect of any cause, then it does not exist.

The establishment of the non-existence of objects depends upon that [establishment of self]; if that is established, what is there to be known? Thus, in the absence of cognition, there is no cause for the sense of "I-ness."

"Therefore, you are pure and liberated; what talk can there be of bondage and liberation? Śikhidhvaja said: "I am enlightened, O Blessed One; what you have spoken is most excellent and endowed with reason."
Due to the absence of a cause, I know that this Brahman is not an agent; because of the absence of an agent, the world does not exist, and therefore there is no perception of objects.
Therefore, neither the mind and so forth, nor the ego-sense and so forth, are its seed; this being the case, I am pure, I am awakened, or I am Śiva.

Having realized that "I" and "the other" are nothing at all, the perception of objects and so forth appears thus as something non-existent; by this, I remain peaceful from beginning to end, like the expanse of space.

Alas! That vision which perceived the manifold divisions of the world’s objects—including the categories of existence, space, direction, time, and the flux of moments and actions—has finally been stilled after a long duration; now only the peaceful Brahman remains, the immutable Self.

I am stilled; I am extinguished; I stand firm; I do not go, I do not rise, nor do I set. I abide; abide as you are, O self established in its own nature! I am auspicious, beautiful, purifying, and silent.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having thus attained rest in Brahman, Śikhidhvaja remained for a moment with his mind perfectly tranquil, like a lamp in a windless place.
While he was intent on a non-conceptual meditative absorption, Kumbha quickly awakened him with the words, "By my own playful sport. He was thus instantly aroused.
Kumbha said: O King, awakened from the sleep of ignorance, you abide as Śiva; for you there is no purpose to be served by either setting or not setting [the sun].

O dear one, you have now become liberated while living—your self shining forth all at once, having destroyed the nature of both the undesirable state and its opposite, and being entirely free from the perception of parts.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus enlightened by Kumbha, he indeed became possessed of awakening; having emerged, he shone brightly from out of the casket of great delusion.
With his intellect at rest in an instant, seeing the very non-existence of the object of perception, the liberated soul spoke thus with ease.
Śikhidhvaja said: "Although this is already largely known to me, let that which I ask be told once more for the sake of my refined understanding, O giver of honor, O giver of joy!"

In the auspicious, peaceful, and non-manifest state, whose nature is not subject to arising, how could there be the cognition known as the seer, the seeing, and the seen—the very soul of the universe?
Kumbha said: "Well asked, O great king; you shine indeed with brilliance. This alone remains for you to know—listen now to that."
Whatever is seen here in this world, whether stationary or moving, all of it—abounding in every variety—is destroyed at the end of the eon.
Then, neither light nor pervasive darkness remains; at the end of the play of the great aeon, only the essential reality persists.
Pure consciousness alone—stainless, tranquil, and manifest as the supreme ether—is liberated from all mental constructs and united with the highest intellect.
That which is manifested as one, utterly transparent, tranquil, pervasive, and radiant—the splendor whose essence is the Supreme Self, motionless and consisting of pure consciousness alone.
Beyond reasoning and unknowable, equal, auspicious, and irreproachable; it is the Brahman-nirvāṇa, completely full, filled with ever-arising consciousness.
It is the most minute of the minute, the largest of the large, the heaviest of the heavy, and the best even among the excellent.
Such is that supreme and subtle [reality], compared to which this sky appears as something gross, like Mount Meru standing beside an atom.
Such is that supreme grossness, before which this world appears like a mere atom; it shines forth in some places, yet does not shine at all.
Know that the manifestation of the universal self within the state of the Creator, who is beyond possibility, is the awareness of "I," which exists as the Virāj-self throughout the world.

Just as no distinction exists between the wind and the movement of the wind, so too there is no distinction between pure consciousness and the sense of "I," which are comparable to emptiness and space.
Just as waves and the like exist in water at the end of space and time with a cause, so too does the world exist in the Supreme—which is non-existent at the end of space and time—without a cause.
Just as bracelets and other ornaments exist within gold at the end of space and time and possess a cause, so too does the world exist within Brahman at the end of space and time and lack a cause.
Such is that most excellent and undecaying sovereignty over the world; it is non-dual, stainless, and peaceful, wherein the entire world is regarded as no more than a blade of grass.
Such is that supreme bliss when the Lord exists; through the knowledge of Him, the splendor of the multitude of objects in the world attains its true being.
O King, that single essence alone exists here, pervasive; it is the one, the singularly beautiful consciousness, which, by virtue of its non-duality, is not even "one."
Therefore, no second conceptualization whatsoever exists; the reality of the Self alone shines forth, which is both full and inexhaustible.
Everything is always established as if arisen in every form; because it is invisible and unattainable, it is neither effect nor cause.

Because it is inaccessible to perception and other means of knowledge, that supreme reality is something indescribable; it is everything, the essence of all, subtle, and consists solely of pure experience.
For that which has the nature of being both named and nameless, and whose appearance is without manifestation—whether it be existent or non-existent—how could it possess causality?

That which is indeed the seed of nothing whatsoever, because it cannot be described, and which is not a cause—nothing at all is born from that, the reality of the Self, such as the means of valid cognition and so forth.
It is without agent, object, or instrument; it is truth, a mass of consciousness, and indestructible. It is the nature of the Self, without appearance, self-knowing, and unimpaired.
Therefore, O Sage, nothing whatsoever is born from the Supreme Brahman; how, what, or by whom could anything be obtained, just as waves and the like arise from their cause?

"Others [say] that at the end of an improper place and time, the world is likewise without a cause. Śikhidhvaja said: "Indeed, that which consists of waves and so forth in water and the like does possess a cause."
"I do not consider that others, the world, the ego, and so forth, are without cause. Kumbha said: "O Lord of the Earth, this truth has now been known by you in its true essence."
This world, consisting of the sense of "I" and so forth, does not exist here at all; devoid of the referent of the word "world," the world exists as being of the nature of Śiva.
It is created within space itself, tranquil, and subtler than space; just as emptiness exists in the sky, so does this world exist in the Lord.
Whether this world is similar to its own essential nature or not similar to any form whatsoever—when understood correctly in such a manner, it becomes auspicious.
By the power of right knowledge, even poison becomes like nectar; but when wrongly understood, the world is most inauspicious and a source of supreme suffering.
Even nectar, when consumed with the thought that it is poison, acts like the essence of poison; and so it is with whatever this Lord of Consciousness perceives.
Śiva exists immediately in that very way, with such a form, just as a flame, through delusion, appears with various illusory shapes.
For the reality of Brahman remains exactly as it is, without any change in its nature; indeed, that which is supreme abides within the self as the essence of consciousness, steady and unmoving.
By that [consciousness], the body, the embodied self, and so forth, as well as the world and so forth, are merely indicated; thus, only the supreme Śiva shines forth as the ultimate reality.
Therefore, it is not appropriate to ask questions such as "Who am I? regarding the world; for a question shines forth only with respect to a thing that actually exists.
As for that which has not been perceived, what is the use of an inquiry or a question regarding it? Just as the existence of gold is not found without its particular configuration.

Likewise, without the sense of "I" in the world, the Lord has no existence; because He is without cause, this world does not exist as something other than Brahman, for it is Brahman alone who thus unfolds.
This world, which exists as if it were not even yawning into being, has its intentions mutually impelled by that very [reality] which consists of me alone.
These states, like a multitude of couples within the pentad, produce wonder; yet pure consciousness alone perceives pure consciousness within pure consciousness.

Though not diverse in their true nature, they appear as if diverse through the self-nature of the knowledge of the Self; from the Full, they draw forth full things, and from the Full, they have fashioned full things.
From the full, full things arise; yet only the full remains—that which shines as pure consciousness alone within the Self, which consists of pure consciousness.
Without even conceiving that name, the perception of creation was conceived; thus, at the very beginning, I, who am consciousness itself, became as if I were myself consciousness.
Without abandoning its own nature, it does not become form; rather, it is composed of light, without beginning or end, the very form of the mind, infinite.

O Emperor, the world appears as if it were your own body; yet, because it is of the nature of Being (*sat*), one sees this as truly existent, or indeed as Being itself. Through the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), the visible world attains the state of reality and comes into being in an instant.

This world, in its state of expansion, is peaceful; it is free from the meanings of words denoting inherent nature, indescribable, and one. It exists as a reality whose form is the vision of its own innate wonder—the essential truth whose nature is experience devoid of the world's own sound.

Kumbha said: Within gold, at the end of place and time, there exists this sequence of produced and producer; nothing whatsoever is born from that which is quiescent, nor does anything whatsoever dissolve.
Brahman, established in its own being, is neither seed nor cause; it is pure experience alone, and nothing other than that exists.

"That which appears as the world, the ego, and so forth, is indeed that very same infinite reality. Śikhidhvaja said: "O Sage, O Auspicious One, I know that the world, the ego, and so forth do not exist."
"How does this perception of creation appear? Tell me this quickly. Kumbha said: "That [reality], which is without beginning or end, exists as if it were consciousness itself in its expansion."

Each respective world is utterly transparent, and each respective subtle element constitutes the body of the universe; there is no object consisting of consciousness, nor is there an external object, nor is there emptiness.

Since its essence consists solely of sensation, it is called "essence-consciousness," just as liquidity is the essence of water; the state of being conscious or unconscious is not the cause [of its nature].

That [reality] is the self-nature, the Lord, and the infinite; it remains exactly as it is, established without any change, because there is no exclusion of its opposite in the case of existence and being.
Because it is non-existent, by that [reason] there is an establishment in the supreme state of pure being; if the peaceful state were subject to the occurrence of causality, [it would not be so].
How could that which is motionless, non-manifest, and beyond inference ever exist? Therefore, Brahman is never a cause, nor is it ever a seed.
There is no creation of any effect whatsoever by that [cause]; nor indeed can the production of this creation be established in any other way.
Apart from that which is pure consciousness alone, no insentient creation exists; whatever is seen here has arisen as if it were a mass of consciousness.
The coloring of the sense of "I," the world, words, and their meanings, as well as aesthetic flavor, cannot be established in an object, because of the absence of a cause.

Due to one's own experience, that which consists of duality, unity, and so forth is like a flower in the sky; because it is ultimately nothing but destruction, it is not established as an object known by a wise person.
How can there be a destruction that brings about perception for that which has arisen? Or else, do you perceive it as being both eternally existent and eternally destroyed?
Why is there distress regarding this flood of objects, even though it is thus of a single nature? Furthermore, this perception which occurs is merely a marvel of the mind.

There exists only the reality of consciousness; duality and unity do not exist at all. Therefore, O Lord of the Earth, when there is an absence of the existence of objective entities, [consciousness alone remains].
Since the cultivation [of an object] is impossible, you have no cultivation of "I-ness"; and because the state of being "I" is impossible, what else can be called "mind"?
Thus, the great form of the mind does not exist; therefore, there is no duality. Free from latent impressions, with a tranquil mind, silent, he consists of the supreme ether.

Whether with body or without body, even while situated amidst objective phenomena, one remains like a mountain; for, through the connection with the vision of pure consciousness, the non-existence of external objects is established.

When, through the cultivation [of insight], there is no longer "I" in the mind of its own accord; when, through the experience of cultivating the meaning of the Vedas, one realizes "This is Brahman"; and because the perceived object is the sole reality—where then can so-called "thought" exist?

Therefore, you are that Brahman—stainless, causeless, primordially liberated, eternal, entire, both manifold and one; it is the void, free from affliction, neither non-existent nor existent, without beginning or middle; it is the whole world, consciousness, and Brahman itself, exactly as it is.

Śikhidhvaja said: "Tell me that other reasoning by which my understanding that 'the mind does not exist' may become clear, or else explain it to me more skillfully, for I have not understood it thoroughly."
Kumbha said: O King, the mind does not exist at all, anywhere, or at any time; that which appears as if it were a mind is the imperishable reality known as Brahman.
Therefore, that which consists of ignorance does not exist as the world at all; how then can there be imagined constructions such as "I," "you," "that," and so forth?
This world that has arisen as something whatsoever does not exist at all; only Brahman exists here as the whole. By whom and how is that realized?
This world was impelled in this very manner at the beginning of creation following the great dissolution; however, I have employed the designation "this" here for the sake of your understanding.
Because causes such as the nature of grasping and so forth do not exist, and because it is impossible for all entities whatsoever to be without a cause.
Thus, because the world is perceived through the intellect of ignorance, it does not exist; therefore, whatever appears here is the radiance of Brahman and nothing else.
To say that "the Lord, who is inexpressible and formless, creates this" is false; such a statement is not logical in nature, it is not true, and it is not experienced.
The statement that "the Lord—who is inexpressible, non-resistant, self-natured, and formless—creates the world" is merely for the laughter of the unintelligent.
By this very practice, O King, the mind does not exist; the world itself is not real, O virtuous one—how much less the mind and its derivatives contained within it?

For the mind is merely a latent impression (vāsanā), and an impression exists only when there is something to be impressed; since that very world which is to be impressed is non-existent, how can the existence of the mind be established?
That which shines as Brahman itself, by itself, within itself, is that very thing which, by that same [Brahman], is given the name "mind" (citta) and so forth.
This world that is perceived is merely a manifestation; it has not truly arisen at all. Since there is no prior cause, how could there even be the state of "mind" (cittatā)?
Therefore, this alone—which is the nature of the mere space of consciousness, named the supreme ether, and is a vast awareness—shines forth; whence could there be a world?
