Whatever slightly glimmers in the supreme space, because it has not arisen within the mirror of consciousness, there is neither mind nor the activity of the world.
This perception of "I," "you," and "the world" is not real; it appears falsely like a dream, surely bringing about my complete destruction.
Since there is no world to be perfumed, and thus no latent impression (vāsanā) exists at all, what kind of mind could there be—of what nature, where, from what cause, and in what manner?
This world, which is the visible object, is understood by the unawakened as the mind; yet that unreal mind is formless and has not arisen at all from the beginning.

Because of the absence of a cause, it has never arisen at any time, even at the beginning of creation; for such is observed through worldly experience, scriptural authority, and direct perception regarding any visible object.
Neither beginninglessness, nor birthlessness, nor even stability can be established for this manifest world, which is gross and characterized by resistance.
Because of the absence of all causes—according to both worldly experience and the scriptures—it is not logical to deny the occurrence of the great dissolution and other such events.
Furthermore, one who claims that even those three [types of dissolution] do not exist, based on the scriptures, personal experience, and the established tenets of the Vedas, is truly a madman.
He whose mind regards neither the world, nor the treatises, nor the Vedas as authoritative is more foolish than the wicked; therefore, a virtuous person should not rely upon him.
Furthermore, that which is non-resistant cannot be the cause of this visible object which is resistant; nor can that which is formless be the cause of that which possesses form.
O Sage, when observed in this manner, each and every thing is thus constantly [devoid of intrinsic nature]; yet it is not the case that this world would thereby fail to perform its causal functions.
Therefore, this [universe] arises from the partless sky of consciousness, which is of unimpeded form, formless, infinite, and through its prior state of being partless.

That which is the equal [state] of Brahman—who possesses all forms, who is tranquil, and who has consumed [all things]—is the self-manifestation by its own nature, assuming the form of creation and dissolution.
By that very [realization], his own body was known in an instant as being like the world; yet, when awakened in the next moment, it remains as Brahman alone within the selfless state.

Therefore, all this is indeed Brahman alone; nowhere is there the notion of a world or the like. Where could there be "that-ness" (tā) and so forth? Where could there be the conceptualization of duality, unity, and so on?

All is without support, unborn, and profoundly tranquil; it is the self, existing as it is from beginningless time. This, however, is neither manifold nor even non-manifold; remain as you are, in the silence of perfect stillness.
Śikhidhvaja said: "O great sage, through your grace, my delusion has perished and my memory has been regained. I stand firm, freed from doubt, with a tranquil mind and self-possessed."

I am one who has known all that is to be known, a great sage of silence, having crossed the vast ocean of illusion; I am peaceful, devoid of the sense of "I," a knower, and I abide free from all affliction.
Oh, for so very long a time have I wandered in the ocean of existence; now, at last, I have attained the state that is imperishable and unshakeable.
This being the case, O Sage, that triple world consisting of "I-ness" and so forth does not exist; I know that which appears as this foolish intellect is Brahman.

Kumbha said: Where even the world does not exist, there how can there be the manifestation of "I" and "you"? Thus, where, from whence, of what nature, and in what manner could this world-existence, which is like the sky, exist?
O sage, remain as you are, acting according to worldly convention, silent and with a tranquil mind; abide like the movement of a whirlpool within the belly of a calm ocean.
This tranquil form of Brahman exists thus as it is; "I" and "this world" are essentially of the nature of space, consisting of the meaning of words.
This entire thing called saṃsāra, devoid of beginning and end, is the self whose name is the wonder of consciousness; it shines like the sky.
Just as gold exists when the perception of its particular configuration has ceased, so too does this Brahman exist when the perception of the world and its primary objects has subsided.
Just as the self-arisen one is indeed called "self" by his own volition, so too are bondage and liberation established as dependent upon one's own awareness.
The conception "I am" leads to bondage that is utterly destructive; the conception "I am not" leads to liberation for the stainless self.
The constant awareness of the true nature of the meanings of the words "bondage," "liberation," and "intention," which are always present, is called both "Reality" (sat) and "Isolation" (kevalatva).
The realization that "I am not" is success; the notion of "I am" is calamities. He who possesses the pure awakening that "I am indeed that which is not-I" is one who has attained the Self.

By the mere absence of mental construction, which consists in the arising of perfect knowledge, mental construction—which is itself unreal by nature—is destroyed of its own accord for the sake of spiritual accomplishment.
Indeed, in the auspicious Śiva, whose nature is beyond conceptualization, there is no causality; and due to the absence of a cause, the category of an effect also does not exist.
When the non-existence of objective entities is fully established, cognition is no longer tenable; due to the absence of its cause, the ego-sense never arises again.
Since the sense of "I" does not arise, whose is saṃsāra, and of what nature? In the absence of saṃsāra, everything remains as the Supreme alone.
That which shines here is the Supreme Reality alone, abiding within the Self; the Supreme, full of the Supreme, unfolds as the Equal within the Supreme.
Know that by him all has been rendered motionless, like a mountain strewn with stones; the world exists as Brahman, appearing as if composed of rays of light.
Know that the form of the city of conceptualization—which appears when the prior volition has perished—is the very nature of the world: clear as space, yet consisting of both being and non-being.
He who sees the world as flickering like a shadow-man, yet peaceful and devoid of mental construction, and who sees it as being free from the referents of the word "world"—he truly sees.
The wise know that Nirvana is indeed the realization of perfect knowledge, which arises when forms, light, and mental attention have become tasteless through the cultivation of the scriptures.
Just as there is wind that is motionless, or as there is [wind] moving through the sky, so too does Brahman exist as the world, like gold in the form of various ornaments.
These forms, light, and mental attentions—which are sapless, appearing as unreal, yet producing the cognition of the world—exist as the very form of Brahman.
Just as water, even in great quantities, is devoid of the meaning of the word "wave," so too is Brahman naturally devoid of the meaning of the word "creation."
Creation itself is the Supreme Brahman, and the Supreme Brahman is the vision of creation; yet, devoid of the meaning of the word "creation," this is the eternal meaning of the sentence.

When the meaning of the word *brahman* was fully realized, the understanding of the meaning of the word *sarga* (creation) was established; when the meaning of the word *sarga* was perfectly accomplished, the understanding of the meaning of the word *brahman* was established.
The pure sky of consciousness, which arises from the cultivation and non-cultivation of all words and their meanings, abides; it is designated by the word "Brahman."
When both [the self and the non-self] are no longer perceived due to the perfection of right vision, speech turns back from that which remains—ageless and tranquil.

The flood of all sensations belonging to the self has been completely stilled; this is the singular nature of one's own true being. It is the true nature of the entire world as it exists, like stone, yet it is the supreme form of consciousness.
Śikhidhvaja said: "If that is so, O one of great intelligence, then I understand this world to be exactly like its supreme cause; the effect is indeed of the same nature as the cause."
Kumbha said: Where there is causality, there an effect is possible; but since that which is not a cause in the first place cannot exist, how could an effect arise from it?
Here there is no cause whatsoever, nor is there ever any effect; all this that exists is entirely quiescent and unborn.
An effect that arises from a cause must possess the nature of that cause; as for that which does not arise at all here, how can there be similarity with it?
Tell me, how can that which has no seed at all be born? And as for that which is inconceivable and inexpressible, how could it possibly possess the nature of a seed?

Due to the influence of place and time, all things possess causes and are established by means of valid cognition; how then can there be valid knowledge regarding the two causes when Brahman is without an agent?
In Śiva, who is devoid of agent, object, and instrument, there is no causality; therefore, that which is known by the word "world" has no cause.
You are indeed Brahman; maintain that very nature which is eternally established. That same [Brahman], when perceived by those of imperfect vision, is what is designated as the world.

That which is cognized is the one, undecaying, and tranquil pure consciousness alone; by that very [consciousness], this world-body is understood as Brahman—real, tranquil, and of the nature of consciousness.
O Lord of the Earth, that very state of the mind which is otherwise [than its usual condition] is declared by the wise to be destruction, and it is experienced by them for themselves.
Know that the mind, O King, has the nature of destruction; it is essentially perishable, since even what is called "the mind of an eon" is said to perish in an instant.
Through the mere absence of volition, which consists in the arising of perfect knowledge, volition—which is by nature unreal—perishes of its own accord for the sake of accomplishment.
O lotus-eyed one, if the universe is said to have its non-existence accepted by its very name alone, how could it possibly exist? Indeed, how could that be so?
How can he who, raising his hands, declares with a loud voice "I am a Śūdra," become a Brahmin? Of what nature, indeed, is his Brahminhood?
Know that for one who, with his elements overturned, cries out loudly, "I am dead," death itself has already arrived; his so-called "living" is merely a delusion.
Whatever exists here that appears in the form of an illusion is like a whirling firebrand, like a mirage, a double moon, and so forth, or like a child’s ghost and the like.
How indeed could that which consists of the burden of effort be real? It is said that it is merely the delusion of ignorance within the mind.
Ignorance is said to be the mind, which exists as if real though it is unreal; ignorance is non-perception, while knowledge would be perception.

Through the knowledge and realization of the nature of the ignorant being, there is the destruction [of ignorance]; O virtuous one, the cognition of water in the mirages of the desert is a vain delusion.
Through the realization that "this is not water," the dense impurity of ignorance within the heart—which conceives "this is mind"—is dissolved by consciousness.
Through the knowledge that "there is no mind," it is destroyed along with its root, just as the state of being a snake in a rope arises from the delusion of ignorance.
Just as the notion of a snake rooted in the heart perishes through the knowledge that "this is not a snake," so too does the delusion born of ignorance regarding the Self vanish from the mind.

The notion that "the mind does not exist" destroys the conviction rooted in the heart regarding consciousness; this persists as long as ignorance exists, [conceiving] the mind, the intellect, and the ego as distinct.
There is no mind, nor indeed anything in this world associated with egoism and the like; there is only consciousness, absolutely pure.
By that deluded woman, the mind of volition and so forth had been created; today, by that awakened one, everything has been abandoned through the absence of volition.
When it moves with volition, O mighty-armed one, it proceeds without volition, like a mass of flames in the fire driven by the wind.
The entire world is pervaded by the reality of Brahman, which is a single, dense mass of the essence of the Self, just as the ocean is pervaded by water.
I do not exist, nor does another exist; neither you, nor these, nor the mind; neither the sense-faculties nor space—there exists only the one stainless Self.
That very same [reality] is perceived in the form of jars and other objects; what kind of false conceptualization is this, that "this is mind" and "I am"?
Nothing at all is born or dies in these three worlds; this is solely the play of consciousness, appearing through the nature of conceptions of existence and non-existence.
Everything is the Self, the Supreme Brahman, once and for all manifest and pervasive; neither duality nor unity exists, nor is there delusion or confusion.
Therefore, O friend, you exist as the very form of the entire collection of sense faculties; thus, O one of great intelligence, you are not burned, nor are you stained anywhere.
O friend, nothing perishes for you, nor does anything increase, for you are of the nature of the stainless sky, whose form is the infinite state of absolute liberation.
The two powers consisting of desire and non-desire, as well as that which is other than them, are you alone; for the moon is not perceived apart from its rays.

That reality of the Self is unborn, undecaying, beginningless, and of an immutable nature; it is eternally pure, ever-shining, and always of one form; it is free from all mental constructions, yet its play is expressed through the so-called "parts" (kalās); it is primordially arisen, the first-born, and unborn.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Reflecting upon these words of Kumbha as being genuine, the king himself, in that very moment, became fully absorbed in that state of the Self.
With his mind and eyes closed, the sage became silent; with the form of his limbs motionless, he appeared as if carved out of a stone slab.
Then, after only a moment, Cūḍālā, who had assumed the form of Kumbha, spoke to him as he woke up with his eyes sparkling, O mighty-armed one.
Kumbha said: "Have you found rest in happiness upon this vast, pure, expansive, and stainless plane, which is the excellent couch for those free from conceptual construction?"
Are you awakened within? Have you abandoned delusion? Has that which is to be known been fully understood, or has that which is to be seen been truly seen?
Śikhidhvaja said: "O Blessed One, by your grace, I have beheld a great state of immense splendor, a vast station situated above all."
Oh, how wonderful! The association with the great-souled ones, who have realized what is to be known, is composed of a unique and unprecedented nectar that bestows the essential fruit.
That great nectar which I had not obtained even by birth has today been attained by me of its own accord through association with you.
O lotus-eyed one, why was this beginningless, endless, and immortal state of the Self not attained by me previously?

Kumbha said: When the mind has attained tranquility, when it remains with the desire for enjoyments abandoned, and when the ripening of the impurities of the entire collection of sense organs has been completed;
The stainless words of the Teacher find rest in the mind, just as drops of saffron water settle upon a pure white cloth.
Today, the ripening of the infinite passions (kaṣāyas) accumulated by your bodies—which are themselves the nature of your own latent impressions (vāsanā)—has arisen for you.
O lotus-eyed one, O virtuous one, all impurities fall away from the body over time, just as fruits drop down from a tree when they have ripened.
O friend, when the impurities consisting of latent impressions have departed, that which the Guru speaks within you enters [you] just as an arrow enters a reed.
Now that the ripening of the astringent [of ignorance] is complete, you have been awakened by me today; therefore, O Mahāmati, the destruction of your ignorance has occurred this very day.
Today your impurities have been ripened; this very day you are fit for discourse on knowledge. Today, with this instruction, you have awakened right here and now.
Today, the exhaustion of all auspicious and inauspicious karmas has been brought to completion through your instruction under the guise of association with the virtuous.
O Lord of the Earth, as long as this was the forenoon of that day, so long did your ignorance of "I" and "mine" persist.
Now that destruction has come upon your mind through the awakening brought by my words, and it has been completely cast out from your heart, O King, you have truly awakened.
As long as the existence of the mind remains in the heart, so long does ignorance persist; when the mind is relinquished through its very nature as mind, the dawning of knowledge occurs.
The mind that perceives duality and unity is called ignorance; the dissolution of these two perceptions is knowledge, which is the supreme goal.

You are awakened, you are liberated; O King, the mind has been abandoned by you. Indeed, you have abandoned the state of being composed of existence and non-existence, as well as the ground of unreality.
Free from sorrow, free from exertion, unattached, without another, and possessed of the Self; a sage of great awakening, silent, abide in your own stainless nature.
Śikhidhvaja said: "Indeed, O Blessed One, the ground of the mind exists only for a foolish being; for one who is awakened and knows that reality, O Lord, there is truly no such thing as 'mind'."
Tell me, how do these people who are liberated while living wander about? For men such as yourself and others likewise have no mind that exists.
Thus, relate this to me in its entirety with the rays of your own words; in this manner, skillfully wipe away the darkness of my heart.
Kumbha said: O knower of reality, it is exactly as you say and not otherwise; for the mind of those liberated while living does not exist, just as there is no sprout from stones.

That latent impression (*vāsanā*) which is capable of producing rebirth is called "dense impression" (*ghanavāsanā*); it is designated by the term "mind" (*citta*), and it does not exist for one who knows that [reality].
Know that habitual tendency by which those who possess such knowledge engage in activities here to be designated as "sentient beings," yet they are free from rebirth.
The great-souled ones who are liberated while living, established in purity and with senses restrained, move about free from attachment; they are never established in the mind.
They say that the deluded mind is "citta," while the awakened is called "sattva. For those who are unawakened abide in the *citta*, whereas those of great intelligence abide in the *sattva*.
The mind is born again and again, but the being is not born again; O King, bondage exists for the unawakened, but not for the awakened.
You have become one possessed of courage; you stand as a great renouncer. I know that today you have relinquished your mind entirely.
O King, liberated from all latent impressions, you shine even today; O sage, I believe your mind has attained equality with space.
You have attained supreme tranquility, perfected and established in equanimity; for this indeed is the great renunciation—that all of that has been utterly abandoned.
O virtuous one, heaven, liberation, wealth, and even the fruits of austerity and charity are attained through awakened intelligence—the supreme awakening of the intellect.
How could austerity possibly bring about the destruction of even a limited measure of suffering, when true happiness consists of equanimity, which is free from both decay and excess?

That reality is that very thing; it is something, yet not heaven or other such perishable things. It is mounted upon existence and non-existence, and is established as the realization of consciousness.

What is called heaven is merely pleasure, and even that remains situated within doubt; for as long as the perfection of one's own Self has not been attained, the section on ritual action may be auspicious.
Would one who has not obtained gold ever abandon brass? Through association with Cūḍālā and others, you will attain knowledge with ease.

Why then have you immersed yourself in this meaningless misery consisting of asceticism, for the sake of that evil deed which is to be accomplished only through the various stages of life and so forth?
O wise one, its beginning and end are suffering; only the middle is happiness for you, since that is the time when it arises and when it transforms.
Establish your footing there within those portions of conceptualization that are the very form of austerity; for from the exceedingly pure sky of consciousness, all phenomena have arisen.
In that very same way they are perceived, yet in that very same place they have gone to dissolution; the notions of "this is to be done" and "this is not to be done" are but droplets of Brahman.
"O Śikhidhvaja, abandon the barren and take refuge in the full alone; ask for what you desire from me, O friend, just as it is requested."
In the same way, how can he be so beloved by the woman that she herself should thus entreat him for these states of being, fashioned by her own imagination and appearing so radiant?
The wise and great-souled do not grasp at anything whatsoever—even that which yields fruits such as heaven and liberation—just as they do not grasp at reflections in water.
Having abandoned [all else], become that very one which appears as equal and uniform; indeed, being free from longing, destroy existence with existence through destruction itself.
Grasping this flood of objects, remain with a mind-ground that is motionless; for one whose mind is without movement, the cycle of existence does not run here.
O virtuous one, misfortune is indeed considered to arise from human effort, just as it is in the mind; whatever sufferings manifest here in the three worlds [are likewise so produced].

O Lord of the Earth, those various [misfortunes] arise solely from the fickleness of the mind; he whose mind is steady, peaceful, motionless, and free from fickleness is forever possessed of great bliss and is the worthy recipient of sovereignty.
Therefore, O knower of reality, having brought both movement and stillness into unity within your mind, remain as you wish, having attained eternal oneness.
Śikhidhvaja said: "O Lord, how have these two—motion and non-motion—attained unity? O You who sever all doubts, tell this to me quickly."

Kumbha said: The entire world is a single reality, pure consciousness alone, like water in the ocean; that very reality vibrates through the functions of the intellect, just as pure water vibrates through its waves.
O dear ones, that which has been sung as Brahman, pure consciousness, stainless, and named "Being"—that very thing the deluded perceive as the world.

The vibration of consciousness alone is the very essence of creation; from that indeed arises the cycle of worldly existence. For this vibration is supreme, being equal to the vibration of words such as "Vindhya" and the like.
If that very consciousness is meditated upon as both vibration and non-vibration through its single nature, then therein lies this stainless Śiva.
Creation, whose essence is merely the vibration of consciousness, dissolves upon right vision; it arises for those with false vision, just as the delusion of a snake appears in a rope.

The designation "mind" refers to that which is characterized by movement; however, this [reality], which is pervasive and free from movement and established in the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), cannot be expressed by speech.
Through the continuous practice of association with the scriptures and virtuous people, the mind attains purity over time, like the moon that has risen.
This alone has appeared, extended through one's own experiences; it is described by oneself within one's own experiences as one's very own form by means of the Self.

You have attained the essence, which is without beginning or middle; remain right here, established in your own state. O virtuous one, you have indeed become free from sorrow, for you are born as the Great Consciousness-Self, whose nature is beyond the differentiation of forms.
Kumbha said: Thus, O Lord of the Earth Śikhidhvaja, everything has been told to you—how all this arose and how it dissolves away.
O Leader of Sages, having heard this, understood it, and reflected upon it, remain as you wish, now that the supreme state has been clearly perceived.
"O Sage Nārada, on this auspicious occasion, I am going to heaven; you have arrived from the world of Brahmā in the assembly of the immortals."
If he does not see me there, he becomes angry; for a worthy disciple should never cause his gurus any distress.
With all mental constructs abandoned and desiring nothing at all, you must always dwell thus; this very vision is purifying.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Even as Śikhidvaja, with flowers in his hand, was about to offer this reply in salutation, he vanished from sight.
Just as an object produced by creative imagination is not seen at the end, so King Śikhidhvaja did not see the jar before him.
When the jar had departed, the protector of the earth was struck with supreme wonder; reflecting upon that very marvel, he became as if fixed in a painting.
He reflected upon this wondrous play of Fate: that by means of the pretext of a jar, I have been awakened to an awakening that has long since arisen.
Where is Kumbha, the son of Nārada, and where am I, Śikhidhvaja by name? It is solely through the power of time that he has awakened me.
"Oh, how well-spoken by the son of the gods! It is indeed logical. Oh, after a long time, I have truly awakened from the sleep of delusion!"
Where was I, submerged in the foul mud of the web of ritual actions, caught in the false whirlpool of delusions such as "this must be done" and "this must not"?
Oh, how cool, pure, and peaceful is this path of my own! Having the appearance of a life-restoring elixir, it cools my being here.
I am stilled, I am fully extinguished, and I abide in absolute bliss; I do not desire even a tip of grass; I remain established just as I am.
Reflecting thus, the king, clearly intent on banishment, remained in silence as if carved out of stone.
Then, having attained a firm and unshakable stability in that very silence—which is free from volition and without support—he remained like the peak of a mountain.

There, with his fear completely stilled, his mind at rest after a long time, equanimous in self, and having after a long time attained his own stainless nature, he then slept in yoga, his soul untroubled.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Through unwavering samādhi, his state became like that of wood or a wall; now hear how King Śikhidhvaja [related this] to Cūḍālā.
Having awakened her husband Śikhidhvaja by means of that disguise as Kumbha, she vanished and swiftly traversed the sky.
In the sky, he cast off the form of a son of the gods created by his illusory power, and assumed a beautiful feminine form, charming and innocent.
He reached his own city through the sky and entered the inner apartments in an instant; he became visible to the world and performed the duties of a king.
Then, after three days, she returned to the sky and, through her yogic power, became a water-jar; she went to the grove of Śikhidhvaja.
Likewise, while there on the forest ground, she saw that king established in unwavering meditative absorption, like a tree carved in relief.
"Ah! Indeed, O friend, by good fortune this one has now come to rest within himself; he stands self-abiding, equanimous, and tranquil," he said again and again.
Therefore, let me first awaken him from this supreme state; why indeed does he abandon his body even now?
Let him enjoy for a short time either sovereignty or the forest; once we have cast off these two bodies, we shall go together as equals.
Instruction for him is difficult and does not reach its fruition; therefore, by means of this yoga of practice, I shall first awaken him.
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā let out a lion’s roar again and again before her lord, striking terror into the forest-dwellers.
When he did not move, remaining like a rock upon a mountain despite that roar being repeated again and again, she then caused him to tremble.
When the king was shaken and even cast down, yet did not wake up, Cūḍālā, who was in the form of Kumbha, reflected thus:
"Aha! This Blessed One has reached maturity in his own state; by what means, then, shall I now awaken him?"
Or rather, for what purpose should I awaken this great-souled one? Having attained awakening, let him remain as he pleases, free from the body.
I too, having abandoned this body of a woman, shall go to the supreme state from which there is no rebirth; for what indeed is equal to this?
Having reflected thus, the highly intelligent Cūḍālā, being intent on abandoning her own body, reflected once more.
I shall look upon this body of the lord of the earth for just this long, to see if there remains within his heart even a trace of vitality, the seed of awakening.
At that time, this Blessed One will attain full awakening, like a cluster of flowers nestled within the sap of the root and the bark of a tree.
Thus, even while living, one becomes truly liberated from separation; if I consider myself liberated, then I shall go along with him.
Having reflected thus, the beautiful Cūḍālā, observing her husband with both touch and reasoning, spoke with apprehension.
There still remains within his heart a residue of goodness that serves as the cause for awakening; through the arising of the causes for awakening, he has awakened that residue of goodness.

Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin, how is one who possesses a deeply tranquil mind, who remains as steady as a piece of wood or a clod of earth, and who is absorbed in meditation, recognized as having only pure being (sattva) remaining?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: He in whose heart there exists a cause for awakening—a subtle essence of being remaining within like the flower and fruit in a seed—is destined for liberation.
Of that which is devoid of the vibration of the mind, whose true consciousness is unshaken, which is free from duality and unity, and which abides equally and immovably.
The body is in a state of even composure; it neither flags nor exults, neither sets nor rises, but remains perfectly equanimous.
The body of one whose mind vibrates with notions such as duality and unity undergoes change; for one whose mind does not vibrate, it never does.
For the vibration of the mind, O Rāma, is the cause of the existence of the entire world and of all modifications of being, just as honey is the cause of flowers.
O scion of the Raghus, as the mind repeatedly departs from this body, neither joy, nor anger, nor delusion comes under its control.
When the mind has attained tranquility, that body which is devoid of a sentient being cannot afflict it, just as changes in the state of the sky do not affect the sky itself.
Just as waves and the like do not arise from a continuous stream of water that is uniform, so too no defect is seen in a continuous stream of beings that is uniform.
There is no perception of a sentient being except through its cessation; as long as reality appears, it remains uniform, and only with time does it subside into solitude.
But in that body where neither mind nor a living being is found, O Rāma, it dissolves into the five elements like snow under heat.
This body of Śikhidhvaja is mindless yet powerful with vital energy; because it is endowed with a portion of pure being (*sattva*), it is not subject to exhaustion.
Beholding her husband’s body in such a state, the excellent woman did not abandon her own body, but reflected with urgency.
Having entered the all-pervading, pure essence of consciousness, I awaken it; for there, established in that state, I shall bring about the lovely awakening.
"If I do not awaken him, he will eventually awaken by himself; why then should I remain alone?"—thinking thus, I awaken him.
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā abandoned her body, which is a cage of the senses, and attained stability in the principle of consciousness (cittattva), which is devoid of beginning and end.
There, having caused the conscious vibration of the living Lord, that consciousness entered its own body once more, like a bird returning to its own nest.
Then, rising up in the form of a water-pot, she settled upon a bed of flowers and began to sing the Sāman chants, her voice sounding like the humming of a swarm of bees.
Hearing that sound of the Sāman chant, she—endowed with the quality of pure consciousness—awakened within the king’s body like a lotus plant in springtime.
Then King Śikhidhvaja, having attained the perfection of inner strength, caused her vision to blossom like the sun causes a lotus to bloom.
He saw a pitcher standing before him, intent on chanting the Sāman hymns, endowed with a supreme form like another Sāmaveda.
"Oh, how blessed we are that the sage has come here of his own accord!"—thus they exclaimed, and the king gave flowers to Kumbha.
"By good fortune, O Blessed One, we have been uplifted by your purifying mind; for what great beings indeed would not remain established in your grace?"
The very purpose of your coming is to purify us; if not, tell me what the second reason for your arrival might be.
Kumbha said: "O blameless one, from the very moment I departed from your presence, my mind has remained here with you alone."
I do not remain in the delightful heaven now, but am present near you, O one with limbs like a rising god; for that which is desired stands before all beautiful things.
I believe there is no one like you in this world—neither a kinsman, nor a trusted confidant, nor a well-wisher, nor a friend, nor a companion, nor even a disciple worthy of my trust.
Śikhidhvaja said: "Aha! Indeed, the merit-trees of our family mountain have borne fruit, since even you, though free from attachment, desire our company."
"This is the forest, these are the trees, and here am I, your devoted servant; heaven does not please your heart, therefore, O Lord, please remain here."
"O holy one, through the yoga-technique bestowed by you, I have found rest; therefore, I consider that there is no such rest in heaven as this."
Relying upon that very same pure and luminous state, wander here as you desire, whether in heaven or upon the surface of the earth.
Kumbha said: "Have you found rest in the supreme state of great bliss? Have you completely abandoned this suffering consisting of duality?"
O King, has your delight in those volitions that are pleasant at first sight utterly vanished, so that you find no taste for worldly enjoyments?

Is your mind established in a state that transcends the conditions of what is to be abandoned and what is to be acquired, which is peaceful, abiding in equanimity, and free from agitation regarding whatever has arisen?

Śikhidhvaja said: "O Blessed One, by your grace, the state that transcends all objects of sight has been seen; the boundary of saṃsāra has been reached, and the certainty regarding that which was to be attained has been gained."
After a long, exceedingly long time, I have finally come to rest, free from ailment; everything that was to be attained has been attained, and I remain here, contented for all eternity.
Nothing whatsoever needs to be taught to us; I am completely satisfied in every respect, I am firmly established, and I am free from all feverish distress.
The known and the unknown, the unattained, the abandoned, the abandonable, and that which is resorted to—the reality, the otherness, and the existence of my own self is nothing at all.

Free from saṃsāra, devoid of delusion and fear, dispassionate, eternally risen, with an equanimous disposition toward all and being entirely gentle; universal in nature, detached from all mental constructions, as clear as the expanse of space—I abide in equanimity.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, with various discourses on the supreme self, those two, both knowers of what is to be known, sat together in the forest for three muhūrtas.
Then, having risen from there, they sported upon a certain mountain peak abounding with cranes and lakes, and in a forest like the Nandana grove.
By that conduct and those conversations, they then spent eight days in the forest paths of those groves.
Then Kumbha said, "Let us go to another forest on the mountain. Thinking "So be it," the king agreed, and they both set out.
Forests of many forms, jungles, riverbanks, lakes, thickets of shrubs, mountain peaks, and dense thickets.
Rivers, regions, as well as villages, cities, and forests; Mañjughoṣas, mountains, groves, sacred fords, and shrines.
Being equal, with equal affection, united, and both remaining steadfast, they stood always praising one another, possessing equal strength and equal energy.
O Raghava, they both worshipped the ancestors and the gods and partook of their meals; with equal minds, they remained the same whether in heat or in moisture.
In the groves of *tāla* trees and in the thickets of *mandāra* blossoms, that couple, whose hearts were tender and who were like dear friends, shone with splendor.
O Rāma, the mental construction of conceptualization—“this is a house” and “this is not”—did not carry away those two, just as a whirlwind cannot move the mountain of the gods.
Those two friends roamed about, sometimes grey with dust, sometimes their limbs smeared with sandalwood paste, and sometimes stained with ashes.
In some places they wore divine garments, in others variegated robes; in some places they were covered by young shoots, and in others adorned with flowers.
In just a few days, through that equanimity of mind and his noble nature of purity, the king shone like a water-jar.
Then, seeing Śikhidhvaja—who shone like the offspring of a god—attained such splendor, the proud Cūḍālā reflected:
This husband is noble-minded, these forest lands are delightful, and this state of being free from exertion is one that has not been deceived by desire.

For those liberated while living who remain established in whatever enjoyment comes to them with a mind of liberation, that which is called "one-pointedness" would be nothing but a trivial and foolish delusion.
A noble-souled husband, freedom from anxiety, youth, and houses filled with clusters of flowers—she is not a woman who is not struck down by these.
That beloved woman who does not take delight in a bower of forest flowers and creepers under the control of her husband is not free from suffering; she is indeed a ruined woman.
Fie upon that wicked woman who, having obtained a charming, handsome, and wedded husband in a secluded place, does not take pleasure with him!
If one who knows the nature of experience always abandons even that which has been attained—which is blameless and of sublime purpose—what could possibly be accomplished by such a knower?
Therefore, I shall quickly devise some artifice to display in the forest, by which this lord of the earth, my husband and bestower of honor, may take delight in me.
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā, wearing the guise of Kumbha and standing among the forest thickets, spoke to her husband like a female cuckoo to a male cuckoo.
Kumbha said: This is the great first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra; today, indeed, Hari’s assembly hall in heaven undergoes a grand inauguration.
I must remain present there in the presence of my father; for destiny, as it has been established, must never be disregarded.
"You must wait for me here in this forest glade while you play among the fresh blossoms, without becoming agitated."
Today, at the end of the day, I have come from the sky in a state free of conceptual thought; indeed, association with you is far more pleasing to me than even the act of creation itself.
Having said this, Kumbha gave a cluster of flowers to Mitrā, as one might give one's own beloved wife born of the trees of Nandana, for the sake of mutual delight.
"When the king spoke thus, 'You must return very quickly,' he then leapt from the forest into the sky like an autumnal cloud."
Moving through the sky, he cast off the handful of flowers born from the garland of blossoms; scattered by the forest wind, it was like a snowy cloud dissolving.
Then Śikhidhvaja beheld him as he was departing until he vanished from sight; like a peacock awakened by the rain-cloud, for the affection of the wise is indeed difficult to relinquish.
At the end of Śikhidhvaja’s gaze, she who had the form of a jar vanished into the sky; like the beauty of water when its whirlpools have subsided, that charming woman returned to her own true nature.
By way of the celestial path, he reached his own city, which was as delightful as heaven, resembling a wish-fulfilling tree in full bloom, and adorned with fluttering banners.
Remaining invisible, she entered the inner apartments crowded with women, just as the great goddess of the spring month enters a tree adorned with shimmering creepers.
Having swiftly completed all the royal duties there, he fell before Śikhidhvaja like a cluster of fruits and flowers.
There, with an unwearied mind, Kāladyuti made her face like a moon shrouded in mist, or like a dark lotus flower withered by the sun.
Seeing him in such a state, Śikhidhvaja rose up; his heart became distressed, and with great respect, he spoke these words.
"O son of the gods, homage be to you! You appear as if troubled in mind. You are Kumbha; abandon your agitation and sit upon this seat."
Those noble ones who have known what is to be known do not resort to a state born of joy or sorrow; established in themselves, they remain unaffected, like lotuses by the moisture of water.

When the lord of the earth had spoken thus, Kumbha, entering his seat, spoke with a dejected voice that resembled the sound of a broken bamboo staff. Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "When the king had spoken thus, Kumbha, entering his seat, spoke with a dejected voice that resembled the sound of a broken bamboo staff."
Those who, throughout the various states of the body, do not remain with equanimity of mind toward the organs of action are not knowers of reality; they are deceivers.
For those fools who do not know reality, O King, out of sheer childishness they flee from the states of existence that have been grasped by their very nature.
Just as oil exists within every sesame seed, so does the state of decay exist within every body; he who does not fall into this bodily state cuts through the sky with a sword.
This indeed is the unsurpassed relinquishing of the suffering of the bodily state: that equanimity of the mind through yoga, and not the mere steadiness of the organs of action.
As long as the body lasts, one who understands the ten limbs according to their proper conduct should remain active through the organs of action, but never through the organs of perception.
All beings, beginning with Parameṣṭhin, though their intentions have already arisen, remain within the states of the body; such is the certainty of destiny.
Indeed, all this collection of visible phenomena, whether consisting of the ignorant or those who know reality, rushes toward destiny just as water flows toward the ocean.
Those who know this [sustain] this unbroken destiny as long as the body lasts, through the equality of intellect and other faculties, and by the movement of the hands and other limbs.

But the ignorant, O dear one, struck by states of pleasure and pain through the agitation of all things, pass their time under the sway of destiny, which is shattered by hundreds of thousands of bodily marks.

O friend, if living beings have realized that they must abide thus in times of happiness as well as in states of suffering, then this fixed play of destiny, manifested by the multitude of both the ignorant and the wise, is indeed impossible to transcend.
Śikhidhvaja said: "O illustrious one, such being the case, tell me, O best among those who know what is to be known, how even you, a god, have come to experience such agitation?"
Kumbha said: "Listen, O lord of the earth, to this purpose of my mind; I shall tell you in its entirety what has occurred to me today regarding creation."
Sorrow, when disclosed to a friend, reaches its ultimate attenuation; just as a cloud, though thick, dull, and dark, is emptied once it has released its rain.
The mind of one who is questioned by a friend attains clarity, just as water quickly becomes clear when treated with *kataka* nut that has been brought into it.
Having first gone from here and given a cluster of flowers to your honor, I have crossed the sky and reached the third heaven.
Then, having stood in due order in the assembly hall of Mahendra and then rising at the time for departure, he was dismissed by his father.
Having abandoned heaven to come here, I have reached the sky; I travel along the path of the wind together with the horses of the sun.
Then, while the sun had gone one way, I returned by another path through the sky, appearing like one who has fallen into the ocean.
Then, amidst the path of clouds filled with water ahead, I saw the sage Durvāsas approaching with great speed.
With its clouds serving as a veil, adorned with circles of lightning, and its sandalwood paste on the body washed away by the rain, it resembled a woman going to meet her lover.
He rushed with speed toward that river, which stood upon the surface of the earth providing excellent shade for travelers, like a beloved goddess of ascetic merit approaching him.
Having paid him homage, I, traveling through the sky, said: "O Sage, you are like a woman going to meet her lover, dressed in garments of dark blue clouds."
Having heard this, O giver of honor, he uttered a curse upon me: "She shall become a lovely woman, possessed of breasts and long hair, and playful with gestures and emotions."
"Go! Because of this ill-spoken word, you shall become a woman at night"—having heard this inauspicious speech uttered by the decrepit brahmin, [she was struck with fear].
"O virtuous one, while I was reflecting for just a moment, the sage vanished; thus, with a mind full of agitation, I have arrived here from the sky."
"All this has been told to you; I have become a woman of the night. How am I to pass through this state of womanhood at the end of the days?"
"Seeing a woman with breasts at night, one should say: 'What must I say to my father? Alas, how treacherous indeed is the course of destiny within this cycle of existence!'"
Alas, that by fate I have today become the prey of gamblers; through my loss, a quarrel is now breaking out.
In heaven, the minds of the divine youths were agitated by desire; here, however, the self was brought under the sway of shame before teachers, gods, and the twice-born.
"How should I properly conduct myself from now on as a woman of the night? Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus, she remained silent for a moment in the posture of a sage.
O descendant of Raghu, relying on fortitude, Kumbha spoke here once more: "Why do I grieve like an ignorant man? What injury has been done to my self?"
"This body, composed of whatever has come together, will experience [its end] as something other than myself. Śikhidhvaja said: "O Devaputra, what is the purpose of such lamentation?"
When it comes, let it come; the self of the body is not defiled by whatever sufferings or pleasures are ordained.
All those [actions] belong to the body, not at all to the embodied self; yet if you, though unworthy of distress, are distressed by these duties.

"O you who are adorned by the scriptures, what other means could there be for others? You have said something to the effect that when one is weary, one should speak what is appropriate for weariness."
"Now, having attained equanimity, remain undaunted as you truly are. Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "With such words as these, the two of them themselves offered mutual consolation."
Having stood there together, the two forest-dwellers, their friends, were mutually distressed; then even the sun, as if producing femininity in this Kumbha, [shone].
The lamp of the world set like a lamp whose oil is exhausted; along with the weight of worldly affairs, the lotuses underwent contraction.
The roads, together with the travelers, and the hearts of the wives of those travelers, were gathered together in one place by him, making all the birds like fishermen.
Rich with a net of star-jewels, the sky attained a state of equality with the world; as if laughing at it, the sky, too, was filled with stars like a bed of blooming night-lotuses.
Then those two friends rose up as the twilight dawned with the rising moon, while flocks of cakravāka birds cried out loudly and swarms of bees buzzed about.
Having paid their respects and performed their prayers in that manner, they remained within the thicket; then Kumbha gradually assumed a feminine form there.
Standing before Śikhidhvaja, she spoke with faltering words: "I seem to fall, I seem to tremble, and my slender limbs seem to melt away."
"O King, it is out of sheer shame that I think I am turning into a woman; behold, O King, these hairs of mine are growing."
Behold, these two breasts of mine upon my chest seem to be facing upward, like the darkness at day’s end with its shimmering garland of stars.
Like two lotus buds on a lotus plant in springtime reaching upward toward the sky, my garments have become so long that they hang down even to my ankles.
O friend, behold how from the body itself there gradually appear, as if from a woman, ornaments, jewels, and various kinds of garlands.
Behold, my dear, how these are born from one's own limbs like flowers upon a tree; behold, this very person today shines with rays as beautiful as the moonbeams.
O giver of honor, a silken cloth has appeared upon my head like mist on a mountain; O bestower of pride, all the embraces of my beloved have come to pass for me.
"Alas! Woe is me! I am despondent; what shall I do? For I am a woman. Alas! Woe is me! Oh, virtuous one, I remain truly a woman!"
"O Kumbha," he said, "I am experiencing within me these very buttocks and hips in this forest," and having spoken thus, he became silent and dejected.
And the king, beholding him, was likewise dejected in spirit; after only a moment, Śikhidhvaja spoke these words:
"Alas! This is that very same Great Being, and she has become a woman of excellent complexion. O virtuous one, you have known all that is to be known; you understand the course of destiny."
Do not let your heart be distressed by this inevitable matter; such various conditions befall even the wise when they concern the body alone.
"These [women] do not enter the mind through the intellect, nor do they enter the body. Kumbha said: "So be it; I shall assume for myself the female form of a woman of the night."
"I do not succumb to despondency; by whom can destiny be transgressed? Having thus resolved, they led away that sorrow as if it were diminished.
They spent that long night in silence upon a single bed; then, at dawn, they cast off their female forms and their youth.
She became Kumbha, possessing the luster of a jar and a form released from the pressure of breasts; such was that queen Cūḍālā of excellent complexion.

Having assumed the form of a jar, she later returned to her female state; by night she sported in the forest depths with the conduct of a maiden, while by day she remained in the company of her husband and friend, assuming the form of a jar.

With her beloved friend Bhava, that woman roamed at will, her yogic movements unimpeded upon the peaks of Kailāsa, Mandara, Mahendra, Sumeru, and Sahya, adorned with garlands, necklaces, and ornaments.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, after only a few days had passed, that virtuous woman, assuming the form of Kumbha, spoke thus to her husband:
O King, whose eyes are like lotus petals, listen to these words of mine: every night, I remain standing right here as a woman.
Therefore, I desire to perfect such a womanly duty: I shall give myself to some husband through marriage.
"Therefore, you alone among the three worlds are pleasing to me as a husband; accept me through marriage to be your wife for all time, even at night."
O virtuous one, I wish to enjoy the pleasure of women together with my dear friend, which has come to me without effort; do not be an obstacle to me.
What fault could possibly arise for one who performs his natural duty—a task that has proceeded sequentially since the beginning of creation, which is pleasant, achievable, and pleasing to the mind?
Having abandoned desire and aversion toward all things on every side, we are neither desirous nor averse; therefore, we perform this desired task.
Śikhidhvaja said: "O friend, O one of great intelligence, by performing this deed I perceive neither good nor evil; therefore, do as you wish."
With a mind that has attained equanimity, I see these three worlds as my very own nature; therefore, act as you wish.
Kumbha said: "If that is so, O protector of the earth, then this very day is an auspicious conjunction; for yesterday, I calculated everything, and today is the full moon of this month of Śrāvaṇa."
O mighty-armed one, tonight when the moon has risen, its digits complete and stainless, the wedding ceremony for both of us shall take place.
Today, on the delightful summit of the peak of Mount Mahendra, in a jeweled cave-palace enriched by the light of jewel-lamps.
It was resplendent with rows of lofty trees bent low by the weight of their blossoms, and enchanting with the dance of forest creepers and flowers like dancing women.
O you with eyes as long as the tips of your ears, may the stars traveling through the sky at night together with their lord, the full moon, gaze upon us both.
"Arise for the sake of our own marriage; let us gather from the hollows of the forest a collection of sandalwood, flowers, and other materials, combined with jewels."
Having spoken thus, Kumbha rose up with that king and gathered flowers as well as a collection of jewels and other treasures.
Then, in just a moment, upon a level and auspicious jeweled peak, they both indeed made heaps of unguents and flowers.
Furthermore, heaps of necklaces, garments, supreme jewels, and other such things lay upon the ground; they were like treasuries of good fortune gathered by Time for the sake of Kāma.
Likewise, having prepared their equipment for the journey, those two great friends went to the river Mandākinī in the golden cave to bathe.
There, Kumbha, preceded by auspicious rites, bathed that great king with great reverence—the monarch whose shoulders were like the frontal lobes of an elephant.
The future husband bathed his beloved Cūḍālā, who was to become his wife, while she was in the form of a water-jar.

Having bathed there, the two of them worshipped the gods, the ancestors, and the sages; they were as indifferent toward the fruits of their actions as they were toward the abandonment of those actions.
Unsatisfied by the essence of eternal knowledge and established in the maintenance of the world, the two of them partook of a sublime meal, each according to the other's desire.
Having put on white silk garments from the wish-fulfilling tree and having eaten its fruits, the two of them gradually proceeded to the place where their bridegroom was staying.
Then, after this much time had passed, while the two were longing for the birth-chamber, the sun swiftly entered the mountain of setting, as if to do them a favor.

Then, when the twilight ritual had been performed and the recitation of the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn completed, the sky became filled with a multitude of stars as if for the very purpose of witnessing the wedding.
The night, the sole companion of the month of Mithuna, smiling with its abundance of white water-lilies, arrived scattering a profusion of networks of frost.
On the mountain, Kumbha properly arranged many jewel-lamps, like the lotus-born Brahmā arranging the celestial bodies together with the sun and moon in the sky.
As night fell, she assumed the form of a woman and adorned the king with floods of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and saffron.
With necklaces, armlets, and bracelets, as well as garments from the wish-fulfilling vine, with garlands, neck-chains, and ear-ornaments, and with various appropriate flower wreaths;
Likewise, with clusters of wish-fulfilling creepers, mandāra and pārijātaka trees, saṃtāna trees abounding in many jewels, and a crown having the form of the moon;
After this much time had passed, Kumbha attained the state of a young bride; burdened by the weight of his thick breasts, he quickly became full of amorous grace.
He reflected thus: "I have attained the status of a bridegroom; for the sake of desire, my very self must be given by me, for indeed, one's duty is that which is appropriate to the occasion."
"Here I am, your lovely bride; you, my husband, stand before me. O Kāma, take me! Come, for this is the time for you, O dweller in the heart!"
Having reflected thus, Rati approached her husband, who stood in the depths of the forest ahead of her like the rising sun, as she would approach Kāma.
"I am your wife, named Madanikā, O bestower of honor; this prostration at your feet is performed by me with affection."
Having spoken thus, she of faultless limbs, her face bowed down with modesty, prostrated before her radiant husband with her head and its dangling locks.
And she said this: "O Lord, adorn me with ornaments; having gradually kindled the fire, perform my marriage ceremony."
O King, you shine exceedingly; you make me sick with love. Having surpassed Madana at the wedding of Rati, you now preside over her.
O King, those garlands of yours are like the clusters of rays from the moon, and the necklace upon your chest bears the luster of the flowing current of the Ganges on Mount Meru.
O King, you shine with your locks of hair interwoven with mandāra flowers, like a golden lotus whose filaments are studded with hovering bees.
O Lord, with your jewel-like rays, flowers, beauty, steadfastness, and splendor, you stand surpassing Mount Meru, the abode of jewels.
Speaking thus, those two future husband and wife, who had previously been a married couple in disguise, became mutually delighted.
Seated upon a couch of golden stone, King Śikhidhvaja himself adorned the Great Queen Madanikā.
With crest-ornaments, as well as garlands, ornaments of jewels and gems, garments, ointments, and flowers placed in beautiful positions;
Adorned, that slender woman shone—intoxicating and bestowing joy—like Pārvatī eager for her wedding, or like a passionate woman beloved by Kāma.
The great king, having adorned the queen, said this to her: "O fawn-eyed one, you shine like the newly risen goddess Lakṣmī."
May that auspiciousness be yours which belongs to Śacī with Śakra, which belongs to Lakṣmī with Hari, and which belongs to Gaurī with Śambhu.
With a heart like the bud of a lotus calyx, with eyes like shimmering blue lotuses, and with the auspicious sound of *jhāṃ* like its fragrance, she remained established there like a lotus pond.
With hands of deeply red sprouts and bearing the clusters of your breasts, I consider you to be the creeper of the wish-fulfilling tree of desire, laden with manifold fruits.
With limbs as white and cool as snow, and a smile that radiates like moonlight, you delight us exceedingly, appearing like the beauty of the full moon, ever-ready and joyful.
Therefore arise yourself, O lady of beautiful hips, to the wedding altar; there, with networks of flowering creepers marked by stone-staffs at every interval, [the rite shall be performed].
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: With clusters of pearl-like flower-bunches resembling bouquets, and with four great coconut fruits on the four sides;
With full jars prepared and filled with the waters of the Gaṅgā, they caused a fire to blaze up in its center using sandalwood logs.
One should circumambulate clockwise the blazing fire with its flames kindled, standing to the south and facing eastward, before a seat of twigs placed at the front of the fire.
Having directed the lovely couple to enter, Śikhidhvaja himself entered after having offered sesame seeds and parched grain into the fire.
Rising again and again, he took his beloved in his own arms; they shone together like Śiva and Bhavānī in the forest.
The couple performed a circumambulation of that fire, offering their own inheritance—the entirety of their knowledge, their heart, and their restless love.
Having performed three circumambulations and offered parched grain into the fire, the two of them, whose faces were beautiful with the splendor of mutual smiles, gave to one another.
The husband and wife, both equally delighted, gradually released their hands; their lovely faces were smiling like two moons newly risen.
They entered upon a new bed of flowers prepared beforehand; meanwhile, the moon descended from the sky by one-quarter.
He slowly advanced as if to behold the beauty of these two, and his gaze moved all around as if to find a flaw in that woman.
Then, as the moon rose, the lover moved his hands through the bower of creepers with various new stories and conversations.
Those two lovely spouses sat together for a short while; then, rising, they entered a golden cave illuminated by blazing jewel-lamps.
The two lovers entered the secret chamber they themselves had previously prepared; there they beheld a new couch fashioned of flowers.
It was completely covered on all sides by heaps of carved golden lotuses, as well as by mandāra and other flowers that were entirely free from wilting.
With flowers of great measure, fashioned high and uniform, resembling the long disc of the moon and cool as a bed of frost;
Resembling a stream of milk from the ocean of nectar, as beautiful as a mass of moonlight, it was like the reflection of the bodiless Love-god bent forward as if standing against a wall.

That couple, fragrant, exalted, and lovely, having arisen after a long time from their former state, sat down upon that pure heap of flowers on all sides, as Mount Mandara rests upon the milk-ocean of equal and expansive extent.

Through those various playful exchanges of affectionate speech, through those endearments suited to the occasion, and through those acts of loving service, that long night passed for the two lovers like a mere moment, filled with ever-new bliss.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, as the interior of the world was colored by the pigment known as the sun, Madanī, the wife of Śikhidhvaja, assumed the form of a water-jar at dawn.
Thus, on Mount Mahendra, both Kumbha and Śikhidhvaja were married by their own accord; having entered into that state, they became a divine couple.
Every day they sported in the various forest groves, which were laden with the weight of fully ripened fruit and abounded in flowers and tender shoots.
During the day, the two friends were most affectionate toward one another, and at night, the beloved couple remained united like a lamp and its light; they were never separated.
They sported in forest groves and mountain caves, amidst thickets of *tamāla* trees and dense thickets of *mandāra* blossoms.
And on the Sahya, Dardura, Kailāsa, Mahendra, and Malaya mountains; and on the slopes of the Gandhamādana and Vindhya ranges, as well as on the ridges of the Lokāloka mountain.
When her beloved had fallen asleep after traveling for three days at a time, Cūḍālā, having performed the duties of the king, returned once again.
During the day, those two friends and allies—the husband and wife who were kings of Kumbha—stood together in mutual joy, adorned with various flowers.
For one month, they were honored by gods and kinnaras while staying in a cave-dwelling with jeweled walls on the delightful Mahendra mountain, which was thick with pine trees.
O you who are garlanded by the unfailing Mandāra forest that is within reach of the hand, likewise, on the back of Śuktimat, there is a fortnight in a house of wish-fulfilling creepers.
For two months, on the southern slope of the mountain Pāriyātra, in the Pārijāta grove within a pavilion of divine flower clusters.
On the surface of Jambūkhaṇḍa, at the foot of Mount Meru on the bank of the Jambū river, he spent a month amidst vessels made of gold, [drinking] the fermented juices of jambū fruits.
They spent ten days in the region of Uttarakuru, and twenty-seven days among the northern Kośalas.
In this manner, those two illustrious friends, husband and wife, remained together at night in various other lands belonging to different rulers.
Then, after several months had gradually passed, Cūḍālā, who possessed the form of a son of the gods, reflected:
I shall test Śikhidhvaja with a burden of beautiful enjoyments, so that his mind may never again find delight in sensual pleasures.
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā, by means of her illusory power, manifested in the forest region Hari, who had arrived accompanied by the gods and apsarases.
Seeing Indra arrived with his retinue, Śikhidhvaja, dwelling in the forest, honored him according to tradition.
Śikhidhvaja said: "O King of the Gods, what has been done by myself that has caused such distress from coming so far? You ought, by your grace, to tell me how this came to be."
Indra said: "We have come here from the sky because of the excellence of your virtues, which cling to our hearts like birds bound by a string while wandering in the forest."
Arise and come to heaven; there all the hosts of celestial nymphs stand, their faces turned toward you, filled with wonder at hearing of your virtues.
Furthermore, having taken up the sandals, the pill, the sword, the elixir, and so forth, proceed by the path of accomplishment and take possession of the realm of heaven.
Having come here, you, as one liberated while living, must enjoy various pleasures in the abode of the gods; for that reason, I have come to you.
Virtuous men such as you do not disdain with contempt the prosperity that has arrived, nor do they long for prosperity not yet attained. O good ones! You are truly virtuous.
By your arrival today, dwelling here in comfort without hindrance, may heaven attain purity, just as the three worlds were purified by Hari.
Śikhidhvaja said: "O leader of the gods, I know the conduct that leads to all the heavens; however, for me, heaven is not restricted to any single place."
For I am satisfied everywhere, O Lord, and I rejoice everywhere; because my mind is free from longing, I am full of bliss in all things.
"O Śakra, there is certainly some such merit for heaven established in one place; I do not know how to go there, nor do I carry out your command."

Śakra said: "O virtuous one, I consider the enjoyment of pleasures to be appropriate and consistent with the conduct of the good—those who have known what is to be known and whose intellects are fully perfected."
When the Lord of the Gods had spoken thus and the king remained silent, Hari said to him, "Why do you not depart from here?"
"O Śikhidhvaja, I do not speak thus only at this moment; may it be well with you, O Kumbha," saying this, he vanished from sight.

Then that entire host of gods, together with the Lord of the Thirty-three, became completely invisible there in an instant—a second [host] like a mass of waves in the ocean when the wind has subsided, where the shimmering sea-monsters, foam, and serpents have vanished.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having brought that illusion to rest, Cūḍālā reflected: "By good fortune, this lord of the earth is not being carried away by his desire for enjoyment."
Tranquil and with even enjoyment, Śakra, in this assembly, conducted his worldly affairs without agitation or pride.
I shall deliberate once more with great care and in detail upon this captivating [work], which is characterized by passion and hatred.
Having reflected thus, at night when the moon had risen in the forest, that virtuous Madanikā, beloved and assuming the form of a woman, departed.
While the wind blew, rich with blossoms and thick with sweet fragrance, Śikhidhvaja stood on the riverbank intent upon his evening prayers.
Intoxicated with passion, she entered the inner chamber of the forest goddesses—a bower of *saṃtānaka* creepers made dense with clusters of flowers.
There, upon a flower-bed prepared by her imagination, she stood adorned with garlands of flowers, holding at her neck the beloved paramour imagined there.
Having arrived and searched through the groves, Śikhidhvaja beheld Madanikā in a bower of creepers with the charming libertine around her neck.
His shoulders were draped with locks of hair, his body was anointed with sandalwood paste, and his crest-jewel was disarrayed by being cast down upon the bed-curtains.
Upon a pillow formed by the arms of a girl with a golden luster, doubled over, her locks of hair were clinging to her ears, the corners of her eyes, and the surface of her cheeks.
Then he saw that couple, their faces smiling at one another, with their mouths pressed together, hidden by the garments of the kalpa-creeper.
Under the pretext of their limbs being entwined, those two—resting on a bed of swaying garlands, agitated and afflicted by passion—offered their mutual love to one another.
With faces turned upward in mutual joy, languid with unrestrained passion, they struck each other with flowers while their breasts were pressed together by their chests.
Beholding that with an unchanging mind, Śikhidhvaja was greatly pleased and said, "Oh, what happiness these two libertines find in their station!"
"Stay as you wish, my dear friend, in comfort and according to your disposition; do not cause any obstacle to us who are afraid," he said, and then he departed.
Then, after only a moment, disregarding that elaborate display, she emerged, revealing her own body blooming and agitated with passion.
He saw the king seated upon a golden stone slab in a secluded spot, established in meditative absorption, with his eyes slightly opened.
Having approached that place, her face bowed down with shame, the woman Madanikā remained silent for a moment, distressed and withered.
In an instant, Śikhidhvaja ceased his meditation and, with an undisturbed mind, spoke these exceedingly sweet words to her.
O slender one, why have you arrived so quickly with your joy obstructed? Whatever beings there may be, they all strive only for the sake of bliss.
Go once more and gratify that beloved with acts of affection; for mutual love desired by both is indeed rare throughout the three worlds.
For this reason, O proud lady, I feel no agitation; for one who understands, whatever is most cherished in the world is exactly that which must be relinquished.
"O slender-limbed one, Kumbha and I are both free from passion, while you, this young woman, are subject to the curse of Durvāsas; therefore, do as you wish."
Madanikā said: "O illustrious one, such indeed is the fickle nature of women; for the passion of women is eightfold, so you ought not to be angry."
"O weak woman, while you were intent on your evening prayers in this dense forest at night, what could I, a wretched creature, do?"
Neither a woman nor a maiden, out of longing, makes her lover—who obstructs her pleasure—rest upon her own body.
Women attain beauty only when there is no union with city men; what will indignation, prohibition, lamentation, or even chastity accomplish?
"I am a weak woman, as well as a child and a foolish offender; O Lord, you ought to forgive me, for the virtuous are indeed forgiving."
Śikhidhvaja said: "No anger exists within me toward you, O young girl, like a tree in the sky; I simply do not desire you as my wife because you are censured by the virtuous."
O lady, through our friendship, let us always take delight together in the forest regions as before, with equal joy and free from passion.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: While Śikhidhvaja remained there in such equanimity, Cūḍālā reflected upon him, her heart stirred by his virtuous nature.
Oh, how great is the supreme equanimity attained by this Blessed One! Free from passion and devoid of anger, he abides as one liberated while living.
Neither enjoyments, nor even great supernatural powers, nor pleasures, nor pains, nor calamities, nor prosperities can carry him away.
All blameless women of great supernatural power, when thought of, go toward this one man alone; I consider him to be like another Nārāyaṇa.
I shall remind you of this entire account of my own life; having abandoned this form as Kumbha, I shall become Cūḍālā once again.
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā, her body Cūḍālā remaining unhurt, quickly displayed herself there, having cast off the body of Madanikā.
Therefore, as if she had emerged from the body of Madanikā, she appeared before him, joined with her, as if she had come forth from a casket.
He beheld that Cūḍālā, whose limbs were faultless, standing there as his beloved once more, tender with affection like Madanikā herself.

The king beheld his own beloved, appearing like a cluster of spring lotuses in full bloom, like the Goddess Śrī herself descended from the surface of the earth, or like a treasure revealed from an open jeweled casket.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, beholding his beloved with eyes wide open in wonder, Śikhidhvaja spoke these words in a voice agitated by amazement.
Who are you, O lotus-petal-eyed one? From where have you come, O beautiful lady? Why are you here, for how long, and for what purpose do you stay?
By your gestures, your conduct, your smile, and your conciliatory manner—indeed, by the very grace of my wife—you are recognized as that very person.
Cūḍālā said: "Know it to be even so, O Lord; I am Cūḍālā, there is no doubt. Today I have been found by you in person with my uncreated body."
It is solely to awaken you that this manifold display of mine has reached a hundred branches here within the forest, through the fashioning of bodies such as Kumbha and others.
Ever since you abandoned the kingdom out of delusion and came to the forest for asceticism, I have been striving for your awakening.
By means of this pot-body, you have been awakened by me alone; the creation of the bodies of Kumbha and the others was solely for the purpose of awakening you.
O Lord of the Earth, nothing such as a jar or other objects created by illusion is real; therefore, you who have known what is to be known, perceive this through meditation as an undivided whole.
"O knower of reality, you see everything; behold it swiftly through meditation. Then, being thus addressed by Cūḍālā, the king girded his loins.
Through meditation, he specifically beheld his own history in its pure clarity, from the renunciation of sovereignty up to the sight of Cūḍālā.
Through meditation for a single moment, he beheld his entire life-story, from the very moment of his renunciation of the kingdom through the succession of every present instant.
Having perceived everything, the protector of the earth ceased from his meditative absorption; having emerged from samādhi, his lotus-like eyes blossomed with joy.
Quickly stretching out his arms, which were radiant with horripilation, he shed tears that flowed from his limbs with intense affection, while his longing throbbed within him.
Nakula embraced his beloved for a long time, as a male mongoose embraces a female; and in that embrace of theirs, a certain state of being arose.
He cannot be described even with the tongues of Vāsuki out of such joy, like two bodies joined together in heaven, as if made of mud.
Like two mountains carved from the same rock, the two lovers remained embraced for a long time; in a moment, their bodies grew heavy with perspiration and became thick with horripilation.
Their two beloved arms, whose hearts were filled with nectar yet resembled empty hearts, slowly and slightly relaxed.
Having remained silent for a moment of intense bliss, with his arms outstretched and his eyes fixed upon Lakṣmaṇa, he spoke words tender with affection.
Placing his hand upon the chin of his beloved, the king spoke to her in a voice exceedingly sweet and affectionate, as is natural for a lover toward the women of his own house.
How great must be the measure of the merit flowing from your delight—the nectar of your name which is sweeter even than the actual ambrosia—O slender-limbed one, enchanting as the young moon!
For the sake of my husband, I have long endured terrible suffering; thus, I have emerged from that cave of saṃsāra which is so difficult to cross.
By what can that intellect by which she was delivered be compared? She is Arundhatī, Śacī, Gaurī, Gāyatrī, Śrī, and Sarasvatī.
O beautiful slender lady, by the splendor of your virtues, all things—intellect, fortune, loveliness, forbearance, friendliness, compassion, and the rest—become as if fragile in comparison.
Among beloved women whose forms are beautiful, you appear as the very first; by means of this supreme resolve, I have been awakened by you.
By what kind of return-favor would your mind be satisfied, [given that it has been drawn] from the beginningless thicket of delusion, even from its endless thicket?
Virtuous women of noble family rescue one who has fallen through their resolve; however, the meaning of the scriptures, the guru, and mantras are not capable of such rescue in that manner.

Just as these noble women of good family are full of affection for their husbands, so too are friends, brothers, well-wishers, servants, teachers, and companions [affectionate] toward wealth and happiness.

The scripture is her sanctuary and she is the servant of her husband; noble women must always be honored with every effort. Noble women are everything to their husband's family. In these [perfections] is established all the happiness of both worlds; for her who is free from desire, they lead to the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra.
How shall I repay you for this kindness? I believe that all noble women in the world have now been surpassed by you.
You shall become the subject of discourse regarding female excellence, surpassing the web of virtues of the Creator who fashioned you.
I believe that Arundhatī and the other women must surely be provoked to anger by you, who are a Satī and a casket for the jewels of beauty, goodness, and virtue.
"Come, grant once more an embrace to me, who am exalted by your virtues. Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus to that Cūḍālā, whose eyes were like those of a young deer, Śikhidhvaja—
Nakula embraced her again firmly, as a male mongoose embraces its mate. Cūḍālā said: "O Lord, while you were intent on a web of dry ritual acts, your own self was agitated."
Again and again, I have been deeply distressed on your account; therefore, by means of that [distress], my own purpose—which consists in awakening you—has indeed been accomplished.
"O Goddess, what honor do you show me here? Śikhidhvaja said: 'O lady of beautiful hips, it is so that your own auspicious purpose may be accomplished by you.'"
"Now, let all these noble women accomplish that accordingly. Cūḍālā said: "O Beloved, O Lord, you have awakened and come to rest upon the shore of the snare of the world."
