Today you perceive that former delusion which persists in the form of the thought: "I am doing this," "I am not doing that," "I have attained this."
Do you perhaps inwardly laugh at that state of your intellect being as fragile as a blade of grass—at those trivialities of craving and those wicked fabrications of conceptual thought?
"O Lord, today you are no longer seen, like mountains in the sky; what has become of you now, my dear? Upon what do you rely, and what do you seek?"

"O Lord, how do you perceive the sequence of bodily movements of one who has passed away? Śikhidhvaja replied: "O you whose eyes possess the essence of garlands of blue lotuses filled with beautiful flowers!"
I have approached whatever being exists within you; I am effortless, I am partless, I am as pure as the sky, and I am free from desire.
I am peaceful, I am the nature of the ultimate reality; for a long time I have remained as "I," having reached that state wherein I abide solely upon the path of the mind.
I am established in my own natural state, resting solely in pure consciousness which is nothing at all—consciousness that even Hari, Hara, and the other gods cannot suddenly negate.
O lady with beautiful eyes, I am now liberated from delusion and from saṃsāra; I am neither pleased nor distressed, neither this nor anything else.
"I am neither gross nor subtle, O beautiful one, and I am the Truth; I am like a reflection of light that has emerged from its source and fallen upon a wall."
I am indeed equal through a radiance free from decay and excess; I am peaceful, I lead to equanimity, I am established in my own self, and I am devoid of latent desires.
O you who are devoted to your husband, I am indeed in the state of final nirvana; I am like that which I am. I can say only what I truly am, and nothing else.
O you whose outer corners of the eyes are tremulous like waves, you are my guru; salutations be to you! By the grace of the large-eyed one, I have crossed over the ocean of worldly existence.
I shall not take up impurity again, like gold that has been smelted a hundred times; I am peaceful, self-abiding, gentle, restrained, free from passion, and possessed of indivisible wisdom.
"Transcending all and omnipresent, I abide like space. Cūḍālā said: "O Great Being, Lord of Life, beloved of my heart, since this is so..."
"Now, O Lord, speak; what pleases you, O Great-minded One? Śikhidhvaja said: "I do not know how to refuse, nor do I know how to desire."
O slender one, whatever you do, I know it to be exactly so; O beloved, may everything that is your wish be fulfilled without exception.
"O Sundarī, I do not know how to pursue anything; whatever you yourself know, O beautiful one, do that."
I shall maintain that very reflection, like a jewel, with a mind free from desire, according to what has been attained, and beyond reproach.
"I neither praise nor blame; do as you wish. Cūḍālā said: "If it is so, O mighty-armed one, then listen to my thought."

Having heard this, O one whose self is liberated while living, you ought to adopt that very state; for you are endowed with the realization of universal unity, which arises from the destruction of ignorance.
We remain indeed free from desire, as clear as space; whatever constitutes our seeking, such is our non-seeking.

Since no one at all practices anything here when there is no desire for vital breaths, who indeed is that pure consciousness? Therefore, O Supreme Person, we are those who exist in the beginning, the end, and the middle.
Having set aside the one remaining [son], we ourselves remain here; having spent this time with our current kingdom, we shall indeed proceed in due order.
"O Lord, after some time we shall attain the state of bodilessness (videhatā). Śikhidhvaja said: 'Tell me, O fickle one, what will we be like in the beginning, the middle, and at the end?'"
"Or how indeed shall we remain, having abandoned the one remainder? Cūḍālā said: "O best of kings, we are kings in the beginning, the end, and the middle."
Abandoning delusion alone, we shall become yours once again; remain as king in your own city, established upon your own throne.
"Am I not indeed the ornament of lovely women? Shall I become your queen, with the intoxicated citizens as my subjects and young maidens dancing before me?"

May that city—adorned with banners, resounding with musical instruments, strewn with showers of flowers, possessing shimmering creepers with their clusters of blossoms, and garlanded by rows of humming bees—be equal for a long time to the splendor of the vine in the month of spring.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having been addressed thus by Cūḍālā, Śikhidhvaja laughed and spoke these sweet words, unperturbed and free from all distress.
"If it is so, O large-eyed one, then those splendors of perfected enjoyments are within our own power in the triple heaven; why then, my dear, do I not dwell among them?"
Cūḍālā said: "O King, I have no desire for enjoyments, nor for riches; by the power of my own nature, I abide in whatever comes to me."
Neither heaven, nor sovereignty, nor even ritual action brings me happiness; rather, I remain established as I am, undisturbed, with my conduct centered in well-being.
When the duality of "this is pleasure" and "this is not" has come to an end, I abide here at ease in that very same state of peace.
Śikhidhvaja said: "O large-eyed one, you have spoken rightly with this balanced wisdom. For what purpose indeed could there be in either the grasping or the abandoning of a kingdom?"
Having abandoned concern for states of pleasure and pain and being free from envy, let us both remain exactly as we are, having attained composure.
Thus, through their conversation and discourse there, the day drew to a close for that couple who had been husband and wife for so long.
Then, having risen, those two blameless ones, though full of longing, performed their daily duties as they occurred, free from anxiety, being experts in what must be done.

Disregarding the attainment of heaven, they remained with their minds fully satisfied; on that very same bed, through various acts of affection, that night passed for those two who were liberated while yet living.

As the two supreme beings themselves expressed their longing for the bliss of enjoying that [union] and liberation, filled with the playful charm of affectionate words, this long night passed for them like a mere moment as it brought their lovers' minds to a state of intense yearning.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, when the sun had risen and stood in the sky free from darkness, that jewel of the world emerged as if from a casket.
The lotus pond blossomed at the edge of dawn as if it were its two eyes, while the rays of the sun spread forth like the worldly customs of men.
Having risen and performed their twilight rites, the two, husband and wife, sat together upon soft and smooth leaf-seats, radiant within that golden cave.
Then Cūḍālā rose up there and, standing before the jewel-pitcher, her beloved, she willed it to be filled with the waters of the seven oceans.
With that auspicious jar, his wife consecrated her husband—who was standing facing the east—in private within his own kingdom.
When he had arrived, seated upon his own throne within a golden vessel brought forth by her own will, that slender Cūḍālā, possessing a divine form, spoke to him.
O Lord, having set aside your mere silence, you ought to sustain this peaceful splendor—the combined radiance of the eight world-protectors.
Thus addressed as "Cūḍālā" in the forest, King Śikhidhvaja, saying "I shall do so," attained the status of a great king.
Then he spoke to the proud lady who stood in the position of a female doorkeeper: "Today I shall consecrate you as queen in the position of the Goddess."
Having spoken thus, and having bathed her in the lake and likewise consecrated her in the office of the Great Queen, the king said to his own beloved wife:
"O beloved, lotus-petal-eyed one, you ought to procure in an instant a vast and formidable army produced by mere thought."
Having heard these words of her beloved, Cūḍālā, the woman of excellent complexion, conjured up an army as formidable as a monsoon cloud.
The two of them beheld that army, teeming with horses and elephants, filling the sky with its banners and making the forest appear dense and continuous.
The mountain caves and dense thickets resounded with the blaring of musical instruments, while the great radiance of the crest-jewels pulverized the veil of darkness.
There, upon that excellent scent-elephant, within the royal circle established and protected by joyful vassal lords, the king and queen were mounted.
Then King Śikhidhvaja, together with his beloved queen, leading a vast army crowded with foot soldiers and chariots, marched forth.
Then he departed from that forest with his army, which caused even the mountains to tremble, as if splitting the earth and its hills with a swift terrestrial whirlwind.
Then that lord of the earth set out from Mahendra, the king of mountains, beholding along the way various mountains, regions, rivers, villages, and wildernesses.
Showing that collection of his own adventures to his beloved, he reached his own city, which was as beautiful as heaven, in a very short time.
There, his neighboring kings, respectful of his arrival, recognized him by the sound of "Victory! and went forth with uplifted hearts.
Accompanied by those two armies, which had joined as one and resounded with the blare of trumpets, the king entered the city.
Showered with handfuls of parched grain and flowers by the city women, he beheld the merchant’s street, which was most excellent and unsurpassed.
Crowded with banners and flags, beautiful with nets of pearls, filled with women devoted to dance and song, it stood immovable upon its own ground.
Then, having entered the palace accompanied by various royal auspicious rites, he duly honored the multitude of subjects who bowed before him.
Having celebrated a magnificent festival for seven excellent days, the king attended to his royal duties within his own inner apartments.
O Rāma, having ruled the kingdom on the surface of the earth for ten thousand years, he desisted from maintaining the body along with Cūḍālā.
Having cast off the body, O Rāma, that one of great intelligence attained nirvāṇa like a lamp without oil, so as not to be born again.
Having enjoyed sovereignty for ten thousand years through that even-mindedness, he attained the state of Nirvana.

Free from fear and dejection, liberated from pride and envy, his actions natural and spontaneous, his intellect having consumed all passion—he who possessed such an even and equanimous vision conquered death and ruled for ten thousand winters as a sole sovereign.

Having enjoyed manifold pleasures on earth and having remained for a long time as the crest-jewel of all sovereign kings, he attained the supreme state of immortality with his essence alone remaining. In this same way, O Rāma, following the course of nature regarding the multitude of duties that have come upon you, remain free from sorrow; arise, whether experiencing them yourself or forcibly, the splendors of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "I have related this entire narrative of Śikhidhvaja to you; by traveling along this path, you shall never again experience weariness."
Firmly grasping this view which destroys passion and hatred, remain with a mind eternally free from passion, having firmly attained that state.
O Rāma, by conducting the affairs of the kingdom just as King Śikhidhvaja did, may you become one who possesses both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Rāghava, understand it in this way: just as Kaca, the son of Bṛhaspati, attained awakening through the very method of Śikhidhvaja.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, please describe in brief how that blessed Kaca, the son of the blessed Bṛhaspati, attained enlightenment.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen, O illustrious King, to this story of how Kaca, the son of the preceptor of the gods, attained supreme awakening just like Śikhidhvaja.
Having transcended childhood and being intent on crossing over cyclic existence, Kaca, who understood both words and their meanings, spoke to Bṛhaspati.
Kacha said: "O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, tell me how a living being, bound by the thread of life, may emerge from this cage of saṃsāra."
Bṛhaspati said: "O son, by renouncing everything, one flies up without agitation from this ocean of saṃsāra, which is a house made of the elements of misfortune."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having heard these most purifying words of his father, Kaca abandoned everything and went to a solitary forest.
That departure of Bṛhaspati did not cause him any distress; for great men of noble character remain equanimous both in union and in separation.
Then, O sinless one, when three or five years had passed, Kaca again encountered his father in a certain great forest.
Having honored and saluted him, and having embraced his son, Kaca again questioned the Lord of Speech with a pleasing voice.
Kaca said: "Today it is the eighth year since I have practiced total renunciation; yet even so, O father, I do not attain blameless peace."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: While Kaca was speaking these words of distress in the forest, the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati), having said "Abandon everything," ascended to heaven.
When he had departed, Kaca likewise cast off his body and even his bark garments; he became like the autumnal sky, from which the moon, clouds, sun, and stars had vanished.
Furthermore, after three years, in a certain forest region, he abandoned the raining of water and other such acts, just as the sky ceases its rain in autumn.
A lay disciple, his body tranquil and empty like the far reaches of space and sighing deeply, reached that very father and teacher with a grieving mind.
Having performed the sequence of worship with devotion, Kaca, embracing his son, questioned him again with a voice faltering from grief.
Kaca said: "O father, everything has been renounced—the patched garment, the bamboo staff, and so forth; yet even so, there is no rest in my own true state. What shall I do?"

Bṛhaspati said: "They say that the mind is everything; by abandoning that, my son, you shall shine. Those who know all things understand the abandonment of the mind to be the abandonment of everything."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus to his son, the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati) swiftly leapt into the sky; Kaca, his mind undaunted, sought to abandon the mind itself.
When he could not perceive his own mind even while reflecting upon it in the forest, he then reflected further and understood through his intellect that he had gone to his father.
The collection of objects, such as the body and so forth, is said not to be the mind; why, where, or for what purposeless reason should I abandon this innocent [world]?
I shall go into the presence of my father to understand the mind, that great enemy; having understood it, I shall quickly abandon it, and thereafter I shall remain free from the fever of affliction.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having reflected thus, Kaca ascended to the celestial realm; having reached the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati), he affectionately paid homage and prostrated before him.
He questioned him in private: "O Blessed One, tell me, what is the mind? Speak of the true nature of the mind so that I may completely abandon it."
Bṛhaspati said: Those who know the mind understand one's own ego to be the mind; that internal sense of "I-ness" which exists within a living being is called the mind.
Kaca said: "O Great-minded One, tell me how this came to pass regarding the host of gods, O Teacher, which consists of thirty-three times ten million."
I think that the renunciation of this [body] is difficult and does not lead to perfection; how indeed, O best of yogis, can it be abandoned?
Bṛhaspati said: Even by the mere plucking of a flower or the mere closing of one's eyes, the abandonment of egoism is easily accomplished; there is not even the slightest difficulty in this.
Listen, my son, as I tell you how this is so: an object established solely through ignorance perishes by means of knowledge.
In reality, O son, there is no such thing as egoism; it is a false delusion, appearing as if existent though non-existent, like a child's phantom.
Just as the state of being a snake appears in a rope, and just as the notion of water arises in a desert, so too does the false manifestation of egoism flash forth, though it is unreal.
Just as duality, though non-existent, is perceived in the moon due to delusion, so too does the ego-sense manifest; it is neither real nor unreal.
There exists a single, beginningless and endless, pure consciousness alone, free from internal impurity, clearer even than the sky, and the knower of all.
That very same single reality shines everywhere, at all times, and in every manner among all living beings, like water shimmering within the restless waves of the ocean.
In this regard, what is this sense of "I," from where does it arise, and how has it emerged? Where is a mass of dust born within water, and where can water rise from fire?
O son, abandon this futile notion of "I am this," which is insubstantial, limited in form, and rendered helpless by space and time.

You are that which is unconditioned by space, time, and the like; transparent, eternally manifest, all-pervading, consisting of all objects yet being the singular object of pure consciousness, and stainless.

Like the sap of fruits, flowers, and leaves situated in every direction, you are ever-present within all worlds; as the stainless conscious self, eternally infinite, who indeed am I compared to you, O embodiment of pure being—what certainty can there be of an "I"?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having thus received this supreme yoga, this unsurpassed instruction, the son of the preceptor of the gods became liberated while yet living.
Free from possessiveness and free from ego, with the knots of bondage severed and the intellect perfectly tranquil—just as Kaca remained, O Rāma, so should you remain, free from all modification.
Know that the ego-sense is unreal; do not rely upon it, nor abandon it. For how indeed can there be the relinquishing or the grasping of the unreal, such as a rabbit's horn?
When egoism is impossible, where are birth and death for you? Likewise, who could gather the fruit sown in the field of space?
Partless, with all mental constructs stilled, pervading and consisting of the essence of all beings, subtler than even the most minute atom, you are pure consciousness alone, composed of mind.

Just as waves and the like arise from water, and bracelets and the like from gold, so too does that very [Self], though not being other than itself, appear as if it were something else, when conditioned by the sense of "I."
Through lack of awakening, the entire world remains as if composed of illusion; through awakening, O sinless one, everything becomes the very form of Brahman.
Abandoning the notions of duality and unity, remain established in what remains and be happy; do not be miserable in vain like a deluded person.
This worldly existence, which has become dense and is like an autumn mist, is an illusion exceedingly difficult to cross; yet, through awakening, it quickly attains attenuation.
Śrī Rāma said: I have attained supreme inner satisfaction through the nectar of your knowledge, just as a cātaka bird, overcome by the fear of drought, finds relief in a refreshing shower.
As if sprinkled with nectar, I enter into a state of inner coolness; yet I abide above all incomparable riches.
I do not reach satiety as I listen to your words, just as the thirsty cakora bird never reaches enough of the moon’s rays.
O Lord, though already satisfied, I ask you this question once more: who indeed, even when satiated, would not drink the unswallowed nectar-liquor?
O best of sages, why is that which is called the "false person" said to be both a reality and a non-reality? Tell me quickly how the entire multitude of things in the world is thus made.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, listen to this beautiful narrative told by me, which produces laughter and serves to awaken you from the delusion of the unreal person.
O mighty-armed one, there exists a certain person composed of illusion and machinery, whose intellect is as tender and deluded as that of a child, and who is concealed solely by ignorance.
Having arisen somewhere in solitude, he remains right there in that void, like a mass of hair in the sky or like a mirage in the desert.

Therefore, nothing other than that exists there; and that which does exist is precisely that itself. Whatever else appears, it is merely an appearance of that, yet the one of dull intellect does not perceive this.
As he grew in that state, a firm resolve arose within him: "I am space, I am space, space is mine; I shall protect space."
"Having established the sky, I myself shall protect the desired object with care"—thinking thus, he built a house for the purpose of protecting the void.
O descendant of Raghu, he placed his trust in its interior, thinking, "The space is protected by me," and was thus satisfied with the space within the house.
Then, in the course of time, his house went to ruin, like a cloud at the end of the season or a wave by the wind.
"Alas, O space of the house, you are lost! Alas, where have you gone in an instant? Alas, alas, you pure one, you are shattered!"—thus did he lament.
Having thus lamented a hundred times, the evil-minded one again made a well right there for the sake of his donkey; he became intent on the empty space of the well.
Then, in the course of time, even that well of his met its destruction; when the space of the well had vanished, he became utterly immersed in grief.
At the conclusion of his discourse on the space within the well, he quickly fashioned a jar; having become the space within the jar, he himself attained final nirvana.
O descendant of Raghu, even Kumbha was brought to destruction in time; for whatever direction an unfortunate person takes, that very direction perishes.
At the conclusion of his prattle regarding the space within the jar, he made a pit for the sake of a donkey; likewise, by that act, he became one who was devoted to the space within the pit.
In the course of time, even his sacrificial pit met with destruction; thus, like darkness vanishing before light, he grieved for the space that had once been the pit.
At the end of his grief, he constructed a great four-winged mansion for the sake of protecting the earth; that mansion then became as vast as space itself.
Time, which devours all creatures, swiftly snatched that away from him as the wind carries off a withered leaf; thereupon, he became consumed by grief.
At the edge of the sorrow of the four-pillared hall, he constructed a granary for the protection of his livestock; it was shaped like a water-cloud, and he remained there, intent upon the sky.
Time swiftly snatched that away from him, as the wind carries off a cloud; he was consumed by the grief over the loss of his granary.
Thus, with houses, four-sided halls, jars, bowls, and granaries, this time of his, which has no end, passes away.

Remaining thus, powerless, he grasps at the sky within the cave as his own home through the dense thicket of self-identification; bewildered by the cycle of coming and going, he moves toward and departs from a mass of suffering that is even denser than the preceding suffering.
Śrī Rāma said: O Lord, why have you described this illusory person (māyāpuruṣa) through the context of a false man? And what is meant by the "protection of the sky"?
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: Listen, O Rāma, as it truly is; I shall reveal this to you—the story of the account of the illusory man that has just been told.
O descendant of Raghu, know that this person, who is said to consist of the machinery of illusion, is the ego (ahaṃkāra) arisen from the empty sky.
O virtuous one, that infinite, unreal void within which this world resides in this sheath of space becomes manifest of its own accord at the beginning of creation.
Then, like sound from the ether, the ego-sense arises from that Brahman which resides within and is exceedingly difficult to perceive, just as vibration first arises from the wind.
Having increased in the sky and attained the state of being the self, that which is non-self strives thereafter by means of the designation "self."
Having fallen into a state of agitation, this non-self, for the sake of protecting its own singular self, repeatedly creates various kinds of bodies even as they perish again and again.
That very person is a person of illusion; he is indeed a false person. For the ego-sense, though non-existent and purposeless, has arisen through māyā.
Having fashioned bodies such as wells, ponds, four-sided halls, and jars, he thinks, "I am protected," and thus his meditation proceeds within that void.
O Rāghava, hear these names of this very egoism, by which delusions in the form of the world it causes one to be infatuated.

It is renowned by such names as the living soul (jīva), intellect (buddhi), mind (manas), consciousness (citta), illusion (māyā), primordial nature (prakṛti), as well as volition (saṃkalpa), conceptualization (kalanā), time (kāla), and a portion (kalā).
Through these and other such names, which have become manifold, the egoity (*ahaṃkāra*), possessing a thousand forms, expands by means of imagined objects.
Within the vast and empty elemental ether, the world is certainly without foundation; yet the person remains there, experiencing pleasures and pains that are truly illusory.
Just as a deluded man, guarding against the fear of his own reflection in the sky, becomes distressed by the space within jars and such, so too you should not become afflicted.
Vaster even than space, pure, subtle, auspicious, and beautiful—how and by whom can that Self be grasped, or even protected?
When the body, which is merely the space within the heart, perishes, living beings grieve in vain out of the suspicion that the Self has been destroyed.
Just as space remains undivided when jars and the like are destroyed, so the embodied soul remains eternally untainted when bodies perish.
This pure Self, consisting of consciousness alone, is subtler than even space; for it does not perish, O Rāma, being like the sky and consisting merely of its own portion of self-experience.
Nothing whatsoever is ever born, nor does anything ever die anywhere; it is only Brahman that expands in the form of the world's manifestation.
Truth is the one state, peaceful, devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and liberated from both existence and non-existence; having realized this, be happy.

Having abandoned through awakening the entire state of egoism—which is the abode of all calamities, unstable, lacking self-mastery, prone to downfall, devoid of discernment, ignoble, and ignorant—you shall remain in the perfectly secure state and attain the highest excellence.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Before the supreme Brahman, the mind first arose; consisting of the nature of thought and expansive, it attained its state while remaining established in that very [Brahman].
O Raghava, as fragrance resides in the calyx of a flower, as a great wave in the ocean, and as a network of rays in the sun, so does the mind reside in Brahman.
O Rāma, this world has come into existence solely through the forgetting of that invisible reality of the Self; it has not come from anything else, like a snake imagined in a rope.
O Raghava, whoever perceives this web of rays as distinct from the Sun, it is indeed as if it were something other than that radiant one.
For one by whom the armlet is conceived as distinct from gold, that [armlet] is indeed just an armlet for him; it is not gold for him.
He by whom the rays are realized as non-different from the sun—that person is indeed the sun itself; he is called one who is free from conceptual construction.
For one who perceives a wave as something distinct from water, only the notion of a "wave" remains for them, and not the ocean.
He by whom a wave is perceived as not distinct from the water, possessing the cognition of its identity with the water, is called non-conceptual.
He by whom the armlet is perceived as not distinct from the gold, possessing the great wisdom that gold alone exists, is called one who is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*).
For one by whom the series of flames has been perceived as distinct from fire, the cognition of "fire" vanishes, and only the cognition of "flames" remains.
That state is colored like a mass of flames or a streak of clouds; the agitated mind, being absorbed in it, adopts that very same instability.
He who perceives the series of flames as non-different from the fire possesses a single cognition of fire; he is called one who is free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa).

He who is free from conceptual construction, who is truly great, and whose great intelligence is undiminished—by him that which is to be attained has been fully attained; he does not sink into objects.
Having abandoned all multiplicity within the hollow of pure consciousness alone, remain established in the reality of awareness, which is utterly free from any object of perception.
When the Self, by itself and through itself, brings forth its own power called volition, it is like the wind manifesting its power of motion through its own vibration.
Then the mind, which consists of the fabrication of conceptual constructions, becomes the soul of the universe, appearing as if separate while itself imagining its own form.
The mind, which consists of volition, causes this entire world to exist; by whatever volitions it conceives, so does it become in an instant.

The mind—known by such names as the individual soul (jīva), ego (ahaṃkāra), intellect (buddhi), and consciousness (citta)—assumes the state of an insect, the state of Brahmā, or likewise the state of Meru or of the gods (maruts).
Through volition, the mind attains duality and unity, and thereby extends the existence of the world; subsequently, within that very extension, it itself undergoes manifoldness.
This expansive world that is perceived is composed solely of mental construction; it is neither real nor unreal, having arisen like a web of dreams.
Just as the mental kingdom of a living being shines forth with various undertakings, so does this vast mental kingdom of Brahmā resplendently manifest.
Because it is cultivated through the perception of things as they truly are, this [duality] dissolves; for when seen from the perspective of ultimate reality, this is indeed nothing at all.
But the visible world, though not ultimately real, undergoes a hundredfold branching as it vibrates, becoming fit for the conceptualization of water, waves, ripples, and so forth.
Just as the ocean naturally assumes its form, so does consciousness; for it performs thousands of actions without anything other than the vibration of the atomic consciousness.
He does nothing at all that was not already present, abandoning even the slightest sense of differentiation; thus he goes, hears, touches, smells, speaks, acts, and sleeps.
Meditating thus, "Nothing whatsoever exists that is not real," know that whatever you do is but the stainless, all-pervading Pure Consciousness alone.
Brahman is of an expanded form; nothing other than that exists, since the entire multitude of objects remains composed of the essence of consciousness.
All this world is indeed consciousness; there is no other conceptualization. Within this mere radiance of consciousness, which is named the "web of the world," [nothing else exists].

Whence arises the false grasping that "this is one thing and that is another," given that there is the possibility of only a single consciousness in all its various forms? Since even the object of cognition does not exist at all, how can there be bondage and liberation?

Forcefully casting aside all fruitless conceits regarding the thought that "this is liberation" or "this indeed is bondage," remain as one who is silent, self-controlled, free from pride and intoxication, a great soul performing his own duty, truly devoid of egoism.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O sinless one, you are a great doer, a great enjoyer, and a great renouncer; having abandoned all doubts, take hold of eternal fortitude.
Śrī Rāma said: O Lord, please explain to me correctly: who is called the "great doer," who is called the "great renouncer," and who is called the "great enjoyer"?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, these three vows were formerly proclaimed by the one who bears the crescent moon on his crest to Bhṛṅgīśa, by which he remained free from all feverish distress.
Formerly, on the northern peak of Sumeru, which resembled fire, the bearer of the crescent moon stood together with his entire retinue.
O Rāma, the highly effulgent Bhṛṅgīśa, who possessed limited knowledge, stood before the Lord of Umā with palms joined in reverence and questioned him.
Bhṛṅgīśa said: O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, omniscient Supreme Lord, please tell me quickly out of compassion that which I am asking.
O Lord, beholding this structure of saṃsāra, as flickering as a wave, I am bewildered, being deprived of rest in the ultimate reality.
Having accepted a beloved and well-established internal certainty, I dwell free from feverish distress in this dilapidated house of the world.
The Lord said: "Abandoning all doubts and resorting to eternal fortitude, O sinless one, become a great enjoyer, a great doer, and a great renouncer."
Bhṛṅgīśa said: What is meant by "the great doer," what is meant by "the great enjoyer," and what is meant by "the great renouncer"? O Lord, explain this to me correctly.
Īśvara said: O illustrious one, he who performs dharma and adharma as they arise, free from doubt and undecaying, is called a great agent.
He who performs passion and hatred, pleasure and pain, merit and demerit, and fruit and non-fruit, without regard for them, is called the Great Creator.
He who acts with silence, free from egoism, pure, and devoid of envy, performing his work without agitation—he is called a great doer.
He whose mind is not stained by doubts regarding dharma and adharma in matters both auspicious and inauspicious is called a great doer.
He who is free from attachment everywhere and remains like a witness, who engages in action without desire—he is called a great doer.
Free from agitation and joy, with an equanimous and pure intellect, he who neither grieves nor exults is called a great agent.
When, at the time of action, the wise sage remains with an unattached mind, abiding in conduct appropriate to the task at hand, he is called a great doer.
He who, remaining indifferent while performing action as well as non-action, attains an absolute internal equanimity—he is called a great doer.
He who is peaceful by his very nature and does not indeed abandon equanimity, even while performing both auspicious and inauspicious deeds—he is called the Great Doer.
He whose mind remains exactly the same during birth, stability, and destruction, as well as during rising and setting, is called a great doer.
He hates nothing, nor does he desire anything; he partakes of everything as it comes to him—he is called a great enjoyer.
He who does not grasp even while grasping, does not act even while acting, and does not enjoy even while enjoying—he is called a great enjoyer.
He whose intellect is unwearied observes the entire worldly transaction like a witness; having his desires departed, he is called a great enjoyer.
He whose mind does not deviate because of pleasures or pains, through ritual actions or their performance, or due to existence and non-existence which cause delusion—he is called a great enjoyer.
He who perceives even old age, death, and poverty within sovereignty as truly delightful—he is called a great enjoyer.
He who receives great joys and sorrows equally, like the ocean receiving its waters, is called a great enjoyer.
Non-violence, equanimity, and contentment are like rays from the orb of the moon; because he has drawn them in, he is called the Great Enjoyer.
He who eats pungent, sour, salty, bitter, unrefined, refined, and excellent food with equanimity—he is called a great eater.
He who perceives with equanimity the flavorful and the flavorless, as well as sexual union and its cessation, is called a gentle one, a great enjoyer.
He whose equanimity remains steadfast toward alkaline matter and sugar, toward the auspicious and likewise the inauspicious—he is called a great enjoyer.
Having abandoned the conceptualization that "this is edible" and "this is inedible," he who eats with all longing gone is called a great eater.
He who experiences adversity and prosperity, delusion and bliss, whether inferior or superior, with an equanimous mind, is called a great enjoyer.
He by whom merit and demerit, pleasure and pain, as well as death and birth, have been completely renounced through wisdom—he is called a great renouncer.
He by whom all desires, all doubts, all impulses, and all certainties have been abandoned through wisdom is called a great renunciant.
He by whom the existence of the body, the mind, and the senses—while they abide in the mind—is truly abandoned through suffering, he is called a great renunciant.
"I have neither body nor birth, nor do I possess actions, whether appropriate or inappropriate"—one who possesses such internal certainty is called a "great renouncer."
He by whom all internal mental constructions, desires, and deliberations regarding both dharma and adharma have been completely renounced—he is called a great renouncer.
Whatever conceptualization of the visible world is observed in its entirety, he by whom that has been thoroughly renounced is called a great renouncer.
Thus was it spoken by the God of gods to Bhṛṅgīśa in the past, O sinless one: "O Rāma, maintaining this vision, remain free from all feverish distress."

There exists Brahman alone—eternally risen, pure in form, infinite, and primordial—not even a trace of any other part or fraction. Meditate thus; having attained the state of stainlessness, reach Nirvana with all your mental fluctuations stilled and purified.

The Brahman is free from ailment, the sole seed for all the effects of every kalpa, and the very form of the Supreme Self; it is vast, having expanded all states of being, and is like the sky—whatever little appears here, O dear one, is that.
"O virtuous one, remain with a firm internal conviction that nothing whatsoever exists anywhere at any time—neither as real nor as unreal—and thus dwell free from the play of doubt."
Being constantly inward-turned while performing the entire multitude of external duties, you never experience weariness and attain the state of one whose egoism has been cast away.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, when the mind—known as the ego—is dissolved, or when its form has vanished, what would be the characteristic mark of the sattva?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For even when produced by force, defects such as greed and delusion do not stain the pure disposition, just as water does not stain a lotus.
The glories beginning with sympathetic joy never leave the face when the mind consisting of egoism dissolves and evil deeds dissolve as well.
The knots of latent impressions (vāsanā) snap completely and gradually as if severed; anger undergoes attenuation, and delusion indeed reaches a state of dullness.
Desire grows weary and greed flees elsewhere; the senses do not exult, and distress does not manifest intensely.
Sufferings do not overwhelm them, nor do pleasures cause them to exult; rather, equanimity arises everywhere in their hearts, bestowing a cooling serenity.
If these things such as pleasure and pain are seen on the face, they are indeed seen; yet, because of their insignificance, they do not smear the mind.
When the mind dissolves into a state desirable even to the hosts of gods, the virtuous person attains it; then there arises within him an equanimity like the cool moonlight.
Thus it bears a great form that is tranquil and lovely, serviceable and unobstructed, modest yet majestic, and pure.
Though it is contradictory as both existence and non-existence, though variegated, and though vast, the delusion of worldly existence brings neither joy nor sorrow to the wise.
Fie upon that lowest of men who, out of delusion, does not apply himself to this reality—which is to be accomplished by the light of the intellect and is free from all calamities.

O friend, for one who desires to cross the ocean of birth—a mine of jewels of suffering—in order to attain the rest that is so fitting, the thought "Who am I? How is this world? What might the beyond be? And what is the use of enjoyments? is the supreme means.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen to how Ikṣvāku, the king who was the first ancestor among you and born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, attained liberation.
A king named Ikṣvāku, while protecting his own kingdom, once went into solitude and reflected thus in his mind.

"What might be the cause of this phenomenal world of appearances, which exists as a state of delusion consisting of the agitation of birth, old age, and death, and of pleasure and pain?"—thus he reflected within himself.
Even though he reflected upon it, he did not discover the cause of the world; then, on one occasion, he questioned Manu, who had come from the realm of Brahmā.
To the Blessed Prajāpati, who was seated in his own assembly and being honored, Ikṣvāku said: "O Blessed One, O treasure-house of compassion, you constrain me with boldness."
This very grace of yours enables me to ask you directly: from where has this creation come, and what is its essential nature?
How much is this world? To whom does it belong? When was it created? By whom? And how may I escape from this treacherous delusion of saṃsāra?
"May I be liberated from this dense thicket, like a bird from a net. Manu said: "Oh, how after a long time, through solitude, [the mind] has become fully blossomed!"
"You have asked an essential question that cuts through false and meaningless things: that whatever is seen here, O King, does not exist at all."
Just as a city of Gandharvas, or water in a desert, whatever is not seen is as if it does not exist at all.
That which transcends the six faculties with the mind as the sixth, which is indeed nothing whatsoever, yet is indestructible—this exists here and is called the True Self (Sadātman).
But this succession of creations, O King, rich with all that is visible, has attained its reflection in that very same great mirror.
Luminosities, arising from their own nature, are powers that cause the manifestation of Brahman; some attain the state of the cosmic egg, while others become living beings.

Others undergo change; thus does the stability of the world exist. There is no bondage, there is no liberation; only Brahman exists, free from ailment. There is neither unity nor duality; it is the essence of consciousness that unfolds.

Just as a single body of water manifests through the breaking of waves, so does consciousness manifest, yet it is nothing at all. Casting far away the conceptualization of bondage and liberation, remain established in yourself; you are the very essence of fearlessness, free from the fear of becoming and non-becoming.
Manu said: O King, when the consciousness of pure awareness becomes oriented toward volitional thought, living beings undergo transformation, just as water turns into waves.
Those living beings wander here in this cycle of existence that has arisen from before; the delusion regarding the states of pleasure and pain exists only in the mind, not in the Self.
Just as the invisible Rāhu is perceived by means of the eclipsed moon, so too is the self, whose nature is pure experience, beheld through the object of perception.
The Supreme Lord is not seen through scriptures nor even by a teacher; the Self is seen by the self alone, through one's own intellect established in purity.
Just as travelers are seen on the road by one who is free from passion and hatred, so too should one's own senses and their objects be viewed with such a mind.
One should not show disrespect toward these, nor should a virtuous person treat them with contempt; let them remain at their ease, occupied merely as objects of experience.
Having completely cast away from afar, by means of the intellect, all objective things such as the body and so forth, remain eternally absorbed in the Self with an utterly cooled inner heart.
The notion that "I am the body" is the bond of saṃsāra; indeed, this notion must never be accepted by those seeking liberation.
"I am of the nature of pure consciousness alone, consisting of nothing whatsoever, subtler than space"—this eternal realization is not a binder in saṃsāra.
Just as light exists everywhere within and without clear waters, so does the Self abide in all things.

Just as gold assumes the various forms of bracelets and other ornaments through its arrangement, so too does the Self assume the nature of the world and so forth, being both identical to and different from itself.
The waves of living beings, which are like the ripples upon the net of the world, flow into the terrifying great ocean of desire, which is overwhelmed by the submarine fire of destruction.
Nevertheless, O King, always contemplate yourself as the great Agastya, who is the one that drinks up the ocean of time which remains even now unfilled.
Having abandoned the notion of selfhood in this non-self—the web of visible objects such as the body and so forth—and having ascended to pure being, remain hidden and abide as you please.
Just as a mother weeps for her son, forgetting that he is sleeping within the hollow of her breast, so too does this person weep for their own sake.
Failing to realize that the self is undecaying and immortal, one weeps at the dissolution of the body, crying out: "Alas, I am slain! I am helpless! I am destroyed!"
Just as water appears in various forms through its own movement, so too does the Consciousness-Brahman expand by the power of volition.

Having established your mind—freed from the stain of volitional construction—within the Self, and being as if completely stilled, remain here as if without vibration even during movement; established in yourself, happy, govern this kingdom.

Manu said: The All-pervasive One himself sports like a child through the vibratory emanations that constitute creation; then, by means of the power consisting of withdrawal, he withdraws [all things] and abides within himself.
In such a way that he is bound, his own power arises within him; in such a way that he is liberated, his own power arises within him.
Just as there are rays from the moon, the sun, fire, heated iron, and gems; just as there are leaves and so forth from trees; and just as there are droplets from waterfalls.

In the same way, this world, consisting of the intellect and so forth, is imagined within the expansive Brahman; it brings suffering to those who do not know it, appearing as if it were something other than that very reality.
"Oh, how wonderful is this illusion, my dear, which deludes the whole world! For even though the Self is threaded through every limb, one does not perceive the Self."
He who remains with his desires stilled, contemplating that this entire world is composed of the mirror of consciousness, is happy, armored in Brahman.
One should meditate that everything is empty, without support, and of the nature of consciousness—a state free from the sense of "I" and devoid of the form of non-existence.
"This is pleasant, this is not"—this is the seed of your continuous stream of suffering. When that seed is consumed by the fire of equanimity, whence can there be any occasion for suffering?
O King, let the distinction between the pleasant and the unpleasant be swiftly cut away within yourself by your own extraordinary human effort, using the weapon of non-conceptualization.
Having cut down the forest of karma through cultivation by means of non-cultivation, and having attained supreme attenuation, remain indeed free from sorrow, O friend!

Having filled the expanse of the world, yet remaining beyond all divisions; with the manifestation of the appearance of mental constructs dissolved, he possesses the play of discernment; having attained the vibration of supreme bliss, he is for long free from ailment; his expansive enjoyment is pure, equanimous through tranquility, and his body is consciousness itself, fearless of worldly existence.

Manu said: One should first increase one's wisdom through the study of the scriptures and association with virtuous people; this is declared to be the first stage of yoga for the practitioner of yoga.

The second is investigation (vicāraṇā), the third is the contemplation of non-attachment (asaṅgabhāvanā), and the fourth is dissolution (vilāpanī), which consists in the dissolution of latent impressions (vāsanā).
The fifth state consists of the bliss of pure consciousness; here, the one liberated while living remains with the appearance of being half-asleep and half-awake.
And the sixth stage consists of self-awareness; it has the form of a single mass of bliss and is a state resembling deep sleep.
Then, with the fourth state stilled, there is liberation alone here; equanimity and clarity—this is the gentle seventh stage.
But the state that transcends the fourth (turyātītā), which is supreme and of the nature of nirvāṇa—that seventh, fully matured state, cannot be an object for those who still live.
In this context, the first three states are established as the waking state alone; the fourth is called dream, wherein the world indeed appears like a dream.
The fifth, called deep sleep (suṣupta), arises from the complete condensation of bliss; then the sixth, characterized by non-perception, is designated as the state of Turiya.
The seventh stage is the supreme state beyond the fourth (turyātīta); it is ungraspable by mind or speech, and its nature is the state of self-luminosity.
If the object of thought has not been clearly dissolved within by the power of withdrawal, there is no doubt that he is liberated through that great equanimity.
A person of such a mind—whether possessing a body or bodiless—becomes one whose full intellect has never before been touched by portions of pleasure or pain derived from worldly enjoyment.
I neither die nor do I live; I am neither existent nor non-existent. A man who dwells in the Self should remain thus; this is declared to be liberation.
Whether engaged in worldly affairs or tranquil, whether a householder or even a solitary mendicant, the living being does not grieve when it realizes, "I am nothing but consciousness."
Thinking, "I am untainted, ageless, free from passion, with tranquil latent impressions, stainless, and the very expanse of consciousness," one does not grieve.
Thinking, "I am devoid of end and beginning, pure, awakened, ageless, and immortal; I am peaceful, the manifestation of the equal and the unequal," one does not grieve.
Thinking that whatever exists on the tips of blades of grass, in the sky, in the sun, or among men, nagas, and gods is precisely that [same essence], one no longer grieves.
"My greatness as consciousness pervades horizontally, upwards, and downwards; knowing this of that which possesses infinite play, who indeed could be subject to decay?"
An object that is pursued with firmly established latent tendencies brings happiness; yet that very same thing which leads to happiness quickly turns into suffering through its destruction.

The inseparable connection between pleasure and pain is well known; for whatever object is pursued, whether it be one that leaves a subtle impression or one that leaves no impression at all, [it results in the other].
O sinless one, that action which is performed with a mind whose latent impressions have been exhausted brings no pleasure, nor does it cause suffering at the time of destruction.
Like a burnt seed, it no longer produces a sprout; yet, by means of the body, senses, and so forth—the multitude of instruments—it is conceptualized as action.
Who indeed, my dear, could possibly be a single agent and enjoyer, having arisen by completely casting off all mental constructions regarding all existing things?
Full and cool as the moon, it shines like the sun; the beauty of the cotton-wool of karma, when being performed, is already as good as done for the silk-cotton tree of the body.
Arising from the wind of knowledge, it flies off and goes somewhere; for every single faculty of a living being perishes through lack of practice.
This digit of knowledge, once born within, increases day by day by its own power, like rice sown in a fertile field.

The one Self, whose form is the universe, vibrates within all things, like pure water in lakes and oceans; O dear one, know that this entire world is but a single portion of existence, wherein the vast multitude of composite parts has been completely stilled.
Manu said: As long as there is a desire for the enjoyment of sense-objects, so long is the self called "jīva"; that desire, being produced by a lack of discernment, does not exist in reality.
When hope comes to an end through the power of discernment, then the self, having cast off the state of being a living soul, attains the state of Brahman, free from all affliction.
Moving for a long time from above to below and again from below to above, do not become a water-jar on the rope of anxiety for the waterwheel of saṃsāra.
Those fools who, out of delusion, cling to this dense illusion of worldly convention—the thought "this is mine" and "I am this"—go downward from the lower realms to even further below.
"‘This is mine,’ ‘I am this one,’ ‘That is he,’ ‘I am thus’—those by whom such delusion has indeed been abandoned through their intellect go higher and ever higher."
O King, resting without delay upon your own self-luminous Self, remain filling the entire space; behold the worlds!
As soon as the nature of consciousness is thus realized as all-pervasive, undivided, and awakened, at that very moment one has crossed over saṃsāra and attained the state of the Supreme Lord.
One should cultivate the realization: "Whatever Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and Varuṇa are prepared to do, I, whose body is consciousness (cidvapuḥ), perform all that."
Whatever is taught in whichever philosophical systems at whatever time, my dear, all of that is indeed true; for the play of consciousness is unrestrained.
By what can that supreme bliss be compared, which belongs to one who has become pure consciousness alone, who has crossed over death, and who is free from the mind?

Meditate upon the world as being neither non-empty nor empty, neither of the nature of insentience nor consisting of consciousness, neither of the nature of self nor of the nature of another. Be thus!
Having attained this true nature, primordial matter (prakṛti) comes to rest; there is no place called liberation, nor time, nor any other state.
Through the destruction of egoism and delusion, this nature known as "cultivation" dissolves; this indeed is liberation.

With the restlessness of investigating the meaning of the scriptures stilled, with the curiosity for various poetic sentiments and dramas ceased, and with the turbulence of all conceptual constructions entirely cast away, he remains at ease, equanimous, and established in his eternal nature.
Manu said: He who is clothed in whatever [garment], who is fed by whatever [food], and who sleeps wherever [he may be], shines like a sovereign emperor.
Abandoning the constraints of the scriptures regarding caste, duty, and the conduct of the stages of life, he emerges from the web of the world like a lion from its cage.
Transcending the domain of speech and abandoned by the state of longing for sense-objects, he attained an indescribable beauty, like the expanse of the sky in autumn.
Deep and serene like a great lake in the mountains, unagitated by the essence of supreme bliss, he rejoices in the Self by means of the Self.
Renouncing the fruits of all actions, eternally contented, and without dependence, he is stained neither by merit nor by sin, nor by anything else.
Just as a crystal is not stained by a reflection, so the knower of reality is not stained within by the fruit of karma.
While dwelling among the multitude of people, he experiences neither weariness nor joy from the cutting up or honoring of his body, as if these were reflections in a mirror.
He is beyond praise and free from change, devoid of both the worshiper and the object of worship; he is both united with and separated from all methods and sequences of conduct.
Therefore, the world does not tremble before him, nor does he tremble before the world; he is neither abandoned by passion, hatred, fear, and joy, nor is he joined with them.
A person of great noble intent does not take root in anything that can be made an object of cognition; yet one of pure intent can be made an object of cognition even by a child.
Let him cast off his body at a sacred ford or even in the house of an outcaste; let it never be otherwise, O King, whether it occurs at this very moment or at any other time.

At the moment of attaining knowledge, he is liberated and freed from all latent desires; for the delusion of "I" leads to bondage, while liberation is the destruction of that [delusion] through knowledge.
He is to be worshipped, he is to be praised, and he is to be reverently saluted; he is to be gazed upon and greeted by one who desires the fullness of prosperity.

O dear one, that supreme purity is not attained through sacrifices, sacred fords, austerities, or gifts; it is attained through devotion by the virtuous who know the Self and whose afflictions of worldly existence have been exhausted.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus, the blessed Manu went to the abode of Brahmā; Ikṣvāku also, having grasped that vision, became steadfast.

Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, such being the case for one who is liberated while living and possesses right-mindedness, what unprecedented excellence does he possess, O best among the knowers of the Self?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In some particular aspect alone does the intellect of the knower attain excellence; ever-contented and with a tranquil self, he abides in the Self alone.

By those perfected through mantras, perfected through asceticism, and perfected through tantras—in great numbers—such things as traveling through the sky have been accomplished; what novelty could there be in that?

Even powers such as *aṇimā* have been attained in great numbers by those very [yogis] because they were accomplished through effort; they are not attained by one who perceives the Self through other means.

This indeed is his distinction; he is not equal to those of deluded intellect. Because he has abandoned attachment everywhere, the mind of that one of great wisdom becomes free from passion and stainless; he does not sink into worldly objects.

This indeed is the sign of one who knows reality—the one whose form is beyond signs (aliṅga), who is stilled from the long wandering of saṃsāra, and who has attained liberation: that his passion, anger, dejection, delusion, greed, and misfortunes daily diminish with skillful precision.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as a Brahmin, by neglecting his own true nature through misguided effort, gradually accepts the state of a Śūdra, so too does the Lord assume the state of a living being.
At the time of re-absorption, beings indeed manifest in two ways; born from the primordial vibration, they are truly without cause.
O dear one, having departed from Īśvara, beings undergo further births and experiences solely through their own previously performed actions.
Such is this causal relationship between birth and action: all living beings arise from the Supreme State without any [other] cause.
Afterwards, it is their own actions that are the cause of pleasure and pain; the volition arising from self-knowledge is the cause of action.
For the state of conceptualization is indeed the cause of bondage; abandon that. Liberation, however, is the state of being free from conceptualization; therefore, be intent upon its practice.
Be vigilant regarding the delusion of the grasped and the grasper, gradually abandoning the states of conceptual construction at all times.
Do not become the nature of the grasped object, and do not become the nature of the grasping subject; having abandoned all mental cultivation, become one with that which remains.
O sinless one, whatever object the group of senses constantly falls upon, there it is bound by attachment; there, through detachment, it is liberated.
If something whatsoever is pleasing to you, you are bound to the state of existence; if nothing at all is pleasing to the mind, you are liberated from the state of existence.
Therefore, from this entire collection of objects, including both the stationary and the moving—from a blade of grass up to the bodies of the gods—may nothing at all please you.
Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give—therein you shall be neither agent nor enjoyer; thus one whose mind is liberated remains tranquil.
The virtuous do not grieve for the past, nor do they worry about the future; they attend to the present and perform the task at hand without interruption.
O Rāma, the states of being such as craving, delusion, and pride, which are knotted within the mind, must be severed by the mind itself by one who possesses discernment.
With the mind itself, as if with an exceedingly sharp iron blade, cut through the mind by means of discernment for the sake of pacifying all delusion.
Those skilled in cleansing wash away impurity with impurity itself; they ward off a weapon with a weapon and poison with poison.
The individual soul has three forms: the gross, the subtle, and the supreme. Among these, worship that which is its supreme form; abandon the other two.
This body, composed of hands and feet, which moves about for the sake of enjoyment—this gross form exists here for the purpose of the living being's experience.

Know, O Rāma, that the mind—which consists of forms created by one's own volitions and which persists as long as saṃsāra exists—is the subtle, transportive body (*ativāhika-rūpa*) of the individual soul (*jīva*).
Know that which is without beginning or end, the truth, pure consciousness, and free from conceptual construction—that is the supreme third form, the universal form.
This is the pure state of the Fourth; take your firm stand here. Completely abandoning the first two states, do not allow the notion of "self" to dwell there.

Śrī Rāma said: O leader of sages, please explain specifically and by distinguishing it, the fourth state (turya) which abides throughout the three states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, yet remains unperceived.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having abandoned both the sense of "I" and the sense of "not-I," as well as existence and non-existence, that which remains unattached, equanimous, and pure is called the Fourth (turya).

That state which is transparent, equanimous, and peaceful—the established condition of one liberated while living—is the state of the witness; in common usage, it is called the reckoning of the Fourth (turya).

This is neither waking nor dreaming, because of the impossibility of volitional constructions; nor is it the state of deep sleep, because of the absence [of that] and because of the persistence of insentience.
To those who are perfectly awakened, this world remains as it truly is—tranquil; yet to the unawakened, they say it is dissolved in the fourth state (turya), remaining fixed and stable.
When the fragment of egoism is abandoned, when equanimity arises, and when the mind is rendered dissolved, the fourth state (turya) manifests.
Now, O wise one, listen to this illustration being told by me, so that even though you are already awakened, you may attain further awakening.
Seeing a certain sage established in great silence within a certain expanse of the forest, the hunter asked him about this wonderful sight.
"O Sage, having arrived later, I saw a deer fleeing, pierced by an arrow; struck by my arrow, the deer has come here."
"Where has the deer gone? the sage replied to him: "O virtuous one, we forest-dwelling sages are of the same character."
"O friend, we possess no ego that is capable of engaging in worldly affairs; for it is the mind alone that performs all the functions of the senses."
Surely that sense of "I," composed of egoism, has long since dissolved within me; I no longer perceive any states whatsoever known as waking, dreaming, or deep sleep.
"Indeed, I abide only in the fourth state (turiya); therein, no object of perception exists. Having heard these words of the Lord of Sages, O Raghava, [Vasiṣṭha continued:]
The hunter, failing to understand his true interest, departed in the direction he desired; therefore I say, O mighty-armed one, that there is no state other than the fourth.
For the mind is indeed non-conceptual; that alone exists here and nothing else. The triad known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep is merely the form of the mind.
The self-mind abides here as terrible, peaceful, and deluded; the mind consisting of the waking state is terrible, while that consisting of the dream state is peaceful.

When the mind is deluded and situated in the state of deep sleep, devoid of the three qualities, it becomes as if dead; yet within that "dead" mind, the single essence (sattva) remains equanimous. Indeed, all yogis strive with effort to bring about that very state.
Free from the play of all mental constructs, remain in the fourth state as the stainless Self; therein abide forever liberated, the great sages who have stilled all distinctions.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The final conclusion of the spiritual scriptures is indeed the negation of everything; here there is neither ignorance nor illusion—this is the peaceful Brahman, beyond succession.
In the luminous consciousness alone—which is tranquil, transparent, the self of perfect equanimity, and inlaid with all powers—the name "Brahman" is conceptually imputed.
Having determined emptiness, some [determine] mere consciousness, and others the nature of God; thus they dispute with one another.
Having renounced everything, O sinless one, become a great silent sage—possessing nirvāṇa, free from mental fabrication, with the mind exhausted and the intellect perfectly stilled.
Abide in the Self alone with a tranquil mind, like one who is mute, blind, and deaf; remaining eternally inward-turned, let your intellect be completely filled within by the Self.
O Rāghava, while remaining awake, abide in the state of deep sleep; perform actions internally renouncing everything, yet externally act as things come to you.

The existence of the mind is supreme suffering; the non-existence of the mind is supreme happiness. Therefore, bring the mind—which is of the nature of pure consciousness—to its end through the absence of sensation.
Whether one sees what is pleasant or unpleasant, one should remain as steady as a stone; by this much effort of the self, the cycle of existence is conquered.
Neither pleasure, nor pain, nor that which is intermediate is to be experienced; by this much personal effort, the infinite end of suffering is attained.

Like the full moon within its orb, the knower of that [reality] attains happiness here and now through the glorious elixir; having realized the essence of all things in the three worlds, he performs no action whatsoever, even when approached by others.
Śrī Rāma said: How is the practice of the seven stages of yoga performed, and what are the signs for the yogi regarding each stage?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Man is of two kinds—the active and the withdrawn. Listen now to the characteristics of these two, who are oriented toward heaven and liberation respectively.
"How small indeed is that so-called nirvāṇa; for me, cyclic existence itself is better. He who acts with such a sense of duty is known as one who is engaged in worldly activity (pravṛtta).
Like the entry of a tortoise's neck through the hole of a yoke amidst the four oceans, at the end of many births, a man of discernment is born.
Alas, the condition of cyclic existence is indeed essence-less; enough of this for me! What is the use of stale karmas? My day is spent on those very things.
"What could be the supreme rest if it were devoid of the excellence of action?"—he who possesses such certainty within is known as "withdrawn" (nivṛtta).
"How may I, having become free from passion, cross the ocean of saṃsāra?"—when the one of noble intellect is thus intent on such reflection, [he attains liberation].
Day by day he attains detachment within his meditations; he proceeds with noble deeds and rejoices daily.
He constantly hesitates regarding vulgar and dull actions; he does not utter words that strike at the vital points, and he cultivates meritorious deeds.
He practices gentle deeds that do not disturb the mind; he constantly fears evil and does not look toward worldly enjoyment.
He addresses him with words that are tender with affection, charming, appropriate, and suited to the time and place.
Then he has attained the first stage; with mind, deed, and speech, he serves virtuous people.

Whosoever, having brought together treatises on knowledge from wherever they may be found, should possess such an inquiry directed toward crossing over the cycle of existence; [he shall attain liberation].
He is said to possess the stages; the remainder is known as "for one's own sake. He has reached another stage of yoga called "Investigation" (vicāra).
He honors eminent scholars who are renowned for their primary expertise in the study, retention, meditation, and performance of the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and the conduct of the virtuous.
One who knows the classification of categories and has mastered what is to be heard understands the determination of what ought and ought not to be done, just as a householder knows his own home.
Like a snake shedding its skin, he easily casts off even outwardly manifest pride, arrogance, envy, delusion, and excessive greed.
One whose mind is thus disposed attains, through service to the scriptures, the teacher, and virtuous people, the entirety of the secret doctrine exactly as it is.
Then that beloved one falls into the third stage of yoga, named Non-attachment, like [falling] onto a pure bed of flowers.
Having firmly established his mind upon the meaning of the scriptural words exactly as they are, he rested in the hermitages of ascetics through a succession of discourses on the inner self.
Likewise, by censuring cyclic existence and following the sequence of practices that produce dispassion, one who sits upon a stone bed wears away his extended lifespan.
Dwelling in the forest retreat, which is graced by the tranquility of the mind and characterized by the gentleness of unattached happiness, the wise man passes his time with propriety.
Through the study of excellent scriptures and the performance of meritorious deeds, a person’s perception of reality becomes clear exactly as it is.
Having attained the third stage, the wise one personally experiences a twofold non-attachment; hear now this distinction regarding it.
This non-attachment is twofold: the general and the supreme. [In this state, one realizes: "I am neither the doer nor the enjoyer; I am neither the oppressed nor the oppressor."
Thus, the non-attachment to objects, which is called "universal non-attachment," is entirely fashioned by prior karma and is dependent solely upon the Lord.
Whether it be happiness or suffering, what agency do I have here? Enjoyments and non-enjoyments are great diseases; prosperities are supreme calamities.
Unions lead only to separation; mental anxieties and physical ailments are the lot of the wise; and Time is ever intent on devouring all states of being without ceasing.
The internal non-contemplation of phenomena through non-reliance—that lack of attachment belonging to one whose mind is fixed upon the meaning of the sentence—is the universal [practice].
Through the yoga of manifold stages, through the union of great-souled ones, through the separation from the non-existent, and through the application of self-awareness;
Through human effort and the yoga of continuous practice, when the reality has become firmly manifest, like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand;
On the far shore of the ocean of saṃsāra, in the essence that is the supreme cause, I am neither the agent nor the Lord; action or its primordial material cause do not belong to me.
Having indeed cultivated the contemplation of the meaning of the word "certainly" at a great distance, that silent and peaceful sitting is called the highest non-attachment.
That which is neither within nor without, neither below nor above, neither in the directions nor in the sky; neither in an object nor in a non-object, neither in the insentient nor in the sentient.
Seated, luminous, peaceful, and beyond appearance, equal to the sky, without beginning or end, unborn, and beautiful—that is called the supreme non-attachment.
Sweet with the fragrance of contentment, possessing the stainless sprouts of virtuous deeds, it is nestled at the tip of the stalk of the mind, though beset by the thorns of obstacles.
The lotus of discernment, having taken root within and blossomed by the radiance of the sun of inquiry, bears fruit in this third stage, which is characterized by non-attachment.
Through the conjunction of pure qualities and the accumulation of meritorious deeds, the first stage arises by way of a chance occurrence, like the falling of a fruit upon a crow.
That ground, as soon as it has been raised by them like a sprout of nectar, must be protected and guarded with effort through the sprinkling of the water of discernment.
One should daily and with effort bring that very part which shines forth during investigation to its full development, just as a farmer tends to a sprout.
For this [second stage] is the sole ground for the cultivation of those whose inner [minds] have been polished; therefore, one should strive to reach the second stage, and from that, the third.
For this third stage here is indeed the most excellent when fully integrated; at this point, the person becomes one who has utterly abandoned all mental constructs and conceptualizations.
Śrī Rāma said: For one who is deluded, born of an ignoble family, engaged in base conduct, and who has not attained the company of yogis—how can there be a crossing over?
Whether it be the first, the second, the third, or the other [state], what kind of destiny awaits one who has died while having ascended [to these stages], O Blessed One?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For the deluded one who has not ascended [to wisdom], the cycle of worldly existence remains extended for as long as hundreds of future births, by the stroke of chance like the "crow and the palm fruit."
Alternatively, if detachment does not arise through association with the virtuous, then once detachment has arisen in a person, the emergence of the stages [of yoga] necessarily follows.
"Therefore, for the embodied being whose life has departed through the stages of yoga, cyclic existence is destroyed"—this is the summary of the meaning of the scriptures.
In accordance with the portions of the spiritual stages, one's prior misdeeds are exhausted; thereafter, one dwells in the celestial palaces of the gods and in the cities of the world-protectors.
He delights with his beloved in the groves and forest thickets of Mount Meru; thereafter, he experiences the consequences of the store of merit and the misdeeds committed in the past.
When their web of enjoyments is completely exhausted, yogins are born on earth in the secret homes of pure, prosperous, virtuous, and noble people.

Having been born, these beings, perfumed by yoga, devote themselves solely to yoga; there, the wise, recollecting the sequence of the stages of yoga practiced through prior cultivation, leap up to the higher sequence of stages.
O Rāma, these three stages are known as the waking state; this is perceived as the waking state because of the cognition of distinctions as they truly are.
In this regard, for those engaged in yoga, there arises solely that state of nobility which, upon seeing it, the desire for liberation arises even in those of deluded intellect.
He who performs what ought to be done, refrains from doing what ought not to be done, and abides by the conduct of the common folk—he is remembered as a noble one (ārya).
He who adopts worldly conduct according to custom, according to scripture, according to his own mind, and according to reality, is known as a noble one (ārya).
In the first [stage] it has sprouted; in the second it has blossomed; in the third, the state of nobility becomes the fruition for the yogin.
Having died while in a state of nobility, the yogi, having enjoyed for a long time the pleasures accumulated through pure intentions, is born again as one possessing yoga.
When ignorance has reached its end through the practice of the three stages, and right knowledge arises in the mind like the rising of the full moon;
Those yogis whose minds are disciplined and who have reached the fourth stage perceive everything as equal—undifferentiated and without beginning or end.
When non-duality has attained stability and duality has come to rest, those who have reached the fourth stage perceive worlds as if they were a dream.
The triad of stages is the waking state; the fourth is called dream. It dissolves away like the vanishing of fragments of autumn clouds.
Having reached the fifth stage, he remains as a mere residue of existence; having attained the fifth stage, which is named the state of deep sleep.
With all particular aspects stilled, he remains in non-duality alone; with the appearance of duality dissolved, the awakened one rejoices within.
Having reached the fifth stage, he remains as one solidified in deep sleep; though remaining inward-turned, he is nevertheless engaged with external activity.
Due to its state of complete tranquility, one who practices this stage appears as if constantly asleep; thus, one becomes free from latent mental impressions (*vāsana*).
He gradually ascends the sixth stage, known as the Fourth (Turyā), wherein there is neither non-existence nor the nature of existence, neither "I" nor even the absence of egoity.
With mere thought extinguished, he remains beyond both duality and unity; free from knots, with doubts stilled, he is liberated while living, devoid of mental constructs.
Though not in nirvāṇa, it remains as if in nirvāṇa like a painted lamp; empty within and empty without, it is void like a jar in the sky.
Full within and full without, like a full jar in the ocean; this has become something, yet indeed it is nothing at all.
Abiding on the sixth stage, he shall attain the seventh stage; indeed, the seventh stage of yoga is described as the state of disembodied liberation (videhamuktatā).
Inaccessible to words, that peaceful limit within the realms of existence is called "Śiva" by some and designated as "Brahman" by others.
By some it was conceived as the discernment between primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa); by others, in various other ways through diverse distinctions imagined regarding the self.
Although it is eternal and inexpressible, it is taught in some way; these seven stages have been described by me to you, O scion of Raghu.
Through the practice of these, no suffering is experienced; there exists one who is utterly intoxicated with joy, moving with gentle slowness.
