If that female elephant, intent on combat and displaying her great tusks, is indeed slain, she will surely cause endless misfortune.
Thus, while these stages are all complete, the man is victorious, so long as that female elephant, intoxicated with rut, has not been overcome by his splendor.
"Who indeed is that brave warrior in the fields of battle where prosperity abounds? Śrī Rāma said: "Who is this intoxicated female elephant, and what are those fields of battle?"

"How is this [desire] destroyed, and where does it find long-lasting delight? Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O Rāma, that which is called 'will' is like an elephant, whose form is the thought, 'May this be mine.'"
In the forest of the body, she is intoxicated, bringing about various delights; her fierce young elephants are the senses, and she speaks with the voice of a female elephant-calf.
Hidden within the thicket of the mind and equipped with the two tusks of karma, its rut is the mass of latent impressions (vāsanā), its body spreading everywhere.
O Rāma, the various views of cyclic existence are its battlefields, wherein a person repeatedly experiences victory and defeat.

This "desire-serpent" (icchānāgī) destroys the miserable multitudes of living beings; it consists of latent impressions (vāsanā), longing (īhā), mind (manas), consciousness (citta), volition (saṃkalpa), mental cultivation (bhāvanā), and yearning (spṛhā).
May this multitude of names, contained within the treasury of her heart, be effortlessly dispelled by the excellent weapon named Fortitude.
One should conquer with one's whole being this serpent-like desire that consists of all things, as long as it expands within [the mind] in the form "this is an object."
So fierce is the great cholera of the poison of saṃsāra; such is this saṃsāra as it is when the mind thinks, "Let this be."
The summary of this knowledge is that liberation is its very pacification; it is clear, producing serenity, free from desire, and pure in form.
The word of instruction comes to rest like a drop of oil upon a mirror; by the mere absence of perception, the sprout of desire for existence does not arise.
Desire, which brings about misfortune, must be severed even when it has only slightly arisen, by means of the weapon of non-perception, just like a row of poison-sprouts.
The living being, though pierced by desire, does not abandon its state of wretchedness; yet the effort of self-awareness remains silently seated within.
Like a hundred corpses sleeping, utterly devoid of attention, catch that fish of desire with the hook of sensory withdrawal.
The supreme ones say that the agitation of thinking "let this be mine" is conceptual construction; the non-contemplation of objects is called the relinquishment of conceptual construction.
Know that recollection is volition; the wise know that non-recollection is Śiva. In that state, both what was previously experienced and what was never experienced are contemplated.
Having forgotten both remembered and unremembered recollections like a piece of wood, and having quickly forgotten everything, remain hidden as one of great intelligence.
With arms upraised I cry out, yet no one hears me; non-attachment is the supreme good—why is it not cultivated within?
It is said, O Rāma, that by remaining in silence alone that supreme state is attained, wherein even sovereignty is regarded as a mere blade of grass.

Just as the movement of the feet of a traveler who is intent solely on the destination he must reach is free from volitional thought, so too is the movement in one's own actions when they are performed with such intent.
What is the use of saying much here? This is stated in brief: conceptualization is the supreme bondage; its absence is liberation.
Seeing all this as unborn, peaceful, infinite, eternal, and immutable—the true nature of reality whose form is consciousness—remain at peace and dwell as you please.
They know yoga to be non-perception, peaceful, seated, and inexhaustible; established in yoga, perform actions without latent impressions, or else do not perform them at all.
They know yoga to be the absence of feeling, the unconditioned cessation of the mind; having become entirely absorbed in that, O sir, remain as you are.

O Rāma, that which is auspicious, all-pervading, tranquil, consisting of the nature of awakening, unborn, and pure—the constant contemplation of that alone is known as "renunciation of everything. Contemplating this perpetually within yourself, perform your duties and actions.
One who perceives "I" and "mine" is not liberated from suffering; one who does not so perceive is liberated. Therefore, practice that which you desire.

Bharadvāja said: Having heard in its entirety this ancient essence of knowledge spoken by the supreme sage, that foremost of the illustrious Raghu dynasty—pure-minded, self-sufficient, filled with equanimity, and established in perfect enlightenment—asked something further.

He is indeed the supreme yogi, worshipped by the universe, the lord of the gods, free from birth and death, whose very nature is pure consciousness; he is the treasury of all virtues, the abode of Lakṣmī, and the sovereign master of the creation, preservation, and grace of the three worlds.
Śrī Vālmīki said: Having heard these words of Vasiṣṭha, which are a compendium of Vedānta, the lotus-eyed Rāma, who had mastered all branches of knowledge, [spoke].
By the power of the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*), the ocean of the bliss of consciousness, dense with pure awareness, was suddenly awakened and manifested its unfolding splendor for a moment.
Free from the formal sequence of questions and answers and so forth, his body was thrilled with horripilation as he was filled with the nectar of bliss.

Because it exists as the pervasive nature of consciousness and is the form of the great universal generality (mahāsāmānya), its desire for the eightfold sovereign powers is eternally regarded as being like a blade of grass.
Having attained and become established in the auspicious state, he said nothing at all. Bharadvāja said: "Oh, how truly wonderful it is that Rāma has reached the great state!"

O Leader of Sages, how can such an attainment be ours—fools, stubborn, knowing only a little like me, and sinful? Where are we, and where is the state of Rāma, which is sought after even by Brahmā and others and is so difficult to obtain?
"O Master, Lord of Sages, how may I find rest? Tell me quickly how that ocean of existence, so difficult to cross, may be traversed."

Śrī Vālmīki said: O Lord, having reflected with my intellect upon the entire account of Śrī Rāma as it has been set forth from the beginning in accordance with the words of Vasiṣṭha, consider it; I too shall relate such a narrative to you here.
This is the proliferation of ignorance; here not even an atom of reality exists. The wise discern this, while those lacking discernment engage in dispute.
There is nothing whatsoever separate from consciousness; why do you obstruct yourself with conceptual proliferation? O friend, become clear through the practice of the secret teachings.
The mental state whose object is conceptual proliferation is proclaimed as "sleep with dreaming"; but he is truly awakened within whom the stainless lamp of consciousness shines.
O friend, this conceptual proliferation has emptiness as its root and emptiness as its peak; because it is empty of essence even in the middle, the wise have no attachment to it.

Due to the defect of beginningless habitual tendencies, this cyclic existence—which is full of manifold delusions and has the appearance of a city of Gandharvas—is perceived as real, though it is actually non-existent.
Why do you become deluded by cultivating the poisonous creepers of latent tendencies, instead of practicing the auspicious kanda-plant of the nectar of consciousness?
While awake, this [mind] does not fall downward due to its grasping at the support of knowledge; nor are there any above all beings who possess consciousness free from support.
The great river of consciousness, whose essence is nectar, remains thus solidified until it is plunged into by the skillful in its true nature as the Self.
O friend, know that this entire world does not exist in the beginning, nor does it exist at the end; it does not exist even in the middle. This world is like the occurrence of a dream.
All these diverse manifestations, whose source is ignorance, arise for a moment like bubbles and then dissolve into the single ocean of knowledge.
Then, having recognized the river of very cool water and plunged into it, let those who have been tormented by the heat of external delusion emerge, their suffering allayed.
And there is one ocean of ignorance that remains, having flooded the world; this is the eldest wave, "I am," which arises from the wind of nescience (avidyā).
The waves of mental lapses and divisions, as well as passion and the like, are merely imagined; the whirlpool of the notion of "mine" proceeds of its own accord and at will.
Passion and hatred are the two over-graspers; once they have seized one immediately thereafter, who can prevent the entry into the abyss of misfortune?
Plunge into the ocean of pure nectar, where the waves are the tranquil nectar of immortality; why do you immerse yourself in the waves of the salt sea of dualistic grasping?
Who remains, or who has gone? Whose is what, and by whom has what been obtained? Why indeed do you sink into illusion? Do not fall; remain vigilant!
Since they declare this entire world to be the one reality, which is the Self, who else could there be beyond that, O dear one, that would be an object of your sorrows?
To the ignorant, this entire world is a transformation of Brahman; the wise, however, always abide in the untransformed bliss.
An undiscriminating person grieves and suddenly rejoices; but one who knows reality remains laughing, for him delusion is a mere mockery.
And this subtle reality is concealed by ignorance, just as people have doubts regarding dry land, water, and their own selves.
When this world, composed of the atoms of the great elements such as earth and the rest, remains [in its natural state], who is there that has departed from it here to be mourned?
There is no arising of the non-existent, nor is there the destruction of the existent, O friend; these are merely the manifestation and disappearance of various configurations.
However, because of the many efforts of the cities, it falls to the enemies; therefore, worship the Supreme Lord, the Teacher of the World, who possesses full abundance.
All his misdeeds have certainly not yet been fully ripened; the nooses of this god have merely become loosened.
Worship with form for as long as the mind is not yet serene; thereafter, one's abiding in the formless, supreme reality becomes uncontrived.
Having surely conquered this unrestrained darkness by means of the strength of your being, follow the path of Yama with a confident inner self.
Composing yourself for a moment, behold the inner self by means of the self; let this night of your former intellect clearly dawn as day.
That which is to be attained by men is obtained not merely through human effort and action alone, but solely through the grace of Maheśa.
Neither noble birth, nor character, nor policy, nor prowess—O friend, only ancient deeds alone are powerful.
Since there is no remedy for what is beyond reasoning, why do you despair in this way? Even the Lord cannot erase the line of letters inscribed upon the forehead.
Where is the speaker, where is his eloquence, and where is this creeper of delusion? If this destiny is inconceivable, how has this pair been brought together?
O Bhāradvāja, clearly abandon your delusion through discernment; now you will undoubtedly attain a knowledge that is extraordinary.
In times of great calamity, a king of great being exerts himself far beyond measure; for a person of small being grieves even when only slightly wounded.
Awakening, which depends upon merit, unfolds over many lifetimes; it may be inferred from its effects in the case of the steadfast who are liberated while living.
O son, by that very same action through which such bondage was incurred when it was hostile, you shall attain liberation when it has become friendly.
This surge of virtuous activity among the good, dispelling the ancient [evil], extinguished the forest fire of living beings like a torrential rain.
O friend, having renounced all actions, become a lover of Brahman, if you wish to bring to rest the whirling of the cycles of the wheel of saṃsāra.
This world arises from conceptual construction only so long as there is grasping at externality; it is like a turbulent ocean when agitated, but merely still water when the waves have subsided.
Why do you embrace this sorrow that causes blindness? Let that very same unbreakable staff of wisdom support you.
Those who are carried away by the waves of joy and sorrow like blades of grass are never counted among the most noble.
This world is mounted upon a swing of ten stages; it is made to play by six kinds of oscillations. O friend, why then do you grieve?
Time alone, full of curiosity, swiftly procreates, withdraws, creates again, and destroys the worlds through many cycles.
There is no perception of distinction whatsoever, nor is there any [particularity] among living beings who are like food; for the serpent of Time has already seized them all.
What need is there to speak of mere mortal bodies that exist for but a moment? Even those classes of gods are within the sphere of ill-timed death.
Why do you dance yourself in joy when your faculties are impaired by calamity? Sit motionless for a moment and behold the drama of saṃsāra.
O Bharadvāja, the wise person does not despond even slightly at this world, which consists of many waves and is subject to momentary destruction.
Abandon inauspicious grief and contemplate auspicious things; meditate upon the Self, which is pure and a mass of consciousness and bliss.
The grace of Maheśa shall befall those whose minds are made tender by the weight of faith in the gods, the twice-born, and the guru, and who take the true scriptures as their authority.
Bharadvāja said: Through your grace, all this has been understood by me in its entirety. There is no kinsman superior to dispassion, and no enemy greater than saṃsāra.
Now I wish to hear the essence of knowledge as it was set forth by Vasiṣṭha, explained in its entirety through the words of the text.
Śrī Vālmīki said: O Bharadvāja, listen to this great knowledge that bestows liberation, by the mere hearing of which you shall not sink into the ocean of worldly existence.
Salutations to Him whose form is Existence-Consciousness-Bliss, who, though being one, exists in manifold ways through the distinctions of dissolution, maintenance, and creation.
I shall explain to you, in brief, according to the teaching of the Vedas, the means by which reality shines forth once the phenomenal world has been dissolved.
How has your memory—which ought to investigate what precedes and follows—perished? By that very memory, everything is known by oneself as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand.

One must investigate this for oneself with one's own mind; that by which it is attained, one no longer grieves. This should be contemplated again and again by one endowed with detachment, through the company of the virtuous, the study of sacred scriptures, and discernment.

Śrī Vālmīki said: He was peaceful, self-controlled, and withdrawn from prohibited and desire-driven actions, as well as from the pleasure derived from the contact between the senses and their objects, and he was endowed with faith.
Seated on a soft seat, having mastered the activities of the mind and the senses, one should utter "Oṃ" until the mind becomes serene.
Then one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) for the purification of the internal organ; afterwards, one should gradually withdraw the senses from their objects.
Having known that from which the origin of the body, the senses, the mind, the intellect, and the knower of the field arises, one should subsequently dissolve them back into that.
Having first established himself in the Virāj, and thereafter in the Self within that, he subsequently abides in the Undifferentiated (avyākṛta), and finally rests in the Supreme Cause.
One should dissolve the earthly portion, such as flesh and so forth, into the earth; the watery portion, such as blood and so forth, into water; and the fiery portion into fire.

One should cast the element of air into the great wind and the element of space into the sky; having thus assigned earth and the other elements, one should then place the sense organs within their own sources.

One should assign the sense of hearing, endowed with its defining characteristics, to the directions for the sake of accomplishing the enjoyments of the agent; one should project the sense of touch into the lightning.
One should dissolve the eye into the orb of the sun, the tongue into the waters, the vital breath into the wind, speech into fire, and the hand into Indra.
Likewise, one should place one's feet in Viṣṇu, the anus in Mitra, and having placed the generative organ in Kaśyapa, one should fix the mind in the Moon.
One should restrain the intellect within Brahman; these deities of the organs are designated by the name of the senses.
Having recollected the words of the Vedas, one should not manifest [the self] by one's own power; thus, having deposited the self within the body, one should contemplate, "I am Virāj."
That Lord who resides within the cosmic egg as Ardhanārīśvara is declared to be the support of all beings and their ultimate cause.
That sacrifice, in the form of creation, is established in the functioning of the world; outside the egg, which is twice its size, is the earth, and the water is twice the size of the earth.
Fire is twice the extent of water; wind is twice the extent of fire; and space is twice the extent of wind—each increasing successively by double in this upward order.
The world is woven together by that which is both individual and collective, and all-pervading; having caused the earth to enter into water, one should cast the water into fire.
Having merged fire into air, one should cast air into space; and space into the Great Space, which is the cause of the origin of all things.

Having remained there for that moment, the yogi, bearing only a body consisting of the subtle linga, [abandons] the latent impressions (vāsanās), the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣmas), as well as karma and ignorance (avidyā).
The wise know this—the ten sense organs, the mind, and the intellect—to be the *liṅga*. Having emerged from that half-egg, one should contemplate there: "I am the Self."

This four-faced one is situated at the forefront, established within the subtle elements; the wise man, having placed the subtle *liṅga* in the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), should then place it in the unevolved (*avyakta*).
Some call that in which the world abides, being entirely free from name and form, "Prakṛti"; others call it "Māyā," while still others call it "atoms."
Others, whose minds are deluded by sophistry, declare it to be ignorance; having gone to dissolution therein, all remain in an unmanifest form.
Devoid of connection and devoid of relish, they arise again from that; for they remain in their own essential nature as long as creation proceeds.

Creation is traditionally taught as proceeding from the direct order, while dissolution proceeds from the reverse order; therefore, having abandoned these three states, one reaches the fourth, immutable state.

To attain that, one should meditate on the *liṅga* and, having dissolved it, enter the Supreme; [having dissolved] the elements, the senses, the mind, the intellect, the latent impressions, karma, and the vital breaths.
Bharadvāja said: "Ignorance and its foundations are the marks [of the unmanifest] when the unmanifest exists; since I am now in every way liberated from the fetters of those marks."
Having entered the ocean of consciousness and bliss because I am a portion of that consciousness, I am the Supreme Self, free from all limiting adjuncts, due to non-duality.

I am the immutable, absolute, all-pervading one, possessing the powers of both consciousness and the unconscious; just as when a jar is absent, there is no distinction between the space within the jar and the space within the pot.
Many scriptural revelations declare with such reverence that unity is exactly thus: just as fire cast into fire follows after it by virtue of its identity.
Having become that very thing and absorbed in it, one is not perceived as distinct; just as grass and other things thrown into *rumā* salt-earth become salt.
The insentient world, when placed within consciousness, becomes sentient, just as a lump of salt from the Sindh region dissolves into the ocean.
Released from name-and-form, it enters into the state of the ocean, just as water poured into water, milk into milk, or ghee into ghee.
These remain undestroyed and are not perceived as distinct; likewise, when consciousness is present, I have entered into all things through my entire being.
In that which is eternal bliss, all-knowing, supreme, and the ultimate cause; which is eternal, omnipresent, peaceful, faultless, and stainless.
I am that supreme Brahman—partless, actionless, pure, and higher than the highest; free from rejection and acceptance, the embodiment of truth, and beyond the senses.
I am the supreme, pure Brahman, whose resolve is solely truth; I am the cause of the universe, liberated from both merit and demerit.
I am the non-dual, supreme light, Brahman, the imperishable bliss; endowed with such qualities as these, yet devoid of the qualities of sattva and the rest.
One who performs their own duties should always meditate on the entire Brahman as having entered [into all things]. For a person practicing in this way, the mind indeed comes to rest therein.
When the mind has set, his own Self shines forth by itself; when there is this illumination, there is the destruction of all sufferings and bliss within the Self.
One realizes bliss as the Self by means of the Self itself; there is no other lord besides me who consists of consciousness and bliss.
"I alone am the Supreme Brahman"—thus the Self shines within. Śrī Vālmīki said: "O friend, having renounced all actions, become a lover of Brahman."
"If you do not desire the cessation of the wandering in the whirlpool of the wheel of saṃsāra," Bharadvāja said, "O Teacher, all this knowledge spoken by you has been understood by me."
The intellect has become pure and worldly existence no longer lingers; now I wish to know what kind of action is performed by the man of knowledge.

"O Lord, whether it be engaged in worldly activity or withdrawn from it, or whether something ought to be done or not—Śrī Vālmīki said: Therefore, that which incurs no fault when performed should be undertaken by those seeking liberation."
One should especially not perform optional or forbidden actions when the individual soul is endowed with the qualities of Brahman and has abandoned the qualities of the mind.

Then the entire collection of the senses becomes completely stilled, and he becomes the all-pervading Lord; he who is beyond the body, the senses, the mind, and the intellect, and who is higher than that which is high.
When one meditates thus: "I am that," then the individual soul (jīva) is liberated—freed from being an agent or an enjoyer, and divested of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
Then, liberated from pleasure and pain, one is fully released; one perceives the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self.
When one perceives [reality] without differentiation, then the individual soul (jīva) is liberated; this occurs when one has abandoned the three states known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
When the individual soul enters the fourth state of bliss, it is then liberated; this state of the soul within the Supreme Self is known as the Fourth (turiya).
This state, which is free from conditions, seeds, sleep, and the like, and whose nature is the bliss of consciousness—this is the culmination of yoga; it is great bliss and supreme awareness.
When the mind has set for men, nothing else is perceived, as they remain in the ocean of pure nectar, where the waves of nectar have become utterly tranquil.
Why do you wallow in intoxication amidst the waves of the salt ocean of dualistic grasping? Devote yourself instead to the Supreme Lord, the Teacher of the World, whose fullness is all-pervasive.
Thus, my son, I have described to you in its entirety the instruction of Vasiṣṭha, by means of this path of knowledge and the path of yoga.
O Bharadvāja of great wisdom, you will certainly come to know everything through your mastery of the scriptures and by understanding the meaning of the teacher's words.
"Through practice, all perfection is attained; such is the instruction of the Vedas. Therefore, casting aside everything else, make your mind steady in practice."
Bharadvāja said: "O Sage, Rāma has attained supreme yoga within his own self by means of the Self; how was he then made by the divine Vasiṣṭha to be intent upon worldly affairs?"
Having understood this, I shall likewise strive for the sake of practice, so that my conduct during the state of emergence will be exactly the same.
Śrī Vālmīki said: When the noble-minded Viśvāmitra had become fully matured in his own true nature, he then spoke to Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages.
Viśvāmitra said: "O Vasiṣṭha, O highly fortunate son of Brahmā, you are great! Your status as my guru was revealed to me in that very instant by the descent of your power."
He who, through sight, touch, or sound, or out of compassion, generates the Śāmbhava immersion within the body of a disciple—he indeed is the true teacher.
This Rāma, too, being pure in soul and detached through his very self, desiring only the cessation of delusion, attained the supreme state through this dialogue.
The disciple's own wisdom alone is the cause of awakening through the words of the guru; if the three impurities are unripened, how can one awaken as if they were ripened?
This knowledge is indeed direct perception, serving the purpose of both teacher and disciple, since both are qualified for all such [teachings].
Now, out of compassion, you ought to bring about Rāma’s restoration; for you have reached the pinnacle of maturity, whereas we are still occupied with our duties.
"O Lord, remember my task for the sake of which I have come, and recall how King Daśaratha himself was entreated by me with great difficulty."
O Sage, do not let all this be in vain; perform the work of the gods with a pure mind, for it is the purpose of our descent.
I have led Rāma, the crusher of Rākṣasas, to Siddhāśrama; from there he will perform the liberation of Ahalyā and [marry] the daughter of Janaka.
Having resolved to marry her by breaking the bow, he will surely restore the lost status of Rāma, the son of Jamadagni.
Free from fear and devoid of desire, he entered the ancestral kingdom of his father and grandfather under the pretext of dwelling in the forest, residing here in the Daṇḍaka wilderness.
Under the pretext of the calamity caused by the abduction of Sītā, he will indeed uplift various living beings and the sacred fords on earth from their state of lamentation.
Through the slaying of Rāvaṇa and others, he will demonstrate to all the lack of composure among those attached to women, as well as the transformation of the monkeys and their ilk.
Seeking Sītā’s purification and seeking the approval of the world, he remained devoted to the path of ritual action, though liberated while living and free from desire.
The union of knowledge and action will reveal the destiny for those by whom it has been seen, or even remembered, or heard, or awakened to.
"It will indeed bestow liberation while living upon those in all states; for it is the task of the three worlds and of me as well, in its entirety."
Homage to this high-souled man, Rāmacandra; by him all has already been conquered. May such a person as he prosper for a long time!
Śrī Vālmīki said: Having heard these words spoken by Viśvāmitra, all those perfected ones (siddhas) and lords of great yogis, headed by Vasiṣṭha, spoke again.
They remained intent on respectfully remembering the dust of Rāma’s lotus feet, while listening from afar to the accounts of the Lord of Maithilī.
The Blessed Vasiṣṭha and the other great sages were not fully satisfied, even as they spoke of and listened to the qualities of that treasure-house of virtues which they had heard.
The venerable sage Vasiṣṭha said to the sage Viśvāmitra: "O sage Viśvāmitra, tell me, who was this lotus-eyed Rāma? Was he a wise being, or was he a human, a descendant of Raghu?"
Viśvāmitra said: "In this very matter, place your trust; for he is that Supreme Person, who churned the ocean for the sake of the universe and whose domain is the profound scriptures."
Rāma is the embodiment of perfect supreme bliss, equanimous, marked with the Śrīvatsa, the bestower upon all living beings, and exceedingly gracious.
When enraged, he slays; he creates those who are unrighteous; he is the origin of the universe, the progenitor of all beings, the Ordainer, the Sustainer, and the Great Friend.
This vast ocean of bliss is plunged into by those free from passion, who have transcended the deceptive and hollow world of saṃsāra with its subtle wiles.

In one place this person (puruṣa) is like a liberated soul abiding in himself; in another, he is designated as the fourth state (turya); in another, his nature is projected outward; and in another, he remains established within that very nature.
This divine being, composed of the three Vedas and transcending the thicket of the three qualities (guṇas), this wonderful Puruṣa whose self is the Veda, triumphs with his six limbs.
This one with four arms is the creator of the universe, the four-faced Brahmā; this very one is Mahādeva, the three-eyed destroyer.
This unborn one is born through yoga; ever-awake and great, the Blessed One, though formless, sustains this universe by assuming manifold forms.
Just as victory is borne by prowess, light by radiance, and the excellence of wisdom by sacred learning, so is this man carried away by Suparṇa.
Fortunate is this Daśaratha, whose son is the Supreme Person; fortunate too is that Ten-necked one (Rāvaṇa), who is even now being contemplated by his mind.
"Alas! Heaven is now empty because of him; alas! Having come here from Pātāla, by his arrival this middle world has attained excellence."
This Person who lies within the ocean has descended as Rāma; this Rāma is the immutable Supreme Self, a mass of consciousness and bliss.
Yogis who have restrained the collection of their senses know Rāma; we, however, are only capable of perceiving his inferior form.
"We have heard that the Blessed One is the one who brings about the destruction of Rāghava's enemies; therefore, O Vasiṣṭha, out of compassion, please cause him to engage in worldly affairs."
Śrī Vālmīki said: Having spoken thus, the great sage Viśvāmitra remained silent; but the highly effulgent Vasiṣṭha addressed Rāmacandra.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one, O Great Being composed of consciousness! This is indeed not the time for rest; become the bringer of joy to the worlds.
As long as the conceptual investigation of the world has not ceased for the yogin, so long will his state of firmly established samādhi never become stainless.
Therefore, O son, having observed that objects such as kingship are perishable, and having taken up the burdens of divine duties and the like, be happy.
Śrī Vālmīki said: Even though he was addressed in this manner, when Rāma did not say anything at all, having entered into dissolution, then he too slowly entered the heart by way of the Suṣumṇā.

The individual soul (*jīva*), whose instruments are engaged with power, vital breath, and mind, and who consists of light, having fully nourished all his faculties through the channels of the *nāḍīs*, slowly opened his eyes; seeing the eminent sages headed by Vasiṣṭha, he remained waiting for them all, free from all desires and devoid of deliberations regarding what ought or ought not to be done.
Having heard the words of Vasiṣṭha as the instruction of his guru, and having heard them himself, the blessed Rāmacandra spoke with a composed mind.
Śrī Rāma said: By your grace, he is no longer subject to injunctions or prohibitions; nevertheless, your word must indeed always be carried out.
O great sage, in the Vedas, Āgamas, Purāṇas, and even in the Smṛtis, it is declared that the word of the Guru is the injunction, and its opposite is the prohibition.
Having spoken thus, that soul of all beings, a treasury of compassion, placed his head upon the feet of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha and addressed them all.
Śrī Rāma said: Listen all, may it be well with you; this is my firm and well-ascertained conclusion: there is nothing superior to self-knowledge, nor even to the Guru who knows that.
The Siddhas and others said: "O Rāma, it is exactly thus that [this truth] has taken its place in the minds of all; and by your grace, everything has been made firm through this correspondence."
"Be happy, O Great King Rāmacandra; salutations be unto you! Having been permitted by Vasiṣṭha as well, we shall now depart as we came."
Śrī Vālmīki said: Having spoken thus, they all departed, intent on praising Rāma; indeed, a rain of flowers fell upon the head of Rāmacandra.
All this narrative of Rāmacandra has been told to you; by means of this sequential practice, O Bharadvāja, may you be happy.

Thus has this accomplishment of the Lord of the Raghus been proclaimed by me to you, variegated like a jeweled necklace strung with the words of the excellent sages; it is a form to be served by the entire assembly of poets and yogis, and through the grace of the Supreme Guru, it bestows the path to liberation.
Whoever should constantly hear this account of the ritual between Rāma and Vasiṣṭha, even in any state whatsoever, is liberated through hearing it and goes to Brahman.

Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahman, through dispassion and the abandonment of mental constructs, the body of the embodied one falls away. How is it possible for this to happen quickly while one is still alive?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The abandonment of mental constructs is possible for one who is living, but not for one who is dead. Listen to its true nature, which is an ornament to the ears.

Those who know conceptualization say that the very cultivation of the sense of "I" is conceptualization; the cultivation of the space-like nature of objects is called the relinquishment of volitional construction.

Those who know conceptualization say that conceptualization is indeed the savoring of the objects of perception; the cultivation of the space-like nature of those objects is called the relinquishing of volitional construction.
The supreme ones say that the conceptualization "this is an object" is agitation; the cultivation of the space-like nature of objects is called the relinquishing of conceptual construction.

Know that recollection is volition; the wise know the absence of recollection to be Śiva. That which is thus contemplated may have been experienced previously, or it may not have been experienced at all.
Having forgotten all memory—whether experienced or not—as if you were a piece of wood, and having quickly forgotten everything, remain hidden, O Mahāmati.
Abide with a nature consisting solely of the non-recollection of all past actions, like the movement of a half-asleep infant toward activities that have become habitual.
Just as the wheel revolves by a flow free from volition, so too does it move through its own actions and its own karma by the power of prior, faultless impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Being devoid of a [substantial] mind, you have entered into the conditioned formations of sentient beings; therefore, move only within your own activities as they fall into the stream of continuity.
With arms raised, I cry out, yet no one listens to me; freedom from volitional thought is the supreme good—why is it not cultivated within?
Oh, the greatness of delusion! That this wish-fulfilling gem called "discernment," which destroys all suffering, is abandoned by people even though it resides within their own hearts.
Without sensation and without volition, become one with that very state; this much is the supreme good—let it be experienced by yourself alone.
It is said, O Rāma, that by remaining in silence alone that supreme state is attained, wherein even sovereignty is regarded as a mere blade of grass.
Just as the movement of the feet of a traveler who is focused solely on his destination is free from volition, so too should you move in your actions.
Having forgotten the stain of striving for the fruits of all actions, move without sensation in whatever task falls upon you like a flowing stream, as if asleep.

Letting go of unformed volitions through the vibration [of awareness], and not dwelling upon pleasure or pain, one remains like a blade of grass released from effort when caught in the current of necessary action.
Let the cultivation of aesthetic flavor (rasa) remain within you during your activities, like that of a wooden mechanical doll performing for the sake of others.
May all perceptions of your sense organs be utterly sapless, like creepers in the winter season, discernible only by their bare outlines.

Moving by means of the essence of the yellow Bodhārka-plant, which possesses the power of the six groups [of enemies], remain like the vibration of a machine, as a tree remains with its creeper in the winter.
By your own effort, quickly restrain the senses—even when they are active—so that they hold only the internal essence of consciousness, just as trees do during the winter season.
Whether you engage or do not engage the functions of the senses with passion, this caravan of worldly misfortunes will never subside.
If you vibrate like the movement of water in a machine or the flame of a windless lamp—free from conceptual construction—then you are fashioned for infinite well-being.
This alone is the supreme fortitude that wards off the fever of birth: the practice of agency in one's own actions without latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Free from latent impressions and free from volitional constructions, following whatever arises as it occurs, move gradually through your activities like the whirling motion of a potter’s wheel.
Let there be no thought of the fruit of action, nor let there be attachment to inaction; either abandon both of these, or take refuge in both.
What is the use of saying much here? This is stated in brief: conceptualization is the bondage of the mind; its absence is liberation.
Here there is nothing whatsoever that is to be done or not to be done, nor anywhere at all; everything is Śiva—unborn, peaceful, and infinite—so remain as you were before.
Perceiving inaction within action and action within inaction, you whose nature is consciousness perceiving reality as it is, remain at peace and as you please.
They know yoga to be the absence of sensation, the unconditioned cessation of the mind; having become entirely absorbed in that, O sir, remain just as you are.
In that which is equal, peaceful, auspicious, subtle, devoid of both duality and unity, pervasive, infinite, supreme, and pure—what indeed is distressed by what?
Let no volitional resolve arise within you, like a sprout in a desert; let no desire arise in you, like a creeper in the heart of a stone.
For one who is without sensation and at peace—whether living or even dead—there is no purpose whatsoever here in what is done, nor any at all in what is left undone.
That which is action and non-action within the peaceful, eternal, and undifferentiated form—therein, there is no action in actions, nor is there agency even in the agent.
Perceiving "I" and "mine," you are not liberated from suffering; by not perceiving them, you are liberated. Therefore, practice that which you desire.
"I" and "mine" do not exist; that which exists is the supreme Śiva. Yet this is even higher than the highest Śiva—the ineffable, whose nature is pure meaning.

Whatever is seen here in this world does not truly exist; it appears like the state of being a bracelet in gold. They know that its destruction is simply non-perception; thereafter, that alone remains—the Truth, the ultimate reality.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Non-dual unity, free from mental constructs, peaceful, and established within the Self—just as an army might be composed of mud, so too is the world composed of Śiva.
And that very mind—consisting of the intellect, ego, and so forth—is composed of that [consciousness], joined with the arrangement of time, form, action, sound, and power.
The sequences of form, perception, and mind consist of nothing but the mud of Śiva; because they are identical with Him and because He is infinite, what is perceived by whom?

The subject, the object, the means of knowledge, and so forth; space and time, the directions and the like; existence, non-existence, transformation, and so on—all of which consist of the essence of Śiva and Prakṛti (the primordial matter).
Therefore, since there is no essence other than the Supreme Lord apart from "I" and "mine," remain with an unattached mind, like the silence within a stone.
Śrī Rāma said: O Lord, for the wise man who does not contemplate the unreal nature of "I" and "mine," what is auspicious—through the abandonment of inauspicious actions or through their performance?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O sinless one, tell me quickly that reality which I ask about; if you know it in truth, what then is called "karma"?
What is the extent of karma, what is its root, and how is it to be destroyed? Tell me skillfully how it is brought to an end.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, that which is to be destroyed is surely destroyed by skillful means at its very root; it is not [destroyed] by the lopping off of branches and the like."
Indeed, a wise person should destroy their own good and evil karma; by grinding away its very root, that karma is thoroughly destroyed.
O Brahmin, I shall describe the roots of the tree of karma; listen to me, for by the rubbing away of which it becomes rootless and does not sprout again.
O Brahmin, this body has indeed arisen as a tree of karma; it has grown in the forest of saṃsāra, adorned with the various creepers of its limbs.
Karma is the seed of this tree, which bears a succession of fruits of pleasure and pain; it is lovely with the youthfulness of a moment, yet it laughs with the flowers of old age.
Every moment, his form was being destroyed by the fierce monkeys of Time, while from within the interior of the winter sleep he had entered, the petals of dreams were emerging.
Of the world-born wilderness, whose succession of leaves—desires—is withered by the autumnal peace of one's own old age, and whose grassy undergrowth is its family;
The parts of the sprouts, such as the palms, backs of the hands, and so forth, are reddish; the leaves are thin, rounded, well-lined with veins, and tremulous.
The fingers, reddish, stirred by the wind, soft, and smooth in form, with their tendons and bones visible and moist, are like young sprouts.
The rows of nail-tips are soft, smooth, with sharp points, rounded, and repeatedly grown; they have the form of the crescent of the second moon.
For it is said that when karma has fully blossomed, it takes the form of the body; thus, the organs of action are its roots—corrupt and knotted.
Bound together by firm joints and ligaments, their very selves are submerged in mud; they are soaked with the essence of latent impressions and possess their own vital fluids as blood.
Know that their roots—the organs of perception—are likewise possessed of joints, firm-limbed, well-sheathed, and smooth.
Even though they have arisen far away, those five pillars are steeped in the mud of latent impressions (vāsanā); they are flavorful and great.
Their root is the vast pillar of the mind, which pervades the three worlds; it is drawn by the five streams and releases the infinite fluid of existence.

They know its root to be the living being (jīva), whose nature is consciousness directed toward objects of thought; the conscious awareness of the object of thought is the root of all, the single cause of every root.
The root of consciousness is Brahman, which has no root; for it is ineffable, infinite, pure, and of the nature of truth.
For all actions, such perception is the supreme seed; having internally willed their own form, from that, vibration proceeds.
O Sage, consciousness alone is said to be the primordial seed of karmas; when that exists, the śālmali tree of the body arises with its great branches.
If this [state] is permeated by the cultivation of the meaning of the word "consciousness," then that action attains the state of a seed; if not, it is the supreme reality.

If consciousness (citi) is enveloped by the latent impression (bhāvanā) of the meaning of the word "consciousness," then it becomes the seed of that karma; if not, it is the primordial, supreme state.
Therefore, in this world, it is feeling alone that is the cause of the form of action; as for what has been declared regarding actions, O Lord of Sages, that was spoken by you yourself.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, for this subtle action which consists of perception, what abandonment can there be, and what performance [of rites] is possible, as long as it remains bound to the body?
Whatever is conceived, by that it immediately comes to exist both externally and internally; whether its form be real or unreal, it becomes so through the imposition of delusion.
If it is not perceived, then enough of this delusion; one is liberated from it. Whether the delusion be real or unreal, what is the use of this inquiry?
This very consciousness unfolds within itself through the delusions of its own arising, under names such as latent impressions, desire, mind, action, and volition.
Whether for the awakened or the unawakened embodied being, within the house of the body, the mind exists as long as there is a body; its abandonment is not possible.

How indeed could the abandonment of those who are living be possible, except when there is the cultivation or non-cultivation of the mental impression (bhāvanā) regarding the meaning of the word "karma"?
Having abandoned both action and inaction, one becomes unborn by oneself; for he who performs action while having truly renounced it is indeed unborn.
This renunciation of duty was not accomplished by him through any external effort; rather, it occurred because this sense of "this-ness" dissolved of its own accord through awakening.

They know that renunciation of the world is non-attachment and is indeed liberation; and perception exists only when there is an object to be perceived, as the vision of the object occurs at the very beginning of creation.

That which has not arisen does not exist at all; therefore, what is there to be felt, and where? Indeed, that which is the very form of sensation consists in its being directed toward the object of feeling.
Neither sensation nor that action is [real]; that which is peaceful is called Brahman. Volition is said to be action, which expands like a cloud within the cycle of transmigration.
They know liberation to be insentient; the teaching is addressed only to the knower. Therefore, the renunciation of actions is not possible as long as the body exists.
Those by whom action is fully honored are not liberated from its root; for the root of one's own action is consciousness, which consists of the mind and its latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
And that [avidyā], O Rāma, cannot be utterly eradicated until enlightenment; it is merely supreme, having its root in karma within the internal mind.

By means of the non-perception of subtle consciousness, it is cut away through one's own effort; that by which consciousness is investigated through the non-perception [of itself] by one's own effort.
By that, the scraping away of the root of the tree of cyclic existence is carried out.
Inconscient space is non-dual, one, and thus exists as this very thing devoid of objects; since it is of the nature of the void, they say that this alone is the stainless essence of consciousness.
Śrī Rāma said: O Lord of Sages, how can the non-perception of perception be brought about? For there is no coming into being of the non-existent, nor is there the cessation of the existent.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The non-existent has no being, and the existent has no non-being; when this is understood, then the perception and non-perception of [reality] becomes easy for oneself.
Know that these two—the word "feeling" and its referent—are unreal, like the delusion of a snake in a rope, arisen and equal to the water of a mirage.
Non-understanding of these two is better; understanding of them leads to suffering. Therefore, O Raghava, understand only what is real; do not understand what is unreal.

For a living being, the understanding of the meaning of words regarding sensations causes supreme suffering; having set aside the understanding of the meaning of words regarding cognition, remain as you truly are.
At this moment of universal awakening, regarding both the word and its meaning, let there be the utterance "Om," the supreme arising of Nirvana; thus, be stilled.

One who possesses discernment must destroy their own karma, consisting of both the auspicious and the inauspicious; this is accomplished through the knowledge of reality, which realizes that such [karmic bondage] does not exist.
Through the grinding away of the root of karma, cyclic existence is stilled; when karma is thoroughly investigated and sought out, it is no longer found.

When that which is of the nature of consciousness, situated within the core of the wood-apple, applies the designation "mind" to itself, it does not differ from the wood-apple even in the slightest degree.
Just as one configuration is not separate from within another configuration, so too space, objects, and the like are not separate from the Supreme in the slightest degree.
Just as water itself possesses internal fluidity and is not separate from it, so too is consciousness itself consciousness, because the objects of that consciousness are of the same nature as it.
Just as liquidity exists in water and light in fire, so too does consciousness exist within Brahman, though it is not its inherent nature, and consciousness exists within the mind.
Volitional action is like a phantom that causes internal delusion; it arises without a cause, for if it has not arisen, it does not exist.
Volitional action appears like the vibration of the wind; when this self is without cause, it is the meaningful consciousness both within and without.
The body is the expansion of karmas; it consists of the ego and is characterized by worldly transmigration. Through the absence of ego, it becomes insentient and subsides like a windless breeze.

Having become infinite in soul through the absence of consciousness, though you are a knower, remain like a stone; like the tip of the snout of a wild boar, perform the weeding of the root of saṃsāra.
In this way, the abandonment of the sheath of the subtle essence of the seeds of karma is accomplished; not otherwise, O Raghava. May there be eternal peace, forever established.
But when this minute portion of the seed of karma has been abandoned in the other self, which does not exist for the living being, [that state] is known by those who have realized the reality.
Nothing is grasped by those who are peaceful, nor is anything abandoned; because they understand through neither relinquishing nor acquiring, their minds are thus at peace.
The wise, whose hearts are as empty as space, abide in things exactly as they are; they act according to what arises, yet even that which is done by them is not truly performed by them.
Everything occurring within the flow vibrates even for one whose mind is peaceful; thus their organs of action are like those of a child who is half-asleep.
When the flavorless state is attained, even flavors become utterly flavorless; they abide neither within nor without, like those who are skilled in ignorance.

The experience of karma is its relinquishment, and that is accomplished through awakening; since it is not a real entity, there is no purpose served by either what has been done or what has not been done.
That which is without sensation, beyond being sensed, free from latent impressions, abiding in stillness, equanimity, and non-conceptualization—that is called the renunciation of karma.
That action which is completely forgotten after a long time, such that it is no longer remembered, remains like the interior of a pillar; that is called the renunciation of karma.
For those of futile understanding who regard non-renunciation as renunciation, that demoness of the abandonment of action devours them like ignorant beasts.

For those who have attained peace through the complete renunciation of actions along with their roots, there is no purpose whatsoever here in this world in what is done, nor any in what is left undone.
Having completely uprooted even the subtlest portion of the seed of karma, those who know that remain in eternal, one-pointed concentration; therefore, they abide in bliss.
When an action occurs as part of the natural flow, they move with slight effort, are not absorbed in it, and are like those reeling from intoxication or like those set in motion by a machine.
As if afflicted by a passion for the playful Goddess of Liberation, they arrived at some unknown land, appearing like those half-asleep and half-awake.
That which is abandoned along with its root is said to be truly abandoned; an abandonment that scrapes away only the rootless [trunk] is like the mere lopping off of branches.
The tree of karma, whose roots and branch-tips have not been uprooted or lopped off, grows again with a thousand branches for the sake of suffering.

O dear one, the renunciation of karma is accomplished through that which is of the nature of non-feeling; it is not achieved by any other means. Therefore, do not grasp at this very [feeling], for that leads to existence.
But those who, without thus renouncing action, perform something else, kill the sky—the very self of renunciation—which is characterized by non-renunciation.
Through the nature of awakening, the renunciation of action occurs spontaneously; like a burnt seed, the highest desirelessness results in action that is truly non-action.

Action performed with the sense organs, when imbued with the contemplation of the essential flavor, bears fruit; it should be undertaken like a well-fastened rope. Any other movement born of the limbs is fruitless.

Established in the renunciation of karma through awakening, liberated while living and free from latent impressions, he may dwell at home or in the forest; let him remain in tranquility or let him encounter rising activity.
For one who is tranquil, even his own home is a secluded place far from the forest; for one who is not tranquil, even the forests are crowded, and a city is as solitary as a wilderness.
For the wise one whose mind is utterly tranquil, the forest ground—untrodden by men, stainless, vast, and heart-pleasing—is as if within his own heart, even in a dream.

For the wise one, for whom the visible world has attained nirvāṇa, the great forest that is the universe consists of the motionless reality, composed of space, wherein all particularities have been stilled.
For the ignorant man who possesses infinite volitions and whose heart contains the entire world, the whole ocean of the earth revolves within his very heart.
For the ignorant and wretched person, the multitude of villages—with its various conflicts and hardships, its active pursuits, and its diverse forms—dwells as if within the heart.

The earth—consisting of various states of activity and transformation, along with its cities, towns, districts, and mountains—is reflected within the heart, just as it is in a mirror-case; thus, though the earth itself is impure, it becomes pure within the heart.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the world, beginning with the sense of "I-ness," has ceased within the awakened state that is the essence of the power of consciousness, renunciation is perfected—resembling a lamp that has gone out; it is not otherwise.
Renunciation is not the abandonment of action; renunciation is known as awakening. It is the undecaying self whose nature is solely the non-appearance of the world, free from egoism and the like.
When supreme nirvana has been attained, like an oil-less lamp, the notions of "this is I," "this is he," and "this is mine" cease; only the self of pure awakening remains.
For one who does not possess the knowledge that "this is he," "I am this," and "this belongs to me"—who has no such [identification]—there is neither peace, nor renunciation, nor liberation.

When the dissolution of "this is mine," "this is this," and "I am this" occurs to such an extent, that which is the nature of awakening—auspicious and profoundly peaceful—is found; nothing else exists beyond it.
When the portion of "I" has been dissolved, everything has indeed gone to destruction; yet nothing whatsoever has perished anywhere, for one remains as a single, solid mass of nirvāṇa.
Simply by realizing "I am not," one becomes tranquil without obstacle; since this [liberation] is accomplished by this much alone, why is there such torment?
The delusion of "I" and "not-I" does not exist apart from consciousness; and since consciousness is as pure as space, where then can this state of delusion reside?
There is no delusion, nor wandering, nor indeed error, nor is there a deluder; this is merely non-seeing, for through seeing, this [delusion] does not exist for you.
Know that this entire expanse, which resembles the nature of the unreal, is indeed nothing but pure consciousness; therefore, enough—remain in silence, for all this is nothing but nirvana.
In the very same instant that one perceives "I am," by perceiving in that very same instant "I am not," one does not grieve.
Abiding firmly in that state, remain with the sense of "I-ness" (ahaṃbhāva) dissolved like an arrow shot into the sky, either continuously, swiftly, or until it is exhausted.
O you who perceive the supreme goal in this way without ceasing, remain unattached to all states of being, having crossed over the ocean of existence.
If one lacks the heroism to conquer even one's own inherent nature, tell me, what talk can there be of that beast attaining the supreme state?
He by whom the sixfold group has been previously conquered through his own superior knowledge is a vessel for great purposes; no other is anything but a human donkey.
He whose internal mental activity is being conquered or has already been conquered is the object of the discerning; he is called a true man.
Whatever object falls upon you, like a stone into the ocean, flee from that very thing, contemplating only: "I am not this."

Even though you have understood that "I am not," and even though you sufficiently know—along with its logical justification—that it is merely a mental representation, why do you still delude yourself like one who is ignorant?

In this world, the object of knowledge does not exist in reality, just as the state of being a bracelet and so forth does not exist in gold; that [appearance] exists merely through delusion, and it is stilled by your non-recollection.
Whatever state arises within you, like a vibration in the wind, lead it to a state of groundlessness by means of the mental modification "I am not."
Why does he who has not conquered greed, shamelessness, pride, and delusion at the outset engage in this futile and harmful endeavor?
That "I-ness" which resides within you, like vibration in the wind, is not different from the Supreme Self; it is just as that vibration is not other than the air.
Through the consciousness of non-creation, creation shines forth most brilliantly in the Supreme; for even that which is of evil meaning appears beautiful through a particular arrangement.
The Supreme Self, however, never rises nor ever sets; and since there is nothing other than this, what could be either existence or non-existence?

In the supreme, the supreme; in the full, the full; in the peaceful, the peaceful; in the auspicious, the auspicious—thus alone is this vast expanse, wherein there is neither "I," nor the world, nor the intellect.
In non-nirvāṇa there is complete nirvāṇa; it is peaceful within peace, auspicious within the auspicious. Nirvāṇa is also non-nirvāṇa; it is neither an existing object nor is it not so.
Blows from weapons are endured, and the pains of disease are borne; what difficulty is there in enduring that which consists merely of the thought "I am not"?
The "I" is the imperishable sprout from which the multitude of objects in the world arises; when that sprout has reached its rootless state, the world itself has become rootless.
Like a mirror soiled by tears, I was rendered turbid by the self—which, though devoid of essence, appears substantial; yet upon the pacification of that self, it becomes perfectly clear.
The referent of "I" resides in the supreme wind; when that [wind] is stilled, however, there remains that which is indefinable, non-manifest, infinite, unborn, and immutable.

The sense of "I" (ahamartha) is that which presents the reflection of objects before consciousness; when that [sense of "I"] subsides, consciousness remains without appearance, infinite, unborn, and immutable.
When the cloud of the sense of "I" has been exhausted, the autumnal sky of ultimate reality shines forth, pure and radiant with the supreme, infinite, and limpid splendor.
O friend, if that unmanifest copper, freed from the impurity of the sense of "I," becomes the supreme, supremely radiant gold, it attains splendor.
Just as the splendor of an object devoid of designation attains a state beyond description, so too does this "I-ness" that is not truly "I" attain the state of Brahman.

Brahman, though established in the state of "I-am-ness," appears as if it were an object possessing a name; though it is tranquil, it appears as if it were existent, and thus it possesses designations.

If the sense of "I," which is the seed of the world, has been burnt away through non-contemplation, then what room is there for such notions as "this 'I-ness' is the bondage of the world"? It is nothing but a mere mental construction.

In the Supreme, which is the True Brahman, the Auspicious, and the Self, the ego-sense arises—untainted by names—just as the forgetfulness of the clay-substance arises from [the perception of] the state of being a jar.
From this seed of the sense of "I," the creeper of existence has arisen, upon which infinite worlds come and go as its fruits.
This earth with its mountains, oceans, and rivers, as well as this perception of forms and the desire for them, are the internal wonder of the "I-notion," which is like a seed of black pepper.
Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions—these are the fragrance of me, the "I," as this fierce flower blooms.
The pervasive sense of "I" reveals the world, just as the day, having begun, manifests the appearance and perception of existing forms.
Just as the purpose of a day is made manifest by its progression, so too is this unreal world created in an instant through the sense of "I-ness."
When that drop of oil-like impurity of the sense of "I" spread within the water of Brahman, this wheel of the three worlds immediately came into existence.
Astonishingly, by a mere opening of its eyes, the "I" experiences the worlds; yet, like sight, it does not experience them even when closing its eyes, for they are both real and utterly unreal.
For when the referent of "I" is projected outward, saṃsāra is experienced; but when it is not so internalized and has been completely exhausted, it is like the pupil of the eye.
When the sense of "I" has been rendered partless by eternal consciousness, this mirage of saṃsāra subsides entirely.

In this supreme reality, which is to be accomplished through the mere cultivation of one's own self-awareness, do not fall into distress or wander aimlessly within the self that is already established as the very essence of attainment.

O sinless one, I see no higher good for you than this: that which is to be accomplished by your own effort alone, through means such as being without assistance, and characterized by the absence of the sense of "I."

Forgive me; you must remain as you are, having manifested your power and filled the entire universe. You are the pure Self, appearing in the form of the mountains on all sides, the sky, the earth, the oceans, and the paths of the winds; established in yourself, peaceful, free from sorrow, devoid of the slightest trace of the impurities of the senses, beyond all conceptual proliferation, motionless yet the soul of all movement—both the whole and the part: such is the essence of the final doctrine.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For one who, being conscious, first conquers their own innate nature and the senses, and then applies themselves to discernment, everything is swiftly accomplished.
For one of burnt intellect who has not conquered within himself even the mere nature [of the self], the attainment of the supreme state is as difficult to obtain as oil from sand.

For even a slight instruction, when given to one who is pure, takes root like a drop of oil on a clean surface; it does not stick to those with upturned minds, just as a pearl does not adhere to a mirror.
In this very context, they cite this ancient history, which was previously told to me by Bhuśuṇḍa on the summit of Mount Meru.
Long ago, Bhuśuṇḍa was once questioned by me during a conversation in a secluded cave on the peak of Mount Meru.
"O dear one, when I asked him, 'Whom do you remember as having lived for a very long time—a person of dull intellect who did not know the Self? he replied to me as follows."

Bhuśuṇḍa said: "In former times, there was a Vidyādhara who was ignorant of the Self and tormented by worldly pleasures; he was a noble man of reflection dwelling on the peak at the boundary of the Lokāloka mountain, yet he remained withered."
Through manifold austerity, self-restraint, and religious observance, he remained with undiminished life-span for four previous kalpas.
Then, at the end of the fourth aeon, discernment arose within him, just as a lapis lazuli gem from Vidūra manifests its brilliance upon the rising of the clouds.
Reflecting upon death again, birth again, and old age as well, he felt ashamed; and pondering thus, he wondered: "What single thing might there be that is stable?"
Having cast off his own [body] and become detached in soul, having realized the lack of essence in worldly existence, he came to me to inquire about the city consisting of eighteen parts.
Having approached me and offered a grand salutation, and having been honored by me, he spoke these blameless words at an opportune moment.
The Vidyādhara said: "One's own senses are like weapons—soft yet capable of causing intense heat, as firm and strong as stone, and skillful in both cutting and piercing."

Agitated, defiled, and bringing about calamity, these senses are filled with waves of suffering because they act as fires to the forest of virtues; having conquered them—though they are dense with the darkness of the heart and composed of gloom—one attains happiness. So, what use have I for worldly objects?
The Vidyādhara said: "Tell me quickly of that state which is noble, effortless, free from decay or excess, purifying, and devoid of beginning or end."
"For so long a time I have been asleep, dull-witted; now, O Sage, I am fully awakened through the grace of my own Self."
The mind is greatly deluded, heated, and agitated by the movements of ignorance; rescue me from this miserable state, from the delusion that persists in the form of "I am."
Even upon one who is illustrious, calamities quickly fall upon the faint-hearted, just as frost falls upon a lotus, however virtuous it may be and however firm its stalks.
Only worn-out beings are born and die, neither for the sake of Dharma nor for liberation, like gnats in a lotus pond.
We are weary from long ago of those very same states of being—those deceptive delusions based on worthless objects—and we are deceived by them again and again.
There is no end to this, nor any state of stability for one whose mind finds no rest as it wanders among the fragile enjoyments of existence, like a traveler in desert lands.
The realms of sensual enjoyment are sweet at their onset, yet fragile and the causes of worldly existence; they undergo transformation in a short time and are ultimately terrifying.
O father, I take no delight in this perverse woman who is devoted to honor and dishonor, whose beloved is wicked pride, and who has destroyed the splendor of the Vidyādharas.
And he beheld the grounds of the Caitraratha garden, tender with blossoms, where the splendor of every kind of luxury was provided by the creepers of the wish-fulfilling trees.
He dwelt in the groves of Mount Meru and in the cities of the Vidyādharas, amidst the rows of excellent celestial chariots and upon the grounds of the wind-spheres.
He rested among the armies of the gods and upon the vine-like arms of his beloveds, as well as in the cities of the world-protectors, which were graced with the play of enchanting necklaces.
"Nothing at all is suitable or good; everything has been burnt by the heat of the poison of mental anguish and turned to ashes, my dear father—I have realized this now."
By this eye, which is restless in its longing to behold forms and greedy for the faces of women, and which is accompanied by such radiance, I have been brought to suffering for my own ruin.
Setting aside the conceptual construction that "this brings benefit" or "this does not," [the mind] runs even toward non-existent things because it follows after mere form.
The mind, intent on various bonds and oriented toward the welfare of others' enemies, does not attain detachment as long as it remains under the sway of calamities.
This sense of smell clearly runs toward objects of no benefit from every direction; O Father, I am unable to restrain it here, just as one cannot hold back a horse.
I have been joined with a sense of smell that follows the breath from my mouth like a conduit for scented water—an exceedingly faulty organ that acts like an enemy.
For a long time, I have been excessively struck by this tongue, devoid of moral conduct, upon the mountains of suffering hidden by elephants and jackals.
And I am unable to suppress my skin's craving for touch, just as one cannot suppress the heat of the sun blazing in the summer season.
The powers of hearing of the sage, longing for the essence of the flavor of auspicious sounds, lead me into this perilous situation, just as the desire for grass leads a deer astray.
The splendor of auspicious sounds was heard—sounds uttered by bowing attendants intent on doing what was pleasing, blended with the resonance of musical instruments and song.

We beheld the goddesses of Fortune, the women, and the very quarters of the sky, as well as the shores of the oceans and the mountains—all of them captivating with their splendor and adorned with tinkling jeweled ornaments.

For a long time, the six flavors—sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent—endowed with excellent qualities, delightful through their aesthetic wonder, and brought by humble beloved women, have been tasted.
In the expansive pleasure-grounds, they were touched on all sides without obstruction by silken garments, lovely necklaces, flower-strewn carpets, and gentle breezes.
O Sage, the fragrances wafted by the gentle breeze—arising from the faces of brides, medicinal herbs, flowers, and unguents—have been experienced by you.
That which was heard, touched, seen, tasted, and smelled again and again has become parched and tasteless once more; tell me quickly, what shall I resort to?
Having consumed this mass of miserable enjoyments for thousands of years, from the Brahma-world down to a blade of grass, no satisfaction arises.
Having ruled over an empire for a very long time, having enjoyed a multitude of wives, and having utterly shattered the forces of the enemy—what unprecedented thing has been attained?
Even those by whom the destruction was never known, and by whom the three worlds were enjoyed—even they have, before long, all together gone to the state of ashes.
One should apply effort, even through arduous exertion, toward that which has been attained such that nothing further remains to be attained.
For those beings by whom beloved pleasures have been enjoyed for a long time, no tree is seen upon anyone's head, nor is there a floating vessel in the sky.
For a long time, I have been deceived by my senses in these endless forest ranges of sense-objects, like a child led astray by crafty tricksters.
Today, however, I have fully recognized these enemies within my own domain; they are the wretched ones called the sense-faculties, who will surely deceive me once again.
In the empty jungle of saṃsāra, the deceitful hunters of the sense-objects and their domains repeatedly console and then slaughter the scorched human-deer.
Those who have not been seen even two or three times in this world, having been burned by these uneven venomous serpents—the sense-objects and the senses—[are truly rare].
[It is] a snare trembling with craving, coiled with the terrifying elephants of enjoyments; it is richly equipped with the fierce swords of greed and marked by the clusters of spears of anger.
It was pervaded by the chariot of the net of dualities, governed by egoism, crowded with the horses of active impulses, and tumultuous with the clamor of desire.
O dear one, those who have risen to conquer the army of wicked senses stationed at the very borders of the body—they alone are truly the noble warriors here.
It is easier to pierce the temples of the rutting elephant Airāvaṇa than it is to restrain one's own senses when they have set out upon the wrong path.
O virtuous one, the subjugation of the senses is the ultimate limit even for those who possess great manliness, great being, and great fortune.
Even a man attains the highest status among the dwellers of heaven only so long as he is not dragged down like a blade of grass by his wretched senses.
Those great beings on earth who have conquered their senses are truly men; the rest, I consider to be merely moving assemblages of flesh-machines.
O Sage, if I have the effort to conquer this army of the five senses belonging to the general of the mind, then I shall surely achieve victory.
For those diseases of the most excellent senses, there are no medicines, no sacred fords, and no mantras for their pacification, other than the casting off of the desire for enjoyments.
I have been led to the utmost distress by my senses rushing toward their objects, like a solitary traveler in a great forest pursued by bandits.
The sense-faculties are like muddy ponds: turbid, lacking clarity, fraught with great misfortune, and filled with the weeds of foul-smelling moss.
The sense-faculties are like dense jungles, difficult to traverse, shrouded in mist, and generating a web of terrors.
The lotuses have holes and their qualities are very difficult to perceive; the stalks have knots and dull parts, and so do the sense organs.
The sense-faculties are like the waters of the ocean: harsh, greedy for jewels, tossed by billows, and terrible with seizing crocodiles.
Deaths cause distress to kinsmen and bring about another body; likewise, the sense faculties produce piteous lamentations.
The senses are like dense, infinite, and empty forests: they are enemies to those lacking discernment, but friends to those possessing discernment.
These terrible clouds and the sense faculties are alike: they are solid yet hollow within, soiled and dull, and possess the fleeting brilliance of lightning.
Those seized by lowly creatures are avoided by those of disciplined self; likewise, one's own senses are like pits when overwhelmed by passion and ignorance.

The sense-faculties are like the edges of abysses: they are exclusively skilled at casting one down, they are filled with the venomous serpents of the defilements, and they are marked by hundreds of thousands of harsh thorns.
One's own senses are like demons: they are self-serving, ignoble, delighting solely in reckless violence, and dwelling in darkness.
The sense-faculties are hollow within, devoid of essence, crooked, and knotted; they are ill-wooded and fit only for the purpose of burning.
The sense-faculties are like wretched, ancient cities: they are bound by dense delusion, difficult to traverse and deep, vast yet utterly empty.
Among infinite objects, the causes for jars and the like are the whirling, mud-stained wheels and the sense organs.

O you whose nature is to rescue, lift me up with the dawning of compassion—me, who am thus sunk in calamity and destitute of anything. For those who are truly virtuous and victorious in the worlds declare that association with them removes the deepest sorrow.
Bhuśuṇḍa said: Then, O Brahman, having heard those purifying words of his, I spoke this in response to what was asked, with speech consisting of very clear syllables.
Excellent, O Lord of Vidyādharas! By good fortune you have awakened for the sake of your welfare; after a long time, you desire to rise from the deep pit of the darkness of worldly existence.
Your purifying intellect shines with a dense form, like a stream of molten gold purified by the fire of discernment.
He grasps the meaning of the words of instruction with effortless ease; just as an object reflects without exertion in a stainless mirror.
"Whatever I say here, you ought to accept it all with the word 'Om'; we have sought this for a long time, so there should be no hesitation in this matter."
Whatever tastes within you, understand it as ignorance and cast it aside; you do not exist even after searching for a long time within, for you cannot be found.
For you who are certain that "I am not," "you are not," and "the world does not exist," everything exists as Śiva; and that [Śiva] leads neither to your suffering nor to your pleasure.
Whether the world was born from ignorance, or whether ignorance belongs to the world—having investigated even this, we do not know, for these two are essentially one.
Like the water of a mirage, the universe, though existing, is non-existent because it lacks substantial reality; that which shines here is Brahman, which is both nothing at all and everything.
The universe does not exist, like water in a mirage; nor do you exist, nor does even the appearance exist here, because that [universe] is absent. Therefore, there is auspiciousness (śiva).
Know that you are the Great Ego, the seed of the universe; for from it is born this world, like an ancient tree with its mountains, oceans, earth, rivers, and islands as its roots.
From the subtle seed of egoity (ahaṃtva), this tree of the universe is born; for its roots are indeed the worlds, rich with the sap of the senses.

The clusters of stars are its buds; the multitude of constellations is its mass of unopened blossoms; the spreading clusters of latent impressions are its flower-bunches; and the full moon is its abode of fruit.
