Heaven and the other realms are its great branches, the vast hollows of its trunk; Mount Meru, Mandara, Sahya, and the other mountains are its rows of leaves.
The seven oceans are its prominent fibers; the netherworld is the hollow of its root; the Yugas are the swarms of wood-boring insects; and the cosmic qualities are the rows of its joints.
Ignorance is the ground for the birth of men, who are like millions of birds; perception is the great pillar, and the forest fire is the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Forms, light, and mental attention have various modes of joyful activity; the vast forest is space, and the surface of the mouth is a net of mother-of-pearl shells.
The seasons are its variegated branches, and the ten directions are its twigs; it is a great flood of the essence of consciousness, with the movement of the wind as its turning point.
The flickering rays of the moon and sun are intent on rising and sinking; the flower clusters are beautiful, while the darkness is the wandering of bees.

Filling the netherworld, the quarters of space, and the intermediate region, that which is unreal stands as if it were real. Yet, when the seed of the ego-sense is consumed by the fire of non-egoity (anahantā), there is no further sprouting of even that which was real.

Bhuśuṇḍa said: "O Vidyādhara, you are the support of the earth, whose dwelling is the mountain caves; you are one who moves with swift motion through the conduct of the sky and the intermediate quarters."
Such is this tree of the world that it arises from the seed of the sense of "I"; when that seed is consumed by the fire of knowledge, nothing at all is born again.
And when it is being scrutinized, that "I-ness" is never found at all; this alone is that knowledge, and by this very [knowledge] it is consumed.
Because of the absence of "I-ness," there exists the "I-ness" which is the seed of saṃsāra; because of the absence of "I-ness," there is no "I-ness"—this is the supreme knowledge.
Since this creation was indeed non-existent at the very beginning of creation, whence comes "I-ness," whence comes "you-ness," and whence arises the delusion of duality and unity?
Having heard the words of the Guru, those who strive by their own effort toward the abandonment of all mental constructs from their very root are victorious in attaining the supreme state.
A cook gains victory through his work in his own craft; likewise, a man of discernment attains his state of discernment only through diligent effort, and not otherwise.
Know that this world here is nothing other than the mere wonder of consciousness; it exists neither in the vital breaths, nor outside, nor within—it is not found anywhere at all.
The variegated world is perceived merely by the opening of volition; when that opening ceases, it dissolves like a painting upon the mind of the artist.
There is a great pavilion with massive pillars, fashioned from pearls and gems, extending for many hundreds of thousands of yojanas and adorned with beautiful gold.
It was surrounded in front by a thousand jeweled pillars reaching up to Mount Meru, beautiful as the clouds at the end of an eon, enriched by a thousand rainbows.
Wherein women, children, men, and others residing there have established various structures here and there for the purpose of play.

Filled with the seeds of past beings and echoing with the humming of the enemy of darkness, these are called the variegated manifestations of light and shadow—the caskets containing the transition between worlds.
Fragrant with the scent of musk, their sprouts being the rows of moving clouds, they were like pleasure-lotus-pools where the wish-fulfilling trees of women's ornaments had been plucked away.
The great mountain ranges were balls shaken by the breath of children; the twilight clouds were ear-ornaments; and the autumnal clouds were fly-whisks.
The clouds at the end of the eon have become fans; the surface of the earth has become a gaming board; and the sky, with its stars, has become a canopy.

In the game of dice where the elements are the stakes and the turning of fortune is the play, the moon and sun are the dice upon the courtyard of the sky, with the illumination of the world as the wager for those dwelling in their homes.
Thus, through long-term cultivation, mere mental resolve within eventually attains a semblance of reality, like an object perceived before one's eyes.
In the very same way, this world-form has arisen from volitions; its essence consists solely of the wonder of consciousness, like a painting created by the mind of a painter.
Everything that manifests is indeed unreal; it both exists and does not exist. This world has arisen from what is non-existent, as if it had emerged from somewhere.

Just as bracelets and other ornaments are nothing but gold, so too this hollow interior of saṃsāra is merely the wonder of consciousness, brought to cessation through the absence of conceptualization.
It is entirely within your own power; do as you wish. For one who has shown disregard in the giving and receiving of food and drink, this is his final birth, yet he does not abandon that karma.

O pure-souled one, you have attained the second holy stage of discernment, which purifies the three worlds; I know that you shall not fall back again with this mind—therefore, abandon this silent state and proceed to the stainless station.

Bhuśuṇḍa said: O sinless one, even though you are of the nature of consciousness, remain as the peaceful mass of consciousness alone, not perceiving objects such as "this" and so forth, like a ray of light within pure water.
The insentient exists within sentience solely because of sentience; though dissimilar to its own nature, it appears similar, just as fire exists within a mass of water.
The cause of the conscious and the unconscious is likewise consciousness because it possesses sentience, just as wind is the cause for the arising and ceasing of a flame.
"I do not exist"—let your consciousness rest within that very consciousness. Thereafter, remain exactly as you are, in whatever manner you may be.
In the form of consciousness, you abide within and without all things, just as water exists both inside and outside a mass of clear water.
O dear one, if the nature of consciousness, which is "I do not exist," is fixed within consciousness itself, and no other form of Brahman is perceived, with what can it be compared?

It was like the entire realm of the earth, the underworld, and the heavens, including the gods and asuras, inhabited together; it was as agitated as the very passage of time, filled with the constant arising and passing away of diverse states of being.
Just as a painting made of colors remains on a wall as if silent, so too does the world, painted by consciousness, abide within the void-wall of the Self.
That which is the mind, whether it be insentient or sentient, exists as that very abundance which is manifested from itself; do as you wish.
These wonders of consciousness flash forth in the void as this world; for those who have realized the Knower, they are transparent and unobstructing, like the rays of the sun.
Just as for those whose vision is overcome by cataracts, a mass of hair and the like appears in the sky, so too does the form of the world appear to those who abide in what is not the self.

Thus, that which consists of the awareness of "the world," "you," and "I" has arisen as a mere appearance, neither truly arisen nor unarisen; it is like a city fashioned from the lattice of the sun's rays, wherein walls and such exist as real, yet not in the sky like a creeper.

Bhuśuṇḍa said: Know that consciousness itself is both conscious and unconscious; just as fire exists within water, consciousness and insentience are not distinct from one another even in the slightest degree.

Since there is no difference between that [object] and the experience of it, remain established in your natural state—unconstrained, like the cognition of a figure in a painting, or like the center of space.
Likewise, because Brahman possesses all powers, non-consciousness exists [within it], just as a future speck of foam exists within undisturbed, pure water.
Just as a fragment of foam does not dispel its cause—the water—so too the creation and so forth do not dispel their cause, Brahman.
And there is no cause here for this uncaused process of creation; therefore, nothing whatsoever is born at the beginning of the world, nor does it perish.
Because there is absolutely no cause, the world is not born as anything at all; like water in a desert mirage, the world does not exist even though it is seen before one's eyes.
Brahman is infinite, unborn, and peaceful; therefore, this notion of creation does not exist. Due to the absence of a cause, all this is indeed the undivided Brahman alone.
Therefore, you resemble a solid stone yet are like the expanse of space; because your form is the single, dense mass of Brahman, you are unborn and without parts.
Whether you know something or nothing at all, remain seated here free from doubt; let the appearance of consciousness subside within the Self by means of the Self, for it is insentient.
Because the Unborn is eternal bliss, there is no cause that produces an effect; since the creation and so forth are impossible, that which exists is the Unborn Śiva.
But for those who revel in ignorance, for whom there is no unborn one whose nature is consciousness, what is there to be deliberated upon when the creation and destruction [of the world] have arisen?
Wherever the Supreme Brahman exists, there indeed are worlds; and such liberated beings exist in the form of the very meaning of the word "world."
In grass, in wood, in water, and in a wall—it stands supreme everywhere; and everywhere the flood of creation remains interwoven with one another.

It is not appropriate to say what the intrinsic nature of Brahman is, because in the infinite, supreme reality, the possibilities of "belonging to oneself" and "not belonging to oneself" are utterly impossible.
Furthermore, since an entity that depends upon non-existence is impossible, fallacious expressions such as "intrinsic nature" do not find a footing in the infinite.

Because non-ownership and non-existence are absolutely impossible in that which is eternal and infinite, once ownership and existence are established, the expression of "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) does not hold.
O virtuous one, when examined through the light of the intellect, "I-ness" is not found; how could this, which is utterly non-existent, have arisen from anywhere, like a yakṣa seen by a child?
That which is liberated from the meanings of the words "I" and "mine" is the Supreme; but that which is joined with the meanings of the words "I" and "mine," when scrutinized, dissolves away.

The difference between the world and Brahman, and their non-difference, are like the playful manifestation of synonymous words and their meanings; they are said to be mere conceptual construction and not real, just as [the difference and non-difference] exist between a bracelet and gold.
Bhuśuṇḍa said: He who, perceiving weapons clinging to his naked body as if they were his own beloved limbs, remains perfectly equanimous, is established in the supreme state.
One should apply effort and fortitude in practice for as long as the state of deep sleep arises with respect to the emergence of objective phenomena.

Just as water does not stain even slightly a lotus, so too mental afflictions do not stain in the least one who knows the reality of things as they truly are, even though those afflictions stand before him.
He who, being of tranquil soul, perceives weapons, women, and the sky—even when they have come into contact with his limbs—as if they were not at all attached, he truly sees.
Just as poison becomes a scorpion within its own interior by itself, and this state of being a scorpion is nothing other than the poison itself; so it is with the mind.
Thus, without abandoning its own essential nature, it presides over living beings; likewise, the Self presides over that [world] which is dissolved solely through the realization of it.

Just as the individual soul (jīva) becomes deluded by death even though its nature is immortal, so too consciousness, without abandoning its own essential form, assumes a form that is both conscious and inert.

Though non-different from Brahman, he appeared as if different; though established within it, he arose at times as if separate. Though situated therein, he remained as if not situated there, appearing as the manifest creation itself.
Just as a worm within poison does not abandon its poisonous nature, it neither truly dies nor is it born; yet it both dies and is born.
By means of one's own consciousness, which has the nature of being immersed in the objects of experience, the ocean of existence is crossed like a cow’s footprint; it is not crossed by fate.
In that state which abides within all things, which transcends all states of being, and wherein there is an inner coolness—how could there be any neglect toward it?
When the existence of all objects in the world has been quickly contemplated in their general form, what stain can there be for the pure Self, which is beyond mind, ego, intellect, and the rest?
Just as you perceive objects such as pots and cloths, so too, O friend, perceive this body; likewise, perceive the "I-ness," the mind, the intellect, and the sensations as well.

The entire multitude of objects in the world, along with the mind, intellect, and other faculties, are established within the Knower alone; therefore, remain as one who possesses no objective consciousness, grounded in perfect steadfastness.
No one ever has any fault whatsoever, nor is there ever any merit here; there is neither pleasure nor pain, neither existence nor non-existence, and there is neither an enjoyer nor any agency.
Bhuśuṇḍa said: Just as the conceptualization that "the sky has become the firmament" is mere delusion and unreal in nature, so too is the cultivation of the sense of "I."
Just as I am the one who imagines through delusion that "space has been produced," so too does the ineffable Self exist, though it is spread out as if it were non-existent.
In the void, there exists only the Self, whose nature is consciousness; it perceives its own form as that which shines forth through the notion of "this-ness," yet it is neither "I" nor "not-I."
Therefore, there exists such a form of consciousness wherein even the gross ether is contained within it, just as Mount Meru is contained within an atom; for that consciousness has consumed the void.
From that [intellect] arises the dense appearance of insentience, which is even more subtle than space; that which knows its own nature exists as this very creation.
For the knower of the Self, the world is the expansion of that which is tasted as "I-ness," just as the expansion of the fluidity of water takes the form of whirlpools and the like.
The expansion of consciousness is tranquil, like water that has ceased to ripple; it has the form of wind that has become motionless, resembling the heart of space.
And it is not possible [to perceive it] within the expansions of the world such as space and time, except for the emanation of pure consciousness, which is dense yet empty and devoid of appearances.
When pure consciousness alone has expanded throughout time—whether in space, on a boat, in water, or on land—in sleep, in waking, or in dreaming, the world appears as if arisen.
For consciousness, neither expansion nor non-expansion is possible, because it is always more transparent than even space, and because it is inherently undisturbed and so forth.
The Knower perceives neither enjoyments nor the like, nor does he conceive "I" within himself; remaining as a secondless unity in the Supreme, he is like fluidity inherent within water.

One who is free from conceptual construction does not perceive the host of qualities such as intelligence, modesty, fortune, fear, mindfulness, fame, and beauty, just as one cannot see the footprints of a snake in the darkness.

The creation, which is a flow of nectar from the rays of the moonlight of consciousness shimmering within the orb of Brahma-the-moon, does not exceed the Lord, because of the non-existence of space and time.
Thus, through self-conceit, one vibrates; as it vibrates, the luminous mind—which is the primordial nature of the world—vibrates within others like a multitude of whirlpools in water.
With the sounds of plunging and emerging, and through the movements of eddying, swirling, and winding, the river of creation appears long exhausted, yet its flow remains uninterrupted.
Just as water shines with whirlpools and smoke shines like a cloud, so does this third creation exist between these two by virtue of its insentient nature.

Just as the grain, swirls, and so forth appear in wood when it is cut by a saw, so too this creation—consisting of both that and what is not that—appears within the Supreme when He is beyond space and other such categories.
Apart from the sprout of volition, there is no difference whatsoever between the plantain trunk of saṃsāra and a stone, even though the former is soft while the latter is hard.
It possesses a thousand hooves, heads, eyes, hands, faces, and private parts; it extends over various mountains, bodies, directions, regions, and rivers, yet occupies no more space than a mere span.
Empty within and devoid of essence, it is colored by manifold passion; yet it is threatened only by the cleansing brought about by the flashing forth of dispassion.

[It is] together with the gods, asuras, gandharvas, vidyādharas, and mahoragas; it is that which moves through the dull matter, the self, and the wind, and is perceived by the consciousness of others.
The world is a beautiful, radiant, and charming manifestation of conceptual construction, like a magnificent kingdom depicted in a painting on a cloth, which cannot withstand close scrutiny.
Falling into the aspect of conceptualization within the nature of vibration—which is unreal in form—consciousness spreads through delusion like a drop of oil upon water.
Through the spreading webs of heart-etchings that revolve in every eddy, and through the chewing upon the dullness arising from the mixture of spreading affection;
When the form of consciousness turns outward through the conceptualization of "I" and so forth, it is not distinct from the Supreme, just as the nature of water is not distinct from its fluidity.
The sun of consciousness, which is one's very own self, is designated as "creation"; having become "I," there is no other creation, nor is there any creator.
Just as vibration exists within the essence of existence, like fluidity in water, so too does the conscious self perceive itself as both the void and the non-void.

The experience of consciousness, preceded by the manifestation of place, time, and so forth, consists in its very nature of creation; therefore, its similarity to water and fluidity is not far-fetched.
Know that whatever perception there is—such as the mind, the sense of "I," or the intellect—is ignorance; it is destroyed quickly through diligent human effort.
Half [of ignorance] is removed through mutual conversation, a portion by means of investigations into the scriptures, and the remainder ceases through self-realization.
When the four parts have been sequentially eliminated through the destruction of ignorance, that which remains simultaneously is the reality of the object, free from names.

Śrī Rāma said: Half [of the knowledge] comes from mutual conversation, a portion from the investigation of the scriptures, and a portion from self-realization; how is that [remaining portion] removed?
O Lord of Sages, what is meant by "simultaneously" and "successively"? Tell me, how can that which is called "the reality of the meaning of non-naming" be both existent and non-existent?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Together with a virtuous person who is dispassionate and seeks to cross over the cycle of existence, one should investigate the nature of worldly transmigration along with those who know the Self.
Therefore, having sought out from wherever possible a person who is free from passion and envy, virtuous, and self-knowing, a wise man should strive to propitiate him with effort.

O best among those who know what is to be known, know that when the meeting with the virtuous one has been accomplished, half of one's ignorance has gone to destruction, due to the arising of the most excellent and supreme state.
Half of ignorance is destroyed through association with the virtuous; a fourth part by the meanings of the scriptures, and a fourth part by one's own effort.
A single desire arises for enjoyments and is restrained; upon its destruction, one-fourth of ignorance is eliminated through one's own effort.

Impurity is diminished by association with the virtuous, by the meaning of the scriptures, and by one's own efforts—either by each one individually, by all together, or even sequentially at the same time.
That which, being of the nature of the extinction of ignorance, is neither anything nor yet something at all—that they call the Supreme, the nameless reality, which is both non-existent and existent.

This Brahman is dense, undecaying, beginningless, infinite, one, a manifestation of volition, and indeed non-existent [as a separate object]. Having realized this, with the delusion of the measurer and the measurable dispelled, dwell in the sorrowless Nirvana, moving about at ease.
Bhuśuṇḍa said: For that which has the nature of pervading the universe, neither space nor time is required for its maintenance, just as light does not require support in the sky.
These three worlds are merely a creation of mental ideation; they are peaceful, subtle, light, and clearer even than the fragrance within the wind.

For the virtuous one, who is indeed a mere atom of the world consisting only of the wonder of consciousness, the fragrance within the wind and Mount Meru exist through the application of the experience of others.
That toward which this creation moves is indeed what perceives it, just as a person perceives their own dream-like configuration of objects.
In this very context, they cite this ancient history, concerning what occurred long ago within the belly of a mote of dust belonging to the king of the gods.
At some time, in some place, on a certain branch of a certain world-age, within a certain wish-fulfilling tree, there appeared the fruit that is the universe, like a fig.

It resounded with the humming of swarms of mosquitoes that were the hosts of gods, asuras, and spirits; its formidable gates were the mountains, the flesh-like netherworlds, the heavens, and the earth.
Exceedingly beautiful with the wonder of consciousness, thick with the essence of latent impressions, fragrant with the aroma of diverse experiences, and captivating as the relish of the mind.
It possesses millions of creepers of the mature existence of the vast tree of Brahman, has the great stalk of egoism, and is brilliantly illuminated by the light of universal perception.

Its mouth is blossomed by the gateway to liberation; it is enveloped by rivers, oceans, and veins; it resides within the sheath of the five elements; and it is sprinkled with droplets from the floating stars.
Worn out by the end of the aeon, now accessible to crows and cuckoos alike, it has fallen into peace and gone somewhere to its final resting place.
Therein dwelt Śakra, the lord of the immortals and sovereign of the three worlds, like a leader of small insects settled within a jar of honey.

Through the instruction of his guru and his own practice, he became one whose veils were destroyed; a great soul who had cultivated his inner self, he was the best among those who know the past and the future.
Then, at one time, when Nārāyaṇa and others who were endowed with prowess had for the most part withdrawn into concealment, there was one [remaining] together with the lord of the gods.
He fought with the great asuras amidst the blazing flames of their weapons; but being defeated by those of great heroism, he fled away in haste.
Chased by his enemies, he fled with great speed through the ten directions; yet he found no place of rest, like a base man in the next world.
Finding a slight opening among those enemies whose vision was deluded, he brought his own bodily intention to a state of tranquility, both within and without.
He entered a certain mote of dust situated within the rays of the sun, by virtue of his nature as pure consciousness, just as a bee enters the calyx of a lotus.
There he quickly took rest and after a long time found relief; then, having forgotten the battle, he attained a state of withdrawal.
Then, in an instant, he experienced a created palace; in that palace, at the center of a lotus, he took delight as if upon his own throne.
Then Hari, in the form of a householder, beheld that fashioned city, with its walls and palaces constructed of gems, pearls, corals, and other precious materials.
Then Hari, having entered the city, beheld the countryside, resplendent with various mountains, villages, cow-pens, towns, and forests.
Then Śakra, experiencing such delight, surveyed the world—comprising mountains, oceans, the earth, rivers, and forests, along with all activity and the conception of time.
Then Śakra, experiencing such delight, perceived the three worlds—along with the netherworld (pātāla), the earth, the sky, the celestial realms, the sun and other luminaries, and the mountains.
There he remained in the sovereignty of the gods, adorned with the weight of enjoyments; then a son named Kunda was born to him, who was full of valor.
Then, at the end of his life, having cast off the body, the blameless Śakra attained nirvāṇa like a lamp whose oil has been exhausted.
Kunda, the king of the three worlds, having begotten his own son, in the course of time, at the end of his life, went to the supreme state.
Then his son likewise, having installed his own son in the kingdom, departed at the end of his life to the supreme, purifying state.
In this way, O handsome one, thousands of grandsons have passed away; even now, among them, a portion remains established in the sovereignty of the Lord of the Gods.

Thus, as long as the world is conceived, he alone occupies the station of Śakra within the lineage of Amareśvara; even when that [station] is impaired, dissolved, struck down, or lost anywhere in the sky, he remains like the purifying atom of the sun’s rays.
Bhuśuṇḍa said: There was once a lord of the gods born into the lineage of that Śakra; he possessed supreme qualities and was glorious, and his body was of the western direction.
Then, there arose for that noble son of Indra an attainment of inspired wisdom, as proclaimed by the words of Bṛhaspati.
Then, having realized that which is to be known and following his natural disposition as it had been attained, he, the sovereign of the drinkers of clarified butter (the gods), ruled over the worlds.
He fought with the Dānavas and conquered all his enemies; having crossed over ignorance, he performed a hundred sacrifices.
Out of necessity, he dwelt for a long time within the fibers of a lotus stalk, and indeed experienced hundreds of other adventures as well.
Once, there arose in him, who was endowed with the power of awakening, the desire: "Possessing meditative concentration, may I perceive the reality of Brahman exactly as it is."
Then, remaining in solitude with his mind stilled by the renunciation of all causes both internal and external, he beheld through meditative concentration.
Brahman is the supreme of all powers, pervading and consisting of all things; it is everything, in every way, at all times, by means of all [means], everywhere, and omnipresent.
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces on all sides, and with ears everywhere in the world, He exists pervading everything.

It is free from the qualities of all the senses, yet endowed with the qualities of all the senses; it is unattached and yet the sustainer of all; it is devoid of qualities, yet the experiencer of the qualities.
It exists both outside and inside all beings, as the unmoving and indeed as the moving; because of its subtlety, it is incomprehensible; it is far away, yet it is near.
Everywhere it consists of moon and sun; everywhere it consists of earth; everywhere it consists of mountains; and likewise, everywhere it consists of oceans.
Everywhere it is heavy with essence; everywhere it consists of space; everywhere it consists of saṃsāra; and everywhere it consists of the world.
Everywhere indeed it is the nature of liberation; everywhere indeed it is the primordial consciousness. Everywhere it consists of all objects, yet from every side it is devoid of everything.
In a jar, a cloth, a banyan tree, a wall, a cart, and likewise in a monkey; in a dwelling, in space, in a tree, in the mountain, in the wind, in water, and in fire.
He beheld the three worlds—possessing diverse conducts and deliberations and various modes of existence—even within a space no larger than a single atom.
Just as sharpness exists within a mirage and emptiness within the sky, so too do the three worlds—both real and unreal—exist within the self that consists of consciousness.
Meditating in this way with pure consciousness that was free from the sense of objective existence, Śakra gradually became a practitioner of meditation in that very same manner.
Beholding everything as one through meditation for a long time, that noble-minded one of great intelligence perceived this creation of ours.
Then, wandering through this creation, he attained the status of Śakra after Śakra and exercised sovereignty over the kingdom, which was adorned with hundreds of historical accounts.
"Know this as it truly is: the king of the gods is the sovereign of the Vidyadhara clans, and he was born into the lineage of that very Indra."
Then, through the practice of yoga focused on the seed-syllable situated in the heart and directed eastward, he experienced the account of his dwelling within the fibers of a lotus stalk.
Just as this Śakra has been described as having his abode within a mote of dust and as having his abode upon the fibers of a lotus stalk, so too is one born of that lineage radiant with splendor.
Likewise, hundreds of thousands of such transactions have passed and continue to exist there in the sky, here and there.
This river flows thus without interruption for a long time; meanwhile, the mature stream remains visible, whether its state has been ascended or not ascended.
Thus, this illusion is beginningless and long-extended, ever-tending toward the conditions [of perception]; it finds its sole delight in total dissolution through the mere vision of reality.
O sinless one, this illusion arises from somewhere or other, or anywhere at all; it is perceived merely as having come into being in whatever manner.
Like mist arising suddenly from a cloud as if seen through the mere wonder of the sense of "I," it perishes instantly upon being scrutinized.

By this [means], the reality of the self is revealed as a manifestation whose nature is free from the long-desired vision, the seer, and the seen; because it is empty of all objects, it is therefore of the nature of emptiness—solely space-like and consisting of nothing but mere mental construction.

Bhuśuṇḍa said: Where there is "I-ness" and the world, it remains having arrived there from before, even within the ultimate atom of Indra, just as [one might find] a mote of dust in the interior of a sunbeam.
The primary root of this worldly delusion, which has arisen like the color of the sky, is said to be the sense of "I," the conceiving self.
From this minute seed of the ego, drenched with the sap of latent impressions (vāsanā), the tree of the three worlds grows upon the mountain of Brahmā in the forest of space.
It is a cluster of flowers that are the stars, with the mountains as its withered sprouts; it is a flood of veins that are the essence of rivers, with latent impressions as its core and its fruit.
This vibration of the world is said to be the water of the ego-sense; it is the flowing liquid of spreading latent impressions, sweetened by the wonder of consciousness.
The stars were its spray of mist, the infinite sky was its bed; it possessed great whirlpools of existence and non-existence, and various mountains were its waves.
It is the brushstroke that paints the three worlds, foamy with its flickering light; it is the bursting bubble of the cosmic egg, as thick as a bolted door-panel.
The surface of the earth is a solid mass of foam for the water-bird of the dense consciousness, characterized by the immersion and emergence of various swift and rapid movements.
It is wondrous with the surging waves of old age, death, delusion, and the like; it is uniquely beautiful with the multitude of droplets that are the bodies which arise and perish.
Let it be understood that the world is the vibration of the wind of egoism; let it be realized that the world is the fragrance of the lotus of egoism.
I am never distinct from you and the world, just as wind is always inseparable from its movement, as liquidity is from water, and as heat is from fire.
The world exists within the object "I," and "I" exists within the world in the heart; these two arise mutually, standing like the container and the contained.
He who, through awakening and not through ignorance, wipes away the "I-ness" that is the seed of the world—by him the impurity of the world is thoroughly washed away, like various stains by water.
O Vidyādhara, that which is called "arhatship" does not exist at all; because it lacks a cause and is a non-entity, it is said to be like the horn of a hare.

In that Brahman which is exceedingly vast, infinite, and devoid of the delineation of conceptual constructs, there is never any reality consisting of "I-ness," because the cause for such "I-ness" is absent.
Since no cause is possible at the beginning of creation due to the absence of any real entity, therefore "I-ness" and so forth do not exist anywhere, just like the son of a barren woman.
In the absence of that [duality], the world does not exist; and due to the non-existence of the world, there is no subjectivity. What remains is only nirvāṇa; therefore, remain at ease in peace.
Thus, due to the absence of a basis for rebirth, the world, the self, and their respective natures are extinguished; for you, O Śānta, these do not exist in any other way.
That which does not exist simply does not exist; the remainder is peaceful and eternal. You have fully awakened; do not again give rise to stainless delusion.

Pure, free from the stain of temporal succession, you are auspicious, you are peaceful, you are the eternal Lord; to you even your own self is like a mountain, and the entire world is but the form of a single atom.
Bhuśuṇḍa said: Even as that leader of the Vidyādharas was speaking thus, his consciousness became utterly tranquil, and he attained the transformation of meditative absorption (samādhi).
Though being awakened by me again and again from this state or that, he did not fall back to the visible world, having attained supreme nirvāṇa.
He attained the supreme state through that much awakening alone, O dear one, and not by any further effort of one desiring excellence.
Therefore, O Rāma, it has been said by me: if the mind is indeed pure, instruction spreads like a drop of oil upon water.
"There is no 'I' within you; do not cultivate this [notion] for the sake of peace. This much is the statement of the supreme instruction; indeed, there is nothing other than this."
This very [truth], when it falls upon an unworthy mind, dissolves away like a pure pearl upon a smooth, upward-facing mirror.
But when the mind of a worthy person has become tranquil, it attains and enters non-falling; having entered within that which is called "discernment," it is like a ray of light entering a sun-gem.
The intense sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāvana) is itself the seed of the silk-cotton tree called suffering; likewise, the notions of "mine" and "this is mine" are the cause for the spreading of its branches.
Beginning with "I" and ending with "mine," from that desire proceeds; it brings about hundreds of misfortunes regarding these objects and is the bearer of worldly existence.
O best of sages, even such fools become long-lived; for indeed, my dear, there is no fixed rule regarding the cause of longevity.
Those whose minds are inwardly pure, having been instructed even slightly, attain the supreme state from [the Buddha] who bestows fearlessness after a very long time.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus to me on the summit of Mount Meru, that lord of birds, his soul liberated, became silent like a cloud upon Ṛṣyamūka.
O Rāma, having taken leave of that accomplished Vidyādhara, I then returned once more to my own abode, which was adorned by a circle of sages.

This method for the pacification of Vidyādharas, arising from the brief awakening taught by Bali-bhuj, has been told to you today. Indeed, eleven great Yugas have passed while I was here in this assembly of Bhuśuṇḍa, the lord of birds.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Through the very absence of the perception of "I," the desire that bears fruit as saṃsāra—which yields the results of both auspicious and inauspicious actions—surely subsides within.

Through the practice of non-identification with the self, having become one for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are equal, and having stilled the afflictions of existence, a person does not suffer.
Propelled by the force of the awakening of another, which has flown up from the hollow of the ego-sheath, I do not know where this stone of the object "I" quickly goes.
Launched from the hollow of the ego-sheath, impelled by the power of the hero Brahmā, I do not know where this stone of the object "I" quickly goes.
Launched from the pouch of egoism, impelled by the force of the hero Brahmā, I know not where this stone of the body-machine quickly goes.
This sense of "I" within me has been dissolved by the flame of consciousness; it seems as if it has flown away, and I do not know where it has quickly gone.
The essence of "I," having dissolved within by the flame of consciousness through the absence of egoity, I know not where it quickly goes from the withered leaf of the body.
The intoxicating juice of the essence of egoity, once its sap has been completely extracted from the leaves of the body, attains the state of transcendence by way of the sun of non-egoity.
Whether on a bed, in mud, on a mountain, in a house, in the sky, on dry land, or in water; whether gross, subtle, formless, or even entered into another form.
Whether situated here or there, asleep, awakened, or reduced to ashes; whether held, led away, submerged, far distant, or nearby—she remains ever present.
The sprout of egoity, situated within the seed-vessel of the body, quickly spreads its net of scriptures known as this saṃsāra in an instant.
I am indeed a vast tree whose body resides within the hollow of a banyan seed; it spreads its multitude of worldly branches extensively here and there.

Indeed, a tree with hundreds of branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits exists within the interior of a seed; it is perceived by the eye. Likewise, the body exists within the atom of the "I-sense" (ahaṃtva), surrounded by the consciousness of all remaining objects of perception; this is seen only through the vision of the intellect.

For one whose body has attained the sense of "I" through inquiry, and whose very form is now the mere expanse of consciousness, the tree of worldly existence does not arise here from the seed-pit of egoism—which is unreal—once that pit has been consumed by the great fire of awakening.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Death, which consists of the total destruction [of everything], never exists. What is called "death" is merely the stabilization within one's own internal volition.
Behold these mountains, like Mandara and Meru, which appear as if being carried away before us, even though they are not mounted by the winds of the quarters, like mountains reflected in a river.
Higher and higher within, like the layers of a plantain leaf, the successions of worlds exist in the sky, some joined and others unjoined with one another.
Śrī Rāma said: "O leader of sages, I do not properly understand the unimpaired meaning of the sentence, 'Behold my cities being carried away'."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Within the vital breath (prāṇa) is the mind (citta), and within the mind is the world, existing in its various forms just as a tree exists within a seed.
When a man has died, the vital breaths merge with the winds of space, for they have flowed into the Self just as the waters of rivers merge into the waters of the ocean.
The worlds within them, though consisting solely of volition, seem to move incessantly here and there, driven by the winds of space.
I see all these directions filled on every side with winds accompanied by vital breaths, containing throbbing volitions within them.
Look here; behold, I see Mount Mandara and Meru being swept away before me by the vision of the intellect within the courtyard of the world born of imagination.
Know that within the wind reside the vital breaths whose life has ceased; within the vital breaths resides the mind; and within the mind resides the world, situated like oil within a sesame seed.
Just as the vital breaths, which consist of mind, are carried along by the winds until they become equal to space, so too are these limbs and even the worlds carried along.
Even the three worlds, along with their collections of real elements such as ether and earth, are carried forward everywhere like a fragrance, even though they are not mounted upon it.
O descendant of Raghu, those things are perceived by the intellect alone and not by the physical eye; they exist before one in the form of mental constructs, like the cities seen in one's own dreams.

Everywhere and at all times, these things exist as something even more subtle than space; because their essence consists of mere conceptual construction, they are not perceived in the slightest degree.
Because they possess a firm nature within their own worlds, those very things are entirely real for the aspect of consciousness, just as you are, owing to its omnipresence.
Like cities reflected in the current of a living river before one's eyes, things are carried away even if they have not taken root, and even those that have taken root are not carried away at all.
O Raghava, fragrances are gathered within the limbs of the wind; the worlds reside within the vital breath, yet they are composed of the nature of space.

Just as there is no difference in the internal space when a jar is carried to another country, so too there is no difference in the delusion of the three worlds within the mind, which consists of movement and other such fluctuations.
Thus, this delusion of the world, though appearing as if real, is truly unreal; it neither perishes nor arises, being in essence nothing but Brahman.
Or even when it has arisen, its various movements are not perceived by those situated within it, just as the motion of a boat is not felt by those inside its hold.

Just as the movement of a boat attached to the body is not perceived by those situated inside it, so too the movement of the earth is not perceived by those who reside upon it and are composed of its very substance.
Just as a house one yojana wide is experienced within a small space, so too does the entire world exist within a single atom of its supporting pillar.

For a person of small character considers even a vast thing to be small and a tiny thing to be immense; just as mice regard the contents of their own two palms as if they were fresh mud, so do children perceive things.
While this world called "the universe" has no real nature of its own, it is a delusion for the knower; that expansive conceptualization consists of the dharmas of other worlds.
"To one who possesses internal ignorance regarding what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, there exists delusion even if they are omniscient."
For just as a conscious whole perceives its own parts, so too does the living soul perceive the three worlds as woven within itself.
O friend, this infinite, unborn, and undecaying supreme space of consciousness is the Self; these worlds are merely the forms of its constituent parts.
Just as an iron ball, though insentient within, perceives the razor, needle, and other objects [placed upon it], so too does the ignorant individual soul perceive the delusion of the three worlds.
Just as a clod of earth, though insentient, is perceived as a bowl, a water-jar, and so forth, so too, my dear, does the living being perceive the world.
Just as the sprout of consciousness and matter within the body conceives itself to be a tree, so too this triple world is Brahman, devoid of the referent of the word "tree."
Whether conscious or unconscious, just as a mirror perceives a city—whether it is reflected within it or not—so too does Brahman perceive the three worlds.
The three worlds consist of nothing more than space, time, action, and substance; therefore, there is no difference between "I" and the world, for they are both of the nature of the Self.
When this is taught by means of a conceptual analogy, the similarity between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison exists only in one respect.
Whatever is seen here in this world, whether stationary or moving, is known as the body of the individual soul (jīva), which does not abandon its supreme atomic nature.
In that state which bestows pure vibration through the relinquishment of all perception, there is not even the slightest difference, like a flawless gemstone free from attachment.
Whatever conceptual portion is projected, wherever, in whatever manner, whenever, and by whatever means—it is consciousness itself that is thus projected.

Because it lacks consciousness, there is no mental construction in the mind, like a sprout in the sky; but because the mind possesses consciousness, know that here it is consciousness itself that constitutes conceptualization.
That splendor of conceptual construction which arises for one of unawakened disposition is not composed of reality, because the sky of consciousness is all-pervading and infinite.

Just as the splendor of conceptual construction arises, it does not actually arise for one who is awakened; because the sky of consciousness is all-pervading and infinite, that [construction] is not composed of reality.
The notion that all mental constructions are real is unimpaired even from childhood; for an object experienced internally within a dream or similar state can be obtained by someone.

Volition, latent impression, and the individual soul—these three objects are inscribed upon consciousness; though experienced, they are unreal, belonging only to that which is non-existent, not to the existent.
When truth is expressed as non-existence, one becomes liberated Śiva himself, characterized by the blossoming that arises from the total dissolution of the subtle body alone.
The worlds are carried by the winds in the sky like the cotton-wool of the silk-cotton tree; yet they are not carried, like stones, nor do they exist at all except through conceptual construction.
Thus, within this treasury containing the multitude of all objects, even in the exceedingly vast sky, there exist worlds—some intermingled with one another, and some not intermingled at all.

Because it is all-pervasive, the Supreme Consciousness assumes infinite forms, filling the quarters of space with abundant manifestations; these are as fragile as the reflection of a city in turbulent waters, yet they resemble the vast and dense cities existing within one's own heart.

Though possessing stability, they are constantly perishing moment by moment; though with eyes clearly open, they are perpetually closed; though filled with light, they are surrounded on all sides by darkness—these are the surging waves of the ocean of the nature of consciousness.

Just as the waters of rivers, though distinct and mingled together in the ocean, or like the lights of the stars, sun, moon, and planetary orbs when they have risen together in the sky; so too are these [realms].

Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, tell me what the nature of the individual soul (jīva) is, as well as its assumption of form; how it possesses the state of the Supreme Self (paramātman), and what its location is.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That which is called "the object of thought" (cetya) by its own volition (saṃkalpa), known by the alternative name "consciousness" (cit), is the infinite space of consciousness (cetanākāśa) that is designated by the term "jīva."
Neither subtle nor gross, neither empty nor anything at all; pure consciousness whose nature is self-experience, all-pervading—this is called the living being (jīva).
The wise know that the life-force (jīva) is the subtlest of the subtle, the grossest of the gross, and indeed not even a mere atom; it is all.
Know that whatever is the nature of any given object, that very thing exists there as its manifestation, because it is known exclusively through the identity of that essence.
O Rāma, in whatever manner, wherever, and whatever it quickly conceives, that very thing becomes of the nature of experience in that manner, in that place, and at that time.

Just as there is vibration in the wind, so indeed is there objective perception in the individual soul; it is to be determined solely by one's own consciousness, and not through instruction, like a yakṣa.
Just as the wind, by ceasing its vibration, becomes the very essence of stillness, so too the living being, by transcending its lack of consciousness while yet living, attains the supreme state.
Because its nature is a mass of consciousness and because of the awareness "I am," the living soul (jīva) remains after having fashioned the powers of space, time, action, and substance.
It is itself embellished or unembellished by place, time, action, and substance; though unreal, it appears as real, expansive, and having that very [unreal] alone as its body.
For with his mind he perceives within himself the form of non-existence as the state of frost-atomization; then, regarding selfhood, he sees it as resembling one's own death in a dream.
Perceiving that [dream-object] as being similar to his own body-parts while differing from them, he forgets his conscious existence and quickly returns to that very state [of non-consciousness].
Awakening in such a manner, he then quickly perceives his own self as being swollen, like the orb of the moon suddenly [emerging].
Then, within the self—which is the nature of the lunar orb—he himself perceives that fivefold consciousness, which has arisen as if by chance, distinct [from itself].
Then, he perceives those five distinct components of the five types of consciousness, and he also experiences the apertures that have their form in them.
He, the Virāt Puruṣa, shines forth afterwards as the fivefold [body]; he is the consciousness of infinite forms, the unmanifest self, free from all affliction.
This mind-made [body] has arisen from the Supreme; it is the first to emerge, as clear as space, tranquil, and consisting of the radiance of eternal bliss.
And he, whose nature is beyond the five elements, yet resembles that which consists of the five elements, is the Virāj-self, the one Puruṣa, the supreme Parameśvara.
It arises by itself and quickly dissolves by itself; it expands by itself and contracts by itself.
By means of a flood of eons created by his own volition, or even in a single moment, he arises again and again at will, and having come into being, he subsides once more.
This body of primordial nature (prakṛti) has as its sole essence the form of mind alone; it is called the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka), the subtle transportable body (ativāhika) of every being.
Subtle and gross, this self of the ether is manifest and unmanifest, devoid of end; it is both outside and inside of everything, yet it is neither anything nor indeed anything at all.

O Rāma, its eight limbs consist of the five [senses] with the mind as the sixth; these are the organs accompanied by the sense of "I-am-ness," and they are composed of both existence and non-existence.
By him these Vedas were sung together with the conceptualization of words and their meanings; by him was established the cosmic order (niyati), which remains even today exactly as it was fixed.
His head is the infinite space above, and likewise his soles of the feet are the space below; the belly of this pavilion of the Brahma-egg is the outer sky.
The endless intermediate worlds were his flanks; blood was his fluid; the mountains were his masses of flesh; and the rivers were his continuous veins.
The oceans are the reservoirs of blood, the islands are the entrails as a binding, the arms are the vast quarters of space, and the stars are the mass of body hair.
The forty-nine aggregates of wind are the vital breaths; the fierce solar orb is the bile, which is the digestive fire of the stomach.
The moon’s orb is the individual soul (jīva), phlegm, semen, and white strength; it is the mind whose essence is volition, the self whose essence is the vital core, and the supreme nectar.
It is the root of the tree of the body and the seed of the tree of karma; through the production of all states of being, it is the moon that causes delight.
That which is called the lunar orb is said to be the sovereign life-principle (jīva); it is the seed, the root, and the source of the body, karma, and the mind.
From this Moon-Virāj-Jīva, there emanate throughout the three worlds living beings, minds, actions, pleasures, and immortals.
O Virāja, these [deities] such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara are his volitions; the gods, asuras, and sky-dwellers are the wondrous manifestations of his mind.
When the nature of consciousness, while awakening, quickly contemplates the state of being like a minute particle of frost at the very beginning, it then remains right there.
Therefore, O scion of Raghu, know that this alone is the abode of the living soul; this body, consisting of five parts, is what is experienced.
From the Virāj, from the Jīva, and from the Moon, the life-principles of embodied beings issue forth as food-born entities in the form of a diffusion of dew.
These very [elements] become the living souls within the bodies of embodied beings; having become the mind, they exert themselves as the cause of action throughout successive births.
In this way, thousands of Virāṭs and hundreds of Mahākalpas have passed, and others will likewise come to pass; they exist with various modes of conduct.

By means of this existence, which consists of universal experience and is non-different from the supreme state, and which possesses the union with the great limbs that are free from limits, he stands as the Supreme Person, the Virāj.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This person of volition (saṃkalpa-puruṣa), whatever he himself conceives, becomes that very thing and of such a nature, like the sky consisting of the five elements.
O Rāma, the wise know that this entire world-born universe is His volition; it is spread out, having such a form, and directed toward the objects of the fivefold self.
The Virāṭ is the cause of the entire multitude of objects in the world; therefore, effects are indeed identical with their cause.
Just as this Virāj himself is the Virāj within each individual self, he expands within his own consciousness as one who possesses awareness, and not as one devoid of awareness.
Thus, from the crawling insect up to the wind-god, this delusion has arisen; even within an atom, it possesses the vast extent of a mountain, like a tree contained within a seed-vessel.
From the crawling insect up to Rudra, the Virāṭ exists within each individual self; yet even in the Supreme Self, it exists through the awakening of the infinite Self, and not through non-awakening.
Just as this expansion has come to be within the Virāj-self, so too is it here within every single being, even down to the size of an atom.
In the ultimate sense, there is nothing whatsoever, whether gross or subtle, anywhere; whatever is extended wherever it may be, that is experienced immediately as it is.
The mind was born from the moon; the moon arose from the mind. Or rather, life arises from life; this is but a single existence, like the fluidity inherent in water.
They know the living soul (jīva) to be the essence of semen, resembling a drop of frost; from that very source, the mass of immovable bliss proceeds.

She perceives that [object] which appears as such, complete and situated within herself by means of her own self; therein she assumes identity with it, and by that means she takes on a form composed of that.
When this consciousness of the living being attains the state of the five elements, there exists therein no cause whatsoever, nor is there any state of being an effect.
Since there is no exclusion of a counter-positive for the two intrinsic natures, the expression of their own nature here does not follow the actual state of affairs.

The living soul (jīva) exists as life itself, and by virtue of its own nature as life, it appears both internally and externally of its own accord; yet it is not perceived [as a material object], just like the wind.
Enveloped as if by mist, intent upon unreal objects, the self consisting of breath does not perceive the path, like one born blind.

Through the world-expansion (jagajjṛmbhikā), the individual soul assumes duality instead of its own unity; like the wind enveloped by the power of vibration (spandaśakti), it does not perceive itself.
The dissolution of ignorance—the great knot consisting of false objects of cognition, which is non-existent yet takes the form of the object "I"—is known as liberation.

With dense consciousness entirely departed, remain indeed without perceiving "I" on all sides; being of a single form characterized by non-conceptual dense consciousness, you are the ground where existence and non-existence, as well as that which is both, arise eternally.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, one should always be a man of knowledge, not a kinsman of knowledge; I consider an ignorant person better than the state of being a kinsman of knowledge.
Śrī Rāma said: Who is called a kinsman of knowledge, and who is called a knower? What is the fruit of being a kinsman of knowledge, and what is the fruit of being a knower?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: He who explains and recites the scripture for the sake of enjoyment, like a craftsman, but does not strive in its practice, is called a "kinsman of knowledge."
He in whom awareness is seen to bear fruit amidst the vibrations of karma is called a "kinsman of knowledge" (jñānabandhu), because he subsists by the craft of awareness.
Those who, satisfied with mere clothing and food, understand the fruits of the scriptures as kinsmen of knowledge—one should know them as artisans of the meaning of the scriptures.
He who abides in the Dharma characterized by active engagement (pravṛtti) as it is found in what has been heard is called a "kinsman of knowledge" because his knowledge is not far removed.
They know self-knowledge to be true knowledge; as for those other forms of knowledge, they are merely reflections of knowledge, because they do not perceive the essential reality.
Those who, failing to attain the knowledge of the Self, are satisfied with a mere fragment of other forms of knowledge, are remembered as "kinsmen of knowledge" despite their arduous efforts.

Without the pacification of the expansion of that which is to be known through knowledge and so forth, one should not cultivate a satisfied mind here; O Rāma, having attained the kinship of knowledge, rejoice, and do not take delight in worldly enjoyments which are like diseases.

In this regard, one should perform blameless work for the sake of food; one should take food for the sake of sustaining the life-breaths; the life-breaths should be sustained for the sake of inquiring into reality; and reality should be inquired into so that there may be no further suffering.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: He who, through knowledge, being established in the object of knowledge, does not perceive the mind or even the non-mind as the fruit of action—he is called a man of knowledge.
He who, having correctly understood the true knowledge, perceives through that knowledge all actions as being devoid of latent impressions—that wise one is called a "knower."
He whose inner coolness is observed by the wise in his desires, being uniquely peaceful and uncontrived—he is designated as a man of knowledge.

That realization which leads to non-rebirth is what truly bears the name of "knowledge" (jñāna); everything else—providing clothing and food, as well as the various arrangements for livelihood through crafts—is merely a means of subsistence.
He who remains free from desire and mental constructs while engaged in actions that have fallen into the natural flow of life, with a heart as vast as space—he is called a wise man.
Entities appear as if they proceed without a cause; though non-existent, they remain as if they were existent.
Through appearances and disappearances, through existence and non-existence, and through becoming and non-becoming, they subsequently become causes for one another through mutual causal activities.
For that which is non-existent, such as a hare's horn or the water of a mirage—which cannot be obtained even by looking—what kind of cause could there possibly be?
Those who search for the cause of non-existent things, such as a hare's horn, are reaching for the shoulder of the grandson of a barren woman’s son.
This alone is the swift cause for the non-appearance of unreal things: namely, that which is called "non-perception," occurring at the very moment of perception's destruction.
When the individual soul perceives the insentient as its own nature, it becomes the Supreme Self; but when it perceives the sentient as its own nature, it remains merely the individual soul.

This living soul is indeed the Supreme Self itself; though perceiving the insentient, it attains the state of a *sahakāra* tree through its transformation into sap, just as a mango fruit becomes a *sahakāra* through the attainment of juice.
Perceiving consciousness, the individual soul (jīva) alone remains; the jīva is worn out through births and lives that have become decrepit.
For those who have attained the supreme vision, their method is like that of water: it is always a state of non-conceptualization regarding form and light, a vibration that is yet without vibration.
For those who have attained the supreme vision and have seen the far shore of the splendor of the visible, even that which exists does not exist as an extended perception for them.
Know that for those who have attained the supreme vision, all movement as well as non-movement here is like water, occurring solely through the power of non-perception.
Unencumbered by the pursuit of form or light, like one whose bonds have been released, the wise engage in actions just as the wind moves through the leaves of a tree.
Those who have attained the supreme vision and see the further shore of saṃsāra do not praise action, just as one living by a river does not praise a well.
O sinless one, those deluded ones who possess bound attachments praise ritual action; through that, they proceed without awakening, even though it is appropriate according to the Śruti and Smṛti.
The senses fall upon an object like a vulture pouncing on meat; having restrained them with the mind, one should sit disciplined and intent upon that [goal].

There is no gold without its arrangement, nor does Brahman exist without its manifestation; however, for one of disciplined intellect, the auspicious [Brahman] is expressed by means of the words and meanings of "manifestation" and so forth.
When a single darkness has arisen at the end of the age, worldly activity becomes undifferentiated and devoid of appearance, just as it is within the dense mass of Brahman.

Just as within the belly of a cloud there exists the nature of moving and non-moving beings consisting of their own self-awareness, so too does the sovereign Mistress exist as the very essence of all beings.

Just as within water there is the vibration of its own nature consisting of both duality and non-duality regarding the various portions of the water, so too within Brahman exists the perception of the elements.
Just as the creation of the portions of the sky appears within the sky—which is both dual and non-dual in nature—so too does it appear within the partless Śiva, who is non-different from it.
The world exists within the form of the "I," and the form of the "I" exists within the world; they are interwoven with one another like the layers of a plantain tree.
Through the apertures of form, light, and mental attention, the living soul perceives the creation as if situated outside, just as a mountain perceives a lake within itself.
This living soul perceives itself as the world without cause, just as gold perceives itself as bracelets and the like; not seeing that [gold], it does not see [the world].
Though living, they do not live; though dead, they do not die; and though existing, they are as if non-existent—those auspicious ones who know the further and near shores.
The awakened one, even while performing all actions, does not perceive them, just as a person staying at home who is preoccupied with the cattle pen does not notice the household chores.

Just as the Virāj is in the heart, and just as the moon resides within every body, so the individual soul (jīva) exists in the form of a drop of frost—large when the body is large, and small when it is small.
I, the Self, undergoes the conceptualization of being a triangle; though non-existent, the conscious body imagines itself to have the appearance of existence.
The self, which is the living soul (jīva), abides in the body within the triangular heart-center and the essence of semen, like its own fragrance in a flower.
The consciousness situated in the seed-syllable "Aham" spreads from the feet to the head throughout the entire pavilion of the cosmic egg, just as moonlight radiates everywhere.
The water of sensation, flowing through the conduit of the apertures of the senses, pervades the three worlds, just as smoke spreads through the sky by becoming clouds.
Although perception exists within and without this entire body, nevertheless, there is a dense latent impression (vāsanā) here in the vital seed (śukra).
The individual soul (jīva) consists of mere volition; whatever volition it forms remains within the heart, and having become that very thing, it immediately and clearly flows outward.
And apart from that which remains as it is, devoid of thought and comparable to a mountain, the delusion of "I" is not pacified by any state whatsoever.
Even as it is being contemplated through reflection, it is to be cultivated like the sky; by means of tranquility, you shall gradually achieve the pacification of the sense of "I."
Those who know that reality conduct themselves here free from the conceived and the conceiving, without form, light, or mental reflection, like silent logs of wood.
He who is the contemplation of nothing whatsoever is said to be liberated; while living, he is as clear as the sky and is evidently free from bondage.
The consciousness established as "I" spreads from the feet to the head throughout the entire body, just as the light of the sun pervades the cosmic egg.
"The eye is vision, the tongue is tasting, and that which is hearing becomes the ear"—having bound oneself with these five such latent impressions (*vāsanās*), one sinks into them.
The state of consciousness arises undiminished as the mind from one part of itself, just as the all-pervading sap in the springtime emerges as a sprout upon the earth.
For one who contemplates the non-existence of entities that have not yet arisen here, suffering will never cease for that effortless person.
Clothed in whatever manner, fed by whatever means, and sleeping wherever one may be, such a person shines here like a sovereign emperor.
Though endowed with all latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he is free from impressions; though empty within, his self is not empty, like the sky filled with wind.
Whether sitting, lying down, or traveling, he remains conscious through effort, like one who is drowsy yet finds rest in the cessation of the mental fabrications of the manas.
For the Puruṣa is pure consciousness alone; though all-pervading, he abides in the clear essence of the body, just as fragrance resides in the filaments of a lotus.
They know that a living being is pure consciousness alone, and the world is its outward expansion; the state of abiding within the Self is the supreme non-world—this is the ground of the teaching.
Become dispassionate toward all things, such as worldly power and prosperity; making your heart like a stone, act in such a way that you may attain ultimate well-being.
O virtuous Rāghava, since you possess no mind, let there be for you both the voidness and the non-voidness of the heart, just as there is for a stone because it lacks a mind.

Regarding all actions, whether existent or non-existent, there is no distinction whatsoever between one who knows that [reality] and one who does not, except for the state of being free from latent tendencies (nirvāsanatva).
This very consciousness, when it is opened, becomes the world; that supreme reality is like the eye, pervasive and nameless, when it is closed.
The entire visible world perishes; having perished, it is born again. That which has neither perished nor arisen—that is the Reality, and that you are.
For the manifestation of existence is rootless; even when cultivated, it does not exist. Like water in a mirage, it does not produce the sprout of existence.

The cultivation of the thought "I am" is severed by the vision of reality as it truly is; once seen, it does not arise again, like a seed that has been burnt within and can no longer produce a sprout.
Whether performing action or not performing it, the person who is free from passion, free from affliction, devoid of mental constructs, and eternally liberated, abides in the Self.
When the mind is stilled, the kinsmen of enjoyments are completely pacified for the sake of peace; yet their inherent nature is not exhausted, for it is said that the mind is their mine.
The wise living being, free from all density and consisting of pure light, attains the Supreme; though it appears as other, it is not other, like the sun at midday within its own heat.
The form that appears entirely within the mind of a person standing in one place after having come from afar—that form belongs to the Supreme Self.
That which is the beautiful camphor of the sky, which itself causes wonder, knows itself as the infinite, internally unmanifest world.

Indeed, even while remaining here, a person who has attained the inexhaustible peace that is radiant with the cessation of the wandering through existence, who is like a lamp left unattended, and who follows the Lord of the World, shines with joy in the sky.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having cast off all worldly tendencies through the impression of dispassion, arise and depart from this nature, like Maṅki who was marked [by the deer].
Formerly there was a brahmin named Maṅkin who was firm in his vows; hear how he attained nirvāṇa after being awakened by me.
Once, having descended from the expanse of the sky to the earth, I was invited by someone for the sake of your grandfather.
Wandering across the earth, I have reached your grandfather’s city and arrived at a certain vast wilderness, scorched by great heat.
O Rāma, it was indeed strewn with dust, its sands shimmering and heated, its further shore and limits unseen, and marked here and there by footprints.
It was characterized by the tranquility of its undisturbed winds, light, waters, and earth; it was pervasive, empty, yet possessed of great activity, like the stainless reality of Brahman.
Like ignorance, it has reached a state of delusion and a mirage through error; it is an expansive dullness, empty, and clouded by the mist of disorientation.
Then, as I was wandering through that great forest, I saw before me a traveler speaking out of exhaustion.
The traveler said: "Alas! The sun, with its intense heat, leads only to exhaustion; this wicked heat causes torment, like an association with a villain."
The vital points seem to throb, and fire seems to flash in the heat; the forest ranges, with their clusters of shriveling shoots, are scorched.
Therefore, I shall first enter this village situated ahead; having quickly dispelled my fatigue here, I will proceed swiftly upon the road.
Having reflected thus, when he desired to enter the Kirāta village situated before him, I then spoke these words.
O friend of auspicious form, who has not yet fully understood the path free from passion; O traveler on the great forest road of the celestial path, welcome to you!
For a long time, O traveler on the lower path, you shall find no rest upon this road through this desolate village in the human realm, even though you are weary.
Resting in a village, which is the abode of the vulgar, does not exist at all; indeed, thirst only increases further by drinking salt water.
These living beings, who take refuge solely in the village, are like trembling sprouts or like deer wandering upon improper paths, fearing even the slightest movement.
They do not quiver amidst discursive thoughts, nor do they blaze within sensory experiences; they do not tremble before misconduct, being as if made of stone and machinery.
Those of burnt intellect, whose manly efforts are entirely devoted to sensual desires, wealth, passion, and hatred, take delight in actions that are sweet only at first sight.
Noble by birth, expansive, cool, and rich in flavor—this speech does not find confidence here, like a bank of clouds in a desert.
Better to be blind and dwell in a cave, better to be an insect inside a stone, and better to be a lame deer in the desert than to associate with vulgar people.
Sweet as the taste of a momentary blink, yet fading in the next instant; solely intent on destruction, they are like drops of poison for those of vulgar mind.
In houses that are dilapidated and crumbling, the unrighteous winds of the villages blow, scattering clouds of ash and busily tossing away grass, leaves, and forests.
O sinless one, when he had spoken thus, I was then addressed by him with these words, which comforted me like a bath in the waters of nectar.

The traveler said: "O Blessed One, who are you? You are a perfect soul, a great soul; how is it that you, possessing self-mastery, look upon the world without agitation, like a wayfarer observing a village festival?"

Have you drunk the nectar of immortality? Are you a sovereign emperor or a universal monarch? For even though you are destitute of all possessions, you shine for a long time as if you were completely fulfilled.
You are empty and you are full; you are as if whirling and yet you are firm. You are not everything, and yet you are everything; you are nothing at all, and yet you are something indeed.
O Sage, why is it that your form is both tranquil and lovely, radiant yet non-obstructive, withdrawn and yet majestic?
Though situated upon the earth, you stand as if above all the worlds in the sky; you are free from attachment, yet you appear as if firmly established.
It does not extend into objects, nor does it exist as the nature of objects; indeed, your mind, pure like the moon, remains composed of nectar.
Possessing the arts yet free from blemish within, cool, radiant, and equanimous, you shine like the full moon filled with the essence of elixirs.
But by your will, I perceive both existence and non-existence within your consciousness; this entire circle of saṃsāra stands within it like a fruit upon a sprout.
"O Brahmin, I am indeed this man named Maṅki, born of the lineage of Śāṇḍilya; O illustrious one, I have come here in the course of my pilgrimage."
Having traveled a very long distance and now beheld the sacred fords, he is prepared to go to his own home after a long time.
And my mind, having become detached from home, had no inclination to go back after seeing the beings within the belly of the world resembling flashes of lightning.
O Blessed One, out of compassion, please tell us truly of yourself; for the minds of the virtuous are indeed deep and serene lakes.
In the presence of great beings who show friendship at the very first sight, living creatures blossom and find comfort like lotuses.
Out of delusion, I consider this mind of mine—which arises from the wandering of saṃsāra—to be incapable of abandoning it; therefore, may you, out of compassion for my awakening, [help me].
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O one of great intelligence, I am Vasiṣṭha; I am a sage whose home is the sky. For some purpose, O royal sage, I have arrived upon this path."
Do not fall into despondency; you have entered the path of the wise. You have, for the most part, reached the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra.
Neither a mind magnanimous with the power of dispassion, nor speech such as this, nor a form characterized by tranquility belongs to one who is not a great soul.
Just as a gem attains a state of stainlessness through gentle rubbing, so too the mind attains discernment through the ripening of austerities.
"What do you wish to know? How do you wish to abandon saṃsāra? I consider that what has been taught is accomplished through actions."

One whose latent impressions are stainless, whose mind is supreme, and whose intellect is thoroughly secluded by the splendor of the people, is indeed fit for the stainless lotus; this is said for one who has resolved to cross over the world.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When I had spoken the word "mine," Maṅki fell at my feet and, his eyes filled with joy, spoke these words while still on the path.
Maṅki said: "O Blessed One, my eyes have wandered extensively through the ten directions, yet I have not found a virtuous man who could destroy my doubts."
Today I have obtained the fruit of the very essence of all bodily constituents; yet, O Blessed One, I am weary from beholding these conditions that bring about the defects of saṃsāra.
Born again and again, and perishing again and again, there is constant wandering through pleasure and pain; for all things are indeed suffering, as they are inevitably destined to reach their end.
O Sage, pleasures are indeed extreme sufferings; therefore, sufferings are better than them. Because they end in firm suffering, pleasures cause me pain.
In this way, O Rāma, just as my very suffering has turned into happiness, so too have my teeth, hair, and intestines reached a state of decay along with my body.
The intellect, intent on falling from a high station, lacks resolve; due to its evil intentions, it does not perceive the dense thicket of beautiful sprouts as something luminous.
Like the hollow of a rotten tree in a wretched village filled with the droppings of woodpeckers, the mind is in a perpetually sinful state, inhabited by vultures in the form of latent tendencies.
The intellect is as fierce and crooked as a thorny tree or creeper; it is like a night blinded by darkness, characterized by the exhaustion of life.
Having reached a state where light has vanished due to incessant anxiety, he extracts no flavor from anything; though already as good as lost, he does not perish.
