For us, craving is neither flowering nor bearing fruit, like a withered creeper; action is submerged within action, that which is called latent impression, leading toward non-action.
Life has grown old among people, yet the ocean of existence has not been crossed; day by day, the hope for enjoyments swells, bringing only fear.
In one whose nature is both full and incomplete, the great calamities of fortune—which cause the fever of anxiety and are like pits, thorns, and trees—are indeed exhausted.
Though it was perfect and uninjured, that [lotus] withered through separation; like a bright cave-dwelling where a jewel shines within, yet remains in darkness.
The discerning do not touch me when my mind is agitated by waves, empty, as wretched as a dried-up ocean, and solely intent upon the objects of the senses.
Like a *śleṣmātaka* tree standing amidst thorns and impurity, this great undertaking is utterly unreal, like a wind that stirs up restless arjuna trees.
The mind, not having reached death, leaps toward suffering while it is still empty; yet it bears the moon and stars of association with the treatises and the company of the virtuous.

The night of ignorance has not merely been diminished, but destroyed by that yakṣa flourishing with the sense of "I"; it is a lion to the intoxicated elephant of the darkness of ignorance, and a fire to the grass of karma.
The sun of transformation has not yet risen, though the night of latent tendencies has ended; from me, the elephant of the mind perceives the unreal as if it were real.
The senses cut one to pieces; I do not know what will happen, for even the vision of the scriptures—which is relied upon by the wise for crossing over—is not being resorted to.

That [ignorance] also, like a lack of vision for one who is blind, causes the onset of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*). Therefore, O Father, tell me—who am asking—as to what should be done here in this terrible state of extreme delusion for the sake of future welfare.

The mists of delusion subside like those in autumn when a virtuous person has arrived; likewise, all directions become stainless. May the word "Truth" be sung by the company of holy men through you, who have awakened me and granted peace from worldly existence.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Perception, ideation, latent impression, and mental construction—these terms, though devoid of objective reality, expand here in the world for the sake of worldly suffering.
Know that feeling (vedanā) is the cultivation of the basis for all defects; in it alone are calamities found, just as creepers exist within sweet nectar.
In the dense path of saṃsāra, carried along by the force of latent impressions, the succession of events unfolds through a diverse flood of occurrences.
For the discerning one, the delusion of saṃsāra together with its latent impressions perishes at the end of Mādhava, just as the moisture of the earth gradually evaporates.
Of this world-plantain tree, which causes the growth of latent impressions, this [desire] is like the sweet sap-streak of a wild vine upon a forest-creeping plantain.

Due to the blindness of saṃsāra, the essence consisting of latent impressions (vāsanā) arises within consciousness, just as the essence of the spring month remains on the earth in the form of a forest.
Apart from the stainless pure consciousness, nothing at all exists; there is nothing else whatsoever, just as in the infinite sky there is nothing other than emptiness.
The firm conviction that "there is no other self than sensation" is ignorance; this is delusion, and it is the pervasive cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
That which is established through non-observation perishes by observation alone; being unreal in nature yet appearing as real, it vanishes in an instant like a child’s phantom.

When all perceptions of the visible are sublated, they attain oneness through their essence being consciousness, just as the full currents of rivers from the entire surface of the earth merge into the ocean.

Just as a vessel made of clay is not perceived when devoid of clay, so too the object of consciousness is not perceived when devoid of consciousness, because it consists of consciousness and originates from consciousness.

That object which is already awakened within awakening is what is designated as "to be awakened"; awakening does not awaken that which is unawakened, because there would be a difference in nature and so forth.
In the seer, the seeing, and the seen, each is nothing but pure consciousness; therefore, that which is other than this has no reality whatsoever, like a flower in the sky.
A homogeneous [cognition] attains unity with that which is homogeneous; therefore, let there be a determination of oneness based on their mutual experience.
If wood, stones, and the like did not possess the nature of consciousness, then they would never be perceived, just like non-existent things.
But when this visible splendor is seen to consist solely of the nature of pure consciousness, then, while being both other than and not other than it, it is realized by that consciousness.
This entire visible world pervading the universe is extended as mere consciousness, just as wind is mere vibration and the ocean is mere water.
For even though these things, such as lacquer and wood, are mixed together, they are not mutually experienced [as one] when mixed; yet they are experienced as a unity only through mutual experience.
For unity is indeed mutual experience, and unity is the mutual awareness of one another; it is like that of two waters or two portions of milk, not like that of wood and lac.
"I am" leads to bondage; "I am not" leads to liberation. Since this much bondage depends entirely on oneself, what incapacity can there be?
Like the cognition of two moons or the perception of water in a mirage, why have I arisen as something non-existent, when in truth I have never arisen at all?
"‘This is mine’ leads to bondage; ‘I am not [this]’ alone leads to liberation. Since this much of reality depends solely upon oneself, why is there ignorance?"
The relationship between the pit and the jujube fruit, or the state of the jar and space—that too is not a distinct relation; for unity is indeed mutual awareness.
Mutual awareness is indeed a unity that persists even when divided into parts; whether non-inert or inert, it never abandons its singular nature.
That which is non-inert does not become inert, for intrinsic natures are immutable; and where that which is non-inert is seen as inert, there is duality, and no unity exists therein.
Enveloped by the force of latent impressions and consisting of hundreds of evil transformations, they go further and further down, like rocks fallen from a mountain that rush downward.
For human straws, driven here and there by the winds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), those sufferings descend; it is impossible to describe them.

Having wandered extensively like balls struck by the palms of the hands, people fall into the hells, impassioned by their cravings; there, worn out by suffering, they eventually become like something else once again after the passage of time.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Indeed, for one fallen into the dense thicket of the path of worldly existence, hundreds of thousands of various events descend like insects at the arrival of the rainy season.
Indeed, all these phenomena are mutually unconnected, like stones in a forest; it is only through mental cultivation that a chain of connection is perceived among them.
Due to the dullness of the mind, it stands like a dense forest with the trees of worldly events, just as a grove in spring is filled with the coloring of aesthetic flavors in this world.
Alas! How strange it is that these elemental beings, rendered powerless by the force of their latent impressions, experience pleasures and pains throughout their births.
Oh, how extremely perverse is this latent tendency (vāsanā), by the power of which people experience within themselves this delusion regarding things that do not even exist!

What difference is there between the moon and the wise man—both of whom bring delight, are as if dead to worldly attachments, are pure, illuminate all things, are cool toward all objects, and possess true knowledge?
What difference is there between a fool who desires whatever he wishes without considering what comes before or after, and a child who lacks all restraint?

Tell me, who among the ignorant would not abandon even their own flesh when it is seized, up to the very end of their life? Who indeed would not do so? Who, like a fish, would not release it? Tell me.
Indeed, all these things—bodies, wives, wealth, and so forth—are as fragile as a bowl of sand that quickly dries up and crumbles.
Even as you wander through hundreds of wombs, from the peak of Brahma down to a blade of grass, for as long as an eon, there is no peace of mind except through tranquility.
Merely by reflecting upon it, even the slightest scent of bondage does not afflict one, just as the unevenness of a path does not trouble a traveler who keeps his eyes fixed ahead.
Desire will devour one whose mind is not attentive; what can a demon do to a Buddha who is ever vigilant?
Just as the expansion of the gaze consists merely in the perception of form, so this world exists as the self that is the mere expansion of consciousness, together with the sense of "I."
O Slayer of the Enemy, just as the closing of the eyes brings the cessation of the perception of all forms, so too does the "covering of consciousness" bring the cessation of all that is visible.
This world, though non-existent, I—the pure consciousness—spreads out within the void; by means of a slight expansion, it quickly manifests like the vibration of the wind.
This very reality, though appearing as if it were a day, does not act otherwise and yet prospers; just as clay attains the state of a jar through gold, which is inseparable from its own nature.
Just as the sky is mere emptiness, just as the wind is mere vibration, and just as waves and the like are mere water, so too is the world mere consciousness.
Know that the three worlds are nothing but uninterrupted, partless pure consciousness—tranquil like the sky, or like a mountain reflected in water.
In that wise one who has attained the tranquility of nirvāṇa, there arises a coolness such that even these moons within him become like sparks from a blazing fire.
In this world, which is void, where the self is the absolute peace of the unextended Śiva, what is produced by whom, and how—when there is no light and no other light?
That which is called the word "Brahman" is the innate form of everything; wherein there is no contradiction whatsoever, all is composed of that, the imperishable.
As for this state of being an object which is experienced as being sublated, and whatever constitutes that sublation—having observed this, we do not know it to exist, just like a flower in the sky.
O Knower, remain peaceful like a great stone, with the internal mind departed; this is neither thought nor the conceit of "I," but is infinite, unborn, and undecaying.
For one who abides in their own nature, which is like space, there occurs a non-perception of the limbs due to the lack of firmness in practice, just like a transformation in a dream.
The Brahma-creator conceives the variegated world even upon a wall-less void, without any material cause or accumulation; indeed, there is no agent whatsoever, nor is there anything at all.
Whatever it expands, that is indeed its own state abiding there in such a way; since the visible does not exist, the visible is non-existent—therefore, who, where, or what could act?

"I am happy," thus one is happy; "I am miserable," thus one is miserable. All beings, though established in their own true nature and being of the essence of space, appear as if they were made of earth.
For all entities, even though they are of the nature of the space of consciousness, their state of being material is entirely false, like that of mountains in a dream.

Existence, when delineated by the sense of "I," is subject to the fluctuations of delusion; in the absence of that [sense of "I"], there is the state of resting solely in one's own nature, characterized by tranquility.

Just as for you, the meaning of the word "bracelet" exists as something distinct from gold, so too, for one whose self is peaceful, there exists no real ego-sense as something distinct [from that peace].
He is extinguished, free from mental activity, silent, both the doer and the non-doer, and cool; he remains as pure awareness alone, utterly tranquil, empty yet completely full.
Free from latent impressions and intent upon the motionless, like the limbs of a mechanical puppet, that knower remains exactly as he is, even while engaged in worldly activity.
Just as the limbs of an infant lying on a couch throb or do not throb at all without any conscious effort of its own, so too are the limbs of one who has realized the Self.

For one who is the singular awakening beyond all awakening, who is free from hope, seeking, and desire, and whose nature is the peaceful and infinite Self—whence could there be any further mental synthesis?
How indeed can there be a synthesis for one who is neither a seer nor an object of sight, whose nature is not vision and who is formless—especially for such a witness who is independent?
Expectation alone is dense bondage; equanimity alone is liberation. For one who has come to rest within that which is endowed with all sounds, what remains to be seen?
Since this earthly body is as unreal as a limb in one's own dream, and consists of nothing but delusion, from where, where, for whom, and what could there be any dependence?
With all worldly desires stilled, with every curiosity vanished, and with sensation cast aside, the wise one abides in pure, absolute knowledge.
Then, by means of that which is heard, even great delusion is entirely abandoned by the one possessed of learning, just as a snake sheds its skin right there.
Performing his duties as they arose in the natural flow of life, he had cast off all latent tendencies; thus, at the end of a hundred years, he remained on the mountain in meditative absorption.
In that state, for as long as it lasts, he remains with qualities like a stone; yet the yogi, whose faculties are completely stilled, awakens when being instructed.

By this word of discernment, O Rāghava, may you attain peace and sport with a radiant mind; let not your passion-laden intellect fall into despondency, for it would vanish in an instant like a cloudless autumnal bank of clouds.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Be liberated and peaceful in soul, following whatever comes to you; O gentle one, though existing, remain as if non-existent, as if fashioned from crystal.
When everything exists within that single, all-pervading Self, how can there be any perception of multiplicity in that which is neither one nor many?

Everything is devoid of beginning and end, a void entirely filled with the reality of consciousness; what impairment could there be to the reality of consciousness during the arising and destruction of the body?
For inert playthings manifest due to the flickering wonder of consciousness; through its lack of flickering, they are perceived like waves in water.
Just as the suspicion that a white cloud is a cloth does not bear fruit, so too this suspicion that "this body is I" is not real.

Do not remain immersed in that which is non-substantial, for it bestows manifold worldly existence; instead, for the sake of your ultimate welfare, contemplate today that which is substantial—the primordial source of infinite bliss.
Within this very Self, which is the infinite sky of consciousness, there exists no limitation whatsoever; may that supreme reality, which is thus, be your highest attainment.
Thus, you who possess such certainty are indeed the stainless one; the meditator, the object of meditation, as well as the act of meditation, and even reality itself, do not exist at all.
The seer, the seen, and the act of seeing are but the manifestations of consciousness alone; apart from that awareness, there is no other meditator nor any object of meditation.
When the moon of the first day of the lunar fortnight rises and the wind of universal dissolution blows, the reality of the self remains equanimous and serene; it neither agitates nor subsides.

Just as one traveling by boat perceives the trembling of stumps, trees, mountains, and so forth, and just as there is the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl, so too is the perception of the body and other objects for the mind.
Just as the body and so forth belong to the mind, so too does the mind belong to the body; likewise, the individual soul belongs to the supreme state—therefore, whence can there be duality?
All this is one, peaceful Brahman, expanded through the realization of consciousness; there is no such thing as the world and so forth, nor does any other delusion exist.
Just as a forest does not exist in the sky, nor moisture in sand, nor lightning in the orb of the moon, so too do the body and other such things not exist in the mind.
Since this world-delusion does not exist at all, do not fear; know this alone to be the supreme truth, O best among those who know the truth.
That delusion of yours which held that "the world exists" or "it does not exist" has today been stilled by my instruction; what other cause for bondage could there be?
Just as pots, water-jars, vases, and so forth consist of nothing but clay, so too this world consists of nothing but mind; and that [mind] is brought to cessation through analytical investigation.

In calamities and prosperity, in existence and non-existence, with a consciousness free from desire, joy, and dejection, liberated through the gentle realization of the "I-notion," remain as you truly are and do not dissolve.

O Rāma, moon of your own family’s ocean, if you remain having realized the reality as it truly is, then—having abandoned joy, sorrow, desire, aversion, and the like—remain as you wish or abide as you please.

Śrī Rāma said: O All-pervading Lord, tell me once more the true nature of seeds and sprouts, of human actions that bring about birth, and of those things which are designated by the term "destiny" (daiva).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This very vibration of consciousness, which ranges from destiny and action down to a jar and its state of being a jar, has attained the form of the "person" (puruṣa) in the world.
Apart from the vibration of consciousness, what could manhood or action possibly be? For this entire world, consisting of jars, pits, cloths, and so forth, has been created by this alone.
The fortune of the world proceeds from the vibration of consciousness accompanied by latent impressions; indeed, saṃsāra ceases from the vibration of consciousness devoid of latent impressions.

For they know that the vibration of consciousness which is without latent impressions (vāsanā) is non-vibration; even when vibrating, it is a non-manifesting vibration, by which one is not carried away by whirlpools and the like.
O Rāma, there is not even the slightest difference between consciousness and its own vibration, nor between creation and human action, except for the portion consisting of conceptual construction.

Just as the duality of water and its waves arises from conceptual construction and is not real, so too here are the living being and its karma, which are of the nature of the movement of consciousness.
O Rāma, action itself is the person, and the person itself is the state of action; know that these two are non-different, just as coldness is inseparable from frost.
As snow is coldness, and as coldness is snow; so is this living being his karma, and as the living being is, so is that karma.
Divinity, action, humanity, and so forth are merely synonymous terms for the very essence of the vibration of consciousness; they do not exist as separate actions or entities.

Through vibration, consciousness becomes the seed of the world; through non-vibration, it attains the state of being seedless. And that very [consciousness] is the sprout, because the beauty of the sprout already exists within it.
And consciousness, by its very nature, is in some respects motionless and in others mobile; it is infinite, like a single vast ocean, established within the sequence of space and time.

The vibration of consciousness, possessing latent impressions (*vāsanā*), is here the causeless seed; having come into being, it attains the state of a cause for the series of sprouts that are the body and so forth.
Even regarding the movement within the seeds of grass, creepers, vines, shrubs, and plants, the seed is nothing but the vibration of consciousness; for that [vibration], no seed exists.
There is no difference between the seed and the sprout, just as there is none between fire and its heat; know that the seed itself is the sprout, and know that action itself is the human being.
The consciousness, throbbing within the sheath of the earth, produces the sprouts of stationary beings—whether gross or subtle, soft or hard—like bubbles upon the water.
Who is capable of causing sprouts as hard as adamant to flourish from the extremely delicate sheath of the earth, were it not for the funeral pyre?
Consciousness, abiding within the essence of the vital energy of living beings, extends the moving and pervasive world, just as the sap residing within a creeper produces flowers and fruit.
If consciousness were omnipresent but not exceedingly powerful, then who would be capable of causing the agitation of gods, asuras, and mountains?
This is the primordial seed of all moving and stationary beings; it consists merely of the vibration of consciousness, and no other seed for it exists.

There is no difference between the seed and the sprout, between conceptual constructions, between action, the person, and karma, or between waves, ripples, and billows; there is no such distinction in reality.
Salutations forever to that Great One, the wise Paśupati, in whom duality exists as the seed and the sprout of both man and karma.
The essence of latent impressions (vāsanā) residing within the seed of consciousness gives rise to the sprouting of the embryo; burn that away with the fire of non-attachment.
Whether acting or not acting, the wise know that non-sinking of the mind amidst auspicious and inauspicious deeds is what constitutes non-attachment.
Alternatively, the eradication of latent impressions (vāsanā) itself is known as non-attachment; by whatever means possible, you must indeed accomplish that within yourself.
By that very method and through human effort by which you understand this, the total uprooting of the sprouts of latent impressions (vāsanā) is itself the supreme Śiva.
By means of human effort, or in whatever way you know how, restrain the portion consisting of the sense of "I"; this is the dissolution of latent impressions (vāsanākṣaya).
There is indeed no other way to transcend saṃsāra than through human effort—this effort which consists in the dissolution of egoism and is known as the exhaustion of latent impressions (vāsanā).

Right from the beginning, consciousness alone exists here; that is the sprout, and it is the seed. That is karma, and that is the person (puruṣa); that is destiny (daiva), and that is the auspicious and the inauspicious.
In the beginning, there is no seed other [than consciousness], nor is there a sprout, nor indeed a person; there is neither karma nor destiny and the like, for it is consciousness alone that arises.

O virtuous one, there is no seed, nor indeed is there even a sprout; neither is there karma, nor is there a person. Rather, it is the single consciousness that has arisen through this splendor of designations, like an actor appearing in the roles of gods, humans, and asuras.

Having cultivated this very certainty free from affliction and having utterly abandoned the doubt regarding the deliberation of human action, remain—free from latent impressions and released from all mental constructions—in the body of pure consciousness, indeed according to your own desired wish.

O Rāma, with all desires stilled and free from doubt, established in pure consciousness alone, you perform all necessary actions; delighting in the Self as your sole pleasure, your every wish fulfilled, be fearless and find joy in tranquility.

The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: Remain eternally inward-turned, free from passion and devoid of latent impressions, contemplating everywhere that action which is pure consciousness alone—immaculate and peaceful.
Clear as the sky, wise, established in the singular density of pure consciousness, equanimous, gentle, and equal in bliss—he is Brahmā, whose inner being is fully expanded.
In sorrows, in terrible calamities, in crises and in pitfalls; in all circumstances as they arise—whether diminished or exalted.
Without being distressed yourself, inflict suffering upon them in due order and according to their location, including everything from weeping and wailing to the experience of dualistic pleasures.
O gentle-souled one, enjoy the bliss during the gatherings of beloveds, at festivals, and at times of prosperity, like one who is deluded and overcome by latent impressions.
In the face of death and in battles and other such tasks, consume all beings like a forest fire consumes grass—like one who is deluded and overcome by latent tendencies.

Without becoming weary when duties come in succession, acquire wealth through careful reflection like a crane; yet remain like one who is deluded and overcome by latent desires regarding the very acts of acquiring wealth.
O destroyer of enemies, forcibly split apart all your foes, just as the wind scatters empty clouds, or as one overcome by latent impressions treats a deluded person.
Maintain fortitude toward people who deserve compassion and toward great souls; with a mind delighting in the Self, remain silent like one who is deluded and overcome by latent impressions.
Be joyful amidst delights; be sorrowful amidst sorrows; practice compassion toward the wretched; and be heroic among the brave.
O sinless one, you are not the agent in that which is performed by one who is inward-turned, ever-blissful, endowed with delight in his own self, and noble through tranquility.
O virtuous Rāma, because you are constantly established in inward-turned contemplation of the self, even the falling vajra-shower becomes blunted for you.
He who dwells at ease within the hollow of his own pure consciousness, free from the activity of conceptualization, is the Great Lord, rejoicing in the Self.
Weapons do not pierce it; fires do not burn it; waters do not moisten it; and winds do not dry it up.
Embracing the unborn, well-supported pillar that is one's own self—ageless and immortal—the wise-souled one should remain, firmly grasping it as one might hold up a palace upon a sturdy pillar.

One should savor within the self that consciousness which is established in its own state, which is inward-turned and infallible, and which possesses the splendor of the fragrance of the flowers—the multitude of objects—that constitute the tree of the world.
For those who constantly perform their duties externally with inward-turned focus, no latent impression arises even while they live, just as it does not arise in stones.
Furthermore, make the mind sleep within, released from outward wandering; performing all actions while remaining without activity, like the limbs of a tortoise.
With a mind that is devoid of internal activity yet appears as if possessing external activity, and which is like one who has just awakened from sleep, perform your duties.
Like the consciousness of a child, a mute, or others, with internal impressions abandoned, your mind is not defiled while performing its activity, being like space.
Remain free from feverish distress with a mind that has dissolved through the renunciation of habitual activity, which spreads only slightly outward while remaining profoundly asleep within.
O sinless one, remaining in pure consciousness—where the stain of volitional thought has vanished and the mind arises as its own cessation through knowledge—do or do not act.
Moving about and conducting the affairs of the waking state with a mental state similar to that of deep sleep, take nothing at all, nor abandon anything whatsoever.
If you are as if in deep sleep even while awake, and if you are awake within that deep sleep, then because of the identity of waking and deep sleep, you exist as one who is free from all affliction.
Thus, through gradual practice, one should attain that state which is devoid of beginning and end, transcendent over all dualities, and beyond all objective entities.
Having reached the certainty that the world is neither duality nor unity, attain the supreme rest with a mind as clear as space.
Śrī Rāma said: "If this is so, O tiger among sages, then tell me: why do you yourself remain here in this world, identified by the notion of 'I' and bearing the name Vasiṣṭha?"
Śrī Vālmīki said: While Rāghava was speaking thus, Vasiṣṭha, the best among speakers, remained silent for half a moment, his movements perfectly composed.
While that great assembly remained silent, fallen into an ocean of doubt as to what might happen, Rāma spoke once again.
For what reason, Blessed One, do you remain silent like me? There is no principle in the worlds that is not capable of providing an answer for the virtuous.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O sinless one, it is not because of my inability to speak or a depletion of reasoning that I have reached this point; rather, the answer to this millionfold question is simply silence."

The questioner is of two kinds: either one who knows reality or one who does not. To the ignorant person, the answer should be given according to their ignorance; but to the knower, it should be given according to their knowledge.
For such a long time, O Mahāmati, you remained ignorant of that state and were a vessel for further conceptualizations.
Now you have become a knower of reality, resting in the supreme state; it is clear that you are no longer fit for further conceptual meditations.
O best of speakers, whatever verbal expression there may be—whether its meaning is subtle or ultimate, and whether it be extensive or very brief—[all of it is encompassed by this].
O virtuous one, that [consciousness] is associated with all delusions—such as the exclusion of counter-correlates, number, and so forth—just as light is associated with motes of dust.
O Sundara, one who knows that [reality] does not deserve an answer that is stained with fault; yet there is no speech that is unstained, and you stand as one who knows it even better.
And I must speak to my wise disciples exactly as it is; those who know reality as it is understand that the silence of wood is free from extremes.
They say that silence, free from discursive thought yet accompanied by volition, is the supreme state; that very thing has been granted to you as a beautiful answer, O knower of reality.
For indeed, my dear friend, a person speaks according to what they consist of; and I, consisting of pure knowability alone, abide in the state that transcends speech.
For how can one who stands upon the plane beyond speech grasp the impurity of speech? Therefore, I do not speak that which is unspeakable; for speech is indeed marked by conceptualization.
Śrī Rāma said: Disregarding those words that proceed from the mouth which cause defects, speak first by means of the exclusion of their opposites: who are you?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, this being so, hear this as it truly is: "Who are you? Who am I? Or what is the world?"—O best among those who know reality.
O dear one, I am indeed this stainless space of consciousness, devoid of the perception of objects of thought, and transcending all mental constructs.
I am the pure space of consciousness, you are space itself, and the entire world is space; everything is nothing but space.

My self is of the singular nature of pure consciousness; within this self composed of pure consciousness, I am free from the perception of any other awareness, and I do not know how to speak of anything else as being distinct from myself.
Those intent on asserting their own position, though striving for the sake of liberation, lead the growth of the "I" and the self to a hundred branches.
They call that supreme state when one, though living and engaged in worldly affairs, remains as tranquil as a corpse.
That which has no external means, which is peaceful, equal with no internal means, and which is neither pleasure nor pain, neither "I" nor "other"—that is Śiva.

This "I-ness" belongs to liberation; where is there both non-existence and cultivation? To seek that very [liberation] by means of that [I-ness] is like a person blind from birth looking at a painting.
Whether in movement or in stillness, that state which remains as motionless as a stone—know that to be the undecaying state of Nirvana for one who is not insentient.
And no one else perceives that; it is experienced by oneself alone, like the state of being a knower within oneself by a wise man who is dispassionate toward worldly desires.
Therein, there is neither "I-ness" nor "thou-ness," neither non-"I-ness" nor otherness; it is simply the state of absolute purity—stainless and auspicious Nirvana.
They say that the consciousness of this conscious being consists precisely in its orientation toward objects; and this very state is saṃsāra, bondage, leading to abundant suffering.
Know that liberation is the insentience of the sentient, consisting in the state of being turned away from objects of thought; it is the supreme, peaceful, and indeed imperishable state.
When one abides in the peaceful Self, which is tranquil and unconditioned by space, time, and the like, an object of cognition is simply not possible; who could cognize what, and in what manner?
O kings, just as a mental construction within a dream-appearance would appear as something other than its true nature—which is pure consciousness—so too does it appear when it has gone outside.

These [entities] such as the mind (manas) and the intellect (buddhi) conform to pure consciousness alone; however, when conditioned by the referents of words such as "mind" and "intellect," they become insentient in nature.
In pure consciousness alone—which is uniform, clear, pervasive both internally and externally, and undivided—what purpose does the notion of duality serve as it expands?
What is the difference between pure consciousness alone and the void? Even the wise do not know that difference; thus, it does not fall within the range of speech.
Just as some appearance, possessing both existent and non-existent forms, is perceived with effort by one who looks into the darkness, so too is this world perceived within Brahman.
If I am pacified and free from latent impressions, I am indeed space itself; yet if you do not bind yourself to latent impressions, you remain as the very sky of consciousness.

Thus, one who possesses internal certainty and knows that [reality] remains like an ignorant person in outward appearance; though existing as the very embodiment of consciousness, he becomes tranquil of himself, as if non-existent.
The fire of ignorance, blazing within living beings due to the wind of nescience that conceals true cognition, is extinguished by those very same means for those who have attained awakening.
That which is the ignorance of those who are not inert, like that of trees remaining still—they call that the unshaken liberation, the state of abiding in the imperishable.
By attaining knowledge through knowledge, a human being becomes a sage; by falling into ignorance through ignorance, one descends to the state of a beast or a tree.
The delusion consisting of ignorance—that "I am Brahman" and "this is the world"—is unreal; through discernment, it is not found, just as darkness is not found by means of a lamp.

Though possessing a complete collection of sense organs, one who is free from volitional thought and devoid of perception—possessing a tranquil mind—experiences nothing whatsoever, whether internally or externally.
Just as a dream dissolves into deep sleep, so all that is visible dissolves within the consciousness of the Knower during samādhi; once again, only one's own Self is perceived.
Just as blueness exists in the sky, so does the nature of earth and other elements exist in Śiva; apart from mere delusion there is nothing else—just as the sky is, so is Śiva.
Though endowed with all latent impressions (vāsanās), he is free from latent impressions; for his intellect is such that it regards all this as non-existent.
O noble one, just as the world-processes are like a marvelous dream, illusion, or a magician’s trick within our volitions, what reliance can there truly be upon them even when they are perceived?
There is no suffering, no happiness, no merit, and no sin; nothing whatsoever is lost to anyone, because neither an agent nor an enjoyer exists.
Everything is empty and without support; even this notion of "mine" is like the double moon or a city in a dream—for us, that [notion] also does not exist.
Whether remaining solely in the state of worldly activity or having attained the silence of wood, by abiding like a piece of wood or a stone, one attains the state of Brahman.
In this auspicious state, which is peaceful, mental, and neither manifold nor non-manifold, there exists no other reasoning for the existence of a whole than that of its parts.
And since it is impossible for that which has attained its true nature to possess a self-nature within this stainless, all-pervading Brahman, there can be no mention of a self-nature in it.

Nor is there existence of consciousness due to the perception of nihilists; nor is it non-existent, for not even the slightest thing exists because of the impossibility of the view of grasped object and grasping subject.

That which is peace—stainless, unassailable, cherished by the noble ones, auspicious, unborn, undecaying, seated, and equanimous; that is the unerring state. Abide in that tranquility; drink, sport, and enjoy, for this "existence" does not exist.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Egoism alone is the supreme ignorance that obstructs the state of liberation; that it is sought after by the deluded is the behavior of a madman.
Enough with this egoism born of ignorance; it is the very hallmark of ignorance. For one who knows the truth and is at peace, the notions of "mine" and "I" do not exist.
Having cast off the impurity of egoism, the wise one, like the stainless sky, remains free from fever—whether with body or without body—having attained nirvana.
Neither the autumnal sky, nor the tranquil ocean, nor the center of the full moon shines as brilliantly as the Knower.
Just as there is composure within an army engaged in a battle of brilliant arrays, so too is there equanimity in the wise man, even while he is occupied with worldly affairs.

For the knower who has realized oneness with nirvāṇa, even latent impressions (vāsanā) are no longer considered impressions; they are like a string of pearls. Yet, the waves and so forth of the ocean are not something other than water.
Just as the ocean, with all its surging waves, is nothing but water, so too Brahman—though appearing as the swelling of the visible world—is Brahman alone and nothing else.
He whose inner [mind] has set and is undisturbed, and whose outer [senses] have set and are tranquil, yet who exists when impelled [by necessity], is said to be liberated.

In the supreme consciousness which consists of pure awareness, consciousness vibrates in the form of the ego and its manifestations, like water within water; what, then, is the nature of this perceived diversity?
Just as when smoke billows in the sky, the formations such as elephants and chariots are not distinct from the smoke itself, so too are the creations not separate from the supreme state.

Through the investigation of consciousness and delusion, you who sport in the non-apprehension of delusion—be victorious! Do not fall into despondency, O knowers, for that very state of knowing belongs to you.
Just as a sprout contains within itself the tree, its leaves, and its fruit, so too does the Knower perceive the world, the ego, his own self, and even the void of the self within himself.
Form, light, mind, and existence are like the appearance of straightness in flames; though they exist, they do not truly exist, being like the illusory powers of a deluded mind.

According to their pleasure, according to their undertaking, according to their destruction, and according to their arising; according to place and according to time—may you, free from decay, remain in peace.
Even while engaging in worldly affairs, one who is tranquil amidst the attainment of the desirable and undesirable experiences nothing else within, being perfectly extinguished like a corpse.
That ego devoid of mental impressions, which sustains the world for a long time—whether one is living or dead—is the conscious life-force; it is the supreme state.
For men bound by the noose, existence itself, carried along by the force of dullness, serves only as a burden of suffering, like young calves in the ocean.
Liberation does not resort to him as it does through the experience of ignorance; for how can one who is alive attain that which is said to be attainable only by one who is dead?
Whatever one conceives through volition, that very thing is subject to destruction by that same volition; that state where this [volition] does not exist is the imperishable reality.
Cultivate the realization that "there is neither another nor am I," and you will become fearless; this truth, when properly applied, becomes like nectar even to poison.
Having investigated the entire body, from the inert physical form down to the mind, one realizes "I am not"; therefore, "I am not" is the truth.
For those for whom all particularities have been stilled through the investigation that ends with the "I-ness," liberation arises as pure alone; yet nothing whatsoever is destroyed.
For in this matter, nothing other than the renunciation of enjoyments, discernment, and personal effort is of use; thus, O ignorant ones, bow down quickly to your own self.

They describe liberation as the state of mental reflection free from latent impressions; yet that does not occur without awakening. The delusion of the world is a failure here, for there is no higher realization than this; since there is no conviction in this matter, bondage persists for a very long time.

Having correctly realized that "I am non-existent" regarding this world, and being entirely indifferent toward people, wealth, wife, and body, he indeed becomes one whose nature is pure consciousness; for liberation does not exist otherwise than as the infinite void.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Within the manifestation of consciousness, which is the self of all, that alone is immediately experienced—whatever internal reality is perceived, whether it be a real entity or a non-entity.
Through prior habituation, that very [consciousness] first manifests as the experience of external objects, appearing as if it were external; one's own dream is the illustration for this.

All this is of the nature of consciousness, and consciousness is clearer even than the sky; since consciousness gathers [all things] and is itself consciousness, therefore none of this exists anywhere at all.
There is no destruction, no non-existence, no misfortune, no birth or death, and no space; there is neither emptiness nor multiplicity—everything is indeed Brahman alone, and yet not even that.

Upon the destruction of the world, egoism, and so forth, nothing at all is destroyed; for indeed, even the destruction of that which is unreal—such as a dream and the like—is there anything that is actually destroyed?
In a false appearance, such as a city of one's imagination, what indeed is lost? Likewise, in the case of the world, the ego, and so forth, no destruction exists in that which is non-existent.
If it is asked, "Whence comes this reproach against the world?", [the answer is: since that [world] is a non-entity, no definitive determination is possible; for what can be said of sky-flowers?
This alone is the final conclusion here: that you remain like a stone, not bringing about any activity whatsoever, but abiding in conduct exactly as it is.

The world is essentially nothing more than a mental construction; therein, that which appears as an object ceases entirely in an instant. This is the certain conclusion regarding the delusion of creation.
In creation, this [world] is indeed unrestrained and imperishable by virtue of its nature as Brahman; otherwise, however, this creation neither exists nor does it exist, nor do they exist.
And for those whose creation exists like that of unreal men in a dream—that creation and those persons are like the waves of water in a mirage.
We know no definitive conclusion regarding those things which, though non-existent, have attained as it were the state of existence, like the words "the son of a barren woman."
There is a certain unprecedented fullness, resembling a perfectly filled ocean; for those who know that, they do not fall into the perception of the parts of the seer and the seen.
Like lamps in a windless place that remain motionless with equal radiance, they abide in perfect composure, whether engaged in conduct or free from conduct.
Resembling a single, full ocean, an indescribable fullness has arisen within; the realization of inner coolness is perceived by the knower as something truly unprecedented.
In this world, the person is seen as nothing but latent impressions (vāsanā), yet those impressions do not exist; and since no one perceives them, from where has saṃsāra come?
That which is established as non-perceived through observation does not exist when observed; the non-perception of blackness and so forth in this context serves as a clear illustration.
The elements, the body, the flesh, and so forth, as well as that which is unreal and delusive—the insentient intellect, ego, and mind—are composed of that [consciousness] alone and nothing else.
If the intellect, ego, and mind, having abandoned their nature consisting of the elements and so forth, attain an absolute state of stability, that is declared to be liberation.

Since it is not established as a distinct entity, what kind of existence can there be here? Therefore, what is the latent impression (vāsanā), from where does it come, where does it reside, and what is its essential nature?
And for one who has this delusion, that which is non-existent appears as if existent; like the water of a mirage, by that [delusion], whose is saṃsāra, what is it, and from where does it arise?
Therefore, in that case, whatever arising of thought there may be for him, that very same delusion of saṃsāra proceeds once again.
Therefore, without relying on anything at all, one should meditate like space; the supreme good here is non-recollection, which is the ultimate forgetting.
Here there is no seer, nor an enjoyer; there is neither existence nor non-existence. This world remains as it is—tranquil, one, and ever-vibrant like the ocean.

When it is clearly realized that the entire visible world is Brahman and is real, the auspicious state arises—just as [the reflection vanishes] upon the drying up of water—when the distinction between the original object and its reflection has ceased.
Or rather, the conventional usage of "quiescence," which is free from passion and hatred, is seen in one who has come to rest in the supreme reality and possesses equal vision.
Alternatively, only the state of peace remains for this Nirvana; since the Sage is indeed free from latent predispositions (nirvāsana), how could he engage in conventional discourse?
As long as his nirvana has not reached full maturity, he continues to engage in worldly activity, with the arising of passion, hatred, and fear still remaining.
Free from passion, fear, and anger, extinguished and with a tranquil mind, the sage remains forever like a stone that has become as solid as rock.
Just as the entire lotus plant exists within the seed of the lotus in its sheath, so too the delusion of a dream exists within the self; it is not something external.

Through the cultivation of externality, the external becomes [the self]; through the cultivation of selfhood, this very thing becomes the self. Indeed, in the supreme reality, cultivation is precisely that which it intends to produce.

This very same internal delusion of dreams and the like is manifested as external; there is not even the slightest difference here between the two, just as there is none between the milk in two separate vessels.
Likewise, stability and instability here, which consist of nothing but delusion, are extended; those two—being the support and the supported—are like water and its waves.

In dreams and similar states, there is the perception of otherness because of the cognition of the self as being distinct [from the objects]; however, when there is the realization of non-otherness, that [perception of otherness] does not arise, for it is not distinct from that.
That form of the Supreme Self which is peaceful and free from temporal succession—by becoming that very thing, it becomes so; by not being that thing, it would not become so.
When cognitions such as dreams have subsided, that pure, sovereign form neither exists nor does it not exist; it is simply beyond the range of speech.
When ultimate delusion has dissolved, one who is thus disciplined realizes his own true nature; for that [nature] is not the object of instruction for the wise man.

It is fitting to abide solely in that one, unborn Nirvana—peaceful, free from fear, pride, despondency, greed, delusion, body, ego-sense, mind, and the dullness of the senses—which has abandoned the notion of "I," is imperishable, and has cast aside all distinctions.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When consciousness expands, then the delusion of "I-ness" and the world arises; though unreal, it appears as if emerging, just as the state of wind arises from its own vibration.

Even when it has arisen, it does not lead to weariness because of the realization of its nature as Brahman; however, it leads to supreme misfortune through the cultivation of the conceptualization of the world as the referent of the word "jagat."
Just as the eye takes on the experience of form through its outward extension, so too consciousness, through its own expansion, assumes the delusion of the world.
That which spreads forth in vain is not real because of the absence of an object of cognition; how can that which is non-existent spread forth? Where does the son of a barren woman dance?
But this person remains experiencing [the world] in vain through mere experience alone, not experiencing that which is unreal, like a child imagining a yakṣa.

The sense of "I" also exists for the sake of suffering, because one perceives only "I"; since there is no perception of an "I" [in the absence of suffering], bondage and liberation depend upon oneself.
That indeed is meditation or that is samādhi which is abiding in non-perception—insentient as it were to those who are sentient, even, peaceful, and free from affliction.
O wise ones, do not despair like the ignorant through the confusions of verbal compositions arising from the distinctions between duality and non-duality; such things lead only to suffering.

One whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are dense experiences suffering based on what is non-existent, like a dream, [perceiving] forms, light, and mental attentions as if they were fashioned by conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa*).
One whose latent tendencies have become subtle does not experience suffering at all, remaining as if asleep, as if toward forms, light, and mental attentions were devoid of conceptual construction.
Having reached a state of extreme attenuation, the latent impression itself attains liberation, just as the mental conception of an object vanishes through the conjunction of place, time, and action.

When a latent impression (vāsanā) reaches a state of extreme attenuation, it attains liberation, just as clouds and the like in the sky reach the state of emptiness through the transformation into atoms.

Through the cultivation of the sense of "I," the latent impression regarding awakening undergoes thickening or thinning, just as ignorance results from the lack of practice in associating with the wise, while wisdom results from such practice.
Through my reasoning, it is known that there is no certainty here of "I exist" whose nature is inner peace; this is called "established awakening," whether one is living or not living.
In the wind, this world and its beginning appear as if in a pair; it is pacified only through inquiry such as, "Who am I? and "How is this?"
"Nirvana is simply 'I am not'—is such ignorance possible? This is quickly understood through the company of the virtuous and through inquiry."
Through association with those who know reality, the bondage of "I" is destroyed, just as darkness is dispelled by light or night by day.

"Who am I? How is this visible world? Who is the individual soul (jīva), and what is life?"—one should investigate these questions throughout one's entire life through association with those who know reality.
The world shines as the individual soul (jīva), and from that, the notion of "I" perishes; that reality is attained by one through service to the sun of knowledge—let it be cultivated.
O friend, attend individually to each and every one who possesses excellence in awakening; for when they meet together, the demoness of disputation arises among them.
Even when the Lord of Yakṣas has arisen, just as in a child, so too in the wise man, the primary delusion "I am" arises, though it is thoroughly joined with reason.
Therefore, a wise person should serve a learned scholar in private on each occasion; having unified those matters spoken by him, one should reflect upon them with the intellect.
One should contemplate the meaning of that teaching with the intellect for the sake of increasing wisdom; one should attain identity with that Reality which is free from all conceptual constructions.
Having brought your intellect to a state of supreme sharpness through association with the wise, let that single creeper of ignorance be utterly cut away, piece by piece.
This matter is indeed possible; therefore, I relate this which we, as children, have personally experienced, for we do not speak what is inconsistent with the truth.

Just as the manifestation of clouds from the sky or the breaking of waves from the great ocean, neither destruction nor arising is possible here for that which is devoid of mental construction, nor does anything perish.

For all this is like the water of a mirage within the undecaying, peaceful, and pervasive Brahman; when investigated, even "I" is not found here—how, where, and from what source could there be the delusion of thought and the like?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: If a person is not led toward the state of knowledge by their own human effort and their own intellect, which has been expanded through the company of the virtuous, then there is no other means.
One's own conceptualization and the conceptualization of another are both taken up as "other" through one's own counter-conceptualization, just as nectar may take on the nature of poison.
Conceptualization ends in non-conceptualization, and liberation is that which is free from conceptualization; this is accomplished by first renouncing worldly enjoyments, and not otherwise.
For one who dwells within, neither articulating with speech nor mentally conceptualizing the word and its referent, the cessation of conceptual construction gradually increases.
Apart from the notion "I am," there is no other form of ignorance; when this [notion] is stilled through non-contemplation, there is no other liberation whatsoever.
You are born and you perish within this ego-sense that is yet not the body; when the desire for the world and its origins is abandoned in it, you become tranquil and you attain perfection.
Salutations to that Great Soul, by whose insentience all this—though existing—stands as if non-existent, and who is as tranquil as a stone.
All this ceases through non-perception, like a mirage, for one whose mind is dissolved in the supreme and who cultivates the nature of consciousness as being called "emptiness."

Whether this [object] exists or does not exist, if it is consciously perceived, it leads to an increase in suffering; if it is not consciously perceived, it leads to happiness, because internal consciousness arises from the absence of [external] consciousness.
There are two terrible diseases for embodied beings: this world and likewise the next; by these two, being afflicted in every way, one experiences dreadful sufferings.

In this world, the wise strive to treat the disease with enjoyments as difficult medicines, exerting themselves to the best of their ability for as long as life lasts, as one would for no other ailment.
The best of men strive for a cure for the great disease of the next world by means of the nectars known as tranquility, association with the virtuous, and awakening.
Those who are attentive to the treatment for the next world conquer through the power of tranquility the great longing for the path to liberation.
He who does not seek a cure for the disease of hell while still here—once he has gone to that place where there is no medicine, what will he do, afflicted as he is by pain?
Let life proceed through medical treatments in this world; let it not go to ruin. Let the ignorant cure the next world with the medicines of self-knowledge.
Life is as fragile as a leaf tossed by the wind or a drop of water; it is a great disease for the next world, so let it be treated with effort and speed.
When the great disease of the next world has been diligently and swiftly treated, the disease consisting of this world subsides of its own accord and quickly.
They know that a living being is pure consciousness alone, and the world is its expansion; even within the interior of a single atom, there exists that [expansion] as vast as hundreds of mountains.
That expansion of consciousness which consists of forms, light, and the mind is experienced within space alone; therefore, the delusion of the world is not real.
Even when the dissolutions of the world are observed, the delusion known as the visible universe neither perishes nor is born, for it consists solely of mere illusion.
If the self, submerged in the ocean of the mire of enjoyments, is not rescued by the wonder of one’s own human effort, then there is no other means for that.
A person who has not conquered the self is deluded and entrenched in the mire of sensual enjoyments; such a one becomes a vessel for calamities, just as the ocean is for waters.
Just as childhood is seen to be the beginning of life, so the renunciation of enjoyments, which brings about the pacification of passion, is the beginning of nirvāṇa.
For one who knows that, the river of life, though full of waves, flows without agitation; it moves with equanimity and gentleness, as if insipid and fixed in a painting.
But for the river of the life of the ignorant, there are whirlpools that are exceedingly terrifying, accompanied by waves of agitation in their course that flow along with the current.
The multitudes of created worlds surge forth as mere fragments of the expansion of consciousness, like the illusion of seeing two moons, a child’s ghost, a mirage, or a dream.
Thousands of creations appear like a surging flood of waves in consciousness; when investigated, they are unreal, yet they seem real due to the delusion of experience.
Even within the expanse of space, the worlds appear as if they exist due to the delusion of the expansion of consciousness; however, they are not truly real.
The delusion of creation is a bubble upon the waters of the expansion of consciousness, possessing the form of the modifications of the existence of "I" and so forth.
Consciousness is nirvāṇa; the world is the unfolding of consciousness. It is neither internal nor external, neither unreal nor real—it is everything.
The Lord is the nature of consciousness, unborn, unmanifest, one, and immutable; He is Brahman, devoid of both selfhood and the state of being, more tranquil even than the void.
For Brahman, who is devoid of intrinsic nature, no external cause is required for the perception of creation, just as no cause is required for the movement of the wind.
Like the experience of a dream, this is an illusion; within the ocean of Brahman, there are waves of Brahman. In reality, however, there is neither dreaming nor the state of creation here.
This alone is non-manifestation, mindlessness, non-inert, and equal; it is neither existent nor non-existent, neither existent-and-non-existent, and is this immutable, non-dual reality.
He for whom, while remaining exactly as he is, there has arisen a cessation of consciousness that is non-perceptive in nature—him they call the best of sages.
He who, though existing, is like something made of clay—characterized by a lack of self-awareness—and from whom the world has dissolved: him they call the best of sages.
Just as a city of imagination subsides through the absence of volition, so too does the world, which arises from sensation, subside within consciousness through the absence of sensation.

Except for intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), all meanings of words are indeed accompanied by causes; however, that which is the cause of intrinsic nature is liberation—the realization of that [emptiness].
In this world, no object whatsoever possesses any intrinsic nature; all experiences are merely the fluidity of the great ocean of consciousness.
These very experiences are the vibrations of the great wind of consciousness; let it be understood that these are the emptiness of the sky of Brahman.

Brahman and the creation are inseparable, like the wind and its movement; yet their perceived difference is unreal, arising from one's own delusion, comparable to the experience of one's own death within a dream.
Error persists as long as the investigation into the true nature of reality remains unclear; however, when the investigation becomes clear, error itself attains the state of Brahman.
Error, however, is unreal; therefore, upon investigation, it is not found as a real entity. Like the horn of a hare, it is utterly non-existent; thus, Brahman alone remains.

Without beginning, middle, or end, infinite, transparent, equal, auspicious, eternal, and truly one—being liberated from the delusion of the burden of all transformations of old age and ignorance, attain the state of space.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: He who perishes when pleasures and pains arrive perishes; he who does not perish is indestructible—for him, enough with the instructions of the scriptures.
For whoever there is an arousal of desire, for that person pleasure and the like necessarily exist; if those are to be properly treated, let desire itself be liberated first.
This world is an illusion; in the supreme state, it does not exist at all. This is peaceful, without support, entirely the inexhaustible Nirvana.
"I am Brahman" and "the world exists"—this delusion born of the confusion of words—by whom indeed has it been imagined within the all-pervading, tranquil space?

Herein there is no "I," nor the world, nor those things denoted by words such as "Brahmā"; since the one who is peaceful is the all-in-all, who here could be an agent or an enjoyer, and from what source?
Because he surpasses all teachers, he has indeed performed a total negation [of all else]; and since that [negation] is of the nature of truth, he alone is distinguished as "I."
The movement of the Siddhas dwelling on the summit is not perceived, nor is it harsh, just as a man sleeping on one side does not perceive the dreams or the thundering of clouds.

Since it does not exist in the state of being made known (*jñapti*), the practice of the perfected ones (*siddhācāra*) is not perceived; for everyone experiences that which abides in the state of being made known as "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*).
Even consciousness is indeed identical with the Self, for everything shines as being composed of that; therefore, I am this entire world, which is non-different from the Supreme Self.
Pure consciousness shines as the world, just as in the case of volitions and dreams; it arises without diverse parts, just as water arises in the form of waves.

At its arising, consciousness is indeed of a single nature, yet through ignorance it appears as if it has attained multiplicity; however, because that [multiplicity] is unreal, it is not perceived when examined.
Just as an aggregate might consist of all its own constituent parts, so too this world is nothing but Brahman—eternal, partless, and peaceful.
The brick of the nature of consciousness holds within it millions of vessels; whatever it perceives, it knows as if it were the world and so forth.

Brahman alone shines forth as this world through its existence and its state as the clear universe; because it is of the nature of consciousness, it is like the ocean appearing as waves and the like due to its fluid essence.
Whatever one wills within, one perceives as if it were the world and so forth; even though it is formless, it appears as its own form, whereas that which one does not will does not appear at all.
The statements regarding his being conscious and unconscious were made for the sake of instruction, because he is the Lord even within his own body; they do not refer to reality in its actual sense.

The world does not exist as real, nor does it exist as unreal; yet it appears because of consciousness within consciousness. Since it does not shine forth from what is insentient, how can there be any apprehension of objects for us here?

The insentient and the sentient, as well as movement and stillness, belong to the Self; yet these are not objects of concern for that which is self-dependent, remaining as steady as a stone situated in its own natural state.
I do not know from where this demon has arisen, who, when looked upon, has neither existence, nor support, nor cause—this one who thinks, "I am."
The very existence of this yakṣa who thinks "I am his" does not exist in reality; oh, how strange it is that you have been rendered helpless by him!

Just like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, the delusion that "I am manifest in Brahman" appears; it is merely one's own form appearing through a visual error, like a mass of floating hairs in the sky.
I am indeed Brahman, and the world here is likewise; whence, then, could there be destruction or origination? Therefore, what possible basis can there be for joy or sorrow?
Because the Lord is the sovereign of all, this world appears to him as both perceived and unperceived; therefore, let it be unperceived by you.

Because the world arises from consciousness, Brahman appears as the void like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence; how then could that [world] be distinct from it, being like a city in a dream or a city of one's own volition?
Just as waves and the like exist in water, or as a carved figure exists in wood, or as jars and other objects exist in clay, so does the state of emanation exist within Brahman.
That which is experienced within the clear, formless, and structureless [reality] is nothing other than that very thing; what, then, is called "I" and what are the worlds?
Just as the Maruts [wind-gods] possess a variety of movements through their very existence alone, so too the world, the ego, and so forth arise from Brahman, who is devoid of intrinsic nature.
Just as the forms of trees, elephants, horses, deer, and so forth are perceived in a cloud, though they possess no real configuration or shape, so too do others perceive the world as a creation.
The entire creation appears as if possessing parts within the supreme Śiva; know its likeness to be just like that of cause and effect.
With a mind inwardly peaceful, effortless, free from limiting adjuncts, and devoid of delusion, remain like the sky—equal [to all] precisely because of the impossibility [of duality] in the world.
Neither you, nor we, nor worlds, nor the elements exist; this Brahman alone remains, entirely peaceful and absolute.

In all things without exception, there is the state in which every distinction has been stilled; realizing "I am that very reality," abandon [the notion of self] quickly and cultivate this for the sake of liberation.
Know sensation to be bondage; know non-sensation to be liberation. Abide as you are, acting as you do, peaceful and free from sensation.
The seer does not become the seen, nor does consciousness become the object of thought; since there is no world due to the absence of anything to be thought, who could perceive what, and how?
Since the states of the seer and the seen do not exist, remain as if in deep sleep even while awake—resembling the expanse of the autumnal sky and comparable to non-existence.

Likewise, within the single form of Brahman-consciousness, just as in the vibration of the wind, there is the non-consciousness of awakening which is creation, and the consciousness of Brahman as one, which is liberation.
The vibration of consciousness (*citspanda*), which is the wind of Brahman, is known as "creation" (*sarga*); that which is the absence of this vibration of consciousness is declared to be "nirvāṇa."
Just as a seed knows its own nature within itself as sprouts and so forth, so does the Great Consciousness know its own nature abiding within it as the state of creation.
Just as a seed remains as leaves and so forth through the experience of those very leaves, so too does the supreme consciousness of creation become the state of creation itself.
Just as the appearances of the modifications of existence are ultimately consciousness, so too all seeds and examples are of that very nature and consist of it.
Know that this entire world is composed of the changeless Supreme Brahman; know it to be changeless, without beginning or end, and free from all affliction.

Consisting of nothing but one's own volition, this world—subject to destruction through one's own volition and characterized by the transformations of duality and non-duality—is like a city created by imagination.
Just as you understand the difference between emptiness and space, know that the difference between Brahman and the creation is likewise devoid of self-nature.
That peaceful existence of Brahman, which from of old was of the nature of my speech and mind, is itself this "I-ness" (ahantva) arising from the lack of awakening that "I am a human being."
In this Brahman, which is the form of the universe, nothing at all is born; and even that which is born and then perishes does not truly perish, like a wave in water.
Brahman alone abides within itself in the form of the objects of the world and as Brahman itself—just as a whole resides in its parts, as space in space, or as water in water.
That form which exists within consciousness when one moves from one place to another in half a blink of an eye—let that very nature be worshipped.
The wise declare that the nature of consciousness is twofold: agitated and unagitated. Be single-mindedly devoted to that which you seek as the supreme good; do not be lacking in discernment.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That stainless form which exists in the interval between consciousness as it moves instantly from one distant place to another—that is the supreme form of the Self.

While walking, hearing, touching, smelling, opening the eyes, closing the eyes, or laughing, you should certainly remain constantly absorbed in this [Self] for the sake of attaining freedom from all affliction.
From that very reality which is free from appearances and devoid of the desire for latent impressions, she remains as she is and as she acts, as immovable as the mountain of the gods.
Such is the nature of ignorance that it cannot be perceived; if it were perceived, it would become supreme knowledge itself.
Since the object of thought arises from ignorance, where and what could possibly arise within the state of non-mind? How indeed can anything be perceived internally? Only peace has arisen with power.
Truth is Brahman and the world is one; though established as one, it appears as many. Everything shines as if it were not everything; though pure, it is spread out as if impure.
The non-empty appears clearly as if empty, and the empty as if non-empty; the expansive appears as if non-expansive, and the non-expansive as if resembling the expansive.

Though changeless, it appears as if changing; though uniform, it appears as if non-uniform; though peaceful, it appears as if unpeaceful; though existent, it appears as if non-existent; though invisible, it has arisen as if it were something other than itself.

Though indivisible, it appears as if divided; though devoid of inertia, it has become like inert matter; though beyond the reach of thought, it seems to possess the nature of an object of thought; and though partless, it shines as if possessing parts.

Though not "I," it appears as if it were "I"; though indestructible, it appears as if it were subject to destruction; though stainless, it appears as if it were stained; and though beyond being known, it appears as if it were carrying the burden of the knowable.
It is like light compared to dense darkness, both new and ancient; it is subtler than even an atom, yet it contains within itself the multitude of all worlds.
Though it is the self of all, it is abandoned through great hardship; though it is not a net, it is richly ensnared; and though it is without end, it appears manifold in many ways.
Know that Brahmā, the lord of the wise, though free from illusion, is like the stainless sun with its orb of illusory rays, and like the great ocean to the waters.
The great treasury of the jewels of the world is lighter than cotton on a scale; even illusion, a mirage, and the moon are not within the range of sight.
Though infinite and shoreless, it does not abide anywhere; within space, it is intent upon the creation of forests, arrangements, and mountain ranges.
The most minute among the minute, the largest among the large, the heaviest among the heavy, and the best even among the excellent.
Without agent, object, or instrument; without cause and without actor—this has been fulfilled for a long time through internal emptiness alone.
The world-receptacle is eternally empty like a wilderness, yet though it is as hard as an infinite mountain, it is as soft as a fragment of space.
Day by day, for the most part, the ancient appears new and the delicate appears old; light takes on the appearance of darkness, and darkness spreads as light.

Even that which is perceptible is difficult to discern, and even that which is beyond perception is foremost; it is the very form of consciousness and yet insentient, and it is indeed insentient and yet of the nature of consciousness.
I alone am the state of non-I, or the non-I is indeed I; that which is other is I, and I am indeed that; I am other than that, and that is indeed other than I.
Within this full ocean, these waves of the three worlds remain as if quivering, consisting essentially of the fluidity of their own nature.
It bears all whiteness situated within its own limbs, like frost; indeed, everything shines by means of this very [whiteness], as if by frost.
Though devoid of space, time, and constituent parts, this Divine Being extends the unreal world day and night, just like a wave upon the water.
In this vast forest of space, these withered clusters of the world are blossoming, their five petals being the spreading leaves.
This one, whose form is utterly stainless, has himself become a mirror out of his own desire to behold his own reflection.
The luminous perception of this creation, which is like the fruit of a tree in the sky, arises as a manifestation of one's own will; as it emerges, it brings wonder within consciousness.

Through that which is internal and that which is external, by means of the manifoldness within the manifold Self, this very [Self] shines forth internally and externally through the manifestation of existence and non-existence.
This splendor of objective entities, being of such a nature, produces wonder within this [consciousness] by its own will, for this very purpose, like the tongue within the cavity of its own mouth.
That which is the fluidity of this water is called the world; it is consciousness, the constituent factor of perception, possessing the revolutions of the whirlpools of the universe.
In this [Self], the splendor of all objective entities subsides within the Radiant One; from Him alone they arise, like the light of a fire from its own radiance.
This entire world is indeed whiteness, just as whiteness exists in snow; from this, these consciousnesses proceed, like rays from the moon.

From this bodiless aesthetic field (raṅga), this variegated world stands; know that it is pervaded by that [reality], which is peaceful, consisting of this [field], and free from non-existence, transformation, and the like.
From this forest tree, which is firmly rooted in the courtyard of the sky, there extend visible branches that are clusters of the world-web.
Indeed, here on this immovable mountain flows a visible river characterized by both decline and rise, bearing a manifold and infinite variety of flowers.
Upon this stage consisting of the void, the dancer of Destiny performs with incessant exertion through the whirls of the dramatic representation of the worlds.
The opening and closing of whose eyes constitutes millions of world-ages and great kalpas, He further causes the child of Time to be produced upon His stage.
Even while these worlds arise, he remains utterly tranquil, like a mirror that, though devoid of desire, reflects hundreds of images.
Of beings that exist, of creations that have come to be, and of those yet to be, this is the causeless seed, like the primary cause of all emanations.
The opening of his eyes is the prosperity of the world, and their closing is the arrival of dissolution; yet, being without such opening or closing, he abides in the Self alone.

As these worlds—so very numerous, immense, and subject to the states of creation, dissolution, and birth—arise, this one whose nature is boundless remains entirely tranquil, like the wind itself amidst its own vibrations.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, all misfortunes manifest as wonders, like whirlpools in water; they are all of one single nature, just like the waves upon the water.
She is the form of both the knowable and the unknowable within this entire universe; she is the nature of the supreme ether and rests upon ultimate tranquility.
Just as the thoughts of a child regarding the sky before them are nothing at all, so too is this universe in reality; yet it is true for the mind of a child.
The mental engagement with form and light is like an army of stone statues; since the mental engagements with form and light appear [thus], what universality can there be here?
Apart from the essence of pure consciousness, form, light, and mental attention cannot be found; other than that, where in this world is there even a trace of the universe, like the void?

The world is an illusion for one who perceives it, but there is no delusion for one who does not perceive it; perception and non-perception are dependent upon you, just as your mind and its absence depend on you.
