Because the sky of consciousness, whose form is vast, is of the nature of the supreme ether, no alteration of its inherent nature can possibly occur anywhere.
For this universe, which consists of that [Brahman], no modification of its own nature exists even when examined; how much less, then, will such a thing come to be?

All this is indeed the sky of consciousness; there is no such thing as "existence" or even "I. Since modification and the like do not exist within pure awareness, one can never find non-awareness therein.
I see nothing at all—neither "you" nor "I," nor the delusions of ego and the like; everything is peaceful, auspicious, and pure, like a forest born of the sky.
Know this word of mine: that which is the emptiness of the space of consciousness abides of its own accord within you, in the space of your own consciousness, within the Self.
They say that the supreme state is that which is seated without the arising of desire, like the posture of a stone statue or one depicted in a painting.
With his mind at rest and observing silence, his movement in the performance of necessary duties was like that of a wooden man—devoid of desire and free from agitation.
To the wise man, life appears like a hollow flute: empty within, empty without, devoid of flavor, and free from latent impressions, even as he lives.
He for whom the visible does not please, yet the invisible pleases within his heart—tranquil in both the outer and the inner—he has crossed over the ocean of existence.

Let the nets of words be spoken, like a flute whose latent impressions have passed away, through aesthetic flavor clinging to the bodiless god of love, with no other instigation than the subject at hand.
Let tangible objects be touched as they come, without mental impression, remaining as unshakable as a peaked pavilion, free from desire and free from mental activity.
Let the networks of flavors be tasted—free from desire, fear, and seeking, devoid of attachment or longing—just as they are obtained, like a ladle.
Let the various arrays of forms be seen again as they have attained freedom from latent impressions—devoid of flavor, beyond the reach of the mind, and free from pride, like a variegated eye.
Let them smell the fragrant flowers, free from desire and latent impressions, so that they may abandon their attachment to the fetters of worldly activity, like a forest wind.

If it is argued that, having been made aware of their lack of essence, the diseases of enjoyment have been treated, and likewise there is no talk at all of a means for their pacification; [then we reply: no.
He who, tasting the poison of sensual enjoyment, finds delight day after day, casts his own body into a blazing fire and abandons an inexhaustible store of fuel.

Those adorned with the scriptures say that composure consists in desirelessness; for the mind does not become tranquil through hundreds of instructions in the same way that it does through desirelessness.
Just as the arising of desire is suffering and the pacification of desire is happiness, so it is neither experienced in hell nor even in the world of Brahmā.
The wise know that the mind is mere desire; its cessation is called liberation. Only this much constitutes all the scriptures, austerities, observances, and restraints.
To whatever extent and in whatever manner a living being's desire arises, to that same extent and in that same manner a handful of seeds of suffering sprouts forth.
Just as the desires of a living being diminish through discernment, so too do the cholera-like fevers of suffering and anxiety subside.
Just as the density of the world's passion increases according to one's desire, so too do the waves of the poison of suffering and anxiety swell.
If this disease of desire is not treated by the medicine of one’s own effort, then I believe there exists another, more powerful medicine for it.
If it is not possible to bring about the complete pacification of desires, one should follow even a small portion of the path; one who stands upon the path does not perish.
That lowest of men who makes no effort to diminish his desires casts himself day after day into a blind well.
Desire alone is the seed of this cyclic existence, which is characterized by the production of suffering; once burnt by the fire of perfect knowledge, it does not sprout again.
For saṃsāra is merely desire, and nirvāṇa is the non-perception of that; let effort be made toward the non-arising of desire—what is the use of vain delusions?
Why do you look upon the teachers of scriptural instruction as useless? Why is the meditative concentration that does not follow after desires not attained?
For one whose intellect finds difficulty in accomplishing anything through the mere absence of desire, the instructions of a guru, the scriptures, and so forth are surely useless.
Birth in the wilderness of this world is sufficient to cause the expansion of suffering within men, for it is like a doe transformed by the poison of desire.
If this [desire] is not made even slightly childish for the sake of self-knowledge, let the cessation of desire be brought about; by that, it is fully attained.
Freedom from desire is indeed nirvāṇa, for desire itself is bondage; one should conquer desire to the best of one's ability—what is so difficult in this?
May the seed of desire within always be consumed by the fire of tranquility—the seed from which grows the forest of *karañja* and *khadira* trees that are old age, death, birth, and the like.
Wherever there is freedom from desire, there is liberation; therefore, as long as one has life and breath, one should destroy every arisen desire.
From whatever direction desire arises, from that very direction come the snares of bondage—masses of suffering consisting of merit and demerit, fraught with widespread afflictions.
When even a single moment of a virtuous person passes without the fulfillment of his desires, it is right for him to lament for a long time, like one who has been plundered by bandits.
Just as the inner desire of this person subsides, so too does his auspiciousness for liberation increase.
The fulfillment of the desires of a person who lacks discernment is nothing other than the watering of the poisonous tree of saṃsāra.

Born from the tree of the heart, the seeds of one's own pleasure and pain—arising from the auspicious and inauspicious actions performed by the body, such as enmity and the like—attain the flames of the fire of evil deeds; these desires, whose ends are sharp, burn the person who is like a sacrificial animal with a crackling sound.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen once more, clearly, to that which is called yoga—the disjunction from the transformation caused by the poison of desire—for the sake of peace, even though it has been explained before.
If that which is distinct from the self exists here, let it be desired according to one's wish; but if it does not exist, why is this difference from one's own self asserted?

Consciousness is partless, devoid of components, subtle, and even more empty than space; yet, being that very same consciousness which takes the form of the "I" and the world, why is it sought as a separate reality?

She is of the nature of space, indeed space itself, the knower and the known whose essence is space; what object of desire could there be here in this manifestation of the world, which is of the nature of space?

As for the claim that the relationship between the grasped and the grasper arises from something [external], we do not accept that; such a thing exists for those who are utterly tranquil, but I do not know who they are.
The relationship between the grasped and the grasper is not found even when established in itself; how can that which is non-existent be obtained? By whom has a black moon ever been obtained?
This indeed is the existence of the grasper and so forth: that they do not reside within themselves. If they are real when their intrinsic nature is examined, I know not where they go.
This indeed is the true nature: that the entirety of the seer and the seen comes to an end; having realized them to be unreal, one attains nirvana within the self.

In nirvāṇa there is no object of perception and the like; in the object of perception and the like, there is no nirvāṇa. There is no mutual experience between these two, just as there is none between shade and sunlight.
Both of these are mutually unreal, and where there is unreality, there is no cessation; for from that [reality] comes Nirvana, which is experienced as ageless and beyond suffering.

The world of appearances and so forth is a mere delusion; it is eternal [in its unreality] and never bestows happiness here. It is non-existent—contemplate this, and do not remain in the unborn state of Nirvana [out of attachment].
That which is perceived as resembling the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is not found; since even the causal efficiency of an object does not exist there, what is the use of denial?
From its existence comes great suffering; from its non-existence comes great happiness. Its absence, when supported by reasoning, attains firmness through meditative cultivation.

Therefore, O base ones, why do you vainly apply cleverness to the Self for the sake of bondage? For [the properties of] increase and so forth are clearly established only in an object that is not the Self.
When the entire world of cause and effect and so forth is indeed Brahman alone, then Brahmanhood truly resides within this all-pervasive reality whose nature is pure consciousness.
Enough with those deer seeking awakening; for when the one all-pervading Self, whose nature is space, truly exists as the sole reality, what need is there for them?
What indeed is the sequence of those very utterances rich in causal relationships, which serve as the cause for the vibration of wind and the fluidity of water?
O gentle one, when the sky is empty and the conscious self is the source of creation and so forth, then Brahman alone is everything, including the relationship between cause and effect.
Then, within Brahman, the cause of all creations is free from shame; there is neither suffering nor happiness, for the world is peaceful and composed of auspiciousness.
Since there is no otherness from pure consciousness, how can there be the arising of desire? Just as in an army of clay bodies, there is nothing other than mere clay.

"There is no attachment to the world, to the ego, or to the visible, nor is there anything other than Brahman. Śrī Rāma said: "O Lord of Sages, if this is so, then let desire arise, or let it not arise."

But since she is indeed Brahman itself, what purpose would there be in enjoining or forbidding her? Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When she is known and fully awakened, her will is Brahman alone and nothing else.
O Rāma, as the Fully Awakened One has declared, that is the truth; however, listen to this: whenever knowledge arises, at that very moment desire subsides.
Just as when the sun rises from the very nature of things, the night merely subsides and does not arise again, so too do desire and the like subside within cognition and do not arise.
To the extent that the arising of cognition brings about the cessation of duality, to that same extent there is the dissolution of latent impressions; how, then, could there be the arising of desire?
For such a person, this stainless liberation has arisen through the subsiding of ignorance; because of the distaste for all that is visible, no desire ever arises in them anywhere.
Neither does detachment from the visible arise in him, nor does attachment toward it; rather, he merely experiences the splendor of the seer and the seen, yet not as an inherent nature.
If, by a chance occurrence like the "crow and the palm fruit," or through the instigation of another, one should at some time desire something rightly—or even if not—[it may happen].
Therefore, whether he has desire or no desire, it is Brahman alone in this matter; of this there is no doubt. Desire does not arise in the knower, either necessarily or otherwise.
If knowledge has arisen in a person, then his desire subsides; these two cannot coexist in one place, just like light and darkness.

But for one who knows that [reality], there is never any scope for prohibitions or injunctions; for one whose desire for all worldly pursuits has been stilled, who is there, what can they say, and for what purpose?
This alone is the sign of knowledge: the complete attenuation of desire, or else the experience of delight for all the worlds.
When the visible world has become tasteless and no longer brings any relish whatsoever, then desire no longer spreads, and at that very moment, liberation occurs.
For one who abides in the peaceful non-duality that is the oneness of awakening, all states such as desire and lack of desire are of the nature of Śiva.
Through awakening, he has set aside duality; he is devoid of both non-duality and unity; he is pure, free from agitation, tranquil, and established in the Self.
He has no purpose whatsoever here through action, nor any at all through inaction; nor does he have any dependence on any being for any purpose.
It is never through lack of desire nor through desire, nor through existence nor through non-existence; it is neither by means of a self nor by another, nor by these things of death and life.
No desire arises in him who is awakened to Nirvana; and if a desire should arise in him, that is indeed the eternal Brahman itself.
"There is neither suffering nor happiness; the world is peaceful, auspicious, and unborn"—those wise ones know him to be awakened who remains inwardly like a stone with such a conviction.
Making suffering into happiness through meditative cultivation, as if turning poison into nectar—having thus resolved, one whose self is steadfast is called "awakened."

That world exists in the sky within the sky, the peaceful in the peaceful, the auspicious in the auspicious, the void in the void, and the real in the Real—thus does the universe abide within Brahman.

When it is established that "all things are not" within the vast expanse of consciousness devoid of perception—tranquil, perfectly equanimous, peaceful, and auspicious—the delusion of egoism comes to an end.
Whatever is seen here in this world, whether stationary or moving, all that is the peaceful void, comparable to a city imagined by another's thought.
Just as your coming and going proceed without obstruction into the midst of another's city of thought because of its emptiness, so it is within this delusion of the world.
Within the Self, which is utterly devoid of the beauty of oceans, heavens, earth, rivers, and mountains, the perceiver and the instruments of perception expand like waves upon the water of a mirage.
Like a city created in a dream, or like a child’s ghost or a palm-tree stump—whatever is seen here, how could it possibly be anything other than unreal?
The unreal alone appears as "I," and the real alone appears; even without one who experiences delusion, this delusion flashes forth as something real.
Neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent—this world, which is beyond the reach of the senses and inexpressible, shines forth undisturbed like the sky.

In this world, for the wise man who has attained equanimity, both desire and non-desire are sufficient for peace; nevertheless, I clearly consider the arousal of non-desire to be more conducive to the highest good.
The cognition "I am the world" is situated in consciousness as if space within space; just as vibration belongs to the wind, there is no other cause for it in the conscious self.

The mind is that state of the consciousness being oriented toward an object of thought; that itself is transmigratory existence. That same [consciousness] is desire, and its freedom from that is liberation. Having understood this principle, be at peace.
Whether there be desire or lack of desire, whether creation or dissolution—there is no harm to anyone whatsoever, for indeed nothing exists here at all.
Desire and non-desire, existence and non-existence, being and non-being, pleasure and pain—none of these mental constructions can possibly exist within the void.
One whose desires diminish day by day, and who is never satiated with discernment and tranquility, is said to be a partaker of liberation.
When the heart is pierced by the arrow of desire, a piercing pain arises; where these prevail, neither jewels, mantras, nor medicinal herbs can overcome it.
I do not perceive those arrays of effects and instruments that he previously created, except as a mass of false delusion arising from my own lack of vision.
If one engages in worldly transaction by means of an unreal object that has become an illusion, then why is the mountain of another's mind not turned into a woolen blanket?
If conventional usage is carried out by means of what is non-existent—which perishes upon mere inspection—then why is the sky not covered by a rabbit’s horn?

Due to its ego-sense and because of its extreme density, the space of consciousness instantly attains the state of a stone; like water, it reaches the condition of a body through the state of the mind and so forth.
Because it is consciousness, it experiences this state of being embodied even though it is unreal; the power of consciousness remains undestroyed, just as one experiences one's own death in a dream.
Just as blueness is unreal in the sky because it lacks substantiality, yet real through experience, so too this creation in this Lord is neither non-existent nor composed of existence.
Just as there is no difference between emptiness and space, or between movement and the wind, so too there is no difference between the creation and Brahman, which are of one and the same nature.
Nothing here is born, such as the world and so forth, nor does anything perish; it merely appears like a dream to one who has fallen asleep.

Since the creation of earth and the other elements does not exist and consists of nothing but mere appearance, what cause for agitation could there be regarding gain or loss within the sky of consciousness?
The body, composed of causes such as earth and the other elements, does not appear; there is only pure Brahman-consciousness alone, established within the Self itself.

The causality of the intellect and so forth is not real, because neither duality nor unity is possible; rather, it attains its status as the meaning of "this is produced by that" through the possibility of such a relationship.

In consciousness, the multitude of mental constructs and activities appears without cause or sequence; just as in a dream, those who are impetuous experience death, birth, and so forth in a mere instant.
The earth is indeed space, the mountains are space, and the firm walls are indeed space; the worlds are space, movement is space, and the perception of creation belongs to consciousness as space.
Upon the wall of the sky, the painting of the universe—composed of the stage of consciousness—is spread out; it neither rises nor sets, neither ceases nor suffers weariness.
In the water of consciousness, which takes the form of the fluidity of the lofty waves of the world—what indeed has arisen, or how; what has ceased, and when, or how?
In the peaceful great space of consciousness, which possesses the emptiness of the world, since there is no possibility of an object of thought, how could there be rising or setting?
Mountains appear like the sky, and the sky appears like mountains; through the application of perception, the state of Brahman remains as the creation.
By the application of the powder of consciousness, yogis in half a blink of an eye can turn the world into space and space into the three worlds.
Just as there are countless cities of perfected imagination in the sky, so too do thousands of creations exist within the sky of consciousness.
Just as whirlpools in the great ocean, though mutually mixed, remain distinct from one another, and the waters do not become anything other than water; so it is with these.
The great consciousnesses and the great creations, though intermingled with one another, remain distinct; they are not separate from that [consciousness].

The words of the wise declare that the attainment by an awakened yogin of another world of the perfected beings (siddha) during the interval between one creation and the next is precisely this [state].
Imperishable beings abide within the supreme Śiva, just as the manifestations of emptiness and the various classes of creations exist without obstruction in the sky.
The innate delusions of creation, which possess the natural fragrance of ultimate reality, neither arise nor subside, like lines engraved within a stone.

Just as the fragrances of flowers, though mingled with one another, remain unmixed, so too are these creations of the nature of space, each being a distinct ground of attainment for the perfected ones.
Because it has the nature of space as its volition and exists like all experience, the thoughts, expressions, and mental constructs regarding the body and delusions are indeed real.
Neither the claim that knowledge exists is true, nor is the claim that external objects exist; these perceptions bear fruit for you exactly according to how they are perceived.

When it is contemplated that "the world exists within consciousness as the very nature of consciousness," then no distinction between them is possible, just as there is none between liquidity and water.

Time, the worlds, the universes, and I—the aggregate of the senses—you and those [objects], and "so it is" therein—all this is one. It is the peaceful, unborn, and undecaying sky of consciousness, the self of the Lord; indeed, passion and the other afflictions do not exist at all.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Awakened by the realization of its own nature, consciousness perceives the world as false, just as an eye smeared with the ointment of illusion sees mountains and other forms within the sky.
The creation of Brahmā and the creation of the mind are considered these two to be similar, because they both consist of the nature of ultimate reality and are eternally undisturbed.
Know that because it is of the nature of cognition, it is not external; yet because it is experienced as external, know that its form as an external object is real, for it is true.

For us, the doctrine of external objects (*bāhyārthavāda*) and the doctrine of consciousness-only (*vijñānavāda*) are indeed one and the same, because they are both always established as existing or non-existing due to their single nature of being of the essence of sensation (*vedanā*).

The very being of Brahman, pervading everywhere, is characterized by the tranquility of the unagitated ether, air, light, water, and earth; it is vast, empty, and the source of all great undertakings.
To him who is everything, from whom everything comes, who is all that, and who is everywhere; to him who is eternally composed of all things, to that Soul of All, salutation!

When the object of cognition attains oneness with the consciousness of the perceiver due to the latter's nature as pure consciousness, then this [object] is cognized by the consciousness through its very aspect as the visible; it is not otherwise.
When this entire process of the seer, the seeing, and the seen is nothing but pure consciousness, then the experience of everything therein remains as its fruition.

If the seer and the seen were not one within the nature of consciousness, then the ignorant person would not experience the taste of the seen, just as a stone does not perceive sugarcane even upon seeing it.

Because consciousness is of the nature of intelligence, the object of cognition sinks into that intelligence like water into water; through this, experience occurs, and not otherwise, as it would between two pieces of wood.
Just as wood does not perceive because of the absence of unity among its homogeneous parts, so too the observer, though non-inert, would not have known the object of perception.

Just as the wood possesses its own existence, so too does the insentient possess its own form; yet it does not know anything other than that. Therefore, the visible object is insentient, being perceived by consciousness.

The states of water, air, earth, and stone exist only through the Great Consciousness-Self; in these, there is no vibration, cognition, or the like, due to the absence of vital breath (*prāṇa*), the individual soul (*jīva*), and so forth.

The vital breath, the intellect, and the other faculties attain their existence through the power of mental cultivation (bhāvanā). This cultivation is the wonder of consciousness itself, and it arises according to one's will.
The Self abides as the reality of Brahman through its state as the world and its state as peace; it has indeed attained masculinity in both semen and the banyan seed.
In the seed composed of all the foremost atoms, that which is the most preeminent atom within it becomes each respective foremost thing; and the seed remains established within itself.
Brahman is the self of all atoms; because it is, in reality, subtler than the subtlest, whatever object it becomes, that very object remains as Brahman alone.
Just as a substance is indeed a substance—whether horizontal, upward, or downward—all is likewise Brahman, in whatever manner and by whatever means.
Just as there is only gold-ness and not otherness in a hundred forms of gold, so too there is only quiescence in the quiescent, despite the multitude of creations and the sense of "I."
Just as no clouds in a dream that appear by your side truly exist for you, so too, for me, the tumultuous activities of creation and dissolution are nothing but the void-self.
Just as that army of sons and banners imagined upon the sky is nothing but the state of tranquility—the sky itself—so too is this world.
The very delusion of mental construction within has blossomed forth as the world, like a tree in a kalpa whose seed was moistened by water and soil.

For the wise one who is free from the sense of "I," who exists as pure being and rests in oneness, even the supernatural powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest are indeed like mere fragments of withered grass.
In the three worlds, including the gods, asuras, and humans, I do not see anything that could excite the greed of that Great-Souled One, even for the sake of a single hair-pore of his body.
Whether remaining as one is or having gone here and there, for one who has realized the Self, the entire mass of dualistic conceptualizations does not exist.
For that Great-Souled One, the entire sky and all things are empty; how, for whom, and in what manner could there be a desire in him who is selfless?
Who is capable of weighing existence and non-existence as equal, when all distinctions have been stilled through the distinction of desirelessness?
Nothing dies by the Māras, nor does anything live by living beings; for this luminosity, which consists of pure consciousness, is like the sky.
Birth and death appear falsely to the world through delusion, even though they do not exist, just like the banks of a river in a mirage which appear to one who suffers from an optical illusion.
As long as there is no delusion and no examiners, that which has been correctly examined is indeed neither birth nor death, but solely the peaceful and imperishable.

He who has attained detachment from the visible world and the like, who delights in the Self and has reached tranquility—he, though existing, appears as non-existent, having completely crossed the ocean of worldly existence.
They know the one who is truly pure as "peaceful," whose extinction is like the extinguishing of a lamp, whose mental activity has set, and who has attained tranquility within the self alone.
The supreme ones call him liberated who, like the tranquil sky, finds no inherent relish for this world of perception beginning with the intellect.
Without inquiry, "I" exists; through inquiry, "I" does not exist. Since the referent of "I" is non-existent, where is the world and where is transmigration?

The sky of consciousness perceives the world—consisting of forms, light, and the nature of the mind—as existing through the very act of conscious perception, appearing with the forms of the intellect and so forth.
For you, whose mind is devoid of all objects and who are the Self of all, every action in every way and at all times is entirely auspicious.
Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give, whatever austerity you practice, and whatever you destroy or seek—that all is Śiva, the immutable.

That which I am, that which you are, that which is hope, and whatever constitutes action, time, space, and so forth; that which the Lokaloka mountains are—that is the pervasive, auspicious expanse of consciousness.

Whatever consists of form, light, and thought; whatever is the world throughout the three periods of time; and whatever consists of the afflictions of old age, death, and so forth—that is the auspicious Great Space of Consciousness.
Free from doubt, free from appearance, free from desire, and free from mind—the sage, having become selfless and entered into nirvāṇa, remains as you do, perfectly established.

Whether you engage in worldly activity or not, let it be as the wind acts through movement and stillness—you who are free from the thought of going or coming, peaceful, abiding in the infinite, and beyond all mental cultivation.
May your state as a person be free from latent impressions, devoid of fragmentation, and peaceful—like a wooden puppet driven by a mechanical device according to the instruction of a teacher.
Let the light of reality be neither affection nor lack of affection directed toward the external; let it remain as an indefinable light, like a multicolored lamp.

For one who is free from latent impressions, devoid of passion, and without desire, what indeed—apart from the scripture—is the cause for the delight of reality? For him who is stainless through the meaning of the scriptures and the approval of the virtuous, and who has no ulterior motive regarding sensory perceptions, his very nature is that [delight].

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: A person in whom the conviction that worldly existence is unreal has arisen naturally and is diminished, being free from volition, does not perceive volition; therefore, for him, it is as if non-existent.
Like the fading of breath upon a mirror, that which stands as "I" from some unknown source is seen by the Knower to be without cause; once perceived, it quickly vanishes and is no longer found.
He whose obscurations are exhausted, in whom all afflictions have been stilled, and whose self is filled with the supreme nectar—he shines by his very being.
By means of that radiant intellect, which acted like a wind for the mist of the dense darkness of all doubt, the region shone like the sky with a full moon.
Free from wandering, free from doubt, having attained the light, and unobstructed—the wise one, as pure as the autumnal sky, is known through what is to be known.
Free from conceptual construction, without support, and tranquil, he bestows purity through his touch; cool within, he is like the wind from the world of Brahmā.
This nature of things—that there is the experience of heaven—is the perception of what has no real form, just like the experience of a dream or the perception of the son of a barren woman.
This world that is experienced is indeed non-existent; this very nature of things is the perception of that which has no real form.
Since the transmigrations themselves are unreal, how could there be any purpose [in them]? The very terms "creation" and "liberation" are like the son of a barren woman.
The world is real as Brahman—uncreated, unconditioned, and unestablished; otherwise, it is neither "I" nor is it understood.
This nature of reality consists in resting in the intrinsic nature of the self; it is the non-perception of egoity, creation, suffering, and so forth.

When the consciousness has reached another location, from a moment's time up to a distance of a hundred thousand yojanas, that form of his which exists in the interval of the path is stainless within the conscious self.
It is like a windless atmosphere, consisting of consciousness that resembles the expanse of space; it is beyond thought, tranquil yet manifest, comparable to the blossoming of a creeper.
The wise know that to be the true nature of the entire multitude of living beings; for the discerning one who abides therein, the perception of creation dissolves away.
In deep sleep there is no cognition of dreaming; in dreaming there is no cognition of deep sleep. The delusions of creation and liberation are like those of deep sleep and dreaming.
This is the intrinsic nature of the object of delusion; it is neither dream nor deep sleep, neither creation nor nirvana, but is the truth that is entirely peaceful.
If delusion, consisting solely of the non-existent, is not found when scrutinized, how indeed can that which is unreal—like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—be attained?
That which is not apprehended does not exist; therefore, there is no possibility of error. There is no other nature than that which is perceived, and for whom [could it exist]? For no one at all.
It is said that intrinsic nature alone is always pleasing to everyone; for it is indeed non-dual, yet appears as if dual—so why not let this be clearly understood through various doctrines?

"In the absence of intrinsic nature there is great suffering; in the presence of intrinsic nature there is only peace. Having reflected thus within with the intellect, let that which is desired be performed.
Just as a large tree exists within a subtle seed, so it is established by observation; likewise, it is the highest discourse that the embodied universe exists within the embodied Śiva.
Form, light, mental attention, cognition, the "I-notion," and so forth are other [factors] that are essentially identical to its own nature, like fluidity in water or the nature of space.

Just as a material object performs actions through its constituent parts which resemble itself, so too the space of consciousness, though non-agent, acts through the elements that have become its own self.

The sound "I" and so forth, which arises from that which resides within the self and is not subject to transmigration for those such as ourselves—this sound, though devoid of any objective referent, is produced in drums and other instruments.
That which appears does not exist when examined; it is eternally non-existent. The form of the world is formless by nature; Brahman is established within Brahman.

For those for whom the world is a dream, they are like dream-people to one another; indeed, they do not exist within themselves, nor do they exist in relation to one another, just as sky-flowers do not exist in us.

In me, your Brahman is of a single form, peaceful like the expanse of space; and through worldly activities that are non-different from it, like the vibrations of the wind, you are likewise absorbed in me.
I, however, am real to them, like a dream to those who are dreaming; they, on the other hand, are surely unreal to me, like the dreams of one in deep sleep.
Whatever worldly transaction I have with them is that Brahman abiding in Brahman; let them see what they see, but enough, quite enough of that for me!
I do not exist at all within myself; this pervasive reality of Brahman arises, as it were, for your sake—such indeed is this very speech.

For one who knows that Self which consists of pure consciousness and is both non-contradictory and yet transcends contradiction, neither the desire for worldly enjoyment nor the desire for liberation flashes within the heart.

Since this sequence of bondage and liberation for human beings depends solely upon one’s own nature, what a mockery it is! Alas, through delusion, people experience the illusion of an ocean even over a mere puddle in a cow’s footprint.
In liberation, which consists in the pacification of non-existence through the realization of intrinsic nature, neither wealth, nor friends, nor ritual actions are of any help.
Just as a drop of oil, once cast upon water, spreads rapidly across the entire surface, so too does consciousness abide swiftly within the mental construction of the objectified world.

Just as the state of experiencing a dream-event possesses a certain flavor while one is awake, so too does the existence of the web of "I-ness" and the world possess that same flavor for the wise man.
By that very yoga of practice, it likewise attains such thinness that neither the "I" nor saṃsāra remains, and only peace is left behind.
Whenever the sun of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) becomes established, at that very moment the darkness of enjoyments (bhoga) dissolves; though it still exists, it is no longer perceived.
Free from the great delusion of the ego, the collection of instruments such as the intellect flashes forth at the time of death, exists, and likewise shines, just as light proceeds from a lamp.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: They know that the perception of forms, sights, mental activity, intellect, and the other senses is the unfading essential nature of the reality that is devoid of inherent self-nature.
When the persistence of intrinsic nature expands through the attenuation of the absence of intrinsic nature, then creation appears as a mere illusion.
When rest in one's own nature attains a state of peace, then the world-appearance subsides like a dream in deep sleep.
Sensual enjoyments are the great diseases of existence; kinsmen are a firm bondage; the attainment of wealth leads to misfortune. Therefore, let the self be stilled within itself.

Creation is the nature of being without self-nature; Śiva is the singular nature of self-nature. May [all] become the supreme void; may they be stilled here, and not suffer. Creation is the nature of being without self-nature; Śiva is the singular nature of self-nature. May [all] become the supreme void; may they be stilled here, and not suffer.
I do not perceive a self, nor the visible world of delusion; I have entered the peaceful Brahman—I am indeed Brahman, free from all affliction.
You alone perceive you, and you perceive the reality that unfolds as the meaning of words; I, however, perceive only the peaceful, absolute, supreme ether.
Within the supreme space of Brahman alone, these delusions of yours—consisting of form, light, and mind—have arisen like the vibrations in the wind, appearing as if they were real.
The Self as Brahman does not know the creation, nor does the Self as the creation know Brahman; one in deep sleep does not know the dream state, nor does one in the dream state know deep sleep.
Awakened to the nature of Brahman and the world as being like the forms seen in a waking dream, the one liberated while living, with a tranquil intellect, perceives their true form as pure light.
The awakened one thoroughly understands all this as it truly is; and with his self purified, he becomes tranquil like a cloud in autumn.

Whether established in memory or established in conceptual construction, the world-appearance is as it is described; likewise, the delusion of "I" and the world consists merely of the error of existence and non-existence.
For even in the self there is no seer of that [error] which has no knower at all; it is neither empty nor non-empty—this error appears as such.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This entire perception of "I-ness" and so forth is by nature devoid of inherent self-nature; let it be naturally extinguished by means of the single nature of its own true essence.
Wherever the sun may be, there let there be light; but where the awakened intellect resides, there let there be a supreme distaste for sense objects.
Without an agent, an object, or an instrument; without a visible world, a seer, or a seeing; this world has arisen as a painting on no wall, with its entire mass of phenomena beyond grasp.
It is neither arisen nor anything whatsoever; it is not tranquilized, yet it remains tranquil as it is. That supreme Brahman is free from affliction, truth, and indeed immutable.
Who is able to count the painted figurines of the world in the sky, which are colored upon the stage of imagination and consist of nothing but the wonder of consciousness?

Rich with aesthetic flavors, emotions, and transformations, they dance with ever-new gestures; for the most part, being of the nature of space, they flash within the sky even within every single atom.
Wearing the crowns of all seasons, with the creepers of their arms reaching out in all directions, they have the netherworld as the creepers of their feet and the world of Brahmā as their necks.
With the sun and moon as their rolling eyes, the stars as the hair upon their bodies, and the seven worlds as their slender limbs, they were clothed in the vast expanse of the sky on all sides.
The worlds, encircled by the oceans and the continents, with the Lokāloka mountain as their girdle, possess life-breaths flowing through living beings that move under the weight of all creatures.
Adorned with forests and groves as their necklaces and armlets, they take delight in the words of the ancient Vedas and the fruits of ritual actions.
This dance of the daughters of the three worlds which is seen before us is but the fluidity of the water of Brahman and the vibration of the wind of Brahman.
Abiding in its own lack of intrinsic nature, it is the cause that constitutes the essence of the cause; it remains in deep sleep like one who is not asleep, appearing as if real within the dream.
Abiding in a state that is neither asleep nor in deep sleep, contemplate your true nature; even while awake, remain free from agitation and do not resort to this dream.

That which is the state of deep sleep even while awake, free from desire and latent impressions through awakening—that is known as the true nature by the knowers of that; liberation is the transformation into that.
Without agent, object, or instrument, without the seen, the seer, or the act of seeing, and without form, light, or mental activity, Brahman exists as the world.
In the beloved, the beloved shines; in the full, the full is established. Devoid of duality and unity, it appears as that which is free from duality and unity.
It is truth, established in truth, peaceful, and itself the very self within the nature of creation; it is like the hollow of space and resembles the interior of a stone.
Having the form of a belly filled with excellent jewels, it is dense yet like the sky; like a reflection, it is unagitated even when agitated, and is both non-existent and existent.
The city that was to be newly created existed as if within his mind; it was Brahman, consisting of expanded light, with its mental faculties rendered undifferentiated.
Just as a city of imagination does not differ at all from the act of imagining, so too this appearance of the world does not differ from ultimate reality.
Like a golden pedestal containing the arrangement of many future worlds, it remained vast, tranquil, and imperishable, even while being perceived.
Abounding in constant destruction and arising, yet uniform and free from affliction; without destruction or arising, undecaying, and appearing as if manifold despite its radiance.

Brahman alone shines forth, having entered into a state of dense tranquility, appearing through the emergence of creation that is devoid of both setting and rising; indeed, when one is awakened, it manifests spontaneously as the dissolution of the attainment of inherent nature, like the sky through its power of emptiness.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That which is the manifestation of consciousness within the tranquil state is not distinct from it; since it is unmanifest and stainless, how can there be the possibility of creation and so forth?

When the lamp of the mind has gone out, the perceptions of forms, light, and mental attention vanish like waves of water; yet while it remains in the sky of consciousness, they appear as if wandering through delusion.
Just as the movement of the wind is independent of any instrument, and just as the radiance of light is its own diffusion, so too is this world within the Supreme.
Just as liquidity is in nectar, emptiness in the sky, and vibration in the wind, so too is this something consisting of the Self within the Supreme.
In the great consciousness, within the vast space, this world that shines forth is nothing but the radiance of consciousness itself, appearing like the purity within a gem.
Just as liquidity exists in water, as emptiness exists in space, and as vibration exists in wind, so does the world exist within the Great Consciousness.
Just as the wind perceives its own vibration, so does consciousness perceive the world; herein, not even the slightest possibility exists for distinctions such as duality or unity.
Through lack of discernment and through discernment, the world appears radiant and fragile; yet upon awakening, it is always the nature of pure being—non-radiant and indestructible.
Apart from pure cognition alone—which is devoid of beginning, middle, and end—nothing else exists here; this is the definitive conclusion regarding that whose nature is great pure consciousness.
To some it is auspicious and peaceful; to some, the eternal Brahman; to some, mere emptiness; and to some, mere cognition.

Then, contemplating its own infinite self as the form of consciousness as if it were an object of thought, that which is established in itself undergoes a state of knowability as if it were ignorance.

There is no existence of the mind apart from consciousness, nor is there consciousness without it; just as there is no "without" apart from "without," or as the wind is the cause within its own vibrations.
Likewise, the great radiance of consciousness always possesses existence or non-existence within the functions of the awareness of creation, because it does not depend on any other cause.
If such were the meaning here, it would exist by virtue of duality, unity, or existence; but who could conceive of duality or unity here in the great void?

The state of being the single, boundless, supreme expanse of space, encompassing the entire universe in every direction, is like the duality of motion and wind; it exists only as a verbal designation and is not real.

The duality of the Lord of All and the universe, as well as that which consists of the nature of non-existence, is indeed non-existent duality; for it is that which is the Great Pure Consciousness alone.

This very world-appearance is that [Brahman] alone; it is neither the universe nor the state of being the universe. Just as gold possesses reality at some time through its possession of space, time, and so forth, [so too does Brahman appear as such].
Furthermore, since the bracelet-ness and the universe are distinct, and since duality and unity are both impossible here, how can there be a relationship of cause and effect?
If it should be argued that this is merely a mental construction and not another real entity—just as emptiness is in the sky or fluidity is in water—then [we reply]: so be it.
The world’s primordial state exists, as it were, non-different from the mere line drawn in the sky; since the form of Brahman is the very form of the world, where in this is there duality or unity?
Whatever is the nature of space, such indeed is the nature of the entire void, within that single, pervasive, pure, and all-encompassing essence of consciousness alone.

How could there be a state of non-spatiality within space, given that a second entity is impossible? It is the self of manifestation alone, whose nature is light, that shines as creation within the Great Consciousness.
Only a semblance of worldly existence remains, appearing like the silence of a wooden statue, just as the mental delusion of perceiving forms persists for one whose eyes are closed.

Just as one who is awake in a dream perceives what is non-existent as if it were existent through the power of mental conception, so too for one with eyes open, there arises the mental delusion of perceiving forms.

Even while awake and situated in the waking state, one is as if non-existent due to the absence of the notion of existence; having brought about the cessation of such mental cultivation, one remains as one is, like a solidified stone.
Let the internal nature, which has indeed become free from agitation, remain equanimous through the offering of solitude and the worship of whatever objects are encountered as they arise.
For the sake of awakening, let the Supreme Lord, who is one's own nature, be worshipped with discernment; when one's own self is honored through discrimination, it immediately bestows vast boons.

In this [state], the worship of Rudra, Upendra, and others is regarded as a mere fragment of withered straw; it is worshipped solely by the flowers of offerings consisting of inquiry, tranquility, and the company of the virtuous.
O virtuous one, one's very own self is the Supreme Lord, whose fruit is immediate liberation; when worshipped solely by the mere vision of reality, he bestows the unsurpassed goal.

Where the Self and the Lord reside, what deluded person would seek refuge in another—especially for one whose soul is honored by the company of the virtuous, tranquility, contentment, and discernment?

Weapons, snakes, poisons, and fires become like *śirīṣa* flowers; even acts such as worshiping the gods, performing austerities, visiting sacred fords, and giving gifts, though performed excessively, become so.
These [worldly activities] turn to ashes for those of great soul who lack discernment, because they are devoid of purpose; yet, if they are performed with discernment, they become fruitful.
Why then is this discernment not clearly cultivated within, so that through the knowledge of things as they truly are, there may be the cessation of latent impressions in the supreme state?
The effort known by the word "discrimination" arises from the clarity of the self; in that same manner, discrimination should be made to increase within by means of the nectar of tranquility.
Furthermore, to the extent that one undergoes drying up through no longer being deluded, by disregarding the existence of the body and seeing things as they truly are;
One should conquer shame, fear, dejection, envy, pleasure, and pain equally. Since the world, the body, and so forth did not exist at all in the beginning, how could they exist today?
Even if this effect belongs to the cause, it is nevertheless nothing but Brahman; it is merely a pure appearance, for jars and the like do not exist apart from consciousness.
Intuition is indeed of the nature of knowledge; the entire world is nothing but cognition. Even this cognition, which is the glory of the reality of the Self, subsides when it is fully understood.
But when the object of knowledge is absent, that which is inexpressible remains—the eternal, auspicious, bodiless, and non-universal Self; all this is pervaded by that Peace.
Free from the knower, the known, and the act of knowing, they remain like the silence of a stone; with their inner faculties stilled, they are self-abiding, like the interior of a stone statue.
Whether moving or causing movement, remain as the very form of consciousness; you are the true nature of the knower of the unknowable, the essence of both being and non-being.
The realms of existence have become as clear as the expanse of space for you; they remain exactly as they are, coming and going just as they came.
The wise attain the supreme state either by performing only those actions that come to them naturally, or else by being radiant with an inner organ pacified through the renunciation of everything.
Let all things remain in solitude, like figures depicted in a painting; when conceptualization has ceased, let everything always be like a city of one's own imagination.
Like one awakened from a dream, the world has always set for the enlightened; yet, like one blind from birth, they perceive it through delusions as if experiencing forms with eyes.
Describing nirvāṇa through the instruction of conceptual fragments, the ignorant person is tormented within and does not find peace; so does the world, whose nature is composed of ignorance.

Due to some form of ignorance, one who has not accomplished his purpose thinks, "I have accomplished my purpose"; thus, being deluded by folly, he perceives himself as having achieved what was unachieved.
Through the afflictions of subsequent moments, one will realize that the goal has not been achieved; the wise know that a means consisting of mere conceptual construction is no means at all.

Having fully understood the delusion of the world through its delusions of existence, non-existence, longing, and error—which, because they bestow suffering, vanish in the blink of an eye—one remains free from latent impressions (*avāsana*); that indeed is called Nirvāṇa, wherein all sense objects have become tasteless.

Having attained the intuitive flash of meaning through this narrative, the essence of consciousness, being fluid by nature, will experience the waters of awareness; seeing the entire stainless form of the knowable as consciousness, you shall attain nirvana in the true nature of the world.

When one has cast beneath one’s feet that state of non-awakening which is understood through the scriptures as being like the experience of forms by one blind from birth, then, having descended into this internal awakening, there arises an experience that transcends worldly existence.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Through thorough knowledge, this world, beginning with the sense of "I," attains unreality; yet through delusion, it appears as real to those whose minds perceive otherwise.
For one who is freed from the fever of ignorance and whose self has been cooled by awakening, this alone shall be the sign: that the water of worldly enjoyment no longer appeals to them.

Enough with other forms of thorough knowledge or the delusions regarding the signified and the signifier; let Nirvana be contemplated as nothing more than the awareness that is free from the notion of "I."
Just as objects experienced in a dream do not truly taste [to us] once they are fully understood, so too, in this delusion of "I" and this world, they do not exist.
Just as a person with an eye disease sees a city with its inhabitants and trees as if they were real when they are actually unreal, so too does the living being perceive cyclic existence.
Just as a yakṣa who is of the nature of delusion and the world of yakṣas are both mutually real in form yet firmly established as false, so too are the delusions of "I-ness" and the world.
In the forest, due to the absence of obscuration, yakṣas appear in delusive forms; just as these spirits manifest, so too do these fourteen [elements].
Realizing and contemplating that "I am merely a delusion and am utterly false," the yakṣa becomes a non-yakṣa; likewise, this mind attains the state of the true nature of mind.
Abandoning all suspicion regarding mental constructs, free from both rejection and acceptance, with all desires no longer spreading forth, remain peaceful and established as you truly are.

This pervasive visible world, which arises from non-existence, is of the nature of the seer; or else, if it is not of the nature of the seer, why remain in this state of being inexpressible despite its existence?
Just as a cluster of branches and shrubs is merely the fullness of the essence of spring, so too is the state of creation merely the fullness of consciousness in its own nature.
This world-appearance is pure, a perception consisting of consciousness alone; what unity or duality is there here? Let Nirvana, which is stainless, be attained.
Let there be dwelling within the space of pure consciousness; let the supreme nectar be drunk; and let one remain without fear in the bliss-grove of Nirvana.
Why do you humans, with deluded minds, wander like deer driven by the wind in these utterly empty wildernesses of saṃsāra?
O you whose intellects are blinded by the mirage-water of the three worlds, do not run with agitated minds, for your hopes have been snatched away by your own inner dispositions.
O deer, do not waste your lives in vain exertion, drinking the water of a mirage formed by forms, light, and mental attention.
Perish with the great pride of this world, which is like a city of Gandharvas; perceive that these things which appear to be happiness are nothing but suffering.

O you who perceive the world as a mass of hair-tufts floating in the midst of the great sky, do not mistake it for such; rather, let your mind be transformed toward your own true nature, which is free from error.
O humans, who are as fragile as the ripples of water caught on the high leaves of a wind-tossed tree, do not sleep upon the beds of the womb within these mortal women.
Remain at rest in the peaceful, beginningless, and endless nature without interruption; let it perish through its lack of intrinsic nature due to the defects of the states of the seer and the seen.
When cyclic existence is realized as it truly is, not even the slightest bit of it remains; and as for that which is the truth, no name for it exists.
Having forcibly torn apart the cage of saṃsāra, which is entwined with the iron chains of craving, remain above all like the king of beasts.
Liberation is merely the pacification of the delusion that grasps at a self and what belongs to a self; for the yogin who abides in suchness, that very state is his own being.

The state of nirvana, the state of being free from latent impressions, the supreme state of freedom from affliction, and the state of omniscience—these are the peaceful grounds of rest for one weary on the path of saṃsāra.

That which is known by the wise is not known by fools, and that which is known by fools is not known by those who possess such wisdom; this purpose of the world exists as a mutual state consisting of an inexpressible meaning.
When all delusion has completely subsided, that which remains is not even perceived; it is like a doll made of water, submerged within the waters of the great ocean.

When delusion has subsided for the awakened one who has attained nirvāṇa, the universal nature of existence remains exactly as it is; it is found to exist just as it stands, yet free from all conceptual constructs.
Just as a heap of ashes from burnt grass is carried away somewhere by the winds, so too the world is carried away somewhere by the sages who rest in their own true nature.
That arrangement of the categories of the world-Brahman is indeed supreme; it has the nature of the referent of the word "Brahman" and does not participate in the function of the word "world."
Just as these objects appear to an ignorant person who does not understand them, so do they appear to the wise man who remains with his latent impressions extinguished.
That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled man keeps watch; that wherein beings keep watch is night for the sage who sees.

That which is his waking state remains indeed uninterrupted, like his deep sleep; for one who perceives the world as a painted picture, his cravings for the objects of the waking state are like those of a dream.

To the wise one, the perception of the world—which is like the experience of forms by one blind from birth, consisting mostly of error and having the nature of the unreal—appears and yet does not appear.
The suffering of the three worlds is delusion; its objects are not real. When a dream is known as a dream, the forms, perceptions, mind, and activities [within it] cease to be true.
Just as they do not taste [the objects], so let them flash forth in waking and dreaming; being undivided, fully composed, and having attained supreme non-contradiction.

With an inner self that has become profoundly cool, the knower abides in nirvāṇa; for one who knows that and is liberated from attraction, his state is one of equanimity even without formal meditation.
Without a low place, no flow of water can occur at all; likewise, there is no mental attention without an object, and no mind without the coloring of an object.
This very manifestation, consisting of both the external and internal, extends as far as the ocean and is composed of hundreds of converging river currents.

Just as the water of rivers flows as a single mass of congealed ice, possessing both external and internal forms and consisting of both the meaningful and the meaningless; so too does this world appear.
It is the mind alone that manifests as the appearance of objects, thus expanded; there is no duality between object and mind, just as there is none between water and its waves.
In the absence of one of two things, both are stilled, like wind and its movement; for in ultimate reality, that which is devoid of essence is certainly stilled through the cessation of even one.
Because they are one, the object and the mind are simultaneously and swiftly stilled; for one who understands, that object whose nature is conceptual construction should no longer be pursued.
Through right knowledge, the mind and [the sense organs] attain peace; for the wise man, these two—the object and the mind—perish of their own accord when [ignorance] has not been destroyed.

Just as one feels fear toward an enemy made of clay through the knowledge that it is not real, so too, for the wise man, the object and the mind always remain exactly as they are, yet free from the fear of the perception of enmity.

When that which is of the nature of pure being has come into existence, everything else becomes something entirely unprecedented; even the time of the world, which is the purpose of the collection [of scriptures], becomes ignorant, a subject for the ignorant, and unreal.

To the wise man, this world does not exist as something with consciousness, just as there is no dream for a man sleeping on his side, nor as there is no malevolent yakṣa for a eunuch; it is like the perception of a demon held by a hero.

The wise man cultivates the ignorant one for a long time, and thus even the barren [intellect] flourishes, as if it had attained the state of an object without even knowing the meaning of the word "object."
The wise know the abiding consciousness to be beginningless and endless by nature, yet as that which enters into creation; it is the mind devoid of word and meaning, free from division and end.
Like a wave of the mind within the pure water of awakening, where indeed can there be an end even for that which arises; for what, truly, are objects and the mind?
Delusion is indeed meaningless; let one remain established in the nature of intrinsic being, like autumnal skies, abiding in the nature of pure awareness.

The state of the mind is not experienced through the boundaries of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; having shaken off infinite multiplicity and the unreal nature, [abide] in that which is free from affliction.

Know that everything without exception is like a rope; abide in your own nature as the dense mass of consciousness. It is pure awareness alone that presides over both the internal and external, manifesting as the state of being an object.
Tell me, how can the seed, the branches, and the fruits exist? Where, then, are the object and the mind? Since the knowable is non-existent, even consciousness has reached the ineffable state.

Because all specific attributes have been stilled, that which remains is the reality whose nature is existence; it is the object itself as mental attention, and that is an illusion consisting of non-existence.
The mind itself is the mental construction of objects, and that is an error consisting of non-existence; because the Unborn One is the self of all, this mind is likewise without a cause.
Due to the experience of delusion, an object appears as if it truly exists, though it is entirely false; the mind manifests as the appearance of an object even without any external cause.
Unstable and flickering like a flash of lightning, you, whose nature is mere mental attention, wander in delusion within the cycle of existence.

Through the thorough knowledge of the single nature of things, you neither exist nor do you wander in delusion; for saṃsāra exists only through the mind, and it is stilled by the awakening to the Self.

People suffer in vain through the form of the delusion that silver exists in a mother-of-pearl shell; but the supreme state is the non-existence of existence, which is the nature of pure consciousness, free from saṃsāra.
Any existence other than Nirvana is the delusion that "I am suffering"; I am like the water of a mirage, having the nature of the unreal and the void.

Thus, through the thorough knowledge of the self, the notion of "I" itself subsides; having known this and becoming composed of pure knowledge, one realizes the nature of all things, both external and internal.
Just as water does not abandon its own nature even when it has become a wave, and just as the existence of a tree extends from the root to the tips of its branches.

Free from modification and impurity, the single end of the object of knowledge shines forth as pure consciousness alone, just as the one stainless sky appears to extend for hundreds of thousands of yojanas.
In that same way, knowledge alone shines forth as undivided, reaching to the very limit of the knowable; because it is empty, it is one and stainless, just as space is all-pervading.
Likewise, having known that one stainless reality even within the states of both the knower and the known, the self becomes solidified like clarified butter and is turned into stone.

In the same way, by being perceived as an object of thought, the Self itself is made into one's own mind; thus, even without space or time, the Self attains the state of being a mind through awakening or non-awakening.

The unawakened are led by means of logical arguments, for this [reality] alone is well-established; although here there is no possibility whatsoever of non-awakening or the like, nevertheless, for the sake of awakening one another, such [distinctions] are conceptualized right here.

Possessing great majesty and free from conceit, they dissolve upon the pacification of the state of delusion; being devoid of error and tranquil through their very infinity, they become eternally composed in meditative absorption.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, tell me of that Being which bestows rest, which possesses the fruit of the lotus from the tree of meditative absorption, and which is adorned with creepers and flowers.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen to the description of the tree of meditative absorption (samādhi), which rises ever higher throughout one's life in the forest of discerning people, and is endowed with leaves, flowers, and fruit.
The wise know that the seed of this [renunciation] is the disillusionment with the forest of saṃsāra, which has arisen in some way through suffering and by itself.
The wise know his field to be that which is ploughed by the furrow of the auspicious net, watered day and night with the essence [of dharma], and possesses channels for the flowing wind.
Disgust for cyclic existence is the seed of meditative concentration; it falls of its own accord upon the ground of the mind, which is secluded like a forest where those who practice solitude dwell.
The seed of meditative concentration that has fallen upon the ground of one's own mind should be diligently watered with these consecrations by one of great intelligence, without weariness.
With pure, gentle, purifying, sweet, and self-beneficial words—like the milk of association with the virtuous, or like the nectar of the moon—[he spoke].
With the excellent waters of the meaning of the scriptures—cool as nectar, pure, full, and bestowing inner emptiness—spread abroad like channels of ambrosia;

Having thoroughly understood with great intelligence that the seed which has fallen upon the ground of one's own mind is the disenchantment with saṃsāra, it should be guarded with effort for the sake of meditative concentration.
By means of various forms of austerity and giving, through the arrangement of ritual objects as desired, and by planning the construction of hermitages, temples, resting places, and extensive groves;
A guardian named Contentment, whose disposition is well-trained, must be appointed for this [tree] once it has sprouted; he should be constantly accompanied by his beloved, Joy.
One should ward off the vultures of lustful pride as they swoop down from this [world] upon the birds of others' affection that have settled there behind one's back.
The dust and darkness [of the mind] must be wiped away from us by the gentle spears of virtuous conduct, by the rays of the sun of discernment, and by those which grant inconceivable light.
Prosperity and women are like waves, fragile in their enjoyment; upon him fall the thunderbolts impelled by the clouds of his own misdeeds.

These [thoughts] should be warded off by means of fortitude, magnanimity, compassion, and mantras, as well as by recitation, ritual bathing, austerity, and self-restraint—by one who wields the trident of the meaning of the *praṇava*.
From this seed of meditative concentration, thus well-guarded, there emerges a new sprout called discernment—glorious, noble by birth, and exalted.
By that, the ground of the mind shines forth, radiant and blossoming; it becomes delightful with light, just as the sky is by the newly risen moon.
Therefore, from the sprout of that [seed], two things blossom of their own accord: the first is the study of the scriptures, and the second is association with the virtuous.
He erects this pillar named Steadfastness, reaching toward loftiness, wrapped in the bark of contentment and dyed with the essence of dispassion.
One whose soul is nourished by the essence of dispassion and who is endowed with the rainy season of the meaning of the scriptures attains supreme exaltation in a very short time.

Nourished by the essence of dispassion through study of the scriptures and association with the virtuous, it does not tremble in the least from the disturbances caused by the monkeys of passion and hatred.
Then, from that being whose form was adorned with consciousness, these creepers, exuberant with sap, were born and spread across the wide regions.
Clarity, truthfulness, existence, steadfastness, non-conceptuality, equanimity, tranquility, loving-kindness, compassion, renown, and nobility.
O ascetic, this powerful tree of meditation, with these creepers of its virtues as leaves and its fame as flowers, acts like a *pārijāta* tree for you.
Thus, this supreme tree of knowledge, possessing creepers, shoots, and flowers, will day by day yield the fruit of future wisdom.
Rich with clusters of flowers of fame, shimmering with the foliage of virtues, spreading the essence of dispassion, and having the form of blossoming buds of wisdom.
It cools all directions like a cloud in the rainy season; it pacifies the heat of creation as the moon does the heat of the sun.
Peace spreads a cool shade like the arrival of the clouds; peace disperses the obstruction like a wind scatters a cloud.
It fastens itself as a pedestal, standing firm like a principal mountain; it produces above it the "vessel" (ghaṭikā) of the fruit, beginning with the auspicious [element].
But as the wish-fulfilling tree of discernment grows day by day, the forest of a person’s heart becomes enveloped in its spreading shade.
The coolness that removes the heat of the soles proceeds forth; it is the creeper of the flourishing intellect, beautiful as the interior of frost.
In her, the deer of the mind—like a traveler worn out since birth and agitated by the clamor on the road—finds rest from its intermediate exhaustion.
Sought by enemies for the sake of his mere existence, his body, and his skin, he was on the verge of being shattered, stripped of his various essential forms and appearances.
Driven by the winds of latent tendencies spreading through the forest of saṃsāra, and constantly scorched by the fire of the river of egoism, [I am ruined].
Worn out by long-standing and far-reaching movements of essential pursuits, he has fallen into a pit through the power of his attachment to sons and grandsons.
His limbs were worn out by the hardships of wallowing in the creeper of Fortune; grasping at the river of the glory of craving, he was struck far away by its surging waves.
Intent on fleeing from the distress caused by that disease and its wicked hunter, he performed his rites without hesitation, as if fearing the fall of the hunter's arrow upon him.
Apprehensive of the arrows of suffering that had reached the seat of the knowable, he was intent on driving away his enemies, marked by the act of fetching stones.
It was violently tossed about by the rising and falling, the surging and subsiding; it was ground to powder through a succession of impacts from the stones of its own transformations.
Wounded by being drawn into the net of the beautiful creeper of craving, his conduct fashioned by his own ignorance, he was thoroughly schooled in supreme deceit.
Having come upon the collection of the senses, he was intent on fleeing, yet he was crushed by the fierce, thundering trampling of the great elephant that is so difficult to seize.
Fainted by the potent venomous hiss of the great python of sense-objects, the lustful man is generally cast down upon the ground of the beloved by the force of passion.
Burning with the eruption and inflammation of boils on his back, scorched by the forest fire of anger, he is constantly tormented by the burning of many long-lasting sufferings of coming and going.
Afflicted by the defects of the portions of desire clinging to one's own self, he has long been pursued by the jackals of worldly enjoyment, greed, vanity, and pleasure.
Chased by the leopard of poverty arising from being deluded about one's own karma as its creator, his body tumbles into the pit of the mountain-peak of blindness caused by the mist of confusion.
Distressed by the trembling of his heart at the sight of Mānasiṃha’s exultation, he regarded death in battle as if it were a *vṛka* flower.
Quickly frequented from afar by people because of pride that swallows them up, it has the sprouts of its bamboo-like tongue spread out on all sides by desires.
Having been embraced for a moment by youth, his friend, he was then abandoned; he was left like one cast out by turbulent winds into places difficult to traverse.
O King, at times the deer of the mind attains peace and tranquility under a certain tree, as if finding its livelihood in the sun.

May the deer of your own mind reach that tree of supreme peace—the very name of whose bliss the deluded do not know, even as they rest among the trees and shrubs such as the *tāla*, *tamāla*, and *bakula*, which laugh with the playful display of abundant flowers.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: O slayer of enemies, having thus come to rest, this deer of the mind finds delight right there and does not go to another branch.
Then, after this much time, that tree of discernment gradually and fully brings forth its internal fruit, which is the nature of ultimate reality.
That deer of his own mind, standing below that tree of merit which is the fruit of meditation, gazes upon it as it reaches the very top.
A man climbs a tree to taste its fruit; he abandons other categories of objects, possessed as he is by an extensive resolve.
Having attained the exalted state, one abandons the worldly activities rooted in the tree of discernment; having reached that height, one no longer desires what is below.
Therefore, for the sake of the supreme fruit, having ascended the tree of discernment, he casts off his former formative predispositions (saṃskāra) like a snake sheds its skin.
Laughing aloud as he beheld himself ascended to such a high station, he thought: "What kind of wretched person was I for all this time?"
Wandering among those branches of compassion and the rest, he shines resplendent like a sovereign emperor, casting down the serpent of greed beneath his feet.
Day by day, craving—the dark iron chain that is the row of throats for the moon of the heart and the mass of darkness for the lotus of suffering—is cast off.
He remains equanimous toward what has not been attained and does not long for what has not yet arrived; gentle as the moon, he is inwardly cool in all his mental states.
He remains seated upon the very sprouts of the meaning of the scriptures, observing the movements of the world as they rise and fall, going downward.
Beholding his former haunts, now bristling with heaps of flowers scattered by fearsome trees and creepers, he laughs inwardly at their wretchedness.
Moving among those regions of the [five] aggregates with a captivating nature that soars and settles, he shines like a king.
One perceives one's children, wife, friends, and wealth as if they were produced in another life, or as if they were born of a dream.
Due to the great power of passion, hatred, fear, intoxication, pride, and delusion, these [defilements] are seen in him—whose mind is cool and pure—as if he were an actor.
The courses of the rivers of saṃsāra, with currents as fickle as waves, appear like the behavior of a madman even as they flow before one's eyes and laugh.
He does not direct his thoughts toward any desires for worldly objects, wives, or wealth; resting in the unprecedented state, he is like one already dead while yet living.
Having fixed one's gaze solely upon that which is absolute, pure, awakened, and most exalted—the Self—one ascends to that supreme fruit.
Constantly recollecting his former states and nourished by the nectar of contentment, he finds satisfaction even in the loss of both gains and losses.
In legal affairs, in undertakings, and even in matters that produce enjoyment, he experiences supreme agitation, as if a sleeper suddenly awakened.
Like one who has traveled a long distance, he—long overcome by the exhaustion of ignorance—desires a noble and unimpeded rest without ceasing.
Even though awakened by exhalation, the fire remains within itself as if without fuel; though equal to the mere breath, it subsides while remaining inside.
He is unable to gradually ward off the aversion toward objects that falls upon him with sheer force, just as one cannot turn back a vision that has already fallen away.
Proceeding toward that great state which bestows the fruit of the ultimate truth, one also attains a stage that is beyond the reach of words.
When enjoyments arrive from some source even while he remains inactive, by the power of destiny, he feels a distaste for them, like a traveler in desert lands.
Reeling as if exhausted, yet blissful and asleep to the fluctuations of worldly existence, with his mind full within, the silent sage attains an indescribable state.
Having attained such a state, he gradually approaches the proximity of that ultimate fruit, just as a bird reaches the path of the sky.
Then, having abandoned that entire intellect and becoming equal to the sky, he grasps, tastes, enjoys, and finally becomes fully satisfied.
The daily expansion resulting from the renunciation of objects of volition, which consists in resting in one's own pure nature, is called the attainment of the ultimate reality.
When the cognition of difference has dissolved its object, non-difference alone remains; the wise know that to be Brahman—pure, one, and without beginning or end.
By one who is dispassionate toward the desire for worldly life, who has abandoned the desire for a wife, and who is liberated from the desire for wealth, rest is found in that state.
