Through a further transformation, the notion of difference between consciousness and ultimate reality dissolves, like a streak of frost under the heat of the sun.
For one who knows that [reality], once it has been drawn forth and released, no state whatsoever can exist within its own natures without a simile, such as that of a garland of flowers.

Just as a carved statue (śālabhañjikā) situated within the interior of a pillar is neither existent nor non-existent [as a separate entity], so too is the existence of the universe within the Supreme.
Meditation cannot be practiced, nor is it of any use; for one who has awakened through non-awakening remains right here by himself.
He in whom an absolute lack of relish for visible objects is observed is a Buddha; for only one who is awakened possesses the power to renounce the visible world.
The awareness of the visible as being awareness itself, which is never separate from that awareness, is designated by the term "concentration" for one who is perfectly concentrated.
When the mental cognition takes the form of the unity of the seer and the seen, it then rests of its own accord in that singular concentration.
For the knower of reality, one's own innate nature is simply a distaste for the perceptible; the supreme ones declare that the very vibration of the perceptible is the state of not knowing reality.
Objects of sense please only those who do not know that [Reality], but not those who know it; for bitter sour gruel does not please one who has drunk nectar within.
For the wise man who is free from craving, established in the Self, and has abandoned the three types of seeking, meditation proceeds spontaneously even though he does not desire it.
Awakening shines forth for one in whom craving no longer exists; having abandoned its own nature, where could that craving remain, what would it be, and how?

May that realization of the object of meditation, which belongs to the wise man who is not a seeker of worldly gain, lead him [to liberation]; for that [realization] is infinite for one free from craving, arising spontaneously as an indivisible whole.
For one who is free from craving, meditation proceeds spontaneously and boundlessly, like the natural stability of a mountain whose wings have fallen away.
Because it possesses the nature of knowing, the state of non-concentration arises within the pure self of awakening; for a drop of ghee never remains in a well-kindled fire.
Supreme detachment from sense objects is declared to be meditative absorption; salutations to that Brahmin among men by whom that has certainly been attained.
Surely, when freedom from craving for sense objects has reached full maturity, even the gods and asuras, including Indra himself, are unable to displace one's meditative absorption.

Therefore, let supreme detachment from sense objects be accomplished through diamond-like meditation; once duality has dissolved through wisdom, what is the use of other meditations that are like mere straw?

The meaning of the word "universe" resides in the ignorant, yet it does not have the ignorant as its object; likewise, it resides in both the knower and the ignorant, and in both the universe and the Lord of the Universe.
O wise ones, rest there where all things shine as one—the ground of awakening for the perfected ones, or the realm of objects for those who possess discernment.

Since existence and non-existence, as well as duality and unity, have been determined here by no one else, there is but one means [to realization]: the purpose of the scripture, and second, association with those who possess knowledge.

The third dhyāna is supreme in Nirvāṇa; therein, each subsequent stage is superior. Through the mirror of the individual soul, one perceives form within one another; this is the Great Body (Mahāvapu).

In this world, through the friction of [opposing] things, there arises a lack of distinction between the equal and the unequal, for one who has previously known the entire world situated like a checkerboard.

When one is established, both are established: the lamp of awakening and the lamp of dispassion. Shaken by the wind of the intellect in the sky of consciousness, everything is consumed by the fire of knowledge.
I do not know where this world-cotton quickly goes into the supreme peace; by that awakening, as if by a variegated fire, dullness is not extinguished.
Even though the delusion of the world is rootless, it does not quickly dissolve; for just as the perception of a world blazes up through ignorance in one who is unenlightened.

Likewise, through the thorough knowledge of the Knower, the non-perception of that [world] is illuminated; for one who knows that, the perception of the ignorant world remains devoid of both word and meaning.
The perception of the three worlds, just as it exists, has arisen like a painting; it is fashioned by emptiness itself, as if constructed by sleep.

The desire for manifestation shines forth as the cognition of the world within the mind of the knower; indeed, for one who is undeluded in awakening, there is neither egoism nor the persistence of the world.
A certain state exists which has the nature of supreme luminosity; the mind, consisting of both awakening and non-awakening, shines like dry and wet wood.

Due to awakening, the world is one; through the state of insentience, it has not attained selfhood. Through mutual awakening they speak to one another, and through awakening they cultivate friendship.
The wise person, by abiding in identity with that which is its predominant aspect, does not perceive the true nature of the existence and non-existence of the world.

Just as one who has reached the fourth state (turiya) perceives the nature of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, so too this mind—which is nothing but latent impressions—is destroyed through self-inquiry.
Therefore, because it is not a real entity, liberation does not proceed from the destruction of the self.

Having gradually attained awakening from the tree of meditation—which had matured of its own accord through time into no small ripeness—the deer of the mind, desiring the primordial supreme awakening as the fruit of the elixir, was released from its fetters.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the fruit of the supreme reality is known and has reached its consummation in liberation, even that "awakening" quickly becomes unreal; for the supreme reality is like a deer of the mind.
Somewhere that state of being an animal vanishes like a lamp whose oil is exhausted; there remains only the vision of ultimate reality, shining with infinite light.
When the mind has attained awakening through the fruition of the tree of meditation, it maintains a state of adamantine essence, remaining as motionless as a bird whose wings have been clipped.
Mental activity vanishes somewhere, while pure awareness remains—unobstructed, undivided, and truly all-pervasive in its nature.
Through its state of perfect seclusion, the existence of consciousness arises as awareness; it is without beginning or end, and it bestows the fruit of pure luminosity.
Then, there, all desires having been cast aside by itself, nothing remains but meditation, which is without beginning or end and free from effort.

As long as Brahman has not been realized and one has not come to rest in the supreme state, so long is that [mental activity] understood as mere cogitation (manana) and not as meditative absorption (dhyāna).
Having attained oneness with the ultimate reality, I do not know where the mind has gone; where are the latent impressions, where are the karmas, and where are the perceptions of joy and anger?
The yogi is seen solely as one who has attained exclusive devotion to meditation; established in the vajra-concentration, he is like a mountain, immovable against adverse conditions.

For the yogi who has become dispassionate toward all enjoyments, whose sensory perceptions and consciousness are stilled, for whom every visible object is devoid of flavor, and who delights in his own self;

For one whose mental fluctuations have gradually dissolved and who has attained rest through sheer force, by whom indeed can that meditative absorption (samādhāna), which has arrived of its own accord, be scrutinized?
Those of refined disposition cultivate a distaste for sense objects to such an extent that they do not perceive them at all, just as a person in a painting does not perceive the objects [within it].
Not perceiving worldly objects due to the absence of latent tendencies, the self-possessed man is forcibly established in the adamantine concentration as if by another.
When that meditative concentration has arrived—like a river in flood during the rainy season—and comes by its own power, the mind does not waver again.

When one has arrived at meditative absorption through the power of the cooling of all objects, and through knowledge there is a distaste for sense-objects, that indeed is true samādhi and nothing else.
The firm distaste for sense objects is declared to be meditative absorption; that very state, through its full maturation, becomes truly adamantine in essence.
This very absence of craving for enjoyments is indeed the sprouting of meditation; when that same [state] is secured by the binding of the seat (pīṭhabandha), it becomes beautiful.
Right knowledge, fully expanded and forever free from latent impressions, becomes meditation; having reached the state of bliss, it becomes nirvāṇa.

If there is freedom from craving for enjoyments, what need is there for the deluded mind of meditation? If there is no freedom from craving for enjoyments, what need is there for the deluded mind of meditation?
For the sage who has abandoned the tasting of the visible world and possesses perfect knowledge, non-conceptual meditative absorption proceeds without interruption.
He for whom the visible world does not taste sweet is known as a perfectly awakened one (saṃbuddha); when enjoyments no longer taste sweet, perfect awakening (samyagbodha) is said to have arisen.

How can there be the state of an enjoyer for one whose nature is at rest? For the state of an enjoyer is indeed without intrinsic nature; when that [nature] has ceased, how and from where could it exist?
At the conclusion of hearing, reciting, and chanting, one should be devoted to meditative absorption; when weary from meditative absorption, one should resort to hearing, reciting, and chanting.

He attained Nirvana, free from all weariness, delightful through the setting of every doubt, as serene as deep sleep, with a mind equally tranquil, and pure within like the expanse of an autumn cloud.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen to this sequence for one who, utterly exhausted by the burden of worldly existence and with his body rolling in calamities, desires rest.
When, previously, a tiny spark of discernment arises within one's own heart—consisting of world-weariness toward saṃsāra—whether through a specific cause or even without a cause;

Then, scorched by the heat, they resort to those who possess true luster and are exceedingly vast in their goodness—just as those oppressed by the sun seek out trees by the roadside that dispel the fatigue of the journey.

Like a traveler avoiding the sacrificial posts of the ignorant, he keeps those who lack knowledge at a distance; following the path of the wise, he performs ablutions, charity, austerity, and sacrifice.
It bears a conduct that is graceful, appropriate, and unartificial, which delights the world like the nectar of the moon's orb.
Following the wisdom of others, fortunate, fulfilling the welfare of others, and delighting in pure deeds, a certain gentle person proceeds.
Like a vessel of fresh butter—clear, smooth, soft, and enchanting—her sweet new acquaintance brings happiness to people.
The cool and pure deeds of the discerning person thoroughly refresh people, just like the clusters of rays from the moon.
One does not rest so free from fear in garden groves filled with heaps of flowers as one does in the company of the virtuous.
Like the waters of the Mandākinī, the associations of the discerning wash away evils and bestow purity.
Among those who possess discernment, who are dispassionate, and who seek to cross over saṃsāra, people attain a state of coolness as if they were in houses made of ice and crystal.
Indeed, that noble passion for the Name which exists in one who possesses discernment is not found even among the daughters of the gods and gandharvas, nor among human women.
The wisdom of one who performs appropriate actions gradually attains clarity; it internalizes the meaning of the scriptures, just as a mirror reflects an object.
Abounding in the essence of the meaning of the scriptures, true wisdom attains its height through the grace of discernment, like a plantain tree in a great forest.
Wisdom, endowed with purity, experiences all objects reflected within itself entirely, like a mirror.
One whose soul is purified by the company of the virtuous and who has been polished by the meaning of the scriptures shines like a cloth cleansed by fire, its impurities removed.
Like the sun that illuminates the world with its shimmering golden luster and stainless light, the virtuous person shines by his own splendor.
In such a way does the wise person pursue the study of the scriptures and the company of the virtuous, that through constant attachment he experiences those two alone.

Gradually attaining the state of a virtuous person and being permeated by the weight of the meaning of the scriptures, he shines while disregarding worldly enjoyments, as if having emerged from a cage.
As he daily cast off the misfortune of failing to obtain enjoyments, his family shone like the circle of stars with the moon.
No trace of miserliness regarding enjoyments ever arose in him; there was an unprecedented luster upon his face, like that of the moon when it is free from Rāhu.
That tree of cosmic aeons becomes an object of mention for those great beings who treat the three worlds as mere straw, just as the sky is an object of mention for the denizens of heaven.
Feeling inward shame even in his mind at the very thought of enjoying pleasures, he finds supreme contentment even in the failure to obtain them.
With a face smiling with weariness, that base man mocks within himself his own young wives of restless movements, like one who remembers his past lives mocking the jasmine flowers.
Then virtuous people, their eyes wide with wonder, came to see him out of sheer affection, like the moon risen upon the earth.
Having always disregarded enjoyment, he does not highly esteem even the enjoyment that has come to him through appropriate exertion, owing to his proper understanding.
First, for one whose inner self has arisen and whose worldly dullness has withered, a distaste for cyclic existence arises from within, like the autumnal tree after its fruit has ripened.
Then, desiring his own well-being, he himself seeks association with the virtuous for the sake of future prosperity, just as one suffering from illness resorts to a physician.
Thus, having become noble-minded, he plunges into the meanings of the treatises, just as a great elephant enters vast, clear lakes.
For a virtuous person, having rescued one standing near them from calamities, establishes them in prosperity, just as the sun places all things within its own light.
Abstention from taking what belongs to others occurs even earlier; and for one who possesses discernment, contentment with one's own possessions arises.
Abstaining from taking what belongs to others and overflowing with the nectar of contentment, the discerning person gradually desires to disregard even his own interests.
For even when asked for mere chaff, oil-cake, or vegetables, he gives them; by that very practice, he eventually gives even his own flesh.
Surely, for those whose minds are dissolved and who pursue solitude, their folly becomes as light as a cow's footprint when they are running.
Having first diligently practiced abstaining from taking what belongs to others for the sake of others, one should then, through discernment, cultivate detachment from one's own interests.
Then, through the renunciation of enjoyments, the wise gradually effect the abandonment of self-interest for the sake of supreme and perfect rest.
There is no such suffering in this world, nor even in millions of hells, as that which consists in the lifelong teaching of the acquisition of wealth.
Whether on a seat, in bed, in a vehicle, while walking, or in the company of people, those who are solely intent on excessive anxiety—surely they are fools; let them know that [state].

Indeed, objects of desire are spread with misfortune; prosperities are continuous with calamities; and enjoyments are great diseases of existence—yet these are perceived by us through a distorted vision.
The bitterness of enmity does not arise from the expansion of objects of thought until one seeks wealth for the sake of trivial ends, which results in great misfortune.
May he for whom supreme bliss has long been pleasing perceive the true goal by viewing the world as a blade of grass and attain peace.

The meaning of "caravan" (sārtha) is traditionally understood as that which possesses manifold transformations of states, the processes of aging and death, and the burning pains of wretchedness and wickedness.
In this world, for living beings subject to old age and death, contentment is the elixir that makes one free from aging and death.
Spring, the Nandana grove, the moon, and the apsarases are remembered on one side; on the other side is the nectar of contentment, all gathered together.
Just as a lake is filled by the rainy season, so too is fullness attained through contentment; it is profound, cool, heart-pleasing, serene, and rich in aesthetic flavor.
Having attained vigor, the virtuous person shines through contentment alone, just as a tree with its well-flowered forest-like form shines through the spring.
A person of base nature who seeks wealth strives like an insect crushed by the touch of a footstool; he goes from one misery to another.
Disturbed by great waves like those fallen into a turbulent ocean, supplicants of deformed appearance cannot attain their natural composure.
Prosperity and women are as transient as high-tossing waves; what wise man would take delight in them, which are like the shade cast by the hoods of a serpent?
That fool who, despite knowing the torment involved in acquiring and protecting wealth, still feels desire for it—one should not even touch that beast among men.
He who cuts away both the external and internal objects of the mind with the sickle of dispassion—equally—his field shines forth.

The world-ness perceived by the ignorant is actually non-existent; yet the Knower, though knowing it as such, perceives it as if it were real—this is the manifestation of a lack of spiritual cultivation.

Having reached a state of world-weariness toward saṃsāra, and having approached the company of the virtuous and the scriptures through that [company], one casts off enjoyments by means of the realization of the meaning of the scriptures; and through the firmness of dispassion, one attains the ultimate reality.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When detachment from worldly existence has taken root, when association with the virtuous is established, when the meaning of the scriptures has been contemplated by the intellect, and when freedom from craving for enjoyments has arrived;
When distaste for sense objects has arisen, when goodness has likewise emerged, when illumination has become oriented toward the heart, and when awakening has taken place within it;
The wise do not long for riches, just as one avoids darkness; even when they are present, they are cast away like withered, impure leaves.
Wives and kinsmen appear as a burden to one like a traveler; yet they are indeed attended to according to one's ability and at the proper time.
Furthermore, even when the objects of the senses are present before the senses, enjoyments are certainly not experienced again and again due to the tranquility of the mind.
In solitary places, at the ends of the horizon, by lakes and in forests, in gardens, in sacred regions, or even in one's own home.
One does not remain for long in the playful diversions with friends, in auspicious gardens, in eating and other such activities, nor in the investigation of the scriptures and logic.

By one who is tranquil, self-controlled, delighting in his own self, and silent—the wise one who speaks with exclusive devotion to realized knowledge—only that which is already known is further investigated.
Thus, through the power of practice, the discerning person comes to rest in the supreme state by themselves, becoming tranquil like water naturally settling in a depression.
Tranquil, both external and internal, pure consciousness alone has arisen as the object; that a separate object exists is impossible—this indeed is the supreme state.
There is no apprehension of objects, nor is there anything empty apart from the nature of awakening; they call that state which abides in internal experience the supreme goal.

Due to the transformation resulting from the connection with the singular awakening, there is neither the state of being an awakening, nor emptiness, nor the nature of objects; know that to be the supreme state.
For the wise who are free from the mind and rest solely in their own self-awareness, sense objects do not provide any pleasure, just as water does not for stones.
Having entered the state of cessation, free from mental activity and slow with the silence of a sage, he remains established in his very nature, like a self-possessed man depicted in a painting.
The heart of the knower of the known is the Great God himself—possessing all objects yet devoid of objects, like a supreme atom; it is non-empty, yet its very nature is emptiness.

For the knower, egoism, the notion of "you," the activity of the world, and the reckoning of space and time—as well as knowledge and the void—do not exist at all, even though they appear to be present.
By means of knowledge established in the stainless state, just as by a lamp, the darkness within the heart as well as external darkness, along with passion, hatred, fear, and so forth, is dispelled.
One should bow to that sun among men, who is free from all stains and directions, who has reached the further shore through his essence, and in whom the nature of darkness does not arise.
When differentiation has been dissolved and the mind has attained invisibility, that state of one who has realized awakening does not fall within the range of words.
O one of great intelligence, the Supreme Lord, being propitiated for a long time with supreme devotion day and night, bestows this Nirvana.
Śrī Rāma said: "O best of sages, who is the Lord, and how is he propitiated through devotion? Tell me this in accordance with the truth, O foremost among those who know all truths."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O one of great intelligence, the Lord is neither far away nor difficult to attain; the Supreme Lord is simply one's own self, whose singular nature consists of great awakening.
To him who is everything, from whom everything arises, who is everything, and who is everywhere; who is within and consists eternally of all things—to that Soul of All, I offer salutation.
Therefore, these transformations of creation and dissolution are produced from that which is not their cause as if from a cause, like the movements of the wind and other elements.
All these classes of beings, both stationary and moving, constantly worship them by granting whatever they desire.
Through many births, according to his own desired wishes, when he has been fully honored by him, he attains grace.
That Mahādeva, the Great Lord who is the Self itself, being well-pleased, swiftly dispatches a pure messenger with auspicious intentions for the sake of awakening.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, by whom is the messenger impelled—the Supreme Lord himself? And how does that messenger perform the act of awakening? Tell me this.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Impelled by the Self, the messenger known by the name Viveka (Discrimination) dwells eternally in the cave of the heart, like the moon in the sky.
This very [Self] gradually awakens the living being whose nature is latent impressions, and it delivers the undiscriminating one from this ocean of saṃsāra.
This very Self of awakening is the innermost self, the supreme, the Parameśvara; the Praṇava, approved by the Vedas, is the name-designator of this very one.
He is constantly propitiated by men, nāgas, gods, and asuras through the sequences of recitation, fire-offerings, asceticism, charity, study, sacrifice, and ritual action.
The sky is his head, the earth his feet, the stars the rows of hair on his body, the elements his bones, and the ether is the heart of that Supreme Lord.
Because it is of the nature of consciousness, it goes everywhere, wakes up, and sees; therefore, it possesses hands, ears, eyes, and feet in every direction.
Having awakened the messenger of discernment and slain the demon of the mind, the living soul is led to some vast state of the Self.
Having abandoned the flood of all conceptual constructions—the transformations that are a mixture of misfortunes—let the self itself be pacified by the self through its own human effort.
In this darkness of the night of saṃsāra, which is agitated by the clouds of mental waves and infested with the demon of the wandering mind, one’s own self alone is the full moon.
Within the hollow of this ocean, turbulent with the waves and whirlpools of deep death, flickering with the ripples of craving, and driven by the fierce winds of one's own mind—
In this great ocean of worldly existence, which is filled with the afflictions of extreme dullness and dense with the thicket of the senses, discernment is the great ship.

Having previously become well-pleased by worship according to one's desire, the Self, acting here as a purifying messenger, bestows discernment; and through association with the virtuous, study of the scriptures, and the supreme awakening to the ultimate truth, it leads the individual soul to the one, primordial, and stainless state.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Within those whose discernment is fully matured and who have cast off the impurity of latent desires, an extraordinary greatness of a truly unprecedented kind arises.
The fourteen worlds do not fathom the intellect of the great, which is vast through its noble boundaries and beautiful in its profundity.
When the conviction that "the world is a delusion of the mind" has taken root among the wise, both the external and internal crocodile-grasp of delusion is stilled.
When the delusion of the world is flashing forth like two moons, like heat-waves in water, or like a mass of hair in the sky, how can there be any causal basis for latent impressions?
When the causal condition of latent impressions is empty, only the empty void remains; since even that state ceases when the mind is non-existent, how could it not be abandoned by the discerning one?
But that state which is devoid of these three states by means of this triad is called the supreme state, whether it be termed "seeing" or even "not seeing."
Like a mass of rays from various jewels, the world is manifold in nature; it is a mere appearance, not a self, not a solid entity, and not composed of earth.
For the world exists as nothing but the perception of forms, which is entirely empty, arising like a web of rays from a collection of various jewels in the sky.
Here there are no real beings, no world-existence, and no emptiness; this is the unfolding of the net of light-rays from the jewel-lord called Brahma.
Creations and non-creations, belonging to Brahmā, appear as nothing but formless, dense masses of conceptual clouds, neither manifold nor subject to destruction.
Thus, in this way, no solidified mass of perception exists; and in that which is conceptually constructed, only emptiness is perceived, like the sky.
Since that [bond] is a non-entity, how can there be a basis for cultivation? What bird could ever rest upon a tree in the sky?
There is no solid mass of elements, nor does emptiness exist; for this very reason, even the mind has set, and what remains is neither being nor non-existence.
Though appearing in various forms, the awakened one remains truly non-dual and equal; with diverse objects dissolved within, he is like a mass of gold.
For the knower who abides as he truly is, the universe and the mind, along with the sense of "I-ness," dissolve; that which is inexpressible—the state of no-mind—remains as his true being.
The intellect is merely distressed by views that fluctuate between higher and lower; for the true reality is understood through reasoning practiced even slightly.
The Virāj is devoid of life, along with its effects, causes, and so forth; it is the source of the world-body consisting of the past, present, and future.
He by whom the Buddha is realized through the nature of awakening is designated as "the Knower. For that non-dual and quiescent one, the universe does not exist.
All these aforementioned instructions and qualifications come to the experience of the knower spontaneously, like the words of a virtuous person.
There is no solid mass to the elements, for they are empty due to their non-arising; therefore, the mind does not exist, and what remains is the abiding state of true reality.

The consciousness of this internal conscious being consists precisely in its orientation toward objects; that which has arisen leads to misfortune, while that which has not arisen would lead to the highest good.
Having arisen, it moves toward externality and there assumes a state of mass; through its own self-perception alone, due to its insentience, it becomes like water turning into stone.

Just like the objects of a dream and so forth, consciousness assumes a state of solidification through its own non-awakening; having become the mind that grasps those objects, it binds itself to a physical body.
In all these states, no otherness arises for consciousness; the distinction is merely imagined through the conceptualization of words.
Within and without consciousness, it is the Self alone that appears through the perceptions of objects; it does not exist as "internal" or "external" in the manner of the mind.

Because consciousness is like space, time, space, and so forth are its very form; likewise, all objects are one's own self, being like a dream—a void that does not possess the nature of external objects.
External objecthood does not become internal by the power of cognition; for that which is insentient can never, anywhere, attain the state of being cognition, as it lacks similarity [to it].
Awareness does not enter the state of the visible; even when it has reached that condition, it remains exactly as it is and does not undergo even the slightest alteration.
When the singular transformation of supremely pure consciousness has fully arisen, even the hearing of words denoting "consciousness," "unconsciousness," or "objects" shall set.
For those with subtle bodies, it is only the minds that develop the perception of materiality through their own firm habitual conditioning.
This state of materiality is falsely imagined by those subtle, ethereal bodies whose minds have been purified as clear as space, just as actors falsely assume the form of demons.
This delusion is known to be pacified by the practice of non-delusion; indeed, madness is said to be quelled by the realization, "I am not mad."

When delusion is fully understood by oneself, its latent tendencies cease; once one has recognized a dream for what it is—a dream—how indeed could there be any further mental cultivation regarding it?
Samsara is pacified solely through the thinning of latent impressions; the wise are intent upon severing these very latent impressions, which are like a great yakṣiṇī.
Just as the intoxication of ignorance in men is cultivated through habituation, so too, through the awakening of one's own practice, it subsides over time.

Just as this subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) is led toward a state of gross materiality (ādhibhautikatā), so too is it led by those who know reality through the grace of the existence of pure consciousness (bodhasattā).
Likewise, even the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha), having led the individual soul (jīva) to the state of the living, should be led to the nature of Brahman through firm practice of awakening.
If origination, which is of the nature of consciousness, is understood through its own object, then how is it that the subtle body (ativāhikī) is also understood?
If that knot does not dissolve through the meaning of the response to that [objection], it is like the word "pratipattṛ" (the performer) in the sūtra concerning the eradication of spirits.

Having realized the oneness of the world with pure consciousness, that which is to be known remains unblemished as long as even that [realization] is not itself perceived through ultimate transformation.
When the mind, both externally and internally, is stilled, its true nature shines forth; relying upon that very nature, which is cool and radiant like the sky, may you find peace.
Possessing knowledge and established in the sacrifice of knowledge, planting the sacrificial post of meditation, he conquers the world by victory, with total renunciation as his sole fee.
Whether a rain of glowing embers falls or the wind of universal dissolution blows, whether he moves upon the earth or in the sky, the wise man remains equanimous within the Self.
For one whose mind is tranquil through the absence of craving and who has attained the purity of cessation, no state of stability is possible except through the vajra-like concentration.

The mind does not become tranquil through treatises, compositions, instructions, austerities, or self-restraint in the same way that it becomes tranquil when there is freedom from craving for external objects.
The fire of non-craving for all objects has been kindled within the grass of the mind by the winds of universal renunciation, through the contemplation that prosperity is itself calamity.
Delusion both within and without, the grasping of a solid mass, and the perception of objects—all shine forth as mere cognition within the Self, like a jewel.
Through the perceptions of humans, *nāgas*, *asuras*, houses, and mountain caves, consciousness alone has spread forth, like smoke appearing as clouds in the sky.

The rivers of one's own transformations, flowing with the essence of the individual soul-power (*jīva-śakti*), quiver within the inert vessel of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) due to their liquid nature as they descend.
The small fish of the vital breath, dwelling in the water of the sky, ensnared by the net of delusion, does not remember its own abiding state within itself.
Having become condensed through its own density, the mass of consciousness manifests within itself, by means of its own self, in the courtyard of the sky in the form of various objects.
All living beings are indeed equal and devoid of latent impressions (vāsanā); they are insentient, like dry leaves blown away by the wind.

Having summoned human strengths and conquered sloth, one should rise up; having dispelled and accumulated the flood of latent tendencies, and having swiftly shattered the dense cage of the snares of saṃsāra, one should emerge on all sides like one who is no longer ignorant.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: These multitudes of living beings that are seen extending through the ten directions, bearing the designations of men, serpents, lords of gods, Gandharvas, and so forth—[are they not all one?]
Some are awake only in dreams, some are awake only in their mental constructs; some abide solely in the waking state, while others remain awake for a long duration.
Others abide in dense waking, while others are in waking-dream; some have their waking exhausted—living beings are thus remembered as being of seven kinds.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, let the distinction between these seven forms of living beings be told to me for my understanding, just as [the distinction is seen] among waters in the oceans.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In a certain former kalpa, in a certain world, somewhere, some living beings possessing the nature of life remained asleep within their bodies.
Know that this world is a dream for those who perceive it as a dream; indeed, they are called the "awake in dreams" who subsist by their livelihoods.
This object before us is the very dream that arose spontaneously for those who were sleeping somewhere; we are the dream-men of them.
Because of their long duration, that dream has attained the state of waking; those living beings who were in that dream-waking state remain situated within it.
Because the Omniscient One is omnipresent, everything exists everywhere; therefore, we who are like dreamers abide as dream-people within those [dreams].
Śrī Rāma said: "In whichever kalpas they were born, those kalpa-constructs have perished; if that is so, then how can there be any continued existence for those who are awakened?"

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Here, at the end of their dream-delusion, they are either liberated from sleepiness or, having attained [new] bodies through volition, they take recourse in other forms just as before.
In the same way, they perceive another world and its imagined constructs; yet there can be no crowding in the sky of the manifestation of conceptualization.
Those who are like worms in the decayed udumbara tree of the world—which is composed of mere conceptualization—are called "dream-awakened"; now hear about those who are "conceptualized-awakened."
In a certain former aeon, in some world somewhere, there were those who remained entirely sleepless within, devoted solely to their mental constructs.
Or else, having slipped from meditative absorption and fallen under the sway of mental fantasies, they reach a state of firm conceptualization, their prior experiences having dissolved away.

For those whose state of waking consists solely of mental resolve (saṃkalpa) due to its long duration and partial manifestation, and for whom all activity has ceased therein, they are indeed "waking through resolve" (saṃkalpajāgara).
Upon the subsiding of their volitions, they resort again to that [state] or another; within their bodies we, these men of volition, remain.

These living beings, who dwell in the world while remaining within the sphere of life, are said to be awake through their mental constructs and to sleep through their mental constructs; now hear about those who are awake in the absolute sense.
They are said to have descended first from Brahmā, whose self is expanded; they are described as being solely wakeful, remaining undiminished even before the creation.
Furthermore, those very same beings who have passed into other births, having long remained awake and attained maturity, are described as moving within the sphere of cause and effect.

Due to the entry of those very misdeeds, they have attained the state of dull, stationary beings; they are called "dense waking" because they have reached a state of density among those who are awake.

But those who have attained awakening, being awakened by the meaning of the scriptures and by the company of the virtuous, see the waking state as if it were a dream; they become those for whom waking is a dream.
But those who have fully attained awakening and come to rest in the supreme state, with the stages of waking and so forth extinguished, have reached the fourth stage.
Thus, the sevenfold division of living beings has been described to you by me, like that of the oceans; having understood this, become intent on the highest good.

Abandon the delusion consisting of the calculation of the world; you have attained the pure state of being a solid mass whose sole nature is awakening. It is free from emptiness and liberated from non-emptiness; therefore, you are the primordial one, whose body is released from both duality and unity.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, how does the purely waking state—causeless and purposeless—manifest from the Supreme, like a tree from the sky?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O one of great intelligence, no effect is perceived without a cause; therefore, for one who is merely awake, nothing at all can possibly arise here.
Therefore, because of the impossibility of its arising, all other varieties of living beings that possess life cannot possibly come into existence, being thwarted by the absence of their cause.
Nothing is born here, and nothing perishes here; the arising of the conceptualization of words and their meanings occurs only for the purpose of instruction and that which is to be instructed.
Śrī Rāma said: Who creates bodies through the consciousness of mind, intellect, and so forth? Who deludes living beings with the bonds of affection, passion, and the like?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: No one ever creates bodies at any time; no one ever deludes living beings at any time.

Consciousness, whose nature is a manifestation without beginning or end, is established within the Self; it appears in the form of various objects, just as [the ocean appears] in the form of waves and so forth.
Nothing external exists; it is consciousness alone that manifests as if it were external. Consciousness arises from the heart of awareness, like a great tree from a seed.
O descendant of Raghu, this entire universe exists within consciousness itself, just as a carved statue is manifest within a pillar.
May the world itself awaken—as the one Self, both external and internal, infinite in space and time, and the spreading fragrance of awakening.

This very world is the supreme realm; let there be the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Let [the mind] be stilled; for what latent impressions indeed come from that which resides in the next world?
It is the locus of place, time, action, the world, form, mind, self, and existence; yet it is devoid of the referents of words such as "place" and "time," and is not a mere void.
O Rāghava, the realization of that state occurs only for those who know the words and for other seers for whom the object of sight has become stilled; it does not occur for others.
Those who have indeed taken refuge in the abyss of a greatness that is both fickle and profound—none of them ever behold that light.
This perception of the world by the knower—resounding with the infinite multitude of fourteen kinds of beings—is comparable to the limbs of his own body.
Due to the absence of a cause, creation neither arises nor ceases; whatever the nature of the cause may be, such is the nature of the effect.

If the effect were already present within the cause, what would constitute its causality? Since the effect is indeed perceived, while that [cause] is non-existent because the two are not experienced [as distinct], [the effect cannot reside therein].
Just as waves, whirlpools, and the like exist within the tranquil ocean, so do the world, the mind, and other phenomena exist within Brahman, which is devoid of agitation.
The stainless Brahman alone is the self of all, existing as a single mass, just as gold exists within various vessels in the form of the objects contained therein.
At the time of dreaming, it is indeed a dream, because one is not occupied with or grasping at the waking state; at the time of waking, it is indeed waking, because of the realization of reality.
Through the nature of mind-only, the Buddha remains like the water of a mirage; when deconditioned by analytical inquiry, it comes to appear as the state of waking and dreaming.
Through right knowledge, the elements, along with the body of the knower, release their binding foundation, just as clouds disperse when their time has passed.
Just as a dense cloud that has begun to dissolve returns to the state of the sky, so too the world, along with its grasping at a self, is stilled through the realization of truth.
Like an autumn cloud that has been torn away, or like the water of a mirage, the state of being perceived dissolves upon awakening, even as it is being touched again.
Just as gold, clarified butter, and fuel, when cast into a blazing fire, attain oneness within that fire, so too do the world, the mind, and perception attain oneness within consciousness.
Through awakening, the sense of solid cohesion in the three worlds becomes attenuated, just as the notion of a house as a "demon" vanishes for a child who has been awakened.
Within consciousness itself, which is infinite in form, the appearance of the world, the mind, and so forth occurs by its own self within itself; what indeed is this "solidification" here?
This world has arisen like the mind itself through the very act of awakening; when that [mind] has set through awakening, what existence can there be for the bondage of the body?
Through the awakening from waking and dreaming, it abandons the solidity of its mass and attains supreme lightness, like gold melted by fire.
Awareness itself, remaining exactly as it is, attains a state of density as if creating space and time out of nothing, like gold.
While one remains thus awake through inquiry, as this fragile state resembling a dream wanes, its intensity diminishes like the sap in the autumn season.
The splendors of the visible world, though they persist, have reached an extreme fragility; like dreams once recognized as such, they no longer please the discerning man.

Where indeed is the repose in one's own self, and where is this perception of objects? How could there be an identity between deep sleep and the waking state, or between the nature of delusion and non-delusion?
When one abides in that which is mind-only, mere illusion, and has the nature of a mere dream, the notion of reality regarding the objects of this world ceases.
Whose untruths are pleasing, O Mahāmati? For how could they be so, when even those things that appear before one are like the waters of a mirage?

When the cognition of reality has dissolved, one of tranquil intellect perceives the world as having the nature of the sky—a single, undifferentiated mass appearing like the web of rays from a lattice-window.
For one who is awake, the cultivation of the relish for the nature of delusion—which consists of the mind’s own error—ceases once that which is in reality empty has been fully understood.
Since that which is known to be a non-entity, how could there be anything to be accepted therein? Who, having fully recognized a dream, would go after the gold within that dream?
When the object of perception is thoroughly understood as being like a dream, attachment to it ceases; the severing of the knot of defects in the states of the seer and the seen then proceeds.

Devoid of worldly flavor, with a tranquil mind and free from the egoism of nirvana, the wise one—having accomplished his task, free from passion, and effortless—abides in peace with a Buddha-like intellect.
When the flavor has become flavorless, latent impressions dissolve, just as the rays of a lamp vanish when its flame is extinguished.
Just as the sky appears dense with a mass of light from a lamp due to awakening, so too the entire world is an illusory form, like a city of Gandharvas.
By seeing neither the self, nor space, nor emptiness, nor sensation—through ultimate transformation—one beholds that state.
Where there is neither self nor emptiness, neither the conceptualization of a world nor the notion of the arising of the mind's objects—there everything exists exactly as it is.

The state of being earth and so forth is realized as non-existent by the wise through knowledge; having set by means of wisdom, it becomes for the knower a mere void, and even though it persists, it does not exist.

He becomes one whose self is tranquil through single-pointed concentration, as pure as the sky; he remains free from attachment, and though established in existence, he is like one who is non-existent.
With his mind set at rest, silent, and having reached the state of cessation, he has crossed the ocean of saṃsāra and come to the end of karmic actions.

Supreme ignorance is that which is intent upon the creation of the body, the world, the sky, and the multitude of mountains; when that has dissolved, all this, though still existing, dissolves as well.

With his inner organ completely stilled and free from conceptual construction, consisting of the essence of his own true nature, the wise one remains unobstructed, satisfied by the nectar of supreme peace.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, by what sequence does consciousness appear as the world? Tell me that sequence again, step by step, for the cessation of duality.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as with a tree, that which is seen by one who is utterly deluded appears within his own mind; but that which is not seen does not exist in the mind of one whose memory is very slight.
A capable person perceives only the meaning of the treatise as it is connected from beginning to end; he does not act upon some object that falls within the range of his vision alone.
Being devoted to the practice of the teachings and with a mind one-pointedly focused on the meaning of the scriptures, become a sage and listen to this instruction, which is an ornament for the ears.
This delusion regarding the weight of the visible world is indeed called ignorance; in reality, it does not exist, just as water does not exist in a mirage.
For the sake of the instruction and the one to be instructed, please listen for a moment to this, relying upon me as if I were the truth itself, out of consideration for my request.
Without raising conceptual constructions such as "from where does this come" or "how is it so," you will yourself understand through awakening that "this is not theirs, nor does it exist."
Whatever is seen here in this world, whether stationary or moving, all of it—abounding in every variety—is destroyed at the end of the eon.

The destruction of this [individual], consisting of the division of its parts, is necessarily unavoidable; for when it is extracted through each individual *bindu* upon awakening, there is indeed its dissolution.
This being the case, since Brahman consists of that very substance, if that substance were destroyed, neither infinity nor existence would at all be possible for Brahman.
The claim that "knowledge is like the power of intoxication" is not established for us; for us, the body arises from consciousness like a dream, but not as an ultimate reality.
The splendor of the visible world perishes; it is that very same splendor, neither something else nor not at all. In this way, the scripture would be rendered appropriate, and not otherwise.
How could there be the possibility of a lost object being grasped as "this is that very same thing," unless it were consistent with its previous form? We follow what has been experienced.
If that very [space] existed as space itself, how could it be non-existent? If it remained as space in that same way, then it has not undergone destruction.
When cause and effect are thus of one and the same nature, then, due to the absence of the relationship between cause and effect, our tradition maintains that they are indeed identical.
That which has reached the state of emptiness or non-apprehension is indeed destroyed; if it were otherwise, tell me, what kind of destruction could it possibly be?
What is it that perceives: "That which was lost has arisen again"? Because this necessarily perishes, another [moment] proceeds once more.

Since there exists a persistence of the seed-essence from the beginning until the body, which manifests as individual parts such as height and fruit at various intervals, how can there be a relationship of cause and effect?

Since the seed alone—possessing a single nature defined by its place, time, and action—exists here exactly as it is perceived, it performs only one specific function; therefore, a jar does not perform the work of a cloth.
In the established doctrine of all philosophical systems, there is no difference regarding the ultimate reality; therefore, what is the use of dispute over this for us?

This is peaceful, without beginning or end, because through investigation it is seen to have that nature; it is like space, consisting of pure awareness alone, according to the authority of direct experience.
How this has not been experienced before, how it is now being experienced, and how it attains perfection—all this shall be explained in due order.
When the entire visible realm has perished at the end of a great kalpa, extending up to the Great God (Mahādeva), all mental, intellectual, and karmic activities come to an end.
Even when the sky has come to rest, when time has ceased its course, when the wind has departed, and when fire has utterly vanished;

When even fire has gone to destruction, and water and the other elements have been worn away for a very long time, until the entire collection of words and their referents has reached its ultimate end;
What remains is the essence of peaceful awakening—eternally pure, free from all that can be sublated, without beginning or end, gentle, indescribable, stainless, and immutable.
Inexpressible, unmanifest, beyond the senses, nameless, the self of all beings, empty, both being and non-being—that is the supreme state.
That is neither air nor space, neither the intellect and so forth, nor the void; it is not anything at all, yet it is the self of all, some other supreme ether.
That is experienced by one who knows it, who stands upon that state, and who is liberated from it; for others, it is described solely through the scriptures as they have been handed down.
There is no time, no mind, no self, neither being nor non-being, nor space or direction; there is no middle between these two, no end, no awakening, and not even that which is unawakened.
Something utterly translucent is indeed perceived by those who have reached the further shore of awakening, who have stilled the expansion of saṃsāra, and who have attained the supreme state.
These objects which have been prohibited by me exist everywhere; they are to be discerned by my intellect, like the waves of the gentle ocean.
Just as various carved figures exist uncarved within a great pillar, so do all phenomena abide exactly as they are therein.
Thus all things abide there, and yet they do not abide in that way; they are the self of all, yet not the self of all; they are that very thing, and yet they are not that very thing.
Just as this state is the self of all, yet devoid of all objects, so do those who are transformed into oneness perceive it therein.
Everything is indeed of the nature of all things, yet that primordial state is seen to be devoid of all objects, while simultaneously being completely full of all objects.
O you of great intelligence, such perfect generosity, which consists in the pacification of all objects of desire, has not yet arisen in you; here, doubt is the proof.
He who is awakened, who has reached the supreme radiance that is free from appearances, whose inner organ is pure and who is tranquil—he beholds that intrinsic nature.
This delusion of the world throughout the three periods of time—consisting of "this," "you," "I," and so forth—exists therein like a network of ornaments within a mass of gold.
Just as a collection of various vessels is not perceived apart from a mass of gold, so too the world is not found to exist as something distinct from the density of ultimate reality.
For one who always perceives that which constitutes their own limbs as distinct from themselves sees this entire world-duality as being like gold in the form of a bracelet.
This world, consisting of space, time, and action, is empty of the meanings of words such as "place" and the like; as it truly exists, everything therein both exists and does not exist.
Just as a painter creates various forms upon calm water with ripples and the like, or fashions a multitude of vessels from a lump of clay, so does this [universe] abide within Brahman.
Thus, this [reality] here is neither different nor non-different; it both does not exist and exists. It is eternally composed of that alone, pure, and likewise tranquil within tranquility.
This statue of the three worlds appears as if it were never carved; it has attained visibility within Brahman, as if by its own inherent nature, like a figure in wood.
The statues fixed upon pillars appear as if they were carved out; within this very Akṣobhya, the waves of perceptions of creation are likewise contained.

In the lake of supreme flavor, showers of the nectar of dense consciousness shine; though undivided, they appear as if divided, and though unagitated, as if agitated. Within the density of consciousness, the visions of creation appear as if manifest, though they are not manifest.
In every single atom here, the entire circle of saṃsāra shines forth with a brilliant manifestation, yet nothing at all truly shines forth.

The collection of categories such as space, time, and wind constitutes its limbs, yet for that which is devoid of limbs, even those are not limbs; they call this the undecaying ultimate reality, which is the self of all and yet empty of all modifications of existence.
Śrī Rāma said: Just as there is consciousness in the object of consciousness, as there is temporality in time, as there is the nature of space in space, and as there is insentience in the insentient;
Just as the nature of air exists in air, non-existence in that which has not come into being, vibration in that whose essence is vibration, and materiality in the material; so it is here.

Just as there is divisibility in the divisible, just as there is infinity in the infinite, just as there is visibility in the visible, and just as there is the state of creation in creations; so it is with all things.
O Brahmin, best among speakers, explain this to me in its proper sequence; for those of limited understanding are awakened only after being instructed from the very beginning.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That infinite great space is called the mass of great consciousness; it consists of the nature of consciousness that is beyond being known, peaceful, one, and established in equilibrium.
When the meanings of words such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara have reached their dissolution in that which is called the Great Dissolution (mahāpralaya), that which remains is pure.
In that regard, no cause for creation is logically tenable—neither impurity (*mala*), nor forms, seeds, and so forth, nor *māyā*, delusion (*moha*), error (*bhrama*), and the like.
There exists that which is exclusively peaceful, utterly pure, and devoid of beginning and end; it is that wherein even space becomes as solid as a stone.
When that which has consciousness as its body exists, it is not fitting to say "it does not exist"; nor is it fitting to say "it exists," for at that time it is utterly tranquil and stainless.
When self-awareness has reached a hundred yojanas in a mere moment, that which is its form in the midst of that [process] is the form of that state.

When both the external and internal have become tranquil, when the delusion regarding objects and latent impressions has ceased, and for one who is awakened and free from all thought, it is as if it were midnight.
That form which is motionless, belonging to the person who abides alone, free from pleasure and pain—that is the form of that state, which is peace.
The universal of existence (sattāsāmānya) is extended throughout grasses, shrubs, sprouts, and so forth; that form which arises from their arising is the form of that [universal] state.
Within that state, this world-form which is clearly perceived—appearing as if it had a cause, as if its form were formidable, and as if possessed of distinctions—is [in truth] that very state.
All that is neither born nor existent due to the absence of a cause; it is not endowed with form, nor is it the world, nor is it joined with duality or unity.
The existence of that which is without a cause is not possible here; for when an object is itself eternally experienced, who has the power to deny it?

Nor can that which is empty, without beginning or end, be the cause of the world; for the formless Brahman cannot be the cause of the formed, visible world which does not possess the nature of Brahman.
Therefore, when the form of the world appears there, it is that very thing which shines by itself as the space of consciousness; thus it is established.
And because the world is the nature of consciousness-Brahman, its appearance as such is like an illusion; everything is one, unborn, peaceful, non-dual unity, and free from affliction.
From the full, the full flows forth; in the full, the full shines resplendent. The full alone has arisen; in the full, the full alone is established.

Peaceful, even, devoid of arising and passing away, free from form, unborn, as pure as the sky, and one; this primordial Nirvana is the nature of supreme awakening, whose self-nature arises always as the unity of all that exists and does not exist.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That which is called the world is the clear sky; it is the existent Brahman situated within the sky. This unborn reality shines as the sky within the sky, and such is the meaning of the word "world."
The referents of words such as "you," "I," and "the world" are Brahman within Brahman; they exist as the peaceful, perfectly equal radiance, which is both abiding and yet non-abiding.
Even though this world consists of oceans, mountains, clouds, and the earth, it is unborn; indeed, this entire universe remains as still as a log in silence within Brahman.
The seer is the seer alone, established in his own self by virtue of the nature of the seen; the doer is the doer alone, due to the absence of anything to be done and being devoid of causes.
Therein is neither knowership nor agency, neither insentience nor the state of being an enjoyer; there is neither emptiness nor substantiality, nor even the nature of space.
Truly, it is like the interior of a stone—solid, one, unborn, and pervasive; all is peaceful, without beginning or end, and one beyond both injunction and prohibition.
Death and life, truth and falsehood, and the auspicious and inauspicious—all are one unborn space, like water consisting of a web of waves.

It is precisely through differentiation that [consciousness] comes to possess the state of being the object seen and the state of being the seer; and this conceptual construction is experienced in dreams, cities [of the Gandharvas], and the like.
Thus, this world shines forth in the supreme ether like a city in a dream; from the very beginning, it is Brahman alone that exists in this manner.
Know this to be such: everything that is of the nature of all things, which, in the movement from one place to another, remains unmarked in the interval for the knower.
And thus situated in the midst of the consciousness-ether, which is utterly tranquil, the world exists just like water in the form of waves and so forth.

That which arises has already arisen, and that which does not arise has never arisen; in the interval between the departure from one place and the arrival at another, it is not differentiated by the wise.
Therefore, it is said that no cause for this creation is found, even when sought with great effort, just like the horn of a hare.
That which appears without a cause is non-apparent and consists of delusion; how can truthfulness be attributed to a delusion that is unreal in nature?
Indeed, how can there be an effect without a cause? That which is the sight of a virtuous son by one who has no son is an illusion, not reality.
That which appears without a cause is the manifestation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); it exists in every form, like a mental construction or a city of Gandharvas.
When moving from one place to another, the body of the Knower shines in the intervening space in an instant, as if not abandoning its own nature, like a transformation of objects.
Consciousness alone shines forth in the form of objects, and it is its own subtle essence; the internal experience of mountains in dreams and mental constructs serves as the illustration for this.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahman, just as a future great tree exists within the seed of a banyan, why does the creation not likewise exist within the atom?"
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: Where there is a seed, there a branch of expansive form may arise; and that branch is produced by causes along with their auxiliary conditions.
In the dissolution of all beings, what form does the seed take? And what auxiliary cause arises for it, by virtue of which the world is produced?

But as for that Brahman which is supreme and tranquil, what conceptualization of form could there be therein? Even the connection with atomhood does not exist here; so what possibility is there for it to be a seed?
Since a cause—such as a seed—that produces both the real and the unreal is impossible, how, by whom, from where, where, and of what nature could the existence of the world be?
Nor is it even fitting to say that the world exists within the interior of the supreme atom; the notion that Mount Meru exists within a mustard seed is merely the imagination of the ignorant.
When a seed exists, views of cause and effect proceed; but for that which is formless, what is the seed, and where is the sequence of the produced and the producer?
Therefore, that which is the supreme reality is itself this world as it exists; herein nothing at all is manifested, nor does anything whatsoever perish.

The sky of consciousness perceives the delusion of the world within the sky of consciousness in the heart; by virtue of its conscious nature, it perceives the pure as impure in the impure, and the pure in the pure.
Only its own form appears to it, like the vibration in the wind; for us, there are no such things here as the conceptualization of the word or the object of "creation."
Just as emptiness exists in space and fluidity in water, so does this pure creation, consisting of the nature of otherness, exist within the Self.
This world, which is of the nature of light and profoundly peaceful, is indeed Brahman spread out before us; it is without beginning or end, the truth, and neither arises nor ceases.
Just as the body of a traveler exists momentarily in the space between two places when moving from one land to another, so too this world is situated within the self of space.
Just as movement exists in the wind, fluidity in water, and emptiness in space, so does this world appear within the Self, without any actual contact with it.

The sky of consciousness is indeed the sky of the universe; where, then, is there a sunless state within the Self that is free from rising and setting? Since the entire visible world is a limb of that reality and is non-different from it, remain as the mere sky, free from all conceptual construction.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Existence and non-existence, grasping and relinquishing, the gross and the subtle, the moving and the unmoving—these were indeed never produced at the beginning of creation, as they lack a cause.
For the formless element of consciousness is never capable of being the cause of material things; it cannot be its own seed, just as the earth is the seed for trees.
Constantly contemplating its very nature, which consists of contemplation itself, the entire element of consciousness remains within the self alone as the possessor of all experience.
The element of consciousness, whose nature is like the sky, relishes whatever state it has attained through its own delirium, just as one intoxicated by agitation becomes agitated.
When everything is unarisen and does not exist at all, yet is nevertheless seen, then know this to be Brahman alone—equal, peaceful, and like unto the non-existent.
Like the sky within the sky, or like liquid water within water, that which shines by virtue of its consciousness—it is that very thing which has created this world.
Just as that very world arises in a dream as something pure, so too does it shine here within the void of creation, beginningless yet appearing as if with a beginning, like the shimmering of glass.
Just as the world appears in a dream through the manifestation of one's own consciousness, so too this waking state is of that same nature; it exists as nothing but itself.
For at the beginning of creation, the dream of consciousness was designated as "waking"; today, the dream of consciousness during the night is likewise designated as "dream."
Just as the ripples on rivers, having set in motion long ago, remain established even now exactly as they were, so too is the arrangement of objects within the range of vision.

Just as the beauty of the waves in water is limited by the configuration of the rivers, so too within the sky of consciousness, the immeasurable creation arises from the internal existence of the seed of consciousness.
If death were absolute annihilation, then that would indeed be the bliss of sleep; yet since saṃsāra arises once more, that bliss is merely momentary.
If there is fear of evil deeds, that [fear] is equal both here and in the next world; therefore, for everyone, death and birth are equal in their resulting happiness.
Whether there be death or life, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of those two is born together; he whose mind rests thus is said to be "internally cooled."
When all forms of cognition have ceased, a certain kind of pure awareness arises; by becoming one with that very awareness, one is said to be liberated.
Through the realization of absolute non-existence, the perception of all that is visible arises as something devoid of any object of cognition, whether a creation exists or does not exist.

That which is neither an object of thought nor of the nature of consciousness, yet is unperceived even by consciousness—those who know that have attained identity with its being; they are peaceful, yet remain engaged in worldly activity.
That which is called "the world" is merely a shimmering, flickering appearance; in the utterly transparent supreme space, how can there be any such thing as the perception of bondage or liberation?

The world, being essentially of the nature of the vibration of consciousness and of the nature of volition, consists entirely of reality; it never consists of earth or other material elements anywhere.
Here there is no space, no time, no substance, no action, and no ether; everything appears as if real—whether expanded or unexpanded—and yet it is unreal.
Thus, there shines only the absolute, the dense mass of ultimate reality, which is neither empty nor non-empty, and which is clearer even than the sky.
Whether with form or without form, it is indeed non-existent yet exceedingly luminous; it is the expansion of pure, singular consciousness alone, like a city in a dream.

Thus, this Nirvana is spread out in this manner within the inner sky of consciousness; it is both turbid and yet of an unturbid nature. It appears as manifold, yet it has not spread anywhere as something manifold; it is emptiness, like fluidity in the ocean or space in the sky.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Everywhere, in every way, everything, and at all times, exists perfectly pure within the all-pervading, consciousness-filled void, just as emptiness exists throughout the entire sky.
Wherever there is consciousness, there is the glory of creation—whether in the non-void or in the void; because all things consist of consciousness, there is nothing unconscious anywhere.
Just as the collection of objects such as mountains and cities in a dream are nothing but consciousness alone—the supreme void—so too is the ground of waking objects.
O Rāma, hear this narrative of the stone, which is a veritable elixir; it is that which was previously seen by me myself, both wondrous and natural.
Having known that which is to be known, my mind was once full; desiring to abandon this worldly conduct, which is a dense delusion.
Having attained one-pointedness through meditation for the sake of long-term rest, he gradually abandoned his restless activity and, seeking solitude, proceeded toward tranquility.
I reflected thus: "While staying in a certain celestial abode, I beheld the various, transitory states of worldly existence."
Truly, this worldly existence is devoid of essence; though beautiful on the surface, I believe it never bestows happiness upon anyone, by any means, or anywhere.
These perceptions of what is seen produce agitation within the observer, due to the distress of intense mental turbulence, as they yield desired and undesired fruits.
What is this that is seen, or what does it perceive? Who am I? Everything is the peaceful, unborn void—a mere ripple within the Self that is pure consciousness.
Therefore, having gone from here to a very auspicious location that is difficult for all the Siddhas, Indras, gods, Daityas, and others to access, one should conceal oneself by means of the self.
Invisible to all beings, having attained the non-conceptual samādhi, I abide in a state that is even, clear, and peaceful, free from all sensation.
Therefore, what region could there possibly be that has reached absolute emptiness, wherein these five perceptions of external objects are not experienced?
Agitated by the floods of water and the roar of the forest of sounds, the mountains, being thus disturbed, become my enemies.
The various regions situated between the lords of mountains, crowded with people, are indeed full of perils, for they are entirely infested by the serpents of sensory objects.
The oceans, their depths filled with water-dwelling creatures, resembled cities crowded with citizens agitated by various undertakings.
The shores of mountains and oceans, the cities of the world-protectors, mountain peaks teeming with living beings, and the caverns of the netherworld.
The mountain caves and deep hollows sing with the humming of the wind, dance with their hands of creepers, and laugh with flowers for the lords of elephants.
The lakes, their lotuses trembling as if from the touch of silent fish-sages, became utterly desolate, resounding only with the cries of water- whirlpools.
With its banners of grass and dust stirred by the touch of the wind, even the earth of the waterfalls cries out with the whistling sounds of the breeze, unrestrained.
Therefore, in some remote corner of the void of space, I shall remain here, firmly established by means of the blameless method of yoga.
Having constructed an imaginary hut in some corner here, I dwell within it—firm as the interior of a diamond—free from all latent mental impressions.
Having reflected thus, I went into the stainless sky; yet even there I beheld that entire expanse, stretching out in every direction.
In some places it had hosts of Siddhas wandering about; in some places roaring clouds; in some places it was the support of Vidyādharas; and in some places Yakṣas were casting down mountain peaks.
In one place a magnificent city was wandering; in another, a battle had begun; in one place there were clouds raining down thunderbolts; and in another, yoginīs were leaping about wildly.
In some places it contained the cities of Daityas and Gandharvas soaring upward; in some places it had hosts of planets wandering about, and in others it was crowded with stars.

In some places it was brushed by flocks of birds in the sky; in some places it was filled with a raging great wind; in some places it was enveloped by portents; and in some places it was adorned with circular patterns.

In some places there was a flood of unprecedented beings coiled like serpents; in some places it was trodden upon by the chariots of the sun; and in some places it was crowded with the chariots of others.

In some places it ends with the burning heat of the sun, in others it is endowed with the coolness of the moon; in some places it is unbearable for base people, and in others it is impassable due to the intense heat of fire.
In one place there was a wildly dancing vetāla, in another a soaring Garuḍa; in one place it was like the clouds at the end of an aeon, and in another like the winds at the dissolution of the world.
Then, having left the hosts of spirits, I went further and further away until I reached a solitary place that was utterly empty and vast.

Know that which is utterly devoid of even a slight breeze, where no elements are encountered even in a dream, free from auspicious or calamitous portents, and inaccessible to the cycle of worldly existence.
Then, I constructed there a hut with an open interior, its walls solid and without gaps, as beautiful as a lotus bud.
Her body was as charming as the interior of the full moon's orb when bored through by woodworms; she was adorned with the beauty of the calyxes of white water-lilies, jasmine, and mandāra flowers.
Having mentally resolved there that I was unapproachable by all beings, I then became inaccessible to all creatures.
Seated in the lotus posture, with a tranquil mind and observing supreme silence, he determined his own time for rising at the end of a hundred years.
Established in non-conceptual meditative absorption, he appeared as if sealed in sleep; equanimous and dwelling in the gentle sky, he was as if carved out from the firmament.

Whatever the mind contemplates for a long time, it perceives that very thing instantly; and when it is expanded over a long duration, like the manifestation of the wind of hope, it sees it as vastly extended.
Then, for a hundred years, the seed of awakening remained within the enclosure of my heart-field, blooming for a certain period of time.
Then my vital breath became fully awakened, its perception perfectly enlightened, like the sap of a tree whose limbs were withered by the cold now flows forth in the springtime.
Those hundred years passed for me there like a mere blink of an eye; even many successions of time seem but a moment to one whose mind is focused on a single point.
The sequence of my cognitive faculties has reached its full expansion and moved outward; like the essence of intoxication in springtime, it has become manifest for me in the form of flowers.

A demon was born from me—me who am filled with vital breath and a portion of consciousness that has arrived as the sense of "I"—and he, surrounded by women of his own desire, suddenly uprooted me like a fierce tree blown by a wind of rising and falling gusts coming from somewhere unknown.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, tell me for the sake of quelling my doubt: why does the demon of egoism afflict even you, in whom nirvāṇa has arisen?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In this world, the maintenance of the body for both the knower and the ignorant occurs without the sense of "I-ness" (ahaṃbhāva); for the supported cannot remain here without a support.
But listen to this distinction here, O you of tranquil mind, by hearing which the demon of egoism shall find peace within you.
This demon of egoism, though non-existent within, has been imagined by this child of ignorance; therefore, it persists.
Even ignorance does not exist at all, for it cannot be found when examined by one who investigates with the lamp of discernment, just as the nature of darkness cannot be found.
Just as it is scrutinized, so it dissolves; thus, when this female demon of ignorance is investigated here, it vanishes.
It is said that when ignorance exists, a perpetual Yakṣī consisting of the delusion of the intellect arises from non-knowing, just as a bodiless spirit appears in the night.
If ignorance exists, its occurrence is possible [only] through creation and not from anywhere else; for when there is a second moon, only then does a second rabbit exist.
