This creation, because it is unborn, does not exist even as something known by the ignorant; it is not born due to the absence of a cause, being like a tree in the sky from the very beginning.
In the beginning of creation within the interior of the supreme space-treasury, which is free from all affliction, what indeed could be the cause for the perception of earth and other elements?
How can that which transcends the six sense-faculties including the mind be the cause of the mind—including its six faculties and the self—which possesses form, yet is itself formless?
It is said that the effect, the sprout, arises from the seed as its cause; but where even the seed does not exist, how could the sprout arise there?
Without a cause, an effect can never logically arise; for when, by whom, and where has a manifest tree ever been seen or found in the sky?
Just as branches and other objects are seen in the sky through mere conceptualization, so too that conceptualization exists in such a manner; therein, there is no substantial reality.
Thus, this unimpeded persistence of creation which is experienced in the beginning of the emanation within the space of consciousness is like the form of emptiness in the sky.
The sky of consciousness shines as such within itself; its very nature is called creation, and because it is consciousness, that consciousness is the Lord.
The creation of dreams is the illustration here, which is experienced every day; in the dream-consciousness itself, the form of mountains and cities manifests.
Just as a creation exists here within the nature of consciousness like a dream, so too did it appear as a creation within the great void of the past, though it was not a creation.
At the beginning of creation, that which is pure, one, unborn, and undecaying—the non-perception of the perceptible, without beginning or end—shines forth; that alone is our established creation.
There is no creation here, nor is there this sphere consisting of the collection of earth and the other elements; everything is peaceful and without support—Brahman alone abiding in Brahman.
That Brahman, whose essence is all-potent, appears in whatever manner it shines; without abandoning its own pure form, it becomes exactly like that.
Just as a city in a dream is a manifestation of pure consciousness for a living being, so too is creation at the beginning of the world-cycle a manifestation of pure, pristine consciousness.
In the pure supreme space of consciousness, that which is established as the space of consciousness is this very creation; it is conceived as such by that [consciousness] itself.
The intense cultivation of the stages of the object to be realized, the realizer, and the act of realization—all this is nothing but the pure sky of consciousness, abiding by itself within itself.
This being the case, whence is creation, whence is knowledge, and where is ignorance? Brahman is entirely peaceful and solid; where do egoism and the like abide?
This complete pacification of the sense of "I" has been described to you; once fully understood, the sense of "I" subsides like a demon.
But when this entire sense of "I" was fully understood by me in this way, then, although it still existed, it became as fruitless as an autumn cloud.

Just as a painted fire is known to be fruitless when applied to things that can actually burn, so too the creation and so forth of the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva), once understood, reaches a state of fruitlessness.
Thus, when I have attained equanimity toward both the abandonment of egoism and attachment, then my state remains the same in every creation, like that of the sky which is not [limited by] the sky.
"I am not the ego-sense, nor does the ego-sense belong to me"; by this, know that all this is but the cloudless sky of consciousness.
Just as it is for me, so it is for other awakened ones here; like the fire-nature of a variegated fire, this delusion of awakening does not exist.
When you have reached the certainty that "I am not, nor is there another, and everything does not exist," remain in the silence of a stone while performing your natural worldly duties.

Remain for a long time with a form as clear as the expanse of space, according to the instruction, having concealed all objective existence; for from the very beginning, indeed, everything is composed of consciousness alone, and thus the entire visible world is nothing but auspiciousness.
Śrī Rāma said: Oh, how wonderful! O Blessed One, for our welfare you have once again described that vision which is expansive, noble, stainless, vast, and immovable.
In every way, at all times, everything, everywhere, and always—reality remains as "Being" alone, equal through the experience of sameness.
O Brahmin, I have this doubt; please dispel it: O Blessed One, why is this narrative called "The Story of the Stone"?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: To establish that everything exists everywhere and at all times, I shall relate this illustration of the story of the stone to you.
It is demonstrated here that even within the hollow of a stone whose body is entirely solid and without gaps, there exist thousands of creations; tell me how this is so.
In this great elemental space, which does not abandon its nature as empty sky, it is demonstrated that thousands of creations exist; thus it is told.
It is demonstrated here that thousands of creations exist for internal growths, sprouts, and so forth, as well as for living beings, wind, water, and fire; tell me how this is shown.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, if it is said that multitudes of creations exist within walls and such, why is it not seen that multitudes of creations shine within this sky?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, I have described all of this to you in its primary essence: this creation which is perceived is nothing but space situated within space.
For that which is visible and appears here has never arisen even from the beginning, nor does it exist even now; it is Brahman, abiding within Brahman.
There is not even an atom of space that is not filled by creations; nor do those creations exist anywhere as separate entities, for they are nothing but the void of Brahman.
There is not even an atom of light that is not filled with creations without any gap; nor do those creations exist anywhere—this is simply the void of Brahman.
Not even an atom of space exists within the wind that is not filled by creations; nor do creations exist anywhere at all, for they are nothing other than the ether of Brahman.
There is not even an atom-sized space that is not filled by creations; nor do those creations exist anywhere—they are nothing but the void of Brahman.
There is no such thing as the nature of the great elements that is not permeated by creations; yet creations do not exist anywhere at all—that is simply the void of Brahman.
Among the mountains, there is not even an atom that is not solid by its own creations; yet no such creations exist anywhere—that is simply the void of Brahman.
There is not even an atom of Brahmā that is not filled with creations; nor do those creations exist anywhere—they are simply the void of Brahmā itself.
In all creations, there is not even an atom that is not always the very self of Brahman; thus, "Brahman" and "creation" are merely a distinction in words, not in reality.

The creation itself is the Supreme Brahman, and the Supreme Brahman itself is the state of creation; there is not even the slightest duality here, just as between fire and its heat or the sun and its light.
These creations and this Brahman are views that are ultimately inexpressible; they appear like the sound of wood being split, devoid of any real object.
Where there is not even the slightest bit of duality or unity, how, to whom, or as what could the meanings of words such as "creation" or "Brahman" appear? To whom indeed would they manifest?
O dear one, for the knower, even while engaged in worldly activity, this silence is as solid as a stone—tranquil, one, without beginning or end, pure, and free from disease.

Thus, Nirvana is entirely like space; the visible world, you, I, the masses of mountains, and the gods and asuras—all this world should be viewed in that same way, my dear, just like the web of worldly activities within a dream or in the mind of a living being.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, after you had awakened from your meditation within the hollow of the hut in the expanse of the sky, what occurred during that hundred-year period?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, awakened from my meditation, I heard a sound there—gentle, with distinct words, and pleasing to the heart, yet not following after any specific object of speech.
Whether it was soft and sweet like the nature of a woman, or resonant yet lacking full resonance due to its smallness of scale—that speech was inferred by me.
It has the form of the humming of bees, is as pleasing as the resonance of lute strings, is neither weeping nor recitation, and its sound is like that of a lotus bud.
Having heard that, I then quickly reflected upon it there; looking toward the ten directions with wonder through the investigation of grammar, I saw this.
This [region] is situated immediately beyond a part of the sky measuring hundreds of thousands of yojanas, which is devoid of the paths traversed by the Siddhas.
Therefore, how could there be the occurrence of such a word here? Even though I look with great effort, I do not see any grammarian [who would provide it].
This infinite, empty, and stainless sky before me—though one strives to perceive what is real within it, nothing is seen here.
Thinking thus and looking again and again, when I did not see Śabdeśvara, I then reflected as follows:
Having become space itself, I have attained oneness with space; within the vessel of space, I produce the meanings of sound, which is the quality of space.
Having established the space of the body here in its natural state through meditation, I shall attain oneness with the sky of the body of consciousness, just as water unites with water.
Having thought thus, I sat in the lotus posture to abandon the body and remained with eyes closed again to enter meditative absorption.
Having abandoned the contact with external objects as well as those internal to the senses, I became the space of consciousness, whose very nature consists of the vibration of awareness.

Gradually abandoning even that, I reached the state of the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*); I became the single mirror for the web of the world within the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*).
Then, by that very nature, I attained oneness with the elemental space, just as water merges with water or fragrance with fragrance.
Then, having become perfected, it pervaded the great space; then, being infinite and all-pervading, though formless and without support, it attained the state of being the support for all objects.
I behold the multitudes of the three worlds and hundreds of transmigrations; therein, I see even countless millions of cosmic eggs.
The pure spaces, unseen by one another, though possessing various modes of conduct and movement, are indeed mutually empty.
Like the dream-forms of sleeping men occurring at the same time, these [visions] were characterized by great undertakings, yet they were empty of one another.
Those being born perish; those growing increase manifold; those existing, those that have passed, and those yet to be, all do so in every way.
Various nets of diverse paintings, great walls, and voids—like formidable kingdoms created by the mind alone—have been fashioned by manifold people.
Forms that are unobscured, as well as those with a single obscuration; those possessed of five obscurations, and those with six or one obscuration.
There are mandalas with ten enclosures, sixteen enclosures, twenty-four enclosures, and thirty-six enclosures.
They are empty yet once filled with beings, composed of the five elements, consisting of the single element of earth and so forth, as well as the four elements of earth and so forth.

There are others consisting of three earths and so forth, as well as those consisting of two earths and so forth; likewise, there are those composed of the seven great elements and those consisting of a single birth.
But those regions which are contrary to the full extent of experience such as yours—being eternally dark and devoid of the sun and other luminaries—are likewise [unreal].

Likewise, their creations were merged together, they were presided over by a single lord, and they possessed diverse conducts due to the various portions of the lords of subjects who were of distinct characteristics.
Likewise, there are treatises on world-weariness and those that are not treatises at all; and they contain worms, insects, and the like, as well as beings such as gods and other living creatures.
But by birth, they possess a lineage and are endowed with conventional conduct; likewise, they are eternally luminous and consist of blazing fire.
Likewise, those filled with nothing but water and those consisting of nothing but air remain motionless in the supreme ether, yet they flow incessantly in that same manner.
Some, being born, nourish [others] and, once fully nourished, spread in all directions; others move horizontally, consisting entirely of everything.
There were worlds consisting solely of gods, those composed only of humans, those made up entirely of hosts of Daityas, and even those that were nothing but gaps between worms.

Within, within, and further within that end—even inside its own sheath, down to the subtle atom—there exist things already born and those currently being born, like the layers of a plantain tree's leaf-stalk.
Indeed, the vast webs of dreams experienced by the soldiers were not seen by one another, nor were they mutually experienced, as if they had arisen independently.
Though they are diverse and infinite, they are entirely composed of the nature of clear space; they function independently of one another, yet they do not exist in mutual dependence.
And those which are mutually distinct scriptures, and those which are mutually infinite; those which are mutual arrangements, and those which are mutually one another.
They saw various other worlds and mutual cities of the perfected ones, with different kinds of great elements and different directions and mountains.
When matters such as these—unfathomable to those like you and yet arrived at through experience—are recounted by people like me, they appear utterly inconsistent.
Within the solar orb of consciousness, the rays of the ultimate glory are like earrings—masses of light-beams shimmering in the sky of the absolute.
Some of those very things, having come into being again and again, eventually cease to exist; others are born exactly as they were before, like the leaves of a forest.
And because they are mutually distinct, some things are similar yet distinct, while others remain entirely different for a certain period of time, even though they appear very similar.
Those fruits of the great tree of ultimate reality are infinite; they are indeed non-different from it, yet different, for they are composed of that very essence.
Some are of short kalpas, some of long kalpas; others are indefinite and vast, while some are definite and vast.
Arising spontaneously by the power of chance, they exist as distinct entities whose times of origin are unknown—growing, flourishing, and remaining firmly established.
Those nets of emptiness have grown within the treasury of the supreme space; they have flourished for an unknowable time within one whose faults remain unrecognized.
Enveloped by hundreds of oceans, suns, skies, Mount Meru, and so forth, the webs of dreams appear without obstruction within the sky of the wondrous play of consciousness.
Because experience is of the nature of error and because causes do not exist, earth and the other elements—being themselves causeless—are both absolutely existent and non-existent.
Like the abundance of water in a mirage, or like the description of two moons in the sky, things that have come into being are not real, even though they appear real through experience.
Like many appearances in the sky of mental construction, driven by the wind of latent impressions, they roll about through the movements of the self.
The gods, asuras, and others, like gnats, [gaze upon] the many fruits of the udumbara tree, filled with nectar and swaying in the winds.
For one whose nature is noble-born and who initiates creation, these cities of imagination appear in the sky for the child-like pure consciousness.
The notions of "you," "I," "he," and "this" have become firmly established by the power of thought, just as clay toys are rendered solid by the light of the sun.
By destiny, which is ever-satisfied and rich in aesthetic flavor, all things have come to pass like forests of fierce fruit brought forth by the spring's essence.
The great agents or non-agents, or indeed the sense-voids, are either not created at all, or they are produced within the sky of consciousness as forms spontaneously perfected.
Even those things described as other than that are indeed composed of the ultimate truth; though unobtained, they are as if obtained, and while always non-existent, they nonetheless exist.
And there are groups of beings of fourteen, ten, one, and other such kinds; these very same ones are again within, while others are outside.
Even hells, heavens, the underworld, enemies, and friends—consisting as they do of great undertakings—are empty from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Like the waters of the milk-ocean, they are everywhere composed of the essence of affection; they are as flickering as breaking waves, and they flow both inwardly and outwardly.
These are merely forms of appearance within the light of the sun-like Self; they have arisen spontaneously like the vibrations of the wind.
The forms of trees belonging to the leaves—which are the intellect, ego, and mind—are non-existent even though they appear; they are like the men projected in a dream.
Lying upon the pillows of the conceptual constructs of the Purāṇas, Vedas, and established doctrines, they sleep in a deep slumber as if bearing the state of corpses.
In the great forest of ultimate reality, within the dense self, there are indeed houses fashioned by the gandharva of consciousness, illuminated by the lamps of the sun.
When beings were being born and dissolving without cause in the infinite sky, I then beheld the worlds as if they were the floating hairs seen by one with cataracts in the eyes.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, wandering all about while reflecting upon such a state, I remained for a long time, having attained the nature of the unobstructed space of consciousness.
Afterwards, I heard a sound resembling the melody of a lute; gradually it became clear in its syllables, and from that it attained the status of Āryā verse.
As the rain fell in the direction of the sound, I beheld a woman whose side was illuminated by a luster like molten gold, making the sky radiant.
With her garlands and garments swaying, her hair disheveled, and her eyes unsteady, she was like another Goddess of Fortune who had arrived with her half-bound braid loosening.
Her limbs were as fair as lovely gold; she was in the bloom of youth while standing on the path, beautiful in every limb and fragrant like a forest goddess.
She had a face like the full moon, a smile like a cluster of flowers, a countenance exuberant with youth, and was graced with long, thick eyelashes.
Dwelling in the expanse of the sky, beautiful as the rays of the moon, adorned with strings of pearls, my beloved follows after me.
With such a sweet voice, that noble and charming woman, smiling softly by my side, recited this verse in a gentle manner.
O Sage, I bow to you alone, the tree upon the shore that serves as a support for those who are utterly bewildered in the river of saṃsāra by their improper, empty minds.
Having heard this and beholding her of the lovely face and voice, I thought, "What is this woman to me? and, disregarding her entirely, I departed.
Then, having beheld that illusion consisting of the multitude of worlds, I was struck with wonder; yet, disregarding it entirely, I prepared to roam through the sky.
Then, completely casting aside that anxiety caused by her, I, whose nature is space, set out to comprehend the illusion of the world as it stood in the sky.
Just as all those worlds, however fierce, and the entire sky are indeed empty—just as in a dream, a mental construction, or a verbal description.
They never see nor hear anything whatsoever, even those [moments] that consist of a single great eon, a great intermediate eon, or a great birth.
[He beheld] the Puṣkarāvarta clouds acting like intoxicated [beings], the Utpāta winds acting like madmen, the great mountains shattered, and the pavilions of Brahmā constructed with firm forms.

[He beheld] the abodes of the Ḍākinīs, where the *eḍaviḍa* [fire] crackles and bursts like the blazing fire at the end of an eon, and which scorch with twelve forms of solar orbs like the Kārttikeya-sun.

Resounding with the gurgling cries of lamentation from the vast throngs of the city of the gods as they rolled about, and formidable for swallowing the entire range of mountain ridges on the battlefield;
[He saw] the great oceans of the sky agitated by the vast turbulence of their own collapse, resounding with the crackling *paṭat-paṭa* sounds of the blazing fires at the end of the eon.
[He saw] the harsh, gurgling wails of gods, asuras, and humans, which filled the great flood of the seven oceans and submerged the orbs of the sun and moon.
They do not perceive the ends of the eons as distinct from one another, like those sleeping in a single chamber who, in a dream, experience the tumult of battle.
There, thousands of Rudras and hundreds of millions of Brahmās were seen by me, as well as hundreds of thousands of Viṣṇūs and countless multitudes of Kalpas.

There, in certain places where there is no sun and the surface of the earth is devoid of day and night, at the end of kalpas, yugas, and years, the destruction and emergence of worlds occur through inferential reasoning.

All is consciousness; all belongs to consciousness; consciousness is all, and consciousness is everywhere. Consciousness is the reality that consists of the self of all—this entire truth was perceived by me therein.
If you say that there is "something" therein, O dear one, it is as if there were something; for that [emptiness] is more empty than space, yet it is not truly nothing at all.
Thus, this space shines forth designated as the "world"; for by that very space of sound, all is indeed the supreme space.
"This perception of the visible world is an illusion, like a cluster of blossoms on a tree in the sky; it is merely a limb of the space of consciousness"—this is what I have experienced therein.
By means of that infinite consciousness, which is of the single nature of the space of the intellect, all-pervading and consisting of pure awareness, this was experienced by me through volition.
The web of the universe is the Brahma-void; the ten directions are the Brahma-void; and time, space, substance, action, and so forth, are the Brahma-void.
In that regard, O lords of sages, just as it appears to me, hundreds of times over in this cycle of existence, there have been seen excellent Brahmins named Vasiṣṭha who were sons of Brahmā.
O Brahmin, seventy-two Tretā ages have all passed along with the Rāghavas; there, a hundred Kṛta ages and likewise a hundred Dvāpara ages have been seen.
Indeed, those various states of creation are seen through the arising of differentiation; yet, through awakening, they are that single, utterly transparent Brahman, like the pervasive sky.

This name "jagat" (world) does not exist in Brahman; rather, this world is indeed within Brahman. Brahman alone is unborn, without beginning or end, and it is that which constitutes all things, such as the word "tat" (That).
That which is like the silence of a stone, unexpressed by anything whatsoever, yet which shines as "that which is something"—Brahman is traditionally known as the world.
In the sky of consciousness, one's own existence alone shines forth as the world—unthinkable, formless within the formless, and resembling the experience of a dream.
Brahman is non-different from the self; everything has the nature of mere appearance. Like light, it illuminates, yet it does nothing at all.
Indeed, among those hundreds of thousands of worlds, there are moon-disks that are hot and suns that possess cool forms.
People see him in darkness, for they do not see him in light; their conduct is like that of an owl, and their voices are similar to his.
From here, they perish through merit and likewise go to heaven through sins; they live by eating poison and die by eating nectar.
In whatever manner it is perceived in awakening, or in whatever way it arises spontaneously, whether it be real or unreal, that very thing immediately attains clarity in that same manner.
A forest appears in the sky with trees that resemble the trunks of branches, shining like vajras, and whirling with foliage that has the luster of flowers.
When sand is pressed, it flows with an oily essence; and from stone slabs, lotuses grow in abundance.
In the wood, the stone, and the wall, the flickering statues, accompanied by celestial nymphs, sing and converse.
Living beings wear the clouds aloft like lofty garments; every year, fruits of diverse kinds spring forth upon the mountain.
With various limbs arranged in non-standard positions, all beings move about upon the earth with their heads [downward].
Certain worlds below, devoid of the Śāstras and Vedas and lacking all dharma, are inhabited by animals; there, people act according to whatever whim arises.
Some were devoid of the experience of desire and lacked women; they were pervaded by spirits with withered hearts, as if they were made of stone.
There were beings who subsisted on air, as well as those made of precious gems and stones; they had not yet attained their purpose, were free from greed, and seemed as if devoid of pride.
In some cases, one perceives oneself as distinct and attains nothing else; yet the world, though consisting of many elements, is also a single element.
Just as [the self] exists in the nails, hair, and so forth, so too does it abide elsewhere; one should cultivate the realization that the self of all beings is one with one's own self.
In some places, there is a vast emptiness that is infinite, shoreless, and without end; through diligent effort, one attains consciousness of it, yet at its limit, the world does not exist again.
Some beings, regarding the meaning and views of the word "liberation," are utterly unawakened by the Buddha, like a multitude of living beings fashioned entirely from wooden machinery.
Some networks of spirits are devoid of the circle of constellations and free from the reckoning of time; they consist essentially of silent conventions.
Some beings were entirely devoid of the perception of sight, sound, and objects, their own radiant splendors rendered useless by the singular thought that they were but elemental forms.
Some are devoid of the consciousness of vital breath and possess useless fragrance; some are mute due to the futility of sound and are bereft of hearing.
Some others are like the mute because they are devoid of the consciousness of speech; some others are like limbs of stone because they are devoid of the consciousness of touch.
Even some things that are seen consist of nothing but pure consciousness; though they appear as objects of worldly transaction, they are eternally ungraspable, like ghosts.
Some were made of earth and others reached to the very summit; some were solid masses, while some were filled with water and others were filled with fire.
Some worlds are filled with wind and possess all possible forms, while others are of the nature of space; indeed, they shine there within the void.
While others remain within the various seats of the earth, embodied beings dwell in them like frogs in the hollows of stones or like insects in the belly of the earth.
While the earth, its forests, and its mountains remain entirely filled with water, other beings wander about constantly like fierce fish.
In other places filled with fire alone, even the elements devoid of water and the rest flash forth intensely, consisting solely of fire like a blazing flame.
In other beings who are filled with wind, even those whose bodies consist of nothing but wind quiver like the wind of Arjuna.
In other creations, there exist living beings whose bodies consist of nothing but space and who are themselves of the nature of space; they perceive and interact within those worlds.

As they fall into the underworlds, soar into the sky, or remain suspended in states of delusion throughout the quarters of the world—in these various realms of existence, what indeed has not been seen by me among the flickering bubbles of the ocean of consciousness?
Śrī Rāma said: Was that which was seen by you at that time situated in only one part of the expanse of consciousness, or was it while you were wandering through the sky?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: At that time, I was indeed the infinite Self, all-pervading like space; in such a state, what kind of coming and going could those two possibly have?
I am not composed of that which abides in a single place, nor have I become composed of movement; therefore, by this, this has been seen by me within my very own self.
Just as I perceive the limbs from head to foot as being the body itself, so too have I seen this with the eye of consciousness, which is yet no eye.

Since that formless one, whose nature is the stainless sky of consciousness, abides without parts and does not exist as such [in itself], those worlds are like a lattice of limbs belonging to me; they have neither fallen away from their own nature nor do they possess substantial reality.
In this matter, your authority is the delusion of the world seen in a dream; for that which is experienced as an object in a dream is nothing other than empty space itself.
Just as a tree perceives its own leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth with the eye of self-awareness, so too have I seen this.
Just as the ocean, whose nature is infinite, knows all aquatic creatures, as well as its waves, whirlpools, and foam, so too have I understood this.
Just as a whole perceives its own parts within itself as non-different from itself, so have I understood these creations.
Even now, O Rāma, having attained the state of pure consciousness, I see those same creations within my body, in space, on mountains, in water, and on land, exactly as they were.
Having attained the state of pure consciousness, I perceive this entire universe before me—both within and without my house—as being filled with multitudes of worlds.
Just as water knows its own fluidity, just as frost knows its own coldness, and just as the wind knows its own movement, so does one of pure intellect know this.
Whosoever is indeed of a discerning nature and has attained oneness with pure consciousness is equal to me, being of one essence; I know my own self to be such as this.
In this vision, there is no cognition of a knower, a knowing, or a known resulting from transformation, because there has arisen the oneness of the self-nature of consciousness.
Just as one with divine vision perceives objects situated on a mountain as well as those located ten million yojanas away, so too do I, having awakened, know all things both external and internal.

Just as the earth-element knows things such as treasures, minerals, and essences through its own nature, so too has that which consists of me awakened to itself as non-different from what is otherwise invisible.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahman, O lotus-eyed one, since you experience it thus, tell me: what did that beloved wife do, she who was so proficient in reciting the noble scriptures?"
Vasiṣṭha said: Reciting that very same noble verse and likewise filled with conciliation, she stood near me with a body of light in the sky, like a goddess stationed in the firmament.
Just as I have a body of space, so too does she possess a form of emptiness; therefore, that woman was never before seen by me with this physical body.
I am the self whose nature is mere space, and she is the embodied one whose body is mere space; at that time, in that state, the web of the world existed as nothing but space.

Śrī Rāma said: From what source does that speech arise—composed of phonemes—which emerges through the body, its positions, the articulatory organs, effort, and the vital breath, yet belongs to one whose nature is otherwise?
"O Blessed One, tell me the truth and the certainty of how form, light, and mental attention arise from the self."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as forms, perceptions, mental activities, sounds, recitations, and words exist within the void of a dream, so too do they exist there in the ether of the sky.

Just as those [objects] arise in a dream through forms, light, and mental attention within the sky of consciousness itself, so too does that which is perceived therein abide as having the nature of space.
Not only is that visible object so, but even we ourselves and this entire world are, within the sphere of our experience, nothing but the pure void; thus it is for us in its entirety.
The great ultimate realm, whose conscious form is liberated from all that is to be known, shines forth by itself in this very way; such is the certainty regarding its own nature.
What proof do you have for the existence of the body, its locations, and its articulations? Just as they [the Mīmāṃsakas] maintain their body and so forth, so too is this established for us.
Just as that is, so is this; and just as this is, so is that. Though non-existent, it has attained the appearance of existence; and though existent, it stands as if non-existent.
Just as in a dream there is the activity of the earth, paths, and so forth within the sky, so too am I, you, she, and this world are likewise the sky.
Just as in a dream, people experience the clamor of battle and the coming and going of others—though these are unreal—so too are the multitudes of worldly existence experienced.
If you say that the splendor seen in a dream is such, why is that inconsistent? This must not be said, for there is no other cause for the existence of experience.
To the questioner who asks, "How is a dream perceived?", it is explained: "It is just as you see it now. This alone is the reason here; there is no other.
From the very beginning of the first creation, the Virāṭ self appears like a creature in a dream within the void; in the sky, it is merely the sky itself, existing in mutual relation.
I employ the word "dream" for the sake of your awakening; yet this visible world is neither existent nor non-existent—it is not a dream, but absolute Brahman alone.
Then, O Raghava, that beloved woman, who was inseparable from me, having established with me a consciousness consisting of that [same essence], appeared in a visible form and asked this.
Just as worldly interaction arises in a dream with those born of that dream, so too did my interaction with her arise at that time.
Just as worldly activity is like a dream and is indeed empty space itself, so too should you know this—me, the self, and the world—to be empty space.
Just as the form of the dream-world is nothing but space, so too is this world; for that which is a dream at the beginning of waking is the emergence of the world at the beginning of creation.
This expansive manifestation of the world is a dream, or perhaps nothing at all, being merely the pure sky of consciousness; thus it is established as pure Being alone.
In an ordinary dream, there exists a perceiver such as yourself who possesses form; however, the perceiver of the dream of creation is the stainless sky of consciousness itself, by its very nature.
Just as the seer is the stainless sky, so too has the visible become that same way; in this world which is essentially a dream-form, the stainless sky exists intensely as the world.
The dream that flashes forth spontaneously within the heart from the formless sky of consciousness—whence could there be a creation for it, and how could it possess form?
That dream-world which belongs to that which possesses form is but the stainless void; how then could the creation of the formless sky of consciousness not be the void itself?
Without any accumulation of causal material and upon no foundation at all, one perceives this world—uncreated like the sky of consciousness—as if it were a dream created by a maker.

Although the pavilion of creation, with its windows of the senses, was fashioned by Brahmā—the Brāhmaṇa—in the void using the soft clay of the ether of consciousness, it was as if it were never made at all.

There is no agency, nor are there worlds, nor is there any state of being an enjoyer; "it exists" does not apply, nor does "it does not exist," for nothing whatsoever [exists] apart from this. Being wise, adopt the silence of a stone and practice conduct according to the natural flow; let the body remain here or not.
Śrī Rāma said: How was it possible for that woman to exist with a body that is not of the nature of sound? And how were the phonemes such as ka, ca, ṭa, ta, and so forth, articulated there?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Within the bodies of living beings, the phonemes such as ka, ca, ṭa, ta, and so forth, never arise at all, just as [the colors] do not arise in corpses for whatever reason.
If the pronunciation of syllables had possessed a manifest meaning, then people standing nearby, even while awake, would have experienced that [meaning] within their dreams.
Therefore, nothing in dreams is real; it is merely an illusion. That manifestation of the space of pure consciousness occurs in that manner within the void, born of its own nature.

In that state, the spaces of consciousness appear as if they have become the blackness of the moon, the body of the sky, a stone, a song, and so forth; likewise, the sounds of the body and other such things appear in the same way.
Know that what is called the manifestation of the space of consciousness during the experience of a dream is indeed the space itself—the manifestation of the void and nothing else.
Just as a dream, so too is this waking state established before one; just as space is non-space, so too is this [waking state].
Just as that beautiful consciousness shines forth with such cleverness, so too does it remain exactly as it is—this very reality, vibrating as if stable and true.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, how is it that this dream itself exists as the waking state? How can that which is unreal attain the appearance of reality?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen to how these worlds exist entirely as mere dreams—neither different from them, nor real, nor stable, nor even enduring.
Experienced seeds are like a heap of seeds in the sky; they are various and distinct, yet they are both the same and not the same.
Likewise, many other various intermediate [worlds] have arisen individually, unseen by one another.
All of them do not perceive anything at all of one another; like inert masses, they even dissolve away like seeds.
Because they are of the nature of space, they do not perceive one another; though they possess the form of consciousness, they remain as if in a continuous state of sleep.
While asleep, they engage in the web of the dream-world during the day; those asuras, though slain by the gods, remain situated within that dream-world.

They have not attained liberation due to ignorance, nor have they reached the state of insentience due to dullness; being devoid of the existence of a dream-world, how could they be possessed of bodies?
Men who, while asleep within the web of the dream-world, conduct themselves according to their own habitual behavior, are slain by other men; yet they remain established in that very same state.
Being devoid of liberation and lacking a physical body, yet endowed with consciousness and latent impressions—where else could they dwell if not within the perceived web of the dream-world?
Those Rākṣasas who were slain by the gods while they were asleep, moving within the established course of the web of the dream-world, remained exactly as they had been situated.
"O Rāma, tell me: what do those who have been thus slain do? If they have not attained liberation due to ignorance, it is because consciousness does not reside in a stone."
All this visible world, including the mountains, oceans, and the earth, remains exactly as it is; these beings experience it for a long time, just as we ourselves do with due attention.
The arrangement of their world-systems and eons is exactly as ours is; and the arrangement of our world-system is exactly as theirs is.
These very dream-people are we who stand here; and those which are called "saṃsāras," know this one alone among them.
Those dream-people are indeed real for them through their own experience, because the conscious self (cidātman) is all-pervading, being both oneself and another.
Just as those dream-people are real within themselves, so too are others; nevertheless, those dream-people are indeed real, and they [the waking people] are exactly like that.
Those citizens of your own respective dream-cities whom you saw remain there exactly as they were even until today, because Brahman is the self of all.
For even upon awakening, dream-states are perceived as distinct according to how they existed; likewise, they are experienced according to their state of being, or else as the Supreme Brahman.
Everything exists everywhere, at all times, as the self of all, just as in the case of space, where nothing is absent, nowhere is it lacking, and nothing is destroyed.
In the boundless supreme space, in the boundless play, in the boundless mass of consciousness, and in the boundless multitude of worlds.

Corresponding to the treasury of every portion of space, corresponding to every circle of saṃsāra, corresponding to the form of every intermediate world, and corresponding to every continent and mountain;
In every mandala, in every village, in every city, for every living being, in every house, in every year, and in every age.
However many beings have died who are devoid of liberation, that many separate and inexhaustible cycles of existence remain there.
Among them, there are those whose minds are directed toward other people; and from those minds, the world arises, and from that world, again, other people.
Thus, this delusion consisting of the visible world is without beginning or end; in the view of the knower of Brahman, it is Brahman alone, and herein there is no limitation whatsoever.

Since pure consciousness alone exists within the wall, the sky, the stone, the water, and the earth—and from that, this entire universe arises—wherever that [consciousness] is, there the world is. What count can there be here? To those who know it, it is the Supreme; to the minds of the ignorant, it is the visible world.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, having observed that woman whose eyes were like a garland of blossoming *mālatī* flowers, I spoke to her playfully.

Who are you, O lady with the luster of the interior of a lotus, and for what purpose have you come to me? To whom do you belong, what do you seek, where have you come from, and what is your dwelling place?
The Vidyādharī said: "O Sage, listen as I relate my own story to you exactly as it is. You ought to question me with confidence, for I am distressed and a seeker of compassion."
Within some corner-cavity of the treasury of supreme space, this house of the world of yours is situated for the time being.
The netherworld, the earth, and heaven are these three chambers here; the Creator’s power of illusion has fashioned this maiden as their sole conceptualization.
There, the surface of the earth, encircled by continents and oceans like bracelets, appeared like the forearm of the Goddess of the World, fashioned from pale-red sandalwood.
Beyond the continents and oceans, situated in every direction, is a ground made of gold extending for ten thousand yojanas.
Self-luminous, bestowing the fruits of one's resolve, as pure as the sky, composed of wish-fulfilling gems, and transparent, her own radiance has surpassed that of the entire world.
It was a ground for the playful excursions of Apsarases, Maruts, and Siddhas, beautiful with every enjoyment brought forth by mere thought.
At the edge of that earth stands the famous mountain Lokāloka, which bears the appearance of a bracelet encircling the forearm of the terrestrial sphere.

In one place it is eternally pervaded by darkness, like the disposition of one with a deluded intellect; in another place it is eternally of the nature of light, like the mind of those possessed of sattva.
In some places it produces delight, like meeting with the virtuous; in other places it produces distress, like association with fools.
In some places it reveals all its meanings clearly, like the mind of the wise; in other places it is extremely obscure, like the mind of a foolish Vedic scholar.

In some places it did not receive the rays of the moon; in some places it did not receive the light of the sun; in some places it consisted of the world itself; and in some places its horizons were utterly empty.

In some places it was pervaded by the cities of the gods; in some places it was filled with the cities of the Daityas; in some places it was as deep as the netherworld (Pātāla); and in some places its peaks rose high like necks.
In some places vultures hovered over the chasms; in others, it was enchanting with its peaks; and in yet other places, the interior of Brahmā’s city was reached upon the summits of its crests.
In some places, there was the wind of the end of an eon blowing through vast empty forests; in other places, there were throngs of Vidyadhara women singing in flower gardens and groves.
In some places it was terrifying with kumbhāṇḍas in caves as deep as the netherworld; in other places it was as delightful as the hermitages of sages, resembling the Nandana grove.

In some places it was filled with inexhaustible clouds of intoxication; in others, rain-clouds were difficult to find; and in some regions, its borders were dense with the hollows of mountain caves and deep chasms.
In some places, it was a land where the spirits were driven away by the reproaches of agitated people; in other places, it was a realm surpassed in goodness by its resident inhabitants.
In some places, the moving and stationary beings were produced by winds blowing eternally; in other places, the moving and stationary beings remained firm, liberated from all destruction.
In some places it was terrifying with the *bhāṃkāra* sounds released by the winds of the great desert; in other places it was adorned by the warbling of intoxicated cranes amidst the lotus ponds.
In some places, it resounded with the gurgling splashes of waves upon the water; in others, it aroused passion through the playful swinging of intoxicated apsarases.
In some places its horizons were filled with restless piśācas and kumbhāṇḍas; in other places its riverbanks resounded with the dances and songs of vidyādharīs and siddhas.

In some places, its banks were washed by the many rivers flowing from clouds that rained down; in other places, it was adorned with excellent cloths in the form of various clouds brought and driven along by the *sata-taga* winds.

In one place, his circle of meditative absorption rested within the opening of a lotus bud; in another, he served as the jeweled ornament for the teeth of the celestial nymphs and the beautiful wives of the Siddhas.
In some places, it was beautiful with the conduct of people whose hands were like sunbeams; in other places, intoxicated night-stalkers danced within the houses of the darkness of night.
In some places, the earth was losing its people due to rising portents; in other places, circles of cities were flourishing through the perfection of excellent governance.
In some places it was utterly empty, in others covered by inhabited lands; in some places it was deep with interior chasms, and in others terrifying like the netherworld.
In some places there was a vast wish-fulfilling tree, in others a waterless wilderness; in some places a great herd of elephants, and in others a troop of rutting lions.
In some places it was devoid of beings, in others it was filled with frantic rākṣasas; in some places there were thickets of karañja trees, and in others vast forests of palm trees.
In some places it had lakes resembling the sky; in others, vast desert lands; in some places, dust was constantly swirling; and in others, forests flourished in all seasons.
Upon its peaks are rocks resembling those of an ordinary mountain; they are like clouds poised for a long duration, composed of jewels, and as pure as the sky.
In these [cities], monkeys born of the lineage of Hari rest incessantly, like lions dwelling in forest thickets that are as white as the milk-ocean or the moon.
In the northern quarter of those [peaks], within the hollow of the eastern summit-rock, I dwell upon a surface whose skin is equal to the indestructible essence of diamond.
Bound there by fate, I dwell within this stone machine; O Sage, I believe that countless multitudes of ages have passed for me here.
Not only am I bound, but my husband there is also bound, like a bee in an evening lotus bud.
Together with that husband of mine, I experienced great hardship for a long time within the narrow cavity of a rock; many years have passed here.
Even now, due solely to the fault of the self, we do not obtain liberation; remaining for a long time in that very state, our dispositions remain unliberated just as before.
In that rocky confinement, not only were we two bound, but our entire retinue was likewise imprisoned there.
"There dwells my husband, a twice-born man who is an ancient being; though bound, he does not move from that single spot even while living for hundreds of yugas."
A celibate from childhood, learned in the Vedas, a reciter of scripture, yet free from indolence; he dwells alone in solitude, straightforward in conduct and without fickleness.
O best among the knowers of the Vedas, I am his wife, devoted to him; without him, I am not capable of sustaining this body for even a moment.
Listen, O Brahmin, how I was obtained as his wife by him, and how this natural affection of ours has reached such growth.
Long ago, when my husband was born, while he was still a mere child, possessing only limited knowledge, he remained alone in his own pure abode.
Having deliberated for a long time, he resolved: "From where can a wife worthy of my status as a Vedic scholar and endowed with noble birth arise?"
O lotus-eyed one, I, whose limbs are themselves faultless, have been brought forth by that Lord as his own, just as the stainless moonlight is produced by the moon.
With my mind, I became the mental wife of Mandara, most beautiful of women; from that time on, I grew like a flower-cluster in the spring.
Clothed in the natural sky, she captivates the hearts of all beings; with a face like the orb of the full moon, she is like the heavens adorned with pure stars.

With her breasts elevated like buds and heavy with their weight, she was endowed with every aesthetic flavor; she was graced by her sprout-like hands, like a choice forest creeper adorned with its shoots.
She eternally captivates the hearts of all living beings; with eyes as dark as a doe’s, she bestows the intoxication of passion.
Her sole delight was in playful grace, her eyes rolling with amorous sport; she was ever fond of song and instrumental music, and her passion was never satiated.

Supreme in the enjoyment of good fortune, she is the dear friend of both Fortune and Misfortune; she is inseparable from the snares of delusion, yet remains undaunted by both prosperity and adversity.
O dear one, it is not only the house of the twice-born that I support; indeed, I sustain this entire abode of the three worlds.
I am a wife who brings honor to my family, capable of supporting my husband, and the sole bearer of the burden of maintaining the household of the three worlds.
Then I became a young woman, with full and prominent breasts, radiant with the essence of grace like a cluster of blossoms swaying on a creeper.
Because of his prolixity, his status as a Vedic scholar, and his devotion to asceticism, my husband has not yet married me, despite some underlying expectation.
Therefore, though endowed with youth and full of the essence of graceful charm, I am consumed by grief without him, like a lotus plant in a fire.
Upon the lotus ponds constantly stirred by cool breezes, I experience a burning sensation in my limbs as if upon a ground of glowing embers.
All the gardens and groves are filled with showers of flowers; the desert lands that were once barren sands have become fertile.
The lakes, tender with ripples of water and clusters of white and red lotuses, and delightful with the cries of cranes, have become tasteless to me.
Though garlanded with clusters of lotuses, mandārakas, and water-lilies, I experience intense burning, as if tossed upon thorns.
The beds of white water-lilies, blue lotuses, white esculent lilies, and plantain trees, once crisp with the heat of summer, turn to ashes from contact with my body.
Whenever I behold that which is lovely, appropriate, sweet, diverse, and captivating to the heart, my long eyes become filled with tears within.
Dripping with teardrops scorched by the fire of calamity, they fall and sink with a *chamaccham* sound into rows of lotuses and water-lilies.
In the cherished garden groves, by the playful swinging upon the trunks of plantain and kandalī trees, I weep with my face covered.
I see a pavilion of plantain leaves strewn with heaps of frost, emitting warmth yet terrifying like the glowing embers of khadira wood.
Beholding the female crane resting upon a male crane amidst the swings of lotus stalks, I look within with a dejected face and reproach my own youth.
I weep when an object is pleasant, I become indifferent toward one that is neutral, and I rejoice over one that is unattractive; thus, wretched as I am, I do not know what state I have come to.
I have seen the kunda, mandāraka, and kumuda flowers, as well as the snows, scattered in every direction like the ashes of those consumed by the fire of desire.

My days of fresh youth have passed in vain as I lay upon a bed of dark-blue sprouts, lotus stalks, creepers, blue water-lilies, white lilies, jasmine, plantain leaves, and *mālatī* flowers, drying them up by the movement of my limbs.
The Vidyādharī said: Then, after a long time, that passion of mine turned into detachment, like a sapless leaf at the end of autumn.
My husband is old, living in solitude, devoid of passion, lacking affection, straightforward-minded, and silent; what do I think of my life? I consider it of no value.
Better is widowhood from childhood, better even is death, better is disease or calamity, than a husband of an unlovely nature.
Such is the fulfillment of this birth and such is unbroken good fortune: that a man is a lover of aesthetic delight, of graceful conduct, young, and the husband of a woman.
A woman is ruined who lacks a husband; the intellect is ruined that is not refined; fortune is ruined when enjoyed by the wicked; and modesty is ruined when stolen by a prostitute.
She is a true wife who follows her husband; she is true prosperity who follows the virtuous; she is true wisdom which is sweet and noble; and she is true goodness which consists in impartial vision.
Neither mental anxieties, nor physical ailments, nor calamities, nor misfortunes cause any affliction to the minds of a couple who are devoted to one another.
The blossoming flower-lands, the grounds of the Nandana grove, act as deserts for women who have lost their protectors and those who are without a lord.
All worldly states may be abandoned at will, even through a mere trace of a quality or out of negligence; however, a wife must never abandon her husband.
O leader of sages, behold the manifestation of misfortune: these sorrows have been endured for many years by me, who possess perpetual youth.
Then, in due course, by that very means, my passion became devoid of passion, as a lotus scorched by frost becomes sapless.
Therefore, O Sage, through your instruction, I desire the extinction of my own self, which is the coloring of all states of being by the latent impressions of dispassion.
For those who have not attained their desired goals, whose minds find no rest in the world beyond, and who are being carried away by deaths, death is better than life.
My husband, desiring nirvana day and night today, strives to conquer his mind with his mind, just as a king seeks to conquer a kingdom with his royal power.
And for the sake of pacifying the ignorance of that Brahmin, my husband, and myself, perform the remembrance of your own self with words consistent with reason. Oṃ.
When my husband remained indifferent toward me, disregarding me entirely, that detachment brought a sense of world-weariness to my perception of existence.
Therefore, having abandoned the influence of the latent impressions of saṃsāra, I dwelt there, having bound myself in the intense and desired meditative concentration on moving through space.
Having thus acquired the power of movement in the sky through meditative concentration, I further practiced that concentration which yields the fruit of association with the perfected ones (siddhas).
Then, having fixed my gaze upon the eastern and western limits of my own world-system and maintaining that concentration (*dhāraṇā*), I remained there until I too attained perfection.
Then, having seen his heart within his own world, I, who had gone outside, beheld the massive rock of the Lokāloka mountain.
O Sage, even after all this time, neither of us, husband and wife, ever had the slightest desire to see another.
My husband, through his exclusive contemplation on the singular meaning of the pure Vedas, knows neither what has passed nor what is yet to come; oh, how he is free from all worldly desires!
Therefore, although my husband was learned, he did not attain that state; today, both he and I desire the supreme state through diligent effort.
Therefore, O Brahmin, you ought to make this request of mine fruitful; for among the great, no supplicants have ever been rendered unsuccessful.
O giver of honor, as I wander always in the sky among the hosts of Siddhas, I see nothing here but this forest fire of dense ignorance, except for you.
O Brahmin, since the virtuous fulfill the desires of those who seek their aid even without a cause such as compassion, you ought not to subject me—who have come here seeking refuge—to rejection.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, having been thus addressed and questioned by me—who was seated upon a mentally fashioned seat—she remained poised in the sky, seated upon a seat likewise fashioned by her own resolve.
O foolish girl, how could those like you exist within the interior of a stone? How could there be movement there, and for what purpose would you have a dwelling place therein?
The Vidyādharī said: "O Sage, just as this vast world shines forth for you, so too does our world exist there, joined with creation and the cycle of existence."
The nāgas quiver in the underworld, the mountains stand firm upon the earth, the waters ripple and surge, and the winds blow through the sky.
The oceans shine with their waters, yet within them living beings move slowly; just as beings are born incessantly and die without ceasing.
The winds blow, the waters flow, and the gods shine and do not shine in the sky; the mountains stand firm, the planets rise, and kings traverse the earth.
The day-lotuses of the lake that is the earth, their petals the moving rows of clouds, remained in full bloom for an eon, repeatedly closing and opening.
Creating moon-like splendors in the four directions with the sandalwood paste of its own radiance, it destroys even the darkness residing within the hearts of the night and Rohiṇī.
Delighting in tasting its own state, well-guided by the mechanism of the wind, this lamp called the Sun shines in the sky, the abode of heaven and earth.
Willed by Brahmā and obstructed by those who move with the flow of the winds, the wheel of the stars revolves incessantly in the sky, turning according to the cycles of the qualities.
From the beginning of creation, the pivot-pin of destiny, set in motion by necessity, grinds the grain of living beings; it rattles like the ocean against the door-panels of heaven and earth.

The surface of the earth was filled with islands, oceans, and mountains; the sky with celestial chariots and cities; and the entire circle of the netherworld with throngs of Daityas, Dānavas, and Nāgas.
The dark blue circle of the earth’s surface is the earring of the Fortune of the three worlds; it remains there like a shimmering gem upon her who is fickle in her conduct.
Taking up the subtle vibration of consciousness—which is devoid of intellect and the like, like the wind—and which constitutes both the stationary and the moving, one is born.
The earth was characterized by the silence of sages, the waters by the fickleness of monkeys, the winds by their capacity for space, and the splendors by their brilliance.
Within trees, the earth, oceans, mountains, and the sky, living beings—worms, gods, asuras, and aquatic creatures—throb intensely, all facing toward birth and death.
Together with the gods, asuras, and gandharvas, Time impels all creatures with its arms—the eons, yugas, and years—just as a herdsman tends his own cattle.
In the ocean of time, which is infinite, vast, unfathomable, and deep, they are born again and again, only to dissolve through the turning of its whirlpools.
The fourteen kinds of elemental dust, tossed by the winds, dissolve into the space of destruction like the play of autumn clouds.
Awakening the world with the fly-whisks of the rays of the moon and sun, she stands with the sky as her garment and a crest of clusters of stars as her ornaments.
The quarters of the sky stand as if paralyzed, enduring wind, earthquakes, clouds, and heat, without abandoning their own regions.
Even when portents such as the roar of calamitous clouds, earthquakes, and the seizing of planets are not understood, the course of beings nevertheless unfolds.
The blazing submarine fire drinks up the waters of the seven oceans, just as Time devours the multitude of beings throughout the intermediate worlds until the end of the kalpa.

The host of spirits enters the underworld, ascends to the hollow of the sky, and wanders everywhere throughout the circle of the directions; it traverses the circles of great mountains and oceans, as well as other continents, following the course of the wind.
The Vidyādharī said: "O Sage, please come to that place of creation; let favor be shown to me. For when wonders have arisen, the great are indeed filled with intense curiosity."
When I said, "So be it," I began to travel through the sky with her—just as fragrance is carried by a whirlwind, or the void by the void within the void.
Then, having traversed a long distance through the empty sky, I reached together with her a multitude of beings situated in the firmament.
Having traversed that expanse of moving beings in the sky for a long time, I have now reached the white cloud in the firmament above the Lokāloka mountain.
Emerging from that seat of clouds, white as the moon in the northern sky, I was brought to this lofty rock fashioned like molten gold.
As long as I beheld that bright rock, it was not this world, but appeared like a lofty ridge of the realm of fire made of pure gold.
Then I said to that beloved woman: "Where is the ground of your creation? Where are Rudra, the Sun, Fire, the Stars, and so forth, and where is the sevenfold series of other worlds?"
Where is the calculation of time for action, and where is the wandering through the worlds of the past? Where are the Vidyādharas and Gandharvas, and where are humans, gods, and Dānavas?
Where are the sages, kings, and seers, and where is the sequence of right and wrong policy? Where are the nights of the five-fold afflictions, and where is the wandering through heaven and hell?
Where is the reckoning of merit and sin? Where are the playings of the arts and time? Where are the enmities of gods and demons? And where are the ways of hatred and affection?
While I was speaking these words, that woman of excellent complexion, her eyes as white as stone, looked upon me with a gaze agitated by wonder and spoke.
The Vidyādharī said: "I see everything here as not my own; I behold all people like the inhabitants of other cities reflected in a mirror."
In this philosophy, constant perception alone is the cause for me; O Sage, I consider the absence of that perception to be the cause of your non-perception.
Moreover, through this long-standing discourse on non-duality, we both have forgotten our state as the pure, singular, transcendental spiritual body.
Since I no longer clearly perceive this world of mine—which, though practiced by me for an exceedingly long time—has become like a creeper upon the sky.
That which was previously my own world, appearing to me with extreme clarity, I now see as indistinct, like a reflection in a mirror.
O Lord, through the mutual pain of our long-standing and futile conversation, we have forgotten our own most pure and pervasive state of well-being.
That practice which shines forth from within by the power of the pure sky of consciousness becomes entirely composed of that very essence, appearing as if it were innate from childhood.

Know that there is no art which cannot be mastered through the study of true scriptures, nor any which cannot be achieved through right reasoning; for nothing fails to be accomplished through the practice of boundless exertion.
"Surely this delusion of discourse has overwhelmed me by the force of my own long-continued habit; for between two [conflicting views], the stronger one indeed prevails."
O Sage, for those seeking their desired object, there is no other refuge than the repeated performance of that action as instructed by one who knows it.
This mature delusion of ignorance here, consisting of the thought "I am," is pacified by the cultivation of knowledge; behold the manifestation of practice!

"I am a young female disciple, a mere child, yet I see; you do not see. Though you are omniscient, you do not perceive this creation of stone, which is manifested through the power of meditative practice."
Even the ignorant attains the state of the knower, even a mountain is ground to powder, and even an arrow reaches its great target—behold the manifestation of practice!
In this way, indeed, the fully matured cholera of false knowledge is pacified by inquiry alone; behold the power born of practice!
O Sage, through habituation even a pungent substance becomes agreeable; the neem tree is pleasing to one person, while honey is pleasing to another.
One who has no kinsman becomes a kinsman through proximity and the practice of intimacy; conversely, through lack of practice, affection for kinsmen diminishes due to distance.
This subtle body (ātivāhika-deha), which is merely the pure space of consciousness, assumes the state of a material body through the practice of mental cultivation.
This physical body, through the cultivation of the practice of concentration (dhāraṇā), ascends into the sky like a bird; behold the manifestation of practice!
Meritorious deeds may go to waste, mothers may go to waste, and fortunes may go to waste; but practice never goes to waste.
Enemies who are difficult to subdue attain success, and they turn into friends; even poisons turn into nectar through the yoga of continuous practice.
He who abandons practice regarding a desired object is the lowest; he never attains it, just as a barren woman never obtains her own son.
Even that object which is desired because it is acquired through one's own habitual practice should be abandoned according to reason, just as life itself must be relinquished until death.
That lowest of men who does not practice toward a desired object attains what is undesirable regarding that which is undesired, passing from one hell to another.
Those who indulge in the worthless flow of saṃsāra cross over the vast river; they alone do not abandon the practice known as self-inquiry.
The appearance of repeated practice is fully capable of revealing the desired object and brings it about without obstacle, just as the light of a lamp reveals a jar.
Just as the wish-fulfilling trees and creepers, and just as the true wish-fulfilling gems, bear fruit in autumn, so too do the stages of practice.
The light of long-practiced meditation upon a desired object illuminates all beings, so that they no longer perceive the night of the earth known as the sense-faculties.
In the illumination of all objects for every class of living being, the sun of practice alone always triumphs loftily.
However, among the fourteen types of beings born of the elements, no one achieves their desired object without natural, uncontrived practice.
Repetition of an action is called practice (*abhyāsa*); it is that alone which constitutes human effort (*puruṣārtha*) here, for without it there is no progress.
Success occurs through one's own action, which is characterized by firm practice and designated as "effort," arising solely from one's own realization; it does not happen otherwise.

When the sun of practice shines upon the earth and in the forest, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished by a hero; through practice, all fears on this earth become fearlessness, even in the most desolate mountain caves.
The Vidyādharī said: "Therefore, let us perform our ancient practice within the stainless state of awakened concentration; by that means, this world shall become manifest to you, O Mountain-dweller."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the Vidyādharī had spoken thus with logical reasoning upon my chest, I then assumed the lotus posture and arose into meditative absorption.
Having abandoned the cultivation of all objects and being devoted solely to pure consciousness, I renounced that impurity consisting of the conceptualization of the meanings of previous discourses.
Then, having attained the state of the sky of consciousness, I reached the supreme vision, just as the sky attains clarity upon the arrival of the autumn season.
Then, through the intense and singular practice of fixing my attention on truth within this body, my delusion regarding the material world has surely come to an end.
Free from rising and setting, yet consisting of perpetual arising, the great consciousness, as clear as the sky, then became as if manifest.
Then, as far as I could see by the very power of my own stainless luster, there was in reality neither sky nor stone; it was only the Supreme.
The pure, solid ultimate reality shines forth as such; indeed, through such contemplation, my own self has perceived it in that very way.
Just as in a dream a very large rock seen within one's house is found to be nothing but empty space, so too is the rock of the sky of consciousness utterly pure.
A man who himself possesses dreams, having entered into the dream-masculinity of another, is in his essential nature just like one who has awakened from ignorance within a dream.
Those whose heads are severed while they remain in the state of dream—remaining thus within saṃsāra—what indeed can they possibly do without the attainment of knowledge through time?
There is a time when even those possessed of great delusion become awakened, because there is nothing whatsoever that is imperishable except for the reality of Brahman.
Therefore, that pure wealth of consciousness, the Brahma-ether in the form of stone, was seen by me there as such; however, earth and other elements were not found to exist anywhere.
That which is pure and ultimate among beings at the time of the first creation—that very body of theirs remains attainable through meditation.
For that which is the primordial, innate form of all beings—belonging to the Self—is what is today called the kingdom of the mind, or volition.
The body that carries the living being beyond is, in the ultimate sense, that which is the supreme direct perception; it is the primordial manifestation of consciousness.

The first body of the living being, whose primary and intermediate senses are active, is called mental perception (mānasa-pratyakṣa); that very thing has been asserted by the dull-witted person this very day.
What has been called "yogic perception" is also called "mental perception"; it is simply the very nature of consciousness itself, having needlessly undergone a change into something else.
Know that this so-called "present" perception, which arises from what is non-existent, is indeed a perception of the non-existent; O dear one, understand that to be perception.
Aha! How wondrous is this illusion: that which was previously manifest has become hidden, yet in this very thing now determined to be unperceived, the notion of being perceived has arisen.
Know that the state of the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha), which was first described as being directly perceived, is real and all-pervading; whereas the material body (ādhibhautika) is merely illusion.

Just as the state of being a bracelet does not exist in gold even when it has been experienced, so too the state of being material (adhibhautikatva) does not exist for that which is purely transmental (ativāhika).
That the living being perceives error as non-error and non-error as error—without inquiry—is it not indeed a state of utter delusion?
This physical body is not found upon inquiry; however, it is said that the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) is indeed imperishable in both worlds.
For the material consciousness, firmly rooted within the subtle body, is indeed false—just as the perception of a body of water in a mirage in the desert.

The consciousness pertaining to the elemental (ādhibhautikī) arises within the sequence of the subtle transportive body (ātivāhika-cit); through the power of the perception of a body, it becomes fully developed, just as the notion of a person arises in a tree stump.

Just as there is the appearance of silver in mother-of-pearl, of water in a mirage, and of duality in the moon [reflected in water], so too does the perception of materiality arise through illusion (māyā) in the subtle body (ātivāhika).
That which is non-existent is made real, and that which is real is made non-existent; oh, how great is the power of delusion born from the lack of inquiry into this living soul!
There exists only the direct perception of the yogin, yet there is also mental perception; for the conduct of both worlds is established by these two alone.
He who, having abandoned the primary perception, establishes himself in this truth, remains happily after drinking the water of a mirage within that very perception.

That which they call happiness is actually suffering, because it is experienced as momentary destruction; the wise know that true happiness to be that which is unconditioned and without beginning or end.
In this way, let perception itself be examined by perception; that which is the primary perception is the real perception—let that be seen by means of perception.
There is no one more foolish than he who, having abandoned the perceptible experience of this world which yields the fruits of the three realms, instead grasps that which is illusory in nature.
For these beings, there exists only a subtle, transportable body; the pervasive presence of the material body here is merely an unreal phantom.
How could that which consists of unarisen conceptualization be a real perception? How could that which is not itself real produce an effect?
Where even direct perception itself is non-existent, what else could exist there? Where could that real entity be found which is established by means of something unestablished?
If existence itself is directly perceived as having perished, where indeed could inference and the like be employed? Where elephants are carried away, what talk can there be of woolly sheep?
Therefore, that which is established by valid means of knowledge—the visible—does not exist anywhere at all; this alone exists as it were, the dense mass of Brahman, utterly solid.
Just as in a dream, the mountain is only space for the dreamer within his house and not for anyone else, so too, for us two who possess that same contemplation, that very stone is consciousness.
"This is a mountain, this is the sky, this is the world, and this is I"—thus the Self, consisting of consciousness, itself performs a wondrous display within the void.
One whose self is awakened perceives this, but never one who is unawakened; the comprehension of the meaning of a discourse belongs to the listener, and never to one who does not listen.
"This is unawakened" is merely an error that has attained the status of reality; to one who is intoxicated, even trees and mountains appear perfectly stable as they dance.

Having realized the nature of consciousness as the directly perceived Śiva—the unimpeded, uniform awareness that pervades all—those fools who here resort to other, inferior perceptions are as good as nothing, being as frail as blades of grass and utterly deceitful.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That which is the limb of the world, appearing as a non-appearance, invisible yet standing as if visible, is seen through the supreme vision as that very Brahman, free from all affliction.
Therein, the wanderings of mountains, river currents, worlds, and the intervals between worlds appear reflected in that supreme mirror of the great sky.
Then, having entered that creation with unrestrained activity, I too entered there along with her, consisting of the nature of volition.
Having reached that world of Vairiñca, she, full of effort and supremely beautiful, sat down before Viriñca.
"O tiger among sages, this one says: 'This is my husband; he protects me, for I was previously conceived by him in his mind for the sake of marriage.'"
Even though he is the Ancient Puruṣa, he has not married me, even though I have now reached old age; because of that, I have become disenchanted.
Even this seeker of dispassion desires to go to that state where there is neither the state of being a seer, nor the state of being seen, nor even emptiness.
The great dissolution is now imminent upon this world, yet he does not waver from his meditation, remaining as immovable as a mountain observing the vow of silence.
Therefore, O Lord of Sages, having awakened both me and him as well, establish us on the supreme path until the beginning of the creation of the next great kalpa.
Having said this to me, he spoke these words in order to awaken him: "O Lord, this lord of sages has arrived at this dwelling today."
This sage, the son of Brahmā, has come to another house in this world; honor him with the hospitality due to a householder who has arrived at home.
"Let the bull among sages be awakened and honored with water for the guest and water for the feet; for the Great Soul takes delight in great and solemn rites of hospitality."
When she had said "So be it," he of great intelligence awakened from his meditative absorption, like a whirlpool in the ocean arising from the nature of the fluidity of his own self-awareness.
Skilled in policy, Madhu slowly opened his eyes, just as a flower opens upon the earth when the cold season has subsided.
