Gradually, those limbs manifested his consciousness, just as clusters of fresh honey-sprouts reveal their new sap.
Multitudes of gods, siddhas, and apsaras gathered from all sides, like restless swans flocking to a lake blossomed at dawn.
He saw me and that playful woman arrived before him; then the Creator spoke these words, beautiful with the resonance of the *praṇava*.

Another Brahmā of the world said: "O sage who has seen the essence within the worthlessness of saṃsāra as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand, O great cloud of the nectar of knowledge, welcome to you!"
We have reached this most distant path; weary from the long journey, please sit upon this seat.
When he had spoken thus, O Blessed One, saying "I salute you," I sat down upon a jewel-encrusted seat that was pointed out by his gaze.
Then, the praises, offerings, prostrations, and rules of conduct were set forth, uttered by the immortals, sages, gandharvas, munis, and vidyādharas.
Then, after only a moment, when the tumultuous display of prostration by the entire host of beings had subsided, I spoke to that Brahmā.
O Lord of the past and the future, what is this that she has come to me and speaks with words of wisdom, urging me with effort: "Awaken us"?
O Lord, Master of Beings, you have reached the further shore of all knowledge; but this woman is a fool driven by desire—tell me, O Lord of the World, what does she say?
O Lord, how is it that she, who was brought forth by you for the sake of being a wife, has not been led here to the state of a wife, but instead led to a state of bitterness?
Anyajagadbrahmā said: "O Sage, listen; I shall relate this to you exactly as it occurred, for that which has transpired must be told in its entirety to the virtuous."
There exists, indeed, a certain Reality that is unborn, peaceful, and undecaying; from that, whose nature is exclusively the manifestation of consciousness, I have emerged as a manifestation.

Another world-Brahmā said: "Now, I, who am the space consisting of consciousness, desire to attain that supreme state which consists of another kind of space; for that reason, my dissolution has arrived here."
"O Lord of Sages, at this time of the great dissolution, I have now begun to abandon her; for that reason, she has surely become distasteful to me."
When, by virtue of being space, I become this primordial supreme space, then there is the state of the great dissolution and the total destruction of latent impressions.
Therefore, having become despondent, she runs toward my path; for what person of noble intellect would not follow their own creator?
Now, at the end of this Kali age, there is the reversal of the four yugas; today indeed has come the end of the subjects, the Manus, the Indras, and the gods.
This very day is the end of the kalpa and indeed the end of the great kalpa; today is the end of my latent impressions and the end of the space of this body.
Therefore, O Brahmin, this latent impression is now prepared to go to its destruction; for where indeed could a trace of fragrance remain when the lotus pond has dried up?
Just as a moving wave arises from a line on the surface of a dull ocean, so too does desire arise in vain from latent impressions (vāsanā), being without cause.
From the very nature of this latent impression (vāsanā) consisting of the conceited body, the desire to perceive the Self arises spontaneously.
Indeed, as she beheld the reality of the Self through the practice of concentration, she saw this creation of yours, unrestrained and occupied with its various categories.
By her, who was intent on moving through the sky, the stone at the mountain peak was seen; yet for us, it is the void-natured space that serves as the support of our own world.
In that world where this world exists, there is the state of being a mountain within the mountain of the world; and within the objects of our own world, there also exist other worlds.
We do not see those [realities], for these people remain fixed in the perception of duality; but having quickly attained the oneness of awakening, we see them through our vision.
In a jar, a cloth, a banyan tree, a wall, in space, fire, water, and light—the worlds exist everywhere at all times, as if within a stone.

The so-called "world" is indeed a vain delusion, comparable to a city in a dream; it is purely false—where is this world? It exists as the very form of consciousness, yet it does not exist [as an object].
Those for whom this [intellect], once fully understood, has attained oneness with the sky of consciousness, do not become deluded; but the rest remain vessels of error.
Furthermore, O Sage, you were seen by her as she accomplished her own purpose through the practice of another form of concentration, which was brought forth by the power of her own dispassion.
Thus the power of consciousness unfolds like an insurmountable illusion; in this way, the stainless power of Brahmā is without beginning or end.
No effects whatsoever proceed or cease here; consciousness alone shines, illuminating substance, time, action, and the rest.
Know that this—space, time, action, substance, mind, intellect, and so forth—is in fact nothing but the single body of the rock of consciousness, which is without setting or rising.
This very consciousness remains in the form of stone, yet it sustains within itself the web of the world, just as the wind sustains its own vibration.

One perceives the world as a self consisting of a mass of consciousness; though beginningless and endless, that consciousness appears to have a beginning and an end because it is consciousness, even though it is indeed consciousness.
Through the realization that this beginningless and endless consciousness is both with beginning and end, it remains established as the body of the world—both with form and yet formless.
Just as in a dream consciousness itself perceives its own form as a city in the void, so too does it perceive this world-body as a stone.
In this state, rivers do not flow, the wheel does not revolve, and objects do not transform within; only this sky of consciousness shines forth.
In the sky of consciousness, the cognitions of great eons and the end of eons do not exist as separate forms, just as one body of water does not exist as distinct from another within water.

The worlds both exist and do not exist within the peaceful sky of consciousness, which is all-pervading and of a single form; just as the spaces within the sky exist within the great sky, so do these beings exist within the supreme ether of consciousness.
O Vasiṣṭha, O sage, go now; you too find peace upon your own seat. Let the forms consisting of intellect and the rest proceed toward the Supreme; we shall depart for the state of the Great Brahman.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus, the Blessed Brahmā, together with the inhabitants of the world of Brahmā, sat in the bound lotus posture and entered into infinite meditative absorption.
The half-measure at the end of the syllable Oṃ, wherein the mind is entirely stilled, assumes a form bestowed by the act of writing, yet its experience remains unextinguished.
Following that very [state], she likewise remained absorbed in meditation; with all portions of her latent impressions extinguished, she became tranquil and took on the nature of space.
When that Parameṣṭhin, free from all volition, had attained that state of attenuation, I beheld him as the form of the all-pervading, infinite, and conscious void.
Just as his conceptualization becomes tasteless in an instant, so too does the earth, along with its mountains, continents, and oceans, quickly become so.
The capacity for the growth of grass, shrubs, creepers, and rice has entirely begun to fade away, little by little.
It is said that the earth bears the status of being a mere limb or part of that Virāj-self; for that reason, [the earth] arises from a lack of awareness of Him.
Devoid of consciousness, she became tasteless and utterly withered, having fallen into the frailty of old age like a creeper at the end of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Just as a finger becomes insensible to us through our own lack of awareness, so too has the earth fallen into a state of distress through the awareness of Viriñci.
It was filled with a multitude of great portents gathered together; its men were turned toward the hells, scorched by the embers of their own misdeeds.
It was filled with famine, sudden calamities, instability, wretchedness, poverty, and misfortune; it was crowded with women of immoral character and men devoid of all restraint.
The sun was dimmed by dust, mist, and grime; the world was agitated by the misfortunes of the diseased, the miserable, the afflicted, and the foolish who live in pairs.
Its territories were devastated by fires, floods, and war; its common folk were reduced to miserable conditions due to drought and the failure of rain.
Where mountains and cities fell unexpectedly due to great portents, and where people wept at the destruction of children, Vedic scholars, sages, nobles, and the virtuous.

In the midst of places where one has no cause for suspicion, deep wells have suddenly appeared; the women of mixed castes have become objects of attachment for the people, and they have become the mistresses of the land.

Where all people have their throats as their only stake, where the crossroads are the stakes of the Śivas, where women have their hair as their sole stake, and where the lords of men have their begging bowls as their only stake.
All the people were afflicted by the pain of dualities and practiced the thorn of suffering; women were the thorn of unrighteousness, and the lords of men were the thorn of addiction to drink.
Enveloped by the trident of unrighteousness, pierced by the hundreds of tridents of false scriptures, rich with the wealth of all wicked men, and struck down by calamities that destroy the virtuous.
The un-noble guardians of the earth disregard the wise; they are devoted to greed, delusion, fear, hatred, passion, disease, and the dust of worldly attachment.
Even those who go elsewhere, whose virtuous twice-born are struck by wrath, and whose base folk are intent on incessant lamentation;

It was a place where bandits had destroyed the cities, villages, temples, and the dwellings of the twice-born; its undertakings were sweet at first sight, yet they resulted in suffering and were as fragile as a broken belly.
Characterized by a failure of duty manifesting as the play of laziness, it will end in the affliction of all calamities, with its array of directions gradually destroyed.
The cities and villages were reduced to ashes, all the regions were devoid of people, and the sky was made terrifying by clouds of ash and howling jackals.
The belly of this wretched woman resounds with the loud lamentation of her grand display; she is a mere handful of people, yet she is obsessed with causing distress to the multitude.
When the earth element has lost its sensation, it becomes devoid of all other regions and is stripped of the qualities of all seasons; such is the state of Brahmā.
The earth, having become vast and desolate due to its imminent destruction, was then abandoned by its consciousness, and the water-element turned toward its own exhaustion.
When his mind was agitated, then, due to the transgression of restraint, the oceans cast aside the boundaries of the noble ones and their waters surged forth.
Like madmen crying out, they have begun to undergo transformation; by the shifting agitation of their waves, they are lopping away the forests on the shore.

The sky and the directions were filled with towering waves tossed upward by the swirling eddies of surging billows, while the vast expanse of the heavens was obscured by the wandering of great clouds.
The mountain caves resounded with vast, gurgling whirlpools and roars, while the peaks were enveloped by dense clouds amidst a great upheaval of flying sprays.
Their interiors were churned by heroes leaping and surging like sea-monsters, and their bellies were filled with forests of trees overtaken by frolicking makaras.
Aquatic creatures were struck down by lions that had fallen from caves split open, while the sky was made starry by the weight of great jewels tossed up by the waves.
The sky was covered by great clouds resembling leaping sea-monsters, emitting harsh *bhāṃ* and *ṭāṃ* sounds from the mutual clashing of their waves.
The trumpeting of the elephants was as resonant as the shimmering sun, while the mountain slopes were split apart by the frantic tossing and turning of one another.
The circles of waves were like plunderers of the mountain slopes on the banks, while the intoxicated elephants emerged from their dwellings in the roaring caves of the mountains.

The kings, having invaded the cities of their enemies, stood as if clinging to them after slaying their foes; they caused the sky-dwellers to flee from their mountain-like dwellings with loud cries of "tāra."
The forests were plundered and the groves laid waste, while the sky was filled with waves resembling winged mountains.
The mountain-like waves were shattered by winds of great roar and tossed about; the masses of trembling coastal mountains caused the waters at their slopes to crash with a rattling sound.
With masses of sea-monsters tossed up by surging, vast whirlpools, and with mountain caves swallowed up by deep, flat-edged eddies;
The jagged rocks, appearing like teeth as they were crushed and shattered, and the elephants submerged in the waters where waves lapped against the edges of caves hanging from the mountain peaks.

Tortoises were impaled upon the branches of trees by the horses of Yama, Indra, and the Guardians of the Earth, which were agitated with fear and had their ears pricked up as they galloped with restless, twisting movements.
The sounds of the mountain ridges falling with a crashing roar were heard, as the swift mountains, severed by the strokes of the fish’s tail, repeatedly sank and rose again.
The masses of water, cooled by showers that had playfully lopped away the forest groves, were joined with rows of flames from the blazing submarine fire.
With their great fires made suspicious by the destruction wrought by the essence of the Lord, they fought against the elephants of the waters atop the meeting mountain ranges.
The water-mountains, pierced by the surging waves, seemed to dance; they were masters at bursting asunder through their mutual collisions with the shifting waters.
Adorned by the circles of living beings in the vast forests and mountain thickets, they resounded with the beating of wild forest-elephant lords as if they were drums.

Then there arose the sound of the trumpeting of the elephants of the quarters, whose upturned trunks resembled the faces of serpents, like the netherworld being thoroughly agitated by the waves of the Asuras.
The earth, its surface and palate split apart by the violent tearing of the underworld, trembled for a moment as it was shaken by the moving mountain-piles.
Then, like a restless creeper of moss tossed by the surging ocean, she was accompanied by a tumultuous roar that could not be resisted and was free from any opposing winds.
The sky seemed to burst as it fell with the wailing cries of the lords of the quarters; and comets, shaped like swirling eddies, fell from the firmament.
Golden and jewel-encrusted pearls emerged from the quarters, the sky, and the earth like vermilion serpents, as the horizons were scorched.
With their massed tresses of flickering flames and rows of various portents, the earth and other elements, as well as the asuras and others, were cast out in every direction by Brahmā.
The two kinds of great elements underwent extreme agitation; the moon, sun, wind, Indra, fire, and Yama were all thrown into tumultuous uproar.
The lords who had reached the world of Brahmā were intent on falling down; with their tremors, they caused rows of trees to fall with a *kaṭakaṭa* sound.

The mountains experienced the intense swaying of the earth; the caves of Kailāsa, Meru, and Mandara trembled from the earthquake, and showers of red flower-clusters fell, released from the Kalpa trees.

As the cities, mountains, oceans, and forests at the ends of the worlds struck one another by the apocalyptic winds of the kalpa, the universe became a scattered and shattered tumult, like the mass of the three cities falling into the full ocean.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, when the Self-born One had withdrawn his vital breaths into the Virāṭ-ātman, the one born of space, who was stationed within the column of wind, abandoned his stability.
For those, it is said, are his very vital breaths; when they have departed, who else could maintain his station upon the circle of stars, which supports all living beings?
When the vital wind (prāṇa-māruta) was stepped upon by Brahmā within the mass of wind, it abandoned its equilibrium and, becoming agitated, began to move violently.
Supportless, the stars fell from the sky onto the surface of the earth like clusters of flowers from a tree, resembling sparks from a fire fanned by the wind or embers from a flaming torch.
The rows of celestial chariots fell down, their roots shaken by the ripening of time, containing the fruits that are fragments of the world, and their supports—the winds—having been stilled.
When the fuel of Brahmā’s creative volition was on the verge of dissolution, the movements of the perfected ones subsided like the flames of a blazing fire.
Wandering in the sky like bits of cotton driven by the winds at the end of an aeon, the lineages of perfected beings fell silent as their own power waned.
The networks of wish-fulfilling trees and the cities of Indra and the other gods fell down as the heads of the mountain of the immortals trembled from the earthquake.

Śrī Rāma said: Since Virāṭ Brahmā, whose body is the universe, consists essentially of the creative intention within consciousness, what part of him is the earthly realm (bhūloka), what is heaven (svarga), and what is the netherworld (rasātala)?
O Brahmin, how do these constituent parts abide within him, and how does he himself abide within his own body?
Brahmā is essentially composed of mere volition and is formless; that this world exists is my firm conviction—what else could it be?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In the beginning, this was neither non-existent nor existent; it existed as the stainless, supreme space of pure consciousness alone, filling the entire expanse of the quarters.
It perceives this object of thought as being of its own nature, namely, space; never abandoning its own essential form, it becomes conscious by virtue of its consciousness.
Know that the individual soul (jīva) is consciousness itself, which, due to its density, exists as the mind; within this entire web of existence, nothing whatsoever exists with a formal shape.
The sky of consciousness remains pure within itself, just as before; yet that which appears here is other than Śiva.
Then that mind, expansive, with its sense of "I" cultivated and throbbing, remains as an indestructible, motionless space whose essence is volition.
The manifestation of consciousness through its volition, conceived as "I am," experiences that which is utterly non-existent, like a configuration within the sky itself, appearing in the sky.
He knows, sees, and even experiences the manifested form; yet it is established that this body, consisting of the nature of mental construction, is indeed empty.
Just as you perceive a city of imagination—which is entirely empty—exactly as it acts, so too the Unborn perceives the body as merely empty space within the sky, having experienced it as such.
Because consciousness is pure, as long as it experiences such and such an experience in this manner, it subsides by its own will alone.
When there is a thorough knowledge of reality for people like us, then know this worldly existence to be spread out—empty, yet standing as if it were real.
Through the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are, latent impressions (vāsanā) are stilled here; from non-duality and the absence of ego, liberation remains as the result.
Thus, he who is Brahmā is indeed this world that exists; O Rāma, that which is the body of Virāj, the Brahman, is this very world.
The delusion that has arisen from that which is of the nature of the space of volition—this very thing appears as the world; it is designated as the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
All this is indeed only space, consisting of the fabrication of mental constructs; in reality, neither the world nor "you-ness" nor "I-ness" exists anywhere at all.
In some pure space that is mere-consciousness, how or by what means could the world arise? What exists here, and what is its auxiliary cause?
Therefore, this has arisen as false; the false is what is perceived; the false is tasted; thus one sees only the empty.
By means of the primordial speech of the world, pure consciousness tastes itself of its own accord, as the wind moves within the sky of the self through its own vibration, even amidst duality.
Know this world to be the space of consciousness—neither something nor nothing, devoid of both duality and non-duality, empty, transparent, and free from affliction.
"O Raghava, I abide as one in whom all distinctions have been stilled; though existing, I am as if non-existent. You too should remain thus, free from the sense of 'mine'."
Free from latent tendencies, with a peaceful mind, silent, and devoid of fickleness, do whatever comes to you; or do not do it—what attachment can there be in this?

That which is the one, beginningless, eternal experience is itself the visible, and not any other visible. Those vast "great visions" of the visible, which are non-experiences within the true experience, are merely that.
Śrī Rāma said: The cognition of bondage, liberation, and the world is neither void nor composed of existence; it neither sets nor rises, for that primordial reality is indeed something indescribable.
"O Brahmin, this Brahma has been sufficiently understood by me through your instruction. Speak further, for there is no satiety for me as I drink this nectar."

O All-pervading Lord, for one whose vision perceives the agitation of creation and so forth, as well as the vision of its own dissolution and so forth, none of these are real, nor are any of them unreal.
This being the case, I have indeed awakened to all that is true; nevertheless, for the sake of further awakening, let the experience of creation be described.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Whatever is seen here—the entire world, both stationary and moving, rich in all its various forms, and characterized by space, time, action, and so forth—[is all of this].
Upon its destruction—the great destruction known as the Great Dissolution (mahāpralaya)—which brings about the transformation of Brahmā, Upendra, the Maruts, Rudra, and Mahendra.
What remains is something peaceful, utterly pure, unborn, and beginningless; from which words turn back—what else can be understood?
Just as Mount Meru is of an immensely vast form compared to a mustard seed, so too is space gross when compared to that which is the immediate void.
Just as these motes of dust are subtle in comparison to the king of mountains, so too is the gross universe-subtle in comparison to that [which it contains].
When that gentle time, long matured, had become measureless, it subsided into that supreme, primordial space which is of the nature of experience.
Free from conceptual construction, profoundly peaceful, and of immeasurable form throughout space and time, the great inner sky of consciousness perceives, as it were, the state of an atom.
Including that very non-reality within itself by its own nature, like a dream, it then understands the meaning of the word "Brahman" as the pervasive nature of consciousness.

The nature of consciousness experiences within itself its own innate atomicity of consciousness because it is consciousness; then, as if seeing that very [atomicity], it remains thereafter as if a seer.
Just as in a dream one sees a dead person by oneself within oneself, and the seer of death is indeed dead along with that death, so too is the atomic consciousness (cidaṇu) within itself.
Then this state of consciousness, though essentially one within, perceives as if there were duality; it remains in its own true nature, yet appears as if situated as the seer and the seen.
Though entirely devoid of the nature of consciousness and utterly formless, it arises as if seeing a subtle body like an object of sight; and at that time, it becomes, as it were, a dualistic seer.
Perceiving itself as a subtle atom of light through its own experience, it becomes aware of a state of swelling, just as a seed perceives its transformation into a sprout.
Place, time, action, substance, the seer, the act of seeing, and the object seen exist as entities distinct from one another, yet they remain unexpressed by names.
Wherever that atom of consciousness appears, that location has attained the status of space; when it appears, then there is time; and that which is its appearance is known as action.
They know that the perceived is the substance; the state of being a seer is the state of perceiving. Illumination is the act of seeing, and the cause of seeing is the faculty of sight.
Thus, this swelling appears—either limited or infinite, or both successively; though unreal, it is like the sky, having the very form of space, and emerging without exit.
The manifestation of the atom of consciousness appears through its extension within the body; that by which one sees is the eye, and this is the summary of the functions of the senses.
Within the reflection of the atomic consciousness, first there is that which is devoid of name; it consists of the mere sound of these [elements], and its nature is like space.

The very mass of space that is the manifestation of the atomic consciousness exists in a state of density; compelled by its own internal continuity, it perceives the five sense organs which transcend the physical senses.

In this way, the continuous connection of the atoms of consciousness sufficiently nourishes the visible world; that very process is called "knowledge" (jñāna) and is designated as "intellect" (buddhi).
Then the mind, having ascended that [intellect] and reached the state of egoism, accepted limitation by space and time as its own nature.
Wherever there is a fresh perception of this atomic consciousness, it will later assign to that [object] the designation of "prior."
In another location, that [consciousness] will produce the designation "above"; in this way, it will gradually construct the designations of the directions and so forth.
Although he will be as clear as space, he will himself come to know the meanings of words pertaining to place, time, action, and substance.
Thus, by its own experience, this internal body of consciousness, bearing the form of space itself, becomes what is known as the *ātivāhika* (subtle) body.
And for a long time, through that very cultivation there, he grasps a full conviction regarding his own material nature.
The delusion that "this has been fashioned by the pure sky within the sky itself" is like the water of a mirage appearing spread across the real ground, though it is non-existent.
Having the form of space within his own body, he assumes various volitions: in one place taking on the meaning of the word "head," and in another, the meaning of the word "foot."

In some places it consists of the meanings of words such as "chest" and "sides," being pure; in other places it also consists of the meanings of words such as "existence," "non-existence," "grasping," and "relinquishing."
[The mind] has attained a state directed toward objects, characterized by a fixed form, constrained by space, time, and so forth, and pierced by the multitude of the senses.
Then Soṇu perceives his own form, imagined by himself, composed of hands, feet, and other limbs, and endowed with the mental construction of the mind and its faculties.
In this same way Brahmā comes into being, and in that same way Hari comes into being; in this same way Rudra comes into being, and in this same way even a worm comes into being.
Nothing at all has been produced; it remains exactly as it is. It is empty, a play within the empty; cognition is merely unfolding within cognition.
It is the root of bodies, the seed of the creepers of the three worlds, the provider of the bolt for liberation, and the rain-cloud for the deluge of saṃsāra.
He is the cause of all effects, the leader in the performance of actions such as the passing of time; he is the primordial Person, acting according to his own will, who, though unarisen, has arisen.
His body is not composed of the elements; there are no bones in his little frame. No one at all is able to grasp him with a fist.
By him, whose soul was as powerful as the roar of a lion in battle amidst oceanic clouds, surely all remained silent, like a man fast asleep.
Just as the perception of warriors and soldiers seen in a dream while awake exists neither as non-existent nor as existent when it has entered into memory, so does this [world] abide.
Though his vast body measures many hundreds of thousands of yojanas, he shines within the interior of a single atom, with the three worlds contained within the pores of his skin.

Although his nature consists of the multitude of qualities of the principal mountain ranges and he is the very soul of the universe, the Unborn One does not fill even a mere grain’s worth of space within his own abode.
Although it extends over the vast expanse of hundreds of millions of worlds, in reality this [mind] does not occupy even an atom’s worth of space, like a mountain in a dream.
He is declared to be the Self-Existent (Svayambhū), he is called Virāj; his soul is the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa) and his body is the world, yet in reality, he consists of space.
He is called Sanātana and is also designated as Rudra; he possesses bodies such as those of Indra, Upendra, the Maruts, clouds, mountains, and the celestial network.
Having first conceived of a body as a mere atom of light through the act of volition, one gradually becomes established as the Great "I," whose consciousness has expanded.
Through the perception of vibration, that which is experienced as "vibration" is indeed that very thing known as wind, existing in the form of a mass of air.
The vibration of the prāṇa and apāna is experienced through sensation; by that [vibration], this mass of wind which is described as being in space is manifested.

Therefore, these [planets] are imagined from the primordial mind by the ignorant, like malevolent spirits; though they are non-existent, these particles of light have attained the state of being celestial abodes.
The swing of the reversal of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, arising within its belly, bears the name "wind-mass"; that great heart is the world.
He is the primary seed of all those who possess bodies according to their own inclinations, and of all those throughout the world who engage in worldly activities until the end of the eon.
Since bodies have arisen from this [consciousness] as the self of the world through its initial impulse, then, just as they exist externally, so too do they abide internally for those [beings].
Just as the consciousness of that primordial seed was described previously, even now it arises within the living being in exactly that same way, according to its own volition.
His phlegm, bile, and wind are the moon, the sun, and the wind; his planets and constellations are his breaths, his spittle, and his droplets.
We see his bones as mountain ranges, his fat as dense clouds, and his head, feet, skin, and body—we do not see him himself.

Know, O limb of the world, that the body of Virāja is indeed the nature of conceptualization belonging to that which has volition as its form; therefore, everything—including the ether, mountains, earth, and oceans—is the tranquil space of consciousness.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Now hear of that particular arrangement within that kalpa and that mental resolve, which was established as his very form and which captivates through its diverse conduct.
That which is the supreme space of consciousness is the body of the Virāj-Self; devoid of beginning, middle, and end, the world is its subtle body.
Brahmā, free from conceptual construction, beholds his own egg—which is composed of conceptual construction—as nothing but luminous space surrounding his body.
This Brahma, whose nature is the Self, being full and possessing a radiant form, divided his own egg of volition into two parts, like a bird dividing its own body.
He realized that one part of the cosmic egg had reached far into space, while the portion situated below the earth was not distinct from himself.
The upper portion of the cosmic egg is called the head of Virāj; its lower portion is termed the feet, and the middle space is the waist.
The junction of the two distant fragments is seen as a vast, infinite streak of sky—dark, empty, and expansive.
The vast sky is his palate; the drops of blood are the stars; and gods, asuras, humans, and others are the subtle particles of consciousness within his body.
Within his body are worms, as well as bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas; the various worlds are the cavities and hollows within his physical frame.
The fragment of the cosmic egg is spread beneath him as the soles of his feet; the cavities of Pātāla are the openings in the hollows of his knee-joints below.
The earth, with its many hollows and cavities, trembles and quivers in the waters; it is unstable within its inner circle, encircled by oceans and islands.

The rivers, with their flowing waters making a gurgling sound, are like veins; they carry the essence of the streams to Jambūdvīpa, which is like a lotus-heart whose pericarp is the Golden Mountain (Meru).
The hollows are the quarters; the liver, spleen, and so forth are the mountains; the soft, oily, and banner-like structures are the clouds; and the dense networks are the fat.
The sun and moon are his two eyes; the world of Brahmā is said to be his mouth; his splendor is declared to be the moon, and the snowy mountain is his phlegm.
The world of fire is his aurva-fire, whose bile is exceedingly difficult to endure; the great winds of the wind-element are his prāṇa and apāna breaths situated in the heart.
In some places there were forests of wish-fulfilling trees and swarms of serpents; there were infinite forests and groves consisting of networks of hair.

Above, the entire fragment of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) serves as its vast head; from it, a blazing crest of light has arisen, its radiance filling the hollow space within the limits of the cosmic egg.

Since this very mind is itself [the agent], his mind is not required; it is said that the self alone attains the state of being the enjoyer—so for whom, how, and from where could there be [an object of enjoyment]?
He himself has established the existence of these sense faculties elsewhere, since it is said that the entire collection of sense faculties is merely a mental construction.

Just as there is no difference whatsoever between a part and its whole, so too there is not even the slightest distinction between the sense faculty and the mind; they possess oneness, being two aspects of a single body.
Whatever activities there may be for the worlds, they are his very volitions; appearing as if endowed with duality, they move by means of the functions of a person.
When that [Self] is known, its birth and death are not perceived as anything other than it; this world is that very Self, consisting of our own volition, and nothing else.

The existence of the world is due to the existence of that [Brahman], and by its death alone the world dies; just as the existence of motion and the wind is one and the same, such is the existence of those two.
The existence of the universe and Virāṭ is one, like that of the wind and its movement; that which is the universe is indeed Virāṭ, and that which is Virāṭ is known as the universe.
The words "jagat" (the world), "brahmā," and "virāṭ" are synonymous; these are merely conceptual constructs, whose true nature is the pure space of consciousness.
Śrī Rāma said: Since that Virāṭ himself, through mere volition, has assumed a form like the sky, how can it be that he remains as Brahman alone within his own body?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as you remain within your body through meditation, so too does the Grandfather (Brahmā), whose nature is volition, abide within his own body.
Likewise, for men and for those who are foremost, the individual soul (jīva) exists within the interior of the city of Brahman; it is the body born of its own origination, resembling a reflection.
If even you, who are limited by a body, are fully capable of acting within it, why then will the all-pervading Brahmā, whose very nature is volition, not act there?
For the immobile resides within the seed, and the mobile resides within that object; why then should that which consists of the imagination of one's own consciousness not reside within the body?

May it be with form, having the nature of space, or indeed formless like a dream; may it abide both outside and inside, and within the distinction between the external and internal, yet remain external.
Delighting in the Self, observing the silence of wood, he is not dull-witted yet is as inert as a stone; though composed of "I," "you," and so forth, he abides within the Virāj-Self.

Like a man who has discarded a vine, grass, or wood after wrapping himself in it, or like the sound of a rushing torrent, he whose limbs are cast off remains with a mind as tranquil as the interior of a stone, even while engaged in various kinds of worldly activities.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, while Brahmā was absorbed in meditation, I, with my eyes fixed upon him who stood before me, slowly beheld that world of Brahmā situated ahead.
At midday, a second sun clearly rose in the west, like a conflagration at the edge of the horizon or a forest fire upon a mountain.
Then, like the world of Agni in the sky or the submarine fire in the ocean, I beheld the blazing sun in the direction of the southwest.
The sun is in the southern quarter; the sun is at the mouth of the south-eastern quarter; the sun is in the eastern quarter; the sun is at the mouth of the north-eastern direction.
I saw the sun in the direction of Kubera, the sun at the edge of the northwest quarter, and the sun in the region of the western direction; because of that, I was filled with wonder.
While I was quickly considering the chaotic failure of the ritual, the sun rose from the earth like the submarine fire from the ocean.
In the eleventh [chapter], there arose within the sky of the quarters, amidst the three suns, something like a reflection of all the suns.
For that was a fierce form, and in its center were three eyes; it was a blazing mass of twelve suns in size.
It blazed intensely in every direction like fire in a dry forest; then there arose a summer day that withered the world into fragments.
O lotus-eyed one, that fireless conflagration, in which the clusters of firebrands were suddenly invisible, was a burning by means of a fire that was no fire at all.
My limbs became as if scorched by a forest fire and exhausted; then, leaving that region, I ascended far away.
Standing in the sky, I beheld the sun of fierce radiance rising in the heavens like a ball struck by a firm blow of the palm.
The twelve-fold host of Ādityas blazes in all ten directions, like the moving circle of stars with its great constellations appearing as if ablaze.
There was a great, tumultuous roar like the crashing of the seven oceans in boil, as the spaces between the worlds and the interiors of the cities were packed thick with flaming firebrands.
The mountain was turned vermilion by the swelling mass of dense flames, and its peaks were like banners of lightning, steady within the blazing great caverns.
It caused the circles of cities to crackle with the swelling clatter of snapping bracelets, while dense masses of stone raised columns of smoke from the surface of the earth.

The pavilion that is the abode of the world was filled with thousands of pillars of glass, and it resounded with a deep gurgling from the cries of the stars—the great elements of living beings—boiling within it.
The earth, cities, and worlds were violently shattered with a loud *caṭa-caṭa* sound, while the surface of the ground was scraped by the falling stars and the scattering of gems.

In every place, the multitudes of people were moving and being consumed by fire; the quarters of the horizon were filled with the foul stench of hosts of spirits who were wailing until their cries were exhausted and then boiling away.

The great ocean, its aquatic creatures distressed by the waters of the scorching clouds; the interiors of the cities, their cries of lamentation exhausted by the conflagrations of fire from every direction.
The earth was propped up by the tusks of elephants of the quarters that had been split and scorched, while the mountain caves were encircled by wreaths of smoke.
The circle of cities was crushed and scorched by falling mountains, while the great elephants and mountain lions let out cries of "pacat-paca-paca."
The oceans and mountains were feverish with creatures rising up, tormented by the heat; the women of the Vidyādharas fell down, their hearts bursting and their vital strength exhausted.
The heavens were emptied as heads grew weary from the sound of wailing and weeping; the surface of the earth was scorched by the blazing flames of the world of the nagas in the underworld.
In that dried-up ocean, where the fierce aquatic creatures were constantly being cooked and tossed about, the submarine fire Aurva—as if unable to find fuel—seemed to fly up in a thousand directions.
Then, having risen and danced as he went, seizing the expanse of the sky, there appeared one adorned with garments of blazing flames like *kiṃśuka* flowers.
Like the fire of the world’s end for a *tāṇḍava* dance, bearing a garland of flickering torches, it was loud with the crackling of its expansion, like a fierce warrior shouting.
With arms of flames and hair of smoke, the actor who plays the decrepit hut of the world caused the forest thickets, cities, and towns to blaze.
Mandalas, islands, fortresses, jungles, and dry lands; all cavities, the great expanse of space, the ten directions, and the summit of heaven.
With its chasms, water-wheels, towers, cities, and vast horizons, its peaks, throngs of perfected beings, mountains, and oceans;
Lakes, ponds, rivers, gods, asuras, humans, and serpents, along with the quarters of space, were filled with the sounds of "śa-na-śa-na" and with men worshipping Śiva’s flames.

There were Rākṣasas with gaping mouths emitting shrieks, their upward-pointing banners blazing with masses of flames, terrifying with the whirling sounds of "bhaṃ-bhaṃ" and "bhāṃ," and covered in abundant ashes.
Flames issued forth from the caves of the chasms, mountains, and the earth; all classes of living beings, dwelling within the bellies of those flames, turned crimson.
The inauspicious [omens] assumed the beauty of lotuses on dry land, appearing like clouds of vermilion, beautiful with the luster of blood suddenly flowing forth.
With masses of flames reaching out into the world, singing "dhagaddhag" as it were, the sky became strewn with red garments like the clouds of twilight.

The region was covered by forests of blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees that seemed as if they were taking flight, and it was filled with flowering *aśoka* groves that appeared as if they were enveloped by the submarine fire (*aurva*).
Like lakes encircled by land-lotuses, or like oceans filled with the setting sun, it possessed an arrangement of smoke and blazing flames of various colors.
Like the fire of youth in the forest, he was like the serpent Ananta, having arranged himself as a support for the painted mansion-creeper, as if to sustain the fire that had taken root there.
Due to the rising and setting [of the sun] and other such phenomena, the Vindhya mountain fell into a state of distress, as if its branches were like glowing coals leaping through a forest of flames.
Slowly, as if slightly agitated, the bearable became unbearable; it was garlanded by swarms of wandering smoke whose blackness shone intensely in their midst.
The sky was seen like a lake, its waters soiled by the flames of the forest fire; upon the mountain peaks in the atmosphere, the tips of the flames stood like crowns.
The celestial nymphs, whose hair was like banners and who bore the flames of fire upon their palms, danced upon the upper surface of the vault of the universe.

With floods of spirits leaping up as she brandished her hand, with the earth-shaking foundations shattered, with rows of tinkling bells, and with earth, water, and fire, she was of many colors and had a face flushed with red.
Then, in the heart and forearm of the Fortune of the World, [the weapon] became as if made of gold; meanwhile, the mountains [shattered] with crackling bursts and the trees with creaking sounds.
The lands were utterly shattered by tumultuous outcries; the oceans took on the appearance of boiling water, thick with the swelling of foam.
In mouth after mouth, they struck the face of the sun with waves as light as the palm of a hand, while the mountains took on the appearance of the earth’s surface with its surging, tossing billows.
With waves upon their bodies, they were as if inert yet enraged; for those who feed on the ether of hope, there arose the deep, cavernous roars from the hollows of their caves.
A fire-born sound, arising from the crackling of flames, resounded; the walls of the mountains became like glowing embers as the cities of the world-protectors fell into ruin.
All ten directions fell into a state of helplessness, behaving like those driven mad; even the great mountains, trees, houses, and caves were drenched with molten gold.
Slowly, Meru, with its beautiful form, became like snow in the heat; in an instant, it was melted by that fire like butter.
Completely cool within and pure, like a virtuous man among the wicked, the Malaya mountain retains its stainless fragrance even in that state.
The noble-souled one does not abandon his supreme quality even at the point of destruction; even while perishing, the Great One bestows joy and not sorrow.
Even when burned, sandalwood serves only for the delight of those who live; a superior thing never becomes a non-thing.
Even when consumed by the fire of cosmic dissolution, gold does not perish; likewise, both gold and the sky do not perish within that fire of dissolution.

The bodies of those two alone are praiseworthy, for they are indestructible even when everything else is destroyed; the sky is indestructible due to its pervasiveness, and gold is imperishable due to its extraction from ore.
I consider goodness alone to be happiness, neither passion nor darkness; for they are like high, trembling forests showering down scattered embers.
The fire-cloud became a great mass of smoke and flame like a scorched mountain for those empty beings with vast bodies who were afflicted by the loss of their vital essence.
Of the withered leaves of the trees of the sky, which had become like vessels for the clouds, now burnt by the flames of the dissolution;
O dear one, just as no ash of faults is ever seen in a wise man, so too the blazing fire does not leap over Mount Kailāsa.
Then Rudra, enraged for that long, burned him with the fire from his eye; there arose the crackling sounds of trees bursting from the heat and of massive rocks splitting apart.
The mountains, their edges trembling with the prideful display of dense masses of flames as their ornaments, seemed to fight with floods of clubs, stones, and clods of earth.
They became like forests of thick lotuses blooming in the sky; the thought that "creation existed only at some time" passed into the realm of the unrememberable.

Recalling the end of the eon, the fires—intent on supreme torment and devoted to the destruction of others—rendered fools incapable of remembering even that which was once profound; they brought about the disappearance of the worlds, just as the wicked conceal their own faults.

Their limbs tormented by the falling of thunderbolts, appearing like circles of shrubs with flickering firebrands amidst their disheveled hair, the hosts of gods fled like the winds at the time of universal dissolution, licking up everything as they reached the end of the fire at the time of destruction.

The winds blew with such speed that they resembled a mass of fire without remainder; their flames were white with glowing embers carried by the strikes of wandering meteors like clouds, made so by the heat of the ashes rising from the forest of *dānala* trees violently shaken and bursting; and they were darkened by the rows of flames flickering amidst the falling mountain peaks.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Now, while the wind at the end of the aeon blew, shaking the mountains, and by its force the ocean waves created whirlpools in the sky;

In oceans that have lost their seals and are thick with the transgression of boundaries; among the wealthy who are not truly rich, fleeing from the affliction of poverty like clouds driven by a storm.
When the surface of the earth was stripped of even a portion of its sovereigns and scorched by fire, and even the netherworld had, in the course of time, sunk further into the depths;
Whether in heaven, or when the multitude of created beings has perished, in a world where the light of the sky has vanished, amidst the quarters of the horizon that have become abodes of sorrow;
From some part of the hollow of the sky, like hosts of arrogant demons, the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds let out a deep "gulugulu" roar.

It was formidable with the bursting of the walls of the cosmic egg shattered by Brahmā, and it was agitated by the roar of the great ocean as it surged and leaped while the waters lashed against one another.
This [sound] is intense with a thick clamor vomited forth from the city of the ocean of the world, and it resounds with a fierce, gurgling roar fixed upon the ridges of the boundary mountains.
Slow with the swirling currents that fill the interior of the cosmic egg like a conch shell, it was densely thickened from the heights of heaven and the earth down to the depths of the netherworld.
It was capable of effortlessly crushing the walls of all distant directions, and it possessed a thirst for drinking the wine of the great dissolution that had arrived.
It was amplified by the trumpeting of Indra’s elephant Airāvata during the onset of the dissolution, and it gathered a roar like that of the ocean of clouds agitated at the end of an aeon.
In this formidable water-wheel of the cosmic egg, it resounded like the roar of the ocean of milk being churned during the great dissolution.
Then, wondering how this cloud could remain while this fire of the kalpa was present, I cast my gaze in all nine directions in amazement.
Until I see anywhere here, in any direction at all, nothing but showers of firebrands like thunderbolts crossing through with flickering flashes.
By that blazing heat, objects within many millions of yojanas are reduced to ashes, even in the ten directions far away.
Immediately thereafter, in an instant, I experienced from afar in the sky a cool wind above and a heat like fire below.
At such a distance along this path through the sky, the clouds of the kalpa remain; they are not even within the range of the heat of those fires, nor are they comparable to it.
Then, from the quarter of Varuṇa, there came a wind like that at the end of an aeon, by which the Vindhya, Meru, and Himālaya mountains were carried away like blades of grass.

Because of that, they fled swiftly toward the direction of fire—a realm where mountains were tongues of flame, where cinders flew like birds from the edges, and where forests were overrun by flickering torches.
Clouds of glowing coals rose with forms resembling twilight clouds; masses of ash-like clouds wandered through the sky, consisting of the dust of purified charcoal.
Moving with a wind shimmering with flames, that wicked one, appearing like fire itself, proceeded as if toward an army of winged golden mountains melting away.

When the entire expanse of the earth and its mountain ranges had become a mass of glowing coals with gentle limbs, and a multitude of garlands of flames arose, shining with the brilliance of the suns;
In oceans that were masses of fire, with waters boiling and surging; in forests where the leaves were no longer remembered, bearing trees ablaze with fire.
When the lords residing in the Brahma-world and the cities of the Brahma-world—along with their women, children, and the elderly—were consumed by fire and fell into the sky.
In the Brahma-foremost lotus pond of the fire at the end of the eon, she remains with her seeds intact, adorned with sprouts of flame and accompanied by blazing torches.
When the roots, the nāgas, and the mountains—whose very essence was wind—had sunk down as far as the netherworld into the great mire of glowing coals;
Perceiving the sky to be near, like a caravan of camels in motion, a mass of clouds at the end of an aeon, dark as collyrium, approached with a rumbling sound.
A mountain composed of lightning equal to the flames of the fire at the end of an eon, bearing the weight of the waters of the seven oceans resting within a single corner.
The horizons were blocked by the weight of mists radiant against the walls [of the sky], while he was skilled at shattering the dense circle of the shell of the cosmic egg.
Like the ocean agitated at the end of an aeon, possessing the motion of circular whirlpools, with lightning for its aquatic creatures and a deep roar, it seemed as if the sky itself had descended.
The moon, though dead and burnt, became twice as cool; having assumed another form, it was as if it had come from the other world.
In the form of its mass of gold, it bore the entire Himālaya as it were, with all its waters frozen by cold and its cardinal directions rendered motionless like mountains of wood.
Then there fell a rain that was as hard as the bursting of the cosmic egg, filling the sky, while the quarters of the horizon were first drenched by a fierce torrent of frost.
Terrifying with the blazing of fires, the roar of the wind, lightning, and flashes of light; with the crackling, popping, and bursting sounds that shatter the entire circle of the universe.
It resounded with the inexhaustible roar of hundreds of rising hisses and shrieks, while its sky was formed by walls of cold spray and mist.
With showers of rain that were radiant with a multitude of vaidūrya pillars from the pavilions of the clouds, she shone like the earth adorned by the Śātaka mountain, the bearer of the world.

The city of burning coals was shattered by the crackling explosions of the earth, while the world was thrown into turmoil by the falling of beings as they were violently hurled from one realm to another by his roars.
Then she became the mistress of the house of the world, which was filled with embers; she was met by the earth, whose splendor of tears blazed forth.

The sky, with its display of leaping fragments of flame, appeared as if it were entirely covered by a mass of petals from the land-lotuses borne there; and the flickering clusters of cool spray-mist there resembled rows of bees wandering amidst the flames.

The terrifying collision of the clouds, filling the quarters with rising, great *caṭa-caṭa* sounds as they discharged water, became like a fierce battle between the forces of the great, where the weapons are sharp-edged missiles and the enemies are as formidable as the irresistible god of death.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, at the end of the eon, when a supreme upheaval had arisen among the earth, water, fire, and wind, these three worlds came to be as follows.
Resplendent with ash-clouds resembling birds soaring from a *tāpiccha* forest, it moved like the great whirlpools of the vast ocean, a swirling mass of smoke.
The playful, flickering blue flames roar with a soft, humming sound, filling the spaces between the worlds with a mass of ash-clouds.
With rising, long-drawn-out shouts of "chama-chama," accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments and the spreading proclamation of victory from the ascending rain-showers.
It was like a mass of fierce clouds of spray, bewildered by the confusion of vaporous clouds, resembling the agitation of great kalpa-clouds, and grey with the whirling smoke of clouds of ash.

By the spreading gusts of wind, terrifying with their thunderous roar against the walls of the cosmic egg, the masses of the cities of Indra and the other gods were blown into the sky and consumed by fire.
The eyes and ears were rendered deaf by the clanging sounds produced by the violent impact of millions of stones bursting forth due to the surging of water, fire, and wind.
With incessant downpours like pillars of water supporting the sky, and with the dragging of the fires of the kalpa, there was a deep, resonant *chamacchama* sound.
The entire ocean was being filled by hosts of rivers possessing waves like the Gaṅgā, resembling clouds terrifying the sky.
The circle of clouds, licked by the scorching suns, appeared like a sacrificial altar strewn with clusters of blossoms resting upon a mass of *tāpiccha* leaves.
It contained mountain ranges, rivers, peaks, islands, and cities; it witnessed the crushing of mountains caused by the violent agitation of the winds at the end of an eon.
With fierce hosts of planets and stars, agitated and difficult to grasp due to their conflict, they fell like doubled whirling firebrands, descending in spirals.
It was struck by the impact and bursting of the masses of great mountains brought forth by the waters, and it resembled the rocky floor of the mountain ranges overturned during the great dissolution.
It was dense and sluggish with darkness that obscured the rays of the sun’s multitude, by means of clouds of thickened tears as massive as the clouds at the end of an aeon.
The ocean was congested with fragments of the shattered surface of the earth, with crumbling slopes falling away, and with mountains being carried along as they tumbled down.
The horizons were shattered by the roar of the ocean, deep as a thunderclap, with gales of passion that tore through dense clouds like rising stones upon the waves.

With harsh clanging sounds from the hammers upon the surface of the wall of the cosmic egg, and with the crashing of the branches of the clouds at the end of the aeon, the roar of the single ocean was struck.
The sky was filled with fragments of heaven, the netherworld, and the earthly realm, intermingled and remaining according to their own nature, along with the mountains and the base of the earth.
With gods and dānavas whose limbs were dead, half-dead, burnt, or half-burnt, their weapons whirled about as they were tossed by the wind from seeing one another.
With the ashes raised up by those winds called the Arjuna-winds, which had begun to scatter the withered straws of other worlds tossed about by the gales at the end of an eon;
Its banks were being overturned by the impact of masses of rocks being swept away; as worlds fell, there arose the harsh, loud crashing of a vast and terrible calamity.
It resounded with the echoing roars from the caves of the mountain ranges shaken by the wind, while the cities of the world-protectors were filled with swirling eddies created by falling [debris].
It was surrounded by forest groves being swept along by winds that produced harsh, grating sounds like those of asuras, with their windows pierced through the dense thickets.
In the sky, it bore a multitude of cities, mandalas, daityas, fires, gods, nāgas, and suns, like a swarm of gnats.

With the masses of the best of mountains perishing and the abodes of the gods shattered into fragments, the water roared with the gurgling sounds of whirlpools, while fire blazed both above and below.
It was crushing the cities of the world-protectors with its friction against water and mountains, and it was toppling the cities of the lords of gods, demons, siddhas, and gandharvas as they fell.
The winds reduce mountains and other objects, which have become like extinguished embers, to a state of worthlessness, like dust particles.
It shatters the ancient walls of the gods and demons as they crumble, while their jewels produce a clinking sound like the waters of the oceans.
The sky was filled with the falling temples of the seven worlds, which, in their whirling forms, resembled the oceans of the gods as they revolved in a circular motion.
It was surrounded by objects, half-burnt and half-unburnt, tossed about by shifting winds as they flew up and down in the sky like heaps of withered leaves.
The sky was filled with palaces made of gold, crystal, lapis lazuli, and excellent gems, falling from heaven with rising *jhaṇajhaṇa* sounds.
Clouds of smoke and ashes surged upward, while floods of water fell upon the cities; masses of waves rose up, and the mountains of the earth sank down.
Roaring with the gurgling sound of whirlpools and striving to crush one another, the massive mountains rolled about like leaves scattered upon the ocean.
The world became difficult to behold, with the hosts of gods crying out, the living beings trembling, and hundreds of portents such as wandering comets appearing.
The sky became densely filled with a continuous succession of beings—half-dead and half-alive, tossed by the wind, and the color of withered leaves.
The world became filled with the thick, falling torrents from the mountain peaks, while hundreds of rivers, swollen by the winds from the city of mountains, flowed on and on.
The fire, with its hundreds of branches of the sounds "śāmyat," "śama," and "śamā," was extinguished; the mountain slopes, swaying from the surging and tossing of the restless ocean, became still.
It is as fierce as a heap of grass mixed with a river, with continents and oceans; it is a forest that can endure the momentary flames of the consciousness-space situated at an extreme distance.
The gods fell [in reverence] at the fragrance of the ashes arising from the fire quenched by the rain; they forgot the creation of the world that had previously existed.

It possesses a roar that surges without obstruction, the process of the cessation of creation, the remainder that shines forth upon the cessation of creation, and is entirely devoid of the cessation of creation.
It was brought to rest by winds that incessantly produce reversals [of perception], yet it was being filled again and again, like a heap of seeds.
The hollow of the sky was revealed as a golden pavement by the scattered dust born from the gold produced by the fire of the mutual friction of the firebrands.

The surface of the earth was filled with vast fragments of the terrestrial sphere fallen along with their continents and oceans, while the circles of the netherworlds rolled about, filling the entirety of the seventh Pātāla.
From the seventh layer of hell up to the surface of the earth and its mountains, reaching all the way to the sky, everything becomes a single ocean, filled with the winds of universal dissolution.
Then the single ocean gradually and swiftly swelled with hundreds of rivers and waves of water throughout the world, just as anger increases within the mind of a fool.
First with a stream like a pestle, then with limbs resembling pillars, and then with a flow having the form of a palmyra tree, she rained down a torrential downpour.
Then, by means of that [power] which fells all with its fierce torrent of river-like waterfalls, and which is like a dense cloud over the entire surface of the earth with its seven continents;

Just as fire, which causes burning when seen, is thus brought to extinction by the study of the scriptures and the company of the virtuous, so too does one who has deeply entered the state of calamity find peace.

The hollow of the cosmic egg became desolate, its mass of objects situated above and below overturned, and the marrow of its mountains reduced to a rattling *khaṇakhaṇa* sound by internal sparks; it was as pure as a *bilva* fruit tossed about in the play of a young child.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the surface of the earth was shattered by the falling of winds, rains, and snows, the force of the inert matter increased like a king in the Kali age.
It was augmented by the falling torrents fallen from the current of the Gaṅgā, and suddenly by thousands of rivers as radiant as Meru and Mandara.
With its caves reaching up to the path of the sun, sluggish and inert, the lordly ocean swelled into a single expanse like a fool.
By the turning of its vast whirlpools, it has swallowed the withered grass of the mountains; with the tips of its shimmering, lofty waves, it has swallowed the orb of the sun.
He is the aquatic creature dwelling within Mount Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Vindhya, and Sahya; he is the lotus-stalk within which the serpents lie hidden amidst the dissolved mud of the earth.
With its dense groves of trees half-burnt, it was choked with moss; mingled with the ashes of the three worlds, it became a loathsome mire.

The sky was a vast lotus-pool with the great pillars of clouds as its stalks and the brilliant sun as its flower; the great ocean was a mass of falling rain, in which the petals of the lotuses had dissolved away.
With intoxicated clouds roaring from the edges of mountains of foam, it filled the cities and towns of Indra, Vāyu, Arka, and Indu as they wandered about.
The fierce multitude of gods and asuras was being swept away like logs; gradually swelling in its progression, it licked the orb of the sun.
The great mountains were being swept away, obscured by bubbles produced from showers of thundering, crashing sounds.
Seeing the clouds at the end of the eon wandering as restless bubbles that have come to rest, he beheld another cloud, towering and without support.
The sky resounded with the gurgling roar of the torrential flood of its great current, while the mountain ranges of the world-system were swept away as a single unified stream.
With mountain-like masses of unprecedented water-torrents driven by fierce winds, it possessed a great, violent, and gurgling speed accompanied by a deep, thundering roar.
Rising up through the collisions and revolutions of the fragments of the cosmic egg, it spread out and rose to heights of hundreds of thousands of yojanas.
The mountains, by their swaying like waves upon blades of grass, caused the orb of the sun to be shattered by the impact of their rocks.
In this nest of the thunderbolt-like waters of the voided universe, the dark, immovable crows are being driven away by the nets of spray from the swans.
[He saw] those agitated by the sinking and emerging of great beings, both dead and alive, as if they were possessed of reflections of waves, sea-monsters, and whirlpools.
He bore the surviving gods, fallen from their cities and exhausted by the force of the waters, upon the edges of the mountain ridges of foam like so many gnats.
Like Indra beholding his own eyes, he perceived the vast water-bubbles, as numerous as the stars, which were as expansive as the space of the present day.

With his eyes fixed upon the clouds, which resembled the autumn sky and were moving along with the currents of the rivers, he seemed as if he were gazing at the clouds themselves as they became filled with copper-colored waters.
With many circles of waves from the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds, which rose up like winged mountains, he seemed to be performing embraces.
Satiated by devouring the three worlds, he seemed to sing with his gurgling roars, and to dance of his own accord upon the fierce mountain ridges and the trees that were the waves of his arms.

It is surrounded above by mountain-like clouds bearing streams of rivers, in the middle by mountains that have been consumed by fire, below by mountains and serpents, and at the very bottom by those dwelling in the mud.
With the incessant downpour of torrents from the overflowing triple-pathed river, the mountain peaks were submerged and emerged like masses of foam and bubbles.
The sky-dwellers cried out as fragments of heaven were being carried away and shattered; meanwhile, the interior of the lotus-like faces of the Vidyadhara women was swept along by the current.
When the great waters were being swept away during the destruction of the fragments of the three worlds, with the speed of a gurgling roar amidst the floods of the single ocean;
There was no protector whatsoever, and he was even slain by the power of the Avīci hell; for who is able to protect one who has been swallowed up by Time?

There was no sky, nor were there the quarters of space; there was nothing below, nor was there anything above. There was no being, nor was there any creation; there existed only the supreme, absolute water.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In the meantime, standing in the sky, I then cast my gaze upon the great world of Brahmā, like the radiance of the sun at dawn.
There I beheld the Supreme Lord, established in meditative absorption, appearing as if carved out of rock, accompanied by his principal retinue.
And there was an assembly of gods and sages of purified souls, including Śukra, Bṛhaspati, Śakra, Vaiśravaṇa, and Yama.
Then Soma, Varuṇa, and Agni, as well as other celestial sages, the leaders of the gods, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Sādhyas;
With forms fixed as if by the hand of a painter, all were intent on meditation; seated there in the lotus posture, they remained as if devoid of life.
Then those twelve Ādityas arrived at that very spot and stood there quickly, just as they had been, with their lotus postures firmly bound.
Then, in just a moment, I saw the Lotus-born [Brahmā] before me, having become wide awake, appearing as if he had been seen previously in a dream.
I did not see any of the inhabitants of the Brahma-world, as if they were merely the latent impressions of great beings, like one awakening from a dream-city while standing at its forefront.
At that time, the contemplation of Brahman was as empty as a forest, like a city on earth utterly destroyed by a sudden calamity.
At that time, none of them—the sages, the ascetics, the gods, the Vedas, the Vidyādharas, and so forth—were anywhere like him.
Then, while remaining in the sky, I perceived with focused attention that they had all attained nirvāṇa, just like Brahmā.
When their latent impressions have dissolved, they have come to non-appearance; like worlds seen in a dream, they have returned to their own true nature for those who are awakened.

This body, though its very nature is space, appears clearly through latent impressions; yet in the absence of those impressions, it does not appear, just as a dream does not appear to one who has awakened.
Just as a body situated in the intermediate space is perceived in a dream, nothing at all is observed upon awakening when those latent impressions have been stilled.
Likewise, even while awake, when latent impressions (vāsanā) have been completely exhausted, neither the subtle body (ativāhika) nor the physical body (ādhibhautika) is perceived here.
This experience of a dream is indicated here as an illustration; it is well-established among children, being experienced, heard, and remembered.
And even that rogue who denies his own experience must be abandoned; for who indeed would wake one who is asleep by means of falsehood?
If it is argued that a dream is caused by the body and thus not seen in the absence of a body, then for those who are bodiless, the next world would likewise not exist.
If this [creation] were to cease upon the dissolution of that body, then this creation would not exist; yet that [body] indeed exists at all times.
Since destruction—which consists of the division of parts—is inevitable, the claim that this world has never at any time been otherwise than it is now is also untenable.
Consequently, the Purāṇas, the Itihāsas, the Smṛtis and other texts which teach the total destruction [of all things], as well as the Vedas, would all become purposeless.
Because these [scriptures] are not authoritative regarding this matter, O Mahāmati, how could other things—such as barren women and the like—possess the status of being authoritative?
And this is not accepted in the world because it would cause the destruction of the universe; but let that be aside for now, my dear friend, listen to this other point of mine.

The state of possessing bodies such as those of piśācas, which is observed in other regions among those who have spread abroad due to the power of intoxication within their own consciousness, is not established [as real].
If it is argued that even this delusion is seen as long as the body exists, then that which is called "delusion" would simply be the truth for you.
If this were so, would not even this cognition—that there is another world consisting of heaven, hell, and so forth—attain the status of truth?
For even the perception of a piśāca is not real for one who possesses the power of intoxication; how then could the appearance consisting of the next world not be unreal?
If the cognition that "a piśāca exists" is a cognition of a real object, then why is there not the same reality in the cognition that "there is a world beyond for the deceased"?
If a ghostly cognition exists within the body by mere chance, like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, why should there not be a causal awareness of the objects of the next world?
In whatever manner consciousness internally knows, it experiences that very thing accordingly; whether it be true or false, it is established as such by virtue of experience.

Knowing that "there is another world for the deceased," one should become composed of such [knowledge]; whether this body exists or does not exist, what is the use of that which is both existent and non-existent?
Therefore, one's own nature first flashes forth as pure consciousness; subsequently, having understood the cause to be latent impressions (*vāsanā*), one perceives the delusion.
Upon the destruction of that [ignorance], the disease consisting of the seer, the seen, and the seeing comes to rest; yet when it exists, this demoness called "saṃsāra" arises.

At first, perception arises, and from that comes the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of Brahman; know that the cessation of that [perception] is *nirvāṇa*, while its existence is the delusion of *saṃsṛti*.

And since it is impossible for that [consciousness] to exist as anything other than the Supreme Brahman, it arises as such; thus, this consciousness arising from the ritual commitment (*samaya*) and so forth is indeed the Supreme Brahman itself, which is real.
The wise know that complete understanding of this much is nirvana; O Raghava, know that lack of understanding regarding this very thing is bondage.
This is indeed a mass of consciousness, whose nature consists of both manifesting and non-manifesting; it manifests by itself within, or else it does not manifest at all by itself.

Since it consists merely of the transformation of a portion of consciousness and is of an exceedingly subtle nature, what room is there for the views of bondage and liberation, or for the effort required to achieve them?

Bondage lies in the awakening of consciousness; when that [consciousness] is not awakened, there is auspiciousness (śiva). The world, though unreal, appears as if real within the womb of the awakening of consciousness.
Non-inert awareness that is dormant is called liberation; when awakened, they call it bondage. Whatever you desire, take that.

Abide in that which is the latent impression of Nirvana—endless, beginningless, a continuous flow of pure awakening, free from constraint, and beyond all doubt; non-dual yet devoid of oneness, with emptiness cast aside, and peaceful with a mind as clear as the expanse of space.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, all those inhabitants of the world of Brahmā who had arrived vanished from sight, like lamps whose wicks are spent.
Then, when Brahmā had attained the state of Brahman, those twelve Ādityas, with their radiant rays, consumed that world of Brahmā just as they consume the world.
Having burned down the city of Virañca and having practiced meditation like Virañca himself, they too attained nirvāṇa, like ten oil-less lamps.
Then the flood of the single ocean, possessing a hollow form, filled the interior of Viriñca’s city at night, just as darkness fills the earth.
The world, up to the realm of Brahmā, became filled with that water, like a ripe grape fruit filled entirely with its uniform juice.
Enveloped by birds that were masses of mountains amidst those various waves, the scattered clouds of the kalpa dissolved entirely back into the water.
In the meantime, I saw from the sky something terrifying rising up; terrified, I looked further into the midst of the heavens.
Kṛṣṇa, whose form was like the world at the end of an aeon and who filled the sky, appeared like the nocturnal darkness accumulated over an entire aeon suddenly risen in bodily form.
It bore a radiant splendor like that of a million rising suns, resembling three suns and intensified by a steady mass of lightning.
With eyes [beholding] the face of Ābhāsvara, emitting a mass of flames, he has five faces, ten arms, three eyes, and holds a trident in his hand.

Though you have reached the end of coming and going, you remain having assumed a body as dark as a cloud, like the sky itself which, though vast in form, persists even within the space that is free from limits.

It remained in the sky outside the cosmic egg, which was filled with the waters of the single universal ocean, appearing like the void itself as characterized by the arrangement of hands, feet, and other limbs.
He was like Govinda, who agitated the Ocean of Milk with his staff-like arms, or like one who has tossed a single great ocean with the reversal of the wind from his nostrils.
The flood of waters of the ocean of the aeon has arisen as if in the form of a male; it is the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra) endowed with a physical form, arrived as the primordial cause.
Like a vast multitude of great mountain ranges rising up with the grandeur of flight, it ascended, filling the entire sky with its mass of wings.
Then, having recognized from afar that "this is Rudra" by means of my trident and eye, I paid homage to the Supreme Lord.
Śrī Rāma said: Is that Rudra of such a kind? Is he Kṛṣṇa? What is his great form? Why does he stand there with five faces and ten arms?
Was he three-eyed? Was he fierce in nature? Was he alone? What was his purpose? By whom was he impelled? What did he do? And tell me, O Sage, what was his shadow?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Kākutstha, this one named Rudra arose as the ego; his nature consists of a singular and uneven conceit, and his form is the pure sky.
That Blessed One has the form of space, the color of space, and great splendor; because his essence consists solely of the space of consciousness, he is called the self of space.
Because he has become the self of all beings and because he is omnipresent, his form is great; the five cavities that are attached to him are the sense organs.
They say those various forms on all sides are his mouths; for the organs of action and their objects are his ten arms.
When he was completely abandoned by all beings and men, together with Brahmā who had ascended to the highest realm, he then returned to his own form.
