And that [self], being of a single part and a single nature, does not exist, for it has no form; nevertheless, it appears as if possessed of a body through mere delusion.
He dwells in the vast elemental ether that has become one with the space of consciousness, and within the bodies of all beings, he eternally abides like the vital air, the Lord.
At that time, abandoned by all beings, he will become ethereal in form; agitating for a moment, he will then be exhausted and attain supreme peace.
Those which are the qualities, forms, times, mind, ego, and intellect; those which are the phonemes of the *praṇava*, as well as the three Vedas.
By the arrangement of that Rudra’s eyes, he stands established; by him, the triple world has been grasped within the hollow of his hand as a trident.
Since nothing else exists apart from that [Self] even among the multitudes of all living beings, therefore the Self alone remains as the body.
Its purpose is a nature characterized by the perception of all sentient beings; this has been proclaimed by Śiva, who is of the nature of the space of pure consciousness.
And having been swallowed by that very [light], he attains supreme peace; this Lord, whose nature is like the stainless sky, is Kṛṣṇa.
Having brought about the dissolution of the entire world and then drunk up that single ocean, he attains supreme peace so as not to return again.
Immediately thereafter, I saw him there, and with all my effort, I began to drag him toward the great ocean with the force of my life-breath.
Then his wide-open mouth, its interior filled with garlands of flames, swallowed him like the great ocean, drawn by its vital breath, swallows the submarine fire.
Having become that very Vāḍava fire in the ocean until the end of the kalpa, Rudra, as the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), then drinks up all those waters.
Like water entering the netherworld, like a serpent its hole, or like the five winds entering space, he entered that mouth with speed in an instant.
Approaching it, Rudra drank that milk in a single moment, his body turning black like the sun consuming darkness, or like the contact with the virtuous destroying vice.
From the world of Brahmā down to the netherworld, everything became peaceful and empty; it was a uniform void, free from dust, smoke, wind, oceans, and the elements.
Only these four objects, as motionless and as pure as the sky, are seen there; listen to them, O descendant of Raghu.
First, there is this one Rudra in the center, appearing in the form of black garments; he stands unsupported in the sky like a motionless reflection of fragrance.
The second part, situated far below the seven netherworlds (pātālas), is like the surface of the earth and sky; it is the foundation of the abode of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).

Pervading the netherworld, the earth, and the heavens—including the great mountains and the celestial dwellers—he partook of the nature of the earthly realm, consisting essentially of nothing but mud.
The third category here was the region above the portion of the cosmic egg; due to its extreme distance, it was beyond the range of vision and its dark expanse was difficult to discern.
That which lies between the two widely separated halves of the cosmic egg is space—beginningless and endless, the pure and all-pervading Brahman.
Then that fourth category was perceived by me; there is nothing here other than these four, nor anything whatsoever apart from them.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, what exists outside the shell of the abode of Brahmā? Tell me, what are the coverings there, how many are they, and how are they situated?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Beyond the two hemispheres of the cosmic egg, there is water ten times greater than that; beyond that lies the infinite twilight sky, situated after having set aside that [water].
Then, in that same manner, the fiery energy consisting of flames remained tenfold; then, in that same manner, the wind, the pure wind, remained.
Beyond that, the pure sky is said to be ten times [the size of] that; beyond that is the infinite, supremely transparent Brahma-ether.
Then, in various other places, his other infinite visions likewise shine in the sky; though situated far apart, they are mutually perceived as creations of their own selves.
Śrī Rāma said: O Lord of Sages, above the shell of the cosmic egg and likewise below it, where, how, and by whom is that vast expanse of water and the other elements supported?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: He stands amidst the objects of the earth like a lotus leaf; they run toward him alone, just as children run to their mother.
Therefore, toward that very great body called the cosmic egg which is nearest, the objects of the world rush forth like thirsty people toward water.
Relying upon that very [consciousness] within, the faculties such as the sense of sight do not abandon their own state of existence, just as the limbs [of a body do not abandon the body].
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, how can it be told how those two remain within the fragment of the cosmic egg? What are their forms, by whom are they sustained, and how do they perish?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That which is not held is indeed held aloft, and that which has fallen may yet fall; though formless, the world appears with form, like a city in a dream.
What is its name that falls away, or by what is it sustained? Just as consciousness manifests, so does this abide.

Just as a mass of hair appears in the sky, and just as emptiness exists in the sky, so too does the vibration of the wind exist in the space of consciousness, and so does the world exist in the space of consciousness.
Upon the funeral pyre lies the city of imagination, the house of the world called the cosmic egg; it is like the sky within the sky, formless yet appearing as if possessing every form.
That which arises from the consciousness of falling remains falling day and night; that which arises from the consciousness of going remains going day and night.
That which arises from stable consciousness remains steady day and night; that which arises from surging consciousness remains surging as it rises.
The knower of destruction goes to destruction through the perceptions of the great aeons and so forth; it is born through the perception of birth in the void by means of all-encompassing perceptions.

A multitude of pearls shines within the autumnal sky; though seen as unreal, they possess a form of supreme reality. Just as it is impossible to count those shimmering [clouds] in the heavens due to delusion, who here is capable of numbering these worlds?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, O Rāghava, I beheld that Rudra in that vast sky, having assumed a massive form, intoxicated and engaged in dancing.
Like the sky having assumed a form without abandoning its own inherent pervasiveness, he was of massive stature, dark as a rain cloud, and filling the ten directions.
With the sun, moon, and fire as its eyes, with the moving ten directions as its garment, it was tethered by a dense and long-reaching web of light from dark-blue flames.
Resembling the submarine fire, radiant with the weight of its surging waves and flickering arms, it rose up as if suddenly assuming a bodily form from the waters of the single ocean.
Immediately thereafter, I saw that from his body there issued forth, like a shadow, something that followed the movements of his dance.
Since the suns are no longer present and the sky is filled with great darkness, it is my thought: "How can this shadow remain here?"
Just as I was quickly reflecting, there stood before him the vast Śrī Trilocanā, dancing.
Dark, emaciated, with limbs covered in veins, she was worn out and stretched out in form; her crest was a mass of forest foliage flickering like a fire filled with flames.
Dark as collyrium and deep darkness, she had assumed the form of the night; she was like the beauty of gloom embodied, or like the radiance of the sky made manifest in a physical shape.
Exceedingly tall with a terrifying mouth, she seemed intent on measuring the sky; with the movement of her long knees and arms, she appeared as if desiring to measure the quarters of the horizon.
Emaciated as if by many fasts, her great body was deeply sunken; dark as collyrium, she was like a line of clouds tossed by the wind.
When she was emaciated and unable to remain standing for very long due to her condition, she was then, as it were, bound together by long, sinew-like cords that resembled veins.
It was so exceedingly long that I could see its head and its hoof only with great effort, after repeatedly moving up and down for a long time.
With its head, hands, and hooves bound by strings of entrails and intestines, it was like a thicket of thorns entwined with thread from the very roots.
Her garland was formed by clusters of lotuses from the heads of the sun and other deities, all possessing universal forms; her borders were composed of pure light, wind, and fire.
With snakes clinging to her long, drooping ears, wearing earrings made of human flesh, and possessing long, swaying, dark breasts like dried gourd-vines and stones;

The circle of his skull-topped staff was marked by the circles of Brahma’s matted locks, which were like a flood of Kumara’s peacock feathers, as well as by the heads of the exalted lords of the gods.
Pure with its garland of ivory tusks, it rolls and turns in circular whirlpools due to the falling of stainless radiance, like a streak rising from the ocean of darkness.
Residing high upon the tree of the sky like a creeper of dried gourds, its knotty joints were tossed by the winds, making a rustling *paṭa-paṭa* sound.
With her arms raised like great waves, she shines with a dark-blue luster; she revolves in the cycles of her dance like a series of billows upon the single ocean.
In one moment she has the form of a single arm, and in another moment she is crowded with many arms; she possesses a pavilion for the dancing of the world, cast forth by her infinite and fierce arms.
Quickly she takes the form of a single face; quickly she has the appearance of many faces; in an instant she possesses infinite fierce mouths, and for a moment she is even faceless.
In one moment she possesses a single foot, and in another she quickly possesses a hundred feet; for a moment she is endowed with infinite feet, and in a moment she acts as one who has no feet at all.
"This is Kālarātri," so I inferred regarding her bodily form; "this is the Blessed Lady Kālī," thus was she determined by the virtuous.
Her three eyes resemble a fierce well filled with flames, and the region of her forehead is like the summit of a blazing mountain of sapphire.

Her two formidable jaws were like the deep blue Indranīla gems of the Lokāloka mountain and the terrifying abyss; she wore a necklace of pearls that were the stars strung upon the thread of the wind’s force.
In the sky, where the intense radiance of archways as high as mountains of sapphire rested, the terrifying crow-like Bhaga appeared, resembling a mountain of glass.
With the flowers of her dancing vine-like arms—the bright circles of light from her nails—she seemed to whirl through the vault of the sky like hundreds of full moons.
With their arms whirling and pervading the circle of the quarters like the clouds at the end of an aeon, they rained down the great radiance of the rows of stars from the edges of living beings.
With their tree-like arms whirling, adorned with nets of vine-like fingers and flower-like nails, they darkened the entire expanse of the sky with their formidable forms.
Moving with a swaying gait, she traversed the ground thick with *tāla* and *tamāla* trees—ground that resembled a vast forest consumed by fire—with her multitude of trembling shanks.
Even with its hair reaching the far shore of the infinite great sky, it seemed to be spreading out a vast garment for the wandering elephant of darkness.
By that breath-wind, which makes the entire circle of directions and the village of the sky resound with a deep *ghuṃghuma* roar, even the Merus are carried away.
As it sang the song of its roar like a battle-cry with the whistling of dense winds, that mountain, as if constrained by conciliation, trembled with its ridges following in its movement.
Then, as her body grew larger through the intensity of her immersion in the dance, she was seen by me, whose attention was fixed upon the vast expanse of the sky.
As long as that garland—composed of the playful coils of her body—is worn upon him, he is encompassed by the Malaya, Kailāsa, Sahya, Mandara, and Meru mountains.
The row of clouds at the end of the eon was her silk headband; and the three intermediate worlds were the circular mirrors upon her body.
On his two ears were silver and golden rings like the Himavat and Meru mountains; his great girdle was a waist-belt of garlands resonant with the humming of the cosmic egg.
The great boundary mountains were like flower garlands, with their peaks, forests, and cities appearing as clusters; the ancient cities, forests, islands, and villages were like delicate sprouts.
Within her limbs were seen cities and towns, the three worlds as the seasons, and the arrangement of months, days, and nights.
The pearl necklaces and other ornaments are the rivers such as the Kālindī and the Tripathagā; both dharma and adharma are the ear-ornaments on his two ears.
Her four breasts were flowing with drops of ghee and milk; they were the Vedas, with nipples established in the fourfold arrangement of the meaning of all the scriptures.
With tridents, sharp-edged spears, javelins, arrows, pikes, double-edged swords, and mallets, she bears emerging nets of weapons like garlands of flowers.
The fourteen kinds of elemental beings, beginning with the gods, exist as the rows of hair upon her body.
And as she dances, the cities, villages, and mountains lying within her body dance along with her; thus they undergo rebirth for the sake of joy alone.
At that time, I realized that this entire world, including all that is moving and stationary, is but a single living soul; it dances, and thus abides in happiness in the next world.
Having swallowed the world and placed it within her own body, she has attained satisfaction; intoxicated, she dances like a female cātaka bird that has digested the world.
The entire world appears as if situated within a mirror-reflection; in her vast, self-natured body, it assumes a form identical to her own.
It does not dance; rather, this entire world—including its mountains, forests, and groves—dances, being manifold in nature, having died and returned again.
Then I beheld for a long time that beautiful dancing of the world, reflected within the mirror of his body; it remained there, undecayed and ever-present.
The net of stars trembled and the circle of mountains whirled; the gods and demons, shaken by the wind, appeared like a swarm of gnats.
The sky was covered by islands and oceans that resembled the wheels released in battle; with effortless whirling and eddies, it treated massive mountain ranges as mere blades of grass.

The sky resounded with the whistling of winds as it was covered by garments of dark-blue clouds, while the quarters of the horizon echoed with the loud "paṭa-paṭa" sounds of the bursting and cracking of wood, bones, and other debris.
Just as a mirror is pervaded by various objects of the world, both mixed and unmixed, so too is [the body] pervaded by limbs that possess expansive forms and by the delusions of limbs.
Mount Meru dances, its great arms being the restless and lofty peripheral mountains, and its fine body-hairs being the whirling masses of clouds.
Transgressing their boundaries, the oceans have overstepped their seals; the trees rise from the surface of the earth toward the sky, and from the sky they descend to the surface of the earth.
Cities are seen submerged below with gurgling sounds; yet nothing—neither houses nor watchtowers nor inhabitants—is rolling down beneath.
As she moved with agility within it, the moon, the sun, day, and night appeared like golden threads shimmering amidst the light of the marks made by her fingernails.
The creations of that [night] shine forth like dewdrops on a web of water, belonging to her who wears dark clouds as a garment and captivates with her frost-like radiance.
Her vast mass of braided hair became the sky; her two feet the netherworld (pātāla), her belly the earth, and her arms the cardinal directions.

The continents and oceans are its rings of intestines; all the mountains are its ribs; and the series of inhalations and exhalations are its swinging cradles, possessing the nature of the masses of wind.
Then, as she danced with her body expanded, the Himavat, Meru, Saha, and other mountains experienced the illusion of being rocked by the movement of her vast form.
As she wound garlands with her creeper-like arms, it was as if the dance of the dissolution of the world were being commenced once again in playful sport.
His body was covered with the hair-like hosts of gods, asuras, and serpents; unable to remain motionless, that small-bodied being whirled around like a wheel.
Adorned with the sacred thread of various manifestations of consciousness, she moved through the sky, making a deep, whistling sound like a thundercloud.
In that state, the ground becomes space and space also becomes the ground; it exists as a reflection within, yet nothing at all undergoes transformation.
From the vast caverns that serve as its interior, thick and resonant roars issue forth; there, fierce winds blow, producing terrifying whistling sounds.
With hundreds of rays from her [the moon] revolving four times across the sky, it shines as if strewn with sprouts tossed up by a fierce wind.
Because of the resulting delusion regarding the multitude of worldly objects born from that limb [of mine], even my firm vision has faltered in this infatuation, like an army in the heat of battle.
Mountains are carried away like machines, sky-dwellers fall down, and the dwellings of the immortals roll about when the mirror of the body is turned.
The Meru mountains were arrayed like leaves, the Malaya mountains like sprouts, the Himalayas like flakes of snow, and the earths like lotus creepers.
They were like birds on the Sahya mountain, like Vidyādharas on the Vindhya range, and like royal swans wandering in the sky over the Vṛkṣāvarta forest.
The continents were like blades of grass, the oceans like bracelets, and the abodes of the gods like lotuses within the waters of his body.
Upon her limbs, which resembled the vast sky and were like cities seen in a dream or through magic ointment, her large shanks possessed a luster equal to the orb of the sun.

The Vindhya dances in the forest of the Golden Mountain; the Sahya, the Sahya mountain, Kailāsa, Malaya, the peak of Mahendra, Krauñca, Mandara, Gokarṇa, the courtyard of the sky, the earth, and the city of the Vidyādharas—all these forest lands have eternally attained mobility within her body.

The oceans dance upon the mountain, and even the mountain leaps high into the hollow of the sky; even the firmament, along with its moon and sun, has moved from beneath the earth. With its islands, mountains, cities, and forests strewn with flowers, the world wanders through the circle of the directions like a blade of grass tossed in the ocean of the universe.

Mountains, oceans, the ends of the quarters, other worlds, and circles of cities and towns wander in the sky, like rivers and lakes within a mirror, by the movement of grass scattered by a powerful wind.

Fish move about in the desert as if in excellent water; cities appear in the sky as if on the earth; mountains stand in the air like clouds at the end of an aeon or peaks whirled by a cataclysmic wind—that is how it appeared.

A multitude of stars revolves by means of the mechanism of a thousand lamps, beautiful with the speed of a shower of jewels; released from within and without on all sides out of affection, it is like a rain of flowers shed by hosts of Vidyādharas and gods.

The multitudes of dissolution and creation, corresponding to the divisions of day and night, appear like drops of silver; the white and black masses of the day likewise shine forth in confusion on all sides, like the stainless white and black circles of a mirror.

The jewel-like orbs of the sun and moon, and the clusters of stars with their necklaces of shimmering circular luster, create incessantly many streaks like whirling firebrands across the clear sky, which is like a vast, billowing canopy.

The various and virtuous ornaments, whose gems tumble through the three worlds at the time of the end of the aeon, suddenly produce a clanging sound as they whirl about; emitting a humming resonance, their radiant energies move upward and downward.

In these days, where all the sunlight and the days themselves turn dark with the wave-like luster of the swords of soldiers intoxicated by battle, the clamor of the throngs of people is heard even as they roll about, though they remain steadfastly firm.

Led by Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, Hara, Agni, the Sun, and the Moon, the gods and asuras arrive in successive turns; they come and go in various ways, like gnats driven by the wind or the flickering of a lightning bolt.

Dissolution and creation, pleasure and pain, birth and non-birth, effort and lack of effort, prohibition and injunction, birth and death, delusion, and so forth—these states always manifest together and separately within creation; though they have entered into a state of intermingling therein, they remain distinct.

In this world, not even the slightest count can be perceived of those whose bodies are as empty as space, which falsely manifest in the sky as the arising, persistence, and destruction of beings, as well as the delusions of creation, dissolution, and the protection of the worlds.

Therein, portents, pacification, death, festivals, war, equanimity, hatred, passion, fear, trust, and so forth—like a collection of jewels in a single treasury—it shines as a succession of creations of various flavors that are unimpeded.

Within her body, which consists of the ether of consciousness, the various states of the world—arising from the nature of indistinct experience—manifest everywhere; yet, because they are subject to total dissolution, they flash forth like the appearance of a tuft of hair in the sky perceived by one with impaired vision.
The world, though agitated, is seen as unagitated, remaining in its established state; it is like a reflection in a mirror being moved, which itself remains unmoved.
With their inner majesty flashing through dance, they abandon and assume their positions for the sake of the world at every moment, like the creations born of a child's imagination.
The power of action, incessantly filling the interior of the body, becomes a mass and scatters the heaps of the world like a shower of mung bean grains.
For a moment she is perceived as something, and for a moment as nothing at all; for a moment she is only the size of a thumb, and for a moment she fills the entire sky.
For that entire Goddess is the power of consciousness (saṃvit-śakti) whose nature is the world; she is infinite, possessing a pure body that is the treasury of the supreme ether.

For consciousness, which exists within the three worlds situated in the three periods of time, shines forth in that very manner; it flashes with such speed in its form—which resembles the web of the world-picture existing within the mind of a master painter—in accordance with how it actually stands.

Because she is the single conscious self whose body consists of all things, and because she is the reality of the single conscious self whose body is the one, utterly tranquil space; thus, bearing a form that is both closed and opened, she shines as an infinite and beginningless singular essence.

Within that infinite treasury consisting of stone, the visible world shines forth like the carvings of lines, lotuses, and wheels; it exists within her whose body is merely the void of space, just as streaks of waves appear in the ocean-treasury due to its consciousness.
The great goddess Bhairavī, filling the sky as she danced, stood before that Rudra of the end of the eon, who possessed a terrifying form.
With its forest lands scorched by the fierce fires resting upon its head-crests, it dances like a garland of trees shaken by the winds at the end of an eon.
She carried a hoe, a mortar, a grass mat, a wooden board, a water-pot, and a basket; she held a pestle, a water-ladle, a cooking pot, and a pillar, and wore garlands and strings of beads.
Scattering heaps of flowers from such nets of garlands, she seemed as if she were weaving together the agitation of the dance with the destruction of the world's decay.
While being thus praised by her, Ākāśabhairava likewise, with his form expanded in that same manner, then danced exultantly.

May Bhairava protect you—he who, being praised by Kālarātri, who dances to the sound of musical instruments while uttering "ḍimbaṃ ḍibaṃ suḍimbaṃ paca paca sahasājhamya jhamyaṃ prajhamya�!", holds in his hand the great horn of Yama’s buffalo, filled with red wine, and wears a garland upon his breast and a crest of Garuḍa feathers upon his head.

Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, what is this that dances during the universal destruction, and by whom is she led? Why does she carry winnowing baskets, platters, jars, and other vessels, and why does she wear garlands and wreaths?"
What has been lost that the three worlds now exist again? What was situated within the body that has been drawn forth by Kālī? How does Nirvāṇa dance, and how has it returned once more?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That was neither a man nor a woman; it was not that dance, nor were those two [performers]; even so, in such a state and such conduct, there were no physical forms belonging to them.
That which is the beginningless sky of pure consciousness is the cause of all causes; it is infinite, peaceful, a mere manifestation, imperishable, and all-pervading.
That auspicious, true Śiva is directly perceived in the form of Bhairava; thus established for the peace of the world, he is indeed the supreme space itself.
Because it possesses consciousness, it is not logical for that [mind] to remain without the manifestation of such an intrinsic nature, just as gold cannot exist without its form.
Tell me, O wise one, how can pure consciousness exist without a conscious subject? Tell me, O wise one, how can black pepper exist without its pungency?
Consider how gold could exist without its bracelets and other ornaments; how could the existence of an entity possibly occur without its own intrinsic nature?
Without sweetness, how could one speak of sugarcane juice? That which is devoid of sweetness is not indeed that juice.
That which is insentient, though appearing as pure consciousness, is not called pure consciousness; nor is it possible for the void of pure consciousness ever to perish anywhere.
Nothing other than its own mere existence is tenable for it; indeed, this [space] is claimed to be non-different from space, yet one cannot accept its being something else.
Therefore, that which is his unagitated state, mere existence, self-luminous, without beginning, middle, or end, and consisting of all powers;
Thus, this creation and dissolution of the three worlds—the sky, the earth, and the directions—known as destruction and production, is in truth nothing but the non-manifestation of space.
Birth and death, illusion and delusion, dullness and unsubstantiality, substantiality and discernment, bondage and liberation, and the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Knowledge and ignorance, bodilessness and embodiedness, the momentary and the long-lasting, instability or stability—all that consists of you, me, and others.
Existence and non-existence, as well as both existence and non-existence, folly and even wisdom; the reckoning of place, time, action, and substance, and the play of conceptual construction.
This world, consisting of form, light, mental attention, action, the intellect, and the sense organs, as well as fire, water, air, space, earth, and so forth, is thus pervaded [by consciousness].
All this is that stainless space of pure consciousness, free from ailment; not abandoning its very nature as space, it thus abides as the self of all.
And all this is nothing but the pure space here; of this there is no doubt. It is not different from this, as the example of dreams and the like remains unimpeachable in this regard.
That which I have described as the supreme space consisting of consciousness—this very thing is called Śiva; this is the eternal one.
He exists as this Hari, he becomes this Grandfather (Brahmā), and he is the Moon, the Sun, Indra, Varuṇa, Yama, Vaiśravaṇa, and Anala.
The wind, the clouds, and the ocean—whatever exists or does not exist—is merely a manifestation of these small fragments of the space-treasury of consciousness that flash forth intensely.
Through such notions, these things are falsely cultivated; however, by the mere awakening to their true nature, they become exactly as they are.
Ignorance and awakening are thus nothing but the space of consciousness (cidvyoma) abiding within itself; therefore, since neither difference, duality, nor unity exists, be at peace.
The individual soul acts as a wave within the great ocean of its own saṃsāra only so long as it does not know its supreme nature and, having attained identity with it, becomes free from affliction.
But through knowledge, he attains peace in such a way that there is neither that ocean nor those waves; and all this, as it truly is, becomes for him the infinite Supreme itself, which is quiescent.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This which I have described as the supreme space of pure consciousness—this very one is called Śiva; therefore, Rudra dances.
O best of the accomplished, that which is its form is not a form at all; it is the sky of pure consciousness alone, appearing in such a manner.
At that time, I saw that very space as having that form; it was understood by me alone, and no one else perceives it in that way.
Just as that end of the aeon, that Rudra, and that Bhairavī are merely illusion, so too have I fully understood all things to be nothing more than illusion.
The supreme void is indeed the sky of consciousness; by virtue of that particular configuration, it appears as such, having assumed the form of Bhairava.
Since no understanding arises without a relationship between the signified and the signifier, I have described to you exactly what was perceived by me.
O Rāma, whatever has been expressed here is always present for you; yet for one whose perception of the material world is firmly rooted, it becomes illusory in nature in an instant.
That is not Bhairavī, nor is that Bhairava, nor is there any destruction; all of that is merely an illusion, appearing as the sky of consciousness.
It is like a city created in a dream, like the impetuous force of a mental construction, like the essence of a caravan of narrative meanings, and like the play of a kingdom of the mind.

Just as a dream-city appears in the clear sky, just as the perception of pearls arises [in the air], and just as a mass of hair appears in the sky, so does the insentient appear within the dense mass of consciousness.
The clear space of pure consciousness alone shines by itself within itself; thus, that which appears as such shines as the self in the form of the world.
Just as the Self shines by itself within the sky of consciousness, so does it shine there upon the canvas, even amidst the dance of the fire at the end of the aeon.
O dear one, the formless nature of Śiva and Śivā has thus been described; now listen, for I shall tell you of the state of the dance that is beyond dancing.
Volition cannot exist anywhere without some degree of contact with the element of volition, just as a thing cannot exist without being a thing.
Therefore, consciousness exists as Rudra by virtue of its own nature, just as gold exists in the form of an ornament through its beautiful configuration.
Whatever is indeed volition, wherever it exists, necessarily possesses the property of movement by its very nature; for substantiality arises from intrinsic nature.
Whatever vibration belongs to this Śiva, who is a mass of consciousness, that alone appears to us as a dance, manifesting through the power of the immersion in one's own latent impressions.
Therefore, know that when Rudra, who is auspicious at the end of the aeon and possesses a fierce form, dances swiftly, it is indeed his own vibration as the mass of consciousness.
Śrī Rāma said: From the perspective of valid cognition, this visible world does not exist at all in reality; whatever appears as if it exists will all perish at the end of the kalpa.
In this supreme sky, which is as utterly empty as at the end of an aeon, how is it that the mass of consciousness, though itself beyond thought, somehow perceives that which is indeed unthinkable?

The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: Even then, my dear, this alone serves to pacify the ocean of duality and unity—if there is nothing whatsoever that is an object of thought within the sky of pure consciousness.
Therefore, nothing whatsoever is perceived anywhere at any time; everything is peaceful, like the silence of stone, a mass of consciousness, and like the sky.
That which is called "the object of thought" moves within its own nature; for the tranquil nature of consciousness remains established in its own being.
Just as in a dream, consciousness itself appears internally like a city or a town, yet that city and so forth do not exist at all; it is merely the space of pure awareness.

Having realized within itself by means of itself that both the knower and the known are entirely devoid of consciousness, it likewise understands its own manifestation from the very beginning of creation.
Shining by itself within the hollow of the sky that is its own conscious nature, consciousness assumes through its own imagination the delusion of the world, whether for a moment or for an eon.
The sky of consciousness, its luster shining within itself in the space of its own nature, performs such conceptualizations as "this is he," "I am this," and "you are this."
Therefore, there is no duality here, nor is there unity, nor is there emptiness; there is neither the conscious nor the unconscious, and that is indeed silence, yet it is not even that.
Nothing whatsoever is perceived anywhere by anyone, due to the nature of the perceived self; therefore, even the perceiver does not exist as it were, and only silence remains.
For non-conceptual meditative absorption is the established conclusion in all scriptural traditions; that is the silence of the living rock, so remain thus in stillness.

Performing your own natural duties according to the flow of worldly convention, remain steadfast through the silence of the ultimate truth; free from pride, delusion, and intoxication, with a heart as pure as the expanse of space, abide in peace, O you whose life is the Embodied One (Kāmadeva).
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, tell me what follows: why does Kālī dance in this manner? Why is she encircled by a garland of winnowing baskets, planks, hoes, clubs, and other such implements?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That Bhairava, the space of consciousness, is designated as Śiva; know that his non-dual power of vibration, consisting of mind, is that very [power].
Just as a single movement of the wind and heat and fire are one, so too pure consciousness and the power of movement are always of a single nature.
Air is characterized by movement, and fire is characterized by heat; pure, stainless consciousness, when tranquil, is designated as Śiva.

That [Śiva] is perceived only through the power of the illusion of His own vibration, and certainly not otherwise; for the wise know Śiva to be Brahman—tranquil and inexpressible even to those who are masters of speech.
The power of vibration (spanda-śakti) extends that appearance of the visible world according to its own will, just as the will of a person possessing form creates a city of imagination.
The will of Śiva indeed acts; it acts this [universe] for Him who is formless. This very will is called Consciousness (cit), because it provides life to those who desire life.

Having herself become the primordial nature (prakṛti) of creation by virtue of being that very nature, she is called "action" (kriyā) because she brings about the manifestation and experience of the perceptible world.

She is called Śuṣkā because she withers [all things] with a form like the crest of the submarine fire; she is declared to be Caṇḍikā because of her ferocity, and she is [called] Utpalā due to her lotus-like complexion.

She is called Jayā because she is solely intent on victory and because she is the refuge of accomplishment; she is called Jayantī because she is victorious, and Vijayā because she is the basis of triumph.
She is called Parājitā because of her prowess, and Durgā because of her form that is difficult to grasp; she is celebrated as Umā because she is the essential power (sāra-śakti) of the syllable Om.
She is Gāyatrī because her nature is that of song; she is Sāvitrī because she abides as the source of procreation; and she is called Sarasvatī because she flows through all philosophical views.

Gaurī, because her body is fair-limbed, is associated with the body of Bhava; she resides in the hearts of those who are asleep as well as those who are awakened through the utterance of the syllable *Am*.
The crescent moon is said to be the eternal essence of the beings of the three worlds; because Śiva and Śivā possess the nature of space, their body appears dark.
For the sky is seen as flesh by these two through their vision; there is a sky within the sky itself, and those two are situated in that sky-of-skies.

With limbs as pure as the sky, they were like two elder brothers of space; yet, due to the distinction between the multiplicity and scarcity of their hands, feet, faces, and heads, they appeared different.
Listen to that diversity—the state of wielding plows, winnowing fans, and so forth, as well as wearing garlands—for that Blessed Lady is indeed action, whose sole nature is vibration.

"One should give, bathe, and offer oblations"—thus [it is said] by the primordial embodied being; the beginningless and endless power of consciousness (cit-śakti) likewise shines by itself within itself.
The beloved one is embodied space, the visible splendor possessing the nature of vibration; for those various dramatic performances and dances of that Goddess Kālī are indeed her own.
These are the modes of creation, old age, and death belonging to Brahmā; this activity consists of the arrangements of villages, cities, islands, and provinces.
Kālī is she who effects vibration and sustains within herself that which consists of imagined parts; Kālī is the lotus-pond, Kālī is action, and Kālī is the Kali age of the cosmic egg.
The Goddess of Consciousness holds within her heart this visible splendor which has become her own limb; yet she herself never possesses any definable limbs anywhere.
Inseparable from the state of Śiva, let Śiva-hood itself be seen in this way, just as emptiness belongs to the sky and movement to the wind, my dear.
Know that the visible aspect of consciousness is indeed like the moonlight, while its activity is like the moon itself; know it to be auspicious, peaceful, effortless, immutable, and stainless.
Therein, not even the slightest inertia exists, for that is the very nature of vibration; when that activity, being of such a form, comes under the power of awakening, [it becomes liberation].
When she remains exactly as she is through that very withdrawal, she is then called Śiva; for the activity of the power of consciousness, the Goddess, is established within the self.
That very state of abiding as it truly is is called Śiva; he is the essential nature of the Goddess’s action, the power of consciousness, whose form is the Great Creation.
These worlds, radiant with light, consist of groups of virtuous beings; they possess no other parts than those who bear assumed forms.
The earths with their six continents and oceans, together with their forests, groves, and mountains; the three Vedas with their limbs and sub-limbs, along with the sciences and songs.

Sacrifices accompanied by ritual injunctions and prohibitions, involving conceptions of the auspicious and inauspicious, together with the sacrificial fees, the sacred fires, and the praise of the *puroḍāśa* cakes and other offerings—[all these are abandoned].
They were joined with kings, mortars, stools, winnowing baskets, sacrificial posts, and so forth; they were battles accompanied by multitudes of weapons, along with spears, arrows, and javelins.

Resplendent with spears, maces, javelins, horses, elephants, and warriors, the fourteen classes of beings beginning with the gods are the kinsmen of the hosts of spirits; likewise, there are the fourteen oceans, continents, earths, and worlds.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Sage, tell me: do those mental constructs of the embodied consciousness—the various creations that exist within its limbs—abide in the Self, or are they unreal?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, this is indeed the power of consciousness (cicchakti); whatever is impelled by it is likewise perceived by it. Therefore, all this is real, as it were.
Reflected from the outside like a reflection in a mirror, that [object] exists truly within consciousness itself; it is not unreal in reality.

Nevertheless, for that which is of the nature of consciousness, there may still exist within it a city of true volitions; how could such a thing arise from consciousness that has been purified through firm meditation?
Whether that creation exists in mirrors, in dreams, or in mental construction, my view is simply this: it is real because it performs its function within the self.
If you say that he is not for my sake, then how could it be so? For at this very moment, all those who have gone to other lands are indeed for my sake.

Just as a village in another region serves a purpose for one who has gone there, so too do all [things] serve a purpose for one who has attained that state, because of the determination of their true nature.
Whatever is seen to perform its function for all purposes exactly as it is, that is true for itself; it does not become untrue for another who has not attained that state.
Therefore, all successions of creations reside within the sheath of the power of consciousness; they appear as real to one who has attained that state of being, but not at all to anyone else.
The hosts of mental constructs and dreams situated in the past, present, and future are all real; since He is the supreme reality and the self of all, how could it be otherwise?
Those [objects] are attained by one who has achieved yoga and entered into that state, just as mountains, villages, and regions are reached by another through travel to another country.
Just as for one who has been shaken while in a deep sleep, a city seen in a dream does not actually tumble, yet it is clearly accepted that it has indeed tumbled.
Likewise, as she moved, the world situated within her body rolled along with her; yet it did not actually roll at all, remaining fixed like a reflection in a mirror.
This great undertaking of the three worlds, though real, is merely an illusion; tell me, what indeed can be said of the rolling or non-rolling of that which is merely an illusion?
When is the city of dreams real? When is the city of dreams false? When is the city of dreams destroyed? When is the city of dreams established?
That very splendor of the visible world which appears before you is nothing but delusion; know that even this worldly fortune is an unreal delusion.
Just as in imagination, in the kingdom of the mind, in a dream, in conversation, or in delusion, so too is the experience of the three worlds according to one's previous experiences.
This internal delusion of "I" and "the world" appears as if it were manifesting from consciousness; yet, when thoroughly understood, that which is called the subtle supreme space subsides.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus that goddess dances with the circles of her long, staff-like arms, making the sky appear like a dense forest through their rhythmic movements.
In that same way, the stainless power of consciousness dances through its activities; its ornaments are the winnowing basket, the hoe, the mat, and so forth.
Arrows, spears, clubs, darts, maces, and so forth; rocks and the like; as well as the multitude of categories of existence and non-existence, the arts, and the sequence of time.

The vibration of consciousness holds the world within itself, just as imagination holds a city within the heart; or rather, that very [vibration] is the world, for it is simply imagination, just like a city [created by the mind].
Just as there is vibration in the wind, so is that will of Śiva; just as vibration exists within the wind, so Śiva remains with his will stilled.
Just as the formless wind spreads a display of sound and movement within the space, so does the will of Śiva create the universe.
Then, while she was dancing there in that supreme ether, by the force of her own impetuosity and through a chance occurrence like the "crow and the palm fruit," [he fell].
Śiva, standing nearby, was touched by him as he approached; like the submarine fire that carries a streak of water for its own destruction, he was drawn near.
As soon as that Śiva, the supreme cause, was touched, she began to slowly return to her original nature, O Urajā.
Having abandoned her infinite forms, she became Girimātrikā; from there she became Nagaramātrā, and then Drumasundarī.
Then, having assumed a form like the sky, she entered the very form of Śiva, just as a river enters the great ocean after its turbulence has subsided.
Then he became truly one, separated from Śivā; he was Śiva alone, peaceful, the tranquilizer everywhere in the sky.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, tell me in truth why that Śivā, the Supreme Goddess who has been touched by Śiva, has come for the sake of peace.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, that is called Prakṛti, the supreme will of Śiva; it is renowned as the "illusion of the world," the uncreated power of vibration.
He is declared to be beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), the Puruṣa whose form is like the wind; he bears the form of Śiva, is peaceful, and possesses the tranquility of the autumnal sky.
Nature wanders in saṃsāra in the form of wandering; it is the will of the Supreme Lord, the power of consciousness, whose essence consists solely in vibration.
As long as one does not perceive Śiva—the eternally satisfied, free from ailment, undecaying, supreme, devoid of beginning and end, and transcending duality—[so long does one remain in saṃsāra].
Because pure consciousness alone is its sole substrate, by way of a chance coincidence, the Goddess Consciousness, having touched Śiva, becomes thoroughly identified with Him.
Having touched the Puruṣa, Prakṛti abandons its state as Prakṛti; having attained oneness within him, it is like the form of a river in the ocean.
For a river consists of nothing but water; when it meets the ocean, it quickly reaches that very ocean and dissolves right there.
Consciousness is the will of Śiva; having reached that very God, it comes to rest, just as an iron blade with a sharp edge is blunted upon reaching the whetstone that is its place of origin.
Just as one's own shadow quickly enters the body of a man who has entered one's own shadow, so does primordial nature (prakṛti) enter the person (puruṣa).
Having willed its own created state called "man," which is eternal, it wanders again in saṃsāra; for it does not attain that true reality here.
A virtuous person dwells among a horde of thieves only so long as he does not recognize them; once he has recognized them, he no longer finds pleasure there.
As long as consciousness does not perceive that supreme reality and become one with it, it delights in and wanders within duality, which is of the nature of unreality.

That which is the nature of the supreme state, whose form is the nirvāṇa of consciousness—having attained that, one reaches identity with it, just as a river reaches the state of the ocean upon entering the sea.

Under the sway of delusion, consciousness wanders through those various states of birth within turbulent creations for as long as it does not perceive the Supreme; then, having seen Him, it immediately sinks deeply into that very state, like a female bee into thick honey.

Who indeed, having attained it, would abandon that reality of the Self? And who, having obtained and experienced an elixir, would discard it—by which, O Rāma, all incessant sufferings consisting of birth, death, and delusion are stilled?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen, O Rāma, how he remains there in that great space; having abandoned that delusion within the body, even that Rudra becomes tranquil.
Then that Rudra, as if depicted in a painting, remained motionless while gazing at those two fragments of the world, even as I stood there watching.
Then, in just a moment, that Rudra beheld those two fragments in the midst of the sky, as if looking upon heaven and earth with the eye of the sun.
Then, in the mere twinkling of an eye, he brought those two fragments together with a snort from his trunk and cast them into his mouth as if into the depths of the underworld.
He remained all alone, like a single void within the entire void, his circle of spheres having devoured the fierce mass of the fragments of the consumed cosmic eggs.
Then, in just a moment, he became as light as a cloud; thereafter, he became the size of a staff, and then the size of a span.
Then he was seen by me in the form of a grain of glass; thereafter, becoming minute, he was seen by me with my divine vision.
Having then become a minute atom, he subsequently vanished; thus he attained tranquility, like a fragment of an autumnal cloud.
"Even such a great undertaking [was accomplished] right before my very eyes"—thus he spoke with a sense of concealment regarding those two door-panels of the cosmic egg.
When the leaf had been swallowed by the deer tormented by hunger, the sky then became stainless, like the absolute Brahman alone, and all was stilled.
"I beheld there that vast delusion of the end of the eon, which is without beginning, middle, or end, and consists solely of the space of pure consciousness."
Then, like a reflection in a mirror within the hollow of a stone fragment, he remembered that woman, that stone, and that delusion.
Having arrived at the palace gate like a rustic, I was filled with wonder; I gazed again upon her, who was like a slab of stone polished by water.
As long as all these creations exist here within this body like the limbs of Kālī, they are seen by the eye of the intellect or by the divine eye, but not in their [ordinary] manner.
Whatever exists everywhere, at all times, and in every way, that indeed exists then and there; if it is perceived as distant by the physical eye, it is simply because it is [conceived of as] a stone.
Only that single rock is seen, and not any creation or the like; it remains as that very same rock, uniform in form and a solid mass.
Then, vast and beautiful as an evening cloud made of refined gold, I was filled with wonder and reflected upon it once more.
In the same way, with that supreme vision, I beheld the other part of the stone as well, appearing as sluggish as the beginning of the world.
In that very same way, as if it were hollow in form and beautiful with various objects, I beheld yet another region just like that.
Whichever region of that rock I beheld, I saw it everywhere to be exactly like that, filled with the intensity of the creative impulse.
Then, with great curiosity, I beheld the entire world reflected upon all the rocks of that mountain, as clearly as in a stainless mirror.
The portions of prosperity, as well as grasses, shrubs, and so forth, were searched for everywhere, exactly as that world exists in its established state.
It is perceived by the intellect alone and not by the eye; it appears in various forms, sometimes as the first creation itself, and sometimes as the Prajāpati being born.
In some places, he calculated the stars, the moon, the sun, the days, nights, seasons, and years; in others, he oversaw the circles of people gathered upon the surface of the earth.
In some places, it was partially excavated by the four fierce oceans; in other places, it was partially unpeopled by gods and populated by dānavas.
In some places, it consists of virtuous beings whose conduct accords with the Kṛta Yuga; in other places, it consists of wicked beings whose conduct accords with the Kali Yuga.
In some places, it was difficult to cross due to the array of cities and the battle with the Daityas.
In some places, the earth was a network of great mountains without any gaps; in other places, it was the emergence of a single lotus, with its creation only partially complete.

In some places, the surface of the earth was inhabited by humans who were free from old age and death; in other places, it was auspicious, with its peaks empty of the moon because none had yet been born.
The ocean of milk was not yet churned; it was filled with death, fish, and gods, but was devoid of nectar, horses, elephants, physicians, cows, lotuses, and poison.
In one place, a host of gods was eager to destroy Śukra, Amara, and Mahāvidyā; elsewhere, the Lord of the Gods was intent on cutting off the limbs of a pregnant woman.
Because its nature is unfading, it is a self-luminous multitude of all things; yet in some places and in some respects, it exists in a sequence of arrangements different from what preceded.
In some places, the investigation into the practice and meaning of unprecedented Vedic scriptures remained as if poised for the upheaval at the end of a kalpa.
In some places, the abodes of the gods were being plundered by throngs of Daityas; in other places, Gandharvas and Kinnaras were singing in the celestial gardens of the gods.
In some places, I have described the grand display of the world—past, future, and present—including the occasional friendship between the gods and the asuras that has been initiated.
Then, within his body—which was the self of the great host of the universe—he experienced all at once the churning caused by the Puṣkarāvarta clouds agitated at the end of a kalpa.
On one side stood the entire multitude of gentle beings gathered together; on the other side were the lords of gods, asuras, and men, all equally agitated.
In one place it is a mass of eternal darkness where light cannot possibly exist; in another place it is lovely, devoid of gloom, resembling the interior of a flame.
On one side was Madhu and Kaiṭabha, reclining upon the stalk of a lotus; on the other was the infant Brahmā, sleeping within the casket of a lotus.
In one place, Mādhava rested upon a towering tree in the midst of the single universal ocean; in another, it was filled with the dense darkness of the void at the end of the kalpa-night.
Motionless like the interior of a stone, it is like the vast expanse of space; it has the form of the belly of deep sleep, unknown and without defining characteristics.
Inconceivable and unknowable, like a state of deep sleep on all sides, the sky was filled everywhere with crows perched upon mountains shaken by the winds of one side.
In one place, it was brilliant with mountains melting from the impact of thunderbolts; in another, mountain ranges were being swept away by the surging, intoxicated ocean.
In one place, it was tumultuous with the battle between the city-dwelling Vṛtra and Andhaka; in another, the earth trembled from the shaking of the intoxicated elephants of Pātāla.
In one place, the earth was being tossed about at the end of the eon by the head of Śeṣa; in another, the Rākṣasa Rāvaṇa was slain by the youthful Rāma.
In one place, Rāghava was obstructed by the *rākṣasa* Rāvaṇa himself, who stood with his feet planted on the ground while keeping his head fixed upon the summit of Mount Deva.
I see the sky pervaded in some places by Kālanemi, and in others constantly protected by the Asuras and Dānavas.
In some places it was protected by the gods who had fallen from their status as asuras, and in others by Viṣṇu joined with Jiṣṇu, guarded by the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas.
In one place, where multitudes of akṣauhiṇīs had been slain in the Bhārata war, Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, tell me, who was I in a previous life?"
"If it did not exist in this very arrangement, how [could it appear]? Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O Rāma, all phenomena indeed revolve again and again."
Just as beans being filled may be done gradually by one means or another, some [moments] are equal to all other sequences, whether they occur through that same sequence or another, mutually.
Certain states of being, equal to their objects, surge forth like the waves of the ocean: again you, again I, and again and again these people.

It is never the case that others do not exist at all within the Supreme; rather, they are either identical to Him or distinct from Him, just as waves are in the ocean—this is the definitive conclusion.
Just as that which is not born [is not perceived], so it is for beings wandering in saṃsāra; infinite beings come and go here through the delusions of existence.
Those very same [beings] and others besides them—both equal and unequal, possessing cyclic existence—are likewise both those and others on every side.
Know that all beings are but sprays of water from the ocean of the world, distinguished only by wealth, kinsmen, age, action, learning, specialized knowledge, and activity.
By those very [karmas], some embodied beings are born again and again; some are similar to them by half, and some are equal to them by a quarter.

Those living beings who possess different bodies become dissimilar from one another; some are equal in all these respects, while others are distinct by time alone; some are similar in time, yet distinct from this [other factor].

In the course of time, with their restless activities, they go up and down like others; moreover, exhausted by the scraping of bodies, they undergo countless and ever-changing existences. They carry the waters of being within this ocean of saṃsāra, which is as fickle as a whirling wheel—who is able to fully enumerate them?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, having pervaded all with my infinite and unblemished body of consciousness-space, I became attentive toward my own form and perceived it somewhere.
To the extent that the internal creation remains established like a sprout, it is like a seed within a granary or like a sprout in the heart when watered.
Just as a sprout swells upward within a seed after it has been moistened, so too does the world—whether possessing form or being formless, whether conscious or unconscious—arise from the mind.

Just as the splendor of the visible world manifests for one who has awakened from deep sleep, or as it appears upon waking from a dream, so does it arise for pure consciousness through its own self-awareness.

In the very same way, within the Self, whose nature has been experienced since the beginning of creation, the arising of creation occurs in the heart and not as something having another form, because its nature is like space.
Śrī Rāma said: O you whose form is space, O Supreme Space, please explain further for the sake of precise understanding how creation proceeds within space.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen, O Rāma, to how I formerly experienced my own self-existence as something unreal yet appearing as real, like a city in a dream.
Beholding that great cosmic agitation, I, whose form is space, caused consciousness to emerge within another part of my own body.
As soon as that stainless consciousness remains with even a slight expansion, at that very moment I perceive myself there somewhere as if it were the nature of space.

O Rāma, just as you, having entered the state of sleep, perceive the dream-world as solid and real, so too does the sky of consciousness perceive its own nature when it enters the waking or dreaming state.

First there is the mere space of the directions; from that arises the cognition "I am. That [cognition] when condensed is called the intellect (buddhi), and when that intellect is further condensed, it is called the mind (manas).
It knows that as the subtle element of sound; then the other subtle elements arise, and from their grossification come the five sense organs—thus occurs the emergence of the group of senses.
Just as for one entering the dream state from deep sleep, the dense manifestation of the world-appearance arises, so too at the beginning of creation does suffering appear in the blink of an eye.
Within this infinite manifestation of the web of the visible, which occurs simultaneously, some speak of a sequence, while others do not speak of one.
Within a lovely atom-sized particle, I experienced myself as consciousness, which in reality is nothing but the stainless sky.
Just as the wind moves incessantly in the sky by its very nature, so too does one perceive the body everywhere by its very nature.
Whatever form has been intended by that supreme power, it is not able to make otherwise, even with great effort.
Then, as soon as I saw that he had become minute in form, because of my own nature as consciousness, I immediately became and remained in that very same state.
Then I perceived a form in the shape of a minute spark of light; subsequently, while contemplating that very form, it appeared to me as if it had attained grossness.
Thinking, "I shall first look at something," he then, through a subtle awakening, set out merely to observe slightly and experienced [it].
O descendant of Raghu, whatever names have been assigned to that [city] there, hear today from me its principal names as they have been devised by those like you.
That through which one proceeds to see is called the eye; that which I see is the visible object, while the act of seeing is the fruit resulting from that.
When I see that it is Time, and when I see it as the Sequence; when I see it as Mature Destiny, and where I see it, that is Space.
When this conceptualization arises, "I am situated in that place," then I am the cause of those subtle elements (tanmātras) through the mere unfolding of consciousness.
Then, the thought "I see" arose in me there as a slight awakening; thereafter, through two apertures, I saw that which was also unobstructed.
"Through those two apertures by which I saw, these two eyes are situated; therefore, I hear slightly"—thus was consciousness declared to me.
Then I heard a very slight humming sound, like the sound of a blown conch shell, which was the natural resonance of the sky itself.
From those two regions where I heard the wind blowing with a spreading sound, these two ears of mine have become wounds.
I have experienced a certain perception of touch here; by virtue of that specific location, it is called "skin."
Whatever limb was touched by that, I experienced it as being of the nature of pure consciousness alone; this is what is known as "air."
When I became aware of what is called the subtle element of the sense of touch, there arose for me the experience of tasting and the sense organ for the flavors to be tasted.
From my vital breaths, the subtle element of smell has arisen, which is of the nature of space; thus, nothing at all has been produced, yet everything has been produced here for me.
If the web of the senses and subtle elements is thus established therein, then for that long, the five knowledges arise in me by their very power.
Having as their sole substance the mere [elements of] sound, form, taste, touch, and smell, they are formless, yet appear as having a nature of their own, consisting essentially of delusion.
Cultivating such a net as I was then established in, that is what is called "egoism" today by people like you.
This very [consciousness], when it has become solidified, is designated as "intellect" (buddhi); and that intellect, when further solidified, is designated as "mind" (manas).
Thus, I am established here as the very nature of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), having the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) as my self, and possessing the form of the space of pure consciousness.
I am void even of the wind and so forth, being nothing but pure space; I am the form of emptiness for all phenomena, unobstructed.
Then, because I remained there for a long time through such contemplation, the conviction arose in me that I was seen as possessing a body.
Then, by means of that notion of "I," he set about making a sound, just as a man who has fallen asleep in a void might cry out while dreaming of a flying man.
Then, as if by a child, the sound was first produced as "Om"; thereafter, this very syllable Om was brought once again to prominence.
Therefore, know that whatever has been spoken by me here is like something uttered by a man in a dream; it is speech brought back from the future.
I have become that very Brahman, the creator of the universe and the teacher of the world; therefore, these creations were fashioned by me through the mind alone.
Thus have I arisen, yet I am not born as anything at all; I have seen the cosmic egg, but nothing exists beyond the cosmic egg.
Thus, although this world appeared to me as being composed of mind, nothing at all was actually accomplished there; it was merely empty space.
Thus, all this is indeed utterly empty, consisting merely of cognition; these entities such as earth and the rest do not exist even in the slightest degree.
The waters of the world’s mirage appear as cognitions within consciousness; there is no external object, nor is there anything external, for that void remains situated like the sky in the sky.
In a desert there is no water at all, yet consciousness perceives it as such; rootedless and inwardly tormented, it experiences delusion through its own agitation.
The world does not exist at all in Brahman; consciousness perceives it as such. Because it is consciousness itself, the world is utterly rootless, and thus there is the confusion of delusion.
This entire world spread out within the heart appears as if non-existent, like a kingdom of the imagination or a mental construction, such as a city seen in a dream.
Just as one does not perceive anything at all in the dream of a person sleeping on their side without the entry of that [dreaming] mind, so too nothing is experienced through the entry of that mind.
In the same way, the world enters into that stone and is experienced; though it appears as a form reflected in a mirror, even when seen, it is otherwise non-existent.
If it is perceived by means of the eye through its material nature, then nothing at all is seen; only the mountain itself is seen.
If one perceives with the subtle body through the vision of supreme awakening, the creation is seen as nothing other than the stainless Supreme Self.
Everywhere, both creation and liberation are perceived through the light of wisdom; for if it were otherwise, nothing at all would be discernible, as Brahman is indeed the Self.
That which the pure intellect perceives through reasoned investigation is not seen by Śiva with his three eyes, nor even by Indra with his hundred eyes.
Just as the sky is covered by creations, so did he perceive it to be "earth"; then I became a meditator, endowed with the concentration on the earth-element.
By that support of the earth, I assumed the form of the earth; yet, without abandoning my nature as the space of consciousness, I became like a sovereign emperor in no time at all.
And through the concentration on the earth, having entered the interior of the earth element, I experienced myself as having a body consisting of continents, mountains, grass, trees, and so forth.
Then I was established upon the surface of the earth, which is covered with various forests of trees, filled with various rows of jewels, and adorned with various cities.

It was rich with villages, thickets, and mountains; its belly was hollowed out by the subterranean realms (pātāla); it was embraced by the arms of the great boundary mountains (kulācala), and it possessed the encircling oceans and continents.

Rich with a body of hair as thick as a mass of grass, it was a cluster of shrubs upon a mountain slope, supported by the hundred heads of Śeṣa, which were like the frontal globes of the world-elephants of the quarters.
The protector of the earth saw it being carried away by creatures with beautiful elephant-like trunks, its limbs being consumed by living beings, yet increasing in size through its established order.

With the Himālaya and Vindhya mountains as its sturdy shoulders and Mount Sumeru as its noble neck, it has a body resplendent with the flowing waters of the Gaṅgā and other rivers, like a shimmering necklace of pearls.
It contained caves, thickets, and marshy banks; it was a circle of oceans like a mirror; and it was beautiful with white sands of desert wastes and the fine cloth of the sky.
Formerly filled and completely purified by great oceans, it was adorned with flower forests and covered with thick masses of pollen.
It was constantly ploughed by farmers, fanned by cool breezes, scorched by the burning rays of the sun, and drenched by the waters of the rainy season.
He has broad shoulders and a chest, eyes like a lotus pond, a white and black cloud-like crown protuberance, and a belly as vast as a ten-directional palace.

Terror-inspiring with its formidable mouth formed by the great circular moat of the world and its surroundings, it possesses as its sole consciousness the movement of the infinite multitude of living beings.
It is pervaded both within and without by various hosts of beings, separately—by gods, dānavas, and gandharvas on the outside, and by insects within.

In the cavities of the underworld and the apertures of the senses, there are multitudes of nāgas, asuras, and worms; and within the treasuries of the seven golden oceans, there are aquatic creatures of various species.

It was pervaded by floods of rivers, forests, oceans, the horizons of the directions, mountains, islands, living beings, territories, lands, and jungles; it was encircled by various rows and consisted of segments of spherical shells, with clusters of lotuses, lakes, rivers, and swarms of enemies.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Mānava, while existing there as the very surface of the earth, I subsequently experienced the state of self-awareness within the roaring rivers and streams.
In one place, there was the piteous lamentation of women crying out at death; in another, the great bliss of a grand festival with women performing wild dances.
In some places there was the ill-fated misery of irresistible famine and wailing; in other places there was the deep affection resulting from an abundance of all kinds of crops.

In some places, there was the terrible agony of bodies being consumed by the great conflagration of fire; in other places, there were fragments of cities and towns swept away by surging floods of water.
In some places, there were circles of plundering created by fickle vassals; in other places, there were circles of Rākṣasas and Piśācas characterized by unrestrained wickedness.
In some places, the tips of its waves were bristling with joy at the splashing of the reservoirs of water, while clouds were tossed about by the winds emerging from the depths of the caves.
With the hair on his body bristling like sprouts arising from the awakening of consciousness, and with his palms slightly lowered due to the agitation caused by the clouds;
The cities, mountains, forests, and towns—including those with peaks, terrifying abysses, and fortresses—possess a gentle trembling marked by the lines of movement within the sphere of consciousness.
In some places, there was the gathering of armies agitated by neighboring vassals in battle; in other places, the entire circle of vassals sat peacefully and calmly.

In one place, the forest was not entirely empty, resounding with the whistling of the wind; in another, the jungle was filled with crops that had been cut down, sown again, and brought to full maturity.
In one place there was a lake filled with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks and blooming lotuses; in another, there was a desert plain where the wind blew through the thick trunks of *nārjunī* trees.

In some places, there was the gurgling sound of rivers and streams effortlessly grinding against their beds; in other places, there was the swelling of seeds sown and moistened, whose limbs were destined to become sprouts.
In some places, there is the sensation of the soft movement of insects within; it is as if awakening me by saying, "Recognize me quickly here and save me!"
In some places, it possessed the full expanse of branches and secondary limbs, while in others, it supported its own boughs by pressing down upon the earth with the weight of its mass of roots.

In some places, the mountains stood densely packed together, having mutually ascended one another's slopes and pressed against the edges of the quarters; in other places, they were tossed by the surging of the ocean.
In some places, there was the squeezing of limbs tightly by the contraction of withered leaves, and the extraction of one's own sap by the intolerant rays of the sun.

In some places, there was a harsh falling down of trees struck by the thunderbolt-like blows of elephants against the temples of their tusks, resulting from the intense stability of their thick-limbed bodies.
It was a new manifestation of the sprouting of the sprouts of subtle delineation, occurring without obstruction for those whose bodies were composed of the bliss of closed eyes.
In some places, it is like a dwelling for flies, lice, and mosquitoes; in others, it is the effortless dragging away of fragments of walls by wall-ants, bees, and ploughs.
In some places it was cold, with waters frozen into stone and skin shattered and flayed by the piercing chill; elsewhere, the wind was harsh and biting.
With its soft limbs becoming swollen and covered in blisters, with swarms of worms writhing within, and with roots such as the feet occasionally emerging, it sank into the water.
In some places, the manifestation of the rain was such that it brought joy by slowly soaking the water within, while outside, it produced a mass of hair-like sprouts of scallions rising upward.
With the soft lotus-leaf carpets gently shaken by the subtle breeze, the lakes have provided for me a wandering that is like liberation upon my limbs.
Śrī Rāma said: Having fixed the earth-dhāraṇā in order to perceive the worlds, you have become this terrestrial world; is it not likewise mental?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "This mind of mine has become this broad earth; yet this is not the mind, nor have I truly become anything at all in reality."
There is no surface of the earth whatsoever that is not mental; whatever you perceive as non-existent or existent, that is merely mind alone.

I am the pure sky of consciousness; for me, whose nature is that supreme state, that which is the manifestation consisting of pure consciousness is known as this world of differentiated mental constructs.
That mind, that surface of the earth, that world, and that Grandfather—all this is the sky of the mind, shimmering in space like a city of one's own volition.
In this way, that which was merely my volition and merely my mind, when expanded and nourished by the practice of concentration, remained as the circle of the earth.
This earth-sphere is not that [reality]; indeed, it is something else, consisting of mind. It is a mere appearance in space, an unperceivable manifestation of consciousness.
That very self, which consists of mere space and has remained in such a state for a long time, abandons its mental nature because it has attained the state of being perceived as "this."
The cognition arises that "this earth-sphere exists, stable, very firm, and expansive," just as [the notion of solidity] arises in the sky due to long-standing habituation.
By this logic, this surface of the earth does not remain as it was; and this very place has now reached the beginning of the first creation.
Just as in a dream it is consciousness alone that appears as the city within the void, so too at the beginning of creation, this world exists as consciousness alone.
Know that the three worlds, as well as this entire visible realm beginning with the surface of the earth, are at all times the kingdom of the mind of the child that is consciousness.

For the Self whose nature is consciousness, there is no volition other than that which consists of it; the world is composed of that. Yet, in reality, it has no true essence, no substantial form, and no luminosity.

The visible world exists when it is not fully understood; once it is fully understood, it is no longer found. That very thing which you have been hearing for so long is what constitutes its full understanding.

Everything, being pure consciousness alone, shines forth, perfectly tranquil, by itself within itself; it is the very self of the terrestrial sphere and the self of the visible world, devoid of both duality and unity.
Just as a gem, by its very nature, produces rays of light such as white, yellow, and so forth even while not acting, so too does the space of consciousness produce the world.
Since it performs no action and does not abandon its form, therefore this is not the mind, nor is there anything at all here upon the surface of the earth.
The infinite space of consciousness alone shines forth like the surface of the earth; within the Self, the sky exists as a pure expanse, just as the netherworld (atala) exists within the sky.
The manifestation of mere intrinsic nature is that very thing as it exists, like the orb of the earth, yet utterly transparent, entering into the midst of space itself.
This terrestrial sphere and that [heavenly one]—both of these are merely the manifestation of the very nature of the Great Consciousness, appearing to you like a city in a dream.
This is of the nature of mere space, and that too is mere space; through the thorough knowledge of the self as ignorance, and through knowledge, neither this nor that exists anywhere.
The agitation of the net of beings in the three worlds, occurring throughout the three times, exists in the state of a mental kingdom as a dream-like construction.
Those beings that have been, those that will be, and those that are currently existing—all those spheres of earth here have attained a state of commonality in their existence.
I alone am all of them, even those that are internal; therefore, they were experienced by me, and everything was seen by me in that way.

This undecaying reality of the Supreme Self is pure consciousness alone; it maintains its state as the pure self while remaining inherent within the body. Though this entire world exists with its perceived distinctions, my dear, when realized as it truly is, it does not maintain even the slightest thing at all.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, tell me what followed; were the worlds then seen by you anywhere within the circles of the earth, or not at all?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, by means of my own nature as the mass of the earth-spheres of the supreme self’s waking and dreaming states, that was experienced within my heart and beheld with the supreme vision.
Just so, the entire web of the world remains everywhere; though everything consists of the visible and is peaceful, it is nonetheless non-dual in nature.
The worlds exist everywhere; everywhere Brahman is established. All is empty, supremely peaceful, and all is slow in its undertakings.
