Everywhere there exists the gross earth and so forth, yet that is nothing at all; it is only the sky of consciousness, like a city in a dream, unborn in the ultimate sense.
Here there is no diversity, nor is there non-diversity; there is neither non-existence nor existence. Since even "I" does not exist at all, how and what could there be anywhere?
Even this which is experienced in the form of "I am" and so forth does not exist at all; or, if it does exist, it is that unborn and undecaying Brahman.

Since this world is merely a city of dreams within the sky of consciousness from the very beginning of creation, what kind of existence or non-existence could there be therein, where, or from what source could it abide?
Just as I saw those worlds assuming the form of the earth, so too did I see them, having become water, in that very same way.
By means of the retention of water, having become water—though insentient as it were—I have long roared with a gurgling sound within the depths of the ocean abodes.
It was mounted upon the stalks of grass, trees, creepers, shrubs, and vines—so subtly that it was unnoticed—as if by a louse upon your own limbs.

In the interior of her natural form, there is a pillar like all the world's pillars; when that is cut, there is a ring-like [structure], and with softness, the arrangement is like the movement of a serpent into the ear.
Having rested upon the sprouts and fruits of the *vallī*, *tamāla*, *tāla*, and other trees, he fashioned a design with lines through his well-nourished form.
Having entered the heart through a mouth that bore the distress of the seasons, the bodily constituents were stolen, impaired, consumed, and cut away from the bodies.
He slept upon beds of sprouts in all directions simultaneously and without weariness, appearing in the form of droplets of frost.
Traversing an unceasing path that seized various lakes, rivers, houses, and villages, he found rest here and there through the favor of his friend, the bridge.
Through the continuous connection with consciousness, that which is insentient does not take refuge in it; yet it manifests within the receptacles of the insentient, like water moving in a whirlpool.
Like a wicked man, though situated upon the high rocks of kings, I have been shattered a hundredfold by falling into the abysses while remaining within my own whirlpool.
Having emerged from the wood in the form of smoke into the ocean of the sky, it remained within the blue sapphire gem by means of the spark-gem situated inside it.
It rested upon the couches of clouds together with its wife, the lightning, like Śauri upon the remaining coils of Śeṣa, which are as dark as split sapphire.
Even within this creation composed of atoms, Brahman alone, as the soul of all, remains unperceived within the forms of composite objects.
Having attained contact with the subtle tips of the tongue, an excellent experience is produced; I consider this to belong solely to the self and to pure knowledge, not to the body.
That which has not been tasted by me, nor by the body, nor by anything else, yet is perceived as an object within—that too is unreal due to ignorance.
Having fully enjoyed various blossoms of many fragrances, possessing the essence and form of all seasons, he left behind the remnants in his abode.
Within the joints of the limbs of the fourteen types of beings, it dwells—though insentient—as if sentient, and though its nature is non-intelligent, as if intelligent.
Having mounted the wind-god's chariot in the form of a mass of spray, he was as if created by the fragrance itself within the paths of the stainless sky.
O Rāma, in that state, this entire world, exactly as it exists, was experienced down to its subtlest atomic particles.
By that net-like Samaya, which is non-inert though appearing as if inert, all internal objects of experience abide, whether known or unknown.
There, hundreds of millions of worlds and hundreds of instances of destruction and emergence were seen by me, established like the stalks within the leaves of a plantain tree.
Thus, whether the world or the non-world, whether with form or formless, everything is but the sky of pure consciousness—purer than space itself.
There is neither "nothingness" nor "this is nothing"; this supreme, pure awakening shines forth. That too is not "nothing," nor is it a void; you are like space itself—be at ease in this expansion.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, through the power of the concentration on light, I became that very light, endowed with diverse limbs such as the moon, the sun, the stars, fire, and so forth.

Because it is eternally dominated by *sattva*, the entire world has arisen with the nature of luminosity; yet, apart from that which is seen, everything is joined with the pervasive darkness of thieves.
With lamps and other offerings, gentle and glistening, illuminating a thousand dwellings, he made all things manifest in every house like a divine king.

And in the Lokāloka mountain, with the hairs of its body being the rays of the moon, sun, and other luminaries bristling with joy, it cast the garment of the sky far away, delighting solely in the supreme light.
For one who possesses all virtues, the visible world is constantly perceived as both real and unreal—like darkness, like wretchedness, and the destroyer of every excellence.
It is the axe that fells the Tamāla tree of darkness, the state that effects supreme purification, and the very life-sustenance for people through gold, gems, rubies, pearls, and the like.
The giver of bodies to all castes—whether white, black, ruddy, and so forth, who eternally rest within the limbs of the moon—is like a father to his sons.
The earth protected it with the essence of thick moisture against the piercing of fire; in every house, the little lamps were surrounded by dense joys.
In the netherworlds, which consist mostly of subtle darkness, fire was seen; on the surface of the earth, adorned by living beings, it was seen only half-visible, consisting of subtle dust.
The Great Being among sentient beings, the permanence within celestial abodes, the lamp for the world’s dilapidated huts, and the great water in the well amidst darkness.
It is the stainless mirror for the brides of the quarters, the wind that dispels the frost of night, the very essence of the moon, the sun, and fire, and the saffron unguent of heaven.
The field of day-lotuses is a favor to those swollen by darkness; it is the shimmering water for washing the vast glass vessel of the sky.
Because it bestows existence upon objects and because it also illuminates them, it is like a younger brother born of the same womb as the ultimate reality of pure consciousness.
The sun that causes the lotus of action to bloom, the very life of the interior of the earth, and the wonder of the mental engagement with the perception of forms—such is consciousness.
It was garlanded with the countless jewel-like stars situated in the vault of the sky, and it was foamy with the submarine fire and other elements augmented by days, seasons, and years.
Dull with the waves of the moon, sun, and other luminaries, it is a vast, muddy expanse; situated within the great cavity of the cosmic egg, it is an eternal, undecaying single ocean.
Gold-ness in gold and the like, prowess in men and the like, the brilliance of gems and the like, and the manifestation of rain and the like;
In the orb of their moon-like faces, where the eyelashes are the decorative markings, there flows a flood of the nectar of affection; their laughter is the manifestation of friendship.
Through his own invincibility, he became a playful lover among women, possessing cheeks, arms, eyes, brows, and hands that were as formidable as those of a jackal.
The valor that treats the three worlds as mere straw, that strikes down enemies with a slap, and that turns their heads into diamonds—this is the courage found in the hearts of lions and the like.
The army moved with fierce clamor, accompanied by the sharp clanging of swords striking against armor and the loud, boastful shouts of the warriors.
Among the gods you are the enemy of the Dānavas; among the gods and others, you are the enemy of the gods. Among all beings, you are vigor; among the stationary and other things, you are height.
Then, O lotus-eyed one, I experienced myself there as a radiant god among the gods within those world-ether-receptacles.

With his webbed fingers spread across the ends of the quarters, grasping the world-bird with its limbs intact, he assumed the state of the sun, having beheld the surface of the earth as if it were a mere village.
The pericarp-wheel in the lotus of desire, the submarine fire in the ocean of darkness, the lamp in the abode of the cosmic egg, and the tree for the succession of fruits of the day.
The face of the sky is the moon, appearing like a pool of elixir; it is the laughter of the night-demoness and the blossoming of the cities of the night.
He was the object of comparison for all the fortunes of beauty in the world, and the supreme beloved of the night, Rohiṇī, women, and white water-lilies.
The cluster of stars was like a soft mass of flowers upon the creeper of the face of the multitude of eyes, and like a swarm of gnats over the flood of heaven.
The quality of being a jewel was tested by the mere merchant as his hand moved the scales, while it was tested by the oceans as their waves tossed it about with their hands.

In the water of the ocean, there is the leaping of fish and the swirling of eddies; in the water, there is a cluster of lotus stalks; at the beginning of the rain, there is the forest fire, and upon his body, the flashing of lightning.
The blazing fire was spread wide, difficult to restrain as it split the wood; it was auspicious for the burning of the sacrificial fire, emitting harsh crackling sounds.
A great splendor consisting of glittering gold, rubies, pearls, and gems eclipsed her asceticism, just as ignorance eclipses the learning of fools.
It was scattered upon the peaks of their breasts by those pearl necklaces belonging to the women of the asuras, uragas, gandharvas, and leaders of men.
I have attained the state of being trampled by feet on the road and the status of a mere tilaka mark on the face of a bride; behold the fickleness of my condition as a firefly!

In some places, among those clouds situated in the sky—which were beautiful yet distorted and resounded like whirlpools in the waters—there was a flash of lightning, as if by a sapharī fish in the oceans.
In some places, having been brought there as lamps by women with limbs as tender as flower buds, he beheld the amorous dalliances of beloveds within the inner apartments.
In some places, within its own hollows, it resembled a massive tortoise due to its attachment to masses of soot that took on the appearance of golden flames, as if weary of them.

At the end of the aeons, in certain places, due to the dense exhaustion from wandering through the entire world, he was absorbed into the sky—which is as black as collyrium—like lightning vanishing into a cloud of Rudra’s elephant.
In some places, having drunk the waters until the end of the eon by means of the submarine fire, he danced at the edges of the oceans within the worlds and the skies.

In some places, I was like one whose teeth were firebrands, with arms of flame for a body, possessing fierce locks of hair in the form of turbulent whirlpools of smoke, and endowed with agitated energy.
During the burning of cities and ponds, he made of wood and other materials—substances fit for consumption—repeatedly into morsels, swallowing all living beings within them.
In some places, sparks and fragments of stone were spat out by the weapons and rocks as they struck iron masses, as if vomited forth for the purpose of burning their own slayers.
In some great stone casket, by means of a stone-jewel, I remained for even hundreds of ages, invisible to all beings.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, bestower of honor, tell me for my enlightenment: in that state, was happiness experienced by you, or was it suffering?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as a man, though possessed of consciousness, falls into a state of insentience while asleep, so too does the space of consciousness (cidvyoma) attain the state of being an object of perception and thus experience its own insentience.
When Brahman perceives itself as the earth and so forth, then it remains within as if asleep and inert; otherwise, this would not be the case for it.
In reality, its earth and so forth are neither of the nature of non-existence nor composed of existence; like the seer and the seen, this Brahman remains uniform.
For one in whom this unbroken thorough knowledge of reality has arisen, there are no five elements, nor is there the delusion of the seen and the seer.
Then, by me alone—pure and possessing the form of Brahman—that was performed; for nothing whatsoever can be accomplished by one who is devoid of the form of Brahman.
When all this visible world was realized as the untainted Brahman, then, abiding in the state of Brahman, I perceived the Self in this very way.
But when I manifest as "the five elements" alone, then I am indeed inert; what, indeed, could I possibly perceive?
Even though he is conscious, having firmly conceived the thought "I am asleep," he enters into a state of profound sleep-like dullness; yet, even in that brilliance of stupor, he perceives something.
But for one whose self is awakened by knowledge, the physical body belonging to the elemental realm subsides, and the pure, transportive body consisting of consciousness alone arises.
By means of that subtle body of transport, which is of the nature of consciousness and either minute or vast according to its will, it abides in the state of liberation.
Having entered the heart even of stones that are otherwise indivisible by means of the body of awakening, it quickly emerges, goes to the netherworld, and traverses the sky.
Therefore, O Rāma, in the past, by me—who was then infinite, consisting of consciousness, and having the nature of the void—this was accomplished through that very body of awakening.
For one who thus swiftly performs the coming and going through diamond, stone, the underworld, the sky, and the atmosphere, no obstacle arises.
As long as that [consciousness] remains within insentient objects by means of its body consisting of pure awareness alone, it persists there in that very state.
If, having moved by its own will, it then proceeds elsewhere, that very thing returns to its state as it was, just like its coming.
The wise know that the body is merely consciousness, subtle, and imperishable; now, as a knower, you yourself experience that very thing here.

Through the realization that "I am of the nature of the void of pure consciousness" regarding the sun and other objects, the self alone is brought to its setting; though existing, it becomes as if non-existent by means of itself.
It remains in the world of dreams and the like, as if by darkness or as if by sleep, or as if veiled; it exists as something unattainable by others, yet visible to the vision [of the wise].
With Taraṅgalekhā clinging to his body like the river of charcoal, he was instantly transformed by her, as if she were the very fortune of his kingdom of desire.

With its rows of soot-like smoke, it was like a forest of fire; with the beauty of its blossoms, it took on the appearance of a bed of full-blown land-lotuses in the form of *kiṃśuka* and *aśoka* trees.
O dear one, though it was ignited by a high-flaming blaze with wide-spreading flames, it fell away effortlessly, like the fortune of a wicked man who has risen to power.

O Rāma, in this very same way, I have seen the splendor of the universe here even within the interior of a single atom; yet that is neither different from the supreme sky of consciousness, just as the multitude of mountains seen there in a dream is your illustration.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, out of curiosity to behold the world, I assumed a meditative concentration consisting of air and extended it with a steady disposition.
I am perfected as the wind, the dancer who delights in gazing upon the vine-like women, and the protector of the fragrance of the clusters of lotuses, blue water-lilies, kunda flowers, and the like.
Intent on effortlessly carrying away sprays of mist like snowfall, it yearned to refresh all the limbs weary from amorous play.

He was skilled in the rhythmic dancing of the leaves of grasses, shrubs, creepers, and climbing plants; he was adorned with the fragrance of flowers and the radiant luster of the fruits and medicinal herbs of the creepers.
Gentle during auspicious times, he was cherished by the glances of women; yet formidable during times of calamity, like a massive mountain with its foliage.
In the Nandana grove, he was ruddy with the pollen of the nectar from kunda and mandāra flowers; in hell, he was radiant with a thick frost amidst heaps of glowing embers.
In the ocean, his movement was inferred from the straight lines of the whirlpools; in the sky, the mirror of the moon was polished and wiped by the shifting clouds.
The chariot of Nakṣatra-kṣatrasainya, increased in speed, was capable of supporting the celestial palaces where the Siddhas of the three worlds travel.
Because his mind moved so swiftly, it was as if he were a uterine brother; though bodiless, he possessed all limbs, being like sandalwood that brings joy through its very vibration.
He was worn out by the aging of his body-hair from the shower of frost-spray; he was the intoxication of the youth of fragrance, and possessed the childhood of silence and softness.
Sweet with the fragrance of the Nandana grove, flowing through a delightful and noble course, released from the beautiful Caitraratha forest, it has removed the fatigue of passion in the wilderness.
For a long time, he was exhausted by the swaying of his body upon the waves of the Ganges; yet, through ignorance of the true nature of fatigue, he did not cease that exertion.
For a long time, he made the creepers of the spring grove—those young women bent low under the weight of flowers—tremble with his touches, their leaf-hands and bee-eyes flickering.
Having long enjoyed the tip of the moon’s orb, she slept upon a bed of full clouds; now, having shaken off the host of lotuses, her fatigue from lovemaking has been dispelled.
He alone is the horse that traverses the sky above all the dusts; he is the great friend who brings forth the exultation of the elephant intoxicated with the fragrance of ichor.
The cloud, acting as a cowherd, reached the peak of the lightning with its slow pace; it was like an enemy to the dust-storms, weaving a thread from the pearls of spray-drops.
It is the fragrance of a flower in the sky, the uterine brother of all sounds; it is the water in the channels and conduits, and that which sets in motion the limbs and members of living beings.

He whose sole essence is the performance of vital actions, the lion within the house of the cave of the heart, is the eternal traveler on the solitary path, the knower of the essence of the fire of consciousness.
A plunderer of the jewels of fragrance, the ground for the city of celestial chariots, a moon to the darkness of burning heat, and a milky ocean for the coolness of the moon.

By means of the rope of the currents of inhalation and exhalation, he is the driver of the machine for living beings; he is both enemy and friend to the continents, delighting in their constant movement from one to another.
Though appearing before one, its nature is invisible, resembling a city of the mind's kingdom; it is like a palm-leaf fan, sesame oil, or a tethering post for a flickering elephant.
In a single moment, he caused all the mountains to tremble, acting as the sole creator of the waves of colored syllables like the flow of the Gaṅgā.
It creates great whirlpools of smoke, clouds, dust, and waters; it is the current of the celestial river, a mass of rain, and a swarm of bees upon the blue lotuses of the sky.
He is the wind that fans away the old grass wrapped around his body; he is the sun for the forest of lotuses that are his quivering limbs; and he is the sole rain-cloud for the downpour of sound.
He is the elephant in the forest of the sky, the whirlpool in the house of the body, and the lover who embraces the grove of kadamba trees in the dust.
Through the six activities of solidifying, drying, supporting, moving, perfuming, and cooling, [the wind] continues until its moment [of cessation] is attained, and thus remains inexhaustible.
Constantly intent on extracting the essences like a brother of the vital heat (*tejas*), he effects the application of the bodily constituents that perform the functions of taking up and discarding.
In the city of the body, moving unimpeded through the pathways of the channels, he is the great merchant of the jewel of life, who turns over the vessel of vital essence.
He is solely intent on the destruction and reconstruction of the city of the body, and is skilled in separating the essence, the waste, the subtle portions, and the constituent elements.
Then, within the body, I perceived the world down to its most subtle atoms; therein, I appeared clearly as a form, expansive and perfectly stable.
In this regard, the creators of the world seem to be carried along atom by atom; yet nothing at all is actually being carried, for when it is one's own doing, what is there to be carried?
Together with the Moon, Sun, Wind, Fire, Indra, Padma, Vaiśravaṇa, and Īśvara; along with Brahmā, Hari, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Mahoragas.

Together with the oceans, mountains, islands, and the far reaches of the quarters like a great sea, and including the intermediate worlds, the world-protectors, their activities, time, and the sequence of its divisions.

[He beheld] the worlds including heaven, earth, and the depths of Pātāla, along with the intermediate realms, together with their states of existence and non-existence, their privations, and the terrors of old age and death.
Thus indeed, O Rāma, at that time I sported there within the interior of the lotus of the three worlds, having assumed the form of the five elements.
The essence of earth, water, air, and fire was drunk and experienced by me while dwelling within the root-systems of trees and living beings.
He rolled upon her limbs, which were like elixirs of immortality and beautiful with the liquid application of sandalwood paste, as if rolling upon the orb of the moon or upon beds of frost.
In the groves of all seasons, he fully enjoyed the various fragrances of clusters of flowers in every direction, leaving behind only the remnants in his abode.
He slept upon soft, well-spread carpets on the courtyard floor that rose and fell in places, like masses of white clouds resting upon beds of fresh butter.
Upon the limbs of the celestial and Siddha women—limbs as soft as jasmine petals, radiant with the splendor of dark blue beauty—the latent impressions of passion were cast far away.
In the forest of lotuses, amidst the white, blue, and red water-lilies, a soft and playful clamor was raised by the female swans.

The mountains were like the abodes of body-hairs, possessing the essence of lakes and rivers as their veins, endowed with the circle of the earth as their roots, and bearing upon their limbs living beings that quivered with life.
The Khādira mountains are renowned for their long river-threads and small seas, which rest upon their limbs like mirrors reflecting images.
The creation of beings—including Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others—rested within my body as if perceived by it, like flies and ants forming a single mass.
By my grace, the Sun and the other planets obtained their bodies, which were joyful and colored black, red, white, yellow, and green, as if they were various types of emeralds.
By means of the ocean-seal, which consists of the seven continents and the sevenfold self-form, the earth was established in the forearm like a bracelet.
Though his slender body was touched by the wives of the Vidyādharas, he experienced a thrill of horripilation within himself as if it were done by one unseen.
The worlds themselves became the networks of my bones—vast, hollow, and filled with the pure, flowing essence of the veins of rivers.
It dwells within my heart like gnats inside a fig, amidst countless sky-elephants with the sun and moon as their moving chowries.
O Rāma, even then, with his feet resting upon all the netherworlds and supporting the belly of the earth, he did not abandon his state as the supreme atom by means of his own head.
It exists in all directions, everywhere, at all times, as the agent of all things; it abides as the void-nature, which is both the self of all and yet not-all.
I have sufficiently experienced being something while being nothingness; having form while being formless; and being conscious while possessing inertia.
Furthermore, thousands of creations have been brought forth by me toward the earth from the ocean, which is as vast and deep as Maināka and remains as motionless as a pillar.
The worlds, whether hidden or manifest, were borne upon his limbs by Maya, like cities of reflection within a mirror that is not insentient.
Thus, by me, through my own nature as space, the states of water, wind, fire, and earth were created—alas, a manifestation of illusion, like that of consciousness within dreams.
Moreover, in that state, I beheld countless worlds within the hollow of space, even within every single atom.
Space exists within every atom, just as a multitude of creations exists within each atom, like a city joined with another dream within a dream.
I myself was the entire circle of the earth with its continents as its earrings; yet, even with my whole self, nothing whatsoever was pervaded by me anywhere.
By producing every shoot of creeper, tree, and grass, I have extracted the very essence from the surface of the earth for the sake of those who bear human form.
When the time for awakening through battle has arrived, which is most pure, some millions of worlds endure, while others do not.
Those who manifest wonder within consciousness, and whose own wonders reside within, these are the visions of creation.
Whatever suffering has been experienced or undergone, however and wherever it may be, nothing is perceived here apart from the wonder of ultimate reality.
Each [individual] is of the nature of the universal form, the creator of all, free from affliction, awakened, and of the nature of pure consciousness, because everything has Brahman as its essence.
All, everywhere, the self of all, all-pervading, and the refuge of all—this is the domain of the awakened; I do not know it as unawakened.

Within the nature of consciousness, which is as clear as the expanse of space, this succession of creations always shines forth; yet that [succession] is indeed within that very [consciousness], like internal heat within fire, appearing as the perception of duality. Thus, there is no existent thing, only the infinite.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, having turned back from such a state of consciousness with great effort, I arrived at that place within the interior of the hut of the sky.
As long as I did not see my own body situated anywhere there, I saw only some other perfected being (siddha) standing before me.
Seated, established in meditative absorption, he had attained his desired goal; he was like the sun at its gentle rising, or like a fire whose fuel has been consumed.
Seated in the bound lotus posture, peaceful, motionless in meditative absorption, with the testicles situated between the two ankles, he has transcended the objects of the senses.
His neck was beautiful with shoulders of smooth, gentle, and even fullness; he was lovely in his posture, which was firm, noble, and resting with perfect composure.
He was illuminated by the radiance of his two hands, which were turned upward near his navel, as if by the splendors of the heart-lotus shining forth externally.
With its eyelashes closed and all vision extinguished, it attained a state of clarity like a lake at the end of day, with its lotuses shut and fallen asleep.
With a steady disposition, he bore within the hollow of his inner organ a state that was unagitated and profoundly calm, like the sky when all portents have subsided.

Not seeing my own body, yet seeing that sage before me, I then thought this with a beautiful mind: idaṃ mayā tadā tatra cintitaṃ cārucetasā // Not seeing my own body, yet seeing that sage before me, I then thought this with a beautiful mind: "By what means shall I behold him? For he is not within the range of my sight. "By what means shall I behold him? For he is not within the range of my sight. iti sañcintya manasā bhūyastenaiva hetunā / Having thus reflected in my mind, for that very reason once more, tasyaivābhimukho bhūtvā sthito 'ham acalendravat // I stood facing him alone, as immovable as the king of mountains. atha tena munīndreṇa kṛtā me 'bhyutthitena sā / Then by that lord of sages, having risen, that [welcoming] gesture was made toward me; arghapādyādikaṃ sarvaṃ vidhinā parikalpitam // the entire offering of water for the feet and guest-offering was prepared according to the ritual rules. tenaiva ca mayā tatra dṛṣṭo 'sau munipuṅgavaḥ / And by that very [vision], I saw there that bull among sages, sākṣāt pratyakṣataḥ śrīmān yathāvad upalakṣitaḥ // the glorious one, perceived exactly as he is in direct, manifest presence. tatas tena mayā tatra pṛṣṭaḥ sa munisattamaḥ / Then I questioned that best of sages there: "O venerable one, who are you? And from where have you come? ity uktaḥ sa mayā tatra prāha māṃ sa mahāmuniḥ / Thus addressed by me, that great sage spoke to me there: "Know me, O dear one, to be the son of the sage Agastya, born of Lopāmudrā. evam uktvā sa mām āha punar eva mahāmuniḥ / Having spoken thus, that great sage said to me again: "Tell me, O fortunate one, what is the purpose of your coming here? iti pṛṣṭas tena tadā mayā proktaṃ mahātmanā / When asked this by him, I then replied to that high-souled one: "I have come here, O venerable one, desiring to see you. ity uktaḥ sa mayā tatra prāha māṃ sa mahāmuniḥ / Thus addressed by me, that great sage spoke to me there: "Enough of this talk of seeing me; it is useless, O dear one. For I am not seen by those whose minds are distracted by worldly objects. iti tena munīndreṇa prokte tasmin mahātmanā / When this was said by that lord of sages, the high-souled one, mayāpi cintitaṃ tatra hṛdaye cārucetasā // I too then reflected in my heart with a beautiful mind: "Alas, what a great delusion is this! That I have come here for no purpose. And from where have you come? ity uktaḥ sa mayā tatra prāha māṃ sa mahāmuniḥ / Thus addressed by me, that great sage spoke to me there: "Know me, O dear one, to be the son of the sage Agastya, born of Lopāmudrā. evam uktvā sa mām āha punar eva mahāmuniḥ / Having spoken thus, that great sage said to me again: "Tell me, O fortunate one, what is the purpose of your coming here? iti pṛṣṭas tena tadā mayā proktaṃ mahātmanā / When asked this by him, I then replied to that high-souled one: "I have come here, O vener
"Someone who is a great adept has arrived here in this region; like me, he seeks solitude for the sake of rest in the vast sky."
With the thought, "May I find a secluded place suitable for meditative concentration," this hut was seen by him, who was endowed with the power of true resolve.
Because he did not consider my arrival for a long time, he has cast off that body of his which had become a corpse and established himself here.
"Therefore, I shall go now to my own world"—having made this resolve, just as I was about to depart, [my body vanished] due to the dissolution of my mental constructs.
That hut having vanished, only empty space remained there; though he was a perfected one endowed with meditative absorption, he fell downward, being without support.

When that small hut—like a city within a dream or a mental construction—was destroyed through the subsiding of my own volition, and with the cessation of that dream-like construction, [the world vanished].
Then that meditator fell from there like a torrent of water from a cloud, like a cloud driven by the wind from the sky, or like the lunar orb at the end of an eon.
Like a demigod fallen from his celestial chariot, like a tree whose roots have been severed, or like a stone cast from the sky, he fell from there onto the earth.
While he was thinking, "As long as this hut exists, so long shall I exist," his [limited] existence was exhausted; when the destruction of the hut occurred, he fell, perfected, in an instant.
As that Siddha was falling from there, out of curiosity born of my innate goodness, I descended from the sky to the surface of the earth by means of my mind alone.
He fell, through the circular whirls of the wind's mass, onto the pleasure-grounds of the gods at the edge of the seven continents and oceans.

Because his vital breaths (prāṇa) and downward breaths (apāna) were moving upward, he remained suspended in the sky exactly as he was; having previously cast his feet upward toward the earth, he fell while remaining in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana).
Wandering about, he remained unconscious and did not wake up; he was like a body made of stone, or as light as if his very self were cotton wool.
Then, striving to understand that [matter], I assumed the form of a cloud in the sky and let fall a thunderous roar.
By that falling of hailstones in that direction, he awakened this [man] with his intellect, as the rainy season awakens a peacock.
With the beauty of his limbs illuminated and his eyes blossoming, he became like a bed of lotuses in the rainy season, its very self in full bloom from the mass of falling showers.
When his vision had become perfectly tranquil, I questioned that awakened one who stood before me, with a clear disposition, as he had turned away from the ultimate reality.
Where do you stand, and what are you doing here, O leader of sages? Who are you, and why do you not fall even from such a great distance, though your mind is so far away?
Thus addressed, he looked at me and, recollecting his former state, spoke these charming words, just as a cātaka bird addresses a rain-cloud.
The Siddha said: "Wait for me while I recall my own history; afterwards, I shall relate to you the account of my later life."
Having spoken thus and reflected quickly, he remembered his own conduct exactly as it had occurred, just as one remembers the day's events at evening.
Then he spoke these words to me—charming, cool as the rays of the moon, delightful, irreproachable, faultless, and bringing about happiness.
The Siddha said: "O Brahmin, you have now been recognized by me; I offer my salutations. This transgression must be forgiven, for forgiveness is indeed the nature of the virtuous."
O Sage, for a long time I have wandered among the grounds of the celestial groves, deluded by the fragrance of enjoyments like a bee among lotus ponds.
Then, as I was being carried away by the whirlpools of the visible river through the play of the waves of the water of the mind, I became distressed and thought:
In the ocean of saṃsāra, I was agitated by the waves of visible objects; in time, I fell into distress like a cātaka bird during a drought.
In these enjoyments whose sole essence is pure consciousness, what indeed is there that is truly delightful? I shall remain only in the sky of consciousness itself, free from all agitation.
Apart from the mere [elements of] sound, form, taste, touch, and smell, there is nothing else whatsoever here; why then do I take delight in this much?
All this is indeed the space of pure consciousness, or rather, it is pure consciousness alone; so why do I, with a ruined intellect, take delight in this unreal form as if it were real?

Sense objects are like the unevenness of poison; they are deceptive and bestow the delusion of desire. Their flavors turn into a distasteful bitterness; who, rolling about in them, has not been destroyed?
The intellect, which is like a decayed female crab in the mud of life, now wishes to seize the body with swift motion; it is like a large female crab desiring old age.
This body is soon to perish, like a bubble in the ocean; though it flickers before one, it vanishes within the city [of the heart] just like the flame of a lamp.
With its various turbulent waves, it creates whirlpools and eddies; with birth and death as its great banks, it has pleasure and pain for its ripples.
Turbid with the splendor of youth, foaming white with old age, and possessing bubbles of happiness produced by chance, like the falling of a fruit upon a crow.

It is crowded with the noise of the dull-witted from the great stream of legal proceedings; it is filled with the dense manifestation of passion and hatred; and its bodies are restless upon the surface of the earth.
Alas! This river called "life," though sounding cool, is a great whirlpool of greed and delusion, where one is tossed up and down and whirled about.
The waters of the river of saṃsāra and the riches that have come together are such that new ones arrive and the old ones depart completely.
Enough with those wretched beings who, having come forth, turn back; for what kind of reliance can there be here upon those unprecedented ones who keep coming forth?
The water of every river flows from the ocean and returns to it; but the water of the river of the body, which is life, flows away and never returns again.
Hundreds of times, moment by moment, for each individual aggregate, entities revolve in the ocean of existence like the rotations of a potter’s wheel.
The four thieves roam about—the treacherous enemies that are the sense-objects; they carry away the entire wealth of one's being. Am I awake here, or am I asleep?
Pieces of life fall away again and again; alas, no one perceives that the days are being consumed by time!
"Today this is mine, and likewise this, and likewise this; this belongs to me"—by such reckoning, alas, the world does not realize what has passed or what has been attained.
I have eaten and drunk, and I have wandered through endless forest lands; I have seen joys and sorrows—what else remains here to be accomplished?
Because of the repeated experience of pleasure and pain, because of the constant turning back [of rebirth], and because all phenomena are impermanent, we remain free from worldly curiosity.
Multitudes of enjoyments have been experienced and the extreme impermanence of things has been witnessed; yet, not even a slight sense of rest is found anywhere here.
Having wandered through the lofty peaks and the grove lands of Mount Meru, and having reached high into the cities of the World-Protectors, what unartificial thing have I found?
Trees everywhere are made of wood, beings of flesh, and the earth of clay; suffering and impermanence are likewise universal—tell me, how can one find comfort in this?
Neither wealth, nor friends, nor pleasures, nor kinsmen are able to protect a person who has been seized by time.
Like water within the belly of a cloud, a person vanishes into the hollows of mountains; as fragile as a heap of dust, he sets into utter emptiness.
Sensual pleasures do not delight me, nor do magnificent riches; even this life of mine is as flickering as the arching glance of an intoxicated woman.
O Sage, where, for whom, how, or from what source could there possibly be consolation? For today or tomorrow, death—the wicked—places calamity upon one's head.
The body falls away like a leaf; life is a worn-out structure; the vital flavors are seized by the lack of fortitude and have become sapless.
My life has been spent merely through dry desires; not even the slightest desired object of my own has produced any wonder for me.
Today delusion has come upon me; this body is of no further use here. Indifference alone is the supreme state; attachment to worldly standing is the lowest condition.
Alas, this calamity has indeed befallen us, producing such delusion; one must always think thus: "I am not attached here in this cycle of existence."
By means of injunctions and prohibitions, both eternal and non-eternal, the world is led according to its desires, like water by depressions and elevations.
Having stolen from the heart-lotus its entire essence of the fragrance of discernment, the winds of the sense-objects induce a swoon.

Just so, that which is indeed non-existent is seen to have attained existence; in such a way that the non-existent itself has become the form of the existent, and the non-existent itself has become the existent.
Just as the wives of the ocean run along the earth, swaying their bodies back and forth, so do people run after sense-objects.

The arrows of the mind, once released toward their target, rush toward sense objects; they do not return to touch the bowstring again, just as ungrateful people do not return to their former friendship.
The wind of calamity is indeed one's life; friends are indeed enemies; kinsmen are indeed bonds; and wealth is indeed extreme poverty.
Pleasures are indeed extreme sufferings; prosperities are supreme calamities; enjoyments are the great diseases of existence; and delight is itself the ultimate aversion.
All calamities and prosperities result only in suffering; life leads only to death—alas, this is the unfolding of illusion!
Beholding many revolutions of time, both desirable and undesirable things, and even slight pleasures, as well as separations from loved ones, a person reaches a state of complete exhaustion.
Enjoyments consist of the indulgence in sense objects; like the hoods of serpents, they bite as soon as they are slightly touched, and having been seen, they vanish every moment.
Life passes away for those who are devoid of attaining the state free from exertion, through formidable and painful activities whose forms are fragile at their conclusion.
For those bound by thirst for the hope of enjoyments, there is humiliation at every step, like wild elephants tethered to a hitching post.
Prosperity and women are as transient as the crests of waves; what wise man would take delight in them, which are like the shade cast by the hood of a serpent?
Truly, sensual pleasures are enchanting; truly, worldly prosperities are delightful; yet life is as fickle as the flickering glance from the corner of an intoxicated woman's eye.
Those who delight in sense objects that are charming only at first sight fall into hells whose ultimate end is utter desolation.
Wealth that is obstructed by the defects of dualities, difficult to acquire, unstable, and fit only for those lacking noble character, has never brought me satisfaction.
Sweet only at first sight and ending in suffering, fortune is a momentary plaything intended solely for the delusion of the world.
Associations with the wicked are pleasant at first sight, but they dissolve upon closer examination; they bestow suffering and bring about calamity.
The splendors of youth are as fleeting as the shadow of autumn clouds; sense objects are pleasant at first encounter but bring torment in the end.
The Ender stands as an obstacle even for the lives of the great; the lifespans of embodied beings waver like water hanging from the tip of a branch.
The hair of one who grows old decays; having offered it as a sacrifice, the teeth of one who grows old decay. Everything decays as one grows old, but craving alone does not decay.
In the entire forest of the body, which is dense with the enjoyment and non-enjoyment of pleasures, there flourishes the supreme, uneven cluster of the single creeper of craving.

Childhood passes away like youth, and youth passes away like childhood; thus, these two possess a mutual relationship of both the standard of comparison and the object compared, as well as a shared fragility.
Life slips away quickly like water from cupped hands; like the current of a river, once gone, it does not return.
The body arrives suddenly from somewhere, like the wind of Arjuna; it sets even as one watches, like a wave, a cloud, or a lamp.
In beautiful things, unloveliness has been seen; in stable things, instability as well; and in objects that are real, unreality. Therefore, we have become disenchanted with this world.
When the mind has attained the state of pure being through rest in the Self, that bliss which arises is not found in any enjoyments whatsoever, whether in the netherworld, on earth, or in heaven.
Even though their objects are entirely delightful, these five functions of the senses still conquer me, just as variegated creepers entice a bee.
After a long time, through a mind free from egoism, I have today attained this state of freedom from craving for heaven and liberation.
For the sake of long-lasting repose in solitude, he came here to this region of the sky; like you, I have arrived here and beheld that hut.
Today this has been fully understood: that this is your hut, and that you will come here again; previously, I did not reflect upon that.
Then, however, I realized here through inference that this was some perfected being (siddha) who, having abandoned his body, had attained nirvāṇa in this very place.
"O Blessed One, this is my life story; 'this is who I am'—I have told you everything exactly as it is. Now do as you see fit."

O Sage, it is the very nature of even the minds of Brahmā and the other gods that as long as the remaining reality has not been investigated and determined by the perfected ones (siddhas) of superior intellect through focused attention, they do not know anything regarding the calculation of the three periods of time.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, upon that great ground as vast as the golden sky, I spoke these words to that Siddha solely out of affection.
Not only by you, but even by me this has not been considered: that for embodied beings, there can be no such thing as a lack of pervasion.
Why did I, having deliberated upon your situation, stabilize this hut in the sky? For had I not done so, you would have remained in a state of instability.
Arise! Let us dwell as we are in the worlds of the Siddhas; for those who abide in their own place, O gentle one, are the excellent means for the realization of their own self.
Having thus resolved, those two, resembling stars, soared high into the sky together with a single bound, like two stones released from a catapult.
Then, having exchanged mutual salutations and taken our leave, he departed for his desired destination, and I too departed for my own desired destination.
Thus have I related this entire account to you, O Raghava; behold the wondrous and manifold variety of the cycles of existence.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, this body of yours has become minute upon the earth; by what body did you wander through the worlds of the Siddhas?"
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: "Listen, I have remembered; hear then the account of my wandering within the house of the universe, among the hosts of Siddhas and in the cities of the world-protectors."
I reached the city of Indra, yet no one there saw me, for I was devoid of a physical body and possessed only a subtle, transportable form.
Then, O Rāma, it is said that he became like the sky; neither support nor supported, his nature consisted of the space of consciousness.
For those like you who have realized the true nature of reality, there is neither a grasper nor anything to be grasped; nor does anything anywhere obstruct the course of space and time.
Consisting solely of the nature of mental ideation, devoid of earth and the other elements, having the form of a person created by volition, it does not obstruct external objects.
And being himself unobstructed by the flood of objects and turned toward his own direct experience, he engages in worldly activity with such beings who are likewise composed of mind.
O Rāma, the experience of dreams is an unassailable illustration in this matter; let there be enough for you who would deny such experience.
Just as a dream-walker is not seen engaging in activities within a house, so too was I not seen at that time by those situated in the sky, even though I stood right before them.
I see others shining with the forms of kings, yet no one at all sees me, the subtle transmigrating self.
Śrī Rāma said: "If you are not seen because of your bodiless state and your body is like the sky, then how was it that you were seen by that Siddha in the Golden Forest?"

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as people like us do not obtain what is not conceived by their own volition—since we possess bodies whose desires are realized through that very conception—so it is with all beings.
By a person whose pure self is immersed in worldly affairs, the subtle body (ātivāhika) of the self is forgotten in an instant.
At that time, he formed the intention, "May he see me"; therefore, he saw me, becoming the recipient of the object of his own volition.

An ordinary person, because of the state of being subject to decay, is not a vessel for the objects of his own volition; yet this very person, through the state of having transcended decay, becomes a vessel for the fulfillment of his true desires.
When two accomplished persons possess powers that are mutually contradictory yet desired, the one who possesses greater purity of self and human effort is the victor.
As I wandered through the cities of the world-protectors amidst the hosts of Siddhas, that nature of my self as a *ativāhika* was forgotten by the flood of worldly affairs.
Whenever I then began to interact with others in the great sky, no one there perceived me as something flickering.
O sinless one, even when I cry out most loudly, my voice is not heard by anyone in the worlds of the gods, like that of a man in a dream.
For me, who am embodied by the thinking of the mind and whose activity is already firmly grasped, not even the slightest thing remains to be grasped by anything else.
Thus, O descendant of Raghu, I became a sky-demon; I experienced this extraordinary state of being a demon in a temple of the gods.
Śrī Rāma said: Piśācas exist in this world; what is their form, what is their dwelling place, what is their lineage, what is their conduct, and what is their appearance and disposition?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen to what kind of piśācas exist in this world; he is not a refined person who does not speak words that arise in the course of conversation.
Certain piśācas, possessing subtle bodies like the ether and endowed with hands, feet, and other limbs, perceive your form just as you do.
By means of a shadow that is terrifying in one place and deceptive in another, they take possession of the mind and awaken the latent tendencies of men.
They swiftly kill, devour, and drink the blood of people of weak character and strength; indeed, having assailed the mind, they destroy the power, the character, and the very lives of beings.
Some are like space, some resemble mist; some have the form of men in a dream, and even those with forms are of the nature of one's own self.
Some resemble fragments of clouds, some have bodies of wind, and some consist of nothing but delusion; all are composed of the intellect and the mind.
They are not fit to be grasped, nor are they able to be grasped; those whose nature is empty like space perceive their own form.
They experience pleasure and pain caused by cold, heat, and so forth; yet they are unable to drink, eat, grasp, or even exert effort.
Endowed with desire, hatred, fear, anger, greed, and delusion, they are brought under control by mantras, medicinal herbs, asceticism, charity, fortitude, and dharma.
By means of a machine that subdues beings, or by a mantra that has been propitiated, they are sometimes seen or even captured by someone somewhere.
For that [state] is indeed a divine womb; therefore, some are like gods and so forth, some possess a splendor equal to humans, and some possess the characteristics of nāgas.
Some, resembling dogs and jackals, dwell in villages and forests; others live in irrigation canals, rubbish heaps, and streets, as well as in hells.
"These are their abodes" and "these are their forms"—such are they proclaimed to be. Piśācas have such conduct; now hear this concerning their birth.
Brahman, which is non-objective and composed of consciousness, exists by its own nature as all-powerful; though it is ever-awakened within, it appears as if conceiving objects of thought.
Know that living principle (jīva) to be matured as what is traditionally called ego (ahaṃkāra); that ego, when fully developed, is designated by those who know the Self as the mind (manas).
He alone is called Brahmā, whose nature is the space of volition; he is the formless seed of the unreal world, arising from the unreal itself.
Thus, Brahmā, though established in the mind and possessing a body, is like the stainless sky; appearing in the form of a man in a dream, he is always existent yet eternally without a real body.
Devoid of material forms such as earth and the rest, he possesses a subtle, transportable body; for how indeed could earth and the other elements exist in the sky for a person of mere volition?
Just as your mind perceives a city imagined within space, so too does it perceive the state of being devoid of mind as something imagined within itself.
Whatever one knows as imagined, that one sees and even experiences as real; why indeed should one not see that which is exactly as it is?
Whatever he perceives is of that same nature: the self is empty, the sky is empty; whether it be Brahman in Brahman or Brahmā, this is what is called the world.
Likewise, at present, through long-term and singular cultivation, this manifestation of his has become dense, stable, and nourished, appearing as beautiful as a very long dream.
Because of his long-standing contemplation of that subtle body (ātivāhika-deha), even though he is Brahman and possesses the nature of Brahman, he experiences the manifold creation of Brahmā.
Having attained the state of a physical body through the excellence of its manifestation, that very [consciousness] is called "creation," shining forth as a continuous stream of differentiation.
That Brahmā, whose self consists solely of Brahman, [perceives] those two—the world and his own self—which are both eternally unborn and identical with that Brahman.
They dwell in a state of absolute identity, being entirely inseparable like emptiness and space, or like the wind and its movement.
One perceives that state as consisting of the elements, yet it is merely false and not real, just as you perceive the existence or non-existence of a person created by your own imagination.
Then, by means of those elements of the body, the five designations beginning with earth were established; nourished by consciousness, they remain as what is called the "world."
Just as this resolve of yours was indeed unreal while that [other resolve] was real, so too did he experience his own resolve as being truly real.
He himself is the sky of consciousness; he is volition, the ether of awareness. Therefore, the entire world is a dream, and within its creation, both destruction and emergence abide.
Just as this mind is real, so too its parts are indeed real; likewise, the rays of the moon, Rudra, and the sun produced by it are real.
This being the case, the web of the world is said to be its mental kingdom; and that is empty, without support, a manifestation in consciousness like the appearance of space.
Just as a city in a dream, as the mountain of one's imagination, and as the sky, so too are Brahman and the world—merely the void, pure and formless.
Thus, for that which is imperishable and shines as mere appearance without ceasing, the perceptions of creation, its middle, and its end have arisen here in vain and remain so.
O sinless one, tell me: within the expanse of space that is yours, mine, or even that of the world, does anything ever truly arise, or does anything ever perish?
Tell me, for what purpose have passion, hatred, fear, and the like arisen—purposeless, meaningless, and useless, leading only to misfortune?
In reality, my dear, there is neither creation nor beginning, nor is there non-creation; this which has once appeared always exists in this very manner.
In the sky of consciousness—which is not empty, possesses vast expansion, is filled with the water of pure awareness, yet is turbid with the mud of mental constructs—it will come to be.
In the field of the inexhaustible intermediate space, from the self that is of the nature of the sky, this vast range of rocks consisting of living beings has arisen from that seed.
There is no field here whatsoever that is sown, nor is there anything at all; there is no seed, nothing has been born, and yet everything remains established.
Those stone rings there that are thick are the gods and so forth; those, however, which are brilliant in color are the Buddhas, established in their own state with awakened intellects.
Those which are half-cooked are these species such as humans, nāgas, and so forth; those which are solidified and free from passion are worms, plants, and the like.
Those [female spirits] who are heavy yet devoid of fruit, empty in form, subject to decay and injury, bodiless yet possessing bodies, are known as piśācas and the like.
For the will of one who intends is never to be questioned; such was the will of Viriñca, and thus they were so named and so produced.

All classes of beings are indeed of the nature of the space of consciousness; they possess subtle, transportable bodies and are devoid of an essence consisting of earth and the other material elements.
Through the power of long-term practice and by virtue of prolonged experience, they attained the consciousness of the physical world, just as one attains the waking state from a dream.

Likewise, these beings such as Piśācas and others, who are of a similar nature and belong to the realm of living entities, remain with contented minds, dwelling within their own respective cycles of existence.
Some look at one another like villagers looking at country folk; these classes of beings are as if inhabitants of a world that exists only in a dream.
Some, like a world produced by the transformations of dreams experienced by many men, do not see one another, though they are situated in various different forms.
Just as these base-born beings such as piśācas exist in the world, so too do these kumbhāṇḍas, yakṣas, pretas, and others generally exist.
Just as water here on earth remains in low-lying places, so too do the piśācas and other such beings abide wherever there is darkness.
If even at midday a piśāca stands personally in the courtyard, his very presence there creates a profound darkness.
The sun does not destroy that [reflection], nor does anything else perceive it; yet the sun itself experiences it—behold the unfolding of illusion!

Just as fire, the sun, the moon, and so forth possess a luminous sphere (*taijasam maṇḍalam*), so too do piśācas and other such beings possess a dark sphere (*tāmasam maṇḍalam*) that is unproduced by external causes.
In light, the lack of vitality prevails, while in darkness, vitality predominates; that owls, piśācas, and the like [behave] in such a way is a marvel resulting from their very nature.

Thus I have described to you, in accordance with the tradition, this birth of one born as a Piśāca; for it was in connection with this that I said, "I am born in the worlds of the guardians of the celestial realm, though equal to a Piśāca."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, with a body consisting of the space of consciousness and devoid of the five elements, I remained wandering in the sky like a piśāca spirit.
Neither the moon, the sun, nor Śakra; neither Hari, Hara, and the others; nor the gods, siddhas, gandharvas, kinnaras, or the hosts of apsarases see me.
"They do not approach me when I approach them, nor do they listen to my words; thus I have fallen into delusion, like a good man who has been sold."
Then I thought: "These hosts of gods desire the truth; let them behold me in that abode of the gods."
All those residents began to look at me from the front, and in an instant, they reached the city which was like a tree of illusion.
Then, having become a fit participant in the dwellings of the gods, I remained there conducting myself according to their established customs, my actions free from all hesitation.
By those who saw me rising from the sacrificial altar without knowing my true history, I am celebrated in the worlds as Vasiṣṭha, the king.
By those who, traveling through the sky, beheld me in the heavens amidst the rays of the sun, I am celebrated in the worlds as Vasiṣṭha the Luminous.
I was seen by those perfected beings (siddhas) dwelling in the sky who had arisen from the wind, and I was addressed by them as Vātavasiṣṭha.
When I emerged from the water, those lords of sages who saw me said, "I am Vasiṣṭha of the waters"; such is the continuity of my birth.
From that time forward, I became renowned in the world as a king in some places, as one composed of water in others, as one consisting of fire for some, and as one of wind in others.
Then, in the course of time, within that very same subtle body (ativāhika), the state of being a physical body (ādhibhautikatā) became firmly established in me, driven by internal impulses.
This state of transcendency and this materiality of space—both of these, being of the nature of a single body, shine forth from my consciousness.
Thus, my self is in some places space; though I am of the nature of light, I am also the sky. I am the supreme formless reality, yet I appear possessed of form within you.
Acting while liberated in this life, he remains thus as one whose nature is the ether of Brahman; likewise, even when liberated after the fall of the body, he persists as nothing but Brahman alone.
I am not devoid of Brahmanhood even through such worldly conduct, because nothing else of that nature is possible; yet, among you and others, I am indeed "I."
Just as an ignorant person perceives a dream-man as having birth and physical form when he is actually unborn and formless, so too do I perceive the world.
In this very way, all the self-existent ones and their creations appear; yet they are not born, but proceed as if impelled.
I am that very same Vasiṣṭha here in the sky; today, through the practice of my own self, I have attained a state of fullness, or rather, your own state of being.
All these are indeed of the nature of space and are self-existent; for just as this is merely mind, so too are these creations.
This creation, of which I am the beginning, has—due to the fault of lack of discernment—attained a diamond-like hardness for you fools, like a vampire.
But once fully understood, it subsides in a very short time, just as affection for a relative who has gone far away diminishes due to the fading of latent impressions.
Having attained density, the creation thus subsides, just as one who has fully understood the nature of a dream-treasure ceases to regard it as something to be grasped.
All views regarding the visible world subside when they are fully understood, just as the notions of grasping the water in the current of a mirage-river subside.
By merely observing this great treatise, which is like the Mahārāmāyaṇa, this [liberation] is eternally attained; what is difficult in such a small matter?
If one's intellect is attached to the non-existence of the latent impressions of saṃsāra, that dull-witted person who has no longing for liberation is either a dog, a worm, or a mere human being.
This very experience of enjoyment is indeed one thing when experienced by one whose intellect is liberated while living; how else would it be for one who indulges in folly?
Merely by beholding this scripture, which is like a great Rāmāyaṇa, an inner coolness arises that is like snow toward the interests of others.
Liberation is the state of a cool mind, while bondage is the state of a tormented mind; yet even regarding this, people have no desire—oh, the delusion of the world!

This person, by nature enslaved by sense objects and mutually greedy for women and wealth, may become happy through the correct perception of reality and through the investigation of the meaning of the scriptures of those seeking liberation.

Śrī Vālmīki said: When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O you who are skilled in action, this narrative of the stones has been told to you; by this very logic, these creations exist in the sky with a shimmering vision.
And nothing whatsoever has ever remained anywhere at any time; Brahman remains as it is, unfragmented within the density of Brahman.
Know that Brahman is pure consciousness alone, just as in dreams; the city that appears never deviates from its own essential nature.
In the attainment of self-existence and likewise in the established state of the visible world, the unborn sky of consciousness remains, never abandoning its own nature.

There is no self-existent being, nor is there a world, nor even a city in a dream; through this great vision of consciousness, all that exists is established as Brahman, which is pure awareness alone.
Just as a city exists within one's own dream, established in the self as the form of consciousness, so too does it remain undivided from the beginning of creation until the great dissolution.
Just as no distinction whatsoever can exist between gold and a golden stone, or between a dream-city and consciousness, so too there is no distinction between consciousness and creation.
There is only consciousness, not creation; there is gold, not its waves. In the mountain of a dream, there is only consciousness, but no mountain-ness whatsoever.
Just as in a dream, the mind alone appears like a mountain yet remains free from affliction, so too Brahman, though formless, appears as the creation and nothing else.
This space is pure consciousness alone—endless, unborn, and undecaying; throughout thousands of great aeons, it neither arises nor ceases.
The person is indeed the space of consciousness; you, O Bhava, are this very space of consciousness; I am the undecaying space of consciousness; and the three worlds are the space of consciousness.
Apart from the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), the body is merely a corpse; that space of consciousness is neither to be cut nor to be burned, and it never perishes.
Therefore, nothing dies and nothing is born; because it is consciousness, the world is experienced as the manifestation of consciousness.
If a living being, who is in reality nothing but pure consciousness, were to die, then his son would undoubtedly die upon the father's death.
If, when one living being had died, all others were likewise to die forever, then the entire surface of the earth would have become empty of people.
O Rāma, pure consciousness has not yet died for anyone, anywhere; nor has the ground become empty. Therefore, the conscious person (cit-puruṣa) is imperishable.
"I am indeed only pure consciousness; the body and so forth are not mine"—when this truth is continuously contemplated, where is there room for birth, death, and the like?
Those who destroy themselves by denying their own self-experience—that "I am pure, stainless consciousness"—sink into an ocean of calamities.
I am Consciousness, clear as the sky, eternal, infinite, and free from ailment; what is life to me, or what is death, or pleasure and pain?
"I am the consciousness whose nature is space; what are the body and other such things to me?"—fie upon that destroyer of the Self who denies what has been directly experienced within!
"I am the clear sky of consciousness; experience is manifest"—he from whom this [realization] has vanished is known as a fool, a living corpse.
"I am of the nature of pure sensation; what are these bodies and senses to me?"—when one is thus clear in the realization that the self has been attained, calamities cannot destroy them.
He who remains steadfast, taking refuge in the pure Self which is pure consciousness alone, is not overwhelmed by mental anxieties, just as arrows cannot pierce a great boulder.
Those who, having forgotten their true nature as consciousness, place their attachment on this wretched body, have in effect discarded gold and grasped ashes.
Strength, intellect, and splendor perish through the contemplation "I am the body," while these very same qualities arise from the firm abiding in the realization "I am consciousness alone."
I am the pure space of consciousness; what birth and death can there be for me? This being so, where could greed, delusion, pride, and the like find their basis?

Apart from the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), if another person were to obtain some other essence distinct from the body, it would be appropriate to tell him that greed and the like exist. But [since no such thing exists], they do not.

"I am not to be cut, nor am I to be burned; I am pure consciousness, as firm as a diamond within consciousness. For one who possesses this certainty that "I am not the body," even the Destroyer at the end of time is but a blade of grass.
Oh, how great is the delusion of those with the eye of knowledge, that they are so utterly bewildered as to think, "We shall perish" when the mere fragments of the body are gone!
When the truth that "I am indeed the infinite sky" is firmly established in one's being, the falls of thunderbolts and the fires of the end of the aeon are like heaps of flowers.
"I am not pure consciousness, nor am I immortal; I shall perish," she weeps. Yet, even though her body has not perished, a previously unknown harshness has arisen within her.
"I am indeed this consciousness alone; I am not the views of the body and so forth"—he who possesses such certainty within never becomes deluded at any time.
I am the conscious space; destruction does not apply to me. The entire world is filled with consciousness; what cause for doubt could there be for you in this matter?
O great fools, if you say anything other than consciousness, tell me: what is it that you deny as being the self?
If that consciousness were to die, then people would die every day; tell me, why do you not die yourselves, for it is said that consciousness has died?
Therefore, nothing whatsoever dies, nor does anything whatsoever live; though the consciousness thinks "I live" or "I am dead," it neither perishes nor is destroyed.
Whatever the mind intends, it perceives that very thing exactly as it is immediately; this experience exists even in children, and that [perception] never perishes anywhere.
He perceives cyclic existence; he perceives liberation. He knows pleasures and pains, yet he does not differ from their true nature.
When the body is not fully understood, it itself assumes the name "delusion"; but when its true nature is fully understood, it itself assumes the name "liberation."
Nothing ever sets nor does it ever rise; for everything is indeed pure consciousness, as clear as the sky.
There is nothing that is not true, and there is nothing that is not false; in whatever manner and by whatever means a thing is determined, it remains established for that person in exactly that way.

Whatever the conscious self perceives in the world in whatever manner, it experiences that very thing in that same way; this is established by direct experience. It is observed that the multitude of objects is like poison or nectar depending on one's vision, and it is well known that there is nothing that does not fall under the governance of consciousness.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Because the world consists of consciousness and is the supreme Self, like a dream, everything is experienced as Brahman alone, by virtue of its being the space of Brahman.
Because delusion is extremely visible while the Great Consciousness is invisible, it is logical that the Self is like the power of intoxication; thus, its reality is also established.

Because of the non-existence of sentient beings, because of the resting [of consciousness] in the visible, because of the unobtainability of the great consciousness, and because of the absence of a perceiver, it is as if called "empty," even though it truly exists.

The Puruṣa is pure consciousness alone and is a non-doer; from the Unmanifest (avyakta), the world arises. This is true for one who perceives thus, because of the direct experience of the object as it is.
Even for those who maintain that the visible world is an illusory manifestation (vivarta) of Brahman, their doctrine remains untenable because objects of such a nature are actually experienced.
Even the view that the world consists of an aggregate of atoms is not real; for whatever is perceived in whatever manner, it is experienced exactly as such.
Just as it is seen, so indeed is this in this world and in the next; neither non-existent nor existent—this is the mature, true, spiritual path.
Other truth-tellers claim that only the external exists and nothing else; yet they do not attain that which is within their own self and transcends the collection of sense organs.
Because they perceive incessant error, the cognition of momentary destruction is indeed logical for those who know that; for that state is the primordial source of all power.

For those who know the Dharma, it is also said that the law is like the analogy of the kalaviṅka bird's cry; thus, because the Self is established in that way, there is no fault in [teaching it] among the mlecchas in their own lands.
Even when facing the death caused by poison, fire, or water, the wise remain equanimous; for to those who know that truth, all this appears as such, since it is of the nature of the All.

For those who know the truth, it is logical that this [world] is established by its own nature; thus, even when investigated, the existence of an intelligent creator of all things does not reach the level of attainment.
It is true that for those whose minds are absorbed in Him, He alone is the agent in all things; he who possesses this certainty attains Him in this state—this is irrefutable.
This world and the next exist, as do bathing, fire-offerings, and so forth, and nothing else; know that such is the truth for one whose contemplation has been cultivated.
For the Buddhists, this alone is true: that everything without exception is indeed empty; for through such investigation, nothing whatsoever is found at all.
Consciousness, whose nature is space, quickly fulfills one's desires within the self by means of the inner self, like a wish-fulfilling gem or a desire-granting tree.
This is neither empty nor non-empty; for those who know it, it is not a non-entity. For that power is all-powerful; yet that [power] does not exist as such.
Therefore, whatever one is established in as one's own conviction, from that one necessarily obtains the corresponding fruit, provided one does not turn back out of childishness.

Having deliberated together with wise scholars on a matter of supreme importance, the conclusion reached by the intelligent person should be accepted; it should not be adopted otherwise or in any other context.
One who possesses supreme wisdom may arise from either scriptural study or practical experience; wherever such a person may be found, one should rely upon that scholar.
Among virtuous people who may be disputing yet conduct themselves according to the true scriptures, he who is blameless and brings joy to all is the best; one should take refuge in him.

All living beings constantly and by force pursue what they perceive as the highest good, just as waters flow toward a lower level; having reflected upon this, one should take refuge in that which is truly so.
For men being swept away by the great waves in the ocean of saṃsāra, their days pass unnoticed, like drops upon blades of grass.

Śrī Rāma said: Even as a creeper once rested upon the vast ground that existed before the world, who, through the investigation of what comes before and after, can perceive the absence of anything else?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In every birth, there are but a few who become truly distinguished—those whose days pass in radiance like those of the suns.
Rushing upward and downward with the revolutions and whirlpools of the wheel, all these deluded ones are swept away like blades of grass in the ocean of existence born of ignorance.
Having lost their stability of self, the gods in heaven burn intensely amidst the fires of enjoyment, like trees being consumed by a forest fire on a mountain.
The Dānavas, filled with intoxication, were cast down by the enemies of the Dānavas into the terrible pit of Nārāyaṇa, like elephants freed from their tethering posts.
Even the Gandharvas do not perceive the fragrance born of solitude; absorbed in song and drink, they wander like deer.
And the Vidyādharas, deluded by their status as the repositories of sciences, show no respect even for those [teachings] that are radiant and sublime.
The Yakṣas, who had shaken the earth, displayed their unimpaired dexterity toward those who were helpless—namely, children, the elderly, and the sick.
Just as the enemy of the deer (the lion) by his speed brought about the destruction of rutting elephants, you shall likewise bring about the total extermination of the Rākṣasas.
The piśācas see intensely with the thought of devouring living beings, like offerings of oblations accompanied by smoke, darkness, wind, and flame.
The lotus stalks of the Nāga-lake were submerged in the surface of the earth, standing there as if they were the roots of mountains or as if they were utterly inert.
For those young asuras who, like insects on the earth, have only a hole for their refuge, what talk can there be of solitude?
For the sake of even a tiny grain of rice, people generally wander day and night, sharing the same nature as ants.
The days of all living beings pass away in distraction and futile longing, like those of drunkards with their evil desires.
Pure discernment does not touch any person within, just as dust does not touch one who has fallen and is sinking in fathomless water.
Men shaken by their vows are led away by the life-breaths of men, like heaps of dust blown by the winds of autumn.
In the dense mire of food and drink, the hosts of yoginīs have fallen like common folk into a foul-smelling puddle.
Only Yama, Candra, Indra, Rudra, Ārka, Varuṇa, Anila, Hari, Brahmā, Guru, Śukra, Anala, and others are liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
The Prajāpatis, the Seven Sages beginning with Dakṣa, Kaśyapa and others, Nārada and others, Kumāra and others, and Sanaka and others—the sons of the gods.
Among the Dānavas were Hiraṇyākṣa, Bali, Prahlāda, Śambara, Maya, Vṛtra, Andhaka, Namuci, Keśin, Putramura, and others.
Among the Rākṣasas were Bibhīṣaṇa and others, as well as Prahasta, Indrajit, and others; among the serpents were Śeṣa, Takṣaka, Karkoṭaka, Mahāpadma, and others.
Dwelling in the worlds of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra are those who have cast off their bodies, those whose nature is liberated, the Tuṣitas, the Siddhas, and certain Sādhyas.
O scion of Raghu, among human beings, kings, sages, and the most excellent brahmins who are liberated while living are indeed rare.

All beings in all directions are numerous, yet those endowed with awakening are rare; indeed, while there are many trees possessed of clusters of fruits and foliage, wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas) truly occur only rarely.
