Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For those who possess discernment, who are dispassionate, and who have found rest in the supreme state, their enemies—greed, delusion, and the like—attain a state of attenuation.
They do not rejoice, they do not become angry, they do not enter [into worldly affairs], nor do they seize anything; they are not agitated by the world, nor do they cause agitation in the world.

Neither out of atheism nor out of dogmatic faith did those followers of the Vedic path perform difficult austerities; rather, they were of pleasing and sweet conduct, speaking words that were kind and gentle.
Like the rays of the moon, they gladden the hearts of those who associate with them; they are discerners of affairs and reach a decision in even a moment.
Their conduct causes no agitation, like that of kinsmen or citizens; they maintain all outward social conventions, yet inwardly they are cool toward all worldly objects.

They take delight in the meaning of the scriptures, know them, and understand the higher and lower worlds; they discern what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, and they pursue whatever comes their way.

The connoisseur, having desisted from contrary actions, abides in the state of the virtuous; through the unobstructed fragrance of their conduct, they partake of the bliss found in the station of others.
Like blooming lotuses honoring a bee that has arrived, those who remove the suffering of people win over the populace as they seek them out.
Affectionate like clouds in the rainy season providing a cool refuge, those steadfast ones [bore] the agitation that causes the destruction of the country and the breaking of the mountains.
Like mountains restraining an approaching earthquake, they restrain the agitation that has arisen; they encourage one in adversity and bring happiness in prosperity.

With forms resembling the lunar orb, they are like wives who are mines of virtue; they make the quarters of the sky pure with the flowers of their fame and serve as the causes for future excellent fruits.

Like virtuous men who possess the melodious warbling of the male cuckoo, or like the spring months, [they enter] that ocean of delusion which abounds with waves and whirlpools and is the dwelling place of sea-monsters.
The great ocean of another's mind, restless with the agitation of its waves, rolls like the winter season and churns the abode of living beings.
And those virtuous mountains, standing on the shore, are able to restrain it during calamities, the loss of intellect, and amidst turbulent waves.

In times of distress and in terminal calamities, the virtuous alone are the refuge for the good; having recognized them as being of noble intent through these and other signs, one should [rely upon them].
One who is weary from traveling the path of saṃsāra should resort to this for the sake of a single rest, because this ocean of the serpent of saṃsāra is exceedingly treacherous.
Without the company of the virtuous, it cannot be crossed by any other means; let alone my own deliberation—whatever may happen, let that be mine.
Thus, having encountered impurity within, one should not remain like a worm in a pit; rather, one should abandon everything in that person who possesses even a single virtue.
Disregarding any other faults, one should rely solely on that [teacher] from childhood, through one's own effort, in order to discern both virtues and defects.

One should first sharpen the intellect through the company of the virtuous and the study of scriptures as they become available; disregarding even the slightest trace of fault, one should constantly serve the good.
One should gradually and sequentially abandon gross defects that have not yet been extinguished; for even the pleasant becomes unpleasant, and the stable becomes unstable.
I believe that just as it is seen, the virtuous man goes to the state of being non-virtuous; this is indeed a supreme calamity, that the virtuous man should fall into wickedness.

Due to the influence of place and time, even great calamities caused by sins may be seen; therefore, abandoning all other activities, one should seek the company of the virtuous. This practice is free from obstacles and is the means for accomplishing the welfare of both worlds.
One should never be far from a virtuous person; endowed with humility, one should serve the holy. For the spreading pollen of their virtues reaches those who stand near them without any effort.

Śrī Rāma said: For the destruction of our suffering, there exist the means of the scriptures, the company of the virtuous, and reasoning, as well as recourse to mantras, medicines, austerities, charity, sacred fords, and meritorious hermitages.
How do worms, insects, moths, and other species of animals and stationary beings exist? What are their activities, and how can there be an end to their suffering?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: All beings here, both stationary and moving, are fully established and at rest within their own appropriate mode of existence.
Even for beings as minute as atoms, desires are just like ours; however, we are obstacles to them only because our own resolve is slight, while they remain as firm as mountains.
Just as Virāṭ exerts himself, so too do the Bālakhilyas in the sky; behold the expansion of egoism even within a tiny body the size of a child's fist.
Birds are born and die in the supportless sky; their sole domain is the void, and for them, there is not a moment of stability.
Just as even a moment equal to our day is not sufficient for an ant due to its own activities, such as seeking food and shelter for itself and its kin; so too is it for us.
The self whose size is that of a mote of dust—whether it be a worm, an atom, or one named a fish—is observed to possess a restlessness in movement similar to that of Garuḍa.
Just as this vast world appears to men through the mental construction of "this is I" and "that is mine," so too does it appear to a worm through its own elevated qualities.
Wasted away by the distractions of place, time, action, and material things, our life perishes like that of maggots in a wound.
The trees have slightly awakened, while the stones are indeed in deep sleep; worms, insects, and the like experience dreaming and waking just like humans in their activities.
For them, the very destruction of the body is happiness, whereas it causes suffering at present; for us, however, that same life is what constitutes happiness.
Just as a person who has been sold to another continent perceives the multitude of objects there, so too do animals, deer, and other such beings perceive the world.
For animals, cyclic existence bestows pleasure and pain just as it does for us; they are distinguished from us only by their lack of discernment regarding the nature of things.

By means of the heart through pleasure and pain, by the nose through the rope's cord, and by the waist through the girth-strap, domestic animals—and even the low-born who have been sold—are dragged along.
Just as we experience sensation when asleep, though our skin is clearly intact, so too do trees, shrubs, sprouts, and the like experience intense sensation.

Just as our perception of objects is for those like us who fall into the cycle of existence through a sequence of desires, so too is the perception of animals—though it is deluded, it is not free from error.

Gentleness exists equally in both Indra and a worm when it comes to mere joy arising from pleasure; this state is free from conceptual construction, whereas conceptual construction is simply the failure to transcend [duality].

The pleasure and pain arising from passion, hatred, fear, food, and sexual intercourse, as well as the suffering of birth, death, and so forth for animals, do not differ in any way [from those of other beings].

Except for the cognition of objects that exist as real entities and of things yet to come, the rest [of their cognition] is equal to that of humans, such as mongooses, snakes, jackals, elephants, and so forth.

While the mountains and other beings remain experiencing their own existence, they perceive the trees—which are composed of sleep—as being insentient, whereas others experience the undivided sky of consciousness.
Trees and other such things are in deep sleep; likewise, mountains abide in their own being. Moving beings and the so-called space of consciousness (cidākāśa) have never been anything at any time.

The existence of mountains and other things consists of an undivided consciousness, as does the sleep of trees; because they are free from the perception of duality, the world is therefore only the one space (ākāśa).
The entire world, as far as it is joined with ignorance, has been fully understood; there is no "you," no "I," nor indeed "existence" or "non-existence," nor will there ever be.
This [reality] is always exactly as it is: a silence as solid as a stone, without beginning or end, uninterrupted, both sleepless and yet possessed of sleep.
Just as it was at the beginning of creation, so it remains as one and the same; it will be thus even now, and likewise for all infinite time to come.
Neither selfhood nor otherness, neither worldliness nor emptiness; neither the state of silence nor silence itself—nothing at all is found here that can be established.
Remain exactly as you are; I remain exactly as I am. In the tranquil, supreme space of equanimity toward pleasure and pain, there is nothing here at all.
Apart from the state of supreme space, tell me, what exists in a city of dreams? Indeed, that is peaceful, the stainless and healthy sky of consciousness.
In that regard, only non-cognition itself causes confusion; yet once this is fully understood, even that [non-cognition] is not found anywhere.

When the dream of the world is fully understood, there is nothing whatsoever that is real; what attachment, then, can one have for it, other than that which one might feel toward the son of a barren woman?
When it is fully understood that the world is a dream within an atom of a dream, what value or stability could there be? Upon awakening, this world is nothing at all.
Wherein there is no awakening whatsoever, nor is there non-awakening anywhere; whatever perception occurs at that time is simply the prior state itself, remaining just as it was.
Presentness, as well as futureness and pastness, awakening and non-awakening—none of these exist; indeed, every thing is entirely peaceful.
Just as when one wave is struck by another wave there is no injury to the water, so too when one body is struck by a body there is no injury to consciousness.
"I am the body" arises only within the space of consciousness; therefore, when the body perishes, what indeed can perish within that consciousness?
It is established that the world is the dream of the awakened space of consciousness; since it is devoid of earth and other elements, the world is therefore of the nature of a dream.

At the beginning of creation, the cognition of objects such as the earth arises from the dream of primordial consciousness; it is a delusion regarding the reality of dream-objects, consisting of nothing but mental construction.
While this dream, which is more ancient than the ancient, remains established in its constituent parts—even though it is unreal—the conceptualization of earth and the other elements was performed.
And that delusion has become so firmly established that, though it is indeed unreal, it has attained a state of supreme reality; yet that reality is utterly stainless.

In reality, however, only the all-pervading Brahman, which is consciousness as it truly is, exists; and there is nothing established therein that could be a rememberer or a non-rememberer—of what nature could such a thing be?
Thus, in this case, the thorough knowledge of the measures (mātrā) alone is the awakener; yet it is in this very [knowledge] that thorough knowledge acts as the opening of the door.
By process of elimination, nothing such as earth or other elements exists anywhere; that which is the seer and that which is the seen is only the stainless Śiva.

Just as a reflection appears within a mirror from an original object, so does the world appear within the space of consciousness; though it shines forth spontaneously, it is reflected even from that which is not an original object.
Just as no reflection whatsoever is seen within a mirror even though it appears there, so too the universe residing in the space of consciousness is not seen at all, even though it appears.
That which is obtained through investigation, that which exists with a cause, and that which remains as a residue—how could that which is mere appearance and non-existent be real?
Even something consisting of error may be capable of causal efficiency; for even a woman in a dream performs a real causal function for men.

"That which is that manifestation is indeed the light of consciousness (cidbhā), and that is the supreme sky of consciousness (cidambara). Thus, where am I, where is the glory of the universe, where are you, and what are the perceptions of the visible?"

If there is rebirth after death, what indeed has been lost? Even if there is no rebirth after death, there is peace. If, by the power of the view of consciousness, there is liberation, then for one of noble intellect, there is not even the slightest suffering here.

Only one who is ignorant truly knows what this state of a fool is like; indeed, we are certainly not experts in that matter. For only the fish that dwells in the waters of a mirage knows the tossing of its flickering waves.

The single sky of consciousness alone shines as the self of all—manifesting as "internal," "external," "you," "I," and so forth—having for its sole essence the void of awareness, like a tree of desire whose body consists of branches, tips, boughs, leaves, and fruits.

Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahmin, what kind of method might there be for the pacification of suffering in this saṃsāra? Let the view of those who hold such a position be heard, and let it then be explained."
One should live happily as long as life lasts; death is not something that can be avoided. Once one has been reduced to ashes and become extinguished, how could there be a return?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Whatever resolution consciousness adopts, unbroken within its interior, it experiences that very thing as a direct perception; such is the universal law.
Just as space is all-pervading and tranquil, so too is the ether of consciousness all-pervading; that alone is non-duality, for the existence of any other object is utterly impossible.

At the beginning of creation, apart from that [Brahman], no other object exists within the state of the great dissolution; because it is devoid of parts, it does not exist at all as anything else—therefore, this entire expanse is Brahman alone.
Those who do not accept the meaning of all the Vedas and Shastras, nor the great dissolution and so forth, are utterly deluded; being devoid of scripture, they are as if dead.
There is no need for further discourse with those who, through experience, remain established in the conviction that "all this is Brahman," in a manner that is not contradicted by any scripture.
Whatever kind of consciousness arises perpetually and without interruption within the heart, a person becomes composed of that very thing, whether they possess a body or not.
If that person were born from consciousness through awakening, he would become a sufferer; for as long as there is contrary sensation, my dear, the living soul remains composed of that.

When it is contemplated that the world is merely the manifestation of the space of consciousness, how can there be any perception? By what would there be awareness, for whom, and from where could it arise?
For those men who possess the consciousness of a single certainty, neither pleasures nor pains run forth toward them, just as dust does not cling to the skies.
Whether consciousness be real or unreal, such is the certainty; this is established even among children, so by whom and how can it be denied?
Neither the body, nor the person, nor even a separate living soul (jīva) is perceived; consciousness alone is all this, and the world exists exactly as that consciousness perceives it.
Whether that [body] is real or unreal, it is experienced by her through her own autonomy, just as in a dream, in the netherworld, in the sky, in water, or in heaven.
Whether consciousness be real or unreal, the person is known as being of that [consciousness] alone; whatever his conviction is, that is indeed the conviction that it is real.
By this alone is the authority of all scriptures established; it is my conviction that this is the final conclusion of all philosophical systems.
Therefore, that state of yours which is non-awakening is exactly as it is perceived; it becomes pure in form and likewise partakes of the fruit.
That consciousness which consists of ignorance regarding place, time, action, substance, the Vedas, the scriptures, and one's desires—never does it perish.
If that [doubt], once diminished, should manifest again in an instant, then by what means and when indeed will the suffering of consciousness ever be pacified?
Consciousness alone is the life-force of human beings; according to how firm one's mental disposition is, so will one become happy or miserable—this is the certainty.

If there exists for those who know it a realization that serves as a refuge for the destruction of cyclic existence, then well; but if it does not exist, then nothing remains but the blindness of a mute stone.
And that which is obtained through that very consciousness, through feeling itself—this internal insentience is like a man [regaining] his own nature through sleep.

Śrī Rāma said: There will be no end to this [world] in the directions or below, nor will there be the destruction of the universe; he by whom this has been realized, having abandoned the notion of non-existence, [is liberated].
Surely, by one who does not see that "this is merely a mass of consciousness," and by one who, though seeing, does not see the cessation of all things as they have been perceived;
What kind of expression regarding Brahman could there be for the destruction of mental anguish? Cut through this doubt of mine so that my awakening may further increase.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In this matter, first there is one appropriate response, and likewise a second; listen now to this second, logical reply that is about to be spoken.
O Puruṣottama, that person whose state has been described by you is experienced as being merely consciousness itself.

And that [body] is subject to destruction through the dissolution of its form; there is no doubt about this. If, on the other hand, the body were indestructible, then what would be the point of suffering here?
If the self were of the nature of parts and divisions, its destruction would be unexamined; indeed, it is surely certain that such destruction must inevitably occur for it.

Having died, he does not experience worldly existence again because his nature is pure consciousness; for that consciousness which has been cleansed by knowledge does not remain in a state of non-transmigration.
Alternatively, if one holds the conviction that "there is no consciousness," then by virtue of such a cognition, one indeed becomes as insentient as a stone.
Just as the mind [is directed] toward objects according to sensation, when the body is destroyed and sensation is lost, death alone is seen to be the supreme good, not experience.
Those who, being pure knowers, become bodiless due to the impossibility [of embodiment], yet remain in a state of dullness, having become inert, they become blinded by an insurmountable darkness.
And for those who, being composed of consciousness, perceive everything like a city in a dream, this entire web of the world proceeds as if it were real.
What unprecedented thing could there be in the mind regarding the stability or instability of the elements? Whether the elements are stable or unstable, pleasure and pain are exactly the same.
Whether stable or unstable, even for the great elements such as the earth and so forth, all this shines as nothing but the light of consciousness as long as ignorance extends.
Enough with those childish people who, having failed to pervade consciousness with the non-existence of consciousness, have either concluded or accepted its insentience.
Those from whose bodies wisdom has emerged are the supreme persons worthy of veneration; enough with those lowest of men from whom only bodies have emerged, while wisdom remains absent.
The flood of the seeds of individual souls, whose nature is consciousness, moves upward, sideways, and downward like a web of insects in the sky, as if filling itself by its own power.
That by which another agent is perceived through the stream of seeds is itself intent upon that; likewise, it experiences within itself and vibrates spontaneously.
Whatever is conceived by whatever living being, that is immediately attained by it through its conscious nature; this is established as true and remains unrefuted even from childhood.
Just as there are various whirlpools of smoke in the sky and of great waters in the ocean, so too are the diverse revolutions of phenomenal existence within the space of consciousness.
Just as the city of the sky of consciousness appears to a person in a dream, so too has this very world existed from the beginning of creation.
Just as the auxiliary causes do not exist at all in a dream, so too the primary elements such as earth and the rest do not exist at the beginning of the world's existence.
The various lands fashioned within the dream-city of the limbs have themselves attained full development in this dream-city of the world.
These beings are nothing but the space of pure consciousness, devoid of duality and unity; for what else could there be to color this space? Whatever appears in the sky is indeed the sky itself.
The moonlight of consciousness, cool and refreshing in the four directions, spreads the light of awareness; this world is its manifestation.

Even today, the vision of creation occurs within the beginningless and endless space of pure consciousness; through the opening and closing of the eyes of consciousness, the self of the void arises and sets.
In whatever manner one knows something, that very thing is experienced exactly as it is; since everything is purely consciousness, what indeed is not found here?
Those whose minds are gentle and whose consciousness is as clear as the autumnal sky remain as if non-existent; the truly existent ones have realized that ultimate state.

Free from pride and delusion, having conquered the fault of attachment, and possessing their own purpose as it arrives in its natural flow, these people remain free from affliction, appearing like mechanical puppets in the performance of their duties and worldly affairs.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The person is indeed pure consciousness alone; it is that very same consciousness existing in this manner. Apart from pure consciousness, what else can possibly exist?
And that pure space is seen by the seer who consists of it; since the world is merely that much, whence can there be the notion of what is to be rejected or accepted?
For that follower of Bṛhaspati who holds that no other world exists, what essence can there be for one who knows nothing else? For such a person, how could passion and hatred possibly cease?

O dear one, tell me: what is the nature of the defects of attachment and aversion arising from the perception of the desirable and the undesirable within this dream called the world, which consists of the void of pure consciousness?
Whether this is to be abandoned or accepted, it shines forth as pure within the stainless void of consciousness in the self; for what room is there here for the perception of "this" or "not-this"?
Consciousness is the man, the immortal, and the serpent; consciousness is the stationary and the moving. Existence, non-existence, and the like are the waves, whirlpools, and movements of this ocean.
I am indeed the space of consciousness, as are you and all people; we never die at all, for when has consciousness ever died?

For consciousness, there is no object of consciousness; it has attained the state of being self-conscious. Therefore, O large-eyed one, because it is consciousness, where could duality or unity possibly reside?
Therefore, tell me: what entity could possibly exist apart from pure consciousness? If it is said that such an entity dies, then why are we here today?
Let it be stated what those disputants—the Buddhists and others, as well as the Lokāyatas and others—who, setting aside the space of consciousness, hold to be real.
This very space of consciousness is called Brahman by some; it is called knowledge by others, and it is called the void by still others.
By some it is called the power of intoxication (mada-śakti), by some the name "Puruṣa," by some the space of consciousness (cid-ākāśa), and by some Śiva and Ātman.
Even when described in this way, pure consciousness never undergoes any change into something else, because it knows itself in this manner and nothing other than itself.
"May my limbs turn to dust, and may they become like Mount Meru; what loss or what gain is there for me, whose body is of the nature of consciousness?"
If our grandfathers and others have died, yet that consciousness has not died and might die [now], then for us whose awareness is of the dead, there would be no such thing as birth at all.
The imperishable space of consciousness is neither born nor does it die; tell me, how could it come to be? For how indeed could there be the destruction of space?
The indestructible sky of consciousness, whose sole manifestation is the form of the world, remains solitary within itself, free from rising and setting.
The crystal mountain of the sky of consciousness, bearing the appearance of the world and its burning heat, remains within itself—transparent, without beginning, middle, or end.
Just as whatever is being looked at in darkness perishes—appearing like some cloud-cluster of limbs—so too does this entire universe vanish within the Self.

Just as the ocean itself moves through its waters, whirlpools, and so forth, yet remains still while sustaining them, even so the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) sustains this world as a limb within itself.
The Puruṣa is indeed pure consciousness alone, and like space, he never perishes; therefore, the grief that "I shall perish" is entirely futile.
When one attains another body from the present body, it is indeed a great festival; why, O fools, do you grieve over that which is essentially death when it is actually an occasion for joy?
If he does not die again, there will be even greater prosperity here; the fever of grasping and abandoning existence and non-existence has come to rest.
Since death and life are therefore neither suffering nor happiness, this very thing does not exist at all; it is said that the space of consciousness merely unfolds in this manner.
If there were a regaining of the body for one who has died, that would indeed be a new festival; yet death is the destruction of the body, and that death is the supreme bliss.
If death is absolute annihilation, then it is the destruction of the disease of existence; if there is the acquisition of a new body, then it is indeed a festival.
If you have fear of evil deeds, know that it exists both here and in the next world; therefore, O friend, do not commit them for the sake of attaining success in both worlds.
"I shall die, I shall die, I shall die"—thus you speak; "I shall be, I shall be, I shall be"—thus you do not perceive.
Where indeed are birth and death? Where are the planes of existence and non-existence? This entire world, which is of the nature of pure consciousness, is but the void revolving within the void.
Your self is nothing but the space of pure consciousness; drink, eat, and dwell without the sense of "mine. For one as beautiful as the interior of the sky, how could desire ever arise?
The fearless and fortunate one experiences those purifying states—attained through the power of his own mental flow and the influence of place and time—which are purer even than the purifier itself.
Disregarding the moderate defects that arise due to the influence of place and time, he remains within himself with an unheeding mind, as if in deep sleep.
He does not come to suffering through death, nor does he come to happiness through life; he neither desires nor hates, for he then abides free from mental afflictions.

Without reflecting on death, life, birth, or old age, free from desire and devoid of latent tendencies, he who has known what is to be known dwells here like an ignorant man—fearless and as immovable as a mountain.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, when the supreme reality—the self that is without beginning or end—is fully realized, tell me, what kind of Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) does one become?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen, O best of men, to what kind of person becomes one who has known that which is to be known; and how does he live for as long as life lasts, and what is his conduct?
Even stones are friends, and forest trees are kinsmen; even for one dwelling in the midst of the forest, the young deer are their own people.
To him, even a crowded place is empty; misfortunes are his greatest successes; and even while established in a great kingdom, calamities alone are his festivals.
Non-concentration is itself concentration; great suffering is itself great happiness; even worldly discourse is true silence; and actions themselves are the state of non-action.
Though awake, he remains as if in deep sleep; though living, he is like one who is dead. He performs all customary conduct, yet he does nothing at all.

He who is a connoisseur of aesthetic flavor is utterly devoid of flavor; he who is merciless is affectionate toward his kin; he who is pitiless is exceedingly compassionate; he who is free from thirst is possessed by craving.
His conduct is approved by all, yet he stands outside of all conventional conduct; free from sorrow, fear, and fatigue, he appears as if he were possessed of sorrow.
Therefore, the world does not tremble before him, nor does he tremble before the world, even though he has reached the highest agitation while still being a connoisseur of worldly existence.
He does not rejoice in what has been attained, nor does he long for what has not been attained; he remains equanimous while experiencing an object, and is subject neither to elation nor to dejection.
When others are suffering, he speaks of suffering; when they are happy, he speaks of happiness; in all circumstances, he remains with an unconquered heart.
Nothing other than well-performed action pleases him; indeed, for the great, it is their very nature not to act otherwise.
He never clings to either aesthetic relish or insipidity; though free from passion, he moves among objects like one still possessed by passion, yet without being a seeker of worldly gain.

Just as one does not experience joy or dejection regarding the occurrences described in the scriptures or the pleasures and pains that arrive in their due course, so too one remains unaffected by what is yet to come.
They are seen to be greatly elated, and likewise they are seen to be suffering; yet these actors on the stage of saṃsāra do not abandon their inner nature.

Those who perceive reality have no affection for things belonging to the self—such as wealth and children—which are falsely conceived as the self, just as one has no attachment to bubbles upon the water.
Though entirely free from attachment, he remains with a heart moistened by profound affection; the wise one abides in due order, manifesting a disposition full of tenderness.
Like those standing in the current touching the winds, fools vainly touch sense-objects; poisoned by the existence of the body, they dissolve within the belly of the sense-objects.
Outwardly, he maintains all conventional conduct; inwardly, he is cooled by the cessation of all worldly objects. Constantly unpossessed within, he remains as if possessed.
Śrī Rāma said: "O leader of sages, who knows such a true nature of his? Tell me, whether it be truth or falsehood; for even one who is ignorant may be like this."
O Sage, those whose minds are not beautiful practice the life of celibacy like horses; such people exist for the sake of strengthening false ascetics.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Whether it be unreal or real, know that such is the excellent nature of the knowers of the Vedas; this is established in the experience of one's own inherent being.

Though unpossessed by [the demon], they act as if possessed; though free from passion, they behave like those with passion; though devoid of laughter, they suddenly laugh at the ignorant, overwhelmed by compassion.

All that is visible, appearing within the mirror of the mind, is a deceptive floor; seeing it as such through the thorough knowledge of its unreality is like perceiving gold in one's hand within a dream.
No one perceives their inner coolness, just as living beings perceive from afar only the fragrance of sandalwood trees.
But those who have understood what is to be known, whose intentions are thus purified—they recognize them just as those with sight perceive the feet of a snake hidden within a hole.
These unsurpassed ones conceal their supreme state; for who would value a priceless wish-fulfilling gem in a marketplace for common riches?
Since their state is one of concealment rather than perception, they are indeed, my dear, free from latent impressions, beyond duality, and devoid of pride.
But solitude, freedom from pride, lack of poverty, and being disregarded by people—these, O Rāma, bring them happiness in a way that great supernatural powers do not.
This state of having known what is to be known, whose essence is to be experienced through self-awareness, cannot be demonstrated; nor is it seen even by one who knows it.
"May people know this merit of mine; may they offer me honor"—such is the striving of those possessed by ego, but not of those whose minds are liberated from it.

O Rāghava, even for those who are ignorant, the fruits of ritual action—such as traveling through the sky of consciousness and so forth—are accomplished here in this world by means of mantras and medicinal herbs.
Whoever is capable of depositing a particular affliction will necessarily experience its fruit, whether they are awakened or indeed ignorant.
Like the fragrance of sandalwood, the fruit of vibration exists within the heart of everyone; it is surely attained by one who possesses that [vibration].
He who possesses the dualistic impression of "I-ness" and the sense of reality regarding visible objects accomplishes the fruits of actions such as traveling through the sky.

The wise one who knows that "this is nothing," or that it is either an illusion or the void—he, being free from latent tendencies (*vāsana*), how could he perform actions driven by the whirlwind of karma?
He has no purpose whatsoever here through action, nor any through inaction; nor does he have any dependence on any being for any object.
There is nothing on earth, nor in heaven among the gods, anywhere at all, that can incite the greed of one whose mental disposition is noble and who has realized the Self.
For one to whom the entire world is but a blade of grass or even a speck of dust, what else indeed could there be that has become worthy of being accepted?
Having brought the journey of the world to its conclusion, the sage, his mind fully perfected, remains as he is and departs just as he came.
Ever inwardly cool, observing silence, with the forest of his mind become a being of pure essence, he has the appearance of a full ocean, his disposition profound yet manifest.
Like one whose heart is filled with the supreme elixir, he experiences joy within himself or bestows it upon another, like the stainless full moon.
The celestial realms, golden with groves of Mandāra blossoms, do not gladden the heart as much as the intellects of the wise.
With moon-like faces and spring-like limbs, those of great and noble intent were the very essence among those who enjoy the world’s fortune, fragrance, and splendor.
"This entire universe is mere delusion, an unreal magical illusion; it is abandoned"—having thus resolved, day after day, one should abandon all desires.
The wise person regards even the sufferings of cold, heat, and so forth occurring within his own body with indifference, as if they were occurring in the body of another.

Through a disposition noble with compassion and through a conduct as steadfast as a creeping vine, he who is himself devoid of worldly sap attains a state of stability that possesses the essence of the sapless.
Practicing worldly conduct as it is commonly observed, he stands preeminent above all beings, both moving and unmoving.
Having ascended the palace of wisdom, the wise man, beyond grief, looks upon grieving people; like one standing on a mountain peak looking down at those on the ground, the wise man observes everyone.
For a long time, the noble-minded one wandered in the ocean, tossed by the waves; but having reached the further shore, he attains supreme rest.
With a peaceful disposition, he remains as if smiling within himself, regarding his former worldly states and the people who are shrouded in dense delusion.
"These perspectives on cyclic existence, which have led me into the depths of the wilderness and stolen my heart, are themselves unreal"—thus he experiences wonder within himself.
"Even the eightfold sovereignty of vision is as insignificant as a blade of grass to me; thus, because of his tranquility, he does not experience pride even when being honored."
One had his home in a mountain cave, another took refuge in a holy hermitage; one lived the life of a householder, while another remained wandering through many lands.
Some followed the conduct of a wandering mendicant, some were exclusively devoted to asceticism, some observed the vow of silence, and some were intent upon meditation.
One was renowned as a wise man; one was a listener of the Vedas and the Smṛtis; one was a king; one was a twice-born brahmin; and another remained like an ignorant man.
Some, having attained perfection through pills, collyrium, swords, and the like, travel through the sky; some live by means of arts and crafts; and some assume the appearance of commoners.
One has abandoned proper conduct; another is a leader among Vedic scholars; one behaves like a madman; and another has taken up the life of a wandering mendicant.
The person (puruṣa) is not the body and so forth, nor is it anything such as the mind; the person, which is called consciousness, never perishes at any time.
This Self is neither cut nor burnt, neither moistened nor dried; it is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and ancient.
Thus, for one who is perfectly awakened, let him remain wherever he stays in whatever manner; what is the use of rules regarding what is appropriate or inappropriate concerning place?

Let it enter the underworld, let it traverse the sky beyond the circle of the quarters, or let it wander about until it is ground to dust; yet this undecaying pure consciousness shall not go to destruction, for it is that peaceful, unborn, and auspicious reality, like the expanse of space.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Whether it is mere light or mere appearance, it shines forth as peaceful; how and when could there be the destruction of that which is pure consciousness, without beginning or end?
And the Puruṣa never perishes to that same extent; for if pure consciousness were to perish, how and from what could it ever be born again?
And pure consciousness is never anything other than itself, nor does it belong to anyone anywhere; when it is identical in the experience of all, what indeed can that "otherness" possibly be?
For everything, snow is cold, fire is hot, and water is sweet; what kind of difference, then, can there be here for that which is pure consciousness alone?
If it is said that pure consciousness perishes upon the destruction of the body, then why is there despair at death—the end of saṃsāra—which ought to be a cause for joy?
Indeed, the sky of consciousness does not perish upon the destruction of the body; even when the body has perished, the state of being a *piśāca* was witnessed by the barbarians among the kinsmen.
If it is said that consciousness exists as long as the body exists, then why does a corpse not move, even though the body remains entirely intact?

If the experience of a *piśāca* were an inherent property of the living soul, why would it not perceive that [state] at all times? And why would it perceive it in such a manner only when a kinsman has died?
If the specific nature of the living being were such [as you claim], why would a person not falsely perceive that very being as a *piśāca* when it has died in another country?
Therefore, since it is the essence of all, that pure consciousness is not restricted; whatever it knows in whatever place and in whatever manner, it perceives that very thing there.
Whatever kind of consciousness arises as entirely undisturbed and monolithic, that very experience is indeed the cause here, for it is its own inherent nature.
Nothing else is possible here as the cause at the very beginning of creation; tell me, what could that which exists now possibly be, and of what nature and how?
The splendor of conceptual construction, appearing as the world, was never produced at the beginning of creation, nor does it appear now; only the sky of consciousness shines forth.
One realizes that this visible world is merely a manifestation; for apart from the realization that it is "visible," where could its visibility exist?

The beautiful artistry of one's own wonder is awakened through awareness by means of the sky of consciousness with delight; thus, the visible world is perceived through awakening, but it is not perceived due to lack of awakening.

Awakening and non-awakening are of that very same nature, likewise free from affliction; here, the distinction exists only in words and not in reality, therefore the state of being an object of perception does not exist at all.
Know that this appearance which was seen by them was due to a lack of inquiry; since it has now been destroyed by inquiry, where can it be seen?
In this very investigation into the knowledge of the Self, let there be an effort of the intellect; through such effort, supreme practice is attained, which bestows the accomplishment of both worlds.
O virtuous one, although this subsiding of ignorance has arisen for you here, it does not attain perfection without practice.

Having completely abandoned agitation and setting aside [worldly distractions] for even a moment every day, let this beneficial treatise, which is conducive to the welfare of both worlds, be investigated.
Even though it has been understood, this knowledge of the Self remains as if unknown for you highly fortunate ones, were it not for your collective practice together.
Whoever desires an object and strives for it in that manner will certainly attain it, provided they do not turn back out of weariness.
Therefore, turn away from this investigation of false scriptures; you shall obtain peace through the true scripture, just as one obtains the fortune of victory from battle.
Whether in solitude or in the lack of solitude, this river of the mind flows; wherever it is directed with effort, there it attains its stability.
Apart from this treatise, there has been no greater good, nor will there ever be; therefore, for the sake of supreme awakening, let this alone be investigated.
By investigating this for oneself, supreme awakening is experienced; it removes the fatigue of the path of saṃsāra, and is not like a boon or a curse.
That which was not accomplished by your father, nor by your mother, nor even by meritorious deeds—that supreme good, once fully understood, will swiftly bring you benefit.
O holy man, this chronic cholera of worldly existence is perilous; it is never cured unless one attains self-knowledge.

This illusion, consisting of great delusion, persists as the false notion "I am"; through the cultivation of the meaning of the scriptures, may this state of supreme wretchedness be swiftly abandoned.
Go; do not fall into that which is sweet only at first sight—the sky, whose sole form is emptiness—licking the void air like serpents licking their own tongues within.
Alas, your days pass away with their coming and going unnoticed; for by those very days, while you wait for worldly affairs, death is brought near.
This consolation is for you who are partakers of fear: it lasts only as long as a few days until the limit of death arrives.
When death approaches, you will experience bitter suffering and torment, wherein there is the severing of limb from limb and the smearing of cold sandalwood paste.
Those deluded by wealth purchase status and riches at the price of their very lives; why then, through their intellect, do they not purchase the ageless state according to the scriptures?
How can those who, with supreme effort, place their foot in the sky, tolerate the foot of the enemy of ignorance upon their own head?
Having attained freedom from pride and delusion, proceed along the path that is not base; by awakening to one's own true nature, the root of great calamities is utterly eradicated.
Having seen and heard this me, who am thus prattling day and night for your sake, let it be realized by yourself as your own self.
If one does not seek a remedy this very day against the calamity of death, what can that fool do when death has actually arrived and he is afflicted?
Apart from this work, no other book is truly effective for realizing one's own true nature; it must certainly be accepted, just as sesame seeds are sought by those who desire oil.
This scripture illuminates the knowledge of the Self like a lamp; it awakens one quickly like a father, and delights one exceedingly like a beloved wife.

Even though knowledge exists, that which has not been understood from the collection of scriptures is difficult to grasp; yet they will understand it from this [work], which is sweet—of this there is no doubt.
This is the supreme narrative among the primary perspectives of the scriptures; it bestows awakening with ease, is heart-pleasing, and is indeed unprecedented.
One should contemplate this supreme scripture with delight through various narratives and diverse stories; a person attains the highest state—of this there is no doubt.
For that awakening which has not yet been attained even now by unimpeachable scholars is obtained from this [work], like gold from the sands.

One should never, at any time or place, pay homage to the author of a treatise; rather, one should always pay homage to the meaning of the treatise itself, which brings about experience conjoined with reasoning.
Oneness should not be practiced by those who destroy themselves—those who, out of ignorance, envy, and delusion, fail to reflect and disregard the meaning of the scriptures.
I indeed know these things exactly as they are—just as I am, and as you are, and as my thoughts are; for such is my very nature, awakened by compassion.
A pure fragment of your own consciousness stands here to speak thus: "I am a man, not a gandharva, nor a god, nor a rākṣasa."
For you are indeed pure consciousness alone; that state of yours is exceedingly stainless. By your merits, it is said, "I am established"—yet I am not, nor is there another.
Until the days of death arrive, turning everything to a dark hue, let the essence be gathered; there is a distaste for the perception of worldly objects.
He who does not seek a cure for the disease of hell while still here—once he has gone to that place where no medicine exists, what will he do, afflicted as he is by pain?
As long as a sense of revulsion toward all phenomena has not arisen, the cultivation of those very phenomena will not reach attenuation.
O one of great intelligence, there is never any means whatsoever to purify oneself except for the thinning away of latent tendencies (vāsanā).
If entities truly existed, then there would be a cultivation of things in reality; however, these do not exist at all here, just like the horns of a rabbit and so forth.
All worldly phenomena, whose beauty vanishes upon investigation, lack any real existence and fall apart when scrutinized.
Those worldly phenomena which do not exist when investigated by means of valid cognition—how can they exist, or what are they that exist eternally?
All worldly phenomena, due to the total absence of a cause, were never produced even at the beginning of creation; that which appears here is the Supreme.

In that state which transcends all sense-faculties, there exists no cause for entities whose nature consists of the six faculties with the mind as the sixth, nor is there any entity consisting of those six faculties with the mind as the sixth.
How can there be a causeless cause for entities that have various designations? How can there be non-substantiality in a substance, or how can there be non-emptiness in space?
For that which has a form must arise from something with a form, like a banyan seed; how else could that object, being itself with a form, be born from something different?
Since there is not even the slightest seed possessing form therein, the claim that the world arises from it as something possessing form is a mere mockery.
In that supreme state, there is indeed no such thing as the relationship of cause and effect; whatever is imagined by means of verbal prolixity is nothing but ignorance.
For it is experienced even by children that in the absence of auxiliary causes, an effect cannot arise from a cause as something distinct.
Furthermore, tell me: is there a cause for the earth and the other elements that consists of mere sensation? And tell me, how can shadow exist in the heat of the sun?
The notion that the world is a collection of atoms is likewise unreal; it is spoken of due to ignorance, like a bow made from a hare's horn.
If a collection of atoms, having come together, creates the world by mere chance, it likewise dissolves into darkness by mere chance.
Then, in every land and in every house, there will daily appear a previously unseen peak of dust, or perhaps a pit dug out from the earth.
And yet nothing such as that is seen; for whom could such an action belong? It would be in vain for one who lacks the capacity [for it], for atoms are indeed insentient.
O dear one, such an action can never occur for anyone without being preceded by intention; for what madman indeed would perform that which is purposeless with full awareness?
In an insentient entity, there can be no purposeful activity preceded by intelligence; without that, an accumulation of atoms cannot occur, nor is any other agent possible.
We ourselves are indeed such as these—empty-souled beings whose nature is emptiness; we stand just as the men in your dream appear to you within that dream.
Therefore, nothing whatsoever is born, nor does anything exist; thus, the pure sky of consciousness alone shines by itself within itself.
The entire expanse of space has come to rest everywhere within the space of consciousness, just as vibration, fluidity, and emptiness reside respectively in wind, water, and the sky.

Know that the nature of consciousness which exists in the interval between one place and another, even when reaching an extreme distance in the blink of an eye, is the very nature of the space of consciousness (*cidvyoman*).
For that is the intrinsic nature of all things, and they are composed of it; being such, they have the form of space, and therefore the universe is space.
The supreme transformation of that intrinsic nature occurs almost instantaneously; being non-different from its own nature, it remains as this very world.
Therefore, there is never any difference between the world and consciousness; the form of these two is one and the same, like that of the wind and its movement.

When one who knows travels from one place to another, that form which exists in the interval—whose nature is the cessation of all particularity—the wise know that to be the primary [form], and not the other.
That is the inherent nature of all beings; therein the wise abide. Therefore, these elements, such as the earth and the rest, do not deviate from their constant meditation.
This entire universe is merely the appearance of space, a manifestation consisting of light alone; the wise know its nature to be immutable and devoid of form.
It is neither born nor does it die; having once existed, it never comes to be anywhere else. The world is not other than the sky of consciousness, just as emptiness is not other than the sky.
The universe does not exist, nor did it ever exist, nor indeed will it ever come to be; this which appears is the peaceful space of consciousness within the Supreme Self.
Just as pure consciousness alone shines forth as the world before one in a dream, so too does it shine forth by itself in this state called waking, which is likewise a dream.
Since entities do not exist even at the beginning of creation, how can there be a physical body? Therefore, how could there be corporeality for consciousness, which is like the sky in a dream?
One's own body is called the self-existent (svayambhū); the previous dream belongs to the Great Consciousness; from this [body] we arise, and following that dream, there is another dream.
Therefore, even with the greatest effort, our minds will not turn toward the pustules that have arisen upon the boil.
Brahman alone exists as the unreal person, yet it is experienced as if real; from that very moment it has remained so, for this extended world is not actually false.
The world, from Brahma down to a blade of grass, arises as something false; just as it is in a dream, so too it is false and thus quickly perishes.

Just as the sky of consciousness itself, having assumed the state of the universe, vanishes within a dream, so too does it do so within that which is called the waking state, without the universe ever having truly arisen.
Even that which is experienced as false remains false, yet it stands as if true; it is consciousness alone that arises in the form of cities and so forth, just as in a dream.
Just as that which is formless appears as if possessing form, so too does the space of consciousness abide as the world; it is subtler than space, just as an atom is subtler than Mount Meru.
Indeed, how could there be atomicity in that which is called "space"? Since there is no other cause, its form cannot be established.
Since he was unborn even at the beginning of creation, from where could this world have been born? That which is a city within the space of consciousness in a dream is exactly what we have here.

There is no difference between the dream-mountain and the consciousness-ether, just as there is none between empty space and the sky; for that which is the ether of consciousness is not a physical sky, and it is precisely that which constitutes the city of the dream.
Just as that which is called vibration is itself the wind, so too the wind—whose nature consists of both vibration and non-vibration—is like space.
Therefore, this entire world is perceived as having the form of consciousness alone; it is all empty, without support, a mere manifestation of the sun of consciousness.
All this is indeed tranquil, devoid of setting and rising; it is once-for-all luminous, stainless, as silent as a stone, and free from ailment.

Therefore, tell me: how do entities exist? From where do entities arise? Where is the cognition of entities? Where is duality? Where is unity? Where am I? Where are entities? And where are mental constructs?

Ever-arisen even while engaged in worldly activity, changeless, with a mind freed from duality and unity, supremely cool within—abide in Nirvana, free from ailment; having attained oneness with pure awakening, O dear one, no entities exist.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Space is the subtle element of sound; wind is the subtle element of touch; fire arises from the intensification of their conjunction; and the subsiding of that [fire] is the state of water.
"Their assembly is vast; yet, while the appearance of the world is like a dream, how indeed can a material form proceed from the formless ether?"

If this [cognition] is postulated as being produced even after having traveled a great distance, then what fault could there be in this case for an object that is already present at the outset, which is as stainless as space?
Since it is pure awareness alone that shines as the self within its own nature, that very thing is called the "world"; and because it is real, it is truly real.
The five elements do not exist anywhere, nor do walls and such; yet, though they do not exist, they are experienced, just as in the state of dreaming.
Just as in a dream, one's own nature alone appears as a city and so forth, so too does this world shine forth during the waking state; yet in reality, it is like space.
"I am indeed the space of consciousness; this world that exists is that very same thing. Thus, "I" and "the world" are one—the single sky, as solid as a stone.
That which produces the initial creation, that which evolves at the end of a kalpa, and the very structure of the worlds—all that is indeed the formless void.
Whether the body exists or not, liberation is the state of being free from suffering and pleasure, which is imperishable; may there be complete rest in this pure, awakened nature here and now.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The state of consciousness remains experiencing its own nature in the form of the world, like a dream arising spontaneously from itself as a non-different mental construction called "imagination."
This world is indeed like the state of deep sleep even while awake, or like the interior of a stone; it is like the empty sky, yet it has not abandoned its appearance as a world.
A dream itself is the illustration here, adorned with the circle of cities; in a dream, the world appears as something shining, though it is not at all real.
This triple world is indeed unreal, appearing just as it does in a dream; likewise, even while awake, this is exactly so, and not otherwise in the slightest degree.

Neither in the waking state nor in dream is there any real existence of the world as a referent of words; rather, it is the manifestation of the sky of consciousness itself that is perceived as the world.

The self-existent one, within the sky of consciousness, perceived his own creative wonder as the world itself—assuming the form of space, time, and other such categories—within the waking and dreaming states.
This world is not anything at all, nor is consciousness (cit) anything at all; these two—consciousness and the world—appear as if they were something, like the sky, in vain.
Just as nothing at all exists in a dream, so too the three worlds appear; likewise, in the waking state, it is entirely empty and devoid of substantial form.
O Greatly Wise One, who possesses manifold emanations, in a dream indeed, even undertakings are not undertakings; the unreal appears as if real, spread out before us.
The vast expanse of space itself, devoid of any limit to the sky, is the very sky; the multitude of various cities is the mass of mountains themselves.
Just as the roar of years, oceans, and mountains is effectively silence, so too one standing nearby does not hear anything at all, even though they are fully awake.
Just as the son of a barren woman is born though unborn, so too, even when born, one remains as if unborn when there is forgetfulness of the Self's death.
That which exists quickly becomes non-existent, just as the experience of the earth [vanishes]; and everything is inverted, just as night becomes day.
Just as night arises instantly from day, and just as the sight of one's own death occurs despite its impossibility, so too does the impossible come to pass.
The impossible becomes possible, like the appearance of the world in the sky; that which is both night and day is itself the great light of darkness.
Just as light enters into darkness when there is sleep, dreaming, or day; or as the earth itself becomes the sky when one falls into a pit or similar chasm.
Just as the world appears in a dream as being nothing but unreal in form, so too does it appear in the waking state; there is not the slightest difference between the two.
Just as two suns are alike, and just as two men are alike, so too are these two—the waking state and the dream state; there is not even the slightest difference between them.
Śrī Rāma said: This is not so; for where there is a sublater, conviction arises immediately. How could that [experience] seen within a dream be equal to waking, even by its appearance?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having sported in the dream-world together with his dream-kinsmen, O Rāghava, that observer of the dream meets his death therein.
Having died in the dream-world and being separated from the dream-beings, the living being awakens here and is said to be released from sleep.
Having experienced many states of pleasure, pain, and delusion, as well as the reversals of day and night, the observer dies within the dream-like cycle of existence.
Because sleep has departed, the end of sleep arises hereafter; one should then become convinced that "this is not real."
Just as a dreamer, having met with death within the dream-world, is born again in order to see another dream consisting of the waking state.
The witness of the waking state likewise undergoes death within the waking world; in order to see another dream consisting of the waking state, he is born again.
Just as one does not consider a dream to be unreal while still within the prior waking state, so too one who has passed from one dream to another takes up a new cognition once again.
There, the person of deluded intellect again grasps that as a waking cognition, and then he experiences yet another vision of a dream even therein.
In the names "dream as waking" and "waking as dream," nothing is born and nothing dies, yet it is both born and it also dies.
One who sees a dream and dies in that dream is said here to be "awakened"; a living being who dies while awake in this world is said elsewhere to be "awakened."
While remaining in a dream, there is the manifestation of a waking-dream; for one who has died and awakened elsewhere, the waking state itself becomes a dream.
Both waking and dreaming consist of history alone; these two have mutually become the standard of comparison and the object compared.
Dream appears as if waking, and waking arises as if dream; yet in reality, both are unreal, and only the space of consciousness shines forth.
The entire range of beings, both stationary and moving, without exception—what else can possibly exist apart from pure consciousness alone?
Just as a vessel made of clay is not perceived when devoid of clay, so too wood, stone, and the like are essentially nothing but the wonder of consciousness.
This entire collection of objects is for us exactly the same in a dream as it is in the waking state; even that stone seen in a dream exists apart from the wondrous play of consciousness.
Tell me more, O wise one: is it not certain that she is indeed consciousness alone? For surely, whatever form appears in a dream, such is the undivided reality of the waking state as well.
Therefore, the entire world that has arisen is pure consciousness, a fragment of Brahman; therefore, the entire world that has arisen is pure consciousness, the very floor of Brahman.
Just as a vessel made of clay is not perceived when devoid of clay, so too an object of consciousness is not perceived when devoid of consciousness.
Just as a vessel made of stone is not found to be devoid of stone, so too the object of thought, which consists of consciousness, is not perceived as being devoid of consciousness.

Just as water exists in a liquid form and nothing devoid of liquidity can be found, so too the object of consciousness (cetya) consists of consciousness (cinmaya), and nothing empty of consciousness is perceived.
Just as fire in the form of heat is not perceived when devoid of heat, so too the object of consciousness, though consisting of consciousness, is not perceived when empty of consciousness.
Just as wind consisting of movement is not perceived when it is motionless, so too the object of thought, which consists of consciousness, is not perceived when it is empty of consciousness.
If something is composed of a certain nature, how indeed can it be obtained without that [nature]? Where is a non-empty space to be found, and where is a solid earth to be found?

Just as objects such as pots and cloths are composed solely of the space of consciousness, so too these mountains and other things are merely the manifestation of the space of consciousness within a dream.

O fortunate one, just as in a dream the sky itself appears as cities, mountains, and so forth, so too in the waking state is everything composed of consciousness. Whether it be called "dream" or "waking," here there is indeed only one peaceful, infinite, pure consciousness; let all debate cease.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, what is the nature of that space of consciousness (cidākāśa), which is the supreme Brahman? Tell me again; for there is no satiety for me as I listen to this nectar.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as two names are given to twins who are identical for the sake of worldly transaction, so too are the states of waking and dreaming, though they are both composed of stone.
In reality, however, there is no difference between these two, like that between two portions of milk; both are indeed this one alone—the stainless space of pure consciousness.
The form of consciousness that reaches from one distant place to another in a mere instant—that which exists in the interval between them—is called the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).
Just as the state of a tree standing still and drawing up its sap is clear, so too is the sky-clear state known as the sky of consciousness (cinnabhaḥ).
The state of the sky of consciousness is said to be just like the equanimous state of a person whose every desire has ceased and whose mind is perfectly tranquil.
That state of a healthy person when sleep has not yet arrived and the objects of the mind have ceased is called the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).
That state which exists as the uprooting of grasses, shrubs, creepers, and the like when they reach their growth at the end of the season, is called the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).
The state of that person who is liberated from form, light, and mental attention, and who is immortal—clear as the autumnal sky—is the space of consciousness.
That which has been created as the substratum for wood, stone, mountains, and sentient beings—the essence of their existence—is called the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).
Know that the space of consciousness (cit-kha), from which the triad of the seer, the seeing, and the seen arises, and in which they set, is free from all affliction.
That from which all diverse experiences of objects arise and in which they fully transform is called the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).
That in which all is, from which all comes, who is all, and who is from every side, and who eternally consists of all—that is called the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).
That which shines as the self-luminous space of consciousness—identical in name whether in heaven, on earth, outside, or within another—is called the sky of consciousness (cidākāśa).
That sky of consciousness, whose limbs are the universe, is that eternal and extended firm thread upon which the entire world—arising from both the existent and the non-existent—rests like a garland.
Since all the transformations of creation and dissolution are produced from it, and into it they are dissolved—whatever consists of that is the sky of consciousness.
That from which the universe proceeds when sleep has ceased, and in whose tranquility it ceases—that is called the ether of consciousness (cid-ambaram).

Know that to be the sky of consciousness (cinnabhaḥ), which consists of self-experience and abides within itself, by whose opening and closing the existence, dissolution, and emergence of the world occur.
Having determined in every way that "this is not it, this is not it," that which is never anything at all is called the space of consciousness (cidvyoma).

That form of consciousness which exists in the interval between the departure from one place and the arrival at another, even when [the distance] is far away in half a blink of an eye, is known as the form of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).

This entire universe, exactly as it has come to be and exactly as it exists, is indeed composed of that [consciousness]; even when joined with form, light, and mental attention, it remains of such a nature.
Through a slight unfolding, this pure, stainless form—the sky of Being-Consciousness—appears as if it were something else, even though it remains non-different from its own nature.
Perceiving objects with the senses while truly being free from latent desires, remain awakened and unified, as if established in the state of deep sleep.
Free from latent tendencies, with a tranquil mind, speak, go, drink, or take; like a living stone, remain forever in profound and solid silence.
This which you see before you as an object of sight is not possible at all; it is like the water of a mirage, or like duality appearing within the moon.
This [effect] was indeed unarisen at first due to the absence of a cause; for without a cause, an effect truly cannot be established.
Or rather, whatever arises does so without a cause; it is the supreme form as it truly exists that appears as if it has arisen.
Just as it exists, O limb, the prior form remains established; it is indeed non-dual and pure, yet it is perceived through duality.
In this regard, that mature experience which arises as a direct cognition is known by the wise to be an adventitious delusion, equal to a woman seen in a dream.
Therefore, the visible object has not arisen, it does not exist, and it will not come to be; nor does it perish—for what can perish that which does not exist?
That very same supreme, tranquil expanse of consciousness remains thus: unswerving from its own nature, established in itself, and serene, yet appearing as if it were the world.

For that which was seen as the object of vision at first does not exist as real at any time; nor indeed is there a seer, for in the absence of an object to be seen, how can there be the state of being a seer?
Śrī Rāma said: "If it is so, O Brahman, then tell me: what is this appearance of the seer and the seen, and how does it manifest? Speak further, O best of speakers."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Since the visible world is always non-existent in nature due to the absence of a cause, even the mature formulation that "it possesses visibility" is utterly impossible.
Know that whatever appears here—consisting of the delusion of the seer and the seen, such as the world and so forth—is the supreme form of the Supreme Self.
Just as in a dream one remains as pure consciousness alone, like the sky or a forest, so too does pure consciousness itself appear within itself in the form of the world.
From the beginning of creation until now, there has never been any material cause whatsoever anywhere; thus, only the absolute Brahman shines forth.
That which is the manifestation of the space of consciousness itself expands within the Self; this very world shines forth as its own manifested form.

Just as there is existence for what exists, just as there is emptiness for what is empty, and just as there is form for that which possesses form, so too is the world [the form] of the sky of consciousness.
Know this to be the reflection of consciousness, a dense mass of ultimate reality; thus situated, it shines by itself, consisting of the seer, the seen, and the act of seeing.
In reality, however, because of the absence of duality, there is neither appearance nor the act of appearing; who can know this something indescribable as being either existent or non-existent?
Śrī Rāma said: "If it is so, O Brahman, tell me then: how has this distinction consisting of cause and effect and so forth arisen? And how has it attained the status of reality?"

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the light of consciousness itself contemplates whatever appears according to its own manifestation, it immediately perceives that very thing as its own self; thus you have seen.
This form is nothing but the sky of consciousness; it does not become deluded within its own void. Just as in a dream, who can question this?
When one state of being reaches another state of being, that form of consciousness which exists in the interval is the sky of consciousness; this entire world is that alone, and nothing else.
Views such as the relationship between cause and effect are but the manifestations of ignorance; this [consciousness] constructs them just like the world—so who is there to question it?
If there were some other entity who is a seer, an enjoyer, or an agent, then it would be logical to ask, "What is this visible world? and so forth; otherwise, it would not be so.
Wherein, in the dream state, only the sky of consciousness shines forth, free from appearances—pure, one, yet manifold in nature—what can be conceptualized there, and where?
This light of creation shines within the Self-born One alone, who is pure consciousness; yet, once fully known, it becomes Brahman itself in an instant.
This very [reality], when not fully understood, is called delusion and illusion; it is termed the world, and is described as the visible object of knowledge.

By the light of the sky of consciousness, the demon of the visible world is perceived by the mind; like a ghost seen by a child, it is understood to be non-existent, even though it appears as if existent.

Although the world does not exist within the Self, it is experienced by the sky of consciousness alone, just as in a dream the state of mountains and cities appears even though they do not truly exist, like a painting with its various parts.
"I am the mountain, I am Rudra, I am the ocean, I am the Virāj"—this is perceived by consciousness alone within the void, just as mountains and cities appear in a dream.
Because there is no cause, no effect whatsoever has been produced; thus does consciousness abide as "this-ness" within the space of consciousness during the great dissolution.

This world, which is merely a void-bodied form within the conscious self, is experienced as the sky by the sky; it is indeed causeless, being of the nature of pure consciousness within the conscious Self.
All living beings are indeed inert and worn out like mirrors; yet, for one who performs investigation while standing right before them, their inner essence is revealed.

Having abandoned those respective forms and realized that the world is the void of pure consciousness alone, one should remain as if made of sentient stone; there is no other superior state than this.

Just as the world-fluid, consisting of water and whirlpools, remains while moving the body, so too does the nature of consciousness remain as consciousness while appearing as the world through the perception of the mind.

Just as the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma) grants one's desires and just as the thought-gem (cintāmaṇi) does, so too does consciousness (cit) instantly fulfill whatever has been cultivated within one's own mind.
Consciousness, whose nature is space, quickly fulfills one's desires within the self by means of the inner self, like a wish-fulfilling gem or a desire-granting tree.

When one reaches another place from one's own land, the body of consciousness remains in the intermediate space; since this visible world consists of that [consciousness], whence can there be the delusion of duality or unity?
Thus, the infinite, clear, and luminous interior shines like its own shadow; though devoid of limbs and empty within, it appears like the blueness in the sky.

The experience of a dissimilar effect does not occur due to the absence of auxiliary causes; therefore, at the beginning of creation, primordial consciousness itself is the visible world, just as in a dream.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The universe, consisting of pure consciousness and devoid of objects of thought, shines everywhere as the sky of consciousness. Herein, consciousness, the act of cognizing, and this object of cognition are likewise of this same nature.
Therefore, everyone remains as if dead even while living; "this one," "I," and "you"—though alive, are like the dead.
Even when engaged in worldly affairs, they are as if dead through the silence of wood; indeed, all beings, whether moving or stationary, are like birds [in their essential nature].
Whatever is extended here, having the nature of a reflection in the glass of space, know that it is nothing at all; for how could anything exist within the void?
Just as in the case of a tuft of hair, the current of a river, a column of smoke, a pearl, and so forth, that which shines forth with effort lacks substantiality even though it is experienced.

In the very same way, within this manifestation of the sky of consciousness called "the world," though it is experienced as utterly empty, what basis for stability could there be, and who could possess the sense of "I"?

In this web of conceptual constructions spun by consciousness, which is empty in essence and devoid of purpose; in earth and the other elements, which are non-substantial and arise as a mere sky of delusion.
"O children, tell me: what is this basis for 'I' and 'mine'? Enough! It is understood: only a child delights in the conceptual construction of a child."
O timid one, by means of futile investigations into the earth and other elements, your life will pass away in vain; you will know nothing at all, being intent on washing the sky.
Since the causes such as auxiliary factors and so forth were absent from the very beginning, how could that which was not produced at the outset come into existence today?
Those fools who engage in worldly discourse with an unborn and non-existent object are like those who care for a son who is either dead or unborn.
Whence have the earth and other elements arisen, by whom, what indeed, and how? This tranquil space of consciousness shines thus by itself within itself.
For those whose minds are agitated by conceptual constructions such as cause, effect, time, and so forth, the earth and other elements exist in this way; enough of such childish views for us.

That which is called the world—both that which consists of earth and other elements, and that which consists of space—is thus a manifestation of the nature of the void, like the jewel of consciousness appearing in dreams and similar states.

That limb of this sky of consciousness which is formless and inferred through one's own experience, appears in the form of the surface of the earth and so forth, designated by the term "the object of knowledge" (*vedya*).

Śrī Rāma said: This ignorance, appearing in the form of the visible world, exists for one who possesses it; though it is seen as a city in a dream within the sky of consciousness, it is actually empty.
O Sage, please tell me again: for how long does that ignorance persist, what is its form, what is its nature, and how extensive is it?
