Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For those ignorant ones for whom ignorance regarding the earth and so forth exists, there is no end to this [ignorance], just as there is none to Brahman; hear now the story concerning this.
Somewhere in a corner of the sky, there exists something similar to this world; somewhere else, by this very same arrangement, there exists some other triple-world.
There is a certain region of the earth that is the ornament of all that dwells upon it; in that land, there is a city named Tatamiti, whose fame is clearly manifest upon the earth.
There was a certain king there, renowned as Vipaścit, who shone by virtue of his wisdom in an assembly of excellent courtiers.
He shone in that assembly like a royal swan among lotuses, like the moon, the lord of stars, amidst the circle of constellations, and like Mount Sumeru among the multitude of mountains.
Since their speech turns back from describing his qualities due to its own inability, the light of poets becomes as immovable in form as a mountain.
From him, who blossoms day after day and strives to illuminate all directions, there arises the glory born of his majesty, as if from a lotus.
Proud and devoted to the Brahmanas, he worshipped Agni alone as the presiding deity; with equal devotion he honored him, and knew no other god.
Arranged in formations of fish and sea-monsters, accompanied by multitudes of elephants and horses, enriched with whirlpool and wheel arrays, and garlanded by the force of surging waves.
Devoted to the maintenance of boundaries and possessing strength greater than Akampana’s, his four ministers were like the oceans situated at the four quarters of the world.
He was Sudurjaya, the conqueror who, like the Sudarśana discus, illuminated the earth as the hub for the entire circle of the quarters.
Once, a swift messenger arrived from the eastern direction and spoke these words in secret, with rapid speed and terrible syllables:
O Lord, from whom the earth—the cow resting upon the tree of your arms—never falls; please listen to me and then do as is appropriate for what has transpired.
The vassal king of the eastern quarter has set due to fever; I believe he has gone to conquer Yama, having been challenged by you, the conqueror of enemies.
While he was attempting to conquer it from all sides, the leader of the southern region was struck down by his enemy, who attacked with two armies from the east and the west.
When he had died, as soon as the Lord of the Western Quarter arrived with his army, intent on seizing those two regions, they met him.
Together with the kings of the eastern regions and the monarchs of the southern path, he was slain in battle by his enemies on the very road.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: While he was speaking thus, another messenger, distressed by haste, entered the palace like a surge of dull-headed calamity.
The spy said: "The commander-in-chief of the northern quarter, harassed by the enemies of the gods, is coming here with his army like a flood of water breaking its dam."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having heard this, the protector of the earth, considering further delay to be unreal, spoke these words as he was departing from the excellent palace.
Let the king’s vassals be arrayed for battle and let the ministers be brought forward; let the armories be opened and let the terrible weapons be distributed.
Let armor be fastened upon the bodies; let the foot soldiers assemble; let the troops be counted quickly, and let the excellent battle arrays be formed.
"Let the commanders of the forces be appointed, and let spies be dispatched everywhere. Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: While the king was speaking thus with haste and agitation, [the sage intervened].

The doorkeeper, having entered with a hurried and bowed mien, spoke thus: The doorkeeper said: "O Lord, the superintendent of the northern quarter stands at the gate; he desires a vision of you, O God of gods, as the sun longs for the lotus."
The king said: "Go, then, without delay and bring him in. We shall learn what has occurred at the ends of the earth from his report."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having been addressed thus, the king saw before him the commander of the forces, who had been ushered in by the doorkeeper and was intent on offering salutations.
With every limb mangled and wounded, his body covered from head to toe with injuries, gasping for breath and vomiting blood, he was overcome by weakness despite his fortitude.
Having prostrated, suppressing his bodily pain and breathing with continuous gasps, he spoke these words with great urgency.
The commander-in-chief said: "O Lord, all three guardians of the quarters, accompanied by a vast army, have gone to the city of Yama at your command alone to conquer Yama."
Therefore, many kings have arrived here with their forces, pursuing me because I am incapable of protecting that region and other duties.
A great enemy force has reached this realm of Your Majesty; let it be dealt with accordingly, for there is nothing that is unconquerable for Your Majesty.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Now, while he was speaking thus, distressed and seeking a livelihood, another man suddenly entered and spoke these words.
O Lord of Men, the vast forces of this mandala stand on high in the four directions, like the play of broad petals.
Will the earth not be surrounded by our enemies with the splendor of their forests of discuses, maces, spears, and javelins, as if by the ridges of the Lokāloka mountain?
There, chariots with banners, weapons, and warriors, crowded with moving attendants, rush forth like a mass of the Triple City flying up into the air.
Raising their trunks like trees in a forest of flesh, the arrays of elephants trumpet like a multitude of rain-clouds in the sky.
Making the earth rise and fall through their galloping, the throngs of horses neighed like a great ocean tossed by the movement of the wind.
The horses' mouths, emitting frothy spray, resound on all sides in circular patterns like the waters of the salt ocean.
With armors possessing the luster of the sky, army after army arises in every direction with massive waves, like the flood of the ocean at the time of universal dissolution.
The luster of the arrows, missiles, weapons, armor, crowns, and ornaments upon their bodies shines like the flames of the fire of your majesty.
With arrays of fish and sea-monsters and the movements of whirlpools, the masses of troops rise up like the surging waves of the ocean.
Through mutual contact, the rows of weapons such as spears and the like blaze and roar with fierce *huṃkāras* born of anger and other emotions.
"O Lord, I have been thus commanded by my master to make this request: therefore, please go forth to clear away the thickets and other obstructions at the boundary of the maṇḍala."
Therefore, O Lord, I am going there, equipped with my spear, sword, and arrows; everything has been reported by me here, and Your Majesty knows what must follow from this.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus and offered his salutation, he departed in haste, making a gurgling sound like a wave of the ocean that has subsided.

With its ministers, kings, warriors, officials, elephants, women, chariots, horses, attendants, and throngs of city-dwellers all thrown into confusion, the king’s palace—where the multitude of weapons was brandished out of fear—resembled a great forest agitated by a fierce wind.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In the meantime, all the ministers approached the king, just as the sages approached Indra when the realm of the sky had been invaded by the Daityas.
The ministers said: "O Lord, we have reached a conclusion: as long as the enemies are not yet within our reach, let the fourth expedient, force (*daṇḍa*), be employed against them."
O Lord, since no request or entreaty was ever made by us before, what talk can there be now for you to act toward them?
The enemies—wicked, barbarian, wealthy, hailing from various lands, well-united, numerous, and having found a vulnerability—are not susceptible to conciliation and the other [strategic means].
This is indeed a great rashness; there is no other remedy except to avoid it. Therefore, let preparations for battle be made immediately.
Let the command be given to the heroes; let the chosen deities be worshipped; let the neighboring lords be summoned, and let the drum of battle be struck.
Let the warriors arm themselves completely and go forth into battle; let the quarters of the sky be made radiant, dense with clouds that tremble at the hour of doom.
Let the bows be strung loudly; let the rows of bowstrings twang; and let the quarters of the sky become dark as rain-clouds with the circles of [shattered] fragments.
May the clouds of heroes—whose lightning is the vibrating bowstring, whose thunder is their deep roar, and who possess the gleaming circles of their bows—release showers of iron arrows.
The king said: "Go quickly; let the preparations for battle be made. Having bathed and worshipped the fire, I shall depart for the field of combat."
Having spoken thus, the king, though engaged in great undertakings, was bathed in an instant by the jars of Ganges water, like a new garden in the rainy season by clouds.
Then, having entered the fire-chamber and worshipped the consumer of oblations with devotion according to the scriptures, the king reflected.
His lifespan has been brought to its end with the splendor of effortless luxury and majesty; he has bestowed fearlessness upon his subjects, sealed as far as the oceans extend.
Having trampled the surface of the earth, his enemies were placed beneath his footstool; the ten directions were bent low, as if they were creepers weighed down by the burden of fruit.
His white fame is inscribed upon the lunar orbs of the minds of his subjects; the creeper of his glory has been planted upon the earth and flows toward the three worlds.
Friends, companions, noble ones, and kinsmen were filled with jewels like treasure chests; on the shores of the ocean, they drank the fermented juice of coconut sap.
The lives of my enemies have become as unsteady as the skin on the throat of a frog; marked by my commands, they have become like the mountain ranges of other continents.
It has roamed through the Siddha armies across the nine lands at the ends of the quarters, and it has rested upon the summits of the kings at the borders of the earth with the grace of a cloud.

By means of his intellect alone—filled with wisdom, characterized by absolute virtue, and accomplishing desired ends—he acquired kingdoms that were both gained and never lost, established upon a high station.
Even the unruly rākṣasas were bound with heavy fetters; and dharma, artha, and kāma existed in mutual harmony, free from conflict or diminution.
My youth has been spent by me in unbroken [purity], drinking in great fame; now it shines like a mass of frost resting upon young grass.
Old age has arrived, sweeping away all the fervor of enjoyments; upon it, fierce, powerful enemies seeking battle have descended.
Having gathered from all sides, our victory remains uncertain; therefore, let us offer this very oblation here to this god who bestows victory.
"Raising up this very oblation of my head, I indeed offer it. The King said: "O God Agni, this head of mine has become an oblation for you."
O Lord of Gods, previously I offered [this] like a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa); if you are pleased, O Blessed One, then by this act of mine—
O Lord, let four bodies of my own arise from the sacrificial pit—powerful, radiant with splendor, like the arms of Nārāyaṇa.
"O wise and all-pervading Lord, may I slay my enemies in the four directions without obstacle, and may you grant me your vision."

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus, that protector of the earth took up his sword and swiftly severed the head, which was adorned with a lotus garland, as easily as a child playfully plucks a flower.
As soon as he had offered his severed head into the fire of the one with the black path (the god Śiva), that king fell into the flames together with his body.
Then, having consumed it, the fire bestowed upon him a body four times greater; for that which is consumed by the great indeed increases instantaneously.
Then, O lord of the earth, the king rose from the fire in four forms, blazing with masses of splendor like Nārāyaṇa emerging from the ocean.
Those four bodies of his shone with radiant luster, naturally endowed with excellent crowns, ornaments, weapons, and garments.
Wearing breastplates and helmets, together with crowns, bracelets, and armlets, and complete with necklaces and earrings—all were of noble character.
All were of identical form, possessed of similar limbs, and stood there as jewels among horses, resembling the swift and noble Uccaiḥśravas.
Those noble-minded ones possessed quivers filled with arrows of gold; they were auspicious, equal in their physical forms, and possessed bows of identical quality.
That man upon whom they mount—whether on an elephant, a chariot, or a horse—becomes entirely inaccessible to the faults of all enemies.
Having drunk and held them for a long time within the womb, they were tormented by the male principle, like the oceans cast upon a sacrificial altar and consumed there by the submarine fire.

With their bodies filled with heaps of jewels, horses, gold, and flowers, illuminating everything with smiles as bright as the moon, these four—whose forms were auspicious like those of Hari himself, or like oceans, or like the Vedas—issued forth from the fire fed by the oblations.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When they had reached the vicinity of the city from the four directions along with their enemies, in that interval, a terrible battle broke out there.
The villages and cities were plundered; the families and great lineages were destroyed; their bodies blazed with the fire of conflagration, enveloped by masses of smoke like clouds.
The sun was obscured by the great smoke of the net of arrows, appearing as darkness; the solar disc was suddenly visible and then suddenly vanished from sight.
The forest of leaves was scorched by the great heat of the fire’s burning; the sky was filled with the sparks of flickering tongues of flame, like a shower of clubs and stones.

With the reflections of flames doubled by the mirrors [of his armor], he possessed a weapon of blazing fire; having routed the great heroes in battle, he attained the nectar-like splendor of Indra’s consort.
It resounded with the cries of wild elephants, bringing joy to those eager for battle, and rained down a shower of *bhuśuṇḍī* missiles, discuses, spears, tridents, and javelins.
It caused the hearts of the base and ignorant to break with the joy of the soldiers' clamor, and it blocked the path to heaven with clouds as white as masses of dust.
The dust rose as the neighboring kings, frantic with the fear of death, raised their shouts, while the people fell here and there, struck down like by lightning.
A cloud consisting of fire, cast out from houses whose roofs were consumed by flames; a cloud consisting of countless showers of arrows that bestowed the joy of death.
The waves of the ocean were surpassed by the surging waves of horses, and it was made harsh by the loud *kreṃkāra* cries resulting from the clashing of elephants' tusks.
Where the walls of millions upon millions of huts were formidable with thorns, and the mass of dancers was shattered by the clashing of blunt-tipped towers and turrets.
With battle-axes flashing with the grandeur of falling and tumbling down, and with the whirring sound of fluttering banners and pennants flapping in the sky like hollow gourds;
With the clashing of weapons against stones, the sounds of tusks striking the tusks, and the loud *tāra*, *kreṅkāra*, and *huṃkāra* cries, the celestial elephant was summoned.
The great ocean of the sky was filled with the floodwaters of the river of falling arrows, and it was harsh with the makaras of whirling discuses, spears, and sword-blades.
The circle of continents was joined together by the fierce clanging of the armor of colliding warriors and by the shimmering *jhaṇajhaṇa* sounds [of weapons].
The ground was turned into mud by the arrows crushed under the falling feet of warriors; chariots and elephants were swept away by the force of the flowing rivers of blood.

There, broad double-edged spears fell and rose again with the ease of Garuḍa’s flight, while weapons—like aquatic creatures—were shattered and distressed by the waves of arrows that blocked their path.
The sky blazed with flames emerging from the friction of meteors, while heroes, freed from wrinkles and grey hair, had ascended to the third heaven.

The dust of the earth was like a flowing stream of white milk, shimmering like the luster of lightning; the sky was devoid of any gaps due to weapons, while the surface of the ground served as the support for those engaged in combat.

It was fierce with rival warriors shouting out in the arrogance of their fierce battalions; it was filled with the clattering of crashing chariots and the rolling of vehicles as their wooden frames were ground to powder.
It was crowded with thorns consisting of headless trunks, warriors, and vetālas; its lotus-hearts were the foremost corpses being devoured by vetālas for their flesh.
The sky was turned into a forest by the swaying tree-like arms of headless trunks (kabandhas), whose heads, half-heads, hands, hooves, and thighs had been severed by heroes.
The chamber was struck by the laughter of vetālas with flickering faces, and it was terrifying due to the frowns of soldiers who were arrogant and fierce in their armor.
It is exclusively for killing, exclusively for dying, and exclusively for ornamentation; it is the giving and receiving of blows, and the ultimate defilement of miserliness.
It dries up the rut-fluid of the elephants of the foremost heroes and increases the joy of Yama, who takes singular delight in slaughter.
For those who do not boast and remain concealed, there is the proclamation of victory; for those who are not brave but remain concealed, there is the supreme proclamation of their power.
The awakening of their own dormant virtues, such as valor and the like, is the wealth of those strong-armed men who serve as the foundation for kingdoms.
It shattered the temples of rutting elephants by the impact of chariots mounted by tuskers, and it warded off the flow of ichor from all the intoxicated, scent-elephants.
The intoxicated elephants were released by the surrounding vassals, who cried out like cranes; the army of aged kings suffered the pain of sword-wounds inflicted by their own ranks.
Like the day belonging to the sun, it had come for refuge to the king; it was filled with men who were half-crushed and half-dead by the throngs of approaching soldiers.
It was a new marketplace for wealth, where life itself is the commodity, where men, intoxicated by the power of their vital breath, begin the act of crushing one another.
With the multitude of banners fastened to him acting as moving trees for his arms, he was like a coral ornament for the Fortune of the Three Worlds, radiant with passion.
The courtyard of the sky was covered with parasols as beautiful as the waters of the milk-ocean churned by Mount Mandara, and was richly adorned with flowers that were the very weapons [of the gods].
He whose heroic intent was sung by the hosts of gods and gandharvas, and who made the Hālāhala weapon his arm with its blade as swift as a flickering palm leaf.
Having devoured the countless Yātudhānas who were striking at the Saṃgha with a clanging of weapons, and having filled the mountain-cave dwellings with unprecedented, hideous trees;
The sky was filled with heads and hands scattered by the clashing forest of spears, while the quarters of the horizon were submerged in a flood of stones hurled from slings.
The great trees were bursting and melting with a massive *caṭacaṭā* sound, while the women’s shrill cries of "ha-ha-la" echoed through the city and its mansions.
Having abandoned their wealth, homes, and hosts of weapons that shone like a forest fire among the Mandara trees, the people fled far across the earth.
Because it carried weapons on all sides, it was abandoned by those who sought to witness it face-to-face; it was shunned by the timid, just as a flock of birds is avoided by serpents.
It was crowded with excellent warriors crushed by the tusks of elephants, like human grapes being pressed in a machine at the threshold of Death.
Its caves were made resonant by the roar of combatants and by herds of trumpeting elephants, while its weapons lay scattered upon the ground, crushed by the impact of mechanical stones.
Amidst the mountain caves, their thundering roars were echoed back by the mountain's interior; they had acquired this wealth, which was the very essence of their lives, through their own exertion.
It was scorched by the burning of weapons and by incessant conflagrations, both through those very same means and others, as well as through various duels that never came to an end.
It was surrounded by elite groups of surviving warriors, who were as pure as Mount Kailāsa and had become the very support of the Lord.
Overwhelmed by those noble ones—who are themselves the death of even Death—death became life for them, and life became death in battle.
In that battle, where the excellent elephants were severed like lotuses from the sky, the exceedingly formidable warriors shone like cranes in a lake.

With the whizzing sounds of stone-tipped projectiles being hurled from machines, with the roars of soldiers whose heads were suddenly struck down as they rushed through the sky like clouds raining arrows, with the clanging of weapons spreading across the heavens, and with the noise of horses, chariot wheels, and elephants—that [battle] reached a state where the ears of the aged grew deafened, becoming as dull as the interior of a solid stone, its joints and bonds utterly shattered.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, during that battle resembling the end of a kalpa, amidst the tumultuous clash of equal forces, the armies shone as they fell and rose again in the fray.
While the musical instruments, kettledrums, great conchs, and swords resounded in the sky, and while the twanging of the heroes' bows produced piercing shrieks, [the battle continued].

In that mass of warriors, formidable with the mutual clashing of their armor, making a cacophony of "kavaṭ-kaṭa" sounds through their grandiose displays, and with their mail-coats fiercely struck together;
As the armies of the wise king’s faction were being broken in battle, they fell into a stupor like creepers being torn asunder.
The drum of the king’s departure resounded, filling the quarters of the sky with a sound as deep as the thunder of clouds at the end of a kalpa, echoing in four ways.
Violent as if occurring simultaneously with the bursting of the great mountain ranges, it deafened all the quarters of the horizon with its crackling and crashing explosions.
With his four forms like the world-protectors, and with his four arms like those of Nārāyaṇa, that lord of the earth went forth in the four directions.
Surrounded by a great fourfold army, he emerged with difficulty from the city, passing out through the circle of watchtowers.
He beheld his own army depleted and the circle of enemy forces powerful, roaring with a form like that of cosmic dissolution—terrible as the ocean agitated by battle.
Dense with the spray of arrows, crowded with arrays of crocodiles, encircled by arrays of elephants, and spread wide with arrays of waves.

Its interior was filled with waves of battle arrays flowing like the whirlpools of a river; it possessed the eddies of hundreds of moving chariots and the swarms of banners like its rows of surging billows.
Rich with the foam of shimmering parasols, resounding with the neighing and whinnying of horses, with the water of flashing weapons and the supreme, glistening mass of flowing streams.

The river of battle had waves consisting of throngs of elephants and horses leaping about, with the glittering weapons as its water and the rising, gurgling bellies of the slain as its churning depths.
Resounding with the humming of winds agitated by the shattering [of mountains], its body was the great trembling of the lordly mountains made to rise and fall.
It was a great body of water, its vast expanse adorned by waves that surged forth as it flowed boundlessly, while its elephants, horses, and men playfully struck down mountains with their ease.
It had the dense form of the onset of a world-ending dissolution at an untimely hour, a single great ocean of blood that filled the entire space between heaven and earth.
Its interior was covered with a flood of fallen gems from shattered sword-blades; its moving battle-arrays were like shifting stones being hurled by mechanical engines.
In some places it was bent by clouds of twilight and masses of frost-like jewel-spray; in other places, its clouds of rays were turned yellow by the flow of dust-storms.
Beholding him, he thought in his mind, "I shall become for him an Agastya for this ocean of battle," and thus resolved to drink up that sea of war.
He recalled the Vāyavya weapon and fixed it upon his bow, which was as firm as a mountain peak, like Śiva intent on the destruction of Tripura.
Then, for the welfare and peace of his own country and army, he paid homage to the Fire-god, recited the mantra quickly, and cast away that terrible [weapon].
Just so, for the sake of assisting him, he discharged the great Parjanya weapon, the weapon of the great lord of gods, to extinguish the heat caused by his enemy.
Therefore, emerging from that terrible bow wielded by the Eight-formed Lord (Śiva), [the arrows] filled the hollows of the quarters in all four directions.
Rivers of arrows flowed forth, as did rivers of tridents; likewise, fierce rivers of spears and rivers of *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons issued forth.
There were rivers of mallets, rivers of spears by their force, rivers of wheels, and the swift currents of rivers of battle-axes.
There were rivers of javelins and great torrents of slings, and streams of stones, while the winds portended the end of the eon.
There were rivers of thunderbolts and likewise rivers of lightning; there were floods of water-bearing streams accompanied by showers of swords.
There were great showers of iron arrows, thick with the joy of their arising like portents, and serpents that appeared as if born from the mountain kings split open at the end of an eon.
By the force of that shower of weapons, the ocean of the enemy's army was instantly swept away, not over time, like a mound of dust scattered on all sides.
Like lakes whose embankments have burst apart due to torrents of water, thunderbolts, weapons, and fierce winds, the armies fled in all directions.
That flood of troops, consisting of the four divisions, turned its back and fled swiftly in all four directions like the great torrent of a mountain river during the rainy season.
The trees of its banners and standards were broken and carried away by the wind; its forest of flickering sword-blades was variegated with the flowers of shimmering rays of light.
It was covered with the liquid blood from large rolling stones, and its heart-shattering roar of ghastly *ghuraghura* sounds was enough to break one's heart.
The thundering clouds were outshone by the crackling *caṭacaṭa* sounds produced by the clashing of the tree-like tusks of massive elephants being swept along.
The clashing of the fierce assembly of weapons produced a jingling sound like that of blossoming flowers; the waves of the four galloping horses were shimmering and surging with a resonant roar.

It was thick with the deep *kreṅkāra* sounds of stones struck by the multitude of chariots and other warriors; it was a perilous place due to the clashing of foot soldiers, chariots, elephants, horses, and rocks.
It was thick with the sounds of "kaṭu," "caṅkāra," "cītkāra," and "kreṃkāra," and agitated by a dense clamor of cries, "We are dead! We are dead!"
It possessed the gurgling roar of moving great whirlpools of the army-ocean; it was a canopy of evening clouds formed by the mist of blood-sprays.
The cloud, whose waters were scattered and severed by the wind, was dwarfed; it was adorned by the shattering of the banks of the earth’s surface, which had become muddy from the rain.
It was wondrous with spears, pikes, maces, and javelins brandished like palm leaves; it scorched the timid folk who cried out in distress, like a young deer.

It was densely covered with the withered leaves of the multitudes of dead elephants, horses, and warriors; it was turned into a mire by the mud formed from the ground flesh, fat, and marrow of crushed bodies.
The thick sands there consist of massive bones ground into powder by hooves; it is a place made treacherous by the tips of wooden beams and stones being carried along by the current.

With oceans roaring like those at the dissolution of the world, with winds blowing like those at the dissolution, with torrents falling like those at the dissolution, and with the perils of thunderbolts at the dissolution;
The entire surface of the earth was mired with mud, its lands inundated by water, while the sky-cages were formed by rain-showers that had frozen white and cold.
By the fires blazing through the entire city, the villages, and the houses, and by the gurgling cries of the subjects, horses, elephants, and foot soldiers;
With the rumbling of chariots like thunderclouds in heaven and on earth, and with the dense, fourfold *kreṅkāra* sounds of the *tārakas* in all four directions;
Through the clashing and friction of the expanding circles of lightning, and through the raining down of arrows, spears, clubs, darts, slings, and other weapons;
The innumerable forces of the powerful kings, extending in every direction, quickly fled and perished like a swarm of gnats.

By the falling showers of thunderbolts from clouds whose mass of weapons resembled forests of unrestrained fire, the armies—powerless like the waters of a turbulent ocean—became utterly distraught, as if entering the submarine fire.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: If the sandalwood forest, which serves as the garment for the serpents that are the world's necklaces, were cut down by the edges of axes and fallen into the southern ocean;
Like leaves swept away by a flood, the Persians, striking one another in their confusion, were destroyed in the Vañjula forest.
On Mount Dardura, in its depths, the Daradas—with their hearts torn by fear—were hidden within the hollows of caves like Dānavas.
The winds, bearing a mist of powder from the tips of the streams of their four weapons, were encircled by lightning and caused the clouds of uplifted weapons to swirl.
With their bodies crushed by the mutual impact of their tusks, the elephants became like lumps of food swallowed by the belly of Death, which devours its prey whole.
Those born of that [lineage], the Raivatikas, were struck at night by fierce *tomara* weapons; their limbs were torn apart and devoured by *rūpikā* female *piśācas*.

In the dense thickets of *tālī* and *tamāla* trees, and in the withered jungles of Daśārṇa, they were caught by lions who placed their paws upon their throats and tore them apart within, so that they lost their lives.
On the shore of the western ocean, in the coconut-bearing lands, the Yavanas, their lives departed, were swallowed by swarms of sea-monsters.
The Śakas could not endure even for a moment that dark mass of iron arrows; like beds of lotuses, their lives were made to dance away.

Mahendra, with its peaks reaching toward the sky as if to hear [the gods], appeared like Mount Meru surrounded by dark herds of elephants fleeing through the heavens, or like it were enveloped by masses of blue clouds.

The army of the Taṅgaṇas, possessing the excellent form of refined gold, was shattered; slain and stripped of their garments by thieves who were night-stalkers, they were devoured in a secluded place.
Then the surface of the earth became like the sky with its burden of stars, due to the weapons of fire flashing and revolving on all sides.

Resounding with the deep humming of echoes from the hollows of the earth and the clouds that held the rain, the sky—acting as a cave within the house of the world—seemed intent on singing a thick song.
The people from other continents, shattered by the wheels, gave up their lives like old fish in a waterless swamp of fish-bones and forest debris.
Once they had conquered as many islands as could fit within their bellies on Mount Sahya, they rested for seven days and proceeded with a slow gait due to their exhaustion.
In the groves of *puṃnāga* trees on Mount Gandhamādana, heaps of saffron were gathered and guarded by young Vidyādhara maidens.
By those showers of discharged discuses from the Hūṇas, Cīnas, and Kirātas, their heads were severed by the forward-moving winds like lotus flowers.
Like thorns on the stalks of lotuses, they remained motionless; out of fear of him, those made of wood dwelt for a long time within every tree.
Upon the mountain and forest grounds, which were the playgrounds of beautiful deer, there then arose a dense agitation from their falling [arrows] in all four directions.
Those named Kaṇṭakasthala were as rough as the thorny ground; they dwelt upon the thorny ground within the region of Kaṇṭakasthala.
The Pārasīkas, having reached the further shore of the ocean by means of boats, fell down, purified by the winds, like stars at the time of universal dissolution.
Winds blew, striking against the oceans and marked by the jagged edges of rocks; they plundered the forests in every direction, as if portending the dissolution of the world.
Dense with the force of rain-showers, drenched in muddy water, and filled with the deep rumbling of clouds, the ten directions became invisible due to the winds of many agitated weapons.
With winds making a roaring sound and carrying a whistling *chapachapa* noise, mists spread across the earth like the currents of the great ocean.
Standing at a distance from their chariots and making whistling sounds like waves, they fell with the breezes from the lake waters like bees from lotuses.
Even amidst the flood of weapons, the infantry force was overwhelmed by the multitude of discuses; like a mass of dust in a heavy downpour, it was incapable of fleeing.
The Hūṇas are submerged up to their heads in the sands of the northern ocean; drenched right there within the mire, they are like impure spikes used for filling.
The Śakas were bound along the strips of cardamom groves on the shores of the eastern ocean; after being held for a day and then released, they did not go to the abode of Yama.
Descending slowly from Mount Mahendra, crying out softly as they fell from the sky, they were comforted by the best of sages like the deer of their own hermitage.
Having entered into a request on Mount Sahya, two [gems] were obtained from a divine cave; sometimes, through misfortune, a benefit arrives by chance, like the "crow and the palm fruit" (kākatālīya).
The Daśārṇas fell into the Dardura forest like withered leaves; having ignorantly eaten poisonous fruits, they themselves died right there.
Having eaten the *viśalyakaraṇī* by a stroke of luck, the Haihayas went home on the Himalayas like Vidyādharas.
The Vaṅgas, who once returned home with bows adorned with *nṛmlāna* flowers, are not seen even today, as if they have turned into demons.
Having consumed the forest fruits that grant the status of a Vidyādhara, the Vidyādharas remain in heaven sporting with Vidyādharīs.
Falling with their limbs shattered into groves of *tālī* and *tamāla* trees, the Pārasīkas fell into a swoon like celestial beings (*vaimānika*) wandering through the sky.
The fourfold army of the Kaliṅgas, with its elephants whose temples were streaming with ichor, was struck down and fell upon the courtyard of Taṅgaṇa, its limbs shattered to pieces.
As he advanced against the enemy forces, the Sālvas fell with their lord into the interior of mountains of arrows and water, where they remain even today like stones.
Countless men fled in every direction, only to meet their destruction in oceans with surging waves.

Who is capable of counting the fallen bad fruits in fields, forests, cities, waters, lands, mountains, riverbanks, canals, villages, lakes, rivers, oceans, cliffs, trees, hamlets, market towns, mountains, wells, caves, and houses?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, as the enemies were thus fleeing in haste, those four wise ones pursued their forces, reaching further and further away.
Sent forth by the one Lord, who consists of all power, they all set out for the conquest of the directions with equal resolve.
Your forces followed you from afar without interruption, just as the currents of rivers follow to the shores of the oceans.
For them, that entire means of accomplishment—both their own and that belonging to others—was exhausted like the water of a wretched river by a vehicle that never rests even from afar.
Having fully beheld their own and others' powers, they were like those seeking liberation who, as they run forward, find both merit and sin exhausted.
Then, as if there were no fuel left to burn, the nets of flames from the fires and the weapons themselves became pacified in the sky, having accomplished their purpose.
In their dwellings—consisting of chariots, horses, elephants, trees, and throngs—the weapons lay dormant, like birds returning to their nests at the end of the day.
Like waves within water, like mists within a cloud, like clouds within the wind, or like fragrances within the sky, they dissolved away.
The aquatic creatures of his weapons were stilled, clinging to the mud of the flowing streams; he was entirely free from the mist of the showering droplets of iron arrows.
Released from hundreds of whirlpools, endowed with clarity and gentleness, it was like a rain of towering waves where the turbulence of the clouds had subsided.
The vast ocean of the single sky became a stainless sea of the water of emptiness, wherein the submarine fire of the sun was situated in its corner amidst a mass of jewel-like stars submerged within.
The sky shone—vast, profound, and luminous, serene and most radiant, and free from dust—like the mind of the great.
Then they beheld those oceans, like younger brothers of the sky—vast, pure in appearance, and filling the entire expanse of the quarters.
Agitated by the great gurgling roar of waves, droplets, and billows, they possess bodies made beautiful and captivating by abundant spray and mist.

Having spread himself out upon the ground like those afflicted by disease, they lay there with bodies trembling from the distress of gasping breaths, their great arms tossing like the waves of a surging ocean.
Even the insentient [elements], consisting of vibrations and possessing millions of waves and hollows, are like the vast expanses of saṃsāra, agitated by the conditions of whirlpools.

The sun was made to appear more intense by the radiance emanating from the slopes of the heaps of jewels, while the humming sounds were challenged by the noise of the wind entering the piles of conch shells.
The vast expanse of the sky resounded with the gurgling roar of masses of fleshy waves, while coral trees whirled about in the widening circles of the eddies.
Resounding with the deep gurgling roar of the array of sea-monsters, and filled with the cries of sinking ships shattered by the lashing tails of fish;
[The waters] resembled the sky filled with seven thousand suns—the horses of the sun—reflected in the waves, and were swarming with throngs of men swallowed by upturned tortoises and sea-monsters.
The wind produced a whistling sound as it struck the door-bolts, while the clusters of jewels tossed by the waves emitted a jingling resonance through their forceful impact.
With their powerful arms like various nets, they effortlessly touched the solar orb, while the circles of rubies and gems with their rays bent down and rose up again.
In some places, with the upraised trunks of elephants, the waters were for a moment turned into forests of bamboo, featuring rising whirlpools of frothing foam and swarms of sea-monsters.
In some places, there were Mādhava trees with creepers like waves upon their trunks; in others, there were Mādhava trees with their attendants resting within their hollows.
[He saw] countless various abodes of asuras situated in one place, with the sky made jagged by the surging waves of falling stars.

He led the coastal mountains to extreme diminution by the surging masses of his water-waves, making those mountains—which had remained as motionless as branches out of fear of the abyss—resemble gnats within caves.
In the fields of the sky, they planted sprouts that were the paths of light from many jewels; these were interspersed with sands separated by pearls released from the mouths of pure oyster shells.
They entered rivers that were like variegated cloths, rippling with various jewels, silks, and fine threads, and strewn from all ten directions.
In some places, marked by hundreds of pearl oysters scattered upon its sapphire slopes, it displays the beauty of a hundred lovely moons as its fingernails.
Reflected upon the surface of the waves, they were obscured by a network of jewel-like rays, as they caused the rows of flowering palm groves on the shore to appear to revolve.
The aquatic creatures, having abandoned their usual movements, seized the garlands of cardamom, cloves, and kaṅkola fruits that had fallen from the creepers of the coastal forest.
The water-dwellers, deceived by the birds reflected [in the water] as they were about to eat the tips of mango, nīpa, and kadamba flowers, snapped their jaws.
For a moment, by the water-dwellers fleeing here and there at the reflection of the sky-goer, the great embankments with their bonds broken were shattered.
He beheld those four formless ones, who by means of their reflections contained the three worlds within their hearts, as vast as space, like so many Nārāyaṇas situated in the cardinal directions.
Like the sky, which by its extreme depth, purity, vastness, and majesty swallows all things and then displays them as if reflected from within its own heart.
The sky, reflected in the waters of the birds moving upon it, was held by their essential depths as if it were a lotus containing a bee within itself.
Their peaks struck by winds from the surging and tossing waves, they resembled the abodes of the clouds at the end of an eon, deep with the echoes resounding from their caves.
He intensely meditated upon the thunderous roars and the rumbling sounds from the mountain caves, which were like the crashing of lightning and seemed as if swallowed by the Agastya and Aurva fires.
The sky was filled with forest-like masses of water, where abundant spray was the blossoming flowers, the surging waves were the trees, and the ripples were the clusters of blossoms.
With nets of shimmering waves and living beings leaping about below, they appeared as if fragments of the sky had fallen due to a delusion.

When it reached the long shore of the salt ocean, its edge fringed by the dancing leaves of cardamom, cloves, bakula, myrobalan, tamāla, hintāla, and palmyra trees, a line appeared upon the mountain-peak of the sky that resembled a swarm of bees.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, at that time and place, he pointed out to them various things nearby—the forest trees, the ocean, the mountains, the clouds, and the forest-dwellers.
"O Lord, behold this peak of the mountain that scrapes the clouds, which has come from the middle regions of Samaramadhyadesa and reached the land of stone."
These ranges of forests, thick with *bakula*, *punnāga*, and coconut trees, waft winds laden with various fragrances.
The ocean mows down the foothills, with rows of rocks as its rice fields, using the waves as sickles, cutting down the forest groves from their roots along with fruits and sprouts.
The young ocean shakes off the rows of clouds upon the mountain ridges as they dance with their own waters, like a houseboy brushing away a line of smoke from the household hearth.

With trees on their banks whose branches are conch shells submerged in the full flood of the ocean of the full moon, these [lakes] shine like wish-fulfilling trees bearing the lunar orb as their fruit.
With hands of red shoots laden with a profusion of jewel-like flowers, the trees, accompanied by their wives in the form of creepers, seem to worship you.
With its cave-mouths acting as the jaws of sea-monsters that swallow the peaks, and its rocky ridges serving as teeth, Mount Ṛkṣavān roars with a deep *ghuraghura* sound like a bear.
Just as the powerful Mahendra, with his thunderous roars, overcomes the roaring clouds, so does the vigorous leader overcome his enemies through the dull-witted.
Anointed with sandalwood, that glorious and lofty Mount Malaya, like a wrestler prepared to conquer the surging waves of the ocean, stood ready.
The ocean, eternally shimmering on all sides with waves of jewels, is perceived by those traveling along the path of the sun as if it were the jeweled ring encircling the earth.
The mountain peaks, with their jewel-like summits and their hollows filled with water, drink the moving wind; they resemble serpents with their undulating crests and depressions.
Wandering upon the crests of the waves, the sea-monsters and elephants, with their fierce trunks, scatter sprays of water like clouds driven by the wind.
A male elephant with a form rippled by whirlpools, scattering masses of spray in all directions, and whose head is unable to lift due to being excessively burdened, dies from over-exertion.
Just as all the oceans are filled with various living beings and contain waters, mountains, and elevations, so too are the lands of the continents.
Though they are not different from oneself, the whirlpools appear as if they were other; though unreal in nature, they are perceived and clearly seen.
Just as Brahmā bears the worlds, so the ocean bears its own restless waves—tremulous, internal, and insentient, yet continuous and devoid of end.
The ocean, like Indra, possesses many sun-gems which, though their entire wealth was seized by Mantha, were protected from the gods.
He saw those of great splendor appearing even from the netherworld (pātāla), as if they were real beings hidden within by the play of reflections.
I believe that each day passes because he casts one of them every single day into the western ocean for disposal.
The gathering of virtuous men from various directions and lands in the ocean is like the clamor of people meeting one another during a pilgrimage.
Indeed, at the confluence of the ocean and the sea, the battle between the foremost aquatic creatures, arising from their mutual surging against one another, never ceases.
The wind approaches, whirling with the grace of dancing waves whose crests are exhausted by fatigue, scattering pearl-like spray as it blows.
The long, shimmering lords of moonstones situated amidst the pearl-lattices of the rivers resound with a *khaṇa-khaṇa* sound as they move restlessly on all sides from the ocean.
Resounding with the roar of the earth as it shook from the ocean paths turned back by the cave-dwellings of Mount Mahendra, the place brought great happiness to the Siddhas and Sādhyas.
Mandara, its forest expanses shaken by the gusts of wind vomited from its caves, spreads clouds of flowers across the sky.
The cloud-deer enter the caves of Mount Gandhamādana, which abound with the fragrance of mango, nīpa, and kadamba trees, their eyes flickering like lightning.
The winds, blowing forth from the caves of the Himalayas, perform a dance within the coils of creeping vines; they move on, parting the waves of the ocean and the clouds.
O dear one, the breezes from Mount Gandhamādana, fragrant from their contact with the tops of the mango and kadamba trees, cause the waves of the ocean to curl.
The wind, encircling the clouds that have become like the curls of Alakā’s hair, approaches from here, fashioning clouds of flowers along the forest paths.
There, one should perceive the breezes, languid with the sweet fragrance of clusters of *kunda* and *mandāra* flowers, and mingled with sprays of frost.
Behold, the winds from the city of the Persians are about to blow, having acquired a bitter fragrance from the dancing of coconut and palm trees.
Shaking the camphor-clouds from the blossoming groves of Īśāna and stirring the lotus-pools of Kailāsa, the winds blow.
These winds from the caves of the Vindhya mountains, their forms slow with the rutting ichor emerging from the temples of lordly elephants, rustle like parrots.
On the mountain, where the bodies of the Śabaras lie amidst heaps of withered leaves, the forest grove, filled with leaf-clad hunters and iron arrows, resembles a city.
The quarters of the sky, whose bodies consist of oceans, mountains, rivers, clouds, and forests, seem to laugh at these rays of the sun through the forces of your majesty.

In the forest groves of Mount Atrapati, they describe flower-beds prepared by Vidyādharīs; there, charming women, having turned around from the ocean situated on both sides, act the part of men in love-play.

The attendants said: "O noble ones, here in these bowers of creeper-circles, women playful with their charms sing songs; and the hosts of Kinnaras, having forgotten the concerns of the day due to the intensity of their emotional passion, rest there with sweet, melodious warbling."

These mountains—the Himalaya, Malaya, Vindhya, Sahya, Krauñca, Mahendra, Madhu, Mandara, Dardura, and others—though situated at a great distance, appear like white clouds to the eye, resembling clods of earth marked by withered leaves and fragments.

These mountain ranges before us, with their masses of great ridges separated by distant vistas, bear the form of city walls; behold the agitated rivers entering the ocean, appearing like thin white threads of the fringe caught within a cloth.

O King, those ten directions, covered on all sides by dense clouds over the mountains, appearing dark as rain-clouds and filled with the warbling chatter of birds, shine before you like the women of your palace; their creeper-like arms are the charming forest-tracts laughing with flowers released from the vines.

The shimmering forest, its lofty peaks crowded with *tālī*, *tamāla*, and *bakula* trees appearing as a single mass, shines forth as it is struck by the restless waves of the ocean, resembling a dense network of moss clinging to the edge of a shore.

Here sleeps Keśava; here lie his kinsmen; here also rest the birds seeking refuge from his enemies; and here too is the submarine fire along with all the clouds of universal destruction—oh, how vast, powerful, and capable of bearing the weight is the body of the ocean!

O King, these entire villages, forests, cities, plains, mountains, trees, pillars, and clusters of hermitages on the banks of the Jambūnadī shine with the rays of the sun; their splendors, licking the interior of the sky encircled by garlands of flames, are released in abundance here, and thus this place is fit to be frequented by gods alone, not by mortals.

These clouds, following the path of the sun, appear like a blanket of Kadamba forest as they pass over; may this mountain slope be like the earth for you, so that you harbor no fear of a mass of clouds in the sky obstructing the sun.

This is that Malaya mountain, where the trees are made to bend by the three [fires] through the intoxicating intensity of the abundant fragrance of sandalwood trees shimmering with the *lavalī* creepers; while the heat from the cheeks of the Rākṣasa women, situated amidst the blazing flames, rises in a frantic dance, just as the heated drops of sweat from women are wiped away by their thumbs and fingers.

This is the mountain named Malaya, whose slopes are washed by the ocean and where sandalwood trees are encircled by the coils of the lord of serpents; its entire rocky surface has been turned to gold by the mass of radiance from the lotus-faces of the Vidyādharīs.

This is Mount Krauñca, where the flocks of birds are silenced by the tumultuous resonance of the hollow bamboo stalks, which mimic the warbling of the rivers in the thickets of the echoing groves; here, the serpents coil upon the trunks of ancient Rohaṇa trees, agitated by the cries of the powerful peacocks as they move about.
On this shore, listen to the widespread nectar for the ears produced by the swaying bracelets of beautiful women sporting in their dwellings of tender golden creepers.

This mass of water droplets, drenched by the ichor flowing from the temples of elephants and surrounded by swarms of bees like flickering waves, seems as if it were being chewed and tormented; thus it cries out within the ocean.
Behold, the spotless moon, embraced by the beautiful women whose bodies are like fresh butter of nectar, performs his water-sports upon the lap of his father in the ocean of milk.

Behold, O stainless one, upon the ridges of the Malaya mountains, the young creepers are dancing; they possess the sweet warbling of intoxicated cuckoos, their eyes are swarms of restless bees, their hands are their red leaves, and their flowers are their blossoms, as they display the particular charms of a spring festival.

The drops of rainwater that enter at the proper time into the hearts of bamboos, into mountains, into the ocean, and into the hearts of pearl-oysters seeking water, attain the state of pearls; or else they may become something else. For purity, these three types of origins possess qualities like those of pearls.

O Lord, gems assume various forms within mountains, oceans, humans, the earth, clouds, frogs, stones, and elephants; and their functions include providing delight, expulsion, killing, fever, fear, delusion, illumination, blindness, exhaustion, burning, movement upon the ground, and the destruction or restoration of sight.

When the moon has risen, these cities chant its praises through the mouths of their windows, balconies, lattices, side-doors, and main gates; while Mount Mandara, by means of its chasms, clouds, caves, caverns, forests, and clusters of bamboo-hollows, proclaims the ocean of nectar.

"Is the wind carrying away this peak?"—thus watched with wide-eyed alarm by the innocent wives of the Siddhas looking upwards, the cloud rises high from every forested slope of the Snowy Mountain, like a pillar of diamond intended to lift the earth up to the surface of the sky.

O King, behold the slopes of Mount Mahendra, cooled by the spray from the waves of the Gaṅgā, where the beautiful rocky surfaces are inhabited by Vidyādharas, and where the flowering forests are filled with clouds of blossoms.

Having beheld forest regions spread across other lands, flower-filled grounds, groves, and cities, as well as the waters that purify the world at sacred fords, the fear of misfortune departs, driven away with speed.

Seeing the mountain peaks whose summits fill the entire circle of the horizons, crowded with chasms, clouds, caves, and groves, and seeing the oceanic coils that resemble the very sky, even the greatest of one's evil deeds dissolve away.

Indeed, there are delightful sandalwood groves on Malaya and Vindhya; elephants blinded by rut on Kailāsa; gold from the Pādaja mountain and moonstones on Mahendra; and divine medicinal herbs on the snowy peaks. O King, jewels exist everywhere; yet like the blind mouse, people waste away in vain within this dilapidated house of worldly existence.
The world, as if a great lake, was enveloped by darkness as if by water; and these lightning-flashes flickered like restless minnows, as at the end of an eon.

O, how the rain-winds blow with a rising roar! Drenching the clouds that pour forth streams of mist, dew, and frost, they cause a profuse horripilation from the cold and bring about a clamor as they surge forth.

Ah, the wind blows, following the expanse of blue clouds, scattering clusters of blossoms from the shoots and branches of trees; it is beautiful as it moves through the interior of the forest of majestic sandalwood groves, carrying the essence of a multitude of spray-drops from the heavy rain.
These breezes, fallen as it were from heaven, increase in strength and carry with them the fragrance of the sighs of lovely women overcome by passion.
These gentle breezes blow, striving to tear asunder the creepers of blooming blue water-lilies; they are skilled at rending thick cloths and have shaken the groves.
In the sky, the winds carry fragments of twilight clouds with their gentle trembling, like excellent servants in a king’s courtyard perfumed by variegated patterns of flowers.

In some places the mountain breezes bear the fragrance of flowers, in others the scent of clusters of lotuses; in some places they rain down blossoms and scatter lovely filaments, while in others they are white as snow or green, yellow, and dark blue—these winds from the peaks dispel the languid heat of amorous play.
In some places, with rays that emit sounds of "hum" and "kāṃ," the sun scatters heaps of burning coals with its hands, like one who associates with fools.

When the woman, who was liberated from satiety by the elixir of manly passion and whose modesty had been dispelled by intoxication, approached him with her body, he could not endure it, as if overcome by the fainting spell of poison.

The forest winds blowing over the woodland grounds—causing the lotuses to close, carrying gentle sprays of water, and parting the waves of moonbeams—seem as if they possess fire and consist of heat before the women separated from their lovers.

Behold, here on the slope of the eastern ocean’s shore, how the Śabara women—clad in garments of broad leaves, their hips adorned with girdles, and supported by the fresh pride of youth—proceed along the banks of the Kaṭakī river!

With a heart distressed by the fear of the approaching night—the end of the essence of the nectar of the nine sentiments—this woman does not abandon her lover even slightly, as if she were suddenly turned back from before by serpents.
Threatened as it were by days made resonant with the morning trumpets, the woman, having hidden upon her lover’s breast, seemed to burst within her very heart.
This forest range on the shore of the southern ocean, with its blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees, appears as if it were ablaze, being drenched again and again by the waves of the sea.
From her, dark-maned clouds emerge with the winds like columns of smoke; her flowers are like glowing coals, and the birds and bees are like extinguished embers.
Behold this very forest range, ablaze with the fire of truth; yet on the mountain peak in the northern direction, it is carried far into the sky by the winds.

Behold this forest on the ground of Mount Krauñca, where peacocks dance to the deep and piercing cries of slow-moving circles of clouds; it is tumultuous, its groves of flowers, fruits, and sprouts shaken by the agitated winds of rain.

Upon the western mountain, its beautiful joints shattered and splintered by the impact of the peaks of vast golden summits, the chariot of the Sun falls down short, emitting a loud creaking from its wheels and a shrill rattling from its pole.

On the mountain that serves as the rampart for the abodes of the world, the moon—like a blooming lotus—is embraced by the swarm of its rays; yet there is nothing here in this world superior to this, which Fate, though struck down, could not in an instant defile with a stain.
This Maṅkola, the great abode of the world, is the loud laughter of the Lord who carries away the three worlds; it is a flood of milk-water, the lunar light from the ocean of the sky.

Behold the quarters of space, their very bodies filled by masses of radiance—like the surging waves of milk rising from the ocean of the moon as it is churned by Mount Mandara at the onset of night—as they spread forth like the floods of a mighty river.

These hosts of Guhyakas, encircled at night by swarms of fierce and restless Vetālas with hands like matchless cymbals, are descending by force to devour the cities of the Lord of the Hūṇas, which have cast off all peace and are destitute of the auspicious sounds of the Vedas.

The full moon shines in the sky only so long as the face of the bride does not come outside the house; once the moon of the young woman's face has risen in the courtyard-sky, what difference remains between it and a fragment of a white cloud?

These peaks of the Lord of the Snowy Mountains have aged with the rays of the moon as their fresh garments; their rocks are washed by the torrents of the Gaṅgā, they are covered with frost, and their fierce matted locks are the creeping vines.

There, that very Mount Mandara is seen in the sky like an ornament for the Mandāra grove; its breezes are spread by the songs of celestial nymphs on swings, and in some places it is variegated with the brilliant luster of jewels.

Great mountains, bearing dense flower-offerings in vessels upon their thick, blossoming *śilīndhra* trees that are ever-blooming and without gaps, possess the splendor of the sky filled with stars within their deep interiors that resound like thick clouds.

From here, Mount Kailāsa appears as if it were the paved courtyard of Śambhu’s son, measured by a vast stream of radiance that fills the sky; and even the moon, though situated in the Ocean of Milk, seems as if it had entered there.
Behold how Vāsava joins together the trunks of trees whose branches have been severed and even those made of clay, though they were far apart, as if their crests were released by the winds.

These winds, fragrant with the scent of *kadamba*, *kula*, and *kunda* flowers, anoint my sense of smell with a thick rain of nectar; dark as swarms of bees, they are like masses of clouds churning the sky with dense perfumes.

In forest regions where the petals of the buds remain unfaded, in jungles thick with shady meadows, and in villages crowded with trees that bear fruit continuously, Prosperity herself seems to dwell as if for the sake of making them her own home.

With breezes that carry the filaments of the *kośātakī* flowers from the palace chambers—covered by creepers reaching through the windows—and which scatter buds up to the ankles across the courtyards, this village shines like a city of forest deities.

Delightful are these mountain villages: where women sway upon swings made of blossoming, stainless campaka trees and creepers; where the streams of waterfalls murmur; where palm trees stand in full bloom all around; where peacocks gleam within bowers of creepers fragrant with clusters of radiant blossoms; and where clouds hang from the towering *sāla* trees at their borders.

Whose pleasure-pavilions of nectar are these delightful mountain villages, filled with dark-green grounds covered by creepers with variegated leaves trembling in the wind; where flocks of quail, ruddy geese, and wild cocks warble; where Pulinda women sing; where young calves are restless; and which shine with the consumption of curd, honey, milk, and clarified butter?
The attendants said: "O Lord, behold here how the masses of weapons flash upon the mountain ranges that form the boundary of the engaged battle, and how the armies advance."
Behold, behold! Having repeatedly lifted up slain and unslain heroes by the thousands who face their foes, they are ascending into the sky in chariots drawn by women.
Furthermore, for one desiring victory, when a manifest crisis has arisen in battle, righteous combat shines forth like amorous play in youth.
Fortune unblemished by the world, health endowed with prosperity, and righteous battle for the sake of others—the supreme fruit of life.
He who, in accordance with the dharma, slays an opponent encountered face-to-face in battle in a manner consistent with his status as a warrior, is a hero destined for heaven; no other is so.

Here, the arrival of night—dark as a lotus garland and a sharp sword held in hand—is brought by the thick dust raised by horses; behold how he advances toward Lakṣmī, who is adorned with the weight of uplifted weapons and ornaments.

These masses of arrows, spears, clubs, *bhuśuṇḍīs*, tridents, swords, lances, sharp *tomaras*, and discuses gleam; they appear like a multitude of lordly serpents with their bodies leaping upon the earth, amidst the restless ocean that is agitated by the hair tossed in a frantic dance of heat.

Behold the sky, filled with powerful masses of clouds; behold the sky, a shimmering necklace of brilliant stars; behold the sky, its essence darkened by thick, clinging mist; behold the sky, sprinkled by the rays of the clear moon.

In that sky where the multitude of abodes for many gods and asuras has come to be designated as stars, and which is the dwelling place of the constellations and of all things that spread upward—yet even now the perception that it is "empty" has not ceased; what other person is capable of wiping away this worldly reproach fabricated by the ignorant?

Even today, the sky has not reached the end of its transformations caused by masses of clouds, the fires of cosmic dissolution, the crashing of mountain wings, floods of stars, and the tumultuous battles between gods and demons; yet, the greatness of those who possess inner qualities of essential strength is not perceived.

O virtuous one, you repeatedly swing in your lap the sun from the sky, Nārāyaṇa, the moon, and likewise other radiant lights such as the brilliant lightning; yet it is a marvel that even so, you do not abandon the inner blindness within.

O Sky, you shine where the orb of the moon appears; yet, because it is soiled by the darkness of the collyrium scattered by you, it attains a dark hue through association. This is truly a great marvel: for who indeed would defile another with their own internal impurity?
I believe that even for one who is filled with the defects of the world, there is happiness in the perpetual unchanging state of space—like that of a wise man—in which all objects are empty.

O you whose intention is unconfused and whose nature is equally pure, you shall be the creator and sustainer of the elevation of the eons, clouds, trees, and creepers, as well as of the sky, moon, clouds, sun, kinnaras, winds, mountain ranges, and gods. Everything beautiful belongs to you; yet, my dear friend, that this world should possess such a nature of burning—alas, it is a primary cause of our distress!

O Space, you are luminous, stainless, and utterly clear; by virtue of your loftiness, you are the supreme support for the highest things. Yet, having reached you, this cloud of hailstones becomes sparse and crushes the world; therefore, you are superior, while the others are base.

O Space, I consider your very nature to be that of a whetstone; I believe you have long been honed, yet nothing else. You are empty, for you carry the clouds, the stars, the celestial chariots, the moon, the sun, the wind, and you shine, yet you are not devoid of purpose.

By day you appear with a red body, at the end of the day you are black during the watches of the night, and yet you always carry nothing at all; even the wise do not understand this illusion of yours, nor how you act like the empty sky.
Even one who possesses nothing accomplishes his tasks if his intention is expansive; even the sky, though empty within, is the cause of the elevation of all things.

There was neither grass nor water, neither village nor even the name of a town, neither a tree with shade as lush as a leaf-burden nor a virtuous water-shed; nevertheless, the sun travels the path of the sky day after day. Even that which is difficult to undertake, those of noble character do not abandon.

The night adorns [the courtyard] with a veil of darkness; the moon with its rays like heaps of camphor; the day with the fresh garment of sunlight; the sky with clusters of stars as flowers; and all the seasons with clouds, frost, and water as their blossoms—all these adorn the courtyard of the sky for the two Lords in the three worlds, who are themselves the essence of the divisions of time.

The atmosphere does not abandon its natural state even through the disturbances of smoke, clouds, dust, darkness, the sun, the moon, twilight, stars, celestial chariots, Garuḍa, mountains, gods, and asuras; oh, how wondrous is the stability of one who has risen to such greatness!

This world is bounded by walls on all sides, with the sky as its upper surface; the earth is its vast vessel, filled with dense cities and mountains; it is the dwelling place for hosts of Vidyādharas, gods, and great serpents, and it teems with the swarms of ants that are the multitudes of beings wandering through saṃsāra.
Time, action, the world, and existence—as if presiding for a long time over a blossoming grove—seem to have perished every day; yet even now they do not perish. Oh, what a wonder is this illusion!

A pair of verses: I consider that space restrains the excessive height of trees and the like; for even in the case of a non-agent, the status of being an agent arises from the greatness of the Great One.
That wherein millions of worlds neither come into being nor arise—that void is called space; fie upon this unimpaired "wisdom"!
They dissolve back into space alone and emerge from space; those who have attained this state of madness are called "Lords," though they are no different from others.

The splendors of creation come and go, fall down and likewise fly up, like droplets of water rising from a fire; that which is stainless therein, I consider to be the one, beginningless, and endless space itself, and not a cause called "God."

I consider myself to be the Supreme Consciousness itself, whose body is space, which bears upon its limbs the infinitely vast foundation of the jewels of the three worlds and contains within its immeasurable interior all things without exception; it is here that this delusion of the world undergoes its rising and setting.

In the forest groves, amidst the dense thickets of enchanting trees, the song of the beautiful lover who wanders the woods is sung; from here, by this traveler on the road, overwhelmed with emotion, it is heard upon the mountain peak.

A song was sung, with deep sighs, by a Vidyadhara woman—stricken by separation and filled with longing—her voice choked as it pressed against her throat from within the hollow of a high branch on the Shringataka tree. O Lord, hearing that name here, this traveler listens with a sigh; yet, his mind wavering like the swaying of a swing, he neither departs nor speaks aloud.

On the tree atop the mountain peak, within a cupped leaf, this Vidyādharī, distressed by separation and her face obscured by tears, sighs and sings in a low, sweet tone: "O Lord, remembering your smiling kiss upon the couch of my lap—your nectar-like touch that I held to my chin—I have spent these years in vain."

"O King, I have heard this from the mouths of travelers on the road: her husband in a previous birth was turned into a tree by a sage’s curse for twelve years; counting those very years, she remains right here, singing with longing, having taken refuge at the foot of that very tree which is her beloved."

Behold! This Vidyādhara, whose curse was pacified by our glance, has released the girl from the tree; now, with those very arms that were disguised as branches, he embraces her neck—his blossoming flowers appearing like a smile.

Upon the trees with their blossoming foliage, a heap of flowers from the elephants of the peaks shines forth; this peak, moreover, possesses the play of stars fallen from the sky, resembling a mass of frost.

Ah, the Kāverī shines like a woman clad in a white garment of flowers; her banks and marshes are crowded with fearless herds of deer, while she is made formidable by the cries of ospreys fluttering amidst the waves tossed by the impetuous leaps of schools of fish.

Behold here, upon the ridge of Mount Suvela, a golden rock shining with entirely stainless splendor, cast by the sun, resembling sparks from the submarine fire scattered by the breaking waves of the ocean tossing against the shore.

Behold the splendor of the cowherd settlements on the mountains, where dwellings are encircled by nearby thick clouds, where forest trees are in full bloom at the outskirts of the homes, and where the sky is veiled by masses of *palāśa* blossoms.

Triumphant are these villages, where clusters of flowers are bright white like blossoms in full bloom; where the banks are lined with baskets of mandāra flowers and peacock feathers; where the music of the playful splashing in waterfalls resounds; and where the people sing amidst the depths of caves from which they emerge.

I believe that even for the gods here, there is no such satisfaction as that which belongs to those men dwelling in mountain caves within the cowherd settlements—men who, intoxicated by the honey of bees humming as they hide among the petals of blossoming kandalī flowers, are themselves blinded by passion.

With their eyes fixed upon the faces of Pulinda women who sing amidst the forest thickets where the creepers are swayed by bees, do these Kirātas—restless in their play and pitiless within the mountain caves—kill the innocent deer as if they were an enemy?

Victorious are the villages amidst the depths of the great mountains, which delight the moon—villages where the limbs of travelers are cooled by the swaying of vine-leaves that have acquired the essence of clusters of various blossoming flowers, and where waves ripple through the spreading expanse of water.

With the warbling of birds as their drumbeats, with fully blossomed palm trees spreading around them, with canopies of sky formed by climbing vines swaying with flowers and shoots playfully tossed upward, and with clouds hanging from the tall *sāla* trees on their perimeters—these delightful mountain villages, where the moon is the sacred fig tree, resemble the garden groves of the city of the Moon.

Victorious are the villages, where flocks of peacocks dance to the deep, rumbling roar of clouds that have turned yellow as they approach; these villages are strewn with the soft plumage of the birds' crests, appearing like clusters of moonstone jewels scattered about.

Where could the playful splendor found in those villages on the mountain slopes—adorned by beautiful moon-discs situated at their sides and sheltered by clouds heavy with water—be found even in the prosperous kingdoms of Brahmā?

May I find delight in mountain caves that are beautiful with the interior of the Nandana grove, filled with its own fragrance; where bower-huts laugh with clusters of *saṃtānaka* flowers, and where the dense *pāribhadra* trees are thick with bees buzzing softly as they wake.
In the mountain villages, delightful with the cries of does and charming with beautiful *hārīta* birds, men find pleasure as if in cities of the god of love.
Behold these peahens dancing in this mountain glen of the village, where the waters of lovely waterfalls cascade down crystal pillars.
Crested peahens and playful vines, bowed under the weight of their flowers, dance here in the groves to the sound of the resonating waterfalls.

In these village settlements hidden within mountain caves, where the trees of the groves are green with the hue of *hārītaka* fruit and the pure, sweet warbling of birds resounds from ponds as large as lakes, I believe this God of Love rejoices here by his own natural impulse.

O Cloud, you possess a glorious form that dispels the heat of great minds with its lofty and profound nature; you are the ornament upon the crests of mountains and the sole abode of the earth’s moisture. Yet this one thing would truly humble the hearts of all: that while raining, out of joy, you distribute your water equally among the saline wastelands, the puddles, the dry ground, and the trees alike.

O cloud, you constantly bathe in the waters of excellent sacred fords while stationed in a lofty position; being pure, you dwell upon the forest floor having undertaken a vow of silence. Even when empty, a great beauty is observed residing in your body; yet you rise up and hurl a thunderbolt—what is this trivial behavior of yours?
Everything, whether auspicious or inauspicious, becomes vast when it has reached its proper place; yet water, having encountered a dark cloud, attains a blackish hue.

"Oh, how the water has been released by the cloud! Oh, how the earth has been filled with that water! Oh, how it nourishes the ground with its abundant waters, like a wealthy man toward a poor friend!"
Cruelty, instability, impurity, wandering in the streets, and utter contemptibility—was this taken from dogs by fools, or rather from fools by dogs? I do not know.
Even one who possesses many faults may indeed become acceptable to someone through just a few virtues, such as valor, contentment, and devotion.

Having cast his form into the pathways of sense-objects, he runs about like one insane, intoxicated, or on the verge of falling; he regards those who possess great pride as mere fragments of straw—let it be investigated whether this is his desire for existence or his dullness.
Even though their nature as animals is the same, the clamor is endured in one way by lions with agitated minds and in another way by dogs with eyes closed.

O you who are ever impure, devoted solely to barking at those dear to you, and who spend all your time wandering through the alleys—alas, I think you have been taught by some fool, for your disposition is exactly like that of a dog!

The Creator, fashioning the entire world eternally as something incomparable, has made everything equal in this dog, his own grandson: its dwelling is a pit of impure refuse; its food is excrement and pus; its mating is a vulgar act in the sight of all; and its body is the object of universal contempt.

To one who asked, "Who is more base than you?", the dog replied with a laugh: "He who indulges in folly, impurity, blindness, and misfortune more than I am superior. For the noble qualities I possess—valor, sincere devotion, and fortitude—are not found even when sought with a multitude of efforts in a fool. To one who asked, "Who is more base than you?", the dog replied with a laugh: "He who indulges in folly, impurity, blindness, and misfortune more than I am superior. For the noble qualities I possess—valor, sincere devotion, and fortitude—are not found even when sought with a multitude of efforts in a fool."

He eats filth and takes constant delight in filth within a great heap of refuse; he silently devours that which has consciousness and cuts away that which is unconscious. When all have come together for pleasure, he is pelted with clods of earth by people like a dog; thus the Creator, having established him in a state of play, has made him utterly powerless in this world.
Above the linga, this crow caws and reveals itself, saying: "Behold me, who have ascended from all base sins to the highest state!"

O crow, you who wander in this lake whose muddy depths have swallowed the harsh cries of the cuckoo and whose virtues are submerged; since you obstruct the humming of the bees, you have become a thorn upon my head.
The crow devours a heap of hell-beings while avoiding a lotus stalk; therefore, let there be no pride in you, for that which is well-practiced always tastes sweet.
At first, he was seen like a swan with a body white as the filaments of various forest flowers; then, as he swallowed a mouthful of moist worms, he was recognized as a crow.
When crows are gathered together with cuckoos of similar color and plumage, by what means can a crow be recognized unless he speaks for himself?
