A crow perched on a stump watches the soil of the forest, just as a thief from a shrine looks toward the ten directions when people are asleep at night.
In this lake, beautiful with the nectar of lotuses blooming amidst the vigorous movement of cranes, how can a crow sport here, its shoulders grey with a mass of shimmering droppings?

Alas, what a tragedy! Upon this lovely body, the interior of a blooming white lotus, a demon with a face fit for striking with a whip—a crow—has sat down in this small pool and performs various antics along with the royal swans. Look!

O crow of harsh cry, marked by a single saw-like scar—where indeed has that self-same suspicion of yours gone today? Why is this fruitless hope for a young cuckoo, cherished as an only son, intended only to bring you ridicule?

Seeing a crow, resembling a dark stain, moving about with playful grace in the lotus grove while shrieking loudly, he—whose every movement was destroyed by hundreds of cries of "Alas! Woe!"—does not weep; let him be torn apart by a saw!
If there were restless owls and crows in this pond, which is filled with fragile reeds and dense with cranes and water-fowls, then this assembly would be complete.
A cuckoo, its form concealed by flocks of crows, becomes manifest through its cries, just as a scholar becomes evident in an assembly.
The flowering creeper is able to endure the crushing of its soft flowers, sprouts, and leaves by the cuckoo, but not by the heron, vulture, water-fowl, crane, cock, crow, and the like.

O sweet-voiced cuckoo, who here listens to your melodious song, a festival for the ears and a messenger for the union of lovers? My hearing has grown deaf from the harsh, gurgling cries of crows and the quarreling owls here in the thickets.

While the young cuckoo, with its soft and sweet voice, tells auspicious tales with such sincerity that it wins over all who are full of passion, the crow—suddenly swooping down from the sky into the grove with terrifying "dhraṅkāra" cries—renders everyone tasteless by incessantly shouting, "This is my son!"

O cuckoo, why do you warble so rapidly with such exuberance? Withdraw your song back into the hollow of your throat; let there be no more delusion on your part for long. This is not the blossoming of spring with its unrestrained flowers; these trees have been withered by the masses of frost brought by winter.

O cuckoo, sweetly warbling with your melodious notes, you of auspicious form—by whom, alas, have you been taught this unfortunate speech that brings such sorrow? In the month of Caitra, amidst the wonderful new sprouts, a woman separated from her lover says to you: "Whose honey is this? To which you, the tree, reply loudly: "It is mine, it is mine! (Or: "It is yours, it is yours!")

Even when silence, movement, conduct, appearance, and form are identical, an individual who is not a crow among a flock of crows—a *kokila* resplendent with beauty—is recognized from afar; for everyone attains greatness in the midst of foolish people, like a scholar among the ignorant, through the wonder of their own noble character and actions.

Brother cuckoo, enough, enough with your warbling! Your priceless quality does not manifest here; remain silent in some hollow cave hidden by a mass of withered leaves. This place is filled with rows of harsh-cawing crows in the caverns of wild trees; this, my friend, is now the season of winter, not the festival of spring.

"Look, Mother! This young cuckoo has abandoned the crow and gone away; she is now pecking at him!"—while I was thus reflecting for a moment, he too, naturally charming, quickly and joyfully embraced his mother-like [cuckoo] to grow, and whichever direction he turns toward, that very one bestows greatness upon him.

The companions said: "Behold before us that leader of the Māras, reflected as if upon a mountain peak, surrounded by a multitude of birds with variegated cries and shimmering lotus stalks—white, red, and blue."

With its expanded, upright thousand-petaled lotus calyx serving as a pedestal for a majestic royal swan, and frequented by bees as its seats and flocks of birds, it was like the earthly abode of the Lotus-Seated One himself.

With the quarters of the sky made formidable by scattered spray, pale with the pollen from the interior of clusters of blooming blue and white lotuses, and filled with the songs of bees intoxicated by fragrance and the warbling of birds, it moved along like a canopy borne through the heavens.

In some places it has the breaking of waves that are reddish and pale; in some places it has bees humming loudly with distress; in some places it is asleep in deep, pure water; and in some places it is hidden by the brilliant blossoms of lotuses.

On its shores, it was thick with fine sand like pearls and radiant with heat; on its banks, it was dense with excellent creeping vines and lions; its rugged marshy edges were shaken by waves and stones; and its vast marshes extended as far as the sky above the earth’s surface.

With the luster of the pollen rising from the lotus-beds shaken by the clouds, and with its interior illuminated by flashes of lightning, the sky—its one part filled with darkness—appeared like the expanse of the twilight sky when it is devoid of light.

With its body covered by swans whose shoulders were weary from devouring shimmering lotus stalks, it resembled the sky filled with fragments of autumn clouds scattered by the wind, where only the air remains; it was like the sky when the moon’s orb has been gathered up by Time.

With the skill of tearing open the pods of mud shaken by the wind, which is fierce with the fragrance of slow-moving nectar, the rising line of great clouds seems to weave a vast cloth, while a rain of flowers falls from the creepers inhabited by agitated birds.

Fanned by the palm-leaf fans of the swaying great lotus petals, with the beautiful foam of whirling chowries, resounding with the songs of bees and cuckoos, it was a king-like spectacle with its lovely multitude of women who were like graceful lotus-stalks.

It possesses enchanting, captivating songs from the foremost of bees; its waters are tawny, strewn with the pollen-dust of lotuses; and it is adorned with groves on its banks, decorated by clusters of white lotuses as pale as masses of foam.
This lake, with its solitary lotus-heart, supremely gladdening the heart, and appearing flavorful and sweet, shines like the company of the virtuous.
O gentle one, this world appears stainless through the medium of the empty sky, just as the minds of the great appear so through their mastery of the meaning of the scriptures.
Seeing this lake, with its waterbirds and its wind harsh with spray-drops, we perceived no distinct object; it appeared like a cloud of snow.
Just as this visible world of Brahmā is nothing other than the immutable and so forth—O King, like waves and the like appearing as if separate from the water.
Alas, what a treacherous succession of waves for those of dull intellect, who are carried along by their own selves and who create whirlpools!
Just as a difference is observed between a well, a pond, a lake, and the ocean, so too should the difference between women, men, and water be understood.

Who indeed is capable of counting the lotuses of this mind—which, like that of a living being, has long been bound by its birth in the water—by means of the swirling eddies of its waves in their state of decay? They are turned back in circles and are exceedingly continuous.

Oh, how marvelous is the manifestation of association with the dull-witted! For even the lotus, having tucked its own virtues within the hollow of its throat as if they were no virtues at all, conceals them from itself while displaying to everyone a wretched mass of thorns.
Enough with qualities that are like those of a lotus: full of holes, unstable, subtle, concealed, joined with dullness, and though not few, utterly devoid of essence.
Even Vāsuki does not have the power to enumerate the majesty of these great lotuses of noble families, who are endowed with the beauty of virtuous qualities.
Since even Lakṣmī, residing upon the chest of Hari, carries a lotus in her hand merely for the sake of beauty, what other hope could there be for excellence?
There may indeed be dissimilarity between a cluster of white lotuses and a cluster of blue lotuses due to their white and black forms; however, these two are equal insofar as both are insentient.

The newly arisen splendor of the blossoming lotus grove does not attain equality with the lakes through the flowering forests, nor with the sky filled with stars, nor with the clusters of moons; rather, it attains it through the beauty of the faces of dancing women smiling in laughter.
Those bees whose lives have passed with undistracted minds on the taste of flower-creepers are truly the most fortunate of all.
Only those bees that wander among the mango trees, experiencing their lovely wonder, are truly possessed of aesthetic rapture; others merely fill out the meter.
Those [lotuses] that resound upon their blossoms with the intoxication of honey-fragrance laugh at the bees who are satisfied with other flavors.

That very bee who dwelt, sang, and flourished while sleeping within the hearts of lotuses as tender as the hollows of the moon—alas, how will he endure his state among the sapless flowers of the trees in this cold season?
The bee upon the magnificent, unopened bud of the jasmine appears like Andhaka impaled on a trident by Kālarudra.

O bee, constantly wandering through the vine-cottages of all the mountains and tasting the honey of various flowers, you are still not satisfied; alas, what a wicked desire you have! I think you do not perceive the true essence from the forests.
O bee, skilled at devouring the clusters of lotuses, go to the lake; do not, O intoxicated one, subject your body to being torn apart by the saw-like thorns in the pits of the jujube trees.
When the flax flower, the circle of blue lotus petals, and the *tāpiccha* tree are in full bloom, a wise man, like honey among them, possesses a distinct excellence.
Behold this pure vine of a row of swans, nurtured by the beauty of the filaments of the navel-lotus and resonant with the singing of the Sāmaveda.
Seeing his mate reflected in the sky, seated within the lotus-nest of a swing, the swan follows her through the circle of the heavens and is no longer conscious of this world.
O King, let no one ever fall into such extreme misfortune; behold this swan who, following his mate, has died as she was reflected in the water.
The warbling cry produced effortlessly by the royal swan is such that even in a hundred years, the crane does not know how to learn it.
Although they are alike in their origin, appearance, birth, behavior, food, and so forth, there is a vast and absolute difference between a common swan and the royal swan.
Established in the sky during the bright fortnight, illuminating the beds of night-lotuses, he gladdens the hearts of all like a swan or the risen moon.
What other bird can attain the splendor of the swans sporting in a forest thick with lotus stalks, lotus fibers, and plantain trunks?
Circled by waves, captivating with its mass of shimmering spray, and beautiful with an abundance of kumuda, utpala, and kahlāra flowers.
Her creeper-like locks of hair were swaying like bees; her tinkling girdle and anklets resounded; her navel was a whirling eddy; and her eyes were like moving waves.
Waiting for her beloved, the giver of the essence of delight, the lake shines like a woman with two beautiful swans.

O swan, do not dwell alone and incessantly in this lake whose essence consists of water-fowls, cormorants, cranes, and ravens; even in times of adversity, association with those of one's own kind—sharing similar character, age, and speech—yields the fruit of prosperity.

This very bee—who once pressed his head against the temples of great elephants trampled by his feet, whose sole abode was a lotus pond, and who possessed the fortune of enjoying the fragrance of white, blue, and yellow water-lilies, jasmine, and campaka creepers—now, by the power of fate, in the cold season, tastes only clods of earth and grass. Alas! When winter is chill, how the mind is surrendered to the wretchedness of calamity!

O friend, having long remembered the shimmering, sparkling luster within the petals of my son’s lotus here, as I moved through the thicket of stalks shaken by the shoulders of a swan, behold clearly now at midday how that cool, blooming [lotus] suddenly scatters a spray of water droplets from its head, like a white lotus shedding its own essence.

As the swan glides silently for a long time through the sky like the gentle moon or through the water, the drops of water that fall from his lotus-bud-like beak—scarred by the steady movement of its stalk—are quickly drunk with joy by the aquatic creatures, just as they are by Brahmā when the drops fall upon him from the vessel of the Gaṅgā.
The companions and their female companions spoke in turn: "Let one virtue of this meritless crane be observed: that by uttering 'prāvṛṭ, prāvṛṭ' (the rainy season), he calls to mind the monsoon."
Like a crane, you appear like a swan dwelling in a lake while maintaining friendship with water-fowl; yet, having abandoned both cruelty and [harsh] speech, become clearly a swan indeed.

Those clever and skillful cormorants, who repeatedly entered the deep interior of the water teeming with aquatic creatures and, having first impaled fish upon their beaks, devoured them with great dexterity—by some stroke of fortune today, brought to the state of dead whales by the majesty of Time joined with destiny, these lame cormorants do not now attack even the easily-seized prey before them, remaining fixed in their place. Those clever and skillful cormorants, who repeatedly entered the deep interior of the water teeming with aquatic creatures and, having first impaled fish upon their beaks, devoured them with great dexterity—by some stroke of fortune today, brought to the state of dead whales by the majesty of Time joined with destiny, these lame cormorants do not now attack even the easily-seized prey before them, remaining fixed in their place.
Demonstrating that "the world is thus ruined for its own sake," the wicked man praises me, saying, "My teacher has attained the status of a teacher."

With its neck outstretched and its broad, pure, beautiful wings spread, this is a swan in the sky—thus it was perceived by people; yet when it catches a small fish from the water of a pond, it is then indeed known by the world as "this is a crane."

Beholding those swans—who were actually deceitful ascetics wandering for an exceedingly long time—and seeing those rogues standing right there in the thicket of darkness, the women on the bank were filled with wonder.
"Look, these women, for whom cold is but a jest, are carrying off white lotuses from this water; do you wish to follow them? I am not your beloved; I am going."

O leader of men, behold this traveler on the path in the forest on the banks of the Keli-tīra, where he is intent on efforts to appease his beloved who is angry with him amidst the bowers of flowering creepers.
"Thus, O King, behold these excellent women as they display their glances, gestures, playful movements, sidelong looks of anger, and smiles."
Even among cranes, water-fowl, and deer, who always dwell in solitary places, there is mutual confusion of their perceptions, unlike that between the ignorant and the wise.
At the tip of the wagtail’s beak, an insect crackles; it stands raised on high like a banner of ancient misfortune.

While the restless crane cries out loudly at the tree on the riverbank, and while the fish plunges its body with force into the muddy water of a puddle as if into the chest of its beloved, it is skillfully saved from fear by the breaking of its heart; for in this world, nothing other than death can grant such relief to one in great distress.

The fortitude that exists in the hearts of creatures such as the *baka*, the *ajagara*, and the *madgu*—those who swallow their prey whole without chewing—I consider it to be nothing other than sleep.

The fear that arises for those dwelling in bodies of water from the gaze of herons, crows, vultures, cats, and snakes—compared to that, the destruction caused by a thunderbolt is like a blade of grass; this was told to me long ago by a wise man who remembered his past lives.
Look here, at the foot of a flower-laden tree on the shore of this lake, upon the dust of the world before you—dust strewn with fresh blue lotuses and ketaka flowers, like a herd of innocent deer.
Because his mind was uplifted, Barhi entreated Indra for water; that Great-Souled One filled his entire earth with it.
These peacocks follow the clouds like suckling infants; thus it is inferred that the dark one is indeed the son of the dark one.
Beholding the deer and thinking of the eyes of his beloved, the traveler turned into a mechanical puppet before the objects standing in front of him.
The peacock does not even drink water, yet he forcibly devours snakes from the earth; I do not know whether this wickedness belongs to the snake or to the peacock.
Having abandoned the great lake that resembles the bed of a virtuous person, the peacock drinks water spat out by clouds; I believe this is out of fear of bowing down.
Behold the peacocks dancing like clouds of shimmering plumage; shaking the moon-like luster of their tails, they are like the young calves of the rainy season.

In this excellent grove, the ocean itself seems to sport here among the peacocks—whose beautiful waves are as lovely as flickering moon-spots—as they spread their plumage, fanned by the forest breeze.
Walk upon the grass, drink water on the forest floor, and take rest in the grove of plantain trees; O startled cātaka bird, excessive pride, when scorched by the fire, does not lead to happiness.

O peacock, this is not a cloud, its belly filled with the floodwaters of the ocean, seeking to ascend into the sky; rather, this is a circle of smoke rising from the mountain, emerging from the hollows and treetops of a forest consumed by a forest fire.

If the peacock, who even during the year of autumn satisfies himself with water from the moon, does not fill the lake even during the rains—though it is a place fit for young children—the virtuous, observing his undertaking, would be moved to laughter; thus, the peacock strives to pass all his time solely through his own thirst.

Having drunk the water as pure as crystal that has issued from the belly of a cloud, the peacock does not drink water again on the path, even when agitated by thirst; rather, it quivers with joy remembering that cloud again and again, and it does not come to ruin. For those whose hopes are fixed upon a virtuous person, even their toil brings happiness.
Here, at the onset of the rainy season, these travelers generally pass the hardships of the road through stories, just as those who are deluded pass their lives away.

Behold here, O Lord, young girls who have set out, having taken up loads of lotuses, water-lilies, night-blooming lilies, lotus roots, and lotus stalks, along with the leaves and water of the *kahlāra* lily from this lake.
When asked, "Why are you taking this? they replied to him: "O traveler, we are the childhood friends of this woman who is tormented by the fever of calamity."

Then, with hearts colored by passion, their forms graced by gracefulness and burdened by the weight of their breasts, the beloveds staying in their own homes once again brought travelers back to the path of memory.
Surely my beloved, seeing the sky so dark with thick, glistening clouds and as void and impenetrable as a forest, laments, falls to the ground, and stumbles.

Alas, the breeze blows—intoxicated by drinking the honey of the lotuses stirred by cups of water encircled by rows of bees and blue lilies; it possesses the quality of being sung to by throngs of birds rendered charming through the dancing of the sprouts of trees on the banks.
The companions said: "Look, this traveler is telling us in the Mandara thicket the story of his long-lost beloved’s life during their separation."
Listen to this supreme wonder that occurred in one place: filled with anxiety, I spoke to you regarding the dispatch of a messenger.

In this separation, which is like the time of the great dissolution, who could it be that goes to my home with her? There is surely no one in this world who would strive so continuously, sincerely, and with affection for the sake of pacifying another's suffering.
Behold, this cloud upon the mountain peak stands like the horse of Smara joined with his mate; encircled by the playful vine of lightning, it remains there as a true connoisseur of aesthetic delight.

"O brother Megha, take up the rainbow of great Indra as a fitting garland for her neck and thunder softly for a moment; show her mercy. That young girl, whose body is as delicate as a tender lotus stalk and slender, is not able to endure it; go to her, O Sugata, and comfort her with the drops of water falling from you and with your own breath."
Having been drawn in the sky with the brush of my mind and embraced, I know not where my beloved has gone from here now, O cloud!

O slender one, while my mind was thus overcome by anxiety, my memory of you vanished somewhere as my thoughts were withdrawn within; I have become like wood or a wall, my body rendered helpless. For who indeed is capable of enduring the crushing pain born of separation?

Thereafter, a clamorous outcry arose among the continuous caravan of travelers; distressed by their calamity, they addressed the clouds with piteous cries: "Alas! The traveler is dead!"—a sound of "Hā hā! produced by great exertion, accompanied by the wide-spread breast-beating of the wives of the wayfarers.

Thinking "he is dead," the world, with eyes filled with tears, performed the funeral rites for me; having gathered wood and piled it up, I was led to the terrifying cremation ground to be burned—a place dreadful with the loud, crackling *paṭ-paṭ* sounds of the vast, blazing pyre erupting into flames.

There, O lotus-faced one, I was placed by some of them—whose eyelashes were drenched with tears—upon a funeral pyre strewn with the dust of the gathered crowd; upon that head thick with dense, rising smoke, like the finest crest-jewel of intoxicated Death, there lay a fragment of fire-gold visible as a mere sliver.

At this moment, a line of smoke, tender as a *kuvalaya* creeper, has begun to enter my nostrils and my soft throat; hot and black, like a young snake pursued by a mongoose, it quickly retreats from afar into the cavity of the earth, shrinking and curling its body for length.

Armored by the nectar of your resolve, I was not pierced by that shower of spears falling with such force, just as a being with a diamond body is not harmed by them; plunging you, who are like the river of passion, into the chamber of my heart, I did not perceive those pangs of agony even during the severing of my vital organs.

O slender one, for this long time, I have experienced within my heart, together with you, the intense playfulness of our inner dalliance; upon seeing which, like emerging from a flood of nectar-pools, the thought arises that even the enjoyment of sovereignty is but a trivial slaughter.

That grace of yours, those playful gestures, and even that speech of yours accompanied by smiles; those side-long glances, which are the sole ornament for one who has reached the far limit of blissful expansion; those moments agitated by the force of movement during laughter at the conclusion of the necklace’s removal—[all these belong to you]. That grace of yours, those playful gestures, and even that speech of yours accompanied by smiles; those side-long glances, which are the sole ornament for one who has reached the far limit of blissful expansion; those moments agitated by the force of movement during laughter at the conclusion of the necklace’s removal—[all these belong to you].

Or rather, what is there that, when remembered, does not bring a joy like the taste of nectar within? O girl, through the elixir of the bliss of love in union with you, I am so exceedingly satiated that I am overcome by exhaustion; I remain there upon the soft surface of your bed, as if upon the lunar orb with its autumnal, cool, and stainless radiance.

In that interval, suddenly, like a thunderbolt from a long stretch of moon-slice cooled by sandalwood paste, I beheld a fire blazing upon the surface of the earth; resembling the submarine fire of the Milk Ocean, it had descended from its own bed into my body.

The companions said: When her beloved had spoken thus, the innocent girl, crying out "Alas, I am ruined! remained in a swoon due to her naivety, suspecting that the bridegroom was turning away from her.
Fanning her with lotus petals and sprinkling her with water, he remained there, holding her in his arms as she lay in that state.
Questioned again by her, he says: "Behold that very same conversation; here he has taken his beloved by the chin as she stands at his side."

"Alas, alas! A fire!"—with these words, while I was speaking with some rising distress and in great haste, that funeral pyre was suddenly plundered by those gleaming travelers, who in an instant set it ablaze with a harsh crackling sound.

Then all the travelers, embracing me—whose body was covered with abundant flowers and who stood there having been raised up amidst the playful music of swaying palm leaves—surrounded me completely and shouted, sang, laughed, danced, and leaped about.

Then he beheld a cremation ground, fierce as a body, which grants happiness to the formidable Vināyakas; it was strewn with heaps of ashes, snakes, and human heads, and its white bones and skulls were as bright as the moon.

There the winds blow, stealing away the shadows from the sides [of the corpses], spreading the stench of shifting, crumbling, and moist skeletons; they waft the dense mist of widespread ashes and shake the hair of the dead, which in the expanse of the sky takes on the form of arrows fallen from the moon; with the clattering sound of the bones of Śiva’s attendants, they produce harsh, grating notes.

With its trees and leaves withered by the heat of the winds issuing from the streams of funeral pyres ablaze, that land bears the likeness of the pleasure-houses of Agni, Vāyu, and the Son of the Sun.

He beheld that cemetery, thick with the foul-smelling corpses and skeletons of boundlessly terrifying beings, and fierce with the howling of intoxicated jackals, crows, herons, vultures, piśācas, and vetālas.

The groves at the ends of the horizon resounded with the wailing of kinsmen and caravans who had arrived, crying out over various corpses; and there were clusters of burnt trees entwined with strings of fresh tendons and entrails dragged down by birds.

In some places it was illuminated by the agitation of funeral pyres; in others, it was filled with masses of clouds formed by great locks of hair; and in other parts, it was like the sunset mountain at night, its slopes resounding with thunder and covered by a canopy of the earth smeared with blood.
The companions said: "O lotus-eyed one, behold this great couple engaged in conversation of such a nature; they have begun to drink the excellent wine."
Various winds blow, skilled at snapping the clusters of plantains and kandalī stalks that are as clear as crystal, and adorned with the filaments of flowers.
The winds blow, rich with the manifold fragrances wafted from the forests; they have drunk the drops of perspiration and have passed over the tresses of beautiful women.
The winds from the salt ocean rush forth with the fury of asuras, driving the lions that emerge from the dwellings of caves in the boundary mountains.
They were cherished by the playful swaying of *tāmāla* and *tāla* trees, and their tender sprouts were kissed by the waves of water tossed up by the wind.
In the gardens, the breezes blow gently, grey with the pollen of flowers cast forth by the swaying creepers of the lips of women, like kings.
This forest breeze, resting upon the bamboo reeds, has begun to sing sweetly, as if instructed by the women of the city of Pāṇḍu.
When an insult was offered to the wind by the karṇikāra tree, even the bees avoided it from afar.
The palmyra tree yields neither fruit nor even a sprout to the seeker; for it is merely a trunk, like a formless beginning devoid of shape.
For passion alone serves as the ornament for those who are devoid of merit and are dull by nature; O King, it is by passion alone that this *kiṃśuka* tree shines like a king.
Come, this Karṇikāra tree is merely a vessel for transformation; what is the use of it, being devoid of fragrance, like a living being devoid of virtue?
The dark tamāla tree, standing amidst a mass of swaying flower-clusters like flashes of lightning, vainly causes the cātaka bird to mistake it for a rain cloud.
With leaves that form dense clusters and providing shade that covers the mountains, these lofty bamboo-like lineages are worthy of great virtues.
The foremost cloud, resting upon the golden mountain peaks along the shore of the Vāta-vyādhi river, wears a yellow garment of lightning like the agitated Hari at the time of creation.
With birds and bees busily engaged in entering and exiting, the blossoming *kiṃśuka* tree shines like a hero drenched in blood.
In the palace of clouds, tawny with clusters of mandāra blossoms, upon the peak of Mount Mahendra, the intoxicated Gandharva lovers lay asleep.
O King, behold the travelers—the Siddhas and Vidyādharas—who, having rested in the extensive shade of the forest of wish-fulfilling trees, sing.
Behold, in this forest, upon every single sprout of this wish-fulfilling tree, celestial beauties rest, sing, and laugh.
This is the temple of the noble sage Mandapāla on Mount Mandara, whose soft abode is a bower; she who is his wife is a bird.
Behold this series of hermitages belonging to sages, filled with trees flowering in every season, where lions and elephants, mongooses and snakes, sport together in mutual friendship.
These water droplets, reflecting the sun, shimmer upon the sprouts of the forest creepers on the ocean shore, which are intermingled with coral trees.
The waves play among the spots of gems and rubies with the circular motion of whirlpools, like graceful women sporting upon the chests of lovers.
Listen: the divine jingling of ornaments, arising from the coming and going of women from the world of the Naga kings, is heard from the sky.
With the sounds of intoxicated female bees falling from the vicinity of their ears, the mountain caves seem to sing of the bathing grounds of Airāvaṇa.
As the ocean diminishes day by day during the dark fortnight, the rows of its coastal embankments appear like the thin crescents of the waning moon.
Breathing with the fragrance of incense, providing cool shade, her limbs were cool to the touch; she revealed her form in solitude and was filled with various flowers.
Clad in the arrangement of forest trees, laughing with the purity of mountain cascades, and spread with carpets of flowers, the blessed woman who sports in the woods is truly fortunate.
Those of noble intellect do not take such delight in the Nandana grove as they do in the pure forest lands where all sounds have subsided.
The delightful, solitary forest lands bring equal delight to the mind of the sage who is utterly dispassionate and to the seeker of sense objects who is full of passion.
The feet of the mountains on the shores of the ocean, whose ramparts are washed by the waters, shine and resound with heaps of jewels as if with tinkling anklets.
Resting upon the Puṃnāga trees, those birds with lovely golden luster and golden crests shine like hosts of gods in the sky.
Behold, the forests of blossoming campaka trees—thick with bees, clouds, and smoke—are shaken by the wind like mountains set ablaze.
Embracing her beloved cuckoo as it swings upon the tips of the *karavīra* creepers, the female cuckoo causes it to utter its sweet, warbling song.
Behold these shores of the Lavana and Sindhu rivers, filled with kings whose hands bear offerings, resounding with the joyful clamor of their laughter.

From the eastern salt ocean to the western, from the north to the south, O King, let those monarchs who remain victorious in fierce battle be made footstools here; and let weapons be bestowed in every direction of the realm according to the scriptures for the protection of the earth, while your incomparable power, preceded by forbearance, long maintains your peaceful edicts. From the eastern salt ocean to the western, from the north to the south, O King, let those monarchs who remain victorious in fierce battle be made footstools here; and let weapons be bestowed in every direction of the realm according to the scriptures for the protection of the earth, while your incomparable power, preceded by forbearance, long maintains your peaceful edicts.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, having sat down upon the ground on those shores of the ocean, these wise ones performed all the necessary duties of sovereignty.
Then, having established their place of residence right there, they remained in due order and set up the boundaries of the maṇḍala so that it was protected.
Then, as if to describe his majesty, the glorious sun entered the interior of the ocean and proceeded to another world.
The night arrived, dark as a streak of cloud and thinning; having completed their daily duties, they rested upon their own beds.
Like the currents of rivers reaching as far as the ocean, they arrived from afar and, their minds agitated with wonder, accomplished this task.
"Oh, how we have reached this distant path without effort, by the power of the God of Gods, Agni, and by means of our own divine vehicles!"
How vast must this expansive beauty of what is visible be! Here is the ocean, and beyond that, the lordly island-land and the sea.
From here an island, from there an ocean—what might lie beyond even that? How great or of what nature is this formless illusion?
Therefore, we pray to the god Hutāśa for his favor; thus, these [sages] gaze upon all directions, tirelessly, until the very ends of the earth.
Having reflected thus, they all remained in their respective places and simultaneously invoked the Blessed One, the Consumer of Oblations.
Then the Blessed One, the sacrificial fire, became visible to them; assuming a physical form, he said, "O sons, choose a boon."
The wise ones said: "O Lord of the Gods, [tell us] the end of this visible world composed of the five elements—first by means of the body, then by the mantra-body, and finally even by the mind."
"O Lord, let this supreme boon be granted to us: that we may behold [Thee] as far as perception extends, as far as existence extends, and as far as the self extends."
O Lord, may we see with our physical bodies that path leading to the unattained goal, and then, at its end, may we see the visible [reality] with the mind alone.
May death not befall us on a path that cannot yet be traversed; rather, let our mind alone proceed on that path where the body does not exist.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, having replied, "So be it," the Fire-god suddenly departed, moving with great haste like the ocean assuming the form of Aurva in an instant.
Then Agni departed and returned; the night lingered and then passed away; the sun also returned and departed; and their desire to cross the ocean of wisdom continued.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then at dawn, having firmly established the order of the earth according to the scriptures, they were as if possessed by passion and as if being restrained by the chief ministers.

Having restrained his entire retinue who were merely wailing and weeping with their faces upturned, and having cast aside pride, envy, greed, and the pursuit of desires through a lack of worldly attachment;

Having surveyed the ends of the earth, they said, "We shall arrive at the far shore of the ocean in an instant"; by those who had attained supreme power through the force of their own mantras, the ocean was then entered with mere footsteps.
Vipaścit, followed by some servants who were entering the ocean with no small number of attendants, went in every direction as if treading upon water with his own feet.
Having placed their footprints within the web of waves, as if upon dry land both on the back and within the water, those four were joined one by one, yet utterly separated from their own army.
Following that very sequence of steps, those Avalokitas entered deep within the great ocean until, standing on the shore, they became invisible, like fragments of clouds in the autumn sky.
Then they traversed that path on foot across the ocean, with their resolve expanded and their girdles tightened like those carrying off a heavy burden.
By ascending and descending mountains with their rises and falls, those forms of Hari carry away the splendor of the waves of the waters.
Like blades of grass whirled in eddies, they wandered for a long time without agitation amidst those [clouds] that shone like circles of moons, flickering and intoxicated with movement.

Invincible with the power of mantras, spells, and vital energy, they carry weapons in their hands; in some places, their bodies have been swallowed and then disgorged by carelessly negligent sea-monsters.
Their forms driven by winds resting upon the waves of the water, they were carried back and forth in an instant for hundreds upon hundreds of yojanas.
By virtue of those limbs raised high like water-waves by the elephants, she bore the splendor of standing upon the backs of the state elephants of her own kingdom.
Like winds, they displayed the emergence from the watery clouds through their skill in tearing asunder the vast city-like expanse of the massed waves.
Though struck by the surging waves of the rushing elephants, they did not abandon their natural steadfastness, like the excellent shores of the ocean.
Reflected in the circles of pearls and rubies released by the great waves, even though they were solitary, they appeared as if surrounded on all sides by a retinue of men.
Making light steps upon masses of pale foam, they bore the beauty of royal swans gliding through white lotuses.
The kings were not afraid there of the roar of the ocean, which was terrifying with its deep thundering sound and surging like the rolling of the tide.
Struck by the falling and crashing of great water-bearing mountains that scraped the clouds, they descended to the netherworld for a moment and ascended to the abode of the sun for a moment.
Covered by the falling torrent of water rising unexpectedly, they appeared as if enveloped by a canopy suddenly blown down by a tempest.

They have entered the ocean together with their companions, the sea-monsters; they are surrounded by whirlpools filled with brave crocodiles and crabs, and their intervals are filled with the spray from the water-trees. With their shimmering bodies, they appear as if adorned with flowers—stray rubies and pearls with visible and invisible webs of rays—while at every step they are accompanied by vast clouds in the form of other waters.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, these people have set out on foot to travel across the ocean and its islands in order to investigate this ignorance that takes the form of the visible world.
Free from any cutting or breaking, they leaped with ease from ocean to island, from island to ocean, and from island to mountain and forest.
The wise Pītā was defeated by the fish-like Mīna, who considered himself immortal, born from the lineage of Viṣṇu-Mīna, and possessed the power of the vehicle Vitastā.
Having reached the Ocean of Milk, he was disgorged by that fish, which was very difficult to digest; having leaped over the Ocean of Milk, he went far away to another quarter of the world.
In the city of the yakṣas, Dakṣiṇa beheld an ocean of sugarcane juice; having been cast into it by the yakṣiṇī through her skill in training, he was made her lover.
When he previously attacked Makara and cut him down, he was carried away by the Gaṅgā and cast ashore at Kānyakubja.
But Uttara, having propitiated the people of Uttarakuru, attained great fortune; and because of that very [fortune], the fears of death do not afflict him even at the ends of the earth.
Having assumed a form that was swallowed and then disgorged by the sea-monster Makara-mātanga, he traversed many principal mountain ranges of other continents.
Placing him on his back, the bird Hemacūḍa swiftly carried Kuśāṅgaśrī across the oceans to Kuśadvīpa.
On the mountain of Krauñcadvīpa, he was swallowed by a rākṣasa in the forest; that rākṣasa was torn apart by him with rendings of the heart and intestines.
Dakṣa, having become a Yakṣa in an instant due to the curse of Dakṣa, attained liberation after a hundred years in Śākadvīpa.
Uttara, having crossed over the excellent river Tārāvarataraṅgiṇī, became a stone upon the golden earth of the great ocean due to a sage’s curse.
Then, after a hundred years, through the grace of the Fire-god, he was released from there by that very Siddha and attained delight.
Varṣa was the king of the inhabitants of Nālikera for eight years; he was exceedingly righteous and subsequently regained his former memory.
In the forest of wish-fulfilling trees to the north of Mount Meru, he dwelt for ten years with an apsaras, subsisting on coconuts.
Knowing the true nature of the birds' breath, he lived for many years in play within the nest of a female bird on a Śālmali tree in Śālmalidvīpa.
On Mount Mandara, in a bower of mandāra trees upon soft ground, a kinnarī named Mandarī attended [him] for one day.

Then the former [king], agitated by desire, spent seventy years together with the deities of the Nandana grove and the rows of kalpavṛkṣa trees in the forest on the shore of the Milk Ocean, along with the apsarases.

Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, since all these beings consist of a single consciousness and possess a single body, how is it that they have come to possess diverse desires while inhabiting one and the same body?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The single, solid expanse of consciousness, though indeed devoid of diversity and all-pervading, has itself become as if manifold, like the mind within the Self during sleep.
Because it is transparent, the Self itself is reflected within the Self in such a manner; for that which is of such a nature, the reflection occurs just as it is, like in a stainless mirror.
Just as mirrors made entirely of the same metal reflect one another, so too do these ultimate entities reflect one another.
Therefore, whenever and whatever object appears before someone, that person is engaged with it for its own sake, because their essential nature consists solely of the wealth of consciousness.

Thus, this is non-different yet different, and both different and non-different in reality; therefore, it is neither different nor non-different, but consists of the nature of both difference and non-difference.
Therefore, whatever object first appears to a wise person, he attains a state of being composed of consciousness through it and comes under its sway.
Yogins, though situated in a single location, perform actions by pervading everywhere; they also experience all things throughout the three periods of time.
Even a single year, possessing pervasion, performs distinct actions at the same time; by means of that foot, it both brings about joy and experiences it.
Simultaneously and in incalculable numbers, those who are the counterparts of Īśvara create and experience the web of karma that constitutes the world.
Viṣṇu alone, by means of his four arms or his various bodies, protects the world while performing distinct activities and enjoys excellent women.
When one who possesses many arms gathers wealth with two hands, he constantly engages in battle with many more.
In that very same way, by those wise ones situated thus in every direction—even though they consist of a single consciousness—transactions were conducted accordingly.
They slept upon the ground, ate in other islands, wandered through forest groves, and traversed desert lands.
I have dwelt among the mountain ranges, wandered within the depths of the oceans, rested upon the lines of islands, and hidden among the thickets of clouds.
He sported amidst the rising gales and the ocean waves, and upon the shores of mountains and seas as well as within cities.

On the shore of the Sunrise Mountain in Śākadvīpa, he slept for seven years in the dense interior of the Vidala forest to the east, deluded by a Yakṣa; having forcibly drunk the water of the rocks there, he turned into stone and remained within it for seven years, born from the earth.
In Śākadvīpa, on the summit of the Sunset Mountain, in a cloud-cave dwelling, the western prince was made a lover for a month by a Piśāca-Apsarās.
In the region called Śāntabhaya, on the great mountain Jaladhāra, in the Harītakī forest, the eastern [Vāsava] vanished.
On this Raivataka mountain, in the region named Śiśira, there was once a lion for ten nights who had been brought under the power of a yakṣa.
There, having become like a frog in a cave of the Golden Mountain and other peaks, he lived for ten years, deceived by the illusion of a Piśāca.
Having reached his youth, the blind man dwelt for a hundred autumns at Andhakūpa on the northern shore of Mount Śyāmā in Śākadvīpa.
In the year Marībaka, he spent fourteen years there; through the science of the Vidyādharas, that latter one attained the status of a Vidyādhara.

Having caught the breeze from the coastal forest, which is moistened by the spray from the gradual movement of the goddess Lakṣmī’s trembling limbs—she who grew weary from her dalliance with Śiva—and which bears the fragrance acquired from embracing the cardamom creepers.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In the region known as Śāntabhaya, on the mountain Jaladhāra, he remained drinking the water of the Kartari river in that manner while on the tree in Śākadvīpa.
Then, after seventy years, he was released by the western [prince] who had come, having been cut from his state as a tree by means of knowledge, like with a saw, yet remaining unhurt.
A Westerner who had turned to stone during the year of Śiśira was quickly liberated by the Southern [tradition] through the application of beef and other such substances.

When Śiva was situated on the far side of the western mountain, year after year, the western [direction] was liberated by the southern [direction] having come there; it was turned into a bull-hide rug by the Gopi-Śākinī.
In this very Kṣemaka year, on the tree at Mount Āmbikeya, the southern one attained the state of a yakṣa and achieved liberation through that yakṣa.
In this very land of Vṛṣaka, on the mountain named Kesara, one who had previously become a lion was liberated by a later person.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, how is it that yogis, though situated in only one place, perform all actions throughout the three periods of time while pervading everywhere?
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, let that which exists for the unawakened here be as it may; we have no need for it. But hear now that which is told concerning those who are awakened.

For those who know it, there is no self other than the universal existence of pure consciousness alone; for when the realization of the absolute non-existence of the visible occurs, both the perceptions of creation and non-creation perish.
For one who rests continuously in the universal existence of pure consciousness alone, there exists here, at all times, the state of being all and the state of having all as one's self.
Tell me: by what, how, where, when, and like what is anything obstructed? For you are omnipresent, the self of all; tell me where, when, and in what manner [it appears].
When it shines forth in that way within the Self of all, what is there for us that does not exist—the past, the present, and the future, the gross as well as the subtle?
Likewise, "far" and "near," "a moment" and "an eon"—all these always remain within the universal (sāmānya) without ever abandoning their own essential nature.
Behold the manifestation of māyā, which resides within the Self of all—unborn, unceasing, and established exactly as it is.
Therefore, these three worlds are indeed a single mass of consciousness; and while not abandoning its nature as space, it remains as space itself, the self of all.

The Self of the world, appearing as the world itself through the states of seer and seen—since that which is the very body of the vision of the Universal Self exists, what could there be, by what means, in what manner, or at what time?
O knower of reality, tell me what is difficult to accomplish regarding the nature of the curable and the incurable; therefore, [speak] concerning this single, constant consciousness of the wise king.
For one who is following toward awakening but has not yet attained the supreme state—whether she be one or many—it is appropriate for everything to be present everywhere.

For what indeed exists in the Supreme Self, whose nature consists of both awakening and non-awakening? Until supreme awakening is attained, it is only natural that there should be a confusion regarding objects.

For one who has entered even a slight degree of awakening, that state of perfection is indeed appropriate; in this way, all those situated in every direction are entirely interconnected with one another.
If the space of awakening should quickly deviate even slightly from its own nature, it perceives, experiences, and swiftly treats the crisis as if it were falling away from its own form.

"Even though it remains exactly as it is, it assumes, as it were, the state of being something else. Śrī Rāma said: "If the wise are truly awakened, how could they assume the form of lions, bulls, and so forth?"
"O Brahmin, tell me quickly for the sake of my awakening: who are these that go in all directions? Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O sinless one, those whom I have described as awakened are the yogins."
The wise are not awakened by means of a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) or through another form; O mighty-armed one, those who are truly wise are not awakened by such subtle [arguments].
For they remain suspended, swinging between the views of enlightenment and non-enlightenment; the signs of liberation are seen on one side, and the signs of bondage on all sides.
For those wise yogins who are awakened to the eternal Dharma through suchness and by means of dhāraṇā, there is no further state to be reached.
For those yogins of concentration have attained the perfections of concentration; they have reached supreme awakening, in whom ignorance no longer exists.
O lotus-eyed one, do those practitioners of concentration behold ignorance? For these are indeed yogins who have attained supernatural powers through their excellence.
Ignorance exists for them; therefore, they do not investigate that [reality]. Listen to something else, O Rāma, concerning those who possess bodies while being liberated in this life (jīvanmukta).
In conventional usage alone does the cognition of distinct objects occur; even liberation is a property of the mind, and it abides in the mind itself.
The property of the body does not exist in the body, nor does it depart from the body; the mind, once liberated, is never again bound.
By what means can a fruit fallen from its stalk be bound again even with effort? Yet the body of those who have attained liberation while living remains subject to the laws of the body.
Their mind, being directed toward that, perceives it as truly immovable; for liberation is not to be known by another, just like the practice of *dhāraṇā* and other [yogic] applications.
This [consciousness] is indeed self-cognizable, like the pleasure derived from tasting honey and the like; it is that which, joined with pleasure and pain, itself experiences bondage.
When that [state] is liberated, one is said to be liberated; for he who bestows his own direct experience and whose mind is inwardly cooled is indeed called "liberated."
Bondage is a state of a scorched mind; it is not seen in the body and such. Even when the body is cut into pieces or when one is appointed to a kingdom, [bondage does not arise].
For one whose mind is liberated while living, even as they weep or laugh, neither sorrow nor joy arises within; that [liberated state] remains established.
Even for one who grasps it, this experience exists only therein and not elsewhere; scholars are seen to be broken, having undergone a transformation of form.

For those liberated while living, by their very nature, there is never [the perception of death] regarding the body and so forth; even when dead, they do not die, and even when weeping, they do not weep.
Laughing, the liberated-in-life one of great exaltation does not laugh at all; those free from passion appear as if possessed by passion, and those without anger appear as if filled with anger.
Those who perceive reality appear to be enveloped by delusion due to their lack of delusion; for such notions as "this is happiness" and "this is suffering" are merely mental constructions.
Enough of those [theories] that have gone too far, like sprouts growing from the sky; for there is no such thing as a "Self of the World" (jagadātman), yet everything exists as one.
The statement that "pleasure, pain, and so forth belong to him" is like a tree in the sky; those liberated while living, endowed with victory, grieve only for the grief-stricken.
Those who perceive reality see the head of the Lotus-born [Brahmā], which is unbroken and of a single essence, intensely devoted to the chanting of the Sāmaveda.
Hara severed it with his fingernail as if it were a delicate lotus; yet even though he was capable, Brahmā did not produce that head again.
For this sky of consciousness, its oneness with the infinite space is sufficient; what is the use of any other head? For it has no purpose whatsoever here through action, nor any through inaction.

Whatever is accomplished by a name, let it be so; what is the use of anything else? Hara bears on his body the fawn-eyed woman and the unceasing tears of Śarada, just as the Ocean of Milk bears the hidden digit of nectar.
Though capable, this noble-minded one does not abandon his state of passion; for the virtues of dispassion were witnessed by him at the time of the burning of the five-arrowed god.
He has no purpose whatsoever here through action, nor any at all through inaction; nor does he have any dependence on any being for any object of interest.
Let this [world] be full of passion for him; what is the use of any other dispassion? Whatever has come to pass in whatever way, let it remain so—what is the use of anything else?
Janārdana, liberated while living, acts and causes others to act intensely; he dies and is even put to death; he is born and grows incessantly.
And although he is capable of abandoning the state of being either slow or swift, he does not abandon it; for there is no purpose served by his abandoning it, nor any by his resorting to it.
"Let it remain exactly as it is here"—thus is the cessation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Hari remains entirely without desire, bearing the form of pure consciousness alone.
The sun constantly and eternally swings his own self, which has become like a ball of time, upon the courtyard of the sky within the house of the world.
The Lord of Day is not capable of obstructing the body; yet, though devoid of desire and extinguished, he remains exactly as he is.
The moon experiences its inexhaustible waning in vain until the end of the kalpa, yet it remains established in its natural state, weary because of its state of being liberated while living.

Just as a fire that has attained liberation while living carries on its existence with equanimity, though it was once distressed by the consumption of the oblations of Marutta, Gaurī, and Śiva, and so forth; [so too does the yogi remain].
Though they were gurus in this world, Śukra and Bṛhaspati remained like two wretched men, possessed by many desires for victory, even though they were liberated while living.
The sage Janaka rules the kingdom with a mind liberated while living, wearing down his body in fierce battles upon this earth.
Nala, Māndhātṛ, Sagara, Dilīpa, Nahuṣa, and others—though liberated while living—ruled their kingdoms for a long time as if they were still subject to worldly agitation.
In conventional practice, the ignorant and the wise are indeed exactly the same; for it is only the presence or absence of latent tendencies that is the cause of bondage and liberation.
Bali, Prahlāda, Namuci, Vṛtra, Andhaka, Mura, and others—though liberated while living and free from passion—maintained their worldly status as if they still possessed passion.

Therefore, whether non-existence or existence arises through the destruction of passion and hatred, there is not even the slightest difference with respect to the sky-like consciousness in its essential nature.
Through knowledge as pure as space, they perceive all phenomena to be like the sky; for those who are liberated while living, how could there be any notion of duality?
Just as the radiant bow of Indra appears as if it were manifold though it is empty, so too this delusion consisting of the visible world is a mere appearance.
Just as various colors shine in the expanse of the sky within a rainbow, so too are the atoms of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) essentially empty by nature.
This world appears as unreal yet manifests as if real; it is unborn and unceasing, just like emptiness in the sky.
The world, though having a beginning and an end, is without beginning or end; though not empty, it is empty; thus born, it is unborn; and though unobstructed, it is indeed obstructed.
That which is born and that which has ceased exists; thus Brahman shines forth like the very sky. As is a pillar made of wood, so too is the statue carved from it.
One should know that the world is composed of that which is free from all temporal divisions, equal, sleepless, the seat [of consciousness], and the singular space of pure awareness.

One should know that the form of consciousness which exists in the interval between the departure from one place and the arrival at another, being the unmanifested sky of consciousness—that is the world, composed of that very essence.
In that regard, whatever non-duality or unity there may be, I consider even that not to exist at all; it appears as mere space, and I consider even that not to exist at all.
This very world is but the sky of the self, or rather, it abides within the self; though it appears vast and manifest, it is seen like a city yet to be.

The entire range of perceivable phenomena remains as silent as the Self, tranquil and as solid as stone, within a disposition as clear as the expanse of space. Alas, what a delusion it is that this very Self, having bestowed upon itself the designation "the world," appears as if bewildered by its own magic!
Śrī Rāma said: O best of sages, what did the Vipracittas do next as they remained at those ends of the quarters, amidst the continents, oceans, forests, and mountains?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen, my dear, to what happened there to these wise ones as they wandered through the mountains, forests, and islands abounding with rows of *tālī* and *tamāla* trees.
On the western shore of the mountain of Krauñcadvīpa, a certain wise man was crushed by an elephant against the mountain slope, like a lotus crushed by its stalk.
The second, his limbs mangled by the Rākṣasa, was carried through the sky and cast into the submarine fire, where he was reduced to ashes.
The third was indeed led to the realm of the Thirty-three by a Vidyādhara; having gone there, he was reduced to ashes by the curse of Śakra, who was angered by his failure to prostrate.
The fourth, moving with great speed, was split into eight pieces by an irresistible crocodile on the bank of a mountain in Kuśadvīpa, at the edge of a river.
Thus those four kings, like the world-protectors, met their destruction at the four quarters when their fourfold power waned, their minds thrown into agitation.
Then, by virtue of his prior mental impressions, he—whose nature was space—beheld within the sky itself, which was of the nature of space, the terrestrial sphere.
[He saw] the world encircled by the seven islands and oceans, adorned with cities and ports, the pedestal for the summit of the divine mountain, and the crest-jewel of the realm of Brahmā.
It has the orbs of the moon and sun for its eyes, the clusters of stars for its pearl ornaments, the drifting clouds for its garment, and various forests for its body hair.
She beheld all four bodies of the wise ones, as pervasive as the sky and the horizons at the end of a kalpa, just as they had been before.
Through their experience of the subtle body, those whose nature was like space perceived before them the manifestations of gross physical bodies within the void.
To examine how great this ignorance might be if it were of such a nature, all four of them proceeded forward by the power of their mental formations.
In order to perceive the ultimate nature of the experience of the earth's orb as both the object seen and the act of seeing, they wandered through other continents to investigate that ignorance.
Having crossed seven islands and seven great oceans, the wise Vipaścit reached Janārdana in the land of Ghana.
Therefore, having attained incomparable knowledge in the various directions, he remained in that very state of meditative absorption for five years.
Then, having abandoned the body as consciousness attained its true being, he entered the supreme nirvana, like that breath [of life] entering the sky.

Long ago, on the day of the full moon, while contemplating his own body situated beside the orb of the cool-rayed moon, he remained for a long time in the City of the Moon after his physical form had vanished.
In Śālmalidvīpa, the southern king, having destroyed his enemies, still exercises his sovereignty today, for he has not forgotten his former resolve toward the virtuous.
In the seventh ocean, where the waves were tossed by northern gales, he dwelt for a thousand years within the belly of a sea-monster.
Eating the flesh from the belly of the sea-monster, he emerged from the belly of the Makara in the ocean like a Makara itself when its leader has died.
Then, having crossed eighty thousand yojanas of the solid earth—whose interior is very dense and which rises from the ocean of waters that resembles snow—[he reached the mountain].
Having reached the great earth, ten thousand yojanas in extent, he died upon that golden path frequented by the gods.
And in that state, and in its midst, Vipaścit attained the supreme state of being unmanifest, like a piece of wood placed in the middle of a fire attaining the nature of fire in an instant.
Having become the primordial deity, he went to the Lokāloka mountain, which stands like a basin for this tree of the earth's orb.
It rises fifty thousand yojanas high; one part of it is rich with light and the conduct of the world, and not the other.
Those situated below beheld him, who had reached the summit of the Lokāloka mountain and stood upon the path of the stars, suspecting him to be a high constellation.
Beyond that region, on the other side of that great mountain, lies a vast chasm extending in all four directions—a void like the sky, infinite and empty.
Then this terrestrial globe is indeed completed in its spherical form; beyond it is the void of space, a great abyss filled with darkness.

In that state, know that there exists neither darkness blue as collyrium or the interior of a tamāla tree, nor earth, nor anything moving; nor is there any object whatsoever, even in the slightest degree, that can ever be perceived as a support.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, tell me this: how is the terrestrial globe situated? How do the hosts of stars move, and what is the nature of the Lokāloka mountain?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as a ball fashioned by the imagination of a child remains in the sky, so too is the earth imagined in the ether by the Child of Pure Consciousness.
Just as those with cataract-afflicted eyes perceive hairs, moons, and so forth, so too does the space of consciousness perceive the earth and other elements at the beginning of creation.
Just as a city of imagination, though being maintained, is not seen, so too the experience of the earth is maintained and maintained by the consciousness.

In whatever manner and to whatever extent consciousness appears, by virtue of its inherent nature as consciousness, it appears in that very way and to that same extent, being of that very essence in each respective instance.
Just as one whose eyes are overcome by cataracts perceives a mass of hair in the sky, so too does the globe of the earth appear to pure consciousness; yet it remains exactly as it is.
If rivers flow upward and fire burns beneath them within the funeral pyre, appearing as if in a dream, then it must be that such things actually exist there.
Therefore, when consciousness appears as falling, the world appears as constantly falling; but when it appears as rising, it likewise becomes manifold in nature.
Appearing as if motionless, she remains fixed; yet, while possessing light, she is luminous, and being without light, she abides within the self of those who perceive the lightless.
Following the singular manifestation of consciousness alone, the circle of stars and likewise the earth—this entire world, though non-existent, appears as if real and remains unbroken.
Then, there was a great expanse of sky, a void of light upon light; therein, the darkness stood like a single vast ocean, appearing here and there in various places.
Due to the distance of the circle of stars and the vastness of the great mountain, there was darkness in some places and light in others, even within that very same courtyard.
From the circle of the sky situated beyond the Lokāloka mountain, the wheel of stars revolves at a vast distance in the ten directions.
That circle of stars, spanning from the netherworld to the heavens in the sky, spreads through the ten directions, falling everywhere except for that which is above.
The earth-world itself, together with the netherworld and the circle of constellations, revolves at the edge of the Lokāloka mountain; it is nothing other than a construction of consciousness.
Beyond the sky, which is twice the size of the worlds of Sālōka and Bhūloka, the circle of stars remained like the parched kernels of a ripe walnut.
The thickness of the circle of stars is twice that of the sky, as it extends in the ten directions with a consistency like the bark of a wood-apple tree.
Just as the manifestation of the plenitude of consciousness consists of conceptualization, so too, indeed, does this worldly condition exist through such a structural arrangement.
Beyond the circle of constellations, there exists another sky twice its size; that is in some places rich in light and in others composed of dense darkness.
At the limit of that sky stands the shell of the cosmic egg; one part is above, another is below, and the space between these two is in the middle.
Extending for a hundred million yojanas, it is nourished and firm as a diamond; it stands in the sky, consisting of pure consciousness, its very nature being space.
In the great sphere of the sky, which faces all directions, there are its own sun and stars; what here could be above or below, or is everything both above and below?
Falling, rising, going, staying, and consciousness—these are mere manifestations, not a real substance. There is no falling, nor rising, nor going, nor coming, nor even staying.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This is directly perceived by people such as ourselves, and is not merely inferential; it pertains to one whose body is pure consciousness, not to one possessing a material form.
I have described this world-dream to you, but not others; for there exist other world-dreams as well, and their conditions are likewise different.
What is the use of describing the structures of other world-dreams? For the wise, there is no discourse other than that which is purposeful.
Meru is to the north of all, and Lokāloka is to the south; by this inference regarding the entire multitude of beings, the wise [determine their locations].

This is directly perceptible to others, wherein those other delusions of the world exist; for they do not exist in that manner within our own domain, yet they appear beautiful through their specific configurations.
For all those residing in the seven continents, Mount Meru is to the north and the Lokāloka mountain is to the south; it is certain that this is not the case for others.
Listen, O Rāma, to what is relevant: that shell of the cosmic egg, and outside of it, water exists ten times its measure.
That shell of the cosmic egg, however, like a mere blade of grass or a common gem, naturally holds water at all times, like a wish-fulfilling jewel.
The earthly element remains present in all things like a wish-fulfilling jewel; because of that, these [substances] fall down here with great force at all times.
Outside the water, there exists a fuel-less fire ten times its size, as clear as space, resembling the interior of a tranquil and steady flame.
Therefore, the pervasive wind is established externally with ten times that [space]; and external to the wind, the stainless ether exists with ten times that [wind].
Beyond that is the infinitely vast, peaceful space of Brahman—neither light nor darkness, the imperishable mass of great consciousness.
In that great sky of Brahman, which is without beginning, middle, or end; which is called the Great Consciousness, the Self of all, and whose nature is unborn liberation.
Far, far away, again and again, hundreds of thousands upon hundreds of thousands of such cosmic eggs flash forth and cease.
Nothing whatsoever manifests here within this even, luminous reality; such is this nature, existing in that very form, established within itself alone.
This entire sequence of the experience of the visible world has been told to you; now hear what happened to Vipaścit on Lokāloka.
Impelled by his resplendent certainty and the previously cultivated impressions of his practice, he fell into the abyss of darkness from the summit of the mountain that illuminates the world.
There he saw his own body, with its mental form, torn apart by birds resembling mountain peaks, yet spreading forth according to his own thoughts.
Because that country was so holy, he, possessing a pure disposition, did not cause his subtle body (ativāhika-deha) to perceive it as a material (ādhibhautika) entity.
Having attained only that much awakening and not reaching a higher realization, he reflected upon his dark deed and became devoted to the welfare of all beings.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, how does this mind, which is bodiless, expand into its objects? What kind of superior awakening arises from the consciousness of the subtle body (ātivāhika)?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as one who dwells within the inner apartments wanders abroad by virtue of being a traveler of his own volitions, so does this mind of his proceed forth once it has been set in motion.
Just as the mind extends itself into delusion, dream, mental projection, false cognition, or the hearing of stories, so does that extended mind persist.
When that body falls away, it is called the *ativāhika* (conveying) body; through forgetfulness, the notion of a material (*ādhibhautika*) body then appears here in the course of time.
When that physical body, which is comparable to the illusion of a rope-snake, has vanished, then only the subtle, transportive body (ātivāhika-deha) remains.
My dear friend, let this subtle body (ātivāhika) be carefully investigated, until it is realized that nothing exists here apart from pure consciousness alone.
That form of consciousness which exists in the interval when one has gone from one place to another is the very nature of this infinite, uniform pure consciousness.
Where is duality, and where is aversion? Tell me, where indeed are passion and the rest? All is Śiva, without beginning or end; it is remembered as supreme consciousness.
The mentalization of the emanation-body is stilled; this is the supreme awakening. One who remains within the subtle transportive body has not yet attained that awakening.
Awakened by the wisdom of Vipaścit, he beheld his expanding mind as a darkness resembling the dwelling in a womb, through the realization of the subtle body.
At the end of the darkness, there is a ground formed by the breaking open of the shell of Viriñca’s egg, made of gold with the essence of diamond, extending for ten million yojanas.
At its end, he reached water eight times greater than that; it stood level with the surface of the earth and the door-panels, like the surface of the ocean.
Having passed beyond that, he then reached a mass of splendor terrifying like a multitude of suns, shining with a hollow interior of dense flames like the fire of universal destruction.
With a mental body free from burning, grief, and other afflictions, she went there and perceived the vehicle she had previously inhabited.
Being carried along, he realized himself to be the subtle body (ātivāhika); for how could that which is essentially mind alone be carried?
Thus, through his awakening, the wise-souled one crossed that ocean of wind and reached the vast sky situated ten times its size.
Having transcended that, he reached the infinite space of Brahman, wherein all is, from which all arises, and which is both nothing and everything.
Wandering there with his mind, he went further and further away; and by him were seen the earth, water, fire, air, and likewise the entire world.
Again the constructions of saṃsāra, again the creations, again the directions; again the mountains, the sky, again the gods, and again human beings.
Furthermore, at the limit of the five great elements is the cloudless Brahman; again within that are the worlds on high, again the creations, and again the directions.
From that [state] comes the ether of Brahmā, and from that, other creations which are not yet finalized; thus, moving through this for a long time, he remains even today.
For he does not indeed turn away from his long-practiced conviction; there is truly no end to ignorance, for that [ignorance] is itself the reality of Brahman.

In reality, ignorance does not exist here within Brahman, whose nature is free from conceptual construction; this visible world and what is called "this ignorance" are merely the Self manifested in this way.
Just as you have seen, see, or will see in waking or in dream, so indeed has that Brahman been, is, and will be—real and tranquil.

This great, sequential manifestation of the world, which is like a wheel perceived within dense darkness, appears as the supreme Self; yet, my dear, it is neither eternally existent nor does it have the form of non-existence.

Within those very same worlds, which have become exceedingly diminished within the belly of Brahmā, O Rāghava, he still wanders like a deer through their vast fragments, because the true nature of reality remains unknown to him even today.
Śrī Rāma said: O best of sages, what happened after that between those two Vipracits, who were both obstructed by him? What followed for those two Vipracits?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Of those two, one, rendered helpless by long-practiced latent impressions (vāsanā), wandered through various islands with a multitude of bodies until he reached that very same path.
In that very same way, having cast off all veils within the hollow of the supreme ether, he remains even now, beholding hundreds of thousands of worlds in saṃsāra.
Of those two, the second, due to his long-standing habit of initial non-attachment, abandoned [his body] while wandering through various forms; today he remains as a deer on this mountain.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, there is but one single latent impression (vāsanā) that is ever-present for the four [orders]; how has it attained diversity, yielding results both inferior and superior?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The latent impression (vāsanā) of a living being, though well-practiced, undergoes a change in its degree of intensity due to the influence of place, time, and action; it becomes weak, firm, or otherwise, but it does not become something else entirely.
Place, time, action, and so forth constitute a single unity, as does the unity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); whichever of these two is more powerful, that alone triumphs in an instant.
Thus, by way of this distinction, these four are established here: two are dragged away for the sake of ignorance, while another is liberated and the other is like a deer.
Even now, those of deluded intellect have not reached the end of ignorance; this ignorance is infinite, being nourished by lack of knowledge.
When the light of discernment has dawned, it quickly becomes tranquil; it dissolves away without root, like the splendor of darkness at sunrise.
Listen now to the account of Vipaschit, born in another world at a later time; in a certain distant region within the wandering of saṃsāra.
Somewhere in the great void of Brahman, within some sphere of the visible, he attained that which is essentially of the nature of Brahman through its appearance as the visible world.
He alone, through auspicious association, having entered into the midst of the wise and understood the perceptible world as it truly is, attained the stainless state of Brahman.
Through the immediate and thorough knowledge of that very [reality], both that ignorance and that body—bound by passion—reach their cessation like the water of a mirage.
Thus, I have clearly related to you all the deeds of Vipaścit; for this ignorance is infinite, since it consists of that [consciousness], just as Brahman does.
Wherever and however many hundreds of thousands of years one may travel, there, by its very nature, something inconceivable is perceived.
That very same [reality], when not fully understood, is called false knowledge; but when it is fully understood, it is peaceful and is likewise called Brahman.

There is no division; yet this division exists there, consisting of that which is indeed Brahman itself as the manifestation of consciousness, for even differentiation is of the very nature of consciousness.
The ignorant man has sought the end of this pavilion of the universe for hundreds of ages, yet he has not found the end of ignorance; whereas the wise man has found it.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahman, best among speakers, why was that door of the cosmic egg not reached by Vipaścit? You have told us this; why did he not enter?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Long ago, as soon as he was born, Viriñci split open the shell of the cosmic egg with his two arms—one below and one above.
From that point, one part has gone upward to an even greater distance; therefore, another part has gone downward to an even more distant interval.
Depending upon those two, the coverings of water and the other elements remain; they themselves are supported by them, and thus they hang suspended within those two.
Know that the space between these two halves of the cosmic egg is the intermediate realm; that which is perceived as dark blue, extending to the furthest limits of the horizon, is this very space.
There, the coverings of water and the other elements do not adhere and do not exist; for that [reality] is stainless and empty, a tethering post for the conceptual constructions of the imagination.
