Proceeding by that path like a wise leader of a circle of bears, he was highly consecrated for the sake of investigating ignorance until liberation.
Since this ignorance consists of that very Brahman, it has infinite forms; therefore, it exists when it is not fully known, but when it is fully known, it does not exist.
Having reached the state of the wise, far beyond the farthest reaches in the supreme ether, others wander among certain other forms of the world that arise from ignorance.
One deer was liberated, another was somewhere still, and those two were wandering even now, rendered helpless by the powerful impressions of their former lives.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, if you have compassion for me, please tell me: in what kind of worlds and at what distances do those Vipracittas wander?
O Sage, how far back in the course of saṃsāra have those births of yours occurred? This which has been told by you here is a great marvel for us.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, those two worlds in which both Vipaschit remained have passed beyond our range of perception, despite our diligent efforts.
The third has become a deer, wherein the wise one resides; at times, accompanied by the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), he does not remain within our range of perception.
Śrī Rāma said: O one of great intelligence, tell me truly where that world is situated in which Vipaścit has become a deer.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having gone from far to even farther, into the great sky of the Supreme Brahman—listen to that world in which that wise deer exists.
Know this: that deer is situated here within these three worlds; this is that supreme space, yet the world remains at a distance from it.
Śrī Rāma said: "How is this consistent? This Vipaschit, having reached that state from this very world, has been born here today as a deer."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as the whole constantly knows all its own parts, so do I know all things established within the Brahman-self.
He saw those many forms of various kinds, some unfinished and others being withdrawn, interwoven with one another and visible to each other, appearing like earthen statues of their own true nature.
O Rāma, whatever occurred on another path similar to this one has been related by me to you.
While those wandering through other worlds in various bodies moved across the quarters of space, Vipaścit remained for that long in the infinite void of the sky, his mind unwearied.
Having wandered through the vast delusions of many worlds, he was born right here as a deer in a certain mountain cave by the stroke of chance.
Wandering far through the worlds, he perceived that this creation—in which a deer was situated—stood in the void like the "crow-and-the-wood-apple" coincidence.
Śrī Rāma said: "If it is so, then tell me, O Brāhmaṇa, in which direction, in which region, on which mountain, and in which forest does that deer reside?"
What does he do, and how does he, dwelling in a field, chew upon the dūrvā grass? When will that man of mature wisdom remember that noble birth?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That pet deer which was given to you by the lord of Trigarta, residing now in the pet-deer house—that, know you, is Vipaścit.
Śrī Vālmīki said: Having heard this, Rāghava was filled with wonder in that assembly and dispatched numerous boys to bring back the deer.
Then that innocent deer, having been brought in, entered the spacious assembly hall; he was beheld by all the members of the court as one who was both well-nourished and joyful.
Mocking the sky with the drops from his body that were joined with stars, and threatening the beautiful women with showers of blue-lotus-like glances, he moved along.
Respected by the lords of the netherworld, dark with the luster of emeralds, they ran restlessly with the desire for grass, their eyes bewildered with startled glances.
With ears pricked, eyes raised, and necks outstretched, he agitated the members of the assembly with his swift movements, which were momentarily unstable due to their flickering nature.
Beholding that deer, the people—including the king, the sages, and the ministers—remained for a long time overwhelmed with wonder, exclaiming, "Alas, this is infinite illusion!"

With all the people utterly amazed by the tasting of such wonders, gazing at Kṛṣṇa—who was showering a dense rain of blue lotuses upon everyone and was covered in a lattice of jewel-rays—that assembly, as it watched the deer, became like a lotus pond depicted in a painting.
Śrī Vālmīki said: Then Rāma asked this sage, "By what means, O Vipaschit, might there be an end to suffering through the awakening of the primordial Self?"

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For whomsoever by whom [an object] has been brought forth, for that person there is no movement without it; it is neither beautiful, nor does it grant happiness, nor lead to welfare, nor yield good fruit.
Fire is the refuge of the wise; by entering it, this deer regains its former form, just as gold becomes stainless.
"I shall do all this; let it be seen, for I will show it to you. Here before us, this deer is now entering the fire."
Śrī Vālmīki said: Having spoken thus, the sage Vasiṣṭha, whose conduct was most excellent, sipped water from his own water-pot according to the prescribed rule.
He meditated upon fire as being without fuel and consisting of a mass of flames; by that meditation, a web of flames rose up from the midst of the assembly hall.
Devoid of the appearance of embers and separated from fuel, it is clear, crackling, smokeless, and free from soot.
With a most charming and radiant luster, beautiful as a golden temple, having the appearance of a blossoming *kiṃśuka* flower, it rose like a twilight cloud.
Beholding that mass of flames which had driven the assembly far away, the deer, out of his former devotion, rejoiced with his glances.
Beholding that fire and desiring to enter it, his evil deeds exhausted, he quickly drew near from behind, springing forward like a lion leaping a great distance.
In the meantime, having reflected in meditation, that bull among sages spoke, purifying the deer with his glances as he rendered its sins exhausted.
O Lord Agni, remembering your former devotion, out of compassion grant this favor to this wise deer.
While the sage was speaking thus, the deer, having run from afar into the assembly of kings, entered [the king] with impetuous speed like an arrow released from a bow hitting its mark.
Having entered the mass of flames, he was seen with his body clearly visible, like a reflection in a mirror, or like evening clouds come to rest.
Then, even as the members of the assembly were looking on, the deer attained human form, just as a fragment of a cloud assumes a different shape within the belly of a flame in the sky.
Then, within the flame, there appeared a man of invisible form, possessing the luster of gold within, pure in appearance, and beautiful in every limb.
He was like the sun within the orb of the arka-flower, like the moon within the lunar disc, like Varuṇa in the great ocean, or like the moon amidst the clouds of twilight.
In the sockets of his eyes, like reflections in a mirror, in water, or in a gem, the fire of devotion shone with the brilliance of the sun.
Immediately thereafter, like a lamp struck by winds in the midst of an assembly, he vanished somewhere with his mass of flames, like an evening cloud from the sky.
When the walls of the hut had collapsed, a man stood there like a god in a reflection, emerging from the cloth like a dancer appearing on stage.
Wearing a rosary of beads, tranquil, and clad in a golden sacred thread, he was draped in garments as pure as fire, appearing like the moon newly risen.
Because he shone with that attire while the members of the assembly exclaimed, "Aho! Bhā!", he was called Bhāsa, possessing a vast splendor like the sun.
"He shall become known by the name Bhāsa because he appears like a personified form (mūrta)"; thus it was said by some members of the assembly, and for that reason he is called Bhāsa.
Then, having sat down right there, Bhasa remained absorbed in meditation and recalled his entire former history within that body.
While the assembly remained motionless and he himself stood with a smile within, Bhāsa, having seen his own story intact after only a moment, [remained there].
He arrived from his previous births and, awakening from the light of meditation, rose up and surveyed the assembly in due order.
Having arrived, he joyfully prostrated before Vasiṣṭha and exclaimed: "O Brahmin, you who are the life-giving sun of knowledge, salutations be unto you!"
Vasiṣṭha also spoke to him, touching his head with his hand: "O King, may the destruction of your ignorance finally come to pass today."
Then Daśaratha, as Rāma was bowing while crying out "Victory to Rāma!", spoke to him as if smiling, rising slightly from his seat.
Daśaratha said: "Welcome to you, O King; please sit upon this seat. Rest here, weary as you are from wandering through the accumulation of many births."
Śrī Vālmīki said: While Daśaratha was speaking thus, the wise one named Bhāsa entered, bowing before the sages headed by Viśvāmitra as they sat upon their seats.
Daśaratha said: "Alas! For a very long time, the wise man has experienced suffering through ignorance, like a wild elephant bound by its tethering rope."
Alas, what a perilous course results from wrong understanding and false vision! This [ignorance] displays the bewildering spectacle of creation within the very sky.
How many wonders are these worlds within the expansive Self! Long have they been spread out and long have they been scrutinized by the wise one.

Oh, what kind of majesty is this of the self-nature of the void-like essence, this manifestation of the power of the conscious self! For within the very emptiness of the dense sky of the Supreme Self, these various worlds shine forth in such a manner.
Daśaratha said: That the wise man suffers for the sake of the unreal due to ignorance—that I consider a mere exertion; what a painful attachment to that which is not a real object!
Śrī Vālmīki said: At that moment, Viśvāmitra, who was stationed there by the side of the king, spoke these words which arose from the context of the conversation.
O King, for many who have not attained supreme enlightenment, there arise in great numbers many such obstacles to the realization of awakening.
Today, having wandered in this very manner for seventeen hundred thousand years with their resolve unshaken, these seeds of the banyan tree remain situated upon the earth.
Even now, they have set out for the sake of beholding the end of the earth, free from weariness; like the currents of a river, they proceed and do not turn back.
Indeed, this great world is circular and situated in the void; it is like a tree born of the imagination of children, yet it is the certain manifestation of the will of Brahmā.
When the ball is confined within the void, ants wander in all ten directions; in this same way, living beings, which are always supported by that [body], wander perpetually.
The lower portions of the terrestrial globe are its members, and those above it are likewise; at that time, the elements remain there and, having entered them, they revolve.
Having entered that very [space], far beyond the circle of the stars and the rivers, they revolve continuously at great heights, untouched by the moon, sun, and other celestial bodies.
Right here, the sky stands encompassing all directions; the firmament extends above all directions, and beneath it lies the surface of the earth.
The states of being fall and run beneath him, toward all his limbs; that from which they spring forth and go upward is designated as "above."
In a certain region there, O King, were those known as the Vaṭadhānas; among them, three sons of kings were born in former times.
For they, being thus of one mind, having resolved with firm determination to go forth for the sake of wandering—to discover what the end of the visible path beginning with the earth might be—set out.
Again and again, water and earth assailed them as they wandered for a long time; for those who had newly acquired bodies, a vast period of time passed away.
Constantly wandering here according to the analogy of a ball and a swarm of bees, they do not reach the end, yet they perceive their own distinctness.
O King, they remain even now as agitated as ants running after a ball tossed in the air, yet they do not succumb to weariness.
And whatever region of this terrestrial globe they reach, there too, just as here, the directions—upward, downward, and across—are likewise perceived.
They say, "O Great King, since we have not yet reached the end despite our diligent efforts, we shall continue to wander from here."
Thus, this entire display of Brahma’s volition is nothing at all; it is a certain, infinite ignorance consisting of mere volition, like the objects seen in a dream.

Conceptualization is that supreme Brahman, and the supreme Brahman is indeed conceptualization; there is no difference between these two, as they are both of the nature of consciousness, like emptiness and space.

Whatever appears as pure consciousness alone, like the transformations of a flowing stream of water, how could that which is of such a nature appear as something else? For it is impossible for one thing to be another.
Non-existence is the sky, and this sky was the supreme ether at the beginning of creation; it appears as the world by itself, for there is nothing else in dissolution or creation.

Just as it grinds away at the nature of consciousness, so too does it attain delight in that; and through its own cycles of existence, both seen and unseen, it remains for a long time, indeed for a very long time.
The visible nature of form is one and the same for this [reality], and thus it is imperishable; it shines forth as unborn by itself, such that nothing at all appears to shine.
Within the belly of the atom of consciousness reside all atoms of experience; like rocks within the belly of a mountain, they are clear and ethereal within the ethereal Self.
They abide in the state of inherent nature when they remain within the indeterminate self; however, they truly do not abide when they have not yet turned away from the supreme state.
Therefore, those of subtle intellect, through careful reflection on what precedes and follows, have declared that very world to be Brahman, which is pervasive and consists of the nature of light.
This is most wonderful: though not lost from the supreme abode itself, the individual soul suffers by means of the notion of multiplicity, thinking "I am a distinct being."
"Speak, O King Bhāsa, you who are named Vipashcit! How much of the visible world have you seen, how much have you wandered through, and what do you remember?"
Bhāsa said: "I have seen much that is visible; I have wandered much without weariness. Indeed, I remember having experienced many things in many ways."
O King, for a long time and at a great distance, I have experienced vast joys and sorrows through various bodies within infinite worlds, having reached that infinite great space.

O Great-Souled One, by virtue of the power of boons and curses, I have witnessed infinite manifestations with diverse bodies—the revolutions within the whirlpools of successive births—with a mind made firm through the grace of Agni.

For one whose vision is obscured by ignorance, seeking to examine the limits of this earthly body which appears as the self, I formerly exerted constant and intense effort, identifying with body after body throughout the world until the dawn of true memory.

For a thousand years, I was a tree, inward-minded and experiencing the suffering of consciousness; yet, without a mind, amidst the profusion of flowers and fruit, I possessed the vibrant coloring of limbs like a bulbous root.

For a hundred years I was a deer on Mount Meru, golden-hued, with ears like tree leaves; devoted to tasting sprouts of *dūrvā* grass and singing songs, I lived as the lowest among those dwelling in the forest.
With my back encircled by eight legs, having brought about my own death through the distress of the waters when dead, I was a Śarabha for five hundred years in the golden caves of Mount Krauñca.

On the peaks of Malaya and on Mount Mandara, within the bowers of Mandāra, sandalwood, and Kadamba creepers, I have drunk the nectar of the arts of love from Vidyādhara maidens, carried by the breeze entwined with black aloe-wood trees and vines.

For fifteen hundred years, I, the son of the swan of Brahmā, have been drinking the waters on Mount Meru—waters turned tawny by the nectar of golden lotuses—while sporting upon the banks of the mountain stream.

For a hundred years, I have heard the song of the beautiful women of Mādhava, which dispels both sorrow and old age, while their dark tresses of hair were stirred like the fragrant breezes from the forests on the shores of the Ocean of Milk.

On Mount Kālañjara, amidst a forest of *karañja* and *guñjā* trees in full bloom, I took on the form of a jackal. There, an elephant was crushed by a lion, and that elephant was seen by me as I lay dead for the sake of food.

On a certain ridge of the Sahya mountains, which laughs with rows of *saṃtānaka* flowers, there dwelt a celestial nymph with a face like the moon of another world; and then, due to the curse of a *siddha*, I became that solitary woman in a dwelling made of clusters from the wish-fulfilling tree during half of the Kṛta Yuga.

In one place, I spent another hundred years with a fearless mind in the caves of the king of mountains and among the thickets of karavīra creepers; elsewhere, on the distant mountain of Jagatīndra, I dwelt alone and constantly in the form of a bird, like Vālmīka.

Elsewhere, on a mountain ridge, I beheld women hanging from creepers entwined in a grove of shady sandalwood trees; they were like fruits swaying with grace, and though they were carried off by wandering *siddhas*, they were nonetheless enjoyed.

Elsewhere, on the slopes of a mountain in a grove of kadamba trees, my days were spent in the highest state of asceticism; yet within, my mind was afflicted by the cholera of obsession with a single object, and thus I reached my end with a weary intellect that was no longer truly wise.

There exists another [world] filling the entire universe, consisting of all the oceans and the infinite reaches of the quarters, wherein fire, ether, wind, and existence are present, and where the earth consists solely of the forms of beings dwelling in water.
In one place, I beheld a certain woman; within her body, the three worlds appeared as if reflected inside a brilliant mirror, complete with their skies, mountains, and cardinal directions.
"O lady of excellent limbs, when asked by me, 'Who are you? and 'What is this body of yours?', she replied: 'O dear one, I am pure consciousness; these great worlds are my body.'"

Just as I am, so too is this daughter of Smaya; indeed, my friend, all of it is exactly like that, and there is nothing wonderful about it. When others do not see the pure nature because they do not perceive it in this way, my friend, then [it appears otherwise].
By all beings in the world, through the medium of the walls of their own bodies, this sound—which is neither enjoined nor prohibited by the Vedas or Shastras—is heard eternally of its own accord.

The very nature of the existence of things is such that even walls, mountains, and the like speak words to you here, as if in dreams or illusions; therefore, there is nothing inconsistent in this regarding you.
While wandering through this world devoid of women, I saw at one place a being from whom many beings were departing and into whom many beings were entering, all with no other desire.
O you of vast limbs, I have clearly seen single clouds in the sky making a *jhaṇajjhaṇa* sound; they fall on all sides as rain, becoming sharp weapons for men in their fragments.

Elsewhere, as far as the eye can see across the sky, blind people here go toward village houses; they enter there, while here it has become dark for you—yet that very same village was obtained from quite another place.
Apart from the distinctions of humans, gods, and serpents, all beings are equal; they arise from space alone, and at that very time, they do not go to dissolution.
I remember a certain world, uniquely beautiful, devoid of moon, stars, sun, and darkness; a multitude of beings self-luminous, resembling the interior of a flame, and free from day and night.

I remember infinite great worlds containing unprecedented beings such as Daityas, serpents, humans, and gods, with unprecedented trees and cities, and possessing the unique activities of other worlds.

There is no direction that we have not traversed, nor indeed is there any place that we have not seen; there is no task that we have not experienced, and nothing else exists apart from our reflection upon it.

I remember the sound of the armlets on Upendra’s arms, jingling together as they were crushed by the tips of the streams falling from the jeweled peaks of Mount Mandara when it was whirled in the milk-ocean—a sound that made me suspect the thundering of clouds.
Bhāsa said: On Mount Mandara, in a bower of soft Mandāra trees, he took with him an Apsaras named Mandarā, whom he had embraced as she slept, like a blade of grass from a river.
Then, having been questioned by me and comforted, she who was overwhelmed by water, with trembling eyes, said to me, "O girl, what is this?"
Here, at the rising of the moon, these rivers born from the slopes of moonstones rejoice at the arrival of night, like beloved women.
"Surely that was forgotten through the power of being immersed in the flavor of union with you. Having said this, she took me up and flew into the sky like a bird.
On the peak of Śṛṅgavat, upon a golden lotus born from the Gaṅgā, I remained for seven years as a bee; though drenched by it, I was not submerged in mud.
Furthermore, I have seen a world devoid of the circle of stars, filled with people who are self-luminous and belong to a single birth while remaining within the womb of the womb.

Therein there is no division of directions, nor days, nor indeed scriptures, nor Vedic doctrines; nor is there any distinction between Daityas and other gods—such is the world as it is, self-luminous through Me.

On the slopes and thickets of mountain ridges that kissed the clouds—the very realm of the Vidyādharas and the celestial chariots of the gods—I dwelt for seven years as a practitioner of austerity, named Amarasoma, possessing equanimity and a mind of even flavor, on the shore of another sea.

It was surrounded by many clouds that served as bodies for horses with various wind-vehicles as their mounts, and by elephants, deer, lions, trees, creepers, antelopes, mountains, serpents, and birds.

Having ascended from the earth into the sky by means of the supreme power of fire, I moved forward like a garuḍa, desiring to behold from every side the infinite expanse of the world and forcibly dispelling ignorance.
Once, having emerged from the world, I fell into a vast single great ocean; there, white as the sky where I seemed to dwell, I experienced both the stillness and the falling.

When I was exhausted, my sole activity being the experience of falling into the void of space, sleep took hold within me and brought me to rest; then, in that state of deep slumber, I perceived the entire universe within myself as if it were the dream-self manifesting in the waking state.

Furthermore, like a bird upon a creeper, being tossed about by the unceasing force of the wind—the world’s instability as it sways through the quarters of space, the universe, the gods, and Mount Mandara—he has indeed fallen into those various caves of the world.
As long as there was hope for sense objects, I went [to them] in an instant; yet, seeing the visible world again just as before, I went again and again.
Thus, as I leaped across regions—both visible and invisible, accessible and inaccessible—many years passed for me with great speed.
I have not yet reached the end of this ignorance called "the visible," which has taken root in my heart as something false, like a child confronted by a demoness.
Although one remains established in the experience of inquiry, thinking "this is not it, this is not it, it is real," nevertheless, the false view that "this is it" does not cease.
Moment by moment, through pleasures and pains, and through encounters with places and times, they come and go like the restless waters of a river, ever new.

I remember a certain mountain whose peaks were incomparably lofty with *tāla*, *tamāla*, and *bakula* trees, where the wind roared with great force; it was devoid of the sun and other celestial bodies, yet by its own radiance it made manifest the entire universe, including all moving and stationary beings upon its rocky slopes.

That which is delightful for dwelling in solitude, free-willed, singular, immeasurable, and devoid of fear—nowhere among the beautiful worlds have I seen its equal; even the splendor of the king of the gods is not its peer.

Vipaścit said: "Listen, what is so wonderful about this which I have seen elsewhere in another unprecedented world? It is like the state of a great calamity, brought about by force through the blindness of ignorance."

Somewhere in the sky, inaccessible to you, there exists a world with a wondrous creation of blazing light; yet even such a thing is like another city within the sky, as unreal as a dream-city appearing in the mind during the waking state.

While dwelling there, I cast my eye toward the quarters of the sky to seek the object held within my heart; as I looked, I saw the shadow of the mountain upon the earth, darkened by swarms of bees, wandering about.

"What is this? Is it merely a marvel? Before I can even close my eyes, O world, I suddenly beheld a mountain-like, incomparable being in human form falling from the sky with whirling circular motions."

Who might this man be, as heavy as a mountain, a cosmic Virāṭ, whose body falls suddenly like a toppled peak? Even though his form fills the sky and he is within the supreme ether, he does not shine at all, having obscured the splendor of the entire day.

Just as I was thus contemplating such a thing in my heart for a moment, Vivasvān suddenly fell from the sky with a speed that possessed a deep roar like the crashing down of the shell of Brahmā’s egg when it is overturned by the winds at the end of an aeon.
As that being of terrifying nature, whose body is as vast as the ocean, falls, he fills the earth with its seven continents in an instant.
Fearing the destruction of my own self along with the worlds and their continents, I then entered the fire that was inevitably present at my side.
That venerable Jātavedas, who had been worshipped through hundreds of previous births, spoke to me with a body as cool as the moon, saying, "Do not fear."
Victory to you, O God! You are our supreme refuge in every birth; since an untimely end of the aeon has occurred, protect me, O Lord!
When this was said, the Fire replied once more, "Do not fear; arise, come, let us go to my world, O sinless one."
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One placed him upon the back of Śuka, and having burned that being which clung to a portion of his body, he leapt into the sky.
Immediately thereafter, having reached the sky, I beheld that terrifying being of hideous form, who brought about such a calamitous and great portent, inspiring fear.

As he fell with great speed, the earth—along with its oceans, mountains, forests, cities, and vast jungles—trembled; it created streams of water from the two wounds on his thighs and formed deep pits from the gashes in his terrifying body.

The broad earth resounded; the northern quarter resounded, the eastern resounded, and the southern direction resounded loudly. The sky resounded and echoed aloud, as did the entire world with its mountains, terrified by the agitation of universal dissolution.

The broad earth, O King, uttered a roar, its entire quarters threatened by the violent onset of his impetuous speed; even the sky made an insurmountable, resonant din, fierce enough to cause the hosts of Indra’s elephants to flee in terror.

A thunderous roar arose on all sides, terrifying and fearsome, born from the violent splitting of mountain caves; it was a menacing challenge, like the sound of the clouds at the end of an eon, stirred by the fierce and terrible winds of universal destruction.

As it fell with such speed, the earth roared and was pierced a hundredfold by its thundering impact; there, the great slopes of the principal mountain ranges shattered, and the peaks of the Himavat entered the realm of Pātāla.
The fall of that [being], who was like a rock from Mount Meru, caused the shattering of mountain peaks and the tearing asunder of the earth.
The agitating of the masses of water, the casting of mountains onto the surface of the earth, the oppression of all living beings, and the sport of those who seek the dissolution of the world.
The casting down of the sun to the earth, the covering over of the succession of continents, the pulverizing of mountains, and the shattering of the terrestrial mandala.
The sky-dwellers beheld that [city] as if it were a second terrestrial plane, like another half of the cosmic egg, or as if the very sky had fallen down in form.
Then I saw that this mountain of flesh was so vast that not even a single limb of it could fit upon the earth with its seven continents.
Having beheld him, O Lord, I approached the deity who was established in grace; I questioned the blessed Fire-god, saying, "O Master, what is this?"
How did that fleshly Arka fall from heaven along with him? For he could not be contained upon the surface of the earth, with its mountains, forests, and oceans.
Agni said: "Wait for a moment, my son, free from haste; let this fault subside, and then I shall tell you."
Then, even as he was speaking thus, all the sky-dwellers belonging to that web of worlds arrived from every direction through the firmament.
Siddhas, Sādhyas, Apsarases, Daityas, Gandharvas, Uragas, Kinnaras, Ṛṣis, Munis, Yakṣas, Pitṛs, Mātṛs, and immortals.
Then all those sky-dwellers, with their heads and bodies bowed low in devotion, praised the goddess Sarveśvarī, the refuge-seeker, the Night of Time (Kālarātri).

The sky-dwellers said: May that stainless Goddess—who, having bound the vast mass of Kapila’s matted locks to the tip of her skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) of the Lotus-born One, and having fashioned a garland for her breast and a crest-jewel for her head from the severed heads of the foremost Daityas with the feathers of Tārkṣya; she who has consumed the universe and now drinks this world together with its mountains, lands, and oceans; may that Goddess, whose slender body is manifest, protect us who are worthy of protection!
Vipaścit said: "In the meantime, I beheld that man falling from the sky, his entire body paralyzed, appearing in the form of a corpse."
That portion of his body known as the belly was so vast that, resembling a great mountain, it covered even the earth with its seven continents, leaving no space for his mother.
Vahni said: "That infinite [being]—my arm, thigh, and head—has indeed reached the further shore beyond Lokāloka, which lies outside the range of human perception."
Then, while the assembly of sky-dwellers was praising the Goddess with reverence, she emerged from the sky; had she not been withered by herself?
Followed by throngs of pretas and cherished by the circle of Mothers, she makes the sky starry with a multitude of kumbhāṇḍas, yakṣas, and vetālas.
With her veined, long, staff-like arms she made the surface of the sky appear like a forest; with her glances, which scorched the quarters of the horizon, she scattered the suns.
In the hollow of the sky, she made the host of birds fall into a hundred fragments with the clanging *jhaṇajhaṇa* sound produced by her flashing various weapons.
With the limbs of her body rich with the heat of the fire of her physical glow, she radiates splendors extending for ten million yojanas, appearing like a vast forest of tall bamboos.
The quarters of the sky were bathed in milk by the moonlight of her teeth’s luster; she filled the heavens with her body, which was emaciated yet exceedingly tall and broad.
Supportless and without abode, like a vast garland of clouds at twilight, she is mounted upon the seat of the departed spirits, yet firmly established in the supreme state.
Vibrant and blazing in form, the twilight was as red as a rain-cloud, bearing the splendor of the submarine fire within the ocean of the sky.
Scattering garlands, she was restless with corpses and body parts, pestles, spears, lances, clubs, stools, mortars, and plows.
Carrying its offspring through the courtyard of the sky with the swelling roar of clashing stones and the gurgling sounds of pebbles, it was like a mountain torrent in the rainy season.
The gods said: "O Goddess, O Ambikā, this one has been offered as a sacrifice; let him be brought quickly along with his own retinue."
While the host of gods was speaking thus, the goddess proceeded to swiftly extract the essence of blood from that corpse by means of her vital breath.
Drawn in by her breath, that blood entered the mouth of the Goddess like a mass of evening clouds entering the interior of a cave on Mount Meru.
Remaining in the sky, she drank that blood drawn from his life-force until she was satisfied; and having become emaciated, Caṇḍikā now stands there full-bodied.
Then she became one whose body was swollen with blood; red like a line of rain-clouds, her eyes flickering like lightning.
The Blessed Lady has a protruding belly and is adorned with venomous serpents; she is intoxicated by the wine of blood and bears all manner of weapons.
She began to dance in the sky, which was half-filled by her own body, while being watched by the gods stationed upon the peaks of the surrounding ranges of mountains.
Then great hosts of Piśācas, Kumbhāṇḍas, Rūpikas, and others obstructed the corpse, just as clouds block a massive mountain.
That mountain of corpses was seized by the Kumbhāṇḍas at its waist, by the multitudes of Rūpikās from its belly, and by the Yakṣas who had been wounded by elephants.
Since his other limbs, such as the arms, thighs, and neck, have reached the furthest limit of the cosmic egg, they are exceedingly vast in extent.
Then those hosts of spirits, though stationed at a distance in the far reaches of the quarters, were not actually able to reach that place, for they were themselves overcome by time right there.
While Caṇḍikā was dancing in the sky amidst a host of spirits crowded with corpses, and while the gods remained upon the mountains, the world then became [as follows].
The mass of quarters was enveloped in a foul stench from the heaps of gathered corpses, while the sky blazed with fires of *khadira* wood amidst the outpourings of clouds with crimson interiors.

It resounded with the "sha-va, sha-va" cries of corpses rising up in the frenzy of chewing flesh, and it echoed with the loud "kaṭa-kaṭa" noise of large bones snapping as they were crushed by creepers.
It possessed a terrifying sound caused by the clashing and separating of the masses of living beings, and it was covered with mountains of bones as large as the Himalayas and Vindhya ranges.
The surface of the earth was smeared with flesh cooked by the flames of fire from the Goddess’s mouth, while the masses of quarters were turned vermilion by the mist of sprays of blood.
The gods, acting as spectators from all sides, beheld the quarters of the horizon enclosed by ramparts, while the earth with its seven continents had become a single ocean of blood.
The entire circle of mountains had completely vanished from sight, and the women of the quarters were clothed in garments of masses of clouds with a crimson luster.

The surface of the sky was covered by weapons whirled by arms that moved with circular grace, while the circles of cities and towns were reduced to a state where they could only be reached by the path of distant memory.
It consists of all things, both stationary and moving, whose forms are absolutely impossible [to conceive], and it is a single convergence of infinite kumbhāṇḍas, rūpikas, and other beings.
With the nets of the movements of his bird-like hands in the dance, he was as if fashioning another world by the measuring lines of the Creator.

With intestines as threads, the piśācas, having reached the earth from the sun, seemed to be measuring the world—horizontally, upwards, and downwards—with the bowers of the quarters as their measuring lines.
Having beheld the world thus submerged by the flood of calamities that had arisen, and having seen the former surface of the earth turned into an ocean of blood;
On the summit of the Lokāloka mountain at the edge of the seven continents, the gods remained, deeply distressed, in a place not yet reached by his limbs.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmā, since your limbs have extended even beyond the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), why then has the Lokāloka mountain not been obstructed by them?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, within this [universe] consisting of seven continents, its belly is situated; its head, hooves, arms, and other limbs are situated beyond the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
From his two sides, from the middle of his thighs, from both sides of his waist, and from the middle of his head and both shoulders, that Lokāloka mountain is perceived.
Seated there upon the mountain peaks, those gods appear like clouds filled with water, their exceedingly pure splendors radiant from the heat.
With its limbs outstretched and its face turned downward, that fallen corpse is devoured by a multitude of spirits while the Mothers dance around it.
As streams of blood flowed and the stench of fat intensified, the gods, each individually distressed, reflected as follows:
Alas, what misery! Where has the earth gone? Where have the masses of water gone? Where have the multitudes of people gone? Where have the mountains gone?
Alas, where has Malaya gone—that pavilion adorned with groves of sandalwood, mandāraka, and kadamba trees, and filled with heaps of flowers?
Even those vast, lofty, and pure regions of the Himalayas were quickly reduced to a state of self-mire by the blood, as if out of a wrathful passion for their whiteness.
Even that great wish-fulfilling tree which stood upon the surface of Krauñca Island in Krauñcadvīpa—its branches reaching as far as the world of Brahmā—has been reduced to dust.

Alas, O Ocean of Milk, Lord of the Pārijāta tree, the lotus, the moon, and the nectar! Alas, O Ocean of Curds, whose coastal forests sprang from the peaks of butter! Alas, O Ocean of Honey, you who possess coconut mountains and are served by the masters of yoga—where will you now come together? And where has that woman gone, who served as a mirror for the directions?

Alas, Puṣkaradvīpa! Where have you gone—O home of the gods and noble men, skilled in the dalliances of Vidyādharīs resting in the caves of the Kadamba forests; O you whose network of directions is densely filled with lotus-pools for the swans of Brahmā in Krauñcadvīpa, which is as firm as a mountain with joints seamlessly joined by the golden, stainless creepers of the wish-fulfilling trees?

Merely by remembering the forests of Svādūda where the heat is fierce yet the flowers are pure and the earth is holy; the caves beautiful with *gomedha* stones, islands of wish-fulfilling trees, and golden creepers; and the white mountains of Śākadvīpa adorned with groves of celestial trees—merit arises for new men, bestowing the bliss of the realm of the gods.

Alas, I know not how the people will find consolation when all those forests—whose every quarter was illuminated by the expanse of young creepers and sprouts swaying in the gentle breeze—are now utterly destroyed.
When indeed shall we see again those groves on the shores of the sugarcane-ocean and upon the grounds of Mount Khaṇḍa, as well as the jaggery-sweets and the sugar-candies for children?

When indeed shall we behold the dance of those beautiful women with sandalwood-paste in the golden palaces on the mountain of groves of *tālī* and *tamāla* trees, which are cooled by *kadamba* and wish-fulfilling trees?

Alas, even those fruits from the very top of the Jambu tree have passed into the realm of memory—those fruits whose juices the river Jambumatī carries, she who girdles the earth with its islands and oceans.

Remembering again and again the shore of the celestial ocean, where the songs and dances of intoxicated celestial women resound within the hollows of dense sandalwood trees and mountain caves, my heart tears asunder like the earth once did for the primordial lotus.

Behold, upon the surface of the ocean of blood, the peaks of hundreds of golden mountains shine with light; reddened by the twilight of the lands of sunrise and sunset, they appear like the buds of the newly risen moon in the faces of the quarters.

Alas, I know not where the earth has gone—she who was encircled by such vast masses of ocean waters, adorned with the intervals between continents, a landmass featuring blue lotuses in the form of clouds resting upon lofty mountain peaks, and whose garment was the rivers, deserts, forests, formidable cities, villages, and royal endowments, and which now possesses only the sprouts and shoots of trees.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the corpse had been reduced to a mere remnant by the intoxicated host of spirits, the gods, together with Indra, spoke these words once more from the mountain in all directions.

Even in the regions of the celestial chariots where the Vidyādharas and gods dwell, the spirits have spread out vast nets of fat to provide cooling relief; these resemble fragments of pure clouds driven by the wind, filling the sky.
Behold how, throughout all seven continents, the waters of fat have been spread abroad by living beings; meat has been eaten and blood has been drunk—now look at the earth as it is.
Alas, the earth now stands with all her limbs enveloped in layers of fat; the forests appear as if covered with blankets by the masses of autumn clouds composed of fat.
These five bones of his have become great mountains, standing as if they were the peaks of the Himalayas, covering the very horizons.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: While the gods were speaking thus, that host of beings, having turned this earth into a ground of fat, danced wildly in the sky in a state of intoxication.
While the hosts of spirits were dancing, the remaining blood from the earth was cast by the gods into the ocean in a single stream.
The gods formed the resolve that this very ocean should be wine; from that time until today, it has remained a sea of liquor.
The beings, having performed a dance in the sky, drink that wine; then they dance again in the sky within the temple of bliss.
Even today, spirits drink from the ocean of wine as if it were those very same waters, and they dance in the sky together with hosts of yoginīs.
Then, those networks of fat belonging to those beings, having spread out upon the earth and dried up, remained there; from this, the earth became known as Medinī.

Thus, when the corpse had gradually attained peace and the succession of day and night began once more, the Lord of Creatures then created new subjects; and so, that creation here became as it was before.
Bhāsa said: Then, O lord of the earth, while stationed at the corner of the parrot’s wing, I asked that great god Pāvaka this: "Please listen."
O Blessed One, Lord of all sacrifices, Master of Svāhā, Consumer of Oblations! What is this that has occurred? Tell me, what is this corpse?
Vahni said: "Listen, O King; I shall describe to you in its entirety and exactly as it happened, the indestructible account of the infinite corpses that illuminated the three worlds."
There exists the infinite, formless, supreme ether consisting of consciousness, wherein these countless worlds are but atoms.
In that all-pervading, omnipresent sky of pure consciousness alone, there arose spontaneously within the Self of all a consciousness consisting of the act of self-awareness.

Under the influence of her sensation, she perceived those [atoms] as being composed of the ultimate particles of fire, just as you, O traveler, perceive a state of being a guest in a dream due to the nature of the object you have contemplated.
Because it lacks consciousness, the atom did not perceive its own atomicity—[a state] which is radiant, like the pollen of a lotus, and consists of mere conceptualization.
Cultivating a state of emaciation, she once again became herself; she spontaneously experienced the sense organs, such as the eyes, within her own body.
And the Eye of the World saw at its forefront the primordial source, which by its very nature consists of the elements like a container and its contents, resembling a city in a dream.
There was a living being there named Asura who was indeed conceited; his very nature was a manifestation of untruth, and he was the father, mother, and grandfather [of that state].
When, due to his arrogance, he trampled the hermitage of a certain great sage—a vessel of peace—there.
The sage pronounced a curse upon him: "Since you have destroyed my hermitage because of its great size, die and become a wretched gnat!"
Then, at that very moment, the fire of his curse reduced the asura to ashes, just as the Aurva fire consumes the waters.
Formless, supportless, and like the circle of space, the mind—though essentially consciousness—existed as something almost non-objective and radiant.
That consciousness attained oneness with the elemental ether due to their similarity; then, through its substrate, it attained oneness with the wind as well.
He was the conscious self of the wind, becoming the one named Prāṇa for living beings; he was pervaded by passion (rajas), water (payas), fire (tejas), ether (nabhas), and the subtle atom (aṇu).
Consisting of the five subtle elements, that minute atom—a mere fragment of pure consciousness—attained vibration by its own nature, like a particle of wind in the sky.
Then that consciousness, situated within the vital air, became awakened, just as a seed on the earth produces a sprout through the action of time, wind, and water.
His consciousness, having become aware of its own pure state as a curse within, and having perceived its limbs as those of a gnat, became a gnat upon realizing it was a gnat.
The lifespan of that mosquito here on earth, which is born from sweat, possesses a tiny body, and whose form is struck down by its own breath, consists of only two days.
Śrī Rāma said: O Lord, for all living beings here, does their origin arise solely from another womb, or can it be otherwise?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The origin of all beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is twofold; one is composed of Brahman, while the other is born of delusion. Listen to these two.

The origin of the elements is said to arise from the coloring of the subtle elements (tanmātras) by the previously established delusion of the world; thus, the birth of beings is born of delusion and connected to the visible.
When the delusion of the world has ceased, he who exists as the very nature of reality, becoming himself, is declared to be composed of Brahman; his manifestation is not born from a womb.
This being the case, O Rāma, listen to the sequence of that mosquito's actions: it arose from the power of worldly delusion, not from Brahman.
Humming amidst clusters of wild rice, sugarcane, young grass, and thickets, he spent half his life for a single day, wandering about as he enjoyed everything.
He himself began for a long time the sport of swinging upon the swing of the center of the grassy meadow with that female mosquito as his companion, like a child at play.
While he was resting somewhere there, exhausted from the journey on the swing, he was crushed by the falling of a mountain brought down by the front hooves of a deer.
Because she had surrendered her life upon seeing the face of Hari, he, having taken up his senses according to their previous sequence, was thereafter born as a deer.
While dwelling in the forest, a deer was struck by a hunter with a bow; because his gaze fell upon the face of the hunter, he was reborn as that very hunter.
While wandering through the forests as a hunter, he arrived at the grove of sages; having rested there, he was awakened by a sage through their conversation.
Why do you, deluded, kill deer with your bow for such long-lasting suffering? Why do you not protect the fragile world order?

Life is as fragile as water hanging from a mass of clouds scattered by the wind; enjoyments are as flickering as lightning flashing amidst a canopy of clouds; the caresses of youth are as unstable as the current of a river; and the body perishes in an instant. O son, becoming terrified of the power of saṃsāra, seek nirvāṇa.
The hunter said: "If it is so, O sage, tell me: what kind of conduct toward the destruction of suffering would be neither harsh nor mild?"
The sage said: "Having now completely cast aside your bow along with your arrows, and having adopted the practice of silence, you should dwell here with your suffering stilled."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having been thus enlightened by him, he cast aside his bow and arrows and remained right there, adopting the conduct of a sage and subsisting on food obtained without asking.
Then, remaining silent, he entered into the discernment of the scriptures with his mind, just as a flower enters the heart of a person through its fragrance in a few days.
Once, O subduer of enemies, he questioned that tiger among sages: "O Blessed One, how is it that a dream is perceived as existing both internally and externally?"
The sage said: "O virtuous one, even in my own mind, when I was a man of discernment, this very same doubt arose long ago from some unknown source, like a cloud in the sky."
Then, desiring to behold this, I practiced concentration and remained firm within that consciousness, having assumed the lotus posture.
Staying there, I drew back my mind, which had been cast far away, by means of that very [thought], just as the sun draws back its heat at evening by means of its own radiance.
Then, by means of the vibration of sensation, the vital breath accompanied by the mind was emitted by me from the body into the external world, like fragrance from a flower.

That vital breath (prāṇa-pavana), which was enveloped by my mind situated in the void, was directed by me into the breath of the living being standing before me, who was positioned at the tip of my own mouth.

The vital breath, enveloped by the power of life-force, was led into the interior of the heart by that [consciousness], like one's own serpent, driven by its own nature, being tormented by a young elephant.
Then, by means of the horse of my vital breath, I entered his heart; situated in that narrow space, I followed those two within with my own intelligence.
It was surrounded on all sides by many channels flowing with the juices of autumn, like the entire outer region [of a city] with its large and small canals.
The dwelling place of the living being is crowded with the cage of ribs, the spleen, the liver, blood, and other such lumps, like a house filled with household utensils and furnishings.
It was covered with all its members hissing and hot, like an ocean filled with networks of waves scorched by the heat of the summer season.
A new and ever-fresh coolness, consisting of consciousness, issues from the tip of the nose; for the sake of life, the mind is incessantly and perpetually carried forth by the vital wind.
It is slippery with the flow of blood, pus, phlegm, and fat; thick with darkness, hot, and crowded like a hell.

Through the clear or unclear indications of the winds associated with the phases of rising and falling, and due to the irregularities in the durations of stability and decline, [the breath] indicates future ailments.
It resounded with the wind blowing through the crevices of the mountain caves, while the submarine fire blazed within the conduits of the lotus-stalk channels.
It was densely packed with objects meeting one another, white and clear, and accompanied by winds; in some places it was calm, and in others agitated, like a city at night beset by thieves.
It was surrounded by winds moving through other channels and paths of the sky-dwellers, uttering songs in half-and-half measures of the vowel *ā*.
Then I entered the heart of that creature, which was filled with internal distress, just as a superior man enters a dense crowd of men crowded together limb to limb.
Immediately thereafter, I attained the element of fire within my heart, which, though situated at a distance, was perceived with effort like the moon or the sun's light in the night.
Since it is the mirror of the three worlds and the lamp for all things in the triple universe, the life-force (jīva) abides therein as the existence of all entities.
The life-force pervades the body just as fragrance resides in a flower; likewise, vitality is present within the filaments, and coolness exists in the mouth even when the sun shines.
I have entered unobserved into that *ojas* which is the support of the life-force (*jīva*), protected on all sides by the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) like a covering.
Then I entered directly, like fragrance entering the wind, as the hot-rayed sun enters the moon, or as water enters an earthen vessel.
Resembling the rays of a second moon, as delicate as a fragment of white cloud, like fresh butter or molasses, and beautiful as a bubble of milk.
Standing there, having abandoned the agitation of entering, I beheld the entire universe as if dwelling within my own vital energy, like a dream.
Together with the sun, the mountains, the oceans, the gods, asuras, and humans; together with the expanse of cities and forests, and including the intermediate worlds and the quarters of space.

[He beheld] the ocean of the seven islands and seas, together with the sequence of time and its instruments, along with all the kalpas, kṣaṇas, and seasons, and including all things mobile and immobile.
That vision of the dream remained fixed and steady there; indeed, I continued to dwell within it even at the end of sleep, because sleep had not yet truly arrived.
"O hunter, while reflecting on this—'Am I seeing a dream even though I am not asleep?'—I, having become awakened, understood this."
Is it not indeed the very nature of this element of consciousness that it designates itself as the Lord, whose own essence is the sky-like nature of what is called the world?
Wherever the element of consciousness resides, there it perceives its own form as the world, yet without ever abandoning its very nature as space.
Aha! Today this has been understood: that this world which is thus perceived is called a dream, being nothing more than the manifestation of one's own consciousness.
That which is the self-manifestation of the element of consciousness is called "dream" in some respects and "waking" in others; yet waking and dreaming are not two distinct things.
Dream is a dream within waking; yet in that dream, there is waking. Dream is indeed waking itself; thus waking alone exists in a twofold manner.
O one of great intelligence, since the person is indeed consciousness, how, whose, and when did he die, even though hundreds of bodies have perished?
That consciousness exists as space itself, manifesting like a body; it is infinite, undivided in nature, and consists of both resistance and non-resistance.

The world is known as the marrow of that which is of the nature of non-obstruction, whose self is eternally and infinitely arisen, and which is called consciousness (cit), even though it is as subtle as an atom.
Within the belly of the sky of consciousness, all atoms of experience shine forth, just as the various atoms of the parts appear within a whole.

Withdrawn from the external world, the individual soul (jīva) abides in the heart, the seat of the living principle; it perceives its own form as this creation of a dream through the radiance of consciousness.
This individual soul perceives its own form, which is directed outward and manifested externally as the waking state; yet when that same form remains within, it is called the dream state.
Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions—the individual soul has spread forth and remains as a single essence both within and without.

Just as the sun, though situated within its own orb, remains here as well by means of its radiance, so too the individual soul (jīva), taking the form of the universe, is established both outside and inside.
If one knows, "I alone am both the internal dream and the external waking state," as the conscious self (cidātman) in its true nature, then, free from latent impressions (vāsana), one is liberated.
This living self (jīva) is indestructible and cannot be burned; yet one who speaks otherwise is surely deluded by the yakṣa of dualistic conceptualization, just like a child.

The individual soul (jīva) remains inward-turned when it perceives the inner self, and outward-turned when it perceives the external world; thus it exists in the forms of both dream and waking within its own interior.
As I was reflecting thus, the thought occurred to me, "What would deep sleep be like? Consequently, I set out to investigate the state of deep sleep.

As long as one remains silent for a long time within the state where seeing and the seen have ceased, there arises the realization "I am mindless"; this tranquility is nothing other than the state beyond deep sleep.
Just as the nails, hair, and so forth in this body are both known and unknown, so too, within the conscious Self, there is neither the insentient nor the sentient during deep sleep.
"Am I weary from exertion? "The mind has resorted to peace. Because of this single transformation, there is no other state than deep sleep.
This thick sleep occurs naturally even while one is awake; "I am not thinking of anything," "I am at peace"—thus it takes on a single, uniform form during practice.
When this state reaches density, it is then released; that which is subtle is called by the word "sleep," while [the other] is described by its own name.
Having determined that this was deep sleep, I set out to seek the fourth state; I became intent on performing that search, engaged with the highest intelligence.
Just as there is no light apart from pure illumination, so too, not even the slightest form of the fourth state (turīya) can be found except through perfect awakening.
This universe, as it exists, dissolves through perfect awakening; yet, as it exists, it remains so, and nothing whatsoever is dissolved.
Therefore, dream, waking, and deep sleep exist within the fourth state; this world exists exactly as it appears, yet truly nothing at all exists.

The world has arisen from a cause; Brahman does not exist in this manner as the world. That which is peaceful in its nature as the world, unborn, and pure awareness—this alone is the state of the Fourth (turyatā).

Due to the impossibility of the causes for its arising, nothing called "creation" is ever born; for the consciousness of creation is grasped by the Intellect itself, just as fluidity is inherent in water.
The ascetic said: "Having thus reflected that I must go, I then set out toward that unity of consciousness, just as a fragrance moves toward another fragrance through the excellence of its lotus."
As long as that consciousness of his does not abandon the element of *tamas* and *ojas*, it proceeds toward external perception through the cognition of all the sense organs.
Grasping consciousness with consciousness, both externally and internally, in an instant I spread forth there like a drop of oil upon water.
Then, while I was thus transforming within that consciousness, I beheld the entire world existing exactly doubled in size.
The quarters of the sky became doubled as both suns blazed; two terrestrial spheres were produced and two heavens arose.
Just as two reflections of a face appearing in a mirror seem to be mixed together, so do the world and consciousness appear as one.
Just as oil appears within two sesame seeds contained in a vessel, so does that dual world appear, intermingled, within that very reality.
Residing within the sheath of dual consciousness, though mixed, those two worlds appear as unmixed, just like milk and water.
Then, by a mere glance in an instant, she—consisting of that consciousness—was led entirely to the state of being his own self, as if measured by that very consciousness.
She was like one season following another, like a small river merging into a great river, like a streak of fragrance carried by the wind, or like a trail of smoke from a cloud.
Through the rapid realization of oneness, the world attained unity for me, just as the moon, which appears double due to faulty vision, becomes one through clear sight.
Then, as I remained within that consciousness, not abandoning my own state of discernment, my own volition diminished and came to abide in that [divine] volition.
Then, observing the external world solely through that mental activity, he performed his daily routine without ever abandoning those respective states of mind.
Then, by chance, he gradually became overcome by sleep, like a lotus that has drunk its fill of water and eaten its food at evening, becoming weary.
He withdrew his mind that had spread through the forest thickets of the quarters, performing the activity of perceiving forms, just as the sun at evening withdraws its radiance.
Together with his mind, all the functions of his sense organs entered the cavity of his heart, withdrawn like the limbs of a tortoise.
Sealed within the form of the heart, those [faculties] such as the eye existed like clods of earth—mere dead matter, as if depicted in a painting.
By that very movement of his mind, I suddenly rose up and remained there; because of my conformity with his mind, I entered into each of those hearts.
Having withdrawn external perception into that inner vitality, I experienced for a moment a void state of deep sleep upon the softness of my bed.
Due to an abundance of fatigue, food, and drink, even though the channels are congested, the wind either does not exit at all or moves only through those that are hollow.
Whenever one is solely intent upon the Self that is identical with that [Reality], one renders this mind—which by its very nature seeks its own objects—subordinate, as it abides within the heart.
Today, for him, there is only his own self-interest; no one else's task shines within him, because this very body exists solely for the sake of its own purpose.
Śrī Rāma said: O great sage, does the mind think only by the power of the vital breath? Does the mind have no nature of its own, and therefore is it merely that [breath]?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Even this body, though experienced by oneself as one's own, does not exist here at all; this form is merely a product of the mind's imagination, like a mountain in a dream.

That mind also does not exist at all, because it is joined with the absence of the object of cognition; because there is no cause at the beginning of creation; and because there is no cause for the non-arising of the visible world.
Therefore, when all this is Brahman and that [Brahman] is the self of all, then this entire universe exists everywhere just as it is, like the sky itself.

For those who know that [Reality], there is indeed the mind and so forth, as well as the body and so forth, yet it is Brahman alone; however, such a state belongs to those who know it, and not within the sphere of our experience.
Just as this triple world is Brahman, and just as it consists of various natures, so too, O Prince, hear now this sequence being described here.

There exists pure consciousness alone, stainless and of the nature of infinite space, which is at all times the self of all forms; it is neither the world nor the state of being an object of perception.
But because of its omniscience, that [consciousness] has by itself perceived this state of mind—pure, awakened, free from mental afflictions, and not abandoning its own nature.
O best among those who know what is to be known, understand that this very vital breath (prāṇapavana) is indeed that refuge for the self which was conceived by the mind.
Just as this vital breath is experienced by one as if it were fashioned by that [Self], so too are the senses, the body, and the like, as well as the measurement of space and time.
Thus, this entire universe is the indivisible, all-pervading mind alone; and the mind, in turn, is the supreme Brahman which is Consciousness. Therefore, this whole expanse is Brahman.
Formless, without beginning or end, without appearance, and without affliction—this very world-body is Brahman alone: peaceful, pure consciousness, and pure existence.
The Supreme Brahman, possessing all powers, exists through the power of the mind; wherever it may be, it fully experiences its own form in that very way.
The mind, whose essence is volition, is Brahman; whatever it wills in whatever manner, it experiences exactly in that way. This is established as true even for children.

Indeed, this very Self, by its own mind, has been made into a living being; it has been made into a body and even made into the three worlds—not as something primordial. It has been made into a body and even made into the sky or into mountains; this has been experienced in dreams within cities imagined [by the mind].
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The mind alone is the creator of the world; in whatever manner it conceives, whether as non-existent, existent, or both existent and non-existent, so does it remain for it.
By him the vital breath was conceived as "the vital breath is my refuge," and thus, without it, he does not exist; therefore, each of those [faculties] has that as its ultimate resort.
"Surely I shall not exist for some time after being deprived of life; yet surely I shall exist again"—thus was it conceived.
Wherever that [mind] is with the body, there this mind, together with the vital breath, quickly beholds the body arisen in an instant like an expansive city of illusion.
"I shall not exist again, deprived of life and body"—when consciousness possesses such a firm conviction, it does not arise once more.
Swinging back and forth due to doubt, one dwells in suffering with an unstable resolve; this state of his will not pass away through mere conceptualization or slight knowledge.
For one who possesses the notion "this is mine" or "I am this," that [notion] does not subside, except by means of the cognition of no-self (anātman) for some reason whatsoever.
Knowledge does not manifest anywhere other than through inquiry into the means to liberation; therefore, one should diligently investigate the means to liberation.
Indeed, this notion of "I" and "this" does not exist as ignorance anywhere; apart from the means to liberation, it cannot be removed by anything else.
Thus, whatever has been practiced and perceived by the mind remains exactly so; therefore, because my life is my vital breaths, my mind is established in the vital breaths.

When the vital breath (prāṇa) is established peacefully within the body, the mind becomes possessed of its proper faculty of reflection; when the breath is agitated, seeing the agitation inherent in the breath, one perceives nothing else.

When the vital breath (prāṇa) becomes intensely preoccupied with the vibration of its own activity, then the breath, being occupied with that which it seeks, will not exert itself for the sake of the Self.
For these two, breath and mind, are like a chariot and its driver; indeed, who would not follow such a pair of chariot and driver when they are in mutual accord?
Thus, at the beginning of creation, his own self was perceived by the Supreme Self; therefore, even to this day, this law of necessity does not cease for the ignorant.
Through place, time, action, and substance, the mind, vital breath, and embodied beings—though not yet firmly rooted in the supreme state—attain it within their bodies once they have reached it.

When one's own vital breath and mind remain in equilibrium, they perform action; when they are in disequilibrium, one action becomes discordant. When [the mind] is stilled, that state of peace is deep sleep.
When the insentient vital breath (prāṇa), having become concentrated somewhere within the channels obstructed by food and other substances, remains in a state of quiescence, then deep sleep arises.
When the channels are filled with food or likewise exhausted by fatigue, the vital breath remains motionless; then, the state of deep sleep arises.

Due to the softness or fullness of the channels within the cavity of the wound, when the vital breath (prāṇa) remains or dissolves somewhere therein, they become motionless; that is the state of deep sleep (suṣuptatā).
The ascetic said: Then, he into whose heart I had entered became, during the night, deeply immersed in a dense, dreamless sleep, fully satiated by his meal.
Together with him, having attained oneness with his mind, I experienced a profound and dense state of deep sleep, becoming as if a subordinate part of it.
Then, when the internal channel-path of this blind man had become clear and established, and the natural vital breath (prāṇa) began to vibrate, his deep sleep grew thin.
When deep sleep had become attenuated, I beheld right here a world containing the sun and other luminaries, as if it had emerged from my own heart.
And that [ocean], being filled by the great waters rising from the agitated sea, was like one filled by the clouds of the kalpa, which had been released and possessed waves scraping the very heavens.
It was swept away by a mountain-flood roaring with great eddies, which, filled with rows of forests and thickets of grass, uprooted elephants as it flowed along.
Even before the three worlds had been utterly consumed, they were completely filled on all sides with vast fragments consisting of cities, mountains, and the earth.
I saw it right there, in a certain dwelling, in a certain city, in a certain cave, where I had remained with my wife.
Together with my wife, my servants, my sons, and my kinsmen, along with my goods, utensils, and house, I was swept away by the waters.
That house and that city were being swept away by the waters of destruction, overwhelmed by trees taking the form of waves, and filled with floods of water.
It was like the ocean rising up to conquer a great clamor of tumultuous noise; its inhabitants were utterly agitated, and it showed no regard for its young.
It was crowded and agitated by movements rich with the tossing of whirlpools, and terrifying with the mire of people crying out and beating their breasts.

With walls crumbling and wooden beams snapping with a rattling sound, the house was filled with a terrifying clamor; the roofs were falling down, and the faces of the women remained visible through the windows and the lattice-work.
Thus, while I was watching for a moment, I fell into that same state; meanwhile, that entire house began to weep, its soul distressed.
Divided into four parts by the breach of the wall, the army—consisting of the old, the young, and women—went in a hundred directions like a mountain torrent over a rocky ledge.
Then I was being carried away in the waters of the dissolution, having abandoned all concern for wife and kin, my mind intent solely on preserving my life.
Cast by the mass of waves from one league to a multitude of leagues, he was shattered as the tips of trees being carried along were obscured by the intervening flames.
Struck by the harsh friction against wood, walls, banks, and seats, he went down to the depths of the underworld, dancing in whirlpools, and after a long time, he rose up again.
In the water with its many waves, where there is a gurgling roar from the surging ebb and flow of shifting currents, he sinks and rises again and again.
For a moment, he was submerged in water made turbid by the clashing of the lords of mountains, like an elephant sunk in a puddle; then he was drawn out by the pure waters.
Just as I was quickly recovering my breath upon the foam-peak of the mountain, I was suddenly struck by the rushing water as if by an enemy.
At that time, amidst the mass of water with its various tossing waves, there was no suffering of a miserable nature that I did not experience.
In the meantime, O one with eyes like a blue lotus, because of his long-standing practice throughout his life and because of his despondency, his consciousness remained there.
I recalled my former form, consisting of meditative absorption: "Alas! While the world has taken on another form, I remain here as an ascetic."
"I have entered here with the desire to see the dream-vision of another; thus, in this dream, I perceive this delusion."

Although I am being carried away by the waves within this self—which consists of false knowledge and is characterized by firm habitual tendencies toward the present—I remain happy because of that [Self].
Or rather, I saw this as water, with the mountains, cities, villages, tracts of earth, and trees being swept away by the surging of the ocean at the time of universal dissolution.
The women of the serpent-king, men, and sky-dwellers were being swept away, as were the cities and abodes of the world-protectors, along with their great undertakings.
Then, repeatedly beholding the destruction of the world—where the waves of water mixed with mountains clashed against those very mountains—I reflected upon what follows immediately after such an end.
It is strange that even this three-eyed one is being carried away like withered straw upon the ocean; alas, for cursed fate, there is indeed nothing that cannot be done!
By breaking through the four walls, I have revealed my inner intent; the rays of the sun display houses within the water like lotuses.

Wondrously, within the undulations of the waves, the ladies of the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, humans, gods, and Nagas shine forth; like lotus ponds filled with bees, these entire moving beings appear as if they were garlands of bees amidst their many wanderings.

The wall-sections of the great mansions of gods, asuras, and nagas—possessing the splendor of lattice-windows made of jewel-nets that form the boundary of moonstone enclosures entwined by the vine-like arms of vidyadhara women—wander amidst the mass of waters like a multitude of golden ships.

Here, Indra—exhausted by the fatigue of love-making, clinging as if out of pleasure to Śacī’s breasts, which are as expansive as the frontal globes of a rutting elephant and marked with saffron—moves back and forth on the swings of the waves while remaining within his palace of shimmering jewels.

Alas! The winds blow, swirling through the sky and scattering heaps of blossoms shaken from the stars; they seem to carry with them the jewels from the falling celestial mansions, as if they had entered the hollows of the garden groves along with the sacrificial grain.

This lotus of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), which is fixed upon its pericarp and centered in meditation, remains in the sky with its petals closed; it is like a golden stone produced by a machine, its form appearing as water tossed upward by the crests of terrifying waves from the agitated ocean of the mountains.

Like clouds terrifying with their exceedingly thick and rumbling roar, these masses of waves—lightnings over the city of gold—wander through the sky, possessing bodies equal to elephants, horses, lions, serpents, trees, mountains, forests, and the surface of the earth.
Being carried away by the waves that possess the luster of flax flowers, even this Yama is led away as if by Yama himself in the form of a flood of water.

All these world-protectors, along with the nāgas, mountains, and cities numbering in the hundreds of thousands, perceive this in the water; their cities are clearly marked by the gurgling sounds of the vast masses of water swirling within the cavernous womb of the ocean, the source of prosperity.

When the netherworld, the earth, the vault of heaven, and the quarters of the sky were filled by the surging of irresistible waters, the multitudes of Indra, Yama, Yakṣas, gods, and asuras wandered about like fish, together with their villages, cities, celestial chariots, and mountains.
As Kṛṣṇa was being carried away, his very body, taking the form of water, became a source of suffering by turning into a bond, like the mother's own shanks becoming a tether for her calf.
Ah! As the gods and demons grapple with one another, the tumultuous roar of "buḍabuḍa" is heard, mingled with the joyful shouts of their respective women.

In all directions, where the sky is enveloped by masses of water agitated by the swift force of the best of cities filled with clamor, and which appear as if thick with a wandering web of clouds, this solid wall-structure composed of water is clearly perceived.

Alas, what a tragedy! Swiftly carried downward by the waters through the churning revolutions of the whirlpools, Kubera, Yama, Nārada, Vāsava, and the others are now losing their lives, distressed by the masses of water and mist.

The wise, having abandoned pride, carry this body here—though it is being swept along as if it were a corpse—only because it is utterly tranquil and inert; for they see it as being violently pounded by the clashing waters of the fragmented cities of Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu.

A multitude of women comes here, half-crushed; alas, what other wretched person is capable of saving them? For this mass of people, being chewed by the teeth of the Ender (Death), is not able to save one another.
Vast masses of water flow along, surging over mountains and winding through valleys; like boats upon them, the cities of the gods, having raised their bodies upward, quickly descend below.

The three worlds—filled with continents, lords of mountains, gods, asuras, serpents, and humans, along with nāgas, apsarases, and cāraṇas, appearing like lotuses whose roots have been severed by the waters of the ocean—now stand as a single sea-lake. Uprooted by Time, alas! Where have you gone, O gods, leaders of the world, who possessed such great supernatural power and majesty?
The hunter said: "O Blessed One, how did you come to such various states? And why, through the practice of meditation, did you not then attain peace?"
The Sage said: At the ends of the kalpas, the worlds—which are of the nature of illusion—perish through various forms of destruction, like appearances in the sky that exist only as manifestations.
Sometimes destruction occurs gradually at the end of a kalpa; sometimes it happens suddenly and unexpectedly all at once through various transformations such as fire and so forth.
Then, at that very moment, as soon as the water was transformed in that way, the gods were carried away by the waters as far as the primordial ocean.
Moreover, O Lord of the Forest, this time indeed wears away everything; whatever is destined to happen at a particular time will necessarily come to pass in that very way.
When the time of destruction has arrived, strength, intellect, and splendor are everywhere and in every way overturned, even for the great.
Furthermore, O Lord of the Forest, I have described this to you; for what indeed is not possible here within a dream that has been seen in a dream?
The hunter said: "O Lord, if this is unreal, being merely a delusion of a dream, then what is the purpose of this narration, O you who are skilled in auspiciousness?"
