The sage said: O wise one, there exists here a great task consisting of awakening you; you perceive this as being of the nature of delusion, but hear my truth.
Immediately thereafter, while that being remained within the vigor of that intoxicated ocean-like speed, I, wandering in a dream, beheld him as he wandered.
Just as when all the water is about to flow out somewhere, like a multitude of great winged mountains terrified by the agitated vajra.
Being carried along, I reached a certain shore by the power of fate; I remained there, clinging to it as it resembled the edge of a mountain peak.
Then, in an instant, that water flowed out entirely, while the sky became starlit with gods appearing like bubbles bursting on the crests of the waves.
Its interior was composed of jewels by the clusters of stars that had entered the netherworld (pātāla), and it was filled with the vast, ancient mountain grasses whirled around in its eddies.
It was filled with palaces of the city of the gods resembling the island of gold, and garlanded by clusters of lotuses where the swarms of celestial nymphs hovered.
It possessed a network of blue moss like clouds being carried through the intermediate space, and it was filled with lightning like yellow orpiment and dark lotuses like the blue clouds.
The edges of the quarters were filled with clouds of shimmering spray and mist, while the rows of kalpa-trees being carried along were indistinguishable from the surging waves.
Then that ocean-bed became a parched hollow, in some places the Sahya mountain having crumbled away and in others Mount Mandara having withered.
In some places, the moon, Yama, Indra, and Takṣaka were submerged in mud; in other places, there were clusters of wish-fulfilling trees whose branches hung down into the mire.
In some places, his hands were strewn with the heads of world-protectors like lotuses; in other places, he was crimson with pools of blood resting upon those lotuses.

In some places, groups of Vidyadhara women were submerged up to their necks and crying out; in other places, it was filled with fierce buffaloes that struck fear by appearing like elephants seen in a dream.
In some places there were formidable mountains of great-bodied garuḍas, and in others, great embankments intoxicated by the staff of Yama as it traversed the earth.
In some places, the ground was mud mixed with the laughter of swans that were actually the gods of Brahmā; in other places, celestial elephants had their bodies half-submerged in the mire.
In the meantime, having reached a mountain peak at that hermitage, when I rested from my fatigue, sleep came over me intensely.
Then, at the end of my deep sleep, accompanied by that same latent impression (vāsanā), I perceived that very same eon-end while remaining established in my own vital energy (ojas).
Seeing that his suffering was doubled, I became distressed here for a long time; once awakened, I saw that very mountain peak situated within his heart.
Then, on that second day, I beheld the world—beautiful with the rising sun, along with its regions, sky, earth, and mountains.
"Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions"—this has arisen in my mind like leaves and such from a branch.
Then, when that ground had been seen by them in such a manner through those objects, I engaged in worldly activity, my intellect somewhat clouded by forgetfulness.
"Today I am sixteen years old since my birth; this is my father, this is my mother, and this is my home"—this thought brought me great joy.
I saw a certain village and a certain hermitage of Brahmins; likewise, I saw a certain house and a certain kinsman in a certain hermitage.
Then, as I remained in the village house together with my kinsmen, as days and nights passed by, that very same reality persisted throughout the states of waking and the rest.
Then, by the power of time, my former conscious wisdom was forgotten there due to such habitual practice; alas, it was just like that fish's state.
Thus, at that time, I became a village-dwelling Brahmin, whose concern was bound solely to the physical body and who had cast far away the ground of discernment.
He whose self is delighted only by his body and wife, whose essence consists only of latent impressions, and who is solely intent upon wealth alone.
His only wealth was an old cowherd’s staff; he had constructed a fence of planted creepers; he had gathered firewood, earth, and living beings; and he had acquired a water-pot.
With his gaze fixed upon a swaying young tree, always delighting in worldly customs, he remained on a patch of dark-green grassy ground situated beside the house.
He spent his days engaged in the cultivation of vegetable gardens and groves, and was devoted to bathing in rivers, lakes, streams, holy fords, and ponds.
He collects cow dung, food, water, firewood, and fuel with great hardship, rendered helpless by the two snares of "this must be done" and "this must not be done."
Thus, as I lived there, a hundred years passed; once, a self-controlled ascetic guest arrived from afar.
Having been honored, he rested in an earthen hut after first bathing; having eaten and stayed upon his bed, he recounted a story during the night.
In the midst of a certain discourse, charming with the worldly affairs of various directions, countries, mountains, and lands, and serving as a repository for manifold aesthetic sentiments;
All this is indeed nothing but pure consciousness—endless and changeless; though it remains exactly as it is, it shines forth in the form of the world.
Thus enlightened by him, I attained a state of pure, undivided consciousness; by the power of mental retention (*dhāraṇā*), I remembered that entire account in its entirety.
Having remembered his own history—that he had once resided within the womb of that very Virāṭ—he feared him and prepared to depart from there.
Then I did not know that my mouth was the gateway for exit, nor that world in which it was situated—vast, and filled with lands, oceans, mountains, and rivers.
Then, without even leaving that place crowded with kinsmen, I entered his vital breath so as to emerge as the external wind.
"Remaining here, I perceive everything—both external and internal—as well as that which is born of another, as belonging to this Virāj; having thus resolved it to be so," so [he said].
Having bound my concentration through conscious awareness, I did not abandon that region; yet with his life-breaths, he departed like fragrance from a flower.
Having reached the mass of air and entered its hollow interior, I emerged by means of the chariot of the external wind and beheld what was before me.
Meanwhile, my body remained exactly as it was, seated in the lotus posture, while somewhere in a mountain cave there was a hermitage of sages protected by their disciples.
While they remained before me, performing the task of protecting me, a period of time lasting but a single moment passed for those dwelling at the end.
That man into whose heart he has entered—even he, though satisfied by the food obtained at the festival, lies happily on his back.
Having witnessed that marvel, I said nothing at all to anyone; out of curiosity, I entered his very heart once again.
I reached that region of vital energy within his heart in order to behold those kinsmen of mine, being pervaded by that latent impression.
Until the extremely terrible end of the Yuga set in there, that world, along with its established order, underwent total transformation.
There, the mountains are indeed different, and the earth is situated differently; the divisions of the quarters are distinct, and likewise the arrangement of the worlds is otherwise.
Those kinsmen, that village, that stretch of land, and that region of the horizon—I know not where it all has gone, as if swept away by winds after being scattered.
Then I beheld another world situated there, with an unprecedented arrangement, as if it were another universe arisen.
The twelve suns scorch, the ten directions blaze, and the mountains, like ice or frozen water, have begun to melt away by force.
On every mountain and in every direction, the forest ranges are burning; all those treasures that were like jewels have been consumed by fire and have become mere objects of memory.
All the oceans have dried up, and the great winds stand before us; the entire circle of the earth has turned entirely into a heap of glowing coals.

Flames began to issue forth from the netherworld, from the surface of the earth, and from all directions; the entire universe quickly became like the clouds at twilight, becoming one single mandala composed entirely of flame.

Having entered that abode of flames as if into a golden lotus calyx with wandering bees, I then approached it from afar like a moth and did not suffer the pain of the transformation caused by burning.

In this great cloud composed of flames, I wander like the wind-spirit as lightning; my body flickers with the movement of the flames, possessing a beauty like that of a bee upon a cluster of land-lotuses.
The sage said: Even while being scorched there, I did not become a partaker of suffering; for, knowing even while falling into the fire that "this is but a dream within a dream," I remained aware.
I wandered alone through the entire sky, which was filled with circles of newly risen masses of flames, appearing as beautiful as a whirling firebrand.
While I, possessing the knowledge of reality and with an undaunted mind and untroubled soul, was investigating that forest fire, the wind arrived.
He let out an exceedingly deep hiss, resembling the roar of clouds, while he was surrounded by the objects of the world that were revolving and being swept away.
In the forest, with the great force of its thundering roars, it doubled the volume of the clouds; with its whirling solar disks arrayed in formation, it was like a mass of intermingled firebrands.
With masses of flames like clouds at twilight, hundreds of great rivers of fire, and cities of Dānavas and gods upon land-masses twice the size of mountains;
A multitude of vessels, doubled in number by the spirits wandering within the belly of the sky, were burning, unburning, and half-burned against one another.
With sparks of fire doubled by the falling celestial nymphs, it was jagged with the spray from the streams of falling showers of glowing coals.
Shaking off circles of fierce, glowing embers like whirling firebrands and lightning, he veiled the withered face of the upper direction with the darkness of smoke.

From the earth, from the sky, and from all directions, clouds like twilight fires emerged on every side; by them, the seven worlds, together with the sky and its inhabitants, stood as if compressed into a single mass of flaming mountains.

In one place, with his mass of hair blazing tawny with scattered sparks of fire tossed by his leaps; in another, with walls flying up, skilled in harsh rattling, and white as a heap of ashes; and elsewhere, wearing the spreading garlands of flames that fell all around him as they were seized—then that wind began its dance-play like the fierce Hara.
The sage said: While that painful and intense agitation was then occurring, being carried away, I fell into extreme distress.
I thought: "This is but a dream within the heart of another; therefore, I shall attain final nirvana. Why should I vainly behold this suffering?"
The hunter said: "Was it merely to quell his doubt as to whether this might be a dream that you entered his heart? What did you resolve for him?"

What is this that has been seen by you? Where in your heart is the great ocean? Is the wind of the cosmic dissolution in your belly, and how is it that the fire of the cosmic dissolution is in your heart?
Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions—tell me how this thing called the "world" exists within the heart, exactly as it is.

The Sage said: Because there is no cause and because it is evident that there was no origination even at the beginning of creation, the word "creation" and its referent do not exist in the slightest degree as unknown entities.
And both these—the word and its referent—are unknown within the Supreme Self; for that state consists of both ignorance and knowledge, and is free from all affliction.

Therefore, O fortunate one, since awakening has occurred within your own position according to this established doctrine, there exists a supreme, most purifying state that is without beginning or end, wherein ignorance has been stilled.
I speak this regarding the consciousness of the deluded, yet I do not truly know it; this is merely the pervasive awareness that appears as both reality and unreality, born from the non-existent.
Where is the body, where is the heart, where is dream, and where is water and the like? Where is awakening, where is the cessation of awakening, and where are birth, death, and so forth?
There exists here only pure consciousness, transparent and clear; compared to it, even the gross physical sky is like a mountain in the presence of atoms.
By its very nature, that sky of consciousness perceives something through thought; though its body is indeed the void, it perceives that very space as the world.
Just as in a dream it is consciousness alone that appears in the form of a city, yet there is no city or anything else at all, so too this world is nothing but pure consciousness within the void.
This is peaceful, unmanifest, and non-dual; it does not exist within the self. It appears to you in consciousness, in vision, in darkness, and in space, like a wheel or other such illusions.
For us, however, there is neither non-manifestation, nor non-existence, nor existence, nor space; it is the single, formless, beginningless and endless, absolute sky of consciousness alone.
In a dream, that which appears is causeless; in its purity, there is only the seer alone. Therefore, in this state, there is an absence of causes; there is neither a seer nor a seeing.
That something pure shines forth, clearly experienced by oneself, which is inexpressible, without beginning or end, one, and devoid of both duality and unity.
Just as a single time may be a kalpa, and light may possess a dual nature, or as a seed extends to its fruit and flower, so too is Brahman the soul of all.
That which appears as a great wall to one is seen as the pure sky by another; this is observed within the realms of stable dreams, mental constructs, and delusions.
Then that single Self shines forth as pure consciousness alone, like the sky; just as it is in a dream, so it is in the waking state, and likewise in the dream-state—it is not otherwise.
Just as fragrance, though invisible, resides within the invisible wind, so too does the non-obstructive universe reside within the non-obstructive pure consciousness alone.
Upon the abandonment of all mental constructs, you are that which you are—free from affliction, the infinite self within and without, eternally and perfectly established.
The hunter said: "Venerable sir, for whom indeed does past karma exist here, and for whom does it not exist? Tell me that, even without [the intervention of] you."

The Sage said: Those self-born ones, such as Brahmā and others, who shine by themselves during the creation and other cosmic phases, possess bodies consisting of mere representation; for them, there is neither birth nor karma.
For them there is no saṃsāra, no duality, and no conceptual constructions; they possess bodies of pure knowledge and abide eternally as the self of all.
At the beginning of creation, no prior karma exists for anyone here; at the beginning of creation, Brahman alone thus unfolds in the form of the creation.
Just as Brahmā and the others shine forth at the beginning of creation in the form of Brahman, so too do other living beings shine forth by the hundreds and thousands.

However, those born of the quality of goodness (sattva) perceive themselves as distinct from Brahman; whereas those lacking true knowledge, having perceived what is called "insentience," conceive this duality for themselves.
In the time following those [actions], their birth is seen through those very karmas; by those things having become thus, they themselves have resorted to the state of being non-substantial.
But those by whom no difference from Brahman was perceived within the Great Self that is Consciousness—these, namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others, are here beyond reproach.

The transparency of all-pervading consciousness is established solely within the Self that is Brahman; that [consciousness], appearing in some places as the individual soul (jīva), perceives itself within itself.

Wherever one perceives the state of being a living soul (jīvatva), there ignorance (avidyā) persists; therein, under the name of transmigratory existence (saṃsṛti), the Self assumes its corresponding form.
For by itself, in due time, having realized its own nature, it becomes by itself none other than Brahman, established in its own true form.
Just as water, due to its fluidity, appears to whirl within itself, so too does this creative power of Brahman, due to its consciousness, appear to undergo the state of emanation.
This creation consists of the manifestation of Brahman; it is neither dream nor waking state. Whose are the actions here, what are they like, or how many are there?
In reality, there is no karma at all, no ignorance, and no notion of creation; through self-awareness, everything proceeds as nothingness alone.
Brahman alone is the creation, the self of all beings, and the notion that it is "action" or "birth"; acting by itself, it appears through its omnipresence as the possessor of imagined objects.
At the beginning of creation, no action whatsoever is possible for the individual soul; later, that consciousness experiences its own actions by means of mental construction.
Tell me, what is the body of a whirlpool, and what are its actions? Just as a whirlpool is nothing but water, so too the world is nothing but Brahman.
Just as for humans, there is no prior karma for those things seen in dreams, so it is for living beings in the primordial creations, whose nature is pure consciousness alone.

When creation has become established as a process of successive emanations, the conception of prior karma arises; subsequently, these living beings wander, brought under the sway of the bonds of karma.
This so-called creation is not truly a creation; Brahman indeed abides thus. Wherever it may be, what are the actions, or whose are they?
That which is merely the lack of full knowledge of the Supreme Self indeed leads to bondage; for one who knows that [Self], it subsides.
To the extent that a wise person's thorough understanding proceeds, to that same extent his karmic bondage is immediately stilled.
What trouble can there possibly be in the pacification of that which, as it is said, does not exist at all? Apart from the ultimate truth, no such thing as bondage exists whatsoever.

Illusion, which causes the fear of worldly existence, persists as long as that scholarship has not been attained—by which scholarship one does not fall again into the wheel of saṃsāra. Therefore, one should exert effort without ceasing toward that scholarship which is sublime through the knowledge of the stainless Self; otherwise, your fear will never find peace.
The Sage said: Of all dharmas, actions, and sources of happiness, the wise man is the ornament, just as the sun is the ornament of the lotuses.
To that destination which those who know the self and are skilled in the nature of goals attain, there, O Śakra, the glory of the wise appears like a mere fragment of withered grass.
Whether in the netherworld, on the surface of the earth, or in heaven, I do not see any happiness or sovereignty whatsoever that surpasses wisdom.
The wise person’s vision of things as they truly are becomes serene, like the sight of the moon with its entire, stainless orb in a cloudless sky.
This visible world, which is of the nature of ignorance, becomes Brahman in an instant; through the awakening of the wise man, it subsides like the appearance of a snake in a garland.
Since Brahman is established within Brahman, truthfulness belongs to it alone; notions such as the creation, destruction, and so forth of the body have as their sole essence its own inherent nature.
This creation indeed exists where nothing at all [of duality] is found; its properties and actions are not even a string of syllables.
If earth and the other elements arise, let them have a cause; but where that [arising] does not exist at all, what cause can there be for them?
That which appeared to Brahmā is called this world; by that very [appearance], how could these things such as earth exist, and where would there be a cause?
Just as for a dreamer, the objects seen by men exist only imaginatively and not as reality, so too in the waking state, the desires of men do not possess prior reality.

Just as prior karma does not exist for men in their state of masculinity during a dream, so too it does not exist for men here in the waking state, even though they appear as such in both dreaming and waking.

In all creations, the individual soul perceives all objects of dreams as mutually real; yet, due to its prior karma, it is false in essence, appearing in these worlds according to its latent impressions.

At the beginning of creation and at the end of the body, living beings appear to one another like objects in a dream; according to their respective perceptions, they are both existent and non-existent.
Therefore, for one who meditates, all things appear exactly as they are perceived; thus, even within oneself in a dream, they exist as mutually bestowing objects, just as in the waking state.

Because it is grounded in an object situated at the forefront of the consciousness of volition, the fruit obtained by you in a dream is indistinct; it is indistinct because it is grounded in the world [of mental constructs].
Pure consciousness, abiding in its own nature, shines forth by itself as luminous; the designations "waking" and "dreaming" are applied to that very shining of it.
Just as consciousness appeared at the beginning of creation and at the end of the body, so it remains until liberation; this is what is called "creation."

There is no difference between the multitude of objects in the waking and dreaming states and consciousness itself, for consciousness is non-obstructive in nature, just like light and its illumination.
Just as between fire and its heat, or wind and its motion, or water and its fluidity, or even between coldness and the breeze that accompanies it.
The entire world, born of the unreal, is non-obstructive and peaceful; thus, it exists as the real alone, and is not joined with any objective entity.

Having emerged from Brahman and having passed away, that which consists of the experience of the visible world is, in truth, nothing but pure consciousness—undecaying, tranquil, one, and stainless—remaining as such alone.
Just as the causal relationship of objects is conceived in the heart by Brahmā, so too does it exist within the city, as if by a person.
This creation exists within the heart of Brahmā, just as a dream-city exists within your own heart; therein, the relationship of cause and effect stands exactly as it has been described.

In this creation, which is the interior of the density of consciousness, the relationship of cause and effect exists; it stands exactly as it has been projected by you or by him, like a city of imagination.
In this creation, which is a city of volition, the entire structure consisting of cause and effect has been established by you alone through your own nature of conceptualization.
That which is the manifestation within the mind, whose nature is one's own self, is indeed like space; because it is a fixed configuration, that which is within it is called creation.
Those states of consciousness that exist within the city of mental constructs in the heart are this very self-established nature, which constitutes the reality of cause and effect.

Whatever appears first, in whatever manner it exists, that very thing exists here as consciousness; it is to that very [consciousness] that the designations "necessity," "time," "space," and so forth are applied.
Just as that emptiness of the space of consciousness appears swiftly according to its name, so too, by way of such substantiality, is it based upon the relationship of cause and effect.

In this mere flash of consciousness, which has the appearance of creation yet consists of pure being, entities first come into operation, and only afterwards does the designation "creation" occur to the wise.

The three worlds, whose nature is emptiness, likewise abide in the space of consciousness; they are non-different from it, just as the inherent reality of vibration is non-different from a gentle breeze.
Just as in the sky there exists a density of voidness perceived as "blue," so too does the density of consciousness manifest as creation within the Intellect.

While this [world] shines forth as already manifest, its state of being a creation is realized with difficulty, just as one realizes again the true nature of the rope in what was perceived as a snake in the rope.
When dead, he perceives the entire world as distinct, like a dream; that [world] is one thing and this [space] is another, for space is eternally unimpeded.
The hunter said: "How is it that this body comes into being for the sake of pleasure and pain from another? What is its cause, and what are its auxiliary causes?"
If they perform dharmas and adharmas by means of that [body] which possesses obstructive form, then it is illogical to say that they perform its non-obstructive form.

The Sage said: "Dharma and adharma, latent impressions (vāsanā), the agent of action (karmātmā), and the individual soul (jīva)—this burden of synonymous terms is merely conceptualized here; it is not real."
Because of its nature as consciousness, within the self which is the sky of consciousness itself, these names have been fashioned by the mind through the thought that "someone exists."

The self, whose nature is consciousness, by virtue of its own intelligence, perceives the body within space as if it were space itself—just as one perceives a real object after death, or as in the case of volitional imagination and dreams.
To one who has died, the perception of the next world appears like a dream; he beholds it for a long time, yet even there, no reality exists.
If another were to create a dead man, how could there be memory for him? Or how could he be that very same person? Consciousness would be as empty as space.
Therefore, upon death he is not born again; rather, by means of the mind alone, he perceives here in this manner that which consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) within the void.
Having long experienced his own habitual state, he remains there; possessing a clear conviction in this regard, he fully understands it to be the truth.
The self, being space itself, perceives within that very space the appearance of a dream; it experiences its own death again, its rebirth again, and the world again.
Seeing the net of falsehoods thus in the sky, established in each [state], one sees, practices, and consumes; yet nothing belongs to anyone.
In this way, there exist millions upon millions of worlds; yet, O Brahman, they are known as such only when perceived otherwise—that is, as mere appearances.
By them nothing whatsoever is obscured for anyone, nor do they exist; and each of them perceives this very world as being such alone.
The elements abide in each of them and likewise in one another; they are indeed real when viewed through the vision of unreality, but through the vision of reality, they are the unborn state.

That which is non-existent and imperishable for one who knows what is to be known is clearly existent for the ignorant; that which is existent for one who is fully awakened is clearly non-existent for the ignorant.
Whatever appears to the mind in whatever manner, that is real in that way; for this reason, all these elements are mutually of the nature of reality.
Therefore, those various [objects] are eternally true to one another, because their form—which is indeed to be determined by consciousness—is non-obstructive.

Since everything is to be determined by pure consciousness alone, what talk can there be of "otherness" or "non-otherness"? When the multitude of objects shines forth exactly as they are perceived, where is there any room for duality or unity?
"This is that very thing"—this [realization] arises sufficiently from cognition; "that is this," "this is that"—such [realization] would occur because of the unreality of cognition.

If that [object] is identical to the cognition, then it does not exist separately from it; but if the object exists as something distinct from the nature of cognition, then it would follow that this [cognition] is devoid of cognition [of that object].
That which is knowledge is itself the object of knowledge, since it cannot exist apart from the object; therefore, just as knowledge is, so the object of knowledge extends itself by means of itself.

Even while seeing and even while meeting one another, those of separate births are nothing at all; for the wise man, the unreal exists only as the real, yet I do not perceive the objects known by the ignorant.

From the perspective of awakening, all is but pure consciousness, the void of the Self; yet through manifold perceptions, that very same [consciousness] appears as a thousand of conscious-and-inert beings.
In the same way, that single pure consciousness exists as a hundred-thousand-fold self within a dream; then, from that dream, it remains as a single hundred-thousand-fold self in deep sleep.

That which is the perception of a dream within the space of consciousness is called the world; deep sleep is declared to be the cosmic dissolution (pralaya); therefore, this alone is the true principle.
Consciousness alone undergoes multiplicity and the state of being a human, as well as emptiness and the state of being an object, just as in dreams and mental constructions.
All this, it is said, is non-obstructive and consists of nothing but sensation; it is pure, and just as it appears in whatever place, so it becomes there.
At the beginning of creation, there is only one consciousness; it becomes fire, water, space, earth, and so forth for the purpose of that creation, just as in dreams and mental constructs.
That which is named earth and so forth appears as nothing other than the very form of the space of consciousness; for that which is indeed this void alone shines forth as the world.
Consciousness appears as having resistance, and likewise it appears as being without resistance; yet in reality there is no resistance, for consciousness ceases within itself.
You go to the eastern and western directions, knowing them for a long time; you have no so-called resistance, nor are you anywhere possessed of resistance.
He who practices for a long time whatever object has been seen or conceived will certainly attain it, provided he does not turn back out of weariness.
Whether one goes to the eastern or western direction, or remains for a long time, knowing this, he who sits or goes abandons that very state and not the other.
For one whose consciousness is unwavering, the object seen and the object conceived—namely, "May I be"—both exist; for another whose consciousness is unwavering, that duality perishes.

For one whose consciousness is unwavering, there is the thought, "I am going from the south to the north"; for another whose consciousness is unwavering, both [the subject and object] arise and both perish.

For one whose consciousness is unwavering in the thought, "May I be a city in the sky" or "May I be a deer on the earth," both [the city and the deer] would exist; yet neither of these two perishes, for that is the world.

From the perspective of awakening, everything is the void of the Self, which is pure consciousness alone; yet through manifold perceptions, that very same [Self] appears as a thousand entities consisting of both consciousness and insentience.
Whether the body be non-obstructive or obstructive, this cycle of existence for the living being consists of the nature of a dream, both in this world and in the next.
This is directly perceived through the sight of those who have died in regions such as those of the Mlecchas, and through their recounting it with full recollection.
Those who have died and been reduced to ashes in the lands of the Mlecchas return once more, and having explained the matter, they depart, being of an unimpeded nature.
If this were the law for one who is alive, then why would it not apply when a person has gone to another land and one perceives that the object [of the transaction] is dead?
If that which is the property of the living were real, why would the property of the dead not also be real? For such is the experience when these two identical lines of reasoning are established.
The appearance of the world as being like a dream is thus unimpeachably true; by this, there is a single consistent voice among the scriptures of the noble ones' experience.
Just as the net of views of the multitudes of people is unimpeded when looking at the moon’s palace, so too is the world, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent.

It conforms solely to pure existence, consisting of nothing but pure, transparent experience; it is pure consciousness whose essence is mere manifestation, the self of all objects yet devoid of any objectivity.
The entire world is non-obstructive, peaceful, and one within the sky of consciousness; let it rest by itself, within itself, unmoving and without appearance.
To whatever extent one makes consciousness itself steady and immovable, to that same extent it quickly becomes so—whether it be something unreal or even something real.
Since bodies, actions, sufferings, and pleasures exist as they do, whether they persist or pass away, who has a claim to what? What attachment can there be?

Let it be thus, or let it be otherwise; let it not be, or let it come to pass—what cause for agitation is there in this? O you who are feeble, abandon the pursuit of fruit; you have understood that which brings true fruition, so enough with these wanderings!
The Sage said: Since all things, whether existent or non-existent, are of the nature of self-perception in a dream and possess an eternally unobstructed form, what is bound and what is liberated?
Just as there is a shimmering of visual appearances in the sky, so too is this world; due to ignorance, it appears stable, though it is incessantly undergoing transformation.
Just as the shape of a city gradually comes to assume a different form, so too does the world incessantly change, like the shifting of whirlpools in water.
This earth, water, sky, mountains, and so forth, becomes non-existent in an instant; yet in that very same instant, designations such as "yuga" and "kalpa" are made based on the flow of events.
The entire world is experienced like a dream, though it is entirely unreal; if that which does not exist were non-existent in its entirety, then consciousness alone would thus shine forth abundantly.
Just as this world of ours exists, so too do hundreds of worlds exist for hundreds of people in the sky; yet their experiences do not overlap with one another.

The lakes, oceans, and wells are seen as the respective abodes of individual beings; they do not know one another, nor do they ever perceive any other destiny regarding their objects of sight and so forth.
Just as the dream-cities of hundreds of people appear within a single chamber, so do the worlds shine in space; they are neither existent nor non-existent.
Just as hundreds of dream-cities appear within a single house, yet do not truly appear at all, so too do worlds exist and yet not exist in the void.
One's own body, the non-dual visible world, is merely the wonder of consciousness; it is both with form and formless, and both with cause and without cause.

Although designations such as "conditioning factors" (saṃskāra) and so forth are applied to that which possesses the nature of manifesting [images], just as in the case of a statue, those conditioning factors do not exist separately from the manifesting power itself.

Memory occurs in the case of things never before experienced, while dreaming occurs in the experience of objects imagined; furthermore, [dreams] such as one's own death arise from experiences resembling those already seen.

At the beginning of creation, this [universe], whose essence is consciousness, unfolds like a reflection; being pure and consisting of nothing but the light of consciousness, no other name for it is possible.
By this aforementioned statement, "The world shines as Brahman itself," it follows that what appears is not something new; therefore, it is established that this is indeed Brahman alone.

That which is called the cause is the effect; it is the former [cause] that is distinguished. Because it is a conditioning factor (*saṃskāra*), this *saṃskāra* is said to be volitional action (*kṛti*).
That unprecedented object which appears as an example in dreams and the like is said to be [produced] by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) and so forth; there is no external object within the mind.
The object is both seen and not seen; it exists like consciousness in the sky. By its very nature, even its own self appears as if seen and expands as if perceived.

The non-existence of the previous creation, which consists of the meaning of the Vedānta, proceeds forth; thereafter, the wise establish the order of objects of knowledge for the sake of accomplishing their own purpose.

But those who know the truth say that the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of waking which exists in a dream is produced by a waking state that was not actually experienced as waking, yet appears as such; thus, it is "newly created" as a semblance of waking within the dream.
Therefore, like the vibrations of a lute, all phenomena abide inherently within the mind; they proceed from themselves—what role for formative action (saṃskāra) is there here?

In this same way, the single pure consciousness exists as a hundred thousand-fold self within a dream; and since that dream of a hundred thousand-fold self arises again from that [consciousness], it remains as the single state of deep sleep.
The perception of a dream within the sky of consciousness is itself called the world; deep sleep is declared to be the cosmic dissolution (pralaya); therefore, this alone is the correct principle.
The single expanse of consciousness alone assumes manifold forms while remaining inseparable from its own nature; that which appears as this world is like a dream.
Thus, this world-existence stands within the atoms of consciousness; it is non-different from them, devoid of objective enjoyment, like reflections in the surface of a dream.
That which is the sky of consciousness, pure awareness alone, vast as an atom yet without beginning, middle, or end—that very thing is called the world.
Therefore, wherever the infinite space of consciousness (cidākāśa) eternally abides, there the appearance of the world exists; for that appearance is non-different from its own constituent part.
By the principle that "the world is indeed pure consciousness alone; you, I, and the universe are composed of consciousness," the unborn world enters even into the interior of a single atom.
Therefore, I am the supreme atomic self, possessing the form of the entire universe; I abide everywhere, even within the interior of a single atom.
This very self of the universe, though consisting of the atoms of pure consciousness, is like the infinite sky; wherever I abide, there I behold the three worlds.
I am indeed of the nature of a conscious atom; through that conscious atom, I have attained oneness with it upon seeing it, just as water merges with water.
Then, having entered its vital energy (*ojas*), I remained as if experiencing it, possessing the form of the three worlds within me, just as a seed exists within a sprout.
Therein, the form of the three worlds shone within me in my own self; thus it exists, but it does not exist externally anywhere by anyone.
Wherever, whenever, and whether in a dream or in this waking state, that which appears as the visible world—both external and internal—is nothing other than one’s own manifestation of consciousness.
When the world, spread with bliss, appears to a living being in a dream, that manifestation belongs to the atom of consciousness itself, appearing as the Self in the form of that state.

The hunter said: "If the visible world were without a cause, how could it be established? And if the visible world has a cause, then from where does the notion of creation and so forth arise in a dream?"
The Sage said: This creation proceeds at the beginning entirely without cause, because the sky of consciousness that constitutes the creation is devoid of all causes.
Since things that lack a cause are absolutely impossible here, no creation whatsoever involving resistance can exist anywhere.
This Brahman shines thus, radiant by its very nature as consciousness; it is synonymous with terms such as "creation" and so forth, yet is devoid of beginning and end.
Thus, in this causeless creation which shines as the form of Brahman, there appears the reflection of the Supreme Self through the nature of its eternal constituent parts.
Though it is non-dual as well as diverse, though it is Brahman yet possesses the form of non-Brahman, and though it is formless as well as having form, it shines forth unimpeded toward every object.

That very Brahman, being formless and having consciousness as its nature, shines with a radiant body; having become the self consisting of both the stationary and the moving, it appears as if possessing form.
He assumes the forms of divine sages and seers and, in due order, establishes destiny, as well as injunctions and prohibitions regarding place, time, action, and so forth.

Existence and non-existence, grasping and abandoning, the gross and the subtle, the moving and the unmoving—these objects deviate; therefore, not all of them are subject to fixed necessity (*niyati*).
From that time forth, the arising of entities is not possible without a cause, just as the production of oil from sand and similar substances is impossible.
Fate and the Leader likewise, as limbs of the Self from Brahman, restrain themselves by their own limbs, just as one's own hand restrains one's own hand.
And it proceeds in this very way without prior cognition and without desire, like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, or like the ripples from the movement of water in a whirlpool.
For the arrangement [of the universe] is indeed destiny; without it, Brahman would be unable to remain as it is, since that [arrangement] is the inexhaustible manifestation of His universal selfhood.
Thus, the entire visible sphere is always accompanied by its cause; for whatever being, from whatever time of creation onward, it has existed in relation to that [cause].
Brahman shines as causeless even to the ignorant, who perceive it as the essence of creation; and for that very person, this delusion of seeing cause and effect in the world appears.

When the creation exists like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, this principle of necessity (niyati) is established, such that "this is thus" and "this is not thus," functioning like the recurrence of events.
Since all entities necessarily possess causes when a sequence is inevitable, waking and dreaming perceptions cannot occur here without a cause.
Just as in a dream, due to the agitation of water, the delusion of universal dissolution is seen—listen and experience the cause of that.

In all things, logical arguments always shine forth like crystals or shells; yet it is the very experience of meditative cultivation itself that, being inherently powerful and the essence of life, triumphs.

The Sage said: Through the external senses directed outward, the individual soul perceives only the external; through those situated within, it perceives the internal as a dream; and through those intensely agitated by both, it perceives both.
When the sense faculties remain agitated by external objects, then the object of conceptualization is experienced as something faded.
But when the senses are indeed turned inward, then the individual soul perceives that entire world, even down to its atomic dimensions, within its own body.
There is never anything whatsoever in the world that possesses resistance; the vision of the eyes of living beings—that is, the vision of the non-resistant sense-faculties—is the non-resistant world.
When the senses, which are the life-breaths and the eyes, are fully externalized, then the living soul perceives within consciousness the world-body as being essentially external.
The aggregate consisting of the ear, skin, eye, nose, and tongue, which is active in nature, is called the *jīva*; it is of the form of consciousness and possesses the nature of wind.
The living soul, consisting of all the senses, abides everywhere and at all times; because it is the imperishable space of consciousness, it perceives everything everywhere.
When the inner life-force is filled with the essence of phlegmatic nature, then that subtle self, in the form of an atom, perceives within those very sensory atoms.
It was like the Milky Ocean surging at the rising of the moon in the sky, with lakes filled with blooming lotuses and surrounded by white water-lilies.
Canopies of flowers were sung over by bees, and inner gardens arose in the sky as the harem of spring.
[He saw] festivals filled with auspiciousness, groups of women restless in their playful movements, and courtyards of houses completely filled with the splendor of various foods, edibles, and drinks.
Bearing flowers, laughing with foam, and possessing tremulous, restless glances, the rivers—intoxicated by their youth—approach the ocean with graceful charm.
The palaces, as white as the peaks of the Himalayas and exceedingly cool, with their walls washed in plaster, seemed as if they were fashioned from the very surface of the moon.
And there were lands covered by the clouds of the dewy season, the cold season, and the rainy season, as well as grounds abounding in blue lotus creepers and verdant meadows.
The grounds of the city gardens were covered with heaps of flowers, where deer and travelers rested, and which were shaded by trees with glossy leaves.
The flower-filled grounds shone with the nectar of the kadamba, kunda, and mandāra trees, and with the luster of the moon, while their seats and locations were beautifully arranged.
He saw dark-blue forest ranges, entwined with lotus-stalks, supporting grounds of flowering trees, and as tender as the clear sky when the clouds have dissolved.
They wore crests fashioned from plantain, kandalī, kunda, and kadamba flowers; they were garlanded with mountain-creepers, delicate as the swaying, beautiful, and playful sprouts.
With their creeper-like jasmine garlands slipping from their hair as it was playfully tossed aside, the slender-limbed young women performed a dance like playful maidens.
The assembly halls of the king resembled blossoming white lotus ponds, covered with hundreds of beautiful chowries, golden ewers, and canopies.
Their limbs were entwined with the graceful arrangement of circular creeper-garlands; their forest garlands possessed the subtle, melodious resonance of shimmering water-channels.
The ten directions were filled with clouds whose formidable bodies bore the weight of the earth, and their interiors were adorned with necklaces of spray and mist.
When the inner living being is filled with the essence whose nature is bile, then the subtle essence, consisting of the measure of a minute atom, perceives right there.
Beautiful with *kiṃśuka* trees dried by the movement of the wind, the rows of flames were as delicate as the petals and sprouts of a radiant lotus.
The rivers were like streams of mist from the sprinkling of scorching sands, and the quarters of the sky were darkened by the smoke, black as the crests of forest fires.
[He saw] suns harsh as fire, with the brilliance of sword-edges sharpened by whetstones, which produced flavors contrary to those of forest fires, poisons, and afflictions.
Or [he may see] the ocean made hot by sweat, the circle of the three worlds perspiring, and even the dense forests of the wilderness dripping with caustic brine.
He saw water like the mirage of a desert, appearing as flowing streams; he saw lands never seen before, yet once inhabited by trees.
To the traveler, who was grey with heated dust due to the intensity of his haste, that tree on the road with its lush shade appeared from afar like nectar.
The world’s appearance was ablaze with fever, like the earth heated by fire; the regions were struck by dust, as were the quarters of the sky and the intermediate spaces.

From the ocean of the multitude of planets, [he beheld] the directions—[the quarters] of fire, sky, forest, water, and earth—endless, immeasurable, and formidable with masses of clouds like jars of ice and frost.
And [he saw] the autumns, summers, and springs that bring heat and scorching sun; and the earth covered by the warmth of masses of clouds, heaps of grass, leaves, and creepers.
The surface of the sky, the earth, and the horizons were golden, as were the vast lakes and the snowy mountain plateaus, all appearing as if heated by fire.
When the individual soul (jīva) is filled with wind after the fluids have been depleted, then that soul, whose essence consists of subtle particles of vital energy (ojas), finds itself right there.
Because his consciousness was agitated by the wind, he saw an unprecedented surface of the earth, and unprecedented circles of cities, villages, mountains, oceans, and forests.
One perceives oneself flying up like rocks from mountain peaks, with deep, resonant roars, and the spinning of wheels and so forth.
There is the mounting of vehicles such as horses, camels, garuḍas, clouds, and swans, and the movement through the coming and going of yakṣas, vidyādharas, and others.
The mountains, the earth, the rivers, the oceans, the forests, the lands, the villages, the cities, and the directions all trembled, their limbs bristling with fear like bubbles upon the ocean.
Or one has fallen into a blind well, or into a vast abyss; or one perceives oneself as having ascended a tree or a mountain that resembles the sky.
When the living being (jīva) is filled with wind, bile, and phlegm, it then becomes afflicted, having fallen under the power of the portions [of elements] governed by wind.
Pārvatī fell amidst a perilous rain of fine stones, while the surrounding circle of trees whirled about with loud cries from the crumbling battlements and ramparts.
With its forest arrangements whirling about, it made the clouds appear indistinct; the quarters of the sky were rendered continuous by lions, elephants, and rain-clouds.
It was filled with the blazing rows of *tāla*, *tamāla*, and *hiṃtāla* trees, and it resounded with the deep, gurgling roar of echoes from within its caves.
The cave was beautiful with the composition of sounds from the churning of Mount Mandara, and it was struck by the irresistible mutual collision of its splitting rocks.
Resembling the clashing of mountain peaks, harsh with a multitude of "kreṃ-kreṃ" cries, the rivers made the surface of the sky appear like a garland of pearl necklaces falling down.
The great ocean, its waters filled with fragments of rock, filled the sky; the mass of dense forests being swept away struck against the very shell of Brahma’s world.
It was jagged with the ten fingers and eyes rubbing against one another, and it resounded with the crackling *caṭat* and *kaṭakaṭa* sounds of splitting metal.
[He saw] the rising forest breeze shaken by the gusts of wind from the falling houses, bearing lotuses variegated with the dust of his own whirling pebbles as they rattled.
With deep, *maramara* sounds arising from the violent shattering of the mountain peaks, the three worlds appear as if resplendent with cruel cries of lamentation.
Thus, when the individual soul (jīva) has been rendered insentient, it remains utterly oppressed, surrounded by these [elements]: wood, stone, clay, fire, wind, and the army.
Like an insect within soft earth, like a frog inside a stone, like an unformed fetus within the womb, or like a seed inside a fruit.
Like a sprout within the belly of a seed, like an atom within a mass of matter, and like the body of a wooden puppet within its unceasing frame;
Due to the impossibility of any cavities, it is devoid of the movement of the vital breath; it is threatened by a surging mass of stones and a flood of pebbles.
Then, as if within a dense mass of light, one experiences deep sleep for oneself, resembling the interior of a mountain cave or the depths of a dark well.
When the effort has matured and once again reached a state of internal voidness, then the individual soul, awakened by the vital breath, experiences a dream.
When those particles fall into the interior portions of that region, transforming within the body, that indeed is the excessive raining upon the mountain.
Due to the predominance of fire, one perceives much as large and little as small; through the combination of wind, bile, and other humors, one experiences agitation both externally and internally.
Just as this inner living soul (jīva), when brought under control, perceives this [external world], so too does it know or experience it externally, enveloped by wind, bile, and other humors.
When the wind, bile, phlegm, and so forth are slightly disturbed both internally and externally, one perceives this visible world as slightly [distorted]; when they are balanced, it is seen as even.
Enveloped by these agitated elements, this individual soul perceives externally the movement of the earth, mountains, and sky, as well as the blazing of masses of fire.
Travelling through the sky, [visiting] the rising moon and the Himalayas, the dense thickets of trees and mountains, and leaping across the heavens over the oceans.
Diving and surfacing in the ocean, amorous dalliance in celestial abodes, and frequent resting upon mountain slopes, groves, and the white clouds.
There is the whirling experience of the hells, crushed by massive saws, as rows of *tāla*, *tamāla*, and *hiṃtāla* trees revolve in the sky.
There was falling by means of revolving wheels and instantaneous leaping into the sky; there were crowds of people even in empty space and submerging in the ocean even on dry land.
In the dead of night, diverse and contrary worldly activities are as difficult to discern as the light of the sun during the day, or as darkness during the day.
One perceives the surface of the earth as being in the sky, solid ground within the construction of a wall, walls in the open air, and friendship toward an enemy.
One should perceive others in one's own kin, and see goodness in the wicked; one should view a precipice as level ground, and level ground as a precipice.
He saw mountains that were smooth with the humming of songs, washed in nectar, beautifully painted, and appearing as if made of white stone or even of fresh butter.
In dwellings formed by clusters of leaves from the kadamba, nīpa, and jambīra trees, they took pleasant rest with their women, just as bees do upon lotuses in heaven.

For these sensory functions, when closed within, see [the internal], but when opened, they see [the external]; thus, due to the imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), the activities of the senses produce delusion.
In this way, those whose elements are unbalanced perceive and experience many such things externally, just as in a dream.
Both externally and internally, many contrary effects are seen, most terrifying, produced by living beings with unbalanced bodily constituents.
Within these identical elements, this inner life-force itself experiences this uniform state of worldly activity, just as fire exists within [its fuel].

He saw the continuous succession of cities, villages, towns, and forests as they truly were, along with the pleasant waters, the shade of trees, the various regions, and the coming and going of travelers on the roads.
Adorned with pleasant sunlight, the moon, the sun, stars, and the cycles of day and night—thus this unreal [world] appears as if it were real.
The perception of the visible within the nature of consciousness is like a vibration in the wind; though non-existent, it appears as existent, remaining undivided yet appearing as if divided.

From the peaceful void-self, the entire world arises; yet nothing whatsoever arises that is called "existent," for it is peaceful. In that sky of infinite consciousness, this very form—mere light, pervasive and of infinite body—shines forth.
The hunter said: "O best of sages, what happened next to you while that vital energy remained within your heart—that which is called the form of delusion?"
The sage said: Listen now, my dear friend, to what occurred there immediately after that, concerning me as I sat within the element of fire, my form enveloped by its vital energy.
At that time, while that terrible agitation at the end of the aeon was occurring, the wind of universal dissolution blew, carrying away even the great lords of mountains like blades of grass.
Suddenly, a rain of mountains arrived from somewhere, carrying with it the expanse of forests, peaks, villages, and towns.
When that [vision] had reached its conclusion within me and had fully transformed, then I, as a subtle being, beheld that very same downpour of rocks.
Compressed by that flood of rising mountains from fragments of food, I experienced a dense state of deep sleep, a blinding darkness.
Then, after experiencing that state of deep sleep for some time, I gradually became inclined toward awakening, like a bed of lotuses at dawn.
Just as a vision appears after a long time in the darkness in the form of a wheel, so too that which was merely deep sleep has come to assume the state of a dream.
Thus, from my rest in deep sleep, I entered into sleep within the dream; I beheld the visible world within the vital energy, just as the ocean manifests its own waves.
The visible world, which consists of the treasury of consciousness, has thus come to me in that same way, just as movement is not other than the wind within itself, though the wind is motionless.
Just as heat exists in fire and the like, as fluidity in water and the like, and as pungency in pepper and the like, so does the world exist within the space of consciousness.
Because its essential nature is solely consciousness, this pervasive world-appearance is born from that which is like the self in deep sleep, just as [a vision arises] for a young child.
The hunter said: "Since it is designated as 'the visible object of that self in deep sleep,' tell me, O best among speakers, what do you mean by 'the visible object of deep sleep'?"
From that deep-sleep self, which is itself an object of perception, what other produced thing could arise—either another deep-sleep self or some other state of deep sleep?

The Sage said: "The jar and so forth, as well as the world and its like, are born, they shine, and they manifest"—this is the delirious chatter of those tormented by duality, consisting of mere conceptual construction.
Listen now as to how the word *jāta* is a synonym for pure existence (*sanmātra*). The root *jan* is said to denote manifestation, while the root *bhū* is the very form of that manifestation.

The root *bhū* is said to have "existence" (*sattā*) as its sole meaning; therefore, that which has arisen from it is called "born. When it is said that something is born from creation (*sarga*), it is designated by the term *sansarga*.
For the wise, such as ourselves and others, nothing at all is ever born, nor does anything ever perish; everything is peaceful, unborn, and real.
Brahman consists of the existence of all beings; the world consists of the existence of all beings. Tell me, what injunctions or prohibitions could possibly apply there?
Whatever power there may be exists both in that very place and does not exist there; because that Brahman is of the nature of that, so too the self is of that same nature.
For the wise who know the ultimate reality of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth, nothing whatsoever exists other than that which remains as it truly is.
Just as there is not even the slightest form existing in dreams or in cities of the imagination, even while they persist as experiences, so it is with the world at the beginning of creation.

Indeed, it is the individual soul (jīva) who becomes the observer of this dream-vision here; yet at the beginning of creation, consciousness, being beyond objects of thought, shines forth more transparently than even the sky.
Here there is no seer, nor is there an enjoyer; everything here is of such a nature that it is neither something nor nothing—a silence that transcends even speech.

At the beginning of creation, due to the absence of any external cause, whatever has appeared in consciousness remains for a long time in that very form, just like the objects of a dream or a mental construction.
Likewise, from this conscious non-duality, one either fears or does not fear, just as a person himself does not fear his own form depicted on a canvas.

Without beginning, middle, or end, infinite, one, and utterly transparent, yet appearing as manifold through extreme transformation; though it exists as it is, luminous yet unquiet, this entire universe is in truth perfectly tranquil.
The sage said: "Immediately thereafter, O mighty-armed one, as I emerged from deep sleep, this world appeared in my dream as if it had issued forth from the ocean."
As if carved from the limbs of space, as if carved from the earth, as if carved from the mind, or as if carved from the very sight itself.
It was like a blossoming from the trees, like a creation arisen in the beginning, or like a mass of waves upon the shore of the ocean—the very manifestation of visions.
It was as if it had descended from the vault of heaven, as if it had come from the cardinal directions, as if it were carved out from the mountains, or as if it had arisen from the earth.
It was as if it had issued from his heart, as if it had entered through the clouds, as if it were born from trees, or as if it had arisen from the earth like a crop.
As if emerging from his limbs, as if carved out by his senses, as if manifested from a canvas, or as if issued forth from a temple.
It was as if it had fallen from somewhere, as if flying down from the sky, or as if it were a gift received from the earth for the next world.
It is like a blossom of the Brahma-tree, or a wave of the ocean of speech; it is a beautiful statue within the pillar of consciousness, made manifest without being carved.
The infinite wall of this city is made of clay from the sky; the city itself is a city of space. The mind is like a rutting elephant; the life of the living being is false.
And a variegated painting without a wall or stage in the sky—this was the entire wealth of a certain one named Avidyā, the lord of Śambara.

Though it involves great exertion and is stable, it is devoid of space and time; though it appears manifold and richly varied, it is non-dual; and though it possesses many selves, it is nothing at all.
The analogy of the city of the Gandharvas is also equal [to this] because it lacks reality; for indeed, even that illusion is perceived during the waking state.
Purely consisting of the light of consciousness, though unoriginated, it remains as if originated, joined with space, time, action, substance, and the processes of creation and dissolution.
It was as enchanting as the womb containing the embryos of gods, asuras, and humans, like a pomegranate filled with a multitude of seeds situated within separate compartments.

It was filled with rivers, mountains, forests, and the like, crowded with the sky, stars, and clouds; it resounded with the humming of the wind, enriched by songs, the ocean’s roar, and the chanting of recitations.
Then, as I looked about there at that circle of visible objects, I beheld that very same village which had been my former dwelling place.
He saw all those very same kinsmen situated in that same condition, those same sons, that same wife, and that very same house at that very time.
Seeing that former vulgar impression, he forcibly drew it out, just as a wave in the great ocean draws out a bystander whose limbs are being overwhelmed.
Then I was there, blissful from that embrace; surely, having taken up this latent impression, I had forgotten my former memory.
Whatever object stands before it, that very image it assumes; by its very nature, this mirror of consciousness is just like an ordinary mirror.
But he who possesses the realization that "all is indeed the sky of pure consciousness," O dear one, is not awakened by duality here; he remains as the Absolute alone.
The demon of duality does not afflict in the slightest that person whose stainless mindfulness, endowed with awakening, does not perish.
Through the practice of yoga and association with virtuous persons and excellent scriptures, there arises in them an awakening intellect which, once risen, never forgets it nor ceases to manifest.
At that time, my intellect regarding awakening was immature, and it was destroyed by that [ignorance]; who today could possibly destroy my intellect, even if they were a malignant planet?
O hunter, know this: even your intellect, being devoid of the company of the virtuous, will attain peace only with great difficulty through the arduous realization of duality.
The hunter said: "O sage, this is indeed true; yet by your purifying enlightenments, even with such as these, my mind does not find rest in the state of the virtuous."
The web of doubt—"it might be thus, or it might not be"—does not subside even today regarding this reality, despite its being directly experienced by oneself.
Alas! This ignorance, though it exists as something already stilled, does not subside; it has been made exceedingly firm by long habituation.

It is my firm conviction that this delusion of the world comes to rest through practice—by means of association with the virtuous whose intellects are awakened to the words and their meanings, and whose limbs [of speech] are captivating due to their investigation of true scriptures and authentic methods—and by no other means whatsoever.
The hunter said: "If it is so, O best of sages, how can there be truth and untruth? This very great doubt of mine remains fixed by the vision of my dream."

The Sage said: That consciousness which arises with certainty through place, time, action, and substance, appearing as if by chance like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, is known by the name of a true dream.
Cognition, which is designated as "true dream," is known to be non-deviant in some cases due to gems, mantras, medicinal herbs, and substances, while in other cases it is deviant.
When such a state of true dream-existence has been established among the worlds, then, by the logic of the "crow and the palm fruit," no other [state] can be found.
Whatever determination consciousness adopts when its own certainty is not firm, it becomes exactly like that, by virtue of having a nature conjoined with the fruit [of that determination].
But if another person were to subvert that very certainty of hers, how could that mature certainty be considered a valid object of perception?
Nowhere do any objects whatsoever exist either externally or internally; consciousness alone exists, abiding in the forms of the world just as it wills.
When one declares "this dream is real" with internal certainty, it immediately becomes so; likewise, through doubt, it turns into doubt.
Even when a result is obtained from another source, it is due to the conceptualization of the dream as real; he simply understands that "this result was indicated by a dream."

In the three worlds, all things—though firm and distinguished by their own consciousness—deviate from their state over time, in space, or through effort, whether after a long duration or in a short while.

At the very beginning of creation, the world appears as an unobstructed manifestation within the sky of consciousness; therefore, consciousness alone, as the subtle body, extends its own substantial existence according to its will.
Apart from the one Brahman, which is pure consciousness alone, know that everything else—whether existing or non-existing, fixed or unfixed—is always unreal.
Since Brahman alone is the self of all, being one and truly real and nothing else, what indeed could be called true, and what could be called false?
Therefore, a dream is sometimes real and sometimes indeed unreal; for those who are unawakened and for those who are awakened, it is neither of the nature of non-existence nor composed of existence.
This delusion of consciousness appears under the name of the world, possessing its own form; yet who here can be certain that "I am myself a delusion"?
It is consciousness alone that, for a long time, causes this mind to shimmer; when it is like water within itself, this world flows like a liquid.
Just as deep sleep is experienced after observing a dream, so too is sleep experienced after observing the waking state.
Therefore, O high-minded one, know this waking state to be indeed a dream; and know the dream to be waking—these two are one, unborn reality.
This single, pervasive manifestation of pure consciousness alone, which is unobjectifiable like the sky, contains here the sequential arrangements known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
In this dream-consciousness, there is no such thing as necessity, nor is there any lack of necessity; tell me, what kind of necessity and lack of necessity could there be?

It is said that for as long as there is the manifestation of an object in a dream, for that long there is the same constraint; the Sage alone can bring about the restriction of that very manifestation of consciousness.
O dear one, just as the movement of a gust of wind is spontaneous, so too is consciousness; since it is entirely without cause, what is destiny, and of what nature could it be?
Now, whatever name such as "A" and so forth is imagined as the cause of consciousness, that is itself causeless; for the creation is not other than consciousness.
In this matter, such is the very nature of necessity: that whatever appears in whatever manner, to whatever extent it manifests, it is exactly so and not otherwise.
Sometimes there is truth in a dream, and sometimes there is untruth; due to the very absence of fixed destiny, it is merely a matter of chance, like the "crow and the palm fruit."
That which shines by its own nature through the essence of gems, mantras, and medicinal herbs—whatever is indeed determined as such is seen even in the waking state.
Waking and dreaming are merely the manifestation of consciousness; what difference is there here? In the waking state, they are identical in nature because of the perception of a city in a dream.
That which is designated by the word "waking" does not truly exist as waking; the world-form is merely a dream of the Self, even though that Self is entirely free from sleep.
Indeed, that which is called "dream" does not exist at all; it is simply the nature of consciousness of Brahman, who is of a single form whether asleep or awake.
These states of waking, dreaming, and so forth do not exist at all times; one perceives the visible world only immediately after the delusion of death has ceased.
Just as the waves of spray incessantly for infinite time, those very same things manifest intensely like something else in the sky of the mind, though they are not different from it.

Likewise, other creations, whether manifest or unmanifest, do not exist as something separate; what then is there of waking, sleeping, and so forth, therein, any more than lines carved within the interior of a stone?

Having the nature of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth state; devoid of form yet possessing all forms; bearing a body that is a creation yet transcends all mental constructs; though pervaded by the body of consciousness, it is nonetheless hollow with the void of the objective world—this sky of pure consciousness is not, even in the slightest degree, different from the mere expanse of space.

At the beginning of creation, the entire visible world—consisting of space, wind, fire, water, earth, and the clouds that mark the ends of worlds—is essentially nothing but the mind. Since it does not experience any external cause, it is purely of the nature of consciousness; it is ultimately devoid of names, endowed with the very form of awareness, pure, and merely perception itself, rather than being a separate entity.
The hunter said: O Sage, tell me next that reality of yours concerning the world—what occurred for you whose worldly existence has been extinguished by hundreds of great accounts?
The sage said: Then listen, O virtuous one, to what unprecedented event occurred at that time within the vital energy of his heart, you who are longing for the account of what transpired.
Likewise, for me, whose wondrous sense of self had been forgotten while remaining there, time passed in the form of seasons and years.
For sixteen years, my mind being delighted by my wife, those years passed for me there in the householder stage of life, O dull-witted one.
Then, on one occasion, a sage of fierce asceticism, worthy of honor, possessed of great awakening, and wise, came to my house as a guest.
Having been thus honored there, he was pleased; then, after eating and sleeping, O dear one, having reflected upon the conduct of the people, he was questioned by me as follows.
O Blessed One, you possess vast awakening and you know the destinies of the world; for this reason, you have never seen anger, nor do you take delight in pleasure.
Pleasures and pains come to those devoted to action through their deeds—whether auspicious or inauspicious—just as crops come to those seeking fruit in the autumn season.
Why do all these living beings perform equally unwholesome karma, when their faults, such as greed and the rest, arise simultaneously?
Why do famine, drought, and calamities ripen for the entire multitude of people at the same time? Whose identical misdeeds bear fruit thus?
Having heard this and looked upon him, as if smiling and with his mind uplifted, he spoke these words, which were worthy of praise and beautiful like a flow of nectar.
Another sage said: "O virtuous one, it is well! Tell me, what is the cause by which you know whether this visible world is real or unreal? Why is it so?"
"Remember your entire self: who are you, and where do you stand here? Where am I, what is this visible world, and what indeed is its essence?"
"O friend, why do you not realize that all this appears as a mere dream? I am a man in a dream to you, and you are like a man in a dream to me."
Formless, inexpressible, beginningless, and beyond conceptualization—this world exists as a mere shimmering reflection within the crystal of pure consciousness.
Such is the innate form of this pure consciousness alone: that which is omnipresent, whatever exists anywhere, that very thing exists within it.
By conceiving of it as having a cause, everything for him has a cause; by conceiving of it as being without a cause, everything for him is without a cause.
But for us, these creatures, that Virāṭ is the pervasive Self; we abide within His heart, and He likewise exists here through the power of our consciousness.
He alone shall become the Virāṭ self of the other women as well; he is the cause of pleasures and pains, and of actions consisting of existence and non-existence.

Through the transformation of the elements of the Virāj, by means of irregular throbbing and so forth, there arises simultaneously this entire web of living beings, consisting of the various limbs and members of his body.
Whether it passes beyond the calamity of famine or returns to a state of peace, that which is the existence of Virāj is the very nature of this creation.
O virtuous one, like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, suffering and the like fall equally upon certain evildoers, just as a thunderbolt falls upon trees.
Through the conceptualization of action, consciousness partakes in the fruit of its own actions; when liberated from the conceptualization of action, it does not partake in the fruit of action.
Whatever conceptualization arises—whether slight or excessive—in whatever [object], it remains there in that very same way, whether it has a cause or is causeless.

In the city of the causal source and so forth, which consists of a dream-like nature, there exists no auxiliary cause whatsoever; therefore, that is the beginningless, auspicious, conscious, undecaying Supreme Brahman.
This thing called the delusion of a dream appears as something causeless; yet another appears as having a cause—empty, and consisting of both being and non-being.
All cognitions of dreams appear like the "crow-and-the-palm-fruit" coincidence; because they are perceived as identical to those [waking cognitions], this extended world is nothing other than them.
That which is established here by way of having a cause is "with cause"; that which is established here by way of lacking a cause is "without cause."

This dream, arising through the sequence of cause and effect, is merely the manifestation of consciousness; it is the very nature of that which is called the great waking state. Therefore, the wise know all this to be the supreme peace.
"O Mahāmati, hear which entities have no real cause: what is the cause of intrinsic natures, and what is the cause of space here?"
Furthermore, what is the cause of the creation of the dense mass of the earth and other elements? What is the cause of ignorance? And what is the cause of the Self-existent One (Svayambhū)?

At the beginning of creation, what could be the cause of the winds and of the fires? What could be the cause of the waters, which consist of nothing but sensation, and of that which is of the nature of space?
What is the cause for the dead to receive a physical body and attain a form? In this very manner, all creations proceed from the very beginning.
In this very way, they proceed and revolve within the world, like wheels in the sky when viewed for a long time by the eye.
In this very way, by means of the emanation proceeding in the form of Brahman, designations such as "earth" and so forth were subsequently applied to his own very nature.
In the prior sky of consciousness, creations appear like the movement of the wind; they themselves bring about the conceptualization of the causes of the body.
In whatever way destiny is conceptualized, it assumes that very form; for this is its own inherent nature, since it belongs to consciousness as it has been imagined.
Whatever form, consisting of light, was first perceived by consciousness, that remains even today exactly as it was, being "I" myself within consciousness itself.
Furthermore, by another effort that is superior to it, that very consciousness is capable of being altered; and again, by a great effort, it can be made otherwise than that.
Where a cause is conceptualized, there the essence is causality; where no cause is conceptualized by the wise, that is a non-cause.
