This world, which first appeared spread out like a whirlwind in a gale, remains even today exactly as it appeared—though it is entirely non-existent.

Some, acting together, perform good or evil deeds that are their own; they obtain a fruit corresponding to those actions. Yet others, numbering in the thousands, encounter suffering quite without cause, as if struck by a stone or a thunderbolt.
The sage said: By such reasoning as this, I was then enlightened by that sage in such a way that I attained the state of one who has known what is to be known.
Therefore, because of her long-standing entreaty, he was not abandoned by me; he remained there even though he was dead, and in that very same manner.
Behold this best of sages standing by your side—he by whom these words, auspicious like the rising of the moon, were spoken.
By him, the destroyer of delusion, who knows all that precedes and follows what is seen, this was spoken even before it was uttered—by him who, like a sacrifice, has assumed a physical form.
Agni said: Having heard those words of the sage, the hunter then became as if visibly struck by a dream-creation; why was he thus dejected, as it were, out of wonder?
The hunter said: "O Sage, oh, how great and wonderful is this that you have told me today—this which is difficult for the mind to bear, yet which removes the torment of worldly existence!"
That which was described in a dream is here said to be perceived directly while awake; and yet that very thing is obtained—O Sage, this is indeed wonderful!
O Lord of Sages, how is it that this great dream-man has become so solid even while awake, appearing as if he were real to one of childish intellect?
Tell me this wondrous narrative in its proper sequence: from where, for whom, and what is this? For it is indeed a supreme marvel.
The sage said: "Therefore, O fortunate one, listen to this wondrous account of mine; I shall relate it to you in brief, so do not make me wait in haste."
By this, that was then described there for my enlightenment; and by those great words, I quickly became wise.
Then, by these words, my former true nature was remembered by me—pure, like the clear sky at the end of the summer heat.
"Ah! Was I indeed that sage?"—with this thought his intention was expressed; and from the heart, having bathed in the swelling [joy] of "I have been," he remained in wonder.
Having reached this state of attachment to enjoyments, I am like an ignorant traveler who, seeking water in the sky, runs about afflicted by fatigue and pain after a vain mirage.
Alas! Though it exists as a mere illusion consisting of the perception of what is seen, even the wise man is deceived by it, just as a child is deceived by a ghost.
"Alas! How strange it is that by this leaping false knowledge, which is empty of all objective reality, I have been led to such a state!"
Or rather, even that "I" which exists is merely an illusion and not composed of reality; nevertheless, it is called a hundredfold variety because it is a mockery of what is non-existent.
I do not exist, nor does she, nor this world, nor even this delusion; yet all of this is a wondrous illusion, appearing as if it were real.
"What must I do now here, since the destruction of my bonds has been achieved? There remains only this sprout to be cut; therefore, I shall abandon it."
Let this be; this ignorance is useless in nature—what is the use of it? This delusion, which is unreal in form, has now been abandoned by me.
This sage here is the instructor; this is merely an illusion. Just as I am Brahman, so does this form appear like a cloud in the sky by day.
"Thus, first I shall proclaim the Great Sage who has arisen with such knowledge"; having reflected thus, that sage was addressed by me there as follows.
O Leader of Sages, I go to see this body of yours which is my own; for I have also set out to behold that very body [of mine].
Having heard this, that best of sages then said to me with a smile: "Whence did those two bodies of yours come? They have gone to a very great distance."
"Go yourself, O you who are skilled in conduct, and observe the events; first see how they have unfolded, for having seen it, you will understand the illustration for yourself."
Having thus reflected, I, the conscious self, abandoned that body—which was composed of the elements and identified with the sense of "I"—and joined its vital breaths to the wind.
"O Sage, as soon as I have looked upon my former body, I shall return; until then, you must remain right here"—having said this, I departed for the wind.
Then, mounted upon a wind-chariot, I wandered through the sky; having traveled for a long time with great speed, I reached the infinite expanse like the fragrance of a flower.
Then, after wandering for a long time, even as I moved toward the opening of his throat, I did not find anything within his interior.
Then, having fallen into supreme despondency, he returned once more and thought: "This very web of the world is my own tethering post."
Having first obtained this here, I then questioned that unsurpassed sage with one-pointed mind; thus it was in my home.
"O Blessed One, best among those who know the past and the future, tell me what this is; you see exactly how it occurred with your supreme eye of wisdom."
I have entered whose body, and he has likewise entered my own body; where have those two bodies gone, and for what reason are they not found?
For an exceedingly long time, I have wandered through the expansive circle of saṃsāra; yet, from the moment of my birth as a stationary being, why was that opening of the throat not reached?
When asked, "Having gone there, what did that high-souled sage say? the lotus-eyed one replied, "O lotus-eyed one, why do you ask as if you yourself already know it?"
If you perceive this yourself through the singular consciousness of yoga, then you will indeed see it in its entirety, as clearly as a lotus in the palm of your hand.
Nevertheless, if you have a desire to hear my words, then listen to this as I shall speak it to you exactly as it happened, without omission.

As long as you do not exist, there is no one like you—neither the sun that warms the lotus of asceticism, nor the source of the lotuses of auspiciousness, nor the navel of Hari from which the lotus of knowledge springs.
Once, while you were established in ascetic practice, desiring to see a dream, you entered the heart of a certain living being with a fully awakened consciousness.
Since you have entered the heart, there you beheld this vast triple world, with its expansive heaven and earth and their wide interior.
While you were thus long occupied, his body nevertheless remained in that great forest in the very place where it had been left, appearing as if fast asleep.
The fire of the world-conflagration blazed forth, its smoke shrouding the sky with a mass of grey clouds, while whirling circles of firebrands moved like the orbs of the sun and the moon.
The sky was covered by clouds of smoke filled with the ashes of burnt clouds, appearing like blankets as white as the petals of a blue lotus.
The quarters of space were numbed by the loud crackling sounds of bursting [fire], which threatened with the roars of lions escaping from their mountain caves.
The clouds, with their crackling sounds like the crashing of thunderbolts, fell like a dense mass upon the rows of palmyra and tamāla trees that had been turned into flaming wood.
To those situated in distant lands, it revealed the sky as a floor of molten gold, through the perception that the steady lightning was liquid gold flowing forth.
With his lovely grains, he made the clusters of stars in the sky appear doubled; he was the delighter of the eyes of the young women resting upon his chest.
The interior of the sky was filled with the roaring sound of blazing flames, while wild forest-dwellers, startled awake, rushed out from their cave-dwellings in confusion.
The lions, deer, hunters, and birds were fleeing as they were half-burnt; the streams of the lakes and rivers boiled, blinding the fierce forest-dwellers.
The tips of the yak-tail fans were beautiful as they flickered in the flames of the forest fire; the clouds were enveloped by the stench of the fat and marrow of forest creatures being consumed.
By that forest fire, leaping like the fire of cosmic destruction, your hermitage has been consumed as if by a spreading serpent.
The hunter said: "O sage, what was the natural cause of that fire? And how did all those excellent young brahmins perish together with that forest?"

The Sage said: Just as the vibration of the mind that forms intentions is the cause for the arising and dissolution of those very intentions, so too, when it is free from vibration, the three worlds likewise cease to exist in an instant.

Just as there is vibration and the absence of vibration in the heart and at the edge of the forest, so too, O cause of agitation and non-agitation, is the vibration of the three worlds here, occurring without delay.
The world is a city of conceptualization within the element (dhātu); its vibration here is the cause of the arising and destruction of beings, as well as of disturbances such as rain and drought.

Even the mind of Brahmā and others is contained within this, and that too is within another expanse of consciousness; thus, this movement within the sky of consciousness is peaceful and one, without end.

The glory of the sky of consciousness shines within the sky of consciousness; thus it is free from affliction for the wise. But for the ignorant, whether this [glory] appears as it does or otherwise, it is not real here, being merely composed of that [delusion].
Another sage said: There, your city, those houses, and those trees—all quickly came to be reduced to ashes like dry grass.
While you were thus asleep and your two bodies had been reduced to ashes, those great stones were likewise split asunder by the intense heat.
That fire, having consumed the forest entirely, gradually subsided; it went out like Agastya returning home after having drunk the ocean.
When that fire had gone out, the wind blew away all those ashes—once glowing but now perfectly cool—bit by bit, like a heap of flowers.
Consequently, it was no longer known where the hermitage had been, nor where those bodies were; where that multitude of chests had gone was as unclear as a dream upon waking.
When your two bodies have thus come to non-existence, as you sleep and are subject to delusion, it is consciousness alone that unfolds.
Therefore, where is that cavity of his throat? And where is that Virāṭ-Ātman? For one who is burnt, his vital energy is burnt; and for one whose vital energy is burnt, his very body is burnt.
Therefore, O sage, you have not obtained a second body; you remain here in this endless dream-saṃsāra as if in a waking state.
Thus, this very dream has attained the state of waking; we are all here, O observer of noble vows, but dream-beings belonging to you.
You are our man of the dream, and we are your men of the dream; this very space of consciousness (cidākāśa) is always established as the Self within the Self.
From that time forth, you became a man in a dream while remaining as you were; yet, possessing the cognition of being awake, you became a waking man firmly established in the householder's life.
All this has been told to you exactly as it occurred, without omission; it was experienced and clearly seen, and you perceive it now through meditation.

Thus, this one who is devoid of beginning or middle, whose form is infinite, and who is a mass of pure consciousness, shines in the void like the brilliance of gold; he, whose body is restless upon his own forehead, is the self consisting of consciousness, manifesting through the blossoming dark and light forms that constitute creation.
The sage said: Having spoken thus, that sage remained silent there upon his bed at night; and I, meanwhile, was as if being carried away, filled with wonder.
Then, after a long time, O great sage, I said to him: "O Lord, it is my conviction that every dream is thus of a real nature."

The other sage said: "Where something else arises from that which is real, there it is appropriate to have the conceit, 'This is real. But where this alone is reality, what proof can there be for its being anything less?"
Just as a dream, so too does this initial creation appear; though devoid of earth and the other elements, it stands as if established by earth and the rest.
"Thus, from this dream of today, a dream of creation has arisen, pure in nature. Listen, O lotus-eyed one, O sage, O great teacher, O hunter!"
Just as a dream arises for a dreamer from objects seen during the day, so too does the dream of creation first shine in the void as an object already perceived.
Thus, why do you speak as if in doubt, saying "this is a real dream," even though it was clearly experienced? How could there be an effort toward meditation on a real dream?
O Sage, when this world of dreams—which is experienced as such and is clearly manifest—is indeed perceived along with its gods, how can there be any doubt regarding it?
When he had spoken thus, I interrupted his speech and asked: "Tell me, what is this 'teacherhood of a hunter'?"
Another sage said: "Listen, O one of great wisdom; I shall relate this other narrative to you in brief, for there is no end to my detailed account."
I am indeed one of long-standing asceticism, while you are exceedingly righteous; having heard these true words of mine, you shall find delight right here.
"You shall not abandon me while I remain here with your worship; I shall dwell together with you—this is my resolve."
O virtuous one, after some years have passed from now, the destruction of all your kinsmen will occur here due to famine.
And at that very moment, through a conflict over the boundaries and the surrounding lands, this entire village, along with all its small creatures, will perish from its home.
Then, no longer perceiving suffering, they rested together for a long time—tranquil, equal in having known what is to be known, and free from desire for all objects.
Right here, in some single thicket of trees, we two shall dwell together in solitude, like the moon and the sun in the empty sky.
In time, this excellent forest will arise in this wilderness, its entire ground covered with a network of *śāla*, *tāla*, and creeping vines.

Its quarters were adorned by the dancing of the leaves of *tālī* and *tamāla* trees; its blossoming trees were praised by groves of fully opened lotuses; its lovely creeper-bowers resounded with the warbling of flocks of *cakora* birds; it shone like the Nandana grove descended from the sky.
The other sage said: "As we two have been practicing penance for a very long time in this forest, a hunter, exhausted from pursuing deer, will arrive."
You shall awaken him with discourses on the merit of one's own true nature; there, in that very forest, he will practice asceticism, free from worldly attachment.
Then, in the midst of those practicing ascetic disciplines, desiring to know the self and wishing to understand dreams, he will inquire about the discourse on dreams.
"You shall explain to him the unbroken knowledge of the Self through the narrative called 'The Dream'; therefore, he will become a fit recipient."
"In this manner you shall become his guru; therefore, my dear, I have addressed you with the words, 'O teacher of hunters.'"
Thus I have explained to you everything: how this wandering in saṃsāra occurs, who I am, what you are like here, and what will become of you.
Having been addressed thus by him, my mind was filled with wonder; after reflecting upon this together with him, I attained the height of amazement.
Then, when the night had passed, at dawn that great sage, having been thus honored by him, found delight in that very place.
Immediately thereafter, O Sthiramati, we remained in that house and likewise in every village house, having established a mutual bond of affection.
Then this time, consisting of seasons and years, flows on; I remain like a mountain, casting off and taking up the states of being as they arrive.
I do not long for death, nor do I long for life; I remain just as I am, free from the fever of passion.
Then, I reflected there upon that circle of the visible world: what could be the cause of this, and what does it perceive with its mind?
What is this collection of objects, and what indeed is its cause, within this vision of a dream whose sole nature is the space of consciousness?
The heavens, the earth, the wind, the ether, the mountains, the rivers, and the directions—these shine forth as the very sky of pure consciousness, established within the Self.
That which spreads its light in all four directions like the moonlight—this very world appears as a variegated, non-obstructive entity within the void.
These mountains do not exist, nor does this earth, nor this sky, nor even this "I"; this appears as nothing but the manifestation of the void of pure consciousness alone.
Alas, what indeed could be the cause of this entire collection of objects? For without a cause for grasping them as a whole, no object whatsoever could possibly exist.
If this were merely an illusion, what indeed would be the cause of that illusion? Who is the seer and the thinker of the illusion, or what is its cause, where, and of what nature?
He in whose vital energy of the heart I dwelt as mere consciousness—indeed, he has been reduced entirely to ashes along with me.

The sage said: Having thus reached a definitive conclusion regarding this visible world, I remain free from feverish distress—devoid of passion, free from doubt, extinguished in peace, and without egoism.
Without support, without that which is supported, free from pride, and without dependence; abiding in its own nature, self-peaceful, the essence of creation, it is manifest in every way.
I shall be the agent of whatever has been attained, yet I am never an agent at all; for what kind of agency can belong to that which is itself like space?
Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions—all this universe is a single self, a sky whose sole conscious form is the web of all beings.
I am stilled, I am completely extinguished, and I abide in absolute bliss; for me there are neither injunctions nor prohibitions, neither the external nor the internal.
Thus, as I remained here established in my natural state, you have today arrived before me by chance, like the "crow and the palm fruit."
Thus everything has been explained to you: how a dream is, how we are, how the world is, how you are, and how this visible world is likewise.
And you are as this visible world is; as this is seen before us, so are all beings, so is Brahman, and so are these multitudes of people before us.
Having understood this, O hunter, O hunter, be at peace; for false is [this world]. Truly peaceful is this very existence, whose form is the void of pure consciousness.
The hunter said: "Whether Nirvana shines forth by itself, or nothing at all shines forth—if this is so, then I, you, and all the gods and others are likewise [unreal]."
The sage said: All dream-men are mutually composed of both the existent and the non-existent; thus all this stands in relation to one another like a dream.
In this way, both the existent and the non-existent are experienced within one another; by whatever means the visible world is perceived, it is experienced by that very means in that same manner.
Therefore, an object is neither one nor many; it is not existent, not non-existent, and not something in between. In the waking state, it is merely a perception, like a city in a dream.
"Like a city being seen from afar that was never seen before—thus everything has been explained to you; you have been awakened without interruption."
"You are yourself wise and you know; do as you wish. Even though you have been thus enlightened, O hunter, such is your mind.
For a moment they rest in awakening, yet they do not rest in the supreme state; without practice, this awakening does not take root in the heart of the mind.
O wise one, it reaches a supreme transformation, like wood in the bearing of water.

Through practice in resting within awakening, by exclusive devotion to the Guru and the scriptures, and through the pacification of the perceptions of duality and non-duality, the mind is said to attain Nirvana.

Free from pride and delusion, having conquered the fault of attachment, ever established in the inner self, with desires turned away, liberated from the dualities of the notions of pleasure and pain, the undeluded go to that imperishable state.
Agni said: Having heard this, the hunter then stood in that forest region, slow with wonder, as if his form had been painted by an artist.
His mind found no rest in that state without his own habitual practice; he felt as if bewildered, as if being swept away upon the ocean.
As if mounted upon a wheel, he was carried away by the wheel of asceticism; deprived of his prowess, he was as if seized by a crocodile.
Due to the doubt, "Is this nirvāṇa, or is it something else?", that fool did not attain peace, just like a youth in the prime of his life.
Contemplating that this visible world is indeed created by ignorance alone, the notion that "the world is ignorance" does not firmly take root in the heart of one who is skillful.
"How far does this visible world extend? I shall observe it from the beginning, using my body obtained through asceticism to measure its height from a distance."
One dwells eternally in happiness at the end of this world, which consists of both existence and non-existence; therefore, even space exists, and where that is not, there I shall go.
Having thus resolved in his heart, he became a fool indeed; for even such a statement, when spoken without practice, is like [pouring] it into ashes.
From that time forward, together with those very sages, he abandoned his state as a hunter and prepared to practice asceticism.
Dwelling constantly together with those beings in that world, he performed very great austerities for many thousands of years.
While performing austerities, he once again questioned that sage, "When will there be rest for my self? Thereupon, the sage replied:

The sage said: "That knowledge which was taught to you has settled in your heart like a small fire with withered wood; however, it is not appropriate for it to remain there without consuming what is to be burned."
Without practice, you have not yet come to rest in the auspicious knowledge; but through practice over time, you will attain complete repose.
Now listen to this future account concerning myself, a wonder of the world that will serve as an ornament for your ears as I describe it.
One whose self is not awakened by this essence of knowledge, though it has been praised, possesses a vacillating consciousness; such a person is neither a fool nor a wise man.
"How vast is this world, which is of the nature of ignorance and full of enjoyment?"—with such a conceptualization of a self, you have set out to perform ascetic penance.
"In this manner, O broad one, you must perform severe penance for a hundred yugas; then Parameṣṭhin, being pleased, will approach you along with the gods."
O bestower of boons, O boon-receiver, you shall seek from that giver of boons a boon for this doubt regarding your own self, born of your unrestrained wickedness.
O God, while this visible form is perceived and the delusion of ignorance persists, there exists nowhere a reflection free from impurity, as in the case of a mirror.
In this mirror of the sky of consciousness, whether it be of the size of an atom or situated within [the heart], everything here is reflected, wherever that may be.
Therefore, how infinite may this visible world, which causes suffering, be? And what might lie beyond its limit? That too is merely the visible sky.
For this purpose, I pray for this boon; listen, O Lord of Gods, and likewise grant it to me quickly and without obstacle.
May this body of mine be free from disease for a long time, possessing death at its own will, endowed with the speed of Garuḍa, and capable of traveling through the sky.
Let this [space] increase by one *yojana* in each individual channel, gradually becoming of the nature of space on the exterior of the world.
O Supreme Lord, may I attain the end of this visible world which appears to have space; let it be my supreme boon that there be an end to what is otherwise infinite.
O virtuous one, when you have thus spoken, the Lord of gods, the sovereign Master, will say, "So be it for you," and the Ishvara will vanish from sight.
When that Great God, the Lord of Heaven, has departed along with the gods, your body, emaciated by asceticism, shall possess the luster of the moon.
Having paid homage to me and taken leave of me at that very moment, he will then leap into the sky with the desire to behold the object situated within his own mind.
Like a second moon, like a second sun, and like a second submarine fire, he has arisen as if to rival the moon and the sun.
Then, by the speed of his flight like that of Garuḍa, he sought to reach the end of the visible sky, as one might seek the end of the world-oceans through the force of a current.
Then, at the end of the world, his body will increase incessantly, filling the shoreless sky like the ocean intoxicated at the end of an eon.
Then, increasing in stature with a vast body, you shall behold [it] in the great void through the unimpeded progression of the sky, which serves as the support for all emanations.
They are wheels of wind consisting of the emptiness of the ultimate great space; they are waves upon the ocean of consciousness, arising from the impulse of the fluidity of intrinsic nature.
Just as cities and other things appear in a dream within the fabric of consciousness while being of the nature of space, so too will these unrestrained multitudes of creations manifest for you then.
Just as masses of leaves flash in the great sky, stirred by turbulent winds, so too shall you, with unshaken resolve, behold infinite creations.

Just as a net of rays from the eyes of those in an assembly, though existing, is non-existent [to others], so too the world-self, though existing in the void of consciousness, is non-existent [to those who have realized it].
Just as the web of the world is seen by all people upon the earth when it is reflected in the orb of the moon, so too is the non-duality of the Self established when the world exists [within it].
"Again creation, again the sky; again creation, again the firmament"—as you perceive it thus, a long period of time will pass here.
Then, after a long time, upon the trembling leaf of creation, you yourself shall experience agitation in the vastness of the sky.
Then you will experience a sense of agitation as you reap the fruit of your asceticism; at that time, you will behold your body filling the infinite sky.
What is this wretched body of mine that stands like a burden, upon which even a hundred thousand mountains such as Meru would seem as light as a blade of grass?
This body of mine is immeasurable; the entire sky is pervaded by me. Even now I am filling the void, and what is yet to come is not at all reached.
Alas, this ignorance is indeed terrible, endless, and immeasurable; it cannot be measured by anyone except through the knowledge of Brahman.
I shall indeed abandon this body with its unrevealed interior; through it, I shall not attain any union with the virtuous or the true scriptures.
What indeed is this body of mine, which is boundless, without limit or end, resting upon the supportless sky, and yet attains objects so difficult to obtain?

Having reflected thus, and having performed the concentration (dhāraṇā) that expels the vital breath from that body, you shall abandon it, just as a bird leaves a dried fruit after it has been enjoyed.
Having abandoned the body, the living soul, endowed with its vital breaths, shall abide in that sky of yours, as subtle as the wind yet moving like the wind.
The body will fall like Mount Meru with its wings clipped; there it will reduce the entire world of earth, mountains, and so forth, to dust.
Then the Goddess Śuṣkā will devour his body along with her circle of mothers; by that means, the earth shall become free from defect.
Thus you have heard my entire life story, O observer of noble vows; having performed penance in the Tālīvana forest, do as you wish.
The hunter said: "Alas, O Blessed One! I must endure inexhaustible suffering for the sake of that which was wrongly sought after for the sake of wealth, resulting in this useless misfortune."
"O Lord, is there some reasoning for this state of affairs, O Excellent One? Or if the matter must be otherwise, let it be told."
The Sage said: An event that is destined to happen can never be made otherwise by anyone; for that which is ordained does not fail, despite all effort.
Just as a man possesses no power to effect a reversal of his left and right hands or feet, so too he has no power to bring about a state of being otherwise than it actually exists.
Through the knowledge of the meaning of the science of astrology, there occurs here the foreknowledge of future events; however, nothing else whatsoever is ever produced that was not already present.

Victorious indeed are those actions of perception by which, having attained their present state through ordinary means, one sleeps as Brahman itself, with consciousness remaining unaltered even by the burning of the body.
The hunter said: "O Blessed One, what will happen next to me when my body falls down upon the earth, while you dwell in the vast expanse of space?"
The Sage said: Listen attentively, O noble-souled one; what will happen when that body of yours has perished within that supreme ether?
When that body has fallen away, the living being, conjoined with the vital breaths, will become a fragment of wind in the atmosphere of expansive form.
In that state where even a slight breath has ceased, you will see the vast surface of the earth—the visible world situated within the heart—standing before you like the universe seen in a dream.

Due to the expansion of the mental fluctuations, the individual soul will then perceive those [objects] and partake in the objects of its own volition, thinking, "I am the king upon the surface of the earth."
There, a sudden and swift intuition will arise within him of its own accord: "I am a glorious king, highly honored by the name Sindhurāja."
When my father had gone to the forest at the age of eight, the kingdom of the earth bounded by the four oceans, which had been granted by my father, came into my possession.
On the frontier there is a king known as Vidūratha, an enemy who cannot be conquered by name alone without diligent effort.
While I have been exercising this kingship, a hundred years have passed; oh, what happiness I have enjoyed together with my servants and the multitude of my wives!
"Alas! This lord of the bordering land has grown powerful; a terrible battle with him is now at hand."
While he was thinking thus, King Vidūratha [reflected]: "A great battle will take place here, destroying the fourfold army."
In that great battle, even though you are deprived of your chariot, you shall slay Vidūratha, whose shanks will be severed by the blade of your sword.
Then, you shall become a sovereign of the earth bounded by the four oceans, whose commands are honored by the world-protectors overcome with fear.
Having become like the ocean and having attained the entire circle of the earth, you shall engage in these conversations together with your learned ministers.
The minister will say: "O King, this is most wonderful—that Vidūratha was thus defeated by Your Majesty in battle and led away to the abode of Yama."
"You shall say: 'O good man, tell me why King Vidūratha, the enemy of this wealthy man who possesses the force of the ocean at the end of an eon, is so difficult to endure?'"
The minister will say: "He has a wife named Līlā, by whom the Mother Sarasvatī—the stainless Goddess who sustains the world—was won through extreme asceticism."
Once she has been accepted as his daughter, that progenitor of the world effortlessly accomplishes for him all his tasks, even those such as liberation.
By a mere word or sound, she can in an instant turn even the world into a non-world; when that [world] perishes, what distress could there possibly be for her?
Sindhur will say: "What you have said is indeed appropriate; if it is so, then Vidūratha is invincible, and his slaying in battle is a marvel."
Thus, being endowed with such supreme confidence in the Blessed One, why did the king not achieve victory in that battle?
The minister will say: "O lotus-eyed one, she was entreated by him at all times without weariness, saying: 'May there be liberation for me from saṃsāra.'"
O Lord, by her and by him, through that very unfailing consciousness, he brought about his own defeat in battle, having relied upon her.
Sindhu will say: "If it is so, then this goddess is always worshipped by me; why does she, the Supreme Goddess, not grant me liberation?"
The Mantrin shall say: "For this petition always resides within the heart of everyone; that very Goddess, whose nature is pure consciousness, is proclaimed as Sarasvatī."
In whatever manner one's own [nature] is desired by anyone, it bestows that very thing immediately of its own accord; therefore, it is experienced as consciousness.
O crusher of enemies, this consciousness was not sought by you for the sake of liberation; rather, it was sought by you for the sake of subduing your own enemy.
Sindhu will say: "Why was this Sarasvatī not sought by me? Why was pure discernment (*saṃvit*) not sought by me here for the sake of liberation?"
O dear one, why does this Sarasvatī, though she has entered my heart and granted me her command, not act—even in her true form—to bring about my liberation?

The minister will say: "O Destroyer of Enemies, you possess a former habit of impurity; because of that, O Lord, although you bowed down, this [teaching] was not requested by you for the sake of liberation."
Since it is established from the very beginning of the world that a living being becomes whatever its mind is, who—starting from childhood—is able to act otherwise?

Whatever is experienced within by one whose self is stainless through stainlessness, and which consists of the power of practice—that very thing, my dear, becomes unimpeded reality, whether it be existent or non-existent, by the complete sublation of all else.

Then Sindhur will say: "What was I in the past, possessing the form of either an Arya or a non-Arya, and being of deluded mind, by whose power does this former negative conditioning of mine exist, which brings about further existence?"
The minister will say: "Listen to the secret, O King, being intent upon it for a moment; being thus urged, apply this today which destroys all dullness."
There exists here something beginningless and endless, real and free from disease, which abides in forms such as "you" and "I," and is designated by the word Brahman.
That Brahman itself, having assumed the consciousness "I am the conscious one," remained as if having attained the state of a living soul; having become the mind, it did not abandon its body.

Know that the mind is the body, whose nature is as pure as the sky and which is of a subtle, transportable (ativāhika) form; that alone exists here, and nothing else such as a material (ādhibhautika) body.
This mind, though formless, exists as if possessing forms; through conceptual constructions such as the next world and so forth, it alone is real—just like dreams and the like.
The wise know that this world is the mind itself, which, though formless, is all-pervasive—just as that which is called "wind" is nothing other than its own vibration.
Just as the world and the mind are one within the emptiness of space, so too, in this state of non-obstructive form, there is not even the slightest bit of difference.
The web of the world residing in the heart is nothing at all; know that the world is formless, being merely the mind and not real.
That very being who was previously born from the station of Brahmā has now become this one who is the most tamasic of the tamasic.
Sindhu will say: "O highly fortunate one, tell me, why is he called the most tamasic of the tamasic? By whom were these designations previously established in the supreme state?"

The minister will say: "Just as in this world the hands and other limbs belong to a sentient being who possesses parts, so too do these [limbs] belong to the *ātivāhika* self, which likewise possesses parts."

Afterwards, that very self will assume various designations within itself: the names of the elemental (ādhibhautika) states, such as earth and so forth, and those of the subtle transportive body (ātivāhika).

In this manifestation of the world, which resembles a dream, he himself will engage in worldly activity through his own conceptualization, which takes the form of the self and consists of the nature of consciousness.
Because that which has manifested as a new form of the subtle, transportive body (ātivāhika) is called "birth" (jāti), this [manifestation] is designated as "great darkness."
O Lord, though Brahman is changeless, when it assumes the state of the individual soul (jīva), various classes with diverse names are conceived as if it were subject to transformation.

When Brahman itself, through its very first manifestation, appears as if it were a living being, then the experiencer [the individual soul] arises through the intellect; that class of beings is the most excellent among the sattvic.
O giver of honor, that birth which is endowed with auspicious qualities in the present existence is declared by the best among those who know births to be purely *sāttvika*.

If, through many births, one becomes a partaker solely of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, that is called by the virtuous who know the truth "the most excellent among the passionate" (rājasarājasī).
O giver of honor, that which is devoid of auspicious qualities in the present existence is declared to be purely rajasic; such a birth occurs within a very brief existence.
That birth which proceeds toward liberation after many, indeed very many, existences is called by the virtuous who know it the *tāmasatāmasī* (the most ignorant of the ignorant).
Experts in the classification of births have declared that, in general, a birth characterized solely by darkness (tāmasī) leads to liberation only after many lifetimes.
By this sequence, there is a manifold conceptualization of the distinctions between castes; O giver of honor, you have been born into that caste which is the most tamasic among all those [castes].
Many births of yours have passed away—those various and diverse ones, O hero, I know, but you do not.
In particular, you have spent this time in vain with this very body of a great corpse, even though you are capable of traveling through infinite space as a bird.
Thus, when you were born from a lineage that was dark and even darker, then liberation from the cavern of saṃsāra became difficult for you to attain.
Sindhu will say: "Noble one, explain by what means this base birth may be overcome; as long as it remains so, tell me that which would purify it."
The minister will say: "O one of great intelligence, there is nothing here in the three worlds that cannot be obtained by a man who is free from despondency."
Just as yesterday’s misdeeds attain beauty through virtuous action today, you should therefore strive with effort this very day to perform good deeds for the sake of the future.
Whoever desires a certain goal and strives for that purpose accordingly will certainly attain it, provided they do not turn back out of exhaustion.
In whatever way one constantly exerts oneself, whatever one cultivates, and of whatever nature one becomes; and however one desires to be, one becomes exactly like that, and not otherwise.
The sage said: Thus addressed by him with a resolute mind, he will then and there utterly abandon that kingdom, even unto its very name.
Though entreated by his ministers, he will indeed go to the distant forest; he will not again resort to that kingdom from which all enemies have been eradicated.
As he remains in the midst of the virtuous, through the power of those discourses on discernment, discernment will arise within him, just as fragrance arises from contact with flowers.
Then, by means of continuous inquiry as to "How has this birth come about? and "From where has this saṃsāra come?", he will attain liberation.

Then, becoming constantly devoted to inquiry through the company of the virtuous, that Sindhu will attain the purifying state where no fortune whatsoever—like a leaf shaken by the wind—attains any semblance of reality.
The sage said: "All this, which concerns both the future and the past, has been told to you. Now, O hunter, do as you wish; let it be properly performed."
Agni said: Having heard these words of his, his mind overwhelmed with wonder, the hunter and likewise the sage stood still for a moment and then quickly went to bathe.
Thus both the hunter and the great sage, having become friends without cause, practiced asceticism there through the study and reflection upon the scriptures.
Then, in a very short time, the sage attained nirvāṇa; having cast off his body at the end of his life, he reached the supreme transformation.
Then, after a long time consisting of hundreds of ages had passed, the Lotus-born One arrived to grant the hunter his desire.
The hunter, unable to restrain the force of his own latent impressions, requested the boon previously described, even though he already knew it.
Having said, "O Brahmā, let it be so," the hunter departed in his desired direction; to enjoy the fruit of his asceticism, he leaped into the sky like a bird.
With his ever-increasing body, he filled the great sky beyond the world for an incalculable time with speed, like a mountain.
As he filled the sky with the great speed of a garuḍa, moving sideways, upwards, and downwards, a vast amount of time passed.
Then, after a long time, when he did not reach the end of that delusion of knowledge, he fell into a state of agitation.
Then, out of agitation, having bound his breath through the practice of exhaling and retention, he released his life-breaths into the sky; his body became a corpse, falling head-first downward.
The mind, endowed with the vital breaths, went into the sky and there assumed the state of the ocean—that very ocean which was the protector of the entire earth in the form of Vidūratha’s enemy.
His body became like a great corpse as vast as a hundred Meru mountains; resembling a second earth, it fell from the sky like a thunderbolt of lightning.
Like a covering for some path upon the earth, or like a tuft of hair in some space, it appears as a delusion within the world.
O best of the wise, that Great Corpse, which fills the entire circle of the earth and its mountains with its forms, has thus been described to you.
In this world-system upon the circle of the earth, wherever a corpse has fallen, this world appears to us just like a city in a dream.
Having tasted this corpse, the goddess Caṇḍikā—once emaciated, now full, with a large belly, red, and filled with red entrails—has become perfected.
The earth has become "Medinī" because it was filled with the fat (*medas*) of this corpse; it is filled with an unprecedented form, possessing the appearance of the Himavat mountain.
At that very time, this great fat attained the state of the earth-element; through time, it further became the earth and reached the condition of being composed of clay.

Forests have once again sprouted upon the earth, and villages have been established together with cities; those mountains have emerged from the netherworld, and the prosperity of worldly commerce has begun to flourish.
Agni said: "O best of the wise, O virtuous one, go now to your desired direction; the circle of the earth shall once again become stable, possessing its natural course of worldly activity."
O Śakra, you are performing the hundredth sacrifice for the multitude of subjects in heaven; I have been summoned there by the mantra. O knower of all courses, I am going.
Bhāsa said: Having spoken thus, the blessed Agni vanished right there, like a flash of lightning moving through a cloudless sky.
In the same way, I too, carrying my own past [deeds] by means of my mind, remain wandering in the sky to determine my own karma once again.
Furthermore, I beheld countless worlds in the sky, possessing various modes of conduct and reflection, and existing in diverse forms.
In some places, O King, bodies made entirely of umbrellas appear as a single mass; they shine, they seem conscious, they move, and they captivate the heart.
In some places, O Raghava, all beings with bodies made of clay shine, perceive, and move about, resembling mountains.
In some places, beings with limbs made of wood appear; in other places, there are numerous beings whose bodies are composed of stone.
In some places, beings were seen in the sky remaining together for the duration of their lives like solid rocks, their interactions consisting of mere words.
Thus, for a very long time, seeing yet not seeing due to the state of my mind, and failing to perceive the end of ignorance, I became distressed in that state of vision.
Once, while he was intent on performing austerities for the sake of attaining liberation, Indra said to him: "Indeed, there is another birth for me as a deer in the sky."
Overpowered by former habit, I became intent on the delusion of heaven; indeed, I was wandering there in the sky within that grove of Mandāra trees.
When I said, "So be it," he replied, "O Lord, I am weary of this cycle of existence; let me be liberated quickly. Having heard this, he then spoke to me.
When the Fire-god said, "I am indeed the pure-souled formless one; choose a boon," I then requested another boon from him.
Indra said: "This consciousness of yours has wandered for a long time within the womb of a deer; I have perceived that this purpose of yours was destined to come to pass."
Having become a deer, he has reached that assembly hall of great merit, wherein this unimpaired knowledge spoken by me shall lead to awakening.
Thus, there in that place, you shall remember this entire futile account of your own life as a deer, while suffering from the affliction of worldly existence upon the earth of rebirth.
It is like the delusion of a dream, comparable to that which is fashioned by all conceptual constructions; it resembles the reality brought forth by stories of things experienced in another world.
But when you become a man released from the state of a deer, then, at the end of this body consumed by the fire of knowledge, that which resides in your heart will flash forth.
Therefore, having abandoned that long-standing delusion called ignorance, you will become completely extinguished, like a wind whose movement has ceased.
When this was said by that god, at that very moment there arose in me the realization, certain and settled: "This deer is mine; I am in this forest."
From that time forth, I became a deer right there in that inner corner of the excellent mountain, feeding on blades of grass and sprouts of dūrvā.
Then, once upon a time, seeing a hunter who had arrived at the border of my territory seeking game, I became afraid and intent on flight.
Then, O scion of Raghu, having approached him and led him to his home, he kept him there for three days and brought him here for your pleasure.
O sinless one, I have related to you this entire account of my own life, which is like the illusion of saṃsāra and filled with the flavor of various wonders.
Thus, this ignorance is infinite and characterized by the spreading of its branches; it is certainly not extinguished by anything other than the knowledge of the Self.
Śrī Vālmīki said: When Vipaścit had spoken thus and remained silent for a moment, Rāma, whose intellect is beyond reproach, then addressed him with these words.

Śrī Rāma said: "O Lord, tell me: how does one who perceives thus without volition—yet who possesses the volition of 'otherness' within the Self—become a deer that has entered the state of being an object of sight within creation?"
Vipaścit said: "That great corpse which fell upon the surface of the earth in this world was [once] that very ground when Indra, traveling with pride over his sacrifices, formerly went there."
Struck by a foot in the sky while established in meditation, Durvāsas—unaware that he had passed away—became enraged and cursed him.
O Śakra, this corpse, as vast as the shell of the universe and like unto the earth itself, shall before long reduce your most terrible [chariot] to powder.
"Since you have passed me by with the thought that I am a corpse, you shall therefore quickly reach the earth through my curse."
Just as that sage had previously spoken for the sake of the deer, saying "O Goddess," so too did she, by means of that very speech, always bring him within the range of her vision.
In reality, however, it is neither existent nor non-dual, nor even non-existent; that manifestation arises in such a way—so, is it existent or rather non-existent?
Furthermore, O Raghava, hear from me another argument for the sake of a very clear understanding of this composition.
O highly fortunate one, in that Brahman wherein all is, from which all comes, which is all, and which is everywhere—in that, what indeed is not possible here?
It is logically tenable that what is born of conceptual construction does not meet with another; it is also logically tenable that what is born of conceptual construction meets with another.
It is understood that what is born of volition meets with another; for wherever there is shade in the universal self, right there is also sunlight.
If that [universe] were not possible, how could it attain the state of being the self of all? Why is it true that a city of imagination does not coalesce with another?
And thus, even as it embraces all forms within itself, there is nothing therein that is not true, and there is nothing therein that is not false.
Everywhere, in every way, everything, at all times, O you who possess every form! Alas, how treacherous is this illusion that brings about the delusion of the mind!
Insofar as injunctions and prohibitions find their locus in one place, such is this reality of Brahman, which by itself constitutes its own self.
By her, ignorance is experienced as both beginningless and having a beginning; for if the three worlds were nothing more than pure consciousness, [ignorance would not exist].
How could the creation of those things destroyed at the end of a great aeon occur directly? How would there be the existence of fire, how of wind, and how of earth?

Therefore, apart from the mere manifestation of intrinsic nature, there is no other world; this is the teaching of the scriptures, experience, and the people of the world, according to those who speak until the end of the great aeon.
The wise know that essence is not other than the body; it is pure consciousness, the very existence of Brahman, yet [it appears otherwise] due to the thought "I am ignorance."
This world-form throbs like the beauty of the wind from its very movement; herein, no one dies, nor is anyone born.
The very appearance that "I am dead" and "this exists" is of the nature of consciousness; if death were absolute annihilation, then it would be like sleep, which is comparable to bliss.
If there is again the perception of the visible object, is that not indeed life itself? Therefore, there is no death here, nor is there any life here at all.

In some mere manifestation, both [existence and non-existence] may be present, or neither may be; that which is conceptualized exists as a duality, while that which is not conceptualized is neither of the two.
And that which is perceived is only one, the infinite consciousness; therefore, tell me, what indeed is life apart from pure consciousness?

Because it is inexhaustible, that [reality] is not suffering; therefore, where could there be suffering for anyone? Everything, including the designator, must be declared as being there only the space of consciousness.

That which is different from it and that which is non-different from it—what are unity and duality there? Just as whirlpools and the like exist in water, so do bodies and the like exist in the Supreme.

The world is nothing but the unagitated manifestation of consciousness—unobstructed like space itself—whose nature consists of the arrangement of that [consciousness's] existence, and whose essence is non-different from its cause.

It is a marvel that there exists a substance so dense, agitated, and characterized by resistance; yet likewise, there is no ground for such manifestation, nor is there a ground for the experience of the present.
In that regard, let it be understood that through delusion this Piśāca appears as the "self" within the void; yet, just as this void is such, so too is this void—this void remains as the void.
Thus, from this [unreal] has arisen the real; from this, the other is the supreme void. That which is the nature of consciousness is itself the world; herein there is neither oneness nor duality.
There is neither any resistance nor any lack of resistance; for one who sees the reality of things as they are, everything that is seen is non-resistant.

In this context, both the knowledge of that and the lack thereof exist neither as real nor as unreal; since both the real and the unreal are non-existent, everything is therefore the single silence of wood.
Whatever is perceived as the infinite Brahman—that alone is the supreme state; all this is established as being nothing but the Supreme Brahman.
In this way, this element of consciousness shines forth within itself; its shining is the world, the unobstructed form of the void.
At the beginning of creation, there are innumerable souls of deceased beings everywhere, even in every single finger-breadth; they are infinite in number, invisible, and do not obstruct one another.

Those inhabitants of the world of the Siddhas, having reached their own respective places where they have gathered together, do not see one another, even though they remain there joined to each other.
This splendor of the visible world is indeed space itself, having the nature of the sky; it is non-different from consciousness, appearing as the seer of its own self, like a dream.
For when this [reality] is fully understood, it remains just as it is: its nature is the extinction of mere appearance, a state of profound stillness devoid of any manifest form.
The entire web of the world—whether existent or non-existent—is stilled through thorough knowledge, remaining as it truly is, its nature being the cessation of all particularity.
Just as there is a momentary separation and reunion of drops of ocean water, so too do the atoms of consciousness flash forth from one another within the ocean of Brahman.
At the beginning of creation, the splendor of the world appears like a dream, consisting of the sky of consciousness; therefore, it is logically established that all this is the peaceful Brahman.

I have seen worlds of infinite splendor and experienced them as they unfold through the transformation of karma; I have wandered through the ten directions for many eons, yet the defect of the perceptible world does not come to an end except through knowledge.
Śrī Vālmīki said: While Vipaschit was speaking thus, the Sun departed for another world, as it were, with his far-reaching rays, in order to observe that event.
A roar of "Victory! Victory! arose, filling all directions like a drum sounding at the end of the day, as if released by the quarters of the sky themselves out of joy.
For the sake of Vipaścit, Daśaratha gradually provided his household, wives, wealth, and other such riches, as well as royal power commensurate with his station.
Having mutually bid farewell and performed the rites of worship in due order, the king, Rāma, Vasiṣṭha, and the others departed for their respective abodes.
Having bathed, eaten, and passed the night, they returned at dawn; that assembly hall remained established in that very same arrangement.
Then the sage spoke in due order that story as it had been introduced, emitting a delight like nectar through the radiance of his face, like the moon.
"O King, this is ignorance; it exists as if real though it is unreal. Even with such an effort, this has not been definitively resolved by the wise."
Thus, ignorance, when not fully understood, appears as long-lasting and endless; but when thoroughly understood, it does not exist at all, just like a river in a mirage.
O one of great intelligence, you yourself have indeed witnessed this history of the wise Bhāsa, who was their minister.
Through these discourses similar to those you have heard from me, he will come to know that supreme state; and when ignorance has been stilled, he will become liberated while living.
Consciousness is sustained by Brahman within the Self through its own existence as ignorance; due to that delusion, even what is non-existent appears to it as if it were real.
When this ignorance consists solely of Brahman and nothing else, then it exists as unknown; once known, it does not differ [from that which was unknown].
Thus, this ignorance is infinite, abounding in manifold productions; it is insentient yet charming, a cluster of springtime blossoms made of passion that brings about delusion.
Hollow within, knotted, smooth, with beautiful sprouts and thorns, dull yet full of sap, and long—she was like a forest bamboo creeper.
The vain hope for fruit, which is utterly fruitless yet captivates the mind, is not welcomed by those seeking the highest good, like a garland of flowers out of season.
It was not at all material, yet it seemed massive, filling various worlds; agitated by living beings and devoid of light, it was like a vast expanse consisting of nothing but darkness.
Like the illusion of a tuft of hair, with its various knots and entanglements, it is seen falsely in the sky; when not seen, it is nothing at all.
Variegated in color, devoid of qualities, and possessing an expansive form within the void, it consists of the movement and agitation of the insentient, like a streak of Indra’s bow in the sky.
Abounding in dull waves, frothing with the rising of turbidity, and consisting of inexhaustible whirlpools, it is like a surging river in the rainy season.
It is like a hundred mirages in a world that flows incessantly toward emptiness—a harsh expanse consisting of heaps of dust, as ill-fated as a field of corpses.
Just as one does not reach an end while wandering for a long time in a city of dreams, so it is likewise when wandering for a long time in this city of dreams called the waking state.

Those nets of conceptual constructions that have fully attained a firm foundation belong to those of steadfast mind who have abandoned the body situated within the net of the singular object of perception.
Those jewels within the casket of the space of consciousness remain without crowding, existing in this manner in the form of celestial chariots, cities, lands, and so forth.
Those very abodes of the perfected ones shine in the sky in relation to one another; though they are uncountable, unseen, and non-existent, they are yet clearly perceived.
And there were lakes made of gold, jewels, rubies, pearls, and lapis lazuli, as well as lakes filled with elixirs and an abundance of various kinds of food, both solid and soft, and drinks.
And [the lands] were filled with streams of honey, wine, curd, milk, and ghee, and were surrounded by women whose forms were composed of elixirs.

They were filled with flowers, fruits, and sprouts of every season; their dwellings were crowded with women moving restlessly in playful grace; and through the mere act of volition, they were at all times teeming with an abundance of every kind of wealth.
Some [worlds] consist of a thousand lunar disks and a hundred suns; some are composed of gold, nectar, clothing, and water.
Some were filled with darkness or light according to their own will, consisting of eternal bliss, and being led along, they were as light as fine cotton.
Some [worlds] arise and perish in a single moment by the power of time; they possess infinite food and drink, and are free from old age and death.
They possess diverse architectural arrangements and manifold splendors; they are delightful with the qualities of all seasons and consist of everything that satisfies every desire.
Since those nets of conceptual constructions arise from the performance of virtuous deeds, how could they possibly serve as a wall for minds that are steadfast?
My dear friend, nothing else whatsoever exists here within the Self, which consists solely of Brahman; therefore, let it be said: what could this [universe] possibly be composed of?
At the very beginning of creation, there was not even this slightest thing whatsoever; since there is an absence of a cause, of what nature could this world possibly be?
Just as those endless things are conceived within consciousness, so do they appear; tell me, what is the wonder in this?
Even now, O virtuous one, you, others, or anyone else—likewise, the cities of intense, fervent resolve exist only in the sky.
If, indeed, by practicing with single-minded focus, they perform those [aerial feats] by chance, then, having abandoned this body, they attain them in the sky before long.
But he who pursues these two imagined entities obtains [the fruit] like heaven and so forth; indeed, one whose mind is focused on a single object attains that very one.
Just as the Siddhas always shine forth in this way by the power of internal conceptualization, so too do the sufferings of hell and other realms appear solely through conceptualization.
Whatever is perceived, that is experienced exactly as it is; whether this physical body exists or not, it is the mind-made body alone that experiences it.
When the living being abandons one cognition consisting of the body due to a certain state, it immediately perceives another cognition consisting solely of that same state right there.

Pure consciousness perceives pure worlds, while impure [consciousness] perceives impure ones; being of the nature of space, it experiences for a long time only those things that are of the nature of space.
The pure consciousness perceives and even experiences the perfected cities themselves; the impure consciousness [perceives] forms and sufferings within the hells.
There, one undergoes the grinding of two revolving mountains of stone like churning boulders, followed by falling into a blind well from which there is no further rescue.
By the harsh and extreme cold, his body has become like stone; his form has become a dwelling place for endless desert paths filled with living embers.
It was filled with clouds of glowing embers raining down burning coals, and it was terrible with a harsh shower of a multitude of heated iron arrows.
It carried stones, wheels, swords, rivers, and moved through the sky; it shattered with blows from axes that resembled clouds raining down pearls upon chests.
There is immersion with the sound "cham-cham" from contact with the harsh surface of heated iron, and the crushing by weapons and machines accompanied by loud, grating "kaṭakaṭa" sounds.
A rain of wheels, vajras, clubs, spears, tridents, swords, and arrows; the seizing of thorny silk-cotton trees, nooses, and the piercing with hundreds of sharp darts.
Sinking into the underworld due to the collapse of heaps of heated sand; the fear of fire concealed by lamps; and being chewed by large crows.
There was the entry into great pits of glowing coals from which there was no exit, and the piercing with arrows, spears, clubs, darts, bhushundis, and discuses.
There, hosts of hungry ghosts, harsh with the agitation of hunger, gnaw at one another's limbs; they fall from palm-trees onto surfaces of exceedingly rough stone with a loud crash.
It is crowded with rivers of pus and the like, mired in the mud of blood and impurities; there, one is ground by rocks, weapons, horses, elephants, and stones.
The multitude of people was scratched by owls from the abyss and struck by pestles; circles of vultures swarmed over the fragments of heads, hands, hooves, and shoulders scattered about.
From the firm conviction that "this fruit arises from this evil deed," one sees it thus—uncontradicted and extensive—due to the stability of the place.

Whatever consciousness has ever appeared in the sky of the mind, or has not appeared, or is indeed unprecedented—that arises from conceptualization and is composed of that very thing; therefore, it moves for a long time by its own inherent impulse.
Śrī Rāma said: "Regarding this conduct of the sage and the hunter, which involved hundreds of various conditions—could this have been caused by something else, or was it born of their own nature?"

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Such whirlpools of creative manifestation perpetually arise spontaneously within the great ocean of the Supreme Self, by themselves, within their own self, having the nature of space.
Just as from wind, whose nature is vibration, incessant streaks of movement arise, so too from the existent consciousness within the sky of consciousness, [thoughts] arise endowed with manifestation.
In whatever manner this radiance of intuition has arisen from this [source] as its own inherent limb, it remains exactly so here, unimpaired by any other.
Just as there is here only one single whole possessing various parts, so too this single space of consciousness-Brahman is of the nature of manifestation.

Certain manifestations in Brahman are stable and others unstable, like reflections appearing as objects; they reside within the Self, just as bodily states reside in the soul, yet remain established in the Self which is the space of consciousness.
The manifestation within one's own self, like a city in a dream, is a wonder of consciousness; what therein is essence and what is non-essence? What might be real, or what might be unreal?
This entire visible world has been fully understood as being nothing but the expanse of consciousness; once awakened, it is neither existent nor non-existent—how can it be described?

In this auspicious world, which is everywhere a mere manifestation of the space of consciousness, what room is there for attachment or non-attachment? Those who know it abide simply according to the natural state of things.

Arising by themselves from the ocean of the Self like waves produced by its own manifestation, these [entities] are essentially identical with their own source—the Divine—by virtue of the perception of cause and effect.

Just as one's own volition creates its own world, that which is the vast and supreme space of consciousness perceives the universe by that very means; for what are "earth" and the other elements here?
Thus this appearance shines forth, yet nothing at all shines; it is Brahman itself, established in Brahman, which by its own nature is designated as "ignorance."
The entire world here is nothing but the sky of consciousness, which is the density of the density of consciousness; this alone is the supreme awakening, and its full maturity is liberation.
The manifestation, which is merely the form of the emptiness of the sky of consciousness, is pervasive; this world appears as nothing but something unobstructed and tranquil.
For one who meditates, whose body has been dissolved, and whose vision remains fixed for a moment in meditation—apart from pure consciousness alone, what power could possibly be said to exist?

In whatever manner a portion of the space of the element of consciousness appears within something, it remains there in that very manner, according to its own inherent nature, for as long as it so exists.

For one who lacks discernment, the delusion of the visible world—which is actually composed of space—does not subside, just like the fault of seeing two moons caused by an ophthalmic disorder known as *timira*.
Whatever is seen here is indeed that very Brahman, free from affliction—the beginningless and endless sky of consciousness; how could it, and what, ever be extinguished?
That which is the manifestation of one's own self—like a dream—which does not abandon its own nature consisting of pure consciousness, is what is called this world.
When one does not engage in mutual conceptualizations regarding the meanings of the treatises through a sharp intellect, one makes oneself as if asleep and is awakened by someone who is awakened.
This consciousness which is known as "ignorance" is indeed non-deviant; surely it does not exist for you at all, like dust upon rivers.
Just as in a dream there is no earth anywhere even though it is experienced by oneself, so too this visible world does not exist, being composed of unreality even though it is experienced by oneself.
Just as in a dream, objects appear as if they were fire within the mere expanse of consciousness, so too in the waking state, fire is perceived as belonging to oneself alone.
There is no distinction whatsoever between "this is waking" and "this is dreaming," because both are experienced as entirely equal within the reality of the ultimate truth.
"Just as the cognition 'this is not so' arises upon waking from a dream, so too does the cognition arise for one who has died and awakened in the next world while in the waking state."
In this world, the cognition that "sleep" and "waking" last for a short or long time occurs because of the similarity between them both in the experience of the present.
Externally, because all qualities such as "thusness" and so forth are entirely equal, neither the waking nor the dreaming state is superior, just like two twins.
"That which is waking is this dream, and that which is dreaming is indeed waking"—the thought "this is certainly not so" arises for both states over time.
Just as hundreds of dreams are indefinite until the end of life, so too are hundreds of waking states indefinite until great awakening and nirvana.
Just as many dreams that arise and then perish are remembered, so too do the Buddhas and the Siddhas remember hundreds of their own past births.
Thus, when there is complete similarity within the nature of total experience, the waking state shines like a dream, and the perception of a dream is like the waking state.
Just as the two words "the visible" and "the world" have always attained the same meaning, so too are these two [states] traditionally understood to consist of waking and dreaming.
Just as a vast dream-city is nothing but the void composed of consciousness, so too is this world; therefore, where is ignorance seen, and from whence does it arise?
If that very self which is of the nature of pure space is called ignorance, then when it exists, that itself is my bondage, consisting of its own mental construction.
Therefore, let this not be done; for this is the bondage of one who is truly unbound. What difference can there be between the stainless sky and the formless self consisting of consciousness?
In this manifestation of the space of pure consciousness, where indeed there is no objective form, how could there be bondage or liberation, known as "the visible" or "ignorance"?
Ignorance does not exist by name; there is no bondage for anyone. There is no liberation for anyone, nor is there any such thing as "existence" or "non-existence"—this is sufficient.
Neither knowledge nor ignorance exists at all; this unborn consciousness alone shines forth, appearing as space within space, like a dream embodied by its own creation.
The nature of consciousness that exists in the interval when one has gone from one place to another is precisely the form of what is perceived in waking and dreaming; this is the certain conclusion.

The form that belongs to one who is in peaceful sleep regarding all that is visible, both external and internal, is the very form of those who perceive waking and dreaming here in this world during the night.
Know that even this perception of difference is of that very same nature; for once one has reached the limit of consciousness, what else indeed could there be in the perception of difference?

The sky of consciousness alone is the perception of non-duality, and the sky of consciousness alone is the perception of duality; both duality and non-duality are one and the same, thus peaceful and indivisible.
Just as the perceiver consists of the perception and its object, so too, whatever is seen is the perceived; thus, the experience of duality is itself a single unity.
They know that Brahman as the void; duality, non-duality, and indeed non-duality itself. Emanation alone is the supreme Brahman; duality and non-duality are truly existent.

Having determined through "not this, not this" that it transcends everything, one should afterwards abandon even that [determination], and remain here having made oneself like a stone within the space of consciousness.

O fortunate one, proceed, drink, eat, and feed others according to their sequence, according to their natural state, and according to their arising; being free from mental agitation and motionless, become a stone for the supreme goal within the pure essence of that which is desired.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Since all objects exist as the reality of the space of consciousness, this world remains exactly as it is; even the perception and reflection of forms are nothing but the space of consciousness alone.
Since nothing other than the nature of a city in a dream exists, the world is therefore the peaceful void; here there is no diversity whatsoever.
The manifestation of consciousness itself appears as if manifold through its own non-manifoldness; it perceives itself as a non-self by means of the self, as if in dream-cities within the sky.

Like the world at the beginning of creation, this world is a city in the sky of dreams within the space of consciousness; it appears as if real, yet it is certainly unreal, though it stands as if it were real.

The meaning of the word "creation" (sarga), which consists of both the real and the unreal, exists for those who know it as known by them, but not for fools; nor does it exist for the ignorant as known by them, nor for those who possess that knowledge [as known by them].
But regarding that which remains within the internal cognition of those two—the one who knows it and the one who does not—they do not know each other, neither to understand nor to speak.
In their own minds, the referents of the word "heaven" are mutually [contradictory], for these two possess stability and instability while awake, like two men—one sober and the other intoxicated.
Just as waves exist within the water of a river by means of its fluidity, so too do the waves of creation exist within consciousness by means of the Intellect.
That which is of the nature of consciousness, though it is nothing at all, appears as this something existing; though invisible, it shines as if visible, like cities in a dream.
This shadow called the "world" shines forth; is it not indeed formless, yet appearing as if possessed of form, like the shadow cast by a material object?
This is merely the body, consisting only of delusion and composed of unreality; it is a firm seat of illusion, mostly like the appearance of a phantom in a state of confusion.

Like a kingdom of the mind, unreal and flickering like a dangling drop of water—since it is experienced as such by these two means of cognition, how can there be any reality in that which is non-existent?

Like the sound of splitting wood or the roar of waves and wind, sounds in the sky appear as the bursting forth of the wind; likewise, objects appear through the arising of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
From the beginning of creation, one’s own conceptualization shines forth like a mountain in a dream; yet in reality, there is no word, no object, and no state of being visible.
Whatever exists and whatever appears—all that is ultimately real; because there is no other cause, it was not produced even at the beginning of creation.
With the distinctions of words and meanings cast aside, yet with all objects of experience uncast aside, let it be understood: "I am stilled, I am fully extinguished; I am indeed like space."
Let this state of agitation, which has arisen from the unreal and is produced by the self within the living soul, be abandoned through resting in the self, whose sole nature is pure awakening.
For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self; if the self is not protected by the self, there is no other means for its protection.
O Ocean, as long as this youth of yours remains, cross over this world called saṃsāra by means of the boat of pure intellect.
Do this very day what is for your welfare; for when one has grown old, what will you be able to do? For even one's own limbs become a burden in such a state of reversal.
Childhood, old age, the state of being an animal, and death itself—these are known as the life of the living being, provided that youth is discerning.
Having entered this saṃsāra, which is as flickering as a flash of lightning, one should extract the essence from the mire through contact with true scriptures and virtuous people.
Alas! How cruel are these men; what will be their destiny? For they seek their own prosperity even while sinking themselves in the mire.
Just as an assembly of clay-made zombies causes terror to a rustic, yet once the true nature of the matter is understood, they are seen to be merely clay and cause no fear; so it is with this.

Thus, for the ignorant person, the visible splendor consisting of Brahman brings about destruction; whereas, when there is the realization of the true nature of reality, Brahman alone remains, bringing no destruction.
This very unpeaceful visible world becomes pacified; though it remains, it dissolves through the thorough knowledge of reality. While being seen, the visible is no longer seen.
Just as during the time of a dream, even though there is a vivid experience, through thorough understanding one reaches the state of truth which is the very unreality [of that experience].
Even while such an experience of creation is being felt within the sky of consciousness, through the realization of reality, only emptiness remains.

In these wildernesses of life, scorched by the fever of birth, these senses have grown old through the process of being carried away like deer by the wind; having conquered them—those which are accompanied by the gusts of the intoxicated wind of the mind—attain victory and abandon rebirth.
Śrī Rāma said: "Without the conquest of the senses, this state of ignorance does not subside. Therefore, O Sage, tell me how those senses are to be conquered."

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For one of narrow vision, there is no light in abundant enjoyments, nor in manhood, nor in life, nor in the liberation of the senses, just as there is no light for a lamp in the dark.
Therefore, listen to this complete method for mastering the senses; by means of this body, one attains perfection through one's own effort and with ease.

Know that the Puruṣa is pure consciousness alone; from consciousness arises that which is called the individual soul (jīva). Whatever it perceives within, it becomes absorbed in that very thing in an instant.
By drawing back the sharp goad of conscious effort and awakening, one conquers the intoxicated elephant of the mind; it cannot be won otherwise.
