The mind is the leader of the army of the senses; victory comes from conquering it. Is not the ground already covered with leather for one whose feet are hidden by shoes?
For one who remains with consciousness firmly planted in the space of consciousness within the heart, the mind itself becomes stilled, like autumnal mist.

My dear, the mind does not become so tranquil through a multitude of austerities, pilgrimages, sciences, and sacrificial rites as it does through the restraint of effort regarding one's own consciousness.
Whatever is experienced, that very thing is surely made forgotten through conscious effort within consciousness; thus, there is mastery over enjoyments.
When consciousness is somewhat restrained from the bait of sense objects through the effort of self-awareness, that state of the wise is attained.
"Whatever comes to me through the practice of my own dharma—that alone pleases me, nothing else. With these words, become firm as a diamond.
He who avoids the engagement of consciousness with conflicting objects, and remains established while cultivating tranquility and contentment, is one who has conquered his senses.
The mind of one who experiences neither agitation toward the inner relish of consciousness nor toward its states of insipidity becomes tranquil.
Through the restraint of consciousness and effort, the mind abandons its own habitual course; freed from mental fickleness, it pursues discernment.
One who possesses discernment and a noble soul is said to have conquered the senses; he is not deluded by the force of the waves of latent impressions in the ocean of existence.
Through constant association with the virtuous and the diligent study of authentic scriptures, one who has conquered the senses perceives the world as it truly is, according to reality.
Through the contemplation of truth, the turmoil of cyclic existence comes to rest; it is like the perception of water in a desert, which brings the suffering of falling into what is false.
This world is established as nothing but unconditioned pure consciousness; for one who possesses such true awakening, how could there be any notions of bondage or liberation?
Just as water that has been exhausted and is formless does not flow again, so too the visible object, when severed by knowledge, does not sprout forth, being without cause.
Sensation is merely space, assuming forms such as "you" and "I"; setting this aside, everything else that exists as "I" and so forth is the world.
This entire world, beginning with the notion "I," is nothing but ignorance; it abides within the space of consciousness alone, peaceful, and having emptiness as its sole body.
In the sky of consciousness, it is only the shadow of consciousness that appears as the world; and this consciousness is indeed utterly void—void even of the void—such is the certain conclusion.
By whom indeed can the analogy of seeing a dream be refuted here? For that which is composed of the unreal is experienced, and even what is personally experienced is composed of the unreal.
Just as that which is honored as a kingdom has as its essence nothing but consciousness, and lacks agent, action, and instrument, so too is the form of the world for the Consciousness.
I am devoid of agent, object, and instrument; I am pure mass of consciousness alone. This world is indefinable, characterized solely by self-awareness.
Just as death experienced in dreams does not exist, so too this ignorance—the desire for water in a desert—though appearing to exist, does not exist.

At the beginning of creation, the sky of consciousness perceived its own shimmering reflection within the void; thus, the world—rootless and arising by chance like the "crow and the palm fruit"—manifested of itself.
This appears entirely rootless, appearing as if luminous even though it is not luminous; therefore, the wise know that which is this luminosity to be the very state [of liberation].
Whatever appears here as the manifestation of living beings and so forth is indeed that very [emptiness]; emptiness itself becomes the sky, just as whirlpools are nothing but water.
Just as the form of a whole possessing parts would be one yet possessed of parts, so too Brahman, though partless, has the individual soul (*jīva*) and other things as its parts.
The object of perception is a mere appearance; it is pure consciousness, peaceful and immutable. Since you are established in this, what is there to be deliberated upon within your own true nature?
In the supreme state, there are no internal mental constructions whatsoever, neither beginning nor end; this very [supreme] nature is what is called ignorance, for here no ignorance exists at all.
Whether entering from sleep into the waking state, or from the waking state entering sleep, or whether awakened or even unawakened, the living being remains in a single uniform nature.

When deep sleep and the fourth state (turya) are present, they always exist; whereas in the dreaming and waking states, the intellect of the awakened one knows the waking-dream as being truly one with the fourth state.
For the awakened one, waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are all the fourth state (turya); for him, ignorance does not exist, and though he appears to abide in duality, he is indeed non-dual.
Duality and non-duality, "I" and "this"—how could such conceptualizations exist for one free from ignorance? How could there be even a trace of space?
The ignorant play with the distinctions between duality and non-duality and the confusions of various scriptural compositions; those mature in wisdom laugh at them.

The sprout of the space of the heart, which puts an end to the dispute between duality and non-duality, does not arise here without this [practice]; for without it, the cleansing of the space of awakening does not occur.

Having become friends through debate, we have engaged in an inquiry into duality and non-duality within the inner chamber of the heart, which serves as a broom for sweeping away the dust of ignorance.
With their minds fixed on that and their lives dedicated to it, awakening one another and constantly speaking of it, they are contented and they rejoice.
For those who are constantly disciplined and who worship with love, this yoga of wisdom arises, by which they attain that supreme state.
If one must exert effort even to conceal a mere blade of grass, how can the concealment of the hosts of the three worlds be accomplished without effort?

Even the world becomes an object of ridicule for that [mind] which, though established in the highest state, is released from internal calamity, yet remains spread out, situated in the heart, base, and powerless.

What indeed is this so-called happiness that sprouts forth as the desire for kingship and the like? When one finds rest solely in the knowledge of reality, even the status of the king of gods is but a blade of grass.
Just as those who are asleep and awake perceive the visible world and take delight in it, so too do the peaceful and virtuous, being detached from the visible, perceive that supreme state.
Without a heavy burden of effort, this is never accomplished; know that the supreme state is the fruit of the great tree of practice.

"This has been said at great length; what is the use of this?"—thus thinks the one of dull intellect. Even when this much has been stated, the one of ignorant mind does not grasp it, nor does he accept it.
If this is repeatedly relished through constant turning back, and if it is heard and spoken by one who knows it, then one becomes like that which is known.
But that lowest of men who, having looked at it even once, should discard it thinking "it has been seen"—he indeed gains from the scriptures nothing but ashes.
This supreme narrative should always be studied like the Vedas; it should be explained and honored, for it bestows the fruits of the goals of human existence.
Whatever is obtained from this scripture is likewise obtained from the Veda; when this is known, both ritual action and knowledge attain purity.
When this is known, the established doctrine of Vedānta and logic is understood; this supreme narrative has been explained according to the perspectives of the scriptures.
I say this out of compassion for you, not out of deceit; but you yourselves perceive it as a deception—let this be investigated.
From the understanding born of reflecting upon this supreme treatise, all other treatises appear like side dishes seasoned with salt.
Disregarding this narrative as ignoble because your intellect is fixed on the visible world, may you not become destroyers of yourselves, partaking in the cycle of existence.
"Thinking, 'This is my father's well,' base men drink its salty water; likewise, O discerning ones, do not remain perpetually ignorant."

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Within the solar orb of consciousness in this world, the atoms of living beings are its constituent parts; since those parts are identical to it, it possesses the nature of being partless.
Having attained supreme awakening, everything abandons its own objective form; yet, because it remains in a state of oneness with that [awakening], nothing else whatsoever exists.
In all these states, however, that which is the object for one who knows reality is none other than the supreme, stainless Brahman; it is never anything else at any time.
That which has as its object one who does not know reality, only he knows that; we, however, know neither "I," nor "you," nor one who does not know reality, nor that object.
The notions "this is that," "I am this," and "this is real" do not arise in one who knows reality; for where is there a mirage on Mount Meru?
Just as when the mind is fixed upon one object, cognitions of other objects do not arise, so too other cognitions do not coexist [simultaneously].
This world was not, nor has it arisen, nor does it exist, nor will it come to be; it is Brahman alone, whose nature is reality, established in this very manner.
The vermilion hue and the shimmering of glass abide in the Self alone; that which is called "the world" is perceived therein solely through the knowledge of that [Self].

Just as in dreams and in cities of imagination, there is nothing else but pure consciousness—the clear sky—apart from that; and just as in formless things there is neither anything nor any form, so it is with this world currently called "waking."

It is said that something called "this" arises previously, yet it does not truly exist; because it is consciousness, it is like the beginningless sky. Since there is neither a cause nor a cooperative condition for it, what kind of statement is this—that a thing arises by itself?

Therefore, nothing here comes into being by itself; for in the beginning, neither Brahmā nor others exist, being unknown to the ignorant. This all-pervading space is this very Self-born One; thus, the sky of consciousness alone shines forth through consciousness.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In the dream within the waking state, the dream itself assumes the nature of waking; and in the waking within the dream-state, the waking indeed attains the condition of dreaming.
Dream enters into waking, and from dream one awakens to waking; waking enters into dream, and the awakened one [emerges] from the dream-waking state.
The dream of one who possesses both waking and dreaming is called "dream"; the waking of one who possesses both dreaming and waking is called "waking-waking."
In this state, waking is indeed waking, and never a dream; in a dream, it is a dream, and while awake, it is indeed waking, and never a dream.
For the dream state is always of a short duration within the waking state, and the waking state is likewise always of a short duration during the time of dreaming.
There is never any difference whatsoever between waking and dreaming; for one, there is no opportunity in the other, and neither is composed of reality.
At the time of awakening from death, the waking dream subsides; and upon the realization of the experience of the dream, there remains only the exceedingly luminous void.
For one who is alive, during the time of dreaming, nothing whatsoever pertaining to the next world is perceived in the waking state, except for the arising of the cognition of death.
While this empty consciousness of life, whose nature consists of various maladies, persists, not even a single dream consisting of a "next world" is perceived.
Just as the three worlds in a dream consist of nothing but the wonder of consciousness, so too do they appear in the waking state, from the very moment of their creation within the heart.

Although they appear vast, these things are indeed unreal from the perspective of ultimate truth; this possession of forms does not exist at all, just as [forms] do not exist in the waking state for one who is dreaming on the earth.
Just as the world in a dream, though appearing diverse and luminous, is empty, so too in the waking state this entire universe is but space, whose nature is consciousness.
For this is the very nature of the sky of consciousness that this world appears here in the expanse of space, expanding like light from a luminous source.
This wonder called the world shines forth intensely as something innate, whether in the sky or on a wall, in an atom, on dry land, or in water.
While delusion—though unreal in nature—persists as if it were a real entity, and its body is nothing more than empty space, who indeed could have any attachment toward it?
The world, consisting of the nature of the grasper, the grasping, and the grasped, is indeed empty; let it be existent, or let it be non-existent—my dear friend, what is the point of attachment here?

"Let this be so, or let it be otherwise; let it not be, or let it come to pass—what cause for agitation is there here? What attachment to fruit is there in a fruit that is insignificant? That [reality] has been understood; enough with conceptual constructions!"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Know this "manifestation of the self" (ātmakhyāti) to be devoid of both the meaningful word "self" and the word "manifestation," as solid and dense as the interior of a stone.
From the very beginning of creation, the sky of consciousness alone has been thus expanded; that which shines within itself is called "creation" by the awakened one precisely because of that.
Rivers do not flow here, nor is there any emerging or submerging; the sky shines within the sky itself, and thus the nature of consciousness shines forth, free from all movement.

They know this as *ātmakhyāti* (self-apprehension), which is devoid of any mention of an external object and entirely free from the conceptualization of an external thing, lacking any subsequent objective referent.
This entire world is indeed the Self alone, wherein there is no such thing as manifestation; for that which is unmanifested is never manifested by manifestation anywhere at any time.
The verbal formulation "manifestation" and "non-manifestation" is unreal in this context; for what indeed could manifestation be there, or what could non-manifestation be?

Non-apprehension (akhyāti), misapprehension (anyathākhyāti), and the apprehension of the non-existent (asatkhyāti)—these other [theories] are merely the manifestations of the visible world, which are the wondrous play of consciousness for that whose nature is pure awareness alone.
In whatever manner, whenever, and whichever they may be, those pure rays of consciousness shine forth from the sun of the sky of pure consciousness; at that time, they appear in exactly that manner.

Self-manifestation (ātmakhyāti), non-existent manifestation (asatkhyāti), non-apprehension (akhyāti), and misapprehension (anyathākhyāti)—these are the wonders of consciousness, the manifestations of self-manifestation.
The meaning of the term "self-manifestation" (ātmakhyāti) is devoid of the term "self-manifestation"; it is without beginning or end, beyond description, and exists as this single, solid mass.
In this regard, listen to this great narrative, which is an ornament for the ears, a refutation of dualistic views, and an illumination of the sun of awakening.
There is a stainless and vast rock, measuring thousands of millions of yojanas in extent, as hard as a wall of deep blue sapphire.
It is without joints or bonds, dense, with the essence of a diamond, expansive, with an utterly robust and firm belly, and as pure as space.
Possessing a solid body that remains undestroyed throughout a multitude of incalculable kalpas, she of lovely limbs appears, by virtue of her stainlessness, as if of the very nature of space.
Its genus is indeed known, yet it is never distinguished by anyone as to what it is, where, or when; thus, it is always unknown.
Within her heart, which is devoid of the elements of the physical world, there is [a nature] dense, infinite, firm, possessing the essence of a diamond, and indestructible.
There exist in great abundance within his own body various lineal patterns, as well as lotus-clusters, conchs, maces, discuses, and so forth.
"Space, air, water, fire, and earth—these are the names assigned; there was no such thing as a 'living soul' (jīva) for those self-written [beings] according to her."
Śrī Rāma said: Tell me, how does this stone possess consciousness? How can that which is called an insentient stone indeed act?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That vast and radiant stone is neither conscious nor inert; who knows its genus, and what else exists therein?
Śrī Rāma said: "Who sees those lines within her womb, and how? Or how and by whom was she broken, and when? Tell me this."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: It is not possible to break that fierce [bond], nor does a breaker exist; likewise, everything is enveloped within this embodied being who is boundless and limitless.
Within that hollow there exist infinite networks of trees and mountains, as well as cities and towns, all composed of writing.
Among them, there are those made of writing, bearing the names of gods and dānavas; they are both subtle and non-subtle, formless yet appearing as if they had form, like little figurines.
There exists a line named Ākāśa, possessing great breadth; and within it there are secondary lines named Candra and Arka.
Śrī Rāma said: Tell me, O Brahman, by whom were those lines seen there, and of what nature were they? Or tell me, how can they be seen when they reside within the hollow of a solid stone?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O Rāghava, those such scribes were seen by me there; if you also have the desire, then you too shall see them."
Śrī Rāma said: Such a stone, as hard as a diamond, ought not to be broken; nevertheless, how was it that you saw those lines situated within its interior?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, I am situated as a line within her womb; therefore, staying there, I see that entire network of lines unimpaired.
"Who else besides me is capable of breaking that stone? Standing there within it, I beheld all of that which was inside it."
Śrī Rāma said: Who is that stone, and who are you? Tell me, where are you situated? What is this you say? Speak; what is it that you have seen?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This Great Being that is the Supreme Self has been described by me to you through this very turn of words; it is not, however, this massive stone.
We are within the belly of the stone of the supreme Self’s great existence; these [beings] are but the flesh of that stone, entirely devoid of cavities.
Know that the sky is a part of that stone; the ever-moving wind is a part of that stone; actions, words, mental impressions, and the conceptualization of time are all parts of that stone.
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, and ego—these are declared to be the various components of the stone.
The Supreme Self is the Great Being, the stone, and the flesh; we all are these very things. Thus we know that although we are non-different from it, we nevertheless appear as different.
This extremely vast stone is indeed of the single nature of pure consciousness; apart from this, where could it exist? Tell me, what can be said?
This very pure sensation alone appears as jars, pits, cloths, and so forth; it shines just as [it does] in a dream, or like water appearing in the form of waves.
The wise know that all this is the solid mass of Brahman, spread out as the solid mass of pure consciousness; it is the solid mass of the ultimate reality, peaceful, and entirely a single mass.

There is one great consciousness, whose very interior is like a solid rock, entirely devoid of cavities, boundless, and without beginning or middle. By that [consciousness], through its own nature as the power of ideation, this creation—known by the name of the "world" or the "universe"—has been fashioned.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Self-apprehension, the apprehension of the non-existent, the apprehension of what is not apprehended, and the apprehension of things otherwise—these views regarding the meaning of words are, for one who knows the truth, like the horn of a hare.
O friend, at some point indeed no mental modifications whatsoever arise; the knower remains as the peaceful, indefinable Self, with all activities having subsided.

These perceptions, such as the misconception of the Self (ātmakhyāti) and others, arise from pure consciousness alone; and that [consciousness] is the most pure ether, perceived as being of the very nature of that [ether].
The internal delusion that "this is the self" and "this is consciousness" does not truly exist; therefore, having abandoned this notion, become one who partakes in the ultimate reality.
Whether walking, standing, or even sitting, everything is therefore peaceful; it is like the silence of space—pure, uninterrupted, and devoid of activity.
Though filled with various great sounds, it remained as silent as a stone; though moving incessantly, it stood like a mountain, as still as the sky.

Though it possesses various kinds of undertakings, it is the great void, unmarked; though composed of the five elements, it is like space, having not attained the state of the fivefold [sensory objects].
Though crowded with objects, it is empty and consists of pure consciousness alone; like a great city seen in a dream, it is composed of stainless consciousness even while being perceived.
Whether with effort or without effort, it is like a city of one's imagination; it is mere space, consisting of delusion, and comparable to union with a woman in a dream.
Even though it is experienced, it is as futile as a woman who is a mere reflection; for an object constructed from various perceptions is, in reality, empty.

Śrī Rāma said: I consider this world, consisting of waking and dreaming, to be perceived through memory alone; here, memory produced by external objects that possess the nature of reality is the very cause.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That which, through the shimmering of the crystal of consciousness, appears as the body of all things by chance—being of the nature of space, the mere existence of phenomena, and without any foundation—is what shines forth.
This very [nature], whose essence is indestructible, exists at all times everywhere within the Supreme Self, just as ripples exist within calm water.
This very state, which is signless and consists of its own essential nature, exists within the Supreme Self, the Universal Self, the Nirvana, the Space-like Self, and the Selfless.
Whenever and however it appears within, by whatever means and in whatever manner—whether always or never, wherever or nowhere—it is nothing at all.
Of that very radiance of Brahman, by means of that very self which is Brahman, and of its own transparent nature, without abandoning its own inherent nature.
"This is waking, this is dreaming, this is deep sleep, and this is the fourth"—these names have been applied by oneself to the Self, which is Brahman, due to its own consciousness.
In reality, there is no dream, no waking, no deep sleep, no fourth state (turiya), nor anything beyond that; everything is the supreme, tranquil space.
Or rather, all this that has the form of waking is always [waking], or it is always a dream, or it is always deep sleep.
Or perhaps that fourth state is always within it, or else it is always this very thing which we, whose forms are but hopes, do not know.
This is nothing but foam, or perhaps a mere bubble; it is the void within the water, the sky of consciousness within the belly of the great ocean.
Whatever is perceived in whatever manner is experienced in that very way; whether it be real or unreal, in a dream it is both real and unreal, like [the appearance of] things in the sky.
This manifestation of consciousness shines forth according to its appearance: the void within the void, the form of consciousness within the form of consciousness, in the pervasive Self.
And consciousness, which is the very essence of the sky of thought, is always of such a nature; it neither sets nor rises, for this world is its own limb.
The great creations beginning with the dissolution, and the nights of the great dissolution, have become constituent parts of her alone, like hair, nails, and so forth.
Its manifestation or non-manifestation, its brilliance or its dullness, is nothing other than the Great Consciousness itself—just as movement is not distinct from the nature of the wind.
Therefore, what indeed could be called waking, what is dreaming, and what is deep sleep? What is the fourth state, what is memory, and what is desire? These are all empty, false views.
Since internal consciousness shines as its own external object, where is duality and where is the wealth of objects? Therefore, how can there be such a thing as memory?
This very thing shines forth without a supporting wall, manifesting by its own nature; it is like the luminous form of the sun in the sky, devoid of material elements.
If an external object exists in the form of reality, then let the memory arising from it serve as the cause for the existence of this world, beginning with names and so forth.
However, this external object does not exist, because it is utterly impossible for the five elements to have existed at the beginning of the first creation, due to the absence of any causal factors.
Just as a hare's horn does not exist, just as a tree in the sky does not exist, just as the son of a barren woman does not exist, so too the dark moon does not exist.
Likewise, objects such as the world, the beginning, and the "I," which appear to the ignorant, exist when not investigated; yet when investigated, none of them exists at all.
Just as this great form exists, or as it exists as nothing at all, so too, O Rāma, does this undivided reality exist as the object of those who know the truth.
Whenever the marrow of the sky of the density of consciousness arises, its supposed rising and setting are merely designated by the conventional expression "perpetually arisen."
At various times, it perceives within the void itself as if it were earth and so forth; thus, through its own manifestation, it assumes the conceptualization of earth and the rest.
The unborn Great Consciousness, which is its own manifestation and nothing but space alone, subsequently designates itself by the names of earth and the other elements.
Just as a child [perceives] a city of the imagination, so does the immutable pure consciousness maintain its own awareness that "this earth is indeed space."
One does not conceptualize whether there is manifestation or non-manifestation for that; know it to have the nature of both vibration and non-vibration, like the wind in the sky.
Just as the sky of consciousness shines, so does this appear; it is formless space within space itself, and these elements such as earth do not exist anywhere as reality.
Just as it shines, so too, by virtue of its nature as the space of consciousness, though it appears fully, it is neither existent nor non-existent; it is nothing at all, yet it is everything.
Whether it be thus or otherwise, whether existent or non-existent, as it truly stands—the wise man understands the history of the world's various successions, and no one else.

That very [consciousness], by means of the perception of the visible world shimmering within the space of the heart, manifests the external cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) in this manner, whether it be real or unreal, exactly as it stands.
What here is external, or what is internal? What is visible, and what is its visibility? All that is auspicious, peaceful, and yet unpeaceful—let it all be stilled with the syllable "Om."

Investigation devoid of the perspective of the signified and the signifier does not come to pass; and that [investigation] is accomplished through the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, no accomplishment whatsoever is possible without that, just as the perception of the eye at night is impossible without a lamp.

Therefore, having cast aside with a supremely pure intellect the internal web of manifold conceptual constructions and mental imaginings, and having established the mind in the great meaning of all the scriptures, fly up and go to the supreme state, being single-mindedly intent upon it.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as a tree, without any prior intention, produces the variety of its branches, so too does the Unborn One produce within the void itself the various appearances of creation, which are as insubstantial as space.
Just as the ocean, though lacking intellect and other faculties, produces whirlpools and the like, so does the Self of all, the Lord of all, produce all perceptions within the void of space.
From those very self-cognitions, he himself then creates various designations such as "mind," "intellect," and "ego."
The manifestation of the nature of consciousness itself occurs without prior deliberation; when the intellect and its functions are conceptualized, they appear like waves upon the ocean.
In the same way, the mind, intellect, and other faculties proceed from pure consciousness alone, just as whirlpools, bubbles, surges, and waves arise from the ocean.
Just as a mere wall is nothing more than the appearance of a painted world, so too consciousness—which is essentially the void of consciousness—is a mere manifestation.

An undertaking that is not preceded by conscious intention, yet possesses a structured arrangement, comes to pass within the process of existence; likewise, the nature of creation resides within consciousness.

Just as another person gives names such as "cluster" (gulucchaka) to the various parts of a tree, so too are names assigned to the flowers and fruits of the tree of consciousness, as well as to the earth and other elements.
Just as flowers, leaves, and so forth are not other than the great tree, even so this world is indeed not other than the supreme self, the sky of consciousness.

In the various parts of the tree, another [agent] produces diverse names; yet within the self of the space of consciousness, it appears as if distinct among all things, though being no other than the nature of the void.

The creations are but the sprouts of the tree of the mind; by virtue of being the mind itself, they do not exist at all. It is that very mind which, like a dream, appears of its own accord as both cause and effect.
If you say, "How is it that this is experienced in vain?", who would deny the existence of the first creation or of dreams and the like?
Just as this conceptualization was fashioned upon a tree that possesses form, so too has this conceptualization been fashioned upon consciousness, which is like the mere sky.

Just as fragrance and other qualities reside in a flower, and emptiness and other qualities reside in space; just as motion and other qualities reside in the wind, so do cognition and other qualities reside in the Supreme.
Just as fragrance and so forth reside in a flower, and emptiness and so forth in space, and just as movement and so forth reside in the wind, so do these creations reside in consciousness.
Just as one perceives the emptiness, movement, and fragrance of space, wind, and flowers, so too does consciousness experience creation and its persistence as being of the nature of emptiness.
Emptiness is not separate from space; fluidity is not separate from water; fragrance is not separate from the flower; and motion is not separate from the wind.

Heat does not exist separately from fire, nor does coldness exist separately from snow; likewise, the world does not exist separately from the Lord, who is the pure, singular essence of the space of consciousness.
That which is seen at the very beginning of creation in the sky, and in the heart as if in a dream, is without cause; for how indeed could it be anything other than the space of consciousness?
Let the dream itself, which is constantly observed here, be considered as the illustration; tell me, what essence can there be therein apart from pure consciousness?

This traditional teaching—that "this [world] is visible only through the mental impressions of the intellect" and so forth—is not possible; for how could that which is a non-entity (atattva) be described as such?
If that which was seen there were to exist here at the time of recollection, then it would not have been experienced there; for how could a single thing exist in two places?
Therefore, this world appears in consciousness like the "crow and the palm fruit" by way of a revolving process; subsequently, this conceptualization of dreams and so forth arises therein.
Just as waves and the like arise spontaneously when a creation occurs without prior intention, so too does the subsequent configuration and stability come about of its own accord.
That which is born is not truly born, for that which is born exists without a cause; since it is unborn, it remains today just as it was, established in that same state.
Just as the rays of jewels and other such things arise without prior intention, so too does the very existence of these perceptions of the world appear through a particular arrangement.
In whatever manner this world first comes into being, it subsequently assumes a fixed order within itself, like a whirlpool in the ocean.
In the sky of consciousness, the dream-webs and the worlds of consciousness proceed and cease without cause, though they are essentially void and empty.
Until finally, after a long time, everything becomes the cause of everything else; thus, entities such as Īśvara and the rest are essentially empty in nature.
This arises as nothing but emptiness, and it grows as nothing but emptiness; indeed, through emptiness itself, it perishes as nothing but absolute emptiness.

The void shines with the appearance of the non-void; he who denies this illustration of a dream and what has been experienced here is a person of evil intellect, like a beast under the control of its master.

This world appears as if it were real, yet it is nothing but an illusion, a mere fabrication; its essence is simply the wonder of consciousness, appearing as a fabrication to the ignorant, but as pure existence to the wise.
This long-standing conceptualization is the delusion of creation and dissolution; knowledge is the radiance of one's own nature, while ignorance is the unfolding of error.
The visible world arises suddenly from Brahman as its self, appearing without cause like a dream arising from deep sleep in the sky; subsequently, it falls under the sway of necessity.

Due to its nature as consciousness, the object of perception appears within consciousness like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence; it exists by its own nature, just as whirlpools and the like exist within the ocean.
Such indeed is this element of consciousness, consisting of mere space, that this very body of consciousness shines forth in the form of the world.

Subsequently, by that conscious being, various designations were imagined within itself—consisting of the conceptualizations of memory and so forth, of earth and so forth, and of the intellect and so forth.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, this being the case, you have stated that memory arises from the impressions of the intellect. Tell me, if memory is not fully awakened, what is attained?"
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: Listen, O Rāma; I shall split this question as a lion splits an elephant, and I shall establish the one non-duality as the sun establishes the light.
This visible world exists as the very self of the universe within the hollow of pure consciousness, like an uncarved statue existing within a tree in the forest.
A carpenter might at some time extract a carved statue from a tree; but who can carve such a figure from a single, solid pillar?

In a pillar, that [consciousness] becomes manifest only through dullness, as it remains uncarved therein; but in consciousness, being internalized, it shines forth fully within itself simply by virtue of its nature as consciousness.
Yet, while manifesting, she remains as if her body were uncarved, consisting of space itself; never falling from her own nature, she abides within the self as pure consciousness alone.

At the beginning of creation, that [consciousness], possessing the power of ideation, brings about the processes of creation by its very nature as consciousness, just as one experiences what has arisen today within the dream-self in the void of one's own being.
In the heart, which is indeed space, the statue of consciousness, taking the form of the supreme space, imagines within itself, by means of itself, various mental constructs.

"This is a portion of Brahman; this here is indeed the manifestation of pure consciousness (cinmātra); this is the intellect (citi), this is the individual soul (jīva), and that is the ego (ahaṃkāra)."
This is intellect, this is mind, this is time, and this is space; this is that "I," this is action, and this is the pentad of subtle elements.
This collection of the senses is known as the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka); here, this is the subtle body (ativāhika-deha), as well as the physical body (ādhibhautika).
I am Brahmā, I am Śaṅkara, I am Upendra, and I am Ravi; this is the external, this is the internal, this is creation, and this is the world.
This entire web of conceptual constructs is nothing but the utterly pure sky of consciousness; therefore, where are these multitudes of objects, where is memory, and where is duality or unity?
The fragment of the world's expanse is indeed without cause; at the beginning of creation, it appears like a dream, as the void itself appearing as if subject to transformation within the void.

Space shines within space itself, for that which is composed of consciousness shines within the consciousness-nature; when it is thus awakened by that very [consciousness], where is that world, since it has been realized through awakening?
Where is memory, and where is dream? Where are the times and what are the mental constructs? This manifestation of consciousness shines, peaceful like the void in the sky.
Whatever exists within the mass of consciousness has attained the state of being external; yet in reality, that is neither external nor internal, for there is nothing other than pure existence.
How could those who are blind otherwise accept that which proceeds from that which is devoid of parts, tranquil, and beyond description, as being an uncaused element?
Therefore, as is the supreme Brahman, so is this supreme visible world; just as the sky of consciousness exists in a dream, so too does the city of the dream exist.
Not even the slightest thing exists here as this visible world; where is there dust in the full ocean, and where is there a visible object in the supreme sky?
Whatever little of this appears to shine, that is merely consciousness, devoid of objects of thought; it shines as if quiescent, established thus within the Self.
From the full Brahman, the full is indeed drawn out, yet it remains undisturbed; this world shines as if it were that very light-form, the manifestation of the Supreme Self.

While I am thus speaking, alas, the inner delusion of people remains profound even as they experience its manifestation; for even now, though they know it instantly, they do not abandon the perception that the world-body is a waking state while they are dreaming.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: He for whom pleasure does not lead to pleasure, and for whom pain does not lead to pain—one whose mind is eternally turned inward—is called liberated.
He whose wisdom does not flicker, remaining unmoving within the sky of consciousness even amidst unfolding enjoyments, is said to be liberated.
He whose mind is unwavering, resting in the Self that is pure consciousness alone, and has attained delight in that very state, is called liberated while living.
He whose mind, having come to rest in the Supreme Self, does not turn back to wander again among these visible objects, is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, I consider that man to be merely dull matter, devoid of consciousness, for whom pleasure does not lead to happiness and suffering does not lead to sorrow.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: He who, being of the nature of pure awakening, does not experience pleasure through effort because he is established in the absolute solitude of the sky of consciousness, is said to be at rest.
He for whom all doubts have indeed been completely exhausted through discernment regarding all objects has come to rest in the supreme state.
He who has no aesthetic relish (*rasikatā*) toward any object whatsoever, even while engaged in worldly affairs, is said to be inwardly at rest.
He whose every undertakings are free from desire and volition, dwelling in whatever comes to him, is known as one who has found rest.
Victorious is he by whom rest has been attained within the Self through its nature as consciousness, on the long path of saṃsāra which is without support and without repose.
Those who, having run for a long time, have attained rest and remain still, appear as if asleep, even though they are engaged in worldly affairs.
For they shine as luminous suns risen eternally in the sky of the manifestation of consciousness; yet they do not remain anywhere here at all.
Even while engaged in worldly affairs with their bodies, these superior ones appear as if asleep or as if dissolved; they possess a semblance of dullness, yet they are not dull-witted.
Those who reside in the city of dreams while lying here upon their beds as if asleep are called "asleep," yet they have not fallen into a state of insentience.
He who, having rested from the long journey, does not speak even when addressed, is said to abide in the bliss of silence; he is not of dull appearance.
That which is night for all beings, consisting of the setting of ignorance—that is the supreme awakening and supreme peace; therein he is established in equanimity.
While all beings remain awake within this visible world that bestows suffering, he remains perpetually asleep therein; thus, he does not perceive it and is happy.
O scion of Raghu, he who disregards the flood of karma and abides in his very self is called one who delights in the self; he is not a dullard.
Having transcended this suffering and reached the further shore of the ocean of existence, that fortunate one remains experiencing the bliss of rest within his own self.
Exhausted on the long journey by the four objects of the senses for a long time, he was afflicted by the nature of enjoyments and beset on the path by cruel and terrifying calamities.
Repeatedly rendered inert by the thunderbolts of the frost of old age, this deer of human existence wanders in vain and restless agitation through the wilderness of birth.
The traveler on the path of saṃsāra is beset by the thorns of suffering; though the shade of happiness is difficult to attain, he wanders there, deprived of the Supreme Self.
Having made his provisions with evil deeds, he stumbles and grows exhausted at every step; rendered helpless by narrow paths consisting of gain and loss, he is driven along.
Having reached the far shore of the ocean of saṃsāra, which is devoid of [the notion of] beings, that self-possessed one, free from sleep and possessed of supreme wisdom, rests in bliss.
Alas, the self-possessed one sleeps happily—withdrawn, cast out from the world, free from dreaming and deep sleep, awakened, yet without outward consciousness or slumber.
Like a noble horse, though born here as a low-born beast, eating, moving, breathing, and speaking in the midst of the world like a great forest, alas, the self-possessed one lies happily.
The profound sleep of those who perceive reality is truly unique; it is not disturbed by the thundering of clouds at the end of an aeon, nor by the laceration of one's own limbs.
For those who perceive reality, there is a certain profound sleep entirely unprecedented, which causes even the eyes of the awakened to close.
He whose eyes remain unblinking and in whom the entire universe dissolves is truly intoxicated in the ultimate sense; alas, that self-possessed one sleeps in bliss.
Having swallowed the entire universe and attained supreme fullness, he who possesses the Self sleeps happily, having drunk the nectar of immortality to his heart's content.
Free from worldly joy yet possessing great bliss, experiencing undecaying non-dual happiness, devoid of external light yet possessing the great light—alas, the self-possessed one sleeps in peace!

With the cessation of the darkness of greed, having transcended worldly attachment, and possessing a dense expanse despite being devoid of material weight—alas, the self-possessed one sleeps in bliss!
While the world remains in a state of unpeaceful and endless suffering, alas, the self-possessed one, a supreme yogi whose mind does not turn outward, sleeps in bliss!
Making himself the smallest of the small and the largest of the large, and making the sky his bed, alas, the self-possessed one sleeps in happiness.
Within every single atom, even hundreds of millions of worlds are contained; alas, the self-possessed man rests happily within that body, which is both atomic and vast.
Whether performing the floods of dissolution and creation or not performing them in any way, alas, the self-possessed one sleeps happily upon the bed of supreme light.

Having fully understood the dream of the accumulation of saṃsāra as a state of deep sleep, and leading [his vision] toward the vast expanse of the manifest directions, alas, the self-possessed one sleeps happily!
Having attained the state of universal existence common to all the purposes of the world, he who is more pervasive than space, the self-possessed one, now lies in bliss.

Having made the sky perfectly clear and having turned the entire world into empty space, he who possesses self-mastery sleeps happily, his speech stilled and his breath suspended—alas! *Acchāccha-ambaraṃ kṛtvā jagad apy ambarī-kṛtam / śānta-śabda-paraśvāsaṃ hā śete sukham ātmavān //*
Beholding this world of ours within a corner of space, he who is himself the essence of the vast expanse of the clear sky—the self-possessed one—alas, sleeps happily!
Just as one who has rested upon a bed of grass finds comfort in the delightful worldly activities that flow on by their own current, so too does the self-possessed man lie down happily.
Through supreme personal effort characterized by thorough knowledge, one lives like the sky within the sky by means of the sky itself, as if through a dream-vision.
Through wisdom that is like space, perceiving all phenomena as resembling the sky, the Fully Awakened One, by means of wise effort, has attained the state of the supreme ether.
Awakened while sleeping, and even while asleep yet awakened, he rejoices constantly; having become as if in deep sleep, he then wakes up together with the friend who is the object of his dream.

Having spent all his days with that ancient friend—sweet with its variegated persistence and intent upon dwelling together through many lifetimes—he shall attain rest for a long time in the supreme state.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, tell me who is his friend with whom he delights; what is the nature of that delight, or is it of the essence of passion?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Its own natural flow, its inclination toward its own nature, and its own karma constitute its one true, unartificial friend.
It provides consolation like that of a father, restraint like that of a wife, and is ever-faithful in times of calamity and insurmountable distress.

He whose conduct inspires no suspicion, who has perfectly accomplished the bliss [of liberation], and who, by remaining unangered even in the face of provocations, has bestowed the nectar of winning over others.
Dedicated to extracting faults that are difficult to traverse, difficult to overcome, and difficult to restrain, it is a treasury of all the jewels of trust, inhabited since childhood.
Having been together since childhood, playing together in the dust, they were united from their very youth; he restrained her from improper conduct and was intent on protecting her like a father.
Like heat is to fire, like fragrance is to a flower, and like the day is to the sun, pure [virtue] is always inseparable from it.
Constantly devoted solely to nurturing, perpetually intent solely on protecting, and ever-ready solely for guarding against the onset of every calamity.
Like fire for gold, it bestows purity upon the body in all its states; it is solely intent on discerning what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted.
Like a citizen with delightful and blameless stories, he was a palace filled with a collection of vessels made of the jewels and rubies of virtuous deeds.
Like the sun constantly revealing what is unpleasant, as darkness does; she, like a devoted great lady, revealed only what was dear.
He made people speak kindly by acting only with kindness toward them; he was graceful, sweet, affectionate, unperturbed, and possessed a joyful disposition.
He is the benefactor of the world, worthy of worship, one who speaks with a smile first, whose passions are stilled, whose nature is virtuous, and the sole cause of the ultimate truth.
In the battle born of ignorance, he was previously intent on striking; now, his locks of hair were dancing with the playful grace of unprecedented acts of charm.
It is the protector of the essence of virtue, of one's wife, and of one's family; it is the nectar-like medicine for a mind overwhelmed by mental anguish and physical disease.
Delighting in discourse through their exceptional learning, wit, and eloquence, they stood as if divided into two, due to their shared lineage and character.
He always caused devoted kings, virtuous men, and generous donors to perform sacrifices, acts of charity, austerities, pilgrimages, and to be intent upon promoting justice and wealth.
Together with his sons, wife, twice-born men, women, servants, and kinsmen, he enjoyed auspicious food and drink in the company of the most excellent and praiseworthy.
Warding off the thirst bound to enjoyments and the like which brings suffering, it is noble with its very affectionate conversation and the supreme refuge for consolation.
Endowed with such a friend in himself and accompanied by his wife, he delights in his own karma by his very nature, impelled by nothing else.
Śrī Rāma said: O Lord of Sages, what is the wife of this friend, and what is her form? Tell me briefly.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O high-minded one, his great-souled sons, named Snāna, Dāna, Tapas, and Dhyāna, are devoted to all their subjects.
Like a crescent moon, she gives delight to the eyes of the world; inseparable from him, his wife Mudita is full of affection for him.
Her companion, who is never-failing, is filled with the wealth of compassion, captivating to the heart, and a generator of joy for him.
Equanimity is considered his constant beloved dwelling in his heart; she stands before him like a female doorkeeper, bowing low and bestowing happiness upon his face.
O virtuous one, that intellect which is ever fixed upon fortitude and righteousness—this intellect of this steadfast, pre-eminent, and fortunate man runs ahead of him.
Always resting evenly upon the shoulder of this king of great majesty, benevolence acts as the provider of counsel in his conquest of the enemies that are the sense-objects.
The noble boundary of all affairs is the teacher of wisdom, and the truthfulness of this venerable one bestows its own purpose upon everyone.
Thus, together with his retinue, friends, and ministers, conducting himself according to his own duty, he neither rejoices nor becomes angry.
That sage remains exactly as he is, his mind extinguished, like a figure eternally depicted in a painting, even while engaging in worldly affairs.
In debates devoid of substance, he was like one made of stone—mute; regarding words that served no purpose, he reached a state of supreme deafness.
Regarding all rites that contradict worldly custom, concerning corpses, and in deliberations on the conduct of the noble, Vāsuki or Bṛhaspati is the authority.

He was one whose speech was constantly engaged in meritorious discourse, possessed of eloquence toward the crooked, capable of reaching a decision in the mere twinkling of an eye, and a speaker who could quickly expound upon many subjects.
He was even-sighted, noble-minded, generous, and sharing; he was refined, affectionate, and sweet-spoken; he was handsome and possessed of meritorious renown.

This indeed would be the nature of those with awakened intellects; however, through effort, they do not become such [as the ignorant]. The moon, the sun, fire, and so forth, are never illuminated by the instigation of another.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This world shines as the manifestation of the space of consciousness; in reality, it is neither the world, nor a mere appearance, nor a void, nor distinct from consciousness.

That which shines as the sky of consciousness called the "world" is not distinct from it; it does not exist as something other than that, just as emptiness is not other than space, even though they appear otherwise.
In the interval between the departure from one place and the arrival at another, that which is the form of consciousness appears as this visible world; no other visible world exists.
Indeed, at the occurrence of the great dissolution, there is a renewed creation from the Supreme; for in the absence of a cause, how could the visible world possibly come into being?
For then not even an atom of the seed of the perceptible exists, since this wheel indeed proceeds again in embodied form.

Therefore, this visible world has never arisen at all; it is not a material object. Like the son of a barren woman, it absolutely does not exist; hence, the cognition of the visible is likewise non-existent.
Whatever appears here as the visible world standing all around, the wise know that to be pure consciousness alone, clear as the sky, the supreme state itself.
Just as one passing from deep sleep into dreaming enters a state of instability, yet the pure consciousness does not abandon its own innate, stainless, and healthy nature.
Likewise, at the beginning of creation, this very Self, by itself within itself, appears as the visible world—a manifestation of consciousness that is essentially of the nature of space.
Just as the mind appears in the form of a prior state, sluggish with its own volitions, so too does the supreme sky of consciousness appear like the visible world at the beginning of creation.

Just as the wind within itself manifests as movement like the circling of a whirlpool, so too, at the beginning of creation, the sky of consciousness remains and exists as the very appearance of the visible world.
Therefore, it is known that the visible triple world is indeed non-manifest; this supreme Brahman alone shines, established thus within its own self.
There is never anything whatsoever, such as earth or other elements, that possesses form; whether it be formal or formless, this is only Brahman that shines forth.
Just as at the time of waking, the mountain of dreams is nothing but formless space, so too, upon awakening, these three worlds are but the void of peaceful pure consciousness.
To those who are awakened, this world is the supreme Brahman, undivided; yet even the wise do not know that which is this state of non-awakening.
That form of consciousness which exists in the interval when one has gone from one place to another is indeed the true nature of all beings; that is the state of the Supreme Self.
That form of consciousness which exists in the interval when one has gone from one place to another—that is the supreme space; in it, everything is established.
Just as that state is, so is this [world], consisting of both being and non-being, wherein nothing whatsoever exists apart from the fivefold objects.
The wise know that form, light, and mental attention are this very state; these are the whirlpools of fluidity within this great ocean of the state.
In the transition from one place to another, that which constitutes the form of consciousness in the interval—apart from this, there is no such thing as the world at all.
States such as attachment and aversion, as well as views regarding existence and non-existence—without relinquishing this very form, they remain as its constituent parts.
Having abandoned the prior and posterior limits, that which is the form of consciousness in the middle is to be known as the supreme nature, designated within the ocean of the world.
Know that the intermediate consciousness occurring when moving from one place to another is the world—another name for the Self that never falls away from its own true nature.
From the very beginning of creation, this visible world has never actually arisen; that it appears to exist here is merely the deceptive display of a magician.
It is a pity that what is visible does not exist at all, yet it persists as if it did; and it is a pity that the Supreme Brahman, which truly exists, persists as if it did not exist.
Where shall I go, for this world has become perverted? That which is unreal is called "real," and thus Brahman itself is not understood.
Nothing whatsoever that is visible has ever arisen, nor does it appear anywhere; that which appears here is Brahman, shining by itself like the empty sky.
Just as a gem shines by its own radiance which is not distinct from itself, so too is the space of consciousness made manifest by a creation that is non-different from itself.
In that very same peaceful state, this sun shines; it is indeed a part of that [reality], for there is no other sun by name.
Even when situated there, neither the sun nor the moon shines; rather, it is this Lord who illuminates the sun, not the sun that illuminates the Lord.
By its light this entire visible mandala shines; it is the illuminator of all things, including the moon, the sun, and fire.
The conceptual construction of the meaning of words such as "it has form" or "it is formless" is, for those who know the truth, as unreal as a flower in the sky; it does not exist.

Just as a single atom, together with its constituent parts, shines within the light of the sun of the individual soul (jīva), so too do the suns and other luminaries either fail to shine or shine there like mere atoms.
Tell me, how could those manifestations—the sun and so forth—which are the radiance of the jewel of the space of pure consciousness, be distinct from it?
That state is devoid even of pure consciousness, yet free from emptiness; it is empty of all selves, yet endowed with all objects.
Even the earth and other elements do not exist there; nothing whatsoever exists there. Furthermore, no living beings exist there, even those who are alive.
Not abandoning the grossness of duality, these are merely atoms therein; yet here, there is no such thing as non-dual unity that does not abandon its own nature.
There is nothing here whatsoever, nor is there anything at all; "nothing" and "not-anything"—this conceptualization is far removed from this state.
The very existence of the sky-like void of pure consciousness—unitary, uninterrupted, infinite, and eternally expansive by its own nature—abides within itself under the name of the world.

When one form of consciousness has been abandoned and another has not yet been attained, that which is the nature of the world is the very nature of this [consciousness], even though it appears as manifold.
This manifold world is indeed not manifold; it is the expanse of consciousness alone, spread out in the form of the five elements, existing like consciousness in a dream.
Just as consciousness, while remaining exactly as it was in deep sleep, enters into a dream upon waking from that sleep, so too does it attain this state of creation.
As deep sleep is, so too is the dream state, and likewise the waking state; and the fourth state (turiya) is exactly like this. Therefore, the world is equal to the infinite sky.
Waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and even the fourth state—all exist as that alone. But I do not know that which the one deluded regarding the lineage of the Knower of Reality perceives.
That which is the incessant, subtle transformation of all objects—both insentient and sentient—yet remains internal and devoid of mind, intellect, and the like; [that is the Self].
The form of the perfectly pure consciousness is the objects, and they are composed of that; they do not exist as having a real nature, for it is that alone which exists in such a state.

Therefore, O sinless one, in this [teaching], not even a trace of the views that perceive the meaning of words such as "transformation" (pariṇāma) and so forth exists within these utterances intended for instruction.
From the very beginning of creation, the single Great Self has remained within itself as the supreme space of pure consciousness, by virtue of its nature as the Great Being.

In the perfectly full, unitary Self, that consciousness is manifest as all-pervasive; by means of that [consciousness], the designations "the world" and so forth are established within the Self itself.
Just as when a dream is fully understood, pleasure becomes pleasant through acceptance, while pain becomes painful in an instant through non-acceptance.
Whether walking or standing, waking or sleeping, the one who knows that [reality] remains eternally established in a single, constant composure, being ever tranquil.
For the wise person who, despite diversity, abides in non-duality; who, even in suffering, remains established in happiness; and who, though existing, is as if non-existent—what else remains for him?
Even while engaged in worldly affairs, he neither abandons nor grasps at anything; though performing external actions, he remains inwardly as one who does nothing at all.
Just as coldness belongs to snow and heat to fire, such is its nature; it would be eternal, for that is not an adventitious quality of it.
But he whose nature were such that he did not [perceive] "name" would not be a knower of reality; this alone is the mark of ignorance: that one's desire is other than its inherent nature.

With his inner heart consoled, his conceptual constructions diminished, consisting of the essence of his own true nature, and satisfied by the nectar of supreme peace, the wise one remains free from all veils.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, devoid of earth and the other elements, I consider that primordial Lord of Creatures to be nothing but the void, consisting solely of mind, like a tree of volition.
By the designation "mind," a subsequent attachment is conceived, just as a whirlpool, having arisen through the turning of the current, subsequently turns back.
How indeed can there be intellect and the other faculties for that which consists of mere existence? When earth and the other elements do not exist, what dust can there be in infinite space?
For him there is no body, mind, and so forth, nor sense faculties, nor latent impressions; although these exist, for him they do not exist at all as anything whatsoever.
O wise one, since the former lord of creatures has been liberated, how could he possibly come into existence again? There is neither memory nor rebirth for him.
For those who are liberated, there is indeed no recollection, nor is there again the arising of a body; nor is there a recurrence of place and time, as occurs with whirlpools that truly exist.
Or even if there were some body and so forth belonging to him through memory, that would be as tranquil as a city of imagination, being devoid of earth and the other elements.
Just as the form of a mountain of one's imagination, though clearly visible, is devoid of earth and other elements, so too is the body of Virāj.
And memory indeed never arises at all; that which exists for worldly intellect does not exist for the intellect of the wise.
Śrī Rāma said: "O best among those possessed of memory, why is it that memory does not arise for these [beings]? And why, O mine of all virtues, is there an absence of memory?"

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Indeed, this relationship of cause and effect exists within the realm of the perceptible; however, memory—which is characterized by the presence and absence of that [perceptual] state—does not truly exist.
From Brahma down to a blade of grass, no visible object whatsoever exists; where, how, of what kind, and from whence could the arising of memory occur?
For memory is said to be the recollection of an object that was previously seen; where the object itself does not exist, how can such mental constructions arise?
Indeed, this visible world is eternally and absolutely non-existent; since "all is Brahman" is the true meaning, how can there be any conceptual constructions arising from the memory of that [world]?
Therefore, memory is simply not possible for Prajāpati from the very beginning; how could there be any possession of form for him whose nature is pure consciousness?

That which is to be remembered exists by virtue of its ontological reality; worldly memory itself does not exist. However, there is another object of memory that possesses a true nature; listen to this from me.
The recollection of a thing that has already existed is called memory; however, such a thing does not exist at all—it neither has existed nor will it ever exist.
For indeed, this Brahman is the supreme and immovable; since it is without beginning, middle, or end, how could there be such things as memory and the like?

That which is the self of all, whose nature transcends all categories, yet is the manifestation of the sky of consciousness—tranquil even in worldly activity—it is that which I have designated by the word "Smṛti."

This so-called "recollection" is indeed the manifestation of its own nature; therefore, an external object, having been practiced [previously], appears [in recollection] due to its similarity [to that nature].
Whatever is experienced, that which makes it its own nature by way of its own-being—that object which shines forth is designated by the term "recollection."
Just as the visible world appears though it does not exist, such is its state; it appears yet is non-existent, like a rising mirage.

Those excellent cognitions which, abiding in the true universal self, shine forth, are called "memories" when their objects have become firmly established through practice due to their similarity [to previous experiences].
In the Supreme Self, all excellent cognitions appear like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence; being its own limbs, naturally established in itself, they alone are designated as "memories."

Whatever aspect of one's own nature, which is the essence of all, shines forth spontaneously as a real form, that is called "memory" by the wise because of its resemblance to an object previously experienced through repeated practice.

Whether the cause has been obtained or not obtained, for the wise, those very [cognitions] whose objects have become firmly rooted through practice are designated as "memories" (smṛti) due to their similarity [to memory].
Those designations called "memory" appear like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit; just as these parts of yours shine forth and yet do not shine forth.
In the same way, all cognitions, which consist of every thing, abide within the Self alone; they are like objects such as jars and cloths, which are composed of false knowledge.

In the same way, what need is there to investigate the object of memory as an error? Since the visible world is impossible for the knower, memory does not exist at all from the perspective of reality.
Because the existence of the world is thus a single solid mass and consists of the space of consciousness, this visible world exists exactly as it appears right now for the ignorant person.
I do not know the teaching on the means to liberation, nor its established nature; therefore, as if out of doubt and desiring to understand, the discourse on liberation is now being told.
As long as his perception of the visible world, memory, and recollection cease—due to the absolute non-arising of ignorance, folly, and delusion.
The certainty residing in the ignorant is never within our range; and whatever does not exist within the scope of a particular object, that the ignorant person does not experience at all.
Tell me, my dear, how can there be the experience of night for the sun? For that which appears as the very nature of an object is nothing other than pure consciousness itself.

Due to the similarity with an object previously practiced, that mental impression (saṃskāra) is known as memory; this applies even to those things whose nature is the self, which are of the form of the space of consciousness.
Since for all things that are conceptually constructed, even their appearance is not established, thus the world does not exist at all, at any time.
Just as water is seen in a mirage but does not exist in ultimate reality, so too does this [world] appear during dreams and at the beginning of creation.
The supreme sky of consciousness alone exists within itself as the succession of creation; thus manifested as the sky of consciousness, it has not fallen away from its true nature as existence.
Whether as form within itself or as that which exists as if having the nature of reality, it remains falsely manifested even while manifesting, having shone forth at the very beginning of creation.
Therefore, how could there be the appearance of anything to be abandoned or accepted anywhere? This is not something possessed of form, nor is it of the nature of memory anywhere.
Due to the absence of causes, the true nature of the Supreme Self shines forth; and whatever suffering would arise from having a formal shape, that very same [suffering] exists within memory.
Since this duality does not exist, that which is called "bondage" is not found; it remains as it is, purely empty within the sky of consciousness, which resembles the elemental sky.

Just as the sun, mountains, and other features of the world remain without abandoning their own essential natures, so too the state of being the universe did not abandon its form, with its fierce directions and time remaining exactly as they were.

The city of the dreamer’s dreams consists solely of the knower, whose nature is nothing but his own self-experience; it exists within the belly of the space of consciousness, never abandoning its own form.

Since there is no earth or other elements there, tell me, how could earth and the rest exist? That which shines there is only the peaceful space of consciousness (cidākāśa), and it is likewise within the Self.

At the very beginning and at the time of sleep, how could there be the arising of earth and the other elements? For [all things] arise, as it were, from the reality of Brahman—which is of the nature of the Self—within the Self, appearing in the form of the world.

It subsequently produces designations such as "earth" and so forth, which appear as if they were bestowers of real objects; yet it is neither of the nature of memory nor endowed with a formal image, because earth and the like do not truly exist. It is neither an illusion nor a transformation (vivarta); the world is solely of the nature of Brahman.

Brahman shines forth as this beautiful form of the world, yet it is one alone, established in the nature of both manifestation and non-manifestation; though appearing as the visible, it is pure like the tranquil sky, eternally risen, and its essence consists of the emergence and dissolution of creation and pralaya.
Śrī Rāma said: For this reality of the Self, which is the nature of all experience, the self of all, and infinite—even within the body, why is there this grasping at "I"?
How could consciousness become like stone or wood in dreams and such states? And how is it that these things, such as stones and wood, neither exist nor do they not exist?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as there is a grasp of "hand-ness" in the hand of an embodied being, so too is there a grasp of "body-ness" in the body of the Universal Self.
Just as there is a grasping for "leaf-ness" in a leaf of a tree, so too there is a grasping for "tree-ness" in the tree that consists of all its parts.
Just as there is a grasping for emptiness within the voidness of space, so too is there a grasping for substantiality within the substance of the Self, which is the soul of all.

Just as there is a grasping of form in a dream-city according to what is appropriate for a dream, so too is there a grasping of the nature of the universal self in the states of dreaming, waking, and so forth.

Just as that same apprehension occurs regarding a stone, a tree, water, and so forth in relation to Mount Aṅganda, so too does that same apprehension occur regarding the state of being the city of Mount Aṅganda in relation to the Universal Self.
Just as there is a perception of the body in things such as hair and nails, so too is there a perception of the universal self in wood, stones, and the like.
Just as in a dream, consciousness itself takes on the form of wood, stones, and so forth, so too at the beginning of creation, the sky of consciousness possesses the appearance of parts and the like.
Just as the body of a person consists of both conscious and unconscious elements, so too does it possess the nature of nails, hair, water, and space, while shining with various forms.
The body of the Universal Self is likewise a single essence consisting of both conscious and unconscious; it comprises all that is moving and stationary, yet it is eternal and formless.
To one who possesses right knowledge, this world subsides exactly as it is, just as the delusion regarding objects seen in a dream ceases for one who has fully recognized the dream.
"This is indeed the space of pure consciousness alone; there is no seer, nor is there anything seen. This silence is sufficient; that which belongs to the dreamer is his awakening.
For thousands of millions of eons, creations come and go; they are both these very ones and others, like whirlpools of water in the ocean within the sky of consciousness.
Just as the ocean produces various shimmering forms such as waves and the like, so does Consciousness produce designations such as "creation" and so forth within its own nature.
This universe, as it exists, is always Brahman itself, free from affliction—except for the conviction held by those ignorant of reality regarding one who knows the truth.
"I am not the wave; I am the water"—by such reasoning, when a wave has realized this, how can it possess the state of being a wave?
Since this [universe] appears as a wave of Brahman, the two powers of Brahman—being a wave and not being a wave—have come to abide [within it].
O Rāma, this very mind—which, without abandoning its nature as the sky of consciousness, experiences manifold perceptions like a dream—is indeed called Brahmā, the Grandfather.
Thus, the primordial Lord of beings is formless and free from affliction; his nature is pure consciousness alone, devoid of causes like a city created by mental resolve.
By this, Hemāṅgada indeed realized that there is no such thing as being a "bracelet"; for how could he possess the state of being a bracelet? His nature is purely that of gold.
Today, within this body of the sky of pure consciousness whose nature is mere volition, that which appears as "I," "you," "the world," and so forth, is nothing other than That itself.
Those vacuities that shine as the wonders of consciousness within the void of the intellect—these are the very perceptions of the intense activity of creation, preservation, and dissolution.
This very manifestation of the sky of pure consciousness is itself; appearing like a dream, it is nothing but the state of the mind—this is that Great-Grandfather (Brahmā).
Just as a wave incessantly surges in that very form or another, so too does this delusion of creation and dissolution, which is without beginning or end, perpetually manifest.
The beautiful manifestation of the sky of consciousness, which is designated as Virāj, would indeed have a mind just like that of a city of one's own imagination.
Creation is a dream, and the waking body is likewise a dream; deep sleep is a dense state, just as perception may become blurred by cataracts and the like.
The night of another eon arose as his hair; light and darkness were known as the joints of his limbs, called the "passing away" (death).
Fire was his mouth, heaven his head, space his navel, and the earth his feet; the moon and sun were his eyes, and the quarters of space his ears—thus was this conceptualization manifested.
Thus, when correctly perceived, the Virāṭ, whose nature is space and whose form is vast, appears like a mountain of our own volitions, abiding in the form of a dream.
And that which shines forth of its own accord within the space of consciousness—this very thing is called the "world"; thus, it is the Self alone that is experienced by the Self.
Thus the Virāj-self shines as the pervasive, consciousness-filled space, a city of dreams that is one's own nature, consisting of mountains, serpents, and all beings.
The experiencer alone experiences the experience as real, even though his own self is as if unreal; he experiences it by way of its limited extent, just as a dream-actor experiences a dream-location.

The creations are the waves of the ocean of Brahman; within them, consciousness is the fluid substance. Another creation consists of pleasure and so forth—where else could there be anything such as duality or unity?
Just as the self in dream and deep sleep is of the very nature of sleep, so too the sky of consciousness consists of the single essence of both the seen and the unseen.
Just as one perceives a city in a dream while awake, so too is this world; once it is fully understood as such, how could a person of discernment have any attachment to it?
At the beginning of creation, because the perception of the creation is a cognition of things as they truly are, the world is exactly like a city seen in a dream while awake.
Just as the various latent impressions of a city in a dream are not real even while one is awake, so too are the latent impressions of the waking state not real.
If a cause were to be postulated here as arising in some other way, why then is such an error not likewise postulated as being closer at hand?

This delusion is indeed experienced directly, just as in the worlds of a dream; however, its cause must be established through inference—wherein does inference ever have authority beyond direct experience?

Even that which has been seen exists [only as a mental construct] if it is not under one's own control and has not been examined by oneself; otherwise, due to the impossibility of its being otherwise, it is of the nature of an internal delusion, like a mountain in a dream.
