The non-conceptual is supreme insentience, while the conceptual is transmigratory existence; therefore, neither meditation nor meditative absorption can possibly occur.

Samsara is meditation with mental objects; however, the state of a stone is meditation without mental objects. Liberation is the manifestation that is not like a stone, and therefore it does not consist of conceptual construction.

And indeed, by means of non-conceptual meditative concentration (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*) which does not perceive any name, nothing else whatsoever is attained; what could possibly be gained by one's own sleep?

Therefore, for the discerning person, through right thorough knowledge, there arises the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti), because of the absolute impossibility of creation, once mere error has been removed.
Non-conceptual meditative absorption is here called infinite; it is the seat that remains as it is, undisturbed, and illuminates all things.
That which is called infinite deep sleep is known as the fourth state (turiya); it is proclaimed as nirvana and designated as liberation (moksha).

That which is the state of being a single mass of perfect awakening is known as meditation (dhyāna); they call that awakening, whose nature is the absolute non-existence of the visible world, the supreme state.

And that [state] is not a dullness marred by obscuration, nor is it like deep sleep; it is neither free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa) nor possessed of conceptual construction (savikalpa), nor is it non-existent.
Because the object of perception is absolutely non-existent, that primordial consciousness alone exists; it is all of that, yet it is nothing at all, and it knows itself in that very way, my dear.
From perfect awakening, that supreme nirvāṇa is proclaimed; herein this entire universe, as it truly exists, has completely reached its dissolution.
Therein there is neither diversity nor non-diversity, neither nothingness nor something; it is described as the ultimate limit of all that exists and does not exist.
Know that supreme state to be the utter impossibility of the visible world, which is indeed established as nirvāṇa—tranquil and the arising of pure awakening.
And that pure awakening, the unsurpassed meditation, is attained by one whose intellect has been produced through the instruction of a teacher who understands the words and their meanings.
This scripture, titled *Mokṣopāya*, should be read constantly by a person who possesses pure intellectual means, and by no one else whatsoever.
Not by sacred fords, nor by charity, nor by ritual bathing, nor by knowledge; not by meditation, nor by yoga, nor by austerities, nor by sacrifices.
This is indeed mere delusion; though non-existent, it appears as if existent. The world-form is like the sky itself—a dream within the sleepless firmament of consciousness.
The delusion known as "name" is never pacified by asceticism or sacred fords; through asceticism, sacred fords, and the like, the heavens may be attained, but not liberation.

Delusion is pacified by correctly perceiving the meaning of the scriptures through right understanding; this occurs here in this very life solely through the means to liberation consisting of self-knowledge, and not from anything else.
All delusion caused by darkness is pacified by the stainless light of the meaning of the scriptures alone, just as total darkness is dispelled by light.
The appearances of creation, dissolution, and maintenance shine within the sky of consciousness, like vibrations in the wind or states of fluidity in water.

Just as the inherent wonder of a substance resides within itself, and just as the movement of the wind is constant, so too this creation exists; its state of being and its dissolution are of one and the same nature within the void.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The primordial sky of consciousness, appearing like a dream, is the cause of the perceptions of the body; since no other object of perception is possible apart from that sky of consciousness, how could there be a physical form?
O sinless one, at the beginning of creation, everything is of the nature of dream-consciousness; neither this creation nor the next world is established, even though they appear to be perceived.
This world appears exactly thus as something non-existent, experienced [only as such]; it is merely the peaceful expanse of consciousness, like union with a woman in a dream.
There exists the element of consciousness (ciddhātu), nameless, without beginning or end, and stainless; though its nature is void and its form is transparent, it manifests as the world.
This impurity remains when it is not fully understood, but becomes transcendent once it is fully understood; for how indeed could there be impurity in the supreme, beginningless and endless, ether?
This very pure perception is itself the city of a dream; that alone is the world. At the beginning of creation, how could there be the arising of earth and the other elements?

The conceptualization of earth and the other elements, as well as the state of mind, intellect, and so forth, has been fashioned from the sky-like radiance of the self of consciousness, which takes the form of creation.
Like a whirlpool in water or the movement of the wind, the appearance of the world within the sky of consciousness occurs without prior intention and without a supporting wall.

Afterwards, by that very same [Being], proclaiming its own sovereignty, there was fashioned the conceptualization of intellect and so forth, as well as earth and so forth, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent.
This great consciousness of one's own, which is utterly transparent, shines by itself; that which is called "creation" is merely its own space, and nothing else.

And yet, my dear, nothing whatsoever shines forth; that is remembered as being purely transparent. It is the singular perception of pure consciousness alone, spread throughout by the Self within the Self.
This very body, which is the sky of consciousness within the sky of consciousness, appears as the mind and as the visible world; it exists just as it does in a dream.

Because no other cause for the object is possible and because there is an absence of external causes, the sky of consciousness itself perceives its own self as the visible world at the very beginning of creation.
And that [state] is devoid of attributes like a dream; it does not differ in the slightest. Therefore, the space of consciousness is the space of consciousness—emptiness like the sky and so forth.
When that supreme Brahman, which is devoid of all forms, exists as that very one in such a manner, it abides as everything in this way.
This is experienced in a dream, for the dream shines as the Self itself; though appearing as manifold cognitions, it is indeed the stainless Brahman alone.

Brahman itself, through its state of consciousness, imagines within itself the condition of being a living soul (jīva); without abandoning its own pure form, it attains, as it were, the state of the mind.
This entire universe seems to expand from that, yet it is of the nature of space alone; though changeless, it appears as the form of the world, as if undergoing transformation.
The mind itself is Brahmā; abiding within the heart of creation, it incessantly performs all things and also perpetually withdraws them.
In that [state], which is devoid of earth and the other elements and lacks even the charming parts of the body, the other three worlds appear as formless, just as in a dream.
I alone, formless and infinite in nature, abide as the mind in the forms of bodies and worlds; I am both consciousness and unconsciousness, and the supreme dissolution.
Here there is no earth or other elements, no body, nor indeed any other object of perception; it is only the void of the mind that flashes forth as the world.
When viewed through the lens of discernment, even this does not exist as anything at all; rather, only pure consciousness shines by itself within itself, devoid of all density.
From which words turn back, silence alone remains; though engaged in worldly activity, one's own Self alone persists like a mute man.
Boundless, shoreless, and limitless, with pure consciousness as its supreme foundation, this awakened Supreme Person becomes silent.
Just as whirlpools and the like are produced in water flowing without prior intention, so too are the insentient mind, intellect, and other faculties fashioned by Brahman.
Just as movement is produced by the wind without prior intention, so too are the intellect and other faculties produced by the Supreme Self, being non-different from it.
Just as the imperishable vibration is not different from the wind, so too pure consciousness is not different from the Supreme Self.
"O best among the wise, one should know that 'the space of consciousness,' 'Brahman,' 'pure consciousness,' 'the Self,' 'the Great One in consciousness,' and 'the Supreme Self' are synonyms."
Like the wind, consisting of the opening and closing of Brahmā’s eyes and of vibration and non-vibration, the world is exactly like his closing of the eyes, and so too is his opening of them.
The manifestation of this [consciousness] is the visible world, and its closing is the absence of the visible; this one is formless, because both of these states are ultimately dissolved.

The Supreme is considered to be of one and the same nature throughout both closing and opening the eyes; therefore, whether the visible world exists or does not exist, Consciousness is eternally both being and non-being.
For Brahman, whose body is creation and who consists of both closing and opening [of the eyes], there is no closing other than the opening, nor is there any opening other than the closing.
Know this world to be exactly as it is: entirely peaceful, unborn, undecaying, like the sky, gentle, and perfectly equal.
The void whose nature is consciousness and non-consciousness shines forth as a form; that which is called "consciousness" appears as this very world, for such is its body.
Neither does it perish, nor is it produced; the visible world is neither seen nor experienced. Pure consciousness alone, being itself, simply wonders within itself.

The light of the great jewel of consciousness, though appearing as non-different from its own source even while manifesting under the name of the "visible," is like the heat inherent in the rays of the sun.
Deep sleep appears like a dream, and Brahman alone appears like a creation; all is one, auspicious, and peaceful, yet it vibrates as if existing in manifold forms.
Whatever is perceived—of whatever nature, whether existent or non-existent, in whatever manner, and at whatever time—it is experienced in that very way, as such, whether it be real or unreal.
If a cause is postulated on the grounds that it cannot otherwise be explained, then this world-existence, appearing like a dream, would not be possible otherwise.
Since the universe has arisen as non-different from that which transcends the subject, nothing whatsoever that transcends the subject has arisen apart from it.
Whatever the mind of one finds delicious, to that it goes accordingly; therefore, the mind that finds its sole delight in Brahman attains that very state.
Whatever a person’s mind is focused upon and whatever their life-force is directed toward at all times, that object is known by them as "this is it," and they clearly perceive it as such.
Whatever the mind may be intent upon as its sole flavor, that very thing it becomes in an instant; whatever a person's heart finds its flavor in, by that alone is it perceived as real.
The mind of that person for whom the ultimate reality has indeed come to rest performs other things for the sake of worldly transaction, following right conduct though devoid of its true essence.
No conceptualization of duality, unity, or the like exists here; this vision is pure existence alone, and if it is seen as such, that is sufficient.

In this world, for those whose vision perceives the invisible and the visible, the existent and the non-existent, the formed and the formless, there is neither a creator nor an enjoyer anywhere at all, nor indeed is there anything that does not exist.
This world-process, without beginning or end, exists within the Self as a single, dense mass of Brahman, utterly tranquil, like a pillar standing upon a path.
That very Brahman which is the intellect and so forth is this very stainless one; know that it is precisely that which is the peaceful, empty sky.

Just as tufts of hair and the like in the sky consist of both the existent and the non-existent and appear as if they have attained duality, so too do the intellect and the other faculties appear within the Supreme.
Likewise, intellect and so forth, the body and so forth, sensation and so forth—whether higher or lower, manifold yet non-different—are all voidnesses, just like space.

Just as for one whose nature is singular sleep, there is neither duality nor unity upon entering a dream from deep sleep, so too for Brahman, even while abiding in creation, there is neither duality nor unity.
In this very way, this clear reflection of one's own great consciousness shines; yet, my dear, nothing at all truly shines, for it remains established as nothing but clarity itself.
For in the sky of consciousness, the sky of consciousness itself is one's own stainless body; it appears as the object of thought, like the visible world, just as it exists, as in dreams.

Due to the impossibility of any other [explanation] and because of the absence of an external cause for objects, the Self, which is the sky of consciousness, first perceives itself alone as the visible world.
At the very beginning of creation, the formless visible world appears as the void-self itself; this delusion surrounds it on all sides, like dreams, mental constructs, and false cognitions.

Like a dream, that [impurity] is devoid of intrinsic nature and does not differ from it in the slightest; even though it is subject to transformation and possesses attributes, it is nonetheless a defilement of the reality of the sky-like consciousness.
That which has the form of a city in a dream possesses both real and unreal qualities; thus it remains eternally non-different from Śiva, ever-abiding.
The visible world is as transparent as a mountain in a dream; it does not differ from it in the slightest. Therefore, the voidness of the sky of consciousness is like that of the physical sky.
That very Supreme Brahman, which is devoid of all forms, exists in this state as the creation, remaining exactly as it is.
This is experienced in a dream; for in a dream, it is the self alone that appears in the form of cities and so forth, and not as something actually constructed by cities and the like.
Furthermore, in dreams, there is no existence of recognition, mental impression, or memory, because the object "this is that which was seen" is utterly impossible.

Therefore, having abandoned these three, that which is the manifestation of the consciousness of Brahman—because of its similarity to perceived objects—is attributed by the deluded to memory and so forth.
Just as a wave goes again and again to that very place from which it arose in the water, so too does the world go to that same non-dual space within the Supreme.
All injunctions and prohibitions, both always and at all times, exist as either distinct or intermingled; they both exist and do not exist in the ultimate sense.
Therefore, since the existent Brahman is the self of all, what indeed is not found here? That very existence is the self of all, and this [world] also has that as its essence.
Just as the wandering of one who is deluded does not mean that the earth itself is deluded by the hosts [of demons], so too, even for a knower, vision here does not cease without practice.
Indeed, for this treatise, there is no other practice for the pacification of perceived appearances than its recitation; it has never existed before, nor will it ever exist in the future.
The mind, being neither living nor dead, does not undergo obstruction within saṃsāra; because it is inseparable from the body, it does not perceive this [obstruction] through awakening.
The mind is always inseparable from the body and its objects of perception; yet here and in the hereafter, it subsides of its own accord at the end of awakening.
The three bodies, which are the objects of the mind's perception, are stilled through awakening, just as the wind, its movement, and the army [of clouds] cease for want of a cause.
The cause of this is indeed ignorance, and that is pacified for those whose intellects have been somewhat refined simply by reading this very scripture.
For one who understands the text, word by word and according to its meaning, first perceives what was previously unknown from the superior scripture; being diligent, such a person does not turn back.
Therefore, know that this very scripture is the means for the destruction of delusion; it is experienced as having attained a uniqueness not shared by anything else.
Therefore, one should investigate this great treatise according to one's ability—whether two parts or even one part—and by that means, the destruction of suffering will occur.
If this [work] does not please you because of the oversight that it is of non-human (āruṣeya) origin, then you should examine some other treatise on the knowledge of the Self.
One should not reduce one's youth to ashes through harmful lack of discernment; rather, by means of awakening—the essence of knowledge—one should assimilate the visible world into the Self.
Not even a single moment of life can be obtained for all the jewels in the world; alas, what a great delusion it is that one should spend it in vain!

And even though this world has been experienced by us, and even though it is accompanied by a perceiver, it appears as if real only while shimmering—like one's own death in a dream or the weeping of kinsmen.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahmin, there have been and will be countless worlds; how is it that you awaken me with stories concerning them?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: You have understood the relationship between words and their meanings within the dreams of the world; it is indeed not non-existent, nor is its description by the world useless.

That discourse which is expressed by means of words and meanings understood by those who have realized the Self is not grasped internally by others; it is precisely that [discourse] which is functional here in worldly transaction.
When you have known that which is to be known and possess stainless vision regarding the three times, then you will perceive those things through direct perception itself.
Just as in a dream, pure consciousness alone shines forth by itself in the form of the world, so it is at the beginning of creation; nothing else is possible here.
In the sky, there exist worlds numbering more than an anāvanā; who indeed is capable of counting the floods of their worldly activities?
In this very place, it was told to me long ago by my father, the lotus-born Brahmā; listen as I relate to you that narrative known as the *Padmareṇumatākhyāna*.
Long ago, I asked Brahmā, "How vast is this web of the universe, and where does it appear? Tell me. Thereupon, Brahmā spoke to me.

The venerable Brahmā said: O sage, all this is indeed Brahman alone that appears as the world; it is infinite for the virtuous through its true being (sattva), yet it appears as the world to those who are unenlightened.
Listen to this auspicious narrative of mine, an ornament for the ears; it is called the *Brahmāṇḍapiṇḍa* and is indeed known as the *Brahmāṇḍa-khyāna*.
In the void there exists the non-dual Self, the supreme atom of the sky of consciousness; it is pure like the form of emptiness in space, and like vibration in the wind.
He perceived within himself, as in a dream, the state of being a living soul; it was like the sky appearing as a void, or like the wind appearing as motion.
Without ever abandoning its nature as space, the living being (jīva) then spontaneously perceived within itself a form consisting of "I," which was of the very nature of space.
He perceived within himself egoism as the very notion of "I," which consists of the construction of a single certainty and conforms to the nature of *māyā*.
Perceiving in a dream the unreal consisting of intellect, mind, and ego, they bend the non-conceptual self by means of conceptualizations through the self.

Then, in that dream, he saw his own mind within the body as possessing five senses; though formless, it appeared to have a solid form, just as the intellect of the ignorant perceives a mountain in a dream.
That mental body beheld its own self as a form consisting of the three worlds—its very self, without any external support, yet manifesting as a vast expanse radiant with the walls [of the universe].
Composed of many elements, consisting of various moving parts, it is fashioned by the power of time and conceptualization, with its mutual associations being imagined.
In this dream, one perceives each of the three worlds individually, like a city reflected in a mirror, enchanting with its ninefold colors.
Then, in each instance here as well, he perceives within his heart the three worlds—more beautiful than the nine dramatic sentiments—as if reflected in his own mirror.
Within the interior of every single atom, there exist vast worlds that are not minute at all, yet they are as densely packed as clouds.
This ignorance is infinite; when it is perceived as ignorance, yet fully understood as Brahman, it becomes the stainless Brahman.
In this way, even the observer who perceives the web of dreams finds nothing at all upon waking; who here is the observer, whence is the object of sight, where is duality, and where is the cause?
Everything appears as utterly tranquil, the void-natured and supportless absolute; established in the self of Brahman, it is translucent and devoid of beginning or end.

The multitudes of millions of cosmic eggs eternally abide within the Supreme Self, appearing as if distinct though they are not different from it, just as these collections of water-atoms remain within water, surging with the force of waves that spread unimpededly.
Śrī Rāma said: If this world indeed proceeds from the supreme state of Brahman without any cause, like a dream or a mental construction, then...
Since it is established that [an effect] arises without a cause, why would another thing not arise as causeless anywhere, at any time?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In whatever manner something is imagined by someone, he perceives it in that very way; otherwise, there would be no such imagination, because it would be devoid of its corresponding cause.
Just as this imagined object of perception is known by one mind in a certain way, so too does that [other] mind know it exactly as it was imagined by another.

That Brahman is by its very nature a single unity consisting of both imagination and the absence of imagination; such is the nature of imagination that a living being appears as if possessed of hair, nails, and so forth.
The state of being a causeless entity and the state of being an entity possessing causes—both of these exist in Brahman, because it is the self of all potencies.
For if there were ever, anywhere, anything other than Brahman, then its conjunction with a causal factor would be possible.
Where everything—without beginning or end, appearing as manifold and yet non-manifold—is but the one peaceful Self, Brahman; therein, what could be the cause of what?
Nothing here proceeds, nor indeed does anything cease; it remains as the one, beginningless and endless Brahman, which is like the ether in its nature.
What is the cause of what? By what means, for what purpose, or in what place might it come to be? What is the cause of what? By what means, for what purpose, or in what place might it not be?
In this Great Emptiness, there is neither emptiness nor non-emptiness, neither existence nor non-existence, nor a middle state; there is nothing that exists, nor "not," nor even "not not."
This is nothing, or it is something; whether it exists by name or does not exist—know that all this is indeed Brahman, both as it is and as it is not.

Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, regarding an effect that arises from a cause within the domain of those who do not know [the truth], how could the Self be without a cause, or in what manner? Tell me this, O Lord.
Śrī Vasiṣ�ṭha said: For one who knows that [Reality], there is no such thing as an "ignorant person" at all; therefore, what kind of inquiry could there be regarding a non-existent tree in the sky?

Consisting of a single awakening and having the nature of a mass of tranquil consciousness, those who know that—how could they engage in investigation regarding an object that is non-existent in form?
And that state of not knowing [the truth] shines within awakening as its constituent part, just as mere sleepiness shines within the states of dreaming and deep sleep.
Nevertheless, even while conceding this, the conviction of the fool is stated by me: "This is the subtle soul of all, because it is the stainless Brahman."
Entities exist as those that are indeed causeless, and likewise as those born from causes; for just as they are conceived in consciousness, so are they obtained.
When all causes have completely subsided for those who possess the experience of everything, there is no cause for creation; therefore, creation is indeed without cause.
Whatever is conceived here as God and so forth, which lacks the quality of being heart-pleasing, is merely a useless web of words that is unpleasant and devoid of essence.

Apart from the perception of appearances as in a dream, there is no perceptibility of the visible world consisting of gross forms that can be established by any other means than the principle of "impossibility otherwise" (anyathānupapatti).

In the experience of the dream-earth and so forth, what cause is there for one who is not awakened? Tell me, apart from the nature of consciousness itself, what indeed is the so-called object of a dream?
For the object of a dream, when not fully understood, bestows a great burden of delusion; yet when fully understood, it leads to no more delusion—just as it is with the process of creation itself.
Whatever cause is postulated that is devoid of experience due to the obsession with dry logic and dogmatism—that is the stubborn adherence of ignorance.
The heat of fire, the coldness of water, and the luminosity of all radiant things—the inherent nature (svabhāva) of all entities—is it the cause for one who lacks understanding?
What is the cause of a single object of meditation obtained by a hundred meditators? And what is the cause for the walls in a city of the Gandharvas?

Since dharma and the like are formless, they cannot be the cause of the embodied body in the hereafter; what, then, could be the cause of the body for one who experiences the fruits of creation and so forth?
For the proponent of cognition (jñānavādin), what is the cause for the repeated arising and perishing of the infinite cognitions that take on forms such as walls and non-walls?
Even when it is said that "this very nature is the cause of nature," that is merely a figurative way of speaking regarding nature.
Therefore, delusion is without cause, yet entities appear as if they have a cause; for the ignorant, it is so, but for the wise, every effect is established as arising from a cause.
Just as one does not experience suffering when being robbed of wealth in a dream because of the recognition that it is a dream, so too is life [without suffering] through the vision of reality.

From the very beginning of creation, this visible world was never produced; rather, it is the sky of consciousness itself that appears as its own form, like a dream—nothing else is logically possible here.
No other conception is seen to be supported by reason; why, apart from this logic, should this ground of experience be Brahman alone?
Just as waves, whirlpools, fluidity, and so forth appear within a pure mass of water, so too does this succession of creation shine as Brahman within Brahman.
Just as the movement of ripples, whirlpools, and eddies appears in a pure wind, so does this vibration of creation appear within the wind of Brahman.

Just as infinity, porosity, emptiness, and so forth exist in the great sky, so too does this creation—both supreme and inferior—consist of the nature of consciousness, which is neither existent nor non-existent.
Even when these entities such as sleep and so forth are clearly perceived, they are essentially non-existent, because they do not possess an independent nature of their own.
Thus, within the Self—which is a mass of consciousness, serene, pure, and dense with sleep—the structures of creation, dissolution, and maintenance appear like the states of dreaming and deep sleep.
Just as a human being passes from one dream to another within sleep, so the Unborn One remains within His own existence, passing from one creation to another.
Although this space of Brahman is devoid of earth and the other elements and is free from affliction, it appears as if possessing those very things, just as in dream-experiences.
Just as sounds such as "pot" and "cloth" remain present while I am perceiving them, so too do all creations—whether born or unborn—remain within the non-dual Great Consciousness.

Just as the Visionary shines while being seen by the Visionary, so too do the worlds shine; for within consciousness, the worlds are nothing but consciousness, composed of consciousness, just like words.

What is the use of treatises or the deliberations of discourses? Liberation is simply life free from latent tendencies (*vāsanā*). Since creation is unreal due to its lack of a cause, it does not exist even while appearing to exist; indeed, there is no such thing as "creation" at all.

And this which is established here as "latent impression" (vāsanā) is indeed that very being of consciousness, continuous and one; devoid of all multiplicity, it appears here in dreams as the city and other forms, though it is nothing but consciousness itself.
Śrī Rāma said: In the three worlds, objects are of two kinds—formed and formless; among them, some possess resistance, while others are without resistance.
Those which do not obstruct one another and do not move against each other are called non-obstructive; those which do move against one another are called obstructive.
In this world, the mutual displacement of things that possess resistance is observed; however, there is no such thing at all for any of those whose nature is non-resistant.
In that regard, what is called "perception" is this which falls from the lunar orb; it is experienced by everyone as being unimpeded.

I speak of this as being constructed from the non-duality of conceptualization and discrimination that is only half-awakened; I do so by way of provisional acceptance, but it does not abide in the state of true awakening.
"O Lord, tell me: which vital breath (prāṇa) situated within the body generates agitation, consisting of inhalation and exhalation? Or how does it do so?"
How can that which is called "non-resistance" (apratigha) be of the nature of resistance (pratighātmaka), yet move this body just as a bearer carries a load?
If a resistant object moves while that which is non-resistant by nature does not, then why does a mountain not leap up for a person through mere consciousness alone?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the tube situated here in the heart undergoes expansion and contraction, then the vital breath comes and goes through its interruptions.
Just as air, whose nature is to occupy space, moves in and out of an external tool such as a bellows, so too does vibration occur here within the heart.
Śrī Rāma said: An iron-smith joins an external bellows together by means of contracting and expanding it; but who is the mover who sets the internal channel in motion?
How can a hundred become one, and how can one become a hundred? How is it that these things—wood, clods of earth, stones, and so forth—are endowed with consciousness?
Why does a stationary object not tremble even when it is moved? Tell me, why is it that only a mobile object here vibrates at the mere act of moving?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as a blacksmith in this world moves the bellows externally, so does internal consciousness move the coiling of the intestines through external activity.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, since everything residing within bodies such as those of air and fire possesses resistance, tell me how consciousness, which is itself non-resistant, can move it.
If consciousness, which is non-obstructive in nature, were to move that which is obstructive in essence, then it could, by its mere will, move even distant water.

If there were a mutual movement between two entities, one with resistance and one without resistance, then that would be mere wishful thinking; for where and what could there be [movement] by means of the agent, the object, and the sense organs?
Just as there is no union between that which possesses resistance and that which is non-resistant externally, I consider it to be exactly the same internally; O Sage, tell me the rest.
Just as this is experienced within oneself or by a yogi, so too, O Lord, may that movement of the formless through the formed be swiftly revealed to me.

The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: Listen to these words, which are an ornament for the ears, serving as the root-scraping tool for all trees of doubt, and intended for the realization of the oneness of all things.
There is nothing here whatsoever that is not called a "thing" possessing resistance anywhere; at all times, all this is entirely peaceful, non-resistant, and pervasive.
The entire collection of objects, beginning with earth, is pure, consisting of consciousness alone, peaceful, and non-obstructive in nature, just like those in dreams and mental constructs.
This entire world does not exist in the beginning or at the end due to the absence of a cause; even while appearing in the present, its nature is delusion, shining like a dream within consciousness.
Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions—through a great multitude of causes, they know his unimpeded awakening.
Know that everything—whether it be the internal organ, the elements, or clay, wood, stone, and so forth—is both empty and non-empty; it is consciousness and nothing else.
In this regard, listen to the narrative known as Aindava, an ornament for the ears; it was previously told by me, and now another portion of it is being described.

Nevertheless, listen to that which is spoken for the sake of awakening you to the question regarding the present, so that all this—the body and so forth—will be understood as being only consciousness.
O Brahmin, in a certain previous cycle of the world, there was a twice-born man known as Indu, who was the very foundation of asceticism and Vedic rites.
He had ten sons who were like the quarters of the world; they were high-minded, great-souled, and the refuge of the great and the virtuous.
In the course of time, their father passed away, like the Blessed Lord Rudra, the eleventh, at the dissolution of the ten.
Fearing widowhood, his devoted wife followed him, her eyes like stars, just as the twilight follows the day with its star-like glances.
Their two sons, overcome with grief, went to the forest; having performed the funeral rites and abandoned worldly affairs, they devoted themselves to meditative absorption.
Among all the dhāraṇās, which one bestows the highest accomplishment? By means of which dhāraṇā may we, being perfected beings, become lords of all?
Thus, having reflected there, those ten, seated in the bound lotus posture within the interior of an unobstructed cave, meditated upon this:
By means of sustaining the entire world as presided over by Padmajā, may we remain, without obstacle, as the form of the world endowed with Padmajā.
Having reflected thus for a long time with the intent of sustaining the world together with Brahmā, they remained with eyes closed, as if painted in a picture.
Then, with their minds fixed in concentration (dhāraṇā), those embodied beings remained there for eighteen months without falling away.
Dried up and reduced to skeletons, their limbs chewed by carnivorous beasts, they met their destruction there like patches of shade by the heat of the sun.
As they perceived, "I am Brahmā, and this world, along with this creation consisting of the worlds, is mine," a long period of time passed by.
Those mind-bodies, through the ten meditative absorptions, then become perfected as the worlds themselves; indeed, they become ten distinct physical bodies.
Thus, their conscious will was fulfilled as the entire universe; yet it remained in a state that is utterly transparent in nature and devoid of form.

Since all worlds consist of consciousness, know that everything—from the earth to the mountains—is of the nature of consciousness; if it were otherwise, what else could be said? For us two, nothing remains unexplained.
It is said that as for the web of the three worlds, what is its essence? It is nothing other than the mere emptiness of the space of consciousness; it is not otherwise.
Just as no wave exists apart from water, so too no movement or the like exists apart from the reality of consciousness.

Just as these worlds, belonging to the lunar realm, are composed of consciousness within the ether, so too, within these worlds, even wood, clods of earth, stones, and the like, are composed of consciousness.
Just as the volitions of Indra became this world, so too has this volition of the Lotus-born One attained the state of the world.
Therefore, here these mountains, the earth, the trees, and the clouds—the great elements and everything else—are spread out as consisting solely of pure consciousness.

The tree of consciousness, the earth of consciousness, the sky of consciousness, the ether of consciousness, and the mountains of consciousness—nothing exists that is not consciousness, just as in those worlds of the moon-god.
By the potter that is the void of pure consciousness, upon the revolving wheel of its own body, why is this creation incessantly fashioned from the clay of its own physical form?
If, in a creation fashioned by conceptualization, stones were not sentient, then tell me: what would this clod of earth, a mountain, and so forth be?

The mental formations of recollection do not hold an object within their interior; for those who possess a family of objects through conceptualization and the like, the object is as if it had rained down from before.
Just as a gem [shines] within a heap of gems in the abode of consciousness, so too does some object arise sufficiently within the mind, which is the self of all.
The purpose of performing what ought not to be done is never distinct from Brahman; since it is its very nature, it is certain that all this is Brahman.
Just as the water of consciousness flows and whirls upon the earth according to its own momentum, it does so through its own extremely intense effort, independent of anything external or internal.
The worlds shine forth like the play of a lotus from Brahman, who is pure consciousness; they are not even in the slightest degree other than that very Self.
This world is Brahman alone—unborn, unceasing, pure existence, whose nature is space; it is peace, the midpoint between being and non-being, consisting solely of the light of consciousness.

One who says that the world of mental constructs—which exists as consisting of consciousness, like a dream or the like—is not consisting of consciousness, is an ignorant person laughed at by the wise.
Just as one perceives worlds composed of volition within the sky as being like one's own self, so too does this world, born of Brahma’s volition, perceive itself as being of the nature of space.
To whatever extent this vision is observed more and more rapidly, to that same extent this suffering dissolves more and more rapidly.
To the extent that this view is scrutinized, before long it becomes a funeral pyre; to that same extent, this suffering becomes dense and solid.
For those long deluded by their evil deeds and lacking this vision, this cycle of existence—hard as a diamond—is never stilled.

Here there is no form, nor birth and destruction arising from becoming and non-becoming; there is neither existence nor indeed non-existence. Only the supreme peace shines thus within itself as Brahman—or rather, even this shining does not exist here at all.

Devoid of beginning and end, its creation is a rootless creeper whose very foundation is unattainable; it is entirely pure, encompassing the entire universe. Within it lies the flood of created beings, yet it remains eternally dense, free from birth and destruction, and devoid of even a trace of space.

I am indeed this entire universe—pure existence alone, devoid of internal distinctions, with all its manifold manifestations, free from limits, beyond calculation, and of unconditioned form; having the nature of the self and the sky, it is firmly established, unborn, silent, and sufficient unto itself, beyond all conceptual constructions.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, the three worlds are nothing but pure Being, which is solely Consciousness alone; no beings whatsoever here arise that are not perceived by the intellect of the ignorant.
Therefore, from where could there be a resistant entity such as a body? Whatever is seen here is entirely non-resistant and pervasive.
The sky of consciousness abides within the sky of consciousness; the peaceful abides equally within the peaceful. Space abides within space; cognition unfolds within cognition.
Everything consists of consciousness, peaceful, and exists like a dream within the waking state; it abides in an unobstructed form—where, then, is this state of obstruction?
Where are the limbs of the body, where the intestinal coils, and where the skeletal frame? Know that the body, though appearing solid, is like space, devoid of resistance.
The hands are consciousness, the head is consciousness, and the entire collection of sense organs is consciousness; all is peaceful and non-obstructive, for indeed nothing exists that is obstructive.
Because the existence of the world has the nature of being like a dream within the ether of Brahman, all this comes to pass—both with cause and without cause.
It is logically untenable that an effect can exist without a cause; for whatever has been determined by someone to be in a certain way, it is characterized as such by that person.
Without a cause, an effect appears as if it were real; one undoubtedly attains the very object exactly as it has been meditated upon through consciousness.

Just as everything exists everywhere and in every way within a dream according to its possibility, so too in the waking state there is the nature of being the self of all, because of the fact that it consists of consciousness.
In the state of Brahman, which is the Self of all, there exists existence—both that which is without cause and that which is born from a cause—abiding within the manifold and the non-manifold.
Just as these sons of Indu became one thousand, so too did they attain the state of being hundreds upon the earth through hosts of worlds born of their own volition.
For indeed, that which constitutes a thousand cognitions becomes a single body through the emanations [of the Lord] in union with Cakrapāṇi and the others.
The ocean remains but one, even with hundreds of rivers; time remains but one, despite the multitude of seasons and years.
This body has arisen like a dream within the very space of consciousness; it is formless like a mountain in a dream, yet it is vividly manifest through one's own experience.

Consciousness alone arises from experience, yet it is itself devoid of the nature of experience; through the triad of the seer, the seen, and the act of seeing, the single void of consciousness thus appears as the world.

Sensation and the self that experiences sensation are one, like sleep, dreaming, and deep slumber; they are non-different, like wind and its movement. Therefore, the world is the single expanse of consciousness.

The seer, the seen, and the act of seeing are the manifestation of consciousness, which is the ultimate void; therefore, the world appears like an empty dream within the single expanse of consciousness.
O Lord, this world is indeed non-existent; through delusion it has appeared since the first creation, but once fully understood, it subsides entirely, like fear in a dream.
Just as a single consciousness appears in manifold ways within a dream, so too at the beginning of creation did it appear in the form of various objects within the void.
Just as many shadows appear as one in a house with many lamps, so too does the single power of the All-Powerful shine forth in manifold ways.

That which is the shimmering of spray in the ocean called Śiva is like the shimmering of a cluster of trees in the sky; that is the creation. This cluster of trees in the sky has a distinct form, but in the ocean of Brahman, there is not even the slightest drop of creation.

Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, dispel this doubt of mine, which is like darkness obscuring the sun, so that there may be a perfect realization of the true nature of the states of existence in the world.
Once, while I was sitting with one-pointed attention in the assembly of the learned at the house of knowledge, a certain ascetic arrived.
A learned and illustrious preeminent brahmin from the realm of Videha, possessed of great ascetic power and radiant beauty, was as difficult to withstand as Durvāsas.
Having entered and quickly saluted the assembly of radiant splendor, he sat upon his seat; while remaining there, he was saluted by us.
Having gathered together the doctrines of the Vedānta and Sāṃkhya schools, I asked this of that most excellent man as he sat comfortably and rested.
Exhausted by the long journey, you appear as if burdened by effort; speak now, O best among speakers—whence have you come?
The Brahmin said: "It is even so, O highly fortunate one; I am indeed possessed of great effort. Listen now to the resolution regarding that purpose for which I have come here."
There is a land named Vaideha, endowed with every form of prosperity, like a reflection upon the earth of heaven situated in the sky.
There I was born as a brahmin and remained one who had attained learning; because my teeth were as white as kunda flowers, I was known as Kundadanta.
Then, having conceived a sense of detachment, I set out to wander for the sake of allaying the fatigue caused by the agitation of gods, brahmins, and great sages.
Once, I reached Śrīparvata, which is unassailable; there I dwelt for a long time, performing gentle and protracted austerities.
There lies a well-known forest, free from grass, woods, and the like, like the expanse of the sky over a ground from which heat, darkness, clouds, and so forth have departed.
In its midst stands a small tree with delicate foliage; it rests in the empty sky like the sun when its rays have faded.
Upon its branch hung a person of purifying form, like the sun caught by its own rays within the sun, appearing as if bound together.
With his feet bound by a girdle of muñja grass and his head perpetually downward, he was like one possessing a large goitre, as if clinging to the base of a great silk-cotton tree.
Having reached that place, I once beheld that man; I observed him closely from nearby, with his hands joined in a hollowed gesture at his chest.
As long as he lives, this brahmin sighs with his form unharmed; he experiences all the touch of cold, wind, and heat that arise according to the seasons.
Immediately thereafter, I did not attend upon him alone for many days; rather, through the fatigue of the sun's heat, he was gradually brought to a state of confidence.
And he was asked: "Who are you, O Blessed One? For what purpose do you perform this terrible austerity, O large-eyed one, having made your life barely perceptible?"
Then he said: "O ascetic, what kind of purpose could possibly be served by this? For the desires of embodied beings regarding their purposes are never very extraordinary."
When he was thus questioned by me with great effort and persistence, he then gave me this reply.
I was born in Mathurā and grew up in my father’s house; standing between childhood and youth, I am a knower of words and their meanings.
"A king becomes a treasury containing the full accumulation of happiness"—having heard this, I, seeking enjoyments and in the prime of my youth, [went there].
Then, the noble-souled one reflected for a long time: "May I become the lord of the earth, as vast as the seven great continents."
Having come to this region for this purpose, O giver of honor, I have remained here in this manner for twelve years that have passed.
Therefore, friend, go quickly to whatever desired land you wish; as for me, I shall remain firmly established in this very way until my goal is attained.
Having been addressed by him in this way, I spoke to him thus: "Listen; the mind of a wise person does not succumb to weariness upon hearing something wonderful."
"O virtuous one, as long as you have not obtained the desired bridegroom, I shall remain here for the purpose of guarding and serving you."
When she said "So be it," he became like a stone, observing silence; with eyes closed, his form diminished, and he was motionless toward the outside.
Thus I lived for six months before him, who observed a vow of silence like wood, remaining free from agitation while enduring the impulses brought about by time.
Once, I beheld a man, radiant as the sun, who had emerged from the solar orb and was standing in another region.
While he was being honored by him with both mind and deed, [the other] spoke words as beautiful as a flow of nectar.
O Brahmin, you who are intent on hanging from a branch, O long-lived ascetic! Withdraw your asceticism, O destroyer, and accept the boon you desire.
With this very body, you shall righteously protect the earth, encircled by the seven oceans and continents, for seven thousand years.
Having thus granted what was desired, that second sun then entered the ocean of the sun to go to its setting, from which it had arisen.
When he had departed, I spoke to that wise ascetic of the Śākha lineage, who was a supreme granter of boons whose excellence had been heard of, seen, and experienced.
O Brahmin, having attained your desired goal by hanging from the branch of a tree, abandon your asceticism and conduct yourself according to the worldly life as it naturally presents itself.
When he had thus consented, I then released his feet from that tree as if they were from a tethering post.

Having bathed with purifying grass in his hand and having performed the *aghamarṣaṇa* recitation, he completed the breaking of his vow by means of the fruit obtained through his merit from the tree branch.
By the power of that merit, we rested there for three days, refreshed and unperturbed by those sweet fruits of the tree which we had obtained.

Having performed austerities with his body suspended from a tree, standing on his head, in order to enjoy the entire earth bounded by the seven continents and oceans, that Brahmin obtained his desired boon from the Maker of Day; then, after three and a half days, he set out for his own home along with my friend.
Kundadanta said: With joyful countenances, the two set out to go to their dwelling within the city of Mathurā, which was like the city of Indra to the moon and the sun.
Having reached the village named Rodha and rested on the mountain of mango groves, they dwelt happily for two days in that city of Sālīsa.
With our hearts gladdened by the journey, we passed the second day among forest trees with cool waters and lush shade.
White with heaps of flowers fallen from the creepers on the riverbanks, they delighted travelers with the singing of the "jhāṃkāra" sounds of their surging waves.
The shadows of the lush trees and forests resounded with the cries of deer and birds; on the tips of the branches covered in thick grass, dewdrops hung like pearls.
On that day, they crossed over forests, mountains, cities, villages, ravines, marshlands, plateaus, and plains, as well as river currents and lakes.
Exhausted and chilled by the frost, we spent the night in a dense grove of plantain trees upon a bed made of plantain leaves.
On the third day, we reached a wilderness adorned with grove after grove, separated from human habitation, appearing like the sky itself brought down to earth.
There, abandoning the path he had been following and entering another forest, he spoke these words concerning an improper act:
"Let us go to this hermitage of Gaurī, adorned by a circle of sages; my seven brothers stand in the forests, seeking their goals in this very manner."
"We eight brothers were born through that singular birth; we are composed of one consciousness and possess one unified resolve."
Therefore, they too have come here and remain for the sake of asceticism, relying on their own resolve; having arrived, they have destroyed their sins through various forms of austerity.
"Previously, having come here with those brothers, I dwelt for six months in this hermitage of Gaurī; therefore, he was seen by me."
In the shade of trees within a grove of flowers, the young fawns slept peacefully; at the entrance of the leaf-huts, the parrots rested while reciting the insights of the sacred scriptures.
Come, for the sake of prosperity, to this hermitage of sages which resembles the world of Brahmā; let us go there, and our minds will become exceedingly pure through meritorious deeds.
For even among the learned, the steadfast, and those who know reality, the mind of men indeed hastens toward the perception of the conviction that "enough has been done."
When he said, "So be it," we both reached that hermitage of the sage, where we beheld one of invisible form within that great forest.
He saw neither tree nor hut, neither shrub nor human being; neither sage nor child, nor anything else, neither the sacrificial altar nor a twice-born man.
That infinite forest was nothing but pure emptiness; it was scorched by heat on all sides, like the sky resting upon the earth.
While he was saying, "Alas, what a tragedy! What has happened here?", we wandered for a very long time and then saw a small tree in one place.
With smooth skin and dense luster, cool as a rain cloud, that aged ascetic remained established in meditative concentration beneath him.
We two sat for a long time on a grassy spot in front of that sage, beneath his shadow, until he turned away from his meditation.
Then, after a long time, out of agitation and impulsiveness, I spoke these words loudly: "O Sage, awaken from your meditation!"
Awakened by my loud voice, the sage stretched himself like a lion at the roar of thunder and spoke.
Who are you two virtuous ones? Where has that hermitage of Gaurī gone? By whom have I been brought here, and what time is this that prevails?
When he said "So be it," I also replied: "O Blessed One, know that it is thus; there is nothing [we do not know]. Why then does even the Buddha not know it himself?"
Having heard this, the Blessed One again became absorbed in meditation; he beheld the entire account of us as well as of himself.
After awakening from meditation, the sage spoke within a mere moment: "Listen to this marvel, for you two noble ones are knowers of what must be done."
"O virtuous ones, behold this young Kadamba tree, which is the abode of my forest and appears like a flowering braid of hair."
For some reason, while he was present, the virtuous Vāgīśvarī dwelt there for ten years, experiencing all the seasons.
Then, by him, this vast forest of trees was created here, known as Gaurīvana, adorned with flowers and the seasons.

O body of the sweet-voiced bird, whose playful and enchanting song captivates the hearts of the female bees; O canopy of the sky with its hundreds of moons and clouds of flowers, scattering the pollen of lotuses across the quarters of space!

The quarters of the sky were made fragrant by the nectar of mandāra and kunda flowers; it was filled with heaps of blossoming flowers reaching to the moon, beautiful with the blooming smiles of clusters of *saṃtānaka* blossoms, and its multitude of vine-like women was perfumed by the fragrant breeze.

The city of Puṣpākara resounded with the songs of bees and was enriched by pavilions formed from clusters of flowers where female bees dwelt; there, throngs of celestial Siddha women were swaying on flower-swinging cradles, as tender as the web of moonbeams.

Its banks were crowded with flocks of hārīta ducks, swans, parrots, cuckoos, ruddy geese, crows, cakravāka birds, bhāsas, and sparrows; it was delightful with the playful frolics of bheruṇḍas, roosters, kapiñjala partridges, golden-crested pheasants, peacocks, and cranes.

The window possessed a kadamba-like pericarp of feet rubbed by the crowns of gandharvas, yakṣas, asuras, and siddhas, and was attended by Sarasvatī; it bore the fragrance of a mass of golden, tender campaka flowers, like clouds in the starry sky.

It was cooled by the rays of the sun, hidden by the arrangement of young creepers and sprouts shaken by a gentle breeze, and it was drunk in by the abundant pollen from the clusters of flowers of the kadamba, karavīra, coconut, tālī, and tamāla trees.

It was filled with clusters of white, night-blooming, blue, and red lotuses, where cakoras, bakas, kokas, kadambas, and swans warbled; it was the abode of various powers dwelling within the hollows of tālīsa, guggulu, sandalwood, pāribhadra, and bhadradruma trees.

In that forest, Gaurī, whose face is like the orb of the serene moon, dwelt for a long time with half her body joined to Hara due to some particular cause; she, the Mistress of Speech, stood amidst the *kadamba* trees like a digit of the moon upon the head of Śiva.
The aged ascetic said: "Having stayed at this very kadamba tree for ten years according to her own will, Gaurī then departed for the abode that is the left half of Hara’s body."
Sprinkled by the nectar of her touch, this young kadamba tree remains as if seated upon her lap; it does not at all succumb to old age.
Then, after Gaurī had departed, that great forest became like an ordinary forest, subsisting upon the multitudes of people.
There is a country named Mālava; there I was the lord of the earth. Once, having renounced the glory of sovereignty, I wandered through the hermitages of sages.
Having arrived at this place, he was honored here by the residents of the hermitage; established in meditative absorption, he remained beneath this kadamba tree.
Then, at one time, you previously came to this hermitage together with your seven brothers for the sake of ascetic penance.
There were eight ascetics living there at that time, known by those very names; they were such ascetics that other ascetics held them in high esteem.
In due course, one of them went immediately to Śrīparvata, while the second departed for penance before the Lord Kārttikeya.
The third went to Vārāṇasī, while the fourth went to the Himālaya; these other four wise ones remain right here, performing supreme austerities.
And for each and every one of these, this is their desire: "May I become the sovereign lord of this entire earth consisting of all its continents."
Then this desired object was accomplished for all of them by means of the most excellent boons granted by their chosen deities, who were pleased by their ascetic penance.
Then, having enjoyed the Age of Dharma upon the earth like the Creator in the City of Brahmā, those brothers departed for their own abode, shining with splendor.
O noble one, at that time, during the rite for granting boons, those brothers of yours diligently entreated their chosen deities as they prepared to bestow boons.
O Goddess, while we remain as lords of these seven continents, may all these subjects and all those dwelling in the various stages of life be established in truth.
Having respectfully accepted that request for the sake of her chosen deity, the Sovereign Goddess said to them, "So be it," and vanished from sight.
Then those residents of the hermitage all went to their own dwellings; they have all departed, and I alone have not gone.
I alone, with my mind solely intent on meditation, stand like a mountain at the foot of the Kadamba tree of Vāgīśvarī.
Then, as this time—consisting of seasons and years—was flowing on, this entire forest was cut down by people living in the surrounding areas.
People worship this unfading kadamba tree with great devotion, saying, "It is the abode of Vāgīśvarī," and they regard me alone as having attained one-pointed concentration.
"Now that you two long-lived ascetics have come to this place, I have related all of this in its entirety as it was perceived by me through meditation."
Therefore, having risen, O virtuous ones, go; you have arrived at home, where all your brothers are gathered together with their wives and kinsmen.
Prosperity shall be yours, all eight of you, in your own abode; it will be like the gathering of the great-souled Vasus in the world of Brahmā.
When he had spoken thus, that supreme ascetic was questioned by me; "O Noble Ones, because of my doubt regarding this marvel, I shall now describe it."
"O Blessed One, this earth indeed consists of only seven continents; how is it that eight lords of the seven continents can exist at the same time?"
The Kadamba ascetic said: "What has been said so far is not at all inconsistent for us; now hear from me something else that is even more irrelevant."
These eight brothers, having become ascetics there at the dissolution of their bodies, will all become lords of the seven continents within their own homes.
Listen to me: these eight kings shall become lords of the seven continents here on this earth, in these various regions and dwellings.
It is said that these eight have an irreproachable group of eight wives, as constant and radiant as the eight stars of the constellation Ursa Major in the various quarters of the sky.
When these had departed for long-term asceticism, their eight wives became sorrowful, for separation from men is as difficult for women to endure as a serpent.
Suffering on account of them, they performed severe penance; by performing a hundred *cāndrāyaṇa* fasts, Pārvatī became pleased with them.
In the inner apartments of the palace, during the occasion of worship, that invisible Goddess, the Sovereign, spoke these words to each of them individually.
The Goddess said: "O young girl, let a boon be accepted for the sake of your husband and for your own sake; you have long been tormented by asceticism, like a flower-cluster by the summer heat."
Having heard these words of the goddess, Ciraṇṭikā, to whom flowers had been given, began to offer praise to the Goddess according to her own latent impressions.
Speaking softly, Ānandamantharā addressed these words to the goddess stationed in the sky, as a peahen addresses a garland of clouds.
Ciraṇṭikā said: "O Goddess, just as you have love for Śambhu, the God of gods, so may I have love for my husband; may he be my immortal husband."

The Goddess said: "Because of the firmness of destiny since the beginning of creation, immortality cannot be obtained; therefore, O lady of virtuous vows, choose another boon instead of this through penance and gifts."
Ciraṇṭikā said: "O Goddess, this is unattainable for me; let not the life-breath of my husband depart even for a moment from the interior of his house to the outside."
"O Mother, let this boon be granted to me: that when the fall of my husband's body occurs, it may take place within my own home."
The Goddess said: "So be it, my daughter; even though your husband has passed to another world, you shall become his beloved wife after the end of this body—of this there is no doubt."
Having spoken thus, the voice of Gaurī ceased within the belly of the sky, like the sound of a mass of clouds rising faultlessly and powerfully.
After the Goddess had departed, after some time, their husbands all returned from the various quarters, having obtained great boons.
Today let this husband also go to his wife; let there be a mutual reunion between brothers and kinsmen.
Now hear this other, extraordinary, and confused account of what occurred—wonderful yet obstructive to the noble task.
While these [ascetics] were performing their penance, their parents, accompanied by their daughter-in-law, went forth filled with grief to visit the series of holy fords and hermitages of the sages.
Disregarding their own bodies and desiring the welfare of their sons, the two became intent on going to that village of Kalāpa.
As they proceeded along the path to the village of sages, they saw a white man, tawny, short, with ashes on his limbs and hair standing erect.
When the two of them disregarded the scattering of dust, suspecting him to be an old traveler, he spoke to them as they went along, filled with rage.
O great fool, accompanied by your wife and seeking a holy place, you pass me by, Durvāsas, without offering the prescribed salutation.
As you depart with your daughters-in-law and your sons, even the great boons obtained through your ascetic penance will turn out to be contrary to your expectations.
While he who had spoken thus was being honored by the king together with his wives and daughters-in-law, the sage vanished from sight.
Then those two parents, accompanied by their daughters-in-law, returned home deeply distressed, emaciated, with dejected faces, and devoid of hope.
Therefore, I say to you: not even a single one of their names is improper; rather, there are hundreds of thousands of improprieties, like pustules bursting upon a boil.

In this great city of the mental constructs of the consciousness-ether, such diverse and incongruous things come into being, even though it is of the nature of emptiness—just as the manifestations of visible objects appear within the sky.
Kundadanta said: Then, I questioned that ascetic of Gaurī’s hermitage there—an ascetic whose hair was withered by old age and as thin as the tips of dried darbha grass.
There is but one earth consisting of seven islands; how can there be eight supreme lords of those seven islands here and there?
How can that living being who has no exit from his dwelling to the outside perform a conquest of the directions as the lord of the seven continents?
How can curses, which were granted by those bestowers of boons, turn into their opposite? For how could a shadow ever become heat?
How can two properties that are mutually incompatible abide in one place? Furthermore, how can a substratum itself become the object supported within its own self?
The ascetic of Gaurī’s hermitage said: "O virtuous one, listen further: when this eighth [day] has fully arrived, you will see him in that place along with his kinsmen."
Having reached that place from here, you two, dwelling in happiness, shall for some time remain established in the well-being of your own kin.
Then those eight brothers will die one after another at home; thereafter, their kinsmen will consign their bodies to the fire.
Their respective spaces of consciousness, situated separately, will remain for a mere moment like those in deep sleep, as if inert.
In the meantime, those actions of theirs—consisting of boons and curses—will, by the nature of things, converge together in the sky within a single assembly.
Those karmas, taking the form of presiding deities, will manifest as a collection of bodies for boons and curses, each individually.
The fortunate ones, with lotuses in their hands, bearing the staff of Brahmā as their weapon, with limbs white as the moon and four arms, shall go there as your attendants.
There, curses will manifest as three-eyed beings holding tridents; they are terrifying, resembling black clouds, two-armed, and have faces with furrowed brows.

The excellent ones will say: "Go far away! Curses have come upon us; their time has arrived. Who is capable of transgressing them, any more than one can bypass the [appointed] times of sacrificial rites?"
The curses will say: "Go far away, O excellent ones; the time for us has arrived, just as [the time] for sacrifices does. Who is capable of transgressing that?"
They will speak excellent words: "O sirs, we have been made by the Sage, we have been made by the Maker of the Day; for the Blessed One was formerly the god superior even to the Munis."
While the excellent ones were thus speaking, the wrathful-minded Vivasvat addressed the boons as curses: "You have been made from a portion of Rudra; we have been made from a portion of Viṣṇu."
"Rudra is superior to the gods; the sage is born from a portion of Rudra. Having said this, they raised their peaks like mountains against them.
While their horns are raised for curses against these enemies of the gods, the excellent ones will laugh and proclaim the certainty that has been made an object of direct perception.
O cursed ones, abandon your wickedness and consider the conclusion of this matter; that which should be considered at the end of a quarrel should have been considered at the beginning.
"Having gone to the City of the Grandfather, a final decision must be made by us at the end of this quarrel; why is this not arranged here first?"
Having heard what was spoken by the boons and curses, he accepted it, saying "So be it. For who, even if a fool, would not accept a statement that is endowed with reason?
Then, along with the boons, the curses shall go to the city of Brahmā; for the path of those of great majesty always leads to the destruction of doubt.
Having first offered salutations, they will relate all that happened to one another to Brahmā; and having heard it from them, he will speak.

Brahmā said: "O lords of boons and curses, those who possess inner essence are victorious. As for the question 'Who possesses inner essence?', you yourselves must surely investigate this among one another."
Having heard this, they entered to examine the essence of boons; for curses are the heart of boons, and boons are the heart of curses.
Having searched for one another and personally understood the essence of their own hearts, they will come together and address the Grandfather.

The Śāpas will say: "O Lord of Creatures, we have been conquered; for we are without inner substance. Only those with inner substance are truly excellent, remaining as immovable as pillars of diamond."
"O Blessed One, these boons and curses are indeed always [mere] mental constructs for us; surely our body is nothing other than consciousness itself."
For that consciousness of the Giver which remains as "the boon has been granted" is itself found by me, the petitioner, standing as "this boon has been obtained."
The body is the manifestation of representation-only; from that, it itself becomes the fruit. Through the delusions of hundreds of places and times, one sees, experiences, and consumes.

Because it is grasped by the self that bestows boons, when this consciousness is accumulated over the course of time, it becomes difficult to conquer due to its internal essence; however, that which arises from a curse is not so.
When the granting of boons by those who grant boons has been practiced for a very long time by those seeking boons, then that becomes the essence of all boons.
Whatever consciousness one practices for a very long time, that alone quickly becomes its essence, and one swiftly becomes identified with it.
Among pure cognitions, consciousness appears as supremely pure; among impure ones, it appears as impure. Due to time, there is no equality between them.
Even by a fraction of a moment, that which is superior is fulfilled according to its own logic; pride is not capable of establishing any other logic regarding the goal.
An object situated at both extremes together becomes a mixed entity, like milk mixed with water through the play of a blessing and a curse.
Through both blessings and curses, or rather through the dual nature of consciousness itself, it experiences its own self-nature just as one does in dreams.
O Lord, that very thing which was learned from you has been recited by us back at you; we depart quickly—salutations be to you!
Having spoken thus, that self-imposed curse, along with its host of curses, vanished somewhere, just as a hair-tuft seen in the sky disappears when the darkness has subsided.
Then another group of boons, which obstructed his departure from the house, fulfilled their purpose like a command issued by a local official at his own station.

Those dwelling in the place of the curse will say: "O Lord of Gods, we do not know the departure of the beings who rule over the seven continents from their abodes of death, just as one does not know the waters within a blind well."
These excellent and noble heroes cause these lords of the seven continents to undertake the conquest of the quarters in battle within their dwellings on these islands.
Therefore, O Lord of the Wise, since this conflict is thus unavoidable, command us what must be performed for our welfare.
Brahmā said: "O you who are the lords of the seven islands and the bestowers of boons for dwelling in the home, your desire has indeed been fulfilled here, as it has been for yourselves as well."
Go away; for even those who have long resided as lords of the seven continents in their homes will, in an instant, come to depend upon this very thing, even in their final hour.
Immediately upon the falling of their bodies, all these supreme ones became lords of the seven continents within their own abodes.
All will say: "From where do these eight terrestrial circles and the seven continents with their riches come? Here, only a single surface of the earth has been heard of and seen, and nothing else."
And how do these remain within some small inner chamber? How can great elephants appear within the subtle calyx of a lotus seed?
Brahmā said: It is fitting that you and we [should realize] that the entire world is of the nature of space; it exists within the supreme atom of consciousness, experienced like an internal dream.
What wonder is there that what shines within the interior of the dwelling of the supreme atom flashes forth? What cause for pride is there in the sequence of nature?
Immediately after death, this world appears exactly as it is; at that very moment, it is the consciousness itself that manifests as the dense form of what is essentially empty.
If the entire world is contained even within an atom, what wonder is there that the earth with its seven continents shines within the interior of a house?
That which appears as this consciousness-essence (*cittattva*) and as the world does not exist as a world anywhere; it appears as pure consciousness alone, like the sky in its emptiness.
Thus were those boons proclaimed by Brahmā, the giver of boons; thereafter, having completely abandoned those bodies which consist of the delusion of the material world, they [attained liberation].

Having prostrated before the Unborn One, those possessing subtle spiritual bodies departed together; they went to the seven continents and to the houses and treasuries of the gods, as well as to the people of Kacajjana.
Meanwhile, those eight kings who were there—rulers of the seven continents, beloved and prosperous—remained for eight days.
Unaware of one another and ignorant of each other as kinsmen, they dwell upon their respective portions of the earth's surface, yet they are devoted to what is considered beneficial for one another.
Among them, one who was as beautiful as a youth lived happily within his very home in Ujjayinī, the great city and capital.
A certain inhabitant of Śākadvīpa, intent on conquering all directions, wanders within the belly of the ocean with the desire to overcome the world of the nāgas.
In the capital city of Kuśadvīpa, a certain king, free from anxiety and having conquered all directions, lay asleep while supported by his beloved queen, together with all his subjects.
In a lake at the city atop the head of the lordly mountain of Śālmalidvīpa, a certain man was engaged in water-sports together with a host of Vidyādhara women.
In Krauñcadvīpa, at Hemapura, which is augmented by seven islands, a certain king began to perform a horse sacrifice for eight days.
In Śālmalidvīpa, a certain king, having uprooted the great mountain ranges by drawing the tusks of the world-elephants, was prepared to fight with a wanderer from another continent.
A certain king of Gomeda-dvīpa, Kaṣatsena, went forth by his own power to bring back the daughter of the lord of Puṣkara-dvīpa; he became the eighth.
A certain king of Puṣkaradvīpa, the ruler of the world bounded by the Lokāloka mountain, set out with an envoy, desiring to see wealth and lands.
Seeing each of these lords of their respective islands exercising such sovereignty within the space of their own homes as was appropriate for their individual creative intuition;

Then, having abandoned the forms of ego-inflation, those two excellent ones attained oneness within the houses by means of their respective consciousnesses, just as the cavities [of space] merge with space itself.
They shall go and become, for a long time, those who have attained their desires; indeed, all eight of them, being satisfied, shall become lords of the seven continents and possess contentment.

Thus, those of expanded intellect shall attain these goals through their austerities, for that which flashes within the consciousness of the wise is the very same thing found externally; indeed, by whom has it not been attained through appropriate actions?

Kundadanta said: Having been asked this, that ascetic living at the foot of the Kadamba tree replied: "How is it that the seven continents and the eight [sub-continents] of the earth appear within houses?"
The ascetic Kadamba said: This element of consciousness is indeed such that, although it has the nature of space, wherever it exists, there it remains of its own accord within the self.
In this way, the Self perceives its own form as the three worlds or in some other manner, without ever abandoning its essential nature as space.
Kundadanta said: In that one, stainless, peaceful, auspicious, and supreme cause, how can a diversity established by its own nature exist as something real?
The Kadamba ascetic said: "Everything is peaceful within the space of consciousness; there is nothing here that is manifold. Even that which appears vast is like the nature of whirlpools in water."
That which appears as objects among these non-existent entities is consciousness; that very essence, whose nature is like dream and deep sleep, is its own pure, innate form.
For that which is in motion is indeed motionless, and even a mountain is not a mountain; just as the nature of consciousness appears as objects within dreams, so too is its inherent nature.
Neither intrinsic natures nor objects exist for that which is appropriate to the nature of all things; whatever form was manifested at the beginning of creation remains exactly as it is.
Indeed, there is no other form whatsoever characterized by luminosity; for the self of substance and consciousness—the sky of consciousness—abides thus as the absolute alone.
Just as the one consciousness alone shines forth in a dream as if it had become a hundred thousand people in an army, so too does its state of being an object shine forth with utter clarity.
