That which is the sky of consciousness, shining brilliantly by itself within its own pure self, is experienced as the world, taking on that very form through that [consciousness] alone.
Just as the cognition of heat appears even when fire is absent, so too does an object appear as its own illuminator within the void that consists of pure consciousness alone.

Just as in a dream one perceives the nature of a pillar in the sky even though no pillar exists there, so too this manifoldness of the world appears as if other than itself, though it is not different from it.
In the original creation, the nature of all things and their inherent tranquility were perceived by the sky of consciousness exactly as they are; even today, it perceives them in that very same way.
Just as a tree exists in its flowers, leaves, fruits, and trunk, so too does the Supreme, which is the Self of all, exist everywhere as both the transcendent and the immanent.
The succession of creations is but water in the ocean of the sky of ultimate reality; emptiness is the consciousness of creation within the great space of ultimate reality.
Ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) and manifestation (*sarga*) are synonyms, like "taru" and "vṛkṣa"; through awakening one realizes this, but through lack of awakening, duality leads only to suffering.
The ultimate truth is this certainty alone: that this world is one. Through the awakening to the inner science (adhyātma-śāstra), this very desire for existence becomes liberation.
Brahman is the body of volition for that which has the form of conscious volition; that very thing is the form of the world. Therefore, the world has Brahman as its essence.
From which words turn back, or perhaps do not turn back at all—so too do injunctions and prohibitions, as well as the perceptions of existence and non-existence.
That which is non-silence yet silence, the individual soul (jīvātman) whose state is like that of a stone, which is being itself yet appears as non-being—that is called by the name Brahman.
Since everything is but the one, dense, and stainless Brahman alone, what is activity and what is cessation? What are entities such as existence and non-existence?
When within a single, undifferentiated state of deep sleep, the delusions of dreaming appear as if variegated and continuous; |||
Within this consciousness-space-existence, which is itself devoid of variety, the many root-creations appear as if variegated and continuous.
Just as one substance joined with another substance brings about a different effect, so too does the internal vibration, whose essence is consciousness, mutually manifest in such a manner.
All objects are always nothing but the essence of consciousness and are non-obstructive; they appear exactly as they do because they are essentially one with pure consciousness alone.
Because their essential core is the single self that is pure consciousness, the powers of substances manifest as they are perceived—motionless and free from mental activity.
This entire world—including Rudra, Upendra, and the Lotus-born—is seen and experienced even though it does not exist at all, like a dream.
Indeed, diverse modes of vibration are seen within the water of consciousness, manifesting as the mobile and immobile self arising from joy, indignation, and despondency.

Alas, how widespread is the diffusion of this wondrous web of the world, which is shaken by the winds of its own inherent nature, and which is like a cloud of dust, mist, and frost within the rays of pure consciousness!
Just as a tuft of hair appears in the sky to one with blurred vision, so too does this delusion of the world appear in the void to one who does not know the Self.
To the extent that it is conceived, it appears exactly as it was conceived; just as this city of imagination shines forth, so does this world appear.
In a city of imagination, as long as the entire existence of that imagination persists, it remains indeed unreal in nature, yet appears as if real while established in experience.
Destiny, which bestows its ordained objects, indeed flows on; both the stationary and the moving remain exactly as they are in their proper order.
From the living being arises the mobile, and from the immobile as well; by necessity, water flows downward and fire moves upward.
The machines of bodies carry [their burdens], luminous bodies blaze, the winds move eternally, and mountains and other such things remain fixed.
The wheel of time (kālacakra), consisting of light, revolving and turning the sky into a downpour of rain, proceeds as the essence of the ages, years, and so forth.

The arrangement of the earth, the oceans, and the mountains remains as a single expanse; and the power of substances, consisting of the grasping and abandoning of existence and non-existence, persists.
Kundadanta said: "That which was previously seen comes to memory through one's own volition; but in the first creation, whose prior vision could there be to appear?"
The ascetic said: Everything is seen as unprecedented in a dream, just like one's own death; yet there is a memory of it as "previously seen" due to habituation to that very experience.

Because it is consciousness, the city of the world's conceptualization shines within the sky of consciousness; therefore, this world is neither existent nor non-existent, since it appears and does not appear by its own nature.
Since whatever is experienced—such as volitions and dreams—is through the grace of consciousness, how could one not remember that the city of volition is the pure sky of consciousness?
Free from joy and resentment, and indifferent to both suffering and happiness, the wise proceed along their natural path like wheels on a track.

Know that the delusion of the three worlds is just like the city in a dream when sleep has passed away, or like [the objects] in memory; it is the supreme Self, whose nature is the sky of consciousness.
Know that which is designated as the "world" to be nothing but the appearance of consciousness; it is the utterly tranquil void of consciousness alone, and nothing else.
That in which all is, from which all comes, which is all, and which is from every side—all that is everything by virtue of its all-encompassing nature; that everything exists at all times.
I have explained to you how this Brahma-cycle of transmigration will come to be, as well as the manner in which the visible world appears.

"Arise, go to your own desired abode this very day; let it be done quickly, like a bee to a lotus. I remain here, established in a samādhi that is pure and free from suffering; indeed, my dear friend, I shall enter into samādhi again for a long time."
Kundadanta said: Having spoken thus, "Even an aged sage," he sat with eyes closed in meditation, his breath and mind motionless, as if fixed in a painting.
Although he was entreated by us again and again with words full of affection, he, not understanding the nature of worldly existence, did not grant us an answer.
Having departed from that place with slow and eager steps, we both reached our home within a few days, where our kinsmen were filled with joy.
Then, having celebrated a festival there and recounted ancient tales, we all remained until those seven brothers had arrived.
Gradually they have reached dissolution like oceans at the time of universal destruction; now only this one friend of mine remains liberated, like a single vast ocean.
Then, in the course of time, he too set like the sun at the end of the day; my soul overwhelmed by grief, I fell into a state of supreme despondency.
Then, becoming even more distressed, I went to the ascetic at the Kadamba tree, intent on asking him for that knowledge in order to destroy my suffering.
There, after three months, he became free from that meditative absorption; then, being questioned by me with bowed head, he spoke as follows.
The Kadamba ascetic said: "I am unable to remain for even a moment apart from meditative absorption; therefore, making haste, I shall immediately enter into absorption once again."
O sinless one, this instruction on the ultimate truth does not take hold without practice; therefore, listen to this supreme reasoning and then act accordingly.
There is a city named Ayodhyā; there dwells a lord of the earth named Daśaratha, whose son is known as Rāma.
Go there into his presence; for it is said that the best of sages named Vasiṣṭha, the family preceptor, will speak in the assembly.
O twice-born one, having heard that divine discourse on the means to liberation for a long time, you will attain rest in the supreme, purifying state, just as I have.
Having said this, I entered this region, which is a great ocean of the elixir of meditative concentration, having come into your presence.
"Here I am; I have related to you this entire account of mine exactly as it occurred, as it was seen, and as it was heard, without omission."
Śrī Rāma said: From that time forth, he—expert in narrating stories beginning with "Kundadanta"—has remained constantly by my side.
This very brahmin named Kundadanta, who is seated here by my side, has heard this entire work entitled *Mokṣopāya*.
"O twice-born one, this man named Kundadanta who stands by my side has today become free from doubt; let him be questioned as to whether this is so or not."
Śrī Vālmīki said: When Rāghava had spoken thus, Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages and foremost among speakers, looked toward Kundadanta and replied.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Kunda-danta, best of the twice-born, O sinless one, tell me what remains to be known by you who have heard and understood my supreme words that grant liberation.
Kundadanta said: "The mind alone, which cuts through all doubts, is for my victory; the cutting through of all doubts has been realized, and the indivisible object of knowledge is known."

That which was to be known has been known as stainless; that which was to be seen has been seen as unimpaired; that which was to be attained has been attained in its entirety; I am now rested in the supreme state.
All this is yours, O Buddha; it is the dense wealth of the ultimate truth, manifested within the space of your own self in the form of the world, as nothing other than yourself.
Because it consists of all things, possesses all forms, and is the self of all, everything arises sufficiently from everything, everywhere, and at all times.
Worlds arise within the hollow of a single grain of mustard seed, and yet they do not arise; this is known in its entirety.
Within the house, the earth with its seven continents truly exists; yet the house remains empty—this is the truth, without a doubt.

Whatever object, in whatever manner, appears here with its aforementioned nature and is experienced by beings, all that exists at that time as the dense totality of Brahman; thus does Brahman exist, eternally free from beginning and end.
Śrī Vālmīki said: While Kundadantā was speaking thus, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha, whose soul is beyond reproach, spoke these words appropriate to the ultimate truth.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Ah! Rest in discernment has arisen for this great-souled one; he perceives the universe as Brahman, like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of his hand.
It is said that this entire universe, whose nature is mere illusion, shines as the unborn Brahman; and that very illusion is Brahman itself—Brahman, which is peaceful, one, and free from affliction.

In whatever manner, by whatever means, wherever, of whatever nature, to whatever extent, whenever, and from whatever source something exists; in that same manner, by that same means, in that same place, of that same nature, to that same extent, at that same time, and from that same source, it truly exists.
Auspicious, peaceful, unborn, silent yet beyond silence, undecaying, all-pervading, both utterly empty and not empty, non-existent, without beginning or end, and eternal.
Whichever state is nourished with the weight of conscious attention, that state branches out into a thousand forms, just as a creeper does when watered.
Since the supreme cosmic egg is but an atom situated within the space of consciousness, and since the supreme atom itself is the cosmic egg containing the world within it.

Therefore, this entire universe is the space of consciousness—without beginning or middle, indivisible, and serene. It is Nirvana, wherein the bonds of birth have set; remain as you are, O healthy Self.
Itself the visible, itself the seer, itself consciousness, itself the insentient; itself neither something nor nothing—Brahman alone is established within the Self.
Just as this world, being Brahman itself, becomes absorbed within the space of the Self—remaining peaceful and not abandoning its own nature—so too does it become absorbed therein.
Brahman and the visible world are never, as they appear, a duality; know that these two are one, like emptiness and space.
The visible world is indeed the Supreme Brahman, and the Supreme Brahman is indeed the state of being visible; this is neither tranquil nor untranquil, neither manifold in form nor devoid of form.
Just as in a dream or similar state during awakening, the body is formless; its nature is pure consciousness alone, it is non-obstructive, and though experienced by oneself, it consists of unreality.
Just as a living being composed of consciousness remains in a state of sleep and becomes inert, so too does this consciousness remain in an inert state when it is called "stationary" (sthāvara).

Because of its immobility and insentience, consciousness attains sentience from the mobile self; the conscious being, whose nature is deep sleep, enters into dreaming and waking through hundreds of worlds.

Until liberation, this existence of the living soul appears as dream-like worlds consisting of hundreds of thousands of universes, manifesting through earth, water, air, fire, space, and the void-self.
Just as a person in a state of sleep accumulates dullness, so too does the mind accumulate insentience; yet the nature of consciousness itself is not truly subject to the power of insentience.
By consciousness, the body of the knower of sensation is made stationary; by consciousness, the body of the knower of sensation is made mobile.
That form of consciousness which, at the initial creation, appeared and remained as the world like a dream, is said to be exactly the same at the end.
And that very [reality] is non-obstructive, peaceful, and remains exactly as it is; nothing has ever come into manifestation, nor was there anything unmanifested that was beneficial.
This appears as the beginning and this as the end of creation, emerging from the chamber of deep sleep within the consciousness that is like a profound, dense slumber.
For I abide alone, without beginning or end, a solid mass of ultimate reality; therefore, even the names of dissolution, maintenance, and creation do not exist for me.
The visible world, consisting of dissolution, maintenance, creation, and so forth, does not exist; nor is it anything other than the Self, just as a painted woman exists only within a painting.

Just as a painting created by Citrasena does not differ from the canvas, so too the various appearances and non-appearances of resistance are, within the nature of mind, nothing other than the state of emanation.
Even though this portion [of reality] is devoid of division by the sleep of the mass of consciousness, it is stolen from those in deep sleep; thus, "liberation" is but a dream of the mind.
This is dissolution, this is creation, and this is dense dream—all these are but the manifestations of consciousness, which possesses a thousandfold radiance and an unimpeded form.
The dream-like portion of the sleeping consciousness is called the mind (citta); that very same thing, when awakened, is called the living being (jīva), which perceives gods, asuras, and so forth.
When this very state is fully realized by itself as deep sleep, then it is called "liberation" by those who long for liberation.

Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, the mind consists of gods, asuras, and so forth; consciousness is sleep, and the vision of one's own self is awakening. What is its extent, and how does the universe exist within its belly?"

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Know that the mind is the man, the god, the asura, the immobile being, the woman, the serpent, the mountain, the piśāca and so forth, the bird, the insect and so forth, and the rākṣasa.
Know that its measure is infinite, wherein this world—from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—attains the state of dust in thousands of ways.
That which moves upward beyond the path of the sun, this is the consciousness; it is the realized state, possessing an infinite and stainless form.
This is the formidable form of consciousness; when the prosperities of the worlds enter into it, then that creation is said to have come from the mind.
They know that the mind alone is the living soul (jīva), devoid of beginning and end; it exists within bodies like space within jars, or it does not exist according to its own will.
Just as the current of a river takes up and leaves behind the low and high parts of the earth, O dear one, so does the mind take up and abandon bodies.
But through the thorough knowledge of this Self, this delusion regarding the body and so forth is quickly stilled by awakening, just like the perception of water in a mirage.
In that [state], the world is as minute as an atom within the mind; since the person is indeed of that same measure, the world resides within the persons.
Whatever is seen here is but that mind, like things in dreams; and that very mind is the person (puruṣa). Therefore, what difference is there between the world and the Self?

This entire flood of objects is consciousness alone; there is no "object-ness" existing apart from it, just as in a dream, or as the state of being a bracelet and so forth does not exist apart from gold.

Just as waters, though undivided from the ocean, manifest everywhere and in every part, so too do the objects of perception exist eternally within Brahman, inseparable from consciousness and consisting of its own nature.
Just as liquidity exists in the ocean and the waters contained within its belly surge forth, so too do all other multitudes of objects manifest from the Knower, being non-different from Him.
This pillar of consciousness, free from movement and devoid of beginning or end, remains as the very form of space, bearing the carved figures of the world exactly as it exists.
This entire universe, as it exists, is established within the space of consciousness; remaining peaceful and never abandoning its own nature, it is like the ground of a dream.
The universal consciousness and the world-consciousness possess equality, reality, existence, oneness, and immutability, as well as the relationship of container and contained between one another.

In this world, there is either no difference, or rather there is a difference, between dreams, mental constructs, the cycle of existence, boons, and curses—just as there is between the waters of lakes, oceans, and rivers.

Śrī Rāma said: How can there be the relationship of cause and effect regarding the cognition of the purpose of a boon or a curse? It is said that an effect cannot exist without a material cause; let this be explained.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The world is said to be the manifestation of the space of one's own pure consciousness, just as the movement of whirlpools occurs within the surging waters of the ocean.
Objects whose nature is consciousness shine like the roaring waters of the ocean; the wise call their names "volition" and so forth.
Through time, through the practice of yoga, through equanimous inquiry, or by virtue of one's birth, or by means of a sattvic and stainless nature.
For the wise one who possesses right knowledge and perceives reality as it truly is, the intellect becomes pure consciousness alone, free from both duality and unity.
She consists of consciousness free from all veils, whose nature is the Brahman of pure awareness; she has as her sole body the light of consciousness itself, yet is devoid of any physical form.
Thus he perceives everything without exception, as far as it consists of mere mental construction—his own self-manifestation, which is peaceful and non-different from the ultimate reality.
For this entire world is merely her volition alone, just like a city of imagination or a great city in a dream.
The self is the sovereign of its own volitions; as it is purified, in whatever manner it conceives, so does that become for it.
Just as a child in a city of imagination perceives the levitation of stones as real, so too does one experience the constraints of one's own actions as being truly real.
In these three worlds, which have become the very substance of his own volition, the Supreme Self knows that blessings, curses, and so forth are real, for they are not other than himself.

Just as oil is produced from sand within a city created by one's own volition, so too, through the volitions of creation, do boons and other things arise here from the Self by means of conceptualization.

Since the cognition of differentiation does not arise because cognition is unobstructed and quiescent, for one who [realizes] the non-duality of conceptualization, even the attainment of boons and the like is not established as a goal.
Whatever conceptualization has become firmly established remains so even now, until it is overturned through effort by means of another conceptualization.

Just as there is a sequence of various parts within a reality that possesses parts, so too, when the two states of duality and unity are released from their constituent parts and remain stable in Brahman, [there is a similar sequence].
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, tell me how those who practice dharma solely out of unobstructed ignorance bestow curses and the like.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Whatever indeed Brahman conceives within itself at the beginning of creation, that very thing it experiences, because nothing else exists therein.
When he knows the Self as Brahman, he is this very Brahman, the Lord of Creatures; and he is not distinct from Brahman, just as liquidity is not distinct from water.
Whatever indeed that first Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) conceives, that very thing immediately comes to be; this world is his mental construction.

Supportless and without a point of reference, having the nature of space, it shines within space—like a mass of hair seen by one with impaired vision, or like a string of pearls perceived by the sighted.
By him were willed forth the progeny, dharma, charity, austerity, the qualities, the Vedas, the scriptures, the five elements, and the instructions on knowledge.
Then, whatever the ascetics might say without delay through their arguments, and whatever those learned in the Vedas might say, he resolved that all of that should be so.
This consciousness-Brahman has then conceptualized as follows: the void as space, the movement as air, the heat as fire, the fluidity as water, and the solidity as earth.
Such is the nature of this element of consciousness that whatever it perceives as being of the nature of space, it immediately experiences all of that—whether as "you," "I," or "he."
In whatever manner the sky of consciousness perceives a thing, it becomes exactly that; just as in a dream the Self, though eternally real, appears as the unreal "you," "I," and so forth.
Just as a lie regarding a stone becomes true within a city of one's imagination, so too is the world—though a city of imagination—true for Brahman according to His will.
Whatever has been awakened by means of the pure nature of consciousness, and whatever it is like—that an impure being is unable to alter is just as [impossible] as for a worm.

Consciousness perceives that which has been frequently practiced as vast, while it perceives the other as small; and even while existing in the states of dream or waking, it perceives everything as real.
Always within the sky of consciousness, this single, innate form—consisting of the seer and the seen—shines forth as it perceives itself within that very sky of consciousness; nothing else appears.
Since the sky of consciousness is all-pervading, being both the single seer and the seen, therefore whatever is perceived anywhere is always truly existent right there, according to one's desire.
Just as the state of fluidity belongs to the body of water and vibration to the body of air, so too does the world constitute the body of the Unborn, just as Brahmanhood belongs to Brahman.
I am indeed Brahman, the Virāj Self; the world has the body of the Virāj Self. There is no difference between Brahman and the world, just as there is none between emptiness and the sky.
Just as from a waterfall, various multitudes of water droplets fall and spring up, ending in diverse places and times.
Having settled into oneness for as long as the world endures, devoid of mind, intellect, and the like, those who possess the consciousness of Brahman shine within themselves alone.
Having themselves fashioned the conceptual constructs of intellect and the rest within their own bodies, they embraced the splendor of creation, just as water embraces its state of fluidity.
Thus, this world exists only through difficult-to-comprehend ignorance; for me, however, it is solely action—causeless, non-dual, and unborn.
Whatever kind of insentient existence is experienced in this body as its eightfold state, such is the nature of the Supreme Self in stones and other inert objects.
Just as both deep sleep and dreaming exist within a single state of sound sleep, so too do these appearances of creation and dissolution abide within Brahman.
Just as light and darkness appear during deep sleep and dreaming respectively, so too do creation and non-creation exist within the same single state of sleep.
Just as a person experiences the state of a stone while asleep, so does the Supreme Self experience this state of insentience.

Furthermore, when there is no contact with wind or other elements by means of the thumb or a finger, that experience of another object occurring in one whose mind is elsewhere—such as in the case of a stone—is [the experience] of the Self.
Just as there are experiences of bodies for the sky, stones, water, and so forth, so too are there today various experiences for us who are without mind.

Śrī Rāma said: From what source does the necessity (niyati) of these diverse and innumerable entities arise? How is it that the inherent nature (svabhāva) of entities remains uniform, stable, and immovable?
Among the innumerable gods, why is it that the sun alone possesses such fierce radiance? Furthermore, what causes the lengthening and shortening of the days?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That which appears spontaneously and necessarily in another, exactly as it is and in its true form while remaining as it is—that is called the world.
Whatever appears from the All-Powerful (Sarvaśakti) is real exactly as it appears; since consciousness is the essence, how could that which has appeared ever become non-existent?

Since Brahman has existed as it is and has shone forth for a long time by virtue of its consciousness, its manifestation—which appears as non-manifestation—is indeed designated as "necessity" (niyati).
That which shines forth as "this is thus" and "this is otherwise," being Brahman itself, is declared to be called Niyati (the Law of Destiny), assuming the form of creation and dissolution.
That which is called waking, dreaming, and deep sleep is the self-manifestation within consciousness; it is non-different from that [consciousness], as pure and singular as liquidity is to water.
Just as emptiness is in space, as fragrance is in camphor, and as heat is in sunlight—and nothing else—so it is with the waking state and the rest in consciousness.

By virtue of its non-different existence within the single continuous flow known as creation and dissolution, it is established solely within the Self of Brahman, which is the nature of the sky of pure consciousness.
That which is the manifestation of consciousness for a moment is perceived as "this creation"; that which is the manifestation of consciousness for a moment is perceived as "this eon."
That time, that action, and that reality—such as place, substance, and emergence—are, by their very nature, merely the manifestation of consciousness, like a dream.

Form, light, mental attention, place, time, action, and so forth—these shine within the sky of consciousness as that which is called "cittva" (the state of mind), though it is itself formless by its own nature.
Just as whatever time is perceived and whatever is conceptualized, by that very means this necessity (niyati) exists, which is likewise of the nature of space.
That which is called a moment (nimeṣa) lasting until the end of a kalpa, and that which is a manifestation of a single form—those of expanded intellect call that inherent nature (svabhāva).
In this way, a hundred objects arise from a single pure consciousness, each retaining its own specific form as a portion of that consciousness.
In that which consists of consciousness, those [powers] which shine forth as if within the supreme consciousness—by means of them, that differentiation of their own bodies was performed by them.
Consciousness, earth, water, fire, motion, and emptiness—each of these is a mine for the others, yet they are like dreams within the sky.
There, the great source of this solid, resistant earth—the support of the multitude of beings—shines forth like a royal court.
The ocean is the primary essence of the waters, the sun is that of the fires, the wind is that of motion, and space is that of emptiness throughout the world.
Since consciousness is the mine for the five elements, those five [senses] are appropriately called "Brahmic"; what question, then, could there be regarding the Sun?
This consciousness, which is called "awareness" (cit), is said to be all-pervading and possessing all forms; by its own majesty, it is experienced everywhere by everyone.

This Brahmā, whose self is Brahman and who is a child of Brahman, being of the form of the sky, expands this manifestation of his own consciousness, which is named the earth—the silken garment of the ether—and which has the appearance of the firmament.

When she, through her unceasing consciousness, consumes this and that for a long time in such a manner, then the flickering [manifestation] of its limbs, such as the sun and so forth, is neither produced nor non-produced.
Preceded by volitional thought, this sky of consciousness appears like a visible object, with its wheel of celestial abodes revolving like a whirlpool, resembling a net of spiders.
In that regard, some objects appear luminous, some appear slightly luminous, and some appear non-luminous; they possess various forms.
This entire collection of objects has neither been born nor is it seen; to the knower, this unborn world appears as the sky-like Self, like the objects seen in a dream.

The Self is pure consciousness alone, the Lord of all, appearing as everything yet transcending the visible; though it seems to perish when its own body is dissolved, it neither shines forth nor perishes.
That which appears like a dream-vision within the sky of consciousness, in the expanse of consciousness—apart from being the sky of consciousness, whence could there be any other form for this world?
In whatever manner that pulsating body manifests throughout the duration of existence, it is here described by such terms as "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) and "necessity" (niyati).
The existence within the body of space, through the conceptualization of the subtle element of sound, remains in an unmanifest form, like a seed within a granary or a sprout within a husk.
"This was accomplished from that" — such is this [work] produced through the effort of composition; it was composed in vain by fools for the sake of awakening the ignorant.
Nothing here ever sets nor does it ever rise; this is eternally peaceful like the interior of a stone, existing yet non-existent.
Just as the atoms that constitute the parts of a whole never cease to exist within it, nor do they rise or set, so too do the worlds neither rise nor set within the state of the Self.
The world-space exists within the space of Brahman, just as one void exists within another void; how, then, can that which is utterly pure ever set or arise?
Of that gem of consciousness, whose nature is infinite light and which is all-pervading, there is a manifestation consisting of pure existence alone, occurring incessantly by its very nature.
In that state, consciousness itself appears as if it were becoming slightly objectifiable; though its nature remains ungrasped, it indicates the movement of reflective awareness.
With the mental constructions of future objects, its form is slightly inferred; it is subtler than space, pure, and the awakening to all that is yet to be.
Then that supreme being, Satī, becoming oriented toward consciousness, becomes fit for the name "Citi" (consciousness) by virtue of its being slightly attainable through her.
Following from that dense perception, there arises the mental construction of a self—designated as the "living being" (jīva) and so forth—which, by its very occurrence, becomes the supreme state.
Encompassing within itself, it abides as the ineffable state of being covered by the space of consciousness; yet now, for that which is utterly pure, it is of a non-dual nature.

At that time, these [faculties], intent on the cycle of existence which has as its essence merely the singular cultivation of the self, proceed by means of that [cultivation] even without an external object.

She is of the nature of emptiness, the one who possesses her own being, containing within her the qualities such as sound; perfected through the cultivation of consciousness, she is the state of the meaning of what is yet to be named.
Immediately thereafter, it arises together with the very existence of time; for you, that is the primary seed for the future meaning of designation and for the persistence of the world.
The web of the world, which is unreal in nature, is merely the self-awareness of the supreme power of consciousness; through that consciousness, it appears as if real.
Consisting of such a nature, that seed of consciousness within the tree of volition cultivates egoity inside; it itself becomes this [world] here in an instant.

This very thing called the "living soul" (jīva) now wanders within the state of the Self through the whirlpools of the surging waves of existence and non-existence, like water within water in the form of ripples.
When consciousness possesses such a state of contemplation regarding the subtle element of space, it gradually becomes dense by itself and perceives the subtle element of space.
That seed of the tree of the flood of words is the form of future objects; it undergoes transformation into the meanings of words, sentences, the means of valid cognition, the Vedas, and so forth.
Therefore, the entire glory of the world will arise from the reality of sound, spreading forth through the transformation of the multitude of objects produced by the flood of sound.
Citi alone, through such a resolve, is designated by the word "jīva"; it is the seed of the tree that is the mass of past beings, through the web of meanings of words yet to come.
From that, the fourteenfold collection of beings, which envelops the sky and fills the ears of the belly of the world, will emanate forth.

Not yet having attained names or modes of conduct, yet conscious by virtue of being alive, it perceives itself as pure consciousness alone, vibrating like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit.
The seed of the tree of skin and touch is the form of the mass of wind; from that, the vibration of the activity of all beings will spread forth.
In that regard, whatever experience of light arises from the play of consciousness is the subtle element of form (*rūpa-tanmātra*), which will provide the objects corresponding to their designations.
Luminous consciousness is light; that light cannot be produced by anything else. The sensation of touch is touch itself; it does not arise from another touch.
The perception of sound is sound itself; it is experienced by itself alone, just as space is perceived by space itself within its own sheath, for there is indeed nothing else that produces sound.
Indeed, in that state, who else could be the creator of sound? Thus, even today, duality and unity are utterly impossible.
In this way, the subtle element of taste and the subtle element of smell, though utterly unreal, are perceived as if they were real, like a dream-vision.

The seed of the tree of light is the brilliance [of consciousness] manifested through the sun and other luminaries; from that, through the differentiation of forms, the cycle of existence will expand.
Then, the tasting of that assembly—which is called "the future" and which is non-existent like space or as if it were self-born—is termed the subtle element of taste.
This entire group, consisting of the mental construction of future forms, is of the nature of volition; it then perceives the subtle elements (tanmātras), such as odor and the rest.
From that seed of the tree of form, which is the soul of all supports and exists as the future terrestrial globe, the cycle of worldly existence will expand forth.
Though unborn, that collection of mere elements has come into being; though formless, it has become possessed of form through the power of conceptual construction.
This group of subtle elements, by its own nature like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit, perceives form through a particular location; that is called the sense-organ.
That region by which one perceives sound is called the ear; that region by which one perceives touch is the tactile faculty (tvagindriya).
That part by which one perceives taste is the gustatory faculty; that part by which one perceives odor, however, is the olfactory faculty.
Due to the distinctions of space and time, this living being has assumed a fixed form; because it lacks the nature of being the Self of all, it does not know everything with every part of its body.

Thus, the infinite reckoning of the Self, which is internal, inferable, non-different, and identical with the Self—it neither rises nor sets; it remains like the interior of a stone, profound and utterly silent.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This beginninglessness that has been proclaimed regarding this mental construction is for the sake of awakening you to the supreme non-dual reality; it is not ultimately real.
Such an innate and uncreated modification of the Self, which is the reflection of consciousness directed toward an object of thought, is designated by the term "jīva."
O descendant of Raghu, there are many names for this *kāla* (time); hear those diverse names of the conscious self (*cidātman*) when it is oriented toward objects of thought (*cetyonmukha*).

That which lives through vitality and consciousness is called "jīva" (the living being); that which is oriented toward the object of consciousness is called "citta" (the mind), and is thus designated as "cit" (consciousness).

Because it possesses the clear cognition that "this is thus," it is called *buddhi* (intellect) here; because of its conceptualization and its nature of reflection (*manana*), it is designated as *manas* (mind).
The internal ego is said to arise from the notion "I am," while the mind, rich in volition, is called the immortal by those who investigate the scriptures.
From the web of mature volitions, it is known as the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka); because it is the primary cause of transmigratory existence, it is known as "primordial nature" (prakṛti).
"Because it does not exist from the perspective of awakening, it is called 'ignorance' by the wise. Thus have these names for this conceptual construction been told to you.
This state, which is without beginning or end, formless and free from affliction, is designated by the wise as the "subtle body" (ātivāhika-deha).
Thus, like a city in a dream or a mental construction, the delusion of the three worlds appears as a substantial entity, yet it is empty and non-obstructive in nature.
Thus has the *ātivāhika* body been described, O best of embodied beings; this body of consciousness is the void, even more empty than space.
Until the consciousness of liberation arises in the world, the mind-ground remains the sole reality for the fourteen-fold creation of beings; it neither sets nor rises.
In this regard, hundreds of thousands of cycles of existence will come to be, are currently coming to be, and have already come to be, just as fruits appear according to the arrangement of time.
This body, composed of mind, exists both within and without the worlds; it is utterly empty like a reflection in a mirror, or like the sky.
At the end of the great eon, when all things have perished and remain stable, in the vast state of great emptiness, which is the stainless self of Brahman;

Being, by its own nature, a mass of consciousness and lacking the state of being an object of thought, this manifestation of consciousness belonging to the Self perceives, through this sequence, as having the appearance of a subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*).
That subtle body, impelled by that light, is called "Brahman" by some and remembered as "Virāj" by others.
One was known by the name Sanātana, another was named Nārāyaṇa; one was celebrated as Īśa, and another was called Prajāpati.
The five cognitions of one's own sense-faculties appear like the "crow-and-the-palm-fruit" coincidence; wherever and in whatever manner they abide, there they remain exactly so.
Thus, when this vast and fully developed delusion of the visible has arisen, nothing at all has truly come into being, because everything is pervaded by emptiness.
The supreme Brahman, which is without beginning, is said to be neither being nor non-being; it is this very same thing, without beginning or end, existing thus as non-cognition.
As that subtle body experiences for itself, its dream—like a lover to one who is afflicted by longing—attains fullness and growth.
Even though it is empty and formless, the shape of a jar is experienced, just as one's own body and the world are experienced in dreams and mental constructions.
It becomes exceedingly exalted as a performer of purpose, like an object in a dream within the sky of consciousness; though its nature is purely space, it appears like a formidable material entity.
This subtle body (ātivāhika-deha), though formless, void, dream-like, and non-existent, experiences by itself in due order, remaining as it is.
The collection of bones, including the thick series of limbs such as the hands and so forth, remains in its configuration of three types of hair, vessels, and sinews.

The delusion of arising exists for the sake of the meaning of existence, which consists of birth, action, the place of effort, transformation, the state of age, and the sequential enjoyment of space and time.

It encompasses the sequence of birth, old age, and death throughout the ten directions; it consists of the states of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower, as well as the experience of beginning, middle, and end.
The ancient Puruṣa perceives his own body as consisting of the earth, water, sky, sun, people, worldly transactions, cities, and peaks, composed of both the support and that which is supported.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This subtle body (ātivāhikadeha) of that primordial Lord of Creatures perceives "as it is" and so forth through its nature as consciousness, like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit.
By its very nature as consciousness, it remains for a long time in that state; alas, this entire universe appears thus—what cause for wonder is there in this unreality?
The seer is unreal, the seeing is unreal, and that vision is pervasive; or else, everything is indeed real, for all is Brahman through its nature as the Self.
Śrī Rāma said: "Thus ends the account of that world of the subtle body (ātivāhika) belonging to that first Prajāpati. How did it attain solidity? And how can there be reality in a dream?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The subtle, transportive light is experienced by itself alone; because it is always and incessantly so, that very light shines forth as if fully nourished.
Just as the intensity of a dream, when experienced for a long duration, appears as if it were utterly real, so too does its own subtle, ethereal nature appear.
When the experience of the subtle body arises after a long time, the notion of materiality emerges like a mirage in the desert.
The world appears as a delusive manifestation of a dream, existing like the water of a mirage; though it is entirely non-existent, it shines forth even while producing the conviction that it is real.
The materiality of the subtle bodies (ātivāhika-rūpa) is itself unreal; yet it is sought by those of limited vision as if it were real, though it is far removed from them.
"This is I," "this is mine," "these are the mountains, the sky, and the directions"—thus a false delusion appears, like a mountain in a vivid dream.
This subtle body (ātivāhikadeha), brought forth by the primordial Creator, perceives this material form as having the nature of the physical realm (ādhibhautikatā).
Having abandoned consciousness, which is like the color of a cloud, one perceives, "I am Brahman"; yet one binds oneself with the mental conception that "this is the body" and "this is the support."
By cultivating the notion of reality toward what is unreal, one becomes bound; by repeatedly cultivating this internally, one pursues manifold diversity.
He produces sounds, conventions, designations, and vibrations; then, when "Om" is uttered, he chants forth the Vedas, the multitudes of words.
By means of those very [conceptions], the mind quickly constructs conventional discourse here and there; for the mind indeed conceives that which it perceives.
For how can one who consists of that very thing not see it? Thus, the unreal delusion of the world has reached such maturity.

"Everything up to Brahmā appears in vain, like a long-lasting dream or a magical illusion"—this [realization] is appropriate for the *ātivāhika* (subtle) body as its state of being *ādhibhautika* (material).
There is no materiality whatsoever anywhere at all; through practice, this very [mind] attains the state of being purely subtle (ātivāhika) by means of meditative cultivation.
"Delusion, which consists of false experience, has come from the very root of Brahman itself; this is what is held by the great-souled ones."
Thus, O Rāma, in this manner, where is there any connection between the states and the aggregate? All this is merely delusion, or rather, it is Brahman alone that appears as such.

There is nothing here other than the eternal; there is no cause apart from that which is indeed the state of being an effect. Since the possibility of being an effect or a cause does not exist in the Unafflicted (the Nirvāṇa), how can this [world] be so extensively spread out?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The state of knowledge becoming an object of cognition is called bondage; the cessation of that very objectivity is called liberation.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin, how does the cessation of the knowability of knowledge proceed? And once that notion of bondage has taken root, how is it here brought to an end?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Through the awakening of perfect knowledge, the dull intellect ceases; thus liberation—formless, innate, and peaceful—comes forth.
Śrī Rāma said: What is that which is called perfect knowledge—awakening in its absolute form—by means of which this living being is liberated entirely from bondage?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Knowledge has no object to be known; it is solely undecaying knowledge. This internal realization that "it is inexpressible" is remembered as perfect knowledge.

Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, tell me, how is it that the knowability of knowledge is distinct? What is its internal limit? Furthermore, does the word "knowledge" (jñāna) denote an action (*bhāva*), or rather an instrument (*karaṇa*)?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Knowledge is merely awareness, consisting solely of the means of apprehending an object; there is no distinction between knowledge and the object of knowledge, just as there is none between the wind and its movement.
Śrī Rāma said: If this is so, then how has this delusion of knowledge and the knowable—appearing like the horn of a hare, yet characterized by the past, present, and future—come to be established?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The deluded intellect described here is to be understood as arising from the error of external objects; yet, neither an external nor an internal object exists at all.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, tell me how this object of direct perception—consisting of you, myself, and others, composed of the elements, and characterized by the nature of experience—does not exist?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O sinless one, even at the very beginning of the process of creation, no object whatsoever was born as the primordial Virāṭ-ātman; therefore, there is no possibility of any knowable thing existing.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, this vision of the world—which abides in the past, present, and future—is constantly being experienced; why then is it said that it has not arisen?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Like the objects in a dream, the water of a mirage, the moon in the sky, or a mentally constructed object, this world and the sense of "I" appear falsely, like the optical illusion of floating hairs.

Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, how was it that at the beginning of creation, even the entire interior of the universe—including "I," "you," and "this"—did not arise as something possessing objective experience?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: It is a certainty that an effect arises from a cause and not otherwise; yet, in the total cessation of all things, there is no cause for the arising of the world.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, how could that which remains at the occurrence of the great dissolution—unborn and immutable—not indeed be the cause of creation?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Whatever effect exists within its cause, from that it proceeds; but what is non-existent does not arise, O Rāma, for a cloth is not produced from a jar.
Śrī Rāma said: When the great dissolution has arrived, the world remains within Brahman in a subtle form; therefore, it proceeds forth once again.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O sinless one of great intelligence, by whom was the existence of creation experienced at the end of the great dissolution? And what was that state like while situated therein?

Śrī Rāma said: Prosperity (Śrī) consists of pure consciousness; when situated therein, it is experienced as such. That which is of the nature of space, however, does not exist, for that which is non-existent cannot have being.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "If it is so, O mighty-armed one, then the three worlds are nothing but consciousness. For one whose body is pure knowledge, how can there be birth or death?"
Śrī Rāma said: "If, in this way, there was no creation from the beginning, then from where and how has this delusion come to be? O Blessed One, tell me."

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Because of the absence of the relationship between cause and effect, neither existence nor non-existence truly exists; and whatever is perceived as an object of thought is merely what one's own self perceives as its own thought.
Śrī Rāma said: If the conscious perceiver perceives the machine, and the seer becomes the object of sight, how can the Lord exist? And how indeed could wood ever burn fire?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The seer does not become an object of sight because of the impossibility of an object; therefore, the seer alone shines, as the singular, solid form of the Self of all.

Śrī Rāma said: That pure consciousness, which is without beginning or end, then perceives the object of perception. From where could this appearance of the world arise, given the impossibility of an object of perception?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Indeed, because of the absence of a cause, nothing whatsoever exists as an object of cognition; and due to the absence of an object of cognition, the state of liberation for consciousness is forever inexpressible.

Śrī Rāma said: If this is so, then how and from where does this object of cognition—such as the sense of "I" (ahaṃtā) and the rest—arise? How is there the perception of the world, and how is there the perception of movement and so forth?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Since no cause is possible, nothing whatsoever was produced in the beginning; for what could have been created? Therefore, all is peaceful, and creation is but an illusion.

Śrī Rāma said: In this state which is free from mental constructs, beyond the intellect, immovable, and so forth—luminous once and for all and stainless—whose delusion could there be, and of what nature?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, due to the absence of any cause, delusion truly does not exist at all; everything—“you,” “I,” and so forth—is but the one, peaceful, and healthy reality.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, having fallen as if into delusion, I do not know how to ask anything further; nor am I entirely awakened. What, then, should I ask here now?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Question the very touchstone of causality until you reach the cessation of causes; then you will yourself find rest in the supreme, ineffable nature.
Śrī Rāma said: I believe that, due to the absence of a cause, the state of creation did not exist even previously; therefore, whose is this delusion of the cognizer and the cognized?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Because it is without cause and because it is everywhere quiescent, delusion does not exist; it simply does not find rest due to the lack of practice.
Śrī Rāma said: From what would non-practice arise, and from what would practice arise? From what has this delusion, consisting of practice, now reappeared?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Because the Infinite is infinite, there is no delusion at present; all that appears as the delusion of habitual practice is, in truth, the undivided mass of the Great Consciousness.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahmin, since all else has subsided into tranquility, tell me what else remains to be said through this wealth of words regarding the teacher, the teaching, and so forth?"

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Brahman, consisting of both the teacher and the teaching, is established within Brahman itself; the certainty is that in the nature of pure awareness there is neither liberation nor bondage.
Śrī Rāma said: For those whose minds perceive distinctions of place, time, action, and substance, how can the existence of everything be established when everything is impossible?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For those whose minds perceive the distinctions of place, time, action, and substance, there was nothing other than mere ignorance; prior to that, no other existence existed for us.

Śrī Rāma said: Since the relationship between the object of knowledge and the knower is absent, how can there be the state of being consciousness? This is so because duality and unity are impossible, and the existence of Brahman as a cause is likewise impossible.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Through awakening, one attains the state of being awake; however, the word "awakening" refers to the state of being an object of knowledge. This [usage] is appropriate only with respect to you, and not for those such as us.

Śrī Rāma said: When consciousness itself assumes the state of "I-ness," then there is the appearance of otherness from consciousness. How could this [otherness] exist in the supreme, infinite, and stainless, which is like exceedingly pure water?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That which is the very nature of consciousness as consciousness is called "I-ness" (ahaṃtva); the duality therein is described as being like that between the wind and its movement or the eye and its sight.

Śrī Rāma said: Just as the waves and other phenomena within the gentle ocean take on their existence as they are, so too has the awakened one realized that the object of knowledge is nothing other than the nature of one's own self.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: If it is so, then what fault could there be from defects such as duality, since [the Self] abides in the infinite, singular, peaceful, and perfect supreme state?
Śrī Rāma said: Who here is the one who imagines this? Who am I? Who is the enjoyer that experiences? And what is the root from which this infinite delusion of the world unfolds?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Indeed, when the existence of the object of knowledge is realized, bondage no longer exists at all; since consciousness itself is the form of all objects, how then can there be bondage or liberation?

Śrī Rāma said: Just as blue and other colors appear from a lamp, the external nature of cognition proceeds [from it]; yet surely the external object exists as a real entity, for it is perceived through direct observation.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This reality of external objects and effects that lack a cause consists solely of the nature of delusion; it has no other basis.
Śrī Rāma said: Whether a dream be true or false, it nevertheless bestows suffering; likewise is this delusion of the world—tell me, what is the remedy for this?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, if this state of the world is exactly like a dream, then the entire perception of objects as solid masses has arisen solely from delusion.
Śrī Rāma said: When all this has been accomplished, what dear thing becomes fully attained? And how does the solid form of objects dissolve even in dreams and the like?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Through the reflection upon what precedes and follows, the sense of solid mass in objects subsides; when even this is so in a dream, gross conceptualization ceases.
Śrī Rāma said: For one whose mental cultivation has reached attenuation, what does he perceive? How is this wandering in the cavern of worldly existence stilled for him?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: One who is free from latent tendencies perceives the world as a false appearance that has vanished, like a city arisen in a dream, or like a painted image washed away by rain.

Śrī Rāma said: What then happens for him when the attenuation of latent impressions has been established, when the grasping of objects as solid masses has ceased, and the state of the world remains like a dream?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Through the gradual dissolution of the world, which is of the nature of mental construction (saṃkalpa), his latent impression (vāsanā) also dissolves; by that means, he quickly becomes one who is free from impressions and attains peace.

Śrī Rāma said: How is this terrible latent impression (vāsanā), which has grown deep through many births, which abounds in branching offshoots, and which causes the bondage of worldly existence, to be pacified?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Through the realization of things as they truly are, when the mere delusion is established within the Self, there occurs a gradual dissolution of this wheel of the visible world, which is devoid of any graspable substantiality.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, when this wheel of the visible world has been gradually liberated from the grasping of the physical body (piṇḍa), what else remains? How is peace produced?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the delusion of grasping at a solid body has subsided and the mind has attained the state of being nothing but consciousness, the world's existence comes to rest, liberated from the weight of its own suppression.
Śrī Rāma said: While this radiant world exists in the form of a child’s imagination, how can there be the pacification of attachment? Why would a man [persist] in such suffering?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When that which is accomplished by mere volition has perished, how can there be suffering? Let that which is merely the mind of volition be investigated for a while.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, what is the nature of the mind, and how is it to be investigated? Furthermore, tell me, what is attained when it has been properly investigated?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That which is the consciousness’s tendency toward objects of thought is called the mind; this very inquiry is its means by which latent impressions are stilled.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin, how much indeed is there of the mind’s orientation toward objects of thought? And how does the state of the mind becoming non-mind arise, which brings about liberation?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: An object of consciousness cannot possibly exist; therefore, what does consciousness perceive, and from where? Since an object of consciousness is impossible, the existence of the mind has long since ceased to be.
Śrī Rāma said: How can this object of thought, which is being experienced, not exist? And how can such a denial be made regarding that which is directly perceived?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: To the extent that the world is an object for the ignorant, it possesses no reality; yet to the extent that it is an object for the knower, it is that which is inexpressible and non-dual.

Śrī Rāma said: What is the nature of the three worlds for those who lack knowledge? Why is it not real for them? And why would it not be appropriate to describe what the world is like for those who possess that knowledge?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For those who lack knowledge, there is duality between beginning and end; for those who possess that knowledge, it does not exist. The world does not truly come into being, as it is eternally unarisen from the very start.
Śrī Rāma said: How can that which was unproduced from the beginning, which never comes into being at any time, which is non-existent in form and devoid of appearance, be experienced?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That which is unreal yet appears as real, unarisen and without cause, arises like a waking dream and is experienced as if it were a functional object.
Śrī Rāma said: That which is perceived in dreams and in mental constructions arises from the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of the waking state, resulting from past performance and experience.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, tell me this: is that which is experienced in a dream of the nature of waking, or is it something else? And what is its nature in a mental construction or a kingdom of the mind?

Śrī Rāma said: In dreams, in mental constructions, and the like, as well as in the delusions of the kingdom of the mind, it is the waking state alone that constantly appears by virtue of its nature as latent impressions (saṃskāra).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: If that very waking state appears as a dream due to the impressions (saṃskāra) of the waking state, then how can a house that has collapsed in a dream be recovered in the morning?

Śrī Rāma said: That which shines in the waking state does not shine in the dream; that [waking reality] is indeed none other than Brahman. Since this has been understood, how is it that it appears as something else, as if unprecedented?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: An object, whether previously experienced or not experienced, appears in the mind; however, that which has been well-practiced appears throughout the beginning, end, and middle of creation.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahmin, having understood that this world shines forth as consisting of dreams, how is this yakṣa of a dream—acting like a planet—to be treated?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: As for this dream of worldly existence, what could be its cause? Consider this: it is observed that the effect is not distinct from its cause.
Śrī Rāma said: The mind is the cause of the perceptions in dreams; therefore, that very mind is for you the universe—devoid of beginning or end, essence-less, and free from affliction.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, O one of great intelligence, the mind is indeed that very mass of Great Consciousness; as it thus abides, there is no dream or anything else of a different nature.
Śrī Rāma said: Just as there is a distinction between a part and the whole, so indeed is that [distinction] present there; yet in that partless Brahman, there is oneness with the world and all else.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, it is simply not possible that the world exists as something eternal, unarisen from the beginning, ageless, peaceful, unborn, and entirely undisturbed.

Śrī Rāma said: I consider the delusions of creation, its end, and so forth, along with the states of being a perceiver and an enjoyer, to be like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence within the Supreme State.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: There is a certain ever-active vision of poets that perceives aesthetic flavor through its sensitivity to rasa, and there is the scholarly vision of the wise which unfolds upon objects of established meaning. Relying upon both of these, the entire universe has been described by us with tranquility; as long as there is no perception of a "seer" apart from the act of seeing, for us there is neither emptiness nor delusion.
Śrī Rāma said: "If it is so, O best of sages, then this world consists of the supreme reality; being the self of all states at all times, it neither arises nor ceases."
This very delusion appears in the form of the manifestation of the world; or rather, it is not even delusion at all, but only the existence of Brahman itself.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When Brahman appears as if by chance (kākatālīya) within the Self by means of the Self, one understands that the world is indeed the Self itself through that very Self.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, tell me, how does the light of a lamp shine at the beginning of creation and in the world beyond, shining even without walls and transcending the directions?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This world shines in such a form through the radiance of the light of consciousness; behold, it exists by itself as that very [consciousness], even through its manifestations of illumination and so forth.

Light appears as if on a wall; that wall and its illumination exist because, in the beginning, there was no possibility of an object to be seen—therefore, let the speaker and the seer themselves be seen.
Therefore, the seer exists, but this visible world does not exist at all; it is the stainless radiance of consciousness itself that, by its own nature, becomes both the wall and the illumination.
The single essence consisting of the seer and the seen shines by itself alone, just as it does here today in dreams and other states, existing as that very essence of seer and seen.

For at the beginning of creation, consciousness alone shines; shimmering, it appears as if it were the creation itself. It is both the object to be manifested and the act of manifestation, wherein its own nature is self-luminous.

Though it is but one, consciousness appears as a triple painting at the beginning of creation, appearing as if it were the creation itself; such is its very nature that it shines forth in this manner, radiant.
This is experienced even within cities of dreams and mental constructs; such indeed is the way this first-arisen radiance of consciousness shines forth.
Just as in the sky, this world shines with the form of the sky; it is without beginning or end, and its creations are merely the manifestation of the nature of creation itself.
To us great-souled ones, this appears as our very own nature; the consciousness of the illuminated and the illuminator, which was perceived [as distinct], perishes.

At that time, indeed, at the beginning of creation, there was neither the object of illumination nor the illuminator; it was solely through the power of false cognition, just as the perception of a person occurs in regard to a post.
Thus, because duality appears within the Self, duality shines forth in the mind; yet at the beginning of creation, there was neither an object to be manifested nor a manifestor.
Due to the absence of a cause, non-duality alone shines as the sky of consciousness; tell me, what indeed could be the cause in reality at the beginning of creation within consciousness?
Due to the absence of any objective perceptions, consciousness alone shines forth in this manner; that which appears as this world is neither the waking state nor deep sleep.
Because it does not arise from sleep, that which is perceived is merely Brahman shining forth; thus, at the beginning of the creation of the sky of pure consciousness, it gleams in this manner.
That which knows its own body as the world, though it is not composed of the world—such is the blossoming of the sky of pure consciousness at the beginning of creation.
That which is called "the world" is indeed like emptiness and space.

And having understood this, one should remain endowed with one's own direct experience, free from conceptual construction; for the "silence like a stone" spoken of by the base person is not to be accepted, as it is merely the talk of an ignorant man who has neither experienced nor realized.
Śrī Rāma said: Alas! For so very long a time we have been bewildered within this supreme sky of saṃsāra, merely because it was not fully understood.
O Buddha, this so-called delusion of the world is nothing at all; it has not existed, it does not exist now, nor indeed will it ever come to be.
Everything is peaceful and without support; consciousness alone remains—endless, a mass of pure awareness, like the sky, free from passion and devoid of conceptual construction.
This very supreme space, merely through being unrecognized, has come to appear as if it were saṃsāra for us; how wonderful, indeed! O, how marvelous!
Thus this duality appears: these worlds, these mountains; yet it is nothing but the pure supreme space, appearing as if impure.

At the beginning of creation, in the next world, in dreams, and in mental constructions, it is consciousness alone that appears as the object of cognition; for how indeed could there be any other notion of an objective world?
If one has the thought, "I am situated in heaven or even in hell," then for that person, the end of that hell is seen as being composed of consciousness itself.
This is neither the visible object nor the seer, neither creation nor the world, nor consciousness; there is no such thing as waking, dreaming, or the like—all this is non-existent.
If it is asked, "O Sage, from what does the occurrence of this delusion arise?", we reply that even this is not tenable, because of the experience of the absence of delusion.
Error is simply impossible within the state of pure consciousness, which is changeless; that which is known as the cognition of error is itself that [consciousness], and nothing other than it.

In the space that is continuous, without beginning or end, or within the interior of a mountain, how could there be any conceptualization of otherness, given that the ground of consciousness is immutable?
The experience of delusion is indeed false, like one's own death in a dream; that which is called "non-perception" ceases through right perception.
This delusion of ignorance is like the optical illusion of a mirage, a city of Gandharvas, or a second moon; through investigation, it is not found to exist.
For even when one is awake, this delusion is not true knowledge; it is like a child’s perception of a ghost. Having grown firm through lack of inquiry, it is pacified by inquiry.
O Sage, the question "from where did it come? does not apply here; for through inquiry, one gains knowledge of that which exists, not of that which does not exist.
That which is not found when scrutinized through valid investigation is simply non-existent; therefore, the experience of that is an illusion.
How can that which has been determined by the means of valid cognition as "non-existent" and thoroughly investigated as being like a sky-flower or a hare's horn be obtained from what exists?
Even when sought everywhere, that which is not found anywhere—what kind of existence could there be for it, being like the form of a barren woman's son?
Therefore, no delusion whatsoever can ever possibly exist; this entire expanse is nothing but a mass of unobscured consciousness.
Whatever appears here in this world today, that is indeed the Supreme; the Supreme abides as the full within the Supreme, which is the supreme plenum.
Nothing here has ever appeared, nor has anything ever not appeared; this body of the world remains as it is—transparent and utterly peaceful.

I am that state which is unborn, undying, unassailable, and cherished by the noble; supremely changeless, entirely free from affliction, exalted, pervasive, pure, egoless, manifold yet non-dual, and ever-expansive.
Śrī Rāma said: Neither the gods nor the sages know that state which is without beginning, middle, or end; yet this world shines forth—where is the world, and where is the visible?
Enough for us with the delusions and doubts arising from statements concerning duality and non-duality; we seek that primordial, stainless form which is utterly tranquil.
Just as the appearance of space within the sky is utterly tranquil, so too is the manifestation of the vast space of the three worlds within the sky of consciousness.
Just as the nature of space resides in space, the nature of stone in stone, and the nature of water within water, so too does the nature of the world reside within the mass of consciousness.
Know that this entire visible world, beginning with "I" and extending through the sky of hope, is the belly of the Great Consciousness—a peaceful void arisen from emptiness.
When this deluded living being [realizes] the Supreme, which possesses immeasurable manifestation, even the throbbing demon of saṃsāra is pacified.
Even for one engaged in worldly activity, the perception of duality completely vanishes—just as it does for the insentient or even for the sentient, like a wave within the belly of the water.
When the sun of ignorance, the great source of heat and power, has gone somewhere far away, the day of the existence of saṃsāra sets, and that arrival of night follows.
Regarding the existence and non-existence of effects, such as birth, old age, and death, the knower, though remaining amidst the state of constant flux, does not truly abide therein.
There is no ignorance, no delusion, no suffering, and no arising of happiness; for that which is called knowledge, ignorance, happiness, and suffering is nothing but the stainless Brahman.
When this is fully understood, it is indeed the stainless Brahman itself; for us, there exists no non-Brahman self that remains uncomprehended.
I am awakened; all my false views have been completely stilled. I behold these three worlds as peaceful, equal, and this very void.
This entire world has been correctly known as nothing but Brahman alone; that which was Brahman when the Self was unknown now abides in the known Self.
Brahman alone is thus undecaying, appearing neither as the known nor the unknown; it is one, like the sky which has the single form of emptiness, unity, and blueness.

In the month of Nirvana, in the month free from fear, in the month of effortless supreme bliss, in the month of the eternally abiding and infinite as-it-is—how could that month not be a state of equanimity?

I am always everything, the one infinite; or rather, I am nothing at all, or else I am utterly tranquil. I am everything and yet nothing, I am the eternal One, and yet I am not—I, oh, what peace this is!

That which was to be realized has been realized; that which was to be attained has been attained; this entire mass of phenomena, which others had not reached, has come to its end. Such is the dawning of supreme awakening, wherein even the name of the rising and setting of things no longer exists.
Śrī Vālmīki said: When the leader of sages had concluded the composition of the discourse on Nirvāṇa and was bringing the final words to a close in their proper sequence, [Vasiṣṭha spoke].
When all the assembly had attained the equanimity of non-conceptual meditative absorption, and their mental activities were peaceful and clear.
When the reality of consciousness has reached the pinnacle of being for all people who possess learning, it attains supreme purity.

Instantly, it was carried away by the sky from the mouths of the perfected ones (siddhas) dwelling in the hollows of the firmament, who, with their minds previously liberated, uttered cries of "Well done! (sādhu).
Likewise, there was a great accumulation of words of praise from the sages of purified soul seated in the assembly, headed by the son of Gadhi.
A tumultuous clamor arose, filling the quarters of the sky, like the sweet sound of hollow bamboos whistling in the wind.
Then, along with the shouts of "Well done! from the perfected ones, the celestial drums suddenly resounded, filling the mountains with their echoes.
Along with the celestial drums, a shower of flowers, beautiful like a downpour of snow, fell from all directions, veiling the entire horizon.
The place was filled with a flood of flowers, its caves resounded with sound, the sky was colored by pollen, and the wind was perfumed with fragrance.
The convergence of the sound of "well-spoken" (sādhuvāda), the resonance of celestial instruments, and the roar of the downpour of flowers shone forth brilliantly.
Its interior was darkened by the rays from the eyes of all the courtiers looking up, and it was heard by deer, elephants, horses, birds, and beasts with ears pricked.
He was gazed upon by children and women with eyes upturned in wonder and fear, while the assembly of kings looked on with faces smiling in amazement.
With an intensity that was the essence of a shower of flowers and surpassed the splendor of sound, he quickly brought the hollow between heaven and earth to an unprecedented state.
Washed by a rain of flowers and nectar, resounding with the "sughuṃghum" cries of shouting spirits, and filled with hundreds of blown conch shells, the sky attained equality with the palace.
The world, resplendent with the abundant sound of "bhāṃkāra," surrounded by gods and celestial musicians, and filled with intoxicated festivities, shone forth, adorned equally with flowers.

The heavy rain of flowers that was the speech of the multitude of Siddhas and Dundubhis proceeded slowly and simultaneously through the space between heaven and earth, like the tide reaching the shore-mountain in the ocean.
When that moment of the gods' agitation had passed in an instant, these words of the Siddhas became manifest:
The Siddhas said: "Throughout the aeon, thousands of means to liberation have been explained and heard among the assemblies of Siddhas; yet none such as this have ever existed."
By the playful charm of this sage’s words, even animals, women, children, and predatory beasts attain peace; of this there is no doubt.
Just as Rāma was awakened through examples, reasons, and logic, so too does Arundhatī herself awaken him—or does she not?
By this means of liberation, even animals have gone beyond disease; they remain liberated—what humans on earth, indeed, will not become so?
Having drunk this nectar of knowledge with the cupped hands of our ears, we have attained supreme glory, our spiritual powers having become fully renewed.
Hearing this, the people in the assembly, their eyes wide with wonder, beheld that hall filled with a shower of lotus flowers.
It had a mass of coverings concealed by great flowers such as the mandāra, and its courtyard ground was densely filled with clusters of *pāribhadra* creepers.
It was resplendent upon the surface of the earth, rich with the blossoms of the pārijāta tree, while the hands of the assembly members were covered by the great clouds of saṃtānaka flowers.
With its tips adorned by crests of crest-jewels and resting upon yellow sandalwood, it had canopies suspended like clouds hanging down from a mass of water.
Thus observing the assembly, the people were filled with abundant cries of "Well done! and endeavored to speak various words appropriate for that occasion.
