Then, bowing with all his senses, he honored Vasiṣṭha with a handful of flowers accompanied by prostrations.
Then, when those garlands of royal prostrations had somewhat subsided, the king, holding the vessel of honorific water (arghya) in his hand, spoke while worshipping the sage.
Daśaratha said: O Lord of Arundhatī, through awakening, supreme fullness has arisen within you by means of the ultimate reality of the self, which is free from decay and excess.

There is nothing on the surface of the earth, nor even among the Daityas or the gods, that is so great as to have not been attained by you, who are worthy of worship, through your own acts of adoration.
Nevertheless, O Brahmin, in order to make this sequence of mine not fruitless, I shall speak as it has come to me; you ought not to be angry.
With myself, with my wife, with the merit of both worlds, and with the entire kingdom and its servants, I worship you.
All this, O Lord, is under your own control like your own hermitage; employ it as you direct, according to your desired will.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O King, we Brāhmaṇas are satisfied by a mere salutation; we are pleased by salutation alone, and that very one has been performed by you."
Only you know how to protect it, and the kingdom shines for you alone; let this remain yours here, for where are the Brahmins compared to sovereigns?
Daśaratha said: "O Sage, we feel ashamed to say how small our kingdom might be; therefore, O Lord, act as you see fit for its expansion."
Śrī Vālmīki said: When the king had spoken thus, Rāma, offering a handful of flowers, bowed down and addressed these words before his great preceptor.
O Great King, O Brahmā, who have rendered all others unsurpassed, I bow to you; I am Rāma, whose essence is merely this prostration, at these two feet of yours, O Lord.
Having spoken thus, she first bowed her head at his feet and cast away the flowers from her joined palms, as a mass of snow leaves a mountain forest.
With eyes filled with tears of joy, that master of statesmanship bowed down again and again to his guru with supreme devotion.
Śatrughna, Lakṣmaṇa, and others who were his equals, standing nearby, likewise quickly bowed down to the lord of sages.
Standing at a distance, kings and princes, as well as sages, paid him homage with prostrations from afar and with handfuls of flowers accompanied by the wafting of the wind.
At that moment, amidst the showers of handfuls of flowers there, the sage vanished like the Lord of the Snow Mountains disappearing behind its snowdrifts.

Then, when the agitation of the assembly had subsided and the multitude of prostrations was likewise concluded, he reflected for a moment upon the teaching regarding the truth of black and white intentions.
The sage, having brushed aside that heap of flowers with his two arms, revealed his face like the moon emerging from white clouds.
When the multitude of the perfected ones' words had become silent, as did the sound of the drum, while the rain of celestial flowers fell and the assembly was in a state of tumultuous acclaim;
Immediately after the prostration, when that assembly of people, including Rāma and others, had become as serene as a cloud when the wind has subsided, [he spoke].
Hearing the cry of "Well done! from Viśvāmitra in a gentle voice, Vasiṣṭha, the leader of sages whose soul was beyond reproach, spoke these words.
O Sage, O Lotus of the Gādhi clan, O Vāmadeva, Nimi, Kratu, Bharadvāja, Pulastya, Atri, Ghṛṣṭi, Nārada, and Śāṇḍilya!
"Bhāsa, Bhṛgu, Bhāraṇḍa, Vatsa, Vātsyāyana, and the other sages—have you heard my words, which are indeed trivial?"
Whatever in this [work] may be improper, whether it be difficult to understand or devoid of meaning, may you now tell me out of your favor.

The members of the assembly said: "O Brahmin, today we have heard for the first time a truly novel statement—that even the words of Vasiṣṭha, which are uniquely endowed with ultimate truth, can become meaningless."
That impurity which had been accumulated by the endless defects of birth has been wiped away by you here today, just as gold is cleansed by fire.
O All-pervading Lord, we have been made to blossom by Your speech, which is expanded by the Brahman and is as cool as supreme nectar, just as night-lotuses are by the radiance of the moon.
We here bow down to you, the leader of sages, the sole teacher, who bestows great awakening upon all sentient beings.
Śrī Vālmīki said: Having spoken thus, they again addressed the Lord of Sages with the single word "Salutations to You! uttered in a loud, resonant voice as powerful as the roar of the ocean.
With multitudes of handfuls of flowers showered from the sky by the Siddhas, they filled Vasiṣṭha, just as clouds fill a mountain with snow.
Thus did those well-versed in the history of Rāghava praise King Daśaratha, as well as Rāghava and Mādhava, who are the fourfold self.
The Siddhas said: We bow to Rāma, the prince who is liberated while living, together with his brother, who is like another Nārāyaṇa of fourfold nature.
To King Daśaratha, the protector of the circle of the earth bounded by the four oceans, who bore the insignia of a sovereign of the three times.
To King Bhāskara, the lord of the sage-army and possessor of great splendor; to Vasiṣṭha, rich in excellent speech; and to Viśvāmitra, a treasure-house of asceticism.
By the power of these very [teachings], we have all heard this supreme method of knowledge, which destroys delusion and agitation.
Śrī Vālmīki said: Having spoken thus, the Siddhas again scattered flowers from the sky; then, with joyful hearts, they remained silent within the assembly hall.
In the same way, the Siddhas traveling through the sky praised that person again; likewise, the members of the assembly there honored them with a profuse hymn of praise.

The sky-dwellers, the earth-dwellers, the lords of sages, the great seers, the hosts of gods, the twice-born, and the kings honored Janma with their very vigor, along with heaps of words and the offering of flowers and water for the feet.
Śrī Vālmīki said: Then, as the cries of "Excellent! gradually subsided and the kings, having received the instruction on knowledge, seemed to shine with great splendor;
When the delusion of saṃsāra has been stilled, one truly laughs within one's own mind at one's own past conduct as it pursues the truth.
The minds of the assembly were subdued, intent on savoring the taste of knowledge; the discerning crowd remained tranquil, as if established in meditative absorption.
Rāma, together with his brother, sat in the lotus posture before the Guru with palms joined in reverence, his eyes fixed upon the radiant face of the Teacher.
The King relished a certain state of meditation within himself—a state consisting of liberation while living, which purifies the beginning, middle, and end.
The sage, who honors those who seek his favor, remained silent for a moment as if to receive the worship of his devotees, and then spoke with clear and composed syllables.
O lotus-eyed Rāma, moon of the sky that is your own lineage, what else do you wish to hear? Tell me your desire and I shall speak.
Tell me, what kind of state do you yourself experience now? And tell me, what is the nature of this worldly appearance that you perceive?
When this had been said by that sage, the prince, looking into the face of his teacher, spoke calmly, gently, and clearly.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Lord, by your grace I have attained supreme purity, like the vault of the sky in autumn when every mark of blemish has been stilled."
All my delusions, which cause the destruction of existence, have been entirely stilled; I abide in my own naturally pure form, like the clear sky.
I stand with all knots dissolved, with every particular attribute stilled; my intellect is as pure as crystal, situated within the abode of crystal.
Now my mind no longer desires to hear or to grasp anything else; it has attained supreme satisfaction and remains as if in deep sleep.
O Sage, my mind is peaceful—its all conceptualizations stilled, its every curiosity vanished, and all volitional thoughts completely abandoned.
While remaining awake for the sake of the world's stability, I enter parinirvāṇa and am stilled; I sleep, as it were, in a state free from affliction, without dreaming and beyond rebirth.
Laughing at my former state of being, which was shaken by desires within this body, I remain established in myself, free from doubt, through the radiance of well-spoken truths.
Neither by instruction, nor by wealth, nor by scriptures, nor by kinsmen, nor even by the renunciation of these things is there any purpose for me now.
I experience right here that very same state which exists in universal sovereignty or in the sky—unperturbed and inseparable from my mind.
Today, with my eyes reaching toward its very essence, I perceive this world as nothing more than a portion of the utterly pure space of consciousness, which is even more transparent than the sky.
"This entire world is nothing but space"—this is my singular certainty. When this sky known as the "visible" has perished, I remain awake, imperishable.
Whatever he says—according to his desire, as it has been obtained, and as if it were already established—I perform without obstacle, free from all longing.
I am neither pleased, nor elated, nor flourishing, nor do I weep; alone I perform what must be done, and my delusion has gone far away.
Let this creation go to its end, or let the wind of dissolution blow; let the region become pleasant; I am well, established in my own self.
I am at rest, I am free from embarrassment, I am beyond perception, and I am without affliction; O Sage, I am bound by my desires as the sky is grasped by fists.
Just as fragrance from a flower on a tree reaches the realm of space and remains there, so too do I abide, having transcended the body and established in equanimity.
Just as all kings dwell according to their pleasure—both those who are unawakened and those who are awakened—in their kingdoms with many duties.
With peace, joy, sorrow, and hope extinguished, possessing steady and singular equanimity, I abide fearlessly within the Self and likewise move about.
O Lord, though I am happy even above all, I do not desire happiness for myself; I remain equal toward all people—employ me as you wish.
O holy one, as long as this body lasts, I shall maintain this worldly existence with a single, stainless vision, casting off all fear like a child at play.
"I eat, I drink, I stand, and I perform my own duties; O Lord of Sages, by your grace I have been born free from all doubt."
Śrī Rāma said: Oh, what great merit has been attained by you, who have reached this state that is without beginning, middle, or end, wherein one does not grieve!
In my own self, which is naturally cool through the effortless application of perfect equanimity, I have attained rest within that which is as tranquil as space within space.
By good fortune you have become free from sorrow; by good fortune you are firmly established; by good fortune the fear of misfortune in both worlds has come to rest for you.
By good fortune, O son of the Raghus, you have purified the lineage of your family—past, present, and future—through your awakening.
Now, O Raghava, having fulfilled the request of Viśvāmitra, the lord of sages, and having enjoyed this earth together with your father, you shall depart.

Accompanied by you, along with their sons, servants, and kinsmen, and together with their circles of infantry, chariots, elephants, and horses—may the Raghavas be free from ailment, devoid of fear, possessed of stable prosperity, ever-victorious, and fortunate, O blessed one!
Śrī Vālmīki said: Having heard these words of Vasiṣṭha in the assembly, the kings attained an inner coolness, as if drenched by a flood of nectar.
Rāma, whose eyes were like lotus petals, shone with his moon-like face, like the full Ocean of Milk filled with a beautiful flood of nectar.
Vāmadeva and all the others, who were experts in the knowledge of reality, said with reverence: "Oh, the Blessed One has spoken of wisdom!"
With his inner self pacified, King Daśaratha shone with joy; his limbs thrilled with contentment, he attained a renewed luster.
Then, amidst many discourses of praise concerning the objects of knowledge already known, Rāma, his ignorance having dissolved, spoke these words once more:
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, our impurity has been thoroughly wiped away by you, just as the blackness of gold is removed by fire.
"O Lord, formerly we were ones who saw only our own bodies; now we have become those who behold the entire universe in all directions."
I stand complete in every way; I am perfected and free from ailment. I am born with all doubts dispelled; as a wise one, I now remain awake.
I am gladdened for the sake of tirelessness, and I am happy for the sake of long duration; I stand firm for the sake of never-setting, as the rising of the eternal truth is mine.
"Aha! I am sprinkled by you with the cool, purifying water of wisdom; I myself rejoice in my heart like a lotus."
Today, by your grace, this state has been attained by me; abiding in which, the entire world has become nectar for me.

With an inner mind serene, all sorrow dispelled, and having attained splendor through tranquility within my stainless heart, I have reached bliss in the Self by the Self alone; I have attained purity—homage be to me!
Śrī Vālmīki said: While the sage and Rāghava were thus absorbed in deliberation, the sun ascended to the midst of the sky as if to listen.
Then the heat quickly attained sharpness in every direction, like the great intellect of Rāma for the purpose of expanding the multitude of objects.
Then, with their heart-lotuses blooming into vast forms, those standing there shone like kings in a playful lotus pond.
Immediately after the clusters of pearls, the net, having eclipsed the sun, seemed to dance as it traversed the sky, as if out of a desire to hear the news of his awakening.
The rays of the young sun, having touched the rubies, sparkled like flashes of intellect—the subtle portions of knowledge—soaring from the surface of the sky.
Thus, when Rāma—the white lotus of his own lineage—had attained liberation and remained as if in full bloom from beholding the face of the Lord of Sages;
When the sky, with its sun and submarine fire as its lotus petals, had become the navel of the great ocean—a blazing mass of light that consumed all essences—[the world was thus transformed].
The blue lotus of the sky shone forth, its pollen falling away, lovely with the sun as its pericarp and its shimmering rays as its filaments.
They are the crest-ornaments of the Fortune of the World and the ear-pendants of the three realms, resplendent with rows of jewels like shimmering stars nestled within them.
As the great waterless clouds, split by the heat of the sun, were held up like mirrors by the quarters of the sky—those brides with their large peaks as hands—[the sun shone].
As if augmented by the fire arising from the excellent sun-gem, it blazes twice as intensely in the expanse of the sky when devoid of the sun.
Filled with the fierce and violent breath from their mouths, the midday conchs blared like oceans swollen by the winds at the end of an eon.
Like the beauty of frost upon lotuses, or like the beauty of summer upon faces, she—resembling scattered pure pearls—set foot [upon the earth].
The splendor of that sound, intensified by the agitation of living beings and reverberating off the walls of the house, filled the ears like the ocean filling its own shore.
A fresh row of pale camphor clouds, raised by the housewives to quench the heat of the summer's onset, shone forth brilliantly.
That king, together with his vassals, his princes, his retinue, Vasiṣṭha, Rāma, and his assembly, rose up all at once.
The kings, princes, ministers, and likewise the sages, having honored one another, departed for their own abodes filled with joy.
At the front of the inner apartments, a fresh garland of clouds was created by camphor dust carried there by the wind from palm-leaf fans.
Then, as the sound of the midday drums resounded against the walls, the leader of sages, skilled in speech, spoke these words.
O Raghava, everything that can be heard has been heard by you, and everything that can be known has been known without exception; indeed, there remains nothing further of superior value to be known.
Just as you have been instructed by me, just as you perceive it through the scriptures, and just as you experience this supreme truth, act accordingly with single-minded resolve.
Arise now for our task, O Great-minded One; this is our midday hour, and the moment for bathing is passing away.
Furthermore, O noble one, whatever you desire to ask for the sake of dispelling your doubts, that auspicious matter should be asked by you again tomorrow morning.
Śrī Vālmīki said: When the Lord of Sages had spoken thus, King Daśaratha himself honored all those virtuous members of the assembly with due reverence.
Together with Rāma, that righteous-souled king [honored] the sages, brahmins, and kings, as well as those who travel through the sky, according to the sequence instructed by Vasiṣṭha and the others.
With the value of heaps of jewels and pearls, with divine flowers, by the gift of precious gems, and by the offering of pearl necklaces.
By means of affection, prostration, and the offering of wealth, as well as clothing, seats, food, drink, gold, and even land.
The blameless lord of the earth honored all those who had come before him with incense, perfumes, and garlands, exactly as prescribed.
Then the giver of honor rose from the midst of the assembly together with the assembly and the divine sages headed by Vasiṣṭha, like the evening moon rising from the sky.
The time of the simultaneous rising shone forth with great excitement, as the ground became muddy from the flowers released by the gods that had reached the height of their knees.
The earth was reddened by the dust of jewels from the colliding armlets, while the night sky shone with the stars of pearls from broken necklaces.
It was crowded with the movement of celestial sages, hermits, eminent brahmins, and kings; its fly-whisks were made restless by the hands of attendants and women who were busily waving them.
Vibrating with the act of making knowledge its object of measurement, he is not harsh; he shines resplendent precisely within the head, hands, three eyes, and tongues.
Then, having consulted with one another, all the kings and sages, beginning with Daśaratha, were honored with elegant words.
The virtuous ones returned to their own hermitages with hearts mutually satisfied and affectionate, like the gods dwelling in the seven worlds returning from the city of Śakra.
Having honored one another in turn out of mutual affection, they were dismissed by him; returning to their own homes, they performed their daily duties.
Then all those beginning with Vasiṣṭha, as well as those beginning with Daśaratha—the kings and the sages alike—performed their daily duties.
Then, after they had performed their daily rites as was customary, the sun, traveling through the path of the sky, gradually reached its setting.
Through that very conversation, by virtue of the awakening of those sages and of the high-minded Rāma, that night quickly passed away.
The sun arrived, turning the world into a palace, filled with flowers that were the stars and the dust of darkness dispelled.
Then the young sun entered the ocean of the sky, reddening the quarters of the horizon with his rays that shone like *karavīra* and safflower.
Kings, princes, ministers, and sages such as Vasiṣṭha and others likewise assembled once more in the assembly hall of the son of Daśaratha.
In due order, according to their positions, their locations, and their seats, she entered that assembly hall like the splendor of the celestial fire-altars in the sky.
Then, while Daśaratha and the others, as well as Sumantra and his companions, were praising the sage Vasiṣṭha who was seated upon his throne, [the king spoke].
In the presence of his father Vasiṣṭha, the wise Rāghava, whose eyes were like lotus petals, spoke these words in gentle tones.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, great ocean of all knowledge, axe to all doubts, remover of sorrow and fear!
Is there anything further for me to hear, or indeed anything to be known? Whatever remains to be heard, you should please explain it all to me.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, you have attained true awakening; there is nothing further for you to hear. This intellect of yours has accomplished its purpose, having reached all that is to be attained and being established in the Self.
First, reflect within yourself with your own intellect and tell me: what is your inner state now, and what remains for you to hear?
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, I think thus: since my mind has accomplished its purpose, I am liberated, I am profoundly peaceful, and no desire remains within me.
What was to be said has been spoken by you; everything that is to be known has been understood by me. May your eloquence, having accomplished its purpose, now find rest.

That which was to be attained has been attained; this entire knowable has been reached by me. Duality has set, and all-oneness remains. The appearance of the manifoldness of the visible has completely dissolved; indeed, the foundation of all worldly existence has been skillfully cast away.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O mighty-armed one, listen once more to my supreme word: a mirror shines exceedingly when polished again and again.
The object is a convention of sensation, and the word is like the sound of water; this visible world is but the manifestation of consciousness—like a dream, where did the universe ever come to be?
Indeed, that which is perceived in a dream while awake exists before one as consisting of memory; it is pure consciousness and mere cognition, yet it is spread out as if possessing another form.
Just as the sky of consciousness within me, though appearing as a city in a dream, is formless even while possessing form, so too is this triple world.
Śrī Rāma said: How did this earth come into being? How did the mountains come into being? How did the waters come into being, and how did the stones come into being?
And how is the fire perfected, and how is the ritual action perfected? How is the time perfected, and how is the wind perfected?
How is emptiness accomplished, and how is the sky accomplished? This has been understood by me further; tell me for the sake of awakening, O Lord.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Tell me in truth, O Rāghava, how did the earth come to be in that great city seen in the dream, and how did the sky come to be?
How is water perfected? How are stones perfected? How is fire perfected? And how are the directions perfected?
How is the time perfected, and how is the ritual action perfected? How are all these factors, such as the signs and so forth, said to be perfected? Please explain this all.
By whom was this created, burnt, brought, fashioned, piled up, produced, and manifested? What is its conduct, and what is its nature?
Śrī Rāma said: The Self of this world, which is like a dream, is purely space; it consists of neither earth, mountains, nor anything else. It is formless and without support.
The Self alone is its form, like space—without support and without shape; for this space that is devoid of form, what need is there for a supporting cause?
This which has arisen is nothing at all, for it is not distinct from consciousness; this so-called "manifestation of the intellect" is simply the mind itself abiding in such a state.

To those who know it, space, time, and so forth are the manifestation of consciousness; the immovable mountains and so forth are the manifestation of consciousness; water and so forth are likewise consciousness through awakening; and wind and so forth are the void of consciousness.
Consciousness alone, indeed, exists as the void, reaching the state of emptiness; it remains as a stone due to its hardness, and like water, it exists through its fluidity.
In reality, however, there is no such thing as earth or the like, nor is there any visibility; that infinite space of consciousness is all, one, and of its own nature.

Just as water from the ocean becomes manifold through its various transformations despite being essentially one due to its fluidity, so too does the non-dual consciousness within the self of the space of consciousness become manifold.

When consciousness attains the state of solidity, it perceives itself as a vast earth, as if it had become a mountain; when it perceives emptiness, the body of consciousness knows itself as void, like space.
Through the perception of fluidity it knows water; through its vibration, the wind; and through the awareness of heat, it knows fire, without ever abandoning its own essential nature.
Thus, this element of consciousness, whose nature is like the sky, shines forth in this way as a sequence of qualities that are without cause.
Apart from these two, nothing else exists here whatsoever, just as there is nothing other than emptiness and water in the sky and the ocean respectively.
Nothing whatsoever exists apart from the sky of consciousness; therefore, remain in the state of utter peace regarding this world, the "you," the "I," and so forth.
Just as you perceive fire, mountains, and so forth while acting within this house, yet see them as having no physical form, so too is the sky of consciousness.

At the beginning of creation, it is the sky of consciousness that shines as the appearance of a body, but not a physical body; since there is no cause for what is non-existent, one should reflect that consciousness alone arises.
The mind, the intellect, the ego, the elements, the mountains, and the directions—all remain as they are, composed of silence like a stone-womb.
Thus, nothing whatsoever has arisen, nor has anything perished; the form of the world remains as it is, abiding within the Self that is Consciousness-Brahman.
That which is called manifestation within consciousness is the unfolding of its own essential nature; this is what is termed the "world," just as fluidity is to water.

This appearance of the world is indeed no appearance at all; it is the void of the sky of consciousness, the ultimate reality itself. For one whose intellect perceives things as they truly are, it is the Buddha; for one whose intellect does not perceive them thus, let it be as it may.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, if there is no web of doubt regarding this—that what is seen in a dream is exactly like the supreme sky [of the waking state] even during the waking state—then it is so.
O Blessed One, tell me this, my supreme and great question: how does consciousness, which is bodiless, become like one's own body during the waking and dreaming states?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Whether in the waking state or in a dream, the visible world has space as its support, consists of space, and is born from space; and space itself is never anything else. There is no doubt about this, for it is established by reasoning.
In that whose nature consists of the total disappearance of all causes and forms, no elements whatsoever come into being even at the beginning of creation.

Therefore, this body is merely composed of earth and the other elements; it is nothing at all. Indeed, these are just the primary elements (bhūtas); the body does not exist as anything distinct from them.
Therefore, this sky of consciousness perceives appearances like a dream; it is the mere shining forth of its own nature, appearing as if agitated by forms.
This form of the world, which is merely a manifestation and a mere appearance, is described by the conscious Self through the metaphors of space and a dream.
This which is called "feeling" (vedanā)—the sky-pure expanse of the sky of consciousness—is the internal form of consciousness; it exists as the dream that is the world.
Then, within this very expanse of the manifestation of its own nature, which is of the form of consciousness, these various designations such as "earth" and so forth were fashioned.
It is the very manifestation of consciousness that is described by the terms "dream" and "world"; and this manifestation is its inherent nature, like space, which never ceases.
The many diverse visions of creation are like Brahma within the ether of Brahma; they abide and dissolve within the void of emptiness, like the wind in the sky.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, you have indeed spoken of millions of creations; some are situated within the shell of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), while others are devoid of such an egg."
Some are situated within the treasury of the earth, some are established in the treasury of space; some are contained within the treasury of fire, and some reside in the treasury of wind.

Some had the surface of the earth situated in the sky, with their certainty regarding what was above and below inverted; they had their hooves pointing upward from the space of the base, with forests and mountains hanging down from them.
Some were like floods consisting of the nature of wind; some were eternally bearing darkness; some had the configuration of the sky; and some were teeming with swarms of worms.
Some were situated within the hollows of space, some within the hollows of stones; some were situated within the hollows of bird-nests, and some remained in the sky like birds.
O Blessed One, best among the knowers of reality, tell me this: among those [worlds], what is this Brahmāṇḍa like and how does it exist?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That which is unprecedented, unseen, unexperienced, or unheard is described through excellent illustrations; it is grasped and inferred therefrom.
But this cosmic egg, O Rāma, has been described hundreds of times by the scriptures, sages, and gods; and all of that has been known by you in its entirety.
Just as this has been understood by you and described according to the scriptures, so does all this stand; what else remains to be described here?
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, tell me how this great space of pure consciousness came into being; what is its extent, and for how long has it existed?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This Brahman exists, eternal and imperishable, without beginning or end; it possesses no beginning, middle, or end, nor does it have forms within the supreme ether.
The space of Brahman is without beginning or end, undecaying, and all-pervading; this entire universe consists of that, being itself devoid of beginning or end in every respect.
That which is the self-manifestation of this supreme sky of consciousness within itself is called "this universe"; yet by that very fact, it is itself illusory.
Just as a person has the perception of a city in a dream, so too does that [universe] appear like a city; this is what is called "this universe."
Here there are no mountains that are solid, nor are there waters that are liquid; this space is not empty, and time is not of the nature of measurement.
In whatever manner and wherever that which is imperishable is conceived by consciousness itself, it remains exactly so and there within the nature of consciousness, as stable as a mountain.

Just as in a dream non-stone may indeed become stone and the sky itself may become a non-sky, so too here the beginning of creation and the existence of perceived objects occur within consciousness, like a dream.
The tranquil consciousness itself, being formless, perceives its own awareness as if in a dream; thus it is said that this world exists, yet it remains truly formless.
Just as the movement within the wind is nothing other than the wind itself in its continuity, so too this Brahman within Brahman neither arises nor ceases.
Just as liquidity exists in water, just as emptiness exists in the sky, and just as substantiality exists in a substance, so does this world exist within Brahman.
Neither has it gone forth nor has it come from a causeless source; neither does this world not exist, nor does it exist as something distinct from the state of Brahman.
Nor can the beginningless, appearance-free, and formless sky of consciousness possibly be the cause of any other perception anywhere.
Therefore, just as the parts of a whole exist only as their own selves, so too does the world-space abide within the partless space of Brahman.
All is peaceful, without support, mere cognition, and free from affliction; herein there is neither existence nor non-existence, nor is there any diversity whatsoever.
All this that is extended is like a mental construction, a dream, a city of the Gandharvas, or a dance; it exists as the same, peaceful, unborn, and imperishable space.

That which, being the heart of the supreme consciousness-ether, shines forth as beautiful and stainless through its own volition—that very thing is conceived as this world; by that [consciousness] alone, it is perceived as its own form until the end of the aeon.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That appearance which shines forth without a cause is nothing at all; for in that manner, O sinless one, the supreme reality remains as the supreme reality according to the ultimate truth.
In this regard, O Mahāmati, listen to this supreme great question which I was asked by someone; I shall explain it for the sake of nourishing right awakening.
There exists a continent known as Kuśadvīpa, which is renowned throughout the three worlds and is situated on the earth like a ring, encompassed on both sides by two oceans.
There, in the northeast, is a golden city named Āstīlavatī, where the surface of the earth and the vault of the sky are fixed upon pillars composed of blazing flames.
In former times, there was a king renowned as Prajñapti, who was beloved by all living beings and was like a second Śakra in heaven.
For some reason, on one occasion, I approached that king from the sky, descending like the sun at the time of universal dissolution.
Having honored me with flowers, water for the guest-offering, and water for sipping, he sat down; then, in the midst of some conversation, he asked this out of affection:
O Blessed One, when all things have been withdrawn, when one abides in emptiness, in the ineffable supreme void where all causes have ceased, [what remains?]
Tell me again: what is the root cause of the commencement of creation? What are the auxiliary causes, from where do they arise, and how do they function?
What is this world, and what is its creation and so forth? Some regions of darkness are eternal; some are oceans situated in the sky, while others are teeming with swarms of worms.

Some are situated within the hollow of space, and some reside within the hollow of stones; furthermore, what indeed are the elements and the like, and from where do cognition and its associates arise? How [could they exist]?
Who is the agent, or who is the observer? What is the relationship between the support and the supported, and how does it exist? It is certain that there is never any destruction of the worlds.
It has been established so as not to contradict the meaning of all the Vedas and Shastras: that just as there is such a thing as consciousness, so too are there experiences corresponding to names.

O Leader of Sages, since sensation would arise from this or that, how could it be indestructible or composed of non-existence? Furthermore, O Leader of Sages, [this applies] today in a region such as Jambūdvīpa.
For those who have died, whether cremated by fire here or having their bodies destroyed elsewhere, the body serves as the instrument for the experience of hell or heaven once they are bodiless.
What could that [result] be, or what would its auxiliary causes be? Dharma and adharma are both formless; for that which is formless, how could there be form?
The argument that one makes something substance-less by means of substances is inconsistent; for since there is an absence of mother, father, and so forth, what could possibly be the cause therein?
What other causes could there be, or how could the existence of substances and so forth arise? For [the claim] that "there is no other world" stands as it is according to direct experience.
Moreover, it is inconsistent because it contradicts all worldly experience and the Vedas; for results are obtained by those who have gone to distant lands through actions performed without desire.

In this case, what sequence can there be for a progeny to be obtained through formless and unrelated things? It would be like a pillar becoming golden by a boon, without any coming or going of actual gold.
If prosperity is achieved there in an instant, how can it be said that injunctions and prohibitions are rendered purposeless and devoid of cause?
Whether they are firmly established or not yet established, tell me what purpose they serve: "The world was non-existent before; immediately thereafter, it became existent."
O Brahman, how is the consistency of this Vedic revelation to be explained? O great sage, tell me how this [universe] could have come to be, and how Brahmā himself came into existence.
Why is it that not everything is produced from such a sky, or why do all medicinal herbs and objects abide within it?
O Lord of Sages, tell me according to your realization: what are the natures of life for a man as a friend and death as an enemy?

How can it be said that what is sought after by dying in a sacred field such as Prayāga will be attained through the fruits of meditation, thinking, "May I become the imperishable full moon in the sky"?

Is the sky not filled with thousands of moons by those who have attained that state simultaneously? Furthermore, how could a single woman be meditated upon in succession by hundreds of thousands of meditators?
Together with their wives, they simultaneously obtained the fruit of meditation; whether virtuous or unvirtuous, each remained at home devoted to her husband through ascetic practice.
And how did their wives become so accomplished, O Great Sage? How did that king depart from his home and travel throughout the seven continents for an entire kalpa?
Where does the end reside for the status of being a boon-giver through boons and curses, and for acts such as charity, dharma, austerity, and rites for the deceased?

For those who reside here and are formless, there exists the fruit of reality consisting of form through affection; yet, no formal agent of worldly transaction exists here in either of the two worlds.
O Sage, whether in another place or after a long interval of time, the fruit of karma arises intensely; yet that occurs without the actual experience of it at the time of its ripening.

"How could that which is indeed inconsistent be perfectly consistent?"—with such a multitude of doubts arisen within me, sever them with your cool and pure speech, just as the moon dispels the darkness of twilight.

Because doubt regarding the supreme reality is destroyed, benefit for both worlds clearly arises; therefore, grant me here the meeting with the virtuous, for no one’s encounter with the good bears fruit that is meager in this world.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: Listen, O King, as I shall explain this clearly to you, so that all your doubts will be completely uprooted.
Indeed, all phenomena in the world are always of the nature of non-existence, yet they are always of the nature of existence, because they abide in accordance with how they are perceived.
O dear one, that consciousness wherein it is declared "this is thus" necessarily becomes that very reality, whether it be existent or non-existent.
Consciousness has such a nature that by it the body is manifested; yet, in its own true form, it remains entirely one, and this is not perceived by one who knows it.
The wise know this very body as such; from states such as dreaming, a certain consciousness arises, and there is no other state of being a body.
Just as this world appears based on the manifestation of a dream, what otherness could there be here at the beginning of creation, given the absence of all causes?
Thus, that very stainless sensation which is designated as Brahman is what appears as this world; so what else could there be other than the world?
Thus, the world's existence is pure from beginning to end and immutable; this has been experienced and declared by the worldly sciences, the Vedas, and the great treatises.
Those fools who deny that which has been firmly established by the great-souled ones as the consciousness of all beings—as one would deny a single blind well—are truly deluded.
Taking as their authority only the delusion that consists in the mere experience of the present, they have fallen into the error that consciousness is the cause of the body.
Those ignorant ones are truly mad; they are not fit for our discourse. What conversation can there be between one who is sober and one who is intoxicated, both being of deluded intellect?
That discourse by which all doubts are not destroyed for the wise—know that such a discourse in the three worlds is merely the talk of fools.
Because he says that this person is merely established in direct perception and thus stands in the position of a fool, his statement is devoid of reason and his conduct is like that of a stone.
He who speaks in contradiction to everything is called ignorant, like a frog in a well; having abandoned the understanding of what precedes and follows, his mind is fixed only on the present.
When questioned, all these—the Vedas, the worlds, and so forth—declare this vision endowed with personal experience, so that all doubts may perish.
To that fool who holds the view, "If consciousness itself is the body, why does a corpse not perceive?", this is now said:
This manifestation of the world is, for now, like a city in a dream to you—the pervasive city of volition belonging to Brahmā, who is of the nature of Brahman.
All this is always, without interruption, of the nature of pure consciousness alone; you should have no delusion regarding this, just as one has none concerning a city in one's own dream.
In that regard, you have personally experienced that the directions, the mountains, the earth and so forth, the cities and so forth—indeed everything—is consciousness alone, which is space.
The dense Brahman is the sky of consciousness; that city of its volition is the Virāj. Brahmā, consisting of pure consciousness, is said to be this very world.
Just as whatever is conceived in the city of Brahmā’s imagination is experienced exactly so, so too is it experienced in the city of your own imagination.
Just as whatever is imagined in a city of one's imagination exists exactly in that way at that time, so too does it exist within the city of your own imagination.
Therefore, just as these two—motion and non-motion—were fashioned by Brahmā through his consciousness for the governance of the body, he experienced them in that very same way.
At the conclusion of the great dissolution, creation proceeds once again; however, due to the absence of all causes, substance does not exist at that time.
Because the Lord of Creatures is liberated, memory does not arise; therefore, this radiance is Brahman itself, which shines as the very world.
Therefore, the world, appearing as its own primordial self by its own nature through Brahman, is realized as a city of mental construction—like space within space.
Just as a city of imagination appears as pure consciousness alone, so too does the world appear without a cause as the unfolding of pure consciousness.
Whether the body exists or not, wherever the sky of consciousness exists, there the self perceives the world consisting of both duality and non-duality.
Therefore, just as one perceives a city in a dream or a city of one's imagination, so does the sky of consciousness perceive the world immediately after death.
The world appears as if composed of earth and other elements, though it is not so composed; just as this entire universe appeared from the very beginning, so it remains even for one who has died.
Just as for one who has awakened from sleep, space and time do not pervade him even to the extent of an atom, so it is for one who has departed to the next world.
Even though this world is clearly experienced by one who is awakened, it does not exist at all within the scope of reality, just as there is no cause for anything in the sky.
Just as this world appears radiant though it is non-existent to one who is unawakened, so too does the void itself appear as a creation to the one who has departed for the next world.
To those who have departed for the next world, the sky itself appears as if it were once before, vast and spread out, though it was never so before, enriched with the earth, mountains, and oceans.
"Dead, I have been born again in the world of Yama; I am experiencing the fruits of my good and evil deeds"—thus the deceased perceives an exceedingly dense delusion.
This delusion does not subside for those who disregard the means to liberation; this delusion subsides through awakening and the state of being free from latent impressions.

The consciousness of one who is unawakened consists of the latent impressions of merit and demerit; that which appears as the very void, having the nature of the void, is precisely what constitutes the existence of the world.

The nature of the world that appears under the name of Brahman is neither of the nature of emptiness nor of the nature of existence; yet, through the power of ignorance, it becomes a source of misfortune, whereas for one who has realized it, it is of the nature of auspiciousness.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen to how good and evil arise for living beings within the context of domestic life—arising from things that are unconnected, non-obstructive, and situated at a distance.
This entire world exists as a city of Brahmā’s mental construction; that which appears as an object of perception is, through the awakening to Brahman, nothing but Brahman itself.
Whatever is conceived in the city of one's imagination, and however it is conceived at any given time, that very thing is experienced then as having a corresponding structure.
When this house has passed away in such a manner, this progeny likewise comes to pass; when the world is thus filled with such mental constructs, it becomes exactly so.
In this city of your own volition, it exists exactly as it is for you; indeed, whatever you conceive, that very thing you perceive accordingly.
Just as pure consciousness is attained through both a boon and a curse, so too does that consciousness come to be conceived as being nothing other than Brahman.
Through the injunctions and prohibitions regarding progeny, by means of a single established conviction, one attains the very same result; such is the conception that it is indeed the Brahmic state.
Because those embodied beings who exist in this world are not perceived [in their ultimate reality], it is understood that the world was previously non-existent; yet, it is perceived as being real.

O dear one, this world exists solely by the power of the volition of Brahman, whose nature is consciousness; the opening and closing of that consciousness are what constitute cosmic dissolution and emergence.
The king said: "What is it that is not perceived first, and what is it that is perceived later—this world, whose body is ever-moving, yet which shines with the appearance of a very stable beginning?"

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Within this city of volition situated in the space of consciousness, such is the nature of existence: that having come into being, it ceases to exist, and yet in an instant, it comes into being again.
Like a city of a child's imagination, or like the optical illusion of hair-tufts in the sky, these creations—appearing as both existent and non-existent—manifest within the conscious self.
Having constructed the city of conceptualization, you destroy it in that very instant; for your own nature is such that it exists by virtue of the consciousness of another, distinct from itself.
Know that the rising and sinking within the city of the mental construction of the space of consciousness is the manifestation of its own nature, and it is likewise stainless.
The density of consciousness is indeed the beginningless and endless void that constitutes the sky of the three worlds; therefore, whatever it performs or perceives today is merely that.
Although this [consciousness] is unobstructed even across hundreds of leagues and through eons, it performs its functions like a dream, as if occurring in the present.
Indeed, what single Self that is eternally unobstructed, whether in another country or even in another world, would not perceive?
Just as the rising and sinking of reflections within a gem is merely a transformation of its own luster, so too is the manifestation of the worlds within the gem of consciousness.
The purpose of injunctions and prohibitions is the maintenance of the world; that very [maintenance], being firmly rooted in consciousness, remains the bestower of fruit even after death.
It never sets, nor does it ever rise; Brahman, the manifestation of the consciousness of Brahman, is eternally established within the Self.
Just as the city of imagination, consisting of the seer and the seen, appears by itself like the world, so too is it said to have been born.
When, having withdrawn its manifestation from its own nature, it abides within itself as the single essence of the space of Brahman-consciousness, it is likewise called "peaceful."
The nature of that which shines and does not shine is pure and inexhaustible; just as these two—motion and stillness—are not other than the self, so they are not other than the wind in the sky.
May these moments, which destroy old age and death, exist here individually, just as they exist within the city of your imagination.
In this city of Brahmā’s volition, the inherent natures of all medicinal herbs, objects, and everything else in the three worlds have likewise arisen.
O King, the one who forms volitions does not himself exist within the city of volitions; rather, like a child with toys, he imagines each blade of grass as something else.
This is clearly the very nature of this mass of consciousness: whatever it conceives of immediately, even its own constituent parts appear therein.

Though they shine as having the nature of consciousness, they appear to themselves as having diverse natures; though they abide with a single essence, they possess the intrinsic nature of various forms.

It is said that within each individual there exists, in the self which is pure Brahman-consciousness, that [consciousness] which is the soul of all; in whatever manner it abides therein, in that very manner it manifests internally.

Without beginning, middle, or end, possessing infinite vigor, it is neither something nor nothing, and though existing, it is unreal; as it abides wherever it may be, it is the self of that very place, becoming the self of all within the entire range of beings, from the elements down to grass and other such things.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen to this: for a single man, life is desired by a friend and death by an enemy; yet that which is sought through dying at a sacred site such as Prayāga—listen to that.
For all fields and objects, Brahmā ordained their respective fruits in his own creation-city of volition.

Wherever merit is performed and for whatever purpose, if that field is treated accordingly by those two [the donor and the recipient], then the merit of that person who applied it rises through its fulfillment.
Therefore, whether it be a portion or the whole of that great sin, that merit—which has the power of consciousness as its essence—subsides after having circulated through the body.
If the evil of those to be converted is slight, yet the excellence of the field is greater, then, having destroyed that evil, the very name of that field resounds triumphantly.
O Lord of the Earth, by virtue of that field-dharma, two bodies shine forth perfectly for this disciple, consisting of the nature of his own wisdom.
Thus, the great fruit of such evils and merits is exactly as it is fashioned by the volition of Brahmā; it is precisely according to that [volition].
That element of consciousness is called Brahman; it is the lotus-born Brahmā, the ego, and so forth. Just as it exists, so is each of those its own conceptualization of the world.

The inspired intuition of the disciple arises in such a manner through the merit of the field [of the teacher], just as that [intuition] of one who possesses the [Buddha-]element arises for one who has turned away from error.
Today I am alone; I am dead, while these kinsmen of mine weep. I have reached the other world all by myself.
In that very place, at that very time, and in that very manner, his perception of even his kinsmen was of exactly the same kind, as if he were one whose elements were in agitation.
Due to their own extremely intense merits or sins, or when observed by great beings, even the destinies of men appear otherwise through the power of mental construction.
They too see him dead, unconscious, and become a corpse; they weep for him and cast him into the fire along with their kinsmen.

Just as that disciple perceives himself as free from old age and death, established and without suffering, through another embodied being who possesses the nature of consciousness; so too does he perceive his own self.
With his body remaining as it was, he perceives the duration of his life; however, death is perceived through another, invisible body, impelled by the merit of the field [of rebirth] known to him.
A turbid consciousness is perceived in an instant by a consciousness that is empty [of objectivity]; for there is no affliction for one whose limbs are armored when striking those who are unarmored.
Even his kinsmen see him likewise attained to immortality; thus he obtains both life and death as equal.
These three worlds are merely an illusion, initiated by that which is non-obstructive; since nothing truly exists, what indeed could be a reversal of illusion within an illusion?
The delusion experienced in the city of one's imagination and in a dream is greater than that which is experienced in the waking state, not less.
The King said: "O Brahmin, how do dharma and adharma become the cause of the consciousness of the body? And how does that which is formless alone attain the state of having two bodies?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O high-minded one, in this world of Brahmā, which is like a city of one's own imagination, what indeed is not possible—whether it be real or even inconsistent?
Just as that which cannot exist here in a city of one’s own imagination does not exist at all, so too, what could possibly exist within this conceptualization of Brahman?
In both a dream and a city of one's imagination, a single thing attains the status of a multitude; likewise, the single consciousness itself assumes the form of an army within a dream.
Thousands become one; likewise, that very state is deep sleep (suṣuptaka). Otherwise, there is the experience and recollection of the army of dreams and mental constructs.
Who has not experienced the cities of imagination and dreams within this world, which is essentially consciousness, consisting of experience alone, and is nothing but the space of awareness?
Therefore, within this world-soul, which is a conceptualization of consciousness in the space of the intellect, what indeed is not possible, or what indeed is even possible?
In this very way, this delusion appears as consisting of the radiant sky; herein there is nothing whatsoever that exists, nor does it not exist, nor is there anything here that is non-existent.

Whatever is experienced exactly as it is, that is how it appears to one who sees reality; for one who is awakened in this regard, what else could there be? He alone is the limb [of the truth]—enough said!
If this dharma were ordained here [on earth], then those mountains of nectar would exist in heaven; why, then, did he not obtain those mountains by forming such a resolve here?
"In this world, whatever action is performed is experienced in the next; thus, in this city of mental construction, everything is entirely inconsistent."

If there were any object whatsoever that was perfectly stable, it would become an object of perception; this is the universal rule. However, because of its nature as consciousness, it remains established within itself.

Thus has this principle been stated; from that, experience is established for those who have attained realization, because the worlds are the volition of consciousness by virtue of its nature as Brahman.
Just as there is no impossibility whatsoever within a city of one's imagination, so too there is no impossibility regarding any object within the creative resolve of Brahmā.

In whatever way something is conceptualized therein, it exists only as far as that conceptualization extends; for it exists by its own nature exactly in that manner, because it possesses that particular configuration.
Therefore, in this case, the mixing [of the two] does not proceed merely through mutual observation; without another effort of the mind, the purpose is not otherwise accomplished.
Just as the world exists as it appears within an unceasing volition for the duration of an eon, so too will another [world] arise through another form of volition.
Consisting of volition, it shines forth by itself as the world in every eon, just as a city in a dream appears within the dream-consciousness of each individual living being.

There is nothing whatsoever that cannot arise from this body of the city of volition, for it is the conscious self; know, O dear one, that the entire universe is none other than Brahman itself, the primordial and supreme nature of the Shaker.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as the sky does not become filled with a hundred moons even when hundreds of meditators attain the state of the moon that wanes at the end of its fruit, listen to this explanation.
Those who meditate upon the lunar disc have attained what is to be attained and are well-established; they have not reached this expanse of the sky, nor have they resorted to this moon.
Tell me, how can one person reach another’s city of mental construction? The attainment of the objects within a city of construction belongs only to its creator, not to anyone else.
They remain within their own respective creations born of individual volition; therein, moons shine, entirely free from the waning of their digits.
The meditator should enter into this very moon, the lord of the night; abandoning the internal self, the intellect, and pleasure, he enters into this very [moon].
"I have entered the moon; I am endowed with the bliss of the lunar disc"—by meditating thus, one becomes a partaker of such bliss; this is the certain conclusion.
Just as this imperishable consciousness connects with its own nature, it experiences that very [nature] in exactly that way, provided there is firm certainty.

Just as the state of being the moon appears individually to every meditator through their own mental construction, even so the attainment of a woman is itself a conceptual construct arising from oneself.
That which appears as the meditator within meditation has become a virtuous wife; that experience of such conceptualization resides within the being of those individuals.

The living being, though not having stepped out from its home, remains as the master of the seven continents; yet even for him, that kingdom is merely a mental construction within his own palace in the sky.

All this is merely conceptual construction arising from the birth of primordial ignorance; it is empty, non-obstructive, and quiescent—otherwise, what else could there be even within those [constructions]?
Listen as this is explained: that which is the embodied fruit in the next world of formless acts such as charity, rites for the deceased, austerity, and recitation.

Those whose intellects are marked by generosity and other virtues perceive the fruit in the next world as being like a dream; though unborn and appearing both formless and with form, they do so through the conceptualization of consciousness as having a form.

Furthermore, this pure consciousness, which consists of both vibration and non-vibration, takes on the form of feeling and the felt; yet, when that delusion subsides, it becomes the tranquil and stainless self.

Since one who is limited by the appearance of pure consciousness obtains the highest state through giving in the hereafter, and since the wise say that [the self] is of the nature of volition (saṃkalpa), why is it not perceived?

In this cycle of existence, which is of the nature of conceptual construction, volition is the uncreated fruit; whether through non-giving or giving, let it be as it has been described, for it is nothing but pure consciousness.
All this has been told to you, O lord of the earth, exactly as you asked: that this entire world, which is unimpeded, is a mere conceptual construction of consciousness alone.
The King said: "O Blessed One, at the beginning of creation, how does this body—which is a mere conceptualization of consciousness—appear? And how can a lamp shine without a wall?"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O high-minded one, that meaning of the word "body" which you have understood does not exist at all for one who knows reality, like the dancing of a stone in the sky.
That which is the meaning of the word "Brahman" is indeed the meaning of the word "body"; there is no difference between these two meanings, just as there is none between water and its waves.
This very body of Brahmā, which is like a dream, is indeed a dream; however, this reasoning is stated for the sake of your awakening, and it is not that the body itself is actually a dream.
Because you have experienced objects within a dream, you are awakened from it; however, there is no similarity between a creation appearing as consciousness and the ashes of a dream.

What indeed is this body there, and to whom do these belong? Where is the dream-consciousness? By means of a dream, one who is ignorant is awakened from delusion by one who has already awakened to the knowledge.
Therein, there is neither waking nor dreaming, nor deep sleep, nor anything else; this manifestation is something indescribable, mere space, stainless silence.

That which now appears as "this" shines as if it were shining, though it is indeed unshining; for it was previously manifest in such a way that it is utterly transparent, unlike the states of waking, dreaming, and so forth.
In the movement from one place to another, that which is the form of consciousness in the interval—this entire world, both dualistic and non-dualistic, consists of that alone.
Elsewhere, the dream-like state consisting of consciousness—whether dualistic or non-dualistic, auspicious or inauspicious—is compared to the sky of unobscured pure consciousness alone.
Emptiness and the perception of objects, appearance and non-appearance, duality and unity, the unreal and the real—all is the supreme sky of consciousness.
From the Full, the full flows forth; the world remains as nothing but the Full. It has neither appeared nor not appeared, being like the interior of a solid stone.
Since the emergence of the world is consciousness, it is therefore of the nature of space and unimpeded; wherever there is pure consciousness, there the world is appropriately manifested.
The sky of consciousness exists everywhere, and all this is composed of the world; everything is composed of Brahman, peaceful, though it is designated by the word "world."
This universe, as it exists, is established in that very way—free from disease, nothing but Brahman, the faultless self, whose form is created by the city of conscious volition.
Because no other reasoning is possible, this very reasoning is the most excellent; however, an experience devoid of reasoning, as described here, does not shine for those who seek the truth.

Whatever is established in the world, in the treatises, or in the Vedas and so forth, that is indeed established; for it is impossible anywhere to establish that which is existent as non-existent, or that which is non-existent as existent, within the Self.
When the entire universe, which exists as identical to that [Self], dissolves, then this very [Self], thus fully known, attains the state of Brahman.
By this principle stated here, all things such as the world and the Vedas are established; therefore, he is entirely liberated while living, and for that reason, this alone is appropriate.
The sky of consciousness is fully known within the tree of ignorance; "I am this triple world"—such is the definitive conclusion regarding bondage and liberation.
This visible world, as it truly exists, dissolves through thorough knowledge; for the knower who has thus set [the mind], only the silence of a stone remains.
Whatever is established in the world, in the treatises, and in the Veda is indeed established; that alone is experienced, and therefore it clearly bears fruit in this very way.
Whatever is experienced for a long time through the complete exclusion of all other objects, that alone is inevitably attained; this is true everywhere, as it is conditioned by nothing else.
Whatever is experienced exactly as it was experienced, that is experienced by its very name; whether it be true or untrue, let it remain so for as long as it is obtained.

Thus, O wise and noble-souled one, I have spoken this investigation of the great questions to you; by means of this, proceed quickly along the path and become exalted, free from anxiety, free from disease, and free from calamity.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having sat there and been honored by that king, I accomplished my purpose and leaped into the sky to go to heaven.
"O best among the wise, what has been spoken by you today—through this right vision—you shall become one whose mind is peaceful and who has realized his own self."
All this is indeed Brahman alone—the stainless sky, devoid of names; something indescribable, unborn, utterly tranquil, and free from beginning, middle, and end.
It is said to be the mere manifestation of consciousness; it is designated by the name "Brahman"; it is proclaimed as "higher than the highest"; yet that state is truly nameless.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, tell me how the worlds—the abodes of the Siddhas, Sādhyas, Yakṣas, Brahmavidyādharas, and the gods—are seen, and how they are supported by the world.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: [He appeared] before the Siddhas, Sādhyas, Yamas, Brahmavidyādharas, and the gods, as well as other unprecedented beings of great soul.
Night after night and day after day, you look before and behind, above and below; though you gaze upon the worlds, you do not truly see them.
These worlds, it is said, are not far from their locations; these are called the worlds of mental construction (saṃkalpa), and by them indeed all is pervaded.
Just as these worlds of conceptual construction are, so too is this world for us; just as the wind is conceptual, so too are the worlds and the lights.
Those worlds of your own volition and dreams which shine for you day and night—they are indeed of that same nature, yet others are likewise made stable by volition.
If you, with a perfectly steady mind, bring even those things that have been dissolved by meditation to a state of stability, then they will quickly attain stability without obstacle.
Enveloped by the power of their own volition, people see things according to their desired extent and desired perfection, as if they were accomplished realities.

However, those [senses] were brought to stability by the Siddhas through the excellence of their celestial vehicles; yet, because those [vehicles] are unstable, they have been rendered [unstable] again by these sufferings during the repose of meditation.
The entire world is always an unimpeded, peaceful sky of consciousness; just as it is firmly realized, so does it appear, and not otherwise.
It does not shine at all when it is not cognized; it neither exists nor does it not exist, nor is it an object of effort. For this is empty, non-obstructive, like the supreme space, and unimpeding.

Manifesting by virtue of its nature as consciousness, it appears like light; yet, within this, there is no conceit of being a conscious self, for that does not exist by way of its own intrinsic nature.

If it is argued that [the world] exists due to the relationship of cause and effect, no such discourse applies here at all; for how indeed could anything be born, and from what, out of the infinite, already established space?
And that which appears as if born in the sky is in fact just the sky itself; therein, how could there be any formless conception of oneness or duality?
For that remains exactly as it was, changeless; it becomes like the sky, immovable even in a dream.

Just as a mountain appears as a form in the mind through the play of imagination, yet that mountain is not real nor is that space [of the appearance], so too is the existence of the world within Brahman.
Maintaining silence like a block of wood, even while speaking, these great-minded sages conduct themselves here like wooden men.
Just as the movements of waves and whirlpools exist within water and revolve without being distinct from it, so do creations revolve within Brahman.
Just as there is motion in the wind and emptiness in the sky, so too are creations in Brahman—non-different from it and likewise formless.
Just as a city of imagination exists as a void yet appears with form, so too does this world exist within Brahman—having form, yet being formless.
Even though this triple world has been experienced for a long time, its purposeful activity is empty and formless, like a city of one's own imagination.
Just as a city is nothing other than a mental construction, so too this pure Brahman is called the world in that very same way.
Although the objects of the world have been experienced by a person for a long time as constant, they do not exist at all here, just like one's own death in a dream.
Just as a man in a dream may see his own cremation even though he is dead, so too is the world perceived by the Supreme as a mere appearance of existence where there is only non-existence.

Both the state of being the world and the state of not being the world are the stainless body of the Supreme alone; and that which is designated as "Supreme" is not, in the ultimate sense, truly existent.

"Let it be thus, or let it be otherwise; let it not be, or let it be—what cause for agitation is there in this? O Phalguna, abandon your grasping for fruit; you have understood, and enough with these exertions!"

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That which, by virtue of its consciousness, perceives itself as "I am indeed the void of Brahman"—that alone is the state of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), and this entire universe is his belly.
This being the case, there is neither Brahmā nor a world that has arisen and persists; rather, it remains exactly as it is—the unborn, supreme Brahman itself, just as it was before.
In consciousness, however, the form of the world appears in exactly this same way; like a mirage, it is entirely false, being unreal even while it is being perceived.
From this point forward, this new delusion has arisen as empty; for where and what indeed is this delusion? It is only the untainted Brahman itself.

The world is but a whirlpool in the waters of Brahman; what indeed are duality and unity here? Where is the duality between the whirlpool and the water, and where is their unity, given that duality does not exist?
That Brahman is dense and profoundly tranquil; by virtue of its consciousness, it perceives itself as "I," knowing its own inherent emptiness which resides within like a sky with vast interior space.
As the wind possesses motion, as fire possesses heat, and as the full moon possesses its own coolness, so does the self possess existence, just as an object possesses its own nature.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, O Sage, when indeed did you not perceive that [reality] which is unobscured and without beginning or end? What is it that perceives now?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: It is exactly so; this very thing, including myself and others, has always been conscious in this way. For this beginningless and unborn reality, there is no dependence whatsoever upon anything other than its own self-awareness.
Brahman, whose nature is like the sky—neither creation nor non-creation—is everywhere and at all times; it is never "this," nor "not this," nor is it anything whatsoever that can be known.
The movement of the wind, the coolness of the moon, the emptiness of the sky, and my own identity as Brahman—which is non-different from the Self—he never fails to perceive.
Such is existence at all times; it has never been otherwise. Since the world is without beginning or end, it is indeed the stainless Self that is Brahman.
But solely because you have not awakened, being pierced by the hearing of sounds, you perceive duality in this non-dual realization of Brahman.
In this world, no one ever fails to perceive anything at any time; nor is there anyone whose self is other than that [consciousness], for such a person never perceives at all.
This appearance of the three worlds always shines in this manner; yet, O Rāma, it is the peaceful and equal Brahman—herein there is not the slightest diversity whatsoever.
Trees and mountains are never born from the sky, nor are they born from Brahman; realizing this, attain supreme peace.
As long as you, being of limited intellect, have not awakened to the truth regarding the purpose of the teacher and the teaching during moments of doubt, so long do you continue to accept duality.
But for the awakened one who has realized consciousness, there is no scripture and so forth, no cognition of words, no notion of difference, and no difference; he is simply this Prajāpati.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahmin, this which you have spoken for the sake of my understanding has been understood by me; now please explain that which is relevant to the subject at hand."
When that egoity has been resolved into the supreme state, what remains? You have understood this; being desirous of hearing more, I truly do not reach satiety.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When this sense of "I-ness" exists, the existence of space proceeds; the existence of the directions, the existence of time, and the existence of duality also arise.
When it appears as "I am here," then even "I am not here" appears; thus, within the sky of the self, the non-sequential duality of its own nature arises.
The cognition that designates these entities as being of the nature of space will occur at a later time; at that point, they will be nothing other than space itself.
When this formless sense of "I," which consists of the perception of space and time, has been fully perfected, there remains only the void that perceives those subtle elements alone.
This luminous form which shines forth, called "the object of perception," namely sensation—though it is in truth only Brahman, unassailable—appears as if it were non-Brahman.

Brahman alone is peaceful, unborn, one, and without beginning or middle; having conceived it as space itself, yet as if possessing the notion of a living soul (jīva), the knower of the Self perceives within that very unobstructed space the pervasive visible world and even his own nature as if it were something else, due to his state of self-knowledge.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O destroyer of enemies, just as you have questioned me today, so previously was I questioned by you when you were my disciple and I was your teacher.
Indeed, in a certain former age, this very consciousness, appearing as the reality consisting of the self and so forth, existed in the forest in the form of a teacher and a disciple.
At that time, I was the guru and you were the disciple; standing before me, you, possessed of a bold and steady intellect, questioned me as follows.
The disciple said: "O Blessed One, sever this great doubt of mine regarding everything: what perishes during the great dissolution (mahākalpa), and what entity does not perish?"
The Guru said: "O son, just as the entire visible world perishes instantly, so too does the city of dreams vanish for one who has entered the state of deep sleep."
Without distinction, the mountains of the earth, the ten directions, activity, time, and sequence—all these perish; nothing whatsoever remains.
All beings perish and even space itself dissolves, because the perceiver of the appearance of the entire world cannot possibly exist.
For even those who are the causes of the causes—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Rudra, and the rest—even their very names are no longer found here at the end of the great kalpa.
For the immutable space of consciousness (cidākāśa) remains; its persistence at that time is inferred by this very cause for the experience of creation.
The disciple said: "There is no being for the non-existent, nor is there non-being for the existent. How is it that this expansive world, while existing, goes nowhere?"
The Teacher said: "This [world] does not perish; therefore, my son, it does not cease to exist. There is no coming into being for the non-existent, nor is there cessation of being for the existent."
O Rāma, how indeed can that which does not exist as a reality at any time whatsoever—which is of the nature of non-existence—ever perish?
Where does the water of a mirage abide? Where is the delusion of two moons stable? Where are the hairs seen in the sky firm? And where is the experience of an error stable?
"O son, all this that is seen is mere delusion, composed of unreality; it appears like a city in a dream—how is it that this does not subside?"
This [world] subsides entirely, in every way and at all times, just as a dream ceases during the waking state, or as the waking state ceases within a dream.
Just as a dream-city is peaceful, and I do not know where it quickly goes, so too this visible world is peaceful; I do not know where it quickly goes.

The disciple said: "O Blessed One, what is this that shines, and what again does not shine? Of what entity is this the form, [that entity] which is the sky of consciousness and whose shape is all-pervasive?"
The Guru said: "O son, this sky of consciousness shines with a brilliant luster; that which is called the world appears, yet no world other than this exists."
This is the form of this very reality, the pervasive expanse of consciousness; it appears in this manner without ever abandoning its own pure nature.
Its own body consists of creation and dissolution, shimmering and non-shimmering; it is of the nature of space, both white and black, just like the body of a whole.
Just as you alone were at first within the white waters by means of your hair, so too is Brahman—the pure Self—thus [the same] during creation and imperishable even at the dissolution of creation.
Just as in dreaming and deep sleep there is but one undecaying sleep throughout the day and night, so too in this creation and in dissolution, there is but one imperishable consciousness, Brahman.
Just as for one who perceives the world in a dream, the world subsides entirely into peace, so too does this world of ours subside entirely into peace.

Therefore, my dear, we do not know how that which is called "space" could exist elsewhere in space; for this is impossible in the space of another, since it arises only within the space of our own consciousness.

Just as here, at the dissolution of creation, there is the manifestation of our own space of consciousness, so too is it with the space of consciousness of others; what proof is there that it is not thus?
