The disciple said: "If this is so, then just as in a dream there exists for the perceiver a cognition of the visible object distinct from himself, I believe that in the same way, elsewhere, there exists a cognition of the world and so forth."

The Guru said: "It is even so, O one of great wisdom; yet that world is not the true nature [of reality]. That which is the true nature shines within consciousness, and it does not shine in the same way as those [objects]."

It does not shine, nor is it anything at all, yet it is not non-existent; it is the manifestation of the space of consciousness—what room is there therein for the notions of "existent" or "non-existent"?
For that indeed exists everywhere, everything, by means of everything, at all times; and yet nothing whatsoever exists anywhere at any time.

Whatever exists at all times and in every way, whether real or unreal, the entirety of it is composed of that; that is the space of consciousness, which is neither subject to destruction nor is it destroyed.
That which is indeed the space of Being-Consciousness, whose nature consists of creation and dissolution—that, when unrecognized, leads to suffering; when fully known, it is supreme peace.
This all exists in every way, everywhere, and at all times; yet this all does not exist in any way, anywhere, or at any time.
This deity is the jar, the mountain, the cloth, the thunderclap, the bank, and the banyan tree; it is the grass, the fire, the stationary, the moving, and indeed everything.

Existence and non-existence, emptiness, action, time, space, and earth; being and non-being, becoming, prosperity, destructions, bonds, and the auspicious and inauspicious—all these are [but manifestations of the mind].
That indeed does not exist which is not eternal, singular, and external; nor does it exist as beginning, middle, or end, nor even as the three divisions of time.
Everything exists here by everything, everywhere, and at all times; yet everything does not exist here by everything, everywhere, and at all times.
O Rāma, when everything exists at all times as the Self of all in this way, then indeed, by virtue of being Brahman, it is like the experience of a dream-city.
Grass is the agent, grass is the enjoyer; because it is identical with Brahman, grass is all-pervading. The jar is the agent, the jar is the enjoyer; the jar is the Lord of all lords.
The cloth is the agent, the cloth is the enjoyer, the cloth is the Lord of all lords; the Seer is the agent, the Seer is the enjoyer, the Seer is the Lord of all lords.
Giri is the doer, Giri is the enjoyer, Giri is the Lord of all lords; Nara is the doer, Nara is the enjoyer, Nara is the Lord of all lords.
He is the creator and enjoyer of every single thing, higher than the highest; he is the sustainer without beginning or end, since everything has Brahman as its self.

But these things, such as grass, jars, and so forth, exist in this form through the Lord’s own omnipotence; for whatever form appears as the Lord, its arising and passing away are likewise [manifested by Him].
The external object exists; it alone is here the agent and the enjoyer of such a kind. For those who know thus, there exists only consciousness as the agent and the enjoyer.
For those who know the truth, there is no agent here at all, nor likewise any enjoyer; for those who do not so know, it is the Lord alone who is the agent and the enjoyer here.
In that state, which is the most supreme of all, everything is possible; what injunctions and prohibitions exist there, and what do not?
In the pure sky of consciousness, like a seer contemplating the appearance of an object, one perceives one's own self as the world; thus remaining, one stays free from affliction.

All perceptions, including all views of injunctions and prohibitions, are preceded by specific volitions and cognitions; they are eternally real in nature, yet not real in themselves, because their true essence here consists in the form [of the object] as it is experienced.

Thus, in the past, you heard this from my presence as a disciple, yet because of that you did not understand it. Consequently, having experienced existence in other worlds, you have now been born here and ask about that very same thing.

All this supreme sacred knowledge is true wisdom, the orb of the moon for the long night of worldly existence. You have been born possessed of sublime and stainless awakening; having dispelled delusion, act according to what you have received.

Abiding then within yourself—the supreme, stainless-natured, and all-pervading Self—blazing forth and free from all objective phenomena, with a mind tranquil through Nirvana and as beautiful as the expanse of the sky, protect the kingdom through Dharma, having crossed over craving.

Śrī Vālmīki said: When the sage had spoken thus, a celestial drum suddenly resounded from the sky like a rain-cloud at the end of the monsoon; and a shower of flowers, white as a fall of snow, fell upon the earth, whitening the faces of all the quarters.

With her thick body-unguent of pollen-masses at the end of the day, wearing white garlands of filaments shaken by the breeze, and her limbs cooled by the soft spray rising from the bellies of flowers—she has arrived like the very Fortune of Merit come in person from the city of the gods.

Stationed in the sky, she mocks the host of stars with her vast laughter as it spreads terrifyingly across the faces of the quarters; she resembles a fruit fallen swiftly from the celestial tree—its dry branches shaken by the monkey that is the time of the world’s end—and she possesses a renowned luster.

Then that rain of flowers, thundering with the sound of drums and possessing clouds of pollen-masses, came to rest; it filled the entire assembly with a flood of snow-white blossoms, causing the eyes of all to open wide in wonder.
Having paid homage to Vasiṣṭha, those members of the assembly, standing below according to their respective places, cast off their grief upon seeing those divine flowers.
Daśaratha said: "Aha! We, whose souls were deeply afflicted by the vast expanse of saṃsāra, have finally found rest after long weariness, like pure clouds settling upon a mountain."
The limit of karmas has been reached; the boundary of calamities has been seen. That which is to be known has been known in its entirety; we have come to rest in the supreme state.
Through the delusions of long-term experience in the supreme void attained through meditation, and through the stages of abandoning the body by resting in the support of *dhāraṇā*.

By means of the constructions of the forest of conceptualization, by the fevers of the world seen in dreams, by the experiences of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, and by the visions of one's own death in a dream;
Not distinct from the movements of the wind, not distinct from the flow of water, like the filling of cities in a magician's trick, or the clusters of cities of the Gandharvas.
Through the enjoyments of cities filled with illusion, through the currents of rivers in a mirage, through the touch of the wind in the future, and through the arising of the experience of two moons;
[One is deluded] by the throbbing of the temples and the city, by the shaking of the earth in vain, by the experiences of children, yakṣas, and the like, and by the sight of hair-tufts in the sky.
"By these and other such examples that bring about one's own direct experience, oh! the vision of the visible world has been wiped clean for me by the Blessed One."
Śrī Rāma said: "O Lord of Sages, through your grace, my delusion has perished and I have attained the supreme state; I have become truly perfected, with a mind that is utterly pure."
I stand with all doubt dispelled in my own nature, which is of the form of Brahman; possessing unobstructed consciousness, I shall carry out your word.
Remembering again and again your words, which grant the bliss of a sprinkling of nectar, I rejoice again and again, as if thrilled, even though I am an Arhat and already tranquil.
Today I have no purpose whatsoever in what is done, nor any in what is left undone; I remain just as I was, free from all feverish distress.
What means or what kind of vision does he have here? Alas, how vast is this ground; how painful is such a state!
I have no enemy and no friend; neither field nor wicked person exists for me. This world, agitated by those of poor understanding, is in truth peaceful and beautiful in all its aspects.
How can people know this without your grace? How could a child cross the ocean without a bridge or a boat?

Lakṣmaṇa said: "By the destruction of doubts accumulated over many lifetimes, and by the awakening brought about by the words of the sage—which have arisen from hundreds of merits accumulated over many lifetimes—a light has been born today in my mind, like the moon."
While such a vision is being perceived, the world is consumed like wood by that very misfortune of its own, through hundreds of states of defect in its sight.
Viśvāmitra said: "Aha! Oh, what great merit and knowledge have we heard from the mouth of the sage, by which we stand as if bathed in a thousand Gaṅgās!"
Śrī Rāma said: "The ultimate limit of all prosperities, of all perspectives, of all scriptures, of all calamities, of all speeches, and of all lands that have been seen has now been beheld."
Nārada said: Having heard that knowledge today which was never heard before in the world of Brahmā, nor in heaven, nor upon the surface of the earth, my two ears have attained purity.
Lakṣmaṇa said: O Sage, by you who have wiped away both internal and external darkness, the state of a supreme sun has surely been revealed to us.
Śatrughna said: I am liberated; I am at peace; I have attained the supreme state. For a long time I have been fulfilled, and I abide in absolute bliss.
Daśaratha said: "O Lord of Sages, through merit acquired over many lifetimes, this steadfast one has spoken to us that by which we have attained purification."
Śrī Vālmīki said: While those members of the assembly were speaking thus along with the king, Vasiṣṭha spoke these words with a voice purified by knowledge.
"O King, the sole moon of Raghu’s lineage, do as I say; for at the conclusion of a historical narrative, the twice-born are worthy of honor."
Therefore, today you should satisfy the multitudes of Brahmins with all their desires; thus you will obtain the eternal fruit of the proper performance of the Vedic teachings.
Upon the conclusion of the discourse on the means to liberation, the honoring of the twice-born should be performed according to one's ability even by a mere insect; how much more so by a sovereign?
Having heard these words of silence, the king had ten thousand twice-born men who were exponents of the Vedas summoned by means of messengers.
Having honored and summoned those twice-born men who dwell in Mathurā, Surāṣṭra, and Gauḍa, he brought them from those families.
At that time, the king fed ten thousand twice-born men who were by nature possessed of knowledge exceeding even the most excellent.
Having thus honored those brahmins, as well as the ancestors, the gods, and the kings, with that gift of desired food and sacrificial fees;
On that day, King Daśaratha was together with his citizens, ministers, servants, and friends, as well as with the poor, the blind, and the wretched.
Having reached the end of his worldly existence, he celebrated a supreme festival in that royal palace, which was adorned with silken garments, jewels, and gold.
And in that adorned city, as beautiful as the mountain of the gods, intoxicated and amorous women, full of grace, danced in every house.
With cymbals, bamboo flutes, bronze lutes, and muraja and mardala drums, they raised a tumultuous roar through their Tandava dance, placing one another upon each other's heads.

The sky was overspread by the flickering illusions of hands moving through the agitated marketplace, while the masses of moonbeam-like rays from their teeth were scattered by their charming, loud laughter.
Their *huṃkāra* cries were agitated by intoxication, their voices tremulous in their playful movements, and they struck the surface of the earth with ease by the mere stroke of a single foot.
They were white with the showers of flowers falling from the garlands and wreaths, and their steps faltered as they stumbled over the pearls of broken necklaces cast down by the downpour.
The women danced with amorous gestures, their ornaments swaying; the Brahmins, the bards, and those very women recited verses with clear articulation.
The drinkers, full of intoxication, drank their liquor amidst a wild dance; adorned and seeking food, they feasted on various delicacies.
The walls of the house, colored by coatings of lime and other substances, shone with the light of the moon-like Rāma, as well as with flowers, incense, and ointments.
Wearing variegated garments and adorned with the finest garlands and ornaments, the attendants and female servants moved about at the king’s sacrifice, fragrant with lovely scents.
Having applied *yakṣakardama* paste to their slender bodies, those women, like dancers in a *tāṇḍava*, entered the courtyard whose very essence was the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).

Out of joy at the end of the long night of worldly existence, King Daśaratha, together with his kin, celebrated a magnificent festival for seven nights, establishing an inexhaustible glory of constant giving and enjoyment.
Śrī Vālmīki said: O Bharadvāja of great intelligence, leader of my disciples! Thus Rāma and the others, having known that which is to be known, have attained freedom from sorrow.
Holding fast to this very beautiful vision, remain as you please—free from passion, without fear, liberated while living, and with a tranquil mind.
For one who has not practiced attachment, O sinless one, like Rāma and others, does not become deluded even when immersed in dense ignorance or though bewildered.
Thus these great beings—such as the princes Rāghava and others, and King Daśaratha and others—have attained the state of liberation while living.
And you, my son Bharadvāja, are yourself one whose intellect is liberated; indeed, having heard this compendium on liberation, you are today even more liberated.
Even a child, upon hearing these meritorious means to liberation which grant the fruit of direct experience, attains the state of a knower; what then need be said of one such as you?
Just as the high-souled Raghus, free from sorrow, followed the path of merit, O virtuous one, so too must you proceed by following the flow of Vasiṣṭha’s words to that very first state.

Through the conduct of the virtuous, service to the supreme, and inquiry into noble discourse, the wise and vigilant attain what is to be known, just as Rāma and others did through association with Vasiṣṭha.

Those knots of ignorance that have taken root in the heart, bound by the firm fetters of craving—indeed, through the investigation of the discourse on liberation, all of them dissolve away; for the ignorant, like those who are no longer ignorant, attain non-duality.

Those who are the most excellent among the knowers of reality will understand the means to liberation that possess great majesty; they shall not enter the cycle of rebirth again. O son, what is the use of further elaboration?

Those who are learned, having investigated and correctly awakened to the meaning, will speak to people; being virtuous, they will not fall back into the state of childishness—so what is the use of other words?

Those who will recite it without regard for its meaning, those who will have it written down as a book, or those who will cause a reciter to be provided with an auspicious commentator in the noble land;

Endowed with the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice, those beings of noble character will repeatedly go to heaven; and by attaining their third birth, they will reach liberation, just as the meritorious attain prosperity.
In ancient times, having reflected upon this well-composed work consisting of liberation, Viriñca, whose form is inconceivable, delivered it through his true speech; and his words never prove false.

When this literary composition titled *Mokṣābhyupāya* has reached its conclusion through the diligent effort of the wise, the Brahmins should be fully honored by providing them with fine dwellings and gifts of desired food and drink.

Indeed, one should give them a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth, according to one's own means and the desire of one's heart; having considered what is appropriate, that person attains the merit of association (*saṅgapuṇya*) exactly as performed in accordance with the scriptures.

This great, stainless treatise, which expands upon the reality of Brahman and is adorned with illustrations and logical reasoning, has been told to you by the Buddhas through hundreds of sequences of discourse for the sake of awakening. Having heard this, attain lasting peace; being one whose intention is liberated while living, enjoy imperishable prosperity endowed with the sequence of knowledge, austerity, and ritual action, and remain yourself undecaying.
Śrī Vālmīki said: O King, this wise discourse of the one born from a jar (Agastya) has been related to you; by means of this path of reality, you will certainly attain that supreme state.
The King said: "O Blessed One, your vision destroys the bondage of worldly existence; by it being beheld, I have crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra."
The divine messenger said: Having spoken thus, the king, his eyes wide with wonder, addressed me with words in a sweet and gentle voice.

The king said: "O messenger of the gods, salutations to you; may it be well with you, O Lord. It is said that friendship among the virtuous is formed by walking seven steps together, and that has been done by you."
Now go, may it be well with you, to the abode of the King of the Gods; by hearing this, I am both comforted and gladdened.
"Thinking over the meaning of what I have heard, I shall remain here free from distress"—when she said this to me, O blessed lady, I was struck with great wonder.
I have never before heard this essence of the Jñānasāra; having now heard it, I am inwardly gladdened as if I have drunk nectar.
Then, having taken leave of Vālmīki, I have come into your presence; all this that was asked of me by you, O sinless one, has been related to you. Henceforth, I shall go toward the abode of Śakra.
The Apsaras said: "Homage be to you, O highly fortunate messenger of the gods! By you, through the proclamation of the meaning and its understanding, I have attained supreme peace."
I have achieved my purpose and am free from sorrow; I shall remain here, rid of all feverish distress. Now go, may you be blessed, wherever you desire in the presence of Śakra.
Agniveśya said: Then that excellent Suruci reflected upon that very matter; she remained on the slopes of the Himavat, near Gandhamādana.
"Have you heard this instruction of Vasiṣṭha, my son? Having fully grasped all of it, then do as you wish."

Kāruṇya said: Just as memory, speech, vision, and existence [are perceived] regarding the son of a barren woman or water in a mirage, so too is the worldly condition known through wisdom to be like that.
I have no purpose here in what is done, nor any at all in what is left undone; I abide in whatever comes to me, for what attachment can there be to inaction?
Agastya said: Having spoken thus, the virtuous son of Agniveśya, out of compassion, performed his duties at the proper times and in the prescribed manner.
No doubt should be entertained here, O Sutīkṣṇa, regarding knowledge and action; for one who doubts falls away from his own goal, and the doubting soul perishes.
Having heard these words of the sage, which reveal the unity of many meanings, he bowed to his teacher and spoke in his presence with humility.

Sutīkṣṇa said: Ignorance and its effects have perished, and unsurpassed knowledge has been attained; [all] actions [are now seen] in the Witness, who is the manifestation of radiance, as constant as a lamp.
When that exists, the desires for wealth proceed preceded by movement, just as bracelets, armlets, earrings, and anklets exist because of gold.
Since the world of appearances vibrates like a series of waves upon the milk-ocean, this entire universe is established as full within the Full.
I follow what has been attained; who would transgress the word of the virtuous? O Blessed One, by your grace, I remain established as one who has known that which is to be known.
My purpose is fulfilled; salutations to you! Prostrating like a staff upon the ground, I ask: by what deed can disciples attain the state of having crossed over from their teacher?
Therefore, by means of body, speech, and mind, disciples should offer themselves to the guru; that alone is their liberation, and not by any other action whatsoever.
"O Lord, by your grace I have crossed the ocean of existence; with all doubts dispelled, I remain, having filled the entire web of the world."
Salutations to that Self which is Brahman, after hearing clearly proclaimed in the Sāman chant: "All this, indeed, is Brahman; it originates from Him, dissolves into Him, and breathes within Him."

We bow to the venerable Vasiṣṭha—the bliss of Brahman, the bestower of supreme happiness, the embodiment of absolute knowledge, beyond duality, resembling the sky, the target of such teachings as "That thou art"; the one, eternal, pure, immovable witness of all intellects, transcending all existence and devoid of the three qualities.
Thus, in the *Ārṣa* Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of Vālmīki, within the section on the means to liberation spoken by the divine messenger, in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa, in the latter half, in the Bālakāṇḍa.
